Combined Comments: "We hereby submit a response to the consultation of the restriction proposal. This response will be digitally added to the form provided on your website for this purpose. This letter also provides general information to inform residents and council members about the context of the restriction proposal. 1. Background On February 7, 2023, the proposal for a European ban on PFAS (Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) was published by ECHA (European Chemicals Agency). Such a ban is also called a restriction. This restriction proposal was prepared by the Netherlands together with Denmark, Germany, Norway, and Sweden. The purpose of the restriction proposal is to ban the production, trade, and use of these substances in order to limit the risks to human health and the environment. The proposal focuses on the entire group of PFAS to prevent the substitution of one PFAS with another. 2. Process There are three stages in the process of banning PFAS. The first stage has already been completed and involved preparing and submitting a restriction proposal. The second stage involves a public consultation. Everyone can have a say in the file and provide information, which will be processed. Subsequently, ECHA's scientific committees will provide their advice. In the third stage, the European Commission will make a final proposal, which the member states will vote on. Then the ban will come into effect. 3. Consultation the consultation is intended to provide ECHA with scientific and technical information to help them prepare their advice. Given the PFAS issues identified in Dordrecht and the surrounding municipalities in South Holland South since 2018, it is important to submit a response to ECHA for each municipality. Subsequently, this response will be formulated, following the structure of the digitally available response form. It is the responsibility of the mayor and aldermen to submit a response on behalf of the municipality. 4. Structure of the response This letter is written from the perspective of the municipalities working together in the Chemours file: Dordrecht, Sliedrecht, Papendrecht, and Molenlanden. In addition to a substantive response, it concludes with a number of conclusions and a plea for a complete ban on the production, trade, and use of PFAS in Europe, including the import and transit of PFAS, including semi-finished and finished products containing PFAS. 5. Response form As mentioned above, anyone can provide a response to the restriction proposal at ECHA (deadline is September 25, 2023 at 23:59 EET). The response must be submitted using a digital response form."

General Comments: The Etienne Lacroix Group is a pyrotechnic systems Integrator, providing applications to the defence in particular with its subsidiary LACROIX  located in the south of France.

A short presentation of the company and the general comment in response of this public consultation on the proposed restriction for PFAS are provided in the section IV.

This general comment was written by several companies, all members of the French Land Defence and Security Industry Association (GICAT). These companies have two main common points: the Pyrotechny and its applications in the defense field. They have been working together in a REACH working group since 2009.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The Annex XV restriction report version 2 does not cover relevant nor essential uses of fluoropolymers in the critical sector of « the defence » . In annex A, table A.1. Pyrotechnics and Defense Industry are mentioned as uses not researched in details.  The target of LACROIX’s reply is to give more details on this sector and on a specific sub-use described below.  Sector : Defence  Use: a complete range of self-protection pyrotechnic systems for airborne applications.  Sub-use: Manufacture of pyrotechnic compositions Manufacture of pyrotechnic compositions integrated in passive countermeasures systems to protect aircrafts against every threat.  A range of flares and decoys are designed to protect combat jets (Mirage 2000, Rafale, Super Etendard) transport aircrafts (C130, C160, A400M) and helicopters (Puma, Super Puma). The current type of pyrotechnic infrared flares used to cover military applications is a composition magnesium, Teflon®, Viton® (MTV).  The paragraphs below explain why Teflon® and Viton® are essential to maintain the capability of our armed forces. Infrared flares are pyrotechnic devices which emit a defined intensity of radiation in the IR region of the electromagnetic spectrum in addition to visible radiation. When ejected from an aircraft, the flares present a more attractive IR signature than that of the target and thus decoy the missile seeker away from the aircraft. The decoy flare emission should be larger than that of the aircraft in the spectral waveband of operation of the IR missile seeker so that the decoy becomes a prominent target for the missile. The targeted aircraft can protect itself from an IR missile attack by ejecting IR decoy flares. Each decoy flare is design to protect one type of aircraft, which is equipped by a specific launcher. Without this protection, no aircraft should be allowed to take off.   For the first time in 1968, literature refers to the use of magnesium/PTFE mixtures in infrared decoy flares and gives details on caloric data and ignition sensitivity (Military and civilian Pyrotechnics, from ELLERN H. (1968). Over the years, improvements have been made in terms of performance and safety of the MTV decoy flares, which are still the most widely used flares.   Why MTV formulations have to be considered as an essential use of fluoropolymers as PTFE and VITON® ?  • To obtain the best performances of the flares : The performance of the flares invariably depends upon both the design and chemical nature of the IR-producing formulations. Parameters such as shape, size, weight, burning characteristics and IR output play an important role at the time of selection of a suitable formulation for a specific purpose. In particular, the IR output of a pyrotechnic formulation depends on the nature of its combustion products, their concentration in the flame, their emissivity and flame temperature and mass burning rate. The particularity of the MTV formulation is its emission of a radiant energy partly in the IR range and partly in the visible range with a minimum amount of smoke.  The main reaction on combustion of magnesium with PTFE is shown in the equation below:  2nMg + -(C2F4)n-  2nMgF2 + 2nC = 23 Kcalg-1  The heat generated heats up carbon black to a temperature  2200°K, yielding radiant emittance values comparable to those of a black-body. Thus MTV spectral distribution displays the peak maximum at 2,0 µ and strong emission bands at 4,3 µ due to carbon dioxide. MTV formulations emit a high order of IR intensity because of the presence of fluorine therein. The last important point is that the MTV formulation does not produce oxygen and does not react with the ambiant air to generate gas as CO and CO2. (High Energy Materials – propellants, explosives and Pyrotechnics » from Jai Prakash Agrawal (2010))  • To assure a good ageing of the flares :  The shelf-life of an ammunition is about 10 to 15 years. It means that the pyrotechnic composition must be very stable over time in hard environmental conditions (high and low temperatures, humidity, vibrations, …). Fluoropolymers are chemically very stable over time and fullfill their mission during the entire life of the ammunition.  In addition, the proposal of restrictions on PFAs concerned also the placing on the market of articles which contains 250 ppb of PFAs. Ammunition and pyrotechnic components are considered in majority as articles. Some of them are only a part of a complex system, integrated later by our customers to be placed on the market. Another consequence of the restriction is that the ammunition and/or pyrotechnic or not components already in stocks of our customers (in particular of the DGA in France) can no longer be used after the date of application of the restrictions and have to be destroyed by fire.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Production site : First and foremost, the production sites of MTV formulations are often located in more remote regions, a combination of a large space and the low urbanization of rural areas. It is necessary to maintain suffisant regulatory hazards zones between the population outside the production site but also between each building of the production site depending on the type of activities realized (production, storage, transport, testing areas…) and the quantity implemented.   Manufacture :  Processing of magnesium Teflon® Viton® (MTV) or magnesium Teflon® (MT) :   Several types of granular PTFE are used to produce about more than 40 different versions of MTV formulations.  • Production process of MTV formulations. The flow chart of MTV flare production line (Metal fluorocarbon based Energetic Materials, First edition, Ernst Christian Koch) is presented in a document called "Production process of MTV" provided in section IV.  It  starts with the weighting out the amounts of PTFE which is granular (the average particle size is between 100 to 800 µm). The weighting out PTFE and VITON do not generate dust nor waste. In conformity with the study of safety for each operation of the production process approved by the french legal authority, the filling capacity of the blender (batch size) is few kilograms of pyrotechnic composition. VITON® is used as a binder in the formulation and dissolved in acetone. The viscous solution is introduced in the blender. The mixture is realized in wetted conditions with no generation of dust and in specific working places with strong walls, where operators are forbidden for safety reasons. They are not exposed to chemicals.  The granulated composition is pressed into its final shape with molding tools.  The drying of the composition is realized in an oven but not completely, also for safety reasons.  A table which sums up the safety information at each working place of the process is presented also in the document called " "Production process of MTV" .  The manufacturing of pyrotechnic formulation is regulated by plenty rules and regulations to protect the employees against a pyrotechnic hazard. Collective protection (screen, strong walls, automatic process), and personal protection equipments (Fire protective clothes, leather gloves, glasses, conductive safety shoes) are ever mandatory to be safeguarded in the case of an accidental ignition of the composition.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The flares compositions are released over a wide geographical area, both from a perspective of spreed of travel of the aircraft and the altitudinal variations.  Ernest Koch has described the manufacture of toxic products of combustion of MTV and points out that the most toxic possible by-products (e.g. HF and MgF3) are calculated to be released at low concentrations due to the speed and trajectory of the aircraft and dispensing system (Metal fluorocarbon based Energetic Materials, First edition, Ernst Christian Koch). In particular, it ought be noted that HF is lighter than air and is less likely to « settle » (Energetic Materials and Munitions - Life Cycle Management, Environment Impact and Demilitarization » by Adam S. Cumming and Mark S. Johnson).  End of life of the flare : Concerning PTFE and VITON® : No waste from the processing production of MTV : very, very low quantity of fluoropolymers is sent to be incinerated by a permitted industrial waste facility per year. These polymers have no shelf life to be used. In consequence, they can be ever kept.  Concerning the MTV composition : pyrotechnic compositions are mandatory destroyed by fire on a specific outdoors area in the production site. This rarely happens. Never more than 100kg of fluoropolymers per year. As decribed by Ernest Koch, MTV will generate hydrogen fluoride and metal fluorides as magnesium fluoride and carbon soot as part of smoke formation. Ernest Koch states the important fact that in the open air, the dispersal of these products is much greater than in enclosed spaces.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Manufacture of MTV not concerned by the recycling.

6. Missing uses: a - Sector of defense - Sub-sector: Pyrotechnic systems integrator Use: a complete range of self-protection pyrotechnic systems for airborne applications. Sub-use: Manufacture of pyrotechnic compositions Annuel tonnage: less than 5 tons of PTFE and VITON  Annuel emission: very low emission (no dust, no waste of raw material) - about 100 kg are eliminated with the wastes of pyrotechnic compositions (see details in paragraph 3)  b - Information are provided in detail in the paragraph 1of this section.  c - In France, LACROIX is the only industrial to provide the Armed Forces with a complete range of self-protection pyrotechnic systems using MTV. There is only one competitor in Europe.  d - Up to now, there were no restriction on fluoropolymers which are not classified for a hazard for the health or for the environment. Finding an alternatives for MTV compositions was never identified as a priority. No study was conducted to find alternatives. Fluoropolymers are the most consistent/unique choice of material from 1970’s.  e - The time expected to be required for substitution (including any relevant certification or regulatory approvals) : More than 25 different ammunitions adapted to different threats and to different IR signatures of aircrafts and helicopters exist today. For each one, the formulation of the MTV composition is adapted (rates and types of magnesium (atomised or granular), type of PTFE (free flowing, recycling, several granulometries). So, it is not one but many alternatives that must be found to meet all the required properties. In the case of alternatives found, the usual time to qualify a solution in one ammunition is around 8 years.   The substitution will be not considered as a minor modification. In consequence, all the performances have to be tested.  f - No study conducted to answer to this hypothesis.  g - Economic impact of non observance of custumers’s contracts : A direct cost : In the case of the restriction on fluoropolymers shall apply 18 months from the entery into force, the impact on the annual sales turnover of LACROIX in the air sector would be estimated as > 70 %. This data is calculated with LACROIX knowledge of the sales planned from 2027 for the French forces and exports to other forces. It is stated that LACROIX will have to pay at least 10 or 20 % of the value of the committed market to repair the damage of the non-observance of the contracts.  Indirect cost : The non-respect of the contracts or the tacit engagements to supply with the « consumable » would be an unmeasurable impact on the reputation of LACROIX and its future markets. Loss of employment : 20 to 50 employees from the production and support services.

General Comments: We, the Medical Technology Association of Japan (MTJAPAN), are an association of manufacturers of medical devices for treatment. Our member companies account for more than 60% of all medical devices shipments in Japan. We also export high-quality medical devices to Europe and other countries around of the world, contributing greatly to the advancement of medical technology and patient care.

　Our medical devices widely contain PFAS, which was proposed to be restricted this time. In particular, PTFE and PFA are used in many medical devices as coatings and membrane materials, and are indispensable materials. In the manufacturing process of medical devices, many PFAS are used as processing solvents, processing aids, manufacturing equipment parts, and mold release agents. As a result, we are able to provide a stable supply of medical devices to patients and healthcare professionals around the world.

　PTFE and PFA, PFAS materials used in medical devices have excellent biostability. When implanted in the body or intravascular treatment, they do not leach out with body fluids or blood, etc., and the toxicity risk to the patient is extremely low. We believe that it is virtually impossible for any chemical substance to replace these materials for all medical devices within the 12-year timeframe of the proposed restriction. Additionally, medical devices must be evaluated for performance and patient safety by national regulations. In Europe as well, clinical investigations are required for new materials (raw materials) and implantable medical devices. Clinical investigations require several years or more from the start and a review period. Before clinical trials, a preliminary evaluation of the feasibility of commercialization is required for a number of years.
　Even in the unlikely event that any one company is able to provide a medical device with alternative materials, it would be difficult to secure the number and volume of medical devices for use in Europe in a 12-year period. The substitutes would not necessarily perform as well or be as safe as the well-proven PFAS. On the contrary, medical technology may decline, increasing the probability that patients will be at risk. Prices of medical devices are naturally expected to rise as well, which could be a significant burden on the health care economy.

Reference number of the previous answer : 4962d054-b85a-4c8d-bee7-a85b6042a92b

GICAT, The French Land Defence and Security Industry Association responded previously to this public consultation to express its great concern about the proposal restriction of Per-and Polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) that strongly impact its members.
Since then the impact analysis of each members (manufacturers of energetic materials components, ammunitions, rockets, missiles,...) have continued and raised the necessity to explain more in details why the chemical and physical properties of fluoropolymers are so suitable to energetic materials  processes and formulations in particular for military applications. Note that most of them have already contributed to the public consultation on their own due to confidentiality and commercial interest, and some others only rely on national association as GICAT and on European associations such as ASD, Aerospace, Security and Defence Industries Association of Europe.
Two tables are enclosed to list the physical and chemical properties of fluoropolymers, essential to answer specifications and performances requested by our military customers and by national and international standards for several decades. The objectives are to demonstrate that fluoropolymers have unique properties that make them the only ones to cover all the extreme conditions required to manufacture, to store, to handle and to work in complete safety and to achieve reliability requirements.
Table 1 lists the properties of fluoropolymers fulfilling the whole scope of requirements in the case of a contact with energetic materials during the process (tools and surface treatment) as well as in the finished product.
Table 2 concerns the key properties of fluoropolymers used to formulate pyrotechnic compositions.
These tables are submitted as a confidential attachment.
Currently there are no substitutes that fulfill all, or even most, of the key properties listed in these tables. Furthermore, even if such substitutes were found, military applications require lengthy and complex processes for qualification and validation.

Given intrinsic hazards of explosive substances and products, safety issues require progressive validation because of the lack of feedback.
To be able to substitute PFAS from our uses we would first need to be able to prove that the substitute is chemically compatible with all constituents and substances. The substitute would then need to be tested in different conditions and environments to ensure their stability and reliability.
Next their performances would need to be tested in products into which they are included, the testing being done through blast tests.
Finally all tests would need to be cross-referenced to obtain a validation according to French instruction DGA 17500 publishing 6. The entire process would take years starting once a substitute is identified during which we would be unable to supply all armed forces.
It has to be noted that gun firings tests are quite expensive and long to be planned.




A major point in the case of fluoropolymers is that there have been no previous regulatory alerts because these polymers do not present any health or environmental hazard classification and therefore no substitution dynamic exists. R&D starts the search for alternatives from scratch: NO KNOWN DEADLINE FOR SUBSTITUTION.

Due to the reliance on products from a wide range of sectors, a sectoral exemption for Defence of fluoropolymers would not protect against widespread obsolescence and unpredictable side effects within the affected industrial supply chains. It is the reason why we request an exemption of fluoropolymers for all sectors of activity.

We remain at your disposal for any questions and exchange on issue.

General Comments: A. About American Pacific Corporation

Note: Exhibit A (additional historical information), Exhibit B (citations either by link to or in pdf form), and Exhibit C (Copies of references for which links were not available) entered in Section 4 augments information in this section.

American Pacific Corp, Halotron Division (AMPAC) is a specialty chemical manufacturer founded in 1955 and located in Utah, USA.  In 1992, AMPAC initiated efforts to identify and commercialize acceptable substitutes for severe ozone depleting substances (ODS) clean fire suppressing agents, Halon 1211 (CF2ClBr) and Halon 1301 (CF3Br).  The screening program included review and analysis of dozens of compounds and blends.  This led to the first generation of products to replace severe ODS, blends of a hydrochlorofluorocarbon (HCFC) and of two hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) (Halotron I and II respectively), commercialized in the 1990’s.

Given the existing international regulations and related limitations of “first generation” HCFC-based halon substitute agents and purported imminent regulations of HFC-based agents, in the 2000-2001 timeframe, AMPAC began research and development efforts for a novel and high-performance next generation clean fire extinguishing agent.  After screening hundreds of chemicals, by itself or through collaborative efforts, 2-Bromo-3,3,3-trifluoropropene (herein referred to as “2-BTP,” CAS No. 1514-82-5, EC No. 627-872-0) became the chemical of choice for many reasons, as described below.  Through AMPAC’s efforts, millions of euros and over 20 years have been spent bringing this clean, highly effective, of low acute toxicity, non-ODS and low-Global Warming Potential (GWP) fire extinguishant to the life safety fire protection market.  The development steps by AMPAC included fire testing, generation of data related to materials compatibility, product stability in standard containers (and the related challenges), and collaborative fire testing with AMPAC’s hardware manufacturer partners to achieve fire extinguisher certification (both Underwriters Laboratories (UL) and US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Minimum Performance Standard (MPS), AC20-42D, EASA, ANAC), as well as many in vitro and live animal toxicity tests.

B. Early Development of Halons

Clean fire extinguishing agents became a necessity with the development of electronic and precision mechanical devices in the early 1900’s.  A clean agent is generally defined as “electrically nonconducting, volatile, or gaseous fire extinguishant that does not leave a residue upon evaporation” (Ref. 1).   The first clean agent was carbon tetrachloride, also known as Halon 104, which was employed in the early 20th century through World War II.

Methyl bromide (Halon 1001) was used in the 1930’s but did not find wide acceptance due to its toxicity.  Methyl bromide would later be employed as a broad-spectrum pesticide.  The Germans developed and used chlorobromomethane (Halon 1011) during World War II as it was more efficient than Halon 104. In this period there was a recognition that agent toxicity to humans was a factor that could be problematic so that a screening process was needed.

In 1948, the U.S. Army commissioned the Purdue Research Foundation to search for a suppressant of high fire suppression efficiency but low toxicity (Ref. 2). The U.S. Army developed the term “halon” to be short for halogenated hydrocarbon and devised the naming system.   During the 1960s and 1970s, two of the compounds tested finally emerged as commercial successes, namely Halon 1301 (CF3Br) which found widespread use as a total flooding agent (i.e., it dispersed throughout a space, quenching flames regardless of location).  To a lesser extent, Halon 2402 (C2F4Br2) was also used in this application but mainly in the Soviet Union and Italy.  Halon 1211 (CF2ClBr) became a commercial success as a streaming agent (where a “stream” of agent is manually directed via a fire extinguisher utilizing a designed pressure and nozzle).  By the 1980’s, most computer rooms and nearly all commercial and military aircraft and numerous museums were protected by halon-based systems because halons were clean, non-toxic, and highly effective against fires without damaging the asset being protected.

The international Montreal Protocol on Substances that Destroy Stratospheric Ozone (Montreal Protocol) was first signed in 1987 and went into force on January 1, 1989. The chemicals of concern included CFCs, methyl bromide, and halons (Halon 1211, Halon 1301, and Halon 2402).

Since halons are some of the most potent stratospheric ozone depleters and have very high global warming potentials, they were phased out of production, which led to the quest to find alternatives.

C. Why Do We Need Halon-like (Volatile, rapidly evaporating) Clean Fire Extinguishing Agents?

Aviation Fire Protection Challenge

One of the most important uses of halons has been on commercial and private aircraft.  The US FAA described the challenges associated with aviation uses of halon and determined that no know chemical had the capabilities to replace Halon 1211 for handheld fire extinguishers in the cabin compartment or Halon 1301 in the engine nacelles/auxiliary power units (APU), cargo compartments and lavatory trash receptacles (Ref. 5).  Consequently, FAA launched a coordinated research program in 1993.   The scope of the program was described as “The FAA program would concentrate on the four application areas, engine nacelle/APUs, cargo compartments, lavatory trash receptacles, and hand fire extinguishers. The basic approach would be to use full-scale evaluation fire tests to study the impact of various parameters on the level of protection provided by alternative agents/systems. Subsequently, a minimum acceptable level of performance would be defined with the research results.  Standard performance tests would be developed and validated for each application and ultimately used as the basis for approval.”   FAA was not tasked to identify candidate agents, but rather looked to industry and other government-funded research programs for alternative agents that the FAA would test against defined performance standards based on known and perceived fire hazards.

The Critical Performance of Halon 1211 - Hidden Fire Performance

In the program description (Ref. 5), FAA stated “A test article would be developed to evaluate the effectiveness of alternate agents used in hand extinguishers as compared to Halon 1211.  The fire hazard against which the hand extinguisher must protect would be a hidden in-flight fire.  It is envisioned that the hidden fire hazard would be patterned after the in-flight fire which occurred on a transatlantic Delta L-1011 flight on March 17, 1991.  In this incident, halon extinguishers were blindly discharged into air return grills, successfully extinguishing a severe electrical fire beneath the floor that was spreading into the cabin, and likely saving the airplane and its 231 occupants.  Although Halon 1211 extinguishers were originally required by the FAA for fighting a seat fire accelerated by spilled gasoline (a hijacking scenario), it is anticipated that a hidden fire hazard criterium would be recommended and the extinguishment capabilities of Halon 1211 would be maintained as the performance standard for hand fire extinguishers.”

Furthermore, the FAA went on to state (Ref. 5) “Alternate agents for hand extinguishers would be expected to be equivalent to Halon 1211 in terms of their effectiveness against hidden fires.  A full-scale test article, as described earlier, would be used to evaluate alternate agents/extinguishers.  Full-scale test results would be used to develop a small-scale performance test for appraising agent/extinguisher effectiveness against hidden fires.  The performance test would form the basis for certification approvals.   A crucial and challenging aspect of the full-scale test article is the development of a realistic and repeatable fire hazard.  In the previously mentioned L-1011 incident, insulation batting, electrical wiring, flooring, and sidewall paneling were heavily involved in the fire, and the accumulation of debris and contamination from years of service contributed to the fire spread.  It is very difficult to attain consistent burns, or even sustained burning in some cases, with such an array of complex, fire resistant materials.  For an agent/extinguisher to be effective against a hidden fire, it must possess properties that promote agent expansion and penetration into voids and throughout empty spaces.  Gaseous or low boiling point agents such as the halons, are highly effective against this type of scenario.  Unfortunately, some alternate agents are more toxic than Halon 1211.  Therefore, agents that are found to be effective against hidden fires would be evaluated under full-scale conditions for their potential toxic threat during inflight firefighting.  Virgin agent and agent decomposition products would be measured and their toxic threat to humans would be calculated based on available data and models.  A worst-case fire scenario that maximizes the agent’s toxicity would be utilized.”

The FAA elaborated (Ref. 5) “A standard small-scale performance test for hidden fire extinguishment using hand extinguishers would be developed.  The testing being considered would define the essential elements which are a controlled fire source, a port or grille into which the extinguisher is discharged, and a convoluted enclosed path between the discharge point and a fire source.  The design of the performance test would be patterned after the full-scale hidden fire test article.   A correlation of test data with the two devices would be established.  Once a prototype performance test has been developed, the next step would be its standardization.  In general, performance test criteria standardization would be accomplished with public participation. If need be, round robin testing would be used to assure conformity of results.”

As part the FAA’s program, they and cooperating agencies established the International Halon Replacement Working Group (IHRWG) (Ref. 6).  The first meeting of this group occurred at the FAA Technical Center in Atlantic City, New Jersey, USA in October 1993. The IHRWG was comprised of a wide variety of attendees including representatives from chemical manufacturers, government transportation representatives, aircraft manufacturers (Boeing, Airbus, Embraer, Bombardier), and fire suppression systems companies. AMPAC was part of the IHRWG.
The FAA established the goal of creating an MPS for each of the four areas (handheld extinguishers, cargo, engines, and lavatory). The IHRWG held meetings multiple times per year over many decades to find solutions for aviation fire protection that met the MPS.

The development of an MPS for handheld extinguishers took an extended period.  In one update given by FAA at a meeting in Germany in 2000, the lead FAA representative, Mr. Harry Webster, notes the elements in the MPS are to include US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) approval, approved by a laboratory such as Underwriters Laboratory (UL) (5-B fire test) and passing the Seat Fire Toxicity Test (at the FAA Technical Center) and the Hidden Fire Test (Ref. 7).

In 2002, the FAA MPS for handheld fire extinguishers was finally published after years of effort (Ref. 8).  All Halon 1211 replacement extinguishers must meet certification requirements of a national testing organization such as UL 5:BC or British Standard BS 3A:34B ratings. This entails repeatedly extinguishing heptane pan fires measuring 5 ft2 (0.465 m2) using a fire extinguisher conditioned to -40°F (-40°C).  The 5-B pan requires 57 liters of heptane.

The other test criteria that must be met as described in the MPS were (Ref. 8):
A. The hidden fire test design and protocol, which was important in testing the effectiveness of fire suppressants on hidden fires such as the one that occurred on a Delta L-1011 aircraft, were developed in Europe by Kidde International Research (UK) under a contract with the Civil Aviation Authority Safety Regulation Group. The established baseline to demonstrate equivalent or better performance compared to Halon 1211 was extinguishment of 9 cups out of the 20 heptane fire cups in the hidden fire test article (Ref. 9).

B. Seat Fire/Toxicity Test: When the agent is applied to a seat on fire, the agent decomposition products cannot exceed prescribed maximums in the fire fighter breathing zone (highest Hydrogen Fluoride over 60 second and 4.5-minute intervals).

The 2-BTP agent incorporated into hardware specifically designed for this suppressing agent has passed the elements of the MPS on multiple occasions at Underwriters Laboratories Inc in Northbrook, Illinois, USA beginning in 2009, and then again in 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2021 in various fire extinguishing hardware.

As noted in references 5 and 8, any candidate to replace Halon 1211 to the same level of safety must demonstrate performance in both a conventional pan fire test as well as the hidden fire test. There are no conventional agents such as water, dry chemical, and carbon dioxide that have demonstrated an ability to achieve these results despite attempts made over the past 20 years (Ref. 10).

The search for appropriate candidates that could meet these MPS requirements started in 1989 and continued for several decades.  As presented, the search for and screening of thousands of chemicals occurred from 1989 until the present day (Ref. 2).  Almost all those chemicals identified in previous efforts have been ruled out for one reason or another.

D. Justification for Extended Derogation

We believe that we have demonstrated the difficulty in identifying alternatives for clean fire suppressing agents required for critical uses such as aviation and dangerous military and industrial applications.  The process to test and certify a new chemical to make sure it meets the performance requirements takes more than 13.5 years (current RO2 proposal is 12 years plus 18 months). If the derogation for 2-BTP is for only 13.5 years, this could mean that airplanes do not have the means to protect against fire scenarios, such as seen on the transatlantic Delta L-1011 flight on March 17, 1991, after the currently proposed derogation period.  We believe a time unlimited derogation period is needed and appropriate for fire suppression agents such as 2-BTP, for the following reasons:

Other Properties of 2-BTP Clean Fire Extinguishing Agent and ODS Substitution Considerations

1. Low Atmospheric Impacts. 2-BTP has a short atmospheric lifetime and a near zero Ozone Depletion Potential and Global Warming Potential, which is favorable compared to other older generation halon substitutes including HFCs (F Gases).

Global Average Atmospheric Lifetime: 7 days (30°N to 60°N) - 4.3 days (60°S to 60°N), (Ref 4)
Stratospheric Ozone Depletion Potential (ODP): 0.0028 where CFC-11=1.0, (Ref. 4)
Global Warming Potential (GWP), 100 yr. time horizon, CO2=1.0: 0.26 (ref 4) 30°N to 60°N emissions scenario, lower for the 60°S to 60°N emissions scenario (Ref. 4)
2. Low Environmental impact
Low water solubility: 1 g/L at 20°C (Ref. 11)
Henry’s Law Constant (H): 14,350 Pa.m3/mole (Ref. 12).  This result (more than 100 Pa.m3/mole) means that, after contact with water, more than 50% of the substance would be lost from the water phase in 3-4 hours.
Octanol-water partition coefficient: Log 10 Pow: 2.7.  Since this value is well below 4.5, it indicates the substance will not tend to bioaccumulate (Ref. 11).
3. Overriding and Critical Life Safety Aspects. The agent is one of a very few that have passed the internationally recognized FAA Minimum Performance Standard demonstrating the ability to duplicate the unique capability of Halon 1211, when in 1991 a fire on a transatlantic flight below the cabin deck was extinguished with a portable Halon 1211 fire extinguisher saving over 200 lives. Carbon Dioxide, water, and most other known halon replacement agents cannot achieve this performance (Ref. 10).  When employed on commercial aircraft, portable fire extinguishers provide the primary tool in case of fire in the unique situation where there is no option for “flight” in the classic “fight or flight” fire scenario – since there is no way to exit an aircraft in flight and any fire threat must be addressed quickly and effectively utilizing the available fire extinguishers onboard.
4.  High Societal Value. Fire suppression articles containing 2-BTP have a relatively high societal value in their enhanced effectiveness in protecting life safety against the omnipresent risk of fires, protection of high value equipment, and key societal functions that rely on such high value (typically electronic) equipment.
5. Product Development Time (25+ years). The length of time and effort expended since 1989 to identify, test, and certify candidate halon replacements has been extensive.  Many chemical candidates were eliminated because they did not achieve the desired and unique properties of passing the FAA MPS, meeting acceptable toxicity profiles and environmental characteristics.  Installation of 2-BTP containing fire extinguishers only began in 2017, more than 25 years after research began for the drop-in replacement for handheld severe ozone depleting Halon 1211 fire extinguishers.
6. Lack of research for new alternatives.  The firefighting applications that still require a halon-like agent due to criticality of the asset or application do not represent a large enough market segment to warrant chemical manufacturers to investigate new alternatives given the extended time and expense to identify, test, and certify new agents.
7. Closed System Filling, Recovery and Reclamation. A robust program for chemical recovery and reclamation is employed in the EU so very little chemical will be emitted outside of firefighting discharges for life safety reasons. When bulk 2-BTP made by AMPAC is used to fill approved fire extinguishers, a closed system with leak detection is used to avoid leakage and avoid unintended emissions.  By design, because of chemical stability testing performed before 2010, the agent life in an extinguisher is limited to 12-14 years, depending on the number of times handled after initial filling, from the date of manufacture to the date of reclamation. Therefore, the life cycle for extinguishers containing 2-BTP is 12 years from the time the chemical is first dispensed in the fire extinguisher equipment.  If the extinguisher is not discharged during its life cycle maximum, the chemical is set to be recovered utilizing good practices into clean containers.  2-BTP can then be reclaimed, tested for purity standards, and recycled into new equipment.  All these processes are performed by select few authorized handlers.
8. Incremental Avoidable Carbon Dioxide Loading for Additional Testing of Candidate Agents
To the extent that new agents can be identified that are worthy of full-scale fire testing to pass the MPS series, agents must be screened, pretested for fire extinguishment capability, and then formally tested for certification by an authorized testing laboratory.  In the past, the US-based Underwriters Laboratories witnesses tests conducted at its facilities in Illinois, USA, or another approved site.

The amount of additive CO2 emissions associated with this testing activity for one chemical can be estimated based on our extensive first-hand experience of over 20 years with these programs. The estimated equivalence of CO2 generated by burning one liter (0.6795 kg) of heptane is 2.1 kg (https://homework.study.com/explanation/for-every-gram-of-heptane-burned-how-many-grams-of-carbon-dioxide-are-produced.html).  Burning one liter of gasoline produces approximately 2.3 kg of CO2 (https://natural-resources.canada.ca/sites/www.nrcan.gc.ca/files/oee/pdf/transportation/fuel-efficient-technologies/autosmart_factsheet_6_e.pdf).

Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Emissions of 2-BTP fire extinguishant can be separated into three phases: during manufacturing and fire extinguisher filling, during use in installed applications, and during equipment maintenance and end of life reclamation.  1) Manufacturing and Extinguisher filling: The final and most important step of 2-BTP manufacturing occurs at a dedicated facility in Utah USA.  The process is undertaken utilizing close system tanks, pumps, hoses, and fittings.  It is then shipped from the U.S. to the fire equipment filling location in Europe in bulk containers typically holding 600 kg each, where it is securely stored.  As needed, original bulk containers are moved from a storage area into the filling station where the extinguisher filling activity occurs, which is a dedicated smaller building or enclosure within a much larger fire extinguisher production area.  This smaller enclosed filling area has a floor area of approximately 24 m2 and a volume of approximately 66 m3.  This smaller dedicated extinguisher filling station is designed to ensure that any trace BTP vapors released during the handling, through fitting connection/disconnections, are controlled.  This control is both in terms of the distance vapors can travel and in the favorable manner of prompt evacuation from the space to the outdoors via a positive pressure ventilation system.  The filling configuration is designed so that the distance between the bulk tank and the point of filling fire extinguishers is minimized so that emissions during disconnecting is minimized.    2) Fire Extinguisher Use and discharge: Fire extinguishers containing 2-BTP are considered high performance and as noted above fulfill an important life safety role in fire protection, however, they are discharged relatively infrequently.  The two primary reasons for discharge would be in the event of a fire that needs to be extinguished quickly, and for training purposes by firefighting personnel.  The primary current use in Europe is for aviation fire protection where discharge occurrences are very low, specifically onboard aircraft from handheld (portable) fire extinguishers with net charge weights of 1.6 kg each of 2-BTP.  Regarding emissions in the aviation industry specifically, information provided by the Boeing Company (Ref. 14) described the known historical frequency of handheld fire extinguisher discharges onboard aircraft. Over the 2000-2012 period, there were an annual average of 28 discharges of Halon 1211 fire extinguishers, with 20 of those at altitude (above 10,000 ft) during flight.  The probability of discharge of a clean agent fire extinguisher on an aircraft is 1.5 in 1x10-6 per flight.  Within that low likelihood, 53% (190/360) of the discharges were on actual fires. When the latter occurs, the agent is transformed to combustion by-products (primarily HF, HBr) within the radiant heat zone while extinguishing the fire, and these combustion by-products are well known to be short-lived in the atmosphere.    These data show that although handheld  extinguishers are installed and ready for use, they are infrequently discharged before the extinguisher’s end of life.   3) Maintenance and Reclamation at End-of-Life Cycle: Fire extinguishers containing 2-BTP for aviation are to be removed from service after 12 years of being installed and returned to an authorized 2-BTP reclamation facility, currently in the US. The reclamation process for returned 2-BTP from the EU utilizes a professional firm with extensive experience.  The technology employed includes single plate distillation, use of molecular sieves, and activated alumina in a closed process with an effective yield in the 95-98% range.  The process is closed and employs recycling of reject heels, so that very little emissions (1.5% maximum) to the atmosphere result from the activity.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: The breakdown of 2-BTP in the atmosphere was studied by Patten, et al. and results published in vol. 116 of the Journal of Geophysical Research, 2011, “OH Reaction Rate Constant, IR Absorption Spectrum, Ozone Depletion Potentials and Global Warming Potentials of 2-bromo-3,3,3-trifluoropropene. “(Ref.  4).   The authors conclude that the most important eventual breakdown oxidation products are the atom Br, CH2O (formaldehyde), CF3C(O)CH2OH, CF3OH (trifluoromethanol) and CF3COOH (trifluoroacetic acid, TFA).   Trifluoromethanol is relatively unreactive in the troposphere. The breakdown mechanism involves photolysis. Reactive materials such as free Br and HBr are temporarily formed.     When 2-BTP is used to extinguish fires, which is its’ designed function, the chemical catalytically reacts with the elements involved in the combustion process to extinguish a fire.  In this process, 2-BTP breaks down to form a limited amount of unique degradation products (or “combustion by-products”) which will be generated because of the interaction of the agent in the high temperature fire zone.  These will primarily be the gases Hydrogen Fluoride and Hydrogen Bromide, which are very reactive, short-lived and are not PFAS.

10. Analytical methods: Current Best Practices used by AMPAC for Quality Control and Certificates of Analysis:  2-Bromo-1,1,1-trifluoropropene (2-BTP) is analyzed for moisture content (Karl-Fischer titration), color (comparison to a Hazen standard), turbidity (nephelometer), acidity (water extraction followed by acid/base titration), non-volatile residue (gravimetric), and purity (gas chromatography using a flame ionization detector).   Quality control for these analyses is monitored using standard materials for all but the purity, which compares the 2-BTP peak area to the combined areas of all other peaks in the chromatograph. Duplicate analyses are performed for each test. Laboratory spiked samples are prepared and analyzed for tests where this procedure is applicable.

Content: Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: EDUR is a specialist for centrifugal pumps made-to-order. As a developer and manufacturer of centrifugal pumps, EDUR produces custom-fit pumps for various individual applications in the field of water/wastewater technology, energy technology, liquid gas conveyance and industrial cleaning technology. At the same time, we are consultant and technology partner for our customers with international orientation and comprehensive service.
Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues
EDUR develops and manufactures its pumps based on specific customer requirements in order to be a successful niche supplier worldwide. Key enabler to master those requirements is a  modular system of different pump types and hydraulics, a wide range of sizes and materials, and a variety of drive solutions and sealing systems, which was  built up since the company was founded in 1927.
The sealing systems with suitable sealing materials play a special role here. To ensure resistance, these must be precisely matched to the pumped medium and its properties in the respective application, as sealing systems are responsible for restricting or preventing the medium from escaping into the environment - in the case of EDUR, conveyed fluids include various liquid gases, refrigerants, industrial cleaners or even water with special temperature or composition properties. Here, fluoropolymers are needed to produce elastic sealing materials such as FKM, FFKM or PTFE. Only these sealing materials, at this point without any proven alternatives, guarantee the best chemical resistance and fuel/high-temperature resistance. That’s why, they are an integral part of EDUR's  pump solutions built upon on EDUR’s modular system described earlier. EDUR has been using these materials since 1960, and pumps supplied with FKM, FFKM or PTFE account for a share of approx. 50%. Of these, approx. 150,000 pumps are on the market. A comprehensive ban of these materials would therefore have serious consequences for EDUR, both in the short and long term:
- Comprehensive restructuring and downsizing of the modular system as the basis of the product range due to a lack of alternatives - approx. 50% of the variants would no longer be available
- Limitation of customer applications served due to lack of sealing alternatives for numerous pumped fluids
- Loss of direct and indirect export markets outside of the European Union where fluoropolymers might be further used - due to lack of technical as well as commercial competitiveness
- Impossibility to serve the spare parts business of pumps in the field that are equipped with sealing materials such as FKM, FFKM or PTFE


For EDUR, those consequences of a comprehensive PFAS ban result in a considerable increase of expense and cost facing a loss of business volume at the same time. It is questionable whether alternatives could be available at all and in what time horizon and even if, supplier relationships probably must be build up from scratch. The damage for EDUR is thus hard to calculate; however, a third of the current annual turnover, the company's existence in an international competition would certainly be at risk.
Even though EDUR defines innovation as the core of its business model and is open to actively seek for alternatives of the described sealing systems: A comprehensive ban would pose a threat to the company's existence, especially because many customers on the German and European markets would be affected to an even higher extant. This would probably lead to a decreasing customer base.
Transitional period
EDUR has built up its modular system since 1927 and has constantly developed it further through a great deal of experiential knowledge of customer applications served. The entire business model is based on this structured expertise and ensures competitiveness in an international context. Granting a transition period of 18 months to find alternatives for one of the most important components of this system (sealing) for all served and new applications seems like an insult in front of almost 100 years of company history and is in any case completely inadequate.
Request for exemption
A comprehensive ban on PFAS would have a significant impact and would severely limit both the competitiveness and innovative capacity of European industry in general and EDUR in special. A general ban would reduce product diversity and would result in a technological step backwards even in emerging industries. A differentiated approach is therefore urgently required for sustainable regulation of the substance. It evaluated whether a PFAS substance and its use pose an uncontrollable risk to the environment and humans before deciding what substances should be banned.
In the applications EDUR serves, the sealing materials (FKM, FFKM, PTFE) can be safely installed, used and recycled, and accordingly the entire pump can be fed into the circular economy. The installed sealing elements (O-rings, flat gaskets) do not have to be exposed to the environment during their entire life cycle by providing for proper disposal. This should be the starting point for reconciling economy and ecology.
We therefore reject a general ban on PFAS substances and call for differentiated regulation of PFAS substances on a scientific basis. In addition, polymers should be exempted from the ban that have been proven to pose a low risk and are not exposed to the environment. This is the only way to ensure that the EU can serve as a role model for other regions of the world without losing its industrial position and place in the world’s economy. A differentiated approach should also be taken in order to prevent functioning technology in the installed based being replaced at the expense of the environment.

A recent project executed by the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) in cooperation with Société Générale de Surveillance (SGS) was conducted to assess that fluoropolymers get fully incinerated under representative European municipal incinerators conditions without any formation of short chain or long chain PFAS.   The study clearly demonstrated that fluoropolymers are converted to inorganic fluorides and carbon dioxide. The inorganic fluorides detected were hydrogen fluoride. A large majority of samples indicated that long chain PFAS were below levels of 1ng/m3 (>99% of samples associated with 860 deg C condition and >98% of samples associated with 1100 deg C condition). There were no short chain PFAS detected post incineration. TFA was non detectable in all samples with a reporting limit of 14 µg/m3. The results confirm that fluoropolymers at their end of life when incinerated under representative European municipal incinerators conditions do not generate any measurable levels of PFAS emissions and therefore pose no risk to human health and the environment.  The main reason to include fluoropolymers in the EU PFAS restriction proposal was persistence (resistance to degradation in the environment) in the environment. The absence of organic fluorides and more specifically PFAS in tests representative of municipal waste incineration confirms complete mineralization of fluoropolymers and provides critical data in support for exempting Fluoropolymers from the EU REACH PFAS restriction proposal. 1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Fluoropolymers are very stable materials, but persistency alone is not an appropriate measure of potential human health or environmental risk. Persistence in the environment does not indicate that the substance would accumulate in organisms, nor that environmental levels would rise to such an extent that exposure would result in toxicity. The PBT criteria established under REACH has always considered the characteristics of both persistency and bioaccumulation together, as indicators of potential risk (i.e., toxicity), which is not the case in fluoropolymers. Moreover, persistency, or stability, is the characteristic behind the much sought after properties that fluoropolymers bring to numerous industrial applications (e.g., related to chemical and temperature resistance or durability of products). Furthermore, any alternative substances that may be considered as potential substitutes for fluoropolymers, and which should perform at levels at least close to those of fluoropolymers are likely to be persistent too.   This is described in a recent (eco-)toxicity read-across report written by GSI Environmental USA, providing information on the lack of concerns related to fluoropolymers. The report is attached.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Construction products (Annex E.2.13.): PTFE thread sealing tape 1. It is widely used in gas industry as a protection of the connection between cylinder valve and cylinder. This is an essential functionality of PTFE tape as it provides lubrication of the thread, guarantee disassembly of the valve when necessary. Easy application and reliable performance in this application is not easy to replace. Historically used solution with cones based on silver and lead (alternatively including tin or aluminum) are not acceptable as they also contain problematic material. Gas companies run millions of cylinders globally and PTFE tape is used on almost every of these cylinders. If there is other solution like PTFE cones or PFPE based liquid lubricant, it is still based on PFAS.  We need further information from suppliers and development work with them to estimate the derogation period that we would need.  2. PTFE thread sealing tape is also used in equipment for cryogenic and low temperature service.  In this use we do not see any alternatives available yet and not under study.  3. PTFE thread sealing tape is used also in many other connections of gas production equipment where different design approach will need to be implemented to eliminate the use of PTFE. This will require time and investment into new equipment.  Availability of spare parts including PTFE tape will be essential for maintenance until the new equipment is available. We need further information from suppliers and development work with them to estimate the derogation period that we would need. Introduction of these lubricants significantly reduced occurrence of oxygen ignitions (fire) and improved safety of our employees, customers and patients. Currently we see no evidence of availability for alternative guaranteeing adequate level of safety and expectation of successful development of such alternative is on very low probability within the proposed derogation time.

5. Proposed derogations: On the ignition coil production BorgWarner uses worldwide Molykote G5008 Dielectric grease containing polyfluoroalkyl (PFAS).   The ignition coil is a component used on gasoline combustion engines and the function is to generate the high voltage to the spark that initiates the combustion. Quantity used per ignition coil is on the range of 0.05g.  The connection of the ignition coil to the spark plug is made through a silicone rubber component part of the ignition coil construction. In order to achieve the dielectric sealing between the rubber and the ceramic a relatively high interference is required. During the normal operation this is a static connection but the lubricant is required not only for the assembly but mostly important for the removal of the ignition coil during engine routine maintenance, in particular spark plug replacement.  Due to the temperatures involved during the application life in excess of 200C, the required dielectric protection and the silicone rubber material, only 2 options were identified over the years, a talcum powder or the Molykote G5008 Dielectric grease. The talcum powder was being discontinued over time because of the lower lubricant characteristics after ageing (exposure to high temperatures), leading most of the applications to the use of Molykote G5008 grease.   In a event that the Molykote G5008 Dielectric grease can not be used, and a suitable replacement not identified, this could lead into an ignition coil replacement every time a spark plug replacement is required. This would incur in a very high cost to final customer and not a safe environmental solution.

6. Missing uses: a. Types of PFAS PTFE, FKMs, Bisphenol AF  b. Major functions of PFAS It is installed in the hydraulically operated cylinder part of construction, industrial, agricultural and robot machines to prevent leakage of hydraulic fluid and to suppress abnormal vibration to prevent damage to the cylinder. They provide function and safety until the product life of the equipment (about 20 years) without deterioration by lubricating oil.  g. Substitution is not technically or economically feasible Multiple seals and wear bands are installed inside hydraulic cylinders of construction, industrial, agricultural and robot machines. These convert the pressure of the hydraulic fluid to reciprocating motion, thus preventing leakage of the hydraulic fluid and enduring sliding heat up to 150 deg C. NBR, ACM and VMQ other than FKM can ensure function and safety until the product life (20 years) when the normal temperature is around 100 deg C. However, the sliding speed increases due to the demand for high performance equipment, and the temperature of these products reaches 150 deg C. As the attached data shows, except for FKM, the product life is reduced to 1/10 at 150 degrees Celsius compared to 100 degrees Celsius. That is, the parts need to be replaced once every 2 years. Thus, the number of 0 replacements increases to more than 10 over the life of the product, and the amount of waste with environmental impact increases by more than 10 times. The replacement of seals and wear bands requires the disassembly of cylinders, which is a significant financial burden. If not replaced, in the worst case, an accident due to broken cylinders or a fire associated with an oil leak could result in a loss of life. Thus, FKM (perfluoro and polyfluoropolymers) is an important material to reduce the environmental impact and protect human life. PTFE (including filled PTFE), which has similar performance to FKM, can also be used for seals and wear bands. PTFE simultaneously has oil resistance, heat resistance, and wear resistance that do not deteriorate due to hydraulic fluid, sliding heat generation, and friction, as well as low sliding resistance, in particular, which can suppress stick-slip occurrence. The use of PTFE is a very beneficial option because stick-slip induces abnormal vibration and causes sudden cylinder failure. Therefore, FKM (perfluoro and polyfluoropolymers) and PTFE (including filled PTFE) are not subject to regulation, and its continued use with Time-unlimited is essential.  Also, banning supply parts from coming to market after a certain deadline violates CE principles and Green Deal goals because it prevents the repair and inspection of vehicles already on the market. Type certification systems and supplies should be recognized as important requirements for exemptions.   In addition, the use of FKM (perfluoro and polyfluoropolymers) to form molded products with rubber elasticity requires the use of bisphenol AF, a type of PFAS, as a cross-linking agent. Proposed regulations for bisphenol AF have been published in the "ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT - BPA and bisphenols of similar concern for the environment". It can be said that the proposed regulations have established upper limits for the release of bisphenol AF into the environment and that the environmental impact has been sufficiently examined. The threshold for bisphenol AF in molded products should be in accordance with the values in this proposed legislation. The use of FKM (perfluoro and polyfluoropolymers) is not subject to PFAS regulations and its continued use with Time-unlimited is essential.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Wear bands used for shock absorbers in suspension of transport vehicles Produced by NOK and supplied to the EU.  a. Types of PFAS PTFE  b. Major functions of PFAS They are used in the shock absorbers of the suspensions in the chassis of the vehicle, which dampen the vibration of the vehicle body to stabilize the attitude and maneuverability of the vehicle body, thereby contributing to the prevention of vehicle accidents. They provide function and safety until the product life of the vehicle (approximately 20 years) without deterioration due to hydraulic fluid, sliding heat generation and friction wear.  g. Substitution is not technically or economically feasible A vehicle chassis requires a suspension to dampen body vibration and stabilize body posture and steering, and shock absorbers are used for suspension components. The shock absorbers consist of a cylinder and a piston, and the piston is equipped with a wear band to stabilize reciprocating motion. Since the wear band reciprocates violently in oil, only PTFE (including PTFE with filler), which simultaneously provides oil resistance, heat resistance, and wear resistance without deterioration due to hydraulic fluid, sliding heat generation, and friction, is applicable. When resins other than PTFE, which do not simultaneously have these characteristics, are used, parts will be repaired and replaced more frequently than when PTFE is used. In other words, the economic burden of repair will increase, and the amount of waste that becomes an environmentally harmful substance will increase as a result of replacement. If not replaced, the running stability of the car body will be impaired, and there is a concern about the impact of traffic accidents on human lives. In addition, PTFE has low sliding resistance and can suppress the occurrence of stick slip. The use of PTFE is very beneficial in preventing accidents and protecting human lives because stick slip induces abnormal vibration and causes sudden suspension failure. Therefore, it is essential that PTFE (including PTFE with filler) be exempted from the regulations and continued use with Time-unlimited. The above is exactly the same for suspensions of construction, industrial and agricultural machines.  It is against the idea of the ELV Directive to prohibit the launch of vehicles after a certain deadline after type approval because it prevents recovery of development costs of vehicles. Banning the launch of supply parts after a certain deadline violates CE principles and Green Deal goals because it prevents the repair and inspection of vehicles already on the market. Missing uses: Medical devices and Medicinal Product are highly regulated and linked through the regulation (EU) 2017/745 Article 117 (which refers in several chapters to Directive 2001/83/EC (EC, 2001b)). Aptar Pharma noticed that, whereas PFASs use in Medical Devices is well described and taken into account in the sector of use and related derogation in the Annex XV restriction report, the understanding  on PFAS in the Medicinal Product sector is not obvious.  Table A.1 of Annex A of the Annex XV restriction report, does not explicitly describe uses for medicinal product whereas it is mentioned later on, in the same Annex in A.3.10 and A.3.10.1.7, A.3.10.1.12  and A.3.10.1.17 (see abstracts hereafter). Therefore, Aptar Pharma seeks for addition of Medicinal products as Use Sector in the Annex XV restriction report with at least the following sub-uses: - Polymeric PFASs used for coating packaging in contact with medicinal products (or “coated primary packaging”), - Polymeric PFASs used as hydrophobic feature of filter membranes to ventilate preservative free systems.   Abstracts of Annex A related to medicinal products: • A.3.10: “ Medicinal products (including pharmaceutical ingredients), anaesthetics and contrast media are considered not in scope of medical devices”… • A.3.10.1.7: “PFAS, especially fluoropolymers, are widely used in medical packaging applications. Packaging components like ampoules, single and multi-dose containers, bottles (also in caps and actuators), cartridges; pressurized containers, syringes and vials are known to (partly) contain PFAS, especially fluoropolymers.  Liquid drug products for injection (e.g. vials, prefilled syringes) are packed in closed container systems. These types of packaging are mostly a combination of glass (vial, barrel) and elastomers (stoppers, plungers, seals). Because of the extended period of contact between the drug product and packaging, elastomer extractables could leach into the drug product. ETFE or PTFE coated elastomeric components are often used to minimize interaction between the drug and the packaging. As this kind of packaging is in direct contact with the drug product, they are part of the drug product registration.  PTFE is also used in ophthalmic solutions packaging. It acts as hydrophobic membrane in certain ophthalmic solutions’ packaging, allowing the venting of air, while retaining fluid within the container, preventing leakage.”  • A.3.10.1.12.  “Membranes based on PTFE and PET with fluorinated C6 based side chain coatings are used for (sterile) venting of several medical devices, for example cell culture devices, analytical devices, blood tube systems for dialyzer systems, tube systems for eye surgery.” •  A.3.10.1.17 “Fluoropolymers used in the pharmaceutical packaging sector are subject to requirements of the EU legislation on regulation of medicinal products for human or veterinary use (i.e., Regulation (EC) 726/2004 (EC, 2004), Directive 2001/83/EC (EC, 2001b), Directive 2001/82/EC) (EC, 2001a).”   II. INFORMATION  A)  ANNUAL TONNAGE AND EMISSIONS (AT SUB-SECTOR LEVEL) AND TYPE OF PFAS ASSOCIATED WITH THE RELEVANT USE.  PFAS associated with the use for coating pharmaceutical product primary packaging are polymeric PFAS. Information on tonnage for medicinal product is provided in Annex A, Table A.39.  B) KEY FUNCTIONALITIES PROVIDED BY PFAS FOR THE RELEVANT USE.  Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) fluoropolymer is used directly as the material of the filter membrane.  Alternatively, PET with fluorinated C6 based side chain coatings is used. The filter membrane is used to ventilate preservative free systems without compromising their sterility. The hydrophobic effect is critical to the ventilation mechanism as liquid with low surface tension can block the filter membrane if the hydrophobic properties are not sufficient. This leads to non-function of the system. Availability is critical because preservatives in the liquid cause unexpected or harmful side effects.   Etylene Tetrafluroethylene (ETFE) fluoropolymer is part of the inert laminated film we add on drug surface contact of our rubber closures (stoppers for vials, plunger for syringes) to limit interaction with the medicinal product from our customer (pharmaceutical companies).  FluoroPolymers (FP) are chemically inert thanks to the electronegativity of fluorine and the strength of carbon-fluorine bonds. As an inert coating, this material does not leach extractables substances and reduces chemical absorption and adsorption of the pharmaceutical product by and on the rubber material of the closure, and increases the stability of the medicinal product over time. The use of a FP coating also limit the amount of free silicon oil, used as lubricant on the rubber closures surface and potential contaminant of the drug.  ETFE is FP with additional interesting functional properties :  - Moldability and adhesion to elastomers after appropriate surface treatment, - Translucency, - Solvent resistant to virtually all chemicals at high temperatures and pressures, - Temperature resistant (up to 200°C), - Low permeability to liquids, gases, moisture, and organic vapors, - Compatibility with steam sterilization and gamma irradiation sterilization. Thus, the choice of ETFE especially adapted to the use with elastomeric components for primary packaging of medicinal products.  C) NUMBER OF COMPANIES IN THE SECTOR ESTIMATED TO BE AFFECTED BY THE RESTRICTION.  Coated Stoppers or coated plungers are used by Pharmaceutical companies to package the medicinal products.  PFS equipped with coated plungers - Estimation 2022 Pharmaceutical companies                      236 Units                                                    0.6 Bn Products                                                       569   Vials equipped with coated stoppers - Estimation 2022 Pharmaceutical companies                         487 Units                                                        1.9 Bn Products                                                        1990   Source : Iqvia Data & APTAR Inj BI&Strategy Analysis  Ophthalmic dispensers, nasal sprays and topical sprays are used by Pharmaceutical companies to package the medicinal products.  D) ALTERNATIVES   To date, no chemical or technical alternative has been identified by Aptar Pharma R&D for the coating of elastomer packaging and for the filter membrane used for ventilation of medicinal products. Alternative products tested up to now by Aptar Pharma for the coating of rubber stoppers used to close the vials of medicinal products are summarized in the attached confidential Appendix 1.  Time for searching and identifying a new technical solution could not be defined at this stage and will most probably depend on the R&D research initiatives of our materials suppliers. Financial investments and development time until a successful completion of the alternative solution all along the supply chain (from raw material suppliers to the medicinal products) is expected to be long. The following steps for the implementation of an alternative for the primary packaging company should be considered:  1. alternative solution screening  2. new coating qualification 3. industrial validation 4. new packaging registration towards Health regulators   Once alternative is identified (step1), it will take at least 10 years to the primary packaging manufacturing company from the R&D stage (demonstration of the technical feasibility) to the commercial batches production and the registration with the relevant Health authorities of the new packaging.  Then, at last 5 years will be needed  for the  pharmaceutical company to qualify and register a new packaging with the relevant Health Regulators (process validation (pilot and/or industrial batches), stability studies, extractable / leachable studies…).  This means that taking into account the estimated timelines all along the supply chain (5 years for the development of an alternative for the material suppliers, 10 years for the primary packaging company, 5 years for the pharmaceutical company), transition period could reach at least 20 years.   E) SOCIO-ECONOMIC IMPACTS FOR CONSUMERS  The lack of technically feasible alternatives and the high societal value of the medicinal product indicates that a full ban would be associated with high socio-economic costs and would have harsh implications on public health.   Availability of preservative free systems of ophthalmic dispensers and nasal and topical spray pumps are critical because preservatives in the liquid cause unexpected or harmful side effects. This is evaluated in detail in the Annex - Studies on impact of preservatives used in ophthalmic dispensers (see A2 non confidential attachment).   Without alternatives and depending on derogations/ exemptions which would be considered for pharmaceutical products, shortage of Polymeric PFAS due to decrease of manufacturing by suppliers is highly probable and could lead to shortage of medicinal products.  This has been confirmed by European Pharmaceutical industry (EFPIA), publication of January 2022, (see A3 non confidential attachment). Aptar Pharma takes into consideration the risks highlighted by ECHA to the environment and human health of the use of PFASs. However according to OECD PLC study recently published (see A4 non confidential attachment), the risk caused by polymeric PFASs is different and far less from the one caused by non polymeric PFAS.
