7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: [a. Type of PFAS] PTFE(Annual usage:65tons)  [b. The key functionalities provided by PFAS] As a sealing material for automotive air-conditioning compressors, heat pumps and waterpumps. The combination of rubber and PTFE in the Radial shaft seals makes it highly compatible with the operating environment, as the properties of both materials complement each other. They demonstrates good sliding characteristics and high sealing performance in a poorly lubricated environment where heat resistance is required. Radial shaft seals are operating in a poorly lubricated environment and generate heat during use, so self-lubricating properties (low coefficient of friction and wear resistance) are especially required. The PTFE seal lip is mainly used in poorly lubricated environments because it is placed behind the rubber seal lip on the sealed fluid/gas side. Due to its molecular structure, which enables it to maintain sealing performance even in system environments where rubber seal lips lead to lack of sealing performance due to wear. PTFE also has a wide allowable temperature range and can function in low temperature environments in cold regions.   [c. The number of companies affected by the restriction] (All Vehicle Manufacturers)  [d. The availability, technical and economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives] There are no alternative material that can provide equivalent functionality.  Only PTFE, which has excellent heat resistance and self-lubricating properties due to its molecular structure, can be used. If alternative materials (non-PFAS) with inferior functionality were to be used, they would not be able to maintain the sealing function due to the inability to achieve both self-lubrication and heat resistance, leading to rapid wear and deterioration. Furthermore, if mechanical seals were used as alternatives, - the amount of fluid leakage would increase approximately 100 times, rendering them unable to maintain their functionality.  - Additionally, the amount of refrigerant leakage would also increase approximately fivefold, resulting in an annual leakage of over 10g of refrigerant from all new vehicles (approximately 10 million units/year) within the EU region after the implementation of regulations. In other words, in the first year of regulation, it would be 100 tons/year, increasing to 200 tons/year in the second year, and 300 tons/year in the third year, and so on. This would have an extremely significant impact on the environment. - The size of the lipseal gives also the opportunity for downsizing of the compressor / waterpump in the case of a mechanical seal this is less easy / not possible. .  Compared to lipseals, mechanical seals have an energy impact based on used materials which is almost 50% higher. The lipseals also show a friction over life time which is 40-80%  lower compared to a mechanical seal   In compressors for car air-conditioning and waterpumps for the cooling circuit Compared to lip seals, mechanical seals are approximately 10 times more expensive. In addition, the width of mechanical seals is approximately twice as wide as that of lip seals, therefore it is expected that costs of the equipment will also increase due to the increased size. (The lip seal : approx. 12 mm、the mechanical seal : approx. 24 mm）  [e. Information on the status of R&D processes for finding suitable alternatives] At present, there is no possibility of developing alternative products from a technical and financial standpoint. - FKM material which has high temperature resistance (required property) was considered as a rubber seal lip instead of PTFE seal lip, but PFAS regulations are the same and the wear resistance was also insufficient.  - There was also an idea to set grease between the rubber lips, but this design caused wear of the rubber seal lip on the non-liquid side, the problem of durability could not be solved. From the above, not only our company but also other companies have generally designed lip seals for automobiles with rubber on the liquid side and PTFE on the non-liquid side. Apart from lip seals, mechanical seals are available, but environmental degradation and socio-economic impacts due to decrease in sealing properties can be expected.   ---If the risks described in section g. below are acceptable, the following statements regarding alternative considerations may be referenced --- If we were to develop alternative materials, even with compromised functionality (Negative environmental impact), it would take several years for development and selection, and an additional five years or more for validation at the material, component, standalone product, unit, and vehicle levels.  The costs incurred during this period are estimated to be approximately 1 million euros per specification for component manufacturers, and vehicle evaluations alone are expected to cost between 50,000 and 100,000 euros per model.  It would require further time and expenses to accommodate multiple vehicle models and manufacturers.  There is also a possibility of requiring modifications and adjustments to peripheral devices, which raises concerns about the impact on consumers due to the increased costs.  [f. Supposition when substitution is technically and economically feasible] At present, it is technically irreplaceable.  [g. Supposition when substitution is not technically or economically feasible] Citizens in areas where PFAS regulations apply will have to live in a deteriorating environment.  Based on the above, there are no PFAS substitutes, and substitution with materials of inferior functionality would cause a variety of adverse effects, making substitution virtually impossible.  Therefore, PTFE in radial shaft seals for airco compressor, heat pumps  and waterpump cooling circuits in passenger vehicles should be exempted from this restriction.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: -

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: We urge time-unlimited exemptions and request better definitions on many of the proposed derogations (or exemptions) for the following applications as these applications are highly regulated and the qualification process is extensive: • Lubricants. We note that there is already a proposed derogation for “lubricants where the use takes place under harsh conditions” or the use is needed for safe functioning and safety of equipment until 13.5 years after EIF. This time frame may not be sufficient to address these applications. • Fluoropolymer manufacturing. • Materials used at industrial sites. Accompanied by reporting requirements on risk management measures and emissions controls, exemptions should be similar to the approach taken in the REACH restriction on intentionally added microplastics. • Military and defense (not covered currently). • Petroleum (oil and gas) and mining. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) and the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement (BSEE) are two agencies that regulate oil and gas companies.  At present, the American Petroleum Institute (API) has over 50 industry standard specifications that reference specific PFAS for their beneficial safety-driven properties, including requirements that critical (pressure- or temperature-protective) components include superior properties provided by PTFE (e.g., Teflon), fluoroelastomers (e.g., FKM and FFKM), fluoropolymers in general, or PVDF.  We note that there is already a proposed derogation for “fluoropolymer applications in the petroleum and mining industry until 13.5 years after EIF.” This time frame is not sufficient for certain applications and is not needed due to API’s standard-setting process and the highly regulated nature of the oil and gas sector. In addition, it seems this derogation does not cover the whole oil & gas sector – and refers only to parts of the exploration/production process, and not the refining, petrochemicals or distribution parts of the oil & gas sector. The scope of the derogation should be extended and clarified. • Electronics and semiconductors.  Spare parts for repair of finished electronic equipment already placed on the market.   Resupply of articles already placed on the market (preowned products).  As mentioned in comments from the Information Technology Industry Council, “The concepts of ’right to repair’ and allowing resale of preowned products have been broadly incorporated into other EU substance restrictions and other EU REACH restrictions, and it is essential to incorporate them into the EU PFAS restriction to avoid major market disruptions.”  Materials used in photolithography, etch, deposition, cleans, and other unit processes that are deemed essential for the manufacture of advanced semiconductors.  Articles used in the manufacturing of semiconductors. • Energy applications, including batteries and hydrogen. • Transportation (manufacturing of transportation, safety, and emissions controls technologies of vehicles).   Currently, alternative solutions for PFAS are poorly understood with respect to several key technical automotive applications. Identifying and validating alternatives take a considerable amount of time. Additionally, reporting requirements for PFAS substances are a recent development.  Resultingly, the development of an exhaustive PFAS inventory of the global automotive supply chain is ongoing and will likely take many years. Therefore, the 18-month time limit after entry into force for applications without a derogation is far too short and exemptions should be considered.  The maintenance and repair of vehicles no longer in production are critical factors to ensuring that customers can continue to get high-quality, reliable parts throughout the life cycle of their vehicles. Redesigning replacement parts for vehicles no longer in production would not be feasible due to technical, economic, and logistical barriers. Replacement parts must function identically to the original part to ensure that vehicle functionality and safety are not adversely impacted. Therefore, a derogation for replacement parts, specifically designed for the service, repair, and maintenance of vehicles is critical.  Fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers should be excluded from the scope of the restriction. Currently, there are no known alternatives available that can provide the desired durability, chemical resistance, temperature resistance, and surface tensions of fluoropolymers. Furthermore, fluoropolymers are vital in the development of electric vehicle battery and hydrogen fuel cell technologies, which both support EU decarbonization policy.  In particular, according to the most recent study “Pilot-Scale Fluoropolymer Incineration Study: Thermal Treatment of a Mixture of Fluoropolymers under Representative European Municipal Waste Combustor Conditions” conducted by Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) in cooperation with Société Générale de Surveillance (SGS) (study summary is provided below):  "There were no short chain PFAS detected post incineration. The results confirm that fluoropolymers at their end of life when incinerated under representative European municipal incinerators conditions do not generate any measurable levels of PFAS emissions and therefore pose no risk to human health and the environment."  Exemptions, derogations, and longer transition timelines are required for the vehicle battery industry to allow it to identify and implement alternative non-PFAS solutions.  Potential replacements for R-1234yf do not have the same or better global warming potential (GWP) value. The use of CO2, propane, or ammonia as a potential substitute also have concerns. Switching away from R-1234yf will require extensive redesign of existing vehicle platforms and the servicing of approximately 1.5 billion vehicles already in commerce to utilize the new refrigerant. Unlimited derogations are also required for existing internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles and existing fleets due to the lack of alternative options.  The automotive industry will require derogations and longer transition timelines for the use of refrigerants for thermal management on battery and e-powertrain equipment, technology that supports EU decarbonization policy.  Unlimited derogations are also required for existing ICE vehicles and existing fleets due to the lack of alternative options.  Automotive electronics applications such as cables, cable harnesses, printed circuit boards, brackets, touch panels, wires, electronic components, and semiconductors rely on PFAS materials, mainly fluoropolymers. This is because of their unique combination of properties, including temperature performance, durability, and chemical stability. There are no known suitable alternatives with the same level of lifetime performance available at this time.  Requirements for the safe dismantling of vehicles exist, which minimize the environmental PFAS risks. • Aerospace.  The aerospace industry should be recognized as a separate sector with a time-unlimited derogation. For space applications in particular, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration implements standards on U.S. industry. • Aviation (individually and as part of aerospace). The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), the U.S. Department of Defense, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration, and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency are examples of primary agencies responsible for regulating different aspects of the aviation sector. The FAA, for example, ensures that commercial aircraft are certified to meet the safety requirements.    As discussed in the recent GCCA white paper (excerpt follows), many considerations must be taken into account when designing or changing the design to any part, component, system, subsystem, or full aerospace product.   The A&D companies that design and integrate the products (e.g., aircraft, engines, radar systems, missiles), are each responsible for their own product qualification, validation and certification, according to airworthiness regulations or defense/space customer requirements. Within a single A&D company, even seemingly ‘similar’ components or hardware used in different systems/models have unique design parameters and performance requirements, driven by the system-level requirements of the final delivered product. A&D products cannot be placed on the market without going through this demanding process irrespective of any REACH legislation. The same rigorous process is in place to approve materials used for the repair and maintenance of these products. Aerospace and defense chemical substitution timelines can vary from a few years under the most optimum conditions (e.g., simple change with full interchangeability with the original design) to multiple decades (e.g., where performance requirements are not fully met by candidate alternatives, such as hexavalent chromium (Cr(VI) or halon fire protection replacement activities). • Industrial applications (not covered currently).  Hard chrome plating industry: Implementation of an exemption or extension of the derogation to 13.5 years to avoid conflicting with EU persistent organic pollutants and other elements of EU REACH. • Chemical processing industry (not covered currently).  • Medical devices and medical products. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) governs medical devices and medical products.  We urge exemptions for two medical propellants currently used in MDIs: HFC-134a and HFC-227ea consistent with the one granted to other medical device sectors. The proposed time frame—18 months after finalizing the proposal—is not technically or economically feasible and would risk the health of patients in Europe and around the world. Prematurely banning these essential products could lead to drug shortages of essential lifesaving medicines. A significant proportion of medicines manufactured in Europe are exported around the world. Adequate time must be provided to allow replacement products to be developed, tested, and approved by medicines’ regulators and for patients to be safely and seamlessly transitioned. Companies are developing next- generation more sustainable propellants to mitigate climate impact. One of these propellants, HFC 152a, is not classified as a PFAS. The current proposal recommends a 12-year derogation for MDI coatings given “the lack of technically feasible alternatives and the high societal value of the medicinal products indicates that a full ban would be associated with high socio-economic costs.” The precise same rationale applies to the existing medical propellants for MDIs.   We respectfully request a permanent exemption for HFO 1234ze as a medical propellant for MDIs. As outlined below (and to be supplemented in the future), HFO 1234ze represents an important alternative option to accomplish the phasedown of the existing medical propellants and will have a long-term role as a potential option for transitioning MDIs away from the existing medical propellants, HFC-134a and HFC-227ea.  We request a permanent exemption for PFAS used in membranes for dialysis equipment and as coatings for medical implants and coatings for surgical instruments as there are no other materials to which blood platelets and pathogens do not adhere.  We urge exemptions for fluoropolymers present in the plant, equipment, and consumables used in pharmaceutical manufacturing facilities. In chemical synthesis facilities PFA, PTFE, PVDF, and ETFE lined components provide corrosion protection against aggressive process solutions. While in biotechnology manufacturing facilities fluoropolymers (FEP, PTFE, EFTE, ECTFE, PCTFE, PFPME, and PFA) are used extensively because these materials are chemically inert, stable, and of very high purity, characteristics that are necessary for aseptic and low bioburden processing. In short, EU manufacturing facilities would not be able to function without fluoropolymers and if these facilities are global suppliers of APIs (active pharmaceutical ingredients), the security of the supply of multiple medicines will be put at risk by the EU PFAS Restriction.    The coalition urges an exemption for Polychlorotrifluoroethylene (PCTFE)-based materials. PCTFE is used as a noncontact layer in prescription and over-the-counter (OTC) pharmaceutical packaging, as well as in medical device packaging applications. 8. Other identified uses: Rotating shaft seals, reciprocating seals, and fixed seals (Including O-rings, packing, gaskets, etc.) used in equipment and equipment used in food processing. Produced by NOK CORPORATION and supplied to the EU.  a. Types of PFAS PTFE, FKM, Bisphenol AF  b. Key functions of PFAS PFAS are installed on moving parts and connections of equipment and equipment used in food processing to protect (keep odors away, prevent leaks, and prevent contamination) processed food. PFAS do not deteriorate due to acid/alkali, oil/mineral content, etc., and do not deteriorate due to disinfectant or high-temperature sterilization at the time of cleaning to provide the function and safety of equipment and equipment.  g. Substitution is not technically or economically feasible   Food processing frequently involves mixing, stirring and transferring food ingredients. In mixing and stirring, rotary shaft seal and/or reciprocating seal are required between the tank and the shaft in order to transfer power from an external motor to the raw materials in the tank. In addition, piping is used mainly for the transfer of food raw materials, and a fixed seal such as an O-ring, packing, gasket, etc. is required for the joint of the piping. These seals do not leak raw materials to the outside and prevent foreign matter from entering from the outside. Of course, high durability is required so that the seals themselves do not become foreign matter.  Fluororesin (PTFE, etc.) and fluororubber (FKM, etc.) are preferably used for these seals. The reasons are as follows. Fluororesin and fluororubber do not deteriorate due to oil/mineral content in food raw materials or acid/alkali aqueous solutions such as hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide used in food processing. Fluororesin and fluororubber do not transfer odors to raw materials because their own odors are very low, and at the same time, they do not absorb odors and transfer odors to other raw materials because their affinity with odor components is very low. When cleaning equipment and equipment, chlorine-based disinfectants and high-temperature sterilization at 120°C or higher are used, but fluoropolymer and fluororubber do not deteriorate by disinfectants and high-temperature sterilization.  Other than fluoropolymer and fluororubber, there is a risk of leakage of food raw materials, contamination of foreign substances from outside, and contamination by the seal itself as a foreign substance due to deterioration during use and cleaning. Infiltration of foreign substances from outside due to seal failure, and health hazard due to ingestion of food contaminated by the seal itself as a foreign substance. In addition, deterioration of the quality resulting in the adhesion of smell to food raw materials occurs, and food destruction due to the occurrence of food quality incompatibility increases. To avoid this, the waste of seal parts increases by replacing seal parts every time. Therefore, if a material other than fluororesin or fluororubber is used, the frequency of replacement of seals increases, and the waste generated by replacement increases significantly. In order to replace seals, it is necessary to disassemble equipment and equipment, which is a heavy economic burden. If seals are not replaced, in the worst case, internal pressure can cause an explosion of food raw materials, etc., or a fire caused by a leak of flammable food raw materials can affect human life. Fluororesin and fluororubber are important materials that reduce environmental impact and protect human life, so they are not subject to regulations and must be used continuously under Time-unlimited.  Banning spare parts from the market after a certain period of time would interfere with the repair and inspection of equipment and equipment already on the market and would violate the CE Principles and Green Deal targets. Spare parts should be recognized as an important requirement for exemptions.  In addition, the use of bisphenol AF, a PFAS, as a cross-linking agent is required for the use of FKM (perfluoro and polyfluoropolymers) to form rubber-elastic molds. The proposed regulation for bisphenol AF is published in "ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT – BPA and bisphenols of similar concern for the environment". The proposed regulation sets an upper limit for the release of bisphenol AF into the environment, and it can be said that the environmental impact has been fully examined. The threshold value of bisphenol AF in molded products should be in accordance with the proposed regulation. The use of FKM (perfluoro and polyfluoropolymer) should be exempted from PFAS regulation and continued use in Time-unlimited is mandatory.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Sector Lubricants: in watchmaking and manufacture of watches a specific substance is used. It is also referred to as an epilame. Epilame is available from different companies but one of them is the biggest and most used by far. It contains partially fluorinated alkane isomers and is applied to watch parts by coming in contact with the solution and dried afterwards. It helps prevent spreading of the oils and lubricants that are applied to those parts. Expected appliances range from just two specific parts to even rinse all watch movement parts in it. Two of the bigges swiss watch brands demand use in their certified service centers or anyone that wants to officially service their products in order to stay conform to their standards. As an independent watchmaker I have the ability to avoid it. Watchmaking is over a hundred years old and epilames were only used since the 1970s and improved upon ever since. Before it was mostly diluted stearic acid that was used to treat the parts. A multi layered stearic acid also has the effect of keeping oil in one place and avoid spreading but not as efficient as modern day epilame. As a side effect of today's epilame it can happen that the coating is scraped off by moving parts and it can form a dust or loose particles inside the movement. To what extent this dust has a negative impact on running and accuracy is researched but I don't have the results. But the assessment of the big brands has apparently ruled the positive effects over the side effects. When a watch is serviced, it is cleaned in a cleaning solution with a rotating basket. These solutions will contain parts of epilame and when the solution is disposed, fluor compounds will enter the recycling circle. The pros and cons of epilame use is sometimes discussed among watchmakers and some independent have even stopped using it in mistrust of the possible dust pollution - not even considering environmental or health issues. I can't name them specifically but I have talked to well known watchmakers and they can see no downsides in accuracy or performance after leaving the epilame away. There might be a potential shortening of the service intervall that would need to be discussed or researched further.  Summary: considering the marginal loss in performance by either leaving epilame away or using the former method of stearic acid, it can be discussed if watch servicing and manufacture are really dependant on the use of fluorinated compounds in order to produce a well working product or if the use of alternatives can instantly be applied to the whole industry and their extended arms with downsides for the consumer that weight way less than the positive effect of one less industry using fluorinated compounds.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:  The use of hydrofluoroolefins (HFO) has many advantages for the production and the long-term use of insulated pipes.  Insulated pipes are mainly used for district heating networks. For the production of such pipes blowing agents are employed for manufacturing of the thermal insulation. Using HFO (CAS numbers: 692-49-9, 102687-65-0, 754-12-1)  instead of the alternatives cyclopentane or pentane has distinct advantages.  Most notably there are significant energy savings over the life time of district heating networks when the insulated pipes being employed are produced with HFO. The energy losses of such insulated pipes is 15 % below the next best technical alternative. District heating is one of the key components with respect to decarbonzation (see for example: Communication from the commission to the European Parliament, the Council, The European Economic and Social Committee of the regions,  An EU Strategy on Heating and Cooling, Feb 16, 2016).  For that reasons it is requested that HFO-1233zd(E), HFO-1336mzz(Z), and 1224yd fluorinated gas uses as as foam blowing agents made subject to the time-unlimited derogation.    REASONING:  Hydrofluoroolefins (HFO) are chemicals which can be used as physical blowing agents for polyurethane foams (PUR-foams).   As an alternative hydrocarbons such as pentane or cyclopentane can be used instead.  However, HFOs have distinct ecological an technological benefits over hydrocarbons. That shall be exemplified with insulated pipes which are employed in district heating networks.  Insulated pipes are used whenever there is a need to keep the transported medium at a defined temperature. In district heating the transported medium is water which is heated up centrally and then distributed to the individual households for the purpose of heating. The central energy source for heating the water to the desired temperature (typically 80 - 120 °C) is advantageous compared to the individual heating of each single residential building (e. g. with oil or gas). District heating allows for the use of waste heat (e. g. from power plants) or the use of energy sources which could not be easily used by individual households (e. g. biomass, wood waste and so on). Furthermore district heating is more energy efficient. For those reasons district heating is at the heart of the energy transformation in order to reach the long term CO2 - targets (net zero).  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_heating  https://www.veolia.co.uk/district-heating-efficiency   It is necessary to understand the following technical details in order to appreciate the advantages of HFO over hydrocarbons as a blowing agent in PUR-foams:  1) The physical blowing agent is a key component for the formation of the PUR-foam. The physical blowing agent is mixed with the two reactive components, a polyol and an isocyanate.  2) The two components react with each other and a chemical network is building up in a matter of a few minutes. During that exothermic reaction the mixture is warming up.  3) The evolved heat causes the blowing agent to evaporate and this gas formation is the cause of the reacting mixture to become actually a foam instead of a firm material.  4) The resulting foam consists of little bubbles of dimensions in the range of several hundred micrometers, those bubbles are also called cells of the foam.  5) The blowing agent does not leave the foam after its formation, instead it remains trapped in the cells of the foam.  6) In addition to the physical blowing agent there is also carbon dioxide which is being formed during the chemical reaction. That carbon dioxide acts as an additional blowing agent and remains in the cells too.  7) All those gases entrapped in the cells are called the cell gases.  8) The insulation properties of a given PUR-foam are mainly determined by its cell gas composition. The ratio of carbon dioxide and the physical blowing agent can be altered within certain limits. Also the type of physical blowing agent can be changed (HFO, cyclopentane, pentane). The insulation properties of a given PUR-foam are improved by  a) a lower amount of carbon dioxide in the cell gas b) a higher amount of physical blowing agent in the cell gas c) having HFO instead of other conventional physical blowing agents (hydrocarbons). That is because physical blowing agents have in itself a lower (i. e. better) heat conductivity than carbon dioxide.  9) The reason for 8c) is twofold:  a) HFO has a lower heat conductivity than cyclopentane or pentane, that means the intrinsic insulation properties of HFO are better than for hydrocarbons b) HFO has a much higher solubility in the two component mixture mentioned above. Therefore it is possible to make foams containing more physical blowing agent and therefore to shift the ratio of the cell gases towards the preferred physical blowing agent.  10) Using HFO as a blowing agent instead of hydrocarbons allows the production of insulated pipes which have a heat loss which is 15 % lower. This translates proportionally to the energy being saved in a district heating network.    To illustrate the magnitude of that energy saving, the situation in Switzerland shall serve as a typical example. The total energy consumption in 2020 added up to 208 TWh (see Annex 1, chapter 2.1, page 9). Out of that 33 % (70 TWh) was used for heating of buildings and hot water. At the moment about 5 % of the buildings are connected to district heating (see Annex 1, chapter 2.2, page 10). Though not all heating needs will be covered by district heating in the future it becomes clear that in order to reach the target of net zero in 2050, huge efforts will be taken to enlarge the share of district heating at the expense of fossil fuels like oil and gas. But for the sake of the argument the 5 % of district heating corresponds to 3.5 TWh of primary energy needed per year. A 15 % reduction due to better insulation of the pipes corresponds to 0.5 TWh per year.  If that is projected to the population of the European Union which has a population which is 50-fold that of Switzerland, that conservative estimation comes to 25 TWh of energy savings per year. And that reflects only the status as of today, the huge expansion of district heating in the years to come is not included in that picture.

6. Missing uses: As a mechanical engineering company in the field of materials handling technology (downstream user), it is foreseeable for us that the PFAS restriction proposal published by ECHA will have a significant impact on our production and products.  Many uses in which certain PFAS play a central role are not mentioned in the restriction proposal, although extensive information was provided by industry in the previous consultations.  In particular, the use of components containing PFASs in industrial plants is not considered, although this is highly relevant for the entire industry and no suitable alternatives currently exist.  All applications not considered without exemptions would be affected by a direct ban of all PFAS after a transition period of only 18 months!  PFAS are present in many mechanical and electrical components that we need to manufacture our machines. For example, in construction and coating materials, valves, seals, motors, sensors, contactors, cables, connectors, belts. For some applications, there are alternatives to products containing PFAS, but often this means sacrificing the service life, performance, and safety of the machines.  Furthermore, the area of spare parts is not considered in the planned regulation. How are existing machines to remain repairable if components containing PFAS may no longer be manufactured? From the point of view of sustainability and cost-effectiveness, it is imperative that exemptions be unlimited or at least adapted to the service life of machines.  From our point of view, the restriction of PFAS should be substance-related and risk-based, as also provided for in Art. 68 (1) of the REACH Regulation, since not all PFAS pose an unacceptable risk that justifies a restriction.  The restriction should differentiate between the different PFAS groups, and the risks posed by their uses and exclude individual substance groups from the restriction proposal altogether.  Industrial applications usually involve the use of fluoropolymers. Some  of these have been scientifically evaluated as "polymers of low concern" (PTFE, ETFE, FEP, PFA, PVDF  and VDF-co-HFP). They have been shown to be chemically stable, nontoxic, non-bioavailable, not water soluble and not mobile. For these reasons, the fluoropolymers are also approved, for example, as materials for food contact or in medical technology. Any deviating classification would have to be scientifically justified.  PFAS groups with low risk (e.g. fluoroelastomers, fluoropolymers, assessed by the OECD as "polymers of low concern"), which do not pose a relevant risk to humans and the environment but guarantee the durability and safety of industrial products and production processes, and uses without relevant risk (e.g. uses in closed systems) should be exempted from the ban.  The planned regulation should clearly distinguish between applications in the consumer sector (B2C) and applications in the industrial sector (B2B).   The chemical scope of the restriction should also be communicated transparently by means of a list of affected substances (including IUPAC names, CAS numbers, EC numbers), so that as a company you can collect the information along your supply chain in a targeted manner.  The proposed restriction is neither safe for companies to comply with nor can it be safely controlled by competent authorities. The limits for the permissible concentrations of PFAS come from the most sophisticated trace analysis, but there are no standard methods for their determination.  The identification of the affectedness is a major challenge for us. The insufficiently harmonized classification of PFAS in the CLP Regulation means that no information is passed on to us as users (e.g. via the safety data sheet), which makes the analysis of the affectedness time-consuming and in many cases almost impossible.  Furthermore, we ask ourselves how it is to be controlled or prevented that products containing PFAS continue to be imported into the EU from outside the EU. This would lead to a competitive disadvantage for us.  Furthermore, it is not comprehensible why applications where PFAS directly enter the environment (e.g. pesticides) are exempted from the restriction and applications where there is no risk to the environment (e.g. components in mechanical engineering) are affected by a ban within 18 months.  The socio-economic effects of the planned PFAS restriction are currently not yet foreseeable for ourselves, our suppliers and customers and therefore lead to considerable uncertainty. Possible effects are:  • Costs due to the identification of affectedness • Costs for the search for alternatives • Cost of switching to alternatives, if available • Impact on machine functionality, life, performance and safety, if applicable • Disruption to supply chains if needed components may no longer be manufactured and alternatives are not available • Loss of revenue due to increased costs or disruption to supply chains • Loss of jobs, if applicable  The indefinite exemption of substances with no relevant risk, such as fluoropolymers, would prevent most impacts before they occur. Competent authorities could focus on the really problematic substances and applications.  Regulations should be limited to a reasonable level and, before they come into force, clear  and pragmatic detection methods should be developed.

5. Proposed derogations: As we have understood the Echa's PFAS ban, a hazard to humans and the environment is to be avoided. This hazard arises only from short-chain PFAS substances and not from long-chain fluoropolymers. This fact was confirmed by the study: Korzeniowski, S.H. et al. (2023), A critical review of the application of polymer of low concern  regulatory criteria to fluoropolymers II: Fluoroplastics and fluoroelastomers. Integr Environ  Assess Manag, 19, 326-354, https://doi.org/10.1002/ieam.4646, in which FKM and FFKM were classified as polymers of low concern under the EU definition of a polymer of low concern and these Fluoropolymers are not a risk for the health of humans and environment. Other short-chain fluorinated substances which are used as a processing aids or emulsifier, on the other hand, should be banned. The Industry has proven that fluoropolymers with identical properties can also be produced without such substances.  According to this statement KACO supports the planned substance ban for PFAS as there are substances among the PFAS family that pose a risk to human health and the environment. A regulation or ban of such substances is right and important.  With the complete restriction of all PFAS products the European industry will no longer be competitive with other global markets, such as Asia. This is why KACO is calling for the exclusion of the fluoropolymers and their monomers needed for their production from Annex XV of ECHA's proposed substance ban on PFAS.

6. Missing uses: e: SHAFT SEALS: KACO does know the alternative materials for shaft seals, which are ACM, HNBR and NBR, as we are using them all in our production. When the application or the customer specification is allowing a different material than a fluoroelastomer KACO is already using the alternative. The alternative materials provides always a benefit in price which helps us to be and stay commercially competitive as fluoroelastomers are the most expensive polymers we are using.  For certain application, like gear box shaft seals for combustion engines, alternative materials are working better than fluoroelastomers.  With higher requirements to temperature, chemical resistance or friction, alternative materials will not fulfil those sufficiently in at lease one of this points. As friction is for the range of battery vehicles a critical criteria, the requirements are getting lower which can not be achieved by alternative materials.  MEMBRANES: KACO uses PTFE based membranes for battery deflation parts, which are helping the battery pack of a car to have always the correct pressure inside. When heat is generated (driving or charging) the membrane has to release the overpressure out of the battery pack. In emergency cases (e.g. burning of a single battery cell) the membrane has to perform a degassing by its permeation or by bursting at a certain pressure. In addition, the membrane must have a certain level of waterproofing and meet a UL 94 fire rating.The most important criteria are: Temperature resistance up to 150 °C or above Classification according UL 94 Water thightness Air permeability  Mechanical properties Membrane materials are available that are not based on PTFE. However, these have all been developed for the textile industry and do not meet the requirements of a membrane for a functional or safety-relevant component in the automotive industry.  KACO does not know a alternative material for our membranes which fulfil all requirements to achieve functionality for the live time of a vehicle.  SHAFT GROUNDING RINGS: Shaft grounding rings are necessary to protect the barring of the shaft from currents which are coming from the electric engine. Currently there are two electric engine architectures used in for battery vehicles.  In first architecture the electric engine is separate from the gear box and shaft is running run dry. We call it dry grounding.  In the second architecture is the gear box and electric engine in one unite and the engine and the shaft are running in oily environment.  We call this wet grounding, which is according to our customers the future For both architectures we are using either a silver coated PTFE disc or electric conductive PTFE compound. Known alternative materials are for shaft grounding rings  Carbon fibre elements in the shaft grounding ring: Only works in dry applications Speed limit of the shaft of 45 m/s Can not run bidirectional, fibres will break while driving in reverse  Non woven disc in the shaft grounding ring: Only works in dry applications.  Non woven materials have a poor resetting properties. Will loose the contact to the shaft. Therefore no life time product Will brittle at temperatures of around 125 °C and have even worse resetting properties

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: • sector: Food contact materials and packaging, packaging for pharmaceutical (pharma packaging), medical devices, cosmetic and hygiene articles • sub-uses: paper and board packaging, plastic packaging, other packaging applications

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: In the consumer plastics packaging industry, very small quantities of polymer processing aids (< 0,1%) based on fluorine-containing monomers are used in polyolefins. These polyolefins will go into the plastic recycling streams with varying PFAS-content. In order to check the TOF-limit of 50ppm (or 50 ppm limit for fluoropolymers) for recycled PE or PP set on the market, a recycler would have to check each recycled batch for PFAS without having the possibility to influence the PFAS concentration during the recycling step. Additionally, currently, there is no standardized analytical method available to check the content of fluoropolymers in plastics, thus the proposed limit for content of fluoropolymers cannot be controlled. Therefore, we ask for an exemption for the output material of the plastic recyclers.

5. Proposed derogations: Some IK member companies have provided detailed information regarding tonnage of PFAS used per year to the Fluoropolymer Group at PlasticsEurope as part of a corresponding survey (Downstream user questionnaire for PlasticsEurope Fluoropolymer Group (FPG) to develop a Socio-Economic Impact Assessment (SEIA) for the European Fluoropolymers Industry). We refer to the data from the Fluoropolymer Group.  Regarding to the issue emissions to the environment we refer to the “Pilot-Scale Fluoropolymer Incineration Study” from Fluoropolymer Group at PlasticsEurope: The study clearly demonstrated that fluoropolymers are converted to inorganic fluorides and carbon dioxide. The results confirm that fluoropolymers at their end of life when incinerated under representative European municipal incinerators conditions do not generate any measurable levels of PFAS emissions and therefore pose no risk to human health and the environment. The study results of the preliminary report of this study have been submitted to ECHA and attached to the report.

6. Missing uses: • Packaging (flexible and rigid) for pharmaceutical (pharma packaging), medical devices, cosmetic and hygiene articles • Agricultural films such as stretch wrapping films (for industrial applications) • Transport packaging (IBCs) for dangerous goods • Technical textiles (Membranes used for the ventilation of IBCs and packagings which must be water, oil and alcohol repellent) • Plastic fabrics for hygiene and medical applications, e.g. nonwovens that also have to be water, oil and alcohol repellent or be highly hydrophilic  • Machinery parts for the production of packaging materials • Lubricants and oils for industrial uses/production • For the construction sector:  geo textiles, roofing applications, building insulation   • Details to medical applications: fabrics for single use pillows, sheet covers, blankets, ostomy bags (Stoma Beutel), Operation room equipment such as aprons, masks, fabrics to cover wounds, and many more • Lab equipment that has to be super hydrophobic, such as special sample and centrifuge tubes, Hydrophobic microtiter plates, pipette tips   Same situation regarding alternatives as for food packaging materials.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Plastic regenerate and internal recyclate use pose a major problem in complying with the proposed limit of 50 ppm. Not only the intended use, but also the indirect use via reclaim in types that are actually PFAS-free, but may contain PFAS at significantly lower levels due to internal reclaim. However, this influence decreases over the years due to the potential limitation in the intentional use of PFAS in virgin materials.   In order to remain deliverable, we propose a longer transition period for packaging placed on the market (food/petfood/health personal care contact: 5 years; flexible packaging for pharmaceutical products/IBCs: 12 years).  We would like to add that this suggested time covers also the development time at the packaging producer as well as the implementation at our food/petfood or pharma costumer. Or food/petfood costumers have to do shelf-life tests, feeding tests, migration tests. Our pharma customers have to carry out risk assessment to assume the leachable and extractables as well as the interaction between the packaging and the pharmaceutical product. The time of each test depends on the shelf-life of each foodstuff, petfood as well as pharmaceutical product.  Regarding "Packaging for dangerous goods", the customer/filler must also test their products for the new (PFAS-free) packaging in a time-consuming and costly manner: e.g., pre-storage of the filling materials for several months and subsequent testing of the packaging materials for several months in accordance with dangerous goods legislation.

8. Other identified uses: Regarding plastic packaging, it is noted in the ECHA proposal that there is sufficiently strong evidence that alternatives for polymeric PFAS as processing aids already exist. Several alternatives (e.g. boron nitride, polyethylene waxes) are available on the market.  From our point of view, boron nitrite is not a solution for thin, flexible plastic films, because boron nitrite is an inorganic, hard particle which has to be added in higher quantities to the polyolefin in order to achieve the same effect as a fluoropolymer-based processing aid. Moreover, this material is not suitable for the production of transparent plastic films due to their colour nature (white colour).   Polyethylene waxes have been used in some experiments that showed that PE-wax-based processing aids where basically ineffective for the blow film extrusion of thin, flexible films.  Other alternatives are currently being tested for its feasibility. According to current knowledge, many proposed alternatives are not approved for food contact applications in Europe but have no food contact approval at all or only an FDA approval. For introduction of such alternatives, it must be considered that industry will have to seek for EFSA approvals and listing as additive in 10/2011/EC. This approval process and listing may take up to 3 years, according to our experience.  From our point of view, there are currently no alternative substances for polymeric PFAS processing aids on the market for which both the technical functionality and the food law safety of the application in the EU can be guaranteed.

10. Analytical methods: There are still many open questions about PFAS analysis. We would welcome the development of standardised analytical methods for PFAS in plastics at CEN level.

These wires are laid around our pipes in order to heat the fluids transported by our pipelines, using resistive heating. The applications are varied, although mostly centred around energy and high temperature processes: extractive (oil & gas), petrochemical, infrastructure (bitumen) and recycling (food oil for recycling).

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Our heated pipeline products, which include high-temperature heating wires as a component, have typical lifetimes of around 30 years (from 20 years to 50 years).  In the manufacturing phase, wires are laid around the pipeline. To manufacture these wires, 69 tons of fluoropolymers have been used by our supplier in the past 6 years (since this product exists). The use phase of our product corresponds to fluid transportation. At this stage, wires are well protected and confined in an annular gap formed by two pipelines welded at their extremities. The wires are energized in order to heat the fluid transported. Consequently, there is no emission of fluoropolymers at this stage. In the end-of-life phase, our clients (the pipeline users) have a legal obligation to recover the pipes and recycle the materials (steel pipes and wires). All the wires will be collected and can be recycled if necessary.

5. Proposed derogations: It is difficult to estimate a true average as the business is very cyclic. We have participated in 6 projects with pipelines containing heating wires; the volumes range from less than 100 kg to more than 20 tons per project and our wire manufacturer has used 69 tons of fluoropolymers to manufacture our wires in the past 6 years. We currently have several projects in our scope with quantities >10 tons. A yearly projection could be 10 tons.

6. Missing uses: Fluoropolymers can be extruded around electrical conductors to make cables with exceptionally high temperature endurance and durability. We have developed a trace heating technology to be included in our very efficiently thermally insulated pipe-in-pipe. The materials used for manufacturing our wires are PFA (perfluoroalkoxy) and FEP (fluorinated ethylene propylene). Trace heating is used to keep the products contained inside the pipes above a minimum temperature even in case of a stoppage of product flow. This prevents the liquid from solidifying and allows production start-up in any situation. The traditional alternative without trace heating is to install a second pipe-in-pipe (at double the cost and double the footprint) and then, connect them in a loop which is flushed in case of a production shutdown. Tanks for both the flushed liquids and the flushing liquids must be maintained, and chemicals which are toxic for the environment are used for pipelines preservation in that case, such as methanol and methylene glycol. Hence, a heat traced pipeline is a more efficient system as it trades a second insulated line with some relatively small cables installed in the protective environment of the pipe-in-pipe annulus. It also saves on flushing liquids which are often methanol-based in quantities ranging up to several 100m3. Fluoropolymers typically have higher usage temperatures than most other extrudable polymers (200°C+ or even 300°C in some particular grades). This provides two advantages: - Some pipeline projects would simply not be possible with other electrical insulation materials, the main example being the CRISP project which conveys bitumen at 230°C between two refineries in the port of Singapour. - In order to guarantee a 20–40-year lifetime, it is necessary to run accelerated ageing tests at conditions specific and representative for a given project. This usually involves running tests at temperatures higher than project specifications. An often-used engineering rule considers that every 10°C temperature elevation leads to a doubling of ageing rates, hence a 60°C temperature margin is required to increase ageing rates by 2^6=64 which allows to validate a 30-year lifetime in a more manageable 6 months. Given that many recent projects announce design temperatures of 110-150°C, a sufficient headroom required a polymer temperature capability better than 170°C.  The heat tracing is also an enabler of a special category of reduced-footprint offshore developments, namely tie-backs to existing platforms or floating production units: these existing production units are often weight-constrained and cannot host additional equipment. A heat-traced pipeline does not require additional pumping, tankage or flushing systems and therefore allows an economical, low-cost development of marginal satellite fields. These tiebacks have been one of the mainstays of the last years’ offshore developments as the operators have shied away from many of the large green-field developments in the face of an unstable political and economic environment.  In terms of technical outlook, the current push is to increase the cable voltage which provides a longer “heating reach” from a single power inlet. This is an efficient improvement as the high electrical properties of fluoropolymers do not call for a proportional increase of thickness. These developments are long-winded and require extended qualification and certification efforts both with certification agencies such as the DNV and with the end-users. We have presented its Electrically Heat Traced Flowline technology in 1999 and installed the first system offshore in 2017, 18 years later. Apart from early proof-of-principle demonstrators, the proposed systems have always involved aerospace-grade fluoropolymer-insulated cables due to the high temperatures and long lifetimes required. Once a pipeline is installed subsea there are no repairs possible, so cable degradation can only be mitigated through redundancy. For projects operating up to 90°C there are existing alternatives, between 90 and 120°C there may be some materials possible such as silicones but this will require a significant multi-year qualification effort for a product that is eventually mechanically weaker, less crush-resistant, than the already-developed fluoropolymer materials. At our level, the cost ranges around 1000k€. In terms of production units for the complete PiP, the required investment is probably a small multiple of this number. For design temperatures above 120°C, PEEK is one of the only available alternatives. However, its handleability and other characteristics are so different to extruded polymers that there is a high risk that no technically viable solution will be found. This comes on top of its high cost which is an issue in itself but, also leads to cables with very thin insulation that cannot be pushed to higher voltages which seems to be the object of the current system technology developments. It is unknown whether the material can be used at high voltages and long durations.  All the current prospects using this technology require design temperatures between 130 and 150°C, and their objective is to extract natural gas from offshore fields. These pipelines should be built between 2026 and 2032, meaning that, without the use of the fluoropolymers included in our heat-tracing technology, ITP Interpipe will not be able to answer to its clients needs. Moreover, as our competitor is using the same type of wires with the same materials, it will mean the impossibility to use this technology, and maybe these projects will never see the light, as they might not be economically viable anymore. That would mean less natural gas available for the energetic transition, with the critical consequences it could lead to.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: As explained in section 6, these developments are long-winded and require extended qualification and certification efforts both with certification agencies such as the DNV and with the end-users. We have presented its Electrically Heat Traced Flowline technology in 1999 and, installed the first system offshore in 2017, 18 years later.

6. Missing uses: We miss the use of "Process Gas Compression". The use of compressors is to compress a (process) gas to a higher pressure state.  The use case is mandatorily needed for example in the energy sector. Here classically natural gas is for example compressed before using it in a gas turbine in a gas power plant. Often the natural gas is available in a lower pressure state than expected by the gas turbine for a high efficiency. In the hydrogen technology usage, piston compressors are used to compress the hydrogen after electrolysers (often less or equal than 30 bar discharge pressure) to the pipeline pressure (often round about 70 bar). Also for hydrogen storage (up to 250 bar pressure) a compressor is needed to press the gas into the salt cavern. Especially for hydrogen, piston compressors are the best suitable technology, as they have high efficiency and high pressure ratio. But this is only possible with PTFE type sealing elemens (piston rings and piston rod packings). The needed properties are high temperature resistance, very high sealing rate, no reaction with process gases, non-toxic and especially the formation of a tribo-film. This film is build up at the beginning of the use of the sealing element on the counter surface and as soon as it is existing, the wear rate is decreasing massivly. At the moment there is no competitive other material existing. Other base sealing materials like PEEK, have to include parts of PTFE as without, no tribo-film would build up. The only material used in the past without need for PTFE was graphite/coal rings. The was the technical standard in the 1950/60s and before. In these days, the compressor had to be stopped every 2 or 3 months for exchange of graphite material. Now with PTFE sealings, the meantime before repair has grown on up to 3 years. Additionally the internal leackages will grow, which will lead in significant amount of additional electric power needed. Attached as confidential attachment is an excel sheet based on an experience calculation (used since more than 40 years in BORSIG) to evaluate the effect of increased internal leackages in the compressor. What can not be evaluated from our side, but needs to be stated is, that also external leackages will increase very significantly. Normally a sealing packing, like a piston rod packing has a standard leackage rate that is very low for normal operation. This leackage rate increases over the time to a max rate with a worn out packing. The max value is depending on the machine and the process 2 to 3 years. Using graphite, this will be every 2 to 3 months. The leackage rate of a  worn out packing is up to 7 to 10 times higher than for normal operation. For process gas this can be for example toxic gas like ammonia or sour gas containing sulfuric acid or gas that part of global warming processes like CO2 or Methane. While all efforts where taken in the last 10 years to decrease the external leackages to a maximum, if not possible to go for zero leackage, this would be made obsolte. Also the now still existing external leackages are treated with own compressor equipment (seal gas compressors) to bring them back to suction side to avoid any leackage to atmosphere. Also those seal compressors are dependent on PTFE and the size needed with the extremly high leackages of non PTFE sealed compressors would make this setup obsolete, as such big seal gas compressors are not available. In fact it would need a process gas compressor just for compressing the leackages, but this machine would have itself high leackages without PTFE.  The main issue for us is that an application in the process gas compressor industry is very hard to name as the applications are plenty and each gas composition is different. So we could name hydrogen compression as application, but i then it would need to be clarified what that is. Only a compression of 100% hydrogen or also 50% hydrogen in the mix or even 1% hydrogen in the mix? It is extremly rare, that an application is exactly the same. But what unites the whole topic is, that PTFE is non dispensable for economic and environmental reasons. Without PTFE the drop in efficiency would prevent our energy transition and the additional leackages of climate harmful gases would hinder our way to achieve the climate goals.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: • sector: Food contact materials and packaging, packaging for pharmaceutical (pharma packaging), medical devices, cosmetic and hygiene articles • sub-uses: paper and board packaging, plastic packaging, other packaging applications

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: In the consumer plastics packaging industry, very small quantities of polymer processing aids (< 0,1%) based on fluorine-containing monomers are used in polyolefins. These polyolefins will go into the plastic recycling streams with varying PFAS-content. In order to check the TOF-limit of 50ppm (or 50 ppm limit for fluoropolymers) for recycled PE or PP set on the market, a recycler would have to check each recycled batch for PFAS without having the possibility to influence the PFAS concentration during the recycling step. Additionally, currently, there is no standardized analytical method available to check the content of fluoropolymers in plastics, thus the proposed limit for content of fluoropolymers cannot be controlled. Therefore, we ask for an exemption for the output material of the plastic recyclers.

5. Proposed derogations: topic Some IK member companies have provided detailed information regarding tonnage of PFAS used per year to the Fluoropolymer Group at PlasticsEurope as part of a corresponding survey (Downstream user questionnaire for PlasticsEurope Fluoropolymer Group (FPG) to develop a Socio-Economic Impact Assessment (SEIA) for the European Fluoropolymers Industry). We refer to the data from the Fluoropolymer Group. Regarding to the issue emissions to the environment we refer to the “Pilot- Scale Fluoropolymer Incineration Study” from Fluoropolymer Group at PlasticsEurope: The study clearly demonstrated that fluoropolymers are converted to inorganic fluorides and carbon dioxide. The results confirm that fluoropolymers at their end of life when incinerated under representative European municipal incinerators conditions do not generate any measurable levels of PFAS emissions and therefore pose no risk to human health and the environment. The study results of the preliminary report of this study have been submitted to ECHA and attached to the report.

6. Missing uses: • Packaging (flexible and rigid) for pharmaceutical (pharma packaging), medical devices, cosmetic and hygiene articles • Agricultural films such as stretch wrapping films (for industrial applications) • Transport packaging (IBCs) for dangerous goods • Technical textiles (Membranes used for the ventilation of IBCs and packagings which must be water, oil and alcohol repellent) • Plastic fabrics for hygiene and medical applications, e.g. nonwovens that also have to be water, oil and alcohol repellent or be highly hydrophilic • Machinery parts for the production of packaging materials • Lubricants and oils for industrial uses/production • For the construction sector: geo textiles, roofing applications, building insulation • Details to medical applications: fabrics for single use pillows, sheet covers, blankets, ostomy bags (Stoma Beutel), Operation room equipment such as aprons, masks, fabrics to cover wounds, and many more • Lab equipment that has to be super hydrophobic, such as special sample and centrifuge tubes, Hydrophobic microtiter plates, pipette tips  Same situation regarding alternatives as for food packaging materials.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: We would like to add that this suggested time covers also the development time at the packaging producer as well as the implementation at our food/petfood or pharma costumer. Or food/petfood costumers have to do shelf life tests, feeding tests, migration tests. Our pharma customers have to carry out risk assessment to assume the leachable and extractables as well as the interaction between the packaging and the pharmaceutical product. The time of each test depends on the shelf life of each foodstuff, petfood as well as pharmaceutical product.  Regarding "Packaging for dangerous goods", the customer/filler must also test their products for the new (PFAS free) packaging in a time consuming and costly manner : e g.g., p re storage of the filling materials for several months and subsequent testing of the packaging materials for several months in accordance with dangerous goods legislation.

8. Other identified uses: Regarding plastic packaging, it is noted in the ECHA proposal that there is sufficiently strong evidence that alternatives for polymeric PFAS as processing aids already exist. Several alternatives (e.g. boron nitride, polyethylene waxes) are available on the market. From our point of view, boron nitrite is not a solution for thin, flexible plastic films, because boron nitrite is an inorganic, hard particle which has to be added in higher quantities to the polyolefin in order to achieve the same effect as a fluoropolymer-based processing aid. Moreover, this material is not suitable for the production of transparent plastic films due to their colour nature (white colour). Polyethylene waxes have been used in some experiments that showed that PE-wax-based processing aids where basically ineffective for the blow film extrusion of thin, flexible films. Other alternatives are currently being tested for its feasibility. According to current knowledge, many proposed alternatives are not approved for food contact applications in Europe but have no food contact approval at all or only an FDA approval. For introduction of such alternatives, it must be considered that industry will have to seek for EFSA approvals and listing as additive in 10/2011/EC. This approval process and listing may take up to 3 years, according to our experience. From our point of view, there are currently no alternative substances for polymeric PFAS processing aids on the market for which both the technical functionality and the food law safety of the application in the EU can be guaranteed.

10. Analytical methods: There are still many open questions about PFAS analysis. We would welcome the development of standardised analytical methods for PFAS in plastics at CEN level.

Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Drug delivery products may include several different constituents, which themselves are differently treated dependent on local regulations: Device components including batteries and electronics, infectious parts (used needles, etc.) and residual drug.  One goal for delivery systems is to simplify their use which includes the disposal strategy. State of the art design must support the most common mode of disposal (household waste, electronics disposal. etc.) but also facilitate waste separation if applicable. More recent trends also include options for recycling parts of the product. Yet, the majority of the products still end up as part of common household waste either in waste deposits or incineration facilities.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Electronic components of combined products are separated and recycled, if they are separable from other (e.g. potentially infectious) components. However, for certain devices that are not easily dismountable, the research of more advanced recycling strategies is currently a hot topic among pharma and medical device industry. Yet, market ready solutions are not expected within the next decade, taking into account the long development period for health care products.  There is no data available on how to recycle electronic components with a PFAS coating. The electronic components may require a washing step to wash off the PFAS coating before they can be re-used. Currently there is no full recycling for the majority of electronic components. There is no information on the potential costs linked with re-use or recycling of the electronic components in question.

5. Proposed derogations: Only a small share of medical devices and combined products include electronics that are  required to be water-proof due to their specified use-environment.  MPP can only give a rough estimation due to lack of detailed information from electronics industry and based on extrapolation of current market share.  The overall worldwide use of PFAS in the target application is estimated in the range of 1 to 100 kg /a.

6. Missing uses: a. N/A b. Long term sealant for electronic components to grant water-proof properties. c. The number of companies is estimated to be low (up to 10 companies). The market share of the applicant is too low to interpolate reliable numbers for overall use.  d. However, non-PFAS alternatives are seen as less effective as coatings in the electronics segment because they do not have the same water repellence that FPs have, hence wetting occurs;”  e. Research on alternative substances is in progress. The major responsibility lies with the electronics industry for whom the authors of this contribution cannot give a statement.  f. Yet the high standards on safety and stability from both device regulation (EU 2017/745) and human medicine directive (2001/83 EC) result in long timelines for any product change or new development. Content: Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues
Combined Comments:
General Comments: -

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Executive summary The ideal refrigerant for every application does not exist!  The choice of refrigerant is always a compromise between environmental impact, safety and cost-effectiveness related to the application and temperature range which is required. Based on that the hydrofluoro-olefins (HFOs) used as refrigerants, in particular HFO-1234ze and HFO-515B make an important contribution to a sustainable and environmentally friendly cooling and heating supply: Based on the available evidence, we conclude that the fluorinated gases HFO-1234ze and HFO-515B used as refrigerants in heat pumps and chillers must be fully excluded from the scope of the proposed restriction: 1. HFOs have an atmospheric lifetime of days or months and are not classified as (very) persistent under REACH. 2. The ECHA assessment for HFO-1234ze results in the PBT status that the substance is not PBT (HFO-R1234ze is not persistent, not bioaccumulate, not toxic). 3. In comparison to HFC-134a and HFO-1234yf, which decompose into Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) in a significant fraction this is not given for HFO-1234ze and HFO-515B. These fluorinated gases have atmospheric decomposition products that are not classified as persistent. 4. HFOs used as refrigerants are operated in a closed circuit system without any contact to the environment. These systems are classified as "permanently technically tight" according to legislative texts and technical rules. Thereof, refrigerant leaks are reduced to minimum.  5. Oil-free systems of chilled water units and heat pumps leads to outstanding energy efficiency and low indirect greenhouse gas emissions: The basic requirement for this is the use of high molecular weight refrigerant, in particular HFO-1234ze. 6. The risks of emissions of F-Gases are adequately controlled through existing EU legislation, in particular the F-Gas Regulation (517/2014, currently under review for heat pump and chilled water unit applications.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Emissions of chillers and heat pumps occur during production, operation and decommissioning. Thereby, the operation of chillers and heat pumps, based on their lifetime of approximately 20 years has the highest impact of their total emissions, i.e. the focus of emission avoidance must be especially here. Thereby, the emission is split into 2 parts: 1-the direct emission by refrigerant leakages, 2- the indirect emission by the electrical power consumption of the chiller or heat pump. Hereby, due to our high efficient devices, the indirect emissions are 95% of the total emission over the lifespan according to the TEWI calculation. Only, 5% resulting by the refrigerant due to our closed "permanently technically tight" circuit system. Beyond that, our oil-free heat pumps and chillers using synthetic refrigerants, are distinguished by production in Germany and supplier in Europe, which reduces the emissions during the production. Furhter on, by looking at the decommissioning process the Eco-friendly design: o No groundwater-polluting lubricating oils with water hazard class (WGK) o No service intervention for oil exchange is required, meanwhile refrigerant can escape into the environment. - High recycling factors for the refrigerant are possible: o recycling factors greater than 95%, as no refrigerant can be bound in the oil ...results into a minium reduced emissions also there.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: In addition to outstanding energy efficiency the following advantages of the oil-free design has to be taken into account: - Retaining the high efficiency values over the whole heat pump/ chilled water unit lifecycle due to: o no friction losses due to magnetic and non-contact shaft-bearing  o no oil deposits in heat exchangers - Eco-friendly design: o No groundwater-polluting lubricating oils with water hazard class (WGK) o No service intervention for oil exchange is required, meanwhile refrigerant can escape into the environment. - High recycling factors for the refrigerant are possible: o recycling factors greater than 95%, as no refrigerant can be bound in the oil

5. Proposed derogations: 4. HFOs used as refrigerants are operated in a closed circuit system When fluorinated gases (HFOs) are used as refrigerants, the circulate in a closed circuit system according to the cold vapor process without any contact to the environment, respectively atmosphere. These systems, especially those for stationary application, as ours, are classified as "permanently technically tight" according to legislative texts and technical rules.  Thereof, refrigerant leaks are reduced to minimum. Tightness is achieved constructively and/or through organizational measures (periodic leak testing) and gas detection in order to detect and remedy leaks at an early stage.  In contrast hereto, applications of fluorinated gas in blowing agents (e.g. fire-extinguishing foam, insulation production) require that the fluorinated gas has to be released into the atmosphere or the environment as part of its use. These kind of applications are to be viewed and evaluated completely differently than fluorinated gases utilized in closed circuit system without a direct contact and effect to the environment.

6. Missing uses: Alternative refrigerants "so-called: natural refrigerants", even if these are synthetically produced (e.g. Ammonia is made by using natural gas), are not covered via risk assessment and will not get an approval for utilization in Data Centers like Hyperscaler, which cooling demands up to 30MW!

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: No substitution - we ask for a lifetime exemption. Further on, the ECHA assessment for HFO-1234ze results in the PBT status that the substance is not PBT  The fact that the HFO-R1234ze is not persistent, not bioaccumulate, not toxic according to previous assessment of ECHA is what matters. The relationship between PFAS and refrigerants doesn’t matter due to:  The term "PFAS" is a broad, general, non-specific term that does not indicate whether a compound is harmful or not, it only indicates that the compounds covered by this term have the same characteristics, namely a fully fluorinated methyl or methylene carbon content. [OECD (2021), Reconciling Terminology of the Universe of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances: Recommendations and Practical Guidance, OECD Series on Risk Management, No. 61, OECD Publishing, Paris.]

8. Other identified uses: The ban of refrigerants containing PFAS would be a major drawback for the competitveness for the industry and the data center business in the European Union. I.e. due to high energy costs the efficiency of chillers and heat pumps especially in these sectors is indispensable to be successfull on the world market. Also the risk assessment may lead to the fact that the approval of the resepctive authorities will not be given by using A3 refrigerants such as Propan or Isobutan with high amounts in densely populated areas.
