Combined Comments:
General Comments: -

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Metal plating and manufacture of metal products (Hard chrome plating, Decorative plating with chrome, Plating with metals other than chrome); Applications of fluorinated gases; Lubricants (Sector as a whole); Missing uses; Others.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The primary sources of PFAS are industrial facilities, particularly those that manufacture or use PFAS-containing products. Obviously, a regulation in this field is important. To the best of our knowledge, fluoropolymers (fluoroelastomers and perfluoropolyethers must be included) which fulfil all thirteen OECD criteria can be regarded as "polymers of low concern" and thus are very safe materials during their use. As we know, fluoropolymers make up 0.1% of the total PFAS class and lead to emissions between 0-1%. Our products based on fluoropolymers have a lifetime typically between 20-30 years. For use phase no emissions are expected during their use because fluorinated polymers are stable during their use phase. Uses of PFAS in products with a long service life and for which there is from today’s perspective no substitute available should be regarded as criteria for a general exception from proposed restriction or at least for long derogations to enable industry work on potential alternatives. Any specific derogation provided must include the entire supply chain (including manufacturing).   Up to know, the main disposal way for PFAS or the main waste treatment process of PFAS is known to be incineration. Nevertheless, we would like to point out that there are also other recycling methods available on large scale. It is possible to close the chemical product cycle through upcycling. Via pyrolysis, 95 % of monomers can be captured, purified and reused to produce new polymers without any loss of quality (see https://multimedia.3m.com/mws/media/907323O/up-cycling-fluoropolymers-brochure.pdf?fn=Up-Cycling_Brochure_EN.pdf). Such recycling methods should not be abandoned and preferred to a fluoropolymer ban. To realize circular economy for fluoropolymers, a general exemption is needed for fluoropolymers (including fluoroelastomers and perfluoropolyethers) otherwise less or no companies would invest into recycling technologies after transitional periods or few years of derogation. We refer to corresponding contributions.    Fluoropolymers waste from industrial applications is already significantly regulated (ELV, Landfill, Incineration, Recycling). In addition, the WEEE Directive regulates the return and recycling of electrical and electronic equipment. Manufacturers and importers of electrical and electronic equipment are obliged to be registered as "WEEE manufacturers" and to comply with the reporting and take-back obligations. This must be linked to recycling of fluoropolymers.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: We know that the main concern related to fluoropolymers is the use of PFAS as polymerization aids in the manufacturing of fluoropolymers and the other concern is the end-of-life fate of fluoropolymers applications. We want to point out that for manufacturing, already non-fluorinated polymerization aids are known (see https://icrl.lexxion.eu/data/article/18899/pdf/icrl_2023_01-006.pdf). It is expected that most of the fluoropolymer production will be developed completely free from PFAS polymerization aids. The use of PFAS-based polymerization aids to continue with the manufacture of FPs (which are safe) in the EU should be allowed by the regulators linked to a commitment to use PFAS-free aids if now possible. Thus, it appears reasonable to claim that fluoropolymers should be exempted from any regulatory initiative, and that their uses should be allowed without any unjustified restriction.   As far as we know, PFAS are typically destroyed at very high temperatures (>800°C). Recent studies have shown that fluoropolymers are converted to Inorganic Fluorides and Carbon Dioxide at standard incineration conditions. We refer to the report of GFL, KIT and SGS. The results confirm that PFAS (long-chain and short-chain) are fully destroyed during incineration without any noticeable levels of PFAS emissions or formation of harmful fluorinated derivatives (see https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9778349/). Additionally, several technologies are still in development. One promising technology is the PFAS destruction by decarboxylation which allows PFCA to be destroyed under mild conditions and in high yields (78-100 % at 40-120°C, see https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.abm8868). Future work should be done to study and use such methods in practice. Another recent study promises a sustainable approach for water purification and destruction of PFAS by metallopolymer sorbents based on ferrocene and cobaltocenium (see https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsami.3c01670). Scale-up of this electrochemical method could represent the next breakthrough for clean, PFAS-free water. Another method is based on the treatment and recovery of PFAS-contaminated water using plasma treatment, see https://www.igb.fraunhofer.de/en/reference-projects/atwaplas.html.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Unfortunately, we do not have detailed knowledge in the field of recycling. We rely on contributions from the recycling sector to get a complete picture. However, the established methods and evidence shows that fluoropolymers are best candidates for upcycling. Promising developments are also ongoing on other PFAS (see Answer to Question 3).

5. Proposed derogations: For durability and safety reasons, there is no alternative to the use of PFPE and PTFE. Even if alternatives might be possible, we expect that fluoropolymers are more suitable for our products and have better properties compared to traditional ones because they are non-flammable and therefore product safety is high, and they are thermally stable in a wide range (low and high). In result, product safety is high also due to retained lubricity. So far, we are not aware of any equivalent alternatives. The properties of fluoropolymers ensure the long-lasting performance of our products required for sectors and applications described in Section V. An increased safety of our products has already been achieved with minimal amounts of lubrication. Without fluoropolymers, we are not able to produce products with high reliability. With alternatives, we expect reduced product performance for the same products being risky for the sectors that we supply. Alternatives will not be able to replace PFAS 1:1. For our applications described, we need fluoropolymers due to their unique properties which cannot be guaranteed by other polymers. All in all, our products are part of digitalization and energy transition and meet critical needs. Less performance and efficiency of our products will block future goals of the EU.   Why short transitional periods or derogation periods will disrupt or damage supply chains: Plastics in EE applications are subject to strict regulations. First, it is needed to qualify suitable plastic materials for production and application of alternatives. Then a completely new approval is required for the re-designed article. We estimate the cost at €5 million and around 2 years for re-registrations if the product series is completely changed, or much longer depending on the series. Changes require high additional costs, effort and time.   The industry is always working on customer-oriented products/solutions, customer requirements can no longer be met. As we know from our suppliers, they say that their production processes for lubricants are closed, which excludes environmental contamination during production. They are working on formulations for fields of application in which the use of alternative substances is possible while at the same time maintaining the required functional reliability. But, from their point of view, lubricants containing PTFE and PFPE cannot currently be substituted for particularly demanding applications (on both product and production site)  On the production site, we are currently determining our concern. We cannot make any statements about cooling/refrigerating agents in systems that are serviced by external companies and refer to corresponding contributions. We use fluoropolymers in machines as lubricants, seals which are installed inside the machine and have no direct contact with the environment guaranteeing safe handling. As we know, there are no polymers which can replace such applications. Also, without spare and wearing parts for machinery and equipment, we expect undefined product standstill. Unfortunately, we do not have detailed knowledge in the field of plant and mechanical engineering and refer to contributions from this sector. We call for a general exemption for fluoropolymers, for spare parts and refurbished products and for products already placed on the market, guarantying re-sale as pointed out by the ZVEI. Alternatively, should PFAS - including fluoropolymers - be subject to regulation, extensions of exemptions should be possible (RoHS directive as basis for this procedure). We call for a distinction between consumer products and industrial applications. We refer to further information attached to Section V (Confidental).

6. Missing uses: PFBS as flame retardant for UL04 V0 certified products: Shorter-chain PFAS such as PFBS (C4-sulfonate) are known to be more soluble in water and therefore more mobile in the environment. We do not support the entry of such substances into the environment, but we would like to take the following into account when making a decision: the entry of PFAS into the environment and thus into the groundwater is largely due to applications linked primarily to the use of fire-fighting foams containing fluorine during firefighting operations and training exercises, to the use of process materials containing PFAS in industrial facilities, e.g. textile finishing. Studies have shown that the concentrations of short-chain PFAS can vary significantly, from which we conclude that the entry of such substances can be controlled and targeted if one knows the entry sources and tries to eliminate them (for example by collecting different PFAS waste). This is supported by the fact that some areas are less polluted by PFBS than others (see https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11783-009-0021-8). As a consequence, the main focus should be placed on identifying causal sources of exposure and on recycling methods which are able to eliminate water-soluble PFAS from groundwater. PFBS has a shorter carbon chain and a significantly shorter half-life than PFOS and PFOA. Studies have shown that the toxicokinetic properties of PFAS often vary with chain length, with shorter, straight-chain non-polymeric PFAS being eliminated faster than the longer-chain, non-polymeric PFAS (see https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6624215/). The study confirms that PFAS with shorter chain lengths have a shorter half-life due to their better water solubility, resulting in rapid bioelimination and therefore lower exposure (should exposure occur). Although the elimination half-life for PFBS in humans is still too long at 26 days, it is important to emphasize that these effects were seen in high-exposure settings with used doses far exceeding the levels to which humans are exposed in the environment. This should be considered by interpretation of the results when attempting to establish cause and effect. Similar results were observed in other studies, see https://pubs.acs.org/doi/pdf/10.1021/jf304680j. It is also criticized that especially short-chain PFAS cannot be removed with common methods (activated carbon filtration). Fraunhofer UMSICHT and Cornelsen Umwelttechnologie GmbH developed a new process with which PFAS can be removed effectively and cost-effectively from the extinguishing water on site, see https://www.interschutz.de/product/perfluorad/309278/N1485753. The process combines activated carbon adsorption with an upstream cleaning stage. Such and other already described methods should be transferred to other use cases.   PTFE-bonded coatings: a silicone coating in combination with PTFE offers or combines several of the outstanding chemical and physical properties of PTFE and siloxane with the dimensional stability and mechanical strength. The products are extremely temperature resistant (high and low), non-flammable and have high chemical resistance, resulting in products with long product life and reliability. Even small amounts enable good coefficients of friction even at high temperatures.   In general, graphite and molybdenum disulfide are used in combination with PTFE micropowders. Without PTFE, bonded coatings do not offer the same coefficient of friction. Micropowder PTFE is chemically more resistant than graphite and molybdenum disulphide. Micropowder PTFE has excellent plastic/elastomer compatibility. Graphite and molybdenum disulfide are not inert or water resistant. Graphite requires water to fully activate its low-friction properties. PTFE can work in different conditions -40 to 260°C, silicone alone would decompose. MoS2 is black, PTFE is white. Additionally, silicones are under discussion to be included in the POP regulation. At this time, we don't know how this would affect products, but it would eliminate the alternative of silicone coating. Alternatives are considered or seen as a reason for banning PFAS, but at the same time alternatives are limited by other regulations and that is in contradiction. Further confidental information are attached to Section V.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: As part of the surface treatment, PFAS are used for hard chrome plating, bright chrome plating and plastic electroplating with chrome but also for plating with different metals such as nickel plating, copper plating, tinning, alkaline zinc and zinc alloy plating.   Since we are not producing plated materials by ourselves, we even don’t know which of the materials are produced with PFAS or can contain PFAS. On inquiries, our suppliers say that they are still in the process of determining PFAS contenting materials and processes. So, we have no information on these materials since there is currently no notification or information obligation. We are not able to estimate which articles would need to be substituted in future. This is also the case for plastics. Therefore, we think, an introduction of an information obligation for intentionally added PFAS is urgently needed to enable downstream users a concern analysis. Further detailed information are attached to Section V (Confidental).

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Various strategies have been developed to manage PFPE oils when they reach the end of their useful life. One prevalent approach is high-temperature incineration, a method employed for disposing of PFPE oils. It is imperative to carry out PFPE incineration exclusively within specialized facilities that are outfitted with advanced pollution control technologies. This ensures the avoidance of detrimental pollutants being released into the environment. Within these dedicated facilities designed for waste incineration, the waste is subjected to elevated temperatures ranging from 850°C to 1100°C.

8. Other identified uses: Manufacturing:  Our company acknowledges the significance of responsible manufacturing practices, even though our current manufacturing operations are not located in the EU. During the manufacturing of PFPE oils, after the polymerization step the low boiling materials are removed by distillation.  The resulting products are further purified by distillation based on the viscosity. Thus, PFPE oils are produced extremely pure. Any production wastes are carefully treated and disposed depends on the nature. With this responsible manufacturing including comprehensive measures to prevent any emissions with well efficient waste management systems, along with targeted and non-targeted residue analysis*, it is possible to bring safe PFPE oils into market. Lubrication:  Under the present proposal, there is a provision for a derogation period of 13.5 years pertaining to the utilization of polymeric PFAS/PFPE oils in lubrication. It has been widely acknowledged that PFAS-based lubrication represents the pinnacle of lubrication technology and is utilized in critical applications where viable alternatives are not feasible. While it may be that individual alternative technology could outperform polymeric PFAS-based lubricants in one certain property, it is crucial to emphasize that the comprehensive combination of properties provided by PFPE oils remains unparallel. It is important to note that, to date, no alternative technology has been identified that can fulfill the complete range of requirements for the specific application in question.  Additionally, it is important to note that at present, there is no conclusive evidence or guarantee that an alternative technology can be developed within the next 12 years, and the duration required for its validation remains uncertain. Therefore, we request a complete exception. Please find further supporting information in the confidential attachement

8. Other identified uses: Semiconductors support all industries and are an indispensable technology. In the semiconductor manufacturing process, UV tape is used to protect the surface or fix the position of wafers and semiconductor packages during processing. The attached document illustrates the specific use of UV tape. Please refer to it as well.  For example, BG tape is used to protect the surface of wafers during the back grinding process, and dicing tape is used to secure wafers and semiconductor packages during the dicing process. Before UV irradiation, the tape has strong adhesion to securely fix wafers, and after UV irradiation, the adhesive strength weakens, making it easy to peel off the tape and pick up chips. These characteristics contribute greatly to improving the quality and reducing the cost of semiconductor devices, and the quality of BG tape and dicing tape also directly affects the yield of semiconductor devices. A small amount of fluorine oligomer including PFAS is sometimes added to the adhesive portion of UV tape. Although there are alternatives such as silicone, etc., in semiconductor product groups with cutting-edge or special specifications, those alternatives have inferior peelability and pick-up properties, resulting in very low semiconductor wafer yields. If this UV tape becomes subject to regulation, the social and economic impact will be extremely large due to the increase in semiconductor prices and decrease in semiconductor supply. Since the tape is used in the semiconductor manufacturing process and is added to the adhesive of the tape, the risk of spillage outside the semiconductor manufacturing plant and into the environment is extremely small.

Missing uses: d) Alternatives: Oxyphen track-etched PET membranes with only a very small amount of covalently bounded PFAS coating would deliver already about 100 times reduction in PFAS use in comparison with ePTFE membranes. e) No alternatives are available for hydrophobic/oleophobic coatings, especially for C6-containing coatings. Corresponding substitution material showing satisfying performance do simply not exist yet. For example, the structural modification of the surface with Si nanoparticles shows still a clearly low performance in comparison with fluorine coatings (see 5.3 in https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4360/13/15/2520).  For example, the siliconization of the surface shows also a clearly low performance in comparison with fluorine coatings (see 5.2 in https://www.mdpi.com/2073-4360/13/15/2520). g) The substitution is not technically feasible. The extremely electronegative property of fluorine has no other known chemical equivalent. The formation of C-F bond makes bonded fluorine atoms extremely inert and the surface atoms of other materials do not form chemical bonds to the bonded fluorine atoms. All possible substitutions are based on other chemical bonds like C-H bond in case of silicones or paraffins for water repellency. The bonded H ions are still interacting with surface atoms of other materials and cannot provide simultaneous good repellency for both water and oils (hydrophobicity and oleophobicity), only one or another.

Modified and/or cross-linked PE materials, the standard in hoses for regular kitchen appliances, do not withstand higher temperatures or require such high wall-thickness that they are no longer considered flexible. 1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Hydrofluoroolefins can be used as a physical blowing agent for the production of thermoplastic foams. A typical example would be foams made from polyethylene terephthalate (PET).  The use of PET has many economic and ecological advantages. Since it is used in great quantities it is relatively cheap. In addition PET is currently one of the few polymers which is actually recycled in significant quantities. A typical application of PET is for bottled beverages, huge quantities of the recycled material are used in the clothing industry. Another example are boards made from PET-foam which are used in the construction of wind mills for power generation or as boards for thermal insulation.  For the formation of PET-foam, a physical blowing agent is injected into the molten PET and on expansion the physical blowing agent causes the foam formation. As physical blowing agent often cyclopentane is being employed. There are numerous disadvantages connected to cyclopentane: It is a highly flammable liquid, its mixtures with air are explosive, it has a global warming potential of 11 (GWP, Randall, D und Lee, S., The Huntsman polyurethanes handbook, John Wiley & Sons, 2002, ISBN 0-470-85041-8, p. 131-134), and its heat conductivity is relatively high. In contrast the use of HFOs has numerous advantages: It is non-flammable, its GWP is only 2 (https://www.opteon.com/en/-/media/files/opteon/opteon-1100-push-bulletin.pdf), and it has a lower heat conductivity. In terms of energy savings and in order to reach net zero CO2 by 2050 it would be preferable to work with HFO instead of cyclopentane because then the PET-foams would have superior thermal insulators and significant amounts of energy would be saved.  It is important to understand that the majority of the physical blowing agent stays in the foam, only a small percentage will be lost during the production process. But once the physical blowing agent is encapsulated in the cells of the foam it will remain there for the lifetime of the product. According to the state of the art the insulating foam is being incinerated at the end of its lifetime. During incineration any HFO will be decomposed, the final decomposition products being carbon dioxide and hydrofluoric acid (like with any fluorine containing organic compound). All acidic gases (as the hydrofluoric acid) are being retained by acid scrubbers. In the end no further HFO is released to the environment.  For that reasons it is requested that the use of the fluorinated gases HFO-1233zd(E), HFO-1336mzz(Z), and 1224yd as foam blowing agents for thermoplastic foams are made subject to a time-unlimited derogation.

The presence of fluorine atoms in PFAS imparts strong electronegativity, resulting in the creation of super acids critical for this process. As a result, all successful PAGs demonstrated so far are fluorinated. Additionally, top antireflective coatings (TARCs) in photolithography necessitate specific properties such as a very low refractive index, low surface energy, and exceptional barrier capabilities. Fluorinated acrylate/methacrylate/styrene-based copolymers are employed to achieve these properties. Furthermore, PFAS surfactants are utilized for various photolithographic materials due to their unique attributes, including very low surface tension and a combination of hydrophobic and oleophobic behavior. These properties make them valuable in forming immersion top coatings with the necessary low surface energy, outstanding barrier properties, and prevention of intermixing with the photoresist. Dielectric Polymers, such as Polyimides (PI) and Polybenzoxazoles (PBO), provide crucial electrical, thermal, moisture, chemical, and mechanical protection for semiconductor devices. They are based on water-insoluble PFAS polymers, enabling water-based development processes. The estimated PFAS consumption in Europe for the aforementioned photolithography activities is approximately 2248 kg per year, with projected emissions of around 1161 kg. As for PFAS discharge into wastewater, comprehensive industry-wide measurements have not yet been compiled. However, a peer-reviewed study featured in the "Environmental Science & Technology" journal in 2021 (Paige Jacob, Krista A. Barzen-Hanson, and Damian E. Helbling Environmental Science & Technology 2021 55 (4), 2346-2356 DOI: 10.1021/acs.est.0c06690) conducted an analysis on wastewater samples from three fabrication facilities in the United States. This analysis uncovered that the overall PFAS concentrations in downstream samples from these three facilities were recorded at 0.623 ± 0.024 µg/L, 0.394 ± 0.018 µg/L, and 0.376 ± 0.024 µg/L, respectively. To assess the significance of these values, they can be compared against the EU PFAS drinking water directive limit values for potable water, which is established at PFAS Total = 0.50 µg/L.

In general, fluorinated tapes are used for their essential and intricate characteristics, such as arc-cracking resistance, temperature resistance, fire resistance, mechanical strength including low abrasion, and compactness. This is why they are primarily found in the aerospace, aviation, and certain military applications. A permanent derogation is necessary for fluorinated tapes, or one that extends beyond 40 years. Fluoropolymers are considered crucial Strategic Raw Materials for aerospace cables, as they offer the best "technical performance/product weight" ratio compared to other engineering polymers. Currently, no precise alternative solutions have been identified on the market. The implications of banning fluoropolymers for the Aerospace & Defence industry would include: ⦁ Halting production and delivery of A&D products  ⦁ Inability to service and repair existing products  ⦁ Compromising the safety function of A&D vehicles  ⦁ Loss of reliability in operations  ⦁ Premature retirement of A&D equipment from service  ⦁ Potential risk of strategic dependency in Europe  ⦁ Job losse Considering these consequences, a time-unlimited derogation is necessary for the entire aerospace and defence domain.   Plastic additive:  Flame retardancy of plastics used in electrical products is key and critical as those materials must prevent fire propagation in case of ignition due to electrical defaults. 1/4 of fire have electrical defects root cause.One can easily understand that fire propagation just after ignition is key for safety. Those last years, the number of flame-retardant solutions for plastics decreased under regulatory pressure. A flame-retardant system for plastic is specifically designed for the standard test to target. In our domain, UL94-V is compulsory and is very difficult to achieve. For some plastics such as Polycarbonate, the standard test can only be achieved with a complex FR system in which one of the components (dripping agent) is a PFAS. The amount of PFAS in the formulation is very low (a fraction of percent) but key for a pass. For safety reasons, we cannot degrade the FR standard tests severity level and the plastic industry needs time to develop new FR systems which is a very long process. The very low level of fluorinated polymer in the formulation, combined to the difficulty to develop alternative solutions means that we need at least a 12 years derogation for that application. As explained for PFAS metal surface treatment case, our experience with current solutions enable us to guaranty the safety of our products for at least 20-30 years. Finding an alternative solution takes time if we want to guaranty the same reliability level. Some plastics show intrinseque tribological properties when others need additives to improcve their friction behaviour. Replacing additived plastics by intrinseque good friction polymers is not feasible in all applications. Alternative solutions proposed in the restriction dossier (siloxanes) are not relevant for our applications. MoS2 can be used as alternative of PFAS in some plastics for better tribological behaviour, but this must be validated and it takes time. A minimum 5 years derogation is required to cover raw materail supplier investigations, evaluation at product level and long term validation.  demolding agent or mould treatment(silicone)  Fluorinated mold release agents show extremely low surface energy compared with silicon and wax. Moreover, silicon mold release is prohibited in automotive industry due to  oligomer release. Our industry needs a derogation of minimum 5 years to validate alternative solutions.

This recognises that “incineration of PFAS containing waste is currently seen as the most effective treatment option for destroying PFASs. Rationale: This amendment ensures that non textile high performance filtration membranes are unambiguously included within the scope of a twelve-year derogation. The PFAS containing polymers used in these filtration and separation media have a unique combination of physical and chemical properties which PFAS-free alternatives are not able to offer. These properties include water repellence, low pore size which retains microbes, high chemical resistance, permeability to air and impermeability to water.  2. By way of derogation, paragraphs 1 and 2 shall not apply to oxidizing liquid tubing and associated connectors in biological decontamination equipment until 6.5 years after EiF. Rationale: Oxidising chemicals are used to decontaminate the surfaces in bio contamination equipment, and in some cases the chemicals can be used inside equipment which incorporates PFAS tubing and associated connectors. Missing uses: Statement of Pfaudler GmbH on the regulation of PFAS within the framework of the REACH regulation  Consultation procedure from March 22nd – September 25th ,2023  Pfaudler GmbH is part of the GMM - Pfaudler - Group, which is a leader in the field of corrosion-resistant technologies. GMM - Pfaudler operates 16 manufacturing sites on four continents, employs 1800 people and has a turnover of 340 million USD p.a. (Annex 15). Pfaudler GmbH is a manufacturer of glass lined equipment, such as stirred tanks (DIN 28136, Annex 13), storage tanks (DIN 28020 and DIN 28021), columns, heat exchangers (Annex 01) and thin-film evaporators (Annex 02), along with glass-lined parts such as agitators, baffles (DIN 28148), immersion tubes, covers (DIN 28153-3), valves (DIN 28140, Annex 12), pipes (DIN 2873) and glass-lined measuring probes. The manufactured glass-lined equipment and accessories are used worldwide in all areas of the chemical, pharmaceutical and food industry. Many of the applications are system relevant. Glass lined vessels are pressure vessels made of steel covered with a vitreous coating (Annex 03) on the entire surface in contact with the product, which is extremely corrosion-resistant to almost all strong acids and alkalis (Annex 04). Many process engineering systems in the chemical industry would not be functional without glass-lined apparatuses and pipelines. The customer list for Europe from Pfaudler GmbH (Annex 05) shows where glass-lined equipment is used in Europe.  Plastic materials are also used in all glass lined equipment, primarily various types of fluoropolymers. These are high-performance plastics that are used under extremely aggressive chemical conditions and high temperatures of up to 230°C. They also reduce friction and prevent substances from sticking, comparable to an enameled surface. Essential components are gaskets with a PTFE envelope (DIN 28148), bellows in valves (Annex 6), form seats (Annex 7), wiper blades of thin-film evaporators (Annex 02), repair sleeves (Annex 08), linings of apparatuses and pipelines (Annex 09), machined construction parts and seals (Annex 10, Annex 11). The plastics used include the widespread fluoroplastic PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene, also known as Teflon), PFA, FEP (Poly fluoroethylene propylene) and FKM (fluor rubber). All sealing elements make a significant contribution to avoiding toxic leaks in process engineering systems and are therefore extremely relevant to safety. The Global Glass Lined Reactor (PTFE) market size was USD 516 million in 2021, USD 645 million in 2022 and is estimated to be USD 825 million in 2028 (Annex 16).  Only components made of PTFE, PFA, FEP and FKM can ensure that systems and employees are protected from high toxic corrosive, pure and ultra-pure liquids, gases and vapors, even under the most difficult environmental and pressure conditions, which occur in the chemical, petrochemical, pharmaceutical – and food industry and process technology. Where glass-lined equipment is installed, there are no alternatives to the PFAS available. The materials are indispensable for the safe operation of all process engineering systems worldwide in which glass-lined equipment is installed. A ban on fluoropolymers poses a significant health risk. If highly stressed seals no longer fulfill their function, there is a risk of substances that are hazardous to health migrating into the environment, means consumers are at acute risk. Without reliable inert seals in the pharmaceutical and food sectors, contamination with germs and bacteria will occur, which would also endanger consumers.  The economic effects of a ban on fluoropolymers should also not be ignored: Glass-lined equipment cannot function without seals, fittings and bellows. Without suitable alternatives, we as a manufacturer cannot guarantee our customers safe use in terms of legal requirements (Annex 14). In the worst case, the result would be a sales stop and nothing less than an end to the supply of consumers and industry with many essential goods of daily use. This threatens the manufacturers of glass-lined equipment and their customers with major upheavals. Furthermore, an emergency in the supply of citizens and industry would be the inevitable consequence.  GMM Pfaudler stands for a sustainable world and supports the central idea of substituting materials and substances that are hazardous to health, as well as the goal of no longer allowing PFAS classified as very dangerous (e.g.CMR, PBT, PMT) to enter the environment. In this respect, regulation of these PFAS, which are classified as very dangerous, seems correct in principle.  Many PFAS uses were not, or not extensively, addressed in the restriction proposal submitted (see uses highlighted in blue and orange in Table A.1 in Annex A of the Restriction Report). The entire sector of the "Chemical Industry" is marked in orange, which means "not researched in detail". Equipment for use in highly corrosive processes, in particular glass lined equipment including components made of PFAS, falls into this area.  Numerous fluoropolymers have been scientifically evaluated as "polymers of low concern" (e.g. PTFE, ETFE, FEP, PFA, PVDF). They have been proven to be chemically stable, non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water soluble and non-mobile. For these reasons, the fluoropolymers are also approved, for example, as materials for food contact or in medical technology. These rather harmless "polymers of low concern" are also safely contained in glass-lined equipment and remain there for many years without any risk to the environment. Even after the end of the product life cycle, all components are recycled as far as possible, but in any case, at least disposed of professionally.  GMM Pfaudler therefore calls for the general exception of fluoropolymers in the context of highly corrosion-resistant equipment, which (by the way also according to the definition of the OECD) are considered as "polymers of low concern", from the PFAS restriction project. In addition, substances such as monomers and process aids that are necessary for the manufacture and production of fluoropolymers should be exempted from the ban, provided that their safe use is ensured. This is also what the study of the British Health and Safety Executive (HSE) provides (https://www.hse.gov.uk/reach/assets/docs/pfas-rmoa.pdf). Therefore, groups with a low risk (e.g. fluoroelastomers, fluoropolymers, rated as "polymers of low concern") or uses without a relevant risk (e.g. uses in closed systems) should generally be exempted from the PFAS regulation.

Sectors and (sub-)uses: Fluoropolymers in drinking water and heating applications The applications of plastic materials in drinking water contact or heat generators primarily involve the use of fluoropolymers. These are high-performance plastics that are characterized by particularly high resistance. They have sealing and water-repellent properties, reduce friction and prevent the adhesion of substances. These include above all the widely used fluoroplastic PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene, also known as "Teflon") or FKM ("fluor rubber"). They are used, among other things, in seals and hose in drinking water installations and not only make a significant contribution to preventing leaks, but also to the success of the climate change. They also provide optimum protection for drinking water quality.  Some fluoropolymers have been scientifically evaluated as "polymers of low concern" (PTFE, ETFE, FEP, PFA, PVDF and VDF-co-HFP). They have been proven to be chemically stable, non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water soluble and non-mobile. For these reasons, the fluoropolymers are also approved, for example, as food contact materials or in medical devices. In addition, Henry et al. (2018) state that all fluoropolymers should be considered “polymers of low concern” .

6. Missing uses: We are acitve in the field of drinking water valves, heating valves and water treatment applications (softeners). In our valves we use PFAS-containing materials in seals, membranes and hoses. Fluoropolymers are primarily used here. These are high-performance plastics that are  characterised by particularly high resistance. They have a sealing, water-repellent and friction-reducing effect in our products and prevent the adhesion of substances. These include above all the widely used fluoroplastic PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene, also known as "Teflon") or FKM  ("fluororubber"). PFAS-containing materials in our products contribute significantly to drinking water and heating valves. Some of the fluoropolymers we use in our valves have been scientifically evaluated as "polymers of low concern" (PTFE, ETFE, FEP, PFA, PVDF and VDF-co-HFP). They have been proven to be chemically stable, non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water soluble and non-mobile. For these reasons, the fluoropolymers are also approved, for example, as materials for food contact or in medical technology. We therefore call for the general exemption of fluoropolymers, which (incidentally also according to the OECD definition) are considered "polymers of low concern", from the PFAS restriction project. In addition, substances such as monomers and processing aids that are necessary for fluoropolymer manufacture and production should be exempted from the ban, provided  that safe use is ensured. This is also envisaged by the study of the British Health and Safety Executive (HSE). Therefore, in general, groups with low risk (e.g.  fluoroelastomers, fluoropolymers assessed as "polymers of low concern") or uses without relevant risk (e.g. uses in closed systems) should be exempted. In this context, we would like to point out that there are currently no alternatives to the use of materials classified as "polymers of low concern" in our area of drinking water and heating valves that have similar resistance over a comparable period of time. These are of enormous importance, especially in the environment of our products, because it is about the safety of drinking water over a long period of time. A ban on these PFAS substances would mean that at the present time we would not be able to use sealings and membranes in our products that comply with the applicable legal and regulatory provisions - and also the required warranty periods - and also do not have the necessary approvals (or certificates, if (applicable). The consequence would be nothing other than a sales stop and a dramatic drop in turnover of about 30-40 percent. Because without sealing and membranes our valves simply do not work. In order to avert such existentially threatening damage, not for us but for the entire industry and society as a whole, fluoropolymers such as PTFE in the context of building fittings must therefore be excluded from PFAS regulation.

6. Missing uses: Many products used in stationary fire protection contain PFAS-containing seals, especially products in gas and water extinguishing systems. Alternative PFAS-free materials are also available for these seals. However, the Construction Products Regulation EU 305/2011 requires that many of these products are tested and certified by a notified body. Otherwise, the products may not be placed on the market in the European Economic Area. If PFAS-containing gaskets are no longer available due to the ban, all the above-mentioned products would first have to be modified by the manufacturer and tested and recertified by notified bodies. This considerable effort can only be carried out by the notified bodies over a long period of several years.  Thus, after a ban on PFAS-containing seals, many products that are needed in stationary fire-fighting systems will no longer be available. The effects would lead to breakdowns and shutdowns of plants, which would inevitably lead to plant closures, as fire protection would no longer be ensured. It is therefore strongly recommended to provide an appropriate transition period of at least 10 years for gaskets and similar parts used in fire fighting products.

6. Missing uses: The proposal for the restriction of PFAS does not sufficiently take into account the requirements for mechanical and plant engineering sector. Our requirement is most comparable to the aforementioned use sector for transportation (transport sector). The mechanical and plant engineering sector is also extremely dependent on PFAS, especially when used in complex products (e.g. seals in hydraulic applications such as cylinders and valves).  "Schuler Pressen GmbH", like the entire mechanical and plant engineering industry, is integrated into a highly ramified network of specialized component manufacturers. The functionality and reliability are the result of a continuous improvement process. The materials used for these components (primary products) are mostly unknown to the machine manufacturers. The percentage by weight of PFAS in the total weight of a machine is very small, but the properties of these materials are all the more important. In the vast majority of cases, they are fluoropolymers that do not have any abrasive behavior during the use phase and therefore do not pose any relevant risk. Fluoropolymers like PTFE are commonly regarded to meet the key internationally recognised safety criteria of the OECD for “polymers low concern” (plc). This means that they are chemically stable, non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water soluble and non-mobile. For these reasons, fluoropolymers are also suitable, for example, as materials for food contact, in medical applications or in the production of high-purity active pharmaceutical ingredients (e.g. vaccines). Therefor the competent authorities of the United Kingdom claim that fluoropolymers, fluoroelastomers and monomers for manufacturing of these do not need to be restricted at all! We demand from the competent authorities of the European Economic Area (EEA) to take over this scientific and simply reasonable approach. In the disposal phase, machines are generally scrapped and fed into a controlled recycling process. The PFAS components remaining in machine parts are melted down in this process, thus destroying the problematic methyl/methylene group. Fluoropolymers (PTFE, FKM, ...) are used in particular in pneumatic and hydraulic systems of "Schuler Pressen GmbH". A restriction or ban of these substances has a restriction on the tightness, friction as well as the service life and thus on the sustainability and energy consumption of the equipment and represents an unforeseeable disruption in the further application of the equipment, with far-reaching effects on many other industries, especially the automotive industry as well as the complete supply industry including the production of battery components and the like for the changeover to electromobility. Given these factors, we would like to request a derogation from the REACH regulation concerning PVDFs used specifically in filtration membranes for wastewater treatment. Content: Scope or restriction option analysis

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Refrigeration: Industrial use of HFC’s as refrigeration agents in the large cooling systems by high tonnage in chemical production sector.

6. Missing uses: Industrial uses of HFCs as refrigerants in the large chemical synthesis industry were not included in the derogations. Most chemical synthesis installations have large (multi-tonnage refrigeration systems) containing HFCs used as agents to significantly reduce the processing and storage temperature of  specific chemicals that require extremely low temperatures, e.g. storage of organic peroxides. HFCs are widely used in the chemical synthesis process due to their physicochemical properties, in particular the fact that they are not classified as flammable, oxidizing or toxic to workers. This is very important in a situation where the production installation contains a number of other raw materials, semi-finished products, auxiliaries and final products classified as posing a risk to human health and the environment. Currently available alternatives to large-volume equipment containing HFCs include only ammonia and propylene. Based on the conducted analyses, the use of non-flammable refrigerants such as CO2 is not possible in standard compressor refrigeration circuits due to their physicochemical properties, i.e. the critical point, which is 31oC and 73.7 bar. At the currently available level of cooling water parameters (temperature of water after cooling 27 oC, temperature of return water to the chillers 37 oC) from the fan cooling tower, by means of which condensation heat is transferred to the environment, it would require the pressure in the condenser and compressor on the discharge to be 73 bar. Such high pressures would require the use of pipes and pipelines approximately 5 times thicker than those currently used, for example, for propylene refrigeration units. In addition, the compressors and heat exchangers would have to be very large to operate effectively at such high pressures (standard versions of such equipment are not available on the market). Capital expenditures required for this task would be approximately six times that of propylene and the cost of electricity consumption almost twice that of propylene-based refrigeration circuits for cooling water and other media to 5oC. Both alternative substances (ammonia anhydrous and propylene) are classified as flammable, and anhydrous ammonia is additionally classified as toxic by inhalation Cat 3. Replacing a refrigerant currently not classified as flammable with a refrigerant classified as flammable is a very big technical, technological and financial challenge for manufacturers. As a result of the use of refrigerants such as ammonia or propylene, new explosion hazard zones will be created on technological installations, posing a risk to service, the environment and property. It should also be taken into account that from the point of view of the HFC's legislation currently in force, i.e. Regulation (EU) No 517/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 April 2014 on fluorinated greenhouse gases and repealing Regulation (EC) No 842/2006 Text with EEA relevance, measures have been taken to replace HFC's with high GWP (e.g. R-507A) with other HFC's with significantly lower GWP. As the restrictions currently stand, it may be that any conceptual work on replacing HFC's with other more environmentally friendly HFC's must be suspended, and the investment incurred to date will be lost. Given the planned inclusion of the restriction on all HFCs (without taking into account GWP factors), a development investment plan should be developed with consideration of alternative refrigerants (ammonia, propylene). In adition, the challenge of allowing additional substances causing the risk of major industrial accidents (as defined by DIRECTIVE 2012/18/EU OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 4 July 2012 on the control of major-accident hazards involving dangerous substances, amending and subsequently repealing Council Directive 96/82/EC) will be a long-term and very challenging process. The new regulations and the need for many users to adapt to these regulations will result in longer investment cycles due to the fact that there are a limited number of entities supplying ammonia or propylene-based refrigeration equipment on the market. The manufacturer's market will not keep up with the needs of users. At the same time, the decommissioning of a large number of units in such a short period of time will cause complications in the disposal of refrigerants. As a result, they will be stored in tanks or other equipment for a long time and will leak into the atmosphere in certain quantities until they are physically decommissioned. In order to minimize the risk of a major chemical accident, emissions resulting from the storage of withdrawn refrigerants and also the restrictions of the equipment manufacturers' market, the process of planning the replacement of refrigerants should not take place under time pressure and be adequate for the entry into force of such restrictive restrictions.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Due to broad safety concerns, we are requesting a 12-year deferral of the derogation of the use of HFCs as refrigerants used in the chemical industry, which will allow manufacturers such as ANWIL S.A. to more effective prepare for the replacement of refrigerants with non-HFC's. As mentioned above, currently available alternative replacements increase the risk of a major chemical accident at production installations in the chemical industry and their implementation should be spread over time. An additional important element is the fact that the current equipment containing a large amount of refrigerants (>500 T/eqCO2) has a continuous detection system for accidental release, and in addition the leakage inspection of the equipment is carried out at least once every 6 months (a legal requirement), which significantly minimizes accidental release and ensures that the HFCs in use are used under strictly controlled conditions with a low likelihood of accidental release.

Their use, as refrigerants and expanders of insulating foams, and the management of the end of life are already regulated by Regulation (EU) 517/2014 which imposes periodic checks of gas leaks, encourages recycling and regeneration and guarantees that the product is treated by expert personnel, effectively reducing the possibility of uncontrolled emissions into the environment. If fluorinated gases were included in the restriction, the impact on the entire value chain of the Refrigeration, Air Conditioning and Heat Pumps (RACHP) sector would be very significant. Substitute products are not feasible in all applications: in some cases for reasons of space, in others due to low energy efficiency ( C02 transicritical system)  or because the risk associated with flammability ( Propane R290) or toxicity ( Ammonia R717)  is not acceptable or minimisable. In most cases, simply replacing the gas is not possible, but the entire system must be redesigned and/or replaced. In fact, "natural" refrigerants are not suitable for replacing HFCs in existing systems and, therefore, if a ban on PFAS were imposed (which include almost all HFCs and their HFO substitutes, with almost zero greenhouse effect), over 90% of refrigeration, air conditioning and heat pump systems should be replaced within a few years, with a very high cost for the community and with an enormous load of products to dispose of. So the carbon footprint of this conversion to natural gas would be impactful and bring more indirect emission of CO2. Therefore, inadequate phase-out timing does not allow the industry to introduce alternative substances into the equipment in time, as the redesign and development of new equipment must be done by addressing issues of safety for the consumer, energy efficiency of the equipment, as well as feasibility. So far, the risks of emissions of F-Gases are adequately controlled through existing EU legislation, in particular the F-Gas Regulation (517/2014, currently under review), by means of regular leak inspections and recovery at end-of-life.  The main substitutes are the so-called “natural gases”, the use of which could impact the environment and be hazardous for the users. General Comments: -

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Restriction on the manufacture, placing on the market and use of PFASs.  Owing to the: 1) PFAS materials (mainly fluoropolymers such as PTFE, PVDF, ECTFE, FEP, VITFEP (FEP-FKM), FKM, PFA) are used for lining in piping, valves and their associated gaskets/ seals, pumps and instrumentation.   Several types of fluoropolymers are use in the gaskets that seal connections and avoid leakages of liquids and gases. These gaskets must be flexible, tight and resistant to the chemicals used in the process.  2) Membranes for electrolyzers are manufactured on the basis of PFAS, when these are a basic element of chlorine production technology. During the development of the membrane electrolysis technology, in the early 1970s, properties were sought which remain relevant today including chemical stability, high efficiency (facilitating high transport of sodium/ potassium-ions with low transport of hydroxyl ions), relatively low electrical resistance and low diffusion of chlorine and hydrogen gas.  The development of membrane technology was initiated after the Minamata disaster as mercury was previously the basis for chlor-alkali production. Since 2017, mercury-based technology for chlor-alkali production is banned in Europe and will be phased out in the rest of the world by 2025.  Examples of specific uses of PFAS in the chlor-alkali industry:  Chlorine drying PFAS materials here include in equipment, piping, valves, gaskets and column internals. Alternative materials are available including titanium (for specific applications), PVC lined FRP and steel (for specific applications). For gaskets and sealing systems, EPDM could be used but this has a shorter lifetime and leads to more chlorinated waste.  Hydrochloric acid production  The main issue here is the gaskets to seal the graphite equipment.  Analysers There is a lot of analytical equipment, particularly in the chlorine loop, which is equipped with PFAS- (mostly as fluoropolymer) containing elements such as sample pumps and valve tubing. These are similar to the process equipment. The size and flexibility requirements of the tubing and valves, in addition to their chemical resistance, make fluoropolymers the only real choice here.  Safe transfer of chemicals Here, PFAS materials (i.e. fluoropolymers) are used due to the required chemical resistance, mechanical strength and flexibility requirements.  Implementation of Alternatives – duration and testing period: In those cases where an alternative has to be developed, more time will be required to account for research and development of the alternative. The required time needed for this is impossible to estimate but can be multiple years if such an alternative can be found at all. When a potential material is identified it has to be confirmed that there are no regrettable environmental/ health and safety effects, which can also take several years. This is then followed by pilot scale testing which usually takes around five years to demonstrate that the materials have the necessary life-span. After this, these materials are tested in operational installations (approximately 5-10 years). Upon completion of this phase the application of the alternative starts. Based on experience, a minimum of 20 years (excluding the time for the R&D work) is normal. This supports the need for a longer derogation period for those cases where no alternatives are readily available and suggests that a review may be needed to verify if developments of alternatives are still progressing as expected.  The alternative materials tested so far did not reach the required lifetime in the area of chemical resistance.  We request a derogation for the use of PFAS-containing materials in the chemical industry,  respectively keeping the possibility of using these materials and keeping their availability in the long term.  Otherwise, the future operation of the chlorine production facility, or their reliability and safety are threaten, due to the unavailability of materials for which no full-fledged replacement is currently known.

6. Missing uses: SODEL is looking to gather information on alternatives to PFAS in its field of activity. SODEL designs and manufactures disinfection products and medical devices. The exceptional surface tension provided by PFAS in our medical equipment disinfection products allows for excellent spreading and maximizes disinfection while reducing usage doses. The alternatives (Annex E.2.5.) to PFAS proposed in the restriction project (especially silicone derivatives) do not offer a suitable toxicological profile for the application areas of our products (human exposure); or do not provide as low a surface tension as PFAS.  In addition, silicone surfactants can remain on the surfaces of certain medical devices because they are difficult to rinse off and can therefore migrate into tissues in contact with these instruments (risk of encystment). To optimize the effectiveness of disinfection of invasive instruments, PFAS allow excellent diffusion and penetration of the biocidal solution containing them into the hollow and serrated bodies of the instruments. The very low surface tension of PFAS enables it to reach the deepest structures of the materials to be disinfected (endoscopes, surgical rasps and gouges).

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Our products are subject to Regulation (EU) No 528/2012 (BPR) and Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on Medical Devices (MDR). These regulations require our products to obtain marketing authorization (MA). However, obtaining the necessary MA involves creating a costly and complex dossier to meet the requirements of both the BPR and MDR. Furthermore, the evaluation process for these dossiers can take several years with the competent authorities. Once the MA is obtained, it is not possible to quickly modify the composition of the products under BPR or MDR regulations since every modification must be evaluated by the competent authorities. Additionally, any modification to a biocidal product or medical device is subject to evaluation timelines of several months or even years before being authorized. Even if there are usable alternatives to PFAS that can meet the requirements of the BPR or MDR, substituting PFAS with these alternatives can only occur after approval from the competent authorities and a revision of the product design dossier. Given that this evaluation process can take years, the proposed timeline (R01) for the restriction is incompatible with the timelines for processing MA applications. Therefore, for products subject to BPR or MDR regulations, and already having MA, a derogation period for the use of PFAS of a minimum of 5 years, ideally 12 years, would allow for the modification of products containing PFAS while still respecting the product evaluation timelines.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: -

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The comments apply to the semiconductor industry and it's downstream markets such as the electronic industry, military applications, mobile communication, computing, power generation and distribution and others.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: None of the fluoropolymers necessary during manufacturing of semiconductor wafers or semiconductor devices is part of the wafer product or device product and none are present in the downstream production and the products used by the end consumers of any electronic product. All uses are part of the production equipment and building infrastructure and do not contribute to any emissions via waste disposal by end users. Emissions can only occur once a manufacturing site will be dismanteled or re-commissioned to other uses, at which stage the equipment or installations would be deconstructed. The typical period of time until this happens is several to many decades and within that time there is no accumulation of fluoropolymers in the manufacturing buliding, equipment or products.

6. Missing uses: No PFAS material is part of any semiconductor wafer or device material but a small number sub-groups of fluoropolymers or -elastomers within the PFAS material group are indispensable to manufacture semiconductor wafers and semiconductor devices, which can be used in the electronics industry. The key functionalities of the necessary fluoropolymers are to protect the semiconductor wafers and devices during manufacturing from any contact with very small particles or even single metallic atoms. Ultrapure chemicals used for etching the semiconductor wafers would absorb single metallic atoms from storage containers, equipment or pipes if not all metal containing parts of the production equipment are protected by a layer of fluoropolymer or elastomer. And because metal atoms get absorbed into the semiconductor wafer and device once they reach it's unprotetcted surface during manufacturing, the acceptable limit for foreign metal atoms in a wafer remain usable for semiconductor manufacturing cannot be maintained without the use of fluoropolymers or -elastomers to protect the wafer or device during manufacturing. For those indispensable types of PFAS material there is to our knowledge currently no alternative material in development not even in research stage, which would be capable to protect the wafers sufficiently to maintain the acceptable limit of foreign metal atoms in the wafer. Due to the change of conductivity associated with already ultra low concentrations of metal in the ppb or ppt range, less powerful alternatives to the used fluoropolymers are not capable to protect the wafer sufficiently to remain usable for advanced electronic devices. Besides preventing foreign atoms such as metals from equipment to be absorbed by process chemicals and hence protect the semiconductor product from becoming unasable, certain  fluoropolymer and elastomers are also necessary to maintain a clean enough and particle free air in critical production areas. This is necessary to ensure that even particles in the nanometer size range cannot come anywhere near the surface of a wafer or device until the circuit structures, which are in a similar or smaller size range are finished. Particles on the surface would make advanced semiconductor device production impossible, because to achieve such advanced functions and speed at low enough energy consumption, the structures for the circuit on the wafer are smaller than such particles which leads to a failure of the whole device if only one larger particle would be on the surface during device production.  Without the properties and function of these fluoropolymers or -elastomers being able to protect the manufacturing equipment or the air quality in semiconductor wafer or device production facilities in Europe, no state-of-the-art semiconductor devices can be manufactured in European fabs any more. While technically, manufacturing may be possible for an interim period as long as a ban is not yet in force or during a derogation period and while the existing equipment and manufacturing infrastructure is still protected by the already existing and applied fluoropolymers or -elastomers , the transfer of semiconductor wafer and device production out of Europe to other continents, where at least the essential fluoropolymers or -elastomers out of the large group of PFAS materials is still available, is expected to start immediatly, because of the long times needed to re-build capacity. The proposed derogation period for semiconductor manufacturing would only prevent the beginning exodus of semiconductor industry, if a realistic chance to have non-PFAS materials with at least the same functionality and properties as the currently used PFAS-materials become available during that period of time, but no candidatea for such materialas are known to be in development or even at least research level.  The immediate step will be a stop of investments in Europe by most semiconductor companies, followed by increasing investiments in countries where the electronic manufacturing will remain possible in future. Despite their strategic importance for high tech, automotive, environment technology, military and other sectors, semiconductor industry will finally have moved out of Europe, latest by the end of the derogation period when necessary equipment or manufacturing infrastructure cannot be maintained any more or spare parts become unavailable or too expensive, but likely earlier, by the time that the non-European newly built capacity will be able to take over. This will lead as well to the loss of jobs in the whole semiconductor industry with a risk of job reduction in downstream industries of the users of the semiconductor devices in the electronics, green energy, automotive, and others, unless the supply disadvantage would be compensated.  With a sufficient derogation period of such type of PFAS or fluoropolymers or -elastomers, an additional global shortage or semiconductor devices might be avoided, if production in Europe can be maintained long enough until all capacity to replace it is online out of Europe. It is, however, more likely that there will be an interim period of some years with also a global shortage of semiconductor wafers and semiconductor devices.  About 30% of European wafer production is used for power electronic devices which are necessary for power generation, transport, renewable energy and also automotive applications. The loss of such wafer capacity for an extended period of time until wafer capacity is re-built outside Europe would lead also to shortages of devices for such applications. The remaining wafer capacity goes into many applications, especially smart phones and computing. With about nine to 10 million square centimeter of semiconductor wafers from Europe being taken out of the market for two to three years until the other regions can replace that capacity, the global automotive production would suffer a shortage of 30% to 35% in that period and global smartphone and computing a shortage of still 20% each with corresponding large negative effects on jobs and private consumers not only in Europe, but especially there.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: No alternatives are known to exist or be in development which can achieve the necessary functions to allow ultra pure and ultra clean wafer or device production. Whether after ten years or more, an alternative material with similar function can be developed is not known and even if it would, the semiconductor industry will long have moved out of Europe and have invested in all the capacity it needs elsewhere. Thus, it will not move back existing capacity into Europe and even if capacity for additonal demand increase would be put into Europe much later, is less likely than in established semiconductor regions with all the infrastructure still existing. For this reason, derogation periods will not prevent manufacturing to be forced to move from Europe to other continents, they can only lessen the extent of an interim global shortage of semiconductor devices. Only an exemption of at least the small number of Fluoropolymers or -elastomers as key materials within the PFAS material group and which are currently classified as Polymers of low concern by the OECD (ACC study) would allow the semiconductor wafer and device industry to have a long term perspective and likely prevent a full scale exit with severe consequences for many industry sectors in Europe and for some years also globally. Failure to exempt the essential group of fluoropolymers or -elastomers within the PFAS materials will therefore also have significant impact on the Green Deal, Electro mobility, or a European Chips Act or Military independence.

6. Missing uses: II. Polysilicon production   b. Fluoropolymers are used in chemical plant engineering, such as gaskets, pipe and reactor inliners, valves, pumps and other devices. In uses relevant to solar technology, PFAS are used for polysilicon treatment during polysilicon production, where plant equipment contains fluoropolymers.   Fluoropolymers are chemically resistant and durable against chemicals necessary for polysilicon and semiconductor production, such as strong acids, or flammable and toxic chemicals under high pressure. Thanks to mechanical stability and durability, fluoropolymers ensure safe process conditions.     There are also other applications of fluoropolymers during production of polysilicon and semiconductors, such as processing materials and protective equipment, and their phaseout can cause serious disruptions in plant operation.   c. Polysilicon producers in Europe, a crucial and highly strategic segment of the PV value chain, would be affected. This is a concern for the industry as a whole; there is a strong indication that potentially up to 100% of valves, gaskets, pipes, column internals, linings, filters, membranes, diaphragms, electronics used in industrial settings contain fluoropolymers. Crucially, fluoropolymers are used in production processes, but not in the manufactured product, meaning that a ban on imports would not affect non-EU production. In other words, EU manufacturers would be disadvantaged compared to non-EU manufacturers.   It is estimated that about 100% of the plants in Europe will be impacted.    d. Another challenge would be in compliance of alternative materials with national legislation of Member States. The effort to entirely re-equip a plant comes close to the construction of a new plant.   g. As there are currently no materials offering the same leak-tightness as PFAS, plant operation with alternative materials will not be approved, as alternative materials lack proper testing, or do not perform in compliance with the limits for gaseous and liquid leakage.    Products will therefore not be manufactured. The PFAS ban would not only affect the usage of fluoropolymers for polysilicon production, but the change would also have far-reaching consequences for European producers of these materials, employment, and consumers. It could potentially lead to job losses and reduced job opportunities within these industries. SolarPower Europe estimates that about 4,500 direct and indirect FTEs were provided by the polysilicon manufacturing segment in the EU in 2021.   IV.Inverters  a.There is some evidence of PFAS present in the connector with some reporting the content of 40 mg per kg. There is an indication that packaging of diodes may have fluorine content, this case is under analysis.   b.PFAS is widely used in semiconductors, wires, cables and PCB boards. Inverters contain the above components. PFAS makes products waterproof, oil proof and high-temperature resistant.    c.Likely all inverter producers in Europe.    d.As of current knowledge, there are no alternatives to PFAS for this use.    f.Due to lack of information about PFAS use along the supply chain, many inverter producers are at the stage of analysis of their products for the PFAS content.    There are verification costs connected to testing about 1,000 parts per model. If the material needs to be changed due to PFAS content, there will be cost of reliability test for new materials and cost of production trial run.    g.To our knowledge, there is no substitute material to PFAS in inverters. It is highly probable that in case of a ban, production of inverters will cease to exist in Europe. The impact of this ban extends beyond the usage of PFAS and encompasses European producers of these materials, employment prospects, and consumers. There is potential for job losses and limited employment opportunities within the inverter industry affected by the ban. According to SolarPower Europe’s EU Solar Jobs Report 2022, inverter manufacturing in the EU provided 31,000 direct and indirect FTEs in 2021.   VI. Battery energy storage systems   b.BESS provide grid-balancing services to help integrate renewable energy sources into the power grid, and also contain refrigerants that prevent overheating of the system. Without cooling, there are major safety concerns for the functioning of BESS.    There is a challenge coming from the fact that BESS are not considered air conditioning systems, and therefore are not subject to the proposed derogation for maintenance and refilling of existing Heating, Ventilation, Air Conditioning, and Refrigeration (HVACR) equipment put on the market before the entry into force (EiF) of the proposed restriction.   d. Li and Tang (2022)1 analysed drop-in alternatives for the currently used refrigerant and found that from the tested alternatives, there is no perfect mixture found that is nonflammable, has low Global Warming Potential (GWP), and has higher system efficiency and capacity than currently used refrigerant.   g. There is no proposed derogation for BESS that are already placed on the market. The retrofitting of cooling systems is especially a concern for existing systems.    The estimated lifetime of BESS products is about 20 years. If existing systems are required to retrofit their cooling system, the cost would place a significant burden on operators.    1 Li & Tang. (2022). A comprehensive study of drop-in alternative mixtures for R134a in a mobile air-conditioning system. In Applied Thermal Engineering, V.203, 117914, ISSN 1359-4311,  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.applthermaleng.2021.117914.   EU Solar Jobs Report 2022. available at: https://www.solarpowereurope.org/insights/thematic-reports/eu-solar-jobs-report-2

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: III.Semiconductors  b. The properties of PFAS which are used by the semiconductor industry are low surface tension, chemical stability and compatibility, inertness, purity, low degree of friction, special electrical properties, non-flammability, high resistance to permeation, extreme temperatures, bacterial growth and an extended service life.   PFAS are present in photoresists, which are used in various stages of semiconductor manufacturing. In the process of photolithography, a thin coating of photoresist is applied to silicon water. Subsequently, this coated wafer is exposed to UV light through a photomask, to create specific geometrical shapes on the silicon wafer. Photoresist is also used in etching and cleaning, where gases are applied to chemically remove layers from the silicon wafer surface. Another use of PFAS in photoresists is to improve properties such as adhesion to the silicon water, durability, resistance to corrosion, radiation and high temperatures.   PFAS are part of the production process of several semiconductor components, such as interconnects, capacitors and insulators, where they improve thermal stability and moisture resistance. Another application is in the equipment and factory infrastructure to manufacture semiconductors (eg. high purity water distribution systems, lithium batteries for metrology tools) and in the equipment components and chemicals.   d. Metal oxide-based materials such as zirconium oxide and titanium oxide are a potential alternative to PFAS in photolithography. These materials offer adhesion and chemical resistance comparable to PFAS-based materials. Another alternative researched is hydroxy styrene-based materials, which are fluorine free polymers. The properties such as patterning performance and environmental safety are promising, but they need to be further optimized and the material needs to have enabled use in industry.   e. Some alternatives described above are being researched in the field of photolithography, however, for most uses of PFAS by semiconductor industry there are no alternatives. There needs to be research and development of alternative substances, which then need to be applied into mass production.    Alternative materials will need special attention from chipmakers, which will have to ensure the performance and reliability of their products while minimizing their impact on the environment and human health.   f. Semiconductors and their manufacturing processes are complex. It can take from several years to decades to market product and process innovation. Semiconductor manufacturers, who work in conjunction with materials and equipment suppliers, can take up to 25 years to complete their innovation cycles consisting of research and development, technology integration, prototyping and manufacturing ramp-up.

8. Other identified uses: V. Batteries and EV batteries  PFAS is widely used in batteries as binders, coatings and more. Alternatives are in development, but not readily available.    a. There are 2 electrode coating processes, wet coating and dry coating. In the wet coating, current selection of materials are PVDF for the cathode and styrene-butadiene-rubber/carboxylmethylcellulose (SBR/CMC) for the anode. In dry coating there is only PVDF in use.   b. PFAS is used in electrode binders in Li-ion batteries. The chemical provides mechanical strength to form and maintain electrode architecture in battery production and use, as well as enables the electrode to withstand hash electrochemical and chemical environment, which secures battery performance and degradation as designed.     There are specific prerequisites for the correct functionality of the binding material. First, binder chemistries for cathode use need to be oxidative stable and resilient to strong acid, so the material needs to be at higher oxidation state without being readily hydrolysable. Second, binder chemistries for anode need to be reductively stable, so the material needs to have a lower redox potential.     e. 30 years of research to find an alternative to PVDF and SBR/CMC used in the wet coating has not yielded an alternative. 15 years of research to find alternatives to PVDF-based dry coating, but none was found. All binder materials tested didn´t meet requirements for manufacturability and electrochemical performance. Once an alternative binder is found and qualified, the material supplier will require at least 5 years for scaling to mass production volume. In case of a ban on PFAS in the current state of art, no lithium-ion batteries for EV could be produced or used in Europe.
