7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: We use various fluoropolymers such as Ethylene tetrafluoro ethylene (ETFE), Fluorinated ethylene propylene (FEP), Perfluoroalkoxy alkane (PFA) and Polytetrafluoroetylene (PTFE) as insulation and buffer materials for our cables.  Fluoropolymers are the only materials that simultaneously possess the excellent features listed in  1) to 5) above. 1) Wide operating temperature range  Fluoropolymers are the only materials that can operate in high-temperature environments of 250°C or higher.  It is the only material that can maintain elasticity in extremely cold environments of -100°C or lower.  2) Higher resistance to weather, chemicals, oil, and flame than other materials   Material with extremely low dielectric breakdown under exposure to ultraviolet rays and ionizing radiation. Extremely little mechanical deterioration due to corrosion from corrosive gases, acids/alkalis, organic solvents, and various types of oil. Corrosive gases, acids, alkalis, organic solvents, various oils, and other corrosives.  High oxygen index of 95% or higher, making it a material that is difficult to burn.  3) Combines lubricity, wear resistance, tensile strength, bending modulus and elongation not found in other materials. Coating materials that combine high tensile strength with high flexural modulus and elongation include alternative materials (silicone materials, polyether ether ketone (PEEK), mica, EPDM, polyvinyl chloride, polyethylene, ceramic based and one confidential polymer).  There are no alternative coating materials other than fluoropolymers, including alternative materials (Silicone materials, Polyether ether ketone (PEEK), mica, EPDM, Polyvinyl chloride, Polyethylene, ceramic based and one confidential polymer).  There are no alternative materials (silicone materials, Polyether ether ketone (PEEK), mica, EPDM, Polyvinyl chloride, Polyethylene, ceramic based and one confidential polymer). The material has water repellency, lubricity, abrasion resistance, and non-adhesiveness at the same time.  Fluoropolymers that combine these characteristics are necessary materials for long-life movable wires.  4) Extremely high voltage resistance and the lowest dielectric constant and dissipation factor among polymers  Lowest dielectric constant and dielectric loss tangent of any alternative material (silicone materials, polyether ether ketone (PEEK), mica, EPDM, polyvinyl chloride, polyethylene, ceramic based and one confidential polymer) The volume resistivity (>1018Ω-cm) is higher than that of alternative materials (silicone materials, polyether ether ketone (PEEK), mica, EPDM, polyvinyl chloride, polyethylene, ceramic based and one confidential polymer)  Lowest dielectric constant (2.1) and dissipation factor (2×10-4) among all polymers. It is an ideal material for high-speed transmission.  5) Thin-wall Formability Unmatched by Other Materials  High elongation allows for excellent thin-wall formability.  About cables for moving parts Cables for moving parts are used in a variety of equipment because they can supply power to the end of the equipment as sensor cables and motor power cables without breaking while the cable is moving. They are mainly used in industrial robots (e.g., articulated robots with multiple axes, scalar robots, and robots that move on XY stages). Industrial robots are required to be automated and highly precise in manufacturing production lines and are responsible for labor production shortages. Fluoropolymers used for cables for moving parts, as explained above, have a high volume resistivity and can reduce the insulation thickness, making it possible to make thinner cables while maintaining the insulation performance than cables using other insulation materials. Robots have been miniaturized in recent years, and cables are required to be moving parts with narrow wiring. Going forward, cables will continue to need to be made thinner. The only resin that can meet this requirement is fluoroplastic. If the cables are too thick, they cannot be routed inside the robot and the robot housing itself will become huge, and the motors to move them will also become larger and use more electricity. As a result, CO2 emissions will increase, worsening the global environment. Since ETFE, FEP, and PFA have high mechanical properties such as tensile strength, elongation, and hardness, the resin will not crack or break due to movement, and wires coated with ETFE, FEP, or PFA can be used as wires for moving parts. If wires made of other insulation materials are made to move, the insulation will crack and lose its insulating properties, making them unusable as wires for moving parts. In particular, FEP has a low dielectric constant and is a material that combines telecommunication characteristics such as attenuation and leakage with a small diameter. In terms of durability under movement, fluoropolymer-insulated conductors are 1.9 times more durable than PVC-insulated conductors and 1.2 times more durable than cross-linked polyethylene conductors. (See Appendix for test conditions and results.) PTFE is also an essential material for cables used in moving parts. PTFE (in tape form), which has a low coefficient of friction, is applied to the inside of the wire. By applying PTFE (in the form of tape) as a buffer between the wire core and the shield, it is possible to prevent the shaving of insulation by the metal shield that occurs when the cable is moved. PTFE also has a high elongation, so it is a material with no alternative that can withstand the violent movements caused by repeated movement and maintain cushioning protection without cracking.  Our Impact Even if we were to switch to an alternative material to PFAS, we would need to replace five extruders, and we would not be able to bear the cost of the equipment. Even if the company could bear the cost, it would take more than seven years to replace the equipment. Our cables for moving parts are designed and proposed in accordance with the operating conditions of each machine and robot, and are used not only in Japan but also throughout the world. We are a manufacturer that supplies approximately 10,000 types of cables for moving parts to the world, More than 90% of its products (cables for moving parts) are made of fluoroplastic. Fluoropolymers are indispensable to our company, and maintaining the same level of performance and sales with non-fluoropolymers is technically and economically unfeasible, and we can expect to be unable to maintain our 180 employees. In addition, it is easy to believe that it would put the entire society at risk of slowing down the pace of development of manufacturing. Based on the above, we advocate the continued use of ETFE, FEP, PFA, and PTFE.

Non-confidential attachment.   a) The annual tonnage and emissions (at sub-sector level) and type of PFAS associated with the relevant use. - Relevant PFAS are used in packaging machines to ensure thermal and chemical stability for example in heating or cooling processes which are necessary for product safety, especially for pharmaceutical products and food processing. - Extrapolating the total tonnage of PFAS material use, as well as estimating it, is not practical or feasible for us as a trade association due to the high percentage of special machinery built by our members.  b) The key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use.  With the investigation in the network of Packaging Valley Germany e.V., the following areas of use of PFAS were identified among the member companies: - Piping and tubing of product (w/o product contact), - piping and tubing to media, - filters, - seals, - O-rings, - gaskets, - tubing and pipes, - expansion joints, - conveyer belts and reject trays (w/o object contact), - valves and fitments, - chutes, - guiding rails, - rollers, - funnels and sliding plates, - tanks, - funnels, - rollers, - lining, - blades of knives, - membranes, - lubricants, - surfaces, - refrigerants.  c) The number of companies in the sector estimated to be affected by the restriction. The main relevant applications of the Packaging Valley Germany e. V. member companies were identified in the two customer sectors of food and pharmaceuticals, which is why the consultation of Packaging Valley Germany e. V. focuses on these two areas. Packaging machinery manufacturers have been identified as being severely affected, as have component manufacturers and automation companies involved in packaging technology. Accordingly, only sales from the packaging technology sector were taken into account.  Food sector: 70 of the member companies of Packaging Valley Germany e.V. provide machines/or solutions for the food industry. The estimated impact of a total PFAS ban on turnover and employees was given as a decrease of 10-30 % for food packaging machines.  Pharma sector: 64 of the member companies of Packaging Valley Germany e.V. provide machines/or solutions for the pharma industry. The estimated impact of a complete PFAS ban on sales and employees was given as a 10-40% decrease in pharmaceutical packaging machinery.  Affected sectors:  - Equipment for industrial production, processing, packaging and filling of food; food contact materials - Equipment for production, processing, packaging, chilling, filling and freeze-drying of pharmaceutical and nutraceuticals products as well as their ingredients. - Equipment to clean or sterilize food, pharmaceutical products, nutraceuticals and their ingredients and packaging material as well as the equipment to produce, process, fill or package it. - Spare parts for already installed equipment of all the above-mentioned sectors.  This information is based on the results of our survey of Packaging Valley member companies. On the basis of the information provided, the overall impact of a total PFAS ban on member company sales and employment is estimated to be between 5% and 25%. Considering a total sales of about 7,24 billion Euro and about 20.000 employees of the Packaging Valley member companies in the packaging sector in the EU.   d) The availability, technical and economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives for the relevant use, including information on the extent (in terms of market shares) to which alternative-based products are already offered on the EU market and whether any shortages in the supply of relevant alternatives are expected.  - Shortages in the supply chain are expected. - For packaging machine manufacturers, possible alternatives are widely unknown. - Known alternatives do not run efficient and can so far not fully replace the requirements. - Substitutes/Alternative substances cannot be fully assessed by mechanical engineering perspective on their application.   e) For cases in which alternatives are not yet available, information on the status of R&D processes for finding suitable alternatives, including the extent of R&D initiatives in terms of time and/or financial investments, the likelihood of successful completion, the time expected to be required for substitution (including any relevant certification or regulatory approvals) and the major challenges encountered with alternatives which were considered but subsequently disregarded.  Processes of materials research and development are widely unknown from the perspective of mechanical engineering companies.  f) For cases in which substitution is technically and economically feasible but more time is required to substitute:  i) the type and magnitude of costs (at company level and, if available, at sector level) associated with substitution (e.g. costs for new equipment or changes in operating costs); ii) the time required for completing the substitution process (including any relevant certification or regulatory approvals); iii) information on possible differences in functionality and the consequences for downstream users and consumers (e.g. estimations of expected early replacement needs or expected additional energy consumption); iv) information on the benefits for alternative providers.  - Unknown.  g) For cases in which substitution is not technically or economically feasible, information on what the socio-economic impacts would be for companies, consumers, and other affected actors. If available, please provide the annual value of EU sales and profits of the relevant sector, and employment numbers for the sector.  With a ban on PFAS, productivity losses are expected due to: - Higher inefficiency of the cleaning cycles (chemical detergents may affect durability or need to be replaced, requiring longer cleaning cycles). - Higher wear of material cause higher downtimes of machines and impact the carbon footprint of products. - Modifications of processes and higher costs for material, changes of material, productivity and cleaning. - Complex processes e.g. high/low temperatures in food/pharmaceutical processing must be revised, modified and revalidated.  Productivity losses affect not only the carbon footprint of the single material but also of the processes and machines. The impact cannot be assessed at this point.  The replaceability of PFAS materials is not yet fully given. Food safety and pharma safety might take losses. Up to now, high temperatures and corresponding cleaning processes have ensured food and pharmaceutical product safety.  Furthermore, new validations will be necessary in the pharmaceutical sector (leads to further downtimes of machines) - the impact on products might change, as well as machine breakdowns can be caused by new processes, which leads to higher drug shortages in the EU. Due to higher productivity and lower complexity relocation of production facilities abroad become more attractive. Machines in the EU could no longer be operated because spare parts are affected by a PFAS ban or spare parts made from new materials cannot replace the required functions. Lower productivity will make investment in the EU more complicated and less attractive, which may lead to relocation of production in the long term. As a result, the security of supply of pharmaceuticals could decline and the dependence on third countries could increase further.  With an assumed service life of at least 15 to 20 years for machinery and equipment, security of supply is absolutely essential for customers (especially in the pharmaceutical industry), otherwise even existing machinery will be relocated to non-EU countries.  The machine building industry strives to act in the interests of the circular economy. Machines do not end up in landfill, as they typically yield a very high scrap value for their components. End of their lifecycle, machines are usually either reprocessed or recycled, which closes the loops, and the materials and components do not end up in the landscape.  The estimated annual value of EU sales affected is between €0.36 billion and €1.81 billion and the number of jobs affected in the EU is between 1000 to 5000, as declared in more detail in point c) above.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: -

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Mechanical engineering, plants and equipment for research, development, small series and start-up production in or around the pharmaceutical, chemical, battery, photovoltaic, food and nuclear industries. The main PFAS-containing parts we use for our facilities are as follows: Containers, pipes and hoses, seals, screw fittings/cables/plugs, compressed air fittings, pipe connectors media resistant, ball valves, pipe coatingеn, safety valves, centring rings.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: As a consumer and as a company that already uses finished products made from polyfluorinated compounds, we cannot determine the extent to which the environment is polluted during their manufacture. What we can say is that the release in the environment of PFASs is considered very low or unlikely when they are built into our machines. The equipment supplied to the customers is usually used for a very long time, well cared for, maintained, and regularly upgraded for new applications under high purity laboratory conditions. Lifetimes more than 30 and often 40 years are the norm, and the rate of disassembly is very low. The substances that customers handle in the equipment are usually more hazardous than the materials used in the equipment itself, and the equipment components must be decontaminated or disposed of as hazardous waste prior to disposal anyway because of contact with customer substances. Proper segregation and disposal of PAFS components is easily accomplished within this framework.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: As mentioned above, we are a company that uses manufactured products containing PFAS to integrate into our facilities.  All we can say is that our systems have been in use for a very long time, well cared for, maintained and regularly upgraded for new applications in high purity laboratory environments. Lifespans of over 30 and often over 40 years are the norm, and dismantling rates are very low. However, when it comes to dismantling they are dismantled and disposed of by appropriate disposal companies, and almost all of the materials used are recycled.

6. Missing uses: The application areas in which our company integrates, installs and uses PFAS are: Machinery, plant and equipment for research, development, small series and start-up production in or near the pharmaceutical, chemical, battery, photovoltaic, food and nuclear industries. The equipment is classified under various European directives as large industrial tools or research and development equipment, which are already exempt from many environmental and disposal regulations. The requirements our equipment must meet: Very high resistance to a wide range of aggressive substances and influences such as acids, alkalis, salts, solvents and UV radiation. Since R&D typically involves analyzing, testing, and evaluating a wide variety of variants, and design based on resistance to a single substance is not possible and would preclude the intended use or make it completely uneconomical, universally resistant materials are essential. In addition, the above is sometimes coupled with requirements for special certifications (e.g. FDA), increased temperature resistance, or flame retardancy. The availability of alternative materials that combine even some of the above properties is currently not given and, based on the current state of research, is not expected within a few months to years. Impact: A ban on PAFS would force our customers to purchase our equipment in multiples or with extremely expensive conversion options to cover a sufficiently broad range of applications and substances. Maintenance intervals would be significantly reduced with alternative materials, in some cases by a factor of 10-100. The total cost of research and development in academia and industry would increase dramatically. Even if the above effects were tolerated, it would no longer be possible to process various substances safely, and the danger to plant operators, bystanders and the environment would increase considerably due to the expected increase in the number of leaks, spills and resulting accidents. In particular, significant locational and competitive disadvantages are to be expected in the highly topical areas of battery technology and photovoltaics, which are currently significantly increasing the demands on plants due to the use of highly modern and sophisticated chemicals. The regularly observed ignorance of existing EU legislation on the part of non-European manufacturers, coupled with incomplete market monitoring and the punishment of deviations, is likely to significantly increase their competitive advantage in the EU in this area. The expected improvements and environmental relief, at least as far as they come from the above-mentioned area, will probably not materialize to a large extent.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: For many of the products we use in our plants, there are no sufficiently good substitutes on the market. Some of the examples we can give are: Vessels, pipes and hoses: pressure vessel, PTFE hose, corrugated ring hose, pipe. Seals: Various O-ring and clamp seals. Many different ball valves.

Inherent dilemmas and trade-offs between environmental concerns of PFAS and climate objectives High-voltage equipment using PFAS gases is typically installed in critical network nodes. Their shutdowns would cause the rejection of renewably generated power. This would equal a tremendous amount of wasted resources. The proposal to restrict PFAS should not prevent either the decarbonisation of the electricity grid infrastructure or the grid development, which is essential to properly deliver the energy transition (by allowing the integration of renewable energies and the electrification of uses). The PFAS currently used for the electricity grid infrastructure contributes to its functionality and high efficiency. Complete restrictions of their placing on the market and use should always be considered in light of the availability of alternatives. Decarbonisation and the protection of human health and the environment are key. ECHA's proposal to restrict PFASs should, therefore, strike for a good balance between both objectives.   2. PFAS in solid components and spare parts of electrical equipment 2a. Solid components PFASs are used in electrical grid equipment, machinery components and parts, such as insulated nozzles, sealings, plain bearings, gaskets etc. The insulated nozzle is a key component for interrupting fault current (the arc of a short circuit current) inside a circuit breaker. More use cases are further specified in the annex. Once manufactured, solid components with PFAS are usually installed within the machinery. The decommissioning and recycling are carried out respecting all applicable legislation and in close collaboration with manufacturers.  TSOs are not aware of any alternative solutions to the PFAS use cases listed in the Annex of this document. Therefore, an undifferentiated restriction of PFAS for these components of grid equipment would signify a ban on new equipment and spare parts for critical infrastructure within18 months after its entry into force. This would effectively bring all current European grid development projects to a halt and then would endanger the ongoing energy transition, as no manufacturer is currently able to supply PFAS-free equipment. As research and development of alternatives is only starting, it is urgently needed that ECHA acknowledges this gap in the current proposal and adds a derogation of 13,5 years for solid components in electrical transmission equipment. More specifically, derogation 6. in the restriction proposal for fluoropolymers and perfluoropolyethers should be extended for use in high-voltage electricity transmission equipment by adding the paragraph “6 g high-voltage electricity transmission equipment”. 2b. Spare parts containing PFAS should be exempted Many PFAS are used in existing electric equipment already installed with a minimum lifetime of 40 years. It is, therefore, necessary that the supply of spare parts is secured throughout this lifetime. The operation, maintenance, repair and extension of existing equipment containing PFAS must be ensured until the end of its lifetime, as PFAS-free spare parts may not work in the originally designed equipment. Otherwise, they would need to be decommissioned prematurely, entailing additional environmental and climate-related burdens, without consideration of circular economy or reparability principles. ENTSO-E reiterates and stresses the importance of being able to use equipment during its lifetime. Therefore, ENTSO-E recommends an unlimited derogation for using spare parts containing PFAS in existing electrical equipment.   3. PFAS in liquids and lubricants Several liquids and lubricants used for the servicing and maintenance of electrical equipment use PFAS. The properties of mineral oils and lubricants are modified with PFAS additives to fulfil the needed quality demands, e.g., on temperature behaviour and ageing stability. They are used, for instance, in circuit breakers, which need to work impeccably when used. TSOs are not aware of any alternative solutions to the use cases listed. An undifferentiated restriction of lubricants and liquids containing PFAS would impede TSOs from carrying out their legal obligation to maintain and service their equipment to ensure proper functionality and efficient operation of the grid, bearing considerable risks regarding grid stability, security of supply and workers’ safety. Therefore, the proposal to allow a 13,5-year derogation for lubricants used under harsh conditions is strongly supported. On top of that, TSOs recommend a 13,5-year derogation for PFAS in liquids, in particular technical mineral oil with PFAS additives, until alternatives have been developed and proven to satisfy comparable quality standards regarding long-term reliability and performance requirements.   4. 1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The scope of this feedback is the application of fluorinated gases (F-Gases) in the refrigeration, stationary air-conditioning and heat pumps sector (RACHP). The submission strengthens the arguments put forward in view of the derogations proposed in the RMOA, and also provides an overview for which applications non-fluorinated alternatives are currently not economically and technologically feasible to replace F-Gases under the RMOA scope, and potentially under the ongoing F-Gas revision.  There is no on-size-fits-all refrigerant alternative for all RACHP applications. Our submission provides further details on this matter. The technical challenges in terms of safety, energy efficiency and cost-effectiveness for switching to alternatives in these applications are explained in details in the attachment.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: For more detailed information on emissions, please refer to Chapter 2 of the submission. The confidential attachment provides internal data on the manufacturing emissions of RACHP equipment in sub-chapter 2.1, on use-phase emissions sub-chapter 2.2. RACHP equipment is usually designed with hermetically sealed systems to avoid leakages, and at end of life, the fluorinated gases are normally collected under controlled circumstances to avoid releases.  Multiple data sets on end of life of refrigerant containing equipment are available at EU level and shed light on the level of end-of-life emissions in certain EU Member States. Sub-chapter 2.3. in the submission provides a non-exhaustive overview of estimated recovery rates at end-of-life according to different recent studies.

5. Proposed derogations: Point i. of the proposed derogations within the Annex XV restriction report states: maintenance and refilling of existing HVACR equipment put on the market before [18 months after EiF] and for which no drop-in alternative exist until 13.5 years after EiF.  The report recognizes that “terminating current HVACR equipment with many years of service life left will likely also cause environmental impacts, as energy and other resources would be needed to replace functional equipment”. Unfortunately, the report does not recognize that the service life RACHP equipment is often longer than the proposed derogations. The European Commission Ecodesign Study Review of Regulation 206/2012 and 626/2011 Air conditioners and comfort fans Task 2 report - Final version (page 51) concludes that the average lifetime of different types of residential & commercial air-conditioners and heat pumps is between 15 to 20 years, and in practice many systems have a longer lifetime.  This would mean that after 12 years, RACHP equipment could no longer be maintained or refilled, leaving consumers and businesses two options: 1) prematurely replace the whole system and equipment; 2) continue using the equipment and systems, and in certain cases without maintained and refilled systems to prolong the life of the equipment, resulting in lower efficiencies and performances thus higher energy consumptions.  To prevent this, the derogation on maintenance and servicing of existing HVACR equipment should be extended to a time-unlimited derogation (instead of 12 years). Further clarifications are provided in sub-chapter 3.2. of the attached submission.  Point j. of the proposed derogations within the Annex XV restriction report states: refrigerants in HVACR-equipment in buildings where national safety standards and building codes prohibit the use of alternatives.  A number of national and local obligations limit the use of alternatives to F-Gases. Therefore, it is necessary to ensure that those buildings can continue to be heated and/or cooled, without compromising energy efficiency, safety of installers, users, inhabitants. It is critical that the proposed derogation point 5 (j) in the Annex XV report is maintained not to contradict national building codes and safety standards, since bans of F-Gases at EU level would be combined with restriction of flammable refrigerants at national level. In sub-chapter 3.1.2. of the attached submission, national case studies are further detailed to strengthen the case for derogation needs.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Electronics and semiconductors (Annex E.2.11.) Electronics

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The PFAS-containing product parts are in the inside of the final product (heavy duty encoder).  Our products including all PFAS-containing product parts are B2B only and do not end in private household waste. Professional recycling by industry end users is standard. PFAS-containing seals are mounted in such a way that they can be dismantled and recycled without problems after end-of-life.

5. Proposed derogations: We produce encoders for use in heavy duty environments, e.g. steel mills, ports and mining industries. In the following we will layout the current use of PFAS-containing product parts in one of our best selling encoder series: FG(H) 40: • Total weight of FG 40 encoder: approx. 3 kg (depending on specific encoder type) • Total weight of PFAS in one FG 40 encoder: 0,83 g • %-share of PFAS-containing product parts of total encoder weight: 0,03%  In conclusion, PFAS-containing product parts only account for a minimum weight share of used raw materials. However, because of their specific properties PFAS-containing sealing parts are needed to achieve the desired product features and reliability for usage in heavy duty environments as we will lay out in the following.

6. Missing uses: We are a manufacturer of encoders for use in heavy duty environments, e.g. steel mills, ports and mining industries. At the moment we use PFAS-containing products parts such as: • Axial/radial shaft seals • O-rings (sealings) • Damping in encoders for railway operation The above-mentioned product parts are used in all our main product lines, which in sum account for a share of turnover of >80%. In compliance with the proposed EU restriction of PFAS we aim to substitute all PFAS-containing product parts with non-PFAS-containing parts, for example NBR or HNBR. However, for some product parts there are no alternatives available that would allow a substitution without a significant loss of product quality. In the following we will describe the used PFAS-containing products and the PFAS properties and features that make a substitution with existing alternative materials not feasible.   1. Axial/radial shaft seals • PFAS-containing material/component: elastomer part made of FKM or PTFE • The shaft seal provides tightness between the housing and the rotating shaft to prevent grease, oil or other lubricants from leaking out and, at the same time, to prevent the ingress of particles that could cause damage to the encoder.  Consequences of grease or oil leakage would be immediate wear of the encoder until its failure.  • Service life of the shaft seal: at least 10,000, in some cases up to 30,000 operating hours • Suitable for ambient temperatures from -40°C to +120°C • Resistance to media such as bearing oils and bearing lubricants as well as chemical cleaning agents, disinfectants, salt water, waste water and cleaning water (high-pressure cleaning) • Resistance to mechanical influences e.g. sand, dust, metal particles • UV resistance • Low coefficient of friction: 0.2 µr or lower • Required protection class: standard IP6x, minimum: IP5x • Suitable for varying speeds up to 8,000 min-1 in highly dynamic applications with frequent changes of direction, load changes and high accelerations. • Shaft seals made of NBR already break down at around 1,800 revolutions per minute • Compared to the standard material NBR, FKM is more expensive, but NBR is not suitable for applications in adverse environmental conditions or in potentially explosive atmospheres. • At the moment no suitable NBR or HNBR axial or radial shaft seals are commercially available.  2. O-rings (seals) • PFAS-containing material/component: elastomer parts made of FKM • Seals with O-ring in the encoder and in attachments such as plug connectors, cable glands, screw plugs to prevent moisture and dust penetration • Service life of the seal: at least 10,000, in some cases up to 30,000 operating hours • Suitable for ambient temperatures from -40°C to +120°C • Resistance to media such as bearing oils and bearing lubricants as well as chemical cleaning agents, disinfectants, salt water, waste water and cleaning water (high-pressure cleaning) • Resistance to mechanical influences e.g. sand, dust, metal particles • UV resistance • Required protection class: standard IP6x, minimum: IP5x • Compared to the standard material NBR, FKM is more expensive, but NBR is not suitable for applications in adverse environmental conditions or in potentially explosive atmospheres..  3. Damping in encoders for railway operation • PFAS-containing material/component: damping buffer made of FKM • Vibration damping for increased durability of the electronic parts • Required Hardness: 70 +/- 5 Shore • Tolerance according to DIN ISO 3302-1 M3 • Suitable for ambient temperatures from -40°C to +120°C • UV resistance • FKM has outstanding damping properties that no other material known to us with comparable other heavy-duty requirements can match  We checked the use of the following alternative materials as possible replacements for the above-mentioned PFAS-containing product parts: PTFE/Teflon Temperature range: -250 … +250 °C Frictional power: very high Resistance against media: very high Comments: almost unlimited resistance to ozone, weathering and ageing. Withstands almost all known hydraulic media, lubricants, chemicals and solvents.  FKM/FPM/Viton Temperature range: -25 … +200 °C Frictional power: high Resistance against media: high Comments: FKM is generally not resistant in hot water, steam, polar solvents, glycol-based brake fluids and low-molecular organic acids.  EPDM Temperature range: -45 … +150 °C Frictional power: intermediate Resistance against media: intermediate Comments: EPDM materials are incompatible with any mineral oil products (lubricants, fuels).  HNBR Temperature range: -30 … +150 °C Frictional power: intermediate Resistance against media: high Comments: higher maximum temperature than NBR.  NBR Temperature range: -30 … +120 °C Frictional power: intermediate Resistance against media: high Comments: good mechanical properties and resistance to mineral oil-based lubricating oils and greases. Good resistance to fuels is usually only given with special compounds. The resistance to ozone, weathering and ageing is low.   Conclusion: HNBR can be used as a replacement material for FKM or PTFE in some applications/products parts where the ambient condition requirements are not as harsh. However, for heavy duty environments, in which the vast majority of our encoders is used, there are no available alternatives to substitute fluorpolymers with the same required product properties.  In the case of a general PFAS ban, it would be impossible for us as a manufacturer of heavy duty encoders to produce products with the same quality, durability and performance and to cover the most important areas of application: corrosive heavy duty environments. For about 50% of our products, the use of PFAS materials is a necessary prerequisite for use by the customer.  Approx. 80% of our products are certified (SIL, Ex, UL/CSA and others). Post-certification would put a great strain on us in terms of personnel and finances. The resources that would have to be expended would deprive us of the opportunity to develop new products for a market that is developing at a rapid pace. Our future viability would be severely jeopardised.  As we have an export share to non-EU countries of >70% and no production sites outside the EU, our products would no longer be competitive on our most important markets (China, USA, South America) compared with the products of manufacturers from outside the EU not falling under the PFAS ban.  In fact, a general PFAS ban would therefore threaten the existence of our company with economic consequences for our customers (spare parts) and suppliers (loss of sales) as well as the loss of jobs.   In case of a general PFAS ban, the productivity of our customers, especially steel mills and ports in the EU, would decrease, as machinery and equipment will experience more frequent maintenance and unplanned breakdowns (due to excessive wear of shaft seals).  As all our competitors’ products would face the same problems under a general PFAS ban, exchanging our products with competitors’ products would not help our customers. The competitiveness of European steel mills and ports against the competition, e.g. in Asia and the USA, would decrease noticeably due to unplanned breakdowns and higher maintenance costs.  To avoid problems caused by a general PFAS ban and to remain competitive on important markets in Asia and the Americas other European encoder manufacturers are likely to move production from EU to non-EU countries. For us, however, such a step would exceed our financial possibilities.  We therefore advocate the indefinite exemption of fluoropolymers from the scope of the restriction for use in seals und damping of encoders and their components.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: During the manufacturing phase there are emissions, around 20% of the manufactured product ends up as scrap as it is off-spec and cannot be used (=2,4 tonnes). There are no emissions during the use phase (=0 tonnes). There are emissions during the end of life phase (=12 tonne).   As far as we are aware all waste is subject to incineration (100%).

5. Proposed derogations: As part of mining operations 10 tonnes of FKM is used. This is all incinerated during the end of life phase (100%).

6. Missing uses: FKM elastomers are used for construction vehicles/machines. 6,6 tonnes (55%) are used each year for construction vehicles/machines.   FKM elastomers are also used in military vehicles (defence industry). 1 tonne (8,3%) is used each year. The remaining 4,4 tonnes (36,7%)  is used in petroleum and mining activities.   In terms of the numbers of companies affected by the proposed restriction – there is one company that supplies military uses and 13 companies which supplies construction uses.   Fluoropolymers are used when a combination of requirements needs to be met and no other alternative material solutions exists. The key functionalities provided by FKM elastomers include: - Extreme temperature range use (-40°C to +250°C) and stability - Outstanding long-term chemical resistance (oils, coolants, water, fuels, acids) - Non-flammable (UL 94 V0), low in friction - Excellent dielectric properties (volume resistance >108 Ohm) - Low H2 and fuel permeation This combination of properties is only possible due to the chemical structure of fluoropolymers (physico-chemical properties). It is therefore not possible to obtain them without the existence of C-F bonds.   Please see non-confidential attachment.   Please also see the confidential attachment.   It is our view that the properties of FKM (long lifetime, excellent stability at high temperatures and in oils/media) are outstanding and cannot be covered by any other elastomeric sealing material, As such, there are not currently suitable alternatives to FKM elastomers for our uses.   This is also supported by the UK Health and Safety Executive report “Analysis of the most appropriate regulatory management options”, March 2023 which states in respect of fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers, that the industry view appears to be that for many or most uses there are no alternatives with the requisite performance characteristics. In addition, it explains that substitution of PFASs may need to take place across different pathways and timescales. It also highlights that many existing possible alternatives present potential human health and/or environmental hazards which require further investigation.   Fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers   The Restriction proposal follows the OECD definition of PFASs meaning – fluorinated substances that contain at least one fully fluorinated methyl or methylene carbon atom (without any H/CL/Br/l atom attached to it) (with certain limited exclusions).   The OECD “Reconciling Terminology of the Universe of Per-and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances: recommendations and Practical Guidance” explains (amongst others) that:  - it should be noted that this general PFAS definition is based only on chemical structure, and the decision to broaden this definition compared to Buck et al. (2011) is not connected to decisions on how PFASs should be grouped in regulatory and voluntary actions.  - PFAS are a chemical class with diverse molecular structures (e.g. neutral, anionic, cationic or zwitterionic; with or without aromatic rings; non-polymers or polymers; low molecular weight or high molecular weight) and thus diverse physical, chemical and biological properties (e.g. involatile or volatile; water soluble or water insoluble; reactive vs, inert; bioaccumulative or non-bioaccumulative). Therefore it is highly recommended that such diversity be properly recognized and communicated in a clear, specific and descriptive manner.  - The term “PFASs” is a broad, general, non-specific term, which does not inform whether a compound is harmful or not, but only communicates that the compounds under this term share the same trait for having a fully fluorinated methyl or methylene carbon moiety.  - in respect of the revised definition of PFASs it does not conclude that all PFASs have the same properties, uses, exposure and risks.   As such, fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers should not be treated in the same way as other PFASs for which there are known concerns (e.g. PFOA).    In addition, the UK Health and Safety Executive report “Analysis of the most appropriate regulatory management options (RMOA)” also considers PFAS. However, it considers a narrower definition on the basis that compounds with a single isolated –CF2- group are generally understood not to degrade to any of the highly persistent substances that have given rise to the environmental and/or human health concerns about PFAS.   The UK Health and Safety Executive adopted an approach of grouping PFASs into further subgroups with fluoropolymers being allocated to their own specific sub-group. This is due to the acknowledgement that not all PFASs give rise to the same environmental and/or human health concerns.   The UK Health and Safety Executive concludes that any restriction it would support under UK REACH need not apply to low hazard groups or low risk uses including fluoroplastics and fluorelastomers. It considers that potentially UK REACH authorization could be considered for PFAS used in processing aids in the manufacture and processing of fluorinated polymers. Industry have currently identified the lack of viable alternatives due to the required performance of these substances. Authorisation would allow controlled use whilst researching a viable alternative.   We support certain of these conclusions, in particular that restriction is not an appropriate option for all PFAS.

8. Other identified uses: In case of O-ring/sealing materials FKM – where it must be used today- cannot be replaced by other elastomers on the market, as other elastomers are inferior and far less resistant against oils/media, sun, ozone and especially heat etc., meaning the service life of a machine operated with other materials than FKM, would be drastically reduced. Seals need to be changed even more frequently, some machines would not run at all with especially aggressive oils. There is no choice for customers, FKM is the only option. 2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Based on the latest ESIA publications from 2023, semiconductor sites have to be considered with an end-of life span of over 25 years. Manufacturing runs in cleanroom conditions, however the level of CR and the usage of chemicals is highly different in a frontend and a backend factory. Some specific installations contain fluoropolymers e.g. pipe linings or specific valves, however a low emission is to be considered to other industries because of the long end of life span. Any kind of waste that has been generated during the operation of the factory is sorted and collected in accordance to the harmonized European waste code numbers for mixed plastics (EU Comm. 2002) and are either sent for disposal or recycling processes to authorized waste treatment companies.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: In the High Power Backend manufacturing processes PFAS compounds in a gas form are only used in closed systems, where practically zero emission is occuring during the normal operation. Any kind of waste containing PFAS compounds in our location is selectively collected in the original manufacturing packaging and transported to waste handling which contains a partial recycling and a waste handling according to the EU laws. There is no burning of such components!

5. Proposed derogations: In recent past there were plenty of proposals that have been accepted by the EU comission in order to have a greenhouse gas reduction  of greater or equal then 55% compared to the 1990 baseline by 2030. Modern semiconductor manufacturing of which our company is part of are contributing to achieve this goal.  Semiconductors from Infineon Technologies help to generate green electricity from renewable sources. They also offer increased efficiency  in generation, transmission, storage, and in particular, in the usage of electricity.  Applications of wide range use them e.g. industrial applications, power supplies, consumer electronics, as well as in motor drives or traction applications.  Production of semiconductors is done under cleanroom conditions. Systems are closed to rovide highest quality. High automation level and practically zero emission at the workplaces characterize a typical manufacturing.  Our location as a Backend factory misses several process steps that are present in the frontend manufacturing where the semiconductor chips are being produced and could potentially contain PFAS. Such technologies that does not exist in the backend are e.g. photolithography or plasma etching.  Adhesives: PFAS can potentially be a component of semiconductor products, e.g. in some electrically insulating adhesives, 70-90 wt% filler content of the PFAS Polytetrafluorethylene (PTFE) may be present to reduce stresses. This filler also prevents moisture destruction effects, which is responsible for corrosion within the semiconductors during operating circumstances (e.g humid/salty seashore environment).  The PFAS remains in the product and does not change its characteristics throughout the service life. At end-of-life, the semiconductor product is sent normally for proper disposal. Therefore, no emissions has to be considered.  Cleaning: Paste soldering relies even nowadays on a organic solderpaste. It requires a specific cleaning with the PFAS hydrogen fluoride ether (HFE) to remove paste residues after the soldering process that would prevent further assembly steps and damage the sensitive semiconductor during the usage. Total removal of such solder flux rests is not possible with alternative cleaning methods or components.  Hence it is to be considered that several years the current chemicals need to be used in the processing. However as mentioned in the previous sections, the chemicals are in a closed system, and after renewal or changing the waste is collected and sent for waste treatment and partial recycling so there is minimal emission or loss during the process.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Even though the backend manufacturing of semiconductors uses less PFAS in form of liquids, solids or gases, as frontend factories the whole supply chain is not possible w/o the front end chip manufacturing where many applications use this and have no proven alternatives. A majority of PFAS cannot be replaced by alternatives according to current knowledge even in long term and it will be extremely difficult. Instead of temporary exemptions -due to the very long lead time of developing alternatives- an appropriate exemption should be granted for the semiconductor manufacturing process, covering the entire semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem and value chain. A restriction on PFAS would have a direct negative impact on our revenue (FY 2022: €3.4 billion in Europe and €14.2 billion worldwide) and employees (FY 2022: 21,703 in Europe and 54,286 worldwide), as production with PFAS is not possible in Europe. In Hungary approximately 1900 Employees and their families and at least as many suppliers and vendors would be affected not to be considered the negative effect of missing key products for the renewable energy and green transportation. EU (but also worldwide) semiconductor manufacturing is currently not possible w/o using PFAS and in the near future alternatives will not be in place. A general prohibition of PFAS for the semiconductor industry, its suppliers and customers should be avoided under all circumstances to eliminate a locational disadvantage for Europe and generating huge problems in key application areas .

Hence, an analysis of alternatives and socio-economic analysis can not be provided. Subdivision of the energy sector as given in chapter 2.8 is urgently needed.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: The use cases given in Table 8 in Annex XV does not address assets operating in the electric power transmission grid. Derogations for the energy sector as given in chapter 2.8 are urgently needed.

8. Other identified uses: TSOs build and operate the critical power grid infrastructure to supply electricity to European industry and citizens. TSOs make sure to keep the environmental impact of the grid to a minimum and even enhance nature restoration and biodiversity in their corridors. The sophisticated high and extra high voltage equipment used in power grids is built to last 40+ years. It is designed to operate and withstand extraordinary and harsh conditions, such as high pressure, extreme voltage levels and temperatures, and to guarantee the functioning and resilience of the grid at any time. The use of PFAS in solid, liquid, and gaseous components of grid equipment is determined by manufacturers to ensure the needed requirements for its performance and reliability.  The sophisticated high and extra high voltage equipment used in power grids is built to last 40+ years. It is designed to operate and withstand extraordinary and harsh conditions, such as high pressure, extreme voltage levels and temperatures, and to guarantee the functioning and resilience of the grid at any time. The use of PFAS in solid, liquid, and gaseous components of grid equipment is determined by manufacturers to ensure the highest requirements for its performance and reliability.   A restriction that does not take into account network-specific use cases could lead to the unavailability of critical assets and, thus, to unpredictable effects with regard to system security.  Due to a lack of data, TSOs do not yet have a comprehensive overview of the use of PFAS in the components of their electrical equipment, nor the PFAS used to manufacture this equipment. Furthermore, there is also insufficient information on possible alternatives to replace them. European TSOs are committed to protecting the public and workforce wherever risks stemming from PFAS are identified. Therefore, typical use cases for PFAS where information exists are highlighted and the need for use case-specific derogations in the restriction proposal in case no alternatives are available is stressed.   1. Inherent dilemmas and trade-offs between environmental concerns of PFAS and climate objectives  High-voltage equipment using PFAS gases is typically installed in critical network nodes. Their shutdowns would cause the rejection of renewably generated power. This would equal a tremendous amount of wasted resources. The proposal to restrict PFAS should not prevent either the decarbonisation of the electricity grid infrastructure or the grid development, which is essential to properly deliver the energy transition (by allowing the integration of renewable energies and the electrification of uses). The PFAS currently used for the electricity grid infrastructure contributes to its functionality and high efficiency. Complete restrictions of their placing on the market and use should always be considered in light of the availability of alternatives. Decarbonisation and the protection of human health and the environment are key. ECHA's proposal to restrict PFASs should, therefore, strike for a good balance between both objectives.   2. PFAS in solid components and spare parts of electrical equipment  2a. Solid components  PFASs are used in electrical grid equipment, machinery components and parts, such as insulated nozzles, sealings, plain bearings, gaskets etc. The insulated nozzle is a key component for interrupting fault current (the arc of a short circuit current) inside a circuit breaker. More use cases are further specified in the annex. Once manufactured, solid components with PFAS are usually installed within the machinery. The decommissioning and recycling are carried out respecting all applicable legislation and in close collaboration with manufacturers.  TSOs are not aware of any alternative solutions to the PFAS use cases listed in the Annex of this document. Therefore, an undifferentiated restriction of PFAS for these components of grid equipment would signify a ban on new equipment and spare parts for critical infrastructure within 18 months after its entry into force. This would effectively bring all current European grid development projects to a halt and then would endanger the ongoing energy transition, as no manufacturer is currently able to supply PFAS-free equipment. As research and development of alternatives is only starting, it is urgently needed that ECHA acknowledges this gap in the current proposal and adds a derogation of 13,5 years for solid components in electrical transmission equipment. More specifically, derogation 6. in the restriction proposal for fluoropolymers and perfluoropolyethers should be extended for use in high-voltage electricity transmission equipment by adding the paragraph “6 g high-voltage electricity transmission equipment”.  2b. Spare parts containing PFAS should be exempted  Many PFAS are used in existing electric equipment already installed with a minimum lifetime of 40 years. It is, therefore, necessary that the supply of spare parts is secured throughout this lifetime. The operation, maintenance, repair and extension of existing equipment containing PFAS must be ensured until the end of its lifetime, as PFAS-free spare parts may not work in the originally designed equipment. Otherwise, they would need to be decommissioned prematurely, entailing additional environmental and climate-related burdens, without consideration of circular economy or reparability principles. TSOs reiterate and stress the importance of being able to use equipment during its lifetime. Therefore, TSOs recommend an unlimited derogation for using spare parts containing PFAS in existing electrical equipment.   3. PFAS in liquids and lubricants  Several liquids and lubricants used for the servicing and maintenance of electrical equipment use PFAS. The properties of mineral oils and lubricants are modified with PFAS additives to fulfil the needed quality demands, e.g., on temperature behaviour and ageing stability. They are used, for instance, in circuit breakers, which need to work impeccably when used. TSOs are not aware of any alternative solutions to the use cases listed. An undifferentiated restriction of lubricants and liquids containing PFAS would impede TSOs from carrying out their legal obligation to maintain and service their equipment to ensure proper functionality and efficient operation of the grid, bearing considerable risks regarding grid stability, security of supply and workers’ safety. Therefore, the proposal to allow a 13,5-year derogation for lubricants used under harsh conditions is strongly supported. On top of that, TSOs recommend a 13,5-year derogation for PFAS in liquids, in particular technical mineral oil with PFAS additives, until alternatives have been developed and proven to satisfy comparable quality standards regarding long-term reliability and performance requirements.   4. PFAS in gases  4a. Gases for operation, maintenance and extension containing PFAS should be exempted  In recent years, TSOs have been using PFAS-containing gases as insulation medium in electrical switchgear to replace SF6, the most potent greenhouse gas, and decarbonise their electric equipment. For the new installations above 145 kV, as well as for specific uses on all voltage levels, TSOs currently have limited possibilities to replace SF6. One key component to do so has been PFAS-containing insulation gases, such as fluoronitrile (C4F7N). The application of the gases in electrical equipment, listed in the annex per use-case, is used in closed cycles and has state-of-the-art leakage detection devices to ensure smooth operation, protect the environment and minimise workforce exposure.  As of today, it is not certain whether PFAS-Gas-free solutions above 145kV and for specific uses on all voltage levels will be commercially available in 6,5 years time, also in sufficient quantity for all ranges of TSOs application. This is due to long development, qualification, and standardisation processes. If PFAS in switchgear insulation gases were banned after the derogation period of 6,5 years, it would mean the already ordered and installed equipment supposed to operate with PFAS gases may not be put into operation, maintained, nor extended after the ban date and that existing equipment would have to be put out of order and become a stranded asset.   It must also be ensured that switchgear operating with PFAS gases that have been lawfully put into operation according to the F-Gases Regulation can be refilled for maintenance purposes or extended with the corresponding gas as long as it cannot be maintained or extended with PFAS-free gases. Therefore, TSOs recommend an unlimited derogation for PFAS gases used for refilling, maintenance, or extension purposes of switchgear. Replacing existing switchgear operating with PFAS gases before their end-of-life would lead to stranded assets, which would contradict the principles of reparability and circularity.  4b. Derogation of PFAS-containing gases will help speeding up the PFAS-free developments  The present draft of F-Gases Regulation forces TSOs to install fluornitril based assets until alternative solutions are available. TSOs believe that derogation of the PFAS Gases within 6,5 years, as proposed by ECHA, would strengthen the developments of the alternative PFAS-free solutions and hence the installations of PFAS-Solutions would be limited to minimum.   Thus, TSOs urge ECHA and policymakers to take into account the ongoing negotiations on the draft F-Gases Regulation.  5. Combined Comments:
General Comments: -

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Our comment applies to: PFAS Manufacturing; Applications of F-gases (refrigeration, air conditioning and heat pumps, foam blowing agents, insulating gas in electrical equipment; transport (Use of PFASs in applications affecting the proper functioning related to the safety of vehicles, and affecting the safety of operators, passengers or goods, mobile air conditioning, transport refrigeration MAC – and refrigeration in military applications). Our submission will cover both fluorinated gases and fluoropolymers.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: a. EPEE is using its EU HFC Outlook model to provide data for this consultation. More details about this model are indicated in the attached documents. Its projections are built bottom up to give an analysis of the stock of RACHP equipment in more than 50 F-gas market sub-sectors.  The modelling shows that the level of emissions and the split between the three stages can vary considerably between the different technology types used in the RACHP sector. Data collected by the industry also shows that there have been significant reductions in emission rates, driven by the controls in the first and second F-Gas Regulation.  This reduction is expected to continue with future and further controls in the third F-Gas Regulation. Many types of small RACHP equipment are factory built sealed systems e.g. domestic refrigerators, standalone retail display cabinets. They have very low operational leakage rate – well below 1% per year. Larger systems such as supermarket’s now have leak rates under 5%. For smaller units such as air-to-air, annual leakage rates are below 2%. For large site installed equipment operating life emissions are dominant (around 60%), whereas for small sealed systems, end-of-life emissions are dominant (around 90%). Figures and data are available in the attached Annexes to this submission. b. Share of waste treated through incineration:  Almost 84% of all fluoropolymer applications (beyond the use in the RACHP sector) were treated with incineration with energy recovery (72%) and thermal destruction (12%), and only 3% was recycled.  For F-gases, Member States are encouraged to develop Extended Producer Responsibility for their recovery, recycling, reclamation or destruction. Recycling and reclamation activities of F-gases have significantly increased since the second F-gas Regulation and the HFC phase down entered into force driven by the increased value which came with the reduced amounts available on the EU market. It is harder to give an estimate of the share as many countries also have specific schemes. In France for instance manufacturers are under obligation to provide empty packaging to users of refrigerants, collect all polluted fluorinated gases for free, and recover them fully. Moreover, data reported by the EEA and by Memer states show significant discrepancies.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: More data will be needed to assess the end-of-life of PFAS and the destruction of PFAS. PFAS are not under mandatory monitoring in EU legislation applicable to incineration plants, contrary to other persistent substances such as PCBs. A study conducted by ivl and Avfall Sverige in 2021, based on monitoring in municipal incineration plants in Sweden found low concentrations of PFAS after combustion in residues. However, there was no apparent relation between high concentrations of analysed PFAS in sampling matrices and operational data (temperature, waste composition) was found, meaning that a high temperature did not guarantee a low concentration of PFAS. Very few laboratories with experience in PFAS measurement and sampling are available. For a more in-depth analysis, please refer to the submission of the Confederation of European Waste-to-Energy Plants (CEWEP).

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: For a more in-depth analysis on the proposed concentration limits, please refer to the submission of the Confederation of European Waste-to-Energy Plants (CEWEP). While EPEE is not a recycling expert, it can share the experience of its members and the legislation applicable at EU level. Recycling and reclamation activities of F-gases have significantly increased since the second F-gas Regulation and the HFC phase down entered into force driven by the increased value which came with the reduced amounts available on the EU market. Recycling and reclamation are two different procedures requiring different equipment and investment. While recycling, a simple cleaning process (e.g. removal of moisture and oil by drying and filtering) is done by installers and contractors, while reclamation requires more technology and includes a final laboratory analysis to confirm the quality of the reclaimed product and is done by companies disposing of the necessary expertise and infrastructure. Concerning the quantities of recycled HFCs in the EU, there is basically no official data available because installers/ contractors are not required to report on the quantities they recycle and reuse. This is also a process very difficult to control.

5. Proposed derogations: The proposed derogation for “Maintenance and refilling of RACHP” (which also falls under the definition of HVACR: heating, ventilation, air conditioning and refrigeration) is very important, and it’s crucial that this provision is included in the final text. Repair and maintenance of existing system is an essential aspect of the circular economy and helps to reduce waste. However, as products have a long lifetime, a full time unlimited derogation is needed for Maintenance and refilling (and maintenance and refilling of fluoropolymers) to ensure that existing, well-functioning equipment are not wasted.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Electronics: corrosion protection coating for electronic devices.  Mainly conformal coating of assembled printed circuit boards. Industrial: Etching of silicon containing deposit for cleaning of plasma deposition reactors Industrial: Plasma resistant materials for plasma reactors Filtration: coating for improving filtration efficiency of filtration materials and/or for making those materials oleophobic

5. Proposed derogations: In §5.2 of the table presented in the proposal summary, a 6.5 year exemption is proposed for the treatment of textile used in filtration and separation.   Our plasma process is one of such applications the combined usage from our equipment is below 50 kg/year.

6. Missing uses: Corrosion protection coating for the electronic industry seemed not to be covered in the original assessment. Conformal ultra-thin (< 5µm) coatings are deposited on circuit printed boards assembly (PCBa) to protect those against corrosion and extend the life of the products and or make those products water resistant.  Water resistance is needed to use equipment in varying atmospheric conditions where condensation might occur. Such products include cell phones, hearing aids devices, automotive ECU, control boards of a wide variety of industrial equipment (pumps, frenquecy drives…) etc.   Non halogenated alternatives exist but do not meet all the properties of the halogenated coatings, mainly the alternatives are not oleophobic and less resistant to harsh (chemical and/or temperature) environments.  We therefore ask that an exemption is considered for application where oleophobicity and/or harsh environment resistance is mandatory. As the coatings are extremely thin the material usage is very low.  Our company and its customer uses less than 200 kg of PFAS monomer per year allowing for the treatment of millions of PCBa.  Fluorocarbon gas as etching agent for plasma reactor cleaning: One of the alternatives to the PFAS containing coatings is silicone-based coatings.  Those coatings have similar low surface energies as PFAS based coating enabling good water repellency properties.  Other alternatives could be organic based coating or inorganic (ceramic) based coatings.  However silicone based coatings have significant advantage over those two alternatives.  Silicone based coatings have better thermal and better chemical resistance than organic based coating.  Silicone coatings are flexible unlike inorganic coatings.   Thin conformal silicone coating are deposited by vacuum based technics (CVD, PE-CVD, ALD).  The coating is deposited on the parts to be treated as well as on the wall of the deposition reactor.  Therefore the reactor must be cleaned of this silicone based coating on a regular basis.  The cleaning is done by plasma etching.  As in semiconductor manufacturing silicone etching is done by fluorine containing gases (CF4, SF6, etc).  The use of fluorine containing gas allows for the transformation of Si containing deposit into gaseous product (SiF4) that are pumped down by the vacuum system and trapped by the scrubber system.  The current assessment mentions the use of fluorocarbon gas for the etching of silicone in semiconductor manufacturing but not for plasma reactor cleaning.  Other available cleaning technics are not able to replace plasma etching.  Mechanical cleaning and/or solvent cleaning are not viable as they do not allow for a very fine cleaning of the reactor.  Plasma cleaning allows for a cleaning down to the molecular level. They will always leave some residue in hard-to-reach places which will lead to contamination during the following coating process.  Furthermore, mechanical based cleaning (dry ice blasting, sanding etc) generates significant amounts of dust that are not easy to capture and might expose the operator as well.  Solvent cleaning is not a viable option as plasma deposited coatings are highly crosslinked and therefore non soluble. Taking all the above into consideration plasma etching is the safest option to clean the reactor as all will take place in a closed environment (vacuum chamber) with all exhaust gases treated accordingly preventing release in the environment.   The combined usage of PFAS gas for cleaning our equipment as well as the equipment sold to our customers is less than 1 ton/year worldwide. Compared to other coating technologies like parylene, dip- and spray coatings that also need PFAS containing chemistry for applications where oleophobicity is necessary, plasma enhanced nanocoatings consume a fraction of the chemistry for similar performance. So as the world wide usage for this application is very low and allows significant reduction of PFAS used for coating applications, we recommend an  exemption to use PFAS gas for cleaning of plasma reactor used for the deposition of Si containing coatings. PFAS polymers as plasma resistant materials: Plasma reactors are used in a wide range of applications from cleaning of surface to deposition of coatings.  Sectors range from medical to defense.  Plasma treatments cover a wide range of application thanks to the unique properties of the plasma state which is an extremely reactive media even at low temperature.  Such reactive media require specific materials to withstand the reactivity of plasma.  PFAS polymers are part of those materials.  Because of their low dielectric constant,  good temperature resistance and good chemical resistance PFAS polymers are the only polymeric materials that can resist long plasma exposure as well as plasma cleaning cycles.  Some examples of PFAS polymer use in plasma reactor are tubing for cooling systems, flexible electrical insulation.  Six alternative materials, meeting the electrical, thermal, outgasing… properties, have been identified and tested for plasma resistance.  Mass loss of those materials upon plasma exposure was studied for up to 16h (data available in attachment).  PTFE presented no mass loss, the mass loss of the alternative materials ranged from 14% to 22%.  Mass loss needs to be negligible otherwise the etched materials will contaminate the plasma and negatively impact the treatment quality. We therefore also request an exception for the use of PFAS polymer in the construction/maintenance of plasma reactors.

6. Missing uses: We are active in the field of pressure gas equipment. We use PFAS-containing materials in seals, diaphragms and O-rings for pressure regulators and valves. Fluoropolymers are primarily used here. These are high-performance plastics that are characterized by particularly high resistance against many gases for the electronical and medical industry (e.g. semi-conductors, hospitals, research laboratories). These include above all the widely used fluoroplastic PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene, also known as "Teflon") or FKM ("fluororubber"). PFAS-containing materials in our products contribute significantly to prevention of leakages, process and plant safety, protection of the user, guarantee of tightness. Some of the fluoropolymers we use in pressure regulators and valves have been scientifically evaluated as "polymers of low concern" (PTFE, ETFE, FEP, PFA, PVDF and VDF-co-HFP). They have been proven to be chemically stable, non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water soluble and non-mobile. For these reasons, the fluoropolymers are also approved, for example, as materials for food contact or in medical technology.  We therefore call for the general exemption of fluoropolymers, which (incidentally also according to the OECD definition) are generally considered "polymers of low concern", from the PFAS restriction project. In addition, substances such as monomers and processing aids that are necessary for fluoropolymer manufacture and production should be exempted from the ban, provided that safe use is ensured. This is also envisaged by the study of the British Health and Safety Executive (HSE). Therefore, in general, groups with low risk (e.g fluoro elastomers, fluoropolymers assessed as "polymers of low concern") or uses without relevant risk (e.g. uses in closed systems) should be exempted.  In this context, we would like to point out that there are currently no alternatives to the use of materials classified as "polymers of low concern" in our area that have similar resistance (or other specific properties to be mentioned here) over a comparable period of time. These are of enormous importance especially in the environment of our products, because here it is about the protection of the workers or the plant, potentially explosive area over a long period of time. A ban on these PFAS substances would mean that at the present time we would not be able to use the seals / O-rings and membranes in our products that comply with the applicable legal and regulatory provisions and also do not have the necessary approvals and certificates. The consequence would be nothing other than a sales stop and a dramatic drop in turnover of about 90 percent. Because without sealings and membranes, our pressure regulators and valves simply do not work. In order to avoid such existence-threatening damage not only for us, but for an entire key industry that enables laboratories, hospitals and production plants to use the pressure gase equipment for their daily work. Fluoropolymers such as PTFE in the context of pressure gas equipment must therefore be excluded from PFAS regulation.

To allow all sectors and companies a legally secure assessment of their affectedness, the scope of the restriction must be communicated in a clear and transparent manner. A list of relevant substances containing IUPAC names and CAS numbers is required for the analysis of affectedness along global supply chains.  The establishment of a comprehensive information obligation for "intentionally added" PFAS for at least five years prior to a comprehensive PFAS restriction represents, from our view, a suitable approach to control PFAS emissions and to prepare a more targeted regulation. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: We are a downstream user of fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers and to our best knowledge all polymers relevant to our activities meet the OECD-criteria of “Polymers of low concern.” Tests performed by an external accredited laboratory using LC-MS showed, for engineered plastics like Ethene-1,1,2,2-tetrafluoro-homopolymer (PTFE) or Tetrafluoroethylene-propylene copolymer (TFE/P) that no measurable low-molecular PFAS was detected with a detection limit of 10 ppb (10 μg/kg). In general, we observe that all manufacturers of fluoropolymers have changed their manufacturing processes to become fluorosurfactant-free or are in the process to do so. We expect that over the short to medium term test results of all fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers will show no detected measurable low-molecular PFAS. As it is common sense that fluoroelastomers are regarded as persistent we assume that these do not pose a risk for human health and for the environment during their lifecycle. Additionally, during use products are installed leading to no exposure to people as well as to the environment. Our view is substantially supported by a detailed comprehensive lifecycle assessment executed by Gujarat Fluorochemicals GmbH in collaboration with Ramboll we are referring to as this assessment proves that fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers are safe! We fully support this study that has already been sent to the competent authorities and represents, to our best knowledge, a contribution of Gujarat Fluorochemicals GmbH to this internet consultation. Unfortunately, we are not able to provide the original report on this assessment as we have no access to it but expect the results will be published in a scientific journal over the short term.  Unfortunately, today there is no established system for industrial scale recovery of materials like fluoroelastomers and fluoropolymers. It’s our opinion that an open consortium of industrial and professional stakeholders would be the most meaningful setup to materialize recycling systems as mentioned above. Today incineration and landfilling represent the main ways to treat waste of products made of fluoroelastomers and fluoropolymers. As shown above our products made of fluoroelastomers and fluoropolymers don’t pose a risk to human health and for the environment this is assumed to be valid also for landfilling. Regarding incineration we would like to refer to a study by Conversio in 2022 (German based consultant) prepared for Pro-K (Fluoropolymer Downstream User Association) and Gujarat Fluorochemicals GmbH. This study has shown that at its end-of-life approximately 85% of all fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers end up in waste-to-energy recovery incinerators. We regard these activities as part of our activities for sustainability as well as to contribute to enhance resource efficiency.
