To allow all sectors and companies a legally secure assessment of their affectedness, the scope of the restriction must be communicated in a clear and transparent manner. A list of relevant substances containing IUPAC names and CAS numbers is required for the analysis of affectedness along global supply chains.  The establishment of a comprehensive information obligation for "intentionally added" PFAS for at least five years prior to a comprehensive PFAS restriction represents, from our view, a suitable approach to control PFAS emissions and to prepare a more targeted regulation. This would also enable companies and authorities to define reasonable targeted risk minimization measures.   The current scope of this proposal is inappropriate and forces us and many others to “guess” how they and their customers are affected. To our best knowledge and available information, the sectors and uses according to Table 9 of the Annex XV restriction report mentioned below concern the following activities:  Manufacturing • Sector as a whole • Manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance of equipment for production of PFAS require seals at least partially consisting of PFAS.  TULAC (textiles, upholstery, leather, apparel, and carpets) • Manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance of equipment for production of textiles, upholstery, leather, apparel, and carpets in general require seals at least partially consisting of PFAS.  Food contact materials and packaging • Industrial food and feed production • Manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance of equipment for production of food and feed assembly, processing and filling in general require seals at least partially consisting of PFAS. • Unfortunately, equipment for processing and packaging of food and feed has not appropriately been considered in the Annex XV report! The harsh conditions of cleaning the equipment as well as assuring hygienic conditions require the use of fluoroelastomers and fluoropolymers due to their unique chemical resistance. Although, we have mentioned the segments and uses as missing as listed below twice (during our feedback to the call for evidence as well as during the 2nd stakeholder consultation) undeniable relevant sectors using PFAS as listed below are still missing:  • Machine manufacturing • Equipment manufacturing • Aerospace • Chemical production • Pharma manufacturing • Agriculture equipment • Processing equipment • Defense • Fluid Power • Machine tools • Marine  • Presses • Robotics • Sanitation • Trains • Ships  Please note the list above is “only” about missing sectors. Concerning the uses there are likely more drastically important aspects missing, due to the less than properly defined “uses” in the scope! For these reasons we urgently claim for a time-unlimited exemption of fluoroelastomers and of fluoropolymers including all raw materials, specifically monomers and processing aids needed for manufacturing. In addition to this we urgently claim for the establishment of a comprehensive information obligation for "Intentionally added" PFAS of at least five years prior to a comprehensive PFAS restriction. From our view this represents the only suitable approach to control PFAS emissions and to prepare for a more targeted regulation. This would also enable companies and authorities to define reasonable targeted risk minimization measures.  Alternatives for fluoroelastomers and fluoropolymers do not exist! Consequences of a total ban of fluoroelastomers and fluoropolymers for uses of manufacturing of seals, bearings and many other products would be dramatic. This ban will greatly affect the standard and quality of living. Future opportunities of the entire society will be lost! A restriction or even ban of fluoroelastomers and fluoropolymers as irreplaceable materials would catapult us all back into the Middle Ages!

10. Analytical methods: Today only around 100 of the more than 4.700 PFAS Substances may be investigated. Meaning the content of around 98% of the known PFAS including all fluoroelastomers and fluoropolymers cannot be investigated at all! In general reference materials and standards are difficult to achieve and, in many cases, not available. Additionally, from the perspective of an analytical laboratory the differentiation of PFAS molecules of the same molecular weight but with different molecular structure is not possible leading to significant uncertainty regarding traceability, reproducibility, and reliability of measured values. In practice per material/product several different analytical measurements each focusing on a specific group of PFAS are performed leading to multiple detection of the same substance and massively higher values as really contained in the specimen tested. It is understood that alone these facts prove that the proposed broad restriction is not appropriate and breaching a great number of principles in accordance with a constitutional state as it is not clear and controllable by companies and authorities!  To date, there are no standardized analytical methods for PFAS existing at all. To detect and analyze the few PFAS possible to investigate requires massive efforts. Tests of different laboratories, lead to different results, as many laboratories are following their own standards for PFAS-measurements, as well as for interpretation of the results obtained! It is understood that these circumstances lead to test reports of different analytical laboratories to be not comparable and contain significantly different to contradicting results! Missing standardized analytical methods are hindering companies from controlling and ensuring their actions are compliant. In addition, this humble stance makes it impossible for authorities to enforce this proposed restriction. From our view, the facts mentioned above represent additional evidence that the proposed PFAS restriction is not appropriate and breaches several principles of a constitutional state because it is not clear or controllable by companies and authorities.  The concentration limits proposed in the Annex XV restriction report are nothing more than unrealistic! These limits are extremely low and impossible to control in a pragmatic manner (on our own) leading to significant uncertainty regarding traceability, reproducibility, and reliability of measured values. Analytical laboratories are forced to take massive efforts in a “Mission Impossible” to avoid contamination, as well as, to achieve and maintain framework conditions for obtaining traceability, reproducibility, and reliability of results. We are greatly annoyed about the simple, unacceptable situation hindering us to control whether our actions are compliant, and about this apparent “humble stance” taking authorities any chance to enforce this proposed restriction. It’s our view the facts presented above provide additional evidence that the proposed PFAS restriction is not appropriate and breaches several principles of a constitutional state because it is not clear or controllable by companies and authorities.

8. Other identified uses: We submit this supplemental information and comments regarding the Annex XV Restriction Report Proposal for a Restriction and the Annex to the Annex XV Restriction Report.  We are a leading global service company in the oil and gas industry. We present the following information to assist in completing the picture of the various applications of solid fluoropolymers in the specific area of oilfield services in the oil and gas development arena (see pp. 498-508, Annex E) for consideration by ECHA, in support of the proposed 12-year derogation for fluoropolymer applications in the petroleum industry.  We also support the need for additional exemptions for other specialty applications, specifically. An indefinite exemption is requested for permanent downhole installations in oil and gas wells as identified in Attachment 1: 1. Downhole Isolation Packers – Downhole production strings 2. Bonded Well Isolation Elements – Expandable Liner Hangers used for downhole isolation in oil and gas production 3. Most equipment for deepwater high pressure/high temperature applications; Packer Elements – Molded seals and engineered sealing configurations 4. Most downhole tools including safety values and most other isolation tools – Primary seals for non-elastomeric sealing systems, spring energized engineered seals and backup support components for elastomeric systems in downhole tools 5. Safety valves – Primary seals for non-elastomeric sealing systems including for the flapper which is a primary barrier for well integrity 6. Production packers, sand control – Downhole pressure and fluid isolation equipment Upstream oil and gas development takes place in extreme conditions not unlike those found in refineries and petrochemical plants, including high temperature, high pressure environments that can also be either acidic or caustic.  Carbon capture and storage, and geothermal wells present similar technical challenges. To responsibly operate in these challenging environments, materials have been developed and selected to withstand these conditions while meeting the required performance criteria of the component and/or piece of equipment.  As identified in the American Petroleum Institute’s (API) submittal and IOGP’s submittal, these solid fluoropolymer materials are incorporated in many of the design specifications of equipment, piping and tools used in the energy industry. Data A summary on the use of solid fluoropolymers in the equipment, piping, and tools manufactured and used by the oilfield services sector of the energy industry is provided in Attachment 1. At this time, there are no alternatives commercially available that would meet the design specifications of the equipment (chemically and thermally stable with extreme temperatures and aggressive environments). While it may be possible to find alternatives to the use of solid fluoropolymers in some applications, this will require significant research and development and could potentially require more than the 12-year derogation period.  With the specific applications listed above and shown in Attachment 1, industry does not have viable replacement materials currently available in the marketplace and development of new materials, testing and refinement, setting performance specifications, and testing against those specifications will likely not be possible.   Economics The upstream oil and gas development sector of the petroleum and mining industry in the EU and EEA accounts for approximately 6.4 billion Euros/year in capital expenditures; the North Sea (UK) is an additional 23.2 billion Euros/year, according to Rystad Energy research.  This sector employs approximately 26,000 people in the EU and there is potential for this sector to be disrupted without the necessary tools and components for new exploration and well construction.  This could result in lower energy production and higher costs leading to energy supply instability within the EU.  Summary The oilfield services sector of the mining and petroleum industry urges ECHA and its member countries to retain the proposed 12-year derogation period for the use of solid fluoropolymers in the petroleum and mining industry.  This derogation period will allow research and development along with the testing and field-trial evaluation of non-fluoropolymers and other potential sustainable substitution materials.  Additionally, we request that the future implementation of the restriction includes a review period, well in advance of the expiration of the 12-year derogation period, to assess the availability of alternatives and the need for future extensions of this derogation period. Finally, we hereby request an indefinite exemption for specific applications that require permanent downhole installation as outlined above. General Comments: -

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Not all members of the PFAS family are harmful. In particular, fluoropolymers’ electronic structure, arising from their stable carbon-fluorine covalent bonding, reflects the unique interactions responsible for their distinct composition and set of properties that make them irreplaceable for industrial applications (Teng, 2012) and safe for humans and the environment (Henry et al., 2018). Fluoropolymers not being on any restriction list are especially, among others: - Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) - Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) - Fluorinated ethylene propylene (FEP) - Perfluoroalkoxypolymer (PFА) - Perfluoropolyethers (PFPEs) Besides its outstanding resistances, the uniqueness of PTFE relies on its non-toxic and safe use, as to break down into a different substance, the compound would have to be exposed to temperatures above 440 °C (824 °F). Moreover, PTFE can be safely used under a continuous temperature at or below 260 °C (500 °F), as stated by Teng (2012). In addition, PTFE is practically insoluble in water and is non-bioavailable, as evidenced by a wide range of toxicology studies including acute and sub chronic toxicity, irritation, sensitization, cytotoxicity, genotoxicity, haemolysis, and thrombogenicity (Henry et al., 2018). Table 3 as attached in Sector 4 depicts a more in-depth description of PTFE's features compared with PFOA as an example for hazardous PFAS compounds.  Taking PTFE's distinguished characteristics and safety profile into account, there is no current one-to-one substitute for this chemical that could be implemented for critical industrial applications such as valves, sampling units, and other piping accessories. The safeness and irreplaceable use of PTFE are strongly corroborated by science and the industry, with both the FDA and the European Food Safety Authority reinforcing the safety and reliability of this compound throughout their manufacturing life cycle (PlasticsEurope, 2021). It is undeniable that using this compound is more beneficial than harmful to human health and the environment, providing that the material is manufactured and used according to the industrial guidance established by regulatory bodies (Teng, 2012). The use of less advanced or capable materials poses the risk of environmental pollution on a larger scale and with more risky chemicals involved in the case of failure of piping accessories (e.g., plug valves, sampling systems, strainers, gaskets). Teng (2012)  [https://www.mdpi.com/2076-3417/2/2/496] Henry et al., (2018)  [https://doi.org/10.1002/ieam.4035] PlasticsEurope (2021) [https://fluoropolymers.plasticseurope.org/application/files/6216/3178/0517/Fluoropolymers_Safe_Hand_EN__June_2021.pdf]  Fluoropolymers enable modern life and help achieve important societal goals such as renewable energy or more sustainable transportation. Therefore, there is a criticality of fluoropolymers for achieving the EU Green Deal.  Beyond enabling modern life, these innovative technologies promote and secure European competitiveness and allow for continued investment in jobs and skills. Fluoropolymers also help enable the EU Hydrogen Strategy, which envisages a drastic expansion of hydrogen production and infrastructure, and sets a 13-20% target for clean ‘green’ hydrogen in the energy mix by 2050.  The different aspects of usage in different industries are not holistically addressed. The focus is too much narrowed down to only some aspects of the direct usage of PFAS, especially on those substance classes which are posing a danger. Hereby the Annex XV Restriction Report neglects the other important usage of products, items and applications which are including non-dangerous PFAS related components, e.g., PTFE, and other chemicals of low concern. As an example, in chapter 1.3.2.15. Petroleum and mining, there is no hint to the applications of industrial valves which are widely used inside the industry. There is no substitute available today, even after almost 20 years of research for substances which combine those unique properties such as PTFE has. A blank ban of all PFAS would lead to complete decommissioning of all mining and petroleum industry activities, because the plants and installation could not be operational anymore (no valves, no operation).

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The OECD considers FPs as chemicals of low concern, mainly due to the following reasons, as they - do not degrade into smaller (dangerous) PFAS in the environment;  - are not mobile (large molecules of > 1000 Dalton size); - are not bio-accumulative (molecules are too big to penetrate biological cells); - are not toxic; - are inert; and - are not soluble in water or other liquids. The certification of FPs for the use in food and beverage (e.g., FDA) and medical applications confirm these facts. Our products use FPs coming from sources/producers which are monitoring the emissions of PFAS in a way that the emission levels are kept. Furthermore, production processes are used where the emission creating conditions are actively avoided by an intelligent process monitoring. During the production of our products and depending on the type and design, several fractions of FP side products are occurring. Namely lumps, turnings or shavings of FPs (e.g., from PTFE, PFA, FEP, TFM, etc.) can be expected. Those materials are pure and clean by nature. Due to a strict production planning, there is no cross contamination between the different grades.  Our products can be refurbished, that means especially the plug valves are taken back into the factory in the case of malfunction or at the end of lifetime. They are then stripped to address the damages.  As every product has a unique serial number, we can trace back to the smallest details of the assembly, hence we know exactly which parts of which material are used. A decision is then taken whether the plug valve can be refurbished and sent back to the client, or needs to be scrapped. In both cases, the contained FP parts can be 98 % - 100 % retrieved from the valve body and collected separately from the metal. As different FPs are in use, the separation also here includes a strict split of the used FP parts in their corresponding fractions. The different grades of FPs allow for different ways forward after the separation process.   For both sourcing routes (production of a new plug valve etc., or in the refurbishing process), the following recycling methods can be applied. In the case of pure virgin PTFE, this material can be re-used in the production of different PTFE products, where a certain amount of recycling PTFE is tolerable. Then, no release to the environment is happening. Thermo-fluoropolymer residuals can also be recycled and reused in e.g., ram extrusion processes.  For grades with fillers, please refer to the statements under Question 3.  Fluoropolymers are a valuable resource which can be sold to appropriate producers of FP products. The recycling involves processes such as cleaning, drying, shearing, grinding, milling, and separation steps. A recycling quota of > 99 % can be achieved.  Therefore, fluoropolymers should not fall under the proposed restriction´s scope, as the safety of FPs contained in our products is guaranteed over the entire lifecycle of our product. Hence, FPs should be fully exempt for industrial applications.  As a side note, the scrap metal parts are also collected and enter the recycling process for metals at a level of very close to 100 %.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: As outlined in Question 2, there is a decent stripping, separation and collection process in place already today. Both for the metal parts as well for the FP parts of our products. The possible routes for recycling of some of the FP grades have been outlined in Question 2 as well. In case there is no direct recycling use of FPs, there are too more options for dealing with the residuals; namely thermal treatment, or landfill.  Producers of PFAS have already set up facilities such as thermal oxidizers to incinerate the FPs in a controlled way. The Fps are completely decomposed and those facilities then produce CaF2 as a product, which can be used as a fluor source for other chemical processes. In the case of landfill, it must be pointed out, that there is no risk of fluoropolymers in leachate since fluoropolymers are inert, non-toxic, and non-mobile.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: This is not applicable for AZ-Armaturen GmbH. We are sourcing from producers which products are compliant with the emission limits of their semi-finished and finished products. Our processing steps are neither changing the material properties in this respect or release PFAS emissions.

5. Proposed derogations: The unique combination of properties of the main industrially used PFAS materials (38 out of 5.000 to 10.000, with PTFE being the most prominent of this 38 materials) make them unreplaceable for the industrial use in industrial valves, strainers, sealings, and alike.  For the time being, and after almost 20 years of research of serious research compagnies, it hasn’t led to any suitable alternative, which could compete with those group of 38. A calculation can be drawn up to determine the amount of PFAS related products which are possibly released to the environment during the usage phase. A conservation assumption (zero recycling rate) based on this calculation reveals, that the possible emissions of PFAS related product in terms of  polymeric PFASs is less than 1 % compared to the entire polymeric PFAS emissions (ca. 100 t/a related to ca. 10.000 t/a),  total PFASs is less than 0,6 % compared to the entire PFAS emissions (ca. 100 t/a related to ca. 54.600 t/a); based on the emission figures to be found in Table 1 of the ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT. All details of the calculation basis can be found in Table 2 in Section 5. Looking on this low emission potential, the potential damage to the environment due to leakages of non-safe piping accessories and/or the impact to the European industry by a blank ban, fluoropolymers should not fall under the scope of the proposed restriction, i.e., they should be fully exempt for industrial applications.

6. Missing uses: While scientific research findings suggest that some fluoropolymers pose a threat to human health, other compounds of the family of molecules are supporting human projects of making our planet a better and healthier place, e.g., in the field of green energy, especially hydrogen-based concepts and the like. PTFE and related substances are proven reliable compounds which are present in a myriad of products in modern times The criticality of fluoropolymers for achieving EU Green Deal cannot be underestimated. Not only for the applications which are already considered, e.g., membranes and the like, but also on a lerger and more basic industrial scale. A prime example are here again (plug) valves, sealings, and other piping accessories. The use of PTFE or related materials parts in those applications is without an alternative possibility. For device manufacturers, the regulatory teams must review previous bans on essential use chemicals and weigh risks versus benefits related to manufacturing industrial appliances with safeness and quality for both human health and the environment. It is also vital to consider the costs to develop new compounds while ensuring the quality and properties are comparable to PTFE and other related materials (PFA, TFM, FEP, etc.).  Scientific studies have historically been proven to be the best path for safety and overall human benefit. The same will remain for certain fluoropolymers like PTFE. But, for the time being, even after decades of research, no new materials with better environmental balance and same or similar combination of properties have been discovered.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Not applicable for AZ-Armaturen case.

8. Other identified uses: The Table 1 and Table 4 in Sector 4 and 5 give an overview on the different industrial fields where piping accessories are in use, plus the consequences on a hole if PFAS related substances are banned completely. In case there are derogations, it will only shift the problem by a certain time. In particular, it is then more likely that industrial plants and operations are moving out of the EU, utilizing the derogation time frame to make the move and keeping operations on until the alternative production site is ready. As already stated, several times in this concern paper, there hasn’t been an alternative material found after decades of research, and business deciders will not take chances and just wait and hope. From Table 1, some industrial sectors should be addressed with a special focus as we feel that several applications are not addressed properly. There is a huge difference between gas, liquids or solids being involved, or mixtures thereof. The variety of (sub) applications in the different industries require a more in-depth analysis, mainly because the different media which need to be considered do not allow a blank approach. This is particular valid for the situation in the following industries:  mining  metals production  food & beverages  drinking water  sewage  nuclear  power generation (& distribution, e.g., distance steam heating systems)  renewable energies  chemical industry where the use of PTFE and related are set as industrial standard.   A complete ban is economically and socially a very difficult situation for the entire industrial environment. As it stands now, manufacturers and suppliers have indicated that it could take a relatively long time (several years to several decades) to transition towards using alternatives that can achieve the same level of performance. Continued R&D increases the chance that alternatives for the relevant applications will be identified. However, it must be pointed out, that even after two decades of intensive research, no appropriate alternatives could be found for the PFAS use in industrial applications in the sector of piping accessories. Furthermore, given the relatively large (up to hundreds or thousands) number of individual products supplied in this sector, all with different specific formulations, this would be a complex undertaking needing sufficient time. Additionally, the is a multiverse of applications with very different process conditions in terms of pressure, media, temperature (level, constant, fluctuating), and chemistry. This is strong evidence in terms of exempt those specific applications and the required PFAS related materials from the ban.  Loss of functionality of products in this sector could have substantial economic implications, including shorter operational lifetime of components, increased frequency and costs of maintenance (and by that also more waste generation of those substitution materials!), and increased operational downtimes (with the effect of increased product prices). The costs of substitution are likely to be borne in full (in the form of reduced producer surplus/profits) by the firms active in the sector. Additionally, product reformulation costs can range from tens of thousands of euros to millions of euros for any single formulation. Product reformulation will also imply costs relating to quality assurance. The market will hardly be able to cater for this, and the cost for final products to the consumer, industrial and hybrid markets will increase dramatically. A recession would be in evadable.  AZ-Armaturen has no direct possibility for research on specific materials. Insomuch we as other piping accessories supplier are dependent on the research of the PFAS manufacturers.  The only indirect way for searching for alternatives is by applying different materials in the industrial applications. Due to the criticality of the applications, plants will not be willing to take those risks, both for loss of production, but moreover also due to the possible environmental implications in case of a test failure and setting free harmful substances.  A blank ban would have severe consequences for AZ-Armaturen GmbH and its subsidiaries in Europe and worldwide.  For the time being there are no substitute substance available in the market, unifying the unique combination of properties, which those PFAS related substance have, which are used by AZ.  The effect is not only on AZ, but also on the competitors active in the piping accessories market, as those use the same set of materials. The social-economic consequences of a blank ban effect not only AZ-Armaturen GmbH as a single company. One needs to take into consideration that one step up and one step down the value adding chain is also affected.  If AZ is not buying anymore due to stop of business, the supplier of AZ will also be affected. Depending on the size, the structure and the turnover share of AZ for this supplier the consequences may reach from little (nothing) to severe (bankrupt). Also here, some add-on effects might happen, if several companies in the piping accessories business source from the same supplier. A similar consideration must be drawn up for the clients of AZ. If AZ is not delivering the process components which are critical for the operation of a plant, the plant/production must be stopped. The add-on effect as outlined for the supplier side is also applicable here, even on a bigger scale as there are more clients (both for AZ and competition) than suppliers. A detailed consideration of the effect on employment and turnover can be found in Table 4 in Sector 5.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: All materials of the PFAS sub-groups which are used by AZ-Armaturen (PTFE, PFA, TFM, FEP, etc.) do not have any degrading potential in the environment under standard environmental conditions.

10. Analytical methods: not applicable

6. Missing uses: e and f) PFPE- and PTFE-based lubricants are considered to be physically and chemically very stable, durable, non-flammable, extremely inert, resistant to radiation and with high electrical resistance .   Due to these outstanding properties, they are specifically used for the following critical applications where other lubricants cannot be performant. All the following applications require the best possible compatibility between part material and lubricant: • High temperature applications: Fluoropolymers are used to lubricate the rolling bearings of corrugating machines or the vulcanising rubber operations to manufacture tyres, where high temperatures and humidity prevail at the same time, or the bearings in ovens for heat treatment of plastic films. Similarly, the bearings in automated furnaces are lubricated with food-grade PFPE-based lubricants.  • Contact with reactive, corrosive or explosive liquids and gases: PFPE is used as sealing and working fluids in vacuum pumps exposed to aggressive environments (chemical and thermal). • Low outgassing applications: in vacuum applications, optical instruments and light housings where lubricant condensation must be minimised, PFPE and PTFE-based lubricants are sometimes the only choice.  • Power generation: In nuclear power plants, PFPE-based lubricants are used as a bearing lubricant for pumps operating in an area where they are exposed to radiation. Radiation quickly degrades ordinary lubricants, but PFPE-based lubricants function for long periods without significant degradation. • Lifetime lubrication in automotive and machinery: PTFE cannot easily be replaced by another solid lubricant without impairing functionality, including noise reduction. Apart from the inertness of PTFE, this is mainly due to its compatibility with plastics/elastomers and its lubricating properties under certain loads and conditions. These lifetime lubrications must cope with a huge range of temperatures from below freezing in the winters to the heat of the summer or when the engine is running (from -60°C to +250°C). • Valves: PTFE offers optimum lubrication, for example in the chemical industry (oxygen valves), without dissolving or chemically reacting under harsh chemical conditions. • Machinery for emergency cases: PFPE- and PTFE-based lubricants are also used for emergency applications when machinery needs to start quickly after years of stoppage (for example: fire doors that need to close, emergency power generators, gear boxes...).  Additionally, due to their excellent oxidation stability and suppression of deposits, PFPE- and PTFE-based lubricants are used in general industrial applications, for example for heavily loaded bearings and pivots. They reduce the number of lubricants changes and thus reduce the volumes of lubricants used.  Eventually, PTFE and PFPE based lubricants are by far more expensive than conventional lubricants and therefore are used only when absolutely necessary.   g) At the current stage of our knowledge, we do not have alternatives that meet the same level of performance of PFPE and PTFE-based lubricants. Potential options available, such as silicones or esters, make our customers redesign their product. Based on the experience of our members and on our customers feedback, we have identified several major drawbacks for the alternatives: • Due to certain toxicological properties and/or stability issues, alternatives cannot be used for certain applications such as food production, medical technology; • Decompose rapidly in aggressive chemical environments; • Cannot be used due to extreme temperatures (heat) because of the decomposition and the volatility of the alternatives; • Increase risks for the health and the environment because of their hazardousness (toxicity, flammability, etc.); • Restrict the safe functioning of equipment because of their physical and chemical properties (vapour pressure, hydrophilicity). For non-metallic polymeric materials, some cause shrinking in parts (PAO) and some cause swelling in parts (Esters), which is a serious safety concern; Or other issues such as spreading and migrating (Silicones). • Lifetime lubrication would become difficult with any alternative; • Result in more dangerous and/or costly maintenance work. There is going to be more frequent relubrication intervals, many more touch points and exposure points for workers and shortened lifetime of parts. Besides, these other options would lead to higher lubricants consumptions and reduce component lifetime due to the shorten lifetime of these alternatives. Thus, much less environmentally friendly, jeopardizing the objectives of the Green Deal.

Org. name: Ministry of Rhineland-Palatinate for Climate Action, Environment, Energy and Mobility
Combined Comments:
"- 9213" "On February 7, 2023, the European Chemicals Agency ECHA published the restriction proposal for the entire group of PFAS substances. In March 2023, a six-month public consultation was launched. All additional necessary information must be provided by all relevant stakeholders during this consultation. Rhineland-Palatinate, as a state with significant industrial sites, agricultural areas, and nature reserves, sees the PFAS restriction proposal as an important measure to counteract new damage cases and the increasing ubiquitous spread of PFAS. The widespread use of PFAS compounds leads to the difficult removal and remediation of PFAS-contaminated soil and groundwater. To date, there are few efficient and cost-effective remediation technologies. Conventional remediation methods are significantly less effective in treating PFAS. Therefore, a high cost is to be expected. As a result, in Rhineland-Palatinate, almost exclusively remediation measures are taken in the form of securing through surface sealing and the installation of the material in security structures to prevent further spread into bodies of water and groundwater. 

Relevant damage cases and sources of contamination for Rhineland-Palatinate:
In 2008, in Rhineland-Palatinate, there was a large damage case due to the use of PFOS-containing fire-fighting foams, which subsequently led to the impairment of a water supply area.
Nationally, many PFAS damage cases in soil and groundwater are primarily related to the use of fluorinated foam extinguishing agents in firefighting operations and exercises, as well as the use of PFAS-containing auxiliaries in industrial production, for example in electroplating and textile finishing plants.
In the neighboring state of North Rhine-Westphalia, the (illegal) application of contaminated organic waste mixtures and so-called "soil conditioners" on agriculturally used areas in the Hochsauerland was identified as a significant pathway for exceptionally high contamination with Perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and Perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) in the Ruhr in 2006.
Another significant source of contamination is certain industries that use PFAS substances to produce products.
Large-scale as well as small-scale PFAS environmental entries of various causes have consequences, which directly impact drinking water supply and agricultural production.
Water suppliers incur considerable costs for water treatment, resulting in an increase in water fees, and farmers may no longer be able to market products or have to change production methods.
In the case of large-scale contaminations, there are also problems with designating building areas and handling contaminated earthmoving. This also affects the provision of landfill capacity, which is still an unresolved task in many places.
In the case of large-scale contaminations, remediation measures are often only partially possible due to the principle of proportionality, with the focus being on damage management.
Significant costs can be incurred, for example, for urgently needed investigation and research projects that serve preventive consumer protection or regional development "despite the damage."

Measures by Rhineland-Palatinate:
As early as 2009, all relevant industries were approached and encouraged to use harmless PFAS substitutes in their production in the future.
The Rhineland-Palatinate municipalities responsible for wastewater disposal were informed and encouraged to investigate their sewage sludge, as a relatively high proportion is still used in agriculture.
Due to a EU-wide ban since June 27, 2011, the use of fire-fighting foams with PFOS, a special group of PFAS, is no longer permitted. This was followed by a ban on the use of PFOS-containing fire-fighting foams for training purposes by the Rhineland-Palatinate Ministry of the Interior in 2009.
In addition to the above, the state is taking further measures to address environmental pollution: In the event of critical damage cases, the first priority is to exclude any risk to humans through precautionary measures. Possible measures include restrictions on the consumption of fish from affected waters, refraining from watering gardens from heavily contaminated surface waters, and prohibiting the application of contaminated sewage sludge on agricultural land.

PFAS Strategy in Rhineland-Palatinate
In 2014, a PFAS strategy was developed in Rhineland-Palatinate, which has since served as a basis for the enforcement authorities to:
- investigate water and soil with the aim of identifying baseline loads and pollution hotspots
- carry out evaluations and assessments of the causes and sources of harmful PFAS contamination
- implement specific procedures from exploration to remediation
- take acute, precautionary, and securing measures

Successes in Rhineland-Palatinate and nationwide:
The latest fire-fighting foam is free of PFAS. Evaluations of the federal environmental sample bank show that the contamination of young adults with certain PFAS has decreased significantly in recent decades. Since 2021, in the context of a federal soil investigation program, soil samples have been taken from agricultural areas (14 arable land and 10 grassland sites from Rhineland-Palatinate) on behalf of the Federal Environment Agency (UBA) to determine PFAS background values. In addition, within the framework of the periodic sampling of the 16 long-term soil observation areas in the Rhineland-Palatinate forests, PFAS background values of forest soils are determined. These are intended to supplement existing event-related investigations at potential pollution hotspots and suspect areas.

According to the Rhineland-Palatinate government, it is important that all additional necessary information is provided by all relevant stakeholders during this consultation. Rhineland-Palatinate is of the opinion that the restriction procedure under REACH for the entire group of PFAS, for which the competent authorities from Germany, the Netherlands, Denmark, Sweden, and Norway have prepared a dossier and submitted it to the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA), provides a great opportunity to drastically reduce the ever-increasing emissions of this group of substances. This is demonstrated by the hard-won successes already achieved at a regional level. Further action is also needed to take into account new findings regarding the health effects of these substances or other PFAS substances, and to improve consumer and environmental health protection.

Background information (for internal use only):
Soil protection/Water protection
PFAS compounds can be detected in soils and waters in Rhineland-Palatinate due to their durable properties and wide range of applications. Extensive contamination has not yet been identified. Extensive PFAS contamination has predominantly been detected in the vicinity of airports, especially in the area of fire extinguishing training grounds due to the use of fluorinated fire-fighting foams in the past. Other possible sources of contamination include production facilities in the metal and paper industry or special chemical industry. Due to the extensive application of PFAS and experience from other federal states, ubiquitous spread is expected. Ongoing monitoring programs, such as the nationwide soil investigation program of the Federal Environment Agency (UBA) to determine PFAS background values on agricultural land or the periodic sampling of the long-term soil observation areas in the Rhineland-Palatinate forests, will provide an initial overview of PFAS background values in Rhineland-Palatinate. The removal or disposal of PFAS-contaminated soil materials can currently only be realized by incineration at high temperatures in the Netherlands, as there are no incineration or landfill capacities for PFAS-containing soil materials in Rhineland-Palatinate. In addition, it should be noted that with regard to an informative assessment of PFAS-containing soil materials, only seven test values will be available to the soil protection authorities from August 2023, when the amended BBodSchV comes into force, for a substance group of thousands of individual compounds. In addition, remediation target values are currently lacking, which significantly complicates the enforcement of remediations against obligors. Against the background of the current situation or problem areas presented, the soil protection division appreciatively welcomes a restriction of the entire PFAS substance group.

Chemical safety
On February 7, 2023, the European Chemicals Agency ECHA published the restriction proposal for the entire group of PFAS. Exception rules are provided. The Federal Environment Agency (FEA) has emphasized the restriction of PFAS. The challenge is to identify uses that require an exemption because the use of PFAS continues to be considered indispensable in these cases despite the problematic properties. Many questions remain unanswered in both analytics and eco-toxicology and human toxicology. The use of these substances in plant protection products and biocidal products is not covered by the REACH PFAS restriction proposal. Possible sources of contamination in Rhineland-Palatinate include the use of PFAS in industrial production in various industries. For example, in the metal industry for surface finishing, in the paper industry for coating papers for food packaging, or in the area of specialty chemicals, e.g. for the production of fluorinated plastics. German mechanical engineers fear that a comprehensive ban on PFAS chemicals will also affect important technologies for the energy transition. The chemicals are indispensable for the production of fuel cells, heat pumps, or solar systems. According to industry experts, a comprehensive ban as planned by the EU would have devastating effects. (FAZ May 24, 2023) Implications for food control (LMÜ): According to our understanding, the restriction proposal for PFAS affects the production, placing on the market, and the use of around 10,000 PFAS compounds. Food is only indirectly affected by the proposal since PFAS are not used in food but can occur there as contamination. Such contamination can occur through environmental pollution (e.g. through contaminated waters or soils) or possibly through a transfer from food contact materials (FCM). The goal from the perspective of consumer health protection is to minimize the contamination of food and consumer products (cosmetic products, articles for daily use) with PFAS that are classified as harmful to health. A further entry of PFAS, classified as harmful to health, into food through the environment or FCM should therefore be prevented. In this context, the regulations of Regulation (EU) 2023/915 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food are crucial. New maximum levels for four priority PFAS have been in place across the EU since January 2023 in various animal-based products for the first time. Knowledge about the contamination of individual foods with the respective substances is a basis for setting maximum levels. Since PFAS are durable and already ubiquitously present in the environment, it is impossible for us to estimate how a ban on all PFAS would affect the contamination of food. It is likely that (like other environmentally resistant contaminants, e.g. dioxins) a continual adaptation of the maximum levels and the regulated foods in the contaminant regulation will be necessary. Since some PFAS compounds are permitted for use in the production of food contact materials (FCM), a restriction of their use would require an adjustment of Regulation (EU) No. 10/2011 on plastic materials and articles intended to come into contact with food.

Concerning cosmetic products:
A partially permitted targeted use of PFAS in cosmetics (e.g. as emulsifiers, antispasmodics, stabilizers, viscosity regulators, lubricants, or as fat-repellent agents) must be declared in their list of ingredients according to specific nomenclature specifications. For this product group, manufacturer-compliant observation of legal requirements generally makes it possible to recognize a purposeful PFAS use. If there were to be a restriction for PFAS under REACH, it is expected that these substance bans, by means of the so-called OMNIBUS procedure, would be transferred to the Cosmetics Regulation (Regulation (EU) No. 1223/2009) similar to other highly toxic substances. A restriction of PFAS would likely also affect their, then no longer permitted, use for the production of textile consumer goods such as functional clothing. Food control is affected in terms of spot checks and risk-oriented inspections to ensure that the requirements of the above regulations are being followed.

Consultation with the ECHA:
In the absence of specific information concerning the concrete restriction proposal, the environmental protection division does not believe there are substantial information that could be helpful during the consultation.

Therefore, no text block for the draft of Rhineland-Palatinate's contribution to the EU consultation is provided by section 4."

Sectors and (sub-)uses: - Gas pressure regulators - Safety devices for gas pressure - Complementary equipment for pressure control stations - Complete stations for pressure control and measurement of combustible gases - Fuel gas odorization systems   The below listed equipment is an essential resource for safe and reliable use of the gas infrastructure and installations: • Pressure Regulators • Pressure Safety Devices • Filters / separators  • Heaters / heater exchangers  • Automatic shut-off valves; • Automatic burner control systems; • Gas/air ratio controls; • Multifunctional controls; • Complete Gas pressure control and metering stations for transmission and distribution; • Auxiliary Devices for Gas Pressure Control Stations; • Odorizing systems; • Etc...

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Gas infrastructure and installations equipment can be disassembled and separated at the end-of-life for processing or re-use in a circularity methodology. The fate of fluoropolymers at the end-of-life in this business sector is controllable and can be any one or more of the following:  Recovery and Recycling:  Fluoropolymers can be chemically returned back to their building blocks for reconstruction without damage to their properties. Melt-processable fluoropolymers, which excludes PTFE, can be recycled through traditional mechanical methodologies. The challenge for non-melt  processable fluoropolymers like PTFE is identifying ways to return materials to a facility that can  perform chemical recycling. This is a difficult problem, but not insurmountable.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: There are available studies that strongly suggest that PTFE, the most stable  fluoropolymer, undergoes complete thermal decomposition at a temperature of about 800°C and is  safe for incineration at municipal incineration facilities. Therefore, it is assumed that most other  fluoropolymers also thermally decompose within similar parameters and are also safe for incineration  at most typical municipality incineration facilities.

5. Proposed derogations:  Incorporation of Gas infrastructure and installation equipment as a missing use. Fluoropolymers are clearly differentiated from other substances in this very broad group of PFAS chemicals. There is strong evidence that suggests that these materials will not give rise to situations of concern for human health or the environment, acknowledging as well that industry continues to make significant progress to limit the use of PFAS polymerization aids and to introduce adequate abatement techniques to keep emissions of potentially harmful fluorinated by-products under adequate control.   Fluoropolymers are known for providing many beneficial properties simultaneously (combined in single products) that allow the continued development of applications critical to society, not only related to technological progress, but specifically in terms of safety to the population and development of green energy alternatives.

6. Missing uses: The equipment that may be affected by PFAS REACH restriction require high performance and high reliability to prevent failures in products that could result in harm to people and the environment. Availability  Non-fluoropolymer alternative materials do not exist today for specific applications due to the harsh operating conditions in which the materials are required to operate. Finding suitable alternatives is extremely challenging and the evaluations require reliable lab and field test, approval, certifications, etc. to verify durability and behavior over time and in any case will be the best secondary and tertiary choices. For example, some industry standards require 5 years of field experience to validate elastomeric materials.  Another consequence concerns the spare parts to be provided for maintenance of already in service equipment originally designed including PFAS materials. The non-PFAS spare parts can compromise the original performances and approvals, leading to a possible replacement of the whole equipment. This situation is critical to align with the European core values of sustainability and economic efficiency, as well as the commitment to fostering a culture of repair and reusability. Non-PFAS Elastomers Traditional elastomers such as Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM), Hydrogenated Nitrile Butadiene (H-NBR), and Silicone were considered as alternatives for seals, but were deemed unsuitable due to their inferior chemical resistance, temperature limitations, and mechanical properties. Most elastomers cannot perform at operating conditions that exceed 150°C. Using materials that are not adequate for the operating condition is not recommended and would, at a minimum and best case, require an unrealistic number of maintenance cycles. Furthermore, safety of workers and the environment could be compromised due to increased probability of failure and possible releases of hazardous materials. All potential alternatives, metals, non-PFAS polymers, and non-PFAS elastomers, may lead to increased maintenance cycles and generation of higher amounts of environmental waste. Economic Feasibility   Cost is not the deciding factor for use of fluoropolymers in gas infrastructure and applications. Fluoropolymers are typically more expensive than non-PFAS materials. They are used because of their technical requirements. The primary consideration for applications in gas infrastructure and installations is performance to ensure that safe and efficient operations are maintained. Even if alternatives were available today, the time needed for careful and comprehensive engineering work that accompanies a material change in a highly regulated segment can be in excess of years with substitution costs. Substitution costs, while substantial, will pale in comparison to the on-going costs of increased production facility downtime due to more frequent maintenance cycles and shorter life of components caused by decreased performance of any alternative. Another significant consideration is the intensive engineering effort that accompanies a material change in components for Infrastructure. Activities to be conducted include finding and evaluating alternatives, modifying designs, re-qualification testing and re-certification (ATEX, Pressure Equipment Directive 2014/68/EU, GAR), supply chain cadence change, and customer relations. Hazards and Risks  Safety is the deciding factor for use of fluoropolymers in gas infrastructure and installations applications. These materials are selected due to their high performance. The use of inferior performing alternatives could lead to a breach of containment and a subsequent release of media, which could harm humans, the environment and critical equipment. Non-Polymeric PFAS Processing Aids in Fluoropolymers Gas infrastructure and installations equipment providers are downstream users of fluoropolymers and do not handle any non-polymeric PFAS. The main concern related to fluoropolymers, in terms of human and environmental exposure, is the use of non-polymeric PFAS as polymerization aids in the manufacturing process, rather than the fluoropolymer itself. The fluoropolymer itself is not toxic, bio-accumulative, and/or water soluble, in contrast to the processing aids. Suppliers are addressing this and making progress on the development of non-fluorinated processing aids to be used in the production of fluoropolymers. It is expected that fluoropolymers will not degrade to other PFAS during normal  conditions of use or in the environment.  Recent indications received from fluoropolymer suppliers suggest that incineration of fluoropolymer waste at industrial incinerators can achieve complete thermal destruction of fluoropolymers under specific conditions; therefore it could be concluded that the environmental impact of their by-products can be controlled.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: UCRS is in favor of safeguard of environment and ban of toxic substances emission and fully committed to comply with all relevant environmental laws and regulations in the country. However, due to need of safety, efficiency, and functionality, the use of PFAS is still necessary and derogations should be then assured for in Gas infrastructure and installation applications.   In closing, UCRS derogation request is:   Incorporation of Gas infrastructure and installation equipment as a missing use. Fluoropolymers are clearly differentiated from other substances in this very broad group of PFAS chemicals. There is strong evidence that suggests that these materials will not give rise to situations of concern for human health or the environment, acknowledging as well that industry continues to make significant progress to limit the use of PFAS polymerization aids and to introduce adequate abatement techniques to keep emissions of potentially harmful fluorinated by-products under adequate control.   Fluoropolymers are known for providing many beneficial properties simultaneously (combined in single products) that allow the continued development of applications critical to society, not only related to technological progress, but specifically in terms of safety to the population and development of green energy alternatives.

8. Other identified uses: The Europe oil and gas infrastructure market from oil and gas segment account for USD 3 billion revenue in 2022 (www.gminsights.com).  Exclusion of fluoropolymers in gas infrastructure and installations as a use sector and implementation of an all-PFAS ban will have significant socioeconomic implications on the European economy.  Furthermore, through the possible elimination of fluoropolymers, the EU could fall behind other countries on technology competitiveness, especially in the area of chemical processing. Potential outcomes include reduction in manufacturing operations resulting in higher imports for everything from food to pharmaceuticals. Material limitations will continue to narrow the scope of technology-related activities that can be accomplished including those critical to Europe’s future, namely alternative energy, transportation, etc.. Materials are critical enablers of these technologies, and a derogation of fluoropolymers will enable Europe to maintain a level playing field, increasing the probability of achieving a successful outcome. 1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Energy sector (Annex E.2.12.) -  Sector as a whole (Electronics and semiconductor (Annex E.2.11.) – Electronics)

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The uses of PFAS in batteries and potential releases of PFAS during battery recycling have recently been investigated for the first time. Additionally, the industrially applied methods for battery recycling are currently undergoing large developments. At this point of time, there are no methods available in the lithium-ion battery recycling industry for specifically preventing PFAS emissions. The service life of LIBs can span between 5-10 years, but the service life can be up to 20 years before the batteries are recycled. Therefore, there will be need to recycle PFAS-containing LIBs many years into the future even though there might be PFAS-free applications on the market in the coming years. Therefore, it is crucial to perform research and investigate emissions of PFAS during battery recycling, and in our view, it is also the responsibility of the battery manufactures and recyclers to provide the funding for such research.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: The EU Batteries Regulation was revised to comply with the European Green Deal and is aiming for more sustainable and safer batteries on the European market under a circular economy. This includes increased recycling capacities of the battery materials (50% by 2027, and up to 80% by 2031 for Li). Therefore, it is in the interest of the recycling industry to reduce the use of hazardous substances in the battery materials for effective recycling. Fluorine contamination can be problematic, but it is also dependent on the used recycling process used for the LIBs. Fluorine in the recycling products can have an impact on the quality of the black mass which ultimately also impacts the electrochemical performance of LIBs that use recovered cathode materials. Additionally, the generated fluorinated inorganic and organic byproducts (including PFAS) can pose a risk to the environment if waste is not monitored and handled according. Also, the generation of hydrofluoric acid (HF) is unfavorable as it causes corrosion of the equipment but is also a safety issue especially for the workers.  There can be direct emissions, but also the release of transformation products (i.e.  some of PFAS used in the LIBs can be transformed into more toxic PFAS transformation products). The pyrometallurgical process that uses temperatures up to 1600 °C is expected to mineralize PFAS such as for instance polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) or polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) used in binders for the electrodes. Destruction of PFAS in the pyrometallurgical process is expected given that the temperature is higher than in the incineration processes where PFAS are also mineralized. The field of recycling LIBs has progressed in recovering and regenerating critical materials, but more development is needed for the recovery of the spent electrolytes. As of now, there is a potential risk for emissions of hazardous substances and PFAS, if there is not appropriate waste management of the electrolytes during the recycling process. There is a benefit for industry to reduce the content of fluorinated compounds in LIBs, as the quality of the regenerated materials can be increased but also the environmental and occupational health risks can be reduced.

8. Other identified uses: In the restriction proposal it is currently stated that there are no viable alternatives available for the use of PFAS in LIBs. We investigated the use cases of PFAS in the electrode (cathode) and electrolyte of LIBs and determined if there are potential substitutes. Our research resulted in the identification of potential alternatives that are also commercially available.  It is our understanding that it is technically challenging to replace fluoropolymers such as PVDF and PTFE that are commonly used as binders in the cathode. There are companies offering possible PFAS-free solutions, but they might not be applicable to every battery cell depending on performance requirements and the given chemistry. But there is much research ongoing in this field and the results are promising. For the electrolyte, PFAS salts, or so-called fluorinated ionic liquids, such as lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI) are added in small amounts to enhance the performance of the battery and safety. Some of these additives have been detected in the environmental already, therefore it is desirable to abstain from the use of these compounds to reduce emissions. In our understanding, lithium hexafluorophosphate (LiPF6; inorganic, does not fall under the PFAS definition) is a necessary salt, and the PFAS additives are rather optional. But again, this ultimately depends on the cell chemistry and required performance. Research is also ongoing to find high-performing fluorine-free alternatives for electrolytes. In summary, the science and technology to generate PFAS-free batteries is available. It is now up to the battery industry to take this research further, and assess its large-scale implementation, and the resulting costs. We understand that the LIB sector is a crucial part in mitigating climate change impacts, but it is important to consider other environmental impacts such as chemical pollution as well.  The restriction proposal can be an opportunity for the battery industry to facilitate the research towards more sustainable and less hazardous chemicals in the used materials to ensure compliance with a desired green energy storage application. Furthermore, it is a chance for Europe to become a leading competitor in sustainable technologies within the energy sector.

In Vat-photopolymerisation, these acrylates-based resin is placed on a transparent vat through which light passes from below. Hence, an analysis of alternatives and socio-economic analysis can not be provided. Subdivision of the energy sector as given in chapter 2.8 is urgently needed.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: The use cases given in Table 8 in Annex XV does not address assets operating in the electric power transmission grid. Derogations for the energy sector as given in chapter 2.8 are urgently needed.

8. Other identified uses: TSOs build and operate the critical power grid infrastructure to supply electricity to European industry and citizens. TSOs make sure to keep the environmental impact of the grid to a minimum and even enhance nature restoration and biodiversity in their corridors.   The sophisticated high and extra high voltage equipment used in power grids is built to last 40+ years. It is designed to operate and withstand extraordinary and harsh conditions, such as high pressure, extreme voltage levels and temperatures, and to guarantee the functioning and resilience of the grid at any time. The use of PFAS in solid, liquid, and gaseous components of grid equipment is determined by manufacturers to ensure the needed requirements for its performance and reliability.  A restriction that does not take into account network-specific use cases could lead to the unavailability of critical assets and, thus, to unpredictable effects with regard to system security.  Due to a lack of data, TSOs do not yet have a comprehensive overview of the use of PFAS in the components of their electrical equipment, nor the PFAS used to manufacture this equipment. Furthermore, there is also insufficient information on possible alternatives to replace them. European TSOs are committed to protecting the public and workforce wherever risks stemming from PFAS are identified. Therefore, typical use cases for PFAS where information exists are highlighted and the need for use case-specific derogations in the restriction proposal in case no alternatives are available is stressed.    1. Inherent dilemmas and trade-offs between environmental concerns of PFAS and climate objectives  High-voltage equipment using PFAS gases is typically installed in critical network nodes. Their shutdowns would cause the rejection of renewably generated power. This would equal a tremendous amount of wasted resources. The proposal to restrict PFAS should not prevent either the decarbonisation of the electricity grid infrastructure or the grid development, which is essential to properly deliver the energy transition (by allowing the integration of renewable energies and the electrification of uses). The PFAS currently used for the electricity grid infrastructure contributes to its functionality and high efficiency. Complete restrictions of their placing on the market and use should always be considered in light of the availability of alternatives. Decarbonisation and the protection of human health and the environment are key. ECHA's proposal to restrict PFASs should, therefore, strike for a good balance between both objectives.    2. PFAS in solid components and spare parts of electrical equipment  2a. Solid components PFASs are used in electrical grid equipment, machinery components and parts, such as insulated nozzles, sealings, plain bearings, gaskets etc. The insulated nozzle is a key component for interrupting fault current (the arc of a short circuit current) inside a circuit breaker. More use cases are further specified in the annex. Once manufactured, solid components with PFAS are usually installed within the machinery. The decommissioning and recycling are carried out respecting all applicable legislation and in close collaboration with manufacturers.  TSOs are not aware of any alternative solutions to the PFAS use cases listed in the Annex of this document. Therefore, an undifferentiated restriction of PFAS for these components of grid equipment would signify a ban on new equipment and spare parts for critical infrastructure within18 months after its entry into force. This would effectively bring all current European grid development projects to a halt and then would endanger the ongoing energy transition, as no manufacturer is currently able to supply PFAS-free equipment. As research and development of alternatives is only starting, it is urgently needed that ECHA acknowledges this gap in the current proposal and adds a derogation of 13,5 years for solid components in electrical transmission equipment. More specifically, derogation 6. in the restriction proposal for fluoropolymers and perfluoropolyethers should be extended for use in high-voltage electricity transmission equipment by adding the paragraph “6 g high-voltage electricity transmission equipment”.  2b. Spare parts containing PFAS should be exempted Many PFAS are used in existing electric equipment already installed with a minimum lifetime of 40 years. It is, therefore, necessary that the supply of spare parts is secured throughout this lifetime. The operation, maintenance, repair and extension of existing equipment containing PFAS must be ensured until the end of its lifetime, as PFAS-free spare parts may not work in the originally designed equipment. Otherwise, they would need to be decommissioned prematurely, entailing additional environmental and climate-related burdens, without consideration of circular economy or reparability principles. We reiterates and stresses the importance of being able to use equipment during its lifetime. Therefore, we recommends an unlimited derogation for using spare parts containing PFAS in existing electrical equipment.    3. PFAS in liquids and lubricants Several liquids and lubricants used for the servicing and maintenance of electrical equipment use PFAS. The properties of mineral oils and lubricants are modified with PFAS additives to fulfil the needed quality demands, e.g., on temperature behaviour and ageing stability. They are used, for instance, in circuit breakers, which need to work impeccably when used. TSOs are not aware of any alternative solutions to the use cases listed. An undifferentiated restriction of lubricants and liquids containing PFAS would impede TSOs from carrying out their legal obligation to maintain and service their equipment to ensure proper functionality and efficient operation of the grid, bearing considerable risks regarding grid stability, security of supply and workers’ safety. Therefore, the proposal to allow a 13,5-year derogation for lubricants used under harsh conditions is strongly supported. On top of that, TSOs recommend a 13,5-year derogation for PFAS in liquids, in particular technical mineral oil with PFAS additives, until alternatives have been developed and proven to satisfy comparable quality standards regarding long-term reliability and performance requirements.    4. PFAS in gases  4a. Gases for operation, maintenance and extension containing PFAS should be exempted In recent years, TSOs have been using PFAS-containing gases as insulation medium in electrical switchgear to replace SF6, the most potent greenhouse gas, and decarbonise their electric equipment. For the new installations above 145 kV, as well as for specific uses on all voltage levels, TSOs currently have limited possibilities to replace SF6. One key component to do so has been PFAS-containing insulation gases, such as fluoronitrile (C4F7N). The application of the gases in electrical equipment, listed in the annex per use-case, is used in closed cycles and has state-of-the-art leakage detection devices to ensure smooth operation, protect the environment and minimise workforce exposure. As of today, it is not certain whether PFAS-Gas-free solutions above 145kV and for specific uses on all voltage levels will be commercially available in 6,5 years time, also in sufficient quantity for all ranges of TSOs application. This is due to long development, qualification, and standardisation processes. If PFAS in switchgear insulation gases were banned after the derogation period of 6,5 years, it would mean that the already ordered and installed equipment supposed to operate with PFAS gases may not be put into operation, maintained, nor extended after the ban date and that existing equipment would have to be put out of order and become a stranded asset.  It must also be ensured that switchgear operating with PFAS gases that have been lawfully put into operation according to the F-Gases Regulation can be refilled for maintenance purposes or extended with the corresponding gas as long as it cannot be maintained or extended with PFAS-free gases. Therefore, we recommends an unlimited derogation for PFAS gases used for refilling, maintenance, or extension purposes of switchgear. Replacing existing switchgear operating with PFAS gases before their end-of-life would lead to stranded assets, which would contradict the principles of reparability and circularity.  4b. Derogation of PFAS-containing gases will help speeding up the PFAS-free developments The present draft of F-Gases Regulation forces TSOs to install fluornitril based assets until alternative solutions are available. TSOs believe that derogation of the PFAS Gases within 6,5 years, as proposed by ECHA, would strengthen the developments of the alternative PFAS-free solutions and hence the installations of PFAS-Solutions would be limited to minimum.   Thus, TSOs urge ECHA and policymakers to take into account the ongoing negotiations on the draft F-Gases Regulation.  5. Resulting additional derogation proposals Based on the explanations above, the following derogation propsals should be taken into consideration in the “ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT – Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs)” in the table “Proposed restriction - Annex XVII entry PFASs (Restriction Option 2)” beginning at the page 4 of the report: - add “4.d. spare parts necessary for operation, maintenance, repair and extension in energy sector.” - add “5.u. Additives in mineral oils and lubricants in high-voltage electricity transmission equipment until 13.5 years after EiF”  - add “6.g. Fluoropolymer applications in high-voltage electricity transmission equipment until 13.5 years after EiF”   Annex: Non-comprehensive overview of the of PFAS in components of TSO equipment  Disclaimer: As users, TSOs currently do not have a comprehensive overview of the use of PFASs in components of their electrical equipment. Moreover, TSOs also lack the data to determine the amount of PFAS contained in their equipment, as well as the PFAS used to manufacture this equipment.
