1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The respondent, Praxair srl, a Company 100% owned by Linde PLC, welcomes the opportunity to provide comments and feedback to a proposal for a restriction of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) as set out in the Annex XV restriction Proposal of March 22,2023. The respondent is active, among other operations, in the field of manufacturing coating systems made with thermoplastic Fluoropolymers (alternatively here named: Polymeric PFAS) and mixtures thereof.  Comparatively to sectors identified in the table 9- RO2 (Page 115) of the Annex XV restriction proposal, the following sectors are served, either directly or through specialized OEMs : 1. Food contact materials (Annex E.2.3) with regard to:  a. Industrial food and feed production  b. Nonstick coatings in Industrial and professional bakeware  In both subsectors, release systems, fully resistant up to 260 °C, made by polymeric PFAS like PTFE, FEP, PFA, are provided, in order to impart high release capability, so to allow automatic demolding and handling of produced goods, as well high cleanliness in operations and no need to add oils for release.  2. Electronics and Semiconductors (Annex E.2.11) with particular regard to: a. Semiconductor manufacturing  In this subsector, high thickness polymeric PFAS Coatings are used (PVDF, ECTFE, ETFE, PFA), in order to impart, at the same time: i. Corrosion resistance against chemicals ii. High temperature resistance iii. High purity The last property is essential for the semiconductor Industry, as leach out of metal cations (coming from metal walls) and TOC (“total organic carbon”) leach out (which may come out from an organic material, like a polymer)  may lead to a complete scrapping of the integrated circuits production. A polymeric PFAS coating, unique among all organic materials, does provide the needed cleanliness and purity , by protecting the process fluids (high purity chemicals and high purity water) from contamination given by a metal wall and not realising anything itself. 3. Energy sector (Annex E.2.12), by considering the sector as a whole. Particularly, the respondent is serving the sector by providing high thickness corrosion resistant coating systems, made by Polymeric PFAS like PVDF, ECTFE, ETFE, FEP for all parts that need corrosion protection in the course of the different processes to generate energy or transforming it. Worth mentioning is the large use of such coating systems to protect equipment used in flue gas handling and desulphurization plants, as ancillary equipment installed in power plants working with fossil sources, to clean from SOx contaminants gases bound to the stack and eventually to atmosphere. Beside an established presence in the Energy Companies working with fossil sources, the respondent has started being active also in other two fields, related to Energy, which have great importance in today European Green Deal: a. Production of green Hydrogen by means of PEM electrolysis processes: coating systems with high purity, in regard to the contact with water and other fluids to be sent to the electrolyzer; b. Production or recycling of components for Li-ion batteries, whereas processes with high acidic conditions are set up.   4. Petroleum and mining (Annex E.2.15)  Even in such a field polymeric PFAS are used as applied coating systems in a variety of applications to protect equipment against presence of sour gas. PTFE, PVDF and PFA polymers are mostly used.    All that said, the respondent must respectfully make the restriction proponents and ECHA  aware that other sectors are not all mentioned in the Annex XV report , in spite of the fact that coating systems, made mostly by the same polymeric PFAS materials mentioned above, have been successfully in place since dozen of years and used for their optimized  balance between outstanding and unique properties and relatively low cost in comparison with other potential alternatives. These sectors, where the respondent is very active as a provider of coating systems, are: 1. The petrochemical Industry, particularly in the production of:  a. Olefins (cracking processes) b. Grey Hydrogen (steam reforming processes) c. LDPE and its copolymers: EVA, etc. d. Synthetic rubber production (Butyl/Butadiene-Styrene, etc.) In these fields a large use of release coatings, manufactured mostly by using PTFE and PFA, is present, to impart, even at very high temperatures (260 °C)  easy-to-clean properties to the process equipment and, particularly,  fight the very damaging fouling effects which hamper rotating equipment (compressors and similar equipment) as well the damaging corrosion effects due to sour chemicals as wet SOx and CO2  present in process stream.  2. The fine and organic chemistry  In this field, acidic corrosion resistance, sometimes at process temperatures in excess of 100 °C and in presence, very often, of large solvent concentration, is best achieved by means of polymeric PFAS like PVDF, ECTFE, ETFE, FEP and PFA. 3. The Pharma Industry Most reactions of the Pharma Industry, with their downstream processes  bound to the production of drugs and active principles, do imply the use of acids and solvents combined together, which require use of materials with very high and broad chemical resistance. At the same time cleanliness is required to avoid contamination into the process. Peculiar attention is then required in the production of markers for nuclear medicine, where, beside, all these requirements, also radiation resistance is required . Polymeric PFAS (PVDF, ETFE, E-CTFE and PFA) offer well proven solutions to all these requirements.        4. The Industries manufacturing paper and woven-non-woven tissue  and the converting Industries related to those web-type products Coatings, with polymeric PFAS, applied onto rolls bound to production of paper, its derivatives, as well in processes bound to produce woven-non-woven webs, is a sound practice to allow higher machine speed (better productivity), lower scraps rate and better preservation of the roll metal against oxidation and corrosion. The unique combination of surface properties, temperature and corrosion resistance, have brought OEM and users to select and use coating systems made of Polymeric PFAS in this field. Processes downstream to the primary production of paper webs or Woven-Non-Woven (WNW) webs, collectively named as “converting industry”, where the paper-based products or WNW webs are used to make finished articles, sometimes in combination with plastic foils, thin metal foils or other materials, do use largely polymeric PFAS coatings onto the process rolls, to impart release and easy-to-clean properties. Two exemplar cases, which do not however limit at all the large variety of applications, collectively grouped under this sector, are: a. The flexographic industry, where changeover of colors is made very easily and, above all, very fast, by means of polymeric PFAS coatings applied onto rolls and ink vats. b. The production of diapers for human beings (babies, ladies, seniors) , where glues used to bond different layers, could lead to a much more cumbersome and difficult process, and therefore much more costly, if polymeric PFAS coatings were not available to protect the process surfaces and make them self-cleaning or easy-to-clean. 5. The automotive Industry. It is well known that polymeric PFAS, both thermoplastic and elastomeric (FKM),  in extruded or molded form, are largely used as components, mostly in under-hood applications, by the car Industry (cables, hoses, gaskets, shaft seals, etc.). It may be less known that also coatings do find important applications to provide dry lubrication to small components whereas the best engineered solution is the use of a dry lubricant, to impart the needed tribological properties, to have a lower friction factor and therefore a lower energy consumption and, at the same time, a better wear resistance.   In such overview, the respondent has covered about only 90% of sectors which are served by means of coating systems, applied onto metal parts, and whose composition consists mostly of polymeric PFAS, namely: PVDF, ECTFE, ETFE, FEP, PFA; PTFE. Given the very high flexibility of the coating technology and the possibility to apply a coating on practically every metal part or component of equipment, it must be taken into account that also minor applications should be included in the scope of defining the uses of polymeric PFAS as base materials for coating systems bound to impart one or a combination of the following properties, that make these materials mostly unique: 1. Very low surface free energy, with related high release properties; 2. Very high temperature resistance, up to 260 °C; 3. Practically universal chemical resistance, against alkali, acids, solvents and almost any other chemical;   4. Outstanding fire resistance and very low flame propagation capability; 5. Cleanliness and purity, so not to leach out anything to a given process stream; 6. Food contact compliance for most the mentioned polymeric PFAS; as set out by Regulations 10/2011 and subsequent modifications; 7. Outstanding electrical properties as: very high dielectric strength; very high resistivity, very low loss factors. All these properties do have also from time to time practical use in coated articles; 8. Some of the polymeric PFAS mentioned above, particularly;  E-CTFE; PCTFE; E-TFE, do have, finally, very high radiation resistance, so that it is possible to use them in environments where radiation exists.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The respondent, as responsible Industry, has been since ever committed to minimize emissions, to provide a robust safeguard to all Associates, to the environment and all living beings. Therefore, the respondent is ready with pleasure to provide available information on emissions generated during the processing of polymeric PFAS into coatings. No or very little information can be given about emissions at end-of-life phase of coated articles as the fate is the same as that of the article in most instances. With regard to the coating, it must be said, first of all, that the respondent is already actively cooperating with all available raw materials suppliers in order to test and qualify polymeric PFAS either free from polymerization aids (in such a case polymeric PFAS are made by technologies like, for example, suspension polymerization and no longer with emulsion polymerization techniques) or with polymerizations aids not falling into the PFAS product group.  The respondent has a large record of past development work made, in partnership with key raw materials suppliers, with polymeric PFAS, which had undergone changes in their polymerization techniques, due to the introduction of regulatory restrictions including:  introduction and qualification of new polymers grades made without use of green-houses gases (mostly R11) used in the polymerization process; and more recently introduction and qualification of new polymerization aids. Therefore, the respondent is ready to do his own expert part to support, foster and qualify any new and final change in the polymerization techniques, such that fully fluorinated polymerization aids will be eventually totally dismissed.   Getting rid of polymerization aids, incoming together with the polymer in very low percentage as additive, means first of all to strongly reduce the risk to have water-soluble or volatile PFAS in the emissions, at the various phases of the manufacturing process to produce coatings made with polymeric PFAS. The spraying process, carried out in dedicated spraying cubicles, generates small amount of solid and liquid waste, which may contain tiny PFAS residuals either present as solid polymeric PFAS particulate, defined as overspray, or water soluble fluorinated polymerization aids residuals (in case they are still present).  Presence of PFAS in off gases from spraying cubicles is realistic to be considered nil. Liquid and solid waste, which may contain PFAS, are normally handled in closed loops and tanks and finally collected by external specialized Companies for treatment. The sintering and film formation process, after the spraying step,  is normally carried out in dedicated ovens, both tunnel-type or box-type. Typical process temperature may range from 240 °C (PVDF) to 420 °C (PTFE). Even in those conditions, which fall under the intended conditions of processing, as set out and prescribed by any single raw material producer, there is negligeable amount of volatile PFAS, coming out of off gases. These off gases are in any case collectively handled and treated to thermally degrade all organic molecules carried on by the fumes, in a dedicated combustion process. Lastly, the stripping of old coatings from their metal wall, as mentioned by the Annex XV restriction report itself, is made by thermal degradation of the coatings, followed by a blasting with conventional grit media, This process is generating : solid waste (the used grit), containing polymeric PFAS residuals, which is  collected by specialized Companies for treatment and off gases, conveyed to a dedicated treatment process. Liquid waste generated by this latter process is then treated as above described for other waste water streams.  Overall, the respondent is therefore in the position to handle emissions, both internally, with dedicated equipment, and by dedicated and specialized Companies, in their different physical forms.

6. Missing uses: Among potential alternatives, for his own activity, the respondent tells apart two distinct situations: 1. Alternatives that can be realized by means of the same technology presently mastered by the respondent: the coating technology. Only raw materials would change and polymeric PFAS would be offset by other materials. As typical case, most of applications related to the food industry can fall into this scenario and there are detailed hereinbelow, as example which may be taken as representative also for other applications. 2. Alternatives which would offer the same functional performance with a different technology.  Under this scenario, one must include all applications where coatings and lining systems, made with polymeric PFAS applied onto metal equipment, manufactured with carbon or stainless steel, to fight harsh acidic corrosion, can be offset by manufacturing the same article with high content nickel alloys. It must be clear from now on that, if such alternatives are to replace polymeric PFAS coating systems, because of whatever restriction may be enforced to them, the respondent will completely lose his market share and related revenues in the very same applications. The respondent, at the present state of the art in the materials science, coating technology and related engineering science, is of the strong opinion that, whenever a joint combination of at least two of the properties, already outlined in section 1 (Sectors and (sub)-uses), is needed in a given application, it is very difficult, not to say impossible, to offset polymeric PFAS as main constituent of coating systems. All that said, the respondent has made a comparison, in terms of performance, costs and also sustainability, among some of the proposed alternatives, that have been mentioned also in the Annex XV restriction proposal. Two cases are presented: 1. coated items for professional bakeware 2. coated articles in harsh corrosion environment  Coated items for professional bakeware In this application, the primary performance requirement is high release, and it must be combined with high temperature resistance, often up to 260 °C, and  good corrosion resistance against acid or alkaline dough compositions. Necessary condition to be fulfilled is, of course, the full compliance to regulations related to food contact, namely the Regulation (CE) 1935/2004, the Regulation (EU) 10/2011 and all related updates, and finally the regulation (EU) 2023/2006. By following the explanations given in the restriction report and, particularly in its Annex E, the following alternatives to coating systems made by polymeric PFAS in such subsector may be conceived. 1. Solgel technologies (based on silicon chemistry)  2. Silicon resin technologies 3. Silicon elastomer technologies 4. No coating systems and return to continuous oiling of straps, molds and trays There is evidence in the respondent’s industrial experience, supported by a variety of cases at many customers, that all coating technologies based on the silicon chemistry have much less duration than coatings based on polymeric PFAS. Apart few niche applications where silicone-based coatings do offer a better release (cakes, sweet dough), all other applications have shown a far better behavior and duration of Polymeric PFAS coatings. Data reported by Mc.Keen L.W. in his ”Fluorinated coatings and finishes Handbook” (Plastics Design Library, 2006) show (pages 210-211) a ratio in life duration, in the industrial bakeware industry,  between silicon-based coatings and those ones made with polymeric PFAS,  up to 1/10.  Indeed, in case coatings made of polymeric PFAS become no longer available to the bakeware industry, one alternative  available to users is to come back to use  oils (normally based on palm oil) as release agent, with subsequent modifications  in the organoleptic and dietary properties of the baked products, and issues related to dirt formation, caused by degraded oil,  all over the straps and molds used for the baking process.  If such solution were to be chosen, as the one giving the least cost/performance ratio, in case the polymeric PFAS coatings would disappear, the respondent is concerned about indications received from members of the European Industrial bakeware Industry that they would be severely impacted and could get back to the situation of about more than fifty years ago.   Coated articles in harsh corrosion and high temperature conditions. As hinted above, for such applications, when potential leach out of metal cations is not an issue for the application, the realistically unique functional alternative to thick polymeric PFAS coatings and lining is the manufacturing of the metal articles (in most cases, heavy and costly vessels, process equipment, etc.) by using high content nickel alloys.  Indeed, other kind of linings (ebonite, epoxy coatings, etc.) do have severe limitations as far as the maximum service temperature is concerned, as well in case the process composition has high solvent concentration. The respondent is aware that pure cost of an equipment manufactured in carbon steel and subsequent coated with a polymeric PFAS is 100-300% cheaper than the same equipment made with nickel alloys. Beside the pure cost comparison, it is expected that an LCA evaluation and comparison, would be also more favorable to a coated solution.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Based on all above considerations, the respondent would like to make ECHA and the European regulators aware that: a. If the Annex XV Restriction Report is finally accepted and converted into a regulation as such, with a restriction to ban the use of polymeric PFAS in the above described coating applications, the economic activity of the respondent would become useless and would lead to a complete stop of it.   b. Similarly, in such an occurrence, the overall downstream supply chain, which, as seen, involves a vast variety of industrial activities, some of them essential for entire critical sectors such as energy, pharma, semiconductor, would be put in serious jeopardy, not to say destroyed. Therefore, the respondent is respectfully asking ECHA and all regulators for reconsideration of the Annex XV restriction report in order to grant the maximum 12 years derogation for all thermoplastic polymeric PFAS used as coating materials in the above-described sectors and applications with opportunity to review if alternatives are not then available. Involved Polymeric PFAS are, in detail: PVDF, ECTFE, PCTFE, ETFE, FEP, PFA, PTFE.

Our PFAS is unique with respect to pH-stability and shows excellent suitability to protect from skin damages including wounds. Thus, it protects from skin damage due to intestine secretions, gastric acid, bile fluid and pancreatic fluid. Protection against these secretions, e.g. is necessary for skin protection in surgeries or in percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy. Our barrier products, containing our PFAS, are also unique with respect to the protection against skin damage related to very long-lasting contact time with faeces (up to 24 hours), even if faeces are loaded with small intestine secretion. Problems like this are typical situations in home care of elderly patients. However, the products are also suitable and used to protect newborns and children from skin damage. All kinds of stoma applications are possible as well. Additionally, our PFAS shows very good skin tolerance. So allergic skin reactions against our barrier products are reduced to a minimum, which is confirmed by tests on atopic skin [Ref.: Certificate for Coryt Protect. 2019 Dermatest and Certificate for Coryt Protect Sensitive. 2018 Dermatest]. c. The number of companies estimated to be affected by the restriction would be a several hundred which are already using our products (mainly university hospitals and clinical centres) and of course those we were not yet able to address or introduce our products. d. – e. We would like to summarize under item e also items f and g, because we are not able to assess the future development with respect to substitution success. Our general needs: Functional stability of the protective film against secretions of low and high pH. Very good resistance against hydrophilic and hydrophobic substances. Low allergenic potential. Our particular needs: Very good skin tolerance in order to allow the application of our products to allergy sufferers. Protection at low pH (gastric acid). Protection against aggressive secretions, such as gastric acid, bile fluid, pancreatic fluid and small intestine secretion. Additionally, our PFAS shows very good skin tolerance. So allergic skin reactions using our barrier products are reduced to a minimum, confirmed by tests on atopic skin [Ref.: Certificate for Coryt Protect. 2019 Dermatest and Certificate for Coryt Protect Sensitive. 2018 Dermatest].  Our R&D has started screening the raw material market. However, there are only few possible alternative candidates which might be able to meet our requirements. Unfortunately, until now, all tested candidates show only partial suitability. The likelihood of success to find a suitable alternative is estimated to be 10 %. The expected time line for a possible successful substitution is estimated to be at least 10 years causing total costs of about 300.000 EUR. Our main concern is, that only practice will reveal suitability during a very long-lasting process.  Some estimation with respect to socio-economic costs: We are assuming average costs in case of wounds due to contact dermatitis of 5.000 EUR per patient (wound treatment and costs for additional care). In addition, according to the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, physical integrity is the right of any human being. If a wound yet has occurred due to inadequate protection of the skin, this means that physical integrity of a patient’s health had been disregarded.  Our estimation is, that the socio-economic savings by using our products are 40 – 50 Mio EUR / year based on our current sales. Thus, in case our PFAS is banned, these savings will turn into costs. In order to give a reference with respect to this topic: Costs associated with urinary incontinence alone are estimated to be more than $26.3 billion annually [Ref.: Zulkowski K., Advances in Skin & Wound Care, 2012; 25, 231-236]. Costs due to faecal incontinence have to be added. A main cost driver is skin damage due to incontinence-associated dermatitis and intertrigo.   Our request to the authorities: To give us further allowance to use Polyperfluoroethoxymethoxy Difluoroethyl PEG Phosphate in our applications including the allowance to manufacture our barrier products in the plant of our toll manufacturers. Alternatively, a transition time of 13,5 years.

Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: Substances covered in the Regulation (EU) No 517/2014 on fluorinated greenhouse gases should be exempted from the PFAS regulation The PFAS restriction proposal overlaps with F-gas regulation. Fluorinated gases are already strictly controlled in the F-gas regulation, and companies have made their investments and planning according to provisions and transition periods in that regulation, also already anticipating those to come soon in the revision of the current F-gas regulation. Overlaps create great uncertainty among those who need to make longer-term investment decisions now.  For the sake of overall sustainability, it is important that expensive equipment, facilities and buildings, for example, can be used up to their anticipated end of life.   The competitiveness of the EU companies and value chains should not be compromised The derogations in paragraphs 4 and 5 do not at present cover the precursors, raw materials, or auxiliary agents of the final products. These need to be addressed in the derogations as well as R&D, so that distributors can continue providing the manufacturing industry in the EU with the raw materials needed for innovations and development of products in the EU.  The list of exemptions should remain open-ended. The unique properties of PFAS substances, including their favorable toxicological profile, make them challenging to replace. Products of lower quality and performance are not well received by customers or consumers. In the worst case, such products would compromise safety and cause loss of valuable resources.  It should be possible to extend the list of exemptions or transition period, if no alternatives, which provide overall comparable or increased safety for the application is found and important value chain as well as in some cases even critical autonomy might be otherwise lost in the EU.  Why are exemptions essential for the field of refrigeration and air conditioning technology for society as a whole and why are no suitable alternatives available?  • Retailors would be affected by a ban on PFAS in the areas of heating, air conditioning and refrigeration. This is because PFAS are used in different forms in the areas mentioned. On the one hand, as a component of refrigerants, in particular in those alternatives that are affected by the amendment of the F-Gas Regulation as a replacement for those affected by the upcoming bans. On the other hand, it is also used as material in technical hydraulic components with special properties. These include compressors, pumps, valves and cylinders. PFAS are used here in seals, hoses, pipes, valves or even in coatings. Substitution of PFAS in these special areas is often not possible. This is because either there is a lack of alternatives or the special performance of PFAS cannot be achieved to the extent necessary to guarantee the functionalities of these components. Due to the complete ban, neither the production of these components in the economic area itself nor their import from outside would be possible. • For the food trade, a ban on PFAS would have the following consequences: o Any refrigeration technology that is used for safe storage and for offering food requiring refrigeration would no longer be permitted after the transitional periods have expired.   This would make it virtually impossible to supply the population with goods requiring refrigeration in compliance with today's hygienic standards. o A large proportion of climate-relevant emissions in the food trade result from refrigeration technology. In this respect, the switch to more climate-friendly refrigerants offers a great deal of leverage for food retailers to minimise greenhouse gas emissions and thus contribute to climate targets in Germany and Europe. However, due to a lack of alternatives, a general ban on PFAS would prevent a switch to more climate-friendly alternatives. A change before the ban is also hindered by the limited personnel capacities at refrigeration companies and industry.  o In addition, the proportion of food waste would also increase drastically, as refrigeration in the market contributes to a longer shelf life of sensitive products. o However, this does not exclusively apply to the production and trade of foodstuffs. Medical products (including vaccines) would also be affected by a PFAS ban.    Are you in favour of exemptions for the entire refrigeration and air conditioning sector? If so, what is the duration of the exemptions?  • Due to the systemically importance of refrigeration technology – including for the supply of the population – exemptions should apply to the entire field of refrigeration and air conditioning technology.

10. Analytical methods: In relation to current testing methods and the textile industry, it should be highlighted the limitations on fluorine content: the methods available for determining total fluorine in textiles and leather (e.g., EN 14582:2016 and ASTM D7359:2018) are unable to reliably distinguish between organic and inorganic fluorine in those substrates. Intentional use of PFAS in the textile sector is likely to result in concentrations of at least several thousand ppm total fluorine in relevant components of articles in most circumstances.   However, PFAS may be present in components of finished articles in the hundreds of ppm even if not intentionally added. The detected fluorine may be present due to unintentional PFAS contamination or the presence of non-PFAS fluorine-containing compounds such as fluoride salts used upstream in the supply chain. For example, chemical formulations utilizing inorganic fluorine compounds, e.g., fluoride salts, are used in various textile manufacturing processes.  For this purpose, the draft restriction includes an exception under paragraph 2. ii) in case the value is total fluorine exceeds 50 mg F/kg and the manufacturer, importer or downstream user submit a proof to authorities demonstrating that the fluorine measured is or inorganic sources.  This situation would lead into legal defencelessness in the industry due to a lack of a proper test method to ensure the compliance of the goods manufactured or sold in EU and a huge uncertainty on the acceptable proof by authorities in case of inorganic fluorine sources in the products.   WE suggest that EU Commission support the rapid development of a validated test method capable of reliably differentiating between inorganic and organic fluorine in textile and leather substrates (including related trims) to avoid inadvertently prohibiting fluorine-containing compounds that are not PFAS.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Sector: Military/defence sector. The Norwegian Defence Sector, Norwegian Armed Forces (NAF), Norwegian Defence Material Agency (NDMA)  Uses (none-exhaustive list): Ammunition and explosives Several substances defined as a PFAS by this restriction proposal have military applications, either directly in energetic material or in proximity such that their performance directly affects the performance of the energetic material or munition. This includes airborne countermeasures, insensitive munitions and solid rocket motors. The list most likely includes several other uses.   Soldier material PPE, military field clothing and equipment, mobility and endurance material are material categories which contain textiles and other products with membranes and durable water repellent surface treatments containing PFAS. PFAS is used for impregnation in textiles and Teflon coatings, which improves the products' oil, water and dirt-repellent properties.  Base material Electronics, tools and HVAC are identified material categories containing PFAS. Challenges associated with HVAC and cooling, ventilation and freezing systems are identified. The supply of old refrigerants will decrease over the years, resulting in more expensive maintenance and repairs with longer lead times. In worst case scenario, entire systems may need to be rebuilt or disposed of due to a complete ban on current gases. If NDMA has to procure new materials and parts to replace the current ones containing PFAS, there is a significant risk that they may not have the same properties as PFAS. Parts and spare parts with specific requirements such as heat resistance, flame-retardant components, components with special surface treatment, and batteries, are difficult to replace. It is important to find alternative materials that can maintain the desired properties while being less harmful to the environment. Research and development in this area is crucial to finding safe and effective alternatives, but is a time consuming process that requires an increasement of both human and financial resources.  Naval Systems Coolants with PFAS are used in all refrigeration and freezer systems, as well as HVAC systems on the Navy’s vessels. There are no easily accessible alternatives for these coolants. If these systems were to be replaced, new systems would likely have a larger volume and weight. Military vessels do not have as much available volume and weight for retrofitting as civilian vessels. Additionally, alternative coolants such as hydrocarbons, carbon dioxide and ammonia have properties that increase the risk in a combat situation (flammability, toxicity, asphyxiation). In addition, materials containing PFAS are used in many parts for engines, hydraulic systems, and other technical equipment, such as Viton in seals and gaskets.  Coolants for refrigeration, freezing and HVAC systems on military vessels are not included in the Annex XV Restriction report, page 134 “MAC- and refrigeration in military applications”. The proposed derogation or derogation for reconsideration only include vehicles in military applications. The exemption should also include military vessels.

6. Missing uses: f.III.  Substances defined as a PFAS by the restriction proposal are used in airborne countermeasures. Details as to why these substances are necessary and why they can not readily be substituted is classified information iaw. The Norwegian security law.  Substances defined as a PFAS by the restriction proposal are used in insensitive high explosive formulas in the form of Viton, a fluoride elastomer. Insensitive explosives are a class of energetic material that is generally characterized by being less sensitive to stimuli than traditional explosives, enabling the production of munition that reacts less violently, i.e. the munition will burn rather than detonate when exposed to rapid heating. The use of Viton contributes significantly towards the insensitive properties of the energetic material, while additionally giving the bulk energetic desirable properties, such as allowing for low temperature casting and machining. Furthermore, energetic materials in use in munitions are expected to endure extreme environments in terms of vibration, temperature extremes and temperature cycling. Viton is crucial in achieving the material properties to endure such environments.  Alternatives to insensitive munitions exists and are readily available. However, reverting to traditional explosives will significantly increase the risk to own forces in terms of severe injury, loss of life and material in a combat environment as well as peace time. There are currently no substitutes that can achieve a similar performance without PFAS. Further details as to why these substances are necessary in particular classes of munition and can not readily be substituted is classified information iaw. The Norwegian security law.  Substances defined as a PFAS by the restriction proposal are used in solid rocket motors and are crucial for performance in the extreme environments associated with the use of a solid rocket motor. Further details as to why these substances are necessary and can not readily be substituted is classified information iaw. The Norwegian security law.  The proposals seeks to restrict the use of functional chemical groups while neglecting to identify each individual substance by e.g. a CAS-number or other appropriate identifier. This makes the job of identifying applicable substances throughout the supply chain hard, within the timeframe of the consultation.  Additionally, a key difference between consumer goods and military ammunition is control throughout the life of a given article. Military ammunition is manufactured and subsequently transported to a storage area. Military storage areas for ammunition are highly controlled environments in terms of access and the risk of unintended release is very low. In peace time, the majority of military ammunition is kept in storage for the duration of the lifetime, in preparedness of and as a deterrence towards armed conflict. In an armed conflict this would be different, but that is considered outside the scope of ECHAs regulatory authority. At the end of the intended lifetime, the ammunition is decommissioned. In peace time, only a fraction of ammunition is used for training and the majority of such ammunition is not known to contain PFAS as this is generally found in more expensive ammunition. Expensive ammunition is used less often for training or substituted with a cheap training version that is a ballistic match. We find that rather than restricting the use of PFAS in military ammunition and energetic materials, a more realistic approach would be to assess suitable methods for decommissioning to limit the release of PFAS.

8. Other identified uses: Products containing PFAS are used on the Norwegian Armed Forces’ aircrafts and helicopters. These products are specified by the aircraft manufacturers. If these products are to be replaced, they must be approved by the respective aircraft manufacturers or by Norwegian Military Airworthiness Authority.  A restriction of PFAS with or without the proposed transition periods and derogations is likely to impact the critical equipment of the Norwegian Armed Forces. The negative impact of reduced military readiness of Norway and other countries in the EU is a mainly qualitative factor, which cannot be quantified.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Answer to Specific Information Request 1:  Annex XV restriction report (Table 9) does not adequately capture the sectors and sub-uses that apply as our energy related industrial systems are used in varied industries including targeted areas of energy transition.  Products and subsystems include industrial compressors, pumps, turbines, motors, electronics valves and vessels.  Specific PFAS applications include seals, gaskets, industrial coatings, cables, transmitters, semiconductors, circuit boards, etc.  Many other components utilize fluoropolymers to ensure durability and product safety with lifetimes of 40+ years. The vast majority of fluoropolymers that are used in our products are in solid form (FKM, FFKM, PTFE, PFA, FEP), which are not prone for PFAS release during their use phase.    It is difficult to identify the extent of PFAS in the supply chain since the majority of the 10,000+ individual PFAS substances covered by the PFAS ANNEX XV report are not currently classified as hazardous or substances of very high concern.  The impact on products supporting both existing energy markets and the development of new green technologies focused on renewables and green hydrogen is readily apparent.  Decarbonisation efforts will also be impacted by a ban on PFAS since this is the primary sealing technology that prevents fugitive greenhouse gas emissions and promotes optimal energy efficiency of the machinery.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Answer to Specific Information Request 2:  PFAS materials which is used in the energy sector are mainly solid state fluoropolymers (PTFE, FKM, FFKM, FEP, PFA) and do not present a substantial source for emissions to the environment as noted during the first consultation phase by ECHA’s impact assessment.

5. Proposed derogations: Answer to Specific Information Request 5:  The proposed derogations do not adequately address that in some applications there are no qualified alternative material available. In some impact assessment sections this is highlighted as “non-availability of alternatives”. Until such alternatives are identified and properly qualified a timetable cannot be identified.

6. Missing uses: Answer to Specific Information Request 6:  PFAS materials have been applied in products within critical applications in the energy and chemicals industry for a long time due to their outstanding properties including extreme temperatures and chemical environments. Due to the process gas constituents containing reactive compounds, FKM and FFKM O-rings are a standard in the industry. The sealing of the compressors is vitally important for containing greenhouse gases and other process gas constituents that may be harmful. A ban on PFAS materials would be either impractical or unsafe for nearly all oil, gas, and petrochemical compression applications. Compressor applications could contain Hydrogen Sulfide (H2S) or Chlorine gases which are lethal even in concentrations of ppm. These compressors are essential in both current and future areas of energy transition.  The proposed ban on PFAS compounds will result in significant safety risks to the operation of industrial process equipment including compressors and will create an environmental impact in terms of an increased carbon footprint during operation. A ban on PFAS compounds works directly against global carbon reduction goals and creates unnecessary safety risks to compressor operations by making compressors less efficient and increasing the risk of leakage of process gases. These very compressors are utilized in carbon capture technology that is being used to help decarburization efforts around the globe, and many energy transition industries (H2, ammonia, CCUS, sustainable fuels, etc.) will need compressors to reduce their carbon footprint.   Currently, alternatives are not available for seals in these applications.  The research and development efforts to find suitable alternatives will come take considerable time, and there is no guarantee that suitable replacements can be quickly found.   The applications in our industry require 50,000 hours of proven service history to become an accepted technology based upon the safety considerations of high-pressure equipment containing harmful process gas constituents and the environmental impact of a failure.  The first item will be to find suitable alternatives and methods that are just as effective in maintaining efficiency and sealing to prevent the leakage of fugitive emissions and in some cases toxic and explosive gases.  Based upon the R&D efforts to develop suitable alternatives and the 50,000 hours necessary to provide a proven service history for industry acceptance, this will take a 10+ year effort to possible develop alternatives.

8. Other identified uses: Answer to Specific Information Request 8:  Exemptions are required for currently installed industrial products in which no suitable alternate materials are available.  These products and applications will continue to require service (potentially with PFAS materials). Exemptions are also required for industrial products that have no PFAS emissions during operation and where no proven alternatives are available. Consideration to the amount of PFAS material quantities in industrial products including compressors, turbines and control systems and its negligible emissions should be taken into account as to not jeopardize essential technologies for chemical processes and the energy transition.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Applications of fluorinated gases/Fluorinated substances used as Foam-Blowing Agents. PU Europe has already commented on the scope of the Restriction proposal (input has been filed under c847c31e-8df9-44a2-8798-218bf9d9ac2a) and see no justification for a ban of Fluorinated Gases notably HFO-1336mzz-Z, HCFO-1233zd-E & HFO-1234ze-E. Concerning the proposed derogation for foam blowing agents, under the application of the F Gas section, we call for a time un-limited derogation with a review clause. The industry needs significant time (more than 5 years) to research new formulations, make them stand the test of time (I.e. ageing of the insulation product to ensure they can deliver performance over the life of the building) and then undergo official certification (in particular for the spray foam products covered by EN 14315 & EN 14318). Furthermore, it is critical to highlight that no assessment has been made on the alternatives to F gases or on F Gas blown insulation products. Furthermore, for products made in factories, a ban would result in manufacturers exiting the business  due to the costs and administrative hurdles to move to pentane and a flammability compliant work environment. For spray foam application, fire safety is a crucial consideration – in most construction/renovation sites it would not be allowed to use flammable (hydrocarbon) blowing agent (spray foam equipment are not even ready for handling them).  Finally, a ban on the use of low GWP F Gases in insulation foam would affect the Renovation Wave (80% of the buildings that will be standing in 2050 have already been built https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/energy-efficiency/energy-efficient-buildings/renovation-wave_en) by not insulating buildings properly (due to the lack of alternative or less energy savings - HCFOs/HFOs have much better insulation properties than these pentanes, in the range of 20-40%).

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Please look at the excel spreadsheet called 2023_08_06 SPF emissions profile. We estimate that a maximum of 10% of the blowing agent (F Gas) is lost during the manufacturing and spraying stage (based on current loadings of HFOs in the formulation compared to earlier HFCs formulations which gave higher number). During the very long use phase (which could last 50 years in certain buildings), the emissions to air could range from 1% up to 31% (based on an optimistic approach and a conservative one- this figure is dependent on the thickness, skin finishing, substrates and so on). As for the emissions to air during the decommissioning stage, as per our internal calculations, these would not amount to more than 1.5% of the remaining gas trapped in the foam. It is therefore assumed that the vast majority of the F Gas (60-87%) will need to be recovered in many decades from now. As for waste management options, according to the final report "Plastic waste from B&C in EU 2018", 65% of the waste is deemed to go to incineration plants.  As Europe moves towards a circular economy, national voluntary or mandatory schemes for the recovery, sorting and recycling of construction and demolition waste will be put into place.  Blowing agent recovery and destruction from household refrigerator’s foam has already been done for years in Europe under the WEEE directive.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: A number of studies have been issued over the past decades on the effectiveness of municipal waste incinerators to treat CFCs/HCFCs. For HFOs/HCFOs, the latest information (RIVM report 2021-0143) indicates that above 850°C the majority of PFASs are removed effectively from flue gas.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Application of F Gas/Foam blowing agents: The spray foam insulation market is estimated to stand at around 100,000 tons of finished products, giving an estimate of around 6,000 tons of HFOs/HCFOs. Using the assumptions presented earlier under section 2, a maximum of 600 Tons of blowing agent would be emitted in the air during the manufacturing stage (with potential for best practices to improve that figure). The vast majority of the remainder of those gases would be trapped in the foam for decades. Concerning the Socio-economic impact due to lack of viable alternatives, please find attached a calculation on the missed energy savings that would result from banning HFO/HCFO on sprayed/poured PU foam and moving to open cell polyurethane products. The untapped energy savings calculated over 30 to 50 years (buildings usually last longer) amount 16.8 TWh – 28 TWh!

8. Other identified uses: To our knowledge, no assessment has been made on the alternatives to F gas and also to F Gas blown insulation products. For a number of applications (like hot water tank or refrigerated truck plants), a ban would result in users of F Gas formulation to get out of business  due to associated costs and administrative hurdle to move to a pentane compliant work environment (necessary safety precautions include explosion proofing of facilities and use of non-sparking tools).

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: We would like to pinpoint to the resources of the EFCTC on the matter, notably the one dated September 2021, https://www.fluorocarbons.org/news/published-evidence-supports-very-low-yields-of-tfa-from-most-hfos-and-hcfos/ . Emissions in the end-of-life phase: High-temperature incineration (HTI) is used as an effective disposal technique for the safe destruction of hazardous PFAS and PFAS-contaminated wastes as stated in the Persistent Organic Pollutants (POP) regulation and the UNEP technical guidelines. HTI is a thermal treatment process that involves subjecting PFAS-contaminated waste to high temperatures, high turbulence, and with sufficient residence times to ensure the destruction and removal of PFAS compounds at a high efficiency.  Eurits members [the European Union for the Responsible Incineration and Treatment of Special Waste] have internal data demonstrating the high destruction efficiency of PFAS in rotary kilns – this data is not yet available to share as members are awaiting a standardised methodology.  The final outputs of incineration are air pollution control residues, fly/boiler ash, and bottom ash/ slag with low POP content which are further treated and eventually landfilled under controlled circumstances.  Recent studies (on an HTI installation within Europe) state that PFAS-containing waste processed at such an HTI installation has no relevant contribution (in terms of impact on human health and the environment). Nevertheless, the current lack of a framework in which reliable, reproducible and validated measurements can be carried out in terms of possible water and air emissions currently makes it impossible to answer the above question scientifically. Therefore, there is a strong need for the development of a standard framework for PFAS air emissions, based on the (eco-)toxicity of the different PFAS, and a strong need for the development of measurement methodologies for guided air emissions. It is essential that PFAS is destroyed for the protection of human health and the environment. HTI provides the needed solution to address PFAS pollution.

6. Missing uses: As a mechanical engineering company in the field of materials handling technology (downstream user), it is foreseeable for us that the PFAS restriction proposal published by ECHA will have a significant impact on our production and products.  Many uses in which certain PFAS play a central role are not mentioned in the restriction proposal, although extensive information was provided by industry in the previous consultations.  In particular, the use of components containing PFASs in industrial plants is not considered, although this is highly relevant for the entire industry and no suitable alternatives currently exist.  All applications not considered without exemptions would be affected by a direct ban of all PFAS after a transition period of only 18 months!  PFAS are present in many mechanical and electrical components that we need to manufacture our machines. For example, in construction and coating materials, valves, seals, motors, sensors, contactors, cables, connectors, belts. For some applications, there are alternatives to products containing PFAS, but often this means sacrificing the service life, performance, and safety of the machines.  Furthermore, the area of spare parts is not considered in the planned regulation. How are existing machines to remain repairable if components containing PFAS may no longer be manufactured? From the point of view of sustainability and cost-effectiveness, it is imperative that exemptions be unlimited or at least adapted to the service life of machines.  From our point of view, the restriction of PFAS should be substance-related and risk-based, as also provided for in Art. 68 (1) of the REACH Regulation, since not all PFAS pose an unacceptable risk that justifies a restriction.  The restriction should differentiate between the different PFAS groups, and the risks posed by their uses and exclude individual substance groups from the restriction proposal altogether.  Industrial applications usually involve the use of fluoropolymers. Some  of these have been scientifically evaluated as "polymers of low concern" (PTFE, ETFE, FEP, PFA, PVDF  and VDF-co-HFP). They have been shown to be chemically stable, nontoxic, non-bioavailable, not water soluble and not mobile. For these reasons, the fluoropolymers are also approved, for example, as materials for food contact or in medical technology. Any deviating classification would have to be scientifically justified.  PFAS groups with low risk (e.g. fluoroelastomers, fluoropolymers, assessed by the OECD as "polymers of low concern"), which do not pose a relevant risk to humans and the environment but guarantee the durability and safety of industrial products and production processes, and uses without relevant risk (e.g. uses in closed systems) should be exempted from the ban.  The planned regulation should clearly distinguish between applications in the consumer sector (B2C) and applications in the industrial sector (B2B).   The chemical scope of the restriction should also be communicated transparently by means of a list of affected substances (including IUPAC names, CAS numbers, EC numbers), so that as a company you can collect the information along your supply chain in a targeted manner.  The proposed restriction is neither safe for companies to comply with nor can it be safely controlled by competent authorities. The limits for the permissible concentrations of PFAS come from the most sophisticated trace analysis, but there are no standard methods for their determination.  The identification of the affectedness is a major challenge for us. The insufficiently harmonized classification of PFAS in the CLP Regulation means that no information is passed on to us as users (e.g. via the safety data sheet), which makes the analysis of the affectedness time-consuming and in many cases almost impossible.  Furthermore, we ask ourselves how it is to be controlled or prevented that products containing PFAS continue to be imported into the EU from outside the EU. This would lead to a competitive disadvantage for us.  Furthermore, it is not comprehensible why applications where PFAS directly enter the environment (e.g. pesticides) are exempted from the restriction and applications where there is no risk to the environment (e.g. components in mechanical engineering) are affected by a ban within 18 months.  The socio-economic effects of the planned PFAS restriction are currently not yet foreseeable for ourselves, our suppliers and customers and therefore lead to considerable uncertainty. Possible effects are:  • Costs due to the identification of affectedness • Costs for the search for alternatives • Cost of switching to alternatives, if available • Impact on machine functionality, life, performance and safety, if applicable • Disruption to supply chains if needed components may no longer be manufactured and alternatives are not available • Loss of revenue due to increased costs or disruption to supply chains • Loss of jobs, if applicable  The indefinite exemption of substances with no relevant risk, such as fluoropolymers, would prevent most impacts before they occur. Competent authorities could focus on the really problematic substances and applications.  Regulations should be limited to a reasonable level and, before they come into force, clear  and pragmatic detection methods should be developed.

The results confirm that fluoropolymers at their end of life when incinerated under representative European municipal incinerators conditions do not generate any measurable levels of PFAS emissions and therefore pose no risk to human health and the environment.  The study provides strong evidence that incinerating a mixture of fluoropolymers under representative municipal waste combustion conditions leads to complete mineralization of the C-F bonds, no significant emissions of long-chain PFAS, and no significant emissions of TFA or light fluorocarbons such as CF4 or C2F6. The absence of organic fluorides and more specifically PFAS in tests representative of municipal waste incineration confirms complete mineralization of fluoropolymers.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: In the plastics industrial packaging industry, very small quantities of polymer processing aids (< 0,1%) based on fluorine-containing monomers are used in polyolefins. These polyolefins will go into the plastic recycling streams with varying PFAS-content. Also some fluorinated packaging or fluorinated gaskets and sealings especially from the croplife sector could end up in the packaging waste stream.  Because PFASs are bound in the polymer, they will not be released from the plastic during mechanical recycling to the environment. They remain in the plastic and can be reused in new plastic products. In order to check the TOF-limit of 50ppm (or 50 ppm limit for fluoropolymers) for recycled PE or PP set on the market, a recycler would have to check each recycled batch for PFAS without having the possibility to influence the PFAS concentration during the recycling step. Additionally, currently, there is no standardized analytical method available to check the content of fluoropolymers in plastics, thus the proposed limit for content of fluoropolymers cannot be controlled. Therefore, we ask for an exemption for the output material of the plastic recyclers.

5. Proposed derogations: We estimate that total emissions to the environment from the contents of fluorinated plastic packaging in Europe are significantly less than 500 grams/year. These estimates are derived from the maximum value of the leach-out studies and the total amount of plant protection products.

6. Missing uses: • Transport packaging (drum, jerrycans and IBCs) for dangerous goods  • Technical textiles (Membranes used for the ventilation of IBCs and packagings which must be water, oil and alcohol repellent)  • Seals and gaskets for dangerous goods packaging.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Plastic regenerate and internal recyclate use pose a major problem in complying with the proposed limit of 50 ppm. Not only the intended use, but also the indirect use via reclaim in types that are actually PFAS-free, but may contain PFAS at significantly lower levels due to internal reclaim. However, this influence decreases over the years due to the potential limitation in the intentional use of PFAS in virgin materials.  In order to remain deliverable, we propose a longer transition period for packaging placed on the market (packaging for dangerous goods/sealing/gaskets: 12 years)  We would like to add that this suggested time covers also the development time at the packaging producer as well as the implementation at our costumer. The customer/filler must also test their products for the new (PFAS-free) packaging in a time-consuming and costly manner: e.g., pre-storage of the filling materials for several months and subsequent testing of the packaging materials for several months in accordance with dangerous goods legislation.

8. Other identified uses: An alternative to fluorination is coextrusion of the primary plastic (typically HDPE) with a thin layer of PA (polyamide) or EVOH (co-polymer of ethylene and vinylalcohol). The barrier properties of coextruded containers are similar as with fluorinated packaging. For the following reasons, these alternatives could only be implemented to a limited extent:- Intermediate container sizes (20-200 L) cannot be produced as CoEx containers. Coextruded packaging could be an extra limitation in the ability to recycle the plastic after use. Fluorinated plastic packagings, on the other hand, can be recycled and possibly used in bottle-to-bottle recycling. In addition to the pure additional costs due to the higher material consumption for the alternative coextruded barrier layer during production, there will also be further additional costs due to the taxes on non-recyclable packaging envisaged in the EU, which would only affect the alternative packaging (multilayer packaging).

10. Analytical methods: There are still many open questions about PFAS analysis. We would welcome the development of standardised analytical methods for PFAS in plastics at CEN level.

The fluorinated fluids used in direct contact, two-phase immersion cooling for high performance computing require a specific combination of thermophysical, safety, and compatibility properties. Fluids such as nonafluoro-2-trifluoromethyl-3-pentanone display not only a high dielectric strength to prevent arcing but also very low dielectric constant to protect signal integrity which is essential in high performance computing. The fluids possess sufficiently low viscosity as well as high enough heat capacity and vaporization enthalpy to facilitate efficient heat transfer. This results in significant reduction in data center energy consumption. The fluids are nonflammable and demonstrate low toxicity allowing their use in an occupied data center. No technology is currently available or in development that can adequately replace the use of a fluorinated fluid in direct contact, two-phase immersion cooling for high performance computing.  Not-in-kind technologies have been used to remove the heat generated in data centers, including air cooling (forced convection) and immersion in a single phase, hydrocarbon oil (both synthetic and fluids derived from natural sources). However, these cooling technologies are insufficient to meeting the heat transfer demands of high-performance computing such as that required with artificial intelligence. The proximity of devices and resulting high power density which enables these computations is not sufficiently cooled by conventional heat transfer methods such as air cooling or single phase, dielectric liquids. Thus, although the demand for high performance computing continues to grow, no alternative to the currently used fluorinated fluids is currently available which can meet the technical, performance and safety requirements . e. Cooling computer hardware by direct immersion in a dielectric fluid has been conducted on a commercial scale for nearly 40 years. The Cray-2 supercomputer debuted in 1985 using liquid immersion cooling with a fluorinated fluid. The extremely high density of components required to achieve the supercomputer performance requirements was not able to be effectively cooled with air or oil. “Effective cooling techniques are central to the design of high-speed computational systems.” (The Cray-2 Series of Computer Systems, Cray Research, Inc., 1988). Through today, high performance computing continues to rely upon fluorinated fluids to meet its intense cooling needs. Decades of research has been conducted as industry searched for safe, environmentally sustainable chemistries for refrigerants and heat transfer liquids (J. Chem. Eng. Data 2020, 65, 4176−4193). New compounds have been developed to overcome environmental concerns associated with ozone depletion and climate change. Some applications have also been able to return to the use of flammable hydrocarbons through system design changes. However, no technology has been able to simultaneously meet the demanding performance and safety requirements of high performance computing applications other than a fluorinated fluid. Traditionally, datacenters have relied on air-based solutions to dissipate heat, primarily employing three methods: (1) chiller-based cooling, (2) water-side economized cooling, and (3) direct evaporative (free) cooling. Chiller-based cooling employs a closed-loop system featuring a water chiller, while water-side economization incorporates cooling towers to lower water temperatures through evaporation.  In response to escalating chip temperatures, liquid cooling has been introduced by cloud providers. Initial implementations typically involve placing cold plates on the most power-intensive components. These cold plates facilitate the flow of fluid through them and the associated piping to effectively dissipate heat from these components. However, this approach demands tailored design and manufacturing of cold plates for each new component, adding complexity to engineering and prolonging time-to-market. Additionally, even with cold plates in use, air cooling is often still required for other components. Microsoft Corporation published a comparison summarizing the advantage of 2-PIC with alternatives (Misra, P.A., et al. (2022). Overclocking in immersion-cooled datacenters. IEEE Micro, 42(4), 10–17.). The comparison demonstrated that 2-PIC provides more than twice the server cooling capacity while consuming less than half the cooling power of the nearest alternative due to its more efficient heat transfer. Please see the attached file for additional details. In our assessment of overall performance comparison 2-PIC was clearly the only technology that can simultaneously meet the demanding performance, economic and safety requirements for current and emerging needs of this societally important technology. The attached file provides a comparison table and additional details. g. According to IEA, the share of data center energy use is significantly higher in countries with growing data center markets: Data centers accounted for 18% of the total energy consumption by Ireland in 2022; Data center energy demand is estimated to rise to 15% in Denmark by 2030. The use of 2-PIC presents a unique opportunity to make the next generation of computing technology and data centers significantly more energy efficient. Reduced energy consumption will result in lower energy-generation emissions and contribute to achieving the EU climate objectives.  Without 2-PIC, development of the most advanced, high-performance computing applications will be severely inhibited. This will have a direct impact on the advancement of technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) and applications of it such as machine learning. A briefing for the European Parliament acknowledges that “Artificial intelligence plays an increasingly important role in our lives and economy and is already having an impact on our world in many different ways.” As OECD stated in its 2023 assessment “Policy makers and actors across research systems can do much to accelerate and deepen the uptake of AI in science, magnifying its positive contributions to research. This will support the ability of OECD countries to grow, innovate and address global challenges, from climate change to new contagions.”  The anticipated benefits of AI through productivity gains and innovation will stall without the continued advancement in computing technology which is currently dependent upon the use of a fluorinated fluid to safely and effectively meet cooling requirements. 6. Missing uses: One PFAS use that does not yet seem to be identified is forensic science, more specifically, fingerprint detection.  Forensic science is a small sector compared to those already identified in this PFAS restriction report, yet an important one in terms of law enforcement, crime resolution and reduction, and public safety.  Fingerprint researchers and forensic practitioners need sufficient time to conduct research and to validate suitable solvent alternatives prior to a complete ban of PFASs.  We are already under a time crunch with 3M’s announcement of their plans to cease manufacturing PFASs by end of 2025.  Currently, 3M Novec HFE7100 and HFE71DE are the primary carrier solvents in all three amino acid sensitive chemical formulations that are used to develop fingerprints on porous exhibit items (e.g., paper, envelopes, cheques, magazines, cardboard) in criminal investigations in Canada and internationally.  These solvents help to carry other reagents to the fingerprint residues that are absorbed into the porous surfaces.  We are aware of one other solvent that is currently used in amino acid reagents for casework by two international police agencies.  Unfortunately, these agencies have also reported explosions in their laboratory facilities when using this solvent.  There are approximately 160 police agencies in Canada, covering federal, provincial, and municipal jurisdictions.  We believe that the majority of these agencies are unaware that a potential PFAS ban is being considered (we were not aware that the Government of Canada was seeking input from stakeholders in 2021; we only found out about this opportunity from a European counterpart a few weeks before the submission deadline) and that HFE7100/DE will no longer be available within a couple of years.  While 3M made their announcement in Dec 2022, we were not made aware until Mar 2023 by a forensic supply distributor, who has direct contact with the manufacturer.  Several Canadian police agencies were unaware in May 2023 at an in-person event and one police agency reached out to us only a couple of weeks ago.  Many Canadian police agencies are not in a position to conduct fingerprint research, as the forensic practitioners (primarily police officers) are occupied with attending and processing crime scenes, processing exhibits, etc.  While our organization found out about a potential PFAS ban in Europe back in 2020, we could not start researching alternative solvents until summer 2023 due to staff shortages, the COVID-19 pandemic (limited access to laboratory, fingerprint donors), and other organization-driven priorities.  We were the first Canadian police agency to conduct a research study investigating an alternative solvent to HFE7100/DE that appeared promising based on three recent peer-reviewed publications (research conducted in three different countries), only to find out in June 2023 that it would also be considered a PFAS, depending on which definition was used.  That being said, the manufacturer stated it does not plan to stop production.  Unfortunately, there were some operational issues that should not be ignored (e.g., laboratory renovations likely required to properly store compressed gas cylinder; more expensive glassware needed to safely store working solutions; access to refrigerator/freezer required; alternative solvent caused an increase in ink diffusion).  Our organization hopes to assess other alternative solvents within the next year.  Multiple research studies are required prior to recommendation for implementation into operations.  While we may not be able to provide you with the exact information desired, we hope the following will provide you with some useful insights or aspects to consider: - When fingerprint researchers/forensic practitioners were looking for an alternative solvent to CFCs (Freon 113) which were being banned in the 1990s, it took about five years before HFE products were considered suitable.  Additional years were required to optimize the chemical formulations for effective fingerprint development. - The amount of porous exhibit items to process for fingerprint evidence can various depending on where a forensic identification unit is located in Canada.  For example, in a past national field trial, a unit only processed one porous exhibit in a year.  During the same time period, another unit processed over 1760 porous exhibits belonging to a single criminal investigation, plus additional items from other investigations.  Therefore, the amount of solvent required will vary depending on caseload.  Please note, our organization alone has ~65 units across the country. - Our organization adheres to the International Fingerprint Research Group guidelines, which break down research studies into four main phases: proof-of-concept, optimization/comparison, pseudo-operational to casework trials.  Therefore, several years are needed to compare HFE7100/DE to other solvents.  Not all fingerprint researchers are able to collaborate with police agencies. - While the focus may be to find an alternative solvent for fingerprint development, it is important that additional research is conducted to determine the impact of/on other forensic analyses (e.g., DNA, questioned documents), as the goal is to maximize evidence recovery.  Not all police agencies have easy access to these other disciplines to collaborate. - Many forensic organizations also need to meet accreditation standards (e.g., ISO 17025).  Therefore, research conducted needs to be scientifically/statistically sound and robust. - While there may be alternative solvents to explore, we may run into issues with manufacturers we have never dealt with before.  Also, forensic science is a niche application and therefore not likely to represent a large portion of solvent manufacturers’ client/product portfolio.  Therefore, additional discussions may be required for alternate packing sizes, etc.

Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: With reference to the ""Annex XV restriction report"" Chapter 2.4.3.3.point g) paragraph (xiv) or Table 13 Applications of fluorinated gases (Annex E.2.8.): Even though there are currently PFAS-free products for gas-insulated electrical switchgear up to 145kV on the market, only one manufacturer (Siemens Energy) can currently serve European switchgear needs now and for the next 10-15 years. The competitors (Hitachi Energy, GE Power & Grid) have indicated that there is currently no development strategy for non-PFAS, gas-insulated high-voltage switchgear for the European market. In times of the energy transition and the massive grid expansion required to maximize feed-in capacity from renewables, it would be an economic-political problem to leave the potential switchgear market throughout Europe to just one manufacturer for the next 10-15 years. Transition periods are also not a solution in the medium term - a comprehensive derogation is needed here. Regarding gas-insulated electrical switchgear above 145kV, there are currently no PFAS-free products ready for the market; especially for circuit breakers, there are currently no discernible development steps at this voltage level. Moreover, there are already physical limits in the development of such switchgear, where even market maturity in the next 10-15 years seems unrealistic at present.   In general, decarbonising industry and district heating is a major challenge if we are to meet our targets for reducing CO2 emissions, in particular Fit for 55 ones. As a result, the deployment of Heat Pumps (HPs) to decarbonise district heating and industrial heat has been identified as one of the main solutions. The impact of the PFAS ban on Refrigeration, Air Conditioning and Heat Pumps would be twofold:  1) All fluoropolymers fall under the proposed definition in the proposal. These substances such as PTFE, FPM etc are critical to most of the components which makes these systems run efficiently and at best performance.  2) Most F-gases, which are a core part of the full portfolio of refrigerants used on RACHP applications are covered by the proposal. Refrigerants are an essential element for the good functioning of their RACHP components, equipment and systems to heat and cool.    In the case of large high-temperature heat pumps, crucial for the decarbonisation of industry and district heating, special refrigerants called Hydro Fluoro Olefines (HFO, e.g. R1234ze) have been developed in order to replace refrigerants according to the F-Gas Regulation (e.g. R134a). These HFOs allow high temperature ranges combined with a high efficiency. They are not ozone-depleting, have a very low GWP and are in case of accidents not so dangerous compared to alternatives like NH3 (toxicity) or propane (flammability and explosion protection). There are already technical solutions to minimise emissions into the atmosphere. A large number of these HFO-based heat pumps with a lifetime of more than 20 years have been recently installed or are in installation. Because the heat pumps are constructed according to the refrigerants’ physical properties, the revamping of the heat pump in order to use natural refrigerants is not possible. It needs to be possible to operate them until the end of their lifetime.   The industrial HP market can be divided into 3 categories depending on heat supply temperature (up to the actual limit of 150°C):  - Standard HPs providing heat up to 85°C - High-temperature (HT) heat pumps providing heat from 85°C to 100°C  - Very high temperature HPs (VHTs) providing heat between 100 to 150°C.  The F-Gas Regulation, under ongoing review, mandates the progressive phasing out of fluorinated gases, including HFCs used in refrigeration systems. In order to meet these requirements, European industrials developed few years ago HFC-free solutions, today mature or very close to maturity (in the process of being demonstrated) for these three markets.  Most of solutions for the HT and VHT markets (supply temperature > 90°C) are designed to use an HFO-type refrigerant (r1234ze(Z); r1234ze(E); r1233zd(E); r1336mzz(Z)), which belongs to the PFAS family. Manufacturers of industrial HPs have chosen this solution for a number of reasons: Zero ODP, extremely low GWP, limited or zero flammability, non-toxic, optimum performance at target temperatures.  For heat pumps providing heat at high or very high level (> 90°C), alternative refrigerants to HFO are still non-existent from a commercial point of view (TRL < TRL 9): the first laboratory demonstrators are under way and the first field demonstrations will see the light of day from 2024/2025 (often using hydrocarbon-type fluids: butane or n-pentane). The use of hydrocarbons will also require time for industries to adapt in order to incorporate these highly flammable refrigerants. The use of water is also an alternative but at laboratory demonstration stage for closed cycles.
