Analytical methods: RISE Research Institutes of Sweden has coordinated the POPFREE Industry project, and collaborated with partners, especially with the Department of Environmental Science at Stockholm University in developing analytical methods to screen products for PFAS-content with focus on polymeric PFAS. Combustion ion chromatography (CIC)-based total fluorine (TF) determination together with pyrolysis-gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (Pyr-GC/MS) have successfully been used for quantification and identification of polymeric PFAS in a wide range of product samples. The combination of these two methods offers a promising strategy for enforcing the 50 ppm concentration limit including polymeric PFAS in materials and products in the class-wide PFAS restriction. Compared to methods that employ extraction before analysis, both CIC and pyr-GC/MS are based on direct thermal breakdown of samples which makes them faster and better suited for detection of polymers. The higher detection limits associated with CIC and pyr-GC/MS make these techniques unsuitable for enforcing the 25 ppb/250 ppb individual PFAS limits that require a more sensitive, targeted approach.   Over 50 consumer product samples have been analysed. Products that are known to contain intentionally added fluoropolymers or side-chain fluorinated polymers display levels between 200 ppm and 630 000 ppm (mg/kg or µg/g). The latter high concentrations are obtained when analysing for example a PTFE non-stick coating or dental floss made of PTFE. Highly fluorinated ski wax measure 57 000 ppm, PTFE as an additive in the plastic measured around 1500 ppm (corresponds to 0.15 w% in the plastic). In know PFAS-treated textiles typical fluorine concentrations are in the range 200 – 1600 ppm. Interestingly all textile with known PFAS-free treatments measured less than 50 ppm indicating that the 50 ppm total fluorine concentration is a realistic value separating the PFAS-free from PFAS-containing textiles. Also, other products that were known to be PFAS-free measured a total fluorine concentration under 50 ppm.    To confirm that the fluorine was organic in nature, and deduce structure, a qualitative pyrolysis-gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (pyr-GC/MS) method was validated using a suite of reference materials. When applied to samples with unknown PFAS content, the method was successful at identifying polytetrafluoroethylene in cookware, dental products, and electronics at concentrations as little as, both when being the main ingredient and as an additive in the plastic at 0.1-0.2 wt%. It was also possible to distinguish between 3 different side-chain fluorinated polymers in textiles.   RISE has employed these two methods in contract work with industry partners. In two projects the samples were textiles. As a first step all textiles were screened for total fluorine and the samples with a total fluorine concentration over 50 ppm were analysed with pyr-GC/MS. The presence of side-chain fluorinated polymers (SFP) was confirmed in all those samples. Most samples contained a C6-SFP but we could also find a couple of samples that contained C8-SFP. In another customer project cookware products were analysed. The total fluorine was less than 50 ppm and we could not detect any fluoropolymer with pyr-GC/MS. This product was designed to be PFAS-free.   For some cookware products and electronic samples such as heat protective coatings/sheets in a coffee maker (and possibly in other household equipment that we have not yet analysed) and cables we measure a total fluorine concentration between 70 – 3000 ppm, but we cannot conclude the presence of PFAS with pyr-GC/MS. Some further investigation indicate that these products may contain the inorganic pigment mica, an inorganic pigment/filler that is commonly used in cookware to provide pearlescent aesthetics and for heat protection in high-temperature applications. Thus, for future compliance pyr-GC/MS is a suitable technique to verify the origin of the quantified fluorine. Although many product samples have been analysed there are more to be tested and further optimization that could be done.   Further method development is planned to be elaborated in PARC - receiving funding from the European Union’s Horizon Europe research and innovation programme under Grant Agreement No 101057014, project 6.4.3.b 2023-2026.  The higher detection limits associated with CIC and pyr-GC/MS make these techniques unsuitable for enforcing individual PFAS limits (25 ppb/250 ppb), which require a more targeted approach with for example LC-MS/MS. The 25 ppb limit is reasonable for individual PFAS. What has to be decided in the final restriction is how many and which PFAS substances that should be analysed for this 250 ppm of total PFAS, but since many products and articles contain polymeric PFAS, the total fluorine detection is more appropriate as a first screening. For example, in a textile sample that was analysed we detected a concentration of 1500 ppm total fluorine (and a C6-SFP was confirmed with pyr-GC/MS) and when analysing the same sample with target analysis of 24 individual PFAS substances, the total sum was 11 ppb. After oxidation and TOPA (total oxidizable precurssor assay) the total sum had increased to 3000 ppb, but still way far from the levels obtained with total fluorine. General Comments: - Our company is engaged in the design, fabrication, and construction of architectural membrane structures, and we are in a position to purchase membrane materials from membrane manufacturers.
- Membrane materials used in architectural applications include PTFE-coated glass cloth membranes, PVC-coated polyester or glass cloth membranes with a top coat of PVDF or titanium oxide, and ETFE films.
- Most of these membrane materials are utilizing Fluoropolymers PFAS, which will not be able to be used if fluoropolymers are restricted.
- These membrane materials are used for architectural roofing & façade due to their lightweight nature, safety, design flexibility, and ability to create well-lit interiors underneath.
- The main applications of membrane materials include stadiums, train stations, gymnasiums, sports facilities, recreational facilities, roofs of large plaza and shopping malls and wall facades of buildings.
- Especially for applications that require durability of over 40 years, such as stadiums, PTFE-coated membrane materials are adopted.
- In recent World Cups (in Germany, Brazil, South Africa, Qatar), the roofs of 23 out of all the 42 stadiums (55%) were membrane roofs, all of which used membranes utilizing PFAS.
- Glass fabrics coated with PTFE possesses high durability, corrosion resistance, light transmission, and antifouling properties, making it an essential material among highly-durable membranes.
- Glass fabrics coated with PTFE membranes have a proven track record of over 30 years of service life, with some projects even exceeding 50 years (project list attached in Section IV).
- There is no alternative to PTFE coating for such highly durable membrane materials, and there are no membrane materials with comparable performance.
- If PTFE is restricted, there will be no viable alternative, and membranes will no longer be used on long lasting stadium roofs.
- PVC membranes are commonly used for architectural structure, but their service life is approximately 10 years when not protected by a PVDF top coat, with the assumption of replacement within 10 years.
- If PVDF Fluoropolymers, is top coated on PVC membranes, the service life extends to 15 to 25 years (depending on the type of PVDF).
- In addition, if titanium oxide is top coated on PVC membranes, the service life is about 15 years. But PVC/TiO2 is already existing for long time and is still representing a very low part of the PVC coated membranes worldwide and especially in Europe.
- If PVDF top coating is prohibited, membrane materials will be limited to applications where replacement is possible within 10 to 15 years and the market for membrane structures will shrink significantly. PVC/TiO2 will not be an alternative for PVDF.
- Pure ETFE foils is a membrane material that can be used as an alternative to glass.  It is transparent, has the same durability as glass, and is lightweight and safe. Its safety even if it breaks, which is a big advantage over glass, greatly contributes to its adoption. ETFE foils is very light and more flexible than rigid glass panels. It is an alternative in challenging environment like earthquake or stormy zones.
- If the use of ETFE is prohibited, there is no other resin that combines transparency, flexibility and durability as an alternative, so traditional glass will continue to be used in atriums.
- ETFE is 100 times lighter than glass and its Environmental product declaration(EPD) is available(See the attached in Section Ⅳ).
- Fluoropolymers are totally different from other PFAS. Their toxicological and environmental profiles is totally different than other PFAS chemicals that are of concern. Fluoropolymers used in Tensile architecture such as PVDF, ETFE, ECTFE, FEP, PFA, PTFE, are inert, stable, resistant to fire, stain resistant, and highly durable. All those characteristics make them unique and non-replaceable by any other alternative because no other material is able to achieve all performances together. And as there is no toxicological and environmental reason to consider them in the same restriction process as other PFAS. We are deeply concerned that the regulation of PFAS would set the architectural membrane industry back by 50 years and we support the statement made by FCJ on the issues of proposed restriction as per attached in section Ⅳ and request an exemption of all fluoropolymers from this restriction proposal under the REACH regulation.

8. Other identified uses: a.  PTFE is used for coating composite membranes with glass cloth. As a manufacturer of roofs we use   Glass/PTFE membrane that represent a total consumption of PTFE is 3.8 tons. Pure ETFE foils are used as standalone architectural membrane. The annual usage of ETFE is 9.7 tons. We use PES/PVC/PVDF membranes. PVDF is thinly coated on the surface of PVC for its antifouling and weather-resistant properties. The annual usage of PVDF is 0.3 tons. b.  ① PTFE PTFE is coated on both sides of glass cloth and used as a membrane material, being the only resin that simultaneously possesses the durability of over 40 years, fire safety, dirt resistance, and light transmittance required for large-scale architectural membrane applications. PTFE is considered an indispensable material for roofs of buildings, such as stadiums, designed to be in use for over 40 years. ② ETFE ETFE is a single film used in membrane structures, having transparency, durability of over 30 years, dirt resistance, and fire safety as a membrane material.  In architecture, ETFE is employed as an alternative to glass, serving as the essential and sole material that combines transparency, durability, and safety.  ③ PVDF PVDF is used as a PVC top coat, providing protection for PVC, enhancing durability and dirt resistance. General PVDF top coated membranes are designed to have a durability of 15 years, while specialized PVDF top coated membranes are designed to have a durability of 25 years. c.  Directly, membrane manufacturers, membrane processing companies, and construction companies within the EU will be affected. Indirectly, membrane manufacturers, membrane processing companies, and construction companies outside the EU that conduct business with EU will also be affected. The number of companies is unknown. d.  Alternatives to PTFE membrane materials: The durability of PTFE membrane is 40~50 years. (1) Membrane material coated with PVC on both sides of glass cloth. The surface of this membrane is thinly coated with titanium oxide as an antifouling treatment. It has a durability of 15 years.  Although it is possible to acquire the incombustibility certification required by Japanese building codes, PVC is two to three times more flammable than PTFE, so its durability is reduced when limited to thinner thicknesses. It exhibits excellent antifouling performance. It’s cost is lower than PTFE. Its tensile strength is low. This membrane material cannot serve as an alternative to PTFE membranes in terms of durability. (2) Membrane materials coated with PVC on both sides of polyester cloth. There are two types of membrane materials within this kind; one is top coated with titanium oxide and the other is top coated with PVDF for an antifouling treatment. Both have a durability of 15 years. They cannot obtain incombustibility certification and therefore cannot be used as construction materials in Japan. They exhibit excellent dirt resistance. It is possible to manufacture ones with high tensile strength. However, as the thickness increases, permeability decreases. These membrane materials cannot serve as alternatives to PTFE membranes in terms of durability and fire resistance. (3) Membrane material coated with silicone on both sides of glass cloth. It is durable for over 20 years. It cannot obtain incombustibility certification. Its antifouling performance is low and has not been improved for 30 years. Since no antifouling coating can be applied over silicone, it is impossible to provide antifouling property to it. It has low tensile strength and poor bonding performance. Although this membrane material has better durability than PVC, due to its poor antifouling and bonding performances, it cannot be used as an alternative. This material has been developed more than 20 years ago and never been a success in tensile roof with only few big project done which have not been success stories.  It is concluded that no material is as durable as PTFE.  Alternative to ETFE: The durability of ETFE is over 30 years. Membrane materials using transparent PVC have comparable transparency to ETFE, but their weather resistance is significantly poor, resulting in a service life of approximately 5 to 7 years. They cannot serve as alternatives for ETFE. There are no other transparent resins that can replace ETFE.  Alternative to PVDF top coated membrane: The durability of a general PVDF top coated membrane is 15 years, while a specialized PVDF top coated membrane can last 25 years.  (1) Acrylic top coated membrane: Acrylic top coat has lower UV blocking performance and a durability of 10 years, which is 5 years shorter than a general PVDF. Additionally, its antifouling performance is lower than PVDF. (2) Titanium oxide top coat membrane: The durability of a titanium oxide top coated membrane is 15 years, which is equivalent to a basic PVDF. However, it is 10 years shorter than a specialized PVDF. It exhibits excellent antifouling performance. e.  Composite membrane material of glass cloth coated with silicone is available, but it has extremely poor antifouling performance. If used as a roofing material, regular cleaning every few months is necessary to maintain its whiteness, which is not practical. If the membrane is initially made gray, the dirt becomes less visible, but it hinders light transmission, negating the benefits of using a membrane. Additionally, special tapes are required for bonding, and the thermal bonding process requires higher pressure compared to PTFE, resulting in the need for facility upgrades costing hundreds of thousands of dollars. f.  Currently, the available alternative membrane material is PVC membrane with titanium oxide top coat, which has a service life of 15 years and good dirt resistance. However, using PVC membrane with titanium oxide top coated as an alternative to PTFE membrane in stadiums is not feasible due to its relatively short service life, requiring replacement every 15 years. Stadium owners are unlikely to accept the cost of frequent replacements within a short period. As a result, membrane solutions will no longer be chosen for stadiums, and alternative roofing materials will be selected instead. Moreover, in the case of existing PTFE membranes that have suffered partial damage from flying objects or other causes, repairs cannot be made with PVC membrane with titanium oxide top coat. Consequently, a switch to non-membrane roofing materials becomes necessary. However, this would involve structural changes, leading to a complete rebuild and placing a significant financial burden on the owners. (Please refer to the attachment in Section IV for the list of existing PTFE and ETFE projects within the EU.)  As for the alternatives to PVDF top coat membrane, the durability of general PVDF is 15 years. Therefore, PVC membrane with titanium oxide top coat can be considered as a viable alternative with similar durability. However, PVC membrane with titanium oxide top coat is already existing for long time and is still representing a very low part of the PVC coated membranes worldwide and especially in Europe. Specialized PVDF membrane materials offer a durability of 20 to 30 years, making them less durable options compared to PVC membrane with titanium oxide top coat . As a result, the replacement cycle for PVC membrane with titanium oxide top coat would be sooner in these cases. g.  In practice, there are no alternative membrane materials that can replace PTFE membrane or ETFE. Therefore, in the EU market, only PVC membranes without PVDF will be available, resulting in a significant contraction of the membrane structure market. It is certain that our group company in the EU (Taiyo Europe) will be greatly affected, and we will have no choice but to consider withdrawing from the EU market.  On the other hand, outside the EU, we plan to continue manufacturing and selling PTFE membranes, ETFE, and PVDF top coat membranes as before. However, we will no longer be purchasing membrane materials from EU-based manufacturers subject to regulations.  In addition, the existing PTFE membrane and ETFE buildings in the EU cannot be repaired if the membrane is damaged, so they will have to be changed to roof materials other than membrane materials. This would involve a complete structural overhaul, imposing a significant financial burden on the owners.

PTFE is considered an indispensable material for roofs of buildings, such as stadiums, designed to be in use for over 40 years.  ② ETFE ETFE is a single film used in membrane structures, having transparency, durability of over 30 years, dirt resistance, and fire safety as a membrane material. (2) Membrane materials coated with PVC on both sides of polyester cloth. There are two types of membrane materials within this kind; one is top coated with titanium oxide and the other is top coated with PVDF for an antifouling treatment. Both have a durability of 15 years. They exhibit excellent dirt resistance. It is possible to manufacture ones with high tensile strength. However, as the thickness increases, permeability decreases. These membrane materials cannot serve as alternatives to PTFE membranes in terms of durability and fire resistance. (3) Membrane material coated with silicone on both sides of glass cloth. It is durable for over 20 years. Its antifouling performance is low and has not been improved for 30 years. Although this membrane material has better durability than PVC, due to its poor antifouling and bonding performances, it cannot be used as an alternative. It is concluded that no material is as durable as PTFE.  Alternative to ETFE: The durability of ETFE is over 30 years. Membrane materials using transparent PVC have comparable transparency to ETFE, but their weather resistance is significantly poor, resulting in a service life of approximately 5 to 7 years. They cannot serve as alternatives for ETFE. There are no other transparent resins that can replace ETFE.  Alternative to PVDF top coated membrane: The durability of a general PVDF top coated membrane is 15 years, while a specialized PVDF top coated membrane can last 25 years. Additionally, its antifouling performance is lower than PVDF.  (2) Titanium oxide top coat membrane: The durability of a titanium oxide top coated membrane is 15 years, which is equivalent to a basic PVDF. However, it is 10 years shorter than a specialized PVDF. It exhibits excellent antifouling performance.  e.  Composite membrane material of glass cloth coated with silicone is available, but it has extremely poor antifouling performance. If used as a roofing material, regular cleaning every few months is necessary to maintain its whiteness, which is not practical. If the membrane is initially made gray, the dirt becomes less visible, but it hinders light transmission, negating the benefits of using a membrane. Additionally, special tapes are required for bonding, and the thermal bonding process requires higher pressure compared to PTFE, resulting in the need for facility upgrades costing hundreds of thousands of dollars.  f.   Currently, the available alternative membrane material is PVC membrane with titanium oxide top coat, which has a service life of 15 years and good dirt resistance. Stadium owners are unlikely to accept the cost of frequent replacements within a short period. As a result, membrane solutions will no longer be chosen for stadiums, and alternative roofing materials will be selected instead. However, this would involve structural changes, leading to a complete rebuild and placing a significant financial burden on the owners. Specialized PVDF membrane materials offer a durability of 20 to 30 years, making them less durable options compared to PVC membrane with titanium oxide top coat . As a result, the replacement cycle for PVC membrane with titanium oxide top coat would be sooner in these cases.  g.  In practice, there are no alternative membrane materials that can replace PTFE membrane or ETFE. Therefore, in the EU market, only PVC membranes without PVDF will be available, resulting in a significant contraction of the membrane structure market. It is certain that our group company in the EU (Taiyo Europe) will be greatly affected, and we will have no choice but to consider withdrawing from the EU market.  On the other hand, outside the EU, we plan to continue manufacturing and selling PTFE membranes, ETFE, and PVDF top coat membranes as before. However, we will no longer be purchasing membrane materials from EU-based manufacturers subject to regulations.  In addition, the existing PTFE membrane and ETFE buildings in the EU cannot be repaired if the membrane is damaged, so they will have to be changed to roof materials other than membrane materials. This would involve a complete structural overhaul, imposing a significant financial burden on the owners.

Org. name: Arbeitsgemeinschaft der Wissenschaftlichen Medizinischen Fachgesellschaften e.V. (AWMF)
Combined Comments:
General Comments: - The Association of Scientific Medical Societies in Germany (AWMF) points out, that PFAS are widely used in the medical field and are central components of modern medical devices.
- There is currently a knowledge gap regarding the composition and harmlessness of PFAS in medical devices.
- The regulation of PFAS use planned by the EU Commission with the aim of a far-reaching PFAS ban is supported in principle by the AWMF. However, two principles must be guaranteed:
1. the medical care of the population must be guaranteed at a state-of-the-art level at all times.
2. the PFAS subgroups must be classified risk-adapted and treated differently to facilitate further use.
-  PFAS have ideal characteristics for use in medical devices with regard to sterilization, long-term exposure and tissue compatibility (biocompatibility, in the case of fluoropolymers). As a consequence a ban on PFAS in the field of medical devices can only be implemented if substitute substances with comparable properties are available and new medical devices can be brought to market approval. For both prerequisites a considerable lead time is necessary.
- Exemptions or derogations from the PFAS ban in the medical field are therefore inevitable in order to ensure modern patient care in a transition phase of sufficient duration.
PLEASE, SEE NON-CONFIDENTIAL ATTACHMENT: AWMF-Position Paper for background, detailed analysis, discussion, references, and current survey results.
Conclusions:
- PFAS possess properties that currently make them indispensable for the production of medical devices and thus for state-of-the-art patient care.
- For obvious reasons of environmental pollution and possible health hazards PFAS should be banned in the European area.
- The transitional periods, that are provided, if an exemption is granted, are very likely to be too short to develop equivalent substitute substances and to bring corresponding new medical devices to market approval, especially under the requirements of the MDR.
- As the safest option for maintaining patient care, the AWMF therefore advocates sector-specific regulation for medical devices in line with the exemption for medical products (pharmaceuticals). Should no agreement be reached on this, at least "PFAS of low concern" must be exempted from the ban.
- In parallel, all efforts must be made by research and development to maximize the proportion of "PFAS of low concern" within the total group of PFAS used and to generate harmless substitute substances for PFAS.
- Efficient control of the production process and the disposal or recycling of medical devices would significantly reduce the discharge into the environment.
- The AWMF points out possibilities for practicable solutions to continue the production of medical devices in the EU while improving the protection of humans and environment from PFAS substances. It is important to consider that a PFAS ban in the EU would mean, that production has to be relocated abroad in order to maintain the indispensable product range for patient care. The consequence would most likely be the continuation of production under lower standards.

General Comments: ・Kyoritsu industries was established in 1944, and has been manufacturing industrial fabric materials and products, mainly to Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corporation, Japan Railway Companies and Japanese Governments. We have currently developed into an engineering company and supplies and builds many kinds of membrane structures and high-performance fabric products. Kyoritsu acquired ISO9001 certification in 2003, and MSAJ (Membrane Structures Association of Japan) highest level certification for our production center in 2007.

・Kyoritsu industries, especially as a professional engineering company, has been developing our unique structures utilizing high-performance fabric products including PTFE‐coated fiberglass fabric, PVC‐coated polyester fabric, and ETFE foil, and supplying the following contents to our customers.
- Design, engineering, fabrication and construction of the Pavilions, Architectural membrane structures, ETFE foil membrane structures, Shade structures, Safety fabric ceiling system, Fail-safe net ceiling system, and Tent warehouses, etc.

・Membrane structures have come a long time to the present in a wide range of architecture around the world due to their lightweight, light transmission, durability, weather resistance, and sustainability. Common applications are the following (see also Josep Ignasi de Liorens(Ed.), Fabric Structures in Architecture, The Textile Institute, Elsevier 2015, ISBN 978-1-78242-233-4);
- Architectural Roofs and Canopies: stadiums, convention center, shopping center
- Exhibition and Event Facilities: temporary or semi‐permanent exhibition spaces, pavilions
- Transportation Facilities: airport terminals, train stations, and bus terminals
- Sports Facilities: stadiums, swimming pool covers, tennis courts
- Environmental Facilities: greenhouse covers, botanical gardens, zoos
- Residential Structure: shade sails, carports, pergolas, etc.
These are just a few examples of the diverse applications of membrane structures, but membrane structures can make them more suitable for a wide range of architectural, commercial, and industrial projects.

▪ The restriction of architectural membranes using PTFE, PVDF, and ETFE foils according to PFAS restriction proposal will have adverse effects in a wide range of other industries. For now, there are no alternative materials in the field of lightweight structures and the restriction would mean the end of lightweight tensile structures using architectural membranes and ETFE foils around the world including Japan. The architectural fields are lately trying to assess the LCA(Life cycle assessment) of membrane structures to achieve carbon neutral aims, and membrane structures will offer solutions to achieve more efficient and less impacting building structures due to their material properties.

▪ According to PFAS restriction proposal, by grouping all various PFAS substances together and restricting them as a single class, the PFAS Restriction Proposal would restrict numerous PFAS substances that have not been risk‐assessed and for which no unacceptable risk has been demonstrated.

▪ Therefore, we request an exemption of fluoropolymers including PTFE, PVDF, and ETFE from the PFAS Restriction Proposal under the REACH regulation. In addition, with regard to the PFAS Restriction Proposal, we also support the statements and replies made by AGC and Chukoh Chemical industries, etc. as membrane and foil producers, coating and weaving companies.

▪ Finally, Kyoritsu Industries also supports the statement made by FCJ on the issues of the proposed restriction, as attached in Section IV.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: “(ee) the semiconductor manufacturing process” is classified as an application that substantial evidence is required to apply to derogation in the Annex XV report. We manufacture and supply a large numbers of fluorine compounds defined as PFAS, which used as semiconductor process materials and their raw materials. We would like to provide information to support that there is no substitute for these fluorine compounds at this time, and it is reasonable to apply the derogation for the stable supply of semiconductor products in EU.
Perfluorocarbons (PFCs) and hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) defined as PFAS, are widely used in semiconductor manufacturing processes in purpose of etching silicon and other silicon-based materials. For anisotropic etch, these gases are introduced to semiconductor manufacturing equipment such as reactive ion etching (RIE) chamber where a radio frequency (RF) field is applied. The RF field creates a plasma of ions including CF3+ ions and highly reactive F radicals. The ions in the plasma are accelerated towards the substrate by an electric field and collide with the substrate, transferring energy to the surface atoms and causing them to break bonds and become volatile. The reactive gas in the plasma reacts with the volatile atoms on the substrate surface, forming volatile compounds that can be removed from the surface by the ion bombardment. For the most advanced chip manufacturing, RIE needs precise control over the etched features, including the depth, shape, and selectivity. To achieve the necessary levels of accuracy, uniformity, and reproducibility, it is especially important to control the types and numbers of ions and radicals generated in the plasma from the PFCs and HFCs defined as PFAS. There are few non-PFAS etch gases such as CCl4 or C2HCl3, which does not have fluorine atom in the molecule, used in certain application such as poly silicon etching. However, since these non-PFAS chemicals tend to have high toxicity and ozone depletion potential, even if the required etching performance are met, it will not be a good substitute to replace PFAS in the etching processes. In other case, there are wet/dry chemical etching processes that does not need plasma to etch silicon-based materials, and other semiconductor materials. However, even in this different etching method, PFAS is also widely used, and it is not easy to find substitutes from the standpoint of toxicity and environmental contamination.
In these circumstances, to meet the potential PFAS restriction it is necessary to develop new etching technology based on non-PFAS chemistry. However, as mentioned above, the manufacturing of semiconductor devices requires extremely advanced etching technology, and it’s not only developing new chemicals, but comprehensive integration is needed. Which will take long term research and development. In addition, after the development of new chemicals and processes, usually it takes 2 to 3 years to install the technology to mass production of chips. In particular for new chemicals, it’s toxicity could be higher than the restricted PFAS, so their material properties need to be carefully examined.

General Comments: “(ee) the semiconductor manufacturing process” is classified as an application that substantial evidence is required to apply to derogation in the Annex XV report. We manufacture and supply a large numbers of fluorine compounds defined as PFAS, which used as semiconductor process materials and their raw materials. ArF immersion lithography is one technology that enhance the resolution of ArF lithography by filling water (refractive index 1.44) instead of air (refractive index 1) between the lens and resist. This technology is essential to achieve resolution below 65 nm used for manufacturing advanced semiconductor devices.
When the resist contacts with water, components in the resist such as PAG and quencher (base) are eluted from the resist to water, and it cause degradation of patterning performance. In addition to it, water containing eluted resist components contaminates exposure equipment, causing equipment failure and long-term maintenance. Fluorine polymer containing PFAS, which has high water repellency, is placed between the water and the resist to protect both of resist and ArF exposure equipment, and can prevent these defects.
There are two methods of protection: one is to coat barrier layer onto the resist with a topcoat material (topcoat process). Another is to impart surface water repellency to the resist composition itself (topcoatless process). In the topcoat process, in addition to high water repellency of 90°or more, multiple performances such as solubility in developer and coating without mixing with resist are required. Also, even in the topcoatless process, fluoropolymers containing PFAS (-CF2- and -CF3) are always used in resist formulation to achieve low elution and high water repellency. The only compound that satisfies these requirements is resin with fluorinated alkyl group substituted on the side chain, and currently there is no substitute. In addition, the fluorinated resin compound has multiple advantages such as appropriate transparency at 193 nm (ArF) wavelength, prevention of swelling during development, and high solubility in organic solvents due to its polarity. These features have become essential for ArF resists as well.
To our knowledge, there are currently no PFAS-free topcoat or topcoatless materials on the market. The production yield of ArF immersion lithography using the current process is 99% or more due to highly accumulated technology and experience. Even if an non-PFAS alternative material is found, if the performance is inferior, the yield will decrease, and there is a concern that it results in increase in waste and adversely affect to the environment.　
In addition to ArF immersion lithography, EB exposure, nanoimprint lithography, or EUV exposure are methods to achieve resolutions below 65 nm, but it is difficult to substitute for ArF immersion lithography. EB exposure is suitable for manufacturing expensive photomasks that require high-precision ultra-fine processing, but its photo-imaging speed is still insufficient, making it unsuitable for mass production of semiconductor chips. Nanoimprint lithography is known to use release agents with perfluoroalkyl chains to release the resin from the mold. So it can’t be PFAS-free alternative. EUV exposure is a lithography technology that uses 13.5 nm soft X-rays as a light source, and is effective as a method for forming ultra-fine patterns below 32 nm. However, EUV exposure tool is very expensive (over $150million). That’s why replacing ArF immersion with it would be too much financial burden. And, it cannot be non-PFAS alternative since PFAS containing photoacid generators and surfactants are used in the EUV resist composition.
As for the PFAS-containing resin mentioned above, it is synthesized from building blocks with optionally fluorinated substituents. Monomers are produced from the building blocks in several steps, which are then used to produce polymers, which are used to produce resist compositions containing the polymers. Resists are not manufactured by direct fluorination of polymers or their compositions. Therefore, in order to maintain a stable supply of resist products, the transportation of these fluorine compounds between companies and between countries must not be impeded. When the semiconductor manufacturing process is placed as the derogation, it should include the entire supply chain including raw materials, monomers and polymers.

An exemption for PTFE thread sealing tape is necessary. PTFE thread sealing tape is used to seal metallic threads in equipment and plant construction to achieve an adequate seal against liquids and gases under high pressure. In addition to chemical resistance, high sliding properties and temperature resistance are very important for creating a secure threaded connection. Often, the only alternatives are adhesives with inadequate chemical resistance, and in addition, adhesive connections are not detachable and lead to enormous maintenance costs for replacing fittings, piping, and even critical components such as pumps, filters, and flow meters." 8255 "See file >>input_ECHA_consultation_2023-09.pdf<<" 8255" "Today, there are already possibilities to reuse polymeric PFAS. For this purpose, 4 rough recycling strategies are available: "1) Mechanical recycling, processing without breaking chemical bonds through crushing and milling processes, 2) Macromolecule recycling through solvent-based processes, 3) Monomer recycling (depolymerization) as a thermal process for the recovery of monomers, 4) Feedstock recycling as a further splitting into chemical intermediates beyond monomer recycling." (Source: >>Chemie Ingenieur Technik - 2023 - Schmidt-Rodenkirchen.pdf<<) At present, a total of 96.6% is thermally utilized or disposed of. Only 3.4% is currently recycled as material. According to general information, a combustion temperature of at least 850 °C will be needed to split PFAS. However, there are contradictory data, so that 1100°C or even 1400°C are needed to completely destroy any PFAS compounds. Source "Fluorochemicals: Durable, dangerous, avoidable" by the Bund für Umwelt und Naturschutz (Page 14) -> File >>chemistry_fluorochemicals_background.pdf<<. In contrast, there is a novel process developed at Northwestern University in Illinois, USA. The newly developed process works with sodium hydroxide and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). Combined Comments:
General Comments: "Merck Electronics is manufacturer of process chemicals as well as provider of delivery systems for process chemicals used in semiconductor manufacturing in Europe and other countries around the globe. Thus, we produce and import various process chemicals and articles – amongst other, chemicals for photolithography (e. g. photoresist, process and patterning enhancement materials), gases for etching and cleaning of vapor deposition chambers (e.g., hydrofluorocarbons, perfluorocarbons) as well as customized delivery systems for corrosive, toxic, hazardous chemicals, and gases in semiconductor manufacturing plants.
Each of these portfolio segments includes products containing PFAS.
Semiconductors are essential components of electronic devices and are integral to modern society . They are of strategic importance for both economic growth and national security.

The initial proposal suggested a limited derogation for the use of PFA substances in the semiconductor industry – however, the very complex production of chips is currently impossible without PFAS. For several applications (e.g., photolithography, plasma etching, wafer cleaning), a replacement that has the same technical properties would be very difficult or impossible to find. Either way, it would require a significant amount of time and in some cases even a completely new technology. Meanwhile, the EU Chips Act ambition to increase the EU’s share of the global semiconductor production from 10% to 20% by 2030 cannot be achieved if semiconductor manufacturers can no longer manufacture, import and use key materials in the EU.
Merck supports the ambition for a smart and targeted PFAS regulation. Notwithstanding, in its current form, the PFAS restriction proposal threatens the resilience of supply chains in several critical sectors and with that the competitiveness of the European Union in a complex geopolitical environment. It also contradicts other European policies and legislative proposals aiming at increasing European competitiveness such as the EU Chips Act, the Net Zero Industry Act and the Green Deal Industrial Plan.

In this comment Merck Electronics is addressing only the use of PFAS in semiconductor industry.
Additional comments are already - and more will be - submitted separately by Merck, to provide also regarding other PFAS uses a better basis for an adequate regulation of PFAS materials.
Merck is additionally actively contributing to industry association comments as e.g. from VCI, Cefic, SEMI, SIA and EFPIA – some comments are already submitted, others will be submitted later in course of the consultation phase.

Content: Environmental emissions Baseline
Combined Comments:
General Comments: “Omgevingsdienst.nl" is the partnership of 29 Regional Environmental Agencies in the Netherlands. The mission of these environmental agencies is a healthy, safe and sustainable living environment. The agencies work on behalf of the provinces and municipalities that are the competent authorities for environmental tasks. The main tasks of environmental agencies are licensing, supervision, enforcement, advice and monitoring. As joint Dutch environmental agencies, we are speaking out in support of the Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) restriction proposal. We do so based on the following considerations:
1) Accumulation of PFAS. As executive agencies, our toolkit is regulation, supervision, enforcement, advice and monitoring. The possibilities of using these mechanisms to prevent environmental and health damage depend on the opportunities offered by legislation. The persistent nature of PFAS means that any emission contributes to a permanent increase in the concentration in the environment. Even if licensing, supervision and enforcement (Vergunningverlening, toezicht en handhaving: VTH) mechanisms reduce and regulate emissions, these persistent substances will accumulate in the environment and contribute to health risks. The executive environmental agency toolkit simply isn’t equipped to prevent this persistent accumulation.
2) Lagging legislation for new PFAS. PFAS cover a large number of substances. Emission requirements can certainly be set for specific substances where health risks have been identified. However, in practice, new PFAS variants, many of which cannot yet be regulated through legislation, are constantly being developed and used. From the perspective of the implementation of licensing and supervision, the possibilities of preventing or reducing new PFAS emissions are then lacking. As legislative change takes time, there is therefore a continuous lag between licensing, supervision and enforcement capabilities and practice.
3) Unknown PFAS. In addition to the use of new PFAS variants, actual practice has shown us that other PFAS variants can also emerge in business processes where PFAS are used. In addition, it is often unclear what the effects of these substances are, or there isn’t any reliable measurement method yet. Thus, the problem isn’t just limited to the PFAS being used but also relates to substances that we may not yet know have been created or formed. From the perspective of the performance of environmental tasks, it isn’t possible to regulate or monitor these unknown PFAS through permits.
4) Point sources and diffuse emissions. The primary focus of the environmental agency toolkit is the environmentally harmful activity, e.g. at companies. Licensing, supervision and enforcement are mainly focused on specific sources and, in addition, reducing risks in industries and company chains. However, the problem of the diffuse release of PFAS goes beyond the capabilities of the licensing, supervision and enforcement toolkit. After all, the multitude of products and applications, both manufactured and imported, also cause diffuse emission after the use phase. Relatively little is known about this diffuse release. Although environmental agencies, as implementers of environmental policy, can reduce and solve many problems, executive agencies can do little in relation to this issue of diffuse emissions and accumulation through regulation, supervision and enforcement. As such, this “diffuse tap” can’t be regulated or inspected, which is why it should be closed.
5) Feasibility and enforceability. With regard to the content of the EU restriction proposal, we draw attention to its feasibility and enforceability. For the authorities responsible for execution, it is crucial that regulations can indeed be applied in practice and are enforceable. In this context, it is essential to be cautious in the number of exemptions. In terms of the feasibility and effectiveness of regulations, it is important that there are sufficient incentives for companies to quickly come up with substitute, non-persistent alternative substances. As implementers of environmental legislation, and from a perspective of feasibility and enforceability, we therefore advocate great restraint and strict temporariness of any exemptions.
6) Environmental and health benefits. Consultation responses from companies and industries point a lot to the financial-economic consequences of the restriction proposal. However, as environmental agencies, we, in turn, would like to highlight the significant environmental and health benefits of the PFAS ban. In our opinion, the ban could provide a major stimulus to innovate and replace PFAS with other substances. As an incentive, it can also contribute to achieving significant health gains.

General Comments: "PFAS" (per- and polyfluorinated chemicals) does not describe a specific substance, but an extensive group of chemicals containing fluor.  These are characterized by grease, water and dirt repellent properties and are correspondingly widespread in everyday life, for example in cosmetics, coffee mugs, dishes and pans, textiles, and hygiene papers.
A group of PFAS is currently subject to restrictions due to applicable EU regulations (REACH): PFOA (perfluorooctanoic acid and related compounds), PFOS (perfluorooctane sulfonic acid and related compounds), PFHxA (perfluorohexanoic acid and related compounds), PFCA (C9-C14 perfluorinated carboxylic acids, their salts, and related compounds).
The ZEISS ophthalmic lens coatings contain extremely small amounts of substances that belong to the group of PFAS but are not yet subject to any regulations or restrictions within the EU.
We do not have any evidence or scientific studies that indicate environmental or health risks from anti-reflective (AR) coatings of eyeglass lenses. It is important to emphasize that compliance with applicable limit values or regulation in areas of application ensures safety, health, and protection of the environment.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Ophthalmic lens products apply to section 6k of annex 15 restriction proposal.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: We don't have information on what consumers do with their lenses at the end of their lifetime. But we know that at ZEISS Vision Care the total amount of PFAS compounds on ophthalmic lens products for whole Europe for one year is about 15 to 100kg only.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: We don't have information on what consumers do with their lenses at the end of their lifetime. But we know that at ZEISS Vision Care the total amount of PFAS compounds on ophthalmic lens products for whole Europe for one year is about 15 to 100kg only.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Ophthalmic eyeglass lens products after their use are not part of an established recycling pathway.

5. Proposed derogations: At ZEISS Vision Care the total amount of PFAS compounds on ophthalmic lens products for whole Europe for one year is about 15 to 100kg only.

6. Missing uses: Affected parts in ophthalmic lens products: Easy-to-clean coatings, surfactants in hardcoating resins, lens cleaning products, all contained in section 6k.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Affected parts in ophthalmic lens products: Easy-to-clean coatings, surfactants in hardcoating resins, Lens cleaning products, all contained in section 6k.

8. Other identified uses: Easy-to-clean effect is combination of high water contact angle (>105°) and high oil (hexadecane) contact angle (>60°). This is important for always clear vision, essential for safety (e.g. to avoid glare and reflection-impaired vision during car driving) and to avoid eyestrain. It reduces sensitivity todust and dirt contamination on eyeglass lens surface that lead to scratches and coating damages, and is thus extending use time of the glasses which improves the products environmetal footprint. It reduces frequency of cleaning and use of chemical cleaning substances, easening use of pure water for cleaning. Easy-to-clean functionalities are among top criteria for consumers to prefer premium AR coatings for branded lenses over low-cost alternatives with basic coating. In comparison to organomodified silicones and straight polyacrylates, fluorocarbon-modified surfactants have clear advantages with respect to flow-behavior and substrate wetting. PFAS based surfactants drive anti-fog effect in lens wipes and cleaning solutions.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: "Piston rings are products that seal the pressure in the combustion chamber in internal combustion engines and slide inside the engine together with the piston.The temperature of the piston and piston rings reaches 200°C as the engine burns. Therefore, it is necessary to apply a surface treatment to the piston rings to provide them with wear and seizure resistance.
A typical surface treatment of piston rings is a method of coating them with a resin with high lubrication properties containing PTFE. The resin coating is applied to the outer circumference, upper and lower surfaces of the piston ring to prevent seizure of the sliding surfaces and adhesion of the piston material, and to blend it with the surrounding parts. This extends the life of the engine and enables it to meet emission regulations from the early stages of use.
TPR has the technology to coat piston rings with this resin coat, which is called TS-1, TS-2, TS-3 coat and Teflon coat and uses a surface treatment containing PTFE. Piston rings without resin coatings limit engine output and shorten engine life. As a result, the life cycle of the vehicle is shortened and the frequency of piston ring replacement increases, which can have a negative impact on the global environment in the process of recycling waste materials and in the product fabrication process. Furthermore, if a resin coating cannot be used, the engine, including the piston rings, has to be redesigned, which requires a great deal of work.
On the other hand, non-PFAS alternatives that meet the lubricating properties of PTFE have not been identified. The establishment of alternative technologies is not in sight due to the time required to develop and demonstrate alternatives. Resin coatings wear away with engine operating time and become worn away during the normal life cycle. Much of the abrasion is discharged into the engine oil and is disposed of with the oil change. It is therefore not considered to have a significant impact on the environment. For the above reasons, a deferment of the regulation of PTFE for resin coatings is desired."

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: “Status of atmospheric aerosol measurements”
We manufacture and sell measuring devices using PTFE(polytetrafluoroethlene) porous membrane filters for the measurement of aerosols in the atmospheric environment such as PM2.5. Japan Ministry of the Environment and local governments nationwide constantly monitor PM2.5 and SPM (suspended particulate matter) in the air environment in accordance with laws and regulations such as the Air Pollution Control Law, and our measuring equipment used here uses a large amount of PTFE membrane filters. Japan public institutions use analyzers using PTFE filters, not only in our company but also in other companies' products. In addition, the globally standardized method for measuring PM2.5 mass concentration is the Federal Standard Measurement Method (FRM) in the United States. （Refer to 40 CFR Appendix L to Part 50 - Reference Method for the Determination of Fine Particulate Matter as PM2.5 in the Atmosphere - Content Details - CFR-2011-title40-vol2-part50-appL (govinfo.gov)）.　 In the FRM method, PM2.5 is collected by a filter and the mass is measured by a balance, and the material of the filter that collects PM2.5 is determined to be PTFE. In addition, PTFE membrane filters are also used to perform component analysis of atmospheric aerosols containing PM2.5.

“Why there is no substitute for PTFE in the measurement of atmospheric aerosols”
There is no conceivable alternative to the PTFE membrane filter used in our equipment described above. There is also no substitute for PTFE membrane filters in the FRM method. The following describes why there is no substitute for PTFE as a filter material for the observation of aerosols in the atmosphere.

(1) The PTFE membrane filter can collect more than 99% of 0.3 micro meter particles, so it has excellent particle collection properties. In addition, even if a large amount of air is passed through the PTFE membrane, the pressure drop is low and the air permeability is excellent.
(2) When measuring the mass of particulate matter collected in the filter, the PTFE membrane does not have an error due to the amount of moisture adsorbed in the filter because it itself is not hygroscopic.
(3) Gaseous substances in the air are rarely adsorbed by the PTFE membrane filter.
(4) Since PTFE membrane filters are extremely thin and lightweight, the measurement error of the aerosol mass can be minimized, which is extremely advantageous.
(5) When analyzing the components of the aerosol collected in the filter, strong acid or strong alkali is usually added to dissolve the particulate matter, but PTFE itself is not attacked and is stable and has excellent chemical resistance.
(6) The PTFE membrane is highly durable, has almost no defects, can be made into a roll tape, and even if the tape is pulled a little harder, it will hardly break.
(7) At present, PTFE membrane is supplied with very stable manufactured products.

Manufacturers of PTFE membrane filters have said us that those with these properties cannot be manufactured with materials other than PTFE and are highly unlikely to be developed in the future. Observations of atmospheric aerosols using these PTFE membrane filters have been going on for many years to protect the air environment and can never be stopped. Not only in Japan, but also in other countries, environmental standards for PM2.5 concentrations of air aerosols have been established, and many continuous monitoring devices are in operation to achieve these standards. PTFE membrane filters are essential consumables for these devices.

“Instruments for measuring trace gas components and water environments in the atmosphere”
We also manufacture and sell analyzers for measuring trace amounts of NOx, SO2, ozone, and hydrocarbons in the atmospheric environment. We also manufacture and sell measuring instruments for COD, TOC, total phosphorus, total nitrogen, ammonia, and cyan in aquatic environments.
These analyzers use components made of PTFE, PFA and PCTFE, as described below, but no alternative can be found because they have little gas adsorption, are highly durable, and are durable even when heated in strongly oxidized or strongly alkaline conditions.
(1) Piping (2) Dust removal filter (3) Valve for switching gas lines (4) Pressure regulating valve (5) Processed product made by turning PTFE lumps into reactors and cells of various shapes

“Requests for PFAS regulations”
PTFE and PFA are indispensable materials for measuring particulate matter and gas components of the air environment and measuring the water environment manufactured by our company. This is true not only for our company, but also for our peers, but we believe that it is extremely unlikely that alternatives will be developed in the future. In particular, PTFE membrane filters are indispensable for PM2.5 measurements carried out all over the world. If the PTFE membrane is lost, the observation of aerosols in the atmosphere, including PM2.5, will be interrupted. This loss is immeasurable. Of course, this will also cause significant damage to PM2.5 observations in Europe. For this reason, we strongly request that analytical instruments including environmental measuring instruments and materials such as PTFE and PFA used for analysis be considered as exemptions from PFAS regulations.

General Comments: "We manufacture and sell pressure sensitive adhesive tapes (PSTs) using PTFE as a carrier,  and a PTFE thread sealant which are used in aerospace applications pursuant to customers' requirements, industry-approved specifications, and regulatory requirements.

We understand that the EU proposes these PFAS/PTFE restrictions to reduce PFAS impact on the environment and human body  to create a sustainable future. We are also committed to these shared goals and to working collaboratively with the EU, our customers, the supply chain and all stakeholders  to find PFAS/PTFE alternatives that balance safety with environmental stewardship. Although the science, technology and socio-economic impacts of these objectives is complex and evolving, all stakeholders benefit from research and development into PFAS/PTFE alternatives while continuing to provide consumers access to products essential to modern life, including medications, medical supplies, devices, computers, alternative energy and transportation. Our company wants to be part of the PFAS/PTFE alternative solutions, innovations and emerging marketplace.  Consistent with EU's goals and objectives, we believe that, given enough time, we can develop an alternative with equal or better safety performance to PFAS/PTFE, and further ECHA's environmental initiatives.  However, there are currently no alternative materials that provide industry safety and mechanical requirements of PTFE.

The purpose of this document is to provide ECHA with comments regarding our manufactured PSTs that use PTFE as a carrier and applied in the aerospace industry, specifically PTFE tapes used in molding carbon fiber reinforced plastic parts.

Two of the most important properties of PTFE in these applications include:

1. Heat resistance: In the molding process of CFRP, there are cases where the environment reach to around 200°C, and the material is required to have a melting point of 200°C or higher.

2. High mold-releasing property: When the CFRP is released after molding is completed, it is required that it does not cause a decrease in mechanical properties by smoothly detaching the member without deformation, and that it can be suitably detached from the core. For this, materials with a high contact angle of water, such as PTFE film, are used.

Details of technical requirements are explained in the documents attached in Confidential Section V.

PTFE is considered a low concern polymer (Ref. 1, 2, 3).   Considering this and that there are currently no alternative materials that provide industry safety and mechanical requirements of PTFE, we request an Exemption from EU proposed rules to restrict the use of PTFE."

Impacts on the recycling industry: " ""Some methods and processes used for PTFE recycling:  Mechanical Recycling: Mechanical recycling involves processes where PTFE waste is mechanically shredded or ground into smaller particles. These particles can then be mixed with new PTFE material to create a blend that can be used in certain applications. Mechanical recycling of PTFE is relatively limited due to the difficulty in processing PTFE's tough molecular structure.  Pyrolysis: Pyrolysis is a thermal decomposition process in which PTFE waste is subjected to high temperatures in the absence of oxygen. This process breaks down PTFE into its constituent elements, primarily fluorine and carbon. While pyrolysis can recover valuable fluorine for reuse, it's a more complex and energy-intensive method and may not be widely used for PTFE recycling.  Chemical Recycling: Chemical recycling involves breaking down PTFE into its basic components using chemical processes. This can include methods like hydrolysis, where PTFE is exposed to strong acids to break the polymer chain into smaller molecules. However, chemical recycling of PTFE is not as common due to the challenges associated with handling the strong acids required for the process.  Reprocessing PTFE Scrap: Some PTFE manufacturers offer reprocessing services for scrap PTFE materials generated during manufacturing. These materials are collected, reprocessed, and used in the production of new PTFE products. This closed-loop approach helps reduce waste in the manufacturing process.  Alternative Applications: In some cases, PTFE waste or scrap can be repurposed for applications where the material's unique properties are less critical. For instance, PTFE waste might find use in applications that don't require the same level of non-stick or high-temperature resistance, such as industrial fillers.  It's important to note that PTFE recycling is not as common as the recycling of other plastics due to the challenges posed by its chemical properties and molecular structure. The durable and chemically inert nature of PTFE that makes it valuable in various applications can also make it difficult to recycle using traditional methods applied to other plastics. As a result, recycling options for PTFE are relatively limited, and the focus often remains on reducing waste through proper manufacturing practices and responsible waste management."""
