Eurovent comments and data collection for the open consultation on the PFAS restriction proposal
In a nutshell
Within this document, Eurovent provides comments and results of the data collection among its members to reply to the open consultation on the PFAS restriction proposal.  The following paper has been jointly developed by the Eurovent task force ‘FGAS’, which groups all Eurovent members active in heating, air conditioning and refrigeration sectors, and the Eurovent Product Group ‘Air Filters’. The latter part on air filters is completed by a separate appendix. Eurovent is also aligned with the Orgalim position paper dated 31 August 2023.
PFAS and the Heating, Air Conditioning and Refrigeration industry
1.Quantity, type and use (application) of PFAS substance or mixture used
PFAS as refrigerants
The PFAS restriction proposal potentially affects several refrigerants currently used by the industry, leaving out only non-fluorinated refrigerants and few other fluorinated refrigerants such as R32, R152a, R23 and some sector-specific refrigerants like R1132.
The main pure refrigerants currently used, included in the PFAS restriction report, are:
- R-125
- R-134a
- R-143a
- R-1224yd
- R-1233zd(E)
- R-1234yf
- R-1234ze(E)
- R-1336mzz(E)
- R-1336mzz(Z)
These refrigerants are part of many refrigerant blends that are widely used and would also be affected by the PFAS restrictions. Some examples are enumerated in the following:
- R-407C
- R-410A
- R-448A
- R-449A
- R-450A
- R-452A
- R-452B
- R-454A
- R-454B
- R-454C
- R-455A
- R-513A
- R-513B
- R-515B
The applications where the virgin refrigerants and their blends indicated above are used vary between Chillers (e.g. comfort or process heating and cooling, marine and reefer applications, …), Heat Pumps (e.g. heating, cooling, sanitary hot water, …), IT Cooling (e.g. data centre applications, …), Air Handling Units (e.g. Industrial Ventilation technologies…), Rooftops, Refrigeration equipment (e.g. Food Cold Chain technologies ...) etc.
Some refrigerants that are not used anymore in new equipment due to F-Gas Regulation restrictions, like R404A and R507C, are currently used when reclaimed or recycled for the service and maintenance of existing appliances and systems.
Degradation to TFA and considering TFA as PFAS according to the UNEP report on Environmental Effects of Stratospheric Ozone Depletion, UV Radiation, and Interactions with Climate Change
Eurovent would like to highlight a recently published report   of UNEP regarding TFAs, which is important to consider. Below is reported an extrapolation from the chapter 3.8 “Conclusions and uncertainties”; TFAs are assessed also within the Executive summary - 6 Air quality and contaminants, and the chapter 3.1.1 “Classification of trifluoroacetic acid as a per- and poly-fluoroalkyl chemical”.
“3.8 Conclusions and uncertainties (pag. 292 of the report)
TFA is a perfluorinated acid that has been included in the class of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). This class of chemicals contains 4730 substances, of which about 256 are in commercial use. […] To regulate these substances as a class (as has been suggested) is not scientifically defensible and TFA should be treated as a unique chemical for the purposes of regulation. […] This persistence is not a major concern because it does not react with biomolecules. TFA and its salts are easily excreted by animals and do not bioaccumulate in food chains. Salts of TFA have low toxicity to animals and plants and there are very wide margins between current/projected exposures and toxicity values. One source of TFA in the environment is the degradation of replacements for chemicals that contribute to the destruction of stratospheric O3. These are the HCFCs, HFCs, and HFOs, all of which are replacements for chemicals that fall under the purview of the Montreal Protocol. […] These releases will add to the existing load of TFA in the environment but predicted amounts are well below the threshold for concern with respect to human and environmental health.”
Considering what above, Eurovent would like to request a time-unlimited derogation for F-gases use in HVACR sector.
PFAS used in components
PFAS are used in a significant number of components, subassemblies, spare parts used within the HVAC/R equipment, most of which do not have alternatives to date. All of the below-listed components are critical for the correct functioning of the units, also from an Ecodesign efficiency and safety point of view.
The following is a non-exhaustive list:
- Compressors
- Cabinet vent / filter
- Coax cables
- Coolant for liquid cooled servers
- Electrotechnical and Electronic components – diodes, capacitors, sensors, motors, switches, etc.
- Exterior cabinet paints and coatings
- Heat Exchanger tubes – hydrophilic coating (potential)
- High Temperature and/or chemically resistant O-rings / Seals / Gaskets
- Lithium-Ion Batteries – electrode substrate and in the electrolyte
- Plumber's tape (PTFE / Teflon)
- Printed Circuit Board Coatings (potential and likely)
- Pumps (using PFAS o-rings, seals, gaskets)
- Semiconductors
- Wire coatings, insulation, foams
PFAS used in suppliers processes
Many of our suppliers also use PFAS in their processes. Examples include cleaning tools, degreasing stamped metal dies, plastic and rubber mould release agents, emulsifiers and electronic manufacturing atmosphere purges. These processes are carried out by specific and highly costly equipment that could require extensive adaptation, if not total replacement, in case that the use of PFAS is banned.
2.Containment measures currently in place or upcoming
Lifetime Emissions: Our industry follows and respects the current F-Gas Regulation and has implemented all the required measures to prevent emissions of F-gases from existing equipment by implementing checks, proper servicing and recovery of the gases at the end of the equipment's life.
The PFAS impurity limits indicated within the restriction proposal do not consider the procedures and processes for the manufacturing, supply chain, recovery and recycle processes and procedures of HFCs, HFOs and HCFOs. The analytical methods included in the restriction proposal are not relevant to the practical analysis of these F-gases and their impurity levels.
A number of F-gases are not, due to their chemical structure and properties, within the restriction proposal, for example, HFC-32 and HFC-152a (referred to below as “excluded F-gases”).  However, they may contain very low concentrations of short chain PFAS (that is, other HFCs and HFOs that are contained within the proposal) and that may be formed during the manufacture of the excluded F-gases. Furthermore, it cannot be ruled out that excluded F-gases could become contaminated with low concentrations of short chain HFCs/HFOs/HCFOs in scope of the restriction, due to the fact that F-gas imposes the obligation of using refillable and returnable containers.
It is recommended that a specific concentration limit is established for fluorinated impurities threshold for the virgin and reclaimed excluded F-gases which, for consistency, should be based upon the AHRI 700 2019 Standard for Specifications for Refrigerants, with allowable fluorinated impurities in F-gases of up to a maximum of 5000 ppm, without any individual limits.
The appropriate treatment of the waste according to WEEE Directive can reduce and prevent disposal emissions. A proper management (collection, transport, depollution, treatment for reuse, environmentally sound treatment) of waste should be supported by a dedicated exemption in the restriction proposal, ensuring preparing for reuse and recycling companies addressing the end of life of the products contributing to the circular economy. Otherwise, a massive and illegal landfill of waste will occur.
PFAS substances contained in solid objects (see the PFAS used in components section above) are not subject to be released in the environment during the product lifetime. Furthermore, these products are properly treated at the end of their life under the WEEE Directive. Therefore, in reason of their negligible PFAS release factor and considering that the majority of the components, sub-assemblies and spare parts currently used by the industry do not have non-PFAS alternatives to-date, a dedicated exemption for this kind of applications (“solid components for the industry”) should be foreseen. In particular spare parts need to be exempted during the whole lifetime. Following the EU Right to Repair principle and the material and resource efficiency requirements embedded in the Ecodesign framework and the upcoming EU Sustainable Product design requirements a circular economy needs to be guaranteed avoiding artificial created obsolescence of appliances.
3.Currently adopted alternatives, and/or activities done to develop alternatives to PFAS substances
In most air conditioning products and heat pumps applications the PFAS-impacted R-410A refrigerant can be replaced by R-32, R-454B or R-452B (the latter two also impacted by PFAS restriction proposal) whereas R-134a, R-513A, R-513B can partially be replaced by R-1234ze (also impacted by the PFAS restriction proposal) and R-152a. Natural refrigerants are still at an early stage of development for these applications.
A considerable share of the stationary refrigeration industry has already adapted its technologies and product portfolio to use natural refrigerants instead of HFCs or HFOs, universally guaranteeing a high level of efficiency.
Some national building codes may prohibit the use of toxic or flammable refrigerants, therefore completely abandoning synthetic refrigerants seems difficult.
4.Percentage of turnover linked to PFAS related substances
Depending on the core business of the company, the turnover linked to PFAS related substances could vary from 5% for air handling units’ and stationary refrigeration manufacturers to more than 70% of the turnover for the chillers, heat pumps, IT cooling and rooftops manufacturers.
5.Impact on the product availability in case of ban
The impact of the potential restriction on PFAS is strictly linked to the new Regulation on F-Gases, still to be finalised.
Therefore, the fluorinated refrigerants are potentially impacted by both the FGAS Regulation and the REACH, with possible mutual impacts.
As an industry we support new technologies, where the application allows it, which already use alternative non-PFAS fluorinated and non-fluorinated refrigerants (as it is already the case in many stationary refrigeration applications) and foam blowing agents in many applications. To secure future innovation (eventually with PFAS) paths it’s recommended to integrate a review clause in the restriction proposal.
Since several years the stationary refrigeration industry has already adapted its technologies and product portfolio to use non-fluorinated and non-PFAS refrigerants, universally guaranteeing a high level of efficiency even in the warmest climatic regions of Europe and without compromising on safety.
Regarding the use of fluorinated refrigerants for servicing or maintenance and the refrigerant stock currently contained in existing systems, the most commonly used refrigerants in the existing HVAC&R equipment are PFAS.
A restriction on PFAS refrigerants could lead to premature obsolescence of equipment.
In the current proposal, a 13.5-year derogation is foreseen for maintenance activities, but this period of time is not sufficient to cover the entire lifetime of some equipment with a lifetime up to 25 or 30 years, particularly for domestic applications. As an industry we recommend integrating a time-unlimited derogation covering the complete lifetime of the appliances.
It must be highlighted though that some PFAS substances are used in some key components and lubricants as shown in the above chapters, widely adopted in the HVAC&R industry to manufacture products and systems, and that have no alternative to date.
For those components a time unlimited derogation for both fluoropolymers and non-fluoropolymers should be developed that also reflects the availability of spare parts for repair in the sense of Ecodesign (e.g. is not acceptable to scrap a compressor due to unavailability of an PFAS free o-ring with interchangeable design).
The PFAS substances are present in minimum amounts/percentages, confined within the molecular structure with no volatility or dispersion possible, and completely recovered when treating these components at the end of their life (as per WEEE Directive).
In any case and based on the above, it’s also proven that the 18 months transition period is far too short. This sector has such a complexity that a least 5 years of derogations is recommended.
6.Expected socioeconomic impacts on the company/business/employment due to a PFAS ban
As for the above point, the impacts are strictly linked to the final provisions of the regulation on F-Gases.
Considering the information given and the data at disposal of the manufacturers, it can be estimated that the potential impact of the PFAS proposal could have a huge effect on the market. It must be noted that, as highlighted in the previous chapters, not only refrigerants will be affected by the proposal but several components, spare parts and processes, and therefore the entire value chain could suffer from this.
On the other hand, it could be predicted that for some sectors that are already using natural refrigerants for their products and systems (as it is the case in the stationary refrigeration sector), a ban on PFAS refrigerants could accelerate the replacement of mature systems using PFAS HFCs, stimulating investments, creating green jobs and increasing employment in Europe, with workers needing to be retrained and upskilled.
Eurovent membership represent several global players with research & innovation centres and manufacturing sites in Europe but with major trade relationships in third countries. Due to the proposed “restriction on the use”, they are also prohibited to export innovative and high energy efficient solutions to those third countries. As a consequence, part or complete manufacturing capacity, including employment, will be relocated outside EU. This is in complete contradiction with the European Green Deal Industrial Plan (e.g. NZIA…). In order to enhance global competitiveness of these global players, an n exemption for the export of equipment to third Countries should be required.
PFAS and the air filtration industry
A key feature of air filters widely used in HVAC applications, besides high filtration efficiency, is their energy efficiency reflected by average pressure drop over their service life.
Ensuring a low pressure drop, and thus reducing energy consumption to overcome the resistance of airflow through the filters, is essential to achieving global environmental goals.
A fundamental impact on the properties of filters, such as durable water repellency and high dust holding capacity, has C6 (PFHxA), which is an additive used in the manufacture of filter media.
Air filters operate in the wide range of ambient humidity and temperature related to weather conditions. This often results in condensation of moisture on the surface of filtration media. In many cases filters may be exposed to direct rain (when installed close to the outdoor air inlet).  Without accurate water repellency, filtration media loses its properties which leads to water clogging air passages and loss of particle separation abilities. This in turn considerably deteriorates filtration efficiency and increases pressure drop (energy consumption).
No less important is the oil repellency. Filter manufacturers use adhesives (e.g., glue) to pleat the filtration media and assemble the filters. The adhesive bonds the pleated media into the filter frame and prevents liquid or air leakages. By providing oil-repellency, C6 ensures that the media is repellent to glue, preventing the adhesive from penetrating inside the media with the risk of clogging air passages, and ensuring shape stability of the filter. In absence of C6, there would be an increased risk of adhesive adsorption and increasing pressure drop properties, which would ultimately lead to a reduced lifetime and higher energy consumption. Oil-repellence is therefore a crucial feature for filter manufacturers.
The REACH PFAS restriction proposal covers the filtration and separation media used in high performance air and liquid applications in industrial or professional settings that require a combination of water and oil repellence, which include air filtration media containing PFHxA (C6). The currently proposed PFAS derogation, covering the PFHxA (C6) containing media air filters is 6.5 years.
Although the entirely equivalent alternatives of PFHxA (C6) containing filtration media do not exist on the market yet, Eurovent members believe that they will be available in the near future and support the proposed 6.5-year derogation. However, given the importance of the PFHxA (C6) impact on key properties of filtration media, Eurovent would like to emphasize that the proposed derogation period should not be shorten.
To substantiate the Eurovent position, we provide an overview of the HVAC filtration sector and information on the potential impact of too early restrictions on air filters with media containing PFHxA (C6) in the attached appendix.
In conclusion, Eurovent supports the proposed ban with a transition period of 18 months and a 5-year derogation for textiles for the use in filtration and separation media used in high performance air and liquid application in industrial or professional settings that require a combination of water and oil repellence.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: [Hazard or exposure]
We would like to explain the hazard information regarding HCFO-1233zd(E) (hereafter referred to as 1233E). Note that 1233E is the fluorinated gas (CAS RN: 102687-65-0, Chemical Name: trans-1-chloro-3,3,3-trifluoropropene) with a boiling point of 18.3°C.
1233E is not readily biodegradable according to an OECD TG301D study. It is likely to partition to the water rather than to the sediment and soil compartments as it has a relatively low partition coefficient (log Pow = 2.2). Furthermore, the high vapor pressure (1,516kPa at 30°C) suggests that the substance will volatilize rapidly from water and partition to the air. The rapid degradation of the substance in the air is supported by a publication from Sulbaek Andersen et al. (2018)1, which shows a lifetime of 36 days by its reaction with OH in the air. Based on all the evidence, it is concluded that the substance is not persistent and bioaccumulative.
Ref. 1 shows that approximately 2% of TFA is produced by the atmospheric decomposition of 1233E. In addition, trifluoroacetic acid, which is a concern in the proposed restriction, has also been shown to pose a low risk of toxicity to living organisms and human bodies in the reports of the Environment Agency of Germany and Norway, who actually submitted this restriction proposal2,3.
1233E is expected not to be mutagenic since it is negative in the Ames test of OECD TG471 and also negative in the chromosome aberration test of OECD TG473. The substance is also expected to have low toxicity to humans since the LC50 (rat) is 120,000ppm in the acute inhalation test of OECD TG403 and the NOAEC = 4,000ppm in the 90- day repeated inhalation test of OECD TG413. Based on these test results, the WEEL for 1233E is determined to be 800 ppm (8-hours, TWA)4.
Reference 1 indicates that 1233E has an ODP of less than 0.00030, a GWP of less than 5, and a POCP of 3.6. Therefore, in the concentrations expected in the environment its atmospheric degradation products will have a

negligible impact on ecosystems. The substance does not adversely affect environmental problems such as ozone depletion and global warming, so it is environmentally acceptable.
Based on all hazard information, we would like to propose that 1233E should not be regulated as a PFAS.

[Request for exemption]
1233E for blowing agent use is mainly used as a raw material for rigid polyurethane foam. Rigid polyurethane foam is widely used as a heat insulator for consumer and industrial applications. Rigid polyurethane foam consists of minute independent bubbles formed by urethane resin, and gas derived from a blowing agent is sealed inside the bubbles. By using PFAS with low thermal conductivity such as 1233E for that gas, rigid polyurethane foam can achieve higher thermal insulation performance than other insulation materials. In addition, urethane resin has high specific strength and good resistance to low temperatures and dimensional stability. Taking advantage of these features, rigid polyurethane foam is mainly used as heat insulating material in the normal to low temperature range. Major thermal insulation applications are in houses, frozen and refrigerated warehouses, refrigerators, vending machines, plants handling low-temperature fluids such as LNG, LNG carriers, and liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen tanks of large rockets.
Rigid polyurethane foam is produced by foaming the raw material with gas derived from a blowing agent in the process of solidifying the liquid material into a resinous state through a chemical reaction. The raw materials other than the blowing agent are polyol, catalyst, foaming agents, flame retardants, and isocyanate. The most common foaming method for rigid polyurethane foam is to vaporize the blowing agent by reaction heat, but the blowing agent used for this method must have a low thermal conductivity of its gas and a boiling point near room temperature. In addition, many other characteristics are required, such as adequate solubility in the urethane raw material, chemical stability and non-toxicity, and non-flammability. There are very few options for blowing agents that satisfy these requirements, and fluorocarbons have been used in the past.
1233E has low gas thermal conductivity (0.0102 W/m·K, at 20°C) 5, a boiling point near room temperature (18.3°C) 5, chemical stability, low toxicity (WEEL=800ppm) 4, and nonflammability 4. Based on the above, we propose that the use of 1233E in blowing agent applications should be completely exempted from PFAS regulations. 1233E is also used as a refrigerant in centrifugal chiller. General Comments: [Non-confidential response – please review confidential attachment for more details]

Our organization, a leader in mitigation and capture of harmful CO2 emissions using high performance membrane systems, welcomes the European Union's proposal for regulating PFAS-containing materials. We recognize the imperative need for comprehensive regulation in the interest of public health and environmental well-being.

While it is crucial to address and regulate certain PFAS compounds due to their well-documented environmental and health concerns, it is equally important to recognize that not all PFAS materials are created equal. Fluoropolymers have uniquely beneficial properties for CO2 capture and mitigation and have minimal impact on health and the environment. Therefore, these materials merit a separate classification within regulatory efforts when used for critical applications that support the European Union’s decarbonization goals.

In this response, we make the case that the use of fluoropolymers for use in high performance membranes for CO2 mitigation should receive a time-unlimited derogation.

Given the technology is still being developed, for competitive and confidentiality reasons, we are currently unable to publicly disclose certain information. We have therefore attached all the requested information in the confidential attachment. Where possible, we have provided information in the non-confidential sections.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: None of the sectors and (sub-)uses identified in the Annex XV restriction report (Table 9) align well with the proposed applications, we therefore seek the creation of a new sector and (sub-)use category.  The closest sectors and (sub-)uses currently listed are: ● “Textile, upholstery, leather, apparel and carpets (TULAC)”, which includes “technical textiles”, which itself includes “high performance membranes”. However, the description of “high performance membranes” has too many qualifiers: "textiles for the use in filtration and separation media used in high performance air and liquid applications in industrial or professional settings that require a combination of water- and oil repellence". This definition therefore does not align well with the proposed applications. ● “Petroleum and mining”, which includes "fluoropolymer applications". However the examples given for fluoropolymer applications do not include membranes. Additionally, whilst membranes can be used in petroleum and mining applications, they can also be used in numerous other industries.  We therefore propose the creation of the following sub-use: “Fluoropolymers for use in high performance membranes for CO2 mitigation”. We propose that this sub-use be applicable to a broad sector called “heavy industry”, which should include (but not be limited to): Steel & Iron, Cement & Kiln processes, Oil & Gas, Petrochemistry, Chemicals, Pulp & Paper, Glass, Power Generation, Transport.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: [Please review confidential attachment for more details]  Manufacturing phase With appropriate controls, membrane module manufacture can be done using processes that are entirely free from PFAS emissions.  It is also public knowledge that all major fluoropolymer manufacturers have committed to responsible manufacturing practices in the production of fluoropolymers. This includes Chemours that plan to ‘eliminate at least 99% of PFAS air and water emissions from [their] manufacturing processes by 2030’ (see reference 1) and Solvay, which are phasing out, by 2026, the use of fluorosurfactants (see references 2 and 3), one of the largest sources of PFAS emissions in the fluoropolymer manufacturing process.  Use phase Fluoropolymers exhibit a markedly different chemical structure compared to other PFAS compounds. It is well known that their strong carbon-fluorine bonds render them inert and non-reactive in most environmental conditions, which is why they have such exceptional thermal and chemical stability, the very reason they are so popular. This stability significantly reduces the likelihood of release of harmful breakdown products and therefore of harmful emissions during the use phase. This is supported by several papers.  One paper by Henry et al (reference 4) concludes as follows: “This paper brings together fluoropolymer toxicity data, human clinical data, and physical, chemical, thermal, and biological data for review and assessment to show that fluoropolymers satisfy widely accepted assessment criteria to be considered as “polymers of low concern” (PLC). This review concludes that fluoropolymers are distinctly different from other polymeric and non polymeric PFAS and should be separated from them for hazard assessment or regulatory purposes. Grouping fluoropolymers with all classes of PFAS for “read across” or structure–activity relationship assessment is not scientifically appropriate.”  A later paper by Korzeniowski et al (reference 5) expands on Henry et al’s study and concludes that fluoropolymers “satisfy the widely accepted polymer hazard assessment criteria to be considered polymers of low concern (PLC). [...] Further, the study results demonstrate that fluoropolymers are a distinct and different group of PFAS and should not be grouped with other PFAS for hazard assessment or regulatory purposes”.  In the proposed applications, fluorinated products are deployed exclusively in industrial applications, and therefore operated in controlled environments by trained personnel. It is therefore highly unlikely that they would be mis-used in a way that could damage or degrade them so as to lead to harmful releases of PFAS-containing materials.  End-of-life phase In the proposed applications, fluorinated products are deployed exclusively in industrial applications and therefore are easy to track, control, and be properly decommissioned.  Several studies (references 6 and 7) have confirmed that incineration at standard conditions and using existing processes and equipment (e.g. municipal incineration) is an acceptable way to dispose of fluoropolymers with no associated harmful emissions. Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: [Summary of our opinions and Request for exemption]
We are a manufacturer and distributor of endoscopes and related products. We have a high level of interest in and respect for the ECHA PFAS regulation and understand that there are certain reasonable concerns about the impact of PFAS on mankind and the environment. On this basis, we believe it is important to scientifically and objectively assess the risks and benefits of PFAS and to properly manage and regulate them. The endoscopes and related products we manufacture and sell utilise PFAS as an essential material, for which no alternative materials currently exist. We believe that a ban on PFAS in 'endoscopes and related products' is likely to have a serious impact on minimally invasive treatment of cancer patients and testing for the early detection of pathology in the EU. We therefore strongly advocate for an exemption from regulation or maximum derogation period for PFAS used in endoscopes and related products, on the basis of the difficulties associated with  substituting this material and the negative socio-economic impact any potential restriction of its use in our products would have.

[Scope or restriction option analysis]
Endoscopes and related products use PFAS as an essential material for which there is no alternative at present. PFAS is used as a material for components such as endoscope tubes, endoscope sheaths and lens covers. PFAS has excellent properties such as heat resistance, abrasion resistance, chemical resistance, slip resistance, transparency and biocompatibility, and plays a role in enhancing the safety and functionality of endoscopes and related products. PFAS is also an essential material for endoscope sterilization and cleaning equipment. Its resistance to the detergents and disinfectants used for the cleaning and sterilization of endoscopes and its ability to withstand the high temperature, high-pressure conditions under which these processes take place help to achieve the required standard of cleanliness.

[Information on alternatives and Transitional period]
Together with manufacturers of materials and chemicals, we have examined potential alternative materials to PFAS, but at the present time there are no materials other than PFAS that fulfil these functions satisfactorily. For example, silicone rubber and polyurethane have lower heat and abrasion resistance than PFAS and are not suitable for sterilization and cleaning. Inorganic materials such as glass and ceramics are heavier and more easily broken than PFAS and may compromise the operability and safety of the endoscope. In addition, for endoscopes and related products, their manufacturers and distributors are required to carry out performance tests on materials as well as biocompatibility tests to ensure patient safety before registering the product with the authorities. We have estimated that material substitution in endoscopes and related products would require at least 14.5 years, even if alternative materials can be successfully developed.

[Hazard or exposure and Environmental emissions]
We manage the risk of exposure to humans and the environment for endoscopes and related products in accordance with the EU MDR, which requires biocompatibility testing to be carried out on the body-contact parts of medical devices and risk assessment of the impact of the product on the human body. Fluoropolymers" and "Fluoroelastmers" (such as PTFE, FEP, PFA, ETFE, PVDF, EFEP, FEPM, FKM, FFKM) are listed by the OECD as "polymers of low concern"[1] and are used in many applications as safe and stable materials. For example, the above-mentioned PTFE is a biocompatible material and has been used in our endoscopes and related products for decades with no reported adverse effects. ([1] OECD Definition of Polymer; https://www.oecd.org/env/ehs/oecddefinitionofpolymer.htm) In addition, EU MDR Annex I, paragraph 14.7, requires that infectious waste from medical devices be treated by a specialized processor and that its disposal be traceable. As such, medical devices are subject to much stricter controls than general consumer goods or general electronic and electrical equipment. For this reason, we consider the likelihood of PFAS contained in our products being exposed or discharged into the natural environment as a consequence of their disposal to be minimal.

[Information on benefits and other socio-economic analysis (SEA) issues]
The PFAS restriction will have a severe impact on patients who would have benefited from minimally invasive diagnostic methods, treatments and early detection testing with endoscopes and related products. It is expected that endoscopes and related products will be used for more than 18.5 million minimally invasive treatments and early detection procedures in five major European countries (UK, Germany, France, Italy and Spain) in 2023 (Source: Our estimation on the basis of multiple sources). If endoscopic examinations cannot be performed, early detection and treatment of cancer will most likely be missed and cancer will be found at later stages, with a significantly lower chance for a survival rate.

If the use of PFAS is regulated, new research, development, testing and analysis of endoscopes and related products will require significant time and cost. Regulation could cause confusion and uncertainty for healthcare organizations regarding the use and management of endoscopes and related products. There is also cause for concern regarding the potential economic consequences, such as shortages in the supply of endoscopes and related products and price increases. Such outcomes would lead to a decline in the standard of care and an increase in healthcare costs, resulting in significant additional burdens, not only for medical device manufacturers, but also for medical institutions and patients.

For these reasons, we strongly advocate for the 'exemption' or 'maximum derogation period' of PFAS used in endoscopes and related products, on the basis of the difficulties associated with substituting this material and the negative socio-economic impact any potential restriction of its use in our products would have.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Medical devices sector:  We request that ”endoscope and related products” in the medical devices sector be newly added to derogation as missing uses.

6. Missing uses: [Technical factors for PFAS free] 1. Endoscope Materials used for endoscopes must possess a considerable range of highly exacting characteristics. They must be biocompatible and resistant to chemicals (i.e. acidic and alkali chemicals), and also provide arc resistance, safe dielectric strength at thin layer thickness, as well as a non-stick-slip effect for movement; low friction for mounting in and on pipes and rods; low friction for moving parts (during cleaning cycles), high temperature resistance for steam cleaning and disinfection; and also a high degree of resistance to chemicals such as hydrogen peroxide and others during cleaning and disinfection. Furthermore, such materials must also be heat-resistant, mechanical strength, flame resistant, smooth, electrically insulating and abrasion resistant. As a global manufacturer of kitchenware (cookware, ovenware, small domestic appliances), we have been applying PFAS-free Ceramic Non-stick coatings on our own brands of products since 2007. For Private Label and OEM customers worldwide, we have progressively worked with them to phase out use of fluoropolymer type coatings such that our wholly owned cookware factory in China is now virtually PFAS-free. The data below show percentages of PTFE type and Ceramic type Non-stick coatings applied by our factory over the last five years.

Year                   %PTFE              %Ceramic Non-stick
2018                  14.7                  85.3
2019                  13.0                  87.0
2020                  15.6                  84.4
2021                  12.8                  87.2
2022                  16.9                  83.1
2023, H1            1.1                   98.0
2023, H2            less than 1       greater than 99

*2023, H2 percentages are projections based on order book for second half of 2023

Thus, we have demonstrated that switching away from fluoropolymer non-stick is feasible without technical or economic barriers. Moreover, no significant investment in new equipment was needed. Our experience is in line with the following evidence: (i) independent market research that projects a CAGR of 5.3% (forecast period 2021-2028) for Ceramic Non-stick[1]; (ii) the Annual Home World Forecast of consumers’ purchasing intentions for 2021 running at greater than 52.2% in favor of Ceramic Non-stick.[2] It is notable that the CAGR of 5.3% was projected in 2020 (i.e. prior to taking into account the potential impact of the European PFAS Restrictions proposal on the production of PFAS or their alternatives).

These Ceramic Non-stick coatings are based on Sol-Gel chemistry, which provides a Sustainable alternative to fluoropolymer non-stick coatings. Sol-Gel that is used for Ceramic Non-stick does not rely on fluorinated chemistry, and no PFAS processing aids (surfactants) are used. Such processing aids that are required for producing fluoropolymer dispersions are: (i) very highly persistent; (ii) mobile in the environment; (iii) bio accumulative; (iv) associated with chronic diseases, cancers and impaired reproductive health. In Europe, health-related costs to Society, linked to PFAS exposure (especially to C4-C14 surfactants) were estimated in 2019 to be between €52 to 84 Billion.[3] The short chain alternatives to PFOA, including PFHxA, GenX and Adona (for example), remain critical to the manufacture of PTFE Dispersions. However, these alternatives are highly soluble in water, more mobile in soil and readily taken up by plants, for which reason they have been termed Regrettable Substitutes for long-chain counterparts.[4] As well as being more mobile, the KEMI report on “Occurrence and use of highly fluorinated substances and alternatives” states that such short chain alternatives need to be used in higher quantities than the substances that they were replacing in order to achieve the same process effects.[5]

Even if the PFAS processing aids, currently used in the manufacture of PTFE Dispersions, could be replaced, fluoropolymer non-stick will still contain PTFE and potentially other fluoropolymer resins such as PFA (Perfluoroalkoxy Alkanes). Both PTFE and PFA are polymeric forms of PFAS. It is incorrectly argued in some circles that these polymeric PFAS are “merely Persistent” and are not mobile in the environment. However, such arguments ignore the impact on the environment of fluoropolymer non-stick coatings, starting from their manufacture (and associated PFAS emissions) right the way through to the end-of-life disposal either at landfill (with potential to leach fluorinated microplastics) or by incineration (generating emission of gaseous, fluorinated PFAS fragments into the atmosphere).[6] It is reported that one of the thermal degradation products of PTFE is TFA (Trifluoroacetate),[7] TFA has been found in the environment, and its concentrations in evaporative wetlands are predicted to increase over time.[7]

Thermolysis in industrial and consumer applications (e.g. ovens, non-stick utensils) is reported as being a likely significant source of TFA in urban rainwater. The same report goes on to state: “Thermolysis also leads to longer chain polyfluoro- and/or polychlorofluoro- (C3-C14) carboxylic acids that may be equally persistent.”[7]

Apart from PFAS surfactants, manufacture of PTFE itself involves polymerization of TFE (Tetrafluoroethylene, C2F4), which is produced from Fluorspar, Hydrofluoric Acid and Chloroform.[8] TFE contains two Fully Fluorinated Carbon Atoms and, therefore, is itself a type of PFAS. Furthermore, TFE is reported to be a Probable Human Carcinogen.[9]

As PFAS are ubiquitous in the environment, it is evident that production of fluoropolymer non-stick impacts the environment and our health and has a high social cost.[3] Moreover, fluoropolymer non-stick is without question a Non-essential Use when applied on domestic and professional kitchenware. In fact, non-stick coatings in general are non-essential: they merely add convenience. Metal and earthenware cookware, without non-stick coatings, have existed since Medieval times. Modern alternatives to non-stick kitchenware include Seasoned Cast Iron, Carbon Steel or Enamelled cookware. These are practical, easily accessible, affordable and sustainable (known to be virtually indestructible). Accordingly, fluoropolymer non-stick coatings on kitchenware should not be exempted from the EU’s proposed restrictions on PFAS, and neither should they be granted a derogation. A transition period of 18 months is sufficient because the PFAS-free alternatives already exist in the mass market[1-2]. Because there are multiple coating suppliers that offer Sol-Gel alternatives, the switch is scalable without impacting supply chains[10-12].

Sol-Gel coatings are based on Metal Oxide Precursors and, in the case of Ceramic Non-stick, these precursors are Alkoxysilanes[13]. The precursors initially undergo hydrolysis and condensation reactions to form Oligomers (Oligosilanes). Although there is no single oligomer of discrete Molecular Weight (i.e. there can be two or more monomers jointed together), these Oligomers are typified by Polymethylsilsesquioxane (CAS No. 68554-70-1], which is a material permitted in both cosmetics and repeated use non-stick food contact surfaces (21 CFR 177.1520).[14]

Socio-Economic Impact Resulting from Adoption of PFAS-free Alternatives?

As noted above, there will be no shortage of supply of Sol-Gel coatings[10-12]. Moreover, the Alkoxysilane raw materials are readily available in the market worldwide at scale as they are supplied by some of the largest international chemical companies, such as, for example, Dow, Shin-Etsu and Wacker Chemie, which as of 2022 have a combined annual capacity for Silicones of 1.2 Million Metric Tons (out of a total global total capacity for Silicone materials of 3.8 Million Metric Tons).[15] Supply of Alkoxysilane raw material is therefore not a constraint when the global fluoropolymer non-stick coatings market (PTFE, FEP, PFA) in 2020 was worth only USD532.09 Million (2020)[16]

Another reference point in terms of scalability is the fact that cookware is reported to account for around only an estimated 10-13% of total PTFE uses (with Industrial Processing, Electrical and Electronics, Automotive, Healthcare, Construction and other uses contributing the majority).[17] Thus, replacing fluoropolymer non-stick coatings with PFAS-free, Sol-Gel alternatives poses no obstacle of scale.

PFAS are widely used in many other types of coatings.[18] Therefore, our own experience of switching away from fluoropolymer non-stick to PFAS-free alternatives, such as Sol-Gel, provides other coating industries with a Case Study and a model for switching to PFAS-free alternative coatings. Thus, the benefits of eliminating PFAS in non-stick coatings may be replicated across a wide range of coating manufacturing and applications. Independent market research by UBS identifies a scenario in which proposed restrictions are adopted (termed “High Regulation”), which encourages innovation and opportunities for early adopters of new technology.[19] Thus, what is perhaps perceived as a threat by some conventional fluoropolymer non-stick suppliers is an opportunity for encouraging innovation within the European Union.

It is very clear that the cost of inaction on regulating PFAS will be very high. The Nordic report already puts the estimated health costs impact as of 2019 between €52 to 84 Billion.[4] Over the next 30 years, without any regulatory action, emissions during the production and use phases are expected to grow significantly[16], which will in turn lead to increases in emissions and higher impacts on society of the associated health costs, which is the negative side of the ledger.

On the positive side, encouraging development and adoption of PFAS alternatives creates economic opportunity. The UBS report describes the opportunities that will be created in the scenario of High Regulation combined with High Innovation.[19] Accordingly, introduction of restrictions for non-essential PFAS uses is an opportunity for regulators to help mitigate the health impacts and costs on society[4] whilst on the other side of the ledger fostering the adoption of new technology in the field of PFAS-free non-stick coatings as well new PFAS-free alternatives in other fields. The UBS report further notes that high regulation will increase resources allocated to alternative development, thus making them more widely available whilst lowering cost and opposition to regulation.[19]

Suitability of Fluoropolymer Non-stick?

Good Housekeeping reported that pre-heated empty pans may reach a temperature of 507⁰F (264⁰C) whereas a pre-heated pan with oil may reach 514⁰F (268⁰C) and cooking of Hamburgers and Steaks requires temperatures up to 577⁰F (303⁰C) and 656⁰F (347⁰C) respectively.[20]

University research also confirms that empty pans on a domestic stove can reach temperatures as high as 700⁰F.[21a]

In contrast, the maximum long-term use temperature advised by the German BfR for resinous coatings such as fluoropolymers, used on non-stick cooking articles, is limited to 230⁰C or intermittently (for 15 minutes) up to 250⁰C[22]

In its FAQs (2005) concerning non-stick cookware and roastware, the BfR formerly warned:[23]

- “PTFE is a cold, heat and chemical resistant, non-stick plastic. PTFE is non-combustible. It decomposes when overheated. At temperatures above 360°C fumes are released that are toxic to man.”

- “Already at temperatures of more than 360°C toxic fumes are formed from fluoridated compounds and particles. If people inhale them, they can cause flu-like symptoms, so-called Teflon fever (polymer fever). Cases of illness have only, however, been reported from the industrial production of PTFE where the contaminant concentrations are higher than in private homes.”

- “Approximately 202 °C was determined as the lowest critical temperature in animal experiments. At this temperature small PTFE particles already flake off which can have a lethal effect on birds.”

For industrial uses, fluoropolymers such as PTFE are reportedly safe up to 500⁰F (260⁰C).[24-25] Above such temperatures, PTFE start to lose weight, releasing products of thermal degradation[24-25]; moreover, the toxicity of substances released increases as the temperature is raised.[21b]

Furthermore, PubMed states that: “Any industrial or household activity in which PTFE is heated above 350-400 degrees C puts nearby workers or residents at risk of illness and is to be avoided without strict industrial hygiene controls.”[26]

In contrast, Pyrolysis of Ceramic Non-stick coatings up to 850⁰F (450⁰C) and subsequent analysis by GC/MS (Gas Chromatography coupled with Mass Spectrometry), carried out by a third-party accredited analytical laboratory, confirms that no substances of toxicological significance are released.[27]

Suitability of the Alternative - Non-stick Longevity of Sol-Gel?

One criticism which has incorrectly been levelled against Sol-Gel coatings is that such coatings have a shorter non-stick longevity in comparison with PTFE. Such arguments may have had some limited merit in 2007 when Ceramic Non-stick first entered the mass market. However, on the whole, manufacturers of Sol-Gel coatings were quick to improve on this aspect of their coatings.

In fact, testing by third-party accredited laboratories demonstrates that the non-stick properties and longevity of currently available Sol-Gel coatings have in some aspects surpassed those of fluoropolymer non-stick coatings across a range of different tests (such as Hardness, Wear Resistance, Scratch resistance and Heat resistance) that reflect common use and abuse conditions of kitchenware.[28]

These third-party test reports form part of a confidential disclosure to the European Regulators (i.e. not made available to the public). However, in summary:

A) Thermogravimetric Analysis (TGA) confirmed that up to extreme thermal abuse conditions of 600⁰C (752⁰F), Ceramic Non-stick only lost 3-4% of its weight whereas four different brands of PTFE type non-stick coatings lost weight in the range 60 to 90%.

B) Pencil Hardness testing at 200⁰C (as per EN12983-1, Clause 8.4.3 (Annex K)), corresponding to cooking temperatures, showed that the Ceramic Non-stick retained a Pencil Hardness of ≥ 9H whereas the PTFE type non-stick showed a Pencil Hardness of only H.

C) Resistance to Wear was measured at 500⁰F (260⁰C), which according to Good Housekeeping[20] corresponds to a high cooking temperature (e.g. for Hamburgers). In contrast, Ceramic Non-stick provided ≥ 10x the Wear Resistance in comparison with the best of the three well-known PTFE type non-stick brands that were tested.

For the following reasons, the use of fluoropolymers as the cladding material for single-mode plastic optical fibers (SI-POF) employing PMMA in the core should be exempted from the proposed regulations.

- Assumptions -
SI-POF uses the principle of total internal reflection when light enters from a high refractive index material to a low refractive index material, exceeding the critical angle.
Therefore, it has a structure where the high refractive index light guiding material (core) is surrounded by a low refractive index material (cladding), and a numerical aperture (NA), as determined by the following equation, of approximately 0.5 is required,

NA = (n1^2 – n2^2)^(1/2)
n1: refractive index of core, n2: refractive index of cladding

- (1) Significance of POF -
Compared to glass optical fibers, plastic optical fibers (POF) possess superior mechanical strength and significantly larger diameters. Therefore, when applied in key applications such as inter-equipment communication cables, optical sensors, medical devices, lighting, and automotive components, the use of POF is essential to mitigate potential issues including damage, communication disruptions, malfunctioning sensing systems, and medical accidents due to fiber breakage within the body.
(*Standard Diameter: POF 1000μm, Glass Fiber 125μm)

Hence, substituting POF with glass optical fibers is impracticable, as POF is the indispensable material for these applications. Inter-equipment communication and optical sensors are extensively integrated into various production facilities, including semiconductor manufacturing equipment and industrial machinery, making POF a critically important material. Additionally, POF finds application in numerous medical devices, including those used in ophthalmic surgery, solidifying its status as an essential material within the healthcare industry.

- (2) Significance of PMMA core -
The core of POF naturally requires high transparency, and among practical resins, PMMA theoretically possesses the highest level of transparency. Applying resins other than PMMA would result in significant performance deterioration. Therefore, the use of non-PMMA resins is extremely limited to exceptional applications, and PMMA remains the only core resin that meets practical performance requirements.

- (3) Significance of Fluoropolymer cladding -
In practical terms, a numerical aperture (NA) of POF is required to be equal to or greater than 0.5. The refractive index of PMMA is 1.492, and when combined with the previously mentioned equation, it is necessary for the refractive index of the cladding to be 1.4 or lower.

NA = (1.492^2 – n2^2)^(1/2) ≥ 0.5
∴ n2 ≤ 1.405

Considering the Lorentz-Lorenz equation, it can be deduced that only fluoropolymers and silicone satisfy this requirement. However, silicone exhibits extremely poor adhesion with PMMA, making it unsuitable for use as a cladding material. Therefore, apart from fluoropolymers, there are no other materials available for use as the cladding.

- (4) Conclusion -
As mentioned earlier, POF is being used as an irreplaceable component in various industries, and its core must be made of PMMA. Therefore, the use of fluoropolymer as the cladding material for POF employing PMMA as the core is essential. Consequently, it is necessary to exempt the use of fluoropolymer as the cladding for POF with PMMA core from the proposed regulations.

*For details about basic principles and characteristics of POF, please refer to [Ref1].
*For details about low refractive index polymers, please refer to [Ref2].

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: 1. About our company and our expertise
Our Company (15 employees, about 3 million Euros turnover) develops, manufactures and sells devices (equipment) for chemical and pharmaceutical research and production outside and inside the EU. Our devices are called to be very sustainable.
All our devices need and use elastomeric sealing materials (usually O-rings). Our experiences and our comments are about:
• FFKM, a completely fluorinated material (most-known trade name is Kalrez), this is the only known elastomeric sealing material that can be used at temperatures of 300 °C or even more.
• FKM, a partly fluorinated material (most-known trade name is Viton)
• FVMQ, a fluorinated silicone material that can be used at very low temperatures, for example down to  60 °C
(Our company also uses PTFE as a sealing or insulation material in some applications, but since this is not an elastomeric material, we skip this point in the current comments to keep the argumentation more comprehensible.)

2. About elastomeric PFAS-polymers as sealing materials
The conditions of chemical reactions for chemical and pharmaceutical research cover all conditions that are known in chemistry – including:
• high and low temperatures
• high and low pH-values
• high pressure
• liquids with various abilities to solve substances/materials
• hazardous substances that must remain strictly sealed
The only way to seal demountable devices against leakage are elastomeric sealings. The only elastomeric materials that withstand such conditions are PFAS-polymers.

3. About possible metallic alternatives
Metallic seals are used as a standard for tube connections – including at our company. But tube-shaped connections are the only type of connection where these sealings can be used. Reaction devices with the ability to be disassembled (an essential feature especially in the field of research) need different types of sealings – O-rings and others.

4. About possible elastomeric alternatives
A simple look into the resistance tables of any supplier of elastomeric sealings proof, that no non-fluorine-containing sealing material is known – not even close. (Proofs from two example sources are attached in section IV.)
This is a fact now and it will be a fact in the future, unfortunately. The unique characteristics of elastomeric PFAS-sealings are based on the unique C-F-bond. The periodic table is well known, and due to the unique role of carbon (the only element with the ability to build molecules in the “organic chemistry”) and the unique role of fluorine (element with the highest possible electronegativity) it is sure that no alternatives with the same or even similar characteristics will be possible.
Of course, there are chemical reactions, that can be performed with sealings made from non-fluorine-elastomers – EPDM, for example. FKM is significant more expensive than EPDM and FFKM is roughly about 100 times more expensive than FKM. We are talking about extreme expensive sealing materials and usually nobody would use them, if a much cheaper non-fluorine-material is suited just as well.

5. About the consequences of a total ban of PFAS-elastomers as sealing materials
• Chemical and pharmaceutical research will not be possible.
• Especially pharmaceutical ingrediencies for medicine usually need advanced chemistry that is impossible without these sealings, so the availability of most medicines will be affected negatively.
• Our company would not be able to sell any devices and will not be able to exist. So there would be a job loss of 15 out of 15 jobs.

6. About the need of exemptions
As mentioned before, no alternatives for most applications of PFAS as elastomeric sealings are to expect. From today’s point of view an everlasting exemption for many chemical applications is necessary.

7. About emissions
There are three phases where emissions may occur caused by PFAS-elastomeric sealings:
1. Manufacturing
We have no knowledge about this, but it will definitely be possible to manufacture these sealings without emissions. The number of companies involved in this is rather small.
2. Use (including storage and assembling)
Environmental emissions do not occur during the use of the sealings in our devices.
3. End of life
Measures to avoid emissions in this phase are possible (see comments below in the section for request 2).

8. About quantities
In 2022 our company bought about 2000 O-rings with a total mass of less than 0,1 kg FFKM and less than 0,2 kg FKM. Even though this is a very small amount, this is an essential part of our devices.

9. About the scope of the PFAS restrictions (personal general comments)
As explained before, alternatives for polymeric PFAS with the same characteristics, but no environmental drawbacks, are not possible. So, the questions are:
a) Can the polymeric PFAS be replaced by a material with more limited characteristics?
If this is the case, all activities to enforce this replacement are very welcome.
b) Can the polymeric PFAS be not replaced by another material?
This is true for many chemical applications.
In this case it must be decided whether this application is not needed or if an emission-free way including manufacturing, use and disposal is possible.
In my opinion chemical research and pharmaceutical production should not and cannot be waived and an emission-free business for PFAS-sealings will and must be possible.

10. Conclusion
Since it is not possible to replace PFAS-elastomers as sealing materials in most cases the suggested alternative is to ensure emission-free manufacturing and emission-free disposal – while use is already emission-free. A proposed measure is to set mandatory colours for PFAS elastomers.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: This information is about (per)fluorinated elastomeric sealings (O-rings) for chemical applications.  The typical end of life scenarios for O-rings in our devices are: • exchange because of change of characteristics (elastomeric behaviour) during the use • exchange because of mechanical damage In both cases the O-rings are usually still complete and able to collect. The lifetime lasts usually up to several years.  Disposal of the O-rings occurs usually in the garbage/waste/litter since no system for collection and recycling exists. PFAS-O-rings and O-rings without fluorine often look almost the same and are difficult to differ as a result. Most O-rings are manufactured in black colour, but special colours are possible. For some fluoropolymers colours are more or less common. If our company uses FKM, we always buy them in green colour, in cases we buy FVMQ, it is usually available in blue.  To avoid fluorinated O-rings to be disposed in undefined ways, it would be helpful to define special colours. Based on a defined colour code the collection of elastomeric fluorine-polymers would be possible. After collection recycling would be desirable or a defined destruction without environmental impact, at least.

6. Missing uses: The missing application of elastomeric PFAS polymers as elastomeric sealing material is described above in the general comments. The answers to the elements listed in this chapter are:   a. The annual tonnage of PFAS as elastomeric sealing material should be known by the rather small number of manufacturers of such sealings. Our company uses much less than 1 kg per year. There are no emissions during use.  b. Sealing of chemical devices under harsh conditions (including very high or very low temperatures, high or low pH-values and other corrosive conditions). c. Almost all companies performing advanced chemical reactions. Many thousands of companies in the chemical and pharmaceutical industry and almost all universities. d. For chemical reactions that need FFKM to seal, no alternatives are available or in sight. For other polymers used as sealings (PTFE, FKM, FVMQ, and many more) alternatives may be available in some cases, but not with the same or even similar functionalities. e. The Carbon-Fluorine-bond is unique in the well-known periodic table. It is not likely that any other type of chemicals can ever be developed, that has the advantageous features of the PFAS, but not their negative environmental features. If chemical research (and production) is desired, fluorinated polymers cannot be banned in general:  • Measurements to limit their use on applications without alternative can be acceptable. • Constraints to collect them at the end of the lifetime can be acceptable.  • Higher prices caused by stricter manufacturing requirements are thinkable, however have to be acceptable.  f. – g. Of course, it is up to the big chemical companies to tell, but I am sure that multi billion Euros of sales and profit with chemical and pharmaceutical products will be impossible or transferred outside the EU without the possibility to use fluorinated elastomers as sealing compounds.  Actually, it is not a single use missing. Every chemical synthesis performed in research or production is a different use case.  In case of large-scale chemical production specific fluorine-free sealings may be evaluated and found. For research and small-scale production sealings that resist without any doubt must be available – the only known option in many cases are fluorinated sealings.

Content: Information on alternatives Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: 1. About the substitution of -CF3 group-containing liquid crystal molecules by -CN group-containing liquid crystal molecules for liquid crystal display application.

Active-matrix liquid crystal displays (hereafter referred to as AM-LCDs) are currently used worldwide as an excellent display system with high contrast sensitivity. The liquid crystal compounds used in the initial stages of AM-LCD development were liquid crystal mixtures, mainly consisting of liquid crystal compounds possessing cyano groups. However, they had the significant disadvantage of low voltage holding ratio (VHR), which disturbs the performance of the thin film transistors resulting poor image contrast of the liquid crystal displays.

Subsequently, it was discovered that liquid crystal compounds with fluorine atoms had a high VHR, so that liquid crystal compounds with cyano groups are not used at all as liquid crystals for AM-LCDs at present.

Figure 2 in literature Mol. Cryst. Liq. Cryst., 1995, Vol 264, pp57-65 shows the data comparing the temperature dependence of the voltage retention of ZLI-1132, whose main components are liquid crystal compounds containing cyano groups, and FB-01, whose main components are liquid crystal compounds with fluorine atoms instead of cyano groups. The figure shows that the VHR of ZLI-1132 drops sharply as T-Tc approaches 0°C from 60°C, whereas that of FB-01 is maintained at almost 100%. From this result liquid crystal compounds with cyano groups cannot be used for AM-LCDs.

For the above reasons, liquid crystal compounds having cyano groups cannot be a substitute for the substances proposed in the PFAS. They are also irreplaceable in terms of practical evaluation and the LCD industry. The proposed no grace period is not appropriate and should be exempted from the proposed restriction.

Multi-folded scientific and industrial efforts about the development of the fluorinated liquid crystal compounds have been provided in these 30 years, and they are now essential for AM-LCDs. The requirements for liquid crystal materials for AM-LCDs and the usefulness of fluorinated liquid crystals are well summarized for example in chapters 2 and 3 of the article Angew. Chem. Int. Ed, 2000, 39, 4216-4235.

The comments of Prof. Dr Dietrich Demus, a member of the German National Academy of Sciences "Leopoldina", on this matter are attached in Section Ⅳ.
The CV of Prof Dietrich Demus is also attached in Section Ⅴ.

2.  Additional substances excluded from PFAS restrictions - Compounds with X'
being cyclohexyl should be added to the structural elements of exempted compounds

Up on the expansion of the applications of the active-matrix liquid crystal displays (hereafter abbreviated as AM-LCD), such as PC monitors, notebook PCs, mobile phones and TVs, the properties required for the liquid crystal materials are diversifying. Among them, the reduction of the drive voltage and the response time (switching speed) are the most important and common factors for any of drive modes.

Among the liquid crystal materials that have been developed so far, a series of liquid crystal compounds, in which a cyclohexyl group is directly connected to a difluoromethylene (-CF2-) (hereafter abbreviated as RHHXF3) in the chemical structures are key components for solving the above mentioned requirements. RHHXF3 makes it possible to realize the liquid crystal mixtures that exhibit the wider mesophase temperature range (TNI) and large increase of the dielectric anisotropy (Δε). Those liquid crystal mixtures provide the LCD showing lower drive voltage, decreased viscosity, faster response (switching speed), and the reduction of the power consumption of the LCDs.

The properties of liquid crystal materials having a structure, in which a cyclohexyl group is directly connected to a difluoromethylene (-CF2-) are described, for example, in the literature Mol. Cryst. Liq. Cryst., Vol. 411, pp. 127 (2004). According to Figure 3 of this literature, the liquid crystal mixture containing RHHXF3 simultaneously achieves higher values of dielectric anisotropy and lower viscosity, and has a wider liquid crystal (mesophase) temperature range than that of the liquid crystal materials with other linkage groups. The liquid crystal compounds having this structural element (cyclohexyl-CF2-) are especially useful for AM-LCD applications. RHHXF3 is currently widely used as a liquid crystal material for high dilution TVs and mobile phones.

Liquid crystal compound namely trans-4-propyl-trans-4'-[4-(trifluoromethoxy)phenyl]-1,1'-bi(cyclohexane) (hereafter abbreviated as 3HP0CF3) is conventionally used for AM-LCDs and is excluded from the definition of PFAS-restricted objects in the recent ANNEX XV. Data comparison of the physical properties of this compound with those of trans-4-[difluoro(3,4,5-trifluorophenoxy)methyl]-trans-4'-propan-1-ylbicyclohexyl (hereinafter abbreviated as 3HHXF3 where R=propyl for RHHXF3), are given in the Japanese Patent Bulletin in Table 2 of the Japanese Patent Gazette (attached). The liquid crystal mixture containing 3HP0CF3 is much inferior to that with 3HHXF3 in terms of the property values (TNI, Δε and viscosity) essentially required for AM-LCD. Therefore, it is incredibly challenging to substitute RHHXF3 with compounds that do not fall under the PFAS definition.

In the more than 50 years since the emergence of displays using nematic liquid crystals in 1968, liquid crystal displays have undergone various technological innovations and are widely used worldwide as a reasonably priced display medium that supports today's electronic information society. As one of the items that support our daily lives, the significance of their existence is high. One of the most common applications requiring a wide display temperature range is LCDs for automobiles, while special applications requiring high resolution include medical monitors. For automotive applications, displays for monitoring the status of electronic control are indispensable as automated driving technology is spread in the future. In this context, if the use of the RHHXF3 is restricted, it will have a significant impact on the socio-economy of various sectors, including the automotive industry and the medical business.

As liquid crystal compounds for AM-LCDs are required to be stable on display, it is a prerequisite that they are persistent. However, even if the liquid crystal compounds are released into the environment, they should have no ecological impact. The result of ecotoxicity tests conducted on 3HHXF3 is attached. 3HHXF3 is persistent, but its solubility in water is below the lower limit of quantification, so the bioaccumulation test result for fish is below the standard value and it has little bioaccumulation potential.

For the above reasons, compounds where R in the definition of PFAS-restricted objects in the recent ANNEX XV is a cyclohexyl group should be added to the structural elements of the compounds to be excluded from the proposed PFAS.

Content: Information on alternatives Information on benefits Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: 1. Arguments for fluoropolymers (PFAS subtype)
The restriction proposal’s approach to group together all fluoropolymers with other PFAS types must be revisited. Henry (2018) and Korzeniowski (2022) demonstrated that most fluoropolymers meet the OECD criteria to be defined as ‘polymers of low concern’. They verifiably do not pose a risk to human health or the environment as they are not water soluble, toxic and bioavailable. In addition, fluoropolymers uses in the hydrogen value chain are restricted to highly controlled industrial environments, where contact with workers or consumers is demonstrably limited and strictly supervised. Therefore, regulatory action should focus on tackling any potential PFAS emissions at all life-stages (manufacturing, use and end-of-life) and not on banning these essential, high-performing and low-concern products. Fluoropolymer production and use shall therefore be exempted from the U-PFAS restriction.

2. Inputs on suggested alternatives
There are some non-PFAS microporous membrane materials on the European market. While such non-PFAS materials were found to provide adequate performance for some vents used in ‘non-harsh’ conditions, these materials were not viable for products used in harsh environment applications. These (harsh) uses require vents made with the combination of temperature stability and chemical resistance (inherent in PTFE) that can be processed into a thin, microporous substrate.
Assuming that a new non-PFAS material in the future may meet performance, manufacturing, and regulatory requirements, it may easily not meet cost and profitability targets. If material costs are increased, or productivity is reduced / limited economies of scale, and market conditions mean that it is not possible to pass these costs onto the customer, then these non-PFAS materials may not be economically viable.
The challenges with finding alternatives to PFAS in venting products used in the automotive sector is also highlighted by the German Association of the Automotive Industry (2021: pg 3) which states that “without PFAS, both existing vehicles and future automotive technologies would be inconceivable”. The reasons given by the Association is that components containing PFAS “satisfy high standards and quality requirements”, including “guaranteed vehicle safety, reliability under large temperature fluctuations, flame retardancy and high durability over the whole lifecycle of 15 to 22 years” (German Association of the Automotive Industry, 2021).
For example, let’s consider ‘automotive electronic enclosures vents.’ Open venting solutions (like tubes) do equalize pressure but cannot protect against liquid intrusion, which would lead to component failure. There are a few PTFE membrane style alternatives (using polymers such as polyether sulfone (PES) and polyethylene terephthalate (PET)) which cannot meet the combination of attributes that PTFE exhibits - specifically around chemical resistance, temperature stability, mechanical robustness, and durability. Membrane alternatives are used in less challenging environments (for example, temperature requirements) or systems (for example, Tire Pressure Monitor systems) or less safety critical electronic applications. Open venting solutions are not an option for electronic enclosures.
3. The proposal does not meet the requirements for a restriction proposal as required by REACH.
According to REACH Annex XV Part II-3, the risk addressed by the restriction must be in the form of a Chemical Safety Report based on the relevant hazard and risk assessment set out in Annex I. In REACH, persistence is subject to risk assessment only when combined with bioaccumulation and in some cases with toxicity. However, this restriction proposal is based on persistence alone, which is not considered a hazard endpoint, as if all PFASs are hazardous. In addition, while exposure assessments should be made for each use by creating exposure scenarios, all PFASs are grouped together, so the assessment for each use is insufficient and does not indicate the existence of unacceptable risks as required by Article 68. Therefore, we believe that this proposal does not meet the requirements for a restriction proposal as required by REACH, and it is not appropriate to discuss a restriction.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: VENT products using PTFE Membrane can satisfy the IP rating of equipment requiring dustproofing and waterproofing because they have micropores and hydrophobicity even when applied only to small-sized parts exposed to the outside. Stretched PTFE is hydrophobic and has a surface energy of 19 dynes/cm. It can easily push out fluids with a surface tension of 40 dynes/cm or more, such as water. In addition, additional fluoropolymer treatment ensures oleophobicity to further lower the surface tension, preventing the inflow of potential low surface tension fluids and pure water. By preventing potential device failures from occurring, you can prevent the increase in waste from vehicle and electronic device parts. Not all polymers are hydrophobic, and none is as inherently hydrophobic as PTFE. Although PTFE Membrane is very thin, it has a three-dimensional microstructure with pores smaller than 1㎛, preventing the inflow of smaller particles. Non-porous materials such as urethane, silicone, or PEEK can be used to seal pores, but because they do not have pores, they do not distribute pressure evenly. This causes pressure to be applied to the membrane, destroying it, compromising the functionality of the equipment, and causing it to be discarded. Therefore, non-porous membranes are not an alternative to PTFE membranes used in VENTs. Woven Mesh provides protection against light rain and liquids but allows small dust particles to pass through. This is because it has a structure of a single layer and regular interval pattern of similar size. Therefore, it is not protected from strong rain or excessive liquid, which may result in the device being discarded due to deterioration in performance. Although various non-PFAS polymers can be used to create porous membranes, these materials do not have sufficiently low surface energy and cannot achieve both oleophobic and hydrophobic properties. This is also not suitable for VENT as it is not water-repellent. For example, polysulfone has a surface energy of 47 dynes/cm, and PET Membrane has a surface energy of 39 dynes/cm, which is too high for VENT use and has poor permeability due to low porosity. Expanded polyethylene and electrospun poly urethane, which have a certain level of hydrophobicity, are not suitable for VENT because they melt or deform at a temperature of 150℃.
