General Comments: 1. Arguments for fluoropolymers (PFAS subtype)
The restriction proposal’s approach to group together all fluoropolymers with other PFAS types must be revisited. Henry (2018) and Korzeniowski (2022) demonstrated that most fluoropolymers meet the OECD criteria to be defined as ‘polymers of low concern’. They verifiably do not pose a risk to human health or the environment as they are not water soluble, toxic and bioavailable. In addition, fluoropolymers uses in the hydrogen value chain are restricted to highly controlled industrial environments, where contact with workers or consumers is demonstrably limited and strictly supervised. Therefore, regulatory action should focus on tackling any potential PFAS emissions at all life-stages (manufacturing, use and end-of-life) and not on banning these essential, high-performing and low-concern products. Fluoropolymer production and use shall therefore be exempted from the U-PFAS restriction..

2. Inputs on suggested alternatives
PTFE’s chemical / physical properties (due to the chemistry of carbon-fluorine (C-F) bonds) are unique, and it is SFTC’s understanding that it is not possible to replace the use of PTFE in any of their filtration products without a negative impact on the performance on the end-products.
The PTFE membrane filter has the capability to collect more than 99.9% of these pollutants, while non-PTFE membrane filters typically show an efficiency of ~50%-99.5%-99.95% efficiency) (EMW Flitertechnik, n.d.). This is one of the reasons filters used in harsh environments almost exclusively use PFAS materials to help maximize capture and control of potential air emissions.
Lower performing filters (e.g. polyester) are already used in less demanding applications, (e.g. to collect coarse, non-hazardous dust from air streams). These non-PFAS alternative filters (to SFTC’s Filters) typically have shorter lifespans and thereby generate more waste. Using alternative filters is also expected to increase the energy used, and due to higher resistance to gas flow, will be more challenging to clean.
As there are no alternatives that have the same performance as PTFE-based filters, any transition to non-PFAS alternatives by 2025 would require the customer to find a different solution that in most cases would decrease their performance, resulting and lower efficiency and (by default) additional emissions and/or reduced savings on the carbon footprint area. Less effective filters would also allow more fine dust to pass through; this means that more dioxins, heavy metals and other toxic or carcinogenic pollutants would be emitted and eventually end up in ambient air, surface waters and in the food chain. In addition, potential replacements would be expected to not meet the performance requirements of environmental regulation and potentially lead to concern with regard to ambient air quality.

3. The proposal does not meet the requirements for a restriction proposal as required by REACH.
According to REACH Annex XV Part II-3, the risk addressed by the restriction must be in the form of a Chemical Safety Report based on the relevant hazard and risk assessment set out in Annex I. In REACH, persistence is subject to risk assessment only when combined with bioaccumulation and in some cases with toxicity. However, this restriction proposal is based on persistence alone, which is not considered a hazard endpoint, as if all PFASs are hazardous. In addition, while exposure assessments should be made for each use by creating exposure scenarios, all PFASs are grouped together, so the assessment for each use is insufficient and does not indicate the existence of unacceptable risks as required by Article 68. Therefore, we believe that this proposal does not meet the requirements for a restriction proposal as required by REACH, and it is not appropriate to discuss a restriction.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Field: PTFE Media filters for high-performance filtration applications used in industrial environments and homes. Use: Filtration applications requiring low gas permeability, chemical resistance, and low pressure loss.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Stretched PTFE Membrane has high air permeability because it creates millions of micropores per ㎠. In addition, PTFE itself is hydrophobic and has a very low friction coefficient. Glass fiber or polyester felt filters have the property of trapping dust particles inside the pores, so they can ensure efficiency above a certain thickness. However, it is difficult to remove trapped dust particles, so the lifespan of the filter is short. Filters made of PTFE have a low coefficient of friction, allowing dust on the surface to be removed with only small vibrations, ensuring a long service life. Due to these characteristics, when comparing the pressure loss of glass fiber material and PTFE material in ULPA specifications with the same filter efficiency of 99.9999%, the glass fiber material has a pressure loss of 500Pa, but the PTFE material has a low pressure loss of less than 300Pa. It possesses excellent characteristics in terms of energy efficiency. PTFE material filters also have excellent characteristics in discharging chemical components. In an experiment conducted by Nitto, residual chemical components were analyzed by exposure to Bibutyl phthalate, Methyl Ethyl Ketone Oxime, Methyl Isobutyl Ketone Oxime, and Fluoro Alkyl Alcohol. In the case of glass fiber materials, residual chemical components were 1100ppm, 1000ppm, 210ppm, and 1240ppm, respectively. Although it was detected, no residual chemical components were detected in the PTFE material. In addition, the total amount of emissions was confirmed to be 7,860 ppm (㎍/㎡) for glass fiber materials and 461 ppm (㎍/㎡) for PTFE materials, which is 6% of that of glass fiber materials. https://ko.snylifilter.com/info/advantages-of-ptfe-materials-77553467.html

Content: Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: 1. Concern of pharmaceutical manufacturers:
Scenario two contains an exemption for active substances in medicinal products (API, Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients) that is not limited in time. However, other substances used in the manufacture of medicinal products (e.g., ingredients, excipients) as well as (manufacturing) processes are not exempted from the restriction proposal:

1. APIs without EU approval, this concerns e.g., PFAS APIs for worldwide export.
2. Chemical raw materials, starting substances for synthesis, catalysts as well as e.g., intermediates and other substances and auxiliaries required for synthesis (e.g., solvents, tubes, filters, liners etc.) for API production.
3. APIs in development. Beyond a production volume of 1 tonne per year, the exemption for scientific research and development no longer applies and both production and further development would be no longer possible in the EU.
4.  Other "non-active" ingredients in medicinal products, such as excipients/auxiliary substances and propellants, as well as substances and auxiliaries necessary for their manufacture (e.g., solvents, tubes, filters, etc.).
5.  Primary packaging materials and sterile barrier systems, even if they are part of the marketing authorisation.
6. Products containing PFAS, such as seals, valves, tubes, filters and membranes which are required, among other things, in production facilities for the manufacture of medicinal products and for their analysis.


2. Concern of medical device manufacturers:
Scenario two includes an exemption for fluoropolymers or perfluoropolyethers in implantable medical devices (e.g., acetabular cups made of Teflon). This exemption does not apply to suture material, mesh, wound care products, tubing and catheters. All other medical devices, substances used in manufacturing as well as (manufacturing) processes are not exempted from the restriction proposal:
1.  PFAS-containing ingredients in medical devices, the following are some examples:
(a) substance-based medical devices (example: ocular endotamponades (perfluorodecalin and perfluorooctane), excipients for sperm transfer in in vitro fertilisation (perfluorooctane)) these contribute to the physical effect of the medical devices holistically.
b) medical devices (example: ventilators, X-ray machines) containing PFAS polymers or polymers with PFAS coatings (e.g., tubes, catheters, films, membranes, or containers for 3D printing).
2.  All substances required to manufacture ingredients/components for a medical device, such as chemical raw materials, catalysts as well as e.g. intermediates and other substances and auxiliaries required for synthesis (e.g., solvents, tubing, filters, films, etc.).
3.  Medical devices under development (including the exceptions mentioned above).
4.  Primary packaging materials and sterile barrier systems of medical devices. These are crucial for the shelf life of the product and are part of the technical documentation of the medical device.
5.  Products containing PFAS, such as gaskets, valves, tubing and membranes required for medical device manufacturing processes and analysis.

Consequences of the restriction proposal:
The supply of medicinal products and medical devices to the population must be the overriding objective of all regulations adopted. Especially under the aspect of the constantly growing problem of supply shortages (Good practices for industry for the prevention of human medicinal product shortages), this goal must not be lost sight of. The restriction proposal also refers to the security of supply of medicinal products for the population in the justification on page 72 for the exemption for active pharmaceutical ingredients (API): "Human MPs are important for the protection of humans from diseases".
In scenario two of the restriction proposal, there is an indefinite exemption for active substances in pharmaceutical products (API) and an exemption for fluoropolymers or perfluoropolyethers in implantable medical devices, this does not apply to meshes, wound care products, tubes, and catheters. All other substances as well as processes in and during the manufacture of medicinal products and medical devices, as listed in detail above, are affected by the restriction. This will have far-reaching effects both in the field of medicinal products and medical devices. For example, many substance-based medical devices (e.g., ocular endotamponades, excipients for sperm transfer in IVF) may then no longer be available on the market without alternative. This also applies to other medical devices (for example: respirators, X-ray equipment) that contain PFAS polymers or polymers with PFAS coatings (e.g., tubes, catheters, films or containers for 3D printing). Since all substances required for the production of the ingredients/components of a medical device, such as chemical raw materials, catalysts as well as e.g., intermediates and other substances required for synthesis (e.g. tubes, filters, films, etc.) are also not exempt from the restriction, massive problems will also arise here. This is also transferable to e.g., PFAS-containing seals, valves, tubes and membranes, which are necessary for the manufacturing process for medical devices.
These problems are just as present for the manufacture of medicinal products, because despite an exemption for active substances in medicinal products (API) that is not limited in time, the (manufacturing) processes (see above: Concerns of pharmaceutical manufacturers) and the necessary substances such as chemical raw materials, catalysts as well as e.g. intermediates and other substances required for synthesis for API manufacture are not exempt.



General demands:
A clear legal structure without double regulations is imperative. Medicinal products and medical devices that have a marketing authorisation (API authorisation, marketing authorisation, MDR/IVDR, etc.) as well as restricted or regulated substances (F-gas, specific Reach restrictions) should generally be excluded from the restriction proposal in order to avoid regulatory conflicts.

Demands regarding Medicinal Products:
In order to ensure the supply of medicinal products to the population and to achieve the goal that the production of medicinal products can remain or even be expanded in Europe, further specific exemptions (raw materials/intermediates, reagents, materials such as PVDF filters, PFAS-coated equipment parts for manufacturing) are necessary in addition to the exemption for active pharmaceutical ingredients in medicinal products, which is not limited in time: Transition periods must not only take into account technical development and substitution, but also take into account the duration/time required for requalification and revalidation, conducting stability studies, regulatory changes (variations) or re-registration (up to ~10 years).
Therefore, we call for a full exemption for the entire finished medicinal product including manufacturing. This includes:

1. API without EU approval.
2. Chemical raw materials, synthesis starting substances, catalysts as well as e.g., intermediates and other substances and auxiliaries required for synthesis (e.g. solvents, tubes, filters, etc.) for API production.
3. APIs under development.
4.  Other "non-active" ingredients in medicinal products, such as additives/excipients and propellants, as well as substances and auxiliaries required for their manufacture (e.g. solvents, tubes, filters, etc.).
5. Primary packaging materials and sterile barrier systems, even if they are part of the marketing authorisation.
6.  Products containing PFAS, such as seals, valves, tubes, filters and membranes which are required, among other things, in production facilities for the manufacture of medicinal products and for their analysis.

In addition to a full exemption, an exemption subject to conditions (see ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT - Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs), Proposed restriction - Annex XVII entry PFASs (Restriction Option 2), Point 8), such as the preparation and regular maintenance of site management plans, would be conceivable.
If a full exemption or a full exemption subject to conditions of the required points 1. - 6. is not possible, we request an additional transition period of 10 years to the maximum transition period of 13.5 years granted in the restriction proposal, i.e., a total of 23.5 years for points 1. - 6. above.
An extension of the proposed transition periods is necessary, as not only technical development and substitution may be considered, but additional periods for requalification, revalidation, performance of stability studies, regulatory changes or re-authorisation are required.


Demands for medical devices:
In order to ensure the supply of the population with medical devices, further specific exemptions are necessary in addition to the temporary exemption for fluoropolymers or perfluoropolyethers in implantable medical devices (PFAS-containing ingredients e.g. raw materials/intermediates, reagents as well as materials such as PVDF filters, PFAS-coated equipment parts for manufacturing): Transition periods must not only take into account technical development and substitution, but must also take into account the duration / time required for requalification and revalidation, the performance of stability studies, regulatory changes or recertification.
Therefore, we call for a full exemption for all medical devices including their manufacture. This includes:

1. All medical devices.
2. All substances required to manufacture the ingredients/components of a medical device, such as chemical raw materials, catalysts as well as e.g. intermediates and other substances and auxiliaries required for synthesis (e.g. solvents, tubes, filters, films, etc.).
3. Medical devices under development.
4. Primary packaging materials and sterile barrier systems of medical devices, even if they are part of the technical documentation.
5. Products containing PFAS, such as gaskets, valves, tubing and membranes required for medical device manufacturing processes and analyses.

In addition to a full exemption, a conditional exemption (see ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT - Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs), Proposed restriction - Annex XVII entry PFASs (Restriction Option 2), Point 8), such as the preparation and regular maintenance of site management plans, would be conceivable.
If a full exemption or a full exemption subject to conditions of the required points 1. - 6. is not possible, we request an additional transition period of 10 years to the maximum transition period of 13.5 years granted in the restriction proposal, i.e., a total of 23.5 years for the above-mentioned points 1. - 6.
An extension of the proposed transition periods is necessary, as not only technical development and substitution may be considered, but additional periods for requalification, revalidation, performance of stability studies, preclinical and, if applicable, clinical studies and their evaluation, regulatory changes or recertification are required.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: 1. If there are many substances involved in the restriction proposal, risk assessment should be carried out separately
The restriction proposal to include around 10,000 substances under control based on their molecular structure alone is contrary to the restriction principle of the EU REACH regulation, which stipulates that substances can only be restricted if they pose an unacceptable risk to human health or the environment.
The physical, chemical and biological safety of PFAS substances of different structures is different, and all substances to be restricted should be subject to a risk assessment in accordance with Annex XV of REACH to analyze whether there is an unacceptable risk and, if not, the substance should be removed from the restriction proposal.
It is recommended to separate fluoropolymers (such as: PTFE, PVDF, FEP, PFA, ETFE, PCTFE...). Individual assessments are made to see if they pose an unacceptable risk to human health or the environment. Such substances should not be placed on restricted lists until clear conclusions have been reached.

2. The whole life cycle risk of fluoropolymer is controllable and should not be included in the scope of the proposed restriction and control
Fluoropolymers have highly stable properties, do not have bioaccumulation, long-distance migration, biotoxicity, and are difficult to pose a threat to the environment and human health. Fluoropolymers are recognized as “polymers of low concern (PLC)” by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), and are not restricted substances under the REACH regulation.
From the perspective of fluoropolymer preparation process, each manufacturer implements strict control over the whole process of fluoropolymer production, and PFAS substances other than fluoropolymers can be controlled within the scope of compliance.
Fluoropolymers meet the OECD classification of "Polymers of Low Concern" and do not require special emission control measures during normal processing and application phases.
After the use of the product, the emission risk can be controlled through recycling, landfill, and standardized incineration.
Therefore, the whole life cycle risk of fluoropolymers is controllable and fluoropolymers should not be included in the scope of the restriction control.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: 1. Introduction
Armstrong International is a fifth-generation family-owned company specialised in solving and preventing thermal utility problems for satisfied customers all across Europe and beyond. Our in-depth experience, knowledge and insight, allow us to maximize energy efficiency especially through industrial waste heat recovery, thus lowering energy use and reducing environmental emissions.

High-temperature heat pumps (HTHPs) allow to recovery industrial waste heat and upgrade its temperature up to 120°C – these allow to generate low pressure steam, which can then be compressed up to 200°C. Our HTHPs use HFO/HCFO working fluids that allow to achieve these high temperatures, while the pressure within the refrigerant circuit remains relatively low. The two substances used in our industrial high-temperature heat pumps, namely HCFO-1233zd(E) and HFO-1234ze(E), currently do not have a safe alternative and therefore should not be restricted under the current legislation.  HTHPs are installed in controlled industrial environment and the working fluid is retained in a closed circuit and is therefore fully recoverable. A critical advantage of these working fluids is their safety classes: A1 for HCFO-1233zd(E) and A2L (slightly flammable) for HFO-1233ze(E) – to be compared with safety class A3 (highly explosive) for hydrocarbons, such as pentane and butane. The additional safety risks related to hydrocarbons make their usage prohibitive for most industrial sites that are not already ATEX or Seveso III.  Furthermore, no high-temperature heat pump having a capacity around 1 MW and output temperature above 100°C is listed at Technology Readiness Level (TRL) of 9 (existing system available for scale up) in IEA Heat Pumps Technology Appendix 58.

The ban that is proposed does not consider the sector of High Temperature Heat Pumps (HTHPs) and might lead to even worse safety consequences both for citizens, the environment as well as for the sector of HTHPs as a whole – by not recovering industrial waste heat, which will result into longer use of fossil fuels to produce industrial heat and the wastage of renewable energy (thus requiring much more infrastructure to produce it).

2. Information on benefits
The currently proposed PFAS restriction proposal poses concerns when it comes to the beneficial environmental impact (presented in the attached charts) of High Temperature Heat Pumps.  Firstly, it is important to emphasize the tremendous opportunity presented by the utilization of waste heat in the European Union (EU). The annual energy content of waste heat available in the EU equals to 30% of the natural gas purchased by the EU. Low-grade waste heat, which constitutes half of the industrial waste heat in the EU, is predominantly found in light industries such as food & beverage, paper, and small chemical plants. The recovery of this waste heat has the potential to reduce natural gas imports by 15%, resulting in substantial cost savings of approximately 50 Bn€ (2022 prices) and a significant reduction in European CO2 emissions by 5%. Additionally, the transformation of industrial sites to recover low-grade waste heat would stimulate over 100 Bn€ in investment, create approximately 40,000 local jobs, and enhance the competitiveness of European industries. It is worth noting that these objectives are aligned with the Green New Deal and RePowerEU policies, further reinforcing the importance of pursuing this vision.

The key technology required to achieve this ambition is the use of closed-circuit industrial High-Temperature Heat Pumps (HTHPs) designed to recover low-grade waste heat. However, the refrigerants, HCFO-1233zd(E) and HFO-1234ze(E), which are essential for the deployment of HTHPs at scale are currently threatened by the proposal. It is crucial to recognize that these refrigerants have a short duration in the atmosphere (less than 40 days) and exhibit very low Global Warming Potential (GWP below 10), as well as an Ozone Depletion Potential (ODP) of 0.005 for HCFO-1233zd(E) and 0 for HFO-1234ze(E). Furthermore, the limited impact of these fluids on Trifluoroacetic Acid (TFA) formation due to chemical degradation (less than 2%) indicates that their use in HTHPs does not present any discernible concerns regarding environmental persistence.

3. Scope/restriction option analysis & information on alternatives
Specific restrictions have been presented in the context of the maintenance and refilling of existing HVACR (heating, ventilation, air conditioning and refrigeration) equipment put on the market before [18 months after entry into force] and for which no drop-in alternatives exist and refrigerants in HVACR-equipment in buildings where national safety standards and building codes prohibit the use of alternatives.  It is important to, once more, note that HTHPs operate on a closed circuit, effectively preventing refrigerant escape into the atmosphere under normal use conditions. Therefore, neither HCFO-1233zdE nor HFO-1234zeE pose any significant environmental persistence concerns when used in HTHPs. On the other hand, the alternatives presented by European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) PFAS proposal (Annex XV, page 246), namely butane, iso-butane, pentane and heptane, are far less appropriate than the current refrigerants used (HCFO-1233zdE and HFO-1234zeE).

According to ECHA’s Substance infocard:
• R601 Pentane (Safety Class A3, H304 Aspiration Toxicity 1, H225 Flamable Luiquid 2 (very high), H411 Aquatic Life Chronic 2 (medium)) may be “fatal if swallowed and enters airways, is toxic to aquatic life with long lasting effects, is a highly flammable liquid and vapour and may cause drowsiness or dizziness” (CLP) and “is an extremely flammable liquid and vapour and causes skin irritation” (REACH).
• R600 Butane (Safety Class A3, Properties of Concern “Carcinogenic (CARC A1) and Mutagenic (Muta. 1B), H220 Flammable Gas 1 (very high)) “is an extremely flammable gas and contains gas under pressure and may explode if heated” (REACH) and is reported by ECHA to have “Carcinogenic and Mutagenic among its Properties of Concern.”
• R603 Heptane is covered by safety codes H304, H315, H225, H410, H336 and H400 – therefore it represents even higher safety risks than the ones described above for Butane and Pentane.
• Another potential alternative refrigerant, ammonia (Safety Class B2L, H331 Acute 3 (toxic if inhaled) and H314 Skin Corrosion 1B (high), H400 Aquatic Life Acute 1 (very high)), “causes severe skin burns and eye damage, is toxic if inhaled, is very toxic to aquatic life and is a flammable gas” (CLP) and “is toxic to aquatic life with long lasting effects, contains gas under pressure and may explode if heated and may cause respiratory irritation” (REACH). Additionally, it is worth noting that ammonia emissions to atmosphere – particularly in the context of agri-food – are (expected to be) targeted by new/upcoming legislation around the EU.

The refrigerants used by the Industrial High Temperature Heat Pumps belong to Safety Classes A1 and A2 (no toxicity and flammability & no toxicity and low flammability). HCFO-1233zd(E) is H412 Aquatic Life Chronic 3 (low) and HFO-1234ze(E) is currently not classified.  Based on these information from the ECHA Substance Infocards, it is clear that in terms of safety, and environmental concerns, the latter are much better fitted than the ‘natural’ refrigerants put forward by the PFAS proposal.

In regard to the impact assessment of TFA degradation, scientific articles on HCFO-1233zd(E) concludes that it is below 2%, and no TFA degradation is identified for HFO-1234ze(E) (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1352231018300906 and https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0045653514008492?via%3Dihub). To recover the 500 TWh/year of low-grade waste heat in Europe – and thus save 100 million tons of CO2 per year – about 100 000 MW of HTHPs will have to be installed. It might take up to 20 years to get there – but these will eventually contain about 20 000 tons of refrigerant. Considering that these HTHPs run below 15 bar, there should be no more than one leak every five years – this will result in maximum 80 tons of TFA/year on average (furthermore, leaks will be often partial). The article mentions an estimated quantity of “natural” TFA in oceans of 268 million tons.  Therefore, the additional yearly quantity resulting from HTHP refrigerant leak should not exceed 0,00003% of the existing global stock of TFA (the yearly quantity generated by natural sources is unknown to us).

4. Request for exemption
In light of the information presented above, it is of paramount importance that the Restriction Proposal carefully considers the HTHPs sector, while also acknowledging and not dismissing the aforementioned environmental and safety concerns. Armstrong strongly advocates for the inclusion of a time-unlimited derogation specifically for HCFO-1233zd(E) and HFO-1234ze(E) when employed in closed-circuit industrial HTHP applications, until a viable alternative can be identified and implemented.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: 1. Introduction
Liebherr-Verzahntechnik GmbH (LVT) develops, manufactures and services highly complex systems for gear cut-ting, gear measuring, automation systems and tools with around 1600 (2023) employees worldwide. We are committed to the development of sustainable and environmentally friendly technology, which is also reflected in our constant investments in research and development. Our customer portfolio includes all major car manu-facturers such as Daimler, BMW, Volkswagen, Ford, GM, Hyundai but also other companies like ZFF, Eaton, SEW, Sany and Caterpillar. As one of the leading manufacturers of industrial equipment LVT must ensure that the strict requirements of all his customers in safety and durability are met. According to that we are certified to ISO 9001 (Quality), VDA 6.4 (Automotive), ISO 14001 (Environment), ISO 45001 (Safety) and TISAX (data protection).

The service life of our products can be up to 20 years. This requires materials that can withstand the highest chemical and thermal stresses, are subject to very low material fatigue and offer reliable corrosion protection. Durability and long maintenance cycles have a positive effect on the consumption of resources and the amount of waste produced. In many cases, however, this can only be achieved by using substances that will no longer be available as a result of the proposed restriction on the manufacture, marketing and use of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances.
Almost all manufacturers in the mechanical and plant engineering sector are affected by a potential future PFAS restriction, either in their products or in their production. There is a very high level of concern, for example, among the manufacturers of hydraulic components, such as. pumps, motors, valves and cylinders, as well as manufacturers of manufacturers of valves and compressors. The list does not claim to be completeness. PFAS, mostly fluorinated polymers, are frequently used, for example, in gaskets, hoses, pipes, valves and coatings. In some cases "only" the performance of many products would massively deteriorate. However many products could no longer be manufactured, imported and marketed, so that many companies would be completely or partially deprived of their business basis by a PFAS restriction would be withdrawn.


2. Applications and Consequences
For a better representation of our affectedness by the impending restriction, we have analyzed and evalu-ated some products regarding PFAS. The following products would be directly affected by the impending re-striction:
• Power cable and control cable
• O-ring pre-stressed PTFE seals
• Backing rings based on PTFE
• PTFE-based guide elements
• O-rings on FKM and FFKM basis
• X-rings on FKM and FFKM basis
• O-ring preloaded translational hydraulic seals
• O-ring preloaded rotary seals
• Radial shaft seal
• Lip seal ring
• O-ring preloaded PTFE wiper
• O-ring preloaded hydraulic rod seals
• Special rotation seal
• Special rotation and linear guideways
Please note that the detailed overview (including consequences) is admitted in the attached presentation.


3. Conclusion
LVT supports the goal of preventing the release of hazardous substances into the environment and adequately regulating the risk to humans and the environment from individual substances.
However, the proposed ban on the production, use and marketing of PFAS (in substances, mixtures and articles) would have a massive and unpredictable impact on the entire industry, which has an essential social responsi-bility.
Further, an enforced abandonment of the use of this substance class would drastically shorten the hollow life of our products and thus have a negative impact on the environment. Far more important, however, is that to date there are no known alternatives that would provide equivalent or greater protection, thus posing a threat to human health and life.

Fluoropolymers like PTFE are commonly regarded to meet the key internationally recognised safety criteria of the OECD for “polymers low concern” (plc). This means that they are chemically stable, non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water soluble and non-mobile. For these reasons, fluoropolymers are also suitable, for exam-ple, as materials for food contact, in medical applications or in the production of high-purity active pharmaceu-tical ingredients (e.g. vaccines). Therefor the competent authorities of the United Kingdom claim that fluoropol-ymers, fluoroelastomers and monomers for manufacturing of these do not need to be restricted at all. We de-mand from the competent authorities of the European Economic Area (EEA) to take over this scientific and simply reasonable approach.

We consider the production sites of European companies as well as their global competitiveness to be seriously endangered in the case of a general restriction. At the same time, the proposed restriction would threaten the development of new, high quality technologies.
Finally, the proposal to ban PFAS fundamentally violates the essential use concept and contradicts ECHA's pre-vious approach to dealing with hazardous substances. For this reason, we call for a revision of the restriction proposal. A regulation of certain PFAS via Annex XVII exclusively for specific, non-professional uses would be a possible alternative.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: 1. Introduction
Rolls-Royce develops and delivers complex power and propulsion solutions for safety-critical applications in the air, at sea and on land. Our products and service packages enable our customers to connect people, societies, cultures and economies together and to meet the growing need for power generation across multiple industries. As a company with strong European imprint, we are a significant contributor to jobs, the supply chain, innovation and export at our European sites. It is important for us to maintain technology leadership and high-quality jobs in Europe and to remain internationally competitive. It is our goal to develop cutting-edge technologies that deliver clean, safe and competitive solutions. Net zero technologies play a vital role to achieve that goal as part of the technologies that we want to offer to our customers, as well as for the decarbonisation of the use of our products. Indeed, we aim at delivering the next generation of sustainable and innovative aviation, maritime and energy solutions, such as engines certified for sustainable fuels, hydrogen propulsion and electrical propulsion applications.
If the broad, wide-reaching and fluoropolymer-inclusive PFAS proposed restriction, was adopted without amendment, it would severely impact all areas of our portfolio, essentially preventing production, servicing and repair of our products in the EEA with the associated consequential impacts to wider society, where our products are used. This includes air travel (passenger and goods), back-up power generators for civil infrastructure (data centres, hospitals), rail travel, marine propulsion, nuclear power and defence fleets.
PFAS substances (fluoropolymers) are essential enablers for technologies to realise sustainability and net-zero ambitions, with no credible alternative technologies in many cases.  As such any restriction on the use of fluoropolymers will be a major barrier to the achievement of essential environmental goals. We see major concerns for the future of such technologies with the PFAS restriction proposal as presented.
In particular, the inclusion of fluoropolymers in scope of the restriction and without adequate derogations, would severely disrupt industry in the EEA, not just in the sectors where we operate but also much wider, and as such the preferred proposal (RO2) in the current form should not be considered as a viable proposition.

2 Comments on the proposed restriction impacts, derogations and compliance challenges
2.1 Challenges for identifying PFAS uses
We would like to highlight some of the concerns and challenges we face to determine the possible impact of the proposed restriction throughout our products and processes and global supply chain. At the current time therefore, we do not have full information to be confident of identifying all critical mixtures and articles that will require derogations in order that disruption to our EEA manufacture, import and continued operation of our products, including to those already in service, is not realised.
Since PFAS, as defined under the scope of the restriction proposal, comprise a large group (over 10,000 CAS numbers) and the majority are not subject to any current requirements for disclosure e.g. via REACH article 33 or meeting requirements to be disclosed on SDS, there is a large unknown in terms of the understanding of all the applications and components relying on a PFAS substance. This presents challenges for identifying all critical dependencies of PFAS in order to ensure necessary derogations covering every use, are provided for.
Derogations ideally should be at sector level and sufficiently broad such that specific applications not currently visible would be covered. Clear sector level derogations will also help to avoid a reliance on many specific and sporadic individual derogations for many different PFAS applications across a sector, with differing expiry dates, that may be confusing to navigate. This could also present confusion and challenges for understanding applicable derogations and managing compliance in the supply chain of super complex articles.
Whilst some potential/proposed sector-level derogations exist e.g. Transport (6o), derogations for power generation and the Aerospace and Defence sector are absent from the proposal. For some individual applications in use e.g. lubricants, there are derogations that may cover uses in the missing sectors (e.g. where the ‘lubricant’ derogation (5s) could cover lubricant use in aerospace and defence/power generation products and processes) but derogation coverage would be partial, leaving many other uses without coverage and thus effects of non-use scenarios would be realised.
In the case that sufficiently scoped derogations at sector levels are not provided for and to prevent non-use scenario impacts from specific PFAS dependencies not currently known, there would need to be a mechanism in the restriction to request late derogations.

2.2 General comments regarding PFAS alternatives
The majority of the known PFAS uses across our portfolio are fluoropolymers.
Rigorous testing, qualification and certification requirements have to be met in order to approve introduction of alternatives for our products. Owing to the large number of affected parts, products and processes for which PFAS alternatives would need to be found, if the PFAS restriction is implemented as proposed, the required alternatives development and substitution work would be a major undertaking and is expected to exceed well in excess of 12 years. However, currently there are no feasible alternatives to even begin testing.
The C-F bond is crucial to providing the essential properties conferred by fluoropolymers, which gives these materials the performance capabilities needed to remain durable under harsh environments and still meet the technical functionalities demanded by our products. There is no other chemistry that can compare to the fluoropolymers (C-F bond) and in most cases it is believed to be likely, that there will never be suitable alternatives to fluoropolymers, which can meet the demands of our products.

2.3 Fluoropolymers vs small molecule PFAS
First and foremost, it should be addressed whether fluoropolymers do indeed meet the criteria to be considered as demonstrating the same hazards and risk concerns as other PFAS. There are studies referenced by the Fluoropolymer group of Plastics Europe (https://fluoropolymers.plasticseurope.org/application/files/7116/7334/1071/Fluoropolymer_Letter_5_January_2023_-_PFAS_REACH_Restriction_2.pdf. ), that point to polymers in this class of widely used and critical materials, meeting the OECD ‘polymer of low concern’ criteria. This does not appear to have been considered or evaluated in the dossier, which considers that persistence alone may give rise to sufficient concerns for regulation of the PFAS group as a whole (PFAS restriction Annex XV dossier, section 1.1.2, page 21)
• If it is shown that fluoropolymers do not demonstrate the same concerns and need for restriction as small molecule PFAS, they should be removed from the scope of this restriction.
• In this case derogations necessary for small molecule PFAS, to allow continued production and supply of those fluoropolymers on the EEA market should be provided for, with the appropriate controls on environmental emissions.
• Derogations for continued use of small molecule PFAS in aerospace and defence will also be needed, to reduce the potential disruption to the sector whilst alternatives are researched and developed and taken through the necessary testing to be qualified and certified for use in affected applications (uses of non-polymeric PFAS identified to date in our portfolio is limited to aerospace and defence products and is low volume/niche).

2.4 Need for exemptions for essential and irreplaceable fluoropolymer uses
If all available information is reviewed and fluoropolymers are determined to warrant EEA-wide restriction, it should be considered, that based on current knowledge many applications are unlikely to ever find alternatives. This is because the very properties of these materials, that make them the only suitable options for use in many modern products (resilience/persistence in harsh environments), is also giving rise to the reason for concern. In these cases, exemptions/time-unlimited derogations for essential and irreplaceable uses of fluoropolymers must be available. Particularly for low volume sectors where there is control of emissions during manufacture at industrial facilities and end of life disposal protocols for the resulting industrial products.

2.5 Derogations/exemptions requested
A summary of the derogations and exemptions necessary to minimise disruption to our operations, including minimising disruption for products already in-service are summarised below. Available information in support of these needs is provided directly in response to the specific ECHA questions.
Scenario 1 – fluoropolymers are separately assessed and determined not to warrant restriction in conjunction with small molecule PFAS
• Exemption of fluoropolymers from this restriction
• Derogations for small molecule PFAS necessary to allow continued production, use and placing on the market of fluoropolymers, with any appropriate controls on emissions.
• Derogation for small molecule PFAS uses in aerospace and defence products and processes, including servicing and repair, until alternatives can be developed (at least 13.5 years after entry into force is needed, assuming alternatives can be developed and all testing is successful).
• Limits for any levels of small molecule PFAS in derogated fluoropolymer products to be proportionate and achievable, in order that this is not still essentially a ban.
• Mechanism to allow extension of time-limited derogations in case viable alternatives are not found by the end of the derogation periods.
Scenario 2 – fluoropolymers are separately assessed and determined to warrant restriction in conjunction with small molecule PFAS
• Derogation for use of fluoropolymers in aerospace and defence products and processes (including spares, servicing and repairs) – time-unlimited whilst there are no viable alternatives foreseen.
• Derogation for applications affecting the proper functioning related to the safety and reliability of internal combustion engine systems and alternative powertrain systems, and affecting the safety of humans or reliability of equipment – time-unlimited whilst there are no viable alternatives foreseen (or at least 13.5 years after entry into force, with possibility for extension).
• Derogation for small molecule PFAS uses in aerospace and defence products and processes, including servicing and repair, until alternatives can be developed (13.5 years at least is needed, assuming viable alternatives can be found and all testing is successful). Possibility for extension, where needed, is also required.
• Derogation for small molecule PFAS necessary to support continued availability and use of derogated fluoropolymer uses, with any appropriate controls on emissions.
• Limits for any levels of small molecule PFAS in derogated fluoropolymer products to be proportionate and achievable, in order that this is not still essentially a ban.
• Mechanism to allow extension of all time-limited derogations in case viable alternatives are not found by the end of the derogation periods.

Additional derogations are also necessary for technologies, that we are customers of, where they are also required to ensure continued availability and operability of our products and operations. The technologies we are aware of, that we rely on, and which also rely on PFAS (fluoropolymers) and may need derogations in the scope of this restriction include:

• Derogation for use of fluoropolymers in PEM (proton exchange membrane/polymer electrolyte membrane) fuel cells
• Derogation for use of fluoropolymers in batteries
• Derogation for use of fluoropolymers in semiconductor manufacture
• Derogation for use of fluoropolymers in electrical cabling, harnessing and components
• Derogation for use of fluoropolymers in chemical transport and processing
• Derogation for use of fluoropolymers in lubricants

2.5.1 Proposed reporting requirements
Additional concerns arise with regard to the ability to manage the reporting requirements that would be required throughout the supply chain:
• Regarding the proposed limits in paragraph 2 of the proposed restriction – as downstream users of formulations and assembler of some articles, we do not currently have visibility of whether those articles may use PFAS in the manufacturing and therefore contain low ppb levels as supplied to us. It is unclear which articles would need to be tested under this requirement.
• Limits for any levels of small molecule PFAS in derogated fluoropolymer products must be proportionate and achievable, in order that this is not still essentially a ban.
• Challenges for the reporting requirements and site-specific management plans proposed in paragraphs 7 and 8 by 18 months after EiF – the supply chains are global and complex and currently PFAS are not required to be disclosed in most cases (unless subject to REACH article 33 or classified on SDS). Experience with obtaining substance declarations across the supply chains suggests that it is likely to take considerably longer than 18 months to identify most PFAS uses. For EEA sites to comply with paragraph 8, upstream suppliers would need to clearly disclose PFAS (including fluoropolymers) present in formulations and articles supplied under the derogations – it may not otherwise be apparent to sites that there has been a change in regulatory status and that associated obligations for using such products apply.
• We have recently carried out a short and targeted PFAS A&D supplier survey to gauge the awareness of the proposed restriction, awareness of PFAS reliance and readiness to communicate this within our supply-chain. Feedback indicates that 18 months will not be sufficient for compliance with reporting and also confirms the lack of potential alternatives for A&D uses:
o 55% of suppliers responding to the survey are not aware of the presence of PFAS (including fluoropolymers) used in products they supply
o 24% of suppliers responding to the survey don’t have visibility of whether they use any PFAS (including fluoropolymers) in their manufacturing process
o 58% of suppliers responding to the survey do not know if their suppliers rely on PFAS (including fluoropolymers) in their manufacturing processes
o 100% of suppliers responding to the survey do not know of any viable alternatives for PFAS substances they rely on in products or processes
Given the considerations and current status of supply chain PFAS awareness, a transitional period for these reporting requirements of at least EiF+5 years is requested in order to have sufficient time to engage the supply chain and try to meet these obligations to avoid non-compliance.

2.6 Non-Use Scenarios
• Products that will be impacted if we can no longer continue use of PFAS-containing formulations, materials and parts include aero engines used in both civil and defence, submarines, naval marine engines, power generation, railway engines and combat (tank) engines.
• Should PFAS-containing mixtures and articles used in our products, processes, repair and maintenance schemes, including within our EEA supply chain, be unavailable due to the restriction (either directly or indirectly), non-use scenarios would come into effect. There will be significant loss of manufacturing, maintenance and repair, including loss of imports, for affected aerospace, defence, rail, marine and power generator parts (to support nuclear power plants, data centres, electricity companies and hospitals) and products in the EEA. Without intervention, back-up power generators for civil infrastructure will be impacted, affected aircraft will be grounded and other affected defence equipment in the EEA will be unavailable to meet military, security or humanitarian mission requirements. Affected in-service products would face premature retirement, where they need PFAS-containing parts or mixtures to enable their maintenance and repair.
• Additionally, development programmes for future technologies would be affected, including:
o hydrogen applications (including fuel cells and fuel)
o electrical aircraft technologies
o systems for use of sustainable aviation fuels
o novel nuclear technologies, including power generation for terrestrial, defence and space use
o novel defence technologies
…such products and technologies reliant on PFAS, would have to continue to be developed exclusively outside of the EEA and would not be able to be offered to this market.
• There are likely to be additional disruptions to product availability and operation in other regions, including the UK, that are currently reliant on EEA-based supply, until supply chains could be reorganised to avoid EEA-based PFAS uses.
• Since prohibition of PFAS, including fluoropolymers, would affect all our business areas and products in the EEA, including non-EEA made imports, it is difficult to see how business in the EEA would continue to be viable in that scenario. As a result, site closures and associated loss of economic and socio-economic benefits in the affected regions of those member states would be realised. There would be a reduction in our business, as we would have to exit the EEA market, since products and maintenance services could no longer be offered to customers in the region. We would also need to relocate any supply chain activity reliant on use of PFAS or PFAS-containing parts, exclusively outside of the EEA, which would mean a knock-on effect to those businesses and the economies of the local areas in which they are based.
• Since other regions are not also prohibiting fluoropolymers, manufacture, repair, maintenance and placing on the market of our products in those regions would be unaffected, leaving the EEA at a severe disadvantage; unable to access the technologies and products available to other regions and with loss of ability to continue to maintain and repair currently in-service products in the EEA.

3 Sector level support
We have also engaged with trade associations to provide responses at sector levels and are in support of the information provided by ASD, EUROMOT and Hydrogen Europe, which also provide information on the sector critical nature, current lack of alternatives and challenges for finding and implementing alternatives, for our many current PFAS dependencies.
We would also suggest that, for Aerospace and Defence uses, recent information provided on the alternatives challenges, typical timelines and socioeconomic costs of non-use presented in the recently submitted ADCR consortium hexavalent chromates Authorisation review reports and new applications (ECHA AfA numbers 0325-01 to 0345-02) may be considered relevant, since the general challenges, process and typical timelines for developing, qualifying, certifying and industrialising alternatives are the same, although it should be noted that for fluoropolymers, there are no foreseen alternatives (unlike the chromates). Additionally, the SEA data presented in the ADCR dossiers may provide a very conservative estimate for the impacts from PFAS non-use, which would be much more detrimental to the EEA market. This is because import and use of articles will also be affected in the PFAS non-use scenario and as such relocation of activities to continue to support the EEA market via imports (as suggested in some cases for chromates) would not be a possible non-use scenario that could also be considered for PFAS.

Proposed derogations: Whilst it is clear our uses do not all fall within the currently proposed derogations, we can try to provide some information on our uses, that do still need to be covered by derogations. Typically, we are very low volume customers of these types of articles.  We do not currently require suppliers to declare any PFAS content in articles they supply to us, other than those PFAS substances listed on the EU and UK REACH candidate lists. In any case, the declaration threshold of 0.1% would not pick up any articles containing PFAS substances below this limit, including at ppb levels.  Where we are using PFAS in mixtures, we only have visibility if the supplier is required to declare the presence of the substance in the region of use e.g. where required to be stated on safety data sheets or where the PFAS substance is also subject to REACH article 33 reporting.  Please also refer to submissions to the consultation by Dupont to illustrate examples of specific fluoropolymer-based parts, that are manufactured by Dupont and used in aeroengines (comment ID 6706 and associated). The submissions include an SEA for the aerospace supply chain of the fluoropolymer parts and also provides commentary for the lack of alternatives and consequences of no derogation.  In terms of PFAS emissions to the environment from our uses, we do not expect this during manufacture, maintenance and repair processes at our industrial facilities, since wastes should be captured and disposed as hazardous waste (for management by licensed waste contractors). In terms of release from specific applications during service life, this will be dependent on the type of product and application.  For fluoropolymer parts used in engines (including seals, bushes, rub strips, O-rings), some abrading of the polymer may occur as part of in-service wear. In addition, some fluoroelastomer parts can degrade over time by thermal and/or chemical exposure e.g. from contact with engine fluids.   Depending on where the part is located within our products, in some cases any abraded fluoropolymer material may be contained within proximal fluids or within complex articles e.g. dust in oil or hydraulic fluid, or remaining as wear debris within a complex article to be cleaned and disposed of (to hazardous waste) during MRO (maintenance, repair and overhaul).  For fluoropolymers used in batteries and PEM fuel cells and electrolysers emissions during service life are not expected since the fluoropolymers are contained.  For uses in mixtures that remain part of complex articles (lubricants, anti-corrosion liquids, grease), information on emissions during service life of those articles is currently unknown but is not typically expected, since a feature of these fluoropolymer-based formulations is that they are not washed off during use e.g., by oils or fuels.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: 1. Introduction
Rolls-Royce develops and delivers complex power and propulsion solutions for safety-critical applications in the air, at sea and on land. Our products and service packages enable our customers to connect people, societies, cultures and economies together and to meet the growing need for power generation across multiple industries. As a company with strong European imprint, we are a significant contributor to jobs, the supply chain, innovation and export at our European sites. It is important for us to maintain technology leadership and high-quality jobs in Europe and to remain internationally competitive. It is our goal to develop cutting-edge technologies that deliver clean, safe and competitive solutions. Net zero technologies play a vital role to achieve that goal as part of the technologies that we want to offer to our customers, as well as for the decarbonisation of the use of our products. Indeed, we aim at delivering the next generation of sustainable and innovative aviation, maritime and energy solutions, such as engines certified for sustainable fuels, hydrogen propulsion and electrical propulsion applications.
If the broad, wide-reaching and fluoropolymer-inclusive PFAS proposed restriction, was adopted without amendment, it would severely impact all areas of our portfolio, essentially preventing production, servicing and repair of our products in the EEA with the associated consequential impacts to wider society, where our products are used. This includes air travel (passenger and goods), back-up power generators for civil infrastructure (data centres, hospitals), rail travel, marine propulsion, nuclear power and defence fleets.
PFAS substances (fluoropolymers) are essential enablers for technologies to realise sustainability and net-zero ambitions, with no credible alternative technologies in many cases.  As such any restriction on the use of fluoropolymers will be a major barrier to the achievement of essential environmental goals. We see major concerns for the future of such technologies with the PFAS restriction proposal as presented.
In particular, the inclusion of fluoropolymers in scope of the restriction and without adequate derogations, would severely disrupt industry in the EEA, not just in the sectors where we operate but also much wider, and as such the preferred proposal (RO2) in the current form should not be considered as a viable proposition.

2 Comments on the proposed restriction impacts, derogations and compliance challenges
2.1 Challenges for identifying PFAS uses
We would like to highlight some of the concerns and challenges we face to determine the possible impact of the proposed restriction throughout our products and processes and global supply chain. At the current time therefore, we do not have full information to be confident of identifying all critical mixtures and articles that will require derogations in order that disruption to our EEA manufacture, import and continued operation of our products, including to those already in service, is not realised.
Since PFAS, as defined under the scope of the restriction proposal, comprise a large group (over 10,000 CAS numbers) and the majority are not subject to any current requirements for disclosure e.g. via REACH article 33 or meeting requirements to be disclosed on SDS, there is a large unknown in terms of the understanding of all the applications and components relying on a PFAS substance. This presents challenges for identifying all critical dependencies of PFAS in order to ensure necessary derogations covering every use, are provided for.
Derogations ideally should be at sector level and sufficiently broad such that specific applications not currently visible would be covered. Clear sector level derogations will also help to avoid a reliance on many specific and sporadic individual derogations for many different PFAS applications across a sector, with differing expiry dates, that may be confusing to navigate. This could also present confusion and challenges for understanding applicable derogations and managing compliance in the supply chain of super complex articles.
Whilst some potential/proposed sector-level derogations exist e.g. Transport (6o), derogations for power generation and the Aerospace and Defence sector are absent from the proposal. For some individual applications in use e.g. lubricants, there are derogations that may cover uses in the missing sectors (e.g. where the ‘lubricant’ derogation (5s) could cover lubricant use in aerospace and defence/power generation products and processes) but derogation coverage would be partial, leaving many other uses without coverage and thus effects of non-use scenarios would be realised.
In the case that sufficiently scoped derogations at sector levels are not provided for and to prevent non-use scenario impacts from specific PFAS dependencies not currently known, there would need to be a mechanism in the restriction to request late derogations.

2.2 General comments regarding PFAS alternatives
The majority of the known PFAS uses across our portfolio are fluoropolymers.
Rigorous testing, qualification and certification requirements have to be met in order to approve introduction of alternatives for our products. Owing to the large number of affected parts, products and processes for which PFAS alternatives would need to be found, if the PFAS restriction is implemented as proposed, the required alternatives development and substitution work would be a major undertaking and is expected to exceed well in excess of 12 years. However, currently there are no feasible alternatives to even begin testing.
The C-F bond is crucial to providing the essential properties conferred by fluoropolymers, which gives these materials the performance capabilities needed to remain durable under harsh environments and still meet the technical functionalities demanded by our products. There is no other chemistry that can compare to the fluoropolymers (C-F bond) and in most cases it is believed to be likely, that there will never be suitable alternatives to fluoropolymers, which can meet the demands of our products.

2.3 Fluoropolymers vs small molecule PFAS
First and foremost, it should be addressed whether fluoropolymers do indeed meet the criteria to be considered as demonstrating the same hazards and risk concerns as other PFAS. There are studies referenced by the Fluoropolymer group of Plastics Europe (https://fluoropolymers.plasticseurope.org/application/files/7116/7334/1071/Fluoropolymer_Letter_5_January_2023_-_PFAS_REACH_Restriction_2.pdf. ), that point to polymers in this class of widely used and critical materials, meeting the OECD ‘polymer of low concern’ criteria. This does not appear to have been considered or evaluated in the dossier, which considers that persistence alone may give rise to sufficient concerns for regulation of the PFAS group as a whole (PFAS restriction Annex XV dossier, section 1.1.2, page 21)
• If it is shown that fluoropolymers do not demonstrate the same concerns and need for restriction as small molecule PFAS, they should be removed from the scope of this restriction.
• In this case derogations necessary for small molecule PFAS, to allow continued production and supply of those fluoropolymers on the EEA market should be provided for, with the appropriate controls on environmental emissions.
• Derogations for continued use of small molecule PFAS in aerospace and defence will also be needed, to reduce the potential disruption to the sector whilst alternatives are researched and developed and taken through the necessary testing to be qualified and certified for use in affected applications (uses of non-polymeric PFAS identified to date in our portfolio is limited to aerospace and defence products and is low volume/niche).

2.4 Need for exemptions for essential and irreplaceable fluoropolymer uses
If all available information is reviewed and fluoropolymers are determined to warrant EEA-wide restriction, it should be considered, that based on current knowledge many applications are unlikely to ever find alternatives. This is because the very properties of these materials, that make them the only suitable options for use in many modern products (resilience/persistence in harsh environments), is also giving rise to the reason for concern. In these cases, exemptions/time-unlimited derogations for essential and irreplaceable uses of fluoropolymers must be available. Particularly for low volume sectors where there is control of emissions during manufacture at industrial facilities and end of life disposal protocols for the resulting industrial products.

2.5 Derogations/exemptions requested
A summary of the derogations and exemptions necessary to minimise disruption to our operations, including minimising disruption for products already in-service are summarised below. Available information in support of these needs is provided directly in response to the specific ECHA questions.
Scenario 1 – fluoropolymers are separately assessed and determined not to warrant restriction in conjunction with small molecule PFAS
• Exemption of fluoropolymers from this restriction
• Derogations for small molecule PFAS necessary to allow continued production, use and placing on the market of fluoropolymers, with any appropriate controls on emissions.
• Derogation for small molecule PFAS uses in aerospace and defence products and processes, including servicing and repair, until alternatives can be developed (at least 13.5 years after entry into force is needed, assuming alternatives can be developed and all testing is successful).
• Limits for any levels of small molecule PFAS in derogated fluoropolymer products to be proportionate and achievable, in order that this is not still essentially a ban.
• Mechanism to allow extension of time-limited derogations in case viable alternatives are not found by the end of the derogation periods.
Scenario 2 – fluoropolymers are separately assessed and determined to warrant restriction in conjunction with small molecule PFAS
• Derogation for use of fluoropolymers in aerospace and defence products and processes (including spares, servicing and repairs) – time-unlimited whilst there are no viable alternatives foreseen.
• Derogation for applications affecting the proper functioning related to the safety and reliability of internal combustion engine systems and alternative powertrain systems, and affecting the safety of humans or reliability of equipment – time-unlimited whilst there are no viable alternatives foreseen (or at least 13.5 years after entry into force, with possibility for extension).
• Derogation for small molecule PFAS uses in aerospace and defence products and processes, including servicing and repair, until alternatives can be developed (13.5 years at least is needed, assuming viable alternatives can be found and all testing is successful). Possibility for extension, where needed, is also required.
• Derogation for small molecule PFAS necessary to support continued availability and use of derogated fluoropolymer uses, with any appropriate controls on emissions.
• Limits for any levels of small molecule PFAS in derogated fluoropolymer products to be proportionate and achievable, in order that this is not still essentially a ban.
• Mechanism to allow extension of all time-limited derogations in case viable alternatives are not found by the end of the derogation periods.

Additional derogations are also necessary for technologies, that we are customers of, where they are also required to ensure continued availability and operability of our products and operations. The technologies we are aware of, that we rely on, and which also rely on PFAS (fluoropolymers) and may need derogations in the scope of this restriction include:

• Derogation for use of fluoropolymers in PEM (proton exchange membrane/polymer electrolyte membrane) fuel cells
• Derogation for use of fluoropolymers in batteries
• Derogation for use of fluoropolymers in semiconductor manufacture
• Derogation for use of fluoropolymers in electrical cabling, harnessing and components
• Derogation for use of fluoropolymers in chemical transport and processing
• Derogation for use of fluoropolymers in lubricants

2.5.1 Proposed reporting requirements
Additional concerns arise with regard to the ability to manage the reporting requirements that would be required throughout the supply chain:
• Regarding the proposed limits in paragraph 2 of the proposed restriction – as downstream users of formulations and assembler of some articles, we do not currently have visibility of whether those articles may use PFAS in the manufacturing and therefore contain low ppb levels as supplied to us. It is unclear which articles would need to be tested under this requirement.
• Limits for any levels of small molecule PFAS in derogated fluoropolymer products must be proportionate and achievable, in order that this is not still essentially a ban.
• Challenges for the reporting requirements and site-specific management plans proposed in paragraphs 7 and 8 by 18 months after EiF – the supply chains are global and complex and currently PFAS are not required to be disclosed in most cases (unless subject to REACH article 33 or classified on SDS). Experience with obtaining substance declarations across the supply chains suggests that it is likely to take considerably longer than 18 months to identify most PFAS uses. For EEA sites to comply with paragraph 8, upstream suppliers would need to clearly disclose PFAS (including fluoropolymers) present in formulations and articles supplied under the derogations – it may not otherwise be apparent to sites that there has been a change in regulatory status and that associated obligations for using such products apply.
• We have recently carried out a short and targeted PFAS A&D supplier survey to gauge the awareness of the proposed restriction, awareness of PFAS reliance and readiness to communicate this within our supply-chain. Feedback indicates that 18 months will not be sufficient for compliance with reporting and also confirms the lack of potential alternatives for A&D uses:
o 55% of suppliers responding to the survey are not aware of the presence of PFAS (including fluoropolymers) used in products they supply
o 24% of suppliers responding to the survey don’t have visibility of whether they use any PFAS (including fluoropolymers) in their manufacturing process
o 58% of suppliers responding to the survey do not know if their suppliers rely on PFAS (including fluoropolymers) in their manufacturing processes
o 100% of suppliers responding to the survey do not know of any viable alternatives for PFAS substances they rely on in products or processes
Given the considerations and current status of supply chain PFAS awareness, a transitional period for these reporting requirements of at least EiF+5 years is requested in order to have sufficient time to engage the supply chain and try to meet these obligations to avoid non-compliance.

2.6 Non-Use Scenarios
• Products that will be impacted if we can no longer continue use of PFAS-containing formulations, materials and parts include aero engines used in both civil and defence, submarines, naval marine engines, power generation, railway engines and combat (tank) engines.
• Should PFAS-containing mixtures and articles used in our products, processes, repair and maintenance schemes, including within our EEA supply chain, be unavailable due to the restriction (either directly or indirectly), non-use scenarios would come into effect. There will be significant loss of manufacturing, maintenance and repair, including loss of imports, for affected aerospace, defence, rail, marine and power generator parts (to support nuclear power plants, data centres, electricity companies and hospitals) and products in the EEA. Without intervention, back-up power generators for civil infrastructure will be impacted, affected aircraft will be grounded and other affected defence equipment in the EEA will be unavailable to meet military, security or humanitarian mission requirements. Affected in-service products would face premature retirement, where they need PFAS-containing parts or mixtures to enable their maintenance and repair.
• Additionally, development programmes for future technologies would be affected, including:
o hydrogen applications (including fuel cells and fuel)
o electrical aircraft technologies
o systems for use of sustainable aviation fuels
o novel nuclear technologies, including power generation for terrestrial, defence and space use
o novel defence technologies
…such products and technologies reliant on PFAS, would have to continue to be developed exclusively outside of the EEA and would not be able to be offered to this market.
• There are likely to be additional disruptions to product availability and operation in other regions, including the UK, that are currently reliant on EEA-based supply, until supply chains could be reorganised to avoid EEA-based PFAS uses.
• Since prohibition of PFAS, including fluoropolymers, would affect all our business areas and products in the EEA, including non-EEA made imports, it is difficult to see how business in the EEA would continue to be viable in that scenario. As a result, site closures and associated loss of economic and socio-economic benefits in the affected regions of those member states would be realised. There would be a reduction in our business, as we would have to exit the EEA market, since products and maintenance services could no longer be offered to customers in the region. We would also need to relocate any supply chain activity reliant on use of PFAS or PFAS-containing parts, exclusively outside of the EEA, which would mean a knock-on effect to those businesses and the economies of the local areas in which they are based.
• Since other regions are not also prohibiting fluoropolymers, manufacture, repair, maintenance and placing on the market of our products in those regions would be unaffected, leaving the EEA at a severe disadvantage; unable to access the technologies and products available to other regions and with loss of ability to continue to maintain and repair currently in-service products in the EEA.

3 Sector level support
We have also engaged with trade associations to provide responses at sector levels and are in support of the information provided by ASD, EUROMOT and Hydrogen Europe, which also provide information on the sector critical nature, current lack of alternatives and challenges for finding and implementing alternatives, for our many current PFAS dependencies.
