Identified essential uses of fluoropolymers in these products include: • Fluoropolymer parts including seals, O-rings and hose linings, which are used throughout power generation products.  o Without continued availability of fluorocarbon seals, current products will no longer be able to be made. Previously (ca. 20 years ago) nitrile rubber materials were used but these would not be suitable in current products because the operating temperatures are now too high for them to withstand and they are not as long-lived (failure of nitrile rubber O-rings in the engines occurs around <100 hours operating time). o At several locations in an engine, even perfluoroelastomer O-rings are required, where fluoroelastomer materials are not sufficient to meet the thermal requirements and are necessary also to meet EEA emission requirements. o Requirements, that alternative materials must meet are detailed in our standard document (MTN5097) that we can share upon request. This standard explains which elastomer materials meet the requirement for different applications within our combustion engines; it informs where we can use non-fluoropolymer materials versus where only the fluoropolymers are suitable and gives a comparison of the differences in the resistance properties between the materials, that gives rise to their suitability for use in different applications/locations within the engine. o In general, the functionalities, that alternatives need to meet, include:  Pressure stability (10 bar)  Maintain effective seals  High temperature fluid and gas management  Withstand high temperature and/or chemical aggressivity environments e.g.  survive high operating temperatures and chemical attack by corrosion inhibitors in cooling water and engine oils.  Longevity in the product • PFAS present in batteries o In batteries there could be some use of PFAS in the separator and as binder for within the electrodes of the cell and potentially in fire retarding polymers of the battery pack around the cells. o Alternatives in the battery application are unknown since we are reliant on batteries as a downstream user. Battery manufacturers would hold information on availability of alternatives. However, if PFAS cannot be replaced and the batteries are no longer permitted on the market, this will have a knock-on impact regarding continued availability of our products. • PEM fuel cells and electrolysers o PEM fuel cells and electrolysers are technologies based on fluorinated membranes. We rely on this technology for new aero electrical applications and applications in power generation. They are an essential enabler towards advancements for reaching decarbonisation aims. A prohibition that prevents availability of these materials or does not provide sufficient timescales to implement alternatives (6.5 years after EiF would not be sufficient) would stop our activities in this important area.  o Whilst there are always other membrane technologies being developed, historically it has taken decades to reach a point where they can be implemented.  o We are aware of HT PEM, that has been looked at. This is another membrane, which has also been in development for 30 years. It uses a polybenzimidazole membrane with phosphoric acid electrolyte. However, even after many years of development, this material is not yet viable for us to consider further developing in our technologies; the performance is currently relatively poor. It also operates at 120C+ rather than 60-90C so the balance of plant would also be different. o Requirements that any alternatives must meet include:  Promotion of proton conduction   High ion exchange capacity  Binder for catalyst  High chemical-mechanical stability and durability  Impermeablity for gases; O2 and H2  For the uses identified, there are currently no acceptable alternatives (i.e. none, which have not already been dismissed as non-viable in our applications) even available for us to start our testing for our affected applications. We are dependent on formulators and materials manufacturers to develop new products demonstrating sufficient initial performance properties, that we can then start to test for potential suitability and further development in our various applications. Typical expected timelines for necessary testing and introduction of an alternative material would be conservatively ca. 10 years. However, there are not even any new alternatives to start such testing programmes with. Additionally, the scale of PFAS (including fluoropolymers) replacement is more significant than any other alternatives replacement programme we have previously or are currently undertaking – it affects every product in multiple parts and applications. Replacement will be a major undertaking requiring many alternatives replacement programmes over decades. In the meantime, certainty for the continued availability of existing materials is needed and so time-unlimited derogations for fluoropolymers are requested.  To give an example, another significant, although less widespread use across our portfolio, is that of hexavalent chromium. Where alternatives have been in development for over thirty years and alternatives programmes to replace all remaining uses will still be ongoing for at least a further decade. Given that there is information indicating that (some) fluoropolymers, which are the primary PFAS substances on which we have critical dependencies, have been shown to meet the criteria to be considered ‘polymers of low concern’ (ref. Plastics Europe Fluoropolymer group communication to ECHA:https://fluoropolymers.plasticseurope.org/application/files/7116/7334/1071/Fluoropolymer_Letter_5_January_2023_-_PFAS_REACH_Restriction_2.pdf), all available information should be considered and assessed to ensure that restrictions only require Industry to begin major undertakings towards novel fluoropolymer replacements where it is warranted. Moreso considering the lack of feasible fluoropolymer alternatives and therefore viability of committing resource to such projects, with no good prospects of success at the onset.  Please refer also to responses from the industry associations for the sectors where we operate, including responses from ASD, EUROMOT and Hydrogen Europe. The challenges and long timelines for alternatives development, qualification, certification and industrialisation specific to the sectors in which we operate are described in those sector level responses.  Q6 (f) ANSWER:  n/a  Q6 (g) ANSWER: Please refer also to section 2.6 (submitted in the general comments section) regarding non-use scenarios. If the uses of PFAS are no longer permitted, not just our company, but the sectors in which we operate – aerospace and defence, transport, marine and energy will be similarly affected. In addition, many other sectors for which we are customers and downstream users, will also be affected. In the case of a non-use scenario, we would no longer be able to manufacture products or support (repair and maintain using PFAS-containing parts or mixtures) products currently on the market eventually leading to the early removal from service of affected aircraft, defence vehicles, marine vessels, rail vehicles and power generators.  Development programmes for new electrical technologies to meet decarbonisation aims and advancements towards sustainable aviation fuels would be effectively terminated, leading to loss of years of development towards commercialisation in these critical areas.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Please see our response to question 6 – there will be overlap. However, none of the currently proposed or potentially warranted derogations adequately provide for the long timelines, that would be required if fluoropolymers have to be replaced across all applications in our portfolio. Nor do the derogations adequately have in scope all of our critical uses.  Necessary derogations are discussed in section 2.5 of this response, submitted in the general comments.  Additionally, contradiction between advancing environmental targets and removing the fluoropolymer technology that is currently enabling significant progress towards these aims is not addressed in the current restriction proposal, introducing significant uncertainty and risk for continued investment and R&D in this area, which needs to be addressed. Particularly in PEM fuel cell and electrolyser applications, potential for emissions from fluoropolymers could also be addressed by consideration of controls for end-of-life treatment and disposal/recycling to ensure no releases occur.  Furthermore, we expect to be reliant on derogations necessary for other sectors/products to continue manufacture, where we may be downstream customers for their applications. These may be currently less visible to us in specific articles we receive (for reasons previously outlined in response to question 5) but would include: • Semiconductors • Electronics and electrical connectors • PPE • Plating and surface technology (incl. Metal plating and manufacture of metal products) • Chemical transportation and containment • Batteries • PEM fuel cells  In addition, derogations to allow such continued uses, must also ensure that the full supply chain is considered i.e. derogations for continued end-use of fluoropolymers in products may also need upstream PFAS derogation provisions to allow the continued manufacture and supply of those materials to the end-users.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: 1. Introduction
The Blood Transfusion Association (BTA), is a non-profit trade association committed to promoting the correct use and safe supply of blood for transfusion. Blood transfusions are an integral part of modern medicine and are used in a wide range of lifesaving treatments, such as,. trauma, cancer and heart surgery. Given the impact and ubiquity of these treatments, the BTA is committed to ensuring patient and donor safety as well as a safe and sufficient blood supply.

The BTA's commitment to patient safety encompasses the phasing out of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) as set out in the PFAS restriction proposal. However, in order to accommodate the demand for blood bag sets, devices and accessories used in lifesaving blood transfusions, the BTA advocates for the maximum derogation period of 12 years to be granted to the blood bag set sector. This extended timeframe is essential to guarantee the safety of donors and patients undergoing processes or procedures involving blood bag sets, while manufacturers research and develop alternative materials that meet quality, cost, and regulatory requirements.

The Association's members constitute approximately 90% of the blood bag set market in Europe, offering valuable insights into manufacturing practices and the challenges the PFAS restriction poses to innovation and supply. The following estimations have been based on the interpretation of potential PFAS contamination in the supply chain, considering the suggested limits of 25 ppb for individual PFAS (excluding polymeric PFASs) and 250 ppb for the total PFAS concentration (excluding polymeric PFASs).

2. Affected components

a. Devices (Equipment)
The analysis by BTA members identified the possibility that PFAS may be found in thousands of components that are integral to critical devices employed in the collection, processing, and safety of blood. These components cover various categories, such as adhesives, cables, wiring, displays, touch screens, lubricants, hydraulics, labels, paint, motors, sensors semiconductors, and coatings. There is uncertainty about the total impact because of the maximum limit of 25 ppb, which could mean that this limit is exceeded due to processing aids, rather than intentionally added to the final article. As it stands now, alternative materials for these components are not readily available which necessitates significant further research and development followed by the necessary clinical and regulatory steps, prior to placing a final product on the market.

The industry would require up to 5 years for the identification of suitable substitutes and another 3 to 5 years for the validation and studies of the potential alternatives. The vast majority of these compromised components are manufactured at the beginning of the supply chain before reaching the blood bag set manufacturers. This process causes the blood bag set manufacturers to depend on other industries to find PFAS-free alternatives to these components, which will still need to go through regulatory processes and safety controls. As a result, blood bag set manufacturers rely on the cooperation of other industry actors along the supply chain to move together towards a transition to alternatives through a time-intensive process, spanning 5 to 10 years. Given these timeline projections, the maximum derogation of 12 years must be awarded to the blood bag set sector so there is sufficient time to adequately assess and ensure patient and donor safety.

The estimated total cost of redesigning these components is substantial and could present a burden in excess of 100 Million Euros. This cost encompasses the labour, time and resources required to formulate new elements that meet the health and safety checks upheld by European and national agencies. The ultimate outcome relies on the efficient collective action of the industry.

b. Disposables
Filters play an essential role in safeguarding patient safety in blood-related medical devices, yet their key components contain PFAS. Currently, PFAS-free alternatives for blood filtration materials have not yet been developed. Consequently, a comprehensive overhaul of filter design will be required, particularly those associated with leukoreduction. The development and certification of new filtration materials with similar properties will require up to 10 years.

Additionally, filter replacement is subject to stringent regulatory requirements that call for 5 to 10 years of regulatory development, taking into account national regulations and European standards. The need for clinical trials in the event of material changes further extends the timeline. Completion of this process is governed by the time required to age the product to meet the minimum shelf-life requirements. Considering these demands, the engineering cost for filter replacement alone is projected at 10 Million Euros for the industry.

c. Packaging
Under the current analysis, it has been found that the packaging of medical devices will also be affected by the upcoming PFAS restriction. For example, the ink used on packaging materials will need to be replaced by a PFAS-free alternative. This change is a relatively less complex task, accompanied by a smaller cost and risk, estimated in the hundreds of thousands of Euros for the Industry.

Because of the significant scale involved, the packaging necessitates a substantial development effort, as it is closely intertwined with the associated devices. This development phase is projected to span over 5 years or more.

d. Unknown degradation of components
It should also be taken into account that the above analysis does not account for the unknown degradation of components which could result in the appearance of PFAS over time in components that were initially PFAS-free.

3. Conclusion
Upon initial analysis, the blood bag set sector has identified PFAS in the equipment and devices, filters, and packaging, and is, at this stage, unable to characterize the unknown degradation of components. To guarantee the availability of alternatives, future substitutes must pass regulatory processes, development processes, validation and studies, and clinical trials. To optimize resource utilisation, changes in the equipment and device must be approached holistically, encompassing the entirety of the medical device segment on a global scale.

The blood bag set manufacturers are committed to working towards the elimination of PFAS in their manufacturing processes, devices and disposables, within a realistic and achievable timeline. The proposed restriction poses a multi-year development project, contingent upon the successful identification of PFAS in the product supply chain, the development of alternative materials, the completion of regulatory checks, and the collective cooperation of the industry.

Considering the critical nature and intricacies involved, blood bag set manufacturers should be granted an extended derogation period of 12 years for disposables and devices. This prolonged derogation period would recognize the distinctive societal significance of blood bag sets and ensure the uninterrupted provision of life-saving blood transfusion services. It would also allow sufficient time to identify and incorporate alternative materials that meet the necessary standards for quality, cost-effectiveness, and regulatory compliance.

General Comments: 1. Kuraray believes that chemical management should use a risk-based approach and, not solely hazard-based. In our view, any justification for a substance ban based on the precautionary principle – in this case persistence alone without any identified hazard – must stem from a thorough assessment of potential benefits and costs of such a ban, as well as the scientific evidence for the risk assessment.
2. Kuraray has grave concern with the idea of basing a potential REACH restriction only on the persistence. Actually, "persistent" by itself is not hazard. It should be recognized that the intrinsic property of persistence confers the desirable properties of high durability and unique functionality to products.
3. Kuraray  believes that, if a restriction on the basis on persistence alone were to be established, this precedent would severely hamper and possibly prevent any future innovation in the chemical industry, in particular innovation aimed at durable materials.
4. Alternative for substance and/or substituent does not mean the direct alternative for products. Products which are used as alternative substances must meet the specifications of the original product. Furthermore, even if alternative substances other than PFAS are found, it is necessary to be mindful of the hazards and risks to human health and the environment. This could potentially lead to a different form of "regrettable substitution."
5. There are numerous examples of PFAS that can provide multiple necessary functionalities as a single substance. The availability of alternatives means to cover these functionalities is limited. It is crucial to ensure that necessary exemptions are not overlooked to avoid societal and supply chain disruptions.
6. Polymer PFAS should be reconsidered for further exemption as fluoropolymers have documented safety profiles; are thermally, biologically, and chemically stable, negligibly soluble in water, nonmobile, nonbioavailable, nonbioaccumulative, and nontoxic.
7. Spare parts: the “repair as produced” principle should be introduced. Products need the same spare parts as those used in the first production of each product. A re-design of spare parts often also requires a re-design of the products, because otherwise the original performance (i.e. safety and durability) cannot be guaranteed.
8. We strongly request to establish the new system to be able to apply for further extension after the termination of the exemption period. We kindly ask to the authorities to take into consideration for the new submission system and process to enable to extend the transition period as for the RoHS exemptions.
9. Kuraray would also like to emphasize the importance of availability of analytical methods. Because of the difficulty in identifying which parts of complex articles to try to measure and the general lack of analysis methods applicable to the broad range of substances and matrices in which PFAS are used, enforcement of a broad PFAS restriction will not be feasible.
10. Kuraray would like to ask the European Chemicals Agency and the European Commission to take the above comments into consideration, and to have discussions with stakeholders and to make decisions in a clear and clear process.

Combined Comments: "1. Weapons systems and the defense sector The Ministry of the Armed Forces in France, like the other defense ministries of the Member States of the European Union, constitutes the final link in the defense sector supply chain. Given the complexity of defense systems (an aircraft comprises several million parts), this supply chain consists of many levels and relies on different areas of expertise within the defense industrial and technological base: mainly naval, land, aerospace and space, and the transverse domain of missiles, weapons, and ammunition. These areas use an extremely wide range of technologies using PFAS, such as electronics, refrigeration, technical textiles, professional clothing (including individual protective equipment), pyrotechnics, and nuclear. Defense sector equipment is therefore particularly affected by the restriction project. The inventory work carried out by the General Directorate of Armament (DGA) since 2021, based on its main direct suppliers, has shown the use of many PFAS applications, despite the currently very partial nature of the communication obligations in the supply chain concerning the PFAS targeted by the restriction project (safety data sheets and Article 33 of REACH). Such a result is not surprising: defense systems consist of an assembly of equipment or products that come from different sectors that use PFAS. Some of these sectors are mentioned above, and the annex XV file of the restriction project confirms such use for each of these sectors. The specificity of weapons systems is that they must operate in very severe environments, especially in terms of mechanical stresses and operating and storage temperature ranges. They must also be able to protect the armed forces against multiple aggressions, especially nuclear, radiological, biological, and chemical. They require the best available technologies to achieve the highest performance, robustness, and reliability in order to have an advantage in combat. All weapon systems therefore use PFAS for their many unique properties, whether it is temperature resistance, resistance to chemical attacks, mechanical resistance, low friction coefficient, electrical insulation, dielectric constant, or use as a refrigerant. They are used in many components, sub-assemblies, or basic ingredients (as refrigerants, extinguishing agents, cables, electronic components, hydraulic hoses, seals and other sealing parts, lubricants, adhesives, sealants…), or in manufacturing processes (coatings and surface treatments, demolding of explosives, vapor phase soldering of electronic cards…). Weapon systems must also be kept in operational condition (MCO) throughout their entire lifespan, which can be very long. Equipment such as surface ships, submarines, fighter planes, or tanks have a lifespan of around 40 years. It is therefore necessary to ensure that the future restriction on PFAS does not, by direct or indirect effects, compromise the performance of defense systems and their MCO throughout their entire lifespan. 2. The challenges of the restriction project as presented for the defense sector In general, the Ministry of the Armed Forces notes that the restriction project has an extremely broad scope, due to the definition retained for PFAS: the substances concerned are very numerous, and all uses of PFAS are targeted by the ban, with very few exceptions." "The uses listed here by the Ministry of the Armed Forces are those considered the most critical, the most specific, or of vital importance for defense. As for the proton exchange membrane (PEM) of fuel cells and electrolyzers, some defense applications use them to avoid the embrittlement of metal structures induced by the hydrogen in the cell and the entire piping.  Lubricants: The use of PFAS as lubricants is essential for the defense sector. The following uses of non-polymeric PFAS have been particularly identified: - Non-fluoropolymer cleaning/solvent agents are used for certain essential electronic systems; - Lubricants in many defense systems.  Other equipment and consumables of the armed forces using PFAS  Among the other equipment and consumables of the armed forces using PFAS and whose uses are not specifically mentioned in Annex XV, the following elements can be cited (non-exhaustive list): - Non-fluoropolymers: adhesives in the production tools of certain munitions; - Fluoropolymers for sensors. In summary, even if the list of defense uses presented here cannot be exhaustive or very precise regarding the equipment due to the sensitivity of this information, it appears that PFAS are used transversely on a wide range of specific defense materials." "Use as refrigerants and for mobile air conditioning (MAC) in vehicles for military applications up to 13.5 years after entry into force (derogation 5.dd) and other specifically military refrigeration uses. This potential derogation calls for the following comments: it is generally considered essential for military applications, given the specific military constraints indicated in Annex XV. It should also be clarified and adapted to the duration of the military equipment concerned. Insufficiency of the term "vehicle": The term "vehicle" used in the derogation is insufficient; it is generally used in reference to only land-based vehicles. It would therefore be appropriate to add warships, auxiliary ships, and aircraft, to explicitly cover the naval and aeronautical domains. Submarines are considered to be included in the term "warships". Insufficiency of the derogation period (cf. "Calendar for the transition," Annex E p. 359): As mentioned in the general part, military systems have a lifespan of around 40 years, which can extend to around fifty years. Even if the study mentioned in Annex XV (Hill, 2003) mentions a transition period of 2 to 4 years for the introduction of vehicles into production, this appears impossible in the military domain. Indeed, the design time for a military system is long, often on the order of a decade. Therefore, ongoing programs with orders to industries have already had to make choices about the use of HFO and HFC; some of these systems will be delivered until 2030, others will not be delivered until around 2040. In addition, especially when these systems are part of the naval domain, maintaining operational conditions cannot be compared to maintaining private cars. Indeed, some systems require two types of maintenance: minor and major. Major maintenance is scheduled approximately once every ten years, and its technical and budgetary planning is not improvised. This explains why the use of HFC and in the longer term HFO remains essential to reconcile regulatory evolution and the life cycle of naval vessels, vehicles, and military aircraft. This is why we believe that derogation 5.dd should be provided until 2040. Additional justifications in response to Annex XV - Military applications for MAC and refrigeration: responses to the limits pointed out in Annex XV (p. 359-360) While it is true that alternatives to PFAS refrigerants are used, for example in civil naval domains where some constraints similar to the military domain may apply, it should be noted first that the military domain can use civilian solutions when possible (for example, for small programs with shorter lifespans not intended for military operations). Secondly, military specificities lie precisely in the presence of additional constraints compared to the civil domain, in particular concerning additional safety constraints arising from the use of certain propulsion systems of warships, or from the enclosed atmosphere conditions of submarines, or from a combination of both. Across all domains (naval, aerial, terrestrial), operational deployment entails additional safety constraints in terms of flammability compared to the civilian domain. Regarding the statement that many activities related to the military domain do not take place in a hostile environment (for example, general public contracts – therefore outside of defense and security –, accommodation for personnel and their families), this is true. However, it should be noted that: - the specificities mentioned in Annex XV, Annex E, section E.2.10 (Transport) mainly apply to "mobile" refrigeration, i.e. used in military carriers (warships, aircraft, vehicles); - when "civil" conditions apply (public contracts outside of defense and security), the rules of general law generally apply; - specific conditions must be applied for cooling certain sensitive electronic systems, whether on land or in military carriers. For these systems and other refrigeration uses mentioned in Annex XV, we believe that this type of use should be able to benefit from the general derogation that we are requesting in the "General Comments" section. Regarding standards specifically developed for the military for which Annex E (p. 359) indicates a lack of information on how these standards affect the possibility of considering alternatives as satisfactory: these military standards reflect the requirement for the best technical performance for weapons systems, in terms of weight, speed, power, robustness of materials, as well as rapid fire extinction, safety of personnel in confined spaces, etc. Indeed, the ultimate goal is to ensure the survival of our armed forces against enemies who are not subject to the same rules as ours. Civil standards do not integrate the need for strategic superiority as a constraint. - Summary of costs and benefits assessment - Military applications for MAC and refrigeration: response elements to the information requested by Annex XV (p. 385-387) Annex XV requests elements regarding the type of applications ("range of applications") where this derogation on refrigerants and MAC for military "vehicles" would be necessary; in response, you will find below a non-exhaustive list: - Naval domain (surface vessels and submarines): refrigeration of onboard provisions, air conditioning of operational premises, living quarters and technical installations, including the propulsion systems; - Aeronautical domain: refrigeration of electronic systems; - Land domain: air conditioning of vehicles.  Main other potential derogations indirectly impacting defense uses In addition, although they do not specifically concern military equipment, the Ministry of the Armed Forces finds interest in the following potential derogations, as the components, equipment, ingredients or applications concerned are an integral part of defense equipment: - 5.ee (semiconductor manufacturing process); - 6.o (applications related to vehicle transport security); The potential derogations concerning medical devices and 3D printing, if justified, are also useful. Indeed, these applications can be used by military medical personnel and in the production of spare parts for military equipment." "Transportation One of the potential substitutes for halons in portable fire extinguishers in aeronautics is the substance 2-BTP. This substance is a PFAS and could be used for mission aircraft in the Air Force. After years of research invested by aerospace industries, the search for alternatives to 2-BTP does not seem to be an economically viable option or practically feasible within the long-standing deadlines for critical uses of halons in the (EC) Regulation No 1005/2009 on substances that deplete the ozone layer. The ongoing review of this regulation also does not foresee any changes to the deadlines for critical uses of halons. Other equipment and consumables used by the armed forces relying on PFAS In addition to the uses of PFAS listed in parts 6 and 7, the following uses, in particular, have been identified by the Ministry of Defense (non-exhaustive list). These uses are either already mentioned in Annex XV or are apparently less specific to defense than those mentioned in part 6. However, these uses remain important for defense equipment. Non-fluoropolymers - Cleaning agents / solvents for military aircraft. - Fire suppression systems for Army vehicles (derogation 5.m) - Personal protective equipment, filtration textiles, and textiles for certain Army vehicles for the protection of the armed forces against NBCR risk (not covered by a derogation, except for filtration textiles and separation media); Fluoropolymers - PTFE-treated surface treatment for weapons; for this type of treatment, no derogation is provided for in the restriction proposal. It is worth noting that this type of treatment is an alternative to commercially available hard chrome plating, which is subject to authorization due to the use of chromium trioxide. The PTFE in this surface treatment reduces the friction coefficient, giving the treated part good resistance to wear and corrosion. - PTFE in adhesives, adhesives, and sealants for various military equipment in the ammunition, aeronautical, land, and naval domains; - Fluoropolymer seals used in many weapons systems, beyond ammunition. For example, in fighter planes, surface vessels; - Tribological coatings; - Radiation resistance. Overall, this list of PFAS uses, in addition to those listed in part 6 - even though it cannot be exhaustive or very precise due to the sensitivity of the information - reinforces the observation of widespread use of PFAS in weapons systems and the need to take into account the socio-economic impacts of the restriction proposal on the defense sector."

Content: Information on alternatives Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: 1. PFAS regulations threaten the Green Deal and Fit for 55 programs. (More details can be found in Hydrogen Europe’s public comments.)
In the context of the Green Deal and the 'Fit for 55' program, the European Union's ambitious targets for reducing CO2 emissions towards climate neutrality relate to the energy transition in almost all sectors, from production to energy transition. This calls for rapid and extensive action. The European Union has recognized that the transition to climate neutrality can only be successful if a hydrogen economy can be successfully established in the European Union. The European Commission has defined this within its so-called Hydrogen Strategy in 2020, with the vision of creating a hydrogen ecosystem starting with research and innovation and extending to production and infrastructure. Hydrogen therefore plays an important role in the decarbonization of industry and heavy transport in Europe. Specifically, the European Union aims to have an annual hydrogen production capacity of 10 million tons by 2030 using 500 TWh of electricity produced through electrolysis. This represents approximately 14% of the EU's total electricity consumption, so a huge amount of hydrogen technology is needed. The intended PFAS ban for PEM fuel cells and PEM electrolysis, with a transition period of 6.5 years, will now impact these technologies and companies currently involved in their industrialization and increasing these products using PFAS. Due to the PFAS ban, products containing the latest technology can no longer be pursued. This will bring all activities to a halt as these companies must first re-enter the non-fluoride product development phase. This will make the goals of the EU's Green Deal and Hydrogen Strategy unattainable.

2) Inaccurate understanding of the hydrogen sector and value chain (more details can be found in Hydrogen Europe’s public comments).
Fluorine polymer membrane technology is also essential in the alkaline electrolyzer value chain. This is because the liquid electrolyte (KOH) required for the process must be manufactured by electrolysis using fluoropolymer membranes, which is the best available technology. The alternative is to use mercury or asbestos. (Both are highly toxic and are banned). It is unclear whether the exclusion of the proposed regulation includes PEM electrolysers or other types of fuel cells and electrolysis technologies (e.g., alkaline, solid oxide electrolyte cells, or anion exchange membranes). These technologies are not as viable without fluoropolymer-based components as PEM fuel cells and are as essential to the EU's decarbonization goals as PEM fuel cells.

3) Claims regarding fluoropolymers (PFAS subtype) (further details can be found in Hydrogen Europe's public comments)
Electrolyzer and fuel cell applications are core technologies in the hydrogen industry. Other process technologies across the value chain are also essential to the deployment of the hydrogen economy (compression, purification, and liquefied storage components). Electrolyzers, fuel cells, and other processes all rely heavily on fluoropolymers (considered a PFAS subtype). No alternatives are currently or in the near future expected to replace these highly specialized materials, which are critical to the EU's transition towards climate neutrality. These fluoropolymers are produced under responsible manufacturing conditions and used in highly controlled industrial environments. Because emissions are high and initial prices are high, reusability and recyclability are actively explored and inherently encouraged. The proposal's approach to grouping all fluoropolymers together with other PFAS types should be reexamined. Henry (Wiley Periodicals, Inc. on behalf of Society of Environmental Toxicology & Chemistry (SETAC), Volume 14, Number 3, pp. 316-334) and Korzeniowski (Korzeniowski, S.H., et al. (2022), A critical review of The application of polymer of low concern regulatory criteria to fluoropolymers II: Fluoroplastics and fluoroelastomers. Integr Environ Assess Manag.) demonstrated that most fluoropolymers meet OECD criteria defined as 'low risk polymers'. It has been proven not to pose a risk to human health or the environment due to its lack of water solubility, toxicity and bioavailability. Additionally, the use of fluoropolymers in the hydrogen value chain is limited to highly controlled industrial environments, where contact with workers or consumers is clearly limited and strictly supervised (included in the first Call for Evidence by one of Hydrogen Europe’s members). Therefore, regulatory action should focus on addressing potential PFAS emissions at all life stages (manufacturing, use, and end-of-life) and not ban these essential, high-performing, low-concern products. Therefore, fluoropolymer production and use should be exempt from U-PFAS restrictions.

4) Comments on PEM electrolysers, other electrolysers, and proposed alternatives to PEM and other fuel cells (more information can be found in Hydrogen Europe's public comments)
Fluorine-free ionomers and membrane materials have existed in the scientific community for decades. However, it was not possible to meet the requirements of hydrogen applications during this period. Research work is ongoing on hydrocarbon membranes, for example the development of sulfonated polyetheretherketone (PEEK) membranes (Chi Hoon Park, Chang Hyun Lee, Michael D. Guiver, Young Moo Lee, Progress in Polymer Science, Volume 36, Issue 11, 2011, Pages 1443-1498, ISSN 0079-6700, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.progpolymsci.2011.06.001; Dong Won Shin, Michael D. Guiver, and Young Moo Lee, Chemical Reviews 2017 117 (6), 4759-4805 DOI: 10.1021/acs.chemrev.6b00586; N. Esmaeili, E. M. Gray, C. J. Webb, ChemPhysChem 2019, 20, 2016.). Oxidation due to oxygen radicals inevitably generated at the cathode electrode often reduces durability. Non-fluorinated membrane concepts have not been proven at industrial scale, primarily at laboratory or pilot scale, and are still immature, lasting only a few tens of hours relative to the 25,000-hour lifetime requirement for fuel cell applications. In PEM electrolysis, the membrane support, aromatic chemicals (e.g. sPEEK), have too low durability. Appropriate chemicals must be found to accommodate these major barriers. Although certain indicators of the performance of non-PFSA membranes may be superior, in electrolyzer applications these non-PFSA membranes (e.g. hydrocarbons) do not have a commercial life (more than 50,000 hours for electrolyzer applications) or associated temperatures (higher than 79°C). In fact, to be considered a truly commercially viable alternative, durability well in excess of 50,000 hours must be achieved. However, to date, few non-perfluorinated alternatives have come close to 1,000 hours, and none have even reached 10,000 hours. Hydrocarbon membranes have problems with certain chemicals they produce on a regular basis, such as hydroxy radicals (.OH) and hydroperoxy (.OOH) radicals, which are produced by HOOH decomposition, which are byproducts of fuel cells or electrolysis processes. These radicals can easily cleave not only C-H bonds but also aromatic and ether bonds. In the 1990s, there was great interest in replacing Nafion and other fluoropolymer-based membranes.
This was because these membranes were more expensive and emitted HF that could attack steel bipolar plates. Nonetheless, neither of these programs offered a viable alternative. The 2010s saw a resurgence of interest in hydrocarbon membranes as companies experimented with non- and partially fluorinated chemistries. Since 2013, the U.S. Department of Energy has spent $30 million on membrane/ionomer R&D, two-thirds of which were on non-PFSA approaches (Cumulative amounts from the relevant years: https://www.energy.gov/eere /fuelcells/hydrogen-and-fuel-cells-annual-merit-review-proceedings). None of these have resulted in commercial polymers for fuel cells or electrolysers. PEM fuel cell membrane electrode assemblies currently have durability issues due to aromatic hydrocarbons. The European Clean Hydrogen Alliance project GAIA (2019-2022) (https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/826097), with €4.5 million in Horizon2020 funding, is developing hydrocarbons for PFSA ionomer membranes. We set out to find an alternative, but we found that similar performance was not possible. In the Solid State Ionics 274 (2015) 94–99Horizon2020 paper, they found a difference from the fluorine-based ionomer when evaluating the hydration levels of the hydrocarbon-based electrolyte membrane, and the limitations of the hydrocarbon-based ionomer can be confirmed. Moreover, in the Materials Today Energy 17 (2020) 100483 paper, since the hydrocarbon-based ionomer cannot use the same antioxidants commonly used on fluorine-based ionomers, serious problems with durability were identified as there are many attack points in the molecular structure itself for radicals. At present, there is no way to improve these problems, making it difficult to apply hydrocarbon-based ionomers. IMMORTAL(https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/101006641), another project with EU funding of 3.8 million euros, and ELECTROHYPEM (https://cordis.europa.eu/), a project with EU funding of 1.3 million euros. project/id/300081) concluded that alternative membrane technologies known to date are far behind in terms of durability. Currently, there are no commercially viable hydrocarbon membranes that simultaneously meet the necessary chemical and mechanical durability requirements (https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1149/2.0131806jes).
As a membrane support in PEM fuel cell applications, PTFE has the required mechanical durability, dimensional stability upon moisture absorption, and chemical inertness upon radical attack. Polyphenylene (PPP) cannot be an alternative because it is thermally and chemically unstable and cannot be processed at high temperatures (higher than 100°C). One member of Hydrogen Europe conducted 15 years of in-house testing on ionomers and reinforcing hydrocarbon materials and concluded that there were significant gaps. It is an unsuitable trade-off between performance and durability, both chemically and mechanically. In the short and medium term, it will be difficult to identify PFAS replacement porous films to replace expanded PTFE (ePTFE) reinforcements for PEM fuel cell applications. Current experience shows that effective additive technologies, including state-of-the-art mobility and fixation additives, are not sufficient to improve the chemical stability of hydrocarbon membrane ionomers. Hydrocarbon ionomers in PEM electrolysis membranes are not technically feasible because they are too hard and the mechanical durability is not sufficient. In Journal of The Electrochemical Society, 155 _2_ B119-B124 _2008, a fenton test was conducted to evaluate the chemical durability of hydrocarbon ionomers and fluorine-based ionomers, and the results showed a higher weight loss (hydrocarbon-based ionomers 24 hours later) than fluorine-based ionomers (16w% weight loss after 96 hours). Afterwards, a 100w% weight reduction was confirmed. This confirms that the chemical durability of the hydrocarbon-based ionomer against radical attack is significantly low, and when comparing cell acceleration durability, it can be confirmed that the durability of the fluorine-based ionomer is stable. Important relevant properties of PFSA polymers, such as proton conductivity, oxidation stability at high anodic potentials during typical PEM electrolyzer operation, and processability (lower glass transition temperature compared to hydrocarbon ionomers) are not achievable with hydrocarbon alternatives. For this reason, the production and use of fluoropolymers in PEM fuel cells and electrolyzers should be exempt from U-PFAS restrictions.

5) The proposal does not meet the restricted proposal requirements required by REACH.
According to REACH Annex XV Part II-3, the risk addressed by the restriction must be in the form of a Chemical Safety Report based on the relevant hazard and risk assessment set out in Annex I. In REACH, persistence is subject to risk assessment only when combined with bioaccumulation and in some cases with toxicity. However, this restriction proposal is based on persistence alone, which is not considered a hazard endpoint, as if all PFASs are hazardous. In addition, while exposure assessments should be made for each use by creating exposure scenarios, all PFASs are grouped together, so the assessment for each use is insufficient and does not indicate the existence of unacceptable risks as required by Article 68. Therefore, we believe that this proposal does not meet the requirements for a restriction proposal as required by REACH, and it is not appropriate to discuss a restriction.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Energy sector (PEM fuel cells and PEM electrolyzers)

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: SFTC's electrolyte membranes are used by fuel cell and electrolyzer manufacturers such as Bosch. We agree and support the information provided by Bosch.  During fluoropolymer manufacturing, PFAS emissions are strictly controlled at the production site. Manufacturing companies already have to adhere to strict environmental standards. It is important to note that, as implied in the general comments in this section and identified in the proposed restrictions, the amounts of fluoropolymers used in the hydrogen sector are small compared to PFAS materials used in other sectors. We would like to inform you of the input provided to the ECHA public consultation by certain Hydrogen Europe members, such as Gujarat Fluorochemicals, on potential emissions during the manufacture of fluoropolymers. PFAS emissions to water or surrounding equipment are negligible during the use of fluoropolymer-containing components in electrolyzer and fuel cell applications. Nonetheless, a number of Hydrogen Europe members are currently undertaking data collection work that provides robust and sufficient data to support claims that PFAS emissions from water or ambient equipment are negligible. End-of-life incineration, including exhaust gas disposal, in a safe and controlled manner is the current standard operation for fluoropolymer membranes used in all types of electrolyzers and fuel cells. All exhaust gases are treated to the highest standards in accordance with EU and local legislation and there is no indication that PFAS remain after incineration under the conditions in which they were used. However, there is no EU-level legislation on PFAS emissions associated with incineration. Mutual standards on this are a prerequisite for future legislation. Industry players have already begun coordinating to come up with proposals on this topic. Addressing potential releases of end-of-life fluoropolymers should be a regulatory priority rather than a complete ban on the substances. Taking fuel cells in mobility applications as an example, at the end-of-life stage, the vehicle equipped with the fuel cells is dismantled, the modules are removed, and the stack itself is disassembled to collect the cells. The cells are then incinerated as described above to recycle the platinum group metals (PGMs), while the ionomers are completely destroyed with the release of hydrogen fluoride (HF). The same thing is done for fluoropolymers in other applications, such as PEM electrolysis. The resulting fluoride-containing emissions are captured and treated, and the results are measured against stringent environmental standards. However, to date there is no systematic data collection on potential emissions (e.g. fluoro-ionomers), so it is important to explore the potential of monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) systems. For fluoropolymers, it must be clear that recycling is the way forward, to gradually replace the aforementioned incineration practices. It is also clear that economic imperatives will lead to more and more recycling of PEM fuel cells, especially once they reach significant volumes at the end of their useful life. In fact, platinum recyclability can reach nearly 100%. There are also examples of recycling where 100% of the membrane is separated from critical raw materials. This means that return and efficient separation of the membrane material is possible. Because the applications are relatively limited, recovery systems that enable such recycling are very realistic. Some members of Hydrogen Europe have already begun systematic recovery of end-of-life products, and some claim that in just five years PFAS, including components of fuel cells and electrolysers, will be diverted from landfill. In addition to incineration, research is underway aimed at recovering ionomers. Although it is possible to separate the precious metals from the membrane, the ionomers are now deformed to the point that they cannot be reused in other fuel cells. Currently, there is no known process to “repair” the material to a sufficiently high grade required for fuel cell applications. Additionally, the risk of ionomer diversity in different PEM fuel cell products raises the challenge of developing slightly modified recycling technologies. A value chain must be established for recycled end-of-life materials, from raw materials for high-demand applications to low-demand applications. Robust recycling processes therefore require both time and sufficient quantities to develop end-of-life components and applications that can use the recovered materials. PEM electrolyzers and PEM fuel cells are based on the same scientific foundation and are developed using similar technologies. Even though they are different products, the restriction proposal did not acknowledge this. Moreover, synergies can be developed where recycled ionomer materials from fuel cells can be utilized in water electrolyzer technology. However, these processes need to be developed, and this requires legal certainty for the industry to continue to use and develop fluoropolymer components. Unfortunately, the recycling of PGMs and fluoropolymers for both fuel cells and electrolyzer systems may be jeopardized by proposed PFAS restrictions because they no longer have end markets. As a nascent market, fuel cell vehicles have not yet reached the volumes required at end-of-life. This is the main reason for the lack of recycling ecosystem development. Even assuming 10% waste along the value chain by 2030, the accumulation would already be significant despite the small number of devices reaching end-of-life. Nonetheless, investments have been made in research on the topic, including the HyTechCycling project and a €500,000 investment from one Hydrogen Europe member. Other members are also devoting additional capacity to projects that expand the entire end-of-life process (e.g. the H2Giga project). The U.S. Department of Energy plans to invest $50 million in recycling research for PEM fuel cells and electrolysis from 2023 to 2027, with additional funding for projects to expand ionomer recovery. Additionally, the Department of Energy is working with industry partners, American Institute of Chemical engineers, universities, and national laboratories to develop technologies related to circularity, recycling, and end-of-life and critical supply chain issues in the hydrogen economy. The Clean Hydrogen Partnership has also funded collaboration to develop projects that address the recycling of end-of-life hydrogen technology. For example, the BEST4Hy project (2021-2023), with an investment of 1.5 million euros, targets high recovery of ionomers (80%) and remanufacturing of at least 70% new cells/stacks. The PEM stack contains 95% ionomer and platinum. Life cycle assessment (LCA) and life cycle costing (LCC) methodologies can be applied to the entire life cycle of electrolysis and fuel cell technologies, providing a factual basis for the potential environmental impacts of the final termination of these technologies. Additional efforts, in close collaboration with research institutes and industry, will be invested in the currently running BReCycle project, with a total of €1.2 million in funding.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: SFTC's electrolyte membranes are used by fuel cell and electrolyzer manufacturers such as Bosch. We agree and support the information provided by Bosch.    Today, there is an economic need to recover PEM stacks (both fuel cells and electrolyzers) at the end of their life cycle to recover and recycle the expensive platinum group metal (PGM) catalyst contained within the membrane/electrode assembly. The same goes for fluoride. Through recycling processes, the fluorine contained in the ionomer can be recovered in the form of calcium fluoride, for example, made from fluorspar or fluorite (on the EU's 2020 list of important raw materials). Calcium fluoride can then be used as a raw material for further production of fluorine-containing substances. Therefore, it is financially inadvisable for the associated fluoropolymer components to enter the general waste stream. Moreover, there is a strong possibility that fluoropolymer ionomers can be recovered at end-of-life and reused in polymer form, as demonstrated by the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) project Frankenstack and Carmo et al. Additionally, several patents exist involving methods for recovering and recycling catalyst coated membranes (CCMs) by dissolving the membrane and separating its components. A recent peer-reviewed study conducted by Aleksandrov (2019) on end-of-life PTFE disposal found that incineration is an appropriate method of disposing of fluoropolymers without environmental concerns. The study showed that combustion of PTFE using best available techniques (BAT) under typical waste incineration conditions (municipal level) does not decompose into PFAS, which are identified as environmental concerns. It has also been shown that under standard municipal waste incineration conditions PTFE is essentially converted to carbon dioxide and hydrofluoric acid. They therefore concluded that municipal incineration of PTFE should be considered an acceptable form of waste disposal. It should also be noted that the Netherlands Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM) has drawn slightly fewer specific conclusions, noting that it can be assumed that polymer molecules are destroyed during the gasification process, but this does not provide sufficient information. Therefore, further research on the topic will be needed to fill this gap.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Recycling of PTFE-based sealing materials for hydrogen compressor systems is already established. Collecting materials by grade allows you to expand your recycling process to cover almost 100% of your in-house waste. There are already specialized grinding companies on the market that allow recycling of these perfluorinated polymers. A Process Technology provides efficient shredding equipment for recycling processes, and Dressler Group provides shredding services for its customers. Basically, recycling of perfluorinated polymers is divided into four steps: 1) Collection of waste by grade 2) Grinding A process of milling particles down to about 20 – 30 microns 3) Blending the ground material with new material (normal powder mixing process) 4) Producing new semi-finished products from a new mixture containing recycled materials. The cost of recycling is about €10 per kilogram. It is equal to the cost of new materials. This means that it is possible from a financial perspective.

5. Proposed derogations: SFTC's electrolyte membranes are used by fuel cell and electrolyzer manufacturers such as Bosch. We agree and support the information provided by Bosch.

Org. name: Siemens Energy Global GmbH & CO. KG // Business Area: Electrolyzer and Fuel Cell
Combined Comments:
General Comments: 1. Scope or restriction option analysis
Siemens Energy supports the EU’s ambitions to cut PFAS emissions by 95% by 2030. However, we have some concerns on very specific applications essential for infrastructure and society and on timelines of the proposal, which we lay out below and in further application specific reports.

The water electrolyzer technology as an essential element of a renewable energy society has not been appropriately considered in the ban proposal. Even though the risk (concerns RAC) of PFAS-release during operation and after end of life are very small to zero. The socioeconomic impact (concerns SEAC) is tremendous, because the PFAS ban dramatically slows down the energy transition by at least one decade, if no derogation time in addition to the 18 months is granted to the water electrolyzer technology. It appears even more inconclusive, as the fuel cells, using the same kind of material, got granted a 5-year derogation time, still insufficient for a transition to alternatives presently not available.
We therefore kindly ask to reconsider the ban proposal in those two respects (electrolyzers and fuel cells) to grant both technologies at least a derogation time of 12 years, the maximum currently possible.

2. Environmental emissions
- PEM water electrolyzers do not emit PFAS into the environment during operation.
After end of life, the membrane material will be recollected and either recycled or incinerated to mineralization stage. There is no release of - PFAS after end of life.
Soon it is likely, that new membranes will be made from recycled materials, which reduces the material consumption and production born emissions.

At end of life, the membrane which contains the majority of the PFAS is extracted from the systems and recycled to recover precious Platinum Group Metals (PGMs) like Iridium and Platinum. The current low-volume process incinerates the membrane material and PFAS is decomposed back to the mineralization stage (CO2, H2O and HF) and therefore not a PFAS anymore. For high-volume recycling, process steps to recover the membrane material have been developed and are about the be qualified for implementation as standard process.
In a general context it is of importance to consider and to recognize, even in a scaled-up scenario with large installed fleets of fuel cells and water electrolyzers, that the amount of PFAS used per annum is by an order of magnitude smaller compared to the commercial / non-professional textile industries. With recycling on top of that, these applications do not represent a significant source for PFAS related environmental pollutions.

3. Information on alternatives
- Currently, there are no alternative materials qualified. Once available, the transition time for implementation will be in the order of 6 - 10 years.

Important for the context is to recognize timelines. -
Fluoropolymers where already known to the industry for many decades when fuel cells and electrolyzers started to become commercial products. It took more than two decades to make them suitable in all necessary technical aspects to the cost of their price. These materials are at least two orders of magnitude more expensive than standard polymers. The natural interest to find substitutes is present since the beginning and remains till now.
The very few alternatives, which are known to today, are promising in some regards e.g., they do sufficiently conduct protons and offer low gas diffusion rates, but do fail completely in others e.g., the membrane electrode assembly still requires PFSA (a PFAS) on the interfaces and technology readiness level (TRL) for implementation is still at or below 3-4. The price most likely will not be an issue but chemical stability / lifetime requirements for an industrial product cannot be met at current. More time will be needed to let the material system mature. Once the polymer material and the corresponding membranes become sufficiently chemically stable, the material (polymer and membrane) would have to be available in large quantities, and furthermore the production processes on the user side must be developed and implemented correspondingly. Such transitions take at least 6 to greater 10 years, before they can become effective. Material production must be scaled up and the implementation into the production needs to be stable and requires a qualification process, too.
Again, the suggested transition time of the ban proposal was even unrealistic, if an alternative would be available any time soon.

4. Other socio-economic analysis (SEA) issues
- The true socio-economic impact should be considered based on the impacts on the society, like derailed energy transition / not meeting CO2 reduction targets in time and their consequences, rather than on individual company impacts.

As outlined before, the energy transition will be significantly slowed down and delays the goals set for the hydrogen industries by at least one decade. With respect to the very small quantities used (smaller than 5t/GW), neglectable release rates, the recycling efforts and with that the incapability for PFAS emissions to the environment, the ban proposal is unbalanced and to be reconsidered for this application.

5. Transitional period
- Since no alternatives are available, a transition period cannot be provided.

For a qualified request for changes on the transitional period/deferred entry into force, the fundamental aspect is missing, there is no qualified alternative material for the membrane of an electrolyzer / fuel cell developed yet. The evidence statured itself by non-availability of alternatives. If available, qualification (2-5years, depends on the application; fuel cell 20.000 h lifetime, electrolyzer 80.000 h lifetime), implementation into the production lines and scale-up of the production capacity will add time on top. A transition time of one decade is typical for such drastic adaption in a product.

6. Request for exemption
- Products in the market and in use should be exempt to allow service.
- Fuel cells and water electrolyzer are essential for renewable hydrogen and thus a major column to decarbonize the society.

An exemption must be granted for products already in the marked, where service and repair is still ongoing. It should last until the technical lifetime of the product has been reached or an alternative is available. Otherwise, the trust in this new market will be destroyed, since the customer will suffer significant stranded investments because the product becomes unserviceable.
The insignificance of the used PFAS material quantities (compared e.g. to the textile market) and with that the neglectable emission potential to the environment on one hand and the delayed energy transition by one decade and more with all its impact on the other hand qualifies hydrogen technologies like water electrolyzers and fuel cells to be reconsidered and to be exempted.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: 1. Scope or restriction option analysis:

Siemens Energy welcomes the EU’s ambitions to cut PFAS emissions by 95% by 2030. As a company, we believe this is the right thing to do and will support you in any way possible. However, we have some concerns with the timelines proposed, which we lay out below.

PFAS materials are used at Siemens Energy in a wide range of products and applications essential for the energy transition. In order to visualize the complexity of our products and the materials used, some examples are described below.

Our energy industrial solutions vary from gas turbines, generators, compressors, high voltage energy transmission and distribution equipment, transformer, fuel cells, electrolyzer, industrial heat pumps, wind turbines, power electronics and many others.

For a wide range of PFAS applications like cables, sensors, tubes, hoses, semiconductors, surface coating of equipment, sealings and many other applications, intentionally added PFAS (mostly Fluoropolymers) are used, ensuring an extreme durability and lifetime in some applications of 40 years or more. Identifying PFAS is a great challenge as the vast majority of the about 10,000 individual PFAS substances covered by the restriction proposal are currently not classified as hazardous in accordance with the CLP Regulation (EC) No. 1272/2008, nor identified as substances of very high concern (SVHCs) under REACH Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006. A communication on those PFAS contained in mixtures and articles along the supply chain is therefore non-existent.  As of today, it is not possible to draw a complete picture of the magnitude of a PFAS ban, as proposed in the PFAS ANNEX XV report. However, an impact assessment for some identified cases was possible and proposals for changes to be considered are provided. On some specific cases like compressors/turbines, PEM water electrolyzer and fuels cells as well as grid technologies, we will provide detailed feedback in separate feedback documents.
The significant impact became obvious during our assessment of PFAS, not only on the business figures and employment but also on the development and market ramp-up for new (‘green’) technologies closely linked to projects focusing on renewables, green hydrogen, net zero technologies and a sustainable society. It is worth noting that R&D and industrialization efforts vary greatly and may not lead to successful outcomes matching required performance criteria with alternatives requiring different development times (e.g.  5, 10, 15 years) before product launch. For cases where alternatives are not yet known, a significant delay is to be expected (development, testing, certification, etc.) which must be considered. There is already a large amount of machinery and applications in operation, where PFAS is necessary for their safe use. During their use phase, this machinery and applications will continue to require servicing, potentially with PFAS. Servicing this equipment with PFAS should still be allowed.

In all other cases, where a replacement is possible, the complex way of identification, finding a replacement, implementing them in products and finally repeating type testing of related products will also exceed the given transition time of 18 months by far. However, when we look at the current state and the quantities of PFAS material used by Siemens Energy in the energy sector, it can be stated that we end up with an annual amount of less than 500t/a of PFAS material. The majority of the used PFAS material does belong to fluoropolymer in solid state form, e.g., FKM, PTFE, PVDF, PFSA, which are not prone for PFAS release during their use phase. the risk of emissions after end of life should be covered by specific recycling / waste handling regulations as already in place within the EU. Concepts are provided in close co-operation between industry and such operators, including disposal methods for PFAS waste through high temperature chemical breakdown, or incineration, taking the responsibility in this.
Therefore, the PFAS ANNEX XV report proposal should extend derogations for energy industrial applications from the current restriction proposal to 5-12 years to give sufficient time for the identification, implementation and certification of PFAS-free alternative materials or solutions.

2. Environmental emissions:
The small amount of PFAS material which is used in the energy sector is mainly to be found in solid state fluoropolymers (PTFE, FKM, PFSA-membrane) and does not present a substantial source for emissions to the environment as noted during the first consultation phase by ECHA’s impact assessment. The energy sector is responsible for less than 0,1% of the annual PFAS emissions in the European Union (Draft_R.16_V3.0 (europa.eu)).
Emissions can further be reduced by improved production processes, implementation of recycling and certified disposal and waste management.

3. Information on alternatives:
Fluoro materials are used by the industry and the energy product portfolio for a long time and are applied due to their outstanding properties like the resistance in harsh temperature and chemical environments. In the PEM electrolyser membrane and fuel cell, PFAS properties like proton conductivity, resistance against chemical radicals (like OH radicals, H2O2 radicals) and temperature resistance are essential elements of the functionality of electrolysers and fuel cells. In parallel, the search of alternatives for fluor materials has been ongoing for decades already, also with a focus on reducing the cost factor of such materials, which are two orders of magnitude more expensive than standard materials.
The very few alternatives which are known today are in a continual evaluation process and a few of them are promising in some respects but do fail completely in others. The technical maturity (TRL) of the alternative PFAS materials for implementation are still between experimental proof of concept and technology validation in a lab. The price most likely will not be an issue but lifetime requirements, as e.g., energy transmission and distribution equipment, generators, compressors, gas turbines covering a lifetime of 30 – 40 years cannot be met and will require more time. After the continuous assessment of alternatives, the new and qualified material then must be available in large quantities to cover previous applications of PFAS material. The production processes on the user side must also be developed and implemented. In total, such transitions take at least 6 to 10 years before they can become effective. In the case that alternatives are not available or known for certain applications, a complete redesign of the product might be the consequence, entailing the entire product development process to avoid PFAS. In case of compressors, it could trigger high gas leak rates and lower efficiency.

4. Other socio-economic analysis (SEA) issues:
The impact on PFAS emission reduction from the energy sector is marginal with an estimated amount of 55t/a out of 74.000t/a PFAS emissions in total. The current proposal of the PFAS ANNEX XV report would however still have a major impact for climate-neutral technologies.
With regards to repair and maintenance for products already placed on the market, e.g., in the high voltage energy generation, transmission and distribution sector, products are heavily impacted as they must be compliant with customer requirements of end-of-lifetime guarantee and considering the EU Green Deal to produce longer lasting products that can be repaired, recycled and re-used. With the current approach to ban PFAS (Fluoropolymer) after Eif + 18month, products which are already placed on the market cannot further be maintained which is in total contrast to the EU Green Deal approach. With proximately 50.000 circuit breakers and ~10.000 gas insulated 3-pole circuit breakers in the grid today, the functioning of the EU energy power grid will be put at risk. The same is true for gas turbines mainly on the sealing and gaskets of bearings and lubrication system.
Major impacts will also develop in other industries like the chemical industry which we supply with chlorine compressors. PFAS containing seals are essential for this application. Such compressors could not be operated without these PFAS containing seals, as they are necessary for both the safe performance and conformity to standards.

Many other examples for professional industrial applications of the material could be provided. They all have one thing in common: at first glance, the financial impact on one company in relation to the entire European economy seems small. However, this is misleading as this does not take into account the ripple effect throughout the entire economy. This is especially true for the energy sector, as this would not only impact the economic performance but could have a lasting consequence on the infrastructure which is necessary for the energy transition.

5. Transitional period:
For a qualified request for changes on the transitional period/deferred entry into force, a fundamental aspect is missing. For some applications there is no qualified alternative material available yet. The evidence is statured itself by “non-availability of alternatives” in certain impact assessment sections. If alternatives would be available, the qualification process would have to start and it would take many years, depending on the Siemens Energy product portfolio application.
Industrial applications demand in minimum a lifetime of over 20 years and thus a sound pre-qualification time in test rigs and test applications are mandatory. The implementation into the production lines and scale-up of the production capacity of the alternatives will add time on top. A transition time of 6 - 10 years is common for such drastic adaptions to an industrial product.

6. Request for exemption:
Exemptions are required for products that are already on the marked, where service and repair is still ongoing. Otherwise, the trust in the market will be destroyed since the customer will suffer significant stranded investments.

Exemptions are also required for industrial and professional products and solutions with no PFAS emissions during operation and where no alternatives are in sight.
The insignificance of the used PFAS material quantities in some sectors and its neglectable emission potential to the environment should be considered in the ban in order not to jeopardize essential technologies for the energy transition, grid technology and chemical infrastructure.

A differentiation should also be made between essential industrial solutions and consumer products. The current proposed restriction for industrial applications in the energy sector could jeopardize the EU’s important ongoing energy transition and decarbonization efforts and should therefore be reconsidered and such applications exempted. With this new approach, together with improvements in the production process, mandatory recycling or qualified incineration, we believe that the PFAS-reduction goal can still be maintained.
