Sumitomo Electric Fine Polymer, Inc. is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Sumitomo Electric Industries, Ltd., supplying polymer products including perfluoropollymer to various industiries such as automotive, aerospace, electronics, etc. Irradiated Products Division handles sleeve products such as heat-shrinkable tubing or heat resistant tubing.
We understand that your agency works continuously to protect EU citizens from harmful substances and welcome this opportunity for public comment. We would also like to emphasize that we are actively working to replace the PFAS in our products from an environmental and health perspective. However, there are no substitutes for some of the applications that are essential to society. Therefore, we propose exemptions or significantly longer transition periods for some essential uses.

1) Request for exemption
We strongly request that perfluoropolymers (e.g., PTFE, PFA, FEP) and those cross-linked by electron beam irradiation be exempt from the scope of PFAS in the proposal for the following reasons.
Perfluoropolymers and those cross-linked by electron beam irradiation are materials that are neither bioaccumulative nor biotoxic. Their unique and outstanding properties have made them indispensable to society, especially in solving environmental problems, as they provide solutions unmatched by other materials.
Perfluoropolymers have totally different properties and hazardous levels compared to other harmful PFAS substances, such as PFOA or PFOS. If perfluoropolymers are collectively banned with those other PFAS simply because their chemical formulas are similar, without closely reviewing and classifying their properties, we may encounter serious consequences in terms of social economic impact. The reasons are detailed in sections 2) and 3) below.

2) Perfluoropolymers are neither bioaccumulative nor biotoxic
Because perfluoropolymers are chemically and biologically persistent and inert, elution of these materials is known to be very limited (Olabisi et al., 2016). Complying with EU regulations on PFOA and PFOS, we have seen a drastic improvement in the production process of perfluoropolymers. According to our analysis performed by a third party testing laboratory, PFOA was not detected from PTFE and PFA (see “PTFE_PFA_ analysis.pdf” as attached in Section Ⅳ). Therefore, no hazardous materials are expected to be leaching from perfluoropolymers, which indicates that animals or plants will not be absorbing PFOA nor perfluoropolymers themselves. If there is nothing being absorbed, then bioaccumulation and biotoxicity do not occur (Henry et al., 2009; OECD, 1993; Beyer EC.1993; Korzeniowski, S. H, et al., 2023; FCJ, 2023, see "FCJ.pdf" as attached in Section IV).
Since perfluoropolymers are chemically and biologically persistent and inert, they have been used as material for implantable artificial organs such as pericardial patches and artificial blood vessels (Henry et al., 2009; Olabisi, 2015; Gangal & Brothers, 2000).
It is also documented in the literature that perfluoropolymers are substances with distinctly different properties from potentially toxic low molecular weight compounds such as PFOA and PFOS, which were the starting point for this proposed restriction (Henry et al., 2009; OECD 1993; Olabisi, 2019; FCJ, 2023, see "FCJ.pdf" as attached in Section IV).

3) Perfluoropolymers are irreplaceable materials that can contribute significantly to solving environmental concerns
Perfluoropolymers have unique and excellent properties including heat resistancy, oil/fluid resistancy, sliding capability, flame-retardancy, etc. that properties have made the substances essential to society. Heat-shrinkable and non-heatshrinkable tubing made of electron beam irradiated perfluoropolymers are widely used for electric insulation, protection, bundling and other purposes in automotive, aerospace, electronics, medical and other sectors. As for heat-shrinkable tubing, there are many choices of materials such as polyethylen, PVC, silicone, PET, etc. other than perfluoropolymers, but there is no alternatives for temperature rating of 150℃ or higher, or oil/fluid resistancy is needed use. Silicone is a potential alternative, however, it has many inferior points such as 1) mechanical strength is weak, 2) no transparency, 3) too thick wall compared with perfluoropolymers, 4) abrasion resistance is weak, 5) fluid resistance is weak, 6) shrink ratio up to 50%, which limit their use. PEEK is another candidate of alternatives, however, PEEK is so hard (stiff), which makes the tubing very difficult to use. Its shrink ratio is smaller than silicone, up to 20%, which also limit their use. In the end, there is no alternative for perfluoropolymers heat-shrinkable tubing.

Sincerely yours,

Comments on Annex XV Restriction Report (PFAS Restriction Proposal)


Sumitomo Electric Fine Polymer, Inc. is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Sumitomo Electric Industries, Ltd., supplying polymer products including perfluoropollymer to various industries such as automotive, aerospace, electronics, etc. Irradiated Products Division handles sleeve products such as heat-shrinkable tubing or heat resistant tubing.
We understand that your agency works continuously to protect EU citizens from harmful substances and welcome this opportunity for public comment. We would also like to emphasize that we are actively working to replace the PFAS in our products from an environmental and health perspective. However, there are no substitutes for some of the applications that are essential to society. Therefore, we propose exemptions or significantly longer transition periods for some essential uses.

1) Request for exemption
We strongly request that perfluoropolymers (e.g., PTFE, PFA, FEP) and those cross-linked by electron beam irradiation be exempt from the scope of PFAS in the proposal for the following reasons.
Perfluoropolymers and those cross-linked by electron beam irradiation are materials that are neither bioaccumulative nor biotoxic. Their unique and outstanding properties have made them indispensable to society, especially in solving environmental problems, as they provide solutions unmatched by other materials.
Perfluoropolymers have totally different properties and hazardous levels compared to other harmful PFAS substances, such as PFOA or PFOS. If perfluoropolymers are collectively banned with those other PFAS simply because their chemical formulas are similar, without closely reviewing and classifying their properties, we may encounter serious consequences in terms of social economic impact. The reasons are detailed in sections 2) and 3) below.

2) Perfluoropolymers are neither bioaccumulative nor biotoxic
Because perfluoropolymers are chemically and biologically persistent and inert, elution of these materials is known to be very limited (Olabisi et al., 2016). Complying with EU regulations on PFOA and PFOS, we have seen a drastic improvement in the production process of perfluoropolymers. According to our analysis performed by a third party testing laboratory, PFOA was not detected from PTFE and PFA (see “PTFE_PFA_ analysis.pdf” as attached in Section Ⅳ). Therefore, no hazardous materials are expected to be leaching from perfluoropolymers, which indicates that animals or plants will not be absorbing PFOA nor perfluoropolymers themselves. If there is nothing being absorbed, then bioaccumulation and biotoxicity do not occur (Henry et al., 2009; OECD, 1993; Beyer EC.1993; Korzeniowski, S. H, et al., 2023; FCJ, 2023, see "FCJ.pdf" as attached in Section IV).
Since perfluoropolymers are chemically and biologically persistent and inert, they have been used as material for implantable artificial organs such as pericardial patches and artificial blood vessels (Henry et al., 2009; Olabisi, 2015; Gangal & Brothers, 2000).
It is also documented in the literature that perfluoropolymers are substances with distinctly different properties from potentially toxic low molecular weight compounds such as PFOA and PFOS, which were the starting point for this proposed restriction (Henry et al., 2009; OECD 1993; Olabisi, 2019; FCJ, 2023, see "FCJ.pdf" as attached in Section IV).

3) Perfluoropolymers are irreplaceable materials that can contribute significantly to solving environmental concerns
Perfluoropolymers have unique and excellent properties including heat resistancy, oil/fluid resistancy, sliding capability, flame-retardancy, etc. that properties have made the substances essential to society. Heat-shrinkable and non-heatshrinkable tubing made of electron beam irradiated perfluoropolymers are widely used for electric insulation, protection, bundling and other purposes in automotive, aerospace, electronics, medical and other sectors. As for heat-shrinkable tubing, there are many choices of materials such as polyethylen, PVC, silicone, PET, etc. other than perfluoropolymers, but there is no alternatives for temperature rating of 150℃ or higher, or oil/fluid resistancy is needed use. Silicone is a potential alternative, however, it has many inferior points such as 1) mechanical strength is weak, 2) no transparency, 3) too thick wall compared with perfluoropolymers, 4) abrasion resistance is weak, 5) fluid resistance is weak, 6) shrink ratio up to 50%, which limit their use. PEEK is another candidate of alternatives, however, PEEK is so hard (stiff), which makes the tubing very difficult to use. Its shrink ratio is smaller than silicone, up to 20%, which also limit their use. In the end, there is no alternative for perfluoropolymers heat-shrinkable tubing.

Sincerely yours,

General Comments: 356mmz (hexafluoroisopropyl methyl ether, CAS. 13171-18-1) has intramolecular CF3 groups and is classified as a PFAS compound in Annex XV of the ECHA restriction proposal. This compound is categorized as HFE, hydrofluoroether, including Novec series, and is widely used as a precision cleaning agent and as a solvent for fluoropolymer resins. Due to its solid structure, the Novec series is known to have a relatively high GWP (e.g., Novec 7100, cas: 163702-07-6, GWP; 421, from IPCC 5th report annex 8. A (IPCC: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change)), a kind of environmental index that means sustainability in the environment. 356mmz has a low GWP value of 14 (from IPCC 5th report annex 8. A), making 356mmz a better choice among HFEs for these applications. Many attempts have been made to adopt HFOs, hydrofluoroolefins with low GWP values, as alternatives of HFEs or Novec to precision cleaners and solvents, but the most of HFOs and their intermediates have been included in the ECHA restriction proposal. Candidate alternatives to HFEs, including Novec, which are currently used in precision cleaners and solvents for fluoropolymer resin seem ordinary hydrocarbons or Halons as non-PFAS compounds. The former normal hydrocarbons are flammable, so a large investment in cleaning equipment would be required to maintain the same level of safety in use. The latter Halons generally have three drawbacks as precision cleaner solvents. First, most of the Halons have been well regulated due to their toxicity and environmental persistence. Secondly, the surface energy induced by the fluorine atoms in the molecule is much higher than that induced by the fluorine atoms in the molecule, making Halons unworthy of use as precision cleaner compounds where low surface energies are required. As same as precision cleaner usage, Halons can not dissolve fluoropolymer resins so that its range of usage as solvents is also limited. Third, compounds containing chlorine, bromine, and iodine atoms tend to swell plastic materials, so Halons cannot be used for precision cleaning of materials containing metal-plastic mixtures. Fortunately, 356mmz has been developed as a compound that is greatly able to mitigate these problematic properties. These means 356mmz has low level of environmental persistence, non-flammability, affinity to fluoropolymer resins and low surface energy with non-polymer attack character for the requirements in the application areas of cleaners in precision cleaning and solvents of fluoropolymer resin. In other words, it can be said that there is no alternative compound for 356mmz in these fields. 356mmz is also useful as a working fluid used in organic Rankine cycle systems or thermal management systems (e.g., heat pipes, vapor chambers), and is essential fluid as non-flammable medium that is available for the thermal control of electronic devices and energy devices or the renewable energy system.
The thermal management system is used for cooling the heat source generated by data centers and electric vehicles and so on. Common fluids such as water and alcohols are also used as working fluids. However, the applications such as data centers and electric vehicles are necessary to be avoided using water and flammable liquids. From the viewpoint of heat conversion efficiency and environmental sustainability, 356mmz is also essential and reasonable to exempt it from the proposed regulation. A closer look at the environmental aspects reveals that 356mmz is susceptible to UV oxidation and breaks down to trifluoroacetic acid (J. Phys. Chem. A 2005, 109, 4766-4771). Trifluoroacetic acid and its salts have been considered hazardous to human life due to its eco-accumulative potential, as explicitly described in ECHA Annex IV, but it has been advised by the German environmental authorities that it should not be (German Environment Agency, Reducing chemical input into water bodies, trifluoroacetate (TFA) as a persistent and mobile substance from many sources, 2021). Considering these points and the fact that there are no suitable alternatives in these areas, 356mmz should be left out of the range of ECHA proposal.

General Comments: A ban on PFAS would be a devastating blow for all industries in Europe as they are needed for all kind of industrial processes and not only in consumer products. Detailed information on these impacts will be given by specific trade bodies such as France Chimie.

For this consultation we specifically wish to bring to the attention of the RAC and SEAC the uses of PFAS in the production of pyrotechnical substances as well as pyrotechnical initiators which are essential solutions without any alternatives for safety and reliability reasons in both civilian and military applications.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The applications we will comment on are not identified in Table 9. They impact both the Pyrotechnics sector and the Defense sector. For the following questions we will consider two different impacted key elements of our activity (listed as A & B from here onwards), both of which have implications for both civilian and military uses:  A - Pyrotechnic compounds synthesis: PFAS binders are used as additives in the formulation of our RED-OX pyrotechnic compositions where they play a critical role for both the safety of manufacturing and handling of the said compositions.  These binders are key to obtain a safe granulometry that will avoid unsafe conditions such as thin deposits on surrounding equipment or clogging in the production process. They will also help guarantee a correct initiation of the pyrotechnical compound and thus safe usage.  B - Pyrotechnic high-performance components: both for civilian and military uses, components that are subject to harsh terrain conditions (extreme temperature, resistance to cuts and friction, etc.) and high stress situations (high speed propulsion, shockwaves from other explosions, etc.). These components may be cables sheaths, electronic components, surface treatments, etc. Their resistance to these conditions is key to the safety of the end users as misfires or malfunctions can gravely threaten the workers, the armed forces as well as bystanders.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: A – Pyrotechnic compounds synthesis:  During the manufacture phase the viton used is not transformed. Some of it will be integrated as part of the compound and the rest will be dissolved under solvent. In any case no waste or pollution is released into the water network or in any other way. During the use phase the pyrotechnic compound undergoes a combustion/detonation and no PFAS are released at this stage. The end-of-life phase corresponds with the use phase for most products. For the ones that are not used the only way to safely dispose of them will be to initiate them or burn them. None of the compounds or byproducts will be recycled and the slag will go to specific landfills. The previous statements are backed by information from the book “Metal-Fluorocarbon based Energetic Materials” by Ernst-Christian Koch.  B - Pyrotechnic high-performance components: The nature of these components can be extremely varied: specific coatings for cables, casings and shells; manufacturing of electronic components; foams; etc. Most of these elements are delivered to our factory as semi-finished products to be incorporated into our initiators. The producers of these components come from very different industries, and it is therefore not possible to obtain data on and cover such varied cases in detail in this consultation. The impacted sectors will respond to the consultation through their respective trade bodies.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The use phase of the pyrotechnic compounds as well as the end-of-life phase both correspond to a combustion / an incineration. No PFAS are released at this stage as the compound undergoes a combustion. The previous statements are backed by information from the book “Metal-Fluorocarbon based Energetic Materials” by Ernst-Christian Koch.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: For safety and/or secrecy reasons pyrotechnical compounds or components are not recyclable through the regular processes. Therefore, the impact on the recycling industry will remain null.

In any case the PFAS would be prohibited even for the very specific needs of our industry, there would be major to critical consequences as follows: - At short term, the development of our activities would stop as our company could not anymore manufacture and sell any initiators containing energetic substances made from PFAS materials, being here clarified that PFAS materials are in the formulation of energetic materials that are used in our most demanded initiators. - By short to mid term, the most critical consequence would be the loss of sovereignty and military independence of several nations of the European Community including but not limited to France. - By short to mid term, around 100 people would lose their job at Davey Bickford as our company would not be capable to honor the demand of our customers. - By short to mid term, our company would have to resiliate several important contracts with defense companies, the financial consequences of such terminations is not evaluated at this stage. - By mid to long term, the ending of defense and safety activities at Davey Bickford would also directly impact the principal activity of the company (detonators for the mining industry) due to losses of internal synergy between our different entities, losses of strategic skills and core competences, uncontrolled turnover of staff , etc…More than 500 people might lose their job.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: A blanket ban on all PFAS could have far reaching implications for the achievement of the European Union’s climate goals and the global objective of restricting global warming to below 1.5 degrees Celsius by 2050. Clean technologies and clean tech manufacturing are crucial for the realisation of these objectives. Many of these clean technologies are reliant on chemicals that are part of the PFAS family.

The restriction proposal is very broad. There’s no structuring or subdivision of more than 10,000 substances, which have very different intrinsic properties and no differentiation that considers the different risk profiles of the substances.

A one-size fits all approach to PFAS regulation could have catastrophic consequences for the development of the clean tech industry in Europe. The restriction should focus on substances that present an unacceptable risk in line with the REACH regulation, and for which alternatives may be available. The materials of most concern are fluorosurfactants, which are persistent and bioaccumulate. High molecular weight fluoropolymers such as membranes that are essential to the use of Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM) electrolysers are inert and non-toxic.

No alternative is foreseen to be able to substitute today or in the near future these highly specialised materials, central to the functioning of the hydrogen value chain. These PFAS are produced and used in a highly controlled industrial environment, where their emissions are negligible.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Our comments apply to industry; specifically, the clean hydrogen sector and clean tech manufacturing, in particular electrolysers and fuel cells.

6. Missing uses: A ban on fluoropolymers used in electrolysers would jeopardise the EU’s hydrogen strategy (reaching 10m tons of renewable h2 production in Europe by 2030) and contradict efforts to scale up net zero clean tech. An estimated €30 billion investments in electrolysers and fuel cell technology by the end of the decade is at risk and up to 200,000 direct jobs and 260,000 indirect jobs within 10 years in a market with a potential value of €820 billion employing 5.4 million jobs by the middle of the century.   In our electrolyser cell stacks and manufacturing processes, we use many fluorinated materials due to their unique properties (chemical and thermal resistance). Examples are:  • FEP – insulation for bolts and dielectrics • Viton – O-rings and gaskets • Tefzel (ETFE) – Seal gasket • Teflon (PTFE) – R2R MFG, legacy  • Nafion – Proton Conducting Membrane  • Kynar (PVDF) – MFG process tanks • Krytox – Tie rod lubricant  The most irreplicable PFAS in our cell stacks is the Nafion for which there is no viable alternative. A multi GW scale per year PEM market will need approximately 500 tons of nafion per year. Nafion membranes used in PEM electrolysers meet the OECDs criteria for polymers of low concern. PEM technology itself is perfectly suited to work hand in hand with renewable power generation due to its defining characteristics: dynamic response and ability to respond to fluctuations in power generation and varying load factors.   Hydrocarbon membranes have been cited as alternatives to nafion membranes but they are not feasible alternatives. Results of our testing hydrocarbon membranes revealed that H2 levels in the oxygen rapidly rose and resulted in cell failure around the 10 hour mark. This is typical of hydrocarbon membrane technology that exists today. Electrolysers need to run at least 5000-8000 hours a year to be economically viable. No hydrocarbon membranes are close to being stable enough, especially at elevated hydrogen generation pressures.  Claimed durability data is typically at atmospheric pressure. Given the state of the art today, widespread deployment of hydrocarbon membranes suitable for electrolysis at scale is at least 10 years out, probably closer to 15-20 unless a major breakthrough is made imminently.   (NB. Please see attached pdf for graph illustration of cell failure).

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: As explained in point 6, alternatives to the use of nafion in PEM electrolysers are at least 15-20 years out and depend on a major scientific breakthrough. The combat against climate change cannot wait 15-20 year for another alternative. Decarbonisation of hard to electrify sectors needs to start happening now, and we need renewable hydrogen for that. Without electrolyser, we cannot have renewable hydrogen.   The derogation periods for fuel cells and electrolysers are not fit for purpose. An exemption should be granted given the lack of viable alternatives on the horizon as well as the low risk factor of the chemicals used in the relevant processes, which remain highly controlled and away from the public, in industrial settings.

Content: Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: A broad restriction of PFAS in test and measurement equipment will have disproportionate negative impacts on the European economy and society.

The Test & Measurement Coalition supports the phase out of PFAS wherever this is practicable. In test and measurement equipment, this requires the availability of technically and economically viable alternatives which are to date not readily available. Finding alternatives is not guaranteed, especially for high performance applications, and substitution (if possible) is a time-consuming process due to the complexity of the affected products. This cannot be achieved in the proposed 18-month transition time.

The expected releases of PFAS from test and measurement equipment to the environment is expected to be negligible as PFAS containing components are predominantly used in closed systems (i.e., encapsulated within the equipment enclosure) and when they finally reach end-of-life they are processed by professional recyclers. Ultimately, test and measurement manufacturers are small consumers of PFAS materials as compared to other industries such as consumer goods, and their equipment have long expected lifecycle (up to 40 years).

The cost effectiveness ratio is thus calculated to be considerable, and the restriction for test and measurement sector highly disproportionate. The high socio-economic cost would only offset a minor contribution of the total PFAS input into the environment.

Therefore, the analysis reasonably justifies a time-unlimited derogation of PFAS chemicals used in industrial monitoring and control instruments and as analytical reference materials to avoid important shortages of these critical instruments. The identified instruments are essential to environmental monitoring, the good functioning of electronic communications networks, heavy industrial processes such as steel manufacturing, the testing of vehicles for compliance with emissions standards, and the monitoring of complex and critical systems of all types. This includes nearly all of the analytical equipment that is used to study and detect PFAS in the environment.

(For further details, see full-fledged Socio-Economic Analysis report attached.)

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Electronics and semiconductor (i.e., test and measurement instruments).

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Please refer to answers to Specific Information Requests No. 3, and to the Socio-Economic Analysis report attached for details on emissions in the end-of-life phase.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The market sectors addressed by industrial test and measurement equipment can in some cases require that the instruments can be maintained in use for decades. The nature of industrial test and measurement instrument applications demand highly accurate and reproducible results throughout their life. With a typical first use of ten years and a total life of up to 40 years, great care is taken during the design and qualification phases to ensure that the stringent performance and reliability requirements are met and must incorporate design for serviceability. This provides a continuous supply chain of equipment for refurbishment with extended life through resale providing great economic and environmental benefit. Whilst the instruments are designed for long-term reliability, failures do occur during such an extended period of use requiring ability to service and replace parts. After market withdrawal, equipment is normally supported for a minimum of five years. Moreover, refurbishing and reselling on the secondary market are crucial in this sector and often account for 4–5% of producer turnover for test and measurement manufacturers.  Due to the costs, reliability, and unique applications of T&M equipment, many customers do not dispose of the equipment, but instead keep it for use at a later date or place it on the secondary market. As a result, test and measurement equipment typically enters the waste stream many decades after it is placed on the EU market. Industrial test and measurement equipment’s contribution to the Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment stream is very small (0.12% by weight of EU WEEE) with industrial WEEE being collected through B2B systems. Consequently, the environmental impact of industrial test and measurement products is negligible compared to the total electronics sector.  As regards PFAS and its restriction, a ban will have no impact on PFAS materials being released into the environment in the short term since they would not end up in the waste stream. These instruments are sold B2B for professional and industrial use only. Thus, equipment that finally reaches end of life will be appropriately processed by professional recyclers who are obligated to have suitable controls to avoid any environmental releases.  Ultimately, according to the academic literature, the process of by-products generated during waste treatment of articles that contain fluoropolymers via incineration is not well understood and no clear evidence of PFAS emission has been found (Lohmann et al., 2020). Furthermore, fluoropolymers at their end of life when incinerated under representative European municipal incinerators conditions do not generate any measurable levels of PFAS emissions and therefore pose no risk to human health and the environment.  (For further details, see full-fledged Socio-Economic Analysis report attached.)

5. Proposed derogations: Test and measurement manufacturers are small consumers of PFAS materials as compared to consumer industries. Overall, on the basis of the information gathered in the context of a survey covering more than 70% of the whole EEA test and measurement equipment market, less than 8,700 kg of PFAS enter the EEA market every year within test & measurement instruments.  Negligible releases of PFAS to the environment are likely during either T&M equipment production or use phases of the concerned products. Under normal conditions of equipment use, PFAS are not released through the use of the product because PFAS containing components/parts are predominately encapsulated within the equipment enclosure and will neither be touched nor released to the environment. Furthermore, due to the precision nature of these high-performance instruments, their internal components are handled infrequently and with care.  TMC member companies have only indicated a minor risk for substances to be released to the environment during the manufacture of the components. These are not produced by TMC members. Thus, data are not available, however the estimate is expected to be bounded by the total use of the substance (i.e., release to the environment is expected to be less than the mass of substance incorporated into the components entering the EEA market every year). In this way, the estimate would be a maximum of 8,700 kg/year.  Ultimately, as mentioned above, T&M products have an expected lifetime of 10+ years, with many products being used for up to 40 years. Therefore, a ban will have no impact on PFAS materials being released into the environment in the short term since they would not end up in the waste stream. These instruments are sold B2B for professional and industrial use only. Thus, equipment that finally reaches end of life will be appropriately processed by professional recyclers who are obligated to have suitable controls to avoid any environmental releases.  (For further details, see full-fledged Socio-Economic Analysis report attached.)

6. Missing uses: Based on available documentation, the main properties offered by PFAS chemicals in T&M instruments include: low dielectric constant, electrical insulation, high thermal stability, chemical resistance, lubrication, moisture resistance, surface tension reduction, anti-sticking properties, flame retardancy and optical clarity.  Thanks to the wide variety of properties offered by PFAS, these materials are used in a variety of safety, electrical performance and mechanical applications within electronics, including semiconductor and cables uses. PFAS are used ubiquitously across the entire TMC member companies’ portfolios (mainly in closed systems). Approximately 86% of the T&M equipment are expected to be impacted by a restriction.  The use of PFAS materials within test and measurement equipment is still being investigated as TMC member companies are currently approaching their corresponding supply chain, which consists of several thousands of vendors from whom these companies source components and assemblies containing PFAS, and an untold number of sub-suppliers who are responsible for including the PFAS into their products, and are gathering the data as to where PFAS are used intentionally (i.e., it was called out in a drawing or purchase specification).  To date, TMC member companies believe that fluoropolymers are the most common use of PFAS in T&M products. TMC member companies are not aware of intentional use of non-fluoropolymer PFAS, even though, based on literature review, this is a possibility.  Due to the unique characteristics of PFAS materials, and based on the current state of the art, there are no known alternatives that are currently available for most of the PFAS uses above. To date, the supply chain for the T&M coalition members (suppliers and producers PFAS based components) have not been able to identify technically suitable and economically viable alternatives to PFAS. As relatively low (downstream) consumers for these parts, and generally not direct customers for the actual suppliers of PFAS based commodities, T&M manufacturers have little influence over their complex and extended supply chain and the identification and development of PFAS free alternatives.  Implementing a re-design requires long timelines and high costs to convert the entire T&M portfolios. As downstream users for PFAS based commodities, substitution timelines are highly dependent on the ability of the supply chain to offer suitable alternatives. Timelines are difficult to predict and highly subject to uncertainty. The whole process of identifying suitable alternatives could take decades.  From the general availability of compliant commodities, it is anticipated that a minimum of 10 to 15 years is needed for re-designing the T&M portfolio. This extends the timing for substitution to > 25 years (minimum) to complete transition activities (i.e., implementing the substitution of PFAS based equipment) in order to retain industrial monitoring and control instruments on the EEA market and globally for products manufactured within the EEA. The change would involve assembling alternative components into a test product, and evaluating the new product for functionality, hardware and software performance, reliability, EMC, safety, manufacturability, and a wide range of additional technical requirements. These timelines are in line with the input provided by the Test & Measurement Coalition to the various consultations related to the RoHS Directive.  A potential broad restriction would have disproportionate socio-economic implications on the EEA T&M equipment sector: the total impact of a PFAS restriction at the level of test and measurement industrial equipment manufacturers is monetized in the range of 4.3 billion EUR to 6.2 billion EUR (conservative estimates in net losses), consisting of social impacts from unemployment in the EEA, substitution costs and economic impacts (EBIT loss) for T&M manufacturers in the EEA.  The estimates reported in this socio-economic analysis should be considered as a minimum (lower boundary) of the expected impacts.  (For further details, see full-fledged Socio-Economic Analysis report attached.)

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: The main properties offered by PFAS chemicals in T&M instruments include:  Low dielectric constant: PFAS-containing materials can have an extremely low dielectric absorption, which means they do not store as much electric charge per unit of volume. This property makes them useful in several electronic components used in low level/sensitive measurement instruments where low dielectric loss is important. This is critical for ensuring measurement accuracy of signals, where losses could result in signal amplitudes falling below the noise floor. Moreover, PFAS offer a stable dielectric constant. Consequently, capacitors utilizing PFAS, for example, are very time and temperature stable; cables with a PFAS dielectric have signal loss, phase and amplitude stability characteristics that are unmatched by other materials.  Electrical insulation: PFAS-containing materials can provide excellent electrical insulation, which makes them useful in applications such as electrical wires and cables, circuit boards, and electronic coatings. For example, PTFE is used in safety applications due to its high insulation strength and Comparative Tracking Index (CTI). This is required in high voltage applications, where the properties are required for cable and connector insulation and physical barriers that enable T&M manufacturers to meet the requirements set out in the Low Voltage Directive (LVD) (2014/35/EU) and harmonised standards (i.e., safety standard EN 61010-1:2010+A1:2019 ‘Safety requirements for electrical equipment for measurement, control, and laboratory use General requirements’).  High thermal stability: PFAS are highly stable at high temperatures, which makes them useful in electronic components that generate heat, such as integrated circuits and power electronics.  Chemical resistance: PFAS are highly resistant to a wide range of chemicals, including acids, bases, and solvents, which makes them useful in electronic components that are exposed to harsh environmental conditions, or require protection from chemical exposure.  Lubrication: PFAS-containing lubricants can reduce friction and wear in moving parts of electronic devices, improving their performance and longevity.   Moisture resistance. PFAS-containing coatings and films can provide low absorption of water, which is often present in PCAs wash during manufacturing, as well as moisture resistance to electronic devices, protecting them from corrosion and other forms of damage.   Surface tension reduction: PFAS-containing substances can reduce the surface tension of liquids, which makes them useful in cleaning process of semiconductor components allowing the liquid to penetrate and remove contaminants more effectively.  Anti-sticking properties: PFAS-containing materials can prevent the adhesion of contaminants and other materials to electronic surfaces, which makes them useful in applications such as semiconductors and electronic packaging.  Flame retardancy: Some PFAS-containing materials have flame retardant properties, which makes them useful in electronic devices and components that are exposed to sources of ignition.  Optical clarity: Some PFAS-containing materials have excellent optical clarity, which makes them useful in applications such as displays, lenses, and optical fibres.  Thanks to this wide variety of properties offered by these materials, PFAS are used in a variety of safety, electrical performance, and mechanical applications within electronics, including semiconductor and cables production applications.   The use of PFAS materials within test and measurement equipment is still being investigated as TMC member companies are currently approaching their corresponding supply chain (i.e., several thousands of vendors from whom these companies source components and assemblies containing PFAS – and an untold number of sub-suppliers who are responsible for including the PFAS into their products) and are gathering the data as to where PFAS are used intentionally (i.e., it was called out in a drawing or purchase specification).  To date, TMC member companies believe that fluoropolymers are the most common use of PFAS in T&M products. TMC member companies are not aware of intentional use of non-fluoropolymer PFAS, even though, based on literature review, this is a possibility.  For instance, in the case of PTFE, the most widespread PFAS material in T&M equipment, the are no known alternatives that have the same electrical and mechanical properties. Other potential substitutions are being managed by T&M manufacturers’ supply chain and the chemical manufacturers who are supporting the supply chain.  There are some applications in which fluoropolymers can be substituted by alternate polymers, but not without technical trade-offs. For example, for some applications, there might be potential alternatives, such as Polyphenylene sulphide (PPS), Polyamide-imide (PAI), polyetherimide (PEI). These substances are not PFAS yet exhibit some of the mechanical properties of PTFE. Nevertheless, these alternatives could work for a limited number of applications within T&M equipment, while most of the uses, especially the high-performance applications, would likely not be covered.  In some applications, non-fluoropolymer wire insulation may be used as an insulator (not as a dielectric) if the thickness was increased, but this would impact its flexibility and thus reliability. Since fluoropolymers are generally more expensive than other polymers, fluoropolymers would not be used unless there was a functional/technical advantage.  Without access to PFAS, it will not be possible to produce equipment reliant upon its dielectric properties in the production of high-frequency, high-speed, signal transmission applications. There is no commercial availability of new PFAS-free commodities that currently are known to be incorporated into T&M equipment.  In general, it must be noted that industrial test and measurement equipment manufacturers are positioned downstream in the context of a global and complex supply chain that involves a large number of players distributed globally. Particularly because of the complex high-mix low-volume nature of their portfolios, it means that they have little influence on the upstream article manufacturer to identify a technically viable alternative. Thus, T&M manufacturers will need to work with each component manufacturer to investigate if an alternative exists, and then test and validate any of these alternatives to assess product performance and long-term reliability.  According to some key suppliers of PFAS containing commodities contacted by T&M manufacturers, the proposed restriction risks to significantly undermine their ability to keep supplying these items. They highlighted, once again, that there is no known alternative material that will provide the same performance and so substitution is currently impossible.  To the best of the knowledge of T&M manufacturers, where substitution is practicable, large suppliers are already working to provide alternative items that are PFAS-free. Nevertheless, small (or unaware) suppliers are unable to influence the material and chemical manufacturers to find unique solutions for their niche intermediate products, requiring T&M manufacturers to search for and set-up alternative vendors and supply chains.  Provided alternatives are available, substitution will take years. There are a number of activities that would need to be performed by manufacturers to substitute PFAS in T&M equipment. These activities include:    Identifying all PFAS in T&M products and supply chain through supplier querying and testing  Researching and testing the functional feasibility of alternatives  Re-designing all T&M products in companies’ portfolios  Re-certifying for safety, EMC, and Environmental Compliance  Re-qualifying for reliability, and Manufacturability  Updating manufacturing processes before implementing design changes  These substitution activities cannot be done all at once but need to be staged, and given the breadth of the portfolios, can take decades to fully adopt and commercialize. From the general availability of compliant commodities, it is anticipated that between 10 to 15 years are needed for re-designing (i.e., implementing the substitution of PFAS based equipment) and completing transition activities and to retain most products on the EEA market.  These are the timelines once an alternative has been identified. The time to find alternatives is unpredictable and will vary greatly. As mentioned above, these timelines are highly dependent on the ability of chemical manufacturers to design and supply safer alternatives with equivalent performances and upon the article supply chain to adopt, requalify, re-certify their manufacturing of their raw materials to the T&M manufacturers. As downstream users, TMC member companies will depend heavily on the capabilities of their suppliers to offer suitable alternatives, in the context of a complex and global supply chain.  Based on previous experiences under RoHS, the importance of PFAS, and the magnitude of the substitution, the whole process of finding a suitable alternative is expected to take decades. Overall, the total timeframe for a replacement of PFAS in monitoring and control instruments could easily take more than 25 years.  These timelines are in line with the input provided by the Test & Measurement Coalition to the various consultations related to the RoHS Directive, which is a major piece of legislation impacting product design of electrical and electronic equipment. Since 2005, the Test & Measurement Coalition has been actively engaged with the European Commission and its consultants, providing data on the time required to substitute the substances restricted under RoHS as well as the exemptions needed. The TMC has authored the initial application for renewal of Annex III for category 9 industrial and has submitted in January 2023 ten exemption renewal applications, providing substantial amount of data, including socio-economic analysis.  Meanwhile, companies have indicated that the PFAS restriction would have significant impacts on their business and customers. Given the broader definition of PFAS, it is estimated that the vast majority of the overall company portfolios in the EEA depends on PFAS-containing components.  Thanks to the wide variety of properties offered by PFAS, these materials are used in a variety of safety, electrical performance and mechanical applications within electronics, including semiconductor and cables uses. As such, PFAS are used ubiquitously across the entire TMC member companies’ portfolios (mainly in closed systems). Approximately 86% of the T&M equipment are expected to be impacted by a restriction.  Accordingly, a potential broad restriction would have disproportionate socio-economic implications on the EEA T&M equipment sector: the total impact of a PFAS restriction at the level of test and measurement industrial equipment manufacturers is monetized in the range of 4.3 billion EUR to 6.2 billion EUR (conservative estimates in net losses), consisting of social impacts from unemployment in the EEA, substitution costs and economic impacts (EBIT loss) for T&M manufacturers in the EEA.  (For further details and examples, see full-fledged Socio-Economic Analysis report attached.)

8. Other identified uses: Please refer to answers to Specific Information Requests No. 6 and No. 7.

10. Analytical methods: The current PFAS restriction proposal could jeopardize its own implementability and enforceability, as described in Annex E.4 of the Annex XV report, because the tools for measuring the presence and quantity of PFAS rely themselves on PFAS. Indeed, Liquid Chromatography (LC) and Gas Chromatography (GC) instruments are highly effective tools for measuring the presence and quantity of PFAS within drinking water.  (For a case example of the essential use of PFAS within analytical chemistry equipment, see full-fledged Socio-Economic Analysis report attached.)

Combined Comments:
General Comments: A coating film formed from a coating agent for a printed wiring board using a fluororesin is extremely excellent in battery electrolyte resistance and acid resistance. As an alternative substance, a coating agent obtained by dissolving a silicone resin, an acrylic resin, a urethane resin, an olefin resin, or the like in a hydrocarbon-based organic solvent can be considered. However, these alternative materials are not highly acid resistant and cannot protect the copper traces on the board when the printed wiring board is exposed to volcanic gases or battery electrolyte. It corrodes copper wiring and cannot be used as a substitute for fluorine compounds.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Conformal coating for printed wired board.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: When incinerated or melted for metal recovery, the fluororesin film decomposes into HF.

5. Proposed derogations: Judging from the results so far, it is estimated to be about 100 tons/year.

6. Missing uses: Fluoropolymer coating is resistant to battery electrolyte. Applying it to the printed wiring board can prevent fire accidents caused by battery electrolyte leakage. Lithium battery fire accidents are occurring frequently. This accident can be prevented with fluorine coating. Preventing fires is an important point from the viewpoint of respecting human life, and the economic effect is immeasurable.

General Comments: A comprehensive PFAS ban should be avoided, as the interactions between key transformation technologies and the EU chemicals regulation REACH reveal major risks for the success of the energy transition and for Germany and Europe as a business location.

Based on the facts mentioned in our attachment, we advocate the provision of unlimited exemptions for commercial and industrial use for all of the below-mentioned applications to achieve the climate protection and decarbonization goals:
• PEM electrolysers
• Process engineering reactors for synthetic and bio fuel production
• Large/industrial heat pumps
• Industrial compressors and expanders
• Turbocharger
• Two and four-stroke engines for shipping and power plants (also emergency power)

This must apply to both new construction and the supply of spare parts. The exceptions provided for in the present restriction proposal, e.g. for the energy sector, must be supplemented and expanded accordingly.

Content: Request for exemption
Org. name: GHC Gerling, Holz & Co. Handels GmbH
Combined Comments:
General Comments: A derogation for the use of fluoropolymers for materials in contact with chemicals, (in the chemical industry) should be included with 13.5 years EiF. For more information, see section 6. Missing uses – Analysis of alternatives and socio-economic analysis.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Chemical industry.

6. Missing uses: The chemical industry needs a derogation for seals, O-rings, valves, fitments, bearing coatings, hose products, tank liners, gaskets, membranes, diaphragm etc. made of fluoropolymers.   Chemical reactions are based on the reactivity of the substances involved. However, the desired reactivity often has the side effect that, firstly, it is not specific and the substance can also react with the equipment used and, secondly, the substance has hazardous properties and must be controlled with appropriate risk reduction measures. Fluoropolymers have proven to be resistant to most chemicals and enable the safe and secure operation of equipment, facilities and plants (plants). Their key functionalities are, for example, their high resistance to chemicals, corrosion resistance, resistance to acidic and alkaline substances, gas-tightness, non-conductive properties and temperature resistance. Fluoropolymers are indispensable for the operation of most modern plants.   Many plant permits demand the use of fluoropolymers in certain parts of the plant. At a first glance, a restriction on fluoropolymers would only affect the licensing and construction of new plants. However, as the restriction would also affect spare and replacement parts, it would also affect existing plants. As a consequence, applications for changes to existing permits would be required. This would lead to an unreasonable additional workload for both, industry and the authorities.   Substitution is often not possible. But even when it is possible, it is often undesirable. The chlor-alkali process is a good example of this. Modern plants use membranes made of PTFE. The PFAS restriction would force those to revert to old process using asbestos-diaphragm or mercury cells. Both, asbestos and mercury, are highly toxic substances. Thus, the restriction would lead to regrettable substitutions.   In addition to plant permits, product approvals and authorisations are also affected. While time- unlimited derogations for active substances in biocidal products, plant protection products and human and veterinary medicinal products are proposed, those derogations do not apply for co-formulants and packaging, which are also part of the product approvals and authorisations. Here, too, applications for amendments to existing product approvals and authorisations would be required. This would also lead to an unreasonable additional workload for both, industry and the authorities.  The restriction report concludes that a restriction of fluoropolymers in seals, O rings and gaskets in the transport sector is not feasible. The same is true for applications in the chemical industry. It should also be mentioned that fluoropolymers in seals, O-rings, gaskets, tubing and pipes, expansion joints, valves and fitments etc. are already considered for derogation for 6.a. food contact materials for the purpose of industrial and professional food and feed production (6.5 years EiF). However, it must be noted that the derogation period of 6.5 years EiF would not be feasible for the chemical industry.  In conclusion, a derogation for the use of fluoropolymers for materials in contact with chemicals, (in the chemical industry) should be included with 13.5 years EiF.

General Comments: A future of medical technology without per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) is a future in which clinical interventions are set back decades. A future in which the well-being of the patient is no longer the main focus. A future of anachronistic patient care.

Although the - still - existing state of the art is proven to be safe, there is a need for political will to ensure that fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers in particular can be used without restrictions in areas where they offer an unquestionable benefit to society. In medical technology, for the well-being of patients, but also in other socioeconomically relevant areas of industry.

The attached position statement from MedicalMountains GmbH provides information on the background and effects of the current PFAS restriction process proposed by the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA). The process is connected to the “Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability Towards a Toxic-Free Environment” published in October 2020. The aim is to provide better protection for people and the environment while strengthening the competitiveness of industry within the European Union. We are firmly committed to these objectives.
More than that, we see it as our duty to intervene with all the means at our disposal when the protection of people, patients and Europe as a center of industry is at risk. That is precisely what we fear will happen if the proposal to restrict PFASs takes effect in its current form.

-- A nuanced, risk-based approach is required --
It is absolutely right to impose strict regulations or even total bans on the use of unsafe low-molecular-weight PFASs, and some have already been initiated. However, it is equally important to take a nuanced view of this highly complex issue. A “Broad Restriction Proposal” does not differentiate between PFASs that are actually hazardous and those that are not. The individual risk assessment and appraisal of “use cases” has been dropped. Rather than banning tens of thousands of substances in one go, what is required is a nuanced, risk-based approach. Fluoropolymers play only a minor role in emissions and, moreover, are disposed of safely.
In this context, it is important to know that: Medical technology is already one of the most strictly regulated sectors, with elaborate approval and control procedures. This includes a requirement to prove the biocompatibility of any medical device that comes into contact with the body. In the case of fluoropolymers, this is required when they are used as materials (such as in tubes) or as coatings (such as in catheters or guide wires). There have been a number of tests showing that they pose no danger to humans. The safety of the products has been confirmed by years of use and large quantities of clinical data, for example from the use of PFAS-containing implants. Finally, Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices (Medical Device Regulation, MDR) sets a very high bar for CMR (carcinogenic, mutagenic or reprotoxic) substances.

-- A general ban has a substantial impact on crucial areas --
PFASs are not all carcinogenic, despite frequent reports to the contrary. Fluoropolymers are chemically and physically very different from unsafe PFASs. They meet the criteria for “polymers of low concern”. This understanding is already widely accepted in places such as Australia and the United Kingdom. Fluoropolymers “of low concern,” which present no potential risk to humans or the environment and are essential for medical technology, should therefore be immediately excluded from the restriction process.
PFASs combine a unique biocompatibility, low friction, thermal and chemical stability and dielectric strength, all properties that are essential in safe medical devices for patients. There are currently no known alternative materials that could combine all the properties of fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers. This means that, even with the longest possible derogation in terms of time, a general PFAS ban would have a substantial impact on crucial areas.

-- Without fluoropolymers, EU’s well-meant efforts would have been to nothing --
Even if a derogation is discussed for certain industries, it will create new problems: The production and availability of high-performance polymers in Europe must also remain guaranteed. Otherwise, we run the risk of creating new dependences, particularly on Asian manufacturers. Some companies have already shifted their production to non-EU countries. This goes against the EU’s current efforts to keep supply chains for future technologies in Europe. Fluoropolymers are essential for medical technology as well as chip production and green hydrogen production. Without them, the targets set out in the European Chips Act and the “Green Deal” would be unachievable and all the efforts made would have been for nothing. We risk losing Europe’s position as a high-tech location and make European resilience impossible.

-- If a nuanced, pragmatic approach is adopted, the various legitimate interests can be reconciled --
In view of the expected impacts, as a society we now need to have a discussion: What are we prepared to give up, and what do we want to gain from doing so? Medical devices will not improve if we get rid of all PFASs. We need nuanced consideration of harmless fluoropolymers in the areas where they are truly important.
The pros and cons need to be weighed up in the public discourse.

If a nuanced, pragmatic approach is adopted, the various legitimate interests can be reconciled: protection of the environment and health, protection of patients, innovation and the leading industries of Europe.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: A number of PFAS are currently on the REACH candidate list of substances of very high concern. With the proposed restriction on the manufacture, placing on the market and use of per-and polyfluoroalkyl (PFAS) substances, all PFAS substances would be banned. This general approach has the potential to be a showstopper for the development of the hydrogen sector. Indeed, PFAS substances are used across hydrogen technologies and equipment, from renewable hydrogen production to hydrogen transport, distribution and storage as well as in various applications. PFASs are used both in the core and secondary components of hydrogen technologies:
• PFAS are used in the membrane of electrolysers and fuel cells from proton exchange membrane (PEM) technologies.
• PFAS are used in sealing materials, gaskets, coating, valves, filtration and lining components throughout the entire hydrogen value chain as well as in other membrane chemistries.

Whether it is a core part or a secondary component, the chemicals used belong to a subcategory of PFAS called fluoropolymers. These chemicals have the required characteristics to operate in chemically and mechanically harsh environments of hydrogen devices whilst ensuring hydrogen impermeability and oxygen permeability.

Having considered existing literature, we believe that the restriction proposal’s approach should reconsider grouping fluoropolymers with other PFAS types. Fluoropolymers should instead be considered as “polymers of low concern” as they meet the criteria defined by the OECD for this category. They verifiably do not pose a risk to human health or the environment as they are not water soluble, toxic and bioavailable. Furthermore, their use in hydrogen technologies is tightly controlled and contacts with consumers or workers is very limited.

Furthermore, the current lack of alternatives to substitute these chemicals from hydrogen technologies adds to the need for an exemption. Currently no promising alternatives to replace fluoropolymers in the membrane of PEM fuel cells and electrolysers has been found. The insufficient properties of hydrocarbon membranes in terms of durability and mechanical behaviour have been documented in literature and projects. For gaskets and sealing materials, no products are commercially available yet. Their development is expected to take 15 to 20 years including technology validation of the options being explored. Distinguishing the treatment of both uses could be problematic considering that the sectoral spillovers are substantial: the ban of fluoropolymers in one area of the value chain can still jeopardise others. Therefore, we believe that fluoropolymers should be all together exempted from the PFAS ban.

It should be considered that the incineration and landfilling of hydrogen technologies containing PFAS is not the most likely case for the end of life of those technologies. Recycling paths are promising and economically incentivised due to the value of the materials to recover (i.e. iridium, platinum, etc.). Both literature and ongoing projects have demonstrated this. Instead of a ban on fluoropolymers, we believe that regulatory actions should be introduced.
Such actions would require the implementation of the best practices observed in industry in order to limit the potential PFAS emissions across the life stages of hydrogen technologies. This is of particular importance for the end of life of materials for which requirements for the sorting and recycling of materials could be proposed. Take-back obligations by manufacturers or distributors of systems as well as the obligation to constantly increase the recycled content of raw materials could be an approach to consider.

Finally, considering that alternatives with a sufficient commercial lifetime are not available or not commercially viable for membranes. The continuation and expansion of both national and European funded research and development activities such as the Clean Hydrogen JU are key to elaborate solutions. Research has still a major role to play to phase out PFAS in its entirety. This is why, further research projects and funding are required to find alternative materials. Topics for such research should explore:
• Development and expansion of the analysis of the PFAS substances in use, including the precursors, process aids, intermediate products and by-products used in terms of detectability within the required detection limits and assessment of their risk potential;
• Clarity about the type and quantity of possible entry paths as well as their limitation and best possible avoidance;
• Sorting of PFAS materials and composites;
• Recycling PFAS materials and composites.

In order to find all the references and data supporting these statements, we refer to the answer to the consultation submitted by our industry partner, Hydrogen Europe, submitted on 25 September 2023, that we support and endorse.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Org. name: European Council of Optometry and Optics
Combined Comments:
General Comments: A rigid gas permeable (RGP) contact lens is a medical device intended to be worn directly against the cornea of the eye to correct vision conditions. RGPs are used by eye care professionals to correct patients’ eye sight conditions such as farsightedness, nearsightedness, presbyopia, astigmatism, keratoconus and corneal ectasia.

RGPs contain PFAS substances, and so would be subject to a PFAS ban. In RPGP lenses, these substances provide ‘non-stick’ qualities, but also make an essential contribution to oxygen permeability, biocompatibility, comfort, wettability, rigidity, lathability, durability, scratch resistance and shape stability. Their introduction into the polymer matrix results in a safer and more efficacious lens wearing experience.

Data from the Philip Morgan periodic survey suggests that worldwide use of RGP lenses is 12% but that it is somewhat higher in Europe, varying between countries from 5 % to 32 %, and that this percentage is growing. (https://www.clspectrum.com/issues/2023/january-2023/international-contact-lens-prescribing-in-2022)

The key concern is that for certain patients and certain conditions RGP contact lenses are the only form of treatment available. On average, respondents to the EuromContact/ECOO survey considered that they would no longer be able to treat 52% of their current RGP patients if RGP contact lenses were no longer available. In particular irregular corneas, keratoconus, high astigmatism, post-surgery patients and myopic with Ortho-K patients (both adults and children) would suffer from the unavailability of RGP contact lenses.

Furthermore, respondents said that on average 29% of patients would only be able to receive an alternative treatment that was less effective. This means that 81% of current RGP patients would either no longer be treated or could only be treated with less effective alternatives. This would translate into a significantly reduced visual acuity for those patients and reduced quality of life. There is also the risk that these patients would continue to use old or outdated medical devices or seek alternative solutions resulting in deteriorating eye health.

We would also highlight that a derogation is proposed for intraocular lenses (IOLs), recognising the severity of the eye conditions that these implants are used to treat, and therefore the importance of such lenses to patients, and the fact that there is no alternative to the use of PFAS in such lenses. RGP contact lenses are used to treat eye conditions of comparable severity and therefore the same considerations and derogation should apply to RGP contact lenses.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Rigid gas permeable (RGP) contact lenses (proposed derogation for reconsideration)

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: As mentioned in section III, there are currently no alternative treatments to RGPs available for a number of eye conditions, in particular: irregular corneas, keratoconus, high astigmatism, post-surgery patients and myopic with Ortho-K patients (both adults and children).   The recent survey of contact lens specialists referred to above confirms that the vast majority of RGP patients (81%) could be no longer treated or would be treated with less effective alternatives.   Soft contact lenses or spectacles are not an alternative for all RGP wearers. This is because, unlike soft lenses, rigid lenses do not mold to the shape of the cornea and in this way they provide better visual acuity in persons with an abnormal corneal shape. In about 10% of lens wearers – an estimated 3.2 million people in the EU - rigid lenses are preferred mainly because of this so-called astigmatism that cannot be as effectively corrected with soft lenses. Indeed, some irregularities of the corneal surface cannot be compensated at all with either spectacles or with soft lenses. For patients with these conditions, rigid gas permeable lenses are the only solution to improve their visual acuity and to avoid them becoming visually impaired. Without RGP lenses, these patients would have to live with deteriorating eye health, significantly reduced visual acuity and their quality of life would be reduced significantly.   From an economic and employment point of view, this restriction could result in an increase in the number of people who become economically inactive due to a visual impairment, and dependent on social security benefits and potentially the social care system. There would also be economic and employment effects on contact lens specialists across Europe, many of who are SMEs. Based on data from the ECOO Blue Book 2020, our members account for 150,000 opticians and optometrists across Europe. At a conservative estimate, at least one third of these will be contact lens specialists, meaning that at least 50,000 eye care professionals would be impacted by this change. If PFAS restriction measures result in RGP lenses no longer being available and there are no other treatment options available to patients, then it is to be expected that they would experience negative impacts such as loss of turnover or even loss of employment.   The amount of additional emissions arising from this derogation would be a very small fraction (estimated 1 t/y in the restriction proposal). There is currently no alternative to using PFAS in RGPs. Fluorinated monomers are used in the preparation of rigid contact lens polymers due to the unique combination of beneficial properties that they confer, including oxygen permeability, deposit resistance, hardness and chemical inertness.  The 3 PFAS monomers which are incorporated into rigid contact lens polymers, HFPM, TFEM and BHI, can be classified as ultra-short chain PFAS. There are today no non-fluorinated alternatives that can meet the same characteristics for the optimisation of lenses in terms of quality, performance, comfort, and the safety of patients.  ECOO therefore considers that the balance between the significant impact for patients and the relatively low quantity of PFAS emission justifies a derogation from the PFAS ban for rigid gas permeable contact lenses.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Baseline Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: A total ban on fluoropolymers is not proportionate. The concerns of persistence raised in the restriction proposal can be appropriately managed through the implementation of responsible manufacturing and EoL risk-management practices.
Although initiated under the ECHA Chemical Strategy for Sustainability (CSS)*, the proposal is – and can only be – adopted under the current REACH rules, which must be demonstrated to be met. Europump believes that there is not enough scientific data and evidence which would justify the complete ban of PFAS.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Generally, it is difficult to sort the pumps into categories and the pre-defined sectors are not fitting well. Pump industry had already problems in the previous consultations to provide information/data, as required categories were missing and the pre-defined ones were only partly fitting.  Pumps containing PFAS containing components are being used in a multitude of sectors mentioned in the Annex XV report, but also beyond. The majority of PFAS chemicals in pumps belong to the group of fluoropolymers. They are used in pump applications where resistance to chemicals, high temperatures, and wear are important. Typical examples of fluoropolymers containing pump components are:  1. Pump seals: Fluoropolymer materials such as PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) or PFA (perfluoroalkoxy) are used as pump seal components. These materials offer excellent chemical and temperature resistance and low friction, which helps to reduce energy consumption, extends the service life of the pump and also assures a higher tightness level along the service.   2. Product lubricated bearings: Fluoropolymer materials like PTFE or mixtures of fluoropolymers with other materials such as metals, ceramics and other polymers are used as product lubricated bearings, as they offer excellent chemical resistance and low friction, which helps to reduce wear and extend the life of the pump.  3. Pump linings: Fluoropolymer linings are used in pumps to protect the internal components from corrosive chemicals or other aggressive fluids. These linings can be made from materials such as PTFE, PFA, FEP (fluorinated ethylene propylene), or PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride).  4. Diaphragms: Fluoropolymer diaphragms are commonly used in pumps that handle aggressive chemicals or other fluids that can attack traditional elastomer diaphragms. PTFE and FEP diaphragms are often used in applications that require high purity or resistance to aggressive chemicals.  5. Coatings: Fluoropolymer coatings are applied to pump components such as impellers, casings, and fasteners to provide protection against chemical attack, corrosion, or abrasion. These coatings can, for example, be made from materials such as PFA (perfluoroalkoxy) or ETFE (ethylene tetrafluoroethylene).  6. Cable sheaths: Fluoropolymers are applied to high voltage cable sheaths of submersible pumps because of their resistance to UV radiation, the excellent insulating properties and the resistance to moisture and water uptake.  7. Gaskets: Fluoroelastomers, also known as FKM or FFKM, are preferred for gaskets, because they offer high resistance to chemicals, such as hydrocarbons, acids and bases, and can withstand temperatures up to 200°C. Furthermore, they provide a low gas permeability, which makes them mandatory for applications where either the fluid being pumped must be kept free from contamination, or where the release of the pumped fluid to the environment must be avoided in any case. In addition to their chemical and thermal resistance, fluoroelastomers also offer good compression set resistance and excellent aging characteristics. These properties make them a reliable and long-lasting choice for use in industrial pumps, especially for applications where safety is crucial.  Overall, the excellent chemical resistance and durability of fluoropolymers make them essential for many pump applications in: 1. Chemical processing, where highly aggressive chemicals are present, because they can withstand the corrosive effects of these chemicals, considering also higher temperature behavior. 2. Oil and gas production, because of their resistance to hydrocarbons, high temperatures, and high pressures encountered in drilling and production operations. 3. Energy production because of their high temperature stability even in the presence of air borne oxygen. 4. Pharmaceutical applications in conventional as well as biotechnological processes, because they are inert and non-reactive and can be sterilized.  5. Food and beverage processing applications, because of their non-sticking properties and chemically inertness, which is relevant for the regular cleaning and disinfection processes, and that the quality of the contacting food and beverage is not negatively changed. 6.
