Combined Comments:
General Comments: A wide variety of PFAS-applied products on the market are closely related to the European Green Deal.
We believe that this proposal to regulate PFAS will have significant implications for the European Green Deal, which is targeted to be achieved by 2050.
In REACH, persistence is subject to risk assessment only when combined with bioaccumulation and in some cases with toxicity. However, this restriction proposal is based on persistence alone, which is not considered a hazard endpoint, as if all PFASs are hazardous. In addition, while exposure assessments should be made for each use by creating exposure scenarios, all PFASs are grouped together, so the assessment for each use is insufficient and does not indicate the existence of unacceptable risks as required by Article 68. Therefore, we believe that this proposal does not meet the requirements for a restriction proposal as required by REACH, and it is not appropriate to discuss a restriction.
In addition to the exclusion of fully degradable PFAS, we think risk of PFAS with potential to degrade (soil remediation potential) would not be “unacceptable risk” and the risk of each substance should be quantitatively assessed and discussed.
The current PFAS regulation will have a tremendous impact on the chemical industry, which provides materials for a wide variety of applications and products, and will affect not only the chemical industry but also the global supply chain.
Since PFAS-applied products cover a wide range, there is a high possibility of a situation that cannot be handled by testing laboratories that carry out tests to prove that PFAS is not contained in products.
In addition, for some PFAS, even analysis methods have not been established.
Furthermore, these tests require a great deal of time and new economic burdens, and many businesses are forced to give up their businesses, which may result in a large number of unemployed people.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Foam blowing agents

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Fluorinated gases are highly safe substances in terms of toxicity and flammability, and are used in many applications due to their efficiency and cost. In particular, on-site foam polyurethane spray insulation exhibits excellent insulation performance, and fluorinated gas is indispensable for preventing fires during spraying work. Refference 1 shows that about 2% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) is produced by the reaction of HFO-1233zd(E) with OH radicals in atmosphere. Reference 2 also reports that the evidence is clear and irrefutable that TFA occurs naturally in large quantities in the environment.Furthermore, according to references3 and 4, TFA which are of concern in the proposed regulations, actually pose a low risk of toxicity to living organisms and humans, even in the reports of the German and Norwegian environmental agencies that submitted this proposed regulation. In addition, according to Reference 5, HFO-1233zd(E) is negative in the OECD TG471 Ames test and negative in the OECD TG473 chromosome aberration test, so it is expected to have no mutagenicity.  The LC50 (rat) in the inhalation test was 120,000 ppm, and the NOAEC (No Observed Adverse Effect Concentration) in the OECD TG413 90-day repeated inhalation test was 4,000 ppm. The working environment exposure limit (WEEL) of 800 ppm (8 hours, TWA) was determined, and toxicity to humans is expected to be low. Further, Reference 6 reported that “UV-driven photodegradation of some of the compounds controlled by the Montreal Protocol (e.g., hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs))produce contaminants such as trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), but concentrations of these breakdown products in the environment are currently deemed too low to be a concern for human health or the environment."  Therefore, we request that fluorinated gas including HFO-1233zd(E) for this application be exempted from the application or given as a special exemption without a time limit. Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: A-Gas questions the added value this proposal will bring since it ignores the existing regulatory framework. In particular for refrigerants, the industry is already extensively regulated via legislation on F-gas, WEEE & eco-design which manages the production, use and lifecycle management of these products and the sectors / appliances within which they are used. The F-gas legislation specifically foresees already an ambitious phasedown which coincides with the development of other lower global warming technologies. Rather than imposing further restrictions, it makes more sense from a sustainability point of view and proper legal governance to focus on enforcing the current regulatory framework and implement an actual EPR system for refrigerants.
Combined with the circularity of reclaimed refrigerants, the opportunity is there to minimise the environmental and human exposure to PFAS containing refrigerants at all stages of their life-cycle. Based on the available data, there is an increase in reclaimed refrigerants (see reference to EEA report) which will only increase under the forthcoming F-Gas Regulation. Rather than imposing restrictions  via new legislation, which will negatively impact the overall circularity  of refrigerants, the logical way forward is the enforcement of the current regulatory framework in order to ensure a compliant end-of-life management of refrigerants, thereby simultaneously closing the loop on potential emissions of GHG and PFAS.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: - Fluorinated gases (maintenance of appliances & clean fire suppressing agents) - Transport (MAC systems)

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The intention of this question, and of the proposal in general, starts from the wrong consideration i.e. that all PFAS variations are identical in technical properties, uses, releases in the environment etc. which would justify one legislation regardless of the type of PFAS and regardless of the products within which they are used.  The approach of grouping chemicals is not only questionable from a legal point of view but also from a scientific perspective. In particular, the study ‘Grouping of PFAS for human health risk assessment: Findings from an independent panel of experts ’ concludes that “[…] “all PFAS” should not be grouped together, persistence alone is not sufficient for grouping PFAS for the purposes of assessing human health risk, that subgroups are appropriate, and that the nature and definition of the subgroups can only be defined on a situation-dependent and case-by-case manner." [source: J.K. Anderson e.a., Grouping of PFAS for human health risk assessment: Findings from an independent panel of experts, Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology, Volume 134, 2022, Elsevier. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0273230022001131?via%3Dihub]    An additional concern which will arise due to the massive scope of this proposal is the inability of the national authorities to do a proper enforcement of the legislation due to insufficient resources. Especially for the refrigerants sector, it can lead to an increase in illegal trade, which in turn, will result in an increase of non-compliant end-of-life management of refrigerants. This will have a counter effect to the initial goal of the proposal. It is therefore appropriate and proportionate to introduce a different approach which foresees a case-by-case assessment which has to evaluate whether additional legislation is required. This assessment should take into account the impact of PFAS in line with its specific properties and the specificities of the product within which it is used and cannot be seen separately from the existing EU policy framework. In particular for the refrigerants sector, a well-defined policy framework is already in place through the F-Gas Regulation, WEEE Directive and the Eco-design Directive.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: A distinction has to be made between the end-of-life management of the equipment in which refrigerants are used and the end-of-life management of the refrigerant itself. The latter does not coincide with the former. A-GAS approaches refrigerants from a life-cycle management point of view which delays significantly the moment PFAS containing refrigerants reach their actual end-of-life stage, and in some cases reduces the need for virgin production in the first place. .  Under the proposed restriction, the recycling/reclamation of refrigerants would collapse in the EU as the economic case supporting the entire waste value chain (recovery, reclamation & resale) would cease to exist. If recovered refrigerants can no longer be reclaimed and re-sold then the incentive to recover them from end-of-life equipment will disappear and the refrigerants will become a liability for the operator. Raising costs for disposal will likely result in higher emissions through illegal venting of refrigerants. As a general principle, the most optimal way for preventing PFAS emissions of refrigerants is to fully recover them from equipment and then make these go through a reclamation or destruction process. Such a reclamation process consist of:  - removing the contaminants from the used gases: mainly oil, moisture, non-condensable; - blend correction: to ensure that the mix of individual components is in line with the AHRI 700 requirements;  - fractional distillation  Reclaimed refrigerant is therefore optimal for re-use in appliances and is a direct translation of the circular economy principles to the refrigerants sector. A study conducted by Daikin showed also that “…the carbon footprint of reclaimed refrigerant reuse lies between 72% and 90% lower compared to that of virgin refrigerant production, depending on the refrigerant”. [Source: Daikin, ‘Assessing the carbon footprint of reclaimed refrigerant for reuse and virgin refrigerant production’. https://www.daikin.eu/content/dam/internet-denv/catalogues_brochures/commercial/226%20-%20Assessing%20the%20carbon%20footprint%20of%20refrigerants.pdf]  In general, reclaimed refrigerants are already common practice in the industry and, based on the EEA  report, continues to rise. [Source: EEA, ‘Fluorinated greenhouse gases 2021’. https://www.eea.europa.eu/publications/fluorinated-greenhouse-gases-2021]  We recognise that there is a large potential to increase it even more especially through the further regulated phasedown foreseen in the new F-gas Regulation which will create an incentive for increasing reclaimed refrigerants. Any prohibition of F-gas will undermine this incentive and will impact the entire recovery process of refrigerants. In the end, a counterproductive effect will be created leading to higher emissions.     Destruction is generally considered the best option in the following cases: • Not economically viable to attempt further processing e.g. contains contaminants that are difficult to remove e.g. complex mixtures of refrigerants containing hydrocarbons, azeotropes or high content of legacy refrigerants like CFCs • Where there is no permitted use for the refrigerant in the market e.g. CFCs, HCFCs  • Where the client/waste producer mandates destruction • Usually the reclaimer will make the decision around destruction   In addition to the end-of-life management, it is also important to note that overall the emissions during the use-phase are decreasing which is expected to continue with the next F-Gas Regulation and which is driven by a better control of leakage. This is concluded in EPEE’s HFC Outlook model and is also reflected in EPEE’s contribution to this consultation:   Finally, we ask ECHA and the five countries having submitted the proposal to review the emissions data on the basis of which they are proposing the restrictions for refrigerants. The data in the EPEE HFC Outlook model shows significantly lower emission values. Also, the EEA report states that for 2019, F-Gases made up 2.3% of total EU greenhouse gas emissions which is much lower than the values used in the proposal. Since the consequences of the proposal are far-reaching for the refrigerants sectors, it is essential from a proper legal governance perspective, that any restriction is based on correct data.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: From a sustainability point of view, it is essential that recycled and reclaimed F-gases, even if deemed to  contain PFAS, can still be used for servicing and maintenance of equipment already placed on the market before the entry into force date of the PFAS restriction as long as they are compliant with Standard AHRI 700(2019) Specifications for Refrigerants which allows impurities up to 0,5% by weight (5000 ppm) for both virgin and recycled refrigerants. This is crucial to ensure that all equipment already in use can remain to be operational since PFAS-free alternatives are either not compatible with the equipment or are subject to a prohibition under the EU F-gas Regulation.  The threshold proposed by the five countries is set at very low values of which it is not even certain that proved methods are available to correctly detect these low impurities within refrigerants.

5. Proposed derogations: Derogation HVACR (Annex E – 2.8.3 (iv)) The maintenance and refilling of existing HVACR equipment should be subject to an unlimited derogation period since the proposed time-specific derogation does not reflect the actual lifetime of these products. Any time limitation for maintenance and refilling would counter the principles set out by the European Commission in its 2020 Circular Economy Action Plan which focuses on waste prevention and the right to repair with the aim of postponing as long as possible the actual waste phase: The proposed derogation period of 12 years (+18 months) will result in a significant amount of installed and still well-functioning HVACR products being scrapped which is in no way compatible with any sustainability principles. In addition to the environmental impact, consumers will be confronted by the financial burden of removing and replacing products which did not yet reach their end-of-life. The time-unlimited derogation can be linked to a review process to evaluate the market development.  Clean fire suppressing agents (Annex E – 2.8.3 (xii)) Clean fire suppressing agents should have a time-unlimited derogation. A-Gas supports the position of HARC (Halon Alternatives Research Corporation) which states that “There is no indication or expectation within the fire protection community that new non-PFAS alternatives will suddenly be discovered. There have been strong economic and regulatory incentives to develop such products for many years. Millions of euros and extensive time has been spent in identifying, testing, and ruling out candidate alternatives before those now in use were commercialized. As all known candidate clean agent chemical groups have already been researched, discovering alternatives that are zero ODP, low GWP, and non-PFAS is highly unlikely”  Derogation MAC (Annex E – 2.10.3 (i)) The derogation of five years (+ 18 months) for refrigerants in mobile air conditioning (MAC)-systems in combustion engine vehicles should also include the MAC systems in electric vehicles. The proposal does not mention anything on the servicing and maintenance of already installed MAC systems in vehicles (both combustion and electric vehicles). In line with the thinking which applies for the maintenance and servicing of HVACR, a similar unlimited derogation will therefore be needed to reflect the lifetime of vehicles

"A) Usefulness and Importance of Fluororesin Products
Our company supplies lubrication systems for machinery, including molding machines, machine tools, and other industrial machinery. These lubrication systems consist of pumps, valves, and pipes that dispense lubricants. Many of the components used to assemble the lubrication system employ tapered threads. To fill the slight gaps when connecting these tapered threads, prevent liquid leakage, and avoid damage to the machinery due to inadequate lubrication, we use a liquid sealant or sealing tape containing PTFE, a type of PFAS.

Performance Criteria, Functions, and Benefits of Fluororesins
To prevent liquid leakage when connecting tapered threads, we use liquid sealants or sealing tape. These products contain the PFAS, PTFE. PTFE is used as a liquid sealant or sealing tape, and it is resistant to high and low temperatures. It is also resistant to a wide variety of fluids (liquid and gas), such as general chemical agents and solvents, and can be used under harsh conditions ranging from vacuum to high pressure. Its non-sticking and low-friction properties make it suitable for moving applications, and it can be used as a sealant for extended periods.

Importance of Fluororesins to Meet Customer Application Requirements
Sealants or sealing tapes containing liquid PFAS (PTFE) are commonly used in the piping connections of lubrication systems, which are installed in molding machines, machine tools, and other industrial machinery produced by our customers. Leakage from these connections would result in insufficient lubrication reaching the necessary components. Additionally, since the machinery is used under harsh conditions, the heat and cold resistance and chemical resistance of PTFE make it an ideal sealing agent for preventing leaks.

B) Existence of Non-PFAS Alternatives that are Technically and Economically Viable
At present, no useful information regarding alternative coating agents is available. Even if alternative products were to emerge in the future, several years or more may be required for practical application, considering the need for verification tests and so forth.

C) Impact and Concerns for the Social Economy
We supply lubrication systems to molding machines, machine tools, and other industrial machinery used by our customers. If lubricating oil leaks occur and lead to machine damage, the disruption in production could have a significant impact on various markets (medical, automotive, industrial equipment, household appliances), causing extensive damage and loss." "Attachment XV Limitation Report (Table 9) includes "PTFE thread sealing tape". However, there is no item related to liquid sealant. The liquid sealant also contains PTFE and has the same function as "PTFE thread sealing tape". Even if alternative products were to appear in the future, it may take several years or even longer to be concerned about the need for practical implementation without conducting verification tests, etc." 4563 "At present, there is no useful information on alternative coating agents. Even if alternative products emerge in the future, it may take several years or longer to worry that practical application may not be possible without conducting verification tests. The purpose of the verification tests is to ensure that the liquid sealing agent or sealing tape used in the piping joints of lubrication systems connected to molding machines, machine tools, and other industrial machines produced by the customers are not prone to liquid leakage from the threaded parts. Leakage from the joints means that the required amount of lubricant does not reach the necessary parts. In addition, the machines are sometimes used under harsh conditions, and the characteristics of fluororesin (PTFE) are excellent in heat and cold resistance, and it is resistant to various fluids (liquids and gases) such as general chemical substances and solvents, and it is suitable as a leakage prevention sealing agent that can be used under harsh conditions from vacuum to high pressure. Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Org. name: The Japan Federation of Medical Devices Associations (JFMDA)
Combined Comments:
General Comments: About this submission:
JFMDA submitted a first submission on September 5th.
This document JFMDA’s second and final submission with detailed information on application for PFAS uses in medical devices.
We added Appendix 1 to Chapter 6, which lists the uses of PFAS in medical devices.

General Comments:  The following is the same as first submission.

We support the gradual strengthening of PFAS regulation within the framework of REACH.  On the other hand, we have strong concerns about the legitimacy and socioeconomic impact of uniformly regulating PFAS by lumping them all together as "common hazards and risks“. PFAS are lumped together on the basis of their "persistent" nature, however, the chemical structure and physical, chemical and biological properties of each sub-group of PFAS differ greatly, and their toxicity profiles are not identical. In addition, the risk to human health, the environment, and the socio-economy varies greatly depending on the application. We request to establish appropriate grace measures for essential use, and also request to regulate on a priority basis PFAS subgroups with greater hazards or PFAS application posing higher environmental risks as well.

For example, fluoropolymers are lumped together with PFCAs and are included in the proposed restriction as posing a high risk to humans and the environment, even though they meet the criteria for a "polymer of low concern" as defined by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). Fluoropolymers are the only materials that combine excellent properties such as biocompatibility, persistence (stability), chemical resistance, repellency from water and oil , low-friction, heat resistance, electric insulation, flame resistance and durability, and are known as essential materials that support social infrastructure functions such as medical devices and their progress. And more, even though disposal is controlled or manageable in medical applications, they are regulated in the same way as in consumer applications with much higher potential risk of discharge into rivers and sewers.

We believe that it is beneficial to European society to establish effective regulations for PFAS after appropriate assessment of health and environmental risks, socioeconomic impacts, risks of exposure to humans throughout the product life cycle, and feasibility of countermeasures for low concern fluoropolymers and fluoroelastmers. In other words, by prioritizing the regulation of PFAS subgroups, including Arrowheads substances, for which there is evidence or strong suspicion of hazards, and applications with severe environmental and health risks, it will be possible to effectively and efficiently reduce risks to human health and the environment with minimal socioeconomic impact.

As an organization supplying medical devices to Europe, we request the following in order to contribute to human health and safety and to socio-economic development in Europe, and to ensure that healthcare professionals and European people do not lose an opportunity to access to the best medical care.
1. Enact effective PFAS regulations in a phased manner based on appropriate risk and socioeconomic assessments
2. Exempt fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers from the proposed PFAS regulation
3. Devices subject to Medical Device Regulation 2017/745 (MDR) and In-Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation 2017/746 (IVDR) shall be exempted as Essential Use
4. Exemptions shall be provided for repair parts.
5. Provide an "extension clause" that allows for an extension of the grace period.
6. Provide exemptions or maximum grace periods for medical device applications for which additional information is provided

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: 1) Annex XV restriction report (Figure 1). Main PFAS subgroups: all of fluoropolymers (FPs)  2) Sectors: E.2.9. Medical devices, ANNEX A.3.10. Uses listed in these sections are limited.  For example, medical electronics is included in electronics (A.3.12), but the viewpoints to be evaluated differ between medical use and general use. Our comments cover all medical devices covered by the MDR/IVDR, including medical electronics etc.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Invasive medical devices such as catheters and syringes are properly disposed of by each medical institution as infectious waste. Disposal of medical devices used in medical institutions must be properly managed according to the regulations of each country. Unlike consumer products such as food wrappings and clothing, they are not, in principle, discharged into rivers or soil. PFAS from medical devices are not released into the environment when properly incinerated.  EEE is controlled by WEEE Directive in the end of life. Waste EEE is properly discarded according to the WEEE Directive.   The EU has legislations requiring proper collection and disposal for all products. End of life shall be controlled by sector-specific legislations, such as, WEEE Directive.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: PFAS such as PTFE can be decomposed by incineration to prevent PFAS emissions into the environment. Fluorine can also be recovered. ( K Aleksandrov et al. Chemosphere, Vol 226, July 2019, P898 )  Further development of such incineration and recovery technologies will benefit all mankind.  The EU has legislations requiring proper collection and disposal for all products, but adding an obligation to do something based on whether or not they contain PFAS will undoubtedly bring up management costs. Rather, it is more efficient to designate PFAS as SVHC, utilize the scheme that provides information to waste disposal companies, and technically standardize beneficial treatment methods when PFAS is contained.  Waste EEE is controlled by WEEE Directive, and the MDR and IVDR, which are medical device regulations, contain provisions on disposal.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Spare parts are necessary to guarantee the expected lifetime (more than 20 years) of Medical device. Especially since Medical device requires high performance and high reliability, we would like to emphasize that the same spare parts are required throughout the life of the product as when it was first evaluated. Without spare parts, waste minimization according to the principles of “Right to repair” and “Repair as produced” cannot be achieved.

5. Proposed derogations: Please find Section 3 of Appendix 1.

6. Missing uses: Please find Section 1 of Appendix 1.   The alternatives of the uses listed and discussed in Appendix are unavailable. And the technical unavailability is also explained in the Appendix.  If the alternatives are become available in the future, a long grace period is required until PFAS become restricted The medical devices are made in small numbers, are produced for long periods without modification or changes, have to be reliable and need long term test for reliability. The supply chains are very long and take time to eliminated restricted substances from the supply chain. If the medical devices mentioned above cannot use PFAS anymore and PFASs are to be substituted, the long grace period is required in order to test the product to comply with the safety requirements defined with ISO10993-1, IEC and other safety standards, and obtain the re-certificates according to the requirements.  As mentioned above, the design change of an existing product to a PFAS-free component would require a considerable number of years of evaluation, and if a sufficient grace period were not set, there would be a shortage of medical devices in the European region. In addition, medical device manufacturers will be forced to concentrate human, financial, and other resources on design changes, which will affect the technological development of medical devices. The launch of medical devices with the latest technology in Europe will be delayed, resulting in lost opportunities for European citizens to receive the latest technological medical care. Since the amount of PFAS used in medical equipment, excluding fluorinated gases, is small and disposal is properly managed, the need to regulate PFAS content in medical equipment in the same manner as in other sectors is extremely low. As a result of such considerations at the time of the RoHS directive, the regulation for medical devices was applied eight years later than for general electrical and electronic products. Since the number of substances covered by this PFAS is an order of magnitude greater than the initial six substances of RoHS, a grace period of 13.5 years or more is considered necessary. Since regulating other sectors first will lead to a switch to PFAS-free in medical devices for general-purpose components even without regulating medical devices, it would be more socio-economically beneficial for medical devices to focus resources on new development and prioritize the introduction of medical devices with the latest technology.  We ask that you consider excluding medical devices from the scope of this proposed regulation and adding them to the scope again at an appropriate time when other sectors have made some progress in becoming PFAS-free.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Please find Section 2 of Appendix 1.   The alternatives of the uses listed and discussed in Appendix are unavailable. And the technical unavailability is also explained in the Appendix.  The derogations for these uses are essential.  Futhermore, as mentioned in 6., we propose not only to limit these uses but also to exclude medical devices from the scope this proposed regulation.

8. Other identified uses: Please find the attachment.  The alternatives of the uses listed and discussed in Appendix are unavailable. And the technical unavailability is also explained in the Appendix.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Access VetMed represents the industry of generic and added value medicines in Europe. We welcome the proposed time unlimited derogation for the specific use of PFAS as medicinal active ingredients (APIs) under EU Regulations. The proposed derogation is important to allow for the supply of veterinary medicines as many active substances contain structural moieties CF3- or -CF2-, which are irreplaceable because of their unique properties.
However, the supply continuity of veterinary medicines in the EAA will be severely compromised if derogations covering their development and manufacturing are not included. Not addressing PFAS materials in the entire -production chain would result in a ban of e.g. certain manufacturing equipment parts, inevitable filters and several primary packaging materials, many precursors, intermediate compounds, and processing aids, which are all necessary to provide essential medications to society and for which no alternatives are available to ensure adequate and sufficient quality and thus safety and efficacy of the medicines.
The ability to develop and manufacture veterinary medicines in the EEA depends on such derogations. Development and manufacturing of APIs classified as PFAS or non-PFAS APIs and involved veterinary medicines will be severely impacted in the EU / EEA if the restriction without further derogations is implemented, which will compromise the supply and availability of veterinary medicines in the EEA and create severe and unacceptable dependence on production outside the EEA.
We therefore request consideration for additional exemptions or changes to already proposed derogations, addressing the PFAS materials in the entire development and manufacturing chain of pharmaceutical ingredients classified as PFAS and non-PFAS APIs and veterinary medicines, including:
• An unlimited derogation for packaging material of veterinary medicinal products as in Annex XV, Proposed restriction - Annex XVII entry PFASs (Restriction Option 2), Column 2: 6.l applicable to all fluoropolymers with approval rather than PCTFE only, and not limited by time.
• Additional derogations for identified specific PFAS uses in the pharmaceutical supply chain. These include starting materials, intermediates, reagents, solvents, catalysts and single or multiple use equipment necessary for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals or related processes such as quality control or diagnostic testing.
Further information is specified in sections 6 (Missing Uses) and 7 (Potential derogations marked for reconsideration).

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: NEW proposal for a Sector: medicinal products.  This sector is missing from Table 9 of the Annex XV restriction report. Only the use as active ingredient (Annex XV, Table 6), and PCTFE-based packaging materials (until 13.5 years after EIF; Annex XV, Proposed restriction - Annex XVII entry PFASs (Restriction Option 2), Column 2) are covered for potential derogations in the draft restriction document.  All (sub-)uses are missing for this sector, and are listed in section 6 (Missing Uses).

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Waste management of the medicinal products is completed in accordance with national requirements after conclusion of the marketing authorization procedure. Disposal of any unused veterinary medicinal product or waste materials derived thereof is performed in accordance with national law and requirements.

6. General Comments: According to Article 67 (1) of the REACH Regulation, restriction “shall not apply to the manufacture, placing on the market or use of a substance in scientific research and development.” Thus, we expect for the upcoming PFAS restriction that the use of non-polymeric PFAS as substance or mixtures in R&D applications will be exempted and that analytical standards will fall under a time-unlimited derogation. Nevertheless, this exemption may not be valid for fluoropolymers or PFAS substances that are part of analytical equipment, so we will provide information on the beneficials and irreplaceability of fluoropolymers for the laboratory use within the following sections.
In analytical laboratories, a variety of PFAS chemicals as well as instruments and equipment that consist of or contain fluoropolymers is used. As part of many analytical equipment, fluoropolymers like PTFE, PFA etc. play a central role in analytical lab applications and are used in various processes where chemical, thermal, and electrical stability is required. Replacing these equipment parts with fluorine-free alternatives would disable a vast number of analyses like HPLC, GC-MS, impurity profiling of materials in low concentrations levels especially in case of ultra-trace analyses for semiconductor applications (i.e. analytical methods enabling detection and quantification of analytes in ppm and ppb and even ppt scale), Karl-Fischer titration etc. The main reason is that none of the currently available fluorine-free materials have equal chemical stability towards chemicals which are mandatory for sample preparation or during analysis (e.g. organic solvents, concentrated acids like fluoric acid). Consequently, such routine analysis would not be conducted within EU laboratories anymore and thus quality measurements required for manufacturing standards and specifications would not be available after entry into force of the EU PFAS restriction if no derogation for PFAS used in analytical laboratories is granted.

Thus, due to the inalienability of PTFE and similar fluoropolymers in analytical laboratory equipment an unlimited derogation for using fluoropolymers in analytical lab equipment is needed. Without such derogation, most of the analytical methods would not be technically feasible anymore, leading to lack of numerous quality measurements and analytical methods employed at manufacturing sites and R&D laboratories.
Consequently, without an exemption for PFAS polymers in analytical and lab equipment, analysis of many chemicals, chemical R&D activities as well as chemical manufacturing would be largely jeopardized in the EU.

In the following sections the use of PFAS materials in laboratory equipment is demonstrated, with practical examples illustrated and evidence for necessity to use these materials is given by information on compatibility of PFAS polymers compared to alternative materials. Information on the waste handling is given as well.

Additional comments will be submitted separately by Merck to provide also regarding other PFAS uses a better basis for an adequate regulation of PFAS materials.
Merck is additionally actively contributing to industry association comments as e.g. from VCI, Cefic, SEMI, SIA and EFPIA – some comments are already submitted, others will be submitted later in course of the consultation phase.

General Comments: Across the globe, climate change is increasingly affecting our lives and the
environment. There is an urgent need for system-wide transformation to limit the emission of greenhouse gases. Currently, many polluting hard-to-abate industries such as steel, fertilizer, and refineries rely on chemical processes heavily dependent on fossil fuels. A report of the European Parliament notes that emission-free hydrogen produced by electrolyzers using renewable electricity is key to decarbonizing hard-to-abate sectors like these.

As the hydrogen industry seeks to play a major role in limiting global warming, systemic support is essential to unlock its potential. Currently, there is an absence of alternative technology solutions to materials containing PFAS. These materials are critical to clean hydrogen electrolyzers. A ban on PFAS could significantly affect the growth of clean hydrogen production and delay the decarbonization of key industries.

We strongly recommend -

1. That the ECHA make an exemption for the electrolyzer industry through an exclusion or maximum derogation. This is because of the lack of current
alternative technology solutions to PFAS.

2. That the ECHA not place a PFAS restriction on the electrolyzer industry. This is because of the absence of analytical methods to measure PFAS compounds.

3. That the ECHA dedicate resources to develop methods to measure PFAS
compounds because of the complications associated with such methods.

4. That the ECHA give the electrolyzer industry maximum time to work on
alternative technology solutions to PFAS because development of new
technologies takes significant time and effort.

The clean hydrogen industry is being built by people who are very passionate about the environment and sustainable energy resources. Development of new technologies to replace the materials critical to electrolyzer technology, however, could take more than 10 years. A PFAS restriction that affects current technology development could have a significant negative impact and hamper the growth of the clean hydrogen industry.

General Comments: actnano supports the European Union efforts to safeguard human and environmental health through the comprehensive ban on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). The lack of regulation for these hazardous chemicals presents health risks on the global scale.

The electronics industry is one the major contributors to PFAS usage, as outlined in Table 1 of the Annex XV Restriction Report. A subset of that PFAS-usage in the industry is coatings for the environmental protection of electronics and electronic devices. Environmental protection is necessary to ensure the longevity and dependability of devices by preventing corrosion and also helps reduce electronic waste. Coatings are utilized in various areas to protect against corrosion, including on printed circuit board assemblies (PCBAs).

There are PFAS-free electronic coatings available on the market today that are readily used in consumer electronics, automotive, industrial and white goods markets. actnano manufactures such PFAS-replacements, which provide comparable environmental protection (please refer to the attached confidential comparison of actnano products vs competitor PFAS-containing coatings). Our products have undergone rigorous testing by our customers, meeting the highest performance standards and regulatory compliance, and demonstrating the ability to replace PFAS without compromising protection. Consequently, there are no performance barriers to eliminating PFAS-containing coatings from the majority of devices. It should be noted that further study is required to assess the replacement of PFAS-containing coatings in medical and aerospace applications, but this testing is currently underway.

While these products are available now, the time it takes to transition to replacement technology depends on the thorough performance testing conducted by product manufacturers to meet their stringent operational standards. If no modifications are necessary for the electronic devices themselves, it is feasible to test and implement alternative coatings during the 18 month transition period.

The coatings market and actnano are poised to replace PFAS in the supply chain, therefore we advocate for the planned 18 month transition period, with limited derogations for high-reliability applications such as medical and aerospace.

Sectors and (sub-)uses: As all PFAS and their residues from the identified sectors and sub(uses) might end up in the water cycle the feedback is provided by the drinking water operators and applies to all sectors listed in table 9.   PFAS are a large group of very persistent and mobile chemicals that tend to accumulate in the environment. Especially there are findings in water resources that are used for drinking water abstraction.    So far, there are a couple of PFAS hotspots in Germany. In the case of Rastatt (Baden-Württemberg)  PFAS-contaminated paper sludge was spread for soil amelioration. All drinking water suppliers in the region are affected and have to treat raw water intensively to ensure that the drinking water they supply complies with the regulatory framework for drinking water quality regarding PFAS levels. As another consequence drinking water wells had to be closed due to the PFAS pollution. In the case of Rastatt PFAS polluted about 1188 ha of soil. The affected groundwater body measures 58 km2 with a total volume of 180 million m3. The costs for drinking water treatment are estimated to be more than 11 million Euros and it remains unclear who will bear the costs for the remediation of the environmental damage as the polluter went bankrupt.   Another well-known case is at the Düsseldorf Airport, where firefighting foams containing PFAS infiltrated the soil and groundwater during a major fire.   Recent research studies showed the problem of seaspray contaminating islands with PFAS. Air deposition is in this context as well a problem, that leads to pollution of for e.g. at the “Nordfriesischen Inseln”.   The PFAS Emissions source vary from point source to diffuse pollution. That means PFAS are found ubiquitous.   A joint journalistic research (NDR, WDR and SZ) in 2023 have found more than 1500 locations contaminated with PFAS for Germany, including more than 300 hotspots. Together with 15 European partner media, the reporters in the "Forever Pollution Project" have located more than 17,000 places with relevant PFAS pollution throughout Europe, including a good 2,000 hotspots with significant risks to human health. The German collected data, measured PFAS pollution comes from the Fraunhofer Institute's SumPFAS project in cooperation with the German Federal Environment Agency (UBA) and from the evaluation of parliamentary inquiries from eight German states and at the federal level.

The consultancy assignment, entitled "Support for developing and drafting technical guidelines on PFAS substances and the recast Drinking Water Directive", aims to assist the Commission and Member States in evaluating and selecting the best available analytical methods for the new parameters "sum of PFAS" and "total PFAS". The study on available analytical methods includes specific (target) and non-specific (non-target) approaches. General Comments: Aero-Sense® NV is Belgium based company, specialized in manufacturing dedicated chemicals with their application in the aeronautical industry worldwide. (www.aero-sense.com)
Our broad range of specialized products contains de-icing & anti-icing chemicals, cabin & exterior cleaning products, disinfectants and aerosolized aircraft disinsection products.

Aero-Sense Aircraft Insecticides assure an essential insect control for all passenger airlines, freight cargo, military and private aircraft required to be treated to prevent the international spread of vector-borne through air travel.
All of these aircraft disinsection products products have been designed and formulated taken into account the requirements of several international recommendations, standards and regulations including:
- EU Biocidal Products Regulation (EU BPR – 528/2012/EC) – Union Authorisation EU-0024297-0000
- EU F-Gases Regulation (517/2014/EC)
- World Health Organization recommendations on Aircraft Disinsection
- IATA regulations – Medical Manual
- ICAO Annex 9 – Facilitation
- Aircraft Material Specification AMS 1450 ‘Disinsectant (Insecticide), Aircraft
- Boeing Specification Support Standard BSS7434 ‘Chemical Compatibility of Cleaning Products and Interior Parts/materials of Commercial Aircraft’

Our company has invested a lot of time and resources in meeting the European F-Gas regulation by replacing its HFC portfolio with HFO technology, resulting in a better performing product with higher added-value to the end user and its environment.
The aerosolized product formulation contains a well-chosen liquified propellant to fulfil some important requirements. The product formulation must be non-flammable and to obtain a maximum rate of efficacy, a space treatment with small droplets that remain airborne for a long time is required.

Before 2018 the non-flammable and liquified propellant that was mainly used for the product of technical aerosols was HFC 134 (Global Warmth Potential value (GWP) higher than 1400).
On 1/1/2018 a restriction on placing on the EU market described in Annex III of the F-Gases Regulation (517/2014/EC) entered into force: a prohibition to place on the EU market technical aerosols based on HFC’s with a GWP value of 150 or more, except when required to meet national safety standards or when used for medical applications.
As a consequence we were forced to adapt our product formulations of the aircraft insecticides and to perform research on an alternative liquified propellant that fulfils the required technical requirements, is non-flammable and has a GWP lower than 150.
We managed to find an alternative liquefied propellant which is currently used for production of the aircraft insecticide aerosols: Solstice 1234ze or HFO 1234ze manufactured by the company Honeywell.
At this moment it is the sole available and alternative liquified propellant that can be used to manufacture technical aerosols for placing on the EU market in accordance with the F-Gases regulation. Moreover, worldwide, there is no alternative available to be used as a non-flammable liquified propellant.
HFO 1234ze has a GWP lower than 1 (and an ODP of 0). It is a liquified propellant that has specific and distinctive characteristics that allow the mixtures that we manufacture to pass the flammability tests established in the EU-standards, acting as propellant and co-solvent in their formulation.
Currently there is no alternative liquified propellant available to manufacture EU compliant technical aerosols for applications where non-flammability and high technical performance or spray characteristics are extremely important. Replacing the liquified propellant by an alternative, non-flammable propellant is also not feasible due to the final product requirements (spraying characteristics, droplet size).

Compressed gases
Non-flammable pressurized propellants or compressed gases such as nitrogen or CO2 cannot be used as they are used to manufacture another type of aerosolized products where the propellant is present in a gaseous form and so can’t act as a solvent or carrier of the other components.
With a compressed gas, the pressure in an aerosol formulation will not remain constant as the product is used. High pressure generally gives a fine, dry spray; low pressure generally gives a course, wet spray resulting in bigger droplets and a less efficient space treatment for aircraft disinsection products.

Also, the product Union Authorisation granted under the EU Biocidal Products Regulation in 2021 and valid until 28th of February 2031, would no longer be valid and cause a lack of authorised aircraft disinsection products.
The importance of using these niche aerosolized products in the aviation has increased exponentially. Due to climate change causing better life circumstances for exotic mosquito types as Culex, Aedes and Anopheles species, the threat of vector borne disease has increased too.
So the control of vectors (insects) getting on board of an aircraft in non-EU zones where vector borne diseases are present, is extremely important.

It is our believe that imposing a new restriction, partially contradicting existing European regulation and based on a too broad interpretation of the chemical component PFAS, with a timeline for implementation too short to be operationally and commercially feasible for the industries involved does not constitute a constructive and realistic route to market, irrespective of the underlying noble and justified intentions.

Due to a possible restriction of PFAS substances including fluorinated greenhouse gases, a lack of specific aircraft disinsection products will occur. Insecticide aerosol sprays will no longer be available on the market for the professional users due to a lack of alternative products authorized under the EU BPR Regulation and due to the technical requirements that can’t be fulfilled. In all cases, these products are the only technical and safe options for this specific application.
Regarding the global export market, our company will not be able to continue competing on those markets where it is currently already present with these aerosolized aircraft disinsection products. As the restriction would be limited to the EU, it would cause a very unfair economic level of competition.

8. Other identified uses: Relevant information will be provided in future submissions.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: Relevant information will be provided in future submissions.

On 13 January 2023, the competent authorities of five EU/EEA countries (Dossier Submitters) submitted the PFAS REACH Annex XV Restriction Report (Proposal) to the European Chemical Agency (ECHA). Honeywell submits the following information and comments to the ECHA 1st public consultation on the Proposal.  Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) is formed in the atmospheric degradation processes for some HFCs and HFOs fluorinated gases. For most HFC/HFO refrigerants, degradation rates/yields into TFA are small,  resulting in de minimis increases in overall TFA concentrations by comparison with pre-existing TFA levels. Only a few commercialized fluorinated gases decompose into fractions of TFA over 30% (including, HFO-1234yf, HFC-227ea, HFC-134a). Nevertheless, these emissions lead only to increases in TFA concentrations that safely remain at orders of magnitude below scientifically established DNEL/PNEC levels and/or food intake or water quality standards for TFA.  According to the trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) REACH registration dossier and Chemical Safety Report (CSR), this substance does not fulfil the criteria for a PBT or vPvB substance under Annex XIII REACH. Neither does it raise equivalent levels of concern under Article 57(f) REACH. In this respect, ECHA already reviewed/evaluated the TFA dossier without concluding that further regulatory actions were needed.  Potential effects of HFC/HFO emissions on TFA concentrations and respective risks to humans and the environment were studied intensively worldwide. In this respect, highly qualified independent assessments of UNEP panels repeatedly concluded that “The current low concentration of trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) produced by the degradation of several hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) and hydrofluoroolefins (HFOs), is currently judged not to pose a risk to human health or to the environment.”  and that “available evidence indicates that this breakdown product [TFA] is of minimal risk to human health”.  The most recent Environmental Effects Assessment Panel (EEAP) 2022 Assessment Report unequivocally cited a common agreement among the majority of experts that “all PFAS should not be grouped together, persistence alone is not sufficient for grouping PFAS for the purposes of assessing human health risk, and that the definition of appropriate subgroups can only be defined on a case-by-case manner” and that “it is inappropriate to assume equal toxicity/potency across the diverse class of PFAS”. According to the same Report, this equivalent  argument applies to the inclusion of TFA, with a two-carbon chain and a single CF3 group, in a class with longer chain PFAS (e.g. PFOS). The Report concludes that “Trifluoroacetic acid has biological properties that differ significantly from the longer chain polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and inclusion of TFA in this larger group of chemicals for regulation would be inconsistent with the risk assessment of TFA”. This Report also concludes that “based on projected future use of these precursors of TFA [incl. HFC/HFO], no harm is anticipated” and that TFA “is unlikely to cause adverse effects out to 2100”.  Moreover, according to the most recent 2022 UNEP/WMO report: “TFA abundance and its environmental impacts have been assessed in many previous Assessments (e.g., Montzka, Reimann et al., 2011; Montzka, Velders et al., 2018; Carpenter, Daniel et al., 2018). Those Assessments concluded that the environmental effects of TFA due to the breakdown of HCFCs and HFCs are too small to be a risk to the environment over the next few decades based on the projected future use of hydrocarbons, HCFCs, and HFOs.”  Environmental fate and distribution modelling of TFA in the freshwater aquatic environment was conducted based on the assumption of constant and ongoing HFO emissions, which through atmospheric degradation in turn leads to a constant deposition of TFA. Initial modelling results demonstrate that within a short timeframe (months) a steady state concentration of TFA is reached, which does not further increase over time. This is illustrated in a case study for the Rhine basin (Germany, The Netherlands), for which TFA concentrations clearly below 10 µg/L are predicted. Importantly, this study invalidates the incorrect assumption in the Proposal that TFA concentrations in fresh water would keep increasing until “inevitably” a toxic level would be reached.  In addition, emissions of HFC are subject to effective Risk Management Measures (RMMs) under the EU F-Gas Regulation, including progressively phasing down their tonnages via quotas (until 2030).  Considering the above, the conclusions in section 1.1.6 of the Proposal suggesting the existence of unacceptable risks from HFC/HFO emissions and their further degradation to TFA that are not adequately controlled and that all HFC/HFO emissions should be used as a proxy for unacceptable risks are erroneous, not proved by science and based on “hypothetical” or “zero risk” assumptions. These conclusions are in contradiction with available solid scientific data, REACH registration information and ECHA practices.  Therefore, in line with the provisions of Articles 68 and 69 REACH, fluorinated gases such as HFO-1234ze(E) as well as TFA as a substance and as a degradation product of certain fluorinated gases must be excluded from the scope of the Proposal.  Information source: Honeywell International Inc.  Further information: please also see attachment.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: For some specific technical aerosols, safety and performance constraints should be recognised. Our company has invested a lot of time and resources in meeting the European F-Gas regulation by replacing its HFC portfolio with HFO technology, resulting in a better performing product with higher added-value to the end user and its environment. The aerosolized product formulation contains a well-chosen liquified propellant to fulfil some important requirements. The product formulation must be non-flammable and to obtain a maximum rate of efficacy, a space treatment with small droplets that remain airborne for a long time is required.   Before 2018 the non-flammable and liquified propellant that was mainly used for the product of technical aerosols was HFC 134 (Global Warmth Potential value (GWP) more than 1400).  On 1/1/2018 a restriction on placing on the EU market described in Annex III of the F-Gases Regulation (517/2014/EC) entered into force: a prohibition to place on the EU market technical aerosols based on HFC’s with a GWP value of 150 or more, except when required to meet national safety standards or when used for medical applications.  As a consequence we were forced to adapt our product formulations of the aircraft insecticides and to perform research on an alternative liquified propellant that fulfils the required technical requirements, is non-flammable and has a GWP lower than 150.  We managed to find an alternative liquified propellant which is currently used for production of the aircraft insecticide aerosols: Solstice® 1234ze or HFO 1234ze manufactured by the company Honeywell. At this moment it is the sole available and alternative liquified propellant that can be used to manufacture non-flammable technical aerosols for placing on the EU market in accordance with the F-Gases regulation. Moreover, worldwide, there is no alternative available to be used as a non-flammable liquified propellant. HFO 1234ze has a GWP of less than 1 (and an ODP of 0). It is a liquified propellant that has specific and distinctive characteristics that allow the mixtures that we manufacture to pass the flammability tests established in the EU-standards, acting as propellant and co-solvent in their formulation.  Currently there is no alternative liquified propellant available to manufacture EU compliant technical aerosols for applications where non-flammability and high technical performance or spray characteristics are extremely important. Replacing the liquified propellant by an alternative, non-flammable gaseous propellant is also not feasible due to the final product requirements (spraying characteristics, droplet size).   Compressed gases  Non-flammable pressurized propellants or compressed gases such as nitrogen or CO2 cannot be used as they are used to manufacture another type of aerosolized products where the propellant is present in a gaseous form and so can’t act as a solvent or carrier of the other components.  With a compressed gas, the pressure in an aerosol formulation will not remain constant as the product is used. High pressure generally gives a fine, dry spray; low pressure generally gives a course, wet spray resulting in bigger droplets and a less efficient space treatment for aircraft disinsection products.  Due to a possible restriction of PFAS substances including fluorinated greenhouse gases, a lack of specific aircraft disinsection products will occur. Insecticide aerosol sprays will no longer be available on the market for the professional users due to a lack of alternative products authorized under the EU BPR Regulation and due to the technical requirements that can’t be fulfilled. In all cases, these products are the only technical and safe options for this specific application.   Concluding: currently there is no substitution potential for fluorinated gases used as a propellant for the production of technical aerosols (conform to the EU F-Gas regualtion) where safety, performance and non-flammability are unquestionable requirements.

Aerzener Maschinenfabrik GmbH manufactures compressors and blowers. Fluoropolymers are included in all machines for various applications:

-Surface coatings Tempcoat, Chemcoat for housing parts, pistons and rotors

We want a general exemption for fluoropolymers and are fully behind the VDMA's position paper.

Since the 1950s, PFAS have been used in a wide range of industrial and consumer goods applications and, at least in the industrial sector, have led to a significant improvement in the areas of operational safety and service life, especially in the use of fluoropolymers. Fluoropolymers do not pose a health hazard in operation, the benefits mentioned outweigh the risks. Therefore, the position of the AERZEN Group with regard to the planned PFAS ban is unambiguous and will be communicated to national and EU institutions as well as to trade associations in all available ways.
Fluoropolymers as a component of PFAS have made the world safer and more sustainable in recent decades. Substitutes with the same positive physical and operational properties are not discernible; a ban now would even stop the necessary climate change, as, among other things, the required hydrogen compressors must also be equipped with fluoropolymers for operational and safety reasons. Fluoropolymers are used in the AERZEN Group in the shape of seals in every blower / compressor / turbo for the above reasons. In addition, fluoropolymers serve in certain applications for the piston/rotor coating, as lubricants or as emergency running materials in air foil bearings.

6. Missing uses: Applications (all fluoropolymers): 1. seal ring / O-ring made of FPM / FKM fluorocarbon rubber or fluoroelastomer, e.g. trade name "Viton" Application: sealing of machine elements in compressors against oil and gases at temperatures up to 150°C, e.g. air sealing for blowing atmospheric oxygen into the aeration tanks of wastewater treatment plants 2. PFPE oil/ PFPE grease made from PFPE / perfluorinated polyether Application: compressor lubricating oil in the compression of technical gases for solar panel and semiconductor production 3. Surface coatings Tempcoat, Chemcoat for housing parts, pistons and rotors Application: protection of metal surfaces against corrosion and decomposition during compression of humid gases (hydrogen/ biogas) 4. Air bearing made of PTFE / polytetrafluoroethylene  Application: air foil bearing without further energy input and maintenance free, top foil serves as a reliable and durable lubricating film  General impact: The ban would have an impact on workplaces and value creation in the EU. Turnover would decrease by about 1/3. Moreover, workplaces and turnover would be relocated outside Europe.  The ban would additionally have an impact on product safety. Despite shorter maintenance intervals, chemical and ATEX plants could no longer comply with today's safety standards and the hazard of leakage would increase by a factor of 5. The degree of innovation of our machines would thus fall back to the level of the 1950s.  In addition, new technologies that are important for renewable energy production could not be pursued further. In this way, the technology of compressing hydrogen, which plays an important role in sustainable industrial processes, would be slowed down. In addition, the supplement leads to a reduction of the maintenance intervals by 1/3. This causes higher resource consumption and higher operating costs of our machines, which has a negative impact on sustainability.
