Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Information on alternatives Transitional period Request for exemption
Org. name: Association of the European Self-Care Industry (AESGP)
Combined Comments:
General Comments: AESGP, the Association of the European Self-Care Industry, represents manufacturers of non-prescription medicines, self-care medical devices and food supplements that together are also referred to as consumer healthcare products.

We support the efforts made to address and mitigate the risks associated with some PFAS as well as the unlimited exemption for active substances in pharmaceutical products (API, Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient) However, we would like to express our concerns about the fact that the term “PFAS” is a broad, general, non-specific term, which does not inform whether a compound is harmful or not” and therefore, without considering the loss of human health benefits due to the restriction and without applying a risk-based approach, the consequences for consumer healthcare products could be detrimental.

The following substances and applications would be subject to restrictions after the 18-month transition period with a significant impact on self-care patients and users in and outside the European Union.
• Primary packaging materials (e.g. tubes, sachets, blisters ) and sterile barrier systems, even if they are part of the market authorization of Medicinal Products and the certification of Medical Devices.
• Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs) without EU marketing authorization, such as APIs that belong to the PFAS family (as defined by ECHA) for global export.
• APIs in development. Beyond a production volume of 1 ton per year, the exemption for scientific research and development no longer applies and both production and further development would no longer be possible in the EU.
• Other "non-active" components in consumer healthcare products, such as additives/excipients and propellants, as well as substances and aids required for their production (e.g., solvents, hoses, filters, etc.).
• Fluoropolymers in industrial settings – both as equipment and consumables:
o  Chemical raw materials, synthesis starting materials, catalysts, as well as intermediate products and other substances and aids necessary for synthesis (e.g., solvents, hoses, filters, etc.) to produce active substances.
o PFAS-containing equipment in production, such as seals, valves, hoses, filters, and membranes, are necessary for producing and analysing essential products.


• Impact of the restriction proposal and recommendation in relation to transition timelines

The restriction proposal refers to the security of the supply of medicinal products for the population in the justification on page 72 for the exemption for active pharmaceutical ingredients (API): "Human MPs are important for the protection of humans from diseases". All the substances as well as processes in and during the manufacture of medicinal products and medical devices (such as chemical raw materials, catalysts as well as e.g., intermediates and other substances required for synthesis e.g., tubes, filters, films, etc.), for which an exemption is not foreseen, are affected by the restriction. This will have far-reaching effects, particularly in the field of medicinal products and medical devices which are likely to negatively impact healthcare systems protecting the health of the EU population.
In order to ensure the supply of medicinal products to the population and to achieve the goal that the production of medicinal products can remain or even be expanded in Europe, further specific exemptions (raw materials/intermediates, reagents, materials such as PVDF filters, PFAS-coated equipment parts for manufacturing) are necessary in addition to the exemption for active pharmaceutical ingredients in medicinal products, which is not limited in time.
Therefore, we call for a general exemption for finished consumer healthcare products, particularly non-prescription medicinal products, and self-care medical devices including manufacturing, covering:
1. APIs without EU approval.
2. Chemical raw materials, synthesis starting substances, catalysts as well as e.g., intermediates and other substances and auxiliaries required for synthesis (e.g. solvents, tubes, filters, etc.) for production and manufacturing.
3. APIs and medical devices under development.
4. Other "non-active" ingredients, such as additives/excipients and propellants, as well as substances and auxiliaries required for their manufacture (e.g. solvents, tubes, filters, etc.).
5. Primary packaging materials and sterile barrier systems, even if they are part of the marketing authorisation.
6. Products containing PFAS, such as seals, valves, tubes, filters and membranes, which are required in production facilities for the manufacture and analysis of consumer health products.

Time-unlimited derogations, which will not be limited to the active substances in pharmaceutical products (API, Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient), would be indispensable to guarantee the uninterrupted supply of medicinal products to the population and to promote pharmaceutical manufacturing growth in Europe. This is especially relevant for raw materials, intermediates, reagents, and all kinds of primary packaging materials.

For instance, using primary packaging materials is crucial in preserving and protecting pharmaceutical and healthcare products, such as tablets, which are classified as medicinal products, substance-based medical devices, or food supplements. Consequently, restricting PFAS packaging which is crucial to deliver the respective consumer healthcare product, as well as failing to allow sufficient timelines for replacing PFAS packaging, will lead to supply and availability issues of crucial medicine for EU citizens.


• Need for time-unlimited derogations for specific packaging used for consumer healthcare products without alternatives

There is a need for time-unlimited derogations for specific primary packaging materials, notably with regard to thermoform blisters used for tablet packaging commonly utilize PCTFE (Polychlorotrifluoroethylene) due to its exceptional properties, including high moisture barrier, transparency, thermoformability, chemical stability, inertness, non-sticking characteristics, non-ageing properties, and sterilizability. Incorporating a layer of PCTFE offers technical advantages for medications requiring enhanced protection for the delivery of safe and sterile products to patients. The self-care industry supports the proper disposal of waste blisters through collection and incineration, ensuring the appropriate handling of medicinal products.

• Need for longer transition periods for specific packaging used for consumer healthcare products with alternatives

For packaging where alternatives could be found the transition periods must account for technological advancements and substitution possibilities as well as consideration of the time required for requalification, revalidation, stability studies, regulatory changes (variations), or new approvals (which can take up to 10 years). The high-level requirements to consider are the following:
• Compatibility / Stability study – shelf-life qualification
• Extractables / Leachable assessment
• Functionality qualification
• Processability qualification
• Re-submission to health authorities

Longer transition periods are necessary for two main reasons: the time needed for the development of alternative options and the qualification and registration process for primary packaging. When replacing a primary packaging material in the market, a thorough and typically lengthy requalification process is required. If the vitamin is used in a medicinal product, this process involves working closely with health regulators to ensure compliance and would fall under exemptions and longer transition periods of medicinal products.  However, it is important to note that, within the EU, the classification of the same vitamin product can vary, with some markets considering it a food supplement while others classify it as a medicinal product. One example is prenatal vitamins which could in some countries be marketed as a food supplement and in other cases as medicinal products. Due to the importance of vitamins as well as to maintain consistency for the same product across the EU, we, therefore, recommend applying the same transition periods for primary packaging for both food supplements, ingested medical devices, and medicinal products.

Likewise, implementing a prohibition on fluoropolymers in industrial settings – both as equipment and consumables – could result in changing our manufacturing processes. For medicinal products, for instance, this could trigger the submission of several variations to update registered manufacturing processes, which would take considerable time and effort for assessment and approval from regulators. Furthermore, certain medicinal products lack substitutes for numerous applications where properties, e.g. chemical resistance are needed. This situation presents a potential risk of shortages if these modifications are not meticulously planned, permitting exemptions are authorised where essential and ample transition periods are provided.

• Conclusion
We call for a general exemption for consumer healthcare products, particularly medicinal products, and self-care medical devices that undergo rigorous registration, market authorization or certification schemes, proving their beneficial health effects and safety of use. Raw and starting materials, intermediates, auxiliaries, equipment, and consumables required for the manufacture and packaging of healthcare products should also be exempt, as these are handled under controlled conditions.

This is justified by the societal necessity of consumer healthcare products, the limited ability for substitution with non-PFAS chemicals, the fact that APIs used in medicines are already subjected to environmental risk assessment, and the low risk that these materials have for impact on the environment due to both limited volume and minimal hazard (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0160412019309493).

Any emission of industrial manufacturing into environments is controlled and regulated via other existing EU legislation and any risk posed by emissions of these substances can be further mitigated through waste management regulations. Fluoropolymers are not volatile or bioavailable. As the only common property is persistence, their emission should be restricted rather than the use of the substances. Moreover, the derogation for APIs as currently drafted would not allow continued manufacturing of many APIs in the EEA, which conflicts with recent EU strategies to reduce dependency on supply chains located mainly outside of the EEA.

• Additional Considerations
There are many complexities involved in fully investigating this proposed restriction with all the self-care industry suppliers and partners throughout the entire supply chain. We rely on information from our suppliers, who themselves might have to investigate with their (raw ingredient) suppliers. Time and resources will be required throughout many levels of the supply chain to fully assess the impact of this restriction. Therefore, we are not able to respond to the specific info requests as a Downstream User industry, however, we would like to emphasize the proposed restriction will have far-reaching consequences that are not fully realized yet including the unintentional elimination of critical uses/processes/products.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The AESGP submission refers to the use of PFAS in consumer healthcare products comprising non-prescription medicines, self-care medical devices and food supplements.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Afaquim is the Spanish Association of Companies Manufacturing Fine Chemical Products, Active Pharmaceutical Ingredientes to be more specific, which brings together a total of 36 companies. AFAQUIM is a heterogeneous Association that has as its members large corporations and also small and medium-sized companies. The Association's companies produce more than 500 APIs, many of them essential in the AEMPS, WHO and FDA drug lists.

The sector employs nearly 10,000 direct workers and 23,000 indirect workers.

AFAQUIM companies have a turnover of 2.5 billion euros and exports worth 2.1 billion euros.

AFAQUIM shares the objectives derived from the European Green Deal and the Chemical Strategy for CSS Sustainability to minimize the risks to human health and the Environment. It therefore supports the proposal for the restriction of PFAS raised in option RO2, although some uses and sub-uses should be reviewed as well as the temporality in their derogations.

Faced with the restriction proposal presented and for which comments are requested, the sector is affected in two fundamental aspects. On the one hand, intermediates, raw materials and auxiliaries classified as PFAS used in the production of already registered active substances, but also products in research and development; and on the other hand in the use of certain fluoropolymers in their activities.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: For active substances covered by European Directive 2001/83, an unlimited derogation is envisaged in paragraph 4c of column 2 of the proposed restriction set out in Annex XV. Although during the proposal in different sections of the same, reference is made to active substances, to their chemical structure, which makes many of them PFAS, or to their regulation even from the point of view of environmental impact, the reality is that as indicated in Annex B.9.17 no impact study has been considered with respect to them,  nor do they appear for example in Table 8: RO1 - Summary table of alternatives and cost impacts for PFAS manufacture and major PFAS use sectors resulting from a full ban of PFASs. or Table 9: RO2 - Summary table of derogations ('proposed' or 'for reconsideration') for PFAS manufacture and major PFAS use sectors, with substantiation for the derogation period (5 or 12 years) and with cost impacts for the 5 and 12 year derogation periods. It would therefore not be a use identified and evaluated in the proposal.  Intermediates, Raw materials and auxiliaries PFAS:  The proposed restriction presents an unlimited derogation, with the provision of information to be determined, for the active substances, regulated by Directive 2001/83, a derogation with which AFAQUIM fully agrees, but the way in which it is proposed and the reaching of it we consider to be incomplete, since intermediates and raw and auxiliary materials, that are PFAS, necessary in the manufacture of active substances, are not included, may affect the supply of APIs in the EU, many of them essential, determined in the AEMPS, WHO and FDA drug lists.the European Authorities after the episodes of shortage of them during the recent COVID pandemic. Among the raw materials used in the manufacture of API's, it is worth mentioning the use of TFA (Trifluoroacetic acid) in obtaining API’s peptides for veterinary and human use, but also cosmetic use  Thus, the use of intermediates and PFAS raw materials and auxiliaries used in the manufacture of active substances, or in R+D activities, would be a missing use for which it is requested to extend the unlimited derogation enjoyed by the active substances to which they give rise.  Use of fluoropolymers: The other point of affectation is all the equipment and materials used in processes, manufacturing equipment, and auxiliary activities such as Quality Control, R+D, Engineering, etc., that may contain fluoropolymers. Regarding fluoropolymers, AFAQUIM considers that an unidentified use such as in the chemical industry in the broadest sense, similar to the Petrochemical and Mining use, as well as the under-use of fluoropolymer applications, should be incorporated into the proposal.  One of the fluoropolymers with more presence in the sector, especially in manufacturing equipment: reactors, pipes, pumps, filters, valves, etc. is PTFE for its properties of resistance and stability against chemical reactions, as well as for its ease of cleaning, etc. It must be said that all these equipment used in obtaining active substances must also be validated within the same Quality system.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Although the proposed restriction does not provide for any impact analysis, as regards emissions, the management of active substances that are subject to unlimited derogation in the proposal, at the end of their useful life, is carried out through the packaging and packaging waste management systems that EU countries have established, for the correct management of medicines not consumed by patients. Likewise, the management of waste of obsolete active substances and emissions to the different vectors during their manufacture is perfectly regulated and controlled, the manufacturing activities of API's are under the umbrella of the Industrial Emissions Directive.  The same good management occurs for intermediates and PFAS raw and auxiliary materials used in the manufacture of active substances. For them it is requested to extend the unlimited repeal.  Regarding PFAS intermediates and raw materials, the volume of emissions in the final phase of their life cycle is not quantified, but in any case, they are very small amounts and therefore the environmental impact due to their PFAS property is minimal since they are transformed practically entirely through chemical or biological processes.  The emissions produced by the use of these raw and auxiliary materials in the manufacture of intermediates as well as active substances are managed correctly and minimized throughout their life cycle. The management of these emissions is perfectly controlled as the activities of the manufacturing sector of active substances and intermediates are covered by the DEI Industrial Emissions Directive.  As for recycling, we cannot speak as such that this management practice is important in the sector since the regulations of the Health Authorities are increasingly strict in order to guarantee the presence of certain impurities and in certain percentages in the active substances, as established by the Pharmacopoeia. The incorporation of these intermediates and/or recycled raw materials from the processes makes it more difficult to comply with these requirements.  With regard to the use of fluoropolymers in the sector, they are part of equipment such as gaskets, filters, valves, pumps, etc. Given the characteristics of chemical stability, temperature resistance or ease of cleaning, it is not possible to speak of emissions in the use phase of the life cycle of these. When this equipment reaches the end of its life, emissions can be controlled in the recycling or disposal operations of such fluoropolymers.

5. Proposed derogations: Most raw materials and intermediates used in the manufacture of active substances, acquire this condition by having in their molecules structures, among others, such as a CF3- often attached to an aromatic ring. This structure is maintained from the initial raw material to the final API active substance.  The CF3 structure, with the substitution of the H atom for a fluorine atom, presumably exerts subtle effects on the absorption, metabolism distribution and excretion of candidate substances given the physicochemical characteristics of the F atom and the properties of the C-F bond. Thus, as indicated in an article in the journal ACS OMEGA in 2020, the number of fluoro-active substances has grown exponentially in the last 50 years. Globally more than 300 fluoro-active substances have been registered, including some block-buster among them.  Likewise, there are certain PFAS substances used in auxiliary activities such as Quality Control, which are subject to the same regulatory scheme for the manufacture of active substances established by the Health Authorities, which must also be included in the unlimited derogation.  Finally, the activities of Research and Development, PPORD, to obtain active substances that can be PFAS, it is essential that they have unlimited derogation in order to maintain within the EU this sector of high added value and that requires a high level of qualification of personnel. The non-possibility of using certain substances in the development of new molecules would imply moving outside the borders of the EU a strategic sector to avoid not only the shortage of medicines in situations such as the one experienced, but also the dependence on third countries.  From AFAQUIM it is considered that the use of intermediates, raw materials and auxiliaries used in its activities, as well as in R+D activities, and that meet the condition of PFAS due to its structure, are not a missing use but must be included in the use of active substances as contemplated in the proposed restriction in its annex XV,  and therefore also be subject to unlimited derogation; otherwise, there would be a shortage of medicines for EU patients, a dependence on third countries and a displacement of R+D beyond the borders of the EU.

6. Missing uses: There are no alternatives for these substances because it is the perfluorinated structure that contributes to the pharmacological activity; Its elimination or substitution would imply the production of a completely different substance and one could no longer speak of an active substance.   In the case of APIs peptides there’s none alternatives to the use of TFA, a key substance for synthesis, despite the fact that many substitutes have been studied for many years without success.  As for fluoropolymers, it is considered that the chemical sector would be a missing use in the restriction proposal and that the same timetable should be applied to it as to the Petrochemical and Mining sector as regards its use in activities.  Regarding fluoropolymers, if sub-use in the chemical industry is included as Petrochemical or Mining, as established in option RO2, it will allow the sector to adapt to the alternatives that appear. It is even more important to have this timetable for option RO2 as it is a sector that is fully regulated by the Health Authorities, which means that it must not only be ensured that they have the same chemical or temperature stability properties, and do not affect the active substances with the consequent risk to the health of patients, rather, these Authorities should oversee all regulatory validation processes for new materials.  With regard to the non-inclusion of PFAS intermediates and auxiliary substances in the unlimited derogation of the active substances to which they give rise, it affects 100% of the companies of the Association depending on the individual impact of the number of PFAS active substances produced, some of them essential in the AEMPS, WHO and FDA drug list. The economic impact can be billions of euros and hundreds of workers affected, being able to disappear the production of more than 25% of the API's produced by the Association, reaching in some cases the disappearance of some companies. However, the greatest socio-economic impact would be the shortage of active substances for patients and the dependence on third countries on some medicines.   For the specific case of peptides, the non-inclusion of the TFA raw material in the unlimited derogation, such as for active substances, would mean the total disappearance of peptides manufactured in Spain, 7 of them classified as essential for the WHO and 4 for the FDA, and obviously throughout Europe.The consequences would be the disappearance of peptides manufactured for use in personalized medicine treatments in oncological cases, as well as the disappearance of peptides manufactured as "custom synthesis" that are being used in the development of new drugs, which would cause the impossibility for new drugs to see the light. All this would result in the closure of companies and the loss of more than 80 jobs.  Regarding the use of fluoropolymers, the most important socioeconomic impact, if the same derogation as the Petrochemical or Mining sector is not applied, would be that of not having time for the validation of the new materials in their equipment, which would imply delays in the production of all types of PFAS or non-PFAS active substances, and of course, an important economic cost of all the regulatory procedures required by the Health Administration

General Comments: After founding in 1954 in Tokyo as a manufacturer of industrial elastomer products, since 1964, DAIKYO SEIKO, LTD. (hereinafter Daikyo) has been a B to B company continuing to develop, manufacture and supply primary packaging for pharmaceutical drugs using elastomer and plastic as raw materials. Since 1964, Daikyo has been continuing the development of materials and technologies, and the manufacture and supply of high-quality products for approximately 60 years to support the supply of safe medicines. Daikyo supplies approximately 1 billion products per year in approximately 2,000 elastomer and plastic products together. Daikyo’s products are supplied to pharmaceutical manufacturers all over the world. Given that many of pharmaceutical drugs in which Daikyo’s products are used as life-saving drugs, Daikyo believes that we are socially responsible for maintaining human health-being and supporting life worldwide.

Of the approximately 1300 items Daikyo manufactures, 300 elastomer stoppers for vials, pistons and nozzle caps for syringes are manufactured with fluoropolymer films. Therefore, they are the subject of this restriction proposal.

Daikyo works with West Pharmaceutical Services, Inc. to supply our products to pharmaceutical manufacturers who supply drugs to EU market (see Question 6. c). Our products have a large share as primary packaging for pharmaceutical drugs used in EU area. For primary packaging components in direct contact with drug contents, multiple characteristics and quality attributes (see Question 6. b) are required. Daikyo responds to these requirements by laminating elastomer products with fluoropolymer film.

Daikyo imparts the characteristics and quality attributes required for primary packaging for pharmaceutical drugs to Daikyo’s products by laminating fluoropolymer film made from PTFE or ETFE, and PTFE and ETFE meet the standards for "polymers of low concern" of Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)1. In addition, fluoropolymers such as PTFE or ETFE are clearly different from a non-polymer PFAS, and it has been confirmed by various studies that there is basically no interaction or accumulation in a living body. Furthermore, since Daikyo fluoropolymer laminated components are primary packaging for pharmaceutical drugs, those are subjected to marketing approval review for the drugs in use. In EU, Daikyo fluoropolymer laminated components are strictly regulated, reviewed and approved by European Medicines Agency European Medicines Agency (EMA) for use.

In response to this restriction proposal, Daikyo has been discussing the potential possibilities for the development of alternative films which have the characteristics and quality attributes comparable to those of the current fluoropolymer film with a fluoropolymer film manufacturer. However, the fact is that no substance with comparable characteristics and quality attributes has been found (see Question 6. d), and there is no stage in which the actual duration, cost, or potential necessary to develop alternative films can be discussed at this time.

As mentioned earlier, Daikyo fluoropolymer laminated components are primary packaging for pharmaceutical drugs, so there are a vast number of patients with many pharmaceutical companies downstream of our products. Assuming that a substitute film with comparable characteristics and quality attributes is found in the future, changes of the fluoropolymer film used at Daikyo will require pharmaceutical manufacturers to evaluate and verify the impact on the pharmaceutical drugs, as well as pharmaceutical procedures (see Question 6. c). If, in the meantime, the exclusion of Daikyo fluoropolymer laminated components from EU market happens, then a life-threatening risk will arise that the pharmaceutical drugs cannot be supplied to patients in EU area (see Question 6. g).

Wastes that occur during the production of fluoropolymer film by the fluoropolymer film manufacturer are recycled (see Question 2. b). And Daikyo incinerates wastes that are generated during the production of our fluoropolymer laminated components at temperatures above 2000°C. Thus, there is no environmental release of recalcitrant PFAS (see Question 2. b). After being formulated and consumed in EU area, primary packaging containing PTFE or ETFE are managed and treated as medical wastes, and Daikyo confirmed that one of the methods is incineration treatment (see Question 2. b).

Daikyo highly appreciates the regulatory framework for non-polymeric PFAS that have been implemented under REACH and POPs regulations. However, it is clear that regulating of primary packaging for pharmaceutical drugs, such as Daikyo fluoropolymer laminated components, by the restriction proposal that uniformly includes fluoropolymers, which cannot always be said to be highly hazardous, will have a significant impact on the supply of pharmaceutical drugs and, consequently, lead to a risk to human life. Daikyo supports the main purpose of this proposal, “environmental conservation”, as a company responsibility to society. However, at the same time, as a manufacturer of primary packaging for pharmaceutical drugs, Daikyo also has an important social role in maintaining human health and supporting lives. Based on the fact that the discharge of fluoropolymers into the environment from upstream suppliers to downstream consumers of fluoropolymer laminated products is very small compared with other industries, and the balance with socioeconomic impacts including the impact on the lives of patients when regulated, Daikyo calls that primary packaging components that directly contact drug contents, such as elastomer stoppers for vials, pistons and nozzle caps for syringes using fluoropolymer film, be classified into unlimited derogation of the restriction proposal.

The specific explanation and rationale for our request is provided in section of Specific Information. Daikyo hopes that all the explanations and rationales underpinning our requests will be reviewed as a series of steps.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: After more than ten years of development, Jinhua Yonghe fluorochemical Co., Ltd. has developed into a national high-tech enterprise specializing in R&D, production and sales of refrigerants and fluoropolymers. With an annual production capacity of 100,000 tons of refrigerant and 5,000 tons of fluorine-containing polymer products, it occupies the leading position in the key generic technology for monomer manufacturing of organic fluorine and other polymers and the high-speed extrusion production technology of fluoropolymers.
Some fluoropolymers are classified as "Polymers of Low Concern" according to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) criteria. They are chemically stable, biologically stable/solubility, negligibly soluble in water, non-bioavailable, non-bioaccumulative and non-toxic.
Persistence is not necessarily a health risk. The risk to human health happens when it can enter the cells. It is mentioned in the literature (Barbara J Henry and et al., A Critical Review of the Application of Polymer of Low Concern and Regulatory Criteria to Fluoropolymers, Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management, Volume 14, Number 3, pp 316-334.) that fluoropolymers are practically insoluble in water and do not migrate over long distances. With a molecular weight greater than 100,000 Da, fluoropolymers cannot pass through cell membranes. Fluoropolymers are not bioavailable or biocumulative, which has been demonstrated in toxicological experiments of PTFE.
In industrial applications, on the one hand, fluoropolymers can be used for 20 years, 30 years or even longer. However, the use of alternative materials will cause the problem of frequent replacement of parts for weeks or a month, which can not only cause additional harm to workers and is not conducive to reducing carbon emissions. From the perspective of waste reduction, it should not be included in the scope of control. On the other hand, cost is a key driver in many industries. For example, in the automotive industry, fluoropolymers are often used in hoses and pipes to transport engines and vehicle fluids (water, oil, biofuels) or gases (air, exhaust gas), with strict safety and emission requirements. Fluoropolymers are relatively expensive, so they are designed for use only when there are no other alternatives.
Polychlorotrifluoroethylene (PCTFE) is a high-performance thermoplastic commonly used in harsh environments. It shows excellent resistance to improvement when in contact with liquid oxygen, liquid nitrogen, and liquefied natural gas, and is also free from the destructive effects of ultraviolet radiation and gamma radiation.​ In all plastics, PCTFE has the lowest water-gas permeability, does not permeate any gas, and acts as a good barrier.
PCTFE has an irreplaceable role in specific fields such as inert lubricating grease, corrosion resistance and low temperature resistant products, electronics and pharmaceutical packaging membrane. PCTFE has many uses in the field of electronics. For example, it can be used as a chemically resistant insulator in the gas etching process, and the components of its materials can be used for the manufacture of semiconductor processing equipment and computer chips. 40% of PCTEE's market demand comes from the electronics field which PCTEE is mainly used for.
PCTFE is used in the field of medical devices. For example, it can be used to manufacture syringes, blood filters and medical devices for ultraviolet sterilization. PCTFE density is lower than glass, moisture resistance comparable to glass, and oxygen barrier performance better than glass and other plastic containers. Therefore, when used as a packaging material, PCTFE can save transportation costs, minimize product loss caused by rupture, and eliminates potential contamination from glass particles or silicone lubricants used with glass. The PCTFE bottle has a three-layer structure, with the inner layer of PCTFE, the middle layer of the adhesive layer, and the outer layer of PC or PET. The PCTFE bottles have crystal transparency, high purity, high chemical resistance, and gamma sterilization performance. PCTFE bottles have been tested in accordance with the US medical grade VI, International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 10993 biocompatibility testing, EU food contact standards and other related standards.​ PCTFE multi-layer co-extrusion bottle is safe and lightweight. It is a substitute for neutral borosilicate glass in drug packaging and can be used for related oral liquids and injections.
Use PCTFE safely in the valve components of oxygen pressure regulators in the long term. The use of fluorinated resin is critical to the safe use of the oxygen pressure regulator under high pressure. As for the nozzle filler connecting the blow pipe, although the pressure is not high, it still requires, besides the compatibility with oxygen, air tightness and flame retardancy at high temperature. When the gas welding and cutting are safely used under the high temperature conditions near the flame, the fluorinated resin must be used to safely separate the oxygen and fuel gas mixture from the external environment at the connection with the blowing pipe. Other resins will have a violent combustion reaction, which is a great risk.
In summary, there is a high probability that complete substitutes for fluoropolymers represented by PCTFE do not exist or fluoropolymers cannot be replaced in practical applications while PCTFE has a good record in the field of medical devices. Therefore, we advocate that PCTFE should be exempted from the regulation of the Act.

Content: Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: After more than ten years of development, Jinhua Yonghe Fluorochemical Co., Ltd. has developed into a national high-tech enterprise specializing in research and development, production and sales of refrigerants and fluorine polymers. With an annual production capacity of 100,000 tons of refrigerants and 5,000 tons of fluoropolymer products, the company occupies a leading position in China in terms of the research and application of key common technologies in the manufacture of monomers of organic fluorine and other polymers, and the production technology of high-speed fluoropolymer extruding materials.
In order to analyse and respond to the PFAS restriction proposal, Jinhua Yonghe analysed the FEP material and component industries that would be affected, assessed material substitutes and impacts, evaluated socio-economic impacts, and described the end-of-life process and recycling methods for PFAS components.
We believe that the PFAS restriction proposal violates the principle of proportionality, which means that if short-term alternatives to PFAS do not become available in the market, the interests of both PFAS-related companies and their upstream and downstream counterparts will suffer significant losses.
We can find a contradictory rationale on which this restriction proposal is based: it recognises that there are no validly available prediction tools, whereas the proposal predicts PFAS concentrations in the environment. On the one hand, all members of the group are considered harmful, while on the other hand, only certain members of the group have been assessed. It follows that many of these conclusions lack scientific evidence and are subject to uncertainty.
Among the products affected by PFAS restrictions, FEP is an important class of fluoropolymers used in industries where resistance to chemicals, extreme temperatures (high and low) and abrasion resistance are important, as thin film printed boards, wire and cable insulation, generator wire windings, electrically insulated fabrics (panels, rods, tubes, frames and insulators), and corrosion-resistant structural products (oil-free lubricated mechanical components), Paint and glass enameled fabrics, equipment, heat exchangers, fractionation towers, pumps, valves, tubes, seals, pipe linings, laboratory clearware, etc.
Specific examples are as follows:
1. Product Lubricated Bearings: Blends of FEP with other materials such as metals, ceramics and other polymers can be used as product lubricated bearings because their excellent chemical resistance and low friction help to minimize wear and extend the life of pumps and valves.
2. Pump and Valve Linings: Fluoropolymer linings are used in pumps and valves to protect internal components from corrosive chemicals or other aggressive fluids. These linings can be made of FEP (Fluorinated Ethylene Propylene) material.
3. Cable Sheathing: Fluoropolymers are used in high voltage cable sheathing for submersible pumps and valve actuators because of their resistance to UV radiation, excellent insulating properties, and resistance to moisture and water absorption.
4. Diaphragms: FEP diaphragms are commonly used in applications requiring high purity or resistance to aggressive chemicals. Because aggressive chemicals or other fluids are often hot enough to corrode conventional elastomer diaphragms, FEP diaphragms are used for pumps and valves that handle aggressive chemicals or fluids.
In short, FEP's chemical resistance and durability make it an indispensable material for downstream industries. At the same time, the downstream industries affected by FEP will further affect the more downstream industries, such as an important downstream application of FEP industry, pumps and valves industry, it is able to affect the more downstream industries are as follows:
1. Chemical processing industries where highly corrosive chemicals are present, because pumps and valves used here should be able to withstand the corrosive effects of these chemicals, including performance at high temperatures.
2. The oil and gas production industry, as the pumps and valves used here should be able to withstand the high temperatures and high pressure conditions that occur during the drilling and production of hydrocarbons, or the low temperatures that occur during the transportation of liquefied gases (such as natural gas or hydrogen).
3. Power generation industry, pumps and valves used here should be resistant to high temperatures, even in the presence of oxygen in the atmosphere.
4. The pharmaceutical application industry for traditional and biotechnological processes, as the pumps and valves used here should be inert, non-reactive and sterilizable.
5. Applications in the food and beverage industry, because the pumps and valves used here should be non-stick and chemically inert, which is important for regular cleaning and sterilization processes, and the quality of the food and beverages with which they come into contact will not be adversely affected.
6. Water and wastewater treatment industries where highly corrosive chemicals are present, e.g. water electrolysis for hydroxide separation or water treatment in the electronics industry.
7. Pumping and circulation of drinking water.
Ultimately, many other industries are also relevant, and FEP is used throughout virtually the entire chemical industry supply chain. Therefore, exemption measures for FEP are imperative to safeguard the production of critical raw materials and commodities.
Finding alternatives to FEP can be difficult. In most cases, expensive FEP is only used in the following situations: All alternatives fail quickly and in many cases lead to safety issues; FEP ensures that the product or component functions effectively (acceptably and for a longer period of time); The conditions under which it is applied are imprecise (e.g., wastewater composition changes frequently (oil, water, bacteria, antibiotics, other drugs, rainwater, pesticides, fertilizers ......)). With the current development and availability of alternatives in the chemical industry, finding an alternative to FEP means that it takes a long time to explore a new suitable design to achieve the desired function, and also after a long trial period. Especially if different properties need to be characterized, the search for alternatives will set back many of the existing state of the art in terms of sealing, chemical resistance, heat resistance, environmental contamination, product purity, process contamination, and friction reduction to the levels of the 1950s. The number of compounds affected by this is in excess of 10,000, and in terms of processes and applications it will surely be several times that number. So this precludes any practical attempt to create an "exemption".
Therefore, we believe that rather than searching for alternatives to PFAS, it is more important to conduct further research into the recycling and reuse of fluoropolymers Typically, when FEP is prepared into finished products such as pumps, valves, cables, linings, etc., its unique chemical stability allows it to remain stable under extreme conditions and therefore no emissions are expected during the finished product use phase. During the end-of-life stage, to prevent improper disposal of PFAS and PFAS-containing components, implementing a traceability system during operation and at disposal is essential, and using a digital product passport would allow for better tracking and proper handling of such products and their associated components at the end of their useful life. At present, it is difficult to provide relevant data, but it would be feasible to establish such a recycling organization on a global or European scale. In the meantime, scientific studies have shown that high-temperature incineration of fluoropolymers using the best available technology would not be a significant source of PFAS, which should also be considered as an acceptable waste disposal method.
Furthermore, FEP is typically considered a Low Concern Polymer (LCPFMs), i.e., polymers with low bioaccumulation, low environmental concern and low health risk. In terms of persistence and accumulation in organisms, FEPs that are considered LCPFMs should be recognized as having low bioaccumulation and manageable health risks. Instead the regulations confuse the stability of FEP with its persistence, which is considered by the regulations to represent the stability of the FEP itself, and persistence does not mean hazardous. In terms of substitution, it is important for LCPFMs to find alternatives that are friendlier to the environment and healthier. However, due to the special characteristics of FEP materials, there are no alternative polymers and materials on the market, so the continued use of fluoropolymers is in line with the principles of sustainable development and environmental protection.

Content: Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: After over a decade of development, Jinhua Yonghe Fluorochemical Co., Ltd. has been a national-level high-tech enterprise specializing in research and development, production and sales of refrigerants and fluoropolymers. With an annual production capacity of 100,000 tons of refrigerants and 5,000 tons of fluoropolymer products, the Company holds a leading position in China and is known for its expertise in organic fluorine monomer manufacturing and high-speed extrusion of fluoropolymer products.
To address the proposed PFAS restrictions, Yonghe conducted an analysis of the PTFE materials and components industry. The objective was to evaluate alternative materials, assess socio-economic impacts, and describe end-of-life processes and recycling methods for PFAS components.
Yonghe argued that PTFE should not be classified as a PFAS due to its unique characteristics. PTFE has excellent thermal stability, biological and chemical stability, non-toxicity, non-biological accumulation, and non-fluid nature. It has also been demonstrated to meet the globally recognized OECD polymer "PLC" standard (Henry et al., 2018). PTFE plays a critical role in safety-related applications such as seals in engine compartments, fuel and coolant systems, and hoses in the automotive and transportation sectors in a variety of industries, including atomic energy, defense, aerospace, electronics, electrical, chemical, machinery, instrumentation, metrology, construction and more. Replacing PTFE in these applications would not only compromise safety but also lead to shorter vehicle lifespans, increased damage rates, and higher emissions during vehicle operation (VDA Position Paper, July 2021). In addition, fluoropolymers, including PTFE, are essential to meet the targets of the European Green Deal. Consequently, classifying PTFE as part of the PFAS limit would impede progress towards environmental sustainability.
Regarding the emissions of PFAS during production, a report by BauA titled "PFAS and PFAS Polymer Production" (July 2021) highlights that PFAS emissions from fluoropolymer production account for only 2.69% of the total PFAS emissions in the European Economic Area. Most of these emissions are attributed to the use of fluorinated polymerization aids in the manufacture of fluoropolymers, whereas PTFE products produced by Yonghe do not produce PFAS emissions.
The restriction acknowledges that PTFE and its degradation products persist in the environment, leading to an increase in environmental concentrations. This persistence is due to the fact that PFASs, which fall under the proposed restriction, do not naturally mineralize. Once in the environment, removing PFAS from various environmental sources such as surface waters, groundwater, soils, sediments, and biota becomes technically difficult and costly. PFASs have also been detected in living organisms, drinking water, food crops, as well as remote and pristine areas. This widespread prevalence of PFASs in the environment makes it inevitable that both current and future generations will be exposed to them. Human biomonitoring studies have also revealed that exposure to PFASs is widespread, with the highest levels present in high exposure communities. As environmental concentrations of PFASs continue to increase, negative effects on both human health and the environment become unavoidable. Furthermore, exposure to PFASs may have a potential intergenerational effect. Some scientists argue that the geographical limits of PFASs have already been exceeded, and that mixed exposure to PFASs in the general population may lead to health risks. It is important to note that persistence does not necessarily indicate harm, and the focus should be on the potential risks associated with PTFE degradation products. To address this issue, recycling and disposal methods for PTFE should be considered. Many polymer manufacturers are already conducting studies on incineration peak treatment, and Aleksandrov et al have shown that PFASs are not produced during the urban incineration of PTFE. Instead, it is almost entirely converted to hydrofluoric acid (HF). Therefore, municipal incineration of teflon can be considered an acceptable form of waste disposal(Chemosphere Volume 226, July 2019, Pages 898-906: Waste incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate the potential formation of per- and polyfluorinated alkyl substances (PFAS) in flue gas, Krasimir Aleksandrov et al.). In addition, the restriction only refers to the detection of PFAS in humans, without providing clear data or reports demonstrating harm to humans. As a result, any speculation about the risks posed by PFAS exposure lacks a solid basis.
Moreover, PTFE possesses distinctive properties that make it irreplaceable in various applications. Here are some key aspects highlighting the irreplaceability of PTFE:
High Temperature Stability: PTFE exhibits exceptional stability at high temperatures, retaining its performance even under extreme conditions. With a melting point of approximately 327°C (621°F), it can endure prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures.
Non-Viscous Nature: PTFE possesses an extremely low surface energy, making it an excellent non-viscous material. This non-stick property is utilized in various applications, such as anti-stick coatings and anti-friction surfaces. PTFE's resistance to adhering to different chemicals also makes it ideal for use in chemical processing equipment and coatings.
Chemical Stability: PTFE demonstrates excellent corrosion resistance against a wide range of chemicals, including acids, bases, and organic solvents. This chemical stability makes it highly suitable for use in the chemical, pharmaceutical, and food processing industries, where it can withstand exposure to diverse chemical environments.
Electrical Insulation Performance: PTFE is renowned for its outstanding electrical insulation properties, including excellent electrical breakdown resistance and low dielectric loss. Consequently, it finds extensive application in electrical and electronic devices, serving as an insulating material, cable covering, and battery isolator.
Mechanical Strength: While PTFE's mechanical strength is relatively low, its flexibility, wear resistance, and corrosion resistance make it suitable for specific applications. Moreover, the addition of filler materials can enhance PTFE's mechanical properties.
In summary, PTFE possesses distinct manufacturing processes and techniques to control the emission of harmful substances during production, use, and recycling. Furthermore, the unique characteristics of PTFE products make them irreplaceable. Therefore, PTFE should not be classified under the broad category of PFAS but should be evaluated and classified separately.
In conclusion, PTFE has well-established processes and methods to control the emission of hazardous substances during production, use, and recycling. Its unique properties make it an indispensable material in various industries. Therefore, PTFE should not be classified alongside PFAS but should be treated separately.

Content: Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period
Combined Comments:
General Comments: After reviewing and examining the restriction proposal regarding the use of PFAS as a solid lubricant in "lubricants under harsh conditions or for safe functioning and safety of equipment", we generally agree with the previously favored restriction after 18 months + 12 years transition period. We see this time as a minimum value that must be proven in practice.
Due to the very specific and sensitive applications, the PFAS used in our products are not easy to replace. Products for safety-relevant applications in particular require extensive testing and approval procedures in field trials. In addition, both the reformulation of the products concerned and the subsequent field tests and customer approvals will each take several years.
Therefore, we plead for the minimum period of 13.5 years from EiF to find suitable alternatives and in addition request ECHA to review and evaluate the data obtained on quantities and uses of PFAS after an appropriate period of about 7 years after EiF in order to decide on a possible extension of the transition period.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Lubricants under harsh conditions and for safety relevant application in heavy duty machinery

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Emissions of PFAS can only occur during the three main life cycle phases of lubricant lifetime: „formulation“, „use“ and „end-of-life“.  During formulation, direct emission into the environment do not occur, because measures to prevent emissions are taken and containment devices and processes are implemented.  During use there are litte to no emissions into the environent dependent on the application. Exposed lubricated machine elements are exposed to environmental conditions, there should be no emissions as PFAS are enclosed into a non-water-soluble matrix and hence are not to be released by weathering. Emissions from closed systems are only expected during filling/unfilling and in the event of a malfunctioning.  Reaching end-of-life, lubricant waste will be professionall disposed of and therefore, emissions are only possible during decanting, refilling and transfer. In this stage, again measures have been taken to prevent emissions and containment devices and procedures have been implemented. Used containers that accumulate during the three life cycle phases are cleaned according to regulations and any process waste is disposed of professionally in accordance with national (AVV and KrWG) and EU legislation (Commission Decision 2000/532/EC and Directive 2008/98/EC).  We encourage the authorities to develop and implement new and advanced strategies for prevention of current PFAS emissions, i.e. separate disposal and renewed circular economy strategies for lubricants containing PFASs.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Regarding emissions in the end-of-life phase we encourage the authorities to consider the recent study of Conversio (*). Herein evaluation and analysis of circular economy data of common polymers in Germany is presented. Through all polymers there is only about 1 % that end up in landfills. The majority of polymers is getting recycled or energeticaly utilized (incineration).  (*) Stoffstrombild Kunststoffe in Deutschland 2021: Zahlen und Fakten zum Lebensweg von Kunststoffen, Conversio, October 2022

6. Missing uses: After reviewing and examining the restriction proposal we noticed several uses and applications that are not or not explicitly mentioned, but have to be considered due to their technical relevance: - Use as defoaming agents in lubricants and metalworking fluids for automotive industry. PFAS here is an alternative for siloxane-based defoaming agents, as siloxane-based defoamers are not approved for process-related reasons. - Application in heavy-duty machinery due to safety reasons (very low friction coeffitient, preventing stick-slip phenomenon) concerning environmental and human health Development and formulation of alternatives is complex and associated with several years of field trials, due to safety requirement.  Therefore we welcome a minimum of 13.5 years after EiF as transitional period as this time is urgently needed to provide proper alternatives, if even possible.

8. Other identified uses: The use of PFAS free altenatives for e.g. defoamers for metalworking fluids for automotive industry or high performance lubricant additives for safety-related applications on heavy-duty outdoor machinery, can be proven possible only in complex and time cosuming (several years) field testing and approval procedures of the customers. Already available alternatives for PFAS are proven not to provide the neccessary performance, e.g. during extreme temperatures. They also provide certain toxicological properties or cannot be used due to insufficient physico-chemical properties, e.g. hydrophilicity, low friction coefficient, alkalinity or low oxidation stability. As a consequence, the use of these alternatives results in more dangerous and costly maintenance, as relubrication intervals become more frequent. Thus, 18 months + 12 years derogation from EiF might not be a sufficient time frame to achieve the prescribed goal for development and reformulation of PFAS free products in the mentioned sectors.

Information on alternatives:
There are alternatives which are currently used in the retinal surgery. The information of these medical alternatives are as follows,
Air

Air: Air can be discovered as first gas tamponade for retinal reattachment in 1911 by Ohm. It is chemically inert, inexpensive, colourless, non-toxic and most importantly abundant in nature and requires no secondary surgery for its removal as its easily diffusible into the blood circulation. The widespread use of expansile gases began in early 1970s[44]. Additionally, the study suggests that the gas tamponades are superior than air tamponade in inferior pathology[3].

Liquid: The first liquids to be used as a vitreous substitute were balanced salt solution (BSS) and water they exert no tamponade effect on the retina due to their short residence time and low viscosity[45].

Subsequently, Chang et al. in 1987, used PFCLs for retinal detachment in patients with advanced proliferative vitreoretinopathy. Three most commonly used PFCLs currently are perfluoro-decalin (PFD), perfluoro-tetradecahydrophenantrene and perfluoro-n-octane (PFO). Currently, PFCLs are used only as temporary tamponades for intraoperative procedures to unfold and stabilize the retina [45].

Silicone oil (SO) is a synthetic polymer pertaining to polydimetilsiloxanes group which consists of differing chain lengths. Since 1960s, SO have been used in vitreoretinal surgery. In mid 1970s, after pars plana vitrectomy progressed, the use of silicone oil also drastically improved and its long-term use as vitreous substitute gained popularity worldwide. Vitrectomy is recommended in case of severe retinal detachment. Silicon oil approved by United States Food and Drug Administration for intravitreal use only in 1994 [45].

Natural polymers: In early 1970s, hyaluronic acid (HA) was used as a vitreous replacement, but unfortunately cannot be used as a prolonged vitreous substitute due to their tendency to degrade rapidly. Attempts have been made to increase the degradation time of HA by oxidizing it with sodium periodate (NaIO4) to form aldehyde functional group and subsequently crosslinking with adipic acid dihydrazide to form transparent and colourless oxi-HA/ADH hydrogel. Moreover, it exhibits good transparency and tamponade effect intraocularly. Collagen and its derivatives such as Gelatine, Polygeline and Methylated collagen have been investigated for their use as vitreous substitutes, but they demonstrated a rapid decrease in viscosity and also short retention time in the vitreous chamber [45].

Synthetic Hydrogels: It is a synthetic hyaluronic acid hydrogel crosslinked with BDDE (1.4-Butanediol diglycidyl ether), with similar physiological properties as that of native vitreous. It is designed for glaucoma surgery as a space-filler and to restrict postoperative fibrosis. The hydrogel was well tolerated by retina and did not impact the morphology and function of the retina negatively [45].

Though there are alternatives present in the market but having some harmful effect. Unlike the subject device, silicon oil needs to be removed from the ocular cavity to prevent its ocular toxicity. That burden the re-surgery. Natural polymers are degraded before complete recovery and air shows inferior results than that of perfluorocarbon gases. The gases used, get diffused over the period of time in the tissues and the liquid perfluorocarbons are removed before surgery completion. Considering the benefit, ease of use and its need in the healthcare sector, subject devices can be derogated from restriction for use.

General Comments: Albeit we support and welcome the effort to restrict the release of PFAS into the environment, the scope with a generic term used by the EU/ECHA, covers a large number of per- or polyfluorinated alkyl compounds of very different usages. Some are used as material of construction due to outstanding properties in e g chemical resistance and durability.
When trying to see how our company fit into the referenced Table 9 (which is hard to find) it is not easy. The best fit is with Construction products (Annex E.2.13.), though we as a manufacturing company for inorganic coagulants for water treatment it is not fully descriptive. (In fact it is easy to imagine quite a few applications not being covered.)
We do not use any PFAS additive to our products. Not for manufacturing purposes or for product performance. No PFAS addition at all. However, with the broad definition used by the EU/ECHA the PFAS definition comes to cover fluoropolymers, fluoro-elastomers and e.g. ion-selective membranes we are concerned as this type materials are very important to us, not to say critical in certain applications.
These type materials are used due to the outstanding performance they deliver and a ban in use can/will significantly induce severe difficulties to ensure processes safety, environmental control, product quality and energy efficiency to mention some properties sought for. By using these materials of construction aggressive chemicals can be manufactured and used. Such chemicals creates value and often beyond the uses already established are together with use of said range of PFAS (fluoropolymers, fluoro-elastomers and ion-selective membranes) used in safety arrangements and technology for emission, pollution and remediation techniques. Further the materials are used in new innovative energy conversion and “green technology” necessary for progressing several of the UN SDGs.
We are further concerned with the absence of alternatives. To be specific a sustainable production of high quality in organic coagulants use concentrated chemicals starting with aggressive acids as sulphuric and hydrochloric acid and is operated under pressure. The use of fluoropolymers and fluoro-elastomers gives a process performance securing the product functionality necessary from e.g. drinking water and waste water treatment. In the process the same pieces of fluoropolymers and fluoro-elastomers are installed, most often may years with intact functionality. The alternatives would be e.g. reverting to the use of lead or asbestoses gaskests, use of glass-lined pipes (still requiring  gaskets!) or utilisation of advanced metals like Niobium or Tantalum (which are rare and not available in amount). Hence due to the lack of viable alternatives it is our firm believe we by using fluoropolymers and fluoro-elastomers can avoid a significant number or accidents, environmental discharges and loss of productivity (note: clean water risk not to be secured).
Further, in development are circular solutions for recovery of not only raw materials but also e.g. phosphorous (a critical raw material per EU definition) from sewage sludge. Again such development would be hindered, delayed and potentially stopped, if these materials can not be used. Hence there is a significant conflict in goals. Further example of applications in jeopardy are in hydrogen production, fossil free steel production, waste recovery and med tech.
Now, the use of fluoropolymers and fluoro-elastomers etc as materials of construction is not trouble free. Correctly selected type of material (and there are many variants) gives a material which stays intact. The corrosion occurring is often e.g. stress corrosion causing cracks and embrittlement rather than thinning by loss of material form the surface. Further some type materials (e.g. PTFE) has a tendency to float and loose it’s dimensions. Hence end of life is components being almost intact in terms of weight of fluoropolymers or fluoro-elastomers – but having lost the performance – enabling scrapping under controlled conditions. This later is however not implemented in the market.
Hence to avoid injuries, environmental impact, loss of ability to produce within the EU and to allow a more balanced legislation we are hoping for the response from the industry to be taken seriously. We are aware organisations like Euro-Chlor, VDMA and other trade organisation and have in principle similar objections.
In short we find;
• The strive to phase out PFAS is welcome and necessary.
• The ban is however too broad. The use of fluoropolymers or fluoro-elastomers (and ion selective membranes) should be exempted.
• The process for consultation for the industry is ridiculously short and it impossible to give input with the granularity asked for.
• The transition and derogation periods too small. There are in many cases not viable alternatives.
• The proposal as it now threatens largely other relevant goals for the environment and society – the ban on PFAS must be more adapted per relevance

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Baseline Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
"As a plant manufacturer in the field of membrane technology, our company delivers membrane systems in various sizes for different application areas: emission control, product recovery, gas separation, and liquid separation. The membrane systems are used to treat process streams in such a way that the overall process can be optimized, and costs and energy efficiency can be improved, while minimizing environmental impact and enabling the recovery of products (e.g. the recovery of VCM or Ethylene in the production of PVC and PE). These systems allow compliance with regulations, guidelines, standards, and laws regarding the emission of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). While our company as a plant manufacturer is only indirectly affected by the 'Restriction of the manufacturing, placing on the market and use of PFAS', numerous seals and other sealing materials made of fluoropolymers are used in the overall system of the membrane systems, for example in various components, machines, and vessels (pressure vessels, compressors, membrane modules, valves, etc.), due to their high resistance to high and low temperatures and pressures, aggressive and corrosive chemicals, and frequent load changes (PTFE, FKM, FFKM, FEP, FEPM, etc.). In addition, these materials have high wear resistance, impact resistance, UV resistance, and good electrical properties. Fundamentally, fluoropolymers fall under the definition of PFAS. However, among the over 10,000 different PFAS, 38 are fluoropolymers.

These seals and sealing materials made of different fluoropolymers are sourced from suppliers. If there is a 'restriction of the manufacturing, placing on the market and use of PFAS', these seals and sealing materials can no longer be sourced from the suppliers and subsequently used in membrane systems, as the suppliers are not allowed to manufacture and place fluoropolymers on the market. Therefore, our company will not be able to produce, deliver, and maintain existing membrane systems. Maintenance and service intervals for the existing membrane systems will also no longer be possible, as new sealing materials will also be needed, necessitating the inevitable shutdown and decommissioning of the systems to ensure safety and regulated operation. Currently, no alternative materials have been found. That is, there are no alternative sealing materials that meet the high and demanding performance specifications for complex membrane applications, as the seals made of fluoropolymers are indispensable due to their unique properties.

Hence, a possible substitution by other materials is not in any way possible due to the harsh conditions in the processes, such as temperature, pressure, friction, aggressive and corrosive chemicals. There are currently no exceptions for the industrial use of fluoropolymers in the field of mechanical and plant engineering in Table 9 of the Annex XV Restriction Report - Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) and the associated Annex A-G. Therefore, we explicitly recommend that all 38 fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers, among the estimated over 10,000 PFAS, be excluded in principle from the 'restriction of the manufacturing, placing on the market and use of PFAS'.

If our company's already delivered and installed membrane systems (product and vapor recovery systems) from recent years, which are operated in the EU, are no longer maintained and serviced, approximately 260,000 t/a (720 t/d) of hydrocarbons will no longer be recovered and will inevitably emit into the environment, in addition to approximately 365 million m3/a (1 million m3/d) of hydrocarbon vapors, mainly gasoline, from the 'emission control' area. This would result in approximately 2.2 billion CO2 equivalents being additionally emitted into the environment per year, which are currently being retained by modern membrane systems.

Furthermore, no new membrane systems can be manufactured, delivered or operated by our company. Consequently, for each subsequent year in which the 'restriction of the manufacturing, placing on the market and use of PFAS' applies, approximately 18,000 t/a (50 t/d) of environmentally harmful hydrocarbons cannot be recovered and will continue to be released into the atmosphere. Additionally, membrane systems are essential for product recovery, gas separation, and liquid separation as well as for emission control in the context of resource conservation and the circular economy. They play a critical role in increasing energy efficiency and cost-effectiveness, as well as in maintaining and promoting environmental protection.

The emissions released due to the 'restriction of the manufacturing, placing on the market and use of PFAS' will have well-known negative consequences and effects on the environment and the climate since this not only violates some EU directives but these substances also have a significantly higher GWP than CO2. As a result, climate change cannot be effectively addressed and will set back the EU's climate goals by decades.

It is also scientifically proven that there is no danger, exposure, or environmental emissions from fluoropolymers, especially due to the materials FKM, FFKM, PTFE, FEP, and FEPM. These materials are not soluble in water, chemically stable, non-toxic, not bioavailable, not mobile, and therefore do not pose an immediate threat to the environment and human health. Therefore, these fluoropolymers are scientifically considered 'polymers of low concern'. The use and application of these materials have already been approved and standardized in some countries.

As a result of the 'restriction of the manufacturing, placing on the market and use of PFAS', there will be socio-economic impacts, such as health and environmental risks due to the release of hydrocarbons. In addition, a clear technological regression is expected in product recovery, gas separation, liquid separation, emission control, and optimization and efficiency improvement of membrane technology upon the entry into force of the 'restriction of the manufacturing, placing on the market and use of PFAS', the jobs of the current 47 employees of the company would also be at risk.

Furthermore, reference is made to the position papers of the German Mechanical Engineering Industry Association e.V. [4] and the European Mechanical and Plant Engineering Association ORGALIM [5] as well as the Federation of German Industries e.V. In these position papers, detailed socio-economic consequences are discussed upon the entry into force of the 'restriction of the manufacturing, placing on the market and use of PFAS', and the resulting restriction of fluoropolymers. A risk analysis by the British authorities and the resulting recommendations provide a good basis for developing suitable regulatory management options for PFAS." General Comments: Although we of course support all efforts to limit the uncontrolled spread of PFAS in the environment, we criticize that the proposed restriction does not differentiate between fluoropolymers (such as PVDF, ECTFE, FEP, PFA and PTFE as wells as fluoroelastomers - FPM, FFKM, ...) and other PFAS.
We request:
- the restriction proposal to differentiate between the various types of PFAS based of their chemical composition, their toxicological profile and the production method. Not all PFAS are the same and there is no scientific basis to regulate them all the same.
- fluoropolymers to be exempted.
Fluoropolymers use brings significant benefits along the value chain, making them essential in numerous technologies, industrial processes and everyday products. Their chemical inertness and resistance to harsh conditions, corrosion and extreme temperatures (hot and cold) are unique properties, required in a wide range of applications. Banning Fluoropolymers will make it impossible be successful with key initiatives of the European Union: the green deal, the sustainable development goals, energy transition and the European Chips Act.
Most fluoropolymer-based products have been developed to support the EU concept of high safety in the chemical industry, e.g. in chlorine and sulfate production itself and in downstream intermediates such as MNB, TDI, MDI, VCM, HF, etc. The end products are used for all critical purposes, such as environmental protection: climate change mitigation/adaptation, circular economy, water supply sustainability, pollution prevention or biodiversity; human health: public health protection.
Society, governments and the military are affected by the lack of the above products, resulting in missing products and significantly reducing global power.
Any alternative polymer, which has an equivalent link to fluoropolymers, has to provide a same or better compound between the atoms. As a result, these alternatives are expected to show the same long-lasting behavior in the environment.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: We are a 80 FTE manufacturer of pumps and pumps with inner coatings made from fluoropolymers (PTFE, PFA) and we are using seals and gaskets made from fluoropolymers (PTFE) and O-rings made from FKM or FFKM in our pumps made from ceramics or metal alloys. Our pumps and parts are used in industrial applications in all industries worldwide, especially in the chemical and pharmaceutical industries. In the chemical and pharmaceutical industries in particular, goods made from fluoropolymers are used in virtually every plant as flange seals for pipelines, in valves as valve body- and spindle seals and in pumps as gaskets or internal coatings to convey highly aggressive or ultra-pure gases or liquids to protect the environment for spills or to fluid itself for dilution. The corrosion resistance and high temperature suitability of fluoropolymers are the key factors for the use of fluoropolymers in these applications. The corrosion resistance of FP is based on the compound between carbon and fluorine, which is the strongest compound in organic chemistry. Other polymers do not achieve this corrosion resistance because their chemical compound is destroyed earlier. The used fluoropolymers are extremely expensive (much more expensive than any other polymers that might also be considered for such applications), but are not replaceable due to their unique characteristics. With a ban of fluoropolymers, we will lose our complete business, which will also affect a wide range of sub-suppliers even for parts not made from fluoropolymers (metal parts, ceramic parts, electric and electronic devices). Moreover, we cannot imagine how the chemical and pharmaceutical industries worldwide can meet their high safety and environmental standards without these components, which are essential for the tightness and safety and have been tried and tested for decades. We therefore expect not only an end for machine and plant manufacturers in Europe, but also a migration of end customers, i.e. the chemical and pharmaceutical industry, from Europe to Asia, South America and the U.S. Further details can be found in the attachment.
