General Comments: APS Coating Solutions applies coatings based on fluoropolymers for the industry as a whole, more particularly on aeronautical and military safety parts, on elements of nuclear power plants, and medical instruments.

There are critical differences between polymerized and non-polymerized PFAS.
While PFAS are concerns about their environmental impact and potential health risks, it’s important to consider why Fluopropolymers should not be banned outright:
- Fluoropolymers have not been demonstrated to have negative health concerns. The OECD classifies fluoropolymers as polymers of low concern, based on their stability, lack of bioavailability, lack of bioaccumulation, and general absence of observed ill effects (cf. Henry, Barbara J, Joseph P Carlin, Jon A Hammerschmidt, Robert C Buck, L William Buxton, Heidelore Fiedler, Jennifer Seed, and Oscar Hernandez. 2018. “A Critical Review of the Application of Polymer of Low Concern and Regulatory Criteria to Fluoropolymers.” Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management 14 (3): 316–34. https://doi.org/10.1002/ieam.4035).
- PTFE is not soluble in water (and other common solvents) and is not mobile in the environment (cf. Korzeniowski, Stephen H., Robert C. Buck, Robin M. Newkold, Ahmed El kassmi, Evan Laganis, Yasuhiko Matsuoka, Bertrand Dinelli, et al. 2022. “A Critical Review of the Application of Polymer of Low Concern Regulatory Criteria to Fluoropolymers II: Fluoroplastics and Fluoroelastomers.” Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management, August. https://doi.org/10.1002/ieam.4646). The others fluoropolymers (PFA, FEP, PVDF) have the same characteristics.

- In addition, studies have consistently shown that fluoropolymers do not pose a risk to human health, largely due to their inertness, insolubility, and lack of reactive functional groups. A 2022 study by Lee et al. shows that fluoropolymers such as PTFE are safe when ingested (Cf. Lee, Sijoon, Kyung-Ku Kang, Soo-Eun Sung, Joo-Hee Choi, Minkyoung Sung, Keum-Yong Seong, Jian Lee, Subin Kang, Seong Yun Yang, Sunjong Lee, Kyeong-Ryoon Lee, Min-Soo Seo, and KilSoo Kim. 2022. "In Vivo Toxicity and Pharmacokinetics of Polytetrafluoroethylene Microplastics in ICR Mice" Polymers 14, no. 11: 2220. https://doi.org/10.3390/polym14112220). The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has repeatedly investigated the carcinogenicity and toxicity of PTFE, finding it has no toxicological impact, and cannot be classified according to its carcinogenicity (cf. International Agency for Research on Cancer. 1987. “IARC Monographs on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans, Suppl 7, Overall Evaluations of Carcinogenicity: An Updating of IARC Monographs”, Volumes 1 to 42.).

- The connection between POPs and fluoropolymers lies in the fact that some fluoropolymers, particularly those use in the past, were manufactured using chemicals such as PFOA or PFOS. However, there has been a concerted effort to phase out the use of PFOA and PFOS in the production of fluoropolymers

So, even if there are negative impacts on the environment and human health from some chemicals within the wide PFAS family, a group approach of PFAS without any distinction between the many different types, which have varied properties and risk levels, would not be proportionate. Anderson et al presented a review of approaches to grouping PFAS based on factors such as toxicity. Most of the experts in the panel agreed that not all PFAS should be grouped together, that persistence alone is not sufficient for grouping PFAS for the purposes of assessing human health risk, that subgroups are appropriate, and that the nature and definition of the subgroups can only be defined on a situation-dependent and case-by case manner. No single grouping strategy was agreed on that would be sufficient for all regulatory or public health risk assessment purposes (cf. Anderson, J. K., R. W. Brecher, I. T. Cousins, J. DeWitt, H. Fiedler, K. Kannan, C. R. Kirman, et al. 2022. “Grouping of PFAS for Human Health Risk Assessment: Findings from an Independent Panel of Experts.” Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology 134 (October): https://doi.org/10.1016/j.yrtph.2022.105266).
The United Kingdom have also proposed Regulatory Management Options for PFAS and suggest a restriction excluding fluoropolymers: “The restriction(s) set out above need not apply to low hazard groups or low risk uses, for example; fluoroplastics or fluoroelastomers (low hazard groups) […]. These could be highlighted as derogations to any restriction proposal” (cf. 22 Health and Safety Executive. 2023. “Analysis of the most appropriate regulatory management options (RMOA)”. March 2023. https://www.hse.gov.uk/reach/assets/docs/pfas-rmoa.pdf).


So, the restriction proposal should take into consideration the difference in risk and exposure between fluoropolymers and non-polymeric PFAS.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Incineration, recycling and landfilling are all likely to adequately address the possibility of PFAS emissions, and consequently manufactured products containing PFAS unlikely to represent a risk to human health or the environment if proper waste management measures are put in place.   RIVM (Dutch National Institute for Public Health and the Environment) incineration review states that PTFE is stable at 260 °C without loss of mass (cf. J. Bakker | B. Bokkers | M. Broekman, RIVM report 2021-0143. https://rivm.openrepository.com/handle/10029/625409).   Guelfo et al also reiterate the inertness of PTFE and its lack of reactivity in the environment (cf. Guelfo, Jennifer L., Stephen Korzeniowski, Marc A. Mills, Janet Anderson, Richard H. Anderson, Jennifer A. Arblaster, Jason M. Conder, et al. 2021. “Environmental Sources, Chemistry, Fate, and Transport of Per‐ and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances: State of the Science, Key Knowledge Gaps, and Recommendations Presented at the August 2019 SETAC Focus Topic Meeting.” Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry 40 (12): 3234–60. https://doi.org/ 10.1002/etc.5182).   Fluoropolymers, including PTFE, are completely destroyed under specific incinerator operating conditions. Yamada et al. studied textiles and paper treated with fluorotelomers at temperatures of 1,000 °C and residual times of 2 seconds. They found that they will be destroyed and will not be a source of PFOA in the environment (cf. Yamada, Takahiro, Philip H. Taylor, Robert C. Buck, Mary A. Kaiser, and Robert J. Giraud. 2005. “Thermal Degradation of Fluorotelomer Treated Articles and Related Materials.” Chemosphere 61 (7): 974–84. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chemosphere.2005.03.025). According to a 2019 study from the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, municipal incineration of PTFE did not result in significant generation of studied PFAS at temperatures between 870 and 1 020 °C. Instead, the PFAS degraded mainly into hydrofluoric acid and carbon dioxide (cf. Aleksandrov, Krasimir, Hans-Joachim Gehrmann, Manuela Hauser, Hartmut Mätzing, Daniel Pigeon, Dieter Stapf, and Manuela Wexler. 2019. “Waste Incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to Evaluate Potential Formation of Per- and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) in Flue Gas.” Chemosphere 226 (July): 898–906. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chemosphere.2019.03.191). According to a 2021 report by the Dutch RIVM, PTFE is reduced to a fully mineralized state after 2 seconds of incineration at 850 °C. At incinerator bed temperatures, which generally range between 900 and 1 100 °C, PTFE and other fluorinated polymers are expected to fully degrade into small fluorocarbon molecules. For a high degree of thermal degradation, temperatures higher than 850 °C are required (cf. Bakker, J., B. Bokkers, and M. Broekman. 2021. “Per- and Polyfluorinated Substances in Waste Incinerator Flue Gases.” Rijksinstituut voor Volksgezondheid en Milieu RIVM. December 8, 2021. https://rivm.openrepository. com/handle/10029/625409).

General Comments: Aquatis Inc is a consulting company for water and wastewater treatment. The scientists working for Aquatis have together more than 50 years of experience in leading positions in membrane development, membrane production, and membrane application. A large part of our activities focused on dealing with membranes made of polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) for various applications in water filtration. These membranes find use as membranes for ultrafiltration (UF), microfiltration and membrane bioreactor filtration (MBR).

We support the efforts of ECHA to reduce the risks associated with hazardous substances to the community and in this specific case the proposed regulations for restriction of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs).

However, we want to emphasize that there needs to be a balance between the potential risk of PVDF as a PFAS and the substantial health benefits that is provided by PVDF membranes.

We are asking for an exception or exemption of PVDF from the proposed restriction because of the merits of PVDF filtration membranes for the public health and because PVDF can be mineralised without forming PFASs.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: We appreciate the opportunity to present this submission to indicate the profound differences between fluorinated polymers in general and specifically PVDF on the one side and  smaller molecules of PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) on the other side.   We would also like to point out that in the whole Annex XV report the important product group of polymeric membranes, especially polymeric membranes for use in water filtration has not been mentioned. These membranes find use as membranes for ultrafiltration (UF), microfiltration, membrane bioreactor filtration (MBR) and in pharmaceutical applications.        a) Difference between polymers classified as PFAS and other PFAS materials  In contrast to the  non-polymeric PFASs, the polymeric PFASs are not water soluble or spread in the environment and the main concern is that these polymers will eventually  degrade to persistent PFASs. The Restriction Report makes exceptions for “... a few specific PFAS subgroups with combinations of key structural elements for which it can be expected that they will ultimately mineralize in the environment. …”  As explained under point e) we recommend using these exceptions for PVDF homopolymers as well, if these PVDF polymers are produced without use of other PFASs, for example by using suspension polymerisation.   B) unique chemical structure of PVDF PVDF has a unique chemical structure  among all other fluorinated polymers. It has the repeating unit [ -CF2-CH2-]. This means the carbon atoms in the chain have alternating either two hydrogen or two fluoride atoms attached. This structure is unique among all other fluorinated polymers crating the only chemical weakness of this polymer. The strong electronegativity of the fluoride atoms is creating a partial polarisation of the molecule and makes the hydrogen atoms susceptible to attack by strong bases, especially at higher concentrations and at higher temperatures.  This will be discussed in more detail in section 3 of the form.  As explained in the introduction, as a hydrophobic polymer, PVDF is not soluble in water in contrast to the non-polymeric PFASs which have some water solubility and which spread in the environment. As such PVDF is not a dangerous material. It is only the potential degradation of the polymer that could generate PFASs. However in the case of PVDF this can be avoided by choosing the proper conditions.     c) Filtration market  Due to its unique combination of properties PVDF is the most used polymer for all kinds of water filtration, like microfiltration or ultrafiltration for the preparation of drinking water; prefiltration for reverse osmosis plants; filtration in membrane bioreactors or for pharma applications. https://www.gminsights.com/industry-analysis/pvdf-membrane-market#:~:text=PVDF%20Membrane%20Market%20size%20was,USD%201624.4%20million%20by%202032.  Compared to polyester sulfone (PES), the second most used polymer in these membrane applications PVDF has much better mechanical properties, and hollow fibre membranes from PVDF are much more robust and less prone to breakage in comparison to other materials. https://www.academia.edu/50725868/Tensile_and_Surface_Mechanical_Properties_of_Polyethersulphone_PES_and_Polyvinylidene_Fluoride_PVDF_Membranes   The PVDF membrane market size had a valuation of USD 721 Million in 2022. It is expected that the market will reach a valuation of USD 1,439.78 Million by 2030. https://www.verifiedmarketresearch.com/product/pvdf-membrane-market/    d) Treatment of PVDF as waste during production and at its end of life  PVDF as polymer does not have the properties of PFASs. But as with all fluoro polymers there is a risk that degradation of the polymer can create smaller molecules with PFAS character.  In contrast to the non-polymeric PFASs the polymers considered as PFASs are easier to keep separate from the natural environment because they are solid polymers which are essentially insoluble in water. As solids they are also easier to collect and to concentrate if they get into the environment. As the collection process can lead to essentially 100% concentration, the disposal or mineralisation of polymers is much easier for polymers than for non-polymeric PFASs. More details will be given in chapter 5.     e) Except PVDF by adjusting the definition of PFAS   The ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT under point  1.1.1. describes the exclusion of substances that only contain the following structural elements is excluded from the scope of the proposed restriction:  CF3-X or X-CF2-X’, where X = -OR or -NRR’  and X’ = methyl (-CH3), methylene (-CH2-), an aromatic group, a carbonyl group (-C(O)-), -OR’’, -SR’’ or –NR’’R’’’. This exclusion exists because components of such a structure are easier to decompose than PFASs. This is at least partially based on the combination of -CF2- and -CH2- groups or other groups presenting an opportunity for chemical elimination reaction of fluoride from the specific molecule leading eventually to complete mineralisation and putting these substances outside the definition for PFAS. PVDF has the alternating groups -CF2- and -CH2- and can be chemically attacked by strong bases as explained further down in the chapter 3 ‘Emissions in the end-of-life phase’. In the case of PVDF the group X is not  -OR or -NRR’ but  -CH2-.  The -CH2- group presents a chemical weakness in the molecule similar to -OR and -NRR’. In addition the -CH2- group provides less polarity than -OR or -NRR. This reduces the water solubility of potential degradation products.  Based on this we suggest to change the formulation of the exclusion to: … substances that only contain the following structural elements is excluded from the scope of the proposed restriction:  CF3-X or X-CF2-X’, where X = -OR or -NRR or -CH2-’  and X’ = methyl (-CH3), methylene (-CH2-), an aromatic group, a carbonyl group (-C(O)-), -OR’’, -SR’’ or –NR’’R’’’.  This would exclude PVDF homopolymers from the proposed restriction.    f) Exemption for PVDF  If it is no possible put PVDF in the group of excepted materials as described in e),  for the reasons laid out above, we recommend an exemption for PVDF from restrictions in the report. This could be further specified by regulating the non-use of PFASs as processing aids in the production of PVDF. The exemption could also be given specifically for the use of filtration membranes with the condition that both production waste and end-of-lifetime products from PVDF membranes must be treated in a specific ways. More details are given in chapter 3 to the specific information requests.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Both production waste from PVDF membranes and membranes at the end-of-life phase can be treated in several safe ways without forming PFASs.    a) Landfill. PVDF membranes can be safely put to landfill. As the behaviour of fluorinated polymers has been part of the discussion process in relation to the restriction of PFASs , this may not be the best option.   b) Incineration. Fluoropolymers can be safely treated in incineration plants without emitting PFASs as described in recent publications.    https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0045653519306435   c) Chemical dehydro-fluorination of PVDF. PVDF has a unique chemical structure with the repeating unit [ -CF2-CH2-]. This means the carbon atoms in the chain have alternating either two hydrogen or two fluoride atoms attached. This structure is unique among all other fluorinated polymers crating the only chemical weakness of this polymer. The strong electronegativity of the fluoride atoms is creating a partial polarisation of the molecule and makes the hydrogen atoms susceptible to attack by strong bases, especially at higher concentrations and at higher temperatures.  This reaction is described in detail here: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0032386199003432   This can be used to mineralise PVDF in an autoclave with a base and a temperature of 250 degrees C. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0014305722007285   d) Recovery of fluoride as CaF2. Driven by the need to deal with waste from lithium batteries, methods are in development that not only mineralise PVDF but which will also recover most fluoride as calcium fluoride at a high yield. https://pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acssuschemeng.9b01546

6. Missing uses: The use of PVDF in filtration membranes is described in section 1 paragraph c).

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Architen Landrell are a designer and manufacturer of tensile membrane structures and iconic features based in Chepstow, UK, with our roots dating back to the 1980s and a portfolio of over 6000 installations in 48 countries. We work primarily in the Construction Sector with projects associated with all building types and in particular roofing and shade structures relating to transport hubs, sports and recreational facilities, educational facilities, office atria and other recreational buildings.

We are active members of the TensiNet Association, including their Working Group on Sustainability. TensiNet is an EU based association which brings together trade professionals and academics across the lightweight structures industry to promote best practice. We support their ECHA PFAS consultation response submission and refer the reader to this for a wider description of our industry and a source of useful industry and academic led research, EPDs and other technical information regarding the performance of the materials we employ in our projects and identified below.

Whilst technically we are not directly affected by the restriction, as we are based in the UK, the proposal would directly impact our supply chain. We have a longstanding relationship with many European-based suppliers, built on many years of trust and mutual understanding. We source significant quantities of our materials from Europe because we respect the quality and reliability of the products. Significant changes to this will not only negatively impact our business, but also constrict trade with the EU. We have also yet to assess the impact on additional transport costs and emissions which are likely to result as we expand our supply chain more globally to compensate.

Architen Landrell request an exemption of all fluoropolymers from the PFAS Restriction Proposal under REACH regulation. By grouping all various PFAS substances together and restricting them as a single class, the proposed PFAS Restriction would restrict numerous PFAS substances which have not been risk-assessed and for which no acceptable risk has been demonstrated. Credible and/or equal alternatives have not been identified in the Consultation documentation and as such, there appears to be no basis for inclusion of the materials impacted (as identified in subsequent sections of this response) or indeed, no basis for an immediate restriction without derogation.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Architen Landrell use a wide variety of membrane materials, selected based on their properties including strength, light transmittance, fire resistance and longevity. Typically, Architectural Membranes (as referenced in Annex XV Table 9) are supplied on rolls which are then cut into engineered pattern shapes. The individual pieces are welded together, using a variety of technologies, in order to form a 3D surface which is then tensioned in conjunction with a structural frame or assembly of members.  The materials which we perceive as potentially falling directly under the proposed PFAS restriction include: - ETFE (Ethylene Tetrafluoroethylene) single polymer foils for multi-layer inflated cushions (eg The Eden Project, Excel London, Bordeaux University Atrium, Leicester City FC training ground). - PTFE (Polytetraflouroethylene) coated glass fibre fabric used for architectural fabric roof structures (eg. Millennium Dome/O2 Arena Greenwich, Brent Cross Rail Interchange (UK)) - FEP (Fluorinated Ethylene Propylene) tape is used as a seam interlayer for joining PTFE coated glass membranes. - PVC coated polyester fabric which may include PVDF (Polyvinylidene Difluoride) coating for extending service life. (eg. Ashford Designer Outlet (UK), Darien Lakes Amphitheatre (US), Butlins Holiday Centres (three sites in the UK).  Architen's usage of each type of membrane varies from year to year dependent on project requirements. Over the past two years, the average split by area between ETFE, PTFE and PVC products has been approximately 4%, 7%, 89% respectively, with about 40% of the PVC throughput carrying a PVDF topcoat.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: We do not have data specifically relating to PFAS chemicals but advise on the Architectural Membranes themselves. Specific emission and impact data is provided by the suppliers and referenced within the Tensinet Association consultation response. From our manufacturing perspective: ETFE foils - During fabrication (manufacture) stage of a project, wastage is small at around 5% due to optimized nesting of cutting patterns. All offcuts and waste are 100% recycled through a scheme with Marubeni in Europe which results in lower grade granulate. In-use stage and maintenance through life time (typically 40 years) result in minimal amounts of waste, which is also 100% recycled. At end-of-life, we offer take-back of old or damaged assemblies which are also 100% recycled. PTFE/Glass - During fabrication of a project, wastage is around 10% due to optimized nesting of cutting patterns but will vary from project to project. All offcuts and waste enter our normal waste stream and until recently, we are advised that this is 100% landfill although latest reports from our waste handler advise a landfill diversion of between 60 to 100%, presumably to incineration. In-use stage and maintenance through life time (typically 50 years) result in minimal amounts of waste. This would be placed in the same waste stream as fabrication waste. At end-of-life, we would offer take-back of old or damaged assemblies although we are not aware of any of our PTFE structures which have reached that stage in recent years, or have not been made aware of such by the Owner. PVC/PES - During fabrication of a project, wastage is around 15% due to optimized nesting of cutting patterns but will vary from project to project. As with PTFE/Glass membranes, all offcuts and waste enter our normal waste stream and until recently, we are advised that this is 100% landfill although latest reports from our waste handler advise a landfill diversion of between 60 to 100%, presumably to incineration. In-use stage and maintenance through life time (typically 25 years) result in minimal amounts of waste. This would be placed in the same waste stream as fabrication waste. At end-of-life, we offer take-back of old or damaged assemblies which enter our usual waste stream. A small percentage of pre-consumer waste is re-used in small local projects. We are currently investigating options for re-use of end-of-life structures, and looking into options for commercial recycling. Unfortunately, schemes which we have used previously no longer exist (Texyloop) and other schemes are potentially cost prohibitive as they are not UK-based. Under current proposals set out in the PFAS regulations, then our understanding would be that the European options for recycling would cease to exist anyway.

5. Proposed derogations: ETFE is not within current proposed derogations so section 5 is not applicable. In any case, the PFAS data would be within the knowledge of the producer.

6. Missing uses: a. To our knowledge, and in line with the information provided by the manufacturers of the roll goods we use, we are not aware of any emissions of PFAS to the environment during our manufacturing phase, use cases over lifetime, or at end of life scenarios.  b. Use case 1, "Architectural Membranes, Pure Fluoropolymers" ETFE film/foil is used in high end applications and permanent buildings as single and multi-layer constructions. This is notably different to the application listed as "Greenhouses" in the ECHA Appendix XV. The key functionalities are: - High strength to weight ratio providing efficient structural use, and better than clear, solid/flexible alternatives - Single material product, providing the most effective end-of-life recycling opportunity of all the range of membranes we use, as it is 100% recyclable and is 100% recycled. - High light transmission, across a range of wavelengths and better than glass. - Long life, minimising average annual environmental impact over time and performing better than other clear membranes - Low maintenance, reducing use of material and impacts from transport to site  Appendix XV does not appear to explicitly reference this application of ETFE foil. Where it is referred to in Annex E, there is a statement regarding the availability of alternatives, but with experience dating back to the 1980's, Architen Landrell are not aware of what these equivalent alternatives could be? We would be interested to find out so as to evaluate them against ETFE solutions though.    Use case 2, "Architectural Membranes: Composite membranes with top coating" Coatings within PTFE/glass and PVDF enhanced PVC coated PES improve the long term performance of the product and add a certain degree of 'self cleaning' (reduced tendency for dirt to adhere to surface when subject to rainwater and clean cycles). This reduces the quantity of detergents and water required during routine maintenance and cleaning, typically scheduled to be yearly after the first 3 years (or sometimes after ' installation' for PVC based membranes). Quantities will be dependent on project specifics, but annual detergent consumption is typically around 200L per year, which could easily double or more if alternatives required more intensive cleaning. The improved coating also translates to a longer life expectancy and more favourable warranties for the Client, providing better risk certainty to underpin their captial and operational expenditure. As a coated fabric option, PTFE/glass is also the goto product for best fire resistance, meeting the highest certification standards in the UK, EU and US.  c. It is not possible to identify specific companies who will be affected by the restriction. Whilst the UK is not currently subject directly to the proposed PFAS restrictions, most of the specialist membrane fabrication companies in the UK using materials affected by the restrictions will rely exclusively or predominantly on products imported from the EU. The restriction would thus force import from other geographical areas. By our estimation, the number of fabrication companies who provide similar services to Architen Landrell and who will be impacted will number in the region of 10 to 20 in the UK, with potential impacts to their third party suppliers or Business-to-Business clients well in excess of 100.  d. Within Annex E.2.13 of Appendix XV, it is stated that alternatives exist for Architectural Membranes under both sub headings of (a) Composite membranes with top coating and (b) pure fluoropolymers. In both cases it states that this would be associated with reduced functionality and consequential shorter life. In our opinion this is not providing an acceptable alternative. Architen Landrell are certainly not familiar with a viable equal alternative for (b) unless changing to a non-membrane product which will either have cost, weight, fire or higher Global Warming Potential (GWP) impact, amongst other considerations.  For (a) - coated membranes - the use of lesser products may be possible should the client wish to replace it two, three or four times more often than would be required for a higher specification (albeit PFAS impacted) product; PVC coated membranes are available widely without PVDF top coats. However, clearly the risk of a resultant higher overall cost, client business interruption or impact, anticipated higher net environmental impact etc, may sway the client not to adopt a membrane solution at all, leading to a more carbon intensive solution (lightweight membrane structures are generally considered to be lower carbon intensive than comparable solutions) with consequent socio-economic impact on the membrane industry as a whole.  Silicone coated fabrics are not widely available in grades to suit architectural applications. Their fabrication process often relies on heat-cured glues and challenges the realisation of smooth 3-dimensional forms. As such it is less practical and more time consuming to use for many structures, and less economically feasible. Also refer to response under f(ii) citing experience in US where Silicone coated glass fibre product failed to achieve market impact in the 1990s as a result of these issues.  e. Architen Landrell would refer to (and rely on) the membrane producers for new product development insights and challenges, but we understand timescales are in the order of many years, and not months. Please also refer to the response in f(ii) for information regarding adoption timescales for new products once put into the market place . As part of our own R&D activity we are evaluating more environmentally conscious materials as a matter of course (although not necessarily PFAS free). As a small company, we do not have a large R&D team, so this activity runs alongside our current operations. Each option may take as little as three months but often a year or more to evaluate, depending on the level of information available from the supplier and risks associated with end use.  f. (i) Since, for the most part, the process of substitution (if indeed such exist) is not within our control as an intermediate user/fabricator we are unable to answer directly regarding roll material production. However, from a fabrication perspective, once new materials have been scrutinised and accepted as viable, acquisition of new machinery (many newer coating developments require different welding machinery to the current options), would depend on the technology required for the particular product. As a guide, these primary machines may cost within the region of €20k to  €100k. We currently have seven primary welding machines of different types, which provides an indication of the level of capital expenditure required if these were to require replacement.  f. (ii) Since, for the most part, the process of substitution (if indeed such exist) is not within our control as an intermediate user/fabricator we are unable to answer directly. However, we are aware that the timescales of introducing new membranes into the construction sector supply chain and for them to be adopted by the sector is a lengthy journey, even after they have been developed. Some examples from our experience: ETFE foil structures took around 10 years or more to be fully accepted as an alternative in the UK (1989 Westminster & Chelsea Hospital to 1999 The Eden Project) even though they were already in use in continental Europe. A similar or longer period was required through the 1990s and 2000s in the US where approvals, especially for fire certification, vary from state to state. The story is similar for newer coated fabrics. In the US, Silicone coated glass fibre as a replacement for PTFE coated glass was developed by DCI in the 1990s over a period of at least 5 years, but failed to break into the market. Even within our company, whilst often early adopters, new membranes will take 2 to 3 years to be evaluated and again take several times that period to reach any significant market share. This is a result of risks to adopting unproven materials driven by the market and insurance provision and relating to longevity and performance in fire. From a fabrication perspective, once new materials have been scrutinised and accepted as viable, planning, acquisition and installation of new machinery (if required) followed by procedural development and training of operatives would be estimated to require a further 1 to 3 years.  f. (iii) In the case of ETFE, we are not aware of any functionally equivalent products and would surmise that any alternative would be incompatible with existing materials. As such it would not be possible to repair any such structures with material sourced from the EU, and no structures within the EU could be repaired (even assuming that existing ETFE products will remain available outside of the EU). Thus all existing Clients/Owners of ETFE clad buildings dating from typically the 1980's (assuming a design life of 40yrs) would be impacted and would be required to replace their structures in the whole, irrespective of the amount of deterioration or damage ie they could not be repaired. This would come at a considerable financial and environmental cost. It will impact all installations over the past 40 yrs, along with projects which will have been in development over the past 5 years but yet to be built/completed, and those structures about to be built where Clients will have an expectation of a 30 to 40 year life for their new investment.  f. (iv) As we are based in the UK, we can identify two groups of providers who would benefit: a. Those companies who can provide alternative products with an equal or near equal performance (although as stated, alternatives are either unknown or limited). b. Those companies outside of the EU who will be able to provide the same/equal products which are no longer available within the EU.  g. As a manufacturer using products which may fall under the PFAS restrictions, we are only able to comment on direct impacts to our own business. Current estimation is that should the PFAS restriction come into force, potentially 50% of our project throughput would be affected. The market share of structures we install or maintain within continental EU is relatively small at around 5%. However, the share of products we source from the EU is significant and amounts to an estimated 80% or more of those affected by the restriction. All of this would initially need to be sourced globally rather than from the EU, at a cost of well in excess of £200k. As the UK will not be directly subject to the restriction, our perception of immediate impact on the business would be: - Turnover: Low impact. Other projects would substitute for lost EU projects, or lower performance membranes would need to be employed. - Employee: Low impact as employee count is unlikely to be affected. - Competitiveness and profit: It is less clear how this may be affected. There will be less competition from EU fabricators as they will be unable to provide structures to UK (unless they moved operations out of the EU). Profits however may be impacted negatively by higher transportation costs, and potentially higher material costs until local (UK) stock holders establish alternative supply chains for non-EU products.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: The derogations listed in Annex XV do not appear to apply to the use cases we are actively involved in as product users/fabricators. However, in reference to our entries under section 6, it should be clear that we would strongly recommend, as a bare minimum, that a derogation be introduced for the use of ETFE foils and repair tapes as architectural membranes in order to enable the repair and or replacement of existing, current and new structures for a period of at least 40 years. This will: i. enable the continued performance of these low impact structures, ii. prevent premature end of life which would have a catastrophic impact on the LCA of these installations iii. mitigate unnecessary CO2e emissions for their replacements, and iv. avoid significant, currently unmeasurable, financial for current and future owners and clients  For architectural membranes generally, short of fully excluding them from the proposed PFAS restriction (as our preference), we respectfully request that further derogations should be considered until such time as reasonable alternatives are made available and proven, which we do not believe is currently the case, despite the statements in the report.

General Comments: Arkema is a global chemicals manufacturer, focusing on innovative and sustainable materials, driven by the challenges of new energies, new technologies, the depletion of resources, mobility, and increasing urbanization. This submission focuses on the proposed restriction for fluorinated gases (F-gases). Arkema manufactures and imports into the EU various fluorinated gases, as pure substances, and blends.
Based on the content of the PFAS restriction proposal, Arkema has submitted a response that provides clarification and scientific and technical evidence to fill some gaps in the current Annex XV report in connection with the modern F-gases that it places on the European market. While information relevant at sectoral level is submitted via our trade association, The European FluoroCarbons Technical Committee (EFCTC), Arkema’s submission focuses on the properties of the modern F-gases and uses which are missing or are poorly covered by the restriction report, and for which derogations are justified.
In the section B.1.3. Justification for grouping of Annex B of the restriction proposal it is stated: “If there are specific PFASs for which sufficient evidence is provided that the perfluorinated moiety is fully degraded at a rate which indicates them not to be persistent, resulting in a substance/ substances which is/ are not a PFAS, then those substances / groups should be considered excluded from the scope”. Arkema would like to emphasize that the inclusion in/ exclusion from the scope of the restriction should be more granular and based on the presence / absence of the “unacceptable risk” in the meaning of REACH, that is, it should consider the risk profile of the substance itself and the degradation products. Moreover, it should be noted that the F-gases included in the scope of the restriction proposal may vary as regards their chemical structure, degradation patterns and yield of TFA resulted from atmospheric degradation.
As regards the uses of F-gases, we note that the report does not contain any detailed assessment of the alternatives identified & proposed. Indeed (i) some of these alternatives are inappropriate from a technical or toxicological point of view, and some other alternatives are based on chemicals which are being phased out under other sectoral legislation ; (ii) for most of the proposed restrictions concerning the F-gases, alternatives have not been identified, neither a socio-economic assessment has been done.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Arkema, a PVDF fluoropolymer producer, welcomes the opportunity to share data and information in the context of evolution of the EU restriction proposal on PFAS. A first submission made in June focused on the data sharing on safety during the life cycle including toxicological and ecotoxicological information, emissions along the whole life cycle, end-of-life management, and socio-economic impacts. In its first submission, Arkema recommended that fluoropolymers produced without PFAS polymerization aids should be exempted.
This second submission focus on sharing available information on applications and markets, product properties, existence and viability of alternatives, emissions along the life cycle by application.
Those data are supported by technical references and provided in respect of the scientific approach of Reach regulation that must remain the rule for risk analysis.
Kynar® FSF® PVDF homopolymers and copolymers are produced without the use of PFAS polymerization aids and are used in industrial applications. They are designed for extreme inertness in harsh environments, flame & smoke properties, weather resistance, durability, and ease of processing. They are of strategic importance for European industry and sovereignty as well as the EU Green Deal, the Chips Act, the Net zero industry act and the Sustainable and Smart Mobility Strategy, the EU water protection and management.
10 key markets are described in detail in this answer to the public consultation:
1. The chemical processing industries
Kynar® FSF® PVDF is used in piping, pumps, valves used for transportation of corrosive chemicals within the chemical process industry ensuring a safe and durable functioning of chemical production plants.
2. Oil & Gas transportation
Kynar® FSF® PVDF is used in Oil & Gas flexibles supporting the development of mobile floating units while resisting to external extreme conditions and to aggressive products preventing leakages during the 20 years+ lifetime required by the standard with which the installation should comply.
3. Semi-conductors manufacturing
Kynar® FSF® PVDF is used for ultra-pure water transportation which is an essential and unavoidable element of semi-conductors manufacturing plants. PVDF is a material of choice in this application due to its unparalleled high purity and inertness properties. As of today, only PDVF is compliant with the specific standards set of this application regarding absence of leachable and metallic contaminants.
4. Construction coatings
Kynar® FSF® PVDF is used in architectural metal coatings formulation providing unparalleled protection against weathering, aging and pollution. Due to its long life (more than 50 years and counting) without mechanical degradation or color fading, Kynar® FSF® PVDF construction coatings offer the best durability and product performance.
5. Lithium-Ion Batteries
Kynar® FSF® PVDF is used as cathode binder and separator coatings in Li-Ion batteries. The separator between the cathode and the anode material prevents short circuit while allowing ions movement, ensuring safety of usage during the whole lifetime of the battery. The cathode binder ensures adhesion of conductive material to the metal substrate and thus the electrode integrity during the whole lifetime of the battery. As it is a quite new application, PVDF has been included since the beginning of the Li-Ion battery technology development and design.



6. Water Filtration Membranes
Kynar® FSF® PVDF is used to produce wastewater filtration membranes. PVDF offers specific properties for high-end membranes like superior resistance to the cleaning chemicals used in the wastewater treatments and in terms of efficiency of pathogen/virus removal, guaranteeing a safety of usage during the whole life time of the filtration membrane.
7. Flexible Photovoltaic Cell Manufacturing,
Kynar® FSF® PVDF is used as a film in the multilayer construction of photovoltaic panels. It provides transparency while UV and moisture protection to other components of the panels during the whole lifetime of the panels.
8. Sterile filtration and aseptic processing for the pharmaceutical industries
Kynar® FSF® PVDF is used in many filtration articles within the pharmaceutical industry: for vaccines production, for sterilization of cancer therapies, for syringe filters used for treatments and blood analysis. PVDF is the only material enabling to reach pore size small enough to remove virus efficiently.
9. Wire and Cables
Kynar® FSF® PVDF is widely used as an insulation material, protecting cables from external aggression (mechanical and chemical) and providing flame & smoke resistance. It is a crucial material that complies with safety standard in building construction.
10. Polymer Processing and Recycling Aids
Kynar® FSF® PVDF is used as an additive in polyolefins allowing a lower processing temperature, reducing waste during extrusion and allowing end of life management with recyclability enabled by better processability.
Regarding the End Of Life management, PVDF, as a thermoplastic polymer, provides the advantage to be mechanically recyclable or fully mineralized through incineration in many of the applications described.
For all those applications Kynar® FSF® PVDF has been selected for its unique combination of properties that enables to guarantee the safety and durable performance during the whole life time.
Based on the Scientific and Economic data provided in this answer to the public consultation, as mentioned in Arkema’s preferred option is to support a more segmented approach based on the level of risk of the substance to facilitate the effectiveness and the implementation of the restriction.
In conclusion, within this approach and as stated in Arkema’s first answer to the public consultation, Arkema considers that fluoropolymers produced without PFAS polymerization aids should be exempted. General Comments: Arnika welcomes the uPFAS restriction proposal, which has high ambition to stop the PFAS pollution from majority of sources. We applaud the dossier submitters to include the entire class of chemicals based on the persistence and include fluoropolymers as well as F-gases in the scope of this restrictions.
There is clear and unequivocal evidence that demonstrates global contamination of the environment, wildlife and human populations by PFAS - the most persistent human-made chemicals known to date. PFAS pose an unacceptable risk for both current and future generations due to their extreme persistence, and the scientific evidence that links exposure to harmful impacts on wildlife and human health.
Widespread PFAS-use has created an irreversible toxic legacy of global contamination. It is therefore vital for the EU to adopt an effective PFAS regulation to become an example for similar restrictions at the UN level (via Stockholm Convention) and in other world regions.
Due to their high persistence and extensive use, PFAS have become a global issue of concern. Scientists have warned against poorly reversible exposures and the overall underestimation of the risks associated with their widespread uses.  For the European Economic Area (EEA) alone, the annual health-related costs associated with PFAS exposure are estimated to EUR 52-84 billion.
We also applaud the dossier submitters to base the restriction on persistence. As the leading scientist on PFAS prof. Martin Scheringer points out: “Persistence has been seen as a property that merely indicates the presence of a chemical in a given environment. It may seem that persistent chemicals are inert and thus relatively benign. However, they still have many ways to interfere with an organism’s physiology and cause adverse effects. Therefore, persistence is a property that makes the toxicity of any chemical much worse because it leads to—as long as uses and corresponding emissions are ongoing—ever-increasing concentrations, and toxic effects will manifest at some point. In other words, persistence acts as a multiplier of toxicity.”
More detailed information to be found in the attachement.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: PFAS Incineration PFAS are almost impossible to destroy, even high temperature thermal treatment does not guarantee their full break down.  To really get rid of PFAS, incineration at 1400 ºC is required. At lower temperatures, PFAS degrade to shorter PFAS and eventually end up as extremely persistent ultra-short PFAS, of which some have high global warming potential. Municipal waste incinerators contribute to the increasing environmental pollution with PFAS. To minimize the emission, PFAS containing products and materials should be handled with great caution. EC, ECHA and member states shall consider treating all PFAS waste like POPs-containing waste as dealt with under the EU POPs Regulation. Facilities manufacturing e.g. PFAS-treated paper emit PFAS into the air and wastewater and pollute the surrounding environment. , ,  Most of the types of fast-food packaging investigated in our studies are likely to end up in landfills or be incinerated, since the food residues prevent them from being recycled. Disposal of PFAS-treated food contact materials in municipal incinerators leads to emissions of PFAS, fluorinated greenhouse gases and other products of incomplete combustion to the surrounding environment. , ,  Some PFAS remain in the after-incineration fly ash,  and then contribute to the further environmental exposures when the fly ash is landfilled or used in construction materials.  Only specialised non-combustion technologies seem to offer some hope in fully destroying them. , ,  The disposal of PFAS-treated products in municipal incinerators leads to the emission of products of incomplete combustion, including PFAS and long-lived, potent greenhouse gases.  Some PFAS also remain in the ash residues, generating further waste contaminated with PFAS.  Some studies also demonstrate the release of fluorinated greenhouse gases from incineration. Discarding PFAS-treated consumer products with general household waste, whether to landfill or incineration, ultimately acts as a source of emissions to the environment.   Because of the PFAS emission from incineration and the very complicated ways and yet to be developed and widely implemented technologies for PFAS destruction, it is vital to adopt as wide universal PFAS restriction proposal, which covers the entire class of PFAS, fluoropolymers and F-gases. 10. Analytical methods: Laboratory methods  Arnika had various consumer product samples analyzed for the presence of individual PFAS substances. In a few studies, we additionally compared the individual PFAS contamination with the total organic fluorine content. We recommend using the methodology of Total organic/extractable fluorine content for determining the PFAS content in consumer products as they better illustrate the width of PFAS contamination.   Total Organic Fluorine (TOF) The TOF method was originally developed for Danish authorities to test compliance with their legal ban of PFAS in paper/board food contact materials and is considered as an accepted proxy for total PFAS content. The accredited lab analysis of food contact paper packaging was performed by Eurofins Product Testing in Denmark using the accredited and validated method DIN 51723.  Fluorinated substances are degraded in a combustion process into hydrogen fluoride, which is quantitatively collected in an impinge with a buffer solution. The amount of collected hydrogen fluoride is determined by ion chromatography. The expanded uncertainty of the method is 30% and the detection limit is 0.33 mg/kg dry weight (dw). The TOF results can be compared with the Danish guided indicator value of 20 mg/kg dw TOF that was established as a means of differentiating between intentionally added PFAS and background levels of PFAS in paper/board food contact materials. In our survey into single-use paper and compostable food packaging and tableware, the total organic fluorine (TOF) test provided an indication of total PFAS content in the samples and helped identify the most heavily PFAS-treated group of samples - compostables made of sugarcane and wheat moulded fibre, followed by takeaway packaging for fatty foods. Gas/liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry provided quantification of specific PFAS present in the samples and specific profiles of the most frequently identified PFAS - 6:2 FTOH. However, based on the mass balance calculations, only 1% of the organic fluorine present in our samples has been identified by targeted, compound-specific analysis of 55 PFAS. It might be relevant to include the method of the total oxidisable precursors (TOP assay) in future research on PFAS in food contact materials, because that analytical technique helps to identify additional PFAS such as the ones built in to the structure of fluorinated polymers. In our next rounds of testing of food contact papers, the sample extraction methods were used to extract organic fluorine and remove inorganic fluorine prior to analysis. The organofluorine content remaining after extraction, i.e., total extractable organofluorine (TEOF) content, was used as an approximation of the PFAS contamination. With this approach, calculation of mass balance better represents the proportion of the organic fluorine presented in our samples identified by targeted, compound-specific analysis of individual PFAS. The TOF results were compared with the Danish guided indicator value of 20 mg/kg dw TOF that was established as a means of differentiating between intentionally added PFAS and background levels of PFAS in paper/board food contact materials.  Targeted PFAS analysis Targeted analysis applied in Arnika studies covered 55 specific PFAS substances and was performed at the Department of Food Analysis and Nutrition of the University of Chemistry and Technology in Prague, Czech Republic. The analysed substances were selected based on the availability of standards and PFAS reported in food contact materials in previous studies.  The analysis of the 55 specific PFAS involved extraction with a methanol: ethyl-acetate mixture and was carried out using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography interfaced with tandem mass spectrometry with electrospray ionization in negative mode (UHPLC-ESI-MS/MS) for all PFAS except FTOHs. The selected FTOHs were analysed using gas chromatography coupled with tandem mass spectrometry operated in positive ion chemical ionization (GC-PICI-MS/MS). The fluorine mass balance was calculated according to the method described in Schultes et al. (2019).  It involved converting the concentrations of the specified PFAS identified in a given sample into their fluorine equivalent and then comparing the sum of the identified fluorine with the total organic fluorine amount measured in a given sample.    The fluorine mass balance calculation is used to identify how much of the total organic fluorine is accounted for by the specific PFAS in a given sample. These calculations revealed that fluorine from the targeted PFAS identified in the samples represents only between 0.01 to 3.4% of the total organic fluorine detected. The average concentrations of specific PFAS in paper and compostable food packaging was 0.15% for the PFAS-treated oil-beading compostables, 0.041% for the PFAS-treated oil-beading takeaway papers and 0.92% for the non PFAS-treated oil-spreading or soaking papers/boards. Only 1% of the organic fluorine present in our samples could be ascribed to specific PFAS chemicals identified with targeted, compound-specific analysis of 55 PFAS.   Similar issue was encountered in another Arnika study of PFAS in textile samples: The limited number of identifiable PFAS in the textile samples highlighted both the current limitations of the employed analytical methods, which are not able to identify PFAS such as fluorinated polymers, and the lack of commercially available standards to allow identification and quantification of all relevant PFAS used for treating textiles. In this regard, the generally identified PFAS are only the tip of the iceberg. Despite not being identified individually, the other potentially present PFAS cause concern due to their ability to persist and accumulate in the environment. It is not only challenging to identify them, but also to control and remove them once they are in the environment.

General Comments: ARTEMA, The French Association for bearings, transmissions, sealing, fasteners and mechatronics has conducted several studies with our sectoral technical centre and our members to assess the PFAS used in our sector and the availability of suitable alternatives We would like to make the following comments on the restriction report :
- Given their special properties of resistance to extreme temperatures, aggressive environments, corrosion and abrasion, as well as their non-stick, lipophobic and hydrophobic properties, PFAS are used in particular to enhance product safety and durability. This concerns professional equipment that must guarantee the safety of operators (e.g. industrial machines), sub-assemblies or mechanical components used in finished products and subject to specific qualification (automotive, energy, aerospace, etc.) or in many products to extend their life and ensure personal safety.

-The derogations currently envisaged are insufficient and do not take into account the relevance of PFAS for a wide range of uses and innovations needed in the technology industry to fulfil other environmental targets and strategic objectives set out by the EU.
- Many PFAS uses in our sector (components manufactured by our sector are present in all the industrial sector and applications)  are not covered by proposed derogations, even when no alternative exists. For example, for mechanical components in friction applications or in the sealing or fastener sector.
- This draft restriction does not include a derogation allowing the reuse or continued use of products that were placed on the market before its entry into force, or to incorporate recycled materials from these products.
- Substitution solutions must be assessed on a case-by-case basis for the various finished products containing PFAS.
- If many substances are presented in the restriction dossier or in scientific publications as having similar functionalities to PFASs, these generally do not take into account the specific constraints of the various products, have inferior properties and do not replace all of the properties required of the PFAS.
- Replacement by alternatives to PFAS, if they exist, would also entail a phase of renewal of equipment qualifications in sensitive sectors (agroaliment approvals, nucear, automotive, aerospace… etc.).
- On the other hand, PFAS substitution is more easily envisaged, in the more or less long term, for products that require one or even two of the many properties of PFAS. Applications requiring a combination of their properties do not appear to be substitutable.
- Mechanical subassemblies and some components   widespread practice of maintenance or repair operations and a high capacity for being re-used or re-purposed. In addition, our sector is subject to increasing demands and requirements regarding the incorporation of recycled materials, reparability, the availability of spare parts and remanufacturing. The restriction report does not include a derogation allowing the reuse or continued use of products that were put on the market before it came into force, or the incorporation of recycled materials from these products. By way of example of such derogation in other regulation, the RoHS directive introduced an additional implementation period of 10 years for spare parts intended for the repair, re-use, upgrading of functionalities or reinforcement of the capacity of equipment.
For fluoropolymers :
- The vast majority of PFAS parts used in the our industry are made of fluoropolymers which are classified by the OECD as ‘polymers of low concern’ (PLC), as they do not lead to a hazardous risk for human health and the environment. That means those PLCs do not meet the requirements defined by Article 68 (1) of the REACH regulationas empowering statute. The legal preconditions for a ban of fluoropolymers are not fulfilled.
- We additionally estimate that the ban of fluoropolymers will likely negatively affect the environmental performance of assets, as this ban will lead to a reduced machinery service life, increased friction (increased energy consumption), increased use of lubricants (with associated risks of environmental contamination), use of larger components (increased carbon footprint), need for frequent maintenance and increased use of spare parts (waste generation).

For all these reasons, we recommend the inclusion of exemptions for the following uses of PFAS :
- We therefore propose the exclusion of fluoropolymers and fluoroplastics  PFAS from the scope of the restriction , including substances required for manufacturing.
- A general exemption for spare parts or components necessary for the repair, re-use, updating of functionalities or reinforcement of the capacity of products put on the market before this restriction came into force or covered by a derogation.
- Also dry and liquid Lubricants are containing Polymers of Low Concern (including PFPE Oils) and shall be completely exempted.
-A derogation for the presence of PFAS in recycled materials, notably for products that do not present a risk of PFAS emissions into the environment during use.
-Sufficient lead times for professional products, to take into account the duration of complete product redesign processes which may be made necessary by the application of this restriction. These processes can be particularly long, from the validation phase of a substitute substance, when it becomes available, to its integration into the design of a new product. from the validation phase of a substitute substance, when available, verification of product performance on a prototype, validation and approval of the product by customers, then industrialization of the manufacturing process.
The most generous derogation proposal (13.5 years) is not enough to substitute fluoropolymers with alternative technologies capable of achieving the same performance for 2 main reasons: The time required to identify new chemicals that offer equal performance at high temperatures and in chemically aggressive environments is at least 20 years. The added length of customers’ approval process for quality and H&S, added to authorities/insurance approval in some cases (civil applications, aerospace & defense and marine for example) can take up to 13 years.

-The introduction of a review mechanism for derogations that will be granted, so that they can be extended when no suitable alternative solution has been made available by the end of the deadline.

Uses of PFAS must remain possible as long as their risks can be sufficiently managed by appropriate containment measures or in case no suitable substitutes are available.
It is important to distinguish between the different PFAS (groups) and the risks from each use.

Hereunder some exeples in a lot of field to explain why we need exemption or more time for derogation in our sectors.  Sealings systems :  They are key components  in a large number of applications and have a safety and environmental protection function. PTFE is used in the sealing sector to reduce or limit fugitive emissions of hazardous substances into atmospher or water (selaing of valves, pumps used in nucear power plants, chemical and pharmaceutical plants...).Industrial seals are used to contain media (powders, gas and liquids) inside hardware (process or storage equipment). Media within non-moving equipment are secured by “Static Seals” such as gaskets, whereas pistons and rotating equipment such as bearings and gearbox use “Dynamic Seals”. Hazardous, toxic, flammable, corrosive and reactive chemicals are media found in different industries all of which require high performance seals to be used efficiently and safely. Seals are used in aggressive environments where they can be exposed to conditions, such as, wear, abrasion, radiation and extremes of temperature. Different types of materials; metals, Inorganics such as ceramics and graphite, and polymers (plastics and cross-linked elastomers) are used in industrial seals. In each case the seal material is selected based on the specific application requirements. Seal materials must:  1.Withstand the environmental conditions of the application, including, media, temperature, pressure, speed,and abrasion 2.Not damage other equipment (hardware) in which the seal is housed 3.Be compliant with the counter surface to maximize sealing efficiency 4. Chemical compatibility with various fluid  (Specially for Connectors, hoses in fluid power sector)  - PFAS used:  Fluoroelastomers : FKM - FMVQ - FFKM ; Fluoroplastics : PTFE - PFA - PVDF - ECTFE – PCTFE - Key functionalities: chemical inertness, friction properties and resistance to a wide range of temperatures - Alternatives:  - PEEK, HDPE and PA have been identified for specific uses but are not suitable for every application, due to inferior performance. PEEK is significantly more expensive and is not a viable alternative for many applications and not adaptable to rotating devices.  - Substitution of PTFE and fluoroelastomers in static seals: Metal seals can be used in rare cases and are not suitable for many uses, notably for pressure equipment and performance duration when intensive use, because of inferior tightness performances that can conduct to leakages with risks of environmental pollutions.  - Substitution of fluoroelastomers: No substitution solution for applications requiring resistance to extreme temperatures has been identified.  - More generally, applications requiring a combination of several PFAS properties do not appear to be substitutable. - Substitution of PTFE for friction bearings : PEEK and PA are not satisfactory (see above) -      Replacing fluoroelastomers, PTFE or PVDF in sealing and hose applications with other polymer classes always come with a loss of performance and/or a significantly reduced lifetime.  Friction applications: - PFAS used: PTFE, PVDF, PCTFE, ETFE, FEP, THE-EFP, PVDF-HFP  - Key functionalities: Tribological properties (coefficient of friction, pressure-velocity limit, abrasion resistance and abrasion volume), extreme temperature and acids resistance, surfactants, improved resistance, antistatic agent, non-stick, resistance to aggressive chemical fluids and extreme temperatures fire resistance, anti-corrosion, insulation, non-wettability. In addition to their physico-chemical-tribological properties, PFAS are also used to guarantee compliance with regulations such as CE1935/2004 for use in food contact. - Bearing industry : The majority of PFAS based bearings are made from PTFE and are used in applications where standard metal bearings cannot be employed due to high coefficients of friction and where other polymer bearings fail due to high loads or temperatures. Unlike other fluoropolymers, PTFE does not melt, has an exceptionally low coefficient of friction and high self-lubricating characteristics, resistance to attack by almost any chemical, and an ability to operate under a wide temperature range. These properties make PTFE an ideal material in applicacions with starved lubrication, aggressive chemicals, and high temperatures. Due to the very low coefficient of friction of PTFE against all kind of metallic shaft material, the application of PTFE containing bearings contributes to the reduction of friction losses and thereby to saving of energy. - For example substituting fluoropolymers with polymers of other nature in industrial gearboxes operating at high speed and with aggressive lubricants will result in the necessity to maintain these assets (replace the seals) at frequent intervals; no seals will be available to chemical plants processing sulfuric acid at high temperatures as there is no compatible non-fluorinated polymer available;   - Alternatives: No alternative solution has yet been identified. Most of the documents studied address the use of PFASs without focusing on the alternative materials that would meet the specifications of each sector.  In particular, substituting nickel PTFE seems impossible at this time. More generally, applications requiring a combination of several PFAS properties do not appear to be substitutable. In addition, solutions based on brass (with lead content) can not be deployed or in a limited way because already regulated under the REACH and RoHS regulations.  Coatings. In this field, we speek principally about corrosion protection to maintain the functionality of the component (prevention of corrosion, enabling defined assembly characteristics, resistance to media, UV influences and mechanical influences such as stone impact.  - Screws seem minor but play a major role with support of PFAS: For example, screw threads on the axle support are coated with PTFE. This pre-vents the accumulation of welding beads and welding slag and enables defined fixing (threshold torque & re-tensioning angle) of the screws. As a result of safety requirements, axle supports have the highest standards in terms of bolting quality. If dirt gets inand is not properly screwed, there is a risk of loosening of the screws and ultimately disintegration of the axle, which can lead to serious accidents. A replacement for the PTFE coating has not yet been found.  This exemple  can also be used for fasteners in steel construction, guaranteeing the safety of workers and vistors.  - Pumps require a multitude of fasteners with defined mechanical strength and corrosion resistance, to ensure tightness and safe operation.  Usually, high strength fasteners are protected from corrosion by means of cathodic protection, either achieved by hot dip galvanizing or electrodeposition of zinc / zinc-nickel alloys. These protection aren’t sufficient in O&Gaz and nuclear industries.  An appropriate method to overcome these problems is applying a PFAS based coating (Xylan) on high strength carbon steel fasteners.  Fluid power: Automotive or off road applications: Brakes could be seen as an safety issue in first place. However, the hydraulic hoses, which carry the brake fluid to the brakes, are connected to the brakes using PTFE seals. These seals must be stable with respect to brake fluid and with stand the high temperatures that can occur at the brakes. In addition, dirt must be prevented from entering and long-lasting durability must be guaranteed. This results more in an application that allows the proper functioning (of the brakes).  No alternative can assure the security needed in this applications.    Others :  Dry lubricants are used as additives in surface coatings in order to obtain surfaces with specific properties (coefficients of friction) for automotive applications as well. Using the example of coating materials in the chassis area, which are undoubtedly relevant to safety, defined coefficients of friction (e.g. according to the VDA coefficient of friction window22) must be guaranteed. For example, screws must be easy to screw in and generate consistently high preload forces. On the other hand, they must not have too low a coefficient of friction so that they do not come loose while driving. Process-reliable screw connections are currently only possible with connecting elements whose surface coatings contain PFAS (e.g. PTFE) as a lubricant component. There is currently no alternative to the procedure. Due to the wide range of possible uses (other examples are pistons, bearing shells) in all practice-relevant application temperature ranges and the different materials of the counter surfaces (steel, aluminium, magnesium, painted and unpainted, plastics, etc.), a short-term change over is not possible. - Solvents: in operation, fluorinated solvents for an aerospace bearing control operation requiring washing and special cleanliness. The solvents in question are used because of their temperature resistance - they are non-flammable - and are boiled to remove all organic pollution, in order to achieve a certain level of cleanliness. - Finished products: use of fluorinated protective solvents for finished products containing fluorinated hydrocarbons (perfluorinated polyethers). The properties sought through their use are pressure resistance, chemical inertness and temperature resistance. - Maintenance greases and lubricants: use PTFE-based maintenance greases and lubricants for applications requiring long-term lubrication and long service life. and high temperature resistance, for which more conventional hydrocarbon-based products are not sufficient.  General comments: As a matter of fact, for the time being there is no feasible alternative to the use of PFAS for such applications. Moreover, PFAS have been privileged by national and international standards for their durability and reliability in terms of mechanical design aiming, therefore, at providing safe end products. Any future sound design alternative shall be validated through performance testing in the first place, and then by standardisation acknowledgement.  Considering the normal standardisation timing, this process is bound to take at least 10 years.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Baseline
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Article 68 of REACH requires that regulators establish an “unacceptable risk” before banning or restricting a chemical substance. The Proposed Restriction fails to do that here. As discussed in our comments (please see attached), the Proposed Restriction impermissibly attempts to ban thousands of substances based on a purported finding that some of those substances may present an unacceptable risk, in violation of the REACH Regulation.

The Proposed Restriction also does not properly follow the science-based guidance documents and frameworks that govern the implementation and evidence-based execution of REACH. Rather, it improperly attempts to group and restrict thousands of substances and subgroups of fluorinated chemistries that have significantly varied physical, chemical and biological properties.

More specifically:
The Proposed Restriction adopts the broad OECD definition of PFAS and, in so doing, attempts to treat thousands of substances with varying properties as presenting the same risks, even though the actual risks associated with the majority of those substances have not been evaluated. This approach contradicts both the plain language of REACH and ECHA’s guidance.

The Proposed Restriction appears to find “unacceptable risk” based largely on the fact that the chemical structure of the broad group of PFAS renders them “persistent.” This approach ignores the EU legislator’s position that persistence, alone, cannot establish “unacceptable risk” warranting a restriction under REACH.

To the extent the Proposed Restriction considers risk other than persistence, it improperly assumes that the hazardous properties of a few PFAS can be imputed to the entire class of PFAS.

The risk analysis that is included in the Proposed Restriction and supporting documents were not conducted in accordance with applicable guidance and best practices for determining “unacceptable risk.” While REACH does allow for regulators to follow a “read-across” approach in certain circumstances – wherein chemicals within the same class are restricted on the basis of their common characteristics – that approach appears to not be properly followed here.  As further elaborated in our comments (see attached), the scientific evidence demonstrates, and numerous experts agree, that it is inappropriate to assume equal toxicity/potency across the diverse class of PFAS for purposes of human health risk and environmental risk assessment.  In other words, the purported structural similarity of various PFAS substances does not support adding all PFAS to one group for risk assessment purposes.

Finally, the Proposed Restriction improperly rests upon uncertain emissions estimates that do not take into consideration recent advancements in control and treatment technologies or the regulatory framework applicable to operations in EU Member States.

As a result of these deficiencies (further discussed in our comments attached), the Proposed Restriction does not reflect an appropriate and science-based regulatory approach.

With the shortage of fluorspar as a raw material looming in the medium term, it is absolutely necessary to implement recycling cycles in the next few years in order to keep the fluoropolymers in the cycle.
