Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: As a company and national distributors of F-gases, we argue that F-gases should be removed from this restriction dossier, since they are already listed in the Montreal protocol and are strongly regulated under F-Gas Regulation No. 517/2014 , which introduces a gradual reduction in the availability of HFC/HFO on the market, restricts the use of HFCs with a high global warming potential, provides tools for the responsible use of F-gases such as: monitoring and preventing leaks in systems, responsible handling with regard to recovery, recycling, reclaim and destruction, communications to the competent national authorities of quantities of fluorinated gases used in the systems, among others.
The tools of the F-Gas regulation promote the reduction of fluorinated gas emissions in the environment and even promote a circular economy of fluorinated gases, making it possible to promote the recycling of F-gases and their reuse in closed refrigeration and air conditioning systems, by as opposed to alternatives such as propane, carbon dioxide or ammonia.
Double regulation must be avoided, as this places a risk on the reliability, safety and efficiency of a wide range of products that make modern life possible.
F-gases play a critical and essential role in many applications including refrigeration and air conditioning systems:
• Guarantee the safety of the systems, since the alternatives pose risks to the safety of users and facilities, such as flammability (propane), toxicity (ammonia) and asphyxiation (carbon dioxide), which require tighter safety and mitigation actions.
• Essential to achieve the EU's green transition, decarbonization and reduction of dependence on fossil fuels.
• Minimize socio-economic impact and operating costs, as alternatives may increase consumer costs and the need for more frequent technical assistance.
• Promote circularity, unlike alternatives, fluorinated gases are currently recovered, reprocessed and reused in systems.
• Guarantee economic growth, unlike the alternatives, they allow maintaining the existing infrastructure and the normal supply chain despite the gradual phase-down foreseen in the F-Gas regulation 517/2014.
• Some F-gases can degrade into TFA, but this phenomenon only occurs in case of leakage into the atmosphere. As F-gases are handled in closed circuits throughout all their supply chain, by implementing leak containment measures, advance inspection of leaks to identify them as early as possible, recovery and management of end-of-life systems and certification and labelling, the risk of leakage is mitigated, and thus the source of TFA emission is eliminated.
We believe that it makes no sense to include in this restriction the fluorinated gases: HFC-125, HFC-134a, HFC-143a, HFC-227ea, HFO-1234yf, HFO-1234ze, HFO-1336mzz and HCFO-1233zd, due to the severe socioeconomic impacts that its eventual restriction may trigger.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Our comments applies on Applications of fluorinated gases (Refrigeration, and Air conditioning and heat pumps), Transport refrigeration and Mobile Air Conditioning (MAC).

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: F-gases are handled in closed circuits, both in refrigeration and air conditioning systems and throughout their supply chain. Therefore, by ensuring inspection and maintenance of fluorinated gas storage and container equipment, the risk of leakage is mitigated. As distributors of fluorinated gases, we maintain regular inspections through external inspection bodies, of our storage equipment and transportable containers, in accordance with the legislation in force. The Portuguese decree-law nº 131/2019 and the ADR agreement for transportable containers, provide for regular mandatory inspection (every 6 or every 10 years) that confirm the tightness of the storage equipment. The chances of leakage are minimal, but in the event of an accidental release, keep in mind that f-gases are not classified as persistent, bio accumulative or toxic. TFA is an atmospheric decomposition product of some F-gases, however, 95% of TFA in the environment comes from natural causes. Therefore, F-gases should not be included in the restriction as their use is safe throughout their life cycle.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: F-gas alternatives have different properties from F-gases and leads to other challenges such as health, safety, performance, energy consumption, etc. The alternatives, known as “natural” refrigerants (carbon dioxide, ammonia, propane) may not necessarily have a lower GWP than certain F-gases and in many cases, they consume more energy than F-gases leading to higher indirect emissions for the environment, and consequently compromises the European objectives of energy efficiency. Additionally, the alternatives are subject to corrosion, toxicity, high pressures, flammability, and in some cases lower operating efficiencies. Although the alternatives are known as “natural”, they depend on industrial manufacturing processes, such as separation and purification processes in order to meet the quality requirements for refrigeration and air conditioning systems: • Carbon dioxide is a by-product of ammonia production, and depends of an additional processing to meet refrigerant specifications; • Ammonia is synthesised by catalytic methane reforming at high temperature and pressure, and also depends on a treatment to obtain refrigerant purity; • Propane is a by-product from fossil fuels in an oil refinery and also needs to be purified on-site to meet refrigerant purity. In terms of personal safety, the use of alternatives drastically increases the risk of accidents due to the intrinsic properties of the alternatives. Hydrocarbons have flammable characteristics such as high heat of combustion, high burning rate and low lower flammability limit. Ammonia is a toxic refrigerant and carbon dioxide, in the event of a leak there is a risk of asphyxia and it is a refrigerant that operates at much higher pressures than F-gases. Knowing the national market, and in general, companies and technicians are not trained to work with alternatives, and this also increases the risk of personal and material damage. Standards such as EN 378 and IEC 60335, also limits the charge of refrigerant allowed in the systems taking into account the flammability and toxicity of refrigerants, and HFC/HFO have properties that allow them to cover all refrigeration and air conditioning applications in a safe and sustainable way. In economic terms, a ban on F-gases will have catastrophic effects, putting companies like ours at risk of continuing their business and thousands of companies such as installers of refrigeration and air conditioning systems in Portugal that depend on F-gases for their operation. These companies run a serious risk of closing their activities and consequently there will be job losses, after a strong investment in the training and certification of technicians and companies in the handling of fluorinated gases. F-gases promote a circular economy. Existing regulations, such as F-Gas 517/2014, allowed the development of new solutions for fluorinated gases that are increasingly sustainable, with similar operational properties over the decades, allowing the use of existing systems, equipment and containers, and so will continue with the development of future solutions. Substituting for alternatives requires a huge investment in the entire refrigeration and air conditioning infrastructure, both in terms of systems and containers, making the existing infrastructure obsolete. Many companies would not have the economic capacity for such a drastic change.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: As a company in China that produces fluorinated fine chemicals such as AHF, HCFC-141b, CTFE, VDF, HFP chemicals, etc., we have been complying with all the domestic laws and regulations in China. PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) are widely used in various fields, such as the semiconductor and automotive parts manufacturing industries, due to their unique properties not available in other materials. A proposal for restrictions on PFAS (Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances), prepared by the authorities of Denmark, Germany, Finland, Norway and Sweden, was submitted to ECHA on January 13, 2023. The proposal aims to reduce the release of PFAS into the environment and to promote safer technological procedures and products. As PFAS are very persistent in the environment, they will have a negative impact on human health and the environment if not limited, we are very supportive of the purpose of this proposal. However, concerns about the safety of individual PFAS (e.g., PFOA and PFOS) have led to some irrationality in this blanket control of all PFAS substances.
1. We believe that this restriction proposal is not conforming to the European REACH regulation ("Registration, Evaluation, Authorization and Restriction of Chemicals", a European Union regulation for the preventive management of all chemicals entering its market, which was officially implemented on June 1, 2007). Article 68 of the European REACH regulation defines "restriction" as "a means of protecting human health and the environment from unacceptable risks posed by chemical substances". The PFAS restriction proposal is based only on the "high persistence of the final degradation products" and assigns more than 10,000 compounds to a whole class based on their manufacturing process and molecular structure. In fact, the hazards (e.g., bioaccumulation, mobility, potential for long-range transport, toxicological effects, etc.) of the substances/groups of substances presented in the proposal are limited to individual substances therein.
2. We believe that the restriction proposal will severely and disproportionately impede international trade, affecting the region's economy while also having a significant negative impact on the livelihoods and social stability.
If the restriction proposal is implemented as currently announced, trade in basic commodities using PFAS will be significantly restricted and supply chains around the world will be severely disrupted.
In our opinion, even if alternative substances are currently being developed, they will need to undergo repeated demonstrations and evaluations, therefore it will take a considerable period before they can be employed. In addition, for alternatives that have not yet been determined, research and development will have to be fostered through future experimentation and mistakes, so even a 12-year grace period may not be sufficient to confirm their availability.
The severe and disproportionate negative impact of restriction proposal on international trade may violate the principle of proportionality under Article 68(1). In particular, disproportionate negative effects violate Article 68 (1).
Article 68(1) of REACH provides that any restriction agreement shall consider "the socio-economic impact of the restriction, including the availability of alternatives". According to Annex XV, this socio-economic impact may include, i) According to Annex XV, this socio-economic impact may include, i) the impact of the restriction on the industry (e.g. manufacturers and importers) and on the business impacts of all other participants in the supply chain, including the impact on investment, operating costs and innovation; ii) the wider impacts on trade, competition and economic development; iii) alternative risk management measures that would meet the objectives of the proposed restriction, and iv) existence of suitable and feasible alternatives. The proposed restriction does not adequately consider these elements of socio-economic impact and fails to balance the negative impacts on international trade and industry with the potential benefits of the proposed measure. Instead, a blanket restriction on the use of all PFAS substances is proposed (beyond some transitional periods, specific applications and routine), which goes far beyond what is necessary to achieve the legitimate goals and control the potential risks posed by individual PFAS through the most burdensome measures. In particular, the proposed restriction fails to provide a substantive assessment of the "availability of alternatives", including i) for identified alternatives, the risks and benefits must be compared with those of the substance to be restricted, and ii) for substances to be restricted whose alternatives are not yet available, the risk of continued use of these substances should be compared with the socio-economic consequences of not having available alternatives.
In view of the above, we ask the EU to limit the scope of the restriction to what is necessary to achieve the objective of contributing to the socio-economic well-being of the EU.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Baseline Transitional period
Combined Comments:
General Comments: As a concerned citizen of the Netherlands, I am a big supporter of the restriction of PFAS. In 2022 my husband was diagnosed with testicular cancer, a cancer associated with PFAS exposure.  Another family member from Dordrecht has also been diagnosed with testicular cancer a few years ago. Though my husband has since been declared cured, we are now worried for the future health of our newborn daughter, due to the persistence and bioaccumulation of PFAS in our environment. I therefore have a personal interest in submitting these comments.
My husband and I grew up and met in the city of Dordrecht, in one of the most populated parts of the Netherlands. Chemours Netherlands (formerly Dupont) is situated on the outskirts of the city. This plant emitted large quantities of PFOA in the surface water and air since the 70s. In 2012 Chemours replaced PFOA with GenX. GenX - a type of PFAS with a different formula - is still harmful for human health and the environment.  As a result, it is no longer safe to consume crops grown on allotments in parts of the Dutch municipalities of Dordrecht, Papendrecht, Sliedrecht and Molenlanden.  In 2023 the province of South Holland decided it was no longer safe to swim in the swimming lake ‘De Merwelanden’ near the plant, due to high concentrations of PFAS in the water.  My husband and I used to go swimming there regularly when we were younger. According to the National Institute for Public Health and the Environment in the Netherlands, the quantity of PFAS ingested for Dutch civilians through food and drinking water is above the health-based guidance value.
I want to stress the importance of hearing people who have been effected by PFAS pollution during the examination of this proposal, especially given the fact that most comments for this proposal are submitted by chemical companies who are financially benefiting from the use of PFAS. I will substantiate this comment with scientific sources that have not yet been mentioned in the proposal.

General comments:
1. Risks of differentiation between classes of PFAS
While a class-based approach to chemical management of PFAS can pose challenges to the traditional paradigm of individual chemical risk assessment, the extreme persistence and potential for harm from thousands of PFAS demand a more efficient and effective approach.  A full ban of PFAS (RO1) Some chemical companies argue that certain classes of PFAS are not as harmful as others, for example fluoropolymers. But fluoropolymers are a group of PFAS too diverse to warrant a blanket exemption from additional regulatory review. Their extreme persistence and the emissions associated with their production, use, and disposal result in a high likelihood for human exposure as long as uses are not restricted.  Let’s not forget it was the production of fluoropolymers and the associated use and release of PFOA that led to the widespread contamination of the US mid-Ohio river valley.  Some chemical companies say that short chain PFAS are less dangerous than long chain PFAS. But research shows that short chain PFAS are more widely detected than long chain PFAS, more persistent and mobile in aquatic systems, and thus may pose broader risks on the human and ecosystem health. Though conventional adsorption, ion-exchange, and membrane filtration can remove short-chain PFAS, these methods are less effective than the long-chain homologues, and are challenged with poor material regeneration efficiency and disposal of process waste residual.  Managing PFAS as a class reduces the likelihood of replacing well-studied hazardous chemicals with poorly studied but structurally similar PFAS that have the potential to be similarly hazardous. A lack of full scientific certainty should not be used as a reason for abandoning measures. The persistence and bioaccumulation of PFAS in our environment warrant an strict application of the precautionary principle (article 191 TFEU).
2. Waste management during transition period and for exceptions.
Though I recognize the importance of the use of PFAS in the production of certain products used for the energy transition or medical devices, we must prevent these substances from entering our environment at all costs. Exemptions are only to be made when absolutely necessary.  If no alternative is available for essential products, waste from the manufacturing process should be stored or if possible, processed in a way no PFAS or their degradation products enter the environment. Products of which the production process requires the use of PFAS should be phased out as much as possible.  During the proposed transition period of 18 months and time-limited derogations, an immediate EU wide ban for emissions of all PFAS in water and air is therefore necessary.

General Comments: As a concerned citizen, I write this consultation input to advocate for the absolute ban of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) across the EU.

PFAS are synthetic chemicals used in a myriad of everyday products, from food packaging to firefighting foams, often referred to as "forever chemicals" due to their persistent nature. Studies link PFAS to adverse human health effects including cancer, hormone disruption, and immune system issues. Additionally, their resistance to environmental degradation raises critical ecological concerns.

Despite efforts in limiting some PFAS types, we must not overlook the fact that there are over 4,700 known PFAS. The 'one-by-one' regulatory approach is inadequate given the chemical similarities, potential for harm, and the rate at which new ones are being introduced.

A complete ban will significantly curb human and environmental exposures, and stimulate the development of safer alternatives. The European Union, as an authority committed to the health and safety of its citizens and the environment, should seize this opportunity to lead in global chemical regulation.

Please consider this urgent matter seriously. We cannot afford to wait until the damage is irreversible.

Content: Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: As a construction company we are a downstream user of fluorinated gases, in particular hydrofluoro-olefins (HFOs) that would be subject to the proposed restrictions.
Based on the available evidence, we conclude that fluorinated gases must be fully exempted from the scope of the restriction proposal:
• HFOs have an atmospheric lifetime of days or months and are not classified as (very) persistent under REACH.
• HFO-1233zd do not decompose into Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) in a significant fraction. Most fluorinated gases have atmospheric decomposition products that are not classified as persistent.
•  It has been demonstrated that TFA is not harmful to humans or the environment in the concentrations likely to occur in years ahead.
• Persistence on its own is insufficient for a broad restriction as proposed by the dossier submitters.
• The risks of emissions of F-Gases are adequately controlled through existing EU legislation, in particular the F-Gas Regulation (517/2014, currently under review), the WEEE directive (2012/19) and End of Life of Vehicles directive (2000/53).
• The F-gases used in rigid insulating materials are confined inside the closed cells, as a result of which their diffusion is negligible over time.
• HFOs provide unique insulating properties to the end products and as a result lead to significant improvements in the sustainable growth of these materials over their life cycle.
• Technological handling and complexity within the design of chemical installations for the-end users are correspondingly easier to set up and assemble compared to the hazardous and flammable substances used in this business field.

Furthermore, the available evidence justifies time-unlimited derogations for most uses of fluorinated greenhouse gases:
• Alternatives for F-Gases have not been properly assessed for their environmental impact
• The socio-economic benefits associated with the use of F-Gases outweigh the theoretical cost to society in terms of energy efficiency, public safety.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: According to their REACH registrations, all significant influence F-Gases are not classified as persistent. None of them are classified as PBT and/or vPvB. Their toxicity and environmental impact have been thoroughly assessed, both under REACH and in international forums such as the UN Environmental Programme (UNEP) and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Only a few F-Gases decompose in significant fractions to TFA. Referring to substances containing a -CF3 group (which includes many F-Gases), the dossier submitters state that “most of these substances are expected to ultimately degrade in the environment to TFA”. There is, however, robust evidence that this is the case for just a few mainstream F-Gases (https://www.fluorocarbons.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/EFCTC_HFC-and-HFO-Substances-degradation-products-and-TFA-yields-Final-26_08_2020.xlsx).  Since there is a limited number of F-Gases that decompose into TFA and the conversion ratios vary between 0% and 100% (theoretical maximum of 2% for HFO-1233zd ), the exposure assessment by the dossier submitters (figure 7) is therefore misleading and irrelevant.

8. Other identified uses: The dossier submitters refer to the alternatives for F-Gases, notably  Hydrocarbons (propane, butane and pentanes) as “natural substances”. In fact, these are all produced at an industrial scale.  Hydrocarbons, notably Propane, Butane and Pentanes are typically produced from crude oil in refineries. They are classified as (extremely) flammable and included in Annex I of the Seveso III Directive (2012/18) on the control of major-accident hazards involving dangerous substances. They are (Very) Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs) which are associated with air quality (revision of the EU ambient air quality directive 2022/0347(COD)). Their Photochemical Ozone Precursor Potential (POCP) is orders of magnitude higher than F-Gases (VOCs and POCPs - Fluorocarbons).  F-Gases combine unique attributes that are highly valued by downstream users: • They are safe in terms of toxicological and physical properties. • They contribute to highly energy efficient Heating, Air Conditioning, Cooling and thermal insulation.  • As a result, the total cost of ownership is considerably lower than the proposed substitutes, due to additional costs required to meet the legitimate safety concerns.

Content: Information on alternatives Information on benefits Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: As a fluororesin film manufacturer, our company faithfully complies with national chemical regulations while manufacturing and selling. We support the EU's efforts to reduce risks associated with hazardous substances.

Fluororesins are very useful materials with various excellent properties such as heat resistance, chemical resistance, excellent electrical properties, and non-adhesive properties. As a result, demand on fluororesin is increasing in the automotive, electronics, chemical, medical, and aerospace industries, and it is contributing to the development of each industry by providing the products unique performance and characteristics.
In particular, semiconductor chips are estimated to require additional growth of up to $1 trillion by 2030 as demand for high-quality chips increases in various applications such as automobiles. (AI, data center, 5G, etc... ) This industry plays an essential socioeconomic role globally.(attached market size)

Recently, the packaging process, which is an essential process in semiconductor production, has become increasingly highly integrated, and fluorine films are essential to produce such highly integrated chips. The types of fluorine films used in the high-density packaging process mainly include ETFE and PTFE, and they are significantly superior to films mentioned as substitutes in High temp elongation, and chemical resistance.(attached packaging develop)

These properties cannot be replaced by other materials, and substitutes that can only be used in a few simple processes should not be considered viable substitutes in highly integrated semiconductor packaging processes.
Therefore, fluorine film, which is essential for producing semiconductor chips to be used in future leading technologies, performs its function. Because there are no viable substitutes, they should be excluded from PFAS regulations.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Semiconductor process status 1) 8 major semiconductor manufacturing processes As shown in the picture below, the semiconductor process is largely divided into a front-end process called FAB, which mainly processes wafers, and a back-end process called packaging, which grinds, cuts and assembles the chips of the processed wafer to fit the shape. Lose. The front-end process includes wafer manufacturing, oxidation, photo, etching, deposition, ion implantation, and metal wiring processes, and the back-end process includes EDS and packaging processes, which are called “the eight major semiconductor manufacturing processes.”  In the case of the front-end process of a semiconductor fabrication (FAB), the operations take place on the surface of a silicon wafer. It is not a single-step process but involves a looped sequence of oxidation, photolithography, etching, deposition, ion implantation, and metal interconnection processes. This loop is repeated multiple times to achieve the stacking and patterning of circuits. In post-processing, a test called the EDS Test (Electrical Design Signature Test) is conducted to verify whether the circuitry on the completed wafer is functioning correctly. This test involves making contact between fine probe tips, often referred to as "Probe Tips," and the pads on the wafer chip's surface to check if normal electrical signals are detected. Information about units that are functioning correctly is stored on a server. This information is then moved to the packaging process along with the physical wafers. In the subsequent wafer separation process, the server information is downloaded again to select the functional chips, which are then attached to printed circuit boards (PCBs) and connected through internal pads. This process results in the production of a single semiconductor package.  2) Semiconductor Packaging Process After the wafer FAB process and EDS testing are completed, along with the information about functional chips, they are transported to the packaging site. Subsequent back-end packaging processes are carried out, resulting in the final product in packaging form.  The packaging process differs from the wafer FAB process in that it is carried out sequentially without looping, ultimately forming the final packaged product. Within the packaging process, there are several stages known as "Front-End" processes, including wafer grinding, wafer separation, chip attachment, wire bonding, and flip-chip mounting. These stages involve inserting the wafer to adjust the chip's thickness, carrying out individual unitization, and establishing internal connections between the chip and the PCB (Printed Circuit Board). The stage in the packaging process referred to as the "Finishing" process involves the "Molding" process, "Marking" process, "Solder Ball Attach" process, and "Package Separation" process. In this stage, a PCB serves as a carrier, and it involves attaching the external shape of the package and intermediaries for customer installation. During the semiconductor packaging process, the molding process, which uses EMC resin, is employed to shape the external appearance. This process involves using molds made of ultrafine materials and heterogeneous films made of EMC resin to facilitate the separation of raw materials.  In order to package rapidly developing, highly integrated semiconductor chips, complex and diverse mold structures are required. In order to safely protect these molds and produce high-quality chips, fluorine films must be used as release films. Fluorine release film is a film made from a single material, and it has incomparable functional differences in high temp elongation compared to films such as PET, PS which are mentioned as substitutes. You can see significantly superior values for high-temperature elongation throught attached data. Because semiconductor packaging work is done at a high temperature of about 200 degrees, it is impossible to work with films mentioned as other substitutes, and it is expected that it will be difficult to find substitutes for a considerable period of time in the future.  It is believed that these functionalities are irreplaceable by other substances in the future as well. Because semiconductor packaging work is done at a high temperature of about 200 degrees, it is impossible to work with films mentioned as other substitutes, and it is expected that it will be difficult to find substitutes for a considerable period of time in the future.  We are currently living in an era where we ride in autonomous vehicles, engage in conversations with AI-powered devices and appliances, and plan for missions to Mars using reusable satellite rockets. All of these are possible only with small semiconductor chips, and the regulation of fluorine films required to produce these small, high-performance, highly functional semiconductor chips can be the biggest factor threatening the development of high-tech industries and should be excluded from the PFAS regulation list.

6. Missing uses: Fluorine-based polymers are mainly used, The name of the PFAS substance most commonly used is ETFE (Cas No. 25038-71-5).  In 2022, global annual consumption of fluoropolymers is approximately 500,000 tons, and the industry itself is expected to generate revenues of 10 billion euros. Although the fluororesin content in the end product is very low, they provide the end product with a specific, irreplaceable combination of performance, creating social and economic value that far exceeds the impact of the industry itself.  In general, some of the alternative materials may have similar properties to fluoropolymers in terms of parameters or performance, but the combination of properties required for the application is what distinguishes fluoropolymers from other alternative materials. The transition to alternative substances can result in performance degradation, reduced durability and reliability, increased weight, and can have a significant negative impact on specific application areas such as semiconductor manufacturing and the telecommunications industry. Economically, the impact can include setbacks in advanced technology, loss of efficiency, and high capital and maintenance costs. The diversity of applications for fluororesins means that material changes can have not only design implications but also significantly affect product quality issues. From an environmental, health, and safety perspective, there can be a decrease in equipment operational safety and an increased risk of releasing hazardous substances into the environment.  Additional verification is needed regarding the impact of fluororesins on human health and the environment. Fluorine compounds can be divided into high molecular weight resins and low molecular weight resins, and within both high and low molecular weight resins, there are various subcategories. Currently, it is known that some low molecular weight fluorine compounds have been confirmed to be harmful from both a human and environmental perspective. However, for high molecular weight fluorine resins (non-volatile, insoluble in water), there is no precise information available on whether they have any adverse effects on the human body. Nevertheless, despite the lack of evidence demonstrating the impact of high molecular weight fluorine resins on human health and the environment, I believe that grouping all fluorine compounds under comprehensive regulations without considering their different characteristics is not a well-considered approach. High molecular weight fluororesins should be exempt from restrictions until their impact on human health and the environment is proven.

We focus here on the use of synthetic peptides used as active ingredients in cosmetic industry.
Synthetic peptides are used as active ingredients in cosmetic industry, mainly in skin care market segment. A significant number of them are produced using solid-phase procedures. Due to cleavage and purification conditions, they are mostly obtained in the presence of trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), CF3-COOH (EC / List no.: 200-929-3; CAS no.: 76-05-1).
The proposed restriction, which is the subject of the consultation, would ban the use of TFA (included in OECD definition for PFAS) in the manufacturing process of synthetic peptides for cosmetic use (#), and it would also ban placing on the market those synthetic peptides as cosmetic ingredients, and any cosmetic product formulated with such synthetic peptides, containing TFA as constituent or impurity (if TFA concentration is not under 25 ppb, as proposed).
We advocate for a 12 year derogation (after the general transition period of 18 months) for the above-mentioned use of TFA and those cosmetic ingredients and products containing it. We provide the following basis to support this derogation.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Sector: Cosmetics (Annex E.2.6)  (Sub-)uses: a) Use of TFA in the manufacturing of synthetic peptides for cosmetic use. (TFA is used as a reagent in peptide synthesis for the cleavage and deprotection reactions, and as a co-solvent for the washing and purification steps). b) Use of synthetic peptides as cosmetic ingredients (containing TFA as constituent or impurity) in cosmetic formulations.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Emissions across the different stages of the lifecycle of synthetic peptides.  Manufacture phase: On average, the ratio of TFA used for the synthetic process of peptides is estimated to be 30 kg of TFA per kg of manufactured peptide (~20 liters TFA/kg; TFA density = 1.49 g/mL). It includes the industrial manufacturing and research scale productions. At the end of synthetic path, at least 99% of TFA is treated as waste. The current standard waste management is incineration. The annual emission volumes estimation is calculated with following data: - 23 tonnes of peptides are produced in Europe in 2023 (see attachment “Doc0201_Euromonitor_EU Peptide Market Size_Forecast 2023-2027”). - from these, approximately 60% are obtained though synthetic process using TFA (see attachment “Doc0202_Estimation of peptide sequences with TFA”). - then, estimated yearly amount of TFA (treated as waste) at the end of synthetic peptide manufacture would be:  23 tonnes of peptides produced in EU x 60% x 20 liters TFA/kg peptide x 1,49 g/mL x 99% to waste treatment = 407 tonnes of TFA treated as waste (industrial standard treatment is incineration)  This represents >99% of emissions of TFA in the lifecycle of synthetic peptides for cosmetic use, which are handled through waste treatment. A maximum 1% of TFA is estimated to remain as impurity (some companies regard it as a counterion) in the synthesized peptide powder.  Use phase: The synthetic peptides are formulated into cosmetic products (either directly as peptide powder or in a commercial solution, both forms are used as cosmetic ingredients, usually in leave-on face and body care applications), with an estimated maximum percentage in finished cosmetics of 0.005% (= 50 ppm) of peptide. Then, expected amount of TFA in the cosmetic product would be 0.00005% (= 0.5 ppm, or 500 ppb) at the most. During the manufacturing of the finished cosmetic, no TFA emissions nor impact on environment is expected since all cosmetic ingredient is incorporated into finished cosmetic.  End of life phase: As mentioned, most of synthetic peptides are formulated into leave-on face and skin care applications. Eventually, these peptides (along with TFA impurities) would be rinsed-off by personal hygiene (impact on sewage water treatment) or discarded into domestic/municipal waste in the case of unused or expired cosmetic products. In order to have an estimation of the maximum amount of TFA that could be released into environment in the end-of-life phase, we consider that all synthetic peptides produced for cosmetic use in EU, and formulated into cosmetic products, would have an environmental impact: → 23 tonnes of peptides (EU year production) x 60% x 1% TFA (maximum in peptide powder) = 138 kg TFA/year This amount of TFA (0.14 t/y), compared to other estimated annual emissions in other sectors (see Table 1 in Annex XV restriction report) is among the lowest.  Furthermore, companies manufacturing synthetic peptides for cosmetic use could easily improve purification steps at the end of the manufacturing process (in relatively short- or medium-term), and thus the remaining amount of TFA in synthetized peptide powder could be much lower than 1%. The total substitution of TFA in synthetic peptides would require years of R&D activity to achieve completeness (see point 6).  • Toxicological profile of TFA Regarding toxicological profile of the TFA, we want to emphasize that no significant risk can be associated to the release of traces of TFA during the use of finished cosmetic products. a) As regards human toxicity:  According to the harmonised classification and labelling described in annex VI of CLP regulation, TFA, as an acid, is classified H314, Skin Corr. 1A. It is also classified “Acute tox 4 - H332 – Harmful if inhaled” which is the lowest category for inhalation hazard and not relevant for the exposure considered under this scenario. TFA does not meet classification criteria on repeated toxicity nor any CMR classification.  No toxicological concern can be associated to TFA at expected concentration in cosmetic products, considering, moreover, that TFA forms salts when released to terrestrial environment and surface water. TFA salts won’t have the same hazardous properties as the acid form.  b) As regards the environment:  TFA is not biodegradable, but, considering its log Kow, the substance is expected to have a low bioaccumulation potential [Log Kow 0.79 (25°C) <4]. Same conclusion is pointed out in ECHA’s restriction report Annex B.4.2.7.3. (No bioaccumulation studies obtained from established experimental protocols are available for TFA.) Regarding aquatic toxicity, TFA is classified H412, Aquatic Chronic 3, but, according to the tests available on ECHA website, there is no observed effect on fish (OCDE 210) nor Daphnia (OCDE 211) at the expected concentrations. Moreover, ECHA does not list TFA as a substance of very high concern (SVHC) according to the toxicological data available in its website. Based on worst-case exposure scenarios for salts of TFA, risks to mammals, to plants growing in soil and to aquatic organisms is currently considered de minimis (see attachment “Doc0203_SOURCES, FATES, TOXICITY, AND RISKS OF TRIFLUOROACETIC ACID AND ITS SALTS”). It is to be noted that EPA does not include TFA in the definition of PFAS, considering it as a “well-studied non PFAS” (see attachment “Doc0204_EPA_National PFAS Testing Strategy_Oct 2021”, page 5).

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: As mentioned in point 2, the industrial standard treatment for mixtures of TFA with other organic solvents collected after peptide synthesis is incineration. Of all the commonly applied solids treatment technologies, incineration offers the only possibility to completely destroy PFAS (see attachment “Doc0301_PFAS thermal destruction at water resource recovery facilities--A state of the science review”).

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Recycling of TFA at the end of peptide synthetic process is difficult since it is always found mixed with other organic solvents. No available info on recycling processes for these mixtures. The current standard industrial waste treatment is incineration.

5. Proposed derogations: TFA use in peptide synthesis for cosmetics is not included in proposed derogations.

6. Missing uses: The use of TFA in the synthesis of peptides dedicated to the cosmetic industry has not been identified yet in the ECHA restriction proposal. Synthetic peptides used as cosmetic ingredients represent a significant market segment in face and body care applications. Although they are used in very low percentage in final cosmetic formulations, their importance as cosmetic active ingredients and the relative weight in the total raw material cost is quite remarkable. According to the current state of the art, it will be very difficult to synthesize peptides without TFA. Time will be necessary to find efficient new processes for all peptide sequences available on the market and for future ones (see point 6.e). So, we consider it is essential for our activity and business to obtain a time-limited derogation to find appropriate solutions.   a. The annual tonnage and emissions (at sub-sector level) and type of PFAS associated with the relevant use:  The PFAS associated with the relevant use is trifluoroacetic acid (TFA). As estimated in point 2, average annual tonnage of TFA for such use amounts to 411 tonnes (range tonnage may encompass 400 – 450 t/y). At least 99% of it is collected after peptide manufacturing process and this waste is currently treated by incineration. Only low TFA emissions in the end-of-life phase of cosmetic products are expected (see point 2).  b. The key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use:   The key functionality of TFA is “Reactant/Co-solvent” in peptide synthetic process. It is used as a cleavage reagent in solid phase synthesis, both to cleave the peptide from its support and to deprotect the side functions of the amino-acid protective groups. It can also be sparingly used in the context of liquid phase synthesis. Both methods (solid + liquid) are being used in the chemical manufacture of peptides. The peptide-TFA salt obtained after cleavage is exchanged to chloride or acetate to avoid the contact of TFA with the skin.  c. The number of companies in the sector estimated to be affected by the restriction:  A large number of peptide manufacturers and cosmetic companies using synthetic peptides would be affected.  According to some estimations from cosmetic sector, it is expected that the following companies would be affected if TFA is banned (making current synthetic peptide manufacturing not viable): ► 10-20 peptide manufacturing companies. ► 500-5000 companies formulating with synthetic peptides. ► Besides that, many other companies would be indirectly affected: distributers, packaging producers… cosmetic industry supports over 3 million jobs across Europe, up & down the value chain (see attachment “Doc0601_Socio-Economic Contribution of the European Cosmetics Industry_2022”). The ratio of cosmetic products formulated with synthetic peptides as cosmetic actives within skincare segment in Beauty & Personal Care, launched during the last 5 years (2018-2022) is around 4.2% (according to Mintel GNPD data: 5 745 cosmetic products marketed, containing as ingredients some synthetic peptides, from a total of 81 992 cosmetic products, including 60% factor for those obtained by synthetic process using TFA; see attachment “Doc0602_Mintel GNPD_Marketed Cosmetics with Peptides”). If we could extrapolate this percentage (4.2%) to the total volume of skincare cosmetic business in Europe during 2022 (€25.6bn, according to Cosmetics Europe, see attachment Doc0601), an estimated €1.08bn cosmetic business volume would be affected by the restriction of TFA.  d. The availability, technical and economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives for the relevant use, including information on the extent (in terms of market shares) to which alternative-based products are already offered on the EU market and whether any shortages in the supply of relevant alternatives are expected:  So far there are no alternatives to the use of TFA as reactant in peptide synthetic process.  e. For cases in which alternatives are not yet available, information on the status of R&D processes for finding suitable alternatives, including the extent of R&D initiatives in terms of time and/or financial investments, the likelihood of successful completion, the time expected to be required for substitution (including any relevant certification or regulatory approvals) and the major challenges encountered with alternatives which were considered but subsequently disregarded:  No ubiquitous key alternatives exist for replacing the TFA in peptides synthesis for the moment. It needs to be adapted for all amino acids with their protecting groups and for most of the resins used in solid phase chemistry. So far, there is no technically feasible global substitution of TFA for such use in view. Since the publication of ECHA restriction proposal for PFAS, some peptide manufacturers have started working on: -  Work on the purification steps in order to have a minimum content of TFA in the peptide obtained. But the 25-ppb threshold is an extremely low concentration. It seems not feasible to have less than 25 ppb of TFA in finished cosmetic products. - Manufacturing processes without TFA. TFA is a convenient solvent, but it is perhaps possible to find other polar solvents that work. Peptide manufacturers are testing currently in R&D stage, more “greener” processes using other solvents instead of TFA. But these greener processes won’t be applicable for the synthesis of all peptides or amino-acid sequences- Each sequence need to be tested. Another step to be checked will be whether the final price of these new types of processes will be relevant for the cosmetics market. Several years are needed to peptide manufacturers to substitute TFA in the synthesis process of the different peptides. The initial R&D work put into manifest that there are clear handicaps on the way. It foresees no easy substitution or finding an alternative suitable for every peptide synthesis. It will take a long time, in the case there is any possibility. For sure, no possible solution at all just after the general transition period of 18 months (for an expert approach in scientific peptide synthesis, see attachment “Doc0603_Confirmation that there is no current alternative to TFA for peptide synthetic process”). Only having an extended time-limited derogation (12-year) will enable further research and development to identify possible alternatives for each sequence. Even if such alternatives would be eventually found, finished cosmetic products manufacturers will have to repeat all stability, toxicology, safety testing (plus administrative work) (See the details in point 8).  f. For cases in which substitution is technically and economically feasible but more time is required to substitute: No substitution feasible at this time without any research work for most of the peptide sequences:  i. the type and magnitude of costs (at company level and, if available, at sector level) associated with substitution (e.g. costs for new equipment or changes in operating costs):  Hiring of researchers to develop a replacement synthetic method for each peptide concerned at research and manufacture scale.  No need of new equipment would be necessary. No major change in the operating costs is expected.  ii. the time required for completing the substitution process (including any relevant certification or regulatory approvals):  Unknown; not less than 5 to 10 years to find out an alternative manufacturing process without TFA for each synthetic peptide currently used as a cosmetic ingredient.  iii. information on possible differences in functionality and the consequences for downstream users and consumers (e.g. estimations of expected early replacement needs or expected additional energy consumption);   No difference in functionality should be observed if TFA substitution is successful.  But, for cosmetics, according to Cosmetic product Regulation (EC) 1223/2009, all changes in the quality of the raw material (process/stability/impurities) have to be checked and the product information file have to be updated (See description below under point 8). An increase in energy consumption may be anticipated as TFA is used at room temperature and some heating should be necessary for the alternative substitution.  iv. information on the benefits for alternative providers:  Unknown at this time.  g. For cases in which substitution is not technically or economically feasible, information on what the socio-economic impacts would be for companies, consumers, and other affected actors. If available, please provide the annual value of EU sales and profits of the relevant sector, and employment numbers for the sector:  Not fully explored yet.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Potential derogation of TFA as reactant/co-solvent in peptide synthesis is not considered yet

8. Other identified uses: Table 8 in the Annex XV restriction report, under ‘Cosmetics (Annex E.2.6.)’, Sector as a whole, it considers that “in absence of new information to the contrary, our assumption is that PFAS can be replaced by other ingredients and do not have critical functions in cosmetics”, but the use of TFA as reactant in the synthetic process of peptides to be used as cosmetic ingredients is not taken into account. These are critical ingredients, and currently there are no alternatives to TFA to obtain them. For cosmetic finished products: The 12-year derogation would allow industry to develop replacement of the synthetic method for each peptide but is also essential to ensure that downstream users can meet their own requirements within this timeframe.  For instance, for cosmetic industry, once a synthetic method at manufacture scale is in place, several steps need to be considered:   - Assessing/validating the new quality of the raw material - Relaunch stability/compatibility tests  for each formula - Potentially: updating labelling  - Carrying out administrative work (update documents, PIF, etc.)  This remains time consuming, especially for SMEs with limited resources.   However, in the absence of derogation, and considering only the general transition period of 18 months defined in the draft documents, all cosmetic products containing synthetic peptides will have to be withdrawn from the market (estimated cost, based on MINTEL and Europe Cosmetics data: see point 6, about total cosmetic segment impacted)  Furthermore, having no time-limited derogation for this use of TFA, it would imply no guarantee of availability of suitable alternatives, and adding up the cost of R&D, testing, packaging, PIF (Product Information File for each cosmetic product), for new cosmetic formulations.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: TFA is not included among trifluoromethoxy, trifluoromethylamino- and difluoromethanedioxy-derivatives, and it is generally recognized as a very stable molecule and not biodegradable, although is expected to have a low bioaccumulation potential. There are, though, some potential degradation pathways for TFA: a) The major products of thermal decomposition of trifluoroacetic acid at 300–390° in silica and mild-steel vessels are carbon dioxide, difluoromethyl trifluoroacetate, carbon monoxide, and trifluoroacetyl fluoride. Decomposition is believed to proceed through elimination of hydrogen fluoride, followed by the formation of difluoromethylene (CF2), which largely adds to trifluoroacetic acid to give the difluoromethyl ester. Reaction orders for decomposition and formation of products are fractional and increase with temperature, suggesting that the decomposition is partly heterogeneous. Source: https://pubs.rsc.org/en/content/articlelanding/1967/j2/j29670000282#:~:text=The%20major%20products%20of%20thermal,carbon%20monoxide%2C%20and%20trifluoroacetyl%20fluoride  b) The environmental fate of trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) is poorly understood. There are no known abiotic sinks for TFA, and there is a controversy on its biological fate. To provide insight into the environmental fate of TFA, a long-term (90-week) study was conducted to assess its biodegradability in an engineered anaerobic reactor. Trifluoroacetic acid was found to be cometabolically degradable in an anaerobic environment. Biodegradation is a potential sink for trifluoroacetic acid and may limit its accumulation in the environment. Source: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/245336353_Biodegradability_of_Trifluoroacetic_Acid  c) Photoreductive defluorination of trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) in the aqueous phase by hydrated electrons Source: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1385894721043023  d) Additional bibliographic references – TFA as an atmospheric breakdown product. Source: https://www.fluorocarbons.org/environment/environmental-impact/tfa-as-an-atmospheric-breakdown-product/  As mentioned in point 2, EPA does not include TFA in its definition of PFAS, and considers it as a “well-studied non PFAS” (see attachment “Doc0204_EPA_National PFAS Testing Strategy_Oct 2021”, page 5)

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: As a manufacturer of compressors, refrigerated compressed air dryers and compressed air filters for industrial use, we would be massively affected by a comprehensive PFAS restriction with regard to all our product groups.

We fully support the consultation contributions submitted by the manufacturers' association Pneurop, in the preparation of which we were involved, in particular the consultation contributions of Pneurop PN2 - Compressors and Pneurop PN14 - Air Treatment, which are particularly relevant for our product groups.

The impacts of a comprehensive PFAS restriction identified in these Pneurop consultation submissions are all applicable to our product range, with the strongest impacts expected in the following areas:

1) Restriction of the use of fluoropolymers (e.g., PTFE, FPM, PVDF, FEP, PFPE) as a base material, component or coating of machine elements such as seals, bearings, and hoses.
2) Restriction of the use of PFAS as a component in lubricants for compressors.
3) Restriction of the use of F-gases, which fall into the PFAS category, in refrigeration circuits of refrigerated compressed air dryers.

In this regard, we would like to provide the following information in addition to Pneurop's consultation comments. This contribution relates to fluoropolymers in machine elements such as seals, plain bearings and hoses.

For cost reasons, such machine elements made of/with fluoropolymers are only used for particularly demanding applications in which a long service life, good dimensional stability, high elasticity and/or permanently good sliding properties must be achieved under the influence of high temperatures, high oxygen partial pressure, aggressive chemical impurities in the air to be compressed and/or high mechanical stresses (e.g. as a result of pressure and pressure cycling). For less demanding service conditions, less expensive polymers that do not fall into the PFAS category are used anyway.

No alternative materials with the same properties available:

Currently, there are no alternative materials available for such machine elements that cover this range of applications, especially in the combination of stresses and requirements, even approximately with the same service life and reliability.


Small proportion by weight, but of high importance:

The machine elements in our products, which are made of fluoropolymers, account for only a very small proportion of the total weight (indicatively well below 0.0005 w/w), but have a high significance for reliability, availability, durability and minimization of maintenance requirements.


Negative impact on service life, reliability, maintenance intervals and competitiveness:

These machine elements are deeply integrated into our products, which means that, unlike typical maintenance parts, they are not easily accessible or easy to replace. On the contrary, replacing these components usually requires extensive disassembly and reassembly of major subassemblies. This is inherent and could only be changed to a small extent by extensive and costly redesign of the products.

A significantly shortened service life of these machine elements, as would occur if materials with significantly poorer properties were to be used due to comprehensive restrictions on PFAS, would therefore not only result in shorter maintenance intervals, but also in a significant increase in the maintenance effort per maintenance cycle.

In industrial plants, which are our most important customers, the availability of compressed air in the required quantity and quality plays an essential role because production can come to a standstill if the compressed air supply is disrupted. The reliability and availability of products, especially compressors, therefore plays an essential role.

In the event of a comprehensive restriction of PFAS, our products would not be competitive in markets outside the EEA, where the above-mentioned machine elements may continue to consist of or contain PFAS.


Improving recycling as a better alternative instead of restriction:

Almost all of our products are subject to the Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE) Directive 2012/19/EU. This regulatory framework provides good conditions for collecting, safely disposing of or recycling the machine elements containing PFAS at the end of their service life.

Furthermore, our products consist to a large extent of valuable and easily recyclable materials (e.g. steel, copper, aluminum), so that there is an economic interest in recycling at the end of the service life.

We therefore recommend not to restrict the use of fluoropolymers for machine elements such as seals, plain bearings and hoses for use in compressors, refrigerated compressed air dryers and compressed air filters, but to introduce additional measures to improve labeling, traceability and recycling of such machine elements.


Time required for qualification of alternatives:

For us as a machine manufacturer, machine elements made of/with fluoropolymers are mostly purchased parts. There are several stages in the supply chain between material production and use in our products.

The development of alternative machine elements without PFAS starts with material development. This is followed by the development of the machine elements. We assume that several years are already required to bring possible alternatives this far.

After that, these machine elements must be qualified for use in our products. Tests in the laboratory or test field have only limited significance in this respect. Accelerated tests under artificially aggravated operating conditions alone are not meaningful. Ultimately, comprehensive field tests in real products, under numerous different real operating conditions and over long periods of time are required.

We assume that at least 5 years after the availability of machine elements made of alternative materials are required before meaningful results from field tests are available. And meaningful results are not necessarily a confirmation of suitability; the opposite is equally possible.

If the use of fluoropolymers for machine elements such as seals, plain bearings and hoses for use in compressors, refrigerated compressed air dryers and compressed air filters is not permitted to remain, we therefore recommend transition periods of at least 10 years.

6. Missing uses: Fluoropolymers in machine elements such as seals, plain bearings and hoses used in compressors, refrigerated compressed air dryers and compressed air filters for industrial use.

When viable, alternative non-PFAS containing materials are already used. The use of PFAS containing materials can in some cases eventually be replaced, however currently not all uses have commercially available alternatives without PFAS’s.

Where PFAS uses occur in the medical device sector, the usage is due to PFAS’s unique performance and combination of critical properties: chemical and heat resistance, durability, lubrication and biocompatibility in the coating of the final medical device. Taking into account for a possible replacement of PFAS by alternatives within our risk management process, it is necessary to consider technical suitability, cost, health effects, environmental concerns effects as well as their capability to meet performance standards.

The materials used in hearing instruments (including cochlear implants) have to survive the harsh environment in and around the human ear. The humidity and the body temperature resemble a tropical climate that together with earwax, sweat and skin fat create an environment that is harsh for materials. This set of specific requirements for chemical resistance for the materials used to manufacture hearing instruments. Furthermore, the salt from sweat (pH 4.5-7), and the humidity together with the voltage potential from the electronic components can create a corrosive environment if the system is not well protected. PFAS-containing materials perform excellent in these conditions. In addition, to prevent the ingress from oily substances like earwax into microphones, only PFAS-containing materials can provide the necessary oleophobic properties.

The products manufactured in the cochlear implant industry are only available with a physician prescription and are only used when necessary.  Many critical components of a cochlear implant system, including implant, sound processor, microphones, switches, suspensions for transducers and semiconductors that are currently impacted by PFAS content are key to the functionality of the product and in some case are already a focus of the effort to remove PFAS. In these cases, a redesign of the underlying components may be necessary to remove PFAS, and that could take a significant time and resource investments. Finally, (Li-ion) batteries are a part of every rechargeable hearing instrument, including cochlear implants. It is beyond the scope of our feedback to go into detail, but if battery technology needs to change due to PFAS restrictions, the hearing industry will also be impacted. An in-depth discussion on batteries and PFAS can be found at https://rechargebatteries.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/RECHARGE-FIRST-submission_.pdf.

Another concern relates to stock management. Currently, all products on our shelves contain PFAS. It takes a long time to exchange stock with non-PFAS alternatives, in addition to actually finding the alternative(s). Some products are needed for spare parts or some market(s) that prefer a specific device. If all stock needs to be scrapped due to the proposed PFAS restriction, we see a big impact on circularity as the majority will not be recyclable. It will be a waste of raw materials and a high resource load on the supply chain to remanufacture products.  Knowledge of a sunset date will require stock management to reduce the potential scrap as much as possible with that in mind. We suggest that a transition period for stock is acknowledged as the complexity of phasing out PFAS is high. This would be in line with the derogation for legacy spare parts in the RoHS directive.

On the matter of fluoropolymers; their inclusion in a group PFAS restriction is inappropriate since these molecules are toxicologically inert. As with any “plastic” they should be handled appropriately in the end use phase, due to their persistent chemical properties. The production of fluoropolymers should instead be optimized by legal instruments to render it safe for the environment. For example with the Stockholm Convention. It is important to introduce derogations that allow the use of fluoropolymers in places where there is no other way to achieve the technical performance shown by fluoropolymers. Examples are harsh environments, including very specific uses seen in use of cochlear implants.

There are currently no substitutes available as alternatives for PFAS-containing components (microphones, suspensions, switches), which can guarantee to give the same acoustic performance of cochlear implants. For any substitution, whether in coating or in components, it needs to be verified that the general safety and product performance is not impacted as defined by the EU MDR. Besides reliability testing, this may also include evaluation and testing for biological safety according to the ISO 10993 series. However, until now alternatives have not been found why it is difficult to give a more precise timeline. We contend that the reliability and extended lifetime benefits for cochlear implant usage of PFAS, with a continued very limited use, would outweigh the environmental impact.

Thus, we request that the 12-year derogation mentioned for the coating applications of medical devices such as hearing instruments (including cochlear implants) in paragraph 6j of Annex XV of proposed restrictions on PFASs substances will include all polymeric PFASs including fluoropolymers, perfluoropolyethers and side-chain fluorinated polymers.

Moreover, we have a request for a new exemption, not proposed in Annex XV. We request that a 12-year derogation will also be applicable for the critical components in hearing instruments (including cochlear implants). In particular for the use of PFAS in implants and sound processor as well as use of microphones with a FEP membrane and for the use of suspension and gaskets made of fluorocarbon rubber and fluorosilicones, switches and batteries. Finally, we request a 5-year derogation for legacy spare parts for service and repair of hearing instruments (including cochlear implants) in order to avoid conflicts with EU MDR transition deadlines.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Sector: Medical devices (Annex E.2.9.): Other coating applications. (Sub-)uses: Components containing PFAS used in the hearing instrument industry.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The implants, sound processors, and batteries are disposed of according to different waste streams.  For example the batteries are disposed of according to the applicable laws for the country or area that the user is within.  Recycling programs are utilized where applicable.

6. Missing uses: Several PFAS uses have not been covered in detail in the Annex XV restriction report:  1. Coating: This is a defined use, derogation marked for reconsideration. Material: Fluoropolymer and perfluoropolyether (Missing material: side chain fluorinated polymers). Use: Coating for medical devices (Missing use: coating for hearing instruments, including cochlear implants) 2. Components: This is a missing use, no derogation proposed.  Material: Polymeric PFAS. Use: Components of medical devices (such as hearing instruments, including cochlear implants) 3. Spare parts: This is a missing use, no derogation proposed.  Material: Polymeric PFAS. Use: Components of medical devices  Our goal is to keep delivering high quality medical devices that help the hearing impaired in their everyday life to remain part of society. In most EU countries costs for hearing instruments (including cochlear implants) are fully or partly refunded by national health insurance programs. Depending on the specific needs and applicable hearing instrument, one or two ears, features and functionalities, costs for the users may exceed € 3,000 per hearing aid. A recent overview was published by the IFHOH – the International Federation of Hard of Hearing People (https://efhoh.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/Hearing-Aids-Reimbursement-2022-edited-version-final-for-publication.pdf). For cochlear implants, costs are much higher and usually fully covered by the national health insurance.  In its recent World Report on Hearing, the World Health Organization describes hearing loss as an “invisible disability (...) not just because of the lack of visible symptoms, but because it has long been stigmatized in communities and ignored by policymakers.” (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240020481). While hearing loss is indeed one of the most prevalent disabling health conditions, for both adults and children, it often remains untreated (see below).  If left untreated, hearing loss can result in a number of physical, mental, financial and social consequences, such as depression, sleep disorders, social isolation, increased falls and a decrease in cognitive performance. Hearing loss has especially far-reaching consequences for children, as hearing-impaired children are unable, or only partially able, to understand words in their mother tongue, thus hampering their intellectual and psychosocial development.  Hearing instruments significantly increase people’s ability to take part in everyday life and communicate with the world around them. Figures show that for over 22 million people living in the EU with untreated, disabling hearing loss, the costs for society are as high as 185 billion euros each year (https://www.ehima.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/Hear-it-Report-Hearing-Loss-Numbers-and-Costs-2019.pdf). Therefore, there is a socio-economic benefit to society to continue providing high-quality devices to the hearing impaired as well as improving their wellbeing.    PFAS in hearing instruments is used to protect the devices, to extend the product lifetime, and provide superior product performance as follows.   (A) Various technical and usability developments have set in, such as wireless connectivity, new sensors and new features. At the same time miniaturization is on-going, as users demand ever smaller devices. This has to do with the stigma associated with hearing impairment: people do not want their hearing instruments to be visible. As a consequence of miniaturization, PFAS-less components, such as thermoplastic elastomer (TPE) suspensions, cannot be used anymore - due to their size - to deliver optimal acoustical performance. It is therefore important to find an alternative(s) with similar properties to obtain products with similar product lifetime. Not to bring significantly more devices onto the market due to a short product lifetime cycle which from a circularity perspective is unwanted as well as from a manufacturing capacity perspective.   (B) If a coating is not applied (with consequences to device reliability), the consumer will experience a hearing instrument that has to be exchanged more often. Perhaps at two or three times the current rate. Today the public health system is not arranged to hearing instruments with a shorter lifetime. This will lead to higher financial cost for the user, as no public health scheme will currently offer hearing instruments at this rate.  (C) If fluorocarbon rubbers or fluorosilicones cannot be used the hearing instrument user will have to wait for products coming to the market that are larger and with worse acoustics that may be much more prone to howling than today’s instruments. A ban would set the hearing instrument industry at least 10 years back and there would be no available instruments to help the hearing impaired until development had taken place.

General Comments: As a manufacturer of temperature control devices, we demand that temperature control devices be largely exempted from this PFAS ban. Since our devices operate at high temperatures (up to 230°C) and high pressures (up to 41 bar), it is difficult to manufacture an entire generation of devices without PFAS. This would affect 170 employees. Therefore, we request that O-rings, hoses, pumps, seals, pipe fittings, and cables continue to be allowed to contain PFAS in temperature control technology. 1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Plastic packaging, Other packaging applications, Packaging of medical devices

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The task of the ECHA is to do this.

5. Proposed derogations: We have no direct evidence of how much PFAS we use as "pure PFAS", but we estimate that the amount as "pure PFAS" is well below 1 tonne.

6. Missing uses: The tempering technology is a crucial component of the plastic injection molding industry, playing a pivotal role in ensuring the efficient production of high-quality plastic parts. This technology relies on the use of specific materials known as PFAS to maintain performance under demanding conditions of high temperatures and pressures.  Seals and O-Rings: PFAS are used in seals and O-rings to create a tight and durable seal in plastic injection molding equipment. Without PFAS, these seals might degrade quickly, leading to leaks and reduced machine efficiency. This could result in production delays and increased maintenance costs.  Lubricants: PFAS-based lubricants are essential for reducing friction and wear in moving parts within tempering devices. This ensures smooth and reliable operation over extended periods.  Pumps, Cables, Hoses, and Pipe Fittings: High-pressure and high-temperature environments in plastic injection molding machines demand robust components. PFAS are used in various critical parts, such as pumps, cables, hoses, and pipe fittings, to maintain their integrity under these conditions.  Global Impact: The European manufacturers of tempering devices and their distribution companies have a significant global presence. These companies contribute to various industries, from automotive manufacturing to electronics production, where precision and reliability are paramount.  Environmental Concerns: While it's essential to address the environmental impact of PFAS, a sudden ban without suitable alternatives in place could lead to unintended consequences. Substitutes for PFAS in high-pressure, high-temperature applications are challenging to develop and test.  Economic Implications: The estimated investment costs of 5 to 10 million euros to transition away from PFAS components are substantial for manufacturers in this industry. These costs could translate into higher prices for end consumers or a financial burden on the companies themselves.  In summary, the use of PFAS in tempering technology for the plastic injection molding industry is deeply intertwined with the reliability, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness of a wide range of manufacturing processes. While addressing the environmental concerns related to PFAS is essential, it is crucial to develop viable alternatives that maintain the high standards of performance and durability currently achieved with PFAS-containing components. Otherwise, the unintended consequences of increased waste and economic strain could outweigh the benefits of such regulation. Balancing environmental protection with the needs of industry and consumers is a complex challenge that requires careful consideration and innovation.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: As I have already mentioned, 130 employees are affected in our company, and approximately 170 employees are affected across Europe.

8. Other identified uses: Tempering devices are indispensable in various industries where plastics are processed into different products, with a particular emphasis on plastic injection molding. Our devices find application in a variety of uses, including:  Medical Technology: In the production of life-saving medical products such as disposable syringes, infusion sets, infusion bottles, pipettes, blood glucose monitors, and insulin needles, tempering devices ensure precise temperature control to guarantee the quality and safety of these products.  Automotive Industry: Tempering devices are used to manufacture high-quality plastic components for vehicles, including dashboards, bumpers, interior trim, and engine components, contributing to the safety and efficiency of automobiles.  Telecommunications Industry: The production of casings and components for mobile phones and communication devices also requires precise temperature control to ensure the quality and performance of these devices.  Consumer Goods Industry: Everyday products such as packaging, toys, and household appliances are often made from plastic. Tempering devices play a key role in producing high-quality and durable consumer goods.  Chemical Industry: In the chemical industry, tempering devices are used to process plastics and chemicals at specific temperatures, crucial for the quality and consistency of end products.  Food Industry: In the manufacture of food packaging, kitchen utensils, and other plastic-based products, tempering devices are necessary to ensure food quality and safety.  Electronics Industry: The production of electronic components and enclosures requires precise temperature control to ensure the performance and reliability of electronic devices.  The application areas of tempering devices are diverse and span industries that have a significant impact on our daily lives and health. By providing the necessary temperature control, these devices contribute to ensuring quality, safety, and efficiency in these key sectors.
