Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: As a research-based, global biopharmaceutical company, we are firmly committed to assessing and minimizing impacts on human health, the environment, and the communities in which we operate that are related to its business activities. While we appreciate ECHA’s dedication to protecting both the environment and public health, it is our position that the current proposal by ECHA to restrict PFAS needs to be amended so that important and often lifesaving medicinal products may continue to be made available to patients in the EU. Without these amendments, ECHA’s proposed rule will create insurmountable challenges to the ability of the pharmaceutical industry to meet the needs of patients in the EU.

The current ECHA proposed regulation (Regulatory Option 2) includes:
• Time-unlimited derogation on EU-approved active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs); and
• Time-limited derogations of 13.5 years for certain medical devices and PCTFE-based packaging.
However, the proposed derogations fail to encompass regulatory starting materials, intermediates, and excipients as well as crucial applications of PFAS-containing articles or materials that are indispensable for pharmaceutical production. Thus, as proposed, the rule would require the phase-out of the materials and articles within 18 months after its entry into force. If left unchanged, this omission would detrimentally affect all pharmaceutical manufacturing activities within the EU, potentially resulting in a grave and unintended outcome of limiting or preventing patient access to essential medicines.

Examples of applications that are crucial to the healthcare sector and that are overlooked in the derogations include, but are not limited to:
• Starting materials and intermediates used in the synthesis of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs)
• Non-active ingredients (excipients and intermediates) used in the medicinal product manufacturing
• Research and Development of new APIs and medicinal products
• Industrial manufacturing equipment including spare and replacement parts (e.g., Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) or Ethylene tetrafluoroethylene (ETFE) coatings on the stainless-steel piping)
• Process chemicals such as reagents, solvents, catalysts, processing aids, and auxiliaries in the production and quality control (e.g., trifluoroacetic acid (TFA))
• Packaging materials including elastomers (e.g., PTFE/ETFE coated vial stoppers)
• Single- or multi-use consumables (e.g., Teflon gaskets)
• Drug delivery devices

As noted, we are firmly committed to assessing and minimizing impacts from operations on the environment and human health. To this end, we have formed a PFAS management team responsible for conducting thorough impact assessments, exploring alternatives, and developing proactive strategies to reduce PFAS use and release. While we are taking proactive steps to adapt, we have concluded that many PFAS applications in the pharmaceutical industry are irreplaceable and integral to medicinal product production or are too complex to be phased out within the proposed timelines. We are especially concerned about the missing uses noted above and the significant impact the proposed rule could have on patient access to medicinal products, as well as on our ability to continue operating in the EU and the associated impact on the local economies in which we operate. Therefore, we recommend that the regulation be revised to provide:
• Exemption for the materials technically not feasible to replace with non-PFAS materials such as API, starting materials, intermediates, excipients, reagents, and certain devices and packaging materials and manufacturing equipment used in the API and medicinal product development and manufacturing. We support ECHA’s response in its Webinar Q&A Part 2 that all preceding steps required in the API manufacture would be covered by the same API derogation and further request that these irreplaceable materials are considered for full exemption. Reporting obligations under the currently proposed time-unlimited derogation would impose a significant administrative burden without a commensurate benefit, particularly concerning materials we lack direct control over. We operate in a highly regulated industry, and as noted below, European Medicines Agency (EMA) oversight is adequate to govern the industry’s use of PFAS and PFAS-containing materials.
• Time-limited derogation with an extended transition period for those materials that might have feasible candidates for replacement with non-PFAS materials but are either not yet available or more time is needed, such as certain packaging materials and plant equipment. This would allow sufficient time to identify and make commercially available feasible alternatives and for our manufacturing facilities to transition to alternative technologies in a controlled and regulated fashion.

It is essential to note that the production of APIs, medicinal products, and medical devices is strictly regulated by EMA, encompassing rigorous validation procedures and regulatory approvals – a process that often spans over two decades. Requiring the substitution of all PFAS-containing components within eighteen months would not be feasible for the industry and regulatory authorities, going through time-consuming and costly re-registration, re-qualification, and re-validation processes. For example, we manage approximately 1.5 million asset classes and spare parts for manufacturing equipment, often containing fluoropolymers. Estimating the time for developing replacements for each piece is challenging. Some parts in direct contact with products need extensive validation and new regulatory submissions, adding several years to the process.

In summary, we support a measured and thoughtful approach to the regulation of the environment, and human health and safety that relies on good science. In our view, the imposed restriction should not negatively impact patient’s health, and the desired outcomes can be achieved by providing appropriate exemptions and derogations to all aspects of end-to-end pharmaceutical manufacturing materials and processes from the scope of the regulation. This can be achieved through a considered balance that takes into account the impacts on patients and the environment as well as on the industry’s ability to operate in an effective and efficient manner.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: • Sector: pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical industry.  • This sector is missing from Table 9 of the Annex XV restriction report. Only three relevant use scenarios are covered in the draft proposal: active pharmaceutical ingredient, PCTFE-based packaging, and certain medical device uses. All other (sub-)uses are missing for this sector and are listed in the General Comment section above and discussed in Question 6: Missing Uses below.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: While we are unable at this time to provide specific or quantified emission data, there may be potential PFAS emissions during normal operation via F-gases and waste disposal. If PFAS materials are used in manufacturing, even for non-PFAS API processes where PFAS reagents are used and for non-PFAS materials where PFAS processing aids have been used in the synthesis, the potential exists for these materials to be present in process waste streams generated during the product manufacturing process.  Moreover, waste management could be significantly impacted.   With respect to solid fluoropolymers used within our facilities, the vast majority fall into the category of Polymers of Low Concern (PLCs) (Ref. https://setac.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ieam.4646). The waste from these products does not pose a significant threat to human or environmental health.

5. Proposed derogations: The current proposal outlines a time-unlimited derogation on EU-approved active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) under Regulatory Option 2 (RO2). This derogation is justified in the restriction report because APIs are (1) subject to rigorous regulation within the EU, involving extensive evaluations and approval processes by EMA and (2) important for human health and necessary to ensure a stable supply chain of essential medicines. While it is not possible at this moment to provide specific tonnage or emission data, the company assessment of the products manufactured in and/or supplied to the EU market suggests that the phase-out of PFAS APIs could potentially result in more than 10 million global patients losing access to vital medicines. The impacted products include those on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (Ref: https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-MHP-HPS-EML-2023.02) and also those currently in clinical development. Although we support the RO2 time-unlimited derogation for the same reasons outlined in the restriction dossier, we anticipate a significant administrative burden associated with the two-year reporting obligation that outweighs the associated potential benefits and, therefore, recommend a full exemption. Given that PFAS serves as a key functional group in medicinal products and is commonly used in APIs, the reporting requirement would inevitably pose a significant challenge in terms of administrative overhead and protection of confidential business information, potentially leading to increased costs for products and reduced efforts in their development. Today about 30% of all APIs contain fluorine (Ref: https://www.efpia.eu/media/1oeldyty/efpia-ahe-pfas_position_june-2023-final.pdf). There have been 360 organofluorine pharmaceuticals approved and used globally between 1954 and 2021, with 107 of them meeting the ECHA PFAS definition (Ref: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35313699/). The use of fluorine (e.g., as -F, -OCF3, –CF3 / -CHF2-) in a medicinal product is related to the unique properties of this element. To design a commercial drug, many parameters of the lead molecule need to be optimized in parallel. The introduction of fluorine to a molecule is often an essential part of achieving this optimally balanced profile. Fluorine atoms are used to block metabolism at certain positions, change overall lipophilicity and alter electron density for specific regions of the compound. In certain structural contexts, the use of fluorine can make a molecule more acidic or less basic (decreasing its pKa).  All of these factors can impact permeability, binding affinity to the target, selectivity, tissue distribution, solubility and drug efflux, which are important to the benefit/risk profile for the product. Due to the unique properties of fluorine, a direct replacement is not always available for medicinal products that contain PFAS functionality. For example, while there are other functional groups with electron withdrawing properties like -CHF2- or -CF3 (for example carboxylic esters, amides, nitro, or cyano groups), their incorporation leads to compounds with different metabolic stability, polarity, cell permeability, and/or toxicity properties. Replacement of fluoro-alkyl by other halo-alkyl groups such as chloro-alkyl can in certain instances lead to reactive agents with toxicity concerns.  These other groups are also sterically different and may not be compatible with potent binding to the target protein.  Even if PFAS APIs coexist with nonfluorinated drugs in the same therapeutic class, it is incorrect to assume that these APIs are interchangeable. Limiting the options in a therapeutic class because some have fluorinated groups would have a profound impact on the ability to treat patients with the safest and most efficacious medicines. In conclusion, a complete ban on API and medicinal products with PFAS key functionality would consequently remove these molecules from the European market, with potentially severe consequences for patients. We recommend full exemption on development and manufacture of APIs, including all materials and processes containing PFAS to make APIs.

6. Missing uses: 1) Materials used in the API and medicinal product development and manufacturing:  The current proposal outlines time-unlimited derogation on PFAS-containing APIs but does not consider the associated PFAS-containing materials used to make those APIs. It is important to note that medicinal products containing PFAS functionality cannot be manufactured in the absence of the starting materials, intermediates, and reagents (e.g., trifluoroacetic acid (TFA)) used to introduce the PFAS functionality. These materials are missing from the proposed derogations and must receive the same derogation or exemption as APIs which aligns with ECHA’s response in its Webinar Q&A Part 2 Question 15.1 that “any proposed derogation is intended to also cover all preceding steps that are necessary to produce the product.” At this point in time, we do not have a consolidated annual tonnage for this PFAS use, however a ban on these materials would impact the industry’s ability to produce the relevant medicines that are essential for the well-being of patients.   PFAS intermediates and reagents are also used to manufacture APIs that do not have PFAS in the final molecule (non-PFAS APIs). Our assessment indicates that the impacted products include critical emergency medicines that treat life-threatening diseases and conditions for which alternatives do not exist, are first-line treatments for various disease areas, or are the last resort for critically ill patients. Ensuring continued supply of these medicines and avoiding shortages will benefit the patients and will not create gaps or disruption in the health care system. The proposed ban would require every manufacturing process which currently uses a PFAS containing material to develop a non-PFAS solution for each impacted product. It may be possible to identify alternative ‘non-PFAS’ reagents via intensive research and development programs; however, given that the use of PFAS is typical in many instances, it would take at least three to five years to evaluate, develop and register updated manufacturing processes across multiple markets with likely supply interruption and associated significant cost. This assumes that viable ‘non-PFAS’ alternatives can be identified that are technically and economically viable to manufacture existing commercial products. No commercial supply would be viable until a new manufacturing process is fully approved by regulatory agencies. In addition, given the use of PFAS containing materials is industry wide, there would be a significant impact and burden on EMA to approve multiple ‘new’ manufacturing processes for existing commercial products to maintain patient access to multiple medicinal products.  Moreover, the proposed regulation with no derogation on developmental APIs would stop the progress of a number of drugs addressing unmet medical needs in various stages of development. PFAS materials used in products currently in R&D, clinical testing, or regulatory review should also be considered within a full exemption scope. Without such an exemption, it could affect ongoing R&D efforts in discovering and developing future medicines that would benefit from the unique chemical and biological properties of fluorine in the API structure. Regardless of PFAS or non-PFAS APIs, all PFAS materials used to develop and manufacture medicinal products are critical and any proposed ban will result in the suspension of supplying medicines to over 10 million global patients according to our assessment. Due to the unique properties of fluorine, a direct replacement is not available and thus, we recommend full exemption on these materials.   2) Materials used in manufacturing equipment and as processing aids: The proposed rule lacks a derogation for manufacturing equipment parts and processing aids used in the API and medicinal product manufacturing and quality control. PFAS protects equipment, prevent leaks, filters product, and tests product. In many cases, there are no substitute materials available. Where substitute materials might be available, extensive validation programs will be required to replace this material. As many individual pieces of equipment will be required to be replaced, assessments will be required to be performed to understand the impact to the regulatory filings for each equipment train. Where it is not possible to replace equipment in conformance with current regulatory filings, new submissions will be required. Fluoropolymers (e.g. Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), Ethylene tetrafluoroethylene (ETFE), Perfluoroalkoxy (PFA), Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), Fluorine Kautschuk Material (FKM)) are used widely in pharmaceutical manufacturing facilities due to their corrosion resistance, mechanical, and other properties. Examples of their uses include: • In coating applications for lined pipework and vessels, including O-rings, gaskets, bearings, and lubricants. This protects equipment and prevents leakage of product contained within this equipment. • PTFE and PVDF are commonly found within in-line product filters.  • PFAS materials such as TFA are commonly used within analytical laboratories in multiple test methods for many products.  The fluoropolymer properties, such as chemical and thermal resistance, mechanical robustness, low permeability, low surface energy, low flammability, and low friction minimize leachable and extractable content from entering the product stream. Alternative materials to fluoropolymers with similar properties are currently available on the market but do not offer the same technical feasibility. For every production process, we select elastomer material based upon the unique set of physical and chemical attributes that the process presents. This elastomer selection is then verified through trials that are run as part of the overall validation process. For example, Hydrogenated Nitrile Butadiene Rubber (HNBR), Alkyl Acrylate Copolymer (ACM), and Ethylene Acrylic elastomers (AEM) rubbers can offer resistance to aggressive fluids (although not as high as FKM), but at the same time, they do not have the same level of heat resistance as FKM (Ref: https://www.fipnet.com/chemical-resistance-guide-final/?lang=en). Similarly, PTFE lined pipework is used to protect equipment from corrosive chemicals. Alternative substances may provide ‘point in time protection’ but would require replacement on a more frequent basis, increasing employee safety risk and impacting plant availability. Increased numbers of changeovers of equipment trains due to the use of inferior PFAS-free material would produce a negative environmental impact because of increased waste generation and increased energy usage.  Replacing laboratory equipment parts with PFAS-free alternatives would disable a broad spectrum of common laboratory equipment including: HPLC, GC and Karl Fischer titration apparatus. We manage about 1.5 million asset classes and spare parts, and it is estimated that greater than 20% of these asset classes contain PFAS – mainly fluoropolymers. The products manufactured through the impacted processes are supplied to billions of patients within the EU. The proposed regulation would require every EU site to work with equipment suppliers to develop non PFAS solutions for each of the 1.5 million asset classes. It is not possible to quantify how long it will take to develop replacement solutions for every piece of equipment. We will be dependent on the R&D success from each of its equipment suppliers to develop these solutions. Once a replacement piece of equipment is available, a typical equipment validation program from procurement to qualification takes at least three to five years. Some asset parts in direct contact with product will require more rigorous validation and new regulatory submissions which will add years. As there would be multiple validation programs taking place in parallel, continued manufacturing would not be possible during this period. In conclusion, where no suitable non-PFAS replacement is available, we would have to move manufacturing locations to outside the EU and this will affect the supply of medicines to millions of patients over a sustained period. Thus, we request that fluoropolymers used in all industrial settings be fully exempted.  3) Materials for packaging, medical device, and single-use systems: PCTFE-based packaging is currently proposed for 13.5 years of time-limited derogation and marked for reconsideration. However, all other packaging materials and coatings for rubber stoppers and single-use system (SUS) components such as filters and tubing are missing from the proposed derogations, and we request full exemption for the materials that do not have suitable alternatives available. Fluoropolymers are frequently used in packaging, devices, and SUS technology due to their properties such as lubricity, inertness/barrier, and temperature resistance. For example, ETFE/PTFE coatings are frequently used for elastomeric components such as vial stoppers and syringe plungers to create a physical barrier between stoppers components and drug products. Certain medicinal products are sensitive to silicone oil and the use of fluoropolymer-based coatings can replace the lubricity typically provided by silicone oil. It is estimated that 5-15% of our elastomer portfolio (i.e. rubber stoppers) utilizes fluoropolymer-based coatings. However, there are currently no known alternatives to fluoropolymer materials for elastomeric components. Fluoropolymers are also frequently used in SUS technology (e.g., filters, tubing) by use of materials such as PVDF which are frequently used in filters due to high heat resistance. Teflon is also used in tubing for inertness. Thermoplastic elastomer (TPE) tubing may be suitable as a substitute for Teflon tubing, but compatibility testing would be required for high alcohol content solutions. For PVDF filters, polyether sulfone (PES) may be an alternative but there has been no analysis performed to date. There are no known replacements for elastomeric components and SUS, except where specified above for SUS.  Restriction of PFAS for elastomeric components and SUS has the potential to render drug products without solutions for manufacturing and packaging as there are currently no replacements available. Further, many new drugs are sensitive and require the use of fluoropolymer materials. The impact to SUS would be extensive since approximately 75% of all SUS contain fluoropolymers. Given that the potential product footprint is large, it is anticipated that the patient impact would be significant. Thus, we request that these materials with no feasible alternatives (e.g., rubber stoppers) receive full exemption and that materials with potential alternatives (e.g., ink) receive an extended time-limited derogation (e.g. 20 years) to allow sufficient time for new components qualification, component validation, and related review and testing. PFAS is also used as a processing aid in packaging materials. For example, it is known that the Dow HDPE used for solid oral dose (SOD) Squeeze & Turn bottles utilizes a PFAS processing aid and implies that PFAS processing aids could be used in other grades of plastic which could impact other components such as poly bags, stretch wrap, pails, closures, and others. PFAS is also used significantly in ink systems as a processing aid and for functionality to provide grease and water resistance and for ink performance. The primary uses of inks are on unit cartons, labels, leaflets, and print on packages. Alternate ink systems, if any, would require further evaluation, testing, and validating prior to implementation. It is notable that when labels and inks are applied to plastic primary packaging, changes are more complex as studies are often required to evaluate migration of substances through the plastic materials and into the drug product.  4) Analytical Materials and Instrumentation The current proposed regulation outlines a time-unlimited derogation on APIs, but it does not list all peripheral activities associated with ensuring continued supply of medicines. The regulation should make clear that analytical testing is covered by the same API derogation or exemption given (1) the fact that these PFAS materials are not present in the final dosage form and are used for testing purposes only and (2) the relatively small quantities used for analysis and (3) the fact that existing waste management processes would control. In the event that alternatives are needed, this would require re-development and re-validation of every analytical method currently using a PFAS containing material (e.g., reference standards, analytical reagents), employing an equivalent non-PFAS analytical method, for each impacted product. It may be possible to identify non-PFAS alternatives, however, given that the use of PFAS is registered within the analytical procedures, it would take an estimated three to five years to evaluate, re-develop, re-validate and register (across multiple markets) alternate analytical methods, with the corresponding impact on both product release and supply. Also, as indicated in point 2 above, replacing lab equipment parts with PFAS-free alternatives would impact ability to support key equipment types such as: HPLC, GC-MS and Karl-Fischer titration, which can impact the routine product release testing and supply. Therefore, we recommend full exemption for its use in analytical testing and instrumentation.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: PCTFE-based packaging is proposed for 13.5 years of time-limited derogation and marked for reconsideration. PCTFE is frequently used for solid oral dose (SOD) blister packaging films as it provides a high barrier to water vapor transmission to protect sensitive formulations. Cold form (foil) blister packaging is a potential alternative, but whether the replacement can be achieved within the 13.5-year transition period is unknown, given the scope of change activities that would be required to be processed through the standard regulatory requirement and approval. Therefore, we request an extended transition period (e.g. 20 years) for PCTFE-based packaging materials to allow sufficient amount of time to substitute the PFAS material across all necessary applications.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis
Combined Comments:
General Comments: As a responsible producer and supplier to the EU, Arçelik submits the following information and comments to the ECHA 1st public consultation on the Proposal aiming to justify exclusions of certain HFC/HFO gases from the scope of the Annex XV dossier in question.
The Proposal does not identify by any appropriate means (e.g., IUPAC names, CAS or EC number) any of the 10,000 substances within its scope, contrary to section II.3 of Annex XV REACH as well as established regulatory and legal practices, including the principles of good administration, certainty, legality and equal treatment.
Moreover, the ban on all “theoretical” substances in order to avoid “regrettable substitutions”, without any objective assessments of the actual threats/risks, is disproportionate, aleatory, discriminatory, unscientific, and legally unfounded. It is contrary to the core principles of the REACH Regulation, the general principles of EU law (proportionality, objective examination, good administration, subsidiarity and non-discrimination) and the wider EU policies, including the Green Deal and REPowerEU.
Furthermore, numerous PFAS substances falling within the scope of the Proposal (i.e., OECD PFAS definition) do not share similar physicochemical, toxicological and ecotoxicological properties, hazards, and exposure (and consequently, do not pose equivalent risks, if any) which can be predicted by virtue of a simple structural similarity (-CF2- or CF3- moiety).6 According to the most recent EEAP 2022 Assessment Report and the majority of international experts “all PFAS should not be grouped together, persistence alone is not sufficient for grouping PFAS for the purposes of assessing human health risk, and that the definition of appropriate subgroups can only be defined on a case-by-case manner” and that “it is inappropriate to assume equal toxicity/potency across the diverse class of PFAS”.
Contrary to what the Dossier Submitters indicate, there is a range of PFAS substances, including various fluorinated gases, that are not (v-)persistent (not P/vP) and do not degrade to vP substances in amounts leading to their risk characterisation as non-threshold substances with properties similar to PBT/vPvB substances. For instance, HFC-125, HFC-143a, HFO-1234ze(E), HFO-1336mzz(E), HFO-1336mzz(Z), HCFO-1233zd(E), HFC-245fa and HFC-365mfc ultimately degrade in the atmosphere to carbon dioxide (CO2), Hydrogen fluoride (HF) and small amounts of the only PFAS arrowhead substance - trifluoroacetic acid (TFA). These amounts are considered as “minor source of TFA”  resulting in de minimis increase in TFA concentrations and “are well below the threshold for concern with respect to human and environmental health”. Also, comprehensive scientific evidence, including from REACH registration dossiers, confirms that many PFAS (comprising, HFC/HFO and PCTFE) are low hazard substances, not classified for any endpoint assessed in the Proposal (section 1.1.4) and are safe for intended uses. Moreover, many of them are already comprehensively/adequately regulated in the EU and beyond.
The above conclusions are equally true for TFA for which the REACH registration data and Chemical Safety Report (CSR) (including, DNEL/PNEC assessments,13 several times reviewed by ECHA) unequivocally demonstrate that it is not a non-threshold substance with similar risks to PBT/vPvB substances. In this respect, the EEAP 2022 Assessment Report also concludes that “based on projected future use of these precursors of TFA [incl. HFC/HFO], no harm is anticipated” and that TFA “is unlikely to cause adverse effects out to 2100.”
Finally, the Proposal lacks any robust study for allegedly new hazards of TFA or any other substance contrary to Part I of Annex XV REACH. The Restriction options (RO) contradict (concentrations, exclusions, derogations) restrictions on certain PFAS (groups) already included in Annex XVII REACH or currently under consideration by ECHA or the European Commission (section 2.2.1.2 of the Proposal). Moreover, the Proposal appears to lack important information submitted by stakeholders during the two previous Calls for Evidence (CfE)16, including: on existing and foreseen risk management measures (RMM) for specific uses, available alternatives and their safety/risks/costs, uses of substances already on the market, spare parts and second-hand articles, as well as on the demonstrated very high costs for society if the proposed PFAS restriction is imposed. In this respect, the Proposal particularly lacks a robust risk assessment of substitutes for HFC/HFO gases and PCTFE. Based on the available evidence and objective assessments both HFC/HFO gases and PCTFE must be excluded from the scope of the proposed REACH restriction.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Applications of fluorinated gases -  Refrigeration & Air conditioning and heat pumps & Foam blowing agents  Arçelik have consumed R134A, R407C, R450 and R32 to produce reliable products. In near future the use of some olefins (HFO) are on the table to be more insulated and produce energy save products.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The  important thing is that the reuse, recovery and recycling (RRR) of F-gases is mandated under the F-gases Regulation and it is happening successfully on the market today. We need to be clear that equipment is designed to not leak. We also need to be clear that emissions is not equal to the risk, which is an assumption in the Proposal. It is also key in this section to highlight that HFOs/HFCs are not persistent, bio accumulative or toxic and are registered as such under REACH with a decision to take no further action. It is critical here to rebut the assumptions of the dossier submitters that HFOs/HFCs have negative effects on human health and the environment.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The important thing is that the reuse, recovery and recycling (RRR) of F-gases is mandated under the F-gases Regulation and it is happening successfully on the market today. There is a move towards circularity in term of reuse of recover gases in maintenance and repair. Unfortunately, the reporting of RRR is not mandated anywhere and there is not a clear official picture.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: The main degradation product of some HFOs is TFA (trifluoroacetic acid). There have been extensive scientific studies of TFA which have demonstrated that it is not a risk to the environment nor human health. In this section it is best to point to the most recent evaluation of TFA by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) Environmental Effects Assessment (EEAP) Panel where in its most recent Report from May 2023 concludes that “based on projected future use of these precursors of TFA [incl. HFC/HFO], no harm is anticipated” and that TFA “is unlikely to cause adverse effects out to 2100”.  In addition, according to the REACH registration dossier and Chemical Safety Report (CSR) for trifluoroacetic acid (TFA)  this substance does not fulfil the criteria for a PBT or vPvB substance under Annex XIII REACH. Neither does it raise equivalent levels of concern as a PBT or vPvB. ECHA has already evaluated the TFA dossier without concluding that further regulatory actions were needed.

General Comments: As a supplier of perfluoropolyether (PFPE) lubricants into many industries in the UK and Ireland, we are deeply concerned about the impact of this proposed legislation to many key manufacturing industries.  These include healthcare, aerospace (including military equipment), semi-conductor, metal manufacture, packaging manufacture, the chemical manufacturing industry, industrial vacuum manufacturing and a wide range of other industries where the specific properties of these lubricants enable key processes to function and where alternatives are proven to be non-viable.
PFPE lubricants are used in relatively small amounts, they are tightly controlled in use and extremely expensive.  The cost of them generally means that they are not used unless they absolutely need to be, as dictated by the operating conditions.
Special properties of PFPEs include: chemical inertness, thermal stability, elastomer compatibility, low volatilty for aviation and space , non-reactive in oxygen rich environments, resistance to radiation exposure.
PFPE lubricants are highly insolube in water and hydrocarbons so they don't transmit in water courses through dissolution.  Many grades of PFPEs are accredited to NSF H1 incidental food contact approval further reinforcing their safety profile.
We believe that PFPE lubricants are vital to many aspects of modern society with minimal environmental exposure.   This is based on the industries and manufacturers we supply.

We believe that this is over 30% of the UK and Ireland market for PFPE lubricants although we don't have firm data on the size of the market (but we do have long experience in the industry).  The vast majority of product is used by professionally trained operators within businesses where they would all need to comply with disposal regulations when removed from the site on which they are used as waste material. Combined Comments:
General Comments: As a supplier to the automotive industry, we require PTFE-containing greases and plastics for applications in the field of functional safety, such as parking brakes, engine controls, brake-by-wire and steer-by-wire applications as well as seat adjustment and seat belt applications.
The customer-specific and legal requirements of 1st tiers and OEMs in this area can only be met through the use of the above-mentioned products containing PTFE.

The PTFE admixture serves to ensure a constant and low-wear power or torque transmission over the complete lifetime and the required temperature range, from -40°C to +120°C.

In the case of processed plastics with PTFE admixtures, the PTFE serves as a lubricant and wear protection, as external greasing is not possible here due to vibration requirements, as this would simply be thrown off after a short time.
Numerous tests were carried out by us in order to be able to meet the customer's requirements with standard greases or plastics, but it was only possible to meet these requirements with the addition of PTFE.

Since we have PTFE mostly in closed systems, there is the possibility to dispose of fluorine-containing products after the life cycle.

A conversion or ban of the currently used PTFE-containing greases and plastics for the aforementioned safety-relevant applications would have a very large economic impact across the entire value chain, as this would require renewed verification and validation costs up to homologation approvals.

Therefore, we need a derogation for current series products for the use of PTFE-containing greases or plastics in safety applications in motor vehicles and trucks.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: As a vacuum technology company, we do not use PFAS directly in our manufacturing process as a raw material. However, PFAS are widely present in components that we use: lubricants, sealings, electronics. PFAS are needed due to the properties they provide, and there are currently no alternatives to PFAS that meet the harsh requirements of vacuum applications. This makes FKM/FFKM/PFTE/PFPE irreplaceable for the vacuum industry.
There are many key products that require vacuum and therefore PFAS in their manufacturing process (e.g., all semiconductor components, pharmaceutical products, batteries for electromobility, nuclear industry, solar panels, …) and while the final products do not contain PFAS, they could not be manufactured without vacuum and therefore without PFAS.

PFAS are included in vacuum pumps for three different usages:
1.  In sealing components used in all pumps:
Sealings/Gaskets/O-rings/Shaft seals made of fluoropolymers (including FKM, FFKM, PTFE especially) are used in vacuum pumps, vacuum valves, vacuum pipeline assembly and other vacuum devices (gauges, leak detectors,…).
Why are there Fluoropolymer Sealings/Gaskets/O-rings/Shaft and tip seals in vacuum pumps?
As a general statement, sealing is essential as soon as vacuum is involved. It provides tightness and prevent external atmospheric air to degrade the produced vacuum, and it prevents process gases – possibly harmful – involved under vacuum to leak and potentially exit the vacuum area.
There are a lot of these applications where the use of traditional elastomers (such as EPDM, NBR) is ruled out. Aggressive chemicals, extreme temperatures or only ageing can destroy conventional O-rings. This ultimately leads to leakage and may lead to environmental and worker safety issues.
There is no adequate replacement for the fluoropolymers used, and it is unlikely to be, due to strength requirements on the material itself. Fluoropolymers have an extremely high price and are only used where no other solutions are available.
2. PFPE oil or grease for specific applications
Perfluoropolyether (PFPE) oil or grease have a very low outgassing compared to other fluids (vapour pressure of 6×10−8 Torr), which is extremely valuable for vacuum applications. PFPE also withstand the harsh conditions (heat, chemicals, solvents, corrosion, toxicity, flammability, etc.) that are needed in the industries of chemical, electronic, cosmetic, machinery, aerospace, nuclear, etc. This combination of properties (low outgassing and resistance to harsh environment) are mandatory for vacuum applications, and there is currently no alternative (known or foreseen) for PFPE in these applications.
3. PFAS used by our suppliers in electronic and electromechanical products or related components
The amount of PFAS in these kinds of components is low and shall be submitted by the sub-sector of electronic and electromechanical suppliers. We will focus on the sealings and PFPE that are directly involved in the vacuum technology.

The proposal for restriction as it is, will lead to major impact on all the listed applications, also creating a major distortion of commercial and industrial competition with countries without restrictions.
We request full exemption (with regulation and control) for manufacturing and recycling of the following fluoropolymers (FKM, FFKM, PTFE, PFPE) from the restriction proposal, for use in the vacuum pumps, vacuum valves, vacuum pipeline assembly and other vacuum devices.
Exemption for “Vacuum technology and its machines and components” as a main application would be better and more comprehensive.
Rather, it is correct to ban specific processes and procedures that lead to environmental damage. The restriction should focus on large number uses (such as manufacture, TULAC, food contact material, …), where the manufacture, use and end-of-life phases emit massively into the environment.

PFAS are included in vacuum pumps for three different usages:
1.  In sealing components used in all pumps:
Sealings/Gaskets/O-rings/Shaft seals made of fluoropolymers (including FKM, FFKM, PTFE especially) are used in vacuum pumps, vacuum valves, vacuum pipeline assembly and other vacuum devices (gauges, leak detectors,…).
Why are there Fluoropolymer Sealings/Gaskets/O-rings/Shaft and tip seals in vacuum pumps?
As a general statement, sealing is essential as soon as vacuum is involved. It provides tightness and prevent external atmospheric air to degrade the produced vacuum, and it prevents process gases – possibly harmful – involved under vacuum to leak and potentially exit the vacuum area.
There are a lot of these applications where the use of traditional elastomers (such as EPDM, NBR) is ruled out. Aggressive chemicals, extreme temperatures or only ageing can destroy conventional O-rings. This ultimately leads to leakage and may lead to environmental and worker safety issues.
There is no adequate replacement for the fluoropolymers used, and it is unlikely to be, due to strength requirements on the material itself. Fluoropolymers have an extremely high price and are only used where no other solutions are available.
2. PFPE oil or grease for specific applications
Perfluoropolyether (PFPE) oil or grease have a very low outgassing compared to other fluids (vapour pressure of 6×10−8 Torr), which is extremely valuable for vacuum applications. PFPE also withstand the harsh conditions (heat, chemicals, solvents, corrosion, toxicity, flammability, etc.) that are needed in the industries of chemical, electronic, cosmetic, machinery, aerospace, nuclear, etc. This combination of properties (low outgassing and resistance to harsh environment) are mandatory for vacuum applications, and there is currently no alternative (known or foreseen) for PFPE in these applications.
3. PFAS used by our suppliers in electronic and electromechanical products or related components
The amount of PFAS in these kinds of components is low and shall be submitted by the sub-sector of electronic and electromechanical suppliers. We will focus on the sealings and PFPE that are directly involved in the vacuum technology.

The proposal for restriction as it is, will lead to major impact on all the listed applications, also creating a major distortion of commercial and industrial competition with countries without restrictions.
We request full exemption with regulation and control for manufacturing and recycling of the following fluoropolymers (FKM, FFKM, PTFE, PFPE) from the restriction proposal, for use in the vacuum pumps, vacuum valves, vacuum pipeline assembly and other vacuum devices.
Exemption for “Vacuum technology and its machines and components” as a main application would be better and more comprehensive.
Rather, it is correct to ban specific processes and procedures that lead to environmental damage. The restriction should focus on large number uses (such as manufacture, TULAC, food contact material, …), where the manufacture, use and end-of-life phases emit massively into the environment.

General Comments: As a work fluid in the Organic Rankine Cycle. HCFO-1233zd(E) may be an alternative work fluid to R245fa in Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) systems[1]. Medium and high temperature heat pumps play a huge role in environmental protection as an energy efficient technology. HCFO-1233zd(E) has a high transition temperature of 166.45℃ and a normal boiling point of 18.263℃, which makes it suitable for medium and high temperature heat pumps, and has broad application prospects in industrial waste heat recovery, replacing traditional coal-fired boilers and high temperature systems such as pasteurization.[2-3]

HCFO-1233zd(E) can be utilized as a heat dissipation medium due to its good thermal conductivity and low to medium boiling point, and has a smaller critical pressure than conventional refrigerants, which can be effectively used in refrigeration, heat transfer, and air conditioning.[5]
HCFO-1233zd as feedstock can be processed for the synthesis of organofluorine compounds, intermediates for pharmaceuticals and pesticides, and other applications. The development of trifluorine-containing intermediates mainly focuses on aliphatic C2 compounds such as trifluoroacetic acid and trifluoroethanol, while the synthesis of trifluorine-containing intermediates such as aliphatic C3 compounds is still in the research stage, and HCFO-1233zd is an important raw material for the synthesis of aliphatic C3 trifluorine-containing intermediates [6-7].

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: As a worldwide active company with more than 5000 employees, manufacturing plants worldwide and an annual turnover of about 1,8 million € we are supporting the objective of avoding emissions of hazardous substances and the appropriate regulation of individual substances that pose uncontrollable risks. It is therefore one of our core values to handle our resources responsibly and leave the next generation a healthy planet.
Particularly when it comes to the topic of the environment, we observe pioneering guidelines at European level, such as the EU Green Deal, material-related regulations such as REACH / RoHS, and we support the objectives of the Paris Climate Agreement. A sustainably produced product requires appropriate processes and structures along the entire value chain.
While we strongly support the investment into sustainability and safety of products and end-of-life waste management, we also see the production, research and development locations of our company in Europe at serious risk in the event of a blanket ban and therefore call for a fundamental revision of the restriction proposal in key areas.

With this contribution we as a company want to express our deep concern regarding the proposed and universal restriction of PFAS.
PFAS are crucial in a wide range of applications at the present time and for the foreseeable future. They are an enabling material not only to sustain our European production and business, but also for the ability to achieve the targets of strategic EU policies set in terms of the European Green Deal, digitalization and decarbonization of European industries.
PFAS are used due to their unique combination of properties and their important characteristics for the wide range of our products and technologies.
- Environment-independent lifetime
- High temperature performance
- Electrical insulation; dielectric strength
- Chemical resistance against aggressive media
- Heat resistance at extreme temperatures and non-flammability
- Resistance against climatic influences (e. g. moisture, wetness, dust)
- Good mechanical properties (e.g. abrasion, surface tension, friction)

The proposed threshold of 25 ppb is far below any manageable reporting threshold for companies in the middle of supply chains. It is also about minor impurities for which even we as the manufacturer do not know the information, unless highly precise and costly measurements are made (for which, according to the information from the chemical industry, no analytical methods for PFAS have been established as international standard yet). We have tried and failed to establish a successfull analytical method in our own laboratory sofar. The measurement of organic fluorine content in only an indirect measure and does not provide safety regarding the desired statement of "PFAS-free" for products.

Even the smallest impurities lead to large quantities of raw materials and products (including those indented to be re-used/recycled and those already placed on the market for the first time) becoming hazardous waste.

Almost all intentionally added PFAS remaining in our products belong to the polymeric PFAS group that is considered thermally, biologically, and chemically stable, negligibly soluble in water, nonmobile, nonbioavailable, nonbioaccumulative, and nontoxic while in the use phase.
In general, the commercially available and used fluoropolymers, which account for about 96% of the overall global fluoropolymer market, are deemed polymers of low concern, e. g. by OECD.

While some chemistries might offer a similar performance to PFAS for a particular parameter or property, it is the unique combination of properties that sets fluoropolymers apart and makes them vital for the industries our company is active in, which include:
electrical and electrical equipment, renewable energy, infrastructure, food & beverage, mechanical and plant engineering etc.
Alternative solutions are only partially available for some specific applications, for some no alternative is known at all.

- PTFE, FEP or PTFA:
Exemplary use cases: electrical insulation on electronic components (cable sheath, shrink tubes, wrappings etc.)
Required characteristics: unique combination of heat resistance, electrical insulation, resistance to chemicals and mechanical properties (abrasion, flexibility, …),
Alternatives: PVC or PP are already in use as wire insulation for low temperature applications, but they cannot be used if high operating temperatures (above 105°C) are required. Polymers like PEEK or Polyimide are suitable for high operating temperature but have different mechanical and/or electrical properties compared with fluorinated polymers.

- FKM or FPM
Exemplary use cases: O-rings and sealings
Required characteristics: unique combination of heat resistance, resistance to chemicals and mechanical properties (flexibility)
Alternatives: EPDM rubber, Nitrile rubber (NBR) or Hydrogenated NBR as sealings are not suitable in most applications due to their insufficient media resistance.

- PTFE tools
Exemplary use cases: jigs and tools in the production of electronic components (e.g. wafer carriers, sealing rings and handling tools).
Required characteristics: unique combination of heat resistance, resistance to chemicals (process aids) and mechanical properties (flexibility and stability) to prevent scratches on e.g. sensitive silicone-wafers
Alternatives: Not known.

For all industry sectors that we as a company are active in the proposed restriction imposes a blanket ban on a huge number of substances in an undifferentiated manner and without proof of a specific risk. It is threatening production, research and development sites and activities in Europe and their competitiveness worldwide.

Also, the "hidden cross-section applications" such as seals, plain bearings and lubricants in components, machines and plant equipment are affected. Here, too, a ban would have far-reaching consequences even if PFASs were not added to the final product, so that the expected overall impact is likely to be much more serious. Currently we cannot even assess the impact the ban would have on our production plants.

We are calling on the regulatory authorities to establish a reasonable and practicable treshold for intentionally added PFAS levels of 0.1 percent by weight and to fully exclude fluoropolymers/-elastomers from the scope of the upcoming restriction.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Our input mainly covers "electroincs and semiconductor (Annex E.2.11).  However, as other sectory also depend on electrical components, connectors, glands etc. which are part of our portfolio, some of our contributions refer to "Plastics (other than packaging) and rubber/elastomer production (including flame retardant) as well as other uses which are not listed in Table 9, but shown as "uses not researched in detail" in Table A1 of Annex A.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The amount of PFAS, which can theoretically be emitted in the End-of-Life treatment, is very limited. PFAS containing articles in electrical and electronic equipment are collected and dealt with in accordance with applicable regulations, e.g. Waste Framework Directive (WFD) 2008/98/EC, ELV Directive 2000/53/EC and WEEE Directive 2012/19/EU. If the components cannot be repaired or directly reused, they are sent for material or thermal recycling. Cables are typically collected and treated/milled in the waste stream. Metal components are recycled and reused for creation of new metal alloys. Polymer fractions are incinerated. In these processes, the polymeric PFAS contained in the articles are either broken down into their original components or mineralized so that the PFAS properties are lost. Latest studies confirm that fluoropolymers at their end of life when incinerated under representative European municipal incinerators conditions do not generate any measurable levels of PFAS emissions and therefore pose no risk to human health and the environment.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Most of the technically used PFAS are stable for a long time and very resistant to chemicals. PFAS waste treatment technologies are mostly investigated and technically evaluated by energy assisted technologies. In the case of polymeric PFAS, incineration technologies were investigated with PTFE waste. Under test conditions in a waste incineration chamber, with a setup in compliance to the requirements of the 17th BImSchV, it was demonstrated that polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) can be almost fully transformed into fluoride (F-) (as hydrofluoric acid (HF)). Samples of the flue gas were analysed for the presence of 31 PFAS and found to be without significant measurable PFAS content.[1] At temperatures above 750°C PTFE decomposed to C2F4 and C3F6 in a pyrolysis process. During further combustion CF4 will be generated. At combustion temperatures above 1000°C CF4 formation is much reduced.[2] [1] Krasimir Aleksandrow, et. al; “Waste incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate potential formation of per- and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) in flue gas“; Elsevier Chemosphere 226, p898-906; 2019 [2] Sandra Huber, et. Al.; “Emissions from incineration of fluoropolymer materials”; Researchgate OR 12/2009 [3] 17. BImSchV

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: PFAS-containing products already placed on the EU market can no longer be supplied after the compliance enforcement date and have to be disposed of as hazardous waste. Also, existing stocks of PFAS-containing components and equipment already placed on the market for the first time have to be disposed of as hazardous waste, incl. almost all electric and electronic devices for second-hand use.  Recycling industry is working with high volume processing, such as shredding, of different types of products with different compositions on a ton scale and not on a single piece scale. Given the extremely low threshold of 25 ppb, even a few components containing PFAS would degrade extremely large quantities of recycled materials into hazardous waste.  High amounts of high-quality material as well as still fully functional devices must be treated as hazardous waste instead of being recycled, reused and conserving resources. Instead, high amounts of virgin materials are required to cover the needs with the related environmental impact and the dependance on the sources, which are often outside of the EEA.

Content: Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period
Combined Comments:
General Comments: As an industry, we agree with the general objective of REACH to avoid harmful substances from entering the environment. However, because of the partial overlap of the PFAS restriction with the ongoing revision of the F-gas regulation  on the use of refrigerants for heat pumps and on the use of foam-blowing agents in insulation tanks, some considerations need to be made.
Indeed, while the new F-gas regulation will progressively introduce bans on the use of fluorinated gases with a high global warming potential as a refrigerant in heat pumps, the PFAS restriction may ban the non-flammable fluorinated gases to which some manufacturers switched as a result of the current F-gas Regulation. Therefore, the new F-gas regulation and PFAS restriction absolutely need to be aligned in content and timing.
Furthermore, the combination of both legislations may only leave natural refrigerants available, which are flammable for residential and small commercial hydronic heat pumps and may need to follow certain safety requirements. Our members are therefore in the process of assessing their full hydronic heat pump product portfolio to ensure that refrigerants are available for all applications.
For monoblock hydronic heat pumps with a rated capacity ≤ 70 kW, that are completely installed outdoors, we can say with certainty that we can agree with a full phase out of fluorinated gases. For these appliances, the applicable national, local or regional legislation or safety rules are limited, because the flammable refrigerant does not enter the house. However, to ensure sufficient time for component availability and redesign of the heat pumps and to avoid stranded investments, this phase-out cannot be introduced before 2030. What do we propose practically? To set the 1st January 2030 as the date of application for the PFAS restriction for monoblock hydronic heat pumps with a rated capacity ≤ 70 kW. In addition, we support derogations for maintenance of existing installations, as well as for buildings where safety standards prevent the use of non-PFAS alternatives.
For the other appliances, we will need more time to evaluate, and we will come back in written in September.
Regarding foam blowing agents here as well the timing of the PFAS restriction needs to be aligned with the revision of eco-design and energy labelling requirements  for lots 1 & 2. Indeed, blowing agents used for thermal insulation of hot water storage tanks contain fluorinated gases considered as PFAS. While non-PFAS alternatives to these blowing agents exist,  making the switch will require manufacturers to adapt their manufacturing process and sites. This will take time and, combined with increasing minimum energy efficiency requirements via the revision of eco-design and energy labelling requirements,  limit further the number of storage tanks available on the market, at least until all manufacturers have successfully made the switch. Thus, we recommend aligning the restriction for PFAS used in foam blowing agents with the timing of the F-Gas Regulation as well as ecodesign and energy labelling delegated acts, . We are in the process of evaluating  how this should be translated in the REACH restriction, and we will come back with additional input in written in September.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Our comments apply to applications of fluorinated gases, in particular a) heat pumps and b) foam blowing agents. a) EHI members manufacture hydronic heat pumps which rely on fluorinated greenhouse gases (F-gases), such as hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) and hydrofluoroolefins (HFOs). Heat pumps are acknowledged by the Commission as key technologies for the decarbonisation of building and for achieving the EU’s 2030 and 2050 targets, and the REPowerEU Plan communication aims at deploying 10 million hydronic heat pumps in the next 5 years. Refrigerants, fluorinated and non-fluorinated, used in heat pumps are essential to their functioning, because they are the working fluid of heat pumps that allow heat to be transferred from source to sink.  When heat pump manufacturers select alternative lower-GWP refrigerants, they take into account the substance’s flammability, toxicity and/or high pressure, but also the intended application and energy efficiency of the heat pump when using the refrigerant. And although natural refrigerants are being used as non-PFAS alternatives, they are not suitable to all heat pump systems due to their high flammability, toxicity and/or high pressure or their inferior energy efficiency. For instance, the safe use of propane requires hermetically sealing, which is not possible in split heat pumps. b) In addition, blowing agents used for thermal insulation of hot water storage tanks contain fluorinated gases considered as PFAS. Hot water storage tanks are a good mean to store energy, as water accumulates a lot of energy per unit of weight. As such, they are an important equipment to reduce the energy consumption from heating in buildings. The insulation foams used in storage tank to keep the heat is made in many appliances using HFOs, such as HFO-1233zd and HFO-1336mzz(z)). While non-PFAS alternatives to these blowing agents exist, making the switch will require manufacturers to adapt their manufacturing process and sites. This will take time and, combined with increasing minimum energy efficiency requirements via the revision of eco-design and energy labelling requirements, may limit further the number of storage tanks available on the market, at least until all manufacturers have successfully made the switch. In turn, this increases the risk of supply disruption, which is problematic for the roll-out of heat pumps that the European Commission aims at: as hot water storagesare highly relevant for heat pumps, a shortfall in storages would dramatically harm the heat pump ramp up.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: We do not have detailed data on the impact of the proposed restriction on the recycling industry. However, here, we would like to stress the role of the current and future F-gas regulation, which already limits the emissions of HFCs and HFOs as much as possible, by setting requirements on leak checking and recovery as well as  installation  and maintenance  by F-gas accredited specialists. In addition, any transfer of refrigerant needs to happen in closed systems in order to minimise or eliminate emissions. At the end of life, HFCs and HFOs needs to be recovered by F-gas accredited specialists so that the gases are recycled, reclaimed or destroyed.

5. Proposed derogations: We do not have detailed data on the tonnage and emissions of PFAS related to the proposed derogations. However, we have the following comments on the proposed derogations:  • Derogation 5.i for maintenance of existing installations: we think that a 13,5 years derogation is not sufficient; Indeed, heat pumps have a longer expected life-time, which can vary from one brand to another and from one product to another, on top of being very sensitive to the way they are installed. A 13.5 years-derogation period for their maintenance and refilling would be too short and contradict the principles of circular economy and right to repair. To accommodate the diversity and ensure that all heat pumps installed before the application date of the PFAS restriction will be maintained during their entire lifetime, we recommend a time-unlimited derogation.  • Derogation 5.j for buildings where safety standards prevent the use of alternatives: We will provide comments to this derogation at a later stage of the consultation.

8. Other identified uses: Regarding non-PFAS alternatives to foam blowing agents: as indicated earlier, non-PFAS alternatives exist, although they require adapting the manufacturing processes and construction site (i.a. non-PFAS alternatives based on hydrocarbons might require additional safety measures by means of e.g. underground tanks). We are in the process of evaluating how this should be translated in the REACH restriction, and we will come back with additional input in written in September. Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: As expressed in the document attached to Section IV, we support the views reported with regard to the proposed restrictions issued by the Conference of Fluoro-Chemical Product Japan (FCJ) and the Japan Fluoropolymers Industry Association (JFIA).
We request that fluoropolymers be completely excluded from the restriction.
Fluoropolymers are extremely useful materials with various outstanding properties such as heat and chemical resistance, outstanding electrical properties, and non-adhesion. This puts them in high demand by the automotive, electronics, chemical, medical, and aerospace industries, and contributes to the development of each industry by imparting their unique performance and properties. Whereas fluoropolymers possess the various features as mentioned above, the proposed alternatives are inferior to them in both functionality and performance.
For example, in semiconductor manufacturing processes that require chemical resistance, heat resistance, and non-adhesion, fluoropolymer products play important roles in supplying high-performance and contaminant-free gas and chemical solutions. If the restriction is implemented as proposed, the semiconductor manufacturing industry in Europe will collapse and almost all semiconductor chips will need to be imported from Asia or North America. As a result, not only would Europe fail to achieve a target market share of 20% set by the European Chips Act, but it also would lose its current share (10%).
Moreover, the supply chains in Europe would stop functioning, thereby triggering an economic loss of approx. 63.4 billion euros, and probably affecting the employment of at least 20,000 people.
As mentioned above, we request that fluoropolymers be completely exempted from the restriction, as their regulation is expected to have a significant negative impact on industrial development in Europe.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Parts of pumps, tubes, and joints using fluoropolymers such as PFA, PTFE, and ETFE are used for transferring various types of chemical solutions in the cleaning, film deposition, and polishing processes in semiconductor manufacturing and flat-panel display manufacturing processes.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: We annually export about 26 tons of fluoropolymer products produced in Japan and overseas regions other than Europe to Europe. We manage that we don't spread PFAS to natural environment through our product manufacturing.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: a) Fluid control equipment containing fluoropolymers such as PFA, PTFE, and ETFE is used for transferring chemical solutions in cleaning or other similar processes in semiconductor manufacturing and flat-panel display manufacturing processes. We export about 26 tons of fluoropolymer products to Europe annually.  b) Equipment and parts used for transferring chemical solutions require various properties such as chemical resistance, high purity, heat resistance, non-adhesion, and weather resistance. Only fluoropolymers have these properties. Because these performance requirements have a major impacts on product yields and equipment maintenance frequencies in semiconductor manufacturing, fluoropolymers are extremely important materials for this application.  c) If fluoropolymers such as PFA become unavailable, it will probably impose significant hardship on semiconductor manufacturers, semiconductor manufacturing equipment manufacturers, and companies related to manufacturing flat-panel displays. It could also affect the upstream and downstream companies. Among them are Lam Research and Infineon Technologies AG in Europe.  d) Cleaning processes in semiconductor manufacturing use high-temperature (approx. 200°C)/highly concentrated acids, alkalis, and oxidants. Because no materials other than PFA or PTFE are as resistant to chemicals with strong oxidative effects, such as hot concentrated acid, hydrogen peroxide, and ozone in particular, there are no alternative resins. In addition, any resins with comparable heat/chemical resistance would need to as pure without additives as fluoropolymers are, otherwise contamination in the liquid due to elution while in use would significantly reduce product yields. Consequently, no materials can replace fluoropolymers in the field of semiconductor manufacturing. If fluoropolymers are replaced with a material with insufficient chemical resistance, long-term reliability cannot be ensured, periodic replacement of parts will be necessary, and as a result, not only will productivity fall due to frequent equipment starts and stop, but waste will also rise.  e) As candidates for alternatives, the heat resistance of PEEK, PAI, and PPS is equivalent to or higher than that of fluoropolymers. However, PEEK is at least four times as expensive, is vulnerable to concentrated sulfuric acid, and is a processing-resistant material due to its high hardness. PAI and PPS, meanwhile, are vulnerable to concentrated sulfuric acid and alkalis, and their elastic moduli are about at least ten times higher than that of fluoropolymers, preventing their use in piping parts that require elasticity. Since they entered industrial use more than half a century, fluoropolymers have been the only materials for which there have been no viable substitutes.  f) At present, there is no prospect of complete technological or economic replacement.  g) The market for semiconductor manufacturing equipment and semiconductor manufacturing systems in Europe is worth approximately 50 billion euros. Almost all of this amount would go to Asia or North America. Moreover, supply chains in Europe would be affected.

Trend forecasts suggest that this figure is likely to increase in the future.We manage that we don't spread PFAS to natural environment through our product manufacturing. b.Because fluoropolymers have a low dielectric constant (2.1) and a low dielectric dissipation factor (0.0002), they have advantages for this application. Figure 1 shows dielectric constant and dissipation factor of the resins used for printed circuit boards. These two properties directly affect the transmission loss of high-speed digital signals (Figure 2). Lower values for these properties are essential to achieve high-speed digital communication application, which is expected to become faster and faster along technological evolution. A PPE-based resin is probably unable to meet this specification in terms of transmission loss; indeed, PPEs result in higher transmission loss. A simple way to reduce this loss would be reducing the distances between communication devices such as CPUs, FPGAs, and switch ASICs. In this case, electric wiring patterns cannot be designed on printed circuit board realistically because these devices are too close to each other. This situation is likely to prevent the design of required functions and performances. In contrast, PTFE-based substrates improves the transmission loss in high-frequency, high-speed signals by 40% or more, which relaxes the requirement to place devices closer to each other to achieve the functions and performances. In addition, this transmission loss also affects energy consumption. Data centers consume huge amounts of electricity; estimates indicate that servers using PTFE substrates account for 50% of all servers, and this share is anticipated to rise to 80% in the future. For example, based on an estimate by the Japan Science and Technology Agency’s Center for Low Carbon Society Strategy, these substrates will help reduce the total power consumption by 10% in 2030 and by 12% in 2050. General Comments: As part of its ordinary working process, ACEM teamed up and aligned with ACEA (European Automotive Manufacturers Association) to express concerns on this restriction which could have severe implications in terms of safety, durability, electrification, fuel economy and CO2 reduction technologies as well as hampering developments of future initiatives due to its broad range of critical applications for our industry.
Fluoropolymers in motorcycles are used in various components due to their characteristics of lubrication, electrical insulation, frictional properties, dielectric properties, flame retardancy, thermal stability, heat resistance, water and oil repellency.
The industry addressed the possibility of replacing FP in products:
-              changing the tubing from fluorine to aromatic nylon tubing,
-              the fuel storage from fluorine to H-NB
-              the oil seal from fluorine to another type of rubber.
However, due to low heat resistance, inability to meet fuel permeability and low fuel oil resistance, the alternatives have not met the quality standards and could not replace currently used materials. Substitutes for these materials are not available for all technical applications and material changes may result in risks like functional losses ( e.g. fuel efficiency, noise, liquid resistance/permeation), vulnerabilities, unsafe operation, increased wear, environmental impact (e.g. exhaust gas emission, oil releases, hydrocarbon) and more frequent need to change parts which will lead to an increase of discarded parts and a higher consumption of raw materials.
In general, it can be said that at the time of writing there is no viable alternative all applications and that to research, develop and test new compounds a lead time of 15 years is the minimum necessary. Further to the necessary lead time, an indefinite derogation for legacy spare parts needs to be addressed. Without the requested derogation, the supply of legacy spare parts will be severely compromised, which is in strong contradiction to the overall strategic goals of the circular economy. We have a responsibility to consumers to support the longevity of their current vehicles by ensuring that these products can be serviced, repaired, and maintained in such a manner as to not be detrimental to their function, safety, and reliability. Extending the lifetime of a vehicle is essential to reducing costs for consumers, as well as conserving natural resources and energy.
