Combined Comments:
General Comments: As semiconductor company, Elmos Semiconductor SE relays on many materials and their applications falling within the definition of PFAS as defined in the EU REACH restriction on PFAS proposal. The uses of PFAS materials are related to the semiconductor processes (CMOS process, assembly, test) along the value chain and the products itself and determined by the special chemical properties of PFAS (chemical compatibility, stability in harsh environments, surface tension, purity, temperature stability, long service life of larger 25 years, …)

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Elmos refers to the following sectors and (sub-)uses, identified in table 9 of Annex XV: - Electronics and semiconductors (Annex E.2.11): Semiconductors  - Applications of fluorinated gases (Annex E.2.8): Refrigeration / Insulating gas in electrical equipment

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Concerning End-of-life phase of equipment and parts in semiconductor manufacturing and testing: The lifetime of tools and equipment in the Elmos fabrication facilities are long with 20 to >25 years. Because of highest clean-room requirements to ensure highest quality for automotive applications, fluoropolymers like Polytetrafluorethen (PTFE), Perfluoralkoxy-Polymere (PFA), Polyvinylidenfluorid (PVDF) are needed to meet given requirements on ultra-purity and stability for chemically resistant sealing discs for liquid and gaseous process chemicals, valve bodies and other wetted components in aggressive liquid chemical process plants as well as flexible, chemically stable hose assemblies for aggressive liquid chemicals. Due to the long life and service life of these components, emissions in the end-of-life phase of tools and equipment containing PFAS are very low.  PFAS emission during production:  Some process steps (etching, cleaning) in the CMOS process requires special process gases like Hexafluoroethane (C2F6) and Octafluorobutene (C4F8). There are no other chemicals available for theses process steps, as they are linked to the specific chemistry of Silicon/Silicon Oxide/Silicon Nitride. Since many years Elmos already has installed abatement tools to destroy critical gases using high temperature, running the exhaust gases with natural gas at temperatures > 800°C. PFAS gases are destroyed at these temperatures and neutralized in subsequent washing processes.  To protect the integrated circuit against corrosion and impurities in automotive harsh environment, ICs are protected by a Polyimide layer. Even polyimide is not falling under PFAS regulation, some variants can contain certain additives containing PFAS (see confidential information). Polyimide is part of special waste management with a low risk of entering the environment. Substitution to a PFAS free alternative would require process modifications, requalification and product release procedures with all effected automotive products, not manageable in short time.  Concerning End-of-life phase of semiconductor products, containing PFAS: For pressure sensors, the sensor cell has to be protected against the environment. For safety critical applications in the automotive industry, high chemical and temperature resistance is mandatory against water, cleaning agents, combustion gases, gasoline, oil, … Fluorinated silicone gels are used in low volumes to protect the pressure sensor cell as well as the electrical connection (bond wires and bond interface). To protect automotive semiconductor ICs a polyimide layer (some µm thick) is used to decuple the IC from the mold and to raise reliability against moisture and corrosion. Even polyimide is not directly falling under PFAS regulation, some variants can contain additives containing PFAS.  Recycling of IC is done with state-of-the art electronic recycling procedures, as demanded by automotive industry and regulations.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Some process steps (etching, cleaning) in the CMOS process requires special process gases like Hexafluoroethane (C2F6) and Octafluorobutene (C4F8). There are no other chemicals available for theses process steps, as they are linked to the specific chemistry of Silicon/Silicon Oxide/Silicon Nitride. Since many years Elmos already has installed abatement tools to destroy critical gases using high temperature, running the exhaust gases with natural gas at temperatures > 800°C. PFAS gases are destroyed at these temperatures and neutralized in subsequent washing processes.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: If needed, PFAS containing materials (e.g. sealing rings, tubes, …) could be collected separately and can be handed over to the recycling industry in a controlled manner.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: There are no known alternatives to Fluorocarbons (Hexafluoroethane C2F6 and Octafluorobutene C4F8) used in Plasma Etch / Wafer Clean and Deposition processes. The complex nature of Si chemistry makes these gases mandatory for the processes. Change to non-fluorinated gases would require a redesign of semiconductors and changing silicon as the fundamental element in current semiconductors. This seems to be unrealistic. Ban of these gases would endanger the complete semiconductor industry and with this, human life and prosperity as is relying on ICs. For pressure sensors, the sensor cell has to be protected against the environment. For safety critical applications in the automotive industry, high chemical and temperature resistance is mandatory against water, cleaning agents, combustion gases, gasoline, oil, … Fluorinated silicone gels are used in low volumes to protect the pressure sensor cell as well as the electrical connection (bond wires and bond interface). In the last 15 years Elmos evaluated a wide range of alternative protections and coatings for MEMS based pressure sensors. Due to many requirements (chemical resistance, corrosion protection, temperature stability between -40 to 150°C, no influence on pressure sensor characteristics, processability, density, …), only few fluorinated silicone gels could meet all requirements and life time stability. These sensors are used in automotive safety critical applications like side impact pressure sensors. Because of the small volume needed (see confidential information), long lifetime >10 years, controlled recycling of automotive electronics and low probability of availability of non-fluorinated silicone gels alternatives, a ban of these gels would prevent future development of automotive pressure sensor systems. In general, changing materials or media in semiconductor manufacturing, especially for automotive applications, is a compels and long lasting process. Even with known materials and already proven compatibility, it requires extensive process releases and re-qualification of current products, lasting 2-3 years. With absent of substitutes, valid for most of the PFAS materials, used in semiconductor industry and products, basic research becomes necessary to invent alternative materials and appropriately modified processes. Before use in automotive applications with highest quality standards, long lasting release processes will become necessary to guarantee no harmful interaction of the new materials with semiconductor production and use. Due to the uniqueness properties of PFAS, no one could guarantee the success of this fundamental research. If successful, research could last 3-10 and more years, followed by 2-5 years of industrialization, release and qualification. Therefore, the 13.5 years proposed in the Annex XV report for the semiconductor manufacturing process is not sufficient. Oils, lubricants and sealants must meet highest requirements, such as resistance under harsh (high/low temperature, chemical resistivity) conditions. This applies in particular to the use in vacuum pumps and vacuum systems, as they are needed in many locations in semiconductor production. Contamination due to outgassing from oils, lubricants or sealants into the vacuum must be avoided at all costs, as this can lead to serious reliability problems and safety risks in the field. A possible time frame for substitution with PFAS-free materials is assumed to be more than 10 years in general areas of application.

8. Other identified uses: For semiconductor manufacturing and semiconductor products, PFAS are essential and a PFAS free semiconductor industry is very unlikely. Without PFAS, Elmos will not be able to develop, produce and market automotive semiconductors like ASICS, ASSPS and MEMS in the future. Additionally, there are a lot of other uses and applications, which have been added to the ‘updated’ list to table A.49 in the consultation feedback of the ESIA (ESIA, 2023).

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis
Combined Comments:
General Comments: As SONOTEC GmbH, we are closely following the European Union's plans to ban per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, or PFAS for short. With over 200 employees, we are a medium-sized high-tech company based in Halle, Germany, specializing in the development and production of ultrasonic measuring and testing equipment for a wide range of industrial applications. Our devices and sensors must meet the highest demands and requirements and withstand aggressive substances.

PFAS chemicals play an irreplaceable role in various applications, including the manufacture of semiconductors, high-tech medical products, medical devices and laboratory equipment. Here are just a few examples where our customers are also active. At SONOTEC, we use fluoropolymers, especially PVDF, to make our ultrasonic sensors, PFA for medical tubing, and FFKM/PTFE/PVDF for seals and gaskets. PTFE serves as a lubricant and PVDF is used for plain bearings.

Potential economic impact of a PFAS ban on SONOTEC. We use PFAS chemicals in the manufacture of sensors for important applications in semiconductor production, high-tech medical devices, medical equipment and the oil and gas industry. The economic impact of such a ban would be as follows:

• Competitive disadvantages: A ban on PFAS substances negatively impacts international competition when there are less stringent regulations in other countries.
• Job losses: cost-cutting measures and job losses may be required due to the higher costs and challenges of switching to PFAS-free alternatives.
• Cost increases: Switching to alternative PFAS-free materials could involve significant cost increases. This affects not only the procurement of raw materials, but also the development of products and manufacturing processes.
• Quality and performance limitations: PFAS materials are used in certain applications because of their unique properties. Switching to substitute materials could lead to quality and performance limitations that impact longevity and customer satisfaction.
• Delays in innovation: The development of substitutes for PFAS chemicals requires time and resources, leading to delays in the introduction of new products and technologies, especially in the critical infrastructure of medical devices, biotechnology, and semiconductors.
• Supply chain risks: the availability of PFAS-free materials is uncertain, posing supply chain risks. Alternative suppliers must first establish themselves in the market and be found.
• Research and development: In order to find efficient and environmentally friendly alternatives to PFAS chemicals, increased efforts in research and development are needed, which requires additional investments.

On behalf of SONOTEC GmbH, we hope that the regulatory authorities will carefully consider the potential impact of a PFAS ban and find ways to enable a smooth transition to PFAS-free alternatives.

A future PFAS ban would affect us both directly and indirectly and would have an impact not only on us, but on nearly every company in the machinery and equipment industry. We recognize the need for a ban on toxic PFAS substances that can enter the environment. However, we must not allow PFAS compounds to be included in the ban if they are proven to have no significant impact on the environment or if they remain in machinery without coming into contact with the environment.

The economic consequences of a general PFAS ban would be considerable. Therefore, we support the exemption proposed by VDMA for certain fluoropolymer compounds and affected components. It is important to emphasize that years of research into the longevity of these chemical compounds have helped to ensure the durability of various products. A blanket ban could put not only industrial companies but also households at risk, jeopardizing jobs and hindering innovation. Despite the importance of environmental protection, we should not enact a European ban without global participation to maintain economic stability and innovation compared to China and the United States.

We call on the EU to carefully consider the economic impact when designing the ban and to take a differentiated approach that takes into account both environmental protection and economic stability.

Content: Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Baseline Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues
Combined Comments:
General Comments: As the Gesellschaft für angewandte Wirtschaftsethik (GfaW), we welcome the proposal to restrict per- and polyfluorinated alkyl substances (PFAS) and support a comprehensive ban on these chemicals. As the standard-setting body for certifications such as Certified Sustainable Economics (CSE), Nature Care Product (NCP), Natural Cosmetics Standard (NCS), and NATURE THANX, we have been advocating for sustainability in businesses and ethical practices since 2011. The protection of people, animals, and the environment has always been our top priority in developing our standards. Therefore, we continuously engage with the latest research on the potential hazards of various ingredients, with a particular focus on relevant product categories such as non-food products made from renewable resources, including detergents, cleaning products, hygiene items, care products for objects, toys, candles, fertilizers, and natural cosmetics. In this context, an in-depth examination of PFAS was indispensable for us.
An article (EEA 2023. Emerging chemical risks in Europe — ‘PFAS’) by the European Environment Agency summarizes the risks associated with exposure to emerging chemicals, including PFAS, emphasizing the concern over PFAS exposure due to their potential to cause kidney damage, liver damage, immunotoxic effects, reproductive disorders, endocrine disruptions, and carcinogenic effects. It also highlights the potential neurological and developmental impacts of PFAS. Overall, the article underscores the need to understand and address the risks associated with PFAS exposure in Europe.
These conclusions align with our findings from comprehensive research on the impacts of PFAS. Following, we would like to discuss some studies in more detail.
One review (Sunderland, E.M., Hu, X.C., Dassuncao, C. et al. A review of the pathways of human exposure to poly- and perfluoroalkyl substances [PFASs] and present understanding of health effects. J Expo Sci Environ Epidemiol  29, 131–147 [2019]) explores the current understanding of human exposure to PFAS [poly- and perfluorinated chemicals] and their effects on cancer, immune function, metabolism, and neurological development. It reveals significant associations between PFAS exposure and adverse immunological effects in children, while dyslipidemia is the most prominent metabolic effect associated with PFAS exposure.
Another study (Zhang et al., 2023. L. Zhang, A. Louie, G. Rigutto, H. Guo, Y. Zhao, S. Ahn, et al.
A systematic evidence map of chronic inflammation and immunosuppression related to per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance [PFAS] exposure. Environ. Res., 220 [2023], Article 115188) investigated the potential pro-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects of PFAS. The results indicate that PFAS exposure is associated with increased cytokine production, indicating chronic inflammation. Additionally, decreased B-cell activation, altered T-cell subsets, and immunoglobulin levels were observed, suggesting PFAS-induced immunosuppression. All these findings suggest that PFAS may possess immunosuppressive and pro-inflammatory properties typical of carcinogens.
The effects of exposure to PFAS [per- and polyfluorinated alkyl substances] on neurobehavioral and cognitive functions were also examined. The study (van Larebeke, N., Koppen, G., Decraemer, S. et al. Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances [PFAS] and neurobehavioral function and cognition in adolescents [2010–2011] and elderly people [2014]: results from the Flanders Environment and Health Studies [FLEHS]. Environ Sci Eur 34, 98 [2022]) primarily found a correlation between PFOA exposure and increased sleepiness in adolescents, as well as gender-specific changes associated with PFOS exposure. Minor impairments in attention and memory related to PFAS were also observed in adolescents.
A meta-analysis (Costello, E., Rock, S., Stratakis, N. et. al. [2022] Exposure to per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances and Markers of Liver Injury: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Environmental health perspectives, 130[4], 46001) combining 85 studies on rodents and 24 additional epidemiological studies identified a consistent association between PFAS exposure and liver damage, as indicated by elevated liver enzyme levels, in both animal models and human studies.
A Swedish study (Borg, D., Lund, B.-O., Lindquist, N.-G., & Håkansson, H. [2013]. Cumulative health risk assessment of 17 perfluoroalkylated and polyfluoroalkylated substances [PFASs] in the Swedish population. Environment International, 59) utilized biomonitoring data and conducted a cumulative risk assessment for 17 PFAS individually and in combination. The results showed low concentrations of PFAS in the general population but higher concentrations among occupationally exposed ski waxers. Some well-studied PFAS congeners already exhibited effects at low doses. Concerns regarding liver toxicity and reproductive toxicity were raised in the occupationally exposed group, emphasizing the need for reduced exposure. Immunotoxicity and disrupted mammary gland development were identified as concerns in both study populations, underscoring the necessity for additional toxicological data on many PFAS congeners.
PFAS are also known as endocrine disruptors. They can interfere with the endocrine system and disrupt the normal function of hormones, leading to hormonal imbalances and other health effects. There is growing scientific evidence suggesting potential endocrine disruptions caused by PFAS. Experimental studies (Elvira V Bräuner and others, Endocrine Disrupting Chemicals and Risk of Testicular Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis, The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism, Volume 106, Issue 12, December 2021, Pages e4834–e4860) , for example, show that PFAS substances significantly impair the proliferation and function of Leydig cells [the interstitial cells of the testes] in rats.
In another comprehensive meta-analysis (Kim MJ, Moon S, Oh BC, Jung D, Ji K, et al. [2018] Association between perfluoroalkyl substances exposure and thyroid function in adults: A meta-analysis. PLOS ONE 13[5]: e0197244) the relationship between exposure to perfluoroalkyl substances [PFAS] and thyroid hormones was examined. The results suggest that PFAS are associated with a decrease in total T4 levels in the blood, with the effect varying depending on the concentration of PFAS. A positive correlation between PFAS and free T4 as well as TSH was also observed in the moderate PFAS concentration group.
This overview (Boyd, R.I.; Ahmad, S.; Singh, R.; Fazal, Z.; Prins, G.S.; Madak Erdogan, Z.; Irudayaraj, J.; Spinella, M.J. Toward a Mechanistic Understanding of Poly- and Perfluoroalkylated Substances and Cancer. Cancers 2022, 14, 2919) examines the potential mechanisms through which poly- and perfluoroalkyl substances can contribute to carcinogenic effects. Although PFAS are not directly mutagenic, various mechanisms of carcinogenicity have been proposed, including metabolism, endocrine disruption, and epigenetic changes. These mechanisms are interdependent and sensitive to dose and timing of exposure. The overview focuses on testicular and prostate cancer as examples to illustrate these mechanisms and emphasizes the need to consider the complex interactions between PFAS exposure and cancer development.
A systematic review (Gui, SY., Qiao, JC., Xu, KX. et al. Association between per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances exposure and risk of diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Expo Sci Environ Epidemiol 33, 40–55 [2023]) of the epidemiological literature indicates that exposure to per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances [PFAS] may be associated with an increased risk of type 2 diabetes [T2DM]. Specifically, exposure to perfluorooctanoic acid [PFOA] shows a non-monotonic dose-dependent association with T2DM risk.
Furthermore, PFAS are persistent substances that accumulate in the environment and can cause extensive ecological damage. A study (Hedgespeth, Melanie L., D. Taylor, S. Balint, M. Schwartz, AND Mark G. Cantwell. Ecological characteristics impact PFAS concentrations in a U.S. North Atlantic food web. SCIENCE OF THE TOTAL ENVIRONMENT. Elsevier BV, AMSTERDAM, Netherlands, 880[1 July 2023]:163302, [2023]) comprehensively examined per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances in a coastal food web in the North Atlantic region of the United States. Twenty-four PFAS were analyzed in 18 marine organisms from the Narragansett Bay and surrounding waters, and significant relationships were found between PFAS concentrations and various ecological characteristics such as species, body size, habitat, dietary habits, and location. While PFAS exposure can have negative ecological impacts on these organisms, especially through toxic effects, many of these species are also important fishing resources for recreational and commercial fishing, potentially leading to human exposure through the consumption of these organisms.
This study (Wang, Z., Cousins, I. T., Scheringer, M., & Hungerbuehler, K. [2015] Hazard assessment of fluorinated alternatives to long-chain perfluoroalkyl acids [PFAAs] and their precursors: Status quo, ongoing challenges and possible solutions. Environment International, 75, 172-179) found that fluorinated alternatives, especially short-chain per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances as well as perfluorinated ether carboxylic acids and sulfonic acids (PFECAs and PFESAs), exhibit high environmental stability and mobility, indicating significant potential for global contamination. Furthermore, specific fluorinated alternatives have been identified as toxic and pose global risks to human health and the environment. The knowledge gap regarding the risks associated with fluorinated alternatives can be attributed to factors such as information asymmetry between the industry and other stakeholders. Based on existing case studies, the study suggests that a non-fluorinated substitution strategy involving chemical or functional substitutions could serve as a long-term sustainable solution. However, further development and assessment of this strategy are required. Overall, the study highlights the need to address the hazards associated with fluorinated alternatives, overcome knowledge gaps, and explore alternative solutions for a more sustainable transition from PFAAs.
Another study (Ian T. Cousins, Robin Vestergren, Zhanyun Wang, Martin Scheringer, Michael S. McLachlan [2016]. The precautionary principle and chemicals management: The example of perfluoroalkyl acids in groundwater. Environment International, 94, 331-340) also indicates that groundwater contamination with PFAS, especially PFOS, has been known since the 1990s but is being addressed slowly. This contamination is scarcely reversible, and the costs of remediation are high. The precautionary principle should be applied as exposure to PFAS is difficult to reverse. All PFAS entering groundwater, regardless of their structure and bioaccumulative potential, result in irreversible exposures and risks, along with additional remediation costs. It is recommended to avoid highly persistent and mobile chemicals like PFAS to protect groundwater resources for future generations.
Considering these [and many other] findings, it is of tremendous importance that actions are taken to restrict the use of PFAS and ultimately achieve a reduction in their release into the environment.
A comprehensive ban on PFAS would be a significant step toward a more sustainable and healthier future. It would promote the development and use of more environmentally friendly alternatives and help reduce the burden of these harmful chemicals on human health and the environment. Furthermore, such a ban would provide incentives for companies to invest in innovative technologies and sustainable production processes, leading to positive change throughout the economy.
As GfaW, we advocate for ethical and sustainable business practices. A ban on PFAS would make it easier for us and our customers to realize these principles and ensure the protection of health and the environment. We fully support the proposal to restrict PFAS and encourage all relevant stakeholders to express their support for such a ban and contribute relevant information to contribute to informed decision-making.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: As the provider of motion solutions, we are an important part of a competitive, future-oriented European industry and an enabler for green energy and sustainable power supply. We manufacture highly efficient electrical motion solutions for industrial applications. Our product portfolio comprises Low Voltage Motors (260 – 690 V), High Voltage Motors (0.38 kV – 13.8 kV) and Medium Voltage Drives (1.4 kV – 13.8 kV). Our motors and converters drive pumps, presses, propellers, mills, shears, extruders, cranes, centrifuges, rollers, compressors, blowers and other machines in the paper industry, the marine industry, mining, mills, steel industry, plastic industry, crane industry, sugar industry, chemical, oil and gas, water and wastewater, offshore industry, food and beverage, woodworking, and other industries. Our applications are subject to demanding environments and include industries where explosive gases (Zone 1 or 2) and explosive dust (Zone 21 and 22) occur.
We strongly support the initiative to reduce any negative impact of our activities on environment and health and are taking continuous action to ensure and improve sustainability in our actions. This includes the definition of processes and implementation of IT-Architectures to systematically fulfill sustainability obligations such as REACH, where hazardous substances are evaluated constantly for their individual environmental and health risks and allow for a precise allocation and substitution of critical substances.
The submitted proposal for the ban of PFAS however, does not differentiate between the individual substances and their specific risks. Instead, a group of thousands of substances is regarded as equally hazardous. In this context, we strongly support the positions of BDI and VDMA stating that the ban requires a differentiation between the different PFAS Substances based on their individual risk.
The proposed ban of PFAS in its current form will significantly affect our business. In our position as a manufacturer of machinery, we do not produce PFAS substances ourselves. However, we do purchase and assemble components which may include PFAS from suppliers in a globally distributed supply chain. We strongly depend on our supplier’s willingness and capability to provide us with the required information concerning used PFAS. This information has not been requested from our suppliers in the past because PFAS were not listed as SVHC previously.
In our applications, PFAS are being used to resist ionization and endure extreme environments such as very high or very low temperatures as well as aggressive chemical surroundings (e.g., exposure to sea water and applications in extreme climates, corrosive gases) in specified product dimensions.
The substitution of PFAS in our products is possible in some areas but will require a substantial re-design of large parts of our portfolio with all related costs and effort. In other cases, substitution is not possible due to technical limitations. In these cases, the ban as proposed will prevent us from bringing our product portfolio on the European market which will strongly affect our target industries who play a major role in fostering green energy and decarbonization.
Furthermore, our products are integrated in large-scale industrial complexes which require long-term investments and are designed for long lifecycles of up to several decades. To ensure the necessary performance of our machinery over such long time periods we must be able to provide spare parts which are compatible with our future and historical product portfolio. A PFAS ban as presented would prevent us from supplying compatible spare parts to our customers leading to financial as well as EH&S-Risks due to more expensive or overdue maintenance. Furthermore, the non-fulfillment of existing service contracts as well as liability issues may be significant risks if spare parts with PFAS may no longer be used. Since already today maintenance is carried out by trained personnel in a controlled B2B environment, the risk of hazards is strongly limited.
For this reason, we suggest the exemption of spare parts from the ban which are required to maintain existing products in the market to follow the “repair as produced” principle.
As a conclusion, we argue for a risk-based and targeted approach to control substances within the group of PFAS in line with other REACH-controlled substances. We furthermore request, that a sufficient amount of time is granted for those components, where substitution is technically feasible as well as a general exemption of spare parts which are required to repair as produced. A clear guidance for the further procedure is needed.

For these uses, no feasible alternatives are known. We therefore argue for an exemption of PFAS such as PTFE for high and low voltage motors components with the named applications. For these uses, no potential alternatives are known. The key component for all frequency converters (Low Voltage or Medium Voltage) are semiconductors. The use of many PFAS is indispensable in chip production and for the most part cannot be replaced by alternatives even in the long term (acc. ZVEI Position Paper, 08.05.2023). If a PFAS ban leads to a situation that no alternative products are available this would immediately affect not only the business of all suppliers of such products but also could affect all industries relying on and using such products for their production processes (oil & gas, metals, mining, water & wastewater, pulp & paper, shipbuilding, food & beverage …). According to the Omdia Market study (Medium Voltage Drives Report from 2022) the market for medium voltage drives in EMEA is approx. 487’0 USD (estimation for 2023) not mentioning the frequency converter market for low voltage converters. We therefore argue for an exemption of Fluorpolymeres from the ban for the insulation, cooling, electronic components, and the wiring of medium voltage drives (1 kV – 20 kV). Content: Request for exemption
Org. name: Aerospace, Security and Defence Industries Association of Europe
Combined Comments:
General Comments: ASD (Aerospace, Security and Defence Industries Association of Europe) represents European Aerospace, Security and Defence Industries, representing directly or indirectly (through our national association members) over 3,000 companies of all sizes from 18 countries.
We note that uses by the aeronautic, space, security and defence (A&D from here on) sector have not been considered by the dossier submitters. The proposed restriction (restriction option 2 (RO2)) was developed without taking the specificities of our sector into account. The restriction as currently proposed would have a catastrophic impact as it would bring aviation, space and defence to a standstill (no production, no imports, no maintenance) already 18 months after the entry into force.
In our comments, we explain that the specificities of our sector need to be considered in the restriction options proposed by the dossier submitters.
A&D products include civilian and military aeronautics (aircraft of all types including all technologies for propulsion, hydraulics, flight control, etc. and associated ground equipment e.g. air traffic control, ground support equipment and maintenance/inspection equipment. They also include a diversity of security and defence products ranging from naval vessels, armoured vehicles to weapon systems and munitions and all associated ground platforms for example involved in surveillance, communication, critical infrastructure protection and ground support equipment and maintenance /inspection equipment. Space equipment includes satellites, launchers and communication systems. All these diverse products have the commonality that they operate under extreme conditions and must comply with very strict safety and reliability requirements over their service lives. These requirements mean that there are stringent performance requirements for the chemicals/formulations/materials that are used in the manufacture of the parts, components, systems, etc. that make up A&D products. There are formal quality management systems in place for the manufacture, operation and maintenance (so called maintenance, repair and overhaul (MRO)) to ensure compliance with these safety and reliability requirements (e.g. AS9100). The qualification and certification processes in place mean that once a product design is approved, there are formal change management processes that need to be followed to make changes to any part. MRO of products can only be done with the parts/components/system manufactured as per the approved design.
In our reply to Q6, we give an overview of the where and why PFAS chemicals are used in A&D products. We explain that PFAS chemicals are integral to their production, operation and MRO. We give examples of the most common uses and include 20 illustrative case studies. Each case study includes an overview of the application, the role of the PFAS chemicals in performance, the availability of alternatives and the impact of the proposed restriction on the application. We explain that fluoropolymers are in particular ubiquitous as seals, sealants, gaskets, lubricants, bearings, bushings, etc. across all the parts, components, systems that make up A&D products. Due to the formal quality management systems in place, change management is in general a lengthy process due to the qualification and certification requirements and likely redesign requirement for MRO. However in this case, there are no alternatives available that can fulfil the performance requirements that underpin the safety and reliability of A&D products. This means that the timeline for substitution depends on the availability of alternatives not yet identified, commercialised or industrialised. For example, it is unlikely that 1 to 1 alternatives to PTFE for all current uses will be identified meaning that multiple new materials will need to be innovated.
We highlight that the scale of the substitution requirement that would be triggered by this proposal has no precedent. It impacts the availability of 1000’s of parts, components, systems etc. across all A&D products needed for their production, operation and MRO. We cannot overstate the impact. The dossier submitters’ assessment is incomplete as it did not consider the impact on aviation, space, defence and security. RO2 would have wider economic impacts that go beyond lost jobs in manufacturing – it would stop all EEA production of civilian aircraft, require scheduled maintenance for in-service aircraft to be done outside the EEA and make the EEA dependent on an aging and depleting fleet that could not be replenished. Defence forces would be crippled as they would not be able to maintain existing products, could not procure new products from either EEA or non-EEA providers and could not replenish depleted stocks of weapons and munitions. This does not describe a plausible scenario as it would be a loss of sovereignty for Europe.
For the above reasons, we ask the dossier submitters to amend their restriction proposal to explicitly include our sector and its specificities in their assessment.
We ask them to consider the following
• The formal quality management systems and in particular the strict certification process that are in place to ensure safety and reliability of A&D products (e.g. AS9100, NATO standards)
• The absence of alternatives that can fulfil the performance requirements that underpin the safety and reliability of A&D products
• The formal change management process in place to ensure safety and reliability of A&D products mean that substitution is in general lengthy. It could take decades for a full phase out if suitable alternatives could even be developed (see detailed response to Q6)
• The scale of the R&D activities as a result of substitution needs that would be triggered by a restriction with the current broad scope
• The complexity of A&D products that are assembled from 10000’s of parts, components, systems etc. provided via multi-tiered global supply chains
• The interdependencies of parts, components, systems, etc. across diverse products mean that the lack of a qualified part can impact products that operate in different market segments (e.g. seals in gas turbine engines where the engines are used in civilian and non-civilian applications)
• A shortage of even a limited number of parts/components will mean the product cannot be produced/operated/serviced meaning that derogation coverage must ensure availability of all parts/components over the entire service life of the product
• A 12 year derogation period is not adequate due to the absence of alternatives, the need to develop new chemicals/materials/formulations and the lengthy substitution process to take suitable alternatives into use for both new and existing products
• A review clause through innovation would always be necessary for derogations as there are no alternatives and the timelines needed for the identification, commercialisation and industrialisation of new chemicals/materials/parts/formulations is unknown
• The ubiquity of fluoropolymers in the seals, sealants, cabling, coatings, hosing, etc. across all the parts, components, systems that make up A&D products and lack of foreseen alternatives to these materials, that do not also possess ‘persistent’ properties (fluoropolymers are often used for their durability/resilience)
• Any reporting requirement of uses relying on derogations would need to consider the administrative burden and allow adequate time to collect the enormous volume of information on all PFAS chemicals in complex A&D products (e.g. naval vessels, aircraft, armoured vehicles)
Specifically we ask them to
• Exclude fluoropolymers (and the precursor PFAS chemicals necessary for their manufacture) from the scope of the restriction given their ubiquity in A&D products and the absence of alternatives that fulfil the performance requirements for reliability and safety
• Include a sector derogation for the use of non-polymeric PFAS chemicals necessary for the production and operation of A&D products with a review clause to allow for an extension/renewal of the derogation if needed due to the non-availability of suitable alternatives
• Exclude the use of PFAS chemicals on their own, in formulations and in articles that are necessary for the MRO of existing products
• Include a time-unlimited derogation for specific PFAS chemicals used fire suppression systems (see case study 5 in Annex 2 of the ASD response)
We highlight that due to our sectors reliance on products from a wide range of industries (electronics, semiconductors, batteries etc.), A&D sector derogations for fluoropolymers would not be sufficient to protect our industry from widespread obsolescence of materials and processes and unpredictable side effects within the related industrial supply chains.
We highlight that a blanket ban on fluoropolymers is a disproportionate risk management option given that the dossier submitters concern is on the conditions of use and risk management measures in place at their sites of manufacture and end-of-life, and not as such from their use. We note that although the dossier submitters group all PFAS chemicals into (1) PFAAs and PFAA precursors (2) Fluorinated gases and (3) Polymeric PFASs, the use tonnages for polymeric PFAS were ascribed to group 1 (see chapter 1.3.1 of the restriction report). In addition, we note that related to PFAS properties of concern given in Figure 4 of the restriction report, the only property relevant for fluoropolymers is “persistence”. There are more proportionate risk management options that would address the concern e.g. specific obligations under the Industrial Emissions Directive. Their potential for emissions at end-of life requires different considerations from non-polymeric PFAS as while they are “persistent” due to their extreme inertness; we understand that they are non-mobile, non-bioaccumulative and non-toxic*. The potential for risk has not been demonstrated from this class of materials.
Fluoropolymers have a unique combination of properties that make them ideally suited to applications with high performance requirements for safety and reliability for extended periods in harsh and extreme conditions of use. They are durable, stable and mechanically strong in harsh conditions, stable in air, water, sunlight, chemicals and microbes, chemically inert, non-wetting, non-stick, and highly resistant to temperature, fire and weather. There are no materials currently available that have this range of properties. A ban on their use will compromise existing safety standards in the A&D sector and in other sectors (e.g. manufacturing, transport and storage of chemicals).
With regards to fire suppression, we would like to point out that, as shown in case study 5 in Annex 2 and summarised in Table 11 in our reply to Q6, years of research to replace Halon to comply with the EU Ozone regulation deadline have demonstrated that PFAS are the only suitable Halon alternative, already implemented in some applications (cabin & cockpit portable and lavatory fire extinguisher systems) and in final stages of development for other (Cargo). The EU PFAS restriction as proposed would have devastating economic and operational consequences for aircraft OEMs and their customers associated with the regrettable substitution scenario. Considering the very high risk of not finding any other better alternatives to Halon 1211 & 1301 in due time, a time unlimited derogation is requested to allow current implemented halon replacement to be maintained and ongoing activities to continue with no disruption and uncertainties that the current proposal would generate.

We also note that the reporting requirements on manufacturers and importers of PFAS or PFAS containing articles as well as formulators of PFAS containing mixtures relying on derogations (paragraphs 7 & 8) did not consider the specificities of our sector. Due to both the complexity of our products and our global supply chains (see chapter 2.2 in our reply to Q6), it is not possible to collect, compile and report the information required under paragraph 7 within 18 months of the entry into force. The site specific management plans requirements given in paragraph 8 also cannot be implemented within 18 months of entry into force as the users will be need to collect information from all tiers of their supply chain and map PFAS in the 1000’s of parts, components, systems etc. that make up A&D products. At least 5 to 10 years would be needed to be compliant with such requirements.
In addition, we highlight that the restriction refers to ppb levels in articles (paragraph 2) – the challenges associated with complying with the requirement were not considered by the dossier submitters as apriori to verify this, we would need to test all articles. This is not feasible for A&D products as 1000’s of parts/components would need to be tested.   In addition, standard test methods are not available for the range of articles that would need testing with this level of detection.

This response is also supported by the Space Restrictions Task Force (RTF), an initiative of the Materials and Processes Technology Board of the European Space Components Coordination (ESCC MPTB), which is a partnership of the European Space Agency (ESA), national space agencies, and space industry represented by ASD-Eurospace. In addition, ASD-Eurospace with the support of the RTF has prepared a complementary response to the present contribution focusing on equipment designed to be sent into space (ref. MPTB-ES-PO-0131), as they have not been considered as such in the current restriction proposal (“missing uses”).

6. Missing uses: The dossier submitters did not consider the A&D sector and the restriction proposal does not adequately address uses by this sector. Some A&D uses would be covered under proposed/potential derogations. However, the scope and durations are inadequate. Many A&D uses are not covered by a proposed or potential derogation. For this reason, we provide input of our sector wide uses together with information on the availability of alternatives and socio-economic impacts in the attachment. A summary of the content is given below.   PFAS chemicals are ubiquitous in the production, operation and MRO of A&D products (Table 1). Fluoropolymers are the most widely reported PFAS type e.g. as parts (seals, cables, hoses, etc.), as surface treatments (paints, coatings, sealants, etc.) as components of mixtures (e.g. lubricants) (Table 1 and Annex 1 of the ASD response). Our derogation assessment shows that there is limited coverage for the vast majority of A&D application areas (Table 15-19 of the ASD response). Table 18 and Table 19 of the ASD response show that there are application areas that were in principle assessed but are not covered by any derogation and there are also a significant number that were not assessed and unsurprisingly not covered by any derogation. From the use and derogation mapping, it is evident that non-use scenario impacts of the restriction as currently drafted would be already apparent 18 months after the entry into force as ca. half of our reported application areas are not covered by either a proposed or potential derogation.  We explain that the A&D sector has specificities that need to be considered by the dossier submitters in their assessment. These include the strict safety and reliability requirements A&D products must fulfil, the very high performance requirements on the parts, components, systems, etc. that make up A&D products due to the harsh and extreme operating conditions they operate in and the qualification and certification requirements that are in place to ensure safety and performance requirements are fulfilled over the service life of the products. A&D products are also highly complex in terms of the number of parts, components, sub-systems, systems. A single major platform such as a ship or aircraft can have millions of parts, many of which are complex assemblies (e.g. engines, landing gear, brake systems, fuel systems). They have very long service lives meaning that spare parts must be available as per the original design for decades. These specificities mean that a regulatory requirement to substitute chemicals currently in use is extremely challenging. In this case, the requirement would impact 1000’s of parts/components/formulations in use across a diversity of A&D products. There are no alternatives currently available that fulfil the stringent performance requirements of A&D products. The list of possible alternatives given in the restriction report (Annex E) are not suitable for our uses as the specificities of our sector were not considered by the dossier submitters in their alternatives assessment. For example, section E2.2.10 for “transport” as defined by the dossier submitters lists alternatives for transportation sector uses does not differentiate between the differing performance requirements. New chemicals, formulations and materials would need to be innovated and then taken through the lengthy qualification and certification processes that are in place to ensure safety and reliability of A&D products. For existing products, introduction of new materials means that the product will need to be redesigned and recertified. Taking the example of a gas turbine engine, hundreds of PFAS containing components would have to be replaced. It would be necessary to have an alternative for each component before launching the re-certification process for the redesigned whole engine. An additional challenge is that it is uncertain if R&D programs will identity alternatives in particular to fluoropolymers for these uses. They are currently the only class of materials that have the range of properties needed for A&D applications. It is unlikely that a 1:1 alternative can be identified for all current uses of PTFE, for example. Considering the range and diversity of A&D products, we highlight that the scale of the substitution requirement has no precedent for our sector. it has been estimated that around 400,000 - 500,000 PFAS-containing components (mostly fluoropolymers) are likely to be present in a smaller short-haul commercial aircraft, whilst in larger aircraft the number of PFAS-containing components will likely be in excess of 1 million.  We explain where PFAS chemicals are generally used in the production, operation and MRO of A&D products and the driver for these uses. We include examples of uses in specific products, systems, components, parts and formulations in Tables 3-5 of the ASD response. We give examples of key functionalities of different types of PFAS (polymeric, non-polymeric) and examples of their specific uses in the A&D sector in Tables 6-8 of the ASD response together with information on the availability of alternatives. We also included detailed case studies as illustrative (but non-exhaustive) examples (see Table 11 and Annex 2 of the ASD response). These include examples from aeronautic, security and defence. The 20 case studies give descriptions of the PFAS use (which PFAS and the role they play in the performance of the part, component, and product as relevant), the availability of alternatives and the impact of the restriction as currently drafted. The case studies illustrate that there are currently no alternatives available and that the entry into force of the restriction as drafted would have a catastrophic impact due to incomplete/no coverage of proposed/potential derogations and/or derogations periods expiring irrespective of the availability of alternative and/or MRO requirements for existing products.   We also considered the socio-economic impacts of the non-use scenario of the Risk Options 1 & 2 (RO1 & RO2) specifically for our sector (see Table 12). Our sector was not considered by the dossier submitters and the consequences of the restriction are not included in their assessment. We considered the impact to the options proposed on A&D companies, their supply chains, third-party MRO facilities, customers (including airlines and defence agencies) and those who rely on the products and services provided by the A&D industry.  With RO1 where all PFAS chemicals are banned with no derogations, the economic impacts would be catastrophic and detrimental to the functioning of the EEA both in terms aviation (passenger, cargo, military) and national security. This option is discarded by the dossier submitters.  With RO2 (all PFAS chemicals are banned with time limited derogations for uses by specific sectors/applications), the impact depends on the coverage of the derogations for uses of PFAS chemicals needed for the production, operation and MRO of A&D products. If the derogation coverage is not complete and/or the expiry periods are not aligned, the impact can be as severe as RO1. From our use and derogation mapping, we have demonstrated that the coverage is incomplete and the derogation periods when given are inadequate for this sector.  We referred to recent authorisation applications submitted for continued use of a limited number of hexavalent chromium compounds for a limited number of surface treatments of parts/components/systems/products by the A&D sector to get an illustrative understanding of the wider economic consequences of non-use scenarios (see Table 13 of the ASD response). From that socio-economic assessment, we can see that the economic impact of the non-use scenario is exceptionally severe. In this case, due to the number of chemicals within scope and the ubiquity of their use in the production, operation and MRO of A&D products, the impact of RO2 would be catastrophic. RO2 would shut down production of new products, stop MRO of existing products, stop the import of products, components, parts etc. The wider economic consequences go beyond lost jobs but would in effect stop all EEA based production of A&D products, stop their imports, stop MRO of existing products, stop import of components, parts etc. Taking civilian aviation as an example, this would mean that aircraft could fly in the EEA but could not be produced, serviced or imported in the EEA. Taking national security as an example, existing defence products (aircraft, naval vessels, land vehicles, munitions, weapons) could be operated but not serviced due to lack of spare parts. Existing stocks once depleted could not be replenished. New products/parts could neither be produced nor imported in the EEA. Defence forces would be unable to respond to security threats. For these non-use scenarios to come into effect is not credible.  Based on our assessment, we can see that the scale of the substitution requirement that would be imposed by the entry into force of this restriction, together with the specificities of our sector have not been considered by the dossier submitters. Their proposed RO2 does not include our sector and is therefore incomplete.   We ask the dossier submitters to amend their proposal to include our sector and to take into account our considerations and requests as given in our general comments.

General Comments: AstraZeneca is a global, science-led biopharmaceutical company that focuses on the discovery, development, and commercialisation of prescription medicines in Oncology, Rare Diseases, and BioPharmaceuticals, including Cardiovascular, Renal & Metabolism, and Respiratory & Immunology.

AstraZeneca supports the EU’s goal to protect the environment and public health. [1,2]  We comply with regulations and ethical and sustainability standards across our manufacturing chain to mitigate risks to people and the environment. [3] We are an industry leader in accelerating sustainable healthcare innovation while lowering the environmental burden of healthcare. [4]

We welcome the chance to respond to the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) public consultation on the per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) REACH restriction proposal, [5] (hereafter ‘restriction proposal’), because PFAS are used across many medicines’ lifespans and play a role in the research, development, and manufacturing of life-saving medicines.[6,7]

Our first response to the consultation focuses on the application of PFAS in respiratory medicines, in particular the use of fluorinated substance HFO-1234ze(E), a novel propellant under development for use in pressurised metered-dose inhalers (pMDIs) that has near-zero Global Warming Potential (GWP).[8,9] pMDIs are an important therapeutic option for the millions of patients globally with respiratory diseases, as these inhaled medicines reduce chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbations and asthma attacks, which are potentially life-threatening events. [10,11] These diseases are difficult and complex to manage and carry a heavy burden for patients, healthcare systems and society.[10,11,12]

AstraZeneca notes that HFO-1234ze(E) has been classified as a PFAS within the restriction proposal based purely on its chemical structure. However, HFO-1234ze(E) is backed by comprehensive evidence demonstrating that this substance is non-persistent, non-bio accumulative and non-toxic.[13,14]

AstraZeneca, therefore, recommends exempting/excluding from the restriction proposal substances such as the novel pMDI propellant HFO-1234ze(E), as it does not fulfil the criteria of persistence, bioaccumulation and toxicity, and to ensure patient access to life-saving and essential pMDI medicines is maintained.

Please consider further information and the references in the attached file.

Further considerations from AstraZeneca regarding derogations for substances used in pMDIs, reflecting appropriate timelines for transitioning such substances without risk to patient outcomes, will follow in upcoming responses to the consultation.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Propellants in Metered Dose Inhalers (MDIs)

6. Missing uses: pMDIs deliver life-saving medicines with essential socio-economic benefits.  pMDIs are an important therapeutic option for patients with respiratory illnesses recommended by international guidelines. [15] These products answer to specific medical needs and include several medicines listed as essential by the World Health Organization. [16]  Nearly 550 million people globally and nearly 60 million people in Europe live with complex chronic respiratory diseases[17,18,19], including asthma and COPD, with increasing prevalence. In 2016, 339,000 people in the EU died from respiratory diseases.[19] These diseases account for approximately 4.1 million deaths per year globally.[20]  Respiratory diseases such as COPD are serious, complex to manage and can take a significant toll on individuals.[10,11,12] COPD is a long-term, progressive disease which can cause obstruction of airflow in the lungs resulting in debilitating bouts of breathlessness.[10] COPD is the third leading cause of death worldwide and is estimated to affect up to one in 10 adults over the age of 40 in the EU.[21,22]  Improving lung function, reducing exacerbations and managing daily symptoms such as breathlessness are important treatment goals in the management of COPD.[10] Inhaled medicines aim to control symptoms, prevent disease progression, reduce mortality and improve patient outcomes overall.[10]  Inhaled medicines delivered to patients by pMDIs are the most used medicines in respiratory care in Europe and worldwide. In 2021, pMDIs accounted for 76% of all inhaler use in Europe, and 78% of global use.[23] pMDIs are an important therapeutic option for patients, particularly where familiarity with the device, limited lung function, young or advanced age or reduced dexterity or cognition are considerations.[24,25,26,27] These medicines are not interchangeable and switching should only be based on clinical need and individual patient assessment.[28,29]   pMDIs contain an active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) either suspended or solubilised in a propellant which delivers the medicine to the lungs of the patient.[30] APIs, which are exempt from the restriction proposal, cannot be delivered without the propellant. Maintaining propellant options for pMDIs therefore, is critical to ensuring the flexibility to formulate APIs whose varying physical properties secure the efficacy and safety of a medicine whilst being compatible with the various device component materials that constitute the device.[31]  The delivery of the therapeutic ingredient relies on the propellant in the pMDI. There are currently two fluorinated greenhouse gases (F-Gases) used as propellants – HFA-227ea and HFA-134a. Both are subject to production and consumption phase-down following the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol and the soon to-be-adopted EU F-Gas Regulation, and in accordance with appropriate transition timelines.[32,33] Maintaining propellant options for pMDIs has been important to ensure flexibility in formulating APIs with widely varying physical properties. In the same vein, it remains important to maintain options for next-generation hydrofluoroolefins (HFO) propellants transitioning away from current hydrofluorocarbons (HFC) gases with high GWP.[34]   There are, currently, two alternative propellants in development for medical use in pMDIs – HFC-152a (which does not fall in the proposed PFAS definition of this draft restriction but is subject to phase down under the Kigali Amendment and EU F-Gas Regulation, see section III), and HFO-1234ze(E) (which falls within the scope of this restriction proposal, but not subject to phase down under the Kigali Amendment and EU F-Gas Regulation).[35] Other alternatives have been investigated by the industry but are considered unsuitable for use in pMDIs.[36]   In accordance with AstraZeneca’s climate ambitions and global and EU regulation phasing down use of F-Gases, AstraZeneca has committed to transitioning its portfolio of inhaled respiratory medicines to the next-generation propellant HFO-1234ze(E) with an ultra-low GWP of 1.37. It has up to 99.9% less GWP than propellants currently used in respiratory medicines, and therefore presents a viable alternative for long-term respiratory patient care with pMDIs.[8,9]  Adoption of these near-zero GWP propellants will enable healthcare providers and patients to be able to contribute to reduced carbon emissions without having to accept a less effective and safe approach to therapy.[37] The proposed restriction proposal, however, could have the unintended consequence of limiting patient options for essential life-saving and innovative medicines.[15]  Please consider further information and the references in the attached file.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: AstraZeneca’s position on PFAS restriction aligns with the United Nations Environment Programme, recognising that not all classed PFAS should be grouped together to assess human health risk.  The universal EU PFAS restriction proposal does not take into account that PFAS substances do not all exhibit the same properties or risks to human health and the environment, nor industry-wide efforts to deliver non-persistent, non-bio accumulative and non-toxic substances.  The 2022 Assessment Report from the United Nations Environment Programme supports the AstraZeneca position with a statement from a majority panel of experts who agreed that “all PFAS should not be grouped together, chemical structure and persistence alone are not sufficient for grouping PFAS for the purposes of assessing human health risk,” and furthermore that “it is inappropriate to assume equal toxicity/potency across the diverse class of PFAS.”[38]  While the next-generation propellant for pMDIs, HFO-1234ze(E), falls under the OECD PFAS definition because of its chemical structure, it is classified according to the ECHA dossier assessment as non-persistent, non-bio accumulative and non-toxic, and its breakdown does not present a risk to the environment.[13,39,40] It is a well-studied and a fully REACH-registered substance, which should not be grouped with all other PFAS for hazard, exposure and risks characterisation purposes.  Please refer to the attached document for full details of the evidence and references.   This touches upon, among others, the following elements as well as information on alternatives. A) Evidence that HFO-1234ze(E) is not persistent B) Evidence that HFO-1234ze(E) does not-bioaccumulate C) Evidence that HFO-1234ze(E) is not of toxicological concern  Given these considerations, it is important that HFO-1234ze(E) is exempt/excluded from the PFAS restriction given the evidence to support its non-persistent, non-bio accumulative and non-toxic qualities and to ensure patient access to life-saving and essential pMDI medicines is maintained.   Specifically, there is a need for the following amendments to Annex XVII Proposed restriction entry PFAS (Restriction Option 2) column 2, paragraph 4. Before being granted, this derogation required the submission of extensive evidence including on the safety of inhaled medicines and absence of viable alternatives.

Paragraph 9 of the Annex XV dossier of the PFAS restriction proposal states that the new restriction “shall apply without prejudice to […] other applicable Union legislation”. It can, therefore, be assumed that existing derogations established under other applicable Union legislation enjoy precedence, including for the use of PFOB for respiratory medicines under the POP Regulation. It is critical to ensure legal certainty and that already adopted derogations, including the derogation for use of PFOB in pharmaceuticals under the POP Regulation, can continue to apply.

In this respect, AstraZeneca requests the Dossier Submitters and ECHA Committees recommend wording for paragraph 9 that provides legal certainty as to the continued application of existing derogations and exemptions in EU legislation, notably as regards the derogation for use of PFOB in pharmaceuticals no later than 2036 under the POP Regulation.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: AstraZeneca supports the EU’s goal to protect the environment and public health and complies with local and EU sustainability standards across our research, development and manufacturing.1,2

PFAS are used across many medicines’ lifespans and play a role in the research, development, and manufacturing of life-saving medicines.3,4  This includes inhaled respiratory medicines used by patients with complex respiratory diseases like asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and cystic fibrosis.5,6 Inhaled respiratory medicines, usually delivered by pressurised metered-dose inhalers (pMDIs), fulfil specific medical needs and include several medicines listed as essential by the World Health Organization.7 Nearly 550 million people globally and 60 million people in Europe live with respiratory diseases according to 2017 estimates, with increasing prevalence.8,9,10

AstraZeneca’s pMDI medicines currently rely upon HFA propellants (HFA-134a and HFA-227ea) which help suspend or dissolve the active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) into droplets, thereby facilitating delivery into the lungs by inhalation.11 Table 8 of the Annex XV’s restriction report summarises the assessment of the existence of alternatives and the degree of cost impact for PFAS use across sectors in the case of a full ban. Regarding pMDIs, the report states there is “sufficiently strong evidence” for the existence of suitable alternatives, resulting in a “high substitution potential at EiF”.12 Furthermore, cost impact of substitution is estimated to likely “be very small”, and “no additional administrative costs for industry or authorities are expected”.12 Based on experience, scientific evidence and data, there are currently no approved alternative medical propellants in pMDIs to HFA-134a and HFA-227ea. Furthermore, these statements do not adequately reflect the significant challenges that need to be overcome to introduce an alternative propellant formulation for a marketed medicine.

Developing a new medical propellant is a lengthy and complex process entailing extensive research and testing, comprehensive pre-clinical and clinical studies, product development studies and review procedures by national and international regulatory agencies around the world, each with their specific requirements to secure regulatory approval.13

In accordance with AstraZeneca’s environmental protection and climate ambition (Ambition Zero Carbon) and global and EU regulation phasing down use of fluorinated greenhouse gases (F-Gases), AstraZeneca has committed to transitioning its portfolio of pMDI medicines to a next-generation propellant (HFO-1234ze(E)) with near-zero Global Warming Potential (GWP) that is under clinical development.14 AstraZeneca is committed to launching its first next-generation pMDI from 2025 onwards and estimate that the global transition will take at least until 2030. However, completing regulatory approvals around the world is likely to go beyond 2030, and during this time there is a need to ensure there is no shortfall in access to medicines, particularly for countries that are dependent on pMDIs.

Adoption of near-zero GWP propellants will enable healthcare providers and patients to be able to contribute to reduced carbon emissions without being relegated to a less effective or safe approach to therapy.15 The proposed restriction proposal, however, could have the unintended consequence of limiting patient options for essential life-saving and innovative medicines. 16 Furthermore, as a major commercial manufacturing hub for pMDIs, approximately 75% of pMDIs manufactured in the EU are exported to the rest of the world.17 The proposed restriction would also therefore impact supply of these essential medicines to patients in the EU and rest of world, including those in low income and/or low-to-middle income countries who rely heavily on pMDIs as their only device option.17

The soon to be adopted EU F-Gas Regulation is expected to recognise that a successful and complete portfolio transition, that avoids supply disruption and patient health impact globally for current pMDI therapies, will take time. The REACH restriction on PFAS should similarly recognise the criticality of patient need by adopting a consistent approach. Specifically, REACH legislation should allow a derogation for the propellants HFA-134a and HFA-227ea in pMDIs in line with the expected F-Gas Regulation phase-down timeline and cover at least a period of 12 years from the time the restriction will become effective.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: AstraZeneca supports the EU’s goal to protect the environment and public health and complies with local and EU sustainability standards across our research, development and manufacturing.1,2 We are an industry leader in accelerating sustainable healthcare innovation while lowering the environmental burden of healthcare.3  AstraZeneca’s innovation and support of environmental goals is evidenced by the development of near-zero Global Warming Potential (GWP) inhaled respiratory medicines.4

Pressurised metered-dose inhalers (pMDIs) are an essential therapeutic option for the millions of patients globally with respiratory diseases, as these inhaled medicines reduce chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbations and asthma attacks, which are potentially life-threatening events.5,6,7,8 These diseases affect nearly 550 million people globally and nearly 60 million in Europe, are difficult and complex to manage and can carry a heavy burden for patients, healthcare systems and society.5,6,7,8

HFO-1234ze(E), a novel propellant under development for use in pMDIs that has near-zero GWP, has been proposed to be banned by the ECHA REACH restriction.4,9 As stated in the company’s first response to ECHA’s public consultation, HFO-1234ze(E) is backed by comprehensive evidence demonstrating that this substance is non-persistent, non-bio accumulative and non-toxic.10,11,12,13 The present analysis predicts formation of low amounts (0-4%) of trifluoracetic acid (TFA) formed from HFO-1234ze(E), further substantiating HFO-1234ze(E)’s suitability as a solution to transition from current high-GWP propellants HFA-227 and HFA-134a.14

Given the comprehensive evidence demonstrating that HFO-1234ze(E) is non-persistent, non-bio accumulative and non-toxic, AstraZeneca therefore recommends the substance is exempt/excluded from the restriction proposal to ensure patient access to essential life-saving pMDI medicines is maintained.10,11,12,13

A restriction on the use of HFO-1234ze(E) in pMDIs without the availability of suitable alternatives could have a detrimental impact on patients’ health not just in the EU, but across the globe, considering that the vast majority of EU-produced pMDIs are supplied to the rest of the world.15,16,17 Thus, if applied to pMDIs, the ECHA PFAS restriction will have a large socioeconomic impact and may have the unintended consequence of limiting access to essential life-saving medicines for those living with chronic respiratory diseases if enforced before safe pMDI substitutions have been found.16,17

There are currently two fluorinated greenhouse gases (F-Gases) used as propellants in pMDIs– HFA-227ea and HFA-134a. Both are subject to production and consumption phase-down following the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol and the soon to-be-adopted EU F-Gas Regulation.18 Furthermore, there are currently two alternative propellants in development for medical use in pMDIs – HFC-152a (which does not fall in the proposed PFAS definition of this draft restriction but is subject to phase-down under the Kigali Amendment and EU F-Gas Regulation) and HFO-1234ze(E) (which falls within the scope of this restriction proposal, but is not subject to phase-down under the Kigali Amendment or EU F-Gas Regulation).

If both legislations are passed, this will likely negatively impact patients who rely on these essential life-saving medicines and who will lose access to all pMDIs, resulting in further significant socioeconomic impacts.
