Combined Comments:
General Comments: At “Jäger Gummi und Kunststoff” (JGK) as well as at the “Artemis Kautschuk- und Kunststoff-Technik GmbH” we supply all different kinds of products to our customers which all have rubber or elastomers as the functional material. While JGK represents the trading activities (including management of several external suppliers) the Artemis stands as a representative of the various production companies within the Jägergroup.
Besides a huge variety of products based on natural and synthetic rubbers the group of polymeric PFAS elastomers (including FKM, FFKM, FVMQ and also several thermoplastic PFAS like PTFE or ETFE) is crucial for the daily business of our customers. Located in almost all fields of industries we deliver to both big as well as small companies. All have in common that they use products based on polymeric PFAS materials to fulfill a specific function within their processes or applications. These uses cannot be fulfilled by other materials without having the risk of failure and much higher maintenance costs as the alternatives cannot withstand the harsh conditions in the field. PFAS elastomers withstand high temperatures, show a broad resistance against various solvents and aggressive chemicals and are unimpressed by ageing effects which makes them ideal for long term process and product stability (“Hofmann, W. (1980). Kautschuk-Technologie. Gentner Verlag“ and “Fernandez, P. (2008). Fluoroelastomers, FKM, and FEPM. in Klingender, R. C. (Hrsg.) Handbook of Specialty Elastomers. 133-154. CRC Press.”).
Having contact to customers in almost all fields within the German, European and even worldwide rubber industry we can say that there are rising concerns towards a broad restriction of polymeric PFAS starting at the food industry dealing with harsh cleaning conditions at elevated temperatures, continuing with pump producers supporting the chemical and automotive industry with dosing pumps for aggressive media, bio-Diesel, glues and many more and stopping at drilling companies which need highly reliable safety units made of FKM that resist the harsh conditions on the oilfield while maintaining its safety functions whenever needed. Especially those industries which would not be covered by exemptions fear of losing their business.
As a future-orientated company the Jägergroup supports a lot of customers which are crucial players in technologies that help to make the Green Deal from the European Union a successful story. One part in the reduction of the carbon foot print might be the use of renewable fuels like Bio-Diesel. Progressive cavity pumps for Bio-Diesel rely on FKM within the rubber component to have a constant and secure material flow. Alternatives will not show such an elongated lifetime and have the risk of failure within the process which might result in leakage and personal health risks for the operators as well as the environment. („Walker, F. J. (2010). Einwirkung von Biokraftstoffen auf statische Elastomerdichtungen., Gummi Fasern Kunststoffe, 63 (9), 560-563.“) Another part is the support of customers in the production of battery electric cars. Electric engines, more precisely the copper coils inside the engine are sealed in certain resins. These materials are highly aggressive for most elastomers. Therefore we use different types of fluorinated rubbers (FKM) including special types like perfluoro rubbers (FFKM) in our dosing stators to secure the process, to guaranty a constant flow of the resins processed and to enable our customers to build high performance engines. The same applies in the area of battery construction where special thermal pastes also require the use of FKM and FFKM. In short, building electric cars would become nearly impossible without the use of polymeric PFAS.
In several investigations we and our customers learned that there sometimes might be alternatives to polymeric PFAS for specific applications. A fundamental aspect at the beginning of a product development and its design is the choice of material. We at the Jägergroup support our customers to use the best material for their specific application. As fluorine containing elastomers are at the top in terms of costs our customers are always interested in alternatives. Likewise, the idea of sustainability has always been and is becoming increasingly important to us and our customers. For example alternative elastomers like EPDM can be used in contact with acids and bases or NBR when an oil resistant Elastomer is needed. But, as can be seen in the ASTM D2000, whenever it comes to high temperatures combined with low swelling values or a combination of different factors most alternatives fail or would need an enormous consumptions of resources due to short-term maintenance. Therefore in many applications FKM and FFKM are the remaining materials to choose. (“https://www.astm.org/d2000-18.html” as of September 22nd, 2023).
We at Jäger understand that one of the positive properties of PFAS, its long-term durability, is also one of the problems leading to an increasing concentration of PFAS in the environment. Therefore we are always searching for alternatives and are open towards new developments in this field. But as polymeric PFAS with high molecular weight, which are non-reactive and fulfill the rules of the CLP-classification or Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008 for being marked harmless, we believe that a distinction between different types of PFAS, e.g. perfluoroalkyl sulfonates and perfluorocarboxylates on the one side and polymeric FKM/FFKM/PTFE/etc. on the other side, has to be made. Several publications deal with this topic (e.g. “Korzeniowski, S.H. et al. (2023), https://doi.org/10.1002/ieam.4646” and “Bougas,K., et al. (2020), https://data.europa.eu/doi/10.2779/890644”). We also support the ongoing investigations of our suppliers to search for PFOA free ways of producing polymeric PFAS. Examples can be seen in the following publications that show, that it is possible to produce polymeric PFAS without creating volatile PFAS. (“https://www.k-aktuell.de/technologie/solvay-fluortensidfrei-zu-fluorkunststoffen-90125/“ as of September 22nd, 2023 and “https://www.fluonox.co.in/pdf/Announcement-on-NFPA-technology-FKM-27-Aug-2022.pdf“ as of September 22nd, 2023).
Summarising it up we support the ongoing task for a reduction of volatile and critical PFAS especially in applications where there are alternatives or where it is only for personal comfort etc., but say that risking an entire industry which is one crucial player to manage the technological aspects which are necessary for the success of the green deal within the EU is from our perspective no option. Therefore we ask the polymeric materials to be generally removed from the proposal.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: As said before we support different customers from a broad variety of industries which, among others, can be located to the following sectors and (sub-)uses as listed in the proposal:   • Food contact materials and packaging - Industrial food and feed production, e.g. in valves and conveyor belts, and for non-stick coatings We at Jäger produce and sell different types of seals, rubber balls for valves, stators for different type of progressive cavity pumps, parts for cleaning devices, etc. to our customers which process all kinds of foods.  • Transport - Sealing applications and combustion engine systems We deliver several dosing stators for sealing resins/glues, different tubes/hoses and seals for automotive combustions engine systems  • Petroleum and mining We produce general equipment for drilling applications with regards to high temperature usage and/or safety related applications.   Apart from these listed sectors we supply FKM to different industries whenever high temperature, long term stability, aggressive media or safety concerns make polymeric PFAS the ideal material to choose.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: As we mainly work with solid PFAS products we do not see a risk of PFAS that evaporate or leak out of our production facility. Dusty particles which appear due to the addition of powder additives on PFAS basis to our compounds are effectively extracted and can then be disposed of as solid waste. We commission an external company with the solid residues and production wastes that occur in our production. This external company sorts the waste and both uses the rubber material for the production of granulates or takes care that the remaining waste is incinerated in industrial waste treatment processes above 850 °C. This procedure is a suitable procedure to transfer remaining PFAS into mineralized forms like Calciumfluoride (“Gehrmann, H.-J. et al. (2023), Pilot-Scale Fluoropolymer Incineration Study: Thermal Treatment of a Mixture of Fluoropolymers under Representative European Municipal Waste Combustor Conditions.”).

5. Proposed derogations: FKM compounds in the range of about 5t used in the production of different food contact articles and articles intended for the use in the oil- and mining sector would be covered by derogations. As these products differ in size and dimensions it is difficult to give discrete numbers.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: At first, MORESCO supports the statement made by Conference of Fluoro-Chemical Product Japan (FCJ) on the issue of proposed restriction, as per attached in Section IV.
We, MORESCO, would like to give comments about lubricants belong to PFAS for the magnetic recording media in this consultation.
A magnetic storage device is a device that records and reads information by using magnetic heads close to magnetic media and applying a magnetic field to magnetize them. The representative devices are, for example, hard disk drives and magnetic tape drives. Because magnetic heads and media shall be closer each other, lubricants are coated on the surface of magnetic media to reducing a friction and wear between heads and media, and to prevent from physical corruption (data losses) [Ref. 1, 2, 3]. Since then, magnetic storage devices have continued to be developed, and the areal recording density has been increased with narrowing the space of heads and media [Ref. 4]. Therefore, the role of lubricants located between heads and media becomes more important and essential. The lubricants employed for the magnetic media are Perfluoropolyethers (PFPEs) and their derivatives, which are some of PFAS. The reason why PFPEs lubricants employed for the magnetic media is the chemical stability they own have, heat resistance, very low vapor pressure, low surface energy etc. and tribology performance in the application [Ref. 5, 6].
The various lubricants have been synthesized, examined and adopted for the media corresponding to the continuous development of magnetic recording devices [ref. 7, 8]. And many patents of lubricants for the magnetic media are applied and registered. The development of PFPEs and their derivatives are also indispensable for the development of magnetic recording devices as ever and for the future.
We would like to give some comments about the future information society. The world-wide digital data is generating now and on, and exponentially growing [Ref. 9] because:
a) IoT (Internet of Things) devices become more common. It needs to be accumulated in somewhere. For example, Smart Home Devices, Automobiles and Industrial Equipment etc.
b) The social media are used for individuals and companies to share and exchange the information on a daily basis. Such platforms accumulate posted contents, messages, images, videos, etc., increasing the amount of data.
c) Big data can create values in various fields such as businesses and research and developments by collecting, storing and analyzing huge amounts of data. In order to utilize such big data, it is necessary to have a large amount of data.
d) AI (Artificial Intelligence) technology can automatically extract patterns from a large amount of data and self-learn to assist humans in their intellectual work. Therefore, in order to utilize AI, a huge amount of data is required.
Many of these data stores in magnetic storage devices such as hard disk drives and magnetic tape drives. The lubricants as the one of PFAS are employed to these media. The magnetic storage devices cannot be available without these lubricants. Therefore, it is estimated that the increasing huge amount of data will not be stored in the future, and the social impact will be extremely serious globally.
In addition, the progress in science and technology and the accumulation of data and information are essential for the achievement of the EU Green Deal.
Specifically, accumulating and analyzing data and information are essential for promoting efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in various fields such as energy managements, transportations, and industries etc. Foe example, it is required for policies and initiatives based on accurate information, such as monitoring corporate energy consumption and emissions, and analyzing the status of renewable energy adoption.
Under the Green Deal, the European Commission aims to have a large number of Internet of Things (IoT) devices in the EU by 2030. Accumulated data from these devices will also support for achievement of the Green Deal.
In other words, in order to achieve the Green Deal, it is important to accumulate a huge amount of data and information, conduct accurate analysis, and promote policies and initiatives based on these analytical results. Therefore, it is expected that the demand for the storage of data and information will increase.
In fact, in the field of magnetic storage devices, they have continued to take on technological challenges for increasing recording density to meet market demands [Ref. 4]. Heat-assisted recording (HAMR) has been proposed as a new technology for this purpose, and its release is coming soon to the market [Ref. 10]. It is essential to develop new PFPE derivatives, and it is necessary to continue developing these new lubricants to realize this kind of new technology in the future.
On the other hand, PFPEs and its derivatives are synthesized from raw materials, fluorinated gases (F-gases), such as tetrafluoroethylene (TFE) and hexafluoropropane (HFP). It is necessary to continue to supply the fluorine-based gases that are the raw materials for these PFPEs.
PFPE lubricants are coated onto magnetic recording media by dipping into the deluted solvent [Ref. 11]. There are some solvents, such as HFC-43-10mee, HFE-449s1, as diluents. These solvents are already trying to be replaced by solvents with much lower Global Warming Potential (GWP) to prevent global warming.
In this way, magnetic storage media employed PFPE lubricants, and related fluorine compounds, which are belong to PFAS, are believed to contribute to achieve to important social goals as explained above.
For these reasons, we do not deny all PFAS alternatives, but we would like to request for exemption of PFPE lubricants, diluents for PFPEs and F-gases as raw materials for PFPEs used in the field of magnetic recording devices to achieve the global economic development and the Green Deal in the EU.
References in this part is attached on Section IV.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Lubricants for magnetic recording media (Hard Disks, Magnetic Tapes)

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: When disposing or incinerating PFPE and its derivatives themselves, it is necessary to incinerate them in a dedicated processing facility because toxic gases are generated by thermal decomposition. The residue is detoxified and landfilled.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Hard disks and magnetic tapes are considered non-recyclable, except for the metallic materials used.

5. Proposed derogations: As this is not public information, it is attached in Section V (Confidential Information).

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: a. PFAS used in this application is perfluoropolyethers and their derivatives as lubricants for magnetic recording media. Attached to Section V for usage.  b. Due to the chemical stability, heat resistance, low vapor pressure, low surface energy, and tribological properties of perfluoropolyethers and their derivatives c. Countries, companies and individuals around the world that use magnetic storage devices d. As lubricants for magnetic recording media, especially in the field of hard disk drives, there are no evidences for the use of lubricants other than perfluoropolyethers and their derivatives since Ref. 1 in 1985 and Ref.2 in 1987were published. Silicone types or Hydrocarbon types may be candidates as the alternatives. But these substances are notorious as killer materials in the field of magnetic storage devices. Silicone compounds can be oxidized to form sand of silicon oxide, and cause fatal damages on the magnetic heads and media [Ref. 12, 13]. It has also been reported that even small amounts of hydrocarbon-based substances can enter the head-disk interface and cause drive failure [ref. 14, 15]. In this way, magnetic storage media employed PFPE lubricants have been released for about half a century. Therefore, no alternatives have been found, and it is considered very hatd to develop them in the future. References in this part is attached on Section IV. e. There are no candidate substances that have performance equal to or better than perfluoropolyethers and their derivatives currently in use, and it is very hard to estimate the time and cost required for development.  f. Alternatives are extremely difficult, and even now, no investigation has been started. g. If the use of PFAS related to magnetic recording devices and their manufacturing, is restricted, it is predicted that hard disks and magnetic tapes will no longer be available on the market. Without these information storage devices, the impact on future information society would be immeasurable, as mentioned in Section III. We estimate that the economic impact will extend not only to the EU, but also to the entire world.

General Comments: At first: Thank you for giving us the opportunity to participate in the public consultation. The more information the ECHA Committees gets, the better a decision can be made.

The longterm planning must be safe for our clients for the supply chain and production facilities (we talk about 40-50 years lifetime of plants). • Strong resistance - to high (+250°C) temperatures
• Increased lifetime and reliability of components (increasing the safety and also sustainability)
• Great compression set at low and high temperatures
• High chemical resistance
• Non-stick properties
• Wear resistance
• Media resistant against most chemicals
For some of the products we use in gaslines, it`s not clear if there will be new materials for the sealing shortly and if this material has the same properties, there is no experience, who will be responsible if it fails? We are forced to use new material without experience about behavior, but we also need a stable legal support.

In multiple cases functionality of the systems will not be given anymore with alternatives.

We use components with PFAS for al long time. Many risk assessments have been done in that time, for all involved parties, there was no specific risks on use of PFA, nor did we ever had a stakeholder that lost its health due to use of such products in our plants.
The products we use, are produced, and handled safely in industrial facilities under controlled conditions, this also applies to the use in the plants.
In recent years, PFAS has been used more and more in the private sector (for example in clothing), where the monitoring of use is not as well controlled as in industrial use. As a result, the use of PFAS materials has spread to many areas of life and is not as well controlled (disposal) as in the industrial environment.

With banning the material we use (FKM, PTFE, PVDF, FFKM, PFA, TPE/P, FPM, ETFE, TFM) the EU will give a major advance to the USA, India and China in production and distribution of necessary products.

The European Union has set itself the ambitious goal of becoming the first climate-neutral continent by 2050. Therefore, the Member States and the European Parliament have agreed in the European Climate Change Act to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% by 2030. We together with our clients are part of this efforts, to bring the European steel industry to the future. The goal is very ambitious and currently ties up a lot of manpower. Socio-economic impacts:
The damage to our further development and our economy will be immense.
Nevertheless, a broad restriction of applications and materials in the EU, will have a massive impact on the business of European companies and may result in shifting of R&D and manufacturing sites. Employees will be blocked with redesign instead of innovation. With this, the strength and attractiveness of Europe will decrease and result in a loss of employees and disadvantage in a global value chain.
If the restriction will come in force than it must be globally valid. We know from the past, if it´s not done in this way, suppliers will buy PFAS from ASIA or elsewhere. There is no benefit for the environment is still harmed in equal extents, yet EUROPE is once more boosting the ASIAN or other foreign economies.

Used in: Sensors, valves, electrical parts, cylinders etc.  For example:  an oxygen sensor may use PTFE as a sealing device (for chemical and thermal resistance, high purity, low outgassing etc) – this could be used for automotive applications, in the energy sector, in a pharmaceutical plant.  How would these commodity items be treated?    Tonnage in use: FKM 10t/y, PTFE 10t/y, PVDF 20 t/y, FFKM 5 t/y, PFA 5 t/y, TFE/P 5 t/y, FPM 5 t/y, EFTE 2t/y, Unifluor 7550 2t/y, TFM 2 t/y

The parts we use has great economic and environmental benefit; they are designed for a long-term reliability. The parts enter the waste stream many decades after it is placed in the EU market. The equipment which is used is only for professional and industrial environment. For these reason each application must be re-evaluated. It will take several years, involving engineering, R&D, production tests, validations. General Comments: At least until the end of the 18-month transition period, PFAS will be used in many materials and products on the market. Complex articles are a combination of many components (articles) which are manufactured in different locations by different manufacturers (inside and outside the EU). In electrical equipment, for example, switchgears, this can amount to several thousand components which are supplied or manufactured on the global market. Some components (assemblies, complex articles) contain subassemblies from different manufacturers, which also contain subassemblies from other manufacturers and so on. All of them can contain materials from different suppliers. Every manufacturing site has an incoming stock and often also an outgoing stock for order fulfilment. The manufacturing date of materials or components (articles) could be months or even years before the top-level product is manufactured and delivered to the market (first placing on the market of top-level articles). The date of placing on the market of lower-level articles (components of the final product) happens much earlier. This easily consumes the 18-month transition time for top-level products, in case contained articles are included in the prohibition.

Following the actual wording of the restriction, it only points to placing on the market at the handover to the customer of the top-level product (in this example the switchgear). But this would mean, that this top-level product must be completely PFAS-free including all components right after the end of the transition period. But at this point in time, it would still be produced with material or components in stock. If this is not permitted, the complete stock would need to be scrapped because of already produced articles containing PFAS (which means no environmental benefit compared to using them) and would close down production lines for top-level articles until stocks are filled with PFAS-free products. This could lead to interruptions in the supply of products for months with significant damage to the industry, society and the environment. For example, if these products support energy transition projects, they could be significantly delayed.

For this, ABB asks for an extended transition time of an additional 5 years to complete the transition to PFAS-free solutions on the complete supply chain and to replace already produced PFAS-containing articles with PFAS-free articles in ABBs and suppliers' stocks.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The comment does not apply to a specific sector listed in the Annex XV restriction report (Table 9) but will be an additional one. In the products also some sectors are subuses, as for example grease.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: As the materials have been in stock, the overall emissions will not be changed by this request, as by a direct ban the materials on stock would need to be scrapped before use instead of after use. The total amount and impact are the same.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: No impact on the recycling except a time shift (see question 2).

6. Missing uses: This request deals with materials and articles where the handover to alternatives not using PFAS is scheduled. It only deals with a transition allowing to empty the stocks by using articles until the stock is emptied and not scrapped before use. Companies have an intrinsic interest in keeping stocks limited as this inventory binds and costs money. Based on product delivery times and minimum order quantities and/or a balance between investment in stock and additional costs due to low quantity orders best economic compromises are defined.

8. Other identified uses: This request deals with materials and articles where the handover to alternatives not using PFAS is scheduled. It only deals with a transition allowing to empty the stocks by using articles and not scrapping them before use. The articles have already been produced, prior to a ban, so the impact on manufacturing is already there. During the use phase, there are no emissions from the PFAS used in this product group. The end-of-life emissions will be the same if it is now treated or after a use phase. It means the only negative impact will be on the additional costs of producing an article twice and also the double waste, which is negative for environmental reasons. It does not make any economic or ecological sense to scrap brand-new articles before they have been used.

Dricksvattenförorening: PFAS har upptäckts i dricksvattenförsörjning över hela världen, särskilt i områden nära industrianläggningar eller där brandsläckningsskum som innehåller PFAS har använts. Dessa kemikalier kan läcka ut i grundvattnet och kvarstå under längre perioder, vilket utgör en betydande svårigheter att på ett acceptabelt sätt klara av vattenreningen. Genom att stoppa PFAS-användningen kan vi minska risken för vattenförorening och säkerställa säkert dricksvatten för samhällen.

Miljöpåverkan: PFAS kan påverka ekosystem och vilda djur mycket negativt. De har visat sig orsaka skador på fiskar, fåglar och andra djur, vilket påverkar deras reproduktionsförmåga och allmänna hälsa. Genom att förbjuda användningen av PFAS kan vi skydda känsliga ekosystem och bidra till att bevara den biologiska mångfalden.

Med ökad medvetenhet om riskerna förknippade med PFAS ökar också ansträngningarna att utveckla och övergå till säkrare alternativ. Genom att stoppa användningen av PFAS uppmuntrar vi utveckling och användning av alternativa material och tekniker som är mindre skadliga för människors hälsa och för miljön, vilket främjar hållbara och mer tillförlitliga metoder.

Ett förbud av användningen av PFAS är AVGÖRANDE för att skydda människors hälsa, skydda ekosystemen och säkerställa en hållbar framtid genom att gynna utvecklingen av säkrare alternativ.

Initial Feedback Universal PFAS Restriction

It is with some interest that we have taken note of the Universal PFAS Restriction proposal. While we are still in the process of reviewing the work performed by the 5 Member States, we would like to provide some initial feedback, mainly surrounding the questions raised in the public consultation addressed to the recycling industry:

4: Impacts on the recycling industry: To get an understanding of the impacts of the proposed restriction on the recycling industry, information is requested on:
a. The impacts that the concentration limits proposed in paragraph 2 of the proposed restriction entry text (see table starting on page 4 of the summary of the Annex XV restriction report) have on the technical and economic feasibility of recycling processes (together with a clear indication on the waste streams to which the described impacts relate).
b. The measures that recyclers would need to take to achieve the proposed concentration limits.
c. The costs associated with these measures.
The question is an interesting one and requires the review of the proposed concentration limits:
i. 25 ppb for any PFAS as measured with targeted PFAS analysis (polymeric PFASs excluded from quantification)
ii. 250 ppb for the sum of PFASs measured as sum of targeted PFAS analysis, optionally with prior degradation of precursors (polymeric PFASs excluded from quantification)
iii. 50 ppm for PFASs (polymeric PFASs included). If total fluorine exceeds 50 mg F/kg the manufacturer, importer or downstream user shall upon request provide to the enforcement authorities a proof for the fluorine measured as content of either PFASs or non-PFASs.

This then requires us to investigate what is a PFAS:

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) defined as:  Any substance that contains at least one fully fluorinated methyl (CF3-) or methylene (-CF2-) carbon atom (without any H/Cl/Br/I attached to it).
A substance that only contains the following structural elements is excluded from the scope of the restriction:  CF3-X or X-CF2-X’,  where X = -OR or -NRR’ and  X’ = methyl (-CH3), methylene (-CH2-), an aromatic group, a carbonyl group (-C(O)-), -OR’’,  -SR’’ or –NR’’R’’’; and where R/R’/R’’/R’’’ is a hydrogen (-H), methyl (-CH3), methylene (-CH2-), an aromatic group or a carbonyl group (-C(O)-).

What is relevant here is that in many of the press releases around this restriction proposal, it is claimed that the proposed restriction would ban more than 10 000 substances. In fact, this is a gross underestimation. With this definition, an infinite number of substances will be banned.

The infinite nature of what is being restricted makes the demonstration of compliance to the first two proposed concentration limits practically impossible. In analytical chemistry, one can only quantify those substances that are being targeted.

For example, it is possible to take a known amount of PFOA, run standard dilution series through a LCMS system to establish the elution time, MS spectrum, and relate the concentration to an area under the curve. Then, it would be possible to take a sample with an unknown concentration of PFOA, run it over the LCMS system and determine the PFOA concentration.

Of course, several testing institutes have now already started offering packages with more than just PFOA, but a range of PFAS substances (e.g. PFOA, PFOS, and their metal salts). This can be done analytically by establishing several calibrations on a single LCMS system. However, there are limitations to what is possible here due to the affinity of the LC column for the substances. This needs to be sufficiently bonding the target chemicals to retard their progress under a constant flow of carrier liquid but also not too much to prevent progression entirely [1]. In a chemically infinite space, there will be molecules that have too little affinity to the column and simply fly through at the rate of the carrier fluid and there will be molecules which are having such an affinity to the column that they will be forever binding or having elution times in the hours.

Note [1]: Small PFAS molecules with too little affinity for the column and/or a too great affinity for the mobile phase will essentially shoot through the chromatographic column at the same time without separation. This would make identification and certainly quantification impossible. Conversely small PFAS molecules with a too great affinity for the column and/or too little for the mobile phase would just bind the column and either not exit during the run or exit days later in another experiment. The latter is the reason why columns need to be cleaned from time to time to reduce background “noise” in LCMS systems (part of the noise is just material eluting from previous injections).

More fundamentally, performing calibration of such a LCMS system is only possible if the substance is available on its own or can be synthesized and this normally takes an amount of time to perform. With a literally infinite number of substances in the scope of the restriction, it would take an infinite amount of time to calibrate the LCMS system. Those that have worked with LCMS know that LCMS systems tend to drift a bit and require periodic cleaning and recalibration.

One possible analytical solution would be to determine the total organic fluorine (TOF) down to the ppb level. If the TOF would be sufficiently below the 25 ppb level, it would not be possible for the individual small PFAS to be present above the 25 ppb level. Of course, such an analytical approach would basically invalidate the last-mentioned concentration limit (50 ppm TOF) and be somewhat against the spirit of the proposed restriction. More importantly, practically this is not possible for plastics materials. Indeed, after inquiring with several laboratories, the best limit of quantification for TOF seems to be around 10 ppm. This is not because the calibration curve was not established for below this level (which would just require a bit of homework on the side of the labs) but is more the result of interference from other constituents of materials that are subjected to such analysis (e.g. under EN 14582 or EN 15408). Since this is a limitation rooted in the laws of physics, improvements in the limit of quantification for TOF should not be expected.

All of the above means that it will not be possible for recyclers to demonstrate compliance to the limit 25 ppb limit for individual small PFAS or the 250 ppb sum total limit for small PFAS. The 50 ppm TOF limit is a measurable limit.

The above statement is made despite the section 2.5.3. – 2.5.4. showing a workable strategy for enforcement bodies to enforce the terms of the restriction. We too appreciated this holistic approach shown here. However, it should be noted that this would be an approach for demonstrating non-compliance. After having followed the approach, a conclusion can be drawn in the form that: “the material or product cannot be shown to violate the terms of the universal PFAS restriction”. But it would not be possible to conclude from the suggested approach that the material is in compliance with the PFAS Restriction.

To give a very practical example, a sometimes-used polymeric PFAS processing aid is “Hexafluoropropylene-tetrafluoroethylene-vinylidene fluoride copolymer” (Cas: 25190-89-0). This processing aid basically is used to prevent the material from sticking to moulds and/or calender. If used outside of the EU or present in a waste stream with long service life, a TOF analysis might result in a value below 50 ppm. These processing aids are used because they are so extremely effective and very little is needed. Furthermore, when articles with such fluoropolymer processing aids are present in certain waste articles in a waste stream, they will be accompanied by waste articles that do not have the substance, thus reducing the concentration in the recyclate.

A targeted analysis of PFHxS, PFOS, PFHxA (if adopted), PFOA and C9-C14 PFCAs would then not reveal the presence of individual small PFAS.  The material would be in a Kafkaesque position of being non-compliant to the restriction, not being shown to be non-compliant to the restriction, and no company, institute, or authority would be able to say that the material is compliant with the restriction. Legal certainty would become an unanswered question in such cases.
For recyclers, the only actionable limit to which compliance could potentially be demonstrated is the third total organic fluorine limit. As such we hereby request an indefinite derogation from the 25 ppb small PFAS and 250 ppb sum total small PFAS limit for plastics recyclates placed on the market as substance or mixture and articles made with plastics recyclates.

Of course, the issue described above is not necessarily unique to recycling. There will be many industries with global supply chains that would face problems with legal certainty. It might be better to forgo the 25 ppb and 250 ppb limit entirely. Alternatively, it would be possible to set up a specific exhaustive list of substances with CAS numbers for which these limits would apply. An exhaustive list of substances could be established based on the substances that would meet the structural definition and have been registered under REACH. We do expect that such a list would probably be quite short (i.e. certainly not 10 000 substances); there will likely be just very few of the molecules being produced at industrial scale. The rest of the to be restricted chemical universe would then still be regulated by the 50 ppm TOF limit.

These derogations are needed because there are no measures that recyclers could take to achieve the proposed limit values. While we appreciate the faith in our industry that the question 4b betrays, we must manage expectations here. Recyclers do not recycle individual articles one by one; recyclers recycle mountains of articles or shredded material batch by batch or even in a continuous fashion. The recycling process allows these materials to be sorted by exploiting differences in material properties that are unique to the specific waste stream.

To give a practical example, PET bottles from deposit collection systems are shredded and put through a washing line. The washing line ensures that the shredded HDPE/PP caps float to the top of the baths while the PET sinks to the bottom of the baths. Here the separation of the material that was originally part of the mountain of PET bottles is separated by density. Other properties/techniques used include:

• Polymer NIR spectrum / NIR sorting where objects are identified and pneumatically shot from the material stream (does not work with plastics containing carbon black)
• Melting point of different materials / extrusion with melt filtration whereby the molten plastics is passed over a metal filter grid in an extruder. Useful to remove polymer particles with higher melting points and residual mineral contamination.
• Washing lines / removes glues, a large amount of mineral (i.e. dirt) contamination, and food residues.
• Density sorting / by adding salt to water baths of varying density can be made to cut material fractions into different density by sink-float.
• Optical sorting / operators (or sometimes experiments are done with robots and AI) sort out based on morphology colour object type. (e.g. an operator knows that all CDs are PC, CD cases are PS, garden furniture is filled PP, etc.)

A piece of material with a few ppm or even a few ppb of PFAS does not change any property of the material to such an extend that would allow for any exploitation of such a property for a separation technology to effectively sort the material to a different (PFAS rich) fraction.

The only way that it would be possible to ensure that the 50 ppm TOF limit would be respected is for the defined input material to have sufficiently low PFAS content to create a recyclate that matches this limit. All plants treating specific input waste streams that give rise to recyclate that exceeds the 50 ppm TOF limit would need to stop operations. To shortly answer question 4c, the cost associated with the evisceration of entire subsectors of the plastics recycling industry would be… not insignificant.

Summary of first key recommendations:
• To prevent an undefined legal state of recyclate either:
• A general derogation from the 25 ppb 250 ppb limits for small PFAS in recyclate and articles incorporating recyclate; or
• A switch to an exhaustive list of small PFAS to be regulated with the 25 ppb and 250 ppb limits.
The latter option would address the general compliance issue highlighted for non-recyclate derived materials and articles, would not create differentiation between the legal requirements for recyclate and virgin material, and therefore has our slight preference. Both options would retain a total regulation of the entire PFAS chemical universe through the 50 ppm TOF limit value.

Third Feedback Universal PFAS Restriction
Since our first submission (#6198 found in Part 32 of the comments submitted to date on the restriction report) which focused on the difficulty of measuring small PFAS and demonstration of compliance and our second submission which focused on the larger PFAS and included results of TOF measurements of representative samples of recyclate from various waste-polymer recyclate streams, a member of PRE generated additional data on small PFAS in WEEE recyclate samples that we would like to share. This data is mainly relevant in relation to the thoughts expressed in the first submission and confirms our assessment on what should be done with the limits proposed in relation to recyclate and articles manufactured with recyclate.

1 Sample selection
The member company collected 14 samples from various other WEEE plastics recyclers.

2 Analysis method
12 samples were provided to a well-known analytical laboratory and subjected to testing according to ISO 23702-1, a method whereby compounds are extracted with a suitable solvent separated by liquid chromatography and detected with a MSMS system. 44 individual small PFAS were included in the package offered by the analytical laboratory, which as discussed in our first submission is not covering all PFAS that are to be regulated under the proposed restriction.
In addition, EN 15408 was used to quantify total organic fluorine in all 14 samples.

3 Results
The results of this work are presented in Table 1.
The values for total organic fluorine (TOF) are roughly in line with the findings presented in the second PRE submission to the public consultation showing ppm level contamination. This analytical laboratory also had issues guaranteeing a certain limit of detection as is shown by the variability in the reported limit of detection.
The detected small PFAS in these samples were Perfluorobutanesulfonic acid (PFS C4; Cas 375-73-5), Perfluorodecanoic acid (PFC C10; Cas 335-76-2), 1H,1H,2H,2H-Perfluorohexanol (4:2 FTOH; Cas 2043-47-2), and 1H,1H,2H,2H-Perfluorododecanol (10:2 FTOH; Cas 865-86-1).
The limits of detection for these substances varied by substance and through time as for later samples the analytical laboratory adjusted their limits of detection upwards. This was due to a change in their extraction method which was introduced to increase sensitivity in other fields. It is observed that the limit of detection was lower for smaller PFAS (e.g. 2 ppb for PFS C4 vs 5 ppb for PFC C10). This is logical since smaller substances tend to be more readily extractable from polymeric matrixes and give sharper peaks in liquid chromatography. For some PFAS the limit of detection was below the 25 ppb being proposed, while for other the limit of detection was higher than the proposed 25 ppb for individual small PFAS. This is another more practical issue when attempting to demonstrate compliance. Furthermore, there is a difficulty for the sum limit since with such limits of detection it is not possible to prove compliance to the sum total limit. This issue is increased when more PFAS are included in the analysis.
Table 1 TOF and selected small PFAS results in WEEE plastic recyclate. In these samples 44 small PFAS were quantified with varying limits of detection based on the capability of the laboratory, those detected in at least one sample are reported below. n.t. means not tested. * PFS C4 = Perfluorobutanesulfonic acid PFBS (Cas 375-73-5), PFC C10 = Perfluorodecanoic acid PFDA (Cas 335-76-2), 4:2 FTOH = 1H,1H,2H,2H-Perfluorohexanol (Cas 2043-47-2), 10:2 FTOH = 1H,1H,2H,2H-Perfluorododecanol (Cas 865-86-1)
[The table can be found in the attachment]
Two sample contained TOF at or over the proposed TOF limit.
Small PFAS were detected in 10 of the 12 samples tested and 5 of these contained a specific individual small PFAS above the proposed 25 ppb limit value. Just one of these samples exceeded the proposed 250 ppb sum-total limit value.

4 Discussion
The results show that recyclate from WEEE recycling will contain small PFAS and sometimes exceed the proposed limit value of 25 ppb. We are unaware of any useful reason for integration of these specific PFASs into plastics materials and suspect that such ppb level contamination may be present in any and all material that has existed for a number of years since PFAS are omnipresent environmental contaminants.
 
5 Recommendations
The recommendations with regards to the TOF limit in our second submission stand and are unaffected by this new evidence (in fact the new TOF data supports the recommendations).
However, in the first submission we argued for:
1. A general derogation from the 25 ppb and 250 ppb limits for small PFAS in recyclate and articles incorporating recyclate; or
2. A switch to an exhaustive list of small PFAS to be regulated with the 25 ppb and 250 ppb limits.
At the time primarily because it is impossible to demonstrate compliance to limit values that apply to an infinite number of substances. This remains our primary argumentation to either grant a derogation for the small PFAS limits in recyclate and articles incorporating recyclate or to generate an exhaustive list of PFAS to be regulated.
However, given the fact that it has now been demonstrated that recyclate can contain small PFAS above the proposed limit values, we would like to clarify that if an exhaustive list is created (e.g. by determining which PFAS are currently registered), we will have to perform testing to determine whether or not any of these PFAS on the exhaustive list are contained in recyclate and at what level. Therefore, we would like to amend these recommendations on the small PFAS limits (i. and ii.) to:
1. A general derogation from the 25 ppb and 250 ppb limits for small PFAS in recyclate and articles incorporating recyclate; or
2. A switch to an exhaustive list of small PFAS to be regulated with the limits to be determined based on the level of their unintentional presence in recyclate.

Second Feedback Universal PFAS Restriction

Since our first submission (#6198 found in Part 32 of the comments submitted to date on the restriction report) our understanding of the restriction proposal has increased, and we have had the opportunity to perform a measurement campaign to determine the TOF content of various waste-recyclate streams. The views expressed in that submission have not changed and for the reasons explained in this first submission with regards to the small PFAS limits (referred to in i. and ii. of the proposed legal text) we recommend:
• To prevent an undefined legal state of recyclate either:
• A general derogation from the 25 ppb 250 ppb limits for small PFAS in recyclate and articles incorporating recyclate; or
• A switch to an exhaustive list of small PFAS to be regulated with the 25 ppb and 250 ppb limits.
Furthermore, we would like to reiterate that there is no possible sorting or recycling technology that can removed PFAS from waste plastics input nor is there any technology that can separate plastics containing PFAS from plastics not containing PFAS.
The above is not new, since we explained this in our previous submission. However, we feel very strongly about this and would like to reconfirm that this has not changed. The remainder of this paper will delineate the research carried out into TOF levels in representative recyclate samples and finish with recommendations thereon.

1 Sample selection
In the past PRE has collected samples of recyclate from its members for a broader substance screening exercise. In this project, recyclers were asked to either prepare samples in the form of extruded plaques or extruded plaques were produced out of the samples they supplied by a specialised service provider. The choice for extruded plaques as the form of the sample can be found in annex I. Submitting member companies were requested to supply more sample material than strictly speaking necessary for the substance screening to create a sample bank of samples that are representative of European Recyclate. For each submitted sample the original waste material stream was recorded, the country of origin (as well as possible), and the polymer that comprised the recyclate was recorded. Various types of analysis were performed on the samples, ranging from XRF, GCMS and LCMS SVHC screening, to specific LCMSMS techniques for flame retardants depending on the waste product stream. The result is a well characterized sample library of 100+ samples of material representative of common varieties of plastics recyclate.
A selection from this sample bank was used for TOF analysis.

2 Analysis method
All samples were provided to a well-known analytical laboratory and subjected to a Total Organic Fluorine analysis according to EN 15408:2011. The principle is that 1 gram of the material is taken and placed in a combustion bomb and the exhaust gases are transferred to water or 0.2 mol/l KOH solution. The fluor in the aqueous solution is subsequently quantified using a liquid chromatography in combination with a suitable detection technique or with ICP-MS.

3 Results
All results will be discussed based on the recycling sector from which they derive.

3.1 Flexible Polyolefin Film Recyclate
Low density polyethylene (LDPE) is mainly used for film applications. LDPE recyclers primarily obtain their post-consumer input material from sorting centres that sort household (plastic) waste. A well-known specification is DSD 310 which is described as: “Used, completely emptied, system-compatible articles made of plastic film, surface greater than DIN A4, e.g. bags, carrier bags and shrink-wrapping film, incl. packaging parts such as labels etc.”.
However, there is also a substantial fraction of LDPE film used in commercial distribution chains. For example, cardboard boxes stacked on a wooden pallet are wrapped in LDPE film to prevent boxes from falling off and to award some protection from (rain)water in distribution chains.
The TOF results can be found in Table 1. 4 out of 5 samples would exceed the 50 ppm TOF limit as proposed in the restriction proposal. The only sample that would pass was described by the submitting company as light green shrink film. The specificity of the description implies that this would be either pre-consumer or commercial film, as post-consumer film is never sorted by colour.
Table 1 Results of TOF analysis of LDPE recyclate. In ppm.
[To see the table, please see the attachment.]

As already alluded to in our first submission fluoropolymer processing aids can be used in film production and are the likely origin of the organic fluorine. Given the stability of these fluoropolymer processing aids, they likely still contribute to the processing quality of the material.
3.2 Rigid polyolefins
3.2.1 HDPE Recyclate
High Density Polyethylene (HDPE) can be used for many types of products. However, the HDPE recycling sector as such focuses primarily on the HDPE in household waste which are normally HDPE bottles, bins, and crates. Sorting centres for post-consumer household waste can produce varying qualities of HDPE rich waste. Under the German system for example:
[Table visible in the attachment with hyperlinks to specifications and their description]

The TOF results can be found in Table 2. The data shows appreciable concentrations of organic fluorine being present, but no sample exceeds the TOF limit. On average it seems likely that household HDPE recyclers would be able to meet the proposed 50 ppm TOF limit. However, it is not possible to exclude that there will be batches of material that exceed the 50 ppm limit.
Table 2 Results of TOF analysis of HDPE recyclate. In ppm.
[To see the table, please see the attachment.]

3.2.2 PP Recyclate
Polypropylene (PP) is quite a versatile material and can be used in many applications such as film (minor fraction compared to LDPE), pots tubs and trays (e.g. margarine tubs), caps and closures (e.g. tick tack cap), and (garden) furniture, automotive, and electrical and electronic equipment. Most recyclers that consider themselves PP recyclers however focus on material coming from households.
PP based articles can be sorted into a specific waste fraction such as 330 for cups: “Used, residue-emptied, rigid, system-compatible items made of polypropylene, volume ≤ 5 litres, e.g. bottles, cups and trays, incl. secondary components such as closures, labels, etc.”. However, PP can be present as an impurity in other fractions (e.g. 310 will contain PP foils as well) or in fractions that are mixed with HDPE (e.g. 323 is mixed polyolefin items). The recycling sector for this material reflects this since PP recyclers tend to have an overlap with HDPE recyclers with many HDPE recyclers being either PP recyclers as well or supplying PP recyclers with sorted PP materials (or at least material from which HDPE has been removed).
TOF results are displayed in Table 3. Sample P0001 is reflective of the typical household PP recyclate derived from caps and closures containing 16 ppm of TOF. This is an indication that this sector similar to HDPE could meet the proposed 50 ppm TOF limit on average.
In the PP recycling value chain, there are operators that combine PP from different waste origins to produce a recyclate with superior quality in terms of physical mechanical properties (this happens in other recycling sectors as well, though perhaps to a slightly lower extend). Sample P0034 is the result of such a practice. And reveals a concentration of 67 ppm exceeding the 50 ppm limit. There is some weak evidence in the form of a single measurement of automotive PP (see below) that this may be due to the addition of a fraction of automotive PP to the recyclate.
Sample P0019 is a bit of an oddity compared to the wider PP recycling market in the sense that it is derived from maritime waste. It is an, as of yet, relatively small but emerging waste input material for plastic recycling reflecting growing collection rates in this sector.
Table 3 Results of TOF analysis of PP recyclate. In ppm.
[To see the table, please see the attachment.]
3.3 PET Recyclate
Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) is the well know material of construction of bottles, but can also be used for trays, textile, carpets, etc. The PET that is collected and directed to recycling consists primarily of food contact bottles, bottles, and more bottles (and a few food contact trays). The highest quality bottles are obtained through deposit return systems in a number of Member States, however PET bottles from separate collection that are sorted out in sorting centres for household waste are recycled as well.
The results can be found in Table 4, showing that 1 out of the 3 analysed samples would exceed the TOF limit. The variation shows that it is possible that on average the PET recycler would comply with a 50 ppm limit. However, recyclers do not need to comply on average, but rather every single batch and the variation clearly shows that the proposed 50 ppm limit would make it difficult or impossible to comply all the time. In an absence of technology to separate organic fluorine containing material from the waste streams this would result in a severe impediment to recycling.
Table 4 Results of TOF analysis of PET recyclate. In ppm.
[To see the table, please see the attachment.]

3.4 WEEE/ELV Plastics Recyclate
Waste Electronic and Electrical Equipment (WEEE) and End of Life Vehicles (ELV) are governed by relatively similar legislation. The WEEE Directive and ELV Directive both specify that there should be collection, a number of very specific depollution steps (e.g. removal of liquids from cars and mercury containing cathode ray tubes from CRT displays), and that certain recycling rates need to be achieved. In practice, there is collection, depollution is done and apart from reusable parts, the material is shred. From the shredded material ferrous metals are recovered by magnetism, non-ferrous metals with eddy current separators, and a number of other materials are recovered as well. Plastics of a great diversity of polymers accumulate in the Shredder Light Fraction (SLF from WEEE) or Automotive Shredder Residue (ASR from ELV), along with fines, textile, wood, and many other materials. SLF tends to be slightly easier to treat in subsequent steps then ASR due to greater macro impurity levels (concentration of PFAS does not have any impact whatsoever in terms off processability).
SLF/ASR can be directed to specialised recyclers that use density sorting to recover polyolefins (PP with some PE impurity) and styrenics (PS and ABS) in two separate steps with different density separation media from the bulk SLF/ASR. The resulting “heavy fraction” (density greater than 1.1 g/cm³) will contain a variety of other polymers as well as polyolefins and styrenics containing brominated flame retardants including PBDEs that result in the requirement to destroy this waste fraction due to exceedance of the low POP content limit (LPCL). The styrenics fraction tends to be separated in PS and ABS by subsequent electrostatic sorting.
The sector is currently actively developing technology to sort from the heavy fraction more polymers in a legally compliant manner (i.e. trying to selectively sort pieces of shred of a particular polymer without PBDEs). It is anticipated that within a few years PC and PC-ABS (a polymer “alloy” that has superior properties compared to the separate polymers themselves) will be recycled. It is unclear how much TOF there would be in this stream.
The results in Table 5 show that both ELV and WEEE derived polyolefins by far exceed the proposed TOF limit of 50 ppm, while both WEEE styrenics samples contain less than the proposed 50 ppm TOF.
Table 5 Results of TOF analysis of WEEE/ELV recyclate. In ppm. SDA: Small Domestic Appliances, S-IT: Small IT Equipment, ASR: Automotive Shredder Residue, TEE: Temperature Exchange Equipment, and LDA: Large Domestic Appliances.
[To see the table, please see the attachment.]

3.5 PVC Recyclate
Polyvinyl chloride (PVC) is a very tough plastic material that can survive for years in relatively demanding applications. As such it is used extensively in Building and Construction applications, with roughly 70% of all PVC being used in this sector. Most post-consumer rigid PVC waste is collected from building and demolition activities (e.g. renovations) and is successfully recycled back into these applications in a controlled loop for another multiple decade service life.
There is however a unique analytical difficulty with PVC. EN 15408:2011 specifies that for samples with more than 1% chlorine 0.2 mol/l KOH solution should be used to capture the halogen containing exhaust gases. However, PVC samples will contain more than 50% chlorine which may saturate the media that captures the halogens. Furthermore, the samples contain perhaps a few ppm of fluorine and more than 500 000 ppm of chlorine, meaning that the aqueous media used to capture the halogens after combustion of the sample will also contain a vast amount of chlorine. In subsequent chromatographic or other techniques used to quantify the different elements in the aqueous solution there will be great interference from the chlorine in the signal for fluorine.
This translates into a substantially higher limit of detection of 100 ppm for PVC samples and reduces the reliability of the results (shown in Table 6). For example, sample C0002 and C0009 are from “window frames” and “construction profiles”, show wildly different TOF results below the limit of detection of 100 and 553 ppm. This is surprising since window frames normally form the primary constituent in construction profile waste and there is little reason to believe that the chemical composition of window profiles would differ substantially from other construction profiles.

The results for PVC recyclate should thus be taken with a grain of salt and primarily serve to illustrate that TOF determinations in PVC samples will be extremely difficult if not impossible with current state of the art methods. Here is should also be noted that: since the interference of chlorine in the fluorine signal is a physical phenomenon governed by the laws of physics, it is unlikely that it is possible to develop a method that overcomes this challenge.

4 Economic impact
Around 7.2 MT of recyclate is placed on the market annually. If we assume the following distributions based on our last market report: Flexible PP & PE (28%), Rigid PP & PE (25%), PET (26%), PVC (9%), Technical Plastics (4%), other (8%) then these sectors would produce the amounts of recyclate shown in Table 7 and discussed below.
Please note that all price level, value added, revenues, and basically any number is by its very nature volatile and will move up and down over time as market conditions change. However, the order of magnitude will remain similar and should be sufficient to base sound policy on.

The flexible polyolefin film recycling sector would be in non-compliance with a limit value of 50 ppm and in the absence of separation technology to remove PFAS would have to discontinue their activity. While each sector will have its specificities and price levels of input and output change over time, it is not an unreasonable estimate to state that over the long run for each ton of recyclate that is placed on the market 1000 EUR in value has been added. This sector currently thus adds around 2 billion EUR of value to the EU’s economy.
Of course, without commenting on whether or not fluoropolymer processing aids should or should not be restricted, a restriction on such processing aids would over time reduce TOF levels in the flexible polyolefin film recyclate. Such time would be measured in years given the recycling rates and the life cycle of the products.
Again here, we would like to emphasise that we do not know if there are technically and economically feasible alternatives to the fluoropolymer processing aids. What we can speculate on is that since fluoropolymer processing aids are so stable, they will likely maintain their functionality as processing aids through their use and waste phase. As such they will likely contribute to the processability during recycling and in the utilisation of the recyclate. Alternative processing aid technologies will likely be inferior in this aspect.
A TOF limit of 250 ppm could likely be met by the sector on average. However, to ensure that all batches of recyclate would meet this requirement much more extensive testing would have to be performed. Given the lead times of commercial laboratories and the space limitation to store recyclate on the premises of recyclers, externalisation of this work would likely be difficult. Expansion of the QC laboratory would thus be required.
For EN 15408 testing a combustion bomb would be between 500 – 1 000 EUR would be needed to transfer the halogens to an aqueous media and an ICP-MS system as a detector would cost around 200 000 EUR. As such the one-off investment needed would be around 200 000 EUR/company.
Such ICP-MS systems may last for 3 years under intensive use (67000 EUR/year), liquid argon consumption would be 1 canister every 3 weeks (300 EUR/canister  5200 EUR/year), the device would need to be operated by a skilled technician (75000 EUR/year) resulting in a running cost of 147 200 EUR/year at least.
With around 350 companies engaged in this recycling sector the one-off investment cost would be 70 million and the permanent running cost would be 52 million EUR/year.
Next to the cost for QC, it should also be factored in what would happen to batches of material that would not meet the 250 ppm limit. In the absence of rules stating otherwise, it is likely that this would be blended with material containing less than 250 ppm TOF. Thus, having no impact whatsoever on the total amount of PFAS placed on the market. There would thus be a significant one-off cost and running cost for no benefit in terms of PFAS release.
If rules would stipulate the destruction of such batches, the recycler will have done all the work required to get the material into shape for use in the traditional plastic compounding/converting sector and thus have a loss of the market value of the recyclate of between 800 and 1 500 EUR/ton. In the event just 5% would be lost this way the cost would be 80 – 150 million EUR/year. In this case there would be a minor benefit of a very small reduction of PFAS that exist for a very high cost that at the very least outweighs the testing cost required to achieve this.
Alternatively, a TOF limit of 350 ppm would likely result in all recyclate being in compliance meaning that no recyclate would have to be tested. From an economic perspective this would seem to be a logical choice.
The rigid polyolefin recycling sector would likely be able to meet the 50 ppm limit on average. In order to ensure that each batch of recyclate would meet the 50 ppm limit batch testing would have to be established similar to that discussed above. The roughly 300 plants would have a one-off cost of about 60 million EUR and a running cost of about 44 million EUR/year. Similar considerations apply as above with regards to the rules on what to do with the recyclate and the consequences in terms of PFAS placed on the market. A limit of 150 ppm would prevent the need for batch testing.
The PET recycling sector would likely need to discard an excessive volume of material with a TOF limit of 50 ppm, meaning that it would have to cease its activity. The PET recycling sector adds an unusually high amount of value to the material of around 1 500 EUR/ton since particularly the food grade material is in high demand, but demand is also supported by other industries (e.g. textile). Elimination of this sector would result in a loss of 2.8 billion EUR gross value added. (Naturally this would also mean that the aim of 30% recycled content in beverage bottles in the EU’s SUP directive will not be met.)
A TOF limit of 150 ppm would likely be met on average but require the roughly 160 plants to invest in QC for an amount of 32 million EUR one off and 24 million EUR annually thereafter. Similar consideration with  regards to the rules on what to do with batches exceeding the limit would apply. However, given the high market value of the recyclate (1700 – 2 000 EUR/ton), a 5% reduction in volume placed on the market would result in a loss of 162 – 190 million EUR. With a limit of 250 ppm such testing would likely not be necessary.
The technical plastics from WEEE/ELV recycling sector would have to discontinue placing polyolefin recyclate on the market (roughly 50% of the output) if a limit of 50 ppm is set. This in itself would result in around 75 million EUR in gross value added lost. However, without the revenues of the polyolefins, it is doubtful whether or not the other 50% of the output can be recycled in an economic fashion, which would thus result in around 150 million EUR in lost gross added value.
A limit of 300 ppm will likely be met on average. The QC investment cost for the 50 companies would be 10 million, followed by 7.4 million EUR annual recurrent cost. A limit of 400 ppm TOF would likely result in all material being compliant to the limit values without the need for excessive testing.
For the PVC recycling industry there is simply an issue with measuring TOF reliably. Any limit value below 0.1% TOF would not be reliably measurable. Thus, a limit of anything less than 0.1% would place a sector that adds roughly 1 billion EUR in value added to the EU economy in jeopardy.
To conclude a limit of 50 ppm TOF would likely eliminate the vast majority of all plastics recycling within the EU and result in a loss of between 5.5 and 8.2 billion EUR.
5 Recommendations
In addition to advice given previously with regards to the small PFAS limits, we would like to recommend one of the following options with respect to the large/polymeric PFAS limit:
1. Set the TOF limit for recyclate substances and mixtures as well as articles manufactured with recyclate at 0.1% (w/w) for all polymers,
2. Set the TOF limit for recyclate substances and mixtures as well as articles manufactured with recyclate at 400 ppm for all non-halogenated polymers and at 0.1% for halogenated polymers, or
3. Abandon the TOF limit value.
These options would permit recycling to continue within the EU.


Annex I Explanation for the choice of Extruded Plaques
The primary reason for desiring extruded plaques as samples instead of samples of recyclate as such is that recyclate is often supplied to the market as regrind (also known as flakes ).
Regrind is a substance/mixture under REACH of cleaned size reduced pieces of the original waste articles. Each individual piece thus has the chemical composition of the article. To obtain the chemical composition of a big bag or batch of such material one would have to ensure that when analysed enough individual pieces are included. If sent in its raw state to an analytical laboratory several hundreds of grams of material would have to be subjected to solvent extraction or other extraction technique prior to injection in chromatographic equipment (e.g. GC or LC) coupled with a detector system (normally MS).
Analytical laboratories and analytical chemists in general tend to be familiar in handling a few grams or even micrograms of material. Equipment is normally not set up to treat such (in their eyes) humongous bulks of material. As such good, involved, and honest laboratories will simply refuse to analyse such samples (or suggest a way to homogenise the samples). Bad or simply poorly informed laboratories that do not realise the need to have such a mass analysed would take just one or two flakes and perform the analysis on this and report the results as being for the entire batch of material; without informing the client that only one or two flakes were analysed.
From a scientific perspective there are two ways to deal with this phenomenon. Firstly, one could take the 100+ gram regrind sample and grind this in its entirety, mix it well, and take a small subsample (e.g. 1 gram) for chemical analysis. Alternatively, one can pull the material through a (lab) extruder and thus mix the regrind in the melt phase. Scientifically these two methods are roughly equal. There may be some scepticism on whether mixing in the melt phase would really produce a homogenous material. However, given the uniform colour that is obtained when mixing material with all sorts of diffident colours, this seems to be the case .
From a practical perspective, however, quite a few recyclers will have a laboratory extruder in their laboratory and the ability to produce plaques of material. Such plaques and extruded material are used to determine to a degree polymer composition (e.g. through differential scanning colometry) and physical mechanical properties (e.g. tear strength, impact resistance). Recyclers do not have the equipment to perform cryogenic grinding.
In chemical analytical laboratories this is the other way around. Quite a few laboratories will have cryogenic mills, while only very few specialised in plastics will have laboratory extruders. However, such cryogenic mills are normally more used to turn a solid material to a powder to increase the surface area prior to an extraction process. Grinding 100+ gram in these devices would still be a chore and quite unusual. The practical risk would remain that the analyst charged with the procedure would simply take one or two flakes, grind this and perform all subsequent steps of the analysis with material thus obtained; with the end result being data not representative of the big bag/batch. Laboratory extruders do not have this risk since they require being fed with 100+ grams to operate.
There are three added benefits from the extruded plaque approach.
Firstly, plaques can also be analysed with XRF a technique that is being adopted by some recyclers for quality control purposes. For example, the calcium content thus obtained is a proxy for calcium carbonate filler content. Lower content of this tends to mean better physical mechanical properties. The XRF guns can also give some regulatory pertinent tacit information. High bromine content tends to be indicative of brominated flame retardants (BFRs) in the big bag/batch, while a low content would mean that BFRs cannot be present above certain levels. (On a side note, unfortunately these XRF guns cannot detect fluorine. In fact, they struggle with chlorine, with order of magnitude greater limits of detection (several hundred ppm to 150,000 ppm) compared to bigger elements such as bromine for which detection limits are in the ppm range.)
Secondly, the regrind in subsequent production steps will be molten at least once. Performing an analysis of the material that has gone through a similar thermal processing step would be more representative of what the final articles will become.
Thirdly, a plaque is simply more convenient to store, ship, and otherwise handle than a fine powder.

Specific Use case: Gas scrubbers

Frequently chemical processes have by-products like Cl, HCl, HF, SOx or PFAs, that are contained in the exhaust air. In many cases these by-products are extremely aggressive and dangerous to health and to the environment. For the protection of the environment and employees, manufacturers are required by law to reduce/eliminate emissions of such poisonous gases. Thus, special, corrosion resistant gas scrubbers are needed, that are fully resistant to the chemicals.

Depending on the industry and process different kinds of gases are created, which vary in the concentration and temperature. Table 1 will show examples of typical processes and created gases in the chemical industry [1]. The combination of media, concentration and temperature generates a strongly corrosive media. Thus, special corrosion resistant gas scrubbers are needed that are fully resistant to the chemicals.

Pickling of standard steel / HCl
Pickling of stainless steel / NOx (NO2/NO), HF
Electroplating / Chrome - VI, Nickel, Aerosol
Hot-dip galvanise / HCl, Ammonium chloride, solidified zinc vapours
Sewage sludge drying / NH3, H2S
Battery production / H2SO4, Aerosol
Ceramic production / NH3
Chemical industry general / SO2
Foundry / Ammonium
Rubber production / Chlorine
Fertilizer production / Chlorine
Production and processing of Fluoropolymers / HF, PFAs

Experience has shown that steel structures, FRP structures or lined equipment (like rubber linings) are not able to handle most of these very harsh operation conditions.

An optimal solution for solving such heavy corrosion problems in gas scrubbers is the usage of fluorinated melt-extruded thermoplastics. Well-established manufacturing methods for the construction of such scrubbers, like solid construction, bonding to steel, FRP lining (dual-laminate), provide solutions suitable up to high temperatures, see ANNEX I,II and III

We therefore request full exemption of all fluoropolymers like PVDF, ECTFE, FEP and PFA from the restriction proposal.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The specific Sector “Gas scrubbers” is not listed in Annex XV.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Depending on the chemicals, their temperature and concentration, the corrosion protective lining is selected. Either PVDF, ECTFE, FEP or PFA is used with thickness typically ranging from 2 mm up to 5 mm. Additionally accessories like welding rod, pipes, fittings and stock shapes are need.  The larger volume of fluoropolymers used in our company is already produced without the use of fluorinated polymerization aids. To further reduce the risk of emitting small molecular PFAS from the fluoropolymers, most of our suppliers have already announced that they will change their production process to non-fluorinated polymerization aids in the future. Our company plans to use polymers produced with non-fluorinated polymerization aids as soon as they become available.  During manufacturing:  There is a certain amount of emissions when fluoropolymers are processes at elevated temperature in the thermoplastic state. While the majority of the emissions is expected to be HF, also some small molecular PFAS are expected to emit. In our facility, the main parts of the extrusion line with the highest temperatures (thus the areas where emissions are most likely to occur) are covered with a ventilation hood to suck of fumes/emissions above the extrusion line. The off gases are then cleaned in gas scrubber (which can be lined with fluorpolymers to prevent them from corrosion), before released into the environment. We are committed to implement an emission control strategy to detect PFAS emission and to capture them during processing.  We have state of the art technologies in place to avoid loss of fluoropolymer during the production our facility. We capture and recover fluoropolymer waste during manufacturing in processing for recycling. In case recycling is not possible the fluoropolymer-waste is fed into the waste stream in line with current laws and regulations. Incineration is said to effectively destroy PFAS if temperatures are above 850 °C.   Storage and handling Proper Packaging avoids PFAS loss during the transportation and storage. After production, products are packed and stored properly.  The use-phase:  Sheets made from fluoropolymers are used for the lining of gas scrubber equipment (typically columns with diameters from Ø 500 mm up to 2500 mm). It must also be considered that fluoropolymers are installed in the inside area of the tank only.  End-of-life:  Equipment which is decommissioned after service life (~10-20 years depending on the application) can be collected and deposited or incinerated according to the state of the art and in line with laws and regulations.
