Why PFA and PVDF sheets for wet benches?

Microchip manufacturing requires high-purity process media and environments to produce smaller and more efficient chips. As the quality of the semiconductor increases (e.g., microchip size decreases), the acceptable limits for particulate and chemical contamination decrease. The production areas of these microchips are called "wet benches" where high purity acids, mixed acids and high purity water are used to etch the surface and clean the silicon wafers. For the etching media such as nitric acid, phosphoric acid, hydrofluoric acid, sulfuric acid, ammonia, hydrogen peroxide in various combinations are used. All of them are extremely corrosive, requiring chemical resistant fluoropolymers like PVDF and PFA.
In this application PFA is usually used for contact with acids. PVDF is used to store and transport the high-purity water. In addition to their high chemical resistance, both materials are very clean (low amount of leachable (metal-)anions, inorganics or TOC’s), resulting in very little contamination of the process media. Metals are typically not suitable for this type of application, as they contaminate the ultra pure water and the chemicals with metal anions.

Those products are included in the use category “semiconductors” as described in Annex XV, Table 8, of the proposed restriction, and identified with a 12 year derogation. We request on exemption for the category "semiconductors" as it will not be possible to develop alternatives with 12 years.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: For the specific use-case mainly PFA and PVDF sheets in a thickness of 4 up to 20 mm are used. Additional products are welding rods, round rods and solid pipes. Additionally, our raw material supplier for PVDF already announced that they are not using any fluorinated polymerization aids what may remain in the PVDF sheet material, thus emissions during the life-cycle are reduced. We have state of the art technologies in place to avoid loss of fluoropolymer during the production our facility. We capture and recover fluoropolymer waste during manufacturing in processing for recycling. In case recycling is not possible the fluoropolymer-waste is fed into the waste stream in line with current laws and regulations. After production, products are packed and stored properly. The expenditures to design such chips can range from €0.5 billion to well over €1.0 billion. Research and development (R&D) intensity in the sector is high with more than a 15% investment percentage with respect to sales.9  It is estimated that in 2021 the capital expenditure invested was close to $150 billion and was expected to rise to above $150 billion in 2022. This trend will only continue as demand for electronics and connectivity grows. In the automotive space, new vehicles increasingly rely on semiconductor devices for fuel efficiency, safety, and other features. The expected growth in electric cars will only further this reliance. In the long term, as semiconductor devices play an even bigger role in an ever-expanding array of products, global demand for semiconductor devices will continue to rise. Specific Use case: Systems in PVDF and ECTFE for surface treatment of metals

Why Fluoropolymers for surface treatment of metals?

Pickling is one of the most important pre-treatment steps in the production of high quality metals, (especially ferrous materials). Pickling removes surface coatings or deposits from previous manufacturing steps or oxide layers formed by chemical reaction with air, especially after prolonged storage. It provides a clean metallic surface prior to coating or joining processes (such as welding).
For steels, hydrochloric or sulphuric acids are usually used, with concentrations and bath temperatures optimized for the specific task. Special care has to be taken with high strength steels to avoid hydrogen embrittlement. Spent pickling solutions can often be economically regenerated or used for other purposes if the concentration of dissolved metals is controlled. Hot worked steel is immersed in a bath of either sulphuric or hydrochloric acid, called a pickle. Steels containing more than 6% carbon require an additional step using nitric, phosphoric or hydrofluoric acid. The metal is immersed in the bath for a specified time to prevent too much of the metal being eaten up by the acid.
In electroplating, aluminium is also pickled with a mixture of nitric acid and hydrofluoric acid. The hydrofluoric acid treatment, which is subject to legal restrictions in many countries, is used to dissolve silicon that is mixed into the aluminium during the manufacturing process and cannot be electroplated.
The pickling of copper, bronze, brass, tombac or gunmetal with chromic acid mixtures is also known as etching.
The surface treatment of metallic materials is based on the use of inorganic acids, which are essential for this process. The main acids used in this process are sulphuric acid (H2SO4), phosphoric acid (H3PO4), hydrochloric acid (HCl), hydrofluoric acid (HF), nitric acid (HNO3) and chromic acid (H2CrO4), surface treatment is very often done by using mixtures of these inorganic acids.
It should also be noted that, in addition to pickling in acid solutions, alkaline solutions (e.g., sodium hydroxide-NaOH) can also be used. Alkaline processes have very specific process advantages. If the substrate is steel, there is no need to use inhibitors as the base metal is not or only slightly attacked, and there are other chemicals used in the process such as pickling inhibitors because the pickling acid not only removes the scale and oxide layer but also attacks the base metal. This results in costs due to increased acid consumption, metal losses and pickling defects. This phenomenon can be compensated for by appropriate pickling conditions and the addition of inhibitors. Pickling inhibitors are usually high-molecular-weight organic compounds and have the property of minimizing the attack of the acid on the base metal, thus preventing hydrogen embrittlement. The inhibitors have varying efficiency depending on concentration, temperature and type of pickling acid. Last but not least the presence of inorganic salts developed or added to the process have to be considered.
This brief description of the various forms of surface treatments of metals shows one main conclusion: piping systems and tanks for storage, for transport and for the process itself must be resistant to a wide range of chemicals from extremely acidic (inorganic acids with concentrations up to 30%) to basic (alkalis such as sodium hydroxide).
The temperature range in the pickling process can reach 80°C-90°C.

For such applications only products made of fluoropolymers are safe solutions for long term application.
Pipes, fittings, tanks made from PVDF and ECTFE have turned out to be this solution and have been showing an excellent performance since many decades.
Please see ANNEX 3 PVDF and ECTFE products applied in steel pickling plants.

Production, storage, transport and use of chemicals and other hazardous materials can inevitably carry potential risks. Moreover, history has shown that accidents can not only have economic impacts, but also irreparable consequences on human lives and the environment. Mitigating such risks through rigorous safety management whilst simultaneously ensuring efficiency and availability is a major challenge for today’s worldwide chemical industry (in this case surface treatment of metals).

In our view, the Annex XV restriction report does not cover relevant and essential uses of fluoropolymers in the critical sector “chemical industry”: Pipelines, storage tanks and transportation containers for the handling of chemicals. Fluoropolymers are mechanically solid, chemically resistant and stable even in harsh and corrosive environments.

We request full exemption of fluoropolymers used in industrial applications from the restriction proposal.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The specific Sector “Systems in PVDF and ECTFE for surface treatment of metals” is not listed in Annex XV.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: For this specific application extruded PVDF and ECTFE pipes, injection molded PVDF and ECTFE fittings and valves are used. Furthermore semi-finished products in PVDF and ECTFE in form of extruded sheets (up to 20 mm thickness), pressed sheets (up to 40 mm thickness) round bars (up to OD = 340 mm) are needed to make tanks for storage/for the process and  to make machined fittings. Welding rods (circular profile: 3 and 4 mm) are needed as accessories. Sheets are used for construction and inside lining of storage tanks and transportation containers.  According to our supplier of the raw material for pipes, fittings, valves and main semi-finished products, PVDF and ECTFE are already produced without the use of fluorinated polymerization aids, thus PVDF and ECTFE have a very low potential for leaching of small molecular PFAS.    During manufacturing:   For the specific use-case mainly PVDF and ECTFE products are used. PVDF/ECTFE products like pipes, fittings, valves and sheets are solid products. We are using only PVDF and ECTFE raw materials without fluorinated polymerization aids. A controlled supply chain from resin manufacturing till installation of the systems in PVDF and ECTFE is fully implemented and ensures zero emission.  Product manufacturing phase  Fittings and valves are produced by injection molding and pipes by extrusion. Semifinished products are produced by extrusion or by a pressing process. All components are specially packed to ensure no contamination is taking place in the supply chain till the products are installed in the semiconductor fab.   During the production of PVDF and ECTFE components (process steps as mentioned before) no environmental pollution (no spraying, no microplastics, no Ionic or non-ionic PFAS from coatings etc./ emissions do appear). Process water analysis of our production water do not show any PFAS contamination.   There is a certain amount of emissions when fluoropolymers are processes at elevated temperature in the thermoplastic state. While the majority of the emissions is HCl and HF, there is no detailed information available if the emissions contain small molecular PFAS. In our facility, the main parts of the extrusion line with the highest temperatures (thus the areas where emissions are most likely to occur) are covered with a ventilation hood to suck of fumes/emissions above the extrusion line. The off gases are then cleaned in gas scrubber, before released into the environment. Measurement have shown that some small molecular PFAS accumulate in the water of the gas scrubber, thus cleaning the off gasses is a proven way to reduce emissions.  Precise work and proper work instructions avoid loss of fluoropolymers during the production in our facilities. Material from the starting process as well as chips from cutting are collected and added again to the extrusion process (internal recycling). Material which cannot be processed again is stored in containers and sent for incineration following Austrian laws for handling waste (>850 °C effectively destroys PFAS during incineration).   Storage and handling  Proper Packaging avoids PFAS loss during the transportation and storage. After production, products are packed sold in sales units like:  • Pipes: OD 20 – 315 mm diameter; Length = 5 m; packed in plastic foil • Fittings and valves: OD 20 – 315 mm diameter; packed in plastic foil and proper cardboard • Round bars: OD 20 – 340 mm diameter; Length = 1 m; packed in plastic foil • Welding Rod 3 -4 mm diameter (2 kg Spool); packed in plastic foil and proper cardboard • Sheets from 2 mm up to 50 mm thickness, wrapped in plastic foil, packed in cardboard boxes  During the production, storage and handling of PVDF/ECTFE pipes, fittings, valves, semi-finished products no environmental pollution is expected. The material is inert and very stable, especially at ambient temperature.  The use-phase:   Products are used in the following specific sub-uses:  • PVDF piping systems (pipes, fittings and valves) and semi-finished products are used for handling for handling of most aggressive process media in this metal industry. No emission are caused by using PVDF piping system for handling chemicals in the pickling processes. In actual fact this piping system ensures high lifetime and excellent and safe performances as required by this industry.  • ECTFE piping systems are used for the transport of most aggressive chemicals in its different forms. Components made of ECTFE ensure the safe transport of most critical media for human beings and environment. All these different media do not leach out any elements, which belong to the group of PFAS. During the use in the temperature range from 20-120°C emissions from ECTFE do not occur (below detection limit), because the material is extremely stable, inert and does not degrade into small molecular substances over the whole lifetime.   End-of-life:  Equipment which is decommissioned after service life (~25 years depending on the application) could be collected and deposited or incinerated according to the state of the art and according to laws in place for handling waste. Incineration destroys PFAS substances.

6. Missing uses: Pickling is one of the most important pre-treatment steps in the production of high-quality metals, especially ferrous materials and absolutely necessary to ensure high quality of metal products, which ensures a high lifetime. Pickling removes surface coatings or deposits from previous manufacturing steps or oxide layers formed by chemical reaction with air, especially after prolonged storage. It provides a clean metallic surface prior to coating or joining processes such as welding.   a) see document attached  b) Various, reliable, internationally accepted chemical resistance lists/tables (e.g. DVS Codes 2205-1, DIBt media list 40.1-1-4, ISO TR10358) , information supplied by the raw material supplier  confirm that PVDF and ECTFE are the only safe and long term solution for the handling of inorganic acids, lyes and processing additives , these fluoropolymers are chemical resistant no matter how the temperature (up to 120°C) and pH value are, while other materials (e.g. PE, PP, PVC, PVDF, ABS, PA, …) are only for short term solutions) including the risk of unexpected immediate  failures (please see ANNEX 1 ISO_PRF_TR_10358, ANNEX 2 Behaelter_Auffangvorrichtungen_Rohre_Kunststoff_Medienlisten_40_2019).   Also, metals (steel, copper) do not enable such a universal chemical resistance, at least not in a cost effective way. In addition to the outstanding chemical resistance PVDF/ ECTFE systems meet all further requirements for such applications:  • Internal pressure resistance of pipes and fittings • Temperature resistance  • UV resistance  • Flexibility  • Weldability • Suitability for below ground applications  • Availability of pipes, fittings, valves and special parts (complete supply range)  c) Apart from our suppliers for PVDF and ECTFE and the companies producing the PVDF/ECTFE products used in the surface treatment of metals for the transport and storage, the largest impact is expected for the shipping industry and the companies in the need of this chemical and steel.   Affected industrial applications in general: Whole chemical industry, steel industry, refinery and petrochemical industry, metallurgy industry, power industry, viscose industry, semiconductor industry and all users of high-quality metal products.  d) Only high grade piping systems made of high grade thermoplastics, such as PVDF, ECTFE, offer safety, reliability and significant improvements in performance, installation and safety during operation. Alternatives like PE, PP, PVC, ABS, PVDF, PA and metal pipes can only handle low concentrations or higher concentrations for a very limited lifetime including the risk of unexpected failures, which would have dramatic influence on the environment. In addition to a chemical attack on the pipe and tank walls, applications by the oxidizing chemicals used in this process (such as nitric acid, chromic acid)  always involve an attack on the weld seams (= zones with high residual stresses) due to the oxidizing effect of the chemicals. Only PVDF, ECTFE have established its selves as safe materials for long-term applications. Please see:  ANNEX 1 ISO_PRF_TR_10358 ANNEX 2 Behaelter_Auffangvorrichtungen_Rohre_Kunststoff_Medienlisten_40_2019  e) PVDF and ECTFE have become established over the last decades and represents the current state of the art, as the old systems has been replaced due to the large number of problems. Currently for this application no other solution based on polymeric products seams feasible due to the extreme operating conditions, that require a special combination of temperature and chemical resistance (in special the handling of various chemicals with different character). In addition to a chemical attack on the pipe and tank walls, applications with the strong acids like nitric/chromic acid always involve an attack on the weld seams (= zones with high residual stresses) due to the oxidizing effect of the chemical. Only PVDF and ECTFE have established itself as a safe material for a long-term application.  f) Alternative piping systems do not offer a sufficient resistance, especially if its special chemical behavior in watery solutions is considered (changing pH-value, development of oxygen, strong oxidizers). Other piping systems than the ones made of PVDF and ECTFE are not resistant in the same way and would corrode and leak. Alternatives would be available but are impacted by the PFAS restriction proposal as well. It would be possible to use FEP or also PFA. Using PE, PP, PVC, PVDF, ABS, PVDF, PA, steel, copper would never have the same performance for these media.   We are in permanent contact with raw material suppliers, and we are always considering to include products made of new developments (regarding the raw materials with better resistance against chemicals used in the process of surface treatment) in the product range. Concerning raw materials with improved resistance to high temperatures up to 80°-90°C in these treatment processes are not available, which are competitive from the technical point of view. Based on this fact/example a material, that withstand these chemicals at high temperatures up to 80°C, will not be available within the next 10-15 years.  g) detailed numbers see document  At first glance the impact for our company, the competitors, the customers and the suppliers seems to be not drastically, banning ECTFE and other fluoropolymers would increase the cost of water treatment/disinfection.   Operational failures in a steel plant caused by cracks, breaks in pipes and tanks often last for days until the process can be resumed.  The economic damage caused by a production stop is estimated in reliable media reports at around 1 million Euro for a period of 5 hours. However, the economic aspect fades into the background when one thinks the danger for people and the environment is considered. Chemicals such as chromic acid, nitric acid and hydrofluoric acid have devastating effects on humans and the environment - see the examples below:  Hydrofluoric acid has a corrosive effect and is quickly absorbed by the skin and immediately penetrates deeper tissue layers. This means that deeper tissue layers and bones can be attacked without the skin appearing visibly damaged. Burns of the skin are painful and lead to ulcers that are difficult to heal. Pain often occurs hours after initial contact. In addition to the corrosive effect, the toxicity contributes to the hazardous nature of hydrofluoric acid. The fluoride ions block the calcium and magnesium metabolism and inhibit important enzymes, which leads to acutely threatening metabolic disorders that can even be fatal with multiple organ failure. Inhalation of hydrofluoric acid vapors can lead to cauterization of the lungs with formation of pulmonary oedema and can be fatal in a short time even at low concentrations (50-100 ppm). Chromium (VI) compounds are extremely toxic (the lethal dose is equivalent to half a teaspoon) and have also long been known to be carcinogenic. On skin contact, the compounds cause irritation to the eyes, skin and mucous membranes. Chronic contact with chromium (VI) compounds can cause permanent eye damage if not treated. Since 1958, the WHO (World Health Organization) has recommended a maximum permissible concentration of 0.05 mg/liter for chromium (VI) compounds in drinking water.  Banning PVDF and ECTFE would not only cause harm to our business and the business of competitors and suppliers, but to all companies and end users in the chemical, agricultural industry, infrastructure, and water treatment industry. Such industries depend on PVDF and ECTFE as a safe material for the most important process and end production for the mankind.

General Comments: August 22, 2023
Comment on Proposed Restriction of PFAS

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed PFAS restrictions.

We have been manufacturing valves for 65 years. We have voluntarily and proactively engaged in environmental conservation activities to continuously reduce the burden on the environment, manufactured and sold environmentally friendly valves by acquiring ISO9001 and EA21 certifications, and contributed to society by providing valves.
By proposing and manufacturing valves with specifications that meet customer requests, the number of end users has increased, and now they are widely used in heavy industry, chemical plants, water supply and sewerage, food and pharmaceuticals, aerospace industries, hydrogen-related facilities, and various research institutes.

Comment
Fluorine compounds are indispensable for valve seals (gaskets, gland packings, discs). In addition, it is often used in fluorine grease, shaft sliding guide parts, lining materials, etc.
Even if we consider the problems of corrosion resistance, sealing performance, strength, temperature resistance, and sliding performance against fluids, there is no substitute at this stage.

For example, we have an acid-resistant valve series that we manufacture more than 100 units a year. It is often used in public water supply and sewage systems and is active in chemical injection. Many chemicals are strong acids and alkaline, and other metal materials are not corrosion resistant.
Therefore, only the outer frame of the valve is manufactured with metal, all wetted parts are made of PTFE, and the bellows themselves are manufactured by cutting out PTFE. There is a lineup of PTFE, PVC, and PP parts in contact with liquids, but there are no alternative materials that can withstand strong acids and alkalis.

PCTFE is also used extensively in the seals of valves for aerospace fuel supply. PCTFE is an indispensable material for gaskets, discs, and guides that are used in low-temperature environments to seal high-pressure fluids. If metal seals are considered as an alternative, the weight of the flange cannot be reduced from the viewpoint of material strength. In addition, from the viewpoint of sealing performance, there is no metal with sealing properties equivalent to soft discs.

We also manufacture many sanitary valves that control food-related fluids. Materials used for valves must meet the standards of the Food Sanitation Law. From the viewpoint of fluid sealing performance and structural structure that can be easily disassembled and assembled, PTFE used for guides and O" rings (FKM) used for sealing parts cannot be changed.

The valve is designed for long-term use for ease of maintenance.
We believe that being subject to regulations will cause significant risks and cause greater damage than the persistent risk of PFAS.

For the foregoing, we request that it be listed in the "Indefinite Exemptions".

Org. name: AVERE - The European Association for Electromobility
Combined Comments:
General Comments: AVERE - The European Association for Electromobility is the only association representing the entire ecosystem of electromobility including both electric light-duty and heavy-duty vehicles manufacturers, EV users, charging points manufacturers, charging point operators, research organisations, and public authorities.

Our organisation welcomes ECHA’s environmental protection objectives and acknowledges the intent and wide-scope approach of this restriction proposal. However, we call on ECHA and the submitting authorities to include targeted derogations for specific use cases – namely lithium-ion batteries and electric vehicles (EVs) –  which are needed for transitioning to zero-emission transport and energy; and for which no substitutes are available.

AVERE stresses that the absence of derogation for the use of fluoropolymers in lithium-ion battery cell manufacturing processes would mean that the EU will no longer be able to produce batteries on the continent, which would directly endanger the transition to zero-emission mobility.
AVERE also calls for explicitly including EVs in the currently proposed time-limited derogation for PFAS used in vehicle mobile air conditioning (MAC).

1) Use of PFAS substances for the cell manufacturing process of lithium-ion batteries:

As there are currently no viable alternatives to PFAS for the cell manufacturing process of lithium-ion batteries despite more than 30 years of research and development into potential substitutes, AVERE calls on ECHA to introduce a blanket and unlimited derogation for all PFAS substances used in battery production to ensure the EU fully switch to EVs on time.

If this full unlimited derogation cannot be granted, AVERE and its members suggest to insert a time-limited derogation for PTFE (Polytetrafluoroethylene) and PVDF (Polyvinylidene fluoride) used as binder materials for the lithium-ion electrode manufacturing process. This time limit should be set to 13.5 years as a minimum starting point which would allow electric OEMs to continue seeking for alternatives. Should no viable alternative emerge after 13.5 years, as AVERE members anticipate, we will call on ECHA to extend this derogation beyond the initial 13.5 years.

Without an unlimited or time-limited derogation for this specific use-case, the battery industry will not be able to produce lithium-ion batteries in general nor at any scale which would be needed for the EU’s transition.  This would directly contradict the EU’s established strategic autonomy and self-sufficiency objectives  under numerous regulatory frameworks (EU Strategic Action Plan on batteries, EU Net Zero Industry Act proposal, EU Critical Raw Materials Act proposal, EU batteries regulation).

Additionally, the proposed restriction would duplicate sector-specific provisions on hazardous substances provided under the EU Batteries regulation. Indeed, Article 6 of the adopted EU batteries regulation already ensures that potential and demonstrated risks to human health or the environment from hazardous substances used in batteries are appropriately managed. Article 47 also includes detailed end-of-life treatment and depollution requirements, which should guarantee that all PFAS components are destroyed during the recycling process.
AVERE therefore suggests introducing explicit tracking of PFAS emissions from battery manufacturing and recycling as an alternative regulatory management tool instead of an Annex XV restriction.

2) Use of PFAS substances for Mobile Air Conditioning (MAC) systems in vehicles

As mentioned previously, the proposed restriction only establish a time-limited derogation for the use of PFAS substances in MACs of combustion engine vehicles with mechanical compressors and not for electric vehicles and a separate derogation for maintenance and refilling of vehicle MACs.

Regarding the  proposed derogation for new cars, the derogation should not differentiate between EVs and internal combustion engines. Therefore, the proposed derogation for vehicles with mechanical compressors should be expanded to all vehicles.

Additionally, AVERE calls for a complete and unlimited derogation to be provided for the maintenance and refilling for MAC of any vehicle placed on the market before the entry into force of the restriction proposal.

See our specific comments below.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: 1) Use of PFAS substances for the cell manufacturing process of lithium-ion batteries:   AVERE provides detailed information under section 2.6.  Our understanding is that this use case would fit under battery applications in the Energy sector (Annex “E.2.12”), under Table 8 of the Annex XV restriction report.  As mentioned in our general comments, there are currently no viable alternatives to PFAS used in lithium-ion battery cell manufacturing. Individual OEMs invested in identifying and evaluating viable alternatives, with associated personnel costs, and R&D, but concluded that, of the alternatives evaluated, none were viable for this use case. AVERE therefore calls on ECHA to introduce an unlimited derogation from the restriction for all PFAS substances used in battery production to ensure the EU can meet its road transport decarbonisation objectives. AVERE also suggests introducing explicit tracking of PFAS emissions from battery manufacturing and recycling as an alternative regulatory management tool instead of an Annex XV restriction.  As an alternative, AVERE and its members suggest inserting a time-limited derogation for PTFE (Polytetrafluoroethylene) and PVDF (Polyvinylidene fluoride) used as binder materials for the lithium-ion electrode manufacturing process. This time limit should be set to 13.5 years as a minimum starting point which would allow electric OEMs to seek alternatives. If after 13.5 years, still no viable alternatives have emerged, AVERE will call on ECHA to extend this derogation beyond the initial 13.5 years.   2) Use of PFAS substances for Mobile Air Conditioning (MAC) systems in vehicles  We believe that this use case would fall under “Mobile Air Conditioning” in Table 9 of the Annex XV restriction report.  As mentioned previously, the proposed restriction only establishes a time-limited derogation for the use of PFAS substances in MACs of combustion engine vehicles with mechanical compressors and not for EVs. The proposed derogation should explicitly include EVs within the scope of the derogation for PFAS substances used in vehicles MACs.   Additionally, AVERE calls for a complete and unlimited derogation to be provided for the maintenance and refilling for MAC of any vehicle placed on the market before the entry into force of the restriction proposal.    Mobile Air Conditioning (MAC) systems use refrigerants, especially “R1234yf” (2,3,3,3-Tetrafluoropropene HFO) which has been established as an industry standard to enable heating and air conditioning for vehicles users. The decision to use R1234yf is the result of a technical solution to comply with Directive 2006/40/EC which effectively banned the use of R134a refrigerant in newly type-approved vehicles. While some vehicle manufacturers have found alternative refrigerants such as R744, and R290, they still require further testing and development to match the performance of R1234yf.  Our OEM members have designed MAC system fitted for the use of R1234yf, which required testing and type-approval (including revalidation, component and firmware changes), before they ultimately started selling vehicles with R1234yf in Europe. It should however be noted that the R1234yf implementation was a much less difficult design and validation task than it is currently with the ongoing design and validation of R744 and R290, which have been identified as alternatives for R1234yf. Our OEMs have notably assessed non-PFAS drop-in solutions for their MAC systems but have not identified any suitable alternatives on the market to date. Additionally, even possible drop-in solutions which include mixtures of R1234yf would not be in line with the proposed PFAS restriction proposal.   Additionally, while non-PFAS solutions (such as R744 and R290) can be developed, they present specific challenges that have not been appropriately addressed up until now, namely:  - high flammability - weak performance in hot climates  - high pressure and low specific volume which do not allow for a direct drop-in (According to the Study from Sanchez et al. : https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0196890422001844   To allow for the large-scale deployment of suitable alternatives, a complete system redesign is needed and would take several years for internal R&D to develop but also for the vehicle to be type-approved under Regulation (EU) 2018/8517.   As all types of vehicles (electrical, hybrid and combustion engines) must follow the same procedure and associated length for their design, testing and type approval and since a large majority of MAC systems use 1234yf, every vehicle, regardless of its type, should benefit from the same derogation period that is currently proposed for refrigerants in MACs in combustion engine vehicles with mechanical compressors, namely 6.5 years after the entry into force of the new restriction.   Moreover, the current restriction proposal does not analyse in detail the challenges linked with the retrofitting of a MAC system in vehicles. Indeed, such a retrofit currently would cost more than the value of a second-hand vehicle and would therefore not be cost-advantageous for users.   A future-proof restriction which works for the industry and users should therefore provide a derogation for Heating, Ventilation, Air Conditioning and Refrigeration (HVACR) in vehicles which includes a complete blanket derogation for the maintenance and refilling of vehicles that are placed on the market before entry into force of the restriction. Another option would be to include a review clause, 10 years after the entry into force, at which time it would be assessed if there are drop-in solutions for 1234yf that would comply with the PFAS restriction proposal. In case no viable alternative exists by the review period, the proposed derogation of 13.5 years should be extended to a blanked derogation.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: 1) Use of PFAS substances for the cell manufacturing process of lithium-ion batteries - End-of-Life phase  In December 2022, the EU adopted the EU Batteries Regulation which provides a framework to ensure that EVs and industrial battery cells and their components are appropriately managed throughout their full life cycle. Chapter VII of this regulation establishes detailed and binding requirements for OEM's Extended Producer Responsibility, associated collection obligations as well as end-of-life treatment and depollution requirements which would ensure that PFAS are removed in the process. The legislation also sets minimum rates for overall battery recycling efficiency and for the recovery of each material. We believe such end-of-life processes, including responsible recycling and disposal, adequately addresses any public health concerns about PFAS exposure.  The PFAS materials used for the manufacturing of battery cells (i.e., PTFE and PVDF) contained within end-of-life cells or scraps can be managed with nascent cell recycling processes. The aforementioned components only comprise a small percentage of the total cell material mass (0.5 - 1.5 wt. %) and currently the future of these materials is not explicitly tracked or monitored. There are several recycling processes, and depending on the recycling process, PFAS components may be destroyed or left intact,AVERE therefore believes  better and explicit tracking requirements of these components could help improve the monitoring and enforcement of efficiency and depollution standards.   Currently, most cell recycling flowsheets begin with mechanical shredding. Foils (Cu/Al) and plastics (i.e., polyolefin separators) are usually then separated from a mixture of active materials (i.e., cathode/anode/electrolyte), referred to as black mass. The distribution of PFAS components between these streams may vary from processor to processor. A minority of PFAS components may be distributed in the Al/Cu foil streams if they are adhered to the foils.   The melting of aluminium or copper foil scrap is an existing management mechanism. High temperatures and long residence times provide a mechanism for destroying PFAS - the fluorinated components should react with a small percentage of the molten metal to form inert, inorganic fluorides that can be disposed of as slag. The performance and practices of different metal reprocessing operations can vary, hence the importance of explicit standards for destruction efficiency. The black mass mixture consists mainly of anode, cathode, electrolyte and trace (undersized) foils. The majority of PFAS materials are distributed in the black mass mixture. Depending on the recycler or refiner, the material is processed by pyrometallurgy, hydrometallurgy or a combination of both.   These downstream processing steps are explicitly used for the reduction and recovery of battery metals (i.e., cobalt, nickel, lithium, etc.) and, possibly, graphite. These downstream processing steps are designed to recover battery components and eliminate hazardous or non-recoverable components. This also provides a basis for PFAS management at end-of-life.  Hydrometallurgical and pyrometallurgical processing of black mass already includes explicit processing technologies to capture and reduce HF and fluorinated phosphorus species originating from electrolyte salts (i.e., LiPF6). Explicit tracking of PFAS in cell recycling could provide a mechanism to ensure the appropriate capture and destruction of PFAS using complementary abatement technologies.  Pyrometallurgical treatment involves heating active battery materials to temperatures well in excess of 600°C. For some battery recyclers, this may be a high-temperature heat treatment step, and for others it may even involve melting or similar operations. Above 600°C, PFAS components degrade to give HF and light fluorinated hydrocarbons. Dedicated combustion or heat treatment at temperatures above 1000°C with moderate residence times enables almost complete destruction of light hydrofluorocarbons. The efficiency of destruction without high-temperature heat treatment is still a matter of debate, and standards are still lacking. Wet scrubbing can be used to manage the off-gas components (i.e., hydrofluoric acid (HF)) from this treatment - the reduction efficiency varies according to the processor.  Hydrometallurgical processing methods for battery materials do not explicitly destroy PVDF or PTFE as pyrometallurgical processing does. However, these components could be sequestered, or even specifically recovered, by flotation and/or filtration - since PVDF and PTFE are water-insoluble and dense. Depending on the quality of these sequestered materials, they can be reprocessed. Alternatively, they can be disposed of in specially designed facilities, in specialized incinerators (high temperature, long residence time) or, potentially, through emerging technologies such as catalytic dehydrohalogenation or mechano-chemical lye treatment.  Pyrometallurgical treatment or sequestration in hydrometallurgical circuits offer technically viable approaches to managing the complete life cycle of PFAS substances in cells. However, investment in research and development (R&D) and explicit tracing will be needed to ensure satisfactory management of these components.   Although some equipment manufacturers are actively seeking solutions to the risks associated with incomplete degradation/combustion products, focusing on solutions that mitigate emissions that pose health risks to the general population, the fact remains that in the control of emissions by pyrometallurgical processing of PTFE and PVDF, some decomposition products (fluorinated organic compounds) are more difficult to destroy than others.  However, they are also easy to detect and monitor, and can be regulated through specific incineration where harmful emissions are minimized and captured. There is little research into the efficiency of mechanochemical degradation of PFAS by ball milling using alkali hydroxide reagents (KOH, for example). However, initial studies have indicated that alkaline hydroxide reagents used in a ball-milling technique can ensure complete or almost complete destruction of PFAS compounds. With increasing research into alternative technologies for the capture and degradation treatment of PFAS or PFAS-containing components, it is essential that applicable technologies are implemented and designed specifically for chemicals of concern. for chemicals of concern.   2) Use of PFAS substances for Mobile Air Conditioning (MAC) systems in vehicles   Currently, on the market there are several recovery, recycling and recharging machines compatible with R1234yf. These systems have a high recovery efficiency (98.5%) and can continuously reuse R1234yf for mobile air conditioning in other vehicles, after filtering.   For more information on refrigerant recovery and recycling in mobile air conditioning systems, please refer to the existing industry standards in the following brochure:  - https://www.ase.com/dist/docs/2019_online_609_booklet.pdf

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: 1) Use of PFAS substances for the cell manufacturing process of lithium-ion batteries - End-of-Life phase  Thermal destruction by incineration or pyrolysis is the most common method for fully managing PTFE and PFAS at end-of-life. There are also several emerging PFAS reduction technologies for PVDF and PTFE. These include catalytic dehydrohalogenation, Fenton oxidation, lye treatment and supercritical water oxidation. These emerging technologies may prove preferable or complementary over time. Given the well-defined nature of cell recycling streams, it is also possible to optimize recycling streams to sequester and eventually reprocess these polymeric materials.  Thermal treatment (pyrolysis and incineration) of PTFE and PVDF has been extensively studied in academic and industrial literature. These studies show that high temperatures (>1000°C), long residence times and appropriate atmosphere composition are important considerations. Thermal destruction generates hydrofluoric acid (HF), carbon dioxide (CO2), light hydrofluorocarbons and light perfluorocarbons - the relative concentrations and speciation are influenced by the presence of metals/catalysts and the moisture content of the material.  From the information available, it is clear that destruction efficiency and the resulting products must be closely monitored to ensure optimal destruction and capture of post-treatment products. Light hydrofluorocarbons and perfluorocarbons can be captured using membrane technology after thermal treatment or incineration.   Although further investment and monitoring are required to ensure adequate PFAS reduction in battery recycling streams, the battery life cycle forms the basis of management. Unlike distributed sources of PFAS (kitchen utensils, lubricants, clothing, etc.), the entire battery life cycle is intentionally managed. Cells have well-defined characteristics and composition, enabling traceability of PFAS components through mass balance and other monitoring techniques. This also enables specific depollution technologies to be put in place, since cells used in automotive or energy storage applications are explicitly recycled in specific facilities where destruction performance can be optimized more effectively than that seen in municipal waste management facilities.  2) Use of PFAS substances for Mobile Air Conditioning (MAC) systems in vehicles   Our members do not incinerate R1234yf and are not aware of such processes.

5. Proposed derogations: As part of this section 2.5, AVERE will only provide information in order to answer questions for PFAS - Refrigerants used in EVs mobile air conditioning systems.    Regarding the proposed derogation for “5.i. Maintenance and refilling of existing Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVACR) equipment put on the market before [18 months after entry into force] and for which no drop-in alternative exist until 13.5 years after entry into force”:  AVERE believes that the proposed timetable for switching to PFAS-free refrigerant for mobile air conditioners (MACs) in electric and hybrid vehicles is not feasible when compared with previous refrigerant replacement efforts.  The most recent refrigerant changeover for MACs, was based on a multinational effort to reduce the refrigerant's global warming potential, and started the first discussions on switching from R134A to R1234yf in 2002 (Council Decision 2002/358/EC) with the adoption of legislation in the European Parliament's MAC Directive 2006/40/EC, which required the phase-out to begin in 2011 and be completed by January 2017.   In the USA, this gradual reduction was not finalized until the 2021 model year.  In addition, this refrigerant changeover was considered a "drop-in", as the properties of the new refrigerant are almost identical to those of the refrigerant being replaced. This change therefore required only a slight modification in the type of oil used, a change in the operating setpoint of the thermal expansion valve, and selective use of the internal heat exchanger hose to compensate for the slight degradation in performance.  Other changes were mainly due to the low flammability (A2L) of R1234YF compared with R134a (A1), including changes to heat exchanger labelling with additional certification and training requirements for service technicians.  The proposal under restriction option 2 would require more extensive system redesign than the previous refrigerant phase-out due to the lack of alternatives, and the proposed 1.5-year transition period for RO2 is not feasible given the 11 years required to phase out previous alternative refrigerants.  Our members have currently identified two types of alternative systems mentioned in the proposal, namely R744 and R290, both of which present problems:   R744 has been used on an extremely limited basis, by Mercedes in the E/S class and by the Volkswagen Group in the Audi A8 (for Europe only), and for a limited time in the ID3/4 heat pump system.  This short experience and limited production illustrate both the challenges and costs associated with these specialized components, which operate at pressures 5 to 10 times higher than those of current R1234yf systems.  These R-744 systems also require constant monitoring and mitigation strategies in the passenger cabin due to the risk of drowsiness caused by leaks.  With these higher operating pressures, the components that carry the refrigerant must be much more robust in R744 systems than in R1234yf systems (pipes with flexible steel inner reinforcements), and fittings cannot follow typical O-ring/washer sealing designs, but require metal-to-metal sealing designs.  R744 fittings are more susceptible to contamination due to the high pressures and small size of CO2 molecules, requiring special handling and care when making connections in the assembly plant.  The efficiency of CO2 systems decreases considerably in high ambient environments, above 31°C, due to the super-critical temperature of CO2, which means that the refrigerant in the external heat exchanger (condenser) does not undergo a phase change and the COP (coefficient of performance) decreases, thus consuming much more energy. This means that, at high ambient temperatures, the energy required to cool the passenger compartment and battery is much greater with R744 than with R1234yf, and may not be able to meet the requirements of maintaining the battery and passenger compartment at safe operating temperatures.  R290 as a secondary loop has been mentioned as a viable alternative, but R290 is not currently used for automotive production in any form. In 2018, Denso, an MVAC supplier, proposed this type of system at the SAE TMSS (Thermal Management Systems Symposium) conference in San Diego.  The proof-of-concept idea has merit, but it's a long way from commercialization, as single R290 compressors are not developed and validated, and lubricating oils require compatibility testing.  It is important to note that the EPA does not allow R290 to be used in MAC systems in the USA in direct expansion or secondary loop, and the cost of developing a single system for the EU is prohibitive, doubling the R&D and capital investment for two unique designs. Additional capital expenditure would be incurred at vehicle manufacturing sites, to handle large quantities of two types of refrigerant. There are also no standards for service valve connections to charge this system, nor is there a risk assessment for this highly flammable (A3) refrigerant system. In addition, secondary loops are less efficient due to the need to add additional heat exchangers to cool/heat the coolant to maintain the temperature in the vehicle cabin, compared to direct expansion systems, and would likely require additional coolant heaters to meet cabin heating requirements. This additional cost and lower efficiency would increase the overall cost of EVs, while creating a price disparity between ICE vehicles and EVs.  Given the lack of alternatives currently available, and the time needed to establish the required safety standards, obtain regulatory approval and market the new MAC systems, AVERE suggests a 13.5-year derogation for MAC use cases, irrespective of powertrain technology. By providing a waiver independent of the propulsion system, we avoid inadvertently placing zero-emission vehicles at a competitive disadvantage compared with combustion engine vehicles emitting greenhouse gases.  Additionally, we call on ECHA to consider an unlimited derogation for maintenance and refilling of existing MACs for which continued use of the product requires the original refrigerant.   If we consider the entire passenger vehicle sector, there are over 250 million vehicles on Europe's roads (Eurostat, 2023). Assuming that, from 2017 onwards, only vehicles equipped with R1234yf are sold, this would represent an annual market of 11 million vehicles per year (ACEA, 2023). Assuming that, until 2029, all vehicles are equipped with R1234yf, this could represent, cumulatively, 135 million vehicles on European roads that will use R1234yf and require servicing of their mobile air-conditioning unit. In terms of demand for R1234yf, this could translate into an annual demand of 10,000 tonnes. Assuming the same leakage rate of 10% in the worst-case scenario, this would translate into R1234yf leakage of around 1,000 tonnes.  Given the relatively small leakeages and long forecasted timeline of vehicles - which are too costly to be retrofited by consumers - we call for ECHA to provide the following derogation to the proposed restriction:   - a complete blanket derogation for the maintenance and refilling of vehicles that are placed on the market before entry into force of the restriction; or - alternatively, inserting a review clause that would, by 10 years after entry into force of the restriction proposal, assess whether and to what extent, if any, drop-in solutions exist for 1234yf that would comply with the PFAS restriction proposal. If no viable alternatives exist by that time, a blanket derogation should be provided.

6. Missing uses: AVERE believes that the EV Lithium-Ion Batteries are missing from the list of use case which should benefit from derogation to the restriction list proposed.   Certain PFAS, specifically polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) and fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC), are critical components used in almost all lithium-ion battery cells on the market. These materials play an essential role in battery performance, and are vital to the overall safety of EVs and their passengers.   PFAS-based binders serve two major functions: 1) they provide mechanical strength to form and maintain the electrode architecture in battery production and battery use as designed, and 2) they function without perturbation to enable battery performance and degradation as designed under the harsh electrochemical and chemical environment experienced by the electrode.  a) Annual Tonnage and Types of PFAS Associated with EV LIBs:   In the European Union (EU) market for EV batteries, the annual use of PVDF is around 5,600 tonnes and is expected to reach 23,000 tonnes by 2026, while the annual use of FEC is around 600 tonnes and is expected to reach 4,000 tonnes by 2026.   For EVs cell applications, PFAS are all contained within the sealed cells and are not accessible to consumers for handling, repairs, etc. Lithium batteries are processed through a highly controlled supply chain, from cell manufacture to end-of-life vehicle decommissioning. End-of-life treatment of EV cells (and therefore of the PFAS chemicals they contain) is carried out at licensed designated recycling sites, which can facilitate proper disposal management and mitigate the risk of accidental release of PFAS into the environment.  b) Key Functionalities of the PFAS in EV Lithium-Ion Batteries  PVDF and PTFE are used as polymer binders for cathode electrodes because of their chemical resistance, high chemical, thermal and electrochemical stability during cycling, and mechanical properties including durability, adhesion and processability.  FEC is used as an electrolyte additive because of its chemical stability, and is one of the keys to enabling vehicles to achieve acceptable autonomy and the required service life (>10 years). Fluorine-containing additives, such as FEC, provide essential stabilization of battery materials, and batteries can become unstable and potentially dangerous without the use of fluorine-containing additives to stabilize internal components.  By removing PFAS from their critical role in stabilizing EV battery performance, vehicles and their passengers can be adversely affected.  c) Estimate of Affected Companies  If the use of PFAS is banned in EV batteries, we believe that this restriction will have a negative impact on the entire battery value chain, which is estimated to generate annual demand in the EU of €250 billion from 2025 onwards, creating some 800,000 direct jobs and up to 3 million indirect jobs according to RECHARGE. (https://rechargebatteries.org/battery-market-and-technologies/) The automotive manufacturing industry would also be largely impacted by such a blanket restriction.   d) Availability and Technical/Economical Feasibility of Alternatives  There is currently no alternative to replace PFAS in cells in the short term (10 years), either for the cathode binder (PVDF) or for the electrolyte additive (FEC). The only commonly evaluated alternative to PVDF as a binder is another chemical PFAS called polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), which is considered the leading contender as a new polymer binder for future cell technology that takes advantage of manufacturing process improvements.  e) Status of Research & Development for Alternatives  The development of fluorine- and PFAS-free cathode binders is very limited and confined to early R&D activities, mainly in research laboratories.  One of the most promising examples of this R&D activity is that of Professor Mickael Dollé of the University of Montreal, who is studying the development of PFAS-free elastomeric binders to replace PVDF.  His research involves modifying both the chemicals used and battery manufacturing processes.  So, assuming his alternative approach is successful, it would take around 5 more years of development, plus at least 5 years of process development and scale-up for commercialization, as well as the necessary modifications to existing manufacturing equipment (i.e., all electrode mixing, coating and calendering equipment would have to be heavily modified or replaced)While scientists continue to explore other options for replacing PFAS, it should be noted that the viability of the alternative under consideration is currently low and does not provide the e-mobility industry with the certainty needed to abandon the use of PFAS in the manufacture of li-ion battery cells.For these reasons, AVERE believes that a derogation is justified for PVDF and PTFE used in lithium-ion EV batteries.  Similarly, when it comes to electrolyte additives, little development progress is currently being made to replace FEC in LIB cells, due to the necessary stability provided by fluorinated compounds during operation to avoid safety issues. The best option for eliminating FEC from lithium-ion battery cells is to increase the use of other electrolyte additives with inferior performance, such as vinylene carbonate (VC) and potential new additives with fluorine-like properties that can provide similar functional benefits, including additives that contain boron or phosphorus elements. One such additive in this field would be tris(trimethylsilyl) phosphite (TMSP). Both of these components (VC, TMSP) are already in commercial use today, but they do not offer the same level of stability and safety as the existing PFAS chemical (FEC). AVERE also recommends an unlimited exemption for the use of FEC in the lithium-ion battery cells of EVs.  Because of the importance it places on safety, the internal combustion engine vehicle industry is known to be conservative and risk-averse when it comes to introducing new technologies.  Consequently, any modifications to battery components to eliminate PFAS chemicals are expected to be a deliberate process requiring substantial periods of development and validation before being considered for use in automotive applications.  For reference, any minor modification to the design of a battery using an already accepted component technology requires a minimum of three years' development to prove the performance, safety and manufacturing stability of the modification.  In the case of a major technological change such as the elimination of PFAS from EV batteries, not only would a minimum of three years of validation be required, but also years of technical development to meet the necessary performance requirements (5 to 8 years). In addition, it would take time to overcome all the associated economic and manufacturing challenges in order to adapt production to EV quantities and bring new technologies to market. We call on ECHA to offer an unlimited derogation for the use of PFAS in EV lithium-ion battery cells and to introduce explicit tracking of PFAS emissions from battery manufacturing and recycling as an alternative regulatory management tool instead of an Annex XV restriction.   To illustrate the need for this derogation, we need only look at the timing of commercialization of new cathode technologies. For example, in 1991 Sony marketed the first lithium-ion cell for its camcorders, using a cathode technology known as LCO.  From then on, it was 15 years before the next-generation improved cathode technology, known as NMC, was finally commercialized in the mid-2000s.  Even in this example, the switch from LCO to NMC technology would be considered less disruptive than the overall elimination of PFAS from EV batteries, as the elimination of PFAS requires the introduction of multiple new components into a battery. In addition, major changes to the chemical composition of existing batteries are not usually introduced directly into EV applications, which may further delay timelines.  Instead, new battery designs (of which PFAS-free cells would be a part) are first introduced into smaller commercial markets with lower requirements (e.g., power tool batteries, drones), then gradually introduced into mobile devices (e.g., cell phones, laptops, tablets) to reduce technology risks before large-scale commercial introduction into EV applications with stringent requirements. Compared with the timescales currently proposed under Restriction Option 2, the maximum 13.5-year waiver is the only realistic route for industry to successfully phase out the use of PFAS in lithium-ion battery cells.  f) Socio-economic impact of Sectoral Disruption  As indicated in the general comments section, EVs are an essential tool in EU and global efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, essential for climate change mitigation and air quality-related public health objectives, which aim to reduce particulate emissions.   The fully electric automotive sector is set for rapid growth over the next decade, with the European Environment Agency reporting over 870,000 new EV registrations in the EU-27 in 2021. Such a growth would not be possible without the use of PFAS in battery cell manufacturing.   In addition, it is important to stress that the battery value chain has the potential to become a very important vector for job creation. Indeed, a 2022 Menon publication on job creation prospects in the European battery industry suggests 150,000 direct jobs in Europe by 2030, or 735,000 if indirect employment effects are taken into account. Any restrictions on PFAS for EV batteries would therefore have a massive impact on job creation in Europe, at a time when the EU is trying to relocate green technology manufacturing and boost employment in these sectors.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: 1) Use of PFAS substances for the cell manufacturing process of lithium-ion batteries:   As there are currently no viable alternatives to PFAS for the cell manufacturing process of lithium-ion batteries despite more than 30 years of research and development into potential substitutes, AVERE calls on ECHA to introduce a blanket and unlimited derogation for all PFAS substances used in battery production to ensure the EU fully switch to EVs on time and to introduce explicit tracking of PFAS emissions from battery manufacturing and recycling as an alternative regulatory management tool instead of an Annex XV restriction.  If this full unlimited derogation cannot be granted, AVERE and its members suggest to insert a time-limited derogation for PTFE (Polytetrafluoroethylene) and PVDF (Polyvinylidene fluoride) used as binder materials for the lithium-ion electrode manufacturing process. This time limit should be set to 13.5 years as a minimum starting point which would allow electric OEMs to continue seeking for alternatives. Should no viable alternative emerge after 13.5 years, as AVERE members anticipate, we will call on ECHA to extend this derogation beyond the initial 13.5 years.   2) Use of PFAS substances for Mobile Air Conditioning (MAC) systems in vehicles  As mentioned previously, the proposed restriction only establishes a time-limited derogation for the use of PFAS substances in MACs of combustion engine vehicles with mechanical compressors and not for EVs. The proposed derogation should explicitly include EVs within the scope of the derogation for PFAS substances used in vehicles MACs.   Additionally, AVERE calls for a complete and unlimited derogation to be provided for the maintenance and refilling for MAC of any vehicle placed on the market before the entry into force of the restriction proposal.

8. Other identified uses: 1) Use of PFAS substances for the cell manufacturing process of lithium-ion batteries - End-of-Life phase  With regards to the use of PFAS in the manufacturing processes of lithium-ion battery cell, we invite you to take into consideration all the previous sections.   2) Use of PFAS substances for Mobile Air Conditioning (MAC) systems in vehicles   As we highlighted above, the process of redesigning a vehicle's thermal system is complex and time-consuming. Every newly sold vehicle, regardless of type - electric, hybrid or combustion engine - needs sufficient time to design and test a new MAC system, which must then be approved under Regulation (EU) 2018/85. approved under Regulation (EU) 2018/85.   Looking at existing vehicles on the market, it is essential to note that the average age of passenger cars in the EU is 11.8 years. These figures are even higher in Romania and Lithuania which have the oldest car fleet in Europe, with an average of 17 years. Trucks are even older, with an EU average of 13.9 years with Greece having an average truck fleet of 21.4 years (Source: ACEA).  Some of our members' vehicles are designed to last longer than the current system, with some OEMs expecting their vehicles to be on the road for over 35 years. If these vehicles are subject to new requirements and have to be retrofitted to adapt to the new MAC system, this is no guarantee that they will fit in well with existing vehicles. A system redesign could cost customers up to 50,000 € for some vehicles ) more than the value of the used vehicle.   Under the assumption that the proposed entry into force of the restrictions would take place in 2027, this could result in millions of EVs to be sold to non-EU countries in order to have a working MAC system. Such a scenario would deeply undermine the goals of the European Green Deal and impact vulnerable households who cannot afford new vehicles.

Org. name: AVR - AVR Italian association of valve and tap manufacturers
Combined Comments:
General Comments: AVR, Italian Valve and Fitting Manufacturers' Association, federated with Anima Confindustria, is the industry association representing Italian companies in the valves and fittings sector
AVR represents the voice of enterprises:
- for civil construction (sanitary fittings, valves for heating systems and fire valves, components and accessories, fittings), for general and special industry (chemical, petrochemical, energy, steel, shipbuilding and food)
- for public utility works (aqueducts, water treatment plants, sewage treatment plants and irrigation).
For nearly 70 years, AVR has been creating the indispensable conditions for members to build products that fully meet the needs of markets, directives and regulations in force. Efficiency, quality, and reliability are fundamental elements of our members' productions, which do not neglect the importance of constant innovation in technology and, in some cases, design. All manufacturers in the mechanical and plant engineering sector would be impacted by the current PFAS restriction proposal, either in terms of their goods or their production lines. Based on this information, it is possible to understand that the impact of PFAS and related substances restriction would be dramatic for industrial economy, as there is currently no alternative to this substance. The use of PFAS as described in the restriction proposal represents a core component for the valve and taps industry referring to fluoropolymers in particular.
A total ban on fluoropolymers will have a wide impact in all the supply chain of main components serving industrial production plants: pumps, valves, instruments, gasket, flanges etc. The concerns of persistence raised in the restriction proposal can be appropriately managed through the implementation of responsible manufacturing and EoL risk-management practices.
AVR believes that there is not enough scientific data and evidence which would justify the complete ban of PFAS, especially referring to fluoropolymers. At the moment there are no alternative materials capable of combining similar performances.
The total ban of PTFE, FKM and FFKM and similar materials would lead to the return to a limited industrial plant operating capacity for multiple production lines with consequent reduction in performance, increase in costs and reduction in the life of the industrial components

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The use of fluoropolymers such as PTFE in valves, junctions and fittings in general offers a unique combination of desirable properties such as chemical resistance, thermal resistance, low friction and chemical inertness. This allows valves to operate efficiently and reliably even in harsh environments and with aggressive fluids, contributing to the safety and reliability of industrial processes. They are often used in industrial applications that require good resistance to corrosives and high temperature levels.  PFAS materials are mainly used in sealing applications in valves and taps, specifically in seals, O-rings, packings, and gaskets. The use of PFAS materials is restricted to extremely necessary situations and where there are no viable elastomeric alternatives available due to their high cost, which can be anywhere between 2.5 times and over 100 times that of other natural or synthetic elastomers.   Standard elastomers/polymers would quickly degrade in very aggressive liquids, however PFAS-containing elastomers/polymers exhibit extraordinary chemical resistance to such liquids. The elasticity and sealing capabilities of PFAS elastomers/polymers can also be maintained at temperatures where those of other common elastomers/polymers would harden, frequently within a few hours or days of use, making them unable to provide an efficient seal. The European Sealing Association (ESA) has created a position paper with more detailed technical information titled "European Sealing Association (ESA) position statement relative to the European proposal for PFAS regulation in relation with the Sealing Industry." You may see and download this position paper at www.europeansealing.com/about-us/position-statements on the ESA website. That document is supported by AVR.   In the components of a valve or faucet, fluoropolymers can be found in various parts. Some non-exhaustive examples include: Gaskets: Fluoropolymer gaskets such as polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) or tetrafluoroethylene (TFE) are commonly used to provide a tight seal between the moving parts of the valve or faucet. These materials are known for their chemical resistance and ability to withstand high temperatures.  Seals: Seals, such as O-rings, made of fluoropolymers offer superior chemical resistance compared to other elastomeric materials. They can be used to provide a tight seal inside the valve or faucet.  Coatings: Sometimes, the internal components of a valve or faucet can be coated with a fluoropolymer film. This coating offers greater chemical resistance and can help reduce wear or corrosion of internal components. Ball valve seal sets: In ball faucets, seal sets can be made of fluoropolymers to ensure a good seal when the ball is closed. PTFE is one of the materials commonly used for this purpose. Greases/Lubricants: using greases or lubricants in PTFE valve production enhances performance, improves sealing capabilities, protects against corrosion, manages temperatures, and facilitates assembly, ultimately contributing to the reliable operation and longevity of the valves. It is important to note that the specific use of fluoropolymers may vary depending on the type of valve or faucet and the needs of the application. In any case, fluoropolymers are often chosen for their chemical and thermal resistance properties, which make them suitable for many industrial applications.  Furthermore, in the valve and fitting sector, PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) have been used in chrome and metal plating processes primarily for their ability to provide a non-stick and water-repellent surface.  Chrome and metal plating processes: PFAS, including certain fluoropolymers, possess excellent non-stick characteristics, which make them suitable for use in chrome and metal plating. They help prevent the adherence of plating solutions to the equipment, ensuring smooth and consistent plating. PFAS can also reduce the surface tension of plating solutions, enabling better wetting of the metal surface and facilitating uniform plating. This property ensures that the plating material adheres evenly and provides a smooth and durable finish. The total ban of PTFE, FKM and FFKM would lead to the return to a limited industrial plant operating capacity for multiple production lines with consequent reduction in performance, increase in costs and reduction in the life of the industrial components.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Specialized businesses frequently maintain PFAS-required valves and taps, ensuring expert treatment throughout their service life. A systematic tracking system during use and at the end of their lifecycle can be developed, harmonizing with current recovery processes like the WEEE (Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment) directive, to prevent incorrect disposal of PFAS and PFAS-containing components.  The creation of a Digital Product Passport provides a practical way to improve the traceability of valves, taps, and the relevant parts that go with them. Utilizing the Digital Product Passport system makes it possible to more efficiently track the lifecycle of these parts, assuring responsible management and reducing the environmental impact of their disposal.
