General Comments: Background:

Liquid Gas Europe is the European association representing the liquid gas (LPG, renewable LPG, bioLPG and rDME) industry. Members of Liquid Gas Europe comprise of producers, distribution companies and equipment manufacturers and national liquid associations representing 17 Member States.
Whilst LPG (which is predominantly a mixture of propane and butane), is derived from petroleum and from natural gas, our industry is intensively involved in sourcing and developing renewable liquid gas which is manufactured largely from biogenic materials.

In Europe, distributors collect some 17 million tonnes of LPG per year from wholesale terminals where LPG is stored in spheres and bullets, large tanks that hold up to 5,000 tonnes each. This is then transported by barge, rail and/or tanker truck to intermediate terminals, from which it is sold to consumers either in bulk (tanks) or in cylinders. European consumers comprise 9 million households and 1 million businesses that use LPG for heating/cooking plus another 8 million households that fuel their automobiles with LPG (Autogas).

The industry’s main pieces of equipment are containers for the storage and transport of LPG: stationary tanks, transportable cylinders and trucks. LPG is a liquid gas: liquid in transport/storage and gaseous in use. To operate safely and efficiently, all of its containers must be hermetically sealed, i.e. ‘gas tight’ to prevent gas/liquid from leaking out or air from leaking in.

In 2021 demand for LPG in the sectors our industry serves (heating, transport, cooking, industrial usage and others) was more than 21 million tonnes, which at 14 kWh per kg is equal to 294 TWh of energy (less than half the total primary energy consumed by Belgium in 2022 at 680 TWh). A restriction on PFAS would affect (directly or indirectly) c.a. 400 companies in the European Union, by extension of the membership of Liquid Gas Europe.

Safety is our number one concern:

In the Economic Commission for Europe, Inland Transport Committee, ADR, LPG is classified as a Class 2 dangerous good. LPG is a flammable gas which is liquid at low pressure and ambient temperature, and a gas at atmospheric pressure and ambient temperature. Because LPG is a flammable gas, it’s safe storage, transportation and use is paramount. Avoiding leaks (liquid or gas) is the preeminent concern of the industry. It is stored in bulk tanks at distributor premises and transported using road tankers, to end-user bulk tanks. LPG is also distributed in reusable, transportable gas cylinders, which are generally available at retail premises. There are millions of end-user bulk tanks in Europe (approximately 11 million) and many more transportable gas cylinders (approximately 250 million), in use in Europe every day.

The main barriers of LPG containers are its wall, floor, roof/lid or valve, usually made of steel or brass. For valves to be gas tight typically requires seals including gaskets and o-rings. Mostly these are made of Nitrile Butadiene Rubber (NBR). However, one type of seal – for threaded pipe – often uses fluoropolymer, usually PTFE (Teflon) in the form of a tape. This tape is wound around the ‘male’ connection, which is then screwed into the ‘female’ connection.

The tape is malleable and so spreads into the crevices between the two joints to completely block the flow of liquid or gas. PTFE is also chemically inert (it does not react or corrode), withstands high or low temperatures and pressures, resists flame or spark ignition, causes very low friction (so as not to glue the joint), and is resistant to penetration of air, water and LPG or other hydrocarbons. All of these add to the increased safety that these tapes provide the end consumers.

A key benefit of tape is its ease-of-use. This is a main reason that ‘thread tape’, as it is commonly called, is widely used in sealing joints of pipes that carry not just LPG, but natural gas, water and various other gases, liquids and mixtures thereof. PTFE tape is  widely available and relatively inexpensive.

Taped joints are very, very common. According to a study sponsored by the European Commission , in the natural gas distribution network of the Netherlands alone, there are 15 million taped, threaded joints. In Europe there could easily be more than 1 billion (1,000 million) such joints. LPG distribution accounts for a small fraction of that total.

However, the use varies between Member States, and even within Member States. As an example of PTFE use there are around 11 million LPG cylinders in circulation in Poland. We estimate  that around 500 thousand cylinders have their valves refitted or replaced every year and PTFE thread tape (and in some cases PTFE liquid sealant) is generally used to provide a reliable seal. Given these numbers, if these valves were to be replaced using PFAS-free materials, it would take the Polish market alone around 22 years to completely phase-out this use of PFAS material.

In France, the estimated number of cylinders in circulation is 68 million with 800 thousand bulk tanks. The number of cylinders used in Italy is over 26 million with about 1,5 million bulk tanks.

PFAS are also present in many components of the LPG fuelling systems in  LPG cars; LPG is the most popular and used alternative fuel in Europe, according to EC data for 2022, there were more than 8 million vehicles operational and, in 2022, over 119.000 new LPG cars were registered in Italy.

Fluoropolymers to maximise safety:

PFAS resistance to atmospheric deterioration or degradation in use have thus made them an obvious choice as a reliable seal.

PTFE thread tape and PTFE paste is widely used both in transportable gas cylinder assemblies (on the tapered threads between the cylinder valve and the cylinder body), road tankers and in bulk tank installations. PTFE has proven itself as one of the most successful and widely used sealants for LPG equipment and joints. This is essential to secure the safety of the industry which uses highly flammable liquid gas. PTFE content is also incorporated into some of the gaskets we use, in larger installations, and we also make use of FKM and FFKM in more demanding applications.

Whilst non-PFAS alternatives are being trialled by some of our members, with some limited success, caution is being exercised to ensure that safety is not compromised. In some instances, anaerobic adhesives, graphite gaskets, or the less common fluoride-free polymers are being explored. However, the safety and efficacy of these is uncertain and their viability is being explored.

Valves, regulators and other subassemblies used in conjunction with transportable cylinders and bulk tanks may also make use of fluoropolymers (including FFKM, FKM, FPM, PVDF, etc.).

In downstream LPG vapour-phase devices, and cars using LPG as a fuel source, FKM is used. This raises the potential need to replace every boiler, regulator or plumbing system. Nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR) is being explored as an alternative, though likely at a high cost.

Fluoropolymers for renewable fuels:

Several of our members are involved in the development of renewable liquid gases to reduce GHG emissions, and one, renewable and recycled carbon dimethyl ether (DME) (which is a promising substitute for 100% fossil-based LPG), requires FFKM or PTFE-based, gaskets and seals. FFKM is used due to its performance on fluids with high solvent properties and chemical resistance.

For pure-DME of high-ratio DME to LPG blends, precluding the use of FFKM and PTFE as materials for sealing applications would effectively eliminate any potential opportunity there is for DME, which can be produced with high efficiency and burns exceptionally cleanly, and it’s benefits in decarbonisation.

Volumes, alternatives, replacement timing and costs of PTFE tape in LPG:

Due to the replacement and inspection of transportable cylinders and bulk tanks the industry uses approximately 15-20 tonnes of fluoropolymers (predominantly PTFE tape and PTFE paste) per year.

There are alternatives to fluoropolymer tape in threaded-joint sealing. There are some tapes made of materials other than fluorocarbons. There also are pastes that can be applied to joints. Some pastes contain fluorocarbons, and some do not – instead using mixtures of alcohols and glycols. Non-fluorocarbon pastes appear to be equally as effective at sealing as fluorocarbon tape; however, this should be confirmed/refuted in future research, because it is critical to ensuring safety.

It is unclear if non-fluorocarbon tapes are equal in performance to fluorocarbon ones. In principle, though, this should be possible.

Based on an initial investigation, it appears that while the sealing performance of non-fluorocarbon pastes and fluorocarbon tapes are similar, the tapes are clearly easier to use. This means that installers are more likely to be apply tapes properly than they are to apply pastes properly. It might also portend a difference in labour costs; i.e. it might take more time to use paste than tape. Non-fluorocarbon tapes, on the other hand, appear at present to be significantly more expensive than fluorocarbon ones. In short, the LPG industry probably can adapt to a phase-out of fluorocarbon tapes, but this should be considered carefully and studied properly.

Which use sector?:

Whilst the Energy use sector, on the surface, might appear to be the most appropriate fit for our industry and the use category of oil and gas application, the sub-uses are less closely matched. Petroleum and Mining, and in particular petroleum exploration and production uses and properties appear to have similarities but again the fit, as described in the restriction proposal, is not well matched.

However, due to the reasons regarding safety outlined above, it would be crucial for derogations or exemptions to be applied for the Liquid Gas sector, as the current use of PFAS materials are keeping consumers safe and the development and trialling of safe alternatives will take a significant time to complete.

Conclusions:

Whilst LPG use represents a relatively small proportion of overall European, primary energy consumption, it meets the specific needs of those who require the provision of a safe, affordable, off-grid energy supply. Fluoropolymers, and in particular PTFE, have enabled the industry to meet these needs and particularly the need for safety, in storage, transportation and use.

The Energy sector would appear to be the most appropriate sector for the broad categorisation of our industry and specifically the sub-sector of Liquid Gases with uses that include the production, storage, transportation, and use of Liquid Gases, using components constructed from materials that maximise safety.

There are areas where the industry can adapt and replace the use of PTFE with alternatives that do not contain PFAS, but this transition needs to be cautious to avoid any degradation in safety. There are other areas where the industry will find it very difficult to find suitable alternatives and this is particularly the case in the development of alternative renewable and recycled carbon, liquid gas fuels.

General Comments: Background/proposal for the restriction of PFAS:
As part of the EU sustainability strategy for chemicals, the Commission 2020 is presenting a comprehensive package of measures to regulate the substance class of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). The declared aim is to restrict the use of PFASs and the marketing of products containing PFASs in the EU as far as possible.
The European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) published a dossier on the comprehensive restriction of perfluorinated and polyfluorinated alkyl substances (PFAS) on March 22, 2023 and launched the public consultation (restriction dossier ECHA). The restriction aims to restrict or ban the production, placing on the market and use of all PFASs on their own or in mixtures and articles.
PFAS are all substances containing at least one fully fluorinated -CF2 - or -CF3 - group (without any H/Cl/Br/I atom attached to it). The scope of the restriction proposal covers more than 10,000 substances. The main uses are textiles (rain jackets, special protective equipment, e.g. fire suits), in food contact (e.g. pizza boxes, Teflon pans), in fire-fighting foams but also in e.g. lubricants. All PFAS are either persistent themselves ("eternal chemicals") or are degraded to persistent PFAS (e.g. PFCAs, TFA, etc.). PFASs remain in the environment for decades and can affect humans and the environment or cause adverse effects. Under the CLP regulation only single PFAS substances are classified in a harmonized way (e.g. PFOS), under the REACH regulation there is a candidate list with 10 PFAS entries.
For some weeks now, the restriction proposal on PFAS has received a lot of public attention. There is currently no legal obligation to notify or provide information. Internally, we have intensified our efforts on the subject of PFAS in the company processes (e.g. development, purchasing, production) and are currently determining how we are affected in any processing procedures or how PFAS in our products are affected (e.g. through corresponding PFAS coatings).
We therefore ask for your understanding that, within the framework of our legal compliance principle, i.e. compliance with the relevant environmental regulations, we are currently also complying with the associated, relevant regulations (e.g. ChemG, REACH-VO), but no separate information is available on PFAS substances. As soon as we have identified relevant information, we will communicate this accordingly.
We hope that the above information gives you a satisfactory impression of our efforts to include PFASs in our business.
If you have any further information on the subject of substance policy, please do not hesitate to contact us.

General Comments: Banning PFAS is not just a matter of protecting our health; it is a crucial step towards preserving the integrity of our environment. By eliminating these hazardous chemicals from our daily lives, we safeguard our well-being, ensure a healthier future for generations to come, and foster a sustainable world. Let us join forces, advocate for change, and work towards a PFAS-free future—a future where our environment thrives, and our well-being is prioritized.

While the ban on PFAS might seem like a daunting task, it is essential to recognize that safer alternatives exist. Investing in research and development of non-toxic substitutes can provide sustainable solutions that do not compromise our health or the environment. By promoting innovation and supporting the adoption of PFAS-free alternatives, we can drive positive change and create a future free from the hazards associated with these chemicals.

Extensive research has linked PFAS exposure to a range of severe health problems. These substances have been associated with increased risks of cancer, liver damage, hormone disruption, immune system dysfunction, and developmental issues in children. The persistence of PFAS in the environment, combined with their bioaccumulation in the food chain, exacerbates the potential harm they can cause.

General Comments: Based on all the data available, including recent positions expressed by different experts on the topic, it appears evident that PVDF and other fluoropolymers should not be grouped with other PFAS for risk assessment or regulatory purposes. If fluoropolymers are to be included in the upcoming PFAS restriction under the REACH Regulation, the most reasonable and proportionate decision would be to include a broad or time unlimited derogation to ensure continued use of these highly valuable materials . 2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: FLUOROSURFACTANT-FREE MANUFACTURING It should be noted, that the used PVDF is manufactured without using PFAS-of-concern. This is confirmed by our raw material supplier (documentation in our follow-up submission). So, the argument of environmental emissions related to manufacturing aids does not apply here!  Emissions are clearly identified in a recent Life Cycle Analysis of our IPC® membrane module.  The membrane module fabrication allows two emission possibilities for fluoropolymers: 1.  Scrap during membrane production or casting solution preparation 2. Process wastewater – the emitted process water is discharged into the sewerage. 3. Membrane drying – membranes are dried in an oven. From the oven there is exhaust air into the environment. Scrap Scrap is only produced as a byproduct waste stream when cutting the edges of the membrane sheet in the right dimensions.  This scrap is <5% of the overall raw material use.  This is incinerated and contains no low MW PFAS components only high MW fluoropolymer Sales [Sales 2022]. There is no scrap in other production processes by design of the lean production process. Membrane drying Membranes are prepared by the phase inversion process where the membranes are immersed in water. Before drying, the membranes are conditioned to avoid pore collapse during the drying process with glycerine. Membranes are dried in an mild warm chamber with warm air.  The water is condensed and is part of the wastewater, the heat is recovered to the maximum to save energy and some water vapor will leave as air emission. As the polymer is not water soluble and no fluoropolymer is detected in these streams. Process wastewater Water samples of process water is discharged into the sewer within the granted volume and restrictions. 6. Missing uses: Membranes generally comprise of a thin surface layer giving the required perm-selectivity on top of a more open, thicker support that provides mechanical stability.  The membranes must be mechanically strong and will normally have some resistance to thermal or chemical attack.  This means resistance to extremes in temperature, pH and/or oxidant concentrations is required [S. Judd].  The only technical and commercial relevant “lower quality” alternative to PVDF-based membranes in water treatment are PES-based membranes. However the large market of wastewater treatment and impaired water treatment membranes are outside-in module configurations.  In this type of installation PVDF type membrane are used because the mechanical properties enable the high mechanical stresses on the PVDF membrane during operation [Wilf et al., 2010].  Furthermore, these application demand frequent chemical cleanings (NaOCl) and PVDF has a significantly larger Cl tolerance [Li et al., 2021 ] than PES . On top of that, both materials differ in fouling tendency and membrane morphology.    In these applications of wastewater treatment (MBR technology), water reuse and filtration of impaired waters, PVDF clearly outperforms PES.  In clean water filtration or RO pretreatment applications PES is advantageous as the feedwater is much cleaner (less need for chemical cleaning) and there is minimal mechanical stress during operation as these are operated inside-out [Li at al., 2008; Lesjean et al., 2004]. This is summarized in the Table 1 below which is published in WEF Manual of Practice No 36.  [extracted from Wilf et al. 2010].  MEMBRANE FOULING  PVDF membranes exhibit a lower fouling potential than PES membranes.  PES contains a negative charge and as such is the membrane surfaces prone to fouling, especially in difficult to treat water feed streams like wastewater, effluent water and impaired surface waters. In e.g. MBR, the fouling components consists of a very broad mixture of various substances with various charges [Lorhemen 2016]. Aging of the membranes result in higher tendency of membrane fouling and this is why membranes need to be cleaned chemically (extreme pH and/or oxidizing chemicals) and have to be exchanged when a certain level of irreversible fouling is reached.  The fouling potential is a key aspect in the operational end economical evaluation of membranes is wastewater treatment and water reuse and PVDF gives a lower fouling potential.  CHEMICAL RESISTANCE Hypochlorite stability (cleaning agent / oxidizing chemicals) is of great importance because this  ensures long lifetimes of the applied membrane modules and optimized economics and sustainability. Furthermore, these membranes are used in the open environment and as such an excellent weatherability and resistance to UV degradation is needed. On these three aspects; chemical stability, weatherability and UCV resistance, PVDF excels as a membrane forming polymer versus PES or PSU/  PVDF raw material supplier [Arkema website] highlights the chemical resistance clearly in Figure 3. Here, the impact of exposure to extreme pH and NaOCl on the mechanical properties of the polymers show that PVDF clearly outperforms PES, which is the main “other” polymer used for membranes in these applications.   Li et al. investigated the effects of hypochlorite aging various membrane properties of PVDF and PES membranes at different pH [Li 2021]. This is very relevant to do it on the membrane products because of the high contact surface area of these porous materials.  During their use, all membranes in water and wastewater applications are often cleaned oxidatively.  For the PVDF membrane, NaClO aging at pH 3–11 caused a moderate increase in permeability and decreased retention due to the oxidation and release of a membrane additive (non-PFAS related).  For the PES membrane, NaClO aging at all pH values, resulted in chain scission of PES molecules, leading to deterioration of the membrane structure (very high permeability with very low retention).   FLEXIBILITY AND MECHANICAL STABILITY OF MEMBRANE LAYER Due to the operation of the flat sheet membranes in the membrane modules, elongation of the membrane enveloppe will take place and the membrane layer is subjected to mechanical stress. Arkema investigated and published the effect of various chemicals on the mechanical behavior of PVDF, PES and PSU [Arkema 2023]. PVDF showed the best mechanical properties in comparison to the others (Figure 5). This means PVDF will stay flexible after contact with chemicals or cleaning agents, resulting in less defects during operation. PVDF showed longer lifetime in halogenated environments.   MEMBRANE PERFORMANCE There are many studies where PES and PVDF are compared related to membrane performance. In many cases, pore sizes are not comparable or different membrane additives (determining the hydrophilicity of the membrane) are used, all resulting in apple- pear comparisons. Acarer et al. [Acarer 2021] studied to manufacturing and characterization of polymeric membranes and did a fair comparison between PVDF and PES (same amount of additive and comparable pore size. It was shown that permeability of PVDF membranes is approximately 2.5 times higher than PES membranes   It is often dependent on many factors why a certain polymer membrane is chosen for a certain application. In some sectors/applications PVDF clearly outperforms PES, e.g. water treatment by MBR technology, in other sectors/applications PES is advantageous. The wastewater treatment membrane market is by far the largest market worldwide. (see above) Major reasons is that the MBR technology enables to achieve the stringent wastewater discharge limits and potential for water reuse.  references and figures are in the non-confidential added document

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Fluoropolymers are part of the PFAS group by OECD definition. For this reason, we understand that fluoropolymers are included in the scope of the restriction proposal that is being developed in the European Economic Area. However, because of their different chemical structure and properties, they need to be considered as a separate family within the broad PFAS group, clearly distinct not only from the non-polymeric PFAS, but also from the other polymeric PFAS. These differences are relevant not only in terms of grouping but more importantly also in relation to the risk for human health and the environment that will be derived from their manufacture and use. The main differences between fluoropolymers and the other members of the large PFAS group of chemicals are based on the following 4 aspects:  • Structural differences • Safety and environmental considerations, • Limited expected potential to degrade into small PFAS molecules during use and/or disposal • Unique combination of properties. This makes fluoropolymers extremely valuable and irreplaceable in extremely demanding uses in a wide variety of industrial sectors. Furthermore In line with the communication of our raw material PVFD supplier, we are stating the following in relation to the public concerns related to PFAS emissions: • The PVDF polymer that BF uses for the production of  IPC membranes is in a category far removed from the Fluorosurfactants (PFOA, PFAS) that originally triggered PFAS concerns. • The PVDF polymer is manufactured by our supplier without the use of Fluorosurfactants as production agents.  The surfactant that is used, is non-fluorinated and non-persistent.  • The PVDF is a polymer of low concern according to the OECD definition.  A peer-reviewed article has been published in 2022 with scientific proof points . • The PVDF polymer is not bioavailable and not mobile. Even if its structure includes Fluoride, its toxicity and ecotoxicity profile is different from small chain PFAS. • The Blue Foot product made out of PVDF polymer will, at end of life, be managed responsibly.  PVDF has proven to be a safe and successful membrane material that is very stable, inert, and highly resistant to breakdown.  PVDF is made with a very high degree of purity.  This enables PVDF products to satisfy stringent leachable limits and other national health regulations, ensuring that they are safe for use in drinking water treatment .         Blue Foot Membranes position on the matter  Based on all the data available, including recent positions expressed by different experts on the topic, it appears evident that PVDF and other fluoropolymers should not be grouped with other PFAS for risk assessment or regulatory purposes. If fluoropolymers are to be included in the upcoming PFAS restriction under the REACH Regulation, the most reasonable and proportionate decision would be to include a broad or time unlimited derogation to ensure continued use of these highly valuable materials . For that reason, Blue Foot Membranes states clearly that it is  necessary to add a time unlimited derogation on PFAS used in industrial settings to avoid banning the use of critical PFAS-containing pieces of equipment in industrial plants. The un-intended consequences by Banning PVDF without consideration of the important concerns from the membrane industry will have far reaching environmental impacts that turn back the clock to achieve water reuse targets and sustainability goals related to access to water for all. We are not against a restriction/limitation of hazardous PFAS-of-concern, and we support a scientific approach differentiating high and low risk substances based on risk assessment. In that way, it should be concluded that fluoropolymers should not be treated in a similar way as other PFAS substances and should be taken out the ECHA restriction dossier.  Polyvinylidene difluoride polymers SHOULD BE EXEMPTED FROM ANY REGULATORY ACTION UNDER THE REACH RESTRICTION

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Based on published scientific documents, such as EFCTC September 2021 , https://www.fluorocarbons.org/news/published-evidence-supports-very-low-yields-of-tfa-from-most-hfos-and-hcfos/ , the OECD Expert Group on PFAS opinion released in 2021 "Reconciling Terminology of the Universe of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances: Recommendations and Practical Guidance, OECD Series on Risk Management, No. 61, 2021", the opinion of the majority of experts in the UNEP Environmental Effects Assessment Panel released in 2022, we call for the fluorinated gases that are used in the industry of polyurethane / polyisocyanurate (PU) foams to be completely and fully exempted from the scope of the restriction proposal.
Differently from what the submitters dossier states, those substances are not classified as (very) persistent under REACH, they have atmospheric lifetime of days or months and, more importantly, they do not decompose in the environment into trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) in a meaningful fraction. Information on hazards, exposure and risk assessments submitted by the manufacturers of these substances should be carefully read by the ECHA experts.
The objective of establishing a very broad definition of PFAS, thereby covering thousands of substances with different (eco-) toxicity profiles, is not aligned with the science and with ECHA's own guidelines on Read Across policy.
In addition, the mentioned OECD Expert Group on PFAS position paper published in 2021, states:"As PFASs are a chemical class with diverse molecular structures and physical, chemical and biological properties, it is highly recommended that such diversity be properly recognized and communicated in a clear, specific and descriptive manner. The term "PFAS" is a broad, general, non-specific term, which does not inform whether a compound is harmful or not, but only communicates that the compounds under this term share the same trait for having a fully fluorinated methyl- or methylene- carbon moiety".
European risk management measures for products containing HFO/HCFO are in place and get continuously strengthened to achieve a European circular economy. In many countries, measures targeting the recovery and treatment of construction products when they reach their end of life (which for insulation products might be in 50 years from now) are discussed at the time of writing. Furthermore, several industry activities at national level aim to put in place take-back schemes for construction waste at first.

Other jurisdictions in the world such as the UK Health and Safety Executive and the US Environmental Protection Agency do not target HFO/HCFO in their efforts to regulate PFAS, and they rather focus on certain groups of substances in certain applications.

We hope that the above comments, that are in tune with the position of the entire industry of PU polymers in Europe through our European PU Industry Association PU Europe, will be taken into consideration, and would like to recall to recall the support of PU foams manufacturers to the EU long-term carbon neutrality goal. Our products are critical in curbing energy consumption and hence carbon dioxide emissions during the life of buildings, here including commercial, industrial, and public dwellings.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Information on alternatives Information on benefits Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Based on the presence of PFAS, the product and component portfolio for low voltage energy distribution can be divided into the following four groups.

1) Products or components where one or more PFAS has been intentionally specified by the equipment manufacturer (i.e., ABB) by design, as a material or as an ingredient of a material mixture, for a specifically defined function.

Examples include (but are not necessarily limited to):

a. Protection devices such as circuit breakers (miniature circuit breakers, residual current circuit breakers, arc fault detection devices, relays, switches, etc., and accessories thereof), whose internal mechanisms are mostly constituted by polymeric parts (e.g., polyamide, PA) where PTFE is added to the compound mixture as a lubricant. These products are produced in volumes of the order of 100 million items per annum.
b. Protection devices, distribution enclosures and energy efficiency devices comprising polymeric parts (e.g., polycarbonate, PC) where PTFE is added to the compound mixture as anti-dripping or flame-retardant agent, which is necessary to grant safety from fires.

2) Products or components where PFAS has not been explicitly specified by the equipment manufacturer (i.e., ABB) but might be contained as an ingredient of a material mixture, based on the definition of the material manufacturer to match the functional requirements specified by the equipment manufacturer.

Examples may include (but are not necessarily limited to):

a. Protection devices such a circuit breakers (miniature circuit breakers, residual current circuit breakers, arc fault detection devices, relays, switches, etc., and accessories thereof), whose internal mechanisms are mostly constituted by polymeric parts (e.g., polyamide, PA) where some PFAS can be added to the compound mixture as a lubricant.
b. Protection devices, distribution enclosures and energy efficiency devices comprising polymeric parts (e.g., polycarbonate, PC) where some PFAS is added to the compound mixture as anti-dripping or flame-retardant agent, which is necessary to grant safety from fires.

3) Components independently developed and supplied by 3rd party suppliers. In this case, PFAS have not been specified by the equipment manufacturer (i.e., ABB) but might be contained as ingredients of a material mixture or as materials, based on the definition of the product/component manufacturer (i.e., the supplier), or of the material manufacturer for the materials used in the component.

Examples may include (but are not necessarily limited to):

a. Capacitors.
b. Relays.
c. Printed circuit boards.
d. Displays, including liquid crystal displays.
e. Other electronic components.

4) Products or components where one or more PFAS is a contaminant from the production process. Due to the extremely low threshold level of 25 ppb, contamination is hard to control, especially if the manufacturing of parts or components are outside the EU, where no restriction on PFAS exists.

Examples may include (but are not necessarily limited to):

a. PFAS as a release agent used in an injection molding process to allow easy demolding.
b. Surface treatment using PFAS or PFAS-containing substances.
c. Electronic components such as semiconductors, micro-processors, etc.
d. Contamination of PFAS in the production machine.
e. Contamination of PFAS due to proximity to the production line of products with PFAS (that could be exempted from the PFAS ban).

For low-voltage energy distribution equipment:

ABB recommends defining a higher permitted threshold level, for example, 1000 ppm (or, alternatively, 0.1%wt) or 100 ppm (or, alternatively, 0.01%wt) for each distinct PFAS, so that intended use is only addressed, i.e., PFAS intentionally added in a mixture of material components.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: E.2.8 Applications of fluorinated gases / Fire suppressants E.2.11 Electronics and semiconductors / Sector as a whole E.2.13 Construction products / Processing aids and polymer processing aids E.2.14 Lubricants / Sector as a whole Other uses are possible but not known or to be investigated. Furthermore, the 25 ppb threshold includes contaminant PFAS that may enter into products during the production process or during the lifecycle in any unknown and unintentional way.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: In the EU, concerned products have to be disposed according to WEEE Directive 2012/19/EU. For batteries and accumulators, disposal is regulated by the Battery Regulation in the EU. National laws such as the German ElektroG and BattG supplement the European legal acts and ensure that electrical installation devices are not disposed of in residual waste. Similar provisions apply in the other EU countries.

5. Proposed derogations: At the moment, the definition of possible PFAS present in the products is still largely incomplete, because inquiries have to be cascaded down the supply chain. Consequently, it is difficult to provide an estimate of tonnage.   As for emissions, to our knowledge the PFAS concerned products are not expected to spontaneously release PFAS in the environment, unless PFAS is intentionally extracted by external agents, for instance by means of mechanical and/or chemical attacks (both not being supposed to happen in the product lifecycle, unless a misuse is concerned). Anyway, given the very low amount of PFAS in the case of contamination, also these theoretical possibilities are assumed to be practically unrealistic and immaterial.

6. Missing uses: Electrical equipment belongs to the energy sector, which is marked green in table A.1 of Annex A of the Annex XV restriction report, but this equipment is not listed sufficiently as a user of PFAS. It must be noticed that a large portion of electrical devices have protective functions, for humans and for equipment, in front of electrical faults as well as their indirect consequences, such as, e.g., fires or falling or drowning after electric shock. A second portion of electrical devices enable energy efficiency policies, either measuring electrical quantities or controlling electrical sources, storages and loads, e.g., connecting renewables to the grid when available, scheduling EV charging, and the like.  a) The annual tonnage is hard to report as in the very much distributed applications where PFAS has been identified up to now the quantities are not easy to get, as the majority of PFAS are additives in materials provided by the supply chain where the kind and quantity has not been specified, but only material properties which rely on PFAS.  b) In the very wide range it is also not possible to give a simple answer. In most cases, the PFAS is required to fulfil the requirement of long lifetime and low wear or similar material properties. In some specific applications where PFAS is intentionally used or added (e.g., PTFE for self-lubricating polymeric parts in mechanisms, and as anti-dripping and fire-retardant agents), the PFAS (PTFE) is mandatory for the technical function.  c) The problem is common to all competitors and relevant supply chains in the electrical compartment.  d) Most likely the majority of the applications can be shifted to alternatives, but the problems are on the identification, substitution, testing, qualifying and certification. This will require significant time and resources.  e) For most applications there was no search for substitutes up to now, as there was no need. The research is starting, but only a few conclusions are available now.   f) Electrical equipment is mandatory for safe and reliable energy supply. Reduction of performance or lifetime, increasing of maintenance, related outages and costs are not acceptable. Substitutes must be able to have the same performance. Product development times are long (years) and investment is high, also due to CapEx intensive automated assembly lines that are necessary for mass production of electrical goods within EU countries. Depending on the product and the complexity, it is of the order of million Euro per product type.  g) For electrical equipment, in addition to the losses of manufacturing companies if they can no longer produce the equipment, a much larger economic impact is associated with the electrical network. If it is not possible to serve the market, the energy supply is endangered, the transformation to green energy slowed down and the extension of the electrical networks is stopped, with negative impact on industry and society.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Considering the "Proposed restriction - Annex XVII entry PFASs (Restriction Option 2)", the potential derogation "5.[the semiconductor manufacturing process until 13.5 years after EiF]." is relevant for an increasingly larger portion of the product portfolio: It has been announced from the electronic and semiconductor industry that it is almost impossible to offer PFAS free solution in short- to mid-term (alternatives are not yet available). ABB is a customer of said electronic and semiconductor industry and the low voltage electric distribution products here concerned embed electronic components and semiconductor for human and equipment protection purposes, and for energy efficiency functions.

Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Considering the "Proposed restriction - Annex XVII entry PFASs (Restriction Option 2)", the potential derogation "5.[the semiconductor manufacturing process until 13.5 year after EiF]." is relevant for an increasingly larger portion of the product portfolio: It has been announced from the electronic and semiconductor industry that it is almost impossible to offer PFAS free solution in short- to mid-term (alternatives are not yet available). ABB is a customer of said electronic and semiconductor industry and the low voltage electric distribution products here concerned embed electronic components and semiconductors for human and equipment protection purposes, and for energy efficiency functions.

General Comments: Baseline/request for exemption
This restriction pertains to our textile finishing treatments to make our products water, oil, and hydrocarbon repellent. These treatments are an integral part of our business, which is the protection of individuals in their workplace (firefighters, police officers, military personnel, and industrial workers).
Due to the ban on PFOA, we had to adapt to maintain a high level of performance. This new restriction on PFAS poses a real danger to wearers who will no longer be able to protect themselves from the risks they face (e.g., gasoline splashes during a car fire extinguishing operation on the wearer; if the protection is insufficient, the firefighter is exposed to severe burns or even death).

Information on alternatives
To date, a few chemical alternatives exist in CO, but they do not meet current specifications.

Transitional period
Regarding Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), my transitional period is quite long (+10 years) and could allow chemical industries to find solutions to meet our markets. However, it is important to review this restriction in case no reliable alternative is proposed.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) : firefighters, police officers, military personnel and industrial workers

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: We do not have a precise study on this subject. However, it should be noted that an obsolete Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), with a loss of performance during use, is replenished by its user. This means that the PPE is produced again and is less durable.  The use of PFAS increases the durability and performance of a product. The longer a product lasts, the fewer PPE items will be produced within a given period.  For example, PFOA allowed a garment to be washed up to 50 times without affecting the material's performance. Current PFAS have seen material performance reduced by half, allowing for up to 25 washes. This means that, within the same period, PFAS-treated garments need to be produced twice as often.  To date, alternative PFAS technologies do not achieve the same durability performance, approximately 1 to 5 washing cycles, which is 25 times less efficient. This results in 25 times more virgin products being produced and 25 times more factories in operation to meet the protection needs of workers.

5. Proposed derogations: To recap the information listed above, the use of PFAS is the last viable solution to protect high-risk workers such as firefighters, military personnel, police officers, and industrial workers. Their health and lives depend on it, and it is dangerous to propose this restriction without a viable alternative for their safety (high level of protection) and for the environment (compromising the durability of PPE)

8. Other identified uses: To support the point regarding PTFE, some high-performance Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) requires good breathability of materials. PTFE membrane is the most high-performing solution available on the market. Its alternatives do not meet the required specifications and pose a risk to high-risk wearers.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Basic assessment of the German Heat Pump Association (Bundeverband Wärmepumpe e.V.) on restriction procedures and regulatory proposals:

Almost all synthetic refrigerants used in heat pumps belong to the PFAS group. The most common refrigerants are fluorine-containing compounds, which are not only PFAS but also subject to the restrictions of the F-Gas Regulation of the European Union (517/2014). BWP supports the progressive market introduction of natural refrigerants (e.g. propane, CO2, ammonia) instead of fluorinated ones in all applications where this is possible and economically viable.

Chemicals that fall within the scope of the present restriction procedure as PFASs are also used in many ways in heat pumps, as in most household and electrical appliances. They are used, among other things, in seals and foams and as lubricants. PFASs are therefore currently irreplaceable for the functionality of heat pumps. In this respect, heat pumps are no different from other energy transition and climate protection technologies such as electric vehicles, wind turbines and electrolysers. This also means that the replacement of synthetic refrigerants by natural refrigerants alone does not lead to a "PFAS-free" product.

It should first be noted that health risks to heat pump operators from the PFAS used in the refrigerant are excluded. In normal operation, the refrigerant is in a closed circuit and does not come into contact with the outside world. Even in the event of a leakage and complete release of the synthetic refrigerant, the conversion of certain F-gases into trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) only takes place with a time delay and after dispersion in the atmosphere. Heat pumps are therefore a safe product regardless of the refrigerant used.

Therefore, both the restriction of PFAS and the F-gas regulation from Regulation 517/2014 are about defining a time path in line with the principle of proportionality, in which heat pumps switch to the use of natural refrigerants in all areas of application where this is technically possible and justifiable in the socio-economic balance.

The importance of heat pumps in combating climate change must be taken into account. This climate protection technology is at the beginning of a massive market growth. Across Europe, 30 million heat pumps are to be installed by 2030. From 1.5 million units at present, the field inventory of installed heat pumps in Germany is expected to rise to 6 million by 2030, and to 14-16 million units by 2045.

In most cases, heat pumps replace heating systems powered by natural gas or fuel oil. The switch to natural refrigerants must not prevent or inhibit this transition in building heating. In applications where natural refrigerants cannot be used or cannot be used economically, the use of heat pumps must not be prevented by the restriction procedure.

The heat pump industry is working to ensure that appliances using a natural refrigerant capture as large a share of the market growth as possible. Politically, this is supported by the F-Gas Regulation as well as funding incentives (refrigerant bonus in the Federal Promotion of Efficient Buildings (BEG)).


BWP demands for the restriction procedure:

1.) Maintenance and service of existing plants must be guaranteed for an unlimited period.

The decision on PFAS restrictions should not sent out signals that undermine climate protection. Instead, it must be made clear that anyone who decides to buy a heat pump with fluorinated refrigerant (PFAS) is buying a safe product and making a significant contribution to climate protection. Under no circumstances should they be placed in a worse position than someone who hesitates now or even has a fossil-fuelled heating system installed and only decides to buy a heat pump in ten years' time or later. This would be particularly the case if he could not rely on the maintenance and repair of the device being guaranteed over its entire operating life.

Heat pumps are designed for the chemical and thermodynamic properties of a specific refrigerant. Therefore, fluorinated and natural refrigerants are not interchangeable. If a specific refrigerant for a running unit cannot be refilled after a leakage, the unit would have to be dismantled and replaced by a new unit.

Seals, foams, lubricants and other components may also not be able to be replaced by PFAS-free alternatives during subsequent repair. For them, too, indefinite allowance for maintenance and replacement of parts is essential.

Moreover, there is an important connection between the refrigerant used and other components containing PFAS, which particularly affects the compressor. For example, propane operates at higher temperatures, which affects the lubricants that can be used. CO2 is used at a higher system pressure, which in turn places demands on e.g. sealings. These interactions must be taken into account when refrigerants or other components are expected to change to alternatives.

A heat pump has an average operating life of 20 years. Therefore, the 13.5-year transition period is too short. In case of doubt, it would lead to systems having to be taken out of operation prematurely if refrigerants or other components were not allowed to be replaced.

In view of serious interventions in the operation and repairability of a budgetary investment associated with high expenditure, the requirements for the use of PFAS-containing refrigerants in repair and maintenance are about the acceptance of heat pump technology and heat pump ramp-up as part of the fight against climate change.

Last but not least, the proposal to only allow the use of PFAS-containing refrigerants for repair and maintenance for a limited period of time also contradicts the European Union's recycling policy. As recently as March 2023, the European Commission presented a proposal to establish a "right to repair" for consumers.

Maintenance and repair with synthetic refrigerants and other components containing PFAS should remain possible indefinitely. At the very least, however, reprocessed refrigerants must be approved for recycling in existing systems.


2.) Double regulation and contradictions with the F-Gas Regulation must be ruled out.

Industry, trade and consumers need planning certainty regarding the rules that will apply in the future for the marketing and installation of heat pumps with refrigerants containing fluorine.

With the F-Gas Regulation 517/2014, a regulatory instrument already exists whose scope of application includes all refrigerants containing PFAS. The F-Gas Regulation, which is currently being amended, ensures a phase-down as well as concrete bans in the marketing and use of synthetic refrigerants.
Even though this instrument is primarily directed at the climate impact of F-gases when they are released, it de facto ensures a market transition from fluorine-containing to natural refrigerants. The regulation is currently being amended. Just like the REACH restriction procedure, the F-Gas Regulation weighs up the need to switch to natural refrigerants as quickly as possible against the need to minimise the impact on the market ramp-up of heat pumps as part of the climate targets.

In the balancing process, the amendment to the F-Gas Regulation makes distinctions according to the proposals of the Commission, the European Parliament and the Council position:
- according to monobloc and split variants
- according to output sizes

References to national safety requirements also allow for complete exemptions from the bans.

The present Restriction Opinion proposes a blanket ban on the use of PFAS-containing refrigerants and only provides for exemptions to comply with national safety regulations and building standards.

The PFAS application ban thus threatens to undermine the careful considerations of the F-Gas Regulation, according to which certain synthetic refrigerants (differentiated by their GWP value) are to be permitted for longer or even indefinitely in certain applications (split, capacity sizes).

In order to ensure planning security for industry, trade and consumers, it is essential to rule out the possibility that the restriction procedure and the F-Gas Regulation lead to contradictory rules that are not coordinated with each other. Unlike the restriction procedure, the F-Gas Regulation is subject to the EU's ordinary legislative procedure with the participation of Parliament and Council. The considerations made there should not be overruled by the results of a restriction procedure that is only subject to comitology. This would significantly damage the legitimacy and acceptance of the associated serious interventions in the market.

The scope of the F-Gas Regulation should be excluded from the scope of the restriction procedure.
Alternatively, at least the entry into force of the restrictions on the placing on the market of heat pumps with refrigerants containing PFAS (EiF) must be aligned with the latest date foreseen for bans in the F-Gases Regulation after the amendment.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The refrigerant in a heat pump is in a hermetically closed circuit and is not used up during operation. Leakage values, according to VDKF statistics, are between 1 and 2% per year, which also includes the possible complete loss of refrigerant due to damage or external damage. In practice, the proper operation of heat pumps is well below this value, as the functionality of the systems relies on a hermetically sealed refrigeration circuit and each individual heat pump therefore also undergoes strict quality controls.  In comparison, automotive air conditioners, for example, have a higher tolerance for annual refrigerant loss. Here, a system is often considered tight if it has less than 10% annual refrigerant loss.  It is important to note that both the installation and dismantling of heat pumps and air conditioners must only be carried out by certified contractors who are specially trained to ensure that no refrigerant is released into the atmosphere.  Recycling of refrigerants of heat pumps is handled by specially trained installers, who at the end of a heat pump appliance's life cleanly transfer refrigerants from the refrigeration circuit into tightly sealed containers, and the refrigerant dealers, who safely either destroy or recycle it to the quality of virgin gas.

8. Other identified uses: (Please, also take into consideration our answers to Section III)  Aplicability of alternative refrigerants in outdoor and indoor use:   In terms of the German heat pump market, about 70 percent of all heat pumps are installed outdoors. In this sector, the industry is already in a transition phase from currently mostly synthetic to in future mostly natural refrigerants (mainly R 290 propane). The main obstacle to this transition is the industry's access to sufficient quantities of propane-fuelled compressors to match the dynamic market growth (supply chain problem). However, there are numerous special cases in outdoor applications, e.g. when installed next to a drainage gully or basement window, in which the use of a propane heat pump is technically or economically not feasible according to the current status.  For indoor installation of monobloc heat pumps and brine-to-water heat pumps for the use of geothermal heat, as well as for all types of air- and water-operated split heat pumps, the use of natural refrigerants is still in its infancy. Even large heat pumps with very large fill volumes (multi-family houses, industry, heat grids) have so far been used mostly with synthetic refrigerants. In the case of water-operated heat pumps alone, these segments account for around 30% of heat pump sales. Suppliers of these products are working on appropriate solutions, so that in many (but not all) cases the switch to alternatives is primarily a question of the time path and the economic efficiency compared to (mostly fossil-fuelled) heat generators. However, a broad availability of corresponding heat pumps is not to be expected in these segments until the assumed end of the restriction ban (2026/27).   Experience with the conversion of split heat pumps to the refrigerant R 32 suggests a development time of six to ten years, depending on the product segment and manufacturer capacities. In some cases, an economically viable conversion to natural refrigerants is still a very long way off, e.g. in complex heat pump ventilation systems (Variable Refrigerant Flow) for residential and non-residential buildings.   A ban on heat pumps containing PFAS must take into account the differentiation between product segments and must not lead to a general ban on the use of heat pumps in those areas where alternatives are not (economically) available on the market.  Safety derogations:  In principle, it is correct that the possibility should remain to use heat pumps with PFAS-containing refrigerants if safety regulations do not allow the use of alternatives. However, it should be noted that the corresponding regulations and their enforcement vary in the Member States. This can lead to legal and planning uncertainty for industry, trade and consumers as well as to unequal competitive conditions. We are therefore critical of the legal feasibility of the exemption without a corresponding control mechanism.  German safety regulations and building standards do not exclude the use of heat pumps with natural refrigerants in indoor spaces from a certain room volume up to a filling quantity of 5 kg, but prescribe corresponding safety precautions for fire protection. Due to the basic permissibility, the exception criteria of the restriction proposal, according to which the use of PFAS-containing refrigerants should continue to be possible if safety regulations exclude the use of alternatives, would not apply.  So far, however, such fire safety requirements for indoor use of heat pumps with the refrigerant propane have often led to a lack of economic competitiveness compared to oil and gas boilers. The development of heat pumps that meet these requirements is thus a business risk as heat pumps have so far shown low demand elasticity. Even slight additional costs for the development and production of corresponding devices can lead to consumers deciding in favour of an alternative heating system. This is also closely linked to the system of heat pump subsidies in the BEG. Although this provides in principle for a 5% bonus for the use of natural refrigerants, the eligibility of additional costs ("eligible costs") will be significantly reduced as of 1 January 2024.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Baseline Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Basically, the present restriction proposal does not take into account the wide range of applications and uses of PFAS or PFAS-containing products in the chemical industry apart from manufacturing those. In case of a comprehensive and timely ban, there will be extensive, negative effects in this branch of industry.
The fluoropolymers are contained in very many applications with fundamentally important functions (sealing, hoses, sliding surfaces, in electronic devices, sensors) and are used as auxiliary materials (lubricants or as chemical and heat protection in personal protective equipment). Therefore, those must - at least for industry - be fundamentally excluded from a potential ban on use. Currently there are no adequate alternatives available for all different uses. These products are irreplaceable for the save and compliant operation of chemical plants.

Fluoropolymers are predominantly installed in the plants of the (chemical) industry in an abrasion-resistant manner. Thus, no emissions into the environment are to be expected within the framework of the disposal of the fluoropolymer-containing parts, which is strictly regulated by law.
Due to low volatility and low solubility, release to air or into wastewater is unlikely. If the national disposal routes specified for industry in the EU are followed, low-emission destruction or recycling is ensured. The stringent environmental regulations on industrial emissions (IED) and in European waste legislation (WFD) ensure that no significant release occurs from industry. The contribution to release and environmental impact from the industrial sector is therefore low.

The replacement of all e.g. PTFE or perfluoroether applications in the affected chemical plants (100%) within the proposed deadlines is neither technically nor financially feasible for the European industry due to the large number of applications. In addition, alternatives for all application areas cannot be developed, tested and approved in the short transition period envisaged (pharmaceuticals, food and feed production, emissions legislation). A general restriction or ban on fluoropolymers classified by the OECD as Polymer of Low Concern (PLC) is not comprehensible.
The focus of the restriction should be on volatile or mobile substances and non-essential or substitutable applications that have relevant emissions and a significant, negative impact on the environment, humans or animals. Irreplaceable industrial applications that make little measurable contribution to overall PFAS emissions would be massively hampered by a ban or restriction, with new risks related to plant safety due to less effective, less chemically resistant, and untested alternatives.
Ultimately, due to the immense investment costs to be expected, the competitiveness of the European chemical industry would be further reduced and the existing, very high safety and environmental protection level of European chemical plants would be endangered due to the lack of adequate alternatives for the diverse applications.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Unfortunately, the chemical industry has not been considered as a separate sector in the present restriction proposal, although the impact on this sector as well as on the pharmaceutical sector is devastating due to the large number of uses, especially with regard to fluoropolymers.  Affectedness of our company for the following applications of Table 9: - Most important application: "Fluoropolymer applications".  An unlimited exemption is needed for this area. A large number of specialized uses are possible only because of the specific material properties (inert, chemically resistant, durable, temperature and pressure stable as coatings for aggregates and piping, hoses and in personal protective equipment) and the approvals granted on this basis for seals, flanges, valves, use in electronic components, equipment, sensors (no 1:1 replacement is possible). In 95-100% of our chemical plants fluoropolymers are used and installed, either directly as coating material for pipelines and aggregates (e.g. in multi-purpose plants when using a wide variety of chemicals) or indirectly when using stainless steel pipelines, which can only be operated safely and in compliance with the law (TA-Luft) with PTFE gaskets and flanges, valves, ball valves (>95%). Furthermore, in 100% of our plants fluoropolymers are used in electronic components and measuring devices.   - The exemption proposed so far only for the production of PFAS active ingredients (animal, human, biocides, pesticides) is not sufficient, but must be extended to include the associated raw materials, intermediates and intermediate products, otherwise further production of the active ingredients by the chemical or pharmaceutical industry in the EU is not possible.  Further applications within our company: - TULAC (Annex E.2.2. incl. PPE): Use as personal protective equipment (production and firefighting), fluoropolymers should be exempted from the restriction in PPE indefinitely, as there is no such durable substitute in terms of chemical resistance and heat - Technical Textiles (Textiles for the use in filtration and separation media used in high performance air and liquid applications in industrial or professional settings that require a combination of water- and oil repellence):  Fluoropolymers are used as filter material in various industrial applications for product extraction, for (ultra) filtration of waste water and as membranes in manufacturing processes (e.g. membrane process hydrochloric acid): 5 years transitional period is too short for the numerous different applications and there should be an unlimited exception, as the risk of emissions is also low due to controlled waste disposal in the industrial sector. - Food contact materials (E.2.3) in industrial food and feed contact production:  Fluoropolymers used in plant components, piping (> 50% of piping and in seals, ball valves, valves and as special lubricants for high performance pumps and equipment with necessary product approvals for this sector) - Use of Paper & board packaging and Plastic packaging (only use, no production): Coated paperboard and plastic foils are used for product packaging. - Applications of fluorinated gases (Annex E.2.8.), Refrigeration below -50°C: In air conditioning and heat pumps (in use in installed equipment, replacements must be tested in detail for each application and has to be provided by manufacturers)  - Insulating gas in electrical equipment (Insulating gases in high-voltage switchgear above 145 kV): Modern electrical distribution stations contain fluorinated gases. - Fire suppressants (largely already replaced as fire extinguishing agents, but indirectly as additives in installed equipment still in use and necessary) - Cleaning and heat transfer, engineered fluids: The use of fluorinated heat transfer fluids in heating cooling systems in chemical plants, substitution and replacement of the heating-cooling-systems must be planned, i.e. at least 12.5 years of exception are necessary. Also in this case, with the exception of rare malfunctions, a release through industrial applications and the strictly regulated waste sector in the industry is very unlikely. - Transport (Annex E.2.10.) --> Use of fluoropolymers for transport of our products in coatings of hoses, use as gaskets, joints and in flanges, in electronic equipment as well as in safety equipment of vehicles, as far as not already mentioned by other parts of the restrictions (e.g. lubricants, electronic equipment and TULAC) - Hydraulic Fluids: These are in use in our facilities and must be replaced. There is no foreseeable release during use or at end of life beyond the strictly regulated waste area. These should continue to be exempted indefinitely. - Transport refrigeration (Refrigerants in transport refrigeration other than in marine applications): Use in refrigerated transport of sensitive chemicals, a release except in case of accidents is not foreseeable and should therefore continue to be exempted indefinitely. - Use of fluoropolymers in electronics and semiconductors (Annex E.2.11.), see Fluoropolymers: In use in all electronic equipment, a release of fluoropolymers is not foreseeable with controlled disposal in the industrial sector. - Energy sector (Annex E.2.12.): Proton-exchange membranes (PEM) are both under development and in planning for the larger plant. An unlimited exemption is inevitable due to the properties for the development of new processes and the energy transition. - Use of Lubricants (Annex E.2.14.):  The use of specialized, oxidation-insensitive (=long-lasting!) fluorinated lubricants in special pumps is prescribed by the manufacturers for safe and long-term operation, approved replacement lubricants must be developed and provided (especially in multi-purpose plants), therefore the extension of the transition period to at least 12 years is mandatory.  Without the multiple use of fluoropolymers, many processes under severe conditions (in corrosive media, at high temperature up to 250 °C and high pressure or the use of volatile solvents such as dichloromethane) are no longer possible in Europe and a relocation of production branches outside Europe takes place. As the environmental protection standards mostly are lower outside Europe, an increased release of chemicals in other regions then will occur (with the release not only of fluorine-containing chemicals, but of chemicals of all kinds) and a negative effect on emissions is achieved. This should be taken into account when restrictions are imposed at EU level.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: - Information can be provided for the production of active ingredients (veterinary medicines) and on the control of emissions generated in the process (compliance with emission limits at the plant and after incineration in the exhaust gas incineration plant after treatment (<0.1 mg/m³ with threshold value of 1 mg/m³ F determined as HF) and on waste from production, that is collected and disposed of via a special plant. The percentage of emissions at all plants is regularly monitored and is below the authorized TA-Luft thresholds. By controlled post-combustion of these collected exhaust gases in a waste gas purification plant with control of the Fluorine values, the emission <0.1 mg/m³ F can be safely maintained (further details on request). - The disposal of plant components containing fluoropolymers is clearly regulated by the German “Kreislaufwirtschaftsgesetz”. For a release during the use of fluoropolymers, the values of the annual analyses of products on impurities such as heavy metals in relation to Fluorine can be used as an evidence that no measurable abrasion to the products occurs during use.   - Incineration at the end of the life cycle (waste incineration above 850°C ensures complete decomposition of the fluorinated polymers) and proper treatment of the residues (exhaust gas and residue) via national disposal routes specified for the industry by the EU ensure that no emissions are to be expected during normal operation.   - In addition during approval procedures for the food and feed sector, it was ensured that no discharge/abrasion or entry of fluoropolymers into the product takes place, as otherwise the approval would not have been granted. In addition the Final Report 92/ 2023 „SumPFAS –Besorgniserregenden neuen per- und polyfluorierten Stoffen auf der Spur“(SumPFAS –Concerning new per- and polyfluorinated substances on the track) from German Umweltbundesamt clearly states that the temporal trend monitoring showed that the PFAS load of suspended solids in German streams decreased between 2005 and 2019. This clearly shows that by conscious handling, a reduction of emissions is possible without a ban.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Since waste disposal in the industrial environment is clearly regulated by law and wastes are specifically separated and sent for controlled disposal (part of the permit for the operation of the plants!), an uncontrolled release of PFAS or fluoropolymers is not to be expected. All fluoropolymer-containing plant components in the industrial environment are disposed of at the end of their life cycle in accordance with the strict waste regulations of the member states, which are also meticulously controlled (see question no. 2). Therefore, a general restriction or ban on fluoropolymers classified by the OECD as Polymer of Low Concern (PLC) is not comprehensible.

5. Proposed derogations: At one of our sites, PFAS are used as intermediates and active ingredients (veterinary medicines and biocides) are produced from them, which would be exempt from the proposed restriction. Emissions and waste from production are monitored across all stages and do not result in the release of PFAS. A limit value of 1.0 mg/m³ for fluorine/-HF is defined for the waste gas purification plant, which has been continuously undercut for years, also during production of the active ingredient. Since 2020, the measured value has been continuously at or below 10% of the measured value at 0.02 to max 0.1 mg/m³ F. Increased abrasion or input via raw materials of Fluorine from other plants at the site would also be detected by an increase in the measured value for HF after incineration.

6. Missing uses: With the currently proposed exemption only for the manufacture of the active ingredients, without including the manufacture of the precursors and intermediates, this exemption is not usable for the industry. Thus, dependence on ex-EU imports will be increased for these products. Manufacturing only the final stage of the active ingredients in the EU will result in moving all production out of the EU for most of the exempted uses.  The inclusion of intermediates and raw materials in the active ingredient manufacturing exemption is strongly recommended, otherwise it is useless and cannot be implemented. 100% of the chemical and pharmaceutical sectors use other PFAS in addition to fluorine-containing raw materials to manufacture active ingredients exempted from the restriction (it is hard to imagine a fluorine-containing chemical handling facility without the use of fluoropolymers in seals, hoses, coatings, and in electronic devices).  The sectors of chemical, pharmaceutical, and biocide/plant protection production are currently not considered as manufacturing facilities in the restriction proposal. 100% of chemical and active ingredient manufacturers (even without Fluorine in the molecule) are affected by a ban on fluoropolymers.  - Without the use of fluoropolymers, neither the production of the above-mentioned fluorine-containing active ingredients in the EU is reasonably possible, nor the production of substances that can only be manufactured under strict conditions (pH, organic solvents, temperature). This means that in addition to PFAS, many other basic and specialty chemicals will no longer be produced in Europe. - To find reasonable substitutes for fluoropolymers with comparable inert properties and necessary approvals (USP, NSF, FDA, TA-Luft etc.) for ALL applications in the given time frame seems impossible (coatings of aggregates, pipes, use in valves and gaskets, electronic devices, hoses, PPE etc.).  The ban on the use of fluoropolymers in the industrial environment, which has not yet been discussed, is incomprehensible, since the use and disposal of waste containing fluorine is also regulated via the various legal areas, and it can be ensured via additional controls or measurements, if necessary, that emissions from industry are minimal.    Without this exemption, massive losses and closures are to be expected for the entire chemical and pharmaceutical industry, and dependence on imports to the EU will increase. And if chemical production is relocated from Europe to countries with less environmental legislation, no positive effect for the environment can be achieved.  Replacing the fluoropolymers in all plants (seals, valves, coatings, hoses, measuring instruments and sensors) would require investments of 25-30% of the annual turnover, if alternatives exist and are available in the timeframe (if all affected companies replace at the same time), which cannot be recovered within the timeframes specified for listed companies and would therefore lead to shutdowns (sites and individual plants or areas). These costs do not yet include plant shutdowns and longer-term supply outages. A medium-sized company like Alzchem would have no chance of surviving this economically. In an international comparison, almost no EU manufacturer would be competitive if the additional costs were apportioned.  In our view, the extension of the exemption to include the use of fluoropolymers in the industrial sector is absolutely necessary, especially since the proportion of direct PFAS emissions from this sector is negligible.  Likewise, the use of PFAS in the laboratory and analytical sector with trifluoroacetic acid for sample preparation for mass spectrometry, as a mobile phase in HPLC and in protein analysis, as well as the use of PFAS standards for quantification is negligible in terms of emissions (the waste is also collected there) and alternatives for the various applications are currently not known.  - An unlimited exemption for all laboratory applications and also for new developments is necessary.  - A general ban on PFAS applications in Europe will lead to research and development in this area no longer taking place, which is to be seen as extremely disadvantageous in international competition and also severely restricts solution approaches for the future. Safe uses and those without or with negligible release and emission of PFAS must be further possible and a restriction of research does not make sense in the long term.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: The direct and indirect effects of the ban on fluoropolymers on the chemical industry have not been considered so far and, if removed, will lead to a collapse of the entire sector.   The low potential for emissions from fluoropolymers must be taken into account when defining exemptions, as must a loss of safety when switching to substitute materials, if available at all (see question 6). Due to the large number of applications and uses, it is hardly possible to find consistent and safe alternatives for all of them and to achieve the necessary approvals within the specified, very short transition periods.  In addition, the production of fluoropolymers in Europe must also remain possible, otherwise dependence on non-European imports will continue to increase. A general restriction of research and development for PFAS seems also not sensible.  In addition, we fully support the coordinated statements of the VCI.

8. Other identified uses: The chemical industry is not yet covered as a separate sector and is nevertheless extremely affected by the restriction if there is no exemption for the use of fluoropolymers (see paragraphs above). We also fully support the statements in the VCI statement.  Use of fluoropolymers as technical textiles: - Personal Protective Equipment: contrary to the statement of the alternatives, it is NOT ensured that suitable fluorine-free substitute materials are available for high temperatures and for handling corrosive and possibly very toxic substances in the production of chemicals, active pharmaceutical ingredients (human and animal) as well as for biocides and pesticides. Any change from known and established fluoropolymers to new groups of substances poses risks for workers in occupational health and safety in case of possible contact and sufficient testing is necessary before the changeover for the complete chemical industry. Due to the large number of substances, an unlimited exemption for fluoropolymers in PPE is proposed. - Filter materials are in various chemical processes for isolation of products or also for treatment/concentration of wastewater fractions. Chemically resistant PTFE are used in membrane processes for the production of basic chemicals (e.g. HCl, sulfuric acid), an elimination will also lead to the fact that these chemicals can no longer be produced in Europe.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: No release from fluoropolymers from the industrial environment due to controlled waste separation and targeted incineration at 850°C with subsequent waste gas scrubbing and treatment.
