Org. name: CISPE (Cloud Infrastructure Services Providers in Europe)
Combined Comments:
General Comments: CISPE comments to the ECHA’s public consultation on Annex XV restriction report-  Proposal for restriction on the manufacture, placing on the market and use of PFASs

Europe’s technology industries support transitioning to safer and more sustainable materials whenever possible.  However, the proposed ban on the production, use, and market availability of per- and polyfluorinated alkyl substances (PFAS) would significantly impact our industries and their operations. We further support – as the positions below reflect – managing that transition in a responsible, safe manner to avoid using unfortunate substitutes that present equal or greater risks to humans and the environment, unnecessarily stifling circular economy efforts, interrupting regional or global manufacturing and supply chains, and imposing hefty socioeconomic costs and burdens on consumers.

A. Revise Unrealistic Timelines to Ensure the Proposal is Based on Complete, Accurate Data and that Articles Can be Safely Redesigned, Tested, and Manufactured.

Based on the unique complexities of electronics articles and supply chains, and the necessary steps laid out below, policymakers should provide at least a 6.5-year transition period (the 18 months already provided in the proposal, plus at least 60 additional months) for the electronics industry to collect PFAS data and evaluate availability of proper substitutes. Derogation requests, which cannot be substantiated until these data-gathering phases are concluded, should be allowed until the end of the transition period.

The period for public input on this first-of-its-kind proposal is grossly inadequate. Manufacturers, importers, and users of complex articles, such as electronics, require substantially more time to provide complete, accurate information that has direct bearing on the proposed PFAS restriction and exemption requests. The proposal and ECHA’s process greatly underestimate the effort necessary to precisely locate 10,000+ substances across thousands of components, perform vetted scientific alternatives analyses for each use, and then implement responsible substitution plans.

With respect to PFAS in articles, entities across the electronics value chain need several years, not months to:

 Map their supply chains for PFAS applications;
 Conduct substitution analyses (and potentially develop brand-new substances);
 Redesign, test, and certify components and end products; and
 Ramp up production and supply chains for new articles.

Step 1: Mapping PFAS in Electronic Articles

The scope of the PFAS mapping exercise alone is staggering for our sector. Our supply chains are global and many tiers deep. Many of the components in electronic articles are not sourced directly by the importer or manufacturer, making identification of all PFAS in these items a task that few companies have ever undertaken or are resourced to perform. Indeed, global suppliers have never been required by any rule or industry practice to assess or communicate the presence of any but a small handful (fewer than 10) of the 10,000+ substances covered by the proposal. Additionally, to identify PFAS in electronics at or near levels of detection (as the proposed restriction would require), we also will have to locate PFAS uses in our manufacturing processes, which can cause cross-contamination in articles.

Across industries, there are real barriers to accurately mapping PFAS and to standing up new systems for that purpose. Because of the general newness of PFAS materials, for instance, there are no established analytical tools or processes in any industry for locating or measuring all PFAS substances. Today, in fact, only a limited number of PFAS compounds can be accurately quantified (and typically only in environmental samples (e.g., soil and water)), due to the lack of reference standards and analytical methodologies for measuring these substances. This measuring challenge means that we not only lack visibility into PFAS presence in complex finished articles, but we also cannot have a comprehensive understanding of PFAS toxicities and environmental impacts across different articles/contexts.  Developing analytical standards and a coherent measuring methodology for different chemistries underlying thousands of PFAS compounds across all PFAS applications will take years (possibly decades) of work.
Information-gathering also is hampered by trade secret/confidential business information protections for PFAS substances.
Accurately identifying PFAS in all complex electronic (and many other) articles will therefore take years, but is a necessary first step before proper substitution analyses can even begin and EU policymakers can make informed decisions about how best to regulate these substances, grant or deny exemptions from PFAS restrictions

Step 2: Finding or Developing Adequate Substitutes
Finding proper substitutes for PFAS also is a uniquely complex and rigorous process for the electronics sector. Where PFAS-free alternatives are available, they are often not drop-in replacements. This is because there is no other material with the same combination of properties as PFAS materials. For instance, commonly used PFAS substances in electronics are fluoropolymers. They are used because of their heat resistance, dielectric constant, breakdown voltage, repellence properties, low friction, chemical resistance, mechanical strength, etc. There is no single alternative material that possesses the same unique combination of properties. If not all required properties can be combined in a single material, then to produce articles with equal safety levels, functionality, durability, and reliability, a combination of materials or a combination of components must be used. This does not necessarily render it impossible to replace PFAS, but it requires more development effort than simply selecting apples-to-apples replacement substances from a catalogue.  And of course, when adequate substitute materials do not already exist, they must be invented and developed from the ground up.
Notably, steps 1 and 2 must be completed before any derogation requests can be substantiated.
Step 3: Redesigning articles
When an alternative material is available and adopted for an article, that article will take on different properties. For example, it could have different dimensions, move with higher friction, or have higher flammability. So, suitable product changes must be implemented, e.g., more space must be created, a stronger motor has to be used for the PFAS-free part in the equipment, etc. Any such changes at the component level then require redesign of end products to accommodate the substitute. Redesigning electronic components – and then end products – to eliminate PFAS can therefore involve substantial time and resources. Alternative materials could also require changes to the manufacturing process because the processability of the alternative material may be different.
Step 4: Testing and certifying new components and end products
After product redesign, it is crucial to follow rigorous testing protocols to ensure consumer/end user safety and good environmental outcomes. Thorough scientific testing helps ensure that the alternatives chosen meet performance, safety, quality, durability and environmental standards required by law and needed by consumers/end users. Testing takes time. For example, fluoropolymers are fire resistant and have a very high breakdown voltage, so replacing them requires life-time and/or safety testing of the alternative. If after six months, the tested article fails, another design and testing iteration is required.
For products that require certification or (mandatory) conformity testing, additional time is needed to re-certify the product. Conformity testing labs have limited testing capacity (both in personnel and laboratory facilities). Even if substitutes are known and implemented, we anticipate long delays at this stage when every producer in the electronics industry starts requesting testing of re-designed models (on top of tests already planned for normal product evolutions).

Step 5: Scaling and operationalizing distribution of PFAS-free articles
Even after the above steps are completed, it will take additional years to operationalize substitution plans for complex articles like electronics (e.g., ramp up production, adjust supply chains, market to consumers, etc.).

To capture this entire process beginning to end, the National Association of Manufacturers compiled an illustrative list of necessary steps to implement alternatives for substances of concern in articles.

B. Include Additional Broad-Based Derogations to Better Balance the Proposal’s Safety and Environmental Aims with Circular Economy Goals and Actual Risk Potential

1. Spare parts and used articles on the EU market prior to the restriction’s effective date

To promote the EU’s own Circular Economy Action Plan, and be consistent with existing EU material restriction regimes described below, policymakers should ensure that this proposal allows for repair, reuse, and resale of existing parts/equipment and does not cause premature product obsolescence and waste generation. Extending the life of existing products and reusing or selling pre-owned goods are essential activities for a more circular economy. The proposal should therefore include broad cross-industry derogations for spare parts and used components/equipment.

Spare parts. The “repair as produced” principle is well established in EU law,  and makes particular sense for long-life capital goods and high-value electronic equipment. It combats premature obsolescence and the need to generate new parts and equipment by allowing products already placed on the market before a key date to be repaired using spare parts that were compliant as of that key date. As noted above, we anticipate that it will take several years to implement substitution plans for PFAS in electronics, so absent a spare parts exemption, components or equipment that fail and require replacement parts after the restriction’s effective date will be rendered irreparable.

In addition to being a poor sustainability outcome, this creates compliance barriers for other EU ecodesign and “right to repair” laws.   It also disrupts warranty and extended warranty agreements that are common in the IT industry. Compliance with warranty service obligations frequently involves replacing non-functional parts as the most economical and environmentally favourable option to restore products back to functional service. If equipment already on the market cannot be repaired as produced, fulfilling warranty claims will more often result in disposal and replacement of the whole equipment.

Notably, a spare parts derogation would not materially add to PFAS emissions in the EU. The entire electronics sector currently contributes a minute percentage ( less than 1%) of total PFAS emissions in the EU, and spare parts represent only a tiny fraction of electronics produced or imported in the EU. Permitting continued deployment of already-produced, PFAS-containing spare parts for repair purposes would result in negligible, and steadily declining, PFAS emissions, but a meaningful impact on extending the lifespan of many electronic products and related environmental and socio-economic benefits.

Reuse, resale, and recirculation of articles already on the market. Similar rationales support a broad-based exemption for articles and equipment already on the market that can be reused or resold to extend their useful life, rather than being discarded. This approach comports with the EU’s policy preference for robust secondary markets, and also facilitates circular economy programs that put valuable used articles back into the supply chain as components in the manufacture of new equipment.

This exemption, which would apply until an article reaches its end user/end of life, would not result in net new PFAS being placed on the EU market. Similar to a spare parts derogation, this exemption would avoid unnecessary creation of waste and reduce the need to manufacture new articles (which entails additional consumption of raw materials, energy and water expended on manufacturing processes, etc.).

2. Semiconductor manufacturing and articles

The proposal contemplates a potential exemption for semiconductor manufacturing processes. The proposal should retain that exemption and expand it to include PFAS in semiconductor articles.  The semiconductor industry, years ahead of other industries in identifying PFAS in their operations and products, has submitted (via multiple trade associations) detailed data and rationale to ECHA to support this approach, including unique PFAS capabilities within semiconductor process chemistries, semiconductor manufacturing equipment and facilities, and semiconductor chips themselves. There are no known equivalent substitutes for PFAS in these use cases, so absent an exemption of sufficient length, semiconductor production – and countless downstream applications/products that rely on it – are at risk of serious interruptions. This degree of product and supply chain disruption would have vast economic and market impacts.


3. Batteries manufacturing and articles

Similar to semiconductors in pervasiveness and socioeconomic reliance on them, batteries also are main enablers for the transition toward low-emission mobility, decarbonized energy generation and digitalization.  Batteries are essential to ensure the sustainable development of society and they provide critical environmental and social benefits.  PFAS ( less than 5% w/w of a battery cell weight) is used in a wide variety of rechargeable batteries in order to achieve high energy, high power, very long life, superior reliability, and ability to withstand extreme temperatures performance.   The current proposed derogation period (6.5 years) is not sufficient for battery manufacturers to identify, evaluate and qualify alternative materials in these articles.   Battery manufacturers estimate it will take at least 10 years to research PFAS alternatives, followed by at least 5 years to commercialize suitable alternatives. Based on current R&D work, it is not clear that any appropriate substitute materials exist today for battery applications.     The derogation period for PFAS use in batteries should therefore be extended to 13.5 years with a clear mechanism to allow additional derogations or derogation extensions where non-alternatives become available.

4. Fluoropolymers

Although the proposal treats all PFAS the same, PFAS are not equal in terms of their risk profile.  Fluoropolymers, a distinct class of PFAS, have extremely low environmental and health hazard potential. They are immobile; they are practically insoluble in water and they do not break down and spread through the air; and their toxicity profile – particularly at the stage in which they have been incorporated into articles -- is therefore fundamentally different from nonpolymeric PFAS. In fact, recent studies suggest that fluoropolymers satisfy widely-used Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) criteria to be considered Polymers of Low Concern.

On the other hand, these PFAS polymers have unique properties (e.g., thermal, chemical, photochemical, hydrolytic, oxidative, and biological stability) that make them extremely valuable in certain applications, including in electronics, and they present real safety and functionality benefits for consumers/end users. The proposal should therefore balance the risks and benefits involved, and clearly distinguish between fluoropolymers – especially fluoropolymers that have been integrated into manufactured articles --  and nonpolymeric PFAS substances that clearly present higher hazard potential.

5.  PFAS used in research and development

This proposal, in whatever form it is finalized, will spawn aggressive R&D efforts to find or invent substitutes that match the safety and performance of PFAS in various applications. It is counterintuitive and counterproductive that PFAS would be banned in those activities. R&D typically involves small quantities of chemicals in highly-controlled environments where risks and chemical release can be managed. Indeed, the REACH regime contains a wholesale exemption from its restrictions for substances used in scientific R&D in amounts below one tonne per year. EU policymakers clearly want to steer the private sector toward non-PFAS alternatives, so they should promote – not stifle – the activities that will get us there.

C. Other General Amendments to the Proposal are Needed to Ensure a Responsible Transition to Safe, Reliable Alternative Substances and to Balance the Proposal’s Policy Aims with Over-Burdening Businesses of All Sizes and Unnecessarily Banning Products from the EU Market

1. The proposal should contain a clear exemption renewal process

The current proposal includes inflexible 5- or 12-year derogation periods for specific PFAS uses. For many PFAS uses in our sector, however, we likely will need additional time to develop safe alternative materials and/or entirely new products. A well-defined derogation extension process, such as the one used in the EU Restriction on the Use of Hazardous Substances (RoHS) Directive (2011/65/EU), should be included here to ensure PFAS restrictions reflect the actual availability of substitutes and time required to – in some cases – invent and test brand new chemical replacements.   The extension process should allow industry to rely on exemptions while extension applications are under review by the European Commission, and when extensions are denied, a  sufficient transition period – accounting for the myriad steps laid out above in Section A – should apply after the final decision.

2. PFAS threshold limits that trigger restrictions should be raised

The proposal’s near-detection-level trigger for the PFAS ban needs to be adjusted upward.  This will avoid scenarios where the mere presence of PFAS in upstream manufacturing operations (often outside of the EU) could trigger an outright article ban, and/or where the very equipment used to test for PFAS cross-contaminates the article sufficiently to ban it from the EU market.  The lack of testing mechanisms and the sheer number of PFAS substances make it difficult to know what a proper threshold would be to screen out accidental contamination (versus intentional additions of PFAS to articles). As a starting point, policymakers could consider using the 0.1% w/w threshold currently used in REACH for other restricted substances.

3. Reporting obligations for exemption-holders for IT equipment and electronic articles should be delayed for at least 5 years to enable businesses of all sizes in the value chain to develop identification, measurement, and tracking mechanisms to manage the reporting process.

For reasons explained above, the entire sector is struggling to identify and quantify – for the first time – PFAS used in complex IT and electronics articles. General Comments: CLEPA's position on the PFAS restriction proposal is aligned with the ACEA submission (submission 4276 of 24 May 2023). This however does not apply to the sub-use automotive mobile air-conditioning as identified in Annex XV of the restriction report, for which CLEPA is submitting below a separate feedback.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The following comments concern the use sector “Mobile Air Conditioning (MAC)” identified in Annex XV of the restriction report. CLEPA members are developing and producing MAC systems in the EU for both the European as well as the export market. These systems are designed specifically for a refrigerant intended for its later use in the vehicle. The two most commonly used refrigerants in MAC are R1234yf and R134a, both containing PFAS. CLEPA members are therefore directly impacted by a potential restriction of refrigerants containing PFAS. CLEPA members would therefore like to highlight specific concerns about MAC systems based on mechanical compressors that have not been adequately reflected in the restriction report. Due to diverging opinions amongst its membership, CLEPA does not have a position on PFAS restrictions in the case of electric compressors.  1. Need to consider the type approval process for vehicles and subsequent distinction between newly approved vehicle types and vehicles already in production  a. Before placing on the market, a “series” of vehicles, manufacturers have to obtain a vehicle “type” approval to certify that a vehicle “type” meets all EU safety, environmental and conformity of production requirements. b. New vehicles can be placed on the market until:  i. the manufacturer makes technical changes to the vehicle “type” to the extent that it does no longer conform to the approval certification ii. new regulatory requirements enter into force mandating performances that the vehicle “type” does not fulfil.  c. The restriction report does not distinguish between “vehicle types” already approved (i.e. current production) and new “vehicle types” that will be approved in future. As a result, all vehicles in production using PFAS-based refrigerants cannot be placed on the market after the transition/derogation period ends, their production will be terminated and the “vehicle type” will need to be re-engineered and type-approved again with a MAC using PFAS-free refrigerants. This would add a significant additional burden on industry.  CLEPA recommends applying the transition and derogation periods only to new “vehicle types” that will be approved after the date of application of the PFAS regulation and recommends exempting all vehicle types existing at that date.  2. Derogation period for vehicles with a mechanical compressor should be aligned with the recently adopted CO2 fleet standards legislation for cars and vans.  a. The EU co-legislators recently adopted a new Regulation 2023/851 amending Regulation (EU) 2019/631 strengthening the CO2 emission performance standards for new passenger cars and new light commercial vehicles.  b. The new regulation sets a -100% target for tailpipe CO2 emissions for all new vehicles registered in 2035. As a result, sales of cars and vans with conventional internal combustion engines are expected to be reduced significantly as of this year. These vehicles typically use mechanical compressors for their MAC systems.  c. The restriction proposal concluded that PFAS-free MAC alternatives are available for electrical and hybrid cars, but not necessarily for combustion engine vehicles with mechanical compressors.  d. The 5-year derogation proposed by the restriction proposal would require vehicles with a mechanical compressor to end production sometime in 2031, four years before the expected phase-out of internal combustion engines.  e. This would result in high additional burden for industry and a loss of purchase choice for European consumers.  CLEPA recommends extending the derogation period for new vehicle types with a mechanical compressor to 2035 to ensure consistency with EU legislation.  3. Derogation for maintenance of existing vehicles with MAC using refrigerants containing PFAS is missing.  a. The restriction proposal includes a derogation of 12 years for maintenance of HVAC systems in buildings, but such a derogation is not foreseen for MAC.  b. Due to the lack of drop-in refrigerant alternatives, this would result in owners of existing vehicles in the fleet having little choice for their next MAC maintenance after the transition period ends to either:  i. Retrofit the vehicle with a MAC using PFAS free refrigerant which implies significant economic, environmental and opportunity costs  ii. Having to scrap their vehicle even well before its average lifetime expectance and thus incurring significant economic losses  iii. Resort to illegal “black market” solutions for maintaining the MAC which creates legal repercussions for the owner and undermines the effectiveness of the PFAS restriction.  c. All these unintended consequences have already been well identified in the restriction proposal.  CLEPA recommends the introduction of a derogation for maintenance of existing MAC systems based on the longest observed lifetimes of vehicles in EU countries (20 years for cars and vans and 25 years for trucks)   4. Differences between cars and commercial vehicles/trucks not recognised.  a. The restriction proposal clearly points out that for trucks and buses the reliability/durability of PFAS-free alternatives have not yet been proven (p. 249).  b. As a result, more time is required for developing and testing alternatives for these vehicle segments.  c. Yet the restriction proposal does not differentiate its recommended transition/derogation periods between cars, vans, buses, or trucks.  d. Bus and truck manufacturers are therefore missing the needed time to develop alternatives and could be forced to stop selling their vehicles after the transition period ends, incurring significant economic losses and reducing consumer choice.  CLEPA recommends establishing separate derogation periods of 12 years for commercial vehicles including trucks and buses using a mechanical compressor.  Similarly, to point 1, the transition and derogation periods should only apply to new types not yet approved and exempt vehicle types already in production.  5. Research and development derogation aligned to longest use case derogations required:  a. Suppliers of MAC need to be able to test and verify their components and spare parts using refrigerants containing PFAS (e.g. regarding durability, material improvements, etc.) for as long as these systems are used in the market.  b. Without a corresponding derogation for R&D uses (does not include placing on the market), components cannot be checked in spare parts production and improvements cannot be validated. This would also greatly limit quality control.  CLEPA recommends introducing a derogation for development and validation activities in line with the latest phase-out date and derogation period for maintenance.

General Comments: Coating agents that use fluororesin have acid resistance that other resins do not have .
Therefore, it is widely used as an acid-resistant coating agent for metals.

As an alternative substance, a coating agent obtained by dissolving a silicone resin, an acrylic resin, a urethane resin, an olefin resin, or the like in a hydrocarbon-based organic solvent can be considered. General Comments: COG is a manufacturer of elastomer seals with specialised expertise in the field of fluorine-containing polymers. These polymers are used worldwide in demanding applications, for example, in medical technology, the food and pharmaceutical industries, and also in the energy sector (hydrogen, electrolysis, photovoltaics, wind energy, etc.), in semiconductor production and generally in mechanical engineering. Either no or only considerably inferior alternatives exist for these applications. For example, high-purity FFKM polymers are used for sealing in the semiconductor industry (wafer/chip production). Alternative materials for these applications do not exist at this time. The same applies to many production facilities in the pharmaceuticals industry. For example, the very purest water (WFI=water for injection) is used here in production so that medications and pharmaceutical products such as insulin of high purity can be produced. In addition to media resistance to WFI and the product, the special FKM material used here features a low migration rate that cannot be matched by any fluorine-free alternative material in this combination.
A general PFAS ban would cause tremendous problems in other segments of the pharmaceuticals industry as well, because alternative materials do not come anywhere close to current service lives. For example, a production facility that currently has a service life of 250 hours could only operated for approximately 90 hours with an alternative material. Production costs would therefore rise significantly due to increased seal wear and additional production stops.
Safe alternative elastomer materials for many sealing applications currently do not exist in medical technology or the food industry either.
The problem is further exacerbated by the approvals required for pharmaceuticals and the food industry (FDA, USP, ISO 10993, 3-A Sanitary, etc.). While these approvals can be obtained for alternative materials that can be considered from a technical perspective, they do not meet the necessary application criteria such as WFI resistance.
A general ban on PFAS for polymers in the sealing technology field would set the technology back by decades and endanger the safety of products and applications. The climate goals set by the EU and Germany for renewable energy can only be realised on the basis of fluorine-containing polymers.
Furthermore, the (per)fluorinated rubber material group sets itself apart with high temperature resistance.
Alternatives in the corresponding temperature ranges do not exist at this time. This is made clear in particular by the ASTM D2000 chart on page 64 of the attached PDF file.
The temperature range covered by fluorinated compounds is coloured blue, notably in reference to high temperatures. This diagram shows that only fluorine-containing sealing materials exhibit a corresponding high thermal stability.
They are compared here to other typical sealing materials that are not fluorine-based.

VMQ materials are not a suitable alternative since they cannot be used in certain fields because of resistance to media.
The table on page 63 of the attached PDF file present the common acids: sulphuric acid, hydrofluoric acid and nitric acid. Here the perfluorinated material FFKM is compared to the typical non-fluorinated sealing materials. This clearly shows that only a fluorinated material (FFKM in this case) can be used in applications with the acids in question. Reliable sealing for these chemicals, ensuring that they cannot escape into the environment, requires the use of this material.
An undifferentiated PFAS ban would not only have serious negative economic consequences for COG, but could threaten the company’s existence. As of 2021/2022, materials based on fluoropolymers (FKM, FFKM, FEPM, FVMQ) account for more than 62% of the company’s sales. If these sales were to be eliminated by a general PFAS ban, only a small proportion could be made up by other materials such as HNBR or VMQ. There are no alternatives to FKM and especially to FFKM sealing materials.
COG would have to dismiss at least 150 employees out of its current staff totalling nearly 300. Since fixed costs based on existing sales budgets cannot be eliminated, the PFAS ban could also threaten the company’s existence because generating sufficient compensating sales quickly is not possible.

General Comments: Comment on Proposed Restriction of PFAS

Japan Chemical Fibers Association (JCFA) much appreciates the opportunity to join this public consultation, and submit our opinions on the proposal to restrict PFAS (Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl substances) under REACH. JCFA is all for the activities to protect human health and environment from toxic chemical substances. However, JCFA has some concerns about the proposed restriction as follows:

(1) We believe that the proposed restriction of PFAS (Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl substances) proposed by 5 European countries is an excessive measure because it restricts more than 10,000 of organofluorine compounds (PFAS) on the grouping basis that they are persistent as substances of concern equivalent to the already regulated PFOS and PFOA.

Article 68 REACH refers to the scope of the restrictions, which regulates unacceptable risks to human health or the environment that need to be addressed by society as a whole. In the proposal, the following issues are shown as concerns and reasons for the restriction: persistent chemicals, bioconcentration, mobility, the possibility of long-distance transport, accumulation in plants, the possibility of global warming, and toxicological effects. Of these, “persistent” is applicable to all targeted organofluorine compounds (PFAS), but other concerns are related to some compounds.

Persistency common to all organofluorine compounds (PFAS) can be rephrased as "high durability" by focusing on its advantages, however, we believe that it is not appropriate to regulate this property alone as an unacceptable risk to human health or the environment. In addition, it is not appropriate to apply the concerns about some fluorinated compounds, such as bioconcentration potential and toxicological effects, by grouping all organofluorine compounds (PFAS) together, and the risk of each substance should be quantitatively assessed and discussed.

(2) PFHxA types (a kind of PFAS) are widely used as fluorinated repellent (C6) for processing textile products (for providing water and oil repellency), and there is no substitute for it. A restriction on use of the fluorinated repellent (C6) can be an obstacle to produce these products, and can create mass confusion in supply chains and society. JCFA believes that the restriction would increase burden upon textile product processors, because the processing businesses are mainly operated by small and medium-sized enterprises.

(3) Therefore, fluorinated repellent (C6) should be allowed if it is essential and determines human safety. JCFA believes that it should be allowed when used in the following applications.

1) Sports, outdoors, and working
In sports, outdoor and working products, they usually require high water repellency and coating processability. Non-fluorinated repellent does not perform as well as fluorinated repellent (C6). If non-fluorinated repellent is used for these products, it cannot protect wearers under severe environment.

2) Vehicle interiors
Products for vehicle interiors are usually provided with high fire resistance. Non-fluorinated repellent does not provide textiles with oil repellency. When a textile not using fluorinated repellent is processed, fire-resisting coating agents leak out of the surface of the textile, by which its fire resistance and quality deteriorate.

3) Protective equipment (for blocking chemical substances)
Non-fluorinated repellent that does not provide textiles with oil repellency cannot protect wearers, because it does not block toxic substances including chemical substances.

As mentioned above, in introducing the proposed restriction, the risk of each substance should be properly assessed and discussed. On that basis, we believe that the covering range necessary for achieving objectives that contribute to the socioeconomic aspects of the EU should be set. Even if the proposed restriction is introduced, we request that the above (3) related to human safety be exempted from the restriction.

General Comments: Comment on the proposal for the ban of PFAS

The Bruno Bock Group welcomes the EU's initiative to ban harmful substances from entering the environment. It is crucial to take measures to minimize potential risks to both humans and the environment.
PFAS play a crucial role in various industrial applications, especially in corrosion-resistant seals and lubricants. In numerous applications, from sealants in pumps to additives for chemical reactors and components of filling systems, fluoropolymer components ensure the safe handling of hazardous substances and prevent material leaks.
The outstanding heat resistance of fluorinated materials is a key factor in many industrial processes. This enables machinery to operate at higher temperatures, leading to increased efficiency. Furthermore, these materials contribute to the safety of workers as they can withstand extreme conditions.
However, it is important to handle the use of fluorinated materials responsibly. We support efforts to explore alternative manufacturing processes to produce PFAS without harmful fluorinated surfactants. Similarly, the development of recycling methods for fluoropolymers is of great importance.
We also welcome industry efforts to expand manufacturer responsibility and establish closed-loop systems for recycling fluorine chemicals. These initiatives are significant steps towards a more sustainable future.
However, it is crucial to identify realistic alternatives before enacting a general ban on PFAS. In several industrial applications, there are currently no equivalent substances known/available, and a premature ban would jeopardize the functionality and efficiency of critical processes.
It is important to conduct the discussion on the use of PFAS on a factual and risk-based basis. Different applications require individual considerations, and equivalent alternatives will not be available for every use.
Bruno Bock is committed to working with our suppliers on sustainable solutions and minimizing the use of PFAS wherever possible. We see regulation as an opportunity to develop innovative technologies that both protect the environment and maintain industrial performance.
However, it is important to emphasize that not all PFAS substances are the same. Some have been proven to pose significant environmental risks, while others are used in deep machine parts without direct environmental contact. Condemning the entire class of polymer materials on a blanket basis falls short in this regard.
It is also crucial to understand that fluoropolymers can predominantly be manufactured without harmful fluorinated surfactants. New manufacturing processes and technologies offer the possibility of producing PFAS without the known risks. Environmental findings from past times should not serve as the basis for present decisions.
A general ban on PFAS could have unintended consequences. For example, it could significantly impact the semiconductor industry in Europe, thereby jeopardizing the goals of the European Chips Act. It is crucial that regulatory measures are well-considered and based on scientific insights.
The search for suitable substitutes is often a complex undertaking. In some applications, it is challenging to find equivalent substitutes that meet extremely demanding requirements. Despite intensive research, there are cases where substitutes have a shorter lifespan and higher leakage rates.
Overall, reducing the use of PFAS without compromising the functionality and safety of industrial processes is a complex process. It requires close collaboration between industry, regulatory authorities, and research institutions to find sustainable solutions.
Our company is committed to participating in this crucial development and supporting innovative approaches. We are confident that through responsible approaches and technological development, a balanced path can be found to minimize the use of PFAS while maintaining industrial efficiency.
It is important to note that some measures for regulating PFAS have already had positive effects. For instance, fire extinguishers containing PFAS-based fire-fighting foams have already been replaced with more environmentally friendly alternatives. This ban was meaningful and has led to a noticeable improvement in the environmental situation.
However, it is important to consider the potential consequences of a widespread ban on PFAS. The replacement of seals and fittings in various industrial applications could potentially lead to increased use of other hazardous substances that have not been studied thoroughly, if suitable alternatives are not available. This underscores that a blanket regulation may not always yield the desired effects and individual considerations are necessary.
Therefore, it is of the utmost importance to pursue a balanced and scientifically-based approach in regulating PFAS. Close collaboration between industry, regulatory authorities, and research institutions is indispensable to find sustainable solutions that protect both the environment and the safety and efficiency of industrial processes. Our company is firmly committed to participating in this crucial development and supporting innovative approaches.
Our company has already taken steps to ensure the safe disposal of materials containing PFAS, such as PTFE. We are actively in contact with our suppliers and have successfully held discussions to support the implementation of a recycling system. This system aims to ensure an environmentally-friendly and safe disposal of these materials.
In addition, our company has already established clear guidelines. Waste containing PFAS-based materials like PTFE must not be disposed of through household waste. Instead, they are disposed of together with contaminated binders, where they are incinerated at much higher temperatures. This process ensures that no hazardous substances are released during disposal.
It is important to understand that a comprehensive ban on PFAS would have not only economic implications for the chemical industry. The replacement of parts in almost all industrial facilities, including all process engineering components, would incur significant costs and time. Furthermore, such a ban could lead to some facilities losing their operating permits. This would have negative economic consequences, it would entail a substantial bureaucratic effort and represent a significant regulatory risk.
Considering all these factors, it is of paramount importance that regulatory authorities and the industry collaborate closely to find realistic and sustainable solutions that protect the environment while also preserving economic stability and jobs in the industry. Our company is committed to walking this path and actively participating in these efforts.

In order to ensure functionality, patient and user safety on a daily basis, the high-performance materials used in these products cannot be substituted according to the current state of technology and science.   A own report by the IKV Aachen, which is enclosed with the consultation, shows that fluoropolymers cannot be substituted for very representative applications for minimally invasive surgery at present.  This conclusion is also reached by the Ministry for the Environment, Climate and Energy Management of Baden Württemberg within the Think Tank "Industrial Resource Strategies". A corresponding report is expected to be published by the end of the year. The specialty of their approach is to use KI screening all technical literature for potential substitution materials. A preliminary presentation within the think tank identified no substitute for high end medical device applications we as KARL STORZ served as a flagship application. The use of these high-performance polymers should be regulated according to a benefit - risk principle. This essential use principle is also described in the European Green Deal and the EU Chemicals Strategy as a prerequisite of a regulation. A description was published by Cousins 2019 (The concept of essential use for determining when uses of PFASSs can be phased out) in Environmental Science - Processes & Impacts.   Many medical devices cover niche markets and the requirements for the materials used are already very high. Various verifications such as biocompatibility according to ISO 10993, DIN EN ISO 60601 etc. must be carried out. These requirements originate from the (EU) 2017/745 Medical Device Regulation, which was created for this purpose. MDR even regulates use of CMR-substances, endocrine disruptors and phthalates in certain situations when the benefit-risk analysis is positive Annex I, 10.4.1.ff. An extension to chemicals of concern could easily be adopted.     As a company we can trace back the use of fluoropolymers for 6 decades. No issue of biocompatibility is recorded. Evidence with (external lab services) biocompatibility tests for each of our products with body contact is available including the proof of very high biocompatibility of fluoropolymers (PTFE, FEP, PFA, PVDF, ETFE, ECTFE, FKM, ) has been kept in the company for more than 60 years. Likewise, scientific studies show that fluoropolymers do not exhibit toxic effects on humans (Anderson et. Al. Grouping of PFAS for human health risk assessment: Findings from an independent panel of experts; Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology 134 (2022) 105226) with reference to multiple further investigations. As the risk of changing quality of materials is unacceptable to the legislator (MDR), supply and inventory of the supply chain must be ensured and qualified. Likewise, changes in materials and even changes in raw material supplier are significant changes. Significant    changes make the existing certificate of the medical device void in the first place. It further leads to recertification of products in the EU and all those countries basing their market access on the “CE-certification”.  Expectable bottle necks.  It is necessary to ensure the supply chain and the resulting availability. Alternatively, there is a risk that, due to changes of the material or the supplier (which are significant changes), the approval bodies in the EU will be further strained and many medical devices, including PFAS free ones, will not be recertified in time. CE-certificates of all medical devices need recertification every 5 years. Capacity of test-labs also needs to be considered. From our experience with the transition to MDR we already know that a year for a waiting list is easily possible.  More information is attached to this contribution

8. Other identified uses: General derogation for Medical Devices General derogation for flouropolymers  Evidence is attached to this contribution

10. Analytical methods: Analysis of polyfluorinated and perfluorinated alkyl substances  (PFAS)  The determination of polyfluorinated and perfluorinated alkyl substances {PFAS) is a great challenge for analytical methods due to the large variety of substances {estimated: > 10000 substances) with different chemical structures and isomer mixtures as well as different polarity. Standard and reference substances, which have to be used for the calibration of analytical instruments, are often not available. Standards available for the analytical determination of {PFAS) substances are mainly in the field of environmental analysis {for example, for the analysis of water and soil samples) and only available for single substances {<100) [1]. With the standard DIN 38409-59:2022 EN [2] a method for the measurement of the sum parameter adsorbable organically bound fluorine {AOF) is available. However, a clear assignment to individual substances is not possible with this method. The Total Oxidizable Precursor {TOP)-Assay offers a further analysis possibility, also for solid samples. The analytical principle of the TOP assay is to oxidatively convert unknown PFAS precursor compounds into periluorcarboxylic acids {PFCA), which are thus quantifiable. This makes it possible to estimate PFAS levels in environmental samples in screening procedures. The concept of the TOP assay is more selective than, for example, measurements of the sum parameters EOF {extractable organic fluorine compounds) and AOF. A detailed study to evaluate in more detail the capabilities and limitations of the TOP assay methodology and its informative value was published in 2022 [3].  In summary, according to the current state of research, and to our knowledge, the analysis of the approximately 10,000 individual substances in medical devices is not possible. There is a considerable need for research in this area, with a focus on the development of suitable method analytics.

1. Introduction of JAMMA
JAMMA was established in 1939 and is the nationwide organization of agricultural machinery manufacturers in Japan and aims at contributing to the sound development and progress of agricultural machinery industry and the growth of national economy. We work on a wide range of activities such as development of technology, safety, environment and standardization.
We are working on solving various problems in collaboration with agricultural machinery industry associations of other countries, and we have a particularly friendly relationship with related associations in EU.

2. Problems of Proposed Restriction and JAMMA’s requests
It is impossible to survey the use of all 1,000 or more types of PFAS, and we have been able to survey only 24 types by CAS number at the moment (the use example list is attached). Most of them were "not replaceable". We oppose blanket regulation of PFAS. We believe that it is realistic to chemically analyze all PFAS, group them according to the degree of risk, and regulate them in sequence, starting with the highest priority group.
We point out the following problems with the proposed "PFAS restriction" and request improvements. Please consider these matters.
(1) Scope of application
Restrictions are too broad to be addressed. We request that the groups with the highest risk first be gradually restricted after conducting a reliable and scientific risk assessment based on data.
(2) Exemptions
We request that the definition of "essential use" be clarified, and the scope of exemptions be specified. In addition, the agricultural sector is an important industry that supports human diets, and we are convinced that it is naturally included in "essential use," and we request that agricultural machinery be exempted from the application.
(3) Transition period
If agricultural machinery is not exempt, we request the same transition period as the automotive industry with which we share the supply chain.
(4) Repair parts
Maintenance is essential for farmers to use machines safely for a long time. If repair parts for agricultural machinery are regulated, farmers will not be able to repair the machinery and will face the risk of going out of business. From the viewpoint of food security, we request exemption from the application of repair parts for agricultural machinery.

General Comments: Comments of the Volvo Group on the Annex XV restriction report related to the Restriction on the manufacture, placing on the market and use of PFASs

The Volvo Group wishes to provide comments on the consultation on the Annex XV restriction report related to the Restriction on the manufacture, placing on the market and use of PFASs.

Introduction:
The Volvo Group manufactures trucks, buses, construction equipment and power solutions for marine and industrial applications. Volvo Group also have a high pace in the transformation with a rapid expansion of the offer of electric vehicles and machines. The Volvo Group products often operate under harsh conditions and some of the materials and substances used in the Volvo Group’s products are potentially hazardous and cannot today be substituted to achieve the high quality and safety demands. The Group works to reduce its dependency on such materials and substances with the aim to protect both people and the environment. In collaboration with partners, the Volvo Group proactively evaluates alternatives in the design and supply processes to minimize and eliminate use of substances of concern.

The intention to reduce the risks of long living and toxic per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) is therefore in line with Volvo Group ambitions. At the same time, the Volvo Group is concerned by both the timeline and the scope of the PFAS restriction as proposed. Many applications in Volvo Group´s current and future products, like e.g. batteries, fuel cells, refrigerants, sealings, and internal combustion engines, are today dependent on PFASs (mainly fluoropolymers) to provide crucial functions like durability, heat- and corrosion resistance, and chemical stability in order to secure safe products with a long operating lifetime.

The Volvo Group main concerns with the proposed PFAS-restriction:
- A very short timeline for phase-out and absence of proper derogations: The development cycles of our products are long and re-design requires sufficient time for verification and validation to secure high quality and safe products.
- The vast majority of the PFAS occurrences in our products would, to our understanding, not fall under any derogation according to the proposal. This would mean that most of our applications would need to be redeveloped, verified, validated and implemented on all our products in production from 2026/2027. For the reasons explained above, this will not be possible. The time to develop alternatives is unforeseeable in various applications where the technology transition has not started yet. Even when an alternative material/part exists, it is not always possible to know beforehand how long the redevelopment and validation will take. Our experience from phasing out hazardous substances from complex engine parts, shows that this could take many years. The change of some parts could as well trigger the need for recertification towards emission legislations and safety type approvals.
- Retroactive application to produced products: We understand that the proposed restriction will apply as well to already produced products. This could mean that PFAS containing products could not be resold but would need to be scrapped. It would also jeopardize our remanufacturing business and our circularity ambitions. This can surely not be the intention of the proposal.
- The assumed awareness of PFAS existence in our supply chain: Traceability of most of the PFASs in scope of the proposal has not previously been required by any regulation. PFAS occurrences are therefore still to a large extent be unknown. It takes time to retrieve such detailed information through long and complex supply chains like ours.
- The assumed availability of substitution (less hazardous alternatives with equal function): The maturity of alternative solutions to the use of PFAS is currently poorly understood within our sectors. Our suppliers are still investigating PFAS occurrences and alternative materials in parts they deliver to us and are not able to give us a timeline for phase-out.
- A clear risk of regrettable substitution: A switch to alternative solutions without proper investigations also comes with the risk of regrettable substitution from a broader sustainability perspective which needs to be avoided. Unfortunately, our investigations show that some of the PFAS (a minor part) used in our products was introduced through our work to phase out Chromium (VI).

In summary, a transition time of 18 months is not sufficient to phase out substances from our complex products with the required validations and verifications. If the draft regulatory text as proposed become final, we would not be able to place trucks, buses, construction equipment and marine- and industrial power trains on the European market from 2026/2027. We therefore request a derogation for:

Applications affecting the proper functioning related to the safety and reliability of transport vehicles, machinery, and marine power train systems, and affecting the safety of humans or reliability of equipment until 13.5 years after entry into force.

Volvo Group will update our response with technical and socio-economic information before the consultation deadline.

General Comments: Comments on exemptions for ETFE from PFAS proposal
After more than ten years of development, Jinhua Yonghe Fluorochemical Co., Ltd. has developed into a national high-tech enterprise specializing in R&D, production and sales of refrigerants and fluoropolymers. With an annual production capacity of 100,000 tons of refrigerants and 5,000 tons of fluoropolymer products, Jinhua Yonghe Fluorochemical Co., Ltd. occupies a leading position in China in the research and application level of key common technologies for manufacturing of organic-fluorine monomer, and the production technology of high-speed extrusion fluoropolymer.

Fluoropolymers are known as “polymers of low concern” as defined by the OECD. They are not high risk materials as they are not water soluble, not bio-available or bio-accumulative, inert, stable and non-toxic.

Persistence is not necessarily a health risk, the danger to human health is whether it can infiltrate cell. Scientific researches show that the high-molecular (molecular weight ≥ 100,000Da) fluoropolymers are thermally, biologically, and chemically stable, are insoluble in water, do not migrate, and are too large to infiltrate cell membranes (Barbara J Henry and et al, A Critical Review of the Application of Polymer of Low Concern and Regulatory Criteria to Fluoropolymers, Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management, Volume 14, Number 3, pp 316-334.). Toxicology of PTFE has been proven that fluoropolymers are not bio-available or bio-accumulative.
On the one hand, fluoropolymers can be used for twenty years, thirty years or even longer time in industrial applications, while the use of alternative materials will have to face the problem of frequent replacement parts for several weeks or a month. This problem will not only cause additional harm to workers, but also be detrimental to reducing carbon emissions. From the point of view of waste reduction, fluoropolymers should not be included in the scope of regulation. On the other hand, cost is the key driver in many industries. For example, fluoropolymers are generally used as hoses and pipes to transport engine and vehicle fluids (such as water, oil, bio-fuels) or gases (such as air, exhaust gases) in automobile industry, where requirements for safety and emissions are strict. Fluoropolymers are very expensive, so they are the last solution to be used only if no other technical alternatives are available.

ETFE is a copolymer of ethylene and tetrafluoroethylene. It exhibits outstanding chemical resistance to nearly all chemical substances, including strongly-acidic and strongly-alkaline substances. Stable mechanical electrical properties are maintained over a wide range of temperatures, -200 - +180°C. ETFE is used in harsh environment to provide high reliability and safety，which is difficult to be replaced by common polymer materials. Statistics show that the global PVC production capacity is about 62.8 million tons and the global PE production capacity is about 126.8 million tons, while the global ETFE production capacity is only one in ten thousand of that, at 15,000 tons.

Fluoropolymers or fluoroelastomers such as ETFE are widely used for sheating industrial cables of ships, trains, large machinery, motors and ironworks, as well as cables and harnesses used to control electronic devices installed in vehicles. These materials require high heat resistance, high flame retardant, flexibility, oil resistance, wear resistance and electrical insulation properties. There are no alternatives to fluoropolymers or fluoroelastomers, for instance, EPDM lacks heat and oil resistance, and the tensile strength, heat resistance and oil resistance of silicone rubber are insufficient.

Fluoropolymers coating are applied to pump and valve components such as casings, impellers, housing, and fasteners to them from chemical attack, corrosion, or abrasion. Fluoropolymers are used for sheating high-voltage cables of submersible pumps and valve actuators because they are resistant to UV radiation, have excellent insulating properties, and resistant to moisture and water absorption. Overall, the excellent chemical resistance and durability of fluoropolymers make them indispensable for pump and valve applications.

Carbon-fiber reinforced plastic (CFRP) is used for the material of aircraft because of its lightweight property together with high strength and modulus. CFRP greatly contributes to saving energy such as the fossil fuel in terms of the fuel economy improvement, so it is thought as a material which is extremely important now and for the future. The method to prepare CFRP is called “autoclave method”, which needs high temperature and pressure conditions. During the process, the release film is covered on the half-cured and so sticky article called prepreg, followed by heat cured in autoclave. The fluorine resin film has been used as release film because of its excellent mold release property and heat resistance.

Development trials of the substitution to cheaper resin films have been attempted repetitively before this PFAS restriction plan has been proposed because these fluorine resins are expensive. However, it is the current situation that changes to other materials are not yet done. As a reason, the autoclave method is necessary to secure reliability such as the mechanical strength for the CFRP used in aircraft, and the only films that can endure the autoclave method are the fluorine resin films.

As the pre-eminent light-transmissible building material, ETFE has the following advantages:
(1) practicality (saving in the quantity and substantivity of secondary structural materials, ease of upkeep and maintenance, supreme durability with no noticeable ageing problems, ease of erection and refurbishment when needed, complete recyclability of the membrane.)
(2) safety (flame resistance, light weight, no known record of human injures or sufferings through material disintegration or molecular volatility.)
(3) environmental sensitivity (sophisticated technologies to engineer the spectral transmission characteristics of the membrane spanning the solar radiation spectrum, in turn controlling the solar heat gain utilizing different structural formats and architectural design ingenuity, greatly reducing the air-conditioning load of the building interior)
(4) the energy consumption caused by frequent cleaning can be avoided due to strong and tough material properties, as well as wear resistance and self-cleaning.

Overall, there are no alternatives to fluoropolymers such as ETFE. ETFE is not bio-available and unable to migrate long distances. Therefore, we argue that fluoropolymers should be exempt from the regulation.

General Comments: Comments on exemptions for PFA(CAS NO. 26655-00-5) from PFAS proposal
Jinhua Yonghe Fluorine Chemical Co., Ltd. has developed into a national high-tech enterprise specializing in the research, development, production and sales of refrigerants and fluorine polymers after more than ten years of development. With an annual production capacity of 100,000 tons of refrigerants and 5,000 tons of fluoropolymer products, the company is in a leading position in China in terms of the research and application of key common technologies in the manufacture of monomers of organic fluorine and other polymers, as well as in the production technology of high-speed fluoropolymer extruding materials.
In order to analyze and respond to the proposed PFAS restrictions, Jinhua Yonghe Fluorine Chemical Co., Ltd. analyzed the PFA material and component industries that would be affected, evaluated material substitutes and impacts, assessed socio-economic impacts, as well as described the end-of-life process and recycling methods for PFAS components.
As a kind of fluorine material with higher added value, PFA concentrates PTFE and FEP and has various excellent properties. Therefore, PFA is not only widely prepared into corrosion-resistant parts, abrasion-reducing and wear-resistant parts, seals, insulating parts and medical equipment parts, high-temperature wires and cables insulation, anti-corrosion equipment, sealing materials, pumps, valves, bushings, and chemical containers, but also in the semiconductor industry has an indispensable role.
The PFAS Restriction Bill assumes that fluorinated materials such as PFA can be replaced in some areas by materials such as ethylene propylene diene monomer (EPDM), polyetheretherketone (PEEK), mica, polyvinylchloride (PVC), polyethylene (PE), ceramic-based materials, and so on, But in fact, this is not common sense, as the market price of PFA is significantly higher than the above materials, and it is unlikely that anyone would pay more to use PFA if it could be economically replaced by the above materials. From an economic standpoint, it is unlikely that anyone would pay more for PFA if it could be replaced by one of the above materials. This also explains the use of PFA material on specific occasions, because the material itself performance decision, for example, in the pump seal PFA material has excellent chemical resistance and temperature resistance and low friction, which helps to reduce energy consumption, to extend the service life of the pump, and to ensure that in the use of the process of higher sealing; And then, for example, in the pump diaphragm PFA material diaphragm is usually used to deal with aggressive chemicals or other fluids pumps, these fluids, these fluids can be replaced by the above materials, it is unlikely that anyone will spend more expensive to use the PFA material. Other fluids that can corrode traditional elastomer diaphragms. If the use of traditional materials, then the life of the equipment will have a significant reduction, not only increasing the risk of use but also making the use of materials increase, which is contrary to the idea of carbon emission reduction.
In addition, PFA materials are mainly used in the semiconductor sector, for which a comprehensive PFAS emission profile is not yet available. However, the average annual tonnage of the EU market for PFA materials over the last ten years has been 3700 tons/year, which includes materials used for both consumables such as filters, fluoroelastomers, drum liners, etc., as well as materials used for the production of PFA materials in the EU, which have a long-life cycle. This includes materials used for the production of PFA materials in the EU, which have a long service life (more than 10 years). It also includes some components required for production equipment such as pipes, valves, filters, tanks, etc., which are long life materials (more than 25 years). If substitutes for other materials (less than 25 years) are used, such as valves that need to be repaired or replaced due to high utilization, this will result in a large amount of waste material. The main reason for this difference is the change in chemical properties during use. Without the use of PFA materials, existing materials would no longer be sufficient for production and the entire semiconductor industry would be paralyzed. In addition, PFA is usually easy to recycle. If recycling is vigorously pursued, the amount of loss can be significantly reduced.
The unique properties of PFA materials, such as chemical resistance, temperature resistance, flexibility, low coefficient of friction, purity, non-flammability, etc., have led to thousands of applications in semiconductor manufacturing, where the precision and purity of highly complex equipment and a wide range of chemicals are required to provide advanced circuits with stringent regulatory requirements. The semiconductor industry has a long-standing commitment to greener solutions, including compliance with restricted materials regulations. However, the prevalence of PFA in this industry's application space, coupled with the lack of suitable alternative materials, makes PFA replacement technology an extremely difficult challenge. The bill only proposes a few possible alternatives and does not provide a detailed comparison and evaluation of the various properties and applications of alternatives and PFA materials, which can never be used as justification or evidence for banning PFA materials. On the contrary, this lack of detailed justification precisely illustrates the indispensable position of PFA in semiconductor manufacturing today.
In summary, PFA should not be included in the control of PFAS

Content: Information on alternatives Request for exemption
Org. name: Shaowu Yonghe Jintang New Materials Co., Ltd.
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Comments on exemptions for PVDF from PFAS proposal
Shaowu Yonghe Jintang New Material Co., Ltd. is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Zhejiang Yonghe Refrigeration Co., Ltd. and specializes in manufacturing fluorinated refrigerants and fluoropolymer products.
PFOA/PFOS substances have a significant impact on human health due to their persistence, bioaccumulation, and toxicity. As a result, the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) has proposed the PFAS Restriction Bill, which we strongly support. We appreciate the efforts of the relevant parties in implementing this bill, which includes over 10,000 substances. Also, considering the environmental and human health risks associated with PFAS substances, we agree that it is essential to impose uniform restrictions and controls on them. Nevertheless, we regret that fluoropolymer products are included in the list of restricted substances. We advocate for the exclusion of fluoropolymer products from the scope of this restriction bill for the following reasons:

1. The Bill categorizes more than 10,000 substances based on their chemical structure and regulates them under the same standard, considering their PBT properties. While we acknowledge that the potential hazards of these substances may not be equal, it is important to note that some substances, like PFOA, have clear hazards while others may have less understood risks. It is our belief that generalizing such a wide range of substances solely based on their persistence without a complete understanding of the hazards of PFAS substances covered by the bill is unreasonable, unscientific, and unsupported. In 2022, an independent panel of experts conducted a study and reached a consensus that "all PFAS" should not be classified together. They highlighted that persistence alone is insufficient for grouping PFAS for human health assessment purposes, and appropriate subgrouping should be done on a case-by-case basis. Furthermore, the panel members agreed that assuming substances in different PFAS groups have the same toxicity is inappropriate. (Reference: J.K. Anderson et al. Grouping of PFAS for human health risk assessment: Findings from an independent panel of experts [J]. Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology, 2022,134,105226.  https://doi.org/10.1016/j.yrtph.2022.105226). In addition, we note that Article 68 of the European REACH Regulation defines "restriction" as "a means of protecting human health and the environment from unacceptable risks posed by chemical substances." It is, therefore, necessary to assess whether each of the more than 10,000 substances in the current legislation poses an unacceptable risk. In this regard, we support the opinion of the Fluorochemicals Council of Japan (FCJ) that a "blanket control" of more than 10,000 organofluorocarbons (PFAS) is an excessive measure. Instead, PFAS should be evaluated according to their subcategories (compounds), and the risk of each substance should be quantitatively assessed and discussed. Only those PFAS for which a clear risk is recognized should be included in the control measures. For more details, please refer to the unclassified annex: https://www.cfcpj.jp/pdf/FCJ_Comment_on_PFAS_submission.pdf.

2.As stated in justification 1, there is a need to evaluate and discuss the different classes of organofluorinated compounds. We believe that fluoropolymers do not possess the characteristics of PFAS as currently defined. The main concern of the draft, which encompasses all PFAS and/or their degradation products, lies in their exceptionally high persistence, surpassing the very persistent criterion of Annex XIII of REACH. PFAS and their degradation products are likely to persist in the environment longer than any other man-made chemical. Additional concerns include their bioaccumulation, transport, long-range transport potential, phytoaccumulation, global warming potential, and (eco-) toxicological effects. PFAS enter the environment through releases during production, use, and waste. A simplified explanation of the hazards of PFAS is that they exhibit PBT properties, namely persistence, bioaccumulation, and toxicity. Fluoropolymer materials possess numerous unique properties, such as durability, high mechanical strength, inertness, thermal stability, and resistance to chemical, biological, and physical degradation. Some fluoropolymers are classified as "polymers of low concern" according to the criteria for chemical stability, biostability/inertness, negligible solubility in water, non-bioavailability, non-bioaccumulation, and non-toxicity outlined by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) ( Henry, B. J., et al. "A Critical Review of the Application of Polymer of Low Concern and Regulatory Criteria to Fluoropolymers." Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management, vol. 14, no. 3, 2018, pp. 316-334, DOI: 10.1002/ ieam.4035.).  Regarding the aforementioned PBT properties of PFAS, fluoropolymers are only highly durable due to their chemical stability and chemical inertness. They do not bioaccumulate because they do not dissolve in water or get absorbed by blood tissues. Currently, fluoropolymer materials are widely used in the medical industry, including for many implanted medical parts. The stringent regulations within the medical industry regarding material safety demonstrate that fluoropolymers are deemed harmless to the human body, which is why they are extensively utilized. Therefore, persistence alone is not a sufficient reason to label fluoropolymers as dangerous. Of course, the bill also mentions the environmental hazards of degradation products, and it is undeniable that no substance remains persistent indefinitely. However, we need to analyze the situation on a case-by-case basis. Fluoropolymers are chosen precisely for their excellent stability, and they degrade very slowly under normal conditions. Hence, it is necessary to assess the quantities before considering the potential hazards. In the case of fluoropolymers, we should investigate whether the rate of degradation is fast enough to cause harm to humans and the environment. We believe that further assessment is needed to determine the extent to which the degradation products of fluoropolymers contribute to PFAS exposure.

3. We hold different attitudes towards the hazards of degradation products. Based on the research conducted by Brittany Trang et al. (Reference: Science 2022,377,839-845, DOI: 10.1126/ science.abm8868) and Ali Alinezhad et al. (Reference: Environmental Science & Technology,2023,57,8796-8807, DOI: 10.1021/ acs.est.3c00294), it has been found that low-temperature mineralization can degrade perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids. This degradation process can potentially be extended to degrade other perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances. Moreover, the degradation occurs rapidly and results in defluorination under mild conditions. These findings suggest that even fluorinated polymers may eventually degrade to trifluoroacetic acid (TFA). The effects of TFA on the environment have been studied extensively and described in more detail. However, we believe that TFA is not of significant concern in terms of its environmental impact (Reference: Photochemical & Photobiological Sciences, 2023,22,1129-1176).

Specific information 6
PVDF products are primarily used in lithium batteries, coatings, injection molding, water treatment films, and solar cell backsheet films. In the lithium battery industry, PVDF is mainly used as a binder for the positive electrode. It is widely utilized due to its excellent oxidation resistance and chemical resistance. Currently, hydrocarbon elastomers have been successfully used as binders for the negative electrode in lithium batteries. However, due to the higher demand for antioxidant materials in the positive electrode, it is not yet possible to replace PVDF with hydrocarbons. Doing so would have a significant impact on the battery's performance and safety. The PVDF is primarily used in the coating industry for corrosion resistance in construction materials, thereby extending the lifespan of buildings. Currently, attempts have been made to replace PVDF with acrylic resin coatings. However, regardless of how the formulation of acrylic resin coatings is optimized, there is still a certain gap in terms of lifespan compared to PVDF fluorocarbon coatings, which is determined by their chemical structures. Additionally, in terms of application costs, using acrylic resin as a substitute costs about 30-40% of PVDF fluorocarbon coatings. However, the lifespan of construction materials is significantly reduced, resulting in a substantial increase in the cost of building maintenance and wastage of construction resources. The accelerated weathering of buildings also poses certain safety risks. PVDF injection molded products are mainly used in industrial fluid transport, especially for some corrosive fluids or high-purity chemicals. This is based on PVDF's excellent mechanical properties, chemical inertness, and permeation resistance. If general-purpose resins such as PE, PEEK, PP, and other materials are used instead, their media resistance and aging resistance cannot be guaranteed. This not only affects the safety of the transported fluids but also increases the risk of high-purity chemical contamination. In the field of water treatment membranes, the only technical and commercial alternative to PVDF-based membranes is polyethersulfone (PES) based membranes. The key factors influencing the operation of the membrane system include membrane performance, energy consumption, maintenance, chemical cleaning, and membrane life (component replacement and waste generation). PVDF demonstrates superior comprehensive performance compared to PES membranes. Therefore, using PES membranes as an alternative would inevitably increase energy consumption, waste resources, raise operating costs of the membrane systems, and decrease the effectiveness of the treatment process, leading to adverse effects. The solar cell backsheet film requires extremely high weathering and aging resistance. Some solar cells installed outdoors are very difficult to maintain. Therefore, we hope to reduce maintenance frequency by improving the material's performance. However, if PET, EVA, or other materials are used to replace PVDF as the backsheet film for solar cells, the expected outcome is an accelerated aging speed of the backsheet, resulting in increased maintenance requirements and potentially even outdoor battery failure.

In summary, the alternatives to PVDF in various fields are unable to meet the material performance requirements in practical applications. The use of fluoropolymer products is expensive in terms of cost, making its substitution economically inevitable. However, there are still many applications where alternative programs are not feasible, indicating that fluoropolymer materials are not completely replaceable. We initially chose PVDF due to its durability, chemical inertness, and lack of degradation. However, these characteristics have now become a concern that needs to be addressed. We hope that relevant departments will carefully consider and conduct further assessments of fluoropolymer products, particularly in terms of their degradation rate and potential harm to human health and the environment. It is worth noting that the current scale of fluoropolymer use worldwide is relatively small, with an annual consumption of only 300,000-500,000 tons compared to the annual consumption of more than 50 million tons of PVC. Additionally, the stability of fluoropolymers significantly reduces the degradation of PFAS substances, which are known to have harmful effects. Considering the current scale of fluoropolymer use and the negligible cumulative amount of obviously hazardous PFAS produced by degradation, we believe that fluoropolymers should be excluded from the scope of control under the Restriction Bill.
