NiKKi Fron Co., Ltd.

We have been molding and processing fluoropolymers for 70 years, producing and selling various products for a wide range of markets including science, automobiles, and semiconductor manufacturing, and thereby contributing to socio-economic development of society.
The PFAS restrictions recently proposed by the ECHA would include linear fluoropolymers because of their persistent property. However, we do not yet fully understand their impacts on human health and the aquatic ecosystem.
The scope of the proposal would place every PFAS substance under a single category. By doing so, it would restrict any number of PFAS substances, of which risk assessment has not been conducted and thereby acceptable/unacceptable risks are yet to be identified. It would breach Article 68(1) of REACH.
We support the statements of the Fluorochemical Products Council of Japan (FCJ) and the Japan Fluoropolymers Industry Association (JFIA) included in Attachments 1 and 2.

Annex XV1.1.4.9. "Oligomeric and Polymeric PFASs notes that there is concern about the effects of pyrolysis products on human health. Also, Annex XV1.1.5.6. "Emissions Conclusions notes that we do not understand well the effectiveness of incineration to destroy PFAS as well as a tendency to form fluorinated or mixed halogenated organic by-products. We recognize the ECHA's concerns from a material chemistry perspective, and if recycling or complete destruction of fluoropolymer waste is legally mandated, as was in the case of Fluorine gas regulation, we will follow such policies. Also as a company, we are attempting to reduce waste by developing technologies to recycle PTFE waste generated during production processes.

1. Products Containing PFAS for Which We Propose Regulatory Exemption
We request a broad range of our products (PTFE, PFA molded or machined products) including both in-house and OEM to be exempt from, as they are yet to be risk-assessed. As described below, we, as a manufacturer, would face extreme difficulties in offering material solutions, if the following substances and product applications are to be substituted:

Substance name: PTFE
Product name: Diaphragm (Diaphragm valve parts)

2. Diaphragm Valve Structure and Features
Diaphragm valves generally consist of a flow path gated by a diaphragm (membrane) made of flexible material such as rubber.
The basic structure of the valve consists of three parts: "actuator," "diaphragm," and "body," as shown in Attachment 3. Fluid flow is controlled by pressing and releasing the diaphragm against the sealing section inside the body.
Features of the valve are listed below. Based on these features, diaphragm valves are chosen for the fields/applications listed in section 3.

① The actuator is isolated from the line by the diaphragm and the diaphragm is airtight.
② Excellent washability with little liquid accumulation
③ Easy to disassemble and maintain
④ By using fluoropolymer for diaphragm and lining, the valve can achieve excellent corrosion and chemical resistance.
⑤ Compared to other types of valves, this simple structure has fewer parts and is more environmentally friendly.

3. Fields Where PTFE Diaphragms Are Used / Applications
• Chemical industry / acid-alkaline processes, corrosive fluid transfer processes, electrolysis treatment facilities
• Water deionization equipment / water lines (to prevent contamination such as by a rubber diaphragm)
• Pharmaceutical production / bioprocess liquid transfer line, CIP equipment*1, SIP equipment*2
• Food production / lines for fermentation equipment, acidic and alkaline processes, filling equipment
• Semiconductor manufacturing equipment / flow control valves in wafer cleaning equipment
• Steel industry / chemical lines for industrial water supply and wastewater treatment for steelmaking, pickling lines for plating solutions
*1 CIP equipment: CIP stands for Cleaning in Place. Cleaning solution is sent through a line to clean it without disassembly.
*2 SIP equipment: SIP stands for Sterilization in Place. Steam or other disinfectant is sent through a line to sterilize it without disassembly.

4. Diaphragm Material Selection
A material selection chart for each chemical and heat resistance condition is attached (Attachment 4). Diaphragms must have excellent flexibility and are commonly made of rubber-based materials such as natural rubber (NR), chloroprene rubber (CR), isoprene rubber (IIR), nitrile rubber (AB), ethylene-propylene rubber (EPDM), and others. These materials are not well-suited to certain applications with strict chemical resistance and heat resistance requirements (as indicated by △ and ✕ ratings in Attachment 4), and therefore PTFE (TX) is specified for such cases. Because it is more expensive than rubber, PTFE is only chosen when strictly necessary. Among non-rubber plastic materials, PTFE’s flexibility is exceptional.

For example, where 5% hydrochloric acid cleaning is to be performed in pharmaceutical or chemical production lines, PTFE is selected because rubber-based materials cannot be used at temperatures above 80 Celsius due to insufficient heat resistance. Where 1% sodium hypochlorite cleaning is to be performed in food production lines, only PTFE (TX) diaphragms can be used at 36 degrees Celsius or higher. Where fluoric acid cleaning is to be performed in semiconductor manufacturing applications, only PTFE (TX) diaphragms can be used at all temperatures. PTFE is also the diaphragm material of choice for semiconductor manufacturing and deionized water applications because purity is required to avoid metal ion contamination as much as possible. We have not found comparable purity data for rubber materials.
In these diaphragm operating environments, flexibility is an indispensable element, and switching to a material with insufficient flexibility would impair function, resulting in damage and serious accidents.

5. Petition to Exempt Selected PTFE Diaphragm Applications from PFAS Regulation
For the use of food contact in industrial production, a 6.5-year time-limited derogation is proposed under RO2 6a. For these use cases, no materials other than PTFE are rated ○ or ◎ in the material selection table in Attachment 4, and as such we recommend an indefinite exemption for PTFE for this application.
In medical applications, a time-limited derogation is proposed under RO2 6 for some medical devices, but no exemption is proposed under RO2 for chemical lines in medical manufacturing. For these use cases, no materials other than PTFE are rated ○ or ◎ in the material selection table in Attachment 4, and as such we recommend an indefinite exemption for PTFE for this application.
No derogations are proposed under RO2 for chemical line applications of the chemical industry and steel industry applications. For these use cases, no materials other than PTFE are rated ○ or ◎ in the material selection table in Attachment 4, and as such we recommend an indefinite exemption for PTFE for this application.
For use in semiconductor manufacturing processes, a 13.5-year time-limited derogation is proposed under RO2 5ee. For these use cases, no materials other than PTFE are rated ○ or ◎ in the material selection table in Attachment 4, and as such we recommend an indefinite exemption for PTFE for this application.
Deionized water processing equipment is used in semiconductor manufacturing, pharmaceutical production, and food manufacturing. Because there are no substitutes in terms of purity and sterility, we recommend an indefinite exemption for PTFE for this application.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Comments to ECHA on Proposed PFAS Restriction from IPEC-Americas

Members of the International Pharmaceutical Excipients Council of the Americas (IPEC-Americas) have reviewed the European Chemical Agency’s (ECHA) Annex XV Proposal to restrict Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs). IPEC-Americas wishes to submit the following comments on the proposed restriction regarding the impact to all ingredients used in the manufacture and processing of medicinal products.

The proposed restriction indicates a derogation that only applies to active substances in human and veterinary medicinal products within the scope of Regulation (EC) No 726/2004, Regulation (EU) 2019/6, and Directive 2001/83/EC. In addition to Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs), PFAS substances can be present in the API precursors, and other components of the drug product such as excipients, colorants, coating, adjuvants, etc. We recommend that all components of the entire drug product manufacturing process be derogated from the proposed restriction.

A limited derogation for APIs will be ineffective in ensuring continuity of supply of existing drugs and could cause potential shortage of drug products due to reformulation, development, and testing costs if the derogation is not extended to all components of the drug formulation.  Medicinal products cannot be formulated without excipients.  Major formulation changes could require cost-prohibitive non-clinical (including the increased use of laboratory animals) and clinical studies to support safety and efficacy.  Appropriate alternatives for medicinal product components may not be readily available at the time of implementation of the restriction and in most cases, do not exist.

IPEC recommends that an approach similar to the precedence of the use derogation for medicinal products that has already been established in the recently proposed Annex XV report on intentionally added microparticles be adopted for the proposed PFAS restriction.  The use specific restriction in the microparticle proposal applies to human and medicinal products inclusive of all drug components.  A similar approach is justified for the proposed PFAS restriction proposal to avoid significant market disruption and drug shortages.

In addition to the components of the drug product, PFASs can be used in the production of APIs and in the manufacture of API pre-cursors, excipients, colorants, coatings, and adjuvants. PFAS substances are found in manufacturing and processing equipment and reagents, including equipment gaskets, protective coatings (i.e., to protect equipment from strong acids), filters, tubing, and lubricants. In many cases, there are no known substitutes for these items as they have unique properties, such as for corrosion prevention and contamination control. IPEC-Americas requests expanding the derogation to include equipment and chemicals used in the production of drug products, APIs, API precursors, excipients, colorants, coatings, and adjuvants to continue to support processing and manufacturing of medicinal products to prevent significant disruption to supply. Restricting PFAS substances used in the manufacture of pharmaceutical products could inhibit manufacturing operations in Europe.

Furthermore, there will be indirect consequences if a PFAS ban progresses for other industrial chemicals which are either used as excipients or are used to manufacture excipients, and which may not have derogations. In many cases the amount of an excipient used in pharmaceutical applications is only a small percentage of the main volume of these chemicals produced by a manufacturer and may not be able to be sustained for pharmaceutical use if the materials are no longer available for use in other industries. There may not be any suitable alternatives for these excipients since they are already difficult to source. The lack of availability of these industrial chemicals could contribute to the lack of availability of medicines that could be considered to be life-saving or life-sustaining.

In summary, IPEC-Americas requests that ECHA expands the currently proposed time-unlimited derogation for APIs to human and veterinary medicinal drug product inclusive of API precursors, excipients, colorants, coatings, adjuvants, and manufacturing equipment. Derogating the entire medicinal product will ensure continuity of supply is maintained within Europe with no impact to patients.

General Comments: Compounds where X is aromatic group should be added to the structural elements of compounds that are not subject to PFAS regulation

This opinion is added to the recently submitted opinion (reference number: 8533cde3-ceef-4cc0-b872-6b49191d24fc).

１．Usefulness of liquid crystal compounds with trifluoromethyl group bonded to aromatic group
As the applications of active-matrix liquid crystal displays (hereafter referred to as AM-LCDs) expand, the properties required of liquid crystal materials are also diversifying. Reducing driving voltage and response time are the most important for any drive mode. In addition, the reduction of driving voltage contributes to energy saving, leading to global environmental protection. Reduced response time contributes to improved display quality of AM-LCDs and enriches people's daily lives.
A series of liquid crystal compounds with trifluoromethyl group bonded to aromatic group can increase the dielectric anisotropy (Δε), which contributes to a reduction of driving voltage, while maintaining the temperature range at which liquid crystal display is possible (TNI), and decrease the viscosity, which contributes to fast response time.
One of the liquid crystal materials excluded from the definition of PFAS-restricted objects in the current ANNEX XV is 2',3,4,5-tetrafluoro-4''-propyl-1,1':4',1''-terphenyl (hereinafter referred to as 3-BB(F)B(F,F)-F). Data comparing the physical properties of this compound and 2',3,5-trifluoro-4''-propyl-4-(trifluoromethyl)-1,1'':4',1''-terphenyl (hereinafter abbreviated 3-BB(F)B(F,F)-CF3) in the same liquid crystal mixture are given in the European Patent Bulletin, 28 Pages 28 and 29 of the European Patent Gazette. (See Attachments (1))
The liquid crystal mixture containing 3-BB(F)B(F,F)-CF3 is significantly superior to the liquid crystal mixture containing 3-BB(F)B(F,F)-F in the property values (TNI, Δε and viscosity) intrinsically required for AM-LCD.
Structural elements with trifluoromethyl group bonded to aromatic group are therefore essential for liquid crystal compounds and are very difficult to substitute with compounds that do not fall under the definition of PFAS.

２．Environmental impact assessment of compounds proposed to be exempt from PFAS regulation
It is a prerequisite for liquid crystal compounds for AM-LCDs to be persistent, as stable display on the display is required. However, if the liquid crystal compounds are released into the environment, it is desirable that there is no impact on the ecology.
In this study, we propose that compounds where R is a cyclohexyl group and X is an aromatic group should be added to the definition of structural elements that are exempted from the PFAS regulation in ANNEX XV.
A compound with both of these structural elements is trans-4-{[3,5-difluoro-4-(trifluoromethyl)phenoxy](difluoro)methyl}-trans-4'-propyl-1,1'-bi(cyclohexyl) (hereinafter abbreviated as S510).
The results of a test on the concentration of the chemical in the bodies of fish and shellfish conducted in accordance with OECD Chemical Guidelines No.305 for S510 and the test facility's certificate of compliance with the GLP standard are presented in Attachments (2) and (3).
The report shows that the enrichment factor (BCF value) of S510 is less than 50-fold throughout 28 days, confirming the low bioaccumulation potential of compounds with these structural elements.
We therefore propose that compounds where R is a cyclohexyl group in the definition of the structural element of the compound and compounds where X is aromatic group should be added outside the PFAS regulation.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Compression Packings are used to seal shafts, stems, and spindles on various types of static or dynamic industrial process equipment. Examples include valves, centrifugal pumps, plunger pumps, mixers, agitators, vessels, and more. PTFE is used in compression packings in several ways:
1. As a blocking agent in low emission graphite valve packings.
2. As a fibrous or structural material for valve packings requiring fugitive emission tightness
3. As a lubricant/blocking agent for rotating equipment packings
4. As a fiber or structural material for pump and valve packings requiring high chemical resistance.
An immediate ban on PTFE would have an enormous impact on the environment resulting from applications where packings are used.
Low-emission valve packing:
Modern low-emission standards have been developed over many years and have become increasingly stringent. This increase in stringency has been accompanied by the development of new sealing materials and products by the sealing industry. PTFE has been a key material in this development process. The refining and petrochemical industries use primarily graphite packing because of the higher temperatures involved and the need for fire-resistant materials. Another requirement of these industries is compliance with local, national, and international fugitive emission standards. Pure graphite packings are not capable of sealing to the low emission levels required today. To achieve these low levels, blocking agents are added to the graphite. PTFE is a critical component of these blocking agents.
New sealing products take 5-10 years to develop. An immediate ban on PTFE in sealing products would mean a dramatic increase in fugitive emissions. The world would return to industrial emission levels dating back to at least the 1970s. This would have a major impact on the environment, and the climate targets currently being set by the European Union will not be met. Therefore, a grace period of at least 12-15 years would be needed to allow industry to develop new products with non-PFAS ingredients.
The same applies to the use of PTFE as a structural base material in low-emission valve packing.
Rotating equipment packing:
Compression packings are primarily used on rotating equipment where light chemicals and water-based media are sealed. In other rotating equipment where alternative sealing methods are not available, packings are still widely used to seal chemicals and aggressive media. Products for rotating equipment have also been developed over many years and the use of PTFE has become a critical component of the packing used in this equipment. A ban on PTFE would mean an increase in leakage. This leakage must be captured and cleaned in water treatment plants, which means an increase in energy costs. The industry needs at least 5 years to develop alternatives to get to the same performance level.

6. Missing uses: Substitution of PTFE is technically and economically most likely feasible but it will take the sealing industry considerable time to come up with alternatives that work as well as PTFE.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Context
The EU is planning a REACH restriction for a broad group of fluorinated substances, the so called per- and polyfluorinated alkyl substances (PFAS). The addressed risk is based on the high persistence of the compounds, resulting in potential accumulation in the environment and food chains.

Time-unlimited derogations have been proposed by the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA), such as for PFAS used as active substances in plant protection products, biocidal products, and human and veterinary medicinal products, as these are addressed under their respective regulations (1).

Here in this position statement, the life science and pharmaceutical industry is further emphasizing that the manufacture of Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (API) using polyfluorinated building blocks or raw materials, and the placing on the market of these APIs and medicinal products containing them should also include this time-unlimited derogation of the PFAS restriction that is under consideration. To make sure that the PFAS restriction does not negatively impact access to therapies critical for human health, this time-unlimited derogation should also include PFAS materials used in validated production processes, for the production of drug products, medical devices or for packaging.

Position
The life science and pharmaceutical industry, in association with industry groups, such as BioPhorum, and the BioProcess Systems Alliance, contribute by generating data and knowledge about PFAS and their uses in API and drug product manufacturing, to support a responsible and adequate use of essential raw materials and manufacturing equipment. The term PFAS is used in this position paper for any compound that is affected by any PFAS regulation.

The life science and pharmaceutical industry is committed to make a positive impact on the lives of human and animal patients, and to adhere to environmental regulations and other agreements. Sustainability strategies consider both social, economic and ecologic aspects of our operations. To identify this position, the raw material, starting material, manufacturing equipment, and pharmaceutical analysis portfolio has been investigated; specifying substances meeting PFAS criteria utilized by the life sciences and pharmaceutical industry.
 
The life sciences and pharmaceutical is aligned with the position of  EFPIA, representing the European Pharmaceutical industry, and AnimalhealthEurope, representing the Animal Health Industry (2). This position statement highlights supporting evidence for the exemption of the following category groups from the PFAS restriction, based on the detailed investigation of the drug development and commercial portfolio of its members:

(1) Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs)
(2) Starting Materials and Chemical Intermediates
(3) Auxiliaries and Production Materials
(4) Synthetic and Analytical Reagents
(5) Primary Packaging Materials

The life science and pharmaceutical industry is aware of their business impact on the environment. The industry members are engaged to implement preventive measures to monitor and reduce environmental impact and encourage a culture toward environmental protection, including materials containing PFAS.

Life science and pharmaceutical manufacturing sites are committed to select and use appropriate raw materials, to reduce water and energy consumption and to minimize emissions to the atmosphere and sewer; to use hazardous materials carefully and to prevent the occurrence of incidents and accidents. Sites shall as well reduce as much as possible waste generation and eliminate it in the most environmental friendly possible way.

Both polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) and polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) materials have been identified as critical for drug manufacturing and drug product sterilization, the overall life science and pharmaceutical industry has understood and aligned with the EFPIA request for exemption of these materials from the REACH PFAS restrictions for the following reasons:
• Essential with no alternatives: Alternatives to these materials are not readily available and may be detrimental to drug quality and yields. Protein therapeutics, such as recombinant proteins, enzymes and monoclonal antibodies would be most affected, impacting the economics of producing accesible quantities of therapeutics for human health.
• Definition too broad: Fluoropolymers, such as PTFE and PVDF, are large, stable, inert molecules, that are not PFOA, PFOS or other long-chained PFAS, nor can they be transformed into those substances. Fluoropolymers are distinctly different from other polymeric and nonpolymeric PFAS and should be separated from them for hazard assessment or regulatory purposes. Grouping fluoropolymers with all classes of PFAS for or structure–activity relationship assessment is not scientifically appropriate. Therefore, fluoropolymers should not be included in the ECHA restriction of PFAS, based on this differentiation and unique definition (3, 4, 5).
• Safe for the environment and human health: Peer reviewed research (6) indicates that fluoropolymers meet internationally recognized criteria to be considered “Polymers of Low Concern” (PLC) for potential risk to human health and the environment. Fluoropolymers are too large to cross biological membranes and therefore do not present significant concerns. In addition, fluoropolymers have been shown to have negligible residual monomer and leachable levels. Since fluoropolymers are insoluble in water, there is no negative environmental impact based on long-range transport.
• Further risk mitigation: Innovative manufacturing and degradation approaches have been shown to reduce the potential risk to operators and the environment.
• Highly Regulated for Pharmaceutical Manufacturing: Regulations are already in place and followed to limit the environmental impact of materials utilized to supply the pharmaceutical manufacturing industry
Environmental Considerations
The life science and pharmaceutical industry, including many raw, intermediate and starting material manufacturers, are subject to company generated, risk-based discharge limits for various chemicals, including PFAS. Whilst the concern with PFAS chemicals is persistence in the environment, controls are put in place to protect workers in manufacturing settings and to minimize emission to the environment. Given the management measures put in place to minimize worker exposure and emissions to the environment in production, the use of PFAS in the chemical synthesis of APIs, along with pharmaceutical starting and raw materials, especially fluoropolymers, should be exempt from any restriction.

Thanks for considering my submission and information.
Janmeet Anant
Independent Pharmaceutical and Biopharmaceutical Consultant
B.S. Chemistry; Ph.D. Pharmacology; Regulatory Affairs Certification (RAC)

Monica Cardona
Independent Pharmaceutical Manufacturing Consultant
25 years of biopharmaceutical raw materials and manufacturing experience

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Pharmaceutical and Biopharmaceutical manufacturing of medicinal products, such as vaccines, plasma-derivatives (i.e., clotting factors, IVIG, transfusions), immunotherapies, oncology products and cell/gene therapies for terminal diseases.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: MANUFACTURER PHASE: The two main fluoropolymers used are PVDF and PTFE. Companies in the industry have shifted to eliminate PFAS raw materials for the manufacturer of PVDF and PTFE. Suppliers are available that do not use PFAS fluorosurfactants in the manufacture of the PVDF and PTFE.  The regulation should restrict the use of these PFAS fluorosurfactant raw materials, since alternatives are already available.  USE PHASE: During use, extensive chemical characterization studies and extractable data indicates that no impact to the environment is evident from PVDF or PTFE, aligned with the fluoropolymer stability scientific literature. END-OF-LIFE PHASE:  Fluoropolymers, including PVDF and PTFE, have been shown to degrade completely when incinerated at greater than 800 degrees Celsius. Fluorinated gases, not considered PFAS, during the incineration are controlled by emission standards and systems such as exhaust filters. The regulations should require these practices, which are in place for many companies already.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: There are no PFAS emissions, when the fluoropolymers are incinerated at > 800 degrees Celsius. Other emissions, not PFAS-related, such as fluorinated gases, are controlled with facility emission standards and control systems (e.g. exhaust filters).

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: As stated, there are no impacts on the recycling industry, since these materials are likely contaminated with bio waste and must be incinerated.  If able to be recycled because of no contamination, then the polymers are recycled for use in other industries. The fluoropolymers themselves are extremely stable and do not have an impact on human health or the environment.

5. Proposed derogations: My position with scientific references cited focuses on exclusion of fluoropolymers, such as PTFE and PVDF, since they have no emissions in any life cycle phase and they are considered polymers of low concern (PLC) by the OECD. Therefore, tonnage and emissions information is not relevant.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Based on the referenced EFPIA position statement, the life science and pharmaceutical industry aligns with a time-unlimited derogation for medicinal products. The industry requests the same time-unlimited derogation for PVDF and PTFE used for pharmaceutical manufacturing (APIs, filtration for sterilization and adventitious agent removal, blister packaging and other critical materials), since (1) these fluoropolymers, PVDF and PTFE, are utilized for critical medicinal products, (2) Specific fluoropolymers, such as PVDF and PTFE, cannot be substituted because they are in validated approved processes for drug manufacturing and slight variations could affect the safety, efficacy and quality of complex pharmaceuticals; (3) Fluoropolymers have been shown to be of low concern for human and environmental health and the 38 fluoropolymers should be exempt from the PFAS restriction (approximately 10,000 total substances); (4) There are tight and high level regulations for the pharmaceutical, biopharmaceutical and medical device industry, such as bioreactivity testing (ISO 10993), Ph. Eur. guidance on plastic medicinal product containers, standards on chemical characterization and various GMPs and quality tests for specific APIs and drug products.

8. Other identified uses: As a leading industry consultant, I have researched over 25 years and understood that the development process for pharmaceutical manufacturing evaluates various different manufacturing tools and processes, including ones that contain fluoropolymers, such as PVDF and PTFE. These manufacturers look at various suppliers and options that are absent of fluoropolymers and contain fluoropolymers. The main decision point is based on selection of raw materials that result in drug safety, efficacy and quality as regulated by global agencies. If they can utilize more than one alternative, then they will do so.  However, in most cases, only one type of material and process is justified. Therefore, alternatives will most likely impact drug shortages of critical medicines if the restrictions include these fluoropolymers (e.g. PVDF, PTFE, etc.) used in pharmaceutical manufacturing.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: Degradation of fluoropolymers occurs as stated previously by incineration at greater than 800 degrees Celsius.

10. Analytical methods: Fluoropolymers are analyzed by multiple pharmaceutical and compendial regulatory standard, based on physicochemical and biocompatibility standards. These include ISO, ICH and European (EMA) regulatory standards on raw materials and pharmaceutical manufacturing equipment.  Recent updates include extensive chemical characterization and extractable standards, linked with toxicological assessments to verify patient and environmental safety.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Coop Danmark welcomes the proposal to restrict all PFAS as a group

Coop Danmark strongly supports the restriction proposal. This is our comments to the annex XV restriction proposal on PFAS.

The restriction proposal is essential. Chemical pollution is one of the main planetary crises and scientist suggest that PFAS in the environment represent a planetary boundary that has now been exceeded (Food Packaging Forum 2022). PFAS are extremely persistent and are harmful to human health. PFAS already contaminate our drinking water and food. PFAS also contributes to biodiversity loss (Sigmund et al 2023) and F-gases harm our climate. We need to address the problem with PFAS to stand resilient and competitive in the future, and no real change will happen fast enough without strict legislation. The PFAS restriction will also make it possible to safely recycle resources and enable a circular economy.

Based on the key concerns in the Helsingør Statement in 2014 (Scheringer et al 2014) we applied a precautionary principle in Coop Danmark. Since then, we have continuously worked to phase out PFAS and shifted our production away from them. We have learned over the years that it is possible to produce packaging and goods without PFAS, often without quality impairments or notable price increases. It is also our experience that, when you ban PFAS or other harmful chemicals, positive innovation happens. We have banned PFAS in e.g. packaging made of paper and board, cosmetics and personal care products, textiles, outerwear, shoes, home textiles and finally we offer our customers a broad assortment of PFAS-free frying pans and bakeware.

Coop Danmark’s key messages on the proposal to restrict all PFAS as a group:

1. It is possible to ban PFAS in paper and board at no extra cost and at the same time increase customer loyalty. In 2015 Coop Denmark banned PFAS in food packaging made of paper and board. We took microwave popcorn of the market because it was not possible to obtain popcorn bags without PFAS. The withdrawal of microwave popcorn resulted in massive media coverage, with more than a hundred positive press cuttings. Later, we were the world’s first retailer to launch microwave popcorn in PFAS-free bags. Alternatives to PFAS in paper and board packaging are available, but often surface treatment chemicals are not necessary - e.g. in popcorn and paper bread bags. We have not experienced price increases switching to PFAS-free packaging (Department of Food and Resource Economics, University of Copenhagen 2015). In our experience packaging makes up such a small part of the total product price that it has no or very little influence.

2. Alternatives to PFAS in textiles are available, but further innovation is needed. In 2015 Coop Denmark banned PFAS in textiles impregnation and switched to alternative impregnating agents, such as e.g. Bionic finish. Alternatives do not match PFAS-based repellents on all technical parameters (Danish Ministry of Environment 2015), but they represent viable alternatives to everyday consumer to move beyond the conventional use of PFAS and to continue taking steps to design and create innovative solutions and safer alternatives.

3. PFAS are not essential in cosmetics and personal care products. Coop Danmark has never allowed PFAS in cosmetics and personal care products sold under our private labels. Due to the increased concern about PFAS, we also decided to ban PFAS in cosmetics and personal care products from all branded trademarks in 2019. We struggled with large well-known brands, but today none of our marketed cosmetics or personal care products contain PFAS.

4. Food contact materials – PFAS in frying pans and bakeware. Since PFAS is firmly bound in the coating in frying pans and bakeware, we have not prioritized a PFAS ban in these products. However, we are aiming to phase out PFAS from these products as well, and we experience an increased demand for PFAS-free food contact materials.

5. It is expensive and resource demanding to be first mover. In Coop Danmark we feel an obligation to phase out and replace chemicals that are under suspicion for negatively impacting health or the environment. However, it is expensive and resource demanding to exceed legislative requirements. First of all, it can be challenging and time consuming to find PFAS-free alternatives in the market. Moreover, Coop Danmark expend extra resources on compliance e.g., explaining our test setup to suppliers and documenting products are PFAS-free. Getting suppliers to understand and comply with our requirements can be a challenge and not infrequently we find goods in our random sample testing that do not meet our requirements. A more restrictive legislation will not only benefit human health and the environment, but it will also remove an unnecessary compliance burden for responsible companies.

6. PFAS-free alternatives can be a market opportunity and innovation may create new jobs. If Europe and the European companies lead the transition to PFAS-free alternatives Europe may become the global leader on the market, where there is a growing demand for PFAS-free products. Also, innovation in PFAS-free products may create new jobs.

About Coop Danmark
Coop Danmark is a nationwide danish retailer with approximately 1,000 retail stores, a market share of 30% and 46 billion DKK in yearly turnover. Coop is owned by 1.9 million members and is a community based on responsibility, diversity, and involvement. Coop Danmark fight for a better and more sustainable everyday life for consumers.

Org. name: Copeland LP, including Copeland Europe GmbH and other affiliated entities
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Copeland believes the optimal approach to addressing fluoropolymers (including fluoroelastomers) in the REACH Per-and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) restriction proposal would be to fully exclude them from the scope of the restriction irrespective of the application in which they are used. This is due to their classification as polymers of low concern that are neither bioaccumulative, water borne, nor toxic. To the best of our current knowledge, they present limited to no risk to human health or the environment under normal use conditions and at end-of-life when proper waste management practices are followed. This differentiates them from fluorinated processing aids, some of which have been shown to be persistent, bioaccumulative, and toxic. It is believed that the invention and incorporation of newly developed safe, non-PBT, non-PFAS processing aids by many chemical manufacturers should largely address the concerns about the emissions of PFAS processing aids during the manufacturing phase of fluoropolymers. However, given that Copeland is not a producer of fluoropolymers, this submission does not comment on the appropriateness of providing a derogation for the fluorinated processing aids used to make fluoropolymers. We will also abstain from further discussion of a broad exclusion of fluoropolymers from the restriction proposal, as other public consultation submissions have already provided evidence that substantiates this position.
THEREFORE, IN THE INTEREST OF MORE CLOSELY CONFORMING WITH THE CURRENT RESTRICTION PROPOSAL, WE ASK FOR THE ADDITION OF A HEATING, VENTILATION, AIR CONDITIONING, AND REFRIGERATION (HVACR) USE SECTOR ALONG WITH A MINIMUM OF A 20-YEAR DEROGATION FOR FLUOROPOLYMERS (INCLUDING FLUOROELASTOMERS) USED IN THIS SECTOR, INCLUDING THOSE UTILIZED IN AFTERMARKET AND SPARE PARTS FOR EXISTING EQUIPMENT. THE REASONING FOR THIS IS ELABORATED UPON IN THE ATTACHMENTS TO THIS SUBMISSION. A SUMMARY OF THE KEY POINTS CAN BE FOUND IN OUR RESPONSE TO SPECIFIC INFORMATION REQUEST 6 BELOW, AS WE CONSIDER THE HVACR SECTOR TO BE A CRITICAL USE THAT WAS OVERLOOKED IN THE PROPOSAL.

6. Missing uses: Copeland has closely reviewed the REACH Annex XV Per-and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) restriction proposal and identified missing uses of PFAS that are critical to the EU. THE ATTACHMENTS TO THIS PUBLIC CONSULTATION SUBMISSION PROVIDE JUSTIFICATION FOR ADDING HEATING, VENTILATION, AIR CONDITIONING AND REFRIGERATION (HVACR), AS A NEW USE SECTOR TO FILL A CRITICAL GAP IN THE RESTRICTION PROPOSAL. Although the dossier does acknowledge the HVACR sector in terms of “refrigerant use” under the sector called “Applications of Fluorinated Gases (Annex E.2.8.)”, it does not acknowledge the equipment used within HVACR, nor the materials of construction used therein.  Furthermore, IT IS HOPED THAT THE INPUT GIVEN IN THE ATTACHMENTS TO THIS SUBMISSION JUSTIFIES GRANTING THE HVACR INDUSTRY SECTOR A MINIMUM OF A 20-YEAR DEROGATION FOR FLUOROPOLYMERS, INCLUDING THOSE USED IN AFTERMARKET AND SPARE PARTS. Even though the derogations described in the PFAS restriction proposal are limited to a maximum of 12 years (plus 18 months from entry into force), Copeland believes that there are grounds to provide a longer derogation for the HVACR sector. We understand that there is a regulatory precedent under REACH for this request, based on CARACAL discussions, even if based on the authorisation process (See Reference 19 in the non-confidential attachment included with this submission).  The key points justifying this request are: It is only derogating polymers of low concern; the emissions of fluoropolymers at end-of-life for the HVACR sector are manageable; there is negligible human contact with fluoropolymers during the use of HVACR equipment; and, no known alternatives to fluoropolymers exist that can provide equivalent performance in harsh HVACR operating conditions. To this last point, it is important to note that fluoropolymers enable the safe operation of HVACR equipment by significantly reducing the likelihood of component failures that could lead to the leakage of (often flammable) refrigerant.  Additionally, the HVACR sector is of significant socioeconomic importance, providing a variety of critical functions including but not limited to: refrigeration for perishable goods ranging from food to medicine; ensuring human comfort such as maintaining habitable temperatures in hospitals, homes, and cars; providing climate control, ventilation, and air quality in critical industrial processes that require extreme temperatures to operate; and, supporting the decarbonization of heating via electric heat pumps.  ALL OF THE ABOVE ITEMS ARE DISCUSSED IN FURTHER DETAIL IN THE ATTACHMENTS TO THIS SUBMISSION. Please do not hesitate to contact us should you have any questions about this submission.

General Comments: CPA (Chemical Pharmaceutical generic Association), the independent association of the Italian Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients Manufacturers Industry (API - Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients), represents a strategic sector of pharmaceutical chemistry which is also considered a global excellence.
CPA proposes the exemption, or time-unlimited derogation, in addition to the active pharmaceutical substances (API), already provided for in ANNEX XV - (Table 6), of the following substances:
a) Raw materials and intermediates constituting the chemical synthesis chain to produce them;
b) All substances involved in the synthesis of the active pharmaceutical ingredient such as e.g. solvents, catalysts, reagents, fluorinated gases and others as essential to this synthesis process;
c) All products under development (e.g. medicinal products used in clinical trials) containing APIs (PFAS) not yet authorized for marketing. It should be noted that the current text of the PFAS restriction does not provide for any exemption for research and development (PPORD = Process Oriented Research and Development) allowed in the pharmaceutical (and other) context by EC Regulation n. 1907/2006 (REACH);
d) Active pharmaceutical substances (APIs) produced in EEA (European Economic Area) but which for strategic/commercial reasons will not be used in EEA  but only exported to non- EEA countries. If this were not the case, these APIs would not benefit from this time-unlimited exemption and could not be produced in EEA with a significant economic and availability damage in non-EEA markets.

CPA deems the application of these time-unlimited derogations a necessary and compulsory measure to mitigate and prevent the inappropriate shortage of related medicines, which already fall within the scope of Directive 2001/83/EC (human), Directive 2001/82/EC (veterinary) and Regulation (EC) No.726/2004 (human and veterinary).

CPA also points out that:

 the development and/or supply of medicines in the EU would be severely impacted by the PFAS restriction as currently drafted, based on a broad definition of "PFAS" and the wide applicability and different uses;
 active chemical pharmaceutical substances (for human and veterinary use) fall within a specific regulatory framework and are subject to marketing authorizations under  Directive 2001/83/EC and Directive 2001/82/EC. Any limitation of the products covered by the authorizations and especially of those granted under marketing authorization would cause regulatory conflicts and economic burdens for the companies operating in the sector.

It should also be remembered that:
 substances belonging to the group of “PFAS substances” do not have common hazardous properties;
 the Restriction option, if it were to be applied, would have an impact on all chemical-pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical production since there are no alternative synthetic processes that can insert the necessary Fluorine atoms into the structure of the API molecule avoiding the use of Fluorine donor molecules similar to PFAS (e.g. PFAS reagents, catalysts and ligants or solvents) and this would lead to the serious and inappropriate danger of "shortage" of medicines throughout the European community.
 the economic damage, for the specific sector, would be very serious, severely impacting employment, the availability of medicines, Research and Development (R&D) and consequently innovation, as well as going against the new European political trends to eliminate or limit dependence on third countries;
 the Restriction exclusion option should apply to the entire supply chain useful for the production of APIs (raw materials, intermediates and approved active ingredients (API), solvents, catalysts and anything else included in the synthesis).
 if the Restriction option were applied, all the chemical, pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical production, of many APIs containing fluorine atoms, would be seriously compromised since the fluorinating ingredients and raw materials would fall within the scope of the restriction.
 The ban of API PFAS following the adoption of the restriction as described in the text of the document would have an impact on the pharmaceutical industry estimated at tens of billions of euros which will cause a devastating effect on the industry in terms of economics and drug availability. This harmful effect on the economy of the sector will also be supported by the fact that the production of medicinal products containing APIs (PFAS) and/or the production of medicinal products containing APIs whose production uses PFAS substances will be drastically moved outside the EU, where a restriction of the same magnitude is not required.
 the transitional period relating to the established replacement times (5 or 12 years + 18 months) is not suitable for setting up a technical replacement as the period only takes into account the R&D times but not the regulatory times for the different regulatory deadlines; i.e. mandatory clinical and stability tests. Furthermore, any change at the PFAS API level could require the need to resubmit the previous marketing authorizations for each single medicinal product already 'approved', which are in turn subject to different times and different regulatory indications.

Requests for exemption or derogation:
CPA requests a time-unlimited derogation for the PFAS raw materials and intermediates necessary for the chemical synthesis of the related APIs and as previously mentioned for all the substances used in the synthesis process as well as for the products subject to PPORD.

Note: a ban as foreseen in the restriction document would limit patients' access to medicines that are safe and approved in Europe (see Table A.110 Non-exhaustive list of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) following current PFAS definition, authorized as medicinal products) including treatments for cancer and for all pathologies that would require PFAS "drugs" for treatment, as well as for medicines indispensable in the "techniques" applied in intensive care and for which there is no alternative.

Furthermore, a ban as foreseen in the restriction document would move production and/or R&D outside European territory, creating a loss of scientific and economic know-how and increasing dependence on non-EU countries. Furthermore, patients would be exposed to unquantifiable damage when the supply chain were to be interrupted or clinical trials could not be conducted in the EU.

Any substitution would require regulatory efforts and a technical implementation which would result in an extension of authorization times, in an economic loss, in a loss of knowledge and in a dangerous dependence on third markets. This should also be considered to avoid disruptions in the availability of medicines.
Derogations should cover the entire pharmaceutical supply chain including raw materials, reagents, solvents, catalysts and disposable or multiuse equipment required for the production of pharmaceutical products or related processes such as quality control or diagnostic testing.
The exemption from the scope of the restriction should cover all approved medicines (human and veterinary) to avoid regulatory conflicts. This would include pharmaceuticals or medicines subject to valid market authorizations under Directive 2001/83 and other regulations.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: CTC is the Professional Committee for Economic Development of the French Leather, Footwear, Leather Goods, Gloves industry. CTC oversees a general interest mission for the benefit of nearly 850 French industrialists in the raw hides, tanning, footwear, leather goods and glove industries. The purpose of CTC is to support companies in developing their performance and in accessing new markets, from product design to marketing, considering the regulatory constraints of market access.

We globally agree with the assessment provided by the Dossier's submitter, the impact on business and employment losses of such measure should be controllable; alternatives exist in leather sector and seems technically feasible even though the impact on functionality is not clearly known yet.

Nevertheless, in our view several points of the proposal deserve a clarification or a reformulation:

(i)In paragraph 2, from the point of view of an article manufacturer, which concentration limit should be followed for an article to be placed on the market: 25 parts per billion or 50 mg of Fluorine/kg? Besides the large difference factor between the two limits, targeted PFAS analysis represents a considerable cost for articles manufacturers (hundreds of euros per analysis and per type of leather and finishing depending on the number of PFAS to be screened) which represent a heavy burden on tanners and leather downstream users. With the entry in force of this measure, it is expected that PFAS based chemicals will disappear rapidly from the European market after 2025; taking this into consideration it seems unnecessary to conduct trace levels analysis of PFAS on articles indefinitely. Instead, we recommend one specific concentration limit for substances in chemical mixtures and one specific for articles. For articles, the total fluorine proposed limit at 50 mg F/kg is enough to prove that PFAS treatment was not “intentionally added” in the articles during the manufacturing process included for the imported articles from outside EU (usually the level of total fluorine found in a PFAS treated leather or textile is in order of magnitude 500 to 1000 mg F/kg and above). On the other hand, trace level concentrations are more relevant to chemical manufacturers who need to eliminate PFAS entirely from their products per the logic of this restriction proposal.  For articles, the term “intentionally added” can be defined in the text, for example: “a chemical in a product that serves an intended function or technical effect in the product or product component …” in order to draw a line between the voluntary use of PFAS based chemicals in material processing and other non-voluntary source of PFAS contamination for which it would be impossible for article manufacturers to determine its origin. In our view, above reformulation is necessary to improve the efficiency and enforceability of this measure and to facilitate its implementation among article manufacturers, notwithstanding other restrictions already included in Annex XVII or other applicable Union legislation.

(ii) In paragraph 2, we shall point out that, as of now, no standard method exists for the quantification of total fluorine in leather matrix and the existing laboratory technics are not harmonised on this topic. Therefore, it is an absolute necessity for the respective European standard technical committees in charge of this work to propose a unique screening method for the quantification of total fluorine in leather matrix. Ideally the method should be simple to implement, rapid, economically reasonable as compared to a targeted PFAS analysis and available at the time of Entry in Force to facilitate its implementation for small scale enterprises and at a larger scale. Targeted PFAS analysis is complex to implement for small scale enterprises because there are countless PFAS, many aren’t classified and labelled in the data sheets of raw chemicals, some other degrades which complicates greatly their analytical research.

(iii)In paragraph 5 concerning the derogations, subparagraph b and c provide a temporary derogation for “textiles used in personal protective equipment” for specified categories of PPE. We would like to emphasize that technical leathers are also, just like textiles, used in the confection of fire protective equipment such as protective suit, gloves and footwear as well as for protecting workers against substances and mixtures dangerous to health. As such the proposed derogations in paragraph 5, subparagraph b and c should also cover "leather" material.

(iv) For some industries, the constitution of stocks happens several years before the entry in force of an Annex XVII restriction and even before the intention. To allow the industry to sell off legally these stocks instead of destroying them with the significative economical losses for the manufacturers and the consequences it has on the environment, it would be welcomed if the Dossier’s submitter could specify in its proposal that the scope of the restriction concerns “the first making available on the market”. It would bring more clarity to the scope of the restriction and align it with the definition of “placing on the market” given in the new regulation (EU) 2023/988 on general product safety, the Regulation 528/2012 concerning the use of biocidal products and even the ‘Blue Guide’ on the implementation of EU product rules (2022) where ‘placing on the market’ means the first making available on the market of a product. This suggestion could be also adopted for other restriction proposal in general where it creates article surplus losses which represent real economic challenges for the industries. In fact, the current definition of "placing on the market" in REACh regulation covers “the supply or making available of a product available to a third party”. Per this definition, how a manufacturer can destroy article stocks that do not comply with a restriction if he cannot transfer them to a company responsible for the destruction?

General Comments: Current end of life options for polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) water and wastewater treatment membranes include incineration and landfilling; however, due to the stable nature of PVDF, recycling is also a potential alternative.  PVDF hollow fiber membranes may be assembled into filtration modules with adhesive potting compounds and structural housing materials, but 80-90 percent of the hollow fiber membrane is typically not confounded by these other materials making the PVDF membrane portion accessible and attractive for recovering and recycling.  In this study, Solvay - a producer of PVDF - partnered with DuPont to evaluate the ability to recover and recycle PVDF from “end of life” ultrafiltration membranes used in drinking water treatment plants.

In an earlier submission to this consultation process (submission 28, number 6017), the preliminary material characterization results of the recovered PVDF material from end-of-life membranes were shared.  This report will provide additional information and an overall summary of the study.  These results support the potential for PVDF used in water treatment membranes as a suitable material for closed-loop or open-loop recycle processes. The end-of-life opportunity coupled to the evidence provided in the earlier submission further support the recommendation that PVDF used in water treatment membranes be given a long (more than 12 years) derogation.  Additionally, accommodations should be made to allow PVDF from membranes to be recycled.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The water and wastewater treatment membrane application of PVDF was not included in the Annex XV restriction report.  It is recommended to add this important sector and use and allow provisions for a long derogation for the use of PVDF.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: The attached document provides results of a study conducted to understand the feasibility of recycling PVDF from used water and wastewater treatment membranes.  The results show that recycle may be a viable end of life option.  Since PVDF is the main component of the membrane composition and falls under the definition of a PFAS, the concentration limits for PFAS set out in paragraph 2 of Annex XV for recycled materials would prevent recycling PVDF membranes leaving only landfill or incineration for end of life options if water and wastewater treatment membranes are given a long derogation from this proposed restriction.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: The attached report summarizes the analysis of PVDF after use for 5 years in a water treatment plant and the results do not show evidence of PVDF degradation after the 5 year use period.

The cost of treating the symptoms and diseasess that follows on a global public health level, and mitigating the trickle down effects due to the disruption of the biological system on earth, is incredibly high, to put it mildly.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Cyclic and branched perfluorocarbons with molecular weight of in the range 300-600 are widely used by especially oil and gas industry, but also in CCS and geothermal applications, as tracer to follow flow in subsurface porous formations.
These compounds satisfy all criteria for a reservoir tracer, especially important properties being stability in the harsh reservoir environment and detectability in extremely low concentrations. For the last two decades active research, sponsored by among others our organization, has been ongoing to identify other substances with lower GWP and acceptable environmental properties that can substitute this group of PFC, without success. Only other alternatives with suitable properties for the application identified have worse environmental effects (e.g. chloro fluoro carbons).
The information from tracer studies is important as a tool to optimize reservoir utilisation in both CCS/CCUS, geothermal and oil and gas. A good understanding of the reservoir can prevent drilling of unnecessary wells and cause less energy to be used for compression of gas used for injection, thereby significantly reducing the carbon footprint of reservoir operation more than the effect a worst case release scenario of the tracers could cause. For oil and gas application the fate of the tracers have been studied in detail in the EU project AEOLOS (https://cordis.europa.eu/project/id/ENK6-CT-2001-00501 ) that concluded that tracers following the gas phase are close to quantitatively co-combusted to fluoride and CO2 when the gas is utilized in gas turbines (0.01 % un-combusted). Furthermore, the small fraction of the tracers following the liquid phase of the hydrocarbons are also co-combusted  more than 99.5%. During the last 25 years R&D has also been driving the level of detection for these tracers downwards, resulting in a 100-fold improvement since the mid 1990ies. A lower detection limit requires less chemical to be injected, and today typical consumption of gas tracer is in the order of 0.5-20kg, compared to tens to hundreds of kg 25 years ago. Combining this reduction with the results from the AEOLOS and the focus on zero discharge of hydrocarbon gases through e.g. reinjection results in typical discharges from the usage as hydrocarbon reservoir tracer will be in the gram range per project. 20 kg injected will result in 100 gram un-combusted (worst case) if a worst case of 100% recovery of injected gas is assumed. The GWP-100y of the tracers are around 7000 relative to CO2 (ref AEOLOS report) resulting in a carbon footprint of a tracer project of 0.1kgx7000 = 0.7 ton of CO2 corresponding to ~3500km by gasoline car or 1.7 bbl of oil.
In CCS the tracers are utilised to confirm safe storage of the permanently sequestered CO2. With the extreme sensitivity of detection of the tracers, reservoir integrity (leak through cap rock) and well integrity (leaks from well head, flowlines, plugged and abandoned wells etc.) can be detected and remediate actions can be put in place. Detection of such leaks using tracer methods are more sensitive than detection of the CO2 itself and is not subject to background variations (as stable isotope ratios and direct measurement of CO2 are), resulting in tracers being able to give an early warning of leaks and thereby reduce the CO2 released. As a permit for CCS with underground storage is granted under the consideration of permanent disposal, any tracer injected with the CO2 should also be permanently stored and use of tracer in these types of applications are hence not expected to result in any discharge of tracer to atmosphere/environment. During injection operation, the tracer is kept in a closed system, ensuring no discharged during injection operation. In the highly unlikely scenario that a CO2 storage is leaking, the value of the tracer information is given above, with the enhanced detection limit of tracer explained above the concentration of tracer in the stored CO2 is typically in the range of 1E-10 to 1E-08 gram per standard litre of CO2. Again considering a GWP-100y of ~7000, and 1000 litre of CO2 corresponding to 1.84kg, the added GWP by the tracer relative to the leaked CO2 would be (worst case): 1E-08 g/l x 1000 l CO2 x7000 (GWP) /1.84kg = 0.0038 %. The benefit of being able to detect a CO2 leakage from a storage site should be considered larger than the insignificant added carbon footprint of the tracer.
The tracers also have application in geothermal reservoirs in which they are used to trace steam through the geothermal reservoirs. The tracer data provides information about the flow channels through the reservoir and will help optimize operation so that zones are not cooled down to quickly which could result in wells being abandoned and new wells drilled and completed with associated carbon footprint

Components contain CF3-X are today used as water tracers and will fall within the new proposal to prohibit certain fluorinated molecules. These chemicals are not partitioning to gas or oil, they are only following the water (no emission to air). Water is injected to keep the high pressure and replace the oil in oil reservoirs. Thereby most of the injected water is left in the reservoir and thus also the water tracer. Seldom more than 10-15 % of the injected tracer is produced. In addition, today most of produced water is reinjected and thereby also the water tracers are reinjected into the reservoir to avoid discharge. Down towards zero water tracer is therefore produced and discharged.

Annual use of these components is around 400 kg, as described above most of it is left in the reservoir due to reinjection and there is no emission to the atmosphere, as this is not moving in the gas or oil phase.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Daikin Chemical Europe welcomes the opportunity to submit comments to the REACH restriction proposal on all PFAS.

PFAS materials find applications in various batteries, including lithium-ion batteries (LiB), where they constitute a significant component.
This submission presents robust technical evidence for specific materials and their applications within LiBs. As illustrative instances of missing uses in the proposed PFAS restriction, we have included this information in Section IV, as non-confidential documents. Enclosed documents consist of a list of missing uses and three comprehensive evaluations of specific materials. In conjunction with these, we formally request your consideration for a time-unlimited derogation that encompasses the broader category of Li-ion Batteries as a whole.

Outlined below are three executive summaries offering a comprehensive evaluation of gasket materials, binders, and electrolytes utilised in LiBs. However, these summaries are not exhaustive and are intended to illustrate the wider scope. These findings together emphasize the fundamental significance of attaining a time-unlimited derogation encompassing all Li-ion Battery applications. This approach is essential to guarantee the enduring safety, reliability, and performance of LiB systems in diverse applications.

1. Gasket Materials for LiBs: The executive summary highlights the supremacy of Perfluoroalkoxy (PFA) as a gasket material for LiBs. Alternative materials, such as Ethylene Propylene Diene Monomer (EPDM), Polypropylene (PP), and Polybutylene Terephthalate (PBT), were found inadequate in replicating PFA's impermeability, sealing properties, and resistance to degradation. PFA's unique attributes contribute significantly to battery safety and operational longevity. Thus, we urge time-unlimited derogation for the usage of PFA gasket materials.

2. Binders for LiBs: Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVdF) emerged as the optimal choice for cathode binders in LiBs, surpassing non-perfluorinated alternatives. PVdF exhibited exceptional coatability, electrolyte resistance, adhesion, long-term reliability, and processability. The comprehensive suitability of PVdF sets a new standard for binder performance, enhancing battery manufacturing processes and overall lifespan. We advocate for time-unlimited derogation for the implementation of PVdF binders.

3. Electrolytes for LiBs: The application of PFAS in electrolytes offers remarkable potential for enhancing LiB performance, safety, and stability. PFAS material, such as 1,1,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl 2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropyl ether (D2), has shown positive impacts on oxidation resistance, cycle capacity retention, and gas suppression. We emphasise the critical role of PFAS materials in advancing battery technology and recommend time-unlimited derogation for their incorporation in LiB electrolytes.

In conclusion, the collective insights from these executive summaries underscore the significance of employing PFA gasket materials, PVdF binders, and PFAS electrolytes without time-limited derogation. By doing so, we ensure the sustained safety, reliability, and performance of LiB systems, thereby contributing to the evolution of energy storage technologies.

To address the potential socio-economic impacts resulting from PFAS regulations on lithium-ion batteries, it is important to emphasise the complex role PFAS plays in battery technology, as highlighted by the Battery Association of Japan (BAJ). We support that quoted Table (Fuji Keizai Report) regarding Lithium-ion. Fluoropolymers have implications well beyond the battery sector and require a balanced and thoughtful strategy. In addressing the potential socio-economic impacts stemming from PFAS restrictions on lithium-ion batteries, it is imperative to underline the complex role that PFAS plays in battery technology, as underlined by the Battery Association of Japan (BAJ). A full ban on PFAS-containing fluoropolymers has implications that reach far beyond the battery sector, necessitating a balanced and thoughtful strategy. BAJ's perspective highlights the complexity involved in finding viable alternatives to PFAS-containing materials. These potential economic consequences could be substantial, placing battery-related enterprises at risk of significant losses, equivalent to a substantial fraction of the global market valuation.
A particular area of concern centres around lithium-ion batteries, which serve as the backbone of modern technology and green energy solutions. These batteries power essential devices such as smartphones, laptops, and contribute indispensably to the success of electric vehicles (EVs) and energy storage systems. A delay in advancing lithium-ion battery technology, precipitated by PFAS restrictions, might severely hinder the progress of EV adoption and the expansion of renewable energy. This is in contradiction to the objectives of initiatives like the European Green Deal and could inadvertently contribute to raise carbon dioxide emissions.

We kindly request your consideration of our proposals above and appreciate the opportunity to discuss this matter further.

General Comments: Dana is a production and development company that is focused on sealing technologies in the combustion engine and in new energy relevant products like bipolar plates for Fuel Cell, Electrolyzer, and Flow Battery. Core unique technology in these products are the seal where Dana is an expert. The EU part of Dana represented as Reinz Dichtungs GmbH in Neu-Ulm Bavaria has a sales turnover higher then 300Mil€ and around 1.250 employees. 70% of the current sales turnover are connected to FKM type rubber as the focus of Dana is on high end technical applications.
Dana use two main technologies for sealing. Metal Bead Seal where rubber is used in thin coatings up to 30µm to give outstanding microseal properties and injection molding of rubber beads for seals with higher dynamical load. Mainly the used rubber in these applications are FKM types as they only fit to the technical specifications of the different applications. A sealing joint always consists out of the seal itself, the clamping system, mechanical properties of the joint, load and temperature profiles and the machined or casted sealing surfaces. This makes a sealing system very complex, and it needs a lot of effort to develop and evaluate such a joint. All the FKM material for sealing is cured to get strong mechanical properties and bound to mainly metal sealing surfaces to hold the FKM seal in place for function. A functional sealing joint will not release PFAS to the environment. In general, the volumes of FKM per seal are very low.
Examples FKM rubber usage:
- Automotive 4 Cylinder Cylinder Head Gasket with FKM Coating: 2,4 g/car
- Heavy duty 6 Cylinder in line Cylinder Head Gasket with injection molding total usage including technical scrap: 68 g/vehicle.
- FC Metal Bipolar Plate with FKM Coating: 0,15 g/plate
- FC Stack with 300 Metal Bipolar Plates: 44,4 g/car
From our experience and material knowledge of such joints, Dana can clearly state, if FKM types get banished as a sealing material all sealing joints need to be reviewed and new developed, also core boundaries of the applications as temperature or power density needs to be adapted. This will end in less efficient and durable joints for combustion engines and new energy application.
As known, temperature and media (Oil, Coolant, Chemicals) resistance are the main drivers for FKM applications. In new energy applications an additional driver is hydrogen permeation that can be decades lower by FKM then by other used material. All these outstanding characteristics force the usage of FKM even at the high price level that is related with FKM. Replacing FKM may also have the consequence to add CRM type materials into production, with higher health risks for employees.
The main impact of a less durable joint in cylinder head gaskets or similar applications are the driver safety and environmental aspects. By the construction and packaging of new engines the early detection of initial leaks in regular maintenance is complicated. If a leak occurs, the oil and coolant will be released to the environment. In case of a critical leaking joint, the engine can overheat by losing coolant or loss of oil pressure. This will lead into a situation that the engine will be broken, and the car is forced to stop immediately which is a driver safety risk. If durability of seal joints is reduced such events are more likely to happen to the drivers.
For the new energy application focused on hydrogen, the permeability and function of the joint is in general a safety concern. In the system application with hydrogen the focus is to minimize the risk for an explosion critical environment. A joint with less permeation and higher durability is here a key safety factor. Permeation comparison see attachment. In addition to the traditional sealing function in Fuel Cell and Electrolyzer comes the challenge that the seal is not allowed to leach out any material that affects the membranes catalyst negatively.
The development of alternative materials at Dana are very specific and time consuming. In case of a coating or an injection molded material 3-5 years to develop a rubber formulation to TRL3-4 then ex-situ and in-situ validation will start in parallel and need also 3-5 years for TRL 6. If validation of the rubber formulation is not according to specification development needs to start at low TRL again. From experience we see a 6 year timeframe for basic development at Dana as a minimum. After basic material development Dana need to adapt the production lines that a running change on each product is possible. This is an extra effort as we need to run both materials over a longer time due to the complexity of the product portfolio. After this timeframe Dana can start with the customer specific development for each customer application separately from prototyping to vehicle testing. New design and tooling are needed to adapt the gasket to the new sealing material. Overall this timeframe will be between 3-6 years depending on customer and potential changes on other parts of the sealing joint. In sum 12 years is already a challenging time period to phase out FKM of current production. Considering the irritation in the supply chain in general and lack of experts availability in the market makes it more challenging.
All this efforts need to be financed out of the running business. As of today, we are not aware of any financial support for development from the EU or locally on this topic so far. This will negatively influence the global competitiveness of our products as focus in maintenance of the current business instead of developing new products and technologies. In addition, it will take capital to install FKM free capabilities in production. That capital is crucial in the new energy products like bipolar plates to enable this move into a carbon free energy environment.
Key Takeaway points:
- FKM is used for high end technical applications and cannot be direct replaced by a other material, an adaptation of the full sealing joint is most likely
- Minimum 12 year period for an controlled phase out FKM sealing materials is required
- Dana and the customer will have critical financial penalties due to this phase out
- Applications with replaced sealing material may run on lower efficiency due material restrictions.
