- Selbstverständlich möchte ich für mich, meine Familie, und vor allem meine Kinder, dass gefährliche, unter die PFAS Definition fallende, Substanzen gebannt werden, die sich in der Natur, beispielsweise im Trinkwasser, einlagern. Die weitere Kontamination muss schnellstmöglich gestoppt/vermieden werden. Dies ist aus meiner Sicht aber nicht mit einer völlig überzogenen breiten PFAS Beschränkung zu erreichen, die nicht die Merkmale einer Beschränkung, sondern einer Zulassung aufweist. In einer Beschränkung sollten alle Verwendungen zunächst weiter möglich sein, bis auf diese, welche explizit beschränkt werden. Hier ist aber per se angedacht die Herstellung, Vertrieb und alle Verwendungen „zu verbieten“, außer denen, welche explizit ausgenommen („zugelassen“) sind, und das nur für eine limitierte Zeit.

- Um alle Daten, welche während dieser und auch früherer Konsultation gesammelt wurden, zu sichten, zu bewerten und, falls erforderlich noch einmal zu verifizieren, gehen Jahre oder gar Jahrzehnte ins Land, in denen (aus meiner Sicht) keine sinnvolle, gesetzeskonforme Umsetzung stattfinden kann. D.h. eine weitere Kontamination mit gefährlichen PFAS findet in dieser Zeit weiterhin statt, während weiterhin über eine Beschränkung von ungefährlichen PFAS, wie Fluorpolymeren, nachgedacht wird, welche für viele Verwendungen essenziell sind und die für das Funktionieren der Gesellschaft zwingend erforderlich sind. Leider sind aus meiner Sicht nicht alle Daten, die in früheren öffentlichen Konsultationen eingegeben wurden, berücksichtigt worden. Wäre dies erfolgt, würden beispielsweise die Sektoren, die im Vorfeld von den Dossierübermittlern (unzureichend) definiert wurden, bereits vor der Übermittlung des Dossiers an die ECHA angepasst worden. Essenzielle und vielfältige Sektoren wie beispielsweise der Maschinen- und Anlagenbau und die Chemische Industrie wurden gar nicht oder nur unzureichend berücksichtigt und vorliegende Informationen zu Verwendungen ignoriert. Dies lag sicherlich an der schwierigen Zuordnung vorliegender Informationen, da diese natürlich (auf Grund von ungeeigneter Sektor-Struktur der Konsultationen) über diverse Sektoren verteilt eingetragen worden waren. Die Übermittelnden hatten vielfach keine Möglichkeit die Informationen sinnvoll einzuordnen, da diverse Produkte in keine der Kategorien richtig oder ausschließlich einzugruppieren waren. Weiterhin ist es zu befürchten, dass viele essenzielle Verwendungen bisher nicht identifiziert wurden, da bis heute viele Betroffene (vor allem SME) nicht oder nicht ausreichend von der geplanten Beschränkung wissen und sich daher bisher nicht beteilig haben. Diese haben in der Regel nicht die Möglichkeiten, viele Kapazitäten aufzuwenden, um erforderliche Informationen zu sammeln, um sich an der Konsultation zu beteiligen. Auch ist es aus meiner Sicht ziemlich wahrscheinlich, dass in vielen EU Mitgliedsstaaten das Thema nicht ausreichend bekannt und diskutiert ist. Sieht man sich die ersten 50 Konsultationsdokumente an, welche die ECHA Mitte September veröffentlicht hat, so finden sich aus diversen Mitgliedsstaaten keinerlei Beiträge.

- Auch das Thema „Reparierbarkeit“ und „Handling von Ersatzteilen“ wurde gänzlich ignoriert. Auf Nachfrage bei Mitarbeitern der Baua, warum Ersatzteile nicht berücksichtigt wurden, hieß es, dass das Thema zwar diskutiert worden sei, aber dazu doch bitte mehr Informationen in der Konsultation zum Dossier übermittelt werden solle, da man da zu keiner Einigung gekommen sei. Dabei ist gerade das Thema „Reparatur und Verbesserung der Reparierbarkeit“ ein großes Ziel der EU. Neben der Verlängerung der Nutzungsphasen schnelllebiger Produkte, um den Müllberg zu reduzieren und Ressourcen zu schonen, ist es vor allem für Produkte, die Jahre und Jahrzehnte im Einsatz sind absolut erforderlich, dass diese weiter repariert werden können. Sieht man sich das Beispiel Automobile an, so ist es mit einer kompletten PFAS Beschränkung nicht mehr möglich diese zu reparieren und weiter zu betreiben, was zu immensen Mengen von Schrott führt. Das gilt auch für die Elektromobile, deren Herstellung ohne Fluorpolymere nicht möglich ist, das diese in Akkumulatoren als Membran zwingend erforderlich sind, bis es möglicherweise alternative, massentaugliche Techniken gibt. Das Verbot v.a. von Fluorpolymeren steht den Effizienzzielen und auch weiteren Zielen des Green Deal klar entgegen, da für High Tech entsprechende Hochleistungswerkstoffe erforderlich sind. Neben den Schrottbergen, die eine Nicht-Reparierbarkeit von Produkten mit sich bringt, führt dies auch zu einem immensen wirtschaftlichen Schaden für die Bürger, da dies einer Enteignung gleichkommt, wenn  Automobile, Maschinen, Alltagsgegenstände und andere Produkte die Basisanforderungen unseres Alltags erfüllen, von jetzt auf gleich  nicht mehr nutzbar sind und gänzlich Wertlos werden.

- Hinsichtlich des weiteren Funktionierens der Gesellschaft, aber auch für mich privat, mache ich mir beispielsweise Sorgen um die medizinische Versorgung. Viele heutigen Errungenschaften hängen mit der Verwendung inerter Fluorpolymere zusammen. Es ist zu befürchten, dass deren Nutzung nicht weiter möglich wird und die Krankenhausaufenthalte deutlich länger werden als es heute der Fall ist. Auch befürchte ich, dass Lebensmittel deutlich teurer werden und das bei sinkender Qualität. Durch Verwendung alternativer Materialien in der Lebensmittelherstellung und Abfüllung kann es zu Geschmacks- und Geruchsveränderungen und teilweise Kontamination von Lebensmitteln kommen. Die Robustheit gegenüber Reinigungs- und Sterilisationsverfahren ist in bekannter Form nicht mehr gegeben. Die häufigeren Wartungen der Anlagen und damit reduzierten Produktionskapazitäten führen zu steigenden Preisen der Lebensmittel. Ein Teil der Lebensmittelproduktion könnte zukünftig außerhalb der EU erfolgen was zu steigenden Transportkosten und vor allem vermeidbaren steigenden CO2 Emissionen führt.


- Weiterhin macht mir die Gesamtsituation der Industrie in Europa und letztlich auch die Zukunftsfähigkeit meines Arbeitsplatzes Sorgen. Bei einem kompletten PFAS „Verbot“ kommt es zu vielen Jobverlusten, vor allem bei den gut bezahlten Industriearbeitsplätzen, ich vermute weit mehr, als bisher abgeschätzt, da sich alles gegenseitig beeinflusst, so dass es zu einer Deindustrialisierung der EU kommt und die Industrie weitestgehend in die NICHT-EU abwandert. Wo sollen die Leute in Zukunft arbeiten? Wer soll die Steuern zahlen? Und warum?

- Darüber hinaus ist das allgemein anerkannt und akzeptierte Ziel – Europa im Jahr 2050 der erste Klimaneutrale Kontinent – dramatisch in Gefahr. Denn auch die dazu notwendige Technologie und Technik kann an vielen Stellen nicht ohne weiteres erstellt und entwickelt werden. Langjährige Entwicklungszyklen, die bereits durchlaufen wurden, um unter den aktuell geltenden Gesetzen zukunftsfähige Lösungen herstellen zu können, würden innerhalb kürzester Zeit Anpassungen und Überarbeitungen erfordern, die oftmals längere Zyklen umfassen, als die Vorgeschlagenen Übergangs- und Ausnahmefristen für PFAS.

- Eine gesetzeskonforme Umsetzung einer PFAS Beschränkung heißt, es muss ein risikobasierter Ansatz Anwendung finden, in dem Gefahren und deren Einfluss auf den Menschen und die Umwelt betrachtet wird und nicht ein „Verbot“ aller PFAS auf Grund ihrer persistenten Eigenschaften, wobei Persistenz (zu Recht) nicht als Gefahr definiert ist. Persistenz ist bei Werkstoffen eine hervorragende Eigenschaft, die eine Verwendung dieser ermöglicht, ohne dass die Umgebung negativ beeinflusst wird. Ohne persistente, oder besser inerte, Werkstoffe (und dazu zählen nicht nur Fluorpolymere sondern auch Rostfreie Stähle, Gläser, Keramiken und andere Kunststoffe) könnte beispielsweise kein Trinkwasser verteilt werden, ohne dass deren Qualität negativ beeinflusst wird. Denn mit einer so weitreichenden und tiefgreifenden Beschränkung führt auch im Falle eines völlig PFAS freien Endprodukts das PFAS-Verbot dazu, dass diese Produkte nicht hergestellt werden können, weil die Produktionsanlagen in aller Regel Komponenten enthalten, die durch die breite PFAS Beschränkung de facto verboten werden.

- Aus meiner Sicht sollte der Prozess neu gestartet werden

o Einteilung der PFAS in kleinere Gruppen
o Fokussierung auf die besonders gefährlichen Stoffgruppen
o Beschränkung zunächst der Anwendungen, die einen direkten Einfluss auf Mensch und Umwelt haben und für die es Alternativen gibt.
o Sukzessive Erweiterung der beschränkten Verwendungen, sofern ausreichende Daten vorliegen.
o Berücksichtigung der aktuellen Rückmeldungen
o Einführung einer machbaren Dokumentationspflicht für PFAS entlang der Lieferkette, um eine angemessene Entsorgung sicherstellen zu können.

Diese Maßnahmen führen aus meiner Sicht am Ende zu einer schnelleren Einschränkung gefährlicher PFAS und erhalten die Verwendung notwendiger PFAS.

Therefore, we demand for mechanical and plant construction: • a departure from the end-product-related exemption catalog, as this does not do justice to the range of industrial special applications. • that PFAS products can be used without restriction where they are permanently installed within machinery and plants and are thus already subject to disposal regulations. • that polymers "of low concern" may continue to be used. • that the supply of spare and wear parts for existing machinery and plants is possible indefinitely, especially since we consider the longevity of equipment to be a very important contribution to sustainability. All this until suitable substitutes are developed and industrially tested, and the PFAS content of imported products can be reliably determined, so that there is no distortion of competition. Because as long as this is not guaranteed and the regulation applies only within the EU, it will not have any effect. On the contrary: the regulation would fuel imports from less regulated economies and lead to companies closing or relocating, and production being moved out of the EU. We request appropriate consideration of our submission."

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Dated 18th August 2023
PFAS (per-and polyfuroalkylsubstances) Statement
Proposal:  A Time-Unlimited Derogation (Exemption) for articles containing fluoropolymers.
Scientific reasoning:
1) Fluoropolymers are a well-defined subgroup of PFAS, OECD (2015).
2) An article is defined in article 3(3) of the REACH regulation, ECHA (2017)
3) Fluoropolymers are highly stable (Persistent), Henry, B.J et al. (2018).
4) Fluoropolymers are non-toxic, Henry, B.J et al. (2018).
5) Fluoropolymers are not mobile, Henry, B.J et al. (2018).
6) Fluoropolymers meet the requirements to be defined as Polymers of Low concern (PLC), OECD (2009)
7) It has been determined that fluoropolymers do not meet all the Persistent Bio-accumulative Toxic (PBT) criteria, Henry, B.J et al. (2018).
Summary of Statements:
“Article 3(3) of the REACH Regulation defines an article as “an object which during production is given a special shape, surface or design which determines its function to a greater degree than its chemical composition.”” https://echa.europa.eu/documents/10162/2324906/articles_en.pdf
“Fluoropolymers are distinctly different from other polymeric and nonpolymeric PFAS and should be separated from them for hazard assessment or regulatory purposes. Grouping fluoropolymers with all classes of PFAS for “read across” or structure–activity relationship assessment is not scientifically appropriate” https://doi.org/10.1002/ieam.4035
“Polymers of low concern are those deemed to have insignificant environmental and human health impacts. Therefore, these polymers should have reduced regulatory requirements.” ENV/JM/MONO(2009)1:Page 10
“Fluoropolymer data developed for other regulatory needs support the predictive value of the PLC assessment criteria and demonstrate the low hazard potential of this class of PFAS. Due to their physical–chemical properties, PLCs are not bioavailable to cause toxicity or to bioaccumulate. Toxicity study data on PTFE in the Supplemental Data (p 15–27), for example, demonstrate a lack of toxicity, including genotoxicity. Although fluoropolymers are persistent, they are not bioaccumulative or toxic and therefore do not meet the PBT criteria.”  https://doi.org/10.1002/ieam.4035
Conclusion:
It is our contention that, during their in-use lifecycle, articles containing fluoropolymers have an insignificant impact on both the environment and human health, and thus fluoropolymers as defined by the OCED do not fulfill the requirements of a PBT substance while in use.
Therefore, while further investigation of the manufacturing and disposal cycle of fluoropolymers maybe required, we propose a Time-Unlimited Derogation (Exemption) for articles containing fluoropolymers.

General Comments: De Dietrich Process Systems GmbH is the German subsidiary of the globally positioned De Dietrich Process Systems Group. Our expertise is the manufacture, development and marketing of apparatus and equipment made of corrosion-resistant materials for the chemical and pharmaceutical industries. We are the global market leader for innovative and customer-oriented solutions based on apparatus using steel/enamel, stainless steel, special alloy and borosilicate glass technologies. At the Mainz site, approx. 200 employees form the QVF® competence center for glass apparatus engineering and process equipment.
Our clientele includes global corporations, but also many medium-sized companies and universities. In addition to our own product materials borosilicate glass 3.3 and steel/enamel, we purchase many products made of plastics. Our most commonly used plastic is PTFE. In addition, we use about 10 other fluoroplastics such as PFA, PVDF and FEP. The use of these fluoropolymers results from the use of our equipment and apparatus in corrosive processes or use in corrosive atmospheres, often coupled with high process temperatures.
Based on our extensive experience with corrosion-resistant materials, we are not only competent in the design and manufacture of key process engineering components, but also have the in-house knowledge of processing these highly corrosive products, such as sulfuric acid, nitric acid and hydrochloric acid.
We supply clean, modern and energy-efficient mineral acid processing equipment worldwide without polluting the environment.
In the supply chain of fluoropolymers, we are a trader and also a process/plant supplier. In some cases, the use of PTFE/PFA, for example, is based on the specifications of our customers. Often we do not know which products and chemical processes the customer uses in the equipment and plants we supply. In these cases, we plan and build according to the customer's requirements. However, we also have our own processes, e.g. for the treatment of mineral acids. These process plants are designed, developed, built and commissioned by us. During this process we also specify all materials for the components used.

Examples
• Reconditioning of highly corrosive acids in general
• Denitration and work-up of mixed acids from nitration processes
• Hydrochloric acid recovery
• Hydrochloric acid cleaning
• Purification of pickling acids
• High purity acids (electronic grade): HCl, HNO3 , H2 SO4
• Sulfuric acid concentration (pre-concentration, high-concentration)
• Nitric acid concentration, also in electronic grade
• HCl concentration by extractive distillation or two-pressure method.
• Sulfuric acid dilution
• Pre-concentration up to 70 wt.%
• High concentration up to 98% by weight
• Chlorine drying with sulfuric acid incl. reconcentration of sulfuric acid
• Nitric acid concentration via the azeotropic point with sulfuric acid
• Hydrochloric acid concentration via the azeotropic point with sulfuric acid
• Denitration, concentration and treatment of sulfuric acid, e.g. from various nitriding processes
• Bromine recovery and recovery from brines and process wastewater
• Debromination of brines and process streams
• Iodine recovery
• Absorption of HCl, HBr, Cl2 , Br2
• Recovery and concentration of HCl and HBr
• Process plants for the processing of highly corrosive halogens such as chlorine, bromine and iodine as well as their salts and acids
Every year, the chemical industry produces large quantities of mineral waste acids that are diluted with water, mixed with other acids or contaminated with other inorganic or organic components. The aim here is to purify and concentrate these waste acids in order to return them to the production cycle. Some of the plants reach industrial scale. For example, a throughput of 150 t/h of sulfuric acid to be concentrated has already been realized.


Generally speaking, we are thus specialized in the treatment of highly corrosive media in the temperature range of up to 200°C, whereby we design and realize the plants.
We are constantly developing our existing processes both theoretically and experimentally in our in-house technical center. An essential factor here is also the development of new process solutions for specific tasks of our customers. As a result, our portfolio for highly corrosion-resistant plant engineering under demanding process conditions (high temperatures, low vacuums) is constantly expanding.
Our internationally built modern and energy-efficient plants also aim to avoid or reduce the disposal of waste materials and to return them to the production cycle. In addition, we supply plants for the purification of exhaust air and wastewater.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Manufacture (Annex E.2.1) - Sector as a whole Construction products (Annex E.2.13.) - PTFE thread sealing tape

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: a) We are not aware of any emissions arising from the use of finished PTFE, PFA, PVDF, ... products. The use of these materials prevents emissions from the chemical-pharmaceutical production facilities. b) Very little waste of fluoroplastics is generated at our plant. The majority of this is replaced components on equipment that has been repaired in-house. The different materials are separated as far as possible (metal, electrical, glass and residual waste). The PTFE ends up in the residual waste. The city of Mainz incinerates the residual waste in the waste-to-energy plant. According to information on the homepage of the combined heat and power plant, the waste is incinerated at approx. 1000°C. Homepage: Kraftwerksinstandhaltungs GmbH (mhkw-mainz.de) We repair approx. 10-15 heat exchangers per year. This produces approx. 450 kg of PTFE as waste. As we are only one part of the chain, we cannot make any statement about our PTFE suppliers and about our customers. We know that a large part of the PTFE chips in the production of our parts is recycled by our suppliers. PTFE parts generated by maintenance and repair of our components, apparatus and equipment by our customers will most likely end up in residual or hazardous waste. However, it is not the PTFE that is the problem here, but the chemical contamination. Furthermore, all our plastic suppliers are not powder manufacturers. They purchase the powder and then process it further. In addition, they purchase blanks.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: We cannot make any statement on this. We dispose of waste through container collection by the waste disposal company of the city of Mainz and through the waste-to-energy plant mentioned under point 2b.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: a) We have the information via our plastic suppliers that a large part of the chips or even 100% during the production of our parts are fed into the recycling process. We have no knowledge to what extent it is possible with contaminated PTFE, PFA, PVDF, ....  We know from some of our customers that, as far as possible, materials are separated and disposed of individually. There, too, PTFE is disposed of via residual waste. We consider it possible to collect the fluoroplastics separately in an extra container. We have tested our parts to see to what extent PTFE, for example, can be separated from metal. With our own products, this would most likely be almost completely possible. For purchased PTFE-lined parts such as piping or pumps, we are not sure and have neither the know-how nor the tooling to do so. This means that we could basically imagine a separate waste collection and thus the feeding into a recycling process. In addition, however, we also have the option of feeding our waste into incineration via the existing route without additional expense. Collecting separately requires several additional steps: Hire additional staff for separation of waste and determination of materials, disassembly, sorting into different containers (not only residual waste), additional space for more containers, clarification/consultation with the city of Mainz.  b) We cannot say anything about the concentrations. We cannot assess the actual combustion process.  In the literature one can find that PTFE should be burned at a temperature > 850°C so that no harmful exhaust gases are produced. For our case it is realized because the waste-to-energy plant operates at approx. 1000°C.  c) If we can continue to let burn, we have no additional costs. For the other option, we would currently roughly assume that we would need at least one additional employee, probably more likely two. These would have to take care of the material separation, collection and disposal. In addition, there would be costs for further containers and their collection by a waste disposal company. Possibly, further costs could be added if we also had to take back the PTFE delivered to our customers. A new process would have to be set up for this. Possibly similar to the yellow bag or the take-back of electronic items in Germany. We would be prepared to do this if it were an argument that fluoroplastics could continue to be used indefinitely.

5. Proposed derogations: We require an indefinite exemption for the use of fluoropolymers in plant construction for the chemical industry, pharmaceutical industry, for universities and training centers. There are no alternative materials. We also do not see any research results so far that would bring an approach from an idea. There is always only one result for usability: either high operating temperature or chemical resistance. Neither is possible with another material. The installed PTFE parts do not emit any emissions. In some cases, they remain in the equipment for up to 30 years or more without having to be replaced. The material poses no danger to people or the environment. On the contrary, the danger to people and the environment would increase if an inferior material were used. There would then be higher emission of chemical vapors, more frequent leakages, more stoppages and more repair work. Every shutdown is a hazard. Employees often have to enter plants in full protection to find and repair leaks. Every shutdown and startup process is an additional hazard. It is not a routine process. When the plants are started up, the process is set and the process is running smoothly, there is little potential for danger. The potential danger then comes mainly from outside interference or component malfunctions or failures. Failures would be increased if fluoroplastics were no longer allowed to be used. PTFE cannot damage the surface of the materials used for our equipment (borosilicate glass and steel/enamel). This would not be the case for metallic materials. Damage to the surface of the equipment can ultimately lead to equipment failure or leakage.

6. Missing uses: a) The missing application for us is the complete chemical and pharmaceutical industry and its consumers. This ranges from the production of active ingredients, their precursors and intermediates, to the production of solvents, their precursors and intermediates, to the various recycling processes that have emerged in recent years for environmental protection. We are part of the process. However, we are neither at the beginning nor at the end of the chain. We purchase the preformed plastic parts and install them in the equipment, which in turn is sold to the end user. We consume an average of 19t of fluoropolymers per year. Of these, the largest share is PTFE (PTFE virginal, PTFE virginal modified, PTFE electrically conductive). This is followed by PFA and PVDF. For demisters, we have ETFE as the main material. For O-rings, we have many FEP jacketed rings. The use of steel/PTFE piping depends very much on the individual projects. We do not have these in our range as standard, but determine their scope anew in each new order. In 2020 it was approx. 7t, in 2021 2.6t and in 2022 1.5t (weight for steel and PTFE, separate specification is not possible). This year the trend is back to the 2020 level.   b) As users of fluoropolymers, we cannot make any statement about PFAS as such. We refer to the properties of the fluoropolymers produced. Their most important properties are the operating temperature and chemical resistance at low and high temperatures. At higher temperatures, PTFE is largely dimensionally stable. This is extremely important for many of the components listed. The high purities of PTFE and especially PFA are also important for use in plants for the production of high-purity acids (electronic grade). Another advantage is the non-existent catalytic effect. PTFE is indispensable as a material for temporary repair of damage to glass lined apparatus (e.g. gasketing under a tantalum gasket/plate).  c) We as De Dietrich Process Systems GmbH would no longer be able to operate a plant engineering business and would be directly affected. We are 200 employees at the Mainz site. We hang together with our parent company De Dietrich Process Systems S.A.S in France (Zinswiller, Semur, Dijon, Schiltigheim with approx. 500 employees) with the main material combination steel/enamel and PTFE). In addition, the group has several subsidiaries in Europe, e.g. in Spain, England, Hungary, Belgium and Switzerland. In the chain ahead of us, it would hit a large number of suppliers. A large number of them have their headquarters in Germany. These are primarily our plastics suppliers, such as IDT and Lahme. But it would also affect the other materials, such as borosilicate glass 3.3, stainless steel, mild steel and bought-in components from measurement and control technology, switch cabinet manufacturers, agitator manufacturers, pump and valve manufacturers. Probably many more, which cannot all be listed here. We have our own glass production at our site and buy in all other materials. For the glass production we purchase finished semi-finished products and fittings. We do not have our own glass tank for glass molding production. In the chain after us, it affects all the customers we serve. These are all those who depend on corrosion-resistant components. Since we produce not only for German but also for European customers, this will be an international problem. We assume that all other markets outside of Europe will look elsewhere for the equipment they need. We also have representatives in the USA, China and India. These will probably go other ways to supply their own market. We therefore suspect that a ban will lead to a decisive competitive disadvantage for the European economy.   d) There are no alternatives on the market that would be suitable for our area of application. For a few isolated areas in the plants (e.g. cold piping), another material would theoretically be possible. In the event of an incident, however, there would then be an additional increased risk if the pipeline were to be exposed to elevated temperatures. In addition, installation and service personnel could mix up the individual gaskets. Storage areas would have to be increased so that the "same" items in different materials could be kept in stock. Many materials are not available in dissipative versions. However, this is absolutely necessary in Ex areas and to comply with the ATEX directive or to avoid dangerous electrostatic charging.  f) We see PTFE reduction opportunities in the conversion of steel/PTFE piping to glass or steel/enamel piping. There are two possibilities here. For new orders/projects, it is possible to plan directly in other materials if this is possible in terms of the application. (However, the gasket must still be PTFE). This results in a partially higher material price. The planning effort is identical. If piping in existing plants has to be changed, we cannot estimate the cost. This data would have to come from our customers.  This affects our customers. They will have to clarify with their inspection authorities (ZÜS) what needs to be approved and certified again. No additional work would be necessary for new projects.  For each individual pipeline, it must be checked whether the other materials cover the same pressures, temperatures and chemical resistance. For retrofitting in existing plants, these must be shut down and cleaned. Longer planned shutdowns must be expected here.  We are an alternative supplier. However, we can only reduce the consumption of fluoroplastics, but not substitute them.  g) At our site in Mainz, 200 employees are directly affected. Almost the entire site would be at risk. Part of the workforce (approx. 50 employees) could become active in other areas (as an engineering office for project planning and process engineering with other materials, our fitters as service providers). Furthermore, all locations of the De Dietrich Group in Europe are endangered. Our employees in our production would be particularly affected. These are specialized glass apparatus manufacturers. They don't really have a free labor market because the supply of jobs is very limited. We operate in a specialized environment. There are not many suppliers here in the world either. We are the only supplier worldwide for glass components in nominal sizes DN800 and DN1000 and for 500L balls. We have a turnover of approx. 40 million €/year as a location in Mainz. In the worldwide operating De Dietrich Group we have a turnover of approx. 200 million €/year. In addition, our suppliers and service providers would be affected. We currently have around 1,500 active suppliers.  In addition, we have about 1900 active customers worldwide, including major corporations in the chemical industry. An example of a customer is Saxonia Halsbrücke in Germany, as a medium-sized company. It is one of our main customers for our 500L sphere. It depends on borosilicate glass 3.3, steel/enamel, PTFE and PVDF. Other materials are not chemically resistant. He works primarily with aqua regia. His recycling process of precious metals would no longer be feasible with the PFAS ban. He also has about 200 employees.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Manufacture (Annex E.2.1) - Sector as a whole  see also additional file with pictures SECTION IV. Non-confidential attachment

8. Other identified uses: Construction products (Annex E.2.13.) PTFE thread gasketing tape We mainly use PTFE thread gasketing tape for repairs of leaking threads in shell and tube heat exchangers at the drain hole from the tube sheet. Here we gasket PTFE threads with PTFE thread gasketing tape. It becomes necessary when the screw connection leaks due to too many load changes, temperature changes or manufacturing tolerances. The repair can be done in the installed condition of the shell and tube heat exchanger. This means that the heat exchanger does not have to be removed from the production line. Other smaller applications include gasketing threaded connections on various pumps in the process plants or gasketing manifold grommets in our grommet manifolds.  We use 12mm wide tape. There are 12m on each roll. Our average consumption over the last 10 years is 58 rolls per year. This includes fluctuations from 23 to 109 pcs/year.

General Comments: Dear colleagues from the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA),
Following the public consultation on the proposed restriction of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), I would like to express my clinical considerations (and concerns) to keep pressurized metered dose inhalers (pMDIs) available to patients with asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
Inhaled medication is the cornerstone of pharmacotherapy in patients with asthma and COPD. A high concentration of drug(s) and low systemic availability result in a very favorable ratio between efficacy and safety. The amount of lung deposition and the pattern of distribution determine the magnitude of the effects, so, optimal use of the inhaler device is critical. Correct and optimal inhalation of medication, however, is difficult. Several steps are involved in order to get the medication at its desired location. These steps include handling the device (e.g. actuation, firing), the breathing manouvre (e.g. forceful inhalation, breath hold) and the coordination between the two.
It is therefore not surprising that a high percentage of patients makes one or more mistakes when using their inhaler. Depending on the number and severity of these errors, lung deposition will decrease and an optimal clinical effect in terms of maximal reduction of complaints and exacerbations will not be reached. [Usmani 2018] Even despite repeated training and instructions, asthma and COPD are associated with a high burden of disease and economic costs.
Matching patient and device is crucial to enable an optimal lung deposition and therefore clinical effect. From a clinical point of view, three factors are essential when making a choice for a specific type of device in an individual patient: 1. is the patient able to inhale consciously; 2. is the patient able to generate sufficient inspiratory flow; and 3. is the patient able to coordinate well. Besides, patient previous experiences and preference are important to ensure optimal adherence in the long term. [Dekhuijzen 2013]
pMDIs are indispensable devices for patients with asthma or COPD, particularly for those with reduced peak inspiratory flow rate (PIFR), inability to hold their breath for 5-10 seconds, children up to an age of seven years, and patients with asthma or COPD with an acute exacerbation. [Levy Lancet 2023] Prescribing these patients with a dry powder inhaler (DPI) will increase the chance of a future exacerbation and even hospitalisations. This clearly impacts on the burden of disease of these patients and increases which in return has negative effects on solid waste and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.
In addition, switching device types for non-medical reasons may have highly variable clinical outcomes, and, if not consented, may adversely impact on the patient/physician relationship. [Usmani 2022]
Propellants are essential in the working mechanism of pMDIs. The current production and use of the fluorinated greenhouse gases (F-Gases) HFA-227ea and HFA-134a need to be reduced according to the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol and the upcoming EU F-Gas Regulation.
Both these propellants in use as well as the next-generation propellant for pMDIs, hydrofluoroolefin HFO-1234ze(E), fall under the proposed PFAS definition in the draft PFAS restriction proposal to ECHA because of its chemical structure. HFO-1234ze(E)is, however, classified according to the ECHA dossier assessment as non-persistent, non-bio accumulative and non-toxic, and its breakdown does not present a risk to the environment. It has up to 99.9% less Global Warming Potential (GWP) than propellants currently used in inhaled medications.
I therefore would like to urgently ask our colleagues from ECHA to allow the production of pMDIs with HFO-1234ze(E). This will allow us to provide our patients their medication via an essential device in order to reduce morbidity and mortality as much as possible.

General Comments: Dear ECHA colleagues
As a healthcare charity working internationally, representing the needs of clinicians working at grassroots level, we welcome the aspiration of the draft restriction of  Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), "forever chemicals".  The scientific evidence is growing about the harm they can cause to the environment and to human health and we applaud the ambition of the EU to tackle this.

However, with any new regulation or restriction comes the risk of unintended consequences. As an organisation with a respiratory focus, we would urge ECHA to explore if there will be unintended consequences for people living with two very common respiratory conditions: asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).  They rely on inhaled medicines to stay well.  Inhaled medicines are listed on the World Health Organization Essential Medicines List for acute attacks and the  long term management of asthma and COPD globally.

Over recent decades, the manufacturers of inhaled medicines have responded to the need to reduce F-gases and continue to develop devices that have a lower carbon footprint.  This is welcomed by the whole respiratory community and we continue to encourage the choice of lower carbon options where choice is available (in many countries prices dictate that there is no choice).

One of the key issues in relation to inhaled medicines is that the drug and the device are equally important and need to be considered together - the device has to be able to be used easily in order for the drug to reach directly into the lungs.  The propellant is therefore a key component; without the right propellant the drug will not reach the right part of the lungs and its effect will be limited and the side effects considerable (as the drug will land in the wrong places eg the air or the mouth).

This brings us to the potential unintended consequences of the restriction.  Currently, manufacturers are working on using two new  propellants to lower the carbon footprint.  These are  HFP1234ZE and HFA152A and we understand these ought to be available by 2025. Under the proposal, we also understand both would be restricted and, as they are not classed as active products, they would not be included in the exceptions for medical use provision.

Therefore there would be no options available for propellants in inhaled medicines that meet other requirements eg in relation to their global warming potential.  This would have a profound impact on people with asthma and COPD across the world because they are health conditions that exist in every country, and 3/4 of inhalers are made in Europe and exported outside Europe.  Thus supply of essential medicines would be completely disrupted, potentially leading to increased morbidity and even death in these patients.

We want regulation to stimulate innovation so we have tried to check if there could be innovation in respect of inhalers.  We have asked industry colleagues if substitute chemicals exist.  It appears that there may be alternatives to some aspects of production eg the coating of the inside of inhalers to preserve shelf life and it appears that with a 5 year time bound derogation of the relevant PFAS this might be possible.  It appears that  another PFAS is used to bind the medicine to the aerosphere, and that with a 12 year derogation this might be possible. However, it appears there are no other options for the propellant.

We are not experts in chemistry or the development of inhaled medicines. Our expertise is in the care of people with asthma and COPD.   We are deeply concerned that there may be supply issues created by the restriction that would severely impact their care by taking the majority of inhaled medicine out of supply.  We therefore urge you to investigate the potential unintended consequences before banning HFP1234ZE and HFA152A.

General Comments: Dear ECHA Committee Members,
We fully support efforts to minimize and mitigate the presence of substances which pose a threat to human health and the environment. However, restrictions to commonly used materials such as
fluoropolymers pose a risk to the EU’s ability to supply itself with lifesaving therapies, both due to
material shortages as well as regulatory approval backlogs from having to revalidate the manufacturing processes of the biologicals due to material/tool changes in their manufacturing processes. The proposed broad restriction of PFAS covering fluoropolymers would have unintended consequences on the global manufacturing of life science and biopharmaceutical products ultimately impacting availability of existing medicinal therapies (e.g., COVID vaccines), development of new medicinal therapies, and cost to patients. Recent assessments of the dependence of biopharmaceutical manufacturing processes on materials impacted by the PFAS ban proposal range from 94% to virtually all biologics medicinal therapies [1] [2] [3]. We propose a new sector for the pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical industry, including single-use bioprocessing consumables, QC analysis and the supply chain critical to the manufacture of these goods, with an unlimited derogation, similar to that for medicinal products. We also propose separate categorization and perhaps subcategorization of fluoropolymers within the broad scope
definition, to differentiate compounds of high toxicity concern (e.g. PFOA, PFOS) from those identified by multiple, credible authorities as polymers of low concern [4] [5].

Categorization of Fluoropolymer vs PFAS
The broad scope PFAS definition groups well-documented hazardous, small molecular weight chemistries (e.g., PFOA, PFOS) in the same group as 10,000+ potential compounds of highly varying properties, including fluoropolymers. This one size fits all grouping, includes fluoropolymers used in bioprocessing, which meet stringent safety testing requirements for use in pharmaceutical processing, including biological reactivity testing (USP 87, USP 88, ISO 10993) as well as toxicological safety assessments of the extractables and leachables compounds that may migrate from these materials. Moreover, such fluoropolymers including PVDF and PTFE, are successfully used as implants for vascular grafts and stents, facial augmentation, trachea reconstruction, pacemaker leads, glaucoma drainage membranes, intestinal sleeves, hernia repair meshes, and intracochlear hydrophones. Additionally, as polymers of low concern are those deemed to have insignificant environmental and human health impacts, polymers which meet these established criteria should have reduced regulatory requirements [7].  Subgrouping and classification strategies for PFAS have been published in peer reviewed literature [8] [5], and industry reports [9]. Additionally, it is noted that some fluoropolymer formulations used commercially today within the bioprocess industry (e.g., PVDF) are already manufactured without the use of PFAS processing aids, thereby mitigating risk during polymer manufacturing. Clearly there are differences in the vast number of materials falling into the singular PFAS grouping, with greatly differing safety profiles, tonnage used in the industry, contribution to environmental concerns, control strategies and socioeconomic value. Hence, we request separate categorization, and perhaps sub-categorization of fluoropolymers to assess their specific material risks, potential environmental impact, lifecycle management strategies, unique functionality and applications, and extensive socioeconomic impact. In an analogy from Solzhenitsyn, “If only it were all so simple! If only there were evil people somewhere insidiously committing evil deeds, and it were necessary only to separate them from the rest of us and destroy them. But the line dividing good and evil cuts through the heart of every human being. And who is willing to destroy a piece of his own heart?” This analogy exemplifies how the seemingly simple, one size fits all approach can be greatly misguided, while yielding enormous socioeconomic consequences.

Request for Exemption or Maximum Derogation Period
Given the enormous impact of the proposed restrictions on the bioprocessing industry, their supply chain, and the availability of patient therapies, we strongly request (i) recognition of Bioprocessing and its supply chain as industry sector under “missing Uses”, (ii) separate categorization of fluoropolymers used in bioprocessing, and (iii) an exemption or time-unlimited derogation for this sector.

Sectors and (sub-)uses: About the Bio-Process Systems Alliance (BPSA) The Bio-Process Systems Alliance (BPSA) was formed in 2005 as an industry-led international industry association dedicated to encouraging and accelerating the adoption of single-use manufacturing technologies used in the production of biopharmaceuticals and vaccines. BPSA is an affiliate of the Society of Chemical Manufacturers and Affiliates (SOCMA). BPSA’s Mission is to facilitate, globally, the development and manufacturing of biopharmaceuticals through the implementation of robust, safe, and sustainable Single-Use Technologies. BPSA presently represents approximately 70 member companies spanning the global single-use bioprocessing industry.   Support for Related Bioprocess Industry Positions BPSA members are also engaged in parallel industry sector groups related to biopharmaceutical processing and supports the positions below, which help to create a more holistic view of the impact of the broad sweeping PFAS definition and ban on the biopharmaceutical processing industry.  ▪ European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries (EFPIA) and Associations and Animal Health  Europe [3] ▪ BioPhorum response to the Annex XV proposal for universal PFAS restrictions [13] ▪ European Sealing Association [14] ▪ American Chemistry Council [15] ▪ American Society of Mechanical Engineers – Biopharmaceutical Process Equipment [19]

A review of United States Pharmacopeia (USP) drug monographs and standards finds 100 references to “fluoro”, 78 to “PVDF”, and 68 to “PTFE”. In almost all cases, the suitability or any alternative materials depends on the material interactions with the pharmaceutical fluid and manufacturing process conditions (temperature, time, flow). This is a central regulatory requirement for pharmaceutical equipment as stated in the European good manufacturing practice (GMP) guidelines. “Production equipment should not present any hazard to the products. In some cases, (i) alternatives such as PES filters, may be available and suitable as an alternative for PVDF filters with the understanding there will be performance trade-offs and a potential impact to the drug product quality that requires additional assessment, and in some cases update of regulatory filings for each medicinal   product and acceptance by multiple regulatory entities worldwide (as process that can easily take 3 to 6 years for each case and filing). In other cases, (ii) the alternative (e.g., PES membranes) may not be suitable and able to be validated as the performance characteristics of biotech components often depend strongly on the nature of the chemistry of each pharmaceutical fluid, reagent, and process conditions. For example, squalene emulsions, frequently used as ingredients for manufacture of vaccines, can result in performance challenges for PES sterilizing-grade filters to achieve the validated state of absolute microbial retention.  ▪ Fluoropolymer-based liquid filtration membranes and devices. Sterile filtration, virus filtration,  particulate/bioburden filtration ensure purity, cleanliness and safety of the biopharmaceutical or  the fluids used to prepare and formulate the pharmaceutical. ▪ Fluoropolymer-based gas filtration membranes and devices. Sterile (i.e., bacteria removing) vent filters on single-use systems, IV sets, bioreactors, etc.  ▪ Fluoropolymer gaskets and seals. Ubiquitous through bioprocessing.  ▪ Fluoropolymer single-use components. Fittings (e.g., tube to tube connectors), bags, tubing clamps, pump parts, valves, mixer parts, tubing, etc.  ▪ Fluoropolymers used as auxiliaries on sites to manufacture single-use products or chemicals vital to the bioprocessing industry. Chemically inert, non-stick, temperature resistant materials used in thermal and sonic welding, pump valves, tubing, material coatings, equipment gaskets, seals, production of bioreactors and storage bags, etc. It is believed there are an abundance of materials in the supply chain and manufacturing operations that require further time to properly understand. ▪ Fluoropolymer membranes and consumables used for laboratory analysis and quality control testing supporting pharmaceutical development and manufacturing.  ▪ Fluoropolymer bags, bottles, and vials for biopharmaceuticals. Bags with relatively inert chemical reactivity properties that are highly suited for freezing and low temperature storage of biopharmaceuticals and cell therapies. Bags are used for cell culture production processes in cell therapy applications, as well as freezing and storage. Key attributes include purity, gas exchange, water barrier, clarity, chemical and biological inertness, as well as low temperature performance critical to storage in liquid nitrogen (-196°C). This is key for safety of drug products which in the case of personalized medicine/cell therapy are considered rare and nearly impossible to replace. ▪ Hydrophobic and/or Oleophobic Filtration Membranes in Pharmaceutical Processing. In these  cases, small molecular weight chemistries are associated with filtration membranes that allow  the flow of gas but prevent passage of microorganisms. The hydrophobic/oleophobic  chemistries are critical to the surface tension characteristics of the membrane, non-binding  properties, and ability to mitigate pore blockage of small-scale membranes by moisture. Many  membranes previously used PFOA or PFOS-based chemistries and were redeveloped using other  chemistries, that are now in scope of the current ECHA PFAS definition. Such  hydrophobic/oleophobic membranes are well suited to venting applications in pharmaceutical  processing requiring moisture repellence and the maintenance of a sterile barrier. As alternatives  will need to be developed, tested, and validated by the supplier, and then by the pharmaceutical  manufacturer, this process will take extensive time (12+ years). The maximum derogation is  requested for these materials. Other identified uses: PFAS Types Common to Bioprocessing Fluoropolymers (PTFE, PVDF, FKM, PFA) as well as PFAS-treated oleophobic membranes are the most common PFAS types understood used in the single-use bioprocess industry. Hence these represent a small volume segment of the biotech materials, but one in which there are few to no alternatives to meet the aggressive chemical and process compatibility requirements. For PVDF, this material is used in a wider capacity throughout bioprocessing including membranes, fittings, tubing, mixers, clamps, and so forth. For applications involving PVDF, there are in a moderate to large number of cases, alternatives (~50%). However, this varies depending on the application type and specific pharmaceutical manufacturing process. Moreover, given that many PVDF manufacturers have moved away from PFAS-based polymeric processing aides, the environmental and toxicologic safety risk associated with categorization of PVDF as a PFAS material is negligible. Due to their relatively inert, low binding, low fouling characteristics they are frequently recommended for complex pharmaceutical formulations and well suited for late stages of the pharmaceutical manufacturing process. Potential alternative types of sterilizing grade filters include PES and nylon filters, each with specific material and performance characteristics that can impact the quality of the drug and viability of the manufacturing process. For example, PES filters may offer higher volumetric flow properties for simple fluids, such as buffers, but pose challenges for many complex drug formulations to achieve a validated state of absolute microbial retention, which is the essential requirement of such filters. The regulatory preparation and approval steps, depending on the application and number of regulatory approvers, can take an additional 3 to 6 years per use case. Any expectation that the pharmaceutical bioprocessing industry has the lab testing resources, budget, subject matter experts, and regulatory reviewers necessary to safely execute these changes over a 13-year period for all cases where filter alternatives are available, is implausible.

General Comments: Dear ECHA Committee,
We welcome the opportunity to contribute to the public consultation process initiated by the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) regarding the proposal for the restriction of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) according to Regulation (EC) No. 1907/2006 (“REACH”).
Regarding the PFAS restriction, we submit that lubricants and mold release agents should have a 12-year derogation from the implementation of the restriction. Currently, there are no suitable alternatives for mold release/lubricants that contain PFAS that meet the required strict manufacturing performances. By having a 12-year transitional period, Stoner Inc. can work with end users to find and develop technologies, formulations, and techniques to reduce and eventually eliminate PFAS in this sector. The products produced with PFAS containing lubricants and mold releases are critical to societal needs, such as molding medical supplies, so the entire sector will need 12 years to find and develop technologies and techniques for PFAS-free production.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: We provide mold releases to customers to be able to remove parts quickly, efficiently, and safely. For some of the mold releases, the main release component contains PFAS materials. These PFAS materials can provide easy release while satisfying strict surface finish qualities to these products, can be non-flammable, and/or stable at the high temperature (up to 400 °C) to mold the material. The main markets that our PFAS containing mold releases are used for are plastics and rubber molding releases. Specifically, most of the mold release for the plastics market goes toward rotational molding, to make hollow parts such as cooler boxes, agricultural tanks, and various industrial housings and covers. These products are essential to everyday life and there is a societal need to continue to produce these products. The rubber parts vary from hoses for automotive applications to rubber belts. These parts not only have to be able to release from the mold, but also have certain requirements, such as being able to be painted, have a matte finish, or no silicones in the release. For these applications, PTFE provides the release and finishing characteristics that these molders require. Some of these products also have fluorosurfactants which help wet out the mold release on the mold. By wetting out the release agent, all the mold is coated with the mold release agent, and a thinner layer can be applied, allowing for less materials required for the same release. This reduces the overall amount of PFAS that are used for the manufacturing process. Additionally, we also use some fluorinated solvents and fluorinated propellants. The propellants and fluorinated solvents allow us to produce products that are non-flammable while allowing the mold release to dry in a short period of time. Non-flammable solvents and propellants also help to protect workers’ safety human health. Applications where high temperatures are used or where there is energized equipment, there is the possibility that the lubricant, or the propellant could cause a fire. Some of these lubricants are used at such high temperatures that other common propellants and solvents, namely hydrocarbon-based chemicals, can ignite and put workers lives at risk. Fluorinated solvents and propellants can help to suppress ignition which reduces the risk of a fire and protects workers. Without these non-flammable options, workers’ safety will be negatively impacted. To completely eliminate PFAS, a significant amount of time is required in order to find and validate a new procedure to ensure workers safety. Additionally, non-flammable solvents are used in the manufacturing process of critical medical devices. The mold releases are used to release medical components, and to switch their manufacturing process to use new solvents, there will need to be a significant derogation period. The biggest sector that uses our products is rotational molding. Rotational molders make products that range from agricultural storage tanks to seals for inflatable oxygen masks to components for the aerospace industry. Globally, this was a 4+ billion euros industry in 20201. This is also expected to have a compounding annual growth rate (CAGR) of about 5.9% between 2020 to 2031. With continued growth, there will be increased demand for PFAS containing mold releases because they are able to provide easy release to intricate parts. To change the entire industry away from PFAS, the 12-year derogation period for lubricants and mold release is a necessity. This will allow us to formulate and work with end-users of our products to not contain PFAS as well as update procedures for end-users. Updating end-user procedures could require significant capital investment to provide a safe and efficient production environment which will require a significant amount of time to achieve.

5. Proposed derogations: As mentioned in the response to Q1, some of these mold release and lubricant products are used to make medical devices. If a switch away from the current approved mold release formulation is required, it will take time to go through the necessary safety testing. Regulatory agencies such as the European Medicines Agency will require extensive testing which will require a longer phase down. For lubricants that are in high temperature environments and molding applications with difficult release, we can have more time to evaluate and find alternatives that meet the customers’ needs and will still be able to provide these valuable products to the market. We need time to trial new chemistries and new alternatives to be able to find a suitable alternative for customers. We believe that the proposed 12-year derogation for lubricants is necessary to provide us enough time to find a suitable alternative for these mold releases and lubricants.  One particular case we would like to discuss is the use of HFO-1234ze. We understand the necessary phase down of R-134a due to its high global warming potential (GWP). However, the offset that has been developed, HFO-1234ze, is on the list of PFAS. HFO-1234ze is not persistent in the environment because it readily degrades in the atmosphere. Because it readily degrades, HFO-1234ze has almost no GWP and is able to create non-flammable aerosols. One application that this is critical for is as a freeze spray during medical procedures. To cool a patient’s skin or an affected area, a freeze spray is used.  HFO-1234ze can provide similar cooling capabilities to R-134a and remain a non-flammable aerosol. We would respectfully ask that HFO-1234ze be exempted from this regulation.

8. Other identified uses: Currently, no alternative has shown acceptable performance of being non-flammable, great release on intricate or difficult to release parts, high temperature stability, and applications where silicones cannot be used. The requirements for these products can be very strict and the alternatives that have been tried either do not release, degrade at the operating temperature of the mold, create a flammable environment, or leave poor surface finishes which increases scrap and waste. Currently our R&D group is investigating PFAS-free alternatives for our mold releases by working with both suppliers of our raw materials, as well as with end-users to understand their requirements for the mold release application/processing. Additionally, we are working on looking into other propellant options for these products that can still provide non-flammable aerosol without the use of PFAS. As we continue to refine and develop alternatives to PFAS containing products, we will need time for production and implementation. Depending on the customer, this could take multiple years to complete, so the long derogation period would be necessary for complete implementation.

General Comments: Dear European Chemicals Agency,

We welcome the opportunity to contribute to the public consultation initiated by the European Chemicals Agency on the Annex XV Report (“Annex XV Report”) on a proposal to restrict Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (“PFASs”), according to Regulation (EC) No. 1907/2006 (“REACH”).

As we further explain in the annexed white paper, we request the following changes to the proposed restrictions on PFASs of the Annex XV Report:

I. Request to exclude fluoropolymers

We request that the following fluoropolymers be excluded from the scope of the proposed restrictions on PFASs:

A. polytetrafluoroethylene (“PTFE”) CAS # 9002-8-0 (CF2CF2)n;
B. perfluoroalkoxy alkane (“PFA”) CAS # 26655-00-5 (CF2CF2)n-(CF2CF(OCF3))m,; and
C. fluorinated ethylene propylene (“FEP”) CAS # 25067-11-2 (CF2CF2)n-(CF2CF(CF3))m

As a result of their very high molecular weight, fluoropolymers have unique properties that distinguish them from all other PFASs.  Fluoropolymers have low impact to human health and the environment, as further detailed in the attached white paper. Grouping fluoropolymers together with all other classes of PFASs for a single approach structure-hazard assessment based on persistence alone is not scientifically appropriate.

II. Request for a temporary exemption for use of specific fluoropolymer PFASs in electronic automotive radar applications

We request that the proposed restrictions on PFASs provide a temporary exemption of at least 15 years for electronic “automotive radar applications” for the following materials:

A   polytetrafluoroethylene (“PTFE”) CAS # 9002-8-0 (CF2CF2)n;
B. perfluoroalkoxy alkane (“PFA”) CAS # 26655-00-5 (CF2CF2)n-(CF2CF(OCF3))m,; and
C.  fluorinated ethylene propylene (“FEP”) CAS # 25067-11-2 (CF2CF2)n-(CF2CF(CF3))m

PFASs, and in particular the fluoropolymers listed above, are critical to a broad array of electronic radar components used in the automotive industry due to a unique combination of the following properties:

I. Low dielectric constant and low dissipation factor enabling superior electrical performance;
II. Stable electrical and mechanical properties over varying environmental conditions such as high humidity and temperatures above 130°C, enabling stable performance during environmental excursions; and
III. Inherent flame retardancy.

Due to this unique combination of properties, PTFE, PFA, and FEP are extremely difficult to substitute in automotive radar component applications without significant tradeoffs in performance and lifetime, as there are no known alternatives that meet all these performance criteria.

Significant invention is required to identify, and then qualify, each specific PFAS-free solution for this application and there is no guarantee that endeavor will be successful.  To date, no other class of materials has been able to demonstrate the collective performance benefits of PTFE stated above. Typical qualification and test cycles for automotive radar applications are in the four-to-six-year range.

The situation for automotive radar replacement parts must also be addressed. There is currently a legal requirement that radar systems must be maintained for a specific length of time after installation. This amount of time varies depending on the country but is generally about 10 years.  Drop in replacement parts must be available for automotive manufacturers to meet this requirement. This obligation necessitates the extended derogation request, to cover the longest maintenance time regulated, and to avoid product availability interruptions that could have significant impact to critical safety requirements. We are petitioning for a derogation period of a minimum of 15 years to provide sufficient time to invent, develop, qualify, and install an alternative product to the current PTFE solution and to enable a sufficient supply of replacement parts for the current product mandated by law.

The white paper substantiates the science-based reasoning behind these requests, outlines the impact of the proposed restrictions on PFASs of the Annex XV Report, and provides the justification of a derogation for the specific application summarized above.

I would like to express my concern about the planned regulation of per- and polyfluorinated alkyl substances (PFAS) under the REACH Regulation. While I support the need for strict regulation of hazardous chemicals, I would like to highlight some important concerns related to the proposed measure.

3. Impact assessment: A comprehensive impact assessment of the proposed regulation is crucial to fully understand potential economic, social and environmental impacts. Regulation should be based on scientific evidence and take into account both short- and long-term effects.
4. Research and development: The regulation of PFAS should take into account ongoing research and development to ensure that innovative solutions are promoted to mitigate risks and address environmental problems.
5. International cooperation: PFAS is a global problem, and coordinated international cooperation in regulation and research is crucial to finding effective solutions.
I call on ECHA to take a balanced approach to developing the regulation of PFAS, taking into account the above points. Informed and prudent regulation will ensure that the risks of PFAS are adequately addressed without causing undesirable consequences for industry, innovation and economic growth.
Thank you for your attention and commitment to the safety of people and the environment.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Dear Madam/Sir

I would be grateful if you would consider my submission for excluding the propellant HFO-1234ze(E) from the proposed European PFAS regulations.

My name is Richard Beasley, and I am a physician at Wellington Regional Hospital, Director of the Medical Research Institute of New Zealand, and Professor of Medicine at Victoria University of Wellington. I am an Adjunct Professor at the University of Otago and Visiting Professor, University of Southampton, United Kingdom. I was previously the Deputy Chair of the Health Research Council of New Zealand, and am currently Chair of the New Zealand adolescent and adult asthma guidelines. I have been the New Zealand Representative of the International Human Frontier Science Program Organization, and a member of the Board of Directors, Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease. My research interests in respiratory medicine are primarily in the fields of epidemiology and clinical management. I currently have over 750 publications, and a Google Scholar H-index of 112. I have both institutional and personal conflicts of interest, in that I have received personal fees, and my employer the Medical Research Institute of New Zealand has received research funding, from a number of pharmaceutical companies which manufacture inhaled asthma medications.
I first became aware of this issue when I reviewed the Global Initiative for asthma (GINA) article for The Lancet.[1] I must confess that prior to this referee’s role I had limited awareness or knowledge of this issue. However, it led me to research the field and draft this submission.

The particular issue I want to address is the proposed banning of HFO-1234ze(E) from manufacture, distribution and use in the European Union, a regulation which I consider will have serious global implications and potentially lead to a marked increase in asthma deaths worldwide.
In many respects I consider that the logic behind the decision making in this issue is straightforward and as a result I have developed a simple sequence of reasoning, as follows:

1. The restriction of the thousands of PFAS chemicals (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) has a sound basis, due to the known adverse health effects, and their accumulation in the environment. However, this restriction can be justified if amended to only include those PFAS chemicals that have adverse environmental and health effects, and persistence in the environment.
Logic 1: As the specific PFAS HFO-1234ze(E) has no significant adverse health effects or adverse environmental effects and does not persist in the environment, then there can be no reason to restrict the manufacture and use of HFO-1234ze(E).[2,3] The judgement of the US Environmental Protection Agency’s Significant New Alternatives Policy (SNAP) Program that HFO–1234ze is an acceptable substitute as an aerosol propellant because it does not pose a greater overall risk to human health and the environment than the aerosol propellants in use is noted.[2]
Solution 1: Exclude HFO-1234ze(E) from the proposed restriction of the class of PFAS compounds.

2. The option to restrict certain PFAS exists, if used for medical purposes, but not if they are non-active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) as is the case with propellants such as the HFO-1234ze(E).
Logic 2: As the active API (asthma pharmaceutical product) requires the non-active API (propellant) to enable it to have its desired therapeutic effect, the non-active API should receive the same exemption as if it was an API.
Solution 2: Provide the same exemption for HFO-1234ze(E) as other APIs to ensure people with asthma have access to life saving medications.

3. The timeline whereby the EU restriction comes into force in 2026, with an 18-month transition period for non-exempt products will most likely result in the markedly reduced availability of inhaled asthma medications globally. This reduced availability relates to the predominant use of pressurized metered dose inhalers (pMDIs) in asthma management (worldwide the pMDI outweighs the DPI in total number of doses sold by a factor of four)[4], the lack of alternatives due to the phased withdrawal of HFC-propellant pMDIs due to their significant global warming potential,[1,5] the restrictions proposed on the future of availability of HFC-152a under the draft EU F Gas Regulation published 5th April 2022, and the lack of sufficient additional manufacturing capacity to meet current demand with dry powder inhaler (DPI) devices, and greater cost of DPI products.[5]
Logic 3: The likely serious reduction in the availability of inhaled asthma medications, in the EU and globally, represents an adverse consequence of sufficient importance to justify the exemption of HFO-1234ze(E). This potential impact cannot be considered an unintended consequence, but an inevitable result of the regulations.
Solution 3: Exempt HFO-1234ze(E) from the regulatory restrictions for the purpose of ensuring the availability of life saving inhaled asthma medications in the EU and globally.

4. Protecting the environment and health of populations requires integration of government policy. The HFO-1234ze(E) propellant was developed as part of an international initiative to reduce the high global warming effects of the current HFC propellants in pMDIs.1 HFO-1234ze(E) has near-zero global warming potential, up to 99% less than current HFA-227ea and HFA-134a propellants, and similar to the DPI products (which would mean a pMDI with HFO-1234ze(E) as a propellant would have greenhouse gas emissions similar to a DPI), and with a reduced plastic burden compared with the DPIs.[3,5] The transition from HFC to the HFO-1234ze(E) propellant will have a marked beneficial effect on the emitted carbon footprint and global warming, and compared with DPIs a reduced environmental impact from plastics.
Logic 4: The adverse impact of the proposed regulations on the EU governmental policy to reduce carbon footprint and associated global warming potential is of sufficient importance to justify the exemption of HFO-1234ze(E).
Solution 4: Approve the use of HFO-1234ze(E) as a priority to enhance the global efforts to reduce global warming.

5. Worldwide, approximately 180,000 deaths annually are attributable to asthma, with most deaths being largely preventable, frequently being related to inadequate long-term medical care or delays in obtaining medical help during the last attack.[6] The up to 100-fold variability in age-adjusted asthma death rates in countries internationally can be attributed to both differences in asthma prevalence, and the lack of access to inhaled asthma medications. If there was a reduced access to inhaled asthma medications globally as a result of the proposed EU regulations, the global asthma mortality rate would be expected to increase significantly. This outcome would particularly impact vulnerable populations, exacerbating the inequities that already exist in asthma outcomes globally.
Logic 5: No matter what ethical, scientific, medical, philosophical or governmental criteria is applied, it can be considered unacceptable to introduce a policy for which it is known that it will likely markedly increase the death rate from a common disorder.
Solution 5: The mandatory approval of HFO-1234ze(E) to ensure guaranteed manufacture and supply of inhaled asthma medications into the future.

Summary: While the current EU PFAS proposal has undoubted good intent, it will inevitably result in the reduced global availability of essential life-saving inhaled asthma medications, potentially leading to a marked increase in asthma deaths globally, and undermine the international efforts to reduce global warming. These cannot be considered unintended consequences, but rather the likely consequences of the proposed EU regulations.

I look forward to receiving your response.

Yours faithfully
Richard Beasley
