Content: Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Dear Members of ECHA, I fully welcome the intention to stop the environmental pollution by perfluorinated substances.
However, we have to distinguish between industrial use of PFAS and PFAS in end user products on the one hand and between low molecular PFAS and polymer PFAS on the other hand.
Polymeric PFAS like PTFE are valuable and indispensible for some industrial applications suchs as sealing applications under harsh conditions, high pressures or high temperatures.
We, STASSKOL, provide material solutions for demanding applications based on high performance polymers like PTFE, PFA, PVDF but also PEEK, Polyimde, PPS and others.
Everytime when high flexibility (low modulus of elasticity and high elongation at break) has to be combined with a demanding set of applicational parameters, there is no substitute available to fully fluorinated polymers.
This lies in the aliphatic nature of the PTFE molecule and in the strength of the C-F bond.
Alternative substances with comparable chemical resistance, pressure resistance and temperature resistance without Fluor are at least semi-aromatic like PEEK, Polyimides or PPS.
Thus, the disadvantage of being a "forever chemical" is on the same time an enabler for multiple application with the energy sector and the sector of sealing technologies including Hydrogen applications and other future energy technologies.
We, as STASSKOL GmbH strongly recommend to the following handling of PFAS:
1) Eliminate PFAS at applications where the benefit is below the risk of environmental pollution.
These are basically applications of weatherproof clothing, coating of kitchen articles, cosmetics and many more.
Here, the risk of environmental pollution is very high and the benefit is at least questionable.
2) The use of polymeric PFAS in industrial applications should be still allowed in the future
Fluorinated polymeric materials are enablers for a broad variety of new technology applications.
On the other hand they are physiologically neutral and harmless to humans and animals.
As for example materials like PTFE are allowed to be used in food and drug applications and also to be incorporated in human bodies (such as stents).
The only risk ist the disposal of such materials into the environment at the end of lifetime of the product.
Therefore,
3) Products out of polymeric PFAS such as PTFE, PFA or elastomers like FKM or FFKM
should be collected and either re-used or disposed in a environmentally friendly way to prevent
any accumulation of such materials in the nature. One example is the PTFE recycling process
established by STASSKOL to reduce the amount of waste during the production preoscess of PTFE sealing elements.
4) It has to be ensured, that the production of polymeric PFAS is carried out by preventing any pollution to the environment.
This was not always follow in history as some cases show a significant environmental pollyution around PTFE production facilities.
In summary, polymeric PFAS are very important substances at industrial applications such as high demanding sealing applications, but also in the energy sector for building electrolyzers, fluel cell membranes, solar modules or other future technologies.
If we can have a clean production of polymeric PFAS and an evironment friendly end-of-lifetime concept, then the benefit of polymeric PFAS is much higher than the risk of pollution.
We, STASSKOL, will show below, that PTFE can be recycled and that sealing elements out of polymeric PFAS such as PTFE are substantial for reducing environmental pollution.
In this way, the ban of polymeric PFAS, such as PTFE will be a thread for future technologies, for sealing applications and in consequence a thread for the environmental protection.
In summary, it is neccessary to exclude polymeric PFAS such as PTFE, PFA, PVDF, FKM, FFKM from this proposal.
Its important to allow these materials to be used ad advanced industrial applications and ensure that they are safely disposed at the end of product lifetime.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Manufacture [E.2.1.] - Sector as a whole Energy Sector [E.2.12.] - Sector as a whole STASSKOL is a supplier of sealing solutions for industrial applications such as seals for rotating shafts (pumps, compressors, blowers, mills, etc.) or for reciprocating compressor applications. These pieces of equipment are mostly designed for industrial applications and the sealing efficiency of such seals is very important for environmental protection. Moreover, a high number of the applications are used in the field of hydrogen compression  as replacement to fossile fuels. The sealing solutions are used at transport, storage & filling of hydrogen and thus for the entire H2 value chain. The sealing elements of these compressors are based on fluorinated polymers (PTFE). This sector of sealing technology has not yet been considered by ECHA. Moreover, also compressors for industrial processes like Hydrogenation, Polymerization and many more need reciprocating compressor systems with sealing elements based on PTFE to maximize operational reliability and to minimize leakage rates to the environment. Thus, its crucial to keep these polymeric materials available for industrial applications.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Sealing elements out of PTFE are produced from semi-finished bushings made by STASSKOL. Bushings are optimized in diameter and height to minimize waste and safe costs as good as possible. Nevertheless, approximately 70 % of the used material is PTFE (because of filler components like graphite, glass fibers and others). Approximately 30 % of the machined bushings are waste during the machining process at the production of the sealing elements. This waste can be recycled and STASSKOL has established a recycling process together with Neuman & Esser Process Technology and Dressler Group. The sealing elements are the used in reciprocating compressor systems within the Hydrogen value chain or biogas applications or other industrial services.  During the service lifetime the sealing element are losing about approx. 20 % of their initial volume due to friction and wear. This material will end up in the gas as small debris particles. The remaining 80 % are removed when servicing the compressor by installing new wear parts. The old wear parts are most likely disposed by incineration or landfilling. A recycling of used PTFE sealing materials could be possible (comparable to the waste at the machining process) if the pollution from the compression process can be removed sufficiently. Again: PTFE recycling is possible, this has been proved by Neuman & Esser Process Technology and STASSKOL, and a recycling by collaboration with a professional grinding company (Dressler Group) is already established. Landfilling should be avoided in the future to stop the accumulation of fluorinated polymers at the environment. It has to be ensured that PTFE is treated by incineration or recycling (preffered) at the end of life-time. The total amount of PTFE sealing materials at STASSKOL in 2022 was around 40 to 50 tons in total (mixtures). Numbers for PTFE raw material purchase in 2021 andd 2022 are included in the confidantal attachment.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: According to studies found in the scientific literature, the incineration of PTFE shows no significant generation of harmul low molecular PFAS. Thereby PTFE is decomposed into Carbon dioxide and HF. HF is then converted in the filter system into CaF2 (flourspar). As example, a very comprehensive article was published in 2019 in Chemosphere, Volume 226, page 898ff. This article is provided as attachment to this consultation. More information is available at the Institute of Technology in Karlsruhe (www.kit.edu). Thus, PTFE can be safely disposed by incineration at the end of the product life-time. However, recycling of PTFE should be always the 1st choice (if applicable for the specific product).

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Recycling of PTFE based sealing materials is already established partly at STASSKOL. If materials are collected grade by grade, the recycling process can be enlarged to cover nearly 100 % of all waste inhouse. Professional grinding companies are already on the market that allow the recycling of these perfluorinated polymers. Neuman & Esser Technology is providing efficient grinding equipment for the recycling process and Dressler Group is providing grinding service for their customers.  Basically, the recycling of perfluorinated poylmers is split into 3 steps: a) Collecting grade-specific waste b) Grinding process with milling particles down to about 20 – 30 micron c) Mixing grinded material with new material (Normal powder mixing process) d) Producing new semi-finished products from new mixture including recycling material  Recycling costs are roughly 10 € per kilogram which is nearly equal to the costs of the new material. This means, that it is doable at a financial point of view.  More information is provided as attachment to this consultation (presentation about the recycling process and literature).

5. Proposed derogations: STASSKOL is processing approximately 50 tons of PTFE-based sealing materials per year into wear parts for rotating equipment and reciprocating compressors. The PTFE content is on average 70 % which gives a total use of PTFE in the manufacturing of about 35 tons. 30 % of the 35 tons are collected in-house as waste from machining (~ 10.5 tons). This material can be recycled as described above. The remaining 24.5 tons are used as sealing elements in rotating equipment and reciprocating compressor parts. Thereby roughly 20 % (~ 5 tons) are wear debris entering the industrial processes. The remaining 19.5 tons are disposed by incineration or landfilling, but they could also be recycled after grade-specific collection and purification. Thus, the whole process of using 50 tons of sealing materials could be reduced to 5 tons of PFAS ending up as waste in industrial processes. Please note that STASSKOL is just one supplier in this industrial sector and the total volume can be higher than this.  There is no derogation planned for PTFE-based sealing materials in the compressor or pump industry yet.

6. Missing uses: As described above, the annual tonnage of PFAS material (mainly PTFE) used by STASSKOL to produce sealing elements for rotating and reciprocating equipment such as pumps and compressor systems is roughly 50 tons. Maximum 5 tons PFAS are lost due to friction and wear; the rest could be recycled by establishing the right processes. STASSKOL already started to successfully implement internally a PTFE recycling process to collect and re-use the waste generated at the machining facility.  It must be considered that the 5 tons that are lost due to friction and wear indeed get into the environment, but this is Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), which is an FDA approved per-fluorinated polymer that can be used in pharma and food industry. There is no harm to the environment due to the material lost by worn out sealing elements.  The key functionalities of the PTFE-based sealing materials are low friction and wear even at severe operational conditions such as high pressures (e.g. Hydrogen compressors at filling stations), high temperatures and high operational speeds in combination with an universal chemical resistance, especially at reciprocating compressor applications. This is unique to highly fluorinated polymers such as PTFE   For the number of companies, we must split between component suppliers, compressor manufacturers and end users. a)  Component suppliers: There are roughly 40 companies worldwide (approx. 5 in Europe) that are specialized in providing sealing solutions for rotating and reciprocating compressor systems as well as pumps. b)  Compressor manufacturers: There are many reciprocating compressor manufacturers in Europe (Neuma & Esser Group is one of the main manufacturers). Its about 10 to 20 companies that provide small, medium or large sized reciprocating compressor systems throughout Europe. c) Manufacturers of rotating equipment: The list of manufacturers of rotating equipment (screw compressors, turbo compressors, pumps, mills, etc.)  is nearly endless. Most of them need sealing materials based on PTFE to achieve maximum sealing efficiency at their products. d) The end-users are the critical part and the number is really not countable. Nearly every industrial process needs rotating or reciprocating compressor systems or pumps, just to name a few: • Hydrogen compressors for H2 pipeline transportation • Hydrogen compressors for H2 filling stations • Compression of biogas at biogas plants • Compression of CO2 in breweries • Compression of monomers prior to polymerization (eg. PE production) • Compression of Hydrogen prior to Hydrogenation or synthesis of ammonia. Thus, the number of customers affected by a ban of PTFE-based sealing materials is just endless and this will have a deep impact into the production processes and the industrial efficiency of European companies. Moreover, a ban of PTFE-sealing materials will have a bad impact to the environment as other sealing materials will lead to increased pollutions.  Alternative material could be non-fluorinated high-performance polymers, such as sealing materials based on Polyetheretherketone (PEEK), Polyphenylensulfide (PPS) or Polyimide (PI) or others. However, these polymers are not establishing a tribo-film on the counter surface of the sealing application (e.g. piston rod or cylinder liner). The tribo-film phenomenon is unique to PTFE-based materials, and it is viable for establishing low friction and a low wear rate and thus, increased operational reliability.   STASSKOL as a supplier for rotating and reciprocating sealing solutions is deeply involved into material developments since decades. To conduct this R&D work we have standard in-house material testing (tensile test, hardness, etc.) as well as a unique rotating and reciprocating tribometer test bed that’s unique to the market. Additionally, we have a large testbed for rotary seals and a reciprocating test compressor installed at the STASSKOL facility in Germany to test different sealing materials and sealing concepts in terms of sealing efficiency and lifetime. The tribological tests with the rotating and reciprocating tribometer as well as the real-life testing with the rotating test bed and the reciprocating compressor test bed have been executed with sealing elements based on different material compositions. One part are PTFE-based sealing elements, but also PEEK-based and PI-based as well as PPS-based recipes have been tested to get a grip on the durability of the materials and the sealing performance. Due to these tests, it could be observed that the so-called “tribo-film” only is established when using PTFE-based sealing materials. The phenomenon of the “tribo-Film” is a deposition of a thin PTFE layer (about 1 to 2 microns) onto the counter surface of the reciprocating movement (e.g. piston rod or cylinder liner). The “tribo-film” is well-known in the scientific literature and its proven in the literature but also at our own tests, that low wear and low frictional forces only can be observed if a sufficient “tribo-film” is generated. Thus, all material testing in the last decades based on other polymers ended up with high wear, which means that reliable sealing efficiency is only possible by using specialized sealing materials based on PTFE. It was shown for example at the reciprocating tribometer and at the reciprocating compressor test bed it has been shown that very high wear rates prevail without tribo-film. The running times of the sealing elements are reduced here in the range of 1-2 years in dry operation to a maximum of 1 - 2 months. This means uneconomical operation of the compressors and low availability of the system. What is worse, however, is that the leakage of a piston compressor increases by a factor of approx. 3-5 when PTFE-based sealing elements are changed to, for example, PEEK-based elements. This means considerable emissions when operating the compressors, which are directly released 1:1 into the environment. This is especially dramatic for the environment at methane and CO2 compressor installations.  We added a presentation about STASSKOL test capabilities as well as literature about tribo-film generation and wear behavior depending on tribo-film generation as attachment to this consultation.  As described, the service lifetimes of sealing elements for rotating and reciprocating compressors, pumps and other equipment will drop dramatically when changing from PTFE-based sealing elements to alternative high-performance polymer systems. The running times of the sealing elements are reduced here in the range of 1-2 years in dry operation to a maximum of 1 - 2 months. This will have a dramatic influence on the performance of industrial processes such as Hydrogen compression for H2 transport, polymerization processes, Hydrogenation processes and many more.  Moreover, PTFE is a relatively weak material which ensures high sealing efficiency beside the low wear. This weakness is only possible with aliphatic polymers. Aliphatic polymers have a low resistance to temperature and harsh chemicals. Only PTFE shows this resistance due to the strong C-F bond. Thus, it’s evident from a chemical point of view that this sealing efficiency at demanding conditions can only be achieved with PTFE-based materials. The sealing efficiency of alternative high-performance polymers is due to increased stiffness much lower. This leads to increased leakage rates from reciprocating compressor installations to the environment. Especially dramatic when talking about methane (Biogas, LNG, CNG, …) and CO2 (Breweries) compressor systems.  A ban of PTFE-based sealing materials would be a severe thread for future energies but especially for the protection of the environment.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: No derogation available for sealing materials based on PTFE, especially at rotating and reciprocating compressor systems, as well as pumps. There are no feasible alternatives available as the efficiency of PTFE-based sealing materials lies in the nature of the polymer molecule. Thus, there will be also no future alternative available.

8. Other identified uses: No alternatives available, this can be scientifically proved by available literature and R&D testing at our test facilities (see attached material). Indeed, the social economic impact will be huge as the ban of polymeric PFAS like PTFE will be a thread for the environmental protection as well as the European industry, especially future technologies like te Hydrogen value chain. This can be prooved by the information provided as attachment to this consultation.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: No alternative materials are available for sealing elements such as sealing for rotating equipment, for pumps, or packing rings, rider rings and piston rings for reciprocating compressors. Only PTFE-based sealing materials can be utilized to achieve maximum reliable operation and lowest leakages for maximum environmental protection. Most of the PTFE material can be recycled and the PTFE material that gets into the environment due to friction and wear is polymeric and categorized by the FDA as “generally recognized as safe” for the environment as well as for food and pharma PTFE is chemically stable, no degradation is expectable and polymeric PTFE is harmless in itself.

10. Analytical methods: In the report it was stated that PTFE recycling is not possible nowadays. That’s not true, as STASSKOL already has established a recycling process for fully fluorinated polymers together with professional partners. Moreover, we are giving this information to third parties (online-seminars, conferences, close contact to other PTFE-using companies such as Trelleborg) to also enable others to step into the recycling process of fluorinated polymers.  Fluorinated polymeric materials are a key factor for establishing renewable energy solutions such as Hydrogen economy or electromobility and they are indispensable for sealing elements at the processing industry, there, reciprocating compressor spare parts are only one but an important example.  Therefore, we have to find ways to avoid waste in the Future such as the recycling process started by STASSKOL instead of a ban for these unique polymers that enable our future technologies.  The basic analytic method to validate possible alternatives to PTFE in sealing applications is the equipment for tribological investigations. By the means of this equipment it can be shown that no alternative materials are available compared to wear resistant compounds based on PTFE.

General Comments: Dear reader,
The attachment in section IV reflects the input from the members of Norwegian Hydrogen Forum and will go further into detail on what types and where PFAS is used in the hydrogen value chain, status on the alternatives and consequences of a PFAS ban in the hydrogen sector. See attachment for more reasons and sources.

PFAS is essential in many crucial technologies throughout the hydrogen value chain, such as electrolyses and fuel cells, storage applications, infrastructure and refueling stations, to name just a few.
There are no alternatives on the market today or in the foreseen future that can replace PFAS in these applications. There are strong R&D efforts going into researching alternatives to fluoropolymers, but they are still significantly inferior in terms of the duration and stability needed.

The fluoropolymers used in the hydrogen value chain meet the OECD criteria to be defined as ‘polymers of low concern’ (PLC), and do not pose a risk to human health or the environment.

Hydrogen is key to decarbonizing the global energy system and hard to abate sectors in order to reach the ambitious climate targets. A rushed PFAS ban without exemptions for applications in the hydrogen sector would jeopardize the achievement of EU’s Hydrogen Strategy, REPowerEU targets and of the Green Deal objectives.

Based on this, there should be an exemption for the use of PFAS in the hydrogen industry.

General Comments: Dear Sir or Madam,

Siempelkamp Maschinen- und Anlagenbau GmbH welcomes the opportunity to contribute to the public consultation initiated by the European Chemicals Agency regarding potential restriction of Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) according to Regulation (EC) No. 1907/2006 (“REACH”).

Siempelkamp Maschinen- und Anlagenbau GmbH is an internationally active German family owned company. Sustainability and resource efficiency are the defining issues of our time. We bundle the answers to these challenges in our corporate claim “Intelligent engineering for future generations”. It stands for the energy with which we align our technologies with the future topics of digitalization and sustainability. “Engineering” refers to our core competence for which the name “Siempelkamp” has stood since 1883. As a technology supplier and systems provider for machinery and plant engineering, our core business is focused on the production of complete plants for the wood-based panel industry, as well as different types of press-systems for a wide range of essential application areas. "Intelligent engineering" in summary illustrates our approach to continuously developing machines and technologies and thus shape the future of our industries. “For future generations” sums up our ambition to improve the world through our actions. Siempelkamp technologies are geared towards the careful use of resources and raw materials. We develop sustainable, durable products and future-oriented services. Our sustainability concept includes, for example, research and development in the areas of alternative raw materials and recycling or usage of our press-systems for future technologies e.g. in the area of light-weight components. Our portfolio is tailored to energy-efficient, sustainable production. In this way, we fulfill our corporate responsibility towards society.

With regard to the proposed restriction on the manufacture, placing on the market or use of PFASs we submit that for Lubricants under harsh conditions (Annex XV Restriction Proposal E.2.14. Lubricants) the proposed restriction does not adequately distinguish between the fields of application and service life time of the components/plants.

Request for exemption

We propose that the following wording should be incorporated into the REACH Annex XV Restriction Report regarding PFASs as Lubricants:
Annex XV Restriction Report E.2.1.14 Lubricants under harsh conditions:
• “In case of applications in a closed environment with defined human interactions an additional derogation period is possible if no alternatives have been established.”
• “In case of applications for plants/components which service life time extends the derogation period an additional derogation period is possible if no alternatives have been established”

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: This consultation for the Annex XV restriction report gives more specific information about the use of lubricants under harsh conditions according Annex E.2.14. Table 9. To produce our sustainable wood-based materials (particleboards, MDF-boards, OSB-boards or even wood-fiber insulation boards), high-temperature bearings are used in our whole form- and pressing-line. Especially with our continuous press system (ContiRoll®), the operating temperature is around 270 °C. Despite the high thermal load within the ContiRoll® these bearings achieve an extraordinarily long bearing life time through the use of high-temperature greases. Currently, there is no adequate PFAS-free alternative that would be reasonable for the plant operation of our customers. As stated by previous stakeholders in the Annex XV Restriction Report (E.2.1.14 Lubricants) there are no alternative lubricants which could ensure the safe functioning, safety of equipment and a comparable service life time for the components under harsh conditions. As soon as PFAS-free alternatives become available that do not severely affect the customer in the operation and maintenance of the plant, we will switch to these alternatives. The used high-temperature long-term synthetic greases are based on per-fluorinated polyether oils. In our respectively our customers’ cases, the use of PFAS substances is restricted to a closed environment that is only accessible to humans during maintenance. Contact with people only occurs when changing the lubricant, where on the one hand our lubrication schedule specifies the quantity and regularity and on the other hand, maintenance is restricted to trained staff including the use of protective equipment. The re-lubrication process involves re-lubricating the bearings by injecting new grease into the bearing. About the same amount that is injected into the bearing is pushed out of the bearing and is disposed properly by the staff. The bearings are sealed in such a way that no/just a small amount of grease leaks out during operation. Leaked grease is disposed in the same way as above.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: To be able to operate our ContiRoll® accurately and safely and ensure our customers a long service life, our customers need to re-lubricate our bearing positions according to our lubrication plan. The number of lubrication spots depends on the length and on the width of our ContiRoll®. As stated under no. 1, contact with people only occurs when changing the lubricant, where on the one hand our lubrication schedule specifies the quantity and regularity and on the other hand, maintenance is restricted to trained staff including the use of protective equipment. About the same amount that is injected into the bearing is pushed out of the bearing and is disposed properly by the staff. The bearings are sealed in such a way that no/just a small amount of grease leaks out during operation. Since the lubricant is paste-like just a tiny amount of grease leaks out. The leaked grease is cleaned with textiles, the total uncontrolled emissions can be estimated as below 5%. After usage the lubricant and contaminated material is collected in a separate container and disposed as required by local regulations.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: In our respectively our customers’ cases, the use of PFAS substances is restricted to a closed environment that is only accessible to humans during maintenance. Contact with people only occurs when changing the lubricant, where on the one hand our lubrication schedule specifies the quantity and regularity and on the other hand, maintenance is restricted to trained staff including the use of protective equipment.  After end of life the bearings are scrap metal and melted down during the production of new material. This prevents the per- and poly-fluorinated alkyl substances from accumulating. The effectiveness of incineration under normal operational conditions with respect to the destruction of PFAS and the prevention of emissions was evaluated in the following studiy: Waste incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate potential formation of per- and poly-fluorinated alkyl substances (PFAS) in flue gas [Aleksandrov et al, 2019]. Additionally, the prevention of emission is regulated in the European industrial emission directive 2010/75/EU.

5. Proposed derogations: For over 200 ContiRoll® plants in operation worldwide, the specified minimum consumption of all our customers is over 8 tons per year (more specified information according to one of our lubrication plans). According to our supplier, our customers even purchase approx. 17 tons of this lubrication grease per year for the whole forming- and pressing-line. Since these greases are PTFE/PFPE mixtures, our supplier assumes a content of 100% PFAS. The use of the grease is limited to a closed environment (the bearing). While the plant is running (>95% of the time), the bearings are not accessible. Re-lubrication is performed using grease nipples in distant from the actual bearing. The above stated overconsumption results in filling of dead space in the bearing housing. The volume of dead-space in the bearings vary and depend on several variables, but the dead space is absolutely necessary for a safe operation.

8. Other identified uses: Since our plants are built to serve our customers for up to 30 years, we are proposing that PFAS-containing greases can continue to be used under harsh conditions if PFAS-free alternatives for harsh conditions do not enter the market within the extended transition period of 13.5 years. Bearings have to be replaced with exactly the same type. Any other option like reconstruction of the affected parts would result in high costs – unless it is possible to reconstruct. Thus ensuring the operation of new built plants or plants currently under construction until the end of its lifetime. Our current bearing lifetime is around 6 years. Using greases without suitable thermo-mechanical properties would result in a tripling of the amount of grease and thereby in a tripling of waste and resources due to alteration. The tripling is due to the larger dimensions of the bearings as our plants are able to produce faster compared to our former plants. Additionally, the lifetime of the bearings are expected to halve without PFAS containing lubricants. Furthermore, due to insufficient thermal stability, the grease would slowly leak out of the bearing and thus contaminate the entire press, especially the press environment and would harm the quality of the sustainable wood-based products. In addition, the triple amount of grease would not lubricate adequately and thus increased wear out still occurs which would reduce the service-lifetime of our plants tremendous.  Without an adequate alternative, the lifetime of our bearings will be reduced by approximately half or more of the time. This would mean that with 200 plants in operation, each containing at least 70 bearings in high thermo-mechanical loaded areas, 14,000 bearings would need to be replaced every two to three years. This would result in a doubling of the consumption of resources, a doubling of the waste and a doubling of the energy-intense disposal by melting down the bearings. This would contradict our sustainable corporate principles. Furthermore, this would result in 100,000€ – 200,000€ additional costs per plant per service period if no PFAS-free alternative is developed after the end of the extended transition period. Not mentioned the costs for additional downtimes for our customers with up to 150,000€ per day. Currently, there are no PFAS-free lubricating grease alternatives on the market. The research activity regarding PFAS-free lubricants for harsh conditions is part of our supplier. Part of our research activity is how we can redesign our plants to reduce the number of bearings that are subjected to high thermo-mechanical loads. In almost every plant, 36 assemblies are affected. Redesigning all the affected assemblies seems unrealistic. Some assemblies are unavoidable in terms of their thermo-mechanical load. Due to the complex interaction between most assemblies, a redesign for existing plants would not be economically justifiable. Additionally to the increased costs for bearings and lubricants, the manufacturing of these goods results in additional consumption of resources und emission of greenhouse gas emissions.

General Comments: Dear Sir or Madam,

We are a medium-sized company in mechanical engineering, especially in the field of machine tool building and metal cutting. On the one hand, we use PFAS sealants, especially FKM and PTFE, in our products. On the other hand, such sealants are installed in our production equipment, for example in pumps, valves and hoses.
We depend on sealants that are resistant to temperature and chemicals. This is also due to the fact that we cannot assess the chemicals with which our products come into contact at the customers. Especially in metal cutting, a large number of coolants and lubricants are used whose composition we do not know. In addition, bacteria can spread in such coolants and lubricants, which in turn produce a number of chemical substances that can attack and destroy the sealants.

There is no prospect of replacing these sealants with PFAS-free materials.

In the event of a restriction, maintenance and the procurement of spare parts for the plants would also pose major problems. If individual sealing elements can no longer be replaced, larger plant components such as pumps would have to be completely replaced and the old parts scrapped.

This would completely contradict the goal of a sustainable economy.


We support the EU's efforts to make production plants and processes as environmentally friendly as possible and to avoid the use of hazardous substances.
However, it is incomprehensible why the use of an entire group of substances should be banned, even though no concrete hazards are known from the majority of these substances.

We urge you to limit the planned restrictions only to those substances that have been proven to be hazardous to health or the environment.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Dear Sir,

Proposed EU REACH Restriction of PFAS - Fluoropolymers

As the Owner and Managing Director of Holscot Advanced Polymers Limited,  I write to you to register our objection to the proposed EU REACH restriction of certain materials currently classified as PFAS, and to request that the proposal is modified, which I will justify in the following pages, to exclude Perfluoroalkoxy Alkane (PFA), Fluorinated Ethylene Propylene (FEP) and Ethylene Tetrafluoroethylene (ETFE).

In line with the published public consultation schedule starting 22nd March 2023 and ending 22nd September 2023, I also register with you our request for a derogation from the restriction for our uses of the following fluoropolymers; PFA, FEP and ETFE, in the event that the modifications are not accepted.


Who is Holscot Advanced Polymers and what do we do?
Holscot is a UK Private Limited Company with registered offices in UK, Netherlands and Germany.  We have manufacturing in England, Scotland and Netherlands.
We buy PFA, FEP and ETFE Fluoropolymers and make/convert/manufacture these into a large portfolio of products, sold business to business.  The products solve the technical problems of industry and greatly benefit society by using the amazing properties of these fluoropolymers that no other materials possess.

Why we are opposed to the restriction ?
The restriction is based on the grounds of materials persistence.  Whereas the scope of EU REACH is to protect from harm, humans and the environment (article 68 (1) REACH.  Persistence is not an indication of harm.  Persistence is out of scope of EU REACH remit and as such their restriction of chemicals for the purpose of persistence is not valid.

The restriction classifies PFAS as “Any substance that contains at least one fully fluorinated methyl (CF3-) or methylene (-CF2-) carbon atom without any H/Cl/Br/I attached to it.”   Whereas the harmful PFAS are a small subset of this classification.  The chemical properties and risk associated with one chemical group does not transmit to every instance of that group when present in another polymer.  The 1995 US Polymer Exemption Rule was introduced to prevent such blanket restriction which it deemed was unnecessary.  Thus the risk associated with a group of concern must be proven in each instance of application in a polymer chemical.
https://www.epa.gov/reviewing-new-chemicals-under-toxic-substances-control-act-tsca/polymer-exemption-new-chemicals

The environmental and toxicological profiles are distinctly different in Fluoropolymers solids than the majority of other PFAS liquid chemicals.  The assumption that chemical properties are transferred to every instance of occurrence is unfounded and as such the restriction is invalid.

Annex 68 of the Proposed Reach Restriction requires that Fluoropolymers which “pose risk to human health or the environment that is not adequately controlled and needs to be addressed”.  Fluoropolymers are inert and do not cause harm to humans or the environment.  Fluoropolymers are used for medical applications where devices are inserted and remain in the human body.   These have been in use for over 60 years which his proof of their lack of harm and toxicity to humans.

https://www.nordsonmedical.com/Components-and-Technologies/Medical-Tubing/PTFE-Tubing/#:~:text=PTFE%20has%20been%20used%20in,is%20an%20ideal%20catheter%20liner.

The CJEU has held that a risk cannot be purely hypothetical: “[ purely hypothetical
risks based on mere hypotheses that have not been scientifically confirmed cannot be accepted. To make the maintenance of the authorisation of a substance subject to proof of the lack of any risk, even a purely hypothetical one, would be both unrealistic in so far as such proof is generally impossible to give in scientific terms since 'zero risk' does not exist in practice”.

Fluoropolymers do not break down to form harmful chemicals, as has been proven by the Danish EPA. They have been classified as polymers of low concern as documented in the Society of Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry by BJ Henry published 9th February 2018.
https://setac.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ieam.4035

Fluoropolymers are also “food approved” by the FDA in America, so viewed as very safe to humans.

Fluoropolymers are certified not to combust and are proven self extinguishing for example used in the fire proofing of wires.  This is an established major use in high rise buildings World wide (“plendum cable”), this application alone uses 1000’s of tons of melt processable Fluoropolymers.

Fluoropolymers meet the OECD Polymer of Low Concern (PLC) criteria.  They are non-toxic, not bio available, non-water soluble and non-mobile molecules and are deemed as such to have no significant environmental and human health impact.
https://www.oecd.org/env/ehs/oecddefinitionofpolymer.htm

The proposed restriction plans enforcement through the concept of “use”.  There are millions of uses of our products, many that we are not privileged to be informed about, owing to non-disclosure by certain customer and national bodies.  So, the proposed method of restriction and derogation is unworkable.


In summary, the proposed restriction is :-

Summary and Conclusions:

Our corporation uses substances, mixtures and articles containing PFAS in controlled production processes and services under controlled conditions if this is necessary for technical reasons and other materials are not available. In certain cases, mixtures containing PFAS are produced under controlled production processes as well if this is necessary for technical and scientific reasons, for instance a PFAS-based immersion oil, which offers groundbreaking microscopic work with live cells to the scientific community.

Examples for these PFAS-based substances, mixtures and articles are described in chapters 5.1 - 5.4 of this statement (please see confidential attachment). The disposal of the resulting waste containing PFAS is regulated so that the PFAS cannot enter the environment and lead, for example, to contamination of soil and groundwater. When these substances are used, the risk to employees and the environment is determined in risk assessments and - if necessary - appropriate protective measures are defined. These measures are regularly checked for effectiveness, e. g. through inspections and audits (according to ISO9001, ISO14001 and ISO 45001 standards).

Our corporation supports the goal of the “Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability” [34] that aims to better protect citizens and the environment from harmful chemicals, and boost innovation by promoting the use of safer and more sustainable chemicals.

Europe would do well to take the lead on PFASs and innovate to replace them wherever possible. Within the framework of sustainable chemicals regulation, substances that pose unmanageable risks due to their properties and use profile should be restricted or regulated based on scientific assessments.

High-performance materials containing PFAS are however doomed for exactly the technical property for which they are needed and predominantly irreplaceable: their durability and resistance, even in essential applications – industrial high-tech products and production processes.

Scientific literature stated that PFAS uses in industrial processes can be highly complex and a thorough evaluation of the technical function of each PFAS and of the suitability of alternatives is needed [35].

The proposed ban on PFAS will affect our corporation severely by lower turnover and in parallel additional costs for finding, qualifying and validating PFAS-free substitutes.

Since our corporation is a company producing not only products for other corporate business units within a corporate structure and external customers as an OEM, but also delivering services to other business units in the overall corporate structure the impact of a PFAS restriction will not only affect the products itself but also the ability to deliver technical services, for instance machine repair and maintenance, measurement, laboratory and development services.

PFAS-free alternatives may have risks concerning safety of employees and the environment as well, besides the fact that they are no ready drop-in replacements for todays PFAS-based solutions. This is described in detail in chapter 6 (socio-economic considerations) of this statement and from a technical point of view in chapters 5.1 – 5.4.

So, if there are no PFAS-free alternatives available for a drop-in replacement of PFAS-based substances, mixtures and articles which have the same technical performance as the today’s solutions, reliable and probably much more additional derogations in number than listed in the current restriction proposal [15] as well as derogations with revised wording are needed which cover the full suite of controlled PFAS uses. In chapters 5.1 – 5.4 we have provided revised wording for some derogations which we kindly ask the EChA to consider.

Additionally, the derogation times should be set in a way, that there will be enough time to test, implement, qualify and validate alternatives, if there will be any at all. We propose changes to the derogation times in chapters 5.1 – 5.4 and ask the EChA to consider these in the ongoing process. We must take into account, that PFAS based substances have been already reported since the 19th century and have been started to being commercialized since the mid 1950ies [37]. Such a long history which led to the development of a huge variety of products, including high-tech polymers, cannot be swept away by rather short derogation periods.

We also would like to kindly ask the EChA to allow for a further prolongation of the derogation times, if there would be no commercially available PFAS-free substitutes on the market during and after the first derogation period, which could be used as a drop-in material.


It is also not quite understandable why the "Essential Use Concept” [34 - 36] demanded by the EU Commission itself was so far not applied to essential areas of application in the PFAS restriction procedure, like industrial processes and industrial products, which are essential for society.

The Essential Use concept aims to ensure that chemicals are only allowed "when their use is necessary for health, safety or the functioning of society. In [34, page 13] it is explicitly stated that, cit: “That is why the Commission proposes a comprehensive set of actions to address the use of and contamination with PFAS. Those aim to ensure, that the use of PFAS is phased out in the EU, unless it is proven essential for society”.

So, the regulators should consider that PFAS uses which are essential for health, safety or the functioning of society must be allowed without any time-limited derogations, especially if there are no drop-in solutions available. Such uses should include the use of all PFAS-based polymers of low concern (PLC) according to the OECD-definition (i. e. all PFAS-based polymers including PFPE).

General Comments: Dear valued ECHA Committee Members!

The general idea of more restricting the use and application of PFAS is important and over due since many years. However, we strongly agree with many of the comments already made here by others, that a number of 10.000 different substances cannot be treated without careful differentiation and responsible weighing up the benefits and consequences.

We are a globally leading and acknowledged pioneer in manufacture and application development of so called "ionic liquids" (ILs) with more than 20 years of experience. In general Ionic Liquids are defined as organic low temperature molten salts, with a melting point below 100 °C, in their liquid state. In many cases these substances are liquid at room temperature and below. As they are salt melts (and not solutions of salts in molecular solvents), their intermolecular forces are predominated by Coulomb forces and strong hydrogen bonds, resulting in a number of totally different properties than conventional fluids, e.g. having an extremely low vapor pressure, closer to typical solids than liquids. In the last 20 years the field of ionic liquids and their applications developed enormously and today a number of approx. 100.000 scientific papers and 26.000 patent families are published world wide. For more information see e.g. [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionic_liquid]. In summary ILs are an important emerging technology with impact in numerous fields of technical applications, including many sustainability and environmental topics, e.g. energy storage, energy harvesting, waste up-cycling, textile recycling, CO2 separation, biomass conversion, Sustainable Aviation Fuels, etc. Today around 50 industrial applications are in their pilot stage or implemented, see [“Toward Industrialization of Ionic Liquids”; Kalb Roland S. In: Shiflett M. (ed) “Commercial Applications of Ionic Liquids”, pp 261-282; Green Chemistry and Sustainable Technology, Springer (2020); https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-35245-5_11].

Typical ions used in ionic liquids are e.g. alkylated imidazolium, ammonium, phosphonium and pyrrolidinium cations combined with e.g. acetate, formiate, dialkylphosphate, chloride, alkylsulfate and alkylsulfonate anions.

Two very special anions with huge importance are Trifluoromethanesulfonate (CF3SO3-, "Triflate", CAS 37181-39-8) and Bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide (CF3SO2-N-SO2CF3-, "TSFI", CAS 98837-98-0), which are subject to the current ECHA PFAS restriction proposal. Approx. 300 scientific papers were published and 300 patent families filed for ionic liquids with TRIFLATE anions, 15.000 scientific papers were published and 4650 patent families filed for ionic liquids with TFSI anions [search results using CAS SciFinder Database, see attached SciFinder search report pdf files]. Also 83 ionic liquids with these anions can be found in the ECHA C&L inventory, of wich 3 are REACH registered as well [see "Triflate and TFSI Ionic Liquids at ECHA.xlsx" attached].

Ionic liquids with these anions show unique thermal and electrochemical stability and usually are non-flammable. They cannot be substituted by other anions like e.g. tetrafluoroborate (BF4-) or hexafluorophosphate (PF6-), as ionic liquids based on these anions are less stable, but for all are hydrolytically unstable and potentially release toxic hydrogen fluoride gas. Due to the high stability ionic liquids with Triflate and TFSI anions are typically developed for and applied in energy storage applications (e.g. non-flammable batteries, thermal storage), as electrolytes for sensors and organic photovoltaic cells, high temperature cooling applications, polymer fabrication, as catalysts or catalyst carrier solvents, as engineering and process fluids, etc.

The affected PFAS moiety in case of Triflate and TFSI is the CF3 group, the smallest possible PFAS with the lowest lipophilic character and presumably lowest toxic effect. Ionic liquids with these anions would not be released into the environment by evaporation, as the vapor pressure is virtually zero and as they are typically non-flammable . Such ionic liquids are quite expensive and would be used in sealed containments (e.g. cellular phones, organic PV cells etc.) or under controlled industrial conditions; also such ionic liquids would be collected at the end of life and be either recycled (high value!) or being incinerated under controlled and compliant conditions.  The available literature on chronic toxic effects of triflate and TFSI is very scarce [source CAS SciFinder Database], which is not a good basis for an restriction or ban.

The Market for these ionic liquids is still early and therefore small, but the potential for many industrial applications - including valuable sustainability applications - is huge and would be cut off completely, if these anions would now be restricted at this stage.

I request for exemption for salts, more specifically salts with organic cations, more specifically ionic liquids with

⦁ CF3SO2 functional group(s) in their anion,
⦁ more specifically with Trifluoromethanesulfonate or Bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide anions.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis
Combined Comments:
"The current EU PFAS ban proposal describes the most far-reaching restriction plan in the world for a very large group of existing and as yet unknown PFAS. Of the slightly more than 10,000 substances already known, only a small part is economically relevant. The vast majority of these substances have only been produced on a laboratory or pilot-plant scale, have not gained economic significance, are controlled and stored, or safely disposed of (special waste incineration with complete mineralization). The properties of economically irrelevant compounds are often only minimally studied. Should these substances become economically significant, they would be subject to an individual registration procedure in accordance with the proven REACh (Registration, Evaluation, Authorization and Restriction of Chemicals) regulation and would be more closely examined and assessed. For all of the more than 10,000 PFAS, as well as for the economically relevant group of PFAS, it applies that these substances can differ significantly in their properties. In addition to extremely dangerous and poorly controllable PFAS, whose necessity must be doubted in many cases and for which a ban is therefore appropriate and necessary (e.g. PFOA, PFOS, etc.), there are many harmless PFAS that can be safely produced, used, disposed of, or destroyed. At the same time, such PFAS carry a high technical, health-preserving / health-restoring, environmental-protecting, and societal value within themselves (e.g. polymeric PFAS in the sense of Polymers of Low Concern such as PTFE Polytetrafluoroethylene, PFPE Perfluoropolyether, fluoroelastomers, etc.). The ban on all PFAS after at most 13.5 years is always justified by the fact that these substances cannot all be individually examined, and the impression is given that the substances cannot be grouped into subgroups. At the same time, all PFAS are illicitly profiled with worst-case profiles of substances such as PFOA, PFOS, etc. However, the PFAS can be grouped by means of structural and functional considerations and methods such as QSAR (Quantitative Structure-Activity Relationship), which can be jointly evaluated via the Read-Across approach. The amount of examination effort can thus be reduced many times over. Furthermore, the urgency of the comprehensive ban is justified by the fact that PFAS are detectable in the environment and in living organisms. The economically irrelevant PFAS will not be found, and of the economically relevant PFAS, only those whose harmfulness is already essentially known and for which restrictions and bans already exist or are in the process of being developed will be found (e.g. PFOA, PFOS). Other substances will indeed be found in the environment, but due to their properties, they are partly not bioavailable, bioaccumulable, or toxic (e.g. PTFE, PFPE). Summative analysis of the fluoride content cannot differentiate and is therefore only of very limited use. The ban proposal ignores the fact that the extraction, processing, use, and disposal of PFAS are subject to a constant process of improvement and innovation. Thus, PFPE has been able to be produced completely free of emissions for many years and also does not require low-molecular PFAS emulsifiers. And in the production of PTFE, the industry is working on the elimination of PFAS-containing process aids. Even in the area of PFAS waste disposal and drinking water treatment, methods have been developed in recent months that can remove substances such as PFOA from drinking water, some methods even allow for the degradation of PFAS. Current studies also show that PFAS can be safely mineralized even in household waste incineration plants that meet EU standards. This alone calls into question the frequently used classification of PFAS as "eternal chemicals", a term that has no scientific validity but is suitable for arousing and reinforcing diffuse fears among the population and political decision-makers. With the almost irreversible ban, the EU cuts itself off from technological developments in the world. Furthermore, the ban proposal abandons established approaches such as risk-based assessment of chemicals. Instead, only hazardous characteristics are cited, and new "hazardous" characteristics such as persistence are invoked, which are supposed to justify a ban on their own. Data on emissions, immissions, migration, exposure, bioavailability, etc., which could be used to assess the risk of a chemical, are not considered. Thus, we are sacrificing valuable chemicals, even though we have learned in the past to deal responsibly and safely with dangerous chemicals if they are beneficial to us. The diverse use of predominantly high-priced PFAS, often in very small quantities, but crucial for the function of materials and components in countless devices, machines, and systems, is hardly comprehensible. Often, they are small, highly specialized companies whose products would suffer extreme performance losses or become unusable without PFAS. The consequences of such a comprehensive and rapid ban are hardly foreseeable for these companies, the EU, and even non-EU countries. It can already be foreseen that countries such as China, India, the USA, and even the United Kingdom will not follow the EU approach of a comprehensive PFAS ban and will take advantage of the EU PFAS ban. PFAS will be increasingly used in countries with significantly less advanced chemical legislation, which means that, especially mobile PFAS, will still find their way into the EU via the environment. It can also be assumed that PFAS will continue to be illegally imported into the EU via complex aggregates or poorly analyzable materials/products. The numerous and never-ending product recalls for consumer products from non-EU countries (e.g. due to Cr(VI), carcinogenic substances, etc.) show how difficult it is to prevent these imports.
The fact that the ban proposal lists PFAS-containing ski waxes, which are technically easily replaceable and whose emissions are low compared to other PFAS-containing products, as a separate use, while essential materials for chemical plant construction, for example, are not even included, shows how difficult it was for the authors of the ban to grasp the significance and scope of the use of PFAS. The current consultation, due to the inherent high complexity of the chosen restriction approach, will not lead to any significant improvement in quality. The present ban proposal is scientifically immature and was developed on the basis of insufficient data. The data situation will not allow for a reliable impact assessment even after the consultation. It is not socioeconomically evaluable and will therefore be vulnerable. Industrially, the restriction proposal runs counter to the EU's goals. Technologically, it leads to a further weakening of the EU. The uncertainties regarding the impact on the industry will further exacerbate and accelerate the already significant migration of companies from the EU. The planned restrictions are unjustifiable and disproportionate in many cases. Due to the numerous inadequacies, the approach, and conflicts with existing legal regulations, it is foreseeable that the law will be reviewed by the courts. This will further impair the planning security of companies and lead to further emigration, especially of larger companies. Many smaller companies dependent on PFAS are at risk due to the fact that they can no longer obtain the materials they need and cannot move to non-EU countries. The restriction proposal should therefore not be supported by RAC and SEAC and should be fundamentally revised.
Dr. rer. nat. Günther Bodesheim Munich, 25.09.2023"

General Comments: Derogation request for exemption to use “ultrashort-chain fluorocarbon C3F6 in low pressure plasma coating processes” from the PFAS restriction proposal
Dear Sir / Madam
We are writing to submit a derogation request on behalf of SEFAR AG to the European Apparel and Textile Confederation (EURATEX) concerning the use of a ultrashort-chain fluorocarbon C3F6, in combination with low pressure plasma coating processes. We kindly request the exemption of this specific application method from the PFAS restriction proposal as stated under the ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT.
Sefar, a Swiss based company, is the leading manufacturer of precision fabrics from monofilaments for the filtration and screen printing market. Sefar products are used in a wide variety of industries, reaching from electronics, graphics, medical, automotive, food and pharmaceutical applications to aerospace, mining & refining and architecture. With its profound understanding of the applications, Sefar helps its customers to achieve optimum results in their industrial processes. Subsidiaries and fabrication centers in 26 countries on 6 continents provide local technical service for the broad range of solutions offered by Sefar.

Sefar has concentrated on producing the finest and most precise square holes based on textiles for over 190 years. With up to 300 monofilaments per cm in warp and weft direction, Sefar produces a textile with 90’000 identical, precise square holes per cm2. This specialization on technical applications has allowed Sefar to successfully survive the severe crisis of the textile industry in Switzerland, and has made us the world leader in this field.

In low-pressure PECVD (Plasma-enhanced Chemical Vapor Deposition) processes, the material or substrate to be treated/coated is placed in a vacuum chamber. After the air has been evacuated from that chamber, a precursor gas or vapor is introduced into it. Subsequently, this gas or vapor is brought into an ionized state (=plasma) by applying an electro-magnetic field to it. These ionized species polymerize on the surface of the material to be treated, thus forming a nano-coating. These plasma-polymers are generally highly branched and highly cross-linked, and adhere well to solid surfaces and less chance to delaminate during application.
Using these processes, it is possible to deposit a very thin nano-coating on substrates, where the properties of the coatings are determined by the used precursor (source material which can be a liquid or a gas), the system’s design and the defined parameter settings for plasma generation.
Low-pressure PECVD systems and processes are used in many sectors, such as filtration, technical mesh and membranes, consumer textiles (apparel), medical plastics, industrial and consumer electronics.

Some of the applications in the before mentioned sectors, as well as other applications in other sectors which are currently not using low-pressure PECVD, require an oleophobic behavior.

Following the restriction on PFOA/PFOS containing substances and the subsequent restriction on PFHxA containing substances and longer chain C9-C14 PFCAs, Sefar invested substantially in the development of mainly halogen-free alternatives, but also in the use of the ultrashort-chained fluorocarbon C3F6, the latter for those applications having the expressed need for oleophobicity, indispensable to the application (and for instance not for use as DWR treatment).

Although the achieved level of oleophobicity, using this gas as a precursor, is in general lower than when applying long-chain fluorocarbon precursors, it has shown to be sufficient for targeted applications, using the low-pressure PECVD technology.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Derogation for C3F6-based PECVD processes Sefar requests an exemption for the use of C3F6 as precursor in combination with a low-pressure plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition process for all applications where oleophobicity is an explicit property for the application.   This is the case for, among others, following products: • Electronic devices: mobile phones, portable media players, high fidelity equipment, tablets, laptops, portable devices and televisions.  • Filtration applications: Electronics, graphics, medical, automotive, food and pharmaceutical applications to aerospace, mining & refining and architecture: eg. acoustic vents, ventilation filters, fuel filtration, water separation, packaging, wound dressings, protective masks.  • Venting & liquid filtration: matrasses, beddings, ventilation filter, surgical coats, intravenous filter sets, pressure filtration equipment, medical devices, room ventilation and venting barrier media for industrial applications. • Others: building and electronic seals, non-woven materials for diverse applications: automotive, transport.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The use of this specific coating method to form fluoropolymer nanocoatings is very environment-friendly for several reasons:  • The processes are dry, the precursor material is used in the gas phase in order to apply the coating. • The process gases are fully contained in a vacuum vessel, the only emission of such system is through the outlet of the vacuum pump, where point-of-use abatement systems can be employed in order to treat/catch potential unwanted species. • Only a very small amount (flow) of pure precursor is needed in order to apply the ultrathin coating and generate the required properties. • Seen the absence of air or pollutants in general, the deposited coating is very pure and will not only be applied superficial, but also towards the core of the material, this way creating functionality with only a few tens of nanometers coating thickness. • No need for post-processing of plasma coating is required: drying, sintering, compounding, post-reaction, crosslinking etc.  The energy consumed in traditional wet chemical processes for hydro- or oleophobic textiles is almost triple in comparison with physical methods such as plasma treatment. According to data provided by FP7 ACTECO project, the energy used to obtain oleophobic materials by wet chemical process is around 25.7 MJ/functional unit while by plasma process the consumption is only 7 MJ/functional unit. Important quantity of wastes and consequent emission of ecologic unfriendly effluents are generated during these wet-chemical treatments contributing to the global warming (Table 1, see in document attached).   Low-pressure PECVD processes are known for their minimal use of precursor material. Calculation example for a C3F6-based process: a machine, capable of treating material on roll having a width of 1 meter, operates at a speed of 2 m/min, using a precursor flow of 200 ml/min C3F6. So, in order to treat 1m² of this material, 100 ml C3F6 gas is used. This represents 0.004 mol or 0.6 g of C3F6.  A part of this amount polymerizes on the substrate, forming a plasma-fluoropolymer nanocoating. Another part does not polymerize and is exhausted. So far, the percentages have not been identified yet. Emission factor to soil/water=0 for fluorinated gases, as stated on p228 AnnexB, so mainly emissions in the atmosphere could be of concern. Half-life threshold of C3F6 is 3.5 days and it’s determined not to be bio-accumulative. See: “Environmental risk evaluation report: Hexafluoropropene [HFP]” and “ECETOC JACC No. 48”.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The likelihood of exposure to C3F6, and any possible hazard related to this, is very limited when being used in low-pressure plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition processes. The gas is used under vacuum as a precursor material in the manufacturing of fluoropolymer nano-coatings. The gas is fully contained in the vacuum chamber and is lead over the vacuum pump to a well-positioned exhaust point, thus avoiding any possible interaction with people. The amounts of gas used are very limited. If 100% of the injected gas would be exhausted (which is obviously not the case, though no exact figures exists, the purpose of the process is to polymerize the gas onto the substrate as a plasma fluoropolymer), this would be 0,012m³/h for a typical machine. The exhaust stream can also be perfectly abated with efficiencies reported over 99%, in order to further limit exposure to the exhausted species. See attachment 1: document about abatement example.  The resulting plasma-polymer coating is extremely thin, highly branched and cross-linked and adheres very well to the substrate, this way limiting exposure throughout the lifetime of the product by release of species. The species contained in the coating are in line with the Oeko-Tex® 100 standard, see attachment 2: analysis report (confidential).  In contrast, the wet finishing methods are environmentally unfriendly multi-steps processing, that consume large amounts of chemical substances, generating hazardous chemical wastes and toxic emissions in air/water/soil with high chemical oxygen demand (COD), imposing expensive purification treatments and government permissions to eliminate or neutralize noxious residues by multiple cleanings with consequently large quantities of water and energy consumed.  Development of a dry resource-efficient process that dramatically reduces or eliminates the use of water (up to 100%) and consequently, energy consumption and CO2 emission of at least 20% along the overall value chain.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: The quantities deposited on the substrate are minimal, almost negligible, and their impact on the environment is limited throughout the lifecycle of coated customer’s products. The usual recycling techniques, as already existing for untreated material, can be employed for treated material.

5. Proposed derogations: As company driven by development of environmental friendly technologies, we are supporting new legislation aiming to reduce the use of and exposure to harmful substances. We believe that technologies limiting the amount of needed source material and the amount of waste should get special attention though, as they can be key enablers to get polluting technologies replaced.  The scaling potential is extremely large, as the C3F6 solution addressed cross-KET (key enabling technologies):  - Nanotechnologies: by creating materials and devices on nanoscale with the involvement of plasma deposition processes for the manufacture of filtering materials.  - Advanced materials: introduce new functionalities and improved properties in filtering materials, while adding value to existing products and processes, in a sustainable approach.  - Advanced manufacturing systems: overcome the problems of the currently available technology for achieving repellence on textiles, such as: water-based methods/toxic resources, poor adhesion of the thick coating/excessive amount of deposited chemicals and, consequently, high environmental impact, high cost due to the extensive thermal energy consumption in the curing step.  The new solution will overall lead to new products and services, capable of enhancing human health, while conserving resources, energy and protecting the environment:  • No air pollutants such as HF/NOx, thanks to vacuum closed reactor and use of a dry scrubber installed in the exhaust line. Traditional processes involve high emission of pollutants contributing to the total global warming. • Low raw material consumption (about 60%), thanks to high density nanoscaled coatings.  • Reduction of energy and chemical consumption by replacing the traditional wet chemical padding process.  • 100% elimination of water and soil pollutants. • Contribution to circular economy, since the coated polyester fabrics can be recycled.

6. Missing uses: The use of fluorinated species is indispensable in certain coating applications requiring explicit oleophobic functionalities. Some of these applications have already been listed in the restriction proposal Annex XV as proposed exemptions.  Low-pressure PECVD equipment and its associated processes require a high initial capital expenditure, which often forms a hurdle to implement this environment-friendly technology.  Although the advantages compared to wet chemical processing (much smaller amount of base material (precursor) usage, low energy consumption, low waste volume) result over time in an -at least- equal cost, it’s nowadays mainly implemented only by the so-called early adopters.   Next to reasons of keeping the status-quo or shorter term visions or objectives, also the high tech aspect of this technology and the possible impact on needed (technical) profiles to operate and maintain the equipment is a, mainly psychological, hurdle.  Exempting this technology as requested, would give the opportunity to convince companies about its potential and enable a further roll-out to other (non-PFAS) processes, where the same advantages apply as well.  SWOT analysis: Strengths: - Environmentally friendly (safe resources / methods): traditional processes involve high emission of pollutants such as PFCs, HCs, NOx, CO, CO2 etc.  - Sustainable growth by reducing energy consumption and emissions of CO2, recycling PET from reclaimed fibers to produce polyester. - Low cost due to the low raw material consumption (about 60% of the input needed for traditional technology). - Robustness: the chemicals are covalently bonded on material surface with no release in water.  - Fabric properties preservation: almost no fabric degradation (plasma interacts on few nanometers depth) and preservation of fabrics haptic due to very thin deposited layers.  Weaknesses: - Washing stability of deposited layers in particular for clothing application has to be improved (Sefar not affected). - If the materials, especially natural polymers (cotton etc.) contain significant amount of contaminants, could eventually influence the plasma process and consequently bad adhesion of nanocoating to the substrate.   Opportunities: - Growing needs of liquid repellent materials using ecofriendly process and materials: technology proposed offers an efficient process for hydro-/oleophobic materials. - Modular deposition (layer by layer deposition) can address very specific needs, demand-driven innovation. - Rapid growth of technical textiles consumption per capita worldwide, ensuring the development of textile, chemical and plastic industries as well. - Increasing demand for recyclable materials to replace traditional, energy intensive processes (padding) and materials (nonwovens, composite materials, filters) consuming non-renewable resources. - Controlled & reliable process: online monitoring process parameters and as a consequence, quality is controlled directly during production.  Threats: - Growing competitions from Asia and Far-East emerging countries with lower manufacturing costs, where environmental impact / legislation are not strictly maintained.  - Scarcity of raw materials and increasing prices of oil mainly for synthetic yarns - Decline in global market purchases of EU fabrics (clothing sector) (Sefar not affected)   Sefar requests an exemption for the use of C3F6 as precursor in combination with a low-pressure plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition process for all applications where oleophobicity is an explicit property for the application.   Fluoro-compounds are widely used in all global industries, especially for water, oil and stain repellency, for example in the textile and machine industry. A replacement did not seem to be possible until now. Most of the effective fluoro-compounds are based on the fluorocarbons which contain chains of more than 6, 8 carbons. When applied via classical “wet-chemistry” these long-chain fluorinated polymers often contain residual raw materials and trace levels of long-chain perfluoroalkyl acids (PFAAs), such as significant amounts of perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), which is a hazardous substance of concern in Swiss and European chemistry restrictions.   Despite substantial efforts invested in research and development, suitable alternatives that comply with the proposed restriction have not yet been identified for specific applications requiring oleophobicity.  The unique characteristics of ultrashort-chain C3F6 fluorocarbon makes it exceptionally effective for the intended purposes, and we have not identified any substitutes capable of replicating the same performance and properties. However, C3F6-based low-pressure PECVD processes do offer an environmental-friendly alternative to wet-chemical fluorpolymer processes.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Some of the applications already listed in the restriction proposal Annex XV as proposed exemptions, are already using ultra-short chain fluorocarbons in combination with low pressure plasma assisted chemical vapor deposition processes to obtain nano-coatings having oleophobic surface functionalities.   Sefar requests a limitation for those exemptions to the use of C3F6-based low-pressure PECVD for the cases where it offers a working solution.    Other methods to deposit fluoropolymer coatings often require not only fluorine containing monomers but also fluorinated production aids, such as polymerization catalysts, surfactants, emulsifiers, additives and dispersion aids. In contrast to PECVD process, wet-chemical process requires thicker coating to ensure the coating uniformity and functionality (micron to mm thick). These wet chemical processes produce a significant amount of PFAS containing liquid waste.

10. Analytical methods: The resulting plasma-polymer coating is extremely thin, highly branched and cross-linked and adheres very well to the substrate, this way limiting exposure throughout the lifetime of the product by release of species. The species contained in the coating are in line with the Oeko-Tex® 100 standard, see attachment 2: analysis report (confidential).
