Combined Comments:
General Comments: EFCLIN follows and support the comments and documents of EuromContact, reference number 580d560d-d3dd-46c9-832f-ac75f30809db

Executive Summary :
EUROMCONTACT requests that by way of time unlimited (unconditional) derogation, the restriction shall not apply to monomers, nor to polymers incorporating them, for the use in RGP contact lenses, on the basis of their essential and critical contribution to the performance and safety of these indispensable medical devices.

1.Vital Need - The RGP contact lens marketplace is small but vital for 3.2 million wearers in the EU who would be at a much greater risk of sight threatening infections, poor eye health and lens intolerance without PFAS
2.No Alternatives - Despite counter-claims, no alternative chemicals have been identified that adequately match the current level of performance
3.PFAS are Unique – The multitude of critical attributes that PFAS confer to RGP contact lenses for wearers is unlikely to ever be replicated, no matter how much research is performed
4.Effectiveness - Substitution with either soft contact lenses or glasses would in many cases be impossible, and in a majority of others would result in a significant reduction in visual acuity
5.Low volumes - PFAS volumes are infinitesimal when compared with other industries
6.Low Risk - The arrowhead species for RGP contact lens PFAS is trifluoroacetic acid (TFA). Small volumes of TFA do not constitute an unacceptable environmental risk
7.Derogation - The ECHA criteria for an unconditional derogation are met
8.Proportionality - Costs per year due to vision impairment without PFAS would be €5.68 billion, which is over 90,000 times greater than the most inflated estimate of the environmental costs that potentially could be incurred per year if PFAS use continues.


Introduction
An RGP contact lens is a medical device intended to be worn directly against the cornea of the eye to correct vision conditions. In contrast to soft lenses, RGP contact lenses do not mold to the shape of the cornea and as a result they provide better visual acuity for people with an abnormal corneal shape. It is estimated that 3.2 million people in the EU wear RGP contact lenses. Some irregularities of the corneal surface cannot be compensated at all with glasses nor with soft contact lenses : for patients with such conditions RGP contact lenses are the only solution to improve visual acuity and avoid them becoming visually impaired.
Contemporary rigid contact lenses are manufactured from complex polymers which are typically composed of around ten different ingredients selected to impart beneficial properties to the finished lenses. All of these polymers incorporate at least one of the fluorinated monomers hexafluoroisopropyl methacrylate (HFPM, CAS 3063-94-3), trifluoroethyl methacrylate (TFEM, CAS 352-87-4) or bis-hexafluoroisopropyl itaconate (BHI, CAS 98452-82-5). Using the OECD PFAS definition, these monomers, as well as the polymers incorporating them, are PFAS substances. This means that the group restriction on PFAS, proposed by five European countries, would affect all rigid gas permeable contact lenses (RGP CL).
Restricting PFAS use in RGP CL will inevitably lead to a decrease in the performance of these lenses, putting the 3.2 million RGP CL wearers at greater risk of sight threatening infections.  In addition, many thousands of current RGP CL wearers who are completely reliant on these lenses for adequate vision would no longer be able to tolerate using them. This would be a tragic consequence of the broad-based restriction being proposed for PFAS. Fluorinated chemicals are unique and can be used to confer a wide range of beneficial properties to materials. Within RGP contact lenses almost all of these beneficial properties are utilised to make lens wear a safe, healthy and comfortable experience for patients. There are no alternative chemicals, or combinations of chemicals, currently available in the contact lens industry or elsewhere, that can be employed to adequately match this level of performance.
This general comment summarises why the use of PFAS in RGP CL should be fully exempted from the PFAS restriction and presents supporting data relating to the EU RGP contact lens sector as a whole.

The Essentiality of Rigid Gas Permeable Contact Lenses
• RGP CL, which include corneal, scleral, hybrid and orthokeratology contact lenses, are needed for vital health reasons.5 Whilst soft lenses are now worn by most contact lens wearers, RGP CL are either the only viable option, or provide the best visual outcomes, for patients who are highly short -or long- sighted, are highly astigmatic, have corneal injuries, have corneal conditions such as keratoconus and keratoglobus, or have had corneal grafts or refractive surgery.2 RGP lenses for orthokeratology are a vital tool in combating childhood myopia, a sight defect which is now reaching epidemic proportions globally, and which brings a greatly increased risk of sight threatening complications such as macular degeneration, glaucoma, cataracts and retinal detachment in later life.8 The myopia epidemic is expected to become a major burden to global healthcare providers in the future. According to a survey run among 513 eye care professionals, 81% of current RGP patients could no longer be treated or would be treated with less effective alternatives if RGP contact lenses were no longer available.7
• RGP CL are irreplaceable for over half of the 3.2 million wearers in the European Union, as substitution with either soft contact lenses or glasses would result in a reduction in visual acuity. Moreover, if RGP contact lenses were no longer available, it is estimated that the consequences for over 1.4 million of these patients would be life-changing, as the ability to drive, work and/or enjoy the same quality of life would be lost.6 94% of surveyed eye care professionals stated that the impact for patients who cannot be treated by means of RGP contact lenses due to a total ban on PFAS would be a reduced quality of life, 89% stated that it would lead to very poor vision, 78% to inability to drive and 74% to inability to work.7


Why PFAS are Used in RGP CL
• 3 PFAS are used in the manufacture of RGP CL as they provide a wide range of performance benefits including ‘non-stick’ qualities (deposit resistance), an essential contribution to oxygen permeability (mainly through -CF3 groups)5, biocompatibility, chemical inertness (to resist tear fluids, UV from sunlight and atmospheric pollutants over 1-3 years), comfort, wettability, rigidity, manufacturability, hardness, durability, scratch resistance and shape (dimensional) stability.5
• The essentiality of PFAS for achieving these beneficial properties in RGP CL materials has been demonstrated in a scientific study,8 and the criticality of these properties for the effective performance of RGP CL has been confirmed by many leading eye care professionals. For example, “If these very important material properties are reduced or eliminated, then a significant number of patients with very challenging eye conditions simply will not be able to function visually and leaving them without being able to maintain their work. It would reduce quality of life dramatically” and “[a]fter years of research to optimize the characteristics of RGP materials, guaranteeing greater oxygenation of the cornea and reducing the interaction of materials with lipid and protein deposits, these indications [banning of PFAS used in RGP CL] from the EU take us back 50 years.” 3,5
• Without PFAS, the oxygen permeability and deposit resistance of RGP CL will be reduced. Wearing lenses with a low oxygen permeability can compromise eye health and increase susceptibility to infections. Deposits on lenses can impair visual clarity and comfort, and act as sites where harmful microbes can adhere.5 It is estimated that without PFAS over 480,000 current RGP CL wearers would no longer be able to tolerate their lenses and that an additional 3,500 sight-threatening cases of microbial keratitis would occur in the remaining RGP CL wearers each year.6

Alternatives
• Despite much research, no non-PFAS contact lens monomer, or combination of monomers, has been identified that comes close to replicating the level of performance which can be achieved using fluorinated species.5,8 In addition, no viable alternatives are apparent from other sectors of industry.5 This lack of suitable alternatives has been confirmed in a study conducted by an independent consultancy (see confidential attachments). Silicone methacrylates/acrylates have been suggested as an alternative to PFAS by the Dossier Submitters,1 however, they are not effective in preventing eye infections and maintaining the eye health of wearers.5,8 RGP contact lenses present a unique challenge as alternatives must replicate not only the inertness and deposit resistance of PFAS, but also the oxygen permeability and hardness, and there is no guarantee of success.5 PFAS are chemically irreplaceable as the element fluorine has unique advantages which cannot be replicated.5 Without PFAS, a detrimental and permanent drop in RGP CL performance is inevitable.5
• The number of scientists actively researching RGP lens materials is small (less than 10 in Europe and US), and the value of the EU market for RGP CL material manufacturers is also small (estimated at €25 million/year). The sector may, therefore, need to look to chemical innovations from other industries for a viable PFAS free RGP contact lens material to become a reality. Such developments will, however, be largely focussed on replicating the inertness and anti-fouling properties of PFAS, which are critical to most applications. Alternatives with such properties may prove to be unsuitable for adoption in the RGP contact lens sector due to low oxygen permeability, low hardness and/or low optical clarity. As a result, when considering PFAS-free alternatives for RGP CL it is more appropriate to question if they will ever be identified, rather than when.5

Risk of the Loss of the RGP CL Sector in the EU
• A PFAS restriction would result in huge costs to both material and lens manufacturers for developing new PFAS free materials and for obtaining regulatory approvals for lenses made from the new materials (estimated to total more than €100 million). It is not clear that the RGP contact lens market would be big enough to support such expenditure, especially as the decreased performance and safety of PFAS-free RGP CL alternatives will be a big concern to eye care practitioners, and the sector may collapse entirely.5 Patients who are reliant on RGP contact lenses for their vision, and cannot be adequately treated with soft contact lenses or glasses, may find they are no longer supported. This effect is not the intention, nor can it be allowed to be a consequence, of a broad PFAS restriction.

Safety and Minimal Environmental Impact of PFAS Use in RGP CL
• The three PFAS monomers which are incorporated into RGP contact lens polymers, HFPM, TFEM and BHI, are all high boiling point liquids that can be classified as ultra short chain PFAS as their chemical structures contain only non-adjacent -CF3 groups (fluorinated chain length = 1).  Predictions generated using the EPI Suite and ECOSAR software programs indicate that the three monomers do not meet the REACH criteria for toxicity or bioaccumulation (and so are neither PBT nor vPvB).4 This conclusion is supported by the available experimental data and is in agreement with numerous studies reporting that as the fluorinated chain lengths of PFAS decrease, so does toxicity and bioaccumulation.4,6,8 HFPM and TFEM have been registered with REACH at a 1 10 tonne/year level, with both being reported to be biodegradable.
• RGP contact lens materials incorporating these monomers are also ultra-short chain PFAS and can additionally be classified as fluorinated side chain polymers. Numerous different RGP lens polymers have undergone safety testing as part of RGP CL regulatory submissions, including cytotoxicity and ocular irritation assessment, without adverse findings. RGP CL polymers are considered to be inert and harmless to RGP CL wearers.
• 4 tonnes of RGP contact lens polymer are manufactured each year for the EU market, typically in the form of solid rods, which are subsequently trimmed down into polymer buttons. Contact lens manufacturers then lathe these buttons into finished lenses. Risks to the workers performing these processes are considered to be minimal as appropriate training, PPE and ventilation/extraction methods are utilised across the industry and as PFAS RGP CL monomers and polymers are not intrinsically more hazardous than non-PFAS equivalents (the factor which distinguishes PFAS, as a group, from typical chemicals is their environmental persistence, and this does not impact people while manufacturing and wearing RGP CL).6
• In the environment, the monomers and polymers used in RGP CL will eventually degrade to the arrowhead species trifluoroacetic acid (TFA). TFA is a naturally occurring PFAS which, though highly persistent, is not toxic or bioaccumulating (and so not PBT or vPvB). A 2023 United Nations Environment Programme report on the risks of trifluoroacetic acid concluded that global emission levels do not pose a concern for the public or the environment, even when extrapolated to 2100.4,6
• The 4 tonnes of RGP CL polymer produced each year will convert to 1.44 tonnes of TFA. This is a tiny percentage of the TFA generated in nature and by human activities: e.g. 0.042% of the 3,432 tonnes/year produced by hydrothermal vents and 0.0029% of the 50,000 tonnes/year generated from two hydrofluorocarbons, HFC 134a and HFO1234yf, alone.6
• If manufacture of RGP contact lens polymer for the EU market were the only source of TFA globally, and output remained constant at 1.44 tonnes/year, this activity could carry on for over 28.9 million years without environmental levels of TFA increasing to a point of concern.6
• Moreover, TFA is not a ‘forever chemical’ as it reacts with hydroxyl radicals in the troposphere to form non-PFAS products. Environmental levels of TFA will reach a steady state rather than increasing indefinitely.4
• The trimming and lathing processes utilised in the manufacture of finished RGP CL generate significant amounts of waste swarf.6 The industry is aiming to reduce waste and improve waste management, and is exploring options for minimising the generation of TFA. The feasibility and environmental costs/gains of using base washes or high temperature incineration to convert -CF3 groups in RGP CL polymer into non persistent HF or F– species are being evaluated.  If applicable, protocols for the collection and treatment of waste swarf and used RGP contact lenses would be developed and implemented.

Socioeconomic impact of a Ban on the Use of PFAS in RGP CL6,7
• If the PFAS monomers in RGP CL polymers have to be replaced by non-PFAS monomers it will lead to a decrease in performance (a form of “regrettable substitution”):
o The resulting economic costs due to vision impairment in current RGP CL wearers within the EU are estimated to total over €5.68 billion/year.
o The costs associated with increased levels of sight-threatening microbial keratitis infections in RGP CL wearers are estimated to reach €100 million/year in the EU.
• If a PFAS restriction also triggered the collapse of the RGP CL sector:
o The economic burden resulting from vision impairment to current RGP CL wearers is estimated to increase to €37.8 billion/year.
o There would be an estimated 20,000 job losses across the RGP CL sector in Europe, with an associated societal cost of €1.67 billion.

o 3.2 million current RGP CL wearers would be negatively affected.
• Potential health and environmental costs of not banning PFAS in RGP CL:
o Currently, these costs are estimated to be €0 as the level of TFA in the environment is well below the threshold to cause adverse effects to the general public or to flora and fauna.
o This is expected to remain the case until at least 2100.
o A highly unlikely worst-case scenario would be that an EU-wide PFAS environmental monitoring and remediation programme is required at this point. The costs of such a remediation programme have been estimated in a report published by the Nordic Council of Ministers to be €16,902 million (best estimate) or €170,821 million (upper estimate).
o Given the relative contribution of RGP CL to TFA levels in the EU, an appropriate proportion of these reported costs would be €0.468 million or €4.73 million. Averaged up to 2100, this equates to €6,074 /year or €61,386 /year respectively.
o The PFAS Restriction Dossier quotes a value of €52-84 billion/year as the health cost of PFAS currently in the environment. Accounting for the lower risk of TFA, the 1.44 tonnes coming from RGP CL manufacture for the EU market each year is calculated to have a total health cost of only €73.71 over its entire lifetime in the environment.
• The balance of socioeconomic costs is overwhelmingly in favour of continued use of PFAS in RGP CL. If PFAS use is restricted, even if this does not lead to a collapse of the RGP CL sector, costs per year due to vision impairment in current RGP CL wearers are over 90,000 times greater than the most inflated estimate of the environmental costs that could be incurred per year if PFAS use continues (or over 900,000 times greater based on the best estimate of PFAS remediation costs).6

Consequences of a Time-Limited Derogation
• A time-limited derogation could have a strongly negative impact through prolonging uncertainty within the eye care sector over PFAS and the future of RGP contact lenses.6 This uncertainty is expected to lead to a reluctance amongst eye care practitioners to prescribe RGP contact lenses to new patients (as practitioners can’t be sure that these lenses will still be available for patients in a few years’ time) and a reluctance to invest in the training required for working with RGP contact lenses.5 47% of surveyed eye care practitioners declared that uncertainty over the future of RGP contact lenses due to the potential PFAS ban would make them less likely to prescribe RGP contact lenses.7 Also, amongst lens manufacturers, it is expected to lead to a reluctance to register RGP contact lens products under the costly new Medical Device Regulation (MDR) framework. Prolonged uncertainty risks causing a major shrinkage of the RGP contact lens sector and making RGP contact lenses unavailable to many patients whose lives are improved by them.5
• A time-limited derogation would also put at risk the safety and quality of life of RGP contact lens wearers through the strong possibility that the performance level of these devices will never be replicated without the unique benefits of PFAS.5,8 Any such permanent drop in performance would result in a negative impact to wearers that far outweighs the potential environmental benefits of ending PFAS use after 13.5 years.6
• The ECHA criteria for an unconditional derogation are met for PFAS in RGP CL,6 and this is the most appropriate and most proportionate management option.

Conclusions and Outlook
The use of PFAS in RGP contact lenses should continue as:
• viable alternatives are currently lacking and may prove impossible to develop,
• without the unique chemical benefits of PFAS there will almost certainly be a significant, permanent and unacceptable drop in the performance of RGP CL,
• the numbers of patients whose lives would be negatively and severely impacted by a restriction are large,
• the economic costs to EU governments and to patients themselves would be large,
• the PFAS related to RGP CL have low propensities for bioaccumulation and toxicity,
• volumes are small,
• the environmental risks of continued PFAS use in RGP CL are negligible at most, even when high persistence is factored in,
• remediation would be cost effective if there ever was a concern, and
• a time limited derogation would be damaging to RGP CL wearers.
Anything other than an unconditional (non-time-limited) derogation would be disproportionately detrimental and harmful to RGP CL wearers and disproportionately costly to the sector.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Rigid gas permeable contact lenses

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: a. The annual tonnage and emissions (at sub-sector level) and type of PFAS associated with the relevant use. • Annual tonnage and emissions at sub-sector level In a survey run from 5th May 2023 to 1st June 2023 among manufacturers of polymer buttons (from which RGP contact lenses are prepared) and manufacturers of RGP contact lenses, the annual estimate tonnage of PFAS waste and emissions generated from the manufacture of RGP polymer buttons and RGP contact lens for the EU market was 2,742 kg / year as a total of 37 respondents. Considering that the sector is composed of approximately 60 companies, taking into account the size and distribution of market shares and considering that finished contact lenses were not included in this analysis, an extrapolation would conclude that the annual tonnage of PFAS is approximately 4 tonnes for the manufacture of RGP contact lenses for the EU market.  • Type of PFAS associated with the relevant use The molecular structures of the three fluorinated monomers widely used in the preparation of RGP contact lens polymers are : - hexafluoroisopropyl methacrylate (HFPM),  - bis-hexafluoroisopropyl itaconate (BHI)  - trifluoroethyl methacrylate (TFEM).  These species are best described as being polyfluorinated, but not perfluorinated, as while each contains multiple fluorine atoms, a majority of the carbon atoms in their structures are not bonded to fluorine atoms. The fluorine atoms in each molecule are located in isolated  CF3 groups (-CF3 groups which do not have a -CF2- group adjacent). The molecules could, therefore, be described as having a maximum perfluorinated alkyl chain length of 1 carbon atom, and are categorised as ultra-short chain PFAS. This is also the case in polymerised form, where the -CF3 groups are found in side chains. The available evidence, including several reports published by the Danish Environmental Protection Agency, indicates that degradation processes in the environment and in vivo will eventually convert any isolated -CF3 groups which are present in a fluorinated substance to the molecule trifluoroacetic acid. Trifluoroacetic acid is a naturally occurring compound which is classified by the European Chemical Agency as ‘low toxicity’ and ‘non PBT’ (persistent, bioaccumulative and toxic) and which the United Nations Environment Programme has concluded poses a minimal risk to human health and the environment. Please see annex D of this submission “Fate and Toxicity of Fluorinated Substances used in CL Materials” for more information.  b. The key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use PFAS are utilised in many industries for their chemical inertness and ability to repel both oil and water. The three PFAS monomers which are incorporated into RGP contact lens polymers not only provide these advantages, but also make an essential contribution to oxygen permeability, deposit resistance, biocompatibility, comfort, wettability, rigidity, lathability, durability, scratch resistance and dimensional stability. A summary of the various aspects of contact lens wear which have been improved by the addition of PFAS monomers to RGP contact lens materials is given in the table below :  Category Complication Potential impact on patients Related material properties  Safety  Microbial keratitis Ulcer formation could permanently damage sight. Discontinuation of contact lens wear until resolved Oxygen permeability, deposit resistance  Corneal neovascularisation Could temporarily affect sight. Discontinuation of contact lens wear until resolved Oxygen permeability  Corneal infiltrates Discontinuation of contact lens wear until resolved Deposit resistance  Endothelial changes Could ultimately affect the barrier properties of the endothelium Oxygen permeability Tolerability Inflammatory red eye Intolerable discomfort, discontinuation of lens wear Oxygen permeability  Deposits on lenses Reduction in visual clarity, discomfort, increased risk of infection  Deposit resistance  Lens scratches Reduction in visual clarity, increased risk of infection Hardness  Poor lubricity Discomfort Wettability  Lens flexure Inconsistent visual quality, glare Flexural modulus (rigidity)  The key functionalities provided by PFAS for RGP contact lenses are :  • Oxygen permeability : Many fluorine containing materials are highly permeable to oxygen, a characteristic which is necessary for all types of RGP contact lens to avoid hypoxic adverse events and both short- and long-term physiological changes, including endothelial blebs, edema, limbal injection, myopic creep, epithelial microcysts, epithelial thinning, corneal vascularisation, polymegethism and pleomorphism. Highly permeable lenses also help to maintain the barrier function of the eye surface, making it less susceptible to bacterial binding and infection. While low oxygen permeability materials, such as poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA), can be tolerated by some patients for a period of time, the constant hypoxic challenge will be detrimental to eye health in the long term.  • Deposit resistance: The uniquely low surface energy and hydrophobic+lipophobic nature of fluorinated materials makes them invaluable for use in an ocular environment where a contact lens is constantly exposed to chemical species with a wide range of polarities including hydrophilic proteins and hydrophobic lipids. Any build-up of deposits on RGP contact lenses has the potential to impair visual clarity, to cause abrasion to the eye surface, to increase risk of infection by providing sites where pathogens can adhere and to render lenses intolerably uncomfortable to wear. It has been demonstrated that even a small level of deposition, forming on contact lenses over a period of only six hours, is enough to more than triple the number of Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteria adhering to lenses.  • Wettability : Also critical to comfort is wettability, which promotes the formation and retention of a lubricious tear film on lenses, preventing irritation to the eyelids and ocular surface during blinking. While PFAS monomers are primarily added to an RGPlens material to confer oxygen permeability and deposit resistance, they are the only species that can do so without having a highly detrimental impact on wettability. Moreover, with PFAS containing wettable RGP contact lenses there is no tendency to dry the eye surface as may occur with soft lenses.  • Hardness, flexural strength and dimensional stability: The manufacturing process for RGP contact lenses involves lathing a button of polymer into a bespoke shape tailored to a patient’s eye. An RGP lens material must be sufficiently hard to facilitate this process and to provide enough durability for lenses to resist scratch formation over 1-3 years of use. Scratches tend to reduce the optical clarity of lenses and provide hard-to-clean sites which enable bacterial adhesion. Resistance to flexure and to deformation is also critical as otherwise optical clarity and comfort are impacted. PFAS monomers are unique in that they can be used to bring hardness, rigidity and dimensional stability to a material while maintaining a high level of oxygen permeability.   • Safety : RGP contact lenses have been demonstrated to be the safest contact lens modality in terms of incidence of microbial keratitis. This level of safety performance is, however, reliant on patients being able to maintain scratch free lens surfaces and to avoid deposit build up throughout the lifetime of the lenses, and will be unachievable without PFAS.  • Chemical inertness: Each pair of RGP contact lenses is typically worn for between 1 and 3 years and must remain chemically unchanged for this duration, withstanding tear fluids, UV from sunlight and atmospheric pollutants. Chemical inertness is therefore critical and is an important advantage of PFAS monomers. The safety and effectiveness of RGP contact lenses is reliant on the use of PFAS. The addition of fluorinated substances to contact lens polymers facilitated the development of lathable materials with high oxygen permeability and good deposit resistance. This advance has enabled RGP contact lenses to be worn without compromising eye health, while minimising the risk of infection and other complications.  Without PFAS, RGP contact lenses would lose performance in several key areas, notably oxygen permeability, deposit resistance and wettability. Please see annex E of this submission “The Essentiality of PFAS for Rigid Contact Lenses” for more information c. The number of companies in the sector estimated to be affected by the restriction. About 50,000 companies would be affected by the restriction :  • Manufacturers of polymer buttons used to manufacture RGP contact lenses : it is estimated that there are less than 10 companies, both in Europe (UK, Germany, Italy) and outside Europe (USA, Japan). • Contact lens manufacturing laboratories : it is estimated that there are approximately 60 companies in Europe (Spain, Italy, Switzerland, UK, The Netherlands, Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Sweden, France, Croatia, Belgium). • 25 machine tool companies. • Eye Care Professionals : The European Council for Optometry and Optics (ECOO) estimate there are 150,000 ECPs within the EU, out of whom 50,000 routinely work with RGP contact lenses.  d. The availability, technical and economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives for the relevant use, including information on the extent (in terms of market shares) to which alternative-based products are already offered on the EU market and whether any shortages in the supply of relevant alternatives are expected. As things currently stand :  • There are no functional alternatives to RGP contact lenses that could adequately treat most current wearers RGP contact lenses are typically employed as a last resort with patients for whom no other method of vision correction will give an acceptable outcome. They therefore have a critical role to play in correcting the vision of patients with the most challenging optical needs. These RGP contact lenses are either the only viable option, or provide the best visual outcomes, for the millions of patients who are highly short or long sighted, are highly astigmatic, have corneal injuries, have corneal conditions such as keratoconus and keratoglobus or have had corneal grafts or refractive surgery. In addition, RGP contact lenses for orthokeratology are a vital tool in combating childhood myopia, a sight defect which is now reaching epidemic proportions globally, and which brings a greatly increased risk of sight threatening complications such as macular degeneration in later life. • There are no suitable chemical alternatives to PFAS for use in RGP contact lenses. There are currently no non-PFAS substances that can be used to replicate the high level of RGP contact lens performance achieved with PFAS, or even to generate rigid lens materials that would be viable for a majority of patients.  Some older non-PFAS RGP contact lens materials, including poly(methyl methacrylate) and silicone methacrylates/acrylates, are used in small numbers in the EU. Although these products could be made more widely available it is almost universally acknowledged that such materials are detrimental to eye health and cannot be safely tolerated by most wearers. See Annexes E and G of this submission “The Essentiality of PFAS for RGP Contact Lenses” and “EUROMCONTACT PFAS Restriction Impact Surveys 2022 and 2023” as well as the responses below for more information about technical feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives. e. For cases in which alternatives are not yet available, information on the status of R&D processes for finding suitable alternatives, including the extent of R&D initiatives in terms of time and/or financial investments, the likelihood of successful completion, the time expected to be required for substitution (including any relevant certification or regulatory approvals) and the major challenges encountered with alternatives which were considered but subsequently disregarded. The size of the R&D capability within the RGP contact lens sector is small, so there is concern that the development of viable non-PFAS alternatives will rely on innovations from other industries and will be a long-term process, potentially taking significantly more than 13.5 years. Few, if any, of these industries will be focussed on replicating the oxygen permeability and rigidity which is achievable with PFAS materials, and which is critical for RGP contact lens performance, so there is no guarantee that an innovation suitable for the RGP contact lens sector will be forthcoming at all. Although it is anticipated that many potential alternatives to PFAS will be identified over the coming years for use in various industries, RGP contact lenses present a unique challenge as a material must be identified that replicates not only the inertness and deposit resistance of PFAS, but also the oxygen permeability and hardness, and there is no guarantee of success. Fluorinated chemicals such as PFAS are unique and confer an extraordinary range of beneficial properties to materials including chemical inertness, thermal stability, resistance to acids and bases, immiscibility, repellence to both oil and water, biocompatibility, low toxicity (for many PFAS), optical clarity, durability, low friction, abrasion resistance, electrical resistance, dielectric properties and oxygen permeability, almost all of which are important for RGP contact lenses. Alternative substances may have a good level of performance in one, or perhaps a few, of these areas but will not perform well in all. Moreover, for some properties, such as chemical inertness or the ability to repel other substances (including both those that are hydrophilic and hydrophobic), there are no other types of organic molecule that match up.  In general, the loss of performance on removing PFAS from RGP contact lenses would result in patients being more likely to suffer eye infections and being put at an increased risk of associated sight loss. In addition, many patients will no longer be able to tolerate the lenses that are essential for their vision. Please find below the major challenges encountered with alternatives which were considered, and in several cases investigated experimentally, but subsequently disregarded (Any viable alternative will also have to be safe, non-toxic, deposit resistant, optically clear and compatible with other contact lens monomers. Focus of R&D is directed to the small number of substances which are permeable to oxygen, a property which will be critical in any PFAS replacement for RGP contact lenses):  • Replacing the fluorinated monomer by methyl methacrylate (MMA), having a closely related chemical structure without CF3 groups : The oxygen permeabilities of these analogues were too low to be viable for use in RGP contact lenses.  • Replacing the fluorinated component with 3-methacryloxypropyl tris(trimethylsiloxy)silane (TRIS), a silicone monomer which is the substance most widely utilised for increasing the oxygen permeability. But the dimensional stability and hardness of these analogues was extremely poor, making them completely unsuitable for use in RGP contact lenses.   • Replacing the fluorinated component with a 1:1 mixture of MMA and TRIS : These materials had sufficient hardness and dimensional stability, but were less permeable to oxygen and also less wettable. Increasing the MMA to TRIS ratio would increase deposit resistance, but decrease oxygen permeability and decreasing this ratio would have the opposite effect. Importantly, there is no ratio that would give an acceptable level of both deposit resistance and oxygen permeability.  • Silsesquioxanes : Polymeric silsesquioxanes and polyhedral oligomeric silsesquioxanes (POSS) are examples of silicone species where potential advantage is greater rigidity. Experimentally, while an increase in hardness was observed on replacing silicone contact lens monomers with silsequioxane species, there was also a corresponding reduction in oxygen permeability. This reduction in oxygen permeability was of greater magnitude than the increase in hardness. Based on this evidence, silsesquioxanes do not confer a performance advantage over conventional silicone contact lens monomers as a replacement for PFAS.  • Hybrid inorganic/organic glasses : Also known as ormosils or ceramers, hybrid inorganic/organic glasses are composed of silicate, or titanate, species bridged by organic linking groups. These materials are postulated to combine the best properties of the inorganic (strength) and organic (flexibility) components and have been investigated for use in contact lenses.  The oxygen permeabilities of these materials were, however, less than 15 barrers, which is very low. Increasing the oxygen permeability of these hybrid glasses would require the addition of another organic component such as a PDMS silicone species, but this type of change would further lower the hardness and potentially cause the material to become opaque.   • Adamantyl methacrylate + PDMS macromer : Investigated experimentally as a possibility for increasing the performance of a PFAS-free RGP contact lens material by utilising a strengthening monomer in combination with an oxygen permeable silicone species to enable high permeability while maintaining enough hardness for the material to be lathable and scratch resistant etc. Polymers were prepared incorporating a highly permeable PDMS silicone macromer in addition to the strengthening monomer adamantyl methacrylate, with and without a crosslinking agent. The uncrosslinked polymer had a hardness lower than typical for an RGP contact material and also a relatively low oxygen permeability. With crosslinking the oxygen permeability further decreased.   • Fluorinated materials : The fluorinated compound 4,5-difluoro-2,2-bis(trifluoromethyl)-1,3-dioxole, and related species, are routinely copolymerised with PTFE to generate polymers that are highly permeable to oxygen.  However, PDD and related monomers, as well as the highly permeable fluorinated polymers incorporating them are, however, classified as PFAS under the OECD definition and so are not appropriate as alternatives.  • Acetylenes : Acetylenes have been explored as possible ingredients for contact lens materials for almost 40 years, but this research is yet to result in a commercial product.   • Poly(trimethylsilylpropyne) (PTMSP) is one of the earliest, and probably the best studied permeable acetylene polymer, with a reported oxygen permeability in excess of 10,000 barrers. In pure form, however, it is too flexible and not wettable enough to be utilised as an RGP contact lens material. Moreover, it is not possible to polymerise trimethylsilylpropyne monomer within a normal contact lens formulation as a metal catalyst is required (and would remain in the final product leading to toxicity issues). Instead, research within the contact lens sector has focussed on combining the polymeric form, PTMSP, with contact lens monomers, but efforts have been hampered by its hydrophobicity. Furthermore, it has been reported that the permeability of PTMSP decreases to 1% of its original value over time. Such changes in oxygen permeability over time would be unacceptable in a medical device such as a contact lens where oxygen permeability is critical to performance and where regulatory requirements dictate that oxygen permeability must remain within +/- 20% of the reported value. Moreover, acetylenes such as PTMSP have been found to be chemically unstable under ambient conditions, making them unsuitable for use in a medical device such as a contact lens.  • Norbornenes : The polymerisation of norbornenes substituted with bulky -SiMe3 groups has been found to yield materials with oxygen permeabilities of over 2,000 barrers. Such norbornenes are not commercially available and require the use of transition metal catalysts to induce polymerisation, which would be a toxicity concern for a contact lens material. Norbornenes are not compatible with other contact lens monomers as they do not undergo free radical polymerisation. Moreover, the oxygen permeabilities of polynorbornenes have been found to decrease over time.   • Polyimides : An advantage of polyimides is their relatively high stiffness, which would be of use in an RGP contact lens. However, the oxygen permeability of the primary commercially available polyimide, Matrimid, is only 1.5 barrers. The additional of fluorinated groups to polyimides has led to oxygen permeabilities an order of magnitude higher, but such species would be subject to a PFAS restriction.   • Polymers of intrinsic microporosity : The original polymer of intrinsic microporosity (PIM) was prepared by reacting 5,5′,6,6′-tetrahydroxy-3,3,3′,3′-tetramethylspirobisindane with tetrafluoroterephthalonitrile. The resulting material, PIM-1, had an oxygen permeability of around 1,500 barrers. Despite the impressive initial oxygen permeabilities, decreases occur over time and all reported PIMs have a vivid yellow colour, which would make a contact lens both impractical for the wearer. Moreover, PIMs tend to be translucent rather than optically clear. In addition, PIMs are not compatible with other contact lens monomers.  • Cyclodextrins : Cyclodextrins are large ring-shaped molecules with a central pore. Over time, they absorb large molecules within the pore, and the free space is lost. For this reason, if cyclodextrins are added to polymers it is not expected to result in any long-term increase in oxygen permeability. β-cyclodextrin containing ethylene-vinyl alcohol copolymers were found to have negligible oxygen permeabilities, even at 30% loading, indicating that cyclodextrins are not inherently permeable to oxygen.  • Cucurbiturils : Like cyclodextrins, cucurbiturils are large organic molecules that form a ring-like structure with free space in the middle. Over time, bound oxygen is replaced by larger molecules with a greater binding affinity. Again, this reduces the free space within the pores of the molecules, thereby removing any permeability to oxygen.  A large number of potential alternatives are included in Appendix E2 of the PFAS Restriction Dossier. The only class of compounds listed which provides oxygen permeability is silicones. While silicones can be employed to prepare materials with oxygen permeabilities suitable for use in RGP contact lenses, other properties of these materials such as deposit resistance, comfort, wettability, hardness and dimensional stability will be inadequate.   Furthermore, the consultancy Fresh Perspectiv (London, UK) were independently tasked with identifying suitable PFAS-free materials or monomers for use in RGP contact lenses. Despite contacting over 25 chemical companies, industry experts and academic institutions worldwide, no promising solutions were identified (see the confidential attachment to this submission). The uniquely beneficial properties of PFAS for RGP contact lenses result from the unique properties of the chemical element fluorine. Fluorine is the most electronegative element, and forms chemical bonds to carbon which are stronger and more polar than between carbon and any other element. Fluorine is the least polarizable element that can bond to carbon atoms, and this confers the unique property of being both hydrophobic and hydrophilic. Fluorine also has the shortest Van der Waals radius of any atom that bonds to carbon apart from hydrogen, which results in minimal steric strain and confers temperature stability. Moreover, fluorine and carbon are light elements and so performance-to-weight ratio is high. No new lightweight elements will ever be available to chemists and no amount of research will ever identify another element which matches the performance of fluorine. From a chemical perspective, PFAS are completely irreplaceable.  In addition to the R&D process of monomer synthesis and polymer development, which is by no means guaranteed to be successful, the regulatory approval for class II medical devices under the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR) to market lens designs in new, PFAS-free materials is estimated between 5 to 10 years by the majority of surveyed manufacturers, including clinical trials, material regulatory testing, clinical work and approvals, customer regulatory approvals and additional clinical work.  The total costs to the five main RGP lens polymer producers, and 60 principal lens manufacturers, of developing a new ranges of PFAS-free RGP lens materials, and obtaining new medical device approvals for lenses manufactured from these materials through MDR, is predicted to be a minimum of €100 million. The total value of the EU market for RGP CL material manufacturers is estimated at €25 million/year. For many of the small businesses in the eye care sector in the EU these costs will be prohibitive. With 4,000 employees and about 60 companies the average size of a company manufacturing RGP lens polymer and RGP contact lenses is 67 employees.  See Annex E of this submission “The Essentiality of PFAS for Rigid Contact Lenses” and the confidential attachment “The Consequences of Removing Fluorinated Compounds from Rigid Gas Permeable Contact Lenses. Journal of Polymer Engineering. https://doi.org/10.1515/polyeng-2022-0189." for more information.  g. For cases in which substitution is not technically or economically feasible, information on what the socio-economic impacts would be for companies, consumers, and other affected actors. If available, please provide the annual value of EU sales and profits of the relevant sector, and employment numbers for the sector. In the case of RGP contact lenses, the substitution is not technically feasible and the ban would have a disproportionate negative impact on patients, manufacturers and eye care professionals.  • Impact on visually impaired patients requiring RGP contact lenses to restore their vision A ban on the use of PFAS in RGP contact lenses would be detrimental to the 3.2 million wearers as PFAS are critical to device performance and no suitable alternatives are available. Without PFAS, the risks of infection for wearers will increase and fewer people will be able to tolerate using RGP contact lenses. For most current wearers, RGP contact lenses provide a level of vision correction that cannot be matched by alternatives such as soft contact lenses or spectacles. It is estimated that for over 200,000 RGP contact lens wearers in the EU a ban on PFAS would be devastating as not only would they no longer be able to wear their lenses, but also they would no longer be able to work, drive and enjoy the same quality of life, as vision correction with soft contact lenses or spectacles would be inadequate (see annexes F and G of this submission). The associated socioeconomic cost of a PFAS restriction has been calculated to be €5.68 billion/year, which is many orders of magnitude greater than the potential environmental cost of continued PFAS use. Even a 13.5-year derogation introduces a level of risk and potential negative socioeconomic impact for RGP contact lens patients that is unacceptable and disproportionate given the unlikelihood of adequately replacing PFAS in RGP contact lenses. An unconditional derogation is the only option which can protect patients and comes with a minimal (and certainly not unacceptable) environmental cost. • Impact on polymer and RGP contact lenses manufacturers There is a significant risk that a PFAS ban would result in the collapse of the RGP contact lens sector as a total ban on PFAS would result in the closure of most companies. Assuming that a ban on PFAS means that RGP materials and all types of RGP contact lenses can no longer be manufactured, the annual turnover of the companies would decrease by 54% on average and the impact in terms of the number of job losses in Europe is estimated at 2,278, out of 4,000 employees today (57% of jobs would be destroyed). The value of the EU market for RGP contact lens material manufacturers is estimated at €25 million/year. • Impact on Eye Care Professionals The European Council for Optometry and Optics (ECOO) estimate there are 150,000 ECPs within the EU, out of whom 50,000 routinely work with RGP contact lenses. A survey run in 2022 revealed that redundancy of staff in these practices would be at least 1/3 if the rigid contact lens sector collapsed, so that approximately 17,000 jobs would be considered as redundant.  The results of the same survey estimated that the turnover of practices would be reduced by a minimum of 30% and up to 85%. According to a survey among eye care professionals working in a practice which supply and fit contact lenses, about 25% of the respondents declared that at least 65% of their patients that use contact lenses have RGP contact lenses. RGP contact lenses wearers represented on average 35% of the CL patients in surveyed practices (see annex G of this submission). The impact on their practice population and their turnover would put at risk of redundancy a significant proportion of eye care professionals. The economic cost of the estimated 20,000 redundancies across the sector would be €1.67 billion. Org. name: European FluoroCarbons Technical Committee (EFCTC) - a Sector group of Cefic
Combined Comments:
General Comments: EFCTC (the European FluoroCarbons Technical Committee) is a sector group of Cefic (the European Chemical Industry Council), representing the European fluorocarbons manufacturers. Based on the information in this submission and on the additional information provided by other key stakeholders of the F-gas value chain, EFCTC would like to propose the following derogations for F-gases:
- A time-unlimited derogation for the substances listed in Annex I and Annex II Section 1 of the F-gas Regulation revision proposal.
- A time-unlimited derogation allowing the use of F-gases for the maintenance and refilling of equipment until the end of its lifetime for all the uses permitted under the EU F-gas Regulation.
- A time-unlimited derogation allowing the use of recycled and reclaimed F-gases for the maintenance and refilling of equipment until the end of its lifetime for all the uses permitted under the EU F-gas Regulation.
- More adequate concentration limits applicable to F-gases
As a sector group of a trade/industry association, EFCTC is bound by EU competition law; therefore, the information submitted cover F-gases in general and all their relevant applications without distinctions.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: • Application of F-gases • Transport • Medical devices

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: EFCTC, in Annex 4 and 7 (destruction and EOL) has provided some additional information about the treatment of F-gases at the end of life stage.  Key aspects:   • Destruction technologies for HFCs are approved under the Montreal Protocol following independent evaluation of performance criteria, including the efficiency of destruction. The performance of approved destruction technologies is well characterised and achieve a high efficiency of destruction (minimum 99.99% for concentrated HFCs). Detailed reports on destruction technologies and applicable criteria have been published since 1992.  • It has been reported that 17 destruction facilities are registered in 2021 for destruction of F-gas Annex I & II substances in the EU (HFCs, HCFCs, HFOs, and HCFOs) in Europe. Municipal solid waste and rotary kiln incineration are approved for destruction of foams containing HFCs. • HFOs and HCFOs, having double bonds, have reduced stability compared to HFCs and technologies approved for HFC destruction are expected to achieve the same efficiency of destruction, if operated under conditions that destroy HFCs.  • F-gases can be recovered, recycled or reclaimed, and reused (RRR) and it is important to guarantee that the PFAS restriction would not impede the use of recovered / recycled or reclaimed F-gases to avoid undermining the EU goals towards Circular Economy.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: In annex 4 to this submission EFCTC has provided further information on incineration of F-gases Key aspects:   • Destruction technologies for HFCs are approved under the Montreal Protocol following independent evaluation of performance criteria, including the efficiency of destruction. The performance of approved destruction technologies is well characterised and achieve a high efficiency of destruction (minimum 99.99% for concentrated HFCs). Detailed reports on destruction technologies and applicable criteria have been published since 1992.  • It has been reported that 17 destruction facilities are registered in 2021 for destruction of F-gas Annex I & II substances in the EU (HFCs, HCFCs, HFOs, and HCFOs) in Europe. Municipal solid waste and rotary kiln incineration are approved for destruction of foams containing HFCs. • HFOs and HCFOs, having double bonds, have reduced stability compared to HFCs and technologies approved for HFC destruction are expected to achieve the same efficiency of destruction, if operated under conditions that destroy HFCs.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Annex 7 (EOL)  to this submission explains how F-gases can be recovered, recycled, and reused (RRR) and will highlight the importance of guaranteeing that the PFAS restriction would not impede the use of recovered / recycled F-gases to avoid undermining the EU goals towards Circular Economy. Banning the use of recovered / recycled F-gases would severely hinder the capacity to service equipment that has not yet reached its end of life, causing a premature decommissioning of the equipment and subsequently unnecessary waste.

5. Proposed derogations: Annex 1 to this submission provides further information on emissions and calculations based on UN recognized TFA yields.

8. Other identified uses: EFCTC has commissioned an independent consultant, Ricardo Energy & Environment, to conduct a Regulatory Management Options Analysis on eight F-gases. The report, provided as Annex 6, includes information based on the literature research and on the outcome of a survey for F-gases producers, importers, and downstream users performed by the Ricardo team.

General Comments: EGMF is the European federation representing major garden, landscaping, forestry, and turf equipment manufacturers. Through its 30 European corporate members and 7 National Associations, EGMF represents about 23 million units placed on the European market in 2021, accounting for around 80% of garden machinery, and EGMF members employ over 120,000 people in the EU.

We welcome the opportunity to comment on the Restriction Proposal of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) submitted by the competent authorities for REACH of the Netherlands, Germany, Denmark, Sweden, and Norway which aim to reduce PFAS emissions into the environment and make products and processes safer for people.

The group of PFAS is not a single substance, but a class of substances containing many thousands of individual chemicals. Not all PFAS are classified as “hazardous” under the CLP Regulation, especially the polymers that we use in our equipment. A general restriction based only on the persistence of PFAS would thus contradict the risk-based approach.

PFAS are used for various applications in the garden and outdoor power equipment, such as fuel hoses, injectors, manifolds, gaskets, and fan wheels. Until appropriate substitutes are found, these substances remain critical to guarantee the durability and safety of our equipment.

Having considered the extensive use of PFAS in our members' products, EGMF makes the following requests in respect of the PFAS restriction proposal:
A further assessment is made on the impact of the proposed restriction on specific types of machinery;
Exemptions are granted for fluorinated polymers that are essential and used for various applications in garden and outdoor power equipment;
Exemptions are granted for applications and equipment where no appropriate substitute is available, including outdoor power equipment, as well as for spare parts to ensure that products could be repaired and reused and to provide safety products to consumers;
Sufficient time is provided to develop and test alternative substances, as other substances do not offer similar properties in similar extreme climate conditions, thus not ensuring the necessary safety and durability of the equipment.

EGMF also wishes to stress that, in the limited time that was available during this consultation, our members have struggled to obtain the necessary information from their supply base that was needed in order to provide comprehensive answers to the specific questions posed in the questionnaire. We have therefore submitted a position paper rather than attempt to answer the individual questions. We trust that this will be accepted and the points made in the position paper are taken into account during the consultation.

Content: Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Org. name: EHI- Association of the European Heating Industry
Combined Comments:
General Comments: EHI members manufacture efficient heating systems, including hydronic heat pumps which rely on fluorinated greenhouse gases (F-gases), such as hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), hydrofluoroolefins (HFOs) and alternatives using natural refrigerants such as propane (R290). Manufacturers of hydronic heat pumps are investing at unprecedented scale & speed in future-proof sustainable heat pumps to meet the REPowerEU targets, including in particular models without any F-gas chemicals.
As an industry, we agree with the general objective of REACH to avoid harmful substances from entering the environment. You will find our detailed position below.
Concerning the PFAS restriction, we have been following the development of the scientific reports and restriction proposal with interest, since PFAS, as defined in the proposal by the 5 Member States, are a very large group of chemicals that are present in many components of our heating appliances. Our reply will focus on the limited use cases where we are the user of the substance, i.e., PFAS as refrigerants in heat pumps and PFAS as blowing agents in the insulation of hot water storage tanks. For these use cases, there is a partial overlap of the PFAS restriction with the ongoing revision of the F-gas regulation , therefore some considerations need to be made.
It should also be noted that our proposal depends on the conclusions of the risk assessment committee on the harmfulness of PFAS in refrigerants for the environment.

1) Refrigerants in heat pumps
Our association represents hydronic heat pumps up to 70 kW, therefore, our suggestions will only cover those products.
Firstly, we would like to note that our industry is taking all possible measures to prevent refrigerants leaking into the outdoor environment. These measures are part of a set of mandatory requirements under the F-gas regulation, currently under revision.
Secondly, the future F-gas regulation will progressively introduce bans on the use of refrigerants for heat pumps with a high global warming potential. Therefore, any impact on the market of the proposed PFAS restriction must be assessed jointly with the outcome of the F-gas regulation revision. Pending this outcome, it is extremely difficult to reply to this survey. Therefore, we request the possibility to submit an updated reply after the deadline for feedback, when a political agreement on the F-gas regulation is reached.
The combination of both legislations could lead to a situation where only flammable refrigerants would be allowed to be used for residential and small commercial hydronic heat pumps. These flammable refrigerants have to fulfill tougher safety requirements compared to traditional refrigerants. The requirements differ depending on the condition of the refrigerant circuit , implying differing impact on monobloc and split heat pumps.
Self contained refrigerant circuits are assembled in a factory and do not face additional risks from downstream processing, hence the safety requirements are easier to meet.
Monobloc heat pumps work already today with a self-contained refrigerant circuit. In the case of split heat pumps the refrigerant circuit has to be closed by an installer at the place of use and cannot be considered self contained.
For this reason, there is a need to differentiate between the two types of heat pumps.
For monobloc hydronic heat pumps, we can agree with a full phase out of fluorinated gases since an alternative is available (i.e. R290). However, to ensure sufficient time for component availability and redesign of the heat pumps and to avoid stranded investments, this phase-out should be completely aligned with the timing of the F-gas regulation for hermetically sealed equipment.
To fully evaluate the impact on split heat pumps, the final F-gas regulation is a necessary building block. Indeed, if the F-gas regulation will phase-out of hydrofluorocarbons, there is currently no safe refrigerant alternatives available for split heat pumps. Split heat pumps represent a large market share in South European Member States, but also in the Netherlands and France. As such, to avoid restricting these appliances without sufficient transition time, we recommend adding a time-limited derogation for split heat pumps. The exact timing and scope of an eventual derogation will heavily depend on the outcome of the F-gas regulation, considering eventual exemption clauses. We therefore suggest to come back with a proposal after its finalization. It should include both, an extended transition period of 5 years and a review clause for an assessment that should evaluate the market and possible alternatives for split appliances well before the end of the derogation. If this assessment is not finished before the end-date of the derogation, the derogation should be prolonged automatically.
In addition, we support derogations for maintenance of existing installations, as well as for buildings where safety standards prevent the use of non-PFAS alternatives provided they are clearly defined and enforceable. We detail the reasoning of our positioning on derogations in section 5 of the present document.

2) Foam blowing agents for insulation in hot water storage tanks
Regarding foam blowing agents, here as well the timing of the PFAS restriction needs to be aligned with the revision of eco-design and energy labelling requirements  for lots 1 & 2. Indeed, blowing agents used for thermal insulation of hot water storage tanks contain fluorinated gases considered as PFAS. While non-PFAS alternatives to these blowing agents exist, making the switch will require manufacturers to adapt their manufacturing process and sites. This will take time and, combined with increasing minimum energy efficiency requirements via the revision of eco-design and energy labeling requirements,  limit further the number of storage tanks available on the market, at least until all manufacturers have successfully made the switch.  Thus, we recommend aligning the restriction for PFAS used in foam blowing agents with the timing of the F-Gas Regulation as well as ecodesign and energy labelling delegated acts. In practice, this would take the form of a 5-year derogation, so that the restriction occurs after the current ecodesign revision and in time for the next revision, expected to take place in 2029.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Our comments apply to applications of fluorinated gases, in particular a) heat pumps and b) foam blowing agents.  a) EHI members manufacture hydronic heat pumps which rely on fluorinated greenhouse gases (F-gases), such as hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) and hydrofluoroolefins (HFOs), along heat pumps without F-gases. Hydronic heat pumps are acknowledged by the Commission as key technologies for the decarbonisation of buildings and for achieving the EU’s 2030 and 2050 targets, and the REPowerEU Plan communication aims at deploying 10 million hydronic heat pumps in the next 5 years and 30 million hydronic heat pumps until 2030. Refrigerants, fluorinated and non-fluorinated, used in heat pumps are essential to their functioning, because they are the working fluid of heat pumps that allow heat to be transferred from source to sink.  When heat pump manufacturers select alternative lower-GWP refrigerants, they take into account the substance’s flammability, toxicity and/or high pressure, but also the intended application and energy efficiency of the heat pump when using the refrigerant. And although natural refrigerants are being used as non-PFAS alternatives, they are not suitable to all heat pump systems due to their high flammability, toxicity and/or high pressure   b) In addition, blowing agents used for thermal insulation of hot water storage tanks contain fluorinated gases considered as PFAS. Hot water storage tanks are a good means to store energy, as water accumulates a lot of energy per unit of weight. As such, they are an important equipment to reduce the peak demand of energy from heating in buildings. The insulation foams used in storage tank to keep the heat is made in many appliances using HFOs, such as HFO-1233zd and HFO-1336mzz(z)). While non-PFAS alternatives to these blowing agents exist, making the switch will require manufacturers to adapt their manufacturing process and sites. This will take time and, combined with increasing minimum energy efficiency requirements via the revision of eco-design and energy labelling requirements,  may limit further the number of storage tanks available on the market, at least until all manufacturers have successfully made the switch. In turn, this increases the risk of supply disruption, which is problematic for the roll-out of heat pumps that the European Commission aims at: as hot water storages are highly relevant for hydronic heat pumps, a shortfall in storages would dramatically harm the heat pump ramp up.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: We do not have detailed data on the impact of the proposed restriction on the recycling industry. However, here, we would like to stress the role of the current and future F-gas regulation, which already limits the emissions of HFCs and HFOs as much as possible, by setting requirements on leak checking and recovery as well as  installation  and maintenance  by F-gas accredited specialists. In addition, any transfer of refrigerant needs to happen in closed systems in order to minimise or eliminate emissions. At the end of life, HFCs and HFOs need to be recovered by F-gas accredited specialists so that the gases are recycled, reclaimed or destroyed.

5. Proposed derogations: We do not have detailed data on the tonnage and emissions of PFAS related to the proposed derogations. However, we have the following comments on the proposed derogations:  ● Derogation 5.i for maintenance of existing installations:  We think that a 13,5 years derogation is not sufficient; Indeed, heat pumps have a longer expected life-time.  A 13.5 years-derogation period for their maintenance and refilling would be too short and contradict the principles of circular economy and right to repair. To accommodate the diversity and ensure that all heat pumps installed before the application date of the PFAS restriction will be maintained during their entire lifetime, we recommend a time-unlimited derogation.   ● Derogation 5.j for buildings where safety standards prevent the use of alternatives:   While we agree with the principle of this derogation, it is important to highlight that in its current wording, the derogation would not be enforceable by market surveillance authorities and lead to legal uncertainty. Therefore, we strongly urge ECHA to collaborate with the European Commission and REACH competent authorities towards reformulating this derogation with the aim of ensuring its  enforceability and establish a procedure which deals with the approval of installations which fall under this derogation. As an example, we could imagine drafting a conclusive list where safety rules apply based on the  standards and building codes. In addition to this, each installation making use of this derogation should require  approval prior to being installed by an authority, e.g. REACH competent authorities.   ● New derogation for hydronic split heat pumps: In addition, we recommend adding a time-limited derogation for hydronic split heat pumps contingent on the outcome of the on-going F-gas regulation revision. This would avoid an inadvertent ban of these appliances, which still cover a large market share in many Member  States (e.g.: South EU, France, the Netherlands, Poland, Belgium) in the EU.  Hence, we recommend adding a time-limited derogation for split heat pumps. Not only will such derogation be enforceable by Market Surveillance Authorities, but it will also create legal certainty for manufacturers of split heat pumps. At the time of writing, the outcome of the F-gas regulation revision is still uncertain, thus we leave the exact scope and the duration of the derogation open. In addition, this derogation should include a review clause, keeping in mind that the assessment should start well before the end of the derogation. In line with our recommendations for monoblocs, the transition time for manufacturers should be 5 years from the date of entry into force of PFAS Regulation.

8. Other identified uses: Regarding non-PFAS alternatives to foam blowing agents: as indicated earlier, non-PFAS alternatives exist, although they require adapting the manufacturing processes and construction site (i.a. non-PFAS alternatives based on hydrocarbons might require additional safety measures by means of e.g. underground tanks).  One of our member companies is currently investigating switching from an HFO thermal insulation foam to cyclopentane. According to their analysis, although the initial economic investment is quite high, the switch can bring economic annual savings in the order of 16%. The savings are driven by two factors: ● Mixing ratios: Cyclopentane has a lower cost than the comparable HFO; considering the total mixing ratios, an economic saving of 14% can be obtained. ● Density: In addition, if we consider that cyclopentane has a lower density than the HFO thermal insulation foam, there is also a reduction in material consumption that has to be taken into account.  As such, it appears that the substitution for a non-PFAS alternative for the thermal insulation of storage tanks is economically feasible. However, as the switch to non-PFAS alternatives will require manufacturers to adapt their manufacturing process and sites, we recommend a derogation period of 5 years for foam-blowing agents.
