Combined Comments:
General Comments: EHIMA, the European Hearing Instrument Manufacturers Association, welcomes the ambition to reduce the amount of PFAS used globally, and we acknowledge the only way forward is to use some sort of grouping of the chemicals, otherwise we will see regrettable substitution without end.

EHIMA’s members produce medical devices, consisting of hearing aids and hearing implant systems (collectively referred to as hearing instruments). EHIMA’s members are among the world’s largest and most advanced hearing instrument manufacturers, producing up to 90% of the hearing instruments manufactured in Europe.
In the proposal for PFAS restriction we find some aspects of the approach to be too harsh and difficult to obtain for the hearing instrument industry seen from both a socio-economic and a technical perspective.

There are two overarching topics for the current use of PFAS related substances in hearing instruments we will focus on in our feedback to the Annex XV restriction report:
1. Corrosion, moisture and oil protection – involving coatings of hearing instruments.
2. Acoustic performance – involving the use of components in hearing instruments.

Hearing instruments fall in the use sector of medical devices for which a derogation is proposed for reconsideration while other uses are missing. EHIMA would like to share technical and regulatory arguments to substantiate this position.

1. Coating for corrosion, moisture and oil protection

Hearing instruments are fitted on patients and placed behind the ear, partially in the ear canal, or fully in the ear canal. This environment is extremely challenging for electronic devices continuously worn on the body. As high-quality devices, one of the fundamental functionalities is to ensure that they have a repellent (hydrophobic and oleophobic) coating, so that water, sweat and ear wax or other oily substances (such as sebum) will not enter the interior of the device. When the coating is absent, water/sweat or oily substances may enter in the interior of the device, causing corrosion, degradation of materials or clogging of microphones and receivers, which in the worst case will lead to complete damage of the device. Hearing instruments cannot be fully sealed as components like battery, microphones, and receivers need regular air exchange. For the hearing aids to work properly through the intended lifetime of 5-6 years, the industry is coating various components of the devices, e.g., housing parts, microphone protection filters, and electronic components with PFHxA related or other (per-)fluorinated substances.

Back in 2020 EHIMA has commented on ECHA’s PFHxA restriction proposal. As a result, RAC and SEAC final opinion was to support a 10-year derogation for coatings in hearing aids. More on the request for a derogation is discussed below.

It is highly critical to have suitable protection that can withstand the environment in and around the ear to have a reliable hearing instrument. The process to replace hydrophobic/oleophobic coatings to a PFAS-free solution are on-going. It has been possible to replace the hydrophobic coating for some accessories which are not worn on the body. However, this solution is unfortunately not a good substitute for the coating in the hearing instruments because they have to survive in a “hostile” environment, worn on or in the body. Several substitutes have been evaluated and the market is still being explored, but no good substitutes have been found for hydrophobic/oleophobic coating yet. A particular challenge is the protection from ingress of oily and fatty substances into the hearing aid, which can only be achieved with an oleophobic coating. To our knowledge, today only coatings based on fluorine chemistry can provide this property.

2. PFAS-related materials for acoustic performance

Hearing instruments have many components inside. We identified a number of critical components containing PFAS. These critical components are essential for a hearing instrument, to ensure product safety and performance requirements and to enable hearing-impaired users to fully participate in society.

For the majority of uses, PFAS containing materials are unique and difficult to replace with other materials. For cost reasons alternative, non-PFAS containing materials are already used wherever possible, e.g., silicones for gaskets and sealings. The use of PFAS containing materials can in some cases eventually be replaced, however currently not all uses have commercially available alternatives without PFAS.

Most relevant critical components we focus on are microphones, switches, suspensions for transducers and semiconductors.

Many hearing instruments use electret microphones, which contain fluorinated ethylene propylene copolymer (FEP)  membranes to hold the permanent electrical charge of the membrane. Depending on the size of the product, the amount of FEP is not more than 0.4 mg per microphone. Our industry is in a transition phase into a newer technology, i.e., micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) microphones.
However, although MEMS microphones themselves do not contain PFAS, the current manufacturing process of MEMS microphones is dependent on PFAS. A recent guide to PFAS in the electronics and semiconductor industry gives a clear overview (https://chemsec.org/app/uploads/2023/04/Check-your-Tech_230420.pdf). That means that we do not have 100% PFAS-free microphones that are suitable for hearing instruments.
It takes time to get the entire product portfolio exchanged and a MEMS microphone is not suitable for all types of hearing instruments. When MEMS microphones can be used redesign and adjustments are needed for each product. It is therefore not a plug-and-play solution to make this change. As there has been no need to exchange the electret microphones in already marketed devices so far and there is a requirement to service and repair these devices according to the MDR (see below), we cannot phase those devices out here and now, and there is little value for hearing instrument users that resources are spent on redesign of old technology.
More information on microphones in hearing instruments can be found in the confidential attachment in Section V of our comments.

Switches need to have mechanical robustness, wear resistance, and chemical resistance.
Some switches are designed with a PTFE membrane that gives these properties. Alternatives do exist but since the printed circuit board (PCB) is designed for the footprint of the specific switch, one switch is not one-to-one replaceable with another. The alternatives require complete redesign of the PCB as well as testing and validating. This will take no less than 2 years per instrument.

Suspensions for microphones and receivers in hearing instruments make use of fluorocarbon rubber and fluorosilicones to dampen vibrations and for impact protection. They are used to shield the receiver, microphone or vibrator of the hearing aid which are sensitive components. The important aspect of the fluorocarbon rubber and fluorosilicones is their combination of acoustical and mechanical properties. Together with their chemical resistance, they present a set of properties which alikeness are hard to find.
The dampening characteristics of alternative materials are not readily available as many industries do not have a need for these properties. Therefore, finding a substitute requires a lot of initial testing to fulfill the requirements for a hearing instrument. Available alternatives are not good enough and the user will experience a hearing instrument with more noise which would make it less desirable to use if fluorocarbon rubber and fluorosilicones cannot be used in the future.

Finally, we mention (Li-ion) batteries as a part of every rechargeable hearing instrument. It is beyond the scope of our feedback to go into detail, but if battery technology needs to change due to PFAS restrictions, the hearing industry will also be impacted.
An in-depth discussion on batteries and PFAS can be found at https://rechargebatteries.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/RECHARGE-FIRST-submission_.pdf.

3. Legacy spare parts and services

We have a concern in relation to the Medical Device Regulation (MDR, EU 2017/745). A hearing instrument has an expected product lifetime of 5-6 years. The MDR requires that a hearing instrument must be available on the market in an MDR-compliant manner – i.e., to support the product for service and repair in its defined expected product lifetime – which is a longer duration than the expected date of the PFAS restriction to enter-into-force. For the demanded period of 5-6 years, no untested alternative spare parts can be used for repairs. This means that a defective device can no longer be repaired and becomes unusable. The hearing instrument user is forced to buy a new device, which is not financially justifiable. The legal two-year warranty period requires the manufacturer to replace the defective hearing aid with a new one, which would then no longer be allowed. Here a conflict between the laws would arise.

Another concern relates to stock management. Looking at our stock, all current products basically contain PFAS. It takes a long time to exchange stock with non-PFAS alternatives, in addition to actually finding the alternative(s). Some products are needed for spare parts or some market(s) that prefer a specific device. If all stock needs to be scrapped due to the proposed PFAS restriction, we see a big impact on circularity as the majority will not be recyclable. It will be a waste of raw materials and a high resource load on the supply chain to remanufacture products. EHIMA members are aware that knowledge of a sunset date will require stock management to reduce the potential scrap as much as possible with that in mind. We suggest that a transition period for stock is acknowledged as the complexity of phasing out PFAS is high. This would be in line with the derogation for legacy spare parts we have in the RoHS directive.

4. A note on Fluoropolymers

We have a different view on regulating the use of fluoropolymers, in a group PFAS restriction, since these molecules are toxicologically inert. As with any “plastic” they should be handled appropriately in the end use phase, due to their persistent chemical properties. EHIMA members do not understand the ambition to control the use of hazardous substances in the production phase by banning the product. We think the production of fluoropolymers should instead be optimized by legal instruments to render it safe for the environment. For example with the Stockholm Convention. We find it is important to introduce derogations that allow the use of fluoropolymers in places where there is no other way to achieve the technical performance shown by fluoropolymers. Examples are harsh environments, including very specific uses seen in hearing devices, as described above.

5. Timeline for alternatives

At the moment, there are no good alternatives (substitutes) for hydrophobic/oelophobic coatings which provide the level of protection required for reliable hearing aids. We estimate it will take a minimum of 2 years to find suitable material(s). It is possible that no PFAS-free alternative coatings can be found for some applications where oleophobic properties are crucial.

As for any alternatives for PFAS-containing components (microphones, suspensions, switches), there are currently no substitutes available either, which can guarantee to give the same acoustic performance of the hearing instruments.

Once alternatives are found, it will take up to 4 years to approve and qualify a substitute as well as potentially invest in new manufacturing equipment. For any substitution, whether in coating or in components, it needs to be verified that the general safety and product performance is not impacted as defined by the MDR. Besides reliability testing, this may also include evaluation and testing for biological safety according to the ISO 10993 series.
However, until now alternatives have not been found why it is difficult to give a more precise timeline.

6. Request for exemption

In 2020 EHIMA has commented on the PFHxA restriction proposal. With respect to coatings, we argued that the reliability and extended lifetime benefits for hearing instruments with a continued very limited use, would outweigh the environmental impact. Both RAC and SEAC agreed to this in their final opinion of December 2021, and recommended a 10-year derogation to be written into the restriction proposal (see https://echa.europa.eu/documents/10162/97eb5263-90be-ede5-0dd9-7d8c50865c7e). This derogation was the platform on which members of EHIMA based their product development. However, the restriction is still pending the Commission’s adoption.

If the Commission adopts both PFHxA and PFAS restrictions, we enter a realm of judicial evaluation on the principles of “lex specialis” versus “lex generalis”. This is because the new, much broader PFAS restriction does not contain a derogation that is similar to the one both RAC and SEAC decided would be to the benefit of the hearing-impaired users.

In Annex XV paragraph 6 under 6j (p. 12) there is a restriction that covers coatings for medical devices as such, but it mentions only fluoropolymers and perfluoropolyethers, which is not reflecting the type of coating we are currently using. We would like the scope of the derogation under 6j to be clarified and broadened to also cover the side chain (per)fluorinated polymers (via polymerization of (per)fluorinated monomers) used as coatings in medical devices. It should also be clearly stated that the proposed derogation, if granted, should be applicable to the whole supply chain contributing to the manufacturing and use of coating applications for medical devices.

Thus, we request that the 12-year derogation mentioned for the coating applications of medical devices including hearing instruments in paragraph 6j of Annex XV of proposed restrictions on PFASs substances will include all polymeric PFASs including fluoropolymers, perfluoropolyethers and side-chain fluorinated polymers.

Moreover, we have a request for a new exemption, not proposed in Annex XV. We request that a 12-year derogation will also be applicable for the critical components in hearing instruments. In particular for the use of microphones with a FEP membrane and for the use of suspension and gaskets made of fluorocarbon rubber and fluorosilicones, but also switches and batteries.

Finally, due to a possible conflict between the MDR and the proposal for PFAS restriction, we request a 5-year derogation for legacy spare parts for service and repair of hearing instruments.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Sector: Medical devices (Annex E.2.9.): Other coating applications. (Sub-)uses: Components containing PFAS used in the hearing instrument industry.  The above topics are discussed in our feedback under Section III. Non-confidential comments.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Suspension and gaskets: These components are made of fluorocarbon rubber that is placed inside the hearing instruments. There is no emission during the use phase. Fluoropolymers are the preferred choice of material because of their unique combination of properties that are not achievable from other materials or via other functions. Fluoropolymers are classified as "polymers of low concern" according to OECD criteria. This means that fluoropolymers and products that contain fluoropolymers pose no risk to human health and the environment when they are used properly and discarded according to EU waste regulations.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Hearing instruments are electronic devices containing batteries, e.g., lithium batteries. As such, their disposal is regulated by European and local laws (WEEE 2012/19/EU). The batteries must be removed from the used hearing instruments and disposed separately. Both parts must be discarded in local recycling programs or returned to the manufacturer for controlled disposal.  Since the hearing instruments are sold globally, they go into different waste streams that will vary from country to country. A hearing instrument weighs below 5 g and consists of hundreds of components. Recycling is done where it is feasible; the utmost is done to preserve the raw materials.

5. Proposed derogations: More information the amounts of PFAS in hearing instruments can be found in the confidential attachment in Section V of our comments.

6. Missing uses: Several PFAS uses have not been covered in detail in the Annex XV restriction report:  1. Coating: This is a defined use, derogation marked for reconsideration. Material: Fluoropolymer and perfluoropolyether (Missing material: side chain fluorinated polymers). Use: Coating for medical devices (Missing use: coating for hearing instruments) 2. Components: This is a missing use, no derogation proposed.  Material: Polymeric PFAS. Use: Components of medical devices 3. Spare parts: This is a missing use, no derogation proposed.  Material: Polymeric PFAS. Use: Components of medical devices  As described under Section III. Non-confidential comments, materials used in hearing instruments have to survive the harsh environment in and around the human ear. The humidity and the body temperature resemble a tropical climate that together with earwax, sweat and skin fat create an environment that is harsh for materials. This set of specific requirements for chemical resistance for the materials used to manufacture hearing instruments. Furthermore, the salt from sweat (pH 4.5-7), and the humidity together with the voltage potential from the electronic components can create a corrosive environment if the system is not well protected. PFAS-containing materials perform excellent in these conditions. In addition, to prevent the ingress from oily substances like earwax into microphones, only PFAS-containing materials can provide the necessary oleophobic properties.  Socio-economic consequences for users: The goal of EHIMA member companies is to keep delivering high quality medical devices that help the hearing impaired in their everyday life to remain part of society.  In most EU countries costs for hearing instruments are fully or partly refunded by national health insurance programs. Depending on the specific needs and applicable hearing instrument, one or two ears, features and functionalities, costs for the users may exceed € 3,000 per hearing aid. A recent overview was published by the IFHOH – the International Federation of Hard of Hearing People (https://efhoh.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/Hearing-Aids-Reimbursement-2022-edited-version-final-for-publication.pdf). For cochlear implants, costs are much higher and usually fully covered by the national health insurance.  In its recent World Report on Hearing, the World Health Organization describes hearing loss as an “invisible disability (...) not just because of the lack of visible symptoms, but because it has long been stigmatized in communities and ignored by policymakers.” (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240020481). While hearing loss is indeed one of the most prevalent disabling health conditions, for both adults and children, it often remains untreated (see below).  If left untreated, hearing loss can result in a number of physical, mental, financial and social consequences, such as depression, sleep disorders, social isolation, increased falls and a decrease in cognitive performance. Hearing loss has especially far-reaching consequences for children, as hearing-impaired children are unable, or only partially able, to understand words in their mother tongue, thus hampering their intellectual and psychosocial development.  Hearing instruments significantly increase people’s ability to take part in everyday life and communicate with the world around them. Figures show that for over 22 million people living in the EU with untreaded, disabling hearing loss, the costs for society are as high as 185 billion euros each year (https://www.ehima.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/Hear-it-Report-Hearing-Loss-Numbers-and-Costs-2019.pdf). Therefore, there is a socio-economic benefit to society to continue providing high-quality devices to the hearing impaired as well as improving their wellbeing.    PFAS in hearing instruments is used to protect the devices, to extend the product lifetime, and provide superior product performance as follows:   (A) Various technical and usability developments have set in, such as wireless connectivity, new sensors and new features. At the same time miniaturization is on-going, as users demand ever smaller devices. This has to do with the stigma associated with hearing impairment: people do not want their hearing instruments to be visible. As a consequence of miniaturization, PFAS-less components, such as thermoplastic elastomer (TPE) suspensions, cannot be used anymore - due to their size - to deliver optimal acoustical performance.  It is therefore important to find an alternative(s) with similar properties to obtain products with similar product lifetime. Not to bring significantly more devices onto the market due to a short product lifetime cycle which from a circularity perspective is unwanted as well as from a manufacturing capacity perspective.   (B) If a coating is not applied (with consequences described in Section III), the consumer will experience a hearing instrument that has to be exchanged more often. Perhaps at two or three times the current rate (lifetime of 5-6 years). Today the public health system is not arranged to hearing instruments with a shorter lifetime. This will lead to higher financial cost for the user, as no public health scheme will currently offer hearing instruments at this rate.  (C) If fluorocarbon rubbers or fluorosilicones cannot be used the hearing instrument user will have to wait for products coming to the market that are larger and with worse acoustics that may be much more prone to howling than today’s instruments. A ban would set the hearing instrument industry at least 10 years back and there would be no available instruments to help the hearing impaired until development had taken place.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: The proposed derogation for coating (6j) is marked for reconsideration. We have supplied information under item 6 (missing uses) and under Section III.  Referring to these comments, EHIMA argues to remove the mark for “reconsideration” and to include the derogation as “proposed derogation”.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Electrical equipment for electrical distribution above 1 kV are complex products consisting of thousands of parts with extreme durability, a long lifetime of 40 years or more and high technical requirements as wide temperature range, resistance against wear, resistance against electrical arcs or others. To allow this, in combination with long maintenance periods or even maintenance free design, high grade materials are used. For some of the technical functions PFAS materials are used intentionally or might be used as components of 3rd -party materials without any further specifications on chemical consistency. The materials used in electrical equipment are divided in the following groups:
1. Articles or components containing PFAS, which have been selected intentionally by the equipment manufacturer, following the design as material or as ingredient of a material mixture for a specifically defined function.
2. Material in articles or components, that has been selected based on technical parameters by the equipment manufacturer, but where PFAS material is contained as ingredient of a material mixture based on the definition of the material manufacturer.
3. Components, articles or assemblies, which are designed and supplied from 3rd party suppliers. PFAS has not been specified by the equipment manufacturer nor direct supplier but might contain PFAS as an intentionally added ingredient of a material mixture or as material based on the definition of the component - or the material manufacturer.
4. PFAS contained as contaminant based on the production process, e.g. as release agent used in a cast moulding process to allow easy demoulding, surface treatment using PFAS or PFAS containing substances, in the production machine or due to manufacturing of PFAS containing products next to the production line.
Add to 1): Articles or components containing PFAS are selected when reliable operation is required in harsh conditions, such as extreme temperatures, an aggressive environment, and mechanical endurance. We use PFAS because of their capacity to resist these harsh conditions, in addition to other applications such as electrical insulation and sealing. We are already active to identify and search for alternatives for some components. This process is actually ongoing. However, no alternative is foreseen for HFO gases which have been identified as replacement for SF6 to reduce the global carbon footprint of the electrical equipment above 24 kV instead of building heavier pressurised electrical equipment not based on a PFAS gas.
Add to 2): It is already more complex, as materials are used in several applications and changes of a material recipe might have impact on the technical parameters. A change in material might result in a requalification of the alternative material. Alternatively, the supplier might decide to stop the production of the material. Then a new supplier for a similar material with acceptable risk profile must be identified and the substitute quantified.
Add to 3): An example for this group could be electronic equipment as control and protection relays, which are a mandatory component for most products used in electrical equipment. They contain semiconductors or other electronics, where it has been announced from the industry that it is almost impossible to offer PFAS free solutions.
Add to 4): Due to limited availability of analytical methods that can reliably quantify substances falling under the wide-ranging definition as PFAS, is effectively impossible to control and ensure the low threshold of 25 ppb. Even more so, if the manufacturing processes uses materials, parts or components manufactured and imported from outside the EU.
It should be stated that the replacement of PFAS substances can potentially worsen safety properties of electrical equipment for electrical distribution, such as fire resistance, as alternative materials may have less favourable characteristics in this regard. Furthermore, PFAS substances are partially used in core components of power electronics and control systems (for example, thyristors and optical fibres). The use of an alternative material requires a development work which may take 5-10 years after alternatives have been made available by our partners and suppliers. The non-availability of products during that time frame would cause shortage of electrical equipment with huge financial impact and direct negative impact on the energy transition plans and the required extension of the electrical networks. Type tests for grid components are mandatory for most markets, including EU. Any function determining material change has an impact on the results and thus does consequently lead to a repetition of type tests. Currently, there is neither guarantee that current performances will be reached, nor overall carbon footprint limited to acceptable levels. This brings high uncertainties in the achievement of EU's 2030 and 2050 decarbonisation targets.
The proposed blanket restriction of all PFAS, regardless of toxicity, risk profile, and respective use, is not consistent with the risk-based approach according to Article 68(1) REACH and substance -based approach according to Article 69 REACH.
A more differentiated regulatory approach has been proposed by the UK’s Health and Safety Executive, adopting a pragmatic approach to limit the use of PFAS and control exposures to human health and the environment. The thousands of PFAS substances have very different physical, chemical, and biological properties, and not all PFAS remain in the environment with a practical degradation at the end of their lifecycle. We support a similar approach to restrict PFAS substances, with a differentiated consideration of the risk for each substance in its specific use, while considering critical use for society, such as electricity security and supply.
For example, fluoropolymers meeting the criteria for "polymers of low concern" and industrial applications in closed systems, equipment components and equipment generally do not cause relevant emissions to the environment when used as intended. Other, non-polymeric PFAS substances like HFOs used for insulation in pilots of electrical distribution equipment above 24 kV are proven not to accumulate in soil or drinking water and thus are of low concern for people, plants and animals.
When PFAS substances are identified as posing an unacceptable risk to human health or the environment, a differentiated regulatory PFAS restriction should consider:
• The risks associated with individual substances, and their application within T&D equipment, including the consideration of vastly different risks of release during manufacturing, operation and maintenance compared to consumer uses.
• The most appropriate measures to manage the risks posed by PFAS used in T&D equipment, such as requirements for recycling and effective waste treatment from manufacturing to decommissioning after its lifetime, which usually is over 40 years.
• The potential for PFAS replacement, including consideration on whether the alternative already exists at a significant scale and has an appropriate technological readiness level while being cost-effective. This is in line with Article 68 of REACH regulation, which states that any new restriction must consider the socio-economic impact, including the availability of alternative solutions. The lifetime of products with the alternatives shall also be compared with the lifetime of current products to avoid uncontrolled refurbishment or replacement rates.
• For any substances or applications where the only available means to manage the posed risk require actual phase-out and substitution, the timeframe for development and certification of substitutes shall be considered appropriately. For those PFAS uses where restriction is the only available option, we recommend including a requirement to assess the availability of a suitable PFAS-free alternative before the end of any relevant transition period. This requirement is in line with what ECHA’s Socio-Economic Analysis Committee (SEAC) proposed for the EU-wide PFAS ban in firefighting foams for substances covered by the Seveso Directive and for offshore installation in the oil and gas industry.
• The criticality of PFAS use for society, in the context of the energy transition, climate impacts, and environment & human health protection. This means a differentiation between PFAS used in essential closed-loop long-life products which are indispensable for society (e.g. critical infrastructure) and those widespread products which have a short lifetime with non-essential use & applications (e.g. cosmetics, consumer products).
• Appropriate and adequate transition periods for PFAS substances used in T&D equipment, where an unacceptable risk posed to human health and the environment has been identified, with no sufficient control measures available, an existing alternative and for which specific derogations are needed.
With the necessity for substantial grid modernization and expansion to meet the Union’s climate and energy transition, it is crucial that a proportional, differentiated, and balanced regulatory approach is applied. We urge regulators to act on securing an energy transition that goes hand in hand with protecting human health and the environment.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Applications of fluorinated gases (Annex E.2.8.) - Insulating gas in electrical equipment

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The use of HFO as electrical insulation gas to replace SF6 is new in the sector but similar to SF6 emission levels in percentage of the filled quantity (once along the lifetime of 40 years) can be reasonable expected. That are: 2% at electrical equipment manufacturing phase; 4% during use-phase of the electrical equipment; 1,5% at end-of-life gas recovery but unknown the percentage released at gas destruction phase, if not directly liberated to the atmosphere, which is not the case for SF6 which is recycled by SF6 gas manufacturers but could be environmentally acceptable for some specific HFOs.

5. Proposed derogations: The use of PFAS gases (in particular HFO) in high-voltage switchgear below 145 kV is not mentioned in derogation of paragraph 5 r). However, it should also include voltages above 24 kV up to and including 40,5 kV, which are used in MV electrical distribution and generation at solar parks and windparks. This range of voltages are today covered with SF6 insulating gas, but posible alternative solutions not using fluorinated gases imply a bigger carbon footprint, heavier equipments, bigger size and/or higher pressures for equipments placed close to public areas and habitation. The size of the EU28 global market for this range of voltages if totally shifted from SF6 to HFO can be estimated in the placement of around 8,55 ton of HFO per year in gas sealed electrical equipment of 40 years lifetime or superior. This number will depend very much on each specific development and customer homologation time of the alternative solutions, which alternatives to SF6 will be consolidated in future, and how quick de EU decarbonisation investments linked to sustainable electrical power generation capacity progress in next years till 2050.

6. Missing uses: a. Current annual tonnage and emissions of HFOs for high-voltage switchgear above 24 kV up to and including 40,5 kV can be considered negligible, because only used at pilot. b. The use of HFOs allows to reduce the CO2e of the insulating gas per functional unit above 24 kV, when compared with SF6, from 25 tCO2e to less than 0,0056 tCO2e, without increasing the filling pressure and the size of the high-voltage switchgear. c. The number of companies affected depends on how are accepted solutions based on HFO as alternative to SF6 or non-fluorinated gases leading to switchgears with bigger carbon footprints and higher pressures for voltages above 24 kV. The impact will be wide because it impacts electrical power generation and distribution at voltages above 24 kV, in addition to all factories, electric vehicles and buildings connected at this level of voltages through distribution power transformer substations. d. Some HFOs are an alternative to SF6. Those ones and other alternatives not based in fluorinated gases are in a preliminary phase for voltages levels above 24 kV up to and including 40,5 kV. Currently the market is based on SF6, which wants to be avoided. The consequences of not using a fluorinated compound are: bigger carbon footprint along lifetime; more costly equipment; heavier swithchgear; higher filling pressures and bigger pressure wave in case of explosion due to an internal arc fault. For estimated tonnage of HFO in future, see question 5. e. Currently, manufacturers of high-voltage switchgear in MV range are focused in the development, homologation processes and investment on manufacturing plants for solutions without SF6 for voltages up to and including 24 kV, which covers about 70% of the market of MV functional units in EU28. Those solutions do not use PFAS gas. For this reason is rather difficult at current time to make estimations of time to develop or investments needed on sustainable, reliable and safe alternatives not based on the use of fluorinated gases. e. Substitution by a non-fluorinated gas is possible but the consequences of doing so are explained in previous points. Economically cannot be evaluated at this point because solutions above 24 kV up to and including 40,5 kV have not still been developed. Further, from an environmental and health point of view is very questionable that those HFOs need to be replaced, considering that the non-fluorinated alternatives have higher impacts due to the increased quantities of material (copper, steel or aluminium, and epoxy resin) they need. We can easily estimate that the weight of the MV switchgear will be between 2,5 times and 3 times the weight of a MV switchgear based on SF6 or PFAS gas , for voltages above 24 kV up to and including 40,5 kV.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Electrical equipment for transmission and distribution are very complex products with extreme durability and a long lifetime of 40 years or more. To allow this, in combination with long maintenance periods or even maintenance-free design, high-grade materials are used. For some of the technical functions, PFAS materials are used intentionally or might be used as components of 3rd-party materials. The materials used in electrical equipment are divided into the following groups:

1) Articles or components containing PFAS, which have been selected intentionally by design as material or as an ingredient of a material mixture for a specifically defined function

2) Material, that has been selected based on technical parameters. PFAS has not been specified by the equipment manufacturer, but might be contained as an ingredient of a material mixture based on the definition of the manufacturer of the material

3) Components or assemblies, which are supplied from 3rd party suppliers, which have designed them on their own. PFAS has not been specified by the equipment manufacturer but might be contained as an ingredient of a material mixture or as material based on the definition of the component manufacturer or of the material manufacturer for materials used in the component

4) PFAS is a contaminant from the production process, e.g. as a release agent used in a cast moulding process to allow easy demoulding. Also, surface treatment using PFAS or PFAS-containing substances can result in such an effect. Contamination because of PFAS components in the production machine or due to the manufacturing of PFAS-containing products close to the production line of intended PFAS-free products can lead to contaminations. Due to the extremely low threshold level of 25 ppb, contamination is hard to control, especially if the manufacturing of parts or components is outside the EU, where no restrictions on PFAS exist

For 1) the manufacturer of the electrical equipment (e.g. we as ABB) is called to identify and search for alternatives. This process has already started. For 2) it is already more complex, as materials are used in many applications and changes in a material recipe might have an impact on the technical parameters. A change might result in that the material can no longer be used. Then another material has to be qualified. Alternatively, the supplier might decide to stop the production of the material. Then a new supplier for a similar, PFAS-free material needs to be identified. At 3) it becomes even more complex and time-consuming, as the process is not under control and can barely be influenced by the electrical equipment manufacturer (e.g. ABB). The responsibility is on the supplier. An example for this group could be electronic equipment as control and protection relays requested from our customer to be used from 3rd party. They contain semiconductors or other electronics, where it has been announced by the industry that it is almost impossible to offer PFAS free solution in short to mid term. For 4.) it is actually unclear how a declaration of PFAS-free could be achieved.
The identification processes 2) to 4) have one problem in common: The vast majority of the about 10,000 individual substances covered by the restriction proposal are currently not classified as hazardous in accordance with the CLP Regulation (EC) No. 1272/2008 nor identified as substances of very high concern (SVHCs) under REACH Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006. Thus, information on PFAS contained in mixtures and articles is usually not communicated along the supply chain. In addition, the extremely low threshold level of 25 ppb not only limits the identification process to intended ingredients but extends it to contaminants during the production process, which can result in that concentration. Analytical processes to prove if an article is PFAS-free will be extremely challenging taking the huge number of related articles into account, especially for polymers. Without a preceding, sufficiently long mandatory information phase based on legal requirements, during which information on PFAS in articles and mixtures had to be communicated in the supply chain, e. g. via safety data sheets or according to REACH Art. 33, it is not possible to determine all PFAS uses.

ABB has the target to replace PFAS in products wherever possible with PFAS-free materials. There might be some applications where this is not possible, which will be addressed separately. In all other cases, where a replacement is possible, the complex way of identification, finding a replacement, implementing them in products and finally repeating type testing of related products will by far exceed the given transition time of 18 months, taking into account that only the time required for full type testing of products can be one year or more. As this would not only affect ABB but all manufacturers of electrical equipment, due to the limited number of accredited test laboratories, this will create a bottleneck in type testing, which potentially causing a shortage of electrical equipment with a substantial impact on EU energy transition. Type tests are mandatory for most markets, including EU and any material change with impact on the test result, requires type tests to be repeated. As these tests are very time consuming and some specific tests are extremely expensive, the tests have to be done after all PFAS replacements in the specific product to be tested have been completed, to avoid repeated testing of the same product for each identified PFAS again and again.

For this, ABB asks for an extended transition time of an additional 8 years to complete the transition to PFAS-free solutions. As the investigation along the whole ABB supply chain is still ongoing, we still see the risk that this might be challenging, especially if the low threshold level is kept and the identification is not limited to intentionally added PFAS. For this, the possibility of a further exemption after 8 years should be offered, if it is proven that the replacement projects are not completed due to missing alternative solutions.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The comment does no apply to a specific sector listed in the Annex XV restriction report (Table 9) but will be an additional one. In the products also some sectors are subuses, as for example grease.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Electrical equipment in general contains high quantities of recyclable materials such as steel, aluminum and copper and are generally intended to be handed over to recycling companies at the end of life. Depending on the product the recyclability can reach levels of 90 %. Epoxy resin is a component which can not be recycled but burnt (thermal recycling). Only a small fraction of the electrical equipment ends up in landfills. The PFAS-containing materials will normally be part of the thermal recycling process. With temperatures >900 °C for sufficient time PFAS are destroyed to non-PFAS.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: The threshold level of 25 ppb results in contamination of 1.000 tons of waste with 25 g of pure PFAS. As waste is always a mixture which will be processed and purified during the recycling process, the effort to remove such low contaminations will be extremely if possible at all. As the contamination especially in waste is very inhomogenous it is not realistic that any recycling process can be established for products which might contain PFAS even in low concentrations.

5. Proposed derogations: The majority of the material used in electrical equipment is (stainless) steel, aluminium, copper and insulating materials like epoxy resin, silicone rubber or porcelain, highly depending on what kind of electrical equipment it is. The weight of intentionally added PFAS will be for the total product weight <1%. Non-intentionally added PFAS will even be significantly lower, as it is only a contamination of a material which is <1%, which means for a product it will be << 1ppm.

6. Missing uses: Electrical equipment belongs to the energy sector, which is marked green in Table A.1 of Annex A of the Annex XV restriction report, but this equipment is not listed sufficiently as a user of PFAS. a) The annual tonnage is hard to report as in the very much distributed applications where PFAS has been identified up to now the quantities are not easy to get, as the majority are additives in materials of subsupplier where the kind and quantity has not been specified, but only material properties which rely on PFAS. b) In the very wide range it is also not possible to give a simple answer. In most cases, the PFAS is required to fulfil the requirement of long lifetime and low wear or similar material properties. In some specific applications where PFAS is intentionally used or added, e.g. nozzles on hard-gas load break switches, the PFAS (PTFE) is mandatory for the technical function. More details are given in a specific contribution on PTFE from ABB ELDS. c) Most of the usages and even the same or similar products from subsuppliers are used in the complete branch. This is confirmed by common statements prepared in associations. d) Most likely the majority of the applications can be shifted to alternatives, but the problems are on the identification, substitution, testing, qualifying and certification. This will require significant time and resources. e) For most applications there was no search for substitutes up to now, as there was no need. The research is starting but only a few conclusions are available now. Insulation gases based on Fluoronitriles or Fluoroketones for example can not be substituted by other gases without significant loss of product performance. If hard-gas switches without PFTE are possible is also open and doubtful. For other applications, first alternatives are tested. Some with positive, others with negative results. f) Electrical equipment is mandatory for safe and reliable energy supply. Reduction of performance or lifetime, increasing of maintenance, related outages and costs are not acceptable. Substitutes must be able to have the same performance. Product development times are long (5-10 years) and investment is high, also due to expensive type testing. Depending on the product and the complexity it is on the level of several million Euro. g) For electrical equipment the question is not how big companies' losses are if they can no longer produce the equipment. Suppose it is not possible to serve the market. In that case, the energy supply is endangered, the transformation to green energy is slowed down and the extension of the electrical networks is undermined, with a negative impact on industry and society.

8. Other identified uses: A group covering electrical equipment is missing and needs to be created. A derogation of 8 years is estimated to be sufficient to replace actually used PFAS with PFAS-free solutions. In some cases, it is not clear if it is possible. For this, they are treated separately in an additional response to this consultation.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Electrical equipment generally has a long lifetime of 40 years or even more and is therefore well prepared for the sustainable targets under preparation by the EU. Technically, economically, and ecologically it is possible in many cases to further extend this lifetime, in some cases with some maintenance or refurbishment. On the other hand, the replacement of old equipment is always related to very high effort for the owner and operator and requires intensive planning of the work and related de-energization of the equipment or the complete substation. Based on the condition of the equipment even service times of 50 or 60 years are possible and targeted by the network operators, for example, air-insulated switchgear (AIS). Some of ABB portfolio products are maintenance-free, while others require maintenance or service over a lifetime. Both categories might be affected by defects based on internal failures or external reasons which require to be repaired.

Within the lifetime of the equipment, the repair or the replacement of components or assemblies is mandatory to keep the equipment running and to fulfil the required function. Maintenance and repair require spare parts to bring the product back in a condition to fulfil the technical requirements and performance needed for the task. As defects in electrical equipment are often linked to outages or at least to preliminary network configuration to bypass the defective equipment, it is of high importance to repair defects in a short time. For this manufacturers or even operators keep the most common spare parts in stock. In the majority of cases, it is required to use the “repair-as-produced-principle”, as otherwise the technical performance might change and/or test certificates become invalid, which will revoke the permission of use.

For products manufactured many years ago and even discontinued many years ago, it is impossible to have an overview of contained PFAS. Even in actual products, the extremely low threshold levels make it very complex to identify PFAS. In case required spare parts of the original design use PFAS, it might not be allowed to use PFAS-free alternatives as this change can invalidate the type tests. A change of material (in that case replacing PFAS-containing materials with PFAS-free materials) would require according to actual standards, that type tests have to be repeated using this new material. This is not possible for products already in use especially if discontinued by the manufacturer, as the required test objects for type test cannot be manufactured anymore. Without a valid type test, the use of the equipment is no longer permitted, in many cases for safety reasons. In addition, it would be non-proportional to re-do type tests for discontinued products of the last 5 decades to be prepared for any possible defect. Taking equipment out of service because a very small component is not available, is non-proportional and the economic and ecological impact of shortening the lifetime is very high. Keeping the “repair-as-produced principle” is therefore mandatory for electrical equipment.

In addition, the current restriction proposal prevents the transition towards a circular economy and undermines fundamental sustainability goals, e. g. the “repair-as-produced-principle" constituted in EU product legislation such as Directive 2009/125/EC, which allows products already placed on the Union market to be restored to their original condition without undergoing a conformity assessment again.

The exclusion of repair and spare parts from the PFAS ban is crucial due to the serious risk of sudden end-of-life for a wide variety of long-living products after the restriction’s application date. In the majority of cases, the affected article to be replaced by a spare part is only a very small portion of the overall top-level article (the product), for example, a nozzle of under 100 g of a load break switch of a medium voltage ring-main-unit (total weight about 600 kg) or a few grams of grease in a circuit breaker mechanism. As these spare parts are often mandatory for the function and need to be replaced to continue the use of the equipment, it would not be proportional to limit the overall lifetime of equipment to the time of the first defect or wear of a single component. Besides the financial impact of such a limitation, many products are not simple to be replaced by new products. This would lead to unacceptable interruption of use of the products with possibly severe consequences such as outages or limitations of electricity supply.

For this ABB asks for a time-unlimited exemption for spare parts and worn parts used for the maintenance and repair of products already placed on the market prior to the validity date of the re-striction, taking care of any exemption for components or technologies, until the equipment has reached its practical end of life.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The comment does no apply to a specific sector listed in the Annex XV restriction report (Table 9) but will be an additional one. In the products also some sectors are subuses, as for example grease.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Spare and wear parts are required to reset a product to an adequate condition to continue to stay in service. The parts are only a small to very small fraction of the complete product. Most likely only a small fraction of the required spare or wear parts contain PFAS, but in case they need to be replaced, the replacement is mandatory. Alternatives can not be used. As the service is done by dedicated service teams, the collection of PFAS-containing parts is possible. They can be added to a waste stream taking care of minimizing the emissions.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: For PFAS materials without general exemption, there will be no recycling of spare parts. As it is clear that the spare or wear parts are made of PFAS or PFAS is an additive or contaminant, these parts have to be added to a waste stream taking care of minimizing the emissions.

5. Proposed derogations: As spare and wear parts of electrical equipment are only a very small fraction of the overall product weight, the yearly tonnage would be very small and can not be easily estimated. Especially spare parts are normally only needed for the repair of defects. Wear parts are also rare as most products of ELDS are maintenance-free or require only low maintenance. The expected amount of PFAS per year will be more at the level of kg than tons.

6. Missing uses: As stated in the general statement or in the attached file, it is not possible to use spare parts made of alternative material different from the original part, due to the validity of type tests and the original technical function and/or performance. The "repair-as-produced principle" has to be used here.

8. Other identified uses: A group covering wear and spare parts is missing and needs to be created. For this, ABB asks for a time-unlimited exemption for spare parts and wear parts used for the maintenance and repair of products already placed on the market prior to the validity date of the restriction, taking care of any exemption for components or technologies, until the equipment has reached its practical end of life.
