General Comments: Fidra welcomes the opportunity to comment on the restriction proposal prepared by the authorities from Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden, on per- and poly-fluoroalkyl substances (PFAS).

Nine processes have been identified that are critical to the resilience and stability of the whole Earth, and are strongly affected by human actions. These have been named the ‘planetary boundaries’, and a recent update of the planetary boundaries framework indicates that six of the nine have been passed, placing the Earth outside the safe operating limit for humans (Richardson et al, 2023) . One of the six planetary boundaries is ‘novel entities’ which are novel anthropogenic inputs to the Earth’s system, including synthetic chemicals such as endocrine disruptors and organic pollutants. While this category would be assumed to include PFAS, it has been suggested that contamination of the environment by this group of chemicals actually ‘defines a separate planetary boundary’ which has in turn been exceeded (Cousins et al, 2022) . The current capacity to address the removal of PFAS and mitigate their impact once in the environment is very poor, and it is therefore highly important to restrict uses and emissions of PFAS as soon and as comprehensively as possible.

Fidra strongly supports the overall aim of the proposal submitters, to restrict PFAS as a group, as also outlined in the EU Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability published in October 2020 (European Commisson, 2020) . PFAS have been described by researchers as probably the greatest chemical threat the human race is facing in the 21st century, and there needs to be movement now beyond addressing them one by one.

We are constantly learning more about the levels of PFAS in the environment and their impacts, and none of it is reassuring. A recently published study of 12 killer whales found that PFAS made up more than half of the contaminants in them (Lee et al, 2022) . Not only do the results found by this investigation show we need to improve monitoring, we also need to urgently address the discharge of all PFAS into the environment and take action to prevent it.  The widespread contamination of the environment by PFAS (Arena for Journalism in Europe, 2023)  and the presence of PFAS in our bodies (Uhl et al, 2023)  are further indicators that urgent action is needed.

These concerns are addressed well by the restriction proposal that is under consideration here. Restricting the manufacture, use and placement on the market of PFAS, with significant reductions by the end of the transition periods, will be vital steps towards a truly PFAS-free economy in the EU.  It is essential that the broad scope of the restriction continues to cover all very persistent PFAS and includes fluoropolymers, and minimal derogations are included. Transition should be ensured for all uses where alternatives are available, in as short a time as possible. Importantly, the use of PFAS as active ingredients in Plant Protection Products, Biocidal Products and Human and Veterinary Products should not be given a derogation for an unlimited timescale.

The potential economic impact of moving away from PFAS production is often cited as a reason for their ongoing use, however, continuing on the current trajectory of PFAS use will inevitably have its own economic impact (ChemSec, 2023) . PFAS are building up in the environment, ultimately threatening food and drinking water security and public health. As more evidence comes to light about the human impacts of these chemicals, the tolerable limits are repeatedly decreased, therefore, we are tending to a point where the levels in food overtake safe levels. Farms and fisheries may be left with products that are unable to be sold because of unsafe levels of PFAS and drinking water will need a higher degree of treatment to make it safe. As a real-world example of this, the state of Maine has retrospectively fitted filters to individual houses to make drinking water safe, with its estimated costs of PFAS drinking water remediation over 2022-2030 of $42.5 million (The Maine Monitor, 2023) . Furthermore, the impacts to human health from long term repeated exposure to PFAS, will inevitably put further strain and economic pressure on healthcare providers. The health-related costs of inaction has been estimated at 52 – 84 billion EUR for the European Economic Area (Nordic Council of Ministers, 2019) .

Justification for a full group approach
Piecemeal regulatory approaches to PFAS management implemented so far have been inadequate in preventing their release into the environment. In addition, ‘chemical-by-chemical’ approaches have led to the substitution of regulated PFAS with other, similarly problematic, unregulated PFAS. They have created a never-ending cycle of regrettable substitution that has undermined genuine progress towards safe and sustainable alternatives. Regulating all PFAS as one group is the only way to end this never-ending cycle of regrettable substitutions and to cover persistent PFAS which may not even be engineered yet. It is also the most efficient way to address the urgency of reducing PFAS emissions. In an ideal scenario, a restriction takes 3 years from the registry of intention until entry into force. A multiplication of regulations for different subgroups would significantly delay action on highly persistent PFAS.

The fluoropolymers subgroup of polymeric PFAS have been singled out by some commentators as being of ‘low reactivity’ and therefore not in need of restriction. However, independent peer-reviewed scientific literature stresses that their production, use and end of life, are associated with emissions of other PFAS posing an unacceptable risk to human health and the environment (Lohmann et al, 2020; Kwiatkowski et al, 2020)   . In addition, as extremely persistent materials, fluoropolymers represent a long-term reservoir for the emissions of associated PFAS in the environment. Therefore fluoropolymers and other polymeric PFAS must be in the scope of regulatory actions on PFAS to achieve the aim of reducing emissions of highly persistent PFAS to a minimum.

It is vital that all sectors which use PFAS come within the scope of a single set of overarching regulations, as regulations applicable to individual sectors such as food contact materials, plant protection products, pharmaceuticals and F gas will not consider the full spectrum of environmental and human health impacts of a PFAS product’s entire life cycle. Rather the sector-specific regulations will address the safety and toxicity around a product’s function. Where this is a consumer product, such as food contact materials, the focus is on human health while using the product, rather than the environmental impact of its production, disposal and end of life. An overarching regulatory approach to restrict the use of PFAS as a group will address such loopholes.

With increasing evidence of PFAS in our environment, there is an urgent need for commitments to stopping PFAS emissions at source by moving towards a PFAS-free economy.

Increasing evidence of PFAS exposure and accumulation
Whilst we wait for visible action to restrict PFAS, the evidence of the harmful effects of PFAS and their accumulation in the environment and human and wildlife populations continues to build (European Environment Agency, 2019) .
PFAS continue to be a serious chemical global threat through their negative health effects in humans and wildlife (Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry, 2022) . The actual risk of PFAS is high, but many people remain unaware of them (Wickham & Shriver, 2021) . Recently published research shows that in 2019, at least one PFAS was detected in 60% of the public groundwater wells and 20% of the private groundwater wells used as drinking water sources in the eastern USA (McMahon et al, 2022) . In England, the Environment Agency found PFAS contamination in 97% of 470 freshwater sites analysed between 2014 and 2019 (Environment Agency, 2021) . The latest reports from the UK’s Water Industry Research (UKWIR) Chemicals Investigation Programme show that effluent from monitored wastewater treatment works is exceeding the Environmental Quality Standard (EQS) of PFOS. In the case of monitoring effluent released in transitional and coastal waters PFOS has been found to be more than 10 times the EQS across all sites monitored. Analysis by The Rivers Trust and Wildlife and Countryside Link has shown PFAS to be widespread in English rivers with 81 of 105 sites surveyed containing PFAS at levels which would not meet tougher new proposed EU standards.

Researchers have also found freshwater contaminants accumulate in plants and animals, where they can be transferred to humans via ingestion (Roth et al, 2020) .  A US study published in January 2023 found freshwater fish with widespread high levels of PFAS, which if eaten would be equivalent to drinking contaminated drinking water (Barbo et al, 2023) . Distributed by the water cycle, PFAS have been allowed to contaminate remote corners of the planet and negatively impact its wildlife. In Antarctica, accumulations of the PFAS perfluorobutanoic acid in snow increased more than 200-fold between 1957 and 2015 (Garnett et al, 2022) .

Researchers have also found high concentrations of PFAS in Arctic algae (Garnett et al, 2021) . Algae are an important food source for zooplankton, with their contamination feeding upwards through the food chain to fish and shrimp, then seals, and finally to apex predators such as polar bears.  For many people, current PFAS exposure levels are unlikely to be high enough to warrant serious concern. However there is increasing evidence that they affect early brain development (Eriksson et al, 2023) . For adults, exposure in some occupations, including firefighting and chemical manufacturing and processing, are likely to be much higher than others (United States Environmental Protection Agency, 2023) . Links between serious health conditions and occupational exposure are increasingly emerging (Shearer et al, 2020; Purdue et al, 2023)    and will continue to do so as worldwide research, knowledge and understanding of PFAS increases, and as long as PFAS are not restricted or replaced.

Development of PFAS-free alternatives is crucial and already underway
The achievement of a PFAS free economy will impact manufacturers of PFAS and to a lesser extent others who import, supply, formulate or distribute mixtures and articles that contain PFAS in the EU. It is therefore vital that the transition to a PFAS-free economy is undertaken in a way that protects jobs and communities as well as the environment, especially for manufacturers of PFAS and small or medium businesses specialised in PFAS-based technologies. There is no one size fits all approach and context-specific solutions to support a job transition will need to be drawn up that centres workers and impacted communities in decision making.

The transition away from PFAS has the potential to bring real economic benefit. As a group of highly persistent, toxic chemicals, the continued use of PFAS is at odds with meeting the sustainability needs of modern businesses and the shift to a circular economy. Regulatory incentives to promote PFAS substitution and identify safer chemical and non-chemical alternatives will drive innovation towards new and emerging markets.

Transition will vary in pace according to the availability and scale of alternatives. Therefore the opportunity for rapid transitions where existing alternatives exist should not be delayed by consideration of substitutions that are not yet possible. The common characteristics of rapid transitions, include where a new and well established technology simply substitutes for an old one, where substitute technologies have been previously used in other markets, benefitting from the experience of early adopters, where the scales, either national or sub-national, are relatively small, and finally where the technologies offer high tangible benefits for adopters such as health, as well as benefiting from well-designed public policies (Grubler, Wilson & Nemet, 2016) .

To achieve a PFAS-free economy it will be essential to have a regulatory framework with policies to restrict PFAS use, to drive demand for PFAS-free products, as well as policies to support a transition with minimal impact on workers and communities affected by the move to a PFAS-free economy, especially those employed by or closely connected to manufacturers of PFAS and small to medium businesses specialised in PFAS-based technologies.

An essential step of the transition away from PFAS is the creation of a substitution hub. It would centralise information regarding PFAS-free alternatives for various sectors and applications, provide expertise and introduce PFAS users to alternative providers (see for instance ChemSec Marketplace as a model (ChemSec, 2023) ). In addition, governments need to play a pivotal role in supporting the research and innovation needed to develop and adopt PFAS-free alternatives. The substitution hub could also coordinate actions around R&D needs by identifying the gaps in PFAS-free alternatives and facilitating the introduction of companies with scientists to develop alternatives (See for instance the model of the Toxics Use Reduction Institute (TURI) at the University of Massachusetts Lowell (UMass Lowell), with the success story of PFAS-free alternatives developed for semiconductor uses in a year (UMASS LOWELL, 2023) ).

Conclusion
Society must end its reliance on PFAS and the encouraging news is that the transition to a PFAS-free economy is already underway. Progressive companies are switching to PFAS-free products, technologies or alternatives, such as the outdoor wear producer Patagonia (Patagonia, 2023) . PFAS-free alternatives have been developed in the past decades for critical applications such as firefighting foams and new PFAS-free alternatives are being found for sectors considered challenging until recently, such as the semiconductor (Sharma et al, 2023)  and hydrogen production sectors (Fraunhofer IAP, 2023) . Regulation is the strongest incentive to push for substitution (Tuncak, 2013)  and the restriction is the best way to ensure a full phase out of all PFAS manufacturing, uses and placement on the market. In addition, a restriction allows the inclusion of derogations for specific uses in need of longer transition periods, allowing some flexibility. Finally by covering imports, a restriction allows a level playing field for all companies.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Finnish Commerce Federation, being one of the co-signers of the views expressed by the Confederation of Finnish Industries (EK), supports the goal of the restriction proposal to cease the emissions of PFAS substances to the environment.

However, we want to highlight our concerns especially from the commerce perspective. The wide overarching ban of substances and articles would heavily affect many business sectors in the EU, including the trade sector. We are concerned about the overall implementability and possibility to proper surveillance of such a wide restriction.

We want to highlight that in setting transition periods the needs of a whole value chain down to wholesalers and retailers have to be taken into account. The farther away a company is from production the longer it needs to adapt itself to legislative changes.

However, the biggest concern is the challenge and unwanted delay in realisation of green transition in the Union.


We find it important that the proposal is reconsidered for some of its aspects:

Substances covered in the Regulation (EU) No 517/2014 on fluorinated greenhouse gases should be exempted from the PFAS regulation
The PFAS restriction proposal is overlapping with F-gas regulation. Fluorinated gases are already strictly controlled in the F-gas regulation, and companies have made their investments and planning according to provisions and transition periods in that regulation, also already anticipating those to come soon in the revision of the current F-gas regulation. Overlaps create great uncertainty among those who need to make longer term investment decisions now.

For the sake of overall sustainability it is important that expensive equipment, facilities and buildings, for example, can be used up to their anticipated end of life.


Competitiveness of the EU companies and value chains should not be compromised
The derogations in paragraph 4 and 5 do not at present cover the precursors, raw materials, or auxiliary agents of the final products. These need to be addressed in the derogations as well as R&D, so that distributors can continue providing the manufacturing industry in EU with the raw materials needed for innovations and development of products in the EU.

The list of exemptions should remain open ended. The unique properties of PFAS substances, including their favourable toxicologial profile, make them challenging to replace. Products of lower quality and performance are not well received by customers or consumers. In the worst case such products would compromise safety and be loss of valuable resources.

It should be possible to extend the list of exemptions or transition period, if no alternatives, which provide overall comparable or increased safety for the application is found and important value chain as well as in some cases even critical autonomy might be otherwise lost in the EU.

Any European legislation and its implementation should support equal treatment between companies established within and outside the EU, including online marketplaces and platforms, and active in the Single Market.  Due to its complexity and overarching nature the PFAS restriction proposal in its current form hardly fulfills that principle.


Finnish Commerce Federation is a nationwide trade organisation whose mission is to promote Finnish commerce - retail and wholesale. We represent around 7,000 member companies together with several Member and Partner Associations, many of which work close to the manufacturing industry.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Fire sprinklers save lives, property and the environment from damage due to fire. The sprinklers themselves are closed with a PTFE seal. This uses 0.03-0.12 g of PTFE per sprinkler, depending on sprinkler type. With 20 million fire sprinklers sold in the EU that represents 0.6 to 2.4 tonnes of PTFE per year. At present the industry does not have an alternative seal material. Even if it did, standards would first need to be update to recognise it and each manufacturer would need to test and recertify each of its sprinkler models. This would take many years.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: It is not obvious which sector is covered by fire sprinkler systems. We recommend it be separately listed. The sector has annual turnover of €4 billion in the EU and employs tens of thousands of people.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: At present some fire sprinklers are recovered because of the value of their brass content. It would be possible to recover the PTFE as well if there were somewhere to return it.

5. Proposed derogations: We estimate the annual tonnage of PTFE used by European fire sprinkler seals at 0.6-2.4 tonnes. At present no alternative material is proven suitable for this application and European standards for fire sprinklers do not extend to the use of other materials for the seals (see EN 12259-14). If another material can be shown to provide a good seal over the decades in which a fire sprinkler is in service, standards would need to be updated to recognise it. At the same time every manufacturer would need to test and recertify each of their fire sprinkler models with this new seal material. Laboratory capacity is limited so this would take many years.

6. Missing uses: Fire sprinkler seals a. 0.6-2.4 tonnes/year of PTFE in fire sprinkler seals. b. PTFE offers a stable seal, resistant to corrosion by water over the decades while a fire sprinkler is in service. c. Eight fire sprinkler manufacturers and 1,000 installers. d. Unknown. No alternative material has been assessed. e. R&D has yet to begin. f. ii. 5-10 years. Each fire sprinkler model from each manufacturer would need to be tested and recertified. Approvals are required by some Member States and in general by insurers, so that each fire sprinkler model would need to be assessed by several laboratories. These laboratories have limited capacity. g. If no substitute could be found, fire sprinkler systems could not be installed. National fire safety regulations require sprinklers in some types of buildings for safety reasons. If these buildings did not comply with fire safety regulations they would not be permitted to open and would therefore not be built. In addition, insurers would be unable to insure some buildings, in particular warehouses, if they were not protected with fire sprinkler systems. Without insurance they could not operate and would therefore not be built. While the sector has EU sales of about €4 billion and employs about 30,000 people the knock-on effects of buildings being refused permission to open or operate would affect a large part of the construction industry and cause major disruption in sectors such as logistics.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Firecomms designs and manufacturers optoelectronic transceivers specifically for use with plastic optical fibre (POF), an optical communication technology that is widely deployed in power electronics, medical and automotive applications.

We would like to draw to the attention of the ECHA’s scientific committees for Risk Assessment (RAC) and for Socio-Economic Analysis (SEAC) to the significance of an economically important classes of speciality optical fibre, that incorporate fluorinated polymers in their structure and that are not addressed in TABLE 9 of the ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT and nor are they addressed in Annex E. These speciality fibres are used in an extensive and diverse range of applications ranging from the control of high-voltage electricity transmission and AC-DC conversion equipment to medical applications such as endoscopy, ophthalmic surgery and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) image scanners. POF has also been extensively use in architectural lighting and ornamental displays but this application lies outside the scope of this submission.

The unique property that these perfluorinated polymers offer for use in optical fibre manufacture is the combination of the lowest possible refractive index for any transparent polymer together with good mechanical properties. For optical waveguiding the refractive index of the fibre cladding material must be lower than that of the fibre core material and in addition the cladding must be able to bind successfully to the core material and subsequently bear mechanical stress. The combination of the perfluorinted polymer cladding and a core of polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) enables an ‘all plastic’ highly rugged optical fibre. Furthermore, the combination of a perfluorinted polymer cladding and a silica (glass) core also enables the manufacture of speciality ‘glass’ fibres with larger acceptance angles and core dimensions that can be achieved with more conventional all silica fibre constructions. To the best of our knowledge silicone is the only alternative chemistry that can provide the required transparency and low refractive index but silicone’s mechanical and adhesion properties are not compatible with fibre manufacture.

The total quantity of speciality fibre manufactured annually that contain per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) is a vanishingly small fraction compared to the quantity of conventional glass fibre or copper based cables, solutions which could arguably be used to substitute the PFAS containing fibres. However, for the highly specific applications for which these PFAS containing fibres are used, conventional glass fibres or copper cables are either incapable of meeting application specific key performance criteria or are simply not economically viable. On the grounds that (i) there is no straightforward alternative chemistry to replace the PFAS fibre cladding, (ii) the critical nature of the applications in which these speciality fibres are used and the importance they play in multiple value chains and (iii) the complexity of any alternative substitution technologies we request that the use of PFAS substances in the construction of speciality fibres should be given a maximum derogation.

While the ECHA’s PFAS restriction proposal rightly aims to protect human health and the environment, it is important that any imposed restriction does not have the unintended consequence of adversely affecting human health and the environment. Given the use of POF and other speciality fibres in the both the efficient management and control of electrical power and in a wide variety of medical applications we would argue that the continued use of PFAS substances should be granted.

6. Missing uses: The first class of fibre, and the most economically important, that is potentially affected by the proposed PFAS ban is commonly referred to as Plastic Optical Fibre (POF) as standardised in IEC 60793‐2‐40 .ed.3:2009: Type A4a.2. This type of POF is constructed from a waveguiding core of diameter 980 um composed of high purity polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) with a 20 um cladding of low refractive index perfluorinated polymer, therefore by volume the POF (unjacketed) contains 3.96% of PFAS material. This fibre type originally developed by DuPont in the 1960’s, is today primarily manufactured in Japan by Mitsubishi Chemical Group, TORAY and Asahi Glass although a number of new suppliers are also emerging from China.   Since the 1980’s POF as a speciality fibre has developed a number of important markets including industrial digital communication networks such as Fieldbus, Industrial Ethernet, Profinet, Sercos, ControlNet and Modbus used for real-time distributed control of machinery and equipment. The large optical core of the POF, its mechanical robustness together with its simple connectivity make it an ideal optical solution particularly for use in rugged and dirty environments where galvanic isolation can be an important requirement. In the 2000’s the car industry and in particular the European car industry (Audi, BMW, General Motors, Honda, Hyundai, Jaguar, Lancia, Land Rover, Mercedes-Benz, Porsche, Toyota, Volkswagen, SAAB, SKODA, SEAT and Volvo) also adopted a POF based communication bus called Media Oriented Systems Transport (MOST), a high-speed multimedia network technology for applications inside and outside the car.   POF is also a key enabling technology used by the major global manufacturers of power transmission and power management equipment to optically control, using pulse width modulation (PWM), the synchronised opening and closing of gates of high-power transistors such as Isolated Gate Bipolar Transistors (IGBTs) which are themselves used in the equipment to control high current and voltages in industrial applications and power transmission. Such applications include High Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) Electricity transmission, static VAR generators (SVGs), motor controllers (electric trains, trolley buses, electric drive ships), inverters, frequency converters (wind turbines, solar) etc. It is the combination of the POFs ease of use and mechanical resilience while still providing galvanic isolation that has made it an ideal technology solution for over 30 years and more recently to support the growth of wind and solar energy production.  Furthermore POF’s unique combination of properties has also led to its adoption in many and varied medical applications and instrumentation such as endoscopy, catheters, MRI scanners, ophthalmic surgery and surgical robots.  A second class of speciality fibre that use PFAS materials is that of polymer clad silica (PCS) fibre. In this case the waveguiding core of the fibre is made from silica (most commonly with a core diameter of 200 um to larger) but the cladding material is made from low refractive index perfluorinated polymer which enables speciality glass fibres to be manufactured with high numerical apertures. Suppliers of such fibre include OFS and Sumitomo and are used in a range of diverse applications including industrial control, medical and sensing.  In 2018 the world total annual for ‘conventional’ optical fibre was 500 million km. In comparison the annual demand for POF for use in communication, control and sensing applications is estimated to be of the order 200,000 to 500,000 km which converts approximately to an annual 0.8 to 2 metric tonnes of PFAS material in the finished product.  The total POF market value is, in some recent market research reports, estimated at USD $4 billion which would include both the fibre manufactures but also the optoelectronic module and systems manufacturers. This POF industry has historically been centred in Japan and the USA, dominated by product divisions within a limited number of large multi-nationals suppliers, particularly in relation to industrial applications, factory automation and power control (Toshiba, Hitachi, Broadcom). However, in the last 15 years as POF has found additional applications in automotive, medicine and sensing and a significant number of additional suppliers of peripheral equipment and components have entered the market (Hamamatsu, TE Connectivity, Harting, Firecomms, KDPOF) while the POF manufacturer remains dominated by Japanese suppliers. In Europe, SME’s such as KDPOF, Firecomms and HomeFibre have invested many 10’s of millions of Euro in POF related technology and together with EU funded research institutes have played a pivotal role in developing and extending the capability of POF technology.

Content: Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period
Combined Comments:
General Comments: First of all, we appreciate ECHA’s efforts to protect human health and the environment. Our stakeholders operate around the world and are committed to protecting human health and the environment, and complying with laws and regulations for chemical substances. After careful consideration of the proposed restrictions on the Annex XV report, we would like to provide the following comments and suggestions. Especially, we would like to share the information about PFAS in raw materials for coatings applied to the highly functional membrane for CO2 removal applications in natural gas industry.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Since it was difficult to categorize the use of this membrane into the sectors and (sub)uses in Table 9 in Annex XV report, we request you to create an appropriate new category. Alternatively, please add our sub-use to A.3.3.1.1. Technical textiles – high performance membranes.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: 1) Usage and Emission (i) Our company produces highly-functional membrane modules for CO2 removal applications in the natural gas industry. These functional membrane modules contain PFAS. We manufacture the membrane modules in the Netherlands. Emission or exposure of PFAS is well managed during manufacturing, and waste PFAS are collected after manufacturing. General consumers do not come into contact with this waste. Since the membrane is fully integrated into a large cartridge element (1m length / 0.2m diameter) covered by a glass fiber cover, there is no release of PFAS to the to the outside environment during transport, storage, and usage.   (ii) The raw materials for the membranes have been selected in order to achieve high functionality and reliability. The PFAS used for the functional coating in the membrane module are specifically selected for the purpose of separation of gases, with the function of blocking permeation of certain gas molecules (e.g. natural gas) while allowing other gases (e.g. CO2, etcetera) to permeate. The PFAS in the membrane are polymers.  (iii) The amount of PFAS in these highly functional membranes is very small, between 0.02 and 0.03 wt%. The total amount which is brought into the EU region is less than 9 kg per year. Compared to the total amount of PFHxA used in the EU of 250,000 t/a*, the amount of PFAS in the membrane is extremely small. (*This is total use in the EU which was calculated from the information of ECHA_Background Document 19694 on the 9th of  June in 2021).    (2) Emissions and exposure All remaining raw materials for the membrane modules containing PFAS (if any) are collected after manufacturing. A certified waste company handles and collects the waste solutions during and after manufacturing process. During production, the PFAS is incorporated in the matrix of the membrane coating. Since the membrane is fully integrated into a glass fiber cover, the PFAS is kept in the end product. The amount used is very small, and users will not disassemble the membrane cartridge element. It is considered that the emission of PFAS to the environment is also very limited.  (3) Emissions and value as social-cultural property The membrane is used in the process of natural gas purification and removes CO2 out of natural gas with less energy consumption compared to other technologies such as the chemical absorption method. As the membrane contributes to a reduction of energy usage (and therefore a reduction of CO2 emissions), the membrane technology is now highlighted as the more eco-friendly option in natural gas industry.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: The membrane itself is a functional medium and this is not expected to be recycled

5. Proposed derogations: The PFAS in the membrane modules are two polymers.  With respect to the amount of PFAS contained in the membrane modules, it is very small, between 0.02 and 0.03 w/w% This contents will not change in the future. The total amount of PFAS which is brought into the EU region is estimated at less than 9 kg per year.   Since waste materials are collected, release to the environment is also limited. Although we are trying to find alternatives, the feasibility studies are still in progress. For the development of the next generation of membranes, which do not contain PFAS, we shall need at least 5 years, maybe 10. We therefore request a 12 year derogation.

6. Missing uses: Function - The function of PFAS used in the gas separation membrane modules is as the main polymeric layer for the separation of gases. The PFAS is particularly selected for (1) separation of gases with function of blocking permeation of certain gas molecules (e.g. natural gas) while allowing other gases (e.g. CO2, etc) to permeate, and (2) improved solubility to enable coating of the thin layer. As the PFAS is enabling both gas permeation property and processability of the membrane, it is essential for achieving high functionality and manufacturing of membrane. - Since PFAS type materials have fluorine substituents which are electron withdrawing, PFAS has the negative charge triboelectric property, by which hydrophobic and non-polar gases e.g. natural gases are repelled while the solubility of polar gas (e.g. CO2) increases, resulting in an enhancement of the separation property.  Benefit of PFAS for environment perspective: - As explained in the previous section, the F-containing group in the polymer is essential for solubility of polymer during productions. The main separation polymer becomes less soluble when the PFAS group is eliminated from the polymer, thus much more aggressive polar solvents (e.g. DMF, NMP) in much higher amounts (50-100 times more than amount of polymer) are needed. Those solvents tend to be harmful chemicals, and what is more, this process requires more heat and more washing water, and therefore significantly increases the negative impact on safety/health, environment, and cost.   Alternatives - As explained in the previous section, PFAS is essential for gas separation properties and solubility of the polymer during production, therefore advanced technology will be required to design a molecule and composition to replace the PFAS. - We have already investigated a reduced amount of F atoms in the polymer and end product and managed to develop polymer materials which contain only CF3 groups (without any -CF2-CF2- chains), with very low amounts of F-atoms (18 to 20 wt %) in the main separation polymer, and therefore an even lower amount (0.004 to 0.005 wt %) in the end product, the membrane module, by which still both gas separation performance and processability (solubility) are fulfilled.  - In our experience, it will take a lot of resources and approximately 10 years to find the alternative, prototyping, customer evaluation (more than two years to get qualified in multiple customers) and develop to the commercial products. The default transition period of 18 months is far too short for a complete replacement.

10. Analytical methods: Elemental analysis can be used to measure the total weight of F-atoms in the membrane modules.

General Comments: First of all, we appreciate ECHA’s long-standing efforts and cutting-edge activities to protect human health and the environment. Measurement film is a tool to check whether pressure, heating, and UV irradiation are being performed appropriately in manufacturing processes and equipment. By performing these checks, it is possible to detect abnormalities in manufacturing equipment at an early stage and reduce the number of defective products, which leads to improved manufacturing efficiency and a reduction in raw material loss due to the occurrence of defective products. For these reasons, there are cases where Measurement films are incorporated into the specifications and management of the customer's manufacturing equipment. If Measurement film become unusable, customers will no longer be able to manufacture it in the same way as before, as our company has a 100% market share in Europe and there are no substitutes. In addition, our customers include the aviation, railroad, and pharmaceutical industries, and if Measurement film become unusable, the social impact will be significant. Content: Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: First of all, we believe that the proposed PFAS regulation in Annex XV is not appropriate because the proposed PFAS regulation in Annex XV covers all PFAS with some exceptions, while some PFAS species are considered to have risks but have no proven hazardous properties. Our company therefore endorses the statement on the issues in Section IV. attached proposed restrictions prepared by the FCJ and the Japanese Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry.
Fluorine-substituted one-carbon PFASs such as lithium=bis(trifluoromethanesulfon)imide and trifluoromethanesulfonates are widely used in the semiconductor and lithium ion secondary battery industries due to their high ionic conductivity, and are also used as antistatic agents It is also used as an antistatic agent. Many of these fluorine-substituted PFAS with a carbon number of 1 have no information on their persistent nature, and we request that they be excluded from the regulation, that their antistatic agent use be specified in the draft PFAS regulation in Annex XV, and that an additional grace period be set.
Polymer-type antistatic agents manufactured by our company are additives that impart sustained antistatic properties to resins, and because of their characteristics, they are used in a wide variety of applications, including automotive interiors, packaging materials for electronic components, trays for electronic components, and anti-static discharge products. Polymer-type antistatic agents consist of a special polymer component and an ionic compound. For polymer-type antistatic agents, which require particularly high antistatic performance and low staining (resistance maintained by washing with water), PFAS, which has one carbon atom substituted with fluorine and has high solubility in the special polymer, is essential as an ionic compound.
Although polymer-type antistatic agents are also manufactured by companies other than our company, they all have lower antistatic performance than our products and do not meet the needs for lower resistance in automotive interiors, packaging materials for electronic components, and trays for electronic components, which require high antistatic performance. In addition, low-molecular-weight antistatic agents bleed out, so they cannot be used for automobile interiors, packaging materials for electronic components, and trays for electronic components because of problems such as lack of persistence in resistance value and significant dependence on humidity.
Carbon material can also achieve low resistance as an antistatic agent for resins, but it cannot replace our products because carbon has poor dispersibility in resins, it cannot achieve uniform antistatic effect, it is dusty and highly contaminating, and molded products turn black, making it impossible to maintain transparency and coloring.
Under these circumstances, antistatic agents are not listed as an application in the proposed PFAS regulation in Annex XV, and no additional grace period for substitution is given, which could cause significant problems in the supply chain.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Antistatic agents are essential materials used in a wide variety of applications, including automotive interiors, packaging materials for electronic components, trays for electronic components, anti-static discharge products, home appliances, and medical devices. Antistatic agents are missing and omitted from the fields listed in the proposed restriction.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: No data available during production or use. Estimated to discharge about 0.05 tons at disposal.

6. Missing uses: a. We use PFAS in permanent antistatic agents added to automotive interiors, packaging materials for electronic components, trays for electronic components, home appliances, and medical devices. We estimate that we use about 0.05 tons per year and emit about 0.05 tons.   b. The PFAS we use is the only component that simultaneously meets the antistatic, persistent, (low staining), and colorability requirements of the application in question.   c. Permanent antistatic agents are used in a wide variety of applications including automotive interiors, packaging materials for electronic components, trays for electronic components, home appliances, medical devices, etc. The number of affected companies cannot be determined, but we estimate there are many.   d. At this time, no technically feasible substitutes have been found.   e. No technology has been established to achieve low resistance values, persistence, and low pollution, although this has been studied.   f. No technically feasible alternative has been identified at this time.   g. Socio-economic impacts on companies, consumers, and other stakeholders are expected to include static electricity problems in automobile interiors and failure of electronic components due to static electricity. Content: Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: First of all, we would like to appreciate ECHA for its kind contribution and activities to protect human health and the environment for many years. Our stakeholders operate around the world and are committed to protecting human health and the environment and complying with laws and regulations for chemical substances in each country and region. After careful consideration of the proposed restrictions on the Annex XV report, we would like to provide the following comments and suggestions. Especially, we would like to share the information about PFAS in magnetic recording tape media for data storage.
Request for derogation;
Our company manufactures magnetic recording tape media for archiving digital data. The latest magnetic tape products use Side-chain fluorinated polymer, which is a type of PFAS. Due to the low surface free energy of Side-chain fluorinated polymer, it is a very important material for use as a lubricant on the surface of magnetic tapes. The superiority or inferiority of this lubricating performance is directly linked to the recording capacity and product life of the magnetic tape, and it is an absolutely indispensable main material of magnetic tape for data archiving, which realizes low-cost and large-capacity recording. If PFAS is not used, practicality the recording density will decrease, resulting in low-capacity tape production. We manufacture and distribute PFPE lubricants. PFPE is considered a polymer of low concern by OECD standards and has no effect on the human body.
In addition, PFPE is used even though it is more expensive than conventional lubricants because it has the following performance characteristics that only PFPE can provide.
Non-volatile: Because it is an organofluorine compound, it has a high specific gravity (d = about 1.9), and even low-viscosity oils do not volatilize more than hydrocarbon oils.
Thermal stability: It does not decompose even at high temperatures above 350°C. PFPE has high heat resistance and WO87/02995 states that it finally decomposes into low molecular weight oil at 500°C. Even silicone oil, which is said to have high heat resistance, has heat resistance up to 250°C.
Post the URL of the silicone manufacturer's oil operating temperature.
https://nihon-resin.jp/products/oil/kf-96/
Chemical Stability: PFPE oil is resistant to strong acids and alkalis due to its CF bond stability.
Other oils are fragile due to their chemical structure, causing chemical structure changes and decomposition due to strong acids, alkalis, etc.
In addition, since it does not dissolve plastics, it is the only oil that can be used to lubricate plastics.
In this way, PFPE is used because of the properties that result from its chemical structure, and oils with different structures cannot produce the same properties and cannot be substituted.
For these reasons, PFPE-based lubricants are not appropriate within the proposed 12-year period and should be exempt from regulation.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Lubricants

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: In general, equipment and bearings that use lubricating oil and grease are recycled as steel scrap. When it is recycled, it is melted in an electric furnace. The melting temperature is 1,600 ° C to 1,800 ° C, the gas emitted from it is 1,500 ° C, and all organic matter is decomposed into inorganic gas. https://worldwide.espacenet.com/patent/search/family/040965236/publication/JP5362983B2?q=pn%3DJP5362983B2 It is judged that in an advanced society where recycling is established, it will not accumulate in the environment as is a concern in the proposed regulation. If we are concerned about the safety of chemical substances, we believe that we should build a recycling system that can incinerate them at an appropriate temperature.

We manufacture and sell PFPE. PFPE is considered a polymer of low concern under OECD standards and has no effect on the human body.
PFPE is used as a masking oil for metallized films used in film capacitors.
We propose that this sector be exempted from regulation.
https://www.j-platpat.inpit.go.jp/c1800/PU/JP-H03-059981/F2DD44F544D662C837AA65707340AE9D4269226048561F1703EA6389EC017CC7/12/ja
PFPE is used because of its performance characteristics:
Non-flammable: Paraffin and silicone masking oils burn, but PFPE masking oils do not. This feature is necessary for film capacitors that require a high level of safety, such as those used in electric vehicle applications.
Non-volatile: Because it is an organofluorine compound, it has a high specific gravity (d = about 1.9), and even low-viscosity oils do not volatilize more than hydrocarbon oils. Therefore, even when vacuumed, the oil remains and the masking effect does not allow metal to be deposited.
In liquid paraffin and silicone oil, the margin part is formed incompletely due to its volatility, and the metal is deposited and remains on the film, resulting in insufficient insulation.
Therefore, capacitance reduction is likely to occur, the overall withstand voltage decreases, and a sharp margin is not formed at the boundary between the margin part and the deposited metal, resulting in insufficient dielectric loss.
Chemical stability: PFPE oil does not dissolve plastics, so when used as masking of PP and PET films, it does not affect the film and does not deform or tear.
In this way, PFPE is used due to the properties that come from its chemical structure, and oils with different structures cannot produce the same properties and cannot be substituted.
As mentioned above, PFPE should be exempted from regulations because there are no substitutes.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Electronics

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Described in section V

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Electronic circuits that use film capacitors are recycled and processed in non-ferrous smelting facilities.  During the recycling process, they are melted in a melting furnace (kiln) at a melting temperature of 1200°C. The resulting gas reaches 900°C, causing all organic substances to decompose into inorganic gases. https://www-cycle.nies.go.jp/magazine/kenkyu/202005.html In a society where an advanced recycling system is established, it is considered unlikely that the environmental accumulation feared in this proposed regulation would occur. If there are concerns about the safety of chemical substances, it is advisable to establish a recycling system that allows for thermal treatment at an appropriate temperature.

6. Missing uses: a. Our information is set forth in Section 5.  b. Already documented in the general terms and conditions in Section 3.  c. While the exact number of film capacitor manufacturers in Europe is not known, electric vehicle manufacturers invariably rely on the self-healing capabilities of film capacitors to ensure safety.  d. Materials other than PFPE have been used in the past, but cannot be used in today's advanced film capacitors. It is expected that the film will become thinner and may deform with oil other than fluorine, the oil will burn and reduce safety, and the basic electrical performance of the film capacitor will be reduced. Currently, there are no examples of film capacitors using anything other than PFPE oil. e. As noted in the General Conditions in Section 3, we believe that no alternative to PFPE can match its characteristics of non-flammability, low volatility, and non-dissolution of plastics.  g. Film capacitors are used in electric vehicles, wind power generation, household appliances and rail vehicles, and any impact on their safety could affect the safety of these sectors.

8. Other identified uses: Described in section V

Combined Comments:
General Comments: FKM and PTFEs are essential for our products ‘rotary shaft seals’, therefore we request for a full exemption of polymeric PFAS for these kind of applications. The rotary shaft seals or namely oil seals are used together with rotating shafts to maintain fluids where they are placed. The main requirements from the oil seals are leakage free sealing under its operating conditions, low friction, consequently low power loss, little heat development.
The main functionality of the seal is provided with the seal-lip design and its elastomeric material. A major factor is the heat generation under the lip. While the seal continuously rotates on the shaft, heat generated by the friction is one of the limiting considerations in the performance of the seal. Shaft rotation speed has a direct effect on the underlip temperature. The materials with higher temperature resistance have higher speed capability.
Therefore, FKMs and PTFEs are used for manufacturing sealing parts such as rotary shaft seals, valve stem seals, piston seals, pressure seals, cassette seals, combined seals, springless seals, flanged seals, where high temperature and high chemical resistance, low friction are required for some of these applications in the engine and transmission systems.
With very exceptional properties of the FKMs and PTFEs like excellent thermal and chemical resistance, ozone and weathering, with low gas permeability, they become an exclusive solution where very high temperatures more than 150°C up to 200°C in aggressive fluids.
It seems that no other alternatives are available today for higher rotational speeds and temperatures and doesn’t seem to appear in the near future. The demands from the customers from automotive industry are increasing for the sub-suppliers day by day, and these requirements are even higher for e-mobility. Potential derogations for polymeric PFAS as 12 years, don’t seem enough as well. The design of the shaft seal is mostly connected to the lip material, and the whole validation process would take more time throughout the supply chain. Since there are not available alternatives at the moment, 12 years wouldn’t be sufficient to provide reliable products to the market. Hence, full exemption is requested for fluoroelastomers (FKM) & fluoroplastics (PTFE), polymeric PFAS and bisphenol AF (which is used to cure FKMs) to be used for producing rotary shaft seals, and other kind of seals for automotive & agricultural and industrial (hydraulic and pneumatic) applications.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Flame retardant polycarbonate compounds used in thin-wall consumer electronics applications plays a critical role in consumer safety and requires the use of PTFE as an anti-drip additive. Our justification for requesting derogation of PTFE as anti-drip agent in flame retardant polycarbonate compounds comprises two elements:
• there are no alternatives to polycarbonate that provide adequate impact resistance and ductility for thin wall (equal or below 1.5 mm) applications in electronic products
• in order to ensure that the polycarbonate thin wall has adequate flame retardancy, it is essential to use PTFE as the anti-drip agent
There is no other engineering plastic available today which provides adequate levels of impact resistance and ductility compared to polycarbonate. These properties are crucial to:
• provide a durable product that does not break during normal use, including drops and other foreseeable events
• ensure safety by avoiding exposure of life circuitry, and
• meet EU regulatory requirements on the safety of electrical device
We have carried out a thorough analysis of the latest available flame-retardant and anti-dripping technology for polycarbonate, via a patent and literature review, as well as our own in-house technical expertise based on decades of experience with plastics. There are no other technologies that provide adequate flame-retardant properties without significantly degrading impact resistance or other mechanical properties.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Electronics and semiconductor Medical devices Transport

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: PTFE (Polytetrafluoroethylene) as anti-dripping additive in flame retardant (FR) engineering polymers. No significant emissions are expected during the manufacturing phase (compounding) and the use phase since PTFE is encapsulated into the polymer matrix. The above mentioned engineering polymers are typically used in sectors where end of life is regulated, for example by the Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment Directive (WEEE 2012/19/EU) or the End-of Life Vehicles directive (ELV 2000/53/EC). We do not have specific information on the end of life treatments for those use sectors.

6. Missing uses: a. We have no data on the tonnages at sub-sector level. Specific information on our company PTFE uses are provided in the confidential attachment. b. Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), a high molecular weight fluoropolymer, is widely used in flame retardant (FR) plastics, e.g. polycarbonate (PC), acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS), polystyrene (PS). PTFE provides anti-dripping performance which prevents the spreading of fire. PTFE is essential to obtain V-0, V-1, 5VA and 5VB flammability rating, and to achieve compliance with strict EU flame retardancy and fire safety standards. The carbon–fluorine (C–F) bond is the strongest bond between carbon and another atom and imparts unique, outstanding, and beneficial properties and extraordinary functional performance to fluoropolymers. Regarding the anti-dripping mechanism of action, PTFE can form fibril structure due to high shear forces during compounding. Upon burning, this fibril structure, in conjugation with the strength of the C-F bond, is very stable, leading to char formation and preventing dripping. c. Please refer to the confidential attachment d. To the best of our there are no available alternatives to PTFE as anti-dripping agent in Polycarbonate. We have performed a review of the available patents and a literature review of the recent scientific publication on FR PC. We have also experimentally tested several alternative substances, and we have not found any suitable alternative to PTFE. The substances tested or reviewed, typically would not allow to achieve the flammability rating required by regulations. When those rating are achieved, the high loading of the additive will impact the mechanical properties of the polycarbonate (for example lowering mechanical properties). Consequently, the polycarbonate will fail to meet the impact resistance requirements mandate by the regulations / safety standards, and the material will not be suitable for use in the final application. More details are provided in the non confidential attachment. g. We do not have data for the whole sector, neither for the value chain (final product manufacturers). In the confidential attachment we have provided specific information on our company.

However PTFE is essential for the formulation of flame retardant (FR) polycarbonate (PC). To the best of our there are no available alternatives to PTFE as anti-dripping agent in Polycarbonate. We have performed a review of the available patents and a literature review of the recent scientific publication on FR PC. We have also experimentally tested several alternative substances, and we have not found any suitable alternative to PTFE. The substances tested or reviewed, typically would not allow to achieve the flammability rating required by regulations. When those rating are achieved, the high loading of the additive will impact the mechanical properties of the polycarbonate (for example lowering mechanical properties). Consequently, the polycarbonate will fail to meet the impact resistance requirements mandate by the regulations / safety standards, and the material will not be suitable for use in the final application. Content: Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Flat panel displays are essential components of electric and electronic devices. Their invention has triggered a boom in IT and consumer electronics leading to the substitution of the huge and heavy CRT displays with lightweight and high-resolution displays. New areas of display applications appeared, that were not possible with CRT (e.g., automotive). As the usage of the flat panel display is widespread, each display must have specific properties which are finely tuned in a multidimensional development process. The decisive component of the Liquid Crystal (LC) display is the liquid crystal substance. These molecules are formulated into LC mixtures, each mixture with its own individual properties. Currently available technical modes are VA, TN and IPS with its own right to exist due to their advantages for the intended use of the display. All modes use highly fluorinated alkyl and fluorinated aromatic substances having a high dipole moment which is relevant for the functionality of LC displays.
Out of these modes, only the IPS mode contains some LC substances with structural moieties in scope of the draft of the universal PFAS restriction in the EU and thus might be banned by end of 2025. The IPS displays possess unique properties and are used in mobile applications, computer monitors and automotive applications without alternative due to requirements regarding usability in a broad temperature range, high image quality and color gamut. IPS displays are used in medical device monitors due to high color gamut and stability from different viewing angles. This property reduces misdiagnosis in the respective medicinal application.
In the explanations presented below, we can show that we minimize the exposition towards the environment and workers during production. As the LC is encapsulated in the display, we can exclude exposition during the normal use of the display. At their end of life, electric and electronic devices are regulated by the WEEE directive and are collected. The display needs to be dismantled and is thermally recycled at temperatures which lead to PFAS decomposition to HF and CO2.
OLED as successor technology is not yet capable to fully substitute all applications. The reliability of LC displays is still unattained. Furthermore, the production capacity is not yet available to fully switch from IPS to OLED.
In this regard, we apply for a 5-year derogation for the use of PFAS LC substances in IPS displays. A derogation is necessary because we are currently working on alternatives to the essential LC substances which are in scope of the universal PFAS restriction. From our experience, this time is needed to find alternative substances usable in IPS LC mixtures to obtain the desired properties in the final display and the subsequent ramp up to mass production.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Electronics

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The manufacturing of the LC substances in Europe is carried out in Darmstadt in a poly production plant. The synthesis of LC intermediates takes place in closed and defined processes during production. Containment is achieved by technical design, i.e., process connections, cask covers, docking fittings. being capable of ensuring adherence to the respective exposure limits. Our customers are using the LC mixtures to manufacture display panels or final displays in controlled and closed clean room processes. Subsequently, displays are built in electric and electronic devices and the LC mixtures are enclosed in the final device. During the use of the LC mixture, we do not expect any significant release of PFAS into the environment because adhesive forces prevent LC mixtures from leaking even if the display brakes.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The display is treated thermally in industrial waste facilities. Organic substances and foils in the display provide enough energy to melt the glass of the display whereas the waste display is heated >1200 °C. This is above the heat of 600-1000 °C that has to be applied to destroy the PFAS compounds and the LC substance of the LC mixture will decompose. Thus, we do not expect significant emissions of PFAS at the end of life.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Flow Batteries Europe appreciates the chance to offer feedback on the proposed restriction of per- and poly-fluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and supports the stated objective to replace the use of fluorinated polymer processing aids, where possible. Flow battery companies, universities and R&D centres are actively looking into alternative solutions. As an example, organic flow batteries use PFAS-free membranes. However, currently market-available flow batteries based on other electrolytes still need fluoropolymers for specific performance requirements. Flow batteries utilise fluoropolymers which are not classified as hazardous under the EU Classification, Labelling and Packaging Regulation.

If the outright ban on PFAS is implemented, the flow battery sector would be deeply affected as a majority of flow batteries use fluoropolymers. These substances are notably present in certain flow batteries’ ionomer and ion exchange membranes. They are also used in several other components of a flow battery stack, as well as being widely used in accompanying subsystems including power electronics, pumps, seals and gaskets. Moving away from these substances can have substantial impacts on batteries’ stability and performance.

It is crucial to distinguish fluoropolymers from other PFASs compounds, recognising them as non-toxic and essential chemicals for the energy transition. It's important to acknowledge that not all PFAS chemicals are harmful, and non-hazardous ones should not face limitations in their applications. We call on the ECHA to exempt fluoropolymers from the restriction. Additionally, to assure a level playing field concerning the use of fluoropolymers, all energy storage technologies should be treated equally when it comes to exemptions.

The outright and immediate ban on fluoropolymers would have a significant socio-economic impact on the EU and would cause innovative technology companies to leave the European market or shift focus from flow battery technology. Without the technology advancement, the EU’s ambitious climate goals will not be achieved.
If the exemption of fluoropolymers cannot be achieved, a derogation period of 13.5 years would be vital for the flow battery sector allowing the research and long-term testing of alternatives, nonetheless the flow battery industry is not able to answer if a successful transition is possible. Several alternatives are being explored, but they are not largely developed on the market. It remains to be seen how effective they will be depending on the type of flow battery, particularly considering the different types of electrolytes available. It is not clear what efficiency flow batteries can achieve without PFASs and further efforts are needed, in line with the carbon footprint and performance provisions from the recent EU Batteries Regulation. Concurrently, we emphasise that the EU would need to prioritise the allocation of sufficient funding towards the R&D of PFAS-free flow batteries and the sustainability and risk profile of current technologies.

We stress that flow batteries are essential for energy storage due to their durability and safety. Their contribution to the REPowerEU and Green Deal objectives, notably by supporting the deployment of renewables, could be hampered by an inadequately implemented PFAS restriction.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Energy sector; Energy storage sector; Flow batteries

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Based on the information provided by the manufacturers of membranes (which is not limited to flow batteries but also includes the whole production of fuel cells and energy products), we estimate that the potential emitted materials are as follows: • Manufacture < 1,5% (and 3% in waste) • Service life < 0,1% (as PTFE does not outgas, erode or degrade during service life) • End-of-life < 1% emissions Components containing PFAS are used within closed systems, preventing the substances from escaping into the environment. In the end-of-life phase, flow battery components will be recycled, ensuring that the recycling company manages the PFAS-containing substances responsibly to prevent any release into the environment.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Recycling information is limited, especially given the remarkable durability of flow batteries. With their long service life, up-to-date data on their end-of-life is lacking. Nevertheless, it has been demonstrated that core PFASs in flow battery manufacturing such as polytetrafluoroethylene can be treated adequately through incineration and emissions are < 1%. * * Aleksandrov, K., Gehrmann, H. J., Hauser, M., Mätzing, H., Pigeon, D., Stapf, D., & Wexler, M. (2019). Waste incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate potential formation of per-and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) in flue gas. Chemosphere, 226, 898-906, available at: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0045653519306435.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: The PFAS-containing products are used in closed systems so the substances cannot escape to the environment. Following their operational life, flow batteries are taken back by the manufacturer or a recycling company that takes care of collecting the fluoropolymers contained in the batteries with precaution.

5. Proposed derogations: According to FBE internal consolidated data, approximately 1 m2 of a membrane is produced per 1 kW of a flow battery. 1 m2 of membrane contains around 20-40g PFSA ionomer and 1-5g ePTFE reinforcement by weight. This means that a 10MW flow battery would contain around 10,000 m2 of membrane, 30kg of PFSA and 3kg ePTFE. (In 1 GW (1,000 MW) of flow battery capacity, there would be approximately 3,000 kg (3 t) of PFSA and 300 kg (0,3 t) of ePTFE.) Based on our assessments, approximately 100 MW of flow batteries are presently in operation across Europe, including the UK, which means around 300 kg of PFSA and 30 kg ePTFE are currently present in the European market. The European Association for the Storage of Energy (EASE) estimates that 200 GW of energy storage must be deployed regionally by 2030 to meet the EU Green Deal’s ambitious renewable energy targets. Approximately half of this target should be long-duration energy storage (LDES) – 100 GW. Flow batteries represent around 3-5% of the LDES market today. Therefore, the estimated installation of flow batteries in Europe by 2030 could be between 3 GW and 5 GW, depending on their market share growth and technology adoption over the next few years. Consequently, if 3 GW of flow batteries are installed by 2030, the estimated tonnages of fluoropolymers used in membranes on the European market will be 9 tons. It's important to note that, even with the support of the EU, achieving these energy storage goals remains highly ambitious. One of the global flow batteries manufacturers indicated that their annual storage of FPM is 0,3t and of PVDF - 0,1t.

8. Other identified uses: One of the main distinctions between flow battery technologies is the type of electrolyte being used to store energy. The dozens of available electrolyte variants can be classified into two main categories, metal-based and organic. The metal-based category has achieved the highest level of advancement in the market. Among metal-based flow batteries, extensively studied chemistries encompass iron/chromium, zinc/iron, and zinc/bromide. It's important to highlight that vanadium flow batteries have emerged as the most prominently developed choice within the energy market. The progress of organic flow batteries is also unfolding; however, this technology is not available on the market yet. New chemistries are being discovered and early results are very promising. Research shows that organic flow batteries can be produced with non-corrosive and readily available material, such as iron sulphates, lignin or bio-polymers. These minimise environmental impacts and safely enable large-scale deployment. Although most organic flow batteries are PFAS-free, market available flow battery models do rely on fluoropolymers that are crucial for the technology performance and durability. The EU cannot afford to slow down the deployment of available flow batteries by introducing an immediate and outright ban on PFAS.  Our research amongst members of FBE and other organisations in the flow battery community indicates that all PFASs contained in flow batteries are part of the fluoropolymers category. Fluoropolymers are polymers made of fluorocarbons that have several carbon-fluorine connections and they should be distinguished from other PFASs due to their specific chemical properties and low environmental impact. These substances are considered to be non-hazardous and they are not classified as dangerous by the EU Classification, Labelling and Packaging (CLP) Regulation. As non-mobile molecules, fluoropolymers do not risk being circulated widely into the environment and their high molecular weight means that they will not be absorbed into the bloodstream. Due to their durability under extreme conditions as well as their electrical and thermal insulation, fluoropolymers can be found in most types of flow batteries, depending on the particular electrochemistry and the manufacturer. Their major use is in the cell membranes and the jointing materials to hold the membrane to the stack frame. The following PFASs can be found in flow batteries: The following PFASs are used in flow batteries:  • Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF): stable material used for the pump-magnetic coating and sensor connection because of its acid and oxidation-resistant properties • Fluoroelastomer (FKM, FPM): rubber employed for gaskets with resistance to high temperatures for thermal stability • Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE): strong resin used in gaskets to preserve the chemical of membranes • Perfluorosulfonic acid (PFSA): used in combination with PTFE to reinforce the membrane. These substances can be identified in membranes, pumps, sealings, and hoses. Fluoropolymers ensure the stability and safety of flow batteries, notably by preventing leaks and ensuring their thermal stability. These aspects are particularly important for the reliability and sustainability of a long-duration storage technology such as flow batteries, therefore also essential for the EU’s energy transition. It is very challenging to determine the exact number of organisations that would be affected by a PFAS ban in the flow battery sector. Nevertheless, there is currently a lack of alternatives to fluoropolymers for market-ready flow batteries. Flow battery companies, universities and R&D centres are actively looking into alternative solutions. As an example, some organic flow batteries are PFAS-free. However, the most durable and currently available flow batteries rely on parts with fluoropolymers (membranes, sealings, gaskets, and others). Effectively replacing fluoropolymers will require large investments that will not be possible in-house for many manufacturers and will fall onto suppliers. An outright and immediate PFAS restriction is thus likely to reduce the price competitiveness of flow battery manufacturers and their suppliers. In particular, we point out that vanadium flow battery, which is currently the most commercialised technology, is relying on parts containing PFASs. Batteries developed without fluoropolymers are generally less stable and durable. To develop alternatives to the flow battery technology relying on fluoropolymers, time and support would be necessary, nonetheless industry is not able to answer if a successful transition is possible. Flow batteries are known for their extended operational life, with some models surpassing 20 000 cycles and lasting up to 20 years. However, when utilising partially developed or tested membranes with alternative elastomeric sealings, the corrosion stability becomes limited. As a result, the durability of flow batteries is at risk. While certain substitutes for PFASs are under investigation, their effectiveness relies on the specific technical requirements of battery models and their membrane needs. For instance, ion-selective membranes offer an example where fluoropolymers may not be necessary to separate monovalent anions and cations. One promising alternative to the membranes used in organic flow batteries is sulfonated poly aryl ether ketone (SPAEK); nevertheless, these membranes are relatively new, and efforts to gather long-term test data are still ongoing. It is also known that these membranes are not compatible with vanadium flow batteries due to their incompatibility with vanadium oxide. Flow Battery Europe recommends exempting fluoropolymers from the restriction of PFAS substances, considering they are not environmentally harmful and non-toxic, and they play a critical role in energy storage technologies, as well as in the deployment of renewable energy. Additionally, to assure a level playing field concerning the use of fluoropolymers, all energy storage technologies should be treated equally when it comes to exemptions (i.e., lithium-ion, the hydrogen sector including electrolysers and fuel cells, and flow batteries). If fluoropolymers are not excluded from the ban, flow battery sector requires the 13.5 years derogation period, allowing the research and long-term testing of alternatives. Concurrently, we emphasise that the EU would need to prioritise the allocation of sufficient funding towards the R&D of PFAS-free flow batteries and the sustainability and risk profile of current technologies. FBE has identified significant socio-economic impacts caused by the potential ban on PFASs. One major repercussion would be the increased operational expenditure, as replacing PFAS-based sealings with alternative solutions is expected to incur additional costs, estimated to be in the range of at least 10%. These higher expenses could potentially trickle down to consumers, affecting energy storage system prices and overall market competitiveness. Moreover, the chemical industry and laboratory sectors, which are vital players in the production of flow battery components, would be directly impacted by the ban, leading to potential job losses and economic strain. The implications of such a ban extend beyond financial considerations. Flow batteries play a pivotal role in facilitating the smooth and rapid green transition towards renewable energy integration. As a long-duration energy storage technology, flow batteries help overcome the intermittent nature of renewable energy sources, providing a stable and reliable power supply during periods of low generation. A ban on fluoropolymers containing parts could threaten the production and widespread adoption of competitive technology, hindering the seamless incorporation of renewable energy into the grid. This, in turn, may delay the achievement of climate goals and the transition to a sustainable energy future, as it may be challenging to efficiently store excess renewable energy without robust and long-lasting capabilities. Therefore, as we pursue an environmentally conscious path, it becomes imperative to carefully balance the environmental concerns associated with PFAS chemicals while considering the potential socio-economic repercussions of a ban. The outright and immediate ban on fluoropolymers would have a significant socio-economic impact on the EU and would cause innovative technology companies to leave the European market or shift focus from flow battery technology. Without the technology advancement, the EU’s ambitious climate goals will not be achieved.
