Combined Comments:
General Comments: Fluorinated gases (FGs) are widely used in industry refrigerants. The GROB-WERKE GmbH & Co. KG as a manufacturer of machine tools and assembly machines depends on the use of very efficient and precise cooling units. Without the presence of a cooling systems the whole milling or assembly process cannot be executed in a proper way within the very low tolerances provided by the customer. The cooling systems used at the moment are mainly used for cooling specific parts of the machine tool or to temperate the cutting fluid in order to guarantee a stable and precise process. Therefore, mainly the refrigerants R143a or R513a are used.
These refrigerants stand out due to their unequalled performance characteristics. The main advantages are the high energy density which results in a lower amount of filling that is needed and the very low risk of inflammability. These refrigerants combine a high energy efficiency with a simple and safe use of the gas. To keep the influence on the global warming as small as possible the use of refrigerants is strictly regulated by the f-gas regulation today. This regulation shows a phase-out-scenario to reduce the GWP-value over the next upcoming years.
Apart from that we do not consider hydrocarbon (HC) and carbon dioxide (CO2) refrigerants to be viable alternatives. Systems based on HC refrigerants indicated as alternatives contain limited charge amounts of the refrigerant, which makes them less energy efficient; likewise, the higher pressures required for CO2 refrigerants reduce energy efficiency. For these reasons, HFO machine tool refrigerants should be excluded from the proposed restrictions on perfluoroalkyl substances and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS).

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The use of FGs for industrial refrigeration in machine tools (or more general: in the machinery and plant engineering industry) is partly covered by the Use sector “Refrigeration” within the Annex XV Restriction Report. The report mentions industrial refrigeration which refers to our use case.  FGs typically account for only a very small share of weight in a machine tool (few kilograms of refrigerant vs. a total weight of 15 … 40 tons for the machine tool). Nevertheless, the refrigeration are crucial for the proper, safe, and efficient operation of a machine tool. We have therefore included corresponding information under # 6.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Manufacture phase: As a machine tool manufacturer, we are not manufacturing refrigeration’s, but are sourcing these as purchased parts. Therefore, we do not have any detailed information about the emissions related to the manufacture of FGs. Use phase: The FGs used in the refrigerant circuit of our machine tool chillers are not consumable material. The cooling circuit is a closed system so that no consume of refrigerant containing FG is expected. Only in case of an unexpected leakage the refrigerant can escape into the environment. The presence of different sensors detects if the amount of filling in the refrigeration is decreasing. So the escape of refrigeration can be detected and stopped before the whole amount of filling escaped to the environment. During the life phase the refrigeration has to be checked at least once a year by a specialist. Due to the ongoing maintenance the risk of a leakage can be decreased drastically. End-of-life: Machine tools are no consumer products, that are simply “thrown away” – but high-quality and durable means of industrial production, which are disposed of / recycled by specialized companies under strict environmental regulations at the end of their lifetime. It can therefore be assumed that no FGs are released into the environment when a machine tool has reached its end of life.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The operator of a refrigeration systems that contains FG gases has to ensure the recovery of the refrigerant at the end of-life phase. So, it is guaranteed that no FG are emitted to the environment. The refrigerant is then either recycled or reprocessed in order to be used for further applications. The restrictions concerning the disposal of refrigerant is contained in the EN378:2016. The refrigerant is either recycled and reprocessed for further use in refrigerant applications or thermally treated. A thermal treatment is necessary if the refrigerant gas consists of different gas types. In this case the refrigerant is split up into its components and used for chemical processes.

5. Proposed derogations: The derogations proposed in table 9 of the Annex XV contain no useable exception for our application. The derogation in the refrigerant sector foresees the further use of PGs for low temperature applications, laboratory test and measurement equipment as well as refrigerated centrifuges. These use cases are not relevant for the machine tool sector that’s why we can not estimate the tonnage of PFAS used per year and the resulting emissions emitted to the environment

6. Missing uses: a & b) As a machine tool manufacturer, we depend on high-performance refrigerant systems in order to guarantee a specific temperature for most of the machine tool components. Only with well-tempered components (e.g. drives, motorized spindle, etc.) the milling process can be executed within the very low tolerances. Refrigerants containing FGs like R134a or R513a are essential because of their high energy efficiency combined with a low risk of flammability. An overview of cooling systems, that are typically applied in machine tools, is given below: • Cooling of machine components (drives, motorized spindle, etc.) • Cooling of the cutting fluid   We do not have specific information about the annual tonnage of FGs used in machine tools. But we can provide an estimation of our annual usage of refrigerant:  Around 650 active chiller are needed for our machine tools every year. This number includes the chillers for the cooling of the machine components and the coolant. The type of chillers differs according to the required cooling capacity and the voltages of the different countries. The average amount of the refrigerant (mainly R134a) for one chiller is 1,2 kg. In total an amount of 780 kg of refrigerant needed for the first filling of the chillers.  c) The German machine tool industry comprises several hundred companies with over 60,000 employees in total. Despite being a rather small sector of industry, its macroeconomic importance must not be underestimated, because it delivers production technology for all sectors of industry.  d - g) According to the F-Gas regulation and the REACH regulation the number alternative refrigerants for our application is very low. Due to these regulations only, natural refrigerants (like propane or CO2) could be used for further projects.   However, all these alternative materials have in common that they do not meet the unique performance characteristics of refrigerants containing FG: • The risk of burning increases drastically with natural refrigerants • Lower energy efficiency of natural refrigerants • Additional sensors / actors are mandatory to prevent the system from burning  Apart from the disadvantages mentioned above the ban from refrigerant containing would cause big problems regarding the maintenance of existing refrigeration units. In case of a damage or leakage in an existing unit the change to refrigerant without FGs might cause problems. So most of the components that are used in the moment for the refrigerants like R134a or R513a are may not fully applicable for natural refrigeration gases. So either some of the components in an existing units have to be changed or in the worst case the hole unit has to be replaced. The consequences regarding the effort and the costs for the maintenance for existing units containing FGs would be severe. Beside the high material and work costs caused by the replacement of existing chiller units it would cause an higher amount of waste. The components of chiller that can not be used in the future due to the REACH regulation have to be recycled. The energy needed for the recycling proves has an negative influence on the environment.  Furthermore, it is important to understand that these risks do not only affect the machine tool industry itself but a much broader scope of industries. Machine tools are a means of production with a widespread use in the European key sectors of industry, such as automotive, aerospace, defence, renewable energies or medical engineering. It must be emphasized in particular that machine tools are crucial for the production of many “green” technologies required for the European Green Deal, such as windmills or heat pumps.  Considering all these aspects, we request the following from the competent authorities: • Awareness of the disadvantages caused by the use of naturals refrigerants o Lower energy efficiency  o Higher risk of flammability o Waste caused by existing chiller units • Reconsideration the use of FGs for industrial applications with a low amount of gas filling The proposed rejection of natural gases does not mean that the impact of refrigerants to the environment should be ignored. In contrast it is very important to limit the or ban the used refrigerants with high GWP-values. Therefore, the F-gas regulation foresees the phase out of the these gases already in these days.

General Comments: Fluorine compounds having both a hydrofluoroether group and a reactive group have been used extensively as antifouling agents for hard coating agents.

A hard coating agent is a coating agent for the purpose of preventing scratches on various surfaces. After coating, this coating agent is cured by UV irradiation to form a film.

A fluorine compound having both a hydrofluoroether group and a reactive group is used by being added to the hard coating agent.

After coating, the hard coating agent to which this fluorine compound is added exhibits both the function of preventing stains such as fingerprints, water stains and adhesives, and the function of low friction.

Oil repellency and a low coefficient of friction are required to prevent fingerprints and smudges. There is no substitute substance because there is no oil-repellent substance other than fluorine-based compounds in the world.
Also, the fluorine compound has an optically low refractive index.
Reflected light can be reduced by coating optical parts such as lenses and transparent films with a hard coating agent containing a fluorine-based compound to a thickness of about 0.1 μm. Reducing reflected light results in a 3-5% improvement in transmitted light transmittance. Other various resins have a high refractive index and cannot achieve such a reflected light reduction rate.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Additives for imparting fingerprint adhesion for hard coats, Low refractive index additive for hard coat, Anti fouling Additives

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: There are no PFAS emissions during the manufacturing and use stages. 100% emissions at disposal stage. The service life is the same as the equipment used.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: This product is often used in plastics at the disposal stage. If the target is incinerated, it will be decomposed into HF

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Fluorine has played a major role in the industrial development of the twentieth century and can be seen as the key to sustainable chemistry, minimizing the negative environmental impacts of chemical processing and manufacturing and providing economically competitive technologies. In fact, fluorine and fluorinated compounds are essential for our daily lives and for high technology. The following consultation is divided into three main parts, based on the usefulness of the products in different fields and technologies (GIANT 100193, preprint, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.giant.2023.100193).

1. Fluorine and its use to prepare novel inorganic materials
Elemental fluorine is a key element in the preparation of electricity for nuclear power plants. Among other applications such as the preparation of NF3 (etching agent in microelectronics), WF6 (CVD deposition), ClF3 (microelectronics, diffusion barrier etching, ...), mixtures of F2 and N2 (waterproofing of gasoline tanks), one of the main uses of fluorine is linked to the manufacture of uranium hexafluoride UF6, which enables the isotopic enrichment of natural uranium. Around 80% of the world's F2 production is devoted to the synthesis of this gaseous fluoride compound UF6 (J. Fluorine Chem. 2007, 128, 285). Molecular fluorine (F2) production has been developed in many countries around the world, reaching a total capacity of 25,000 tons per year (J. Fluorine Chem. 2021, 244, 109746). F2 gas is produced industrially by electrolysis of molten KF-2 HF salt at 85 to 100 °C on a non-graphitized carbon anode (Orano in France). It should be remembered that the production of electricity by nuclear power plants does not contribute to the emission of pollutants such as sulfur dioxide (SO2), nitrogen oxides (NOx) and carbon dioxide (CO2), all of which contribute to the greenhouse effect. This type of energy production avoids CO2 emissions in France. For nuclear power, only 4 grams of CO2 equivalent is produced per kWh. By way of comparison, according to the French Agency for Ecological transition’s carbon database, the average equivalent CO2 per kWh produced in France is 418 grams (730 g with fuel oil, 1060 g with coal, 6 g for hydraulics, 15 g for offshore wind, 14 g for onshore wind, 45 g for geothermal and even 43 g for photovoltaic panels). Since 1970, nuclear power has prevented the release of more than 60 Gt of CO2 worldwide, equivalent to five years of emissions of CO2 from the electricity sector (Société Française d'Energie Nucléaire – Octobre 2018).

Friction and wear are the main causes of the decrease in performances and durability of mechanical systems. Friction and wear losses represent between 3.5 and 4% of the Gross domestic product (GDP), and in a modern automobile more than 25% of the motor power is lost in friction (Jean Frêne et Hamid Zaïdi, Introduction à la tribologie, Techniques de l’Ingénieur, TRI100 V1, 2011 up-dated in 2018). Metal parts manufacturing techniques must meet growing economic market demands, such as improved material durability, lower maintenance costs and reduced energy consumption. Consequently, the reduction of friction and wear is essential and represents a major economic challenge. When fluorine atoms are covalently intercalated in a carbonaceous (nano)material, and whatever the level of fluorination (F/C atomic ratio), nanocarbons exhibit good tribological properties and can be excellent precursors of the tribo-active phase in lubrication. Hence, the incorporation of fluorine in metal containing parts will be a decisive beneficial factor in the sustainability of the automobile industry (J. Fluorine Chem. 2012, 144, 10-16).

Fluorinated materials also play, and will continue to play, an important role in energy conversion and electrochemical storage technologies. Fluorinated (nano)carbons offer the highest energy density as cathodes in primary lithium batteries and are used commercially for medical and military applications. The enhanced stability of fluorine-based inorganic or organic compounds makes them the electrolyte salts of choice in widespread commercial Li-ion batteries (LiPF6, LiTFSI, LiFSI, etc...). Fluorosalt Na3V2(PO4)2F3, which offers a high reversible capacity (125 mAh.g-1) at 4.2 V combined with high cyclability (more than 500), is today considered one of the reference materials for Na-ion batteries about to be commercialized (T. Broux et al, High-Rate Performance for Carbon-Coated Na3V2(PO4)2F3 in Na-Ion Batteries, Small Methods 2019, 3, 1800215). Conceptually like Li-ion batteries, these new generation batteries, using sodium as a more sustainable and economic alternative to lithium, will be based on the fluorinated electrolyte salt, NaPF6.
Research has focused on the development of anode and cathode materials operating at relatively high potential to avoid problems of electrolyte reduction and oxidation, respectively. Electrolyte instability leads to secondary reactions and, subsequently, to the formation of a solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) on the surface of the negative electrode. The creation of a SEI consumes Li+ ions and increases the impedance of the battery, but at the same time, the formation of a stable, Li+-conducting, and electronically insulating SEI is essential to guarantee high coulombic efficiency, good lifetime and safety (Electrochim. Acta 1999, 44, 2879-2888). In the late 90s, fluorine was first considered as a potential electrode protection agent against SEI formation on graphite material. Subsequently, studies were carried out on LTO (Spinel Li4Ti5O12) fluorination using F2 gas or by solid-state reaction with NH4F (Applied Surface Science 2020, 527, 146834; J. Fluorine Chem. 2009, 130, 810-815; ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces 2017, 9, 17145-17154). Fluorination of the active material leads to reduced reactivity with the electrolyte, so the products of electrolyte degradation are deposited in smaller quantities on the fluorinated electrode surface, thus prolonging the lifetime and increasing the performances of the battery.

Fluorinated inorganic materials (crystals and glasses) offer undeniable advantages for many optical applications. They indeed display low phonon energy and high rare-earth solubility, especially compared with silica. The low phonon energy guarantees IR transparency down to 8-10 µm, long luminescence lifetime and low non-radiative transition probabilities for rare-earth ions (Chem. Rev. 2002, 102, 2461-2476). Efficient lasers with fibers or single crystals have been demonstrated at wavelengths not available in oxide, particularly in the near-IR and mid-IR. Mid-IR lasers are used for gas detection and laser surgery (Chinese Optics Letters 2021, 19-9, 091407). Passive optical applications of fluorinated glass fibers include astronomical and broadband interferometry for telescopes (Science 2006, 311, 194).

The advantages of covalent grafting of fluorine atoms onto carbon materials are also evident in the design of new electrocatalysts for low-temperature fuel cells. Polarity and surface tension, changes in pore size distribution, the effect of codoping with fluorine, as well as bond formation caused by fluorination can all be tailored. A recent review (Adv. Energy Mat. 2023, 13, 2657-2669) summarizes recent advances in the development of various fluorinated electrocatalysts for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in fuel cells, including noble and non-noble metal catalysts, where fluorination plays a key role in tuning the hydrophobicity/hydrophilicity property of the catalyst layers and affects the activity and stability/durability/lifetime of the catalysts. The improvement of fluorination on the performance of the platinum group metal (PGM) catalyst and the PGM-based electrocatalyst is discussed.

Upconversion spectroscopy coupled with rare earth nanoﬂuoride technology continues to bring new discoveries not only for biology, diagnostics and therapy, but also for energy harnessing applications. Upconversion processes in rare earth ﬂuoride nanosystems can also be used for other societal goals such as reducing air and water pollution (Ledoux, G., Joubert, M.F. Mishra, S., Upconversion Phenomena in Nanofluorides, Photonic and Electronic Properties of Fluoride Materials, Progress in Fluorine Science Series,Elsevier 2016 Pages 35-63).

Regarding synthetic routes for inorganic nanoﬂuorides used in photonic and electronic applications, coprecipitation from aqueous solutions clearly emerges as one of the most promising methods to obtain various ﬂuoride materials, namely NaREF4 (RE=rare earth), for industrial use as upconversion luminophores, optical ceramics, including their precursors (Elaboration of nanofluorides and ceramics for optical and laser applications. P.P. Fedorov, S.V Kuznetsov, V.V. Osiko, Photonic and Electronic Properties of Fluoride Materials, Progress in Fluorine Science Series, Elsevier; 2016; Pages 7-31).
Two members of the fluoroborate family, namely potassium beryllium fluoroborate KBe2BO3F2 (KBBF) and rubidium beryllium fluoroborate RbBe2BO3F2, are today the only crystals capable of producing deep-UV (DUV) harmonic generation beyond 200 nm using a simple phase-matching second harmonic generation (SHG) method. The first sixth harmonic generation at 177.3 nm is obtained from a Nd-based laser using a KBBF-PCD (prism-coupled device) with optical contact. This device is successfully used in many state-of-the-art instruments, such as laser photoemission spectrographs with very high energy resolution and the DUV laser photoemission electron microscope. The combination of KBBF crystal and PCD technique promotes DUV laser applications and, to some extent, opens the door to a new field of DUV laser technology (Appl. Phys. Lett. 1996, 68, 2930-2932).

In light-emitting diode (LCD) technology, new advances are linked to the use of fluorinated molecules, such as fast switching modes - like the blue mode - which are being developed to facilitate high-frequency drive, which is a prerequisite for 3D LCD and 8-4K ultra-high-resolution TV. Beyond displays, fluorinated liquid crystals have recently found applications in microwave switching and "smart windows" (P. Kirsch, Fluorinated Nematic Liquid crystals, Chapter 8, Photonic and Electronic Properties of Fluoride Materials, Progress in Fluorine Science Series, Elsevier 2016 Pages 159-176).


2. Fluorinated compounds used in medicinal and agrochemical applications
Fluorinated organic molecules often lead to unrivalled bioactivities compared to their non-fluorinated analogues. Fluorination of bioactive compounds has emerged as a striking trend in drug discovery research in medicinal chemistry. A literature review revealed that the introduction of fluorine into engineered scaffolds led to improved efficacy following the impressive clinical effect of fluorinated corticosteroids and fluoroquinolones between the 1950s and 1980s. Today, fluorinated derivatives are used to treat a wide range of diseases, including viral infections, various types of cancer, multiple sclerosis, cardiovascular disease, migraine, and inflammatory diseases such as vasculitis. Another trend in approved compounds is the increased proportion of chiral fluorinated drugs. The potential of fluoropharmaceuticals should increase in the future, due to their hydrophobic and lipophilic characteristics, improved membrane permeability, its influence on pharmacokinetic properties and the compound's enhanced therapeutic effect (Eur. J. Med. Chem. 2023, 260, 115758).
Consequently, 16% of agrochemicals (iScience 2020, 23, 101467-101467) and 18% of pharmaceuticals (ACS Omega 2020, 5, 10633-10640) on the world market contain at least one fluorine atom. Regarding the drugs, this percentage is continuously increasing. In a context where biological entities are taking prevalence over small organic molecules in pharmaceuticals, fluorinated organic compounds remain, furthermore, highly prized in therapeutic innovation. They are as numerous as the biologics; the latter being often described as rising stars.

Thanks to the 18F isotope, fluorinated molecules can be used in medical imaging via PET (positron emission tomography) technology (Chem. Rev. 2008, 108, 1501; Eur. J. Med. Chem. 2020, 187, 111979).
PET is a powerful imaging technique that uses 18F-labeled molecules to obtain quantitative information on metabolic processes, enabling early diagnosis of diseases such as, for example, cancer or neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, ...) (Cancer Lett. 2017, 387, 25; Cancer 2014, 120, 3433; Chem. Soc. Rev. 2014, 43, 6683; Semin. Nucl. Med. 2021, 51, 196).
These 18F-labeled probes can only contain a single fluorine atom and are therefore not yet covered by this regulation. Nevertheless, the precursors of these compounds, required for advanced labelling, often feature a perfluorinated group, for example a triflate group (CF3SO3), which must be replaced by an 18F atom. The best illustration is [18F]FDG, the 18F tracer most widely used in medical diagnostics for cancer detection. It is prepared by substitution of a triflate group on triflate-mannose by an 18F atom to produce the expected PET probe (Int. J. Radial. Appl. Instrum. Part A 1988, 39, 699).
Moreover, in recent years, thanks to active scientific research in fluorine chemistry, new 18F probes, carrying an [18F]CF3 group, have been developed to extend the field of medical PET imaging (Molecules 2021, 26, 6478; Nat. Rev. Methods Primers 2021, 1, 47]. Examples include octreotide [Trp(2-[18F]CF3)] for imaging acromegaly and gigantism [J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2020, 142, 1180] and [18F]TFMISO for imaging hypoxic tumors [Bioorg. Med. Chem.2011, 19, 2287).

MRI is also a well-known medical imaging technique, widely used for a variety of diagnostic purposes. This method is based on the observation of the 1H atom. To increase sensitivity, MRI may require the use of metallic contrast agents in relatively high concentrations, which can lead to toxicity problems.
To overcome these problems, the use of 19F MRI appears to be a valuable complementary alternative. This requires the use of 19F molecular probes. One of the main advantages of this approach is that only trace amounts of 19F are present in the human body, enabling very good contrast to be obtained. However, to achieve good sensitivity with a shorter acquisition time using only low doses of fluorinated tracers, highly fluorinated probes are required (Chem. Rev. 2015, 115, 1106; Chem. Eur. J. 2022, 28, e202102556]. One example is PERFECTA®, a highly fluorinated molecular probe (C21H8F36O4) used in various applications for highly sensitive in vivo 19F MRI [J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2014, 136, 8524; Nanoscale, 2021, 13, 2373).

3. Fluoropolymers
Fluorinated organic materials are used in a wide range of high-tech applications (e.g. in the energy, electronics, aerospace, automotive and biomedical sectors) (Macromol. Chem. Phys. 2020, 221, 1900573). These specialized niche polymers have high molar masses (up to several million g.mol-1 (Chem. Rev. 2019, 110, 1763-1805)) and therefore do not cross the cell membrane, are non-toxic, non-bioaccumulative and insoluble in water (and therefore non-mobile). In fact, they stand in stark contrast to low-molar-weight PFAs. What's more, these fluoropolymers meet the criteria for polymers of low concern (PLCs) (Integr. Envron. Assess. Managem. 2023, 19, 326-354; J. Biomed. Mater. Res. Part B 2022, 110, 302−320). In addition, fluoropolymers have outstanding properties and are stable thermally, chemically and against UV and aging (Ameduri, B.; Fomin, S.; Progress in Fluorine Science, Volume 2: Fascinating Fluoropolymers and Applications, Elsevier, Oxford, 2020). Thus, they meet the criteria for polymers of low concern (Integr. Envron. Assess. Managem., 2023, 19, 326-54) and are unlikely to face any of the hazardous issues mentioned above. In terms of their usefulness, several key examples can be highlighted:
i) The catastrophic accident of the space shuttle Challenger on January 28th, 1986 led to the modification of seals and gaskets, now made of fluorinated elastomers.
ii) Hundreds of kilometers of PTFE-coated cables per aircraft to ensure fireproofing.
iii) Millions of km of submarine cables (Morel, C.; Les câbles sous-marins : Enjeux et Perspectives du XXIe siècle ; 2023, CNRS Editions, Paris), (many of which are graded-index perfluoropolymer optical fibers - including cores and claddings (Koike, Y. ; Fundamentals of plastics optical fibers ; pp.119-137, Wiley VCH, 2015).
iv) The energy transition requires fluoropolymers:
- separators and cathode binders for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), resistant to low and high voltages in LIB charging and discharging (Goldbach, J. T. et al. Commercial Synthesis and Applications of PVDF, Ameduri & Sawada, eds, in Fluoropolymers; chapter 6, pp; 127-157; RSC, 2017).
- Fuel cell vehicles are equipped with Perfluorosulfonic acid (PFSA) membranes, which need to be durable (7000 h requirement) and stable in concentrated acidic media (Y. Tanaka, Development of the Mirai Fuel Cell vehicle; In Hydrogen Energy Engineering, A Japanese Perspective in K. Sasaki, H.W. Li, A. Hayashi, J. Yamabe, T. Ogura, S.M. Lyth, Eds; chapter 34; pp 461-476, 2016, Springer, Tokyo) is the essential component for fuel cell vehicles. The Chemours Company is on the way to start a new 200 million $-manufacture of such PFSA in France. In fact, hydrocarbon alternatives to these membranes suffer from many problems, including poor conductivity and lower performance.
- Backsheets for photovoltaics, which are highly UV resistant and durable.
- Electroactive ferro- or piezoelectric polymers (Nature Comm. 2021, 12, 675; Science 2023, 380, 1-12).
v) Specific durable and efficient membranes for seawater purification (Scientific Report 2023, 13, 8076).
vi) Internet of things and smart technologies (such as artificial intelligence, fast data transmission with higher bandwidth and lower latency (Adv. Eng. Mater. 2018, 20, 1700743), etc.....
vii) Durable paints and coatings, some with a 30-year guarantee without VOC emission (Fluorinated Specialty Chemicals - Fluorinated Copolymers for Paints and Perfluoropolyethers for Coatings, T. Hoshino, T. ; Morizawa, T., In Ameduri, B.; Sawada, H., eds. Fluoropolymers; Vol. 2; chapter 5, RSC, 2017).

In addition, the last five years have seen profound changes and significant improvements in the manufacture of FPs (Fluoropolymers) in more environmentally friendly processes by many companies, following three main strategies:
i) The use of non-fluorinated polymerization aids (or surfactants) in aqueous polymerization processes.
ii) The effective elimination of gas and effluent emissions; iii) the announcement of their actions in the media and to the scientific community (ITRC Intern. Chem. Regul. Law Rev. 2023, 6, 18-28).

The tiny production volume of FPs (330,000 tonnes in 2021) compared with the huge volume of plastics/polymers (more than 460 million tonnes in the same year) is less likely to release microplastics than commodity polymers. In addition, increasing fluoropolymer (FP) recycling strategies (Chem Soc Rev. 2023, 52, 4208-4247) are currently being applied by FP manufacturers such as Dyneon for PTFE, FEP and PFA (3M Dyneon, Fluoropolymers Up-Cycling brochure, 2018; Invertec, Pilot project: Recycling of fluoropolymers (PTFE), https://www.invertec-ev.de/en/projects/environmental-care/ptfe-recycling/, (accessed November 2022)), Arkema and Solvay for PVDF.


4. Can we expect alternatives to F-compounds?
Possible alternatives should guarantee safety, efficiency, and performance. Presently, in the three above domains, no alternatives can be found.
The unique properties of fluorine atoms make possible the reduction of the quantities of drugs prescribed to a patient and limit side effects. For the time being, no alternative can be offered to treat many pathologies.

As mentioned above, aerospace seals (made of poly(thioether)) unfortunately failed in 1986. What other materials can maintain their high performance at low and high temperatures, under aggressive conditions (resistance to oils, kerosene and fluids of aerospace (e.g., Skydrol®) for automotive and aerospace industries may compete with FPs (Bouharras, F.; Lopez, G.; Raihane, M.; Ameduri, B.; in Gnanou, Y.; Matyjaszewski, K.; Hadjichristidis, N.; Muthukumar, M., eds.; Macromolecular Engineering: From Precise Synthesis to Macroscopic Materials and Applications, Wiley-VCH GmbH, 2022, chapt. 26, pp.1371-1402), or like car tanks or pipes for extracting petrol from oil wells)? To date, no alternative has been found. Similarly, no substitutes for the durable, mechanically resistant membranes used in fuel cells have been proposed.

On the energy production side, uranium hexafluoride UF6 is the only gaseous species of uranium at low temperature (sublimation temperature of 65°C). Moreover, because fluorine element has only one stable isotope 19F, only 235U19F6 and 238U19F6 are formed; the difference in their molecular weights allows their separation by centrifugation or diffusion processes for enrichment purpose. With the U-based actual technology for nuclear reactors, nuclear electricity cannot be produced without fluorine.

On the energy storage side, there is no alternative to LiPF6 in Li-ion batteries and the same can be applied with the future sodium-ion batteries with NaPF6. As for cathode binder, PVDF is still the unique stable material able to withstand many electrochemical cycles.

What about the fate of the economy with or without F compounds and the societal impact? Many of fluorinated drugs will be at least indirectly impacted in the proposed ban, yet they are generally left out when it comes to regulating fluorinated compounds (Org. Process Res. Dev. 2023, 27, 1421-1421). Banning their use without alternatives, as proposed by the EU, would put an end to the production and development of many medicines. Another perverse effect will be the relocation of production to areas of the world less constrained by regulation. This will lead to higher costs, risks of supply disruptions and additional dependence for Europe. However, the Covid19 period clearly demonstrated the importance of independent production on European territory. These risks for human health are not only limited to fluorinated medicines. Many syntheses of non-fluorinated molecules (small organic ones, peptides, small proteins) use fluorinated intermediates or reagents. There are many cases where the use of fluorine-containing compounds is difficult or impossible to replace (Org. Process Res. Dev. 2023, 27, 1422-1426). In any case, if alternatives can be found, it will take a long time. For this long period of academic research, researchers must have all the resources they need for their studies, starting with all the existing fluorinated reagents and intermediates.

The EU proposal will ban extensively fluorinated groups. However, close examination shows that, although fluorination is often used to reduce susceptibility to degradation (metabolic or environmental) at a specific site in the molecule, a fluorinated group may also behave as a degradation site itself, or facilitate degradation elsewhere in the structure, depending on its chemical environment and the conditions to which it is subjected. The general idea that polyfluoroalkyls will be terminal residues in the degradation of polyfluoroalkyl-substituted compounds assumes erroneously that cleavage of the C-F bond is an unlikely event under biologically relevant conditions. Polyfluoroalkyl-substituted compounds can be degraded under a variety of conditions (Leroux, F.; Pazenok, S.; Bernier, D.; Donnard, M.; Hanquet, G.; Panossian, A.; in Marek, I; Gouverneur, V.; Gandelmann, M., eds.; The Chemistry of Functional Groups (founded by S. Patai), The Chemistry of Organofluorine Compounds, Wiley-VCH GmbH, Chichester, 2022; DOI: 10.1002/9780470682531.pat1013.

In terms of the added value of fluorochemicals, markets have been estimated at billions of euros, and the pharmaceutical industry in the EU employs over 860,000 people.

As an example, regarding the fuel cell membranes: As no substitutes are available today, an imprudent general ban on PFAs would have a direct and significant impact on the hydrogen industry and jeopardize the achievement of the objectives of the EU hydrogen strategy, REPowerEU and decarbonization. A hasty ban on PFAs without granting an exemption for hydrogen applications would have destructive effects on the industry's €30 billion investment over a decade (including electrolyzers and fuel cells alone). Such a ban would also jeopardize up to 200,000 direct jobs and over 260,000 indirect jobs within 10 years in a market with a potential value of 820 billion euros, employing 5.4 million people by mid-century (Hydrogen Europe Position Paper on PFAS; The importance of fluoropolymers across the hydrogen value chain, and impacts of the proposed PFAS restriction for the hydrogen sector, 2023).


5. Conclusion
All fluorinated products have recently come under strong pressure from regulators, the press and the media (Ameduri, B.: Hori, H. ; Proceedings of the Internat Symposium in Fluorine chemistry, Invited talk, Quebec, Canada 23-28 July, 2023). Education is needed to raise awareness of the usefulness of these specific organic products and plastics. The main concerns related to the industrial production of FPs have been addressed. These high value-added polymers have exceptional properties, meet PLC criteria, are essential to our daily lives and have no alternatives. In addition, they are non-soluble, non-toxic, non-bioaccumulative and cannot cross the cell membrane of humans and mammals, demonstrating that they are different from conventional PFAs and are irreplaceable materials. Restricting these specialized polymers would be a real loss for the global economy, safety and security, with increased dependence and importations from China.

The current pivotal importance of fluorinated compounds and the absence of any viable replacements to date should refrain any hasty or excessive action towards their ban. Certain PFAs are indeed the source of legitimate concern and alternatives should be developed. Don't cut off the whole leg if you have a blister on your foot. Education is required to raise awareness of the usefulness of fluorine, but also of the need for its smart and responsible use.

Content: Information on alternatives Information on benefits Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Fluorine-free alternatives are available and in limited use for decorative hexavalent chrome plating. The functionality to minimize fumes and exposure is inferior compared to PFAS-based surfactants as the alternatives rely on creating a foam blanket. PFAS-based surfactants minimize fumes and exposure by reducing the diameter of gas bubbles formed during the electrolysis. Smaller size gas bubbles do not create fumes when bursting at the surface of the solution. Additionally, some PFAS-based chrome surfactants may form foam, but foam-free products are preferred as the foam is a safety concern for many installations being explosive as containing hydrogen and oxygen.
Fluorine-free alternatives decompose rather rapidly in hexavalent chrome solution. The higher the solution temperature is, the faster the breakdown takes place. In decorative hexavalent chrome solution continuous dosing, including idle times is required unlike with PFAS-based, stable surfactants. Undesired breakdown products are formed that partly can be tolerated due to high solution drag out rates typical in decorative chrome plating compared to much lower drag out in hexavalent hard chrome plating.
The strong oxidizing character of hexavalent chrome solutions results in formation of Sulfate, Phosphate and Nitrate from Sulfur, Phosphor or Nitrogen as elements contained in Fluorine-free alternatives. The maximum tolerance for Phosphate and Nitrate is 50 ppm, Sulfate is part of the catalyst system used in the hard chrome plating process. Access amounts of Sulfate require removement by precipitation as Barium-sulfate. This treatment results in undesired sludge formation and is not feasible for certain types of plating equipment. Carbon as an element in fluorine-free alternatives is mostly oxidized to volatile CO2 while forming undesired trivalent chrome as metal impurity, reducing conductivity of the process solution. Methods exists to control trivalent chrome concentration in the process solution, increasing complexity of the operation but feasible.
Short chain organic substances can form Acetate when oxidized, a rather stable breakdown product with a maximum tolerance of 50 ppm in the process solution. Longer chain organic substances typically result in formation of oily breakdown products before being further oxidized. Oily breakdown products can cause defects on the surface of the component to be plated.
Fluorine-free alternatives were subject to unsuccessful research for hexavalent hard chrome plating for several decades. Such research continues with low probability of success. As previously stated, foam is a poor method for emission control and unsuitable in hard chrome application as much higher current per surface area of the tank is applied. Foam-free zones form around the areas where large amounts of gas are developed (anodes and plated part) and fumes are created. The breakdown rate of fluorine-free alternatives is a multiple of the breakdown rate in decorative application due to the higher temperature with at least 55° compared to typically 40°C in decorative application. Under industrial conditions fluorine-free alternatives cause unsuitable levels of breakdown products, requiring regular solution replacement. With 500 g/L chromic acid replenishment per year and without solution drag out, a monthly solution replacement must be expected, compared to a typical solution lifetime bigger than 5 years using PFAS-based emission control.
Advertisement on fluorine-free alternatives for hard chrome application ignores the typical industrial use conditions and is considered misleading. We have no knowledge of any successful industrial use since advertisement started several years ago.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: PFAS-based surfactants for functional (hard) chrome plating are mentioned under E.2.4. Metal plating and manufacture of metal products in the ECHA ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT - PROPOSAL FOR A RESTRICTION.

Content: Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Fluoroelastomer(fluorine rubber), fluoroplastic(fluorine resin), fluorinated grease/oil should be exempted from the regulations because there is no evidence of harm. Most fluoroelastomer(fluorine rubber) also contains bisphenol AF, a type of PFAS. The draft regulations for bisphenol AF are published in "ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT - BPA and bisphenols of similar concern for the environment". It can be said that the proposed regulations set an upper limit for the release into the environment and the environmental impact has been sufficiently examined. The threshold for bisphenol AF in moldings should follow the values in this proposed regulation.

Six months is not enough public consultation. Fluoroelastomer(fluorine rubber), fluoroplastic(fluorine resin), fluorinated grease/oil are used in various parts of industrial products and perform as essential parts. Public consultation covering all of these takes more than 12 months.

A transition period of 18 months is too short. Fluoroelastomer(fluorine rubber), fluoroplastic(fluorine resin), fluorinated grease/oil are used in various parts of industrial products and perform as essential parts. A short transition period not only disrupts the market, but can also cause accidents that affect the environment and human life because the necessary products are not available. A transition period of 36 months or more is probably necessary.

This regulation conflicts with the CE Principles and the Green Deal goals because it prevents the repair and inspection of vehicles already on the market. Fluoroelastomer(fluorine rubber), fluoroplastic(fluorine resin), fluorinated grease/oil contribute to the safety of vehicles and contribute to the decarbonization and decontamination of industries. Therefore, Fluoroelastomer(fluorine rubber), fluoroplastic(fluorine resin), fluorinated grease/oil and greases should be exempted with Time-unlimited.

Instead of targeting more than 10,000 PFAS from the start, as in the German-proposed "ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT - BPA and bisphenols of similar concern for the environment" for which public consultations are currently being conducted, a realistic approach would be to create a list of substances or groups of substances with unacceptable risks, and then set conditions for adding them to the list.
PFAS can be divided into several “subgroups”, so for example, “PFCA” such as PFOA and “PFSA” such as PFOS are PFAS with unacceptable risks to human health and the environment. Because of the evidence, we include these two subgroups in the first list and add them to the list with the condition that they are not only "extremely persistent", but also comply with the CLP regulations for human health and environmental hazards. should add categories in the harmonized classification (eg reproductive toxicity, endocrine disrupting, etc.).

General Comments: Fluoroelastomers (FKM) are well known for their resistance to high temperatures (up to 250 °C) as well as a broad resistance to various chemicals. This includes e.g. engine or gearbox oils that contain aggressive additives for high performance applications in use sectors like transportation, petroleum and mining or medical devices.
Fluoroelastomers are also resistant to acids and organic solvents, which makes them the preferred choice in general industry applications.
It is well known that other elastomers are available that provide oil resistance even in the case of high performance oils, e.g. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber (NBR) or Acrylate Ethylene Rubber (AEM). There are also elastomers known for applications in acids or organic solvents, e.g. Ethylene Propylene Diene Rubber (EPDM) or NBR. The ASTM D 2000 classifies elastomers acc. to their heat resistance and swell resistance against a standardized oil and it can be seen that only the fluoropolymers FKM and FFKM show highest temperature resistance combined with high heat resistance (see reference below).

Refernce: Rubber classification by heat resistance and oil-swell resistance acc. to ASTM D 2000

All known candidates to replace FKM or FFKM do not show sufficient heat resistance and start to decompose at elevated temperatures (above 170 °C). Even the very high temperature resistant silicone elastomers cannot withstand combinations of aggressive media (e.g. engine oils, acids, organic solvents) and high temperatures and would swell significantly and consequently would lose its strength and elastomeric properties. Only the combination of heat resistance and chemical resistance while maintaining elastic properties guarantees safe operation and proper function of devices containing rubber parts.
(More details on the elastomer selection for various applications can be provided upon request).

Sectors and (sub-)uses: The compounds RADO is producing based on fluoropolymers are supplied to the following use sectors (acc. to Table 9 of the Annex XV restriction report): • Use sector “TULAC” (Annex E.2.2.) / sub-sector “Technical Textiles” • Use sector “Food contact materials and packaging” (Annex E.2.3.) / sub-sector “industrial food and feed production” • Use sector “Metal plating and manufacturing of metal products” (Annex E.2.4.) / sub-sector “addressed elsewhere” • Use sector “Medical Devices” (Annex E.2.9.) / sub-sector “diagnostic laboratory testing” • Use sector “Transport” (Annex E.2.10.) / sub-sector “Use of PFASs in applications affecting the proper functioning related to the safety of vehicles….” • Use sector “Electronics and semiconductor” / sub-sector “semiconductors” • Use sector “Energy sector” (Annex E.2.12.) • Use sector “Construction products (Annex E.2.13.) / sub-sector “coil coating” • Use sector “Petroleum and Mining” (Annex E.2.15.) / sub-sector “Fluoropolymer applications”  In addition, RADO compounds are also used in the following use sectors in general: • Chemical Industry, Plastics (other than packaging) and rubber / elastomer production, Defense industry and other niche applications.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Data on emissions of PFAS during the manufacturing of compounds containing fluoropolymers at RADO have so far not been collected and analyzed. Furthermore, data on emissions during the vulcanization of compounds containing fluoropolymers for the production of rubber articles can only be given by the manufacturers.  In the rubber compound production, only small amounts of waste are generated, mainly consisting of unvulcanised material. Due to the high material costs of fluoropolymer compounds this waste is directly recycled in the process of compound production. Alongside with the compound production, waste of vulcanized rubber material is generated from rubber tests that are performed as quality inspection. This residual material is sorted and waste of vulcanized fluoropolymer rubber is handled by a service supplier for waste disposal. The annual amount of this waste is approximately 300 kg per year. Another 43 % have been burned in incineration plants or used as fuel substitute and only 10 % were deposited (UMWELTBUNDESAMT 2023).  Other applications e.g. electrical appliances are dismantled after end-of-life and the plastic fraction containing all elastomers is recycled or reused as fuel substitute (UMWELTBUNDESAMT 2022).  When vulcanized fluoropolymer compound waste is burned in incineration plants, no critical PFAS substances are generated. This has been proven by GEHRMANN 2023 (p. 8): “The results confirm that fluoropolymers at their end of life when incinerated under representative European municipal incinerators conditions do not generate any measurable levels of PFAS emissions and therefore pose no risk to human health and the environment." These results also close the gap of knowledge to the study of LOHMANN mentioned in the ECHA proposal. Waste incineration can therefore not be used as an argument for the restriction of PFAS like in the existing proposal.  In general, the recycling of parts made from fluoropolymer rubber is possible. It has already been established in the past in specific cases. Acc. to SCHUSTER 2022 “two methods could be identified to perform in an industrially acceptable way: The deposition of fine milled fluoro-rubber powder in virgin rubber and the mechanical devulcanization of FKM and successive compounding with virgin rubber have proven to be viable recycling methods providing good thermal stability by maintaining the mechanical properties of original FKM.” However, since properly sorted waste rubber, clean from residues, is a prerequisite for the reuse in freshly produced compounds of fluoro rubber this process is not used very often.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Data on emissions of PFAS during the manufacturing of compounds containing fluoropolymers at RADO have so far not been collected and analyzed. Furthermore, data on emissions during the vulcanization of compounds containing fluoropolymers for the production of rubber articles can only be given by the manufacturers.  In the rubber compound production, only small amounts of waste are generated, mainly consisting of unvulcanised material. Due to the high material costs of fluoropolymer compounds this waste is directly recycled in the process of compound production. Alongside with the compound production, waste of vulcanized rubber material is generated from rubber tests that are performed as quality inspection. This residual material is sorted and waste of vulcanized fluoropolymer rubber is handled by a service supplier for waste disposal. The annual amount of this waste is approximately 300 kg per year.  As another consequence of RADO´s position in the above mentioned supply chain data cannot be provided on the use, impact or after end-of-life of parts made from RADO compounds containing fluoropolymers. However, acc. to a study by BEYLAGE 2022 (p. 41) 84 % of articles made of fluoropolymers are incinerated after usage, 13 % are landfilled as waste and 3 % recycled.  Furthermore, the European directive 2000/53/EG on the end-of-life use of cars is defining a ratio of 95 % of recycling for cars. This directive has been transferred into German legislation and acc. to a study of the German “Umweltbundesamt“ the fraction of shredded waste containing all elastomers has in 2020 been recycled by 47 %. Another 43 % have been burned in incineration plants or used as fuel substitute and only 10 % were deposited (UMWELTBUNDESAMT 2023).  Other applications e.g. electrical appliances are dismantled after end-of-life and the plastic fraction containing all elastomers is recycled or reused as fuel substitute (UMWELTBUNDESAMT 2022).  When vulcanized fluoropolymer compound waste is burned in incineration plants, no critical PFAS substances are generated. This has been proven by GEHRMANN 2023 (p. 8): “The results confirm that fluoropolymers at their end of life when incinerated under representative European municipal incinerators conditions do not generate any measurable levels of PFAS emissions and therefore pose no risk to human health and the environment." These results also close the gap of knowledge to the study of LOHMANN mentioned in the ECHA proposal. Waste incineration can therefore not be used as an argument for the restriction of PFAS like in the existing proposal.  In general, the recycling of parts made from fluoropolymer rubber is possible. It has already been established in the past in specific cases. Acc. to SCHUSTER 2022 “two methods could be identified to perform in an industrially acceptable way: The deposition of fine milled fluoro-rubber powder in virgin rubber and the mechanical devulcanization of FKM and successive compounding with virgin rubber have proven to be viable recycling methods providing good thermal stability by maintaining the mechanical properties of original FKM.” However, since properly sorted waste rubber, clean from residues, is a prerequisite for the reuse in freshly produced compounds of fluoro rubber this process is not used very often.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Fluoroelastomers (FKM) are well known for their resistance to high temperatures (up to 250 °C) as well as a broad resistance to various chemicals. This includes e.g. engine or gearbox oils that contain aggressive additives for high performance applications in use sectors like transportation, petroleum and mining or medical devices. Fluoroelastomers are also resistant to acids and organic solvents, which makes them the preferred choice in general industry applications.  It is well known that other elastomers are available that provide oil resistance even in the case of high performance oils, e.g. Nitrile Butadiene Rubber (NBR) or Acrylate Ethylene Rubber (AEM). There are also elastomers known for applications in acids or organic solvents, e.g. Ethylene Propylene Diene Rubber (EPDM) or NBR. The ASTM D 2000 classifies elastomers acc. to their heat resistance and swell resistance against a standardized oil and it can be seen that only the fluoropolymers FKM and FFKM show highest temperature resistance combined with high heat resistance (see reference below).  Reference: Rubber classification by heat resistance and oil-swell resistance acc. to ASTM D 2000  All known candidates to replace FKM or FFKM do not show sufficient heat resistance and start to decompose at elevated temperatures (> 170 °C). Even the very high temperature resistant silicone elastomers cannot withstand combinations of aggressive media (e.g. engine oils, acids, organic solvents) and high temperatures and would swell significantly and consequently would lose its strength and elastomeric properties. Only the combination of heat resistance and chemical resistance while maintaining elastic properties guarantees safe operation and proper function of devices containing rubber parts. (More details on the elastomer selection for various applications can be provided upon request).

Content: Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Fluoropolymers (FPs) are very long-chain PFAS and are widely used in industry for high-performance sealing applications. FPs stand out due to their unequalled performance characteristics. Moreover, FPs are also used in numerous medical devices – even in those implanted into the human body.
As there are currently – and foreseeably – no equivalent alternatives to FPs, a ban on these would have severe technical and socio-economic consequences. Please find more detailed information about our use case of FP seals in machine tools and the implications of a total ban on PFAS under # 6.
While we fully support the regulatory actions to restrict harmful PFAS, we are pleading for a differentiated and risk-based assessment of long-chain polymeric and short-chain non-polymeric PFAS – acknowledging the different risk profiles of the different groups. Peer-reviewed scientific papers supporting this approach are cited below; although we are well aware that the authors of the latter two are affiliated with FP manufacturing companies.

Ameduri, Bruno: Fluoropolymers: A special class of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) essential for our daily life. In: Journal of Fluorine Chemistry 267 (2023), 110117
Henry, B. J. et al.: A Critical Review of the Application of Polymer of Low Concern and Regulatory Criteria to Fluoropolymers. In: Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management 14 (2018), Nr. 3, pp. 316-334
Korzeniowski, S. H. et al.: A critical review of the application of polymer of low concern regulatory criteria to ﬂuoropolymers II: Fluoroplastics and ﬂuoroelastomers. In: Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management 19 (2022), Nr. 2, pp. 326-354

In this context, it should also be considered that the risk of environmental contamination largely depends on the specific application: An FP seal in a machine, that is virtually a closed system, is highly unlikely to contaminate the environment. Whereas, for instance, the fluorinated wax at a ski will inevitably be released into the environment.
FPs (not PFAS in total!) meet the OECD´s criteria for “polymers of low concern”. This means that they are chemically stable, non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water soluble, and non-mobile. In this context, it should also be noted that the use of FPs is quasi self-limiting due to their high cost.
Considering the above aspects, we suggest permanent exemptions for industrially applied FPs.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The use of FPs for high-performance seals and gaskets in machine tools (or more general: in the machinery and plant engineering industry) is covered only marginally by the Annex XV Restriction Report.  FPs typically account for only a very small share of weight in a machine tool (few hundred grams to few kilograms of FPs vs. a total weight of 15 … 40 tons). Nevertheless, FP seals are crucial for the proper, safe, and efficient operation of a machine tool. We have therefore included corresponding information under # 6. [The elaboration for the transport sector (Annex XV, table 8, p. 101-102) could essentially be applied to the machinery and plant engineering sector as well.]

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Manufacture phase: As a machine tool manufacturer, we are not manufacturing FP seals ourselves, but are sourcing these as purchased parts. Therefore, we do not have any information about the emissions related to the manufacture of FPs. Use phase: The FPs used in our machine tools are not consumable material but extremely durable sealing components applied in hydraulic / pneumatic / cooling-lubricant systems. Hence, no significant PFAS emissions are expected during the use phase of a machine tool. At the most, very minor abrasion of the FP seals is conceivable – which will, however, not escape from the machine tool as a closed system.  End-of-life: Machine tools are no consumer products, that are simply “thrown away” – but high-quality and durable means of industrial production, which are disposed of / recycled by specialized companies under strict environmental regulations at the end of their lifetime. It can therefore be assumed that no FPs are released into the environment when a machine tool has reached its end of life.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: As the FP seals used in our machine tools may be disposed of by incineration, we may cite a recent scientific paper: Aleksandrov et al. (2019) found that PTFE, combusted under standard municipal waste incineration conditions, is mainly transformed into CO2 and HF – and does not degrade into PFAS of concern. The authors therefore conclude that “municipal incineration of PTFE […] should be considered an acceptable form of waste treatment”.   Aleksandrov, K. et al.: Waste incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate potential formation of Per- and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) in flue gas. In: Chemosphere 226 (2019), pp. 896-906

6. Missing uses: a & b) As a machine tool manufacturer, we depend on high-performance seals and gaskets for the use in pneumatic, hydraulic, and cooling-lubricant systems. Due to their unique characteristics, fluoropolymers / fluoroelastomers are the material of choice for high-performance sealing applications with respect to: • chemical resistance (especially to cooling lubricants) • tribology / friction properties • pressure resistance (high-pressure hydraulic applications) • wear / abrasion resistance  Relevant FPs in this context are PTFE and FKM / FFKM.   Generally speaking, there are three key functionalities provided by the FPs in a machine tool: • to prevent (aggressive / hazardous / high-pressure) media from leaking from mechanical components, such as cylinders, pumps, tubes, etc. • to prevent aggressive media from intruding into sensitive components, such as spindle bearings, measuring systems, etc. • to guide mechanical components moving relatively to each other and to reduce the friction between these  An overview of sealing systems, that are typically applied in a machine tool, is given below: • O-ring preloaded seals for pneumatic applications (PTFE) • support rings for high-pressure hydraulic applications (PTFE) • guide elements for pistons (PTFE) • O-rings (FKM / FFKM) • X-rings (FKM / FFKM) • O-ring preloaded translational seals (PTFE / FKM) • O-ring preloaded rotatory seals (PTFE / FKM) • rotatory shaft seals (PTFE / FKM) • lip seals (PTFE / FKM) • O-ring preloaded wipers (PTFE) • O-ring preloaded rod seals (PTFE / FKM) • special rotatory seals (PTFE / FKM)  Due to their high cost, FPs are only used if other materials do not suffice because of the high requirements. We do not have specific information about the annual tonnage of FPs used in machine tools. But we can provide an estimation of our annual FP usage: Our annual usage of FPs is in the range of few hundred kilograms. Extrapolated to the German machine tool industry in total, the annual tonnage of FPs should be in the single-digit to low double-digit range. For the PFAS emissions related to FPs in machine tools, see # 2.  c) The German machine tool industry comprises several hundred companies with over 60,000 employees in total. Despite being a rather small sector of industry, its macroeconomic importance must not be underestimated, because it delivers production technology for all sectors of industry.  d - g) We are in intensive exchange with our sealing suppliers regarding possible alternatives for FPs. According to our suppliers, there are indeed some alternative materials that could potentially substitute FPs: • UHMW-PE • (H)NBR • (T)PU • POM • PA • PEEK  However, all these alternative materials have in common that they do not meet the unique performance characteristics of FPs: • reduced chemical resistance • increased friction / wear  • reduced temperature / pressure resistance   Especially the resistance against cooling lubricants, that are widely used in metal cutting, is a crucial issue in machine tool applications. Up to now, FPs (PTFE, FKM, e. g.) are the only polymers known to be highly resistant against cooling lubricants. Nor is it conceivable that equivalent alternatives will be available in the foreseeable future. Due to that, profound – and therefore costly and time-consuming – analyses and research activities in close cooperation of machine tool industry and sealing suppliers will be required. It is, however, likely that – even after a long derogation period of 12 years – no equivalent alternatives to FPs will be available.  Against this background, the substitution of FPs with alternative (inferior) materials in machine tool sealing applications is afflicted with serious technical and socio-economic risks: • reduced durability resulting in increased maintenance efforts / replacement frequency • increased energy consumption (due to increased friction / due to potentially required additional sealing air) • leakage of hazardous substances, such as oil or cooling lubricant, resulting in increased environmental, health, and safety implications • premature replacement of legacy machines, if spare parts not available any more  Furthermore, it is important to understand that these risks do not only affect the machine tool industry itself but a much broader scope of industries. Machine tools are a means of production with a widespread use in the European key sectors of industry, such as automotive, aerospace, defence, renewable energies or medical engineering. It must be emphasized in particular that machine tools are crucial for the production of many “green” technologies required for the European Green Deal, such as windmills or heat pumps.   Considering all these aspects, we request the following from the competent authorities: • differentiation between long-chain polymeric and short-chain non-polymeric PFAS in the regulatory context – acknowledging the different risk profiles of the different groups • recognition of FPs as “polymers of low concern” in accordance with the OECD classification • permanent exemptions for industrially applied FPs

8. Other identified uses: We have extensively elaborated our use case in # 6.
