Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Baseline Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Fluoropolymers are essential materials for the manufacturing of several components of water treatment technologies. Due to their key functionalities, they are mainly used in sealing applications (e.g., seals, O-rings, gaskets), pipes, valves, pumps, reactors, metering tubes as well as part of other components including gas monitoring equipment, electrolysis cells and membranes. Notably, there are no PFAS-free water treatment technologies suitable for disinfection/oxidation purposes at municipal or industrial water treatment level. Consequently, all treatment plants for drinking water, swimming pool water, process water and wastewater (at municipal and industrial level) in the EU rely on installed PFAS-dependent water treatment technologies. Given the classification of fluoropolymers as polymers of low concern (PLC) and the absence of PFAS-free alternatives to water treatment technologies using fluoropolymer-containing components, the EurO3zon members request a time-unlimited derogation for the use of fluoropolymers in water treatment technologies, namely the ozone-based technology, the UV-based technology, the chlorine dioxide-based technology, electrochlorination, the active bromine-based technology, and dosing systems/pumps for chemicals. Notably, both new installations and spare parts for existing technologies fall under the scope of the requested derogation.

A lack of such a time-unlimited derogation from the PFAS restriction would result in several critical effects for the EEA society. From a public health perspective, the supply of adequately treated drinking water in the EEA would be compromised, leading to an increase in the spread of water-borne diseases, the safety of using swimming pools could no longer be ensured, while there would be an increased risk of food poisoning from consuming potentially contaminated food products. Meanwhile, a shortage of essential products such as food and beverages and medicines, to mention only a few, would significantly decrease the quality of life in the EEA, whereas an increased reliance on non-EEA exports coupled with potentially higher product prices would be the consequence. From an environmental point of view, such a restriction scenario would lead to an increased level of contaminants in EEA aquatic environments due to a reduced efficiency for removing such chemical and microbiological materials from urban wastewaters. Additionally, wastewater could no longer be re-used to save water resources (e.g., in agriculture for irrigations), whereas there would be an increased environmental footprint due to the use of more energy-intensive and less efficient water treatment methods not relying on PFAS. From a socio-economic standpoint, such a scenario would lead to job losses, foregone profits as well as additional one-off costs associated with business shutdowns in the supply chain as well as increased operating costs due to the use of less efficient technologies and additional one-off costs for decommissioning and replacing current installations relying on fluoropolymers and other PFAS in the EEA.

Based on the data availability, the attached impact assessment could only monetize the socio-economic effects associated with one-off costs for eventually displacing existing technology installations in the EEA in a worst-case scenario due to the absence of spare parts and maintenance services as well as foregone profits and job losses experienced at the level of some stakeholders in the supply chain. These impacts only are evaluated at 35.32 – 58.40 billion Euros (NPV 2025). Notably, without capturing due to data constrains the severe broader societal and environmental consequences qualitatively described above, this monetized value largely remains a significant underestimation of the real impacts in case of a restriction, as water treatment is absolutely indispensable for the functioning of the EEA society.

6. Missing uses: Based on the available data, information with respect to the following elements is being submitted by EurO3zon in the form of an impact assessment (see attachments under sections IV and V):  • Annual tonnage and risks at sub-sector level and type of PFAS associated with the relevant use (as requested under point a.)  • Key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use (as requested under point b.) • The availability and technical feasibility of alternatives for the relevant use (as requested under point d.)   • (For cases in which alternatives are not yet available) the time expected to be required for substitution (as requested under point e.) • (For cases in which substitution is not technically or economically feasible) information on socio-economic impacts; the annual value of EU profits of the relevant sector and employment numbers for the sector (as requested under point g.)  The present comment serves to provide a summary overview of the submitted impact assessment. It should be noted that information with respect to tonnage, individual monetized socio-economic impact categories as well as baseline financial and employment data is only provided in the confidential version of the submitted impact assessment (see attachment under section V).  Annual tonnage and risks at sub-sector level and type of PFAS associated with the relevant use: The submitted impact assessment provides an estimate of the annual tonnage of fluoropolymers used for the manufacturing of components for water treatment technologies in the EEA.  Several factors minimize the environmental risks associated with the use of fluoropolymers in components for water treatment technologies: • Only solid-state fluoropolymers are used for manufacturing components. • No soluble, short-chain, or volatile PFAS substances are required or released during the production or processing of components. • Very small quantities of fluoropolymers are used for manufacturing of components. • There is a limited number of fluoropolymer-containing components directly in contact with treated water. • Only certified fluoropolymer-containing components are in contact with drinking water. • There is a limited risk for fluoropolymers leaching into the treated water. • All handling procedures, including maintenance throughout the value chain, are performed by highly trained professionals.  Notably, a non-exhaustive list of fluoropolymers covered under the scope of the submitted impact assessment includes PTFE, ETFE, ECTFE, PVDF, PFA, FEP, PFEP, THV, FKM, FFKM and PFPE. Although no recycling system is currently in place, a future collection and appropriate disposal system of fluoropolymer-containing components used for water treatment technologies could be implemented, given that the handling of such components is already being carried out by trained personnel, while the individual parts can be collected as such.  Key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use: Fluoropolymers are essential for various components in water treatment technologies (e.g., pipes, valves, seals, reactors, monitoring equipment, electrolysis cells), thus ensuring worker safety, providing operational efficiency and improving equipment lifetime. Key functionalities provided by fluoropolymers in this sense include high chemical stability against strong oxidizing and toxic agents, high temperature resistance, dielectric strength, and a very good limiting oxygen index, to mention only a few properties. Fluoropolymer-based components play a critical role in water treatment technologies, ensuring high-quality water in various professional applications such as the treatment of drinking water, wastewater as well as process water, consequently leading to a high quality of products (e.g., medicines). These technologies effectively disinfect and oxidize, leading to an efficient removal from the treated water of microbiological (e.g., bacteria, viruses, yeasts) as well as chemical (e.g., micropollutants, persistent substances, pesticides) contaminants. Moreover, PFAS removal from water relies on technologies using fluoropolymer-based components, while the implementation of EU standards and regulations concerning water quality also depends on these technologies.  The time expected to be required for substitution / The availability and technical feasibility of alternatives for the relevant use: To date there are no alternative materials available that meet the key required functionalities of fluoropolymers and thus would not compromise the quality, safety, lifetime and performance of water treatment technologies once implemented. Finding alternatives for components in direct contact with water is especially challenging due to the limited and highly regulated substances allowed for (drinking) water contact. Any potential future alternatives would require at least 10 years for validation and obtaining the necessary certifications, time during which fluoropolymer-containing spare parts would still need to be provided for existing installations. Notably, this 10-year timeline explicitly does not account for any prior research and development activities required to identify such a potential new material, nor does it cover the extended timeframe necessary for conducting human health and environmental toxicology assessments of the respective material. Additionally, there is no guarantee that the potential new material would pass all testing, validation and certification steps during the process.  Concerning other water treatment methods, technologies based on activated carbon and flocculation-based filtration, which do not depend on PFAS, cannot achieve water disinfection when used in isolation from technologies dependent on PFAS-based components. Biological water treatment for swimming pools, while not relying on fluoropolymers, does not result in water disinfection and is limited by the availability of high-quality water. Additionally, biological water treatment is not appropriate for use in settings where vulnerable population groups may be exposed (e.g., therapy pools in hospitals). Other technologies relying on PFAS, such as thermic methods and membrane-based technologies, are considerably less-efficient when not combined with fluoropolymer-based water treatment technologies. No PFAS-free water treatment technologies suitable for disinfection/oxidation purposes are available at the municipal or industrial water treatment level.  The annual value of EU profits of the relevant sector and employment numbers for the sector: The value chain of water treatment technologies using fluoropolymer-containing components consists of fluoropolymer producers and processors, component manufacturers and original equipment manufacturers delivering the respective technologies to various downstream customers. The latter include a variety of public and private stakeholders relying on such technologies for treating drinking water, swimming pool water, process water as well as wastewater, with the benefiting end industrial sectors covering, among others, the pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, pulp and paper, food and beverages, agriculture and aquaculture sectors. Notably, all municipal plants in the EU treating wastewater and drinking water rely on water treatment technologies using fluoropolymer-based components.  To provide a market and financial overview for the producers of water treatment technologies relying on fluoropolymer-containing components, the submitted impact assessment presents aggregated data collected from EurO3zon members with respect to earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT), number of employees and shares of revenues attributable to the different customer segments.  Information on socio-economic impacts: Given the classification of fluoropolymers as polymers of low concern and the absence of PFAS-free alternatives to water treatment technologies using fluoropolymer-containing components, the EurO3zon members request a time-unlimited derogation for the use of fluoropolymers in water treatment technologies. The absence of such a derogation would lead to several consequences in the supply chain; In such a restriction scenario, fluoropolymer producers and processors, components manufacturers as well as water treatment technology producers would have to shut down the parts of their businesses dependent on fluoropolymers. For some of these companies, this may effectively translate to a complete business shutdown. Meanwhile, all downstream customers using treatment technologies based on fluoropolymer-containing components in the EEA for treating drinking water, swimming pool water, process water and wastewater would have to switch to less efficient water treatment methods. An exception is constituted by industrial stakeholders, such as pharmaceuticals and cosmetics manufacturers, which would no longer be able to obtain via less-efficient methods pure or ultrapure water for the manufacturing of their products and would thus need to shutdown the concerned business operations in the EEA.   As a result of such a restriction scenario, the supply of adequately treated drinking water in the EEA would be compromised, which would lead to an increased incidence of water-borne diseases in the EEA. The safety associated with consuming food and beverage products produced in the EEA would decline, while the risk for food poisoning from the consumption of potentially contaminated products would increase. The safety associated with using swimming pools would also decrease, which could potentially lead to a higher incidence of gastrointestinal infections and in the long-term, a significantly reduced availability of swimming pools in the EEA. At the same time, there would be a decreased availability of essential products on the EEA market, including food and beverage products but also medicines, further negatively impacting the population health. Meanwhile, the dependency on non-EEA suppliers would increase and the competitiveness of EEA companies would be significantly reduced, while EEA consumers may have to pay higher prices for essential products, if bottlenecks in supply persist.   From an environmental perspective, reduced removal rates of contaminants from treated wastewater in such a restriction scenario would lead to increased levels of aquatic pollution in the EEA. Meanwhile, treated wastewater would no longer be suitable for re-use, for instance for irrigation purposes in agriculture, which would impede addressing water scarcity by saving water resources. Furthermore, the use of less efficient methods could result in an increased environmental footprint. Methods based on activated carbon for instance, while not achieving disinfection, require frequent recycling of the carbon material, which is an energy-intensive process. Moreover, producers and processors of activated carbon are mostly located outside the EEA, which would lead to longer transportation distances for  recycling in addition to an increased reliance on non-EEA suppliers to ensure water treatment in case of a restriction scenario as well as challenges due to an already limited supply of activated carbon, such as long delivery waiting times and fluctuating prices.  With respect to further socio-economic effects resulting from a restriction scenario, as a consequence of business shutdowns, foregone profits, one-off investment costs for dismantling and clean-up of facilities as well as job losses would be registered in the EEA at the different levels in the supply chain. Furthermore, there would be significant additional one-off investment costs for decommissioning and replacing existing water treatment technologies with less efficient methods where feasible at the different downstream users in the EEA due to lack of spare parts. Ultimately, the use of less efficient methods may also result in increased annual operating costs for treating drinking water, swimming pool water, process water and wastewater.   Based on data received from EurO3zon members, by following conservative assumptions and using the latest methodologies developed by ECHA where applicable, the following impact categories could be monetized in the submitted impact assessment, amounting to an overall value of 35.32 – 58.40 billion Euros (NPV 2025): additional one-off investment costs for decommissioning and replacing existing water treatment technologies in the EEA in a worst-case scenario due to the absence of spare parts and maintenance services; producer surplus losses and the social cost of unemployment for the EEA society resulting from job losses at the level of water treatment technology manufacturers; the social cost of unemployment derived from the number of jobs expected to be lost at component manufacturers. Distributional impacts such as severance payments as a result of job losses in the EEA as well as fines potentially incurred by downstream users of water treatment technologies for becoming non-compliant with EU regulations and standards after switching to less efficient treatment methods were only addressed qualitatively. Overall, due to data limitations and by following a conservative approach, the impacts monetized in the submitted impact assessment remain largely underestimated, especially due to a lack of data for estimating the negative effects pertaining to public health and environment in case of a restriction scenario.

General Comments: Fluoropolymers are unique materials due to their high-performance properties: non-wetting, high dielectric, non-stick, fire resistant, temperature resistant, weather resistant and with near universal resistance to chemicals. It is their specific combinations of properties that are not matched by any of the alternatives, and which thus make them so valuable in applications such as chemical process industry, batteries for EV, water and atmosphere purification, water electrolysis, energy/hydrogen storage, applications in pharmaceutical manufacturing equipment, electronics, aerospace, military & defense, transportation, semiconductor manufacturing and high-end niche applications etc.
Moreover, Fluoropolymers and more precisely PVDF homopolymer and specific ferroelectric copolymers such as P(VDF-TrFE), or P(VDF-TrFE-CTFE/CFE) relaxor ferroelectric terpolymers, attract an increasing intensive high level scientific and development interest for their unique electroactive properties, flexibility, printability, low CO2 footprint, biocompatibility, recycling ability. In addition, based on all the (toxicological and (eco)toxicological) studies carried out that have demonstrated that PVDF are not bioavailable and non-mobile, they are considered not to pose risks to human health, have favorable (eco)toxicological profile, and meet the OECD definition for polymers of low concern.
There is no alternative that offers such a rich set of properties. The most used electroactive ceramics (Lead Zirconium titanate PZT) are toxic and are already difficult to substitute by others inorganic materials, that will remain however (if nontoxic), brittle, weighty, hard to recycle and with a very high CO2 footprint. For a typical device, the use of fluorinated polymers as electroactive material reduces CO2 footprint by a factor greater than 400 compared to inorganic counterparts.
Other polymers have by far too low electroactive and other performances (one order of magnitude lower electroactive coefficients, low thermal and chemical stability etc.) to be used in real applications. Therefore, fluorinated electroactive polymers are high value materials that make possible strategic emerging technologies in medical devices (from vital sign monitoring to cancer treatment), biomedical, sustainable electronics, virtual and & augmented reality, energy storage, energy safety management (such as safety monitoring of hydrogen tanks) or low environment footprint energy technologies for the future such as efficient and zero GWP heat pumps and cooling systems.
These innovations are at the heart of European industrial & green-deal strategy. Thanks to the high involvement of European specialty materials industrials, excellence of European R&D on materials and support from European research organizations, Europe is the world leader for these materials.
Based on the scientific and economic data provided in this answer to the public consultation, Arkema’s preferred option is to support a more segmented approach based on the level of risk of the substance to facilitate the effectiveness and implementation of the restriction.
In conclusion, within this approach, Arkema considers that fluoropolymers produced without PFAS polymerization aids like ferroelectric copolymers should be exempted. The potential emissions as well as the end of life can be effectively managed through alternatives and appropriate regulations such as the Waste directive, the Landfill directive and the industrial emissions directives.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Fluoropolymers do not degrade under intended use conditions or under environmental conditions, as published in the report, ‘Survey of PFOS, PFOA and other perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances’ by the Danish EPA in 2013 (report attached). It clearly states that, “the degradation of fluoropolymers cannot lead to the formation of long chain Perfluoro carboxylic acids (PFCAs) and they are not included in the OECD list of possible precursors of short chain PFAS”.

Fluoropolymers are polymers with carbon-only backbone with Fluorine atoms directly bonded to it. The exceptional strength of the C-F bond in fluoropolymers make them not degrade to small molecular weight PFASs. This has been further elaborated in another publication by Chemservice for Pro-K (report attached) confirming that fluoropolymers are not only different from non-polymeric PFAS, they also exhibit completely different properties from other polymeric PFAS like side-chain fluorinated polymers, particularly in relation to possible environmental degradation into smaller PFAS. This report highlights the main differences between fluoropolymers, perfluoropolyethers and side-chain fluorinated polymers, highlighting how those differences justify considering fluoropolymers as chemicals posing no relevant risk for human health or the environment.

Due to their chemical structure (carbon backbone with polyfluoroalkyl side chains bound to it), side-chain fluorinated polymers can degrade to hazardous non-polymeric PFAS during the intended use or under environmental conditions at the end-of-life phase of their applications. Moreover, these substances are used mainly at the consumer level, which is considered an open and dispersive use. Therefore, side-chain fluorinated polymers could develop effects on human health and the environment that would never be exhibited by fluoropolymers. In the case of perfluoropolyethers, degradation potential during the use phase is limited and therefore, potential risks related to their use are expected to be limited.

6. Missing uses: We are active in the field of industrial valves. In our valves we use PFAS-containing materials in seals and gaskets as well as material for body lining. Fluoropolymers are primarily used here. Those are high-performance plastics that are characterised by particularly high resistance. They have a sealing, water-repellent and friction-reducing effect within our products and prevent the adhesion of substances. These include above all the widely used fluoroplastic PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene, also known as "Teflon"), PFA (Perfluoroalkoxy alkane) or FKM ("fluororubber"). PFAS-containing materials in our products contribute significantly to reduction of fugitive emissions, tightness of the valves and compatibility in food grade applications.   Some of the fluoropolymers we use in our valves have been scientifically evaluated as "polymers of low concern" (PTFE, FKM and PFA). They have been proven to be chemically stable, non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water soluble and non-mobile. For these reasons, the fluoropolymers are also approved, for example, as materials for food contact or in medical technology.  We therefore call for the general exemption of fluoropolymers, which (incidentally also according to the OECD definition) are considered "polymers of low concern", from the PFAS restriction project.  In addition, substances such as monomers and processing aids that are necessary for fluoropolymer manufacture and production should be exempted from the ban, provided that safe use is ensured. This is also envisaged by the study of the British Health and Safety Executive (HSE). Therefore, in general, groups with low risk (e.g. fluoroelastomers, fluoropolymers assessed as "polymers of low concern") or uses without relevant risk (e.g. uses in closed systems) should be exempted.  In this context, we would like to point out that there are currently no alternatives to the use of materials classified as "polymers of low concern" in gaskets or body linings that have similar resistance over a comparable period of. Those characteristics are of enormous importance, especially in the environment of our products, because it is all about safety and emission reduction over a long period of time.  A ban on these PFAS substances would mean that at the present time we would not be able to use seals, gaskets and lining materials in our products that comply with the applicable legal and regulatory provisions and also do not have the necessary approvals. The consequence would be nothing else but a sales stop and a dramatic drop in turnover of about 15 to 20 percent. Because without these substances, our valves simply do not work.  In order to prevent such existentially threatening damage, not only for our company but for the entire industry and society as a whole, we ask to exclude fluoropolymers such as PTFE or PFA in the context of industrial valves from PFAS regulation.

General Comments: Fluoropolymers meet the criteria of polymers of low concern as established by the OECD. Fluoropolymers have thermal, chemical, photochemical, hydrolytic, oxidative, and biological stability. Fluoropolymers are practically insoluble in water and not subject to long-range transport. With a molecular weight well over 100,000 Da, fluoropolymers cannot cross the cell membrane. Fluoropolymers are not bioavailable or bio-accumulative, as evidenced by toxicology studies on polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE): acute and sub chronic systemic toxicity, irritation, sensitization, local toxicity on implantation, cytotoxicity, in vitro and in vivo genotoxicity, hemolysis, complement activation, and thrombogenicity. They have negligible residual monomer and oligomer content and low to no leachable.  Since risk is defined as hazard in combination with the level of exposure, the absence of hazard means risk cannot be directly attributed to fluoropolymers, let alone an unacceptable risk.

The attached two scientific papers bring together toxicity data, human clinical data, and physical, chemical, thermal, and biological data for review and assessment of fluoropolymers (4+14) to show that fluoropolymers satisfy widely accepted assessment criteria to be considered as “polymers of low concern” (PLC). It also concludes that fluoropolymers are distinctly different from other polymeric and nonpolymeric PFAS and should be separated from them for hazard assessment or regulatory purposes.

Therefore, in general, groups with low risk (e.g. fluoroelastomers, fluoropolymers assessed as "polymers of low concern") or uses without relevant risk (e.g. uses in closed systems) should be exempted.  In this context, we would like to point out that there are currently no alternatives to the use of materials classified as "polymers of low concern" in our area of industrial valves that have similar resistance over a comparable period of time. Those characteristics are of enormous importance, especially in the environment of our products, because it is all about protection both of the operator using the equipment as well as protection of the atmosphere and the process itself over a long period of time.  A ban on these PFAS substances would mean that at the present time we would not be able to use PTFE packing rings in our products that comply with the applicable legal and regulatory provisions - and also the required warranty periods - and also do not have the necessary approvals. The consequence would be nothing else but a sales stop and a dramatic drop in turnover of >20%. Because without PFAS, many of our industrial valves will not be suitable nor accepted for service.  In order to prevent such existentially threatening damage, not only for our company but for the entire industry and society as a whole, fluoropolymers such as PTFE in the context of industrial valves must therefore be excluded from PFAS regulation.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Information on alternatives Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Fluoropolymers, encompassing fluoroplastics and fluoroelastomers, hold pivotal roles in a myriad of applications, most notably within the oil and gas recovery sector. These materials boast unique properties that are essential for ensuring safety and operational efficiency across various industries. Given their widespread deployment across a diverse array of products and components, the prospect of achieving large-scale replacements is a highly impractical endeavor, potentially spanning decades, even if viable alternatives were to emerge.

In the context of the petroleum and mining industries, foundational sectors crucial to the European Union's societal advancement, fluoropolymers assume a critical function. These industries underpin economic progress, transportation, and the overall functionality of modern society, aligning with the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goal of ensuring universal access to affordable, sustainable, and reliable energy resources. The EU's energy sector, which employs approximately 1.6 million individuals involved in energy extraction, production, and distribution, contributes a substantial EUR 250 billion in added economic value. Europe's significant investments in renewable energies, combined with its vast consumer base of around 513 million people, establish the EU as a global leader in the energy sector.

While acknowledging the legitimate concerns associated with certain PFAS substances due to their impact on human health and the environment, it is crucial to distinguish that subgroups like fluoropolymers can be employed in a manner that simultaneously safeguards both the environment and human well-being. These materials excel in mitigating leaks of methane, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), hazardous fluids, and oil and chemical spills across a wide array of industries. Their applications span hydrocarbon extraction, chemical and petrochemical sectors, power generation and supply, nuclear safety, aerospace, wastewater management, and natural gas or hydrogen compression. Furthermore, fluoropolymers and analogous compounds exhibit attributes such as insolubility in water, non-toxicity, and limited bioavailability, rendering them unequivocally safe choices that pose no discernible threat to human health or the environment.

In summary, advocating for a blanket ban on PFAS, encompassing fluoropolymers, emerges as an unattainable and undesirable endeavor, given the expansive reach, intricate nature, and potential adverse consequences for existing supply chains and future economic prospects. A focused and deliberate approach is warranted, supplemented by rigorous monitoring, control, and emission reduction measures throughout manufacturing and disposal processes, with a concurrent emphasis on the implementation of material recycling systems where feasible.

The repercussions of enforcing the proposed ban on fluoropolymers would be profound, imperiling European commerce, thousands of industrial jobs, and the interests of countless customers and suppliers, potentially leading to losses in the billions of euros. This outcome represents a disproportionate response, particularly in light of studies by Henry (2018) and Korzeniowski (2022), which underscore that the majority of fluoropolymers meet the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) criteria as 'polymers of low concern' (PLC).

Furthermore, such a ban would constitute a substantial impediment to progress toward EU climate targets and key objectives delineated in legislative frameworks such as the EU Critical Raw Materials Act, EU Net-Zero Industry Act, REPowerEU, Hydrogen Strategy, Air Quality Agenda, and EU Methane Regulation. Identifying alternative chemicals for specific uses is a resource-intensive endeavor, encompassing processes like redesign, retesting, and recertification, alongside the revision of numerous standards. Even if all research programs were redirected toward developing PFAS-free alternatives, meeting the proposed deadlines for substituting compounds across all products would remain an exceedingly challenging task. Moreover, the rush to qualify materials and products under applicable standards would overwhelm qualified laboratories. Our commitment extends to exploring and embracing alternative solutions as they emerge in the market, adapting proactively to evolving regulatory landscapes to continue providing high-quality products to our esteemed clients.

Moreover, the maintenance intervals for equipment relying on fluoropolymer components have been meticulously established over decades of data collection. Recent advancements driven by the Internet of Things (IoT) and Artificial Intelligence have substantially enhanced the efficiency of maintenance cycles, facilitating predictive fault analysis and reducing equipment downtime. A ban on PFAS would entail the forfeiture of a substantial repository of accrued data, effectively resetting industrial installations by decades in terms of maintenance knowledge.

Considering the minimal risk profile associated with fluoropolymers, their suitability for safe production and utilization under existing regulatory frameworks (e.g., Industrial Emissions Directive), the absence of alternatives meeting stringent environmental conditions, and the profound socio-economic ramifications of a ban, we assertively advocate for the exemption of fluoropolymer production and application within industrial contexts. Instead, we recommend the judicious utilization of tools outlined in the EU's Transition pathway for the chemical industry.

For exempted applications, we propose the establishment of a framework that encourages:

- Adherence to best practices throughout the manufacturing, usage, and end-of-life phases of fluoropolymers, integrating circular economy principles across value chains.
- A concerted research effort to identify alternative substances capable of meeting current standards in terms of performance, quality, durability, efficiency, availability, and economic viability.

We urge the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) to re-evaluate the comprehensive ban on fluoropolymers for the aforementioned reasons. We are available to arrange meetings and technical sessions to further explore the use of PFAS in specific industrial applications.

Please note that, due to the complexity of products and global supply chains, an exhaustive investigation into the impact of these restrictions on all product lines has not been possible.

Furthermore, we request clarity from ECHA on several aspects of the proposed restrictions:

- Confirmation that derogations for fluorinated materials necessary for fluoropolymer production extend to the entire upstream value chain, encompassing the use of monomers and polymerization aids.
- Inclusion of spare parts necessary for repair and maintenance within derogations, as the exclusion of spare parts may result in significant additional costs for equipment replacement before the end of its service life.

In conclusion, fluoropolymers, meticulously designed for demanding high-temperature and chemically aggressive environments, exhibit unparalleled properties that outclass other polymers, such as NBR (nitrile rubber), HNBR (hydrogenated nitrile butadiene rubber), EPDM (ethylene propylene diene monomer), and silicone. These exceptional characteristics position fluoropolymers as the exclusive viable choice for applications necessitating elevated temperatures exceeding 150°C and the presence of highly aggressive chemistries, even in scenarios where hydrogen sulfide concentrations exceed 5%.

In recent years, the oil and gas industry has witnessed significant advancements in drilling technology, enabling the exploration of wells that were previously considered inaccessible two decades ago. As drilling operations push the boundaries of depth and efficiency, they frequently encounter environments characterized by extreme temperatures and aggressive chemical compositions.

Fluoropolymers play a pivotal role in maintaining the integrity of such critical applications by providing unmatched temperature resistance and chemical inertness. They act as formidable barriers, effectively containing aggressive chemistries within the drilling fluids and wellbore, thus preventing contamination of the drinking water table and safeguarding the surrounding environment.

In summary, the unique combination of high-temperature resistance and exceptional chemical inertness positions fluoropolymers as the indispensable choice for preserving the safety and environmental integrity of drilling operations in the evolving landscape of the oil and gas industry. Their use ensures that aggressive chemistries remain confined within the well, even under the most demanding conditions, thereby upholding the stringent standards of environmental stewardship and safety in modern drilling practices.

Content: Baseline Information on benefits
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Fluoropolymers, including fluoroelastomers, are thermally, biologically and chemically stable, nonbioaccumulative, nontoxic, nonmobile, nonbioavailable and have been demonstrated to meet the globally accepted OECD criteria for polymers of low concern "PLC" (Henry et al., 2018).  Especially in the automotive and transport sectors, fluoropolymers are used for safety-relevant applications, such as for seals in the engine compartment or for fuel- and coolant systems and hoses. Substituting these substances would not only endanger the safety of operators, passengers or goods, but would also reduce the vehicle lifetime, increase the rate of damage as well as the emissions during vehicle operation (VDA position paper, July 2021). Fluoropolymers will remain crucial for fulfilling the targets of European Green Deal. For these reasons, fluoropolymers (including fluoroelastomers) should be exempted from the PFAS restriction proposal.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Transport: applications affecting the proper functioning related to the safety of transport vehicles, and affecting the safety of operators, passengers or goods.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: 1. Manufacture phase: PFAS emission from fluoropolymers are only 2.69% of the total PFAS emissions within EEA (Report summary PFAS and PFAS polymer production July 2021.pdf, published by BauA). Out of these 2.69% most of it can be attributed to the use of fluorinated polymerization aids in the manufacturing process of fluoropolymers. When processing fluoropolymers and -elastomers for example during extrusion with state-of-the art technologies such as in our company, no PFAS emissions are expected (pro-K Response to Registry of Intention by the fluoropolymer user industry, 23.09.21). Additionally, we are using semi-finished parts made of fluoropolymers or PTFE-containing lubricants where also no PFAS emission is expected.  2. Use phase: Our products are used in the automotive area. Vehicle life-cycle is around 15-22 years (source: VDA). During the entire life-cycle PFAS are encapsulated. Volatile fluorine compounds can only be released during combustion where they are removed from the exhaust gases, e.g. by gas scrubbers. There is no uncontrolled release of PFAS. (Source: VDA position paper, July 2021).

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Fluoropolymer manufacturers are currently working on an incineration study. Furthermore, Aleksandrov et al. have shown that no PFAS are created during municipal incineration of PTFE but can be almost fully transformed into hydrofluoric acid (HF). Therefore, municipal incineration of PTFE should be considered an acceptable form of waste treatment. (Chemosphere Volume 226, July 2019, Pages 898-906: Waste incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate potential formation of per- and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) in flue gas. Krasimir Aleksandrov et al.)

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: The impacts on the recycling industry is currently investigated by several fluoropolymer manufacturers. The results of the study will be submitted during the course of the public consultation period.

5. Proposed derogations: In the transport sector around 18500 tons of fluoropolymers are used in the EU (2018). As demonstrated in question 2 PFAS are encapsulated during the use phase for this particular application and therefore no PFAS are released into the environment.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: In the transport sector fluoropolymers (including fluoroelastomers) are essential for the safety of operators, passengers or goods. Fluoropolymers in fuel line applications such as tubes and hoses not only enable fuel savings but also minimize the risk of health damages from emissions. Alternative materials such as polyamides lead to a significant higher fuel emission which are both harmful to health and lead to a fast failure of the fuel lines. Additionally, they would not meet the emission requirements. The current and future European CO2 and other emission legislation could also not be fulfilled. The resistance against aggressive media such as fuels, oil or heat and moisture as well against friction, abrasion and wear makes the usage of fluoropolymers essential and not replaceable in current as well as in future technologies.

Content: Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Fluoropolymers, including PTFE, play a critical role in numerous industries, and granting an exemption would enable the ongoing utilisation of these materials. PTFE is a crucial material with significant contributions to various industries, and granting an exemption would allow for the continued benefits it offers while maintaining a low environmental impact.
PFAS substances encompass a diverse range of more than 10,000 synthetic chemicals that have been commercially produced since the 1940s. The chemicals in question demonstrate a range of physical and chemical properties, encompassing characteristics such as being in liquid or gaseous states, as well as high-molecular weight polymers. These substances find extensive utilisation across diverse industries, including pharmaceuticals, biopharmaceuticals, automotive, textiles, electronics, energy, and food processing.  PFAS substances, are desirable due to their unique properties, including thermal and electrical insulation, water and oil repellence, and durability. Common uses include non-stick cookware, furniture, waterproof clothing, food packaging, textiles, cabling, rubber, and plastics.
Fluoropolymers, a subset of PFAS, are widely utilised in technologies, industrial processes, and everyday applications across sectors such as aviation, transportation (including electric vehicles), medical devices, energy production, and technical apparel. Within the pharmaceutical industry, fluoropolymers, particularly PTFE, play essential roles with gaskets, valve seat materials, and in lined products such as piping and valve systems. The durability, chemical inertness, and mechanical strength of fluoropolymers make them valuable, ensuring that PTFE does not release harmful substances during use or disposal. Moreover, PTFE's durability reduces the need for frequent replacements, minimising waste generation. Viable substitutes for PTFE in these industries are scarce, if not non-existent.
Importance of PTFE in Industries: An Overview of Key Factors
1. Chemical Resistance: PTFE exhibits exceptional chemical resistance, making it ideal for handling corrosive substances and maintaining the purity of sensitive products in industry. It can withstand a wide range of aggressive chemicals without degradation, ensuring the integrity and quality of pharmaceutical formulations.
2. Purity Assurance: PTFE-lined pipes, valves, and fittings provide a nonreactive and inert surface, minimising the risk of contamination in pharmaceutical and chemical processes. This is of utmost importance in maintaining the purity, efficacy, and safety of pharmaceutical products and chemical compounds.
3. High Temperature Resistance: PTFE can withstand extreme temperatures, making it well-suited for applications in the energy and nuclear industries. PTFE-lined products can safely handle hot fluids, steam, and aggressive chemicals in power plants, ensuring reliable and efficient operations even under high-temperature conditions.
4. Corrosion Resistance: PTFE's resistance to corrosion is crucial in industries where aggressive chemicals are present. PTFE-lined pipes, valves, and fittings protect against corrosion caused by acids, alkalis, and other corrosive substances, thereby extending the lifespan of equipment and reducing maintenance costs.
5. Nonstick Properties: PTFE's exceptional nonstick characteristics prevent the adhesion of substances, reducing the risk of blockages, clogging, and contamination. In the pharmaceutical and chemical industries, this property allows for easy cleaning and prevents cross-contamination between batches, ensuring product purity and maintaining process efficiency.
6. Sealing and Insulation: PTFE gaskets, seals, and insulation components are widely used in various industrial applications. PTFE's excellent sealing properties help prevent leaks and maintain the integrity of systems, crucial in pharmaceutical, chemical, and nuclear processes. Additionally, PTFE's electrical insulation capabilities make it valuable in electrical systems within these industries.
7. Safety, Reliability & Sustainability: The unique properties of PTFE-lined products contribute to enhanced safety and reliability in critical operations. In the nuclear industry, for instance, PTFE-lined pipes, valves, and fittings help prevent leaks of hazardous and active materials, ensuring the safety of personnel and protecting the environment. PTFE-lined products contribute significantly to sustainability throughout the lifespan of factories and plants. Their durability and long-term viability make them an environmentally preferable choice, aligning with sustainable practices and reducing the environmental impact over time.

While we acknowledge concerns surrounding certain PFAS compounds, it is crucial to distinguish fluoropolymers, from other substances within the PFAS category. Fluoropolymers, offer socio-economic value to European industries and demonstrate low risk to human health and the environment. They are considered polymers of low concern (PLC) due to their physical-chemical properties, which prevent bioavailability, bioaccumulation, toxicity, and degradation. In many applications, fluoropolymers contribute to reducing environmental harm compared to alternative materials. Furthermore, they are pivotal to emerging technologies aimed at mitigating the effects of global warming, including solar, wind, and hydrogen technologies. Fluoropolymers should be exempted from the regulatory action proposed. An outright ban on fluoropolymers without providing viable alternatives would have significant consequences for industries heavily reliant on its exceptional properties. Progress in critical sectors would be hindered, technological advancements impeded, and important applications compromised, negatively impacting various facets of everyday life.

6. Missing uses: PTFE tubing, known for its unique properties of chemical resistance, is widely used for delivering liquids in high-tech applications. These tubing are connected and installed to storage tanks that contain harsh chemicals such as hydrogen fluoride (HF) or hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). These chemicals are crucial for rinsing semiconductor processor chips used in computers and other semiconductor applications in order to purify their surfaces. Purification and achieving ultimate purity, along with chemical resistance, are paramount in adopting PTFE tubing for these high-tech applications. Without these specialized tubes, the economical and efficient production of microprocessors would be jeopardized, as computer chips cannot be produced without thorough cleaning with hydrogen fluorides and/or hydrogen peroxides. There are five objects that need to be purged from the semiconductor materials during the rinsing process: 1. Particles 2. Metal ions 3. Organic matter 4. Oil 5. Oxide film None of these objects should be eluted or found before etching a microprocessor chip, as the purity of the chemicals and surfaces is crucial to ensure the quality of the final product. Due to its unique characteristics, PTFE is the ideal solution for maintaining the purity of the chemicals during the delivery process. PTFE tubing does not react with the chemicals and does not release any metal ions, making it the only suitable material for this application. The delivery hose must also be pure and stable, as it should not introduce contaminants or react with the chemicals being transported. In conclusion, PTFE tubing is essential for the safe and efficient delivery of harsh chemicals used in semiconductor manufacturing. Its unmatched properties of chemical resistance, purity, and non-reactivity make it the preferred material for ensuring the high-quality and purity of semiconductor materials during transportation and processing.

General Comments: FLUX is a manufacturer of a wide variety of pumps, volumetric flowmeters and accessories with a focus on drum and container pumps. The products are used worldwide in a wide range of industries. This includes the chemical industry, surface technology, mechanical engineering as well as pharmaceutical, food and cosmetic applications.
Our products are not used in the consumer sector but exclusively in industrial applications.

We regard the planned PFAS restrictions as very critical for various reasons and cannot understand the general restriction, even of fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers classified as harmless, for which we are applying for an unlimited exemption.

The majority of our products are hand-operated pumps used specifically for liquids and in environments where conventional pumps fail.

Fluoroelastomers play an essential role as sealing materials. For many of these materials, there is no known or foreseeable alternative in terms of chemical resistance. Inferior alternatives lead at least to an early failure of the pumps and with high probability to injuries / burns of the operator, which would make the use of the products impossible due to the risk.

Fluoroplastics are not only relevant as a sealing and housing material, but also as a bearing material due to their unique chemical and tribological properties. So far, we have not been able to find any PFAS-free sliding couples that ensure sufficient dry-running protection and thus meet explosion protection requirements for our products.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: As a pump manufacturer, it is not possible to limit ourselves to the given sectors. Our products are used in all sectors where difficult and aggressive media have to be transferred, dosed, filled over, .... An essential sector is the chemical industry, but also areas such as oil and gas, surface technology, mechanical engineering, pharmaceuticals, food, cosmetics, ... are included. PFAS affects our products mainly in the form of fluoropolymers as  - Sealing material (FKM, FFKM, PTFE, FEP)  - Housing and rotor material (PVDF, ETFE)  - Wetted bearing and seal materials (PTFE) The extent to which PFASs are also relevant as auxiliary materials in production has not yet been conclusively clarified for us.  What all the sectors mentioned have in common with regard to our products is that a high level of chemical resistance, in some cases under thermal stress, is necessary in order to fulfill the large number of tasks. Non-PFAS containing materials do not meet these requirements according to the state of the art today.  Our products are exclusively B2B products and are not used in the consumer sector. Exposure does not occur during normal operation.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: No exposure to PFAS is to be expected during the manufacture and use of our products. We cannot assess the disposal itself, however, with legal framework conditions such as WEEE and SCIP database, sufficient tools should be available to dispose of substances of concern in a targeted and sustainable manner.

6. Missing uses: At the moment we are not able to make statement about tonnage. Emissions do not occur in the normal use of the products.  For our products PFAS are mainly used in the following areas:  - FKM, FFKM, FEP for static and dynamic seals.    ○ Due to the very good chemical properties in particular, the materials cannot be replaced for a wide range of applications.    ○ Alternative materials with poorer chem. Properties lead to earlier pump failure and failure when using different pumping media. Since our core products are hand-operated, this would result in an immediate hazard to the operator.   ○ We alternatively offer our products with e.g. EPDM. And NBR seals. However, the share of core products sold with these variants is only about 16%, despite the lower cost. The remaining 84% included PFAS as a sealing material, as application requirements cannot otherwise be met.  - PVDF, ETFE as materials for housing components and rotors    ○ To the best of our knowledge, there is no economical alternative that offers comparable chemical resistance with comparable mechanical properties. resistance with comparable mechanical properties. Without these materials, various applications with aggressive chemicals cannot be served.  - PTFE as bearing, diaphragm and sealing material   ○ In addition to the chemical advantages already mentioned, PTFE offers unique thermal and sliding properties. In addition to the chemical advantages already mentioned, the material offers unique thermal and sliding properties, without which dry-running properties and explosion protection requirements could not be implemented in our products. Alternative materials such as ceramics could not meet these requirements in tests. Our suppliers are not in a position to comment on possible future alternatives to these materials, as no alternative materials with the necessary properties are known to date or will be available in the foreseeable future.  Based on our knowledge of sales figures and customer applications, if these materials were banned, we would no longer be able to serve 80-90% of our customer requirements, which would inevitably lead to the loss of the business basis and the associated jobs.  Due to the chemical properties of these materials alone, a number of customer applications could no longer be solved, or only at great expense and with a large number of media-specific systems and pumps, which would no longer allow economic production.  Even if alternatives to fluoropolymers were developed in the near future, 18 months would be far from sufficient to adapt all production processes to them and to adequately qualify the new products. Different shrinkages in injection molding, for example, would very likely lead to a reworking of the molds with extensive qualification and recertification of the end products, which in turn would be associated with high costs and time expenditure.

Use of fluoropolymers in plastics masterbatches and compounds
Due to their unique chemical and physical properties, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) have been widely used in various industrial and commercial applications. Within the masterbatchers and compounders sector, we have registered the following fluoropolymer uses:
• PTFE for (missing use):
o High performance thermoplastic compounds for injection moulding articles of small dimensions, such as gears, lever arms, bushings and bearings, cams, pins, sliding surfaces, etc.; in a variety of industrial applications, mainly for chemical industries; and
o PTFE is a non-dripping agent often used together with a flame retardant polymer applications (E&E).
• PVDF HFP (Poly(vinylidene fluoride-co-hexafluoropropylene CAS 9011-17-0) ;
• 1-Propene, 1,1,2,3,3,3-hexafluoro-, polymer with 1,1-difluoroethene and tetrafluoroethene, CAS 25190-89-0)
o Those 2 fluoropolymers are used as additive allowing thin polyolefin film extrusion (identified use not derogation proposed). See our brief on fluoropolymers in plastics packaging and food contact materials and fluoropolymers in construction. We will therefore not focus on those in this briefing.

Toxicity
Fluoropolymers are very stable because of their intrinsic physicochemical properties. If lost in the environment, they are therefore currently considered as persistent. However, they do not display any hazardous property/property of concern referred to by the dossier submitter; i.e., bioaccumulation, mobility, long-range transport potential (LRTP), accumulation in plants, ecotoxicity, endocrine activity/endocrine disruption, effects on human health and concerns triggered by a combination of these properties.
Moreover, PTFE, as a fluoropolymer, meets the OECD criteria for polymers of low concern [1]. Regarding residual monomers in articles made from fluoropolymers, it is theoretically possible that small quantities of residual monomers can migrate from finished products.

[1] Henry, B.J., Carlin, J.P., Hammerschmidt, J.A., Buck, R.C., Buxton, L.W., Fiedler, H., Seed, J. and Hernandez, O. Fluoropolymers should be excluded from the scope of the restriction
Based on the non-toxic properties described above, fluoropolymers should in our view be excluded from the scope of this restriction. We however provide additional information showing both its negligible emission and the disproportionate socio-economic impact that would be linked to its substitution.

In case fluoropolymers would not be derogated, the following minimum transition periods should be considered:
High performance thermoplastic compounds for injection moulding articles of small dimensions: Minimum 10 years
Use as non-dripping agent in combination with flame retardant (E&E): 3 years
Use of fluoropolymer additives for thin polyolefin films extrusion (see separate submission on packaging and FCM):

Related emissions during converting and service life Concerning the fluoropolymer manufacturing stage, the Fluoropolymers Product Group (FPG) of Plastics Europe established a program focusing on the emission reduction of non-polymeric PFAS chemicals from European fluoropolymer manufacturing, including average emission targets, promoting state-of-the-art technologies to minimize emissions and a commitment to inform downstream users of fluoropolymers on their safe handling of fluoropolymer resins [10]. During the masterbatching, compounding and converting stage, the spillage of pellets is negligeable, there is only presence of dustiness; although air filters reduce the risk of emitting dust, as well as the presence of filters in water drains prevents the emission into water. Regarding potential emissions during the service life, the risk is negligible given the low migration rate of PTFE from the polymeric matrix. Moreover, the risk of emissions during the end-of-life is low if properly handled. Missing uses: 6.1 Analysis of Alternatives: technical properties PTFE is used in plastic compounds due to their low friction, chemical resistance, high temperature, resistance, electrical insulation, flame retardancy, chemical inertness, etc; which makes them hard to be substituted in many cases. For the aforementioned applications, using alternatives would lead to different products, changing the characteristics of these, and in some cases, bringing very different products to those with PTFE.  High performance thermoplastic compounds for injection moulding articles of small dimensions  One potential alternative to be analysed is Ultra-High Molecular Weight Polyethylene (UHMWPE). While UHMWPE shares some similarities with PTFE (Polytetrafluoroethylene), such as low friction properties, there are important differences between the two materials that make them suitable for different applications. Whether UHMWPE can replace PTFE depends on the specific requirements of the application.    Here are some key points to consider: • Friction and Wear: Both UHMWPE and PTFE have low coefficients of friction and excellent wear resistance. However, PTFE typically has a slightly lower coefficient of friction, making it an even better choice for applications where minimizing friction is critical. • Chemical Resistance: PTFE is known for its exceptional chemical resistance and can withstand a wider range of chemicals compared to UHMWPE. If the application involves exposure to aggressive chemicals, PTFE may be the better choice. • Temperature Resistance: PTFE has a higher temperature resistance compared to UHMWPE. PTFE can handle continuous temperatures up to around 260°C, while UHMWPE has a lower continuous use temperature, typically around 82°C. • Load-Bearing Capacity: UHMWPE tends to have a higher load-bearing capacity and impact resistance than PTFE. This makes UHMWPE a better choice for applications involving heavy loads or impact forces. • Processing speed: Similar processing speed may not be achieved with UHMWPE. This leads to higher reject rates or risk in compromising final product quality.
