General Comments: For more than 100 years, pharmaceutical companies such as Pfizer have utilised chemical synthesis for the production of what are now known as ‘small molecule’ pharmaceuticals. The more recent biotechnology processes produce by biological synthesis large protein molecules and hence are considered as ‘large molecule’ production facilities. However, despite the strides made by biotechnology, ‘small molecule’ production remains a key subsector of pharmaceutical manufacturing with new products continuing to being developed. As an example, the Pfizer, Ringaskiddy manufacturing site, continues to be an important production resource within the Pfizer network. In the Republic of Ireland as a whole, there are a dozen such facilities known to PM Group, with several hundred located in the EU at large.  PM Group’s experience running globally to some hundred such facilities.
In the EU Commission’s own ‘Best Available Techniques Reference Document for the Organic Fine Chemicals Sector’, it is stated in its ‘scope’:
- The chemical industry is Europe’s third largest industry, employing 1.7 million people directly and with an additional 3 million jobs directly supporting the chemical industry. The Organic Fine Chemicals sector employ over 0.6 million people with a turnover of EUR 125000 million. Typical employers include large multinationals with organic fine chemical business units, but over 90 % of all sector companies are either middle-sized or SMEs.

The Pfizer, Ringaskiddy facility, along with other production sites for small molecules, falls within the scope of organic fine chemicals. Indeed, many companies in this organic fine chemicals sector operate equipment and utilise chemicals in a similar fashion to those dedicated to the manufacture of ‘small molecules’. The importance of this sector for ‘small molecules’ can be deducted from a 2009 report of the EU Commission entitled ‘ Pharmaceutical Sector Inquiry’, which was a time when ‘small molecule’ production still dominated pharmaceutical manufacturing.

- "The pharmaceutical sector is essential for the health of Europe's citizens who need access to innovative, safe and affordable medicines. On average approximately € 430 was spent on medicines in 2007 for each European and this amount will likely continue to increase as the population in Europe ages. Overall, in 2007, the market for prescription and non-prescription medicines for human use in the EU was worth over € 138 billion ex-factory and € 214 billion at retail prices. Put differently, the pharmaceutical market accounted for close to 2% of annual EU GDP."

As is explained in the next sections, a total ban on PFAS threatens the viability of the whole sector above.

The production of such ‘small molecules’ by chemical synthesis is a batch process. In a step by step process intermediates are reacted together and purified with isolation steps, such as crystallisation, to produce the ‘building blocks’ of the desired molecule. While these compounds are characterised by the carbon – carbon bonds of organic chemistry, the intermediate steps and compounds frequently contain inorganic compounds as side chains, which are the reactive sites for the subsequent chemical synthesis. A frequent by-product of such synthesis are salts, such as sodium chloride or other halogenated inorganics, formed from the reaction of these inorganic side chains. These have to be rinsed out of the crystallised organic compounds, which ultimately form the desired product.

Materials of Construction
Metallic Systems
Purity is an essential parameter with pharmaceutical production, which requires rigorous attention to ‘Good Manufacturing Practices’ (GMP). Product contact surfaces must therefore be smooth and cleanable. Such facilities manufacture products on a campaign basis and the equipment must be fully cleaned and free from residues before reconfiguration for producing a different product. Contact surfaces must therefore be smooth and free from penetration while also being highly chemical resistant to the aggressive nature of the chemicals it is exposed to. PTFE lined pipe and gaskets, Kalrez and Viton seals are all PFAS utilised in such facilities. While production equipment, such as reactor vessels, are either carbon steel with glass lining or highly polished metallic surfaces. This prevents materials adhering to the surfaces and facilitates the cleaning of the rig between batches.
Halogen compounds, particularly chlorides, are a regular feature in the reaction chemistry for production of ‘small molecules’. Such chlorides, even at low concentrations, will cause corrosion pitting of stainless steel, in which small cavities are eaten into the metal. Alloys like stainless steel, which are resistant to corrosion due to a passivation layer, are actually the most susceptible to pitting. If the passivation film is compromised and subsequently attacked by corrosion, the corrosion will not spread on the metal’s surface, but will instead penetrate inward. Pitting may cause stress cracking, and – if a pit occurs as a critical point – it can cause immense damage.

The most commonly used austenic grade stainless steel in pharmaceutical production is 316L (European designation 1.4404). This has 2% manganese, 16.5% to 18.5% chromium, 2% to 2.5% molybdenum, 10% to 13% nickel with the balance being iron (ferric). Yet it is highly susceptible to pitting corrosion once exposed to chlorides. To obtain corrosion resistance to chlorides one has to turn to Alloy 22, which is also sold under the brand names Hastelloy® C-22 and Inconel® 22. This is a fully austenitic nickel-based super alloy containing some 56% nickel, 22% chromium, 13 % molybdenum and 3% tungsten and 2.5% cobalt. While this is resistant to pitting corrosion, a corrosion rate is still occurring for Alloy 22 when exposed to halogenated inorganic compounds, such as chlorides. This rate being dependent on the operating temperature and properties of the compounds within the equipment.
Nickel is an expensive element, as are chromium, molybdenum, cobalt and tungsten. Therefore, it is not surprising that Hastelloy can be some five to eight times more expensive than equivalent components in stainless steel. Furthermore, with the advent of electric battery technology, there is greater competition for the available nickel and cobalt resources, leading to increased price pressure. In the pharmaceutical sector, Hastelloy is used to fabricate equipment, such as filter dryers and centrifuges, which have complex geometries and / or are involved in heat transfer.  However, the gaskets and seals used on flanges, valves and rotating shafts comprise elastomers made out of PTFE and other PFAS such as Kalrez and Viton. Without these, such flanges, valves and rotating shafts would be a source of regular leaks.

Piping Systems
Piping systems requiring corrosion resistance are generally assembled out of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) lined carbon steel pipe segments. These are available in straight sections, bends, tee pieces, etc., and are bolted together to achieve the required piping system. It is also possible to get flexible hoses made out of PTFE or similar corrosion resistant materials. While valves and similar fittings are also available made out of solid PTFE or similar PFAS, such as Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF).

Atmospheric Vessels and Scrubbers
In addition to lined piping systems, vessels not subject to heating requirements and scrubbing systems are fabricated out of sheets of PTFE or PVDF, supported by an outer body of Glass Reinforced Plastic (GRP). Such scrubbers are essential to treat process off gases and enable compliance with the stringent environmental emission limit values set for this sector

Sealing Compounds
PFA compounds are also used as elastomers for sealing, such as gaskets and O-rings. These offer excellent corrosion resistance and longevity, while being ductile enough to form a good seal. The requirement for such effective sealing is to fulfil a number of objectives. Environmentally it is necessary to prevent leaks of hazardous material occurring at rotating seals and equipment and piping joints. The effectiveness of such sealing also being an environmental objective to reduce diffuse emissions of Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs). For example, the Best Available Techniques (BAT) Conclusions for the ‘Common Waste Water and Waste Gas Treatment/Management Systems in the Chemical Sector’ require ‘High-integrity equipment’, which is highly sealed, and additional Leak Detection and Repair (LDAR) programmes.  Where such ‘high-integrity equipment’ includes:
- "high-integrity gaskets (such as spiral wound, ring joints) for critical applications;
- corrosion-resistant equipment".

In addition to purely environmental considerations, effective sealing is essential from the perspective of occupational hygiene. The manufacture of active pharmaceutical ingredients and intermediates by chemical synthesis requires the usage of aggressive chemicals, which often have low exposure limits and are frequently carcinogenic, mutagenic or toxic for reproduction. These latter legislative require a ‘closed system’ of processing, which cannot be realised without effective sealing compouds.

Alternatives
With regard to alternatives to pipe and equipment lined with PFA compounds and elastomers comprising of PFAS, these are limited.  A greater use of Hastelloy could be applied, but this comes with a significant cost penalty and delays to project schedules, while it is not suitable for highly acidic solutions of hydrochloric acid. For example, the Engineering Toolbox reports a price ratio of 1.5:1 for stainless steel to carbon steel piping, which increases to 3:1 for PTFE lined carbon steel and 4.5 to 1 for Hastelloy piping.  Therefore, there is a 150% price penalty in changing from PTFE lined pipe to Hastelloy. While as previously mentioned gaskets and seals would still need to be manufactured of PTFE and similar PFAS. In a similar fashion, for vessels constructed with a PTFE liner, an alternative would be Hastelloy, but this comes with a significant price penalty, while to reiterate the gaskets and seals would still have to remain as PTFE and similar PFAS.  These cost increases and delays to project schedule associated with the greater usage of Hastelloy will inevitably result in some projects being cancelled or relocated to other jurisdictions where PFAS are not banned.
For PFA elastomers, such as Kalrez, there is no effective replacement. As the Du Pont website claims with respect to the advantages of Kalrez:
- Resists over 1,800 different chemicals
- High temperature stability up to 327°C
- Maintains seal integrity
- Reduces maintenance and operating costs
- Long seal life
- Meets safety standards for pharmaceutical and food processing
- Available in standard and specialty compounds formulated for custom use

Implications of a Total Ban on PFAS
A total ban on PFAS would therefore severely affect pharmaceutical facilities operating in the ‘small molecule’ sector. In some cases, more expensive materials and longer schedules could offset this impact, but in other cases, there is no direct replacement. The net result of this blanket ban on PFAS would be to hamper investment in this sector in the EU and even lead to plant closures and relocation of manufacturing to outside the EU.

Life Cycle
To date limited consideration is given by the pharmaceutical sector to the life cycle of PFAS. In particular to the disposal of PFAS at the end of their life cycle. During the construction and installation phases and the piping / equipment usage, there are no direct emissions of PFAS to the environment. The potential for emissions only arises during the disposal of the system. To date the Pharmaceutical Sector adopts no special measures regarding disposal of PFAS, but these could be developed and implemented. In particular, as this sector has already sophisticated measures in place for dealing with hazardous waste. For example, the procedure for in line filters containing PFAS would already be removing them, bagging them up and disposing them by off-site incineration.

The first step in adopting such control measures would be to complete an inventory of PFAS on site. Then adopt suitable disposal methods when they have reached their end of life. In this manner, the impact of the PFAS on the environment would be greatly reduced.

Conclusion
A 2005 report by the Irish Pharmaceutical Healthcare Association, at which time the pharmaceutical sector was still dominated by small molecule production, documented how the sector formed 44% of the Republic of Ireland’s exports amounting to €34.7 billion.  The number of US Food and Drugs Administration (FDA) approved manufacturing facilities in the Republic of Ireland was 24, while 14 out of the 15 largest worldwide pharmaceutical companies were present in the Republic of Ireland.

For the sector as a whole in the EU, Eurostat was reporting in 2005 how in 2002 more than half a million people were employed in the pharmaceutical industry in the EU.  This corresponds, on average, to more than a quarter of the total number employed in the whole chemical industry.

A total ban on PFAS would severely threaten the viability of this sector in the EU and investment would more likely flow to outside the EU, where no such ban is applicable, such as to the USA or Singapore.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The Annex XV restriction report did not identify the sector to which Pfizer Ringaskiddy belongs, which is the chemical synthesis of pharmaceuticals. PM Group, who have prepared this submission on behalf of Pfizer Ringaskiddy, are one of the largest design and construction management companies for pharmaceutical facilities with offices in the EU, UK, Switzerland, India, China, Singapore and USA.  The production of pharmaceuticals and their intermediates can be based on either biological processes, which leads to large molecules like proteins, or chemical synthesis, which leads to complex small molecules. Chemical synthesis is the more traditional route, which utilises reactive chemicals requiring advanced materials of construction for equipment, such as for piping and vessels. Pfizer, Ringaskiddy, is one of a dozen significantly sized pharmaceutical manufacturing sites in the Republic of Ireland, with several hundred located in the EU as a whole. The importance of this sector to the European economy can be seen from a 2009 report of the EU Commission, which was a time when small molecule manufacturing still dominated this sector:  - "The pharmaceutical sector is essential for the health of Europe's citizens who need access to innovative, safe and affordable medicines. On average approximately € 430 was spent on medicines in 2007 for each European and this amount will likely continue to increase as the population in Europe ages. Overall, in 2007, the market for prescription and non-prescription medicines for human use in the EU was worth over € 138 billion ex-factory and € 214 billion at retail prices. Put differently, the pharmaceutical market accounted for close to 2% of annual EU GDP".  Therefore, this submission reflects the concerns of a wider sector rather than just Pfizer, Ringaskiddy. A sector characterised by a requirement for advanced materials of construction, which include PTFE and PDVF. While elastomers such as Perfluoroelastomer (FFKM/FFPM), e.g. Kalrez®, are also essential for ensuring sealing of equipment containing reactive chemicals.  Indeed, the absence of such materials of construction due to a ban on PFAS would effectively wipe out this sector of ‘small molecule’ manufacturing, as substitutes in these applications are not available for all of these PFAS. The importance of this sector now under threat is visible in other initiatives of the EU Commission, such as its pharmaceutical strategy for Europe.  In particular its Section 3.1 ‘Providing a fertile environment for Europe’s industry’:  - "A competitive and resource-efficient EU pharmaceutical industry is of strategic interest for public health, economic growth, jobs, trade and science. The EU aims to support industry to be competitive and resilient so that, in turn, it can better respond to patients’ needs".  Without access to PFAS as a construction material, ‘small molecule’ pharmaceutical production in the EU would have to close or relocate to other jurisdictions, which do not have such a ban on these materials of construction.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The use of PTFE and similar PFAS in the sector of chemical synthesis of pharmaceuticals is restricted solely to materials of construction. The only emissions arising occur when the equipment is disposed of. This could be either by incineration, landfilling or recycling. To date no special requirements are employed with the disposal of PTFE and similar compounds.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: No detailed information is available on this topic. However, to date most of the PTFE and similar compounds are disposed of when life expired.

5. Proposed derogations: Such tonnage is not available to Pfizer Ringskiddy as one of many end users. It would have to be obtained from the manufacturers of PTFE lined equipment and elastomers.

6. Missing uses: a. The tonnage of PFAS used as a construction material for pharmaceutical facilities is currently unknown.    c. PM Group would be aware of several hundred such pharmaceutical facilities operating in the EU. However, exact number not published.   d. The alternative to PTFE and PVDF as a material of construction is for certain, but not all applications, the use of high nickel alloy called Hastelloy. As the document submitted as an appendix shows, this is 1.5 times the cost of PTFE lined systems, such nickel alloys being in scarce supply. There are no equivalent materials for the use of PFAS in elastomers for sealing purposes.  e. PM Group is not aware of any R&D ongoing to the use of PFAS for elastomers for sealing purposes or as materials of construction in general.   f.i. The increased use of hastelloy as a construction material could potentially replace PTFE in this application, as could glass lined carbon steel. However, this would significantly add to the cost, with hastelloy being 1.5 time that of PTFE lined carbon steel and subject to longer delivery times.   g. For cases in which substitution is not technically or economically feasible, such as for the elastomers use as sealants, The consequences for Pfizer, Ringaskiddy and similar facilities would be increased failure of sealing systems, such as on pumps and agitators, leading to leakage of hazardous process fluids. Which is unacceptable from both an environmental and occupational hygiene perspective. Specific costs to the sector are not available, but over time, it would make the sector in the EU uncompetitive and lead to the relocation of investment to jurisdictions where PFAS were not banned. The importance of this sector having already been documented in the answer to Question 1 and the attachment to the submission.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: As an end user of PTFE and PDVF materials of construction and PFA based elastomers, Pfizer Ringaskiddy and similar facilities in this sector would find itself compromised on new projects and the maintenance of existing equipment, if the proposed ban on PFA products was to proceed. This would affect its ability to produce pharmaceutical products with the necessary quality and protection of the environment. Such a derogation is necessary to allow for upstream manufacturers to develop suitable alternatives to PTFE and PVDF materials of construction and PFA based elastomers.

8. Other identified uses: While nickel based alloys such as Hastelloy can be used for some, but not all, chlorine based chemistry it has a cost basis of 4.5 times that of steel and is subject to longer delivery times. Furthermore, new battery types also utilise nickel-based chemistry, so as the switch to electric vehicles occurs, there will be increased supply pressure on nickel resources.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: For more than fifty years FlexiFrance, subsidiary of TechnipFMC  , has been a leader in the design and industrial production of Subsea Flexible Pipes. These products, which are used in the oil and gas production fields offshore, are made of an assembly of polymeric barriers with corrosion-resistant steel wires. In many applications, they are the only viable solution for subsea oil and gas field development.
Since 2022, European Union has established the reduction of its energy dependencies as a priority. This objective will be met by establishing a new balance in the energy mix between conventional energy (oil and gas) and renewable energies, but also by diversifying our supply of conventional energy and in particular of gas. The maintenance   in Europe of industries such as Flexible Pipe Manufacturing is a key enabler to allow the continuation of the development of offshore fields that will participate to in this diversification, and to reduce our dependency to current state-controlled suppliers of offshore oil and gas.
The function of the polymeric barrier is to ensure the leakproofness    of the Flexible Pipe (hence preventing safety and environmental hazards incurred by oil or gas leakage in offshore environment) and is highly technical as it has to sustain exposure to aggressive fluids, high temperature and pressure variations, along with severe mechanical loadings. In case of operating temperature above 90°C, the use of fluoropolymer PVDF is compulsory. Today the proportion of Flexible Pipe with a PVDF polymeric barrier layer represents 30% of the market and this proportion is expected to increase taking into account the geological properties of the fields to be developed.
Any restriction of fluoropolymers in general and of PVDF in particular would consequently affect the manufacturing of flexible pipes in a very large proportion.  In most of the cases this will lead to the impossibility to develop new fields or to extend existing fields. Moreover, for existing fields, the impossibility to replace ageing Flexible Pipe may lead to premature field closure which could affect energy security and energy affordability for decades to come.
In the “Answer to Consultation” FlexiFrance is principally addressing the case of PVDF, this fluoropolymer being the main polymeric component for High Pressure High temperature flexible pipe. However, it should be pointed out that other components of flexible pipes with specific key functionality like thermal insulation, active heating, sealing with end fitting, etc.…, also require fluoropolymer and / or fluoroelastomer.
Since more than 10 years FlexiFrance is engaged in a program to reduce PFAS. Intensive work has been done to remove and qualify non friendly PFAS like PFOS and FlexiFrance is now in a position to use only  PVDF  PFAS surfactant free. In parallel several projects have been launched and are still active to find alternatives to PVDF, with no success yet to cover the required temperature range
PVDF,  and more generally fluoropolymers, due to their unique characteristics combining flexibility and high chemical resistance in temperature and pressure , are still the only known solutions to provide the safest operating parameters for remote subsea offshore oil fields where maintenance and intervention is extremely complicated.
FlexiFrance is also engaged with all the stakeholders to fully recycle or destruct PVDF waste avoiding accumulation of very persistent polymer in the environment.
For the reasons stated above FlexiFrance encourage to exclude fluoropolymers from the ban. At least the derogation period shall be increased to allow alternative materials /technology availability.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Sector: Petroleum and mining industry Sub-use: Flexible Pipes Principal components   1.  A wide range of fluoropolymer and fluoroelastomers are identified as being used in the oil and gas industry. The most common use for these materials in this sector is in the components of the equipment and piping used in extraction, transport, and storage of petroleum resources.  In particular, fluoropolymer and fluoroelastomers are essential material for key components in unbounded flexible pipe. For instance, Polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) is used as a pressure sheath which its primary function is to ensure containment of fluids and gases in the bore of the pipe throughout the service life for the pipe. PVDF is a chemically resistant polymer commonly used in flexible pipe design especially suitable for use at high pressure and temperatures.  Despite significant research, currently, there is no known substitute for PVDF.  Significant part (more than 50%) of offshore Gas and/or Oil fields could only be developed thanks to flexible pipe.  Any restriction or ban would have a devastating effect on energy accessibility, affordability and security  .   2. Other components of flexible pipes with key functionality : -Sealing systems at the end fitting of flexible pipes also commonly use fluoroplastics and fluoroelastomers. Specifically, the Fluoroelastomer (FKM) and Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) materials are used to maintain sealing systems functionality throughout pipe service life due to their unique properties such as High temperature resistance, High mechanical strength chemical resistance, corrosion resistance Inertness Non-adhesive/low friction resistance Low permeation Flexibility/ductility Light weight and Non-flammable. -Internal thermal screen made up of wrapped PTFE tapes can be used to protect the flexibles pipe layers against very high temperature (> 150°C) conveyed fluids. Without this technical solution some new high temperature fields development will be jeopardized   .  -In order to limit the use of chemicals injections for field flow assurance management, and thus limit environmental impact, pipe heating technologies have been developed to maintain the conveyed fluids at the appropriate temperature. These technologies rely on heating cables for which fluoropolymers, like FEP, are once again the only safe and efficient material to act as protection of the cable core. -PTFE based coatings are mandatory either for manufacturing process of flexible pipe or for anti corrosion purpose.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: 1°) Manufacturing : -Manufacturing of PVDF pellets.  TechnipFMC has engaged with its PVDF materials suppliers a transition to phase out the use of Fluorosurfactant from the formulation of the PVDF grades used for Flexible Pipe. The transition will be 100% complete in 2024. More data to be supplied by PVDF raw material suppliers.  -Extrusion of PVDF sheath layers from pellets.  As part of Flexible Pipe manufacturing, TechnipFMC is performing extrusion of PVDF in accordance with processing guide given by materials suppliers and association of plastic manufacturers. Especially the process temperature is kept between 200°C and 250°C which is a range of temperature at which there is no risk of decomposition (Ref: « Guide for the Safe Handling of Fluoropolymer Resins », June 2021, Plastics Europe)    .  -Thermoplastic wastes generated as part of Flexible Pipe manufacturing in France are totally handled by a company specialized in industrial waste management and recycling   .  2°)Use phase     -Flexible pipes are used for transporting hydrocarbons, and injection of fluids and water offshore. Flexible pipes are considered for the transport of CO2 and H2.   -As part of PVDF qualification for Flexible Pipe, ageing tests are performed in conditions that simulate transport of oil and gas in subsea applications. These tests indicate no loss of weight that could be related to PVDF decomposition even at high temperature (130°C and above). Consequently, no emission throughout typical 20-to-25-year service life of flexible pipes is expected.  3°) End of life phase Worldwide  -Section covered by end users (Oil and Gas Companies responsible for decommissioning in compliance with their local regulation).

5. Proposed derogations: For confidentiality purpose FlexiFrance will not share its consumption of PVDF. Nevertheless it is worthwhile  to emphasize that for the past 10 years the global annual consumption of PVDF within flexible pipe industry is estimated between 1,050 tons to 1,500 tons per year.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: PVDF fluoropolymers are one of the main material family used for the key extruded leakproofness   layer for flexible pipes conveying oil or gases in offshore fields. These materials have been selected and qualified through a very long (>10 years) and extensive process that demonstrated the unique performances of these polymers to resist to the harshest fields fluids conditions: high temperatures (up to 150°C) high pressures (up to 1500 bars) and highly chemically aggressive fluids. PVDF fluoropolymers are used whenever the others oil and Gas qualified polymers (HDPE, XLPE, PA) are no longer suitable due to technical limitations. PVDF fluoropolymers are one of the main enabler for the transition towards the Gas exploitation, more sustainable than Oil, as offshore Gas exploitation requests very high performances materials due to higher pressure and temperature of the fluids. The leakproofness layer of the flexible pipe (also called pressure sheath) requires a suitable level of stiffness and elongation properties to stay compatible with the requested flexibility of the overall flexible pipe product. Mechanical property of material such as metallic materials, ceramic, but also high stiffness and low ductility polymers like PEEK are not compatible with these constrains. The other alternative polymer materials are not compatible to the use at high temperature and high pressure under oil or gas fluid environnementenvironment. As PVDF is an expensive material we are already using alternative polymer materials whenever it is possible. But above approximately 100°C we do not have any alternative solution but PVDF. Once a strong technical alternative for pressure sheath material is identified, which is clearly not the case today (and should take many years or even will never happen), API 17J requires an exhaustive material characterization, including many small-scale tests, but also many full scale tests to demonstrate the good behavior of the polymer layer within the flexible pipe. These full scale tests request to first manufacture full multilayer lengths of flexible pipe, and then to perform various long term tests representing the oil & gas fields conditions. This overall qualification test campaign request 3 to 5 years to be completed. It should be highlighted that Flexible pipe materials must be qualified according to a number of international standards such as API 17J, ISO 13628, NORSOK M-710 ...   , and certified by third parties. Flexible pipe must also be validated according to some customer’s technical specifications. PFAS prohibition would be detrimental to the continuity of Flexi France business. Flexi France is employing 820 people, with a regular revenue of 150M€. Between 30 to 50% of its Projects are manufactured with PVDF raw material and would therefore be removed from its business with the prohibition.

General Comments: For technical reasons, GEA’s Heating and Refrigeration Technology Division is highly dependent on the materials PTFE, EPDM, and FFKM. Without these materials, key components of our products will not meet regulatory and technical requirements and the development of innovative, sustainable products to reduce fossil energy consumption will be affected. Our products provide heat and cold in many key industries worldwide. These include the food and beverage industries, pharmaceutical applications, renewable resources, chemical applications, ware housing and logistics, marine, oil and gas applications and many other similar industries, as well as heating and cooling in real estate.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: These include the food and beverage industries, pharmaceutical applications, renewable resources, chemical applications, ware housing and logistics, marine, oil and gas applications and many other similar industries, as well as heating and cooling in real estate.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: I do not have information about the emissions during production of the materials.  In our production, almost no further processing takes place, apart from rare, minimal machining of surfaces. Debris is collected, no further emissions. During service/operations no emissions occur, particles from minimal wear of the materials will be collected in system filtration. At end of life, materials are disposed and mostly incinerated, but could be collected separately in the future, and recycled if processes are available.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Incineration temperatures need to be high enough to degrade the materials, in countries, where waste is disposed in land fills, these products will remain solid (persistent) and are not expected to harm the environment.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Material containing PFAS is very small compared to total mass, and respective materials could be separated in recycling process.

6. Missing uses: 1. Affected Component PTFE  Shaft seals /Bushings / Seal Seats / Piston Rings / Flat Seals / Gaskets FEPM  Seals / O-Rings  FFKM  Seals / O-Rings  AFM  Flat Seals / Gaskets … in industrial heating and refrigeration systems and gas compression facilities.  2. Sector of the affected Component Industrial and large-scale refrigeration: Refrigeration for industrial processes e.g., food, beverage, pharmaceutical, chemical, ware housing, marine, as well as for climatization in larger building complexes and recreational facilities.  Industrial and large-scale heating: Heat pumps for industrial processes e.g., food, beverage, pharmaceutical, chemical, as well as for heating of communal neighborhoods or in larger building complexes and recreational facilities.  Industrial gas compression e.g., chemical, petro-chemical industries.  3. Key Functionality of the affected Component Static and dynamic sealings, seal seats and bushings: Heating and refrigeration systems consist of screw or piston compressors, oil separators, various heat exchangers, vessels, valves and fittings in the complex distribution and control system, as well as electric propulsion, actuation, sensors, and electric and electronic controls. Static and dynamic sealings, seal seats and bushings play an integral role for the safety and efficiency of the equipment, as they guarantee system tightness and separation of refrigerants, lubricants, and other media at low friction. Depending on the application of the respective system, hot components on the high-pressure side of the systems can reach 120 - 160°C already today, and in our research, we are even experimenting with temperatures >200°C to make heat pumps available for certain industrial applications. On the cold side of the system, temperatures can go down below -60°C. System pressures vary between 26 bar up to 60 bar and more, which causes respective mechanical loads on sealings. Chemical resistance against refrigerants e.g., ammonia, hydrocarbons, and lubricants need to be ensured over the entire range of conditions.  Reliability and longevity of refrigeration systems and heat pumps are very important to ensure continuous supply of cold and heat in these large-scale processes at a maximum of energy efficiency. The service life of our products is typically more than 30 years and customers expect wide maintenance intervals with predictable measures, hence the availability of spare parts must be guaranteed over the entire life cycle of the products.  4. Amount of Fluoropolymers used for the affected Component The amount of fluoropolymers and their compounds is very small compared with the total mass of heating and refrigeration systems, but still they play an integral role in the functionality. The total mass of PTFE components in our products is in the order of 1000 kg per year, the remaining sealings containing fluoropolymers and their compounds have a total mass in the order of 100 kg year.   5. Replacing PFAS in the affected Component Alternative materials do not exist.  5.1. Materials which may be used as alternatives: none 5.2. Amount of material replaceable with 5.1. none 5.3. Amount of material not being replaceable All 5.4. Problems and Risks if Material(s) 5.1. is used:  PTFE: No alternative over the same range of applications/conditions is available. PEEK might be a candidate for some applications, but has not been validated, yet. The mechanical properties of PEEK are different from PTFE. FEPM and FFKM: We are using these compounds only when our standard materials HNBR and CR are no longer compatible with the physical and chemical conditions in the respective applications. These applications include more extreme temperatures and increased pressures to widen the range of heat pumps and refrigeration systems to further reduce the use of fossil energy in the industries. These applications have partly been made available because of the beneficial material properties of fluoropolymers.  6. Consequences of Banning Fluoropolymers in the affected Component A ban of PTFE would be a large throwback in the heating and refrigeration technology and would require significant re-design, validation, and certification of alternative materials, once these are available. It would also add significant costs to a variety of our products. Spare-part availability over the next decades is also important for the systems in operation already, to ensure a reliable supply of cold and heat. A loss of high-performance sealing materials e.g., FEPM and FFKM would limit the range of applications in the heat pump business significantly. This would have an impact on the entire industry transformation away from fossil energy towards a more sustainable future using excessive heat for processes and heating. These technologies offer a great opportunity to reduce CO2 emissions and are already factored into the assumptions and models to reduce global warming.  The before mentioned materials play an important role in GEAs Heating and Refrigeration Technologies Division with an annual revenue of 524 M€ in 2022, and approximately 1750 FTEs. Not only the future of our industry, but also our customers’, is depending on a reliable and economically feasible supply of cold and heat over a broad range.

8. Other identified uses: The machinery industry provides equipment to the entire industry. This large segment with all its sub-uses has been ignored in the proposal. This has to be reconsidered including the feedback from respective industries. Additionally, during my research, I got the impression that also the electric and electronic industries have not been taken into account, but will highly be affected as well. I assume respective feedback will be given from these parties. However, a ban of PFAS will have a very negative impact on the supply of this equipment.  These industries are the motor for the EU's economy.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: For the following reasons, the use of fluoropolymers as the cladding material for single-mode plastic optical fibers (SI-POF) employing PMMA in the core should be exempted from the proposed regulations.

- Assumptions -
SI-POF uses the principle of total internal reflection when light enters from a high refractive index material to a low refractive index material, exceeding the critical angle.
Therefore, it has a structure where the high refractive index light guiding material (core) is surrounded by a low refractive index material (cladding), and a numerical aperture (NA), as determined by the following equation, of approximately 0.5 is required,

NA = (n1^2 – n2^2)^(1/2)
n1: refractive index of core, n2: refractive index of cladding

- (1) Significance of POF -
Compared to glass optical fibers, plastic optical fibers (POF) possess superior mechanical strength and significantly larger diameters. Therefore, when applied in key applications such as inter-equipment communication cables, optical sensors, medical devices, lighting, and automotive components, the use of POF is essential to mitigate potential issues including damage, communication disruptions, malfunctioning sensing systems, and medical accidents due to fiber breakage within the body.
(*Standard Diameter: POF 1000μm, Glass Fiber 125μm)

Hence, substituting glass optical fibers with POF is impracticable, as POF is the indispensable material for these applications. Inter-equipment communication and optical sensors are extensively integrated into various production facilities, including semiconductor manufacturing equipment and industrial machinery, making POF a critically important material. Additionally, POF finds application in numerous medical devices, including those used in ophthalmic surgery, solidifying its status as an essential material within the healthcare industry.

- (2) Significance of PMMA core -
The core of POF naturally requires high transparency, and among practical resins, PMMA theoretically possesses the highest level of transparency. Applying resins other than PMMA would result in significant performance deterioration. Therefore, the use of non-PMMA resins is extremely limited to exceptional applications, and PMMA remains the only core resin that meets practical performance requirements.

- (3) Significance of Fluoropolymer cladding -
In practical terms, a numerical aperture (NA) of POF is required to be equal to or greater than 0.5. The refractive index of PMMA is 1.492, and when combined with the previously mentioned equation, it is necessary for the refractive index of the cladding to be 1.4 or lower.

NA = (1.492^2 – n2^2)^(1/2) ≥ 0.5
∴ n2 ≥ 1.405

Considering the Lorentz-Lorenz equation, it can be deduced that only fluoropolymers and silicone satisfy this requirement. However, silicone exhibits extremely poor adhesion with PMMA, making it unsuitable for use as a cladding material. Therefore, apart from fluoropolymers, there are no other materials available for use as the cladding.

- (4) Conclusion -
As mentioned earlier, POF is being used as an irreplaceable component in various industries, and its core must be made of PMMA. Therefore, the use of fluoropolymer as the cladding material for POF employing PMMA as the core is essential. Consequently, it is necessary to exempt the use of fluoropolymer as the cladding for POF with PMMA core from the proposed regulations.

*For details about basic principles and characteristics of POF, please refer to [Ref1].
*For details about low refractive index polymers, please refer to [Ref2].

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Not listed in the Table 9., however, fluoropolymers are generally used as cladding layer of Plastic Optical Fiber, what cannot be replaced by any other materials not containing fluorine.

6. Missing uses: a) Fluoropolymers; estimated from the market size, approximately 100 tons/year.  b) The fluorine polymer cladding layer covers the PMMA core of Plastic Optical Fiber.  Fluorine polymer exhibits the characteristic of low refractive index; which allows for total internal reflection to occur at the interface due to the refractive index difference with the PMMA core. This enables the realization of plastic optical fibers using PMMA core.    c) Several companies as Plastic Optical Fiber manufacturers. Hundreds of companies as primary users. Because Plastic Optical Fiber is widely used; for industrial sensors, medical equipment, data communication, illumination, automotive parts, endoscope products and so on, it is difficult to estimate the number of final users who will be affected by the restriction. For example, fiber optic sensors are used in almost all semiconductor manufacturers.  d) Because the refractive index of PMMA is about 1.492, the refractive index of the cladding layer should be 1.40 or lesser to achieve NA 0.5 or more. There is no material that achieves such a low refractive index without fluorine.  e) Considering the Lorentz–Lorenz equation, it would be impossible to achieve such a low refractive index without fluorine.  f) Impossible to be replaced by non-fluorine polymer.  g) Because Plastic Optical Fiber is widely used; for industrial sensors, medical equipment, data communication, illumination, automotive parts, endoscope products and so on, it is difficult to estimate the number of final users who will be affected by the restriction. Combined Comments:
General Comments: For the manfacturing of medicinal products, there needs to be an unlimited exemption for the use of fluoropolymers.

Specifically, for the manufacturing of sterile medicinal products, the inertness of fluoropolymers is essential for the quality of the products. Fluoropolymers are used in tubing for the transfer of product solution in compounding and on filling lines, so as a manufacturing aid (mainly PTFE), and for the sterile filtration of solutions (PVDF). Furthermore, PTFE-coated stoppers in vials and syringes play a significant role in the stability of the products by blocking the interaction of the product with constituents of the rubber stoppers (direct product contact over the full shelf live). For the manufacturing of sterile medicinal products, purified water is needed for preparation steps and as feedwater for the distillation units for water for injection. The manufacturing of purified water is usually done by reverse osmosis, and the membranes for this process are made of PTFE.
The machines for manufacturing processes also use PFAS, in regard to their inertness, their low friction characteristics and heat resistance in sterilization processes.
There are no alternatives available for PTFE and PVDF in the manufacturing of sterile medicinal products.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Table 9 in Annex XV of the Restriction Report lists many uses but does not cover the manufacture of medicinal products.  The section on medical devices does not cover medicinal products.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: a.) This needs to be answered by organisations like VCI, vfa or EFPIA. b.) Manufacturing aids such as PTFE tubes are disposable materials and are incinerated or thermally destroyed as pharmaceutical waste. The same applies to the filled dosage forms after use (contaminated hospital waste). Recycling and landfilling are therefore not applicable.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: See previous section: no emissions due to incineration of all waste.

5. Proposed derogations: See previous section: no emissions due to incineration of all waste.

6. Missing uses: Annex A only describes a general research on the use in Medicinal products and lists active pharmaceutical ingredients (API) i.e. drug substances. The use of fluropolymers as manufacturing aid in the form of gaskets, valves and tubing are not mentioned. Also not mentioned is the use of fluoropolymers as filter membranes for the sterile filtration of sterile medicinal products. Finally, the use of fluoropolymer-coatings on primary packaging components like stoppers for syringes and vials is not mentioned and application in membranes for the reverse osmosis process. All uses are essential for the quality and purity of sterile medicinal products. a.) Needs to be answered by the associations like VCI, vfa or EFPIA b.) The key functionality of the fluoropolymers in the uses described above are the inertness and barrier function.  c.) Needs to be answered by the associations like VCI, vfa or EFPIA d.) There are no alternatives available, nor are we aware of any alternatives being developed by the suppliers. Vetter did interview all key suppliers and this was confirmed (please see the attached exemplary statement by a supplier). Besides, all direct and indirect product contact parts are described in the pharmaceutical dossiers and consequently would have to go through world-wide time-consuming and expensive change control processes. If alternatives were available, these would have to be tested for compatibility with the medicinal products, including stability studies, issuance of the change controls to the regulatory bodies and approval. This is a process which in general takes 3-5 years for global products. e.) Vetter has no information on the status of R&D for suitable alternatives, none of the suppliers was indicating that they are working on alternatives. This is particularly true for PTFE as direct product contact material and tubing/gaskets/valves used in the fill-finish process of sterile medicinal products. f.) See point e.) g.) The socio-economic impact for patients is enormous. The medicinal products that Vetter fills for the pharma-and biopharma companies are used in indications like:  • Cancer • Diabetes • Rheumatoid Arthritis • Multiple Sclerosis • Macular Degeneration • Atopic Dermatitis • Hemophilia • Growth disorders • Migraine • Asthma • Anemia • Alzheimers Disease • Hepatitis • Immunological Disorders • Morbus Crohn • Collitis ulcerosa • Osteoporosis • Psoriasis • Thrombosis • Prevention of transplants (organs) • Infertility • Liver Diseases • Erectile Dysfunction • Enzyme Replacement • Many orphan indications • Etc. If these products were no longer available, millions of patients would remain untreated. Sterile medicinal products currently represent more than half of the prescription medicines market worldwide by value.  The impact on the pharmaceutical industry would be devastating.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: As mentioned above, there are no alternatives available or under development that could replace fluoropolymers as processing aids in the manufacture of sterile medicinal products and as parts in direct contact with the product, such as stoppers for vials and syringes.

8. Other identified uses: For the use of fluoropolymers in the manufacturing of sterile medicinal products, an unrestricted exemption is mandatory.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: For the specific uses of R-513A and other F-gases in refrigeration systems which are used in Nuclear Power Plants ("NPP"), we hereby demand an exemption. These safety chillers are essential for the safe operation of nuclear power plants. To protect against external influences, the refrigerant systems are installed inside the power plant building. Therefore, alternatives with higher toxicity and flammability are not accepted to implement by the operators and authorities of Nuclear Power Plants. Nuclear safety standards and building codes complicate the use of existing refrigerant alternatives. The design and qualification of the chiller takes several years. Any retrofitting suggestion of existing chillers from F-gas refrigerants to natural refrigerants are especially for Nuclear Power Plants chillers not thinkable - not only for technical, but especially for safety reasons. It should be noted that the quantities of F-gases required for chillers for Nuclear Power Plants are very small in relation to the total quantity of refrigerant required in the EU.
For the above reasons and in context with the EU-wide security of energy supplies, this exemption should be valid time-unlimited.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Refrigeration

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Due to the long service life of Nuclear Power Plants, the selected refrigerant remains in the refrigeration circuit for a long time (use phase up to 60 years). After this time, the refrigerant is professionally removed by refrigeration specialists and handed over to specialist companies for reprocessing. Refrigerant quantity per chiller to be recycled at end-of-life-phase: dependent on chiller type, refrigerant charge varies from few kg to several tons per chiller.  For safety chillers, the leak tightness is constantly monitored by a permanently installed gas detection device (leakage detection system). Additionally, leak tests of the chillers have to be carried out by an expert (skilled/trained person) at least every six months in accordance with EN517/2014. Tightness criteria according to EN378 (max. 3 g /year) is given. Gas detection devices of the safety chillers are usually connected to the emergency power supply. It can therefore be assumed that almost the total charge of each chiller will remain in the chiller until the end of the system's life (up to 60 years), provided no unforeseen damage occurs. Refrigerant disposal at the end of lifetime of each chiller must be carried out by a certified recycling company in accordance with EN517/2014.

5. Proposed derogations: In chillers the fluorinated refrigerants are not consumables in the sense of constantly causing emissions to the environment. Instead, the refrigerant is cycling through the closed refrigerant circuit. PFAS products may only be built in the environment if any leakage occurs and refrigerant escapes from the closed circuit.

6. Missing uses: to g) A ban of safety refrigerants (F-gases) for chillers which are installed in NPPs would negatively affect the European efforts to decarbonize the power generation. Without a safe and long-lasting permission for service works on NPP chillers and the commissioning of new chillers containing safety refrigerants for new NPP, we as chiller manufacturer are not able to guess what monetary and socio-economic impact this would have on the EU as a whole.   The potential alternatives of safety refrigerants for chillers are hazardous in the sense of flammability, explosivity in certain concentrations with ambient air or requirement of high pressures. The latter alternative however requires plant-specific features which do either not correspond with the safety philosophy of NPP.  In the unlikely, but potential possible situation of a hazardous situation in one of the European NPPs it would make the situation worse if chillers with the aforementioned alternative refrigerants would tighten the already exceptional situation.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: For chillers that do not have to meet the high safety requirements in a nuclear power plant, there are reasonable alternatives.  However nuclear safety standards and building codes complicate the use of existing refrigerant alternatives: the alternatives are not in line with the otherwise very high safety standards.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: For twenty years, we have been manufacturing heating blades providing cutting and welding functions for tubes made of thermoplastic elastomer.
These heating blades are mounted on a device which allows welding to be carried out. The heating part of these blades made via a thin steel sheet (0.2 mm), measuring 125 x 40 mm, is coated on each of these faces with PTFE.
We sell around 1000 pieces per year of these heating blades fitted to our welding devices because these blades have a limited lifespan (200 welding operations).
This tube heat-sealing process is mainly used by the pharmaceutical industry. It ensures and maintains sterility throughout the welding cycle, the latter being carried out with a blade temperature around 210°C.
The PTFE coating helps prevent molten thermoplastic from sticking to the blade during the welding cycle.
This welding process has been approved by our customers who are companies in the biopharmaceutical industry and changing it will involve an approval period which could be very long.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: As explained above, it seems difficult to remove the PTFE coating and replace it with another type. We have carried out tests with ceramic deposits but the non-adhesion performance is much lower and remains unacceptable.

Combined Comments: Forbrugerrådet Tænk (The Danish Consumer Council) warmly welcomes and supports the proposal to restrict all PFAS. The proposal thoroughly outlines the crisis that the use of PFAS is causing. The proposal speaks for itself. The effects on the environment and our health are well documented. The Swedish NGO Chemsec recently calculated that the costs for society (€16 trillion) easily exceed the profits for the industry (€26 billion) globally. Indeed, also from an economic perspective it is time to act.  This restriction is overdue and desperately needed.  Scope and environmental emissions We generally support the restriction proposal, which will ensure better environment and safety for human health. We support the scope, but would wish that it also included biocides and pesticides. . Spreading PFAS directly into nature via biocides and pesticides makes no sense, and ultimately may cause harm in the environment. Allowing PFAS in the future would also go against the principles of circular economy. PFAS will contaminate future products if they are recycled in them. Another important reason to ban them all together.  Information on alternatives Forbrugerrådet Tænk Kemis testing for PFAS in consumer goods confirms that these substances are used in a wide variety of products that consumers are in daily contact with, but the tests also show that are many widely available alternatives that do not contain PFAS. In 2015 and 2016 we tested food contact materials and found PFAS in a lot of products. This among other tests and knowledge gathered by the Danish Food Authorities resulted in a ban on all PFAS in food contact materials in Denmark in July 2020. Today Danish consumers do not lack any of the products they had before the ban, which means that substituting PFAS in food contact materials is indeed possible.  A test conducted in 2021 with our consumer NGO colleagues in Europe we showed that it is indeed possible to phase out the PFAS, and that bans work. The test showed, that in Denmark, where the use of PFAS in paper and board food packaging had been banned since July 2020, none of the sampled French fries’ bags from McDonald’s, for example, exhibited any PFAS treatment. This is in contrast to the results for the same items sampled in the Czech Republic and the United Kingdom. These findings illustrate that regulations are an effective tool to protect people from exposure to harmful chemicals and to push industry players to find safe replacements. However, this also highlights the lack of EU-wide harmonised regulation and protection when it comes to food contact materials. "Consumer products"

General Comments: Forensic science currently uses a PFAS called HFE7100 for the recovery of fingermarks from porous surfaces. The manufacturer, 3M, has declared that this product will be discontinued from the end of 2025 and a new alternative is required. In 2018 I published some work about an alternative that provided good results, Solstice PF from Honeywell which had a much lower GWP and persisted in the environment for a period of days rather than years. Unfortunately Solstice PF however falls under the definition of PFAS. Currently we are undertaking some research related to other alternatives but there are certain requirements for these, they must be volatile, non-flammable, readily available, low GWP, non ozone depleting. Some countries have reported the use of petroleum ether however this is flammable and considering the evidence is then processed in an oven, there are clear issues with this. Current research is aimed at removing the use of solvents completely and to apply the active ingredient via other means such as fuming/transfer/vacuum.

Combined Comments: "Elevated levels of PFAS have been found in Östersund municipality in Storsjön, especially around Frösön, in Göviken, and in Lillsjön. It is primarily in perch, but also partially in whitefish. The data for grayling and pike is more limited, but has also shown elevated levels in some fish and locations. Therefore, these are also included in the recommendations. However, the levels of PFAS in trout and Arctic char in Storsjön were low. Our national agency has measured the levels of PFAS in freshwater fish in Storsjön, the area where my family and I live and fish. The nationally allowable threshold is currently 8 ng/g wet weight in fish muscle tissue for PFAS4, that is for the combined levels of PFOS, PFOA, PFHxS and PFNA, and unfortunately the measured levels exceed this. The suspected source of the PFAS is a military and civilian airport where fire extinguishing training exercises have used substances containing high levels of PFAS. That this set of chemicals is found in northern Swedish lakes and rivers, where the main water source is runoff from the relatively pristine mountain and alpine range between the borders of Norway and Sweden an hour away, is devastating. The region prides itself on access to clean nature areas and resources, and is thus attractive for nature tourism and sustainable sport fishing. The national recommendations are now NOT to consume fish from these areas more than once or twice a year. Both my family and our fellow villagers have eaten fish from the nearby rivers and lakes almost weekly - even in the winter, when we ice fish - for generations. That we now risk our own health and the health of several generations after us because of a fire extinguishing substance used in training is the definition of unsustainable development. This chemical must be stopped immediately and replaced with something that does not cause harm. There is NO acceptable motive for creating and using such substances when the damage is so apparent, widespread, and long-lived. We implore you to place a total ban on PFAS substances immediately."
