General Comments: Founded in 2009, Rivian is an independent company headquartered in the United States with a growing European footprint. With over 14,000 employees across the globe, Rivian’s focus is the design, development, manufacture, and distribution of all-electric vehicles, including both passenger vehicles and commercial vans. Our vehicles will displace some of the most polluting passenger vehicles on the road today.

As an electric vehicle (“EV”) manufacturer with an eye toward decarbonization and the stewardship of our planet for future generations, Rivian recognizes the importance of this proposal and ECHA’s efforts for environmental protection. However, we are concerned that, as proposed, Restriction Option 2 puts zero-emission powertrain technology at an unnecessary disadvantage to internal combustion engine automotive technology, contradicting broader EU climate and sustainability goals. Given the emissions reductions associated with the electrification of the passenger vehicle fleet, it’s important that this restriction not counteract the ongoing global policy efforts to lead industry toward EVs [see: https://www.europarl.europa.eu/news/en/headlines/economy/20221019STO44572/eu-ban-on-sale-of-new-petrol-and-diesel-cars-from-2035-explained ]. Accordingly, Rivian is concerned about the exclusion of EVs from the proposed derogations where ICEVs are included, such as that for mobile air conditioning (MAC) refrigerants, and the absence of use cases and proposed derogation for EV lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) in the proposed restriction of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) under the REACH regulation.

The socio-economic analysis of the proposed PFAS restriction should consider the role of EVs as a tool to mitigate climate change. Delaying the benefits of EVs by banning the materials used in lithium-ion battery cathodes, enabling an unfounded competitive advantage for internal combustion engines (“ICEVs”) through one-sided derogations, and bottlenecking critical parts of the automotive supply chain could result in missed emissions reduction targets. While Rivian recognizes the need for action on PFAS, it’s critical that this action doesn’t come at the expense of the transition to a low-carbon economy.

The lack of readily available drop-in alternatives for refrigerant 1234yf, without complete system redesign, is not unique to ICEV MAC systems, and by only offering a derogation to combustion engine vehicles the restriction creates a competitive disadvantage for EVs. We are currently developing our next generation platform of vehicles and need to make decisions for the thermal system in the next 3-4 months. Uncertainties about the ability to utilize a single system for both US and European regions impacts our sourcing strategies and may delay our execution as much of the industry is not ready to implement the recommended system designs. An ICEV-only exemption is counter-productive to transportation decarbonization and could shift ICEV volume to the EU. Similarly, there are no readily available replacements for PVDF, PTFE, and FEC as they are used in lithium-ion batteries, again setting the terms of RO2 oppositional to other environmental policy efforts. Rivian encourages the commission to explore offering these use cases the maximum 13.5-year derogation to avoid delaying electrification at the expense of climate change mitigation efforts. Additionally, we ask that ECHA plan to re-evaluate the availability of alternatives as the derogation approaches expiration, to ensure that the restriction’s entry into force is aligned with technological feasibility.


Rivian believes that the analysis of the socio-economic impacts of the proposed restriction should consider the role of EVs in mitigating climate change and the potential risks of delaying their proliferation through (1) banning the use of essential cell materials and (2) by inhibiting competitiveness with ICEVs through powertrain-dependent derogations for the industry standard refrigerant. To avoid disruption of electrification efforts which are crucial for transportation industry decarbonization, we ask that these EV-specific use cases receive the maximum 13.5-year derogation and that ECHA re-evaluate the technological readiness of alternatives before the derogation expires.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Transportation (sub-use: Mobile Air Conditioning) and Energy (missing sub-use: EV lithium ion batteries) sectors

5. Proposed derogations: Timing, Availability and Technical/Economical Feasibility of Alternatives The proposed timeline to change to a PFAS-free mobile air conditioning (MAC) refrigerant for electric and hybrid electric vehicles is infeasible when compared to prior refrigerant replacement efforts.  The most recent refrigerant change for MACs, in an effort to reduce the Global Warming Potential of the refrigerant, saw the first discussions of a switch from R134A to R1234yf in 2002 (Council Decision 2002/358/EC) with passage of legislation in MAC Directive 2006/40/EC of the European Parliament, which required phase out to begin in 2011 and be completed by January 2017.  In the U.S., this phase down was not finalized until model year 2021.  Furthermore, this refrigerant change was considered a drop-in, with properties of the new refrigerant almost identical to that being replaced. This switch therefore only required slight modification to the oil type used, a TXV (Thermo expansion Valve) operating setpoint change, and selective use of Internal Heat-exchanger pipe to recover the slight performance degradation.  Other changes were mainly due to the mild flammability (A2L) of R1234YF compared with R134a (A1), including alterations to heat-exchangers labelling with certifications and additional training requirements for service technicians. The proposal under Restriction Option 2 would require greater system redesign than the prior refrigerant phase-out due to the absence of drop-in alternatives and the RO2 1.5-year transition period proposed is not feasible given the 11 years required to phase-out earlier “drop-in” refrigerant.  The two types of alternatives systems referenced in the proposal, R744 (CO2) and secondary systems using R290 (Propane), both present issues:  R744 has been used in extremely limited capacity, by Mercedes in the E/S Class and the Volkswagen group in the Audi A8 (for Europe only) and for a limited time in the heat pump system of the ID3/4.  This short track record/limited production illustrates both the challenges and the costs associated with these specialized components that operate at pressures 5-10X higher than current R1234yf system.  These R-744 systems also require constant monitoring and mitigation strategies in the passenger cabin due to risk of leakage-caused drowsiness.  With these higher operating pressures, the components that transport the refrigerant must be much more robust in R744 than R1234yf systems (hoses with inner flexible steel reinforcements) and connections cannot follow typical O-ring/seal washer designs but require metal-to-metal sealing designs.  The R744 fittings are more sensitive to contamination due to the high pressures and small molecule size of CO2, requiring special handling and care when making connections in assembly plant.  The efficiency of CO2 system decreases dramatically in high ambient environments, above 31°C due to the super critical temperature of CO2, meaning the refrigerant in the outside heat exchanger (condenser) isn’t undergoing phase change and the COP (coefficient of performance) decreases therefore consuming much more energy. This means that in hot ambient temperatures the energy needed to cool the cabin and the battery is much greater in R744 than in R1234yf systems and may not be able to meet the requirements to keep the battery in safe operating temperatures along with the cabin.  R290 as a secondary-loop was referenced as a viable alternative, however R290 is not currently in use for auto production in any form. In 2018, Denso, an MVAC supplier, proposed this type of system at the SAE TMSS (Thermal Management Systems Symposium) conference in San Diego.  The proof-of-concept idea has merit but is far from commercialization as unique R290 compressors are not developed and validated and lubrication oils require compatibility testing.  Importantly, R290 is not allowed for use in MAC systems in the US by the EPA in direct expansion or secondary loop system, and the cost to develop a unique system for EU is prohibitively expensive thereby doubling the R&D and capital investment for two unique designs. Additional capital expenditures cost would be incurred in the vehicle manufacturing sites, to handle large quantities of 2 types of refrigerants. There are also no existing standards for the service valve fittings to charge said system, or risk assessments that have been completed on this (A3) highly flammable refrigerant type system. Additionally, secondary loops are less efficient due to the need to add additional heat exchangers to cool/heat coolant to maintain the temperature in the vehicles cabin, compared with direct expansion type systems, and would likely need supplemental coolant heaters to satisfy the heating requirements of the cabin. This additional cost and lower efficiency would add to the overall cost of EVs while creating a price disparity between ICEVs and EVs.  Time required for completing the substitution process Given the lack of currently available drop-in alternatives, and the time required to establish required safety standards, get approval from regulatory agencies and commercialize new MAC systems, Rivian recommends a 13.5-year derogation for MAC use cases, regardless of the powertrain technology. Providing a propulsion system-agnostic derogation avoids inadvertently placing zero-emission vehicles at competitive disadvantage relative to greenhouse gas emitting combustion engine vehicles.   Furthermore, the use of the MAC system to cool EV batteries is unique and integral to the overall powertrain and thermal development and execution compared with ICE vehicles. Direct current (DC) fast charging times are directly proportional to how cool the battery is kept during a charging session. This metric of recharging speed is often compared with how long it takes to fill an ICE vehicle with gasoline and is a key factor for mass adoption of EVs. An ICEV-specific derogation for MAC threatens the transportation sector’s ability to electrify, and therefore to decarbonize.  In addition, ECHA should consider an unlimited derogation for maintenance and refilling of existing MACs for which continued use of the product requires the original refrigerant.

6. Missing uses: Missing Use Case: EV Lithium-Ion Batteries Certain PFAS, including polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) and fluoroethylene carbonate (FEC), are critical components that are used within almost every lithium-ion battery (LIB) cell on the market. These materials play essential roles in battery performance and are critical to the overall safety of electric vehicles and their passengers.   Annual Tonnage and Types of PFAS Associated with EV LIBs Within the European Union (EU) market for EV batteries, PVDF annual usage is around 5,600 tons and expected to grow to 23,000 tons by 2026, while FEC annual usage is around 600 tons and expected to grow to 4,000 tons by 2026.   For electric vehicle (EV) cell applications, the PFAS are all self-contained within the sealed cells and are not accessible by consumers for handling, repairs, etc. LIBs are handled through a very controlled logistics chain from cell manufacturing through vehicle end-of-life decommissioning. End-of-life processing of the EV cells (and therefore PFAS chemicals contained within) are handled at designated appropriate recycling sites which can assist appropriate disposal handling and mitigate risks of PFAS being accidentally released into the environment.  Key Functionalities of the PFAS in EV LIBs PVDF and PTFE are utilized as polymer binders for cathode electrodes due to their chemical resistance; high chemical, thermal, and electrochemical stability during cycling; and mechanical properties including durability, adhesion, and processability.  FEC is used as an electrolyte additive due to its chemical stability and is one of the keys to enabling vehicles with acceptable range and required lifetime (>10 years). Fluorine-containing additives such as FEC provide critical stabilization of battery materials, and these batteries can become unstable and potentially dangerous without the use of fluorine-containing additives to stabilize the internal components.  By prematurely removing PFAS from their critical roles to stabilize performance in EV batteries, vehicle and passenger may be impacted.  Estimate of Affected Companies If PFAS are prohibited from use in EV batteries, we estimate that this restriction will negatively impact 10-20 major component manufacturers within the lithium-ion battery space, around 10 major battery manufacturers, and the vehicle manufacturers that integrate these battery cells.  Availability and Technical/Economical Feasibility of Alternatives It is our understanding that no alternatives currently exist to replace PFAS within cells in the near-term (next 5-10 years), for either the cathode binder (PVDF) or electrolyte additive (FEC).  The only commonly evaluated alternative to PVDF as a binder is another PFAS chemical called polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), which is considered the top contender as a new polymer binder for future cell technology that leverages manufacturing process improvements.  Status of Research & Development for Alternatives There is very limited development of non-fluorine/PFAS-containing cathode binders, and the development is limited to early R&D activities primarily in research labs.  One of the most promising examples of this R&D activity comes from Prof. Mickael Dollé at the University of Montreal who is examining the development of PFAS-free elastomeric binders to replace PVDF.  His research involves changes to both the chemicals that are used as well as the processes that are performed to create the batteries.  As such, assuming that his alternative approach is successful, it would take an estimated 5 additional years of development time, plus at least 5 years of process development and scale-up for commercialization, as well as the related required modifications to existing manufacturing equipment (i.e. all electrode mixing, coating, calendaring equipment would need to be heavily modified or replaced) that would likely cost billions of dollars across the industry. For these reasons, Rivian believes that a 13.5-year derogation is justified for PVDF and PTFE used in EV LIBs.  Similarly on the electrolyte additive front, there is little current development effort underway to replace FEC in LIB cells due to the necessary stability provided by fluorine-compounds during operation to prevent safety issues. The best option to remove FEC from LIB cells is to increase the usage of other electrolyte additives with inferior performance, such as vinylene carbonate (VC) and new potential additives with fluorine-like properties that can provide similar functional benefits including additives that contain boron or phosphorous elements. One such additive in this field would be tris(trimethylsilyl) phosphite (TMSP). These two components (VC, TMSP) are already commercially used today, but do not provide the same level of stability and safety that is provided by the incumbent PFAS-chemical (FEC) and therefore discovery of a suitable replacement still would need to be undertaken. Rivian similarly recommends a 13.5-year derogation for the use of FEC in EV LIB cells.  Due to its high regard for safety, the LIB industry is known to be conservative and risk-averse when it comes to introducing new technologies.  Therefore, it is expected that any modifications to battery components to remove PFAS-chemicals will be a deliberate process requiring substantial periods for development and validation before being considered for use in vehicle applications.  For reference, any minor change to a battery design using already accepted component technology requires a minimum of 3 years of development time to prove the performance, safety, and manufacturing stability of the change.  The case of a major technological shift such as PFAS-removal from EV batteries would not only require the minimum 3 years of validation time but would also first require years of technical development to achieve the necessary performance requirements (5-8 years). In addition, there would be time needed to overcome any related economic and manufacturing challenges to scale production to EV quantities and bring the new technologies to market. We urge ECHA to offer the maximum derogation (13.5 years) for the use of PFAS in EV LIB cells to allow for the industry’s necessary performance and safety validations, and to re-evaluate the technological feasibility of alternatives before the derogation expires.  To illustrate the need for this requested derogation, consider the historical commercialization timeline required for new cathode chemistries. For example, in 1991, Sony commercialized the first LIB cell for use in their camcorder devices using a cathode technology known as LCO.  From that date, it took 15 years before the next-generation of upgraded cathode technology known as NMC to be finally commercialized in the mid-2000s.  Even in this example, the transition from LCO to NMC technology would be considered less disruptive than the overall removal of PFAS from EV batteries, since PFAS removal requires the introduction of multiple new components into a battery. Moreover, major changes to existing battery chemistries are typically not introduced directly into EV applications, which can further delay timelines.  Rather, new battery designs (which PFAS-free cells would constitute) are initially introduced into smaller commercial markets with less requirements (e.g. power tool battery, drones) and then gradually introduced into mobile devices (e.g. cell phones, laptops, tablets) to de-risk the technology before large-scale commercial introduction into the EV applications with strict requirements. In weighing this against the timelines currently proposed under Restriction Option 2, the maximum derogation of 13.5 years is the only realistic pathway for the industry to successfully shift away from PFAS use in LIB cells.  Socioeconomic Costs of Sectoral Disruption As discussed in the general comments section, EVs are regarded as an essential tool in global efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, critical for climate change mitigation and air-quality related public health goals to reduce particulate matter emissions. The industry is expected to grow quickly over the next decade, with European Environment Agency reporting over 870,000 new EV registrations in the EU-27 in 2021 [see non-confidential attachment: new registrations of electric cars, EU-27]. A 2022 publication by Menon on the outlook for job creation in the European battery industry suggests 150,000 direct jobs in Europe by 2030, or 735,000 when including indirect employment impacts [see non-confidential attachment: Outlook for jobs creation in European battery industry].

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Fritz Driescher KG is a manufacturer of gas and air-insulated medium-voltage switchgears and switching devices up to 36 kV. Our products are used in the transmission and distribution of electrical energy and are an essential component in the expansion and new construction of modern energy networks, as they are also required for the expansion of renewable energies and thus for the energy turnaround.

The switchgears are complex and consist of hundreds of single parts, optimised for a long and low-maintenance service life up to 40 years. PFAS such as PTFE, FKM, FFKM and fluoronitrile (alternative for SF6) are part of this and are of great importance due to their special properties as seals, sliding bearings and in the area of arc quenching. Finding alternatives is difficult. The cost of substitution is not easy to estimate.

First of all, the 10,000 PFASs in our products have to be identified. These can be present in direct form, e.g. as PTFE plain bearings, but can also occur in purchased parts as coatings or as production-related very small concentrations (25 ppb). Here, an extensive exchange with our suppliers and sub-suppliers is needed. So far, they are not obliged to inform us about PFAS in the delivered components. For this reason, a complete analysis of all components does not seem possible at the present time and within a reasonable time frame.

If PFAS are identified in our products, substitutes can be developed and, if possible, authorised. This requires development work and finally complex type tests according to the applicable product standards. Experience shows that such a process can take 2 to 4 years and, depending on the complexity and development effort, up to 10 years or more. During this time, no PFAS-free products will be available, which will reduce the offer and slow down the needed grid expansion.

The planned ban also affects the availability of spare parts. The maintenance or service of existing installations cannot be carried out without the necessary spare parts. Existing switchgears have to be taken out of service because of a missing spare parts supply or can only be operated to a limited capacity. Inadequate maintenance and service can endanger the security of supply of the energy grids. In our opinion, such a ban would run counter to the sustainable and economic use of existing energy infrastructures.


Proposal:

- Suppliers are not obliged to provide information about PFAS in supplied components. Without this information or the assistance of our suppliers, it will not be possible to carry out an analysis within a reasonable timeframe.
A legal regulatory framework is needed that obliges suppliers to share the required information.

- The planned transition period of 18 months is not sufficient for the changeover of our products. Derogations are needed for our products, especially if no alternatives are available. We propose a basic derogation of 12 years for our power transmission and distribution products. Furthermore, a procedure must be defined to extend an exemption if no alternatives are available.

- Existing energy infrastructures should be able to be operated until their end of life in terms of sustainable and economic operation. Spare parts as well as auxiliary and operating materials for maintenance and repair should be excluded from PFAS regulation.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Energy sector, transmission and distribution, switchgears

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: We estimate the emission risk to be very low. According to the current state of knowledge, PFAS are largely used as solids in our switchgears. Switchgears are operated under normal operating conditions and in closed operating facilities. We estimate that emissions during the operating lifetime are therefore unlikely. At the end of their life, units are dismantled and disposed of or recycled in accordance with the applicable disposal regulations. This also applies to the fluoronitrile used as an SF6 substitute. This remains in the hermetically sealed gas tanks of the switchgear during its service life and is collected again at the end of its service life and disposed of or recycled.

5. Proposed derogations: A complete analysis of which components contain PFAS is currently not possible. See general comments. For those where it is known, see specific information 2 above.

General Comments: From the application of products containing PTFE anti-dripping agents, their use in conjunction with flame retardants is added to engineering plastics such as PC, ABS, PA, PBT, etc. By processing and dispersing them into PTFE reticular fibers, they prevent further fire spread caused by molten droplets during plastic combustion, making engineering plastics reach the UL94 V0 flame retardant grade of 1.6mm or thinner products. These engineering plastics are widely used in electronics, cables, new energy vehicles Industries with fire protection requirements such as network communication equipment. In these industries, products do not use PTFE anti-dripping agents, resulting in a decrease in flame retardancy and the spread of fire caused by combustion droplets, posing a huge threat to people's lives and property. According to the annual report released by the World Fire Statistics Center, fires caused by electronic appliances account for about 10-30% of the total number of fires in the world, and even become the largest cause of fires in some countries and cities. In 2020, the global production and sales of PTFE anti-drip agent were approximately 8600 tons. It is expected that the global production and sales will reach 12500 tons by 2025. Based on its typical addition of 0.5% in engineering plastics, if the use of PTFE anti drip agents is prohibited, it will directly lead to a decrease in the flame retardancy of engineering plastics to 2-3 million tons, causing significant losses to human life and property. At present, there is no development, use, or sales of its substitutes in terms of technology and economy.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: We would like to clarify the definition of “semiconductor manufacturing process”. We believe that the “semiconductor manufacturing process” must include all steps of the semiconductor value chain. That is, it consists of the synthesis of the raw materials used for the ingredients, the formulation process of “process chemicals” such as photoresists, the inspection process, the delivery process of chemicals to device manufacturers, the process of using chemicals at device manufacturers, such as Front End of Line (FEOL) Fab manufacturing process steps, Back End of Line (BEOL) Fab manufacturing process steps, and Back End Assembly, Test, & Packaging operations.  The Dossier Submitter developed “Annex A Table A.49” as part of its initial research into the semiconductor industry’s uses of PFAS.  During this consultation, SEMI-E and E-SIA submitted "Updated Annex A Table A.49", based on the semiconductor industry’s broader investigation. It will be updated by the end of this consultation.  E-SIA has also published the following important downloadable papers:  https://www.semiconductors.org/pfas/  Detailed description of the photolithography process and materials used, their required properties are summarized in these papers. They also contain comparisons and timelines of socio-economic impacts, alternatives in each technology.    1.The Impact of a Potential PFAS Restriction on the Semiconductor Sector 2.Background on Semiconductor Manufacturing and PFAS 3.PFAS-Containing Photo-Acid Generators Used in Semiconductor Manufacturing 4.PFOS and PFOA Conversion to Short-Chain PFAS-Containing Materials Used in Semiconductor Manufacturing 5.PFAS-Containing Surfactants Used in Semiconductor Manufacturing 6.PFAS-Containing Materials Used in Semiconductor Manufacturing Assembly Test Packaging and Substrate Processes 7.PFAS-Containing Articles Used in Semiconductor Manufacturing  For “process chemicals” by photolithography, used for “semiconductor manufacturing process”, FFEM provides photoresists, photo-patterning materials for the color filters, buffer coat materials. This photolithography process consists of coating, exposure, and development steps. They require several PFAS related substances, such as surfactants, PAGs, polymers, pigments, initiators, to achieve specific functions. It will take 15 to more than 20 years to develop PFAS-free alternatives for most of the photolithography uses, while for photoacid generators (PAGs), it is expected that this process takes more than 25 years.  As the semiconductor process requires “ultrapure” chemicals, whose metal contamination below “ppb” order. “Ultrapure/ultraclean” condition is a critical environment within the semiconductor industry.  Even trace amounts of metal contamination can negatively impact device yields. To achieve this critical environment, fluoropolymers such as PTFE are used for liners of reactors, vessels, containers, sealings, valves, gaskets, filters, bottle liners, and dip tubes, to avoid contacting metal surfaces. Not only PFAS substances used for PAGs or photoresist polymers, PFAS substances are essential components to handle wet chemicals within the “semiconductor manufacturing process”. As mentioned by JEITA, it is unfeasible to stably and accurately manage the limit values in the supply chain of stakeholders of Electric and Electronic Equipment (EEE). Other types of plastics are not suitable because they cannot withstand the required temperature range. Metal tubing cannot be used because it is too rigid and will split after a few repeated freezing cycles.  e. There are no commercially available non-PFAS substitutes that will meet the performance requirements for these types of aircraft hose assemblies.  f. Electronics coolant hoses cannot be supplied so military radars and electronic warfare components cannot be built or maintained.  These restrictions would have catastrophic impact to the entire aviation industry.

General Comments: GEA Farm Technologies GmbH, headquartered in Bönen/Germany, is providing key products and equipment to dairy farmers. The core product is the fully automated milking machine which is a very complex construction.
The basic milking principle is that milk is being extracted from the udder by means of a vacuum and passed through different components and pipings of the milking machine until it is collected in the milk tank. Milk is a food that can easily coagulate and get sour. This process is accompanied by an increase of germs. To maintain the hygiene requirements of a milking machine, it needs to be cleaned and sanitized in between the milking times on a regular base by means of a CIP & sanitizing line.
The CIP & sanitizing line itself consists of different components, such as valve blocks which are sealed by FKM and FFKM rubber gaskets. FKM and FFKM rubber materials are Fluoro-substituted polymers which have been cross-linked to obtain elastomeric properties. In the synthesis of these Fluoro-substituted polymers, PFAS are being used, e.g. as monomers. As a consequence, PFAS might still be present in the FKM and FFKM rubber gaskets which are used, though at an extremely low level which will not significantly contribute to PFAS emissions into the environment also due to the fact of the minor contact surface of the gaskets to the cleaning solution.
In the past, alternative rubber materials such as NBR, SBR, NR, EPDM or VMQ were evaluated which are significantly cheaper in price but do not provide a sufficient resistance against CIP chemicals and sanitizers. As a result, the life expectancy of the rubber components became negligible and service intervals were dramatically decreased by up to 95%.
A general PFAS ban resulting in the unavailability of FKM and FFKM gaskets would lead to a replacement of these gaskets on a more or less daily base on the farms. Increased waste and CO2-emmissions as well as increased cost for the farmers and milk consumers would follow. Also, it is to be expected that farmers will switch to uncontrolled grey market products which are available on the internet for all original milking equipment manufacturers. To avoid these circumstances, alternative rubber-free sealing solutions need to be developed affecting also the adjacent components (e.g. housings, pistons, valves). This development process is accompanied with the redesign of a broad amount of technical equipment, the investment in a high number of new injection molding tools and the final implementation into the milking machines. It is not guaranteed that these alternatives will show a similar performance and we expect at least an effort of 5 years and 10 Mio. € for development, validation, testing and implementation of these newly developed rubber-free sealing solutions.
The implementation of the rubber-free sealing solutions could be done for a new version of a milking machine. However, for the broad amount of the installed base of milking machines it will be impossible to retrofit these. They are completely designed to use nowadays equipment with PFAS-containing rubber products as pointed out and have an average product life of 25 years. A farmer who invests today in a milking machine must have the opportunity to get spare parts for a longer time than the proposed 6.5 years of transition period.
We appreciate if ECHA will consider these circumstances with a sufficient long transition period much longer than 6.5 years to make the milking equipment manufacturers able to serve spare parts to the market of already installed milking machines.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Industrial food and feed production

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Our yearly turnover of PFAS-containing rubber products is about 500 kg/a. On the emissions of PFAS through our products we have no specific information but usually the PFAS-containing rubber products in our milking machines come only in contact with the rinsing solution with a marginal surface. Also, the PFAS concentration in these products are expected to be extremely low. Therefore, we expect the emissions as insignificant during the use phase.

6. Missing uses: The actual use of our PFAS-containing rubber products in milking machines is missing as they are not being used in direct milk contact. However, we anticipate that this use does fall under "Industrial food and feed production". Therefore, please find our main feedback under "SECTION III. Non-confidential comments".

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Please find our main feedback under "SECTION III. Non-confidential comments". From our point of view the grandfathering of the installed base of milking machines needs to be secured in combination with the possibility to supply PFAS-containing rubber products as spare parts for these.

8. Other identified uses: Please find our main feedback under "SECTION III. Non-confidential comments".

This response will be digitally added to the form provided on your website for this purpose. Background On February 7, 2023, the proposal for a European ban on PFAS (Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) was published by ECHA (European Chemicals Agency). Such a ban is also called a restriction. This restriction proposal was made by the Netherlands together with Denmark, Germany, Norway, and Sweden. The aim of the restriction proposal is to ban the production, trade, and use of these substances to limit the risks to human health and the environment. The proposal focuses on the entire group of PFAS to prevent the replacement of one PFAS by another. 2. Process There are three stages in the process leading to a ban on PFAS. The first stage has already been completed and consisted of preparing and submitting a restriction proposal. The second stage involves a public consultation. Everyone can have a say in the dossier and provide information. This information will be processed. Subsequently, the scientific committees of ECHA will provide their advice. In the third stage, the European Commission will produce a final proposal, which the member states will vote on. The ban will then come into effect. 3. Consultation The consultation is intended to provide ECHA with scientific and technical information to help them in preparing their advice. Due to the PFAS issues identified in Dordrecht and the surrounding municipalities in South Holland since 2018, it is important to submit a response to ECHA for each municipality. This response is then formulated, following the structure of the digitally available response form. It is the responsibility of the municipal council to submit a response on behalf of the municipality. 4. Structure of the response This letter is written from the perspective of the municipalities working together on the Chemours dossier: Dordrecht, Sliedrecht, Papendrecht, Molenlanden, and Alblasserdam. General Comments: General comment in response of the PFAS Consultation
Contact : Joëlle Pinchot (joelle.pinchot@etienne-lacroix.com)

Dear Sir/Madam,

The French Land Defence and Security Industry Association (GICAT) is a trade association created in 1978 and which today represents more than 420 members. A GICAT’s detailed presentation is joined in annex.
GICAT has decided to respond to this consultation to express its great concern about the proposal restriction of Per-and Polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) that strongly impact its members.
Non-polymer PFAS compounds are found in many types of formulations used by the defence industry, from coatings to greases, lubricants or hydraulic fluids. They confer specific key properties required for reliability and thus user safety in rough and demanding environments and are usually found in very low concentrations.
However, the  purpose of this comment for manufacturers of pyrotechnic components, ammunition, rockets, missiles (1)… is to address our industry’s specific uses of fluoropolymers, more specifically, PTFE (Teflon®), PVDF and fluorinated elastomer (Viton®). They are used extensively throughout our supply chains in the manufacture of many pyrotechnic mixtures and articles,in our industrial process (in particular as surface coating in direct contact with pyrotechnic compositions) and are essential for new technology development programmes across the sector
The most critical uses of these substances for the national defence interests is to formulate pyrotechnic compositions used in numerous devices and components where other materials would not satisfy the requirements. For example, the following applications are concerned: Countermeasures flares, heating devices, igniters, obscurants, propellants, tracers, tracking flares, underwater flares, explosive charge, warhead anti-tank system (2) etc.
While the uses of pyrotechnic applications are mentioned in the annex A as “fluorine containing oxidizers, primarily polymers, are extensively used in pyrotechnic compositions » (tables A1 – A77), they are not covered by the restriction dossier due to limited information available. However, the ammunition and other pyrotechnic components impacted by the restrictions under consideration are essential to maintain the operational capabilities of our armed forces on land, sea and air.
For this reason, GICAT decided to target and to develop its response to the PFAS consultation on these strategic and specific uses of fluoropolymers in our range of activities. Many other uses are also essential but are less specific and supported by other sectors of activities.

In the manufacture of pyrotechnic compositions for ammunition, granular PTFE, PVDF, HFP are mainly used.
- Low quantities are used each year per production site: few kilos to 5 tons maximum.
- No transformation nor chemical degradation of the fluoropolymers takes place during the manufacturing process (composition pre-mixing under wet conditions) (2).
- No emission of particles or dust occurs during the manufacturing process (composition pre-mixing under wet condition or dissolution in solvent).
- No waste or pollution of the water network results from the process.
- No emission of PFAs results from the ignition of the ammunition or pyrotechnic component. The combustion products are fluorometal, carbon and HF (2).



Fluoropolymers’ characteristics, in particular their excellent resistance to thermal or chemical attacks, are perfectly adapted to severe environments as required for defence applications.  Fluoropolymers also present an extremely low coefficient of friction which gives them an optimal compatibility with the high sensitivities of pyrotechnic substances or mixtures.
In addition, fluoropolymers are the only molecules chemically compatible with all families of pyrotechnic mixtures which ensures the highest level of safety during the manufacturing, the handling, the functioning and the storage of ammunition in all conditions.
For all these reasons, companies of the defence industry have been using fluoropolymers in pyrotechnic compositions and in components which are in contact with pyrotechnic compositions since the 1980s and no extensive research for alternatives exists today.
Subject to identifying substitute formulations with equivalent performances, the inclusion of fluoropolymers in the restriction would lead to a requalification for each case of use (ammunition and pyrotechnic components). The usual time to qualify a new formulation in one ammunition is around 10 years and the overall cost is assessed at several million euros.

In addition, this restriction would prevent the defence industry from honouring:
- the ammunition orders already committed for deliveries spread over  several years (more than 10 years) leading to break contracts,
- the request of the French State to constitute stocks within the framework of the war economy (Military Programming Law 2024-2030 (LPM)).

Following this restriction, any sub-assembly already in stock (pyrotechnic or not, containing a fluoropolymer) awaiting to be integrated in ammunition or into another complex article to be placed on the market should be destroyed. In addition to the financial and technical impacts (for destruction of pyrotechnic products), national interests can no longer be respected.
All these points will be developed and documented in the other parts of the consultation by each GICAT’s members concerned by pyrotechnic activities.

Nevertheless, fluoropolymers shall be considered as a distinct subset of PFAS related to chemical hazard. Fluoropolymers are inherently safe, non-mobile, non-bio accumulative and non-toxic. Fluoropolymers are different from other PFAS as they do not share the toxicological and environmental profiles associated with PFAS of concern. Fluoropolymers have a unique set of physicochemical properties, they meet OECD polymer of low concern criteria, and are considered to have insignificant environmental and human health impact.
Considering the safety and reliability benefits of fluoropolymer applications for the defence industry, and to prevent significant risks of wide-spread obsolescence for materials and processes, the very low PFAS emissions risk and initiatives being taken by the processing industry to further minimize emissions and closing the loop by implementing circular economy wherever possible, we request a full exemption of fluoropolymers from the PFAS restriction proposal to maintain our major critical uses such as:
- Formulation of pyrotechnic compositions contained in military equipment and ammunition components.
- Surface coating of processing tools and parts of ammunition in direct contact with pyrotechnic compositions.
Sincerely yours.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: GICAT brings together over 430 French air-land defense and security manufacturers. They operate in all joint fields, including intangible ones: land vehicles, weapons, explosives and ammunition, detection and localization, personnel equipment, infrastructure protection, information and communication systems, and so on. As an association, and given the scope of our members' business sectors, we are unable to provide detailed figures. However, GICAT members concerned by the restrictions on PFAS will also submit their responses to the consultation on the ECHA website.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: GENERAL COMMENTS

Scope or restriction option analysis:
The Power Transmission & Distribution (T&D) technology, for which Siemens Energy - Grid Technology stands for, is an essential element of the renewable energy transfer and distribution chain. The consideration of the T&D sector in the proposed ANNEX XV restriction report on PFAS seems limited in its approach, as only switchgear insulation gas is considered with a derogation time of five years, which we as Siemens Energy Grid Technology do fully agree with.  However, the restriction report proposal does not fully consider the other elements of the T&D sector, e.g. converters and transformers by any form of derogation or exemption, with its fluoropolymer components (made of e.g. PTFE, PVDF, FKM, FMQ, FEP, etc.) which do play a vital role in T&D equipment (e.g. for sealing, gliding, protection to withstand extreme heat, pressure, aging, etc.)
T&D equipment includes complex products, like high voltage switchgears and circuit breakers (GIS- gas-insulted switchgear, AIS- air-Insulated Switchgear), converter and power– and distribution transformer. With a long lifetime of 40 years, all these products do consist of thousands of components with an extreme durability, and high technical requirements (e.g. must withstand temperatures of up to 1000°C or in close to switching arc up to 9.000°C, wear-and high pressure resistance 30bar…80bar and chemical resistance, etc.). To ensure these products meet their requirements, in combination with long maintenance periods, highly sophisticated materials are used, which may include PFAS.
Beyond T&D product components itself, PFAS can also be found in essential secondary equipment such as control systems (optical fibre) or critical core components for power electronics (thyristors), necessary for T&D equipment control and monitoring. In case of a PFAS phase-out, a significant hardware and software adjustments will be entailed for the entire T&D equipment, whether already placed on the market or in new design.
As such, we believe further considerations (particularly derogations) for this sector are needed within the context of proposed ANNEX XV restriction report on PFAS.

Information gaps present a challenge to complete phase-out:
The vast majority of about 10,000 different PFAS substances in scope of the proposed ANNEX XV restriction report on PFAS are not classified as hazardous according to the CLP Regulation (EC) No. 1272/2008, nor identified as substances of very high concern (SVHCs) by REACH (EC) No 1907/2006, article 57. Currently, suppliers are not obligated to give information on the presence of PFAS in components or materials. Therefore, we currently do not have exact information on where PFAS are included across the T&D supply chain. This information is only available for those types of products where we specify the use e.g. of PTFE or PVDF (see point I below). As a result, analyzing which components are, or can be, PFAS free seems almost impossible at this point in time. In addition, a far more challenging process will be the identification of so called fluorotensides, used as intermediate in production of some of the PFAS, at threshold level of 25 ppb (see proposed ANNEX XV restriction report on PFAS) or even lower.
Four categories for PFAS including material have been identified by T&D industry stakeholders (members of ZVEI = association of Germany's Electro and Digital Industry), illustrating the challenge for the T&D industry when it comes to a PFAS phase-out:
I. PFAS used following the material specification of the user* – information on PFAS is available and phase-out can be controlled by user*.
II. PFAS added by the material manufacturer according to the technical requirement definition of the user – information on PFAS is required from material manufacturer but phase-out results in a material requalification.
III. PFAS used due to 3rd party design and definition – information on PFAS is not available to user* and phase-out is impossible.
IV. PFAS contaminated material based on the production process - information on PFAS is not available to user* and analysis and thus phase-out is impossible.
*T&D industry

This clearly illustrates that reliable information along the supply chain on PFAS in components and materials can only be sufficiently collected and analyzed if there is a legal framework in place that requires suppliers to disclose this information. This is considered as a necessary precondition to ensure the proposed ANNEX XV restriction report on PFAS, can be implemented.

Testing requirements mean longer timelines are needed:
For other cases, where PFAS are clearly identified and a phase-out seems feasible, the entire transition process – from re-design and implementation into the product followed by a required T&D product type test repetition – clearly exceeds the proposed transition time of 18 months as proposed in the ANNEX XV restriction report on PFAS.
In a best case-scenario, a full T&D product type test itself, including the production of type test models, the type tests and the final certification may take already approximately 1.5 to three years per portfolio type. In the worst-case scenario, taking type test failures and multiple test iterations into account, this can take approximately 2.5 to four years, w/o taking the repetition of new material search process into account.

All T&D product type tests have to be performed in accredited laboratories which means all EU manufacturers of T&D electrical equipment will face the additional challenge of limited availability of test laboratories. This lack of availability will also impact the timeline of the planned PFAS phase-out and will prevent T&D industry from reaching the proposed transition time of 18 months.
For example, when developing Siemens Energy PFAS-free natural-origin gas alternative for our switchgear portfolio, it took about a decade to transition from gases with a high global warming potential. This past experience indicates that a similar amount of time would be needed to transition switchgears, circuit breakers, converters and transformers to PFAS-free equipment.

A lack of current alternatives could impact Europe’s electrical power grids:
The natural interest to find substitutes is present in the T&D sector since the beginning and remains still valid. Currently, there are no alternative materials qualified for the required T&D applications such as cooling pipes and tubes, nozzles, sealing and gliding parts. Currently a 1:1 PFAS material substitution is considered as non-existent. Siemens Energy and others in the T&D sector remain invested in finding PFAS substitutes also together with material suppliers but as we do not manufacture those materials, we do fully rely on our suppliers for this.
When new materials are found, material suppliers will first have to scale up their ability to produce these and initially there will be high demand e.g., by the T&D industry, and not enough supply. Material production must be scaled up before a definite shift from the industry to PFAS-free alternatives to ensure no gaps in capacity.
A short-term phase-out of PFAS containing components in T&D products before alternatives have been properly tested and approved can lead to a tremendous reduction in safety properties of the respective equipment, thus increasing the risks of human and environmental harm. Some PFAS-free alternatives already identified have unfavorable material properties, for example, in areas where fire protection or pressure resistance is required.

Consequently, efforts in R&D are required to find adequate alternatives. This necessitates high costs and time-consuming repetition of type tests, estimated to take between seven to 10 years, during which time PFAS free T&D products will not be available. This would lead to a shortage of electrical high voltage T&D equipment with a financial impact and direct negative impact on the EU’s energy transition strategy for 2050 and the required extension of the electrical networks. For projects of long durations in the electrical T&D system business, (EU projects of common interest (PCI) - cross border infrastructure projects that link the energy systems of EU countries) of sometimes 10 years, the implementation of an alternative PFAS material solution will cause an additional prolongation of already ongoing electrical EU grid projects. In general, additional or unplanned changes in T&D system equipment within this project phase are very limited. For example, due to space constraints on offshore windfarms and onshore wind turbines, there are no opportunities for an additional change on switchgear, transformer or converter once the layout for all stakeholders is fixed right at the beginning of the commissioning.
Therefore, the suggested transition time of 18 months, after EiF, for fluoropolymer is unrealistic. Given that PFAS are found in several components of T&D products and systems and identification of all uses has not yet been possible, coupled with the fact that a phase-out before identification risks resulting in safety, environmental and issues with supply for Europe’s electrical grids, we urge policymakers to grant at least a derogation time of 12 years (after EiF + transition time) for the T&D sector with a clearly defined procedure for the reapplication, review and extension of derogation, in terms of no PFAS-free alternatives are available.

Environmental emissions:
We estimate that environmental emissions from most uses of PFAS in T&D equipment during operation is negligible. For example, PTFE, PVDF, and FKM are mainly used in solid form as components inside T&D products or a protection by special coating. As a result of their solid form, and the fact that they are used in enclosed spaces, they are not exposed to environment (such as rain) and therefore cannot end up in rivers and soil, and do not lead to environmental emissions during operation.
After end of life, components made from, e.g. PTFE or PVDF, will be sorted out during disassembling, following the specified disposal framework and guidance as well as local regulations, further minimizing any chances of environmental impact.

Other socio-economic analysis (SEA) issues:
The proposed ANNEX XV restriction report on PFAS as it stands would hinder the advancement of technologies to meet EU CO2 reduction targets in time as all workforces and resources will be bound to PFAS phase-out, rather than on other efforts to reduce e.g., emissions. This will risk deaccelerating our Siemens Energy roadmap to achieve net zero in time, resulting in delays for reaching overall EU targets towards a climate neutral future as well as the EU energy transition strategy for 2050.
Furthermore, the proposal as it stands risks impacting global efforts towards emission reduction as well as Europe’s competitive advantage abroad. As a result, European companies who are no longer able to provide PFAS containing T&D equipment would lose their footprint in markets outside the EU. These companies would be able to re-enter these markets once alternatives are found but their prolonged absence as credible market players for so many years will have a massive effect on the competitiveness of European companies. This will hinder efforts to convince markets to transition to PFAS-free alternatives as they will have grown to rely on companies from markets where a PFAS restriction is not considered or in force (e.g. Asia, South-East Asia, South America, Africa, Australia).

Transitional period:
As we are not able to propose a common transition time which at the end has to fulfill the requirements for all EU industrial applications, we do only concentrate on giving a proposal on the derogation time (after EiF + transition time of 18 month) required for the T&D sector.
For a qualified request for changes on the transitional period/deferred entry into force, the fundamental aspect of alternatives is missing. If PFAS-free materials were available, the time for a phase out of critical components would be at least seven to ten years (based on time for re-design of product with new material, type testing, and certification). Implementation into the production lines and scale-up of the production capacity will add additional time to this process. A transition time of one decade is typical for such drastic adaption in a T&D equipment portfolio.

Maintenance of existing equipment poses challenges:
Maintenance and repair require spare parts to enable the T&D equipment to fulfil the technical requirements and performance in its application and during operation. The inability to provide maintenance with spare parts would result in interruption times with a long downtime for the T&D equipment and thus the EU power grids. The consequence might be electricity outages within the EU for an indefinite time generating damages and cost that cannot be quantified yet. Therefore, in most cases the use of “repair-as-produced-principle” should be applied, as otherwise the technical performance might change and/or test certificates become invalid, later resulting in a withdraw of permission for operation and repetition of time-consuming type tests.

We therefore urge policymakers to consider to exempt spare parts, refurbished parts and equipment from proposed ANNEX XV restriction report on PFAS, used for the maintenance and repair of T&D equipment already placed on the market and being in operation or to have the proposed ANNEX XV restriction report on PFAS applied once the equipment has reached its practical end of life. This will be the key to guarantee continuous service, to enable safety for maintenance staff, environment and society, as well as to prevent possible power outages within the electrical EU power grid in case of component and thus T&D equipment failure. Such exemptions would be necessary until the technical lifetime of the product has been reached or an alternative material to PFAS covering the technical requirements is available.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: General comments
General company information
Kunststofftechnik Lahme specialises in the manufacture of sophisticated, machined plastic parts. All articles of Kunststofftechnik Lahme are manufactured on customer request. These are mostly small series in the range of 1-50 pieces. With a total of 20 employees, the company generates around 3.2 million euros in sales a year. Of the total sales of 3.2 million euros in 2022, some 2.2 million euros were accounted for by products made from the PFAS-containing materials polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) and polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF). On the basis of expected roughly constant sales and a constant distribution of sales among the raw materials, a ban on PFAS would inevitably lead to a loss in sales amounting to 2.2 million euros a year.

Application areas

The product portfolio includes around 7000 articles in various sizes. These include pump components in diameters from 15cm to 30cm, bellows in lengths between 2.8cm and 45cm, as well as small items such as seals and connecting elements. The most common area of application for these articles is in the pharmaceutical and chemical industries, where they are in regular contact with highly corrosive media. Among others, we supply such articles to the GEA group of companies. After final assembly, our products can be found in chemical plants as well as in medical systems for the production of medicines, where they are used by major companies such as Bayer AG, Wacker Chemie AG, Merck KGaA, and BASF SE in their manufacturing processes. In general, our articles are installed in various application systems. On the one hand, in those for the production of pharmaceuticals and, on the other hand, for cleaning these production facilities. Medical equipment for the production of medicines is used for the production of general medicines as well as for the production of special medicines. These include, for example, insulin, antibiotic agents such as penicillin, rheumatism drugs, painkillers, e.g. Ibuprofen®, cold remedies such as ACC Akut®, disinfectants, injectable generics, vitamins, proteins and biologics, as well as their imitators biosimilars. The more specific area of application is the production process of cancer drugs, new vaccines and vaccines, or the enrichment of cell cultures for research and development purposes. Away from production facilities, cleaning equipment for medical technology is also equipped with PTFE articles, as they are characterised by unique temperature and chemical resistance and are excellently suited for contact with aggressive acids, alkalis and cleaning alcohols. As things stand, there are still no alternative materials that are equally suitable for this purpose. In addition to the areas of application in the pharmaceutical and chemical industries, PTFE components are also needed in the renewable energy sector. For example, for the construction and operation of photovoltaic systems to generate “green” electricity.

Problem description
A possible PFAS ban would affect all articles manufactured by us from PTFE for the above branches of industry. As of today, there are no alternatives to it with comparable material properties. PTFE is used due to its material characteristics and demanding application areas. It should be emphasised here that both high temperature and simultaneous chemical resistance are required. According to current knowledge, the market does not yet offer the user an alternative material with comparable material properties. In the meantime, materials are available that have similar but not identical properties to PTFE. Simultaneous temperature and heat resistance is not yet combined in any alternative material. Here, PTFE still remains the only practicable solution.
In the current PFAS ban proposal, the substance group of (long-chain) fluoropolymers, which includes PTFE, is not considered in a differentiated manner but is included in the general ban. However, many different and varied scientific studies have classified them as non-harmful and non-toxic. The fluoropolymers classified by the OECD should therefore be exempt from the PFAS regulation now and in the future as "Polymers of Low Concern" (PLCs) and thus as safe materials.

Production process

Kunststofftechnik Lahme has been manufacturing plastic parts according to customer requirements in various processing steps for 60 years. This includes the pressing and sintering of blanks, sawing and drilling, subsequent machining on CNC-controlled lathes and milling machines, as well as the joining of assemblies. As part of these processes, we produce flow chips and compact material residues in addition to the manufactured products. They are always collected and sent for recycling.

Recycling
As a company, we are integrated in the time sequence between the production and use phases, which means that no direct emissions are generated by the material as such in the course of our processing. In the machining steps, an average of 6.65 tonnes of chips and offcuts are collected in our company every year, shipped to European partners, mostly based in Italy, where they are 100% recycled, according to our own statement. In this particular case recycling means the production of new PTFE sheets. Our partner manufactures seals for various fittings from the PTFE sheets produced using a stamping process. The leftover pieces arising at its end are also recycled. This applies to all virgin PTFE and PTFE-modified types that we use. The PTFE we purchase and process is therefore part of a closed system.

Handling and possible alternative disposal options, emissions behaviour
As things stand, the market is not aware of any emissions containing PFAS being released into the environment during the use phase of any of our products. If our articles are disposed of properly in the end-of-life phase, all plastic parts containing PFAS can be recycled. If our items are not provided to the appropriate recycler and end up in incineration instead, there are legal and workable processes in place to prevent PFAS from entering the environment. This means that our articles can also be disposed of in a waste incineration plant without posing a risk to people or the environment, provided certain requirements are met. However, it should be noted that our products are not sold to the end consumer, but only to business customers in the mechanical and plant engineering, pharmaceutical and chemical industries. Therefore, our articles are not and will not be found in municipal waste from private individuals, but exclusively in waste from other businesses. According to their own statement, they also have the possibility to collect our articles separately and recycle them. In conclusion, it can be said that recycling PTFE is always feasible and above all more environmentally friendly, but incineration is also possible in case PTFE ends up in the usual disposal system.

Request for exemption
Kunststofftechnik Lahme is appealing to ECHA to reconsider the PFAS ban proposal and grant an exemption for the PTFE and PVDF materials. This is specified below. In the exemptions of the “RO2” ban proposal, large areas of use are not considered separately and proven harmless substances with high socio-economic added value are equated with potentially hazardous substances.

Furthermore, in the general interest, Kunststofftechnik Lahme proposes a much more detailed basis for regulating exemptions. The network for filtering potential exemptions on the basis of Table 9 of Annex XV is extremely coarse-meshed, especially in the area of technical products. Mostly only very broad applications (other packaging applications) or very specific uses (e.g. ski wax) are addressed, whereby the boundaries of the application areas are often fluid. Suppliers of PFAS-containing articles for the B2B sector are often not only active in one industry. The industries overlooked by such a coarse-grained filtering system, which are overlooked in the drafting of exemptions, cannot be counted. Since, according to the current state of knowledge, PTFE is neither toxic nor harmful to the environment in its processing and use, it is imperative that aspects of economic risk and benefit be taken into account for sound decision-making. We also have customers with tens of thousands of employees across Europe who work with PTFE parts that cannot be replaced. A general PFAS ban will result in enormous financial losses and inevitably high job losses. It should also be taken into account that large, economically strong companies may abandon their German locations and move outside Europe. This means an economically damaging exodus of important know-how and increased dependence on non-European markets.

In our above “Application area” item, uses are mentioned that are predominantly in plants and systems from medical technology, for the production of medicines and for cleaning these plants. Our products are not included in any of the exemption rules noted in Annex XV. What is certain is that the components installed, especially those made from PTFE, cannot be replaced according to the current state of knowledge due to their unique material properties.
PFAS-containing PTFE is thus extremely important for human and veterinary medicine, research and the chemical industry.

For this reason, we request an exemption for the production and processing of components and technical articles made from PTFE.
