Combined Comments:
General Comments: General comments
Our company is an OEM manufacturer of plastic pipes, where the product applications are divided into two groups: pipe systems installed inside buildings for hot and cold water, surface heating and cooling, and below ground pipe systems for e.g. secondary district heating and snow melting. The company is part of a privately owned group of SME companies, which was founded in early 1900´s with headquarters in Sweden. The group is mainly active in the building and construction sector, with international sales and heavy focus on the Nordics.
We are submitting comments on the Annex XV restriction report, focusing on technical information on the PFAS in our operations, status regarding alternative substances and the socio-economic aspects of a PFAS restriction as proposed.

Use
As producers of plastic pipes (crosslinked polyethylene, PE-X) for pressurized applications, we rely on the use of fluoropolymers, mainly PTFE, in our production processes.
The use of PTFE is critical in our manufacturing equipment/process for extrusion of pipes. The high-speed production lines require PTFE based coatings on the tooling and other metallic parts to reduce friction and achieve high-quality single and multi-layer co-extruded plastic pipes. No PTFE or other PFAS is added as a processing aid in the actual product formulation but is exclusively applied to the machinery tooling parts of the processing equipment.
PTFE based coatings is the only lubrication solution that have been found to fulfill all process requirements, which include low friction, resistance to high temperature and pressure, resistance to abrasion and chemicals, and mechanical durability. The PTFE coating is drastically improving polymer flow during production resulting in much lower occurrence of melt fractures and build-up of polymer in the die, while also giving a smoother surface of the extruded pipe. Furthermore, the anti-stick properties of the coating facilitate cleaning of the equipment parts. Non-PFAS alternatives have been evaluated but have been found not to meet the requirements of the use.
From the Sectors and sub-uses in the Annex XV restriction report, the production of plastic pipes is not clearly specified in any of them. Thus, there is uncertainty if the use in an industrial setting of fluoropolymers/PTFE for manufacturing equipment in this application is covered by any of the derogations described in Annex XV restriction report.
If the intention in the Annex XV restriction report is for sector Lubricants to include the sub-use described above, the proposed derogation 5s would be relevant. Lubricating coatings of machinery parts for plastic pipe extrusion clearly fulfills the definition of “harsh” conditons, as use conditions include e.g. high temperature (150-220 °C), high pressure (over 200 bar), exposure to oxidizing substances and also requirement on continuous operation (24 h per day). However, as lubricant derogations are very generally described and lack sufficient clarity, risk for conflicting interpretations by different actors exists, and could result in applications not being covered by a derogation. Possible derogation 5s.

Hazards
Use of fluoropolymers/PTFE for coating of machinery equipment/production tools is an industry-only use, where the risk for workers/operators is controlled and safety measures are implemented.
Production tooling parts with inferior performance in the extrusion process, e.g. caused by damage to the coating layer, are being regularly submitted for re-coating. The fluoropolymer lubricant coating is then removed, replaced and disposed of through controlled incineration. Thus, the manufacturing as well as the end-of-life stage stage of the PFAS for this use is fully handled in an industrial setting with professional users and exposure to the public is very limited; indicating also that corresponding waste management and emissions can be handled in a well-regulated and effective manner for hazardous waste.
As priorly mentioned, the use involving PFAS is limited to the production process stage. PFAS is not a part of the product composition and final products/articles as delivered to downstream users or consumers will not contain PFAS.

Alternatives
The use of PTFE for coating of machinery equipment for plastic pipes extrusion cannot be readily substituted. There are no viable alternatives offering the same key performances (mainly durability, resistance to friction, high thermal and chemical resistance, resistance to pressure, purity,…) as delivered by PTFE. Without access to PTFE coated tooling, the production lines cannot produce pipes of the quality as specified by product standards and customers.
In the last 10 years, our company has evaluated several alternative coatings (e.g. chrome based, ceramic) without success. Upstream stakeholders, e.g. machinery manufacturers, have investigated potential alternatives to PTFE for a number of years. The consensus is that there is no alternative offering the performance and securing required quality and performance of the produced pipes. A direct quote from a major manufacturer of extrusion machinery is;
“We deliver extruders and heads for more than 20 years. And we always looked for alternatives to [PTFE], but for processing reasons. I don`t know how many different materials and coatings we have already tried without success. From ceramics to paint nothing worked. I am pretty sure to tell you there is no alternative to [PTFE]”.
The pipe product formulations and properties are regulated by a high level of international standards on product composition and performance. Any changes to the products require a significant long-term testing and certification efforts. Products are used in pressurized applications with high performance requirements and long expected lifetime (50+ years), where premature system failures are costly and can potentially lead to safety incidents affecting human health. In addition, any alternative material for drinking water applications must meet all the specifications arising from EU (recast Drinking Water Directive, Art 11) as well as other international legislations. All these factors pose further limitations for alternatives.

Socio-economic
A restriction of fluoropolymers as proposed in the Annex XV restriction report would impact all pipe products manufactured. Without a derogation, the direct impact will be closure of company with corresponding loss of all revenue and employees. The necessary investments in R&D, machinery, process and product reformulation and certifications to find alternatives and substitute PFAS in a very limited time will not be possible to bear, considering the size of the company and the annual revenue.
A further socio-economic effect of a restriction for this use is that corresponding plastics pipe systems produced outside EEA will still be possible to sell in the EEA market (as the final products do not contain PFAS). The world-wide emissions related to the use will therefore likely not decrease, only shift geographically. In addition, negative environmental impact due to longer transports of voluminous pipe products from outside EEA is to be expected when pipes can no longer be produced locally in the EEA.

Transition
Considering the current R&D status, where no viable alternatives to replace fluoropolymer coatings have been identified, as well as the significant requirement for time and resources to optimize production processes and final pipe products once a potential alternative is developed, the proposed transition times are not realistic in any way.

Adapting new processing technology and potentially also new pipe formulations will require evaluation of long-term application performance and subsequently securing needed certifications in all relevant geographical areas (also outside EEA) for the modified products; this will comprise testing according to multiple product performance standards and requirements for hygienic approvals, depending on market. Nationally based product approvals and certification schemes is the norm for these pipe system applications. The time frame for developing a functioning alternative to PFAS for the described use will be very long, based on the lack of potential candidates for coating as well as the subsequent requirements for long-term pipe testing to verify the performance of the re-designed products and the regulatory framework for both application performance and hygienic assessment of materials in contact in drinking water. The re-cast Drinking Water Directive (DWD) currently under implementation will already lead to large constraints in the testing capacity for hygienic approvals of existing products. Adding testing needs in the same short time for a large number of re-formulated pipe products brought about by implementation of PFAS restrictions will result in an intolerable market situation and an unproportionally large load for manufacturers, especially SME ones.

An estimated substitution process for PFAS for a pipe used in drinking water application is outlined below:
◼ R&D efforts for identification of potentially suitable lubricating coating material that fulfils all the key performance requirements of the process and is available in industrial scale. This is the most difficult phase and is estimated to take at least three to five years, likely more, considering the unique performance of fluoropolymers A note is that if part of the lubricating layer will transfer to the final product, only the use of substances that are on positive lists for drinking water applications will be allowed.
◼ Evaluation and verification of the alternative in the pipe production process, including process optimization for different products and production lines. Full-scale process testing will be costly and potential generate significant amounts of off-spec products. Estimate one to two years.
◼ Product performance and long-term testing for certification, which typically take at least one to two years per product formulation. If these tests fail the process moves back at the beginning, with the identification of a new potential alternative.
◼ Migration tests to ensure compliance with legislations for hygienic aspects (for each relevant country worldwide), which can also take approximately one year. Again, if the material fails the migration tests the process again moves back to the first phase.

Request for exemption
Based on the lack of identified alternatives and high application requirements as well as regulatory load resulting in very long transition times, in combination with industrial-only use with good control of exposure, low emissions and possibilities for efficient end-of-life waste management, an exemption from the proposed restriction is motivated for this use.
An unlimited derogation for use of fluoropolymers, specifically PTFE, in industrial settings (i.e. manufacturing equipment and processes for production of plastic piping systems in industrial environments, including the process for coating of the metal parts) should be granted.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The use of PFAS for manufacturing of plastics piping systems is not specifically described under any of the Sectors and (sub-)uses. A main application for plastics piping systems is building and construction; thus, relevant sector could be Construction. A major application of PFAS in the plastics piping systems is fluropolymers/PTFE used as coating, lubricant or processing aid in the manufacturing equipment/process for extrusion of pipes; relevant sector Lubrication. Another potential sector could be the application sector Plastics and rubber/elastomer production, which was not researched in detail according to Annex A of the restriction report.   Overall, it is unclear whether the specific application of plastics piping systems fits into the description of above sectors and uses, and if it is included in proposed derogations (e.g. 5s for lubrication) or not. This would need to be further clarified

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Use of fluoropolymer/PTFE for lubricant coatings of production tools for plastics pipes is an industry-only/professional use. Coatings are being regularly applied, removed, replaced and disposed of through controlled incineration. The emissions in both the manufacturing step of the coating and in the end-of-life stage can be efficiently controlled.   As no low-molecular weight, volatile PFAS is used in the coatings the emissions during the use stage in the extrusion line is extremely low and presenting no health hazards to operators.  No significant amount of PFAS is emitting to the production air, as evidenced by measurement of air quality performed by accredited third party at several occasions (total volatile organic carbons, VOC, and GC-MS screening/identification).

6. Missing uses: As stated under Information Request 1 Sectors and (sub-)uses, it is unclear whether ‘Use of PFAS for manufacturing of plastics piping systems’ fit into the description of specified sectors and uses and if it is included in proposed derogations (e.g. 5s for lubrication) or not.  Potential missing sub-use under Sector Lubricants is – Fluoropolymer lubricant coatings of production tools for manufacturing plastic piping systems for heating and sanitary inside buildings and below ground   a) Type of PFAS associated with the use is fluoropolymers, mainly PTFE. The volume of PTFE used for coating of machinery/tools is difficult to assess exactly but it is negligible in relation to the volume of pipe product output from the process. Estimate of annual consumption is less than 0,01 kg PTFE per ton plastic pipe produced. b) Key functionalities include lubrication and reduction of friction, resistance to high temperature and pressures, resistance to abrasion and chemicals, non-stick properties and high mechanical durability.  c) As fluoropolymer coatings have been almost exclusively used for the last 20 years, a restriction could be estimated to affect 75-100 % of the plastic pipe manufacturing companies.  Trade association TEPPFA, The European Plastic Pipes & Fittings Association, represent 350 companies that manufacture plastic pipes and fittings and around 65 % of EU market share. TEPPFA members’ final products have an annual production volume of 3 million tonnes directly employing 40,000 people with €12 billion combined annual sales.  d) There are no known alternatives that can fulfill the key technical functionalities offered by fluoroploymers/PTFE. Upstream stakeholders, e.g. machinery manufacturers, have investigated potential alternatives to PTFE for a number of years. Our company has evaluated internally both chrome based and ceramic coatings without success. The consensus is that there is no alternative offering the performance to secure required quality and performance of the produced pipes. Economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives cannot be estimated as no alternatives have yet been identified. e) The status of R&D processes for finding suitable alternatives is that no viable options have been identified by machinery manufacturer, despite continuous efforts in the last 20 years trying to find alternatives for technical reasons. Thus, the likelihood of successful identification of alternatives and implementation of substitute(s) in the next 5 years is estimated to be low. The R&D activities cannot be handled by the pipe manufacturer but would be the responsibility of the machinery manufacturer.  Furthermore, any need for process adaptations and optimization for an identified alternative would add minimum 1-2 years, assuming alternatives will be readily available in the market. Currently, lead-times from order to machinery delivery are typically 12-18 months. As pipe products are used in pressurized applications with expected lifetime of 50 years, long-term performance testing is required by standards and customers. Process changes affecting the final product compositions and/or properties would require new product testing (minimum 1 yr) as well as new certifications and regulatory approvals, especially for pipes intended for drinking water applications where hygienic approvals are required. Plastic piping systems is a heavily regulated application and re-certification of the full product portfolio in all markets in a short period of time would not be financially possible for an SME company to manage. f) Not applicable g) The socio-economic impact of a restriction would be closure of the company as annual sales is fully dependent on the processes affected by the proposal. Direct impact 20 M€ and approx. 60 employees. Downstream actors in the value chain would have larger impact, e.g. largest customer 100 M€. Furthermore, unavailability in the market of plastic pipe systems fulfilling national standards and regulations would have a huge negative impact on the building and construction sector. The full impact on the plastics pipe industry as a whole and corresponding value chain on EEA scale would naturally be several orders of magnitude larger than this.

General Comments: General Comments
Volvo Cars wishes to provide comments on the consultation on the Annex XV restriction report related to the Restriction on the manufacture, placing on the market and use of PFASs.
Introduction
Volvo Cars manufactures premium vehicles, SUVs, station wagons, and sedans and aim to offer full electrification of our vehicles in foreseeable future. Volvo Cars have high standards regarding sustainability and fully shares the ambitions to reduce the use of PFAS substances to protect both people and the environment. However, Volvo Cars have some concerns regarding the restriction proposal when it comes to timeline and proposed derogations for appointed products and sub-uses.
Main concerns:
Volvo Cars main concerns with the proposed PFAS-restriction:
• Impact on vehicle type approval:
Automotive industry is a major downstream user with complex products, having thousands of applications with dependencies where PFASs functionalities have crucial impact on the vehicles safety and reliability. Cars require type approval according to the vehicle type approval regulation ((EU) 2018/858) before the product can be offered for the European market. Substituting PFASs could require product redevelopment, re-design with validation, approval, and implementation phases for crucial components, which take years to conduct and have its dependencies along the supply chain. It could also trigger the need for renewed vehicle type approval. This must be considered when regulating vehicle related PFAS applications and its functionalities.

• Timeline and implementation:
A very large number of PFASs are covered by the suggested restriction proposal, and phasing out that many substances will require time and effort. However, the timeline for the implementation of the restriction proposal is very short to cover all necessary steps of new development and approval phases where needed. For a successful implementation of this restriction proposal that minimizes the risk of regrettable substitution, we suggest taking a stepwise approach.
1) In a first stage, we suggest adopting communication requirements for PFAS in the value chain, with the purpose of getting a clearer view of how these substances are used. Traceability of most of the PFASs in scope of the proposal has not previously been required by any regulation, and therefore PFAS occurrences are still partly unknown.
2) When current uses of the PFASs in scope have been identified, the functionality of the uses and possible substitutes need to be assessed. A switch to alternative solutions without proper investigations could risk regrettable substitution from a broader sustainability and health perspective, which needs to be avoided. After that, potential derogations can be considered for the uses where there are no alternatives available with focus on risks and technical prerequisites.
3) When relevant derogations have been identified, the phase out of PFASs not covered by any derogations can start. Substitution of PFASs in our products require redevelopment, verification, validation, and implementation. The change of some parts could, as well, trigger the need for recertification towards emission legislations and safety type approvals.
4) Suggested derogations should be subject to review after a selected period, to assess the maturity of alternative solutions. Additional derogations can be needed as more information on uses appears. We therefore suggest that the restriction list should not be considered as a static document, but instead be updated as new information comes into light and depending on the maturity of alternative solutions.

• Derogations for products placed on the market before entry into force (EiF):
From our understanding, the proposed restriction will affect products already in production and their spare parts. This could mean that PFAS containing products placed on the market before EiF could not be resold but would need to be scrapped in advance. The restriction could also affect the safety, reliability and lifetime of products placed on the market before EiF, as it might hinder maintenance and reparations, and access to spare parts. This would be in contradiction with the goals of the Green Deal. It would also impact possibilities to act in line with own company objectives to limit use of resources if components cannot be reused, for example by remanufacturing and other ambitions related to circularity. We therefore propose a derogation for products placed on the market before the restriction EiF and for its spare parts during its lifetime.

• Spare Parts & Maintenance, Legacy spare parts
Vehicles have long lifetimes, and must be serviced, repaired, and maintained to guarantee their function, safety, and reliability. Producers of vehicles must ensure availability of service and spare parts for many years. Within the ELV directive, this has been resolved via the decided “repair as produced principle”. With the suggested restriction proposal on PFASs, availability of spare parts and maintenance can no longer be ensured after EiF for products in production or after production. Volvo Cars therefore suggest a full derogation of all spare parts to enable long lifetimes and circularity.

• Appropriate substitutes
It must be recognized that there can be multiple uses of a single PFAS substance with different purposes/functionality. Thus, there is likely not a single substitute that can be applied to all functionalities of a PFAS. Each application needs to be verified based on its requirements and functions.

• Identification of PFASs in scope of the restriction:
Previous substance restrictions have used CAS numbers to identify the substances to be restricted. Here, no CAS numbers have been included in the restriction proposal to identify the substances with, but instead chemical structures have been used. Our current systems of identifying substances in our value chain are based on CAS numbers. Time and guidance from the authorities are needed to update these systems to allow for searches based on chemical structure.

Fabrication of LIB electrodes and function of binder  The binder makes the slurry viscous and bonds and adheres materials in electrodes LIB is a secondary battery that uses a metal oxide such as lithium cobalt oxide (LCO) as the positive electrode active material, a carbon material such as graphite as the negative electrode active material, an organic solvent and lithium salt as the electrolyte, and a separator between the positive and negative electrodes. The active material is usually powder composed of particles of about 1 to 20 μm diameter. The active material is mixed with a binder and a conductive material such as carbon black to form a slurry, which is applied onto a metal foil such as aluminum or copper and dried to form an electrode. (Nagai 2009) The binder is a polymer material that imparts an appropriate viscosity to the organic solvent-based slurry and imparts dispersion stability to the filling material such as the active material when producing the electrode. When the organic solvent in the coated electrode dries, the binder binds the active materials in the electrode together and adheres the active material to the metal foil current collector. At this stage, the binder coats the surface of the active material and affects the electrochemical properties of the battery (resistance, rate performance, battery life, etc.). (Nagai 2009, Yoshino 2010, Amin-Sanayei, He 2015, Despotopoulou, Burchill 2002, KKS 2021)  Organic solvent application is essential　 In water-based slurries, Li ions in positive electrode materials (lithium transition metal oxide compounds, LCO, etc.) are replaced with hydrogen ions in water, degrading the performance of the material. Therefore, there is no substitute for PVDF binders in organic solvent electrode systems. (Watanabe et al 2021)  Binder is a key material that affects various battery performances In the cell, Li ions move between the positive electrode active material and the negative electrode active material through the electrolytic solution, thereby repeating discharging and charging to transfer the electric capacity. Li ions are intercalated and deintercalated at the interface between the electrolyte and the active materials. The greater the amount of active material, the greater the electric capacity of the cell. The resistance of the cell depends on the movement of lithium ions in the electrolyte and the active material, and the intercalation/deintercalation at their interfaces. Therefore, the smaller the active material, the larger the specific surface area, and the larger the coating area of the electrode layer, the better the input/output characteristics of the cell. Binders hold the components in the electrode together to ensure ionic and electronic conductivity.  Electrochemical oxidation resistance at positive electrode Since Li metal has the most noble potential, the potential of the positive electrode is as high as 4.2 to 4.5 V (Li/Li+), so the surface of the positive electrode material becomes an electrochemically highly oxidizing atmosphere. Therefore, the non-fluorine-based polymer has low oxidation resistance and is easily oxidatively decomposed on the surface of the positive electrode material. PVDF has excellent oxidation resistance and does not decompose for a long period of time. (Kurihara, Nagai 1998, Inaba et al 2013, Nagai 2009)  In addition, organic solvent molecules in the electrolytic solution are likely to be oxidatively decomposed when the potential of the positive electrode becomes high. The PVDF binder thinly coats the surface of the positive electrode active material, absorbs several tens of percent of the electrolyte, and swells. It does not interfere with the disinsertion and insertion of Li ions at the interface between the positive electrode active material and the electrolyte and acts as a passive film, ‘SEI (Solid Electrolyte Interphase)’, suppressing the decomposition of the electrolyte solvent. It is essential to suppress the redox reactions of the organic solvents in the electrolyte to prevent deterioration of battery performance (lifetime, ionic conductivity, etc.). (Inaba et al 2013)  Since PVDF binders have excellent properties that are indispensable especially for positive electrodes, even after commercial production began in 1991, numerous developments have been made by companies and research institutes. No alternative to PVDF binder has been found yet. Alternatives to PVDF binder for LIBs:  (a) No alternative binder for lithium metal oxide cathode materials In general, LIB binders use PVDF for the positive electrode, and styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR)/carboxymethylcellulose (CMC) and acrylic resin for the negative electrode. An organic solvent (N-methyl pyrrolidone, NMP) and water are used as solvents for electrode slurries for coating with these binders, respectively. An electrode slurry is prepared by mixing a lithium metal oxide, a conductive carbon material, a binder and a solvent as an electrode material. A coated electrode is obtained by coating the slurry on a metal foil and volatilizing the solvent. The binder binds the members together in the electrode. A cell consists of a positive electrode, a negative electrode, a separator, an electrolyte, and a container (metal can, aluminum pouch, etc.). SBR (Styrene Butadiene Rubber) and acrylic resins can be dissolved or dispersed in an organic solvent to prepare a slurry, which is then applied to a current collector foil and dried to prepare an electrode. However, in the battery, electrochemical oxidative decomposition occurs on the surface of the positive electrode to generate gas, etc., and the battery performance deteriorates, making it impossible to maintain the initial performance. (Kurihara, Nagai 1998, Inaba et al 2013) In addition, since alkaline components (such as LiOH) derived from the raw materials remain in the positive electrode material, there is also the problem of corrosion of the aluminum current collector when the electrode is coated with a water-based slurry. (Watanabe 2021) A carbon material with a large specific surface area is used for the conductive agent, and because it is generally fine particles and hydrophobic, it is difficult to disperse it evenly in an aqueous slurry. This impairs the manufacturing process and product functionality. (Kondo, Ohnishi 2014) Therefore, it cannot be replaced with the non-fluorinated resin binders used in current water-based slurries. CMC cannot be used because it is insoluble in organic solvents. Cellulosic resins such as hydroxypropyl cellulose (HPC) are soluble in organic solvents and are effective in imparting viscosity to slurries. However, it dissolves in the organic solvent of the electrolyte in the cell, so that the binding function as a binder cannot be maintained, and the SEI function on the surface of the positive electrode material cannot be imparted. Therefore, cellulosic resins cannot be used in organic solvent slurry systems. In organic solvent-based slurries, even if slurries and electrodes can be manufactured, no binder other than PVDF has been found that satisfies the requirements for electrochemical stability in cells, battery life characteristics, and safety.  Even if a substitute is found, it is necessary to reconsider an electrode coating device and a solvent recovery system. Commercially produced in 1991, and subsequent developments have not found a better oxide cathode material than the PVDF binder. Therefore, it will take a long time (probably more than 5 years) to confirm the suitability of cathode materials, formulations, manufacturing processes, development, etc., and further verification (battery functions, safety and life) and facility construction. It is expected that it will take 10 years or more.  Many LIB storage batteries are installed in electric vehicles such as EVs and PHEVs and have a proven record of accomplishment as automotive batteries. However, since the alternative battery has no record of accomplishment in small equipment applications, it is necessary to confirm safety and reliability after completing the development of materials and processes for automotive applications. Therefore, it is expected that demonstration tests for another 5 to 10 years will be required.  (b) Improvement of LIB cathode material Appropriate methods and materials need to be developed, such as a coating technology that suppresses oxidative decomposition of the organic material on the material surface by allowing Li ions to enter and leave the surface of the metal oxide of the positive electrode material.　 Coated electrodes and LIBs are highly complete systems, so if one key component is changed, it will have a significant impact on various parts such as LIB materials, manufacturing processes, battery performance, and quality control. This means that it cannot be changed easily.  As mentioned above, no substitutes for PVDF binders currently exist. LIB is a secondary battery that uses a metal oxide such as lithium cobalt oxide (LCO) as the positive electrode active material, a carbon material such as graphite as the negative electrode active material, an organic solvent and lithium salt as the electrolyte, and a separator between the positive and negative electrodes. The active material is usually powder composed of particles of about 1 to 20 μm diameter. The active material is mixed with a binder and a conductive material such as carbon black to form a slurry, which is applied onto a metal foil such as aluminum or copper and dried to form an electrode. The binder is a polymer material that imparts an appropriate viscosity to the organic solvent-based slurry and imparts dispersion stability to the filling material such as the active material when producing the electrode. When the organic solvent in the coated electrode dries, the binder binds the active materials in the electrode together and adheres the active material to the metal foil current collector. At this stage, the binder coats the surface of the active material and affects the electrochemical properties of the battery (resistance, rate performance, battery life, etc.).  In water-based slurries, Li ions in positive electrode materials (lithium transition metal oxide compounds, LCO, etc.) are replaced with hydrogen ions in water, degrading the performance of the material. Therefore, Organic solvent application is essential and there is no substitute for PVDF binders in organic solvent electrode systems.  In the cell, Li ions move between the positive electrode active material and the negative electrode active material through the electrolytic solution, thereby repeating discharging and charging to transfer the electric capacity. Li ions are intercalated and deintercalated at the interface between the electrolyte and the active materials. The greater the amount of active material, the greater the electric capacity of the cell. The resistance of the cell depends on the movement of lithium ions in the electrolyte and the active material, and the intercalation/deintercalation at their interfaces. Therefore, the smaller the active material, the larger the specific surface area, and the larger the coating area of the electrode layer, the better the input/output characteristics of the cell. Binder holds the components in the electrode together to ensure ionic and electronic conductivity so that it’s a key material which affects various battery performances.  Since Li metal has the most noble potential, the potential of the positive electrode is as high as 4.2 to 4.5 V (Li/Li+), so the surface of the positive electrode material becomes an electrochemically highly oxidizing atmosphere. Therefore, the non-fluorine-based polymer has low oxidation resistance and is easily oxidatively decomposed on the surface of the positive electrode material. PVDF has excellent oxidation resistance and does not decompose for a long period of time.  In addition, organic solvent molecules in the electrolytic solution are likely to be oxidatively decomposed when the potential of the positive electrode becomes high. The PVDF binder thinly coats the surface of the positive electrode active material, absorbs several tens of percent of the electrolyte, and swells. It does not interfere with the disinsertion and insertion of Li ions at the interface between the positive electrode active material and the electrolyte and acts as a passive film, ‘SEI (Solid Electrolyte Interphase)’, suppressing the decomposition of the electrolyte solvent. It is essential to suppress the redox reactions of the organic solvents in the electrolyte to prevent deterioration of battery performance (lifetime, ionic conductivity, etc.).  Since PVDF binders have excellent properties that are indispensable especially for positive electrodes, even after commercial production began in 1991, numerous developments have been made by companies and research institutes. No alternative to PVDF binder has been found yet. In general, LIB binders use PVDF for the positive electrode, and styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR)/carboxymethylcellulose (CMC) and acrylic resin for the negative electrode. An organic solvent (N-methyl pyrrolidone, NMP) and water are used as solvents for electrode slurries for coating with these binders, respectively. An electrode slurry is prepared by mixing a lithium metal oxide, a conductive carbon material, a binder and a solvent as an electrode material. A coated electrode is obtained by coating the slurry on a metal foil and volatilizing the solvent. The binder binds the members together in the electrode. A cell consists of a positive electrode, a negative electrode, a separator, an electrolyte, and a container (metal can, aluminum pouch, etc.). SBR (Styrene Butadiene Rubber) and acrylic resins can be dissolved or dispersed in an organic solvent to prepare a slurry, which is then applied to a current collector foil and dried to prepare an electrode. However, in the battery, electrochemical oxidative decomposition occurs on the surface of the positive electrode to generate gas, etc., and the battery performance deteriorates, making it impossible to maintain the initial performance. In addition, since alkaline components (such as LiOH) derived from the raw materials remain in the positive electrode material, there is also the problem of corrosion of the aluminum current collector when the electrode is coated with a water-based slurry. A carbon material with a large specific surface area is used for the conductive agent, and because it is generally fine particles and hydrophobic, it is difficult to disperse it evenly in an aqueous slurry. This impairs the manufacturing process and product functionality. Therefore, it cannot be replaced with the non-fluorinated resin binders used in current water-based slurries. CMC cannot be used because it is insoluble in organic solvents. Cellulosic resins such as hydroxypropyl cellulose (HPC) are soluble in organic solvents and are effective in imparting viscosity to slurries. However, it dissolves in the organic solvent of the electrolyte in the cell, so that the binding function as a binder cannot be maintained, and the SEI function on the surface of the positive electrode material cannot be imparted. Therefore, cellulosic resins cannot be used in organic solvent slurry systems. In organic solvent-based slurries, even if slurries and electrodes can be manufactured, no binder other than PVDF has been found that satisfies the requirements for electrochemical stability in cells, battery life characteristics, and safety.  Even if a substitute is found, it is necessary to reconsider an electrode coating device and a solvent recovery system. Commercially produced in 1991, and subsequent developments have not found a better oxide cathode material than the PVDF binder. Therefore, it will take a long time (probably more than 5 years) to confirm the suitability of cathode materials, formulations, manufacturing processes, development, etc., and further verification (battery functions, safety and life) and facility construction. It is expected that it will take 10 years or more. This commentary concerns polymer optical fibre (POF) and its use for gigabit digital networks and the development of the gigabit society.

The special properties and advantages of POF cable helps people to install a stable and reliable gigabit network technology in a) existing houses without large construction effort and b) for new houses to provide a comprehensive optical data infrastructure in buildings and homes. POF cable is an important product for digitalization in multiple market areas. Installation properties and advantages support the optimized usage of WiFi systems and wide spread integration of 5G, 6G and new up coming data transmission technologies. Since PFAS in POF cable is long-term bound it is practically not released into the environment.

Fluorinated Polymer cannot be substituted today by any other material due to the specific requirement needed for the cladding in polymer optical fibre for optical signal transmission. It is mandatory to ensure a required and guaranteed stable performance of the cable for the entire lifetime of an installation.
POF cable is installed and integrated in buildings and homes in combination with the electrical installation or concealed surface installation. This means that around 80% of installations are protected in the conduits of the electrical infrastructure. Therefore, the very small amount of PFAS used in the thin coating layer of POF (Polymer Optical Fibre) is unlikely to enter the environment or the human food cycle.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Polymer Optical Fibre is used in the sector Electronics and Semiconductors and sub-use wires and cables.   In the current version of Annex XV in “Table 2. PFAS main applications and sub-uses”, cables and wires are only mentioned in the table of sub-use of the section electronics and semiconductions (page 54). Since Polymer Optical Fibre is used in various applications like data cable, light-pipe, sensors, lighting and various sectors as e.g. medical devices, industrial devices and systems, construction products (e.g. lighting, light guide) and semiconductors (optical on-board data transmission, signal coupling etc…) we would like to recommend to create a main application for cables and wires. Polymer optical fibre is used in all these applications and sectors since the advantages of POF have a high specific importance, such as immunity to EMF, galvanic isolation, noise immunity, robustness, flexibility, small mechanical dimension, easy installation and connectorisation and many others. In our case we are using POF cable for data transmission in building- and home networks and for industrial data transmission.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: a) Usage phase: -> The service life time for POF cable depends on environmental conditions. In home- and building installations the lifetime is considered to be more than 100 years or the estimated lifetime of a building (home or office).  Since in most cases the Polymer Optical Fibre (in cable) is installed in conduits or under frame boards, there are no emissions during the usage phase.  b) At the end of Polymer Optical Fibre's life, no emissions to the environment are expected as the material is either thermally recycled or disposed of in a landfill. We expect that 80% are disposed of in landfills with no further emission of PFAS expected.  20% could be disposed of through professional incineration The amount of PFAS used in the cladding of the POF cable is not more than 2%wT.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: No uncontrolled PFAS emission is expected at the end of lifetime.

5. Proposed derogations: Answer to specific info request 5:  The annual consumption of PFAS containing material for POF cable used in data communication is estimated to be between 500 and 4000 km of POF cable per year. The cable weight is approx. 8gram p/m. Thus, the total weight of cable for 500km and 4000km are equals 4T and 32T. The amount of PFAS used in POF is less than 2%wt. thus, the values under 4T and 32T become less than 0.08T p/y and 0.64T p/y

6. Missing uses: In our specific use it is the building- and home network where Polymer Optical Fibre is playing an important role to allow future proof data backbone installations for comprehensive infrastructure coverage in buildings and homes as well as for installations under difficult circumstances. A generic ban would have a very strong impact for the system up-grade of in building- and home networks with Gigabit infrastructure for digitalisation and digital connectivity. It is feasible, that future new wireless technologies with higher frequencies or data transmission over light and infrared would have significant problems to be installed since the benefit of POF cabling, to be installed in one conduit together with electrical wires could not be used. Furthermore, it would not be possible to provide advanced, comprehensive connectivity as required in the future for homes and buildings.

8. Other identified uses: At this time there is no alternative available.

However, the long-term effects of exposure to these persistent chemicals are not well understood, and toxicological data are limited. The underlying chemistry of PFAS (strong C-F bond) contributes to their persistent nature, which in turn leads to greater potential that they could cause serious and/or irreversible damage to the environment.

PFAS families may be divided into two primary categories; non-polymeric and polymeric.
Polymeric PFAS:  Polymers have a somewhat special status in UK and EU REACH in that they are exempt from the registration requirements. Instead of registering polymers, the monomers and other reactants that comprise the polymer are registered in their place. However, polymer substances are not exempted from other parts of REACH. As such polymers – including polymeric PFAS – may be subject to restriction under REACH. The monomers that comprise the polymers may also be covered by the restriction provisions of REACH, if required… It is noted that because monomers used to create polymers are de facto intermediates, these monomers would be exempted from any authorisation provisions of REACH.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: General comments:
After reading the report, our strong overall opinion is that it fails to differentiate between distinctly different materials within the self-labelled ‘PFAS’ umbrella. Throughout the report, it mentions on multiple occasions the many differences between Perfluoropolyethers (referred to as ‘oligomeric/polymeric PFASs) and other, smaller PFAS substances. These differences include, but are not limited to, water solubility, chemical classification and hazard labelling, toxicity, global warming potential, bioaccumulation and mobility.
Regarding water solubility, the fact that oligomeric/polymeric PFASs are water insoluble is mentioned in section 1.1.4.4, however this point is then not discussed in any detail pertaining to how this distinguishes it from other PFASs, and how this negates/limits some of the hazardous characteristics which the report is trying to attach to all PFASs. Additionally, when looking at supplementary documentation, in B.9.22.4 it states that no suitable biomonitoring studies were identified for these materials, which points to a significant lack of evidence to support such drastic action.
Oligomeric/polymeric PFASs do not require REACH registration, and no toxicity information could be found in the REACH registered substance database. It is also stated that for Oligomeric/polymeric PFASs ‘properties within the group can vary considerably’. Within the same paragraph one study for one material (PCTFE) is used in an effort to justify the banning of all PFASs, which is extremely contradictory. There is also no evidence provided for the breakdown route from PFPE to PFAS/PFAA, despite a general statement being provided that this will happen ‘at any point in their lifecycle’. Additionally, in section 1.1.3, it is referenced that around 6600 PFAS’s carry a classification element, and that most are self-classifications. This implies that the proposed ban encompasses at least 3400 substances which hold no hazard classification whatsoever.
The global warming potential of PFASs is detailed in section 1.1.4. However, specific mention is only made to fluorinated gases. It is another contradiction that this is taken into consideration when proposing a ban for over 10000 PFAS chemicals.
It is explained that there are large uncertainties regarding bioaccumulation due to the lack of data for the majority of compounds. Perfluoropolyethers will be unable to accumulate due to their high molecular weight, which are typically in the region of 5000-8000 Da.
Due to the high molecular weight and water insolubility of Perfluoropolyethers, these chemicals should be considered non-mobile or extremely low mobility.

Alternatives:
Perfluoropolyethers have a wide range of beneficial characteristics which make them suitable for a large number of industrial applications. These include:
• Chemically unreactive
• Thermal and oxidative stability
• No flashpoint
• Low friction
• Water and oil insoluble
These characteristics make Perfluoropolyethers unique and arise due to the extremely strong carbon-fluorine bonds present in PFAS materials. Therefore, the requirement to find a replacement solution within 1.5 to 13.5 years (18-month initial period with up to 12-year derogation) is impossible. These products have been available for over 60 years, with a (relatively) very high market price. In this time no alternatives have been found, so to expect a replacement to be found in the next 13.5 years is not realistic.

Request for exemption:
In summary, it is evident that the proposed ban is going too far in order to remove a small number of hazardous chemicals from industry in one region of the world. Perfluoropolyethers have been proven to not share the same hazard characteristics as other PFASs which the report focuses on. Their physical and chemical characteristics make Perfluoropolyethers essential and irreplaceable for a wide range of industries. These uses include but are not limited to: steel manufacturing, aerospace equipment and medical / commercial diving breathing apparatus. Perfluoropolyethers also play a vital role in the manufacture of semiconductors used in technology such as computers and electric vehicles and also act as vital lubricants in the nuclear energy industry. Growth and advancement in these sectors is necessary to secure the security and economic future of EU citizens. By restricting the use of these polymers, advancements and growth in these sectors will be heavily restricted and this will lead to less ability to compete with other world economies and therefore poorer outcomes for EU citizens. We therefore request that Perfluoropolyethers be exempted from the ECHA regulation.

PWN drinkwater supply company in the Netherlands strongly supports the proposed PFAS restriction. PFAS measurements in drinking water, as reported by RIVM in October 2022, emphasize the need for action to protect the sources of our drinking water, the water system in general and our consumers.

PFAS is a serious risk for drinking water
Based on the 2020 EFSA report on “Risk to human health related to the presence of perfluoroalkyl substances in food”,  the Dutch national institute for Public Health (RIVM)  derived a health-based guidance value of 4,4 ng/l PFOA Equivalents.
In the mentioned study by RIVM, PFAS concentrations exceeded this threshold in over half of the measurements of  drinking water produced from surface water. For drinking water from groundwater, this was the case for 1 in 10 measurements. These concentrations need to be brought down to ensure people’s PFAS intake from drinking water does not become too high.
Areas with the highest PFAS concentrations in drinking water are located in the Western part of the Netherlands, where drinking water is mostly produced from river water. Concentrations the environment slowly decline because PFAS are widely present, do not or barely degrade and are difficult to remove in water treatment. Given this fact, a precautionary approach based on source-protection like a the proposed PFAS restriction, is the way forward.
Projections of future PFAS concentrations in ground- and surface water as a source for drinking water indicate that without tackling the source of PFAS  all drink water sources will eventually surpass these threshold values . KWR research in 2022 on PFAS in European waters   suggests that PFAS is raising similar high concern in other EU countries as well.

PFAS is a risk for the water system in general
In addition to the risks for drinking water specifically, it is important to stress that PFAS is a serious risk to the water system in its entirety. If people would only come into contact with PFAS through drinking water, the problem would be less serious. However, there are several other ways in which people are exposed to PFAS.
Furthermore, several examples can be mentioned in which PFAS has negative consequences for the water quality. Additional sources of PFAS in the water system, for example, are the supply of PFAS from upstream rivers and the deposition of PFAS through the air. PFAS has a negative effect on ecology, including toxic effects, accumulation in organisms and subsequently within the food chain.
PFAS also has a negative impact on other water functions like swimming, recreation in general on or close to the water, fishing, irrigation and livestock watering. We see waters in which the concentration of PFAS is already ten thousand times too high, and it is very difficult or even impossible to eliminate PFAS once it is present in the water system.
PFAS also contains  a risk to water soils and circular ambitions. Dredging activities are sometimes necessary to preserve the water system including the water quality. When PFAS accumulates within water soils, the dredge should ultimately be disposed which is very expensive. When it comes to sludge which can be derived from sewage treatment plants, it becomes impossible to reuse the wastewater. In reference a circular economy this is an undesirable effect.

TFA as an extreme threat
Especially the occurrence of the ultrashort PFAS TriFluoroacetic Acid (TFA) in surface water, groundwater and drinking water is an extreme threat. Data from Rijkswaterstaat and RIWA as stored in the Norman database (June 2023) show concentrations of TFA up to 3 microgram/l. The drinking water advisory threshold value for TFA as a single compound is set to 2200 ng/l (RIVM, 2023)  , but combined with other PFAS the proposed threshold-value is in the Netherlands is 4,4 ng PFOA Equivalents (PEQ)/l. In which TFA is given relative potency factor of 0,002.  Neuwald (2022) and Sadia (2023) found concentrations in the order of 1 microgram/l which exceed the limits as given by the European Drinking Water Directive    . In this directive,  which took effect on 12 January 2021,  a limit of 0.5 µg/l for all PFAS is included.  TFA alone exceeds this threshold. This TFA originate from various industrial use, domestic use and degradation products and are found in high concentrations in the environment and drinking water.  illustrating once more that only a (global) ban can be the way forward to prevent the ubiquitous emissions of this compound and its precursors  .
The claim that TFA is of natural origin is convincingly refuted by Joudan (2022)

Clean, deeper groundwater reserves for drinking water will be lost in the future without a ban
At this moment especially drinking water produced from river water is strongly affected by the PFAS pollution. Inevitability, drinking water from groundwater will also be affected without a ban.  Given the ubiquitous presence of PFAS from air-emissions and deposition at the soil-surface, this amount of PFAS will gradually and continuously infiltrate to the deeper aquifers, polluting  the previously unaffected reservoirs of clean drinking water for the Dutch and European costumers, leading to extreme purification costs and efforts. The infiltration-rate of PFAS to the deeper underground is modelled by KWR . This might take decades, but will, without a ban, eventually end up with the pollution of all existing European Groundwater bodies up to levels that exceed the threshold values for PFAS that are proposed in the current revision of the Water Framework Directive (WFD) and its daughter Directives on Environmental Quality Standards (WFD-EQSD) and Groundwater Directive (WFD-GD)), where Environmental Quality Standards (EQS) are proposed for a group of 24 PFAS on al level of 4,4 ng/l PFOA Equivalents.

Banning PFAS in is crucial for several reasons
Health Risks and Consumer Protection
PFAS have been associated with numerous adverse health effects, including developmental issues, liver damage, thyroid disruption, immune system impairment, and certain types of cancer. These substances can enter the human body through various routes, including drinking water. By banning PFAS in Europe, the aim is to reduce exposure to these harmful chemicals and protect public health. The Dutch National Public Health Institute (RIVM) has already calculated that Dutch citizens take in too much PFAS already. A ban on PFAS is absolutely necessary to ensure a safe living environment for European citizens now and in the future.
Water Treatment Challenges and Costs
Removing PFAS from water sources is challenging and costly for drinking water treatment facilities. Due to their unique properties, PFAS are resistant to traditional water treatment processes, making their removal extremely difficult, and moreover, advanced treatment methods, such as activated carbon filtration or reverse osmosis, require 5-20 % more source water, where (groundwater) sources of drinking water are becoming more scarce as a result of climate change and drought.
In addition to this, there are currently no efficient techniques available to eliminate PFAS from waste water through sewage treatment plants. In most cases, existing techniques to reduce PFAS are very expensive and little effective in case of a small source, especially considering the high contribution of additional sources of PFAS through the air and upstream supplies. These techniques are also require a huge amount of energy, which is not desirable in relation to climate change. It is much more effective and environmentally friendly to prevent PFAS from getting into the environment in the first place.  As the vast majority of PFAS in river water (Rhine and Meuse) entering the Netherlands is emitted somewhere in the international river-basin, a European, cross-border approach is the only logical approach to minimize this pollution.
PFAS removal techniques are insufficient and mostly moving PFAS from one medium to another
PFAS is a very persistent group of chemicals with no natural decay.  PFAS removal from drinking water is moving PFAS from one medium to another. Waste streams of PFAS containing activated carbon or membrane concentrate is the result. Removal of PFAS from water might be the solution for drinking water, but leads to extra pollution of (surface) water, air and landfills, as the waste-streams of standard purification (PFAS containing activated carbon, sludge or concentrate) ends up somewhere in the environment.  Verma at al. (2023)  described low performance of thermal and non-thermal treatment technologies in large scale applications.

The need for a ban on PFAS
Banning PFAS in Europe would lead to a reduction in their presence in water sources, easing the burden on water treatment facilities. This, in turn, can alleviate the costs associated with the specialized treatment required for PFAS removal. By preventing further contamination, it allows resources to be focused on enhancing overall water quality and improving treatment efficiency.
In conclusion, banning PFAS in Europe, particularly in the context of drinking water production, is essential for protecting public health, safeguarding the environment, and limiting public costs and even droughts. Droughts, because additional purification with for example membranes, requires  extra source waters from rivers and aquifers that are threatened for over-exploitation during long dry periods like the summer of 2023, where drinking water facilities throughout Europe feared for shortages.  Furthermore, banning PFAS aligns with global efforts to regulate and restrict these substances. It demonstrates Europe's commitment to environmental protection and encourages international harmonization in the control of PFAS. By taking decisive action, Europe can lead the way in creating a safer and more sustainable future, ensuring clean and healthy drinking water for its population and setting an example for the rest of the world.

All PFAS  are a  threat
As we have learned, PFAS are emitted along various pathways and are ubiquitous: everywhere in the world PFAS are found. Unwanted emissions occur during production, use, and disposal.
The total occurrence and emissions of lots of PFAS and precursors are not well known.  According to the Pubchem classification browser  , there are more than 6 million various PFAS that fit the OECD PFAS definition of the Restriction dossier. Removal and remediation is practically impossible. Even burning leads to smaller PFAS-fragments and transformation products like TFA.  Claims of industry that there are less harmful PFAS have led to regrettable substitutions, for example from PFOA to GenX (HFPO-DA). Similar claims of harmless PFAS-subgroups like fluoropolymers are refuted in literature by Lohmann et al.  .  Somewhere in the process of production, use and disposal PFAS will enter the environment and accumulate in water, soil, air and the foodchain. The supports the conclusion that the only way to prohibit further emissions and accumulation of PFAS in our environment is a complete ban.  PWN strongly supports the broad scope of the PFAS definition in the restriction proposal.  The need for a broad scope is also necessary as the health based drinking water advisory level as derived by RIVM has no limitation and contains every PFAS (Including TFA) with an established Relative Potency Factor (RPF-value) translated to PFOA equivalents and should not exceed the level of 4,4 ng/l PFOA equivalents per litre. This list of PFAS is theoretically enormous.



The need of fast implementation and no exemptions
This restriction-proposal does not come as a surprise or unannounced. The societal risks and costs of the use of PFAS have been described many times, for example by Chemsec in 2023  . Given the time between the (announcement of the) proposal (2022) and suggested start of the implementation (2025), there will be enough time for industry to prepare. Therefore exemptions should not be tolerated and only be granted under very strict conditions and for a period as short as possible
Textile, paper and firefighting-foam industry have proven that there are always alternatives available for PFAS. It takes some years of a transformation period, but it is possible, as proven by the H&M group during the ZeroPM workshop in February 2023  .  Recently (june 2023), Martin Scheringer published a comment in science, with the same conclusion  .
Claims that PFAS are essential for societal favourable transitions like the energy transition should be critically assessed, The fact that PFAS are used for “essential” and high valued products, doesn’t automatically mean that PFAS are essential in these products. There will always be an alternative that will also better fit with the European ambitions of a circular economy. PFAS containing products are probably impossible to re-use. In order to prevent further pollution of the European environment and the sources of our drinking water a fast implementation with no exemptions is the way forward.

Only restriction of emissions is an illusion
Claims that the PFAS containing products are not the problem, but only the production, and that the emissions during production could be regulated is misleading. As stated by Lohmann (2020), emissions occur during production, use and disposal  . Removing of PFAS is an illusion. Removal of PFAS from air or water moves the PFAS from one phase to another, for example from water tot activated carbon or membrane concentrate. These PFAS containing waste-streams ends up in landfills or are burned at standard temperatures, leading to new/other and unmeasured smaller PFAS compounds that will re-enter the environment by leaching to soil and air. Again supporting the proposal for a complete ban.

Additional supporting documentation
Commissioned by PWN, KWR has compiled an overview of recent relevant scientific literature information that is important for the current restriction proposal. This report is attached as appendix 2. Relevant conclusions from this research are:
- PFAS have documented adverse effects on human health and the environment, and that (drinking) water is an important exposure route for humans to PFAS;
- The amount of literature and evidence on adverse health effects of PFAS is still growing;
- Many of reported removal methods have the potential to efficiently remove PFAS from water. Nevertheless, it should be noted that these findings are novel and sometimes promising, but it remains yet unclear if their implementation on a large scale is feasible;
- The restriction of PFAS can indeed result in lower exposure and thus risks to humans and the environment;
- It is argued that all PFAS, including fluoropolymers, give rise to emissions of harmful PFAS at some stage of their life cycle. Therefore, some authors support the broad definition of PFAS used in the restriction proposal and the resulting ban on fluoropolymers and other PFAS alike.
- It was noted that the authors supporting the exemption of fluoropolymers from a ban represent or are affiliated with PFAS-producing companies;
- 97 % of China’s PFOA/PFO emissions originated from the production of fluoropolymers;
- Emerging PFAS can induce toxicity like legacy PFAS like PFOS and PFOA;
- The justification for managing PFAS as a single chemical class to reduce PFAS-related risks is provided in the scientific literature. It is argued that a class-based approach can be implemented to eliminate non-essential uses of PFAS more effectively, develop safer alternatives, and clean up highly contaminated areas.
- A restriction of PFAS can indeed result in lower exposure and thus risks to humans and the environment;

The overall conclusion of PWN is that there is strong scientific support for a complete ban of all PFAS according to the proposed PFAS definition, including subgroups as TFA and fluoropolymers.
