General Comments: Guarniflon SpA is an Italian Company, founded in 1982 and based in Castelli Calepio (BG).
The company , since the very beginning,  has been focused on exclusive transformation of PTFE powders (virgin and filled PTFE) used to produce semifinished and machined finished parts .
Guarniflon SpA (with their Divisions FLONTECH - Compounds production-  and PATI - films in Fluoropolymers like ETFE, FEP, PFA, THV) is owned by Mazza Holding, an Italian group established in 1982 which counts about 700 people employed in Europe (Italy, Germany, France, UK, Spain and Romania) , Asia (India) and America (USA and Canada), with a consolidated turnover of 200 million Euro.
Guarniflon Group has now a leading position in transformation of PTFE and in extrusion of Fluoropolymers like ETFE, FEP, PFA transforming more than 5.000 tons of Fluoropolymers/year .
Guarniflon is able to re-use their manufacturing scraps, with an approx. quantity of re-used material of 1000 tons/year.
Guarniflon management system is based on the requirements of the UNI EN ISO 9001: 2015 standard for quality and IATF 16949:2016 standard for automotive sector.
Guarniflon group has its own internal R&D team that closely cooperates with some of the most important Universities specialized in Fluorine Chemistry such as Florence, Milan, Padua, Pisa, Rome and Venice Universities. All the R&D activities are developed in different laboratories located in the Headquarters in Castelli Calepio (BG), and Ospitaletto (BS), in Northern Italy .
Guarniflon group counts in Europe more than 500 employees.

Based on this information, it is possible to understand that the impact of PFAS and related substances restriction would be dramatic for Guarniflon economy , leading it to closure as there is currently no alternative to the conversion of the machinery to produce other materials

Guarniflon is aware of the potential danger of some substances classified as PFAS, but at the same time it is also convinced that an exemption for Fluoropolymers should be adopted, because Fluoropolymers is a family that is profoundly different from the substances for which it is right to request a restriction.

Fluoropolymers are different to other PFAS for the reasons listed below:
• They do not exhibit the toxicological and environmental profiles associated with non-polymeric PFASs that could be considered of concern.
• They have unique physical-chemical properties, which let them very different from non-polymer PFAS and therefore should have a distinct class within them.
• They meet the OECD criteria of Polymer of Low Concern (PLC) and are non-toxic, biocompatible, insoluble and immobile molecules, which are deemed to have insignificant environmental and human health impact.

Industrial production of Fluoropolymers can and has to be handled safely in industrial facilities under controlled conditions.

Fluoropolymers transformed by Guarniflon SpA is used in many different sectors (we supplied PTFE and related Fluoropolymers in several different sectors) that are explained in Annexes.

Main implications for downstream users:

• No alternative allows a complete replacement with performances of equivalent quality; there are some possible alternatives for some properties but there’s no one material that present all the specific and unique properties of Fluoropolymers (no 1:1 alternatives are available)
• Costs will arise due to necessary amendments of machinery and equipment when switching to alternative substances. The industrial application process on products using non-fluoropolymers material is much more complicated.
• Due to the greater quantity of product necessary for this application and the reduced service life of the treated articles, a significant environmental impact must be considered in terms of nanoforms (microplastic) and CO2 emissions.

General Comments: GVS S.p.A consists of three business segments with activities in different industrial sectors. We are manufacturers of filter solutions for applications in the Healthcare & Life Sciences, Energy & Mobility and Health & Safety sectors.

GVS provides our customers with membranes, equipment (filters) and knowledge that are critical and essential for many sectors.

Our three business sectors are critical for society in different ways. Each business sector will therefore provide detailed, data-based, and substantiated input for applications where the use of PFAS (in polymer form) is currently and in the near future without alternative to maintain the function and the purpose of specific critical products.

PFAS have several unique properties that make them very useful yet also difficult to replace with more sustainable solutions. At the same time, very persistent PFAS may lead to adverse effects for the environment and humans.
PFASs are valuable compounds which fall into two main families:
• the low molar-mass PFASs
(including fluorinated telomers, perfluorocarboxylic acids, oligomers and surfactants) which are toxic, persistent, bioaccumulable, mobile and are under severe restricted (several products are already banned) and drastic regulations and
• polymeric ones. Among the latter, polymers bearing fluorinated side moieties have also undergone such above issues.                                                                                    But, fluoropolymers (that is what we use) are niche specialty bio-inert and safe polymers, stable thermally, chemically and against UV and aging. They display outstanding properties, their molar masses being able to reach several million g.mol−1. They fulfill the Polymer of Low Concern criteria and are not prone to face such above hazardous issues. This fluoropolymers must be separated from conventional PFASs and are irreplaceable materials.


We are strictly convinced that this proposal must be readjusted in order to differentiate the restrictions between monomers and polymers and not to consider the PFAS as one big group. We expect to reconsidering, withdrawal or deadline extension/review clause of the regulation.

We, of course, support the search for substitutes for PFAS and conduct active research ourselves. Yet, we do not know whether alternatives with the same technical properties can be found in 5, 10 or 20 years from now or if a different technology is required.

Our industry uses polymeric fluoropolymers PFAS, like PTFE and PVDF in all 3 sectors for filtration solutions. We also use polymeric PFAS as post treatment on our membrane to give the membrane the oleophobic or emophobic properties
We ask that derogations are clarified when it comes to uses of polymeric PFAS in the chemical industry, in Life Sciences, Energy and mobility and Safety sectors.
At the moment:
- "No alternative technology exist at this time."
- "Alternative technologies that are currently conceivable will lead to a decrease in industrial efficiency, and there is concern that it will have an adverse impact on energy problems."

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Table 9 refers only to derogated areas. Many uses and sectors are not taken into account like filters and vents for energy and mobility sectors or filtration media for personal protective devices  GVS currently relies on fluoropolymer components in filtration application. Replacing these throughout all chemical manufacturing infrastructure will be extremely complicated and not feasible in a short period of time.  Table 9 identifies some uses with potential relevance: Industrial food and feed production, medical devices; diagnostic laboratory testing, membranes used in venting of medical devices.  In addition to the uses and sub-uses above, PFAS are used in medical devices (including but not limited to venting membranes), diagnostic devices for quality control in production processes, packaging of substances and mixtures, reagents for manufacture of fine chemicals, pharmaceuticals, plant protection products, biocides etc.  Our comments focus on several industrial filtration and purification devices (as membranes and other components)

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The analysis of emission should be divided for business sector, because the end of life emissions are strongly dependent with the type of use that has been done and with the contacts with substances.  Life science: The solutions provided by GVS are used in laboratories and medical devices applications. The most applications are disposable because they are contaminated with biological substances. Therefore the end of life of these products are treated by incineration or landfill. This could potentially be mitigated by recycling, but this option has not been considered viable due to fears of cross-contamination   Energy and Mobility: our filters and vents cointains PFAS fluorpolymers and they are multi-use and long-term use. Since their durability and long-life, producing limited amount of waste over their long lifetime. They are used for several years before they are replaced, thus waste is minimized and thus volumes of PFAS-containing waste are very low. Furthermore, the PFAS equipment waste is separately collected at its end-of-life phase and is subject to hazardous-waste incineration.  Health & Safety: our personal protection equipments (PPE) cointains PFAS fluorpolymers. The market considers two possible disposal scenarios: incineration with energy recovery or landfill. In both cases, significant impacts are achieved both on the environment and on human health. In the last period recent studies* suggested a new alternative to the incineration and landfill.  The use of waste PPEs  that can be included in the mix for preparing a bituminous conglomerate as reinforcement was studied in an innovative circular economy scenario.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Different strategies can be implemented to reduce emissions, production, and use of specific PFAS.  Manufacturers have been phasing out the production of certain PFAS, replacing them with new PFAS or chemical substitutes or direct destruction. For example, many polymers containing long perfluoroalkyl side chains (more than 7 perfluorinated carbons) were replaced by analogues containing short perfluoroalkyl side chains (6 or 4 perfluorinated carbons) or fluorine‐free moieties (e.g., siloxanes) [15]. The wastewater streams in the production of fluorinated polymers can be recycled as well as the problem of emissions in the atmosphere can be addressed using thermal destruction to reduce the risk of PFAS trace [16].  The most common remediation scenarios for PFAS include:  1) the PFAS destruction of concentrates of PFAS with incinerators that operate under a range of conditions that depend on the application and technology, with multiple hearth furnaces and fluidised bed furnaces used in sewage sludge incineration, and moving grate, rotary kiln and liquid injection incinerators more common for handling municipal and hazardous waste [17]. Generally, the PFAS destruction may require temperatures between 600 to 1400 °C; 2) The PFAS treatment technologies such as ion-exchange resins (IER), granulated activated carbon (GAC) and reverse osmosis loaded with adsorbed PFAS extracted from contaminated water. These can remove PFAS from water but do not destroy them [17,18].   The thermal technologies for PFAS removal include incineration, pyrolysis, gasification, supercritical water oxidation, hydrothermal liquefaction and carbonization; other innovative treatment are vitrification, electrochemical oxidation and plasma-assisted sludge oxidation [19]. Halocarbon welcomes this opportunity to respond to the ECHA Annex XV proposal for the restriction of Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs).  Throughout our 70+ year history, we have always believed in the responsible use of fluorochemistry. We believe that the products we manufacture, and sell can ensure the safety of people and the environment when used properly.  In many cases, no suitable alternatives exist wherein the benefit of the alternative outweighs its own environmental and human safety risks when compared to a fluorinated material. Some critical facts pertaining to Halocarbon’s position on PFAS:
• For 73 years, Halocarbon has been committed to the key industrial applications (business-to-business sales into hazardous operations) where low-volume specialty fluorochemistry is critical due to its unmatched safety, performance, non-reactive properties, and that there are no other suitable non-fluorinated equivalent materials.
• Halocarbon is the only US-based supplier of many critical fluorochemicals currently used in defense, aeronautical, space, and naval applications focused on national and regional security.
• Halocarbon products are manufactured in low volumes that are still commercially relevant and sold into business-to-business applications for use by trained professionals.  In many of these applications no suitable non-fluorinated products exist or can provide the safety, nonreactivity, and containment of extremely hazardous and/or toxic chemicals (e.g. chlorine, nitric acid, liquid oxygen, etc.).
• Halocarbon seeks to engage in open dialogue with regulators, subject matter experts, and public officials to help create meaningful fluorochemical regulation, grounded in the best available science and will abide by and protect all established regulations.
• Halocarbon is and will continue to work with customers to develop cradle-to-grave product strategies and lifecycle solutions.  We seek to establish a circular economy around our fluorinated products, to establish and drive more risk based responsible use and disposal consumption of fluorinated materials.
• Throughout our history, Halocarbon has never manufactured, used, or sold products containing fluorinated surfactants like perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) or perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS).
• Throughout our history, Halocarbon has never manufactured or sold fluorinated materials into non-essential applications such as food-packaging materials or cosmetic products.
Halocarbon believes that the PFAS definition currently proposed by ECHA is too broad to have regulatory utility.  Instead, we believe that regulators should be specific in defining chemicals by structure (e.g., PFOA and PFOS) or in groups of closely related structures (e.g., perfluoroalkyl acids).  Regulators should also focus on specific applications that pose the greatest environmental or consumer risk (e.g. AFFF, food packaging, cosmetics products, etc.), and exclude lower risk chemicals that are used in highly controlled industrial applications and chemicals that are already highly regulated.  We also encourage regulators to evaluate risk by excluding chemicals that are not environmentally mobile, not water soluble, and those that are designed for use in contained (immobilized) applications.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Lubricants and Greases, PCTFE, 9008-83-9 EU Sector is Lubricants. Halocarbon and its EU distributors have several significant applications for PCTFE to mitigate the dangers of reactive gases such as LOX (liquid oxygen), Hazardous MRO (maintenance, repair, and operations), hydrogen, chlorine, and fluorine gases. 1. Maintenance work in chlorine production.  a. PCTFE Oils and greases are used in several applications within the chlorine industry, they are essential to guarantee safe and effective production:  i. greases are used for maintenance of valves, valve assembly bearings.   ii. Inert oil is needed to assemble pumps, compressors, and vacuums.  iii. Used as lubricants for seals, gaskets, and O-rings. b. Please refer to pamphlet 164 provided by the Chlorine Institute. The information in this pamphlet is CONFIDENTIAL so we have attached it in Section V, Halocarbon PCTFE-based lubricants are specified as safe for use in the hazardous operations involving the production, transportation, and use of chlorine.  These products include Halocarbon® HC25-5S, Halocarbon® MT-3I (used as a sealing grease for threaded connectors), InfinX MRO 2505, HC-56 oil, HC-4.2 oil, and HC-6.3 oil. c. These lubricants need to be resistant to the effects of chlorine.  Non-fluorinated hydrocarbon- or silicone-based lubricants react with elemental chlorine and chlorinated species like hydrogen chloride.  Such reactions with non-fluorinated lubricants are extremely exothermic, and can cause uncontrolled self-propagating reactions, explosions, and fires.  Using hydrocarbon- or silicone-based lubrication in chlorine service applications can also lead to catastrophic asset failure: causing the valves to seize in either open or closed positions, bearings in motors and pumps to lock, seals, gaskets, O-rings to embrittle and leak, etc. Such catastrophic asset failures can lead to significant environmental release of chlorine and its byproducts, affecting larger areas of populated communities and natural resources.   For this reason, fluorinated lubricants are essential to the safe handling and containment of other essential hazardous chemical processes. d. PCTFE lubricants have also been codified by industry trade organizations recognized for their application in chlor-alkali chemical applications due to the safety they provide.  One example includes the Chlorine Institute Pamphlet #164 – Reactivity and Compatibility of Chlorine and Sodium Hydroxide with Various Materials (link to pamphlet - https://bookstore.chlorineinstitute.org/pamphlet-164-reactivity-and-compatibility-of-chlorine-and-sodium-hydroxide-with-various-materials.html?Session_ID=6fa6b7adca3af7d7a18117e7ac0b7888 ).  Also added as an attachment.  2. Hazardous chemical reaction processes using highly reactive gases and liquids. The flammability, reactivity and potential for dangerous, explosive reactions mentioned above exist here as well. a. Membrane compressors are used in the production, storage and uses for industrial and syngases:  i. Oxygen ii.  Hydrogen iii. Chlorine iv. Fluorine v. Ammonia  vi. Any related compounds to those above vii. Any very clean gas which must be put under high pressure. b. Membrane, diaphragm, and rotary pumps are used in the production, storage and uses for liquids: i. hydrogen peroxide and similar harsh, highly reactive liquids.   c. In practice, membrane compressors and pumps are used as a safety/control measure for these potentially dangerous systems. i. The gas/liquid is isolated from the pumping piston by a membrane, so the gases have no direct contact with any oil or abrasion. ii. The pumping forces are transported by a hydraulic fluid such as PCTFE Oils. This hydraulic fluid must be extremely non-reactive. iii. This prevents abrasion or an adverse chemical reaction which could result in a deadly explosion.  3. Lubricant for LOX (liquid oxygen) pump. a. Halocarbon PCTFE is used as a lubricant in a LOX pump for military applications, supporting national security. The lubricant for a LOX pump must be non-reactive/inert to prevent a reaction with the liquid oxygen, resulting in extremely exothermic self-propagating reactions, which lead to combustion and/or explosion.   b. Liquid oxygen (LOX) is used in aircraft and Maritime vessels. Oxygen is serviced to aircraft and ships in a liquid state. The advantage of LOX is that it has a nine hundred-to-one expansion ratio. General Comments: HARC comments on an Annex XV Restriction Report on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)

Disclaimer: Nothing in this submission relates to firefighting foams or the chemical agents used in firefighting foam.

Note on Terminology: In this submission and our previous submission in June we use the term halogenated clean agents (HCAs) to refer to the fluorinated chemicals used in total flooding fire suppression systems and portable fire extinguishers. HCAs used in total flooding fire suppression systems are also commonly referred to as gaseous fire extinguishing agents.

The Halon Alternatives Research Corporation (HARC) appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on an Annex XV Report that proposes a restriction on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) under REACH. HARC is a non-profit trade association that serves as an information clearinghouse and focal point for cooperation between government and industry on issues of importance to special hazard fire protection. HARC members encompass all levels of the fire protection industry including agent manufacturers, equipment manufacturers, distributors/installers, recyclers, and end-users.

The fire protection industry has a strong record of taking voluntary actions and supporting regulations to reduce the environmental impact of halogenated clean agents (HCAs). In the early 1990s when informed that halons were potent ozone depleting substances (ODS), the industry immediately stopped any testing and training with halons, developed a voluntary code of practice for halon use, and supported the accelerated 1994 phaseout of halon production under the Montreal Protocol. To reduce the impact of the high global warming potential (GWP) hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) used as alternatives to halons the industry developed a voluntary code of practice to minimize emissions (1) and a recycling code of practice (2), created a data collection program to estimate emissions (3), and supported the phasedown of HFC production under the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol. The HFC phasedown has reduced the use of HFCs in new fire suppression systems significantly in the US and to near zero in the EU.

HARC fully supports efforts to reduce the use and emissions of PFAS to protect human health and the environment. However, unlike previous regulations that allowed for a transition to in-kind alternatives and the continued use of recycled stocks, the proposal contained in the Annex XV report would basically eliminate the use of all HCAs for total flooding fire suppression in occupied spaces after 12 years without alternatives for some technology-based and historical preservation uses. It would also have a devastating effect on the ability of the aviation industry to meet current International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) requirements for the replacement of halons on aircraft. As outlined below, HARC does not believe that the environmental impact of HCAs supports such drastic action. Instead, we support a more targeted approach where the use of PFAS agents would be limited to applications for which alternatives cannot meet safety standards, and where PFAS agents could be recycled for future use to maintain existing equipment.

HARC PERSPECTIVE ON THE SCIENTIFIC BASIS FOR REGULATING HCAS AS PFAS

The proposed PFAS definition is too broad and combines chemical classes with very different characteristics

The proposal treats all PFAS-defined chemicals as being equally deserving of regulatory action. Many environmental organizations are taking parallel actions against some PFAS, but most other stakeholders support targeting only those chemicals which are known to be PBT (persistent, bioaccumulative, and toxic). The short-chain PFAS which are used as fire extinguishing agents do not share the same bioaccumulation and toxicity potential of long-chain non-polymeric PFAS and have not been treated as the same class of chemical by other environmental agencies. Three examples where this distinction is used are found in documentation issued by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), United Nations Environment Program (UNEP) Environmental Effects Assessment Panel (EEAP) and US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

OECD Short-chain vs Long-chain (4)

The OECD definition of PFAS is cited by the restriction proposal and can be found on the OECD web page. The OECD distinguishes between polymeric and non-polymeric PFAS and distinguishes the risk of non-polymeric PFAS by their chain length:

“Based on the length of the fluorinated carbon chain, short and long chain PFASs can be distinguished. Long chains refers to:

• perfluorocarboxylic acids (PFCAs) with carbon chain lengths C8 and higher, including perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA);

• perfluoroalkane sulfonic acids (PFSAs) with carbon chain lengths C6 and higher, including perfluorohexane sulfonic acid (PFHxS) and perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS); and

• precursors of these substances that may be produced or present in products.

The length of the fluorinated carbon chain can result in different physicochemical properties that influence the substance behavior in the environment and in organisms, and its bioaccumulation and (eco) toxicity.”

The OECD has clearly stated that its definition of PFAS does not inform on the hazards of individual substances and was not intended for regulatory purposes. (5)

UNEP EEAP Report, May 2023 (6)

The HCAs used for fire protection fall into the same category as other F-gases that ultimately degrade in part to trifluoroacetic acid (TFA).

“The increases in trifluoroacetic acid concentrations due to replacements of the ozone-depleting substances are not expected to pose significant risk to humans or the environment at the present time. Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) continues to be found in the environment, including in remote regions, although concentrations are so low that they are currently very unlikely to have adverse toxicological consequences for humans and ecosystems [105,106]. The accumulated amount of TFA is expected to increase because of the planned replacement of ODS with short-lived fluorinated chemicals (Fig. 11). However, based on projected future use of these precursors of TFA, no harm is anticipated. There is a large uncertainty associated with the magnitude of other sources of TFA (e.g., potential natural sources, fluorinated pesticides, and pharmaceuticals), which do not fall under the purview of the Montreal Protocol. Trifluoroacetic acid has biological properties that differ significantly from the longer chain polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and inclusion of TFA in this larger group of chemicals for regulation would be inconsistent with the risk assessment of TFA.”

April 2023 US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Significant New Alternatives Policy (SNAP) Program Listing 25 which included expanded acceptable uses of 2-BTP (7)

“EPA understands that currently, there is no single commonly agreed definition of PFAS, and whether or not HFCs or HFOs are classified as PFAS depends on the definition being used. EPA's PFAS roadmap, available at https://www.epa.gov/pfas, sets timelines for specific actions and outlines EPA's commitments to new policies to safeguard public health, protect the environment, and hold polluters accountable. This rule does not in any way establish a definition of PFAS, nor do the listing decisions depend on a specific definition. In evaluating alternatives using its comparative risk framework, SNAP already considers potential risks to human health and the environment. Regardless of what definition of PFAS is used, not all PFAS are the same in terms of toxicity or any other risk. Some PFAS have been shown to have extremely low toxicity, for example. If a chemical has been found to present lower overall risk to human health or the environment, it might be found acceptable under SNAP regardless of whether or not it falls under a particular definition of PFAS. Likewise, SNAP might not find a potential alternative acceptable if it presented greater overall risk, regardless of whether or not it falls under a particular definition of PFAS. As described in the risk screens for alternatives found in the docket for this rulemaking, potential risk to human health or the environment has been considered directly for each chemical, and the risks are not assumed to follow from a chemical falling into any particular category of substances.”

The more targeted approach of the US EPA’s PFAS Strategic Roadmap, May 2023 (8)

These three examples from OECD, UNEP and US EPA share a common approach, which is that the presence of a -CF2- or -CF3 moiety in a chemical is not valid basis to regulate it in the same manner as the longer chain non-polymeric PFAS that have been the subject of significant environmental restriction. HARC recommends instead the approach recently published by the US EPA, which distinguishes Persistent, Bioaccumulative, and Toxic (PBT) PFAS. By targeting PBT PFAS, it should be possible to reap the maximum benefits to the environment and society. Those PFAS that are outside of this category could still be used for their very important positive benefits while harmful PFAS receive the regulatory focus they deserve.

NEED FOR A TIME-UNLIMITED DEROGATION FOR CLEAN FIRE EXTINGUISHING AGENTS

HARC supports the proposal in the Annex XV report for a derogation for clean fire extinguishing agents. As outlined in our previous submission, the information contained in the Annex XV report and its annexes provide ample justification for such a derogation. The Annex XV report acknowledges that alternatives for many important uses of clean fire extinguishing agents do not currently exist and are not in development. We understand the dossier submitters are assuming that 13.5 years is enough time for new alternatives to be identified and developed, and while that may be a reasonable assumption for many uses of PFAS, it is highly unlikely to be the case for clean agent fire extinguishing agents.

The development of new substances has been aggressively pursued within this application for more than 30 years, well before the phaseout of halons, with millions of Euros and extensive time and efforts of myriad private and public organizations spent on development with very limited success. An expectation that new options not already considered in the past can be developed and brought to market in 5, 10, or 20 years is not supported by historical experience. Several important fire risk applications still require halon even after pursuing alternatives for 30 years. Most applications that can use alternative, non-HCA technologies have already migrated, reducing the potential market opportunity for a new, non-PFAS alternative, raising the cost and timeline for development. While the capital costs for a new fire suppressant may be lower due to smaller volumes, the low potential market for sales of a new extinguishing agent will limit interest in commercialization of a new product without viability in ancillary markets.

As an example of the significant resources spent on finding alternative clean agents with limited success, we enclose a history of the Advanced Agent Working Group (AAWG). (9) AAWG was a consortium of industry, government and academia that carried out research to find a drop-in replacement to the use of Halon 1301 for total flooding fire extinguishing and explosion inerting applications in occupied spaces. Over a 10-year period from 1994 to 2004 the group evaluated 24 candidate agents for fire performance, physical properties, atmospheric lifetime/ODP, and availability. Eventually the 4 most promising candidate agents were tested for extinguishing ability, inerting capability, and genetic toxicology. Two of the agents were also tested for cardiac sensitization, a key toxicological endpoint for halogenated fire extinguishing agents. Based on the results of this testing, none of the agents was found to be acceptable for total flooding fire extinguishing in occupied spaces.

It is this history that leads to the consensus within the fire protection community that it is highly unlikely new non-PFAS alternatives will suddenly be discovered. Below is a quote from the 2023 Progress Report of the Montreal Protocol Technology and Economic Assessment Panel (TEAP) that sums up this consensus: (10)

“Furthermore, all known candidate clean agent chemical groups have already been researched, such that discovering alternatives that are zero ODP, low GWP, and non-PFAS is highly unlikely. Based on these factors, there is little to no financial incentive for companies to invest in the research and development of potential new fire suppression agents. As there are no new candidate fire suppressants available for consideration that are not PFAS under these broad definitions, it is anticipated that the only options that will be available after the 12-year derogation are the same ones available today.”

The original phasedown of halons for fire protection migrated many use applications to not -in-kind (non-fluorinated) technologies. Thus, where users can shift to alternative technologies most have already done so. HCAs remain an optional technology to protect those hazards where the risk of loss, be it life, asset, or operational continuity, exceeds the significant cost of adding additional protection measures. The removal of this vital risk management strategy at any point in the future will of necessity increase the probability of loss of life and high valued property, or interrupting the ongoing operation of critical infrastructure, be it transportation, communication, or manufacturing supported by the internet. This, in turn, will discourage EU investments in critical technology infrastructure, impacting global competitiveness in this sector.

NEED FOR REVISED WORDING OF THE DEROGATION FOR CLEAN FIRE SUPPRESSING (EXTINGUISHING) AGENTS

The current wording of the clean fire suppressing agents derogation does not adequately reflect the multiple reasons that a non-PFAS alternative may not work in any specific fire or explosion hazard situation. While damage to assets and risk to human health are clearly important parameters, there are others including speed of extinguishment, time required for agent discharge, weight of the agent and equipment, and space required for the agent and equipment. Any of these factors, alone or in combination, can impact whether an alternative is suitable to protect a specific hazard.

One constant across all sectors of fire protection is the requirement to meet safety requirements such as those given in EN, ISO, NFPA, EASA and ASTM standards. In addition, fire suppression systems and agents are generally required to be listed by an approval agency such as LPCB, CNPP, VdS, BSI or CNBOP to EN standards. HARC would recommend incorporating the requirement to meet safety standards into the derogation by using the same wording as the prohibition on HFCs for fire suppression in the proposed revisions to the F-gas regulation. (11)

“Date of prohibition: 1 January 2024 - Fire protection equipment that contain or rely on other fluorinated greenhouse gases listed in Annex I, except when required to meet safety standards”

We believe this is appropriate as both regulations would cover some of the same clean agents. Tying the derogation only to situations where alternatives do not meet safety standards would significantly limit the size of the derogation.

PROPOSED TIME-UNLIMITED DEROGATION FOR CLEAN FIRE SUPPRESSING AGENTS

Column 2, 5.m. clean fire suppressing agents where required to meet safety standards

OVERVIEW OF PFAS CLEAN AGENTS

The following overview of PFAS chemicals used for fire suppression and their possible alternatives is broken down into three use categories: total flooding fire suppression, onboard aircraft fire suppression, and military.

Background on total flooding fire suppression

HCA fire suppressants occupy a specialty market where there is a need to protect items that otherwise would be damaged by a fire extinguishing agent itself or a slow extinguishment process, and in enclosed spaces where many other fire suppressants would pose a risk to human health and safety. These specialty applications have unique challenges to providing fire and life safety. Each protected hazard using a chemical clean agent provides its own unique set of circumstances and challenges that need to be overcome to use an alternative agent or technology. While some uses may migrate to alternative technologies with modest challenges, others cannot and are still trying to migrate to the last generation of fluorochemical agents without significant success. Even within similar uses such as data centers, the ability to transition to alternatives varies significantly depending on the unique requirements of individual protected hazards.

The diversity of applications and the unique requirements of individual facilities makes it very challenging to claim that an alternative, non-PFAS technology is viable across a general use category such as data centers or control rooms. Each data center, for example, will have different criteria and requirements for the fire protection technology selected.

Clean agent fire systems are not normally required by code. They are an added expense to mitigate an unacceptable risk of losing assets, data or incurring downtime for a high-tech or historical preservation facility as a result of a fire. This risk analysis includes high value assets and business continuity, but also societal impact and security with the loss of critical services in the event of fire. In the interconnected electronic world, loss of telecommunications and internet access can pose significant societal impacts. This makes the grouping of applications for regulation within the category very difficult. In some cases, the assets within the protected hazard are critical, in others it is the function of those assets within the protected space that are of value, not necessarily the assets themselves.

PFAS used in total flooding fire suppression

The HCAs used for total flooding fire suppression that are now defined by OECD as PFAS are: HFC-227ea, HFC-125, FK-5-1-12, and HB-55 (a blend of FK-5-1-12 and HFO-1233zd). The chemical, physical, and thermodynamic properties, especially vapor pressure, differ among these agents and affect their storage, transport, atomization, and vaporization characteristics. These agents are stored as liquids in nitrogen-pressurized containers. Upon actuation of the fire extinguishing system, agent liquid is released into a pipe distribution system and discharged from nozzles into the protected enclosure as a vaporizing spray forming a uniform gaseous agent-air mixture throughout, thus the term “total flooding” fire extinguishing. Widely accepted standards require that the discharge time for systems using HCAs be completed in 10 seconds or less, which assures rapid flame extinguishment thereby minimizing damage to protected assets. The minimum design concentration (MDC) of agent in an enclosure is based on test procedures for the hazard type, described in an applicable national standard such as ISO-14520 (12) and EN 15004 (13) in the EU, or NFPA 2001 (14) in the US and is further tested and validated by approval agencies such as LPCB, CNPP, VdS, BSI, CNBOP, UL and FM .

Fire extinguishing systems containing HCAs are used to protect a wide array of asset types in the EU and around the world, including:

1. Server rooms
2. Power supply rooms
3. Electrical switch gear rooms
4. Hospital (e.g., MRI labs)
5. Document storage vaults.
6. Cultural heritage structures
7. Anechoic chambers.
8. Chemical storage rooms
9. Flammable liquids
10. Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS)
11. Marine
12. Oil and gas exploration
13. Military
14. Naval ships
15. Aerospace

NON-PFAS CLEAN AGENT ALTERNATIVES

Inert gases

IG 01, IG 100, IG 55, and IG 541 are approved for use in total flooding fire extinguishing systems in occupied spaces. Inert gas agents are stored in high-pressure cylinders at pressures up to 300-bar or with technology activated by chemical reaction (energetics). Standards require that inert-gas fire extinguishing systems discharge in at most 120 seconds for Class A hazards (solid substances), and in at most in 60 seconds for Class B hazards (flammable liquids). Use of inert gas agents is permitted for occupied spaces provided that exposure of personnel to reduced oxygen concentrations is limited to 5 minutes where oxygen concentrations are 12% or greater.

Technical limitations affecting use of inert gas agents in place of HCAs are mainly due to (1) increased space and weight burden of inert gas cylinders, (2) where the inert gas agent concentration exceeds 62 percent at sea level equivalent they cannot be used in occupied areas.

Carbon dioxide (CO2)

Carbon dioxide has a long history as an effective gaseous fire extinguishing agent in limited circumstances to protect against class B hazards. It is used in both total flooding and local-application fire extinguishing systems. However, carbon dioxide is fatally toxic at fire extinguishing concentrations, which severely limits its use in normally occupied enclosures except where certain requirements are met (ISO 6183, NFPA 12). (15), (16)

TRENDS IN CLEAN AGENT USE

The use of HFCs for fire suppression in the EU has decreased by 95% since 2014 as a result of the F-gas regulation and is now very small. (17) Remaining volumes are used in applications that do not currently have alternatives such as military vehicles and aircraft, to service existing equipment, and to supply export markets. New clean agent fire suppression systems in the EU are served mainly by FK 5-1-12 and inert gases. Demand for FK-5-1-12 and inert gas systems has been strong for the last several years as they have replaced the use of HFCs. The inclusion of FK-5-1-12 in a proposed PFAS REACH restriction will likely significantly reduce growth going forward.

NOT-IN-KIND ALTERNATIVES TO PFAS CLEAN AGENTS

Water-based systems

Sprinkler systems and water mist systems are both fire suppression systems and are widely used in hazard spaces where water is available at an adequate supply rate and quantity. Note that sprinkler systems are not tested and approved as fire “extinguishing“ systems. Ordinary sprinkler systems are intended to protect the facility and not necessarily the assets contained in it. Collateral damage to protected spaces and assets by water itself is, in some cases, a significant risk.

There are tested and approved total flooding type water mist fire extinguishing systems. Water mist systems are special hazard systems developed for the protection of specific hazards. There are no generally accepted design criteria for water mist systems, thus their effectiveness must be proven by fire testing on the hazard of interest. Collateral damage to assets by water itself is, in some cases, a significant risk.

Hybrid systems (water and inert gas)

These systems simultaneously discharge a fine water mist and inert gas such as nitrogen. They are approved for use as fire extinguishing systems in normally occupied spaces. The inert gas effects extinguishment through the dilution of oxygen while the fine water droplets provide cooling which also contributes to fire extinguishment. As with inert gas systems, personnel exposure times to reduced oxygen concentrations is limited to 5 minutes where oxygen concentrations are 12% or greater (NFPA 770). (18) Collateral damage to protected spaces and assets by water itself is, in some cases, a significant risk.

Powdered aerosol agents

A powdered aerosol fire extinguishing unit discharges a fixed amount of fine extinguishing powder, forming a flame-extinguishing powder cloud, which acts in a total-flooding manner. Powdered agents, as such, are not “clean” agents and can damage certain assets such as electronics. Under the US EPA SNAP program, two powdered aerosols are listed as acceptable for use in occupied spaces.

APPLICABILITY OF ALTERNATIVES TO PFAS AGENTS

For an alternative agent to be an acceptable replacement for a PFAS fire extinguishing agent (a “clean” agent) in an application it must be able to meet the critical regulatory requirements including:

1. Safe for human exposure at the agent fire suppression design concentration.
a. At or below the No Observable Adverse Effect Level (NOAEL) concentration exposure to gaseous agents is limited to 5 minutes.
2. Extinguishment time at the minimum design concentration compliant with applicable standards.
a. Class A fire (involving ordinary combustible materials, such as wood, cloth, and paper): Extinguishment time of 10 minutes or less.
b. Class B fire (involving flammable or combustible liquids, petroleum greases, tars, oils, oil-based paints, solvents, lacquers, and alcohols): Extinguishment time of 30 seconds or less.

Other non-regulatory requirements may be deemed essential in some applications including:

1. Agent must be “clean,” i.e., electrically non-conducting volatile liquid or gaseous agent which leaves no residue (liquid or solid).
2. The physical size of installed equipment (agent containers, piping, control equipment) must be able to fit in the available space.
3. The weight of the installed equipment must be less than the maximum allowed floor loading or vehicle capacity, as applicable.
4. The agent must be able to achieve the required “hold-time,” i.e. the duration of protection after the end of agent discharge.

IN WHAT CURRENT APPLICATIONS OF PFAS AGENTS COULD ALTERNATIVES BE USED?

There are many variables to consider in attempting to assess the technical fitness of alternative agents to PFAS fire extinguishing agent. Making such assessments can be highly subjective, and reasonable disagreements can arise. Nonetheless, the applications list above have been divided into general groups for hazards that likely fall into the class A or class B categories. The fitness of alternatives is somewhat generalized but may be a useful starting point for decision making.

Class A fire applications total flooding

Of the applications listed above, the following are most likely to involve class A fire hazards, including energized electrical equipment: server rooms, power supply rooms, electrical switch gear, hospitals, document storage, cultural heritage, anechoic chambers.

Inert gas would likely be a technically acceptable alternative to PFAS agent in many of these occupancies. Like PFAS agents, inert gas agents meet human exposure requirements, and contain no contaminants that may harm protected assets, i.e., they are clean agents. For a given occupancy, the number and weight of required inert gas cylinders will generally be greater than that of required HCA cylinders, thus a relatively large floor area with sufficient structural integrity must be available to allow use of inert gas rather than HCA. Inert gas agents may, depending on the location of enclosure leak points, provide longer agent hold times, which determines the duration of fire protection, than PFAS agents owing to their lower agent-air densities, which in turn results in slower gravimetric loss to the ambient through enclosure leak points.

Water mist may be technically acceptable if the protected assets can tolerate mist exposure. Water mist can damage protected assets the same as a sprinkler discharge can; for example, protection of paper documents including historical documents and books using water may be problematic.

Hybrid systems may also be technically acceptable if (1) the protected assets can tolerate mist exposure and 2) sufficient floor space with requisite structural strength is available to hold the water mist equipment.

Powdered aerosol acceptability depends on the sensitivity of assets to particulate contamination.

Class B and Class C (EU) fire applications total flooding

Of the applications listed above, the following are most likely to involve class B or C fire hazards: chemical storage, flammable liquids, flammable gases, battery energy storage systems (including BESS using lithium-ion batteries), marine, oil and gas, military, naval ships, aerospace.

Inert gas would likely be a technically acceptable alternative to PFAS agent in many of the above occupancies. Like PFAS agents, inert-gas agents meet human exposure requirements, and contain no contaminants that may harm protected assets, i.e., they are clean agents.  However, the clean aspect of gaseous agents may be less important in some applications. Space and weight considerations would likely preclude the use of inert gas in some marine, military, naval, and aerospace applications. As noted above, inert gas agents may provide longer hold times, which determines the duration of fire protection, than PFAS agents owing to their lower agent-air densities, which in turn results in slower gravimetric loss to the ambient through enclosure leak points.

Water mist and hybrid systems would likely be technically acceptable alternatives to HCAs in some of the above occupancies.  As with inert gas systems, the floor space and structural strength required to house the water mist or hybrid system equipment will often be greater than that required for HCA agent cylinders.

Powdered aerosol may be a technically acceptable alternative to HCAs depending on the sensitivity of assets to the aerosol particulate.

OVERVIEW OF ONBOARD AIRCRAFT FIRE SUPPRESSION

Although the incidence of in-flight fires is low, the consequences in terms of loss of life are
potentially devastating, and the use of HCAs to help guard against such events has been a key aspect of aircraft fire safety for over 50 years. Aviation applications are among the most demanding and critical uses of the fire suppression agents and require every one of their beneficial characteristics. Particularly important are the following:

• dispersion and suppression effectiveness, which must be maintained even at the low temperatures encountered at high altitude,
• minimal toxic hazard to the health and safety of ground maintenance staff and passengers and flight crew, who could be exposed to the agent and any decomposition products for periods as long as several hours, and
• weight and space requirements of the agent and associated fire protection system.

Also significant are short- and long-term damage to aircraft structure or contents resulting from the following:

• the agent or from its potential decomposition products in a fire,
• avoidance of clean-up problems,
• suitability for use on live electrical equipment,
• effectiveness on the hidden fire (the ability to indirectly extinguish fires), and
• the installed cost of the system and its maintenance over its life. (19)

Historically halons were used in active fires suppression systems to protect lavatories, engines nacelles, auxiliary power units (APUs) and cargo compartments, and in handheld extinguishers in the passenger cabin. After 30 years of research, testing and standard development, Halon 1301 systems are still being installed in the cargo compartments, engine nacelles and APUs of all new production aircraft. With the runout date for supplies of recycled halons possibly less than 10 years away, it is critical that alternatives begin being used as soon as possible. At a time when airframe manufacturers and OEMs have been acting with urgency and are close to gaining approval for halon replacements, the PFAS issue has the potential to set those efforts back several decades. Below is a quote from the 2023 Progress Report of the Montreal Protocol Technology and Economic Assessment Panel (TEAP) that expresses this concern: (10)

“A new factor that may affect the halon 1301 and 1211 run-out dates is the proposed PFAS regulations. There are many fluorine containing fire suppression agents which may be regulated under the pending PFAS regulations that only have halon as an alternative.  Destruction of PFAS fire suppressants in lieu of recovery and re-use or a reluctance to decommission existing halon systems and convert to alternatives that would be considered PFAS may put additional pressure to continue reliance on halons.”

OVERVIEW OF PFAS USED FOR ONBOARD AIRCRAFT FIRE SUPPRESSION AND POSSIBLE ALTERNATIVES

HFCs

HFC-227ea and HFC-236fa are currently used in lavatory fire suppression systems on commercial aircraft as a replacement for Halon 1301. There are other HCAs in development for this use, but no non-PFAS alternatives have passed the Airworthiness Authorities minimum performance standard (MPS). Based on the nature of the hazard and the small size of the required system, it is possible that a non-PFAS agent such as inert gas or water could be made to work in this application, however, no testing of these agents for this application has been successfully completed to date. Given the long lead times required to gain approval for the use of a new fire suppressant on aircraft, HFCs are likely to still be installed in lavatories on commercial aircraft after 12 years.

2-BTP

In the discussion above of the research done by the AAWG, we noted that an acceptable alternative for use in total flooding fire suppression systems in occupied spaces was not discovered. However, one of the agents tested, 2-bromo 3,3,3-trifluoropropene (2-BTP), was found to have extinguishing capability and a toxicological profile similar to Halon 1211 making it a good candidate for use as a streaming agent alternative. The first testing of 2-BTP by the AAWG took place in 1998 and after significant efforts by multiple private companies the agent with approved hardware was finally approved, on what was characterized by US regulators as an “expedited basis” for use in handheld extinguishers onboard aircraft 18 years later in December 2016 (20), again providing evidence of the long lead times for development of fire suppression alternatives.

The statement in Annex A, A.3.9.1.6 that 2-BTP is a frequently applied substance for fire suppression is not accurate. Currently it is used in the EU only in handheld extinguishers onboard aircraft. 2-BTP is not a candidate for total flooding fire suppression in normally occupied spaces due to its toxicological profile, so its potential for future growth outside of aviation is limited.

2-BTP handheld extinguishers are currently being installed on most new production aircraft, and all existing aircraft in the EU are expected to be retrofitted to 2-BTP extinguishers before 2026 as required under Regulation EC 1005/2009. (21) There are currently no other candidate agents for this use that are not also PFAS. Non-PFAS alternatives such as CO2, dry powder, and water have been tested for this use and failed to pass the handheld extinguisher MPS tests.

Under the proposed PFAS restriction, after the 12-year derogation for clean agent fire suppression ends, 2-BTP cannot be placed on the market even in recycled form. While it is our understanding that 2-BTP extinguishers would not have to be immediately removed from service after the 12-year derogation period, they could not be refilled and the purchase of spares would be prohibited. Under these circumstances maintaining equipment for any length of time after the restriction takes effect would be problematic.

HARC would ask that ECHA in conjunction with EASA and the Commission provide clear guidance to the industry now while it is making this transition to 2-BTP to meet the requirements of Regulation EC 1005/2009. Will the aviation industry be allowed to maintain and service that equipment for at least the life of the aircraft? Otherwise, we have concerns that airlines may balk at the idea of replacing all of their existing Halon 1211 extinguishers in their fleet with a PFAS agent that is restricted under REACH, and instead ask for a derogation from the required halon end date as allowed under Regulation EC 1005/2009.

2-BTP is also under development to replace Halon 1301 in cargo compartments of commercial aircraft as part of a blend with CO2. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) completed proof-of-concept testing for the 2-BTP/CO2 blend in 2018 (22) and cargo MPS testing was successfully conducted by the FAA in 2019 (23). Additional testing to an updated cargo MPS mixed fuels fire (flammable liquid / lithium battery class A) was successfully completed in 2023. A non-PFAS alternative in the form of a hybrid water mist/inert gas system using nitrogen passed a previous cargo MPS in 2017, but has not been subjected to the latest version of the MPS and would require modification to pass the newer test standards.(24) Further detailed information on the status of efforts to replace Halon 1301 in A/C cargo fire extinguishing systems is available in the International Coordinating Council of Aerospace Industries Associations (ICCAIA) Aircraft Halon Replacement Working Paper presented at the 41st Assembly of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) in 2022. (25)

OVERVIEW OF MILITARY FIRE SUPPRESSION

Military fire protection systems are unique in that they must protect personnel and platforms from the consequences of combat damage and also protect against ‘peacetime’ fires. Fires due to combat events are generally very fast-growing and relatively large. Fire protection systems are required to counter these threats, often while allowing occupants to remain in the affected spaces. A point to consider when choosing extinguishing agent for spaces that are normally occupied is whether the enclosure must remain operational during combat operations or can be evacuated. If the enclosure must stay occupied during a fire event, then a limited number of agents are available for consideration due to toxicity concerns. However, if evacuation of the enclosure is an option, a wider range of agents is available similar to commercial applications.19

OVERVIEW OF PFAS USED FOR MILITARY FIRE SUPPRESSION AND POSSIBLE ALTERNATIVES

The full range of HCAs and non-PFAS alternatives have been investigated for military applications, including CO2, inert gases, HFCs, dry chemicals, and other gaseous
chemicals. For some of these specialized applications, HFCs have been the only alternatives demonstrated to meet these stringent requirements. HFC-125, HFC-227ea and to a lesser extent HFC-236fa are used for fire and explosion suppression in critical military applications including the following:

• Protection of engine and crew compartments on military ground vehicles
• Protection of machinery spaces, engine spaces, command centers, fuel pump rooms and flammable liquid storage compartments on naval ships and submarines
• Protection of crew compartments and engines on military aircraft

Like civil aviation, 2-BTP is currently replacing Halon 1211 in handheld extinguishers on military aircraft.

Significant research has shown that there are no alternatives to HCAs that meet all
military performance requirements. Thus, many of today’s fielded weapon systems and support equipment will remain in service for the foreseeable future. Barring mandatory decommissioning, these mission-critical HCA-based fire protection systems will need to be supported to at least 2050 and likely beyond. Fire protections systems on military vehicles, ships and aircraft can realistically only be replaced when major maintenance or modifications/upgrades are carried out since they are normally in service and operating all over Europe. System replacements plans are therefore usually established many years (decades) in advance. For example, the transition from halons to HFCs on ground vehicles in Sweden started in 1993 and wasn’t completed until 2022. Given that the military sector is not a significant user of these chemicals in terms of global demand, industry sources have informed militaries that they have no plans to invest additional resources to develop alternative chemicals specifically for these unique applications. Therefore, military investigations into alternatives are limited to those chemicals that are used for other commercial applications.

USE AND EMISSIONS OF PFAS AGENTS IN FIRE SUPPRESSION

Annex A, page 71

Table A.36. shows 863 t of PFAS sold in fire suppression equipment annually. The 2022 EEA report on fluorinated greenhouse gases shows 112 t of HFCs sold into fire protection uses in 2021. The difference between these numbers we are assuming represents sales of FK-5-1-12 and possibly 2-BTP. The table shows stocks of 20,201 t and annual decommissioning of 208 t. Assuming these numbers are correct that would mean that stocks are growing by about 650 t annually and would be 28,000 t in 12 years.

Annex XV Report, page 171, Table 13

The report states that a 12-year derogation of all fluorinated gases used in fire suppression will lead to 102,183 t of additional emissions. HARC does not know the source of this estimate, but we believe it is either a typo that was meant to be 10,218 t or it is overstated by a factor of 10. Using stocks of 20,201 t from Table A.36. of Annex A, assuming growth of those stocks of 650 t annually, and using the annual emission rate of 3.5% contained in the Exponent F-gas report, would result in emissions over a 12-year period of 9,982 t. To produce 102,183 t of emissions over a 12-year period at a 3.5% emission rate, stocks of PFAS in fire protection would have to be 243,000 t. Clearly the statement in Table 13 that fluorinated gas use in fire suppression would account for 14% of emissions of all fluorinated gases with derogations is also overstated by a factor of 10, as it is based on the 102,183 t figure. Historically fire protection uses of F-gases were about 2-3% of all F-gas use. Using the data in Table A.36, fire protection annual usage represents 2.8% of total F-gas usage in the EU.

The Exponent F-gas report uses an emission rate for fire suppression of 3.5%, which we used in the above calculations. The Fire Suppression Technical Options Committee (FSTOC) 2022 Assessment Report uses an emission rate for HCAs of 3%. (26) This is a worldwide estimate that would include both developed and developing countries. The latest installment of the US EPA Vintaging Model, which estimates use and emissions of ODS alternatives in the United States, uses a 1.5% emission rate for HCAs in total flooding fire protection systems between 2003–2019 and 1% after 2019. (27) HARC believes that emission rates in the EU would be similar to the US and that using an emission rate lower than 3.5%, possibly in the range of 2%, would be justified. Using a 2% emission rate rather than a 3.5% emission rate would lower the expected emissions from a 12-year derogation from 9,982 t to 5,704 t.

CONCLUSION

HARC is an advocate for human and environmental health, as shown by our 30-year history of coordinating industry compliance with environmental regulations. However, the REACH restriction proposal, in adhering to the broadest possible boundaries for substances to be regulated, creates a regulatory framework that would require the removal of important HCAs from use.

Non-PFAS replacements for many of these uses are not likely to be forthcoming in the coming decades. Further, scientific analysis and shared opinion from the OECD, UNEP, and US EPA agrees with HARC’s best scientific assessment - that the HCAs used for fire protection do not present a significant risk to human health and the environment.

To move forward with the REACH restriction as proposed without a time-unlimited derogation for fire protection brings limited health benefits while removing a needed, irreplaceable means for protection of the many important high-tech and historical assets in installations with stringent requirements.

HARC urges EU REACH to adopt a time-unlimited derogation for clean fire extinguishing agents.

Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Currently end-of-life emissions from the decommissioning of fire suppression equipment are extremely low as most of the agent is recovered and reused to service other equipment. HCAs are recovered and reclaimed using modern, closed-loop equipment that should have emission rates of less than 1%. Under the proposed restriction we would expect end-of-life emissions of HCAs to increase significantly as they lose their value and become a liability that requires destruction.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: The recovery and reclamation of HCAs in the EU is performed by fire equipment distributors/installers and by the primary halon recycling companies. Due in part to their low emission rates and high value, the vast majority of HCAs used in fire protection have historically been recycled and reclaimed for reuse at the end of life. Evidence of this can be seen in the continued availability of significant quantities of recycled halons for critical uses such as aviation even now after 30 years since production for fire suppression ended in the EU and 14 years since it ended worldwide. An October 2022 report from the US EPA on HFC reclamation commends the fire suppression industry for its management of halons over the last 30 years: (28)  “The management of halons in the United States over the last several decades demonstrates a model of collaboration between industry, government, and key users, effective regulations to reduce emissions, a smooth transition to safer alternatives through revisions to industry standards, voluntary industry codes of practice, maintenance of halon banking, and government halon reserves.”  HARC believes this management model extends beyond halons so that most HCAs installed in fire protection equipment in the US and EU are recovered from decommissioned equipment and reused. Data from our HFC Emissions Estimating Program (HEEP) show that over the past decade 75-80% of the HFCs used to recharge fire protection equipment in the US was sourced from recycled agent. This means that only a small amount of newly produced HFCs is used for servicing fire protection equipment. In consultation with EU-based members, HARC understands the situation in the EU is very similar to the US.  Under the proposed restriction, the recycling of HCAs in the EU would collapse within a few years. Used HCAs that cannot be placed on the market and cannot be used to service existing equipment in the future will have no value and would quickly go from an asset to a liability. Companies that currently purchase used HCAs would have no incentive to do so in the future as they would have no outlet to sell them. Rather than obtaining value for their used agent, users would be in a position of having to pay for costly destruction.

General Comments: Hazard or exposure:
Hazards of PFAS-containing F-gases
With five exceptions, all fluorinated refrigerants belong to the group of PFAS chemicals and they would therefore be affected by the PFAS ban. Their use is already strictly regulated and continuously restricted under the European F-Gases Regulation because of their greenhouse effect. However, the F-gases themselves are not unhealthy or toxic and do not have any properties that are harmful to soils, waters and living organisms. They are therefore rightly referred to as safety refrigerants and are even used as propellants in medical dosage sprays.
The focus in relation to refrigerants is on TFA (trifluoroacetic acid or trifluoroacetate), the persistent degradation products of F-gases, and not the F-gases themselves. The UNEP Assessment Report (United Nations environment programme) "Environmental Effects of Stratospheric Ozone Depletion, UV Radiation, and Interactions with Climate Change" published in 2022 proves, taking into account and after evaluating numerous international studies from the last four years, that a TFA ban is not scientifically justifiable due to its low environmental risk. The assessment of the environmental impact of TFA or F-gases must therefore be subjected to a renewed review by ECHA, which would have to conclude that a complete exemption is made for PFAS-containing F-gases.

Quotes from the UNEP Report:
„TFA has a long environmental lifetime, accumulates in surface and ground waters, and has been found in blood, drinking water, beverages, dust, plants, and agricultural soils. However, it does not interact with biological molecules and, due to its high solubility in water, it does not bioaccumulate. It is unlikely to cause adverse effects in terrestrial and aquatic organisms. Continued monitoring and assessment are nevertheless advised due to uncertainties in the deposition of TFA and its potential effects on marine organisms.“

„Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), has no obvious pathway of degradation and might accumulate in some water bodies, but is unlikely to cause adverse effects out to 2100. On the one hand, the safe and continuous operation of refrigeration, air-conditioning and heat pump systems is mandatory in almost all applications (data centre, hospital, blood bank, supermarket, etc.). It must therefore be ensured that immediate repair is possible even in the event of sudden refrigerant leaks. On the other hand, it is not possible to convert systems with F-gases to so-called natural refrigerants. Complete new installation with associated high investments would be necessary. This affects all economic sectors in which refrigeration and air conditioning systems are used, and also private customers who have installed heat pumps with F-gases or will do so in the next few years. Replacing the installation before the end of the systems' service life represents an unacceptable financial burden for all operators. Especially in the case of system-critical applications, a new installation must also be planned for the long term and cannot and must not become necessary at short notice in the event of a repair due to the unavailability of the refrigerant. Depending on the size of the system, months can pass before a new refrigeration or air conditioning system is installed. During this time, the downstream processes that are absolutely dependent on the refrigeration systems would be massively affected, which would result in production downtimes, damage to goods and storage, server downtimes, etc. As a result, many operators would be forced to replace their equipment as a precaution due to the unavailability of refrigerants, as they cannot take the risk of being without cooling or air conditioning for an extended period of time. All these investments and risks pose a great threat to the business location. For many operators, a new installation would also be unreasonable because they have only recently retrofitted their refrigeration systems with the refrigerant R404A with corresponding investments. Due to corresponding specifications in the F-Gas Regulation, the availability of R404A in case of service is not ensured. Therefore, many operators have had their systems converted to the refrigerants R448A orR449A as a precautionary measure, because they cannot take the risk of being without cooling or air conditioning for some time in the event of a refrigerant loss. Since these systems cannot be converted to a PFAS-free refrigerant, the only option would be to completely re-install a system, which would require a lot of planning and new costs. Many operators are not financially able to do this.  Request for exemption:  Temporally unlimited exemption for spare parts in refrigeration, air conditioning and heat pump systems: Numerous components in refrigeration, air conditioning and heat pump systems contain PFAS - gaskets, bearings, sensors, etc. Above all, the coatings and sealing materials used in sealing systems of all kinds serve to maintain function, interchangeability and ease of maintenance and to prevent environmentally harmful substance releases. Their material properties are specifically designed for the refrigerant used in the systems. Replacement with gaskets made of other materials is therefore not possible. Approvals would lose their validity and there would be a danger for the operator's employees and specialists who are entrusted with the maintenance and servicing of the systems if the leakage of refrigerant (flammable/toxic/greenhouse-effective) can no longer be prevented 100% reliably by inferior seals. A single component that is no longer available on the market due to the PFAS ban would possibly result in the replacement of a complete refrigeration, air conditioning or heat pump system. In this context, the same argumentation applies as explained above for the exemption regulation for refrigerants for service and maintenance (unreasonable financial burden for operators as well as ensuring uninterrupted operation especially for system-critical applications).
