Combined Comments:
General Comments: Hazard or exposure:
The so-called hard dimensionally stable gas permeable (RGP) contact lenses consist chemically of hydrophobic components or raw materials. This applies very uniformly worldwide. The weight proportions and the exact chemical structure of the components vary slightly from manufacturer to manufacturer. In principle, however, the synthetic polymers consist largely of the following type of starting substances.

General type of monomer-mixture in RGP material:
- Siloxane acrylates,
- Alkyl acrylates,
- Fluoroacrylates,
- Additives such as UV absorber acrylates and dyes.

The formulation components are therefore fluoroacrylates, among others, which are present in the produced polymer after the polymerisation process of the liquid monomer mixture as polyfluoroacrylate in the copolymer network, thereby enriching the material properties. Quite predominantly, and in our company exclusively, these are low proportions by weight, which are contained in the products at significantly less than 20%, usually even less than 10%! The components in RGP contact lenses are therefore statistically linked together in a three-dimensional, partially cross-linked, very high-molecular copolymer. The hazardous material properties of the monomeric starting materials no longer apply in the polymer state! The polymer, usually a rod-shaped plastic body, is produced under strict conditions in a chemical laboratory in closed facilities. This rod polymerisation is a very long thermal growth and cross-linking process, usually lasting several days. The fluorine compounds do not come out of the polymer again and are therefore very durable as a plastic product overall, which is very advantageous for medical devices. This plastic production is aimed at maximum conversion of the monomeric raw materials, as this is the only way to achieve an overall successful biocompatibility test.  It is important to validly test and fulfil the several years of use (from storage and application). The small products should be used for at least 12 to 18 months without changing their shape or losing properties! The biocompatibility has been comprehensively proven with the most modern trace analysis by independent certified testing laboratories at great expense as part of the approval process. This includes the applicable standards of the ISO 10993ff series, whereby 10993-5, 10 and -18 are to be mentioned in particular. Additionally GC/MS, HPLC/MS and ICP/MS analytics have proven that no fluorine compounds or fragments can be determined from the lens polymer by extractation. The method even uses partially easily destructive solvents such as n-hexane or dichloromethane to expand the polymer structure and analytically detect any unbound components (EN ISO 18369-4). In addition to the aforementioned organic extraction, an aqueous extraction is always carried out to simulate the physiological conditions on the eye. However, the dimensionally stable polymer products are all far too hydrophobic for an extraction of the superhydrophobic fluoroacrylates to take place. This confirms the expectations that the conditions in the storage solution or care product have no influence on the extraction of the cross-linked high-molecular polymers mentioned.
This kind of modern chemical product characterisation is the basis of the risk assessments and the biological evaluations within the scope of the technical documentation. The contact lenses are thus analytically tested down to the lower microgram range on the basis of applicable standards and toxicologically assessed for health risks.
Health hazards for both the plastic manufacturer and the user of the resulting medical products are thus clearly excluded as far as possible with compliance with the standard specifications.
The waste from the manufacturing process and from customer applications belongs in a controlled collection and also incineration as hazardous waste. Halogen-containing compounds (chemicals) have long been collected separately and disposed of by specialist companies. Plastic waste is a separate process waste that is not diffusely released into the environment through extraction.

Environmental emissions:

In contrast to various environmentally harmful applications of fluoropolymers, dimensionally stable contact lens plastics are not a recognisable and somehow significantly measurable ecological and long-term problem. The production of fluoromonomers by raw material manufacturers is a chemical synthesis in closed facilities, the synthesis residues of which are sent to hazardous waste incineration. The volume is extremely small, as these are niche products.
Which fluoromonomers are used for RGP contact lenses in Europe?
The options are very clear due to availability. They have to be acrylate compounds to allow copolymerisation into the network and there are only a "handful" of these. At Wöhlk and at the major suppliers in the USA, the following monomers are primarily used according to information in the approvals:

- TFPM:   2,2,3,3-tetrafluoropropyl methacrylate (CAS 45102-52-1).
- HFiPMA:  Hexafluoro isopropyl methacrylate (CAS 3063-94-3)

These fluoromonomers are therefore a minor polymer component in the contact lens products after the plastic has been manufactured. The weight proportions are to be classified below 20%, mostly even below 10%. Each raw material share has an important contribution to the required material properties in the products. The fluoromonomers are used in the contact lens compound without any further processing procedures, so there are no undetected emissions in the manufacturing process in the chemical production laboratory. Cutting and lathing processes are used in lens production from the plastic rods. Here, too, the process chip is extracted directly at the lathing process and does not enter the breathing air, but goes directly into the special waste collection container. There are no uncontrolled processes and risks as emissions.
These RGP-lens products especially are no short-term disposable products, which makes these kind of products in this market very sustainable and saves the raw material resources quite considerably in direct comparison with the modern soft mass products, which are increasingly common as one-day lenses for single use only. As explained separately, these soft mass products cannot come close to replacing the high-quality special contact lenses discussed here. Users and patients have significantly different and more specific optical requirements that necessitate the use of dimensionally stable contact lenses!

What are the production volumes of hard dimensionally stable contact lenses?
Basically, it should be noted that, contrary to all aspects, it can be seen as an advantage if an enormously helpful and for a long time efficient product is extremely small and light, which per se saves resources. The raw material-effectiveness/benefit ratio of RGP annual contact lenses is exceptionally favourable for the vast majority of ecological load criteria. This extremely small and light product achieves a particularly high-quality improvement in the quality of life for a very long period of use to cope with everyday life for at least 12 months and often for much longer.
As shown separately, hard dimensionally stable gas-permeable polymers are a class of materials that have been developed specifically for the more specialised and very demanding eye applications. The mass-market soft hydrogel lenses are generally less noticeable in-vivo due to their water content and are quicker to acclimate for most people. Nevertheless, the industry has had a stable market share for decades for the water-free hydrophobic RGP products. This is because the many different eye diseases, corneas and changes due to age and influences mean that sufficiently good visual performance can only be achieved with special hard and gaspermeable lenses that are custom-made. This demand will not disappear and continues to require products that are healthy and environmentally friendly. As can be seen, we are not talking about problematic volumes of raw materials and no effective potential for savings, but about very eye-specific-made products based on high-performance hydrophobic polymers.
At this point, our company provides in the confidential section exemplary calculations based on the current production volumes, which show the real use of fluoropolymers.


Information on alternatives:

In the medium-sized company Woehlk, founded by Heinrich Woehlk, the inventor of the contact lenses in 1947, we have been involved in the development of contact lenses and their plastics for decades. The possibilities are of course limited for smaller companies. Nevertheless, we at Woehlk have had great success with our own polymer developments for the production of soft and also various hard dimensionally stable contact lenses. The new European and also worldwide expectations are already prompting us to start working on alternative plastics without fluorine. Each material component always has an urgent requirement in the product formulations. In order to completely dispense with fluorine components in the future, it will be necessary to find completely new substances or to change the current quality of the products in several aspects. From today's perspective, a new development should leave the product quality at the highest current level, or at best even increase it. Since, according to the current state of knowledge, there is no equivalent substitute available for the fluorine components, these quality objectives are a very open-ended, time-consuming task. In any case, it is important to understand that water-containing contact lenses are not a substitute or alternative solution for users of hydrophobic products. The separately mentioned advantages of these products as a whole are entirely dependent on the specific plastic material. In our current assessment, the slight material modifications that only slightly reduce the desired consumption of a fluorine material are on the one hand conceivable and can be implemented with sufficient longer transition periods, but on the other hand the larger modifications of the product formulations (if formulation proportions are approx. 10% fluorine components) are by no means certain to be substituted in a quality-neutral way in a longer transition period. This applies in part to our own products and certainly also to the majority of competitor products and thus also to Wöhlk as a processor of commercial materials. However, substitution of formulation components and the associated new developments are already very time-consuming and very cost-intensive in the approval process for medical devices. Our extensive experience in polymer synthesis suggests that future "alternatives" to this particular polymer chemistry challenge will have significant cost, processing and quality implications. Degraded material quality will mean higher resource requirements, and most likely shorter product life. Shorter product life cycles are a step backwards and mean a loss of desired long-term product applications and higher costs and burdens.

Information on benefits

RGP lenses rely upon PFAS for their technical function which include up to at least 12-months wear time and are a separate and distinct product from disposable 1-day or monthly contact lenses which this statement does not address. Contact lenses provide an important societal function, with up to 30% of citizens in European countries wearing contact lenses.  Currently there are no technical alternatives to PFAS in RGP lenses, with any potential alternative likely to be softer and less chemically resistant due to the absence of the strength of the C-F bond. This will have the result in a product with unsuitable technical characteristics such as the reduced durability of lens and faster agglomeration of film deposits like lipids, lipoproteins and bacteria leading to irritation and higher risks for inflammation. This is a very significant drawback for these modern and successful highly biocompatible products of today. Often, the precorneal eye segment and tear film of patients with a need for individual special lenses is already damaged or at least preloaded. An inferior polymer material of the lenses then additionally worsens the tolerance. Contact lenses always represent a kind of foreign body and have therefore been developed to this level of chemical composition over many years through experience gained in clinical practice.
Hydrophobic, softer, and more adhesive polymers are less comfortable and biocompatible with a higher health risk. This may lead to the development of specialised coatings, cleaning regimes, alternative polymers, or other solutions. However, as yet it is not known which or even if, any of these potential alternatives will be able to offer the necessary technical requirements. It is also important to note that if alternative polymers are developed utilising siloxane, that siloxane toxicity increases as their molecular size decreases . In addition to this, cyclic and low molecular weight siloxane monomers  are extremely lipophilic and essentially dissolve cell membranes and cause cytotoxicity through release of the cell’s contents.  As such a suitable length of time is required to investigate potential alternatives with suitable technical characteristics is critical.
A derogation will allow for the development of suitable processing parameters of the lenses and clinical trials, which alone take 2 years and costs at least €1M (e.g. for orthokeratology lenses). Otherwise the company’s manufacturing such lenses, would expect to lose up to 30% of their sales or even go out of business!
Without a derogation RGP lenses which are the preferred solution in the following instances, would no longer be able to be supported:
• Refractive abnormalities in the paediatric population.
• Non-surgical treatment of keratoconus (thinning and expansion of the cornea).
• Non-surgical treatment to reshape the cornea for vision improvement (Ortho-Keratology).
• Patients with strong corneal astigmatisms as soft lenses cannot be used for fittings, especially those with irregular astigmatisms such as scars and corneal injuries.
• Management of myopia (progressive eye disorder which affects vision, quality of life and increases eye health risks across a person's lifetime).
• Patients after refractive surgery as soft lenses cannot be used.
• Advantages in presbyopia fitting (a refractive error limiting near sight) due to the changed fitting behaviour of RGP compared to soft lenses.
• Patients which do not tolerate corneal contact lenses.
• Patients which do not tolerate soft contact lenses due to “Dry Eye Symptoms”, due to dry eyes or severe deposition problems.


Transitional period:

A differentiated approach to the restriction is essential, with derogations permitting the suitable time for the qualification of potential alternatives, as outlined in the following table. For a substitution to be successful, it must pass through all the technical qualification stages successfully and the potential alternative offers a benefit to either the environment or human health otherwise it can be considered a regrettable substitution.

Total time to develop 10 - 14 years only after a viable alternative material has been identified!

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Wöhlk is a manufacturer of contact lens polymers and of all variations of contact lenses (medical devices). The ECHA annex XV sector is:  6k Rigid gas permeable contact lenses, plano lens and ophthalmic lenses (page 130, table 9)

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: We have submitted a confidential file with a detailed calculation of the amount of PFAS in our contact lens polymers and in our contact lens products. These amounts are very low compared to almost most of the other PFAS application. The contact lens is very small and light and the market is small but very relevant. The waste from the polymer production in our lab and from the contact lens production is also not a high volume, but the waste from the production process is given to incineration.  There is no measureable emission during the manufacturing process with is checked for safety reasons. This means the whole waste from production is collected. At the end of life the lens products are collected and returned or disposed by incineration too.  To understand what we are talking about: Our company has produced in total about 630 kg of RGP PFAS-polymer during 35 years! Resulting from this production, there are made about 17kg of contact lenses in Europe in the market in total during these 35 years. This is much less than 1 kg PFAS from lenses per year at the end of life phase. RGP lenses are very sustainable due to a use of these individual product for at least one year, which is a main advantage to disposable mass products, reducing waste.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Halogen compounds are incinerated as hazardous waste separatly.  This is much more expensive and given to the disposer as a separate waste. Customers only have the option to dispose in the municipal waste (standard incineration).

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: RGP Contact lens polymers and lens products are duroplastic polymers! These crosslinked acrylic copolymer mixtures based on alkyl-, siloxanyl- and fluoroacrylates components are not possible to recycle in current technologies! There are strong chemical bondings between these very long macromolekules from the polymerisation process, reaching a homogeneous and useful material property contributed by each of the formulation components at every point of the copolymer material. There is no way to separate the polymer components from each other afterwards. This kind of stability and durability is what is wanted, but is a disadvantage from the recycling point of view. The keep quality for a long time on the eye and in the storage and in the stock this polymer long-term durability is needed for a successful product approval.

5. Proposed derogations: There is a separate file submitted confidentially. In short: There are very low amounts used to produce these very special RGP polymer materials at Woehlk. The amount of contact lens products is due to the size and weight even much lower. We are discussing about only 500g of PFAS polymer by contact lenses per year in Europe.  One lens weighs about 15 to maximal 40 mg! We are producing the special polymer (in rods) which are used for the lens production. All our RGP products together are weighing less than maximal 20kg PFAS per year!  Large suppliers from the USA are producing much higher volumes for the worldwide market, but it still only means kg amounts PFAS. The smaller the product the less is the waste, and there are only two lens products needed for one year of application!

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Hazardous Waste Europe (HWE) welcomes the PFAS Restriction proposal under the REACH regulation. PFAS represent a very broad family encompassing thousands of substances that can be found in very various applications and forms (fluorosurfactants, fluoropolymers and fluorinated gases). They share similar properties and associated risks and hazards. The grouping approach chosen to address that family of substances is therefore justified and was supported by HWE in past consultations.

However, from the point of view of the end-of-life of products containing PFAS, it is important to make a distinction between these different forms and their impacts on human health and the environment, and to take into account the toxic equivalent of each PFAS.

As a preliminary remark, we would like to stress the current focus on persistence as a criterion deeply intertwined with toxicity. PFAS compounds are chemically stable, so they do not degrade in the environment and this element of stability challenges the way we use, assess and regulate substances in general. Indeed, persistence in the environment can increase the hazardousness of a given substance by leading progressively to a higher concentration. Once a specific concentration level is exceeded, the presence of PFAS might lead to toxicity for the environment and human health. Persistence is more than a factor modulating exposure and should therefore be acknowledged and assessed as an element of chemical hazard.

The scope and the case for restriction are clear and we do not have specific comments regarding the three concentration thresholds proposed in the report. Similarly, three thresholds should be defined for the waste stage to indicate whether waste streams need to be treated in a specific way or decontaminated. This is particularly important in the context of the circular economy, in which waste is reintroduced into the production process.

It is essential to develop PFAS-free alternatives for the vast majority of current PFAS applications. In particular, dispersive applications should be targeted in priority as they are the most problematic ones. As far as essential applications are concerned, they are addressed by means of specific derogations in the report but should be duly justified (lack of alternatives, specific performances, severe operating conditions etc.) to avoid the unnecessary dispersion of pollutants for a longer period of time.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: PFASs are a large family of substances found in many applications. Estimates suggest that several thousand substances will potentially end up in waste streams at the end-of-life stage of products. Of these thousands of chemical compounds, only a small fraction is covered by the regulations (mostly the POP regulation): PFOA, PFOS, PFHxS and C9-C14 PFAS.   It is therefore important to stabilize a clear definition and identify the PFAS that can be found in waste streams, so that we can better assess the chemical footprint of waste streams and therefore direct these wastes to the appropriate waste treatment facilities according to various factors (concentration, toxicity, matrices...).  PFAS can be found in both hazardous and non-hazardous waste streams and can therefore be present in solid, aqueous or gaseous discharges from various industrial facilities (incineration, cement kilns, co-incineration plants, landfill sites, sorting centers and recycling plants, as far as waste treatment plants are concerned). It should also be noted that some specific mixtures or matrices make the work complex and will require significant investment to obtain solid data on their PFAS content.  The ‘no data no market’ principle should be given substance and thoroughly implemented, as the full life cycle of chemicals needs to be taken into account from cradle to grave and back to cradle. As market operators strive to make their products less linear, the fate of chemicals along the value chain needs to be recorded and made available to each step of the value chain. Current initiatives such as the SCIP database and digital product passport bode well for the future, but they have to rely on accurate information and be practicable. To this end, the registrant has a crucial role to play in fulfilling its obligation to provide information in the dossier but also along the value chain by issuing documents such as Safety Data Sheets SDSs or technical documentation. It goes without saying that SDSs and labels must comply with existing requirements and display useful, up-to-date information for downstream users.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: 1/ Measuring PFAS, needs for norms and standards   To date, there are no specific regulations governing the measurement of all PFAS. For incineration, operators usually refer to what is recommended in the Basel Convention technical guidelines on POPs. The technical performance of POPs destruction technologies is based on the level of destruction and irreversible destruction they achieve. This requires consideration of all waste and release output streams from the rotary kilns. Destruction Efficiency (DE) is the percentage of total mass of POPs entering the kiln which is destroyed or irreversibly transformed by the technology. Destruction and Removal Efficiency (DRE) is the percentage of original POPs which is destroyed, irreversibly transformed or removed from the gases released to the atmosphere. United Nations Environment Program (UNEP) recommends that POP destruction technologies reach DE >99.99% (4 nines) and DRE>99.9999% (6 nines).  In all cases, measuring PFAS would require reliable measurements of PFAS entering and leaving industrial plants, whether in gaseous, solid or liquid form. In the case of solids and liquids, standards on this subject are still far from complete. For emissions, this is also complex (there is no standard yet on the method) and potentially more costly. For other types of waste treatment (landfill, composting, recycling, etc.), there are no reference values for assessing treatment performance in terms of PFAS emissions. For recycling, in particular, the question of their presence in the materials resulting from recycling would require more knowledge and data (see above).  From a technical standpoint, many challenges remain for PFAS analysis in order to obtain accurate, representative, comparable, complete and sensitive methods. Differences in regional regulations on PFAS make it difficult to select the analytical method(s) that should be prioritized. Several analytical approaches exist today: target analysis of positive lists of 20 to 50 molecules, non-target analysis, Total Oxidisable Precursor Assay, Total Organic Fluorine, etc. These approaches require different types of equipment, laboratory requirements and hardware configurations to ensure that different compounds can be detected in different matrices. In addition, further work on the environmental and health impacts of individual PFAS compounds, which is poorly understood until now.  The lack of regulations, norms and standards is an obstacle to the effective measurement of PFAS. As far as measurement techniques are concerned, hazardous and non-hazardous waste management operators are launching studies to assess the potential of the various existing technologies and protocols. It should be stressed, however, that the effectiveness of these measurement campaigns depends on the transfer of information on the types of PFAS present in the products (which become waste), in order to be able to better frame the scope of this field of research.  2/ Treatment of waste containing PFAS   The aim of REACH is to ensure that substances are placed on the market without impact on health and the environment, throughout the life cycle of the substance to meet the challenges of the EU’s "Toxic Free" chemical strategy. It is essential to ensure that substances placed on the market can be treated in accordance with current best available techniques. This would align the rules on use, authorisation and restriction with broader issues such as R&D on treatment and traceability. To this end, the work on registration/authorization/restriction shall be linked to the ‘treatability’ potential of the substance.  HWE calls for emission limit values (ELV) to be set for PFAS discharges from waste treatment plants.  a) Hazardous Waste  Incineration   Waste containing PFAS may require special attention during incineration, as some PFAS can release harmful compounds if burnt incorrectly. Regarding hazardous waste incineration, HWE members have conducted and continue to conduct DE/DRE test campaigns to demonstrate the capability of rotary kiln technology for the efficient destruction of PFAS-containing waste. The industrial trials already carried out demonstrate that we are meeting the targets set by the technical guidelines of the Basel Convention (DE and DRE) in such installations.  These results are consistent with existing data concerning the destruction of POPs waste by hazardous waste incinerators. On the other hand, data concerning PFAS cannot be disclosed in the framework of this consultation, given the lack of standardisation of sampling, measurement, and analysis methodologies.   b) Hazardous waste landfilling  In the case of PFAS, the aim of landfilling is to contain the PFAS in order to avoid discharges into the natural environment. Analyses carried out on the presence of PFAS in raw leachates and aqueous effluents demonstrate the effectiveness of effluent treatment technologies (activated carbon, resins, reverse osmosis, etc.).   Waste containing PFAS can thus be disposed of in efficient landfills designed to treat the waste. In addition, long-term management and monitoring of landfill sites may be necessary due to the persistence and potential environmental risks associated with PFAS.  c) Innovation   Research and development work is underway to identify effective treatment technologies for waste streams that contain PFAS. In some cases, additional and final treatments may be required specifically for residues generated where PFAS may be concentrated.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: First of all, in order to preserve the objectives of the restriction and to live in a healthy environment, the restrictions applicable to virgin products must also apply to second raw materials.  To produce high quality second raw materials and guarantee production cycles free of dangerous substances, it is essential to provide for "decontamination" of waste containing PFAS beyond a certain threshold before their final recycling. This decontamination must consist of extraction of heavily polluted fractions.  However, managing these “old substances” will remain a challenge for the waste management industry. It is necessary to clarify and broaden the chain of responsibility, so that each product producer must transmit information on the chemical composition of its products to waste management operators until the waste is transformed into new products by recycling channels. Indeed, responsibility goes hand in hand with information, and the entire value chain must work towards it, otherwise valuable information is lost, making it more difficult to implement total toxic-free circularity. The current set of tools (MSDS, digital product passport, labelling and SCIP database) is useful, but not sufficient to guarantee a sufficient level of traceability and information.  Another key element to consider is the eco-design of products to ensure their elimination and substitution as quickly as possible, in order to minimize the impact on the downstream part of the process.

Org. name: HepcoMotion®, the trading name of Hepco Slide Systems Limited
Combined Comments:
General Comments: HepcoMotion manufactures automation components and systems which support a number of key industries, including factory automation, medical applications, semiconductor and electronics manufacture and food production. We are a downstream user of products containing PFAS, which are fundamental to certain lubricants, coatings and seals, and critical for the proper function and longevity of these components and systems. Where products containing PFAS are used, we are not currently aware of sufficiently good alternatives, and our suppliers are in the same position. The ultimate manufacturers of these PFAS are sceptical that good alternatives can be made and we are guided by their opinions. We are fearful that, if we no longer have access to critical PFAS, our ability to win business will be damaged. In a world market where many countries may not restrict PFAS in the same way, there is a risk that we will lose business to competitors who will be able to use PFAS. Given that many PFAS materials were in use for several decades before the concerns about potential harms were recognised, we are concerned that even the longest 12-year derogation may not be long enough to develop materials whose performance is good enough, if that is possible at all, and to confirm they would not be potentially harmful when used in place of PFAS materials.

HepcoMotion supports the restriction of harmful PFAS based on a risk-based approach. The restriction proposed by the ECHA covers a broad range of uses of PFAS, some of which we view as not having readily available alternatives. Additionally, the ECHA Annex Report omits derogation for use of products containing PFAS in automation components and machinery, an area of industry which is the foundation of many of the sectors and sub-uses listed in the derogation proposals.

In a recent journal paper (J.K. Anderson et al., 2022), experts agreed that “the lack of consistent interpretations of human health risk for well-studied PFAS and the lack of information for the vast majority of PFAS present significant challenges for any mixtures risk assessment approach. Most experts agreed that “all PFAS” should not be grouped together, persistence alone is not sufficient for grouping PFAS for the purposes of assessing human health risk, and that the definition of appropriate subgroups can only be defined on a case-by-case manner.”

Fluoropolymers, for example, fulfil the OECD criteria as Polymers of Low Concern (PLC) and are deemed to have insignificant environmental and human health impacts. Klüber Lubrication München GmbH & Co KG have commented that PFPE oils, as well as PTFE, are high molecular weight polymers (more than 10.000 Da), “not soluble in water, not bioavailable, not toxic and fall outside the definition of hazardous products”.

Recently published ‘Analysis of the most appropriate regulatory management options (RMOA)’ for PFAS by the UK Health & Safety Executive (March 2023) advises that “the restriction(s) set out above need not apply to low hazard groups or low risk uses, for example; fluoroplastics or fluoroelastomers (low hazard groups)”.

Fluoropolymer toxicity data, human clinical data, and physical, chemical, thermal, and biological data was reviewed and assessed in a journal article  by (S. H. Korzeniowski et al., 2023). The paper concluded that that “fluoropolymers satisfy widely accepted assessment criteria to be considered as “polymers of low concern” (PLC). This review concludes that fluoropolymers are distinctly different from other polymeric and nonpolymeric PFAS and should be separated from them for hazard assessment or regulatory purposes. Grouping fluoropolymers with all classes of PFAS for “read across” or structure–activity relationship assessment is not scientifically appropriate.”

The quantity (as a percentage weight) of PFAS used in our products is low, with minimal anticipated emission to the environment in the end-of-life. Whilst the quantity of PFAS in these products is small, the impact of the removal of PFAS would be significant. We would be reliant on our suppliers to develop suitable alternatives within the transition or derogation periods. Without an equivalent alternative product, sensitive industries (for example semiconductor manufacturing) are likely to be negatively impacted and suffer supply chain issues, which will in turn affect a number of other industries and ultimately consumers.

The choice to use substances or products which contain PFAS is driven by performance rather than cost; PFAS-containing substances cost considerably more than the equivalent product when not used in a harsh environment.

According to comments submitted by Precision Polymer Engineering on the ECHA PFAS restriction report, the inherent thermal and chemical stability of FKM seals “make them the only technical solution for SIP (steam-in-place) and CIP (clean-in-place) processes for cleaning and sterilisation of equipment, which involve a combination of steam, acids and bases”. FKM seals outperform any other sealing material that exists on the market and reduce the frequency of maintenance/replacement, which promotes economical and sustainable use of resource ‒ a primary aim of the EU’s Circular Economy Action Plan ‒ as well as ensuring contaminants do not escape into the food manufacturing process. Certain grades of FKM are US FDA regulation compliant.

Usage is increasing year-on-year due to the implementation of stricter regulations to reduce migration into food streams and through the employment of ever more demanding conditions for cleaning and sterilisation of food processing equipment and plants. Fluoropolymers are a key enabler for this; in case of restrictions in the use of fluoropolymers, no sealing material would be available to meet these market needs.

In the manufacture of semiconductors, PFPE is a key ingredient in lubricants which have been developed to suit aggressive chemical environments, extreme temperatures and vacuum environments. These high-performance lubricants are specifically engineered for applications where the environment presents lubrication problems. DuPont de Nemours, Inc. has commented that they have been unable to identify or develop alternative chemistries which work around the fundamental physical-chemical properties of PFAS materials essential to semiconductor manufacturing.

In February 2023, the European Semiconductor Industry Association (ESIA) announced that yearly semiconductor sales in the European market reached the record figure of $53.809 billion in 2022, a 12.3% increase on 2021. Customer demand for products with these performance characteristics will not lessen as a result of the restriction on the use of PFAS. The reliance of EU companies will increase on manufacturers not subject to a restriction on the use of PFAS, who will still use PFAS in their processes and products. We believe this will have a detrimental effect on the ability of EU-based companies to compete with those outside the EU, who are not subject to the same restrictions, and this will also conflict with the European Chips Act, reducing the competitiveness and resilience of Europe’s semiconductor technologies and applications.

The ESIA have also commented that “even though PFAS-free lubricants exist, they do not meet essential performance requirements, i.e. inertness under harsh conditions, low off-gassing, and low particle generation. These properties are critical due to the cleanliness requirements during manufacture. Furthermore, these PFAS-free alternatives have increased failure rates and human health and safety impacts.”

We support the evidence submitted by industry trade associations and consortia in favour of the proposed derogations and exclusions covering the use of fluoropolymers in lubrication, sealing components and coatings for industrial applications. We propose that the aim of preventing the release of potentially harmful substances into the environment at the time of manufacture and at end-of-life could be realised through regulated processes and disposal systems. Many of the uses of PFAS in the contexts described above are in industrial and professional settings (i.e. not consumer-based). Thus, regulation in end-of-life disposal would be more easily implemented, monitored and controlled.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Baseline Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Org. name: Heraeus Precious Metals GmbH & Co. KG
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Heraeus Precious Metals GmbH & Co. KG as a provider of products and services in the Precious Metals industry supports the PFAS restriction. However, the current scope is far too broad and not based on hazard nor risk related to the different substances. This means that the impact on the precious metals industry using directly or indirectly the PFAS to produce and recycle precious metals will be significant. Indeed, the Precious Metals industry has identified direct (electroplating) or indirect (industrial equipment, PPE and analytical equipment) uses of PFAS but also some uses intrinsically related to the use of precious metals (green hydrogen). These uses occur in a well-controlled (industrial) environment, with negligible potential for release / exposure to humans and the environment.

It is worth noting that the PFAS is a huge group of substances with different levels of hazard. A lot of these substances are considered of low concern (cf. OECD1), such as the fluoropolymers.

For most of the uses related to precious metals, PFAS are selected because of their unique properties and there are no alternatives available today with a comparable performance. If these uses were no longer allowed and/or the exemption time is not sufficient to find alternatives, this might have significant impacts on the precious metals manufacturing and recycling activities in the EU, and thus be incompatible with e.g., the EU Green Deal.

PFAS are also present in recycling streams containing precious metals (‘PM’). The PFAS are all being destroyed during the recycling process, trapped from the flue gas and duly disposed of. Any limitation on the use of PM recycling streams containing PFAS will restrict PM recycling activities in Europe.

It is worth noting that the PGMs (Platinum Group Metals) have been identified at Critical Raw Materials. The Critical Raw Materials act sets targets to allow Europe to be resilient. The ban of all PFAS in the EU at short notice will for sure jeopardize the success of the Critical Raw Materials act.

Hence, we would like to request that:

- the hazard profile of the PFAS is considered to prioritize the PFAS included in the restriction.
- the scope of the restriction is limited and that substances of low concern (as per OECD criteria) are exempted from the restriction.
- if the exemption must be use driven, the uses of PFAS outlined above must be exempted for at least 12 years and a mechanism to renew these exemptions must be put in place.

For further details we refer to the comments made under "Specific Information Requests" as well as to the attached statements.

Regarding the preparation of the contribution to this Public Consultation, Heraeus Precious Metals GmbH & Co. KG is supported by the European Precious Metals Federation (EPMF) and the International Platinum Group Metals Association e.V. (IPA).

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: This submission relates to the use of fluoropolymers (fluoroelastomers and fluoroplastics) as seals, gaskets, vessel liners etc, within processing equipment used in the refining and recycling of metals, specifically platinum group metals (PGM). Such use is not recognised within the Annex XV restriction report (Table 9).

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The International Platinum Group Metals Association (IPA) and its member companies do not possess empirical emissions data for PFAS.  The solid fluoropolymer-based articles, such as seals and gaskets used in PGM refining processing equipment are used for their durability and ability to withstand the extremely aggressive conditions necessary to refine noble metals. Such fluoropolymer components typically undergo routine replacement only after many (e.g. 20-25) years, and even then the components are fully intact with no indication of degradation. Hence in-use emissions are expected to be zero.  Due to the high value of PGM, it is common practice for end-of-life components such as the fluoropolymer seals and gaskets used in PGM processing equipment to themselves be put through the PGM refining process to recover any adsorbed PGM. Based on information published in the scientific literature (Aleksandrov et al, 2019; Taylor et al, 2014), it can be confidently expected that the fluoropolymers will be completely degraded and mineralised with negligible and likely zero emission of PFAS.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: IPA does not itself possess any data on thermal degradation and mineralisation of PFAS under municipal waste incineration conditions. Scientific research papers (Aleksandrov et al, 2019; Taylor et al, 2014), though, support the view that such incineration does degrade PFAS and that any PFAS going through the PGM refining process will be thermally degraded and mineralised. PGM refining pyrometallurgy employs temperatures of over 900 °C and in most cases over 1,100 °C, and Best Available Techniques (BAT) dictate its air treatment systems achieve 1,100 °C for at least 2 seconds followed by several treatment steps to clean the air.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Annex E of the Restriction report acknowledges (page 196, Section E.2.4.2.2 Manufacture of Metal Products) that “there are other applications where other properties of PFAS are important, for example durability, resistance to chemical attack, thermal properties and sealing properties. Stakeholders did not identify alternatives that fulfil the performance of fluoropolymers e.g. for chemical and temperature resistance.”  The proposed Restriction would likely end the recycling of Platinum Group Metals (PGM) within the EU, due to the inability to obtain and use fluoropolymer components within processing equipment used in PGM refining and the lack of any suitable alternatives. This would force the EU to become entirely dependent on imported PGM and PGM-based products and contradict the EU’s strategic objective as outlined in the Critical Raw Materials Act proposal to achieve by 2030 40% processing and 15% of recycling of PGM within the EU.  PFAS as defined in the Restriction proposal may also be present in low concentrations within PGM recycling feedstocks (e.g. within electronic wastes). Precise concentration ranges are not known – the heterogeneous nature of the feedstocks prevents practicable representative sampling until after thermal treatment which destroys any PFAS that was present (see responses to Questions 2 and 3) – but as those feedstocks are considered waste they themselves are exempt from Restriction under REACH.  It is vital that any future regulatory developments to embed the circular economy and invigorate the hydrogen economy and use of PGM within electrolysers and fuel cells do not inadvertently alter the status of PGM recycling feedstocks and inhibit the continued success story of PGM recycling.

5. Proposed derogations: The use of PFAS (fluoropolymers) to which this submission relates is not covered by the derogations listed under Paragraphs 5 and 6 of the proposed Restriction.   Precise volumes of fluoropolymers used within componentry of processing equipment used in the recycling and refining of Platinum Group Metals (PGM) are not known. Data on environmental emissions are likewise not available, and we would welcome further research into analytical methodologies for detecting and quantifying PFAS in environmental media. Despite the lack of verifiable supporting data, it can be confidently expected (see answers to Questions 2 and 3) that environmental emissions of PFAS from the uses to which this submission relates will be negligible and likely zero.

6. Missing uses: The critical use of fluoropolymers within industrial chemical processing equipment, and specifically in the refining and recycling of Platinum Group Metals (PGM) – identified as critical and strategic raw materials by the EU – is not recognised in the Restriction proposal.  Fluoropolymers are able to survive the extremely aggressive chemical conditions necessary for refining of noble metals. They are used inter alia as vessel linings, seals, and gaskets; their chemical stability ensuring the hazardous contents of the processing equipment remain contained and secure.  The annual tonnage of fluoropolymers used within PGM processing equipment within the EU is not known but will be modest considering both the amounts required for the fluoropolymer components and their typically decades long service life. Specific fluoropolymers used in PGM processing equipment include PFA (perfluoroalkoxy alkanes), PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride), ECTFE (ethylenechlorotrifluoroethylene / Halar), PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene), FKM (Fluorine Kautschuk Material / Viton), and FFKM (Kalrez).  Europe is a significant player in the global PGM supply chain, providing approximately 40% of global PGM recycling. Within Europe, there are four major PGM refining and recycling companies that would be significantly affected by the Restriction – likely forcing them to relocate outside of Europe and causing the EU to become entirely dependent on import for these strategic critical raw materials.   In addition, there are an unknown number of additional and downstream companies that may require equivalent specification processing equipment to manufacture PGM products.  It is expected that for some of these the use of fluoropolymers in processing equipment ancillaries is similarly necessary and not possible to substitute; hence the current Restriction proposal would also significantly impact the broader PGM products industry in Europe.  No viable alternatives to the use of fluoropolymers in the described applications within PGM processing equipment are known.  Historically, gaskets requiring thermal and chemical stability were made of asbestos. Due to the well-known carcinogenicity of asbestos, these were replaced by fluoropolymer alternatives.  For some processes, use of glass equipment to replace fluoropolymer-lined vessels would theoretically be possible, but this presents its own hazards, and moreover even in those processes seals and other components would still need to be made from fluoropolymers.  Suppliers of industrial chemical processing equipment have engaged in R&D to identify suitable alternatives to fluoropolymers that could deliver the necessary performance, but no alternatives have been identified.  Annex E of the Restriction report acknowledges (page 196, Section E.2.4.2.2 Manufacture of Metal Products) that “there are other applications where other properties of PFAS are important, for example durability, resistance to chemical attack, thermal properties and sealing properties. Stakeholders did not identify alternatives that fulfil the performance of fluoropolymers e.g. for chemical and temperature resistance.”  PGM are categorised as critical raw materials. They provide a critical function within PEM electrolysers and fuel cells that are the basis of the hydrogen economy, and their unique properties have for a long time been utilised in numerous other important applications providing enormous health and societal benefits, including inter alia, anticancer drugs, medical devices such as pacemakers and cochlear implants, catalytic converters that prevent the emission of harmful chemicals from vehicle exhausts, electronic equipment, jet engines, and fertilizer production. The value chain for PGM in Europe (excluding complex end products) has recently been estimated at approximately €95 billion (Eftec, 2023). In the absence of any suitable alternatives to fluoropolymers within PGM processing equipment, the Restriction proposal can be predicted to have the following socioeconomic impacts directly related to this: - Cessation of PGM recycling and refining in the EU and the EU becoming entirely dependent on import of these strategic and critical raw materials - Closure of PGM refineries sited in the EU, with the loss of business revenues in the single-digit billions of euros (Eftec, 2023), and the direct loss of jobs in the single-digit thousands (Eftec, 2023) - Cessation of production of PGM products where dissolution of PGM is necessary in the production process and the EU becoming entirely dependent on imports of those products - Closure of a larger number of sites and companies that utilise PGM to make products that requires dissolving PGM, with the loss of jobs in the thousands.

8. Other identified uses: The specific uses of fluoropolymers that are the subject of this submission, i.e. their use in PGM processing equipment, are not included in Table 8 of the Restriction Report.  The importance of fluoropolymers for metal plating and manufacture of metal products more generally is acknowledged in the report. Annex E of the Restriction report states (page 196, Section E.2.4.2.2 Manufacture of Metal Products) that “there are other applications where other properties of PFAS are important, for example durability, resistance to chemical attack, thermal properties and sealing properties. Stakeholders did not identify alternatives that fulfil the performance of fluoropolymers e.g. for chemical and temperature resistance.”

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: IPA does not possess data on the environmental degradation potential of any PFAS sub-groups. As described earlier, though, environmental emissions of any form of PFAS from the use of fluoropolymers within PGM processing equipment are expected to be zero both during use and at end-of-life

General Comments: Herbert Hänchen GmbH is one of the leading german manufactueres of hydraulic cylinders worlwide. Please note that fluoropolymers contribute significantly to meeting the objectives of the EU Ecodesign Regulation for Sustainable Products (ESPR), which generally requires products to have a long service life. Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Hereby, we as a medical device manufacturer and medicinal product marketing authorization holder are responding to the PFAS restriction proposal so far comprising all compounds without taking into consideration their chemical properties, e.g. solubility / insolubility in aqueous media. Thus, we intend to participate in the official consultation.
In our opinion it is beyond doubt that a complete ban of PFAS is neither appropriate nor feasible within a few years of research for potential alternatives. Therefore, in our statement only scenario two of the restriction proposal including derogations for certain industrial sectors is taken into consideration.
Hereafter, we would like to point out the consequences of a complete restriction of PFAS for us as a pharmaceutical company and as a consequence for the patients depending on our products if the pharma industry is not exempted.
Regarding medicinal products, to date only active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) are excluded from the restriction. Moreover, in the case of medical devices, no derogations are foreseen and might only be potentially reconsidered (i.e., for venting valves in ophthalmological products).
However, PFAS are widely used in different steps of the manufacturing process of medicinal products and medical devices and PFAS are not only necessarily restricted to be potentially present in finished products. For instance, PFAS are included in process aids for manufacturing, the manufacturing itself or in analytical techniques used for product release in the form of pipes, valves, (sterile) filter membranes, packaging material, analytical equipment and more. A ban of PFAS with no exemptions other than APIs will displace the pharmaceutical production outside of the European Union and will clearly restrict the release of drugs produced in the EU to the EU market.
As a consequence, it is likely the EU is threatened once more with supply shortage, this time only on a much wider scope of products. This is not only in contradiction to the European ambition to prevent the supply shortage of medicinal product/medical device but also to the newly introduced German Drug Supply Shortage Control and Supply Improvement Act (Arzneimittel-Lieferengpassbekämpfungs- und Versorgungsverbesserungsgesetz (ALBVVG)).
We share the opinion of the German association of the pharmaceutical industry BAH (Bundesverband der Arzneimittel-Hersteller e.V.): The assurance of population’s supply with medicinal products and medical devices should be the overall objective of all regulatory purpose. It is of utmost importance to have a clear legal structure without unnecessary regulatory overlap. Medicinal products or medical devices having PFAS in their manufacturing process or containing PFAS themselves have been approved for market release for several years already by a competent authority or notified body. If the pharmaceutical industry will not be exempted from the PFAS restriction, these products will completely vanish from the European Market even though they have market approval. The replacement of PFAS in the manufacturing process is time consuming and will take several years. Worst case scenario could be that no alternatives to PFAS are available. If there are potential alternatives, their development, testing and validation for the use in the pharma industry are time-consuming and will exceed by far the planned transition period of 18 months.
Specific exemptions for the pharma industry are urgently required. Medicinal products and medical devices already approved for the market or in late-stage development phase as well as restricted and regulated compounds (e.g. fluorinated gases, chemicals having specific REACH restrictions) should be exempted from the PFAS restriction. Furthermore, specific exemptions are needed for raw material/excipients and intermediate products, reagents, and materials used in the manufacturing process such as filter membranes or other equipment used for manufacturing or product release analytics.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: HEROSE GMBH does not recommend a blanket ban on the entire PFAS group of approx. 10,000 different individual substances, because it presents HEROSE GMBH and important parts of the German and European economy with challenges that are almost impossible to solve. The substance group of PFAS is required by HEROSE GMBH in a wide variety of applications. In the field of valve technology, these range from applications in cryogenics, in oxygen-carrying systems to materials that come into contact with food. In the industrial sector, PFAS are considered high-performance materials that are indispensable in many processes, especially under extreme conditions at both low (e.g. -196°C) and high temperatures.
The PFAS high-performance plastics are indispensable for affected industries in order to comply with legal regulations, e.g. in the field of fire protection, safety standards or norms. A broad PFAS restriction would result in significant gaps in the safety, performance and reliability of assets and products across many industries. Using the example of HEROSE GMBH with the use of seals reinforced with PFAS, a loss of this would endanger the safety of plants, systems and people and lead to more emissions or leaks of gases and chemicals. As a result of this and the shortened service life and more frequent maintenance intervals, the environmental impact would also increase.
In this context, chemicals should only be considered as an alternative to PFAS and thus as a justification for a restriction if they have also been adequately evaluated with regard to safety-relevant aspects, service life, energy consumption and other factors. In addition, the use of alternatives should not be systematically restricted by the requirements of other technical regulations in order to avoid conflicting regulations. In addition, the alternatives should be functionally equivalent, i. H. PFAS-based solutions can replace in terms of form, suitability and function. However, if alternative chemicals are tested that can chemically replace PFAS in an equivalent manner, there is a likelihood that they will be chemically resistant and persistent in equal measure.
Since the development of alternatives, if at all possible, will take years or decades, HEROSE GMBH recommends making broad exemptions from PFAS for industrial applications. The time span of the exemptions should be based on the state of research in order to make the implementation of the restrictions possible. Where alternatives are already available or at a late stage of development, temporary transition periods would be appropriate. In those cases where no real alternatives are yet available, the exceptions should apply indefinitely. At the same time, research into alternative substances should be provided with more research funding in order to enable the gradual substitution of the PFAS substance group. In this way, the EU could take on a global pioneering role on the subject of PFAS and impress with innovations.

General Comments: High pressure ball valves have high dependence on PFASs, including usage in sensible applications such as process, chemical and semiconductor industry.

Our valve designs are based on  different parts from FKM/ FFKM and parts from PTFE.

Fluoropolymers provide exceptional properties, making them irreplaceable in valve applications. Some key features are:
- Chemical resistance: Fluoropolymers exhibit outstanding resistance to a wide range of chemicals, including acids, bases, and other aggressive substances.
- Thermal stability: Fluoropolymers can withstand extreme temperatures without significant degradation.
- Non-stick properties: Fluoropolymers are renowned for their non-stick characteristics. This property is particularly evident in polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE).
- Low friction coefficient: Fluoropolymers have an extremely low coefficient of friction, which means they offer excellent lubrication and reduce wear and tear in mechanical systems. This feature is essential for applications like bearings, seals, and sliding components in valves


Transitional period:
Even if substitutes are available a transition period of at least 10 years must be available to search for alternatives an evaluate design changes.

Those components can be clearly separated from our valves in case of maintenance and therefore can easily be brought to a potential recycle process.

6. Missing uses: a.Membrane materials are used for building roofs and other structures and require durability. While PTFE and ETFE are in use for membrane materials for permanent buildings, PVC-coated membrane materials are often used for other structures designed for long-term use, such as warehouses, event tents, and awnings. This is because PVC resins are low cost and, when plasticizers are added, enable the production of sheet membranes which allow for design flexibility and are soft thanks to its feature as thermoplastic resins. As such PVC-coated membrane materials have used for many years. As for these materials, PVDF, which falls under the category of PFAS, is used in surface coatings to provide surface protection and antifouling properties for PVC resins and enhance their flame resistance.  b. As a material used for surface coating of PVC-coated membrane materials, PVDF has a variety of properties. One example is its flame resistance. Not only Japan, but other countries also have regulations in place that require membrane materials for buildings to be flame-resistant. PVDF’s limiting oxygen index (ISO 4589), an indicator of flame resistance, stands at 43, which shows that the material is highly flame-resistant, contributing to the enhanced flame resistance of PVC-coated membrane materials. As the LOI of PVC and polycarbonate resins, for example, is 37 and 25, respectively, PVDF plays a significant role in providing PVC-coated membrane materials with flame resistance. Meanwhile, the LOI of acrylic resins and silicone resins, which are materials referred to as potential alternatives to PVDF, stand at 18 and 26, respectively, which means that a large quantity of flame-retardant agents must be added to these resins in order to use them as substitutes while making such PVC-coated membrane materials sufficiently flame-resistant to meet the regulations of various countries. This would lead to the reduced strength of PVC-coated resins, making them unfit for long-term use. Another feature of PVDF is its antifouling properties. PVDF has water-repellent and oleophobic (oil-resistant) properties; therefore, when raindrops containing dust fall onto PVC-coated membrane materials, the drops will flow down without sticking to the materials, making them stain-resistant. Furthermore, when these drops flow down, they also wash off stains due to dust, providing the materials with high antifouling properties.  d. Should PVC-coated membrane materials be used without PVDF coating, it would lead to these materials to become stained after a short period of time, resulting in their needing to be replaced more often because they would adversely affect the scenery. In addition, the lack of oleophobic (oil-resistant) properties would speed up the degradation of flexible vinyl chloride resins, making it the maintenance of the necessary strength difficult and thereby requiring them to be replaced more frequently. The increased frequency of the replacement of such materials would lead to the increased generation of industrial waste and the imposition of a greater burden on the environment.  e.f. Acrylic resin coating is widely adopted as a substitute material with antifouling properties; however, it is less water repellent than PVDF and thus has poorer antifouling properties. Its lack of oleophobic (oil-resistant) property makes the coating unsuitable for long-term use. Hence, acrylic resin coating cannot be used as a substitute material. Some refer to photocatalysts (titanium oxide) as a substitute, but photocatalysts decompose not only staining substances but also the PVC coating itself through oxidation, raising concerns due to reductions in durability. Moreover, if the intensity of ultraviolet rays is insufficient, it would hinder photocatalysts from fully exhibiting their antifouling properties, posing a problem in terms of usage environment. Silicone coating, which prevents raindrops from remaining on the material by adding hydrophilic properties to it, is another potential alternative. However, it is impossible to add oleophobic properties to silicone coatings, meaning that the migration of plasticizers is unavoidable and thus making the coating unfit for long-term use. Thus, silicone coating cannot be used as a substitute material. In searching for substitute materials, sufficient verification is required based on the assumption that such materials will be used over the long term; therefore, it is essential to introduce a grace period that is long enough to permit their development.
