On 13 January 2023, the competent authorities of five EU/EEA states (Dossier Submitters) submitted the PFAS REACH Annex XV Restriction Report (Proposal) to the European Chemical Agency (ECHA).

Although considered very persistent (vP) by design, PCTFE is a fluoropolymer that satisfies all internationally recognised criteria of Polymers of Law Concern (PLC). In particular, they do not exhibit hazards identified in the Proposal as “supporting concerns” applicable to all PFAS, i.e., bioaccumulation, mobility, long range transport potential (LRTP), accumulation in plants, ecotoxicity, endocrine activity/endocrine disruption, effects on human health and concerns triggered by a combination of these properties. The Dossier Submitters erroneously attributed these hazards to all substances in the “PFAS group”, including PCTFE. Grouping PCTFE with all other PFAS for REACH read-across and restriction purposes is scientifically unjustified and contrary to the provisions of Annexes I, XI and XV REACH.

PCTFE fluoropolymers are manufactured both from non-PFAS raw materials and the non-PFAS monomer Chlorotrifluoroethylene (CTFE), and polymerized without involvement of other PFAS substances ( processing aids, surfactants, additives, or agents). ©Aclar is a medical grade, high-purity, intrinsically stable, inert material with extremely low levels of residues, impurities, and negligible leaching characteristics throughout its full life cycle. Its end-of-life disposal in landfills and by municipal incineration are proven to be safe and recommended by national and international regulations. Incineration at end-of-life above 800 °C does not release PFAS-related materials nor detectable levels of Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA).

Considering very small tonnages of PCTFE imported into the EU for uses in medicinal and medical devices packaging (app. 2.3% of the total PFAS uses in the medical devices sector and ca. 0,36% of the total polymeric PFAS tonnages used on the market in 2020), negligible emission levels (1%) and its PLC properties, the respective risks to human health and the environment could not be considered “unacceptable” and are disproportionate vis-à-vis the proposed REACH restriction.

Furthermore, any potential safety risks are adequately controlled by the applicable EU legislation, including EU medicines and veterinary laws, requirements of the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and national medicines authorities, EU Pharmacopoeia, Medical Devices Regulation (MDR), Food and Food Contact Materials (FCM) rules, EU waste and packaging laws and other regulations. It is noteworthy that relevant risk management measures (RRMs) cover both the final packaging and the starting (input) materials to fully ensure that all risks are adequately controlled through the full life circle of PCTFE (©Aclar). Hence, “double RMMs” on PCTFE-based inputs/materials for medicines and medical device packaging are excessive.  In this respect, ECHA should consult, exchange information and coordinate with EMA respective activities to ensure coherence in scientific opinions/evaluations to avoid potential contradictions.

There are no alternatives to PCTFE that provide similar moisture/chemical barrier and clarity properties, essential for preserving the quality, safety, and efficiency of drugs and medical devices over a range of temperatures as well as cryogenic conditions. Other materials will inevitably deteriorate and impact the stability characteristics of pharmaceuticals, increase packaging sizes, and exhibit dangerous features, e.g., PVC/PVDC polymers.

Therefore, the conclusions regarding PCTFE exposure assessment and risks characterisation in the Proposal are manifestly erroneous and the proposed REACH restriction on PCTFE fluoropolymers is not justified.

The derogation would be similar to those granted in the Proposal to active substances in biocidal, plant protection, or medicinal products and will be in line with previous RAC/SEAC practices.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Honeywell is a global manufacturer and importer of various fluorinated gases to the European Union (EU), including hydrofluorocarbons (HFC) and hydrofluoroolefins (HFO) refrigerants and their mixtures (blends), primarily used in commercial, industrial as well as domestic refrigeration, heating, ventilation and air conditioning (RHVAC or HVAC, including heat pumps) applications.

Contrary to what the Dossier Submitters claim, there are a range of PFAS substances, including various fluorinated gases, that are not very persistent (vP) as such and do not degrade to vP substances in meaningful amounts. For instance, the gases HFC-125, HFC-143a, HFC-245fa, HFO-1234ze(E), HFO-1233zd(E), HFO-1336mzz(E), HFO-1336mzz(Z), HCFO-1233zd(E) degrade in the atmosphere to carbon dioxide (CO2), Hydrogen fluoride (HF) and insignificant amounts of the only PFAS arrowhead substance - trifluoroacetic acid (TFA). Also comprehensive conclusive scientific evidence, including from respective REACH registration dossiers, confirms that many PFAS (comprising, HFC/HFO) are low hazard gaseous substances that do not exhibit risks similar to PBT/vPvB substances under Article XIII REACH. Thus, they should be excluded from the scope of the Proposal.

According to the REACH registration dossier and Chemical Safety Report (CSR) for TFA, although the substance fulfils certain criteria for persistency, it has scientifically established DNEL/PNEC thresholds and is not classified as PBT or vPvB substance under Annex XIII REACH. It does not raise equivalent levels of concern under Article 57(f) REACH. In this respect, ECHA already reviewed and evaluated a TFA dossier without concluding on the need for further regulatory actions.

Moreover, according to the most recent 2022 UNEP/WMO report: “TFA abundance and its environmental impacts have been assessed in many previous Assessments (e.g., Montzka, Reimann et al., 2011; Montzka, Velders et al., 2018; Carpenter, Daniel et al., 2018). Previous Assessments concluded that the environmental effects of TFA due to the breakdown of HCFCs and HFCs are too small to be a risk to the environment over the next few decades based on the projected future use of hydrocarbons, HCFCs, and HFOs.”

The most recent EEAP 2022 Assessment Report also concludes that “based on projected future use of these precursors of TFA [incl. HFC/HFO], no harm is anticipated” and that TFA “is unlikely to cause adverse effects out to 2100”.

Detailed analysis on HFC/HFO degradation products and relevant hazard, exposure and risks assessments of TFA is provided in the Honeywell submission reference no: 76bb3d12-2101-4390-82cf-3498b47e8015.

In addition, many HFC/HFO gases are already comprehensively/adequately regulated in EU and beyond, including via effective Risks Management Measures (RMMs) under the EU F-Gas Regulation, MAC Directive (F-Gas Regulation), ELV Directive, Industrial Emissions Directive and other legislation. These laws mandate inter alia progressive limitations on placing on the market (e.g., HFC (F-Gas) quotas and certain equipment bans), comprehensive containment measures (leaks controls, servicing certification for HFC/HFO in RHVAC), product (eco-)design and safe use standards (e.g., ISO 5149-1:2014, EN 378, disposal and end-of-life requirements (e.g., recuperation and re-use of F-gases)). These regulations could be strengthened at any time, if warranted.

Therefore, even those HFC/HFO gases that degrade to TFA in substantial rates, such as HFO-1234yf, HFC-134a or HFC-227ea, should be excluded from the PFAS restriction scope due to the absence of unacceptable or not adequately controlled risks within the meaning of Articles 68 - 69 REACH.

Furthermore, contrary to the requirements of Part II, Section 3 of Annex XV REACH Regulation, the Proposal is missing an objective, credible and specific enough assessment of “information on the risks to human health and the environment related to the manufacture or use of the alternatives” as well as on consistency of these alternatives with wider-EU decarbonization and sustainability policies (including, European Green Deal, Fit for 55, REPowerEU, etc.). These assessments are particularly important as far as certain key RHVAC uses of HFC/HFO are concerned.

In this respect, the “careful and impartial” assessment of all available information, including submitted by stakeholders during two Calls for Evidence (CfE) preceding the Proposal, unequivocally demonstrates the scarcity of safe and sustainable alternatives for many uses of HFC/HFO fluorinated gases including in commercial, industrial, and domestic RHVAC applications. Bans on such uses as suggested in the Proposal will result in very high costs on the society and the environment (climate change) and will be contrary to wider-EU policies as well as principles of the EU law.

In this respect, alternative refrigerants referred in the Proposal (often misleadingly called “natural refrigerants”), including CO2 (R-744), ammonia (R-717) and certain hydrocarbons (e.g., propane (R-290), isobutane (R-600a)) are suggested by the Dossier Submitters without adequate assessments of corresponding safety risks such as flammability, toxicity, very high operating pressures, etc. In the meantime, objective assessments of their intrinsic properties and reported incidents (Annexes II-IV) involving those refrigerants demonstrate that respective risks are considerably higher, and often cannot be adequately controlled, than from “fourth generation” HFC/HFO refrigerants specifically designed for these respective uses.

Moreover, two comprehensive studies in Appendixes 1 and 2 of our submission demonstrate that in case of substitutions proposed by Dossier Submitters for RHVAC sector the electricity consumption and respective GHG emissions will result to additional annual 6.9 TWhr/yr of demand and 2.7 MTonne/yr of CO2eq GHG emissions, and will incur additional electricity cost of 1-3.4 Billion €/yr for ~44% of the overall EU air conditioning and heat pumps (AC/HVAC) sector. The proposed substitutions will also add 5.7 TWhr/yr to annual demand on the electricity grid, 2.4 MTonne/yr of CO2eq emissions and additional electricity costs of 0.8-3 Billion €/yr in ~64% of the total commercial refrigeration sector. These costs, combined with potential losses or damages from potential incidents (see above) are too high and disproportionate in comparison with alleged concerns due to persistency of the TFA substance, which is negligible and we have demonstrated in our submission to ECHA with reference. This approach to alternatives is also against wider EU policies on climate change, decarbonization and sustainable energy. It will also add, as we state above 1-3.4 Billion €/yr for ~44% of the overall EU air conditioning and heat pumps (AC/HVAC) sector.

Considering all available information, Honeywell submits that the following HFC/HFO fluorinated refrigerants should be excluded from the scope of the Proposal: HFC-125, HFC-143a, HFO-1234ze(E), HCFO-1233zd(E), HFO-1336mzz(E), HFO-1336mzz(Z), HFC-245fa, HFC-365mfc, HFO-1234yf, HFC-134a, HFC-227ea, HFC-236fa, or their uses in commercial RHVAC/HVAC applications should be subject to time unlimited derogations in line with the provisions of Articles 68 and 69 REACH.

In line with previous practices this exclusion or derogation should also cover maintenance or repair, refitting and reselling activities involving second hand RHVAC systems already placed on the market or installed.

General Comments: Honeywell is a global manufacturer and importer of various fluorinated gases to the European Union (EU), including hydrofluorocarbons (HFC) and hydrofluoroolefins (HFO). In particular, Honeywell plans to supply EU pharmaceutical companies with the gas HFO-1234ze(E) for uses as an excipient in medicinal products, including among other the use as propellant agents in Pressurised Medical Dose Inhalers (pMDIs).

However, contrary to what the Dossier Submitters claim, there is a range of PFAS substances, including various fluorinated HFC/HFO gases that are low-hazard, have low-Global Warming Potential (GWP), not (v-)persistent (not P/vP) and do not degrade to vP substances in any meaningful amounts. For instance, the REACH registration dossier and Chemical Safety Report (CSR) for the fluorinated gas HFO-1234ze(E) contain conclusive scientific evidence demonstrating that it is not persistent and does not exhibit risks similar to PBT/vPvB substances under Article XIII REACH.

According to the most recent scientific data, upon release HFO-1234ze(E) ultimately degrades in the atmosphere to carbon dioxide (CO2), Hydrogen fluoride (HF) and trifluoroacetic acid (TFA). The TFA is a PFAS arrowhead substance: this happens in approximately 19 days and leads to an insignificant/negligible amount of TFA. The respective TFA amounts results in de minimis increases in overall TFA environmental concentrations by comparison with pre-existing TFA levels.

In this respect, highly qualified independent assessments ongoing for several years already by UNEP panels repeatedly conclude that “The current low concentration of trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) produced by the degradation of several hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) and hydrofluoroolefins (HFOs), is currently judged not to pose a risk to human health or to the environment.” and that “available evidence indicates that this breakdown product [TFA] is of minimal risk to human health”. The most recent EEAP 2022 Assessment Report also concludes that “based on projected future use of these precursors of TFA [incl. HFC/HFO], no harm is anticipated” and that TFA “is unlikely to cause adverse effects out to 2100”.

Q&A 10 of Addendum to the EEAP Assessment Report states that “Now and in the distant future, predicted TFA concentrations in surface waters and terminal basins are thousands of times less than thresholds of concern for human or environmental health.”

Detailed analysis on degradation of HFC/HFO and relevant hazard, exposure and risks assessments of TFA is provided in the Honeywell submission reference no: 76bb3d12-2101-4390-82cf-3498b47e8015.

In addition, there is solid scientific experimental and modelling body evidence demonstrating that atmospheric decomposition of HFO-1234ze(E) does not result in formation high-GWP substances like HFC-23 (CF3H).

Therefore, the Dossier Submitters erroneously consider (in section 1.1.6 of the Proposal) HFO-1234ze(E) together with other PFAS (i.e., as a group) for the hazard, exposure and risks characterisation purposes. They also erred when concluding that HFO-1234ze(E) is among “non-threshold substances” with the overall concerns “very similar to those of the PBT/vPvB substances” and using its emissions “as a proxy for risk”.

Moreover, HFO-1234ze(E) as a propellant in pMDIs is subject to rigorous risk management measures (RMMs) and assessments under the current EU legislation on medicinal products and medical devices, including Medical Devices Regulation (MDR), rules and procedures of European Medicines Agency (EMA) as well as relevant provisions of the EU medicines and veterinary laws. Therefore, all respective risks are already adequately controlled and the proposed REACH restriction (i.e. ban) is disproportionate and would result in “double regulation”.  Hence, ECHA should consult, exchange information and coordinate with EMA respective activities to ensure coherence in scientific opinions/evaluations to avoid potential contradictions.  The EMA has approved the running of larger-scale human, clinical trials with pMDIs using HFO-1234ze(E). At present both HFO-1234ze(E) and HFC-152a are at clinical trial stage, preparing for possible marketing authorisation with the EMA.

The fluorinated gas HFC-152a is suggested in the Proposal as the only available non-PFAS alternative in pMDIs. HFC-152a is classified as an extremely flammable gas (Cat. 1A) resulting in significant safety issues from both a manufacturing perspective and patient use. Moreover, HFC-152a has 1.6 years of atmospheric lifetime as well as GWP of 164 (i.e., much higher than 1.37 of HFO-1234ze(E). Generally, according to the Montreal Protocol, Kigali Amendment and EU F-Gas Regulation. Its use should be phased down from 2024 via progressively decreasing volumes of permitted quotas in the ongoing revision of the F-gases Regulations. Therefore, the widespread use/emissions of this gas, including in pMDIs, is contrary to wider-EU decarbonization and climate change policies.

This alternative propellant is a “regrettable substitute” in pMDIs applications, while HFO-1234ze(E) is not a regrettable substitute, but rather a “safe substitute”. In these circumstances, the introduction of the proposed REACH restriction (i.e., total ban in 1.5 years after the entry into force of the future restriction) for HFO-1234ze(E) uses in pMDIs applications:

 is not justified under REACH Regulation,
 is clearly disproportionate (see section 4 below) with any alleged risk from persistency of TFA
 will result in very high costs to society, including shortages and safety of vital medicines.

Honeywell submits that fluorinated gas HFO-1234ze(E) must be excluded from the scope of the Proposal. Alternatively, its uses in pMDIs applications should be subject to time-unlimited derogations, in line with the unlimited derogations already included into the Proposal and previous RAC/SEAC practices in similar circumstances.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Honeywell supplies EU based customers inter alia with fluorinated gas HFO-1234yf (or refrigerant R-1234yf, trademark Solstice® yf) widely used as a refrigerant in MAC, vehicle heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) and thermal management systems (TMS) in EV systems applications. This substance formally falls within the definition of PFAS in the Proposal. HFO-1234yf is a low toxic, non-bioaccumulative, very low persistent (atmospheric lifetime 5-15 days), mildly flammable gas with very low-GWP, no-ODP and with well-established DNEL/PNEC levels as well as no noticeable health or environmental hazards or PBT/vPvB equivalent concerns. Its only PFAS breakdown product is trifluoroacetic acid (TFA).

According to the TFA REACH registration dossier and Chemical Safety Report (CSR), this substance fulfils the criteria for persistency, but it is not classified as a PBT or vPvB substance under Annex XIII REACH and does not raise equivalent levels of concern under REACH. ECHA has already reviewed and evaluated the TFA dossier concluding there is no need for further regulatory action.

A substantial body of scientific data on health and environmental effects demonstrates limited (de minimis) effects of HFO-1234yf emissions and resulting TFA on humans and the environment. Comprehensive independent assessments of UNEP panels repeatedly concluded that “The current low concentration of trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) produced by the degradation of several hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) and hydrofluoroolefins (HFOs), is currently judged not to pose a risk to human health or to the environment.” and that “available evidence indicates that this breakdown product [TFA] is of minimal risk to human health”.

Moreover, the most recent EEAP 2022 Assessment Report also concluded that “based on projected future use of these precursors of TFA [incl. HFC/HFO], no harm is anticipated” and that TFA “is unlikely to cause adverse effects out to 2100”. The EEAP Assessment Report also confirmed that “Now and in the distant future, predicted TFA concentrations in surface waters and terminal basins are thousands of times less than thresholds of concern for human or environmental health.”

In addition, HFO-1234yf used in MAC systems is thoroughly controlled via containment requirements in the EU’s MAC and ELV Directive. Therefore, conclusions in the Proposal suggesting the existence of unacceptable risks from any HFO-1234yf emissions are erroneous.

The industry changes anticipated in Annex E of the Proposal are massive and complex. Carbon dioxide (CO2 or R-744) based MAC and TMS in EVs systems represent only a tiny portion of the overall MAC/TMS systems used in serial vehicles production due to control, safety, reliability and cost related issues.

Annex E also stipulates that highly flammable refrigerants like R-152a (1,1-difluoroethane, HFC -152a) (or R-290, propane) “have been shown to be efficient and safe with secondary loop refrigerant systems”. There is no evidence that hydrocarbon based secondary loop systems are efficient or appropriate in any automotive application, particularly due to very strong safety concerns.

Moreover, the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol obliges developed countries to reduce HFC consumption (including HFC-152a) by 85% vs their baseline by 2036. Accordingly, the MAC Directive already prohibits uses of F-gases with GWP 100 more than 150 in automotive MAC/HVAC applications. However, according to the most recent assessment of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR6 of 2021), HFC-152a has atmospheric lifetime of 1.6 years (vs HFO-1234yf atmospheric lifetime of 5-15 days) and GWP 100 figure of 164, exceeding the MAC Directive 150 limit. This questions the rationality for further development of this refrigerant in all RHVAC systems.

According to numerous research papers, CO2 refrigerant systems are significantly less efficient than fluorinated refrigerants in warm to hotter weather. According to a recent 2023 study published in the International Journal of Refrigeration: “The main feature of using CO2 as the refrigerant is that the refrigeration system works as a transcritical cycle at high ambient temperature due to the low critical temperature. Additionally, the high operating pressure of the CO2 system and large pressure drop in the isenthalpic throttling process leads to significant irreversibility loss and low performance.” These efficiency losses lead to increasing energy needs and thus to higher fuel and electricity consumption of a vehicle.

It is stated on pages 356 and 369 of Annex E of the Proposal that “A barrier to introduction of CO2 is its lower efficiency at medium to high temperatures”. This evidence is mentioned as relevant for the shipping of refrigerated containers but is not acknowledged in the Proposal for MAC applications. The MAC related section of the Proposal simply suggests that CO2 is more efficient than existing refrigerants. This approach is drastically contradicted by the study from Technical Institute of Physics & Chemistry of Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) that compared several refrigerants in automotive applications. The study reviewed refrigerant performance under a variety of ambient conditions including heat pump (heating) and AC (cooling) points. Applying typical weather distribution patterns it is evident that the inefficiency of CO2 and hydrocarbon based secondary loop systems in warmer weather is an approximately 18 to 22 percent yearly power increase required for these systems over HFO-1234yf.

Due to the additional power needed to run CO2 systems in EVs (more electricity generation) and additional fuel burned to run secondary loop - hydrocarbon systems in internal combustion engines (ICE), the above losses in efficiency, would result in additional annual GHG emissions of up to ten million tons of CO2 in Europe. Therefore, HFO-1234yf substitution by other refrigerants in MAC/TMS systems contradicts wider EU decarbonization goals and is disproportionate to alleged risks from HFO-1234yf and persistency of TFA.

HVAC and TMS systems are readily available for use in EVs. This conclusion incorrectly assumes that CO2 hardware can be quickly scaled and that millions of systems could be supplied quickly based on a limited number of CO2 systems in the field. World scale CO2 component production will take many more years than Annex E contemplates. The conversion from HFC-134a to HFO-1234yf refrigerant took more than 10 years. Automotive manufacturers are in the beginning of the transition to EVs and the refrigerant transition periods proposed are very short. Failures or malfunctions may mean forcing a vehicle to the side of the road to avoid fires caused by battery thermal runaway.

Similar to CO2, secondary loop systems using flammable gases like R-152a (or propane) have been studied and no light duty commercial vehicles have ever been mass produced in this configuration. R-152a or propane will increase the fire risk for consumers (over current refrigerants) based on ignition energy, increased combustion energy, flame propagation and wider flammable concentrations. Suggesting such a short implementation timing for an unproven system seems reckless.

Finally, robust end-of-life reclamation of refrigerants and documentation could help with tracking refrigerant supplies and return more refrigerant to the field reducing the need for new refrigerant entering the service market. All the above are responsible means to reduce emissions. Respective Risk Management Measures (RMMs) are already provided in the MAC Directive and ELV Directive (including, on containment, recovery, reclamation and reuse of refrigerants) and could be enhanced at any time.

The introduction of a REACH restriction on HFO-1234yf as suggested in the Proposal, will violate requirements of the REACH Regulation, EU general legal principles and wider EU policies, resulting in very high, unjustified costs on society. Honeywell submits that fluorinated gas HFO-1234yf used as a refrigerant in MAC systems of all types as well as in all EV applications should be excluded from the scope of the PFAS REACH restriction.

Alternatively, considering that the EU plans to ban sales of new vehicles with combustion engines from 2035 and that the estimated service life of a vehicle is around 20 years, a transition period for the full application of the restriction for all vehicles should be at least extended to 2055. In line with previous practices, this time-limited derogation should also cover maintenance and repair activities involving second-hand vehicles placed on the market before this date. This derogation could be also conditional to allow the industry to work towards development of alternatives with a transitional review by ECHA and the European Commission by the end of 2035.

General Comments: Hueck Folien GmbH specializes, among other things, in the coating and printing of transparent roofs, facades and greenhouses made of ethylene tetrafluoroethylene (ETFE), a fluoropolymer. This type of roof is installed all over the world in a wide variety of climatic and environmental conditions. It must withstand extreme temperatures from -50 to 50°C, various chemicals and high UV radiation. Only materials that are mechanically, visually, chemically and fire resistant are suitable for long-term applications. Fluoropolymers such as ethylene tetrafluoroethylene meet all these requirements. No other polymer simultaneously offers optical transmittance greater than 90%, mechanical strength greater than 40 N/mm^2, fire performance certification to European standard EN 13501-1, no outgassing to AGBB, and no leaching. It does not require toxic or unknown additives for its stability. ETFE does not age, neither at high temperatures nor under UV irradiation. Mechanical stress in stormy weather does not affect any of these properties over time, making ETFE the ideal material for architectural applications.

Hueck Folien GmbH collects all ETFE waste generated during the coating process and returns it to its suppliers, where it is recycled. Our customers are also committed to establishing a closed material cycle. Our customers recycle not only cutting residues, but also materials from refurbished or dismantled projects. Because of all these reasons, Hueck Folien GmbH is calling for a timely, indefinite exemption of fluoropolymer films for architectural purposes from the PFAS ban.

Although at first glance there seem to be polymers with similar properties to ETFE, currently no equivalent substitute for ETFE can be found. In particular, polyolefins such as polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP), mentioned in earlier considerations, are not stable long-term under UV exposure, even when additives against aging by UV light are used. Thus, banning fluoropolymer films would have clear negative environmental impacts due to the reasons mentioned above, as no material with comparable properties is currently available.

ETFE films enable lightweight transparent roofing solutions. Glass and ETFE films can achieve a low thermal transmittance (U-value) close to 1 W/m2K. However, glass has a much higher weight per unit area of about 20 kg/m2. Glass allows only smaller window sizes, while ETFE allows spans of about 4 meters in width and over 100 meters in length. The high weight of glass also requires a more robust primary structure, resulting in significantly higher consumption of steel and concrete, compared to the primary structure of an ETFE envelope. As a result, an ETFE roof has a significantly better carbon footprint compared to glass.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: our application requires sector ETFE film/foil for greenhouses

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: see document "2021_MA_CE_Sonmez_Gulhan_S1_June_reducedresolution". ETFE films are good recyclable. PIR and PCR ETFE wastes are currently already recycled in the extrusion process during the production of ETFE films.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Huntsman is a producer of formulations for expanded foam sprayed on site for building insulation. We are using blowing agents that fall under this restriction proposal, namely HFO/HCFOs.
As a result of a restriction, we will need to choose a lower thermal performing or an unsafe alternative.
Huntsman is not using any other substances that are covered in the PFAS restriction proposal.

Huntsman is also producing polyol blends and components used by the overall thermal insulation sector. While most of our customers are using pentane to achieve high performing thermal performance, several of our SMEs customers are still relying on the use of HFO to achieve competitive thermal performance. For them, achieving a safe environment for using a flammable substance such as pentane, is economically extremely challenging and make them uncompetitive towards larger players.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: - Foam blowing agents in expanded foam sprayed on site for building insulation - Applications of fluorinated gases (F-Gases) as Foam-Blowing Agents. PU Europe already commented on the scope of the Restriction proposal (see is c847c31e-8df9-44a2-8798-218bf9d9ac2a). We share this opinion and see no justification for a ban of F-Gases with low GWP notably HFO-1336mzz-Z, HCFO-1233zd-E & HFO-1234ze-E.   For closed cell spray foam which has high thermal performance, and which is applied on the building site, the option to move to pentane blown foam is not possible for safety reasons.  Concerning the proposed derogation for spray foam blowing agents, under the application of F-Gas section, we call for a time unlimited derogation with a review clause. Since there are currently no physical blowing agent alternatives to HFOs, the industry will need more time to both develop them and implement in spray foam. Once alternatives will be made available, the foam industry will have to revise the EU harmonized product standards (spray foam products are covered by EN 14315 & EN 14318) to include these new blowing agents and finally undergo the official certification process.  Last but not least, a ban on the use of low GWP F-Gases in spray foam, which are particularly suitable for building renovation applications, would affect the success of the EU Renovation Wave program and affect achieving the Fit for 55 targets to reduce energy consumption of the existing building stock (80% of the buildings that will be standing in 2050 have already been built)  For a number of other insulation applications (e.g. hot water storage tanks or prefabricated building elements), a ban would result in users of F Gas formulation, typically SMEs to get out of business due to associated costs and administrative hurdle to move to a pentane compliant work environment.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The spray foam is technically recyclable, and we are aiming to capture most of the HFO/HCFO emissions during recycling. The goal is to use similar infrastructure as in the refrigeration sector that extracts the blowing agent for destruction and to recover the PU foam and find recycling outlets. The waste disposal code for construction waste is 170604.  According to the EU F-Gas Regulation and respective Guidance, operators of products and equipment that contain F-Gases should arrange for the recovery of gases “to the extent that it is technically feasible and does not entail disproportionate cost”. (see Honeywell reference a4dd1eeb-c3ee-414c-bdc5-2e87a0748191 page 34 bottom and 35 top)   Please look at the PU Europe excel spreadsheet called 2023_08_06 SPF emissions profile. we estimate that a maximum of 10% of the blowing agent (F Gas) is lost during the manufacturing and spraying stage. During the very long use phase (which lasts more than 50 years in buildings), the emissions to air would range from 1% up to 31%. An important application is under concrete floor slabs and therefore emission is to be expected very low during the use phase. As for the emissions to air during the decommissioning stage, as per PU Europe’s internal calculations, that would not amount to more than 1.5% of the remaining gas trapped in the foam. It is therefore assumed that the vast majority of the F Gas (60-87%) will need to be recovered in many decades from now. As for waste management options, according to the Final report "Plastic waste from B&C in EU 2018", 65% of the waste is deemed to go to incineration plants.  As Europe moves towards a circular economy, national voluntary or mandatory schemes for the recovery, sorting and recycling of construction and demolition waste are being put in place. Huntsman has already recycled post-industrial rigid foam insulation waste streams and has approved products on the market and is working on implementing recycling solutions within a circular economy scheme to treat EOL spray foam.  For the other applications such as hot water storage tanks or prefabricated building elements, solutions for collection and treatment would need to be considered but could follow in principle also similar routes as the end-of-life treatment of refrigerators & freezers that used to contain CFCs/HCFCs/HFCs.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Several studies have been issued over the past decades showing the effectiveness of municipal waste incinerators to treat CFCs/HCFCs. This technology has also been approved by the Montreal Protocol to destroy these ozone depleting substances contained in a foam matrix.   For HFO/HCFO, that are replacing CFCs/HCFCs, the latest information (RIVM report 2021-0143) confirm that above 850°C no PFAS/TFA is formed.  We would also like to refer to the submission from Honeywell (reference a4dd1eeb-c3ee-414c-bdc5-2e87a0748191 p 35: Safe incineration is an existing option) which provides additional evidence on the safe and effective incineration (destruction) of insulation materials containing fluorocarbon foam blowing agents.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Today, the experience gathered with the extraction of blowing agent gases contained in the insulation foam in refrigerators/freezers (WEEE obligation) shows that this insulation foam can be post-treated in the so-called matrix degassing to ensure a CFC-residual content of 0.2 %. We are not aware of techniques to achieve lower levels.  Setting a limit at 25 ppb (2.5 10-6 %) also on the PU foam wastes used as secondary resource that would contain residual HFOs would prevent their recycling into new products and will force energy recovery. See kuehlgeraete_engl_14072015.pdf (urt-recycling.com)

5. Proposed derogations: See table in the confidential attachment for the specific numbers on tonnage per year and emissions.  Emissions: Production 10% + use 1 or 31% + dismantling 1.5% + EOL scheme (grinding with capturing 0.2% or without capturing 1.5%, incinerators 0%)

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Substitution potential: i) Non-flammable, high performance F-gases used as blowing agents such as HFO/HCFOs are indispensable due to their: (1) Safety in use; (2) Best in class insulation values, especially in applications where space is limited; and (3) Unique mechanical properties, where specific properties are required that only foams blown using HFOs can provide. This is recognized by UNEP as well. In the PU category for the spray foam application, there is no valuable alternative to HFO for closed cell spray foam. Flammable blowing agents are not allowed, and CO2 or water blown spray foam result in worse mechanical properties. Finally, the HFO/HCFOs are best in class to achieve energy efficiency. See table in reference: Honeywell submission a4dd1eeb-c3ee-414c-bdc5-2e87a0748191 page 11.   Further info on safety: For safety reasons, Spray Polyurethane Foam requires a non-flammable blowing agent due to its onsite application. This does not allow for traditional engineering controls used in manufacturing facilities to be consistently available. One specific point of importance is the application equipment. Spray foam can be applied through high pressure or low-pressure devices. The largest volume of product is applied through high pressure devices. There are two types of high-pressure spray foam, closed cell and open cell. Closed cell foams typically use HFOs as the blowing agent as the combination provides the best insulation value (lambda) possible for this application. Further info on mechanical properties: The closed cell spray foam under concrete floor requires HFO to achieve the mechanical performance specification, which water/CO2 blown foam cannot meet.  This application is expected to disappear if HFO cannot be used anymore. Because this application involves pouring concrete over the foam, minimizing lateral movement over time (compressive creep) is an important requirement. In France, specification NF DTU 52.10 specifies the maximum amount of compressive creep that is allowed. A list of products that have been tested and approved by the certifying body, CTSB, is available online (ATec or DTA : in-situ polyurethane - Find - CSTB Evaluation). Analysis of the listings for each of these products confirms that only foams that utilize HFC or HFO blowing agents are approved. There are no foams blown with CO2 (generated from the reaction of isocyanate and water) that have passed this compressive creep test. This illustrates one of the applications where the use of HFOs is critical with no alternatives available. See also Honeywell submission reference a4dd1eeb-c3ee-414c-bdc5-2e87a0748191 page 31. ii) There are currently no alternative blowing agent materials available for closed cell spray foam. Research & development, adaptation of the product standard and certification will take easily 12 years or more.  Application of F Gas/Foam blowing agents: The spray foam insulation market is estimated to stand at around 100,000 tons of finished products, meaning that the HFO/HCFOs used in the industry would be around 10,000 tons since 2023 (and the transition to HFCs). Using the assumptions presented earlier under section 2, a maximum of 1,000 Tons of blowing agent would be emitted in the air during the manufacturing stage (with potential for best practices to improve that figure). The vast majority of the remaining of those gas would be trapped in the foam for decades. Concerning the Socio-economic impact due to lack of viable alternatives, please find attached a calculation on the missed energy savings that would result from banning HFO/HCFO on sprayed/poured PU foam.  In the section confidential we share socio-economic impact for Huntsman and its customers:  In France, for under concrete slab no alternatives for this market exist in case of HFO exit. Most of the companies will have to close the business and lay off all people.

8. Other identified uses: For a number of applications (like hot water tank or prefabricated building), a ban would probably result in users of HFOs/HCFOs formulations to get out of business due to associated costs and administrative hurdle (difficulty to obtain permit to store and use flammable products) to move to a pentane compliant safe work environment.  To achieve high thermal performance, the only known physical blowing agent alternative to f-gas is pentane, which is flammable, and needs specific explosion proof equipment and permit to use.  In the section confidential we share socio-economic impact

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: We would like to pinpoint to the resources of the EFCTC on the matter, notably the one dated September 2021, https://www.fluorocarbons.org/news/published-evidence-supports-very-low-yields-of-tfa-from-most-hfos-and-hcfos/ . according to scientific studies, HFO/HCFO used in the insulation foam sector would not degrade in any meaningful amount as TFA. There is additional info in the confidential attachment.

General Comments: Hydrogen is forecasted to play a critical role in the green transition and is essential for the European Green Deal. Even with extensive deployment of renewable energy sources, such as photovoltaic (PV) and wind power, several industries (e.g., steel, cement and ammonia production, petrol refining, and shipping) will be difficult to decarbonize as they are challenging to electrify directly.

"Rethink Energy" predicts the green hydrogen market to reach a $850 billion valuation in 2050, driven by the installation of over 5 TW of electrolysis capacity. Green hydrogen is projected to be the leading hydrogen production method by 2039.

Water electrolyzers are typically categorized into three main technologies: alkaline water electrolysis (AWE), proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE), and solid oxide electrolysis cells (SOEC).

AWE relies on the conduction of hydroxide anions through the liquid electrolyte potassium hydroxide (KOH) between two electrodes separated by a permeable diaphragm, which avoids short-circuiting and mixing of the hydrogen and oxygen produced. The temperature is mainly limited by the structural stability of the diaphragm, and therefore AWE is generally perceived as a low-temperature electrolysis technology. Typical operation parameters for commercially available AWEs are listed in Table 1.

In the context of AWE, operation at higher temperatures (e.g., 120 °C and higher) and improvements in the stability and conductivity of the diaphragm separators will lead to major efficiency increases, further boosting the affordability of green hydrogen.

Previous projects and extensive material testing have shown that polypropylene tanks and piping systems are suited for temperatures well below 90°C and KOH with a concentration of ~ 25%.

However, above those temperatures, and especially for temperatures above 100°C Fluoropolymers like ECTFE, FEP and PFA are clearly superior to other polymers like PP or PE. Fluoropolymers like FEP ensure a safe and reliable operation for a much longer period of time, which cannot be reached if these parts would be manufactured from metal.

In our view, the Annex XV restriction report does not cover relevant and essential uses of fluoropolymers in the critical sector “energy industry”: ECTFE, FEP and PFA pipelines and storage tanks for KOH electrolyte in alkaline electrolysis of hydrogen.

One also must consider that in the electrolyser unit itself, fluoropolymers are important. On the one hand they are essential for the membrane and on the other hand depending on the operating conditions of the unit, they are used for various parts that are in contact with KOH. Depending on the operating conditions PP can be used, but in order to increase the efficiency fluoropolymers are needed.

Various chemical resistance lists (e.g. DVS Codes 2205-1, DIBt Media list, ISO TR 10358) confirm the superior chemical resistance of fluoropolymers against many chemicals. While other materials (e.g. PE, PP, rubber, …) can only handle mild chemicals and lower concentrations. For many applications only the combined properties as exhibited by fluoropolymers enable feasible and economic solutions. Also, metals do not show such a universal chemical resistance, at least not in cost effective way: • Outstanding chemical resistance to a broad range of chemicals from -200 °C up to 260 °C (e.g. KOH, H2SO4, NaOH, HNO3, HF, HCl, NaOCl, …) • Easy installation inside of tanks and leak tight welding lead to high safety and long life-times. • Fluoropolymer linings offers simple repair options since the sheet can be welded again in case repair or system changes are necessary. • Toughness of the fluoropolymer ensure high safety, even in the case of accidents. • Flame resistance (UL94 classification V0)  c. Missing uses: 1) Gasket (PCTFE sealant) a)  Fluoropolymer (PCTFE) is used as a sealing material for cryogenic bulbs used in LNG transportation tanks and LNG bases. b) Fluoropolymer (PCTFE) are the only materials that can be used as sealants for resins at low temperatures (-100°C to-196°C). 　In the cryogenic range, resin, rubber and metal become hard and lose their elasticity. However, fluoropolymer (PCTFE) has a function as a sealing material because it retains elasticity. 　In addition, it has shape stability against high compression, so it does not distort due to deformation, and it is also excellent in gas permeability, making it essential as a member.   c)  When the fluoropolymer (PCTFE) cannot be used, there is a fear that a trouble in supplying LNG may occur. d)  As a substitute member for fluoropolymer (PCTFE), a metallic sealing material is considered, but it is difficult to use it at a bulb site where there is no elasticity and repeated opening and closing is performed. PCTFE is rigid and elastic under low-temperature and high-compression conditions. It is dimensionally stable.   e) Dimensional stability and high compressibility may be substituted for other resinous PEEK, PPS, but dimensional stability after machining is not good. Due to their recalcitrant (durable) characteristics, they may be technically needed and are difficult to replace.  f) At present, there is no technologically economically substitutable prospect. g) The transportation of LNG in EU area is hindered.   From the above, PFAS substitute materials should be exempted because they are highly likely not to be substituted and are not substituted.  2) Parts of ECM (FEP, PTFE ) a) Fluoropolymers (FEP, PTFE) are used as components in electret condenser microphones.  b) Fluoropolymer (FEP, PTFE) has permanent charging properties and is the only material that can be used as a core component in electret capacitor microphones. c)  As fluoropolymer (FEP, PTFE) can no longer be used, it is necessary to review the designs of microphones. Directional microphones have a car or IC record. In addition, the small microphones used in measuring noise accounts, conferences and press conferences, and classic concerts are no longer available. d)  Some electret condenser microphones are replaced by semiconductor-processed MEMS microphones, but when directivity is required, more than one microphone is required. Also, because MEMS microphones are specialized for structures that automatically solder together for mass-production, small MEMS microphones are not practical for applications with structures that require lead routing.   e) Resins such as PP(polypropylene) can be charged, but their permanent charge is lost at high temperatures, so the use temperature range is limited (60°C or less). In addition, these resins are indispensable as materials that can maintain their charging property against moisture.   It has been used for over 50 years and it is not easy to prepare substitutes. f)  Although the amount used is small, it is used as a key part member, and at present, there is no prospect that it can be technically and economically substituted. g) We believe that there is an impact on applications that use sound components in EU regions.   From the above, PFAS substitute materials should be exempted because they are highly likely not to be substituted and are not substituted.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: 1) Semiconductor manufacturing process a) Fluoropolymers (PTFE, PFA, FEP, PCTFE) and fluoroelastomers (FFKM, FKM) are indispensable in the manufacturing of semiconductors. Specifically, they are used in equipment for chemical cleaning processes and film formation processes (Diffusion, Etcher, CVD), as well as in tanks and plumbing components in plants that supply chemicals in semiconductor plants. b) Fluoropolymers (PTFE, PFA, FEP, PCTFE) are used in chemical cleaning processes, chemical tanks for supplying chemicals at plants, and equipment that uses piping components and chemicals. It is used in fields requiring chemical resistance such as sulfuric acid and hydrofluoric acid, and is an indispensable material to satisfy functions at the same time from the viewpoint of heat resistance (use temperature (normal temperature to 160 ° C)) and cleanliness. 　Fluoroelastomers (FFKM,FKM) is used as the only material to satisfy gas-resistance (NF3, 02, etc.), heat-resistance (ambient temperature to 300℃), and cleanliness by sealing members of film-forming-process (Diffusion, Etcher, CVD) equipment. c) It is an indispensable material in the process of manufacturing semiconductor devices. When fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers cannot be used, it is presumed that there is an impact on the manufacturer's Infineon to make semiconducting devices.   d) As a substitute member for fluoropolymers, PE(polyethylene) is considered from the viewpoint of chemical resistance, but cannot be used in a process in which the use temperature (normal temperature to 160 ° C.) is increased because deformation of the material occurs. Although some resins such as PEEK(polyether ether ketone) and PI(polyimide) are heat-resistant, they are inferior in chemical resistance, so they can be used only in some parts.   　As an alternative member to the fluoroelastomers, a member such as a metal sealing material or silicon may be considered. It is difficult to use metal because it has heat resistance but no elasticity to maintain airtightness. In addition, since it is necessary to maintain sealability under an atmosphere of an active gas, a sealing material of a recalcitrant fluoroelastomers is indispensable. e) Within the 60 years of the semiconductor industry, it is not considered that a substitute can be made in 12 years because it is a material used and a substitute has not appeared so far. Due to their recalcitrant (durable) characteristics, they may be technically needed and are difficult to replace.  f) At present, there is no prospect of being technically and economically viable for substitution. g) Because semiconductor devices can no longer be made, they affect not only those who are engaged in the direct semiconductor industry, but also the industry that uses the devices. The semiconducting industry is centered in Asia and the United States, not in EU.   Based on the above, PFAS substitute materials should be exempted from the present limitation proposals because they are likely not to be substituted and are not substituted.

General Comments: I am an assistant professor at University of Southern Denmark, and in the past 10 years I have studied PFAS health effects in humans with a particular focus on child and maternal health. I am writing to express my support for the proposed EU PFAS restrictions.
PFAS are highly persistent chemicals accumulating in our bodies. Due to the global pollution, we now all have PFAS in our bodies, and these chemicals are transferred from mother to child through the placenta during pregnancy and through breastfeeding [1-5] putting infants at high exposure [6, 7]. In addition, infants are particular sensitive to the immunotoxic effects of PFAS [8-10], and we therefore have to do everything in our power to protect infants and their mothers from PFAS.
I therefore support stopping all unessential uses of PFAS as soon as possible. While time-limited derogations may be necessary for certain PFAS applications, it is important to motivate the development of safer alternatives so that exposure to all PFAS is minimized.

Best regards,
Amalie Timmermann

The PFAS chemicals don't break down easily over time and are able to dissolve in water. Since PFAS cannot be removed from the body, we as consumers must avoid PFAS containing products which are very common in many, many food stuffs. A ban on PFAS would reduce quantities of PFAS in the environment over the long term. It would also make products and processes safer for humans. If the European Commission adopts the proposal, companies will be forced to find alternatives for PFAS in applications in which these substances are used. A total ban will force corporations and states to seek acceptable alternatives to PFAS.

General Comments: I am writing to express my deep concern regarding the continued use and presence of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in our environment, products, and everyday life. As an individual deeply committed to environmental and public health, I strongly urge the European Union to take immediate and decisive action to phase out PFAS chemicals across all industries and applications.

PFAS chemicals, known for their persistent nature and widespread contamination, pose significant risks to human health, wildlife, and the environment. These chemicals have been linked to a wide range of adverse health effects, including developmental delays, immune system disorders, liver damage, hormone disruption, and an increased risk of certain cancers. Moreover, PFAS have shown resistance to degradation, accumulating in the environment and bioaccumulating in organisms, thus creating a long-lasting and far-reaching threat.

While the European Union has taken commendable steps in recognizing the hazards posed by PFAS chemicals and implementing certain restrictions, it is imperative to address the urgency of this issue with a comprehensive and expeditious approach. The current measures fall short of adequately protecting human health and the environment, and further action is needed to safeguard future generations.

I propose the following actions to be taken by the European Union:

Immediate phase-out: Implement a ban on the production, use, and importation of all PFAS chemicals, including legacy PFAS and newer replacement compounds, with an accelerated timeline for elimination.

Alternative assessment: Encourage and support research and development for safer alternatives to PFAS chemicals, focusing on non-toxic and environmentally friendly solutions across various sectors, including firefighting foams, textiles, food packaging, and industrial applications.

Strict regulation: Strengthen and harmonize regulations governing PFAS chemicals, ensuring that limits for permissible levels in air, water, soil, and consumer products are set at the lowest feasible levels based on the latest scientific evidence.

Public awareness and education: Launch widespread educational campaigns to inform the public about the potential risks associated with PFAS chemicals, enabling consumers to make informed choices and encouraging behavioral changes that minimize exposure.

Collaboration and international cooperation: Facilitate collaboration among EU member states, scientific institutions, and international bodies to share knowledge, resources, and best practices for addressing the PFAS crisis collectively.

By taking swift and decisive action, the European Union has the opportunity to lead the global effort in eliminating PFAS chemicals and protecting the health and well-being of its citizens and the environment. I implore you to prioritize the urgent phase-out of PFAS and to enact stringent regulations that ensure a toxic-free future.

Thank you for your attention to this critical matter. I trust that you will consider the gravity of the situation and take immediate action to address the risks associated with PFAS chemicals. Together, we can build a safer and healthier world for present and future generations.

Firstly, it would contribute to a healthier environment. PFAS are known as 'forever chemicals' because they do not break down naturally and can accumulate in the environment. By phasing out these substances, we would be reducing their prevalence in the environment, which could lead to healthier ecosystems.

Secondly, halting the use of PFAS would lessen the exposure risk to humans and wildlife. These chemicals can infiltrate our food chain and water sources, posing potential harm to human health and wildlife. Some PFAS have been associated with adverse health effects in humans, including increased cholesterol levels, effects on the immune system, and potential increased risk of certain cancers.

Furthermore, phasing out PFAS can stimulate innovation and development of safer alternatives. A shift away from these substances would encourage the development of new, safer products and technologies. Although this might initially lead to changes in our products, such as a less waterproof raincoat or a slightly larger mobile phone, over time, innovation could lead to comparable or even superior alternatives that do not rely on harmful substances.

So, while there might be temporary inconveniences, the long-term benefits for human health, wildlife, and the environment outweigh these short-term trade-offs. It's a worthwhile transition that would usher in a more sustainable and healthier future.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period
Combined Comments: General Comments: I have no general comments, besides what is written below.

General Comments: I have no general comments, only answers for Specific Information Requests

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Fluoropolymers and fluororubbers are contained in many plant components in the plants we operate for energy generation and disposal (energy and waste management). PFASs are contained in particular in mechanical seals, pipe and equipment seals, and stuffing box packings. They are thus used in a wide range of equipment and machinery such as valves, pumps, agitators, pipes and containers. PFASs are also used as lubricants and components of corrosion protection systems or for internal coatings. Furthermore, fluoropolymers are also used in refrigerants in the systems we operate for building air conditioning and process cooling.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: We ensure that in normal operation PFAS is not released into the environment from the disposal and energy supply facilities we operate. Waste and waste water are of course disposed of in accordance with the relevant regulations. At the end of their service life, the plants are disposed of in accordance with the state of the art and recycled as far as possible. This also applies to the refrigerants used. Waste containing PFAS, such as sealed gaskets or cables that need to be replaced, is also recycled or disposed of properly. As a rule, this waste can be safely disposed of in our own incineration plants, which are operated according to the state of the art. Of course, the waste of all companies located in Industriepark Höchst can also be disposed of there.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: A recent study involving, among others, the Institute for Technical Chemistry (ITC) at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) and Pro-K confirms that fluoropolymers do not produce measurable PFAS emissions at the end of their life when incinerated in representative European incinerators (as our own residual waste plant) and under representative conditions and therefore do not pose a risk to human health and the environment. This demonstrates that no relevant emissions are produced in the end-of-life phase when incinerated properly. Study The study "Pilot-Scale Fluoropolymer Incineration Study: Thermal Treatment of a Mixture of Fluoropolymers under Representative European Municipal Waste Combustor Conditions" is attached under "SECTION IV. Non-confidential attachment".

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Recycling plants are already in operation for the recycling of PFAS.  Our company is aware of a recycling plant operated by the company Dyneon in Gendorf, which was developed by the research institute InVerTec (University of Bayreuth) together with the Dyneon as part of a project funded by the Deutsche Bundesstiftung Umwelt (German Federal Foundation for the Environment) to process PFAS by means of a depolymerisation process.  On 26 March 2015, Dyneon GmbH opened this world's first fluoropolymer upcycling plant together with the cooperation partners Deutsche Bundesstiftung Umwelt, the University of Bayreuth and the Research Institute for Innovative Process Engineering (Invertec) in Burgkirchen. The plant is the world's first fluoropolymer upcycling plant that uses a chemical recycling process to turn old products into new ones without compromising on quality. The plant can process up to 500 t of fluoropolymer waste annually. This plant thus makes a relevant contribution to the realisation of a circular economy for fluoropolymers. (https://www.invertec-ev.de/projekte/umwelt-ressourcen-schonung/ptfe-recycling/).  The process used in the plant enables significant CO2 savings in fluoropolymer production and is the first example of a true circular economy for fluoropolymers. The process was developed with funding from the BDU, the German Federal Environmental Foundation, and the German Federal Ministry for the Environment, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety.  In the meantime, Dyneon plans to phase out the production of PFAS and thus also decommission this plant. This means for the Chemical Park Gendorf that with the shutdown of this plant and all subsequent productions, about 1000 jobs will be lost. (https://www.chemietechnik.de/markt/dyneon-bleibt-die-pfas-produktion-in-gendorf-doch-erhalten-594.html)  Finally, on the subject of recycling, we would like to refer to the article "Strategies for Closing the Material Cycles in the Recycling of Fluoropolymers" from "Wiley Online Library": https://doi.org/10.1002/cite.202300039). See also Non-Confidential Attachment. The article shows different processes for recycling fluoropolymers and describes their possible application to close the fluorine cycle by mechanical, chemical or raw material recycling.

6. Missing uses: PFAS compounds are ingredients of various components or equipment in the plants we operate. Not all uses relevant to us are described in Annex XV of the Restriction Report. Therefore, we would like to present here the other relevant applications of components with PFAS in our view and finally the socio-economic effects of a ban.  For the following components or materials relevant to us, we do not recognise any classification in Annex XV: Seals mechanical bearings and sliding bushes linings of pipelines and vessels Hydraulic and other hoses Paints for surface treatment of metallic objects e.g. as corrosion coating Insulation of power cables Transformers These components require special properties such as high abrasion resistance, chemical resistance, sliding properties or temperature resistance and others. The requirements that the currently used components meet are a prerequisite for safe operation in many of the components we use, such as engines, generators, turbines, filters, pumps, compressors and apparatus such as valves or flaps, and are therefore indispensable.  We started testing alternative components that do not contain PFAS at an early stage. For some of the components used, alternative materials such as ceramics or UHMW-PE are already available. However, for many applications, such as seals containing PTFE, there is no comparable alternative available today or in the foreseeable future. Therefore, we cannot operate our plants without these components or materials in an estimated period of at least 10 years. Alternatives to PFAS are also considered in the following report: https://www.k-zeitung.de/pfas-diskussion-alternativen-zu-ptfe The planned ban on the use of PFAS would mean that we would no longer be able to operate our facilities for the supply and disposal of Industriepark Höchst. We are endeavouring to examine and use alternatives to PFAS, but do not see any substitute solutions to meet our requirements in the foreseeable future. Shutting down our plants would have far-reaching consequences for our customers in Industriepark Höchst, who produce vital medicines or chemicals, for example. In "SECTION IV. Non-confidential attachment" we have attached a table with the PFAS-containing components and alternatives we have considered and their properties relevant to us. In "SECTION V. Confidential attachment" we have attached a table with the socio-economic impacts considered.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: As new technoloiges will come, we should reconsider the usage of alternatives in about 15 Years. We estimate that it will take at least 15 years for modern hydrogen technology to do away with PFAS.

8. Other identified uses: In "SECTION IV. Non-confidential attachment" we have attached a table with the PFAS-containing components and alternatives we have considered and their properties relevant to us. In "SECTION V. Confidential attachment" we have attached a table with the socio-economic impacts considered. In addition to our consideration, we would like to refer to the following article : https://www.k-zeitung.de/pfas-diskussion-alternativen-zu-ptfe

Combined Comments:
General Comments: I represent a company in Denmark who uses perfluoropolymers for manufacture of electrochemical cells in contact with corrosive and oxidizing chemicals for manufacturing purposes and for water purification processes.  We utilize polytetrafluoroetane (PTFE), polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), and polytetrafluorethylene membrane (Nafion) polymers which do not currently have suitable alternatives.  If there are no exemptions for this subclass of polymers which are quite stable and do not degrade in the environment to hazardous perfluorinated substances, our business will be severely affected and in fact will not be able to exist.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Our sector is only concerned with perfluoropolymers such as PTFE. PVDF, and PTFE membranes (Nafion, used in fuel cells and electrochemical processes.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Perfluoropolymers have very limited perfluorinated emissions during manufacture, use phase and end-of-life phase.  Information is attached in regards to Nafion membrane materials.

6. Missing uses: There are cases where substitution is not technically or economically feasible.  The use of perfluorinated polymers in electrochemical cells as ion exchange membranes is required for a large number of electrochemical processes.  For the chlor-alkali industry, a membrane is required to be stable to both high concentration sodium hydroxide at high temperature, and chlorine which is a highly oxidizing chemical which can be used to make chlorine bleach and other products.  There are no non-perflorinated materials that would be stable to both chemicals.  There are many other oxidizing chemicals prepared using the perfluorinated membranes (permanganate, perchlorate, periodate, and others) which would not be able to be produced.  The absence of these membranes will end the electrochemical industry in Europe.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: One of the derogations was to give some time for alternatives to perfluorinated polymer membranes for use in fuel cells  to be developed.  It is possible that alternatives to some fuel cells may be found.  However, our request goes to these polymers for the more corrosive and oxidizing materials produced in similar cells.  There is currently no good alternatives for those applications and we therefore request a full exemption for these materials.

General Comments: I think the proposition is satisfying as it is and I hope the proposition will  be accepted and admitted without beeing "washy" or bland. There are several compelling reasons to stop the usage and production of PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances). Here are some:


Environmental Impact: PFAS are persistent in the environment and do not break down easily. They can accumulate in water, soil, and living organisms, leading to long-term contamination. This poses a significant threat to ecosystems, wildlife, and human health.


Human Health Concerns: PFAS have been linked to numerous adverse health effects. Studies have associated them with increased risk of cancer, liver damage, immune system disruption, hormonal imbalance, and developmental issues in children. Stopping PFAS use can help protect public health and prevent further exposure.


Drinking Water Contamination: PFAS contamination in drinking water sources is a widespread concern. These substances can leach into groundwater and contaminate water supplies, posing a risk to communities. Stopping PFAS production and use would help prevent further contamination and protect the quality of drinking water.


Consumer Product Safety: PFAS are commonly used in consumer products, including food packaging, textiles, and non-stick coatings. By stopping the use of PFAS, we can ensure the safety of consumer products and reduce the potential for human exposure to these harmful substances.


Alternative Solutions Available: There are safer alternatives to PFAS that can be used in various applications. Investing in research and development of alternative materials and technologies can provide effective substitutes without the environmental and health risks associated with PFAS.

5. Proposed derogations: Firstly, PFAS have been linked to numerous adverse health effects in humans. These chemicals are known to be persistent, meaning they do not break down easily and can accumulate in the environment and the human body over time. Studies have shown associations between PFAS exposure and increased risks of various health problems, including developmental delays in children, immune system dysfunction, hormonal disruptions, and an increased risk of certain cancers. Discontinuing the use of PFAS would help protect human health and reduce these associated risks.  Secondly, PFAS pose a significant threat to the environment. Due to their persistent nature, PFAS can contaminate water sources, soil, and wildlife habitats. These chemicals have been detected in drinking water supplies around the world, including both surface water and groundwater. The long-term presence of PFAS in the environment can lead to bioaccumulation in organisms, affecting the entire food chain and potentially harming ecosystems. By discontinuing PFAS use, we can prevent further contamination and reduce the environmental impact on delicate ecosystems.  Furthermore, the potential alternatives to PFAS, such as safer and more sustainable alternatives, exist. The development and adoption of these alternatives would not only eliminate the risks associated with PFAS but also encourage innovation in safer chemical manufacturing. Several parts of our product (most likely) contain PFAS. This is mainly released during the production of our raw materials at our suppliers (including the process for PVC, PTFE). The following parts of our product may contain (possibly) PFAS.
- Lubricants; (for the continued and proper functioning of our product and to guarantee the transition resistance of our product because of their low coefficient of friction) the PFAS on the SVHC list are for now not on the list as an component, with the restriction mostly all lubricants will be prohibited.
- Plastics; PTFE as an insulator with outstanding weather-resistant and dielectric properties;
- Seals; Rubbers and silicones
- Diodes; (semiconductors)
- Electronics components;
Quantity information is not available at this moment.

So far too little is known about PFAS in products and what the impact is for companies like mine. Much more research is needed regarding the consequences for the environment and climate, also many assumptions are made in the bill and little substantiation is provided. Many companies are not aware that a change in the law (with such a major impact) like this is planned. This makes it unrealistic to think that companies will phase out everything that contains PFAS within 18 months. It is really necessary to reassess the timetable befor introducing this legislation.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Refering to Table 9 of the Annex XV restriction report our comments apply to”:  Metal plating and manufacture of metal products (Annex E.2.4.) Electronics and semiconductor (Annex E.2.11.) Energy sector (Annex E.2.12.) Lubricants (Annex E.2.14.) Our product falls under the following sub-use: > Stationary electrical industrial high Voltage equipment. (RoHS Definition) For our sector(sub-use) there must be a full exemption, or at least 12 years, otherwise it’s not possible for us to sell our products before they are tested.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: During the production-phase and the use-phase of PTFE, the release of PFAS is unlikely due to the decomposition temperature of 350 degrees, these temperatures are far from being achieved in our operations and regarding the use of our product. Therefore no emissions of PFAS are expected. During end-of life stage 100% all PTFE plastics we use will be treated as incineration, landfilling waste. Just because this data is difficult (or impossible) to obtain, a ban in the short term would be unrealistic and the consequences for our sector (Energy sector / High Voltage) would be disastrous. In our sector there are currently few potential substitutes for the resources/products we use, if they are available we will have to test them, which results in high costs.  In addition, if it is not known how much PFAS is contained in products, it is impossible to determine emissions. When there are so many unknown factors, a total ban, even a postponement of 12 years, is not justified. The reasoning that if there is no response (no consultation is submitted) it is assumed that the restriction (both RO1 and RO2) will not cause any problems, this is not based on anything. Furthermore the requirements according to Art. 68 (1) REACH for such a far-reaching restriction proposal are not met. For this reason, a corresponding regulation on the part of the Commission would be unlawful. The ECJ will determine this at the latest.  Art. 68 (1) states:
When there is an unacceptable risk to human health or the environment, arising from the manufacture, use or be amended in accordance with the procedure referred to in Article 133(4) by adopting new restrictions, or amending current restrictions in Annex XVII, for the manufacture, use or placing on the market of substances on their own, in mixtures or in articles, pursuant to the procedure set out in Articles 69 to 73. Any such decision shall take into account the socioeconomic impact of the restriction, including the availability of alternatives.
Thus, a lawful restriction requires an "unacceptable risk" to human health or the environment. Such a risk was not presented in the Annex XV dossier. Nor was it defined what is meant by the term "unacceptable risk" as distinct from a risk or concern. In the submitted Annex XV dossier, the term "unacceptable risk" was even used only twice. However, it is precisely the task of the applicants to explain this. There is already a lack of definition of what is to be understood by an "unacceptable risk" as compared to a mere risk. It is clear that here risks must exist to such a high degree that only a restriction of a substance or substances can be considered as an appropriate means. Moreover, these risks must relate to all substances in the PFAS substance group. However, sufficient information on the hazard characteristics of all substances is not included in the Annex XV dossier either.
Furthermore, the legal system of the restriction procedure is not designed for the restriction of entire groups of substances with more than 10,000 individual substances (not all of which are even known). Already Art. 68 para. 1 REACH does not refer to groups of substances, also Art. 69 ff only refer to individual substances. The restriction procedure according to REACH is structurally - e.g. with regard to the deadlines regulated therein - recognizably not suitable to regulate a restriction procedure for entire substance groups. The implementation of a restriction procedure for a whole group of substances is therefore not covered by the procedure according to Art. 68 ff. REACH and therefore inadmissible. This is also shown by the fact that thousands of comments have already been received during the consultation. According to the German Federal Environment Agency (UBA), this already exceeds the previous maximum value in a restriction procedure by a factor of ten as of September 6, 2023. A processing of these comments in the individual case has to take place in any case, as far as different uses of PFAS are addressed. Clustering of the comments is only permissible from the outset if the uses of a substance in the substance group are identical.
