Combined Comments:
General Comments: I worked at a ski resort. In spring, when the snow melts, the ski wax on the tips is exposed. I regret that ski wax is being released into the environment.
The ski wax that can be visually confirmed is probably wax that has been scraped off on the snow. Wax that peels off during skiing and leaks into the environment may not be visible to the naked eye.
Competitive skiers melt and apply wax to the running surface of their skis. Waxed skis create more friction. Therefore, the applied wax will be peeled off. Competitive skiers remove wax at the starting point in cooler temperatures to remove as much wax as possible. When the ski cools, the microcracks and amorphous crystals contract, pushing out the wax. You can remove the most amount of wax by peeling it off in that state. In my experiments, over 95% of the applied wax is removed at this stage.
The remaining wax remains in microcracks and amorphous crystals on the ski's polyethylene running surface. Some of that residual wax is released into the environment by friction with snow and ice. It's a very small amount.
Waxes containing PFAS have very low frictional resistance. Discontinuing this use will have a major impact on the sport characteristics of skiing. I would like to request a limited exemption for the use of PFAS in ski wax for athletes.
Many casual skiers do not use melt-and-apply wax.
They apply liquid wax or solid wax melted in a solvent to the skis.
Melt-and-apply waxes, which require specialized tools and are time-consuming, are used by a small number of competitive skiers. I would suggest an exemption for melt-applied waxes.
In addition to regulating substances, we also propose that ski organizations regulate wax scraping on snow and outdoors. Performing wax scrapes indoors and collecting shavings should be added to competition regulations.
As a result, environmental emissions of PFAS can be significantly reduced.
Sports are not essential to life. However, traditions and culture should be preserved.
I would like to see a flexible response rather than a "full ban of PFASs."

Combined Comments:
General Comments: IGBCE - Industriegewerkschaft Bergbau, Chemie, Energie - supports the goals of the EU Green Deal and the environmental and climate protection targets it sets out, and is committed to achieving a sustainable and equitable transformation. This includes developing a balanced and equitable approach to the regulation of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). Of paramount importance is to consider environmental, occupational and health protection while maintaining innovation and competitiveness. A comprehensive ban would have a massive impact on the German and European industrial base. Preserving value chains in Germany and Europe not only safeguards jobs and locations, but also technology leadership in transformation industries. In addition, dependence on other regions of the world is reduced, which is of great importance especially against the backdrop of changing geopolitical conditions.

The IGBCE represents the interests of around 580,000 employees in Germany. To this end, the IGBCE engages in dialog with employers and politicians in a spirit of social partnership. Because only constructive cooperation can set the course for the future.

The members of the IGBCE are employed in a wide variety of industries in Germany. They develop and manufacture the future technologies and products needed to achieve the European Union's climate targets. Many of these necessary products are only possible because of the unique properties of PFAS materials and thus form the basis of the industry's transformation. The critical infrastructure of energy generation, transportation and storage, as well as the chemical, pharmaceutical and electrical industries, currently function only with products containing PFAS. They are also found in many large-scale industrial facilities, medical devices, semiconductors, electrolyzers, pharmaceuticals and high-purity packaging. To do this, the materials used must withstand extreme temperatures, corrosive acids and be durable for safety-related reasons. However, these special properties of PFAS substances can also lead to negative effects for the environment and humans. Therefore, not only the input into the environment has to be stopped, but also the intensive research and development of alternatives is of great importance. However, this requires a lot of time if similar processes are used as a comparison to find substitutes with the same technical properties. The proposed deadlines in the EU restriction proposal are generally too short and need to be adjusted and exceptions granted in certain areas of application.

The IGBCE is committed to a sustainable and responsible approach to chemicals that makes production safe and prevents their release into the environment. Also against the background of occupational health and safety, there is a need for a targeted strategy in dealing with PFAS. This includes more targeted monitoring and better control so that potential inputs into the environment are prevented and no further accumulation takes place in the food chain.

However, the restriction proposal of the EU chemicals agency ECHA includes about 10,000 PFAS substances with overall very heterogeneous properties. The proposal thus does not do justice to a targeted strategy. Among others, fluoroplastics are affected, which, according to the OECD definition, almost all fall into the category of "polymers of low concern" for human health and the environment due to their properties.

Therefore, the IGBCE advocates a revision of the current, largely blanket restriction proposal and a differentiated and risk-based assessment and regulation of the group of chemicals. The proposal must be based on the manufacturing conditions and areas of use, which must be safe and clean, and must be flanked by comprehensive education and training, so that the appropriate qualifications are guaranteed to protect workers.

The IGBCE advocates a balanced approach to PFAS substances that takes into account all three pillars of just transition - social, environmental and economic.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Description of analytical methods Information on alternatives Information on benefits Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: IIn the Advanced Packaging industry many of the substances containing PFAS are in use because of their specific mechanical, electrical, physical and chemical properties.
Mechanical properties include low thermal expansion and low friction. E.g. chip adhesives, component underfill, glob top, mold compound.
Electrical properties are low dielectrical constant that is needed for signal quality and losses at high data speeds making them necessary for modern needs of data exchange (e.g. base materials for printed circuit boards in high frequency applications).
Physical properties include low water absorption, low material shrinkage, good heat transfer and thermal stability. E.g. chip adhesives, component underfill, glob top, mold compound, Thermal interface materials.
Chemical properties include excellent resistance against corrosive substances, good adhesion (glues) and non-sticking to molding compounds and mold toolings.
For already existing machines and products, the spare parts and wear parts used for the maintenance and repair need to be exempted from the regulation without time limitation until the equipment has reached its practical end of life, assuming there is no reliable substitute.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: As a packaging supplier in the semiconductor sector we refer to the following sectors and (sub-) uses identified in table 9: Electronics and semiconductors (Annex E.2.11.) Semiconductors Wires and cables / Coating,  solvents, and cleaning / Electronic components / Heat transfer fluids / Advanced  semiconductor packaging / Photolithography

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: We dispose only materials like tapes, mold compounds or adhesives which are not disposed to the environment by our production processes. Furthermore the semiconductor manufacturing sites and equipment have a long lifetime, so the emissions in the end-of-life phase of the PFAS-containing equipment is relatively low compared to the amount found in a fab and is collected according to the European harmonized waste key-numbers for mixed plastics (European Commission, 2002).

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: When PFAS materials are disposed correctly by incineration they will be thermally destructed to less harmfull components (broken down into their original components or mineralized) and lose their PFAS properties. A recent study by Conversio has shown that at its end-of-life approximately 85% of all fluoropolymers end up in waste-to-energy recovery incinerators. Our majority of waste containing PFAS is solid material. PFAS containing articles in electrical and electronic equipment are collected and dealt with in accordance with applicable regulations, e.g. Waste Framework Directive (WFD) 2008/98/EC, ELV Directive 2000/53/EC and WEEE Directive 2012/19/EU. It was confimed by latest studies that flouropolymers, when incinerated under representative European municipal incinerators conditions, do not generate any measurable levels of PFAS emissions at their end of life and therefore pose no risk to human health and the environment.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Products that have no PFAS intentionally added are PFAS free, or the concentration by contamination will be very low under the threshold of 25ppm. As the wide PFAS prohibition will severly limit PFAS containing products, the likelihood of contamination is low. Products that contain PFAS intentionally may have to be disposed as hazardous waste after the complinance enforcement date. That would also effect existing stocks of these products as well as Products that are already placed in the market. As the recycling industries are working with high volume of waste, most times mixed of different products with different compositions from various suppliers, contaminations will happen during these recycling processes. Given the extremly low threshold of 25ppm, these contaminations will degrade large quantities of recycled materials into hazardous waste and make the recycling process more complex than nowadays.

5. Proposed derogations: In 2022 Swissbit had 5.7 tons of waste that could contain PFAS materials. Even with an estimation that 5% of our direct materials contain PFAS with a PFAS content of 100ppm, the PFAS materials emitted by Swissbit would be less than 28,5g per year.  For the vapor phase soldering systems used in the semiconductor industry, the substances are needed for the process itself – the heat transfer for heating up the most varied products for electronics or other applications. There are no PFAS free alternatives known now. The machines filter and reuse as many of the heat transfer fluids as possible. Vapor phase soldering has some big advantages over other soldering techniques like reflow soldering and are indispensable for today’s applications and future innovations. Mostly affected will be electronics for the energy sector (production of energy, storage, power electronics), automotive (electro mobility, charging infrastructure), medical, aerospace and communication technology (5G, networks, data storage).

6. Missing uses: The availability of PFAS free materials for advanced packaging materials and processes is expected to last years due to the lack of substitutes in many areas like tapes, heat transfer liquids, molding and underfilling compounds, PCBs, Components, etc. In some products the replacement of PFAS by other additives may be possible, with fundamental research of new materials and compositions. Espacially in consumer products with lower requirements regarding the environmental conditions and lifetime, PFAS free alternative materials may be a possible option. For advanced products like automotive, aviation, medical etc. the transition will take a lot longer, because product lifecycles are usually way longer, often more than 20 years, and qualification for new processes and materials, which are long term safe, can also take many years, assuming it is possible at all to find suitable alternatives and the test results are positive, because the qualification process has to start again.  Taking the vapor soldering as an process example, the physical and chemical properties of the PFAS heat transfer liquid are essential for the process of vapor phase soldering and fluid heating. This technique is extensively used for electro mobility and semiconductor industries. At the moment, there is no known material that offers the same heat transfer capabilities, but also providing a inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation of solder contacts. There has been permanent searching for alternative substances that are not based on PFAS and have the properties of PFAS as a heat transfer liquid. A ban on PFAS as the heat transfer liquid for the use in vapor phase soldering systems leads to the "end" for the technology.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: In the semiconductor packaging area most materials like adhesives, tapes, glues and molding compounds are available for decades, and the search for alternatives already started for many materials years ago. As an example, for package related adhesives it is expected to take more than 20 years to find and implement an alternative. As the stated materials influence each other and interact with the PCB, silicon dies, components, etc. the devices need to be re-qualified which can take, depending on the application, multiple years. For changes in the final product, the customers need to be notified and every change need to be approved as well, which can also take prolongued amounts of time. For heat transfer fluids, depending on the application, there can be different cases. For modern refrigeration and chiller application, qualification and implementation would take at least 8 to 14 years. In many cases it will be needed to redesign the equipment and retrofit or exchange completely existing machines. For more complex applications like vapor phase soldering, it is not known if there may be a possible replacement, and even with fundamentel research it is questionable if such a replacement can be found and implemented in the next 25 years.  For lubricants in semiconductor manufacturing equipment it is expected to take more than 10 years, to find alternatives, at they need to fulfill the special cleanliness requirements of the clean room during manufacturing, while keeping their inertness even under harsh conditions. Changes will also effect specific parts of the machines which may need to be replaced. For mold release tapes, which are used to protect the mold tooling from the liquid compound sticking, there is no known suitable replacement, even though suppliers have been researching for many years. Tested alternatives lead to contamination of the toolings, highly increased maintenance times and strong yield losses and were not suitable for industrial use in mass production.

8. Other identified uses: We use the typical semiconductor advanced packaging materials like: adhesives, coatings, lubricants, encapsulation of semiconductor products. Only few suppliers of these materials already confirmed a PFAS content in their product.  See attached list of materials with confirmed or supposed PFAS content.  Determining the PFAS content of a material may proof difficult. If the PFAS substance is not stated in the material content list a chemical analysis will be necessary. For small PFAS amounts in the material (threshold level of 25 ppb) the analysis effort will be quite high and the results will be hardly reproducible. A clear PFAS declaration on the products from the manufacturer would help in this case.

10. Analytical methods: So far no suitable test method for determining the PFAS amount in an inhomogeneous product or article has been developed. With commercially available analysis methods for homogenous substances, only about 1% of PFAS substances being restricted can accurately be determined.  The lack of analysis methods for detecting and quantifying PFAS chemicals in products and components may hinder the producer to comply with the proposed restriction proposal.

In marine sector, Wärtsilä technologies enable transport of passengers and goods ( over 80% of the volume of international trade in goods is carried by sea), and provide essential technology for fishing vessels, navy, tugs, dredging vessels and offshore support / construction vessels.

Wärtsilä uses extensively PFAS containing fluoropolymer materials (e.g., FKM, FFKM, PTFE, ETFE, PVDF) in high-performing components to guarantee the safety and reliability of the products. PFAS materials are essential in eliminating leakages of highly flammable or toxic fuels, preventing fires in electrical systems, securing the energy generation in critical applications (e.g., nuclear plants, hospitals, airports, and data centres) and ensuring manoeuvrability of marine vessels. Failures in these critical components could lead to catastrophic consequences, impacting human lives and the environment severely.

PFAS materials have been selected due to the properties for chemical and temperature resistance, long-durability (thermal aging), abrasion / wear resistance, oil & water repellence, withstanding pressure, oxygen tolerance, low permeation, lubrification, insulation, and fire resistance. In many Wärtsilä applications more than one of these properties are needed simultaneously, and only PFAS materials can currently fulfil these material requirements. Without PFAS containing materials, majority of Wärtsilä technologies can no longer operate safely and reliably. Therefore, the current PFAS restriction proposal will have a major impact and disruption on Wärtsilä´s customers’ assets, which are already subject to strict regulations to ensure safety of operational conditions and emission control in EU.

Wärtsilä is committed in developing technologies supporting EU and global decarbonisation  goals (European Green Deal, etc.). Wärtsilä already has and is further developing technologies and solutions that enable the transition to decarbonised shipping and 100% renewable power systems. PFAS containing materials are needed to enable these technologies to work safely and reliably. As an example, PFAS containing fluoropolymer materials are required for storage and handling of carbon-neutral fuels, like methanol, ammonia, and hydrogen, for the   lithium-ion batteries in energy storage systems, as well as in carbon capture technologies.

The core technologies containing PFAS materials for marine sector are:
• main and auxiliary engines, generating sets, turbochargers and   related auxiliary systems
• onboard fuel supply systems
• technology for hybrid or all-electric shipping (battery powered)
• propulsors, gears (such as water jets and thrusters), and shaft line solutions
• exhaust gas treatment (SOx, NOx, particulates, and black carbon) and carbon capture
• ballast water systems
• cargo handling, reliquefication, regasification and VOC recovery systems to gas carriers and FSRUs.
Wärtsilä is a market leader in medium speed main engines, with 69 GW of engines installed in marine vessels, 17.5 GW under service agreement, and over 43,000 Wärtsilä equipment installed in 18,000 vessels.
The core technologies containing PFAS materials for energy sector are:
• gas, liquid fuel and multifuel engine power plants
• auxiliary technologies for power plants, including exhaust treatment, fuel storage and supply systems and electrical and automation installations
• large scale energy storage (battery) systems
• power-to-X, liquefaction, and biogas solutions
On land-based installations, Wärtsilä has delivered 76 GW power plant capacity and over 110 energy storage (battery) installations in 180 countries around the world.

Wärtsilä´s position on the proposed PFAS restriction and derogations

Wärtsilä is committed to seeking alternative materials in co-operation with the component/material suppliers in case PFAS materials enter the REACH authorisation or restriction schemes. However, based on the Wärtsilä´s assessment, there are no alternative materials available today to replace many of the PFAS containing materials (fluoropolymers) for both our innovative and critical applications.  For many use cases, the period required for a conversion cannot be meaningfully determined due to a lack of technically mature alternatives. In case a potential alternative material(s) is identified, the process to replace a safety critical component(s) in a large-scale industrial installation is a long process. The technology is needed to be redesigned, tested in laboratory, tested in-situ, certified and approved by class-society (marine vessels) or by national regulatory bodies (land-based installations) to fulfil all the safety and reliability requirements. As the fluoropolymers are present in a large-scale installation in hundreds of different critical components and applications, it would require a complete re-design and new technology development in case new materials would be identified, and this would take minimum 10 years.

Wärtsilä is requesting maximum derogation time for fluoropolymers and perfluoropolyethers in:
• applications affecting the proper functioning related to the safety of transport vehicle (potential derogation marked for reconsideration after the Annex XV report consultation, 6 o.)
• applications affecting the proper functioning related to the safety of engine power plants, energy storage systems, power-to-X and fuel storage, handling, and distribution systems (major use cases missing, and no derogation proposal existing in the Annex XV report)

Wärtsilä also requests developing a mechanism to prolong the derogation time if alternative materials have not been found when the derogation time ends.

Wärtsilä product´s life expectancy is from 30 to 50 years, and our company is required to guarantee spare parts for products with long service life. Wärtsilä is requesting a full exemption for the spare parts both for ‘transport’ and ‘energy’ sector technologies which are placed into market before PFAS restriction would enter into force and/or a specific derogation would expire. Wärtsilä sees that the “repair as produced” principle shall be respected in PFAS restriction. In Wärtsilä case it´s practically impossible to perform redesign, in-situ testing, certification, approval, and conversion with new materials, as it would require unreasonably long downtimes for critical installations / vessels. As an example, there are hundreds of different PFAS containing seals in engine systems and replacing them with new materials in existing customer installation is extremely difficult.

In overall, Wärtsilä is concerned about the ability of its suppliers and sub suppliers to continue operating and providing the materials and components needed in the assembly and maintenance of Wärtsilä products, should the PFAS restrictions come into effect. Wärtsilä is in this response focusing on PFAS use cases in Wärtsilä´s technologies, but there is no visibility how the restriction would impact on the PFAS material producers and Wärtsilä´s suppliers or sub-suppliers. Wärtsilä considers that if the PFAS restriction comes into force (without proper derogations for the whole supply chain), a significant portion of the spare parts needed in operating and maintaining the equipment currently installed in vessels, power plants, and processing facilities, will become unavailable and make these installations inoperable.

General Comments: In 1635, the nickel smelter was founded as a blue dye factory. Various cobalt-based blue pigments were produced, which were used, among other things, to decorate Meissen porcelain. Cobalt was originally a waste product of silver mining, as was nickel, which was also processed in the nickel smelter from the middle of the 19th century and used in the cutlery industry. Since 1991, Nickelhütte Aue GmbH has been part of Siegfried Jacob Metallwerke GmbH & Co. KG.
Since its inception, the company has grown continuously and established itself both in the region and worldwide. Above all, it has always been possible to adapt to changing market conditions and to develop innovative processes and products. Today, the company specialises in the recycling of non-ferrous waste containing nickel, copper, cobalt, vanadium, molybdenum and/or tungsten, which is produced in a wide range of industrial sectors, such as pharmaceutical, chemical, petrochemical, automotive or surface industries. In the pyrometallurgical and hydrometallurgical plants, chemicals and concentrates are produced from them, which are fed back into the material cycle. The product range extends from Ni-, Cu-, Co-salts and Na-vanadate solution to intermediates of the metals Co, V, Mo, W or Cu and copper-based master alloys. In this way, we make a sustainable contribution to the conservation of resources and the environment. For more than ten years now, we have been involved in the recycling of Li-ion batteries from the automotive industry and can count ourselves among the market leaders in this field.
In addition to the core business, there are many other departments that contribute to the success of the nickel smelter. These include transformer dismantling, non-ferrous metals trading and alloy operation. For the supply of the administrative and production areas with electricity and heat, there is a separate department for energy generation, which also covers the needs of surrounding companies and residents. To ensure product and process quality, we employ employees in our own laboratory and sampling, as well as technologists in R&D, who not only monitor the processes, but also continuously develop improvements and new procedures. For repairs, maintenance of existing systems as well as the construction and installation of new systems, there is a separate maintenance department.
The workforce is therefore very broadly positioned; it includes chemists, chemical technicians, chemical plant specialists, electronics technicians, plant mechanics, engineers, IT specialists, business people, laboratory technicians, metal workers and many more. Young people are trained themselves, and career changers are also happy to be trained.
The work in the company is physically and mentally demanding. In some areas, work is carried out on a rolling week. The processes run all year round, seven days a week, 24 hours a day. A stop at the weekend is neither technically possible nor economically viable. To ensure the health and well-being of employees, a comprehensive health management system has been implemented in recent years.
But the region is also very important to the company and it is aware of its responsibility in this regard. The nickel smelter is involved in social, cultural and sporting activities. Old company buildings were renovated. This resulted in a cinema and a gym as well as an ice skating rink and a bowling alley for Aue, which are operated by the company itself. In the meantime, the former company sports association has grown into an independent club of SG Nickelhütte Aue e.V. Girls and boys will find a meaningful leisure activity in the sports sections of handball, football, taekwondo, kickboxing, ski jumping and bowling. The commitment to young talent also serves above all to preserve high-class sports in the region, such as ski jumping as well as the Auer Bundesliga teams in football and handball. All this contributes to the fact that the region remains livable and attracts people.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: For us, the usage phase mainly plays a role. When using ready-made PTFE, PFA, PVDF-, ... Products do not produce any emissions. The use of these materials reliably prevents emissions from chemical-pharmaceutical production plants. In the end-of-life phase, the PFAS products are fed into our waste treatment plant and thus recycled and destroyed.   We use fluoropolymers in the form of seals, pipes and containers in our wet chemical plants. In the supply chain of fluoropolymers, we are thus end users. In our systems, both corrosion and temperature resistance play a decisive role. This mainly includes the following procedures:  - Preparation of copper sulphate from spent copper etching solutions - Production of nickel sulphate, nickel chloride and cobalt sulphate from various secondary raw materials (e.g. electroplating sludge, spent catalysts, etc,) - Production of nickel nitrate from nickel metal - Production of sodium vanadate from filter dusts  Among other things, fluoropolymers are used in various parts of the plant:  - Shell and tube heat exchanger  Built-in PTFE parts: • Deflection segments (baffle) • Tube sheet • Pipe fittings for fixing/fastening the pipes in the tube sheet • Seals • Sleeves for spacer rods • Seals  - O-rings: O-rings are mainly coated with the materials FFKM, FKM, FEP, but PFA and PTFE are also used. Here, in addition to the resistance problem, the temperature problem also plays a role. For EPDM, the application limit is a temperature of 120°C or 130°C.  In the case of fluoropolymers, it goes up to 260°C.  O-rings are installed in fittings, heat exchangers, pipelines, etc.   - More with PTFE/PFA use In addition, other equipment with PTFE, PFA, PVDF, ETFE components is used in the plants we operate. In principle, the reason for the use of PTFE is always the same: universal applicability, very often only PTFE/PFA resistant and usable, no use of many different materials for better and safer maintenance and compliance with various legal regulations when operating chemical production plants (TA-Luft, FDA, ...). Examples include: • Valves: Housing borosilicate glass 3.3, valve bellows PTFE (open/close valves, control valves) • Safety valves: Borosilicate glass 3.3 housing, PTFE bellows • Ball valves: seat rings made of PTFE, ball PFA coated • Flap: PFA lined • Ball check valve: seat, ball and safety plate made of PTFE • Non-return valve: flap incl. gasket made of PTFE • Strainer: filter/support filter made of PTFE, filter sock made of ETFE • Bellows: metal flanges, PTFE bellows • Rupture discs: Graphite with PTFE coating • Stirrer: stirrer shaft and stirrer head steel/PTFE • Mixer Settler: Doppelstauwehr aus PTFE • Column internals: PTFE hold-downs, glass support grate with components made of PTFE, PTFE support ring, PTFE guide funnel, ETFE demister, PTFE grommets for grommet distributors, PTFE discharge tubes, PTFE seals/sealing tapes, PTFE bells for bell bottom columns, PTFE/PFA/PVDF packing or structured packings, PTFE nuts, PTFE washers • PTFE Vortex Crusher • Steel/PTFE lined piping • PTFE/PFA lined fittings • PTFE/PFA lined pumps • PVDF Pumps • Etc.  Compliance with the ATEX directive, reduction of the explosion potential Another great advantage of PTFE, in addition to the normal design and the version of modified PTFE, is the possibility of producing dissipative PTFE. If the installation site is in an explosive atmosphere or if explosive mixtures are produced in the product room in the system, the ATEX directive must be complied with. For this purpose, seals, fittings bellows, pipeline bellows, stirrers, etc. are made of dissipative PTFE. This can then be grounded via grounding connections. For this purpose, there is an elaborated concept for glass plant construction.  Result: Without PTFE, many of our systems will no longer be operational. PTFE is the only material that can be used for gaskets and internals at high temperatures and high chemical resistance. Another important aspect of PTFE is its lower diffusion compared to other plastics. This is very important for the emission values in the plants. Perhaps it would be possible to reduce the large number of different fluoropolymers. In addition, it would be possible to replace some of the steel/PTFE piping with borosilicate glass 3.3 or steel/enamel piping. As a result, only the seals and bellows would be made of PTFE and PFA, but not the entire pipeline.   Construction products (Annex E.2.13.) PTFE thread sealing tape For repairs of leaking threads, for example on various pumps in the process plants, we use PTFE sealing tape.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The PFAS are incinerated in our waste incineration plant in accordance with the 17th BImSchV at temperatures of 850 to 900 °C. We produce very little waste of fluoroplastics. These are mainly replaced gaskets. These are disposed of directly in our waste incineration plants (100% incinerator).

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The PFAS are incinerated in our waste incineration plant in accordance with the 17th BImSchV at temperatures of 850 to 900 °C.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: In any case, limit values in the ppb range are primarily an analytical challenge, because they are at the detection limit of normal measuring instruments. The limit value of 50 ppm, on the other hand, is to be regarded as realistic and practicable.  In the literature it can be found that PTFE should be burned at a temperature > 850°C so that no harmful exhaust gases are produced. This is the case in our pyrometallurgical plants. If we can continue to incinerate the PFAS we produce in our plants, we will not have any additional costs.

5. Proposed derogations: We need an indefinite derogation for the use of fluoropolymers in the chemical industry. There are no alternative materials available. In addition, there are no research results that would change this in the foreseeable future. There is always only one result for usability: either high operating temperature or chemical resistance. Neither is possible with any other material. The built-in PTFE parts do not emit any emissions. In some cases, they remain in the systems for up to 30 years or more without having to be replaced. The material therefore poses no danger to humans or the environment. On the contrary, this would even increase if an inferior material is used. This would result in higher emissions of chemical vapors, more frequent leaks, more downtimes and more repair costs. Every shutdown and start-up process is an additional hazard. When the plants are started, the process is stopped and the process runs smoothly, there is little potential danger. The hazard potential then comes mainly from external interventions or malfunctions or failures of components. The losses would be increased if fluoroplastics were no longer allowed to be used.

6. Missing uses: The missing application for us is the entire chemical industry and its consumers. This ranges from product manufacturing, their precursors and intermediate products to the various recycling processes that have been developed in recent years for environmental protection. Here, PFAS are mainly used in the form of chemically and thermally resistant seals. As a user of fluoropolymers, we cannot make any statement about PFAS as such. We refer to the properties of the fluoropolymers produced. Their most important properties are the operating temperature and the chemical resistance at low and high temperatures. At higher temperatures, PTFE is largely dimensionally stable. This is extremely important for many applications. The high purities of PTFE and especially PFA for use in plants for the production of high-purity products are also decisive. Another advantage is the non-existent catalytic effect.  We would no longer be able to operate our wet chemical plants and would have to shut them down. Like ourselves, a ban would affect many companies in the chemical industry that rely on corrosion-resistant components. To make matters worse, the proposed ban is a purely European project. Its implementation would therefore also lead to a further decisive competitive disadvantage for the European economy. There are no alternatives on the market that would be suitable for our area of application. For a few areas in the plants (e.g. cold pipelines), a different material would theoretically be possible. In the event of a malfunction, however, there may be an additional increased risk if the pipeline is exposed to elevated temperatures. In addition, there could be confusion of the individual seals by the assembly and service personnel. Storage areas would have to be enlarged so that the "same" items in different materials can be in stock. Many materials are not available in a dissipative version. However, this is absolutely necessary in hazardous areas and in order to comply with the ATEX directive or to avoid dangerous electrostatic charges. We see PTFE reduction opportunities in the conversion from steel/PTFE piping to glass or steel/enamel piping. In the future, it would be possible to plan directly in other materials if this is possible in terms of application technology (but the seal must still remain PTFE). However, this would be associated with a higher price of materials.  We would have to clarify this with our ZÜS. No additional effort would be necessary for new projects. For each individual pipeline, it must be checked whether the other materials cover the same pressures, temperatures and chemical resistance. For retrofitting in existing systems, they must be removed and cleaned. Longer planned downtimes must be expected here, which will lead to severe sales losses,  If we were only able to operate our hydrometallurgical plants to a limited extent or at a higher cost due to the PFAS ban, this would further weaken our international competitiveness. In the global market, we cannot pass on the additional costs to our customers. At our site in Aue, about 50 employees are directly affected. Without the hydrometallurgical plants, our pyrometallurgical plants would also be affected. The intermediate products produced by the latter are further processed into various metal salts and solutions by wet chemistry. This would drastically reduce our product range. This would affect another 250 employees.  We have a turnover of approx. 200 million €/year as a location in Aue

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: In a modern chemical industry, it is necessary to transport chemical safely from the point of manufacturing to the point of use. This can be done by trucks, various types of containers (including ISO-Containers) and also in tanks onboard of ships. Depending on the chemicals that need to be transported, different types of tanks are used, such as steel tanks, FRP tanks, rubber lined tanks or tanks lines with polyethylene on the inside. However, these tanks are not corrosion resistant for all types of chemicals, thus for the harshest chemicals (e.g. highly concentrated sulfuric acid, hydrofluoric acid, sodium hydroxide, …) fluoropolymer linings made from PVDF, ECTFE, FEP and PFA are commonly used. The fluoropolymer lining additionally ensure that the tanks are easy to clean (non-sticking properties) and that the transported chemicals are not contaminated during transport (fluoropolymers are essential when electronic grade chemicals for the production of computer chips are transported).

When it comes to the chemicals industry, fluoropolymers allow for the safe production, storage, handling and use of chemicals through protective equipment and linings. Their chemical stability allows them to be resistant to some of the most corrosive substances on the market and as a result protecting works and equipment from harm.

Production, storage, transport an use of chemicals and other hazardous materials can inevitably carry potential risks. Moreover, history has shown that accidents can not only have economic impacts, but also irreparable consequences on human lives and the environment. Mitigating such risks through using the safest and best materials on the market is essential for today’s worldwide chemical industry.

We request full exemption of fluoropolymers from the restriction proposal.

In our view, the Annex XV restriction report does not cover relevant and essential uses of fluoropolymers in the critical sector “Transportation”: Trucks, Containers and Ships carrying the harshest chemicals need to have tanks lined with fluoropolymers for corrosion protection.

Fluoropolymers meet the OECD’s key internationally recognized safety criteria identifying them as polymers of low concern: They are not toxic and not mobile; they do not dissolve in water or contaminate water and they can not enter or accumulate in a person’s bloodstream. They do not present significant toxicity concerns and not degrade into other PFAS (see link: New Study Demonstrates Vast Majority of Commercial Fluoropolymers Meet Criteria for Polymers of Low Concern Designation (americanchemistry.com)

Fluoropolymers are quite expensive. Thus, they are only used in applications where no other products/materials provide a feasible solution. Their chemical inertness and resistance to harsh conditions, corrosion and extreme temperatures (hot and cold), are unique properties, needed in a wide range of applications. The assessment of alternative materials has shown that, when available, they frequently cannot meet the critical performance characteristics of fluorinated materials and are not safer.

Using fluoropolymer is generating significant benefits along the value chain, making them critical in numerous technologies, industrial processes, and everyday products. Banning Fluoropolymers will contradicts the European Green Deal and European Chips Act. The dependency of Europe from products manufactured in other parts of the world is expected to increase in case fluoropolymers are no longer available.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The specific use of “fluoropolymers used for lining of tanks to transport chemicals (trucks, containers ships)” is not listed in Table 9.R02 of Annex XV.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Depending on the chemicals, their temperature and concentration, the corrosion protective lining is selected. Either PVDF, ECTFE, FEP or PFA is used with thickness typically ranging from 2 mm up to 5 mm. Additionally accessories like welding rod, pipes, fittings and stock shapes are need.  The larger volume of fluoropolymers used in our company is already produced without the use of fluorinated polymerization aids. To further reduce the risk of emitting small molecular PFAS from the fluoropolymers, most of our suppliers have already announced that they will change their production process to non-fluorinated polymerization aids in the future. Our company plans to use polymers produced with non-fluorinated polymerization aids as soon as they become available.  During manufacturing:   There is a certain amount of emissions when fluoropolymers are processes at elevated temperature in the thermoplastic state. While the majority of the emissions is expected to be HF, also some small molecular PFAS are expected to emit. In our facility, the main parts of the extrusion line with the highest temperatures (thus the areas where emissions are most likely to occur) are covered with a ventilation hood to suck of fumes/emissions above the extrusion line. The off gases are then cleaned in gas scrubber, before released into the environment. We are committed to implement an emission control strategy to detect PFAS emission and to capture them during processing.  We have state of the art technologies in place to avoid loss of fluoropolymer during the production our facility. We capture and recover fluoropolymer waste during manufacturing in processing for recycling. In case recycling is not possible the fluoropolymer-waste is fed into the waste stream in line with current laws and regulations. Incineration is said to effectively destroy PFAS if temperatures are above 850 °C.  Storage and handling  Proper Packaging avoids PFAS loss during the transportation and storage. After production, products are packed and stored properly.  The use-phase:   Sheets made from fluoropolymers are used for the lining of tanks in trucks and ships as well as used for lining ISO Containers. It must also be considered that fluoropolymer is on the inside of the tank only. During the use phase at ambient temperatures, emissions from PVDF, ECTFE, FEP and PFA do not occur (below detection limit), because the material is extremely stable, inert and does not degrade into small molecular substances over the whole life-time.   End-of-life:   Equipment which is decommissioned after service life (~10-20 years depending on the application) can be collected and deposited or incinerated according to the state of the art and in line with laws and regulations.

6. Missing uses: The missing use discussed in this statement is related to the transportation of chemicals, that require specialized corrosion protection layers on the inside of trucks, containers and ships in case harsh chemicals are transported.  In the past few years in addition to trailers (for trucks) and containers made from metal, also solutions using FRP were introduced to the market. The advantage is that FRP tanks with an inside lining of thermoplastic material, such as PVDF, ECTFE, FEP and PFA have less weight, thus more payload is possible. Further information about this specific applications and why fluoropolymers have benefits and are in some cases the only solution, can be found in the following information:  See link #1 to website (confidential)  See link #2 to website (confidential)  See annex 1: L. Djukic, Specialized dangerous goods tanks for the transport of highly corrosive chemicals, JEC Composites Magazine, Nr. 107, Aug-Sep. 2016  See annex 2: A. Ushakov, Composites tank container for multimodal transportation system, JEC Composites Magazine, Nr. 107, Aug-Sep. 2016  See annex 3, 4, 5 and 6: various successful project descriptions  See annex 7: Application Spotlight: Tank Liners, Arkema, January 2020  b. The key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use.  Various chemical resistance lists (e.g. DVS Codes 2205-1, DIBt Media list, ISO TR 10358) confirm the superior chemical resistance of fluoropolymers against many chemicals. While other materials (e.g. PE, PP, rubber, …) can only handle mild chemicals and lower concentrations, for many applications only the combined properties as exhibited by fluoropolymers enable feasible and economic solutions. Also metals do not show such a universal chemical resistance, at least not in cost effective way: • Outstanding chemical resistance to a broad range of chemicals from -200 °C up to 260 °C (e.g. H2SO4, NaOH, HNO3, HF, HCl, NaOCl, …) • Easy installation inside of tanks and leak tight welding lead to high safety and long life-times. • Fluoropolymer linings offers simple repair options since the sheet can be welded again after proper preparation in the case of mechanical or thermal damages. • Easy to clean (very small amount of residues remain in the tank after draining) due to not sticking properties because of very low surface tension. Less water is needed for cleaning. And cross contamination in case different chemicals are transporter are reduced to a minimum. • Extremely low leach-out of fluoropolymer lining does not contaminate high purity chemicals during transport (essential for semiconductor industry) and in compliance with Semi F40, Semi F57 and Semi C90, etc. • Toughness of the fluoropolymer ensure high safety, even in the case of accidents. • Flame resistance (UL94 classification V0) • Physiological non toxic  One must consider that fluoropolymer are a quite costly solution. Thus, fluoropolymers are only used in applications where no alternatives exist or where alternatives are extremely costly.   c. The number of companies in the sector estimated to be affected by the restriction.  Apart from our suppliers for ECTFE (Solvay), our company and our competitors, also the entire downstream value chain will be effected in case fluoropolymers are banned.  d. The availability, technical and economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives for the relevant use, including information on the extent (in terms of market shares) to which alternative-based products are already offered on the EU market and whether any shortages in the supply of relevant alternatives are expected.  Where alternatives to fluoropolymers are available, they are already used today because fluoropolymers are high priced. Thus, for harsh chemical environments it will extremely difficult to develop alternatives. Especially if you want to use the tank for transporting chemicals for different chemicals. Also impossible is to substitute tanks that are used for electronic grade chemicals. These specialized chemicals are needed in semiconductor industry in a very pure form and if they are in contact with metals the chemicals will be contaminated with metal ions. Test for leach out from metals to ultra-pure chemicals are standardized in SEMI F40, SEMI F57 and SEMI C90. Furthermore, semicon production companies have a stringent copy exact process. Using tanks without fluoropolymers could jeopardize the production yield of computer chips, thus any changes in the supply chain are evaluated and need to be approved.  Availability:  - Various Steel compositions (stainless steel, high-alloy steel like nickel-alloy, titanium alloy, hastelloy, special grade steel…) o The chemical resistance, availability, cost-benefit ratio is much poorer as compared to fluoropolymers  o For example: The chemical resistance of selected fluorpolymers is better in the long term, compared to most of the available steel compositions o For specific applications, steel equipment can be used, with reduced life time and less safety. o For the stated chemicals, fluorpolymers are offering significantly longer service times and safety compare to steel grades: Hydrofluoric acid, high concentrated Hydrochloric acid, Sodium-Hypochlorite, Sodium chloride - Other polymers (PE, PP, PVC, FRP, PA) are showing reduced chemical and temperature resistance.  Technical and economic feasibility:  - Reduced service life and reduced operation safety (z.B. Tabelle Numbers needed, Corrosion Guide) - High-Alloy steels are much more expensive compared to fluopolymer solutions, which will have an direct impact to the price of the down stream users - Processes requiring high purity chemicals can not be performed due to contaminated chemical … - Equipment weight higher CO2 pollution   Hazards and risks:  - Reduced service life of equipment and plant safety - Environmental food print of steel production: Studie - PVC Bann in Scandinavia  g. For cases in which substitution is not technically or economically feasible, information on what the socio-economic impacts would be for companies, consumers, and other affected actors. If available, please provide the annual value of EU sales and profits of the relevant sector, and employment numbers for the sector.  The influence of banning fluoropolymers on transportation of chemicals is difficult to assess. While the impact for our supplier, our company and our customers is not that big looking at the pure numbers, banning fluoropolymers would have a big impact on a vast number of downstream users and in the end also on end user prices.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: In addition to stainless steel and aluminum for vacuum chambers, various diverse low outgassing, vacuum-suitable, cleanroom-suitable and temperature stable PFAS materials are widely used in vacuum technology. For example for sealing, connection, feeding, auxiliary materials, semi-finished product and jigs.
At the moment no alternative materials are available, especially for UHV (UltraHighVacuum) and UCV (UltraCleanVacuum) applications, when production speed (throughput) is crucial (for example: loadlock applications in semiconductor production).

The challenge in this industry is the use of materials in an environment of vacuum as well as increased process temperatures. This is necessary to enable possible clean (particulate, organic, biological, molecular) conditions for high-tech applications. By using low pressure, the evaporation energies of all materials are reduced, so that they start to boil, evaporate or give off parts already at room temperatures. This makes the use of high-temperature und vacuum-suitabke plastics necessary.

Currently, PFAs are used for the following applications:
- Pipes and insulation materials (PVDF)
- Hoses and piping (PTFE)
- Tooling (HALAR)
- Seals (FKM and FFKM)
- Lubricants (PTFE greases)
- Plastic components made of PTFE for bearing and insulation purposes

For all the above applications, the only alternatives are silicone-based. In UHV and UCV applications, however, silicones are not permitted, since outgassing of silicone can have negative effects on, for example, optics or motor lifetimes in these applications. This particularly affects the semiconductor, medical, coating, analystics and aerospace industries.
Below you will find some publicly available literature articles on how outgassing silicon compounds contaminate optics or other semiconductor processes:

General Comments: In Europe, Heraeus Comvance is the main producer of fluorine-doped synthetic quartz glass for fibre optic applications on an industrial scale. Other manufacturers are located in the USA and China and are not affected by the planned restrictions.

Our contribution to the Public Consultation relates to the use of carbon tetrafluoride (CF4) as a doping agent for the manufacturing of special glasses.

For this purpose the CF4 is used as raw material.

The use of CF4 is carried out in compliance with strictly controlled conditions.

In addition, the plant to produce glass at Heraeus Comvance site in Bitterfeld is authorized in accordance with the Bundes Immissionsschutz Gesetz (BImSchG).

This contribution to the Public Consultation aims to obtain an exemption from a restriction or ban of the use of carbon tetrafluoride as doping agent in the production of glass fibres.

1. Substance used Name of substance: Carbon tetrafluoride EC: 200-896-5 CAS: 75-73-0 State / form: gas  Contributing activity / technique for the environment Environmental release category (ERC): ERC 5: Use at industrial site: The substance or its transformation products are included into or onto article ERC6a: Use of intermediate  Contributing activity / technique for workers Process Category (PROC):  PROC 1: Chemical production or refinery in closed process without likelihood of exposure or processes with equivalent containment conditions. PROC 8b: Transfer of substance or mixture (charging and discharging) at dedicated facilities.  Technical function: Other: Doping agent Sector of end use: SU16: Manufacture of computer, electronic and optical products, electrical equipment Subsequent service life relevant for this use: no Substance supplied to that use in form of: as such

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The following information essentially relates to the use phase of Carbon tetrafluoride (CF4) as doping agent in the production of special glasses. Further information can be found in section 6 of this consultation.  The doping of the porous SiO2 body takes place in a closed high-temperature reaction chamber.   Fluorine is incorporated into the SiO2 solid stoichiometrically as SiO1,5F. The fluorine is covalently bound to the SiO2 glass matrix. During the reaction, gaseous CO2 is formed. Subsequently, the porous and fluorine-doped body is sintered to a transparent glass. In the manufacturing process, the gas stream passes through an exhaust gas combustion. During the entire manufacturing process of the doped glass, no CF4 is emitted into the environment.  For quality reasons, no traces of CF4 may be present in the product. The fluorine itself is chemically bound in the transparent glass and is neither released during the intended use as an optical fibre nor at the end-of-life phase.   Fluorine-doped glass fibres have special optical properties, which are essential for the use as bending resistant fibres, ultra-low loss fibres and other applications in comparison to non-doped glasses.  Depending on customer requirements, the glass used to manufacture optical fibres for telecommunications may contain fluorine in the range of 0.1 to 2 percent by weight. The glass fibre itself, on the other hand, consists only partly of fluorine-containing glass. Depending on the type of glass fibre, the final glass fibre can contain approx. 0.015 up to 0.8 percent by weight.  The plant to produce glass at Heraeus Comvance site in Bitterfeld is authorized in accordance with the Bundes Immissionsschutz Gesetz (BImSchG). All wastewater and exhaust air purification systems are state of the art. Plant operation activities are carried out in accordance with existing legal requirements of occupational safety and environmental protection. In addition, the operation of the plant is surveyed in accordance with the Industrial Emissions Directive (IED Directive 2010/75/EU).

6. Missing uses: Comments to element a.: With the anticipated expansion of the global and European telecommunications infrastructure, fluorine-containing glass fibres will be required in particular for FTTH (Fibre To The Home) applications and energy-efficient ULL (Ultra Low Loss) fibre applications.  Therefore, a continuous volume growth of fluorine-doped products is expected for the next years.   Comments to element b.: Doping with fluorine gives quartz glasses special optical and bending characteristics.   Comments to element c.: In Europe, Heraeus Comvance is the main producer of fluorine-doped synthetic quartz glass for fibre optic applications on an industrial scale. Other manufacturers are located in the USA and China and are not affected by the planned restrictions.  Comments to element d.: Alternatives to CF4 have been tested but currently no other doping agents have yet been found to meet customer-specific requirements as stated in section b.  Comments to element e.: Potential alternatives to fluorine doping of fused silica have been under investigation. These included SF6, SiF4, HF, NF3 and F2. However, the required glass fibre properties could not be met with any of the alternative materials mentioned. Statements on potential alternative substances: - Sulfur hexafluoride (Molecular Formula: F6S; CAS No. 2551-62-4) is not applicable to substitute the above mentioned PFAS, because Sulfur containing precipitates are generated in the doping process, which cover the reaction chamber and scrubber and degrade the glass material properties. - Nitrogen trifluoride (Molecular Formula: F3N; CAS No. 7783-54-2) is not applicable to substitute the above mentioned PFAS, because it etches SiO2. Furthermore, NOx, NOF and other substances are generated which must be removed or cover the reaction chamber with hazardous precipitates. - Hydrogen fluoride (Molecular Formula: FH; CAS No. 7664-39-3) is not applicable to substitute the above mentioned PFAS, because it etches SiO2 and is not incorporated in the glass as a dopant. - Silicon tetrafluoride (Molecular Formula: F4Si; CAS No. 7783-61-1) is not applicable to substitute the above mentioned PFAS, because the high requirements on the glass material properties are not met. - Fluorine (Molecular Formula: F2; CAS No. 7782-41-4) is not applicable to substitute the above mentioned PAFS, because it strongly etches SiO2, the reaction chamber and the integrated assemblies.  Comments to element f.: Substitution is technically and economically not feasible (see also sections d and e).  Comments to element g.: The fluorine-doped glasses are an essential, supporting pillar for Heraeus Comvance in general, as well as for the Heraeus Comvance site Bitterfeld located in Germany. If these glasses are no longer allowed to be produced, there is a risk of the Bitterfeld site being closed in the medium term. Consequently, a migration of the production of fluorine-doped glasses to outside Europe would have to be expected. Furthermore, a ban on the use of carbon tetrafluoride as doping agent in the production of glass fibres would have a direct impact on securing the IT infrastructure of Germany as an industrial nation.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Transitional period Request for exemption
Org. name: DECHEMA Expert Group Single-Use-Technologies for Bio-based Applications
Combined Comments:
General Comments: In February 2023, the ECHA (European Union Chemicals Agency) presented a proposal to restrict the use of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). According to the proposal, the production and use of more than 10,000 persistent chemicals in these substance classes will be banned with a transition period until 2026/27. PFA polymers are used in a wide range of industries, including bioprocessing and biopharmaceuticals, due to their unique functional properties (thermally, biologically and chemically stable, negligible water solubility, non-mobile, non-bioavailable, non-bioaccumulative and non-toxic) and low reactivity. This comprises mainly fluoropolymers such as PTFE, EFTE, PVDF, FKM, FEP and PFA. Their use is crucial in biopharmaceutical production (vaccines, monoclonal antibodies, proteins): among other things, they are used in hydrophobic filtration membranes (sterile filtration), seals, hoses, bags and pumps. This includes, in particular, the single-use components that are important for biopharmaceutical production. A ban on PFAS would make active ingredient production virtually impossible, as almost all peripheral and necessary individual components would be eliminated from the supply chain. So far, we are also not aware of any certified alternatives. The resulting considerable restrictions in production would lead to supply bottlenecks and higher prices.
The DECHEMA Expert Group Single-Use-Technologies for Bio-based Applications supports efforts to minimize the use of these and other substances of potential concern in production processes and products and to prevent their release into the environment. Both in the manufacture of disposable components and in biopharmaceutical production itself, the release of PFAS is already legally excluded due to the special requirements for hygiene and cleanliness or disposal. During the prescribed thermal disposal, PTFE, for example, is completely thermally decomposed at over 870°C (Wexler et al.: Waste incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate potential formation of per- and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) in flue gas). Disposal is carried out by the end user in accordance with local legal requirements. Provided that the proper procedures defined by the manufacturer of the disposable components are followed, fluoropolymers can be disposed of without risk to humans or the environment.
Although the ECHA proposal already includes some exemptions, e.g. for materials used in medical devices and pharmaceutical ingredients, biotechnological production facilities and related components are not included in these exemptions. The DECHEMA Expert Group Single-Use-Technologies for Bio-based Applications therefore calls on ECHA to grant appropriate exemptions to the already heavily regulated biopharmaceutical industry:
• Instead of a comprehensive ban on carbon-fluorine bonded molecules (PFAS), we suggest that PFAS be differentially regulated on a scientific basis
• Substances that the OECD classifies as "products of low concern" (PLC), and for which the risks of emission to the environment in the context of production and use have been evaluated and corresponding preventive countermeasures and disposal concepts defined, should be exempted
• PFAS products that do not come into contact with the environment, e.g. because they are fixedly installed, should be excluded
• GMP processes already approved for the manufacture of biopharmaceuticals should be exempted from the ban.
Without adequate exemptions, there is a risk that the production of vital biopharmaceuticals and vaccines in Europe will come to a standstill. This would have a dramatic impact on the already strained supply of medicines not only in Europe, but globally, as Europe is home to important production facilities for the global supply of medicines.
At the same time, research into alternatives to PFAS must be accelerated in order to make alternative materials available to the pharmaceutical industry for future production processes. This applies in particular to single-use components such as filters, bags or tubing. To this end, we recommend developing a roadmap together with developers, manufacturers and users that formulates research needs and defines time targets. Currently, alternative materials are not yet available for numerous applications in biopharmaceutical production; their development, validation and approval require adequate resources and time. This must be taken into account in the discussion on bans and transition periods.
We, as the DECHEMA Expert Group Single-Use-Technologies for Bio-based Applications, are well aware that there are PFAS that are harmful to human health and the environment and that their use must be restricted or regulated. However, a distinction should be made between low molecular weight PFAS, which are released regularly when used, and polymeric PFAS that are permanently incorporated into apparatus or products. In assessing the risk of these products, it is critical to look at the proposal with careful consideration of the impact on biopharmaceutical manufacturing of vital vaccines and medicines. The development and manufacture of these products involves complex processes and certifications that require meeting stringent quality standards, regulatory compliance and extensive testing. Any significant rapid change has far-reaching implications for patients, innovation, and the robustness of our industry's supply chains, preventing adequate response to global pandemic threats in the future, for example. Single-use systems are used in the production of all covid-19 vaccines; on average, 60-70% of biopharmaceutical production is estimated to occur in single-use systems.
The pandemic preparedness project contracted and initiated by CEPI in Germany, among other countries, with the German government, which comes into effect on July 1, 2023, would thus be reduced to absurdity.
It cannot be in the EU's interest to weaken regional biopharmaceutical production and further increase dependence on third countries. The common goal must be to stabilize the supply of medicines also through production sites within the EU and to prevent further gaps in supply.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: In following this grouping approach, the proposed PFAS Restriction would restrict PFAS that
have not been risk-assessed and for which an unacceptable risk has not been demonstrated,
in breach of Article 68(1) REACH.
Article 68(1) REACH provides that substance(s) can be restricted only if they pose an
unacceptable risk to human health or the environment. This unacceptable risk must be
positively demonstrated by conducting a risk assessment that follows the conditions of Annex
XV to REACH (and by cross-reference of Annex I and Annex XIII). Such risk assessment
comprises hazard identification and characterisation, exposure assessment and risk
characterisation.
By grouping all various PFAS substances together and restricting them as a single class, the
proposed PFAS Restriction Proposal would restrict numerous PFAS substances that have
not been risk-assessed and for which no unacceptable risk has been demonstrated, in
breach of Article 68(1) REACH.
More specifically, the scope of the proposed PFAS Restriction is based on the OECD
definition of PFAS. That definition is only based on chemical structure and does not take into
account hazardous properties or risks of PFAS, as the proposed Restriction itself
acknowledges (p. 19). As a result, it covers approximately 10,000 substances with very
diverse physical, chemical and biological properties and behaviour. That broad definition
does not take into account the specific, distinct properties of different individual PFAS or
PFAS subgroups and is therefore not suitable for regulatory risk management purposes.
OECD itself acknowledges that this definition "does not conclude that all PFASs have the
same properties uses, exposures and risks" and that it can only serve a starting and
reference point as it "may be viewed as too broad" (OECD, 2021, Reconciling Terminology
of the Universe of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances: Recommendations and Practical
Guidance).
In particular, the very broad scope of proposed Restriction –which is based on the OECD
PFAS definition- does not enable a legally and scientifically sound risk assessment. By
grouping all PFAS together in a single group for risk assessment, the proposed Restriction
fails to identify and consider the specific, distinct properties of each individual PFAS or PFAS
subgroup and, in turn, to assess and characterise the hazards and risks related to those
properties in order to demonstrate that they pose an unacceptable risk to human health or
the environment.
For example, fluoropolymers are thermally, biologically, and chemically stable, barely
soluble in water, immobile, insoluble (Water, Octanol, etc.), and too large to migrate to cell
membranes, so they are not incorporated into the body and are considered low concern
from a human and environmental health perspective1,2. The findings demonstrate that
fluoropolymers are a distinct group from PFOA and PFOS and should not be combined with
them for hazard assessment or regulatory purposes. Fluoropolymers are the only materials
that simultaneously possess heat resistance, weather resistance, chemical resistance,
water repellency, lubricity, and unique optical/electrical properties, and they have become
indispensable materials in many fields, including the energy field (Fuel cells and lithium-ion
batteries), semiconductor field (Clean members, etching gas), electrical and electronic
communications field (Wire cladding and liquid crystal materials), transportation field (Cars,
airplanes, railroads), and medical field (Catheters, protective clothing). It is necessary to
carefully re-examine whether the uniform regulations for PFAS are appropriate in light of
the chemical hazards and risks of the substances in question. In particular, fluoropolymers
should be excluded from the current regulations because they are highly stable materials
and have no concerns about bioconcentration or toxicological effects.
Reference:
1: Barbara H et al., Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management, Vol14(3),
p316–334.
https://setac.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ieam.4035
2: Stephen K et al, Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management, Vol19(2),
p326–354
https://setac.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ieam.4646

This industry sector concerns laboratory equipment outside the group of medical devices, which are used for the precise measurement and dosing of liquids not only for research, as described in Annex A Table A.101, but also, among others in analytical laboratories, pharmaceutical production and food production. Products used for dosing highly pure and/or extremely aggressive liquids up to hydrofluoric acid, are made of PFAS especially PFA, ETFE, PTFE and PVDF in the components in contact with the media. Most of the applications in this area cannot be carried out with the same performance without this group of substances. 6. Missing uses: 6a) Within the scope of the production of liquid handling devices and volumetric devices made of plastic, a total of 11 t of PFAS were used in our company in 2020. This quantity was 2022 nearly the same. The distribution of the affected polymers was as follows: PFA 6.6 t, PVDF 1.425 t, ETFE 2.983 t and PTFE 0.025 t. These materials were used in particular to manufacture bottle-top dispensers, bottle-top burettes and volumetric flasks. These instruments are used in analytical laboratories for dispensing either high-purity liquids in trace analysis or aggressive liquids such as concentrated acids and alkaline solutions up to hydrofluoric acid in soil analysis and other applications. We do not have any information about emissions during production as we are processors and purchase the materials from the original manufacturers.  Waste generated during the manufacturing process is disposed of by certified companies.   6b) The properties of PFAS used in connection with the laboratory instruments mentioned under a. are in addition to their temperature resistance, above all their extremely high chemical resistance, the good machinability combined with their inertness and high purity are indispensable especially in trace analysis.  6c) The manufacturers affected in direct connection with the products mentioned are manageable. There are less than 10 manufacturers worldwide, of which 6 companies are located in Europe.  6d) Currently, there are no known alternatives. So far, there are also no alternatives from the raw material manufacturers. Immediately after publication of the proposal which we support in principle despite the considerable risks for our company (see confidential documents), our company started the release of a preliminary project. General Comments: In general, the association stands behind the idea of regulating and banning the chemical substances that form PFAS substances when they break down. Chemical breakdown products in the form of forever chemicals cannot be considered to belong in our environment. The big challenge is to do this in a controlled and well-thought-out way. The time span of 18 months must generally be considered too short a period of time for a complete transition to environmentally friendly alternatives. This is even if the exempted areas are included in the assessment. That is, the areas that have 5 years, 12 years or have exceptions without a time limit.

The proposal does not include a ban on the use of the refrigeration, freezer, air conditioning or heat pump equipment that is already "placed on the market". The proposal provides the opportunity to top up refrigerants needed for service and maintenance for up to 13.5 years after entry into force (EIF), provided that there is no commercial " drop -in" replacement. This applies to the HVACR equipment mentioned in the proposal. We interpret this as all refrigeration, freezing and heat pump equipment found today. In order not to lead to confusion, the concept (HVACR) must be clarified under definitions in a possible regulation.

While allowing for the ability to add refrigerant to existing equipment up to 13.5 years after entry into force, we are concerned that manufacturers may not have a commercial interest in manufacturing and distributing all of today's commercial options needed to maintain existing cooling and heat pump equipment in operation over time. Something that will naturally lead to a lot of difficulties for the market.

A transition to environmentally friendly alternatives means a transition to refrigerants that are more challenging in terms of high pressures, toxicity, flammability or even explosiveness. This transition requires a great deal of effort in the form of skill development by people active in the refrigeration industry. Today the market lacks broad competence in the alternative technologies. Competence development of those operating in the refrigeration and heat pump industry takes time. Something that also suggests that the time limit for implementation should be longer than 18 months.

Account must also be taken of the challenges found in various national legislations which very far place restrictions on where the environmentally friendly alternatives can be installed. From that perspective, carbon dioxide may appear to be a good alternative, but carbon dioxide is not always a good alternative in terms of energy efficiency. For larger stores, the overall energy efficiency can be good, but for small facilities where the need for heat recovery is small, the overall energy efficiency can be poor and the carbon dioxide systems therefore burden the external environment more in the form of a greater need for purchased energy.
