Combined Comments:
General Comments: In general, the member companies of Deutsche Bauchemie do not use PFAS as primary formulation components for the manufacture of construction chemical products and see both the obligation and the technical possibility to substitute PFAS in a timely manner for the rare exceptional cases, where they are used as primary formulation components.
Due to the lack of labelling or declaration obligations on PFAS in raw materials so far and the immense scope of substances to be regulated under the planned restriction, formulators of construction chemical products are currently unable to make any statement on the scope of PFAS "introduced" into construction chemical products via raw materials.
Due to this situation, the construction chemicals industry cannot currently assess, whether PFAS-free alternatives are available for raw materials containing PFAS and whether these would have a technically comparable performance in the corresponding products. The necessary technical application tests must be carried out in each individual case and are costly and time-consuming.
Against this background, it is of upmost importance that the affected actors in the supply chains can use sufficiently long transition periods to identify the relevant cases, check the availability of PFAS-free alternatives and, if necessary, investigate their technical applicability.
From a formulator's point of view, it is therefore important that not only PFAS themselves but also the raw materials containing PFAS must be tested for their substitutability. In this sense, the "essential-use concept" must be applied not only at substance level, but at all levels of the supply chains concerned. This should be taken into account conceptually when reviewing and assessing "essential uses".
Products, that were produced before the restriction comes into force - and where the formulator may have been unaware that they contained PFAS - should be exempt from the restriction.
It should also be noted that the necessary transition periods should not be set across the board for the entire supply chain, but rather in such a way that each of the actors concerned has sufficient time to initially identify and then fulfil their obligations.
The problem outlined from the point of view of downstream users not only arises relating to the planned PFAS restriction, but also with other general substance group related regulatory risk management measures in European chemicals legislation and is becoming increasingly important in the course of the foreseeable development.
An example is the recently adopted restriction on synthetic polymer microparticles. Again, formulators (industrial downstream users) cannot assess with certainty whether a raw material contains synthetic polymer microparticles and falls under the scope of the restriction without corresponding additional information from their raw material suppliers.
Unfortunately, the transition periods by which raw material suppliers must inform their customers (industrial downstream users) about possible obligations under the restriction and by which industrial downstream users have to fulfil their obligations are identical. This leads to a situation where, in the worst case, the industrial downstream users do not have time to identify and implement the fulfilment of their own obligations after receiving relevant information from the raw material supplier. This situation is unacceptable from the formulator's point of view and should be avoided at all costs in future.
Irrespective of the product-related problems described above, PFAS play an essential role in many industrial production facilities in the chemical industry. Due to their chemical and thermal persistence and durability, fluorinated polymers are essential components of chemical plants in the form of seals, valves, coatings, membranes, hoses, or lubricants. In this way, they make a significant contribution to the safe operation of chemical production plants and to protect the environment and the chemical product from contamination. Due to their properties, fluorinated polymers are difficult to replace in these areas of application, if at all, without restricting the functionality and safety of industrial plants. This also applies to production plants in the construction chemicals industry without restriction.
NACE_label: Manufacture of chemicals and chemical products

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: In general, the planned restriction of PFAS is to be welcomed.
The main focus should be on applications that, due to the intended use, can be expected to release the substances into the environment.
However, it should be urgently reconsidered whether a general and comprehensive ban on PFAS is expedient.
In our view, the intended use of the substances should be considered in conjunction with the resulting - and non-resulting - health and environmental hazards.

In our case it is about the following application:
We use PTFE hoses and seals in our equipment. The material PTFE is used because it is resistant to the processed materials and withstands the temperatures required in the process without damage.
No PFAS are released from the material during use. The parts only need to be exchanged if they are destroyed by mechanical force.

According to the current state of the art, I am not aware of any materials that meet the required flexibility of the hoses while at the same time being resistant to temperature and materials. Replacement materials would have significantly higher environmental impact as they are corroded over time and would need to be frequently exchanged.
This example can be applied to all use cases where PFA are used due to their exceptional chemical stability as a sealant or containment of aggressive chemical substances.

A general ban on the substances will further endanger Europe as an industrial location. Industries that rely on the use of PFAS to produce their PFAS-free products will inevitably seek other manufacturing options. And they are not only in the substitution but above all in the relocation of processes to other locations.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Use of fluoropolymers as sealants or for containment of chemical substances at high temperatures, where metal encasings are not suitable due to needed flexibility (hoses, seals etc.)

Combined Comments:
General Comments: In general, TRUMPF Hüttinger GmbH + Co. KG and Trumpf Huettinger sp. z o.o.,  (henceforth referred to as TRUMPF Electronic) is aware of the concerns about PFAS and supports the substitution of hazardous substances for human health and the environment.
Companies such as TRUMPF Electronics are situated near the end of the supply chain. We use PFAS in terms of parts in the production process of our power electronics.

We note that the sector of “power electronics” is not listed in the Table A.1 of Annex XV in the restriction proposal, although about 2.5 million Europeans work in the branch “power electronics”. The sector of “power electronics” in Europe realizes a turnover of 705 billion euros, comprises circa 86 000 companies and represents one of the largest branches measured in the EU (Source: European Environment Agency – Europe’s consumption in a circular economy: the benefits of longer-lasting electronics 2020).

Inadequate harmonized classification complicates information gathering.

Even though we are trying very hard to identify our PFAS applications and to substitute PFAS where possible, we are facing a challenge.
However, we rely on supplier information to identify the extent of the impact.
Therefore, we need detailed information of our suppliers to answer most of the specific questions. Almost all relevant suppliers are not able to collect that extent of information within six months (see responses of some suppliers in the confidential attachment) because there is no legal requirement which standardizes the information transfer of all PFAS to its customer. Besides, it would be nearly impossible to find a suitable substitute for most of the PFAS within 18 months or 6,5/13,5 years in case of an exemption. Normally, finding a substitute with the same specific characteristics in the product development process takes several years (for further information, see our use cases in the confidential attachment). That is why the legislative proposal should provide a formal mechanism to extend or renew exemptions in case a substitute for a PFAS is not feasible within set derogation times. Otherwise, a complete ban of PFAS would affect us because machine tools could not be built in the same quality as usual. In the high-tech sector, a market shakeout in the European industrial production is expected as a result of the significant competitive disadvantage.

The inadequate harmonized classification of PFAS in the CLP Regulation means no disclosure of information (e.g. via the safety data sheet), which makes the analysis of the impact time-consuming and in many cases impossible. To obtain information along the supply chains, conclusive lists of the substances concerned, including CAS numbers, would be required.
However, even with harmonized classification, gathering information is difficult, as there is currently no law on the information of PFASs and suppliers are therefore not obliged to inform us about them.

It is not clear how a restriction of a certain PFAS can be controlled by national or local authorities due to a lack of accountability of PFAS-free parts. Especially imported power electronic devices from third countries can contain PFAS in individual parts, while it would be not allowed to produce power electronic devices in the EU with parts including a PFAS.

Restriction option 1 (RO1) of the restriction proposal, an unlimited full ban on PFAS, would be a disaster for the entire industry.
Therefore, we prefer Option 2: Ban with use-specific, time-limited derogations. and plead for an derogation for SMREs at least for 13,5 EiF.
We are investing heavily in the development of alternative materials to be able to completely replace PFAS in the future. But this takes time.

At present there is no alternative to PFAS in many of our applications due to their unique properties.

However, and even with the derogation for 13.5 years of EiF, it is not certain that we will find an adequate replacement for all applications.

Topic of Complexity of the equipment.

In addition to the transfer of information in the supply chain, the complexity of our equipment also poses a challenge in the identification of PFAS:
For a company like TRUMPF Electronics, which relies on over 500 suppliers, and a system which contains more than 600.000 parts, gathering information on PFAS substances that are not yet regulated is a major challenge. The majority of PFAS used are not yet listed in the SVHC list. Accordingly, there is no legal basis for obtaining the necessary information from suppliers. And even if the suppliers are willing to cooperate, they face the same challenges with their suppliers and do not receive the necessary information. This is especially true for our suppliers in the electronics sector.
Environmental emissions
In general, our products mostly are made for semiconductor industry – therefore, they are handled by trained personnel under controlled conditions. In any case person working with the equipment is well trained.

They are manufactured, used and disposed of in a controlled environment in accordance with applicable regulations.

Description of analytical methods
The analytical methods for detecting are still inadequate. Also, the methods listed in Annex E4 do not include all possible PFAS that may occur in our products.

In order to be able to make a well-founded statement about the presence of PFAS, we cannot rely solely on analytical methods. We also rely on detailed information along the supply chain. Which presents us with great challenges.

Information on alternatives

A restriction should only concern a PFAS involving an unacceptable risk to human health or to the environment in accordance with Art. 68 of the REACH Regulation. In the restriction proposal, a profound risk assessment of every single PFAS with regard to its potential danger for human health or the environment has not been performed. As a consequence, applications of PFAS (such as fluorpolymers, so called “polymers of low concern”, and fluorelastomers) without a scientifically evidenced unacceptable risk to human health or to the environment, should still be used in the near future, until a suitable substitute with the same characteristics will be detected and tested (Source for “polymers of low concern”: Henry/Carlin/Hammerschmidt i.a., “A critical review of the application of polymer of low concern and regulatory criteria to fluorpolymers”, Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management – Volume 14, No. 3, pp. 316-334).

With respect to the specific characteristics, the listed alternatives in the restriction proposal have only been assessed for their technical feasibility in replacing some PFAS at a general level. In reality, the proposed substitutes are not feasible based on the specific needs to the same effect as the characteristics of the PFAS in question. Especially in the sector “High-Voltage and High-Frequency”, applications of PFAS are used under extreme conditions (e.g. ultrapure condition, very high/low temperature, high electric fields, high electro-magnetic fields).


Although some alternatives in Appendix E2 can offer comparable properties to fluoropolymers, they are not replaceable for several key applications.

In many use cases for Power Electronics, a combination of the properties of fluoropolymers are used, which the alternatives cannot cover.

We replace Fluoropolymers in new developments wherever possible, but a 1:1 replacement is often not possible due to the unique environmental and performance requirements of our industry.

It can take more than a decade to develop an alternative with no guarantee that it will meet the requirements of performance, health and safety, raw materials, energy and water consumption, etc. The transition period should reflect this.
Assuming we find viable alternatives for specific applications, it will take more than 10 years to develop industrialized PFAS-free designs.

And yet, even after this time, there can be no guarantee that a viable alternative will be found that meets the requirements.

If no suitable alternatives can be found, we will no longer be able to produce our equipment, which means that the entire Power Electronics system for the industry can no longer be produced and operated. This would be a big step backwards for the global, but especially for the European industry.

In addition, the Power Electronics supply chain is highly specialised, which may further impact schedules if alternatives were not available in sufficient quantities to meet demand.

The sector of “power electronics” in Europe realizes a turnover of 705 billion euros, comprises circa 86 000 companies and represents one of the largest branches measured in the EU (Source: European Environment Agency – Europe’s consumption in a circular economy: the benefits of longer-lasting electronics 2020).

We serve a number of key applications and end-user markets that are crucial to the global economy and to managing Europe's environmental and digital transformation, e.g. power generation (f. ex.: solar industry), healthcare, communications and mobility, energy storages (batteries).

A blanket ban, or a limited derogation, would have profound negative consequences for the global competitiveness of the European economy and European citizens.

This is only possible if we can supply the right spare parts at any time and continue to use used machines effectively and efficiently.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis
Combined Comments:
General Comments: In its current form, the PFAS restriction proposal aims to group and restrict over 10.000 substances, without introducing any differentiation between the different PFAS categories.

PFAS should however be regulated based on a more precise segmentation of the different PFAS categories and only restricting those that present a critical hazard and risk profile for human health and/or the environment.

Article 68(1) of the REACH Regulation requires a demonstration of (i) hazard, (ii) exposure and (iii) availability of alternatives, and the Proposal should reflect instances where either of these criteria are not met.

Articles 68 and 69 of the REACH Regulation relate to the existence of an “unacceptable risk” or “a risk to human health or the environment that is not adequately controlled and needs to be addressed”.

Section 3 of Annex XV relates to information on “hazard and risk” (emphasis added). An Annex XV dossier is used to “initiate the restrictions process” (Article 69(4) of REACH), which is then checked for conformity with Annex XV by the ECHA Committees for Risk Assessment and Socio-economic Analysis (Article 69(4)(3) of REACH). The Annex XV dossier cannot and does not restrict nor limit the risk assessment which the Committee for Risk Assessment (“RAC”) is legally required to carry out in accordance with Article 70 of REACH. The RAC must formulate an opinion “based on its consideration of relevant parts of the dossier” (emphasis added) (Article 70(1) of REACH).

However, the RAC opinion itself must address whether “the suggested restrictions are appropriate in reducing the risk to human health and/or the environment” (Article 70(1) of REACH). It is therefore clear that the RAC opinion is not, and must not, be confined or restricted to the information that the Member State has chosen to include in an Annex XV dossier. The RAC is legally required to carry out a full and valid risk assessment assessing all issues relevant to the appropriateness in reducing the purported risk.

As such, RAC must not:
(i) Restrict the assessment to the issues set out in the Annex XV dossier; and
(ii) Proceed on an assumption that it was not possible to conduct an assessment of the risk and exposure.

The general presumption that any chemical substance which is a purported persistent substance poses the same hazards and same risks, and that those hazards and risks always preclude and prevent any hazard or risk assessment from being carried out is manifestly wrong in law and demonstrates a clear and manifest misunderstanding and misappreciation of the facts, particularly in the present case.

A core part of an Annex XV dossier is the requirement to provide “Justification for [a] Restriction at community level” (Part 3, Annex XV to REACH) which includes a requirement to determine whether a restriction is the most appropriate Community wide-measure by assessing “(i) effectiveness” and in particular whether: the restriction is: (a) “capable of reducing these risks to an acceptable level within a reasonable period of time” and (b) “proportional to the risk” (emphasis added). It therefore follows that the risk must be quantified.

The raison d'être of the ECHA Committee for Risk Assessment is to assess risk, which it failed to do in this case. Risk is a “function of […] probability” (Case T-13/99, Pfizer Animal Health v Council, EU:T:2002:209, paragraph 147) and relates to the specific hazards and exposures relating to a specific chemical substance. The hazardous properties of all chemical substances differ and are not the same. The whole purpose of a chemical risk assessment is to assess whether a specific chemical in particular, poses a risk – taking into account the properties of the chemical substance itself, and exposure. Merely because a particular chemical substance is, purportedly, persistent does not mean that substance has the same hazardous properties and/or exposure/risk, as other purported or actual persistent substances.

The failure to conduct a risk assessment as required by EU law (there must be consideration of, for example, whether there were any relevant unacceptable risks; what the “critical probability threshold for adverse effects” were; and/or whether that threshold was exceeded in the case of all the products subject to the Proposal), and to use all actual and possible emissions potentially impacted by the proposed restriction as a proxy for unacceptable risk materially impacts the outcome of the assessment. By working from the presumption that any emissions – even potential emissions – potentially in scope of the proposal, should be used as a proxy for risk, means that for those emissions only zero emissions, or no emissions at all, would constitute no “unacceptable risk”. Further, by working from the presumption that (i) any such emissions were a proxy for risk; and (ii) all emissions should be eradicated and minimized, the Commission and ECHA are unable to properly consider the proportionality of the proposal and whether it addressed the activity giving rise to the perceived risk.

The risks arising from exposure and use of alleged persistent substances can be properly and sufficiently controlled. This is clearly accepted and foreseen in the REACH Regulation itself (For example, Article 58(2) of REACH provides that certain uses or categories of uses may be exempt from a REACH Authorisation requirement, provided that, amongst other things “the risk is properly controlled” (emphasis added). Where the risks arising from uses of Annex XIV substances are “properly controlled” it therefore follows that those uses may be exempted from a REACH authorization requirement pursuant to Article 58(2) of REACH. In other words, REACH clearly provides that the risks arising from alleged or actual Annex XIV substances can be controlled and can be properly controlled, such that they have no adverse effects (Article 1(3) of REACH)). Where the risks are properly or sufficiently controlled such they do not adversely affect human health or the environment in accordance with Article 1(3) of REACH and pose no relevant risk, there is no relevant risk and no “unacceptable” risk for the purposes of Article 68(1) of REACH. The notion that it is not possible to characterize or control the risk of an alleged P/M substance is not correct in law or fact.

Neither the Commission nor ECHA have any legal competence to decide that all actual or possible emissions intended to come within the scope of a proposed REACH Restriction automatically constitute “unacceptable risk”. This is particularly the case where there has been no risk assessment assessing or establishing whether such emissions do pose unacceptable risk. By using all actual and possible emissions within the intended scope of a REACH Restriction as a proxy for unacceptable risk, the Commission / ECHA imposes a zero-emissions and zero-risk policy as regards those emissions.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: In January 2023, the national competent authorities of five member states submitted to ECHA a proposal to reduce per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (so-called PFAS) emissions into the environment. The restriction proposal, published on 7th February 2023, included a very broad definition of PFAS encompassing any substance that contains, at least one fully fluorinated methyl (-CF3) or methylene (-CF2-) carbon atom (without any H/Cl/Br/I attached to it). This definition covers approximately 10,000 substances. PFAS are used in a wide variety of consumer products and industrial applications because of their unique chemical and physical properties, including oil and water repellence, temperature, and chemical resistance, as well as surfactant properties. According to the submitters, the risk to humans and the environment arises from production, use and disposal of PFAS substances and is based on the concern that all PFASs and / or their degradation products meet the criteria for classification of at least one of the three environmental hazard classes: very persistent (vP), bioaccumulative (B) or mobile (M).
Our company fully supports the efforts of the Commission to minimize the impact of hazardous substances to human health and environment. However, we would like to raise our concerns regarding the very broad definition of PFAS currently in scope of the restriction proposal.
The current PFAS definition adopted in the proposal is solely based on molecular structure, and, accordingly, many substances are categorised as PFAS despite not exhibiting the environmental and toxicological characteristics which are in focus of the restriction. Not all substances covered by this broad PFAS definition share the same properties and not all are equally persistent, bioaccumulative or mobile. In particular, due to the extensive scope of the definition, some colourants, mainly used for the colouration of polymers in very specific applications, fall under the definition, even though they only bear one or two aromatic -CF3 groups in their chemical structure. These substances are non-toxic, not bioavailable, non-water soluble and thereby do not fulfil the criteria for PBT, vPvB, PMT and vPvM and, as such, are considered to have no significant impact on the environment and human health.
Colourants imported or manufactured over 1 tonne/year in Europe are REACH registered and their properties are well documented in the registration dossiers. For these substances, specific regulatory measures are already in place where applicable, and should therefore not be included in this restriction proposal.
Colourants bearing -CF3 groups display unique colour shift properties and exceptional stabilities, highly desired characteristics for specific applications, and cannot be replaced. The use of these colourants is often mandatory for safety purposes, to protect consumers and professionals. In the confidential section of this letter, we have specified the two substances registered under REACH which are used for the colouration of polymers for such application and included some supporting arguments to substantiate our request.
Considering that colourants have distinct properties from those targeted by the restriction, this group of chemicals should not be in scope of the legislation, and we ask that an exemption from the definition of PFAS be granted for colourants to avoid unnecessary restrictions and disruptions in many supply chains.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis
Combined Comments:
General Comments: In line with our culture of nuclear safety, occupational safety, and environmental protection, Orano supports any initiative aimed at preventing and limiting the risks of hazardous substances for human health and the environment.

Alternatives to hazardous substances should be pursued when equivalent properties (especially safety properties) are available under acceptable economic conditions. This should be done considering the necessary time for certifying certain equipments under accidental conditions, in accordance with regulatory requirements on nuclear safety (Directive 2009/71/Euratom establishing a community framework for nuclear safety of nuclear installations). In doing so, we are merely emphasizing a requirement of the regulation (EC) 1907/2006 (REACH itself), article 68, which states that any new restriction "must take into account the socio-economic impact, including the availability of alternative solutions".

In practice, the presence of PFAS-containing equipment in installations (e.g., seals, lubricants) serves important functions, particularly in heat and corrosion resistance, and contributes more broadly to safe conversion and enrichment processes or radioactive materials transport where there are no alternatives. Without PFAS-containing equipment in installations (e.g., seals, lubricants), nuclear fuel production in Europe would no longer be possible and without PFAS-containing equipment in radioactive materials transport, nuclear activities would no longer be possible at all.

PFAS-containing equipment are also more relevant in our spent fuel treatment plant in comparison with alternatives. Indeed, our main use on this site (La Hague) is for sealing of stainless-steel faucets. Substituting PFAS-containing equipments (PTFE) for these uses would generate a greater volume of waste, additional maintenance costs, and have  impact on radioprotection for staff workers  in radiological zones due to replacement every 5 years for more conventional seals, as opposed to 15 years for sealing in PTFE and degrade safety by increasing the risk of leakage (degraded performance of materials without PFAS). These consequences are to be compared with the absence of PTFE release during the use phase and the end-of-life phase for nuclear waste.

The response time for the public consultation is too short to map all our uses. We focused on our specific uses in nuclear material transport and sealing, as well as lubrication and sealing in nuclear fuel cycle plants. Our specific uses concerned especially fluoropolymers (e.g PTFE, PCTFE, PVDF, PFA, FKM, FFKM…).

All the uses that could be substituted were done so because of the high cost of PFAS. Residual uses are not substitutable for radioactive materials transport, conversion and enrichment processes (front-end nuclear fuel cycle), as they require a combination of properties that only PFAS can provide.

Our PFAS requirements remain limited in quantity, of few tons per year maximum, for the specific uses mentioned above.

During the use phase in nuclear material transport and sealing, as well as lubricant and sealing in nuclear fuel cycle plants, there is no release into the environment. During the end-of-life phase, nuclear wastes are disposed of in nuclear repositories involving no release into environment. Potential discharges are therefore very low.

Fluoropolymers are stable, inert, solid materials. Fluoropolymers resist degradation by acids, bases, oxidants, reductants, photolytic processes, microbes, and metabolic processes. For this reason, they are thermally, chemically, and biologically highly inert. Fluoropolymers are not expected to degrade under environmental conditions or normal use and processing conditions (Wood report 2020). They are stable and remarkably durable and therefore  persistent.

However, persistence alone does not imply that there is a present or future risk to human health or the environment (Rüdel report 2020). Persistence itself is not an intrinsic hazard, as it does not in itself imply or inform the potential for an adverse effect (toxicity).
New hazard categories had been introduced by the commission delegated regulation (EU) 2023/707:
- Persistent, Bioaccumulative and Toxic or Very Persistent and Very Bioaccumulative,
- Persistent, Mobile and Toxic or Very Persistent and Very Mobile.
However, the persistence alone is not a hazard category in the regulation (EC) 1272/2008 (CLP regulation). Therefore, persistence on its own does not justify the need for specific risk-management measures. Fluoropolymers themselves are persistent, but they are not bioaccumulative, not mobile, and not toxic and therefore not SVHCs from a regulatory perspective (Ruwona and Henry 2021).
Proposing a restriction for fluoropolymers which meet the OECD criteria to be classified as “polymers of low concern” would be in breach of the regulation (EC) 1907/2006 (REACH), article 68. This article specifies that Annex XVII shall be amended “when there is an unacceptable risk to human health or the environment, arising from the manufacture, use or placing on the market of substances”.

Orano therefore requests that fluoropolymers which meet the OECD criteria to be classified as “polymers of low concern” (e.g PTFE, PCTFE, PVDF, PFA, FKM, FFKM…) should be excluded from this proposed restriction for industrial uses.

In addition, we request an unlimited derogation for our use of PFPE as lubricant (oil, grease) in front-end nuclear fuel cycle plants.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The sector is the energy sector, more precisely nuclear energy.  The uses are concerned by TULAC, metal plating and manufacture of metal products, applications of fluorinated gases, transport, electronics and semiconductors, construction products, lubricants sectors. Our response will not cover all these uses. The response time for the public consultation is too short to map all our uses. In addition, many of these uses can be replicated in most industrial sectors. We focused on our specific uses in nuclear material transport and sealing, as well as lubrication and sealing in nuclear fuel cycle plants.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: It is very difficult to answer this question in the absence of information from our suppliers or subcontractors. The best source of information could eventually be the national authorities. In France, for example, a new regulation requires (06/20/2023) ICPEs (classified facility for environmental protection) to assess their aqueous PFAS discharges. Another way of obtaining data is to canvass manufacturers and the waste sector. Perhaps you will find some relevant data among the responses to this consultation. We asked our suppliers to assess PFAS emissions during the manufacturing phase. We have not received any useful data. In the use phase in nuclear material transport and sealing, as well as lubricant and sealing in nuclear fuel cycle plants, there is no release into the environment. The end-of-life phase, there are two types of wastes in nuclear sector: - Nuclear wastes which are disposed of in nuclear repositories and involve no release into environment, - Conventional wastes which are managed as classic industrial hazardous wastes. We have not any useful data. In France, the waste sector is highly regulated (ICPE regulation) and controlled. Nevertheless, our PFAS requirements remain limited in quantity, on the order of few tons per year maximum, for the uses mentioned above. Potential discharges are therefore very low.

5. Proposed derogations: In sealing, as well as lubrication uses our PFAS requirements remain limited in quantity, on the order of few tons per year maximum. Potential discharges are probably very low (no data for manufacturing phase): - Low quantity used, - No release in use phase, - Potential release in the end-of-life phase limited.

6. Missing uses: We prepared 2 confidential attachments for cases in which substitution is not technically feasible: - Use of FKM/FFKM o-rings for the transport of nuclear materials, - Use of several fluoropolymers for sealing and lubricant applications in front-end of nuclear fuel cycle plants. In addition, the use of PFAS for sealing is also possible in back-end facilities. PTFE is listed in over 400 items on our spent fuel treatment plant. On this site, PTFE can be found in certain items, where it is mainly used to seal stainless steel faucets, via fitting seals, valve seals, gaskets, valve seats and so on. It is currently the main type of seal supplied by faucets manufacturers. PTFE is widely used in sealing due to its unique characteristics in this field. First of all, it is the best material for sealing between metals. The material is flexible enough to deform, but not too much, allowing a large number of valve and join operations without the risk of leakage. What's more, it is highly resistant over time, requiring replacement every 15 years, as opposed to 5 years for more conventional seals (some lightly used PTFE seals are still effective 50 years after their installation on site). PTFE is also stable and well-suited to the high-concentration chemicals used on site, notably acids (nitric acid 13.6 N), soda and formaldehyde. Substitution would generate a greater volume of waste, due to the more frequent replacement of seals (every 5 years vs. 15 years).  The work would also entail major technical constraints for maintenance operations, particularly those carried out in radiological zones. Combined Comments:
General Comments: In line with our culture of safety, worker protection, and environmental protection, the European nuclear energy sector supports any initiative aimed at preventing and limiting the risks of hazardous substances for human health and the environment. Alternatives to hazardous substances should be pursued when equivalent properties (especially safety properties) are available at acceptable economic conditions. This should be done considering the necessary time for certifying certain equipment under accidental conditions, in accordance with regulatory requirements on nuclear safety (Directive 2009/71/Euratom). In doing so, we are merely emphasizing a requirement of the REACH regulation itself, which states that any new restriction "must take into account the socio-economic impact, including the availability of alternative solutions" (Article 68).
As far as the proposed restriction on PFAS is concerned, not only the nuclear sector but also the entire electricity sector would be affected due to the essential presence of PFAS in equipment necessary for the proper functioning of installations in this sector (such as photovoltaic panels, rotors for wind power, electrolysers and fuel cell applications for hydrogen production, heat pumps thermal and decarbonized thermal, batteries, switchgear, etc.).
In the nuclear sector, as in many other industrial sectors, the presence of PFAS-containing equipment in installations (e.g., seals, lubricants) serves important functions, particularly for heat and corrosion resistance, and contributes more broadly to the safe production of low-carbon electricity (e.g., sealing, operation of backup pumps, safe transport of radioactive materials enrichment process of uranium).
Then, the implementation of the proposed restriction, without specific derogations or exclusions, would immediately impact the maintenance of nuclear power plants, their safety and the production of low-carbon electricity in Europe. The deployment of new low-carbon generation capacities would also be affected.
Additionally, there are risks:
• of manufacturing relocation for activities requiring the use of PFAS in the production process but not present in the final product (e.g., uranium enrichment process that requires PFAS not found in enriched Uranium: possibility of importation into the EU without domestic production capability)
• to lose the capacity to produce (separation and enrichment) stable isotopes for health care (cancer diagnostics and treatment), as well as for industrial applications (semiconductors, by using gas centrifuges)
• to lose main parts of the enriched uranium products supply chain for 21 countries who decided to go for nuclear as an option to reduce CO2 emissions
• Maintenance of electrical networks (cables)
Besides, it is important to consider and expand upon the concept of “essential uses” for the society, as proposed in the European Commission’s communication of October 14, 2020, titled “Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability Towards a Toxic-Free Environment”, which provides for a phasing out the use of PFAS in the EU, “unless their use is essential”. This concept is also mentioned in a 2022 article by Glüge et al., which acknowledges that the utilization of PFAS in industrial processes can be highly intricate, requiring a comprehensive evaluation of the technical functionality of each PFAS compound and the suitability of alternative substances.
The nuclear energy industry plays a crucial role in helping the EU achieve its decarbonization objectives. It currently supplies about a quarter of the EU's electricity and nearly half of its low-carbon electricity, making it an essential contributor to the EU's energy transition. Moreover, the nuclear sector enhances the EU's energy security by reducing dependence on third countries. As the EU engages in ongoing discussions about enhancing the competitiveness of net-zero technologies and strengthening energy resilience, the nuclear sector emerges as a critical player. It is vital to safeguard this role by ensuring uninterrupted access to essential components and substances necessary for nuclear operation in a safe manner, especially in the form of fluoropolymers and fluorinated gases.
With regards to fluoropolymers, several studies (Chemours, 2021; Henry et al., 2018; EPA, 2021) have found that they do not pose significant risks to human health or the environment. These studies demonstrate that the majority of fluoropolymers meet the OECD criteria to be classified as "polymers of low concern" (PLC). Therefore, it is recommended to exclude these fluoropolymers from the list of PFAS affected by the proposed ban. The UK government, for instance, has already decided to exempt fluoropolymers, along with other groups of chemicals of lower concern, from their forthcoming PFAS restriction proposal. Despite this classification of low concern, the nuclear industry considers further research into the possible risks of fluoropolymers to be important.
As a consequence and considering nuclear energy as essential for society, in particular to secure electricity supply and to fulfil decarbonization objectives, the PFAS restriction should provide a special regime for any article or mixture containing PFAS that contributes to nuclear facility safety, electrical supply security, or low-carbon electricity production.

This circuit must always remain available, and its unavailability leads to preventive reactor shutdown. In practice the RIS circuit utilizes mostly PTFE-based Teflon tape (15,530 pieces consumed between 2018 and 2022) and specific PTFE-based stainless steel washers (252 pieces consumed between 2018 and 2022). • The EAS circuit is the Containment Spray System circuit used in case of an accident to spray soda ash in the upper internal part of the reactor building to neutralize radioactive gaseous iodines emanating from a breach in the primary circuit. This circuit must always remain available, and its unavailability leads to a preventive reactor shutdown. The EAS circuit mostly uses PTFE-based Teflon tape (12,696 pieces consumed between 2018 and 2022), ERTAFLUOR plates based on Teflon specific to the EAS circuit (31 pieces consumed between 2018 and 2022), sets of PTFE-based rings and seals (141 pieces consumed between 2018 and 2022), and subassemblies of seal-bearings for EAS injection pumps (75 pieces consumed between 2018 and 2022). • The TPA speed control circuit's main objective is to maintain a certain water level in the steam generators. It is an essential circuit for steam production to power the turbine. The TPA circuit mostly utilizes PTFE-based Teflon tape (15,576 pieces consumed between 2018 and 2022) and specific ERTAFLUOR plates based on Teflon for the TPA circuit (38 pieces consumed between 2018 and 2022). • In addition, concerning polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF)-based seals, 5,800 O-rings were consumed between 2018 and 2023 for all circuits combined, including a significant number (1,500) on equipment or circuits qualified for accident conditions. On the other side to strong or total ban of PFAS may have some unwanted consequences such as significant deterioration of the quality of life, the introduction of some regrettable substitutes, or may have a great negative impact on the scientifical, technical, or medicinal development of EU.

Instead of a ban, other ways should be introduced in some economic sectors to prevent or at least reduce the release of PFAS into the environment. In my personal opinion it is neccessary first to identify economic sectors where the use of PFAS does not significantly affect the utility of the products and the sectors where the use of PFAS is crucial. In the first group of sectors the ban is reasonable, and should be introduced stepwise, but in the second a system of consistent collection and recycling or safe destruction of waste PFAS, should be established and used throughout the product's life cycle from production to final removal from use.

An example of the economic sectors where the use of PFAS is critical is certainly the use in pharmaceuticals. A fluorine atom is small and can be compared in size to a hydrogen atom. In biologically active compounds, it can thus replace a hydrogen atom without significantly changing the steric interactions. In addition to its favorable size, replacing of hydrogen with fluorine in the molecule drastically changes the chemical properties of the molecule due to its electronegativity and low-lying C-F bond orbital. In the case of active substances, this is mainly reflected in increased interaction with target enzymes and higher lipophilicity, which significantly improves the biological availability of active substances. Since fluorine atom forms a strong C-F bond with carbon, it is strategically attached in pharmaceuticals to certain sites of planned compounds, as metabolic enzymes have a harder time metabolizing such compounds. Thus, the active ingredient stays in the body for a longer time before being excreted, which makes it more potent . This properties of fluorine atoms makes also compounds with CF3- and -CF2- structural moiety (which are actually PFAS) very useful as active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs). (sources: a) E. P. Gillis, K. J. Eastman, M. D. Hill, D. J. Donnelly, N. A. Meanwell: Applications of Fluorine in Medicinal Chemistry. J. Med. Chem. 2015, 58, 8315–8359. b) D. However, if we want to ensure the full availability of such medicines also in the EU area, it is necessary to ensure that the production of both medicines and the active ingredients needed for this medicines will also be fully enabled in this area. This is only possible if it is also possible to access and use the starting materials, intermediate compounds and reagents and they could be processed to the final medicine.

The influence of the PFAS ban is even more drastic if we take in consideration that at the moment the unimpeded and high-quality production of both active substances and medicines is currently only possible by using equipment that contains key elements (gaskets, seals, filters, sometime even vessels or piping) made mostly of polymeric PFASs, which have become dominant due to their universal resistance, and often also the only suitable material for making equipment.

Further, it is crucial to enable unhindered development of synthesis processes of reagents, intermediates and future active substances. Obstructing any of these may make the production of such a medicine in the EU impossible, and the result will be that the production and the development of new APIs will be carried out outside the EU. The final effect may be periodic drug shortages or even complete unavailability of certain drugs, even further consequence would be a significant decline in EU economic activity and a decline in inventiveness in the field of pharmacy in the EU. Some of these effects are well known to us from the recent times of the COVID epidemic.

Consumables for the production of pharmaceuticals - The production of pharmaceuticals requires, among other things, a wide variety of consumables (e.g., sterile filters). Intermediates and precursors for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals - The indefinite exemptions proposed in the restriction proposal relate to the active ingredients themselves and do not cover their manufacturing process. Excipients as components of medicinal products and combination products - In some medicinal products or combination products, PFAS-containing coatings are considered excipients as part of the medicinal product or combination product itself, even if they are partially removed before use (e.g. protective films in transdermal systems). Likewise, PFAS-containing coatings are used in primary packaging materials. It is therefore imperative to implement open-ended exemptions for all PFAS-containing components in pharmaceutical products or their primary packaging. Sufficient time must be allowed for exemptions. After all, if the need for an exemption is seen but then defined to an insufficient degree in terms of time, the goal of ensuring patient care cannot be achieved. Content: Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits
Combined Comments:
General Comments: In principle, a regulation to protect the environment for perfluorinated substances is welcomed. Nevertheless, ECHA overlooks the following aspects in the current draft ban:
1. industrial use of the substances; predominantly useful and harmless versus use in products for end consumers; limited usefulness/replacement.
2. distinction between low molecular weight PFAS and polymeric PFAS; polymeric PFAS are mandatory in many industrial applications.
Polymeric PFASs are essential for almost all applications under high pressure and temperatures and cannot be replaced. Applications include seals, for example. With a combination of a required high flexibility (low elastic modulus and high elongation at break) and demanding application parameters, there is no substitute material for fully fluorinated polymers. These include high-performance polymers such as PTFE, PFA, PVDF, PEEK, Polyimde, PPS, etc.
High-conductivity polymers and polymeric PFAS are enablers for numerous applications in the energy sector, sealing technology for hydrogen applications and other future energy technologies that are part of/the basis for the energy transition (European Green Deal).
Based on all these facts, the following solution is preferable to a blanket ban:
1. the benefit of a PFAS application must be greater than the risk of environmental contamination. PFAS applications in question include coated kitchenware, cosmetics, etc.
2. polymer PFAS should and must be exempted from the ban for industrial applications for existing and new technological advances. The materials are irreplaceably necessary for the energy transition, physiologically neutral and harmless to living beings. This is proven by the use of PTFE in the pharmaceutical and food industries, some of whose products are used inside the body (e.g. stents).
3. attention must be paid to the environmentally compatible disposal of the materials by recycling or incineration.
At the end of life/production scrap of high-performance polymers and polymeric PFAS should apply:
1. products made of polymeric PFAS (PTFE, PFA) or elastomers (FKM, FFKM) must be collected, recycled or disposed of in an environmentally sound manner. Accumulation of the materials in nature must be prevented. The recycling process is explained later in the consultation paper.
2. contamination of the environment must be excluded in the production of polymeric PFAS. This has not been ensured in the past; despite existing possibilities.
Polymeric PFAS are without more advantageous alternative for industrial applications, also and especially for the energy transition. These include sealing applications that reduce leakage, the energy sector with electrolysers, fuel cell membranes, solar modules or other future technologies. In the further use of the materials, environmentally friendly production and disposal should preferably be ensured through recycling.
Conclusion: The use of polymeric PFAS in the industrial sector outweighs the risk of contamination. Polymeric PFAS (PTFE, PFA, PVDF, FKM, FFKM etc.) are to be excluded from the blanket ban of ECHA!
• Already now, polymeric PFAS contribute to higher tightness and lower leakage. A ban is a step backwards in environmental impact.
• Applications for the energy transition would be almost impossible, as no alternative materials exist in the future either. This applies to fuel cells, hydrogen applications, electromobility, etc.
• Environmentally sound recycling processes and disposal is possible.
• Polymeric PFAS are not a hazard for animals and humans, even mandatory for medical and pharmaceutical products.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Manufacture [E.2.1.] - Sector as a whole Energy Sector [E.2.12.] - Sector as a whole The NEA Group is a manufacturer of, among other things, compressors, electrolysers and corresponding equipment in a wide variety of applications. Common to all applications is that sealing solutions for industrial applications are used in the products. The equipment used (seals, etc.) are designed for industrial applications, guarantee operational reliability and are irreplaceable for sealing efficiency, especially regarding environmental protection. The problem includes both leakage to applications that national and international policies for the energy transition as a solution. Example: Hydrogen applications instead of fossil fuels. Alternative sealing solutions for hydrogen applications will not be available with the required properties in the future. Sealing solutions are mandatory for the entire and safe H2 value chain (transport, storage and filling). In addition, many hydrogen compression applications are/will be used to replace fossil fuels. Further essential application examples, also for the energy turnaround, can be found in biogas plants, applications of electrolysers and many more. The sealing elements in these industrial applications are based on fluorinated polymers (PTFE). On the part of ECHA, these use cases of this essential industry have not been considered. Polymeric materials must be kept available for industrial applications for safe operation, environmental protection and in view of the energy transition.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The sealing elements are used by NEA Group in various industrial products, including the hydrogen value chain, biogas applications and other industrial services.  The sealing elements used in the industrial application listed here are made of PTFE. The manufacturing processes are optimized to such an extent that the material utilization is almost optimal. Waste and costs are minimized as far as possible. Sealing elements used in compressor systems exhibit wear of about 20% of their original volume during operation. The 20% wear ends up as tiny particles in the gas during operation and is bound there. No uncontrolled leakage into the environment. During maintenance and servicing work, the sealing elements (remaining 80%) are removed. Depending on the application and contamination of the material, a recycling process can be connected. Alternatively, proper disposal takes place. Landfilling should be avoided in the future to prevent the accumulation of fluorinated polymers in the environment. Due to the large number of suppliers, it is not possible to state the actual quantities of PTFE used in the products.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: No harmful low molecular weight PFAS is formed when PTFE is burned. This fact can be found in studies in the scientific literature. PTFE decomposes into carbon dioxide and HF during combustion. HF, in turn, can be converted into flour spar (CaF2) by a filter.  In this regard, the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (www.kit.edu) offers further information on the subject.  Conclusion: The disposal of PTFE by incineration is possible and harmless. Recycling of PTFE is preferable to disposal.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: In some cases, the recycling of materials with PTFE is already installed in the process at the suppliers. Here it is obvious to integrate all suppliers into a recycling process. Companies are established on the market that also offer a grinding service for recycling.  Possible value chain Recycling process:  1. waste must be collected sorted by type 2. particle size reduction to 20-30 microns 3. powder blending process; mix ground material with new material 4. manufacture of new products from recycled material Based on feedback from suppliers, the cost of recycled material is similar to new material, so a recycling process is an obvious alternative to an impending ban with all its environmentally damaging consequences.

5. Proposed derogations: As a customer of the industry affected by the PFAS ban, only limited information on volumes and emissions is available.  Data from one supplier is available: • 50 tons of gasket material/year (PTFE) for rotating machinery and reciprocating compressor applications only. • 70% PTFE content, therefore 35 tons for production, 30% of it waste from processing. • Approx. 25 tons used as sealing elements in industry. Considering the recycling possibilities, the waste from industrial processes is reduced to a minimum. Under the exemption of PTFE from the ECHA ban, a safe and environmentally friendly industry would still be possible, which also serves the energy transition. Details of other suppliers are not currently available.

6. Missing uses: The ban of PTFE materials, e.g. seals, is a decision against future energy supply, energy transition and protection of the environment. Explanation follows: The application of sealing elements is elementary in rotating and reciprocating equipment, among others. These include compressors, pumps, motors, etc. As already explained, out of 50 tons of PTFE material, at most 5 tons are lost through friction and wear. It is still important to remember that PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) is FDA approved and can be used in the pharmaceutical and food industries without hesitation. No environmental pollution is expected from worn sealing elements. For disposal, a recycling process is preferable to incineration. PTFE and highly fluorinated polymers, as a unique material, offer low friction and low wear under difficult operating conditions. Difficult operating conditions include high pressure, high temperature, and high speed along with universal chemical resistance such as compressors. PTFE and highly fluorinated polymers are a unique material that offers low friction and low wear under difficult operating conditions. Difficult operating conditions include high pressure, high temperatures and high speeds along with universal chemical resistance such as compressors. There are and will be no alternatives for PTFE and highly fluorinated polymers with roughly similar properties. This is due to the unique strong C-F bond.  Regarding the socio-economic aspects, a distinction must be made between component supplier, machine/equipment manufacturer and end user. Component supplier: Globally, there are about 40 companies for sealing solutions for rotating and reciprocating equipment, compressors and pumps. Of these, approximately 5 companies are located in Europe.  Machinery/equipment manufacturers: In Europe, there are approximately 10-20 compressor manufacturers offering small to large compressors. Neuman & Esser is one of the leading manufacturers in the market. The number of rotating equipment manufacturers is much higher. All products require PTFE-based seals for optimum sealing efficiency.  End users: the number of end users is impossible to capture in numbers, as rotating and reciprocating equipment is needed in almost every industrial process. To name a few examples:  • Hydrogen compressors for H2 pipeline transportation and refueling stations. • biogas plants • CO2 plants (breweries) • PE production • etc.  It follows that a ban on PTFE-based sealing materials will have a profound impact on production processes until they are shut down and on the industrial efficiency of European companies. Particularly noteworthy are the negative consequences for the environment due to higher leakages and shorter maintenance intervals including replacement of components. Fluorinated high-performance polymers (PEEK; PPS; PI, etc.) are also not an alternative, as these polymers do not form a tribo film on the mating surfaces of the sealing applications. Only PTFE materials form a tribo film. The tribo-film ensures higher operational reliability and lower environmental contamination due to low friction and low wear rate. The "tribo-film" is well known in the scientific literature. It can be read in the literature as well as proven by experimental tests that low wear and low friction forces are only given with a sufficient "Tribo-Film". The supplier STASSKOL is active in materials development and has proven with appropriate tests that the formation of the tribo-film is exclusively reserved for PTFE materials. It is further stated that the running times of the sealing elements without tribo-film are reduced to a multiple. The leakage rates of the systems increase by a factor of 3.5 when PEEK materials are used. The higher emissions are released 1:1 into the environment; this is particularly serious in the case of Co2 and methane plants.  Reduced running times, higher leakages and increased emissions lead to a low available plant, which in turn leads to uneconomical operation and affects the environment.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Currently, ECHA does not foresee any exemption for PTFE-based sealing materials for rotary, reciprocating and diaphragm compressors, pumps and electrolyzers.  No alternatives to PTFE-based materials exist now or will exist in the future because they are based in the polymer molecule.

8. Other identified uses: For PTFE, no alternatives exist now or in the future. Evidence of this can be found in the available literature and tests by suppliers to the sealing industry, see STASSKOL. A ban on polymers PFAS and PTFE has enormous consequences on many levels, not for the best. Of the consequences, environmental protection (e.g. higher leakage, tighter maintenance), European industry, especially future technologies such as hydrogen, electrolysis, etc. are significantly affected. Not to mention the socio-economic impacts.  Evidence can be found in the annex of the consultation.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: There are no alternative materials for sealing elements now or in the future. Only PTFE-based sealing elements provide reliable, safe operation in rotating equipment, pumps or reciprocating compressors, achieve minimal leakage and the highest level of environmental protection.  As already explained, PTFE material can be largely reprocessed and reused in the recycling process. The small percentage of materials that end up in the environment are polymeric. These polymeric materials are classified by the FDA as "generally recognized as safe" for the environment, food and pharmaceuticals. Polymeric PTFE is harmless to the environment and life because it is chemically stable and not expected to degrade.

10. Analytical methods: Recycling of PTFE is possible. For example, one of the suppliers, STASSKOL with partner, has established a recycling process for fully fluorinated polymers. Experiences and information on the recycling process can be communicated, shared and sustainably established in the industry. An established recycling process is preferable to a general ban on these essential materials.  Fluorinated polymer materials are irreplaceable, especially in view of the industry's elementary share in the climate change associated with hydrogen, biogas, electrolysers and electromobility. Sealing elements are indispensable for many sectors of the manufacturing industry and contribute great guarantees for safe and environmentally conscious operation.

General Comments: In response to risk management measures, when considering alternatives or possible replacements of PFAS, their technical suitability, costs (economic feasibility), environmental and human health impacts, and their ability to meet the relevant requirements must be considered.
{Performance criteria}
For fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers, the industry view is that there is no substitute with the required properties in many or most applications.
Fluoropolymers are widely used because they have proven chemical resistance, temperature range, durability, and vibration resistance.
Currently, there is no substitute for PTFE, which can withstand different substances, different concentrations, and operating temperatures. At this time, it is unclear whether a technically and economically viable alternative to PTFE fluoropolymer can be developed within a 12-year timescale.
Fluoropolymer materials such as PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) have excellent chemical resistance, temperature resistance and low friction resistance.
The material, also known as fluoroelastomer FKM, is suitable for gaskets because it is highly resistant to chemicals such as hydrocarbons, acids and bases and  can withstand temperatures of up to 200°C.
{Food and Beverage Applications}
Non-stick and chemically inert, therefore associated with regular cleaning and disinfection processes, the quality of food and beverages in contact is not adversely affected.
Regulated fluoropolymers include substances that do not need to be regulated in terms of their impact on human health and the environment, but which would have a significant negative impact on the social economy if regulated. Examples include PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene), PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride), and FKM (fluorine elastomer).
Fluoropolymers (1) do not enter the human metabolic system and do not cause accumulation problems in the human body, (2) have a long lifespan and low waste generation. (3) Fluoropolymers are used for important applications in society, are non-fungible, and have a significant negative impact on the social economy if regulated.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: In response to the consultation on the Restriction on the manufacture, placing on the market and use of PFASs in the EU, the Royal Society of Chemistry (RSC) is submitting three documents for reference: our policy position on Risk based regulation for per- and poly-fluoroalkyl substances, our policy position on PFAS in UK drinking water, and our report When the science is uncertain, what is the role of risk-based approaches and precautionary control in chemicals policy?
A summary of our approach to chemicals regulation and PFAS follows:
To direct risk assessment in the most useful, efficient, timely and relevant way there needs to be (i) criteria for prioritising those substances that require a full scientific safety evaluation and (ii) a pragmatic way of performing a risk assessment for a single PFAS or ideally for a PFAS that is defined as representative of a group/category of PFAS. Banning all PFAS on persistence alone would take little scientific resource but could have massive unintended consequences for society with loss of important products and disruption of vital processes. Similarly doing nothing, when we have good evidence of the toxicity of some PFAS, is not an option as we must protect public health and the environment.
A framework based on a multi-step ‘traffic-light’ decision-tree approach around PFAS use in society and on the basis of safety risk and impact assessments may be useful for regulatory action. We put forward a green, amber, and red list approach (further explained in the policy position) to take appropriate regulatory action based on a defined level of acceptable risk according to an agreed set of criteria, as defined by the regulator working with science advisory mechanisms within government. This approach is designed to be proportionate, iterative, and agile, to ensure it accounts for evolving scientific evidence on PFAS.
We do acknowledge and agree with the need to take a precautionary approach where the science is uncertain, and the lack of toxicity and exposure data for many PFAS makes this concept applicable. The idea of essential use may be useful here, and it is included as a step in our risk assessment framework. The following could be considered when applying the essential use concept:
• An authorisation system could be used for essential uses.
• Uncertainty should not prevent action if there is some evidence of harm.
• Regulate chemicals in groups to increase efficiency.
• Transparency from industry will make regulation using the essential use concept more efficient.

However, care should be taken in banning PFAS without understanding the alternatives (which also may be manufactured at less than 1tpa and thus be missed by REACH regulation) to avoid unintended and potentially worse consequences from the use of other more harmful or equally persistent substances. There should be a continuous review of the alternatives used to quickly identify new evidence on safety.

We have also attached our policy position on PFAS in drinking water. Although partly covering the case for tighter drinking water standards in the UK, it is relevant to the regulation of PFAS because it recommends that companies that manufacture or use PFAS should be required to submit data to a central and public database. Compiling such data in a central and accessible database will allow regulators to make decisions based on complete information about the sources of PFAS. It is also important for companies to have better knowledge of their own PFAS use to fully control emissions. Requiring annual reporting will increase awareness in company management of the potential benefits and harms of PFAS use, transparency with regulators and the public, and opportunities to phase out PFAS and/or substitute to other substances. Regardless of the outcome of the proposal to ban PFAS, this action could be implemented in support of other PFAS control policies.

The RSC works with a broad network of scientists in industry, academia, and government with expertise in this area, across Europe and globally. We would welcome any questions on our position or requests for more information.

About us
With about 50,000 members in over 100 countries and a knowledge business that spans the globe, the Royal Society of Chemistry is the UK’s professional body for chemical scientists, supporting and representing our members and bringing together chemical scientists from all over the world. Our members include those working in large multinational companies and small to medium enterprises, researchers and students in universities, teachers, and regulators.
