Combined Comments:
General Comments: In response to the invitation to provide comments to the restriction on the manufacture, placing on the market and use of PFASs, the Polish Chamber of Chemical Industry (PIPC) would like to express, its position and concerns regarding the implementation of such  broad restriction.

Below we provide our detail coments in regard to three usses identified by our members. It is essential to recognize that while the current regulatory proposal incorporates a certain level of detail, it only reflects a fraction of the current use of PFAS. The proposed restrictions will significantly impact numerous products and supply chains, as PFAS are used in various ways across many industries. This complexity is further exacerbated by the unprecedented number of substances within the PFAS group covered by the proposal.

We would like to emphasize that within the scope of such extensive restrictions, the industry encounters difficulties in fully identifying all potential uses, particularly when PFAS are utilized as components within more intricate systems or installations. Therefore, we advocate for the necessity of introducing a time-unlimited derogation for spare parts in critical industrial applications ex. (In sealing elements used in applications where high resistance to aggressive chemical media and demanding temperature conditions are required.) Implementing such a derogation would enable the preservation of essential industrial processes and systems that depend on the presence of PFAS in vital components.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Please find below comments in reference to specific uses:   I) Use in foam blowing agents in PU spray foam. There is limited evidence for finding substitutes for foam blowing agents in PU spray foam. So far, no non-PFAS alternatives have been developed in our sector. While water-blown foam is employed, it serves as a chemical alternative only, and its insulation capability falls short of that provided by physical blowing agents. For instance, dimensional stability deteriorates when using water-blown foam. Additionally, hydrocarbons are not as effective in this applications. We assert that non-PFAS alternatives to fluorinated gas blowing agents, such as cyclopentane, isobutane, and pentane, are unsuitable due to concerns related to fire performance (high explosion risk), energy efficiency (inferior insulating properties), and durability (diminished dimensional stability). They do not match the same level of thermal performance, potentially necessitating a thicker layer of foam, which could be counterproductive to energy-saving objectives. We propose that the potential derogation period for foam blowing agents be reconsidered and extended to a minimum of 10 years.   The PFAS foam blowing agents that we use are not considered persistent, bioaccumulating, and toxic (PBT), nor are they classified as very persistent and very bioaccumulating (vPvB), as indicated in the Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) provided by major supplier.  Furthermore, based on a review conducted by the Environmental Effects Assessment Panel (EEAP) (please find attached a summary of the findings on the following website: https://www.fluorocarbons.org/news/eeap-2022-tfa-yields-from-hfcs-and-hfos/), the TFA yield from the processing of used HFO is estimated to be at 2%.  II) Industrial use of HFC’s as refrigeration agents in the large cooling systems by high tonnage in chemical production sector.   The derogations did not encompass the industrial applications of HFCs as refrigerants in the large-scale chemical synthesis industry. In many chemical synthesis facilities, extensive refrigeration systems, often involving multiple tons of HFCs, are utilized as refrigerants to significantly reduce the processing and storage temperatures required for specific chemicals, such as the storage of organic peroxides. HFCs are widely used in the chemical synthesis process due to their physicochemical properties, in particular the fact that they are not classified as flammable, oxidizing or toxic to workers. This is very important in a situation where the production installation contains a number of other raw materials, semi-finished products, auxiliaries and final products classified as posing a risk to human health and the environment.  Currently, available alternatives to large-volume equipment containing HFCs are limited to ammonia and propylene. Based on the conducted analyses, the use of non-flammable refrigerants such as CO2 is not feasible in standard compressor refrigeration circuits due to their physicochemical properties, specifically their critical point, which is at 31°C and 73.7 bar. Given the current parameters of the cooling water from the fan cooling tower used for transferring condensation heat to the environment, achieving the required pressure in the condenser and compressor discharge at approximately 73 bar would be necessary. Such elevated pressures would demand pipes and pipelines approximately five times thicker than those currently in use, such as those employed for propylene refrigeration units. Furthermore, the compressors and heat exchangers would need to be considerably larger to operate effectively under such high pressures, and standard versions of such equipment are not readily available in the market.  The capital expenditures required for implementing this solution would be approximately six times greater than those for propylene, and the cost of electricity consumption would be nearly twice as high as that for propylene-based refrigeration circuits for cooling water and other media down to 5°C.  Both alternative substances, anhydrous ammonia, and propylene, are classified as flammable. Additionally, anhydrous ammonia is categorized as toxic by inhalation (Category 3). The transition from a refrigerant not classified as flammable to one classified as flammable presents a substantial technical, technological, and financial challenge for manufacturers. The adoption of refrigerants like ammonia or propylene will result in the creation of new explosion hazard zones within technological installations, introducing risks to personnel safety, the environment, and property. It's essential to consider the current legislation regarding HFCs, specifically Regulation (EU) No 517/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 April 2014 on fluorinated greenhouse gases, which includes measures to replace high Global Warming Potential (GWP) HFCs (e.g., R-507A) with other HFCs having significantly lower GWP values. Given the existing restrictions, it's possible that any ongoing efforts to replace HFCs with more environmentally friendly HFCs must be halted, and the investments made so far may be rendered ineffective.  In light of the planned inclusion of restrictions on all HFCs (regardless of GWP factors), there is a need to develop an investment plan that takes into account alternative refrigerants such as ammonia and propylene. Furthermore, addressing the challenge of introducing additional substances that pose the risk of major industrial accidents, as defined by Directive 2012/18/EU OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 4 July 2012 on the control of major-accident hazards involving dangerous substances, will be a long-term and highly complex process.  The introduction of new restrictions and the necessity for many users to comply with these restrictions will lead to extended investment cycles. This is primarily due to the limited number of entities supplying refrigeration equipment based on ammonia or propylene in the market. The manufacturers' capacity to meet the demands of users may not keep pace with the increasing need. Simultaneously, the decommissioning of a large number of units within a short timeframe will pose challenges in the disposal of refrigerants. Consequently, these refrigerants may be stored in tanks or other equipment for extended periods and may gradually leak into the atmosphere until they are ultimately physically decommissioned. This situation underscores the importance of carefully managing and addressing the transition to alternative refrigerants to minimize environmental impacts. In order to minimize the risk of a major chemical accident, emissions resulting from the storage of withdrawn refrigerants and also the restrictions of the equipment manufacturers' market, the process of planning the replacement of refrigerants should not take place under time pressure and be adequate for the entry into force of such restrictive restrictions. Due to broad safety concerns, we are requesting a 12-year deferral of the derogation of the use of HFCs as refrigerants used in the chemical industry, which will allow manufacturers to more effective prepare for the replacement of refrigerants with non-HFC's. As mentioned above, currently available alternative replacements increase the risk of a major chemical accident at production installations in the chemical industry and their implementation should be spread over time. An additional important element is the fact that the current equipment containing a large amount of refrigerants (greater than 500 T/eqCO2) has a continuous detection system for accidental release, and in addition the leakage inspection of the equipment is carried out at least once every 6 months (a legal requirement), which significantly minimizes accidental release and ensures that the HFCs in use are used under strictly controlled conditions with a low likelihood of accidental release. To minimize the risk of a major chemical accident and address the challenges associated with the storage of withdrawn refrigerants and limitations in the equipment manufacturers' market, the process of planning the replacement of refrigerants should not be rushed and should align with the effective implementation of these restrictive regulations.  III) Hydronic heat pumps for residents  Based on the AnaFgas analysis, which models only one technological sector, based on an 11 kW air-to-water heat pump. This analysis assumes that from 2024 to 2036, 97% of these heat pumps can use propane (100% by 2025). PIPC supports the concerns of the European Partnership for Energy and the Environment (EPEE) regarding the possibility of using F-Gases containing PFAS in:  Air-to-water heat pumps with 11 kW power. (a) Only outdoor monoblock hydronic heat pumps can safely use propane. In the case of split hydronic heat pumps and ground-source heat pumps, the use of propane will be very limited due to safety constraints. EPEE's modeling assumes that heat pumps in residential buildings will quickly move away from R-410A and HFC-134a and use a combination of refrigerant solutions, including propane, but also many other lower-GWP refrigerant options, including HFC-HFO blends. (b) In 2021, only a small portion of domestic heat pumps sold in the EU used propane (less than 10%). A report published by Umweltbundesamt (the German Environmental Agency) included a forecast for propane use in heat pumps in Germany – in 2030, the estimate was 30%, which is much lower than the 100% value used in AnaFgas. EPEE agrees that most outdoor monoblock pumps can transition to propane, but it will take time and a gradual phase-out. EPEE's modeling assumes that outdoor air-to-water monoblock heat pumps can transition to propane by around 2030. There is a rapid shift away from R-410A, mainly towards HFC-32, followed by a gradual increase in the use of propane in monoblock pump systems and a slower increase in the use of HFO-HFC blends in split system types (slower because more technical development is required).  Air-to-air conditioning and heat pumps less than12 kW: (a) Modeling the entire important and large market sector using only one technology type is unrepresentative. EPEE's modeling includes six sectors (three sizes: 3.5, 7, and 12 kW; two configurations: single split and multi-split). The optimal choice of refrigerant depends on the size and configuration. (b) This market has already transitioned from R-410A to HFC-32, and the sale of air-to-air devices using propane in the EU is close to zero. It is possible that within a small size range for single-split devices, propane will gain some market share, but the transition will require significant technological development and subsequent technician training. A transition by 2027 is not a realistic forecast. For multi-split devices and larger sizes (above 6 kW), the optimal choice of refrigerant is still difficult to predict. EPEE's model assumes a transition to lower-GWP HFO-HFC blends instead of propane, ensuring safety while achieving maximum energy efficiency. This view is supported by the Commission's analysis of refrigerants in split-type air conditioning systems (presented in the 2020 document), which found that while propane can be used in systems below 7 kW, for larger systems, propane is not suitable, and HFC use (the Commission assumes HFC-32, with an expectation of a future shift to lower-GWP HFO-HFC blends) is still necessary. (c) Transitioning to HFC-32 would require more than 10 years of development. Further transitioning to propane and/or HFO-HFC blends is technically more complex than transitioning to HFC-32. (d) Some published reports and recent presentations oversimplify this market and contain erroneous statements about the potential use of propane in the market for air-to-air devices less than12 kW. The EPEE organization has published three documents stating that these assumptions are unrealistic (e.g., the analysis of the GIZ report).  Air-to-air conditioning and heat pumps greater than12 kW  AnaFgas models two technological sectors, based on a 30 kW rooftop unit and a 27 kW VRF system. EPEE models four sectors, including two significantly larger options (150 kW RTU and 100 kW VRF) in addition to small sizes similar to those proposed by AnaFgas. There is a significant market for heating and cooling in commercial buildings using air-to-air devices greater than12 kW. If larger device sizes have not been adequately considered in the model. The AnaFgas estimations of the HFC quota will be too low. All these larger systems cannot use propane and will require other less flammable alternatives with lower GWP. The above examples clearly show why EPEE's modeling points to the need for a larger HFC quota.

General Comments: In response to the public consultation on the proposed PFAS regulation (hereafter referred to as the regulation) published by the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) in March 2023, we hereby submit our opinions as follows:
Our company uses fluorinated ethers as part of the refrigerant in our cryogenic heat exchange system. We primarily utilize 3M's Novec7000*1, Novec7200*2, and currently considering the usage of China's Noah7000A*3, Noah7200*4. These refrigerants are not classified as hazardous substances and are typically used within enclosed space as refrigerant sealed with inert gases. Our system is equipped with safety system which works in various conditions; when there are volume changes due to temperature fluctuations, any pressure drop is automatically supplemented with inert gas, and excess pressure is released by relieving inert gas through a dedicated automatic exhaust line.
Additionally, these refrigerants exhibit excellent fluidity and insulation properties at low temperatures, making them widely used in the manufacturing of pharmaceutical raw materials, chemical products, semiconductor materials, and various other applications with no alternative option available at the moment.
As it is deemed to be save for environmental and non-toxic according to the test result of Safety Data Sheets (SDS) for these refrigerants, we believe that these refrigerants should not be target of PFAS regulation.
Despite the lack of sufficient data to appropriately assess the impact on human health and environment caused by substances subjected to PFAS, current regulation proposal indicates a direction to prohibit the manufacturing, marketing, or use of "PFASs" solely based on their chemical structures. (Currently, regulation proposal evaluates PFAS substances to have "hazardous properties" due to their characteristics of low degradability and high persistence, but lacks empirical evidence of the harm to human health or the environment). We believe that instead of a full ban on the production, marketing, or use of all "PFASs," a more sensible approach should be applied; assessing the risks based on scientific evidence for each individual substance and banning only substances that clearly harm human health and the environment.
We further believe this sensible approach should be applied as REACH regulation proposal also stipulates that restriction(s) or amendment(s) might be made if there are unacceptable risks to human health or the environment arising from the manufacturing, marketing, or use of substances. (We especially believe that substances with high molecular weights, such as fluoropolymers, should not be subject to regulation as these substances practically insoluble in water so it is hard to be absorbed into human body and have no confirmed harmful effects even in pure liquid form)
A full prohibition on the production, marketing, or use of "PFASs" will affect economic and society significantly. Eliminating "PFASs" from the market in a situation where alternative substances are difficult to come by could disrupt global supply chain and international trade of products containing PFAS. Additionally, this regulation will add additional burdens for the identification and development of alternative substances to various companies within unreal and short time. Considering these uncertainties and additional burdens, it is not wise to adopt a regulatory approach that apply full ban over a thousand different "PFASs."
As mentioned above, we believe it is crucial that the scope of regulation is limited to substances that have been assessed for their impact on human health or the environment based on scientific evidence, taking into consideration the economic and societal implications. Moreover, the selection of substances subject to regulation should be made carefully, considering a wide range of knowledge, including opinions from public consultations, and assessing the availability of alternatives. Additionally, necessary measures should be taken to allow for the exclusion of substances from regulation or extensions of grace periods if it becomes clear after the implementation of the system that there are significant impacts on the economy or society, or if the development and social implementation of alternative substances cannot be sufficiently anticipated during the transition period.

The following topics will be dealt with:

1. Industrial emissions data
Attached to this document we have provided an excel file (named: "1. Industrial PFAS Emissions data Flanders") with the latest industrial emissions data from the Flemish region. This data specifically covers measurements from 2020 until 2022, for earlier data we refer to previous communications to the DS.
The following data can be consulted in the excel file:
- Overview of the total PFAS emissions per site measured over the last years
- Yearly emissions of PFAS from the different companies
- PFAS concentrations found in the waste water of the different companies
In the first tab of the excel file you can find a short explanation of the different tabs.

An important factor to take into account with this data is that it clearly links the emissions of specific PFAS with specific sectors. For each emission point the company name is provided, as well as the NACE code, thereby linking the emissions with the sector of use and production.
Interesting to note is that if one looks at the total PFAS emissions from 3M over the years, one can clearly see that the total emissions have drastically been reduced, from almost 264 kg in 2020 to less than 1 kg in 2022. This drastic reduction proves the effect of imposing strict management measures on PFAS production and use sites. It must be noted that part of this reduction is explained by the temporary stop of production during 2021 and 2022, however this only further substantiates the effectiveness of a full ban on PFAS. This data thus clearly shows that limiting the production and industrial uses of PFAS would be an effective measure to reduce the emissions of PFAS into the environment.

2. PFAS Pollution mapping – EU wide risk
Since the discovery of the large scale PFAS pollution around the 3M site in Zwijndrecht (BE), the Flemish regional authorities have been working on mapping al potential sites of PFAS pollution in the region. The result of this work can be consulted on the Flemish PFAS site (https://www.vlaanderen.be/en/pfas-in-flanders). Most of the identified sites are related to the use of fire-fighting foams (training sites and incident sites), however several sites have been indicated based on industrial activity and legacy landfill sites in Flanders. On some of these locations high PFAS concentrations are being found, even if the industrial activity or landfilling has been stopped for some time. One can also see on the Flemish site that so called “no regret measures” have been defined for the majority of the potential pollution sites. These measures are meant to prevent exposure to PFAS as much as possible, for example by advising against eating vegetables and eggs from home gardens and not letting children play on the ground.
The long lasting presence of PFAS in these polluted sites, as well as the measures that need to be taken to prevent exposure at these sites, clearly illustrate how PFAS can pose a problem to society for long after they have been used or disposed of.
Recently the Forever Pollution project (https://foreverpollution.eu/) has illustrated that this problem is not limited to Flanders alone, and that pollution sites of PFAS can be found all over the EU. If one would extrapolate the no regret measures implemented in the Flemish region to these other sites around the EU, one cannot argue the fact that these substance pose an EU wide risks, and that emissions should be minimized as fast as possible.
The region of Brussels has also conducted measurements on several potential pollution sites, a press release with results can be found via the following links:
https://press.environment.brussels/des-pfas-retrouves-sur-5-sites-en-region-bruxelloise
https://press.environment.brussels/pfas-gevonden-op-5-sites-in-het-brussels-gewest
The Walloon region is also investigating potential pollution sites. At the moment 16 polluted sites have been identified, mainly with sources from use of firefighting foams, but also linking to industrial activities like textile and paper production.

3. Air emissions from incineration plant
In 2022 waste incineration company Indaver has conducted measurements on the air emissions of PFAS from their incineration plant in Antwerp. The study has been requested by the Enforcement Section of the Department Environment (AHH) and under the guidance of the Flemish Environment Agency (VMM) and the Agency for Care and Health (AZG). Indaver is known for processing PFAS waste from PFAS producing compagnies. The full study is attached to this comment (named: "3. PFAS Air Emissions study Indaver_2022").
The results from this study indicate the high uncertainty that still remains on the effectiveness of incineration. In this report it is insinuated that not only the incineration stage can be an emission point, but also the prewashing stages can generate PFAS emissions. It must be noted that these PFAS emissions are potentially generated due to contaminated groundwater that is used for the prewashing step. This indicated that the whole process of waste incineration – including prewashing steps – should be carefully considered when looking at incineration as a method to dispose of PFAS containing waste.
In the study indications have been found that PFOS does not completely degrade during the incineration process. The Flemish authorities have been conducting follow-up studies together with Indaver to further look into the exact ways at which PFAS can be emitted during the incineration process, therefore we might come back at a later stage with more information on this subject.
Furthermore there are indications that the incineration of PFAS waste at this particular site is generating ultra-short chain PFASs, which pose a concern since they might contribute significantly to the total Belgian emissions of greenhouse gasses.

4. Study on PFAS in Belgian household textiles
The Federal Public Services of Health and Environment have commissioned a study on the use of PFAS in home textiles industry in Belgium. For the study chemical suppliers, textile producers and traders have been surveyed on the use of PFAS in their products. This study shows that PFAS have been largely phased out in home textile uses. However for the following uses PFAS are still being used:
- Use in outdoor furniture and furniture for boats. It has been confirmed by the supplier of these products that alternatives are being developed.
- Use in textile wallpaper for the contractors market. PFAS are used for cleaning and removing glue from the wallpaper. For this use no alternatives have been identified yet, although this use only covers limited (high-end) applications.
- Care sprays in shoes, coats and bags. These products were found to be strongly PFAS based.
Furthermore, the study indicates that alternatives are available for water repellent properties, however for dirt repellent industry indicated that alternatives are less readily available. The full study report has been attached to this comment (named: "4. Eindverslag_Gebruik van PFAS voor huishoudtextiel in België_finaal").

5. Human biomonitoring around 3M site
The Flemish authorities have conducted a local HBM study on teenagers living near the 3M PFAS production site in Zwijndrecht. The study looked at the presence of PFAS in humans (blood sampling) as well as the presence in house dust and in gardens and eggs etc. A total of 303 teenagers were included, all living within a 5 km radius around the 3M site for at least 5 years. The study showed that exposure to PFOS was significantly higher compared to the mean exposure in Flanders, with only 1 in 4 teenagers having safe levels. PFOS, PFOA and PFHxS were found in all blood samples and PFNA, PFBA and PFDA in most samples.
The study also showed that main exposure routes are the location (closer to 3M equals higher exposure), consumption of eggs and locally grown vegetables and fruits, but also other sources like use of lubricants and to a minor degree house dust. Especially consumption of eggs was found to be the highest exposure route (of PFOS specifically).
Lastly, the study also investigated the link with PFAS exposure and health impacts. The results show that there are clear links between PFAS exposure and the immune system, as well as  effects on growth and puberty. Higher exposure to PFAS was linked with a lower amount of immune cells, as well as higher risks for infections and suppression of the immune system. Furthermore, PFAS exposure was linked with a slower growth and delay of puberty. No signs were found for abnormal development, however the delay in growth and puberty confirm the endocrine disrupting effect of PFAS.
More information and the full study report can be found on the study website:
https://www.hbm-pfas.be/resultaten/

In 2022 the Flemish Institute for Technological Research (VITO) has finalized a study on the presence of PFAS in seafoam. Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: In the Annex XV report “Proposal for a restriction of Per- and polyfluorinated substances (PFAS)” several structural exclusions based on evidence from scientific literature are formulated concerning substances which can mineralize under decomposition of the perfluoro moiety: “A substance that only contains the following structural elements is excluded from the scope of the restriction:CF3-X or X-CF2-X’, where X = -OR or -NRR’ and X’ = methyl (-CH3), methylene (-CH2-), an aromatic group, a carbonyl group (-C(O)-), -OR’’, -SR’’ or –NR’’R’’’; and where R/R’/R’’/R’’’ is a hydrogen (-H), methyl (-CH3), methylene (-CH2-), an aromatic group or a carbonyl group (-C(O)-).).”
The authorities noted that the restriction proposal is not entirely based on sufficient comprehensive data and, therefore, further input from the industry is necessary to fill knowledge data gaps. According to the OECD definition a large variety of molecules are considered to be PFAS and, thus, are in scope of the EU restriction proposal. Although several structural elements are excluded, the restriction as suggested has a massive impact on many sectors, but industry has only a period of six months to comment on uses and degradation pathways. Depending on the complexity of the supply chain, the consideration of all use conditions is difficult within the consultation period but the generation of scientific data on potential degradation pathways is impossible. We are facing a variety of structures having a variety of metabolites which would need to be analyzed by using a suitable degradation test and development of new analytical methods to provide scientific evidence. Therefore, we screened literature for missing degradation pathways of further molecules which should, in our opinion, also be excluded from the PFAS restriction.
The set of groups which are already excluded from the EU PFAS restriction comprises for example methyl, methylene and aromatic moieties, but does not contain the methine group (-CH-). From a chemist’s point of view, aromatic groups are generally more stable compared to methine groups. Thus, a CF2-O- group adjacent to a methine group should mineralize more readily compared to a CF2-O- group adjacent to aromatic groups. We screened literature for potential degradation pathways of cyclohexanes and branched alkyl chains to provide a basis for the exclusion of methine groups from the proposed PFAS Restriction. Based on examples found in literature, the degradation of methine groups adjacent to the -CF2-O- moiety can lead to carbonyl compounds which are already considered for an exclusion because of their ability to fully degrade to CO2, H2O and HF, leaving no persistent fluorinated organic metabolites.

9. Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: In the Annex XV restriction report for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs), there is mention of propellants and there being substitution potential, so I would like to reiterate the importance of using R1234ze as a propellant in our industry.

We are a GB-based manufacturer of spray adhesive aerosol dispensers and canisters (chemicals under pressure) who export into the EU. To achieve a safer, non-flammable classification, we need to use R1234ze in our formulations. For adhesive products, it is not as simple as replacing the liquefied propellant with compressed gas, such as nitrogen and carbon dioxide, as the high viscosity and cohesive properties of the adhesive need liquefied propellant to break up the particles to achieve the required spray. The expansion from liquid to gas gives the mechanical break up necessary to spray the adhesives in an even film, important for good and permanent bond strength. The application of adhesive is just as critical as the adhesive properties itself. Alternative delivery systems such as bag-on-valve are not suitable as they do not provide this mechanical break-up. Another essential property of using the liquefied propellant, R1234ze, compared to compressed gases, is that the pressure of the product is maintained throughout use due to the equilibrium which is maintained between the vapour and liquefied phases. In a compressed gas aerosol or chemical under pressure, the pressure drops significantly towards the end of the product, meaning it no longer functions as required and results in product waste or poor adhesive performance.

A specific example of using R1234ze as a propellant in spray adhesive applications is in polyurethane foam application. R1234ze is used as a blowing agent to give the polyurethane the correct cell structure on application. It is important that the polyurethane expands and foams for gap filling properties and to increase surface area for adhesion. Alternative blowing agents are flammable, such as R152a, pentane, dimethyl ether and liquefied petroleum gases, so they are not suitable for use where non-flammability is required. Blowing agents are covered in the restriction report but not in relation to spray applications.

The main propellant used in the aerosol industry is liquefied petroleum gases (LPG). Restricting alternative PFAS propellants would mean increased use of LPG from North sea gas fields, which may be worse from an environmental view. Within our company, 9000kg of R1234ze was used in 2022, which would be replaced with products containing LPG if R1234ze was restricted.

In the attachments, I have included video evidence to demonstrate that R1234ze is necessary to achieve non-flammable spray adhesive with the required spray quality:
Aerosol A – A combination of R1234ze and compressed gas
Aerosol B – Compressed gas only
In both examples, the adhesive is the same and the pressure of the aerosol can is the same, but as can be seen in aerosol A, R1234ze gives a wider, even spray pattern. In Aerosol B, the adhesive is sprayed as a bead. Applying the adhesive as a bead will cause uneven coverage leading to weak spots. The thicker spray will also lead to increased drying time and not allowing the adhesive to dry fully will cause adhesive failure. When working over large areas, a narrow spray is not practical either as will take longer to apply.

Summary:
1. The exemption for technical aerosols (‘where non-flammability and high technical performance of spray quality are required’) is required as there are no alternative non-flammable liquefied propellants.
2. The exemption should also apply to ‘chemicals under pressure where non-flammability and high technical performance of spray quality are required’. Chemicals under pressure are effectively larger versions of aerosol dispensers, so the exemption should cover both.
3. Include a comment that the PU foam blowing agent exemptions includes sprayable applications.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Propellant

6. Missing uses: Missing use: propellants in chemicals under pressure for non-flammability and/or high technical performance of spray quality. The associated PFAS is R1234ze.  Chemicals under pressure make up 80% of sales within our company and up to 20% of that is exported into the EU. Currently, we use 9 tonne a year of R1234ze which is critical for 5% of the business. This is expected to rise due to the need for reduce the flammability of our products.   At present, there are no other non-flammable liquefied propellants alternatives that can be used in sprayable adhesives.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Information on alternatives
Combined Comments:
General Comments: In the Annex XV restriction report, certain exceptions to the restriction proposal are noted for some applications. For example, active pharmaceutical ingredients containing PFAS are explicitly excluded from the restriction proposal, which we strongly support. However, this exemption only refers to the active pharmaceutical ingredient and disregards raw materials, precursors and intermediates required in the manufacturing processes for pharmaceutical products. In the case of pharmaceutical manufacturing, the entire manufacturing process should in our view be exempted from the restriction, so that manufacturing in the EU is still possible, also taking into consideration second sourcing requirements and stock out scenarios during COVID-19.

Please find attached detailed information related to our companies manufacturing process.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: All comments are related to the production, manufacturing process of active pharmaceutical ingredients.   The dossier sets out exemptions from the restriction proposal for some applications. For example, active pharmaceutical ingredients are explicitly excluded from the restriction proposal, which is very much to be supported. However, this exception only refers to the active pharmaceutical ingredient and does not take into account the necessary raw materials, precursors and transported intermediate stages. In the case of very complex and multi-stage manufacturing processes, the entire manufacturing process must also be expressly excluded from the restrictions, so that production in the EU is still possible.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Pharmaceutical manufacturing can be divided into different life-cycle phases:  1. Production of raw materials,  2. Processing of raw materials into active pharmaceutical ingredients,  3. Processing of the active pharmaceutical ingredient into a dosage form, 4. Further packaging of finished product, 5. Use of the medicines by the patient.  As manufacturer of active pharmaceutical ingredients and finished products, only the phases 2, 3 and 4 will be dealt with below.  There is no risk during further processing of the active pharmaceutical ingredients into a finished product, because: 1. The production takes place under the high standards of GMP manufacturing.  2. Any dust that occurs is filtered out of the exhaust air by filter systems.  3. Waste is fed into a thermal waste disposal process.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The legal requirements for handling of waste are laid down and described in numerous legal regulations. For the disposal of hazardous waste, disposal permits (see above), disposal certificates must be available in accordance with the requirements of the Closed Substance Cycle Management Act. It describes the waste and the permitted disposal facility. The supervision and approval of such evidence is the responsibility of the competent authority. Monitoring of waste disposal facilities by the competent authorities covers all processes, i.e. from the reception of waste to storage and incineration to the emissions emitted.   In combustion processes of 800 to 1000 °C, an emission of PFAS, especially the trifluoroacetic anhydride, is avoided.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Baseline Information on alternatives Information on benefits Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: In the context of electrolytic PEM ozone generators for pure water production and storage, the use of a few fluoropolymers and fluorinated ionomers cannot be avoided. Due to the anodic evolution of hydroxyl radicals, ozone and other reactive oxygen species, an ionomer with an extraordinary (electro-) chemical resistance is required and the scientific literature does not indicate any substance class that would be able to cope with such harsh conditions except for fluorinated ionomers such as Nafion™. In order to provide pure water for the semiconductor and pharmaceutical industry, the use of highly oxidative-resistant construction materials in aqueous media is required. We therefore intentionally source fluorinated polymers (PTFE, FEP, FKM, Nafion™) without any processing except for PTFE and value them for the following reasons:

- Extremely high resistance to radical species, ozone and other reactive oxygen species
- Hygienic low-friction material avoiding microbial adhesion
- High resistance to gas permeability (safety issue)
- Low electrical resistance (efficiency)
- Long-term mechanical stability contributing to longer part lifetimes

As the selected construction materials are used in a closed, clean environment, an even partial release of PFAS as degradation products is avoided due to strict regulations derived from international pharmacopoeia. A re-use or recycling of the produced parts has already partially implemented in our company.

We apply for the exclusion of the substances mentioned (Fluoropolymers, fluorinated ionomers and highly fluorinated sealing materials) from the PFAS ban, as there are no alternative materials both in research or production.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: In the Annex XV restriction report (Table 9), we do not find our products represented. In the area of semiconductors and electronics, we do find hints given for PEM fuel cells, which differ in their operation compared to PEM electrolyzers. Membranes used in fuel cells can be operated under moderate conditions and allow for a substitute material known from current literature. In contrast to that, the mentioned PEM electrolyzers intentionally produce larger amounts of oxidants which are known to rapidly disintegrate any known membrane materials except for poly- or perfluorinated ones.    We apply for the inclusion of PEM electrolyzers onto a list of derogations.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: During the production of ozone generators, several (per-)fluorinated compounds are processed. In total, the mass of all fluorinated materials makes up approx.. 300 kg/a:   PTFE: Main compartment of electrolysis cell: subtractive manufacturing, valued for chemical resistance and electric isolation.   FKM/FEP: Sealants requiring the same high chemical resistance in a pressurized and oxidative aqueous environment.   PEM/Nafion™: As a core material, this ionomeric membrane serves as the solid electrolyte in the water purification process that can withstand the in situ produced and highly concentrated, reactive oxygen species.   During manufacturing, PTFE is used as a pre-material and subtractively processed. Waste emerging during this process is collected and disposed by a specialized waste disposal company. The aim is to prevent any release into the environment.   During use, emissions from the manufactured products are below the limits given by international pharmacopoeias. (Pharmacopoea Europaea, United States Pharmacopeial Convention, Japanese Pharmacopoeia).   End-of-life phase: Fluorinated components are collected for an intended re-use or recycling process. In direct marketing for product distribution, this has already been implemented. Regarding fluorinated components from products sold by distributors/intermediaries, the responsibility for the accurate disposal is currently left to the end consumer.

5. Proposed derogations: With the low tonnage mentioned in request 2, it is possible to beneficially treat large water volumes with the lowest possible usage of fluorinated construction materials As with industrial partners, a thorough return or recycling system is already being implemented, a tracking of the produced parts is possible and enables a correct disposal or even re-use.   Concerning emissions, a strict PFSA ban would force pure water plants to return to hot water storage and sanitization which is inherently tied to enormous amounts of precious energy compared to the currently used, energy-efficient cold water storage.

6. Missing uses: a) 300 kg/a fluoropolymers, fluorinated ionomers, sealants (Innovatec alone)   b) The polymer electrolyte membrane poses as the key component of the PEM electrolyzer for ozone evolution. At the anodic interface to catalytically coated electrodes, an especially harsh environment is produced to achieve significant amounts of dissolved ozone for the subsequent process of water purification. Reactive oxygen species (i.e. hydroxyl radicals) emerge during this process and affect all construction material nearby. As a result, the construction materials in an ozone-evolving PEM  electrolyzer must be especially resistant against these extreme oxidative conditions. Accounting for the electrolytic part of the ozone evolution, the insulating properties of the materials are appreciated and constructively considered.   c) In the field of electrolytic ozone production, only a few companies are directly affected by the PFAS ban concerning the production of ozone generators. However, a large branch of the entire industry and economy relies on the production and storage of sanitized process water. The specific value of ultrapure water is estimated to grow from 1.8 to 3.9 B USD annually (2021 – 2030) (Ultra-Pure Water Market: Information by Application (Cleaning, Etching, Ingredient), End-User Industry (Semiconductor, Pharmaceuticals, Power Generation), and Region – Forecast till 2030, Straits research https://straitsresearch.com/report/ultra-pure-water-market).   d) In the past, the most widespread alternative for pure water storage was the so-called “hot storage” with water kept at 75°C. Nowadays 20°C cold water is doped with up to 50 µg/L ozone as “cold storage”, consuming orders of magnitude less energy. Due to the currently tense situation in energy supply, wasting unnecessary amounts of precious energy is unfavoured and the cold storage is preferred. Additionally, ozone is also the disinfectant of choice whenever other chemicals (e.g. chlorine) cannot be introduced into processes for various reasons.   e) At the current state of R&D, no other chemical class of materials except for fluorinated materials provide a sufficient resistance to the harsh oxidative environment while sustaining a suitable ion conductivity that is required in the extreme conditions of electrolytic ozone generation. Current research evaluated the most promising substitute materials that are perfectly fine for fuel cells with the conditions that emerge during water electrolysis. The membranes degraded within hours (even in the absence of ozone) which shows that long term stability is the crucial part that cannot be resolved without the use of fluorinated membranes. Additionally, non-fluorinated membranes - which are often SPEEK-based - suffer from a comparably low conductivity at the desired, moderate temperatures of 20°C. (Salleh, Muhammad Taufiq, et al. "Stability of SPEEK/Cloisite®/TAP nanocomposite membrane under Fenton reagent condition for direct methanol fuel cell application." Polymer Degradation and Stability 137 (2017): 83-99.), Sarirchi, Somayeh, Soosan Rowshanzamir, and Foad Mehri. "Simultaneous improvement of ionic conductivity and oxidative stability of sulfonated poly (ether ether ketone) nanocomposite proton exchange membrane for fuel cell application." International Journal of Energy Research 44.4 (2020): 2783-2800.    f) N.a.   g) A PFAS ban without the derogation for PEM electrolyzers would lead to an immediate end of the electrolytic ozone generation for process water sanitization. In consequence, cold water storage cannot be applied in the future and will have to return to highly energy consuming sanitization processes. This in turn would also lead to increased production costs resulting in a migration of industrial plants to other, non-regulated countries.  However, the migration of high tech companies would hold against the EU’s aims and strategies to de-globalize supply-chains which was a direct result from the global economic crisis during the COVID-19 pandemic. For this exact purpose, agreements such as the European Green Deal und European Chips Act were signed. A restriction and ban on PFAS in the current version would negatively affect these agreements. By a sensible and deliberate use of PFAS in certain applications, the emission into the environment can be successfully avoided or at least reduced to a minimum by the implementation of e.g. return and recycling processes. This ecological aspect would be enabled by the addition of PFAS in PEM electrolysis applications onto the derogation list.

8. Other identified uses: In the current proposal, PEM electrolysis as a whole is not considered and therefore not listed in Table. 8.  As stated in the sections above, there is no perspective for a substance class that may replace fluorinated ionomers in the future in the application of PEM electrolyzers, especially intended for ozone evolution. We consider a derogation for PFAS in the context of PEM-based ozone generators justified, as small amounts of traceable and recyclable PFAS allow for a beneficial mass production of pure water in the various applications already mentioned.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: In the context of the discussion and evaluation regarding the possible ban of PFAs, we would like to take a stand against a ban in which the fluoroplastics PVDF, PTFE, FKM and FEP are excluded from Annex XV. The EXNER control valve type 650 is used as the subject for the report. In this case, the valve body is made of either PVDF or PTFE, the O-rings used for sealing are made of FKM or FEP and the bellows are made of PTFE. The broad spectrum with regard to the areas of the applications and the properties that only fluoroplastics can cover, is discussed. This will be done in order to describe the justification for use of the fluoroplastics mentioned and to show the impossible substitution of these materials with supposed alternatives.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: please see attachment "1:Sectors and sub uses" in Sector IV

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Use/application: If used properly and within the application limits, there is no risk of fluorine compounds escaping from fluorine-containing plastics during their service life. Due to the strong chemical bond of fluorine to carbon, fluoroplastics are very inert and exhibit high temperature stability (measured against other plastics and comparable materials for common industrial applications).   End-of-Life phase: Customers have the option and are encouraged to return the control valves at the end of their service life so that the plastic components they contain can be recycled. This is possible without significant restrictions, if the components are properly returned, as thermoplastics can be mechanically and/or thermally reprocessed due to their molecular structure and the interaction of the polymer chains.

6. Missing uses: a) Annual tonnage and emissions please see attachment "Annual tonnage" in Section V  b)  The key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use Control valves with valve bodies made of PVDF or PTFE are used to regulate the volume flow and are of fundamental importance for numerous industries and applications.  Due to their high chemical resistance to acids combined with high temperature resistance, these materials are indispensable for use in steel pickling, for example. As soon as highly concentrated sulphuric or hydrochloric acid is used here, other materials reach their limits in terms of chemical resistance. This also contributes to the longevity of the product, which prevents regular replacement of the valves. This in turn contributes to the conservation of resources and enables a more environmentally conscious implementation when planning industrial plants.   With fluoroplastics, a high degree of purity can be realised in the production process. Control valves with PTFE valve bodies are therefore also used in the pharmaceutical and chip/semiconductor industries. The materials that come into contact with the media must not contain any metal particles, as these can escape during the process and be released into the media. Impurities with metal particles cause defects in the wafers that are produced in the semiconductor industry. Furthermore, fluoroplastics are anti-adhesive, which avoids residues of the medium on the component surface. This is of great importance when precise dosing quantities of the media are required. PVDF is also highly resistant to hydrofluoric acid, which is a commonly used chemical in the semiconductor industry.  The control valves are also needed in the water treatment process. The chemical resistance of the fluoroplastics is also needed here for the implementation of the process.  When controlling the volume flow of media containing chlorine, control valves with valve bodies made of PTFE are also used, as other materials tend to form stress cracks when they come into contact with chlorine.  c) The number of companies in the sector estimated to be affected by the restriction please see attachment "Companies that are affected by the restriction" in Section V  d) Possible alternatives  In the following paragraph, alternative materials or products for selected elements of the control valve are discussed. The discussed products are already used in industry or are traded as potential replacements for fluoroplastics.  Research is currently being conducted on UHMW-PE bellows. However, these are not a universal substitute for critical applications involving highly concentrated chemicals and high temperatures. The operating temperature of UHMW-PE for such applications is 80°C at max. The operating temperature of PTFE in conjunction with control valves with PTFE valve body and PTFE bellows is 140°C at max. The chemical resistance of UHMW-PE is also much more limited than that of PTFE. PTFE is resistant to almost all chemicals, including highly concentrated acids and alkalis at high temperatures. The few exceptions are molten or dissolved alkali metals and hydrocarbons containing fluorine. According to previous experiences, UHMW-PE can be used as bellows for low concentrated acids and alkalis. However, in contrast to PTFE, bellows made of UHMW-PE must be excluded from highly concentrated acids and alkalis due to a lack of chemical resistance.   Furthermore, PE is flammable and drips off while burning, whereas PTFE is non-flammable. When using PTFE, this enables an additional elimination of a potential source of danger during the use of the product.  It is thus clear that when considering the complete spectrum of applications, which includes applications in high temperature ranges and contact with aggressive chemicals, UHMW-PE does not yet represent an adequate alternative to PTFE for the use of bellows.   With regard to the valve bodies, it is possible to manufacture metallic valves made of for example tantalum or of nickel alloys (e.g.: Hastelloy). Metals that are not specially treated tend to corrode when they come into contact with aggressive chemicals and are therefore not suitable for chemically demanding applications. Metal valves with appropriate treatment have the necessary chemical resistance and thermal resistance for the processes described, but there are still reasons for disqualification. The very high energy input in manufacturing compared to plastics and the high weight argue against their consideration as a permanent substitute to fluoroplastics. The energy expended in melting the metals due to the high melting temperatures of metals (approx. 1000°C to 1500°C) is significantly higher than with plastics (melting temperature PVDF = 165° - 180°C  melt temperature during injection moulding approx. 220 °C - 300°C). Machining is also significantly more energy-intensive due to the high hardnesso oft her metals. The following illustration shows the comparison of energy consumption in production between common metals and common plastics. Although the fluoroplastics mentioned are not explicitly listed here, the comparison of energy consumption in production between metals and plastics is very clear.    For mentionted illustration please see attachment "Figure 1 energy comparison metals and plastics" in Section IV   The high weight of metals also requires higher amounts of energy during transport due to the consumption of fuel and requires additional support structures during operation, which also consume resources.  Since every company should pursue a policy that conserves resources as much as possible so that naturally occurring raw materials are also preserved for future generations, products made of plastic should not be indiscriminately substituted by very expensive metals for the reasons mentioned.  e) Indication of why there are no alternatives See above. In summary: Chemical resistance, temperature resistance and purity.  f) Cases, in which substitution is technically and economically feasible but more time is required to substitute No comment possible, since there is no adequate substitution   g) Socio-economic impacts • Control valves with PVDF/PTFE are important products for the implementation of customer-specific requests and the identity of the product portfolio of the company FRANK GmbH. A discontinuation would lead to a loss of sales and a shrinking of the product portfolio. This could potentially lead to the loss of jobs of various employees. • Since in case of a ban, the needs of the industries mentioned can not be met anymore, projects will also be cancelled by customers, which will affect employees in the same way on both sides.  • Technological decline in the German sector of the e.g.: semiconductor industry since the processes cannot be realised without fluoroplastics as already explained. This can lead to a strong gap between Germany and other countries in the area of technological advancement and economic growth.

General Comments: In the current discourse surrounding potential regulatory restrictions on various materials, it appears that our specific market segment—revolving around the usage of compact chlor-alkali electrolyser units for disinfection with a lower CO2 footprint—has not been addressed.

The core of our units relies on Fluoropolymers: PTFE, PVDF, FKM, and Fluoropolymer-based Nafion™ ion-exchange membranes, which are indispensable in the manufacturing and functioning of these units. They do not degrade into smaller PFAS are not mobile, bioacumulative or toxic and therefore should be treated differently.

A blanket restriction would not only compromise advancements in our sector but also inadvertently elevate the CO2 footprint due to reliance on less efficient alternatives. Hence, we advocate for a more nuanced approach in the regulatory landscape, one that distinguishes between materials based on their actual impact and their indispensable role in promoting sustainable technologies.

We strongly urge an exemption for the use of Fluoropolymers such as PTFE, PFA, FKM, and PVDF, and Fluoropolymer membranes in the chlor-alkali industry, as there are no functional substitutes available. We would support the concept of a reporting portal for yearly amounts used.

Org. name: Japan Ship Machinery and Equipment Association
Combined Comments:
General Comments: In the current draft, it is pointed out that there is technical evidence on the sea and on land for alternatives to CO2 and NH3 refrigerants for transport refrigerators, so a derogation period is not required for marine use, but this is a misunderstanding. CO2 and NH3 refrigerant are used as refrigerants under certain conditions, but there are technical and safety hazards for using them on all ships, which are not easy to solve.

CO2 refrigerant is used in limited fields such as heat pumps on land, but the pressure as a refrigerant is very high. There is a suffocation hazard in enclosed spaces on board in the event of a leak. It is very dangerous to use it in accommodation areas where people are present on ships where it is difficult to evacuate from overboard. It is never used in marine refrigeration equipment and air conditioners. In addition, since both CO2 and NH3 systems become large, there is an impact on economic efficiency, such as a decrease in cargo loading capacity.

NH3 refrigerant, which can be used in a wider range of fields than CO2, is more toxic than CO2 and is flammable. Strict leakage countermeasures (see attached ship classification regulations, 　yellow highlighted part of ClassNK RULES FOR CARGO REFRIGERATING INSTALLATIONS and DNV Rules for Classification) are required for its use, and its use on ships is extremely limited. NH3 refrigerant is used in large-scale freezing and refrigerating systems where crew members do not stay for long periods of time, such as the refrigerated holds of fishing boats and refrigerated carriers.(See attached files “News ammonia leak 1 & 2”) For this reason, NH3 refrigerant is not used in air conditioners and refrigerators in the accommodation area.
It is unimaginable to use a refrigerant in the accommodation area that is not only toxic, but also emits an objectionable odor even with the slightest leakage. In trucks, railroads, etc., which are used in an open space, it is possible to release leaked toxic gas to the atmosphere or to evacuate outside the vehicle. Different from other modes of transportation, the indoor and outdoor units of the ship's refrigeration system are both installed on board, and there is a risk of toxic refrigerant leakage, which has resulted in fatal accidents. The use of systems with inherently toxic NH3 refrigerants in confined spaces onboard commercial ships is dangerous and another safe alternative must be developed. Regulation of transport sector refrigerants in the maritime sector is difficult as there are currently no safe alternative refrigerants available.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: In the industrial system of Ningxia Huayu Chemical Co., Ltd, the production of chlor-alkali by ion exchange membrane method is the most front-end and basic part. It is the most important link in the entire company’s industrial chain, which provides basic raw materials for downstream printing, dyeing and chlorine consuming fine chemicals. As the basic condition of our company's operation and survival, the production of chlor-alkali by ion exchange membrane method is the basic condition of providing high-quality products to the world, and the ion exchange membrane process has huge economic and safety advantages compared with the diaphragm process. Different from the ion exchange membrane method, the main equipment used in the diaphragm method is a diaphragm electrolyzer, which is characterized by a porous permeable diaphragm separating the anode chamber and the cathode chamber, and the diaphragm prevents the passage of gas, but only allows water and ions to pass. This can not only prevent the hydrogen produced by the cathode from mixing with the chlorine gas produced by the anode to cause an explosion, but also avoid the reaction of chlorine gas with sodium hydroxide to produce sodium hypochlorite and affect the quality of caustic soda. However, the investment and energy consumption of the diaphragm method is high, and the product caustic soda will contain impurities salt. At the same time, the asbestos diaphragm is short-lived and carcinogenic, seriously polluting the environment. In addition, compared with ion exchange membrane method, the main equipment of the mercury method, electrolytic cell, is composed of electrolytic chamber and mercury chamber, which is characterized by mercury as the cathode, obtaining electrons to produce liquid sodium and mercury alloy. In the mercury lysis chamber, sodium amalgam reacts with water to produce sodium hydroxide and hydrogen. The biggest disadvantage of mercury method is that it will bring mercury pollution to the environment, so this method has been gradually reduced, and there have been many pollution accidents around the world (a major pollution poisoning accident occurred in Japan).

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis
Combined Comments:
General Comments: In the last months a bitter dispute evolved about planned PFAS restrictions. The main argument was "There are PFAS-tensides, which are dangerous. But there are also PFAS substances, used inside machines, like PTFE and flouro-elastomers, which did not cause problems, are not spread in the environment, are not replaceable in a lot of tasks, and which might be forbidden, too - and these ECHA guys show no sign of understanding".
My background: Working for some 30 years as an engineer and designer for long-living machinery.
I know the discussion about using PTFE and flouro-elastomers for static seals (like O-rings) and dynamic seals (like shaft-seals). The PFAS-seals are more expensive than others, usually with a factor of 3. So the economists in the firm wanted us, not to use them.
But they are better with respect to longevity and resistance. So they are preferred when machines shall be leak-proof and long-living.
At the end of their life, after 10 000 to 100 000 hours of operation, these parts go into a melting furnace or (less often) into a waste incineration, both with filtering of exhaust gases (which will be improved in future).
A transition time will not be a help - there has been a search for alternatives with similar endurance for decades - but the problem of lower heat resistance, lower resistance to aging (embrittlement / loss of elasticity) higher coefficient of friction etc. of other substances could not be solved.
If there is a concern about new PFAS substances, a look to a successful former legislation would help:
When coloring substances for food were developed some 150 years ago, several substances were dangerous.  Banning only those substances, found to be dangerous, was not helpful. Legislation was improved, Only substances with a good record of being harmless were allowed for coloring food.
What about a list of PFAS substances with a good record of being harmless ?
(perhaps with an easy, low-cost test that no tensides from their production evade from them)
For larger parts made from PFAS (like big membranes in hydrogen electrolysers to be built)
a "bottle deposit" rule like that for lead-acid batteries might be a solution.
And, after all: Banning seals made of PFAS would be a disadvantage for the EU-industry compared  to imported machines. It will NOT be practical to analyse the seals inside imported machines. There may be declarations - but remember all these goods from unknown companies in China imported to the EU. Some of them have a declaration and follow the rules. Other have a declaration and do not follow the rules (for example about lead) - and nothing happens, no effective control, no fine.
With best regards

Content: Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues
Combined Comments:
General Comments: In the regulatory process under PFAS' "REACH restrictions", it was stated that exemptions would be widely sought.

The exemption proposals submitted in the public consultation will be decided after they have been deliberated, but it can be imagined that the deliberations will be like a simplified examination of authorization approval under the REACH Regulation, and can also be understood as an integrated process of authorization and restriction.

This is related to the description in Annex XV, in particular "2.2.2. Discussion of possible regulatory measure".

Therefore, with regard to PFAS restrictions, I would like to propose that an approval process be established so that proposals for exemptions can be accepted and deliberated even after the proposed restrictions have been finalized.

This also alleviates the possibility of unnecessary socio-economic impacts on PFAS restrictions due to the difficulty of ascertaining their use, and provides a forum for dialogue with stakeholders.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: In the restriction proposal is no risk related differentation between PFAS in consumer products (where unnecessary PFAS could be substituted) and PFAS in the industrial sectors with crucial applications without any idea of a substitute.  In the industry the risk for human health and the environment is controlled and there are protection measures implemented already since many years.
In our company - which is the only European manufacturer of III-V semiconductors - only the Fluorpolymer subgroup of PFAS is present in the infrastructure and in components of the equipment (e.g. PTFE). This is the result of the development in more than 50 years and established state-of-the art. If their functionality and process stability are not given any more due to material changes (no stable PTFE inside) we cannot produce semiconductors.
A transitional period is useless at a time when not yet even an idea of an alternative substance exists.
We ask for an exemption for the use of Fluorpolymers for industrial applications as described above.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Semiconductors

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: manufacture phase: Fluorpolymers , mostly PTFE , are present in the infrastructure (e.g. pipelines) and equipment (e.g. sealings, etching tanks) only. They do not react with the crystals and wafers produced . Hence, they are not part of the final products. The emission of PFAS/PTFE at industrial stage is zero.  use phase: III-V semiconductors are present in special electronic components with very low quantities (µg) and encapsulated e.g. in amplifiers in a mobile phone. These compounds do not contain any PFAS. For that reason the emission volume of PFAS via III-V compounds in the use phase is zero.  end-of-life-phase: If parts made from PTFE have to be replaced during maintenance the removed pieces are disposed off according to legal requirements via an accredited special waste company. No emission into the environment.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: end-of-life-phase: If parts made from PTFE have to be replaced during maintenance the removed pieces are disposed off according to legal requirements via an accredited special waste company. No emission into the environment. The incineration is managed by a special accredited company for waste management.

5. Proposed derogations: In our company PFAS - Fluorpolymers are used in infrastructure and equipment only. These are highly standardized parts and components which are replaced only when they are defect or according risk management rules. This is done during maintenance only. Their summarized weight is far away from 1 t/year (ca. 300 - 400 kg/year only). They are disposed off via an accredited special waste management company. There is no emission of PFAS in our company.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: For the use of highly standardized parts and components made from Fluorpolymers/PTFE in the infrastructure and equipment no alternatives exist - not even an idea which might be a substitute to generate the crucial stable properties needed in our processes.  Zusätzlich sei noch erwähnt, dass in den PFAS-Stoffen Verbindungen mit Fluor als elektronegativstem (reaktivstem) Atom des Periodensystems vorliegen. Genau das macht die Verbindungen so stabil. Andere Elemente mit gleicher inerter Wirkung finden zu sollen, ist nicht möglich und wird immer bedeuten, dass kurzlebigere Versionen genutzt werden müssen, die aber die Natur durch den höheren Verbrauch noch mehr belasten würden. Hier würden jedoch auch neue Risiken entstehen. Beispielsweise sind Dichtungen insbesondere für aggressive Chemikalien bzw. bei erhöhten Temperaturen immer eine Schwachstelle in technischen Systemen. Ein Versagen kann zum unkontrollierten Austritt großer Mengen gefährlicher Stoffe in die Umwelt führen. PFAS werden im Halbleitersektor wegen ihres inerten Verhaltens – sie reagieren nicht mit den Produkten (= verunreinigen sie nicht) - häufig in industriellen Anlagen in Dichtungen, Schläuchen, Leitungen, Ventilen und anderen Anlagenteilen eingesetzt. Hier tragen Sie zur Sicherheit und Langlebigkeit der Anlagen und industriellen Infrastruktur bei. Aufgrund der Rahmenbedingungen (z.B. hohe Temperaturen, hohe Drücke, extreme pH-Werte) bestehen hierfür häufig keine geeigneten Alternativen. Wenn die Beschränkung im vorgesehenen Umfang in Kraft treten würde, stünden die Unternehmen im Halbleiterbereich vor einer Vielzahl von Problemen, wenn nicht vor dem Aus in Europa. Weitere Erläuterungen finden Sie im angehängten Positionspapier des IMAT e.V.

8. Other identified uses: Socio-economic impact of this restriction proposal on semiconductor industry - please see position paper of IMAT e.V. attached: PFAS werden im Halbleitersektor wegen ihres inerten Verhaltens – sie reagieren nicht mit den Produkten (= verunreinigen sie nicht) - häufig in industriellen Anlagen in Dichtungen, Schläuchen, Leitungen, Ventilen und anderen Anlagenteilen eingesetzt. Hier tragen Sie zur Sicherheit und Langlebigkeit der Anlagen und industriellen Infrastruktur bei. Aufgrund der Rahmenbedingungen (z.B. hohe Temperaturen, hohe Drücke, extreme pH-Werte) bestehen hierfür häufig keine geeigneten Alternativen. Wenn die Beschränkung im vorgesehenen Umfang in Kraft treten würde, stünden die Unternehmen im Halbleiterbereich vor einer Vielzahl von Problemen, wenn nicht vor dem Aus in Europa: - Reduzierte Verfügbarkeit von Stoffen in Europa führt zur Verknappung von betroffenen Prozesschemikalien und Bauteilen. Möglicherweise werden im Extremfall sogar Lieferketten dauerhaft unterbrochen (z.B. durch Betriebsschließungen von europäischen KMU’s). Man würde auf Lieferanten aus nicht-europäischen Ländern ausweichen (müssen). - Mittelfristig wird die Sicherheit und Funktionalität von Anlagen beeinträchtigt, so dass die Qualität der Produkte darunter leidet. - Die durch die Substitutionsforderung entstehenden Kosten limitieren die finanziellen Mittel der Unternehmen, die in der Folge andere Ausgaben z.B. für Forschung & Entwicklung einschränken müssten. - Legal Compliance kann nicht als Preisargument gegenüber Kunden verwendet werden, d.h. die Kosten für die Substitution von PFAS sind für Unternehmen nicht auf die Produkte umlegbar. Dies schwächt die Wettbewerbsfähigkeit europäischer Unter¬nehmen gegenüber der nicht-europäischen Konkurrenz. Dies widerspräche den Zielen der REACh-Verordnung, wo der Beschränkungsvorschlag rechtlich angesiedelt ist. - Würde die vorgeschlagene Beschränkung so umgesetzt werden, könnte die Halbleiter-industrie nicht mehr im vorgesehenen Umfang und Zeitrahmen zu den Zielen des Green Deals und der industriellen Transformation beitragen. Im Gegenteil – es bestünde ein hohes Risiko für die Stärkung der europäischen Souveränität. Subventionierte Investitionen wie z.B. die Ansiedlung von Chipfabriken, die Umsetzung von geförderten innovativen Projekten wie z.B. des milliardengeförderten IPCEI ME/CT (Important Project of Common European Interest Microelectronics/Communication Technology), European Chips Act oder Critical Raw Materials Act würden torpediert. - Ganze Industriezweige, welche elektronische Bauteile verarbeiten und gesellschaftlich genutzte Anwendungen wie z.B. Automobile, Flugzeuge, Raumfahrt, Kommunikations-netzwerke (z.B. Glasfaserkabel), die Medizintechnik sowie die Verteidigungsbranche wären in Frage gestellt. Dasselbe gilt für die Tätigkeit der Forschungseinrichtungen. - Im Beschränkungsvorschlag wird für den Halbleiterherstellungsprozess eine Über¬gangsfrist von 13,5 Jahren genannt. Hier stellt sich die Frage, was genau umfasst der Begriff „Halbleiter¬herstellungsprozess“? Abgesehen davon ist es bewährter Stand der Technik in unserer Branche, die Infrastruktur und Anlagenbauteile mit Bauteilen aus Fluoropolymeren auszustatten. Alternative Stoffe müssten ähnliche Eigenschaften haben, um dieselbe Funktionalität und Sicherheit zu gewährleisten. Daher erscheint es unwahrscheinlich, dass innerhalb der 13,5 Jahre ein Substitut gefunden, getestet und qualifiziert werden wird. Ist für diesen Fall eine Verlängerung der Ausnahmefrist vorgesehen? Wenn nicht, müssten viele Unternehmen ihre Geschäftstätigkeit in Europa einstellen. - Da PFAS in den Endprodukten oftmals nicht mehr enthalten sind, sondern nur als Prozesschemikalie oder Bestandteil von Produktionsanlagen verwendet werden, wäre ein Import von konkurrierenden Produkten aus dem nicht-EU Ausland problemlos möglich. Damit wäre auch ein weiterer Kostennachteil für europäische Firmen verbunden, wenn nicht mehr mit langjährig erprobten und zuverlässigen Produktionsmethoden gefertigt werden kann. Die erheb¬lichen Zusatzkosten für die Qualifizierung von Ersatzstoffen haben diese Wettbewerber nicht. Es dürfte klar sein, was dies für künftige Investitionsentscheidungen bedeuten wird.
