Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Description of analytical methods Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: In the restriction proposal, the permitted threshold level for single PFAS has been set to 25 ppb. This level is more a contamination level than an intended quantity with functional impact. At SVHC, which are substances where the negative impact has been proven, the information level is over 0,1%wt.
The main problem at this extremely low concentration is the possibility of the supplier and sub-supplier giving a statement that their product does not contain PFAS. The only way is to perform a chemical analysis of a material sample in a specified lab.
Such kind of analysis can only be performed in the way that it is searching for a known substance, indicated for example as a peak in a GC-MS spectrogram. Then it needs to be quantified, which requires reference measurements with the same chemical substances (in this case the PFAS). Since the PFAS component, that needs to be quantified, is unknown (as only a fragment of the chemical structure is given), the quantification with a reference material will be impossible. The result of this analysis will for this not be able to guarantee that no other PFAS is above the 25 ppb level. The alternative would be to analyse and quantify the total Fluorine content, but this will not give any information on which PFAS is contained or if the Fluorine originated from chemistry containing Fluorine but not falling under the PFAS definition.

This request for extremely sensitive and expensive analytics will create a high burden, as the total quantity and the total investment for the analysis of millions of articles would be extremely high.

In our industry, PFAS is added intentionally in materials or in production processes because of specific material parameters defined by ABB or by the manufacturer of the material. The amount of PFAS added in material recipes is above 0,01%wt (100 ppm) and it is known by the material manufacturer which specific PFAS has been added to the material. These levels representing intentionally added PFAS to a production process or a material recipe will lead to the possibility of reviewing documents like recipes and/or bill of material for stating if PFAS is contained or not. The need for costly analysis will disappear. The process is much faster and does not require external resources.

It is recommended to define the permitted threshold level, for example, 0,1%wt (1000 ppm) or 0,01%wt (100 ppm), for a single PFAS in a way, that it is only covering intended use, e.g. in a mixture of components of a material.

The contamination of the environment is not based on products and articles containing extremely low levels of PFAS slightly above 25 ppb, but on substances containing a high percentage of PFAS or even pure PFAS. For this reason, a threshold level of 0,01%wt for example will not lead to a high contribution of PFAS in the environment.

Articles with very low, not intentionally added PFAS or even contaminations with PFAS are widely unknown and hard to specify. As these low concentrations will not have a functional impact, it is most likely nothing where a substitute needs to be searched for, it is more about the elimination of a contaminant from the manufacturing process if the root cause is known. Higher threshold levels would give clearer and easier controllable rules, as the PFAS content is intentional and therefore can be easily identified. In this case, replacements can and must be investigated, as the added PFAS has a technical
function.

Also recycling companies will not be able to analyse material received within the given limits of the extremely low threshold levels. 25 ppb would mean adding 25 kg of PFAS to the waste of 1 million tons. This would block a huge amount of material for recycling. Calculating this down to 1 ton of recycling material, the contamination would be 0,025 g of PFAS per ton. It is doubtful that any recycling of material will be possible until absolutely no waste containing PFAS exists, which means the complete installed base needs to be PFAS-free.

In addition, the analytics of waste material is even more complex, as it is not homogenous. In liquids and gases, it could be managed to homogenize them, but with polymers it is impossible. A mixture of materials needs to be qualified by a probe and the result is heavily impacted where the probe has been taken.

For this, ABB asks to replace the threshold level of 25 ppb per PFAS by a level of below 0,01%wt and the possibility to proof this by checking material recipes and production bill of materials and a certificate given by the manufacturer of the material or the article (as it is state-of-the-art e.g. for SVHC).

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The comment does not apply to a specific sector listed in the Annex XV restriction report (Table 9) but will be valid for all sectors and products.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: For all intentionally added materials, the emissions on the manufacturing do not differ from the proposed restriction. Also non-intentionally added PFAS are at a specific moment in time intentionally manufactured. During the use phase the differences in articles where PFAS have not been added intentionally but might exist as contamination are extremely low. For T&D products anyhow use-phase emissions are negligible. Also at the end of life, practically the difference is negligible, as if a PFAS is not intentionally added, it has no technical function and it is not planned that the article is contaminated. Somewhere in the process, the contaminant must be present because it is intentionally manufactured. It is clearly questionable why and how the contamination should occur.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: In the majority of cases, articles with no intentionally added PFAS will be PFAS-free. When the material is contaminated by non-intended PFAS, the concentration will be very low. It is quite doubtful why contamination should happen as with a wide prohibition of PFAS with intended use the likelihood of the presence of a contaminant is low.

8. Other identified uses: The process of identifying if a material or an article contains PFAS is very much influenced by the proposed change. If only intentionally added PFAS need to be identified, the identification is straightforward. Substances which are added must appear on the bill of material (BoM) or in the recipe of a material. For this, the identification is easy and can be automated. In the case of the threshold level of 25 ppb the only way to check and proof is a chemical analysis. The effort (time and costs) is immense with respect to the huge amount of materials in the market, as an information system if materials contain PFAS is missing. There is almost an infinite number of articles which can be generated out of the materials. As contaminations do not follow clear rules in most cases, the analytic is just for a moment in time and the same material might be PFAS-free in one sample and PFAS contaminated in the next. The validity of the analysis is highly questionable.

10. Analytical methods: This request deals with all materials and articles. It does not deal with exemptions of PFAS substances or applications, but with the replacement of a threshold level from material analysis by a restriction of intentionally added substances. As for influencing a technical performance usually higher amounts than 0,1% are added, it can be proposed that for proof that no PFAS have been added intentionally a threshold level of 0,1% or 0,01% is sufficient.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: In this comment, we will report on the use of the ALTEF®-procedure and the use of the EMATEF®-procedure. Although most of our products will not exceed 50 mg F / kg since we only apply a thin coating on much larger quantities of aluminium, we want to submit a derogation for a use not yet described int the sector of “Metal plating and manufacture of metal products”. Specifically, we will report on the use of polytetrafluorethylen (PTFE) in the anodic oxidation (anodising) of aluminium products.

The specific uses of our products are generally not known in detail to Altefco. However, known are  uses in the following sectors:
• Printing Industry
• Food industry
• Packaging machines
• Pneumatic and Hydraulic
• Motor sport
• Medical equipment
• Army devices
• Precision apparatus engineering
• Optical devices
• Watch Industry
• Vacuum valves
• Handling devices

We can thus only describe our coating procedures and their advantages without specific information on the exact durability of our coatings in their respective, final uses. We will make assumptions in the following to assume emissions during the life cycle of our products and to estimate their respective positive and negative socio-economic impacts.

ALTEF® is a durable anodised aluminium oxide coating with a PTFE embedding. The coat thickness ranges from 15 – 70 µm, depending on the aluminum alloy used. The recommended coat thickness lays at 40 µm. Half of this layer thickness ‘grows’ into the base material, resulting in an application of 20 µm on top of the aluminium.
The tolerance ranges are for wrought plates ± 5 µm, for cast plates ± 7 µm and for cast and die-cast alloys ± 10 µm. This information applies to a coat thickness of 40 µm. Tolerance range varies with larger or thinner coats.

EMATEF® is an extremely low-porosity aluminium oxide coating with a PTFE embedding that is produced through a special anodising process, a hard ematal coating process. Coat thicknesses ranging from 10 to 25 µm, depending on the aluminium alloy used. The recommended coat thickness is 15 µm. 80% of this layer thickness ‘grows’ into the base material, resulting in an application of 3 µm on top of the aluminium.
The tolerance range of an EMATEF® coat is ± 4 µm depending on the material used and the selected coat thickness.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: We provide information about uses of PFAS in the sector of “Metal plating and manufacture of metal products”. Specifically, we will report on the use of polytetrafluorethylen (PTFE) in the anodic oxidation (anodising) of aluminium products.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: a)  Details on the calculations can be found in annexe 1 uploaded as an additional document to this submission. Manufacturing phase (ALTEF and EMATEF procedure)  For anodising aluminium products with PTFE, we use a semi-finished product, a liquid solution containing 44.5% of solid components (PTFE and other additives). We assume that it contains about 45% PTFE. We use about 40 kg of this semi-finished product per year and, therefore, about 18 kg of PTFE per year. About 5.4 kg of this PTFE ends up on our products. The remaining about 12.6 kg of PTFE will remain in solution since the temperature of the solution is not high enough (< 70°C) for PTFE to become instable and for fluorocarbon gases to be released. The used solution is treated in our own wastewater treatment plant. In this plant, PTFE in wastewater will be precipitated together with aluminium hydroxide. The resulting aluminium hydroxide sludge with the PTFE contamination is treated as hazardous waste and is burned in waste incinerator in accordance with Swiss regulations. The ALTEF procedure accounts for approximately 75 % of waste, the EMATEF procedure for ca. 25 %.  In the remaining wastewater, we determine heavy metal concentrations in accordance with Swiss regulations. PTFE or total fluorine is not determined and there are no regulations for such measurements in Switzerland.  Use phase –  ALTEF-products   One of the main advantages of PTFE-anodised aluminium products with the ALTEF-method is their high wear- and scratch-resistance and their good sliding properties. ALTEF-Products are generally used for products that – without a PTFE coating – would require lubrication and wear-off much quicker with mechanical abrasion. We only have limited or no knowledge at all about how our customers use our products. Thus, it is difficult to know how quickly an ALTEF-coated part is worn off. We have customers who sell ALTEF-coated valve spool combinations, which easily exceed the limit of several million cycles. To our knowledge, the majority of our clients can use the ALTEF-products for years to decades. To estimate the emissions during the use phase, we assume that an ALTEF-product can be used until half of the ALTEF-layer that is not grown into the aluminium is worn off. Half of the layer is growing into the aluminium. We therefore assume that a quarter of the layer can be worn off mechanically until the product cannot be used anymore. As the ALTEF coat does not degrade in the environment, there is no secondary emission coming from this release of PTFE. From the assumptions (above) that about 5.4 kg PTFE are placed on products and that about 75% of the PTFE load stems from the Altef-products, we conclude that about 1.0 kg will be worn off until the end of the use phase. The worn off PTFE will probably remain inside the machines that will be turned over to the waste system. The fate of this PTFE is not possible to determine. A conservative assumption is that the PTFE is transferred to the Aluminium recycling system and will there contribute to emissions of toxic gases.  Use phase – EMATEF-products  EMATEF-products are not used in applications with high-wear potential, but in uses where chemical resistance to goods in contact with the coated surface is important. We assume that EMATEF-products must be replaced if they are scratched. A few scratches will likely not affect more than 1 % of the PTFE layer growing out of the product (20% of the total layer). Therefore most of the PTFE layer on EMATEF-coated products will be turned over to the waste system in the waste phase.  Waste phase – ALTEF and EMATEF-products  The products might to a large percentage be treated as aluminium products in the waste phase since they are made of aluminium. These waste pieces might: a) be recycled b) go to a (municipal) waste incinerator c) be landfilled  In the recycling process (a: our assumption: about 75%), Aluminium will be smelted at about 650 degrees Celsius and the PTFE will likely be transformed into fluorocarbon gases. Most aluminium smelters are equipped with filtration systems, but the country of aluminium recycling is not known. We thus make the conservative assumption that all of the PTFE will be treated in an aluminum smelter without a filter system and will thus transformed into fluorocarbon gases, such as PTFE monomers (H4C2F2). This results in about 5.7 kg of fluorocarbon gases.  In a municipal waste incinerator (b: our assumption: about 12.5%), the waste pieces are burnt at a level of about 1’100 °C with enough oxygen to transform the PTFE into CO2 and HF. The strong acid HF is filtered out of the flue gas, neutralized and transferred into the wastewater in the form of fluorides. This results in a release of about 10.0 kg of fluoride salts in wastewater. In a landfill (c: our assumption: about 12.5%), the PTFE load will not react but simply be transported into the landfill body. There it will not interfere with human processes but remain inert for a very long time. This results in a release of about 0.5 kg of PTFE into a landfill.  b)  If we assume a steady state, where the same amount of ALTEF and EMATEF products is produced and delivered as goes out of use, we can conclude that the numbers calculated above apply for one year. Therefore we find (for ALTEF and EMATEF together):   - Underground landfill for hazardous waste or waste incinerator:  0 kg of PTFE per year - Uncontrolledly emitted into the environment: About 0 kg of PTFE per year - Uncontrolledly emitted from Al-Smelters: About 5.7 kg of fluorocarbon gases per year - Emitted into the wastewater of MSWI’s: About 10.0 kg of fluorides (F-) per year - Transferred into landfills: About 0.5 kg of PTFE per year  The amount of PTFE uncontrolledly but cold (inert) emitted in the environment could be up to 1.0 kg of PTFE per year. This would reduce the amount of fluorocarbon gases emitted from the Al recycling processes. The worst case is the case with the biggest emissions of fluorocarbons.

The emissions of the two procedures in their three life cycles can be found under point 2: Emissions in the end-of-life phase.  b)  ALTEF General key functionalities provided by a PTFE-coating aluminium applied by the ALTEF-procedure are the following: - Highly corrosion-resistant - Highly scratch-resistant - Highly wear-resistant - High dielectric strength - Easy to clean - Good sliding properties  Key functionalities vary for the different uses of compared to other aluminum coatings achieved by anodising. For the following examples, there are no suitable alternatives: - ALTEF-pistons used in pneumatic/hydraulic systems do not require lubrication or only initial lubrication. - ALTEF-laboratory equipment needs no lubrication and moving parts experience very limited abrasion. - ALTEF-components in electric motors need no lubricants and do not lead to the stick-slip phenomenon due to the tribological characteristics of PTFE. - ALTEF-fluid valves that are for instance used in respiratory devices are highly resistant to  various gases.  - ALTEF-components of all kinds that are used in the outdoor area are highly resistant to corrosion and weathering and are often used in petrochemical and chemical plants. - If ALTEF-components are used during food processing, the main advantage is that components are easily cleaned and only require mild cleaning agents.   EMATEF EMATEF has established itself as the best internal coating for parts used in the field of plastic injection moulding and in the handling of post-plastic injection moulding parts handling. The coating of surfaces with PTFE results in a fine-pored surface with outstanding non-stick properties, which are used: - in the case of KS injection moulding tools, which enables demoulding of two plastic components without them sticking together - in handling units (grippers, trays, shelves) where plastic components that have not yet cooled down can be transported without sticking to the handling units.  c)  We estimate that there are about 40 – 80 small- and medium-sized companies (applying PTFE coatings) that will be affected by the restriction. The number of companies affected by the fact that PTFE coated aluminium parts are no more available is much bigger.  d)  To our knowledge, alternatives with comparable key functionalities have not been found yet. This is also confirmed by our yearly meetings of the world IHAA association.   e)  Altefco AG is testing alternatives and is currently increasing its R&D capacities to find such alternatives. To date, real alternatives to PTFE have no been found yet. This is mainly due to its outstanding tribological and hydrophobic characteristics.   f)  ALTEF or EMATEF coating could be replaced by other coating, but following disadvantages will occur: - pollution inside medical and life science devices through abrasion and needed lubricants - need of high risk chemicals to clean devices in food, life science and medical applications resulting in risk of contamination and corrosion – reduced usage life cycle - need of massively more lubricant and grease in hydraulic and pneumatic valves and actuators resulting in more frequent maintenance and higher life cycle cost - higher failure rate in de-casting of plastic parts in various injection mould application resulting in higher failure rate and longer cycle times (performance loss) - faster corrosion and/or wear off of mechanical parts in demanding applications   g)  The advantages of an ALTEF- or EMATEF coating apply to parts where lubrication or chemical resistance are important. This means that many of the machines that use PTFE-coated aluminium parts could not function anymore after a short lifetime due to corrosion or wear-off. General Comments: In vat polymerization, a subtype of 3D printing technology stereolithography, non-stick process films are necessary as a process surface. To enable the processing of UV resins, the process films must have the following properties: Anti-sticking, inert against the chemicals of the 3d-pringn resins, wear resistant, UV-stable and high UV-transmission. All films available in the state of the art with the required properties (Perfluoralkoxy-Polymere PFA, Tetrafluorethylen-Hexafluorpropylen-Copolymer FEP, Ethylen-Tetrafluorethylen-Copolymer ETFE, or other fluoropolymer with similar properties) are PFAS substances.
Over the last two decades, fluoropolymers have established themselves as the best suitable polymerization surface. Just about the entire industry of stereolithography-based vat 3D printing and other stereolithography-based 3D printing technologies use such materials in the printing process. Since these films are relatively expensive, the entire industry has always searched for alternative ones with similar properties, but without success. There are no alternative film materials with even remotely good properties, nor is there any prospect of such materials.
Replacement by non-fluoropolymer would result in a significant reduction in process stability, 3d-printed component quality and the elimination of many established applications. If the manufacturing process can still be used in certain areas with alternative films, this would be accompanied by a sharp increase in consumables/waste of other plastic films or other anti-sticking substances like silicones.
Socio-economic impact: Many individual medical products (dental splints, dental surgical guides, dental prostheses, hearing aid shells...) are nowadays produced with vat-polymerization processes on fluoropolymer films. The discontinuation of this technology would make access to customized medical devices unaffordable for many people. This restriction would hit poorer sections of the population harder, as the fluoropolymer films are predominantly used in lower-cost 3D printing (small to mid-size) devices. In Europe, for example dental laboratories are mostly small- to medium-sized companies that rely on this class of equipment. Alternative 3D printing technologies are often only available on an industrial scale. Which would lead to a concentration of the production of individual medical devices in a few large players. If the device class for small to medium sized companies disappears from the market, also the digitization efforts of the last years would be undone, as 3d printing plays an essential role in the digitalization of manufacturing processes in medical sector.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Individual views on the Annex XV Restriction Report  as follows，
1. The proposed restrictions will hinder the development of the fluorine chemical industry, which will also bring a great risk of unemployment to the individuals who work in the fluorine chemical industry.
PFASs have the characteristics of repelling water and oil, heat resistance, chemical resistance, and non-absorption of light, and have been widely used in waterproofing agents, surface treatment agents, emulsifiers, fire extinguishers, coatings, etc. We have also communicated with upstream and downstream customers, the main component of non-stick coating is Teflon (PTFE), which is a non-toxic, odorless, high temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, anti-aging polymer material. Even if the coating is scratched or dropped, it will not cause any harm to the human body because it will be excreted directly from the digestive tract. Non-stick pans coated with fluorocarbon coating have the best response during the use of people, and there are several reasons: a. If you use an ordinary iron pot to stir-fry, due to the uneven heating of the bottom of the pot, there will be a certain place where the dish sticks to the pot, then this place will be too high temperature, resulting in the dish in this place to burn. If the people eat it into the stomach there may be a risk of cancer, and it is quite inconvenient to clean up. the non-stick pan with fluorocarbon coating will not have the situation where the dish sticks to the pot because of its uniform heating and strong stability; b. It is now said that ceramic coatings can replace fluorocarbon coatings, however, as far as we know, ceramic coatings use silicone oil as a release agent to achieve the so-called non-stick effect. When heating the pan, silicone oil will also migrate to the food and enter the human body because of the high temperature. The shampoos we use are advocating the use of silicone-free series products, but what we eat into the mouth still contains silicone oil. Therefore, we cannot think that this ceramic coating can be used as an alternative to fluorocarbon coating.
Any restriction decision should take into account “the socio-economic impact of the restriction, including the availability of alternatives.” The alternative of ceramic coatings is completely unviable, so we believe that the proposed comprehensive restriction on all uses of all PFAS would be a catastrophe for the fluorine chemical industry, which in turn would lead to socio-economic setbacks, leading to job losses for a large portion of population and economic disaster for these families.
2. Summary，Socio-economic analysis (page 2 of the main text):
The Dossier Submitters have identified main PFAS uses in which the largest amounts of PFASs are used and emitted. This has been done by literature research, stakeholder consultations, and a call for evidence. Fourteen sectors and/or applications - subdivided in numerous sub- uses - have been addressed in detail in this report. For the EU, this resulted in an estimated amount of 140 000 to 310 000 t of PFASs introduced to the market in 2020, which - due to the expected economic growth in several sectors - is expected to increase even further under the baseline scenario. Over a 30-year period the expected mean PFAS tonnage in the EEA is 49 million tonnes, leading to emissions of about 4.5 million tonnes during the manufacture and use phase when no action is taken. The emissions during the waste phase, which may be significant, are not accounted for in that estimate as they are highly uncertain. Hence, it can be assumed that emission estimates are severely underestimated.
Regarding the use of PFAS, the research of this proposal is not sufficient and needs to be more extensive and deeper. Emission projections are used as the only indicator and natural decomposition is not considered. It is recommended that the ban on PFAS should be carried out in different chronological order and priority, and on different trajectories, and cannot be achieved overnight. Fluorine-containing gas decompose into trifluoracetic acid in the atmosphere and precipitate whose impact is little. The proposal also lacks in-depth study of specific use areas, such as fluoropolymers, fluorine-containing gases, etc.
3. Scope (page 2 of the main text):
The chemical scope of the restriction proposal is defined as: Any substance that contains at least one fully fluorinated methyl (CF3-) or methylene (-CF2-) carbon atom (without any H/Cl/Br/I attached to it). There are however a few exceptions (see para below).
This definition is consistent with the OECD’s definition of PFASs, which was published in 2021, has been carefully reviewed by the international scientific community and has been widely accepted. This definition covers more than 10 000 PFASs, including few subgroups of fully degradable PFAS. For these fully degradable subgroups, which can be described in terms of their key structural compositions, they do not meet the high persistence concern basis (see para above), and they are excluded from the scope of this restriction proposal. Examples of public views and comments:
I believe that the scope of the proposal is not clearly defined in the scope section of the proposal, and the exceptions are not listed, resulting in the scope is not clear. The quoted description, like see para below, should be removed, and exceptions should be listed directly, indicating whether they are complete and exhaustive.
The OECD 2021 definition itself is unclear because its description is made through positive and negative examples, without saying whether it is a complete exclusion; its Executive Summary (second paragraph on page 8) states that the term PFASs is broad, general and non-specific term, not to inform the compound that it is harmful or harmless, but only for communication, and the compounds under this term hare the same characteristics of fully fluorinated methyl or methylene carbon structure. The proposal directly quotes the OECD definition beyond the understanding of OECD experts themselves.
4. Summary，Regulatory risk management options (page 1 of the main text):
The irreversibility of the process of a growing environmental stock of PFASs, with associated exposure of humans and the environment, make it necessary to reduce emissions of PFASs to a minimum. Different regulatory risk management options have been considered, e.g., CLH and authorisation, but these options follow a substance by substance approach. In contrast, a restriction offers the possibility to define a broad chemical scope, thereby avoiding regrettable substitution of one PFAS by another PFAS (which may not even be engineered yet). At the same time, it allows to tackle the problem of ongoing, uncontrollable emissions at the source, as manufacture and use can be banned, instead of an end-of-pipe solution that is not achievable, as PFASs are ubiquitously present in a wide range of products intended for industrial, professional and consumer uses. A restriction can cover a wide range of uses and can address the risks arising from the manufacture and use of the substances as such as well as in other substances, in mixtures and in articles, including imported articles from outside the EU. Hence, a restriction is the most appropriate and effective option to adequately control such a large and complex group of substances which are used in numerous applications.
Does the risk come from the increase of PFASs in the environment, or from entering the human body to act on the human body? PFOS and PFOA are two substances controlled by international conventions, but many substances covered are different from their properties, so they cannot be simply extrapolated. Moreover, there are already decomposition methods for these substances, indicating that there is no irreversibility. Scientists support subgroup management because it is unreasonable for all PFAS to be grouped together. They should be classified differently according to their different properties, and reasonable control measure should be taken.
5. The proposal should exclude F-gases used as refrigerants.
Fluorinated gas (i.e., F-gas) is used as a refrigerant. These substances fall under the jurisdiction of the Montreal Protocol and its amendments. Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) is the terminal decomposition product of a variety of F-gases.
As far as we know, TFA is risk-free. The protection of stratospheric ozone in climate change is associated with changes in tropospheric air quality.
S. Madronich and et al, Changes in tropospheric aid quality related to the protection of stratospheric ozone in a changing climate, Photochemical & Photobiological Sciences, Published online 13 June 2023.
Final sentence of the abstract: “one such product, trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), has no obvious pathway of degradation and might accumulate in some water bodies, but is unlikely to cause adverse effects out to 2100.”
Therefore, we do not consider it appropriate to control F-gases as a whole of PFAS.
6. Problem identification (paragraph 1, page 13)
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) are a group of thousands of synthetic chemicals that are used widely in the EU as well as in the rest of the world, in a broad range of applications such as textiles, food packaging, lubricants, refrigerants, and electronics. All PFASs in the scope of this restriction proposal are either very persistent themselves, or degrade into very persistent PFASs in the environment. This is the key hazardous property common to all PFASs in this restriction proposal. Consequently, if releases of PFASs are not minimised, humans and other organisms will be exposed to progressively increasing amounts of PFASs until such levels are reached where effects become inevitable. In such an event these exposures are practically irreversible as it is technically extremely difficult, if at all possible, to remove PFASs from the environment.
However, persistence is necessarily a health risk, the danger to human health lies in whether they enter the cell.
In Barbara J henry and et al, A Critical Review of the Application of Polymer of Low Concern and Regulatory Criteria to Fluoropolymers, Integrated Environmental assessment and Management, Volume 14, Number 3, pp 316-334, it is stated that fluoropolymers are practically insoluble in anyone and do not migrate long distances. Its molecular weight is higher than 100 000 Da, and it cannot pass through cell membranes. Fluoropolymers are not bioavailable or bioaccumulative, which have been demonstrated by toxicological experiments with PTFE.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Industrial pumps carry a wide variety of fluids such as foods, inks, pharmaceuticals, etc. with different features and conditions. Thus materials for the pump’s liquid-contact parts need to tolerate these features and conditions. PFASs (especially PTFE, FET, ETFE and FKM) are compatible with these features and conditions. Applications of the pumps will be limited without using PFASs. Consequently, it will not be able to fulfill some of the roles that the pumps have played until now.
In addition, PFASs (especially PTFE) in the pump industry are used in lubricants to reduce frictional wear and melting. There are no substitutes for PTFE nor fluorine-based lubricants. Without them, lubricity is inhibited and resulting in a significant decrease in pump durability. In the restriction proposal, paragraph 5, part s mentions the derogation of the lubricants where the use takes place under harsh conditions. However, the definition of “harsh” is not specified and there are many more occasions which require PFASs as lubricants than the term “harsh” can generally recall.
Based on the above, PTFE, FEP, ETFE, and FKM are essential for industrial pumps and cannot be substituted. Therefore, an exemption for industrial pumps from the restriction is necessary.

Our product GLINDEMANN PTFE Sealing Ring is essential for challenging work in chemical and pharmaceutical laboratories, where our sealing ring provides almost hermetical seal when using vacuum grease for conical glass joints is no option.

I suggest yet another new scope – Taxation of Fluoropolymer production. Content: Environmental emissions Baseline Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Initial situation

Modern machine tools form the basis of industrial production. They enable the production of increasingly efficient drives (e.g. for aerospace and other mobility applications) and are an important foundation for the implementation of the EU’s Green Deal (wind and hydropower plants, hydrogen production and storage, fuel cells, heat pumps, photovoltaics, etc.)

In order for machine tools to perform, a variety of process and auxiliary fluids are used in them. These range from cooling lubricants (metalworking fluids – MWF), bedway oils and hydraulic fluids to bearing lubricants and greases as well as forming lubricants and dielectrics. In addition, chips and dusts are generated during mechanical processing, which can mix with the aforementioned media to some extent. The materials used in the corresponding areas – e.g. for seals and plain bearings – must be able to withstand both, the mechanical loads and the media used (and possibly their mixtures) over long periods of time. In addition, they must prevent stick-slip effects and ensure the required accuracies (e.g. plain bearings). When equipping their machines, machine tool manufacturers typically opt for the most cost-effective solution that can withstand the expected mechanical and chemical stresses. In the material class considered here, these are mainly conventional materials (e.g. NBR, HNBR, PUR, PA, PC, PE, PP), but in some cases also fluoroplastics such as FKM, FFKM and PTFE.

Impact of the EU chemicals regulation REACH to date

The use of fluoroplastics has become increasingly necessary in recent years, as the EU chemicals regulation REACH (Regulation EC No. 1907/2006) initially regulated the ingredients and additives in coolants and lubricants. For example, many of the biocides previously used in water-mixed MWF are now prohibited. As a common practice to prevent the growth of microorganisms and fungi, MWF emulsions are now operated at pH values above 9, that means in the more alkaline range. This generally has negative effects on conventional polymeric materials, which is why high-performance polymers and therefore PFAS have to be used in some cases.

Fluoropolymers are “polymers of low concern”

Fluoropolymers (FP) are long-chain polymeric PFAS materials that differ significantly from non-polymeric PFAS. FP meet the internationally recognized OECD criteria for “polymers of low concern”. Therefore, authorities in the UK, for example, see no need to restrict FP, including their manufacturing processes. FP behave in a chemically stable manner, they are non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water soluble and non-mobile. In addition, they are used in machine tools in enclosed spaces, which inherently prevent environmental contamination.

Information on alternatives

Machine tool manufacturers, as downstream users, are familiar with fluoropolymer chemistry only to the extent that they know in which cases they must use FP for their applications to still function. Precautionary use of FP does not take place for cost reasons alone – rather, efforts are made to avoid FP wherever possible (FP are 10 times more expensive than conventional polymer materials). However, it has been shown that the changes in the lubricant sector caused by the REACH regulation partly require the use of FP. When speaking with the manufacturers of FP, it becomes clear that currently – and also in the foreseeable future – there are no equivalent alternatives to FP.

Aspects of the socio-economic analysis (SEA)

A general ban on FP would lead to disadvantages in the entire mechanical and plant engineering sector with corresponding socio-economic consequences. These disadvantages range from a lack of competitiveness compared to non-EU machinery to higher energy and resource consumption (e.g. increased friction values, additional sealing air requirements) to shortened maintenance intervals (increased wear and more frequent seal replacements) as well as reduced availability / increased downtimes.

In principle, we welcome the regulatory measures to restrict hazardous PFAS. However, we argue for a differentiated and risk-based assessment. It must be taken into account that long-chain fluoropolymers have a different risk profile than short-chain non-polymeric PFAS. From our point of view, it is essential to differentiate between applications that emit large amounts of PFAS into the environment and that can be easily prevented (e.g. PFAS in consumer articles) and those that are less critical and also cause hardly any emissions (e.g. high-performance seals in enclosed installation spaces of machinery).

If no differentiation is made here, it will no longer be possible to manufacture or operate high-performance technology in the EU. Although we cannot quantify the exact socio-economic consequences, they are likely to be severe. Both the manufacturers of high-performance machines with their jobs and the operators of such systems would be affected. It is to be feared that these jobs will shift to non-EU countries. In the German machine tool industry alone, more than 300 companies would be affected (EU-wide, it would be 1,500 companies with around 150,000 employees and a turnover of over 25 billion euros). Since machine tools – as mentioned at the beginning – form the basis of industrial production, the impact is multiplied when considering the operators as well.

We find it particularly concerning that our application area is only mentioned marginally in the restriction dossier, issued on March 22, 2023. We therefore fear that the authors did not have the urgently required high-performance applications in mechanical and plant engineering, and especially in machine tool manufacturing, on their radar. This may also be due to the fact that our applications fall far behind other applications in terms of volume. According to estimates, the German machine tool industry uses an annual tonnage of FP in the single to low double digits range.

Environmental emissions

Machine tools are capital goods that are used in industry over long periods of time (lifetimes of 30 years or more). Machine tools are permanently repairable and are also refurbished at certain times. In many cases, they are thus given a “second life” and are exemplary in terms of environmental protection and the circular economy. At the end of the machines' lifecycle, up to 98% of the materials they contain can be recycled. Recycling is already carried out because it is economically viable due to the high mass of the machines. Machine tools are in the hands of professionals throughout their entire lifecycle, who can ensure proper recycling and proper disposal of critical components such as FP.

FP seals are mostly used in machine tools in enclosed spaces. A possible small amount of abrasion therefore also accumulates in these installation spaces. Machine maintenance and seal replacements are exclusively carried out by skilled personnel. Due to the long lifespan of the machines, an assured spare parts supply over long periods of time (in this case decades) is of great importance. If spare parts are not available (e.g. due to a ban), there is a risk that the machines will have to be taken out of service and replaced long before their actual end of life. We believe that this environmental effect must also be considered in the rulemaking on FP.

Request for exemption

Against this background, we propose a permanent exemption for all fluoropolymers used in machinery and plant engineering.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The mechanical and plant engineering sector, and specifically machine tools, are not actually listed in table 9 of the Annex XV Restriction Report. Only certain subsectors are mentioned that also have significance for the mechanical engineering industry. Examples are:  - Manufacture of metal products (although PFAS are not used directly in the manufacturing of metal products, they are used indirectly in the machine tools used for this purpose – for the explanation why fluoropolymers are important for the safe, proper and efficient operation of machine tools, please refer to our comments submitted)  - Refrigeration (refrigeration systems are partially used in machine tools, e.g. for temperature control of the coolant and/or for control cabinet air conditioning)  - Hydraulic fluids (machine tools also have hydraulic components, e.g. for workpiece clamping)  - Electronics and semiconductors (modern machine tools use a wide variety of electronic and microelectronic components, ranging from sensors and drive technology to computerized machine control)  - Lubricants (please refer to our submitted commentary, paragraph 2, for more details)  Similar to the general remarks on transport (Annex XV, Table 8, p. 101/102), the mechanical and plant engineering could have been included in the restriction report. This would have prevented a gap for this in our view important area from occurring.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Manufacturing phase: As already stated in our commentary, machine tool manufacturers are downstream users of fluoropolymers who purchase these components and only use them where conventional solutions are not sufficient anymore. As downstream users, we naturally have no knowledge about the emissions in the manufacturing phase of fluoropolymers.  Use phase: The fluoropolymers used in machine tools are used as extremely durable seals in enclosed spaces (some examples are given in the slides we have included as non-confidential annex). Any potential minimal abrasion therefore also accumulates in these installation spaces and does not escape from the machines.  End of life: When machine tools have reached the end of their long service lifes, they are disposed of by specialized companies that must comply with environmental regulations. Due to the high metal content of the machines alone, the material recycling rate is up to 98%. Non-recyclable materials are incinerated, either directly in a blast furnace or in common waste incineration plants.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: As already mentioned in the answer to question 2, non-recyclable materials from machine tools disposal end up in incineration, either directly in the blast furnace or in common waste incineration plants. At the high temperatures in these plants, it can be assumed that the fluoropolymers are completely destroyed and mineralized. This is confirmed by the scientific work cited below:  Aleksandrov, K.; Gehrmann, H.-J.; Hauser, M.; Mätzing, H.; Pigeon, D.; Stapf, D.; Wexler, M.: Waste incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate potential formation of Per- and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) in flue gas. In: Chemosphere, Vol. 226, July 2019, pp. 898-906, ISSN 0045-6535, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chemosphere.2019.03.191

6. Missing uses: For a. and b.) In our opinion, the sub-sector of high-performance seals and plain bearing applications for mechanical and plant engineering and, in particular, machine tool engineering has not been adequately addressed. These applications are of great importance because metalworking fluid (MWF) systems, as well as hydraulic and pneumatic applications of machine tools, place high demands on the chemical resistance, wear behavior, pressure resistance and tribological properties of seals and plain bearings. Moreover, in the last decade further bans on substances in MWF, resulting from the REACH regulation (Regulation EC No. 1907/2006), have created an additional need for the use of fluoropolymers such as FKM, FFKM and PTFE. If these are now removed from the market, there is a risk that machine components will leak prematurely (endangering personnel and the environment), sensitive components such as high-precision measuring equipment and spindle bearings will come into contact with damaging media, and the guides of mechanical components, which are essential for the accuracy of the machine tools, will be impaired.  As already stated in our commentary, the German machine tool industry annually uses an estimated single-digit to low double-digit tonnage of fluoropolymers (FP) in its machines and manufacturing equipment. In a working group of the German Machine Tool Builders’ Association (VDW), the following sealing applications requiring FP were identified, among others (for more detailed information, see the slides we have included as a non-confidential attachment): - O-ring preloaded PTFE seals for pneumatic applications - Support rings based on PTFE for high-pressure hydraulic applications - PTFE-based guide elements for pistons - O-rings on FKM and FFKM basis - X-rings on FKM and FFKM basis - O-ring preloaded translational hydraulic seals (PTFE / FKM) - O-ring preloaded rotary seals (PTFE / FKM) - Radial shaft seals (FKM / FFKM) - Lip ring seals (FKM / FFKM) - O-ring preloaded PTFE wipers - O-ring preloaded hydraulic rod seals (PTFE / FKM) - Special FKM and FFKM rotary seals  Emissions from the use of fluoropolymers in machine tools have already been addressed in question 2.  For c.) For this we quote from our commentary: “In the German machine tool industry alone, more than 300 companies would be affected (EU-wide, it would be 1,500 companies with around 150,000 employees and a turnover of over 25 billion euros). Since machine tools – as mentioned at the beginning – form the basis of industrial production, the impact is multiplied when considering the operators as well.”  For d. to g.) A working group of the German Machine Tool Builders’ Association (VDW) has started discussions with seal manufacturers on possible alternatives. More detailed information on alternative materials for individual sealing applications is provided in the slides we have included as a non-confidential attachment. However, these alternatives, which are already used in less critical areas in machine tools, have lower temperature and pressure resistance and, in particular, lower chemical resistance. They wear more quickly and lead to increased friction in the rotating/moving machine elements. In the past, these materials were partially used in areas with metalworking fluid (MWF) contact, which is no longer possible today, as the MWFs now attack these materials more severely as a result of the revised requirements of the REACH regulation (Regulation EC No. 1907/2006). Therefore, the current use of (expensive) fluoropolymers is already partly due to stricter environmental regulations.  For many of the alternatives that may be considered, in-depth studies are needed before they can be used, including R&D on the one hand, but also long-term practical trials on the other. In principle, the seal manufacturers have reported back on requests that it is unlikely that there will ever be truly equivalent alternatives to fluoropolymers. This is precisely due to the extreme durability of fluorocarbon compounds.  A ban on fluoropolymers in mechanical and plant engineering would thus inevitably lead to the use of poorer-performing alternatives with the corresponding socio-economic consequences, some of which we have already outlined in our commentary: - Lack of competitiveness compared to non-EU machinery, which is still allowed to use fluoropolymers. - Higher energy and resource consumption during machine operation (e.g. due to increased friction and additional sealing air requirements). - Reduced seal durability and consequently increased maintenance effort (more frequent seal replacements). - Higher probability of unintended leakage of process and auxiliary fluids such as MWF and oil (safety risk as well as environmental and health hazard). - Decommissioning of machines long before their actual end of life, as spare parts are no longer available.  As already mentioned at the beginning of our commentary, machine tools form the basis of industrial production. Consequently, they are used in a wide range of industries, including many key and future industries of the EU. A ban on fluoropolymers therefore not only affects the approx. 1,500 machine tool manufacturers in the EU, but also a multiple of these companies – from the producer of the simplest plastic components to household appliance, medical technology and automotive manufacturers, to aerospace and defense technology, as well as all the companies that are supposed to enable the EU’s Green Deal (wind and hydropower plants, hydrogen production and storage, fuel cells, heat pumps, photovoltaics, etc.)  Against this background and the fact that fluoropolymers meet the internationally recognized OECD criteria for “polymers of low concern”, we propose a permanent exemption for all fluoropolymers used in machinery and plant engineering.

Content: Environmental emissions Baseline Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Initial situation
The company is a manufacturer of tool sharpening machines (machine tools) for the machining (sharpening) of tool cutting edges. The processes used for this are grinding, eroding, laser ablation or the combination of grinding and eroding. Grinding requires the use of cooling lubricants (KSS), whereby water-miscible and non-water-miscible cooling lubricants are used. In EDM, media are used that act as dielectrics in the gap between the electrode and the cutting edge of the tool. Machines that are suitable for grinding and eroding are equipped with a medium that allows both processes. The materials used in the machines must therefore have a high chemical resistance to different media.

When sealing rotating shafts (e.g. tool and workpiece spindles using so-called V-rings or radial oil seals) or linearly moving components (e.g. piston rods of pneumatic or hydraulic cylinders using rod seals) against the housing, there are additional requirements in addition to chemical resistance, such as good sliding and wear properties, low friction and no leakage. Wear resistance is necessary to ensure sealing over several years of operation. Low friction is a necessary prerequisite to achieve exact motion transmission (no stick-slip) on the one hand and to avoid unacceptable heating of the rotating shaft at high speeds on the other. Both are necessary to achieve the accuracy required for machining.

For the cooling lubricants, mainly non water miscible substances (low viscosity oil) are used to achieve lubrication with simultaneous cooling of the process zone. The rotation of the grinding wheel causes the cooling lubricants to swirl, creating an aerosol-air mixture in the machine interior that can be ignited by an ignition source (e.g. heating of the process zone or components). During the deflagration (low pressure explosion), temperatures of several hundred degrees Celsius are briefly generated in the machine room. In addition to the above-mentioned necessary material properties of the sealing material (chemical resistance, wear resistance and low friction), there is also the temperature resistance. These necessary properties are fulfilled by fluorinated rubbers (FKM) or polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) for some exposed sealing components. Seals made of FKM are always used when the properties of the standard material made of nitrile rubber (NBR) are no longer sufficient. Seals made of FKM are used in consideration of the technical necessities, as the costs are approx. 10 times higher compared to the standard material.

FKM is also used for sealing cable gland in machine tools. For the power supply of the drive motors and for the transmission of sensor signals, electric cables must be led from the control cabinet into the working area of the machine. The process media, some of which are supplied at a pressure of up to 20 bar, are located in the working area. So called cable glands, in which the sealing part is made of FKM, are used to seal the cable bushing. Of the above mentioned material properties, chemical and thermal resistance are required for this application.

The quantity of FKM and PTFE used in the company across all machines sold is approx. 390 kg/year (basis 2022).

Information on alternatives
At present, there are no known alternative materials to FKM or PTFE that have all these necessary properties. If these materials are no longer available, materials with less favourable properties would have to be used. For example, the use of NBR in cable glands in the past has led to media penetration into the control cabinet, which has endangered the safety and functionality of the machines.

Other socio-economic analysis (SEA) issues
The use of materials with unfavourable properties would result in shorter maintenance intervals with significantly higher costs and resource requirements. It can be assumed that the components protected by the seals (e.g. precision bearings, measuring systems and motors) will have to be replaced frequently. In the area of electrical installations (cable glands), it can be assumed that the reliability of the components will be reduced. Since the sharpening companies have to pass on the higher maintenance costs for the tool sharpening machines to the processed tools, it is to be expected that tool production and a significant part of the resharpening of used tools would move out of the EEA. Sales of tool sharpening machines in the EEA would collapse.
Furthermore, it can be assumed that tool sharpening machines with an increased maintenance requirement would no longer be sold outside the EEA, as the production of tool sharpening machines would also move to countries outside the EEA where FKM and PTFE can still be used.
It can be assumed that the company would lose approx. 80% of its current turnover in the medium term, which would acutely endanger the existence of the company.

Environmental emissions
There are no emissions from the sealing materials used during operation. At the end of their service life, the machines are usually disposed of in an orderly manner.

Request for exemption
It is therefore requested that FKM and PTFE for use in seals be exempted from regulation for at least 10 years and that a review be carried out thereafter to determine whether new sealing materials with comparable properties are available in the meantime.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Initially, We IDEMA JAPAN supports the statement made by FCJ on the issues of proposed restriction, as per attached in Section IV.

We, IDEMA JAPAN, as an industry group for data storage related industries, have been complying with the chemical substance regulations of various countries. We support the EU's ambitious attempts to reduce risks from hazardous substances and have taken seriously the practical measures to meet the requirements of EU chemical regulations such as REACH.

However, we are convinced that the proposed restriction of PFAS (Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl substances) by the five European countries is a proposal that does not offer any significant advantages in terms of increasing the capacity and performance of data storage systems. We are entering an era in which the use of digital technology will continue to advance and become more deeply ingrained in society and people's lives. The proposed restrictions will inevitably become an element of resistance to the development of such digital transformation, and is considered a measure that will hinder the development of the global economy and, by extension, the progress of humankind. In addition, we believe that the proposed restriction is an excessive measure, as it will restrict more than 10,000 kinds of organo-fluorine compounds (PFAS) on the basis of their persistence as substances of concern equivalent to PFOS and PFOA, which are already regulated.

Therefore, we intend to present the following views in the ECHA public consultation, which is one of the actions recommended by IDEMA Japan.

In order to achieve high-density, high-capacity HDDs, the lubricant used to prevent friction and wear between the magnetic head and the media must have an extremely thin coating thickness. Furthermore, reliability must be ensured even under sliding conditions of high temperature and high speed rotation. Lubricants containing organic fluorine compounds such as phosphazene and perfluorinated polyethers are widely used as lubricants that can be used under such severe conditions.

These lubricants are characterized by their ability to form a thin film in the nm range, and they do not scatter or migrate to the head due to high-speed rotation, nor do they evaporate. They are also persistent under high temperatures, and have high purity, narrow molecular weight distribution, and uniformity. In the long history of HDDs, no alternative materials have been found, thus organo-fluorine compounds are indispensable materials for HDD manufacturing.

On the other hand, the amount of information produced daily around the world is growing exponentially and is expected to reach 175ZB (175 trillion GB) by 2025. The amount of data that can be stored for the data produced will reach 10% of the total. HDDs, SSDs, optical disks, and magnetic tapes are used as data storage systems to archive information according to its use, and it is expected that about 85% of this explosive information volume will be stored on HDDs. In terms of volume, 203.04 million HDDs have already been shipped by 2022.

In addition, the thickness of the lubricant applied to the HDD media is about 1 nm, which is an extremely small amount of less than 100 ppb of product weight. The total amount of lubricant used in HDD media is about 10kg for all HDD shipments in 2022.

As a central component of data storage systems, HDDs are lubricated with organic fluorine compounds. We request that lubricants used to prevent frictional wear between HDD magnetic heads and media be exempt from the regulation.

Article 68 (1) REACH refers to the scope of the restrictions, which regulates　unacceptable risks to human health or the environment that need to be addressed by society as a whole.
The proposed restriction lists persistent chemicals (which may remain in the environment longer than any other man-made chemical), bioconcentration, mobility, the possibility of long-distance transport, accumulation in plants, the possibility of global warming, and toxicological effects as concerns and reasons for the restriction. Of these, persistent is applicable to all targeted organo-fluorine compounds (PFAS), but other concerns are related to some compounds.

Persistency common to all organo-fluorine compounds (PFAS) can be rephrased as "high durability" by focusing on its advantages, however, we believe that it is not appropriate to regulate this property alone as an unacceptable risk to human health or the environment. In addition, it is not appropriate to apply the concerns about some fluorinated compounds, such as bioconcentration potential and toxicological effects, by grouping all organo-fluorine compounds (PFAS) together, and if the need for new regulations is to be considered in the future, the risk of each substance should be quantitatively assessed and discussed.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Lubricants for magnetic storage media (hard disks, magnetic tapes)

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: When PFPE and its derivatives are disposed of or incinerated, they must be incinerated in a dedicated treatment facility because they produce toxic gases through thermal decomposition. The residue is detoxified and disposed of in landfills.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Hard disks and magnetic tapes are considered non-recyclable, except for the metal materials used.

6. Missing uses: a. The PFAS used in this application is Perfluoropolyether (PFPE) and its derivatives, which are used for coating the media surface of HDDs. The total amount used was estimated in the file attached in Section V for the quarter.  b. Improved properties of perfluorinated polyether and their derivatives, such as chemical stability, heat resistance, low vapor pressure, low surface energy, and tribology.  c. All countries, companies, and individuals worldwide that use HDDs.  d. No alternative has been found to date and no switch to PFAS-free products is possible in the future.  e. It is also difficult to estimate the time and cost required to develop alternatives because PFAS has been used for about half a century and it will be difficult to develop alternatives in the future.  f. There is no certainty that a substitute can be found because the development of a substitute is very difficult.  g. If the use of PFAS for coating the media surface of HDDs is banned, HDDs will no longer be available on the market. The economic impact would be felt by countries, companies, and individuals around the world that use HDDs, and the impact on the future information society would be immeasurable.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Transitional period
Combined Comments: Introduction On 7 February 2023, you published and opened for public consultation the Restriction Proposal for PFAS, submitted by the Netherlands, Denmark, Germany, Norway, and Sweden. At the European level, work is now being done on a ban on the entire group of PFAS. The ban will apply to the production, use, sale, and import of over 10,000 chemical substances, which are present in thousands of products that we use daily. The official process also includes a consultation. We would like to take this opportunity to give our view on this proposal. 1. Viewpoint The viewpoint has been jointly prepared with the municipalities of Dordrecht, Sliedrecht, Molenlanden, and Papendrecht. Four municipalities that work together on the Chemours file. Coordination has taken place with the South Holland South Environmental Service, the South Holland South Public Health Service, and the province of South Holland. In addition to sharing our knowledge and experiences with PFAS, in the viewpoint, we also express our great concerns about the living environment for our residents as a result of years of PFAS emissions. We conclude with a plea for a total ban on the production, trade, and use of PFAS in Europe, including the import and transit of PFAS, including semi-finished products and end products containing PFAS. Below is our substantive viewpoint. 2. General concern about PFAS PFAS is used in the manufacture of a wide range of products for use by industry, professionals, and consumers. The main concern regarding PFAS is that they are very persistent and, once in the environment, have significant consequences. PFAS is bioaccumulative. These substances have negative effects on the state of the environment, the quality of nature, and the health of humans and animals, due to their dispersion and accumulation in soil, water, and air. The fact that they are persistent and bioaccumulative makes these substances even more worrisome. Municipalities are responsible for a healthy living environment for their residents, a clean environment, and the protection of vulnerable nature. Therefore, municipalities also feel a responsibility regarding combating the harmful effects of PFAS. Especially due to the societal unrest about PFAS. Media attention contributes to increased awareness among residents of the negative effects of PFAS and a decreased societal support for this group of substances. The industry continues to produce and use PFAS. The process of permitting, monitoring, and enforcing business processes using PFAS is highly labor-intensive. Unfortunately, the focus on permitting, monitoring, and enforcement does not provide a proportionate result in controlling and reducing the negative effects of PFAS. Completely reducing the emission and discharge of PFAS is a process that has taken many decades and has not led to a reduction to zero emission/discharge so far. Another concern is that products containing PFAS end up as waste at the end of their life cycle. PFAS cannot be separated. Even in incineration plants, PFAS is not destroyed. Consequently, PFAS will continue to exist in our living environment for a very long time, even after a ban, with all possible harmful consequences. We cannot undo what has already been created. PFAS is present worldwide in the environment and in humans, as a result of the long-term emissions of PFAS by factories. What we can and want to achieve is preventing PFAS from causing new damage in the future. In this context, the current restriction proposal is seen as a good step towards a global ban on this group of substances. Because PFAS does not adhere to the boundaries of a continent, contamination from other continents will continue. The next step should be a global ban. An important factor in this is that (in the Netherlands) applying the precautionary principle in permitting and enforcing PFAS production processes has not been approved by the courts so far. Removing PFAS from soil, groundwater, and surface water is - if possible at all - technically extremely difficult and very costly. Based on the above, the restriction of all PFAS is seen as the most suitable and effective way to eliminate the negative effects on the environment, nature, humans, and animals. Below, this position is further substantiated with specific (local and supra-local) information and various research results. 3. Source of local and regional PFAS contamination In the municipality of Dordrecht, there is a chemical industry complex. This complex includes the establishment of Chemours Netherlands B.V (formerly DuPont; hereinafter: Chemours). Since 1967, Teflon PFTE, Teflon FEP, and Viton have been produced at this location. Dow Chemical Dordrecht (polymers) and Delrin Netherlands B.V. (thermoplastic plastics) are also present at the complex. From 1967 until October 2012, DuPont, later Chemours, used the auxiliary substance PFOA in the production of various fluorine compounds (including fluoro-polymers, homopolymers/co-polymers, and fluoro-elastomers) in the Teflon factory. The use of PFOA was discontinued because PFOA was designated as a Very Concerning Substance (VCS) at the European level from 2013 onwards. The GenX technology (HFPO-DA) was developed to replace PFOA in the production of fluorine-containing plastics, including Teflon. This technology has been used since the end of 2012 in the production of fluorine-containing plastics, with the auxiliary substances FRD-902, FRD-903 being emitted into the air and water, and E1 into the air. GenX substances - belonging to PFAS - were designated as a potential VCS at the national level on 2 February 2018 and at the European level on 26 June 2019. 4. Local concern about PFAS The municipalities of Dordrecht, Sliedrecht, and Papendrecht have been investigating the harmful effects of the PFAS group since 2015, and the municipality of Molenlanden since 2018, and have also signaled to the national government that the problem is larger than just our municipalities. It is now widely known that, due to their persistence, bioaccumulation, and poor degradability, PFAS have caused a harm that is difficult and in many places impossible to remediate. The soil, groundwater, and surface water in our area are contaminated. Swimming is no longer possible everywhere. People can no longer eat from their own gardens without concern, and PFAS in nature leads to an accumulation of the substance in animals. Both the municipalities and the residents of our municipalities are deeply concerned about this. 5. Studies on the consequences of PFAS Below is a chronological overview of the most important studies (and their consequences) on PFAS. These studies support our position to come to a total ban of the entire PFAS group as soon as possible. Since 2018, measurements of surface water have been carried out by the Rivierenland Water Board in its work area. Based on these measurements, the National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM) advised against consuming fish caught in the surface water, due to exceeding the risk threshold for fish. In 2022, the RIVM conducted a study on crops from vegetable gardens in Dordrecht, Sliedrecht, Papendrecht, and Molenlanden. Based on this study, the RIVM advised vegetable garden owners in Sliedrecht within 1 kilometer of Chemours not to eat crops from their gardens. A large number of vegetable garden owners in complexes in Papendrecht were advised to alternate eating vegetables and fruit from their gardens with those from the store. Fruit growers in the affected municipalities are also experiencing adverse consequences due to concerns among citizens. The agricultural sector in the area of the four aforementioned municipalities is also concerned about the consequences of PFAS for the cultivation of crops and the quality of grassland as feed for livestock. While two studies in 2020 and 2021 into meat samples and agricultural products (meat, eggs, milk) by the Dutch Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) established that hardly any exceedances of the current European standards for PFAS occur in eggs, meat, and fish, our farmers are concerned about what the real consequences of PFAS in the soil, grassland, and air will mean for their livestock, the grass and silage feed from their own land that they consume, and for the products they grow on their land. This ongoing uncertainty is having a serious impact on the economic security of the agricultural sector in our municipality. In 2021 and 2022, the RIVM conducted a study into PFAS in vegetables and fruit from vegetable gardens in the municipalities of Papendrecht, Dordrecht, Sliedrecht, and Molenlanden. The same vegetable gardens' soil and water from ditches, rain barrels, and groundwater were also tested for PFAS. The advice was that all vegetable garden owners can use rain and tap water for watering their gardens. Not everyone can use water from ditches. It is advised to minimize the use of ditch water, and to first use rain and tap water. Since PFOA was also found in rain barrels before 2012, it is advised to replace these. There is a relationship between PFAS in the soil and groundwater and PFAS in crops. The higher the PFAS in the soil and groundwater, the higher the PFAS in the crops. Not all crops absorb the same amount of PFAS, so a clear relationship with all crops cannot be established. Groundwater is absorbed by the plants themselves, so no advice can be given for this. The Safety Investigation Board (OVV) published the report "Industry and residents" on 13 April 2023. One of the industries investigated is Chemours. This report provides answers to the questions of how residents living near industry are protected against adverse health effects and exposure to industrial emissions, and which measures offer better protection. The Safety Investigation Board concludes that the health of residents living near industry deserves better protection. The board also advocates that the competent authority should act based on the precautionary principle. Until now, the Dutch courts have not approved the application of this principle. Recently, the RIVM calculated in its report "Risk assessment of exposure to PFAS through food and drinking water in the Netherlands" that people ingest PFAS through food and drinking water. This study shows that the amount of PFAS that people can ingest through food and drinking water exceeds the so-called health-based guidance value. If people ingest more PFAS than this health-based guidance value for a long time, adverse health effects are possible, according to the RIVM. Municipalities also have a strong recreational sector. The landscape, water, and our cultural heritage contribute to the recreational value of our municipality. Recently (July 2023), the RIVM conducted research into PFAS in swimming water in the neighboring municipalities of Alblasserdam and Dordrecht. Although it was established that most of the researched swimming water is safe for swimming, a negative swimming advice was given for a busy recreational lake in Dordrecht, called the Merwelanden. The residents of Papendrecht also rely on this recreational lake. 6. Sub-conclusion 1 We support the concerns about PFAS expressed in the restriction report. As municipalities, we are confronted daily with the consequences of PFAS for our residents, our entrepreneurs, the environment, and nature. PFAS is not only present in the soil of our territory, but also in the surface water and groundwater. The consequences of exposure to PFAS are irreversible and not limited to the borders of our municipality or the Netherlands. This calls for action at the European level, and certainly an initiative for, in our view, a much-needed global ban. 7. Response to the content of the restriction proposal Below are specific remarks on the content of the restriction proposal. They are addressed by topic and, if necessary, a connection is made with the restriction proposal of the submitters. 7.1 Scope of the restriction According to the proposal (pages 50, 68), the restriction concerns the manufacture, trade, and use of PFAS in the EU as such and as a component of other substances, in mixtures, and in products above a certain concentration. We would like to point out that the ban should also apply to the import of PFAS (in all its forms and product forms) from a country outside the European Union for further processing, production, or transit to or through an (other) EU country. Furthermore, the ban should also cover production, trade, and transit between a factory with a branch in the EU and one or more branches outside the EU, in order to achieve a comprehensive ban on PFAS. 7.2 Essential use"
