Content: Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Org. name: Inner Mongolia Yonghe Fluorochemical Co., Ltd.
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Inner Mongolia Yonghe Fluorochemical Co., Ltd. is a professional fluorine chemical enterprise engaged in deep processing of local fluorite ore resources. The main products include fluorite block ore, fluorite powder, hydrofluoric acid and green, safe and environmentally friendly refrigerants.
To analyze and respond to the PFAS Restriction Proposal, Inner Mongolia Yonghe conducted an analysis of the fluorocarbon chemicals industry that would be affected.This analysis involved evaluating material alternatives and their impact, assessing socio-economic consequences, the end-of-life process and recycling methods for PFAS components.
We believe that the PFAS restriction proposal breaches the principle of proportionality. Specifically, if short-term substitutes for PFAS cannot appear in the market, the interests of companies both upstream and downstream in the PFAS supply chain will face significant losses, especially in the semiconductor field and electronic technology industry, which will bring global technology problems and limit the progress of global science and technology.
We observe that this restriction is based on a contradictory rationale: while admitting that no predictive tools are available, the proposal nonetheless predicts the concentrations of PFAS in the environment. On the one hand, all component of the group were considered harmful, while on the other, only certain component of the group were assessed. Many conclusions lack scientific evidence and are subject to uncertainty.
Yonghe's fluorocarbon chemicals affected by the PFAS Restriction Proposalinclude perfluorohexanone, dimer/tri-hexafluoropropylene, perfluoropolyether and tetrafluoroethylene trifluoroethylene ether products.
(1) Perfluorohexanone, also known as perfluoro (2-methyl-3-pentanone), molecular formula C6F12O, is an important substitute for halon fire extinguishing agent, it is a compound of fluoroketone, it is a clear, colorless, odorless liquid, supercharged with nitrogen gas, and stored as part of the fire extinguishing system in high pressure cylinders. Typical applications include fire incidents in settings such as computer rooms, data centers, aviation, ships, vehicles, libraries, oil and gas production areas. Another outstanding feature of perfluorhexanone fire extinguishing agent is its excellent environmental performance. With an ozone depletion potential (ODP) of 0, a global greenhouse potential (GWP) of 1 and an atmospheric life (year) of 0.014(i.e., 5 days), it can be a long-term and durable alternative to fire extinguishing agents such as Halon, hydrofluorocarbons (HFCS) and perfluorinated compounds (PFCS).
Perfluorohexanone is a liquid at room temperature, because its heat of evaporation is only 1/25 that of water, and the vapor pressure is 25 times that of water, these properties make it easy to vaporize and exist in a gaseous state, it mainly relies on heat absorption to achieve the effect of fire suppression. In terms of protecting the environment, it is a veritable green fire extinguishing agent. Because the fire extinguishing concentration of perfluorohexanone is 4-6%, the safety margin is relatively high, and making it safer for humans during use. Perfluorohexanone is a liquid at room temperature and is not classified as a hazardous material, and can be safely stored and transported in ordinary containers under ambient pressure across a broad temperature range (including air transport), rather than requiring pressure containers for storage and transportation like other halon alternatives.
In addition, perfluorohexanone can be used as a wet cleaning agent for steam reactors and their components. It can also be used to clean unwanted deposits accumulated in gas-phase reactors, etch dielectric or metallic materials, and dope various materials within these reactors, and has certain applications in the semiconductor industry.
In short, perfluorohexanone is a green and environmentally friendly fluorocarbon chemical with a short lifespan, low toxicity, and lacking characteristics of persistence, high toxicity and accumulation, which  should not be included in the scope of PFAS control.
(2)Dimer/trimer of hexafluoropropylene is transparent, tasteless, non-flammable, non-oil-based, low toxicity, non-corrosion, wide operating temperature range, high thermal stability and chemical stability, with excellent dielectric constant, ideal chemical inertness, excellent thermal conductivity, ODP 0, low GWP value, environmentally friendly, safe without flash point, non-flammable, and very high safety. It has strong performance compatibility and is applied in industries like electronic and other industry products, for the Internet of Things, big data processing centers, 5G, and high-end electronic devices, require chips that need efficient heat dissipation.
As we all know, data is the basic strategic resource of a country and an important factor of production. I believe that all European countries understand that the development of science and technology and data storage and processing have great strategic significance. Since the 21st century, with the rapid development of information technology (IT) and the emergence of big data applications like the Internet of Things, the importance of data centers responsible for computing, storage and data information interaction has become increasingly prominent. Data centers will serve as pivotal platforms for global strategies like "new infrastructure construction" and "Internet +", and the data center is an important cornerstone of the global transformation of industrial digitization, intelligent life and service informatization, which can support the high-quality development of the global economy and society in the future, and the data center industry is valued by all countries in the world.
However, a major challenge for current data centers is the significant heat generated by equipment, especially under conditions of high density and computing power, which cannot meet the current data calculation requirements, and the core technology of heat dissipation is temperature control technology. At present, in the data center put into operation, the cooling system is mainly air cooling, and the energy utilization rate is low. The cooling technology needs to solve two problems, one is that the heat of the equipment increases, and the cooling capacity of the cooling system needs to be improved accordingly to achieve the matching of heat production and heat transfer rate; Second, the energy utilization efficiency is low, and it is necessary to develop green and energy-efficient cooling technology with industrial application prospects.
Following the evolution of data center cooling technology, we've seen transitions from air conditioning refrigeration to fresh air cooling, indirect liquid cooling, and now, submerged liquid cooling. Currently, submerged liquid cooling stands out as the most effective solution for data centers and the best solution for heat dissipation technology, which has been promoted in computer technology enterprises such as China and the United States. The most ideal refrigerant for submerged liquid cooling in data centers is dimer/trihexafluoropropylene. Due to the special system architecture, the refrigerant needs to be in direct contact with the heating device, so the submerged liquid cooling can support higher power density IT deployment, greatly improving energy efficiency. Dimer/trihexafluoropropylene as the best refrigerant, has a good chemical inertia, and electronic components contact, will not cause any corrosion. There is no need for specific cleaning steps after use, and at the same time, it has excellent thermal conductivity and insulation and non-combustible inertia characteristics. In data center immersion liquid cooling applications, the working principle of fluorinated liquid immersion coolant technology is to immerse the heating equipment (such as servers) in the fluorinated liquid, and transferring the heat produced by electronic devices/systems to the external environment via the circulation of the fluorinated liquid, which is the ideal choice for single-phase and two-phase immersion liquid cooling applications in data centers. The PUE can be reduced to 1.02, which can significantly increase the power density and computing power per unit area of a single rack in the data center.
Some environmentalists might argue in favor of using the most basic and time-tested fresh air cooling technology, they do not need the development of science and technology, they need human health, because air cooling is the most primitive and the most environmentally friendly way. However, it's worth noting that air cooling demands significant mechanical equipment, occupy a lot of land resources, will produce a lot of noise pollution, while the preparation and production of large fan equipment will also be detrimental to the environment, but I think what is more unfavorable is the electrical energy generated by the operation of mechanical equipment, and the source of global electrical energy is still relying on coal power generation, so there will be more coal to power. According to data, China's data centers consumed a total of 160.9 billion kWh in 2018, which is comparable to the electricity usage of 25 million residents in Shanghai, if 10% of the data center uses immersion cooling technology, it can save at least 2.87 billion Kwh, equivalent to saving nearly 1 million tons of standard coal. Reducing emissions by about 2.5 million tons of carbon dioxide. Currently, data centers worldwide account for over 1.0% of global electricity generation, and astonishingly, over 90% still rely mainly on air cooling, I believe that it is 2023, with the speed of world economic development, the power generation of the global data center is doubled, at least in China, the power consumption of the data center is growing by more than 15% per year. As a result, data centers are still primarily air-cooled, which is expected to burn more coal for electricity and produce more carbon dioxide emissions that contribute to global warming. Therefore, I think the use of air cooling is the least environmentally friendly alternative, if the world's data centers can use dimer/trihexafluoryl immersion cooling to replace all air cooling, then more coal resources can be left for the future, reduce energy consumption at the same time reduce carbon dioxide emissions, I think this is a very meaningful thing.
One might then inquire about the feasibility of substituting the fluorine refrigerant? Yes, prior to this, researchers and scientists in related fields have conducted research and practice on the replacement of fluorine-containing refrigerant. Historically, the initial refrigerants were water and ethylene glycol solutions, which utilized indirect cooling technology. However, when these solutions are contaminated with certain impurities, they gain electrical conductivity, corrosive to the pipeline, there are major security risks, once water seepage or leakage, in large data centers, its water seepage or water leakage caused by equipment loss is incalculable, even there will be injury accidents.
Furthermore, the commonly used substitutes for refrigerants currently include aromatic substances, silicates, aliphatic compounds, and silicone substances, among others. For example, the aromatic substances include p-diethylbenzene, diphenylmethyl toluene and hydrogenated terphenyls. However, due to their inherent toxicity and potential carcinogenic properties, and most of them have a strong irritating odor, there are certain restrictions on users and applications, the program was eliminated.
Aliphatic compounds include mineral oil, polyalpha-olefin, etc., which are mainly products of petrochemical industry. Such substances have certain thermal conductivity, but they have flash points. Moreover, its viscosity is high, volatile residues are more and difficult to clean, which has a certain impact on the operation of maintenance. The most significant risk, however, is the flammability of hydrocarbons. In substantial data center servers, there might be dozens or even hundreds of tons of this refrigerant. A leak or fire would be akin to a ticking time bomb, leading to catastrophic consequences.
Silicone substances include dimethylsiloxane, methylsiloxane, and silicone oil. While these substances may have high boiling points and low surface energies, they still share the characteristics of mineral oil with regards to flash points and viscosity. At the same time, silicone substances decompose again under certain conditions, and the decomposition products have certain toxicity. At the same time, there are certain residues that require additional cleaning treatment. The risks associated with them are similar to those previously mentioned, including the potential for explosion.
In short, on the replacement of coolant, scientific researchers have done a lot of work, aromatic substances, silicates, aliphatic compounds, silicone substances and other substances have toxicity and flash points, with explosions and other adverse safety risks to humans and the environment, and they also fall short in meeting the demands of high computational power and energy efficiency.

Dimer/trimer of hexafluoropropylene has excellent electrical insulation and thermal conductivity. It possesses ideal chemical inertness and thermal stability, making it suitable for a wide range of temperature control heat dissipation occasions; It offers excellent material  compatibility, remaining unreactive with the majority of metals, plastics and polymers; Good fluidity, good flow heat dissipation in the temperature control system; Non-dangerous goods, non-combustible and non-explosive, no ignition point, flash point, non-toxic, harmless and non-irritating. The use of dimer/trihexafluoropropylene can reduce the PUE to 1.02, meeting the current and future requirements for high-density, high-power data processing, and is the most ideal refrigerant for data centers.
Regarding production emissions, there's little cause for concern as waste liquids and materials are incinerated, ultimately producing hydrogen fluoride and carbon dioxide. As for recycling and utilization, I think it is easy to achieve. With the existing distillation technology allow for simple purification. The service life of the general data center is more than 10 years, and the entire server is closed, there is no need to worry about the emission of fluorine compounds during use. Once the server reaches the end of its service life, it can simply be replaced, and the valuable fluorinated liquid in the tank can be repurposed.
In conclusion, there's no viable alternative for Dimer/trimer of hexafluoropropylene application technology in data centers. Even if potential substitutes were available, they wouldn't be able to fulfill all the necessary criteria. Moreover, these fluorinated compounds are used in key applications to meet the EU and UN climate goals and are drivers of the European Green Deal, the Chip Act, the Hydrogen Strategy and the Sustainable and smart Mobility Strategy. The proposed restrictions create widespread uncertainty that will undermine investment decisions and innovation for these and other important EU ambitions. Therefore, I believe that given its potential to further global technological advancements safely, propel human civilization forward, and champion green, energy-efficient solutions, dimer/trimer of hexafluoropropylene should be exempted from the PFAS list for a long time.

General Comments: Innolith has developed a breakthrough battery technology, which enhances the energy density and performance of lithium batteries by over 30 %. Consequently, there are significant benefits for this very important field: reduction of battery weight of cars and aeroplanes, less environmental impact (critical raw materials) and full recyclability of the batteries. Innolith’s technology (“I-State-technology”) uses PFAS-like compounds as raw materials and electrolytes. For this reason, the planned full PFAS ban would prohibit commercialization of this breakthrough technology. Therefore, we request a derogation of a few specific perfluorinated compounds (namely perfluorinated tertiary alcohols and their aluminium derivatives), limited specifically for use in lithium-ion batteries, which by definition are closed and encapsuled systems for security reasons. Those compounds are safely enclosed in the batteries during the full lifetime, are not released into the environment, are not in human or animal contact during use and can be fully recycled at the end of the service life. Therefore, there is no significant environmental or human impact caused by the use of those compounds in batteries. Rather the advantages and benefits of using this technology will greatly outweigh the risks.
The key benefits of this new breakthrough technology “I-State” are:
- increase in energy density by enabling 30% reduction of battery weight
- the technology allows efficient recycling of batteries as the electrolyte can be easily removed, purified and re-used in new battery production.
- 30% reduction of nickel, cobalt and manganese (critical raw materials with high environmental impact)
- higher performance of batteries in a wider temperature range, compared to classical Li-ion batteries
- some applications such as energy source in aviation due to weight reduction become possible
- the electrolyte does not propagate fire – currently, uncontrolled flammability of classical Li-ion batteries is a massive acceptability issue in society.
- recharge times can be significantly reduced, increasing acceptability of electrical vehicles.
- this technology has been developed entirely within the EU allowing EU industry to outperform Asian innovators and regain a technological advantage in electrical mobility. The full-scale production of batteries is planned to be located in the EU to protect the technology.
- the technology has been globally patented during the last years and massive resources in research and development would be at stake if the restriction proposal, as is, would come into force.
Therefore, our proposal and request is to amend paragraph 5 in column 2 of the restriction proposal by the following entry: “By way of derogation, paragraphs 1 and 2 shall not apply to:
perfluorinated tertiary alcohols and their aluminium compounds for use in encapsuled batteries.”
We propose not to define an expiration period for this derogation, as there are no alternatives to this technology. The required enhanced voltage stability and performance is intrinsically linked to the per-fluorination of the compounds. Only perfluorinated compounds can withstand this high voltage (5.0 volts) in the battery cells. Therefore, it is highly unlikely that other chemical alternatives can be found, as extensive research in the last 20+ years has demonstrated. The manufacturing of lithium-ion batteries takes place under fully controlled industrial conditions, the batteries provide a safe encapsulation during use, and are recyclable after service life. This allows to mitigate the risk for health and the environment to an absolute minimum, greatly outweighed by the benefits of this technology.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: With reference to table 9 of the restriction proposal, the application/use for which an exemption is herewith proposed (lithium-ion batteries for energy storage), is currently not addressed in this table. The entry that comes closest to our application is the entry “Energy sector (Annex E.2.12.), Sector as a whole” that focuses solely on Proton-exchange membrane (PEM) in fuel cells, which does not cover the application/use we propose for exemption. Please see further sections for more details.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: : Innolith has developed, patented worldwide and piloted a breakthrough new technology for energy storage and improvement of commercial lithium-ion batteries, so called “I-State battery technology”. This I-State technology, using an entirely new battery chemistry, will reduce significantly Electrical Vehicle (EV) costs and increase vehicle range through an unmatched energy density of 300 - 350 Wh/kg while improving both safety and performance. This is made possible through its high voltage, high conductivity, non-flammable electrolyte that also enables a greatly improved temperature range of -40 to +60 °C for charge and discharge. The I-State Technology relies on a new type of electrolyte which uses a new substance as main electrolyte component. The used electrolyte / conducting salt consists in part of PFAS-like chemical components which formally fall under the proposed PFAS restrictions. There exist no known alternatives to the use of those PFAS-like compounds. We have registered the conducting salt of our electrolyte as a new substance (for details please see confidential section) in January 2022 in the 1 – 10 tons/annum tonnage band. Currently, a dossier update to cover the 10 – 100 tons/annum tonnage band is in preparation, as market demand increase is already foreseeable, once full commercialization has started. However, Table 9 and the entire restriction proposal does not foresee any exemptions for electronics or battery technology and the restriction, if coming into force as is, would not allow to introduce this new technology in Europe. Remaining markets would thus be only outside the EU for a new innovative technology developed entirely in the EU. Also, the manufacturing facility, currently planned to be established within the EU, could and would not be established here in the EU but elsewhere, outside the EU. Thus, we see this proposal with respect to our I-State battery technology achieving the opposite of the REACH goal as addressed in recital No. 1 “This Regulation should ensure a high level of protection of human health and the environment as well as the free movement of substances, on their own, in preparations and in articles, while enhancing competitiveness and innovation. This Regulation should also promote the development of alternative methods for the assessment of hazards of substances.” The I-State battery technology, from the beginning of research already, includes a recycling concept for lithium-ion batteries to ensure that all precious material used in such batteries can be collected from end-use applications and recycled to ensure a circular economy by design. More than 10 years of research investment would be lost, in case the restriction proposal would come into force as is. We are very much concerned that investors and customers may step back from further investments and interest in this technology due to the public discussion about this restriction.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: : Our I-State-Technology makes it possible to fully recycle the battery components, including the electrolyte. No parts of the electrolyte would be lost during recycling. This is a significant advancement over existing technologies and batteries. Especially the existing and widely used electrolyte (based on LiPF6 and flammable solvents) cannot be recycled or only with great difficulty. The PFAS-like electrolyte parts will be fully recyclable and therefore, will not be released into the environment. Recycling will be done in a chemical plant environment, ensuring safety and minimizing the loss of PFAS-like components to almost zero. Thus, recycling rates will clearly outperform currently available battery technologies.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: : Since the I-state technology of Innolith is currently only entering commercial phases, there is no commercial recycling plant established, yet. But the recycling industry will be clearly benefitting by widespread use of the I-state technology, because the recycling itself will be much easier than with the currently commercially available batteries (see previous section). Clearly this new technology is designed to enable the EU Council call in its conclusions from October 2019 on 'More circularity – Transition to a sustainable society', in line with the transition to electro-mobility to be accompanied by coherent policies supporting the development of technologies that improve the sustainability and circularity of batteries. This technology is now available and at risk through this proposed restriction on PFAS without a derogation for batteries. The EU Council in July 2023 just adopted a new regulation on batteries and waste batteries (REGULATION (EU) 2023/1542 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 12 July 2023 concerning batteries and waste batteries, amending Directive 2008/98/EC and Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and repealing Directive 2006/66/EC, OJ L 191/1, 28.7.2023). The ambitious recycling targets defined therein will become achievable through this new I state technology and thus, implementing this technology into full commercial scale will be a significant milestone in achieving these goals, economically. However, the Article 6(1) in this Regulation prohibits the use of restricted substances, according to Annex XVII to Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006, unless restrictions are complied with. The proposed PFAS restriction, without a derogation for batteries, would prohibit use and commercialisation of this new technology and prohibit all benefits that come with it. It is noteworthy, that recollection systems for batteries are already well established and particularly for lithium-ion car batteries not only recollection systems are in place but the high cost of such batteries makes it economically attractive for society to recollect and recycle them, to reuse the valuable materials therein, making Europe more independent from the global lithium and transition element market.

5. Proposed derogations: Once fully commercialized, we expect that the volume of PFAS-like components used in the I-state-technology will be > 1000 tons per year. Currently, there are only pilot scale volumes being used. For details, see comments to chapter 6 below. Based on the clear benefits of the technology and no significant environmental or human impact, Innolith requests that the I-State technology and our REACH registered electrolyte (as well as its precursor substances) fully deserves a long-term exemption from the planned PFAS restrictions.

6. Missing uses: Once fully commercialized, we expect that the volume of PFAS-like components used in the I-state-technology will be > 1000 tons per year. Currently, there are only pilot scale volumes being used. The electrolyte containing PFAS-like compounds will be strictly confined in the commercial batteries, and is fully recyclable with very little or no emissions into the environment. There will be no human contact during the use, nor any release into the environment. The electrolyte itself containing PFAS-like components will be fully recyclable in a shielded, chemical plant. We believe that the use of the I-State technology including PFAS-like components will be of high benefit for the society: the weight of the batteries in electrical cars will decrease by almost 30 %, and consequently the use of expensive and critical electrode raw materials like nickel, cobalt and manganese will also decrease by 30 %. The acceptance of electrical cars will generally be much higher. The technology also enables a milestone with respect to lithium-ion battery recyclability, as the electrolyte, containing the PFAS like compound can be recycled and reused, as well as the remaining components of the battery, in line with a circular economy towards a sustainable society. There will be no significant release of PFAS-like components into the environment during use or recycling, nor any human contact during use. The electrolyte is non-volatile, highly shielded and therefore not being released during use of the batteries. Therefore, Innolith requests that the I-State technology and our REACH registered electrolyte (as well as its precursor substances) fully deserves a long-term exemption from the planned PFAS restrictions.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: The known lithium-ion technologies (mostly based on LiPF6) are providing only a limited energy density of 200 – 250 Wh/kg battery weight. This makes electrical cars (and aeroplanes) very heavy, and the use of expensive and critical electrode materials (transitional metals) is high. For the last 20 years there was an ongoing debate about the so called “solid state battery technology” which was very much hyped and always declared “close to commercialization”. However, the battery industry is currently very sceptical whether solid-state batteries will ever reach commercialization. Our I-state technology gives a 30 % overall benefit in weight and energy density and is ready for scale-up and commercialization. Many samples of batteries are already tested at automotive and aeroplane customers. There is no known alternative battery technology ready for scale-up, which will provide the same benefits (energy density up to 350 Wh/kg, 30 % less weight, etc.). The I-State technology relies on PFAS-like compounds as electrolyte. The elevated performance (stability up to 5.0 V) can only be reached by using fluorinated electrolytes. Any other non-fluorinated substances will chemically break down under these extreme conditions. Despite decades of use and screening, no other non-fluorinated alternatives have been found.

8. Other identified uses: : As discussed above, the whole battery industry is excluded from the Annexes and from the PFAS discussions. This is because Innolith’s new I-State-Technology is the first to use PFAS-like compounds in Li-ion batteries. Therefore, the battery industry must be added to the list of industries affected. A ban of PFAS as proposed would render the whole I-State technology by Innolith impossible because it can only be realized using PFAS-like substances (see above). The major and breakthrough benefits for the battery sector resulting from I-State technology clearly outweigh the relatively minimal to non-existing environmental risks (no release in the environment, no human contact). Therefore, the I-State technology clearly deserves a long-term derogation from the planned PFAS ban.

General Comments: Innovationsallianz Baden-Württemberg (innBW) is an alliance of 12 application-oriented research institutes that is unique in Germany.
Together, the 12 research institutions of innBW offer a unique range of services across the entire development process from the idea to market entry. In doing so, they orient their work to the future growth fields along which the federal state government aligns its technology policy.
With more than 4,500 company projects per year and over 500 public research projects in the future-oriented fields of health and care, sustainable mobility, energy and environmental technology, and information and communication, innBW is a beacon of innovation and technology transfer. As a link between science and industry, innBW brings both sides together and ensures the transfer of findings from basic research into industrial practice.
Together with companies, innBW develops market-ready products, processes and services and fulfills its role as a thought leader so that the federal state can maintain its top position as a European technology region. The innBW network of 12 independent research institutes is more than the sum of its members.
PFAS and especially PTFE is a material, which since many years has been tested and been compared to other materials. For industrial applications and especially as sliding material in medical devices it has been proven for outstanding performance with the ability to sterilize reusable medical probes and devices. In photonics applications it serves as diffuse reflector material and has such an outstanding performance that it is irreplaceable.
Without PFAS our research activities are no longer possible, because there are no substitution for PFAS e.g. in many analytical instruments. Our suppliers are not able to guarantee spare/wear parts in case of a restriction. PFAS (PTFE) are used e.g. in exhaust pipes for clean rooms, which are essential for our research. For example the Hahn Schickard institute Villingen Schwenningen, working  in the field of semiconductors, uses many materials falling under the definition of PFAS for manufacturing of semiconductors/MEMS including process chemistries, manufacturing equipment, manufacturing infrastructure and manufacturing support equipment. Actually there are no substitutes so the research work is no longer possible.

PFAS in Li-Ion Batteries:

PFAS, including materials like PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride) and PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene), are used as binders in Li-Ion battery electrodes. These binders play a role in influencing the battery's performance, including formation of the Solid Electrolyte Interphase (SEI) layer and conductivity.
L-Ion batteries are necessary for the green deal of the European Union
Usage and Growth:

PVDF was introduced by Sony in the 1990s for Li-Ion batteries in phones and laptops. Its usage has since expanded to various applications, from portable batteries to industrial ones. The RECHARGE association estimates that PFAS-containing polymers, mainly PVDF, were present in batteries in Europe in 2020 (~ 1.500 t), with an expected significant growth in tonnage by 2030 (~ 15.000 t).

Recycling Concerns:

There's a debate over the release of PFAS during the recycling of PFAS-containing Li-Ion batteries. RECHARGE and Stephen H. Korzeniowski et al. suggests negligible releases, but some researchers, like Ian Cousins, express concerns about the potential for PFAS emissions during recycling processes. Further research is needed to understand the actual impact of polymeric PFAS in recycling.
Regarding PFAS in Lithium-Ion Battery Cell Manufacturing, it is suggested that the proposed restriction consider a derogation (exemption) for PFAS substances employed in the manufacturing of lithium-ion battery cell processes. Actually no practical alternatives to PFAS-based binders currently exist for the production of lithium-ion batteries. A potential solution involves either an unlimited or time-limited derogation for specific PFAS substances like PTFE and PVDF, which are utilized as binder materials. In cases where suitable alternatives do not materialize within the designated time frame (minimum of 13.5 years), there is a suggestion to explore the possibility of extending the derogation.

PFAS-containing coatings are crucial for their longevity, particularly in architectural applications like metallic facades. These coatings, such as FEVE or PVDF, have proven to last for over 50 years, far surpassing other binder systems that degrade quickly when exposed to UV radiation and weathering. This durability not only ensures aesthetics but also maintains the coating's protective function. Furthermore, PFAS-free coatings have a hydrophobic effect, making them resistant to graffiti, dirt, and environmental damage. They can also contribute to energy efficiency by reducing building envelope heat. While alternatives have been explored, the cost-effectiveness and performance of PFAS-containing coatings remain unmatched, as confirmed by an OECD study (OECD (2022), Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances and Alternatives in Coatings, Paints and Varnishes (CPVs), Report on the Commercial Availability and Current Uses, OECD Series on Risk Management, No. 70, Environment, Health and Safety, Environment Directorate, OECD).

The proposed restriction is overly broad, covering more than 10,000 substances with varying properties and without considering their individual risk profiles. It lacks a risk-based approach and fails to assess substances or groups of substances for their potential risks adequately. The justification for the restriction primarily relies on persistence and other hazard properties, but a comprehensive risk assessment has not been conducted as required by the REACH Regulation. To address this issue appropriately, a more differentiated approach is necessary, taking into account the specific properties of each substance and assessing whether it poses an uncontrollable risk to the environment or human health. We believe that certain uses of PFAS can be safe, and a complete ban is not justified if there is no environmental exposure risk. It's crucial to allow the continued safe use of PFAS when suitable alternatives are not available to avoid disproportionate restrictions.

Due to the insufficient data in Annex XV on oligomeric/polymeric PFASs, it would be more than desirable for the regulatory criteria for low concern polymers to be applied. At least until reliable results are available. Korzeniowski et al. 6. Missing uses: e) In a research and development project conducted at our research institute, we employed Nickel (Ni) as a metallic binder, and the outcomes yielded promising results. In addition, we are also developing acrylate-based separators for lithium-sulfur batteries, due to the rapid lithium ion transport and ionic shielding of polysulfides. It's essential to note that these developments are currently in their nascent stages, making it challenging to predict the precise timeline for practical implementation. MEMS should be explicitly incorporated to the sector “Electronics and Semiconductor” because MEMS are manufactured by techniques similar to those used in microlelectronics fabrication. Not covered by this regulation is a derogation for spare parts/maintenance e.g. for industrial equipment for semiconductor/MEMS production. As well for re-use of equipment / re-Manufacturing e.g. repair as produced. The concepts of ’right to repair’ and allowing resale of preowned products have been broadly incorporated into other EU substance restrictions and other EU REACH restrictions, and it is essential to incorporate them into the EU PFAS. Equipment and infrastructure in high-tech research areas such as MEMS are expensive. Due to low investment funds, research institutes and universities are dependent on being able to use equipment and infrastructure for longer (>20 years) than is usual in industry and also to be able to repair and maintain them during this period. Otherwise, there is a risk of extinction of research institutions in in high-tech research areas field in Europe.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: If PFAS were to be excluded generally in medical devices, much more of such devices would become single use (due to actually sterilizable PFAS materials would be replaced by non-sterilizable materials) and explode the total waste volume and environmental burden by non-reusable products.  Photonics products (some of them incorporating diffuse reflectors made of PFAS), today one of the core competencies and growth drives for European companies, would suffer in their performance against Asian competition and pass over the leadership role in such high tech products over to companies outside EU. With PTFE being only a small component in optical measurement devices or lasers playing a significant role for the overall performance of a complete machine or much larger product, banning would lead to a huge loss within our photonics industry. Paragraph 5 of the proposed restriction entry text includes "ee.[the semiconductor manufacturing process until 13.5 year after EiF]" as a potential derogation for reconsideration after the consultation. We appeal to keep the above derogation for at least 13.5 years after EiF and to add explicitly the equipment used for semiconductor/MEMS manufacturing. When deciding on a derogation for the semiconductor/MEMS manufacturing process please consider the consultation comments #4304 by SEMI (RCOM part 13), #4449 by ESIA (RCOM part 18), #4543 by JEITA et al. (RCOM part 21) and the papers published by SIA PFAS Consortium under https://www.semiconductors.org/pfas/. These explain the background of the semiconductor manufacturing process in detail and describe the impact of a potential PFAS restriction.

Analytical methods: The determination of polyfluorinated and perfluorinated alkyl substances (PFAS) represents a major analytical challenge due to the large variety of substances (estimated: > 10,000 substances) with a wide variety of chemical structures and isomer mixtures, as well as a wide variety of polarities. Standard and reference substances that must be used to calibrate analytical devices are often not available. Standards that are available for the analytical determination of (PFAS) substances are mainly in the area of environmental analysis (e.g. for analyzing water and soil samples) and are only available for individual substances (<100) [1]. The standard DIN 38409-59:2022 DE [2] provides a method for measuring the sum parameter adsorbable organically bound fluorine (AOF). However, a clear assignment to individual substances is not possible. The Total Oxidizable Precursor (TOP) assay offers another analysis option, including for solid samples. The analytical principle of the TOP assay is to oxidatively convert unknown PFAS precursor compounds into perfluorocarboxylic acids (PFCA), which can therefore be quantified. This makes it possible to estimate PFAS levels in environmental samples using screening procedures. The concept of the TOP assay is more selective than, for example, measurements of the sum parameters EOF (extractable organic fluorine compounds) and AOF. A detailed study to more precisely assess the possibilities and limitations of the TOP assay methodology and its significance was published in 2022 [3]. In summary, it can be said that according to the current state of research and our level of knowledge, the analysis of the approximately 10,000 individual substances in medical devices is not possible. There is a significant need for research here, with a focus on the development of suitable method analysis. In case of a restriction it is not pssible to analyze if and which PFAS are part of e.g. a medical device. General Comments: Instruments used in the automated measuring and checking of geometrical quantities of machinery products (HS code 903180) including Touch Probes, Styli and Fixturing is harsh where products are expected to perform with high reliability at elevated temperature in high-speed precision applications.

The stable properties of FKM and similar long chain PFAS are well suited to these applications.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Integer manufactures complete medical devices as well as medical device components for many of the largest medical device companies in the world.  Integer also manufactures batteries ranging from small implantable medical batteries to large industrial lithium batteries.  Fluoropolymers such as PTFE, FEP, ETFE, ePTFE, and PVDF are all integral materials across our product portfolio.  Integer, as well as the medical device and battery sectors as a whole, will be heavily impacted by a restriction of PFAS that includes fluoropolymers.  Therefore, Integer would like to submit the following commentary on the proposed PFAS Restriction.

Our first request would be that fluoropolymers are excluded from the scope of the restriction.  Fluoropolymers have a range of properties that make them extremely beneficial to society and these materials have become ubiquitous.  They are extremely inert, highly chemical resistant, nearly frictionless, and very biocompatible, which is why they play a major role in our medical devices.  Fluoropolymers are also a vital constituent in our battery and capacitor products.  There are numerous examples where fluoropolymers play important roles in the fit, form, function and/or even safety of these products.  A restriction on fluoropolymers will have far-reaching impacts on society that could set back quality of life improvements not only on medical devices, but also on medical procedures for many years or even decades.  Fluoropolymers are undeniably useful and are arguably the safest of all PFAS, so some consideration should be made for exempting them from the broader PFAS restriction.

Additionally, it should be noted that both waste medical devices and waste battery products are regulated under other EU regulations.  These regulations could be amended to ensure that resulting fluoropolymer waste is properly disposed of.  For example, medical device waste is biohazardous and is often sterilized by incineration.  The current regulations could be expanded to ensure fluoropolymers in medical devices are fully incinerated before disposal as well.  Similar emission laws could be placed on fluoropolymer manufacturers to limit PFAS emissions during production.  This sort of approach would allow the full benefit of fluoropolymers to continue in certain products while ensuring PFAS emissions to the environment are minimized.

If fluoropolymers must be included in the scope of the PFAS regulation, then Integer requests that our products utilizing fluoropolymers be provided derogations.  Fluoropolymers are utilized in our devices because their unique characteristics are fundamental to their function.  There are no other materials that we are aware of that could be considered direct alternatives for most of our fluoropolymer uses.  Finding and employing alternatives, if even possible, will take many years due to the amount of testing and approvals required in the medical device industry.  Therefore, Integer requests derogations of the longest term for all of our products listed below:

IMPLANTABLE MEDICAL DEVICES
- Stents
- Hernia meshes
- Implantable batteries
- Implantable Pulse Generators (IPG’s) and components
- Leads
- Feedthroughs

INVASIVE MEDICAL DEVICES
- Guidewires
- Introducers
- Catheters and other medical tubing
- Hypodermic tubing / Hypotubes
- Mandrels
- Other associated instruments and tools

BATTERIES AND CAPACITORS
- Lithium primary medical batteries
- Lithium primary industrial batteries
- Capacitor cells and packs

Many of our medical devices use components made directly of fluoropolymers, but fluoropolymer coatings are also very common.  Often metals in medical devices are coated with a fluoropolymer layer to reduce friction.  For example, a guidewire coated in PTFE is less likely to cause damage to a patient’s interior artery wall compared to an uncoated wire.  For similar reasons, hypodermic tubes, introducers, mandrels, and other instruments and tools are often coated to improve functionality and patient safety.  A large group derogation for “coated medical devices” would be much appreciated and would ensure all of these life-saving, coated medical devices can continue to be produced while alternative materials are explored.

It was noted that a derogation for implantable medical devices was already included in the proposal.  This covers many of our products, however, hernia meshes was specifically excluded from this derogation description.  Integer would like for this exclusion from the derogation to be reconsidered as fluoropolymers play a valuable role in implantable meshes.  Making implantable meshes with fluoropolymers helps prevent body tissues from adhering to the mesh device which can result in tearing.  Since fluoropolymers can be crucial to the safe use of these devices, they should be included in the implantable devices derogation.

Lithium primary batteries should also be provided a derogation.  Integer’s position on this is in alignment with RECHARGE.  Fluoropolymers are used as electrode binder materials within all of Integer’s industrial lithium batteries.  Binder materials are important in the function and manufacturability of these batteries, and fluoropolymers are ideal due to their mechanical, thermal, and dispersive properties as well as their electrochemical stability.  These materials will not be easy to replace, and time will be required to explore new chemistries.  The modern world is dependent on batteries, and fluoropolymers have aided in their advancement.  Our large industrial batteries are heavily used by the oil and gas industry, the military, and in environmental surveying equipment.  A derogation is needed to ensure these lithium batteries are not sorely impacted.

In summary, Integer believes that fluoropolymers should be excluded from the scope of the PFAS restriction.  They present less risk to the environment and human health than non-polymer PFAS while also being the most beneficial to society.  The medical device and battery products discussed in this commentary depend on these materials.  Integer requests that our use of fluoropolymers in our medical device and battery products be provided derogations to ensure sufficient transition times to find and implement alternatives.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Integer’s commentary applies to our medical device and battery products that we manufacture.  These would pertain to the “Medical Devices” and “Energy” sectors listed in Table 9 of Annex XV.  We would like to provide additional information on some sub-sectors up for derogation reconsideration as well as propose new sub-sectors be included in the derogations.  Our comments include specific fluoropolymer use and function within these products as well as a discussion on the feasibility of alternatives.  Also included is commentary on disposal of these products.  Our comments apply to these specific sectors and uses: Medical devices: - Implantable medical devices, specifically hernia meshes - Other coating applications, with specific product listing. Energy: - Lithium primary batteries.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Medical devices, once used, are considered biohazardous waste and disposal of such products is already regulated.  The waste must be sterilized before disposal to remove infectious pathogens and is often incinerated to achieve this.  In addition to destroying biohazardous pathogens, incineration has shown to be an effective method of destroying fluoropolymers like PTFE as well.  A 2019 study released in Chemosphere by K. Aleksandrov et al. states that PTFE can be transformed into hydrofluoric acid through PTFE combustion.  Carbon tetrafluoride, the simplest perfluorocarbon, decomposes at 1400 °C.  Regulations can be implemented to ensure that all fluoropolymer-containing medical devices are incinerated before disposal to prevent PFAS from being released into the environment.  Similarly, battery waste is regulated under WEE, Directive 2006/66/EC and the new European Battery Regulation.  While these regulations focus on heavy metals, the scope of these regulations could be expanded to include fluoropolymer recycling or disposal requirements as well.  As recommended for medical device waste, incineration could be a required method of disposal for the fluoropolymer component materials.  A disposal cost will incur that could be absorbed by consumers and manufacturers, but ultimately regulating fluoropolymer waste on a per-product type basis would allow critical fluoropolymer applications to remain in use while meeting the goal of preventing PFAS emissions to the environment.

6. Missing uses: Lithium primary batteries should also be provided a derogation within the PFAS restriction because fluoropolymers are crucial to the function and safety of these batteries.  PTFE is currently used as the electrode binder material within all of Integer’s lithium-oxyhalide batteries.  Due to its unique properties, PTFE is the only known material that can be used as a binder to produce this type of battery.    PTFE consists of very long polymer chains that effectively entangle the cathode material particles so that these particles become bound together without chemically reacting with the binder. PTFE is extremely chemically resistant and does not react at all with the highly oxidizing electrolyte liquids (thionyl chloride and sulfuryl chloride) over a very wide temperature range. PTFE is physically stable and does not melt or soften at the very high temperatures at which the batteries operate (up to 200°C).  A binder material must meet all of these conditions in order to function safely.  There are no alternative binder materials currently known that meet all the physical, chemical, and thermal requirements.  Any alternative would need to be inert to highly oxidizing electrolytes and would need to remain physically unchanged through the entire operating temperature range of -55C to over +200C.  If these parameters are not met then there is high risk that the binder will decompose, releasing the cathode particles and causing very hazardous shorting within the batteries.    Integer is not aware of any research being done to design alternative compositions for these battery applications.  Even if alternatives did exist today, rigorous testing would need to be conducted to ensure that the new binder material would remain physically and chemically unchanged under the conditions in which these batteries operate.   Testing would need to be conducted over the wide operating temperature range and the battery products would need to undergo shock and vibration testing.  More importantly, some of these batteries remain in use for over 10 years once deployed.  Testing would need to be conducted to demonstrate that the alternative binder would remain stable in the electrolytes for more than ten years.    Even if a non-PFAS binder material existed today, it would require the longest derogation duration to prove feasibility and safety of these products.  Using an alternative material that has not been thoroughly tested could severely impact the performance of the batteries.  And when dealing with such high-energy batteries, battery failures can possibly lead to severe injuries or even death.  Therefore, a derogation is requested for our lithium primary battery products to ensure new designs are implemented as safely as possible.    Other missing uses Integer would like to submit are for specific product types listed below that we manufacture using fluoropolymer materials.  These product types were not mentioned specifically within the proposed restriction, but fluoropolymers are essential to their function and derogations should be considered.  However, the typical application of fluoropolymers for these devices is as a coating and would fall under the “other coating applications” sub-use derogation.  Therefore, further information is provided in the next section covering derogations marked for reconsideration.   - Guidewires - Introducers - Hypodermic tubing / Hypotubes - Mandrels - Other associated instruments and tools

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Hernia meshes was specifically excluded from implantable devices derogation description and marked for reconsideration.  Integer would like for this exclusion from the derogation to be reinstated because fluoropolymers play a valuable role in implantable meshes.  PTFE, ePTFE, irradiated PTFE, FEP, and PVDF are the common fluoropolymers used in hernia meshes.  Lightweight meshes have been used for internal repairs for decades now and different materials have shown to have various inherent complications.  Polypropylene and polyester meshes have a low risk of infection, however, these have a high risk of adhesion.  In contrast, fluoropolymers, while having a higher risk of infection, have a very low risk of adhesion formation and can be utilized to mitigate this particular negative outcome.  Depending on the conditions and location of the repair, a surgeon may often choose one material over another.  Many modern meshes are actually composites incorporating multiple polymers with the aim to leverage the benefit of each material.  Since fluoropolymers can be crucial to reducing adhesion risks in these vital medical devices, they should be included in the implantable devices derogation to ensure sufficient time to explore alternatives.  In stark contrast to many non-polymer PFAS which are known to be hazardous, fluoropolymers like PTFE are extremely biocompatible and are intentionally introduced into the body regularly through medical devices.  Integer manufactures a plethora of medical devices, and a portion of our devices get coated with fluoropolymers to attain a set of desired properties.  For example, a guidewire coated in PTFE is less likely to cause damage to a patient’s interior artery wall compared to an uncoated wire.  For similar reasons, hypodermic tubes, introducers, mandrels, and other instruments and tools are often coated with fluoropolymers to improve functionality and patient safety.  Integer therefore highly encourages that derogations are reconsidered and granted for all coating applications within medical devices.    Many desirable properties for medical devices are present in fluoropolymers like PTFE, PFA, and ePTFE.  Some of these attributes of fluoropolymers is low friction, chemical resistance, temperature resistance, flexibility, and biocompatibility.  A table comparing various polymers for these characteristics can be seen in the attached letter.  There are polymers like PEEK, silicone, and polyurethane that exhibit some of these properties, however, most all of these desirable traits are present in the fluoropolymer materials being used.  When considering alternatives, the Appendix to Annex E.2 lists many materials as alternatives to fluoropolymers for medical devices.  Integer’s cognizant team has reviewed the list and decided to comment on the list of “alternatives” identified, specifically for the medical devices tab.  Comments for each particular material is noted in the table at the end of the attached letter.  To summarize, many materials listed are simply not suitable substitutes for the particular applications in which fluoropolymers are currently utilized within our medical devices.  When considering the time required to implement alternatives, the qualification/validation for any alternative material could only start once a suitable substitute is identified. Identifying a substitute and determining its feasibility could take from 18 up to 24 months; lab sample review, pre-feasibility and feasibility studies would need to be executed through each iteration (rarely the first selection works as a “drop-in” substitute). Once the appropriate substitute is chosen, validation activities include Process Characterization, Operational Qualification, Product Qualification need to be executed, extending the timeline for another 12-18 months. Once Integer has validated a replacement, then our customers need to perform their own qualifications and submit regulatory approvals, adding 18-24 more months to the project timeline; worst case scenario you are looking at ~72 months (6 years) from beginning to end to have a suitable qualified and regulatory approved substitute material.  Additionally, switching to a new material/process/technique would make Integer equipment/investment redundant or obsolete and would also results in more expenditure and, if new equipment needs to be introduced, Installation Qualification (IQ) and Software Validation (if applicable) would be necessary, adding another ~3-6 months to the effort.  Integer has five manufacturing sites that perform fluoropolymer coatings by different techniques: Reel-to-Reel, Electrostatic Spray, Dipping and Film Casting; these capabilities mean a multi-million USD investment not only in equipment but also in facilities, utilities, manpower and resources.  Two of these coating facilities manufacture guidewires within the EU and would be severely impacted by a ban on these types of coatings.  For guidewires in particular, coating with PTFE is standard practice and these medical devices are not currently covered by an existing derogation.  A derogation group for other coating application is needed to ensure that these life-saving medical devices can continue to be produced while alternative materials are explored.
