General Comments: Integrated DNA Technologies, a Biotechnology company, develops, manufactures, and markets nucleic acid (DNA and RNA) products that support the life sciences industry. IDT supplies synthetic biology products used in genomics research, diagnostics, specialized reagents, consumables, and medical device products. Our customers use our products in applications ranging from fundamental biological and genomics research to making lifesaving vaccines, biologic drugs, and novel cell and gene therapies. We supply the tools and services that help our customers do their work better, faster, and safer. IDT designs, builds, and then deploys proprietary manufacturing equipment into the European Union to manufacture nucleic acid products. We have over 1400 associates across nine countries worldwide including manufacturing sites in Belgium, Singapore, and the USA.

General Comments
According to ECHA’s Press Release, the purpose of the consultation is to give anyone with information on PFAS the opportunity to have their say. Of particular interest is information relevant to the risks, socio-economic aspects, and alternative substances. ECHA’s scientific committees for Risk Assessment (RAC) and for Socio-Economic Analysis (SEAC) will use the consultation input to evaluate the proposed restriction and to form an opinion on it.

However, due to the rather high volume of the information that must be collected and analysed with regard to the economic and health impacts of the proposed restriction, we request a 6-month extension to the consultation period, in order to gather detailed data on these points.

Currently, IDT is in a position to offer some comments on the following points:
1.) The health and economic impact of sourcing, developing testing, and validating PFAS alternatives in manufacturing processes and equipment.
2.) Consideration of environmental stewardship and waste management for fluoropolymers rather than outright ban.
3.) Fluoropolymers' exclusion from PFAS categories. We request an exclusion of fluoropolymers from the scope of the restriction.
4.) Request for exemption or maximum derogation, recognize critical Biotechnology manufacturing as a significant use case with appropriate consideration for derogation.
5.) Biotechnology is a missing use case in Annex XV. The current proposal does not address economic impacts to the EU and does not consider appropriate derogations for life sciences and biopharmaceutical manufacturing sectors and markets.

A. Request for Extension to the Consultation Period

Because of the scope and scale of the proposed restriction and its unknown impact to synthetic nucleic acid manufacturers with applications in the genomics markets (outlined below), we request that ECHA extend its consultation period by six additional months to enable more companies like ours to fully map out and quantify the impacts this restriction poses to our industry, the downstream users of our technologies, and to patients using biopharmaceutical products. Additional time is required to access the impact and develop an implementation strategy that encompasses more than 10,000 substances and polymers that fall within the scope of this restriction. These materials are distributed throughout our supply chain, consumables, and manufacturing equipment. Once these consequences have been fully mapped out and quantified, our company and others like us would be in a better position to provide more comprehensive feedback to ECHA regarding the consequences of the proposed new restriction. It is only then that the public consultation procedure can be truly useful for ECHA and all the affected parties.

This request is also based on our right to good administration pursuant to Article 41(2)(a) of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (“Charter”), which entails one’s right to have one’s affairs handled “impartially, fairly and within reasonable time”. The volume of the requested information and the fact that our company would have to assess 10,000 components in order to provide ECHA with comprehensive feedback makes it impossible to provide the necessary information to ECHA that would allow it to handle this case fairly within the prescribed 6-month public consultation period.

The specific reasons justifying our request for the extension of the public consultation are the following.

1. No Managed Registry or List of PFAS Materials
Fully mapping out the impact of this broad restriction for our industry’s entire supply-chain in 6 months is extremely challenging and requires the generation of massive amounts of new data. In addition, most PFAS used in polymeric materials do not have CAS numbers. This means manually assessing more than 10,000 components used to manufacture hardware and consumables, and then evaluating the risk of finding alternatives. Only then can we determine potential alternatives and begin developing replacement timelines.

2. PFAS Footprint Mapping Challenges
Mapping our PFAS footprint goes beyond PFAS added to our products, as it requires working with equipment vendors to conduct a thorough assessment of all materials used in our manufacturing equipment. For example, fluoropolymer O-rings in a chemical system, critical coatings used in our production equipment, and printed circuit boards used in our safety control systems. In addition, we will need to work closely with direct and indirect suppliers to complete a thorough impact assessment, as the proposed restriction could cause such auxiliary products to become unavailable, risking our customers’ ability to manufacture biopharmaceuticals, molecular diagnostic tests, pharmaceutical development and other life science products in the EU.

3. Identification of PFAS Additives to Other Plastics
The challenge of identifying and quantifying PFAS additives in other plastics, often required to add necessary product safety properties, such as adding small quantities of PTFE to enhance properties of polymers used in electronics and hardware. To adequately capture all such cases, each specific compound will require testing in certified labs. This work is not feasible in the limited consultation period.

Therefore, the scope of the restriction extending to auxiliary and indirect products means it is impossible to fully assess the impact of the proposal while generating sufficiently accurate data. All input must be viewed as the current best knowledge, but not the complete picture of the impact of the PFAS restriction.

As such, at a minimum, also broad industry-wide exemptions and/or derogations that cover uses across the entire supply-chain will be necessary to avoid key materials becoming unavailable in the EU in the near term.

B. IDT Endorses related ECHA Submissions. As a member of the genomics industry committed to sustainable solutions, we also support related industry group sector responses, including those from BioPhorum, ASME-BPE, ESIA, and Cytiva.

C. Substantive comments

1) The health and economic impact of fluoropolymers

According to the proposal, final active pharmaceuticals ingredients are proposed to be derogated, but process chemicals and raw materials used in their manufacturing are not included in the derogation and therefore proposed to be banned 18 months after the proposal’s entry into force. The derogation also fails to extend to R&D operations, which will directly impact the possibility to carry out clinical trials in Europe going forward.

However, according to Article 68, paragraph 1 of the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH) Regulation, the restriction of PFAS must be substance related – listing specific CAS numbers and differentiating amongst PFAS where different properties and behaviours exist – and risk based. Restrictions of substances should be based on unacceptable risks stemming from exposure to recognised hazards. However, the Classification, Labelling and Packaging of Substances and Mixtures (CLP) Regulation, which sets out the relevant hazard classes does not recognize as hazardous substances displaying persistent properties alone, in the absence of additional, proven concerns around bioaccumulation, mobility and toxicity.

This is the case with fluoropolymers which may be persistent but do not have any other hazardous properties as well. Fluoropolymers are high molecular weight substances that meet the definition of PFAS because of their structure, but are non-bioavailable, and therefore, of low concern for human health and the environment.

Therefore, restricting fluoropolymers alongside other, harmful, PFAS is a disproportionate restriction that is not compatible with REACH and the CLP Regulation.

2) The impact from sourcing, developing testing, and validating PFAS alternatives for fluoropolymers on manufacturing processes and equipment

As regards the impact on health, certain fluoropolymer materials deemed in scope by ECHA definitions and used in the manufacturing processes and equipment in biotechnology industries, which do not include small molecule (less than C16) PFAS chemicals, do not pose the same risks as their more dangerous PFAS chemical relatives. To group these types of fluoropolymers together with lower grade and small molecule PFAS materials is not proportional to the risk they pose and punishes industries that have invested in preemptively phasing out small molecule PFAS. We understand that these fluoropolymers still fall under the broad scope definition of PFAS by ECHA, but these materials pose no meaningful level of PFAS-related environmental pollution during manufacturing, use, or end of life. At a minimum, any references suggesting a meaningful PFAS-related environmental impact from these materials are highly misleading, and warrant additional review given the enormous social and economic impact to the biotechnology manufacturing industry.

In addition, the current proposal does not address the risks and economic impact of re-validation, regulatory approvals, and supply chain disruptions. Examples of Fluoropolymers materials used in biopharmaceutical processing can include, but are not limited to, gas and liquid fluid system components, liquid filtration membranes for removal of bacteria, filtration membranes for removal of viruses, tubing fittings, gaskets and seals, bearing races, tubing clamp, etc. Developing or finding alternate materials requires extensive testing revalidation and establishing robust supply chains. In particular:

a. Substitutions & Alternatives
[1a] Potential replacement materials for certain components, such as fittings and tubing clamps can be developed and manufactured from polypropylene or PBT in three to five years.
[1b] For materials used in gas and liquid flow management and filtration used in bioprocessing (typically PVDF or PTFE),
few if any approved alternatives are readily available for testing and validated in our biotechnology manufacturing processes. Development of economically feasible alternatives is questionable and may depend strongly on the various chemistries and temperatures of individual pharmaceutical processes. This can require extensive development times (3-8 years) to revalidate each manufacturing process and establish robust supply chains.
[1c] Gaskets, seals, ball bearing seats, etc.: These biotechnology manufacturing components are designed, developed, and validated for compatibility with organic chemistries, leakage prevention, and potential contamination or loss of critical product during manufacturing processes. Replacement of these types of materials is strongly dependent on how well candidate alternatives perform within the chemical and process conditions of each manufacturing process. There are no existing substitutes to replace these materials. Each application of these new materials would require extensive evaluation and testing, establishing reliable supply chains, then complete revalidation for each product application.

b. Requested Derogation.
Given the expected low toxicity concern of fluoropolymers manufactured without the uses of small chemical (less than C16) PFAS processing aids, and in consideration of the enormous socio-economic impact to our industry, the EU and our customers, and considering the regulatory requirements for managing materials that contact diagnostic and therapeutic products, we request that such materials that contact or are incorporated into diagnostic and therapeutic products be removed from scope or given a permanent derogation.

3) Consideration of environmental stewardship and waste management for fluoropolymers used in biotechnology manufacturing processes and equipment rather than outright ban.

In any case, based on expected low volumes of the rare fluoropolymer materials with no alternatives that we use in our manufacturing processes and equipment, end of life incineration needs to be considered as an environmental stewardship option. According to some studies such as “Waste incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate potential formation of per- and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) in flue gas” published at ScienceDirect, PTFE, for example, can be effectively incinerated above 800°C reaching complete thermal decomposition, demonstrating that effective disposal methods are available to prevent accumulation of waste fluoropolymer products in landfills. Like the derogation of microplastic restrictions for industrial use, reporting requirements on amounts of polymeric PFAS purchased annually combined with reporting requirements on disposal at end of life could be implemented to monitor the amounts placed on the market and reduce the release of these materials to the environment.

4) Exclusion of fluoropolymers used in bioprocessing applications from the scope of the restriction.

Fluoropolymers (including those which may use small chain PFAS precursors) such as PTFE, FEP, FKM, FFKM, PVDF, PFA are also widely used in bioprocessing applications. Most scientific data indicates that low level, intentionally added PFAS residuals are biologically unavailable and are not impactful to human health. The assumption that PFAS molecules within these polymers may be liberated in meaningful levels over the product lifecycle and become bioaccumulative, rely on speculation, and at a minimum require further evaluation given the relatively small volumes used in the bioprocessing industry and the enormous socio-economic impact. Based on input from our product and material experts, there are today no good PFAS-free replacements for these materials.

a. Substitutions & Alternatives
[3a] Gaskets and seals: Like [1c], candidate alternatives will need to be identified and evaluated on a case-by-case basis. In addition, given that this category includes PTFE, which has unique chemical resistance properties, the likelihood of finding and validating suitable alternatives for each application is low, based on input from material experts.
[3b] Other applications. There are many similar impacted applications, however, given the unique nature of fluoropolymers in this class (e.g. PTFE, PFA, etc.), restrictions on these materials used in bioprocessing applications will likely pose significant hurdles to current and evolving pharmaceutical innovations, including a number of genomics applications, Other examples include valve rotors currently using PEEK CF30+PTFE15 material which will not work without PTFE due to wear. Today we have no alternative materials to replace these rotors. Glues containing PFAS which form fluoropolymers while hardening used to glue optical components will also be challenging to replace. Today there are no PFAS-free alternatives that are known to work for our applications.

b. Requested Derogation.
Given the low toxicity concern of fluoropolymers including those manufactured with PFAS processing aids, the enormous negative socio-economic impact to industry and healthcare, and considering the regulatory requirements for managing materials that contact diagnostic and therapeutic products, we request that fluoropolymers be removed from the scope or given a permanent derogation. Without this derogation, there is a significant risk these materials will become unavailable to Life Science industries, resulting in significant economic impact to the European biotechnology sectors. Exemptions for fluoropolymers used in the biotechnology industry would minimize these risks. In consideration of the enormous socio-economic impact to the EU, our industry, and our customers, and considering the regulatory requirements for managing materials that contact or are incorporated into diagnostic and therapeutic products, we request such materials be removed from restriction scope or given a permanent derogation.


5) Biotechnology is a missing use case in Annex XV and critical Biotechnology manufacturing should be recognized as a significant use case – Request for exemption or maximum derogation

a. Fluoropolymers used as auxiliaries on sites to manufacture chemicals are vital to the biotechnology industry
Biotechnology is a missing use case in Annex XV and critical Biotechnology manufacturing should be recognized as a significant use case. In the same way fluoropolymers are used as components in products described in sections [1] and [3], components like O-rings, pumps, gaskets, and seals are also used on chemical manufacturing sites to create chromatography resins and other chemical products that are vital to the bioprocessing industry. PTFE coatings are also standard in reaction vessels for highly oxidative reactions. At this point suppliers have indicated they would need at least 10 years to develop PFAS-free alternatives to these types of reactor coatings.

b. Collective socio-economic impact of restricting missing uses
If, at the very least/minimum, derogations are not offered for the above uses, we estimate that more than 80% of biopharmaceutical manufacturing campaigns in the EU will be impacted, resulting in impact on the scale of €20+ billion a year for an industry whose fluoropolymer usage contributes to no more than 0.01% of the world’s total plastic waste. The cost in finding and revalidating alternatives, which will be unique and specific to different drug manufacturing processes, will impact availability of resources to bring current and new drugs to market thereby potentially resulting in drug and therapeutics shortages. In addition, it is likely that these enormous costs will be passed down to healthcare systems. Even if derogations are offered for these uses there will be a massive risk of these materials becoming unavailable as the Life Sciences industry represents as a small fraction of the overall use which may otherwise be restricted. Exemptions for fluoropolymers used in industry would minimize these risks.

c. Requested derogation.
We request a minimum derogation of 13.5 years for development and transition to PFAS-free equipment and processes for Synthetic Biology manufacturing where alternatives are available (estimated 80%). We request an indefinite derogation for applications where suitable alternatives cannot be identified (estimated 20%).

6) The current proposal does not address economic impacts to the EU and does not consider appropriate derogations for life sciences and biopharmaceutical manufacturing sectors and markets.

In 2022 the Global life sciences industry was valued at USD 1,224.31 Bn (https://www.precedenceresearch.com/biotechnology-market) and the Biotechnology Market size estimated at USD 823.5 Bn with an expected growth to USD 1848.5 Bn by 2030. Biotechnology employs nearly one million EU citizens (Measuring the Economic Footprint of the Biotechnology Industry in Europe, EuropaBio – WifOR Institute Research Report February 2021). Biotechnology is more than an economic engine, it was responsible for the unprecedented rapid development of a SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. According to the NIH “We estimate that COVID-19 vaccination was associated with over 8 million fewer confirmed cases, over 120 thousand fewer deaths, and 700 thousand fewer hospitalizations during the first six months of the campaign” (The impact of COVID-19 vaccination in the US: Averted burden of SARS-COV-2-related cases, hospitalizations, and deaths). The vaccine produced a proportional impact in the EU. Climate change is another challenge facing the EU economy. Development of crop genomics that can improve crop resilience will significantly improve the sustainability of EU member state’s food supply and reducing economic instability risks.

As written the proposed restriction will reduce innovations in biotechnology, with potentially negative impacts to pandemic responses and climate change challenges.

Org. name: Intel Research and Development Ireland Ltd
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Intel is a global manufacturer of semiconductors in addition to electronic devices.  From a European perspective, the largest manufacturing site outside of the United States is based in Ireland.  Intel is appreciative that the semiconductor industry has been put forward for a derogation for reconsideration relating to “the semiconductor manufacturing process”.  PFAS is used in chemical formulations, components of manufacturing process tools, facilities infrastructure and packaging used to make semiconductor devices. Given the critical and widespread uses of PFAS, the majority of which have no viable non-PFAS alternatives, Intel understands that the proposed derogation covers all uses of PFAS to enable the continuation of both the manufacturing and importation of semiconductor within the EU.  This must include all uses identified in the attached “Annex A Table A.49 – Annex XV Final” which includes process chemistries, manufacturing equipment, manufacturing infrastructure, manufacturing support equipment and semiconductor devices.
Should this comprehensive derogation not be granted to the semiconductor industry, then once the entry into force and the proposed 18-month transition period expires (~ 2028), the ability to maintain semiconductor manufacturing with the EU would simply not be possible.
Such a scenario would lead to very serious consequences for the EU economy, EU citizens and indeed the many EU policy objectives.   The EU Industrial Strategy which supports the EU’s global competitiveness, enabling the EU to be the first geo-political entity to be climate neutral by 2050 and shaping the EU’s digital future are heavily dependent upon semiconductors in addition to the Net Zero Industry Act and the Chips Act.
Intel is firmly committed to the EU and in strengthening its semiconductor ecosystem.  Consequently, Intel has announced significant financial investments within Ireland, Germany and Poland to the tune of billions of euro.
Ireland – €17 billion investment to double Intel’s manufacturing space in Europe.  This will provide 1,600 permanent high tech jobs in addition to 6,000 construction jobs.
Germany – €33 billion to expand Intel’s manufacturing capacity in Europe.  3,000 permanent high tech jobs in conjunction with 7,000 construction jobs.
Poland – €4.3 billion to establish a new semiconductor assembly and test facility.  2,000 permanent high tech jobs in addition to several thousand construction jobs will be created.
The ambiguity regarding the ability to manufacture and import semiconductors as a result of the proposed PFAS restriction is complicating matters such as the planned and in progress expansions noted above.  It cannot be emphasised sufficiently that companies such as Intel that are willing to heavily invest in Europe must have this cloud of uncertainty lifted as soon as possible.
As noted earlier, Intel is also involved in electronics devices.   It was extremely disappointing that the Electronics industry was not put forward for relevant derogations.  Based upon supplier data and insight into the lack of a PFAS substitution roadmap for cables, connectors and capacitors, Intel is requesting derogations for these electronic products.  The duration of the derogations is 12-years.  Please refer to the attached derogation requests for further details.
In addition, with the growth rate of data volume, the use of very low global warming potential F-gases is a pragmatic electronics cooling technology for data centres.  Current cooling methodologies will simply not be able to cope with the greater cooling demands of advanced semiconductors.  It is therefore imperative that these data centres utilise a superior and sustainable cooling technology such as that provided through the cooling distribution systems outlined in the attached derogation requests.
Consequently, it is critically important that this technology including its refrigerant chemistries (HFOs) and hardware (fluoropolymers) are granted an appropriate derogation of 12-years from the proposed REACH Restriction on PFAS.
Intel like most of the semiconductor industry has been using PFAS since the 1980s.  Despite many years research into PFAS alternatives, much more effort will be required.  Given the complexity of PFAS use within the Semiconductor industry, collaborative research will be needed.  It is imperative that research funding for PFAS is put forward by the EU Commission.  In addition, it is critical that companies within the Semiconductor industry and its associated supply and value chains that have legal entities with the EU can apply for such funding and not just those companies that are headquartered within the EU.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Intel’s comments apply to the following sectors and sub-uses as identified in Table 9 of the Annex XV restriction report: Applications of fluorinated gases (Annex E.2.8.) - Refrigeration Electronics and semiconductor (Annex E.2.11.) -Electronics Electronics and semiconductor (Annex E.2.11.) - Semiconductors

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Due to the critical and widespread uses of PFAS across the different stages of the lifecycle of products, i.e., the manufacture, the use and the end-of-life phases for semiconductors, it is not feasible to obtain (sub-)use-specific information on emissions. In terms of emissions from semiconductor manufacturing facilities, these have been separated into emissions from the photolithography process, perfluorocarbon compounds (F-gases) and wastewater.  Photolithography process Intel submitted its data to the PFAS Consortium as it was developing a total use and estimated emissions dataset for the EU based semiconductor manufacturers.  That effort estimated the total PFAS use in photolithography processes in the EU was 2,248 kg/year with an estimated emissions profile of 1,161 kg/year.  Perfluorocarbon Compounds (F-gases) Intel has invested significant amounts of funding in recent years (millions of US$) to expand the number of Point of Use (POU) abatement systems within our manufacturing facilities.  Such POU abatement destroys greenhouse gas compounds to form less harmful byproducts.  Since 2020, POUs have reduced input process PFC emissions by 95% across all of Intel’s manufacturing sites.   This reduction in PFC emissions is also observed across the EU based semiconductor manufacturers.  The European Semiconductor Industry Association (ESIA) quantified PFC emissions that fall under the scope of the proposed PFAS Restriction from the industry to be 12.982 kg in 2022.   Wastewater There is no EU industry wide PFAS in wastewater data currently available.  However, Intel contributed to a peer-reviewed study published in “Environmental Science & Technology” collected and analysed wastewater samples from three fabs in the United States (Paige Jacob, Krista A. Barzen-Hanson, and Damian E. Helbling Environmental Science & Technology 2021 55 (4), 2346-2356 DOI: 10.1021/acs.est.0c06690). The authors found that the sum totals of the PFAS concentrations in the downstream samples from the three fabs are 0.623 ± 0.024, 0.394 ± 0.018, and 0.376 ± 0.024 µg/L, respectively. Intel has employed a new wastewater treatment technology known as Wastewater and Treatment Recovery (WATR) and based upon current data from Intel facilities removes in excess of 90% of PFAS from process wastewater.   Intel’s manufacturing waste that contains PFAS is segregated into general solvent waste, surface modification waste and waste articles.  Intel does not send any of its waste to landfill apart from those facilities that generate sludges from the WATR process. In a typical year, the wastes generated within our EU manufacturing facilities are noted as: • General solvent waste = 3,855 tonnes.  Key solvents are recovered for reuse while the remainder of the waste stream is used as boiler fuel for the distillation process at the solvent waste facility or is sent to a fuel blending process. • Surface modification waste = 22 tonnes.  This waste is incinerated. • Waste articles = unknown tonnes.  Hazardous waste articles are processed by different facilities.  These facilities will engage in either incineration, burn waste to energy or for WEEE are taken apart with components recycled.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Incineration is a waste management technique employed by the Semiconductor industry as a means of destroying PFAS.  Intel has provided a synopsis of several research studies regarding the destruction of PFAS by means of incineration.  The first three papers relate to studies that have concluded while the last two are still in progress.     1. Report on PFAS Destruction Testing Results at Clean Harbors Aragonite Utah Hazardous Waste Incinerator  The results of this comprehensive third-party study demonstrated that its Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) permitted incineration facility destroyed greater than 99.9999% of the 49 target PFAS analytes included in the study.  2. SIA PFAS Consortium Background Paper  This paper provides an overview of the liquid organic liquids generated from the manufacturing process that are managed as hazardous wastes through licensed treatment and disposal facilities that will either reclaim solvent constituents, manage the solvent for energy recovery as fuel for cement kilns, or incinerate the waste. Technical details of cement kilns and incinerators are provided and concludes that based on the high temperatures and long gas residence times associated with these facilities, that PFAS destruction or removal efficiency should be very good.  This information is found on page 30 of the “SIA PFAS Consortium Background Paper” attached to this submittal.    3. Pilot-Scale Fluoropolymer Incineration Study This study was conducted by the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) in cooperation with Société Générale de Surveillance (SGS).  The focus of the study was to ascertain if   fluoropolymers get fully incinerated without any formation of short chain or long chain PFAS.  The results confirm that fluoropolymers at their end of life when incinerated under representative European municipal incinerators conditions do not generate any measurable levels of PFAS emissions and therefore pose no risk to human health and the environment.  The study “Pilot-Scale Fluoropolymer Incineration Study: Thermal Treatment of a Mixture of Fluoropolymers under Representative European Municipal Waste Combustor Conditions” in its entirety is attached to this submittal.   4. SRC PFAS Incineration Kinetics Study   This three year project is part sponsored by Intel through the Semiconductor Research Corporation (SRC) and is a collaboration between principal investigators at Brown University and the EPA Research Triangle Park (RTP) research team.  This project’s aim is to develop a thermokinetic model for the incineration of fluorinated organic chemicals and gases that result from photolithography solvent waste streams.  The model will be validated against experimental data obtained from the RTP pilot incinerator. This project is currently in its data-gathering phase, with results anticipated for publication in the second half of 2024.    5. United States EPA Technical Brief This technical brief highlights knowledge gaps regarding the effectiveness of incineration to destroy PFAS compounds as few experiments have been conducted in conjunction with the lack of measurement methods that are suitable for a comprehensive characterisation of fluorinated compounds.  The EPA is targeting research to gain an understanding of the thermal stability of PFAS compounds, the ability to fully capture and identify PFAS compounds and their thermal decomposition byproducts, and the efficacy of emission control technologies.  The technical brief is attached to this submittal. It is noteworthy to add that Michal Freedhoff, a senior executive within the USEPA called out the need for the Semiconductor industry to use PFAS in relation to an article posted on InsideEPA.com website when discussing the US CHIPS act.

5. Proposed derogations: The proposed derogation for the semiconductor industry utilising the terminology of “the semiconductor manufacturing process” has resulted in the ongoing development of a profile of the industry’s uses of PFAS and their associated emissions within the European Union.    As a typical semiconductor manufacturing facility has approximately 1,000 uses of PFAS from the discrete manufacturing steps to produce semiconductors to the semiconductor manufacturing equipment and support infrastructure, it is not possible to derive a full profile at this time.  However, through ongoing research/investigations by the European Semiconductor Industry Association (ESIA), SEMI Europe and the PFAS Consortium several uses of PFAS including their emissions have been identified and quantified.    As a semiconductor device manufacturer, the use of PFAS in what is known as the Photolithography process is an integral part of the manufacturing process.  The ESIA has estimated the total PFAS used in this process within the European Union for all semiconductor manufacturing facilities is 2,248 kg per year with emissions to air in the range of 1,161 kg in 2022.  Another use of PFAS but in a gaseous form is with Perfluorocarbon compounds (PFCs).  These gases are utilised in the Etch and Chemical Vapour Deposition processes.  The consolidated emissions to air from ESIA members in 2022 was measured to be 13 kg.  The European based semiconductor industry does not have a collective measurement of PFAS emissions in manufacturing process wastewater.  However, Intel in its constant drive to minimise emissions to wastewater has applied best available techniques through what is known as the WATR process that removes PFAS from such process wastewater.  Current measurements indicate a PFAS removal rate in excess of 90% is achieved by this water reclamation technology. Focusing upon lubricants utilised in semiconductor manufacturing equipment, data produced by SEMI has noted that within EU based semiconductor manufacturing facilities, there is approximately 56.7-59.8 mt/year of oil and approximately 4.5 mt/year of grease utilised.  The used oils are recycled by pump service companies while the grease goes to segregated waste collection to be incinerated. Note “mt” above refers to metric tonnes.

6. Missing uses: Intel wishes to highlight a critical and ever developing use of hydrofluoroolefins (HFOs) in the necessary cooling of electronics in data centres.  In an effort to sustain the data demands of the current growth rate of data volume, there needs to be an equivalent increase in computational power.  The growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the high performance compute has resulted in generating significant increases in silicon or processor thermal design power (TDP) beyond 1 kW/each processor and semiconductor package thermal density.  These developments have resulted in an increase in heat generated from these powerful semiconductor devices.  Current cooling technologies such as airflow and water-based have become increasingly inefficient with the cooling load required for today’s demands but will certainly fail in attempting to cater near and longer term future cooling needs. There are no commercially available alternatives that address the future needs for high TDP, high heat flux silicon and global energy efficiency demands that have no PFAS chemistry.   In terms of missing uses in Table A.1 of Annex A of the Annex XV restriction report, this specific use of PFAS falls between both the “Application of Fluorinated Gases” and “Electronics and Semiconductors” applications.  Please note that this use of HFOs to cool electronics in data centres is different to the use of PFAS in immersion cooling in data centres. The annual tonnage of the use of HFOs for electronics cooling in data centres is currently less than one tonne globally.  In terms of emissions, there are no intentional releases of HFOs with this technology as the cooling system itself is a closed system.  The functionality provided by HFOs in this application is a sustained low energy cooling technology with superb Global Warming Potential (GWP) characteristics (GWP <1 to 573) when compared with the more commonly utilised F-gases in data centres such as R134a (GWP 1,430) and R410a (2,088). Based upon data developed by Savills (2022), there are greater than 1,240 data centres in Europe, totalling 8.3 million sqm of space and a power capacity of approximately 8,300 Mw. This represents about 18 watts per capita in Europe. Most of these data centres are located in Western Europe, accounting for 76% of the total power capacity in Europe, more specifically in the FLAP-D markets, named Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris and Dublin. There are over 300 data centre operators in Europe amongst all types of data centres (wholesalers, carrier-neutral colocation, bandwidth providers, proprietaries and resellers).  All of these operators will be negatively impacted by the proposed PFAS restriction.   The application of HFOs to perform such a cooling function in data centres is the outcome of many years research and development efforts.  There are no alternative cooling methods that come close the efficiency provided by HFOs, especially for future cooling needs.  Traditional   forced air cooling has already been optimised within the practical limits of data centre airflow delivery.  Established propylene glycol-water based fluids support high TDP but fall short on supporting high package thermal density as compared to pumped refrigerant 2-phase cooling.  Also, due to the lower effective heat transfer of legacy liquid cooling methods, more power is required for primary loop water chillers and secondary loop fluid pumps.  It’s important to note that water or air chillers used for current data centre cooling is already or will be shortly using one of these hydrofluoroolefins (HFO) refrigerants.      It is true that non-PFAS alternatives currently exist as noted in the previous paragraph.  However, it is clear with the increased heat generated from the more advanced semiconductors, the existing cooling methodologies will simply not be sufficient enough to cool them appropriately.  The inability to cool semiconductors will lead to overheating.  Once this occurs, its functionality can slow down or fail completely, leading to data loss and system crashes within this application in data centres.  Should HFOs not be derogated from the proposed PFAS restriction, it is expected to see exponential growth in data losses and or system crashes arising from data centres.  Intel therefore requests such uses of HFOs be exempted from the proposed PFAS restriction.  More detail concerning this derogation request can be found in the attachment “Electronics Cooling in Data Centres”.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: The use of PFAS within the Semiconductor industry is widespread.  These uses include the discrete steps of the manufacturing process in addition to the necessary supply and value chains that enable such complex manufacturing to take place.  In essence, the proposed derogation for reconsideration referencing “the Semiconductor manufacturing process” must incorporate process chemistries, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, semiconductor manufacturing infrastructure, semiconductor manufacturing support equipment and semiconductor devices otherwise known as semiconductor chips.  The attached Table A.49 to this submittal illustrates all of PFAS uses that must be under the scope of the proposed derogation.  Within the same table, a significant number of the industry’s PFAS uses have been assigned a status as to the probability and estimated timeframe of substituting PFAS of which most uses will require a non-PFAS invention in the first instance.  Some notable PFAS uses include the following: 1. Photolithography applications – the proposed Photoacid Generators (PAGs) by the Dossier Submitters were reviewed by the industry (SEMI, ESIA and the PFAS Consortium) and were found not to be suitable on numerous technical grounds and therefore cannot be considered meaningful candidates as PAG alternatives.  Please refer to the PFAS Consortium’s PAG white paper for a more detailed breakdown of this review on the Dossier Submitters’ proposed PAG alternatives attached to this submittal.  In terms of substituting PAGs for non-PFAS alternatives, the industry expects that it would take in excess of 25 years to invent, qualify and integrate for high volume manufacturing purposes.  For the remaining photolithography uses, it is estimated 15 to 20 years will be necessary to develop and integrate non-PFAS alternatives. 2. Etch and Chemical Vapour Deposition (CVD) applications – Perfluorocarbons (PFCs) and Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) are utilised predominantly in plasma etch and chamber cleaning.  To date, no feasible alternatives have been developed.  It is acknowledged that substances such as nitrogen fluoride (NF3), sulphur hexafluoride (SF6) etc. have been proposed as non-PFAS alternatives, however, when used in conjunction with various hydrocarbons or fluorine gas can create serious environmental and/or safety concerns.  In addition, the global warming potential of these non-PFAS substances is 13,400 and 18,300 respectively.     3. Wet Surface Modification Chemistries – there are many uses of PFAS in this application.  The primary properties required involve wetting agents and selective metal oxide removal.  In terms of possible non-PFAS alternatives, the industry understands the timeline to develop solutions for high volume manufacturing ranges between 3 to 15 years post the identification of suitable alternatives.  4. Heat Transfer Fluids – these substances are used in semiconductor manufacturing as they provide meticulous temperature control amongst a great number of processing and testing steps.  Much investigation has been conducted into non-PFAS alternative heat transfer fluids.  Substances such as synthetic hydrocarbon oils and combinations of ethylene glycol/deionised water mixtures have not been successful in achieving the necessary performance parameters.  The PFAS consortium has developed a white paper titled “PFAS-Containing Heat Transfer Fluids (HTF) Used in Semiconductor Manufacturing” which contains more detail on this use of PFAS within the Semiconductor industry. 5. Pump Fluids and Lubricants – it is acknowledged that non-PFAS lubricants are available on the market today.  However, the semiconductor industry through the PFAS consortium has investigated these PFAS alternatives in an effort to determine their suitability for substitution purposes.  The use of lubricants is multifunctional in nature e.g., reduction in friction, inert in harsh conditions, low off-gassing, minimal particle generation, UV stable etc.  Consequently, any proposed non-PFAS alternative would need to cater for these required functions.  Unfortunately, the research undertaken by the PFAS consortium has identified that the non-PFAS alternatives simply did not meet the necessary technical performance requirements.  The primary issue found was related a significant increase in heat generated as the lubricant breaks down, which leads to an increase in the wear and tear of the associated equipment which in turn increased the defect rates.  In addition, silicone based oils and lubricants do not have the required temperature range required for the semiconductor industry and have been identified as being prone to off-gassing and sources of contamination within the manufacturing process.  Please refer to the attached white paper “PFAS-Containing Lubricants Used in Semiconductor Manufacturing” for more detail on this matter.    6. Articles – it is estimated that PFAS in the form of fluoropolymers accounts for some 60% of PFAS used in the semiconductor industry.  These components include tubing, piping, gaskets, valves, filters etc.  Even the simple O-ring which is a fluoroelastomer is an integral component in semiconductor manufacturing equipment.  Discussions with industry suppliers have noted that research to develop non-PFAS alternatives is in its infancy and due to the vast number of PFAS containing articles, this will take many years (estimated to be approximately 15 years) to accomplish, assuming that suitable alternatives can be invented.   It is difficult to assign specific socioeconomic impacts to the discrete uses of PFAS undertaken by the Semiconductor industry.  However, should all of the uses of PFAS currently required to manufacture semiconductors be not included in the proposed derogation for reconsideration of “the semiconductor manufacturing process”, then downstream users of semiconductors which are ubiquitous will be severely impacted.  The knock on effect of this will result in significant economic consequences both within and external to the EU given the global and interdependent nature of the semiconductor supply and value chains.

8. Other identified uses: The Electronics sector was not put forward for a derogation under the proposed PFAS REACH Restriction.  The basis for this is outlined with the text of the Annex XV report which noted the following conclusion - “…with the inconclusive evidence pointing to the non-existence of technically and economically feasible alternatives at EiF in all other uses, no derogation is proposed.” Intel has highlighted three components - Cables, Connectors and Capacitors under the Electronics sector that based upon input from our suppliers, they will not have non-PFAS replacements by the EiF timeframe or indeed within several years of the EiF.  In addition, a supplemental document “Derogation Request For Electronics Cables, Connectors and Capacitors” attached to this submittal has demonstrated that there is distinct lack of research and development concerning non-PFAS alternatives for these components.  This is an indicative metric that illustrates that there is no line of sight or a roadmap by the Electronics industry that it will be in a position to replace such critical components with non-PFAS alternatives.  Consequently, there is simply no data on non-PFAS alternatives that can be shared as part of this consultation process for these electronics components.   It is therefore considered unreasonable that the Dossier Submitters structured their conclusion on electronics alternatives in Annex E based on speculative comments such as “that it is likely that alternatives are already available or might be found” rather than the facts of what is transpiring within the Electronics industry.  Another use of PFAS within the Electronics sector is the much needed electronics cooling in data centres.  The growth rate of data volume globally is nothing but astonishing.  Information produced by the EU Commission as part of its EU Data Strategy illustrates a phenomenal 530% increase predicted from 2018 to 2025.  In an effort to sustain or meet such data demands, there needs to be an equivalent increase in computational power.  It’s not just a case of doing more of the same as what’s been done in the past to augment the necessary computational power.  The growth rate of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and high-performance compute has driven the need for more powerful processors and hardware accelerators.  This has resulted in generating significant increases in silicon or processor thermal design power (TDP) beyond 1 kW/each processor and semiconductor package thermal density.  To put it simply, the heat generated from these powerful semiconductor devices is also growing. Issues with Current Cooling Technologies  Cooling of data centres is frequently the largest energy loss in the facility and as such represents a significant opportunity to improve efficiency.  The primary cooling methods employed in date centres are air and water based. The objective of airflow management is to circulate only the necessary amount of air through the data centre at any time that is required to remove the heat actually created by the IT equipment. This means no air returns to the cooling system without absorbing heat and no air circulates more than one time through the IT equipment.   When considering water-based cooling methods, the water utilised needs to be sufficiently chilled which can have a significant impact on the data centre’s energy efficiency.  Due to the changing climate, water is becoming a precious commodity in several geographies across the globe including the EU and several regulations are being imposed on data centre operators to limit the use of water for data centre cooling applications such as towers or evaporative air cooling.   Also, to cool high wattage processors, water needs to be chilled using chillers therefore reducing the overall efficiency of cooling solutions. These air and water cooled methodologies are becoming increasingly inefficient with the cooling load required for the greater demands of server products.  Consequently, alternative cooling methodologies have been investigated to cater for today’s requirements but more importantly future needs as well.  Alternative Cooling Technologies Unfortunately, there are no commercially available alternatives that address the future needs for high TDP, high heat flux silicon and global energy efficiency demands that have no PFAS chemistry.  Traditional forced air cooling has already been optimised within the practical limits of data centre airflow delivery.  Traditional propylene glycol-water based fluids support high TDP but fall short on supporting high package thermal density as compared to pumped refrigerant 2-phase cooling.  Also, due to the lower effective heat transfer of legacy liquid cooling methods, more power is required for primary loop water chillers and secondary loop fluid pumps when compared with the pumped refrigerant 2-phase cooling method.  It’s important to note that water or air chillers used for current data centre cooling is already or will be shortly using one of these hydrofluoroolefins (HFO) refrigerants.   To summarise, there are existing non-PFAS technologies that are used in electronics cooling in data centres today.  However, with the additional heat generated from the more advanced semiconductors needed for the constant growth in data volume, alternative forms of cooling are needed as the conventional non-PFAS cooling technologies will not be able to cope with the demands placed upon it.  This alternative form of cooling is facilitated by HFOs which have superior global warming potential characterisation than the current F-gases used in data centres.   Please refer to the attached document “Derogation request for Electronics Cooling in Data Centres” for more detail.

10. Analytical methods: Analytical tools and methods that are currently commercially available to detect PFAS in wastewater are believed to allow visibility to only a small fraction of PFAS constituents that are found in semiconductor manufacturing wastewaters.  This is due to the limitations of current analytical method libraries, and the large number of PFAS species in use. The industry has reviewed what it considers to be a short list of analytical techniques that are capable of detecting some PFAS species within semiconductor wastewater.  However, it was not possible to identify an analytical method that would detect all of the PFAS in a comprehensive manner.  Consequently, it is essential that further research is conducted to advance such analytical techniques noted below so that a more complete series of methods will be available to the semiconductor industry.  1. US EPA 537.1 (modified) The detectable PFAS was C4-C13 species.  In semiconductor wastewater, the limit of detection was found to be ~ 1ppt.  The primary gap highlighted with this method related to almost all of the species included in the analytical library are not used in semiconductor manufacturing, with PFBS being the only exception. The applicability of this method is limited mainly to the detection of PFAS by-products that result from use in semiconductor manufacturing.  2. US EPA draft 1633 (EPA method in development) The detectable PFAS was C4-C13 species.  The limit of detection was ~ 1 ppt.  This method is not yet commercially available.  3. US EPA 1621 AOF The detectable PFAS for this method was the total organic fluoride content.  The limit of detection was unknown but was assumed to be in the ~100-900 ppb range.  The gap identified with this method for semiconductor wastewater was the fact that most short and ultrashort PFAS species will not be detected, as they must first absorb to the GAC column, and most C1-C5 species absorb in an inadequate manner, if at all.  4. Liquid Chromatography-High-Resolution Mass Spectrometry (LC-HRMS) For this method there were ~ 30 PFAS with standards and ~1000 PFAS from a spectral software library without standards.  The limit of detection was ~1-10 ppt for those PFAS species that have standards.  In terms of gaps, the ~1000 PFAS derived from the spectral software library only allows for the positive identification of the structural category and or PFAS species, but not the numerical concentration.  In addition, the availability of this analytical service is very limited, and analyses require many hours processing and review prior to making results available.  5. 19F Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) The detectable PFAS was total PFAS.  The limit of detection was ~ 1 ppt.  With respect to the gaps with this method, the availability is very limited, and it is unknown whether we can gain access (University of Toronto).  Also, each sample requires a six-hour run.  6. BS EN 14852 The detectable PFAS for this method was total fluorine.  The detection limit was 50 ppm.  With respect to identified gaps, although the standard is commonly used in the semiconductor industry’s supply chain, the results are not reliable for solid materials or chemicals in the liquid form.

Content: Environmental emissions Baseline Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Introduction

Machine tools are at the heart of all industrial manufacturing processes. Their use allows strategic sectors such as aerospace, energy, and automotive to build highly efficient parts and components, playing a pivotal role in achieving the Green Deal goals.

A variety of process and auxiliary fluids  are used in machine tool. The materials used in crucial components, such as seals and plain bearings, must resist mechanical stresses and the chemical properties of the auxiliary fluids (and potentially their combinations e.g. auxiliary fluid with chips and dusts resulting from the mechanical process) over extended periods. Furthermore, these materials must avoid stick-slip phenomena and ensure precision and accuracy.

The most cost-effective, reliable and resistant solutions available for machine tool manufacturers are conventional materials like NBR, HNBR, PUR, PA, PC, PE, and PP, and in certain instances, fluoropolymers like FKM, FFKM, and PTFE.

Growing demand for fluoropolymers driven by Regulations

The demand and use for fluoropolymers have increased due to the impact of the EU chemicals regulation known as REACH (Regulation EC No. 1907/2006). For example, many of the biocides previously used in water-mixed MWF are now prohibited. As a common practice to prevent the growth of microorganisms and fungi, MWF emulsions are now operated at pH values above 9, that means in the more alkaline range. This generally has negative effects on conventional polymeric materials, which is why high-performance polymers and therefore PFAS have to be used in some cases.

Currently, machine tool manufacturers do not have any alternative or equivalent products on the market that would allow them to continue their production without fluoropolymers.

Low concern polymers

Fluoropolymers represent a category of long-chain polymeric PFAS materials distinct from non-polymeric PFAS. Fluoropolymers adhere to the OECD criteria as "low-concern polymers", demonstrating their safety for utilisation in industrial applications, equipment, and components. Furthermore, fluoropolymers behave in a chemically stable manner, they are non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water soluble and non-mobile.

Consequently, regulatory authorities in countries like the UK do not perceive a need to impose restrictions on fluoropolymers, including their manufacturing processes.

Impact of PFAS restriction

Implementing the proposed PFAS ban will put the fulfilment of the Green Deal goals at serious risk and have significant drawbacks for the entire mechanical and plant engineering sector. Such restrictions will endanger the global competitiveness of the European manufacturing industry sector.

In addition, from a consumption and maintenance point of view, machine tools will have:
- Higher energy and resource consumption (e.g., increased friction levels and additional air-sealing requirements),
- A more frequent need for maintenance and part replacement (e.g. increased wear and more frequent seal replacements) leading to increased downtimes.

Our industry supports the objective of avoiding emissions of hazardous substances into the environment and the proposed measures to restrict hazardous PFAS. However, the proposed PFAS ban does not consider the individual toxicity and risk profile. Therefore, it is crucial to recognize that long-chain fluoropolymers carry a distinct risk profile compared to short-chain non-polymeric PFAS.

Policymakers must recognize the difference between applications that release substantial amounts of PFAS into the environment, such as PFAS in consumer goods, and those that pose lower risks and generate minimal emissions, such as high-performance seals within the closed space of the machinery installations.

Failure to make this differentiation would harm the business environment and operations  for the EU manufacturers of high-performance machinery.

Based on the CECIMO membership, we can foresee that over 1,500 machine tool industries and their approximately 150,000 workers would suffer serious consequences if the ban was implemented, as indicated in the proposal. In addition, as machine tools have a critical role in any industrial production we can expect a much greater impact, involving all the users (for example aerospace, energy, defence, automotive, healthcare etc) of these technologies.

Finally, it is concerning for our industry to see that the proposal’s specific application domain is only briefly mentioned. Our concern is that the five countries that developed such a proposal may have not considered the applications of certain PFAS in sectors such as machine tool manufacturing. On the other hand, the lack of specific analysis and consideration of the machine tool sector might also be the result of the low consumption volume of fluoropolymers used by this industry.



Environmental emissions

Machine tools are key enabling technologies that directly impact the productivity and competitiveness of almost every manufacturing process. They are used to manufacture different objects such as home appliances, bicycles, cars, planes, medical devices and wind turbines. Therefore, this technology has a big role in transitioning towards more circular and sustainable manufacturing. Machine tools can be considered sustainable products. They are designed to last, with ease of maintenance in mind (retrofitting and remanufacturing are standard practices in the sector). Although each machine tool can be considered a unique product, around 83% of the machine tool is made from metallic materials, allowing high recycling levels and high reuse levels of the materials to produce new products in an almost never-ending loop without loss of quality. Data provided to CECIMO by different machine tool manufacturers also shows that, on average, 80% of the machine tools are still in service ten years after their installation, while 65% are still in service after 20 years. This clearly shows that machine tools possess great durability and a long lifetime.

If spare parts are not available (e.g. due to a ban), there is a risk that the machines will have to be taken out of service and replaced long before their actual end of life. Such a consequence will have an additional environmental impact that must also be considered when evaluating the environmental impact of the fluoropolymer ban.

In addition, Machine tools, as products only destined for the B2B market, are in the hands of professionals throughout their entire lifecycle, who can ensure proper recycling, proper disposal of critical components such as FP and perform machine maintenance and seal replacements.


The importance of a risk-based approach

The proposed restriction on all PFAS, does not consider the individual level of toxicity and risk profile. In addition, using the one-ban-fits-all approach on a hugely diverse group of PFAS with varying risk profiles creates a disproportioned burden for a huge portion of the supply chain.

Given the substantial role of PFAS in many industries (including machine tools), the use of low-concern polymers should be permitted as long as their risks can be effectively controlled through appropriate containment measures or until suitable alternatives are  available.

To tackle the issue of high-risk PFAS and maintain high industrial competitiveness in the EU, our policymakers must adapt the proposal to a risk-based approach so that the restrictions will only be applied to those PFAS with an identified high risk.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The mechanical and plant engineering sector, and specifically machine tools, are not listed in table 9 of the Annex XV Restriction Report. Only certain sub-sectors are mentioned that also have significance for the mechanical engineering industry. Examples are:  - Manufacture of metal products (although PFAS are not used directly in the manufacturing of metal products, they are used indirectly in the machine tools used for this purpose – you can find our justification of the importance of fluoropolymers for the safe, proper and efficient operation of machine tools in the non-confidential comment section.  - Refrigeration (refrigeration systems are partially used in machine tools, e.g. for temperature control of the coolant and/or for control cabinet air conditioning)  - Hydraulic fluids (machine tools also have hydraulic components, e.g. for workpiece clamping)  - Electronics and semiconductors (modern machine tools use a wide variety of electronic and microelectronic components, ranging from sensors and drive technology to computerized machine control)  - Lubricants (more details available in the non-confidential comment section)  Similar to the general remarks on transport (Annex XV, Table 8, p. 101/102), the mechanical and plant engineering should have been included in the restriction report. This would have avoided a major gap in a very relevant industry sector.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Manufacturing phase: Machine tool manufacturers are downstream users of fluoropolymers. They purchase these components and only use them where conventional solutions are not sufficient anymore. Therefore, our sector is not involved or has knowledge of the emissions in the manufacturing phase of fluoropolymers.  Use phase: The fluoropolymers used in machine tools are used as extremely durable seals in enclosed spaces. Therefore, any potential minimal abrasion of fluoropolymers would accumulate in these enclosed installation spaces and not leak from the machines.  End of life: Machine tools are durable goods (lifespan of over 20 years). Specialised companies take care of the machine tool disposal following the requirements set in the environmental regulations. Due to the high metal content of the machines alone, the material recycling rate is up to 98%. Non-recyclable materials are incinerated, either directly in a blast furnace or in common waste incineration plants.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Non-recyclable materials (from machine tools disposal) are incinerated, either directly in the blast furnace or in common waste incineration plants. At the high temperatures in these plants, it can be assumed that the fluoropolymers are completely destroyed and mineralized. This is confirmed by the scientific work cited below:  Aleksandrov, K.; Gehrmann, H.-J.; Hauser, M.; Mätzing, H.; Pigeon, D.; Stapf, D.; Wexler, M.: Waste incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate potential formation of Per- and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) in flue gas. In: Chemosphere, Vol. 226, July 2019, pp. 898-906, ISSN 0045-6535, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chemosphere.2019.03.191

6. Missing uses: Point a. and b. According to CECIMO, the sub-sector of high-performance seals and plain bearing applications for mechanical and plant engineering and, in particular, machine tool engineering has not been adequately addressed. These applications are of great importance because metalworking fluid (MWF) systems, as well as hydraulic and pneumatic applications of machine tools, place high demands on the chemical resistance, wear behavior, pressure resistance and tribological properties of seals and plain bearings. Moreover, in the last decade further bans on substances in MWF, resulting from the REACH regulation (Regulation EC No. 1907/2006), have created an additional need for the use of fluoropolymers such as FKM, FFKM and PTFE. In case of a ban of these fluoropolymers, there will be different risks, for instance: the machine components will experience premature leakage (endangering personnel and the environment), sensitive components such as high-precision measuring equipment and spindle bearings will come into contact with damaging media, and will impair the guides of mechanical components (essential for the accuracy of the machine tools).  According to CECIMO members (national machine tools and manufacturing associations) our industry uses annually an estimated a low level of tonnage of fluoropolymers in its machines and manufacturing equipment. Our members identified the following sealing applications requiring fluoropolymers: - O-ring preloaded PTFE seals for pneumatic applications - Support rings based on PTFE for high-pressure hydraulic applications - PTFE-based guide elements for pistons - O-rings on FKM and FFKM basis - X-rings on FKM and FFKM basis - O-ring preloaded translational hydraulic seals (PTFE / FKM) - O-ring preloaded rotary seals (PTFE / FKM) - Radial shaft seals (FKM / FFKM) - Lip ring seals (FKM / FFKM) - O-ring preloaded PTFE wipers - O-ring preloaded hydraulic rod seals (PTFE / FKM) - Special FKM and FFKM rotary seals  Regarding the emissions from the use of fluoropolymers in machine tools an answer can be found in question 2.  Point c  Based on the CECIMO membership, we can foresee that over 1,500 machine tool industries and their approximately 150,000 workers would suffer serious consequences if the ban was implemented, as indicated in the proposal. In addition, as machine tools have a critical role in any industrial production we can expect a much greater impact, involving all the users (for example aerospace, energy, defence, automotive, healthcare etc) of these technologies.  From point d to point g Alternatives to fluoropolymers are already used in less critical areas in machine tools and they have lower performance and resistance. In particular, they have lower temperature, pressure and chemical resistance. They wear more quickly and lead to increased friction in the rotating/moving machine elements.   For many of the alternatives that may be considered, in-depth studies are needed before they can be used, including R&D and application trials. According to the information we have collected from seal manufacturers, it is unlikely to discover an equivalent alternative to fluoropolymers (particularly the extreme durability of fluorocarbon compounds).  A ban on fluoropolymers in mechanical and plant engineering would thus inevitably lead to the use of poorer-performing alternatives with the corresponding socio-economic consequences, some of which we have already outlined in the non-confidential comment section: - Lack of competitiveness compared to non-EU machinery, which is still allowed to use fluoropolymers. - Higher energy and resource consumption during machine operation (e.g. due to increased friction and additional sealing air requirements). - Reduced seal durability and consequently increased maintenance effort (more frequent seal replacements). - Higher probability of unintended leakage of process and auxiliary fluids such as MWF and oil (safety risk as well as environmental and health hazard). - Decommissioning of machines long before their actual end of life, as spare parts are no longer available.  Given the information provided and the OECD recognition of fluoropolymers as “polymers of low concern”, we propose a permanent exemption for all fluoropolymers used in machinery and plant engineering.

General Comments: Introduction

These comments are submitted by Mexichem Fluor EU BV on behalf of Mexichem Fluor Companies d/b/a Koura (“Koura”). Koura is  a global leader in the development, manufacture and supply of energy-efficient, low global warming potential (GWP) refrigerants for refrigeration, air conditioning and heat pump (RACHP/HVACR) markets, medical propellants used in metered dosed inhalers and critical fluoropolymers used in lithium-ion batteries. Koura also develops and manufactures fluorinated electrolyte additives used for improving lithium battery performance. Koura is a responsible manufacturer, with a commitment to reduce emissions by 2030 and net zero by 2050.  Koura has long-established development and production facilities in the United Kingdom, United States, Mexico and Japan. Koura supports responsible life cycle management as the basis for sustainable products that meet a range of socio-economic needs.

Summary

Koura supports the principles of controlling the use of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) that are harmful to human health, bioaccumulate and persist in the environment. Such characteristics, however, are not applicable to all substances that have been classified as PFAS under the OECD definition that ECHA adopted in the Restriction Proposal, which includes a comprehensive ban of the entire substance class of PFAS through a definition that spans over 10,000 different fluorinated compounds ranging from gases to liquids to solids with widely different environmental and toxicological profiles. Many PFAS substances are persistent in the environment, and it is this concern over persistence that is the basis for the Restriction Proposal. Historically, persistence alone has not been a sufficient justification for restricting a substance under REACH, or in any other jurisdictions.

Koura and other Fluorinated gas (F-gas) manufacturers have strongly supported the Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol. We view this structure as a responsible approach to manage these materials. Double regulating on F-gases and overregulating fluoropolymers would lead to regression from the advanced technologies that enable modern life, a curtailment in the EU’s workforce and ability to attract investors, a reduction in the reliability, safety, and efficiency of a wide array of products as well as their forced early obsolescence.

Koura supports science-based regulation that is consistent and which benefits society and the environment. The Restriction Proposal’s treatment of PFAS as non-threshold substances and consideration of release as a proxy for risk is not scientifically justified. If the Restriction Proposal were adopted in its current form, the socio-economic loss would be significant. Based on Ricardo’s Socio-economic Analysis report  (SEA), for the Refrigeration, Air Conditioning and Heat Pump (RAVHP) sector alone, the EU economy could suffer 6,000 -27,000 job losses between 2025 and 2040, economic losses for producers and importers associated with F-gases alone could be between €550 to €640 million annually, and the loss of downstream users’ revenues is estimated to range between €2.2 and €4.1 billion per year. Based on the Global Research and Evidence Lab’s study report, the PFAS regulation has global impact to not only the fluorochemical market of €18-25 Bn/year, but it also has potential impact to all the industries that use PFAS in manufacturing downstream products in the amount estimated at €27 trillion.

Koura thanks ECHA for the opportunity to comment on the Restriction Proposal and urges ECHA to allow appropriate derogations for the specific applications discussed. To summarize the general comments and supporting arguments below in the form of concrete recommendations, Koura confirms that R-152a, R-1132a and R-32 are not PFAS per OECD definition. Vinylidene Fluoride, VDF, R-1132a was wrongly referenced in Annex Table B.13, it is NOT a PFAS based on the ECHA definition.

Koura respectfully and strongly advocates for the following positions:
• We request time-unlimited derogation for R-1234zeE used as a refrigerant or exclude it from the definition of PFAS.
• We request a time limited 5-year derogation for HFA-134a used as propellant in pressurized metered dose inhalers (pMDI).
• We request time-unlimited derogation for PVdF and fluorinated solvents and additives for use in batteries, including batteries used in electric vehicles and energy storage systems.
• We request time-unlimited derogation for perfluorosulfonic ionomers & polymers and PTFE used in fuel cells and electrolysers.

The comments that follow address in greater detail and with clear supporting evidence Koura’s concerns that restrictions placed on products in three important use categories – refrigerants, metered dose inhalers, and battery manufacturing – should not interfere with the orderly HFC phasedown in the first two use categories, or with the transition into fluoropolymers for battery manufacturing, which would undermine RePowerEU goals. For each sector, Koura can provide supplementary data that supports the derogations needed to ensure that these important societal operations are not disrupted.

Conclusion

As noted at the outset, Koura supports the EU member state proposal to restrict the use of PFAS that is harmful to human health, bioaccumulate and persist in the environment. Careful evaluation of materials that meet the definition of PFAS is necessary, as are scientific and socio-economic impact assessments of alternatives, to grant the proper derogations necessary to avoid major disruptions.

We respectfully request the following derogations:
• Time-unlimited derogation for R-1234 zeE used as refrigerant.
• 5-year derogation for HFA-134a used as propellant in pressurized metered dose inhalers.
• Time-unlimited derogation for PVdF and fluorinated solvents and additives used in batteries, including batteries used in electric vehicles and energy storage systems.
• Time-unlimited derogation for perfluorosulfonic ionomers & polymers and PTFE used in fuel cells and electrolysers.

Koura, with production facilities in the United Kingdom, the United States, Mexico and Japan would be impacted to a relatively lesser extent than our European counterparts under the proposal. Nevertheless, we believe a science-based regulation with overall social-economic assessment is needed to promote the circular economy, to ensure energy efficiency, operational continuity and to avoid unnecessary waste due to premature disposal.

To that end, we welcome a rapid transition in the marketplace, while also maintaining that an appropriate timeframe for transition as well as time to assess the environmental impacts from the use of non-fluorinated alternatives to avoid regrettable substitution is reasonable and justified. We believe careful consideration of the concerns addressed above, and amendment of the PFAS Restriction Proposal to grant proper derogations, would not undermine the global competitiveness of the European industry and would serve the greatest interest of both European citizens, and the competent national authorities acting and putting this proposal forward on their behalf.

Koura believes that double regulation on hydrofluorocarbon gases (HFCs) and overregulating  fluoropolymers used in batteries and green energies would lead to a regression in the advanced technologies that enable modern life, a curtailment of investment in research and development, and a weakened competitiveness for the European industry. It could result in the complete relocation of many industries outside the EU with significant impacts to the standards of living of Europen citizens, prosperous societies and sustainable economies, and could seriously impair achieving the ambitious goals of the EU Green Deal, RePower EU and climate neutrality by 2050. We respectfully request the competent authorities to consider and grant the derogations requested.
