General Comments: Lely welcomes the opportunity to take part in this consultation on the proposed restriction of PFAS. We understand the concerns on PFAS. Whilst certain PFAS are currently critical to our products, we aim to take responsibility by reducing and eliminating the use of PFAS to the fullest extent possible; and by addressing the required steps to achieve this in our upstream value chains. However, as described in this document, we have significant concerns over the restriction as it is currently proposed.

Lely manufactures and sells agricultural machinery since 1948 and has a rich history of innovations in the dairy industry. Our flagship product, the Astronaut milking robot, makes us a leader in our sector, and the first to launch a commercial milking robot in 1992.

In the harsh environment of the barn, in which all our robots (dairy robots, manure collectors, nitrogen-capture installations, etc.) operate, specific technical problems call for specific solutions that permit 24/7 operation with minimal downtime, allowing for a serviceable installed base. This is critical, since downtime of our robots can have a very direct impact on the health and wellbeing of the cows being served and thus on food safety- and food security. For instance, downtime of a milking-robot must be solved in a matter of hours to not cause distress to the cows.

Similarly, having unexpected issues in the feed supply for the herd is a direct cause for concern that requires immediate intervention. In both examples, service technicians must be able to service or repair the relevant machine efficiently, with low downtime and with long service intervals.

For certain engineering applications, such as (static or dynamic) seals in mechanical-, hydraulic-, pneumatic-, or electromechanical applications, PFAS-derivative materials are currently essential in ensuring endurance of these specific engineering functions performed by those parts and providing technical solutions required to fulfil essential food- and safety-related standards and certifications. In many applications, specific, certified materials must be used. In certain applications, no materials are currently available or in sufficient state of development (let alone certified for food-grade applications) to be implemented as PFAS-free alternative.

Especially in applications where hygiene is critical, Viton, FKM and similar compounds present solutions that yet have no suitable alternative that can ensure the service-life required in all applications. Applications where thermal- and chemical loads (steam-in-place and clean-in-place applications) are currently seen as PFAS-critical applications.

Additionally, specific PFAS-containing chemicals are used as lubricants, for reasons analogous to the ones mentioned above.

In some applications, changing the materials of certain engineering-specific functions may be possible. This can be the case where over-specified materials have been incorporated and lower specifications do not limit functionality. However, it is certain that for specific functions, certain vital functionalities cannot be performed, or only with very significant and uncertain R&D trajectories.


Such redesign efforts would result in engineering projects that take a minimum of 2 years and would require long-term field testing to be validated as suitable. Depending on the complexity of a change, this can take in excess of 5 years until implementation. While for new machines being developed, this is more realistic and may be manageable in ongoing developments, for the installed base of machines this is unlikely. With over 86.000 active robots globally, some over 20 years old in the field, not being able to offer replacement components (or to develop drop-in-replacement alternatives) without risking severely reduced performance levels will result in a significant portion of those machines becoming effectively un-serviceable, forcing farmers to write them off.

Resale of whole goods (robots) is an important pillar of Lely’s sales and operations, with robots being designed for long service lives (10 years by design, but 20+ years of on-farm use in practice not being exceptional). Refurbishing programs are an important aspect of this model and require legacy parts to remain available. The restriction as currently proposed makes such refurbishment programs unfeasible, resulting in unnecessary waste-streams due to early decommissioning of machines that could otherwise be refurbished or simply serviced.

Selling of refurbished machines is made even more difficult due to the fact that placement on the market of re-used articles is not excluded from the proposed restriction, meaning that effectively, the waste-streams from these machines, including the end-of-life emissions of PFAS are preponed.

With our machines being a key asset to farmers that rely on them to run their business, having to write off their machines will result in financial distress in an industry (dairy farming) that is already under severe regulatory pressure. Lely identifies a significant risk of increased pressure on the dairy-industry due to the foreseen restriction, which in turn will have a risk of societal impact. We hope you will consider this considering the burden and uncertainty placed on farmers in current times already.

The analysis we performed to arrive at our reported annual consumption of PFAS within Lely (as provided under our answer to question 5), allows performing in-depth analysis and prioritization of items that have disproportional consumption-rates compared to their technical criticality for R&D-activities. This enables a focused strategy concerning reduction of actual PFAS consumption whilst reserving time for the most critical application types, which can then be researched in detail. In certain cases, this will fit well with the proposed derogation timeline foreseen for food-contact materials. However, as further elucidated below, it is our opinion that the definition of the sector and the specific sub-uses is not complete and lacks explicit mention of those specific sub-uses that are critical.

This lack of definition is interpreted as an operational risk, since Lely would be forced to implement redesigns at a time where alternatives for certain materials are expected not to be available2, certified for our uses, or fully tested. For other sectors that closely relate to our operational continuity, such as “Electronics” we also foresee risks of value-chain interruptions presenting risks that are hard to quantify.
With Lely’s reputation in the sector requiring non-stop attention to quality improvements, our continuous improvement practices already allow us to implement pro-active and ambitious PFAS-reduction programs. Given the current knowledge of PFAS and the relevant societal-, environmental- and health implications, Lely has no doubt that prioritizing the elimination of PFAS use to the furthest extent possible should be our aim. However, we strongly emphasize the practical complexity of the topic, considering both the technical challenges that specific sub-uses relevant to the engineering of Lely machines present, but also the challenges imposed by the highly complex global value-chain that we are dependent on.

Although it is not possible to provide quantified detail of the end-of-life emission (question 2), it is clear that in case of foreseen emissions from PFAS-containing seals or other replacement parts, the replaced part will be substituted with a new one. The old part will subsequently end up in the usual waste-streams, meaning that it will end up in waste incineration. This incineration process, which is the default waste treatment option in European context, has no end-product1.
 
Request for Exemption

As also highlighted by the consultation provided by ASML (4473), Lely would find it more reasonable to implement a measure analogous to the “Blue Guide on the implementation of product rules 2022”, wherein re-used products are exempt from restrictions by addition of the wording “for the first time” added to Condition 2 (p4 Annex XV), which states “shall not be placed on the market”. Even though the Blue Guide does not apply to agricultural products, the reasoning seems more sound and would circumvent unnecessary short-term increase of PFAS waste-stream emissions.

It is our opinion that not including an exemption for PFAS-related materials required for maintenance of our installed base of machinery is not proportional to the socio-economic consequences imposed on our industry (dairy robotics), but also on the dairy-producing industry (farmers, our end-customers) and society. This is especially true for sub-uses for which no clear alternative materials are available, or which result in such significant redesign efforts that these are unrealistic to pursue or require more time than is available. More specifics related to this are included further in this document.

Since our machines are engineered to be serviceable and refurbish-able to allow for product lifespans of 10 years (with use in practice often exceeding 20 years), and especially since farmers have to invest significantly in the purchase and upkeep of their machinery, forcing them to replace machines with new-bought machinery has disproportional socio-economic consequences for farmers. Additionally, Lely aims to support its installed base with suitable spare parts for a period of 10 years after the product lifespan has lapsed (meaning after the last machine of a certain version is sold). Given the magnitude of the investment the farmer has to make, we aim to support this long lifetime of the product.

We have described specific viewpoints related to the definition of the sector that we classify ourselves under, which connect to our requested exemption as just described in our answer to question 1.

Considerations
In recent weeks, it has become apparent that certain suppliers of seals and gaskets are already struggling to provide certain compounds commonly used in machinery. Momentarily, it seems that only specific chemicals for producing specific compounds resistant to high chemical loads and for medical applications are affected by these supply-chain issues, stemming from base material suppliers phasing out certain materials.

This seems to take place in anticipation of the proposed restrictions, and without alternative material solutions being available, let alone tested, validated or certified for use in our sector and sub-uses. While no direct effect is anticipated yet, it is clear that if more PFAS-containing sealing and gasket manufacturers go into this direction, it could have severe implications on the industrial value chain.

It is our understanding that the elastomer industry parties involved in PFAS compound manufacturing and processing are preparing commercial- and strategic measures in anticipation of the proposed restriction. It is uncertain whether or not this effect will create further risks for supply-chain instabilities, but this is not to be ruled out. While this could accelerate the desired outcome of the restriction even before it becomes applicable, the consequences of not allowing a carefully planned phase-out for mechanical applications are not to be underestimated. These effects are not factored into our current analysis of the problem.

The risk that certain essential parts of the value chain will be significantly affected poses potential continuity risks for the industry as a whole that are impossible to quantify. Within an increasingly uncertain geopolitical landscape in relation to critical raw material supply, the potential effects that the proposed PFAS restrictions introduce to the European industrial sector at large are highly unpredictable and therefore present potentially far-reaching socio-economic risks.

This does not alleviate the industrial sector, or for that matter the legislator, to take responsibility of eliminating the effects of PFAS emissions by the industry to the furthest extent possible in a calculated manner, but it stresses the need for a well-considered and programmatic effort that factors in the potential downstream side-effects on the agricultural mechanization sector-, on the industrial sector as a whole-, and on society at large.

It is our belief that sufficient efforts should be dedicated to R&D aimed at finding alternative materials for the applications that are affected. And although it seems that the relevant parties for the sub-uses directly affecting manufacturers such as Lely are focused on this, the result of such efforts are not yet leading to applicable materials. As also stated by EHEDG in their Position Paper1, “… no suitable alternatives exist for some of these uses as we speak and the development of suitable alternatives will probably take decades. Meaning that the 6.5 year grace period will probably not be sufficient for the industry to develop commonly usable safe alternatives”. This reflects Lely’s understanding of the technological risk as it exists for the sub-uses, and our sector, based on internal expertise, but also based on discussions with our supply-chain partners. Similar comments are provided by “The Rubber Group” (ID 4099) and the “European Sealing Association” (ID 4472). The risks highlighted above therefore seem to be based on false assumptions that the industrial sector will be able to mitigate the downstream effects of the restrictions by means of relying on innovation.

Lely will pro-actively strive to reduce its use of PFAS and promises to make an active contribution to the industrial changes required to implement this to the furthest extent possible, respecting its responsibilities to its customers and their cows, considering the socio-economic aspects as addressed in this public consultation text.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Based on the contents of Table 9 of Annex XV, Lely classifies itself as a company operating in the “Industrial food and feed production” sector as presented in Table 9 of Annex XV. This means that our milking-robots, but also feed-management-, manure management- and nitrogen-capture robots (and all other peripherals related to our physical product portfolio) are interpreted by Lely to fall under this sector definition, even though it is to be observed that this definition is by no means explicit in Annex XV Table 9.   Lely is of the opinion that the definition of the sector should be broadened to include said product categories, for instance under the following descriptions:  1. Machinery related to feed production (already covered) 2. Machinery related to food production (already covered) 3. Machinery related to manure and/or nitrogen collection and treatment (not explicit yet), including but not limited to machinery used for waste-stream capture, storage and/or nutrient recovery  Additionally, in our machines, food contact materials are by far not the only material applications that require materials that contain PFAS, or that involve PFAS at some step of their production, which are critical to machine performance and operations.   It is our suggestion to extend the list of product categories considered for the derogation of the sector (column 2 of Table 9) with the following sub-uses:  1. Food contact materials (already listed) – interpreted as specific (sub-)components in direct physical contact with food- or feed materials. 2. Seals and gaskets used in products within the sector. This includes seals with chemical- or thermal- and/or dynamic loads, and for which no alternative materials are apparent or suitable in the foreseeable future. 3. Lubricants used in products within the sector.    Furthermore, we identify overlap in our activities with several other sectors:  1. “Electronics”  While Lely as a robotics company puts on the market a considerable amount of electronics, it is not under our direct control and therefore extremely difficult to understand the true use of PFAS in our electronics. As such, we cannot be certain that the absence of a derogation for this category as a whole, based on “inconclusive evidence pointing to the non-existence of technically and economically feasible alternatives at EiF” (p.134 of Annex XV) will not pose a significant supply-risk to us as a machine manufacturer, or a reliability-risk if we were to be forced to substitute all PFAS integrated in our products value-chain in time.   In fact, it is our expectation that due to the complex nature of the electronics value-chain, there will be a disruptive amount of currently unidentified components that will result in obsolescence and/or redesign efforts currently unforeseen. While mitigating such incidents is a part of our daily operations, the criticality lies in our need to perform extensive testing on system-level for most of such incidents, creating possible disruptions for our operations if the quantity of incidents would see an unexpected and unpredictable increase. The result is an operational risk that cannot be ignored, even though it cannot be quantified at current time.   Specific sub-uses of PFAS in the electronics industry in general that we could identify as being potentially critical and difficult to fully eliminate from PFAS usage in the near future are: a) Corrosion protection sub-uses, especially in prevention of chemical-load related corrosion effects on electronics (manure), it is likely that certain specific sub-uses of PFAS in electronics can be hard to substitute. Mainly, we are considering protective coatings of electronics hardware (sensors and other delicate components). b) Insulation and wiring and heat-resistance – PFTE as a material used in electrical insulation is unparalleled in terms of resistance against chemical-, thermal- and electrically conductive loads. Additionally, protection of specific electronics components against heat-induced degradation is expected to involve PFAS-related materials (PTFE specifically) in many sub-uses. Substituting its use in all specific sub-uses in the electronics sector seems like inherently complex. It is foreseen that for Lely, the impact in this particular case could lead to extensive test programs. However, no specific analysis has been performed on its prevalence in our current designs, as it requires non-automated research efforts on component-level. For more specific insight of such matters, we refer to the consultations provided by key players in the electronics industry, such as ASML (4473).  2. “PFTE thread sealing tape (no derogation)” PTFE thread-sealing tape is a very common and practical material that is often used in installations. While there are gel- and adhesive-type materials that can substitute its functionality in some specific cases, a generally applicable alternative that won’t significantly affect serviceability of machines is not apparent. Since no derogation is proposed, this could become a bottleneck for serviceability of our installed base.  3. “Coil coating (no derogation)” For motors, electronic components and general robotic applications, copper coils play an important role in actuation, mechanization and sensor technology. It is unclear what the impact of the restrictions will be in this sector, and what the side-effects will be for Lely.  4. “Polymeric PFASs used in processing aids for production of non-PFAS polymers/plastics” Similarly as for point 3, we have no direct view on the impact of this topic on suppliers that produce for Lely.  5. “Lubricants (12-year derogation)” While it is clear that some lubricants can be replaced relatively easily, it is not clear what precise impact will present itself upon an eventual full ban of PFAS-containing lubricants.  6. “Metal plating and manufacture of metal products” No concrete information is available on the impact in the (sheet)metal supply-chain that we work with.

5. Proposed derogations: We have performed detailed analysis of the PFAS use within Lely based on data available within our systems. Several limitations on the representativeness of these figures have to be noted:  1. Figures do not include PFAS consumption of components bought as finished assemblies, as long as those assemblies do not contain spare parts. Due to the functionality and nature of PFAS use in our machines however, the fraction of PFAS in such items is expected to be relatively low, especially since those uses (mainly seals), often require replacements over time, and are thus detailed in our design-systems and databases in an accurate manner. For good measure, we estimate that 10% of the PFAS use in practice is missed due to this particular limitation. Examples could be mechanical components that contain seals engineered for lifetime, such as bearings. It is likely that components that require no service or engineering attention from Lely are currently not identified. This itself is cause for concern for serviceability of our installed base. 2. Lubricants are not measurable in our system. This is seen as less critical for our input provided with this consultation, since there is a broad derogation for “lubricants where the use takes place under harsh conditions”, which certainly applies to our products and specific uses of such lubricants. If we want to estimate, we project about 5% of the PFAS use in our machines to be missed in our analysis due to this particular limitation. 3. Items not found due to mis categorization (i.e. type errors) of material description or a missed material based on the query performed in the databases. Due to the care taken in the analysis, and since several experts within Lely have reviewed the data, it is not expected that important or dominant uses have been missed.  For good measure, let’s assume this accounts for an additional 10%. 4. The PFAS-fraction of whole goods (machinery) placed on the market after refurbishment is not counted, to the extent that the PFAS components in those machines have not been replaced. Since machines are refurbished after resale, only the spare-parts used during refurbishment are relevant to be counted (and have been considered in our analysis), since the PFAS placed on the market again remains in the machine and is not released into the environment. While we would not include a correction-factor related to this limitation, we note that placing on the market of refurbished machines is not part of any derogation or exemption, and thus should be counted under “placement on the market”. It is not possible for us to quantify this fraction, nor do we think any effort in attempting this is proportional given the limited overall PFAS placed on the market by Lely. 5. Due to technical limitations, it is not straightforward to divide the specific use of PFAS related materials down to their technical sub-uses identified (we refer to the 4 sub-uses identified under our answer to question 1). Given that the determined quantity of total PFAS-related materials placed on the market being relatively low, and given the fact that most of the 204 items we have identified containing PFAS exist in various (sub-)assemblies and often in multiple products, sometimes performing multiple sub-uses, it is technically very complex to categorize and quantify the sub-uses and their criticality or proportionality for a given sub-use in detail without significant investment of resources. While this effort is planned in order to detail our PFAS-reduction strategy as a company, it is not feasible at this stage, and is also seen as disproportional to the additional information it would provide to support our reasoning.  Our analysis shows that in 2022, Lely has placed on the market a total amount of PFAS-related materials of 1.369 kg, of which 51% is related to new sales of whole-goods (machines), and 49% related to spare-parts provisioning. This quantity is accounted for over 100 unique components, which often occur in various machines and (sub)assemblies of such machines, and even for various sub-uses for the individual components counted. Corrected for the 25% of “missed” PFAS consumption in our analysis, this totals at 1711kg of PFAS placed in the market in 2022, noting the limitations mentioned above.  The quantity identified is not expected to be released to the environment in the form of hazardous emissions, assuming correct use and correct disposal of robots and spare parts at the end of their lifecycle2.  Taking into account the total weight of the products (including spare parts) we placed on the market in 2022, namely 1711kg, the quantity of PFAS-related materials is limited.   A significant fraction of this quantity can be mitigated by changing to suitable novel alternatives, given sufficient analysis and testing is performed.  However, for a certain fraction it is not currently clear whether suitable replacements (will) exist. If their use is restricted before a replacement is technically and economically viable, the impact on Lely as a company and the dairy value change will be significant - even though the actual weight of PFAS whose use would be restricted is limited.

6. Missing uses: As already covered in our answers to questions 1 and 5, several nuances are suggested to both the sector definition, in order to ensure that important societal aspects are not disregarded or ignored entirely. Related to the specific nuances put we see explicitly missing in the current restriction proposal as it has been presented in Annex XV. In our answering of question 6, we detail our viewpoints regarding the specific sub-uses we see as relevant, but not (fully) recognized in the restriction- and derogation proposal. We emphasize once again that we find the definition of the sector as described in Annex XV too narrow to provide a fully insightful opinion. We hope you recognize this aspect, taking into account that the sub-uses identified and the detailed reasoning provided should be seen in the context of the broader sector-definition as we have set forth in our answer to question 1.   It is foreseen that, for specific sub-uses, no suitable alternative may be found in the foreseeable future1. Since no accurate description of food-contact materials is provided, and since we are convinced that socio-economic side-effects are likely, the sub-uses addressed in section 3 should be seen as integral to the definition of the (sub-)uses relevant to the sector we represent.   As such, please refer to our answering to question 5 for more detailed elaboration also related to question 6.   Summarizing the 3 sub-uses identified: 1. Food contact materials (already listed) – interpreted as specific (sub-)components in direct physical contact with food- or feed materials. Food contact materials certified for use in harsh environments are critical to our installed base and newly developed machines and are not easy to substitute without severe impact on machine functionality. We foresee a realistic, but hard to quantify risk of substitute materials without PFAS being unavailable in time to serve as alternatives at time of lapsing of the derogation timeline. Furthermore, we emphasize the risk that the scope of the sub-use is not broad enough (see question 5), creating ambiguity and consequent issues in planning a structured phase-out adhering to the proposed timelines.  2. Seals and gaskets used in products within the sector.  This includes seals with chemical- or thermal- and/or dynamic loads, and for which no alternative materials are apparent or suitable in the foreseeable future. While sometimes classifying as food-or feed contact materials, not all applications of seals and gaskets fall within that category. As mentioned earlier, it is our opinion that the interpretation of the sector should be broadened to cover the missing uses discussed, or to add new categories falling under derogation. Inability to apply technically appropriate and certified materials for specific uses besides the food- and feed-contact material definition (if interpreted in the strict sense) will pose significant serviceability concerns for the dairy-machine industry, and the mechanical engineering domain in general.  3. Lubricants used in products within the sector Although less precisely researched or quantified, the use of PFAS-containing lubricants for specific applications in the sector is important. It is unclear to what extend alternatives are appropriate and directly applicable without extensive testing and redesign efforts.  The most direct consequences imaginable in case alternatives are not developed in time, or in case of sudden unavailability of critical PFAS-containing sealing materials for the sub-uses and sector as described are; 1. Reduced machine performance  2. Reduced machine reliability 3. Inability to provide spare parts for our installed base of products 4. Inability to plan sufficient development time into redesigning of functionality to circumvent or mitigate early phase-out of certain materials 5. Increased service requirements and time required for installation and maintenance, both by farmers and technicians in the field. This could have a severe impact on the profitability of farmers, and on the industry and sector we operate in. 6. Societal impact of the abovementioned points can be significant or even severe, considering the fact that food security and food safety are highly dependent on agricultural mechanization and automation. (2023), Pilot-Scale Fluoropolymer Incineration Study: Thermal Treatment of a Mixture of Fluoropolymers under Representative European Municipal Waste Combustor Conditions). 2. 6. Missing uses: Fluoropolymers are a unique class of synthetic materials that possess exceptional properties, making them irreplaceable in numerous industrial and commercial applications. Here are some of the key reasons why fluoropolymers are considered irreplaceable:  Chemical resistance: Fluoropolymers exhibit outstanding resistance to a wide range of chemicals, including acids, bases, solvents, and other aggressive substances. This makes them invaluable in industries dealing with corrosive materials, such as chemical processing, oil and gas, and semiconductor manufacturing. Thermal stability: Fluoropolymers can withstand extreme temperatures without significant degradation. They have a high melting point and can maintain their properties at both high and low temperatures, making them ideal for applications in aerospace, electronics, and automotive industries, among others. Non-stick properties: Fluoropolymers are renowned for their non-stick characteristics. This property is particularly evident in polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE).  Low friction coefficient: Fluoropolymers have an extremely low coefficient of friction, which means they offer excellent lubrication and reduce wear and tear in mechanical systems. This feature is essential for applications like bearings, seals, and sliding components in valves . Biocompatibility: Some fluoropolymers, like perfluoroalkoxy (PFA) and fluorinated ethylene propylene (FEP), exhibit biocompatibility, meaning they can be safely used in medical and pharmaceutical applications, such as catheters, surgical instruments, and drug delivery systems. Inertness: Fluoropolymers are chemically inert, meaning they do not react with most substances, making them ideal for applications that require a material to remain unaffected by its environment.  Durability and longevity: Due to their resistance to chemicals, temperature extremes, and weathering, fluoropolymers have a long service life and require minimal maintenance. This durability contributes to their cost-effectiveness and reliability in various applications. The combination of these exceptional properties makes fluoropolymers difficult to replace with alternative materials in many critical industrial and technological applications. Fluoropolymers are generally considered materials of low concern due to their unique properties and inert nature!

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Alternatives to fluoropolymers would be just as persistent and thus classified in the same way

Combined Comments: General Comments: Limitations on use of PFAS should not be watered down, PFAS as a substance group must be utterly restricted, i.e. its use must be forbidden. Potential negative effects on consumer goods or other goods are non-relevant and pale in comparison to the negative effects on the environment and human health if PFAS and other persistent organic pollutants are not removed from the market. The fact that end-of-life is not included in the environmental assessment and the lack of data on, for example, emissions from waste incineration, are huge drawbacks and is likely to lead to an underestimation of the risks posed by PFAS. This has to be taken into account and speaks for hardest possible restrictions.

General Comments: Linde Hydraulics is a supplier of hydraulic pumps, motors and valves for off-highway machinery mainly used in the construction and the agriculture sector. Hydraulic drives offer the unique properties of high power and force density and can be controlled with high dynamics. Especially in linear drives, there are no alternatives available that can provide the same performance.
Linde Hydraulics asks to continue using PFAS-based sealing materials until an alternative material with comparable performance is found. Linde Hydraulics will continue to work on the development of such alternatives in close cooperation with its suppliers. The PFAS based material for seals used today in hydraulic components does not leave the hydraulic unit until it is recycled and therefore does not pose any threat to the environment or the food chain.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: In use no material is exposed to the environment. After use 100% of the material can be separated from the product

Missing uses: When using hydraulic components in mobile machinery the temperature requirements of all parts are between 60°C and 90°C, mainly driven by high ambient temperatures that can occur and the high power density of the components. In general, hydraulic components provide sufficient cooling since the working fluid is also used to dissipate the heat. However, inside the unit there are hotspots e.g. in tribological contacts or at sealings with a high relative movement, that are 10°C to 25°C higher than the oil itself. The oil temperature is dominated by the hydraulic oil cooler of the machine, that transmits the thermal energy to the ambient air. This cooler requires an additional temperature difference of 15°C to 30°C. Finally, parts in hydraulic units heat up to 60°C to 90°C in normal operation. This temperature and the resistance to fluids is a high demand for the material of a sealing. It is expected to last as long as the hydraulic component to prevent the mobile machine from contaminating the environment. An exchange at a service of the machine would mean a nearly 100% disassembly of the hydraulic unit which can only be done by experienced staff in a protected and clean environment.  In the past, before PFAS-based materials were used in seals, users of hydraulically driven machines were used to small leaks after a certain period of operation. At the time, this was accepted. Fortunately, this property is a thing of the past and PFAS-based sealing materials are now able to ensure leak-free operation over the lifetime of the component. Users expect hydraulic units to function maintenance-free for the period of their specified service life. A seal installed in the hydraulic system does not release any material into the environment during its entire service life. During assembly or during operation, there are no clue effects that would make it difficult to dispose of the sealing material from the steel housing. Thus, the sealing material can be removed and disposed without any problems when the hydraulic component is recycled. In close cooperation with our suppliers Linde Hydraulics tried to develop alternative materials for sealing without using PFAS. In 2022 Linde Hydraulics took efforts to analyze in which applications a sealing without PFAS could also be sufficient. Unfortunately, the endurance tests already showed leakage at the rotary sealing of the pump at around 100h. At this point in time, we must therefore state that there is no sealing material without PFAS available that can meet the requirements of hydraulic systems. On the other hand, reducing the service life an entire hydraulic component according to the life time of a sealing without PFAS would mean enormous efforts for service and would significantly increase the operation cost of the entire machines. E.g. for combine harvesters with high ambient temperatures during operation it would mean rework of the entire hydraulic system for every harvest season. Finally, Linde Hydraulics asks to continue using PFAS-based sealing materials until an alternative material with comparable performance is found. Linde Hydraulics will continue to work on the development of such alternatives in close cooperation with its suppliers. The PFAS based material for seals used today in hydraulic components does not leave the hydraulic unit until it is recycled and therefore does not pose any threat to the environment or the food chain.

General Comments: Low-voltage devices or electrical installation devices are very complex products with daily stress and a long duration of more than 25 years. To make this possible in combination high level of safety and quality, high-quality materials are used. For some of the technical functions PFAS materials are intentionally used or they can be used as components of materials from other manufacturers. The materials used in electrical equipment are divided into the following groups:

1) PFAS-containing products or components that have been intentionally selected as a material or as a ingredient of a material mixture for a specifically defined function.

2) Material, that has been selected based on technical parameters. PFAS has not been specified by the equipment manufacturer but might be contained as ingredient of a material mixture based on the definition of the manufacturer of the material.

3) Components or assemblies, which are supplied from 3rd party suppliers, which have designed them on their own. PFAS has not been specified by the equipment manufacturer but might be contained as ingredient of a material mixture or as material based on the definition of the component manufacturer or of the material manufacturer for materials used in the component.

4) PFAS is a contaminant from the production process, e.g., as a release agent used in a cast mould-ing process to allow easy demoulding. Also surface treatment using PFAS or PFAS containing substances can result in such an effect. Contamination because of PFAS components in the production machine or due to the manufacturing of PFAS containing products close to the production line of intended PFAS free products can lead to contaminations. Due to the extremely low threshold level of 25 ppb, contamination is hard to control, especially if the manufacturing of parts or components is outside the EU, where no restrictions on PFAS exist.

For 1) the manufacturer of the electrical equipment (e.g. we as ABB) is called to identify and search for alternatives. This process has already started.

For 2) it is already more complex, as materials are used in many applications and changes in a material recipe might have impact on the technical parameters. A change might result in that the material can no longer be used. Then another material has to be qualified. Alternatively, the supplier might decide to stop the production of the material. Then a new supplier for a similar, PFAS free material needs to be identified.

At 3) it becomes even more complex and time-consuming, as the process is not under control and can barely be influenced by the electrical equipment manufacturer (e.g. ABB). The responsibility is on the supplier. An example for this group could be electronic equipment as control and protection relays re-quested from our customer to be used by 3rd party. They contain semiconductors or other electronics, where it has been announced by the industry that it is almost impossible to offer PFAS free solutions in short to mid term.

For 4.) it is actually unclear how a declaration of PFAS-free could be achieved.

The identification processes 2) to 4) have one problem in common: The vast majority of the about 10,000 individual substances covered by the restriction proposal are currently not classified as hazardous in accordance with the CLP Regulation (EC) No. 1272/2008 nor identified as substances of very high concern (SVHCs) under REACH Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006. Thus, information on PFAS contained in mixtures and articles is usually not communicated along the supply chain. In addition, the extremely low threshold level of 25 ppb not only limits the identification process to intended ingredients but extends it to contaminants during the production process, which can result in that concentration. Analytical processes to prove if an article is PFAS-free will be extremely challenging taking the huge number of related articles into account, especially for polymers. Without a preceding, sufficiently long mandatory information phase based on legal requirements, during which information on PFAS in articles and mixtures had to be communicated in the supply chain, e. g. via safety data sheets or according to REACH Art. 33, it is not possible to determine all PFAS uses.

ABB has the target to replace PFAS in products wherever possible with PFAS-free materials. There might be some applications where this is not possible, which will be addressed separately. In all other cases, where a replacement is possible, the complex way of identification, finding a replacement, implementing them in products and finally repeating type testing of related products will by far exceed the given transition time of 18 months, taking into account that only the time required for full type testing of products can be one year or more. As this would not only affect ABB but all manufacturers of electrical equipment,  due to the limited number of accredited test laboratories, this will create a bottleneck in type testing, which could cause a shortage of electrical equipment with a huge financial impact and a delay of the green deal. Type tests are mandatory for most markets, including EU and any material change with impact on the test result, requires type tests to be repeated. As these tests are very time-consuming and some specific tests are extremely expensive, the tests have to be done after all PFAS re-placements in the specific product to be tested have been completed, to avoid repeated testing of the same product for each identified PFAS again and again.

For this, ABB ELSB asks for an extended transition time of an additional minimum 12 years to complete the transition to PFAS-free solutions. As the investigation along the whole ABB ELSB supply chain is still ongoing, we still see the risk that this might be challenging, especially if the low threshold level is kept and the identification is not limited to intentionally added PFAS. For this either the possibility of a further exemption after the 12 years should be offered if it is proven that the replacement projects are not completed.

General Comments: Lubricant PTFE (fine powder) compound with rubber, and used as a dry lubricant for the tooth facing fabric of high-load transmission toothed belts used in various general industrial machines such as electric injection molding machines.
In addition, the  PTFE fiber made of fluororesin film is woven into the tooth facing fabric and used as a dry lubricant for the tooth surfaces of high-load transmission toothed belts.

The fabric treatments containing PTFE fine powder used as a dry lubricant, or the tooth fabric woven with PTFE fibers made from fluororesin films are used in high-load transmission toothed belts used under severe conditions. It is used for the protective tooth fabric and improves the slidability with the pulley. Improved slidability contributes to improved wear resistance of toothed belts, and by dramatically improving transmission capacity and durability in the same belt width, the functionality and safety of equipment can be secured over the long term.

As described above, PTFE as a lubricant is an indispensable material for achieving long life, compactness and safety in toothed belt power transmission systems.
As a result, the long life and compactness contribute to the reduction of resources and post-use waste when manufacturing toothed belts and pulleys, the reduction of CO2 emissions, and the securing of economic efficiency for EU-affiliated companies. 　By restricting the use of PTFE as a lubricant, the EU Green Deal target will be hindered and the socioeconomic loss will be enormous.

As no alternative technology has been found after many years of research and development, the proposed grace period of 12 years is not appropriate and PTFE lubricants used in toothed belts shall be exempt from this proposed restriction.

Scope or Restriction Option Analysis
Our Company supports the statement made by FCJ on the issues of proposed restriction, as per attached in Section IV.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Lubricants / Sector as a whole

Emissions are calculated from the amount used and the yield rate of materials, and are estimated to be approximately 1.0 ton per year.  The amount of emissions during use of the product was estimated from the wear amount in the actual machine evaluation results of the injection molding machine. As a result, the wear rate of the tooth fabric is approximately 2.4% over the product's average life span of 8 years. Calculated from this result and the annual amount of PTFE used, the annual emission amount due to wear during use is estimated to be approximately 0.4 tons. In addition, it is presumed that most of these abrasion powders remain inside the equipment, and the amount of discharge to the external environment is much smaller than this.  The amount of product waste after use is estimated to be approximately 15 tons per year, which is landfilled in a controlled environment as industrial waste.  From the above, it is estimated that uncontrolled emissions into the environment during the product lifecycle from manufacture to disposal are negligible relative to the amount used.

Moreover, it is economically more expensive than PTFE and is not a realistic option. Annex E.2.14.2.3 also proposes an alternative to use thickened silicone oil as a lubricant, but toothed belts are mainly used in a greaseless dry environment and are not realistic. Not a substitute. Please refer the attachment to Section V. f. Even after many years of research and development, no substitutes have been found, and at present there is no prospect of technological or economic substitution. g. The socio-economic impacts on businesses, consumers and other stakeholders are enormous, and we are unable to grasp the impacts across all relevant sectors.  [Impact on our EU business] We estimate that approximately 5 million euros in the sales and dozens of jobs will be lost. It will also affect the sales and employment at dozens of our distributors in EU. [Impact on users and customers in the EU market] If it becomes impossible to design a compact transmission device including pulleys, the overall size of the device will increase, resulting in a decline in economic efficiency and a decline in the international competitiveness of EU companies. In addition, it is predicted that the energy loss will increase due to the reduction in the transmission efficiency of the system, and the economic efficiency will decrease. In addition, the deterioration of durability makes it difficult to ensure the functionality and safety of the equipment over the long term. [Impact on achieving the EU Green Deal target] Losing the compactness of the equipment increases the consumption of resources, including related parts such as pulleys, and also increases the amount of industrial waste after product use. It is further increased by the short life cycle. In addition, it is expected that energy loss and CO2 emissions will be increased due to lower transmission efficiency of the drive system. 　 　 From the above, the proposed grace period of 12 years is not appropriate and PTFE lubricants used in toothed belts shall be exempt from this proposed restriction.

General Comments: Maflon SpA is an Italian fluorochemical Company, founded in 1996 thanks to a collaboration with the Fluorine Chemistry Laboratory of Padua University.
Since the beginning, the research project has been focused on fluorinated products and their applications i.e. coating solution for surfaces such as leather, textile, stone, tile and wood.
Maflon SpA is owned by Mazza holding, an Italian group established in 1982 which counts about 700 people employed in Europe, Asia and America with a consolidated turnover of 200 million Euro.
Maflon management system is certified in accordance to the requirements of the UNI EN ISO 9001: 2015 standard for quality and UNI EN ISO 14001: 2015 for the environment.
Maflon has its own internal R&D team that closely cooperates with some of the most important Universities specialized in Fluorine Chemistry such as Florence, Milano, Padua, Pisa, Rome and Venice Universities.
All the R&D activities are developed in Maflon laboratories located in the Headquarter in Castelli Calepio (BG), Northern Italy.
Maflon portfolio and business are mainly based on fluorosurfactants, textile and leather protective products, stone protection products, PTFE and PVDF micro-powders and ski waxes.
Maflon is aware of the potential danger of some substances classified as PFAS, but at the same time it is also convinced that an exemption for Fluoropolymers should be adopted, because Fluoropolymers is a family that is profoundly different from the substances for which it is right to request a restriction.
Fluoropolymers are different to other PFAS for the reasons listed below:
• They do not exhibit the toxicological and environmental profiles associated with non-polymeric PFASs that could be considered of concern.
• They have unique physical-chemical properties, which let them very different from non-polymer PFAS and therefore should have a distinct class within them.
• They meet the OECD criteria of Polymer of Low Concern (PLC) and are non-toxic, biocompatible, insoluble and immobile molecules, which are deemed to have insignificant environmental and human health impact.
Industrial production of Fluoropolymers can and has to be handled safely in industrial facilities under controlled conditions.
Fluoropolymers is used in many different sectors (we supplied PTFE dispersions and PTFE and PVDF powders and in several different sectors) that are explained in Annexes.
Main implications for downstream users:
• No alternative allows a complete replacement with performances of equivalent quality; there are some possible alternatives for some properties but there’s no one material that present all the specific and unique properties of Fluoropolymers (no 1:1 alternatives are available)
• Costs will arise due to necessary amendments of machinery and equipment when switching to alternative substances. The industrial application process on products using non-fluoropolymers material is much more complicated.
• Due to the greater quantity of product necessary for this application and the reduced service life of the treated articles, a significant environmental impact must be considered in terms of nanoforms (microplastic) and CO2 emissions.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: MAG IAS GmbH, Salacher Strasse 93, 73054 Eislingen, Germany is a mechanical engineering company that produces machines and systems for the production industry. The machines are extremely robust and are used in 3-shift operation in most cases and have a service life of approx. 20-50 years. The accuracy requirements for the machines used to manufacture products are high and are becoming ever more stringent. For example, workpieces for combustion engines require accuracies in the ten-micron range, while workpieces for electromobility require accuracies in the one-micron range.
The turning and milling machines have electric drives for the movements and the machining process. In order to be able to carry out the machining process and maintain the required accuracies, cooling, pneumatic, lubrication and hydraulic circuits are necessary in the machines. Numerous pumps, hoses and pipes with connecting elements are installed in it. These components have seals and sealing elements between stationary and moving components.
The machining process in particular is operated with cooling lubricants, which contain numerous chemical additives that pose a major challenge for sealing materials in terms of long-term behavior.

For this reason, components containing PFAS are used in highly stressed seals and linear slideways. The service life of these components has proven to be long-lasting. This results in a long service life for both the sealing components, the machine components and machines themselves. We consider this to be much more sustainable and more resource-efficient, energy- and environmentally friendly than producing shorter-lived machines.

Many of our customers purchase our machines according to their specified customer specifications. The majority of these customers require seals with PFAS content. According to customers, it is more effective to use maintenance-free components in the harsh machine environments and therefore more sustainable.
The design of our machines is based on existing sealing materials with given properties. Replacing the used construction elements by PFAS free elements which are not identical concerning size and tolerances will no longer allow the same functionality and installation space. Numerous redesigns would be necessary. We consider the chance of regaining the performance of our products to be very low.

As a machine manufacturer, we have of course not carried out any particle emission tests regarding environmental emissions. However, we are confident about the assessment for the operation and the exchange.
During the operation of our machine tools, the PFAS sealing materials naturally wear out. Wear occurs in the sealing surface. This means that parts of cubic millimeters containing PFAS are released and introduced into cooling water, lubricating oil or cooling lubricant. These materials are then processed in cycles or disposed of by the machine operators. Therefore, at our discretion, there is no direct entry into air, water or soil.
In case of replacement/repair, our experience has shown that seals are replaced a decade at earliest as part of major component revisions. If disposed of/recycled properly, no PFAS enters the environment.^

A ban on PFAS would completely or partially remove the business basis for MAG. New machines would no longer be sellable. Existing customers could not carry out repairs due to a lack of spare parts.

MAG supports the fundamental goal of preventing dangerous PFAS from entering the environment. In order to move towards a sustainable economic future, exceptions to the restriction are necessary. Three prerequisites are necessary for this:
Firstly, a transition period is necessary. In relation to the product life cycles of our machine tools, we therefore require a transition period of at least 13 years. For new designs, we will develop PFAS-free machines together with our suppliers.
Secondly, it must be ensured for our customers that existing machines can continue to be operated at all times and for the life of the machines. We are guided by the repair-as-produced principle according to Directive 2011/65/EU.
Thirdly, it must be possible to place spare, wear and used parts on the market at any time. These must be granted for an unlimited period or at least over a significantly longer period of time than the transition periods currently provided for.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: MAHLE position on the PFAS restriction proposal is aligned with the submitted positions from the Associations representing the automotive sector ACEA, Clepa and VDA (excluding MAC).
We request the removal of fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers from the scope of the restriction considering that the risks of PFAS emissions are mainly during the manufacturing phase and therefore it can be controlled and monitored. During the use phase they are considered non-toxic, non-bioaccumulative, non-mobile and as such, are classed as polymers of low concern, as per the definitions of OECD.
Also dry and liquid lubricants are containing Polymers of Low Concern (including PFPE Oils - also often meeting the criteria as polymer of low concern) and shall be completely exempted. PFPE are high molecular weight polymers, molecules are bigger than 10.000 Da, it is not soluble in water, not bioavailable, not toxic and fall outside the definition of hazardous products, both for human and for the environment.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: In the automotive sector the use of fluorpolymers enable low friction between materials when used as coatings. Flouroelastomers have very good properties at high temperatures and high chemical resistence. These properties are fundamental for the automotive industry. The following basic substances were identified:  PTFE  PVDF  FKM  PFA  FEP  FVMQ  ETFE  POM+PTFE  PVF  FMQ  FMACP  FAA  PA66+PTFE  ECTFE (25101-45-5)  FPAK   Please note that due to our position as downstream users, we are also highly impacted by the  ban on several sub-uses such as: - Lubricants - Uses of fluoropolymers in batteries and fuel cell - Uses of PFAS in electronics and semiconductors

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: During the end-of-life phase, incineration of fluoropolymers does not contribute to environmental PFAS emissions and is a safe method of disposal. A study* looking at the incineration of fluoropolymers was published in Chemosphere and showed that: • PTFE was incinerated at typical incineration temperatures of 870°C (for 4 secs) and 1020°C  (for 2.7 secs) and determined that PFAS products were generated during the incineration process.  *Krasimir Aleksandrov, Hans-Joachim Gehrmann, Manuela Hauser, Hartmut Mätzing, Daniel Pigeon, Dieter Stapf, Manuela Wexler,Waste incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate potential formation of per- and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) in flue gas, Chemosphere, Volume 226, 2019, Pages 898-906, ISSN 0045-6535

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Charles River Labs in the Netherlands performed tests to investigate if  the persistence of PTFE implies future degradation, release, or transformation into a continuous source of substances of concern.  Studies to Address Potential Partitioning to Water – Studies showed that PTFE is insoluble in  water and is not biodegradable. Studies to Address Potential Partitioning to Soil – The molecular weight of PTFE is above  500,000 Daltons and although the soil adsorption and phototransformation studies are not yet  finished, it can reasonably be expected, based on the high molecular weight, that no  partitioning to soil is anticipated. Studies to Address Potential Partitioning to Air - The vapor pressure was determined to be very  low less than 1 x 10-10 mm Hg at 20°C. No decomposition or chemical reaction was observed  at less than 150°C. No observable weight loss below 549°C, however at 549°C a 5% weight  loss was observed. This data supports the lack of inhalation exposure potential at  environmentally relevant temperatures. Conclusions from the Charles River Laboratory and ALS study: These results support the stability of PTFE and lack of transformation to other PFAS,  such as perfluoroalkyl acids. PTFE will not partition to air, water, or soil. Potential  inhalation, oral or dermal exposure to PTFE for biota or the environment is unlikely  based on this data. Additional studies are also being conducted by fluoropolymer producers and results will be  made available in due course.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: After acceptance of the end-of-life vehicles at a certified dismantling facility, the vehicles are drained of all liquids, collected and recycled properly. Subsequently, useable spare parts, the traction battery and components containing pollutants such as the starter battery are re-moved before the remaining body is pressed and taken to the shredding plant. After shred-ding the car bodies (along with other consumer items such as refrigerators), the materials are sorted and sent to the specific material loops. Materials that cannot be recycled (often plastics, rubber, glass) are thermally recycled. This is already regulated in different waste and recycling regulations in the EU.

6. Missing uses: Finding alternatives requires assessing a number of parameters for the candidate  materials. Such an assessment is a complex process which requires several tests and final customers validation. This assessment involves physical testing of products for durability, temperature, humidity,  crash etc. Such testing requires time and can result in high costs (several millions of Euros per  substance). A systematic assessment of all possible alternatives per restricted PFAS in order  to conclude on the essentiality of a derogation is therefore an unrealistic expectation on  industry. It would also impede our ability to develop new products and solutions for clean mobility.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: The current restriction proposal would require the majority of fluoropolymer/fluoroelastomers  to be  replaced 18 months after entry into force. This timescale is woefully insufficient to allow a safe transition to alternative materials. • Alternative polymers may require additional additives to approach the performance  requirements of fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers. • Alternatives do not currently meet the same level of performance as fluoropolymers. • It is anticipated that the durability of components will be reduced, reducing service life,  increasing servicing intervals and increasing cost of ownership for consumers
