General Comments: material name:CZL-2000-R2

The relevant material will be a resin material used in turbochargers for turbocharged engines for automobiles.
The more boost pressure a turbocharger has, the more power it produces, but if the boost pressure is too high, the fuel injector cannot keep up with the control system, leading to engine blowout. Also, if the turbocharger speed exceeds its limit, the turbine will blow.
To prevent this, the structure is designed so that if the turbocharger is subjected to exhaust pressure above a certain level with an increase in boost pressure, the exhaust pressure is bypassed to the exhaust pipe side and the turbocharger is not boosted above a certain level. The relevant material is used as a plastic bearing component in the wastegate valve that opens this bypass path.
Resin bearing components are required to have stable wear resistance and low friction in low to high temperature environments without lubrication, and the PTFE filling in the relevant material makes it possible to meet the wear resistance and low friction requirements.
If the bearings are not filled with PTFE, they will wear out faster and the turbocharger's supercharging function will not function properly.
As a result, engine damage or shorter engine life and increased replacement frequency may have a negative impact on the global environment.
Furthermore, if PTFE is not available, turbocharged engines have to be redesigned and re-evaluated, which requires a great deal of effort.
On the other hand, non-PFAS alternatives that meet the wear resistance and low friction properties of PTFE have not been identified. As it takes time to develop and demonstrate alternatives, there is no prospect of establishing alternative technologies.
Resin bearing components, used within the turbocharger and not replacement parts. They are not discharged from manufacture to disposal and, if properly treated at the time of disposal, have minimal impact on the environment.
For the above reasons, we wish to defer the regulation of PTFE.

General Comments: Medtech & Pharma Platform (MPP) is a European industry association representing medtech, pharmaceutical and tech companies active in the field of combined products.
We are bringing to your attention the need for an extension of the definition of medical devices as used in section A.3.10.1 of the current proposal of the PFAS regulation. The current definition does not cover single integral products (=combined products) as specified in regulation 2017/745 Article 1(9) second paragraph.
Combined products represent the small intersection between medical devices and medicinal products that comprise a drug and at least one device part. The following information focuses on applications of combined products dedicated for the delivery of drugs, which make the majority of applications among combined products. The drugs delivered by such products span a wide variety of applications including solid, liquid and gaseous active dosage forms dedicated to support therapies with low criticality up to emergency applications (e.g. emergency pen injectors for the treatment of anaphylactic shock). This contribution focuses on combined products dedicated to the accurate delivery of liquid drug dosage forms (henceforth injectors), which are under development and already on the market.
Depending on the injector design, the final combined product is either solely governed by the directive 2001/83/EC relating to medicinal products for human use (single integral product) or the product consists of several separate entities which are considered as separate pharmaceutical product or medical device under directive 2017/745 as applicable.
State of the art injectors with sophisticated delivery mechanisms often require lubricants to ensure their functionality. They support the most critical functional parameters of the device (delivery force, dose accuracy). These lubricants must remain stable over extended storage and shelf life of the medical device and must ensure the functionality upon the first actuation thereupon.
PFAS are used in such applications to utilize their longevity and inertness. A replacement of the PFAS requires thorough planning and testing to guarantee the maintained functionality of the medical device.
Alternative lubricants to PFAS in injectors may exist, but their implementation requires an extended transition period for planning and design to meet the strict product safety and stability requirements.
Therefore, we recommend adding a derogation to directive 2001/83/EC for the application of lubricants in medical devices and device components of single integral products.

General Comments: MedTech Europe, the European voice of the medical technology industry including diagnostics, medical devices and digital health, thanks the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) for the possibility to comment on the proposed EU REACH restriction of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), as published in January 2023 and subject to initial exchange at ECHA’s scientific committees for Risk Assessment (RAC) and for Socio-Economic Analysis (SEAC) in June 2023.
MedTech Europe is committed to the ambition of the EU Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability to boost innovation for chemicals that are safe and fully sustainable. As such the sector is committed to highest chemicals risk management measures and is continuously working with its suppliers to improve the performance of its products and processes, including through the phase out of uses of PFAS where this is technically feasible and at the same time securing the timely availability of lifesaving and life-sustaining technologies to satisfy patients’ health needs.

PFAS in the medical technology sector:
Where PFAS uses occur in the medical technology sector, this is due to their unique performance and combination of different and essential properties, such as chemical and heat resistance, durability, lubrication or biocompatibility. PFAS uses in medical technologies can occur
• either in a component or coating of the final medical device (MD) or in vitro diagnostic device (IVD), including investigational and research use only devices;
•or as a processing aid used during device or upstream manufacturing;
• or in the device part of an integral drug device combination, or as cell replacement therapies, or biomaterials,
PFAS substances play a key role in achieving the required high performance and durability of the technologies which are critical e.g. for precision and reliability of medical applications, especially in the light of the applicable sectoral legislations, Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on Medical Devices (MDR) and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 on In-Vitro Diagnostics (IVDR). These regulations lay down strict requirements for the design, safety, quality, performance, alternatives assessment and validation of MDs and IVDs to ensure the protection of patients’ lives.

Particular challenges in the medical technology sector
Given the need for such a combination of essential properties, there is often no technical or viable alternative available to the use of PFAS in many medical technologies, their (sterile) packaging or manufacturing process, which would deliver similar functionalities or deliver equivalent safety or quality requirements. Often the only viable alternative is another type of PFAS. In addition, an alternative must also fulfill all other aspects, i.e., required validations, aging tests, change of tools and production processes, clinical trials for certain devices, regulatory approvals or registrations, etc. according to the stringent sector-specific legislation mentioned above. Without a successful completion of the required regulatory assessments and having the necessary time to carry them out, a potential alternative material is neither able nor allowed to replace PFAS in MDs and IVDs.

Consequently, MedTech Europe’s consultation response substantiates the following sector specific needs to prevent supply shortages of medical technologies stemming from the proposed PFAS restriction:
1) A transition pathway to non-PFAS alternatives for medical technologies (including manufacturing and supply chain) with a realistic timetable that allows sufficient time to first identify all PFAS uses in medical technologies, and for subsequently identifying and moving to alternatives where these are technically viable, available and in conformity with the sector specific MD and IVD Regulations.
2) A safeguard mechanism for cases where no alternatives are available, and for newly identified non-derogated cases to ensure quality and continued access to essential life-saving and life-sustaining technologies containing PFAS or requiring PFAS for their manufacturing, as well as their upstream supply chain.
3) A differentiation between high risk and low risk PFAS considering that Article 68.1 REACH requires a proof of “unacceptable risk” for enacting a REACH restriction.
4) A patient-centric approach whereby patient safety needs are considered when transitioning away from PFAS (where technically and economically feasible).

A ban would cause problems that cannot be overlooked, as many technical systems in chemical parks, pharmaceutical production and food production rely on the use of PTFE products. We use the PFAS group of substances in all of our fittings, valves and seals, which must have basic chemical resistance to acids and bases under high temperatures and pressures (chemical and physical).  A general ban on the substance group PFAS without a transition period for the chemical industry would mean that the production of pulp as a basis for the further production of paper would have to be stopped. This would also involve the production of bioelectricity (388,232 MWh/a in 2022), tall oil and lignin, as a C-based raw material alternative to petroleum. These economically important products would also not be made available to the market if PFAS were fundamentally banned.  The suppliers of the fittings/valves/seals we use must be given sufficient time so that they can provide alternatives of the same quality, with the same properties (durability and service life) and in sufficient quantities. Current product alternatives have not yet been tested and therefore cannot be assessed conclusively. It is currently unknown whether the currently available alternatives are suitable alternatives and must be tested. Given our dependence as a downstream user, a transition period of at least 20 years is required for adequate testing due to our presence in the production process (at least 90%).  Since it is currently not known whether the use in fittings/valves/seals results in PFAS being released into the environment with the product pulp or with wastewater or other by-products and waste materials, there is interest in participating in a research project on this has already been stated. The results are not yet available. It has been analytically proven that the amount of PFAS released from our use via our pulp product is insignificant or undetectable (see appendix laboratory analysis). For this reason, substitution of fittings/valves/seals with PFAS appears to be sufficient in connection with progressive/regular maintenance and service work. In this respect, it is proposed to specify the exchange of PFAS-based equipment without a deadline. At the same time, foregoing a specific time limit would correspond to the approach of giving suppliers enough time to provide alternatives of equivalent quality in the required quantities.  Flat gaskets made of pure PTFE or reinforced PTFE are part of our factory standard for aggressive acids and alkalis, and are also temperature-resistant up to 250°C. Ensuring the production of kraft pulp, bioenergy, tall oil and lignin, as C-based raw material alternatives to petroleum, is fundamentally of macroeconomic importance. If production comes to a standstill due to the ban on the PFAS group of substances without an appropriate transition period for the chemical industry, the securing of the building blocks that are important for the European energy and climate transition will be at risk.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Merck calls on the European Union to develop a balanced approach to the regulation of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) that safeguards the environment while keeping the internal market of the EU a strong, resilient economy with a competitive industry.

Merck is a global company with its headquarters and roots in Europe. Established in 1668, our ambition is to become the global 21st century science and technology pioneer – and we are uniquely positioned to do so, thanks to our three diverse and distinct sectors: Life Science, Healthcare, and Electronics.

Merck is strongly committed to the European Union and supports the goals of the European Green Deal. To find the best strategy for a digital and sustainable future, politicians, authorities, and industries must work together and stay in constant dialogue. We want to be part of this dialogue and contribute to the best possible solution. The EU needs a holistic approach to secure its resilience and competitiveness, avoid supply chain disruptions and safeguard its strategic autonomy. The proposal to ban virtually all PFAS in the EU threatens to jeopardize this.

PFAS have several unique properties that make them very useful yet also difficult to replace with more sustainable solutions. At the same time, very persistent PFAS may lead to adverse effects for the environment and humans. We therefore support the search for substitutes for PFAS and conduct active research ourselves. Yet, we do not know whether alternatives with the same technical properties can be found in 5, 10 or 20 years from now or if a different technology is required.

Our three business sectors – Life Science, Healthcare and Electronics – are critical for society in different ways: From providing products and services that accelerate drug development and manufacturing as well as discovering unique ways to treat the most challenging diseases to enabling the intelligence of devices. Each business sector will therefore provide detailed, data-based, and substantiated input for applications where the use of PFAS is currently and in the near future without alternative to maintain the function and the purpose of specific critical products.

• PFAS are critical for the European health systems, in drug and vaccine production and development as well as other fields in life sciences. As a result, they enable innovation for a better life of mankind. Merck products are used by thousands of European companies in the pharmaceutical, medical device and biotechnology industry. This makes the availability of medicines and medical devices in the EU more independent from global supply chains and hereby increases our resilience and preparedness for the next public health emergency. Even if a more sustainable alternative with the same properties will be found, substituting a material or substance from these uses often takes several years, due to regulatory approvals or quality management needs.

• The draft restriction proposal recommends exemptions for Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs) – but not for pharmaceutical formulations, manufacturing or the necessary supply chain and packaging. Not addressing PFAS materials in the entire value chain is a general problem in all exemptions or derogations within this proposal. Here, it would ban e.g., precursors, processing aids as well as production equipment, such as filters and primary packaging, which are all necessary to provide patients with much-needed medications. For regulated products, re-submissions and approvals must be regarded as well: On top of the time needed to find a substitute, it usually takes 5-10 years if sufficient resources are available on submitter and authority side. Ultimately, companies would be forced to stop producing and supplying important drugs in Europe. The same applies to the development of future treatments.

• The initial proposal suggested a limited derogation for the use of PFA substances in the semiconductor industry – however, the very complex production of chips is currently impossible without PFAS. For several applications (e.g., photolithography, plasma etching, wafer cleaning), a replacement that has the same technical properties would be very difficult or impossible to find. Either way, it would require a significant amount of time and in some cases even a completely new technology. Meanwhile, the EU Chips Act ambition to increase the EU’s share of the global semiconductor production from 10% to 20% by 2030 cannot be achieved if semiconductor manufacturers can no longer manufacture, import and use key materials in the EU. A ban, including an import-ban, therefore threatens long-term investments in the region.

Merck supports the ambition for a smart and targeted PFAS regulation. Notwithstanding, in its current form, the PFAS restriction proposal threatens the resilience of supply chains in several critical sectors and with that the competitiveness of the European Union in a complex geopolitical environment. It also contradicts other European policies and legislative proposals aiming at increasing European competitiveness such as the EU Chips Act, the Net Zero Industry Act and the Green Deal Industrial Plan.

We therefore require smart derogations that
1. include the complete value chains necessary for the production of critical products,
2. take into account regulatory timelines,
3. and with a review at the end of derogation periods to cover applications for which – despite best efforts – no alternatives could be found within the given timeframe.

General Comments: Merck KGaA consists of three business segments with activities in different industrial sectors. This submission provides information specifically about Merck Life Science KGaA (Merck LS). Separate submissions will be made by our corporate organisation, our Electronics and Healthcare sectors regarding their operations.
Merck Life Science provides our customers with materials, equipment, and knowledge that are critical and essential for the European health systems, scientific progress, innovation in drug and vaccine discovery, development, and production as well as many other important applications in life sciences.
We supply the pharmaceutical and medical device industry, and we have a crucial role in Scientific Research and Development. Our products serve many uses and applications that are not covered by proposed exemptions that may apply to parts of these sectors.
We note with concern that the information submitted during the calls for evidence is not reflected in the proposed restriction and the entirety of the fine chemicals and life science manufacturing sector have been omitted from impact assessment.
We welcome the possibility to respond to the public consultation on the restriction proposal for PFAS in the hope that this omission can be addressed.
We ask that derogations are clarified when it comes to uses of polymeric PFAS in the chemical industry, especially in Life Sciences. This sector is a key part of the EU supply chain for pharmaceutical, medical device and biotech production, and provides essential and strategic technologies in the EU regarding EU innovation and technology to address both current and future health and sustainability challenges.
The proposal does not allow sufficient time to substitute PFAS without compromising supply chains for this critical industry. In highly regulated areas such as pharmaceuticals, medical devices, and  diagnostics , changes to production processes performed under GxP requirements must be validated, qualified and in some cases also approved by authorities. These steps require significant time and may be subject to multiple iterations. We must avoid transitions to PFAS-free alternatives that lead to shortages or disruptions of supplies for critical pharmaceuticals and life-saving therapies. Therefore, we ask that the proposed derogations are revised to avoid negative societal impacts and if necessary also reviewed well ahead of their expiry, in case substitution activity for essential uses has been unsuccessful.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Table 9 refers only to derogated areas. The chemical industry and its life science sector have been omitted from consideration in the Annex XV report and information was provided by Merck Life Science during the calls of evidence. An updated form of this information is provided again in the confidential attachment alongside some preliminary SEA information.  Merck and other chemical manufacturers currently rely on fluoropolymer components in chemical reactors (liners, seals, gaskets, cabling and sensors, lubricants etc). Replacing these throughout all chemical manufacturing infrastructure will be extremely complicated and not feasible in a short period of time. We refer to details submitted by Merck Electronics showing how PFAS containing materials are used in the production environment, including in Merck Life Science operations. Table 9 does identify some uses with potential relevance: Industrial food and feed production, medical devices; diagnostic laboratory testing, membranes used in venting of medical devices. In addition to the uses and sub-uses above, PFAS are used in medical devices (including but not limited to venting membranes), diagnostic devices for quality control in production processes, packaging of substances and mixtures, reagents for manufacture of fine chemicals, pharmaceuticals, plant protection products, biocides etc. Our comments focus on various industrial filtration and purification devices (as membranes and other components), and process equipment such as reactor liners used in bioprocessing. Our answer to Question 6 on missing uses provides details of the uses relevant to Merck Life Science and our customers.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: b) The solutions provided by Merck Life Science are used in laboratories and chemical manufacturing plants (especially in pharmaceutical and biotechnological environments). We do not supply consumer markets. Collection of low volumes of PFAS containing polymeric industrial waste from the chemical sector is well managed (A.3.18.2.1 of the proposal) and therefore the benefit from the proposed restriction is likely to be limited and certainly disproportionate to the impact on customers of Merck Life Science (shown in confidential attachment).

5. Proposed derogations: The entries describing the various derogations are not clear. We have provided tonnage information regarding relevant applications of Merck Life Science products in the confidential attachment. These uses are downstream of PFAS substance or polymer manufacturing. It should also be noted that these entries reflect uses in chemical manufacturing (fine chemical, pharmaceutical, etc) and so typically have well defined end-of-life due to contamination with other chemical and biological materials during our customers’ processes.

6. Missing uses: These comments concern the use of fluoropolymers at Merck Life Science: 1. Using fluoropolymers as raw materials for the production of articles used in the development and production of critical therapies, general drug production, monoclonal antibodies, vaccines and other biotech products. 2. PFAS contained in the equipment used for manufacture of products used in any area of pharmaceuticals, medical devices, biotechnology and laboratory activities. Merck LS is both a user of PFAS containing industrial equipment and a manufacturer of some types of equipment. We are currently collecting information from other products and uses of PFAS that will be submitted later in the public consultation. The two main fluoropolymers used by Merck LS are PVDF and PTFE.  Our fluoropolymer suppliers have already moved away from the use of fluorosurfactants in the manufacture of the PVDF and PTFE resins.  Table A.1 of the proposal shows that impacts on Chemical Industry has not been considered despite being identified in the Annex (A.3.2.1.1) . The chemical industry underpins the supply chain to medical products, plant protection products and biocides, laboratory equipment and filtration, therefore the impact of the restriction proposal underestimates the impact on society through loss of these uses.  Our uses of PFAS, especially the use of fluoropolymers such as PVDF and PTFE, are critical for the European health systems, in drug and vaccine development and production securing the progress achieved by scientific research and development as well as other important fields in life sciences, hereby enabling innovation for a better life for European citizens.  We provide filter devices that remove microbial impurities or viral contaminants from production of biopharmaceuticals (e.g. vaccines). Fluoropolymers are used to produce membranes and in other components of the filter units, e.g. housing. The manufacture of (bio)pharmaceuticals appears to be missing derogations or is not clearly included in the proposed entries. As a consequence, we consider the proposed restriction to significantly underestimate the impact on society and we ask that this is included as a consideration of any restriction to be proposed in future. Regarding question (b), the high variety of applications in the Life Science sector and the wide scope of substances and materials proposed for restriction makes it impossible to concisely describe the key functionalities provided by PFAS in all these different applications. The membrane or device that is used in an application should always be considered to be a part of a solution. Combined Comments:
General Comments: Merit Medical is a leading manufacturer and marketer of proprietary disposable medical devices used in interventional, diagnostic, and therapeutic procedures, particularly in cardiology, radiology, oncology, critical care, and endoscopy. Merit has made it a priority to understand customers, innovate, and deliver life-changing products and services.
We support the concepts and objectives of REACH to contribute to human health and the environment. We would like to express the gratitude of having the opportunity of stating our opinion to the proposed restriction on Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFASs).
PFAS are critical for the European health systems, in production and development of medical devices. As a result, they are critical to the provision of life-saving devices and devices which improve patient's quality of life within the EU. Merit products are used by thousands of European doctors and nurses in the medical device industry. This makes the availability of medical devices in the EU more independent from global supply chains and hereby increases our resilience and preparedness for the next public health emergency. Even if a more sustainable alternative with the same properties will be found, substituting a material or substance from these uses often takes several years, due to technical development, testing and regulatory approvals. This may not be economically viable for some key products.
While we see the need to regulate critical substances, such as some low molecular weight PFAS that are known or likely to be harmful, we believe that a broad and undifferentiated approach as used in the current proposal is not appropriate. In particular, the inclusion of fluoropolymers that are considered polymers of low concern (PLC) according to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development’s (OECD) definition does not align with the overall goal of this proposed legislation.
Fluoropolymers are not considered ‘short-chain’ or ‘long-chain’ chemistries but rather polymers of low concern, meaning they are  stable in the environment and do not degrade. Fluoropolymers do not dissolve or contaminate water, cannot enter, or accumulate in a person’s bloodstream, and do not pose a significant risk to human health or the environment. Fluoropolymers are not bio-available, toxic, or even mobile. Therefore, fluoropolymers meet the OECD's criteria for ‘polymers of low concern’ as they do not present significant toxicity concerns and cannot degrade into other PFAS. (Henry, et al. Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management 14.3 (2018): 316-334.)
Fluoropolymers’ unique combination of properties set them apart from other chemistries and make them vital to the medical devices and interventional  procedures. Their properties make them durable, efficient, reliable, versatile, and fundamental to the products they enable. There are no known alternatives to fluoropolymers.
As an examples of the importance of PTFE properties in relation to implantable devices, Sartipy et.al (Vasc Endovascular Surg. 2015 Apr-May;49(3-4):79-83. doi: 10.1177/1538574415595209) have shown that when you compare polyester stent grafts with PTFE stent grafts for endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR), the PTFE coated devices perform better. Standard EVAR with polyester stent grafts appears to result in a trend toward a more pronounced inflammatory reaction than similar EVAR using PTFE and is associated with a longer in-hospital stay. This is just one example that highlights the importance of very safe material that is included in the proposed PFAS ban, where the ban will have a direct negative impact on patient health and safety within the EU.
The proposed legislation would regulate all PFAS as one large group of chemicals simply based on structural characteristics, ignoring the safety profiles, societal benefits, and existing regulatory frameworks governing such substances. Medical devices are already regulated through compliance to standards and guidance including;
• Medical Devices Regulation (EU) 2017/745
• ISO 10993-1: Biological evaluation of Medical Devices
Merit Medical are of the position that the expanded definition of PFAS being applied in the proposal is overly broad to enable effective, science-based assessment and regulation. PFAS can be separated into distinct classes for regulatory assessment using established scientific standards, including physicochemical properties and exposure conditions.
Consideration should be given to a more targeted approach, considering responsible manufacturing, including reducing air and water emissions of fluorinated organic compounds, and that manufacturers be more heavily regulated and monitored for emissions of known dangerous PFASs.
We respectively therefore request that medical devices are not included in this proposed ban.
Failing that. we therefore require smart derogations that:
1. include the complete value chains necessary for the production of medical devices,
2. take into account regulatory timelines,
3. and with a review at the end of derogation periods to cover applications for which – despite best efforts – no alternatives could be found within the given timeframe.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Section E.2.9 Medical Devices • Implantable medical devices • Tubes and catheters – Merit strongly argue that guidewires should also be included within this group of products, tubes and catheters are rarely used in medical procedures without a guidewire. Guidewires, which are mainly coated, are used in hundreds of thousands medical procedures each year. • Other coating applications

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: For the use of medical devices manufactured by Merit Medical, all PFAS would be in the form of a poly-fluorinated substance, either PTFE or FEP (Fluorinated   Ethylene Propylene). These are used in medical procedures and the use at this temperature range and purpose would not produce any emissions of PFAS. In the  poly-fluorinated form listed above, these meet the OECD criteria of PLC ( = polymer of low concern) are non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water soluble and non-mobile molecules and are judged to have no significant impact on the environment and humans. Looking at each sub-use individually -  Implantable medical devices:  Manufacture phase emission = no emission (we use semi-finished PTFE parts) Use phase emission = no emission (since the PTFE covered stent (implant) does not emit into the environment);  end-of-life phase = no emission (It either gets cremated with the patient or buried, depending on the type of funeral. As funerals have very high criteria regarding emissions into groundwater, it is impossible that ePTFE, which is not soluble in water, emits into the environment. Crematoria are highly regulated and fulfill respective requirements regarding filtration of flue gas.  Tubes and catheters:  are single-use-devices and are disposed via biohazard waste bins after being used for implanting devices such as stents. They are burned after usage in waste incineration plants, where PTFE is essentially converted to carbon dioxide and hydrogen fluoride, which is converted to non-toxic fluorspar in the filter systems. Manufacture phase emission = no emission (we use semi finished PTFE parts),  Use phase emission = no emission End-of-life phase = no emission .  Other coated devices: We use PTFE coating solutions to coat medical guidewires, which involves a solvent coating, drying and sintering process. Use and end of life phase would be similar to tubes and catheters stated above, i.e. no emissions.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Medical waste products are treated as hazardous waste and are destroyed at end of life by incineration. PTFE is burned after usage, where PTFE is essentially converted to carbon dioxide and hydrogen fluoride, which is converted to non-toxic fluorspar in the filter systems.  • Taylor et al. (2014) examined whether combustion of gasified fluorotelomer‐based polymer would emit PFOA at 1,000°C, in an oxidizing atmosphere, with a 2 s residence time to reflect municipal and medical waste incinerator conditions. No detectable quantities of PFOA were measured in the exhaust gas, and qualitative HF (Hydrogen Fluoride) emission suggested complete mineralization occurred. (Chemosphere, 110, 17-22. 10.1016/j.chemosphere.2014.02.037).  • Additionally, municipal incineration of PTFE using best available technologies (BAT) is not a significant source of the studied PFAS and should be considered an acceptable form of waste treatment. In appendix E2, an alternative was listed for guidewires but there was not sufficient data for evaluation. We agree we could not find any further data in the scientific literature or elsewhere to be able to assess this substance as a potential alternative.  Without PTFE coated guide wires, these types of surgeries would be more challenging for the physician, more painful for the patient with reduced level of successful outcome and would take longer resulting in more cost to the hospital. In some case, minimally invasive surgery may not be possible at all resulting in either no treatment or high-cost invasive interventional surgery, requiring anaesthesia. The socio-economic impact of on PTFE coated guidewires would be high. Additionally, if a ban for these products does transpire, a minimum derogation of 12 years would be required. Based on our past experiences, we estimate it would take at least 5-6 years to develop an alternative if possible. Then 2 years to incorporate in a manufacturing line, 2 years to develop into specific product family and another 2 years to complete registration in EU via MDR.

8. Other identified uses: Section E.2.9 lists sub uses for medical devices. One such use listed is for “Tubes and catheters.”  Merit Medical are of the position that this sub-use should be expanded to include medical guidewires. Guidewires are used to allow placement of catheters and tubes into the vasculature of the body and the use of them is critical to allow the use of catheters. Based on this critical interdependence, the two device types should be listed together in the sub-use.

General Comments: Microfluidics is an innovating and powerful technology which consists in the manipulation and analysis of small volumes of liquid (10-6 to 10-12 litres) through the use of devices, systems or structures with micro-meter sized channels[1]. This technology emerged at the beginning of the 1980s, and is now used in many fields of research for transformative industrial applications in health, diagnostics and personalized medicine, green chemistry, transformation of biomass, bio-prospection, etc [2-8]. Its market is today estimated at 30 billion USD and could reach 60 billion USD by 2030 [9,10].

One of the main driver for microfluidics at the industrial level is the biomedical field and the pressing needs to downsize and automatize at increasing rates biological assays. In the two last decades, microfluidic technologies have pushed the boundaries of molecular biology with ultra-high throughput methodologies for DNA analysis for diagnostics (e.g., polymerase chain reaction, high-throughput sequencing), and proteomics[11-13], for screening in immunology and drug development (antibody discovery, development of novel therapeutic solutions, enzymes, antibiotics…).
Droplet-based microfluidics is the manipulation of aqueous droplets used as microreactor in oil. It is a Key Enabling Technology at the origin of an on-going breakthrough in the development of new therapeutic solutions for many pathologies with very early in vitro cancer diagnostics and monitoring, leaning towards personalized therapy and medicine[14-16].

Europe has a leading role in these crucial developments and represents almost half of the market with many worldwide collaborations, well-known and expert researchers and many highly innovative companies in the field. This puts Europe in a leading position in terms of advanced technology, cancer research, and medical device industrialisation[17].

However, to reach the high performance wanted for all of these in vitro diagnostics, this technology requires the use of chemical products based on fluorine chemistry. This chemistry ensures the biocompatibility needed for the manipulation of biological elements, for example oxygen supply for cell incubation. It is at the centre of  platforms and methodologies usable to miniaturize and automatize assays, far beyond what is achievable with other chemicals[18].

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Mitsui Chemicals manufactures and sells a product called "Pellicle," which is used in the semiconductor manufacturing process. Pellicles are produced outside of Europe and are distributed globally. In the European region, it is sold through the European sales office (Mitsui Chemicals Europe GmbH). Pellicle is an assembled product, which contains fluorinated compounds A, B and C that fall under the PFAS definition. Below, we will explain the importance of Pellicles in semiconductor manufacturing and the necessity of the fluorinated compounds comprising Pellicles.
The Pellicle and its cross section are shown at Figure1 in Section IV. Pellicles are attached to photomasks (also known as reticles) used in the lithography process of semiconductor manufacturing, serving as a dust cover (Ref. Figure2 in Section IV). On the photomask, intricate and complex electronic circuit patterns are drawn. These patterns are accurately reduced and projected onto a silicon wafer, and by exposing the wafer to this pattern through a photolithography process, various electronic circuit diagrams underlying different electronic functions are delineated on the silicon wafer.
The lithography process is one of front processes in semiconductor manufacturing. For more details, please refer to Figure 3 in Section IV. Particles on the photomask can cause circuit failure because they are projected onto the silicon wafer just like circuit patterns. Pellicles prevent contaminants on the photomask, thereby preventing circuit failure caused by particles. Particles on the Pellicle membrane surface do not project onto the silicon wafer, thus avoiding circuit failure. (Ref. Figure4 in Section IV)
The schematic diagrams of semiconductor circuits have been continually miniaturized over the years, contributing to the downsizing of high-performance electronic products and supporting the convenience of modern society. The ongoing miniaturization of electronic circuit diagrams further emphasizes the necessity of Pellicle. If Pellicles were not to be able to use by the restriction, it is conceivable that it could lead to a decrease in the quality of semiconductor chips and an increase in defect rates. The rise in defect rates across semiconductor factories worldwide could reduce the productivity of semiconductor production and potentially impact the supply of semiconductors to the global market.
According to research firm, the global semiconductor market continues to grow annually, now approaching $500 billion (Ref. Figure5 in Section V). The decrease in semiconductor productivity due to the absence of Pellicle is expected to result in losses equivalent to a portion of this market size.
As previously mentioned, in the advanced field of semiconductor manufacturing, a shorter wavelength ultraviolet light at 193nm is used in the lithography process to create finer circuit patterns. The performance required of the Pellicle film goes beyond being a dust cover to prevent particle attachment on the photomask. It also needs to have high transparency to this ultraviolet light and exhibit resistance to light degradation. Due to the high energy of the 193nm exposure wavelength, conventional resin films tend to decompose and lack light resistance. Film A has a structure which robust C-F bonds are distributed in whole molecule and is an amorphous solid. This film can transmit nearly 100% (over 99%) of the 193nm light and remains stable without decomposing. These characteristics are achievable only with a chemical structure featuring stable C-F bonds (perfluoro structure, PFAS). Consequently, an alternative material exclude PFAS compounds for Pellicle film has not yet been identified.  This film is adhered to a metal frame to function as a Pellicle, necessitating the presence of an adhesive. Materials with perfluoro structures do not mix or bond with almost any substances other than fluorinated compounds. Even the adhesive that bonds with the film (Adhesive B) is PFAS compounds, and as of now, non-PFAS alternatives for this adhesive have not been found. Additionally, to assemble a Pellicle with these materials, films and adhesives must be handled as a liquid. To dissolve them effectively, a solvent is necessary, but any solvents other than fluorinated compounds cannot effectively dissolve fluorinated compounds. Therefore, Solvent C should be also a PFAS compound, and non-PFAS alternative solvents have not yet been discovered. Solvent C is removed through heating during the Pellicle manufacturing process. Trace amounts can remain in the Pellicle product.
In conclusion, the materials essential for constructing Pellicles in the advanced field include PFAS-based film A, adhesive B, and solvent C. Non-PFAS alternatives for these components have not yet been identified. If a film made from non-PFAS materials were used in the 193nm exposure process, the decomposition of the film could lead to contamination on the photomask due to the generated decomposition products, resulting in decreased transparency and significantly reduced productivity, leading to substantial losses.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Manufacture stage Because Pellicles are produced outside of Europe, the emission of PFAS at the manufacture stage is zero in Europe. General Comments: Mobile cranes are strongly affected by potential PFAS restrictions. Both components and lubricants are affected. Three examples where a ban would have a major impact are given:
These types of cranes, which are needed to erect wind turbines, for example, require a large number of hydraulic cylinders. PFAS seals and guide elements are used in these hydraulic cylinders to create the lowest possible and defined friction conditions. This low friction is of utmost importance for safe operation, so that the load weighing can be determined via the oil pressure of the hydraulic cylinder. Similarly, jerk- and shock-free movements of the cylinders and thus of the crane components are of paramount importance for safe crane operation. Alternatives to PFAS seals and guide elements are not known.
The hydraulic fluids also impacts the friction behaviour. PFAS is used in the fluids to guarantee the safe operation of the hydraulic system.
In order to enable the aforementioned jolt- and backlash-free operation, the components that are moved by the hydraulic cylinders must be lubricated. Here, too, PFAS-containing lubricants have proved to be without alternative.

Often some things do not seem important but they are and the missing property comes up in the lifetime of the product. Combined Comments:
General Comments: Nanoimprint lithography is an advanced process used in the manufacture of semiconductors, microlenses, etc.

Nanoimprint lithography　is capable of molding fine features of 20-1000 nm using fine-feature molds .

the size of the molded object obtained by nanoimprint lithography is 20-1000 nm, the accuracy of the molded object and mold surface is important . On the other hand, since it has a fine shape, there is a problem that the molded product is easily broken when released from the mold.

In order to improve the surface precision and yield (=productivity), it is necessary to use a release agent on the surface of the mold.

An oil-based mold release agent such as silicone oil cannot be used for this purpose because the release agent component is transferred to the molded product.

A dry release agent containing solid particles will not transfer to the molding. However, dry release agents cannot be used in this method because the film thickness of the release agent itself is 1 micron or more.

Perfluoroether-based mold release agents are chemically bonded to the surface of the mold, so there is no transfer to the molded product, and since the film thickness is about 10 nm, nm-size mold shapes can be faithfully reproduced .

is the only mold release agent that can be used in this process , and there is no substitute material.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: release agent for nanoimprint lithography

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: There are no emissions during manufacturing or use. When the mold is discarded, it seems that it adheres to the mold and is discarded. However, if recycled, it is assumed that there will be no PFAS emissions. Almost all molds are recycled, so it is assumed that PFAS emissions are zero.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: At high temperatures when recycling molds, it is believed to all decompose to HF.

5. Proposed derogations: Past performance is estimated to be less than 10 tons per year.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Org. name: French Federation of mechanical engineering industries
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Note: Corrigendum to the contribution submitted on July 14

The French Federation of mechanical engineering industries has conducted several studies with our sectoral technical centre and our members to assess the PFAS used in our sector and the availability of suitable alternatives. Related reports will be attached to this contribution as soon as available. We would like to make the following comments on the restriction report:

- Some of the proposed derogations have a particularly short transition period, which seems difficult to achieve given the alternatives available.
- The restriction report does not propose derogation for many uses of PFAS in our sector for which no alternative solution is available at this stage (for example for sealing applications, mechanical components in friction applications, fluorinated gases and cookware described in section 6 to 8 below)
- The F-gas regulation provides for the phasing out of certain fluorinated gases with a high global warming potential (GWP) and the replacement by alternatives with a lower GWP. The definition adopted for PFAS applies in particular to HFOs and HFCs, which are the alternative to certain fluorinated gases that are banned or about to be banned under the F-gas regulation. The only known alternatives are CO2 and propane, which are either technically impossible to use in installations or create significant risks for installations and users (higher pressure or flammability).
- Mechanical equipment are characterized by a long service life, widespread practice of maintenance or repair operations and a high capacity for being re-used or re-purposed. In addition, our sector is subject to increasing demands and requirements regarding the incorporation of recycled materials, reparability, the availability of spare parts and remanufacturing. The restriction report does not include a derogation allowing the reuse or continued use of products that were put on the market before it came into force, or the incorporation of recycled materials from these products. By way of example of such derogation in other regulation, the RoHS directive introduced an additional implementation period of 10 years for spare parts intended for the repair, re-use, upgrading of functionalities or reinforcement of the capacity of equipment.

For all these reasons, we recommend the inclusion of exemptions for the following uses of PFAS :
- A general derogation for spare parts or components necessary for the repair, re-use or upgrading of functionalities of products placed on the market before the entry into force of this restriction or covered by a derogation.
- A derogation for the presence of PFAS in recycled materials, in particular for products that do not present a risk of releasing PFAS into the environment during the use phase.
- A derogation for all fluoropolymers for which no suitable alternative solution is available.
- A derogation for the presence and use of Hydrofluoroolefins (HFO) and Hydrofluorocarbure (HFC) in refrigerants used for professional food refrigeration applications and non-road mobile machinery.
- 12 years transition period for the presence of PFAS cookware and bakeware and the exclusion of fluoropolymers from the scope of the restriction for these products including professional and non-professional ones.
- Adequate transition period for professional products, in order to take account of the duration of the complete product re-design processes that could be made necessary by the application of this restriction.
- In addition, we consider it is necessary to introduce a review mechanism for the derogations that will be granted, so that they can be extended when no suitable alternative solution has been made available by the end of the derogation period.

The restriction proposal should take into consideration the difference in risk and exposure be-tween polymeric and non-polymeric PFAS and the absence of environmental risk from various product categories during production and end of life phase, for the following reasons:

As accounted for by the restriction dossier, there are critical differences between polymerized and non-polymerized PFAS. Unlike non-polymeric PFAS, which are mobile, can bioaccumulate, and can have toxicity concerns, fluoropolymers have not been demonstrated to have negative health concerns and are a material of choice for various applications, notably necessary for the ecological transition and the decarbonization of economic activities.
The production of products containing fluoropolymer does not result in significant PFAS emis-sions into the environment, due to the absence of exposure and release of substances into the environment, the limited content of non-polymeric PFAS in raw materials and effective envi-ronmental management measures where appropriate. Additionally, non-fluorinated polymeri-sation aid technologies have the potential to greatly reduce the use of non-polymeric PFAS in the production process. As described below, the end-of-life phase of products containing PFAS in our sector is an unlikely source of PFAS emissions from fluoropolymers.

A REACH restriction requires to demonstrate an “unacceptable risk”. According to available da-ta, fluoropolymers do meet the standard. The OECD classifies polymers with “insignificant en-vironmental and human health impacts” as polymers of low concern and
fluoropolymers have been found to meet all the OECD characteristics of polymers of low con-cern, based on their stability, lack of bioavailability, lack of bioaccumula-tion, and general ab-sence of observed ill effects (cf. Henry, Barbara J, Joseph P Carlin, Jon A Hammerschmidt, Rob-ert C Buck, L William Buxton, Heidelore Fiedler, Jennifer Seed, and Oscar Hernandez. 2018. “A Critical Review of the Application of Polymer of Low Concern and Regulatory Criteria to Fluor-opolymers.” Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management 14 (3): 316–34. https://doi.org/10.1002/ieam.4035). PTFE is not soluble in water (and other common solvents) and is not mobile in the environment (cf. Korzeniowski, Stephen H., Robert C. Buck, Robin M. Newkold, Ahmed El kassmi, Evan Laganis, Yasuhiko Matsuoka, Bertrand Dinelli, et al. 2022. “A Critical Review of the Application of Polymer of Low Concern Regulatory Criteria to Fluoropol-ymers II: Fluoroplastics and Fluoroelastomers.” Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management, August. https://doi.org/10.1002/ieam.4646).

In addition, studies have consistently shown that fluoropolymers do not pose a risk to human health, largely due to their inertness, insolubility, and lack of reactive functional groups. A 2022 study by Lee et al. shows that fluoropolymers such as PTFE are safe when ingested (Cf. Lee, Sijoon, Kyung-Ku Kang, Soo-Eun Sung, Joo-Hee Choi, Minkyoung Sung, Keum-Yong Seong, Jian Lee, Subin Kang, Seong Yun Yang, Sunjong Lee, Kyeong-Ryoon Lee, Min-Soo Seo, and KilSoo Kim. 2022. "In Vivo Toxicity and Pharmacokinetics of Polytetrafluoroethylene Microplas-tics in ICR Mice" Polymers 14, no. 11: 2220. https://doi.org/10.3390/polym14112220). The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) has repeatedly investigated the carcino-genicity and toxicity of PTFE, finding it has no toxicological impact, and cannot be classified ac-cording to its carcinogenicity (cf. International Agency for Research on Cancer. 1987. “IARC Monographs on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans, Suppl 7, Overall Evaluations of Carcinogenicity: An Updating of IARC Monographs”, Volumes 1 to 42.).

Even if there are negative impacts on the environment and human health from some chemicals within the wide PFAS family, a group approach of PFAS without any distinction between the many different types, which have varied properties and risk levels, would not be proportionate. Anderson et al presented a review of approaches to grouping PFAS based on factors such as toxicity. Most of the experts in the panel agreed that not all PFAS should be grouped together, that persistence alone is not sufficient for grouping PFAS for the purposes of assessing human health risk, that subgroups are appropriate, and that the nature and definition of the subgroups can only be defined on a situation-dependent and case-bycase manner. No single grouping strategy was agreed on that would be sufficient for all regulatory or public health risk assess-ment purposes (cf. Anderson, J. K., R. W. Brecher, I. T. Cousins, J. DeWitt, H. Fiedler, K. Kannan, C. R. Kirman, et al. 2022. “Grouping of PFAS for Human Health Risk Assessment: Findings from an Independent Panel of Experts.” Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology 134 (October): https://doi.org/10.1016/j.yrtph.2022.105266).
The United Kingdom have also proposed Regulatory Management Options for PFAS and sug-gest a restriction excluding fluoropolymers: “The restriction(s) set out above need not apply to low hazard groups or low risk uses, for example: fluoroplastics or fluoroelastomers (low hazard groups) […]. These could be highlighted as derogations to any restriction proposal” (cf. 22 Health and Safety Executive. 2023. “Analysis of the most appropriate regulatory management options (RMOA)”. March 2023. https://www.hse.gov.uk/reach/assets/docs/pfas-rmoa.pdf).

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Please find below the sectors and (sub-)uses to which our comment applies according to the sectors and (sub-)uses identified in the Annex XV restriction report (Table 9 & 2).  - Food contact materials and packaging: Consumer cookware, Industrial food and feed production. - Metal plating and manufacture of metal products: Hard chrome plating, Decorative plating with chrome, plating on plastics and plating with metals other than chrome (use as a surfactant for worker protection and emission reduction). - Applications of fluorinated gases: Refrigeration and non-road mobile machinery. - Medical devices. - Transport (aeronautical, automotive, railway, space…): Body-, hull- and fuselage construction (blades, engine, nacelle, landing gear, braking, clutch, attachment) , Sealing and gaskets applications, Combustion engine systems, Coating and finishings. - Energy sector: Photovoltaic cells, Wind energy, Nuclear power plant, Green Hydrogen use deployment: Membranes, equipment (pumps, valves, gaskets and sealing systems, bearings, etc.). - Construction products: Sealings, taps and sanitary fittings, pumps, valves, etc.  - Lubricants: Low viscosity lubricants, Solid/dry-film lubrication, Release agents, Greases. - Petroleum and mining: Lining of piping, machinery used by this sector.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: We emphasize that supply chains of complex products include various operators and that the entire manufacturing process for products and components involves multiple stages. The use of PFAS, including their integration into components, takes place in a limited number of these stages. Adequate management of the risks posed by PFAS to human health and the environ-ment could be achieved effectively through a combination of measures rather than a general ban of the use of PFAS. Such combination of measures would minimise the associated socio-economic impacts. The use of non-fluorinated polymerisation aid (NFPA) technologies to pro-duce fluoropolymers without the use of fluorinated polymerisation aids have the potential to greatly reduce the use of non-polymeric PFAS in the production process, effectively addressing any concerns about the release of PFAS into the environment during the manufacturing stage. NFPA technology already exists, but to the best of our knowledge is not generally available on the market and would not enable all industrial sectors to switch to this technology within the timeframe set out in the restriction report. Releases from production sites could be minimized by regulating industrial emissions, for example under the Industrial Emissions Directive (IED), 2010/75/EU. Additional measures on waste treatment of waste containing PFAS could also ad-dress the possibility of PFAS emissions.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Incineration, recycling and landfilling are all likely to adequately address the possibility of PFAS emissions, and consequently manufactured products containing PFAS unlikely to represent a risk to human health or the environment if proper waste management measures are put in place.   RIVM (Dutch National Institute for Public Health and the Environment) incineration review states that PTFE is stable at 260 °C without loss of mass (cf. J. Bakker | B. Bokkers | M. Broekman, RIVM report 2021-0143. https://rivm.openrepository.com/handle/10029/625409).   Guelfo et al also reiterate the inertness of PTFE and its lack of reactivity in the environment (cf. Guelfo, Jennifer L., Stephen Korzeniowski, Marc A. Mills, Janet Anderson, Richard H. Anderson, Jennifer A. Arblaster, Jason M. Conder, et al. 2021. “Environmental Sources, Chemistry, Fate, and Transport of Per‐ and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances: State of the Science, Key Knowledge Gaps, and Recommendations Presented at the August 2019 SETAC Focus Topic Meeting.” Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry 40 (12): 3234–60. https://doi.org/ 10.1002/etc.5182).   Fluoropolymers, including PTFE, are completely destroyed under specific incinerator operating conditions. Yamada et al. studied textiles and paper treated with fluorotelomers at temperatures of 1,000 °C and residual times of 2 seconds. They found that they will be destroyed and will not be a source of PFOA in the environment (cf. Yamada, Takahiro, Philip H. Taylor, Robert C. Buck, Mary A. Kaiser, and Robert J. Giraud. 2005. “Thermal Degradation of Fluorotelomer Treated Articles and Related Materials.” Chemosphere 61 (7): 974–84. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chemosphere.2005.03.025). According to a 2019 study from the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, municipal incineration of PTFE did not result in significant generation of studied PFAS at temperatures between 870 and 1 020 °C. Instead, the PFAS degraded mainly into hydrofluoric acid and carbon dioxide (cf. Aleksandrov, Krasimir, Hans-Joachim Gehrmann, Manuela Hauser, Hartmut Mätzing, Daniel Pigeon, Dieter Stapf, and Manuela Wexler. 2019. “Waste Incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to Evaluate Potential Formation of Per- and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) in Flue Gas.” Chemosphere 226 (July): 898–906. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chemosphere.2019.03.191). According to a 2021 report by the Dutch RIVM, PTFE is reduced to a fully mineralized state after 2 seconds of incineration at 850 °C. General Comments: Nozzles and atomizers made of PFAS polymers (PTFE and PVDF) have a broad scope of application across diverse industries and processes, including petrochemicals, chemical manufacturing, power generation, electronics, agriculture and more. These polymers are preferred for their temperature resistance, chemical inertness, and ability to withstand harsh environments. Alternative materials lack the same combination of advantageous properties as PFAS polymers.

Lechler GmbH, based in Metzingen, Germany, is a family-owned business that specializes in developing and producing precision nozzles, nozzle systems, and droplet separators made from a wide range of materials. The company is a market leader in Germany and Europe and is considered one of the most important players in the global atomization technology market. As of the year 2021, the Lechler Group of Companies employs approximately 785 people worldwide, with around 380 at Lechler GmbH's headquarters in Metzingen. The Lechler group's annual turnover amounts to 130 million euros.
The company's atomization technology products find applications in a broad scope of application across diverse industries and processes, in various industries, including petrochemicals, power generation, agriculture, metallurgy, chemical industry,  pharmaceuticals, electronics, food and beverage, and more. Since many of these applications involve the use of chemicals, these nozzles must be made from chemically resistant and thermally tolerant materials. Lechler uses the fluorpolymers PTFE and PVDF, depending on the customer's requirements and specific application.

If fluoropolymers could no longer be used as nozzle material, it would significantly impact a large number of industries and applications where nozzles are a core process component.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The assignment to one of the listed sectors is not possible because nozzles and atomizers of any kind and shape are not included. The mentioned sectors do not fit to the business sector of Lechler GmbH. Nozzles and atomizers cannot be assigned to any of the existing categories. In our opinion, the list of predefined categories is incomplete and insufficient. The main application markets for nozzles and atomizers include, but are not limited to, the following areas. : - Petrochemicals and Refineries: In the processing of crude oil and petroleum products, spray nozzles are used for applications such as cooling towers, desulfurization, and chemical injection. - Chemical Manufacturing: Spray nozzles are used in chemical processing for mixing, coating, and reacting chemicals. They are also employed in spray drying processes. - Steel and Metal Manufacturing: Spray nozzles are used for cooling, quenching, and lubrication in steel mills and metal manufacturing facilities. - Power Generation: In power plants, spray nozzles are used for cooling processes, such as in cooling towers and gas turbine inlet air cooling. - Aerospace and Aviation: In aerospace industries, spray nozzles are used for coating, cleaning, and surface treatment applications. - Electronics: as in aerospace and aviation, spray nozzles are used for coating, cleaning and surface treatment in crucial processes. - Glass Manufacturing: Spray nozzles are employed in glassmaking processes, including cooling and tempering glass products. - Food Processing and beverages: In food manufacturing, spray nozzles are used for applications like coating, cleaning, and flavoring. - Environmental Control: Spray nozzles are used in environmental control processes such as air pollution control systems and gas scrubbing. - Automotive and Transportation: Spray nozzles are used in car washes, surface treatment, and painting processes in the automotive industry. - Pharmaceutical and Biotechnology: Spray nozzles are used for coating tablets, encapsulation, and spray drying in pharmaceutical manufacturing. - Agriculure: Spray nozzles are used to apply plant protective chemicals and pesticides.  In all of the above sectors (and even more) we can find applications where spray nozzles must perform in high-temperature and/or chemical aggressive environments, making PTFE and PVDF the main choice. The key advantages of PTFE are temperature resistance, chemical inertness, non-stick properties, low friction coefficient, electrical insulation, UV and weather resistance, biocompatibility making it suitable for medical and pharmaceutical applications, dimensional stability over a wide temperature range as well as easy fabrication. Due to these advantageous properties and their unique combination, Fluorpolymers (PVDF and PTFE) are commonly used in nozzles that need to be capable of withstanding high temperatures and harsh chemical environments.

5. Proposed derogations: Raw material usage for spray nozzle production  PTFE: 2.300 kg in 2022 for machining PVDF: 19.000 kg in 2022 for machining and moulding In order to provide data on what proportion by weight remains in the actual end product, further internal investigations are necessary.

6. Missing uses: Raw material usage for spray nozzle production  PTFE: 2.300 kg in 2022 for machining PVDF: 19.000 kg in 2022 for machining and moulding In order to provide data on what proportion by weight remains in the actual end product, further internal investigations are necessary.   Nozzles play a crucial role in various chemical processes and are commonly used for fluid handling and dispersion. These devices are designed to control the flow and direction of liquids, gases, or mixtures within the chemical processing industry. The use of nozzles can significantly impact process efficiency, reaction rates, and product quality. Here are some common applications of nozzles in chemical processes: Mixing and Blending: Nozzles are used to introduce reactants or chemicals into a reaction vessel, ensuring thorough mixing and blending. They can create turbulent flow or introduce jets to enhance the contact between different substances, promoting faster and more efficient reactions. Spray Drying: In spray drying processes, liquid materials are atomized into fine droplets using nozzles. These droplets are then exposed to hot air, allowing rapid evaporation of the solvent and converting the liquid into dry particles. Spray drying is widely used to produce powdered products such as detergents, food additives, and pharmaceuticals. Gas Scrubbing and Absorption: Nozzles are used in gas scrubbing systems to spray liquid solutions or solvents into gas streams. This allows the absorption of gaseous pollutants or contaminants by the liquid phase, resulting in cleaner emissions and safer air quality. Coating and Surface Treatment: Nozzles are employed in coating processes to apply thin films of liquids onto surfaces. Whether it's painting, electroplating, or applying protective coatings, the controlled spray pattern of nozzles ensures even distribution and minimizes wastage. Cooling and Quenching: Nozzles are employed to spray cooling liquids, such as water or coolant, to control the temperature of chemical reactions or to quench hot materials, preventing damage or thermal shock. Foam Generation: Nozzles can be designed to generate foam, which is utilized in various chemical applications, including fire suppression, flotation processes, and as a medium for separation techniques. The choice of nozzle type, size, and material depends on the specific application, the properties of the fluids involved, and the desired process outcomes. Proper selection and maintenance of nozzles are essential to ensure efficient and safe chemical processes. Additionally, advancements in nozzle technology continue to offer innovative solutions for improved performance and reduced environmental impact in chemical processing industries.  Nozzles are widely used in electronic manufacturing processes, particularly in the assembly of printed circuit boards (PCBs) and electronic components. The precise and controlled dispensing of materials is critical in electronics manufacturing to ensure high-quality and reliable electronic products. Here are some common applications of nozzles in electronic manufacturing: Solder Paste Dispensing: Solder paste is a crucial material used to attach electronic components to PCBs during the surface mount technology (SMT) assembly process. Nozzles are used in solder paste dispensing machines to accurately and uniformly deposit the solder paste onto the designated pads on the PCB. Proper solder paste deposition is essential to achieving good solder joints and reliable connections between components and the board. Adhesive Dispensing: Various adhesives, such as epoxy or UV-curable adhesives, are used in electronic assembly to bond components or seal sensitive areas. Nozzles are employed in adhesive dispensing equipment to apply precise amounts of adhesive onto specific locations with consistent accuracy. Component Placement: Nozzles are used in pick-and-place machines to handle and accurately position electronic components onto PCBs. These machines utilize specialized nozzles designed to grip and hold components of different shapes and sizes, ensuring precise placement on the board. Flux Application: Flux is used to clean metal surfaces and facilitate soldering during the reflow process. Nozzles are used to apply flux selectively to specific areas, ensuring proper solder wetting and minimizing soldering defects. Underfill Dispensing: Underfill is a specialized adhesive used to reinforce the mechanical integrity of semiconductor packages by filling the gap between the chip and the substrate. Nozzles are used to dispense underfill material with high precision, preventing voids and ensuring optimal performance of the electronic component. Conformal Coating: In some applications, electronic components and PCBs require a protective conformal coating to guard against moisture, dust, and other environmental factors. Nozzles are used in conformal coating machines to apply a uniform and controlled layer of the coating material. Cleaning and Rinsing: Nozzles are employed in cleaning processes to spray cleaning agents or rinse fluids onto PCBs or electronic components to remove residues, contaminants, or flux residues after soldering. The use of nozzles in electronic manufacturing is essential to achieving consistent and high-quality results in mass production. The automation and precision provided by nozzle-based dispensing systems contribute to increased efficiency, reduced waste, and improved product reliability in the electronics industry. Continuous advancements in nozzle technology further enhance manufacturing processes, allowing for greater flexibility and adaptability in response to evolving electronic designs and requirements.  Nozzles play a crucial role in modern agriculture by facilitating the precise application of pesticides, herbicides, and fertilizers, which, in turn, optimizes crop management, enhances efficiency, and reduces environmental impact. Two important technologies that have revolutionized nozzle performance in agriculture are Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) and the use of PFAS polymer materials. Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) technology allows for more precise control of nozzle flow rates by pulsing the flow instead of relying solely on pressure changes. This method enables more accurate application rates, particularly when operating at varying speeds or in irregularly shaped fields. By using PWM, farmers can apply chemicals more efficiently and target specific areas, reducing waste and potential environmental harm. PFAS Polymer Materials: Nozzles used in modern agriculture are often made of durable materials such as PFAS (Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances) polymer materials, including PTFE (Polytetrafluoroethylene) and PVDF (Polyvinylidene Fluoride). These materials are designed to withstand the harsh chemicals used in agricultural operations and maintain consistent performance over time. The chemical inertness of PFAS polymers ensures that the nozzles remain unaffected by the substances they deliver, thus preventing degradation and prolonging their lifespan. By using nozzles made of PFAS polymer materials, farmers can maintain efficient and accurate application of chemicals, ultimately reducing the overall environmental impact of agricultural practices. Precise application allows for the right amount of chemicals to be delivered in the right places, minimizing chemical runoff and leaching. This preservation of soil health and water quality is crucial for sustainable agriculture and environmental protection.   2.400 customers have ordered nozzles or parts containing PFAS in 2022. We expect all of them affected, but the number of processes oder end-customers affected can only be guessed.  At first glance, PEEK could be considered as an alternative to PVDF and PTFE. But at a closer look, PEEK has many disadvantages. Thermal Conductivity: PEEK has higher thermal conductivity compared to PTFE. While this can be an advantage in certain applications, it can also be a disadvantage in situations where low thermal conductivity is required. Wear Resistance: PEEK has good wear resistance but may not be as superior in this regard as PTFE, which has excellent low-friction and anti-wear properties. In some high-wear applications, PTFE might be a more suitable choice. Chemical Resistance: While PEEK has good chemical resistance, it may not be as chemically inert as PTFE. PTFE is known for its exceptional resistance to a broader range of chemicals and solvents. PTFE is also suitable for use with strong mineral acids such as concentrated sulphuric acid, concentrated nitric acid and hydrofluoric acid.  Molding Complexity: PEEK can be more challenging to process and mold compared to PTFE. The molding of PEEK parts requires more precise control of temperature and pressure, which can add to manufacturing complexity. Water Absorption: PEEK has a higher water absorption rate than PTFE. This can be a concern in certain applications where moisture absorption can affect the material's properties. Surface Finish: Achieving a smooth and high-quality surface finish on PEEK parts can be more difficult compared to PTFE, which has excellent release properties and non-stick characteristics. Electrical Insulation: While both PEEK and PTFE are good electrical insulators, PTFE has slightly better electrical properties, making it more suitable for certain electrical and electronic applications. FDA Approval: PEEK may not have as widespread approval from regulatory bodies like the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in food contact applications compared to PTFE. Wear Resistance: While PEEK has good wear resistance, PVDF is known for its excellent wear and abrasion resistance. In high-wear applications, PVDF might be a more suitable choice. Chemical Resistance: PVDF offers excellent chemical resistance, but PEEK may not be as chemically inert as PVDF. PVDF is highly resistant to a wide range of aggressive chemicals and solvents. Water Absorption: PEEK has a higher water absorption rate than PVDF. In applications where moisture absorption can affect the material's properties which is always the case with spray nozzles, PVDF is preferred. Electrical Properties: PVDF is known for its excellent electrical properties, including high dielectric strength and low dielectric constant. It is widely used in electrical and electronic applications.  Other alternatives, such as UHMWPE, are not feasible simply because of their low temperature resistance. Alternatives to the PFAS polymer materials are currently not known due to the required properties as well as their combination. Many applications in the food sector, where materials actually come into contact with food, require special approvals, such as those provided by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA).  Lechler GmbH currently makes a good part of its total turnover with nozzles made of PFAS polymers, calculated across all the markets and sectors described above.  For other materials to be used in the future, adjustments to all injection moulds used would be necessary due to different shrinkage properties. In total, going to other materials would mean adjustment and redesign of injection moulds and cores. This alone would result in costs of approx. 9 million €. This does not take into account any internal expenses (design, adjustments, re-sampling, drawing changes, documentation, production testing and test samples, adjustment of test plans, injection moulding parameters, etc.). In addition, the revision, redesign and new procurement of moulds and cores would take an rough estimate of more than 10 years. All in all, the entrepreneurial sense of this effort must be seriously questioned. Loss of annual value of sales, profit, and increased effort endangeres approx. 30 jobs. Loss in efficiency leads to lower nozzle performance and therefore lower product quality in customers processes. The absence of nozzles made of appropriate material would have devastating effects. Many processes would simply not run properly without nozzles made of PFAS. Consequently, we request exemption for the product group of spray nozzles made from PTFE and PVDF.
