Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Baseline Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: On 7 February 2023, the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) published the REACH restriction proposal on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS).
The proposal was prepared by the Authorities of Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden and submitted to ECHA on 13 January 2023. It aims reducing PFAS emissions into the environment and make products and processes safer for people, through a restriction on the manufacture, placing on the market and use of PFAS.
More in details, the proposed conditions are:
— the ban of the production, use and placing on the market of PFAS as substances;
— PFAS cannot be placed on the market in another substance, as constituents of other substances, in mixtures or in articles above certain concentrations;
— transitional period of 18 months for entry into force;
— a series of derogations limited in time (from 5 to 12 years);
— the only unlimited exemptions concern active ingredients in biocides, plant protection products, human and veterinary medicines;
— everything that does not fall under the previous cases will be banned at the end of the transitional period (e.g., medical device).
ECHA's Scientific Committees for Risk Assessment (RAC) and for Socio-Economic Analysis (SEAC) will verify that the proposal meets the legal requirements of REACH and, if so, the committees will initiate the scientific evaluation of the proposal.
A six-month public consultation was launched on 22 March 2023.
RAC will issue an opinion on the adequacy of the proposed restriction in reducing risks to human health and the environment, while SEAC's opinion will address the socio-economic impacts, i.e., the benefits and costs for society, associated with the proposal. Both committees formulate their opinions based on the information contained in the restriction proposal and the comments received during the consultations.
Once adopted, the opinions will be sent to the European Commission which, together with the EU Member States, will decide on the potential restriction. This short overview highlights that this is not a "regular" European legislative procedure, which allows political positioning of the Commission, the Council and the Parliament in trilogue negotiations, but "secondary legislation" under the REACH Regulation. Indeed, the Council and the Parliament are formally involved at the end of this procedure. However, the possibility of providing comments under a public consultation is always welcomed and gives to the stakeholders the possibility of tabling their considerations and suggestion on the matter.
Having said that, in this document, Confindustria Dispositivi Medici, with its usual collaborative spirit, intends to present its observations on the proposal under discussion for the sector of medical devices and in vitro diagnostics, with the hope that a reconciliation of the worthy interests at stake can be achieved, through their balancing which also takes into account the technical feasibility of the new forecasts covered by the aforementioned proposal.

1. Confindustria Dispositivi Medici and the Italian medical technologies’ sector:
Confindustria Dispositivi Medici is the main trade association in Italy which units, represents and enhances companies in the medical device sector, including diagnostics, digital health, medical imaging, radiotherapy, electromedical industries, borderlines, and complex and hearing aids. It represents almost 470 companies, from start-ups and small-medium enterprises up to multi-national ones and plays a vital role in advancing innovation in the health technology space.
In Italy, the medical devices sector generates a market worth about € 17.3 billion between exports and domestic markets and has about 4,500 companies, with more than 118,800 employees. Particularly, the export activities of Italian companies are worth approx. € 9.2 billion, with a ranking that sees the USA in the first place as export market, followed by Germany and France [https://www.confindustriadm.it/il-settore-in-numeri-2023/].
The association plays a vital role in advancing innovation in the health technology space, providing educational and advocacy assistance to medical technology companies. The overall activities of Confindustria Dispositivi Medici are focused on the shaping of policies that impact the sector of medical technologies in its complex heterogeneity. To achieve this, the Association represents the interests of its members at both national and EU level. The entire sector is now facing with a Union legislation based on two different European Regulations (i.e., Regulation (EU) 2017/745 and Regulation (EU) 2017/746). Ultimately, the Association welcomes and supports within its members the goals set out in the new legislative framework, with the aim of ensuring that only safe and effective medical devices can reach the market and, thus, the European healthcare systems and patients.
In this context, the association also supports the goal of the “Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability” that aims to better protect European citizens and the environment from harmful chemicals, and boost innovation by promoting the use of safer and more sustainable substances.
2. PFAS definition: the objective of the restriction
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are substances containing one or more fully fluorinated carbon atoms and represent a large and diverse group containing thousands of chemical compounds with physical/chemical properties, health and environmental profiles, uses and benefits widely diversified. These substances are used in the manufacture of products in many industries, including medical devices and in vitro diagnostics.
For the purpose of the restriction here discussed, the five Authorities previous mentioned submitted a dossier under Annex XV of REACH which include a PFAS definition. This definition starts from the one proposed by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), while extending it to all substances derived from PFAS: “Any substance that contains at least one fully fluorinated methyl (CF3-) or methylene (-CF2-) carbon atom (without any H/Cl/Br/I attached to it)”.
Indeed, OECD published a report which summarizes the work carried out by the OECD/UNEP PFC global group between June 2018 and March 2021 for the revision of the universe and terminology of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances [https://one.oecd.org/document/ENV/CBC/MONO(2021)25/En/pdf#:~:text=cd%2F2M9).-,This%20report%20summarizes%20recent%20efforts%20by%20the%20OECD%2FUNEP%20Global,%2C%20industry%2C%20academia%2C%20civil%20society]. The objective of the report is to provide recommendations and practical guidance to all interested parties regarding PFAS terminology. The OECD highlights that the term "PFAS" is broad, general and non-specific, which does not define whether a compound is harmful or not, but only communicates that the compounds under this term share the characteristic of having one or more atoms of fully fluorinated carbon. Therefore, it strongly recommends that this diversity is adequately recognized and communicated in a clear, specific and descriptive manner by Authorities and other stakeholders. The report clearly shows how PFAS have different molecular structures and therefore different physical, chemical and biological properties (e.g., non-volatile or volatile; soluble or insoluble in water; reactive vs. inert; bio-accumulative or non-bioaccumulative, etc.). It is also interesting to underline how the OECD indicates that the chemical definition of PFAS provided is not connected to how these compounds should be grouped for regulatory actions, suggesting the risks in using such a broad definition to regulate chemical compounds that have very different properties.
In the proposed PFAS restriction, the original OECD definition, which included around 4,700 substances, has been expanded to include around 10,000 substances.
However, in such a broad group restriction, the diversity of the molecules that are part of it is not taken into account, as instead suggested by the OECD report. PFAS substances have very different properties and risk profiles: for example, fluoropolymers meet the OECD criteria for polymers of low concern. They are chemically, thermally and biologically stable, thus they do not break down or release potentially harmful chemicals in the environment. They are stable in air, water, solar light, chemical and microbial environments and are non-bioaccumulative (as extremely large molecules) and non-toxic.
The basic reason why PFASs have been grouped together is that they have characteristics of persistence which, however, does not represent a risk as such. The term “persistent” refers to substances which, once released into the environment, remain unchanged (or stable) for long periods of time. Thanks to their unrivaled durability, fluoropolymers can be considered persistent from an environmental point of view, but this characteristic makes them critical and irreplaceable materials for the products they constitute. Fluoropolymers also do not break down into potentially harmful chemicals once released into the environment and are not bioavailable.
In the light of these considerations, the proposed PFAS grouping for the purpose of the restriction is not scientifically valid, and a more balanced approach should be adopted which takes into consideration other aspects than the mere chemical structure. In this regard, while we understand the motivation of the Competent Authorities to avoid "deplorable substitution" (replacing a substance with one with similar characteristics of concern), we believe it is essential that the restriction is based on scientific data and on a risk assessment, thus defining a narrower group of substances that is also more easily manageable from the point of view of restriction. Against this backdrop, it is important to clearly focus on those PFAS that pose an “unacceptable risk” according to Article 68 (1) of REACH. Substances such as fluoropolymers that have proven not to pose such an “unacceptable risk” should be exempted.
While Confindustria Dispositivi Medici strongly support the use of safer and more sustainable chemicals, we want to express our concerns on such a broad restriction for PFAS substances when considering the medical technologies, because it could potentially have a great impact on the availability of medical devices and diagnostics in EU healthcare systems and also because there is no such comprehensive restriction of the PFAS substance group outside the EU. Other possible ways can be evaluated for a risk-based grouping of PFAS, such as the one proposed by the UK Health and Safety Executive (HSE). HSE published a Regulatory Management Option Analysis (RMOA) for PFAS under UK REACH that will assist UK Authorities in their regulatory decision-making regarding PFAS [https://www.hse.gov.uk/REACH/rmoa.htm].
The UK's approach appears to be more pragmatic and science-based than the proposed PFAS restriction currently under discussion at EU level. In essence, the definition of PFAS considered by UK is the following: "Fluorinated substances which contain at least one fully fluorinated methyl carbon atom (with no hydrogen, chlorine, bromine or iodine atom attached to it) or two or more contiguous perfluorinated methylene groups (-CF2-)”. The UK Authority has therefore adopted a narrower definition of these substances, excluding the criterion according to which a single isolated methylene group (-CF2-) is sufficient for the classification as PFAS. With this definition the number of PFAS involved in a possible restriction would be smaller compared to the 10,000 substances contemplated in the current European proposal.
The UK Environment Agency, working with the HSE, has concluded that certain risk management measures (restrictions) may be appropriate for certain uses of PFAS such as:
a) use and disposal of firefighting foams where non-PFAS alternatives are available;
b) other widely dispersive uses such as the application of coatings or the use of detergents;
c) the manufacture and placing on the market of consumer items from which PFAS are likely to be released into air, water or soil or transferred directly to humans.
The same Agency also states that the restrictions must not be applied to types of PFAS or to their uses if considered low risk such as, for example: fluoroplastics or fluoroelastomers, intermediates, uses in sealed/confined systems (including use as heat transfer fluids in heat pumps and refrigeration systems), contemplating them as exemptions.
Instead, it recommends, among others, action on consumer items from which PFAS are likely to be leached and the authorization of PFAS used as processing aids in the production and processing of fluorinated polymers but requiring further evaluation and investigation of substances of concern and ongoing collaboration between different government agencies and with external stakeholders.
We believe that, given the lack of information on the dangers of some PFAS and on the real extent of use of PFAS in the various value chains and downstream sectors as the one of medical technologies, a risk-based approach similar to the one adopted by UK should be considered also in EU. The risk of such extensive restriction is likely to endanger directly medical devices and in vitro diagnostics availability, but also the production processes required for their manufacture.
3. Use of PFAS in medical technologies:
Thanks to their chemical and thermal stability, PFASs have a large use in different sectors, varying from everyday consumer products to special applications, such as in medical devices and in vitro diagnostics, including semiconductor production, photonics, analytical, bio- and laboratory technology, ophthalmic optics or medical technology to mention few. Importantly, PFAS are both used directly in the products because of their high performing properties and indirectly (e.g., for intermediates production or during the manufacturing processes). What distinguish the use of PFAS in medical device is that medical devices are healthcare products, daily used in hospitals by healthcare professionals and in home-stages by lay users, saving lives and curing patients all over Europe.
Thus, it is not reasonable that the "essential use" concept, described by the European Commission, was not applied to the very significant socioeconomic benefit of medical devices and in vitro diagnostics (essential areas for the health) and, thus, why it is not adequately reflected in the PFAS restriction procedure. The “essential use” concept aims to “ensure that the most harmful chemicals are only allowed if their use is necessary for health, safety or is critical for the functioning of society and if there are no alternatives that are acceptable from the standpoint of environment and health” [ https://eur-lex.europa.eu/resource.html?uri=cellar:f815479a-0f01-11eb-bc07-01aa75ed71a1.0003.02/DOC_1&format=PDF]. Medicinal products for humans and animals as well as plant protection products are largely exempted, although these examples involve a high level of release to the environment, but this is in line with the principle above. A similar approach should be considered also for medical devices and in vitro diagnostics given that, as explain above, they contribute for health and safety of the European population. For these reasons, Confindustria Dispositivi Medici disagrees with such a broad ban, that encounter entire substance groups, regardless of their proven risk.
Confindustria Dispositivi Medici actively collaborated with its member to gather and consolidate data about uses and applications of PFAS in the medical device sector. Given this, we refer to their contributions for further details. Indeed, Confindustria Dispositivi Medici members have been working with their suppliers to map PFAS uses in medical technologies, and they continue to find further use cases as time goes on, in order to update this map.
Up to now, PFASs find large applications in medical devices at different levels, thanks to unique combination of specific properties, including, but not limited to, chemical and heat resistance, lubrication, or biocompatibility. Hence, PFAS substances strongly contribute to achieving the required high performance and durability of the technologies, which are critical when considering the medical device sector, as an examples for precision and reliability of medical applications. Indeed, below we list the cases of few examples of medical technologies where PFAS are applied and in the concern of our members (non-exhaustive list):
— Implantable and invasive medical devices, including as an example occluders and endoprostheses, surgical vascular grafts, cardiovascular patches, surgical sutures, implantable ophthalmic applications, hernia mesh, endoscopes.
— Active medical devices, such as devices use for replacing organs’ functions. Generally, this type of device is composed of hundreds of parts and components that together contribute the medical purpose of the device and where different PFAS can be found (e.g., O-rings, lubricants, valves, electronic components, single-use components or their packaging).
— Devices and systems use in intensive care environment, including ventilators (as the ones fundamental during the COVID-19 pandemic), anesthesia machines, incubators, patient Monitoring Systems or hospital gas management systems. In these products, fluoropolymers such as PTFE, PVDF, PFA, FKM are essential materials in ubiquitarian components (e.g., hoses, seals and other gas-carrying parts, electrochemical sensors, lubricants, valves, different type of coatings).
— Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) systems, where large PFAS molecules, as the PTFE, is used in cables and sleeving at low temperatures due to insolation action. Indeed, the very low dielectric constant of PTFE allow to absorb much energy from electromagnetic fields, creating a good insulation in low-temperature environments, where other materials may be prone to electrical breakdown.
— IVD analytical equipment, reagents and home-use self-analyzer (e.g., blood glucose meter). In clinical chemistry, in vitro diagnostics and their reagents are daily used in assaying of blood, tissue samples for diagnosis purpose or for assessing the evolution of a particular pharmacological treatment (as in the case of companion diagnostics). As an example, large molecules PFAS can be found in the maintenance system of cuvette temperature, the place where the reaction between the samples and the reagents shall take place or in the complex tubing systems due to the chemical resistance, while small PFAS (e.g., acetonitrile, trifluoroacetic acid) are used in chromatographic analysis as mobile phase. Another example is the one of glucose meter, a device directly used by the patient for monitoring the glucose level in case of diabetes. PFAS are used in electrical appliances and in printed circuit boards (PCBs) due to their flame retardant and heat resistance properties.
— Pre-filled syringe stoppers are generally coated by ETFE, a large molecule PFAS that provides a barrier effect against extractables from the rubber of the stopper. Ultimately, this polymer protects the drug or the substance-based medical device (generally in a liquid state) inside the syringe from a contamination with other substance that can be extract from the rubber stopper upon contact.
— Cables used in different active devices, such as of robotic arms for different surgeries, IVD instruments, blood gas systems and others. In this application, polymers including FEP, EFTE, PFA and PTFE are used mainly for their electrical properties.
— Printing inks for markings on medical devices and on the device part of an integral drug-device combination, for identification, scale, measurement, size or other attributes marking. Scratch resistance, rub and abrasion resistance, matting effect and hydrophobicity are key characteristics for these applications that impact the safe use of the device or device part by the user.

4. How to make a sustainable PFAS transition for the medical technology sector:
The stringent transition proposed for PFAS-free articles risks to danger the availability of medical devices in the Union market. The reasons rely on different sector-specific factors that encompasses both the requirements to be fulfilled in compliance with the sectorial legislation of MDR and IVDR and the difficulties in mapping all the PFAS included in parts, components, and entire medical devices. Indeed, the examples provided here or the other presented by other stakeholders of the medical device sector do not represent the entire use of PFAS in medical device and in vitro diagnostics, given the so broad definition of PFAS. And the exercise of mapping their use requires time, since for most PFAS there is not the obligation to provide to the supply chain the relevant information regarding their presence, nature or other information. As a consequence, and considering how complex the supply chains are, with the actual proposed restriction we risk the ban of substances to be used in the manufacturing of medical device without a valid substitute. Speaking about substitutes, in line with MDR and IVDR, alternative substances need to be validated in terms of performance, quality, toxicity, biocompatibility, requiring years of R&D works, also to find out the best alternative that is not PFAS-based. As a final consideration, a PFAS phase out without an appropriate derogation will impact the quality of the treatment provided to European patients, in terms of treatments’ appropriateness, timely treatments, treatments availability or even causing adverse event after an alternative treatment.
In the light of these considerations, we propose:
a) To review the definition of PFAS, as the actual broad definition include substances with extremely different physico-chemical properties and, thus, different impact on the environment. This would allow to better identify acceptable vs. unacceptable risks upon the use of these substances, in accordance with art. 68(1) of REACH and, definitely, to prioritize the substitutions in the final products. As a consequence, substances that do not pose an “unacceptable risk” to Art. 68 (1) such as fluoropolymers should be exempted from this restriction procedure.
b) In line with the high socioeconomic impact of medical devices, broader exemptions must be created for their continued use, not only for pharmaceuticals or plant protection products.
c) To discuss a sufficient time for conducting a realistic assessment of the PFAS uses at the different levels that impact the final product (medical device or in vitro diagnostics) and, consequently, a sufficient time to identify, evaluate and validate feasible substitutes, in compliance with MDR/IVDR. Realistic transition periods are needed to ensure the best possible transformation. The proposed transition periods of 18 months and the time-limited derogations of 6.5 and 13.5 years for a few medical devices should be significantly prolonged. In this context, the product redesign, certification and authorization process have to be properly reflected.
d) To include a safeguard mechanism to be applied in case a suitable alternative substance is not available (or it is not possible to find it in the proposed transitional period) for the moment in time or for newly identify uses of PFAS in medical device that were not previously included in a derogation. As mentioned, the applications and uses of PFAS in the entire medical device sector is extremely vast and their identification requires time and constant updates. A fix and stringent restrictions applied now, as proposed, risk that applications will be missed. For this reason, it is fundamental to have a mechanism that permits ensuring the access to essential and life-saving medical technologies containing PFAS or requiring PFAS for the manufacturing process. Indeed, the possibility to find a substitute substance for a specific PFAS does not mean that all the other applications are covered or that it is possible to reach the same level of performance, safety, and quality.
e) To apply the consideration at point d) also to spare parts and manufacturing needs for medical devices. As a matter of fact, PFAS are not only included in the final product, but also in spare parts or single components intended to replace an identical or similar integral part or component of a device that is defective or worn and in aids or special needs applied during the manufacturing processes. All these cases, if not appropriate considered and included in the safeguard mechanism, could determine the impossibility of manufacturing and placing on the market essential medical technologies. Indeed, specific product derogations are useless if raw materials, components or processes needed for the manufacturing of the final products (e.g., medical devices and in vitro diagnostics) are no longer available. We should look at the derogations to be applied from a more holistic point of view, considering the entire supply chain and the relations between the industrial sectors, other than the many common applications that PFASs have nowadays.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The comment applies for Medical devices (Annex E.2.9.) sector, including in vitro diagnostics. Confindustria Dispositivi Medici is the main trade association in Italy which units, represents and enhances companies in the medical device sector, including diagnostics, digital health, medical imaging, radiotherapy, electromedical industries, borderlines, and complex and hearing aids. It represents almost 470 companies, from start-ups and small-medium enterprises up to multi-national ones and plays a vital role in advancing innovation in the health technology space.  In Italy, the medical devices sector generates a market worth about € 17.3 billion between exports and domestic markets and has about 4,500 companies, with more than 118,800 employees. Particularly, the export activities of Italian companies are worth approx. € 9.2 billion, with a ranking that sees the USA in the first place as export market, followed by Germany and France [Data elaborated from Confindustria Dispositivi Research Center, https://www.confindustriadm.it/il-settore-in-numeri-2023/].

6. Missing uses: 4. Challenges for medical device sector: Medical device and in vitro diagnostic sectors are now subject to a strict sectorial legislation governed by Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR) and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (IVDR). Confindustria Dispositivi Medici members are committed in supporting the use of the safest chemicals, supporting the European chemical strategy. However, the search of PFAS alternatives for all the uses reported above (medical technology, their packaging and their manufacturing process) is not free of challenges. As an example, fluoropolymers are largely used in implantable medical devices, and they are being in use in survey for 45+ years in a safely and effective manner for the patients. This specific application of fluoropolymers runs over such a long time because fluoropolymers are biocompatible, bioinert, stable when implanted, durable, non-toxic, chemically and heat resistant, provide a low coefficient of friction, strong, and flexible and, at the moment, there is not a technically feasible alternative which is not PFAS-based. Indeed, MDR and IVDR impose stringent requirements for material selection, biocompatibility, design validation, safety, quality, and design change upon necessity. Obviously, the final goal is to ensure that only effective and safe devices are placed in the European market.  In this scenario, one of the main challenge the sector will face is that PFAS physico-chemical properties are at the same time the very reason why they are widely used in medical technology and the concern for the environment (mainly the persistence). Thus, often the only viable alternative to a given PFAS use is another type of PFAS, not fitting with the purpose of the proposed ban. Alternatively, if a valuable alternative material is available, it would be necessary to assess its adequacy for the purpose at least at the same performance level provided by the PFAS it intends to substitute and its short- and long-term safety and performance. All these stages can take several years, starting with material scientists that find a new material, moving to product design experts that update the design of the medical technology, evaluating the new performances during the relevant time period, and to clinical experts that confirmed the in vivo performances in order to meet the medical purpose of the product. However, this is not the end of process because the change shall be register and approved by the Notified Body, the third-party entity responsible for the issue and maintenance of the CE certificate. Against this backdrop, the transition periods proposed in the PFAS restriction procedure are unrealistic and far too short. Since alternatives for PFAS in the relevant medical devices are not readily available today, the proposed 18-month transition period and the time-limited derogation periods of either 6.5 or 13.5 years proposed for very few medical devices need to be significantly prolonged to ensure a safe transition.

General Comments: On behalf of Anhui Contango New Energy Technology Co, Ltd., we would like to greet the five countries of ECHA and PFAS draft control proposals. We have been making unremitting efforts to comply with domestic and international regulations, and continuously conduct strict self-audits for the compliance of products planned to be exported to the EU. Anhui Contango New Energy Technology Co, Ltd. is a Chinese enterprise mainly engaged in PEM electrolysis of water to hydrogen membrane electrode. We use perfluorosulfonic acid resin membrane PFAS as one of the key materials for membrane electrode preparation to isolate hydrogen and oxygen, prevent gas reactions between the anode and cathode channels, and control proton exchange. PFAS substances of perfluorosulfonic acid resin film have the characteristics of good heat resistance, strong chemical stability and high mechanical strength, and there is no relevant evidence to prove their harmfulness.

PFAS compounds in perfluorosulfonic acid resin membranes assist membrane electrodes to achieve the necessary heat resistance, mechanical properties, electrochemical properties and chemical stability. Specifically, under the conditions of 60 °C, normal pressure and 25cm2, the activity of the membrane electrode can reach 1.957V@3A/cm2; At 60°C, normal pressure, 0.4 mgpt/cm2-1.0 mgir/cm2, 2A/cm2, 25 cm2, the stability of the membrane electrode can reach 4.52 μV/hr.

At present, there are no suitable alternative products on the market, and the products are only used in industrial hydrogen production sites and do not have direct contact with the human body, so we require products for this use to apply for a full exemption in the draft PFAS.We apply for the exclusion of the substances mentioned from the PFAS ban.

FOR DETAILED DISCUSSIONS, PHYSICAL PROPERTY COMPARISON DATA AND CITATIONS, PLEASE REFER TO THE ANNEX: Request for Exemption Request for Draft PFAS, which will be submitted to section V.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Manufacture

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: a. Manufacturing stage：It does not involve emissions in the European region and is produced in China. b. Usage stage：Using electrolysis of water, water is split into hydrogen and oxygen through a proton exchange membrane without any emission pollution. c. Recycling stage：Perfluorosulfonic acid proton exchange membrane (PFSA) can be recycled into perfluorosulfonic acid resin solution, environmentally friendly, simple steps, low recovery cost, the steps are as follows: (1) the perfluorosulfonic acid proton exchange membrane, the boiling point of 80~90 organic solvent and water mixed, filtered, collected filtrate, dry to obtain the first solid; (2) the first solid, organic solvent, water and police agent mixed, filtered, collected filtrate, dried to obtain the second solid; (3) the second solid, boiling point of 300~350 organic solvent and water are mixed to obtain perfluorosulfonic acid resin solution. There is basically no pollution discharge.

6. Missing uses: a. Perfluorosulfonic acid resin film (PFSA) is used in the electrolysis of water to hydrogen production section in the green hydrogen manufacturing process. b. Because this section requires high proton conductivity, low gas permeability, high mechanical and structural strength, good thermal and chemical stability, and high durability, it is used as the only material part that can meet the requirements. The performance of the above requirements directly affects the activity and stability of PEM electrolyzed water hydrogen membrane electrode, which is an extremely important component for the green hydrogen manufacturing industry. c. If perfluorosulfonic acid resin film (PFSA) cannot be used, it is expected that nearly 100 companies in the European green hydrogen manufacturing industry will be affected. d. The alternative available on the market is sulfonated polyimide film, but this substitute is compared with perfluorosulfonic acid resin film (PFSA) and found that its mechanical properties and conductivity are inferior to perfluorosulfonic acid resin film (PFSA), and are only suitable for some working conditions in this section, so it is an incomplete alternative. At the same time, a complete replacement for perfluorosulfonate resin film (PFSA) must meet at least tensile strength (transverse/longitudinal) ≥25/25MPa, elongation at break (transverse/longitudinal) ≥200/200%, Young's modulus (TD/MD) ≥180/180MPa, dimensional change rate (TD/MD/Z) ≤25/25/25%, and proton conductivity ≥140mS/cm. However, at present, except for perfluorosulfonic acid resin film (PFSA), there is no alternative that meets the performance requirements and circulates in the market. e. On the alternative route, there are several alternative substances such as partial fluorinated proton exchange membrane, non-fluorinated proton exchange membrane, composite proton exchange membrane and so on. In the future, the total number of alternative development, mass production samples, and certification and approval procedures is expected to exceed 12 years. f. At present, there are no possible alternatives that meet the technical-economic requirements. g. Businesses, consumers, and other stakeholders will be expected to be affected by the socio-economic impact of electrolyzer installations, green hydrogen manufacturing output, the development of a hydrogen common market, and the expansion of hydrogen applications. At the same time, it will affect the sales, profits and employment of green hydrogen manufacturing related industries in the EU.  In summary, there is a high probability that a complete replacement of PFAS in this use does not exist, or the replacement cannot be completed in practical applications. Therefore, we argue that this use should be exempt from the Act.

General Comments: On behalf of BOE Technology Group Co., Ltd, we would like to extend our greetings to ECHA and five countries that proposed the PFAS control draft. All along, BOE has made unremitting efforts to comply with domestic and international regulations, and continuously conducted strict self-examination on the compliance of the European Union(EU) products to meet the requirements of EU chemical regulations, including REACH.
Based on the analysis of objective facts and social and economic impacts, BOE recommends that PFAS used in display devices and electrical and electronic components for special functions (such as insulation, waterproof, high flame retardant, high temperature resistance, etc.) be fully exempted or at least given an additional 12-year transition period. The specific reasons are as follows (including specific information questions and answers).
1)BOE is a display device manufacturer, which provides intelligent interface products and professional services for information interaction. Display devices and their terminal products are the necessities of people's daily communication, which are widely used. Display devices as pan-semiconductor products, product components and materials need characteristics: heat resistance, cold resistance, wear resistance, impact resistance, chemical resistance, electrical performance, insulation, water resistance and other reliability performance. If characteristics cannot be fully met in accordance with the standards, the quality and performance and safe use of the product will produce unpredictable hidden dangers.
2)In terms of PFAS identification, there are more than 110 kinds of materials used in each display device, most of which involve the secondary and tertiary raw materials of PFAS components. Manufacturing factories are concentrated in foreign countries (Japan, South Korea, etc.), and they cannot give a definite substance classification and PFAS content at this stage. For pan-semiconductor products with long and complex supply chains, this situation increases the difficulty of identifying PFAS-related materials, and we may not realize that some raw materials may contain PFAS.
3)In terms of alternative materials, most manufacturers indicated that they were looking for alternative materials. Due to there were no suitable alternative materials that could meet all the required performance, manufacturers had no choice but to say that they could not give a clear alternative. A small number of electronic materials manufacturers said that in the current UL standard, some PFAS-related materials must be used in accordance with the safety specification design requirements. Therefore, BOE faces the situation that there are no mature alternatives in most materials markets, most of which are still in the research and development stage, and there are many external uncertainties about whether their research and development progress and final performance can meet the needs of products. This makes us face considerable external force majeure whether we can successfully find substitutes and replace them within the 18-month transition period given by the European Union.
4)In terms of process test and verification, the manufacturing of display devices involves more than 30 processes, which involve both physical and chemical reactions in vacuum environment and general processing at home and abroad. Each process involves the mixed manufacturing of multiple materials, and the whole process involves many characteristic monitoring points and process parameters to be adjusted. In general, it takes 3 years to replace and test only one kind of front-end process material in one factory, and 6 to 8 years to replace and test all factories. Materials with the same performance, such as optical materials and electrical materials, need to be replaced one by one in an orderly manner in order to avoid mutual interference of performance test results. In this case, it will take enterprises at least 10 years to arrange all the tests in an orderly manner and gradually replaced. Therefore, with only an 18-month transition period, we are unable to complete the replacement within the estimated time range.
5)In terms of capacity impact, for products that have been experimentally proven to be substitutable, it generally takes several years to build a batch production capacity that meets the needs of the industry according to experience. This means that even if substitutes are eventually found over a period of several years, they will face a situation where they cannot be successfully replaced because there is not enough capacity in the market. Therefore, for pan-semiconductor products, which involve a large number of materials and complex manufacturing processes, an 18-month transition period is obviously extremely inadequate.
6)In terms of PFAS content testing, many manufacturers indicated that the draft did not specify the internationally recognized analytical methods, so it is impossible to judge whether the test method is appropriate and whether test results are recognized. For pan-semiconductor products involving many materials, it is difficult to accurately judge the total amount of PFAS contained in products.
7)Most of the components that make up display products can be recycled. Generally, there is no toxicity spread through water, air, etc., and there is no biological accumulation or long-distance migration of hazardous substances.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Display devices and terminal electronic products including display devices (such as mobile phones, tablets, TVs, notebooks, etc.).

5. Proposed derogations: Due to the large number of products, the number of parts contained in the products is large, it is difficult to accurately calculate the amount of PFAS used in our products, which are mainly used in display device products and some electronic and electrical components.

6. Missing uses: In terms of electrical properties of electronic and electrical components, fluoroplastics are obviously superior to other materials in dielectric loss, and are widely used in high-quality cables, antennas, coaxial lines, etc. Some ultra-fine cables have higher physical requirements for materials (such as MRF, breaking strength and elongation), and no other materials can meet the processing requirements except FEP(CAS No:25067-11-2). BOE has tried to use the PE and PP instead, but it will cause unstable cable diameter, uneven wall thickness, and electrical performance, which cannot meet the requirements. In addition, due to the safety control of electronic and electrical components, only specific fluorine-containing compounds can meet the safety requirements, and there are no effective alternatives for the time being.  For polarizers used in display devices, adding specific fluorine compounds to polarizers can play an anti-static role, and this technology is widely used throughout the polarizer industry chain, without exception. Since static protection is crucial for polarizers and display devices, there are no effective alternatives in the industry for the time being.  For liquid crystal used in display devices, adding specific fluorine compounds to liquid crystal can play a better dispersion and emulsification of the entire liquid crystal mixture system to ensure that the liquid crystal in the display device to achieve the normal function. Due to the technical difficulty, there is no effective substitute in the industry.  In addition, other materials used in the production of display devices, such as photoresist, are also widely used. In order to ensure its unique coating and etching performance, it is necessary to add specific fluorine compounds, and there is no effective alternative.  To sum up, if the bill restricts all PFAS used in display devices and electronic and electrical components for special functions (such as insulation, waterproof, high flame retardant, high temperature resistance, etc.), it will have a serious adverse impact on the production and manufacturing of the whole display devices and terminal electronic products containing display devices (such as mobile phones, tablets, TVs, etc.). The display device industry is a personnel-intensive industry. If products cannot be produced or sold due to the restriction on PFAS, it will lead to a large number of people in upstream and downstream of the industry chain losing their jobs, which will result in a serious socio-economic impact.

10. Analytical methods: At present, BOE mainly judges the presence or absence of PFAS in materials by measuring the total fluorine and declaring the composition of substances from suppliers.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: On behalf of Solenis, I would like to highlight and bring attention to the analytical method chosen to analyze PFAS under proposed Annex XV restriction. Wrong choice of methodology leads to the risk of false positive result of articles where inorganic fluorine is present. In our opinion, proposed restriction will raise a disproportional burden on the manufacturers of such materials making an equal sign between intentionally added PFAS and presence of inorganic fluorine.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Food contact materials and packaging (Annex E.2.3.): -Industrial food and feed production -Paper & board packaging -Other packaging applications

10. Analytical methods: To test compliance with the ban of PFAS in paper and board food contact materials, the total organic fluorine (TOF) method was developed for the Danish authorities. The TOF method screens for just fluorine by combustion of the total sample, in which any fluorinated compound is converted to hydrogen fluoride, followed the absorption of HF into an aqueous media and the amount of fluorine is measured by ion chromatography.  The TOF method is a non-specific method, which means it can’t distinguish organic fluoride (OF) from inorganic fluoride (IF), so the separation of the two fraction is needed. The method is quite simple, and the cost is rather low, which makes it suitable for compliance testing and enforcement. Since this method measures all organic fluorides in a sample, it can be considered as an accepted proxy for the total PFAS content for paper and cardboard, as other fluorinated compounds than PFAS, like for example antibiotics, are rarely used in food packaging. Therefore, the Danish authorities has set an indicator value of 20 mg/kg total organic fluorine measured as a guideline to differentiate between intentionally added PFAS and background levels due to environmental contamination, because PFAS residues are already persistently present in the environment. However, there are two disadvantages to this TOF method. One, high chloride content and earth alkali elements may cause interference, but most importantly, the extraction of inorganic fluoride and method thereof used is crucial for the accuracy of the results. Therefore, Solenis analytical department in Wilmington suggested to use nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy or NMR. This analytic technique observes the local magnetic fields around atomic nuclei. The sample is placed in a strong magnetic field, a radio wave at a certain frequency is radiated at the sample and a signal is produced by excitation of another radio wave from the nuclei. The weak intramolecular magnetic field around an atom (caused by its surroundings) in a molecule will change the frequency of this waves and thus this so-called “chemical shift” gives details of the electronic structure of a molecule and its functional groups. Detailed description of the work done by the Solenis researchers can be found in the attached paper.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: On behalf of the Surgical Working Group on Hernias (CAH) of the German Society for General and Visceral Surgery (DGAV), we hereby comment on the present draft of the planned ban on PFAS and the implications for the surgical treatment of hernias.
We are aware of the potential impact of different PFAS materials on the environment and the negative long-term consequences. Nevertheless, banning certain medical devices has immediate adverse effects on patients’ health, and these also have to be considered in the decision-making process. This is particularly true for implants, especially those intended for long-term use such as hernia meshes. In these applications, the long-term stability of the products is essential for safe patient care. International guidelines clearly indicate that PVDF has the highest resistance to degradation. All other available materials show signs of degradation. [The HerniaSurge Group. International guidelines for groin hernia management. Hernia (2018) doi:10.1007/s10029-017-1668-x].
In addition, certain surgical techniques can only be performed with products affected by the planned ban (e.g. the Chimney-Technique for the treatment of parastomal hernia) and for which there are no alternative products available.
A loss of the products affected (e.g. Composix mesh, Ventralex, Dynamesh IPST, Dynamesh CICAT, Dynamesh IPOM, Omyra mesh) would therefore have a negative impact on patient care both in the short and long term. For this reason and in the interest of the best possible patient care we ask ECHA and the European Commission to refrain from the planned ban of the hernia mesh implants affected.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues
Combined Comments:
General Comments: On October 14, 2020, the EU Commission adopted its Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability, which aims, among other things, to better protect citizens and the environment from harmful chemicals.
August Rüggeberg GmbH & Co. KG fully supports the protection goal of the EU Commission to keep potentially harmful substances out of environmental systems as well as human, animal and plant life.
However, the restriction proposal submitted to the European Chemicals Agency ECHA in February 2023 to regulate PFAS goes far beyond this.
The aim of the planned PFAS regulation is to largely restrict the use of these substances and their placement on the market as substances and in mixtures and articles. The background to this is the high chemical and mechanical resistance of the substances and their poor degradability, which lead to an accumulation of substances of this substance group in the environment as well as bioaccumulation of some PFAS in humans and animals.
Due to a far-reaching general chemical definition of the compounds to be restricted, the substance group of PFAS comprises an order of magnitude of approx. 10,000 substances irrespective of their respective actual harmfulness to humans and the environment and of which therefore only a few have been classified as "hazardous/harmful" so far.
However, the proposed restriction does not distinguish between the different types of PFAS. Fluoropolymers such as PTFE as well as fluoroelastomers such as FKM/FFKM are classified as PFAS, based on their molecular structure. But their toxicological and ecotoxicological profiles differ substantially from the majority of PFAS substances. Fluoropolymers, including fluoroelastomers, are thermally, biologically and chemically stable, non-bioaccumulative, non-toxic, non-mobile, non-bioavailable and have been shown to meet the globally recognized OECD criteria for polymers of low concern, as so-called "PLC, Polymers of Low Concern".
The majority of PFAs are neither harmonized according to the CLP regulation nor listed as REACH candidates. Therefore, no communication along the supply chain is required with regard to any PFASs contained. This might lead to uncertainty regarding possible non-compliance and/or unexpected unavailability of important materials.
With the implementation of the present restriction proposal, the availability of a large number of products with technically unique properties would no longer exist in the EU. In addition to products for consumers, whose orderly use and disposal cannot be fully ensured, this would also affect products for industrial applications, for which the protection goal - the prevention of the introduction of potentially harmful substances into the environment - is nevertheless ensured due to regulated processes and disposal systems.
Fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers are often used as industrial production aids for, among other things, adhesion and friction reduction in equipment and intermediate processes or in chemically and thermally stable seals. They thus contribute directly to energy efficiency and environmental safety in the production of all kinds of goods and then do not become part of the finished products that are sold later on. As things stand today, these substances can already be disposed of safely through orderly incineration processes, including the elimination of the so-called " forever properties".
In addition, spare parts containing PFASs, as well as reconditioned and used products, would no longer be allowed to be placed on the market, which is not in the interest of an economical and sustainable use of resources. This directly contradicts the EU goal of circular economy.

From our point of view, all this means that the present draft
- equates the use of PFAS in consumer products and the use as auxiliary and operating materials in industrial applications in a way that does not serve the protection objective.
- by regulating an extremely high number of substances, does not meet ECHA's own requirement of "no restriction without classification". Unacceptably, substances and products not appropriate for restriction and not considered harmful substances are included.
- poses the direct risk of relocating safely managed production processes from the EU to non-European countries, which runs directly against the protection objective of the regulation, since an unregulated discharge of PFAS into the environment is to be expected there.
- leads to companies being subject to the legal uncertainty of unintentional non-compliance, as necessary information in the supply chain is not available.

We therefore request the exemption of fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers from the restriction as industrial production aids that do not become part of ready-to-sell finished articles, so that they may continue to be traded and used in the European Union. The approach of the restriction proposal to group all fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers with other PFAS types needs to be reconsidered.
Furthermore, we believe it is essential that an obligation to provide information within the supply chain for intentionally added/contained PFAS is implemented before general restrictions are introduced, as without knowledge of relevant uses it is impossible to apply for necessary exemptions.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Currently, there are no adequate sectors and sub-uses available.  We propose to implement them:  Sector: „Industrial use/application of PFAS-materials“ Sub-uses:   - Industrial use/application of fluoropolymers as general auxiliary and operating materials during the production process.  - Industrial use/application of fluoroelastomers as general auxiliary and operating materials during the production process.  - Industrial use/application of fluoropolymers as component or machine element in production machinery.  - Industrial use/application of fluoroelastomers as component or machine element in production machinery.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: August Rüggeberg GmbH & Co. KG does not manufacture PFAS. As a downstream user, we mainly purchase products containing PFAS, which are used as auxiliary and operating materials for the manufacture of tools and tool holders. The use also covers machine elements in production machines. In the manufacture of our products, we ensure that emissions are generally kept to an absolute minimum. No emission of PFAS is expected from the fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers during the use phase, and use with water is not foreseen. At the end of the use phase, the materials are collected separately in accordance with European and local waste regulations and sent for disposal (e.g. PTFE glass fabric as plastic waste, AVV key 070213) or, in the case of coatings, returned to the coater for recoating. Small quantities of materials containing fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers which are considered PLC by OECD are disposed of with residual waste for example due to contamination e.g. by friction. The limitation of exemptions to selected industrial sectors (e.g. "food contact materials and packaging" or "petroleum and mining", see Annex XV Report, Table 9. RO2, from page 116) raises questions regarding definitions and justifications related to the underlying criteria. Emissions can generally be controlled in industrial use and are therefore limited to the waste phase. Furthermore, in our opinion, there are no emissions from fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers without an incineration process. Appropriate specifications would make more sense here than a general ban on use. Furthermore the effects of many PFAS during EOL phase have not been estimated in the proposal. Persistence as only common effect of the defined substances alone does not justify the restriction of nonhazardous materials of low concern such as fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers. Persistence becoming a “negative criteria” for use of common technical materials furthermore would be a direct contradiction to the means of sustainable product design and resource consumption.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: To support specific disposal by incineration, we propose to assign a waste code number for materials containing PFAS and to fix disposal by thermal treatment.  During controlled incineration, PTFE mainly produces carbon dioxide and hydrogen fluoride, which is converted into non-toxic fluorspar by filter systems in waste incineration plants with European standards. (W.L. Gore & Associates, 2019, https://www.ispo. com/maerkte/gore-tex-no-danger-when-burning-ptfe).  According to other sources, polymeric PFASs are also completely thermally degraded when properly incinerated (e.g. "ETC/WMGE Report 9/2021: Fluorinated polymers in a low carbon, circular and toxic-free economy", https://www.eionet.europa.eu/etcs/etc-wmge/products/fluorinated-polymers-in-a-low-carbon-circular-and-toxic-free-economy).

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: No significant effects are expected due to the existing EU legislation and the national regulations of the EU member states, in Germany by the Kreislaufwirtschaftsgesetz (KrWG).  If necessary, PFAS specific waste code numbers incl. defined disposal/recycling routes have to be considered in the future, but this is the daily business of professional waste treatment/recycling companies.

6. Missing uses: Missing PFAS use: „Industrial use/application fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers as general auxiliary and operating materials during the production process “ Therefore, we propose to implement the sector "industrial application of PFAS materials", as well as the sub-uses:   - Industrial use/application von of fluoropolymers as general auxiliary and operating materials during the production process.  - Industrial use/application von of fluoroelastomers as general auxiliary and operating materials during the production process.  - Industrial use/application of fluoropolymers as component or machine element in production machinery.  - Industrial use/application of fluoroelastomers as component or machine element in production machinery.  August Rüggeberg GmbH & Co. KG develops, manufactures and sells tools for surface finishing and cutting of materials. These tools are used in various industries, such as chemical, medical and process industry, railway, apparatus and tank construction, steel mills and foundries, wind and solar energy, vehicle construction, aerospace, mechanical engineering, and others. Especially most of the key industries for the implementation of the green deal goals of the EU as well as the sustainability goals of the UN directly depend on reliable and efficient processing of metals as construction materials provided by machining tools.  In the manufacture of resin bonded grinding tools, materials containing PTFE are used as auxiliary and operating materials, both in direct use and as part of components of the necessary manufacturing equipment. These include PTFE-coated glass fabric, metal plates and containers, PTFE hoses, etc., which are required due to the combination of various properties such as high temperature and pressure stability, non-stick properties, in some cases flexibility, chemical resistance and durability. In addition, the production lines in all areas contain seals made of fluoroelastomers (FKM, trade name Viton), which are also vital due to similar properties as mentioned above.  Due to the high price and costs of fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers there have been a long term ambition and continuous activities to find substitutes for these materials independently from the now existing restriction proposal. Numerous substitution tests have been carried out up to now, which have only been successful in a few exceptional cases.  For example, PTFE coatings for metal plates and containers may possibly be substituted by solgel coatings for few specific applications, so far a positive result. However, the cost of such a coating compared to a PTFE coating is not predictable yet. No statement can yet be made about the service life of the new coating compared to the PTFE coating and the resulting waste quantities. Therefore, any economic effects cannot be evaluated at this stage. Attempts to substitute PTFE-coated glass fabrics, in particular with various silicones, have not been successful because alternative materials have never been able to cover all the necessary properties of PTFE.  In general, a ban on fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers would have a devastating impact on our business. Depending on the final decision on exemptions, the effects range from additional costs and profit reductions up to the technical unability for further production and therefore loss of important business areas. Taking our company as an example, we see more than 130 jobs in the production of abrasives at the Marienheide site alone directly endangered and others in the administrative area indirectly affected if the draft regulation is implemented as it stands and the above-mentioned auxiliary and operating materials are no longer available. A relocation of important production areas to non-EU countries would be the only possible consequence, as the finished products are PFAS-free and can therefore be imported into the EU without any problems. The continuous use of the mentioned materials by competitors from outside the EU probably under low environmental standards in combination with the possibility to export these articles into the EU would (additional to negative environmental impact) also bring a non-compensable disadvantage in competition.

General Comments: Opinion against the EU/ECHA PFAS Restriction Act
Sanming Hexafluo Chemicals Co., LTD (China)


Sanming Hexafluo Chemicals Co., Ltd., a manufacturer of fluorinated chemicals in China, has been committed to the R&D and production of environmental-friendly oxy-composed fluorinated chemicals, and has made certain contributions to the replacement of PFOA and PFOS. We continuously support national & international chemical regulation and EU's efforts to reduce the risk of hazardous substances. We are also seriously striving in order to meet ECHA’s requirements of chemicals.  However, we believe that the PFAS restriction proposed by five EU members is too radical & excessive, as it proposed to restrict more than 10,000 organic fluorinated compounds (PFAS).
Therefore, we intend to make the following comments on ECHA’s open consultation, which expresses the concerns about the radically proposed PFAS restrictions:

REACH Term 68 (1) refers to the scope of unacceptable risks on human health or environment that need to be restricted.

The proposal cites “persistent chemicals, biological concentrations, mobility, potential for long-distance transport, accumulation in plants, global warming potential, and toxicological effects” as the arguments/reasons for the restriction. Among all these properties, “persistence” applies to all targeted organic fluorine compounds (PFAS), but others are only associated with certain compounds. Therefore, we hold against the proposal to mark all the PFAS as “risk to human health or the environment” and restrict solely according to the attribute of “persistence”.
In addition, some arguments regarding fluorinated compounds are also incorrect. For example, it would be inappropriate to mark all the organic-fluorinated chemicals as having the properties of biological concentration potential and toxicological effects. To implement new restricting regulations over PFAS, there has to be quantitative analysis and discussion on each type of PFAS’s risk on human health and the environment.

The proposed PFAS restriction would be violating some of the in-force European/international rules and agreements for the following reasons:

1.The proposed restriction will hinder the implementation & accomplishment of the EU Green Deal:

Having features such as anti-water/oil, heat-resistance, chemical-resistance, non-absorption,etc., PFAS have been broadly used in waterproof agents, surfactants, emulsifiers, fire extinguishers, coatings and extensive industrial applications such as semiconductors, automobiles and batteries. Many of these applications are considered as "basic applications" in modern society.
Making full use of PFAS is critical to the EU Green Deal, which is a comprehensive initiative, including a series of policies and regulations in different fields that were made to achieve Europe climate neutral by 2050. For example, the "Horizon Europe" project has supported research and innovation activities in the area of transportation, including batteries, clean hydrogen, low-carbon steel manufacturing, and periodic biological environments.
Therefore, we believe that the proposed restriction on all PFAS, including the PFAS that have essential benefits to the EU Green Deal, will be intrinsically blocking the implementation and accomplishment of the EU Green Deal.

2.The PFAS restriction proposal is based on classifying all the PFAS as one single category.

When classifying PFAS as one single category, the proposed restriction would be restricting most of the PFAS that have not been evaluated as “having unacceptable risks”, which is a violation of the REACH Term 68 (1):
REACH Term 68 (1) made it clear that, only when a specific substance has been proved to have unacceptable risk to human health or the environment risk according to annex 13 and annex 15 (and by cross-reference annex 1 and annex 13) can we implement a restriction. The risk assessment includes hazard identification, feature recognition and exposure risk assessment.
By classifying PFAS as one single category, the proposed PFAS restriction would be restricting many PFAS that did not been through a risk assessment and do not have unacceptable risks, which is a blatant violation of REACH Term 68 (1).

Specifically, the proposed PFAS restriction is based on OECD (Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development)'s definition of PFAS, which, as the proposed restriction acknowledged themselves, merely based on chemical structure and did not take the hazardous features or risks of PFAS into consideration.
Consequently, the definition covers about 10,000 substances that have very different physical, chemical, and biological properties. This extended definition did not take specific PFAS or subgroups of PFAS with distinct features into account and is therefore not suitable for regulatory risk management purposes.
Actually, even the OECD itself acknowledges that this definition "does not draw conclusions that all PFAS have the same use, exposure and risk attributes" and that it can only be used as a starting point for reference as it "may be seen as too extended".
In particular, based on OECD’s PFAS definition, it is legally and scientifically impractical to conduct risk assessment. By classifying all PFAS as one single category without considering specific and different attributes of different PFAS subsets, the proposal recognized “persistent” as the “critical hazardous attribute” that "triggers equal hazards".  However, "persistence" is neither a sign of hazardous attribute nor a indication of a risk. Being persistent does not justify a determination that a substance is of same concern as PBTs/vPvBs. It also can not be considered as an"unacceptable risk" defined by REACH Term 68 (1) to justify the proposal.
Therefore, “persistence” can only be used to support the proposal when it’s in conjunction with other attributes included in REACH/CLP regulations, such as bio-accumulation, eco-toxicity and not separately.

Except the property of being persistent, the proposed PFAS restriction did not identify any other hazardous attributes of PFAS in common. It only complemented some of the properties of non-PFAS substances. In fact, the evidence provided on the proposal only refers to some subsets of PFAS (mainly long-chain PFAS) and lacks of other PFAS subsets’ data, which is not convincing to restrict all the PFAS.

For example, on page 28, the proposed restriction acknowledges that "for most PFAS, data on bio-accumulation behavior is absent, or insufficient," so the provided data on the bio-accumulation potential of PFAS is insufficient to confirm the bio-accumulation of all PFAS in the environment.
As for the eco-toxicity, the proposal was noted that PFAS includes a large number of different substances with heterogeneous properties and their eco-toxicity assessment is very complicated. It then concludes that bio-accumulation potential and eco-toxicity are expected to differ between different PFAS due to the "high diversity" of PFAS, and yet did not draw a comprehensive conclusion with B/Vb & T criteria for each PFAS substance (page. 47).

Lacking of sufficient evidence, the proposed PFAS restriction have failed to conduct risk assessments (including hazard identification, feature recognition and exposure risk assessment) to demonstrate the unacceptable risks of all PFAS substances that are proposed to be restricted. In some applications,PFAS can be used in enclosed spaces, where the exposure to the environment is extremely limited, and the risk for human health and environment is even smaller. It is also possible that, without describing the specific risks of each PFAS , the proposed restrictions will eventually lead to non-PFAS alternatives, which are likely to be even more harmful to human health and the environment.

Sanming Hexafluo Chemicals Co., Ltd. has realized industrialization in the R&D and production of Perfluoroisobutyronitrile, which is the alternative for sulfur hexafluoride (SF6).
SF6 is an insulating gas with the advantages of high dielectric strength and low global warming potential(GWP), which is broadly used as an insulating medium for high voltage electrical equipment, and is widely used in ultra-high voltage and UHV power systems and distribution networks (SF6 insulated switchgear and ring-grid power supply units).
However, study found that, regardless how many contributions sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) can bring to modern society, this kind of gas also has serious environmental demerits:

1. Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) is uneasy to decompose and has a long atmospheric lifetime. Long-term accumulation of SF6 leads to serious greenhouse effect:
Having a strong chemical stability, SF6 is inert when reacting with other substances after being released into the air. During its ultra-long life cycle of more than 3,200 years, although it can photolysis and slowly settle in the stratosphere and above, it still accumulates in the atmosphere, resulting in a continuous increase in the greenhouse effect.

2. Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) has remarkable global warming potential (GWP):
In order to directly compare the effects of different greenhouse gases on global warming, scientists have come up with a method to measure the global warming potential (GWP values).
The Global Warming Potential (GWP) was developed to allow comparisons of the global warming impacts of different gases. Specifically, it is a measure of how much energy the emissions of 1 ton of a gas will absorb over a given period of time, relative to the emissions of 1 ton of carbon dioxide (CO2). The larger the GWP, the more that a given gas warms the Earth compared to CO2 over that time period. The time period usually used for GWPs is 100 years. GWPs provide a common unit of measure, which allows analysts to add up emissions estimates of different gases (e.g., to compile a national GHG inventory), and allows policymakers to compare emissions reduction opportunities across sectors and gases. It is a relative value comparing with carbon dioxide’ GWP value, which is “1”.
In this case, the GWP value of Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) is “23500”, which means, its Greenhouse effect is 23500 times of carbon dioxide (CO2)’s.


Perfluoroisobutyronitrile [2,3,3, 3-tetrafluoro-2 -(trifluoromethyl) propanitrile, CAS number: 42532-60-5] is an ideal insulating arc extinguishing gas that can replace Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) and has already been developed and industrialized so far. Perfluoroisobutyronitrile has excellent insulating arc extinguishing performance and its breakdown strength is 27.6KV, which is twice that of SF6.
With zero Ozone depletion potential (ODP) and a low global warming potential (GWP) of 2210, (which is only one-tenth of SF6‘s), Perfluoroisobutyronitrile is used to replace Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) as insulating gas, which can and will be greatly reducing the greenhouse effect. In the practical application of gas insulated switch-cabinets, Perfluoroisobutyronitrile is used in the form of mixing with carbon dioxide, and the GWP value of the mixture gas is only 328, which is much lower than the GWP value of SF6(which is as high as 23500).

Replacing SF6 with Perfluoroisobutyronitrile could achieve a reduction of more than 99.9% of carbon emissions:
The globally used volume of SF6 is about 20,000 tons/year, and let’s estimate the leakage as 2,000 tons/year. In this case, if the SF6 is completely replaced, we’d be equivalently reducing 46.34 million tons/year of CO2 emission.
As an ideal alternative for SF6, perfluoroisobutyronitrile is necessary and even urgent to be used.
While SF6 is a persistent substance and has a significant greenhouse effect, perfluoroisobutyronitrile is neither persistent nor bio-accumulative, and has no harm to the ecological environment, which can and will effectively protect the environment and curb global warming.

In summary, we sincerely suggest that, instead of radically restrict beneficial substances like perfluoroisobutyronitrile, EU/ECHA should be paying more attention to the control and replacement of substances such as Sulfur hexafluoride (SF6), which are not in PFAS list but have great negative impacts on the environment.
