General Comments: Opposition to the EU's PFAS Restriction Proposal

I. Compliance Aspects of the Proposal
1.Uncertainty of the EU's PFAS Proposal
The PFAS proposal is based on a "precautionary principle" and encompasses over 10,000 compounds. However, ECHA does not have the CAS and PBT data for these 10,000+ substances. The proposal relies on data from PFOA, PFOS, and other PBTs to infer about other substances including fluorinated polymers that fit the PBT definition. This kind of legislative proposal is not rigorous and is unenforceable.
Supporting Document 2: According to the independent expert panel  in Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology 134 (2022) 105226 regarding the scientific grouping of PFAS, given the current state of knowledge and data gaps, most PFAS risk assessments will need to rely on a significant number of assumptions and shortcomings. These, along with the resulting uncertainties, need thorough and explicit discussions. Indiscriminate validation of PFAS proposalwould lead to over-regulation, causing irreversible harm to industry development and Europe's economy.
Numerous PFAS products have already become an indispensable part of people’s daily life . Moreover, the application of PFAS substances is crucial for the realization of European Green Deal, especially in areas that Europe is actively promoting such as the hydrogen industry, electric vehicles, low-carbon steel manufacturingand green transportation. We believe that the draft proposal, which aims to restrict all uses of all PFAS, will essentially hinder the realization of the goals of European Green Deal.

2.The PFAS Proposal Violates Article 68 of REACH
Article 68 of the European REACH regulation defines "restrictions" as a means to "protect human health and the environment from the 'unacceptable risks' posed by chemicals." The regulation mandates a risk assessment, as specified in the annexes, to demonstrate this "unacceptable risk." Such risk assessments include hazard identification and characterization, exposure assessment and risk characterization. However, it is evident that over 10,000 PFAS  included in the proposal do not necessarily fit this "unacceptable risk" as described. Furthermore, many of these substances currently lack the necessary risk assessments to support the proposal's claim that most PFAS present an "unacceptable risk."

II. Definition of PFAS
1.PFASs are used by various scientists, organizations, and countries, each referring to different ranges of substances. The use of "Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances" and "PFASs" in the EU legislation under these circumstances can lead to confusion among the public. There is a need for clearer terminology and expression. The substances covered by the legislation need to be redefined and specified more clearly.
Supporting Document 1: Hammel et al., Implications of PFAS Definitions Using Fluorinated Pharmaceuticals, iScience, 25, 104020, April 15, 2022.
Content of Document 1: A total numberof 360 organic fluorine drugs were studied. Based on their structures, they were screened against 9 definitions of PFAS as follows:
1)by Buck et al., 2011: 8 organic fluorine drugs met this definition (2.2%).
2)by OECD (2018) : 5 organic fluorine drugs met this definition (1.4%).
3)by OECD (2021) : 107 organic fluorine drugs met this definition (30%).
4)by Glüge et al., 2020: 22 organic fluorine drugs met this definition (6.1%).
5)by TURA (2021a) : 6 organic fluorine drugs met this definition (1.7%).
6)by TURA (2021b) : 4 organic fluorine drugs met this definition (1.1%).
7)by US EPA OPPT (2021) : 5 organic fluorine drugs met this definition (1.4%).
8)by  ≥1% perfluorinated carbon atoms: 337 organic fluorine drugs met this definition (94%).
9)by  encompassing all organic fluorine: All 360 organic fluorine drugs met this definition (100%).
Supporting Document 14: Integr. Envir. Assess. Manag. 2021 - Buck,Identification and classification of commercially relevant per-and poly-fluoroalkyl substances (PFAS).
It is strongly recommended that a comprehensive industry study be conducted on the definitions of PFAS to ensure clarity in future policy decisions and to avoid the implementation of policies based on misconceptions or confusion.

2.The OECD's definition of PFAS (2021) does not specify whether the substances are harmful or harmless; it is solely for communication purposes. Compounds under this terminology share the same characteristic of having a perfluoromethyl or a sub-methyl carbon structure. This point is explicitly mentioned on page 8, paragraph 2. The proposal from the five European countries now references this definition and presumes that the substances in the definition involve risks. The policies established based on this presumption are logically flawed and unreasonable.
Supporting Document 5: OECD (2021) Reconciling Terminology of the Universe of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances: Recommendations and Practical Guidance,OECD Series on Risk Management No. 61, OECD Publishing, Paris.
Supporting Document 6: Zhanyun Wang and et al, A New OECD Definition for Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances, Environmental Science & Technology, November 2021.

III. Toxicity and Persistence
1.Statement on page 32 regarding fluorinated gases:
Some fluorinated gases (such as certain HFOs) ultimately degrade into PFAAs, for instance, TFA or PFBA. Hence, these gases also contribute to the overall exposure and risks of PFAAs. (Annex B.4.1.3.2.).
Supporting Document 12: Changes in tropospheric air quality related to the protection of stratospheric ozone in a changing climate, by S. Madronich and et al, published in Photochemical & Photobiological Sciences online on 13 June 2023.
The atmospheric degradation pathways of the second, third, and fourth generation of refrigerants into TFA are discussed. Table 3 provides the annual production figures for TFA and predicts the concentrations of TFA in the form of sodium salts in oceans for the years 2050 and 2100, estimated at 244-246 ng L-1 and 266-284 ng L-1, respectively. The last sentence of the abstract mentions that TFA lacks significant degradation pathways and can accumulate in some water bodies, but it does not pose adverse environmental effects.
Supporting Document 9: 2022 Assessment Report: Stratospheric Ozone Depletion, Environmental Effects of Ultraviolet Radiation, and Interactions with Climate Change, by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) Ozone Secretariat. The report covers an analysis of climate change, including the decomposition of refrigerants into TFA. It also presents predictions and reasoning that TFA will not have adverse effects on human health and the environment up until 2100.

2.Fluoropolymers exhibit characteristics of low concern. Fluoropolymers with a molecular weight exceeding 100,000 daltons cannot pass through cellular membranes and do not possess bioavailability or bioaccumulation potential. In particular, PTFE is a safe substance, a fact supported by toxicological experiments conducted on PTFE. Essentially, fluoropolymers are insoluble in water and do not migrate over long distances.
Supporting Document 11: A Critical Review of the Application of Polymer of Low Concern and Regulatory Criteria to Fluoropolymers by Barbara J Henry and others, published in Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management, Volume 14, Number 3, pp. 316-334.
The attribute of being "very persistent" is not inherently hazardous and does not, by itself, indicate a risk. Persistence cannot serve as a justification for attributing a substance with a level of concern equivalent to PBT or as representing an "unacceptable risk" under the meaning of Article 68(1) and as a rationale for restrictions. For these reasons, persistence should only be viewed in combination with other characteristics in REACH and CLP, such as bioaccumulation and toxicity, and not in isolation. Apart from the claimed very persistent attribute of PFAS, the proposed restrictions have not identified any other common hazardous properties of PFAS. Persistence does not necessarily equate to a health risk.
Supporting Document 2: Grouping of PFAS for human health risk assessment: Findings from an independent panel of experts by J.K. Anderson and others, published in Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology, Volume 134 (2022), 105226.

3.There's Insufficient Information on the Impact of PFASs on Human Health and the Environment
The EU proposal on page 13 states, the most extensively studied PFASs (PFOS and PFOA) are suspected carcinogens, have harmful effects on developing children (as a result of intergenerational exposure), and trigger effects in the liver or immune system at low concentrations. There's also data suggesting some PFASs as potential endocrine disruptors, and the environmental impact of some PFASs (like 6:2 FTOH) is substantial enough to classify them as hazardous to the aquatic environment. However, for most PFASs, there is insufficient data to adequately assess their impact on human health and the environment, but an increasing amount of research, beyond PFOS and PFOA, reports similar adverse effects for other PFASs."
The proposal clearly specifies that even the most extensively studied PFASs (PFOS and PFOA) are only "suspected" to be carcinogenic. For the majority of PFASs, there is not enough data to comprehensively evaluate their impact on human health and the environment. The fact that the EU's five nations have put forth a restriction proposal despite such significant lack of evidence raises serious concerns about the scientific and fair foundation of the EU legislation. It's also highly irresponsible towards manufacturing enterprises relying on these substances for their livelihood and scientists who have dedicated decades of research to this field.
Supporting Document 2: Within "Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology 134 (2022) 105226", when summarizing the toxicological effects attributed to PFAS, it is essential to avoid overly broad statements. Instead, one should specify when a statement applies only to particular PFAS (e.g., Perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and cancer risk), is applicable to specific subgroups, or generally pertains to PFAS as a category. The ATSDR provided a comprehensive review of the toxicological profiles of a few PFAS (ATSDR, 2021). Some reported health effects of PFAS differ between humans and animals. The consistency of these effects between humans and test species, and among different PFAS, is often inconsistent (ATSDR, 2021; Fenton et al., 2021; Steenland et al., 2020; Zodrow et al., 2022). Even between the most studied PFAS, Perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) and PFOA, a broad consensus on what adverse human health impacts or diseases might be associated with their exposure has not yet been reached (ATSDR, 2021; Australian National University, 2021; Fenton et al., 2021; Steenland et al., 2020). The understanding of human health issues potentially related to PFAS is dynamic and the subject of extensive ongoing research. The lack of a consistent interpretation of human health risks for thoroughly studied fluorinated chemical safety assessment systems, coupled with the absence of information for the majority of such systems, poses significant challenges for any mixed risk assessment method.

IV. Emissions and Socio-economic Aspects
1.Summary, Socio-economic analysis:
"The submitter of this document has identified the main uses of PFAS, where the largest quantities of PFASs are used and lead to the highest emissions. This was accomplished through document retrieval, stakeholder inquiries, and calls for evidence. Fourteen sectors and/or application areas—divided into multiple sub-uses—have been discussed in detail in the report. In terms of the European Union, between 140,000 and 310,000 tons of PFASs entered the market in 2020—with anticipated economic growth in some sectors—further growth is expected under baseline scenarios. Within the EU economic area, the expected median PFAS tonnage over 30 years is 49 million tons, which, without intervention, would result in emissions of about 4.5 million tons during production and use. Emissions during the waste phase will be significant but are not currently included in this estimate due to high uncertainties. Thus, it can be inferred that the emission estimates are grossly underestimated."
Firstly, the proposal's collection regarding use is insufficient. Supporting Document 7 studied 200 applications and 1,400 substances, whereas the proposal from the five EU countries only considered 14 applications, which is far from adequate. It's recommended to further collect data in this aspect. Furthermore, the basis for estimating the socio-economic impact involved in this proposal is lacking, and there should be further comprehensive research.
Secondly, the estimated value of waste emissions is also highly uncertain, indicating that the proposal has not scientifically calculated and evaluated emissions in this regard. There are many ways to discharge waste, and technological advancements must be taken into account. Considering the reported degradation, mineralization, and other emission treatment technologies, simply stating that "emission estimates are grossly underestimated" lacks persuasive reasoning and might seem like an intentional exaggeration of facts.
Supporting Document 7: An Overview of the Uses of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS): Juliane Glüge and et al, Environmental Science and Processes & Impacts, 2020, 22, 2345-2373.
This proposal also lacks in-depth research in certain specific application areas, such as fluoropolymers and fluorinated gases. Therefore, the following document is provided:
Supporting Document 8: Socio-economic information on fluoropolymers, covering various properties of fluoropolymers and information indicating no harm to human health. It also includes an analysis of the socio-economic impact of fluoropolymers. Pages 51 to 81: CHEMService, REGULATORY MANAGEMENT OPTION ANALYSIS FOR FLUOROPOLYMERS, 4 NOVEMBER 2021.

V. Degradation
1.From the Proposal Summary, Concerns, second paragraph:
"When these substances and their degradation products continue to be released into the environment, environmental concentrations will increase, as the PFASs within the scope of this restriction proposal do not undergo mineralization under natural conditions."
The above argument is based on the technological level before 2020. We must adhere to the principle that technology is constantly evolving. For instance, as published in "Science", Perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids (PFCAs) undergo mineralization via a defluorination pathway promoted by sodium hydroxide. Low-temperature mineralization degrades perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids and can be extended to degrade other per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances. The degradation rate is rapid, defluorination occurs under mild conditions, and this can fundamentally solve the environmental problems of fluorinated substances. The pyrolytic decomposition mechanisms of perfluoroalkyl ether carboxylic acids and short-chain perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids demonstrate the effectiveness of thermal degradation of PFASs.
Supporting Document 3: Low-temperature mineralization of perfluorocarboxylic acid, Brittany Trang and et al, Science 377, 839-845 (2022), 10 August 2022.
Supporting Document 4: Mechanistic Investigations of Thermal Decomposition of Perfluoroalkyl Ether Carboxylic Acids and Short-Chain Perfluoroalkyl Carboxylic Acids, Ali Alinezhad and et al, Environmental Science & Technology, 2023, 57, 8796-8807.

VI. Alternatives
1.The proposal's alternative solutions lack operationality, which is highly unprofessional.
The proposal's description regarding alternatives is ambiguous. There are clear alternatives, but their usability is questionable. For those without alternatives, there's no specific introduction on the progress and direction of research and development. Even if PFAS materials must be replaced in the future, the proposal should develop feasible plans. For example, in the substitution of fluorinated refrigerants, let alone whether they can fully replace the original usage, the current technology to replace the equipment still poses significant challenges. Other less-developed countries are blank in the research and development of devices operating with natural working mediums. How to implement this proposal smoothly and effectively is a matter for the EU to consider.
Moreover, the migratory nature of PFAS indicates a global restriction, not just within the EU. When formulating proposals, can the EU share alternative technological information, enabling less-developed countries to restrict or ban them?

VII. Exemptions
1.Unscientific exemption period for substitutes.
In the absence of sufficient information, the RO2 scheme in the proposal only provides a maximum exemption period of 12 years, except for a few long-term exempted usages. We believe that even for currently under-development alternatives, these materials need repeated demonstration and evaluation, requiring a considerable period for implementation. For substances without determined substitutes, research and development must be promoted through trial and error in the future, and even a 12-year grace period may be insufficient to confirm their usability. This is very impractical for a restrictive proposal and will inevitably harm certain industries.

2.Please list the RO2 exemptions in the proposal: Which substances should be excluded? Which should be permanently exempted? Which should have a 5-year exemption? Which should have a 12-year exemption?
We request the EU provide reasons and evidence for the exclusion and exemption of PFAS materials in various uses and present solutions. Otherwise, PFAS applications in regions outside the EU will continue to impact globally, and the EU cannot remain unaffected.

Org. name: The Knowledge Center on Organic Rankine Cycle technology (KCORC)
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) power systems are an emission-free technology suitable for the conversion of thermal energy into electricity. ORC systems can be used to harvest waste heat, generated from industrial processes and engines for example, which would otherwise be wasted to the environment. In Europe, this has the potential to generate as much as 150 TWh/year of emission-free electricity using industrial waste heat alone. As of 2019, this could abate 46 Mt of CO2-emissions per year, taking national emission factors into account. Low temperature waste heat (less than 200 C) has a share of up to 40 TWh/year of green electricity, but for these temperature levels it is much more challenging to harvest.
Many of the commercially available ORC systems are currently using PFAS fluids in a closed loop, which is sealed from the environment (comparable to a refrigeration system). All HFCs and HFOs are indexed as PFAS fluids, and these fluids are used as working fluids in ORC systems. PFAS are only emitted due to leakages or improper handling of the working fluid. When properly disposed, potential PFAS compounds are decomposed and do not pose any further threat to the environment. Therefore, the impact of PFAS can be minimized effectively by safety measures during operation and maintenance, which are already in place through compliance with existing regulations, such as the F-Gas Regulation. Beyond this, many different sealing materials, used for O-ring and flat gaskets for example, are affected by the proposed PFAS ban.
Replacing PFAS fluids with a natural refrigerant is possible and desirable but requires significant amounts of development and adjustment time for the industry and certifying bodies. All natural refrigerants (except CO2) are flammable, and explosive or toxic in some cases. In sectors such as the maritime industry, the current regulations do not allow installations with flammable fluids of any kind. The realization of systems with flammable fluids might be a viable option in other sectors, and for large scale ORC systems in the MW-scale, as the costs for additional devices have a lower impact on the installation costs, while this is not the case for the smaller scale. Using CO2 as a working fluid requires a transcritical power cycle that suffers the drawback of high operational pressure levels. This might be feasible in small dimensions for small scales (size of few kW) and very large scales, but it is not a viable option for medium scales in the range of a few kW up to 1 MW. This drives up the cost for the installation and may prevent some installations from realization due to longer pay-back periods. Consequently, reducing the potential for CO2 mitigation means a lost opportunity for power generation and for saving CO2 emissions.
The proposed ban of fluorinated greenhouse gas refrigerants has an impact on other laws, rules, and regulations. While a regulation is highly desired and necessary, its implementation requires time and so does the development of alternatives.
It may also impact existing plants which can no longer be serviced and subsequently may need to be shut down. The investment horizons in terms of energy efficiency measures are rather long term, typically between 15-20 years.
The most beneficial path for the environment must be taken in this transition process, where different aspects of climate change and environmental pollution concerned. The reason to ban PFAS is that they are reported to be toxic, persistent and bioaccumulative. However, the toxicity and the environmental impact of ORC working fluids has been properly assessed3 and this should be considered in any future regulations. For example, most of the fluids applied in ORC systems are not classified as persistent. Independent of this, the fluids are already adequately regulated through the F-Gas regulation.
Therefore, we suggest a permanent derogation for using fluorinated greenhouse gases as working fluids in waste heat recovery applications using ORC technology, in the same way exemptions have been proposed for the HVACR sector. This should also include the maintenance and service of such systems.
As mentioned, ORC systems can generate annually up to 150 TWh of electricity from industrial waste heat in Europe. With energy consumption data from Eurostat based on the year 2019, this could lead to a reduction of approximately 46 Mt of CO2-emissions per year.
A total of 9 kt of CO2 can be abated by a single 200 kWe ORC unit over an operational lifetime of 20+ years (this estimate is sector-specific and takes the country specific CO2 emissions into account). To quantify the advancements implied by the F-Gas regulation, the figures below (only available in the pdf version of the document attached) compare R245fa (GWP=1030) with R1233zd(E) (GWP=5), a low-GWP working fluid. Both fluids perform similarly, enabling similar efficiencies, and they are both indexed in PFAS appendices.
It can be seen that the global warming potential of fluid loss due to leakage over the lifetime (20 years) of a system working with R245fa is compensated within 20 to 30 hours of operation. With R1233zd(E), the time reduces to 6 to 10 minutes. With respect to entire fluid charge, the global warming potential for R245fa and R1233zd(E) would be compensated within 3300 – 6600 hours and 16 – 32 hours, respectively. At the end of life of the ORC system the fluid can be recycled and re-used, or it can be disposed properly. In the latter case, the fluid is thermally destroyed and no PFAS compounds are emitted following combustion.
In the absence of a comparative base for PFAS with the global warming challenge of today, it needs to be kept in mind that reducing the potential for CO2 mitigation is a lost opportunity for power generation and for saving CO2 emissions.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: ORIXHA is requesting a time-unlimited derogation for Perfluorooctylbromide (PFOB) as a Medical Device for Total Liquid Ventilation clinical applications in Critical Care. Such a derogation will allow to treat and improve the recovery outcomes for 60,000 resuscitated cardiac arrest patients per year in the EEA, with 9,000 lives expected to be saved per year once the therapy is fully deployed (3,000 saved lives per year by 2030).

________

1-bromoheptadecafluorooctane (EC / List no.: 207-028-4, CAS no.: 423-55-2, Mol. formula: C8BrF17), is also known as Perfluorooctylbromide (PFOB) and referenced as Perflubron in the US Pharmacopeia.  PFOB is liquid at ambient temperature and atmospheric pressure. Its properties as a breathable liquid have been demonstrated and are linked to its high solubility for Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide and its low surface tension that enables it to cover the lung tissues and protect the alveoli.

In a Total Liquid Ventilation solution, PFOB is used as the breathable liquid medical device together with a liquid ventilator, where PFOB is administered by the liquid ventilator into the patient’s lungs. This sub-use has not been identified in the Table 9 of the proposed restriction. Total Liquid Ventilation and its therapeutic applications are described in section III.1, with life-saving benefits for patients in critical care.

In the scope of the Total Liquid Ventilation, PFOB is not a pharmaceutical substance but a medical device, regulated by EU Regulation 2017/745. As such, it is not within the scope of Directive 2001/83/EC nor in the scope of Regulation 726/2004 for active pharmaceutical ingredients (API) in human medicinal products. However, PFOB is the only molecule of the breathable liquid and could be as such considered as an API-like substance.

PFOB has a very unique set of properties which are required in Total Liquid Ventilation: high O2 and CO2 solubility, low surface tension, minimal absorption through pulmonary administration, lack of toxicity, high stability…  Decades of research failed to identify any suitable alternative to PFAS, and more specifically to PFOB, for liquid ventilation. More detailed information is provided on technical issues for substitution in section IV.

A restriction on PFOB would thwart the Total Liquid Ventilation development and clinical use, and represent an important loss-of-chance for thousands of patients (see section IV). This is the reason why we believe a time-unlimited derogation should be considered for the use of 1-bromoheptadecafluorooctane (PFOB) for Total Liquid Ventilation.

More details are provided regarding PFOB, its applications in Total Liquid Ventilation, the impact of a restriction on patients and economic impacts in the following sections.

_____

It is important to mention that PFOB is manufactured from Heptadecafluoro-1-iodooctane (aka Perfluorooctyl Iodide (PFOI), EC / List no.: 208-079-5, CAS no.: 507-63-1, Mol. formula: C8F17I).
As such, PFOB contain may traces of different PFAS molecules when imported (see section V for complete specifications), among which PFOI and Pentadecafluorooctanoic acid (aka PFOA, EC/List 206-397-9, 335-67-1, C8HF15O2). PFOI and PFOA are already restricted as per Commission Regulation (EU) 2017/1000 but an exemption has been delivered for PFOB containing PFOI up to 200 ppm. Despite manufacturers’ efforts to lower the concentration of such residues, traces of impurities are inevitable.
Thus, any derogation for PFOB should also take into account the presence of other PFAS impurities in PFOB.

_____

Our company is involved in a process of limiting as much as possible the tonnage of PFOB used for Total Liquid Ventilation through a voluntary recycling process, partly funded by the European Innovation Council. In conjunction with a thorough management of wastes all along the life cycle, we believe that the use of PFOB for Total Liquid Ventilation is compatible with environmental concerns and that emissions per patient could be maintained at a low level. As per our forecasts on Total Liquid Ventilation and assumptions on such processes, 16.2 to 27.0 tons per year need to be imported by 2030 in the EEA to treat and significantly increase the survival odds in good neurological condition of 20,000 cardiac arrets patients. Only a fraction of this quantity would be released into the environment (see section V).

_____

In conclusion, considering :
- the therapeutical benefits of PFOB in Total Liquid Ventilation giving a chance of survival in good condition for thousands of cardiac arrest patients,
- the absence of alternative for substitution,
- the significant socio-economic impact on Orixha of a ban of PFOB from 2027 leading to the complete destruction of the Total Liqud Ventilation value chain in Europe,
we believe a time-unlimited derogation for PFOB as a medical device for Total Liquid Ventilation is relevant. Such a derogation should include a tolerance for PFAS trace impurities which are likely to be found in PFOB.

Significant R&D efforts will be developed to reduce the actual imported tonnage and associated emissions (see section V).

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Our comments apply to Medical Devices.  The sub-use our comments apply to - Total Liquid Ventilation - is not part of the listed sub-uses in Table 9 for medical devices.   Total Liquid Ventilation is a therapy where a breathable liquid is administered into a patient’s lungs with inspiratory and expiratory volumes being pumped into and from the lungs by a liquid ventilator, several times per minute. In this therapy, the breathable liquid itself is a stand-alone medical device, composed of 100% PFOB.  Total Liquid Ventilation has clinical applications in post cardiac-arrest syndrome, respiratory support for patients with Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome, with life-saving benefits for patients.   For the sole application of hypothermic TLV for post-cardiac arrest syndrome, 60,000 patients could benefit from the Total Liquid Ventilation therapy in the EEA per year, with a potential of 9,000 saved lives with improved neurological outcomes once the therapy is fully deployed (3,000 saved lives by 2030).  See Section IV for more details on the therapeutic benefits of Liquid Ventilation.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The use of PFOB in Total Liquid Ventilation is associated with a specific life cycle, including the end-of-life management. Orixha is engaged in a process to reduce as much as possible the environment impact of PFOB-based Total Liquid Ventilation.  Please refer to section V (§ ‘Life cycle, recycling, waste management, tonnage’) where emissions of PFOB in the end-of-life phase is evaluated as per different scenarios.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: By managing the whole life cycle of PFOB from sourcing to destruction, Orixha will be able to recover all liquid PFOB wastes and eliminate them appropriately with selected partners.   Please refer to section V (paragraph ‘Destruction’) where Orixha’s strategy on the management of PFOB wastes is detailed.

5. Proposed derogations: The sub-use of Total Liquid Ventilation has not been identified in the proposed restriction.  For this new sub-use, forecast and assumptions lead to request on a derogation to import PFOB into the EEA to treat 60,000 resuscitated cardiac arrest patients per year once the therapy is fully deployed  (20,000 patients by 2030).   By 2030, 16.2 tons of PFOB would be imported per year (with a worst-case scenario of 27.0 tons, see section V). R&D and industrial development would allow to properly manage the whole life cycle and to limit the associated emissions to as low as 2.7 tons per year for 20,000 treated patients and 3,000 saved lives.  Please refer to section V for forecasts and assumptions.

6. Missing uses: Section IV details the key properties of PFOB in Total Liquid Ventilation and why substitution has not been technically feasible despite decades of academic and industrial research.  As a summary, decades of development have failed to find alternatives to PFAS as breathable liquids. A very unique combination of properties is required to meet both the performances, the safety and the lack of toxicity that are required to perform Total Liquid Ventilation. Scientific state-of-the-art considers that this set of properties can only exist in PFAS. Among these molecules, PFOB is deemed the most suitable compromise both in terms of performances/safety/toxicity and for its environmental impact. This systematic review leads us to believe that there is no appropriate chemical alternative to PFOB for Total Liquid Ventilation and that such alternative will not exist in any foreseeable future.  A restriction on PFOB in the scope of Total Liquid Ventilation would force Orixha to close or re-establish itself out of Europe. Besides the loss of chance for 60,000 cardiac arrests patients per year, this would be synonym of 255 M€ lost revenues in the EEA for years 2027 to 2030, the destruction of 49 direct jobs and a loss of opportunity to the hiring of 200 employees all located in the EEA by Orixha.  It would have significant impact on Orixha’s Tier 1 strategic partners with dozens M€ lost revenues for the years 2027-2030 and the loss of opportunity to hire around 200 employees.  Please refer to section V (§ ‘Socio Economic Impacts for Orixha and its industrial ecosystem’) for detailed socioeconomic impacts.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: The sub-use of Total Liquid Ventilation has not been identified in the proposed restriction. Socioeconomic impact of this sub-use is detailed in Section V.

8. Other identified uses: The sub-use of Total Liquid Ventilation has not been identified in the proposed restriction. Socioeconomic impact of this sub-use is detailed in Section V.

10. Analytical methods: Orixha has developed with Eurofins a GMP analytical method for the quantification of impurities in PFOB, in relation with Orixha’s PFOB specification (see Section V).  Orixha is also developing an analytical method for the quantification of PFOB traces in the human blood.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our comments concern the use of PFAS as refrigerants in HVACR, notably in hydronic space and water heating heat pumps as defined in EU energy labelling Regulations 811/2013 and 812/2013. We do not comment on other uses.

The Dossier Submitters predominately base their justification for a proposed derogation on the lack of suitable non-PFAS alternatives. In the case of F-gases used in HVACR applications, domestic air conditioning, and heat pumps, the Dossier Submitters conclude based on the provided evidence that suitable and safe alternatives exist for most applications and therefore generally propose to restrict the use of PFAS. This general restriction (i.e., ban) is warranted and a step in the right direction towards more climate and environmentally friendly HVACR.

There are two derogations from that general restriction. Firstly, the use of PFAS for maintenance and refilling of HVACR equipment for which no drop-in alternative exists (transition period of 13.5 years), and secondly, a time-unlimited derogation for refrigerants in HVACR-equipment in buildings where national safety standards and building codes prohibit the use of alternatives).

The time-unlimited derogation based on national safety standards and building codes is not properly justified for heat pump applications and goes against the objective of the restriction, considering that:

- PFAS create an unacceptable risk for human health and/or the environment and EU/EEA level measures are needed to reduce the exposure to a minimum. Such Union-level action also guarantees a level playing field in the internal market as compared to action undertaken by individual Member States. Derogations applicable only in a few Member States, and/or certain unspecified criteria would therefore lead to a fragmentation of the internal market and undermine the entire logic of the restriction.

- National standards do neither address nor provide for management measures and regulatory incentives to reduce the risk of PFAS to the environment and health. Furthermore, national standards are not assessed against key criteria applicable to EU regulatory measures.

- Furthermore, state-of-the-art standards (IEC 60335-2-40:2022) allow for the safe use of natural refrigerants in hydronic space and water heating heat pumps at least for the mass market up to 70 kW heat output, as defined in EU Regulations 811/2013 and 812/2013.

- Examples from other policy areas show that national standards are inefficient due to a faulty standardisation process, lack of comprehensive implementation, and ambiguous relationship to EU and national legislation.

- The Dossier Submitters do not properly take into consideration the continued PFAS emissions that result from a time-unlimited derogation.

- The derogation is too broad as the HVACR sector encompasses a very large group of products with very different applications, performance requirements and most importantly status of alternatives. Derogations should be proposed for very specific applications where there is strong evidence of absence of suitable alternatives

- For hydronic space and water heating heat pumps as defined in EU energy labelling Regulations 811/2013 and 812/2013, no derogations are needed because there are no refrigerant-related “national safety standards and building codes” that would render installation of a hydronic heat pump with PFAS alternatives impossible, vs a PFAS heat pump.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The comments provided in this submission refer to the use of PFAS as refrigerants in HVACR applications in  heat pumps, and our input focuses on hydronic space and water heating heat pumps as defined in the EU energy labelling Regulations 811/2013 and 812/2013, i.e. equipment for space heating and water heating using energy e.g. in ambient air or ground for a heating system based on water, coupled e.g. to radiator or floor heating system (air/water, brine/water, water/water “hydronic” heat pumps). REPowerEU targets roll-out of 10 million / 30 million new mainly hydronic heat pumps by 2027/2030, because they are a direct replacement for gas and oil boilers operating hydronic heating systems. A major part will be in air/water configuration in existing buildings with radiators, with an “outdoor unit” installed outside of the building.   F-gas is one of the 3 main groups of PFAS which were subject to the impact assessment (IA), the other two being PFAAs & PFAA precursors and polymeric PFAS. The impact assessment does not only focus on the substance, but also covers the precursors and its degradation products. In this sense, although HFOs are the latest generation of drop-in fluorinated refrigerants, with low GWP, it is clear they pose a risk, as HFOs - a subgroup of PFAS - degrade in the environment to persistent substances.  The existence of other EU legislation regulating F-gases, such as the FGR Directive are not considered as sufficiently addressing the environmental concerns The main objective of the FGR concerns the GWP of the substances in scope and their contribution to global warming (and not their volumes per se), while other concerns are not considered, e.g., atmospheric degradation to TFA which precipitates and causes exposure to humans and the environment. The impact assessment quotes several academic publications and also ECOS (2021) confirming the risks related to the degradation of F-gases and pointing out the existence of natural alternatives.  While most F-Gases have been included in the PFAS definition used for this restriction, the decision was taken to exclude the substances HFC-23 (CHF3), HFC-32 (CH2F2), HFC-152a (CHF2-CH3), HCFC-141b (CCl2F-CH3) and HFO-1132a (CH2=CF2). The exclusion is based on the chemical structure of these substances; however, the assessment confirms that they are used in blend with other fluorinated gases that are within scope. In our view, the exclusion requires further clarification by the Dossier Submitters, especially since it is acknowledged that the overall volume of the different applications (including both PFAS and non-PFAS gases) is of relevance as a shift to a different specific gas could affect the whole application volume. In particular, the exclusion of HFO-1132a should be reconsidered, because there is a risk of unintended market transformation to a substance with unforeseeable consequences.

8. Other identified uses: Alternatives to PFAS refrigerants in hydronic space and water heating heat pumps  Natural refrigerants, such as R290, are a safe, technically and economically feasible alternative to PFAS and other synthetic refrigerants for all use cases of hydronic space and water heating heat pumps up to 70 kW, as defined in EU Regulations 811/2013 and 812/2013. The thermodynamic properties of R290 ensure energy performance that is at least as good as for F-gas based heat pumps, with superior performance at operating conditions requiring higher heating water temperatures in the building stock. Thus, an accelerated transition to safe and sustainable R290-driven heat pumps supports accelerated replacement of boilers by heat pumps, as foreseen by REPowerEU, and fast GHG reductions in the buildings sector facilitating achieving the 2030 GHG target. Ramping up heat pumps using sustainable and natural refrigerants with ultra-low GWP, such as R290 avoids trade-offs with F-gases and their GWP and PBT concerns.  In particular:  - A ban of PFAS refrigerants in hydronic space and water heating heat pumps up to 70 kW heat output is possible, justified and beneficial, because it has positive socio-economic impacts, in addition to positive environmental impacts compared to a “no ban” scenario.  - The ban should apply for all hydronic space and water heating heat pumps up to 70 kW rated heat output, as being readily defined in Commission Delegated Regulations 811/2013 and 812/2013.  - For this heat pump category, all use cases can be covered by alternatives to PFAS refrigerants, such as R290 / propane, enabled by state-of-the-art safety standards.  - The ban supports REPowerEU objectives for adding 10 million/30 million hydronic heat pumps by 2027/2030 in the EU, because it accelerates market transformation to R290 heat pumps that are particularly suitable for operating conditions in the building stock, while reducing the need for installer qualifications, and contributing to investment certainty in times of unprecedented scale and speed for adding production capacities.  - The ban should be effective from 1 January 2028 - for consistency with the F-gas Regulation, and for allowing sufficient time for re-design of heat pumps in particular for indoor installation.  - No derogations for hydronic heat pumps “in buildings where national safety standards and building codes prohibit the use of alternatives” should be foreseen - from a technical perspective they are unnecessary, and from a legal and environmental perspective they create loopholes that lead to unfair competition and unnecessary pollution.  - This picture is in line with the general heat pump market trend to natural refrigerants and in particular R290, with larger and smaller, EU and non-EU makers expanding their offering (cf. e.g. ISH trade fair March 2023).    Additional comments related to the time-unlimited derogation in HVACR equipment in buildings where national safety standards and building codes prohibit the use of alternatives (paragraph 5 j)):  The time-unlimited derogation for “refrigerants in HVACR-equipment in buildings where national safety standards and building codes prohibit the use of alternatives” is not properly justified and goes against the objective of the restriction, and the CSS policy objectives.  From a manufacturer’s perspective, for hydronic space and water heating heat pumps as defined in EU Regulations 811/2013 and 8212/2013 no derogations are needed, because we are not aware of refrigerant-related “national safety standards and building codes” that would render installation of a hydronic heat pump with PFAS refrigerant alternatives impossible, vs a PFAS heat pump.   As a consequence, unspecific and unjustified derogations due to “national safety standards and building codes” undermine legal certainty, create loopholes and unfair competition, and - due to the conflict between CE marking REACH legislation and local rules targeting individual installation situations - risk rendering the restriction meaningless.  In general, a restriction under REACH is necessary when community level regulatory action is needed to address the risk. The justification for the need for the risk management action to be taken on a Community-wide basis needs to be based on risk-related considerations and needs to consider market-related aspects. According to ECHA Guidance document2 for the preparation of Restriction proposal, “the higher the hazard and the extent of the risk the more important it is to take measures to ensure the protection of human health and the environment throughout the Community”. The market related considerations assess if distortion of the internal market could be created if the risk are addresses at national level.  In the PFAS restriction proposal the DS state that PFAS create unacceptable risk for human health and/or the environment and EU/EEA level measures are needed to reduce the exposure to a minimum (1.2. Justification for an EU-wide restriction measure); “Union-wide action avoids trade and competition distortions within the EU/EEA, thereby ensuring a level playing field in the internal EU/EEA market as compared to action undertaken by individual Member States.” In this context, it is difficult to explain how the proposed time unlimited derogation for refrigerants in HVACR-equipment in buildings can help achieve the above-mentioned objectives of risk reduction and level playing field.  According to the ECHA Guidance document for preparation of restriction proposal, if the analysis proves that action at the Community level is not needed but the identified risk should rather be addressed at national level the DS is requested to document the identified risk and this conclusion in the relevant parts of the restriction format and submit this documentation to ECHA and Member State. In the case of the HVACR derogation thorough analysis and documentation have not been provided. The only risk management measure referenced at national level is the safety standards. However, these standards do not address nor provide for management measures to reduce the risk of PFAS to environment and health.  National standards and building codes cannot be considered as an adequate risk management option, unless proven otherwise by the DS, as their adaptation to new available standards is far from certain in terms of timing, ambition and coherence across the Member States.  Moreover, the national standards have not been assessed against the key criteria of: - effectiveness and proportionality - practicality and monitorability - information on the distribution of the chemical (manufacture and use) in markets across the EEA - effects of the national standards and their future potential updates on the internal market.  In addition, the efficiency of the national standards in the construction sector has been seriously questioned by the Impact assessment prepared by the EU Commission in March 2022 for the revision of Regulation (EU) No 305/2011 on harmonized conditions for the marketing of construction products. The IA points out that the underperformance of this Regulation is due to several overarching issues, number one being the “malfunctioning standardization process,” followed by “hampered implementation on the ground in EU countries”, “over-complex and unclear rules” and “ambiguous relationship between the Regulation and other EU legislation, and/or national rules”. It can therefore be concluded that national standards cannot be considered as adequate risk management option, unless proven otherwise by the Dossier Submitters.   The Dossier Submitters also do not seem to properly take into consideration the potential emissions of PFAS from the products that will remain in the market as a consequence of this time-unlimited derogation. While it is stated that emissions are expected to be medium and decline over time, the Dossier Submitters also clearly acknowledge that there is no evidence to evaluate the emissions. They furthermore declare that the expected decline will depend on the speed in which national safety standards are adopted to allow alternatives, while arguing that the actual time period this would require is unknown. The inclusion of this derogation appears even more inconsistent when considering that the major contributor to PFAS emission is the HVACR sector (Annex F, figure 4).    There is also an incoherent approach of this time-unlimited derogation with the other proposed time-unlimited derogations. Other time-unlimited derogations proposed are justified by either an objective reason for the use of PFAS in calibration of measurement instruments and as analytical reference materials or by the existence of EU level legislation which provides for risk management measures – environmental risk assessment of the active substances (PPP, BP, VM, MP). However, even in this case the DSs acknowledge the fact that the predominant concern for the restriction, i.e. persistence, is not sufficiently taken into account during the current authorization processes following PPP, BP and MP regulations. Therefore, the derogation comes with a recommendation to the European Commission to address these concerns in the respective regulations, in order to reduce the use and emissions of PFASs as much as possible. This logic however is not mirrored in the case of the derogation for refrigerants in HVACR-equipment in buildings, where there is no EU level legislation  Incoherent approach regarding alternatives:  The Impact Assessment is entirely based on availability of alternatives which, in absence of strong quantitative data, becomes the key criteria for grating derogation. This approach is in line with the objectives of Chemical Strategy for Sustainability and the essential use concept, which is very much centered around the existence of suitable alternatives. Following this logic, derogations have been proposed for very specific applications in medical devices, where strong evidence of absence of suitable alternatives have been submitted. However, for some other uses in medical devices derogation was warranted but not proposed, because of insufficient data. DS judge necessary not to grant general derogation for all medical devices’ applications, but to encourage substitution where possible, regardless of the importance and the criticality of the application.  In contrast, the DS decided to grant time-unlimited derogation for refrigerants in HVACR-equipment in buildings. The HVACR encompasses a very large group of products with very different applications, performance requirements and most importantly status of alternatives. This is incoherent with the approach taken for the other sectors and conflicts with the CSS objectives to transition to non-toxic alternatives.  The goal should be to limit the derogation only to the applications for which there is strong evidence of lack of suitable alternatives.  For comparison with other restriction dossiers of similar broad scope – Microplastics, the DS (ECHA) proposed 6 y of transition period for leave on products. The Commission proposed a 12y transition period only for very specific products from the leave-on category – make-up, lip & nail products, for which alternatives are not available.  For the HVACR industry, we would foresee a similar scenario. Natural refrigerants have always been considered as alternatives to the use of fluorinated gases in HVACR applications which are under the scope of the PFAS Restriction. They are safe, energy efficient, safe, and particularly suited for the building stock (higher system temperatures) in all heat pump segments and sub-sectors of HVACR industries. Given the progress in technology and engineering processes, natural refrigerants are technically feasible in all applications. This is also supported by different studies (Hafner and Ciconkow, 2021) used by the DS, which investigated the current state and market trends in technologies with natural refrigerants and concluded that all temperature levels and most applications can use natural refrigerants. There is no technical barrier to replace currently used synthetic fluorinated gas refrigerants with natural working fluids. Notably, for heat pump applications (HVACR sub-segment), hydrocarbon-based alternatives are already on the market.  Related to the availability of natural refrigerants for heat pumps, the DS assessment concludes that suitable natural refrigerants are available for many heat pump applications. These refrigerants have a low environmental impact and perform comparably better than synthetic alternatives, with acceptable and stable costs It is fundamental to distinguish between air-conditioning with heating function, and hydronic heat pumps. Potential limitations e.g. for natural refrigerants in the former must not be generalized to the latter. For hydronic heat pumps, we would like to reiterate: Natural refrigerants are a suitable, and very often ideal, material for hydronic heat pump use cases, small and large. State-of-the-art safety standards set out safety measures for product design and installation.  We conclude: The time-unlimited derogation for “refrigerants in HVACR-equipment in buildings where national safety standards and building codes prohibit the use of alternatives” is unjustified as there are technically and commercially alternatives already available on the market.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our company creates signalling solutions (optical and acoustic) mainly for the machinery and equipment industry. The signalling devices help optimising manufacturing processes, provide safety for workers, ...

Our products simplified  consist of a PCBA in a plastic housing and terminal.
Regarding the PCBA we received little information regarding PFAS contained or involved. A typical reason is there was no declaration/information obligation on PFAS beforehand. We suppose no PFAS are contained in the PCB and most of the electronic components, but there is a considerably residual risk. Focusing on the production processes way upstream the supply chain: we are sure PFAS play a critical role.
Regarding the housing plastic materials we got information from our suppliers, that no PFAS are included in the granulates, but they should be involved in the basic production processes more upstream in the supply chain/chemical industry as well.
Since our products serve in different environments outdoors and indoors certificates of tightness (IP-rating) is critical.
To achieve the required goals (waterproofness,...) we use sealings, typically NBR, but also FKM and NBR O-Rings coated with PTFE.

We don't know if we can substitute the FKM sealings by using PFAS-free materials and especially if O-Rings with other PFAS-free coatings are suitable.
A substitution is complex because the automated manufacturing process depends on the PTFE coating , plus the coating helps preserving the O-Ring in use/in special environments: ensuring a good sealing throughout the long lifetime of our products and the possibility of dismounting modules of our signalling towers and replacing them with e.g. an energy saving LED module...

Our partner who does the coating could not present us a PFAS-free solution yet, that achieved the same performance regarding manufacturing handling and preservability of the O-Ring.

With a fast and broad ban of PFAS, especially PTFE,  our products will be much more short-lived, our production process for signalling towers (that make up most of our revenue) will be in danger and the recertification (CE - safety assessment- requirements for tightness) will take a big toll on our locally-engaged and family-owned company and its some hundred employees.

This was only accounting for the direct consequences of a PFAS ban, taking into consideration the implications further up the supply chain, the aftermath may be much more drastic. We hope our suppliers (formulators of technical plastic granulates and batches, sealing manufacturers/coating service providers, PCB manufacturers and electronic components distributors and production companies) commented on the consequences of a general PFAS ban themselves.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our company develops and manufactures parts from elastomer materials, often based on polymers such as FPM, FEPM or FFKM. Articles made of these materials are usually effective under the most extreme installation conditions, especially where other materials fail. In addition, many machine parts are installed in our production lines that are also basic for the manufacture of non-floor materials, such as guide elements, hoses, printed circuit boards, seals or parts for optimising friction and wear behaviour.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Seals made of elastomer materials are used, among other things, in heat pump technology. Here, the requirements for seals made of high-temperature resistant materials are indispensable. In specific cases, FEPM-based formulations are essential. Other tested non-floor materials based on HNBR or EPDM fail at temperatures of 200°C when simultaneously exposed to strong alkalis and oils. Parallel high pressures aggravate the application properties immensely. Seals made of FKM are also indispensable, as they have to seal in CHP units at temperatures of up to 200°C and under the influence of special condensate consisting of sodium nitrate, sulphate and chloride. Resistance must be proven according to EN 16241. No other elastomer can meet these criteria. Parts made of FKM, which are used in airfield refuelling, are equally regarded as safe sealing solutions. It is well known that only pile-based elastomers are sustainably stable against paraffin. In addition, additivated iokraftstoffe are the reason for anchoring high-floor FKM types in the installation space. Plasma-treated seals, previously PTFE-coated in the processing step, become necessary to minimise wear behaviour. Here, too, alternative OF coatings are not effective, as integration into the surface to be coated is inadequate.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our company has a significant role in the Hungarian pharmaceutical sector. Our activities involve active pharmaceutical ingredient manufacturing, medicinal product manufacturing and researh and developement. The company mainly focuses on developing and manufacturing central nervous system, cardiovascular and gynaecological products but manufacture more than 200 drugs including original, generic and licence products in almost every therapeutic area.
The restriction of use/manufacture of PFAS substances would affect seriously not only our production of drug substances but also the research and developement.
Despite that active substances which qualify as PFAS are derogated from the restriction, such active substances still cannot be manufactured within the European Union as the intermediates necessary for active substance manufacturing could neither be produced nor purchased from other sources due to the PFAS-containing molecule parts. The substitution of these molecule parts is not possible as it would modify the therapeutical effect of the API. If the restriction proposal were adopted as currently is, manufacturing of these active substances would be forced outside of the EEA, potentially resulting in a shortage of medicines and dependency on third countries. Quality problems often arise in the case of active pharmaceuticals imported from third countries.
From an R&D point of view there is a great potential in the pharmacological effect of PFAS containing molecular parts. Though in general, research is derogated from REACH restriction, the development and manufacture of these substances can only occur outside of the EEA.  As original research and development usually takes about 10 years, there are several potential candidates in the pipeline that is itself can be considered a PFAS or cannot be manufactured without the use of PFAS substances due to it's chemical structure or technological reasons.
In general the pharmaceutical industry releases a minimal amount of PFAS substances during manufacture and use and the benefits of manufacturing and using PFAS substances for drug products is much bigger than the risk posed by the incidental minimal emission into the environment.
Taking into consideration the information above we kindly ask the legislators to please consider our propositions below regarding some additional derogations for the pharmaceutical sector.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Pharmaceutical industry

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: According to REACH the use and manufacture of a substance as intermediate is only possible under Strictly Controlled Conditions (SCC). The SCC requirement (that is applicable for both transported and on-site isolated intermediates) is maintained during the whole life-cycle of the intermediate in question. The life-cycle of an intermediate ends inside the production plant. Therefore if a PFAS substance is used as intermediate the emission to the environment (water, soil, air) is minimised with technical means.  Due to this reason, subjecting these intermediates to restriction would not mean any benefits and would not lead to the expected results emphasized by the legislators.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: While using PFAS substances as intermediates, waste is not generated, therefore no incineration is required.

5. Proposed derogations: • PFAS active pharmaceutical ingredients and the intermediates generated and used during their synthesis, including transported isolated intermediates and manufacturing reagents, as well as excipients (for example, solvents and catalysts) used during the manufacturing process, adding these to the particulars described in restriction option 2 so that these products may still be manufactured and marketed in the EEA.  Despite that active substances which qualify as PFAS are waived from the restriction, such active substances still cannot be manufactured within the European Union as the intermediates necessary for active substance manufacturing could neither be produced nor purchased from other sources due to the PFAS-containing molecular parts. • Extending the waiver specified in the previous section to non-EU (not registered as per Directive 2001/83/EU) active pharmaceutical ingredients and developmental (product and process orientated research and development [PPORD] according to REACH) products as well. • Fluoropolymers (reactor lining, sealings, tube lines, non-adhesive coatings, surfaces, filtration units, filters, sachets, tubes, insulation material, mechanical parts) for industrial use, according to financial management plans specified in Section 8 of restriction option 2. • Packaging materials of medicines and devices according to the particulars specified in Section 6.l of restriction option 2, however the scope of the waiver should be extended not only to the PCTFE substance but to all fluoropolymers approved by drug regulatory agencies, without time limitation. Besides technical feasibility, any substitution requires regulatory measures which should be considered in the roadmap in order to prevent any disturbances affecting the availability of medicines, and which are unlikely to be resolved in 13.5 years. The deadline specified for the replacement depends on the technology and cannot be defined in a uniform manner, furthermore all changes are followed by a validation period. • Regarding the individual use of PFASs identified in the pharmaceutical industry supply chain. These include starting materials, reagents, solvents, catalysers as well as single-use or repeat-use devices necessary for drug manufacturing and any related processes, including quality control or diagnostic testing. • Each and every already approved medicinal product in order to prevent regulatory contradictions. This includes medicines or medicinal products with a valid marketing authorisation obtained according to Directive 2001/83/EU, as well as medical devices as per the MDR.

6. Missing uses: Fluoropolymers for industrial use: equipment and disposables     • Chemical industrial, pharmaceutical industrial, biotechnological, sterile manufacturing: fluoropolymers in manufacturing equipment (reactor lining, sealings, tube lines, non-adhesive coatings, surfaces, filtration units, etc.) where fluoropolymers come in contact with the product and affect its quality, including spare and replacement parts:     • Chemical industry, pharmaceutical industry, biotechnology sectors: PFSA disposables and single-use goods (filters, sachets, tubes, etc.) where fluoropolymers come into contact with the product and affect its quality.     • Manufacturing: fluoropolymers not contacting the product in complex equipment, including insulation material, mechanical parts, including spare and replacement parts.     • Analytical laboratory equipment, for example teflon tubes, valves, sealings, filters, etc.  Raw and starting materials, chemical intermediates, reagents, solvents, excipients used in production, including storage, transportation and quality control      • Chemical and biotechnological manufacturing of PFAS and non-PFAS active substances: PFAS reagents, catalysers and ligands or solvents which do not become integral part of the active substance molecule, for example homogenous catalysers, i.e. the Crabtree/Pfaltz-type catalysers or other noble metal catalysers containing CF3 substituted ligands, trifluoro-acetic acid, hexafluoro-isopropanole, anhydrous trifluoro-methane-sulphonic acid, trifluorotoluene, etc.     • Chemical production of PFAS active substances: PFAS raw and starting materials, as well as intermediates as building blocks of the active substance molecule.     • Chemical production of excipients: PFASs used as processing excipient for the manufacturing of functional excipients.     • PFAS substances and reagents used during quality control activities set out in product authorisations and specifications, e.g. European Pharmacopoeia monographs. These include, for example, trifluoro-acetic acid (TFA) in the mobile phase of high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC); perfluorobutanoic acid (PFBA) as ion-pairing reagent in chromatography; N-methyl-bis(trifluoroacetamide) (MB-TFA), N,O-bis(trimethylsilyl)trifluoroacetamide (BS-TFA) and N-methyl-N(trimethylsilyl)trifluoroacetamide (MS-TFA) for the production of silyl derivatives in gas chromatography or other methods.     • Storage, manufacturing and transportation: non-polymer PFASs in equipment, for example in electric parts, cooling media in HVACR equipment and low-temperature refrigerators, cooling media in storage and transportation, including spare and replacement parts.     • Quality control and research & development: non-fluoropolymer PFASs in equipment, for example in electric parts, diagnostic laboratory tests, in cooling media of laboratory equipment and temperature-regulated centrifuges.  Packaging of medicines or medicinal products: immediate packaging and closing foils     • Immediate packaging of medicines and active substance, like containers or closures coming into contact with the product, using approved fluoropolymer substances or coatings like PCTFE, ETFE or PTFE. Applies for blisters, sachets, tubes, other metal or plastic containers, vial stoppers or other coated elastomers – according to Section 6.l of restriction option 2, this is not a missing use, in case the legislators consider medicines as “medicinal preparations” too. For medicinal products, the terminology needs to be clarified. Currently, the draft wording is limited to PCTFE-based packaging, which is insufficient in the pharmaceutical industry to ensure that their products are always packaged in a manner that is compliant with drug safety and quality requirements.     • Packaging containing fluoropolymer foil that protect medicines or medical devices from air, humidity and other contaminants or maintain their sterility and stability, in accordance with Sections 6.m and n of the restriction proposal, but not limiting the wording to certain products or materials – this is not a missing use (it is included in Table 2 of the relevant REACH Annex CV report), although a general waiver is missing.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our company has been producing reliable products for our customers in the residential and commercial HVACR sector for many years. PFAS also contributed to this through their outstanding properties.
We fully support the initiative to restrict the use of certain PFASs which are a risk to human health or the environment.
But we strongly believe that the restriction proposal should differentiate between the various types of PFAS on the basis of their chemical composition and toxicological profile, manufacturing method and their particular uses. All PFAS are not the same and we therefore believe that a “one size fits all” regulation is simply too broad. The restriction proposal’s approach to group together all fluoropolymers with other PFAS types must be revisited.
We use fluoropolymers primarily for sealing applications, where e.g. EPDM, silicone and graphite seals are not an alternative to FKM due to their inferior properties. FKM sealings are normally used in the appliance over the lifetime of more than 10 years and are not exposed to the user.
FKM is one of the fluoropolymers that are classified as polymers of low concern according to the OECD. Their high molecular weight prevents penetration into cells and therefore does not cause any damage to health.
The general ban on PFAS has major economic consequences for companies, perhaps entire business areas may have to close or relocate to non-European countries. We therefore request that fluoropolymers be removed from the scope of the restriction or at least be granted an exemption for a period of at least 12 years.
Attached you will find a more detailed description of one of many applications in our business area.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on benefits Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our company has developed and is currently selling electrochromic glass for international commercial and residential markets.  Electrochromic windows are an important component of the overall approach to lower total energy use in commercial buildings by an estimated 25% due to optimized heating and cooling.  Our electrochromic window device architecture may be conceptualized as a thin film lithium ion battery.  As such, a critical component is the electrolyte that separates the cathode and anode and provides both a source and a reservoir for lithium ions during charge/discharge cycles.  Unlike conventional lithium ion batteries, however, the optical characteristics of the device in all electrochemical states is of primary consideration and the electrolyte used plays an important part.  Further, the electrolyte must be stable under exposure to direct sunlight and applied voltage for product lifetimes that are warrantied for 20 years.  PFAS salts, specifically lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (CAS 90076-65-6) , are the only electrolytes tested by our company that have demonstrated both the electrochemical stability and high quality optical characteristics under repeated cycling.  Furthermore, electrolytes of this type were developed explicitly because they are less hazardous than alternatives such as lithium hexafluorophosphate or lithium tetrafluoroborate.   In addition to electrochromic devices, this salt is a known component of perovskite solar cells and is preferred in electric vehicle batteries.  All of these applications explicitly exist to advance green energy concepts.  Hence we request an exemption for lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (CAS 90076-65-6), LiTFSI, in these applications.

We fundamentally appreciate the importance of controlling the release of any chemical recognized as being damaging to human health and the environment.  We do not believe, however, that the current scope of the proposed restriction is appropriate because the current proposal to ban all PFASs does not discriminate between materials demonstrated to be dangerous and those that are not.  Further, we do not believe that the intent of the ban is to force industry to return to more toxic materials that have been intentionally replaced due to safety considerations.

In the hazard assessment of any chemical, both a relevant biological mechanism for harm and a reasonable exposure mechanism capable of delivery of a harmful dose is important.  In addition, the exposure mechanism necessarily includes concepts related to rate and time.

In the specific case of LiTFSI,
(1) the material is not considered to be bioaccumulative.  The molecule is water-soluble and has been selected for the applications above specifically because of the highly ionic, non-coordinating character.  Unlike other PFAS materials, LiTFSI is chemically unique and not a long-chain perfluouro compound and is thus not expected to build up along food chains.  In comparison with molecules of concern such as perfluorooctanoic acid, the partition coefficient (commonly associated with bioaccumulation) differs by approximately 8 orders of magnitude.  This fact is recognized in UNEP Report 2016-1 (attached below) which indicates that only those perfluorinated chemicals with a chain length of more than six carbons are of toxicological concern.  Further, also due to the high water solubility, materials of this nature are noted to be readily eliminated via the kidneys into the urine.
(2) Although the rate of biodegradation is slow,  hydrolysis is known to occur followed by mineralization.  In combination with the lack of bioaccumulation noted above, this rate of degradation should be considered adequate.  This factor is noted in the IMDG shipping requirements for LiTFSI where, unlike other PFAS materials, LiTFSI is not considered to be a marine pollutant.
(3) the primary hazards associated with LiTFSI are due to the corrosivity and thus reactivity with organic material.

Considering that LiTFSI may be viewed as non-bioaccumulative, of limited persistence and not a marine pollutant, the magnitude of the risk should be assessed further based on scale of emissions both quantitatively and in the context of the scale of other exempted PFASs.  This may be further examined when one takes into account end-of-life considerations.  Although electrochromic devices and EV batteries remain generally unique and new to the market, end-of-life recycling is expected if only because of the value of the raw materials present.  Although imperfect, a comparison may be made to the continued presence of lead in automotive batteries.  Although the health and environmental risks associated with lead have been well known for decades, the continued use in automotive applications is feasible because of the high level of recycling.

An exemption for this material in the context of the information above is proposed to be merited.  This chemical should both continue to be manufactured and allowed into the market.  Because the material is fully contained in the products where it is used, no emissions are possible during the life of the product.  All necessary efforts should be addressed to control emissions during manufacturing and end-of-life.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: These comments apply to the Energy Sector and the Construction Products Sector.    The Energy Sector, in particular, appears underrepresented in the Annex XV restriction report.  Limited information is been included regarding lithium ion batteries especially for electric vehicle applications.   In the Construction Products Sector, electrochromic devices do not appear to be included.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: a. Lithium salt of bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide is purchased from European suppliers.  We do not have information on emissions from the preliminary Manufacturing phase.  Our utilization occurs at a secondary Manufacturing phase in which this molecule is added to a chemical formulation for use in the preparation of electrochromic windows.  The material in question is purchased as a solid or aqueous solution and added directly into our manufacturing process.  The vapor pressure of this compound is effectively zero under our handling and utilization conditions.  No more than 1-5% of our purchased material is lost during our process.  This process loss does not comprise emissions, however, as our chemical formulation process is closed-use under an inert atmosphere.  Any losses in our process are handled as chemical waste by a waste handling company.  This chemical formulation is used directly in the preparation of electrochromic devices, again in a closed-use process.  Any process losses or non-compliant materials are captured and handled as chemical waste by a waste handling company.  The end of life phase is not well developed.  The PFAS molecule is contained within an electrochromic Integrated Glass Unit (IGU) which comprise glass, sealant, spacers, etc., like any commercial window, and also very small quantities of proprietary thin films which include the PFAS.  Based on chemical assessment, the metal components comprising the thin films are present at ppm levels thus allowing disposal in a conventional landfill.  The PFAS is encapsulated in a polymer matrix that provides additional resistance to leaching.  Because our product is warrantied for 20 years, no product has reached end-of-life.  Recycling models remain under development. b. We cannot speak to waste associated with the initial manufacture of the PFAS in question.  In our process, 1-5% of material is incinerated in a facility that includes post-incineration scrubbing to the US EPA-level requirement.   Glass devices comprising ppm levels of PFAS may be ground into aggregate for the preparation of concrete or disposed of directly in a landfill.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The effectiveness of incineration is reported to be greater than 99.99% by Clean Harbors, a US-based waste handling firm.   Incineration is viewed as a first-option and landfilling as a second option.  The US EPA is developing guidance including calls for additional research is support of PFAS management.   Data is largely lacking however because PFASs and PFAS-containing waste has not been consistently defined as a hazardous pollutant to date.  This gap interferes with the reliability of existing data.

6. Missing uses: In the use case of electrochromic devices, the magnitude of annual use cannot be readily assessed as this is a nascent product incorporated into energy sector and construction applications in order to lower energy use.  The molecule in question enables a 20 yr lifetime of the product.  We have not demonstrated that any technical alternative exists that meets our required product specifications.
