Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our company imports 2-bromo-3,3,3-trifluoroprop-1-ene (generically known as 2-BTP; CAS# 1514-82-5) for use as a ‘clean fire suppressing agent’ in handheld extinguishers for use in aerospace industry. These special life-safety extinguishers are replacing the halon 1211 extinguishers, which are being phased out due to the ozone depletion properties of halon 1211 as decided in the Montreal Protocol 1987. It is only since 2016 that the commercialization of extinguishers containing 2-BTP is implemented in the aerospace market.

The 2-BTP extinguishing agent, based on its combination of properties, is the sole substance that has been accepted to replace halon 1211 for aviation handheld extinguishers. The aviation industry continues to work on additional aircraft model approvals to complete its full transition away from halon 1211 by the December 2025 Critical Use End Date under Commission Regulation (EU) No. 744/2010.

We have been involved in the creation of special fire extinguisher hardware, but the halogenated agent which we are using in the fire extinguisher was developed by industry groups, academics, and chemical companies.  Over the last four decades, there has been significant activity in the identification and development work to find alternatives to the halons that have been used for aviation.  This work has led to identifications of HCFCs, HFCs, HFOs, and fluorinated ketone compounds which have succeeded the halons 1211 and 1301. The specific extinguishing compound that we currently use, stabilized 2-bromo-3,3,3-trifluoropropene (“2-BTP”), evolved from an identification effort started in 1994 by the Advanced Agent Working Group.

As some contextual background here, water was the original extinguishing agent used in the cabins of aircraft in the early days of aviation.  However, this was not adequate to fight the types of fires that might occur onboard today`s commercial passenger aircraft.  “The requirement for Halon 1211 had its origin with enhancing in-flight firefighting capability, including the need to deal with the hijacking/arsonist threat which was prevalent in the late 1970s.” (Ref: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Handheld MPS, DOT/FAA/AR-01/37) After the industry move to halon 1211, additional benefits were determined.  The halon 1211 agent distinguished itself by extinguishing two aircraft fires that were inside wall or cheek areas of the aircraft, which saved lives (Ref: (FAA).  Halon Replacement Performance Testing.  Notice 93-1.  Federal Register Vol. 58, No. 115, Thursday, June 17, 1993.  pp. 33477-33481.).  This capability for the agent to suppress these “hidden” fire events is now required.

After the Montreal Protocol went into effect on January 1, 1989, restricting production of ozone depleting compounds, there was significant industry and academic interest in identification of halon alternatives. Several HFC compounds were identified which had the appropriate physical properties, including being non-flammable.  A few HCFC compounds were also identified which had low ozone depletion values, although even at the time these were considered as transition chemicals.  All the new compounds, with the exception of CF3I, which falls outside the ECHA definition of PFAS, required significantly more weight and volume than these new compounds and research continued.

CF3I was first evaluated as a fire suppression agent in 1947 by researchers at Purdue University during a study of halogenated compounds sponsored by the US Army.  This was the study that identified the halons 1211 and 1301, which eventually became industry standard for aviation due to their significant fire extinguishing capabilities at lower weights combined with better toxicity profiles than previous clean agents.  After the production stop for the halons was announced, there was renewed interest in CF3I, and the CF3I Ad hoc Working Group was formed to complete the data gaps that were missing for it.  While this was a promising agent, due to the cost, stability, and especially toxicity, its use in fire protection has been negligible.

The CF3I compound has a LOAEL (lowest observable adverse effect level) of 0,4%vol, while a safe extinguishing of a fire requires a concentration of about 4 to 5%vol. This means that CF3I makes the minimum safe volumes for a discharge very large. Therefore, the use in small volumes in areas such as galleys, lavatories, cockpits and especially helicopter cockpits or in general smaller aircraft might result in toxic and lethal concentration for humans. [Toxicity review for Trifluoroiodomethane (CF3I) W. C. McCain and J. Macko Toxicology Directorate April 1990]

There are significant requirements that fire extinguishing agents for aircraft need to meet. In fact, there were several halon 1211 alternative options available for aircraft to use, but these had drawbacks in terms of requiring a much larger amount of agent (which significantly impacts storage locations, added weight, and ease of use for flight attendants), and/or having a high global warming potentials, and/or having an undesirable toxicity profile for use onboard aircraft in handhelds (such as CF3I).

However, based on the investment to create the CF3I Ad hoc Working Group, this group morphed into what became known as the Advanced Agent Working Group, which formed in 1994 (Ref: New Mexico Engineering Research Institute report, NMERI 1994/40/31790).  Its members were academia, fire suppression companies, chemical companies, laboratories, military, and end users (petroleum companies that had extensive halon 1301 total flooding systems). This group funded extensive studies of chemical families by the New Mexico Engineering Research Institute. The most promising candidate compounds were synthesized in small quantities (typically a very expensive step) in order to confirm their physical, extinguishing, and sometimes acute toxicity properties.

In a 2001 paper presented at the annual Halon Options Technical Working Conference, it was stated “For the last 5 years the Advanced Agent Working Group (AAWG) has been funding research into ‘second generation’ halon alternatives. One avenue has been that of tropodegradable bromocarbons, which retain the chemical fire suppression properties of halon, but incorporate functional groups that promote rapid atmospheric degradation, thus minimising both ozone depletion and global warming.” (Ref: Grigg, et al, 1994 Halon Options Technical Working Conference Proceedings).    In the end, the working group had helped to identify 2-BTP as a promising halon 1211 candidate but were unable to identify a halon 1301 candidate.

In 2001, American Pacific Corporation (AMPAC) took over development from the Advanced Agent Working Group to commercialize 2-BTP. Development (fire testing, toxicity tests) continued on and off for several years and began again in earnest in 2009 based on support from Boeing.  In 2016, the 2-BTP extinguishing agent was finally ECHA approved, available in UL listed fire extinguisher hardware, and FAA/EASA approved for use onboard aircraft. So, from start to finish, this compound took roughly 21 years to reach the market from the time the compound was identified. Please note that while the fire extinguisher containing 2-BTP was commercialized in 2016, for aviation, each aircraft model must go distinctly through its own approval process which adds additional time, and this will be discussed later.

According to the recent December 2022 United Nations Environment Program’s Fire Suppression Technical Options Committee, “For portable extinguishers, no new agents have been developed to commercialization since 2018.”  We have reached out to all known chemical companies involved in fire protection and there are no new fire halon alternative extinguishing agents in the developmental pipeline that we are aware of.

A fire onboard an aircraft is quite a scary event and stopping the spread of the fire has significant life safety ramifications.  EASA European Technical Standard Order (ETSO)-2C515, Aircraft Halocarbon Clean Agent Hand-Held Fire Extinguisher, requires the use of halocarbon alternatives to replace halon 1211.  This ETSO flows down and incorporates the following requirements and standards: SAE AS6271, UL 711, UL 2129, U.S. FAA AC-20-42D and DOT/FAA/AR-01/37. The last document listed is entitled Development of a Minimum Performance Standard for Hand-Held Fire Extinguishers as a Replacement for Halon 1211 on Civilian Transport Category Aircraft and contains requirements that the combination of fire extinguisher and extinguishing agent must go through in order to be approved for use onboard aircraft. The extinguishing agent must be able to achieve Class A and Class C ratings, as well as extinguish a 5B sized heptane pool fire, under UL 711, Standard for the Rating and Fire Testing of Fire Extinguishers. Class A covers the ability of the extinguishing agent to extinguish fires involving ordinary combustibles (paper, cloth, plastics, etc.) and Class B covers the ability to extinguish flammable liquids and gases. A Class C rating confirms the lack of electrical conductivity, so the user is protected from electrical shock and allows the use of the agent on fires involving energized equipment. The document also requires an evaluation of the severity of any toxic byproducts produced during a simulated in-flight fire event.  Additionally suitable extinguishing agents which are to be regarded “clean” must be electrically non-conducting volatile liquid or gaseous agent which leaves no residue (liquid or solid).

Beginning in the 1990’s and formalized in 2002 with the publication of DOT/FAA/AR-01/37,
the UK CAA and the US FAA developed a special hidden fire test. In the development report for this special fire test (CAA Paper 95013), it is indicated “Fires have occurred behind cabin side walls, where the only access is by prying up the edge of a panel and discharging an extinguisher. In these examples it may be necessary for the extinguishant to travel up or down and/or across aircraft frames in order to reach the fire. There have been other examples where the fire has been below the floor in the relatively large and open cheek area between the cargo bay and the fuselage skin. Halon 1211 has been discharged through the floor level air grilles and averted what would have otherwise been a major catastrophe.”  So, to avert major catastrophe, all halon 1211 replacement agents need to have the ability to extinguish fires that are obscured and behind walls.  This specific requirement relies on the discharge agent vaporizing and there being sufficient vapors to extinguish the fire.  The 2-BTP extinguishing agent has a much higher boiling point than halon 1211, thus leading to slower vaporization of the agent, making the hidden fire a more difficult test to pass at an acceptable agent weight.  Based on all the tests, while passing the test in the same smaller size extinguisher as used with halon 1211, 2-BTP requires 50% more agent weight than halon 1211 for the standard UL 5B:C rated handheld.

In terms of toxicity, the FAA has developed a special seat-fire test, which simulates a terrorist event where gasoline is poured across a row of passenger seats.  The extinguishing agent must be able to have an acceptable throw range to reach the seats from a distance and extinguish this fire event.  When halogenated extinguishing agents decompose in a fire event, they create hydrofluoric acid (HF), and this must not exceed a specific acute emergency exposure limit.  Certain agents that contain bromine, such as 2-BTP, will also produce some hydrobromic acid (HBr), which is also evaluated.  2-BTP was tested against this seat fire event by the FAA, and it has been shown to effectively extinguish the fire and be safe for use in the cabin based on level of decomposition products being below the maximum established by FAA [Morrison, FAA Presentation, International Aircraft Systems Fire Protection Forum, May 2011].

In addition to the decomposition products, the neat extinguishing agent levels must also be found acceptable for use in aircraft compartments based on the amount of extinguishing agent, the volume of the compartment, the ventilation of the compartment, and the allowable arterial blood level of the extinguishing agent.  This guidance is found in FAA Advisory Circular 20-42D, Hand Fire Extinguishers for use in Aircraft.  Acceptable exposure levels are modelled using a physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model simulating the breath-by-breath uptake and expelling of the agent covering the most sensitive of the population based on various organ and blood partition coefficients.

Classic extinguishing agents will not meet these requirements for a variety of reasons.  Water cannot extinguish a class B gasoline fire and has no capability to extinguish hidden fires.  AC 20-42D “…recommends that dry chemical. dry powder, and carbon dioxide hand extinguishers, in general, should not be used in aircraft.”  Dry powder is a specialty extinguishing medium (normally sodium chloride based) for metal fires and not normally of any use onboard aircraft.  For dry chemical (normally monoammonium phosphate or sodium bicarbonate based), the AC states that it is “…not recommended for hand extinguishers for internal aircraft use, due to the potential for corrosion damage to electronic equipment, the possibility of visual obscuration if the agent were discharged into the flight deck area, and the cleanup problems from their use.”  Carbon dioxide is not effective against ordinary combustibles (carries no Class A rating) and the FAA has concerns about life-threatening hypoxia (low oxygen) potentially associated with its use.

In addition to all the above, the extinguisher must operate properly well below freezing, -40°C (FAA AC 20-42D). This alone discounts all water with additive extinguishing agents.

So, in summary, EASA requires the use of a halogenated extinguishing agent in handheld fire extinguishers onboard an aircraft, and that extinguishing agent should: not limit visibility, have an acceptable acute toxicity for both the neat agent and its decomposition products, be capable of achieving a Class A , B, and C rating, have the ability to extinguish fires in hidden areas, still operate properly at extremely low temperatures, and be able to accomplish all this at a reasonable weight penalty compared to halon 1211.

We have detailed the full process timeline above for the 2-BTP agent, which is not an unusual case.  A portion of this timeline is simply the US EPA and EU ECHA timelines for new chemical approvals.  For 2-BTP it took roughly 3 years for the physical property, environmental fate, and toxicological studies to be completed in order to file the new chemical submittals.  For our industry, both US and EU chemical approvals are crucial.  While the EU ECHA new chemical process was relatively quick, the US process took 3 years to complete.  Therefore, once a candidate compound has been identified, the time to complete the list of required studies in order to submit the new chemical application, assuming the results of all these studies are acceptable (which is not a certainty, as observed with other failed candidates in the past), and then receive the approval can be 6 years in length.

In addition to the other regulatory processes, extinguishers onboard aircraft is not as simple as unbuckling one extinguisher and replacing it with another.  EASA ETSO-2C515 discussed above, calls out five other requirement documents.  However, the process continues as the new extinguisher hardware will have a different weight, dimension, and agent, such that a full evaluation including updates of drawings, part numbers, wall stress calculations, and minimum safe volume calculations for each compartment, need to be accomplished.  This evaluation will result in an update to the Supplemental Type Certification (STC) for a specific aircraft model.  To streamline the STC update process, we worked with the EASA, and they issued ETSO EASA.21O.10077848 in December 2021.  With commercialization of the fire extinguisher in 2016, this streamlining document took 5 years to issue.

The aviation industry continues to work on additional aircraft model approvals in order to complete its full transition away from halon 1211 by the December 2025 Critical Use End Date under Commission Regulation (EU) No. 744/2010.

The ECHA PFAS restriction draft contains wording that seems to have captured the changing dynamic and the needs of our industry.  For example, language in the PFAS restriction states:

• “5m) The derogation applies to fire-suppressing agents in the form of fluorinated gases used for extinguishing fires in high-risk situations where alternatives pose significant risk to health or the assets to be protected. These situations may include aviation, data centres and cultural/historic resources. Such agents are different from fire-fighting foams which are aqueous mixtures.”
• “Alternatives available, but for some applications they have a range of drawbacks, for example risk of asphyxiation (e.g. CO2), potential to damage protected assets (e.g. water), slower speed of action than fluorinated gases. Critical applications include aviation and military vehicles.”
• “Price already provides a mechanism favouring alternatives to fluorinated gases and has led to a significant shift in the market where they are not considered necessary. Remaining users which include safety critical applications such as fire prevention on aircraft and in military vehicles, and protection of cultural assets, consider the benefits of fluorinated gases sufficient to accept higher prices indicating potential for significant consumer surplus losses. [sufficiently strong evidence]”

Based on the above, we think it is already well understood in the PFAS draft that halogenated fire suppressants are used in niche areas, like the aviation industry, where they are critical for saving lives and protecting assets.  We hope that this detailed description of our case will help you to better understand how important the use of 2-BTP is for us and the entire aviation industry. One concern raised in the 2023 Progress Report of the Montreal Protocol Technology and Economic Assessment Panel (TEAP) is that, should PFAS regulation come into force now, it may seem more attractive to continue to rely on halons.

The 13,5-year derogation proposal for clean fire suppressing agents cannot be met based on lack of alternatives in the development pipeline due to the wide array of extinguishing performance requirements, significant regulatory time to achieve new chemical approval, and lengthy aviation regulatory process to approve fire extinguishers for each model of aircraft.

Therefore, we would request a full exemption for onboard aviation use.  At the very least, we would ask that instead of a 13,5-year derogation, that the derogation align with the F-Gas phase out date for HFCs of 2050.  HFCs are used onboard aircraft and as they are allowed to continue through 2050 since they are ‘required to meet safety standards’ under the recent F-Gas amendment.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Our comments relate to Fire Suppressants in Table 9 of Annex XV restriction report. More specifically, our comments relate to clean fire suppressing agents used onboard aircraft in handheld fire extinguishers, and as contemplated, for fixed system lavatory fire extinguishers.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: A detailed emission calculation (EmissionCalculation.pdf) with effective mass and percentage as well as a process flow chart (Process Flow Chart.pdf) for the whole lifecycle is provided in the confidential attachment.   The 2-BTP clean fire extinguishing agent that we use is a replacement for halon 1211, which has been successfully recycled and reused in new fire extinguisher hardware for the last 29 years since production stopped in 1994. Allowance for recycling and reuse of the 2-BTP, similar to halon 1211 will be important to not immediately disrupt the market.  2-BTP, as we purchase it, contains a small amount of stabilizers and has a lifetime of 12 years once transferred into the extinguisher.  At the end of this lifetime, the agent will be cleaned, re-stabilized, re-certified and expected then to be reused in new extinguishing hardware.    Manufacturing Phase  The 2-BTP is produced by our supplier in the USA, where it is filled into 600 kg bulk tanks and stored safely. The original bulk containers are transported to our partner in Italy for further processing. The filling process is generated with vacuum, so in general there is no emission except a small amount through connecting and disconnecting. The filling station is designed to ensure that any 2-BTP vapors released during the handling, through fitting connection/disconnections, are controlled.   The empty tanks, which have small rest amount of 2-BTP, are shipped back to our Supplier in the US where they run through some process steps and will be refilled. Another point where emissions occur is quality control in Germany at our production site.  At specified intervals, a fire extinguisher is removed from the production line and discharged to prove the proper function of the fire extinguisher hardware and validation of extinguishing agent discharge pattern and spray duration. The liquid phase of the extinguishing agent is collected in a container and later fed into the recycling process. The evaporated part is collected by an extraction system with an activated charcoal filter and is not released directly into the environment.   Use Phase  Our specific use is handheld fire extinguishers for use in the aerospace industry. Fire extinguishers containing 2-BTP are considered high performance and fulfill an important role in fire protection. Based on the known frequency of handheld fire extinguisher discharges onboard commercial airplanes, the probability of discharge of 2-BTP from a handheld fire extinguisher in flight is anticipated to be approximately 1,5 x 10-6 per flight; based on reported discharges, 53 percent of those releases are expected to be on actual fires (Boeing 2013 via US EPA, Significant New Alternatives Policy Program Fire Extinguishing and Explosion Prevention Sector, Risk Screen on Substitutes, As a Streaming Agent in Civil Aviation Applications, Substitute: 2-bromo-3,3,3-trifluoropropene (2-BTP), March 25, 2016, Final). We assume 47% to be caused by misuse or accidental release. Due to the immense cost of the agent and to further reduce the amount of emission further discharges for training purposes do not take place. These special life-safety extinguishers for use in the aerospace industry must not be allowed to produce permanent emissions due to leakage. Our fire extinguishers are designed to be on board an aircraft for 12 years and to be always operational. Accordingly, a permanent leakage would not be acceptable for extinguishers.    End-of-life Phase  We as a sustainable company are working on a general return system for all our products including those products that contain PFAS as there are our fire extinguishers. We plan to establish a worldwide functioning “Deposit System” so that our extinguishers are returned to our premises at their end of life which happens after 12-years in service. We understand the challenge to overcome financial hurdles for transportation cost and the motivation of the end user that need to be solved in a smart way. We are working on and hope to have established such until 2029 when the first of our fire extinguisher reach their end of life.  The emissions for the end-of-life phase have a large variance depending on which year is considered. Many Halon extinguishers will still be replaced until the phaseout in 2025. This results in fluctuating emission values for the years that hit the 12-year lifetime cycle.   At this time, we do not have knowledge of destruction.  A detailed emission calculation (EmissionCalculation.pdf) with effective mass and percentage as well as a process flow chart (Process Flow Chart.pdf) for the whole lifecycle is provided in the confidential attachment.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: For the end-of -life phase, no information is known for our specific case regarding waste management in terms of incineration or similar. Our waste management plan is to produce no “waste” at all, rather we plan to reuse all circulated extinguishing agent through a recycling process already established for halon 1211. Due to the immense cost of the agent, we have no interest in scraping and wasting the agent but rather in creating a fully cradle to cradle process.  Should the proposed restriction be implemented it seems probable that the end-of-life emissions will increase significantly as the agent loses its value.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: The extinguishers that we provide in the aerospace industry are filled with 2-BTP that have small quantities of stabilizers. The material can be considered as pure substance and there is nothing to separate out to meet an upper PFAS limit.  Our company worked with the extinguishing agent supplier to have a program for recycling, recertification, and re-use of this PFAS agent, which has been described in box 2 above.

5. Proposed derogations: For an estimate of annual estimated emissions, which can be considered for the evaluation of the industry of clean fire suppressants, but which are not fully applicable to our specific case, we can look to a few documents from Exponent, US EPA, and the UN Technical Economic Assessment Panel. In all of these documents, they provide a total percent of the installed base that may be released as emissions over the course of a year.  This will include releases of the agent for any and all uses: use to extinguish fires, training, testing against standards to achieve ratings, handling, leakage when filling containers, leaking when recovering material, etc.  A detailed emission calculation (EmissionCalculation.pdf) with effective mass and percentage as well as a process flow chart (Process Flow Chart.pdf) for the whole lifecycle is provided in the confidential attachment.   To further reduce the amount of emission due to strong technical training requirements have even designed and produced a trainer which is a fire extinguishing dummy using pressurized air and or water to avoid discretionary emissions during trainings when possible.  As noted prior, 2-BTP is currently the only accepted alternative to halon 1211 for this use. And, as the EU has a looming deadline at the end of 2025 to replace all halon 1211 extinguishers onboard aircraft, we can make an assumption that starting in 2026, all extinguishers for aviation will contain 2-BTP.    Based on the entry into the market, the first extinguishers sold will hit the 12-year mark in 2029.  Also, a large portion of the general aviation market is still transitioning over the next two years in order to meet the end of 2025 phaseout requirement for halon 1211 extinguishers.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Annex E has a section (E.2.8.4.7., page 252) on fire suppressants which correctly identifies that there are no currently identified chemicals that can replace clean agent fire extinguishing agents.  This Annex also contains a statement that it may take well over 10 years for a substance to be available for a transition.    Due to GWP (Global Warming Potential) and ODP (Ozone Depleting Potential) values Halon 1211 handheld fire extinguishers used onboard aircraft are still phased out and replaced by extinguishers containing the 2-BTP agent.  Since the Montreal Protocol 1987, which went into force 01.01.1989, replacement investigations are ongoing. In 2016, the 2-BTP extinguishing agent was finally ECHA approved, available in UL listed fire extinguisher hardware, and FAA/EASA approved for use onboard aircraft.    There are no new extinguishing agent options in the development pipeline of major chemical companies.  EASA specifically requires a halogenated clean agent to be used, and this is because of the unique performance and acceptable toxicity levels of the agents being used.    More information on these unique performance requirements and regulatory process are included in our general comments.  The 13,5-year derogation proposal for clean fire suppressing agents cannot be met because of the lack of alternatives in the development pipeline due to the wide range of aviation authority requirements for extinguishing performance, significant regulatory time to achieve new chemical approval, and lengthy aviation regulatory process to approve fire extinguishers for each model of aircraft.  As this application is critical for life safety and the extinguishing agent we use, is not bio accumulative, nor persistent on its own and captured only as an arrowhead for trifluoracetic acid (TFA).  We believe it will take at least 20 to 30 years before another acceptable candidate is identified and commercialized (see ongoing Halon 1211 replacement). We note that HFCs are currently used onboard aircraft, and these agents are covered under the F-Gas regulation, (EC) No 842/2006.  Recent amendments to this regulation ban the use of these agents in 2024 “except when required to meet safety standards.”  Therefore, use of HFCs onboard aircraft would be allowed to continue through the amended phase out date of 2050. While we believe unlimited derogation is reasonable, we believe that at the least, a match to the 2050 F-Gas regulation 2050 date would potentially allow time for the next generation of compounds to be identified.  Therefore, we would request a full exemption for onboard aviation use.  At the very least, we would ask that instead of a 13.5-year derogation, that the derogation align with the F-Gas phase out date for HFCs of 2050.  HFCs are used onboard aircraft and as they are allowed to continue through 2050 since they are ‘required to meet safety standards’ under the recent F-Gas amendment.

8. Other identified uses: As in our case substitution is not technically feasible, we submit our statement regarding socio-economic impacts under SECTION V. Confidential Attachment.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: The 2-BTP agent has an atmospheric lifetime in the order of days, it has an extremely low solubility in water, and has boiling point just above room temperature which makes it vaporize and quickly partition out of water.  The neat substance is not bio accumulative.  The agent has an acceptable toxicity which allows its use in occupied spaces onboard commercial aircraft.  This information can all be found in the REACH dossier for this compound.  2-BTP will react in the troposphere, where the most important eventual oxidation products to be bromine atom Br plus CH2O (formaldehyde), CF3C(O)CH2OH, CF3OH, (trifluoromethanol) and CF3COOH (trifluoroacetic acid, also called TFA), in proportions that depend on the speed of CF3C(O)CH2OH wet deposition versus OH reaction.  [Ref: Patten, Wuebbles, et al., Journal of Geophysical Research, 2011, Vol. 116, D24307].

10. Analytical methods: Further analytic methods for PFAS are unknown for us.   After consultation of our extinguishing agent supplier and Prof. Dr. Sebastian Hasenstab-Riedel (Technical University Berlin), who is advising us in fluorine-chemical concerns, the analytical methods applicable for 2-BTP are as follows.  The ASTM D26 committee publishes purity and analysis method standards for halocarbon fire extinguishing agents.  For the extinguishing agent use, 2-BTP, the appropriate standard is ASTM D6060, Standard Specification for 2-Bromo-3,3,3-Trifluoro-1-Propene (CF3CBr=CH2).  Target analytical methods are in general possible for 2-BTP. Most common techniques are based on LC- or GC-MS/MS and have a very high selectivity and sensitivity. As the 2-BTP is a pure substance the analytic process is possible. However, it is a highly reactive species which will decompose in the atmosphere and form TFA which of course can also analytically be characterized by analytical PFAS techniques. Further techniques would be so called non-target screening (NTS) separation systems which are coupled with high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS).

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Information on alternatives Information on benefits Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our company is a globally active, medium-sized family-owned company that offers high-quality functional solutions made of plastic and rubber for automotive and industrial companies.
In the automotive sector we focuse on the product areas Noise Vibration Harshness and Sealing, Thermal Management, Drive Technology and Air Guides.
We cover a broad portfolio of products, which are used in particular for sealing, vibration and noise reduction, for regulating cooling circuits, as engine and drive components, and for absorbing and cleaning air in engines.
In the non-automotive sector we concentrate on the industrial vibration technology, functional solutions for measurement and control systems, piping components and railway.
We produce products – mainly sealings - made of Fluoroelastomers (FKM and FVMQ). We also use PTFE Film in our products for Thermal Management.
Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers can be classified as PFAS based on their molecular structure. However, their toxicological and eco-toxicological profile is essentially different from the majority of PFAS substances. Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers are recognised by the OECD as safe materials: "PLC" = polymer of low concern.
Polymers which fulfil die OECD criteria for polymers of low concern also fulfil the polymers of low concern criteria proposed by CARACAL (CARACAL, 2021). Fluoropolymers are not classified as hazardous substances under the CLP regulation3.
Vulcanized elastomers have special mechanical properties which differentiate them from other polymeric or inorganic material. They are flexible (elastically deformable) and stretchable to multiple of their length (high elongation at break).
For our products the essential properties of the used Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers are:
a) High flexibility
b) Chemical inertness regarding a big variety of medias, including harsh chemicals like chlorine gas, hydrofluoric acid and others
c) thermal resistance against low and high temperatures (higher than 150°C)
There is no alternative material currently available, that combines all these properties.
Based on the recognition by the OECD as safe materials: "PLC" = polymer of low concern we request to exempt the Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers from PFAS regulation or use restrictions.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Manufacture of rubber and plastic products for automotive industry and industrial applications. Mainly use Fluoroelastomers in sealings, gaskets, grommets, membranes in the own production. Fluoroelastomers are also part of the components which we buy from our suppliers for example hoses, O-rings. Additionally to this we use PTFE film in our Thermal management applications. Fluoropolymers can be also part of some plastic materials which are used in our production.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: There is no emission of FKM polymer possible during production process of seals. There are closed systems (mixing process) and the thermal stress (max. 230 °C) is below the decomposition temperature (> 360 °C). The waste occurs in a solid, fully vulcanized form. 100 % of the waste is collected. The waste is handed over to a disposal company or reused as recyclate.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Fluoropolymers an Fluoroelastomers should not be treated as monomeric PFAS. There are no emissions of momeric PFAS into the environment at the end of life of items made with fluoropolymers.  For the automotive sector there are IMDS and ELV directives. Both regulate the separation of waste and the end-of-life treatment of such products.  At the end, a fluoropolymer gasket is not creating any kind of emission because of its molecular structure: it has a short saturated chain, no emissions in the environment, is not biodegradable.

5. Proposed derogations: We currently process 250 tonnes of Fluoroelastomers per year (as raw material or purchased parts). Due to the fact of the special requirement profiles of the uses, we do not see any possibility of substitution in these applications.

6. Missing uses: Fluoroelastomers find application in scenarios demanding an elastic material capable of withstanding elevated temperatures, a diverse array of chemicals, harsh weathering, or a fusion of these challenging conditions. They need to be reliable which translates to extended lifespans. Presently, no other polymers or polymer blends have been identified that exhibit comparable physicochemical properties to those of fluoroelastomers like FKM and FFKM. The restriction proposal lists some elastomers which could be considered as alternatives for certain applications, namely - HNBR and NBR - ACM and AEM - silicone rubber (non-fluorinated) - tribo-modified polyurethane - CR -EPDM. All those elastomers differ from fluoroelastomers (FKM, FFKM) mainly by their resistance which results in a shorter lifetime. NBR has approx. 10% of the lifetime of FKM, in applications above 100 °C it is even lower. There is no alternative material currently available, that combines all necessary properties. Considering all of these factors, the transition period towards adopting fluoropolymer-free rubber components for their respective applications is likely to extend beyond 15 years.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: There are no alterntives available that meet the requirements for applications where seals with FKM/FPM/FVMQ material are used. Adopting fluoropolymer-free rubber components for their respective applications is likely to extend beyond 15 years. PTFE film and lubricated polymers for friction application is not substitutable. As a substitute for PTFE film, we have tested alternative materials in the confined friction case, but have not found any suitable substitute materials.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our company is a leading European manufacturer of reefer trailers, and we rely on fluorinated gases (F-Gases), specifically hydrofluoro-olefins (HFOs) such as R1233zd(e), as blowing agents in insulating foam. These substances are proposed to be restricted, and we would like to provide evidence specifically on this subset of substances.
Refrigerated transport capability is crucial for successfully shipping products, particularly food and pharmaceuticals, while complying with the required cooling conditions set by the authorities. In Europe, the cooling conditions are regulated by the ATP agreement (ECE/Trans/322), which mandates a minimum insulating capability of a reefer trailer of at least k of less than or equal to 0.4 mW/(m²*K) for frozen goods (FRC). Simplified, the k-value is roughly proportional to the thermal conductivity of a material divided by its thickness (k ~ lambda/d).
In Europe, the dimensions of trailers are also regulated by the Council Directive 96/53/EC of July 25, 1996. According to this directive, the width of a trailer for temperature-controlled transportation units with wall thickness over 45mm cannot exceed 2600mm, which is already an exception to the nominal vehicle width of 2550mm.
Additionally, the euro pallet, measuring 1200x800 mm², is the most common standard goods carrier in Europe. Considering these dimensions, a refrigerated trailer must have a minimum clear inside width of 2400mm, plus some extra space (around 60mm) for movement clearance during loading, etc. These dimensional restrictions result in a maximum insulating wall thickness of 70mm on each side.
Furthermore, trailer sidewalls, roof, and floor must contain recessed and flush technical elements for load securing, as per §22 of the German STVZO. These elements, necessary to avoid damage to the transported goods or the trailer during loading, reduce the overall insulating capability of the sidewalls, roof, and floor by locally reducing the insulating thickness. To compensate for this reduction, significantly thicker roof and floor panels are used.
To meet the requirements of the ATP agreement within these limitations and other restrictions, it is essential to minimize the thermal conductivity of the insulating material as much as possible. This is achieved by utilizing low lambda blowing agents, such as HFOs.
Our company utilizes HFOs as blowing agents in the insulating foam to provide superior thermal insulation and achieve the lowest possible k-values. This approach enables us to take environmental responsibility by reducing fuel consumption and emissions of pollutants from the cooling unit's engine, particularly CO2, CO, and NOx. Additionally, it maximizes the load capacity of reefer trailers.
If HFOs were included in the PFAS ban and alternatives like cyclopentane were used, the thermal conductivity would increase by approximately 20%. This would result in reduced thermal insulating capability at the given dimensions and restrictions.
Consequently, compensating for this loss in insulating capacity would require either increasing the wall thickness of the remaining large areas (e.g., sidewalls), omitting some securing features mentioned above, or increasing fuel consumption and emissions of the cooling unit by running it for longer periods or more frequently to maintain the desired temperature.
Our company strongly believes that the latter two options are not viable. Furthermore, we are convinced that it is not feasible to easily change the external dimensions of reefer trailers or the dimensions of goods carriers in the next few years. Such changes would necessitate significant redesigns of reefer trailers and the logistics infrastructure (warehouses, gates, etc.) required to ensure a secure cooling chain for food.
This leaves trailer manufacturers with the only viable option of increasing the sidewall thickness at the expense of the clear inside width.
Reducing the internal width of a trailer would inevitably result in a loss of six pallet spaces, which is about 19% loss in transportation capacity per trailer. Consequently, more trailers (or runs) would be needed to transport the same amount of goods from one destination to another. This would increase road load, traffic, and the emission of pollutants (CO2, CO, NOx, etc.) from truck engines and cooling units' engines, without considering the potential need for increased transport capacity.
Additionally, reducing the inner width of reefer trailers would decrease the efficiency of cooling units, as they would need to cool empty space without payload.
Considering these points and the arguments listed in the attachment provided in section 4, our company, as a European market leader in temperature-controlled logistics concepts, demands that the liquid blowing agent R1233zd(e) be exempted from the PFAS ban.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Transport refrigeration

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our Company is a leading timeless high-end watch manufacturer. We do appreciate the possibility to submit comments regarding the proposed restriction of PFAS under the REACH Regulation. We would like to express our concerns regarding the absence of derogations for our use sector, i.e the watch industry.
This industry has a certain number of challenges, starting from the extralong product lifetime, the research of high precision and reliability as well as comfort for the client.
Within this scope, lubricants with high performances are necessary and some, to this date, contain PFAS substances such as Polytetrafluorethylene (PTFE) powder.
Scope of the exemption request:
5. By way of derogation, paragraphs 1 and 2 shall not apply to:
xx: the use of PTFE powder in lubricants (liquid or solid) for the mechanical movement of timepieces, until 13.5 years of EiF

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: This contribution applies to the following use sectors: lubricants (sector as a whole). More specifically, it addresses the use of PTFE powder in lubricants, as additives (in oils or coatings), including the process of manufacturing the lubricant and its distribution.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: a) Emissions by the producer of PTFE powder are not known by the author. Less than 50 kg (upper estimation) per year of this PFAS substance are at stake for the whole watchmaking sector in order to guarantee production, use, servicing and end of life of timepieces. Most of the product stays within the timepieces. The remaining (residue from production or servicing), estimated at less than 10% of the whole tonnage, is treated through special equipment and dedicated services.  b) Special waste treatment companies are authorized by national authorities to collect the waste of chemical compounds (including the concerned PFAS-substance), according to their categories. Regarding the described substances, 100% of the waste of these substances are subject to high-temperature incineration for other industries.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Most mechanical timepieces using PTFE-based lubricants are not destroyed but serviced and kept operational for decades. The great majority of the products are not disposed as domestic waste.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: a) The concentration limits proposed in paragraph 2 of the proposed restriction entry text would impede the recycling of the residual powder of PTFE during its production or at the end of its use in after-sales services branches.  b) Not relevant, as it would not be possible to achieve the proposed concentration limits.  c) Not relevant, as it would not be possible to achieve the proposed concentration limits.

5. Proposed derogations: The annual tonnage of PTFE powder for the whole watchmaking sector is estimated at 50 kg. Emissions are limited due to the fact that the end-product is not considered as domestic waste and has a long life-expectancy. The residual wastes (during production of lubricants and servicing) are collected by dedicated companies and incinerated for other industries.

6. Missing uses: a) The annual tonnage and emissions (at sub-sector level) and type of PFAS associated with the relevant use.  1. Production of PTFE powder In the context of the watchmaking industry, the PTFE powder used in lubricants is sourced from  dedicated industrial partners. No emissions are directly linked to the watchmaking industry at this stage and we do not know the emissions tonnage by the producer. The annual tonnage is estimated (with no guarantee due to a confidential context) at less than 50 kg   worldwide, in order to produce the necessary lubricants for the watchmaking sector (and associated servicing). More than 99% of this annual tonnage goes to the realization of greases, using PTFE powder as thickener.   2. Use of PTFE powder in the realization of lubricants for the timepieces It is estimated that 95% of the implied PTFE powder to produce lubricants are efficiently used. The residual product is found in the equipment, in a laboratory environment where chemical wastes are properly disposed of (by a local specialist of the treatment of chemical products). The annual tonnage is estimated as more or less the same amount than in the previous paragraph: less than 50 kg. The residue to be treated is then estimated at 2 kg.  3. Use of PTFE powder added to lubricants in timepieces The lubricants are provided to end users for industrial and professional uses only. These lubricants  are not accessible to consumers through retail outlets.  Due to its form as an additive in coatings or oils, PTFE powder, once deposited within the timepiece, is not released under normal use, for several years   (until servicing). No emissions or estimation of tonnage can be linked to this stage.  4. Servicing of timepieces using PTFE powder added to lubricants During the service of a timepiece, the product is opened, disassembled and completely cleaned. During this process (and especially its last step), the PTFE powder is washed away, collected, and properly disposed of through dedicated equipment and protocols.   The annual tonnage associated to this servicing procedure is estimated at less than 25 kg   worldwide mainly in the form of transit from the production site to the aftersales services for relubrication of timepieces.  5. End of life of timepieces using PTFE powder in lubricants Most timepieces using PTFE-based lubricants are not destroyed but serviced and kept operational for decades. The great majority of mechanical timepieces are not disposed as domestic waste.  No emissions or estimation of tonnage can be linked to this stage.  b) The key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use PTFE powder, added to solid or liquid lubricants provides: - Excellent anti-friction properties, reducing energy loss in mechanical systems; - Protection against wear by smoothly separating surfaces sliding on each other; - Good miscibility/compatibility with its chemical partners (oils for the greases, liquid solutions for its deposition in coatings); - Inertness regarding the materials in contact with it; - Easiness of deposition.  c) The number of companies in the sector estimated to be affected by the restriction.  PTFE powder is vastly used as thickener or additive in lubrication. Therefore, as far as we know, we assume that all companies involved in the watchmaking industry, producing mechanical timepieces, will be concerned to some extent.  d) The availability, technical and economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives for the relevant use, including information on the extent (in terms of market shares) to which alternative-based products are already offered on the EU market and whether any shortages in the supply of relevant alternatives are expected.  There are only a handful of producers of lubricants for the watchmaking sector worldwide. Some alternatives of PTFE powder as thickener or additive can be found on the market, but no lubricants incorporating such alternatives can directly replace our current solution.  In order to meet the technical requirements of high-quality timepieces, 7 to 10 years of tests are necessary, with potential iterations regarding modifications of the conception of the systems, chemical composition of the lubricants and materials. To this date and despite strong efforts in this direction, no accelerated tests provide high confidence results that can be extrapolated. The 13.5 years-long derogation period asked within this document is directly related to this context.    e) For cases in which alternatives are not yet available, information on the status of R&D processes for finding suitable alternatives, including the extent of R&D initiatives in terms of time and/or financial investments, the likelihood of successful completion, the time expected to be required for substitution (including any relevant certification or regulatory approvals) and the major challenges encountered with alternatives which were considered but subsequently disregarded. As stated previously, no direct alternatives of lubricants without PTFE powder that meet the stringent requirements of reliability and quality of the watchmaking product are available. R&D initiatives will be conducted in this direction in order to provide suitable long-term efficient lubricants that will guarantee the performances of the timepieces. In this respect, full substitution is estimated at between 7 to 10 years.  f) For cases in which substitution is technically and economically feasible but more time is required to substitute: i. the type and magnitude of costs (at company level and, if available, at sector level) associated with substitution (e.g. costs for new equipment or changes in operating costs); At company level, the costs are estimated at 1 human resource (HR) the first year of R&D actions and then 0.5 HR over the 7 to 10 years of qualification of the product.   At first sight, no new equipment is necessary and no changes in operating costs are expected. ii. the time required for completing the substitution process (including any relevant certification or regulatory approvals); As stated in a previous paragraph, the estimated required time is between 7 to 10 years, according to our experience and potential necessary iterations. To this date, no accelerated tests are available to shorten the qualification time. iii. information on possible differences in functionality and the consequences for downstream users and consumers (e.g. estimations of expected early replacement needs or expected additional energy consumption); Differences in functionality would mean less performant timepieces (accuracy, autonomy) with shorter intervals of servicing and important loss of confidence of the clients in the company. iv. information on the benefits for alternative providers. To this date, no information can be provided related to this topic. We do not expect more or less benefits for the alternative provider(s), as the cost engaged are relatively small due to the quantities of product at stake.  g) For cases in which substitution is not technically or economically feasible, information on what the socio-economic impacts would be for companies, consumers, and other affected actors. If available, please provide the annual value of EU sales and profits of the relevant sector, and employment numbers for the sector. i. impact on consumers The lubrication of mechanical timepieces is central to its short- and long-term performances. If substitution is not found in due time, consumers will be affected through lack of accuracy and autonomy of their products, resulting in more complaints and servicing that will not be guaranteed (due to the lack of substitution). ii. impact on the watch industry  If we estimate that the whole sector is dependent on PTFE powder in the lubrication of their timepieces, the restriction under consideration, without derogation, could put at risk between 167,000 and 188,000 jobs and potentially lead to €3.0 billion in loss of export revenues and €1.3 billion in loss of tax incomes and social security contributions.  Considering the low amount of  the PFAS substance used to guarantee the quality of timepieces, as well as their limited impact in term of emission thanks to controlled environments and dedicated protocols of treatment, we can conclude that the socio-economic impacts (of an absence of derogation) are largely disproportionate. iii. annual value of EU sales and profits of the relevant sector  In 2020, watches generated €2.44 billion in export revenues for the EU, despite the significant impact of the Covid crisis (-19.6% compared to 2019). In addition, €536 million of EU watch components and straps were exported to Switzerland in 2020. Furthermore, according to these figures, the taxes generated in the EU by the analogue watchmaking industry could be estimated as follow: €780 million for VAT, €210 million for direct and indirect taxes on household income, and €70 million for direct and indirect corporate taxes. Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our company is a manufacturer of corrosion-resistant machines such as corrosion-resistant pumps and blowers, exhaust gas treatment equipment such as scrubbers, and supplies products to many factories in the semiconductor, steel, and chemical industries.

Our product, the corrosion-resistant pump, is used to transport highly corrosive fluids that immediately corrode even corrosion-resistant metals such as stainless steel.
fluoropolymer and fluoroelastomer such as PFA, PVDF, PTFE, ETFE, and FKM, which are used for parts exposed to chemicals, including sliding parts, are indispensable and irreplaceable materials for corrosion-resistant pumps due to their characteristics.

Fluoroelastomer sealing materials (O-rings, gaskets, etc.) are also used as parts of corrosion-resistant blowers. Corrosion-resistant blowers are sometimes used in production lines where highly toxic gases cannot be allowed to leak, and other sealing materials cannot provide the same level of sealing performance.
If such gas leaks, serious accidents will occur in factories using corrosion-resistant fans. Fluorine-based materials are also used to impart high water repellency to parts for safe long-term operation.

Manufacturers of semiconductor processing equipment and chemicals that use our corrosion-resistant equipment tend to use chemicals and gases with higher concentrations and temperatures to increase processing capacity. Corrosion resistance, heat resistance, and water repellency are getting higher and higher, and it is no longer possible to deal with anything other than fluoropolymer and fluoroelastomer.

Our company, which manufactures and sells corrosion-resistant equipment that uses fluoropolymer or fluoroelastomer parts, and our customers in the semiconductor, steel, and chemical product industries will not be able to manufacture state-of-the-art equipment such as semiconductors due to the disappearance of these excellent corrosion-resistant machines. We will lose business, experience significant impairments, and suffer across the board from the resulting losses. Furthermore, investments in employees and sustainable production equipment will go unrewarded.

There are many plastics that are harmful to the environment and health. These too need to be examined, heavily regulated, or banned. However, fluoropolymer and fluoroelastomer are paramount for safely transporting harmful substances such as highly toxic chemicals and gases without leakage. Due to their excellent properties, these highly toxic chemicals and gases are indispensable for the manufacture of semiconductors and cutting-edge equipment. Without fluoropolymer and fluoroelastomer, these highly toxic chemicals and gases would leak into the environment, making it impossible to manufacture safely and causing environmental destruction. The damage to our economy and further development would be immeasurable.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Information on alternatives Request for exemption
Combined Comments: General Comments: Our company is a manufacturer of high pressure hydraulic pumps. Various sealing components are used in these pumps, which contain, among other things, PFAS. Specifically, these are shaft seals, support rings and axial seals. As consultation with our suppliers of these components has shown, it is not possible to replace PFAS with other chemical compounds without having to accept massive restrictions on the functionality of these components and, finally, of our pumps. As a result, this would lead to a significant shortening of the maintenance intervals of our pumps or to a failure of the pumps with corresponding effects on the environment (contamination with hydraulic oils). For these reasons, we reject the general ban on PFAS for our area of application. Instead, we propose to establish a sustainable circular economy for PFAS with a focus on proper end-of-life disposal.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our company is a manufacturer of hydraulic equipment, mainly for industrial drive and control applications e.g. in the metal forming and press market. With a workforce of ca. 80 employees, an annual turnover of ca. 15m € is being generated. The product portfolio comprises slip-in cartridge valves, servocartridge valves, valve accessories and control manifolds manufactured in-house as well as complete hydraulic systems incorporating hydraulic cylinders, power units, and piping in cooperation with external partners.
Literally all of our hydraulic products contain some type of sealing elements to isolate cavities or channels of pressurized hydraulic fluid against adjacent channels or the ambient environment. Mostly, these seals are ring-shaped rubber compound components, partly supported by back-up rings for stability. Additionally, linear moving parts like cylinder pistons are equipped with guide ring elements supporting external forces while minimizing friction losses.
All the aforementioned components are subject to a collective of technical requirements regarding their properties and performance within defined ranges of boundary conditions. Key criteria include pressure and load stability, deformation characteristic and elasticity, fluid compatibility and resistance, friction properties, temperature range, long-term stability and ageing behaviour. Common combinations of these requirements in our industrial applications impose an ambitious challenge on the material used in sealing, guiding and supporting components.
Currently, in ca. 80% of our products, these challenges can only be met technically through use of materials containing certain types of PFAS; mainly this applies to PTFE and FKM. PFAS-free alternatives are not available to us through our suppliers, and are not expected to be available in the foreseeable future. A full ban on PFAS would affect the major part of our products, which means we would no longer be able to serve our customers with new products and spare parts. Use of other materials with inferior technical performance would not be accepted as it would not allow customers to deliver their products compliant to performance requirements.
The consequences of this for our business model are hard to predict. We expect that they would be severe, given that the current business climate is already extremely challenging and likely to remain like this in the next years. With an additional non-availability of PFAS components on top, the worst-case scenario would see the business model collapsing with a direct impact on income revenue and financial strength of the company. Overcapacities throughout all areas of the value creation chain, but particularly in machine shop and assembly & test, would need to be approached by measures such as short-time work and redundancies. In the best-case scenario, our customers would be able to modify or downgrade their products to a lower level of performance and still be able to compete in the market. This could potentially allow us to adapt some of our products to non-PFAS alternatives. However, this does not apply to all our products, and since our customers commonly are facing strong competition in international markets particularly also from non-EU countries, this scenario is more than questionable.
Comparing the benefits of a restriction to the effort and negative impact, we consider a PFAS ban in these types of hydraulic components to produce a very disadvantageous cost/benefit ratio. This is mainly due to the fact that the industrial applications and use-cases we are serving exhibit extremely low probability of PFAS being released into the environment. They are chiefly being used in closed actuation systems or machines with no potential of accidental emission, and the installation and disposal can be and is normally well controlled by defined processes and trained expert personnel.
From our point of view, a full and non-derogated ban on PFAS is strictly not feasible and not reasonable. A derogation period of 12 years as proposed in RO2 is an absolute minimum to realistically expect viable alternatives to be made available. However, this would still not warrant that such alternatives are economically suitable for our types of products and business models.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Baseline Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our company is a small medium sized enterprise with about 50 employees and an average revenue of over 10 million Euros per year.
We are in the business of building and selling handheld and automatically operated spray valves and extrusion applicators as well as the peripheral equipment to make use of the above mentioned (e.g. pumps, pressure tanks or pressure regulators).
Our customers and the end users of our products come from various markets such as the automotive branch, the mechanical engineering sector (glass, wood, plastics, paper and packaging, electronics and foundries), the food industry and the pharmaceutical industry.
Our products are used to apply various media such as release agents, paints and rust inhibitors, oils, greases or other lubricants, flux, glues and sealants. In special cases they are even used to spray acids or lyes for chemical processes.
In this comment we focus on our use of fluoropolymers.
In our products we use sealings (static as well as dynamic) to prevent leakage of the materials which are to be applied and for the accurate functioning of valves, pressure tanks and pressure regulators.
Our default sealing materials are FKM and PTFE which we use because of their unique qualities like low friction coefficients and their high chemical resistance. The chemical resistance is needed for working with release agents or lubricants based on mineral oils or for applying solvent-based paint, primer or glue. These media often damage seals made from non-fluoropolymer materials such as NBR or EPDM which results in shorter service life, malfunctions or even safety risks.
In special cases with the use of aggressive media we use sealings made from FFKM which has an even higher chemical resistance than FKM. In those applications with aggressive, often caustic and flammable materials every small leakage because of defective sealings results in hazardous situations.
As of now we do not know of any feasible (neither technically nor economically) alternatives to fluoropolymer sealings. As it is not known whether it is possible to develop useful alternatives and if it is even possible how long this process will take: Fluoropolymers as well as the materials necessary for their production should be exempted from all regulatory activities under the REACH restriction.
Fluoropolymers can be classified as PFAS based on their molecular structure. However, their toxicological and eco toxicological profile is essentially different from the majority of PFAS substances.
Fluoropolymers that meet the OECD criteria of PLC (= polymer of low concern) are non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water soluble and non-mobile molecules and are judged to have no significant impact on the environment and humans.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: a. Industrial food and feed production b. Packaging application c. Manufacture of metal products d. Fluoropolymer applications e. Lubricant applications f. Sealing applications

5. Proposed derogations: All fluoropolymers should get permanent derogation.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: According to our OEM clients there are no viable technical alternatives for PTFE components in Medical devices or friction management applications. Furthermore there are no viable technical alternatives for PTFE, FKM or FFKM components in sealing devices.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our company is a specialist in sealing industry and a member of the French Federation of Mechanical Engineering (FIM). We would like to submit our comments on the restriction report:
- Some uses are not taken into account in the document. Indeed, our PFAS containing products are used in many sectors. Not all of them have been assessed by the restriction proposal.
- The proposed derogations give short transition period when few or no alternative exist. It should be highlighted that once a proper alternative will be found, new approval  campaigns must take place according to each sector requirements.
- Many uses of PFAS with no derogation have no alternative solutions available in short notice

The following is a non-exhaustive list of PFAS we use in our production:
- PTFE (CAS No. 9002-84-0): mixing formulations as liquid dispersion and powder, gaskets, O-rings, adhesives, fibers, yarn for braided packing, struts
- FEP (CAS No. 25067-11-2): O-rings (FKM)
- VDF-HFP (CAS No. 9011-17-0): o-rings (FKM, FFKM)
- TFE (CAS No. 204-126-9) : o-rings (FKM, FFKM)
- PMVE : o-rings (FKM, FFKM)
- PFPE : high temperature lubricant (used during mechanical seals assembly)
As end user, our suppliers are not under obligation of information about PFAS that are yet unregulated. For this reason, it is difficult for non-chemist/non-specialist people in the supply chain to narrowly identify which of our supplied materials will be under the restriction.
We ask for a distinction between polymeric and non-polymeric PFAS. Evaluation risk should be classified by groups instead of a global restriction only based on the presence of CF3– or –CF2– bonding.
Fluoropolymers, due to their chemical inertness, are not harmful for human health. Indeed, there is an exposure risk difference between polymeric and non-polymeric PFAS.
As part of a risk assessment process, we asked our polymeric PFAS suppliers, to prove their production does not release non-polymeric PFAS in the environment. We also checked that our own PFAS-containing final products do not release short-chain PFAS, such as PFOA, in a concentration above 25 ppb.
PTFE waste from manufacturing is processed by specialized companies.
As the FIM, we recommend the inclusion of exemptions for the following uses of PFAS:
- A general derogation for spare parts or components necessary for the repair, re-use or upgrading of functionalities of products placed on the market before the entry into force of this restriction or covered by a derogation.
- A derogation for the presence of PFAS in recycled materials, in particular for products that do not present a risk of releasing PFAS into the environment during the use phase.
- A derogation for all fluoropolymers for which no suitable alternative solution is available.
- A longer transition period the presence of PFAS in industrial food and feed production (12 years instead of 5) in mechanical components.
- Adequate transition period for professional products, in order to take account of the duration of the complete product re-design and renewing approvals processes that could be made necessary by the application of this restriction.
We also support a derogation renewing process in case no sustainable alternative is found by the end of the derogation time.

6. Missing uses: Following FIM’s position, it is impossible for our company, as downstream users, to collect data on tonnage and emissions (at sub-sector level) of PFAS associated with the relevant use. In addition, and due to the extreme complexity of identifying the presence of PFAS in products (except for PTFE and fluoropolymer materials) and processes for downstream users, it is not yet possible to provide data on the socio-economic impacts for each specific use. Confidential attachment regarding the specific impact in our activity is will be add to our response. Several sectors are not mentioned in the restriction report: - Chemical industry - Defence industry: Navy, army - Other niche applications: Water treatment, paper mill, pharmaceutical industry - Original equipment manufacturer (OEM) that covers lots of sectors  In addition to the uses/sub-uses mentioned in the Annex XV restriction report, we provide sealing solutions for mechanical equipments of these sectors: pumps, valve (flanges, body/seat seals…), rotary machines, industrial stirrer, industrial cookers, bottling, filling, sealing solution specific to ATEX environment, stuffing boxes, seats, flanges, bodies/bonnets: - Braided packings: mainly PTFE as fibers, powders and dispersion - Gasket: PTFE - Mechanical seals : O-ring/Strut made with fluoroelastomer (FEP, VDF, HFP, FKM, FFKM, PMVE, TFE) - High temperature lubricant : PFPE  Key functionalities: - Low friction coefficient - Resistant to a large amount of aggressive fluids such as strong acids, strong bases, alcohols, cetones, and hydrocarbures - Thermal resistance - Corrosion resistance - PFAS are also used to guarantee compliance with regulations such as CE1935/2004 for use in food contact (e.g. PTFE) - Forms (powder, dense material, dispersion) - Prices Some alternative exists but the properties are lower: - PEEK is mainly mentioned as PTFE replacement but has a nearly 4 times higher friction coefficient. Moreover, PEEK costs ~500€/kg while PTFE ~30-50€/kg. - HDPE and PA have also been identified but have a lower thermal resistance than PTFE (respectively ~130°C vs. ~250°C) - Metal is cited for static seals but is not suitable for high pressure applications - No suitable alternative have been yet identified for high temperature PFPE greases. As mentioned by FIM position, applications requiring a combination of several PFAS properties do not appear to be substitutable. In addition, solutions based on brass (with lead content) cannot be deployed or in a limited way because already regulated under the REACH and RoHS regulations. Moreover, a wide deployment of multiple substitutions to PFAS would mean renewing all of our already approved materials containing PFAS (FDA, CE1935/2004, WRAS, ACS, BAM, DVGW, TÜV, PMUC, API…). This process will cost time and money with no guarantee that the substitution materials will fully check the entire specification requirements (migration tests, fugitive emissions, service life, costs etc…)

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our company is a specialist manufacturer of industrial rubber components, with products such as O-rings and rubber seal used in the automotive, electric and industrial equipment sectors. The company can propose high quality materials, solve problems and ensure smooth production and supply to meet customer needs.

O-rings are ring-shaped rubber parts with a circular cross-section and are used for sealing. O-rings are usually assembled into grooves and compressed to fill gaps and prevent leakage of liquids and gases. O-rings are made from various types of rubber, the most common being NBR (nitrile rubber). NBR is a petroleum-based synthetic rubber with excellent oil and wear resistance. However, other materials may be more suitable depending on the operating environment.

Fluoropolymers and fluororubbers are among the materials used for O-rings and gaskets. Fluororesins include PTFE (Teflon), PFA, and FEP. Fluororubber includes FKM (fluororubber). These materials have excellent chemical and heat resistance and can be used for long periods of time under harsh conditions. PTFE also has non-adhesive and low-friction properties. These materials are indispensable in fields such as automobiles and semiconductors. In addition, there are no materials that can replace them with current technology.

Bisphenol AF is an important substance not only as a raw material for plastics, but also as a cross-linker for FKM. Cross-linkers are substances that link rubber molecules together to increase their strength and elasticity. Bisphenol AF is an irreplaceable cross-linking agent for FKMs.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Transport, Medical device

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Amount used: approx. 12 t/year (our annual FKM consumption). Share of waste: Unknown

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: a) PTFE: quantity used 0.25 t/year FKM: quantity used 12 t/year Bisphenol AF: quantity used 0.12 t/year  b) Heat resistance, chemical resistance and low sliding resistance can be met for use in industrial machinery, agricultural machinery, robotic machinery, medical and transport equipment.  d) Replacement deemed technically or economically unfeasible.  g) Substitution is considered technically or economically unfeasible. FKM has the best heat resistance as an elastic material and is the only rubber material that can be used for a long period of time at temperatures below 200°C. There is no alternative material. The chemical stability of FKM makes it resistant to various oils, solvents and chemicals, and no other material can replace it. Bisphenol AF is an important constituent (cross-linker) of the above-mentioned FKM and cannot be substituted. PTFE has excellent chemical resistance and low friction, which prevents stick-slip. The good processability of PTFE can be used in combination with rubber to provide properties not found in rubber. The above characteristics of PTFE cannot be substituted by other materials.

8. Other identified uses: See Section 7
