General Comments: Our company manufactures Polyurethane, Polyester Polyols and Speciality Chemicals systems mainly for the residential and industrial insulation markets. As a System House company, one of our core businesses in Europe is the manufacture and formulation of systems for spray polyurethane foam (SPF), the market for which is focused on products with high thermal insulation performance, high mechanical performance and processability, as well as safety in application and fire performance in use. The application of SPF by contractors is an in-situ (on site) activity.
To achieve the above-mentioned properties and performance the use of blowing agents such as HFO/HCFOs in our formulations is the key factor. The inclusion of flammable blowing agents is not an option because current product application equipment used by contractors is not designed to handle flammable products. For our own formulating operations, the high cost of adapting a chemical plant, where SPF systems are manufactured and formulated, to handle flammable products must also be considered.
In addition, the use of flammable foaming agents worsens the fire behaviour of the foam itself in its installed form, requiring a higher amount of expensive flame retardants to be included, such as halogenated fire retardants, to maintain the same properties of fire performance. This is clearly an undesirable outcome from both an economic and wider chemical safety perspective. It should also be noted that it does not make the manufacture and application of flammable formulations any safer in itself, since the flame retardants address the product performance, not the processability.
Additionally, the fact of not being able to use HFO/HFCO would lead to sacrifice some products with very good thermal insulation performance. This goes in the opposite direction to the policy of energy saving and reduction of emissions in Europe. This is especially relevant for buildings where there are space constraints (Please refer to the Confidential attachment num 5 ittem) , mainly in building renovations, where SPF technologies have proved particularly versatile with strong examples of benefits in Spain, Benelux and France in both roofing retrofits and the insulation of cellars and other ground-level spaces. and where very good thermal insulation is required to comply with insulation regulations like the long-term strategy for energy renovation in the building sector in Spain (ERESSE) which follows the Article 2a Directive 2010/31/EU, and which would save space in newly built buildings.

(https://cdn.mitma.gob.es/portal-web-drupal/ERESSE/ERESEE_2020version_ingles.pdf)

SPF based on HFOs/HCFOs are providing lambda values ranged from 0.025-0.028W/mk, the CO2-water (1) based blowing agent alternatives have lambda values higher than 0.038, that is, they are about 40% worse. This would affect the impact Renovation Wave significantly as it seeks to target 35 million buildings between now and 2030.

(https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/energy-efficiency/energy-efficient-buildings/renovation-wave_en).

The mechanical properties are another important point to take into account for insulation foams, especially in certain applications, such as passable roofs of buildings or residential houses in markets such as France or Benelux, where there are specific mechanical resistance tests that the foams must pass to ensure a good resilience of the thermal insulation to frequent foot traffic  throughout the lifetime of the building. There are no foams using water as a blowing agent that passes such mechanical tests.
In the case of a HFOs/HCFOs ban, new formulations would have to be developed, with alternatives that do not exist today.  Under the best of circumstances, where alternatives are already available, it takes more than 5 years, to develop new formulations and assess that they are in compliance with European mandatory product regulations in order to achieve CE Marking based on standard EN14315, and country-specific regulations, as well as to carry out the current and expensive voluntary technical assessments per product and country, such as BBA (UK), CSTB (France), Marca N (Spain), ATG (Belgium), etc… It is highly unlikely that alternatives with similar performance can be adopted within the deadlines of the proposed Restriction even if alternatives where already known to exist. However, with nothing currently on the horizon to provide the alternatives required, our company believes that either an exemption or unlimited derogation is required to avoid the unintended consequences highlighted in this submission.
Considering all existing information, our company formally requests that the HFOs/HCFOs (HFO-1336mzz-Z, HCFO-1233zd-E & HFO-1234ze-E.) should either be excluded from the scope of the Proposal entirely or all their uses as foam blowing agents in SPF made subject to a time-unlimited derogation. This goes beyond the current time-limited derogation being considered by the proponents of the Restriction Proposal.

(1). These rely on the reaction of water in the formulation to react with excess isocyanate to generate CO2 in-situ

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Blowing agents for polyurethane and polyisocyanurate foams for thermal insulation. We agree with the document issued by PU Europe, and submitted to ECHA with reference c847c31e-8df9-44a2-8798-218bf9d9ac2a, which highlights the lack of persistence of HFOs/HCFOs themselves, the limited tri-fluoroacetic acid (TFA) generated from breakdown mechanisms and the fact that most other national jurisdictions have no plans to restrict HFOs/HCFOs in foam blowing applications, especially in the area of use in SPF where no demonstrated alternatives are available.   Accordingly, our company sees no justification for a ban of Fluorinated Gas notably HFO-1336mzz-Z, HCFO-1233zd-E & HFO-1234ze-E for use as foam blowing agents.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The vast majority of blowing agent (HFO) remains within the cellular structure of the foam until the end of the product’s useful life, estimated typically at 50 years, Please refer to the Confidential attachment. This retention level is important to maintain the thermal performance of the foam. There are various existing techniques and initiatives to recover, reuse or destroy the blowing agent depending on the product type and its location. These are described in the EFCTC (the European Fluoro Carbons Technical Committee) submission to ECHA consultation on U-PFAS.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: The use of flammable blowing agents as alternative to HFOs/HCFOs is not an option because current product application equipment is not designed to handle flammable products at the contractor level. This issue was heavily explored back in the 1990s, particularly in the USA, as detailed below. In addition, the high cost of adapting a chemical manufacturing and formulating plant to handle flammable products, where SPF systems are produced, must also be considered.  Challenges in ensuring a safe working environment for contractors  Under the guidance of the UNEP Technical Options Committee on Flexible and Rigid Foams, the UNEP Fact Sheet No. 13 on Insulation Foams, published in 2013 stated the following:   “PU-spray foam: This type of foam is always blown at the site being insulated. It is not considered safe to use flammable blowing agents.”   Even in jurisdictions where the use was initially legally permitted, namely in the USA, the experience has not been positive, and activities have required extraordinary levels of training to make them possible at all. The US Environmental Protection Agency explained the situation in its Federal Register as follows:    “The flammability of hydrocarbon blowing agents… are of particular concern in spray foam applications where a controlled factory environment is not possible... Without adequate ventilation, several situations could lead to explosion or fire. Examples include, but are not limited to, equipment wells on roofs, roofs enclosed by high parapet walls, and interior applications (especially where a basement or other confined space is beneath the spray area). Therefore, it is critical that application in enclosed areas be accompanied by adequate forced ventilation, flammable vapor monitoring and the elimination of all possible ignition sources.   The potential for explosion or fire highlights the need for safety training.  Exxon will sell Exxsol blowing agents only to systems manufacturers who have contractually guaranteed to provide training on safe storage, handling and application to their customers, contractors, and applicators.  Because of the US EPA concerns on the use of hydrocarbons in spray foam, only one manufacturer has been listed as an acceptable source of hydrocarbon blowing agents for spray foam (Exxon) as this manufacturer has committed to providing the necessary training. As a result, hydrocarbons and other flammable blowing agents are not considered acceptable in this application (1).  In addition, although, the use of Exxsol material has been approved for spray foams since December 1999 (2),  no SPF equipment manufacturers have commercially proposed such equipment because they are not prepared to assume the risk and no spray foam system supplier has commercialized SPF systems that contain hydrocarbon blowing agents.  Manufacturing/formulating facilities not set-up for use flammable materials   • Page 38, Flexible and Rigid Foams Technical Options Committee, 2022 Assessment Report, January 2023.  “The necessary safety precautions for handling flammable blowing agents include explosion proofing of facilities and use of non-sparking tools.  Capital costs have been reported to range between $250,000 USD to $1,000,000 USD per operating facility.  Hydrocarbons have lower operating costs, but the significant capital investment has made them less attractive for smaller enterprises.  This is a very significant issue for small to medium enterprises (SMEs).”     (1) - See section 3, UNEP Fact Sheet 13, Insulating Foams. April 2015.     (2) - Federal Register / Vol. 64, No. 233 / Monday, December 6, 1999 / Rules and Regulations

General Comments: Our company manufactures products for Public Health Security (to protect people during a health, environmental, or industrial crisis), Patient Safety (for infection control for medical devices, including implantable devices, such as pacemakers or hip replacements), Occupational Health (personal protective equipment, i.e. PPE), and Indoor Air Quality (mold prevention in homes).  There are over a quarter million distinct products and billions of individual units, which incorporate our products, that are sold in these human health end-uses in Europe annually.

COVID-19 is the ultimate example of Public Health Security.  Being a European based manufacturer and a key supplier of Public Health Security solutions during the pandemic, our production capabilities helped assure EU autonomy as borders were closing.

For many end-use applications, substitutes for our products are not available.

The products our company manufactures are not PFAS. PFAS is neither an ingredient nor intentionally added to the final product we sell. Our process to manufacture the products requires the use of PFAS to achieve proper performance properties in these end uses. As the Universal PFAS Restriction Annex XV publication focuses on end-use for derogations, most of our product end-uses (and our specific use for our manufacturing process) have not been listed for derogation.

No test method exists for detecting the PFAS discussed above, and so targeted test method development is underway.   Although results are preliminary, for products used for Patient Safety, the targeted analysis shows potential PFAS concentration to be below the REACH Annex XV limit applicable to articles, set at 25 ppb for a targeted PFAS.  Based on our current knowledge, the total quantity of PFAS traces in our total volume of products manufactured annually in Europe is estimated to be less than 1 kg/year.

According to the criteria in Annex XIII of the REACH Regulation, the PFAS used are non-toxic, and are not classified as PBT, vPvB, PMT or vPvM, and are also not classified as endocrine disruptors (ED) in either mammalian or non-mammalian species based on available data.

In 2021, our company staffed an R&D program to identify substitutes for PFAS used in our manufacturing process.  However, our company requires additional time (through end-use and/or use derogations) to achieve successful non-PFAS alternatives for our manufacturing process for these Public Health Security, Patient Safety, Occupational Health and Indoor Air Quality products.

The R&D program to identify non-PFAS substitutes has significant efforts (double digit manpower and multi-million euro/year budget).  However, derogations to continue existing manufacturing use are needed for 12 years to commercially scale-up and qualify products manufactured with the non-PFAS alternatives in these critical end-uses.

We are requesting 12-year derogations based on previous successful efforts to requalify products with replacement chemistries, where timing to achieve commercial scale and end use requalification is extensive (over 10 years).

Total costs for the non-PFAS conversion are forecasted to be above 100 million euros.

In this non-aqueous process, with no emission sources to the soil or water compartment, there are limited emissions, which are to the air compartment.   With derogations for use to continue to manufacture these products, our company has also used our mass balance to develop a PFAS air emissions reduction plan.

Taken as a whole, for the billions of product units using our material, which are critical to human health and for which substitutes are not available, the total quantity of PFAS traces is less than 1 kg/year.  Our company has initiated an R&D program to develop non-PFAS manufacturing and a program to further reduce PFAS emissions.

General Comments: Our company supplies safety-critical transfer devices to several different markets and these are typically used in the transfer of potentially explosive, potent, and sterile powder ingredients - requiring high containment or sealing. These markets include pharmaceutical, food, medical, battery production & metallic powder transfer – all of which require specialist equipment to ensure the safety of the operator or powder being transferred. A key requirement of the device is utilising effective sealing materials such as PTFE, FKM and FFKM seals.
Our customers are global and span multiple sectors, ranging from small-scale drug discovery and development to major international pharma companies. The devices and the materials used go through rigorous process validation and control procedures as part of our customers’ manufacturing implementation and management. The seals manufactured from PTFE/FKM/FFKM are a critical element of these validation processes. Many of the processes in question use chemicals (e.g. toluene, methylene chloride, methyl isobutyl ketone) that require superior chemical compatibility to other certified materials available as alternative. Using any of these alternatives would provide inferior chemical compatibility and therefore would result in unsafe and unreliable devices with a dramatically increased risk around operator and product safety.
The device seals are in direct contact with the products within a safety and process critical device, meaning that any change in product or manufacturing process requires our customers to follow a rigorous change control process including re-validation. This is to mitigate any risk in relation to process operators and ultimately, potentially, patients taking the end drug product - oral or injectable. Because of this, we have agreements in place with our customers that, pharmaceutical customers especially, require a minimum 6 month notice period for any changes in material, manufacturing processes, device construction or operation to enable an appropriate amount of time to safely transition ensuring the right validation has been completed (including FDA compliance, USP VI 88 & 87,  Triboelectric testing to EN ISO 80079-36:2016 & EN 60079-32-2:2015), even when implementing material of “equivalent” grade.
For our customers, the continued use of FFKM/FKM/PTFE is critical to the safety of the products they are producing and without an exemption for ourselves (as manufacturers) and our suppliers (as distributors) there is a risk that our customers will not be able to continue production and risk the safety of products across a range of industries – a key sector being pharmaceutical products being used directly by patients.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our company supports reasonable activities and measures to prevent potential risk and protect the environment and human health and fully agrees with the dossier submitters that the emission of demonstrably harmful substances should be prevented due to their lasting global impact on environment and organisms. However, we disagree with a blanket ban of a substance group of over 10 000 substances as this does not meet the requirements of a risk-based assessment and is therefore not reconcilable with Article 68 of the REACH Regulation. In many cases, especially concerning fluoropolymers, the use-phase is admittedly unproblematic. Safe industrial uses of fluoropolymers where the risks can be controlled by appropriate measures via occupational safety, emission control or waste legislation must remain available. For issues that arise from the production and end-of-life-phase, appropriate measures should rather be regulated via waste legislation or emission control instead of a general ban.
Our main concern is a possible broad and short-termed restriction with serious downstream consequences, mainly endangering the availability of extremely relevant high-tech materials, technologies and products made in Europe. Affected are many materials with relevance to numerous varying national and international product quality standards (e.g., electrical insulation, UV exposure, tracking resistance, temperature resistance, fire resistance etc.). Modification of the material composition will require a time-consuming re-design and re-qualification with new approvals and testing for thousands of materials, components, and articles to guarantee that the requirements for technical and human safety are met. Recertification will therefore take a large share of additional cost, time, and effort for substitution of the products along the whole supply chain. These efforts are to be expected by the companies themselves as well as the certification bodies, laboratories, and authorities since the requirement will be needed at the same time for the entire industry in Europe. This will contribute to resource shortages, supply bottlenecks and possible allocations and will put the industry under severe pressure.
With the complexity of the products and supply chains in the E&E sector, as well as the large number of substances that are proposed to be restricted, there is a risk that despite the huge determination efforts applications of PFAS will remain undiscovered and subsequently turn out to be relevant. As a downstream user and manufacturer of articles, we are in the middle of the supply chain and rely on statements and knowledge of our suppliers for thousands of components but also on the alternative possibilities and aspirations of the material manufacturers. There is still missing information on PFAS in products in the European and global supply chain as there is no declaration or information obligation for products according to REACH Article 33 for all PFAS substances and no uniform legal basis at international level, which also weakens the influence and control over EU imports. A complete, gapless risk assessment for manufacturers of complex articles and an endless number of substances at a time when the legislation is not yet in force is practically impossible, as the information in the supply chain is not yet available, know-how protected and not mandatory to declare, which means that it is also not available or provided in the supply chain even upon request. Since the concrete requirements of the PFAS restriction proposal have only been announced in February 2023 and the outcome of the PFAS restriction proposal is not yet clear, which means that the specific conditions remain changeable, there will be difficulties to start with full substitution of all products through the entire supply chain and timely enforcement of the requirements within the short deadlines that the dossier submitter have proposed for the restriction. The situation is similar for industrial machines and systems, where PFAS containing materials are indispensable as extremely relevant seals, valves, lubricants, or hoses, where we also expect sudden material and producing performance failure through the years.
Assumption for a development and qualification of a new product is a technically suitable alternative with similar performance which, according to our knowledge based on supplier requests and conversations as well as information exchange with several European and international associations is currently not fully available for fluoropolymers on the market for all applications. It should be noted that new solutions are mostly niche products, which are normally produced in much smaller volumes with less capacities, so additional shortages and supply bottlenecks must be expected in the material manufacturing industry. Considering the wide use of fluoropolymers in the industry, there is a high risk of a domino effect with similar consequences multiplied along the supply chain. This has been confirmed by the enormous participation in the public consultation of the current universal PFAS restriction proposal.
Although our products are less affected by the restriction of low-molecular PFAS, we want to emphasise that E&E companies depend on material that is produced with the help of such substances, e.g., fluoropolymers and semiconductors. With the displacement of the respective manufacturers for such materials from the EU, the E&E industry will have to rely exclusively on non-EU suppliers. In analogy to regrettable substitution, this outcome is very undesirable since the production will then be beyond the influence of the EU while potential emission of PFAS still affects the shared environment.

Our request on the PFAS restriction proposal:
Due to the wide industrial application of PFAS in combination with the specific characteristics of the substances we believe that a general ban would seriously endanger European production and development sites as well as their global competitiveness. It requires more time to find suitable, effective substitutes for such numerous and technically specific applications, close information gaps and enable development re-design and re-certification for substitutes for existing applications or innovations.
We therefore call for a fundamental revision of the restriction proposal and ask for consideration of the following aspects and key requirements of the current state of the PFAS restriction proposal:

a. Transition period of at least 48 months after entry into force to allow for the time-consuming re-design and re-certification of the product with available substitutes.
b. Long-term derogation for the manufacturing and use of fluoropolymers of “low concern” in safe industrial applications.
c. Information obligation for "intentionally added" PFAS (e.g., by inclusion in the REACH Candidate List) to close information gaps about substances in articles.
d. Concentration value of 1000 ppm of “intentionally added" PFAS for articles to exclude impurities.
e. Procedure for renewal and re-applying of exemptions, to ensure important existing applications or innovations when substitution is not possible.
f. General exemption for products already placed on the market to prevent unnecessary disposition of products and warrant use in complex products.
g. General exemption for placing on the market of spare, wear and used parts to ensure sustainability and cost-effectiveness according to the repair-as-produced principle.
h. Reporting obligation to the Agency within at least 48 months after entry into force in accordance with the transition period (Point 7 of the restriction proposal).

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our company supports the statement made by FCJ on the issues of proposed restriction, as per attached in Section IV.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Polychlorotrifluoroethylene (PCTFE) fluoropolymers are used in medicinal and medical device packaging.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: PCTFE fluoropolymers are manufactured both from non-PFAS raw materials and the non-PFAS monomer Chlorotrifluoroethylene (CTFE), and polymerized without involvement of other PFAS substances (processing aids, surfactants, additives, or agents). PCTFE fluoropolymers are medical grade high purity and intrinsically stable inert materials with extremely low levels of residues, impurities, and negligible leaching characteristics throughout its full life cycle. Its end-of-life disposal in landfills and by municipal incineration are proven to be safe and recommended by national and international regulations.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Its end-of-life incineration at temperature above 850 °C releases neither PFAS-related materials nor detectable levels of Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA).

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Most pharmaceuticals/medicinal or medical device packaging wastes in the EU are collected and incinerated under municipal waste conditions (i.e., statutory recommendation) or disposed in landfills. Considering the low hazard profile as defined by polymers of low concern (PLC) criteria, the use of non-PFAS raw materials and monomers, the absence of processing aids/additives/impurities/residues, and the lack of water solubility for PCTFE, there are no PFAS emissions or mobility concerns for Polychlorotrifluoroethylene (PCTFE) fluoropolymers within pharmaceuticals or medical devices packaging when landfilled. In addition, municipal or medical waste incineration does not create TFA or other PFAS-related compounds of concern.

5. Proposed derogations: Considering very small tonnages of PCTFE imported into the EU for uses in medicinal and medical devices packaging (app. 2.3% of the total PFAS uses in the medical devices sector and ca. 0,36% of the total polymeric PFAS tonnages used on the market in 2020), negligible emission levels (1%) and its PLC properties, and the respective risks to human health and the environment could not be considered “unacceptable” and are disproportionate vis-à-vis the proposed REACH restriction.

6. Missing uses: a) Polychlorotrifluoroethylene (PCTFE) fluoropolymers are used in medicinal and medical devices packaging. PCTFE fluoropolymers are Honeywell’s products, marketed under the trademark © Aclar and PCTFE (© Aclar) is not produced in the EU/EEA. Therefore for use of polychlorotrifluoroethylene (PCTFE) fluoropolymers in pharmaceutical and medical device packaging applications within the EU, polychlorotrifluoroethylene (PCTFE) fluoropolymers must be imported from Honeywell or PCTFE films supplied by Honeywell are laminated to other materials such as polyethylene, PVC or polypropylene (as thermoformable films) into blister packaging, other laminates, bottles, vials, etc. by manufacturers outside the EU and then are supplied to the EU. There are no other PCTFE producers or importers in the EU/EEA for the above use. According to Honeywell’s customs data and estimates, the annual import of PCTFE fluoropolymers into the EU was ca. 1000 tonnes in 2015-2020. Moreover, PCTFE is an expensive material, with very low levels of emissions during the manufacturing/processing and use phases. Its use is considered only when absolutely necessary to meet packaging barrier needs for specific pharmaceutical products. Therefore, the total weight of PFAS-related materials from PCTFE (© Aclar) production, use, and disposal/end-of-life stages did not reach 10 tonnes in 2020. b) For more than 50 years, Honeywell’s PCTFE (© Aclar) thermoformable films have been used in originator and generic pharmaceuticals primary packaging (blister packs). PCTFE (© Aclar) thermoformable films provide the highest moisture barrier when compared to other extrudable thermoplastics films (ETF). These unique characteristics substantially increase stability, storage and usage life of medicinal products and devices and are consistent across a large range of temperature and humidity conditions. The latter attribute of drug packaging can decrease medical wastes and potentially reduce improper disposal of pharmaceuticals to the environment. c) In the pharma (medicines) sector, Honeywell’s PCTFE (© Aclar) is used in over 600 oral solid therapies, across all therapeutic areas, including the nervous system, cardiovascular, metabolic, hormonal, antipsychotic, and oncology treatments. It is estimated that if PCTFE (© Aclar) were to be banned, it would affect these drugs and about 20 companies that produce them. d) Unique PCTFE film properties relevant for medicinal and medical device packaging are: • The best moisture barrier of any clear thermoplastic film (highest WVTR protection) • Bio-chemical inertness (very low leaching/migration) • Chemical-resistance (practically to a broad range of chemicals) • The highest crystal clarity of any thermoforming film on the market • Non-flammability; Plasticizer and stabilizer free • Highly flexible, enabling deep draw packaging designs; Cryogenic stability PCTFE (© Aclar) provides the best barrier at the lowest material usage rates, while also exhibiting unparalleled performance in high barrier moisture protection when compared to any other polymers (please see below Section V for details). In the meantime, cold form foils (CFF) are not transparent (opaque) in comparison to PCTFE (© Aclar) and increase packaging sizes up to 55%, negatively affecting the EU’s Green Deal and resource efficiency goals. Creating a smaller pack size with PCTFE fluoropolymers directly reduces raw material (film/foil) usage, waste production, warehousing expenses, and transportation/energy costs along with CO2e emissions. e) There are no acceptable chemical or functional substitutes to PCTFE films for use in medicinal and medical devices packaging available on the market. Other materials do not provide the required properties/benefits and characteristics specified in the respective marketing authorizations/certificates. Because substitutes (like PVC, COC, COP, etc.) do not have as high moisture barrier as PCTFE films and deterioration due to moisture from packaged medicinal products goes on, use of substitutes will inevitably result in shorter storage times and use periods of medicinal products as well as reduced functionality of devices, which are crucial characteristics for many drugs and medical equipment or devices. The substitute, such as PVDC, has similarly high moisture barrier properties and can provide some protection against moisture degradation of packaged pharmaceuticals. However, PVDC film itself has the characteristic of turning yellow over time due to long-term storage, and cannot be used as a substitute material for PCTFE film as a packaging material for pharmaceuticals that require long-term storage. f) At present, there is no prospect of technical or economic substitution. g) The costs associated with changes to packaging formats (technology, machinery, tooling, etc.) are borne by producers of packaging, pharmaceutical and medical devices companies and ultimately patients. If PCTFE materials were to be banned, pharmaceutical producers would be required to identify, develop, and qualify potentially inadequate human and veterinary alternative packaging formats, resulting in adding R&D costs, stability testing, and other regulatory costs for each drug currently packaged in PCTFE materials. These costs would inevitably be passed on to national healthcare systems, insurance companies, and end-use patients. In the meantime, the inferior moisture barrier and migration properties of other packaging materials will decrease quality, storage and use periods of medicinal products and devices. This will directly affect the safety, health, and environmental characteristics of medicines, as well as elevate costs on the industry and undermine patient affordability of medical treatments due to medicine expiration and increased product returns. These consequences could have significant impacts on the population in specific situations (emergency stocks, highly sensitive formulations/devices, transportation, and cryogenic storage conditions for vaccines, etc.). For instance, REACH restrictions on PCTFE uses in medicinal packaging (for humans and animals) will require additional “stability testing” and approval of changes/variations by EMA and/or national medicines authorities for each existing active substance and dosage of final medicinal product (currently over 600). This will not only require substantial development time (i.e., tests normally performed for long time periods with regular intermediate controls) but also considerable human resources from the industry and authorization authorities. According to available information, the cost of “stability testing” for each medicinal product could reach 100.000–500.000 euro, excluding EMA and/or national authorities' fees (26.000–86.000 euro per product/dosage) for the approval of potential variations. All the cost will be passed on to final consumers and public budgets. In the case where alternative packaging would not provide satisfactory stability characteristics to active substances or final medicinal products, changes to medicinal formulations will be required and as such implies that considerable costs and time for developing new medicinal products and obtaining marketing authorizations (additional testing, preparation of valid applications, evaluations by the authorities, etc.) will need to be invested. This will also trigger additional costs for processors/producers of packaging materials to retool and retrofit their machinery for other barrier materials. According to Honeywell’s dedicated estimates, new packaging changes alone will potentially add over 3 mln. Euro of additional costs for one drug and 1,896 bln. euro. Euro for the entire © Aclar product portfolio. Considering the average annual PCTFE (© Aclar) supply tonnages in the EU (ca. 1 000 tonnes), substitution costs would reach over 18 mln. (euro per kg) of PCTFE. However, the overall socio-economic impact of the REACH restriction on PCTFE uses in pharmaceuticals and medical devices sectors, but also on medicinal products and devices diversity, are difficult to estimate. These restrictions would considerably limit the innovative capacity of the EU pharmaceutical industry, including the development of vaccines and other new drugs/devices/implants. It will also undermine the EU's economic goals and would hinder or jeopardise goals within the EU Green Deal. Based on the above, PFAS substitutes should be exempted from this proposed restriction rather than the 12 year grace period because they are highly likely not to be fully substituted and are practically non-substitutable.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our company understands the health concerns with respect to PFAS and the need to reduce their uncontrolled release to the environment and to the human food chain.
However, certain industrial processes where hazardous or strongly oxidizing materials are handled rely on the availability of those materials. About a quarter of the electricity and half of the low-carbon electricity in the EU is generated by nuclear energy (see https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/nu-clear-energy/nuclear-safety_en). Enrichment is, quite obviously, a prerequisite for using nuclear energy. Nuclear energy is subject to the most stringent and demanding safety requirements, given the high damage potential which calls for reducing the probability of a substantial release of radioactive substances to an extreme minimum. Within the high-level safety principles made mandatory by the Nuclear Safety Directive 2009/71/Euratom, national regulations in Euratom member states install strict requirements on the required safety characteristics of nuclear systems, structures and components. In this context, PFAS are in many areas essential for achieving compliance. Due to their inherent qualities, they guarantee the functioning and durability of components in the very harsh environment and stressful chemical environment. A compromise in nuclear safety by lowering the required safety characteristics in order to allow replacement of PFAS with other sub-stances is neither allowed by Euratom and national legislation and regulations, nor would it be compatible with the respondent’s safety culture.
Here, PFAS often cannot be replaced due to the lack of alternatives. This includes the nuclear fuel cycle, where radioactive materials are handled in closed systems and where release of waste is already controlled by particularly strong regulations. Extensive R&D is being done to find nuclear-grade alternatives to PFAS in the long-term; in many areas, however, as yet there is no prospect of such alternatives being identified. As long as there are no alternatives, therefore, PFAS should be allowed in the nuclear sector.
We urge the EU to consider a more nuanced approach to regulating PFAS, one that takes into account their essential role in industrial processes, the lack of viable alternatives, and their use in closed systems rather in applications that are uncontrolled and open to environment. A general ban on these substances would have severe consequences for industry and could hinder progress towards a more sustainable future.
Here, the important role of the nuclear energy has to be highlighted, which is acknowledged by IPCC, IEA and other major institutions as being a vital supplier of low-carbon energy and therefore a major asset in the global fight against climate change. About a quarter of the electricity and half of the low-carbon electricity in the EU is generated by nuclear energy (cf. https://energy.ec.europa.eu/topics/nuclear-energy/nuclear-safety_en). Content: Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our company values the opportunity to submit comments regarding the proposed restriction of PFAS under the REACH Regulation. With this contribution, we would like to express our support to derogation 5(ee) for the semiconductor manufacturing process.
In order to support our request, we are submitting information on the volumes used by our company for the semiconductor manufacturing process and the potential PFAS emissions that our production processes can generate, as well as on the technical and time requirements associated with the transition process. In addition, we are providing examples of PPE used at our facilities and for which we support a derogation.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: This contribution applies to the following use sectors identified in the Annex XV restriction report (Table 9): • Electronics and semiconductors (Annex E.2.11.)    o Semiconductors’ wires and cables    o Coating, solvents, and cleaning    o Heat transfer fluids    o Photolithography • Applications of fluorinated gases (Annex E.2.8.)    o Refrigeration • TULAC (Annex E.2.2.)     o Professional apparel (including PPE)

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Question 2.a: Please refer to quetsion 7.a.  Question 2.b: The fluorinated gases that we use are not recycled. They are destroyed using abatement systems. For additional information on emissions, refer to Question 7(a).

5. Proposed derogations: Under this question, we would like to address derogation 5(b) for textiles used in personal protective equipment (PPE) intended to protect users against risks as specified in Regulation (EU) 2016/425, Annex I, Risk Category III (a) and (c). This derogation falls under the TULAC sector. Our voluntary firefighting brigade uses PPE that contains PFAS, due to the oleophobicity and compatibility with flame-retardant properties that these substances have. For information on volumes and emissions, we differ to the information provided by EURATEX, ESF and ATCS.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Under this question, we would like to address derogation 5(ee) for the semiconductor manufacturing process, which covers the following sectors: (1) electronics and semiconductors, and (2) applications of fluorinated gases.  a) The annual tonnage and emissions (at sub-sector level) and type of PFAS associated with the relevant use.     i. Volumes  • Wires and cables Several articles necessary for the semiconductor manufacturing process contain PFAS, mainly fluoropolymers. These include valves, O-rings/seals, piping/tubing, among others. The fluoropolymers contained in these articles are PTFE, PVDF, PFA, FKM, and FFKM. It is not expected for these articles to release any PFAS into the environment. The following table presents an average lifespan, in years, of these articles at our company, which provides an indication of the timeline for replacement:  Table 2:  Lifespan per fluoropolymer-based article used for semiconductors’ production at our company:  O-rings: Lifetime = 1 to 10 years Tubes: Lifetime = 1 to 2 years Valves: Lifetime = 5 to 10 years  • Coating, solvents, and cleaning  We use different F-gases *  in the production of semiconductors at our company’s manufacturing site. These gases are used in the processes of wafer etching and chemical vapor deposition (CVD). While these come in contact with the wafer during etching and chemical vapor deposition (CVD), the wafers undergo a thorough cleaning process afterwards that removes all undesired particles. Therefore, none of the PFAS mentioned above are expected to remain in the final products.  * Other F-gases consumed for semiconductor manufacturing are SF6 and NF3, which do not qualify as PFAS based on the proposed definition.  • Heat transfer fluids This type of fluids are used in frontend and backend operations.   • Photolithography:  Some photoresists, light-sensitive materials used to form patterns on the wafers by photolithography, contain PFAS. At this stage, it is not possible to share the content or the specific PFAS, given that manufacturers do not disclose this information.  • Fluorinated gases used for refrigeration At our company, we also use F-gases as refrigerants for our heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) equipment. Our equipment suppliers are responsible for the handling of these substances, which are only contained in the equipment, and the proper maintenance to avoid leaks.  For information on quantities used at EU or global level, please refer to the contributions of ESIA and SEMI.     ii. Production process An integrated circuit (IC) is a microelectronic chip made of silicon, designed for various applications, such as microcontrollers, sensors, communication, LCD drivers, and energy management, among others. The surface of the finished chip (die size) and the complexity of technology node used to fabricate an IC depend on the application.  Its manufacturing starts with a bare, polished, silicon wafer (called “wafer”) which is processed hundreds of times through different operations. For technologies up to 110nm (being the size of one transistor), the process comprises cleaning steps, deposition of different materials on the whole wafer surface, photolithography, etching and ion implantation steps. These are described below:  • Cleaning is required to prepare the surface before the following step or after an operation creating undesired compounds or particles. It can be done either with liquid chemicals, ultra-pure water or plasma. • Deposition involves different materials, either dielectric (e.g., oxide, nitride), semi-conductor (e.g., polysilicon) or conductor (mainly tungsten and aluminium). • Photolithography is used to physically reproduce the design of the chip made by computer onto the wafer through masking operations: the masks themselves are produced from the chip design to a physical quartz substrate with chromium pattern reproducing the design.  • Etching removes materials which were not intended to stay in the final product and then reproducing physically the design onto the desired material. • Ionic implantation is used to introduce ions into the materials to locally modify the electrical properties of said materials. All these operations are repeated from ten to forty times.  Finally, several measurement and inspection steps guarantee that the wafers progressing within the flow are optimal and that they reach the targeted quality objectives. All these wafers are grouped in lots by 25 and are controlled by a Manufacturing Execution System.     iii. Emission minimization techniques  Our abatement systems consist in burn/wet systems from our supplier. The abatement systems reach destruction removal efficiencies (DRE) higher than 95% for most PFAS used in production, with an operating time higher than 98%. This allows us to comply with the emissions limit imposed by the national law.     iv. Emissions at use stage As the final products from our manufacturing do not contain PFAS, no emissions during the use phase are to be expected. In addition, it should be noted that our company integrated circuits have an average lifespan of 10 years.     v. End-of-life Final equipment containing our products falls within the scope of the Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE). These devices are a valuable form of e-waste since they contain an array of precious metals and most of their components can be recycled. In addition to these precious materials, electric and electronic devices can contain hazardous materials such as mercury, lead, or cadmium. In this context, EU and national laws require that manufactures and distributors contribute to ensuring they are disposed of and treated properly:  • Registering with the responsible national authorities ("registers") in each country where you distribute or sell equipment; • Filling a regular report on the amount of sold electrical and electronic equipment; and • Organising or financing the collection, treatment, recycling and recovery of products.  Distributors, in particular, must provide a take-back service, whereby customers can return electric and electronic waste free of charge. For information on emissions at EU or global level, please refer to the contributions of ESIA and SEMI.  b) The key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use.  • Electronics and semiconductors:  o Semiconductors wires and cables: Chemical, thermal resistance and heat resistance, high stability, and flame retardance. o Coating, solvents, and cleaning: Optimal cleaning properties through the provision of reactive fluoride.  o Heat transfer fluids: High precision temperature, viscosity, and electrical conductivity.  o Photolithography: Strong electronegativity, low refractive index, low surface energy, very low surface tension, hydrophobic and oleophobic behaviour.  • Applications of fluorinated gases:  o Refrigeration: Current equipment in place not adapted to non-PFAS refrigerants. For further information on the key functionalities provided by PFAS in the semiconductor industry, please refer to the contributions of ESIA and SEMI.  c) The number of companies in the sector estimated to be affected by the restriction.  For information on the EU or global semiconductor value chain, please refer to the contributions of ESIA and SEMI.  d) The availability, technical and economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives for the relevant use, including information on the extent (in terms of market shares) to which alternative-based products are already offered on the EU market and whether any shortages in the supply of relevant alternatives are expected. Currently, our company is not aware of successfully proven PFAS-free alternatives in the production process of semiconductors that would allow an immediate transition. Besides the quality standards expected by customers, manufacturing standards for semiconductors must be respected; for example, the SEMI International Standards and the American National Standards Institute’s (ANSI) Semiconductor Fabrication Standards. A phase-out of PFAS could be incompatible with these standards, preventing the process of being both effective and resource efficient, as well as safe for human health and the environment. In addition, it is impossible to state whether the current machinery would be able to support these changes. Based on current information, machinery prices range from hundreds of thousands of euros to millions. The economic burden that partially or fully replacing semiconductor manufacturing equipment could represent would not only put at risk the economic stability of the semiconductor industry, but also the successful implementation of the European Chips Act. **  ** European Parliament, European Parliamentary Research Service, European Strategy and Policy Analysis System, Global Semiconductor Trends and the Future of EU Chip Capabilities, 2022, https://espas.eu/files/Global-Semiconductor-Trends-and-the-Future-of-EU-Chip-Capabilities-2022.pdf  e) For cases in which alternatives are not yet available, information on the status of R&D processes for finding suitable alternatives, including the extent of R&D initiatives in terms of time and/or financial investments, the likelihood of successful completion, the time expected to be required for substitution (including any relevant certification or regulatory approvals) and the major challenges encountered with alternatives which were considered but subsequently disregarded. As stated in our response to question 7(a), the manufacturing process for semiconductors is highly complex and iterative. Assuming that PFAS-free alternatives are developed in the future, the performance of each will affect all the steps in the process. Research and development for requalification would have to take place for every single step of the manufacturing process, in a holistic perspective; not only for the substances themselves, but also for the way that they could affect the different expected performances of each step. To exemplify some of the steps, we are focusing on heat-transfer fluids and coating, solvents and cleaning applications.  Based on information from the SIA PFAS Consortium***, it is not possible to quantify the time necessary to invent an alternative to the current heat transfer fluids. If a potential alternative is invented, it must follow a period of 2 to 5+ years of research, 2+ years of demonstration, 2+ years of integration and 2+ years of high-volume manufacturing (HVM). We received information from a supplier regarding an alternative to the heat transfer fluid Fluorinert™; while the alternative shows a much lower global warming potential (2.5 compared to 9000), it is a hydrofluoroolefin-based (HFO), fluorinated fluid, which still falls under the PFAS category.  Regarding the application of coating, solvents and cleaning, we are focusing on F-gases used for etching and deposition. The SIA PFAS Consortium was not able to identify a timeframe for the invention of PFAS-free alternatives, due to the critical properties to process silicon for the manufacture of semiconductors that the current F-gases provide. Furthermore, they consider that it would take 10-15+ years to implement each etching and cleaning type after their invention.  *** SIA PFAS Consortium (2022). The Impact of a Potential PFAS Restriction on the Semiconductor Sector.  We would like to note that while these gases have a high global warming potential, the implementation of point-of-use abatement systems reduces their impact on the atmosphere. We are currently running a project aimed to replace (or improve) the abatement systems of the F-gases used in production, with following objectives: • Decrease or cease the use of natural gas (scrubber oxidation). • Decrease or cease NOx production during burning phase. • Minimize greenhouse gas emissions into the atmosphere, which includes the F-gases. This project includes the study of different solutions from the following point-of-use abatement technologies:  • Dry bed adsorption: The process gases are adsorbed by a reagent, such as activated charcoal, becoming a waste solid to be disposed.  • Thermal treatment: The process gases are destroyed at high temperatures using either fuel gas or electricity and then scrubbed into a wet stream for their disposal.  • Wet scrubber: The process gases are scrubbed and absorbed into a wet stream for their disposal.  The selection of one of these technologies depends on different factors, such as physical space, technology effectiveness and efficiency, as well as operational inputs. At the end, we expect to reduce our PFAS emissions into the atmosphere as close to zero as possible. However, we are uncertain about the timeline required for this project, which will depend on whether a complete replacement of the systems is required. If so, we consider a period of around 10 years is required. For further information on each manufacturing step, please refer to the contributions of ESIA and SEMI.  f) For cases in which substitution is technically and economically feasible but more time is required to substitute.  Not relevant, as there are no alternatives available.   g) For cases in which substitution is not technically or economically feasible, information on what the socio-economic impacts would be for companies, consumers, and other affected actors. If available, please provide the annual value of EU sales and profits of the relevant sector, and employment numbers for the sector For information on the EU or global semiconductor value chain, please refer to the contributions of ESIA and SEMI.  For information on the watchmaking sector, please refer to contributions 4575.

Content: Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our company values the opportunity to submit comments regarding the proposed restriction of PFAS under the REACH Regulation. With this contribution, we would like to express our support to derogation 5(k) for industrial precision cleaning fluids.
Amongst our manufacturing sites, some use PFAS mixtures for the precision cleaning of watch parts. The present contribution summarizes the information regarding PFAS used within our company for this application.
In order to support our request, we are submitting information on the application itself, emissions from this use, the requalification process, as well as the negative consequences that the absence of a derogation would imply.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: This contribution applies to the sector “Applications of fluorinated gases” (Annex E.2.8.), more specifically to the sub-use “solvents” and the proposed derogation for industrial cleaning fluids under paragraph 5(k).  The watchmaking industry needs hydrofluoroethers (HFEs) based solvents for precision cleaning because the dimensions of watch parts are extremely small, (tolerances in the micron range). A typical product that is concerned is the balance wheel, in particular high-end balance wheels. Such balance wheels are an assembly of different components: an axis, a roller, a balance wheel, charge screws, regulating screws, etc. Very small holes are machined through the balance wheel rim and a thread is created. To clean these very small and complex cavities, the exceptional properties of the PFAS containing solvent are necessary: low surface tension, ability to dissolve grease and lubricants, fast evaporation. The measurement of the dimensions for the regulating screws is also a challenge. The very small screws need to be perfectly clean to allow a precise measurement with tolerances in the micron range.  The use of suitable precision cleaning fluids is mandatory to ensure the proper function of the watch parts. Without a cleaning process, a mechanical watch or a quartz watch will not function properly.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Question 2.a: Please refer to Question 5.  Question 2.b: Wastes from our production are collected and sent back to the supplier for treatment.  At this stage, they are either properly destroyed or recycled. They are never landfilled. Special waste treatment companies are authorised by national authorities to collect the waste of fluorinated compounds according to existing waste codes. When these substances cannot be recycled, they are subject to high-temperature incineration. When recycling is possible, distillation or condensation processes are applied.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Question 4.a: As explained under Question 2(b), we recycled all the substances used for this application to the extent possible. However, the concentration limits proposed in paragraph 2 of the proposed restriction entry text would impede the recycling of this substance.  Overall, we believe that for derogated uses, it should be possible to allow recycling of PFAS such as fluorinated gases.  Question 4.b: Not relevant, as it would not be possible to achieve the proposed concentration limits.  Question 4.c: Not relevant, as it would not be possible to achieve the proposed concentration limits.

5. Proposed derogations: a) Identification of the substance(s) and volumes We use hydrofluoroethers (HFEs) for this application.  b) Emissions during production All our cleaning agents are monitored and manipulated according to the SDS, identification labels and the national legislation, especially regarding waste management operations. In addition, our equipment is designed to maintain the emission of greenhouse gases as low as possible, as it is mandatory by national legislation, as well as by the European Regulation EU No 517/2014. With regards to waste, as explained in Question 4, all our cleaning fluids are subject to recycling processes.  Furthermore, it should be noted that no water is used during the production processes relying on PFAS cleaning fluids and no emissions to water can be expected.  c) Emissions during use of watches Due to their nature of cleaning agents, the PFAS mixtures used will not remain on the watch parts placed on the market as finished watches; they will evaporate because they are volatile solvents and any remaining traces will be removed by the subsequent rinsing operations.  d) Emissions at end of life of watches There will be no PFAS emissions at end-of-life, as this application does not result in the presence of PFAS in the final articles (i.e., internal watch parts, mechanical and quartz watches).   Additional information on cleaning fluids:  Question 1: The key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use. The PFAS solvents used have some key properties which are critical to fulfil the technical criteria during the precision cleaning of watch parts: • These cleaning solvents have a direct impact on the precise chronometry of watches. A perfect cleaning of the very small watch mechanical parts is essential for the proper functioning of watches. • Impact on the surface energy of the components: Due to their low surface tension, the solvents penetrate in holes, voids, etc. The use of these solvents allows a very precise cleaning, rinsing and drying, especially when some parts of the components are difficult to access, with complex geometry. • These solvents are efficient for the light-duty cleaning of oils, greases, waxes, and fingerprints on the very small watch parts. • The fact that these solvents can absorb any moisture residue is reducing the risk of corrosion of metal parts. • These solvents can be used to clean many different components, they are compatible with all metals used for watch components and act as very good degreasing agents. • These solvents have a good compatibility with the epilame of watch parts. • Because of their high evaporation rate, no stains remain on the parts after cleaning. It allows to obtain a surface without spot or polluting residues. • The process time is very short, allowing cleaning and drying with a co-solvent. • These substances make it possible to apply a cold cleaning process. • They are thermally and chemically stable in use. • The mixtures uses are azeotropic formulations, which guarantees a controlled cleaning with an optimal solvent quality.  Question 2: The availability, technical and economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives for the relevant use, including information on the extent (in terms of market shares) to which alternative-based products are already offered on the EU market and whether any shortages in the supply of relevant alternatives are expected.  a) Alternative solvents: Compared to other compounds, these solvents present not only strong advantages in terms of safety, but also in terms of toxicity and environmental impact: • The use of solvents which present a risk of flammability cannot be considered for safety reasons. • Substitutes should have a lower toxicity for human health and the environment, to avoid a regrettable substitution. • Also, it is important to assess the environmental impact of the solvents. In this regard, it should be noted that compared to HFCs, HCFCs and CFCs, the HFEs solvents that we use have a low Global Warming Potential (GWP). At our company, we are constantly looking into alternatives. At present, we are assessing the possibility of transitioning to non PFAS substances. However, it is still unclear whether the candidates under assessment will be able to fulfil the application requirements and, if so, when the transition could be completed.  b) Alternative cleaning processes: While aqueous cleaning processes exist, these pose a major risk of materials corrosion. Therefore, they cannot be considered a suitable alternative process.  c) No cleaning process: Critical loss of chronometric properties of watch movements has been detected if this specific process is not applied.  Question 3: For cases in which alternatives are not yet available, information on the status of R&D processes for finding suitable alternatives, including the extent of R&D initiatives in terms of time and/or financial investments, the likelihood of successful completion, the time expected to be required for substitution (including any relevant certification or regulatory approvals) and the major challenges encountered with alternatives which were considered but subsequently disregarded. Given that it is not possible to disperse with cleaning process nor to transition to a different procedure, our R&D processes focus on identifying potential alternatives solvents.  Research for substitutes is ongoing, but at this stage it is too early to conclude that the potential alternative cleaning mixtures assessed will fulfil all requirements needed, as specified under Question 1 of this section. A new substance qualification process requires a certain amount of resources (e.g., equipment, workforce, adaptation time, investments), and the global effort is expected to be considerable. The process can take up to several years and has important impact on the manufacture production, as production machines need to be stopped in order to be emptied, loaded with the new substances and to do the tests.  The results of the global qualification process can also have many consequences on the production. Best case, there is no impact and the new substance can be introduced; worst case, processes need to be changed in order to introduce the new substance, and/or a change of equipment is required if the new substance is not compatible. For these reasons, and given the current uncertainties regarding the technical feasibility of PFAS substitution for industrial precision cleaning, we support the exemption of at least 13.5 years for industrial cleaning fluids, to allow industry to finalize its ongoing assessment of alternatives and implement them if technically possible.  Question 4: For cases in which substitution is not technically or economically feasible, information on what the socio-economic impacts would be for companies, consumers, and other affected actors. If available, please provide the annual value of EU sales and profits of the relevant sector, and employment numbers for the sector  i. Impact on consumers: Critical loss of chronometric properties of watch movements has been detected if this specific process is not applied, as well as when using non-PFAS solvents. A deterioration in the quality of the industrial cleaning processes in the watch industry would, resulting from the absence of a derogation, lead to premature wear of the mechanical components and a loss of reliability of watches, leading to a loss of confidence on the part of consumers, who might turn to electronic products that also use PFAS in their manufacture.  ii. Annual value of EU sales and profits of the relevant sector: Watches generated €2.44 billion in export revenues for the EU in 2020. In addition, €536 million of EU watch components and straps were also exported to Switzerland in 2020*. * Federation of the swiss watch industry, 2022.  iii. Employment numbers for the sector: In 2020, the watchmaking industry and jewellery industry and downstream sectors employed 167,000 workers in the EU**.  In Switzerland, around 61,000 workers are employed in the watch production (including 21,000 cross-border workers, mainly from France, Germany, and Italy) ***. ** EuroStat, 2023. *** Convention patronale de l'industrie horlogère suisse, 2022.  iv. Essentiality considerations: The craftsmanship of mechanical watchmaking in France and Switzerland was inscribed in 2020 on the UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. We understand that this is in line with the Commission’s definition of essentiality, which will allow for the use of certain substances when they are critical for the functioning of society and while no alternatives are available****.  **** https://ich.unesco.org/doc/src/LHE-20-15.COM-Decisions-EN.docx

General Comments: Our company would like to emphasize that from an environmental and health perspective, we are fully committed to replacing PFAS in our products. However, there are no alternatives available for some applications that are essential to society. Therefore, we suggest either an exemption or a significantly extended transition period for some essential uses.
Hard Plastic Clad Fiber (hereinafter referred to as "H-PCF") is used for the short-range transmission system. H-PCF is comprised of a pure silica core potion and the fluoropolymer cladding potion. However, there are no alternatives available for the fluoropolymer and our company cannot produce H-PCF If PFAS restriction becomes effective. The short-range transmission system with H-PCF is used in a wide variety of applications such as a railroad car control, a production control in factories and flame-monitoring systems in thermal power stations. Therefore, PFAS restriction affects socioeconomic impacts.
On the other hand, in terms of emissions to the environment, H-PCF Users do not touch a cladding portion directly because the cladding portion of H-PCF is covered with coating materials and PFAS are not released to outside of H-PCF. Used products are collected and ultimately end up in a landfill, therefore, the anticipated emission risks to the environment from a landfill are low.
The cladding polymer is meet the definition of essential-use. Therefore we request that cladding polymer is exempted from PFAS restriction until appropriate alternatives are provided.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Main : Electronics and semiconductors  Sub : Wires and cables Datailes : The cladding polymer of optical fiber

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The types of fluoropolymers used in H-PCF are made from PFHxA-related substance, tridecafluorooctyl acrylate and tridecafluorooctyl methacrylate or made from PFBA-related substance, nonafluorohexyl acrylate and nonafluorohexyl methacrylate. The weight of the PFAS related substances accounts for less than 3% of weight of H-PCF. The cladding portion is covered with coating materials and fluoropolymers are thermally, biologically, and chemically stable, therefore the release of PFAS related substances from landfilled H-PCF is of very little concern. Fluoropolymers and H-PCF are produced only in Japan and during production stage, there are no emissions within the EU.

PFAS related substances are used generally as the only materials which can reduce the refractive index of polymer. Refractive index of silica glass: approx. 1.45 Refractive index of polymer including PFAS related substances: approx. 1.40 ･An all-glass Optical fiber is joined by the fusion splicing generally, but the fusion splicing is not applicable for H-PCF because the cladding portion consists of polymer. A connector is used to join H-PCF and the cladding polymer should have adequate strength to assemble the connector. Typical tensile strength of H-PCF cladding polymer:10MPa or more.　 ･The chemical stability is required for the cladding polymer for long-term use. Fluoropolymers have chemical stability and are suitable for the cladding polymer.  c. The number of companies in the sector estimated to be affected by the restriction. PFAS restriction will have socioeconomic impacts on numerous companies in the EU.  d. For cases in which substitution is technically and economically feasible but more time is required to substitute. A transmission system used all-glass fibers is an alternative. It is assumed that the total cost difference between the all-glass fiber systems and the H-PCF systems will be millions of dollars per year. ･When H-PCF is damaged, system users must replace it with alternatives. Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our company, which is small but efficient, is the distributor of German made ETFE (ethylene-tetrafluoroethylene) in China since 2016.  Between 2019-2022, we have distributed more than 200 tons (half a million square metres) of German made premium quality ETFE, all of them deployed for architectural projects within China.  Individual project sizes vary from a few hundred up to 83,000 square metres.  The structural formats vary from single layer membrane structure to multiple-layer air-inflated cushions for roofing and/or façade of shopping centres, sport stadiums, horticultural enclosures, recreational buildings (including those for schools), exhibition halls, civic plazas, municipal landmarks and pedestrian precinct overhead covers connecting sometimes multiple historical or listed buildings etc.  The number of projects designed for ETFE materials is increasing all the time.

In China, as demonstrated already on a global scale, the preference of using ETFE as the pre-eminent light-transmissible building material in recent years stems from the industry acceptance of the fact that such structures bring

- practicality (savings in the quantity and substantivity of secondary structural materials, ease of upkeep and maintenance, supreme durability with no noticeable ageing problems, ease of erection and refurbishment when needed, complete recyclability of the membrane)

- safety (flame resistance, light weight, no known record of human injuries or sufferings through material disintegration or molecular volatility)

- environmental sensitivity (sophisticated technologies to engineer the spectral transmission characteristics of the membrane spanning the solar radiation spectrum, in turn controlling the solar heat gain utilising different structural formats and architectural design ingenuity, greatly reducing the air-conditioning load of the building interior)

- visual beauty and sensual aesthetics (the wealth of colour choice, the scope for different attribute combinations, the tensile and bending characteristics allow for breath-taking designs of curvatures and profiles, clever interaction of meteorological conditions and membrane optical characteristics by design)
Scanning over all the other known membrane materials as we know them, there is simply no viable substitute to ETFE, considering all the advantages offered by the latter.  If one wants the same level of fire resistance as ETFE, no alternative membrane type can offer the same light transmission performance.  The strength and abrasion resistance of ETFE and its “bending/softness” performance are unique to this material.  When coupled with its self-clean characteristic, by virtue of its chemical inertness, a viable substitute just does not exist.  The building industry knows this, no wonder the interests and usage increase year-on-year, as we have noticed first hand in this market for a considerable time.
The two production houses of premium quality ETFE are located in Germany and Japan respectively.  The German production started nearly 40 years ago and by virtue of this immense experience and knowledge, its products are at the pinnacle in this industry as they offer the widest choice and best stability of colour, the most durable print frit quality (for light transmission engineering), the strongest material, extensive and comprehensive knowhow in light transmission engineering.  Now within the last 6 months at least two new ETFE resin producers and three ETFE membrane makers have emerged in China.  If fluoropolymer product production and usage are banned in Europe, the rest of the world will just turn to the remaining producers for source of supply.  In so doing, Europe is forced to give up on a technology and product which they had had a head-start and accumulated immense experience, not through fair competition, but by merely surrendering without a decent fight.  Further, German production meets a very high standard of quality and environmental conformance, and maintains auditable high standard of health and safety.  When the German production ceases, productions else-where will take its market share but they may not keep to the same management standard as in Germany.  Not only that in our humble view ETFE should not be restricted, even if it were banned in Europe it would not help the cause for this product class world-wide.

We make the comments above based entirely on our own business and trade experience, and we declare that these are given voluntarily and honestly.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Our input, mainly on electric and electronic equipment (hereinafter EEE), is included in this questionnaire as much as possible, but on some topics, details are given in the Annexes. To our first input, following annexes are attached:
1．Japan 4EE Comments on draft Annex XV restriction report on PFAS (Detailed explanation in addition to those provided in the questionnaire);
2. The unfeasibility of “possible substitutes” in the dossier in the actual EEE;
3. Essential Application list A: Explanation starting from PFAS as chemical materials;
4. Essential Application list B: Explanation starting from the functions of EEE needing PFAS;
5. Supplementary Explanation in Relation to Japan 4EEIA Input on PFAS Dossier.
Please see our detailed input as attached. We would like to call the Dossier Submitter’s attention especially on following issues:
(1) We would like to request the Dossier Submitter to carefully re-examine whether the proposed uniform restriction for PFAS is reasonable in view of hazard and risk of the substances.
PFAS only falls into category ‘P’ among Persistence (P), Bio-accumulation (B) and Toxicity (T). We would like to urge the Dossier Submitter to, upon the implementation of a detailed reassessment of risk and socioeconomic impacts, reconsider the need of uniform restriction for PFAS, which is not even listed as an SVHC.
Particularly in the case of complex articles, unless PFAS is listed as an SVHC, even components that may contain the substance cannot be identified. If there are concerns about PFAS, it should be proposed for the SVHC list and appropriate regulation should be investigated step by step.
In addition, UK recently published the regulatory management option analysis (RMOA).　In the RMOA a narrower definition is used than this proposed restriction, with exemptions for fluoroplastics or fluoroelastomers (low hazard groups) and intermediates, uses in sealed/contained systems (low risk uses). It is based on a group approach, which differs from the current restriction proposal. The issues on the risk of PFAS would be covered in details by the opinions from the chemical industries such as Conference of Fluoro-Chemical Product Japan (FCJ). Please refer to their input.
(2)　The threshold for PFAS in the articles should be reconsidered.
If a certain restriction is planned, the restriction on articles should be separately reconsidered. Widely-used industrial chemicals in articles should be restricted only when they can be replaced by substitutes or alternative technologies with less negative environmental impact, according to the results of technical and socioeconomic impact assessment. In current dossier, investigation on substitution is not sufficiently described. In particular, proposed threshold of 25 ppb for PFAS in articles is not feasible and not commensurate with the risk. In our view, this threshold follows that for PFOA, but the suitability was not shown in the risk assessment also in PFOA case. We would like to request the Dossier Submitter to determine a threshold of PFAS that is proportionate to the risk by conducting a proper risk assessment, not by simply copying PFOA.
Generally speaking, under normal use, substances in articles have a significantly lower risk of being released as they are, or of being exposed to the human body or the environment, unlike substances on their own or mixtures.
