(According to a study conducted for the U.S. Consumer Electronics Association (currently, CTA) by researcher Technology Forecasters Inc. (TFI).) The study found that the RoHS Directive cost the global electronics industry more than $32 billion for initial compliance and about $3 billion annually to maintain compliance. However, the cost for restriction of PFAS would be far higher because there are so many PFAS to be restricted and the threshold is extremely lower and the necessary derogations have not been established.  Please also see our section 3 of Annex 1, Annexes 5 and 4. Premature restriction may would prevent the ICT-based life that EU citizens currently enjoy.  PFAS is widely contained in many critical components such as semiconductors horisontally used in EEE but in very small volume. According to Eurostat, imports of ICT products and Electrical machinery totaled EUR 249 billion in 2020 then these sales would be lost from the global EEE industry. If PFAS is uniformly restricted as currently-proposed, almost all the EEE cannot be manufactured and used. Huge amount of unemployment may occur in all over the manufacturing industry because no EEE can be made without PFAS. Semiconductors or thin film device manufacturing will do nothing but move outside EU, because there are no options to avoid making use of PFAS. This means that the employment in conjunction with EEE is lost in EU. Furthermore, such uniform restriction of PFAS may lead to defective substitution which cannot attain necessary performances but also ensure safety, reliability and durability of the whole products. The end-users will be affected most seriously. This may lead collapse of the whole social infrastructure based on IT and semiconductor technologies.  If only semiconductors listed as “potential derogations marked for reconsideration” in current dossier are finally derogated and the adequate derogations for other applications listed in our Annex 4 are not set for electronics, the functions necessary for EEE described in Annex 4 and uses exampled in its Column G become non-available, or could be only used in a condition where their performances are remarkably inferior. From about 1970s, PFAS became used in EEE industry widely. Therefore, if PFAS is uniformly restricted, the level of the performances of EEE may return to those at the late 20th century.  For example, about display function, the performance of the thin liquid crystal displays such as TV or monitors, which are widely used today, would return to the level at the latter half of the previous century. More concretely, if the flat panel displays are not able to be manufactured because of PFAS ban, display cannot but return to the cathode ray tube technology which does not use PFAS. We wonder whether EU and its consumers would really accept such inferior level of performance or not. If accepted, long time has passed since global industry stopped production by such an analog technology, and the supply chain for it has been also abolished, and the production factory does not exist anymore either. If PFAS is banned uniformly, the factories for the old-type products without PFAS must be rebuilt, but it will take several years.  If the large-capacity communication becomes unavailable by PFAS ban along with the inferior display performance, current technologies such as the street view, the surveillance camera or automatic driving by using information via satellites will become also unavailable. If the piezoelectric function is not usable by PFAS ban, the touch panel would not function, either. In addition, the modern minimisation and mobilisation by making use of the high functional materials using PFAS would become completely impossible, then the smartphone with current performance cannot be produced anymore. Please also see page 2 of our Annex 5, which illustrates the essential applications of PFAS used in a smartphone. If the minimisation becomes impossible, many products would inevitably return to bigger and heavier ones, and the resulted wastes would remarkably increase. In addition, as operating the bigger products needs more electricity, uniform PFAS ban would cause negative effect also from the point of view of energy efficiency. Furthermore, the degradation of performance of the motors or the medical equipment, etc. would directly have significant effect on the human safety issues.  Unachieved "intended function" leads to "lowering the performance". We sincerely recommend the dossier submitters and ECHA to examine carefully what degree of deterioration of performances relating to EEE would be acceptable in the modern society.  Also for products which are already in use in the EU, if PFAS is kept restricted as currently-proposed without exclusion for spare parts for old products, social infrastructure based on electronics cannot be maintained in subsequent 10 years, because maintenance or repair cannot be done without original spare parts.  In current technical situation EU would not be able to use the state-of-the-art or future technologies without PFAS. The whole EU society may be left behind from other areas of the world as a result. In this sense, the premature PFAS restrictions would turn down the competitiveness of EU. Such situation would run counter to existing policies of EU including “Shaping Europeʼs digital future”, “2030 Digital Compass”, Regulation (EU) 2021/694 establishing the Digital Europe Programme, and the proposal for a REGULATION establishing a framework of measures for strengthening Europe's semiconductor ecosystem (Chips Act), COM (2022) 46 final and so on. EU authority should properly recognise such possible negative effects from the total ban of PFAS, and show the fact clearly to the EU citizens.  Considering the possible impact at the uncountable level mentioned above, we believe that the essential PFAS applications should be kept usable under the reasonable management and that the society had better to keep obtaining the benefit from it. We consider that THIS would be a better measure balancing with the socio-economic aspects and in line with the environmental policy along with the economic growth, promoted by the EU Green Deal policy.

10. Analytical methods: The Annex XV report states that “Shall not be placed on the market in mixtures and articles in a concentration of or above 25ppb for any PFAS and 250ppb for the sum of PFASs (polymeric PFASs excluded from quantification) and 50ppm for PFASs (polymeric PFASs included). However, we think we can’t manage materials and products in this very small amount range, even if chemical and material manufacturer in upstream supply chain, as it is technically unfeasible to distinguish polymer and not-polymer PFAS, and also applied and non-applied PFAS at present.  There are two ways to analyze the amount of PFAS in the materials: “liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry” and “Combustion-Ion Chromatography”.  The first step in performing targeted analysis on article is a process called extraction, in which PFAS is dissolved into a fluid, such as water or organic solvent, which is suitable for the analytical method. More concretely, it is necessary to establish an extraction methods by optimizing the organic solvent used for extraction, extraction time, extraction temperature, etc., according to the type of polymer that constitutes the molded product and the type of PFAS to be analyzed.  Establishing this extraction method has the following difficulties. (1) There are many types of PFAS, and it is not easy to consider all PFAS. (2) It is necessary to examine the extraction conditions for each polymer that uses PFAS. (3) A polymer containing a predetermined amount of PAFS to be used for the study must be prepared.  Especially this time, it is necessary to prepare a polymer containing PFAS at ppb level of concentration, but it is not easy to produce such a polymer. (4) At extremely low concentrations like this time, the influence of adsorption during pretreatment on the analysis results is relatively large.  If PFAS is extracted successfully from the article, analysis using instrument such as “liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry” is performed as the second step. The “liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry” can theoretically detect PFAS at ppb order by comparison of material to be analyzed and the reference materials which structure and concentration of PFAS have been identified. To obtain the accurate results, we have to understand the exact structure of all PFASs and obtain all PFAS’s reference materials. We think it would be impossible, because there are so many kinds of PFAS covered under this draft regulation. On the other hand, if using “Combustion-Ion Chromatography”, we can determine total fluorine content on the order of a very small amount without its reference materials, but we can’t distinguish polymer and not-polymer PFAS, and also applied and non-applied PFAS.  For these reasons, even if upstream chemical and material manufacturer, it is technically impossible to control at suggested concentrations. EEE industry is manufacturing our products as (complex) articles. Generally, we downstream stakeholders cannot analyse themselves without proper information from upstream manufacturers. In addition, due to the industrial structure of the value chains, it takes long time to deliver the information of articles/components containing specific chemical substances.  From the consideration above, it is unfeasible to stably and accurately manage the above limit values for the stakeholders in EEE supply-chain. Unreliable data getting out of control might cause misunderstanding and confusion throughout the global supply chain.

General Comments: Our understanding is that the European Council and the Parliament will have a F-Gas 'trilogue' meeting to negotiate the final regulations.  We would like to raise some questions to be considered:

⁃ When will Industrial Waste Heat be specifically included in European policies, such as REPowerEU? It is a free, local and decarbonized energy that can significantly lower the bar for Decarbonization - representing about 30% of European natural gas use, or around 1000 TWh/year (half of it below 100°C, the other half above)

⁃ When will Industrial High-Temperature Heat Pumps (HTHPs) greater than 70°C and greater than 100 kW be recognized as their own category? They are a very different technology than residential and commercial heat pumps; and different even than very large heat pumps (greater than 10 MW). There are 30,000 industrial sites in Europe needing HTHPs to produce up to 5 MW of heat less than 200°C. It is unclear in which current F-Gas category these are included.

⁃ Currently, most industrial companies exclude "natural refrigerants" from their HTHP specifications due to safety risks (toxicity and flammability, as declared by producers to ECHA) assessed using EN378.

⁃ Which science-based, peer-reviewed study proves "natural refrigerants" have a lower environmental impact over their lifecycle? Despite their name, these are not collected in nature and are not necessarily good to be discharged in nature in large quantities. Ammonia is produced by fertilizer plants (1.8% of global CO2 emissions); hydrocarbons and CO2 are fossil-fuel based and produced by oil refineries. Frequency of leaks due to higher circuit pressures in HTHPs and the additional metal needed should be taken into consideration to assess the total environmental impact.

⁃ Which "natural refrigerant" alternative allows the generation of steam up to 5 MW? The IEA HTP Annex 58 lists none at TRL=9. Water as refrigerant might be the future, but it is still at a fundamental R&D stage.

⁃ If the goal is to reduce the GWP impact of refrigerants, why try to promote hydrocarbons for high temperatures? Propane / pentane / butane have a GWP=5, while HCFO-1233zd(E) has a GWP=4.

⁃ Will ultra-low TFA degradation be taken in consideration by the future PFAS legislation? Fluids such as HCFO-1233zd(E) and HFO-1234ze(E) have TFA degradation less than 2%, thus resulting into potentially 80 tons/year of TFA from 100 GW of HTHPs that could be installed in Europe. The global stock of TFA is estimated to be currently above 200 million tons.

The "Heat Pump Accelerator" of the European Commission is a great initiative. However, policy uncertainties related to F-Gas and PFAS are limiting investments by both industrial sites and HTHP manufacturers. The result is continued use of fossil fuels and the risk of a future switch to "renewable waste heat", which represent as much as 70% of the primary energy used by light industrial sites.

Industrial HTHPs using fluids having GWPless than 10 and TFA degradation less than 2% should be allowed by both F-Gas and PFAS until a viable alternative is available.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
"About VNCI
The Royal Association of the Dutch Chemical Industry (VNCI) is the industry association for the chemical industry in the Netherlands. In the chemical industry in the Netherlands, 45,000 employees work at 390 companies. These companies are important for many other industries because they supply commonly used basic raw materials. VNCI supports balanced regulation in the field of PFAS to address concerns about these substances. VNCI therefore welcomes the opportunity offered by ECHA to respond to the general PFAS restriction proposal through the public consultation.
Industrial use
The chemical process industry is not treated as a user sector of PFAS in the restriction proposal, unlike, for example, the electronics and semiconductor, medical devices, energy and petroleum, and mining sectors. However, the restriction proposal also has a major impact on the chemical sector. The sector is not only a producer of PFAS, but also a (final) user of, among other things, fluoro-polymers. Fluoro-polymers fall under the definition of PFAS in the restriction proposal. Therefore, it is necessary to pay separate attention to, and conduct further research into, the industrial use of fluoro-polymers within the chemical sector.
Why fluoro-polymers? Fluoro-polymers are water-, grease-, dirt-, and dust-repellent, heat-resistant, and chemically inert. The combination of these properties is an important reason for the use of fluoro-polymers in chemically and thermally demanding process conditions. Their use prevents corrosion/wear of process installations and the unwanted release of chemicals from installations. The applications therefore contribute to process safety. In addition, applications of fluoro-polymers can protect product quality from, for example, contamination by metal ions.
Applications
There are many applications of fluoro-polymers that fall within the broad scope of the restriction proposal. These include tubes, valves, gaskets, pipes, internal parts of columns, linings, filters, membranes, diaphragms, and electronics. Identifying all applications in chemical process installations proves to be a complex task, as companies partly depend on information from suppliers. It is therefore likely that not all applications will have been identified within the (short) six-month consultation period. Suitable alternatives for all these applications will then have to become available in a timely way and in sufficient quantities. This is currently unclear.
Assessing alternatives
Due to the extremely large amount of PFAS variants and applications that fall within the scope of the proposal, it is impossible for us as an industry association to - in general - say something about the availability of suitable and applicable alternatives. The companies in the chemical sector have therefore received advice from VNCI to specifically respond to the consultation for their own processes and to provide relevant data that can be assessed by RAC and SEAC.
Continuity and safety
We are concerned that the continuity of production will be at risk if essential parts of production processes unexpectedly disappear because specific applications of fluoro-polymers are no longer allowed while suitable alternatives (still) are not available. Depending on the specific application, this can have far-reaching and negative consequences for the safety of production, the environment, and/or product quality.
Generic exemption
This must be prevented, and therefore we argue - by analogy with the exemption (derogation) included in the restriction proposal for the petroleum and mining sector - for a generic exemption for the chemical sector for applications of fluoro-polymers in industrial installations. This should be done at least for the period needed for the companies in the chemical process industry to identify, become available, and apply suitable alternatives for the current applications.
Term
The proposed exemption period for the petroleum and mining sector of 13.5 years may be insufficient to ensure suitable and applicable alternatives for all applications of fluoro-polymers within the chemical process industry, and therefore we propose a timely interim evaluation with the possibility to extend the exemption, if and to the extent necessary. This has been done, for example, in the restriction of perfluorinated carboxylic acids C9-C14 (REACH Annex XVII Entry 68).
More information
For further details and data regarding specific applications of fluoro-polymers in industrial installations within the chemical process industry and further underpinning and explanation of our position, we would like to refer to a European study conducted by Accenture on behalf of Cefic, the European Chemical Industry Council. Several Dutch companies participated in this study. We also refer to the response of Cefic to this public consultation and to the individual responses of companies from the chemical sector."

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Overview
We are a global leader in fuel, solvent, and acid leak detection solutions, with a large installed base spanning 30+ years of installations in in commercial and industrial applications such as production, transportation, storage, refining, or consumption of fuels; semiconductor, chemical, paint or pharmaceutical manufacturing; distillery, brewery, wastewater, food processing, and infrastructure such as airports/airfields.  Fuel, solvent, and acid leaks cause damage to property, customer goodwill, and the environment. In the worst cases, leaks cause safety issues to the environment and emergency responders and can result in environment fines. In all cases, leaks benefit from early detection and rapid remediation to improve outcomes for environmental health and safety by ensuring that leaks are discovered before any significant damage can occur.
Leak detection cable is a common form of large area or direct pipeline leak detection. It is a specialized electric cable that is able to detect and report the location of leaking fuel, solvent, or acid to the facility owner / operator across large areas because leaks emerge in indiscriminate places of large areas (berms of tanks) or along pipelines. Use of large area or direct pipeline leak detection cables enables rapid response to unexpected fuel, solvent, or acid leaks protecting commercial and industrial infrastructure from damage, property loss, environmental damage, and owner/operator penalties.
This submission requests a derogation, until 13.5 years after EiF, for the use of fluoropolymers within jackets of fuel, solvent, and acid leak detection cables which are designed to both:
a) be used at temperatures below 65°C; and
b) protect property and environment space against unexpected fuel, solvent, or acid leaks by providing detection and location information of the leak
being the “Fuel Leak Detection Cables”.
We have separately submitted a derogation request for certain Water Leak Detection Cables. The rationale behind the making of multiple submissions is because we see various distinctions between the two classes of products, how PFASs are used by them, and how they are used more generally (amongst other matters).
Form of cable and PFAS use
Leak detection cables, including Fuel, Solvent, and Acid Leak Detection Cables and components, consist of sensing elements are made of a resistive wire jacketed with a conductive fluoropolymer. In Fuel and Solvent sensing cables, two conductive sensing elements are wrapped concurrently in a helical fashion with two fluoropolymer jacketed detection wires around a fluoropolymer structural carrier along with the length of the cable. Sensing and location detection is accomplished via electronics connected to the cable (connections and electronic controller) which puts the two sense wires at different voltage, such that when electrical connection between the two sense wires closes the sense circuit at the location of the detected leak. An electrical connection between the two sense wires is caused by a conductive jacket layer that is sensitive to fuel or solvent which swells inward into the sense wires by being constrained by a constraining mesh.  In Acid sensing cables, two acid sensitive jacketed sensing wires are wrapped concurrently in a helical fashion with two fluoropolymer jacketed detection wires around a fluoropolymer structural carrier along with the length of the cable. Sensing and location detection is accomplished via electronics connected to the which puts the two sense wires at different voltage, such that when acid etches the sense wire jacket, an electrical connection between the two sense wires closes the sense circuit at the location of the detected leak. Location determination is readily determined via the resistance measured because of the know resistivity of the sense wire.  The helically wrap construction embedded within the structural carrier enables reduction of false alarms.  The use of fluoropolymers provides durability and resilience to other potential contaminants such as solvent, oil or other spills that could potentially occur in the local area of deployment (often under flooring).  The sensors can be cleaned, dried, and redeployed successfully (except acid sensors which are destructively etched and must be replaced after detecting an acid leak).
In Fuel and Solvent Leak Detection Cables, fluoropolymers are used to create sensing, to provide dielectric integrity as jackets, as structural carriers, and as the constraining mesh as part of the sensing construction. In Acid Leak Detection Cables, fluoropolymers are used to provide dielectric integrity as jackets, as structural carriers, and as a wicking mesh to enhance the sensing construction. Fluoropolymers are also used in the connection systems to enable the system integrity and durability in these demanding applications.  These unique designs requiring the entire portfolio of fluoropolymer properties to ensure durability and function; specific properties are addressed in the application description.
Applications
Details of how Fuel Leak Detection Cables are used are set out in the “Sectors and (sub-)uses” part of the submission below. Key uses include, however:
(a) in high consequence locations along underground pipelines
(b) along batch and transfer lines at fuel depots, airports / airfields, gas stations (automobile), and other commercial / industrial infrastructure;
(c) airport/airfield hydrant systems;
(d) tank farms; and
(e) above ground piping at terminals, refineries, and oil fields.
Leak detection cables, components, and controllers work together as a system to play a vital role in the European Union’s ongoing efforts to secure energy supply as well as implementing the European Green Deal as they are used within LNG transport, decarbonization, hydrogen production, storage and distribution just to name a few applications supporting the energy transition as well as protecting property and the environment.
Substitutes
In fuel, solvent, and acid leak detection of commercial and industrial applications, we have not conducted extensive evaluations for non-fluoropolymer alternatives, recognizing the fluoropolymers meet the broad range of material requirements needed especially for durability.
We do not believe it is possible to develop a suitable fuel, solvent, or acid leak detection system by shifting from fluoropolymers to non-fluoropolymers for the sense wires, detection wires, carrier cable, or constraint mesh due to the need for comprehensive chemical resistance, especially to fuels, solvents, and acids.  These demanding applications also require mechanical ruggedness and durability such as water, biological, UV, temperature, flame, abrasion, and impact resistance, along with lubricity and sufficient in-line strength for the carrier cable.
We set out further details on the substitution analysis of the available alternatives in our response to information request 8.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: By reference to Table 9, the Fuel Leak Detection Cables would most naturally fall within the sub-use “Electronics” in the “Electronics and semiconductors” sector.   In Table 2 (“PFAS main applications and sub-uses”) of the Annex XV report, the Fuel Leak Detection Cables would most naturally sit under the sub-use of “wires and cables” in the “Electronics and semiconductors” sectors.  It should be noted, however, that the Fuel Leak Detection Cables are used across multiple sectors and in multiple industries to detect fuel, solvent, and acid leaks in commercial and industrial applications such as production, transportation, storage, refining, or consumption of fuels; semiconductor, chemical, paint or pharmaceutical manufacturing; distillery, brewery, wastewater, and food processing.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: a) Usage phase: As fluoropolymers are high molecular weight molecules and meet the global standards as polymers of low concern, it is believed that there is extremely low possibility that leak detection cables under ordinary use will create material emissions during the usage phase. b) End of life phase: A recent Conversio-study has shown that “at its end-of-life approximately 85 % of all fluoropolymers end up in waste-to-energy recovery incinerators” (Conversio-study can be acquired via “https://www.pro-kunststoff.de/fachwissen/conversio-studie-end-of-life-von-fluorpolymeren.html”).  Following on that study, the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) in cooperation with Société Générale de Surveillance (SGS) set out to investigate whether fluoropolymers get fully incinerated without any formation of short chain of long chain PFAS.  Preliminary results of that study demonstrate that (i) fluoropolymers are converted to Inorganic Fluorides and Carbon dioxide at standard incineration conditions; (ii) the inorganic fluorides mainly include Hydrogen Fluoride and Silicon tetrafluoride; and (iii) total organic fluorides (PFAS) were non-detectable with a reporting limit of 0.08 ppm and Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) was also not detected with a reporting limit of 0.04 ppm.  The study concluded that “fluoropolymers at their end of life when incinerated under representative European municipal incinerators conditions do not generate any measurable levels of PFAS emissions and therefore pose no risk to human health and the environment.” See Non-Confidential Annex 01. Additionally, Aleksandrov et al. already concluded in 2019 specific for PTFE that “municipal incineration of PTFE shows no significant generation of studied PFAS. See Non-Confidential Annex 02.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Concerning the effectiveness of fluoropolymer incineration, we would like to reference the ongoing research project by the Federal Institute for Materials Research and Testing (BAM) and the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT), funded by the German Federal Environment Agency:   “Basic investigations on thermochemical degradation of PFAS in laboratory and pilot plants to determine optimum combustion conditions for the thermal treatment of PFAS-containing waste materials.” See Non-Confidential Annex 03. The study involved application samples of the four most sold Fluoropolymers (PTFE, PVDF, PFA and FKM) provided by Pro-K (German association of polymer processors), which were incinerated under standard operating conditions for municipal and industrial waste incineration (850°C – 1100°C for two seconds residence time respectively) and consulted by the German Federal Environment Agency (Umweltbundesamt). The final data sets and methodology used are being reviewed and validated by Environmental Standards Inc. The absence of organic fluorides and more specifically PFAS substances in incineration flue gas confirms complete thermal destruction of Fluoropolymers during incineration and therefore it should pave the way for exempting Fluoropolymers from the EU REACH PFAS restriction proposal.

6. Missing uses: Please refer to Question 8 where we discuss alternatives and socio-economic impacts.

8. Other identified uses: a. Annual tonnage and emissions As discussed in Question 2 above, there is not believed to be any material emissions from the intended use of our leak detection products nor in their end of life recovery. b. Key functionalities provided by PFAS In fuel, solvent, and acid detection of commercial and industrial applications, fluoropolymers are used in five (5) ways in leak detection cables and components to function robustly and durably:  (a) creation of sense wires via percolative conductive fluoropolymers, (b) detection wire jackets providing dielectric integrity of the signals, (c) creation of the structural carrier for deployment into harsh environments, (d) compression / wicking mesh to complete the sense circuit, and (e) protective connection systems to electronics. Leak detection cable is a common form of large area leak detection. It is a specialized electric cable that is able to detect and report the location of leaking water to the building or facility owner / operator across large areas because leaks emerge in indiscriminate places of large areas including water ingress associated with climate related disasters. Use of large area leak detection cables enables rapid response to unexpected water leaks protecting data, historical treasures, and property loss.
This submission requests a derogation, until 13.5 years after EiF, for the use of fluoropolymers as sensing elements, jackets for detection wires, and as a structural carrier for the deployment of leak detection cables which are designed to both:
a) be used at temperatures below 65°C; and
b) protect space against unexpected water leaks by providing detection and location information of the leak,
being the “Water Leak Detection Cables”.

The rationale behind the making of multiple submissions is because we see various distinctions between the two classes of products, how PFASs are used by them, and how they are used more generally (amongst other matters).
Form of cable and PFAS use
Leak detection cables, including Water Leak Detection Cables, consist of sensing elements are made of a resistive wire jacketed with a conductive fluoropolymer. In each sensing cable, two conductive sensing elements are wrapped concurrently in a helical fashion with two fluoropolymer jacketed detection wires around a fluoropolymer structural carrier along with the length of the cable. Sensing and location detection is accomplished via electronics connected to the cable (connections and electronic controller) which puts the two sense wires at different voltage, such that when water touches both of the sense wires concurrently it closes the sense circuit at the location of the detected leak.  Location determination is readily determined via the resistance measured because of the know resistivity of the sense wire.  The helically wrap construction embedded within the structural carrier enables reduction of false alarms.  The use of fluoropolymers provides durability and resilience to other potential contaminants such as solvent, oil or other spills that could potentially occur in the local area of deployment (often under flooring).  The sensors can be cleaned, dried, and redeployed successfully.
In Water Leak Detection Cables, fluoropolymers are used to create sensing, and to provide dielectric integrity as jackets, and as structural carriers requiring the entire portfolio of fluoropolymer properties to ensure durability and function; specific properties are addressed in the application description.
Applications
Details of how Water Leak Detection Cables are used are set out in the “Sectors and (sub-)uses” part of the submission below. Key uses include, however:
(a) under floor deployment in computer rooms, data centers, museums, hotels or other commercial buildings;
(b) in cabinet deployment in sensitive computer rooms and electronic installations;
(c) in building areas subject to water ingress that need pumping to minimize property damage.
Leak detection cables, components, and controllers work together as a system to play a vital role in the European Union’s ongoing efforts to secure energy supply as well as implementing the European Green Deal as they are used within data centers supporting the energy transition as well as protecting property with increasing threats from climate change.
Substitutes
In water leak detection of commercial and industrial applications, we have not conducted extensive evaluations for non-fluoropolymer alternatives, recognizing the fluoropolymers meet the broad range of material requirements needed especially for durability.
We believe it is possible to develop a suitable water leak detection system by shifting from fluoropolymers to non-fluoropolymers for the sense wires, detection wires, and carrier cable due to the low voltage and moderate temperature requirements, however, durability may be compromised against unexpected contaminants that fluoropolymers inherently protect against. In relation to Water Leak Detection cable systems, we have not yet conducted extensive evaluations for non-fluoropolymer alternatives. However, we believe it may be possible to develop a suitable water leak detection system by shifting from fluoropolymers to non-fluoropolymers for the sense wires, detection wires, and carrier cables due to the low voltage and moderate temperature requirements.  However, doing so (in each case) will require a product redesign with careful material selection to achieve the portfolio of requisite performance attributes (including chemical, water, biological, temperature, flame, abrasion, and impact resistance, along with lubricity, durability, and sufficient in-line strength for the carrier cable. We are aware that we have installations of our water leak detection products that have been operating for 30 years.   The risk of introducing less durability (chemical, UV, abrasion, impact, strength), or compromised lubricity, to the carrier cable is that it creates the potential for an inadvertent breach of either or both the sense or detection wires during installation (cables are pulled into position) or otherwise during the lifetime of the product due to erosion (which could create false alarms or lack of alarm that lead to system disablement and thus no leak detection or system replacement).   The cost of lessor durability will be borne by owners / operators, as more frequent replacements of water leak detection cables would be required.  We estimate this cost to be associated with pulling old cables and systems (connections and electronics) and replacing them with new cables and systems (connections and electronics).  We anticipate that this to be about, ~2x, including labor and materials. It is likely that iteration will be required to achieve overall system performance comparable to the current products made with fluoropolymers.   e. For cases in which alternatives are not yet available  We have not embarked on any R&D activities in this area; and/or details of the likelihood of successful completion of possible R&D initiatives is unknown.   f. Cases for which substitution is feasible, yet more time is required As noted in d), in relation to Water Leak Detection cables and systems an iterative approach will likely be required to find non-fluoropolymer substitutes which strike an acceptable balance vis-à-vis the products’ mechanical ruggedness-related characteristics (of chemical resistance, impact resistance, abrasion resistance, lubricity, strength and durability). General Comments: Overview
We are a global leader in thermal management solutions, with a large installed base that includes more than 1.8 billion feet of installed heat tracing cable.
Self-regulating electrical heat tracing cable is a common form of heat tracing cable. It is a specialized electric cable that is able to regulate its temperature, and, in turn, the temperatures of the items, vehicles, pipes, machinery, installations, and equipment into which it is incorporated. It has many applications.
One of these applications is that it can be used to maintain the heat of objects that are exposed to very low temperatures. These objects include, for example, pipelines, piping, valves, vessels, tanks, silos, antennas, electrical panels, safety sidewalks, stairs, guardrails, safety showers, roofs, and gutters.
This submission requests a derogation, until 13.5 years after EiF, for the use of fluoropolymers as the outer protective jackets of electric heat tracing cables which are designed to both:
a) be used at temperatures below 65°C; and
b) protect any substance, mixture or article against frost, snow, and/or freezing,
being the “Freeze Protection Cables”.
We have separately submitted a derogation request for certain Process Maintenance cables and connection systems, which are for use at temperatures above 65°C and below 260°C. The rationale behind the making of multiple submissions is because we see various distinctions between the two classes of products, how PFASs are used by them, and how they are used more generally (amongst other matters).
Form of cable and PFAS use
Self-regulating electrical heat trace cables, including Freeze Protection Cables, consist of two parallel conductors embedded in a heating core made of a conductive polymer. The core is radiation-cross-linked to ensure long-term reliability. Heat is generated as electric current passes through the conductive polymer core between the cable’s conductors. As the ambient temperature drops, the number of electrical paths through the core increases and more heat is produced. Conversely, as the temperature rises, the core has fewer electrical paths and less heat is produced.
In Freeze Protection Cables, these heat trace cables in some products are protected by fluoropolymer outer jackets. These jackets provide chemical resistance, biological resistance, flame resistance, UV resistance, impact resistance, abrasion resistance, flexibility, lubricity (i.e. an anti-stick/slip quality), and durability.
Applications
Details of how Freeze Protection Cables are used are set out in the “Sectors and (sub-)uses” part of the submission below. Key uses include:
(a) in-pipe freeze protection for drinking water;
(b) freeze prevention in rails and switch points to ensure safe railway traffic;
(c) use in underfloor heating applications; and
(d) general pipe freeze protection for outdoor spigots and outdoor water piping (e.g. sprinkler systems, building connections, cooling towers, drainage lines, livestock troughs, heat pumps, safety showers, fire sprinkler lines, waste water applications, and other industrial water feed lines.
Heat tracing cables, heat trace components, and heat trace controllers work together with heat tracing cables as a system to play a vital role in the European Union’s ongoing efforts to secure energy supply as well as implementing the European Green Deal as they are used within heat pumps, LNG transport, decarbonization,  hydrogen production, storage and distribution just to name a few. In addition, they serve to protect safety systems such as safety showers / fire sprinkler lines and enable safe passage of people on walkways, steps, stairways, and under eaves
Substitutes
In our ongoing R&D-efforts we failed to find suitable replacements that show similar portfolio of properties of fluoropolymers and match our applications needs. This applies especially for applications that are not only subject to our industry standards for electrical heat tracing systems (e. g. IEC 62395) but for applications specifically for use in explosive environments (IEC 60079-30) posing even higher demands on material performance and safety.  Freeze protection heat trace is used in industrial / chemical / energy transition processes to protect water lines in many applications, including hazardous areas.
For some applications, we believe that substitution of fluoropolymers used for the protective outer jackets of Freeze Protection Cables will be very challenging. For example, there is currently no known substitute to fluoropolymer-jacketed Freeze Protection Cables for in-pipe freeze protection for drinking water applications; this is because only fluoropolymer jacketed products have passed the stringent chemical extraction tests associated with drinking water applications (Kiwa: We create trust around the world) (https://www.kiwa.com/nl/en/).
We set out further details on the substitution analysis of the available alternatives in our response to information request 8.

It should be noted, however, that the Freeze Protection Cables are used across multiple sectors and in multiple industries.   As a producer of electrical heat tracing systems, we use a variety of fluoropolymers in self-regulating heat tracing cables. Electrical heat tracing systems are used for either freeze protection or to maintain a temperature above freezing. This is done in order to prevent frost damage, maintain the viscosity of liquids and ensure the smooth operation of chemical processes.   • Oil and gas industry: Electrical heat tracing plays an important role in the transportation of oil and gases such as LPG/LNG or H2 through pipelines. General Comments: Overview of Tesla’s response
Tesla’s comments cover the following PFAS (Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances)-associated use cases:
1. PFAS substances used in lithium-ion battery cell manufacturing processes:
• The proposed restriction does not provide any form of derogation – either unlimited or time-limited – for this use case. Due to the demonstrated lack of viable alternatives for this use case (see supporting evidence in our confidential attachment), a blanket, unlimited derogation for all PFAS substances used in battery production is necessary and appropriate.
• Alternatively, we propose to insert a time-limited derogation for PTFE (Polytetrafluoroethylene) and PVDF (Polyvinylidene fluoride) used as binder materials for the lithium-ion electrode manufacturing process, namely 13.5 years as a minimum starting point. If no viable alternatives emerge within that time period, Tesla will seek to extend this derogation beyond 13.5 years.
• Comments on socio-economic impacts and on the lack of available alternatives are provided under Section 2.6 (see confidential attachment).
Immediate factual challenges if no unlimited or time-limited derogation is provided for this use case:
The proposed PFAS restriction in its current form, i.e., without any form of derogation for PFAS used in lithium-ion battery cell manufacturing, will eliminate altogether the battery industry’s ability to produce lithium-ion battery cells in general, and at a large scale, because there are no suitable alternatives for such substances for this use case. Indeed, more than thirty years of research and development have shown that PFAS-based binders are the only option to produce lithium-ion batteries.
In turn, such an effect on the battery industry directly contradicts, both in regulatory and geopolitical terms:
• The established objectives under the EU Strategic Action Plan on batteries1;
• The established “strategic autonomy” and “self-sufficiency” objectives under the EU Net Zero Industry Act proposal2 and the EU Critical Raw Materials Act proposal3; and The EU Commission’s established objectives of promoting and supporting the production of green, EU-made electric vehicle and industrial batteries within the Union, in particular under the umbrella of the EU Batteries Regulation4.
The negative impact of the proposed restriction on the battery industry would in turn directly slow down the EU’s transition to electric vehicles, jeopardizing the EU’s commitment to phasing out internal combustion engine vehicles by 2035 at the latest under the adopted EU CO2 Emission Standards for Cars and Vans Regulation5.
Further, the proposed restriction would duplicate sector-specific provisions on hazardous substances provided under the adopted EU Batteries Regulation, which already ensures that potential and demonstrated risks to human health or the environment from hazardous substances used in batteries are appropriately managed (Article 6)6.
2. PFAS substances used in Mobile Air Conditioning (MAC) systems in vehicles:
• The proposed restriction only provides for a time-limited derogation for PFAS substances used in MACs of combustion engine vehicles with mechanical compressors, and not for electric vehicles (EVs). EVs should be expressly included within the scope of the derogation for PFAS substances used in vehicle MACs.
• In addition, a complete, unlimited derogation should be provided for the maintenance and refilling for mobile air conditioning of any vehicle placed on the market before the Entry into Force (EiF) of the restriction proposal.
• Comments on socio-economic impacts and on the lack of available alternatives are provided under Section 2.6 (see confidential attachment).
3. PFAS substances used in cooling systems in Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS):
• The proposed restriction should provide an unlimited derogation for this use case or for the maintenance and refilling of refrigerants used as cooling for Battery Energy Storage Systems that were placed on the market before the EiF of the restriction proposal.
• Comments on socio-economic impacts and on the lack of available alternatives are provided under Section 2.6 (see confidential attachment).

Halocarbon welcomes this opportunity to respond to the ECHA Annex XV proposal for the restriction of Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs).  Throughout our 70+ year history, we have always believed in the responsible use of fluorochemistry. We believe that the products we manufacture, and sell can ensure the safety of people and the environment when used properly.  In many cases, no suitable alternatives exist wherein the benefit of the alternative outweighs its own environmental and human safety risks when compared to a fluorinated material Some critical facts pertaining to Halocarbon’s position on PFAS:
• For 73 years, Halocarbon has been committed to the key industrial applications (business-to-business sales into hazardous operations) where low-volume specialty fluorochemistry is critical due to its unmatched safety, performance, and non-reactive properties.
• Halocarbon is the only US-based supplier of many critical fluorochemicals currently used in defense, aeronautical, space, and naval applications focused on national and regional security.
• Halocarbon products are manufactured in low volumes that are still commercially relevant and sold into business-to-business applications for use by trained professionals.  In many of these applications no suitable non-fluorinated products exist or can provide the safety, nonreactivity, and containment of extremely hazardous and/or toxic chemicals (e.g. chlorine, nitric acid, liquid oxygen, etc.).
• Halocarbon seeks to engage in open dialogue with regulators, subject matter experts, and public officials to help create meaningful fluorochemical regulation, grounded in the best available science and will abide by and protect all established regulations.
• Halocarbon is and will continue to work with customers to develop cradle-to-grave product strategies and lifecycle solutions.  We seek to establish a circular economy around our fluorinated products, to establish and drive more responsible use and disposal consumption of fluorinated materials.
• Throughout our history, Halocarbon has never manufactured, used, or sold products containing fluorinated surfactants like perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) or perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS).
• Throughout our history, Halocarbon has never manufactured or sold fluorinated materials into non-essential applications such as food-packaging materials or cosmetic products.
Halocarbon believes that the PFAS definition currently proposed by ECHA is too broad to have regulatory utility.  Instead, we believe that regulators should be specific in defining chemicals by structure (e.g., PFOA and PFOS) or in groups of closely related structures (e.g., perfluoroalkyl acids).  Regulators should also focus on specific applications that pose the greatest environmental or consumer risk (e.g. AFFF, food packaging, cosmetics products, etc.), and exclude chemicals that are used in highly controlled industrial applications and chemicals that are already highly regulated.  We also encourage regulators to consider excluding chemicals that are not environmentally mobile, not water soluble, and those that are designed for use in contained (immobilized) applications.  Regulators should also consider commercial availability (or lack thereof) of suitable non-fluorinated alternatives versus the environmental and human safety impacts of those alternatives.  Lastly, we encourage regulators to consider the total annual production and consumption of these chemicals versus their risk of environmental release and contamination when properly and safely handled and disposed of.

General Comments: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are increasingly detected as environmental pollutants and some are linked to negative effects on human health.

They resist degradation, most are also easily transported in the environment covering long distances away from the source of their release. They contribute to unequal distribution of environmental and health impacts. The actors that either enjoy the benefits (users), and make revenues on the production (producers) are not necessarily those that are hardest hit by the negative side effects.

PFAS have been frequently observed to contaminate groundwater, surface water and soil. Cleaning up polluted sites is technically difficult and costly. If releases continue, they will continue to accumulate in the environment, drinking water and food.

Given our global commitment to Agenda 2030 and in particular goals 3, 10, 12, 14 and 15 the continued use of PFAS must be limited. No softening of the proposal should be done.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) are at present indispensable substances in the processing of semiconductors.

Based on three application examples, we explain the current indispensability of PFAS.

Example 1: Processing of next generation semiconductor silicon carbide
Silicon carbide (SiC) is regarded as the next generation key semiconductor material. Due to its outstanding properties, it offers the advantage of faster switching at higher voltages and temperatures with enhanced energy efficiency.

A smooth and damage-free substrate surface is crucial for the desired applications. However, SiC brings its own challenges when it comes to surface treatment as it is extremely hard and chemically inert.
Several manufacturing steps are needed to maintain a SiC substrate. At the end of the process chain is the chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) which combines chemical reaction with mechanical loose-abrasive treatment for a smooth, uniform surface. The chemical inertness of the SiC makes it necessary to use a strong oxidation agent in combination with an abrasive to ensure that a suitable removal rate is obtained despite SiC’s extreme hardness.
While the chemical attack is desired on the workpieces, it is not wanted on the components of the polishing machines. Machine parts that unavoidably come on contact with the polishing medium must withstand the chemical attack as well as the abrasion.
It is essential to coat corresponding components made of steel that are at risk of corrosion. Coatings contain polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) or ethylenechlorotrifluoroethylene (ECTFE).
Up to date we are not aware of any alternative to chemically resistant coating containing PFASs.

Example 2: Processing of silicon semiconductor substrates
Double side polishing is a well-established and indispensable processing step for producing silicon substrates which fulfill the demands on excellent geometry and surface finish.
In the double side polishing process, the substrates are guided in so-called carriers through two rotating polishing wheels. A carrier is a steel disc of similar thickness as the silicon substrates. It contains round recesses into which the substrates are placed. The substrates can rotate freely inside of the recesses and both sides of the substrates are polished simultaneously under the use of a polishing liquid.
The edges of the silicon substrates are delicate and can chip off, which means the destruction of the substrates. Therefore, the insides of the steel carrier's recesses are lined with a so-called insert out of plastic.
High demands are placed on the insert since it not only protects the substrate but also affects the quality of the finished substrate.
The insert material must be chemically resistant to the polishing liquid and must not swell when in contact with it. It must have a high compressive strength, and it must be possible to be injection molded so that the carrier insert can be manufactured at all.
Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) is currently the only known material that fulfills the requirements on the inserts.
 
Example 3: Production of silicon and silicon carbide substrates
The cutting of silicon and silicon carbide ingots by means of wire saws is an established process in the manufacturing chain of silicon and silicon carbide substrates. In this process, substrates are produced that have to meet very high accuracy requirements in order to enable further processing. In order to meet these accuracy requirements and to keep them stable over a long period of time, the positioning and guiding of the wire guide rollers in the wire saw, among other things, is of decisive importance. These wire guide rollers guide the cutting wire with the utmost precision and must be easy to remove and reinstall for reprocessing purposes without any loss of accuracy.
To ensure this, spherical plain bearings with a sliding layer based on PTFE are used in the bearing units. This sliding layer is characterised by freedom from maintenance, low friction, maximum pressure resistance, dimensional stability and freedom from swelling against the cutting fluids used. Currently, only this sliding layer fulfils these requirements.


In our opinion, the desire to regulate the use of PFAS and in particular their release into the environment is appropriate. Nevertheless, it should be born in mind that semiconductor applications rely on the use of mechanically and chemically stable compounds with currently no alternatives to PFAS. Furthermore, it should be mentioned that semiconductor applications take place in closed areas, usually clean room environments.

General Comments: Perfluorinated n-propyl vinyl ether (PPVE) is one of the main raw materials for PFA resin, and there is currently no substitute, requiring long-term exemption under the PFAS Act.
The importance of perfluorinated n-propyl vinyl ether (PPVE) raw materials Heptafluoropropyl trifluorovinyl ether (PPVE) CAS code: 1623-05-8 It is a fluorinated polymer copolymerization and modification process additive, mainly used in fluorinated polymer products such as PFA and modified PTFE. PFA contains 1wt% -10wt% perfluoropropyl vinyl ether (PPVE) in its composition, significantly improving the flexibility of PFA polymer chains, reducing the crystallinity of PFA, and making PFA have good thermoplastic properties. After adding perfluorinated n-propyl vinyl ether (PPVE) and modifying the properties of this type of fluoropolymer resin, it has been widely used in the fields of chemical anti-corrosion and microelectronics production. Fusible polytetrafluoroethylene (PFA) is an important new type of fluorinated resin, With excellent chemical stability, physical and mechanical properties, electrical insulation performance, lubrication, non adhesion, aging resistance, non flammability, and thermal stability. Similar to PTFE, its high-temperature mechanical strength is about twice that of PTFE; And it can be processed using general thermoplastic molding processes such as extrusion, blow molding, and injection molding. The rapidly growing market demand in the PFA industry chain provides the most dynamic growth space for the development of chip technology, which reflects the importance of perfluorinated n-propyl vinyl ether (PPVE) raw materials. If prohibited under the PFAS Act, the entire PFA industry will disintegrate and cannot be produced. The stability of mature production processes from the early stages of the development of the chip industry is the foundation for promoting the development of the chip industry. Therefore, in our strategy for the chip industry, we need to further emphasize the importance of PFA resin. In the absence of other alternatives, it is unrealistic to maintain the rapid development of chip technology in terms of stability and inheritance, and to ensure that chip technology requires rapid replacement of other plastics in terms of innovation and applicability. Global chip factories are unable to establish an evaluation of PFA product replacement plans and the risk results after replacement in the short term. PFA products can be recycled and reused, and their reasonable recycling and reuse have good economic value, ensuring that a large number of PFA products are not abandoned and cause damage to the environment. PFA is widely used in the manufacturing of wires and cables, semiconductors, and thin films. The semiconductor industry is developing rapidly, with a significant increase in demand for PFA. The semiconductor industry has widely applied PFA materials in areas such as chip carriers. Compared with other fluorinated polymers such as PVDF, PFA has a higher degree of fluorination, can withstand stronger acidity and corrosiveness, and performs better in terms of performance. PFA will continue to be the preferred material for cutting-edge semiconductors in the future (there are currently no alternative solutions), continuously unleashing the vitality of various industries. The production capacity of international electronic chips is gradually being released, and PFA production capacity is mainly concentrated in this field for growth. Due to the higher cleanliness level of PFA materials (metal ion dissolution and impurity particle dissolution are very, very small) compared to PTFE, PFA has been widely used in the semiconductor industry in recent years, mainly for handling containers, baskets, pipelines, valves, etc. used for ultra large scale integrated circuit silicon wafers. PFA resin is required to have high purity and is suitable for electronic grade reagents (such as ultrapure hydrofluoric acid) storage purposes. From the perspective of global PFA consumption structure, chemical, petroleum and natural gas industries, and electrical insulation materials are the top three application areas of PFA. Semiconductor is a key element in modern electronic products and an important component of many commonly used electronic devices, including smart phones, tablets, and personal computers. These are basically modern devices that many of us rely heavily on in our daily lives. It is precisely due to the core position of the semiconductor industry that it has broad competitiveness. Due to the extremely high specification requirements in the production process of electronic products, minor pollution or impurity can seriously affect the yield, electrical performance, and reliability of fine semiconductor materials. Whether it is wet etching or chemical mechanical polishing (CMP), even a small amount of impurities will have a significant impact on the final product throughout the entire integrated circuit manufacturing process. Therefore, electronic component manufacturers should be responsible for raw materials, transportation pipelines, and reactions. This means that throughout the entire manufacturing process, there are high requirements for containers, etc. It is difficult to find an extreme chemical environment that can withstand strong acids, alkalis, high temperatures, and pressures, and the important role of PFA resin is highlighted. Chips are the cornerstone and heart of the entire information industry, as well as the engine driving the development of the entire information society. The chip itself is an industry with high technological barriers. Although a chip is only the size of a nail, it integrates over 10 billion transistors. The chip industry has a very long industry chain, and each link in the industry chain must be interconnected, with extremely high requirements. Any error in any link may lead to the chip ultimately failing to meet standards. In exploring the development path of the chip industry, we must respect the scientific laws that require PFA resin in the chip production process, deeply understand the value of PFA resin in the chip industry, correctly distinguish the connotation of environmental development and the laws of product value, fully understand the independence, dependence, and adaptability of PFA resin application, maintain reverence for the chip production process, and gradually construct a scientific, reasonable, and complete PFAS proposal, Allow the indefinite use of PFA resin, the "crown jewel" of modern fluorinated industrial polymers, in the chip industry chain structure. Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Baseline Information on alternatives Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: PFAS are a huge family of synthetic compounds characterized by the presence of an alkyl chain and the bond carbon–fluorine.
Due to their unique chemical structure, PFAS have incomparable properties, such as oil and water repellence, high chemical, physical, and temperature resistance, and the ability to act as surfactants. Because of such properties and the structural variability due to the functional groups, PFAS have been widely used in a variety of products and industrial applications.
At the current state of the art, the purpose of our participation in ECHA’s public consultation is to support the unfeasible substitution of certain PFAS like fluoropolymers (such as PTFE, FKM, PFPE, and PFA), fundamental for different components intended for automotive uses (brake hoses, rings, coatings, friction materials,...) and manufacturing processes. Furthermore, the “PFAS” term used for the identification of an entire chemical family should specify which are the impacted substances and polymers for suitable regulation and effective controls because more than 10,000 substances fall in the OECD definition of PFAS with different behaviors and they are not detectable by a single analytical method.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: We highlight the following applications in which PFAS are essential for our sector: - Brake systems for transport, including racing vehicles. - Auxiliaries involved in the manufacturing processes that remain on the finished product. - Auxiliaries for the proper functioning and maintenance of the vehicles. Additionally, in this consultation, we will provide our available data regarding the products themselves, but also we want to stress the point that the manufacturing processes are impacted by the use of PFAS as lubricants, refrigerants, and material of the components of the machinery (such as cables, semiconductors, insulators, rings, seals, valves, and coating). In general, for the design of industrial processes, it is necessary to foresee investment and maintenance costs, as well as the timing for the return on investment, which may take several years. These are factors that contribute to the final economic balance of the Company. For the manufacturing industry is not feasible to redesign and substitute machineries and equipment in a short time. Furthermore, the maintenance of old machinery would halt entire production lines if spare parts are not available and alternative components have not been validated and approved. Our company is configured as end-users of products containing PFAS, therefore we are heavily dependent on a supply chain that at this moment is not able to provide us with any solutions to substitute components, auxiliaries, machinery, and equipment.

5. Proposed derogations: Our company inquired its supply chain to estimate the tonnage of components containing PFAS involved in our assemblies. Our investigation will continue after the end of the open period of the public consultation. Based on the current collected feedback, we estimate an average volume in the last year of more than 7 million components per 98,000 tons for O-rings, backup rings, brake hoses, gaskets, wear rings, guide rings, boots, diaphragms, brake wear indicators, brake pads, and lubricants. We would like to highlight that this is an initial estimation, based on the responses received and it is not yet complete. As a parallel insight, we evaluated the available data from the International Material Data System (IMDS), a platform dedicated to data exchange on which the automotive sector relies, and we extracted more than 20,000 of our part numbers containing components with PFAS, in particular with fluoropolymers.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: At the current state of the art, there are no alternative possible substitutes to PFAS. To guarantee essential safety characteristics, the use of PFAS is required. For example, PTFE is part of Brake hoses because it resists higher realistic temperatures instead of other polymers available on the market. Our company inquired about the supply chain to assess new alternatives, but no one of the involved suppliers, that replied, has found yet suitable substitutions in terms of technical specifications and physical-chemical characteristics. Furthermore, the supply chain is not able to provide neither alternatives and innovative solutions nor a timeline for the phase-out. If we consider the best case in which there will be new technologies and alternatives to substitute PFAS in a few of years, the internal evaluation and validation processes within the company, the suppliers, and the customers can take several years before the effective introduction into production. Based on these considerations, we would suggest, at least, maintaining the proposed restriction of a 13,5-year period after EiF in the Annex XV Restriction Report, Restriction Option 2, condition of restriction n°6(o) “applications affecting the proper functioning related to the safety of transport vehicles, and affecting the safety of operators, passengers or goods” marked for reconsideration because it is still a short time for the automotive sector. Given the uniqueness of PFAS in automotive applications and the controlled supply chain of vehicle end-of-life management, we suggest considering as appropriate to provide an exemption for fluoropolymers in the proposed restriction, as it has been granted to other sectors and applications, or providing an exemption with a timeline to review it as Annex II of ELV Directive when effective and functional alternatives will be consolidated. Furthermore, we suggest also avoiding setting a phase-out timeline for PFAS used in the machinery and equipment and reconsidering the exemptions when there will be available more reliable studies and evidence on fluoropolymers and the R&D will offer new comparable alternatives in terms of performance.
