General Comments: PFAS play a key role in the safe and efficient operation of manufacturing sites for both medical devices and pharmaceuticals. PFAS are used e.g. in seals, coatings, valves, membranes, lubricants and protective clothing. They can keep their functionality even under extreme conditions like high temperatures or pressure or in contact with acids or leaches. Their properties make them essential for a safe and efficient operation of manufacturing sites.
Numerous regulations are in place for the operation of industrial manufacturing sites . They also cover the use of perfluorinated compounds and products in manufacturing processes and the requirements for their impermeability. Regarding the latter, fluoropolymers play a crucial role. To obtain permission for operation, manufacturing sites have to fulfill strict and complex requirements including environmental authorization procedures as well as complex safety and quality requirements by product legislation  (e.g. Good Manufacturing Practices, hygiene rules, process validation etc. to ensure product safety). Therefore, any change made to existing manufacturing sites requires a complex and time-consuming process and is not easy to realize. It goes without saying that, before such a process is being started, the existence of appropriate alternatives has to be guaranteed. Finding alternatives for a safe and efficient operation of industrial manufacturing sites with the same properties PFAS substances like fluoropolymers have, takes time and the results with regard to their effects on health and environment have to be proven before use.
Furthermore, the availability of spare parts for existing manufacturing sites has to be guaranteed in order to ensure their functionality.
Under all circumstances the operability of manufacturing sites for medical devices and pharmaceuticals has to be maintained. The availability of curing and life-saving high-quality products for patients has to be ensured. Last but not least the economic impact a general ban of PFAS would have to be taken into consideration. The European Union openly strives for a strengthening of its economic resilience and for a reduction of being dependent on imports from third countries. A non-differentiated regulation of PFAS without taking into thoughtful consideration every aspect of the whole production and supply chain of medical devices and pharmaceuticals puts not only the life and well-being of patients, but also the economic strength and competitiveness of Europe’s economy at risk. European countries will have to turn to third countries if PFAS are not regulated in a differentiated way with regard to their properties, with regard to their essentiality for the function of the society, with regard to their benefit-risk-assessment and with regard to timelines for the development of adequate alternatives. Furthermore, a regulation of PFAS should be aligned with other existing legislation and regulations.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Medical Devices: Implantable Medical Devices Tubes and Catheters Membranes used for venting of medical devices Packaging of Medical Devices Electronics: Wire insulation

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Manufacture Phase: Implantable Medical Devices, Tubes and Catheters, Membranes used for venting of medical devices, Packaging => PFAS containing components received from the suppliers and for the medical devices, the components, more or less are assembled and no more processing of these components. Therefore, negligible emissions. Electronics: Wire insulation => PFAS containing wire insulation received from the suppliers and for the medical devices, the wires, more or less are assembled and no more processing of these components. Therefore, negligible emissions. Use Phase: Implantable Medical Devices, Tubes and Catheters, Membranes used for venting of medical devices, Packaging => As the PFAS components used here are in the solid matter form and not in the liquid or gaseous form, the emissions are negligible. Also, in case of interaction with the medicine or body fluids, this has been tested under biocompatibility. It is safe to use for the patient and safe for the handling by the medical professional or end user.  Electronics: Wire insulation => As per the safe usage of the active pumps, there are negligible emissions as the wire insulation is in the solid state. Also, the periodic servicing takes place to keep the control of the wear and tear of the product as they are placed in the field for 10 years. End of Life Phase: Implantable Medical Devices, Tubes and Catheters, Membranes used for venting of medical devices, Packaging => These products are single use and after the application, gets disposed off as per the hospital protocol. As per our knowledge, the products get incinerated under regulated conditions. But we do agree that we do not have the information over the emissions. Electronics: Wire insulation => In case of end of life of the pumps, as per the condition of the components, either they get recycled or gets disposed off. No more information available over the emissions for now.

5. Proposed derogations: Implantable Medical Devices, Tubes and Catheters, Membranes used for venting of medical devices: 10 - 100 Tons Packaging: 100 - 1000 Tons *Electronics (Wire insulation): 100 - 1000 Tons  No information over the emissions are available

6. Missing uses: Table A.1 of Annex A of the Annex XV is not applicable for our Business Unit.  Our Disposable Medical Devices are covered with Annex XV Table 9. But our Active Medical Devices have the components that are neither covered in Annex XV Table 9 nor Table A.1 of Annex A of the Annex XV. Therefore, for all the components not covered, we need it to be considered for the derogation. Besides the Wire insulation, there are more components that are required to be covered, for example the Friction Seal.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Medical devices differ greatly with regard to the components they are being made of. Even routinely used devices may have hundreds and thousands of components which means that supply chains can be long and complex. Currently, there is no obligation to disclose whether products or materials provided by suppliers contain PFAS. That means that the medical technology sector is not and cannot be aware of all uses of PFAS, especially in complex medical devices with a lot of components and a sophisticated manufacturing process for these components itself.  One example of concerned complex equipment are devices which are used to replace essential body functions in case of acute or chronic organ failure, keeping hundreds of thousands of patients alive worldwide.  Given the extremely broad scope and low thresholds in the currently proposed restriction, existing data gaps cannot be quickly closed with the needed reliability by the sector or concerned suppliers. In case of a ban of a single component due to a missed identification of its PFAS relevance or a too tight or short derogation medical devices and related therapies might become unavailable for years.  While we appreciate the proposed derogations for certain applications, we are concerned that many crucial medical applications remain disregarded or uncovered.  If no alternative is available or a PFAS is discovered in a medical device in future, the absence of derogation would adversely affect not only PFAS manufacturers and medical technology producers but especially patients and practitioners throughout Europe and worldwide. The medical technology sector is also dependent on its supply chain for alternative materials and components, which, when available, still need to pass lengthy regulatory approval processes.

8. Other identified uses: We produce millions of pumps for enteral and infusion applications that is used by the healthcare worldwide in more than 90 countries.  Complexity: Tight, detailed exemptions cannot cover all relevant uses of PFAS in medical devices and pharmaceuticals and its supply chain. With the current approach it can be expected that relevant uses will be (unintentionally) banned with serious Socio-economic impact on the availability of these products, i.e. putting patients’ lives at risk. Much broader, generic exemptions for medtech/healthcare are needed. No alternatives: PFAS, especially fluoropolymers, are often intentionally used due to their unique chemical/material properties. Alternatives are missing, would not fulfill required technical criteria or would have equal environmental impact.

General Comments: PFAS PUBLIC CONSULTATION: INITIAL BRIEF PCTFE IN MEDICAL PACKAGING

Brussels, 10 August 2023

EuPC is the leading EU-level Trade Association, based in Brussels, representing European Plastics Converters. EuPC now totals about 51 European Plastics Converting national and European industry associations, it represents close to 50,000 companies, producing over 50 million tonnes of plastic products every year. The European plastics industry makes a significant contribution to the welfare in Europe by enabling innovation, creating quality of life to citizens and facilitating resource efficiency and climate protection. More than 1.6 million people are working in about 50,000 companies (mainly small and medium-sized companies in the converting sector) to create a turnover in excess of 280 billion € per year


Introduction
Following our initial submission, EuPC intends to comment on specific applications. Since those are very diverse, each will be covered in a separate submission. This brief is the initial brief for PCTFE used in medical packaging. We intend to further complete this submission by the end of the consultation period.
This submission is built upon a survey conducted in collaboration with Honeywell, the supplier of PCTFE film from outside the EU, as well as key market leaders responsible for producing multilayer packaging utilizing this film within the EU. This survey is anticipated to encompass approximately 90% of the total usage of PCTFE in medical packaging, ensuring a robust representation of industry insights and practices.

Use of PCTFE in medical packaging
PCTFE (Fluoropolymer PolyChloroTriFluoroEthylene, EC number: 618-336-7, CAS number: 9002-83-9) is a long-chain polymer used in pharmaceutical blister packaging for Oral Solid Dosage Form (more precise than ‘Medical Devices’) and to package and make MEDICAL DEVICES such as parenteral containers and to manufacture MOLECULAR DIAGNOSTIC KITS. The report summaries listed above in this questionnaire did not yet include the use of PCTFE in packaging for medicinal preparations, medical devices and molecular diagnostics. In these applications, PCTFE film is used for several decades as a reliable high-performance moisture barrier. It enables to prevent contamination and loss of product integrity and efficacy of medicinal preparations. PCTFE film is laminated to PVC and other materials to become part of a laminated thermoformable film which is used to shield critically sensitive pharmaceutical substances, medical devices and diagnostic kits. The packaging materials used for these products are strictly regulated in the incumbent regulatory ecosystem (EMA, Pharmacopeia standards, etc.). PCTFE-based films are a critical primary packaging and their composition is an integral part of the submission package in order to obtain approval for market authorisation of the medicinal product. From a regulatory perspective, it is of equal importance as the excipients (1) of the medicinal product (2).
Critical use for pharmaceutical packaging includes blister-packaging of moisture-sensitive substances. Examples of moisture-sensitive are contraceptive drugs, acyclovir, erythromycin, antibiotics, ciprofloxacin, HIV-antiretroviral drugs, cancer-chemotherapeutic drugs and some of the corticosteroid substances which are used to treat COVID-patients. Without sufficient protection moisture-sensitive pharmaceutical compounds will be affected by hydrolysis, they can degrade, the crystalline order can be disturbed and intermolecular interactions can affect the integrity of the product. The inherent overall risk of exposure to moisture is the loss of therapeutic effectiveness of the drug, thereby jeopardizing the reliability of the pharmacokinetic response, potentially leading to illness and loss of life. The use of high-performance barrier film is critical to keep pharmaceutical drugs safe from ambient moisture, especially during transportation and storage and in unstable climate conditions.

(1) Excipient: Constituent of a medicine other than the active substance, added in the formulation for a specific purpose.
(2) Directive 2001/83/EC on the Community code relating to medicinal products for human use; and Regulation (EC) 726/2004 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 March 2004 laying down Community procedures for the authorisation and supervision of medicinal products for human and veterinary use and establishing a European Medicines Agency.

No hazardous properties justifying a restriction
PCTFE whilst it is very persistent by design does not display any hazardous property/property of concern referred to by the dossier submitter; i.e., bioaccumulation, mobility, long-range transport potential (LRTP), accumulation in plants, ecotoxicity, endocrine activity/endocrine disruption, effects on human health and concerns triggered by a combination of these properties.
PCTFE fluoropolymers are manufactured both from non-PFAS raw materials and the non-PFAS monomer Chlorotrifluoroethylene (CTFE), and polymerized without the involvement of other PFAS substances (processing aids, surfactants, additives, or agents).
PCTFE adheres to the OECD definition of a polymer of low concern (1) (2) (3). It demonstrates characteristics of being insoluble in both water and fat (see Honeywell submission Nº 4083). Moreover, no reactive functional groups or functional groups of functional weight have been identified. Oligomers content is negligible as well as monomer content (one has to note that the starting monomer is not a PFAS).

(3) Korzeniowski, S. H. et al. A critical review of the application of polymer of low concern regulatory criteria to fluoropolymers II: Fluoroplastics and fluoroelastomers. 2022.
URL: https://setac.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ieam.4646

PCTFE should be excluded from the scope of the restriction
Based on the above, PCTFE should in our view excluded from the scope of this restriction. We however provide additional information showing both its negligible emission and the disproportionate socio-economic impact that would be linked to its substitution. In the event it is determined that PCTFE shall not be excluded from the scope of the restriction, then our analysis suggests that the industry would need a minimum of a 12-year transition period to discover suitable alternatives.

Note: the following sections numbers correspond to the sections numbers from ECHA’s Comments for Annex XV restriction report for Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS).

1. Sector and sub-use
This comment is related to the following use: PCTFE-based packaging for medicinal preparations, medical devices and molecular diagnostics.

2. Emissions during the end of life
According to a recent study conducted by Conversio on behalf of ProK (4), it has been found that the disposal of medical and pharmaceutical waste predominantly involves incineration, accounting for approximately 90% of the total waste generated. On the other hand, landfill disposal constitutes only 7% of the overall waste generated in this sector – see p. 39, ratio recalculated excluding metal. Additionally, there are some recycling efforts, 3%, particularly in the form of mixed plastics recycling sourced from household waste.

It is essential to highlight that, according to WHO guidelines (Table 2: Methods of disposal of uncontaminated packaging, pp. 140, Guidelines on packaging for pharmaceutical products, WHO Technical Report Series, No. 902, 2002. source: https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/medicines/norms-and-standards/guidelines/regulatory-standards/trs902-annex9.pdf?sfvrsn=82b4c57d_2), incineration is highly recommended for the disposal of uncontaminated medical packaging.

Emissions in the landfill would be negligible given PCTFE is not soluble in water (5mg/l) or oily media (1-octanol). It is based on non-PFAS monomers (CTFE), has negligible impurity and its manufacturing does not involve the use of any PFAS substances (processing aids, surfactants, additives, or agents).

For behaviour in incineration, see the next section.

(4) Fluoropolymer Waste in Europe 2020 – End-of-life (EOL) Analysis of Fluoropolymer Applications, Products and Associated Waste Streams." Final Report Made on Behalf of pro-K, Conversio. July 2022.
URL: https://www.ft.dk/samling/20222/almdel/euu/spm/49/svar/1951975/2698345.pdf

3. Emissions from incineration
Incineration above 850 °C does not release PFAS-related materials (5) (6) (7), nor detectable levels of Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) (Bakker, J., et al. (2021)  ibidem). Those temperatures can only be found in municipal waste incinerators, as they are mandatory according to the Industrial Emissions Directive 2010/75/EU (Article 50), which prescribes that waste incineration plants must be designed to ensure that flue gases reach a temperature of at least 850 °C for at least 2 seconds in order to ensure the proper breakdown of toxic organic substances).

(5) Aleksandrov, K. Waste Incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to Evaluate Potential Formation of Per- and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) in Flue Gas. 2019, 226, 898-906.

(6) Taylor, P. H. Investigation of Waste Incineration of Fluorotelomer-Based Polymers as a Potential Source of PFOA in the Environment. Chemosphere 2014, 110, 17-22.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chemosphere.2014.02.037
(7) Bakker, J., et al. Per- and Polyfluorinated Substances in Waste Incinerator Flue Gases. Rijksinstituut voor Volksgezondheid en Milieu (RIVM) Report 2021-0143.
DOI: https://doi.org/10.21945/RIVM-2021-0143

5. Proposed derogation tonnage and emissions
In July 2023, a comprehensive survey was conducted, specifically targeting the primary converters of medical packaging. The companies interviewed collectively account for approximately 90% of the EU's PCTFE-based film production. Based on the insights gathered from this survey and supplementary information, we can reasonably estimate that the volume of PCTFE utilized in medical packaging across the EU amounts between 1000-2000 tonnes/year – an average of 1,500 tonnes/year. This results in between 4,000 to 8,000 tonnes/year of multilayer film placed on the market – an average of 6,000 tonnes/year; the balance being other polymer layers such as PVC, PE, PA, EVOH, and PET; which are materials without PFAS content.

5.1. Emissions during manufacturing of PCTFE (Aclar®) film
The PCTFE film utilized in this context is imported into the EU as it is not manufactured within the region. Notably, Honeywell, conducted film extrusion at a temperature of 250°C, revealing no signs of degradation in PCTFE. Indeed thermal degradation is expected at temperatures above 350°C. This confirms the film's robustness and suitability for its intended application in medicinal packaging, providing assurance of its high-performance characteristics.

5.2. Converting of PCTFE film into multilayer film and related emissions
PCTFE film serves as a high-performance barrier layer, and it is efficiently laminated with other polymer layers such as PVC, PE, PET, and EVOH for medicinal packaging, particularly blister packs. The lamination process takes place within the temperature range of 15 to 80°C, ensuring that the PCTFE film remains stable without experiencing any degradation.
As PCTFE enters the converters' facilities in the form of a film, the possibility of solid losses, including microplastic pellets, is estimated to be negligible. Moreover, converters have proactively committed to the Operation Clean Sweep (OCS) pledge, aiming for zero pellet and microplastic losses within their facilities. Additionally, any internal waste generated during the conversion process is effectively recuperated and directed towards recycling.
Considering these efforts, emissions at this stage are estimated to be minimal and, consequently, pose no significant environmental concerns.

5.3. Blister manufacturing
Medicinal blister packs are produced in-house by the pharmaceutical company using a thermoforming process on supplied multilayer films. The thermoforming of PVC, at temperatures ranging between 110 and 170 °C – depending on the polymer combination; i.e., PVC, PE, PET, PA, EVOH –, allows the creation of the blisters. 7. Derogation for reconsideration: information on socio-economic impact and analysis of alternatives
7.1. Analysis of Alternatives
7.1.1. PCTFE
For several decades, PCTFE film is the barrier material of choice used in blister packaging due to its outstanding properties: biochemical inert, transparency, and high moisture barrier. It is stable and has an enhanced shelf life. It may withstand varying environmental conditions (wet, cold, heat) ensuring the stability of medicines and drugs. The film is very flexible and enables also deep cavities to receive the pills. It also results in less material to be used than alternatives.

7.1.4. Discussion of technical properties of alternatives compared to PCTFE
a) PVDC offers remarkable process stability, rendering it comparable to PCTFE. Its mechanical properties are medium, similar to PCTFE under ambient conditions, but it can exhibit brittleness at temperatures below 10°C. While PVDC provides good moisture protection, it falls slightly short of PCTFE in this aspect, resulting in a medium shelf life. This reduction in shelf life could potentially lead to increased film wastage or impact drug validity. On a positive note, PVDC showcases high transparency, akin to PCTFE.
However, it is important to note that PVDC is not fully compatible with current operational process conditions used for PCTFE-based films; this would necessitate investments for the implementation of the alternative, such as installing new production coating lines and/or adopting different processing methods and equipment for the thermoforming form/fill/seal medical packaging operation.
b) Aluminium (Cold Foil Forming, CFF) has high process stability, but it falls short in terms of compatibility with the operational process conditions of PCTFE. The mechanical properties of Aluminium-based films are medium – against PCTFE, needing a much larger blister layout. Its moisture/oxygen protection is very high, offering a high shelf life, comparable to PCTFE. In terms of bio-chemically inertness and chemical resistance, it scores lower than PCTFE due to its vulnerability at acid/basic pH exposure. Moreover, it is not transparent – for a discussion of the negative on patient compliance to treatment see section 7.2. It is typically layered with PVC, and increases all pack sizes 2X; this is because the cavity needs to be of enough size to allow the forming of aluminium. Additionally, the processing speed may be reduced by a factor of 2X against PCTFE film thermoforming, thus adding to the cost and complexity.
When Coil Foil Forming (CFF) technique is used, aluminium is usually layered with PVC, and the thermoforming speed may be reduced by a factor of 2.
CFF compatibility with operational process conditions is low. It would need major reinvesting for a technology that was superseded decades ago by PCTFE film solutions.
c) Cyclic Olefin Copolymer (COC) has high process stability. Its compatibility with operational process conditions is medium, as well as its mechanical properties. However, its moisture/oxygen protection is low. On the positive side, COC exhibits high transparency, but increases material thickness 3X, and material usage doubles compared to PCTFE.

7.1.5. Availability of alternative materials
There is an indication that alternative materials such as PVDC are in short supply compromising those as a substitution option for industry. This alternative is the one that might be implemented with fewer process modifications than others.

7.1.6. Cost of substitution
PVDC: Cost of substitution to PVDC would be limited both in capital investment, 100,000-1,000,000 €/company, for the packaging lines and an additional cost for film producers to lay out PVDC coating lines which typically would sum up for the sector to 4 x 6,000,000 €; and raw material cost; i.e., overall cost under 5,000,000 €.
However, it does not display the required properties enabling enough flexibility for the pharmaceutical industry; i.e., brittleness under 10°C – according to industrial converters.
CFF: This is not a really plausible alternative due to low thermoforming speed potentially decreasing the throughput by a factor of 2X. In case investment would be considered, one should consider an investment of 5 million € per line (one line is assumed to package two drugs); i.e., a capital investment of 2,5 million € per drug.
Requalification cost
The cost of requalification by pharma companies is important. We estimate a cost of about 500,000 € per drug and per dosage tested – including testing, registration cost, and tooling –, this means that if a formulation is offered in multiple dosages, each of them requires a requalification application.  Typically the testing takes 24 months in non-accelerated stability tests.

7.1.6. Time needed for substitution/potential socio-economic effects
In case PCTFE use in medical packaging would not be derogated, one has to consider the time necessary for substitution.
Depending on the availability of the alternative, changes to film manufacturing equipment could take 1 to 3 years. Adaptation to cold forming would also take at least 3 years. Requalification of packaging takes a minimum of 2 to 3 years. The main issue is the capability to test all drugs (625 packaged in PCTFE, Aclar®) in combination with the new packaging. The process would have to be repeated by every pharma company for every film supplier. The needed cumulated time to requalify currently packaged drugs would take 10 to 15 years at the minimum.

7.2. Socio-economic impact
Based on our interviews, it is unlikely that, in case PCTFE would be banned, activities would stop at the film converters level. The overall turnover for such applications is estimated at 120-150 million €/year.
We have indicated substitution costs ranging between 317-1,875 million € across the supply chain, including pharma companies.
The main risks are however for patients and would create additional societal costs.
To begin in case of a derogation period shorter than the intended 12 years and given the high requalification cost by the pharma industry it is likely that some drugs especially “generic drugs” or drugs with low volumes of patients (orphan diseases) would cease to be offered in Europe at least temporarily.
In case one would go back to aluminium packaging, this would not only lead to increased cost (twice as much material used) but could also decrease patient compliance when taking treatment. Indeed, there is evidence indicating that non-transparency and the increased size of aluminium packaging lead to difficulties with patient compliance (8), an increase in incorrect medication dosage and an overall increase in healthcare costs. PCTFE-laminated blister films enable higher therapeutic compliance – especially for the ageing population, in part because a visible inspection of blister packaging containing tablets/capsules is possible. PCFTE is the only known barrier material that retains its color and transparency in specific applications where moist sensitivity is critical. In an era of active and healthy ageing, clear blister packaging of pharmaceutical oral solid dosage reduces the risk of ‘overlooking’ or ‘forgetting’/‘wrong dosing’, this is supported by independent studies (8) (9) (10) (11). This is important since up to one-third of the patient may be made more compliant by the development of adequate compliance strategies, packaging design being one of the contributors to the behavioral/ educational strategies put in place.
The very high clarity without impact on optical properties of PCTFE may not be guaranteed for the same shelf life or as enabler patient compliance (retaining of colour) with alternative plastics solutions. For storage and shelf life, it is of vital importance that medicines, in the form of pills, are not exposed to environmental moisture. Products with compromised stability have reduced therapeutic effects. Furthermore, toxic degradants formed due to the degradation of the drug(s) and/or excipient(s) can seriously affect patient or consumer safety (12).

7.3. Proportionality
We have demonstrated above that PCTFE, a polymer of low concern, is unlikely to lead to the release of hazardous PFAS compounds, whilst the substitution cost is prohibitive, 300-1,900 million €, not to talk about the potential impact of withdrawn drugs or decrease in patient compliance.

8. Conclusion/Summary
Based on the above, PCTFE should in our view excluded from the scope of this restriction. We, however, provide additional information showing both its negligible emission and the disproportionate socio-economic impact that would be linked to its substitution. Additionally, the transition to alternative substances necessitates an adjustment period in terms of industrial practices and requalification procedures to meet the regulatory standards applicable to medicinal and medical devices applications. For this, certain time lapses exist that, if not provided with a minimum transition period of 12 years, will compromise the supply of some medicinal/medical devices which are essential for society and human wellbeing.

General Comments: PFAS REACH Annex XV Restriction (Public Consultation)
Comments Submitted by the American Thoracic Society


As President of the American Thoracic, I appreciate the opportunity to comment on ECHA’s proposal:  PFAS REACH Annex XV Restriction.  The American Thoracic Society is the world’s leading medical society dedicated to accelerating the advancement of global respiratory health through multidisciplinary collaboration, education, and advocacy.  The core activities of the ATS’s more than 16,000 members worldwide are focused on leading scientific discoveries, advancing professional development, improving global health, and transforming patient care.  Key areas of the member focus include developing clinical practice guidelines, hosting the annual ATS International Conference, publishing four peer-reviewed journals, advocating for improved respiratory health globally, and developing an array of patient education and career development resources. In short, we are respiratory health experts.

As respiratory experts, we are keenly aware of how access to metered-dose inhaler (MDI) respiratory drugs is essential for helping patients with respiratory conditions like COPD and asthma manage their disease.  It is with professional expertise as respiratory experts that we offer the following comments.

Climate change is a pressing global health threat and requires urgent action.
The ATS agrees with the general intent of the policy proposal to reduce the global emission of powerful greenhouse gases.  We further recognize that current propellants in MDI, while low in overall volume of emissions, do have disproportionately long global warming potential and that policy steps are needed to curb their overall emissions and develop alternative propellant options. We further recognize that the uncontrolled emissions of PFAS pose unique and lasting environmental and health threats.  We support the general intent of the policy proposal to significantly reduce overall PFAS emissions.

The global patient population impacted by the proposed policy is significant.
It is estimated that globally, more than 300 million people suffer from COPD, and an additional 260 million have asthma.  Prescription respiratory drugs, delivered through MDIs, play an essential role in treating these patients with COPD and asthma, both in treating acute asthma and COPD exacerbations and providing long-term disease management.  Given the essential role that MDIs play in treating COPD and asthma and the very large global patient population directly affected by the proposed policy, we urge ECHA to move cautiously in adopting policies that directly impact access to essential respiratory medications.

While alternatives to MDI respiratory medications exist, they are not yet interchangeable with MDI medications.  As clinicians, we appreciate the effort drug manufacturers have made to bring to market alternative formulations of asthma and COPD drugs. Dry-powered inhalers (DPIs) have expanded the options of essential medicines needed to treat serios respiratory conditions like COPD and asthma.  However, DPI respiratory drugs are not yet interchangeable with MDI medications.  The correct use of DPIs requires training and continuous execution of proper technique. DPI technique requires the mouthpiece be placed between the lips and inhale forcefully and deeply. Patients are required to hold their breath for 10 seconds after completion of the inhalations. There is significant literature documenting concerns about the efficacy and consistency of DPI delivery in children under the age of approximately 14 years.1

Based on our clinical experience, the experience of our colleagues, and support from available literature, we have significant concerns that pre-adolescent children will not be able to generate adequate inspiratory flow, achieve adequate mouthpiece seal, coordinate actuation, and/or hold their breath for sufficient time to assure adequate and consistent medication delivery.  While we expect future advances in DPI delivery, education, and adoption, DPI formulations of MDI medications are not yet interchangeable options for MDI respiratory drugs.

Adoption and implementation of the proposed policy will have significant global impacts on respiratory drug availability.  As detailed in industry comments, the EU is a major manufacturer of respiratory drugs used worldwide.  EU-based facilities make constituent components of respiratory medications, including propellants, valves, canisters, and active drugs.  Patients and healthcare professionals around the world use these products.  The policy under consideration will impact treatment options in the EU but also will impact respiratory drug availability and patient care worldwide.

Extend the phase-out period for HFA-134a and HFC-227ea.
The ATS strongly recommends that ECHA finalize the policy, extending the phase-down period of MDI propellants HFA-134a and HFC-227ea. The proposed 18-month phase-down period is woefully insufficient to ensure appropriate access to essential MDI respiratory drugs.  The ATS is concerned that a period of insufficient transition will lead to significant supply chain and access issues to essential respiratory medication.

Exempt HFO-123ze from PFAS REACH Restriction Proposal
It is well recognized that the current approved propellants for MDI products (HFA-134a and HFC227ea) have high GWP impacts, and alternative propellants are urgently needed.  The ATS is pleased that industry is investing resources to develop and test alternative propellants with significantly lower GWP.  The ATS is concerned that one of the most promising candidates as a next-generation MDI propellant, HFO-123ze, would be adversely affected by the PFAS Reach Restriction Proposal.  The ATS strongly recommends that HFO123ze be exempted from the PFAS REACH Restriction proposal to allow continued development and testing of the safety and viability of HFO123ze as an alternative MDI propellant.

The ATS appreciates the opportunity to comment.  We hope you will consider our comments as ECHA moves forward with promulgating the final policy.

Sincerely,

M. Patricia Rivera MD, ATSF
President
American Thoracic Society

Content: Baseline Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments: "PFAS materials are an integral part of sealing and bearing materials used in our hydraulic products, and their use allows for specific necessary product properties to be achieved. 1. Excellent chemical resistance: PFAS materials are known for their exceptional resistance to a wide range of chemicals, including aggressive acids, bases, and solvents. This makes them ideal for applications where seals and bearings may come into contact with aggressive chemicals. 2. Temperature resistance: PFAS materials retain their physical properties well at higher temperatures, making them necessary for components subject to higher temperatures and large temperature variations. 3. Durability and low wear: PFAS materials are characterized by their high wear resistance. 4. Low friction: PFAS materials have low friction, leading to reduced heat generation and more efficient operation of bearings. 5. Low reactivity: PFAS materials do not react with other materials, reducing the possibility of corrosion or chemical reaction with surrounding components. 6. Low risk of leakage: Due to their excellent sealing properties, PFAS materials help prevent leaks, especially important in hydraulic systems. However, due to their persistence, they are used in closed systems and in very small quantities. Based on the current proposal to restrict PFAS, all manufacturers in the machinery and plant engineering industry would be affected, either in their products or in their production line. For example, hydraulic components, pumps, motors, valves, as well as fittings and compressors are heavily affected and are commonly used in the industry. PFAS, mostly fluorinated polymers, are frequently used in seals, hoses, wires, and coatings. While in some cases, the performance of the products would be immensely affected, other products may no longer be able to be manufactured, imported, or placed on the market, potentially depriving companies of their business foundation. Machinery and plant engineering companies are often in the middle of the supply chain. Therefore, identifying an affected party is a significant challenge. The inadequate harmonized classification of PFAS in the CLP Regulation means that no information is passed along the supply chain (e.g. through the safety data sheet), making it time-consuming and in many cases impossible to obtain information along the supply chains about which substances are included in formulations or intermediates. Final lists of particularly concerning PFAS (with CAS numbers) are needed in order to obtain information along the supply chains. The proposal to restrict the use of PFAS-containing seals and bearing materials in valves and coatings is only temporarily exempted and is only allowed in certain industrial applications (e.g. industrial and commercial food and feed production). However, these components are highly relevant for the entire industry (chemical plants, tool, printing, paper, textile machinery, etc.). For industrial applications, mainly fluoropolymers are used. Some of them have been scientifically evaluated as "safe polymers" (PTFE, ETFE, FEP, PFA, PVDF, VDF-co-HFP). They have been proven to be chemically stable, non-toxic, non-biologically available, water-insoluble, and not mobile. For these reasons, fluoropolymers are also approved, for example, as materials for food contact or in medical technology. Furthermore, Henry et al. (2018) have classified all fluoropolymers as low-concern polymers. A different classification should be scientifically justified. When assessing potential alternatives, it must be carefully considered as part of a holistic approach whether there are actually suitable; equivalent uses affected by the restriction. In addition to existing technical regulations (e.g. legal requirements or standards), technological maturity, safety aspects, energy consumption, service life, and other factors must be considered. So far, only a few and mostly very specific temporary exemptions have been proposed for industrial applications. Many uses have not yet been considered. PFAS-containing materials are needed in machinery and equipment when extreme conditions (high or low temperatures, high friction resistance, aggressive/corrosive/toxic chemical conditions, or a combination thereof) prevail. Therefore, most existing industrial plants and applications - including future technologies (e.g. fuel cell, water electrolysis, heat pump, solar plant) - often do not have equivalent alternatives to the expensive PFAS, which are not used carelessly due to their high price alone. Another problem is that machinery and equipment are built for a lifespan of decades. Against this background, it is important that replacement and used parts are taken into account in the restriction proposal. There are no basic exceptions or longer transition periods planned. This means that after the 18-month transition period, repairs or regular replacement of wear parts in durable products, such as the replacement of seals or hoses in industrial plants, would no longer be possible. Even if there are exceptions, they are only proposed for five and twelve years. It is not clear whether, and if so, how an extension of the existing exceptions can be requested. Due to the lack of standardized, simple analysis methods, it is not possible to control how the implementation of the restriction proposal can be ensured by market surveillance in the future, e.g. especially with regard to imported PFAS-containing products. This would lead to uncontrolled imports of PFAS-containing products into the EU. Uncontrolled imports of PFAS-containing products would lead to significant competitive disadvantages. As a supplier to the machinery and plant engineering industry, we strongly support the goal of preventing the very dangerous PFAS from entering the environment (e.g.: CMR, PBT, vPvB, PMT, vPvM or as ED). In this respect, the regulation of these very dangerous PFAS is fundamentally correct when there is a risk of exposure." Content: Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: PFAS, specifically PTFE and FKM as part of the 38 substances of low concern regarding OECD criteria, play a crucial role in the hydraulic industry, in this case in hydraulic cylinders. Key factors that make them vital materials include: Compatibility with different fluids (hydraulic oils, specificly HFDU as flame resistant), very low friction coefficient (when used as guide elements for moving parts) and degradation resistance. They are primarily used in sealings and guide elements. Sealings made from non-PFAS materials are available as a possible substitution, but especially when used with more aggressive fluids (e.g., specialized hydraulic oils used for extreme temperature ranges, flame resistant, ester-based fluids) they do not reach the same lifespan as PFAS-based sealings do.
Like sealings, guide elements made without PFAS are available and in use already, but they share some of the issues. The resistance towards some hydraulic oils is questionable, although this needs further research to pinpoint the exact combinations that are critical. Another issue with non-PFAS guide elements is friction, because in many cases, the possible substitutes do suffer from stick-slip-effects, louder noise, and shorter lifespan. This is crucial in applications where smooth movement and reduced noise are important, examples include cranes and wheel loaders. Stick-slip-effects while lifting heavy objects can cause dangerous and unpredictable movement of the load.

When used in products such as hydraulic cylinders, it is unlikely that PFAS will spill into the environment, because they are contained inside the cylinder and only come into contact with the hydraulic oils used. These are part of an enclosed hydraulic circuit where leakage is considered an issue and needs to be taken care of. Experience shows very low abrasion of the used parts, which supports the assumption that environmental emissions of PFAS from hydraulic cylinders are negligible.

Taking the aforementioned arguments into account, we propose the following considerations:
At least specific PFAS, like PTFE and FKM, should be exempt, because a substitution is not possible in every case yet.
If an exemption is no option, these use-cases should receive a transitional period of at least 12 years. The possible combinations of materials, fluids, temperature and environmental conditions are enormous and the research into substitutes is just starting to gain traction.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The hydraulic sector, in our case hydraulic cylinders, covers a whole range of uses. It doesn't fit clearly in one or more of the given use sectors. Possible use sectors are: Metal plating and manufacture of metal products (since we also do some plating inhouse), Transport (some cylinders are used in transport vehicles, although that is a small percentage), energy sector (hydraulic cylinders are used in all kind of installations that generate or distribute energy), petroleum and mining (hydraulic cylinders are a crucial part in most mining systems and machines). A very important use case is the mobile crane sector, which is essential for shifting towards a more sustainable energy mix (wind turbines can't be erected without mobile cranes).

5. Proposed derogations: The used tonnages of PFAS, in this case PTFE and FKM, can only be roughly estimated. The reason for this is that few parts only consist of the PFAS. Most parts consist of mixed materials where no exact distinction between PFAS and other substances can be given. The used tonnages were roughly estimated to around 30 to 50 t/y for PTFE and 0,7 to 0,8 t/y for FKM.  The expected emissions are unknown, but should be negliglible, because the parts are contained inside the hydraulic cylinders and do not come into contact with the environment. They usually don't show large material loss even after years of use, so even the contamination inside the closed hydraulic circuit should be low.

6. Missing uses: Our use case - hydraulic cylinders for all kinds of customers - is not clearly defined within the given uses. This is to be expected - the tonnages of PFAS in our sector is rather small, compared to other industries. Nevertheless, if the functionality and longevity of hydraulic cylinders - and other hydraulic components - would degrade, a lot of industries would suffer the consequences. Hydraulic systems are used in all kinds of environments, to name just a few: Mining, Offshore, Dams, Mobile cranes, Hydraulic presses. Especially mobile cranes are essential for the change towards a more sustainable future of generating energy. All these market sectors demand specific functionalities, e.g. longevity, lightweight, resistance to aggressive environmental conditions. PFAS - specifically PTFE and FKM - are therefor used in all these mentioned sectors, since they make these functionalities possible. Substitution is not yet possible in every use case, especially guide elements have no viable alternative. The possible impacts of a ban would be: Loss of revenue, loss of customer satisfaction, reduction of the average lifespan, general reduction in quality.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: As mentioned above, a complete substitution of PFAS in the hydraulic industry is currently impossible, because alternatives suffer from a range of issues: Lower temperature tolerance, incompatibility with specific hydraulic oils, reduced lifespan, more friction.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Information on benefits Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: PFASs are essential in paints and coatings. The most important function of paints and coatings is to provide long-term protection to the materials they are applied to, enabling buildings, bridges, and other structures, as well as automobiles, to be usable for extended periods of time. The use of PFASs in paints and coatings further improves this long-term durability, thereby increasing the long-term durability of painted objects and making a significant contribution to reducing environmental impact.
Furthermore, the use of PFASs in paints and coatings changes the smoothness and surface tension of the material's surface, providing the material with processability and anti-contamination properties. This functionality will greatly contribute to energy savings in material processing and cost/energy reductions related to the retention of coated materials.

The majority of PFASs used in paints and coatings are fluoropolymers.
Substances such as fluoropolymers, which are not absorbed by the human body due to their large molecular weight and almost insoluble in water, and fluorine gases whose toxicity cannot be confirmed should not be subject to regulation.
The requirements of Article 68(1) of the REACH Regulation are not fulfilled in terms of uniformly subjecting to regulation even PFAS that pose no significant risk to human health or the environment.
In addition, the substance should be regulated after providing appropriate analytical methods to control it within the thresholds and limiting thresholds consistent with the already regulated standards for highly hazardous PFOA and PFOS.

Replacing the use of PFASs in paints and coatings, which contribute significantly to environmental sustainability and energy reduction, is expected to take a long time and be extremely costly, but no clear development time has been identified at this time. It is highly unlikely that the entire transition will be completed within the same transition period (18 months) as the previous limitation proposal. It is likely that not all transitions will be completed and should be extended to a realistic timeframe.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: PFASs must be allowed without restriction where they provide undeniable benefits to humanity. The patient's well-being must be paramount. A differentiated, risk-based approach is imperative. Medical Devices are in some cases no longer manufacturable because there are no alternatives. In principle, there must be a complete exemption for medical products, analogous to the exemption of the pharmaceutical industry, because otherwise medical care as we know it today will no longer be possible in the future. At least not in Europe.
PFAS must be banned where they are not absolutely necessary and alternative materials make a compromise acceptable. However, these acceptable compromises are not possible for large sectors of the medical device industry.
PFASs exhibit unique properties. It is precisely these properties that have contributed significantly to today's advanced and safe treatment of patients. To do without them in medical technology is to do without safe treatment options for patients.
It is completely incomprehensible that all PFAS should be put on an equal footing and treated in the same way (namely banned), regardless of any scientific evidence about their actual hazardousness in the environment. There must always be a weighing between danger and benefit. In particular, PFAS used in the medical device industry do not pose any hazards or risks according to current knowledge. All manufacturing, use and destruction steps can be carried out without any emission. Therefore, a ban here is scientifically not comprehensible.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Implantable medical devices Other coating applications Membranes used for venting of medical devices Packaging of medical devices

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: It must be stated in advance that the overall proportion of PFAS in medical devices is extremely low. PFAS is only used in those places where it is actually required for the function of the medical devices or its packaging (e.g. Tyvec). Therefore, the quantities at the "end-of-life phase" are also extremely low. Similarly, the medical device industry is not a "manufacturer" of the materials, but a "user", therefore no statement can be made about the manufacturing process. Three product categories are presented below: a. Tubing consumables in the clinic, as well as function-relevant packaging of medical devices: Production: initial production can be made without emissions (Manufacturer issue). Processing into a medical device: no emissions occur here Use: no emissions to be expected Destruction: this takes place by the clinic through incineration. It can be assumed that the combustion parameters are set in accordance with the valid regulations, therefore no emissions are to be expected (or well below the permissible limits). b. Functionally relevant coated units in an electrical medical device: Manufacture: initial production can be made without emissions (Manufacturer issue).. Processing into a medical device: no emissions occur here Use: no emission to be expected Destruction: a return shipment is foreseen, thus ensuring a regularity-compliant feed into a destruction process. No emissions are to be expected (or well below permissible limits). See also: WEEE-guideline is valid. c. Implants: Production: initial production can be made without emissions (Manufacturer issue). Processing into a medical device: no emissions occur here Use: no emission to be expected Destruction: If implants remain in the body of the person until death, the emission depends on the burial method. In the case of burial in the ground, the implant remains in the earth and the substances are gradually released. In the case of cremation, no emissions are expected (or well below permissible limits). In the case of implants that are removed from the human body again, they are incinerated by the hospital. It can be assumed that the combustion parameters are set in accordance with the valid regulations, therefore no emissions are to be expected (or well below the permissible limit values). 5. Proposed derogations: The quantity of PFAS used for medical devices is so small that this quantity is not relevant. In particular, the predominant method of destruction at the end of the life cycle is incineration. Provided that correct incineration is carried out, which can be assumed, this is not expected to cause any emissions. Therefore, the use of PFAS in medical devices can be considered risk-free. Alternative materials are not available for these applications. This has been tested for a long time and no alternative material could be found. Therefore, a ban would lead to the disappearance of the medical devices, and subsequently to the abandonment of the entire business field and thus to the loss of jobs. Furthermore, patients could no longer be treated adequately. At least one PFAS use cannot be compensated with another material, so that this business area would inevitably lead to the abandonment of the business area in question. And thus to the loss of hundreds of jobs, as well as to a deterioration in patient care. The sterile packaging of medical devices is also affected. Here, the medical device industry uses the same materials as the pharmaceutical industry, for which an exemption exists. If an exception is not also allowed for sterile medical devices, this would mean a considerable step backwards for the sterile safety of patients and the number of nosocomial infections in hospitals would increase significantly. A risk-based benefit assessment must therefore inevitably lead to an exemption, since the supposed benefit (lowest conceivable burden on the environment) in no way outweighs the harm (patients can no longer be treated, loss of jobs).to consider the use of PFAS in medical devices as risk-free.

Content: Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period
Combined Comments:
General Comments: PFP members took note of the restriction proposal for Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) and welcome the opportunity to contribute to the ECHA consultation on the matter. While not a producer, or direct user, of PFAS, PFP sectors would have to count on equipment and materials producers to ensure a smooth transition. Here below are our views on the impact the proposed restriction would have on primary food processing.

The following three comments summarise the PFP views on ECHA’s proposal on PFAS:

1) The impact of a ban/restriction on PFAS on the EU food production should be carefully considered. Alternatives are needed to maintain the quality and quantity of EU food production.
2) All materials for food contact should be granted the same time-limited derogation in line with the current horizontal legislative framework for material intended for food contact. A proper transition period is required to validate alternatives for packaging materials and technical equipment in the production process lines – 18 months would be challenging in most cases, if not impossible.
3) Regulatory mechanisms in place to set limitations and restrictions on the use of certain substances (e.g., monomers and additives) in the manufacture of food contact plastics are already well covered under EFSA scrutiny and duplication/overlaps of settings should be avoided.

Below some detailed explanations for the bullet points above:

1) Need to maintain the quality and quantity of food production in the EU:

PFAS are used in various materials and equipment of industrial processes and participate to food quality, as they are used in many production applications from quality control in the laboratories to flowmeters and sealings of pipes.
No restriction should take place before suitable alternatives are readily available. The alternatives developed will need to be as efficient as PFAS. Otherwise, industries could face risks:
- Chemical/Environmental impact: Industries would have to use for example other sealing material which may not be as effective as the existing ones. This entails a higher risk of leakage, leading to chemicals and environmental impacts.
- Food quality impact: If industries have to use other material or coatings, e.g. hemp fibers for sealing, food quality problems may arise, as those natural materials will denature over time and can be a source of mold or yeast infections and other quality problems.
- Quality control will be impacted by replacing existing laboratory equipment with PFAS free equipment and the development of new control mechanism in the industry and the official control of foodstuffs.
- Economic feasibility: A complete ban on the use of PFASs could weaken European food production in international comparison, as production would become more costly, e.g. through increased cleaning intervals, reduced durability of materials, increased maintenance, etc. Overall, this could lead to an increase in food imports or even encourage production to move outside the EU. Thus any actions should be balanced carefully.

To ensure the continued production of foods via safe production processes in the EU, suitable alternatives to PFAS should be developed and made available on the market before restrictions are taken. There will also be the need for downstream users to evaluate the suitability and robustness of the alternative materials and articles in the industrial setting when they are available, which in itself could take more than 18 months to complete and implement.

2) Need to grant the same time-limited derogation to validate alternatives for packaging materials (more 18 months):

We share concerns for the packaging material that are not covered by the proposed time-limited derogation. Indeed, in absence of any other decision, the applicable provisions of the regulation and related restrictions on the manufacture, use, or marketing of packaging materials containing PFAS above specified limits would come into force only 18 months after the effective date. Applicable limitations include:
(1) 25 ppbs for any individual PFAS substance;
(2) 250 ppbs for the sum of all individual PFAS in the substance; and
(3) 50 ppm for polymeric PFASs.

With regard to food packaging, Annex B, Section B.9.4 of the Proposal describes significant known or historical uses of PFAS in packaging:
(1) use of PFASs in the manufacture of paper and paperboard (e.g., as moisture, oil and grease repellents)
(2) to a lesser extent, in generic (thermoplastic) packaging as processing aids, in fluorinated high-density polyethylene (HDPE) materials and articles, and as components of coatings for beverage cans, printing inks, and lacquers.

About the use of PFASs as processing aids in particular, the impact assessment (Annex E to the proposal) says:
For thin film plastic extrusion, production without PFAS processing aids was said in the CfE to be possible but to lead to (much) lower yield and lower product quality. Alternatives were also criticised in the 2nd stakeholder consultation on economic grounds due to:
o Whilst the substances identified for the consultation process were generally cheaper than PFAS they do not impart the same properties as PFAS and don’t fulfill all roles of the PFAS PPAs.
o These lower costs for alternative PPAs were offset by additional costs due to the higher material consumption for the alternative coextruded barrier layer during production and additional costs due to the taxes on non-recyclable packaging envisaged in the EU.
o The use of other polymers (e.g. polyamide) in addition to polyethylene results in multi-layer packaging, which unfortunately is currently difficult to recycle, leading to further additional costs (PFP would add that this would be against the spirit of the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation proposal from 2022).
o Metal packaging as an alternative to packaging produced using PPAs is more expensive than plastic packaging (PFP would add that it would not be suitable for all products).

Alternatives that are technically feasible appear to be available already for many applications, though not all, where PPAs are used. However, no data on the costs of these alternatives relative to PFAS has been identified. No data has been identified to establish the availability of alternatives of the appropriate quality in sufficient quantities for the EU plastics market at the present time.
Whilst alternatives are available little is known if non PFAS processing aids are available to keep high yields and good product quality without PFAS being used. 5 companies stated that they were actively working on alternatives, 2 were not and 1 did not reply to the question.

About substitution potential:

With respect to plastic packaging, PFAS are used as polymer processing aids (PPAs) to assist in the extrusion of plastic sheet and other forms, and also to provide improved moisture protection. A number of alternatives that are already on the market have been identified. However, most respondents for this use in the 2nd stakeholder consultation considered that alternatives were not technically feasible on grounds including provision of inferior moisture, reduced processing speed and limits on the quality and thickness of thin plastic film. Precise details, and information on the performance of alternatives were, however, lacking. The Dossier Submitters consider that there is weak evidence to conclude that the substitution potential is low under a full ban with a transition period of 18 months. As a result, a derogation is considered for the use of PFAS-PPAs in the production of plastic packaging.

From the data evaluated by ECHA to support the proposed restrictions on the use of PFAS in food contact applications, we detect substantial uncertainties that suggest the need for a longer transition phase than only 18 months, taking into account that when the packaging manufacturers will have worked out the transition steps, food manufacturers will also need time to complete their own duty, i.e. identify the packaging materials to change, qualify the alternative materials, proceed to stability/shelf-life tests and deplete the existing stocks, etc.

From this perspective, a transition phase of 18 months looks very short to identify the packaging materials to change, qualify the alternative materials, proceed to stability/shelf-life tests and deplete the existing stocks. This is especially true when substitutes are not readily available. For the cost of implementing alternative chemistries, the agency notes that “… extrapolation from the data that have been collected to the full market is thus prone to substantial uncertainty, even for those elements where data …” evaluated by ECHA to support the proposed restrictions on the use of PFAS “… are available.”

3) Existing regulatory mechanisms should be favoured to avoid redundant regulation:

While the relevance of excluding packaging materials from the time-limited derogation foreseen for food contact materials is questionable, the need for separate and potentially redundant regulation on food materials by ECHA should be considered. Appropriate regulatory mechanisms are already in place to set limitations and restrictions on the use of certain substances in the manufacture of some food contact materials. For the food contact plastics regulated under the Regulation (EU) No. 10/2011, EU recognized risk-based assessment principles are considered and for which similar exposure and safety considerations as described in the ECHA’s proposal apply. In this case, a double regulation needs to be avoided and the regulations on food contact materials would at least need to be amended accordingly or restrictions should directly apply through these regulations.

General Comments: PFPE and PTFE are used in medical device lubrication. These lubricants are not metabolized and show no toxicity according to our tests (see confidential data).
The products are extremly expensive (up to several thousand €/kg) and therefore are only used, where necessary in the lowest necessary amount. Therefore the potential emission is also extremely low.

In our opinion, due to the huge socio-economic impact of a restriction of PFPE and PTFE on the medical care (hospitals and doctors could not work any more, like before; see below), together with the low toxicity risk, an exemption should be considered:
- total exemption without any transition period for PTFE and PFPE used in all sectors or
- total exemption without any transition period for PTFE and PFPE used in medical sectors

Additionally, we plead to derogate the use of the monomers for the above mentioned polymers in the production of PFPE and PTFE.
If only the above mentioned polymers are exempted in the EU, the products have to be produced in other countries which leads to a marked disatvantage for the EU. And in other countries the awareness for the environment might be not that high, as it is in the EU. In the end this could lead to higher pollution of the world as a whole.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Sectors: Medical devices and Lubricants  PFPE and PTFE are important components in lubricants for medical industry. They are not metabolized and have one of the best toxicity-profiles (see confidental data for information on cytotoxicity, hemocompatibility, systemic toxicity, pyrogenity).

These 100 g are carefully cleaned up and disposed to incineration, so usually there should not be an emission to the environment at all.  Estimated emission share for use phase: <0,01% (the PFPE/PTFE-based lubricants in medical devices are made as a lifetime lubricant, so emission is only due to loss on leakages. Leakages are rare, as the medical devices are usaually sealed).  Estimated emission share for end of life phase: <0,1%  PFPE and PTFE based lubricants that are used in medical applications (implants, medical devices) are disposed together with the parent device. As these typically are either potentially infectious (e.g. removed implants) they are incinerated. As the incinerators have HF-filters, total emissions are supposed to be low.  Non-infectious devices are usually diposed together with electronic or general hazardous waste. As these are also incinerated or molten, where the PFAS decompose, here also total emissions are supposed to be low.

5. Proposed derogations: Taking into account our market share (in our oppinion we are one of the three main producer for special PFPE/PTFE lubricants in medical applications) for PFPE/PTFE lubricants in medical applications, we estimate the amount of these PFAS as a lubricant in medical devices to be 1-10 tons/year. 7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: We suppose, that for PFPE/PTFE based lubricants for medical applications the derogation 5s is suitable, as without these lubricants no safe use would be possible. As product development time for medical devices can be quite long, even 13.5 years could be a quite short transition time. Please check for the comments of medical device manufacturers.

8. Other identified uses: PFPE/PTFE-based lubricants for medical applications might fall in a first instance under "lubricants not used under harsh conditions", as temperature and atmospheric conditions are not harsh. However, the requirements for those lubricants are extremely high: a) long time stable for life-time lubrication (especially in implants) b) non-soluble in water or in body liquids c) not mobile in the body d) non metabolizable in humans and animals e) non-cytotoxic f) hemocompatible g) non-pyrogenic h) not systemic toxic i) do not form decomposition products during application j) do not contain unwanted impurities from raw material production product maufacturing k) can be sterilized for re-use in hospitals and at doctors  All these requirements can only be fulfilled with PFPE/PTFE based lubricants. There is no other chemical composition known, that fulfill all the requirements at once.  Therefore, without PFPE/PTFE-based lubricants no surgery with the help of electro-mechanical devices (power tools, saws, drills,... surgery robots, ecmo-systems,...) would be possible any more and also mechanically active implants (pumps, screw drives,..) would not be available in the known situation.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Information on benefits Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Pharma Industry Finland (PIF) represents the interests of research-based pharmaceutical industry operating in Finland.
While acknowledging the general environmental goal of the PFAS Restriction Proposal to minimize the impact of PFAS to the environment and to reduce human exposure, we have serious concerns of the detrimental impact of the Proposal, as drafted, on the development, manufacture, availability and supply of human medicines in the EU.
The restriction proposal appears to be in complete conflict with the Commission’s focus to promote innovation, access to and affordable medicines, European strategic autonomy and any attraction for investment in Europe.
Perfluorinated substituents, which consist of fluorine atoms bonded to carbon atoms in a molecule provides various benefits when added to a drug molecule. These benefits arise from the unique physicochemical properties of fluorine atoms and the resulting impact on the drug's interactions with biological systems.
While active pharmaceutical ingredients are derogated from the Restriction proposal, critical chemicals and equipment needed to develop and manufacture medicines (chemical and biological) are in scope of the Restriction. We are concerned that, if not significantly revised, pharmaceutical development and manufacturing in the EU will be severely impacted. Additionally, under the current Restriction proposal, non-active product components will restrict sales of medicines in Europe that are under valid market authorizations. This applies to fluoropolymer in primary packaging, excipients, and propellants.
Below are some reasons why perfluorinated substituents are added to a drug molecule:
1. Metabolic Stability: Perfluorinated substituents, especially widely used -CF3, -CF2-, -CHF2 and -OCF3, are highly resistant to metabolism by enzymes in the body. This increases the drug's stability and duration of action by reducing the rate of degradation.
2. Hydrophobic Interactions: Perfluorinated groups are extremely hydrophobic and lipophilic. This improves a drug's ability to cross cell membranes and distribute within tissues leading to enhanced target engagement.
3. Enhanced Binding Affinity: The addition of perfluorinated groups enhances the drug's binding affinity for its target protein. Fluorine atoms forms strong, specific interactions with certain amino acid residues in the target binding site, leading to increased potency.
4. Blood-Brain Barrier Penetration: The lipophilicity of perfluorinated groups enhances a drug's ability to cross the blood-brain barrier, which is crucial for drugs targeting the central nervous system.
5. Reduced Drug-Drug Interactions: Perfluorinated groups reduces the likelihood of drug-drug interactions by minimizing interactions with other drugs and endogenous molecules, leading to improved safety profiles.
6. Tuning Physicochemical Properties: Perfluorinated substituents are used for fine-tuning the drug's physicochemical properties such as solubility, lipophilicity, and pKa to optimize its pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics.
7. Improved Bioavailability: Perfluorinated substituents increases a drug's bioavailability by enhancing its absorption, distribution, and overall stability.
8. Reduced Toxicity: In some cases, perfluorinated modifications might mitigate the toxicity of a drug by altering its interaction with cellular components, metabolic pathways, or off-target proteins.
Based on the information provided above, it's important to note that the utilization of groups such as -CF3, -CF2, -CHF2, or -OCF3 in the chemical structure of active pharmaceutical ingredients offers advantages that are difficult or sometimes even impossible to achieve with other functional groups. The effects of such modifications can significantly depend on the specific drug, its target, and the physiological context. Furthermore, drug molecule candidates advanced to the clinical testing phase feature a thoroughly optimized chemical structure. They have successfully undergone numerous safety and toxicity studies over years of research and development, accompanied by substantial financial investments. According to Tufts Center for the Study of Drug Development (CSDD) a typical development cost for NCE in clinical phase is around 2.6 billion €. Hence, requiring the discontinuation of the development of such active pharmaceutical ingredients is unreasonable, it would require starting already from discovery phase. This would result in several development programs to be stopped. Patients with unmet medical needs, particularly in several life-threatening disease conditions, would face substantial delays in receiving appropriate treatment for many years or even miss out on effective treatment.
In addition to the above-mentioned reasons to add perfluorinated substituents to a drug molecule, fluoropolymers are also used in manufacturing equipment and primary packaging when materials must be resistant against heat, light and chemicals, and if their inertness allows for high purity of any material that is processed. The required time to find, test and implement replacements followed by regulatory processes to re-acquire approvals exceeds the proposed transition periods.
To allow for the continued research, manufacturing and patient access of medicines, pharmaceuticals should generally be derogated from the PFAS restriction that is under consideration.
As a general comment a union-wide proposal is necessary in EU for any restriction to ensure a harmonized approach in different member states as the mobility and persistence of PFASs lead to cross-border pollution that cannot be adequately managed by several national regulatory actions while acknowledging that the long-term goal of reducing emissions can only be achieved by a global restriction of PFAS.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Piping Systems made from Fluoropolymers (FPs) are used for conveyance of critical media (e.g. high purity water and/or harsh chemicals) from high-tech industries (related to Green Deal, digitalization etc.) to basic chemical industry uses. Irrespectively of the used pipe materials (polymeric/non-polymeric), piping for these specific uses do need Fluoroelastomer gaskets and diaphragms for valves. Industrial FP piping are designed for 25 years lifetime, can be handled safely in industrial facilities.
We can prove on selected practical use cases in this document with our research (see confidential/non-confidential attachment), that there are currently no technical alternatives (polymeric/non-polymeric) in the upper tier of our specific uses, neither are there any alternatives visible to cover the given FP performance range in piping system incl. worker and environmental safety.
Fluoropolymers constitute a specific group of substances within PFAS, as their properties are completely different. These substances are considered polymers of low concern and therefore their use does not pose any risk to human health and the environment. The proposed PFAS restriction does not differentiate between relevant PFAS and Fluoropolymers /-elastomers (US and UK PFAS restriction proposal is excluding FPs).
Furthermore, as reported by industry/fluoropolymer suppliers, progress is being made in relation to manufacture of fluoropolymers without the use of PFAS polymerization aids, introduction of abatement techniques during manufacture, and incineration conditions to grant full mineralization of fluoropolymers at end of life. For this reason, a broad exemption for this group of substances should be considered within the PFAS restriction proposal.
