General Comments: Position paper of Surfactis Technologies, a leading provider on the market of Epilames.

SURFACTIS TECHNOLOGIES is a SME company based in Angers (France) created in 2004 as a spin off from an INSERM academic group. The company has acquired a strong expertise and know how in chemistry and physic-chemistry obtained through first class collaborations with industrial and academic groups.
The mission of the company is to develop, manufacture and sale high performance coating solutions that bring to treated surfaces hydrophobic and oleophobic properties.
Surfactis Technologies products, which are the result of our R&D pipeline and produced in our facilities, are partially or totally composed of PFAS. They are niche products used to very specific industrials need and produced in volumes comprised between tens of kg to less than 10 tons per year.
This document describes our comments regarding the proposed restriction of PFAS under the REACH regulation and expresses our concerns regarding the absence of derogation for epilame products which are essential coating agents in the functioning of mechanical movements.
Epilame are coating agents for micromechanical movements parts. These products are applied by spraying or dipping and bring to the treated parts oleophobic properties to avoid lubricants creeping / migration.  Epilame products are essential to ensure long-term efficient lubrication.

Surfactis Technologies supplies its customers with epilame products in several industrial domains:
- Watch industry: Our customers watchmakers, manufactures and service centers, in Switzerland and around the world, are using epilame during the manufacturing or servicing of timepieces.

- Mechatronics industry: Mechatronics products combine elements of mechanical engineering, electronics, computer science, and control engineering to create integrated systems that can perform a wide range of functions. These products are prevalent in various industries and use epilame products to manufacture micromotors in :
o Automotive Systems: Modern vehicles rely heavily on mechatronics for features like advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS), engine control units (ECUs), and electronic stability control (ESC) systems.
o Aerospace: Mechatronics is used in the design of aircraft control systems, avionics, and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) for tasks such as surveillance and data collection
Epilame products bring more value to micromotors in terms durability and reliability.

- Manufacturers and users of measuring instruments for the oil industry. Epilame limits the surface contamination by hydrocarbons on metallic and ceramic surfaces.
A ban of PFAS under the REACH regulation would affect drastically:
 our customers because they would then be unable to manufacture durable and reliable high-end products.
 our company with a sharp fall in sales and in our ability to maintain employment.
If the regulation of PFAS is necessary in numerous applications because of the dangerousness of some PFAS or due to the large quantities that are produced and emitted in the environment, the specific industrial applications targeted by the PFAS provided by Surfactis Technologies do not enter in those categories. Our products are non-toxic and they are produced in very small amounts and in controlled environments.
As described in the chapters below, regarding the low impact of our epilame products on the environment public health, and the socioeconomical impacts, we request a permanent derogation for the manufacture and the sale of epilames to our industrial customers for their uses for the surface treatments of :
- watch movements and timepieces.
- micromotors (mechatronics).
- instrumentation for the oil industry.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Epilame products are surface agents that bring to treated surfaces hydrophobic and oleophobic properties. Obtaining oleophobic surfaces is an essential factor for an effective lubrication of micro mechanism. Without epilamisation (i.e. the functionalization of an element by an epilame), these micromechanisms would break down after only few weeks of use.  Epilame products are used in 3 distinct industrials sectors:  -  watch industry manufacturing by supplying the watch groups, manufactures and service centers all over the world. - mechatronics for automotive and aerospace. Epilames products participate to efficient lubrication necessary for and optimal reliability to control major function in automotive and satellites. They ensure the smooth running of the lubrication in the mechanisms during the whole life of the vehicle.  - instrumentation for oil and gas industry to improve the reliability of sensors, by avoiding the clogging of viscous hydrocarbons on the instruments. This phenomenon generates a lack of reliability. The consequence is an increased frequency of maintenance and replacement of the impacted materials. Epilames avoid contamination and ensure a longer period without maintenance of the sensors. Without efficient epilames, all these sectors would be drastically impacted by a default of lubrication and/or oil contamination. This contribution applies to the following sectors: lubricants (sector as a whole) and applications of fluorinated solvents. More specifically, it includes the use of PFAS molecules in the synthesis of epilame active compounds (lubricant sector) and fluorinated solvent (solvent sector) for the production of epilame products and their uses in the lubrication process of micro mechanisms.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Epilames products synthesized and formulated by Surfactis Technologies are solutions composed of fluorinated active molecules dissolved in fluorinated solvents. They are produced in our facilities, distributed to manufacturers that apply the products to treat their parts which are finally sold to end users (timepieces, micromotors, instruments). During all these phases, the product is processed as follows:  - Our collaborators involved in the manufacturing of epilame products have a solid background in chemistry and work following the Good Manufacturing Practices.   - The synthesis of fluorinated active principles is performed in vessels dedicated to chemistry under chemical fume cupboards. At this stage, none of the used PFAS is volatile.  - The formulation is performed in a fluorinated solvent in a controlled area, the solutions are bottled without discharge into the environment.   - All the byproducts and waste are disposed of by a company specialized in waste treatment and subjected to high temperature incineration. Waste treatment companies are authorized by national authorities to collect the waste of fluorinated compounds. All the records of waste elimination are archived in our quality management system.  - The product is applied by dip or spray on the surfaces by professionals wearing individual protection equipment in controlled environment. Specific machines are used to condense the product vapors. No leakage of PFAS in the environment is allowed as specified by the Safety Data sheets of our epilame products.  - Once grafted to the surface (watch mechanism, micromotor, sensor), the product forms a nanolayer of less than 2mg of PFAS compound per square meter. The grafting is stable for years and no leakage/emission occurs.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: We are currently studying with our solvent supplier and our industrial partners the introduction of recycling of the used epilame products. The technical feasibility has already been validated. More than 90% of the fluorinated solvent can be recovered in the production cycle. The by-products of recycling are eliminated in the same process as the one used in synthesis and formulation of epilames. Recycling the fluorinated solvent would decrease drastically the amount PFAS solvents produced for epilamisation processes.

5. Proposed derogations: Based on our estimation and on our knowledge of the market, the annual tonnage of epilame products manufactured in Europe, including Switzerland, represents 10 tons.  Our estimation is based on our annual production of epilame and on the market share of our products.  As described in paragraph 6, regarding the low tonnage of the lack of replacement solution, and the benefits for the end users and for the environment, we request a permanent derogation for the production, the sale and the use of epilames.

6. Missing uses: a. The annual tonnage and emissions (at sub-sector level) and type of PFAS associated with the relevant use.  As described above, epilame products are composed of 99,9% of PFAS solvent and less than 0,01% of active PFAS compounds that bind the treated surface.  The epilame production level is estimated to be 10 tons per year. These products are not available to consumers and are only sold to end manufacturers (watch industry, mechatronic industry, oil and gas industry).   Epilame products are only used in an industrial environment during epilamization of micromechanisms.  -The waste of the epilamisation process is collected by specialized waste treatment centers and then properly eliminated by high-temperature incineration. The PFAS waste could be recycled in the near future (see paragraph 4). -All the fabrication and use steps of epilame are only performed by industrial actors, which use adapted recycling apparatus (activated carbon filters, vapor condensation). We estimate that less 0.5.% of the total amount is released to the environment, i.e. 50kg per year in Europe. -Active molecules represent 0,01% of the epilame product, ie approx. 10kg per year. These compounds are strongly grafted to high-end timepieces or instrumentation which are never discarded in the household waste.  b. The key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use.  Epilame are coating agents for micromechanical parts. These products are applied by spraying or dipping and bring to the treated parts hydrophobic and oleophobic properties to avoid lubricant.  Epilame products are essential to ensure proper lubrication of movements.  For example, oil is necessary between an axis and a bearing to lubricate the assembly. Without the epilame barrier product, the oil will migrate everywhere in the movement, decreasing drastically the efficacy of lubrication. The absence of epilame would lead to premature wear of the components and consequently would bring the system to a rapid and complete stop after only few weeks of use.  The PFAS epilames bring to the treated surface the essential property to repel oil and any contaminant by decreasing drastically the surface energy.   The key benefits of epilames on micromechanisms are the following : 1) Hold the lubricant to the exact place where it is to be deposited. 2) give the lubricant droplets an adequate contact angle (which is an essential characteristic for a good lubrication). 3) Avoid the surfaces to be contaminated by oil. 4) Ensure a chemical compatibility with a broad variety of materials 5) Protect from corrosion  c. The number of companies in the sector estimated to be affected by the restriction.  - Epilame manufacturers and distributors. To our knowledge, less than 10 companies are providers of epilame products. Watch manufactures and watch service centers all over the world. Europe has a rich tradition of watchmaking, with countries like Switzerland being particularly well-known for its watch manufacturing industry. Other European countries like Germany, France, and the United Kingdom also have notable watch manufacturers. Today, there are some 800 watchmaking companies in Europe, of which 5 employ more than 1’000 people. According to the Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry, 16 millions of watches were produced in 2022 in Switzerland corresponding to a market of 24 billions of euros.  This prestigious industry brings together several hundred thousand enthusiastic workers in Europe.  - The automotive OEMs that produce micromotors and the car makers (data not available on the % of micromotors epilamized). - The oil and gas majors and their maintenance subcontractors that ensure the reliability of sensors (data not available).  d. The availability, technical and economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives for the relevant use, including information on the extent (in terms of market shares) to which alternative-based products are already offered on the EU market and whether any shortages in the supply of relevant alternatives are expected.  Epilame products are composed of active molecules that bind to the treated surface and bring to the oleophobic property. This property is due to the chemical nature of fluorine.  According to the chemistry state of the art, there is no technical alternative to fluorine to bring oleophobic property to limit the spreading of oil or the contamination by hydrocarbon.  The use PFAS is mandatory to obtain oil repellency that makes epilamisation effective.  Complete evaluation of hydrocarbonated fatty acids (i.e. stearic acid) and of silicone family coating agents has been performed in the past by academic and industrial groups and by our R&D team to avoid the oil spreading on surfaces. If they can form a conformal layer on the surface, their oil repellency is far too low to avoid the oil spreading. It makes them inefficient for epilamisation.  e. For cases in which alternatives are not yet available, information on the status of R&D processes for finding suitable alternatives, including the extent of R&D initiatives in terms of time and/or financial investments, the likelihood of successful completion, the time expected to be required for substitution (including any relevant certification or regulatory approvals) and the major challenges encountered with alternatives which were considered but subsequently disregarded.  No information available  f. For cases in which substitution is technically and economically feasible but more time is required to substitute: i. the type and magnitude of costs (at company level and, if available, at sector level) associated with substitution (e.g. costs for new equipment or changes in operating costs); ii. the time required for completing the substitution process (including any relevant certification or regulatory approvals); iii. information on possible differences in functionality and the consequences for downstream users and consumers (e.g. estimations of expected early replacement needs or expected additional energy consumption); iv. information on the benefits for alternative providers.  No information available  g. For cases in which substitution is not technically or economically feasible, information on what the socio-economic impacts would be for companies, consumers, and other affected actors. If available, please provide the annual value of EU sales and profits of the relevant sector, and employment numbers for the sector. - Impact on the epilame manufacturers and distributors.  - Impact on the mechanical watch manufacturers and the watch service centers all over the world.  - Impact on the automotive OEMs that produce micromotors and the car makers.  - Impact on the oil and gas companies and their maintenance subcontractors that ensure the reliability of sensors.   For detailed information see paragraph c.

General Comments: Potential safety risks of non-fluorinated refrigerant alternatives

Ammonia, one of the refrigerant alternatives listed in the E2 annex, is classified as B2L – that is, toxic and flammable – in the GB/T 7778-2012 specification. In safety technology, the most effective and direct technology is intrinsic safety - refers to the safety performance of the machine and equipment itself, that is, when the system fails or human misoperation, the machine and equipment can automatically prevent operation errors or accidents. The special properties of ammonia refrigerants themselves make the initial risk in the process of use much higher than R134a (the specification is defined as A1 - non-toxic and non-flammable), so the application of ammonia refrigerants will inevitably encounter the following related accidents:

First: Jilin Province Changchun Baoyuanfeng Poultry Co., Ltd. "6•3" particularly serious fire and explosion accident

Description of the accident: At about 6:10 on June 3, 2013, a particularly serious fire and explosion accident occurred in the main plant of Jilin Baoyuanfeng Poultry Industry Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Baoyuanfeng Company) located in Dehui City, Changchun City, Jilin Province, resulting in a total of 121 deaths, 76 injuries, 17,234 square meters of the main plant and the production equipment in the main plant were damaged, and the direct economic loss was 182 million yuan.

Cause of the accident: The upper electrical circuit of the women's changing room of the first workshop of the main plant of Baoyuanfeng Company and the adjacent power distribution room of the second workshop was short-circuited, igniting the surrounding combustibles. When the fire spread to the ammonia equipment and ammonia pipeline area, the high temperature generated by combustion caused a physical explosion of the ammonia equipment and ammonia pipeline, and a large amount of ammonia gas leaked, which intervened in the combustion.

Second: Shanghai Wengpai Refrigeration Industrial Co., Ltd. "8•31" major ammonia leakage accident

Description of the accident: At about 10:50 on August 31, 2013, Shanghai Wengpai Refrigeration Industrial Co., Ltd., located in Baoshan Urban Industrial Park (No. 1258 Fengxiang Road), had an ammonia leakage accident, resulting in 15 deaths, 7 serious injuries and 18 minor injuries, resulting in direct economic losses of about 25.1 million yuan.

Cause of the accident: At about 8 o'clock on the same day, the employees of Weng Pai Company entered the processing workshop one after another, and at about 10:45, Pan Zexu, the operator of the ammonia compressor room, carried out hot ammonia defrosting operation at the ammonia adjustment station. From 10:48:20, surveillance video in the production line area of the single freezer showed that about 7 minor vibrations occurred at the scene, and the duration of the single vibration ranged from 1 to 6 seconds. At 10:50:15, the cap at the north end of the return gas header of the single freezer that was undergoing defrosting work fell off, resulting in ammonia leakage.

Third: Ammonia leakage accident of Shandong Rushan Hopewell Food Co., Ltd

Description of the accident: At 17:13 on November 28, 2013, liquid ammonia leakage occurred in Shandong Rushan Hehe Food Co., Ltd., causing 13 people to be poisoned, of which 7 died after ineffective rescue, 1 was critical, 3 were seriously injured and 2 were slightly injured.

Cause of the accident: The cap of the liquid ammonia pipeline system in the company's production plant fell off, causing liquid ammonia leakage.

Fourth: Meishan City "4.21" liquid ammonia leakage accident

Description of the accident: At 20:05 on April 21, 2013, the Jinfeng Food Factory in Fengling Township, Renshou County, Meishan City, Sichuan Province. The liquid ammonia leakage occurred in the head of the liquid ammonia pipeline in the frozen storage of the pig slaughterhouse of the food factory, and the accident has caused 4 deaths and 22 acute ammonia poisoning.

Fifth: Wanquan County Jialu Agricultural Products Company liquid ammonia leakage accident

Description of the accident: At 22:15 on August 28, 2011, the liquid ammonia refrigeration pipeline of Jialu Agricultural Products Company in Wanquan County, Zhangjiakou City, Hebei Province burst, resulting in liquid ammonia leakage, resulting in 4 deaths and 4 injuries.

Sixth: Baoding Dayang cold drink plant liquid ammonia leakage accident

Accident description: At 22:30 on July 11, 2003, the Dayang Cold Drink Plant in Xincheng City, Baoding City, Hebei Province, suffered a liquid ammonia leakage accident due to the bursting of the refrigeration pipe and valve connection, killing 3 people and injuring 1 person on the spot.

Seventh: Ruilin Food Co., Ltd. liquid ammonia leakage accident

Description of the accident: At 13 o'clock on March 6, 2003, a large leak of ammonia occurred in the refrigeration workshop of Ruilin Food Co., Ltd., Tianyuan Development Zone, Deyang City, Sichuan Province, when 4 technicians were overhauling the workshop, 4 technicians were trapped, and 2 of them died.

Cause of the accident: The valve was washed away by ammonia gas due to disrepair, corrosion and aging.

Eighth: An ammonia leak occurred at a factory in the Kedah Kulim Hi-Tech Industrial Park, Malaysia

On the evening of February 2, 2022, an ammonia leak occurred at a factory in the Kedah Kulim Hi-Tech Industrial Park in Malaysia, causing 59 employees to have difficulty breathing and vomiting, 27 of whom were hospitalized.

Ninth: 2•3 Leakage of liquid ammonia in Philippine ice factory

On the afternoon of February 3, 2021, a liquid ammonia leak occurred at an ice plant in Navotas City, Metro Manila, the capital of the Philippines, killing a male employee of the ice plant and sending at least 61 others to the hospital.

Tenth: Waterless ammonia leakage accident at Millard refrigeration service station in Alabama, USA

On August 6, 2022, an ammonia water leakage occurred at the Millard refrigeration service station in Alabama, USA. The amount of ammonia leaked in the accident was about 14.5t, resulting in more than 120 people being poisoned to varying degrees, 32 people being sent to the hospital for treatment, and 4 people being treated in intensive care.

Although ammonia refrigerants can be controlled multiple times during use and strengthen patrol detection to reduce the possibility of accidents, accidents are still very common due to their special characteristics and the combined effect of accidents. And once an accident occurs, due to its flammability and toxicity characteristics compared with general refrigerants, ammonia refrigerant accidents will always be accompanied by major casualties and huge economic losses, and the environmental impact around the accident site is also huge.

General Comments: Pro-K, a fluoropolymer downstream user association has published the attached brochure on ‘Recycling of fluoropolymers’ highlighting different possibilities and processes to recycle fluoropolymers.

Another article (report attached) on ‘Chemical recycling of PTFE (as a model for other polymers)’ by Achim Schmidt-Rodenkirchen, Klaus Hintzer, Thorsten Gerdes provides an important aspect of recycling fluoropolymers using chemical composition of the polymer. PTFE and other perfluorinated polymers consist solely of carbon and fluorine. Efficient recycling of the material can close the fluorine loop and will reduce the consumption the mineral fluorspar, which is considered as a critical raw material for the European economy.

Fluoropolymers can generally recycled according to three main categories: thermal, chemical, and mechanical. Chemical recycling can be integrated into a common recycling process between combustion (thermal recycling) and mechanical recycling. Chemical recycling can be done by three ways - Molecule recycling, Monomer recycling and Feedstock recycling. This article describes the recycling process in detail along with environmental aspects of the process.

With all the new recycling options, the fluoropolymer industry can establish closed loops throughout the whole value chain with close to zero emissions for fluoropolymers.

Please also find attached the recently published review paper on ‘Recycling and end of life assessment of fluoropolymers’ by Dr. Bruno Ameduri and Dr. Hisao Hori. This paper presents the state-of-the-art technology on the recycling, reuse and thermal decomposition and the lifecycle assessment of fluoropolymers.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Product description:
PTFE, CAS NO.: 9002 – 84 – 0
PTFE thread sealing tape

Request for exemption:
We request that the above product be exempted from the PFAS draft.

Grounds for exemption:
PTFE, CAS NO.: 9002 – 84 – 0
PTFE thread sealing tape

Poly Tetra Fluoro Ethylene (PTFE) thread sealing tape and its raw material PTFE belong to the substances of low
concern, and there is no scientific data to prove that they are harmful to the human body or the environment, so
they should be fully exempted from the PFAS ban.

Detailed description:
I. Questions about the rationality of the PFAS bill
1. Unreasonable package control regulations
In the bill, the definition about PFAS substances is not clear, and the classification is only based on simple chemical
formula. It adopts the “package control’ measures for more than 10,000 organic fluorides (PFAS), which are
excessive, especially considering that PFOS and PFOA substances that are harmful to the human body and the
environment have been effectively restricted by REACH regulations. Relevant agencies, when promulgating
management and control legislations, should not judge whether organic fluorides are toxic or harmful to the human
body through simple reasoning. Instead, they should collect more scientific data and relevant information, and carry
out classified and hierarchical management for all PFAS substances through scientific means.
2. Whether fluoropolymers are harmful
Fluoropolymer materials, including PTFE, have many unique properties, including long-lasting durability, high
mechanical strength, inertia, thermal stability and high resistance to chemical, biological and physical degradation.
According to the standards of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, some fluoropolymers
are classified as "polymers of low concern" because they have chemical stability, biological stability, inertia, negligible
solubility in water, abiotic availability, abiotic accumulation, and no toxicity. (Refer to the documents by Henry et al. 2018).
The Fluoropolymer Products Branch of the Plastics Europe once commissioned the consulting firm ChemService to
formulate an independent third-party Regulatory Management Options Analysis (RMOA) for fluoropolymers, so as
to ensure that the decision about the final bill shall be based on solid scientific facts and evidence. The above
third-party regulator argued that "PFAS should be grouped into sub-categories for evaluation, namely, the
compounds with high environmental stability such as fluoropolymers should be discussed in a separate category."
3. Evaluation on the feasibility of alternatives
At present, the exemption extension terms stipulated in the draft are relatively harsh, and exemptions are only
granted for a few kinds of PFAS substances under the circumstance that there is not sufficient discussion about the
alternatives for each use. There is no any data or document to prove that the alternatives listed in the relevant
documents have scientificity and feasibility, and there is no guarantee that the relevant alternatives would cause
other safety hazards or ecological pollution. PFAS substances are widely used in all corners of global industrial
production, and a huge disaster would be incurred if they are blindly replaced with alternatives.
II. Advantages of PTFE thread sealing tape
1. Introduction to PTFE thread sealing tape
Since the 1940s, PTFE thread sealing tape has been widely used for the sealing of oil, natural gas, high temperature
gas, and mechanical pipes. In the past 70 + years, PTFE thread sealing tape is widely used by users from all walks
of life due to its properties of being easy to use, good sealing performance, no aging, not easy to damage, non-toxic,
and excellent corrosion resistance. The use of PTFE thread sealing tape has brought significant benefits throughout
the industry chain, and is an excellent product that cannot be replaced by other materials.
2. Evaluation on the feasibility of alternatives mentioned in the Bill
Why PTFE thread sealing tape can't be replaced by fiber products such as hemp silk:
a. The sealing effect of fiber sealing materials such as hemp silk is not as good as that of the sealing tape. Fiber
products such as hemp silk usually need to be wrapped on the thread or joint, which is likely to cause small
gaps or gaps. These gaps may further cause leakage of gas or liquid, resulting in an incomplete sealing.
b. Fiber sealing materials such as hemp silk are easy to be corroded, and some chemicals may erode fiber
products, leading to leakage or malfunction, as well as reducing the sealing effect.
c. Fiber sealing materials such as hemp silk cannot be used alone, and they need to be used together with other
chemicals for thread sealing. However, these chemicals used in the water pipe would cause a direct impact on
the human body.
d. Fiber products such as hemp silk are usually not suitable for the sealing under high pressure or high
temperature environments. Under these conditions, the hemp silk may not be able to withstand the
deformation or rupture caused by high pressure or temperature.
e. In history, the use of fiber sealing materials such as hemp silk is a backward sealing means, and the adoption
of a backward technology to replace an advanced one is apparently not in line with scientific laws.
Why fluid sealants cannot replace PTFE thread sealing tape:
a. The fluid sealant itself is also a sealing product using chemical raw materials, and its sealing performance is
also far inferior to that of PTFE thread sealing tape.
b. The application process of fluid sealants is relatively complex, and it requires more skilled application
techniques and tools. The coating process may require a specific glue gun or scraper so as to ensure uniform
and continuous coating, and a lot of attention needs to be paid to the thickness and uniformity of the sealant
layer during application.
c. Many fluid sealants require a certain curing time to achieve the best sealing effect, which may lead to

Importance of Fluoropolymer in our sector - end use application:

The halobutyl substrate is a first prerequisite for medicinal rubber closures as they have the lowest permeability for air and moisture, and can be chemically seen be crosslinked in a clean way.
The additional FP coating (via film deep drawing) or (via tumble spray coating) applied on top of the halobutyl functions as a barrier for the remaining chemical substances that can migrate from the rubber stopper (e.g. oligomers, anti-oxidants, plasticizers, cross linking residues,…). The FP coated stoppers have proven their performance throughout the years: where expensive stability studies of new drugs at the big Pharma failed in combination with a standard halobutyl stopper, the FP coated version appeared successful.

General Comments: Proposal of Zhejiang Yonghe Refrigerant Co., Ltd. on the Fourth Generation Refrigerant and Blowing Agent

Zhejiang Yonghe Refrigerant Co., Ltd. is an enterprise headquartered in Quzhou, Zhejiang, China with commitment to providing high-quality, safe and environmentally friendly fluoropolymer materials and refrigerant products for the benefit of mankind.

On January 13th, 2023, the authorities (dossier submitters) of five EU/EEA countries submitted the PFAS REACH Annex XV Restriction Report (proposal) to the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA). According to the definition of PFAS in the proposal, there are currently about 10,000 PFAS which encompass almost all the fourth-generation HFO refrigerants /blowing agents.Our company proposes to exclude the fourth-generation HFO refrigerant/blowing agent from the jurisdiction of the proposal for two main reasons: one is that the most typical characteristic of PFAS lies in the properties of PBT, while the fourth-generation HFO substances, especially HFO-1234yf, HFO-1234ze, HCFO-1233zd and their degradation product TFA do not have or have just small amount of PBT properties that could be barely noticed; the other is that there already exist Montreal Protocol, F-GAS regulations, mac instructions, Kigali Agreement and other regulations governing ODS and GWP substances’ production, consumption, storage, recycling, destruction, reduction etc.
there are already a series of regulations governing the production, consumption, storage, recovery, disposal, and reduction of ODS and GWP substances, such as the Montreal Protocol, F-Gas Regulation, MAC Directive, and Kigali Amendment.

1.On Persistence
The major concern core focus of the proposal is the high persistence, long range transport potential, accumulation, and toxicity of PFAS on the environment, while the fourth-generation refrigerant/blowing agent has very low persistence, and according to physical property data of HFOs and HCFOs on EFCTC website,the atmospheric lifetime of HFO-1234yf is 12 days,HFO-1234ze(E) 19 days,HCFO-1233zd(E) 42 days,HFO-1336mzz (Z) 27 days and what’s more,the olefinic bonds in HFOs are vulnerable to the attack of OH free radicals thus making its atmospheric lifetime relatively short and concerns on its persistence unnecessary.
According to the description on page 48 of Annex B of the five-country proposal report , the main degradation product the dominant product of degradation of HFOs is TFA, which is not a substance defined as PFAS in the report a reported PFAS-defined substance, and the impacts of TFA on the environment have been thoroughly studied and described ——in UNEP/WMO report: "TFA abundance and its environmental impacts have gone through have been evaluated in many previous assessments(e.g., Montzka, Reimann et al., 2011; Montzka, Velders et al., 2018; Carpenter, Daniel et al., 2018), and the conclusion is that based on the prediction of the future use of hydrocarbons, HCFCs and HFOs, the environmental impact of TFA produced by the decomposition of HCFCs and HFCs is too small to pose a risk to the environment in the next few coming decades." Additionally, Ozone and TFA Impacts in North America from Degradation of 2,3,3,3-Tetrafluoropropene (HFO-1234yf), A Potential Greenhouse Gas Replacement  published in Environmental Science & Technology in 2010 ( doi.org/10.1021/es902481f ) reached an evident conclusion that the TFA produced by the degradation of HFO-1234yf and brought along by rainfall will not cause adverse effects on the environment. And a similar conclusion is also reached in Projections of National-Gridded Emissions of Hydrofluoroolefins (HFOs) in China (DOI: 10.1021/ acs .est.2c09263 ).

2、On Carbon Reduction
The Kigali Agreement, adopted in Kigali, Rwanda, on October 15th, 2016, advanced the control of ozone-depleting substances (ODS) to the control of global warming potential (GWP) substances, ushering in an era of coordinated handling of ozone layer depletion and climate change. In order to avoid the use and emission of hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), the official website of the European Commission lists alternatives to HFCs commonly used in different industries based on their thermodynamic and safety characteristics.Hydrofluoroolefins (HFO) and HFC-HFO mixtures are included in the list and the widespread use of these substances will also strongly further the accomplishment of European Climate Law and European Green Deal to reach peak carbon dioxide emissions in 2030 and carbon neutrality in 2050. reach the goal of carbon peaking by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2050.

Attention must be paid to the safe application of HFO and its mixtures in the process of substituting HFC. On January 1st, 2015, European (EU) 517/2014 came into effect,which encouraged the use of climate-friendly alternatives when attainable easily.Compared with the figures of 2015 as a baseline, the F-gas phase-down quota mechanism will reduce the amount of HFC that can be sold on the European market in 2030 to roughly 21% that of CO2. HFO will play an important role in commercial and stationary refrigeration.

China is currently a major HFC manufacture and consumption country in the world, and HFO will also be gradually introduced in the production and consumption fields after 2025. According to the forecast of Projections of National-Gridded Emissions of Hydrofluoroolefins (HFOs), The use of China's HFOs will rocket from 2.8kt to 148.8kt and the replacement of HFOs will bring about 5.4Gt of reduction of CO2-eq emission. HFOs in China will grow from 2.8kt to 148.8kt from 2025-2060. Alternative applications of HFOs will result in 5.4 Gt CO2-eq emission reductions.

There is no doubt that the use of natural refrigerants,such as carbon dioxide and ammonia, has  been the trend of refrigeration applications. However, certain properties of them limit the scope of applications. For example, carbon dioxide has poor refrigerating performance at normal temperature and pressure, requiring higher power and energy consumption to achieve the same refrigeration effect.It naturally entails more powerful compressor and more sturdy piping system for refrigeration equipment which adds to the cost and complexity of refrigeration system.  As for ammonia gas,its refrigeration performance at normal temperature and pressure is relatively low, in higher temperature range it can perform better. As a result, it may require higher power and more energy consumption to achieve the same refrigerating effect when at lower temperatures (see Annex 1 ).

Carbon dioxide and ammonia also have their disadvantages respectively in terms of safety. Carbon dioxide is a colorless, odorless, non-toxic gas, but at high concentrations it may pose a suffocation hazard to humans. Due to the high pressure requirements of carbon dioxide as a refrigerant, it is necessary to ensure additional measures regarding gas emission detection and safety assurance. And ammonia is highly toxic and flammable, requiring higher standard safety measures and equipment to ensure safe use. For the above reasons, the use of these refrigerants  cost more and much more complex. In contrast, HFO refrigerants are more universally applicable.

Therefore, in consideration of energy efficiency ratio, safety and usage scenarios, the large-scale application of HFOs and their mixtures is still one of the most effective measures to achieve the goal of carbon emission reduction and comprehensive carbon control in refrigeration foaming and other relevant fields. Besides natural refrigerants,it is reasonable to make room for a healthy development of HFOs and their mixtures, which is an endeavour in the field of refrigeration to curb global temperature rise within 1.5℃ as stipulated in The Paris Agreement.

General Comments: Proposed Derogations
On 13 January 2023, the competent authorities of five EU/EEA states (“Dossier Submitters”) submitted to the European Chemical Agency (“ECHA”) the PFAS REACH Annex XV Restriction Report (“Proposal”).  The Proposal covers all PFAS and their uses, including in all Gas Sensor applications.
Who is CoGDEM?
The Council for Gas Detection and Environmental Monitoring (CoGDEM) was founded in 1974 by the UK's leading gas detection manufacturers as a trade association; CoGDEM’s activities are wholly financed by its members . CoGDEM is the co-ordinating body of the gas detection, gas analysis and environmental monitoring  Industries, representing the collective interest to Government, EC Commission, BSI, and other trade and professional bodies.
An original objective was to be represented on BSI committees involved in gas detection and to address issues raised by the Coal, Electricity, Gas (CEG) committee's draft gas detection standard. CoGDEM joined BSI committee GSE/29 (now EXL/31/1) which created BS 6020 for flammable gas detectors.
CoGDEM now sits on the sub-committees that have worked, or continue to work on flammable and toxic gas safety and air quality standards. CoGDEM is represented on CENELEC, ISO and IEC committees , drafting documents used to create EN and global IEC and ISO standards.  CoGDEM has good relations with the UK Health & Safety Executive (HSE) and others, and contributes to reducing the number of incidents and improving the standard of available gas detection equipment for both industrial safety and domestic CO alarms in residences.
CoGDEM membership includes more than 50 companies (www.cogdem.org.uk); most of the member companies have global sales networks and many have multinational manufacturing sites.
CoGDEM have engaged the services of Graham Wardman of SSC Consulting Ltd, to make this submission (and the later submission in September) on their behalf.
Objectives of this Report
To present data from the Gas Detection and Environmental Monitoring Industries on the usage of PFAS chemicals and materials within the range of Gas Detectors and Environmental Monitoring equipment sold by Companies within the Trade Industry.
We have used this data from our members to present a derogation listing by PFAS chemical family, for inclusion in the full Socio-Economic review in September.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Gas sensors, gas detectors and domestic CO alarms do not fit neatly into a single sector.  The critical PFAS materials are fluoropolymers, specifically expanded PTFE (ePTFE), solid and powder fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers. The most relevant sector is Medical devices with sub-use Diagnostic laboratory testing. An alternative sector is Energy sector, with sub-uses Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM) fuel cells and Electrolysis technologies (not PEM) being relevant to the internal construction and mechanism for certain types. Annual usage of fluoropolymers in Europe for gas sensors, gas detectors and domestic CO alarms is <10t/y, which is less than 0.015% of the EU usage of 75,000 t/y of fluoropolymers.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Note: For references to data tables and literature, please see full report. Identity of the Substances The PFAS materials used in the gas sensor/detector industry are exclusively confined to the subset known as fluoropolymers (FP) defined in as ‘a carbon-only polymer backbone with F atoms directly attached to it, though some ﬂuoropolymers also have Cl or O directly attached to the backbone’.   Two recent RMOAs (Risk Management Options Analysis)  ,  recommend that exemption of FPs from the proposed ECHEM restrictions is warranted due to their low hazard and low risk because ‘substances containing only a -CF2- group are not considered to degrade to arrowheads that have given rise to the environmental and/or human health concerns about PFAS’ 2, due to the absence of reactive functional groups. Further, it is strongly argued  the lack of sound scientific evidence of ‘insigniﬁcant environmental and human health impacts’, is entirely in line with the definition for Polymers of Low Concern (PLC) as defined by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) definition .  However even for a PLC compliant substance, emissions harmful to human health and the environment could still arise during manufacture, use and eventual disposal . In the case of FPs, these life cycle emissions exist in a fast-changing landscape as abatement technologies to remove any polymerisation aids based on the non-polymer PFAS of that provoked the regulatory action are developing rapidly, along with greater understanding of incineration conditions for safe disposal .  This section addresses these life cycle emissions starting at receipt of supplied FP parts to the factory, covering the following finished articles (depending upon the Manufacturers product offering: (a) Gas Sensors -gas sensors/factory test appliances  (b) Appliances - devices with embedded gas sensors, namely, domestic CO alarms and industrial gas detectors  Further to this definition, it means that CoGDEM Gas sensor/detector manufacturers fall into three broad categories: (i) manufacturers of sensors who supply to gas detector/alarm companies  (ii) manufacturers of gas detectors/alarms who manufacture their own gas sensors, and  (iii) manufacturers of gas detectors or CO alarms who purchase gas sensors.  The process of making gas sensors is common to all three categories and we treat it as such for the purpose of emissions (Table 1). We consider emissions in three phases of the life cycle:  Manufacture of finished articles  Use in the field.    Disposal at end of life covering landfill, incineration and recycling Raw Materials Manufacturing and forming of FP materials are omitted from our analysis because FP manufacturers have made their own submissions to ECHA which, due to proprietary knowledge, they were unable to share with us. Emissions during raw material manufacture are therefore already covered, and should we try to enter values here, we would run the risk of double accounting as well as providing potentially erroneous values. In the discussion that hereby follows, all quantitative data is based on replies from CoGDEM members to a detailed questionnaire. Manufacture of Finished Articles For the gas sensor/detector industry (especially the highly dominant amperometric electrochemical gas sensor sector), PTFE is by far the important FP and is supplied in a variety of forms (Table 1); it has been integral to these gas sensors since their inception in the 1960s . FPs of lesser usage in the sensor construction are PVDF, PFA, FEP, fluoroelastomers (FKM, FFKM, VitonTM, Kalrez TM) for seals/gaskets in the gas sampling lines, and perfluoroether polymer-based greases, used as internal sealants in electrochemical gas sensors.    Table i Table 1: Annual global usage of FP materials in the Gas Sensor and Gas Detector industry for 2022 Table 2 shows how the different FP material parts are represented in the three product categories of gas sensors, gas detectors and domestic CO alarms. Feedback from members is that the industry uses two main major suppliers for ePTFE and dust filters and one supplier for PTFE powders. This avoids the issue of variability in PFAS impurities; for the same FP part, purity levels will depend on the individual supplier‘s manufacturing processes6. The gas sensor/detector manufacturing process operates stringent safety measures to protect workers from the release of the hazardous electrolyte liquids, toxic lead (Pb for oxygen sensors) anodes, and poisonous or explosive gases. Also of particular importance is that materials are carefully selected on the basis of low outgassing (release of volatiles); otherwise, the sensor performance is compromised, e.g. generation of bubbles in the liquid electrolyte of amperometric electrochemical gas sensors. PTFE has a history as a material of choice for NASA due to low outgassing amongst other properties . Manufacture of Gas Sensors (a)  For the gas sensor manufacturing process, the as-received FP parts are either used unchanged from the as received state or processed further.  Parts are mostly used unchanged, the exceptions being fabrication of the electrodes and a sealing step, both of which involve stamping out membranes from supplied sheets and heating during electrode manufacture. All heating is done under extraction and at temperatures in excess of 150°C but below 327°C, the melting point of PTFE, ensuring the structural form of the parts are retained. Fabrication of the electrodes is a highly specialised operation, critical to the sensor performance. It is usually a 2-step process involving sintering (250-310°C) a mixture of catalyst and PTFE powder, followed by depositing onto an ePTFE membrane. It is the unique characteristics of this optimised 3-component assembly that enables the sensor to function . Release of entrapped monomers or oligomers of [CFx]n may occur during sintering and would be removed by the oven extraction system. Sintering is a process used by five of the CoGDEM members, and each will use company confidential heating profiles and the process of sintering the electrode and forming the catalyst structure onto the ePFTE as single or combined processes is also company confidential.  Setting aside those parts contaminated by contact with the catalyst and the electrolyte, the supplier’s Safety Data Sheet is valid during the gas sensor manufacturing process. The sensor is assembled by stacking the component parts in a specific order in a small cylindrical plastic (non-FP) pot, done automatically or manually with workers using appropriate protective clothing and tweezers for handling the parts. The pot is sealed as a final step with only the dust filter exposed to the external atmosphere, meaning that most of the FP parts are encased. For sensors assigned to detecting flammable or explosive gases, an additional process step embeds the sensing components in a specialist metal housing with flame-retarding properties.  This manufacturing sector operates a just-in-time production model so stock is always kept minimal. Manufacture of Factory/Laboratory Appliances for Testing Gas Sensors In the second category of finished articles (a), namely, gas sensors, preformed or machined FPs are used as production tooling to hold arrays of gas sensors during testing.  It is general practice to clean machined parts before first use, typically involving degreasing in an ultrasonic bath followed by baking the entire assembly at 110 - 150°C to finish driving off possible contaminants.   We conclude that PFAS emissions of concern do not arise during the sensor or  test appliance manufacturing phases. Product Scrap and Returned Gas Sensors: Sensors that failed or scrapped during manufacture/ test or returned by customers vary in total between CoGDEM members from 0.5% (lowest case) to 6% (highest case). The dominant procedure is not to dissemble the sensors but simply to dispose of them as hazardous waste, due to contamination by the electrolyte (and Pb for galvanic oxygen sensors). Specialist metal refineries (e.g. Johnson Matthey) can recover the metal catalyst and dispose of the (mostly non-PFAS) polymer housing. Disposal as hazardous waste at treatment centres must be in line with guidelines under Article 8 of the WEEE Directive 2012/19/EU , which outlines the criteria for specific materials and components. For incineration protocols, all PFAS materials should be incinerated at temperatures in the range 850°C-1100°C  with proscribed residence times, causing cleavage of the C-F bond by hydrogen radicals , . In this way, the PFAS is mineralised to HF and CO2. Emitted acid gases are scrubbed in stacks (usually using calcium compounds) that are properly designed and maintained. Manufacture of Gas Detectors and Domestic CO Alarms (b) These processes are best described as assembly and calibration operations. For gas detectors, the gas sensor is a component that is connected to custom electronics embedded with the company’s firmware, and typically includes an LCD/OLED display, audio alarm and if portable, batteries all of which are encased in a non-PFAS plastic enclosure. FP tubing and gaskets may form part of the assembly for some gas detectors.  As with (a), we conclude that PFAS emissions of concern do not arise during the gas detector/ CO alarm manufacturing phase. Product Scrap: For those respondents that replied, the combined manufacturing scrap and warranty returns are typically <1%. As with finished article (a), we assume that PFAS components specific to gas sensors will be incinerated as hazardous waste while tubing and gaskets are treated as non-hazardous waste and disposed as landfill waste.  Use Phase  During use, the sensors are enclosed inside devices, modules, monitors, and other various instruments Wear and tear does not occur within these enclosures. The sensor is designed to operate up to 50-60°C so will not be subjected to temperature extremes over its working lifetime of 2 – 5 years. We can conclude that FPAS emissions of concern do not arise during the product use phase. End of Use Phase  UK and EU wide regulations under the WEEE Directive require disposing domestic CO alarms (a consumer product) at local recycling centres. Equally, end-of-use procedures for industrial detectors follow the disposal guidelines under the same WEEE Directive.  Of the three phases covered here, article manufacture, product use and end of life, it is end of life where emissions could occur. There is currently no legal obligation to recycle and so when products enter the waste management stage, they are either incinerated or go into landfill. In Appendix 1, the total FP tonnage going to disposal is calculated to be in the range 5.9 – 8.8 t/y (Appendix 1). According to Annex XV of the Restriction Report , Plastics Europe estimates 80% of fluoropolymer waste goes to incineration and only 15% to landfill, while European waste statistics for 2018 suggest landfill waste is as high as 38%.   As mentioned earlier, incineration municipal treatment centres using the correct firing conditions and with appropriate scrubbing can prevent PFAS emissions arising14. This of course places the onus on these regulated treatment centres to be rigorous in operating to the required protocol and in maintaining their incinerators.  This leaves landfill as the primary source of waste emissions. Studies on leachable material have focussed on PTFE fine powders with <1 ppm being quoted in the most recent work for a ‘wet’ state5. Fine powders have by definition high surface areas for contact with the surrounding environment whereas most PTFE waste is lower in surface area, e.g. dust filters, ePTFE membranes, solid membranes. Furthermore, fine powder features only in making the sensing electrode and will have undergone coarsening, resulting from the sintering step. They will be delayed in interacting with the environment due to the time taken to degrade the outer plastic pot (polycarbonate or acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS)) – here we are assuming that under WEEE, the gas sensors will be removed from the detectors/alarms for separate disposal. t is worth noting that the PTFE powders are present in only 3 of the 5 sensor product categories (Table 3, Appendix 1), giving a weighted average of 17.7% when volume of UK/EU sales for each sensor type is taken into account. So, the available information on leachable material is arguably an overestimate. Therefore, we will assume a high case of 1ppm and a low case of 0.18 ppm, both well below the proposed limit of 50ppm for polymeric PFAS 15 .   The actual quantities of FP waste entering the UK/EU landfill waste stream on an annual basis are estimated (Appendix 1) to be between 844kg and 1,316kg (best case scenario) and on 2,240kg and 3,334kg (worst-case scenario). These quantities in turn produce as little as 0.2g (best case) to as much as 3.3g (worse case) of leachable material. 3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Incineration:  Incomplete conversion of the FP parts to HF and CO2 is the primary risk with incineration. It is argued ,  that if incineration treatment facilities use the correct temperature and residence times, complete conversion should occur; with appropriate scrubbing, no fluoride gaseous products should be present in the flue gases. Temperatures at the front end of an incinerator bed range from 900 – 1100°C , well above 800°C, the temperature concluded from a detailed literature study  by a Dutch national environmental and public health institute, for complete degradation of PTFE.  Less stable FPs than PTFE such as PVDF, PFA, FEP should equally undergo complete degradation at 800°C. As mentioned in Section 2, this of course places the onus on the treatment centres to be rigorous in operating and maintaining their incinerators. Routine analysis of the incinerator exhausts as required to maintain their license would ensure compliance with the permissible PFAS emission levels being proposed.  Landfill:  The risk with landfill revolves around (i) the amount of leachable material, which in turn depends on the form (fine powders) and purity (presence of any residual PFAS polymerisation and processing aids) and (ii) bio-inertness or persistence. Fine powders have a high surface area and as interaction with the surrounding soil occurs only at the surface, fine powders have increased interaction. While the gas sensor/detector industry does indeed purchase fine powders, their form is changed to a sintered skeleton-type framework during the product manufacturing process to make electrodes for the sensor cells. The sintered form has a lower surface area, resulting in reduced leachable potential, reduced further by being encased in a sealed plastic pot. The risk of fine particulate matter entering the atmosphere is very low, due to the conversion of the particulate form to a sintered skeleton framework, and burying preventing weather erosion.   Regarding FP purity, the fluoropolymer industry in Europe  is committed to improving purity through minimising the use of non-polymer PFAS compounds. Section 2 discusses estimates of leachable material based on different scenarios, with concentrations well below the proposed threshold level of 50ppm for polymeric PFAS.  FPs satisfy very persistent (vP) criteria and will persist for decades if not centuries. With the present state of knowledge, there is no awareness of risks to the environment other than the < 1ppm of leached material and the build-up of landfill waste, i.e. persistence. The solution to arresting the build-up of stock is to reduce the volume of landfill waste, meaning moving towards a situation of 100% incineration.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Presently, recycling plays an insignificant part in the gas sensor/detector industry. Extracting the components from the discrete sensors for reuse is challenging due to tearing of the seals in those parts thermally sealed and corruption of other parts through contamination with Pb or electrolyte. Therefore, any recycling of the sensor parts would have to be directed to other uses following a cleansing step followed most likely by a milling step to convert them to powders. This would be an involved process and therefore cost effectiveness could be a determining issue here. Setting cost viability aside, the disposal of these powders would follow the scenarios described earlier in Section 2, generating emission levels which fall below the emission concentration threshold of 50ppm.  For gas detectors, the additional FP parts of tubing and gaskets parts (Section 2, Table 1- 4), are disposed through landfill rather than incineration based on CoGDEM members feedback, but there is no obvious impediment, apart from costs, to recycling these parts following a cleaning treatment into new gas sampling products. Costs would relate to collection and the cleansing treatments. Ultimately with repeat recycling, they would become unusable, but a successful recycling strategy would reduce the quantity of tubing and gaskets in circulation for gas sampling instruments. WEEE requires that tubing be disposed of correctly. Residual monomers are <50 ppb for ETFE, FEP and PFA, and < 1 ppm for PTFE with PTFE suppliers striving for even lower residuals . Gas detector usage by CoGDEM members is 1115 kg/y for tubing and 1178 kg/y for gaskets based on sales into the UK/EU market (Section 2, Table 4) For the third usage category of factory and laboratory test equipment (Section 2, Table 2), machined connectors have long lifetimes (>10 years) although the practice of recycling is low.  Disposal is through WEEE controlled landfill or incineration, but the potential to cycle the UK/EU portion of the 1,318 kg/y used worldwide (Section 2, Tables 1-2) members is high as regeneration in a simple heat treatment to remove any built-up contaminants during service is possible. Overall, there is no additional burden placed on the recycling sector because the FP materials highly pure with at most low ppm leachable discharges in water which will only improve in time based on commitments made by Plastics Europe, the trade body representing manufacturers .

5. Proposed derogations: We are requesting an exemption rather than a derogation for ePTFE and powder PTFE used in the gas sensor/detector industry.  We are requesting a 12 year derogation for fluoro-elastomers, dust filters and fluoro-greases used in the gas sensor/detector industry.  Tonnage and emissions information has been provided in Section 2. Tonnage:  The tonnage of FPs used per year was calculated from the cumulative responses of CoGDEM members to a detailed questionnaire. Based on quantities of FPs bought in, a value of 8.8 tonnes is estimated for 2022 (Section 2). For purposes of corroboration, the tonnage estimate was also calculated by a different route. The same questionnaire provided information to enable determination of the number of sold sensors (Section 2, Table 3) for each different type (Toxic, Oxygen, CO, NDIR/PID). Knowing the weight of FPs in the different gas sensors (Section 2, Table 6), we were able to calculate the quantity of PFs in end-of-life sensors, i.e. going to disposal. The value resulting from this calculation was 5.9 tonnes, 67% of the ‘FP quantities’ figure. The discrepancy between the two figures is due primarily to stock retention in the gas detector segment and to a minor degree, manufacturing waste, which apart from one component, ePTFE, at 10% wastage due to membranes being stamped out of a sheet, is in the range of 0.5-6%.  Emissions:  According to Annex XV of the Restriction Report  Plastics Europe estimates 80% of fluoropolymer waste goes to incineration and only 15% to landfill, while European waste statistics for 2018 suggest landfill waste is as high as 38%. As we have two estimates of tonnage for waste disposal, 8.8 and 5.9 tonnes, we’ll assume an average of 7.3 tonnes.  If incineration municipal treatment facilities apply the correct firing conditions with appropriate scrubbing, PFAS emissions are preventable , although further studies may be necessary for greater reassurance. Operation of treatment centres is a regulated activity and therefore it is assumed that operators will be rigorous in applying the proscribed firing protocols for optimum combustion of FPs.  Assuming incineration delivers FPAS emissions at the permissible levels, landfill is the primary source of waste emissions (recycling is too limited currently to be considered as an emission source). For the averaged 7.3 tonnes of FP waste, we have either 1.1 tonnes for 15% landfill or 2.8 tonnes for 38% landfill. Next, using the worst-case scenario of 1 ppm leachable material  and best case of 0.18ppm (see Section 2 for details), we arrive at the value range of 0.2 – 3.3 g of leachate going into the soil.

6. Missing uses: Fluoropolymers are critical components in gas sensors, but are not specified as a sub-use in the Main applications of ANNEX XV. See our comments to Information Request 1.  For this reason, Information Requests 6. 7. and 8. Are combined in this report for Gas Sensors. Gas sensors are often used in safety critical situations.  Domestic carbon monoxide alarms save lives and the industrial safety related applications include gas monitoring in confined spaces for oxygen, combustible atmospheres and toxic gases; gas sensors mitigate risks to human safety and save lives. In this section we first consider revenue from the gas sensor/ detector/ alarm industries, including the number of employees and customers. This section then details alternative materials, their feasibility, timing and cost implications. Gas Sensor/ Detector/ Alarm industries  As described earlier, this gas safety industry consists of three types of suppliers: industrial and CO gas sensors, gas detectors for industrial safety, and domestic CO alarms.  Some detector manufacturers also manufacture sensors for use in their gas detectors. Alternative Materials: feasibility, timing and cost   The alternatives listed below are not drop-in substitutes for ePTFE, PTFE or other FPs. Each would need significant further development before it could be substituted for FPs in gas sensors. Ultimately, gas detection manufacturers rely upon their material suppliers for this development, but indications from the raw material suppliers are that replacements for these unique family of PFAS will be cost prohibitive and have timescales longer than the proposed maximum derogation period before replacement technologies become commercially available. Realistically, it is uncertain whether the FP alternatives known today will be capable of achieving equivalent technical performance while meeting the relevant regulatory standards. Therefore, replacing PTFE and other FPs in electrochemical gas sensors in a specified time frame is not feasible.   Note that we have focused our evaluation of ePTFE/fluoropolymers for use in both electrochemical gas sensor applications and as dust filters for all gas sensors. While some fluoropolymers are used in other gas sensor technologies, the large majority of fluoropolymer usage is in amperometric electrochemical gas sensors.  A blanket prohibition on PFAS would require a similar evaluation of the components in other gas detection technologies: metal oxides, photo-ionization detectors (PIDs) and NDIR optical absorption for CO2 and combustible gases.  Alternatives for ePTFE for gas porous substrates and solid barriers Alternatives to PTFE and expanded PTFE (ePTFE) have been identified that can meet some but not all of the attributes required for gas porous substates and solid barriers.  Electrolyte leakage of gas porous (expanded) substrates can occur by seeping through microcracks that develop during use, especially during thermal cycling. This failure mechanism has been conquered with ePTFE and would require a very long time of material development and extended safety field trials for any alternative material to meet safety reliability requirements. PTFE and similar fluoroplastics can withstand high processing temperatures. Electrochemical gas sensor electrodes require one, two or three elevated temperature stages, depending on the manufacturing method. These sintering/ bonding/sealing operations require temperatures in excess of 150°C, which either eliminates certain alternative materials or requires new sensor designs and electrode manufacturing operations that would already be used now if they were able to meet performance requirements. Developing new low temperature designs and processes for alternative materials will be a significant challenge.   Alternatives to Fluoroelastomers as gaskets, O-rings and sealants Fluoroelastomers are used to seal components inside the gas sensor and in the gas sampling lines.  Alternative materials must resist oxidation and not react with acidic gases (ozone, nitrogen dioxide, chlorine, sulfur dioxide, hydrogen sulfide). Manufacturers of Digital Mass Flow Controllers (DMFCs) provide two grades of DMFCs for gas control: normal nitrile seals for most gases and Kalrez fluoroelastomer seals for reactive and acidic gases.  Manufacturers have not found a satisfactory alternative to expensive fluoroelastomers when using reactive or acidic gases, so likewise, replacing fluoroelastomers in gas sensor applications will be a technical challenge that to date has not been achieved. Alternatives to Fluoroether greases  Specialist fluoropolymers can be found as greases inside of gas sensors because of their ability to withstand the extreme acidic conditions. These fluoro-greases also maintain the correct viscosity over the wide temperature range from -40°C to +60°C, a requirement that again will take time to provide a formulation with low viscosity-temperature dependence. Usage is very small- less than 250 kg per year. Review of alternative materials The alternatives listed below are not drop-in substitutes for PTFE or other FPs. Each would need significant further development before it could be substituted for PTFE in gas sensors. Expanded Polypropylene (ePP)  • Expanded polypropylene membranes are hydrophobic, but with a higher surface energy than PTFE, limiting their use as gas porous substrates because of the potential to leak electrolyte.  • Unlike PTFE, ePP is not resistant to sulfuric or phosphoric acid, the standard electrolytes in electrochemical gas sensors.  If they are manufactured as thicker substrates to improve lifetime in electrolytes, the gas diffusion and hence response time is too slow to provide a safe alarm. • ePP lacks the thermal stability of FP; the melting point of polypropylene is 160°C versus 327°C for PTFE, so thermal processing during manufacture would require new developments.    • Mechanical performance is poor at low temperatures or after cyclic temperature exposures; this would need improving to avoid microcracks, leading to electrolyte leakage.    • While there may be the potential to improve the chemical resistance and possibly the thermal stability of expanded polypropylene via “surface cross-linking” this process may reduce the ability of this material to be recycled and introduce new problems within REACH. This approach has not been tested in sensors, so is a theoretical concept (TRL1) at this time. Expanded Polyethylene ePE)   • With a melting point of only 120°C, expanded polyethylene lacks the thermal stability and processing temperature range required from an ePTFE replacement.  • ePE may offer relatively better electrolyte compatibility through improved acid resistance but is not as acid resistant as ePTFE..  • With a surface energy greater than ePTFE, ePE may leak electrolyte through the membrane, leading to the gas sensor failing unsafe (ie. it does not generate a signal when exposed to a toxic gas, so the gas detector decides that there is no gas present, which is unsafe). Acrylic Copolymer  • The hydrophobicity and porosity of acrylic copolymer membranes are equivalent to that of PTFE and other fluoropolymers and have replaced FPs in some medical applications. • The critical limitation is its chemical incompatibility with strong acids, which will limit its use with the electrolytes within electrochemical gas sensors.  • Limited processing temperature range means it is not suitable for replacement where elevated temperatures are required for sensor manufacture. Polyether-ether-Ketone (PEEK)  • PEEK offers good temperature and chemical stability so  it could be a suitable replacement in applications where there is direct, prolonged contact with corrosive electrolytes. • The main limitation is the high surface energy, so it cannot be used as a gas porous substrate but could be used as an internal barrier. • Not available as a liquid dispersion, limiting processing and manufacturing opportunities. Polyurethanes (PU) • Similar to PTFE, polyurethanes have both high thermal stability and hydrophobic behaviour.   • PU is not chemically compatible with strong acids, excluding it from internal sensor usage. • Polyurethane will degrade is exposed to certain acid-type gases including hydrogen cyanide (HCN), hydrochloric acid (HCl), chlorine (Cl2) and sulfur dioxide (SO2), so cannot be as universal replacement for FPs. Ceramics   • Some electrochemistry research has been published on ceramic membranes subjected to hydrophobic surface treatment, which offer good temperature and chemical stability.  However, this technology is not mature and has not yet been scaled up to commercial volumes. • Ceramics are inherently brittle and rigid; their mechanical properties need improving to meet commercial gas sensor reliability requirements. Although estimates varied from optimistic to pessimistic, the accepted conclusion was that performance and reliability would be degraded with a significant cost to European gas sensor manufacturers at a time when the focus should be on zero carbon factories. Socio-economic Impact and Conclusions It is clear that moving from fluoropolymer PFAS to alternative materials will have significant impact in the gas detection market, summarised below. • There is no evidence that fluoropolymers are toxic. • Emissions from manufacture and disposal are below REACH requirements and can be monitored and regulated. • Fluoropolymer use in the gas detection industry (gas sensors, industrial gas detectors, domestic CO alarms) is a very small percentage of total European fluoropolymer usage (<10 t/y of the total 75,000 t/y usage). • Fluoropolymers are critical components in gas sensors, especially amperometric gas sensors which are the universally accepted technology for industrial toxic gas detectors and domestic CO alarms. Alternative materials will not meet the performance and safety requirements. Fluoropolymers are expensive, so their use by all manufacturers underlines that there are no reasonable alternative materials. • If fluoropolymers are banned in Europe, then manufacturers in ROW will increase their market share (approximately 50:50 between Europe and ROW) at the cost of a European market valued in excess of 200M€.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: The FP materials, primarily PTFE and to a lesser extent PEPE (perfluoropolyether) are distinctly different classes of chemical compounds; they are not derivatives of the tri- and di- fluoromethoxy compounds.

10. Analytical methods: Fluoropolymer (FP) emissions can be either: • airborne as gases from incineration or particles from degradation • in groundwater by monomer leachate or chemical breakdown Unlike small molecule PFAS, specific FP emissions are not easily isolated. However, FPs used in gas sensors and gas detectors have a common chemical structure of a fully fluorinated backbone and high molecular weight and incineration and degradation products are common to the group of FPs used in gas sensors (PTFE, ETFE, FEP, PFA, fluoroelastomers).  To ensure consistency in measurements and uncertainty calculations, Test standards from national and international standards bodies should be followed. Our company manufactures and sells titrators as our main products.

Our titrators consist of a device that automates volumetric analyses; a sensing unit that detects pH and potential difference; and a burette unit that adds a reagent into a sample solution by increments.

The burette unit consists of a glass burette with a precisely manufactured inside diameter and a stepper motor-driven PTFE piston, which enables precise dispensing of reagents. The unit needs to be chemical-resistant as reagents of strong acid, strong alkali or organic substances are used. To achieve performance of our instruments, our company takes advantage of features of PTFE such as excellent heat resistance, chemical resistance, smoothness, workability and reasonable prices.

Volumetric analyses have widely been used to check the performance of petroleum products and to check the concentration of drugs and medicines or the salt content of food, and are known as an easy-to-operate and reliable method of analysis. If use of PTFE is banned, no other material is currently available to replace it.

Other instruments our company produces also use parts or components that are made of PTFE. These parts or components are processed and used by taking advantage of features of PTFE such as heat resistance, chemical resistance, smoothness. It is no exaggeration to say that PTFE parts or components are used in all our products. Should use of PTFE be banned, there will be a significant impact that will endanger the continuity of our company’s business.
