Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: PSG  Germany GmbH generally supports measures to protect the environment and humans and supports a sensitive handling of hazardous substances . Furthermore, we support a strict regulation of individual PFAS substances in consumer products, with human toxicological properties.

However, the ECHA's intended ban on all PFAS substances, a group of almost 10,000 compounds , goes much too far . A general ban endangers the business basis of tens of thousands of companies in the EU . PSG Germany GmbH, as a manufacturer of highly specialized air diaphragm pumps with the use of Teflon, is one of them.
Therefore, we urgently plead for a differentiation of individual substance groups and state forms and to refrain from a general ban.

Our  pumps are used in numerous industrial processes in which the highest demands are placed on quality and material properties. Heat resistance and media resistance, against acids, alkalis, alkali compounds or solvents and many other critical media are indispensable material properties of our pumps and are only guaranteed to the extent by polyfluorinated plastics according to the current state of the art. The use of substitutes therefore proves to be extremely difficult or impossible in many areas.
Without the use of PFAS, in our case Teflon, large parts of our customers' production and process chains would come to a standstill, which would have a devastating effect on the economy in Europe and on Europe as a business location overall.

In addition, the PFAS material that is used to manufacture our pumps and is used by our customers is applied in industrial processes under strict safety regulations and is present as a solid block, so that the ingestion of PFAS by humans is impossible.
We therefore appeal to the sanity of the committee  to reject a blanket ban on all fluorinated methyl (-CF3-) and fluorinated methylene (-CF2-) compounds and to consider alternative approaches.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The applications of our products, go far beyond the listed uses in Table 9 of Restriction Proposal XV.  As a manufacturer of plastic pumps, including PTFE, for highly specialized and demanding applications, our products are used in a wide variety of sectors. Our customers use our products, which contain PFAS,  in a wide variety of applications due to their unique nature. Our products are in use in the carwash, laundry, horticulture, animal health and warewash sector.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: As a component manufacturer (pumps), we have only a limited overview of the entire life cycle because we are neither users nor disposers, so we can only provide estimates. Since the question does not define exactly what is meant by emissions, we assume that the release of PFAS, in our case PTFE, into the environment is meant.   a. We have no information about the process and the emissions in the production of the raw material. During the production of the finished parts, mechanical processing generates minor amounts of loose material (less than 1% of the mass), but this is collected and, if possible, recycled or incinerated.   There are no significant emissions of PFAS into the environment during the use of our products. The material is in a solid block and cannot be released into the environment in particulate form.   After the use phase of up to 20 years, the material is then present as hazardous waste due to the conveying media and is usually thermally recycled and fed into the energy cycle via an combustion plant.  Overall, emissions to the environment are non-existent or very low in all phases. Potential emissions generally occur only as a result of improper handling.    b. Disposal takes place thermally in all areas at the sub-use level. The media pumped by our pumps are usually aggressive, toxic and hazardous chemicals that contaminate the material and make it necessary to completely incinerate the pump components. In addition, due to the material properties and inertness of the material, it is not possible to transfer it to other uses after use, which more or less eliminates recycling to a downstream resource chain. As a result, PTFE is among the 42.6 percent of all plastic waste in the EU that is thermally recovered (energy recovery) and fed into the electricity grid. (Source: www.europarl.europa.eu)

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Since in almost all cases the waste is hazardous waste, residual components are neutralized after use in special hazardous waste combustion plants. Here, in contrast to normal combustion plants, the incineration takes place at significantly higher temperatures, well above 1000°C. In this combustion process, not only are residual materials completely incinerated, but the [-CF2-] and [-CF3-] compounds are broken up and made harmless.

6. Missing uses: As  described under section 1 Sectors and sub-uses, the sectors put forward by ECHA in the Restriction Report Annex XV Table 9 do not cover all sectors and uses of our products. Therefore, two subdivisions are provided below. First, a breakdown based on the sectors defined in the Restriction Report, with the chemical and bio-pharmaceutical industries included in manufacturing as a whole. Then a further detailed overview is provided, based on the industries as they represent our business areas for PTFE pumps. A tabular overview can be found in the appendices.   a. The companies affected by the PFAS ban in our field can be divided into three categories.  1. suppliers (manufacturers of PTFE components that find application in our products/pumps).  2. processors, manufacturers of plastic pumps using PFAS materials (this includes ourselves and our competitors)  3. customers who use our pumps for hundreds of different applications due to the unique combination of properties of PTFE and cannot replace them for a variety of reasons. They either use the pumps themselves or integrate them into their own products. These customers depend on being supplied with special pumps made of PTFE for their applications and manufacturing processes.  b. Due to the specific properties of PTFE mentioned under 6.b. and their combination, PTFE can be replaced in some applications only to a limited extent  and at high financial cost and in most cases not at all, because the chemical resistance in combination with the temperature resistance and the cleanliness of the pumped medium are not guaranteed. Unfortunately, the properties of PTFE, due to its molecular bonding, which generally give PFAS its high chemical inertness, are exactly the properties that matter in the applications in which our pumps are used.  We considered and rejected the use of PEEK as an alternative because, although it has very good thermal resistance, it cannot be used in most applications because it is not resistant enough to the media for which our PTFE pumps are used . In particular, its susceptibility to strong acids and to some halogenated compounds and aliphatic hydrocarbons are exclusion criteria. The availability of larger quantities of PEEK is also limited and the material is many times more expensive than PTFE, which means that applications are no longer economically feasible in the EU.    For the above reasons, there is no alternative on the market to the use of polyfluorinated plastics, so that the market share in the special applications of the chemical industry and semiconductor industry is around 100%.    c. As an in-between supplier (processor) in a large supply chain, we are financially and technically not in a position to develop new materials. We are dependent on the large raw material producers, manufacturers of PTFE, to bring equivalent materials to the market.  We can only evaluate the use of alternative existing materials. However, efforts to date have been in vain because there are no PFAS-free alternative materials to PTFE that have the chemical resistance under simultaneous thermal stress that PTFE does.  In our view, it is also unlikely that any alternatives can be expected within a reasonable period of time.  Although PTFE can be produced without PFOA today, in contrast to 20 years ago, this is not very likely for PFAS, because according to the ECHA definition of PFAS, this substance is the main component/structure of PTFE.  Furthermore, it is not clear whether alternative materials do not have an even stronger negative impact on the human organism or the environment.  Because the required properties of these materials, are exactly the properties that cause the problems in the environment.  Our own efforts to use alternative materials, e.g. in the form of PEEK or high-alloy steels such as Hastelloy, failed for technological and/or economic reasons.  d. It is only possible to a limited extent to predict the socio-economic impact for the entire supply chain. However, it is clear that the impact would be devastating.  First of all, our suppliers would be affected, for whom the PTFE business accounts for a large part of sales.  If the business there were to disappear completely, many people would lose their jobs.   The same problem affects us, PSG Germany GmbH, and in particular the Hydro brand. The PTFE business accounts for about 45% of sales. Approximately 32 employees can be directly assigned to the Hydro brand. If the PTFE business were to be discontinued, around 20 of these employees would have to be laid off.   Total tonnage in 2022 - approx. 4,000kg.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: PSG Germany GmbH, operating under the brand name Almatec, is a subsidiary of PSG Dover and specializes in the production of air-operated double-diaphragm (AODD) pumps. We utilize Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) for the manufacture of components such as housing parts, valve seats, valve balls, diaphragms, O-rings, and face seals of our pumps. These pumps are important to various industries, including the chemical, semiconductor, food and beverage, and biopharma sectors.

A complete ban on PFAS would lead to substantial financial losses, job dismissals, and potential disruptions in critical industries. If the proposed restriction is executed, it is planned to shut down PTFE-dependent business activities in the EEA, resulting in the loss of workers. Currently, no viable alternatives to PTFE are available that can maintain the required performance specifications for the broad range of sectors and applications in which the pumps are used.

Regarding emissions, we only use pre-manufactured PTFE parts and do not manufacture PTFE itself. As such, no significant emissions are likely to occur during product assembly and use. Emissions during the end-of-life phase are expected to be negligible since the waste is disposed of as hazardous materials considered to be incinerated at high temperatures.

We therefore request a derogation period of minimum 12 years to identify and develop suitable alternatives to PTFE. This request accounts for research and development, testing for biocompatibility and physiological safety, upscaling production, adapting to production facilities, and market introduction of new materials, if identified.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: PSG Germany GmbH's AODD pumps are essential components in numerous manufacturing processes across different industries. In the food contact materials and packaging sector, they are used for hygienic pumping processes and conveying foods and end products. In the electronics and semiconductor sector, the pumps convey critical media in electrical, semiconductors, solar, and battery production industries, including acids, caustics, and other reactive liquids. The biopharmaceutical sector relies on these pumps for various processes involving primary, secondary, and final products while maintaining the highest hygienic standards. In the energy sector, these pumps are utilized for hazardous waste disposal and thermal recycling of liquid hazardous waste, such as paints, varnishes, medicines, and chemical manufacturing residues. The chemical sector uses AODD pumps for manufacturing and processing critical chemicals, acids, alkalis, solvents, oxidizing agents, elemental chlorine, and production of activated carbon and personal protection clothing. The critical need for these pumps arises from their unique properties such as high chemical resistance, thermal resistance, flame retardancy, and antibacterial effect.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Relevant considerations on emissions are provided below for each stage. It should be noted that there are only limited measurement data for the assessment of emissions during the life-cycle. Additionally, emissions occurring as a result of improper handling, possible leakages, or degradation of the material during use cannot be completely excluded but are considered minimal. Further studies and research on the fate of PFAS substances in the environment can help minimize uncertainties and improve the understanding of potential emissions and risks associated with the life-cycle stages of AODD pumps.  1. Design and Assembly Phase: We do not manufacture PTFE but assemble pumps from pre-manufactured parts. Therefore, we only have a limited overview of the entire PTFE life-cycle. During the pump assembly, there is only limited exposure of workers to PTFE. Furthermore, no PFAS-containing air emissions, waste, or wastewater emissions are expected from the assembly of the pumps.  2. Use Phase: During the use phase, AODD pumps are used across various sectors and applications, often with aggressive and hazardous pumping media. While minimal emissions to air or wastewater may occur, they are considered almost negligible. The pumps' use phase can extend up to 20 years with minimal wear and tear.  3. End of Life Phase: After the use phase, the material is considered to be disposed of as hazardous waste due to the hazardous conveying media used. The waste is assumed to be thermally recycled and fed into the energy cycle via a combustion plant. Based on the tonnage used for pump assembly in 2022, around ~25,000 kg of PTFE will end up incinerated after 20 year of service life.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: We are a processor and assembler of air-operated double-diaphragm (AODD) pumps that include components made from PTFE. However, we are not manufacturing PTFE. Therefore, we can only provide a limited overview on the whole lifecycle of PTFE. As we assemble pumps from pre-manufactured parts supplied by their external suppliers, we are positioned as an in-between supplier (processor) in the supply chain of AODD pumps.  Regarding emissions from waste, after the use phase of up to 20 years, the material is considered to be disposed of as hazardous waste and incinerated. It is assumed that after 20 years of use, an amount of around ~25,000 kg of PTFE will end up incinerated. Releases and by-product formation from incineration of PTFE is subject to scientific discussion. The formation of fluorinated by-products during the incineration of PTFE cannot be fully excluded but is considered to be low. However, more research is required to estimate actual emissions. We acknowledge and support the need for further studies. This is expected to contribute to the reduction of emissions from waste products. Emissions during the assembly and use of the parts are considered negligible.

6. Missing uses: Tonnage and emissions:  In 2022, the total tonnage of PTFE used in the EU by our pumps was 24,812 kg. The majority of PTFE is supplied to the chemical sector, accounting for 71.5 % of the distribution of PSG Germany’s PTFE material. Other sectors include food, electronic, energy, and biopharmaceutical industries.  Regarding emissions, we do not manufacture PTFE and only assemble premanufactured parts, resulting in limited exposure to PTFE during the assembly and use of the pumps. Emissions during these phases are considered negligible. The end-of-life phase of the pumps is assumed to be mainly disposal via incineration. Emissions from this process are assumed to be very low, based on reported studies, but cannot be completely excluded. We acknowledge the need for further studies to understand the fate of and emissions potential from treatment of PTFE.  Key functionalities:  PTFE is used in the production of our air-operated double-diaphragm (AODD) pumps due to its unique properties that make it an ideal material for various industries and applications. The key functionalities provided by PTFE for the relevant use include:  1. Very high chemical resistance: PTFE is highly resistant to a wide range of chemicals, making it suitable for use in situations where the pumps come into contact with aggressive chemicals, acids, bases, and solvents. 2. High thermal resistance: PTFE can withstand high temperatures, which is essential for applications that involve high heat or extreme temperature fluctuations. 3. Flame retardant: PTFE is inherently non-flammable, making it a safe material for use in the pumps even when exposed to high heat or potential fire hazards. 4. Anti-adhesive: PTFE has a low coefficient of friction and a non-stick surface, which enables smooth functioning of the pumps and prevents materials from adhering to the pump components. 5. Antibacterial effect: PTFE's chemical composition and structure provide an inhospitable environment for bacterial growth, which is important for applications in food and beverage, biopharma, and other sectors with strict hygiene requirements. 6. Biocompatibility and physiologically safe: PTFE is compatible with biological systems, making it suitable for use in pumps that handle or come in contact with sensitive materials, such as food, beverages, and pharmaceutical products.  Companies estimated to be affected by the restriction:  The PFAS restriction is estimated to affect around 10 to 20 PTFE suppliers, 20 to 40 processors or manufacturers of pumps, and approximately 500 to 800 customers in Germany, as well as 500 to 1,000 customers in other European countries from diverse industries. The most affected markets would be the semiconductor manufacturing and chemical industry.  The proposed restriction may have significant impacts on multiple actors in the field of AODD pumps, resulting in substantial financial losses, job dismissals, and potential disruptions in critical industries. The significant impacts on various businesses along the supply chain could also disrupt the market and lead to shortages.  R&D efforts:  As part of our R&D efforts, we considered Polyetheretherketone (PEEK) as a potential alternative. However, it was found that PEEK could not meet the same chemical resistance standards as PTFE, particularly against strong acids, some halogenated compounds, and aliphatic hydrocarbons. Additionally, PEEK has higher costs and limited availability compared to PTFE, making it economically unfeasible.  Another alternative, Polyethylene (PE), was also examined, but it was found to lack the required thermal stability and adequate chemical resistance for certain aggressive chemicals compared to PTFE.  High alloy steels like Hastelloy were briefly considered but promptly dismissed due to their limited applicability, high costs, and restricted manufacturing capabilities.  Given that no suitable alternatives have been found, we request a minimal derogation period of 12 years to accommodate potential research, development, testing, certification, and market introduction processes for any new, feasible alternative materials that may emerge during that time.  Socio-economic impacts:  The proposed PTFE restriction would cause us financial losses because of the discontinuation of the PTFE-dependent business processes in the EEA. Also, many workers could be dismissed because of the restriction, leading to total social costs of unemployment for us in the EEA as estimated in the confidential report. Thirdly, we would face one-off investment costs, including decommissioning costs for our EEA site and potential fines for not fulfilling contractual obligations, though these costs are not assessed quantitatively but considered qualitatively. Lastly, the restriction could cause significant impacts on several actors in the AODD pump field, including PTFE suppliers, processors or manufacturers of pumps, and hundreds of customers across different industries in the EEA. This would result in significant financial losses, job dismissals, and potential disruptions in critical industries, such as the chemical and semiconductor manufacturing sectors.

Content: Information on alternatives Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: PTFE and PFA are used for the surface coating of medical device guidewires.
In addition, PTFE liners are used for the inner surface of medical device catheters.

Guidewires are medical devices for guiding therapeutic devices such as catheters into hollow organs (blood vessels, gastrointestinal tract, urinary tract, etc.).Guidewires are used in luminal organs either alone or within a therapeutic device. The performance required of guidewires includes anti-thrombogenicity, low sliding resistance, and low change in outer diameter to ensure smooth sliding with the treatment device. For this purpose, they are coated with PTFE or PFA.
As for the sliding properties of PTFE and PFA, as is well known, there are no resin materials with equivalent or better low frictional resistance to replace PTFE and PFA, and there are no alternative materials available due to the requirement of good sliding properties with the combined device.
PTFE and PFA are also very good in anti-thrombogenicity. Blood has the property of coagulating when it senses a foreign substance, which can form a thrombus. If a thrombus adheres to the surface of the guidewire during the procedure, not only is sliding with the treatment device compromised, but there is also a risk of not being able to insert or remove the guidewire into the treatment device. This increases the physical burden on the patient and physician due to the extended procedure time, and if the thrombus adheres to the point where the device cannot be used, the device must be replaced or added, leading to increased medical costs. PTFE and PFA have excellent anti-thrombogenic properties and have been shown to form very few thrombi in blood vessels.
Furthermore, PTFE and PFA have extremely low hygroscopicity and absorb almost no moisture from the blood, resulting in little change in outer diameter.
As a substitute for PTFE and PFA, hydrophilic polymers could be coated as an alternative to resin materials, but hydrophilic polymers are known to absorb moisture in the blood and swell, resulting in a thickening of the outer diameter. Although this provides lubrication, the increased outer diameter reduces the overall sliding performance, which, as mentioned above, leads to prolonged procedure time and physical burden on the patient and the physician. In addition, the physician grasps the PTFE-coated portion of the guidewire and rotates (torques) the tip of the GW to follow the vascular motion, but the hydrophilic polymer-coated guidewire is slippery in the grasping portion, making it difficult to rotate (torque) and difficult to access the lesion. This leads to difficulty in accessing the lesion and prolongs the procedure time.
When oil-based coating is applied as a substitute for PTFE or PFA, adhesion to the underlying substrate becomes an issue. If the oil is removed, the underlying substrate is exposed, resulting in a significant decrease in slipperiness and increased tendency for thrombus to adhere to the substrate.

This results in prolonged procedure time. Currently, there is no technology to adhere the oil to the substrate so that it does not peel off.
In light of the above, there are no resin materials or other technologies that can replace PTFE and PFA, and PTFE and PFA must continue to be used.

Catheters are hollow (tubular) medical devices used to insert drugs, treatment devices, guidewires, etc. into affected areas. In order to ensure smooth sliding with the treatment device, the inner surface must have anti-thrombogenic properties, low sliding resistance, and little change in outer diameter.
For this purpose, a PTFE liner is used.
As mentioned above, there is no resin material with equivalent or better low frictional resistance to replace PTFE in terms of PTFE's slipperiness, and there are no alternative materials available because of the requirement for good sliding properties with the treatment device.
As mentioned above, PTFE is also very good in anti-thrombogenicity. If a thrombus adheres to the inner surface of the catheter, not only is sliding with the treatment device compromised, but there is also the risk that the device cannot be inserted or removed. This increases the physical burden on the patient and physician due to the extended procedure time, and if the thrombus adheres to the point where the device cannot be used, the catheter must be replaced or added, leading to increased medical costs. PTFE has excellent anti-thrombogenic properties and has been shown to form very few thrombi in blood vessels.
Furthermore, PTFE has extremely low hygroscopicity and absorbs virtually no moisture from the blood, resulting in minimal dimensional changes. Therefore, no shrinkage of the inner diameter due to moisture absorption during the procedure is observed.
As a substitute for PTFE, hydrophilic polymers could be coated as an alternative to resin materials, but hydrophilic polymers have been found to absorb moisture in the blood and swell, resulting in a narrowing of the inner diameter. Although lubricating, this leads to a reduction in overall sliding properties due to the narrowing of the inner diameter, which, as mentioned above, leads to prolongation of procedure time and physical burden on the patient and the physician.
If an oil-based coating is applied as a substitute for PTFE, adhesion to the base material (resin) becomes an issue. Once the oil is removed, the resin is exposed, significantly reducing slipperiness and making it easier for thrombus to adhere. This results in prolonged procedure time. Currently,
there is no technology to adhere the oil to the resin so that it does not peel off.
Both hydrophilic polymers and coil-based coatings have been found to be very prone to peeling off due to abrasion caused by the harsh sliding action with the treatment device being inserted. To maintain sliding properties, the inner surface must be made of a material with a certain degree of hardness.
In light of the above, there is no resin material or other technology that can replace PTFE, and PTFE must continue to be used.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: PTFE is a polymer of low concerns by the OECD standards that displays a unique combination of properties that cannot be found in other materials.

- Thermal stability
- Electrical insulation
- Low friction
- Self-flame retardant
- Biocompatible / non toxic
- Durable

lease find below the markets information that lead us, 3P, to request a full exemption of fluoropolymers, and especially PTFE, from the ongoing PFAS restriction study.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: I) Aeronautics Market  In aeronautics, fluoropolymers are used as security parts, especially  for electrical insulation applications for flight control commands  (cable insulation). Replacing PTFE by alternatives would lead to a  consequential reduction of flight safety. Fluoropolymers are also used whenever sliding and durability properties  are needed, for instance for the flap and slat technology of airplanes.  This enables huge fuel consumption optimization during take-off, flight  and landing procedures.  The chemical inertness properties of PTFE is usually exploited for fluid  handling, especially for gas hoses. In addition to this, PTFE  mechanical properties, heat resistance and flame-retardant make it a  central material in handling safely critical fluid in planes. PTFE low coefficient of friction also ensure high flow rates in new low  consumption engines.   Potential alternative(s):  o Electrical insulation: Other materials are already being used to  insulate electrical cables. Silicone, Polyethylene, PVC… However, they  usually are either not performant enough (in terms of electrical  insulation), or are not even PLC according to the OECD. For instance,  the PE is not flame retardant.  Additionally, these “potential” alternatives being considerably cheaper  than PTFE, would already be used if they satisfied the safety  requirement of modern aircrafts.  o Gliding properties: other polymers have gliding properties comparable  to PTFE. It is the case of polyethylene. However, this polymer is not  flame retardant, and could propagate flames. Moreover, polyethylene is  much less resistant to UV light, especially when they are not filtered  by the atmosphere, in high altitude. This does not rend this material totally not usable, but it would imply  some additional maintenance, plastic wastes and energy consumption.  o Fluid handling: While existing polymers (silicones, polyurethanes)  tubes could not be used for fuel hoses for safety reasons (flammability,  chemical resistance…), the most immediate alternative to fluoropolymers  in fuel hoses would be metal, which was the historical technical  solution. Metallic tubes would mean heavier assembly and would increase the craft  gas consumption.    II) Automotive Market  For automotive applications, PTFE is used to reduce friction and improve  engines efficiency. Replacing PTFE would lead to more consuming engines  (both gas and electric), due to frictions. Several PTFE parts are safety related, for instance motorbike brakes or  in ESPs. It is additionally impossible to design a battery for electric cars  without fluoropolymer membranes (usually PVDF-HFP). The same goes for  hydrogen fuel cells, where proton exchange membranes properties can  exclusively be reached with fluoropolymers (usually FKM).   Potential alternative(s):  Polyethylene is often named as an alternative to PTFE for dynamic seals  applications. Its good gliding properties and high stretchability would  make it a suitable replacement of PTFE. However, its much lower thermal  resistance would lead to more maintenance and part change (or oil and  polluting fluid release in the environment when the part is worn out). For applications above 100°C, like in the engine compartment,  polyethylene would not even be suitable at all. Other highly thermally resistant material could not be equivalent of  PTFE, due to their high coefficient of friction (PI, polyphenylenes…).  More friction would decrease the efficiency of the engine, and increase  fuel consumption. Other alternatives composed of polyolefins (High molecular weight  polyethylene) could also be considered, but with lower durability,  especially to temperature, and would need frequent maintenance and  replacement.   III) Energy Market  PTFE and fluoropolymers also are integrant parts of alternative energy  sources, coatings for solar panels, low friction coating of wind turbine  blades…  Potential alternative(s):  To our knowledge, there are no alternative to PTFE for this application.   IV) Communication Market  PTFE as the lowest dielectric constant of all materials, except for air  and vacuum. Dielectric constant, also known as relative permittivity, is  the key characteristic for high frequency data transmission, and  inevitable in 5G applications and IOT.  Potential alternative(s):  To our knowledge, there are no alternative to PTFE for this application.   V) Chemistry Market  PTFE is exclusively composed of carbon and fluorine atoms (the  carbon-fluorine bond being the most energetic and strong bond in organic  chemistry). Therefore it is extremely resistant to most chemicals,  especially strong acids (nitric, sulfuric). This is why PTFE is used to coat chemical tanks for aggressive  chemicals.  Potential alternative(s):  Other materials exhibit high chemical and thermal resistance, such as  ceramics and noble metals. In many cases, they are however not suited  due to feasibility or safety reasons. Glass coated tanks and chemical reactors already exist, but the  temperature must remain relatively stable or cracks will appear in the  glass coating (difference of coefficient of thermal expansion between  glass and metal). PTFE has elastic properties that can withstand the  metal deformation, while still protecting it from the corrosive  chemicals. Noble metal coating would rise other pollution concerns, since this  process involves the cyanide salt of the metal.   VI) Foodstuff applications  PTFE and globally fluoropolymers are high purity polymers, from which  there is no migration of chemicals even at high temperatures. Most of  these polymers are compliant to food contact norms such as EU10/2011.  Potential alternatives:  Amongst alternatives for alimentary fluid transportation, the principal  known alternatives are silicone and polyurethanes tubes.  Silicone could be used in some low requirement cases, considering they  do not contain plasticizers or mobile small molecules. Polyurethanes are  however well known for their terrible thermal and hydrolysis  resistance. Using PU tubes in hot and / or watery applications would  lead to a depolymerization of the tube, generating isocyanates (almost  all known as carcinogenic and/or toxic to humans). These materials  already are regulated by REACh Annex XVII, for instance entry 74.   VII) Healthcare applications  Due to their outstanding biocompatibility and non-toxicity, PTFE and  fluoropolymers are widely used in healthcare applications. Most PTFE  grades comply with medical contact norms, such as USP Class VI, or  oxygen resistant applications (norm BAM). PTFE coated stents for  arterial implants are recommended by the French national health comity  (Haute Autorité de la santé) https://www.has-sante.fr/upload/docs/application/pdf/2018-06/avis_du_15_mai_2018_endoprotheses_coronaires_couvertes__stents_couvertes_de_ptfe.pdf   Conclusion  In all cases, the parts manufactured by 3P are used for their  durability. The part lasts longer, therefore reducing maintenance. Hence, the use of PTFE in these applications avoids using raw materials  and energy to remake the worn out part, as well as the maintenance  itself (especially for big remote parts, for instance offshore wind mill  blades and components). PTFE parts are wildly used in safety applications (Electrical  insulation, flame retardant, brake systems…). They are essential for future technologies (5G, IoT…) and renewable  energies (Solar, wind…), in which 3P is actively involved.  It is also important to note that in all cases the substitution of PTFE  should not even be considered, since PTFE is a safer and cleaner  solution that its alternatives. However, pure PTFE (without filler) can be grinded back into a  processable powder called “reprocessed PTFE”.  Considering the high price of PTFE (PTFE price ~15x polyethylene),  recycling opportunities are developing very fast.  For instance, several  works are in progress to reuse incineration outgassing to regenerate  close to 100% of PTFE wastes.   The recycling yield of 3P PTFE wastes is approximately 24%.  All plastics included, the average percentage of recycling of plastics  is around 15%.  Please find all detailed confidential data in the attached "confidential document" of section V

It is the case of the study Waste incineration of  Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate potential formation of per-  and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) in flue gas, Krasimir  Aleksandrov and al., which final conclusion is “municipal incineration  of PTFE using BAT is not a significant source of studied PFAS and should  be considered an acceptable form of waste treatment”.  Above 800°C, no PFAS are generated by PTFE incineration.

Content: Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: PTFE is different than other PFAS
Fluoropolymers and PTFE among the others, are also different from the other families of polymeric PFAS, such as SCFPs or PFPEs, on the basis of their nature, structure, properties, uses, and applications, as well as from the point of view of safety and expected environmental impacts.
PTFE is firmly settled in some fields since its discovery and is safely used in critical applications including medical and public safety. A substantial number of applications lack viable alternatives, raising concerns about their operations and ability to meet market demands. In some cases, the industry could try to meet the restriction, but provided additional transition time is granted.
Transition period
A significative transition period for the use of PTFE in the sector and sub uses Plastics (other than packaging) and rubber/elastomer production (including flame retardants) is necessary to allow the long supply chain to gradually find viable alternatives and set up new products and safety standards. A derogation of at least 13.5 years after entry into force of the proposed regulation may mitigate the impact that an abrupt general ban would bring about.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Plastics (other than packaging) and rubber/elastomer production (including flame retardants)

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Regulators and researchers have an additional reason for concern regarding fluoropolymers, which is associated with the end-of-life (EOL) stage of products that are made using these polymers. The uncertainty lies in the fate of these persistent polymers when they are disposed of in landfills, as well as the potential for the production of additional per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) during the incineration process. It is important to highlight that PTFE find specific applications in industrial sectors. As a result, the waste generated from these sectors is already subject to substantial regulation. Therefore, waste containing PTFE is managed in accordance with specific legislations, such as those governing electronics recycling (see WEEE Directive). Additionally, it is worth considering that PTFE has an exceptionally lengthy lifespan in its designated applications, often exceeding 30 years. This extended lifespan leads to a considerably lower rate of PTFE waste generation compared to other types of polymers (such as other single use plastics items).

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: It is very well renowned that high-temperature incineration would be expected to result in destruction of the PFAS molecular structure and vapor capture and processing is commonly used during recycling efforts. The use of high-technology fluoropolymers such as PTFE allows for the long life of articles, which in turn reduces the need for material replacement. The reduction in waste and material consumption would be expected to result in lower carbon usage. The extraordinary resilience of fluoropolymers means that relatively little of the material would be released over the long product lifespan and product warranties up to 40 years.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: All possible alternatives come with significant shorter lifetime cycles. This requires regular repair cycles for the equipment due to failures, which are costly and produce more waste. For low‐cost consumer products this would most likely result in that repair costs are higher than buying new product which results in immense waste and recycling challenges. For higher end products for industrial use, the cost of the final product produced will most likely be higher due to more maintenance and labour cost involved. Even here, the consumer buying the final product (coffee, juice, tomato puree, soups, etc.) will pay the higher price, generating increased inflation in the EU zone in the long term. Eventually, EU would lose competitiveness, especially to Asia-Pacific countries where cost is not high and circular economy is not yet a prioritised topic. More low‐cost problems would be imported, and the amount of waste would increase as cheaper products (like household coffee machines) will be disposed instead of putting them into service/repair. Trends will get removed from circular economy back towards “use and trash – then buy new” as it was the case in the past.

5. Proposed derogations: Considering the long term stability of PTFE and having no risk to be spread in the environment such as, on the opposite, other gaseous or liquid PFAS, it shall be exempted from other PFAS restrictions and in any case the sector Plastics (other than packaging) and rubber/elastomer production (including flame retardants) need to granted a derogation to at least 13.5 years after entry into force of the proposed regulation.

6. Missing uses: The use Plastics (other than packaging) and rubber/elastomer production (including flame retardants) is considerably wide as includes different scenarios and it is highly advisable to divide it in sub uses. The uses of PTFE as such, as a polymer additive or antidripping for flame retardancy, having different functions, physical forms, environmental impacts, market volumes, usages, concentrations and fates need to be properly taken into account and addressed with adequate derogations and eventually different alternatives, if any. In any case, at the state of art, no feasible alternatives to PTFE are envisaged.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Alternatives do not meet the performance required by the different application including public safety. The non-use of fluoropolymers and in particular PTFE would result in a severe decline in the life quality of people, or in the worst-case scenario, an increase in mortality because of the lower efficiency of safety devices and long term warranty, therefore human health would be significantly compromised. EU companies manufacturing medical devices would most likely relocate outside of the EEA to other countries where such restrictions do not apply, which could result in an increase in illegal importation and unfair competition. Furthermore, it would have a severe economic impact on the safety sector including healthcare industry, resulting in increased unemployment and dissatisfaction among the population.

8. Other identified uses: The impact of a general ban of fluoropolymers and in particular of PTFE is widely underestimated as in many sectors the involved actors do not even start to consider its substitution because of the lack of alternatives and an abrupt unavailability may cause a severe disruption. It is then required a long transition period with a specific derogation for PTFE in the sector Plastics (other than packaging) and rubber/elastomer production (including flame retardants) and related sub uses of at least 13.5 years after entry into force of the proposed regulation.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: PTFE is used as material for nozzles in load break switches in medium voltage (MV) switchgears of air insulated and gas insulated type. Load break switches are comparable simple switches for voltages of 12, 24 and in GIS 36 kV. They can interrupt the load current, but not the short circuit current. This principle has been widely used in the medium voltage market for decades, as it is simple, cost-effective and reliable. No complex electronics, auxiliary power or drive mechanisms are required. In the open position the AIS designs allow a simple verification, that power is disconnected.

The switching principle is the following:
- After the electrical contact opening an arc between the contacts is ignited.
- By a combination of contact separation and arc blowing with the insulation gas (ambient air in AIS or SF6 in GIS) the arc is cooled.
- The nozzle has as its first function to guide the gas in the area of the arc to improve cooling. PTFE can fulfil this function, as it is a very robust material which will not be ignited by the arc and is neither melting nor burning due to the high melting point of 327°C. It keeps the shape for a high number of operations.

- As a second, but very important function, small quantities of the PTFE material are evaporated by the arc, which has a temperature of several 1000°C, when it gets in contact with the surface. This is releasing Fluorine, which was bound in the PFTE nozzle material, in the area of the arc. The fluorine supports the quenching of the arc and finally the interruption of the current. Without this effect, the arc will not be extinguished.

This switch principle is also known as a hard-gas switch and is widely spread in the lower end of electrical distribution systems. It is not only used by ABB but also by many other electrical equipment manufacturers. As PTFE is a PFAS, it is planned to be restricted, which has a severe impact on this type of switch.

The search for replacement materials is very complex for this kind of function. Insulators with a high-temperature resistance and melting point can be identified, e.g. ceramics. But these materials are only guiding the flow of insulation gas for cooling the arc but are not giving the required support to interrupt the current by releasing Fluorine. Known materials which might release Fluorine are all PFAS. As Fluorine has a very high arc quenching performance a full replacement has not been found up to now and might not be identified in the future. The search for an alternative in that case does not mean a search for a replacement material, but a search for a completely different technology.

There are other technical solutions available, which can interrupt currents, e.g. vacuum circuit breaker. But these technologies are much more complex in design, require much more material and are significantly more expensive. Taking into account that a vacuum interrupter needs a disconnector in series, auxiliary voltage to be operated and a more complex protection relay, the system costs can be up to 10 times higher.

For this, ABB ELDS asks for an extended transition time of an additional 8 years to complete the transition to PFAS-free solutions. As of now, it is still unclear if a technical solution can be identified, the possibility of a further exemption after the 8 years should be offered, if it is proven that the replacement projects are not completed. Alternatively, a non-limited exemption should be considered.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The comment does no apply to a specific sector listed in the Annex XV restriction report (Table 9) but will be an additional one.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Electrical equipment including load break switches in general contains high quantities of recyclable materials such as steel, aluminum and copper and are generally intended to be handed over to recycling companies at the end of life. Depending on the product the recyclability can reach levels of 90 %. Epoxy resin is a component which can not be recycled, but burnt (thermal recycling). Only a small fraction of the electrical equipment ends up in landfill. The PFAS containing materials will normally be part of the thermal recycling process. With temperatures >900 °C for sufficient time PFAS are destroyed to non-PFAS.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: The threshold level of 25 ppb results in contamination of 1.000 tons of waste with 25 g of pure PFAS. As waste is always a mixture which will be processed and purified during the recycling process, the effort to remove such low contaminations will be extremely if possible at all. As the contamination especially in waste is very inhomogenous it is not realistic that any recycling process can be established for products which might contain PFAS even in low concentrations.

5. Proposed derogations: The majority of the material used in load break switches is steel, aluminium, copper and insulating materials like epoxy resin, highly depending on the design. The weight of the used PTFE will be approximately 1...5% of the total weight of the load break switch (without drive mechanism).

6. Missing uses: Load break switches belong to the energy sector, which is marked green in Table A.1 of Annex A of the Annex XV restriction report, but this equipment is not listed sufficiently as a user of PFAS. a) The annual tonnage depends on many factors but is assumed to be in the range of 10...50 t/year. b) The key functionality is described in detail in the general statement or the attachment. As it is a combination of two functions there is at the time no other material known, which can fulfil this requirement and have a functional hard-gas LBS without PTFE. c) Hard-gas switches have been on the market for a long time and are a standard product at a low-cost level, manufactured by many global companies. d) In case no drop-in substitute can be identified, the simple and cost-effective solution can no longer be offered, which will have severe consequences on the affected applications. e) Based on the theoretical knowledge and the perfect functioning solution with PTFE, no intense research programs are running. There was no need for this up to now and it is questionable if the impact of this product justifies the effort. First investigations have confirmed that the chances for a drop-in substitute are not very high. f) As in this case basic research will be required, an extended time of an additional 8 years should at least be enough to answer the question if there is a technical solution possible or not. g) As mentioned in the general comments or in the attached file, the consequences will be more on the network operator and the customer side. When significantly more expensive solutions like vacuum circuit breakers need to replace the hard-gas load break switches, the cost impact would be significant.

8. Other identified uses: A group covering PTFE in load break switches is missing and needs to be created. A derogation of 8 years is estimated to be sufficient to investigate if alternative solutions are possible.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Description of analytical methods Information on alternatives Information on benefits Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: PTFE used in optical applications is a fluorocarbon solid material that has undergone a sintering process to provide an optically reflective surface for absolute and relative calibration of spectroscopy and metrology instruments. In addition to laboratory and field applications, this material has a critical use in space flight for radiometric calibration of Earth-Observing (EO) satellite imagers and is critical in the quest for understanding climate change. This material is used by national metrology institutes such as PTB, NPL, VSL, and the other EUROMET partners as well as space agencies and their supporting contractors; ESA, ESTEC, Airbus, OHB, Leonardo, etc. The reflective properties of this material are unparalleled in both reflectance (99%) and scattering properties approaching a near-Lambertian reflectance pattern that scatters light in all directions. There are currently no materials that compare with the ideal optical scattering properties of this material. These materials are typically re-surfaced in the US when required due to contamination or degradation and are therefore rarely disposed of in a typical landfill situation. Other reflective coatings are prepared with PTFE in a suspension prior to spraying the coating on the reflective target. These coatings retain the PTFE within the dried surface with negligible release of any particles. This spray process is performed in the US. The lifetime of this material spans decades and since the bulk material is made from a sintering process of raw PTFE powder, the emission during usage and end of life are negligible. 100% of the solid PTFE material can be recovered for recycling, and with a simple scraping process, 90-96% of the PFAS material in the spray coatings can be recovered for recycling.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Diagnostic laboratory testing – The majority of our PTFE materials fall into this category as reference reflectance material traceable to National Metrology Institutes (NMIs), or as optical reflectance material where capturing stray light is essential to the performance of the instrument. Electronics and Semiconductors – no sub-sectors apply. Applications include laser cavities and laboratory metrology instruments. Any material in these applications is in bulk form as a solid component for optical performance, and not embedded in the electrical/electronic components, but may be present as a calibration standard in an electronic or opto-electronic assembly.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: a) Raw PTFE powder is sintered in US. Emissions in the EU are zero for the Manufacturing, use-phase, and end-of-life. b) No waste treatment is performed in the EU. In the US, any waste or scrap material derived from the manufacturing process is recycled. Upon enactment, future shipments will apply to new reach requirements for identification of recycling. No current by-weight breakdown of material is provided but can be provided as regulations require for disposal/recycling in the future. In the manufacturing process in the US, 17% of the total material is scrap. 100% of which is recycled.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: This material is provided in bulk form, or as a coating on metal components. Waste management at end-of-life for these materials and equipment is performed by users in the EU and is typically performed as part of a scrap metal process and therefore it is not believed that any of this material would have gone through, or will go through, an incineration process. Upon enactment, future shipments will apply to new REACH requirements for identification of recycling. Instruction will be provided in the future for the manual and/or mechanical scraping process to separate this material from recyclable metal or other material as per the required regulations. It is estimated that 90 – 96% of the material can be reclaimed for recycling.

5. Proposed derogations: Table p. 4 – Proposed restriction - Annex XVII entry PFASs (Restriction Option 2) Derogation 5n, “diagnostic laboratory testing until 13.5 years after EiF” Derogation 5t, “calibration of measurement instruments and as analytical reference materials.”  Tonnage used per year in EU: 899lbs. (0.41 metric tons) Emissions to environment is negligible as the material is inert and does not go through any further processing as it is in its final form upon arrival to our European customers. Average tonnage/yr taken from a 3-year average of exports of the material to our European customers.

6. Missing uses: a. Annual tonnage and type of PFAS: 899 lbs, (0.41 metric tons) PTFE b. Key functionalities are optical reflectance material for metrology, photometry, and calibration of imagers including space applications for earth-observation satellites. c. Number of companies in the sector that will be affected: XXXX d. There are currently no alternatives that provide the level of performance required in many applications. Risks of using alternatives are improper characterization of lasers (eye safety), unreliable calibration of satellite imagers for earth observation and climate monitoring, and human hazards in autonomous vehicles. Alternative products are used in less-demanding applications with no foreseeable shortage. e. R&D continues for alternative materials, which included bubble glass and ceramics, but these materials are limited in their size, shape, performance, and space heritage. Development of materials that are consistent with the current material performance are estimated to be in 10-20 year range at a minimum and may still not provide the performance that is required for space applications and other high-end optical applications. f. The global market for these materials is less than $40M, and therefore the incentive to develop new materials is not as attractive as other markets making the time to market for anything new very long term. Large companies may have resource to develop materials, but the ROI may not be as attractive for a smaller company that would require a longer development period. 1. Type and costs: Costs for developing new materials are estimated to be >5 years @ $20M for terrestrial and laboratory applications. Time requried to complete space-qualified material development will be on the order of decades as some material will require approval for specific space missions. A space agency, subcontractor or  vendor will need to financially support the development and launch of such material with a  dedicated test plan and instrumentation. Costs for this type of program would exceed $100M. 2. The time requried to substitute existing materials in the field will be on the order of decades as many applications are in use in laboratories with sunk costs where the usage life of such equipment spans decades. Replacing these devices will be on the order of tens of millions of dollars. Certification and approval for materials to be used as reflectance standards will require additional time at National Metrology institutes (See EUROMET partners list) and span decades depending on the priority of each laboratory or agency. 3. Differences in functionality will increase the uncertainty of measurements and calibrations for critical applications such as climate monitoring, laser eye safety, earth observation, autonomous driving, and medical device monitoring. The consequences of using lower-performing materials are added error in climate models, potential human harm, and more stringent pass/fail criteria of safety standards to account for the higher uncertianty in measurements resulting in higher development, produciton and testing costs. 4. The potential benefit of alternatives is that consumers may have more choices in their materials, and there may be potential for lower costs. The price/performance decision exists now, but in many applications if the performance is not adequate, the reduced cost will never justify the savings. g. The socio-economic impacts for companies would be delayed time to market of products, and stunting the development of EU companies as compared to the rest of the world. There are some manufacturers of similar materials in the EU, but we do not have their financial information. We estimate about 40-50 companies in the EU that would be severely impacted by this ban.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: See Attached report for details and data.
