General Comments: QUERCY REFRIGERATION is a contractor specialized in industrial cooling applications such as agro-food, fruits preservation. We install and maintain refrigeration equipment for our end-users’ customers.
Our headquarter is located in Moissac, south ouest of France, we also have 7 branches and partners across France. In Moissac we also have a R&D department with a laboratory. We mainly use for our installations R1234ze, but also CO2 for subcritical applications.
Quercy Refrigeration is a downstream user of fluorinated gases (“F-Gases”), in particular Hydrofluoro-olefins (HFOs) R-1234ze are used as refrigerant in our installations and Chillers (Q-REF), which are equipped with Turbocor compressors that would be subject to the proposed restrictions.
With this paper we would like to share publicly our view on the proposal for a Restriction for Per-and Polyfluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFASs). QREF Chillers and installations designed with HFOs (R-1234ze) provide cooling solutions at lower CAPEX and OPEX vs. existing alternatives such as ammonia solutions, our COP is twice higher that NH3 solution, that allows our customer to reduce their electricity bill by -45% and are safe for the people and environment, based on their properties.
Executive summary
For Quercy Refrigeration using the HFO 1234ze is best working fluid for applications because of several reasons:
The safety aspect: this fluid presents no risk to technicians or end-users, is very easy to use, and does not require extensive risk/safety training for our technicians,
This fluid is ideal because it works at very low pressure, which means less risk for the user and far fewer fluid leaks.
One of the great advantages is also the COP, which gives very high energy efficiency to refrigeration systems, and even more so when associated with cycle improvements (subcooler, desuperheater, etc.) that are not possible with other fluids.
The result of the less dangerous nature of this fluid is that it can be used in installations that consume less metals and rare materials, and, ultimately, to offer installations at prices that are affordable for farmers, retailers and other industrialists, and that correspond to their economic activity.
This fluid is ideal because it's the only one that allows direct expansion at very low pressure, compared with other fluids that require much more energy for the same cooling capacity (glycol water cascade, transcritical CO2, minimum 20% more energy).
With a GWP close to 1, Solstice® ze (HFO R-1234ze) fluid will be around for years to come, and Quercy Réfrigération uses a single fluid for all its positive installations.
Turbocor, what this new technology brings to companies is very simple:

• Historic efficiency in the world of refrigeration, with a reduction of up to 50% in power consumption for food storage compared with all the most modern technologies on the market (c02/propane and nh3).
• New reliability and ease of operation by eliminating oil and friction in compressors, which are major reliability problems in traditional refrigeration systems.

Clearly, with our revolutionary cold generation system, we offer food chain companies a guarantee of very low power consumption combined with very high reliability.
This technology is obviously applicable to the storage of fruit and vegetables, meat, etc., but also further down the cold chain to logistics platforms, food processing plants and even supermarkets.
The aim of our society and our generation is to reduce our environmental footprint, and our impact on climate disruption, and a large part of the solution lies in improving energy efficiency, i.e. reducing electricity consumption to produce, store and distribute our food.
That's exactly what our new Q-REF Chillers working with Solstice® ze (HFO R-1234ze) fluid offer.
• Which have already demonstrated, through measurements on industrial sites, a reduction in electricity consumption of the order of 50 % compared with the dominant technology.
• Another important aspect is the simplicity of our design, which drastically reduces the amount of metal needed for manufacturing: with our technology, we do away with very large traditional equipment such as oil separators or oil coolers, which is very important in terms of the environmental impact in terms of CO2 generation during manufacturing,
• Finally, eliminating the oil, which is a fossil hydrocarbon component, solves the problem of oil recycling during the life and service of the plant, but especially at the end of its life.

To sum up, with the Q-REF chillers range we're meeting environmental challenges, reducing up to  50% of power consumption; extremely limit use of metals; and no hydrocarbon oil in our machines.

Based on the available scientific evidence and literature available, we conclude that the fluorinated gases Solstice® ze (HFO R-1234ze) and F-Gases used as refrigerants in refrigeration installations and chillers must be fully and permanently excluded from the scope of the proposed restriction:
1. HFCs have an atmospheric lifetime of years and HFOs of days or months and are not classified as (very) persistent under REACH.
2. Only a few fluorinated gases, notably HFC-134a and HFO-1234yf, decompose into Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) in a significant fraction. Most fluorinated gases have atmospheric decomposition products that are not classified as persistent.
3. It has been demonstrated that TFA is not harmful to humans or the environment in the concentrations likely to occur in the decades ahead.
4. The grouping of an extremely broad range of substances with very different (eco-) toxicity profiles is in breach with ECHA guidelines on Read Across.
5. Persistence on its own is insufficient for a broad restriction as proposed by the dossier submitters.
6. The risks of emissions of F-Gases are adequately controlled through existing EU legislation, in particular the F-Gas Regulation (517/2014, currently under review), the WEEE directive (2012/19) and End of Life of Vehicles directive (2000/53).
7. The design of our chiller, which drastically reduces the amount of metal needed for manufacturing as it’s a oil free system, therefore there is no oil separators nor oil coolers, which is very important in terms of the environmental impact in terms of CO2 generation during manufacturing processes.
Finally, eliminating the oil, which is a fossil hydrocarbon component, solves the problem of oil recycling during the life and service of the plant, but especially at the end of its life.

Furthermore, the available evidence justifies time-unlimited derogations for most uses of fluorinated greenhouse gases:
• Alternatives for F-Gases have not been properly assessed for their environmental impact
• The socio-economic benefits associated with the use of F-Gases outweigh the theoretical cost to society in terms of energy efficiency, public safety.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: According to their REACH registrations, all mainstream F-Gases are not classified as persistent. None of them are classified as PBT and/or vPvB. Their toxicity and environmental impact have been thoroughly assessed, both under REACH and in international forums such as the UN Environmental Programme (UNEP) and the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Referring to substances containing a -CF3 group (which includes many F-Gases), the dossier submitters state that “most of these substances are expected to ultimately degrade in the environment to TFA”. There is, however, robust evidence that this is the case for just a few mainstream F-Gases (https://www.fluorocarbons.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/EFCTC_HFC-and-HFO-Substances-degradation-products-and-TFA-yields-Final-26_08_2020.xlsx). A generalization as used by the dossier submitters is therefore unjustified. Since there is a limited number of F-Gases that decompose into TFA and the conversion ratios vary between 0% and 100% (for one individual substance), the exposure assessment by the dossier submitters (figure 7) is therefore misleading and irrelevant

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: There are several benefits of using Turbocor oil free systems:   • Historic efficiency in the world of refrigeration, with a reduction of up to 50% in power consumption for food storage compared with all the most modern technologies on the market (C02, R290 and NH3). • New reliability and ease of operation by eliminating oil and friction in compressors, which are major reliability problems in traditional refrigeration systems.  Clearly, with our revolutionary cold generation system, we offer food chain companies a guarantee of very low power consumption combined with very high reliability.  This technology is obviously applicable to the storage of fruit and vegetables, meat, etc., but also further down the cold chain to logistics platforms, food processing plants and even supermarkets. The aim of our society and our generation is to reduce our environmental footprint, and our impact on climate disruption, and a large part of the solution lies in improving energy efficiency, i.e. reducing electricity consumption to produce, store and distribute our food. That's exactly what our new Q-REF Chillers with 1234ze fluid offer. • Which have already demonstrated, through measurements on industrial sites, a reduction in electricity consumption of the order of 50 % compared with the dominant technology.  • Another important aspect is the simplicity of our design, which drastically reduces the amount of metal needed for manufacturing: with our technology, we do away with very large traditional equipment such as oil separators or oil coolers, which is very important in terms of the environmental impact in terms of CO2 generation during manufacturing,  • Finally, eliminating the oil, which is a fossil hydrocarbon component, solves the problem of oil recycling during the life and service of the plant, but especially at the end of its life.  So, to sum up, with the Q-REF range we're meeting environmental challenges in terms of: 50% lower power consumption; extremely limited use of metals; and no hydrocarbon oil in our machines.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: According to the REACH Registration of TFA, the substance fulfils the criteria for persistency, but the available data indicate that it is neither fulfilling the criteria for toxic and bioaccumulative (PBT-substances), nor the criteria for very bioaccumulative substances (vPvB-substances) according to REACH directive, Annex XIII and as laid down in the TGD R.11 of the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA).  A recent publication on the mammalian toxicity of TFA concluded that the Margin of Exposure (MoE) to most humans is 4,000 to 476,000 times,  indicating that the levels of TFA in the environment are several magnitudes below what would be considered toxic. [Dekant, W. and  Dekant, R. (2023). "Mammalian toxicity of trifluoroacetate and assessment of human health risks due to environmental exposures." Arch Toxicol 97(4): 1069-1077.] In a series of reports from 2016 to 2022 the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) concluded that TFA has been found at levels that are  below those that would be considered toxic to humans or aquatic environment and will continue to be below these levels for decades. [(https://ozone.unep.org/science/assessment/eeap, https://ozone.unep.org/science/assessment/sap]  There is also overwhelming evidence that TFA is a naturally occurring substance. [EFCTC, Naturally Occurring TFA, https://www.fluorocarbons.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/EFCTC-TheEvidenceThatTFAoccursNaturally_A4.pdf]

5. Proposed derogations: The ECHA Read-Across Assessment Framework (RAAF) clearly states that “(a)pplying the grouping concept (…) means that REACH information requirements for physicochemical, human health and/or environmental properties may be predicted from information from tests conducted on reference substance(s) within the group, referred to in this document as source substance(s), by interpolation to other substances in the group, referred to as target substance(s).” A separate assessment should be conducted for each information requirement intended to be fulfilled by the read-across approach. It is clear that defining PFAS as a group based on the presence of at least one fully fluorinated methyl (CF3-) or methylene (-CF2-) carbon atom (without any H/Cl/Br/I attached to it) does not meet the RAAF criteria.   This is also confirmed by the OECD Expert Group on PFAS (including experts from the dossier submitters) which clearly states that “As PFASs are a chemical class with diverse molecular structures and physical, chemical and biological properties, it is highly recommended that such diversity be properly recognized and communicated in a clear, specific and descriptive manner. The term “PFASs” is a broad, general, non-specific term, which does not inform whether a compound is harmful or not, but only communicates that the compounds under this term share the same trait for having a fully fluorinated methyl or methylene carbon moiety. [underlining added, OECD (2021), Reconciling Terminology of the Universe of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances: Recommendations and Practical Guidance, OECD Series on Risk Management, No. 61, OECD Publishing, Paris.]

6. Missing uses: Many materials, natural and man-made (water, steel, concrete, minerals, polymers) are persistent. That in itself cannot be a justification for a broad restriction with time-limited derogations. The burden of proof that a restriction is justified is on the dossier submitters. They assert that “(t)his is the key hazardous property common to all PFASs in this restriction proposal. Consequently, if releases of PFASs are not minimised, humans and other organisms will be exposed to progressively increasing amounts of PFASs until such levels are reached where effects become inevitable.” We suggest that the term PFAS is replaced with “concrete, steel, water or silica” and ask the reviewers if they would agree.  The economic consequences would be that it would be impossible for local businesses to invest in refrigeration systems, which would put all local shops and food manufacturers at risk of bankruptcy, because refrigeration systems using other fluids such as C02 or R290 or NH3 cost around 40-70% more than 1234ze units, and often have a higher environmental impact, the French food industry would be in immediate difficulty, with a cascade of plant closures.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: The control on in-use and end-of-life emissions of F-Gases is adequate under a variety of EU legislation and has not been properly assessed by the dossier submitters. For example, the EU F-Gas regulation (517/2014, currently under review) requires regular leak inspections and recovery at end-of-life. Similarly, the Waste of Electronic and Electrical Equipment directive (2012/19) and the End of Life of Vehicles directive (2000/53) address/require the minimization of emissions of hazardous substances. Moreover, the mainstream F-Gases have been subject to the REACH registration (and evaluation) provisions which require the registrants to submit detailed and rigorous Chemical Safety Assessments, including end-of-life. In view of their increasing scarcity and relative high market value vs. their assumed alternatives, there are additional and sufficient incentives for the recovery, reclamation and re-use of F-Gases which are a fundamental part of the EU’s Green Deal and its Circular Economy objectives. A prohibition on the placing and use of F-Gases would effectively eliminate the economic incentive for their recovery and reclamation at end of life and could well lead to higher emissions.

8. Other identified uses: The dossier submitters refer to the alternatives for F-Gases, notably Carbon Dioxide, Ammonia and Hydrocarbons (propane, butane and pentanes) as “natural substances”. In fact, these are all produced at an industrial scale. As indicated above, TFA would have a greater claim to the epitaph “natural” (or, in the case of Ammonia, equal). As noted by the dossier submitters, these alternatives are much lower in cost compared to F-gases, and it would have been appropriate to assess their end-of-life emissions since the economic incentive for recovery, reclamation and re-use is virtually absent. • Carbon dioxide (CO2, R-744) is currently exempt from registration under REACH. It is a very persistent substance and the single most important contributor to Climate Change. [IPCC] It is also the single most important contributor to acidification of oceans causing irreparable damage to coral reefs and therefore broader sea-life. [NOAA] In concentrations over 5000 ppm it is a life-threatening substance (asphyxiation). [UK HSE]. • Ammonia (NH3, R-717) is predominantly produced in large scale plants reacting natural gas (CH4) with water (H2O) and then subsequently with air (~78% N2), with CO2 as a by-product. Under CLP it is classified as flammable and toxic:   (Brief Profile - ECHA (europa.eu)  Ammonia (anhydrous) is listed in Annex I to the Seveso III Directive (2012/18) on the control of major-accident hazards involving dangerous substances. The safety issues associated with the use of Ammonia are well documented.   In addition, Ammonia contributes to acidification and eutrophication (OECD 2013), and is also implicated in Air Quality issues (revision of the EU ambient air quality directive 2022/0347(COD)), and its atmosperic breakdown products with both stratospheric ozone depletion and climate change (N2O). Ammonia. A recent study concluded that Ammonia contributes to 50% (EU) and 30% (US) of PM2.5 air pollution, PM2.5 causes chronic respiratory illnesses and can lead to premature mortality and that Regulating NH3 as a precursor to PM2.5 is cost efficient, and will protect human health.   • Hydrocarbons, notably Propane, Butane and Pentanes are typically produced from crude oil in refineries. They are classified as (extremely) flammable and included in Annex I of the Seveso III Directive (2012/18) on the control of major-accident hazards involving dangerous substances. They are (Very) Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs) which are associated with air quality (revision of the EU ambient air quality directive 2022/0347(COD)). Their Photochemical Ozone Precursor Potential (POCP) is orders of magnitude higher than F-Gases (VOCs and POCPs - Fluorocarbons). The atmospheric degradation of Propane results in various carbonyl compounds, with acetone, acetaldehyde, and propionaldehyde among the most prominent. Carbonyl compounds are relevant because of their toxicity and ability to produce free radicals. (Atmospheric oxidation pathways of propane and its by‐products: Acetone, acetaldehyde, and propionaldehyde - Rosado‐Reyes - 2007 - Journal of Geophysical Research: Atmospheres - Wiley Online Library) Based on this evidence, we conclude that a ban on the use of F-Gases could lead to regrettable substitution.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: The economic consequences would be that it would be impossible for local businesses to invest in refrigeration systems, which would put all local shops and food manufacturers at risk of bankruptcy, because refrigeration systems using other fluids such as C02 or R290 or NH3 cost around 40-70% more than 1234ze units, and often have a higher environmental impact, the French food industry would be in immediate difficulty, with a cascade of plant closures.  As noted in the proposal, the submitters of the restriction dossier recognize that F-Gases have a considerable cost disadvantage compared with the putative substitutes. There must be good reasons why downstream users opt for F-Gases and they have every incentive to minimize their use and emissions. Contrary to the assertions by the dossier submitters, F-Gases combine unique attributes that are highly valued by downstream users: • They are safe in terms of toxicological and physical properties. • They contribute to highly energy efficient Heating, Air Conditioning, Cooling and thermal insulation.  • As a result, the total cost of ownership is considerably lower than the proposed substitutes, due to additional costs required to meet the legitimate safety concerns, especially in applications widely used by the general public, as well as the, sometimes substantial, incremental energy consumption. Moreover, the dossier submitters have failed to provide an accurate estimate of the cost associated with the continued responsible use of F-Gases. The graph below provides the Pressure Temperature curves for the most important F-Gases used in Heating, Air Conditioning, Cooling applications.  The graph shows that: • CO2 (R-774) has much higher operating pressures and is ineffective at ambient temperatures above 25oC. It is therefore not an acceptable substitute in large parts of the EU with high ambient temperatures during the summer. • Ammonia (NH3, R-717) and Propane (R-290) have higher operating pressures than F-Gases at higher ambient temperatures, which suggests lower energy efficiency and greater need for engineering expense     Similarly, the dossier submitters refer to a table (E.91) presented by EFCTC as evidence of the thermal conductivity of the main options for thermal insulation. The table shows that the next best non-F-Gas substitute for HFO-1233zd has a 30% penalty in energy efficiency. Delivery of the optimal energy efficiency is critical for the energy transition in the EU (RePowerEU). Forcing downstream users to convert to more energy consuming solutions would require additional investment in power generation capacity, transport and distribution to meet demand at times of peak load in summer (Refrigeration and Air Conditioning) and winter (Heat Pumps). Much of that additional capacity will be sitting idle when demand is below peak load and will place an additional cost burden on society. The associated additional investment will come on top of the already very challenging target of a full conversion to Electric Vehicles by 2035. The dossier submitters have made no effort whatsoever to assess these implications.

10. Analytical methods: The control on in-use and end-of-life emissions of F-Gases is adequate under a variety of EU legislation and has not been properly assessed by the dossier submitters. For example, the EU F-Gas regulation (517/2014, currently under review) requires regular leak inspections and recovery at end-of-life.  Moreover, the mainstream F-Gases have been subject to the REACH registration (and evaluation) provisions which require the registrants to submit detailed and rigorous Chemical Safety Assessments, including end-of-life. In view of their increasing scarcity and relative high market value vs. their assumed alternatives, there are additional and sufficient incentives for the recovery, reclamation and re-use of F-Gases which are a fundamental part of the EU’s Green Deal and its Circular Economy objectives. A prohibition on the placing and use of F-Gases would effectively eliminate the economic incentive for their recovery and reclamation at end of life and could well lead to higher emissions.  Based on the available evidence we conclude that F-Gases must be exempted from the definition of PFAS in the restriction proposal. In addition, there is sufficient technical and socio-economic evidence to justify time-unlimited derogations for the production, placing on the market and use of F-Gases and products containing or relying on F-Gases.

General Comments: Quintessence in case of ban of tubings made of PFA, FEP and PTFE ("Teflon®") in the EU:

1. semiconductor industry:
Without tubings made of PFA, FEP and PTFE the production of semiconductor technology will migrate to non-European countries. Thus, the EU becomes a developing country.

2. food:
Without tubings made of PFA, FEP and PTFE the production of (mainly) liquid foodstuffs is becoming so expensive in the EU that farms are increasingly having to be abandoned due to unprofitability and consumer prices are rising at an inflationary rate.

3. control technology and painting technology:
Plant engineering and vehicle production, are migrating to non-European countries - like the semiconductor industry. As a result, the EU, which is poor in raw materials, is losing its much-vaunted technological edge and thus also its scientific underpinnings.

4. medical technology:
The ban on tubings made of fluoropolymers in the field of medical technology means that patients can no longer receive optimal care. The quality of life and life expectations will be lowered without necessity, and thus the ban on these high-performance plastics contradicts the principles of Hippocrates' oath. The elites will seek treatment in non-EU countries. Consequence: hospital death, thinning out of medical care.

6. Missing uses: 1. semiconductor production In the semiconductor industry, these acid-resistant tubings made of PFA, FEP and PTFE are used wherever, for example, stainless steel and other apparent alternatives cannot be used.  In wafer production, for example, if even the smallest quantities of steel particles come loose from the piping when stainless steel is used, the entire production batch is unusable because of the risk of short circuits in the chips.  2. food In the food industry (dairies, breweries, coffee or beverage vending machines, etc.), inert fluoropolymer tubing is required because it does not contain (toxic) plasticizers which outgas over time and thus contaminate the liquids carried in the lines. The known very smooth surface of Teflon also minimizes contamination of the pipes/hoses, which means that much smaller quantities of cleaning agents have to be used for germ-free operation than with other apparent alternatives.  3. Control technology and coating technology In both pneumatic control technology and painting technology, the chemical resistance and high thermal load capacity of hoses made of PTFE, FEP and PFA are of inestimable value. They ensure trouble-free (sustainable) operation of the systems even with critical media and in aggressive environments. There are only minor maintenance intervals and the lines also have to be replaced much less frequently than with all other plastics. The flexibility of the material up to 260°C, which is particularly required in plant construction, is not achieved by any other thermoplastic. The service life of the products is significantly extended by the above-mentioned properties, which benefits not only the economy but also the environment.  4. medical technology Tubings made of PFA, FEP and PTFE are used primarily because of their sterilizability, UV resistance and for minimizing friction. They are therefore used for coatings of surgical instruments, as additives to minimize friction of polymers in injection devices, or as seals and filters in biotechnical equipment for drug production. These properties cannot be replaced with any other polymer family. Treatment methods and procedures that cannot be performed optimally by not using fluoropolymers, implants of inferior quality or durability mean that patients are deprived of the best possible treatment.   Conclusion While in the consumer goods production (e.g. textiles, kitchen utensils) it is often possible to switch to alternative solutions (polyamide and polyurethane for textiles, ceramics and iron for pans), an alternative to the use of tubings made of PFA, FEP and PTFE is often not possible in technical and medical industry, which is why a general ban on fully fluorinated plastics has serious disadvantages for the EU-oriented location. When properly used and subsequently disposed of, fluoropolymers are much more life and environmentally friendly, but also more sustainable than seemingly simple and cheaper "alternatives" in the short term.

General Comments: Raman spectrometers are used for detailed chemical and structural characterisation for use in varied and far-reaching fields of technology and research. With the manufacture and use of spectrometers and their accessories, careful consideration must be made with the selection of materials to ensure no contamination of results from analysis is possible due to the manufacture of the equipment, and therefore results from such work having a high level of integrity. This includes subcomponents used with the manufacturing process, especially O rings, seals, adhesives and lubricants, finishes, fibre optics plus bespoke optical components which are otherwise unavailable on the market. All must be resistant to a wide range of chemicals and environments, including high vacuum environments. The stable properties of FKM and similar long chain PFAS are specifically necessary to support the fundamental purpose of the equipment to these applications.
Repeated evaluation of alternative materials has shown that the overall performance of PFAS is unmatched. Based on work carried out while selecting and qualifying materials, alternatives result in reduced reliability (an increased safety hazard) and shorter product lifetimes (resulting in higher levels of environmental waste).
Raman spectrometers are not adequately covered in section E.2.4 of the Proposal for Restriction and should be considered separately due to their broad impact on key and wide-ranging research fields and industry, requiring the need for detailed and highly specific structural and chemical characterisation, plus their long lifetime being used for such work.
We recommend that consideration is given to the risk vs benefit of the use of larger fluoropolymers and that the ban targets high polluters and substances likely to cause environmental harm first, phasing in control of less harmful PFAS over a realistic timeframe.
The timeframe for finding and qualifying alternative materials is very short.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The industry and research sectors that use our Raman analytical products are wide ranging and include (but not limited to) healthcare support (research, diagnostics and medicines), renewable energy generation and storage (solar cells, novel battery technology, energy storage and delivery materials), research into materials with novel properties (2D materials such as graphene), biological, forensic science, art and historical artefact conservation, semi-conductor manufacture, particle and liquid analysis, microplastics (the identification and monitoring of microplastics within ecosystems and manufacturing processes) plus manufacturers of all products where materials science is required to determine the composition, distribution and understanding of materials in a wide range of applications. In all these cases it is also important that our products do not leak or leach contaminants that will affect the results of such work and subsequent conclusions, including critical processes for manufacture (such as Li+ battery production) or damage of sensitive or rare samples (such as works of art). The resistant, passive nature of FKM and similar PFAS provide this.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: a) Usage phase: The service life of products typically exceeds 20 years and is supported by repair and upgrade packages. There are only low levels of emissions during the usage phase, typically through loss of PFAS contained in certain lubricants.   b) End of life: PFAS only form a small percentage by weight of the product, the main constituents are metals, mainly steel. Our products are recycled as scrap metals (Electronical and Electricals are managed under WEEE). PFAS are not separated from metal parts and processed at high temperatures along with the metals. Processing temperatures exceed the temperature at which PFAS will be destroyed.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Recycling does not result in PFAS release or formation.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Due to the relatively low volume of PFAS and the long active life of this product type there are no significant impacts on the recycling industry. Our suggestion is that consideration is given to collection and recycling of items that include PFAS. Control of collection and recycling can be implemented easily in B to B environments. Regulations could be implemented through parallel legislation such as the Waste Framework Directive.

5. Proposed derogations: The total annual consumption of PFAS is unknown. Calculations show that an annual mass of O rings and seals used within Raman spectrometers amounts to 2,5kg maximum (combined weight of all physical O rings and seals) with negligible amounts of PFAS within other materials used in the production of Raman spectrometers. Limited amounts of PFAS emissions in manufacturing – industrial cleaners (derogation). Aside from recycling at end of life, there is negligible release of PFAS.

6. Missing uses: Key functionalities provided by PFAS are based on the unique properties of PFAS materials including their stability in hostile environments, resilience, and low friction. To the best of our knowledge and from the results of our own testing and evaluation, indications show that suitable alternatives are not yet available. For certain niche applications substitution is not technically or economically feasible. Use of PFAS in analytical equipment (Raman spectrometers) is important to ensure there is no possibility of contamination from the materials used within the manufacture and use of the equipment (O rings, seals, adhesives and lubricants, finishes, fibre optics plus bespoke optical components which are otherwise unavailable on the market) to ensure spectral results originate from the materials of interest only, and results have high integrity.

8. Other identified uses: Alternative materials are being sought and further work is being done work to evaluate alternatives where they are found. To date no materials adequately meet the mechanical, thermal, and chemical stability offered by PFAS solutions.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: No information to add on the degradation pathways.

Combined Comments:
"Response in the context of the consultation "proposal for a restriction Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs)" of the municipality of Molenlanden (Netherlands) 1. Introduction of submitting organization The municipality of Molenlanden has over 45,000 inhabitants and is located in the Dutch province of South Holland. The municipality has a rural character, consists of 20 cores, and has an area of 192 km2. Approximately 80% of the territory is used for agricultural activities, mainly dairy farming. The municipality also has a thriving recreational sector, with Kinderdijk (UNESCO World Heritage) as the most famous attraction. 

2. General concern about PFAS PFAS is used in the manufacture of a wide range of products for use by industry, professionals, and consumers. The main concern regarding PFAS is that they are very persistent and once in the environment, they have significant consequences. PFAS is bioaccumulative. These substances, due to their dispersion and accumulation in soil, water, and air, have negative effects on the state of the environment, the quality of nature, and the health of humans and animals. The fact that there is persistence and bioaccumulation makes these substances even more concerning. Municipalities are responsible for a healthy living environment for their inhabitants, a clean environment, and the protection of vulnerable nature. Therefore, municipalities also feel responsible when it comes to combating the harmful effects of PFAS, especially due to the social unrest surrounding PFAS. Attention in the media contributes to increasing awareness among residents about the negative effects of PFAS and decreases the societal support for this group of substances. The industry continues to produce and use PFAS. The process of permitting, monitoring, and enforcing business processes using PFAS is very labor-intensive. Unfortunately, the focus on permitting, monitoring, and enforcement does not yield a proportional result in controlling and reducing the negative effects of PFAS. Completely reducing the emission and discharge of PFAS has been a process of many decades and has not led to a reduction to zero emissions/discharge to date. Another concern is that products containing PFAS end up in waste at the end of their lifespan. PFAS cannot be separated at that point. PFAS is also not destroyed in incineration plants. Therefore, even after a ban, PFAS will continue to be present in our living environment for a very long time, with all possible harmful consequences. We cannot undo what has already been created. Worldwide, PFAS is present in the environment and in humans, as a result of the long-term emission of PFAS by factories. What we can achieve and want to achieve is to prevent PFAS from causing new damage in the future. In this context, the current restriction proposal is seen as a good step towards a global ban on this group of substances. Because PFAS does not adhere to the borders of a continent, contamination from other continents will continue. The next step should be a global ban. An important factor in this is that (in the Netherlands) so far, the application of the precautionary principle in permitting and enforcing PFAS production processes has not been approved by the court. Removing PFAS from the soil, groundwater, and surface water is technically extremely difficult and very expensive, if possible at all. Based on the foregoing, the restriction of  all PFAS is seen as the most suitable and effective way to remove the negative effects on the environment, nature, humans, and animals. This position is further substantiated below with specific (local and supra-local) information and various research results.

3. Source of local and regional PFAS contamination The municipality of Dordrecht is home to a chemical industrial complex. This complex includes the establishment of Chemours Netherlands B.V (formerly DuPont; hereinafter: Chemours). Since 1967, Teflon PFTE, Teflon FEP, and Viton have been produced on this complex. The complex also houses Dow Chemical Dordrecht (polymers) and Delrin Netherlands B.V. (thermoplastic materials). From 1967 until October 2012, DuPont, later Chemours, used the auxiliary substance PFOA in the production of various fluorine compounds (namely fluoro-polymers, homopolymers, copolymers, and fluoroelastomers) in the Teflon factory, among other places. The use of PFOA was terminated because PFOA has been designated as a Substance of Very High Concern (SVHC) at the European level since 2013. The GenX technology (HFPO-DA) was developed to replace PFOA in the production of fluorinated plastics, including Teflon. This technology has been used since late 2012 in the production of fluorinated plastics. In the process, the auxiliary substances FRD-902 and FRD-903 are emitted to air and water, and E1 is emitted to the air. GenX substances, belonging to PFAS, were designated as a potential SVHC at the national level on February 2, 2018, and were designated as a SVHC at the European level on June 26, 2019.

4. Local concern about PFAS The municipalities of Dordrecht, Sliedrecht, and Papendrecht have been researching the harmful effects of the PFAS group since 2015, and the municipality of Molenlanden since 2018, and have also alerted the national government to the fact that the problem is larger than just our municipalities. It is now generally known that due to the persistence, bioaccumulation, and poor degradability of PFAS, they have caused a harmful effect that is difficult, and in many places impossible, to remove. The soil, groundwater, and surface water in our area are contaminated. Swimming is no longer possible everywhere. People can no longer eat from their own gardens without concern everywhere, and PFAS in nature causes accumulation of the substance in animals. The municipalities and the inhabitants of our municipalities are deeply worried about this.

5. Studies on the local, regional, and national effects of PFAS Below is a chronological overview of studies conducted on the local, regional, and national level regarding the (consequences of) PFAS. These studies support our position to achieve a total ban on the PFAS group as soon as possible. The municipality of Molenlanden commissioned a comprehensive study of PFAS concentrations in 2018 and 2019. Based on this study, it was determined that elevated concentrations of PFAS (specifically PFOA) were found throughout the entire municipality. The highest concentrations are located in the part of the municipality that is located in the southwest direction from the location of Chemours. The highest measured concentration of PFOA in the soil is 75 µg/kg of solid substance and in the groundwater is 3.4 µg per liter. Furthermore, this study made it clear that the average PFOA concentration in the topsoil (up to 0.5 meters) of studied pastures is 65 µg/kg. Since 2018, the Rivierenland water board has been conducting measurements of surface water in Molenlanden. Based on these measurements, the National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM) advised against consuming fish caught in the surface water due to the exceeding of the risk limit for fish. In 2022, the RIVM conducted research on crops from vegetable gardens in, among other places, Molenlanden. Based on this research, the RIVM advised owners of vegetable gardens in five cores (Wijngaarden, Oud-Alblas, Molenaarsgraaf, Brandwijk, and Bleskensgraaf, totaling about 10,000 inhabitants) not to consume vegetables and fruit from their own garden year-round due to the high PFAS concentration in these crops. Consumption of own crops should be alternated regularly with those from a store. Research firm Arcadis concluded in a study conducted in 2022 on soil and water in vegetable gardens in the municipalities of Dordrecht, Papendrecht, Sliedrecht, and Molenlanden that in these municipalities, food from your own garden can be consumed without restriction up to a contamination of 4.6 µg/kg of PFOA. Above this level, there may be a risk in consuming food from your own garden. In the immediate vicinity of Chemours, it is recommended not to use ditch and shallow groundwater for irrigation of vegetable gardens. The agricultural sector (Molenlanden has about 500 agricultural companies) also has concerns about the consequences of PFAS for growing crops and the quality of the grassland as food for animals. Although two studies in 2020 and 2021 on meat samples and agricultural products (meat, eggs, milk) by the Dutch Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) found hardly any exceedance of the current European standards for PFAS in eggs, meat, and fish, our farmers are wondering about the real consequences of PFAS in the soil, grassland, and air for their animals, the grass and silage from their own land that they eat, and for the products they grow on their land. This constant uncertainty is putting a great strain on the livelihood security of the agricultural sector in our municipality. 
The Safety Board has published the report "Industry and residents" on April 13, 2023. One of the industries examined is Chemours. This report provides answers to the questions of how residents living near industrial emissions are protected from adverse health effects and exposure to industrial emissions, and what measures provide better protection. The Safety Board concludes that the health of residents living near industry deserves better protection. The board also advocates for the competent authority to act based on the precautionary principle. To date, the Dutch court has not approved the application of this principle (see 7.3). 
Recently, the RIVM has calculated in its report "Risk assessment of exposure to PFAS through food and drinking water in the Netherlands" (July 2023) that people are exposed to PFAS through food and water. This study shows that the amount of PFAS that people could be exposed to through food and water exceeds the so-called health-based limit value. If people are exposed to more PFAS than this health-based limit value for a long period of time, harmful health effects are possible, according to the RIVM. Molenlanden also has a strong recreation sector. The landscape, water, and our cultural heritage (Unesco World Heritage Kinderdijk) contribute to the recreational value of our municipality. Recently (July 2023), the RIVM conducted research into PFAS in swimming water in our municipality and in the neighboring municipalities of Alblasserdam and Dordrecht. It was established that the tested swimming water in Molenlanden is safe enough to swim in. However, for two of the three tested swimming ponds, this assessment is based on a measurement dating back to 2019. Moreover, measurements by the Rivierenland water board over the period 2018-2022 show that at one swimming pond in Molenlanden, an increased concentration of PFOS (up to three times the norm of 0.65 ng per liter) is present. 

6. Sub-conclusion 1 We endorse the concern about PFAS expressed in the restriction report. As a municipality, we are confronted daily with the consequences of PFAS for our residents, our entrepreneurs, the environment, and nature. PFAS is not only present in the soil of our territory, but also in the surface water and groundwater. The consequences of exposure to PFAS are irreversible and not limited to the border of our municipality or the Netherlands. This requires action at the European level, and certainly an initiative for, in our opinion, a much-needed global ban. 

7. Response to the content of the restriction proposal Below are specific comments on the content of the restriction proposal. They are addressed by topic. If necessary, the relationship with the proposal of the submitter is made. 

7.1 Scope of the restriction The proposal (page 50, 68) states that the restriction applies to the manufacture, trade, and use of PFAS in the EU as such and as a component of other substances, in mixtures, and in products above a certain concentration. We note here that the ban should also apply to the import of PFAS (in all its appearances and product forms) from a country outside the European Union for further processing, production, or transit to or through a (other) EU country. Furthermore, the ban should also apply to the production, trade, and transit between a factory with an establishment in the EU and one or more establishments outside the EU. This is necessary to achieve a comprehensive ban on PFAS.

General Comments: Referring to the use of HFOs as a blowing agent for the production of insulated pipes, most notably for the manufacturing of the insulation material of such insulated pipes: Insulated pipes for the use of district heating and cooling (DHC) are composed of so called medium pipes which are surrounded by a thermal insulation material (most typically polyurethane foam) which is covered by a jacket of typically polyethylene. The medium pipes consist of steel or are of a polmeric nature. Those insulated pipes are at the heart of any district heating (or cooling) network. The pipes are laid underground and remain in service for 30 - 50 years. During operation hot water (the energy transporting medium) is transported from the centrally located heating station towards the consumers (typically residential buildings to be heated).
In this use case HFO can be used as a blowing agent for the insulating foam. It is important to understand that the HFO remains inside the foam for the entire life-time of the insulated pipe and is not emitted to the environment. The HFO is a functional part within the insulated pipe and serves the specific purpose to reduce the energy losses during operation, and it performs that task better than any known technical alternative available today. The energy savings over the life-time of the products are significant, especially when looking not only at one specific network which is already in operation but when taking into acount the increase which is planned for DHC solutions in the coming years in order to save reach the EU climate targets.

General Comments: Refining operations and refinery product distribution chains were not included in the restriction proposal baseline study/information provided for Petroleum and mining sector.

Therefore, Concawe carried out a study, with Accenture support, to acquire an overall view of PFAS applications, potential release, alternatives, and impact of the restriction proposal in refineries and its distribution segment.
The results of the industry survey, interviews, advanced analytics and patent analysis lead to conclusions that this industry is not adequately covered by the Petroleum and mining outcomes outlined in the initial restriction proposals.
The following conclusions for the use of PFAS in Refineries and Fuel Distribution were found
1. refineries do not manufacture PFAS.
Their use is mostly in solid form contained in industrial equipment, with low risk of exposure to the environment during operations also due to HSE measures in place.
Despite challenges in collecting information on the use of PFAS, we have conducted an inventory of PFAS in Refining and Fuel Distribution Equipment as detailed as possible due to the limited timeline given by the OPC showing that PFAS (mostly fluoropolymers) have been detected in a large share of refineries’ equipment, s such as joints, valves, pumps, etc.
2. We have observed a growing effort in the industry to develop environmental management plans for PFAS, especially related to managing emissions of PFAS in wastewater.
Today, there is a lack of alternatives to PFAS for most industrial equipment. For the uses identified, potential substitutes lack combined properties needed for critical safety requirements (e.g., hydrocarbon leakage avoidance) limiting the ability to adopt alternatives.
3. A PFAS ban in refinery and Fuel Distribution equipment today would have severe impacts across the energy value chain, putting at risk fuel supply in Europe.
Given the results of the study by Accenture contracted by Concawe on PFAS applications, the derogation proposed for fluoropolymer applications in petroleum and mining industry (until 13.5 years after EiF) is not applicable to the Refining and distribution sector, which is currently out of the scope of the derogation.
For all above findings, we ask for an exemption for all PFAS application in Refineries and distribution industrial segment, until proven replacement technology is available for each and every application.
More can be found in Chapter 7 “Conclusion” of the report.

Sectors and (sub-)uses: The Refining operation and refineries´ products distribution were not included in the restriction proposal baseline study/information provided for Petroleum and mining sector. The overview studies used as baseline for the restriction proposal for petroleum and mining sector was only focused on exploration, exploitation and associated offshore processing oil. Refining downstream operation is fundamentally different from the Petroleum and Mining activities: it transforms petroleum crude oil and feedstocks from other origins (vegetable oil, used cooking oil, animal fat, pyrolyzed waste plastics, …) into refined products by a number of processes which operate at high temperature and pressure, that are not met in the upstream activities of petroleum and mining. Most refining processes are relying on controlled chemical reactions, with the presence of catalysts, which can be corrosive (sulfuric acid, hydrofluoric acid) and generate corrosive products that needs to be further transformed using other secondary processes. The refining sector is also the biggest consumer (and producer) of pure hydrogen in Europe, as Hydrogen is both produced from the petroleum feedstock and consumed to purify the petroleum products to meet market’s specification. Hydrogen is , highly flammable, which requires specific handling conditions and equipment. The other feedstocks (other than petroleum crude oil) also require specific processes and handling conditions.  Due to the complexity and specificity of numerous distinct processes (each carried out in a discrete facility, or process unit), Refining operation and refineries´ products distribution has multiple PFAS´ critical applications ranging from nozzle applications through valves, gaskets, pumps etc.  Consequently, Refineries´ operating conditions and applications are not be exhaustively covered by the current Petroleum and mining sector uses identification. General Comments: Refrigerant gas and solid state fluoropolymers are essential materials without suitable alternatives.
a) The global reefer container fleet is estimated to exceed 1.8 million reefer containers rising to about 2 million units by 2026 Ref: Drewry Maritime Census.
b) Two thirds of global reefer container cargo is carried by shipping lines headquartered in Europe.
c) Global shipments of perishable refrigerated commodities were 307 million tons in 2022. While some of this cargo is intra-regional and carried overland by road or rail, half of the global trade is carried in reefer containers on fuel-efficient ocean-going container ships.
d) The EU provides 23% of the global refrigerated cargo trade consisting of 10% of global refrigerated exports and 13% of imports. EU reefer exports are mostly high value meat, fish and dairy products plus fruits and vegetables as well as chemicals and pharmaceuticals.
e) Much of the world’s fresh produce cargoes are exported from developing countries such as Central and South America, Africa and South Asia as well as from Europe and the USA.
f) Servicing of reefer containers must be undertaken, prior to shipment, by a network of qualified technicians located in Europe and other global port areas. Servicing of complex reefer machines and refrigerants requires training to a high level and adherence to safety regulations.
g) The operating life of a maritime reefer container is 18 years. The average age of today’s fleet is 6.5 years. On eventual disposal from maritime service, reefer containers might be used for another 10 years in static, land-based applications. By comparison, road based refrigerated trailers typically operate regionally for 9 to 12 years.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: SECTOR:  Maritime Intermodal Containers SUBSECTORS:   Reefer containers  Refrigerated intermodal containers   Intermodal containers  Transport Refrigeration  Transport by road, rail and sea  Refrigeration servicing and repairs  1.1 Table , Annex E.2.10   The table does not include the specialism of the global maritime reefer container industry or its subsectors.   ECHA are requested to consider the global reefer container as a separate sector to “Transport Refrigeration”  because of the unique special requirements of the global reefer container.  a) The global reefer container fleet is estimated to exceed 1.8 million reefer containers rising to about 2 million units by 2026 Ref: Drewry Maritime Census. b) Two thirds of global reefer container cargo is carried by shipping lines headquartered in Europe. c) Global shipments of perishable refrigerated commodities were 307 million tons in 2022. While some of this cargo is intra-regional and carried overland by road or rail, half of the global trade is carried in reefer containers on fuel-efficient ocean-going container ships. d) The EU provides 23% of the global refrigerated cargo trade consisting of 10% of global refrigerated exports and 13% of imports. EU reefer exports are mostly high value meat, fish and dairy products plus fruits and vegetables as well as chemicals and pharmaceuticals.  e) Much of the world’s fresh produce cargoes are exported from developing countries such as Central and South America, Africa and South Asia as well as from Europe and the USA. f) Servicing of reefer containers must be undertaken, prior to shipment, by a network of qualified technicians located in Europe and other global port areas. Servicing of complex reefer machines and refrigerants requires training to a high level and adherence to safety regulations.  g) The operating life of a maritime reefer container is 18 years. The average age of today’s fleet is 6.5 years. On eventual disposal from maritime service, reefer containers might be used for another 10 years in static, land-based applications. By comparison, road based refrigerated trailers typically operate regionally for 9 to 12 years.  1.2 Reefer container unique operating criteria a) Reefers must be designed to operate in ambient temperatures varying from -30o C to +50o C. This is a much higher and technically challenging range than for other modes of transport refrigeration. b) The ambient temperature where reefers are stowed on a container ship can be between 35oC and 45oC for long periods. Most shipping routes carrying refrigerated cargo transit the tropics where high ambient temperatures combine with heat emissions from on-board equipment to cause a high stowage ambient temperature.  c) Cargo temperatures vary from -30o C to +30o C which covers the requirements of the great majority of cargo types. For example, 17 kW needed when cooling hot stuffed cargo with 20 m/t of Durian, compared to 1.8 kW when maintaining frozen fish at 25°C ambient. d) 'Super frozen’ cargo is shipped at temperatures of - 80o C to -30 o C carried in specialised “super-freezer” reefers which use different system designs and refrigerants. e) Power consumption of the reefer machine design must be low to enable up to 2000 reefers to operate on-board a ship using the ship’s power generator capacity. In addition to the ship’s power requirements, the generators provide electrical power for the reefer containers and ventilators for removing hot condensing air from the stowage areas.  f) Limiting power consumption is a strong focus of the shipping industry both to comply with the IMO 2023 regulations as well as to mitigate the substantial cost of fuel for powering the ship and its electrical generators. Accordingly, it is essential for reefer containers to have a low power consumption. g) R134a refrigerant is used for 96% of the existing reefer fleet. R134a is a low-pressure refrigerant and provides efficiency and a low power consumption over a a wide operating temperature range. R134a yields a low total carbon footprint in reefer containers but it is an F-gas and the GWP (Global Warming Potential) exceeds the target level for many refrigeration applications set in EU F-Gas regulations. h) Carbon impact calculations (ISO 14067) of reefers using R134a over an 18-year operating life indicate that 89.5% of the carbon impact is from power consumption and 10.5% from refrigerant loss.  i) Reefer machine dimensions are designed to fit within the exterior limits of the container (ISO 668).  The reefer machine is also required to be designed to the minimum depth thus optimising the container interior space to transport the maximum amount of cargo.  1.3 F-Gas Refrigerants The reefer container industry is a down-stream user of manufactured refrigerant gases.  a) Of the 1.8 million reefer container machines in the global fleet, around 1 million units, because of the design system, cannot practically be charged with a different refrigerant. b) R134a refrigerant gas is used for 96% of the 1.8 million reefer containers, each charged with between 4 to 6 kg. R134a provides the required operating range, and efficient COP (coefficient of performance) in the wide operational envelope of the reefer container. The demanding operating conditions limits the refrigerants that could replace R134a. c) R404A or R452A is used for approximately 4% of reefers. A small quantity of reefers are charged with R454A, R513A, CO2 and R1234yf. R23 or R473A are used in super-freezers. d) R134a, R404A, R452A and R23 are HFCs while R513A and R473A are HFC blends with HFOs and their continued use is affected by F-gas regulation restrictions because of their global warming potential (GWP). R1234yf and R454A are HFOs and are outside current F-Gas regulations given their very low GWP. e) R1234yf cannot be charged into a reefer designed for R134a because of its mild flammability A2L class (ISO 817) but is potentially a better refrigerant: • ultra-low GWP of just 0.5  • meets performance criteria and has low electrical power consumption. • used in other industries such as the global automotive industry and is widely available. • could be introduced in new reefer container machines in a lead time of 2 to 3-years. f) The reefer container industry has been trialling the use of lower GWP refrigerants such as the natural refrigerants R744 carbon dioxide (CO2) and R290 Propane but there are operating challenges with their use. R717 Ammonia (NH3) might be a long-term possibility too though its toxicity may present a challenge for carriage of food. g) R513a is a blend of R134a and HFO 1234yf with a GWP of 673 which is less than half that of R134a. Most reefer machines manufactured before 2018 can be modified to replace R134a with R513A and from 2018 onwards, reefer machines can be charged with R513A as a replacement to R134a without modification.  h) R513A is a practical replacement for R134a, offering high energy efficiency and low GWP but it is an F-Gas and subject to regulatory restrictions and is not currently widely available globally. i) R744/CO2 cannot be charged into a reefer designed for R134a because a R744/CO2 refrigeration machine design is completely different. Solid state fluoropolymers are irreplaceable materials that are crucial to the manufacture and servicing of refrigerated machinery.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: 2 EMISSIONS IN THE END-OF-LIFE PHASE  2.1 Manufacture stage  The reefer container industry is a down-stream user of F-Gas and sealing elements manufactured of solid-state fluoropolymer materials such as PTFE (Polytetrafluoroethylene), ETFE (Ethylene tetrafluoroethylene) PVDF, (Polyvinylidene fluoride), PFA (Perfluoro alkoxy alkane), FEP (Fluorinated ethylene propylene). As a downstream user, the COA do not hold information concerning any emissions that might occur during the manufacture of F-Gas and solid-state fluoropolymers.  The manufacture and supply of F-Gas and sealing elements is undertaken by specialist manufacturers who directly supply the reefer container and component manufacturers and service providers (repair and maintenance depots). Seal and gasket manufacturers purchase solid stock materials and machine or extrude and form to the required dimensions.     2.2 Emissions During Use Phase  2.2.1 Refrigerant Gases The loss of refrigerant gases from the global reefer container is minimised by ensuring the high quality of proper maintenance procedures and leak detection practiced in the shipping industry as well as the use of special sealing materials.  Reefer containers are examined and serviced in Europe and other global locations before each loading: they must be fit for a long, intercontinental sea voyage carrying high value, sensitive cargoes.  Technicians use specialist leak detection equipment and techniques, such as ultrasonic leak detectors or electronic leak detectors, to locate and repair refrigerant leaks quickly. The ongoing availability of refrigerant gas is crucial to the reefer service centre.  ISO 20854 Table C.1 provides an estimation of fugitive emissions equalling 7% annual leak rate per year. For a reefer charged with 5 kg and 18 lifetime, this amounts to: 5 kg * 0.07%/a * 18 a = 6.3 kg Training programmes are in place to ensure that personnel responsible for reefer container operation and maintenance are aware of the importance of leak prevention and how to identify and address leaks. Record-keeping procedures ensure accurate records of refrigerant usage, leak repairs, and maintenance activities. This information helps track trends and identify areas for improvement.  2.2.2 Solid-State Sealing Elements Sealing elements are compressed within the reefer container machinery system and not exposed to the atmosphere. There is no wear, erosion or abrasion. The materials are used in the solid form and do not shred or degrade into particles during use – or at end of life.   2.3 End-Of-Life Phase  2.3.1 Refrigerant Gases  A unique environmental benefit of the global reefer container is that the maximum use is made of the refrigerant gases before the need for recycling and eventual disposal. It is important that regulatory provisions allow the continued use of the global refrigerated container for the duration of its planned life to avoid premature disposal of refrigerant gases and the detrimental impact on the environment caused by disposal and manufacturing replacements. An 18-year service life is common and many of the main components are not replaced during the strictly applied servicing and maintenance programmes. However, where materials are replaced at end of life, used materials are disposed as licensed industrial waste.  The reefer container industry recognises the work of ECHA to identify pollutants and the COA, the trade association for the reefer container industry, is seeking to develop projects to ensure enhanced responsible processing of used materials and recycling.    2.3.2 Solid-State Sealing Elements  The unique properties of solid-state fluoropolymer sealing element material is that it ensures a long service life and is not vulnerable to degrading into particles.  18-year service life is common and many of the main components are not replaced during the strictly applied servicing and maintenance programmes. However, where materials are replaced, end of life, used materials are disposed as industrial licensed waste.  The reefer container industry recognises the work of ECHA to identify pollutants and the COA, the trade association for the reefer container industry, is seeking to develop projects to ensure enhanced responsible processing of used materials and recycling.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: 3 Effectiveness of Incineration  3.1 Refrigerant gases  Incineration of F-Gases (fluorinated gases) can be an effective method for preventing their release into the atmosphere.  Premature disposal driven by restriction of refrigerants needed for servicing the reefer machine, when the reefer may otherwise continue operations, is a detrimental environmental step. Enabling the 18-year life of a reefer container by regulators permits the usage and servicing of existing reefer containers as opposed to regulations forcing a premature disposal of the global reefer container fleet because of its use of an existing F-Gas. Efforts are made to reduce F-Gas emissions through practices such as recovery, reclamation, and recycling before considering incineration and the principles of waste hierarchy, which prioritises reduction, reuse, and recycling over incineration or landfilling.   Destruction Efficiency:  When F-Gases are incinerated at high temperatures in specialized incineration facilities, they can be broken down into less harmful compounds, primarily through combustion processes. The destruction efficiency of incineration for F-Gases is generally high, meaning that the vast majority of the gases are converted into other compounds, including carbon dioxide (CO2).  Environmental Benefits: Incineration of F-Gases and its conversion into CO2, has benefits as a last resort. Proper Facilities: Incineration of F-Gases must be conducted in specialized facilities designed to handle hazardous gases safely. These facilities should be equipped with appropriate pollution control devices to minimize the release of harmful by products and ensure that the incineration process is environmentally sound.  Regulatory Compliance: The incineration of F-Gases is subject to environmental regulations and guidelines. Compliance with local and national regulations is essential to ensure that the incineration process is carried out safely and legally.  Costs: The incineration of F-Gases can be expensive due to the need for specialized facilities and equipment.        3.2 Solid-state fluoropolymers  The global reefer container industry responsibly disposes of used sealing element materials through appointed service providers (maintenance depots) who are controlled by local government and hold an environmental licence to manage waste material.  Used sealing elements are responsibly disposed as licenced waste at government approved facilities.  The percentage that is disposed in a landfill or municipal incineration is not known. Sealing elements are solid-state materials and could be separated for disposal at approved facilities if required by the authorities.  Municipal incineration of PTFE shows no significant generation of studied PFAS.  Using pilot scale equipment and testing minimizes background interference.  PTFE produced mainly hydrofluoric acid and carbon dioxide during incineration.  A study of PTFE combustion under typical waste incineration conditions was undertaken at the BRENDA (German acronym for “Brennkammer mit Dampfkessel”) pilot plant at Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT).  The study showed that polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) can be almost fully transformed into fluorine (F) (as hydrofluoric acid (HF). The study also investigated the possible generation of low molecular weight per- and polyfluorinated alkyl substances (PFAS). The results indicate that, within procedural quantitation limits, no statistically significant evidence was found that studied PFAS were created during the incineration of PTFE.  Therefore, municipal incineration of PTFE using best available technologies (BAT) is not a significant source of the studied PFAS and should be considered an acceptable form of waste treatment. Source: Chemosphere in 07.2019 (Volume 226, pages 898.906, Sciencedirect.com Krasimir Aleksandrov , Hans Joachim Gehrmann,  Manuela Hauser, Hartmut Mätzing, Daniel Pigeon, Dieter Stapf,  Manuela Wexler

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: 4.a Recovery:   The global reefer container industry undertakes best practice in accordance with the strictest regulations to control the production, use, and management of F-Gases to minimize their impact on climate change.   F-Gases are recovered from the refrigeration system by skilled technicians working in specialist reefer servicing facilities. This involves using specialized recovery equipment to capture and remove the refrigerant gas from the system. The recovered gas is stored in a pressure cylinder for further processing.  Reclamation:  After recovery, the collected F-Gases are sent to a reclamation facility. Reclamation involves purifying the refrigerant to remove impurities, contaminants, and moisture. This process is essential to ensure the gas meets industry standards and can be reused in refrigeration or air conditioning systems.  Filtering and Separation: During the reclamation process, the F-Gases are often passed through filters and separation systems to remove any solid particles or oil residues. These impurities can degrade the performance of the refrigerant and the equipment in which it is used.  Testing and Analysis:  After purification, the refrigerant is subjected to various tests and analyses to verify its quality and ensure it meets the required specifications. This may include checking for chemical composition, moisture levels, and acidity.  Reuse or Destruction: Depending on the quality of the reclaimed F-Gases, they can be either reused or destroyed. High-quality reclaimed refrigerants can be reintroduced into refrigeration and air conditioning systems, reducing the need for new F-Gas production. Lower-quality refrigerants may need to be destroyed in an environmentally responsible manner to prevent their release into the atmosphere.  Record-Keeping:  Proper record-keeping is crucial throughout the recycling and reclamation process. Detailed records help track the source and quantity of recovered F-Gases, the purification processes applied, and their final disposition.

5. General Comments: Refrigerants are a type of chemical called fluorocarbons, including chlorofluorocarbons, hydrochlorofluorocarbons, hydrofluorocarbons, and hydrofluoroolefins. Due to ozone layer destruction, global warming, and climate protection, the Montreal Protocol, the Kyoto Protocol, and the Kigali Amendment have come into effect and implemented planned controls over the production and use of these compounds and mixtures. Therefore, the REACH PFAS regulation does not need to cover the use of these chemicals in gas states again.
These compounds can form trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) through atmospheric degradation pathways. For example, HFC-134a can form CF3CFO and further form TFA; HFO-1234yf can form CF3CFO and further form TFA; HCFO-1233zd (E) can form CF3CHO and further form TFA. In general, after being used, fluorocarbon gas substances enter the atmosphere and undergo intermediate processes before being degraded to produce TFA.
TFA forms as an acid when it is formed in the atmosphere, and when it reaches the surface (soil or water), it forms salts with alkali metals (such as sodium, potassium, and calcium). TFA salts lack reactivity and remain persistent in the environment with an estimated half-life ranging from hundreds to thousands of years. As it doesn't react with biomolecules, its persistence is not important. TFA and its salts are easily excreted by animals and do not bioaccumulate in the food chain. TFA salts are of low toxicity for animals and plants, therefore pose little risk. HFC-134a, or 1, 1, 1, 2-tetrafluoroethane, is a gaseous halocarbon that is considered a leading candidate for replacing other halocarbon materials such as Freon 12 (dichlorodifluoromethane) and Freon 22 in air conditioning and refrigeration systems, and may be used as an aerosol propellant or foam expansion agent. As the federal regulations require switching from CFCs to other suitable compounds, these compounds either do not damage the ozone layer or have less damage to the ozone layer than CFCs.

General Comments: Refrigeration, Air Conditioning and Heat Pump (RACHP) products play an essential role in ensuring not only the safety, security and health of users in extreme climate conditions, but also maintaining food sustainability, while also supporting the Fit for 55 and REPowerEU policies for reducing CO2 emissions and achieving carbon neutrality.
Therefore, we would like to request an exemption from the restrictions on the use of PFAS for socially necessary RACHP products. In addition, we also kindly request to take into consideration the extensive research time required to trace back the components and materials used in RACHP products. We urge you to carefully consider the legislation regarding this matter.
In RACHP products, PFAS is an essential material used in various applications such as refrigerants (F-gas applications), electrical and electronic components (electronics applications), surface coatings, metal plating (plating applications, etc.), as well as in functional components such as refrigerant circuit components and structural materials that make up the chassis (other applications).
The unique properties of PFAS make them a popular choice in RACHP products, where they provide the necessary durability that consumers demand. In summary, materials using PFAS are vital in RACHP products that are essential to people's everyday lives. Thus, an exemption for RACHP products is necessary to ensure their continued use.
Regarding the disposal of electrical and electronic products including RACHP products, the WEEE Directive enforces the collection and disposal of these products, as well as the provision of information to recycling facilities, specifically problematic components. We kindly ask Member States to enhance guidance on the proper operation of recycling facilities.
In addition, when considering the circular economy and efficient use of resources, use of all maintenance related items required for product maintenance and repair should be permitted with no expiration date.
JRAIA intends to submit additional comments and evidence. However, the number of chemical substances that fall under the definition of PFAS is enormous. We are currently conducting surveys with our suppliers to determine the presence or absence of these substances and their applications in each part. This process requires time to investigate the possibility of substitution and to evaluate their applications. It is imperative to conduct investigations that cover not only risk assessment and socioeconomic impact of substances but also span from upstream to downstream, starting from materials, components, and final products, which make up the final RACHP product. We recommend including the time frame for such a study in the legislative review process.

Lastly, we would like to bring attention to refrigerants and refrigerant circuit components:
Refrigerants:
Not all refrigerants can be easily replaced, and the "S+3Es" concept (which is considering not only Safety, but also Environmental performance, Energy efficiency and Economic feasibility) is crucial for successful transition to alternative refrigerants. In this context, "environmental performance" refers specifically to a refrigerant's low global warming potential (GWP), which may have a negative impact on the environment.
In addition, we would like to point out the impact on the two types of Air Conditioning and Heat Pump as shown below:
1. Direct expansion
The market favors direct expansion systems due to their high efficiency and ease of installation. However, the use of R290 (Hydrocarbon), a potent refrigerant, in such systems is premature and is not feasible yet. This is mainly due to concerns about product safety, as well as a lack of social systems such as qualification programs for installers and maintenance / repair technicians handling higher flammability refrigerants.
2. Indirect expansion
Among indirect expansion systems, large size equipment charged with large amount of refrigerant such as centrifugal chillers have a safety issue when converting to higher flammability refrigerants such as R290. While the transition of refrigerants in small-capacity centrifugal chillers is making progress, applying R290 to all indirect expansion systems is difficult due to installation restrictions and safety regulations.

Refrigerant Circuit Components:
PFAS materials are used for components that make up the refrigerant circuit of RACHP products, such as compressors, four-way valves and shut-off valves, because they are required to have long-term reliability (durability) as a maintenance-free feature, which is considered essential for the design of hermetic systems. Therefore, transition to alternatives is not easy.
