Electrolysis: Essential usage of fluoropolymers
The needed scale up of electrolysis production capacities to ensure industrial decarbonization and to contribute meeting climate goals is not possible without fluoropolymers. hence, a European transition towards climate-neutrality is only possible with fluoropolymers. Specifically, we as thyssenkrupp nucera need fluoropolymers as an important substance in our electrolyzers to ramp up our capacities.

thyssenkrupp nucera uses fluoropolymers, a class of PFAS polymers, in all products in the field of Alkaline Water Electrolysis, Chlor-Alkali Electrolysis, NaCl-ODC Electrolysis and HCl-ODC Electrolysis. In the field of all chlorine production technologies, PFAS are essential especially for utilization in membranes as well as for gas diffusion electrodes in the ODC technologies. Furthermore, due to the highly aggressive conditions in all electrolyzer technologies, utilization of PFAS is essential for continuous and safe plant operation. (see annex for list of PFAS in thyssenkrupp nucera technology)
Furthermore, the diaphragm electrolysis also uses PFAS materials or asbestos which represent next to the amalgam electrolysis no sustainable and feasible alternatives and end up in technological drawbacks an drastic competitive disadvantage for Europe.

Key benefits of PFAS regarding our applications are: very high corrosion resistance, plant safety (due to hindered leakages), little / no leaching, excellent oxygen index values, hardly inflammable, low specific weight, easy processing for specialist companies. There are no alternatives available as our supplier’s tests show, which possess the same product properties as required for our applications.

Therefore, thyssenkrupp nucera is currently forced to utilize the given technological state of the art. Of course, we are highly interested in technically and commercially comparable alternatives which might require changes in our technology and could take decades of development.

Low risk of fluoropolymers
According to the restriction proposal, all PFAS are treated equally, without differentiation. However, as Henry et al. 2018 (Note 1) and Korzeniowski et al. 2022 (Note 2) point out, most fluoropolymers can be defined as ‘polymers of low concern’ (PLC) following OECD criteria. Polymers of low concern are those deemed to have insignificant environmental and human health impact. Therefore, “these polymers should have reduced regulatory requirements”, as OECD states. (Note 3)

More specifically, environmental and human health risks of fluoropolymers are extremely limited across the electrolysis technology value chain (both in terms of environmental and human exposure). (Note 4)
• They are not bio-available, toxic, or even mobile.
• They do not dissolve in or contaminate water or generate microplastics
• They cannot enter or accumulate in a person’s bloodstream.
• They do not present significant toxicity concerns and do not degrade into other PFAS

Regarding thyssenkrupp nucera in particular:
• Since thyssenkrupp nucera’s products are not foreseen for the consumer sector, there is no contact to private, nor professional individuals. It is only used in a highly controlled and supervised industrial environment.
• Almost all PFAS are within the closed loop of the electrolysis, i.e. that no PFAS is released to the environment. Furthermore, only experienced and professional personnel is allowed to handle those.
• We use PFAS almost entirely in solid form inside our electrolyzers. Consequently, no uncontrolled entry of PFAS to the environment is happening.

In summary, used PFAS of low concern in thyssenkrupp nucera’s technologies will not harm the environment and human health. During the application there is no dissolvement or erosion.

Consequences of a ban
As pointed out, electrolyzer manufacturers, in particular we as thyssenkrupp nucera, are forced to use fluoropolymers in their technologies. Consequently, a rushed PFAS ban without granting any derogations for electrolyzers would have destructive effects on the industry, leading to deindustrialization within Europe and a slow-down of the European electrolyzer industry. A ramp up of capacities to reach climate goals, as urged by the European Commission, would be impossible without fluoropolymers – dealing with the lack of alternative materials. Moreover, a ban would result in a disbalance between Europe and other regions and thus in a massive competitive disadvantage and economical damage for Europe. More specifically, electrolyzer capacities will be reduced in Europe and transferred to other regions (e.g. USA and China). Precisely, a potential PFAS ban would endanger the entire business for thyssenkrupp nucera.
Even if the ban is implemented, it does not solve the overall problem that PFAS are emitted: The electrolyzer industry does not emit PFAS (fluoropolymers of low concern).
To develop alternative materials, R&D, product development, testing and industrial qualification will take decades of efforts over the entire supply chain impacting all stakeholders (e.g., raw material suppliers, fabricators, placers on the market and users).

Electrolysis importance
Electrolyzers are key to reaching our climate goals. Therefore, electrolyzer manufacturers need to ramp up their capacities to meet the market needs. A possible ban of PFAS would be a severe setback to these efforts.

According to the IEA, 850 Gigawatt (GW) of electrolysis capacity need to be in operation by 2030 to meet the net-zero emission scenario. “Policymakers across the world have been stepping up their efforts to facilitate the market ramp-up by committing to ambitious electrolysis capacity build-out targets, amounting to about 210 GW of pledged build-out by 2030,” (Note 5) as Roland Berger reports. Europe’s recent RePowerEU package includes doubling the previous target for green H2 use in the EU to a total of 20 million tons by 2030. Thus, the European Commission urged European electrolyzer manufacturers to scale up their production capacity. The overall deployment target is 100 GW by 2030, with a share of 40% of all installed electrolyzer capacity “made in Europe”. (Note 6)

Global demand for Chlorine and Caustic Soda grows in line with gross domestic product. Chlor-Alkali electrolysis is a fundamental technology for the chemical industry and the starting point for various value chains of day-to-day products (e.g. Soap / Detergents, Aluminium, Sodium Hypochlorite / Disinfection, Polyurethane foam / Polycarbonates / PVC, Hydrochloric acid, Hydrogenation of Alkenes, Fats and Oils).

As thyssenkrupp nucera, we offer world-leading technologies for high-efficiency electrolysis plants. We have a strong track record of more than 600 projects with a total rating of over 10 gigawatts already successfully installed. More specifically, with our AWE technology to produce green hydrogen based on our experience as a world leader in C/A electrolysis technology, we offer an innovative solution on an industrial scale for green value chains.

By 2050, we expect the water electrolysis market to increase sevenfold. In 2050, there could be a total need of around 26,000 terawatt hours per year. This is almost one fifth of today’s worldwide primary energy consumption comparable to the total primary energy consumption of the USA in 2020 (24,386 TWh). (Note 7)

By now, we have contracted orders with more than 3 GW of AWE. Currently, we offer production capacity of more than 1GW per year and we have a clear commitment to ramp up to 5GW capacity by the end of 2025. A possible PFAS ban would prevent this growth.

thyssenkrupp nucera supplies the electrolyzers (capacity 700 MW) for Swedish company H2 Green Steel to build one of the largest integrated green steel plants in Europe. Furthermore, we partner with Shell to build a 200 MW hydrogen plant in the port of Rotterdam.

Additionally, we are partnering with OxyChem to install the latest generation eBiTAC v7 electrolyzers to support the conversion of its Battleground plant in LaPorte, Texas, from the diaphragm to membrane chlor-alkali technology.

We delivered NaCl-ODC electrolysis technology to our customer Covestro to site Tarragona in Spain. It is the first world-scale production plant for chlorine based upon the highly innovative and energy efficient ODC (oxygen depolarized cathode) technology (up to 25% less energy consumption, 1,550kWh/mt NaOH at 6kA/m2), invented by thyssenkrupp nucera and Covestro.

Request for exemption
Based on our descriptions and in line with suggestions by other affected companies in or organizations at the interface to our industry, we strongly insist on electrolyzer industry (with fluoropolymers as essential and low-concern substances) to be exempted from a ban and the overall PFAS restriction. A PFAS restriction should focus on potential hazardous PFAS substances with a clear exposure to human health and environmental risks.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: 1. Alkaline Water Electrolysis (AWE) -  Energy sector, subuse “Electrolysis technologies (not PEM)“ 2. Chlor-Alkali electrolysis including NaCl-ODC, Hydrochloric acid electrolysis - Sector not yet considered. It shall be reflected by chemical industry, sub-sector basic chemicals (chlor-alkali, HCl electrolysis)

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: 2a) The possible PFAS emissions during manufacturing of fluoropolymers can be more detailly provided by our fluoropolymer components suppliers. However, we are aware that a group of fluoropolymer member companies of FPG committed to responsible manufacturing principles and are continuously improving the manufacturing process and managing environmental emissions. Major fluoropolymer manufacturers have demonstrated emission reduction by recovery of fluorinated polymerisation aids for reuse or 99% removal of fluorinated polymerisation aids by wastewater treatment (Note 2). One of our main membrane suppliers for chlor-alkali electrolysis and HCl-ODC electrolysis, company Chemours, has successfully started up and tested already a thermal oxidizer destroying PFAS gaseous emissions from manufacturing processes with an efficiency greater than 99.99%. (Note 8) The high stability of fluoropolymers is based upon the carbon-fluorine bond, the strongest bond between Carbon and another atom. As a result, fluoropolymers are highly inert and have an exeptional chemical stability (Note 9). For example, polytetrafluoroethylene, the most used fluoropolymer within our applications, is insoluble in all known solvents (Note 10). Fluoropolymers used within our electrolyzer technologies (maximum operating temperature up to 95°C) under normal operating conditions are thermally stable. The typical maximum continuous service temperature for PTFE is 260°C, for other fluoropolymers within our application such as PFA, FEP, ECTFE, PVDF in the range of 140-260°C and thereby far above our typical operating temperature (Note 11). Fluoropolymer components applied within our electrolyzer technologies are carefully inspected and often reused after operating intervals of 4-6 years as they are found to be highly stable and immaculate after the named operating cycle. After many decades of experience with fluoropolymers within our electrolyzer technologies we did never find any hint on significant leaching of PFAS from the polymers to the product streams. Several of our clients within the chlor-alkali business analyse liquids from the electrolyzer unit to proof there is no PFAS release. We hope to submit further insights on these measurements within a later contribution to this ECHA public consultation.  For emissions during end of life, please consult our answers to question 2b and 3 of this questionnaire.  2b)  The fluoropolymer waste at our clients’ electrolyzer plants is collected separately from other waste. For most of the waste, end-of-life incineration with exhaust gas treatment is the current standard treatment. Small quantities e.g., PTFE/TFM are already recycled either by the fluoropolymer manufacturer or by other external companies. Based on the information from some fluoropolymer suppliers, there is research and development ongoing for partial or full recycling of components that are fundamental for thyssenkrupp nucera electrolyzer technologies. First developments are highly promising and will result in increased recycling rates of fluoropolymer components required within our electrolyzers.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Waste management of fluoropolymer components is dominated by incineration with careful exhaust gas treatment. PTFE as the major used PFAS component in our technologies was investigated in detail by Aleksandrov et. al. (Note 12) during municipal incineration using best available technologies. It was shown that while PTFE was almost fully transformed to Fluorine (as hydrofluoric acid), 31 potential harmful low molecular weight PFAS materials were studied. None of them was within quantifiable amount in flue gas during incineration. As such, although recycling is clearly the optimum solution for end-of-life phase of fluoropolymers and recycling rates should be increased within the upcoming years, also current municipal incineration using best available techniques can be considered as a transitional acceptable form of waste treatment.

6. Missing uses: Not answered questions we will deliver detailed information resp.  evidence in later contribution.  As already mentioned during the second call for evidence on PFAS (year 2021), the sector of chemical industry, including our sub-sector on production of basic chemicals such as caustic soda/potash and chlorine via chlor-alkali electrolysis (including also the chlor-alkali ODC technology) and HCl-ODC electrolysis was not considered up to now. a. The annual tonnage and emissions (at sub-sector level) and type of PFAS associated with the relevant use. Typical PFAS utilized within our chlor-alkali and HCl-ODC electrolyzer technologies include PTFE, PFSA/PTFE copolymers, PFCA/PTFE copolymers, PTFE-M, TFM, PVDF, ECTFE, FEP, FKM, PFA, PFPE. A full list of the PFAS materials including the main use within our technologies can be found as a confidential attachment. In addition, an estimation of the yearly amount of fluoropolymers provided by us to our clients is attached.  b. The key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use. For chlor-alkali electrolysis (including ODC technology), the state-of-the art technology is the membrane electrolysis with operating temperatures of ~90°C (upper operating temperature within electrolyzer unit up to 95°C) and strongly corrosive conditions with ~pH 0 for acidified brine to pH 14 for concentrated caustic solution and saturation with corrosive gases such as chlorine or oxygen. Similar, for HCl-ODC technology the utilization of concentrated hydrochloric acid (~10-15wt% in electrolyzer unit up to 60°C) and chlorine/oxygen gas requires utilization of stable materials for all components with medium contact. The key functionality of the fluoropolymers utilized here is to secure plant safety. Leakages of hazards such as hot concentrated caustic needs to be hindered as well as leakages of gases such as chlorine (Note 13), which may cause serious damage for humans and nature. In case of severe leakages due to unreliable, unstable material, the plant personnel as well as residents of nearby areas will be affected by hazards. Furthermore, for the chlorine electrolyzer technologies, two essential components need to be highlighted: 1. The thin membrane implemented in the electrolyzer is an essential component that combines all the following unique features. It shows an outstanding stability under extreme corrosive conditions with (in case of chlor-alkali) acidic concentrated chlorine saturated brine on the anode side while there are highly caustic conditions on the cathode side, all at ~90°C. In addition, the membrane is gas tight and hinders mixture of the gases on anode and cathode side, thereby ensuring a good product quality and preventing highly dangerous explosive conditions e.g. by mixture of hydrogen and chlorine. Furthermore, the membrane has a high conductivity (low electrical power consumption) and allows for transport of cations and at the same time prevents the transport of anions resulting not only in excellent product quality but also low corrosion rate of element internals. In the past, there have been 3 different techniques available for production of chlorine via electrolysis. Next to the state-of-the-art membrane technology, these are the diaphragm and the mercury-cell technology. Since both the mercury-cell technology as well as the diaphragm technology by utilization of asbestos diaphragms are already banned in Europe, for diaphragm technologies utilization of PTFE-diaphragms again containing PFAS would be no feasible alternative to membranes. According to information from membrane suppliers, there is no other non-PFAS alternative available for the membrane except for the above-mentioned already banned production methods. 2. Gas diffusion electrodes (ODC) are one essential feature for the NaCl-ODC as well as HCl-ODC technology. The utilization of this component allows to consume oxygen on the cathode side instead of hydrogen evolution (where H2 cannot be processed as a side product) and thereby immensely decreases the electrical power consumption. In the case of both technologies the fluoropolymer PTFE is utilized as a hydrophobic binder and enables an electrochemical 3-phase reaction of liquid electrolyte and gaseous oxygen at the solid ODC catalyst. Therefore, the ODC properties need to be designed so that both oxygen and liquid can access the active sites of the catalyst without e.g., flooding of the active sites by the liquid medium. Therefore, there is no alternative for the PTFE component available due to its unique properties at highly corrosive conditions.  c. The number of companies in the sector estimated to be affected by the restriction. Within Europe, there are more than 70 sites of various companies to produce chlorine and caustic soda (caustic potash) via chlor-alkali electrolysis. In addition, there are two sites for chlor-alkali electrolysis using ODC technology as well as two sites for HCl-ODC electrolysis. General Comments: Regulatory needs
Exchange of a PFAS containing manufacturing device (e.g. tube, filter ...) with a PFAS free alternative
Many medical devices may be affected by the restriction of PFAS in different ways. The following description shows different possibilities for being affected, without claiming to be complete.
• Some medical devices may contain PFAS as an intentionally added ingredient (e.g. some ophthalmic devices or devices containing PFAS-surfactants). The technical and regulatory challenges for a PFAS-replacement must be analyzed product by product (or product class) and are not in scope of this document.
• Many medical devices may contain PFAS-polymers or polymers with PFAS-coatings as constituent parts if the device (e.g. tubes for respiratory pathways, for blood, urine, nutrient, or pharmaceuticals transport, catheters, foils or containers used in 3D-printing etc.). Even if the technical issues for a replacement in such cases could be very challenging, the regulatory requirements are mostly the same as shown in this document.
• A more indirect affectedness is given for medical devices, for which PFAS-containing devices are used in the manufacturing process (e.g. tubes, filters, foils etc.). The regulatory requirements for the replacement of such parts are discussed in detail in this document.
• As well only indirectly affected are medical devices using substances either as constituents of the medical device or as production aids, that are manufactured by using either PFAS-containing aids (e.g. catalysts) or additives or PFAS-containing manufacturing devices. Even if in these cases the major technical challenges are on the side of the substance manufacturer, the regulatory challenges for the manufacturer of medical devices may be comparable to the requirements described below, if the impurity-profile of the substance is changed by the PFAS-replacement.
Even if there are no substantiated data available yet, it can be expected that a high number, if not even most, of the medical devices on the market are affected by at least one of the last three bullet points.

Conclusion
For the case of replacement of a PFAS-containing manufacturing device with an PFAS-free alternative, no fix timeline can be established. A minimum and a maximum need of time for such a process from the regulatory perspective is given below.
If
- all steps lead directly to a favorable result
- there is only one or a very low number of medical devices affected by the replacement
- there are no multiple changes of manufacturing devices that would complicate the process
- no new constituents are identified by the chemical characterization
- no preliminary involvement of the notified body is needed
an absolute minimum of about 18 months is needed. If a longer shelf life as 18 months is required by customers, this minimum period will increase up to 33 months.
In case of
- many medical devices affected by the replacement
- identification of new constituents by the chemical characterization
- complex situation for chemical characterization
- need of long-term biological testing (e.g. subchronic toxicity (9 months in vivo) or
implantation (min. 9 months in vivo)
the time period needed to fulfill the regulatory needs will increase to about 18 months till start of shelf-life testing plus 9 – 24 months of shelf-life tests. In parallel to these tests up to about 29 months are needed for the chemical characterization and biological tests. Additionally, about 6 months are needed for finalization of the steps 11, 12, and 14. This means that the total amount of time needed for the regulatory requirements of such an exchange can increase up to about 53 months (more than 4 years).
In this calculation some aspects are not regarded:
- if a replacement fails due to unfavorable results at any time point, new replacements must be
found. In a worst case this can more than double the time needed.
- if many manufacturers need at the same time chemical characterization and/ or biological testing the bottleneck could be the capacity of the contract labs, leading to delays of some months to 1 year or longer.
- if many manufacturers need to involve the notified bodies at the same time for verification of
such replacements in the technical documentation, the notified bodies may become as well a bottleneck (this fact already led to the extension of the time frame for implementation of MDR). Additional time up to some months or a year would be possible.
- in some cases, especially (but not limited to this) if a PFAS-constituent of the medical device is replaced, additionally to the regulatory steps shown in the flowchart above, a clinical trial could be necessary. In these cases additionally to the given timeline other ca. 2 – 5 years could be needed for the replacement.
Based on these considerations the derogation of 13.5 years for medical devices is very short, especially considering that the replacement would be available probably at the end of the derogation period for the manufacturing devices (probably 6.5 years, in some cases possibly 13.5 years). For this reason, for highly regulated products like medical devices a longer derogation is needed. We propose an additional derogation time of 5 - 10 years or at least an additional derogation time of 3 - 5 years for medical devices of class I, IIA and IIB and 5 - 10 years for medical devices of class III or devices with replacement of a PFAS-constituent. Even this will not cover fully the absolute worst cases that may occur. Only by such a longer derogation time the supply of vital medical devices to the health system can be guaranteed.

When the proposal itself does not have a qualitative and quantitative document that can be referenced, and the internal theoretical support data is not perfect, then in the process of trade implementation, through cultural differences and many other reasons, the unclear part will be differentiated amplification, which will not only cause many communication problems in the world, but also further affect the EU's own international trade market.
So if the five countries need to move forward with the proposal, we hope to have clear and complete implementation guidance documents, such as CAS for all restricted substances and CAS for exempt substances.

（2） There is a significant difference in the physical and chemical properties between the substances included in the definition, and the data provided cannot match the proposed restrictions
The controlled substances in the proposal include PFOS, PFOSF and PFHxS that have obvious effects on human health, but also fluoropolymers (stable, not bioavailable or bioaccumulative, such as PTFE2) that have little effect on human health. Is it reasonable to include substances with far deviations in physical properties into uniform and exaggerated monitoring and control (RO1, RO2 and inspection standards)?
In the chemical community, substances of S and R configuration need to be differentiated and analyzed to demonstrate the risk of different substances, and just the chiral structural characteristics of S and R alone will lead to different changes in the toxicity of substances (e.g., S, R type Thalidomide). Is it reasonable to rely only on local functional groups - CF3 and -CF2 - as a division of the controlled range? Where does the basis come from? And where is the data for the poisonous argument of matter?—I hope that the proponents will share concrete, complete and powerful information with stakeholders.
To quote ANNEX XV, page 28: "Yet in conclusion, considering the increasing lines of evidence from modelling, laboratory and monitoring studies, there is a justified concern for a subset of PFASs being. bioaccumulative while large uncertainties remain for the majority of compounds due to lack of data"—we do not deny that there are indeed some functional groups - CF3, -CF2- substances that have a huge impact on human health, but not all substances are like this. At present, there is a lack of data on the bioaggregation and biotoxicity of most compounds. On the basis of the lack of data support, all a little bit of similar substances are controlled, this behavior is obviously unreasonable, and the control strength (RO1, RO2) is also too exaggerated, which is completely ignoring the future potential of these undemonstrated substances, which is obliterating all possible research of these substances.

（3） The degree of justification for some explicit restricted substances is not sufficient to support the proposed restriction means
The reason for the control of fluorine gases (HFCs, HFOs) is that related substances will produce TFA that is difficult to decompose after atmospheric degradation. And the existence of special characteristics such as durability, biological toxicity and water solubility of TFA is indeed difficult not to attract the attention of researchers. But is the relevant research data on TFA in the proposal sufficient? Can these data support control measures (RO1, RO2)? —If the proponents continue to insist on controlling TFA, we hope to see stronger and more conclusive data arguments in the proposal, rather than vague and unreasonable toxicity research data.
At the same time, it is also suggested that the proponents can summarize and share the specific data of relevant toxicological studies to facilitate stakeholders' discussion and judgment.

2. Conflict between the proposal and the REACH rules
Quoting Article 68 Introducing new and amending current restrictions from the initial draft of the REACH Act:
“When there is an unacceptable risk to human health or the environment, arising from the manufacture, use or placing on the market of substances, which needs to be addressed on a Community-wide basis" —We see "unacceptable risk" for only some substances in your proposal, not all. And for the rest of the substances that demonstrate incomplete data, you use "considering the increasing lines of evidence from modelling, laboratory and monitoring studies”‘s conjecture is extrapolated as evidence (p.28). As we suggested earlier, we need more conclusive, scientific, and reasonable evidence to support the "unacceptable risk" of the substances you want to restrict.
In addition, the F-gas regulation is considering reducing the use of fluorinated gases, and from a dual regulatory perspective, we do not believe that the PFAS regulation should consider it.

General Comments: REINTJES Benelux BV appreciates the opportunity to provide the following comments in response to the proposal of this PFAS restriction. REINTJES supports the EU's efforts to protect human health and environment. However, this proposal does not seem to adequately address the impact on a wide range of industries. For this reason, we comment on this proposal as follows.
A blanket restriction of the entire PFAS substance group without a differentiated, substance- and application-specific risk assessment and solely due to the persistence of some PFAS is not appropriate. In order to ultimately achieve a sustainable overall balance of resource conservation and environmental impact,  a restriction is only justified in cases where the risks to humans and the environment cannot be controlled.
It should be taken into account that the PFAS definition includes substances with different properties and that neither all PFAS are equally persistent. This puts almost risk-free chemicals on an equal footing with substances of very high concern with properties that require regulation. As part of a differentiated approach, it is urgent to ensure that only those substances whose use poses an unacceptable risk to the environment or human health are banned. Otherwise, there is a risk that chemicals that play a crucial role in innovative technologies will be driven out of the market.
For example, manufacturers of hydraulic components such as pumps, motors, valves and cylinders as well as manufacturers of valves and compressors are affected. PFAS, mostly fluorinated polymers, are often used in seals, hoses, pipes, valves and coatings that we absolutely need for our products. While in some cases "only" the performance of some products would be massively affected, some products could no longer be manufactured, which would mean a very high impact on not only our company, our customers and our market but the entire shipping industry.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Request for additional Derogation of Fluoropolymers for use in Laboratory Equipment for 13.5 years
For details, please refer to section 6 «Missing uses. »

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Please refer to Section 6 as our sector and sub-uses are not listed in Annex XV Table 9.

6. Missing uses: We are a company with headquarters in Switzerland and subsidiaries in more than50 countries, more than 20 thereof in the EU. We are a leading company with more than 3200 employees worldwide specialized in developing and manufacturing of analytical laboratory - and testing equipment and we miss completely our area of applications in the current restriction proposal (Annex XV Table 9 and Annex A Table A.1.)  One of the listed intended derogations of the proposed restriction is diagnostic laboratory testing. It only deals with testing biological or medical samples. Equipment for analytical laboratory testing is a completely different application sector. Application fields are very widespread but mainly deal with analysis of chemical parameters in chemical industry, pharmaceutical industry, environmental monitoring and control, monitoring and control of drinking water and food and many others. As clarified with our legal department analytical laboratory equipment is not covered by diagnostic laboratory testing. Therefore, it is important to make a clear distinction between these application fields and to discuss analytical laboratory testing separately. Our products are not covered by the Medical Devices Regulations 2017/745 or In Vitro Diagnostics Regulations 2017/746.  We would like to answer the other points:   a.) As laboratory equipment manufacturer we only process, but do not manufacture raw materials with fluoropolymers. As a downstream user we do mechanical machining of plastics or use pre-fabricated components made from fluoropolymers in our assembly such as seals, O-rings, plastic housings etc. For note we use only fluoropolymers which are considered to polymer of low concern (PLC) according to the widely accepted OECD criteria, ,e.g.  PTFE, ETFE, FEP, PFA , FPM, PCTFE, PVDF. We consume about 15 tons of fluoropolymers per year to manufacture our laboratory equipment. During mechanical processing no emissions of volatile and/or low molecular PFAS are generated. In general, all possible airborne releases are minimized by exhaust and ventilation systems. Air quality is regulated in national air pollution control ordinances. All types of mechanical processing material waste are recycled. Waste is regulated in national waste ordinances. Disposal of laboratory equipment as end-user product is subject to the WEEE Directive 2012/19/EU. As a consequence it is disposed of in hazardous waste. No other releases are known. Use of laboratory equipment: Fluoropolymers do not leach hazardous substances due to their chemical stability, no exposure known on and for the user side.  b.)  In analytical laboratory equipment and analytical laboratory testing fluoropolymers are used for a wide range of applications and purposes. Requirements for such equipment cover extreme ruggedness, the ability for reliable intense operation (24/7) over long time periods without servicing, expectations for a lifetime of more than 10 years under such extreme conditions. This goes hand in hand with extreme requirements to chemical properties of the used materials: The materials must show excellent chemical resistance against a wide range of chemically aggressive solutions, organic solvents and/or gases, the surfaces must be not-wetting and must not show adsorption effects for organic as well as inorganic chemicals. As a third point a high percentage of the used (mechanical) components must  have excellent mechanical properties: High dimensional precision with very low tolerances (in the range of ±50 µm or below for accurate dispensing of very small solution volumes down to the sub-microliter range), long-term mechanical stability in a wide temperature range, excellent manufacturing properties (flow-injection molding or mechanical machining).   c.) Analytical laboratory testing equipment is indispensable in a number of key industry sectors: Chemical & pharmaceutical industry, food testing, water & environmental analysis, energy supply, petroleum industry, etc.  The global market size of laboratory instruments was estimated with 66.2 Bill. USD in 2020. With a growth rate of 8 – 15% depending on the regional sales and industry sector, a sales volume of more than 100 Bill. USD is expected for 2025. [refer to: Instrument Business Outlook 2021, March 2021 © Kalorama Information]  The instrumentation is highly system relevant for analytics in human and public health & safety, starting from chemical safety over food & drinking water to reliable supply of pharmaceuticals.  As an example: EU Directive 2018/725, also known as the “Toy Safety Directive”, stipulate strict limit values for hazardous substances in toys, e.g. the carcinogenic chromium (VI). These tight limits can be verified with our laboratory testing equipment. Also an important field in which analytical laboratory testing equipment is used, is the monitoring of the environment, e. g. air, water, soils. This also includes analytical equipment for testing PFAS, PFOA, PFOS.  As another example, in the field of water & environmental analysis, one of the major issues is to ensure drinking water quality. With our laboratory testing equipment for ultra trace analysis, it is possible to determine contents of toxic heavy metals down to the lower ppt level. Dimensions become clearer if one considers that one ppt is the equivalent of a little cube of sugar dissolved in a reservoir containing 2.7 billion liters of water. Also other areas in the society are affected, such as energy supply which includes electrical power production and petroleum products.  d.) For our products no alternative materials are available yet. Therefore a massive impact of the availability of laboratory testing equipment is expected. In case fluoropolymers have to be replaced by materials with lower performance there is a high likelihood that the maintenance frequency in our manufacturing processes and of our instrumentation in the field will increase and the manufacturing maintenance intervals and the service repair intervals in the field will decrease. Decreasing of chemical resistance can lead to reduced safety and reliability of the equipment, e.g. increased risk of leakage in the chemical application. There is a risk that this leads to human damage,  decreasing precision or loss of data. A result of this are significantly increased costs of ownership for the instrument users but also for the internal manufacturing costs. If alternatives material do not have the same broad chemical resistance, it is possible that different versions of the products have to be developed, manufactured and maintained. This leads to higher development costs, manufacturing costs, increased prices and lower competitiveness. Additionally, as downstream user we are dependent on the availability of fluoropolymers in our whole supply chain. Numerous components that we source from 3rd party suppliers come with built-in subcomponents made from fluoropolymers. Examples are electronic and electric components, motors, valves, seals, connectors for gases or liquids and many more.  e.) There is currently no alternative polymer in prospect for the fluoropolymers that are considered to be polymer of low concern (PLC) according to the widely accepted OECD criteria. As a downstream user we need to rely on plastic research and development for this. But in case that such an equivalent alternative material will be made available, the number of suppliers is expected to be limited (single source). Due to the fact that such materials with similar properties as fluoropolymers will be needed in high quantities by numerous industry sectors a shortage of the delivery amount and high lead times can be expected, going hand in hand with increased material price.  With the publication of the PFAS dossier the supply chain of fluoropolymers has already become an issue. The situation may even get worse in case a ban of the substances is adopted.  f.) Such a forecast is relatively difficult, because currently are no prospect of a fluoropolymer alternative is known or expected soon. For all the reasons mentioned above fluoropolymers are an integral key component of our products. Our products rely on this key material to provide proper functionality, safety, performance and quality to our customers. The various components made from selected material interact in a highly optimized and well-tested manner. Developing such high-tech equipment involves big working groups and typically takes 5 - 10 years. Simply exchanging a material in a complex instrumental setup by another material does not work. If materials have to be replaced it usually means a complete redesign of the complete assembly - which takes several years in a big working group again. The PFAS restriction will increase the development time for every product in our portfolio because experiences of 80 years in developing laboratory testing instruments cannot be used anymore. The fluoropolymers have been used for several decades, the behavior under temperature change, pressure, chemical load (pH changes, concentrated acids and bases, organic solvents) are well known and integrated in the developed setups. Such an impact would mean to hire additional staff to compensate for the massive re-design impact of our product portfolio. We have a tight development and innovation roadmap until 2030 which needs full involvement of our current number of employees in R&D. All these projects will have to be stopped. For the re-design our development staff must be duplicated. Another challenge is finding qualified staff for the development and manufacturing of our products, we need highly educated experts, who cannot be found in the European Union (EU) or Switzerland (CH) easily. In consequence we may have to shift development and manufacturing activities to countries outside the EU or CH, e.g. India. In the mid- and long-term perspective this will result in job losses in EU and CH.  g.) No statement can currently be made on this point   In the attachment we would like to share the following documents:  1. Our statement 2. Our assessment of alternative materials required by our products, with the statement that currently no alternatives are available. 3. A published study which shows that no harmful PFAS emissions occur with well-operated incinerators

10. Analytical methods: Laboratory equipment is also used to analyze PFAS substances. Today Combustion Ion Chromatography (CIC) is one of the most promising analytical methods for PFAS analysis [see Attachments; Monitoring PFASs in water sources and Adsorbable organic fluorine (AOF) – a sum  parameter for non-targeted screening of per- and  polyfluorinated alkyl substances (PFASs) in waters]. This technique allows the quantification of the total organic fluoride content in gas, liquid and solid samples. As a non-target analysis technique CIC determines the sum of all PFAS substances independent from the chemical structure or availability of standard substances. Different standards are already referring to this method [refer to DIN norm (38409-59), upgrade to ISO in progress (TC 147/SC2), EPA method draft (EPA draft 1621)]. Without a derogation for laboratory equipment the analysis of PFAS substances will be impossible.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Request for exemption of "industrial, high temperature, large capacity heat pumps" and " safety chillers for nuclear power plants" from PFAS restriction proposal.
"Industrial, high temperature, large capacity heat pumps" deliver renewable energy into district heating systems, cut greenhouse gases discharge, and improve energy emissions. They play an essential role in the decarbonisation of district heating systems and carbon neutrality transition in big cities.
The "safety chillers for nuclear power plants" ensure the safe operation of nuclear power plants by providing emission-free electricity.
The "industrial, large capacity heat pumps" and "safety chillers for nuclear power plants" are built so that they are tight and do not lose refrigerant throughout their lifetime (in german technisch dauerhaft dicht) and do not pose a risk of environmental pollution.
Therefore, we are strongly convinced that the "large capacity, high temperature heat pumps" and " safety chillers for nuclear power plants" play a crucial role in EU energy transition and should be excluded from the PFAS restriction proposal.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The comments apply to Use sectors "Air conditioning and heat pumps" and "Refrigeration".  Our company is a supplier of industrial , high temperature, large capacity industrial heat pumps in capacity range from 3 to 35 MW per unit. Our heat pumps are widely used in district heating and industrial processes and play a key role in decarbonisation of the EU energy sector and achieving the goals of Repower EU Plan.  Our heat pumps are using HFO refrigerants (R1234ze, R1233zd), which are safe, non-toxic, energy efficient and have no alternatives in most of applications. Our company is also a supplier of safety chillers for nuclear power plants.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Our "industrial, high temperature, large capacity heat pumps" are built so that they are tight and do not lose refrigerant throughout their lifetime (in german technisch dauerhaft dicht). All possible connections are welded, and the mechanical seals of large compressors are equipped with a double mechanical seal with seal oil system enabling refrigerant recovery. Heat pumps machinery rooms are equipped with stationary leak detection systems both in atmospheric and water site. If a refrigerant leak is detected, the heat pump is shut down and the refrigerant is trapped in the evaporator, allowing the leak to be repaired immediately.  After an end-of-life cycle of at least 30 years, refrigerant can be reused, recovered, or recycled what is mandated under the F-gases Regulation and is happening successfully on the market today.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: After an end-of-life cycle of at least 30 years, the refrigerant can be reused, recovered, or recycled what is mandated under the F-gases Regulation and is happening successfully on the market today. The heat pumps with HFCs and HFOs refrigerant have a very long life-time and require little maintenance.  In Section IV, we attached an extract from the references of FRIOTHERM heat pumps with the number of operating hours > 90'000.  The leakage rate of refrigerant in all these installations is lower than 0.5% per year and proven availability time is higher than 99%.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: This point is not directly relevant for HFO refrigerants as these products are being placed on the market.

5. Proposed derogations: In recent years, our company has supplied heat pumps with a heating capacity of 100MW per year. For 1MW heating capacity, the heat pump needs approx. 600kg of R1234ze refrigerant as working fluid. This means that the annual demand for HFO refrigerants is approx. 60'000 kg. The heat pumps are normally operated approx. 8'000 operating hours per year. It means that the installed heating capacity of 100MW operated for 8'000 hours, can reduce natural gas consumption by approx. 72'730'000 m3 yearly and corresponding emission of 141'828 tons of CO2.

6. Missing uses: "Missing use "are "industrial, high temperature, large capacity heat pumps" for district heating, district cooling and industrial applications.  This sub-uses of HFOs SHOULD BE considered separately in the Table 8 .and Table 9.  in the Use Sector of "Air conditioning and heat pumps".  "Missing use" are also" industrial safety chillers for nuclear power plants", which use HFC and HFOs refrigerants. As already explained in 2 and 3, the industrial heat pumps and industrial chillers are technically permanently sealed to do not lose refrigerant and after an end-of-life cycle of at least 30 years, the refrigerant can be reused, recovered, or recycled what is mandated under the F-gases Regulation and is happening successfully on the market today.  a) In recent years, we have supplied heat pumps with a heating capacity of 100MW per year. For 1MW heating capacity, the heat pump needs approx. 600kg of R1234ze refrigerant as working fluid. This means that the annual demand for HFO refrigerants is approx. 60'000 kg.  b) Mainly HFO refrigerant R1234ze and R1233zd are used as working fluid in refrigeration closed circuits.   c) The number of companies located in EU suppling industrial heat pumps is > 80.  d) Large ammonia, high-temperature heat pumps (> 75°C) have not proven to be reliable, trouble-free technology for continuous operation. Furthermore, ammonia is toxic, and its by-products N2O have significant GWP=265 (IPCC5) and ODP=0.017. Hydrocarbons require very significant precautions due to the risk of flammability and explosion. In large heat pumps where an important hydrocarbon charge is needed, the equipment should be ATEX conformed and the acceptance of such a solution in habited areas is very limited. The large capacity heat pumps with hydrocarbons are at least 100% more expensive than the standard heat pumps with HFOs refrigerants.  Efficient application of CO2 is limited to water heaters and heat pumps with very large delta T in the heat sink (the differences between inlet & outlet water temperatures) and there are no references for large capacity heat pumps operating in district heating applications yet. The required operating pressures for high temperature heat pumps with CO2 will be > 100bar, what would require much more expensive equipment.   Without HFOs refrigerant the application areas of the industrial heat pumps contributing positively towards the EU's goals of decarbonisation, as set out by the Green Deal and REPower EU would be dramatically limited.  e) Currently, there are no satisfactory refrigerant alternatives to HFOs refrigerants for "industrial, high -temperature, large capacity heat pumps" for district heating application and safety chillers for nuclear power plants.  Prototype projects using the so-called alternatives have failed, dissatisfying customers, and providing very poor references for heat pump technology in district heating applications. The required supply temperatures were not achieved, and extensive maintenance work was required. More detailed information on request. It is difficult to estimate how long it will take for the chemical industry to develop a PFAS-free refrigerant.   f) Replacing the HFO refrigerants with ammonia, hydrocarbons or CO2 is not a matter of time because the toxicity, safety and thermodynamic properties of these fluids significantly limit their use in "high temperature, high efficiency industrial heat pumps" to certain very narrow applications.  Large ammonia, high-temperature heat pumps have not proven to be reliable, trouble-free technology for continuous operation. Furthermore, ammonia is toxic, and its by-products N2O have significant GWP=265 (IPCC5) and ODP=0.017. Hydrocarbons require very significant precautions due to the risk of flammability and explosion. In large heat pumps where an important hydrocarbon charge is needed, the equipment should be ATEX conformed and the acceptance of such a solution in inhabited areas is very limited. The large capacity heat pumps with hydrocarbons are at least 100% more expensive than the standard heat pumps with HFOs refrigerants.   Efficient application of CO2 is limited to water heaters and heat pumps with very large delta T in the gas cooler of transcritical refrigeration cycle (the differences between inlet & outlet water temperatures) and there are no references for large capacity heat pumps operating in district heating applications yet. The required operating pressures for high temperature heat pumps with CO2 will be > 100bar, what would require much more expensive equipment.  Without HFOs refrigerant the application areas of the industrial heat pumps contributing positively towards the EU's goals of decarbonisation, as set out by the Green Deal and REPower EU would be dramatically limited.  g) The socio-economic impact of this PFAS restriction proposal would be a loss of jobs of  190 people only in our company. On the other hand, customers would lose safe, proven, affordable technology for the environmentally friendly heat production, which plays a key role in decarbonising the EU energy sector and achieving the goals of Repower EU Plan.  Moreover, there will be no acceptable refrigerant for safety chillers for nuclear power plants, which for safety reasons cannot accept either ammonia or hydrocarbons as a working fluid nor CO2 due to very high delta T required in the gas cooler in the transcritical refrigeration cycle.   According to Heat Roadmap Europe 4 (HRE4), large capacity heat pumps are essential in Smart Energy Systems, and the total installed capacity of large-scale HPs represents a share of 23% heat generation in district heating networks (HRE 2050 scenario) corresponding to 95'000 MW(th). Therefore, the value of the "large capacity heat pump sector" until 2050 according to HRE4 is approx. 50 billion EURO.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: The "Industrial, high temperature, large capacity heat pumps" for district heating and industrial applications as well as "safety chillers for nuclear power plants" should be excluded from the PFAS restriction proposal. There are enough evidences that in these applications the HFO refrigerants cannot be substituted either by ammonia, hydrocarbons or CO2. These fluids are either toxic, explosive, or thermodynamic properties of these fluids significantly limit their use in "high temperature, high efficiency industrial heat pumps" to certain very narrow applications.  The "industrial, high temperature, large capacity heat pumps" as well as "safety chillers for nuclear power plants" are built so that they are tight and do not lose refrigerant throughout their lifetime (in ger. technisch dauerhaft dicht). All possible connections are welded, and the mechanical seals of large compressors are equipped with a double mechanical seal with seal oil system enabling refrigerant recovery. Heat pumps machinery rooms are equipped with stationary leak detection systems both in atmospheric and water site. If a refrigerant leak is detected, the heat pump is shut down and the refrigerant is trapped in the evaporator, allowing the leak to be repaired immediately.  After an end-of-life cycle of at least 30 years, refrigerant can be reused, recovered, or recycled what is mandated under the F-gases Regulation and is happening successfully on the market today.  Therefore, the risk of refrigerant leakage into the atmosphere is minimal.  Please find in SECTION IV, the reference list of "industrial, high temperature, large capacity heat pumps" with number of operating hours > 90'000.  The yearly, proven refrigerant leakage rate is lower than < 0.5%.   Since more than 30 years "industrial, high temperature, large capacity heat pumps" deliver renewable energy into district heating systems, cut green house gases emissions and improve energy emissions. They play an essential role in the decarbonisation of district heating systems and carbon neutrality transition in big cities.  The "safety chillers for nuclear power plants" ensure the safe operation of nuclear power plants by providing emission-free electricity.   Therefore, we are strongly convinced that the "large capacity, high temperature heat pumps" and " safety chillers for nuclear power plants" play a crucial role in EU energy transition and should be excluded from this PFAS restriction proposal.     The entrance in to force of proposed restriction would result in the loss of jobs for thousands of people, would destroy the market of large capacity heat pumps, worth EURO 50 billion until 2050 and ruin one of the most effective technologies needed for achieving EU's goals of decarbonisation, as set by Grean Deal and REPower EU.

8. Other identified uses: "Missing use "are "industrial, high temperature, large capacity heat pumps" for district heating, district cooling and industrial applications.  This sub-uses of HFOs SHOULD BE considered separately in the Table 8 .and Table 9.  in the Use Sector of "Air conditioning and heat pumps". Prototype projects using the so-called alternatives have failed, dissatisfying customers, and providing very poor references for heat pump technology in district heating applications. The required supply temperatures were not achieved, and extensive maintenance work was required. More detailed information on request. Large ammonia, high-temperature heat pumps (>75°C) have not proven to be reliable, trouble-free technology for continuous operation. Furthermore, ammonia is toxic, and its by-products N2O have significant GWP=265 (IPCC5) and ODP=0.017. Hydrocarbons require very significant precautions due to the risk of flammability and explosion. In large heat pumps where an important hydrocarbon charge is needed, the equipment should be ATEX conformed and the acceptance of such a solution in inhabited areas is very limited. The large capacity heat pumps with hydrocarbons are at least 100% more expensive than the standard heat pumps with HFOs refrigerants.  Currently, more than 90% of "industrial, high temperature, large capacity heat pumps" and 100% of "safety chillers for nuclear power plants are" are using HFOs and HFCs refrigerants, which are safe, non-toxic and energy efficient.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: The main degradation product of some HFOs  is  TFA  (trifluoroacetic  acid).  According to the manufacture of refrigerant, TFA is only 2% of degradation product  of R1234ze.   There have been extensive scientific studies of TFA which have demonstrated that it is not a risk to the environment nor human health. According to the most recent evaluation of TFA by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) Environmental Effects Assessment (EEAP) Panel where in its most recent Report from May 2023 concludes that “based on projected future use of these precursors of TFA [incl. HFC/HFO], no harm is anticipated” and that TFA “is unlikely to cause adverse effects out to 2100” *.  In addition,  according  to  the  REACH  registration  dossier  and  Chemical  Safety  Report  (CSR)  for trifluoroacetic acid (TFA)* this substance does not fulfil the criteria for a PBT or vPvB substance under Annex XIII REACH. Neither does it raise equivalent levels of concern as a PBT or vPvB. ECHA has already evaluated the TFA dossier without concluding that further regulatory actions were needed.   *Please see pages 25 and 259 of the EEAP 2022 Assessment Report  Below an extract from EEAP 2022 Assessment Report page 25: "The increases in trifluoroacetic acid concentrations due to replacements of the ozone-depleting substances are not expected to pose significant risk to humans or the environment at the present time. Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) continues to be found in the environment, including in remote regions, although concentrations are so low that they are currently very unlikely to have adverse toxicological consequences for humans and ecosystems [105,106]. The accumulated amount of TFA is expected to increase because of the planned replacement of ODS with short-lived fluorinated chemicals (Fig. 11). However, based on projected future use of these precursors of TFA, no harm is anticipated. There is a large uncertainty associated with the magnitude of other sources of TFA (e.g., potential natural sources, fluorinated pesticides, and pharmaceuticals), which do not fall under the purview of the Montreal Protocol. Korzeniowski et al. - 2022 has presented data demonstrating that the fluoropolymers meet the widely accepted criteria for polymer hazard assessment to be classified as a PLC. The data presented indicate that the fluoropolymers studied exhibit thermal, biological, and chemical stability, are minimally soluble in water, have low mobility, limited bioavailability, no bioaccumulation potential, and are non-toxic, with low levels of impurities. These findings further underscore the need to treat the fluoropolymer class as a distinct entity and not to categorize it with other PFAS for the purpose of hazard assessment or regulatory considerations.   A statement in the EoL question is not feasible. Most of our customers scrap our products themselves. We are currently carrying out a PFAS inventory but cannot make any precise statements before this is completed.

6. Missing uses: A) We don't have information on this topic  B) The Use Sector involves the assembly of Industrial robots, which is not explicitly listed in Annex XV. Generally industrial machinery and the production process are not considered and should be added as a use sector. We agree with the demands of the VDMA in their position paper. (attachment 1) In our manufacturing process, we incorporate a range of essential components such as seals, lubricants, electronics and cable sheathing. These components play a crucial role in ensuring the performance, durability, and safety of our industrial robots.  Our suppliers are held to strict standards, ensuring that the materials exhibit specific properties such as friction resistance, heat resistance, wear resistance, and resistance to various media.  Some of our industrial robots act under harsh environmental conditions, e.g., foundries, clean rooms, or hygienic environments. Some of our industrial robots are optimized for the extreme conditions in washing cells. These industrial robots need the high protection class IP69 suited for wet chemical cleaning, immersion, and high-pressure cleaning processes - even in combination with highly active cleaning agents and disinfectants.  To assure a product usable under these conditions, sealings are used which can withstand such mediums and can handle high rotational speed and resulting friction at the same time. Evidence can be found in the attachment 2 & 3. Right now, we have no alternative except PTFE and FKM. These sealing prevent leakage of oil, which is important in the industrial food industry.  For the robotic industry special cables are manufactured to withstand the 3-dimenisonal movement and the Influences of e.g., cleaning agents. For the winding and isolation outside of these cables PTFE is, under harsh conditions, the only alternative.   C) We don't have information on this topic  D) At present, we do not have information on any technically and economically feasible alternatives for the components in question. However, we maintain an ongoing and active dialogue with our suppliers, exploring the possibility of identifying alternative materials that can meet the same rigorous standards for safety and functionality as the current components. Our commitment to providing durable and high-performance industrial robots remains unwavering, and we are diligently investigating the availability of alternatives for seals, lubricants, and cable sheathing that do not contain PFAS. While we are open to exploring new possibilities, it is important to note that, as of now, we have not found substitutes that fulfill the required criteria for safety and durability without incorporating PFAS. One possible alternative proposed in Annex E for PTFE in sealings is NBR. However, as shown in our attachment 2 & 3, NBR does not meet the criteria for some applications our industrial robots are built for. Under harsh conditions PTFE currently is the only material which can withstand such conditions and last for a reasonable long use phase.   E) Given that our search for alternatives and discussions with suppliers are still in their early stages, it is challenging to determine the exact timeframe and potential financial implications of finding substitutes for all the components. As we prioritize providing safe, durable, and high-quality industrial robots, we propose seeking for industrial machinery a PTFE / FKM derogation for seals, cable sheathing, and electronics an unlimited exemption.  We will continue our efforts to explore viable and sustainable alternatives that meet the required safety and performance standards. The derogation will provide us with the necessary flexibility to conduct thorough research, conduct testing, and make informed decisions without compromising on the quality and functionality of our industrial robots.  Leakage, which could be caused by seals with inadequate requirements, would cause oil or grease to escape from the robot into the environment.  F) See point E)  G) The durability and functionality of industrial robots could potentially be compromised to a lower level if we are unable to find suitable substitutes for PFAS-containing components. It is important to recognize that robotics is a significant global megatrend, and if competitors outside the EU can offer industrial robots without PFAS restrictions, they may gain a competitive advantage and expand their market share.  This situation poses a considerable challenge to the European robotics industry, as it could lead to a disadvantage in the global market and hinder its growth and innovation potential. Moreover, it may adversely impact Europe's overall future viability as a technology leader.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: We are not aware of any alternatives to PFASs in the electronics industry. According to our electronics suppliers, there is also no comprehensive overview of which products and processes might contain PFAS. This poses a significant challenge for our company, as the use of PFASs could be widespread in numerous electronic applications. The socio-economic impact for our company could be catastrophic, as a possible supply shortage or even a production shutdown would accompany a PFAS restriction. Additionally, we are subject to a 30-year spare parts obligation. We therefore propose an unlimited exemption for PTFE and FKM in electronic components in industrial machinery.

8. Other identified uses: We talked in a personal dialogue with multiple people from our main electronic supplier. They not only have no overview about PFAS used in components, nor are they capable of providing substitutions or alternatives in the next years. It is impossible to identify PFAS in the electronic components bought on the market. We, as a downstream user, strongly suggest an unlimited derogation, otherwise the electronic industry can not handle the shift to a more transparent policy. Otherwise, it is impossible to fulfill a full material declaration, needed for compliance with a regulation of this extensive scope.
