General Comments: SANG-A FRONTEC CO., LTD is a Korea-based company that specializes in processing with fluororesin.
We request that automobiles using fluororesin such as sealing and tubes be completely excluded from ECHA's PFAS restrictions.

· Engine equipment such as passenger cars, trucks, bases, motorcycles, lawnmowers, ships, airplanes, etc. have many parts made of fluoride rubber and fluoride plastics.
The energy of these engines is primarily gasoline or diesel. Recent gasoline and diesel include alcohol, MTBE, etc. for environmental efficiency.
Fluorinated rubbers and fluoroplastics are highly resistant to gasoline, diesel, alcohol, MTBE, etc. Therefore, many fuel system parts are made from fluorinated rubber and plastics.
· Previously, fuel system parts were made of NBR rubber or metal. However, there are several problems in this area : photochemical oxidants. One of the causes of this problem was the evaporated gas from the vehicle.
Although many NBR rubber parts have been used in fuel systems, the NBR does not have sufficient fuel gas permeability.
Fluorine rubber or fluoride plastic has a very good permeability of 100 times or more, so we use fluoride rubber or plastic as a countermeasure.
･ Of course, metal penetration is better. However, metal is much heavier than rubber or plastic, which results in poor fuel efficiency.
The engine also has vibrations and requires flexible parts at the connection.
The strength of the carbon-fluorine bond and the polymer structure of these polymers are unmatched. In the years since its development in the 1950s, it has not succeeded in finding alternative materials that can replace or improve performance for nearly 70 years. There are no technical alternatives available for fluoropolymerization in all applications. In the near future, e-fuel and/or biomass-made fuels should be used commercially. This should include chemicals similar to gasoline, diesel, ethanol, etc.
Therefore, the fuel system of the engine needs fluorine rubber and fluorine plastic, so we ask for an exemption.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Engine fuel system parts: application of passenger cars, motorcycles, lawnmowers, ships, planes, etc.

6. Missing uses: For fluorinated rubber and fluorinated plastic gaskets, there is no alternative material to provide an essential combination of chemical resistance, heat resistance, compression and non-polluting properties. Gasket for sealing chemicals and corrosive fluids requires chemical resistance and purity that does not contaminate chemicals. In addition, proper compression properties are required to maintain confidentiality. Fluororesins are flexible and can be used at low clamping pressures, which are essential for stable sealing of these fluids. Currently, there is no material other than fluororesin that has these characteristics. Chemical resistance cannot be satisfied with a joint sheet in which inorganic fibers or organic fibers are bound with a binder. For example, chemicals such as aqua, perchloric acid, chromic acid, chromic acid, chromic acid, hydrobromic acid, nitric acid, hydrofluoric acid, and bromine cannot be used in conventional joint sheets, and these fluids are highly corrosive. Leaks have a huge impact on people and the environment. Therefore, these seals require a reliable gasket. Rubber gasket is also used, but it is less chemical resistant than fluorine resin, and silicone rubber with heat resistance and chemical resistance is not enough to replace. The relatively chemical resistant graphite sheet is fragile and can contaminate the chemicals (gas, liquids) used in the application. Metal and semi-metal gaskets are less chemical resistant and require excessive load when tightened, and cannot be handled by conventional flanges due to strength. It is expensive to review the design specifications of the piping part of the equipment. Heat-resistant PEEK materials and low-friction ultra-high molecular weight PE can be considered as packaging materials, but they have disadvantages of lack of flexibility, poor sealing performance, and are also expensive materials. It's too expensive and less practical. Additional materials with rubber flexibility and low friction properties are required to maintain seal performance. By integrating it with PTFE, it can complement the chemical resistance and sliding properties that cannot be satisfied with rubber alone, so it is used as a sealing material such as food and medicine. However, due to the structure, vulcanization adhesion to the rubber material is required, the processing temperature of the silicone rubber is about 150~250℃, and a material that does not change chemically at this temperature is required. However, no material can withstand these temperatures, such as heat resistance, flexibility, and chemical resistance required for packaging. Fluororesin is the only substance with insulation and chemical resistance and a continuous use temperature of 260℃. For the reasons described above, there is no substitute for sealing materials with fluororesin. Even if there are materials that can be applied to individual conditions, the equipment is highly likely to be altered or redesigned, and it is highly likely to be costly. In addition, sealing materials represented by gasket, packing, etc., are often used in various drug solutions and various environments even if they have the same structure and shape.  For this reason, the proposed restrictions should be waived.

SEMICON APPLICATIONS FLUOROTUBING TUBES  Fluorotubing, known for its unique properties of chemical resistance, are widely used for delivering liquids in high-tech applications. These tubing are connected and installed to storage tanks that contain harsh chemicals such as hydrogen fluoride (HF) or hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). These chemicals are crucial for rinsing semiconductor processor chips used in computers and other semiconductor applications in order to purify their surfaces.  Purification and achieving ultimate purity, along with chemical resistance, are paramount in adopting tubing for these high-tech applications. Without these specialized tubes, the economical and efficient production of microprocessors would be jeopardized, as computer chips cannot be produced without thorough cleaning with hydrogen fluorides and/or hydrogen peroxides.  There are five objects that need to be purged from the semiconductor materials during the rinsing process:  Particles Metal ions Organic matter Oil Oxide film  None of these objects should be eluted or found before etching a microprocessor chip, as the purity of the chemicals and surfaces is crucial to ensure the quality of the final product.  Due to its unique characteristics, Fluortubing is the ideal solution for maintaining the purity of the chemicals during the delivery process. Fluortubing does not react with the chemicals and does not release any metal ions, making it the only suitable material for this application. The delivery hose must also be pure and stable, as it should not introduce contaminants or react with the chemicals being transported.  In conclusion, Fluortubing is essential for the safe and efficient delivery of harsh chemicals used in semiconductor manufacturing. Its unmatched properties of chemical resistance, purity, and non-reactivity make it the preferred material for ensuring the high-quality and purity of semiconductor materials during transportation and processing.

Combined Comments: "Decontamination of pollutants is part of an efficient circular economy, and therefore we support the aim of reducing pollutants in the environment. However, there is an increasing conflict between the Zero Pollution goals and the Circular Economy Action Plan (CEAP), through which the Commission seeks to create a closed loop system for resources and thus decouple economic growth from resource consumption, which is detrimental to the circular economy. The tightening of pollutant limits, without a risk-based approach or comprehensive assessment of legal consequences, leads to products that need to be disposed of rather than circulated, and instead must be energetically recovered or eliminated. In order to achieve the goals of pollutant minimization and circular economy in parallel, certain requirements must be met: pollutant restrictions should be based on a risk-based approach rather than a generic approach (intrinsic substance properties), a comprehensive assessment of legal consequences that weighs the measures considered in light of the goals of zero pollution and substance policy on one hand, and the goals of circular economy policy on the other, appropriate transition periods until the implementation of new substance restrictions to allow for the development and investment in new technologies, and the comprehensive availability of concrete and usable information about these products for waste management." "Entsorgungs-und Abfallwirtschaftssektor 9424" "If waste is no longer allowed to be recycled due to only a potential PFAS content, but instead must be energetically used or disposed of, it would no longer be available for the material cycle. Insufficient transitional periods, which would be necessary for the development of new recycling technologies, exacerbate the trend of valuable resources being phased out. The present PFAS restriction proposal presents a particular problem for the circular economy: since there has been no notification obligation so far, it is often not possible to determine whether the waste to be recycled contains PFAS. The eternal chemicals can only be destroyed by very high temperatures, which are not reached in the course of extrusion (a plastic recycling process in which thermoplastic plastic is pressed through a shaping opening under high pressure and high temperature). Through a complete ban that does not differentiate between the individual PFAS subgroups or allow realistic limits and reasonable transition periods, many otherwise recyclable products would in any case no longer be available for mechanical recycling from the product cycle. Sustainability and resource conservation must be brought into line with the EU's Zero Pollution goals as important components of the Green Deal. In the spirit of the EU's Green Deal and its requirements for a sustainable circular economy, both must succeed: reducing pollutants and optimal recycling. Future regulations must not lead to sustainable recycling for certain materials being restricted or even prevented."

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Scope
Mass flow meters and controllers (MFCs), pressure meters and assemblies thereof are used in all sectors of industry, as well as healthcare and various laboratory applications. These devices are often critical for safety and are also widely used to achieve general environmental goals by reducing waste. These devices require O-rings, membranes, plungers etc. containing FKM and FFKM elastomers (which classify as PFAS according to the proposal). In addition, PFAS-containing lubricants such as Synthetic Perfluoropolyether lubricants (PTFE-filled) are essential to prevent these devices from malfunctioning quickly and to enable proper functioning. Also, PTFE and PcTFe polymers are used for certain applications where their properties are critical for the performance of our instruments.

Information on alternatives
For many applications, there are no suitable replacement materials able to fulfill all of the essential functions of the currently used materials. Please note that materials equivalent or superior to PFAS are also not available. Relevant applications for which this is a serious problem include high pressure applications, and applications where exposure to natural gas may occur. We do not know of any materials in development that will reliably fulfill the essential functions of the currently used materials.

Request for exemption
It is not possible to achieve development, certification and regulatory approvals within a 5-year derogation period. In addition, due to the many different applications and the fact that the market desires devices that can be used for more than one application, it is not feasible to limit a derogation to special applications or industries. Therefore we respectfully request a derogation of 18 months + 12 years for all devices. We commit to proactively change to available PFAS-free alternatives, but we acknowledge this is a complex, long term process, in which we are entirely dependent on third party developers of new materials. A requirement to stop the use of PFAS in flow-related applications would also adversely affect international competition by European companies.

Information on benefits
We would like to offer ECHA information on the benefits of the products mentioned under Scope. In general, MFCs can accurately determine how much fluid flows through a tube. Obviously, this can be used in dosing applications to reduce waste, but it also makes many applications much safer.
Socially relevant applications where mass flow meters and controllers (MFCs) are an essential part of the manufacturing process include:
- Surface coating, especially plasma spray coating, for example:
o Green energy applications
 Coating of windmill blades
 Manufacture and coating of solar panels
 Manufacture of Fuel Cells
o Medical devices
 Coating of prostetic devices, such as artificial hips
 Coating of glasses
- Utility sector
o Addition of mercaptane (odorization) to natural gas/ the gas network (all alternatives leak significantly more than PFAS, or may degrade entirely in a short amount of time)
o Waste water management
- Pharmaceutical and medical industry, for example:
o Preparation of vaccines, including for COVID-19 inoculation
o Manufacture of active compounds (human and vetinary)
o Preparation of medical pills
- Bioreactors, for example:
o For cell cultures
o For the manufacture of food and fuel
o For the manufacture of bioactive compounds including medical and veterinary compounds
- Food
o Accurate dosing of high value ingredients to avoid waste
o Sterilization of food packaging
- Semiconductor
o Leaktight valves (metal does not seal sufficiently)
- Glass fiber
In addition, there are many analytical or laboratory applications
- Medical
o Non-life critical healthcare appliances
- Scientific
o Development of organs on a chip
- Quality assurance
o Testing of PPE
Depending on the precise application, at best replacement of PFAS would reduce accuracy, causing more waste of resources, or more maintenance, requiring more downtime and less energy efficiency, or increasing hazards. In some applications, PFAS cannot be replaced at all, our customers would have to make do without MFC’s or move their production to a location that continues to allow PFAS.

Hazard or exposure
The PFAS-containing components remain inside the devices. The devices are not easily opened by a layperson and are accompanied by a manual instructing users that the devices should not be opened, except by persons that have received special training specified in the manual. The devices are not being sold to consumers. Thus, exposure is extremely unlikely.

Environmental emissions
Environmental emissions can only occur during repairs and at End-of-life. Please note that our products are not disposable items; they are extremely durable, and we continue to service devices made in the early eighties. The shortest Mean Time Between Failure  for any of our current product series is 78 years [MTBF Statement Bronkhorst]. At end-of-life, we recommend that our devices be incinerated above 800 °C, thereby ensuring all PFAS is destroyed without emissions. Customers can send devices back for that purpose.  (Scientific report on waste incineration and thermal recycling: Chemosphere Volume 226, July 2019, Pages 898-906: Waste incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate potential formation of per- and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) in flue gas. Krasimir Aleksandrov; Hans-Joachim Gehrmann; Manuela Hauser; Hartmut Mätzing; Daniel Pigeon; Dieter Stapf; Manuela Wexler).  PFAS waste from production and repairs is disposed of through a certified waste management company.

Sectors and (sub-)uses: Sectors and (sub-)uses:  MFCs are used globally in all sectors of industry (e.g. wastewater management, chemical industry, food&beverage, pharmaceutical industries, life sciences, utilities, agricultural, care&hygiene), as well as various laboratory applications. Various research agencies estimated the global MFC market at about 8 billion dollar in 2021 (Flow Meter Market Size & Forecast, [Latest] (marketsandmarkets.com)).

5. Proposed derogations: Tonnage:  We are a manufacturer of MFC’s, and while PFAS-containing materials are essential to the functioning of our devices, any device only needs a small amount. In our devices, a typical O-ring weights ~10 grammes. Considering the very long life of our devices, yearly emissions are essentially impossible to determine.

6. Missing uses: Missing uses – Analysis of alternatives and socio-economic analysis: Annex XV does not cover MFC’s adequately, including devices for flow and pressure. These devices are used globally in industry, especially the industries mentioned above under “Scope”. In most of these industries, but especially in Pharma, Food, Wastewater management, Utilities and Medical Devices, devices have to comply with standards (IEC, GMP,  ATEX, EC1935:2004 ...) which require testing and approval. Thus a redesign is necessary if we substitute a part containing PFAS, followed by a requalification in the application. The time period needed for a redesign of a product is much longer than the suggested transitional period of 18 months. Just getting an ATEX certificate after a design is completed takes on average 6-9 month (ATEX Certification (Explosive Atmospheres) - CE Marking, Ce Mark, Product Marking, System certification (qvccert.com)), that is nearly half the derogation time!

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Scope (substances): based on existing and potential hazards of long and short chain PFAS molecules, the properties in focus are persistence and (potential) biological adverse effects. In the published draft version the definition of “PFAS” has been amended on both ends of the chain length based on the OECD 2021 PFAS definition. By including both fluoropolymers and molecules with a single CF3 group, non-bioavailable and non-hazardous substances were brought in scope of the restriction. Some have food contact approval or are rated Polymers of Low Concern according to OECD criteria. Molecules with a single CF3 group, on the other hand, have a huge range of properties. They are usually not persistent themselves. The common concern is formation of the degradation product trifluoro acetic acid (TFA), which again is persistent, but not bioaccumulative, and is also the only PFAS occurring in nature. Both subgroups do not have the concerning properties initially raised in the restriction, and their inclusion in the definition is not justified by the existing body of evidence, as the “PFAS” as defined here have no common properties. The OECD 2021 report describes the broad, general, non-specific term PFAS “based only on chemical structure, and the decision to broaden this definition compared to Buck et al. (2011) is not connected to decisions on how PFASs should be grouped and managed in regulatory and voluntary actions.” (https://www.oecd.org/chemicalsafety/portal-perfluorinated-chemicals/terminology-per-and-polyfluoroalkyl-substances.pdf)
Scope (regulatory): the restriction is also applicable to products that are not chemicals, but have approvals under sectorial legislation (such as a pharmaceutical market authorisation). The legal consequences of REACH banning products under explicit market authorisations are complex and cannot be resolved by the industry.
Scope (industry sectors): the Restriction lists “identified” industrial sectors in tables (Table 8 or Table 9). It is unclear by which criteria sectors were included, as heavily impacted industries who responded to the Call for Evidence do not appear on the list. The public consultation does not ask for the inclusion of additional sectors, and all Specific Information Requests starting with question 1 refer to this table as being exhaustive. The lack of justification for the inclusion or exclusion of sectors causes confusion:
- If non-listed sectors are out of scope of the restriction, this needs to be clarified. NGOs (ChemSec), Consultants (3E) and authorities (BAuA) communicate that “pharma is exempt” (or pharmaceuticals are exempt) from the PFAS restriction. We cannot verify either claim in the legal text beyond the highly specific derogation for EU API.
- If non-listed sectors are in scope and are supposed to provide information to this public consultation, the questionnaire needs adaptation. The “Specific Information Requests” refer to Table 9 in a way that does not allow for addition of further sectors.
- If the ability to comment on the proposal or a certain use derogation depends on the industrial sector, this raises concerns in terms of definition of sectors, transparency of the process, competition laws and fairness.
Hazard or exposure: We are not aware of a substantiated risk of PFAS overall as defined in the restriction proposal, as the substance group as described has no common properties. Existing risk assessments for certain PFAS subgroups are inapplicable if the PFAS definition is changed or extended afterwards. The presence of non-hazardous fluoropolymers in materials and products is often unknown, as there is no registration, disclosure or labeling requirement, which complicates data collection, substitution and enforcement.
Information on benefits: Our company manufactures and delivers (bio-)pharmaceuticals to patients in the EEA and abroad. Net Sales (2022) were 7,839 mio € (https://www.merckgroup.com/en/annualreport/2022), and we have a strong manufacturing footprint in the EEA with sites in Spain, France, Italy, Germany, and Switzerland. Although the pharmaceutical industry is not mentioned in the restriction proposal, a time unlimited derogation for the specific use of PFAS as active ingredients under EU Regulations was granted in Restriction Option 2 under § 4. c. We consider this derogation important and warranted to allow for the supply of selected medicines. However, the supply continuity of medicinal products will become impossible without derogations covering the production and development of pharmaceuticals in Europe, conflicting also with the European strategic autonomy for medicines. For the sake of structure, we will submit this information in section 6: Missing Uses in the Specific Information Requests of the consultation, although we cannot allocate our sector in section 1.
Transitional periods: the proposed time-limited derogations look at availability of potential alternatives and their technical implementation. No additional transitional periods are proposed to cover regulatory timelines, when stability testing, validation and variations of market authorisations are required. In the pharmaceutical sector, this can require another 10 years, if sufficient regulatory workforce is available by both the industry and the regulators.
Request for exemption, products: to avoid regulatory conflicts that cannot be resolved, products under specific approvals, authorisations or other explicit marketing allowance cannot be banned. This applies to all products regulated by sectorial legislation, such as, but not limited to: approval as API or excipient, existing Market Authorisations as well as related starting materials, intermediates, reagents, ancillaries and other materials supporting the approved product, approved medical devices under e.g. EU BPR or EU IVDR and other approved medicinal and diagnostic products.
Request for exemption, manufacturing and development: the ability to develop and manufacture pharmaceutical products in the EEA, which is a clear strategic priority for the EU, depends on derogations listed under 6: Missing Uses in this consultation. The most urgent derogation relates to API development products (PPORD), which are not derogated and not covered under the drafted API exemption. Manufacturing and clinical testing cannot happen in the EU / EEA if the restriction is implemented, which is damaging to the EU as a development location, and damaging to EU patients, who cannot participate in clinical studies of non-treatable diseases. This can happen as soon as 2027. As clinical studies are planned a few years in advance, the uncertainty caused by this draft restriction already affects these plans. If the intention of the EU is to keep the development within the EU, this should be communicated as soon as possible.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Sectors: pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical industry, medical devices (used for drug delivery).  The sector (bio)pharmaceutical industry is missing from Table 9 of the restriction report. All (sub-) uses are missing, and are submitted through 6: Missing Uses in this consultation. Sector Medical Devices: All (sub-) uses are missing, and are submitted through 6: Missing Uses in this consultation.

5. Proposed derogations: Terminology used in the derogations raises multiple questions on definitions and applicability. For example, we could not determine whether “textiles for the use in filtration” (5. e) cover sterile filtration membranes, if the “petroleum industry” (6. f) also includes the chemical industry and consequently also chemical API manufacturing, at least when depending on fossil starting materials, or if “medicinal preparations” (6. l) include medicinal products. Due to the unclear scope, we cannot collect volume and emission information for these categories. We do so for the necessary derogations we identified and submit under 6: Missing Uses.

6. Missing uses: We will submit detailed information to this consultation on each missing use, in the above format, as soon as we have collected this information. Missing uses we have identified in our company to date: Fluoropolymers in the chemical, pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical production equipment (with product contact and approval). A time-unlimited derogation is required and justified with emission control measures. Fluoropolymers in production equipment without product contact (electrical or mechanical equipment, HVACR refrigerants). Time-limited derogations should be applicable in most, if not all cases. However, existing equipment including spare and replacement parts should be excluded throughout the service life, as highly complex products can be affected. Fluoropolymers in single or multiple use consumables in production, such as sterile filters, bags or tubes. A time-unlimited derogation is required and justified with emission control measures. Active ingredients (API) in development prior to EU registration (PPORD). A time-unlimited derogation is required. Fluoropolymer coated elastomers for immediate (primary) injectables packaging such as vial stoppers. We will submit information substantiating that a time-unlimited derogation is proportionate. Any time-limited derogation should not be applicable to 1. Products under valid market authorisations, or 2. Fluoropolymer uses where emissions are managed throughout the life cycle. Fluoropolymer coated elastomers used in medical drug delivery devices such as injector pens, with the same rationale applying to immediate packaging. PFAS material and reagents used for analytical, quality control or diagnostic procedures as stipulated by pharmaceutical regulations. The derogation should not be limited by time, but relate directly to the existence of the regulatory procedures in question. Starting materials, reagents, intermediates required for the synthesis of API. A time-unlimited derogation is required, as the synthesis of PFAS API requires a PFAS building block.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Terminology used in the derogations raises multiple questions on definitions and applicability. For example, we could not determine whether “textiles for the use in filtration” (5. e) cover sterile filtration membranes, if the “petroleum industry” (6. f) also includes the chemical industry and consequently also chemical API manufacturing, at least when depending on fossil starting materials, or if “medicinal preparations” (6. l) include pharmaceuticals. Due to the unclear scope, we cannot analyse the socio-economic impact and the feasibility of alternatives for these categories. We do so for the necessary derogations we identified and submit under 6: Missing Uses.

8. Other identified uses: Detailed collection of all information including substantiation needs some more time. We will submit this information at a later point to the public consultation.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Information on benefits Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Scope of restriction
On 7th February 2023, the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) published the Annex XV REACH restriction report for per-and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) which had been prepared by 5 Competent Authorities from Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden.  The restriction dossier proposes a near-total ban of all PFAS substances.
The British Coatings Federation recognises the public and political concern about PFAS.

However, the current restriction proposal is very broad, impacting more than 10,000 organofluorine compounds on the grouping basis that they are persistent.  There is no structuring or subdivision of these substances which have very different properties.  No differentiation that considers the different risk profiles of the substances is made.  The proposal thus includes substances for which a restriction may be reasonable as well as substances that can be used safely.  For example, persistence does not equate to toxicity, bioaccumulation or mobility with the environment. Research has shown that fluoropolymers are not bioavailable, non-bioaccummulative, non-bioavailable, not water soluble, non-mobile and non-toxic during their intended use and thus they meet the current OECD definition of Polymer of Low Concern.

According to REACH Article 68 when there is an unacceptable risk to human health or the environment, arising from the manufacture, use or placing on the market of substances, Annex XVII shall be amended.  Article 68 refers to substances (not groups of substances) which pose an “unacceptable risk”.  This principle should also be applied to any proposed restriction on PFAS and should only target uses that actually pose risks to humans and/or the environment should be substituted.  No risk assessment of individual substances or (at least) individual substance groups with uniform properties has been carried out.  As such, the restriction approach does not meet the requirements of Article 68 (1) of the REACH Regulation, which provides that restrictions may be adopted in the presence of “unacceptable risks”.

The restriction proposal is mainly justified by the persistence of the substances and other possible hazard properties such as mobility or bioaccumulability. The actual risk assessment required by Article 68(1) of the REACH Regulation, which considers not only hazard properties but also exposures from the various uses, has not taken place. For a lawful, appropriate, and proportionate regulation of the substances, a differentiated approach is required. This must take into account the different properties of the substances and include an assessment of whether a PFAS substance or its use poses an unmanageable risk to the environment or human health. In particular, if no environmental exposure occurs in specific applications, a ban is not justified. Safe uses of certain PFAS that cannot be replaced by suitable alternatives must continue to be possible in Europe. Otherwise, the restriction proposal is disproportionate.  Persistence alone does not imply that there is a present or future risk to human health or the environment; persistence itself is not an intrinsic hazard, as it does not in itself imply or inform the potential for an adverse effect (aka toxicity).  As such, there is no language in REACH supporting the notion that persistence alone justifies risk-management measures.

Fluoropolymers do not break down into potentially hazardous chemicals once released into the environment (i) and their durability means they do not need to be replaced as much as their alternatives.  This implies less waste, as they contribute to extending the lifespan of a range of products.  Given their benign hazard profile it is disproportionate to include fluoropolymers that meet the current OECD Polymer of Low Concern (PLC) Criteria within the restriction proposal.  In some cases, the fluoropolymers themselves may be persistent, but they are not bioaccumulative, not mobile, and not toxic and therefore not SVHCs from a regulatory perspective.

BCF believe that the restriction of PFAS must be substance-related and risk-based (Art. 68 para. 1 of the REACH Regulation). Not all PFAS pose an unacceptable risk that would justify a restriction.  The restriction must differentiate between the various PFAS groups and the risks posed by their uses and must exclude individual substance groups from the restriction proposal altogether (including certain fluoropolymers such as PTFE).

Uses in the paints, coatings and printing inks industry
The proposed PFAS restriction is the first to adopt a completely generic approach which would have a massive impact on companies in the coatings and paint industry which rely on a wide range of raw materials.  A large number of the substances in scope of the restriction are not classified as hazardous substances under the CLP Regulation. As raw material manufacturers are not obliged to pass on information on non-hazardous substances in the supply chain, it is difficult at this stage for companies in the coatings and printing inks industry to estimate how extensive the actual extent to which their individual company is affected by the proposed PFAS restriction.  In order to enable a legally sound assessment of the regulatory impact, the scope of the restriction must be clearly defined. To analyse the affectedness along global supply chains, a list of substances in scope containing IUPAC names or CAS no. is required. This is the only way to evaluate all affected PFAS uses to avoid supply chain disruptions and ensure that important applications are not unintentionally excluded.

Another application of fluoropolymers is as binders (FEVE polymers). These enable extremely durable coatings to be applied outdoors.  Many fluoropolymers relevant to industry, such as PTFE, help impart important properties to coatings, such as scratch and abrasion resistance, as well as thermal and chemical resistance, which are essential for the specific end uses.  Fluoropolymers are used in anti-friction coatings for the automotive, mechanical engineering and cutting equipment industries, as well as in non-stick coatings. PFAS-containing coatings are used to increase abrasion resistance on aircraft wings. In the powder coatings sector, PFAS are used, among other things, as structuring and matting agents, and also for functional applications such as slip and friction properties or as pigments for colouring.

Due to the durability of fluoropolymers, they do not need to be replaced as much as their alternatives and thus with their unique combination of properties they play an important role in extending the lifespan of a range of products coated with fluoropolymer coatings and thus produce less waste.

The BCF thus supports the position that fluoropolymers which meet the current OECD Polymer of Low Concern (PLC) Criteria should be excluded from the proposed restriction on PFAS.  This is in agreement with the Fluoropolymer Product Group of Plastics, the European European Coil Coating Association (ECCA) and the Verband der deutschen Lack- und Druckfarbenindustrie (VdL).  In addition it is consistent with the approach of the UK Government as published in their detailed RMOA on PFAS chemicals (ii), which could highlight fluoropolymers as derogations from any restriction proposal.

However, should ECHA decide to retain fluoropolymers within the proposed restriction, then the BCF request longer transition periods as detailed below.

Transition Periods
In order to comply with all the relevant information for an exemption from the basic PFAS ban - especially for PFAS applications for which no alternatives currently exist or are not even foreseeable - companies need a reasonable amount of time to comply with the restriction.

Appropriate transition periods are required. The general period of 18 months is too short for the conversion of all applications within the supply chain for which no alternatives currently exist, and no exemptions are provided.  The transition period does not seem to take into account that applications may have to be redesigned and potentially to meet stringent standards before the use of potential alternatives would be accepted within the supply chain.

Thus, existing stocks of PFAS substances, or mixtures and articles containing PFAS already placed on the market for the first time should be exempted from the restriction.  This will allow coatings to be formulated to existing market standards whilst the approval of replacements is undertaken.  Additionally, it will prevent the disposal of existing stocks of PFAS substances or mixtures as the process of making these available to third parties would be considered placing on the market.

Due to the wide-reaching nature of the proposed restriction and the inclusion of substances which are not classified as hazardous under the CLP regulation and thus not communicated through the SDS, it is proposed to extend the proposed transition periods after EiF to include an additional initial 12-month time period whereby the suppliers of PFAS substances are required to notify downstream users of their presence of PFAS within products and provide instructions for use and disposal to avoid releases of PFAS to the environment.  Within this time period, downstream users would be required to ensure the instructions for use and disposal were complied with and to communicate the presence of PFAS to their customers. As such, all the transition periods would be extended by 12 months to ensure adequate communication within the supply chain prior to the start of the transition periods.

PTFE is used in aerospace coatings to provide wear resistance and surface lubricity.  Even if alternatives could be found which would depend on a number of variables including resistance to UV, corrosion, fluids, as well as comparable wear resistance and surface lubricity, the transition periods for use applications within aerospace need to consider the Aerospace OEM approval process.  It typically takes around 5 years for an Aerospace OEM to approve a new product or change in a raw material for an existing approved product.  In addition, a period of time is required for the coatings manufacturer to develop the product to submit to the OEM.  As such where a coated product is required to meet standards or requirements set by the manufacturer of the coated article, a 12-year transition period after Entry into Force for such coated products is required.  This is the case in applications relating to the use of fluoropolymer coatings within the aerospace industry. As such BCF request a 12-year derogation for coatings requiring approval by the article manufacturer such as those fluoropolymer coatings for Aerospace applications, because of the research on existing non-PFAS polymers, the development of replacements and the time period for approval of new coatings within the industry.

Within the coil coating sector, fluoropolymer-based coatings (FBCs) offer superior durability and performance, unparalleled by other coating technologies. These coatings containing PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride) or FEVE (fluoroethylene vinyl ether), prolong the lifespan of coated surfaces, thereby decreasing the need for substrate recoating, repair, and replacement. The coil coating industry produces pre-painted metal products for the construction, automotive, appliance and engineering markets.  The PVDF/FEVE coatings are specifically formulated for the coil coating industry chain a process that produces a multi-layer product with the layers designed to deliver the required properties, e.g. corrosion resistance, durability and surface appearance of the final high value products. Pre-painted metals that are coated with these fluoropolymers meet the most demanding levels of UV (Ruv5) and corrosion resistance (RC5) as set out in EN10169 and EN 1396; these are the European standards that define product performance for the coil coating industry. As such they are suitable for specific, harsh building environments, including high humidity climates, high UV, marine and chemical environments.  The coatings are also used in high-rise buildings and other significant architectural structures, due to their durability alongside the difficulty to maintain these inaccessible structures.

This extended lifespan and ability to withstand extreme environmental conditions aids in the upkeep of high rise buildings, and other significant architectural structures. If an alternative product was used on these buildings, then the owner would be faced with the need to repaint the building after a shorter period, leading to higher upkeep costs.  This is especially the case in high-rise buildings, which face technical challenges to upkeep and repaint the structure.  The coil coated FBCs are especially crucial for significant architectural structures and structures like bridges and skyscrapers where preserving structural integrity is paramount. These coatings provide a level of protection essential for maintaining the safety of these structures.

This potentially reduces waste by lengthening the useful life of the coated structures.  Furthermore, by diminishing the need for frequent recoating, FBCs will contribute to lower the environmental impact associated with the production and application of coatings.

In addition, coil coated FBCS are manufactured and applied in industrial settings under well controlled conditions. These coatings are not used by consumers. At the end of life, the PVDF/FEVE products are recycled established supply chains which result in the coating being incinerated at high temperatures in metal manufacturing processes.  These processes are subject to the Industrial Emissions Directive, and they deploy extensive abatement technologies to deal with a wide range of hazardous substances to minimise emissions to the environment.

To date no alternatives have been identified that meet the proven performance of coil coated FBCs in challenging exterior environments.  While work is being undertaken to identify alternatives to FBCs, even if a suitable alternative could be found, the transition period needs to consider extensive and prolonged testing to ensure that the durability and extended lifespan of the coatings is maintained.  As such, a 12-year transition period after Entry into Force is required.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Scope of restriction option analysis

The primary objective of this argument is to advocate for the preservation of the industrial use of PFAS (Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances) in specialized applications, particularly in the production of PTFE (Polytetrafluoroethylene)-lined valves. The objective is to present a compelling case against a blanket PFAS ban, emphasizing the critical role of PFAS in ensuring the quality and safety of our products and highlighting the potential adverse consequences a ban could have on our company, our employees, and the industries we serve.

Hazard or exposure

It is essential to recognize that the production of PTFE (Polytetrafluoroethylene), the key component in our PTFE-lined valves, can be carried out without posing significant hazards or environmental exposure risks. Advanced manufacturing processes and stringent safety measures are in place to ensure the responsible production of PTFE. These processes can effectively mitigate potential risks associated with PFAS, such as emissions or discharge into the environment. Moreover, the industrial applications for which PTFE is indispensable often involve closed systems, where the PTFE lining remains contained, reducing the likelihood of exposure. By focusing on responsible manufacturing practices and implementing strict control measures, we can continue to meet industry demands for high-performance materials like PTFE while minimizing any potential adverse effects on the environment and human health.

Information on alternatives

It is crucial to acknowledge that there are currently limited alternatives to PFAS, especially for specialized applications like PTFE/PFA-lined valves. PTFE (Polytetrafluoroethylene) is a unique material that offers exceptional resistance to aggressive chemicals and extreme temperatures. These properties are indispensable in many industrial processes. Finding materials that can match the performance of PTFE is extremely challenging.

Most alternative materials come with significant drawbacks. For instance, using silicone or plastic-based substitutes. These materials often exhibit less chemical resistance and cannot withstand high temperatures, which is unacceptable in many industrial applications. Additionally, alternative materials may have higher environmental impacts as they might require more energy and resources during production.

Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues

A blanket PFAS ban would have substantial repercussions on the economic viability and job security of our company and other businesses in the industry. We employ a significant number of workers and contribute to the stability of the local and regional economy. A ban would significantly impede our ability to retain existing jobs and create new ones.

Considering the potential negative impact of a blanket PFAS ban on manufacturing companies and industry in general, it is important to note that many companies may consider relocating their production sites to non-European countries during the bridging phase. This decision would be the result of uncertainty about the availability of suitable alternatives and could have significant consequences for local economies and jobs in the European Union.

Such a relocation would result in Europe losing technological and economic competence in these key industries, as companies could move to countries that have less restrictive regulations. This could ultimately lead to Europe falling behind in terms of innovation and competitiveness.

Request for exemption

The European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) must differentiate between industrial and private use when deciding on a PFAS ban. PFAS compounds are utilized in a variety of applications, including industrial processes. They are often indispensable for industries to ensure specific functions, such as the production of PTFE-/PFA-lined valves, which are critical products in various sectors, including the chemical, petrochemical, and food industries. A blanket ban would significantly impact industrial productivity and competitiveness.Therefore, we strongly urge the ECHA to carefully consider these factors in its decision-making and ensure that a PFAS ban does not encompass industrial use in specialized applications such as PTFE-/PFA-lined valves. Instead, the ECHA should ensure that the use of PFAS in these specific applications continues under strict regulations and controls to minimize environmental impact while preserving industrial performance. This will allow companies like ours to continue producing high-quality products and securing jobs without endangering the environment.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: 1.) Pharmaceutical and Food Industry: In the pharmaceutical and food industry, PTFE-lined valves are of critical importance. These sectors deal with highly sensitive and often biologically active substances. The use of PTFE ensures the purity and integrity of products since it is inert and does not release any contaminants. A ban on PTFE could jeopardize the quality and safety of medications and food, posing serious health risks to consumers.  Semiconductor Industry: The semiconductor industry requires extremely precise and clean conditions for manufacturing microchips and other electronic components. PTFE-lined valves are used in cleanroom environments to prevent contaminants that could affect the quality of semiconductor products. A ban on PTFE valves would significantly disrupt semiconductor manufacturing and impact the availability of electronic devices.

General Comments: Scope of restriction:
The proposed ban encompasses the refrigerant we currently use: R1233zd (Trans-1-chloro-3,3,3-trifluoropropene) a fourth generation HFO refrigerant which has been developed as a replacement to R-123 currently being phased out of industry under the Montreal protocol by 2030. The refrigerant has a GWP of 1 which is among the lowest in its class. It is currently included as a ‘PFAS’ only due to its chemical structure. The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) emphasizes that the term “PFAS” is a broad, general, non-specific term, which does not inform whether a compound is harmful or not and should not be a basis for regulation. That being said such a broad, class-based regulatory approach ignore the diversity of the chemical.

Hazard or Exposure/ Environmental Emissions
Trans-1-chloro-3,3,3-trifluoropropene is not listed in either the EU F-gas, the EU ODS regulations or the EU restriction of hazardous (RoHS) directive. EU Reach classifies it as a non PBT/ non vPvB molecule. Persistence should not be a sole criterion for banning a particular molecule. The molecule has a log Kow value of 2.2 which is well below the screening criterion of 4.5. The substance is therefore considered not B/vB (bioaccumulative) according to screening criteria. The substance’s critical aquatic effect values are a 96-h LC50 of 38 mg/L in fish and a 72-h NOErC of 115 mg/L in algae and the substance is not classified for CMR or other chronic toxicity endpoints according to Directive 67/538/EEC or according to Regulation EC No 1272/2008. The substance is therefore considered not Toxic.

Trans-1-chloro-3,3,3-trifluoropropene degrades to TFA at levels (less than 2% TFA) that are not considered harmful to humans or the environment (UNEP EEAP).

Information on alternatives
The alternatives in case of an all HFO ban will be natural refrigerants whose disadvantages outweigh their advantages in the industry:
• Ammonia is toxic to humans, animals and the environment, and contributes significantly to photochemical smog. The high pressure requirements for implementation in refrigeration cycle significantly increase costs.
• Hydrocarbons contribute to photochemical smog and are extremely flammable, limiting their application in the industry.
• CO2 is persistent, global warming gas with a lifetime of more than 1000 years. Again requiring high pressure implementation as well.

Information on benefits
Trans-1-chloro-3,3,3-trifluoropropene is an environmentally preferable alternative for its use as a refrigerant for high temperature heat pump applications. It maximizes energy savings and dramatically reduces environmental impact. It is a EU Reach-registered and U.S. SNAP-listed alternative to R-123 and R-245fa designed to make a significant contribution to reductions in global warming:

• GWP = 1
• Non-flammable
• No impact on ozone depletion

It can provide higher efficiency when compared to R-245fa in the renewable heat recovery market and in the waste recovery market.

Request for exemption
We request that Trans-1-chloro-3,3,3-trifluoropropene be exempted from this regulation.

General Comments: Scope of restriction:
The proposed restriction does not differentiate between fluoroelastomers (FKM, FFKM, etc.) and other PFAS. Fluoroelastomers have unique properties that distinguish them from other PFAS and they do not have the environmental and toxicological profiles associated with some PFAS that are of concern. We declared that the restriction proposal should differentiate between the various types of PFAS based of their chemical composition, their toxicological profile and the production method. Not all PFAS are the same and there is no scientific basis to regulate them all the same.

Information on benedits and alternatives:
In terms of heat resistance, fluoroelastomer has the best high-temperature performance among existing rubbers. Fluoroelastomer also has excellent plasma resistance, and is widely used in semiconduct industry, like dry etching or CVD process. However, ordinary rubber has poorer plasma resistance, is easier to be etched, and its sealing performance fails. In summary, ordinary rubber cannot become substitutes for fluoroelastomer in plasma process. Meanwhile, based on previous comparative evaluation data, it can be seen that non-PFAS substances cannot be ideal alternatives in practical applications.

Request for exception:
Fluoroelastomers have brought enormous benefits to the semiconduct industrial chain due to their unique properties (high temperature resistance, plasma resistance, etc.). Otherwise, it does not possess the environmental and toxicological characteristics of PFOA, PFOS, C9-C14 PFCAs. We request that the ECHA-PFAS restriction draft should distinguish and regulate the chemical composition and toxicological characteristics of various types of PFAS accordingly. Exemptions should be granted for low concern substances such as fluoroelastomers.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Fluoroelastomers like FKM & FFKM have excellent high-temperature resistance and plasma resistance, and are widely used in semiconduct industry.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: PFOA, PFOS and C9-C14 PFCAs are not intentionally added in our production of fluoroelastomer.

6. Missing uses: We use fluoroelastomers as mainly sealing material like FKM & FFKM. In a few cases we can replace them by other material such as EPDM, NBR, or Silicone. But in most cases where chemical or temperature resistance is so critical that fluoroelastomers are necessary. Without these it is not possible to keep the life time of sealing product.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: We do not see chemical resistant alternatives on the market by now. And there is no information for develop new material alternatives. The sealing parts made from fluoroelastomers are still nessesary for semiconduct industry as long as no alternatives are available. If we can not use fluoroelastomers for product, we have to stop our business activities.

WMFTS uses fluoropolymers in the manufacture of many of its products.  The volume of products can be found in the confidential attachment report.

Hazard or exposure
WMFTS fully supports the restriction of specific, hazardous PFAS that pose a danger due to bioavailability, bioaccumulative and toxic properties e.g. PFOA, PFOS, GenX and C9-14 PFCAs.  However, to implement a restriction on a broad group such as PFAS means applying these restrictions to substances that exhibit significantly different properties and characteristics.  Fluoropolymers are structurally different to PFAS of concern and have very different properties.  Further differentiation can also be made to separate commonly used fluoropolymers such as PTFE, PVDF, FKM from side-chain fluorinated polymers.
Fluoropolymers do not exhibit bioavailability, bioaccumulative or toxic characteristics and should therefore be separated from hazardous PFAS and exempt from legislative restrictions.  PTFE for example, does not oxidise, hydrolyse, photolyze, degrade by microorganism attack, is not mobile in water and is non-volatile.  Fluoropolymers processed by suspension polymerisation (granular PTFE and PVDF) do not require PFAS-based processing aids.

Environmental emissions
Fluoropolymer waste is known to be chemically inert, and any fluorinated compounds that may leach from fluoropolymer waste would be contained within landfill leachate collection systems.  Furthermore, the most stable fluoropolymer, PTFE, can be effectively incinerated at over 800°C reaching complete thermal decomposition, demonstrating effective disposal methods are available to prevent accumulation of waste fluoropolymer products in landfill.
More information can be found in sections 2 and 3 of the confidential attachment report.

Baseline
Please see the confidential attachment report.

Description of analytical methods
No comment

Information on alternatives
Information on alternative materials has been provided for each sector and sub-use.  Please see sections 6, 7 and 8 of the confidential attachment report.

Information on benefits
No comment

Other socio-economic analysis (SEA) issues
Please see information provided for specific applications and industries in sections 6, 7 and 8 of the confidential attachment report.

Transitional period
WMFTS uses various fluoropolymers across a wide range of products (more than 150 different products) for use in multiple sectors and for multiple uses.  While transitional periods and derogation periods will be essential to allow alternative materials to be assessed, designed and implemented where possible, consideration is also needed for businesses such as WMFTS who will need to conduct these investigative activities for many different products, across many different industries and uses within these periods.  Sufficient time will be required to enable businesses such as WMFTS to effectively research suitable alternative materials for all affected products.

Request for exemption
There is a shortage of data to demonstrate the amount of hazardous PFAS generated from manufacture (when using non-PFAS polymerisation aids), in-use and end-of-life cycles for fluoropolymers.  Appropriate restrictions should still be placed on hazardous PFAS, but there is the opportunity to introduce emission restrictions and reporting requirements of hazardous PFAS for the manufacture, use and end-of-life cycles for fluoropolymers and fluoropolymer products.  Once this data is generated, a decision can be made on the safety of fluoropolymers and if restrictions are necessary.
In addition, the comments and evidence that have been provided here and in the confidential attachment report, show that fluoropolymers are a key material to provide solutions for many applications.  The materials that have been covered within this report are:
• PTFE (Hose liners, seals, gaskets, diaphragms, pump components)
• ePTFE (Tubing, tubing elements)
• PVDF (Tubing, tubing elements, tubing assemblies, pump components, pump connectors, pump cartridges, pumpheads)
• FKM (Gaskets, seals, O-rings, pumpheads, pump drives, nozzles, diaphragms, pump components)
• TFM (Diaphragms)
• Fluoropolymer oils and greases (PTFE, PFPE)
These fluoropolymers are materials of low concern and do not pose a risk.  In many cases these materials are utilised precisely because they are inert and do not break down in otherwise highly chemically aggressive environments. As such, these fluoropolymer materials do not pose a risk to human or animal health, or the environment.  This group of substances should therefore be given a broad exemption within the PFAS proposal.

General comments
ECHA have advised that the property of highest concern with PFAS is the very high persistence due to the very strong C-F bond, with PFAS being known as “forever chemicals”.  For the applications that WMFTS products that contain fluoropolymers are required for, it is this very strong C-F bond that is critical to achieve the chemical, heat and mechanical resistance required for the application.  Suitable alternative materials are not currently available for many applications, but if new materials can be developed, these will need to have the same very high persistence to achieve the required chemical, heat and mechanical resistance, resulting in the same high persistence challenges.  Any newly developed alternative materials are also at risk of posing additional hazards causing regrettable substitutions.  If fluoropolymer materials are restricted, a wide range of products critical to many industries may no longer be available.  Where alternative materials can be developed, the significant costs of development, evaluation, validation and registration of these new materials will likely be passed onto the individual consumers, making medical treatment, energy and transport among others unfeasible for many people, significantly reducing quality of life for the majority of individuals.  Fluoropolymers are also seen as key materials to achieve global sustainability goals.  If fluoropolymers can no longer be used, our goals for working more efficiently and sustainably may not be possible.
As fluoropolymers do not exhibit bioavailability, bioaccumulative or toxic characteristics, these materials themselves can be considered as polymers of low concern (PLC) (see A critical review of the application of polymer of low concern regulatory criteria to fluoropolymers II: Fluoroplastics and fluoroelastomers - Korzeniowski - 2023 - Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management - Wiley Online Library).  Placing the focus of restrictions on the emissions of hazardous PFAS for the lifecycle of fluoropolymers including, manufacture, in-use and end-of-life cycles would control the impact to the environment, without the extensive development activities, costs and resources required to identify alternative materials (if this is possible) and significantly reduce the disruption to multiple industries and global economies.  Fluoropolymers should therefore be given a broad exemption within the PFAS proposal.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Scope or restriction option analysis
• The restriction proposal is very broad. A structuring or subdivision of the more than 10,000 substances, which have very different intrinsic properties, is not apparent. A differentiation that takes into account the different risk profiles of the substances is not made.

• The group-based approach of the restriction proposal is legally questionable. According to Art. 69 of the REACH Regulation, a substance-based approach is required for restrictions.

• Furthermore, the restriction proposal is not risk-based, as no risk assessment of individual substances or (at least) individual substance groups with homogeneous properties has been carried out. Thus, the chosen restriction approach does not meet the requirements of Article 68(1) of the REACH Regulation, which provides that restrictions may be adopted in case of "unacceptable risks". Therefore, a restriction of substances in applications that do not pose a risk exceeds the legal framework provided by the REACH Regulation. In particular, if there is no environmental exposure in specific applications and handling or it can be strongly minimised, a ban is not justified.

• The restriction of PFAS must be substance-specific and risk-based (Art. 68 (1) of the REACH Regulation). Not all PFAS pose an unacceptable risk that justifies a restriction.

• Thus, a more differentiated assessment and regulatory approach that bans only uses that pose a risk is needed. Therefore, the restriction must differentiate between the different PFAS-groups and the risks posed by their uses.

• Certain groups of substances should be entirely excluded from the restriction proposal (e.g., fluoropolymers), as their use is safe and does not pose a risk. Potential risks that may arise during manufacturing or in the end-of-life phase can be controlled through other regulatory approaches (BAT process, IED requirements).

• The restriction must take into account the interlinkages in global supply chains. Derogations for socially important uses are inappropriate if raw materials, processing aids and other preliminary stages in the production process are not covered by the derogation.

• Double regulation must be avoided. Groups of substances that are already regulated by other regulations or restrictions should be removed from the scope of the restriction (e.g., F-Gases, already restricted PFAS, PFAS regulated under the POP-regulation).

Information on alternatives/Information on benefits
• Assessments of many sectors show that a complete substitution of PFAS in many applications is not feasible. In many cases the use of PFAS has specific benefits due to the specific properties of the single compound.

• PFAS are used in many industries whenever extreme conditions such as high or low temperatures, high frictional resistance or aggressive chemical conditions require it. They therefore play an important role in industrial plants and in the field of future technologies (e.g., fuel cells, hydrogen electrolysis, heat pumps, solar plants).

• Fluoropolymers are widely used in industrial plants in many sectors because the production conditions require a combination of the special properties of these materials. Most industrial production plants and infrastructures are therefore equipped with highly standardized components made of fluoropolymer. A lack of these components would have a considerable influence on the service life, functionality, and safety of industrial plants, which are also defined by standards and guidelines.

• Since alternatives must fulfil similar requirements in plants or production processes, it can be assumed that suitable alternatives will and must also have similar properties in terms of persistence.

• Within the assessment of alternatives, a comprehensive approach is required that ensures the inclusion of all relevant technical, functional, and regulatory criteria.

Other socio-economic analysis issues
• A comprehensive and undifferentiated ban on PFASs would have a massive impact on European companies and the innovative capacity of industry in Europe.

• High-tech applications would no longer be possible without the use of certain PFAS, so that the transformation of industry and the goals of the Green Deal cannot be achieved.

• Since a comprehensive ban on the production and use of PFASs would increase dependence on imports from non-EU countries, European sovereignty would also be massively endangered, especially in critical products and applications (e.g., medical products, semiconductors, heat pumps, etc.).

• Due to the broad scope of the current restriction proposal, it will have a massive impact on companies' investment decisions and thus on Germany and Europe as a business location well before it enters into force.

Transitional Period
• Appropriate transition periods are needed. The general period of 18 months is clearly too short for the transition of all applications for which no derogations are foreseen.

• The time limits of 6.5 and 13.5 years for derogations are also too short. In many areas, these periods will not be sufficient for the identification /evaluation of alternatives and the transformation of production processes and supply chains.  When setting transitional periods for exemptions, it is imperative that long-term timeframes for longevity testing, certification and authorisation procedures are also taken into account. In many sectors (e.g., medical devices, plant engineering) authorisation and certification processes of products and plants require very long time periods.

Request for Exemptions
• The restriction proposal does not take into account numerous important uses for which exemptions are urgently needed and no suitable alternatives are available.

• Comprehensive derogations are needed for highly important social applications such as medical technology, as well as for high-tech and industrial applications, in order not to endanger the operation of numerous industrial plants, the continued existence of entire value chains in Europe, the green transformation of industry and the goals of the Green Deal.

• In order not to dramatically increase dependencies and unequal competitive conditions vis-à-vis non-European markets and to ensure that the production of the products exempted from the restriction will continue to be possible in the EU, there must be clearly described,  derogations for all stages of the supply chain including precursors, processing aids and intermediate products . These should be formulated in the restriction dossier in a clear and legally secure manner.

• The possibility to review, renew and reapply for derogations is needed due to the technical importance of PFAS.

• For the placing on the market of spare parts, wear parts and used parts, derogations are necessary for the purpose of sustainability and economic efficiency (repair as produced principle). These should be granted for an unlimited period or at least for a significantly longer period than the transitional periods currently provided for.

• Products already placed on the market for the first time are to be exempted from the restriction. Otherwise, existing stocks of substances, mixtures and articles at downstream users would have to be disposed, since under REACH every process of making available to third parties is considered as placing on the market.

General Comments: Scope or restriction option analysis
ASML fully supports the European regulators’ objectives of environmental and public health protection. We are actively exploring substitutions and alternatives. However, as it currently stands, PFAS remains a necessary component of the Semiconductor manufacturing process and equipment. The derogation, as currently envisaged, is, therefore, an important step in the right direction. To properly assess the implications of the proposal as it currently stands, we deem important that the following clarifications are made:
Firstly, we would like to clarify the definition of “semiconductor manufacturing process”. It is our understanding that it covers all steps of the semiconductor value chain, from the process of chemicals required to manufacture raw material to semiconductor manufacturing equipment and facilities, as well as those used in the manufacturing process. This also encompasses any system, hardware, device composition or improvement, for or relating to the manufacture, assembly or test of a semiconductor device.

Secondly, we would like to clarify the conditions of the restriction. The condition of point 2 “shall not be placed on the market” poses a potential discrepancy with  REACH [1]  and RoHS [2] . The wording “for the first time” (RoHs Directive) has significant implications for compliance. The absence of it in the proposed restriction implies that placing of re-used articles, as well as spare parts, used for repairs and modifications to extend the life of a product, needs to meet conditions of the proposed PFAS restriction. Although the “Blue Guide on the implementation of EU product rules 2022” does not formally cover the REACH Regulation, we believe that it is important to take a coherent approach and treat repairs and modifications prior to the restriction in the same way as the “Blue Guide”, where such products are not considered new [3] and excluded from the scope of the restriction. Such a disposition would allow the extension of the lifespan of existing products and reduce the number of products having to be disposed of and recycled.
Thirdly, it is our understanding that “harsh condition” definitions in point 5s of current condition restriction for lubricants also covers “ultrapure/ultraclean” condition, which is a critical environment within the semiconductor industry.

Environmental emissions
ASML products and processes produce low emission from PFAS containing articles relative to other sectors. ASML products are produced, used and disposed of in a controlled environment, according to applicable regulations. They are designed to be very long-lasting and to minimize the rate of emission by avoiding hazardous materials. ASML’s “reuse” program is contributing to extending the lifetime of our products and parts. 96% [4] of systems sold are still in use, thereby further reducing waste and its associated environmental risk.

Description of analytical methods
Analytical methods to detect the presence of PFAS are being rapidly developed but are still limited to only 40 targeted PFAS. The other method presented in annex XV is applicable for both PFAS and non-PFAS substances and, therefore, relies on extensive supply chain-related information. For a company like ASML, that relies on over 5000 suppliers, gathering information on as-yet unregulated PFAS substances is extremely challenging, particularly in the absence of an adequate analytical method.
Currently, there is no regulatory obligation to highlight the presence of most PFAS in our products. The majority are not yet listed in the SVHC REACH list. However, adding PFAS to the SVHC (with an exhaustive list of concerned substances, incl. CAS#) would expand the scope of art. 33 by providing information on substances and enhancing supply chain communication. This could help in identifying the presence of PFAS.
The proposed condition in point 7 on annual PFAS reporting, if made public, could be a beneficial tool for gathering information on PFAS, provided downstream users, like ASML, would not be included in the requirement and could see it in an ECHA database, similar to the SCIP database [5].

Information on alternatives
Based on our research, and the wider industry work that we are aware of, the proposed alternatives in Appendix E2 are suitable only for very limited applications. While some alternatives might offer similar properties to fluorpolymers, they are not replaceable for a series of key applications.
ASML products use fluorpolymers due to their, currently, unique properties. We strive to replace them wherever possible, but 1 to 1 replacement is not possible because of the uniquely specific environment and performance requirements of our industry. It can take over a decade to develop an alternative, with no guarantees that it will meet the requirements regarding performance, health & safety, raw material, energy and water consumption etc. The transition time should reflect this.
Provided we can find feasible alternatives for certain applications, ASML estimates that it will take 10 years or longer to develop industrialized PFAS free designs. There may ultimately be applications where no viable alternative is available that meets the performance requirements. Furthermore, the semiconductor supply chain is highly specialized, which may further impact the timelines if alternatives were not available in sufficient quantities to meet demand.
Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues
The semiconductor industry serves a number of key applications and end-user markets that are crucial to the global economy and to meet the dual green and digital transitions in Europe , e.g. energy production, healthcare, communication and mobility.
ASML products play a critical role in various European initiatives, (e.g. EU’s Green Deal, EU’s Chip Act) and in securing the EU’s competitiveness. A blanket ban, or a limited derogation, would have profound negative consequences for the global competitiveness of the European economy and European citizens.
We hope that, based on the research and the evidence provided, you will recognize the importance of the semiconductor manufacturing process, including its entire supply chain, as a critical building block of the European Union’s future prosperity and strategic autonomy on the global stage.
Transitional period
It is ASML’s firm intention to meet the deadlines of 13,5 years from the current proposal and to continue to identify and operationalize PFAS alternatives wherever possible. Over that time, we aim at developing a strong understanding of possible substitutions and the research needs and timeframes.  Given the particular challenges of our industry, we ask the regulators to provide a formal mechanism to extend or renew exemptions (currently possible under the RoHS directive) in case a PFAS alternative is not feasible within set derogation times
We would appreciate clarification of the different timelines for derogation in current Annex XV proposal, as those might be mutually exclusive. For the derogation to be effective, derogation for the required materials (fluorpolymers 6,5 years after EiF) should match the derogation for the use (semiconductor manufacturing process 13,5) to avoid inconsistent legislation.

Request for exemption
ASML products, if properly maintained, can continue to productively operate for at least 25-30 years. 96% of the products placed on the market by ASML are still in use at the present day. Regular maintenance of parts avoids premature obsolescence of these legacy products and considerably reduces waste generation. Therefore, maintenance parts, intended for use in the existing products (including those produced before EiF), should also be excluded from the proposed restriction.
