General Comments: Scope or restriction option analysis
Our company uses fluor polymers to cover rollers that are mainly used in the printing industry (offset printing). We use polymers with a molecular weight more than 1000. This includes FKM and PTFE. Both substances are used as emulsion or dispersion on aqueous basis. The coating is covalently bonded to the roller substrate.
The rollers are used as pan rollers and ink rollers in offset printing. These rollers have been established on the market for many years and have become the standard under the brand name "LotoTec", especially in the "pan roller" sector. FKM has an extremely low surface tension. Products coated with FKM acquire a special wetting behavior and thus uniformly introduce a defined amount of water into the printing process. The printing process is a very sensitive system that reacts sensitively to changes in the ink-water balance. With FKM-coated rollers, this process can be controlled more precisely than with conventional rollers. In addition, the rollers with the LotoTec coating have up to twice the service life when used correctly
Another reason for using FKM is that this polymer is one of the high-performance polymers. Its chemical, oxidation, aging, extraction and temperature resistance is far superior to those of traditional roll materials based on nitrile butadiene rubber (NBR).
Moreover, the surface roughness of the coated rolls is significantly lower than that of the traditionally grounded rollers. The outstanding properties (hydrophobicity, resistance, swelling behavior and smoothness) - seriously interfere with the offset process, in some contexts individually, in others jointly.
In the printing industry, rollers come into contact with different media. By using FKM coated rollers, interactions between the substrate rubber and the chemicals can be reduced or avoided. Particular advantages that could not previously be achieved with other materials are: Cleanability of the rollers, less waste due to a quickly achieved and stable ink-water balance, reduced use of printing chemicals as well as the avoidance of volume increase of rollers and premature failure of these machine elements. The particular advantages of such rollers in the offset printing process can be seen in detail in the attached files (Annex_01, Annex_02, Annex_03).
In the context of current EU discussions, fluoropolymers are being considered as "Polymers of Low Concern." The proposal suggests that polymers earn this classification if they meet specific criteria. These criteria include a molecular weight exceeding 1,000 Da, the absence of reactive functional groups, non-cationic properties, and the presence of specific elements (e.g., fluorine) exclusively covalently bonded to carbon. Furthermore, these polymers should not be designed for degradation and should not be classified as hazardous substances under the CLP Regulation. CARACAL (2021) A recent study examining fourteen fluoropolymers, including FKM and FFKM, affirms their adherence to the above mentioned criteria Korzeniowski, S.H. et al. (2023). Notably, these fluoropolymers do not undergo degradation processes leading to the formation of hazardous long-chain PFAS or PFAC. This information is supported by a report commissioned by the EU Commission. Bougas, K., et al. (2020)
We use polymers and not low molecular weight substances. The macromolecular structure means that this class of materials has a lower potential for environmental damage than low molecular weight materials/end products. We therefore propose to generally exempt from the restriction. This approach would be consistent with the EU classification of fluoropolymers as "Polymers of Low Concern" (see earlier in the text). The general approach is not expedient at this point. In addition, it is important to consider whether a PFAS (FKM or PTFE) is permanently and ideally covalently bonded to a substrate (as in our case) or only adheres to the surface through weak physical interactions. Furthermore, it is important whether the PFAS is also cohesively bonded to itself and thus forms a cohesive continuum (crosslinking). A FKM is not only macromolecular, but in the cross-linked state the chains are also bound together with a wide mesh. Detachment of individual macromolecules from the FKM or "breaking out" of entire clusters is unlikely under normal conditions, and so is exposure to the environment.

Hazard or exposure and environmental emissions
At this point, it is again important that polymeric materials are used and not low-molecular subastances. The fluoropolymers are available as solid rubber, or as stabilized latice, or as dispersion.
All employees who get into contact with the materials are advised to wear typical safety equipment. This includes gloves, goggles and work clothes. Even in the case of direct contact with the skin, a polymer is not considered to be "hazardous".
The same applies to the product in use. The rubber is cross-linked and has a structural strength that makes exposure to the environment unlikely. In our case (roller coatings), the FKM is covalently bonded to the elastomer substrate. There is no exposure to the environment under normal circumstances.
In our production, the FKM rubber is sprayed onto the rollers from aqueous phase. When the material is applied to the roller substrate, there is a certain amount of "overspray", as is common in painting technology, for example. This overspray has already been reduced to a minimum for cost reasons. In addition, an exhaust system with a suitable filter system is installed. Emissions to air, water and soil are thus excluded. The filter mats are disposed of properly. Disposal is dealt with in more detail in the specific section.
By using our coated rollers, printing chemicals can be saved in the printing industry. The rollers make the process more efficient, more stable and with significantly reduced consumption of organic solvents and VOC emitters. Washing processes are reduced, the use of 2-propanol is significantly reduced, and the lifetime of the rollers under certain conditions can be significantly extended. The use of FKM therefore creates a real ecological advantage over conventional rollers over the lifetime of the roller.

Information on alternatives
In considering alternatives to fluor rubber (FKM) and the proposed restrictions on PFAS, it becomes evident that while various substitutes like (H)NBR, EPDM, VMQ available, they possess distinct characteristics that differentiate them from FKM.
Some of the most important reasons are:
Temperature Resistance: FKM stands out for its remarkable resistance to high temperatures. It boasts a continuous service temperature of 200°C and can withstand short-term exposure temperatures of up to 260°C for 1000 hours (Hofmann 1980). Comparatively, when evaluated against other elastomers such as NBR, ACM, and FVMQ, FKM consistently exhibits superior performance under elevated temperatures, as corroborated by data in Fernandez's work (2008).
Chemical Resistance and Swelling Behavior: The exceptional chemical resistance of FKM is well-documented in Fernandez's research (2008). FKM showcases a remarkable ability to withstand exposure to various chemicals, surpassing the performance of other elastomers.
Aging Behavior: FKM vulcanizates display an impressive resistance to aging, weathering, and ozone, as noted by Hofmann (1980). Recent investigations conducted by Morsbach and colleagues in 2022 provide valuable insights into the aging behavior of different materials. Their research unequivocally establishes FKM's position as the material with the lowest adsorption of hydrogen among the materials studied.
Permeation Resistance: FKM vulcanizates exhibit remarkably permeability (Hofmann 1980). This characteristic is further emphasized by their extended breakthrough times when exposed to various chemicals, as demonstrated in the context of glove materials, as per data from IFA (2020).
Hydrophobic nature: We use FKM because of its hydrophobic properties, which play a crucial role in the process (printing) in which the rollers are used. Other materials do not have these properties. Surface modifications such as plasma treatments do not last (in our experience) and lose their effectiveness over time as the functionalized layer is removed and the underlying substrate can interact with the surface. In addition, these surfaces do not achieve the desired property profile.
In summary, the potential replacement of FKM in various applications with alternative elastomers is a multifaceted decision. While there are apparent alternatives to some extent, they cannot reflect all the unique properties of FKM, particularly its exceptional temperature and chemical resistance. Due to its property profile, FKM is a unique material that cannot be easily replaced.
Silicone rubber could serve as an alternative to FKM in the long term, even if its properties do not match those of FKM in various respects. However, silicone rubber is not available in aqueous dispersion and must be laboriously dissolved in organic solvents before use. Assuming that both polymers are not released into the environment and that the waste/residues are sent for thermal recycling, the use of silicone under the same general conditions would lead to a significantly higher environmental impact due to the use of organic solvents. Therefore, although this material would be significantly cheaper, it is not an alternative.

Transition phase
Timeframes for development and approval can vary widely depending on the customer and the application. However, it can be assumed that the market launch of a product based on alternative materials will take at least 5 years, if not more.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Our products find broad application in the Printing area. Further more in special applications/spinning machines in which the main material of the roll (e.g. a transport roll) must be protected against certain media.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Our FKM production waste is collected and sent to a local waste recycling plant for recycling. The same happens with the filters of our exhaust systems, in which residues from the coating process settle. To the best of our knowledge, these materials are sent for thermal recycling or incineration. In addition, there is a kind of closed-loop system/refuse system in the production chain of rollers for the printing industry. At the end of a roller's life, it is picked up by the coater and the "old rubber" is peeled off from reusable core. This ensures that the rubber is returned to the material cycle at the end of its life in accordance with European standards. In this context, the following research results are significant: The predominant end-of-life disposal method for fluoropolymer products in Europe is incineration, which accounts for more than 80% of cases (Beylage 2022). The reassuring finding is that under typical municipal waste incineration conditions in Europe, no significant amount of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) is generated. A mixture of PTFE, PVDF, PFA and FKM was studied. This result allays concerns about possible PFAS emissions and confirms the safety of incineration as a disposal method. Consequently, this approach poses no discernible risk to human health or the environment (Gehrmann 2023). This is also done, for example, in the context of end-of-life vehicle recycling in Germany, where a significant proportion of elastomers are sent for material and energy recovery. About 47% of these materials are recycled as valuable materials, and another 43% are recovered for energy. (Umweltbundesamt 2023). In summary, the multi-faceted approach to end-of-life management of fluoropolymer and fluoroelastomer products in Europe reflects a commitment to responsible waste management and environmental protection. The findings on safe incineration practices for fluoropolymers and other recycling options for fluoroelastomers are contributing to a more sustainable and environmentally conscious approach to handling these materials. These findings are evidence of ongoing efforts to minimize the environmental footprint and improve the recyclability of these valuable materials in the European context. (2023), Pilot-Scale Fluoropolymer Incineration Study: Thermal Treatment of a Mixture of Fluoropolymers under Representative European Municipal Waste Combustor Conditions.

5. Proposed derogations: No, our products are not currently covered by any of the exemptions.  Because we only apply very small layers and do not manufacture products that are made entirely of FKM, we only use small quantities of less than one ton per year.

6. Missing uses: The application fields that are missing for our purpose are especially the "printing industry" and here in particular "offset printing". In addition, the area of rollers in the broader context would have to be covered. This means, for example, machine components that transport a special material. In this context, rollers can be full FKM rollers or rollers that have a non-FKM polymer as substrate and are provided with a covalently bonded layer of FKM.

Our technical molded articles division utilizes FKM compounds for the production of elastomeric products. These vulcanizates find applications in various fields. Many of our products are designed for gas control technology, such as membranes, very high temperatures are encountered. Therefore, it is not possible to replace them with alternatives like HNBR or ECO. "The heat resistance of FKM vulcanizates is the best among all elastomers, with a continuous operating temperature of 200°C and reaching 260°C after 1000 hours of use" [Hof80]. The maintenance of FKM's mechanical properties at high temperatures, when compared to other elastomers, demonstrates its superiority in terms of compression set and sealing force over other rubber types such as NBR, ACM, or FVMQ [Fer08].
The second and largest application area is seals and gaskets used in sealing various media. FKM exhibits excellent resistance to a wide range of chemicals, even at high temperatures compared to other rubber types [Fer08]. Particularly noteworthy is its oil resistance at high temperatures, which is unmatched [Bes13]. Additionally, the maintenance of FKM's mechanical properties after exposure to biofuels remains unbeaten, as shown in a comparative study with VMQ, FVMQ, AEM, ACM, HNBR, and NBR [Wal10].
Furthermore, the aging behavior of FKM is outstanding and surpasses most other rubber types. "FKM vulcanizates are not affected by aging, weathering, or ozone" [Hof80]. In studies examining the aging behavior in hydrogen of TPU, PEEK, PU, and FKM using electron microscopy, thermal analysis, and gas sorption measurements, FKM exhibits the lowest adsorption [Mor22] and is indispensable for the energy transition.

The EU is currently working on the definition of "Polymers of Low Concern". According to the current proposal, polymers are classified as "Polymers of Low Concern" if they meet several specified criteria. These include a molecular weight of more than 1,000 Daltons (Da), the absence of reactive functional groups, the non-existence of cationic structures or the ability to form cations, the restriction to the elements carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, silicon, sulphur, fluorine, chlorine, bromine or iodine, each of which must be covalently bonded to carbon. Environmental Emissions
During the manufacturing of products, vapors from crosslinking chemicals may be released into the air. However, these vapors are also present in all other rubber types with similar crosslinking systems and do not contain volatile components of the actual PFAS/FKM. Generally, the emerging vapors can be effectively treated through exhaust systems and filtration units. Throughout the process chain from rubber compounding to the final product, both unvulcanized and vulcanized waste may be generated. These waste materials are thermally processed by external companies under the standard conditions of European municipal waste incinerators. This process does not result in the production of harmful PFAS compounds [Geh23].
"The results confirm that fluoropolymers, when incinerated at the end of their life under representative European municipal incinerator conditions, do not emit measurable levels of PFAS and thus do not pose a risk to human health and the environment."
In the study, a mixture of PTFE, PVDF, PFA and FKM was analysed, thus closing the knowledge gap mentioned in the proposal to restrict PFAS. [Loh20]:
"The municipal incineration of fluoropolymer waste has not been shown to produce any deleterious degradation products."

We feel that certain components such as o-rings, seals are not very clearly identified with alternative options, especially these in PTFE, PVDF and FKM or FFKM.


Environmental emissions

General Comments: Scope or restriction option analysis:
In machine tools pneumatic and hydraulic functions are used with the support of different sealing elements in order to be able to realize rotational and linear movements without leakage losses. PFAS are used for this purpose whenever extreme conditions such as high or low temperatures, high frictional resistance or aggressive chemical conditions, e.g. due to cooling lubricants, require it.

Other areas of application include the refrigerants used today in machine tools which are used in closed circuits of the cooling units.

Further areas of application for PFAS-containing design elements are bush bearings and also movable cover systems in machine tools, which separate the interior (machining environment) from the rest of the machine and at the same time compensate for the movement of the axes through their mobility.

In pneumatic applications these are primarily pretensioned PTFE seals in cylinder systems, support and guide elements, and rotary seals. Here leaks, increased friction and also wear have a considerable influence on the accuracy and energy efficiency of the machine.

In hydraulic systems, these are primarily static (O-rings) as well as dynamic sealing elements (rotary shaft seals, lip seals, rotating seals), which today run at circumferential speeds of up to 50 m/s and can only function over the service life of a machine tool due to their high thermal stability, high resistance and chemical resistance, and thus also make a significant contribution in terms of energy efficiency and sustainability through significantly longer service life.

Hazard or exposure:
Fluoropolymers like PTFE are commonly regarded to meet the key internationally recognised safety criteria of the OECD for “polymers low concern (plc)”. This means that they are chemically stable, non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water soluble and non-mobile. For these reasons, fluoropolymers are also suitable, for example, as materials for food contact, in medical applications or in the production of high-purity active pharmaceutical ingredients (e.g. vaccines). Therefor the competent authorities of the United Kingdom claim that fluoropolymers, fluoroelastomers and monomers for manufacturing of these do not need to be restricted at all! We demand from the competent authorities of the European Economic Area (EEA) to take over this scientific and simply reasonable approach.”

Environmental emissions:
The above-described applications of PFAS in machine tools do not emit any pollutants due to organized end-of-life recycling and closed-loop systems, abrasion does not enter the environment.

Baseline:
Bans on PFAS in machine tools create significant limitations in terms of service life, leak tightness, friction, energy consumption, sustainability, safety as well as spare parts supply in older designs/machines.
This also includes a considerable number of spare parts requiring specific special forms.

Information on alternatives:
All the above-mentioned PFAS elements in pneumatic and hydraulic applications do not have adequate substitutes today and lead to significant losses in quality and safety in our systems. From our point of view, in-depth investigations are required in order to be able to achieve a comparable status here.
Alternative refrigerants with low GWP are explosive and therefore associated with increased, non-permissible risks, especially in machines with large cooling systems and multiple interlinked machines.

Transitional period:
Transition periods are mandatory for all PFAS in machine tools, even if the deadlines for this must be agreed with the manufacturers of the end products we use.
A transition period of 12 years for systems delivered from 2025 is not sufficient to meet our obligations to our customers. An adjustment is imperative here.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Phase1 (manufacturing phase) --> Products with PFAS are used/installed in our machines as a finished product, no emissions are generated in the process. Phase 2 (Use phase) --> No significant emissions are generated, neither in static nor in dynamic applications. Phase 3 (End of Life) --> In the presence of organized recycling, no emissions are generated. The proportion that can be treated by incineration, landfill and recycling is 100%.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Scope or restriction option analysis:
The restriction proposal of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) currently under evaluation by the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) applies to a large group of chemicals that fulfill the criteria of the most recent PFAS definition by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD, 2021).
In the pharmaceutical industry, fluorinated substances represent an important group of drugs and about 30% of all active pharmaceutical ingredients (API) contains fluorine (de la Torre & Albericio, 2023; O’Hagan, 2010). An API is the active substance in a pharmaceutical formulation administered to medical patients and is the molecule that is used to treat a certain condition or disease. Fluorinated moieties are frequently incorporated in APIs to enhance specific properties, potentially making these APIs meet the PFAS definition. Time-unlimited derogations are proposed for APIs as they are already regulated by other legislations (Directive 2001/83/EC and EC 726/2004). Nonetheless, the manufacturing process of an API consists of a multitude of steps involving other fluorinated substances, such as starting materials, solvents, reagents and polymeric materials. These are all categorized as PFAS and are within the scope of the restriction proposal, but are essential for API synthesis. A time-unlimited derogation for APIs will therefore only be sensible when the use of fluorinated substances in API manufacturing is derogated as a whole.

Hazard or exposure: Confidential information on this topic is provided in the attachment.

Environmental emissions:
As a company manufacturing active pharmaceutical ingredients and its registered starting materials, the ICH Harmonised Tripartite Guideline for Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) is applied in order to meet the quality and purity requirements for Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients. Since the manufacturing and use of intermediates is performed in multipurpose installations, in which sometimes highly toxic and/or volatile substances, such as azides, are applied, the set-up of the installation essentially requires closed equipment. The purpose and efficacy of APIs also requires that formation and/or contamination of the final product by undesired impurities is avoided by all means. This can be achieved by charging/discharging the isolated intermediates or APIs by means of continuous liners, gloveboxes, use of inflatable bellows when connecting bags to the manhole of reactors etc., but also by performing the various synthesis steps under strictly controlled conditions; the latter is by definition required as the process steps in closed reactors are conducted under inert conditions (i.e. N2-atmosphere, vacuum). Hence, it can be concluded that application of strictly controlled conditions during the production of isolated intermediates and APIs prevents any exposure or interaction between substance and workers/environment.
It should be noted that emissions to air and water, including type and frequency of monitoring, are regulated by the local, national and European environmental legislation, incorporating Directive 2010/75/EU on Industrial Emission (IED) by implementing the Best Available Techniques (BAT). The specific “license to operate” conditions are part of company’s environmental permit. In addition, operation under GMP requires that analytical quality checks are conducted on waste streams (filtrates, phase separations). Liquid streams that are loaded with the product or other hazardous/persistent substances are shipped to certified off-site waste processors. Solid waste streams that are potentially contaminated by an isolated intermediate (e.g. packaging materials such as bags, drums, PPE that were worn during the handling of the material) are collected in closed bags, placed in closed containers for chemical waste and also destroyed off-site by certified waste processors. In addition, preventive, predictive & periodic maintenance (PPPM) is implemented for daily, weekly, monthly or yearly time-based inspection to assure the integrity of the equipment.

Information on alternatives:
In order to make APIs containing a CF2- or CF3- moiety, the functional group(s) must be incorporated into the molecule at a given point during API synthesis. This fluorination is generally never executed in the final API-forming step since fluorination typically requires harsh conditions and would be an unselective reaction, forming many impurities, and would additionally destroy the API molecule. Therefore, fluorination in the final step of API synthesis is not compatible with the very complex and sensitive structure of APIs. The introduction of the CF2- or CF3-group is typically done using a relatively simple molecule (a commodity chemical or a simple building block) already containing the functionality very early in the synthesis. As a result, many different starting materials and intermediates containing the same functionality of concern are required to manufacture the target drug.
In order to be able to synthesize a fluorinated API (proposed derogation in the restriction proposal) without the use of a fluorinated starting material and the formation of fluorinated intermediates, it would require fluorination on the API molecule itself. For the abovementioned reasons (i.e. harsh fluorochemical reactions on a sensitive API molecule), this would technically be extremely challenging, if not unfeasible.
Fluorinated reagents and solvents are chosen for their unique properties. In many cases, alternative chemistry will therefore be suboptimal and less efficient. The solubility of some intermediates in a fluorinated solvent, for example, can be several orders of magnitude higher compared to the solubility in traditional non-fluorinated solvents (e.g. ethyl acetate). Specific information can be found in the confidential attachment of this comment.
Less efficient chemistry would imply a lower manufacturing yield and consequently the manufactured drugs will become more expensive for the patient as more resources are needed for the same yield. Furthermore, increased resources (e.g. higher volumes of less efficient reagents and solvents) will drastically increase the amount of generated waste. The latter is in contrast to the ambitions of companies and EU authorities to reduce the CO2 impact of manufacturing. In contrast, if the use of a fluorinated reagent or solvent reduces waste and the CO2 footprint, this might be a beneficial scenario.

Information on costs:
The whole process of changing the chemistry (from fluorinated to non-fluorinated) carries considerable costs. If a change of a fluorinated reagent or solvent into a non-fluorinated alternative would be sufficiently successful in the laboratory, a resubmission of the filing of the drug is required (European Medicines Agency, 2000).
The pharmaceutical market is a market that is highly protected in the interest of the patient’s safety. Authorities such as the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for EU, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for US, and the Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency (PDMA) for Japan, together with many other governmental authorities strive to maximize assurance that the patient is taking drugs that are safe. To this aim, companies are requested to provide authorities with extensive dossiers and information, which is called the filing of a pharmaceutical product. Such a filing carries a cost of at least € 1 million, and this amount increases with the number of markets where the dossier is submitted. Typically, the submission process is slow and time-consuming: authorities review the dossier very thoroughly, often ask questions triggering more development work, and moreover request that major changes to a manufacturing process are re-submitted. In addition, it is possible that specific process redevelopment steps will be required. E.g. if the process change results in a changed impurity profile, including new trace impurities in the API, a number of toxicity tests will need to be repeated.
Overall, a process change will require at least 3 years of work and will result in a cost estimated around € 2.8 to 3.6 million. The latter represents a best-case scenario and is most likely a serious underestimation of the actual costs.
Besides these high cost for the API developer/manufacturer, the cost for the pharmaceutical industry will be even higher. Based on the estimated Research & Development costs for a new medicine, which range between US$ 1 and 3 billion (Simoens & Huys, 2021), a conservative process development cost is estimated to be 10% of the total development cost, i.e. US$ 100-300 million.
The redevelopment cost for the pharmaceutical companies is lower than the development cost, but there is also the cost of double synthetic routing for the pharmaceutical industry and cost of non-valorization of the intellectual property (IP). The latter two processes are estimated to amount to tens of millions, if not even more. In total, the cost for the pharmaceutical industry is expected to be in the order of magnitude of US$ 100 million. This cost is not economically manageable or responsible and will force the pharmaceutical companies to take the process and drug manufacturing to non-EU countries, a strategy which will not require redevelopment and/or toxicological risk.

Other SEA issues:
EU-based suppliers will be directly impacted by the current PFAS restriction proposal. In case of a PFAS restriction as currently drafted (according to restriction option 1 or 2), manufacturing of derogated APIs will not be possible since:
1) the manufacture, placing on the market (including imports), use and release of PFAS as building blocks, intermediates, reagents and solvents in API manufacturing will be prohibited within the EU/EEA;
2) the manufacture, placing on the market (including imports), use and release of fluoropolymers, essential to the (bio)pharmaceutical industry due to their resistance properties, will be prohibited within the EU/EEA.
As a consequence, the EU-based supply of life-saving medicine to patients would be discontinued and, in many cases, leaving no alternative drug for the patient.
A restriction on the manufacture, placing on the market (including imports), use and release of fluorinated building blocks, intermediates, reagents, solvents and fluoropolymers essential to API manufacturing would greatly impact the EU pharmaceutical supply chain. Non-EU manufacturers will still be able to use these substances, endangering industrial drug manufacture within the EU (Tyrrell, 2023) and increasing the dependence of the EU on foreign supply chains. This is in contrast with the recent EU strategy on increased resilience and robustness of EU pharmaceutical supply chains and the reduction of direct dependence on API and drug manufacturing in non-EU countries, a weakness which was already exposed before and during the COVID pandemic (European Commission, 2023).
Finally, it is expected that the discontinuation of API manufacturing involving PFAS will have a severe negative impact on employment in the EU, as many companies may relocate their industrial activities outside the EU.

Request for exemption:
A time-unlimited derogation for APIs as currently described in the PFAS restriction is not feasible and meaningless unless all associated development and manufacturing processes are derogated simultaneously. Therefore, a time-unlimited derogation is required for all uses of PFAS related to the development and production of APIs, including manufacture, placing on the market (including imports), use and release of starting materials, intermediates, reagents, solvents and fluoropolymers. This derogation is required to assure EU-based manufacturing and supply of these APIs, and ultimately life-saving medicines, to patients in the medium- to long term.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Sector: pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical industry  Time-unlimited derogations are proposed for APIs. The manufacturing process of an API consists of a multitude of steps involving other fluorinated substances, such as starting materials, solvents, reagents and polymeric materials. All these (sub-)uses are essential for API synthesis but are missing in the current restriction proposal.

6. Missing uses: -Building blocks and intermediates used in API manufacturing -Solvents used in API manufacturing -Reagents used in API manufacturing -Polymeric materials essential to production of APIs  For specific information, we refer to the confidential attachment.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: For information on this topic, we refer to the confidential attachment.

8. Other identified uses: For information on this topic, we refer to the confidential attachment.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Scope or restriction option analysis:
We are quite surprised that the chemical industry has not been considered at all when looking at the derogations of the PFAS ban in Table 9. We do not produce PFAS, nor do we use them as an additive, but the presence of PFAS in our plants is very important for environmental protection and occupational safety.
We do not agree with the proposal of a full PFAS ban (RO1). We favor the ban with use-specific derogation (RO2). In our specific case, we prefer a time-unlimited use of PFAS. We produce titanium dioxide under strongly acidic and high temperature conditions. No alternatives for that conditions exist.
Hazard or exposure:
There is no direct danger to our employees from PFAS. The opposite is the case: thanks to PTFE and FKM, our systems remain tight and are not attacked by the aggressive chemicals. The protection of the employees from leakages due to strongly acidic media is guaranteed.
Environmental emissions:
PFAS do not pose a direct threat to the environment. The opposite is the case: thanks to PTFE and FKM, our systems remain tight and are not attacked by the aggressive chemicals.
Request for exemption:
The PFAS ban should be accompanied by restrictions (RO2: ban with use-specific derogations) that should be worked out individually for the specific areas of the chemical industry. Plants that manufacture products under conditions requiring high temperatures and strongly acidic media should be allowed to continue using PTFE and FKM.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: We produce titanium dioxide, which is a white pigment mainly used in coatings and plastics. The pigment gives the products not only colour but protection against weathering, making these products durable. Aggressive media with strongly acidic pH values and high temperatures are used in our plant. To prevent the equipment from corroding and to keep it tight, our equipment contains PFAS in coatings and seals. We mainly use PTFE and FKM in pipes, pumps, fittings and seals. In addition, we produce copperas as a by-product, which is essential for drinking and waste water treatment. With 350 000 tonnes of copperas per year, we supply drinking and waste water treatment plants as the largest copperas producer in Germany.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: b: PFAS components in plant parts are separated from the metal during disposal and are prepared for incineration with energy recovery.

6. Missing uses: b: We mainly use PTFE and FKM in pipes, pumps, fittings and seals. d: There is no alternative for PTFE and FKM available for our specific purposes. We work partly with concentrated acids and with temperatures of 150 °C. g: A complete PFAS ban without alternatives for PTFE and FKM would most likely lead to the closure of the plant, as there are no alternatives to PTFE and FKM and we would no longer be able to comply with the legal requirements of immission protection and occupational health and safety.  We employ 350 people at our plant and the city of Nordenham receives trade tax from us. Furthermore, we are a client for small and medium-sized, regional companies. There are permanently 30 external company employees on site. During major maintenance shutdowns, there are even 120 external company employees. Our expenditure on external companies amounts to about 20 million per year. Closing the plant would severely weaken the region economically. Our plant belongs to the critical infrastructures according to § 2 (10) BSIG. In view of the current shortage of precipitants, the warning level orange has been declared for the area of wastewater treatment. Since our plant produces the precipitant copperas, a shutdown of our plant would endanger the supply of the wastewater plants and drinking water treatment plant.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: An alternative to PTFE is UHMW-PE. The chemical resistance is comparable to PTFE. The mechanical strength is even better than that for PTFE. Only the temperature is limited. Since the melting point of UHMW-PE is 130°C, a maximum temperature of 85°C is recommended for use. For our company, however, the use of UHMW-PE is out of the question, as we need a temperature resistance of up to 150°C for certain plant components. Without the heat resistance of PTFE, we cannot maintain the tightness of plant components. It is therefore very important that alternatives to PFAS are tested for specific use in the chemical industry.

8. Other identified uses: see number 7.

General Comments: Scope or restriction option analysis:
We strongly oppose the broad definition of PFAS used in this restriction proposal. The inclusion of fluoropolymers within this proposal will risk to miss the more important goal of restricting un-necessary PFAS used in our clothes and cosmetic products, worn and used by consumers.

Fluoropolymers are used in an extremely wide range of industrial products. The choice of fluoropolymers are often done based on data from literature and/or in combination with knowledge from earlier experiences, hence it is rare that the choice is based in extensive studies and comparison between different materials. Due to the unique combination of properties of Fluoropolymers, it is often the only tested, suitable and approved material.

It is therefore very unfortunate that this very common way of working has been so totally neglected and not understood by the authorities behind this proposal and also behind the questions and unrealistic requirements of documents comparison studies behind the choice of fluoropolymers.

With that said, we sincerely hope that the very many participants and calls from the fluoropolymer industry will be heard and taken into account, even though there may not always be extensive studies and academic reports supporting these statements, but instead decades of knowledge and experience in these low and medium size companies.

Additionally, the possible risk reduction with restricting fluoropolymers is not proportional to the potential gain, which is supported in existing life cycle analysis. The restriction does hence not respect the principle of proportionality regarding risk versus consequence, based on the many documented evidence of fluoropolymers as polymers of low concern.

The fact that fluoropolymers are neither bioaccumulation nor toxic, supports that they should not be part of this suggested restriction.

Hazard or exposure:
PTFE is not bioaccumulative and not toxic and it does not degrade to smaller PFAS-substances in the environment. In regular municipal incineration plants, PTFE will be completely demineralized.

In order to handle the remaining concern in the life cycle of fluoropolymers, responsible manufacturing, in all stages of the supply chain, would in an efficient way minimize any emissions to air and water. There are already very good examples of what the industry is doing and planning to do, to continue this work. We believe that it is very important that we can keep these industries in Europe, run and controlled by responsible actors, instead of letting the manufacturing and processing of fluoropolymers be made in our regions where environmental control may not be as controlled as in Europe.

Environmental emissions:
By responsible manufacturing, the industries in all different steps could increase their awareness and control of emissions during the process. By controlling all air and water emissions in regards to PFAS compounds, fluoropolymers could still be manufactured and used without any unacceptable risk for our environment and peoples health.

There are already today, possibilities to purify water with carbon filters and to recue air emissions with high temperature incineration. These are both well proven and used techniques.

Org. name: TRUMPF Lasersystems for Semiconductor Manufacturing GmbH
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Scope or restriction Options Analysis
TRUMPF Lasersystems For Semiconductor Manufacturing Gmbh is aware of the legitimate concerns about PFAS and supports the EU plan. We are committed to fully replacing PFAS in our products. We are already seeking to use alternatives to PFAS in applications where substitution is possible.

Our company supplies essential equipment that is needed for chip production, so called Semiconductor and Related Manufacturing Equipment (SMRE). That is why we are in the "Semiconductor industry".

Restriction option 1 (RO1) of the restriction proposal, an unlimited full ban on PFAS, would be a very harmful for the entire industry.
Therefore, we prefer Option 2: Ban with use-specific, time-limited derogations. and plead for a derogation for SMREs at least for 13,5 EiF.

We are investing heavily in the development of alternative materials to be able to completely replace PFAS in the future. But this takes time.

At present there is no alternative to PFAS in many of our applications due to their unique properties.


However, and even with the derogation for 13.5 years of EiF, it is not certain that we will find an adequate replacement for all applications.

We would like to take this opportunity to clarify a few points according to our understanding:

1. “Semiconductor Manufacturing Process” and SMREs

In our understanding, the "semiconductor manufacturing process" includes all steps of the semiconductor value chain: from the process of the chemicals needed to produce the raw material to semiconductor manufacturing equipment and devices, and those used in the manufacturing process.

This also includes any systems, hardware, device assemblies or improvements for or in the context of manufacturing, assembling, or testing a semiconductor device.
“The Semiconductor Manufacturing Process includes all the direct and indirect equipment and materials required to manufacture semiconductor "chips". [PFAS Explainer - Semiconductor Manufacturing and Markets | SEMI]

2. Discrepancy with existing regulations

Furthermore, we would like to point out a possible discrepancy with existing regulations:
The wording in point 2 "shall not be placed in the market" differs from the wording in REACH and RoHS.
The phrase "first time" has a significant impact on compliance. The absence of this implies that the re-placing on the market of used machines, as well as spare parts to extend the service life of existing machines, fall under this restriction of PFAS and must therefore meet the conditions.
Even though the "Blue Guide on the implementation of EU product rules 2022" does not officially cover REACH, a coherent approach should be taken here, and repairs and changes should be covered in the same way.
In detail, this would mean that these products, used machines and spare parts, would not be considered new and would therefore not be affected by the restriction.
This would extend the lifespan of existing products and significantly reduce the number of machines that would have to be disposed of due to a lack of spare parts.

1. Definition of "harsh conditions"

Note on paragraph 5s: The definition of "harsh conditions" for lubricants should also include "ultrapure/ ultraclean condition" and “vacuum”, which is also a critical environment for the semiconductor industry.
2. Inadequate harmonized classification complicates information gathering

Even though we are trying very hard to identify our PFAS applications and to substitute PFAS where possible, we are facing a challenge.
Like other companies in machinery industry, we are in the middle of the supply chain.
However, we rely on supplier information to identify the extent of the impact.
The inadequate harmonized classification of PFAS in the CLP Regulation means no disclosure of information (e.g. via the safety data sheet), which makes the analysis of the impact time-consuming and in many cases impossible. To obtain information along the supply chains, conclusive lists of the substances concerned, including CAS numbers, would be required. [Position paper VDMA 23.05.2023 Memo (vdma.org)]
However, even with harmonized classification, gathering information is difficult, as there is currently no law on the information of PFASs and suppliers are therefore not obliged to inform us about them.
3. Complexity of the equipment

In addition to the transfer of information in the supply chain, the complexity of our equipment also poses a challenge in the identification of PFAS:
For a company like TRUMPF Lasersystems For Semiconductor Manufacturing Gmbh, which relies on over 300 suppliers, and a system which contains nearly than 500.000 parts, gathering information on PFAS substances that are not yet regulated is a major challenge. The majority of PFAS used are not yet listed in the SVHC list. Accordingly, there is no legal basis for obtaining the necessary information from suppliers. And even if the suppliers are willing to cooperate, they face the same challenges with their suppliers and do not receive the necessary information. This is especially true for our suppliers in the electronics sector.

Environmental emissions

In general, our products are made for semiconductor industry only – therefore, they are handled by trained personnel under controlled conditions.

They are manufactured, used and disposed of in a controlled environment in accordance with applicable regulations.

Description of analytical methods

The analytical methods for detecting are still inadequate. Also, the methods listed in Annex E4 do not include all possible PFAS that may occur in our products.

In order to be able to make a well-founded statement about the presence of PFAS, we cannot rely solely on analytical methods. We also rely on detailed information along the supply chain. Which presents us with great challenges.

Information on alternatives

Although some alternatives in Appendix E2 can offer comparable properties to fluoropolymers, they are not replaceable for several key applications.

In many use cases for TRUMPF Lasersystems for Semiconductor Manufacturing Gmbh, a combination of the properties of fluoropolymers are used, which the alternatives cannot cover.

We replace Fluoropolymers in new developments wherever possible, but a 1:1 replacement is often not possible due to the unique environmental and performance requirements of our industry.

It can take more than a decade to develop an alternative with no guarantee that it will meet the requirements of performance, health and safety, raw materials, energy, and water consumption, etc. The transition period should reflect this.
Assuming we find viable alternatives for specific applications, it will take approx. 10 years to develop industrialized PFAS-free designs.

And yet, even after this time, there can be no guarantee that a viable alternative will be found that meets the requirements.

If no suitable alternatives can be found, we will no longer be able to produce our equipment, which means that the entire EUV system for the semiconductor industry can no longer be produced and operated. This would be a big step backwards for the global, but especially for the European, semiconductor industry.

In addition, the semiconductor supply chain is highly specialized, which may further impact schedules if alternatives were not available in sufficient quantities to meet demand.

Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues

The semiconductor industry serves a number of key applications and end-user markets that are crucial to the global economy and to managing Europe's environmental and digital transformation, e.g., power generation, healthcare, communications and mobility.

A blanket ban, or a limited derogation, would have profound negative consequences for the global competitiveness of the European economy and European citizens.

We hope that, based on the research and the evidence provided, the importance of the semiconductor manufacturing process would be recognized, including its entire supply chain, as a critical building block of the European Union’s future prosperity and strategic autonomy on the global stage.

Transitional period

Similarly, to the Semiconductor Process, we strongly advocate a 13.5 years derogation for SMRE for after EIF.

TRUMPF Lasersystems for Semiconductor Manufacturing Gmbh wants to meet the deadline of 13.5 years EiF and until then identify and substitute all PFAS where possible.
During this transition period, we can develop an understanding of which alternatives are suitable, as well as the research needs and timeframes.

Given the challenges of our industry, we ask the regulators to provide a formal mechanism to extend or renew exemptions (currently possible under the RoHS directive) in case a PFAS alternative is not feasible within set derogation times.

Request for exemption

We guarantee a 7-year lifetime for our systems. However, our systems will continue to be operated for a long time beyond that, as long as they can be used in an economically viable way.
We have been delivering systems since 2012 and approx. 90% of the delivered systems are still in use. This is only possible if we can supply the right spare parts at any time and continue to use used machines efficiently.

The replacement of fluoropolymers in spare parts and maintenance parts would require the fundamental redesign including all cost with it and we cannot guarantee the redesign would maintain the existing performance or allow existing products to function properly.

If the PFAS ban would apply to spare parts, we would not be able to ensure that our active systems could be supplied with the appropriate spare parts, as often a new development and change of infrastructure would be necessary for alternatives.

If the spare parts can no longer be supplied, we expect that after 2-3 months of usage, the systems would no longer be able to be operated and would have to be disposed of.

Maintenance parts intended for use in existing products also significantly extend the service life of the systems.

An exemption for spare parts and maintenance parts is therefore necessary in terms of sustainability, efficient use of resources and economic efficiency (repair as produced principle). Used machines produced before EiF also need an exemption. These are to be granted for an unlimited period or at least for a much longer period than the transitional periods currently planned.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: TRUMPF Lasersystems For Semiconductor Manufacturing Gmbh produces an essential part of the EUV lithography system for the semiconductor industry.  Thus, our products fall under the definition of Semiconductor and Related Manufacturing Equipment (SMRE). In our understanding, we therefore also fall under semiconductor sector and sub-use (please see section III Scope or restriction option analysis).  If SMREs are not included in the semiconductor sub-use, as assumed so far, they represent a missing use (see Q6).  We also make use of other sub-uses, e.g.  • Lubricants  • Metal plating and manufacture of metal products  • Applications of fluorinated gases

6. Missing uses: a. The annual tonnage and emissions (at sub-sector) and type of PFAS associated with the relevant use  Semiconductor and Related Manufacturing Equipment (SMRE) using PFAS containing articles, especially polymeric PFAS.  SMREs are complex systems. Our Laser Amplifier contains nearly 500.000 parts [EUV Drive Laser | TRUMPF].  Emissions are typically during EOL: Decommission takes place in a controlled and regulated way according to local regulations.  b. The key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use. In our machine, mainly fluoropolymers, a subgroup of PFAS, are used. These fluoropolymers have several unique properties and a combination of them are absolutely essential for many applications, e.g. purity, chemical resistance, dielectric properties, mechanical and optical properties. For a more detailed description, please check the confidential appendix for a list of selected use cases where we go into detail about the applications and functionality of the PFAS.  Here are some of the major properties for TRUMPF Lasersystems For Semiconductor Manufacturing Gmbh products which are critical: 1. Outgassing: Outgassing results in a release of contaminants that are damaging for mirrors and lenses used in state-of-the-art photolithographic systems.  Semiconductor manufacturing facilities have very strict cleanliness requirements as its essential for the process. Fluoropolymers are known to release much less of organic and inorganic contaminants than other polymers. In fact, it has been observed that the use of other materials can cause (permanent) damage to our optics. 2. Dielectric properties PTFE is an electrical isolator with high temperature resistance, good creepage and prevents arcing, so it is often used as holders, distance holders and other isolator parts for electronic parts. 3. Resistance to radiation (RF) High-frequency electromagnetic radiation is generated in the Laser Amplifier. The materials used must be resistant to this radiation to ensure both machine safety and human safety. 4. Thermal stability In our systems, temperatures can exceed 200°C, these must withstand the materials without loss of performance, otherwise safety issues can occur (e.g. gas leakage). 5. Low friction  The use of PFAS, especially as a sealing material, also serves not only machine safety but also human safety, as it prevents toxic laser gases from escaping into the service area.  Due to the extreme conditions (vacuum, high voltage, radiation, high temperatures), PFASs, especially fluoropolymers, are irreplaceable in our products today, as there are no alternatives for the required properties.   c. The number of companies in the sector estimated to be affected by the restriction. So far, communication about the presence of PFASs within the supply chain is not required by law. This makes it very difficult for SMRE manufacturers to find out how many companies are affected.  Indirectly, the impact on the ecosystem can be determined from the ESIA report: “The European semiconductor ecosystem supports approx. 200.000 jobs directly and up to 1.000.000 induced jobs in systems, applications and services in Europe [Semiconductor industry forecast, ESIA, Nov. 2022].” TRUMPF Lasersystems For Semiconductor Manufacturing Gmbh itself has about 300 suppliers, but it is not possible for us to find out how many of them will be affected by the restriction. D. The availability, technical and economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives for the relevant use, including information on the extent (in terms of market shares) to which alternative-based products are already offered on the EU market, and whether any shortages in the supply of relevant alternatives, are expected. The listed substances in Appendix E2 are not in all applications (use cases) a technical alternative, because a combination of properties is required, e.g. outgassing and resistance to RF radiation. For more detailed examples, please check the confidential appendix for a list of selected use cases where we go into detail about the applications and alternatives.   Where alternatives in specific use cases are feasible (ie PEEK or PC) those alternatives are already integrated within new designs or development projects are already planned.  In addition, the use of PFASs is particularly relevant to safety in sealing applications. The seals separate the gas compartment, where toxic laser gases are present, from the ambient air. This is particularly important, as otherwise the toxic laser gas can accumulate inside the system and the service area and endanger the lives of service engineers and operators. Unfortunately, none of the substances listed in Appendix E2 have the necessary properties to provide the required gas tightness in the environment (clean room, radiation, vacuum, high temperatures, corrosive gases) to ensure safety.  e. For cases in which alternatives are not yet available, information on the status of R&D processes for finding suitable alternatives, including the extent of R&D initiatives in terms of time and/or financial investments, the likelihood of successful completion, the time expected to be required for substitution (including any relevant certification or regulatory approvals) and the major challenges encountered with alternatives which were considered but subsequently disregarded If alternatives are not available, only an estimation can be given for the timeline: A time frame of 5 to 25 years is within the scope of possibility. „ For some applications, it is not currently possible to demonstrate that a non-PFAS alternative can fulfil the application-specific performance requirements. In these cases, it may be necessary to invent and synthesize new chemicals, and/or develop alternative approaches to device fabrication that provides the necessary electrical and computational performance. Invention is an open-ended endeavor without a fixed timeline or guarantee of success.” [SIA PFAS Consortium The Impact of a Potential PFAS Restriction on the Semiconductor Sector, RINA, 2023]  Aspects such as the following further increase the uncertainty of the timelines. [SIA PFAS Consortium The Impact of a Potential PFAS Restriction on the Semiconductor Sector, RINA, 2023]: - Technical aspects: • The alternative may not be a drop-in replacement and alternative design changes need to be made, solution may not be backward compatible to designs of equipment which are already in service. • The technical requirements at each stage must be met and may require multiple iterations of testing and development. • The solution may not address the long-term reliability of the alternative, which may only introduce additional design needs or technical limitations once the alternative has been used for a considerable length of time. • The solution may need to be qualified by a certified body which can add additional time. - Supplier factors: • Difficulties in identifying a new supplier and their qualification can add considerable additional time to envisaged timeline  • The alternative substance needs to be available in sufficient quantities to meet demand.  • The supply chain for semiconductors can be narrow and varied, and highly, highly specialized. An impact to any one of these unique supply chain elements can have dramatic impacts to downstream customers. For instance, only a handful of chemical suppliers have the research and materials capability to support the critical lithographic materials needed for the entire semiconductor industry. - Delays in testing: Unavailability of testing labs due to the expected increase in the demand for testing of other applications/alternatives, or delays in receiving test material from supplier or prototypes for testing. - Environmental: PFAS articles are exposed to hazardous substances during use which might contaminate the proposed alternatives differently, and thus impact recyclability. Therefore, alternative waste management streams would need to be identified.  - Technical resources: Significant additional specialized highly educated technical resources will be required in the innovation and commercialization of PFAS replacement materials. As such there may be additional time required to recruit and train additional people.   As example; We use hoses with PTFE inlay for water supply. New materials must be tested from scratch. New hoses need to be qualified (TOC, chemical stability), perhaps adjust frequency of water conditioning. New pressure drop, new flow, possibly significantly higher costs due to special solutions, because we have to put new hoses in the current available volume. Otherwise even higher effort to change surrounding (thickness, connections, avoidance of volume conflicts with other components).  A sufficiently long transition time is crucial to ensure proper research into alternatives.  f. For cases in which substitution is technically and economically feasible but more time is required to substitute: It is difficult to provide data at company level on this in the short time available, as this is influenced by various factors.  But, according to a study by RINA on the impact of a PFAS restriction on the semiconductor sector, it could take from 3 to more than 10 years to develop, qualify and implement alternatives when an existing non-PFAS alternative is available or may be viable. If a non-PFAS alternative is available that does not require changes to the infrastructure and if it meets the technical requirements, then it can be expected that it will take at least 3 to 4 years before this alternative can go into high-volume manufacturing .“ [SIA PFAS Consortium The Impact of a Potential PFAS Restriction on the Semiconductor Sector, RINA, 2023]. g. For cases in which substitution is not technically or economically feasible, information on what the socio-economic impacts would be for companies, consumers, and other affected actors. General Comments: Scope or restriction options analysis:
Although the actual proposal report contains a high number of sectors and uses for PFASs, there are sectors and uses missing which concern our company and surely also a lot of other companies.
PFASs are actually used in a wide range of machinery parts, like seals, O-rings, gaskets, tubing and pipes, expansion joints and sensors.
One of the most important part / application type for our company is seals made from fluoropolymers, like FKM, FEPM, FFKM or PTFE. Those seals are often used in contact with different mineral or synthetic oils and have to withstand temperatures that go far beyond the temperature resistance of non-PFFASs-containing rubbers like HNBR. The excellent combination of high temperature resistance (up to 300 °C) and substance compability is needed in our and other hightech machinery. The fluoroelastomers in particular additionally offer mechanical properties required for use as O-rings or flexible media connections.
Since our machinery processes material with up to 400 °C, the option to seal heating and lubricating oils at high temperatures is vital.
The use of fluoropolymers for machinery parts like seals is underrepresented in the actual restriction proposal. Seals are only mentioned in specific sector / uses, like „Food“, „Petrolium and mining“, „Transport“, „Thread sealing tape“. Machinery parts are not mentioned. In addition, no exemption from the ban is planned for this application.
Derogations proposed for the sectors mentioned above range from 5 years (Industrial food and feed production) to 12 years (Petrolium and mining – Fluoroploymer applications in general / Transport – Use of PFASs for the proper functioning and safety of vehicles)
We propose that the use of polymeric PFASs as material for machinery parts (like seals, O-rings or flexible joints), at least for the use under harsh conditions, shall either be excluded from the ban or mentioned as additional sector / use in the final draft. This sector could generally be described as machinery parts used in harsh conditions (similar to the mentioned sector and application „Lubricants where the use takes place under harsh conditions“) and should benefit from the longest possible derogation to allow for intensive search for alternatives.

Hazard, exposure and emissions:
The PFASs used by our company (all polymeric PFASs) are not classified as hazardous.
See Excel-table for details.

This sector could generally be described as machinery parts used in harsh conditions (similar to the mentioned sector and application „Lubricants where the use takes place under harsh conditions“) and should benefit from the longest possible derogation to allow for intensive search for alternatives.


Information on alternatives:
Fluoro-elastomers:
According to different main manufacturer and supplier of elastomer seals (e.g. Trelleborg), there is actually no alternative available for fluoroelastomers like FKM, FFKM, FEPM or PTFE. If those materials would be banned, many applications were affected, espacially when a combination of elastic behaviour, high temperature resistance and oil compability is necessary. EPDM and HNBR have been checked as possible alternatives but up to now, with negative results:
- Too low maximum service temperature (up to 150 °C for HNBR / up to 180 °C for EPDM)
- Too little oil compability (No compability with synthetic oils for HNBR / no compability with mineral oils for EPDM, compability with Held-specific synthetic oils unclear).
Search for alternatives at Held continues by means of literature research, supplier and manufacturer discussions and feedback and own tests (e.g. compability and temperature tests).

Information on costs:
See excel table for details

Information on benefits:
According to different sources (e.g. Fluoropolymers Safe Handling (plasticseurope.org)), fluoropolymers don’t share the toxicological properties that are associated with other PFASs, since they are not water nor oil soluble and not cell-compliant.  According to other sources (e.g. „ETC/WMGE Report 9/2021: Fluorinated polymers in a low carbon, circular and toxic-free economy“ https://www.eionet.europa.eu/etcs/etc-wmge/products/fluorinated-polymers-in-a-low-carbon-circular-and-toxic-free-economy/) polymeric PFASs are fully thermally degradaded when incinated properly.
From this follows that we don’t see any benefits in a ban of fluoropolymers.

In general, a ban of polymeric PFASs would have a high impact on the business of our company. Depending on the final decision on derogations, the effects can range from additional costs / less profit to loss of nearly all of our business / turnover.

Our company demands an exemption from the ban for all polymeric PFASs like FKM, FFKM, PTFE, FEPM since they are unsubtitutable materials for vital machinery parts.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Scope:
- The substances jointly included in the proposal are very diverse. Substance properties within this huge group differ a lot. Not for all of them the prerequisites for a REACH restriction are fulfilled, thus the proposal goes beyond the basic principles of REACH and exceeds the given legal framework.
- In particular, if there is no environmental exposure in specific applications and handling or it can be strongly minimised, a ban is not justified.
- A more differentiated assessment and regulatory approach that bans only uses that pose a risk is needed. A use for which no risk is identified must not be covered as a matter of principle.
- With the F gases regulation, the restriction of PFAS in firefighting foams and several restrictions under POP (e.g. PFOS, PFOA), an efficient framework already exists to ban or manage certain uses with identified risks.
- The focus should be placed on the applications with the greatest environmental impact, whereby the entire, possibly global, value chain must be considered. We consider the differentiation between substances of low molecular weight and polymers to be a first target-oriented approach. In the legal text it must be made clear that the entire manufacturing processes of products or uses, which are derogated or exempted from the restriction are not covered by the restriction so that manufacturing in the EU will be still possible.
- Raw materials, precursors and transported intermediates for basic and temporary derogations must explicitly be exempted from the restriction in the legal text.
- The exemption of fully degradable PFASs must be clarified in the legal text. The description in the explanations on the scope of the restriction proposal is not sufficient. Fully degradable PFASs must not be covered by the restriction - regardless of the chemical structure.


Information on benefits: In many cases the use of PFAS has specific benefits due to the specific properties of the single compound.
- In certain cases, they enable safer and environment-friendly processes compared to former processes (e.g. chlorine production).
- They allow to synthesise specific substances under moderate conditions and avoiding unwanted by-products.
- Due to their persistence, they ensure a long and economic service life e.g. in plants or transport or enable the handling at all (harsh conditions, corrosive substances).
- In a lot of processes, the use of specific PFAS is required by other legislation.
- Especially many high-tech applications, productions, and products are highly dependent on the use of certain PFAS as there are no suitable alternatives.
Please see our detailed position, that contains more examples.


Other SEA issues:
- We have the impression that many more very important applications would have to be listed as exemptions and many uses might be missed due to just rising awareness within different industry sectors, especially those without much REACH experience.
- The approach of requiring specific information on potential derogations means a high burden to companies. They have to provide information (preferably in a level of detail equivalent to that of an authorisation dossier and also with a view to the entire value chain) for multiple applications within a very short time. This is not feasible for industry. We consider the approach to be disproportionate and, as we understand it, it contradicts the principle that in the case of a restriction, the responsibility for corresponding information lies with the authorities. The potential derogations must remain as real derogations, even if no extensive data can currently be submitted by industry in the context of the consultation.
- It has to be kept in mind that even if in some cases theoretically other substances can be used or alternative processes applied, this does not mean that such a possible alternative finally is “better”. In due time before the end of the time limit of a derogation, it must be carefully assessed whether suitable alternatives are available and an environmental assessment on these alternatives should be provided. If this is not the case, the derogation must be extended. It must be ensured that no compromises are made with regard to safety, e.g. occupational safety.
- There is great uncertainty on the future use of PFAS in industrial processes and by professionals. With a long-lasting discussion about necessary exceptions, the danger of fatal consequences grows, as decisions on future investments are made at an early stage. Even if a ban finally is not imposed for certain applications in the end the loss of R&D and production in Europe might happen.


Transitional period
- Many applications and end products additionally underlie specific regulations. It has to be ensured, that in case of a ban the time for implementation of the transformation is sufficient and double regulation with existing EU sectorial legislation is avoided.


Request for exemption
- The whole manufacturing process of the excluded products (whether they fall under the definition of PFAS or not) must be exempted. This has to be made clear in the legal text.
- The use of PFAS in plants should be excluded completely. Manufacturing processes and plants underlie multiple regulations and must fulfil strict requirements. A full ban of PFAS would cause severe problems without having positive effects on overall emissions. The production and use of PFAS-containing equipment as well as necessary spare parts must remain possible in the EU.
- The use of PFAS in chemical synthesis, e.g. as catalysts, intermediate or protective group, as well as its use in associated analytical procedures, should be excluded from the restriction. For industrial use the socio-economic impact must take into account both the final products and their uses as well as their production and supply chains. The same applies for well-regulated professional uses and equipment.
- PPORD has to be excluded from the scope of the restriction to further enable research in the EU.
- All potential derogations (marked by [..]) should be kept as real derogations for the above-mentioned reasons.
- There is an urgent need for clarification, which uses were not intended to be included in the scope of the restriction to end uncertainty for investments in the EU industry.

The restriction proposal for PFAS does cover an extremely wide range of chemical compounds including fluoropolymers. For fuel cell systems as well as for green hydrogen production and use there are no proven substitutes known or even available. For lined reactors needed in chemical processing, for special electrical insulation parts and media pipes PTFE and fluoropolymers are essential, too.
A perhaps less known but very essential use of PTFE is industrial dust filtration applications. The reasons for the ongoing need and the lack of alternatives will be explained in detail in the attached files.
