Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Baseline Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Section 1: Introduction
The European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) published the final version of the REACH restriction dossier on Per- and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) on March 22, 2023 (in the following called “the Proposal”).
This initiative by the authorities of the five EU member states Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark and Norway calls for an EU-wide ban on manufacturing, bringing to market, making use of and importing all substances defined as PFAS, which also include all fluoropolymers such as PTFE, FKM and FFKM. The following text is based on the ECHA information note regarding the Annex XV restriction report consultation as well as the ECHA consultation guidance.

Section 2: Organisational information
With operations in more than 25 countries and sales in 140 countries, SPX Flow Inc. is a global company with approximately 4000 employees working in manufacturing sites, innovation centres and service centres in the Americas, Europe/Middle East and Asia/Pacific regions, developing and manufacturing more than 140.000 products for the Food & Beverage market, the Chemical, Pharmaceutical and Medical markets and many industrial applications including Automotive, Marine, Oil & Gas and Construction.

SPX Flow has a vital interest in the use of certain PFAS, such as, but not limited to, PTFE and FKM in the form of O-rings, gaskets, diaphragms, tape and paste to perform sealing and lubrication functions in our machinery products, such as pumps, mixers, homogenizers, heat-exchangers and industrial tools.

Our machinery products are used to process a wide range of fluids, that may be chemically aggressive (acidic, caustic or alkaline) and/or at high-temperature / high pressure, from water-based to oils and fats and from industrial fluids to foodstuff for human consumption. In order to safely process such fluids, warrant the integrity of our machinery, protect the operators and the environment from spillage and first-and-foremost guarantee that no harmful substances may leach into the processed foodstuff, the use of PFAS-based or PFAS-containing components in our machinery is inevitable due to the exceptional properties of these PFAS materials.

Section 3: Non-confidential comments on the Proposal
SPX FLOW has the following concerns with the Proposal:

(i) The restriction Proposal in general
Substances classed as PFAS are defined as any molecular structure with at least one carbon atom being fully fluorinated ( -CH2- or -CH3 ). This definition covers more than 10.000 different substances with different reactive groups, from non-polymeric to polymeric and from toxic and/or possibly carcinogenic to harmless for the human body. Although the Proposal holds an additional transition time for certain applications, the Proposal ultimately treats all PFAS in the same way and does not provide a sufficiently granular distinction between various groups of PFAS.


(ii) Missing specifications to reduce currently accumulated PFAS
PFAS have been in use since the 1940’s and have accumulated in the environment ever since. Evidence suggests that certain PFAS can cause harm to humans, animals and the environment; consequently actions need to be taken to halt the ongoing pollution and to reduce the amount of PFAS that have accumulated. The Proposal fails to provide measures or guidelines establishing an active process to reduce accumulated PFAS in the environment, such as cleaning-out PFAS from sewage water and/or drinking water , as has been proposed by the EPA and for which the nano-filtration technology is readily available.

(iii) Legal position of the Proposal
There are more than 10.000 PFA substances known and in use. Many, but by far not all, of these PFAS are considered to be toxic, carcinogenic and/or otherwise harmful. The vast majority of PFAS are only persistent, but that criteria alone does not substantiate an unacceptable risk to human health or the environment because the presence of such PFAS does not constitute any directly harmful or adverse effect on humans, animals or the environment.

Secondly, for many PFAS that are currently used in critical applications, such as the Food & Beverage industry  in our case, there are no alternatives (yet) available that would both provide the same mechanical / physical performance as PFAS-based components and guarantee the compliance with food-contact requirements regarding migration-limits of certain chemicals and elements.
Since non-harmful PFAS like PTFE and FKM are included in the Proposal in an indifferent approach, the Proposal does not meet the prerequisites for a Community-wide restriction of such substances according to Article 68.1 of the REACH Regulation (EC) 1907/2006 (* unacceptable risk to human health or the environment, * non-availability of alternatives). Consequently, without a clear distinction between harmful and non-harmful substances respectively substances to which there are no application-specific alternatives, the Proposal violates its own legal foundation within the REACH Regulation and is thus not enforceable. (1)

(iv) Lack of alternatives in the Proposal
The Proposal holds provisions for the restriction and/or ban of PFA substances, but it does not include more appropriate alternative measures like collection and recycling of certain PFAS. PFA substances like PTFE or FKM can be collected in separate mono-fraction waste streams. (2) demonstrates that Secondary and Tertiary Recycling (Up-Cycling) of PTFE is technically feasible and will directly support the purpose and provisions of the circular economy.
Through secondary recycling, PTFE can be reduced in chain length to approximately 1% of the original length. The resultant PTFE – Micropowder can then be used as an additive to non-PTFE elastomers to improve their machining, friction and non-stick properties.
The pyrolytic treatment of PTFE and other fluoropolymers under inert-gas atmosphere (tertiary recycling) produces monomer Tetrafluoroethylene and Hexafluoropropylene, which can then be used again in the polymerisation process of new per- and polyfluorinated elastomers.
Both recycling processes will significantly reduce the waste and thus the accumulation of PFAS.

(v) Socio-economic effects of the Proposal
Although the Proposal includes longer transition timelines and additional consultation for certain applications and markets, the restriction of PFAS in certain markets will inevitably affect the availability as well as the global market-price of PFAS such as PTFE & FKM.  Specifically, because PFAS manufacturers are likely to stop producing a broad range, if not all, PFAS long before the end of the transition period, as some have already announced, we foresee that there will not be sufficient PFAS to meet demand through the proposed transition period. Consequently, manufacturers of machinery products and equipment for the Medical as well as the Food & Beverage market, where the development and approval process of alternative materials may take more than a decade, will suffer from supply shortages and increased costs for PFAS-based components, ultimately to the detriment of all EU consumers.
Secondly, and due to the broad restriction of PFAS without alternatives being available and without taking alternative measures into account, the Proposal will place the EU outside of the supply-market for PFAS and may put EU manufacturers of machinery products in a commercially disadvantaged position compared to non-EU manufacturers.

(vi) Loss of performance by substituting materials
Based on the current state of material-science, many applications, especially in the Food & Beverage industry as well as the Chemical and Pharmaceutical industry, will not find alternative non-PFAS materials that have the same or at least approximately similar physical and chemical properties that would make a direct substitution possible. Those inferior alternatives come with an increased risk of failing, for example through leakage and/or through leaching of harmful ingredients. The direct consequences are an increased risk for food safety and thus for public health and, at the same time, the risk of increased cost for the manufacturing as well as for maintenance of affected machinery products. This will make the European marketplace significantly less competitive in the global comparison by adding undue costs and complexity to the sourcing of elastomeric components and the manufacturing & maintenance of machinery products for a wide range of markets and applications.
(vii) Sweeping-blow approach of the Proposal
On the same topic of controlling the manufacturing, bringing to market, making use of and importing of PFAS and consequently combatting the negative impact of PFAS on human & animal health and the environment, other jurisdictions have taken a more moderate and sustainable approach, that not only focuses on specifically harmful substances but also includes measures such as monitoring and reporting of the manufacturing, bringing to market, making use of and importing of PFAS.

PFAS pollution is a global health & environmental issue and thus shall best be dealt with in a coordinated and cooperative global approach rather than a sweeping-blow whilst others are significantly more focused and driven by technical and commercial feasibility.

We insist that fluorocarbon polymers including PTFE and PVDF, used as  filtration media for solid-liquid separation can be used without any safety and health concerns in our applications. In particular, fluorocarbon polymers like PTFE do not show any environmental and toxicological concerns which are observed in PFOS, PFOA, PFNA, PFHxS and others.  Additionally fluorocarbon polymers satisfy standards of low concerned substances specified by OECD.
Filtration membranes which can remove solid particles from turbid water or liquids are essential products for human life.  Our argument is that substances, which affect health and environment, are the only chemicals to be regulated and not all chemicals of similar structures.
Filtration membrane products help
-improvement of public health for healthy and safe life
-improvement of environment and conservation of water body not only in EU but on our whole planet
-Stable supply of water to areas of water shortage
and contribute improvement of human life.  Furthermore, recently these filtration membrane products are expected to show outstanding performances in distillation as an alternative to current water or liquid treatment processes which consume a big volume of heat, and in carbon neutral technology to separate CO2.

Exemption or unlimited derogation for all Polymeric PFAS materials used in the sealing industry.

Polymeric PFAS, also known as fluoropolymers are used in the manufacturer of high performance sealing solutions for all industries, including critical applications.  Material selection for seals is based on individual application details, taking in account several criteria to meet extreme operating conditions including extremes of temperature, pressure and corrosion etc.  The properties offered by fluoropolymers make these materials ideal for use as sealing solutions due to their:
Chemical resistance
Thermal resistance
Mechanical properties
Low permeability
Low leachable and extractable content
Low surface energy
Low flammability
Low friction
High levels of cleanliness.

There are no alternative materials available offering the same level of performance as fluoropolymers.  The high cost of these materials means that they are only used where their performance is significantly superior to the currently available alternatives.

Fluoropolymers are used to seal aggressive and toxic media, substances which are harmful to human health, and the environment if leaked.  This media if leaked, for example radiation, would be far more damaging to human health and the environment than the fluoropolymer, with potentially serious consequences.  The very things these products are designed to protect.  In fact we know that fluoropolymers are not bioavailable or bioaccumulative and have negligible residual monomer and oligomer content.  Fluoropolymers are not mobile in the environment and due to their high molecular weight and meeting specific criteria, have been classed as polymers of low concern.

The strength of the C-F bond in fluoropolymers contributes to their persistent nature, however, persistence alone does not imply that there is a present or future risk.  Although fluoropolymers don’t degrade, there is considerable data demonstrating that fluoropolymers such as PTFE do not release substances of toxicological or environmental concern.    If these materials were not persistent, they would not have the necessary chemical resistance for their intended uses.



A restriction on the use of fluoropolymers would be damaging not only to the industries we serve, but to the environment and human health too.  They play a vital sealing role by protecting humans and the environment from the potentially dangerous emission of process fluids across multiple industries.  Fluoropolymers have already been subjected to and met material approval requirements, specific to certain industries.  Particular fluoropolymers have been approved by the FDA for food and drug contact use.  In the oil and gas industry, certain fluoropolymers have been approved for NORSOK and API use.  NORSOK and API have cost this company alone over £50,000 for material approvals, as a manufacturer of components only.  The cost of these approvals will be much greater for the valve manufacturers.   Any fluoropolymer restriction will require new approvals for any alternative material, and there is no guarantee these materials will pass the tests.  Even if another material does pass the tests, there will be greater limitations on temperature, chemical compatibility, pressure and seal life, etc.  This will mean that the subsea valve on the ocean bed will need servicing more frequently which may impact on warranty, the integrity of the valve may be compromised and the potential for leakage increased.  Not to mention any hardware modifications (if modifications to existing valves can be made) in order to accommodate an alternative.  Attached is a technical report containing data supplied by the BVAA (British Valve and Actuator Association) members, including us.

Automotive and Aerospace are other examples of heavily regulated industry with research, development, and obtaining approvals taking 20 plus years.  Any design change needs to be carefully considered and tested without time limitations.

Fluoropolymers are critical to the continued safe development of the low carbon economy.  The safe operation of processes using hydrogen gas is a critical issue for the world’s adoption of zero carbon technologies and the European Green Deal.  Industrial valves containing fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers stem/shaft seals are needed to perform a vital role in safely containing this explosive gas in the transport, electrolysis, gas transmission and storage, energy, and petroleum and mining industries.

I urge ECHA to pay particular attention to data supplied by the European Sealing Association, Fluoropolymers Product Group, and other related associations as they represent the voice of the entire sealing industry.

Vewin, the Association of Dutch drinking water companies and the Dutch Water Association (UvW) strongly support the proposed PFAS restriction. PFAS measurements in drinking water, as reported by RIVM in October 2022, emphasize the need for action to protect the sources of our drinking water, the water system in general and our consumers.

PFAS is a serious risk for drinking water
Based on the 2020 EFSA report on “Risk to human health related to the presence of perfluoroalkyl substances in food”,  the Dutch national institute for Public Health (RIVM)  derived a health-based guidance value of 4,4 ng/l PFOA Equivalents.
In the mentioned study by RIVM, PFAS concentrations exceeded this threshold in over half of the measurements of  drinking water produced from surface water. For drinking water from groundwater, this was the case for 1 in 10 measurements. These concentrations need to be brought down to ensure people’s PFAS intake from drinking water does not become too high.
Areas with the highest PFAS concentrations in drinking water are located in the Western part of the Netherlands, where drinking water is mostly produced from river water. Concentrations the environment slowly decline because PFAS are widely present, do not or barely degrade and are difficult to remove in water treatment. Given this fact, a precautionary approach based on source-protection like a the proposed PFAS restriction, is the way forward.
Projections of future PFAS concentrations in ground- and surface water as a source for drinking water indicate that without tackling the source of PFAS  all drink water sources will eventually surpass these threshold values . KWR research in 2022 on PFAS in European waters   suggests that PFAS is raising similar high concern in other EU countries as well.

PFAS is a risk for the water system in general
In addition to the risks for drinking water specifically, it is important to stress that PFAS is a serious risk to the water system in its entirety. If people would only come into contact with PFAS through drinking water, the problem would be less serious. However, there are several other ways in which people are exposed to PFAS.
Furthermore, several examples can be mentioned in which PFAS has negative consequences for the water quality. Additional sources of PFAS in the water system, for example, are the supply of PFAS from upstream rivers and the deposition of PFAS through the air. PFAS has a negative effect on ecology, including toxic effects, accumulation in organisms and subsequently within the food chain.
PFAS also has a negative impact on other water functions like swimming, recreation in general on or close to the water, fishing, irrigation and livestock watering. We see waters in which the concentration of PFAS is already ten thousand times too high, and it is very difficult or even impossible to eliminate PFAS once it is present in the water system.
PFAS also contains  a risk to water soils and circular ambitions. Dredging activities are sometimes necessary to preserve the water system including the water quality. When PFAS accumulates within water soils, the dredge should ultimately be disposed which is very expensive. When it comes to sludge which can be derived from sewage treatment plants, it becomes impossible to reuse the wastewater. In reference a circular economy this is an undesirable effect.

TFA as an extreme threat
Especially the occurrence of the ultrashort PFAS TriFluoroacetic Acid (TFA) in surface water, groundwater and drinking water is an extreme threat. Data from Rijkswaterstaat and RIWA as stored in the Norman database (June 2023) show concentrations of TFA up to 3 microgram/l. The drinking water advisory threshold value for TFA as a single compound is set to 2200 ng/l (RIVM, 2023)  , but combined with other PFAS the proposed threshold-value is in the Netherlands is 4,4 ng PFOA Equivalents (PEQ)/l. In which TFA is given relative potency factor of 0,002.  Neuwald (2022) and Sadia (2023) found concentrations in the order of 1 microgram/l which exceed the limits as given by the European Drinking Water Directive    . In this directive,  which took effect on 12 January 2021,  a limit of 0.5 µg/l for all PFAS is included.  TFA alone exceeds this threshold. This TFA originate from various industrial use, domestic use and degradation products and are found in high concentrations in the environment and drinking water.  illustrating once more that only a (global) ban can be the way forward to prevent the ubiquitous emissions of this compound and its precursors  .
The claim that TFA is of natural origin is convincingly refuted by Joudan (2022)

Clean, deeper groundwater reserves for drinking water will be lost in the future without a ban
At this moment especially drinking water produced from river water is strongly affected by the PFAS pollution. Inevitability, drinking water from groundwater will also be affected without a ban.  Given the ubiquitous presence of PFAS from air-emissions and deposition at the soil-surface, this amount of PFAS will gradually and continuously infiltrate to the deeper aquifers, polluting  the previously unaffected reservoirs of clean drinking water for the Dutch and European costumers, leading to extreme purification costs and efforts. The infiltration-rate of PFAS to the deeper underground is modelled by KWR . This might take decades, but will, without a ban, eventually end up with the pollution of all existing European Groundwater bodies up to levels that exceed the threshold values for PFAS that are proposed in the current revision of the Water Framework Directive (WFD) and its daughter Directives on Environmental Quality Standards (WFD-EQSD) and Groundwater Directive (WFD-GD)), where Environmental Quality Standards (EQS) are proposed for a group of 24 PFAS on al level of 4,4 ng/l PFOA Equivalents.

Banning PFAS in is crucial for several reasons
Health Risks and Consumer Protection
PFAS have been associated with numerous adverse health effects, including developmental issues, liver damage, thyroid disruption, immune system impairment, and certain types of cancer. These substances can enter the human body through various routes, including drinking water. By banning PFAS in Europe, the aim is to reduce exposure to these harmful chemicals and protect public health. The Dutch National Public Health Institute (RIVM) has already calculated that Dutch citizens take in too much PFAS already. A ban on PFAS is absolutely necessary to ensure a safe living environment for European citizens now and in the future.
Water Treatment Challenges and Costs
Removing PFAS from water sources is challenging and costly for drinking water treatment facilities. Due to their unique properties, PFAS are resistant to traditional water treatment processes, making their removal extremely difficult, and moreover, advanced treatment methods, such as activated carbon filtration or reverse osmosis, require 5-20 % more source water, where (groundwater) sources of drinking water are becoming more scarce as a result of climate change and drought.
In addition to this, there are currently no efficient techniques available to eliminate PFAS from waste water through sewage treatment plants. In most cases, existing techniques to reduce PFAS are very expensive and little effective in case of a small source, especially considering the high contribution of additional sources of PFAS through the air and upstream supplies. These techniques are also require a huge amount of energy, which is not desirable in relation to climate change. It is much more effective and environmentally friendly to prevent PFAS from getting into the environment in the first place.  As the vast majority of PFAS in river water (Rhine and Meuse) entering the Netherlands is emitted somewhere in the international river-basin, a European, cross-border approach is the only logical approach to minimize this pollution.
PFAS removal techniques are insufficient and mostly moving PFAS from one medium to another
PFAS is a very persistent group of chemicals with no natural decay.  PFAS removal from drinking water is moving PFAS from one medium to another. Waste streams of PFAS containing activated carbon or membrane concentrate is the result. Removal of PFAS from water might be the solution for drinking water, but leads to extra pollution of (surface) water, air and landfills, as the waste-streams of standard purification (PFAS containing activated carbon, sludge or concentrate) ends up somewhere in the environment.  Verma at al. (2023)  described low performance of thermal and non-thermal treatment technologies in large scale applications.

The need for a ban on PFAS
Banning PFAS in Europe would lead to a reduction in their presence in water sources, easing the burden on water treatment facilities. This, in turn, can alleviate the costs associated with the specialized treatment required for PFAS removal. By preventing further contamination, it allows resources to be focused on enhancing overall water quality and improving treatment efficiency.
In conclusion, banning PFAS in Europe, particularly in the context of drinking water production, is essential for protecting public health, safeguarding the environment, and limiting public costs and even droughts. Droughts, because additional purification with for example membranes, requires  extra source waters from rivers and aquifers that are threatened for over-exploitation during long dry periods like the summer of 2023, where drinking water facilities throughout Europe feared for shortages.  Furthermore, banning PFAS aligns with global efforts to regulate and restrict these substances. It demonstrates Europe's commitment to environmental protection and encourages international harmonization in the control of PFAS. By taking decisive action, Europe can lead the way in creating a safer and more sustainable future, ensuring clean and healthy drinking water for its population and setting an example for the rest of the world.

All PFAS  are a  threat
As we have learned, PFAS are emitted along various pathways and are ubiquitous: everywhere in the world PFAS are found. Unwanted emissions occur during production, use, and disposal.
The total occurrence and emissions of lots of PFAS and precursors are not well known.  According to the Pubchem classification browser  , there are more than 6 million various PFAS that fit the OECD PFAS definition of the Restriction dossier. Removal and remediation is practically impossible. Even burning leads to smaller PFAS-fragments and transformation products like TFA.  Claims of industry that there are less harmful PFAS have led to regrettable substitutions, for example from PFOA to GenX (HFPO-DA). Similar claims of harmless PFAS-subgroups like fluoropolymers are refuted in literature by Lohmann et al.  .  Somewhere in the process of production, use and disposal PFAS will enter the environment and accumulate in water, soil, air and the foodchain. The supports the conclusion that the only way to prohibit further emissions and accumulation of PFAS in our environment is a complete ban.  Vewin strongly supports the broad scope of the PFAS definition in the restriction proposal.  The need for a broad scope is also necessary as the health based drinking water advisory level as derived by RIVM has no limitation and contains every PFAS (Including TFA) with an established Relative Potency Factor (RPF-value) translated to PFOA equivalents and should not exceed the level of 4,4 ng/l PFOA equivalents per litre. This list of PFAS is theoretically enormous.



The need of fast implementation and no exemptions
This restriction-proposal does not come as a surprise or unannounced. The societal risks and costs of the use of PFAS have been described many times, for example by Chemsec in 2023  . Given the time between the (announcement of the) proposal (2022) and suggested start of the implementation (2025), there will be enough time for industry to prepare. Therefore exemptions should not be tolerated and only be granted under very strict conditions and for a period as short as possible
Textile, paper and firefighting-foam industry have proven that there are always alternatives available for PFAS. It takes some years of a transformation period, but it is possible, as proven by the H&M group during the ZeroPM workshop in February 2023  .  Recently (june 2023), Martin Scheringer published a comment in science, with the same conclusion  .
Claims that PFAS are essential for societal favourable transitions like the energy transition should be critically assessed, The fact that PFAS are used for “essential” and high valued products, doesn’t automatically mean that PFAS are essential in these products. There will always be an alternative that will also better fit with the European ambitions of a circular economy. PFAS containing products are probably impossible to re-use. In order to prevent further pollution of the European environment and the sources of our drinking water a fast implementation with no exemptions is the way forward.

Only restriction of emissions is an illusion
Claims that the PFAS containing products are not the problem, but only the production, and that the emissions during production could be regulated is misleading. As stated by Lohmann (2020), emissions occur during production, use and disposal  . Removing of PFAS is an illusion. Removal of PFAS from air or water moves the PFAS from one phase to another, for example from water tot activated carbon or membrane concentrate. These PFAS containing waste-streams ends up in landfills or are burned at standard temperatures, leading to new/other and unmeasured smaller PFAS compounds that will re-enter the environment by leaching to soil and air. Again supporting the proposal for a complete ban.

Additional supporting documentation
Commissioned by Vewin, KWR has compiled an overview of recent relevant scientific literature information that is important for the current restriction proposal. This report is attached as appendix 2. Relevant conclusions from this research are:
- PFAS have documented adverse effects on human health and the environment, and that (drinking) water is an important exposure route for humans to PFAS;
- The amount of literature and evidence on adverse health effects of PFAS is still growing;
- Many of reported removal methods have the potential to efficiently remove PFAS from water. Nevertheless, it should be noted that these findings are novel and sometimes promising, but it remains yet unclear if their implementation on a large scale is feasible;
- The restriction of PFAS can indeed result in lower exposure and thus risks to humans and the environment;
- It is argued that all PFAS, including fluoropolymers, give rise to emissions of harmful PFAS at some stage of their life cycle. Therefore, some authors support the broad definition of PFAS used in the restriction proposal and the resulting ban on fluoropolymers and other PFAS alike.
- It was noted that the authors supporting the exemption of fluoropolymers from a ban represent or are affiliated with PFAS-producing companies;
- 97 % of China’s PFOA/PFO emissions originated from the production of fluoropolymers;
- Emerging PFAS can induce toxicity like legacy PFAS like PFOS and PFOA;
- The justification for managing PFAS as a single chemical class to reduce PFAS-related risks is provided in the scientific literature. It is argued that a class-based approach can be implemented to eliminate non-essential uses of PFAS more effectively, develop safer alternatives, and clean up highly contaminated areas.
- A restriction of PFAS can indeed result in lower exposure and thus risks to humans and the environment;

The overall conclusion of Vewin is that there is strong scientific support for a complete ban of all PFAS according to the proposed PFAS definition, including subgroups as TFA and fluoropolymers.

Other identified uses: The societal risks and costs of the use of PFAS has been described several times, for example by Chemsec in 2023 ( https://chemsec.org/reports/the-top-12-pfas-producers-in-the-world-and-the-staggering-societal-costs-of-pfas-pollution). The costs of PFAS to the world are estimated to be €16 trillion, per year. And thats a conservative estimate, not including damages to animals or reduction of property prices

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: Short chains PFAS like TFA from industrial use or degradation products are found in high concentrations in the environment and drinking water, illustrating once more that emission reduction is practical impossible and a (global) ban, the way forward. See: https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/acs.est.1c07949 or https:// pubs.acs.org/doi/full/10.1021/acs.est.2c06015    As described in Appendix 1 and Appendix 2, the overall conclusion of Vewin is that there is strong scientific support for a complete ban of all PFAS according to the proposed PFAS definition, including subgroups as TFA and fluoropolymers.

10. Analytical methods: Drinking water laboratories in the Netherlands are capable to measure the 20 PFAS as given in the Europan Drinking Water Directive (DWD) on a level of 1 ng/l

Combined Comments:
General Comments: See attached file (Hager position paper PFAs)

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The electrical and electronics sector relies on the use of articles and materials (solid, liquid and gaseous) containing substances falling within the definition of PFAS.   Our comments therefore relate to the following uses and sub-uses identified in Table 9 and 2 of Annex XV: -  Energy sector: Photovoltaic cells; Wind energy, nuclear power plant - Construction products: Sealings and adhesives - Lubricants: Low viscosity lubricants, Solid/dry-film lubrication, Release agents, Greases - Electronics and semiconductor - Insulating gas in electrical equipment - metal and plastic plating and manufacture of metal Products: Hard chrome plating - Plastic packaging - Polymeric PFASs used as processing aids for production of non-PFAS polymers/plastic Application Annexe E, 5.8, 131, 124, 2.11, 2.8

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Electrical equipment is in general containing high quantities of recyclable materials as steel, aluminum and copper and are generally intended to be handed over to recycling companies at end of life. Depending on the product the recyclability can reach levels of 90 %. Epoxy resin is a component which can not be recycled, but burnt (thermal recycling). Only a small fraction of the electrical equipment ends up in landfill. The PFAS containing materials will normally be part of the thermal recycling process. With temperatures >900 °C for sufficient time PFAS are destroyed to non-PFAS.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Fluoropolymers meeting the criteria for "polymers of low concern" ,  and industrial applications in closed systems and equipment components and equipment generally do not cause relevant emissions to the environment when used as intended. Due to the high industrial importance, indefinite derogations are necessary, especially if not technically suitable and environmentally safer alternatives are known. Risks in the manufacturing and waste phase are better addressed in the relevant legislation (emissions/occupational health and safety, waste legislation). In the electrical and electronic sector, there is the WEEE Directive, which already imposes requirements concerning end-of-life product management. This legislation regulates the collection, recycling, and recovery of waste electrical and electronic equipment, aiming to reduce their environmental impact. Manufacturers and distributors are obligated to establish selective collection and recycling systems for end-of-life products, in order to prevent improper disposal and promote a more sustainable circular economy. As a result, there is already a risk management for emissions established by the directive.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: The threshold level of 25 ppb results in a contamination of 1.000 tons of waste with 25 g of a pure PFAS. As waste is always a mixture which will be processes and purified during the recycling process, the effort to remove such low contaminations will be extremely if possible at all. As the contamination especially in waste is very inhomogenous it is not realistic that any recycling process can be established for products which migh contain PFAS even in low concentrations.

5. Proposed derogations: The majority of the material used in electrical equipment are steel, aluminum, copper and insulating material like epoxy resin, silicone rubber or porcelaine, highly depending on what kind of electrical eqiupment it is. The weight of intentionally added PFAS will be for the total product weight <1%. Non-intentionally added PFAS will even v significantly lower, as it is only a contamination of a material which is <1%, means for a top level product it will be << 1ppm.

6. Missing uses: Electrical and electronic equipment and components are not taken into account as such, or only to a very limited extent, in this Annex XV report.  Indeed, electrical, and electronic equipment and components depend on the use of PFAS for several applications as detailed hereafter due to their unique properties: - PTFE as metal surface treatment and PTFE as plastic surface treatment - Plastic additive (Flame Retardant) - Plastic additive (friction, processing aid additive…) - PTFE/PVDF - Specific lubricants  - Cables insulation and connectors PTFE/PVDF/ PFA/MFA - Electronic components  Electrical T&D equipment belongs to the energy sector, which is market green in table A.1 of Annex A of the Annex XV restriction report, but this equipment is not listed sufficiantly as user of PFAS. a) The annual tonnage is hard to report as in the very much distributed applications where PFAS has been identified up to now the quantities are not easy to get, as the majority are additives in materials of subsupplier where the kind and quantity has not been specified, but only material properties which rely on PFAS. b) In the very wide range it is also not possible to give a simple answer. In most cases the PFAS is required to fulfil the requirement of long lifetime and low wear or similar material properties. In some specific applications where PFAS is intentionally used or added, e.g. nozzles on hard-gas loadbreak switches, the PFAS (PTFE) is mandatory for the technical function.  c) Most of the usages and even same or similar products from subsuppliers are used in the complete branch. This has been confirmed by members of the industry with a membership at ZVEI. d) Most likely the majority of the applications can be shifted to alternatives, but the problems are on the identification, substitution, testing, qualifying and certification. This will requre significant time and resources. e) For most applications there was no search for substitutes up to now, as there was no need. The research is starting but only a few conclusions are available now. If hard-gas switches without PFTE are possible is open and doubtful. For other applications first alternatives are tested. Some with positive, other with negative results. f) Electrical T&D equipment is mandatory for save and reliable energy supply. Reduction of performance or lifetime, increasing of maintenance, related outages and costs are not acceptable. Substitutes must be able to have the same performance. Product development times are long (5-10 years) and investment is high, also due to very expensive type testing. Depending on the product and the complexity it is on the level of several million Euro per company. g) For electrical equipment the question is not how big the losses of companies are if they can no longer produce the equipment. If it is not possible to serve the market, the energy supply is endangered, the transformation to green energy slowed down and the extention of the electrical networks is stopped, with negative impact on industry and society.

8. Other identified uses: A group covering electrical T&D equipment is missing and needs to be created. A derogation of 12 years is estimated to be sufficiant to replace actually used PFAS in case a PFAS-free solution is available. It has to be added, that in some specific cases it is yet not clear if a PFAS phase-out and replacement with alterantive materials is possible at all.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: See attached letter for non-confidential comments submitted on behalf of the ASME Bioprocessing Equipment Standards Committee.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: While there are many other industries affected with real concerns, ASME-BPE (The Bioprocessing Equipment Standard of the American Society of Mechanical Engineers) wishes to comment within the scope of our organization, the bioprocessing equipment, components, materials and spare parts which are used to manufacture biologics A small subset of bioprocessed medicinal products (MPs) are mentioned in section 2.2.3 Active substances in Plant Protection Products (PPP), Biocidal Products (BP) and Medicinal Products (MP) and in Annex A - A.3.17. Active substances in Plant Protection Products (PPP), Biocidal Products (BP) and Medicinal Products (MP). However, the equipment to manufacture these MPs, and indeed all MPs, PFAS containing or not, are not given the same exemptions or time-unlimited derogations or any other consideration.  The closest sector the prepared comments would relate to is the medical devices sector, but in a sub use of biotechnology and pharmaceutical manufacturing processes.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: PFAS emissions during the manufacture, use and end-of-life of the Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers themselves is outside the scope of ASME BPE. ASME BPE’s submission is concerned about the continuing availability of Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers in order to produce Medicinal Products (MPs).    Annual emissions are not in the scope of the ASME BPE Standard.  As stated in the attached letter, Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers used in bioprocessing are proven to be very stable for long periods of time over a wide range of bioprocessing conditions during drug qualification.   As stated previously, disposal and end-of-life issues are out of scope for ASME BPE.  We rely on material manufacturers to provide guidance on best practices and appropriate disposal methodologies.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Incineration byproducts of commercially available Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers is not in the scope of ASME-BPE.  We rely on material manufacturers to provide guidance on best practices and appropriate disposal methodologies.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Recycling of Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers is outside the scope of ASME BPE.

5. Proposed derogations: As stated in the letter, ASME BPE is requesting a new exemption for the use of Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers in all bioprocessing equipment, supporting systems, components and spare parts modeled on the current exemption of PFAS containing Medicinal Products (MPs).    This new exemption (or time-unlimited derogation) would apply to all such bioprocessing equipment, supporting systems, components and spare parts used in bioprocessing systems in order to make all MPs, both PFAS and non-PFAS containing MPs, including the ingredients used to manufacture them.  It is outside of the scope of ASME BPE to track the total tonnage of Fluoroplastics and Fluoroelastomers used in bioprocessing.

6. Missing uses: As stated in Question 1, the missing use this submission relates to is the bioprocessing equipment, components and spare parts which are used to manufacture medicinal products, in particular biologics.  Although a small subset of bioprocessed medicinal products (MPs) are mentioned in section 2.2.3 Active substances in Plant Protection Products (PPP), Biocidal Products (BP) and Medicinal Products (MP) and in Annex A - A.3.17. Active substances in Plant Protection Products (PPP), Biocidal Products (BP) and Medicinal Products (MP), the equipment to manufacture these MPs, and indeed all MPs, biologics or otherwise, PFAS containing or not, are not given the same exemptions or time-unlimited derogations or, for that matter any consideration.  With the current proposal, it would be impossible to manufacture most medicinal products.  Please see the attached submission of ASME BPE which explains the key functionalities required from Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers (chemical resistance, thermal resistance, purity, mechanical performance).   This submission also explains the socio-economic impact, the fact that the Proposal in its current form would devastatingly impact the manufacture of most MPs, affecting patients of these lifesaving and life-altering medications, the biopharmaceutical companies and the companies that comprise the supply chain providing the equipment, the components and the spare parts worldwide.  The attached document explains that there are no foreseeable alternatives to the use of Fluoroplastics and Fluoroelastomers for these rigorously tested and validated drug substances and their concurrently qualified processes and equipment.    Several PFAS uses not covered in detail (see Table A.1 in Annex A) and some relevant uses may not have been identified yet – For such uses, information on alternatives and socio-economic impacts is requested including:    a) The annual tonnage and emissions and type of PFAS:  The total amount of Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers used in bioprocessing in terms of tonnage is unknown and beyond the scope of ASME BPE.  Suppliers of these materials to this industry may be consulted.  b) The key functionalities provided by PFAS: Please refer to attached submission letter. c) The number of companies affected: Please see answers above and in the attached submission letter.  d) The availability, technical and economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives; Please see answers above and in the attached submission letter. e) Alternatives are not yet available; information on status of R&D processes and time required for completing substitution: Please see answers above and in the attached submission letter. f) For cases where substitution is technically and economically feasible but more time is required to substitute – Type and magnitude associated with substitution – Time required for completing substitution  – Functionality differences and consequences for downstream users and consumers– Benefits for alternative providers:  Please see answers provided earlier in these questions and the attached letter.  g) Substitution is not technically or economically feasible:  Please see answers above and in the attached submission letter.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: As stated earlier, there are currently no exemptions or derogations for the Bioprocessing equipment needed to produce MPs, both PFAS and non-PFAS containing drug-substances.  The ASME Bioprocessing Equipment Standard representing the combined consensus of parties from all segments in the manufacture of biologics is requesting an exemption from the PFAS restrictions as it relates to Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers used in the bioprocessing equipment, components and spare parts which are used to manufacture medicinal products, in particular biologics.  If an exemption cannot be granted, the industry is requesting a time unlimited derogation, as there are no foreseeable alternatives that will preserve the potency, purity and safety of these rigorously tested and qualified drug products during manufacture.  Without an exemption or time-unlimited derogation, thousands of drug products and their processes would require reevaluation, retesting and revalidation.  This would place an immeasurable burden on the public and the companies which supply these medications in a timely manner.

8. Other identified uses: Since Bioprocessing Equipment does not exist as a sector in the current Proposal, this application does not exist in Table 8.  As stated in the document and in the submission questions, there are no foreseeable equivalent alternatives for the production of most MPs at this time.   This is the reason an exemption or time unlimited derogation is being sought for bioprocessing equipment, components and spare parts.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: The attached letter form ASME BPE indicates the types of Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers typically used in Bioprocessing Equipment.   These materials have little impact on the process, the MP and the patient in part because of their long-lasting properties.  It is outside of the scope of ASME BPE to research the degradation potential of these materials after use.

10. Analytical methods: It is outside of the scope of ASME BPE to develop methods to analyze for PFAS.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: See attached RINA Report

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The relevant sectors are: i) Analytical equipment ii) Nanoscience and plasma technology equipment.  Analytical equipment is used both inside laboratories and outdoors (for example archaeological sites) and in non-laboratory settings such as production environments museums and art galleries. The equipment is used in research and development underpinning key EU policy such as the Green Deal and environmental policies such as REACH and RoHS and to ensure compliance to the regulations, including PFAS testing. Plasma technology equipment is used to manufacture both semiconductors and optical devices and the design and production of these are closely linked industrially. This is because optical devices are increasingly being combined with semiconductors in optical electronic devices such as machine human interaction interfaces.  PFAS materials are used in critical parts and calibration materials in this equipment. Additional time to utilise PFAS-free alternatives is required. Derogations are requested to allow the continued use of the equipment until the necessary design, testing and validation stages of the PFAS replacement process can be completed.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The life cycle of the analytical and nanoscience and plasma technology equipment is evaluated in the attached Impact Assessment report in accordance with the guidance document (ECHA, 2023). The end-of-life phase of the equipment is controlled under EU regulations, with parts containing the PFAS incinerated under the EU rules applicable to WEEE. The use is entirely in the commercial and professional sector, which is often highly regulated. These are not general consumer products, and it is very unlikely that PFAS will be released into the environment during use or disposed of in landfill because of the legislative controls users of the equipment must adhere to.   Most of the equipment represents a high capital investment by the end user. The number of equipment items sold per year is relatively small as these are not consumer items. The equipment has a long service life (in some cases up to 20 years). It is very unlikely that any of the equipment would be sent to landfill due to its retained relatively high value at end of life arising from recyclable component materials such as metals, refrigerant gases, and heat transfer fluids. Equipment will also be taken back as part exchange agreements and then disposed of in accordance with correct procedure. End users of the equipment have well-developed waste disposal procedures in place. Due to the relatively high raw material retained value in the equipment, almost all is believed to be recycled within the EU and the recycling processes used are regulated by EU waste legislation including the Industrial Emissions Directive (2010/75/EU). Therefore, there is negligible exposure of PFAS to humans or the environment at end-of-life.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Evidence is presented in the attached Impact Assessment report that incineration under Best Available Techniques EU requirements, is the best method of disposal of PFAS currently available. This conclusion is supported in Annex A of the restriction proposal under A.3.18.2.7. Incineration. This recognises that “incineration of PFAS containing waste is currently seen as the most effective treatment option for destroying PFASs. The fluorine in the PFASs will end up in either the bottom/fly ash or the flue gas.”

5. Proposed derogations: The tonnage of PFAS used in the equipment could not be estimated because there is insufficient available data.

6. Missing uses: Oxford Instruments supports the following Proposed Derogations without amendment of the text, with the technical rationale and socio-economic impacts assessed in the attached report:  A) By way of derogation, paragraphs 1 and 2 shall not apply to:  5.s. Lubricants where the use takes place under harsh conditions or use is needed for safe functioning and safety of equipment until 13.5 years after EiF  5.t. Calibration of measurement instruments and as analytical reference materials.  Rationale: Oxford Instruments relies upon PFAS containing materials having a unique combination of physical and chemical properties which PFAS-free alternatives are not able to offer. These properties include, low outgassing, low coefficient of friction, chemical and physical stability under harsh conditions of electromagnetic radiation, high voltages and high and low temperatures and pressures and electrical and thermal insulation properties. There are currently no suitable alternatives to PFAS containing calibration and reference standards.  Oxford Instruments requests the following additional derogations with the technical rationale and socio-economic impacts assessed in the attached report: B) By way of derogation, paragraphs 1 and 2 shall not apply to:   Semiconductor manufacturing process, related equipment and supporting processes until 13.5 after EiF.  Refrigerants in semiconductor manufacturing process, related equipment and supporting processes until 13.5 years after EiF.  Analytical equipment for at least 13.5 years after EiF.   Rationale: The manufacture of semiconductors is increasingly being integrated with the manufacture of optical electronic devices. Oxford Instruments plasma technology equipment is designed and used for both semiconductor and optical device manufacture. The derogations are requested to include both optical devices and semiconductors within their scope. PFAS containing materials are used because of their combination of the following unique properties. Low outgassing, low coefficient of friction, electrical and thermal insulation properties and high chemical and physical stability under harsh conditions of electromagnetic radiation, high voltages and high and low temperatures and pressures. Without the above derogations, industrial development in high technology products will be impeded within the EU. There is the risk that such development will then proceed more rapidly in areas outside of the EU.   Analytical equipment is used in research and development, and across most areas of industrial activity including those associated with healthcare. The restriction proposal does not include non-biological testing uses. The equipment is used for cultural, industrial, and scientific research activities, a derogation is therefore, requested that is not constrained by a particular use setting such as a laboratory. The PFAS containing polymers used are the only technically suitable materials. If analytical equipment is no longer available in the EU to support these industrial activities and the cultural applications of the equipment, there will be a significant negative socio-economic impact to the EU. C) Spare parts Oxford Instruments would like to highlight the necessity for the continued use of PFAS in spare parts and repairs of products already placed on the market. Rationale: Oxford Instruments products require servicing and repair and may have a service life of up to 20 years. Without the general consideration to permit the use of PFAS in these applications, this will cause the premature end-of-life and scrappage of products which otherwise could be serviced and maintained in service with PFAS-containing parts. It is therefore vital that the restriction proposal does not impact products already placed on the market.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Oxford Instruments supports the following Proposed Derogation (marked for reconsideration in the restriction proposal after the Annex XV report consultation) without amendment of the text, with the technical rationale and socio-economic impacts assessed in the attached report: 5.v. [Hard chrome plating until 6.5 after EiF]. Rationale: Oxford Instruments relies upon PFAS containing materials having a unique combination of physical and chemical properties which PFAS-free alternatives are not able to offer. These properties include, nonmagnetic properties, hard wearing surfaces, low outgassing, chemical and physical stability under harsh conditions of electromagnetic radiation and high and low temperatures and pressures.

6. Missing uses: a.  Fluoropolymer waste from end-of-life machines and service parts: The fluoropolymer waste we generate today 2023 in the EU, coming from end-of-life machines and service parts, is estimated at < 5 ton yearly.  - Our machines and spare parts contain > 90% recyclable metal. At end-of-life, the majority of our machines and spare parts are sent to metal recyclers, and PFAS that is attached to these metal parts (coatings, seals,…) are hence burnt at > 1300 degrees, meaning that all PFAS is destroyed.  - Certain small PFAS containing parts, such as O-rings, that are replaced during a service, are gathered in industrial waste, and are hence burnt as well at high temperatures (> 850 degrees). Although at these temperatures, PFAS could still be present in rest fractions, but the PFAS weight in these O-rings is marginal versus the total PFAS weight in machines and spare parts.  Fluoropolymer waste gathered in our production:  The production waste amount is marginal as compared to the waste from end-of-life machines and parts. PFAS waste generated in our shops (from coating etc.) is gathered as chemical waste, and burnt at > 1000 degrees, so all PFAS is destroyed.  After our waste handling, only a marginal PFAS fraction is left.  Fluoropolymer emissions during in-use: No emissions are expected.  b. The main functionality of fluoropolymers in our parts is to make compressors leak tight (guarantee safety and performance) and resistant against very low and high temperatures (-260 up to 425°C), high pressures (0-1000 bar), aggressive gas/liquid mixtures (air, oxygen, oil, chloric, acids, glycols, condensate,…), and reduce the friction (to reduce wear, increase lifetime, and to increase performance) under those conditions. Fluoropolymers, such as PTFE, FEP, FKM, viton,… are used in compressor elements, filters, dryers, motors, bearings, valves, electrical components, hoses,… as coatings, seals, O-rings, insulating material, anti-bacterial, hydro/oleophobic material,… The key functionalities of fluoropolymers are required in these parts, we only use PFAS where absolutely necessary, see examples of flow charts and drawings in our attached position paper (confidential).   d. Compressed air is known as the “fourth utility”, apart from electricity, gas, and water. This is not well known, because compression mainly occurs in an industrial environment. 10% of the electricity consumption in industry is related to compression. A compressed air net is required in almost any manufacturing facility, among which in essential sectors such as medical, pharma, food/beverage,... Compressing air/gas is intrinsically coupled to heating and pressure build-up. Compression also needs fast-moving parts, and happens in aggressive environments (gas and liquids). It is the unique combination of properties that makes fluoropolymers indispensable in compression. We only use fluoropolymers on parts where it is absolutely necessary for performance, safety, reliability.  Replacing PFAS by currently available alternatives (PEEK, HNBR, EPDM,…) will lead to shorter lifetime, more failures, more service (parts), lower performance, leaks,… because these alternatives do not have the combination of properties PFAS have. See position paper for an example (confidential).  - More failures and shorter lifetime lead to more spare parts needed, and hence more waste in total. Moreover, more service intervals lead to more transportation and a higher GHG footprint. - Lower machine performance leads to more energy-usage for the same output (air pressure) and hence a higher GHG footprint. - Air/gas leaks not only lead to a lower performance, but also cause unsafe situations (explosion & health risks).  As almost all of our machines contain PFAS (as well as competitor machines), we expect major shortages on the market for these (inferior) PFAS-free alternatives. Moreover, the stricter legislation in Europe creates an uneven level playing field for companies with customers worldwide.   e.  We rely on suppliers for alternatives. Our suppliers have informed us that alternatives with similar properties are not available/developed yet (“essential”) or even not possible at all (“critical”) within the current scientific knowledge state, due to the unique combination of properties which is indispensable in compressing air/gas.  In those “essential” uses, we require multiple years (6.5-13.5) for: - Development (new formulation, new chemistries,…) - Redesign (making sure that running conditions are less harsh) - Testing  - Implementation  R&D costs for new product development in case alternatives are possible but not developed yet (“essential”): ~5.000.000 euro/product type (for +/- 150 types) For “critical” uses, we require time-unlimited exemptions.  Spare parts are designed for a particular machine setup. PFAS-free spare parts need to be designed in such a way that they at least fit 100% geometrically and moreover keep the original functionality/performance of the part. Doing this for an immense installed base is impossible (research, design, validation, sourcing & production, logistics). Existing machines will hence become inferior, irrelevant and/or stop working in the applications of our customers. We, therefore, ask for specific exemptions for spare parts for already installed products in the field.  See position paper for a detailed overview of uses and requested exemptions (confidential).  Discarded alternatives have lower performance, higher energy-consumption (higher GHG emissions), more and sooner failures, leaks,… Examples are mentioned in the position paper (confidential).   f.  If alternative chemistries are possible and would be available right now, then it would take us in any case more than 18 months (as is currently proposed) i.e. 36 months to phase-in, due to: - Lead times (an order placed today often takes over 18 months to be manufactured and delivered) - Administration (converting drawings, manuals,…) - Testing (a typical redesign project takes more than 18 months) - A massive number of parts affected (PFAS is present throughout our portfolio, which means 1000’s of affected part numbers) Product development cost: If alternatives would be available: 500.000 euro/product type (for a few hundred types) Operational cost:  Lower performance leads to higher energy consumption and hence higher energy cost. The best candidate technology to be made PFAS free currently uses 20% extra energy, hence a 20% higher GHG emission. Moreover, if a customer requires an air delivery which cannot be met with the current machine anymore, he must buy an oversized machine.  More failures and shorter lifetimes lead to more service and more spare parts.   g. Fluoropolymers are used in most of our equipment. Only for machines that operate in mild conditions, we would be able to phase-out PFAS over time (however, 18 months is not possible, see section f above). This is true for about 30% of our product portfolio.  If the proposal is accepted (taking into account the time extension of the standard phase-out period, i.e. 36 months), we expect a business revenue loss of 70% and employee loss of 70%. (Remark: the effect for us is worldwide, because in our chemical strategy, we dedicate to follow worldwide the most stringent legislation for all our products, also for products manufactured and sold outside of EU.)  This is only the direct impact for our company. But as we deliver compressed air installations to enable production in other companies, complete industries will be impacted by the lack of compressed air. In other words, the indirect effect of a lack of our equipment will be huge.

General Comments: see below

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: - The TULAC sector, more specifically on the sub-uses “technical textiles”, focusing on filtration and separation media, and “textiles used in engine bays”. - Uses of PFAS in Lacquers. -      Uses of PFAS in H2 technology. - Air conditioning systems. - PFAS in production of automotive – tools, machines, equipment and machinery. - PFAS in electronics used in the automotive industry.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: When incinerating PTFE, which is considered a highly stable substance with bonds that do not easily break, at between 870 and 1020ºC and with a residence time of between 4.0 and 2.7 seconds, complete mineralization of the carbon bonds is realized if BATs are used 1.    1 K. Aleksandrov et al., “Waste incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate potential formation of per- and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) in flue gas,” Chemosphere 226, Issue No. (2019): 898-906. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chemosphere.2019.03.191.  It can be deduced that high-temperature incineration of C6 side-chain fluorinated polymers (SFPs)-treated articles combined with high-efficiency incinerator effluent gas scrubbing ensures the full mineralization of carbon-fluorine bonds. Therefore, it is guaranteed that no emissions are released into the environment.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Batteries are collected, dismantled then Pyrometallurgy destroy PVDF or Hydrometallurgy allow recovery. For a more detailed answer on the issue of PFAS in batteries, please refer to the “RECHARGE” submission, comment n°3925.

5. Proposed derogations: Sub-use: Technical textiles – Filtration and separation media under paragraph 5(e) The filtration and separation industry estimated the volumes of C6 SFPs annually placed on the EU market in filtration and separation media to be approximately 67 t/y 2.   Media manufacturers measuring PFAS in wastewater detected either no emissions or a level close to the detection limit. The detailed test results can be found in stakeholder input of the PFHxA restriction proposal. Furthermore, C6 SFP-based filters used in automotive are expected to be collected separately and incinerated in line with waste codes 150202*, 150203 (both for i.e., absorbents, filter materials (including oil filters not otherwise specified), rags and protective clothing) and 160107 (applicable to oil filters) 3.   Finally, we would like to add a few comments on the proposed wording. Firstly, we understand that the reference to ‘high-performance’ raises enforceability questions. The concept “high performance” means the same as media “that require a combination of water and oil repellency”. We, therefore, suggest removing the terms “high performance” from the wording.  In addition, the term ‘textiles’ should be removed, as filtration media does not only cover woven materials but also nonwovens, polyurethane membranes and cellulose-based media, which do not fit under the current wording. In absence of a definition for textiles, support the changes proposed by the filtration and separation value chain 4.   2 Comment #961, Comments on SEAC Draft Opinion on REACH restriction proposal on PFHxA, its salts and related substances, p. 10-11, https://echa.europa.eu/documents/10162/f1a33a2f-e008-b3d0-1c46-96d1c9eadf10.   3 Directive 2008/98/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 November 2008 on waste and repealing certain Directives, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02000D0532-20150601&from=EN; Commission Decision 2000/532/EC replacing Decision 94/3/EC establishing a list of wastes pursuant to Article 1(a) of Council Directive 75/442/EEC on waste and Council Decision 94/904/EC establishing a list of hazardous waste pursuant to Article 1(4) of Council Directive 91/689/EEC on hazardous waste, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A32008L0098.  4  Comment #920, Comments on SEAC Draft Opinion on REACH restriction proposal on PFHxA, its salts and related substances, p. 95-96, https://echa.europa.eu/registry-of-restriction-intentions/-/dislist/details/0b0236e18323a25d.

6. Missing uses: During our discussion with our suppliers, it appears that PFAS are also used in lacquers. The main substance is PTFE, which is added to guarantee a low friction profile for horn and buckle spring, screws, and metal pillar loop. The durability of the lacquer is also increased by the addition of PTFE. Due to lack of available information, assessment need to be fine tuned in the years ahead. PFAS are also used directly in mixtures for painted parts, such as car’s interiors and lighting applications. Due to its property, currently no alternatives are qualified to substitute PTFE in lacquers for the automotive industry. More details about which substances are used can be found in the annex of the joint document. As mentioned by other professional associations, PFAS are also used in H2 technology. This also impact the automotive industry as H2 storage system are used for emerging new type of mobility. The details of the PFAS used and the parts are detailed in annex of the attached document. It has also been notified to ACEA that PFAS are used as flame retardant additives in polymers.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Understanding the financial implications of such a wide-ranging restriction proposal are extremely difficult, given the wide variety of applications impacted, the availability of substitutes, the research and development that needs to be conducted. Based on our engineering knowledge, and discussions with our supply base, initial estimates on the potential costs per vehicle, are identified below.  Please be aware that these are only initial estimates and could vary significantly when we come to implementation: - Refrigerants: moving to R744 will cost in the region of €300 / vehicle. - Batteries: high investment in research required, adverse impacts on performance, potential increase in cell weight for same performance.  Costs could be upwards of €500 / vehicle. - Powertrain: high investment in research required, adverse impacts on performance and durability. Costs could exceed €300 / vehicle. - Others: research in joining technology / joint performance, research in membrane technology, research in coating / plating technology, research into textiles, unknown impacts etc.  Cost could exceed €200 / vehicle.   This would give a conservative estimate €1300 per vehicle. Based on 2019 data, new registrations in the EU exceeded 2.5 million vehicles.  This would give a potential cost estimate to the automotive industry of €3.25 billion/year.  Sub-use: Technical textiles We welcome the derogation recommended for reconsideration by the Dossier Submitters. However, we would like to propose a series of modifications to the proposed wording. Firstly, we believe that referring to the functions of the textiles and not to their location in the vehicle allows to set an effective and enforceable limitation to the scope, while covering all the relevant applications. This is because the current wording leaves out textiles used for ignition protection, which constitutes a key safety feature in case of accident, providing more time to rescue people before the vehicle starts to burn out. With regard to NVH insulation, the current wording also leaves textiles used in other parts of vehicles e.g., as isolator between dashboard and engine compartment (front engine), between seats and the rear engine, or at the transmission tunnel. In addition, while this is not a primary concern for the automotive sector, we support the request of ATCS to extend the derogation to other types of vehicles, such as motorcycles or non-road mobile machinery that are used for construction or agriculture, in line with the position of the SEAC Committee in the context of the PFHxA restriction proposal  5. Volumes In the EU the annual consumption of C6 SFPs for initial textile finishing is estimated at 200-300 t/y, which translates to 10 kg of impurities (PFHxA) per year. This applies to all technical textiles and is not only limited to automotive applications. Emissions during textile production The European textile industry is committed to decrease emissions across its industry. Additionally, more stringent regulations, implementing measures to minimise releases of PFAS and other substances to the environment such as the Best Available Techniques (BREF/BATs), already significantly reduce emissions during textile production. The BREF/BATs determine that process baths should be reused to the highest extent possible, after which they should be collected separately and sent for professional waste management. As a result of the existing BATs, current measurements conducted by companies using C6 SFPs in textile finishing estimate emissions of 100-300 ng/l in water for all technical textiles (not limited to the automotive applications). Production scraps are incinerated in line with the European Waste Catalogue (CER 04 02 22) 6. Emissions during use of textile articles Technical textiles have an estimated C6 SFP concentration of 0.2-0.5%, as identified in the report by Ramboll and Wood on the use of PFAS in textiles 7 For further information on degradation of C6 SFPs, please refer to the studies cited by ATCS. Emissions at end of life The end-of-life, removal and disposal are covered by the End of Life Vehicles (ELV) Directive (2000/53/EC), which ensures proper handling and treatment 8. To the best of our knowledge, C6-treated technical textiles are subject to treatment in modern high-temperature incineration plants. High-temperature incineration is the most widely accepted method to handle PFAS-containing textile waste and is applied in the following manner: • 850ºC or higher for at least two seconds for non-hazardous waste; • 1100ºC or higher for at least two seconds in case of hazardous waste or co-incineration. 9  Incineration facilities commonly come outfitted with flue gas purification systems, which incorporate multi-stage wet scrubbers employing calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)2). Through this process, hydrogen fluoride is converted into calcium fluoride (CaF2). Hydrogen fluoride, a vital commodity chemical employed in the production of a diverse array of materials, primarily derives from this transformation into calcium fluoride. C6 SFPs provide several combined performance benefits to the sector, specifically:  • water repellence based on ISO 4920 and ISO 811; • oil repellence based on ISO 14419 (grade 3); • stain-resistance/soil protection based on AATCC 130; and • flame retardancy 10 .  Approximately 300 automobile assembly and engine production plants operate in Europe today.  As discussed, C6 SFPs’ properties include a combination of stain, oil, grease and water repellence, which are imperative to manufacture the high-performance technical textile in these applications.  The Danish Environmental Protection Agency reported that many different agents providing water repellence are marketed, namely: Wax-based repellents consisting of paraffin-metal salt formulations, resin-based repellents consisting of fatty modified melamine resins, and hydrophobic modified polyurethanes. None of the identified agents provide efficient repellence against oil, alcohol and oil-based stains. Therefore, these agents cannot be considered as suitable candidates.  In addition, the report by Ramboll and Wood concluded the following: For (textile) applications requiring repellency against blood, solvents, fuels (petrol, kerosene, diesel and resistance of components in motor to oil and diesel /gasoline) and liquid chemicals (Figure 5.3), PFAS-free finishing agents are not currently able to meet the same levels of performance 12.  The lack of adequate performance by any of the alternatives examined suggests that removal of PFAS could lead to increased risks, with potential high societal costs. Complex products, including cars or non-road mobile machinery, undergo an extensive and meticulous validation phase, typically spanning a minimum of 5 years from the initial concept sketches to market release 13. During this period, suppliers engage in testing to establish material specifications, while original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) undertake essential verification tests. In the case of novel materials, customers may also opt for third-party, independent laboratory testing and certification to enhance their confidence in the material's performance. No viable alternatives have become available. As such, we support a minimum transition period of 13,5 years after EiF to allow sufficient time to identify prospective candidates, conduct testing, gain approval, execute implementation, and subsequently introduce them into the market through novel products. We understand that no suitable candidates have been identified at this stage, and there is therefore not sufficient visibility as to when the transition from PFAS will be possible. Socio-economic impacts  C6 SFP-treated technical textiles provide advanced insulation, compatibility with fire retardant products and resistance to water, fuels, extremes of temperature and abrasion. Overall, they contribute to extending the product lifetime and making cars safer, more cost-effective and more durable.    5  RAC & SEAC, Opinion on the Annex XV dossier proposing restrictions on Undecafluorohexanoic acid (PFHxA), its salts and related substances, June 9, 2021. 6 Directive 2008/98/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 November 2008, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32008L0098&from=EN. 7  Ramboll and Wood, (October 2020), ‘The Role of PFAS and Fluorine-free alternatives in Textiles, Upholstery, Carpets, Leather and Apparel’, European Commission, https://echa.europa.eu/documents/10162/13641/pfas_in_textiles_final_report_en.pdf/0a3b1c60-3427-5327-4a19-4d98ee06f041. 8  Directive 2000/53/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 September 2000 on end-of life vehicles, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32000L0053&from=EN. 9   Directive 2010/75/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 November 2010 on industrial emissions (integrated pollution prevention and control), https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32010L0075&from=EN. 10  We would like to stress that C6 SFP  does not provide flame retardancy but, unlike other chemicals, it is compatible with flame retardant products. 11  Lassen C. et al, (2015), Alternatives to perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in textiles, Survey of chemical substances in consumer products, p. 137, https://www2.mst.dk/Udgiv/publications/2015/05/978-87-93352-16-2.pdf. 12   Ramboll and Wood, (October 2020), ‘The Role of PFAS and Fluorine-free alternatives in Textiles, Upholstery, Carpets, Leather and Apparel’, European Commission, p. 95. 13  Shashank, Modi. n.d.
