9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the PFAS restriction proposal and raise a specific question regarding PFAS related to mobile air conditioning systems. This comment of Ford-Werke GmbH (Germany) fully supports the ACEA contribution on mobile air conditioning and makes an important additional comment on the refrigerant R-1234yf, based on the United Nations Environmental Program (UNEP Trifluoroacetic - TFA) Study, please see reference at the end of this submission.  This additional comment is related to the “PFAS” defined chemical refrigerant R-1234yf which is widely used for air conditioning systems in the automotive industry for mobile air conditioning as replacement for R-134a to address global warming concerns. R-134a has a high Global Warming Potential of GWP 1430.  R-1234yf is a common replacement with the recently described GWP of 0.5 CO2eq (IPCC 6th Assessment Report). This means R-1234yf has only the half of the impact on climate compared to CO2 itself. This favorable property of R-1234yf is a side aspect also worth considering in a holistic assessment.  We want to point to the global UNEP TFA reputable and reliable study to constructively support your PFAS investigation. This scientific study released recently by UNEP related to R-1234yf is identifying its quick atmospheric degradation to form TFA and is assessing risks as very minimal. Not comparable to risks of other PFAS Substances.  The UNEP EEAP study provides a detailed review of the literature relating to TFA and concludes:  “However, it does not interact with biological molecules and, due to its high solubility in water, it does not bioaccumulate. It is unlikely to cause adverse effects in terrestrial and aquatic organisms” [p. 5].  To minimize the social and economic impact while optimizing the risk to the environment and society, we would also like the SEAC and RAC consider revising the definition of the PFAS to restrict only PFAS chemicals which are determined to be Persistent, Bioaccumulative and Toxic. The United States Environmental Protection Agency (US EPA) has developed a definition which focusses only on the most harmful PFAS. This Definition is also shown in the attachment. RECOMMENDATIONS  We like to ask ECHA - specifically RAC and SEAC - to review this UNEP study’s findings on TFA and consider it in respective assessments for use of R-1234yf and for proper scientific-based regulatory advice. We think, this UNEP study’s findings on TFA will add valuable input to your risk assessment and socio-economic analysis and recommend a deeper analysis with respect to future R-1234yf use.  Furthermore, we strongly believe this study, result and conclusion is of general interest, and we recommend making ECHA (RAC & SEAC) perspective made public, e. g. as a Q&A. We trust this will happen and would very much appreciate this input to a well-considered scientific-based discussion and decision-making process.  Finally, we recommend a more precise definition similar to the proposed definition of PFAS by the US EPA to minimize risk with the lowest social and economic impact.   US EPA Technical Framework Document PFAS Definition. PFAS or per- and poly-fluoroalkyl substance means a chemical substance that contains at least one of these three structures: (i) R–(CF2)–CF(R′)R″, where both the CF2 and CF moieties are saturated carbons; . (Excludes R-1234yf Includes R-134a) (ii) R–CF2OCF2–R′, where R and R′ can either be F, O, or saturated carbons; or (iii) CF3C(CF3)R′R″, where R′ and R″ can either be F or saturated carbons. SCIENTIFIC REFERENCE UN environment program - Environmental Effects of Stratospheric Ozone Depletion, UV Radiation, and Interactions with Climate Change 2022 Assessment Report, March 2023 – therein: Environmental effect of R-1234yf and TFA https://ozone.unep.org/system/files/documents/EEAP-2022-Assessment-Report-May2023.pdf EXTRACT: Chapter 6 “CHANGES IN TROPOSPHERIC AIR QUALITY RELATED TO THE PROTECTION OF  STRATOSPHERIC OZONE IN A CHANGING CLIMATE” Subchapter 3, “Trifluoroacetic acid in the global environment with relevance to the Montreal Protocol” 3.8 Conclusions and uncertainties: “… One source of TFA in the environment is the degradation of replacements for chemicals that contribute to the destruction of stratospheric O3. These are the HCFCs, HFCs, and HFOs, all of which are replacements for chemicals that fall under the purview of the Montreal Protocol. Some of these products are greenhouse gases and contribute to global climate change. Because of this, there is a trend to replace long lived HCFCs and HFCs with HFOs, which have very short atmospheric lifespans and do not contribute to climate change. The use of these replacements is monitored under the auspices of the Montreal Protocol and estimates of current and future releases of TFA are regularly assessed. These releases will add to the existing load of TFA in the environment but predicted amounts are well below the threshold for concern with respect to human and environmental health.” … “Current and projected (to 2100) concentrations of TFA in the oceans provide a very large margin of exposure (thousand-fold) when compared to thresholds of toxicity and risks to the environment and human health are de minimis.” -> UNEP suggests a negligible risk of TFA / R-1234yf [p 278]: "More recently, a majority of a panel of experts agreed that “all PFAS should not be grouped together, persistence alone is not sufficient for grouping PFAS for the purposes of assessing human health risk, and that the definition of appropriate subgroups can only be defined on a case-by-case manner.” [184]. In addition, the majority opinion with respect to toxicology was that “it is inappropriate to assume equal toxicity/potency across the diverse class of PFAS”. -> Maybe there is an opportunity to at least group PFAS substances according their “Group risks”. For example, besides R-1234yf, Polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) plays a crucial role in the manufacturing of lithium-ion batteries used in electric vehicles (EVs), where it is used as the cathode electrode binder without any suitable alternatives beyond lab-scale R&D. Both (R-1234yf & PVDF) deserve an individual risk assessment.

Analytical methods: As noted in the Restriction Dossier, it is currently not analytically possible to distinguish between PFAS and non-PFAS organofluorine substances when measuring the total fluorine content of a product 14. This would require highly sophisticated procedures that would be able to make the distinction which, to the best of our knowledge, are not yet available. In the SEAC Final Opinion on the restriction proposal on PFHxA, its salts and related substances, the Enforcement Forum of ECHA drew attention to the need to come up with standard methods for the analytical testing of the content of the substances covered by a proposed restriction, i.e., PFHxA, its salts and C6 fluorotelomers, elaborating that some standard methods are currently only available for water matrices.  The measurement of C6 presents a notably greater challenge compared to measuring PFHxA, especially when these substances are bound within larger molecules or present in environmental mediums, biota, and similar contexts. Precursors inherently possess a notably higher level of complexity than singular substances like PFHxA or any PFCA. Consequently, this circumstance underscores the necessity for tests that are tailored to the specific characteristics of each substance. 14  ECHA, Annex XV Restriction Report on Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs), p. 171.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: As mentioned in the attachment, it is not clear whether the amount of PFAS in paper and board exceeds the maximum concentrations of reach and to what extent. Depending on the scenario however it is likely that it would take several years to phase out the PFAS from the paper and board value chain. The introduction of the PFAS restriction without a transition period would therefor risk the circular character of the paper and board production. Recycled paper may account for more PFAS than allowed under the new value limits and could therefor be discarded as a resource in the production of new paper and board.   In the recycling process it is not possible to remove the PFAS that may be present in the collected paper and board. In the collection of paper and board, items containing PFAS such as laminated to-go food packaging material is not accepted. However this is not a guarantee that not a single of such items will be discarded with paper and board. Alternative is to analyse all recovered paper that is to be used in the production process of new paper and board. However since there are no guidelines yet for analysis it is administrative and financially burdensome to analyse all recovered paper and board on PFAS.  The introduction of the PFAS restriction without a transition period would have as a possible consequence that no recovered paper is used in the production of new paper and board. For the situation in the Netherlands this would have severe consequences for the circular nature of the paper and board production process:  • Only in the Netherlands approximately 2.500.000 tonnes of paper and board is put on the market on a yearly basis. For the production of these materials as much as 87% recycled fibres are used. • In the Netherlands approximately 2.000.000 tonnes of paper and board is recycled every year.

Combined Comments: "Dear Sir or Madam, we, bdtronic GmbH, would like to submit our comprehensive statement on the planned EU chemical ban of PFAS substances. As a renowned company in the field of mechanical engineering for adhesive technology, we strive to deliver the highest quality and technical innovations while also fulfilling our responsibility for environmental protection and sustainability. However, the proposed measures to ban PFAS substances present a number of challenges, which we would like to explain below. Our activities in process engineering and mechanical engineering are closely linked to electromobility and other key industries for decarbonization. As a supplier to these industries, we significantly contribute to developing innovative solutions for the production of electric vehicles. Our machines enable the precise processing of adhesives and sealants that are essential for the functionality and safety of these vehicles, especially for the battery electric powertrain. Currently, there are several major projects under construction for a well-known German OEM. For example, this project could not be realized by us or our competitors without the availability of fluorinated elastomers. In this context, fluorinated elastomers play a critical role. These materials are currently used in our process engineering to process highly sophisticated adhesive and impregnating materials. The unique properties of fluorinated elastomers, such as their chemical resistance and flexibility, are crucial for the performance and lifespan of the pumps we use. In particular, when processing complex adhesives, fluorinated elastomers are often the only option to ensure sufficient resistance and functionality. We estimate that approximately 50% of our total revenue depends on the availability of these materials. We understand the need to reduce harmful chemicals to protect human beings and the environment. However, we would like to point out the challenges associated with a sudden ban on PFAS substances. Abandoning these materials would have immediate effects on our ability to manufacture products that meet the strict requirements of our customers. The development and qualification of alternative materials require time and resources to ensure that they meet the necessary standards. At present, we do not see any alternatives for this class of elastomers in the medium term. Our presence as an essential supplier in the electromobility industry means that delays or restrictions in our production could inevitably have an impact on the supply chain and the progress towards sustainable mobility. Electromobility plays a crucial role in reducing emissions and promoting environmentally friendly transport solutions. A ban on fluorinated elastomers could hinder this progress and make efforts towards a clean future more challenging. We are prepared to collaborate with relevant authorities and partners to find solutions that take into account both environmental protection and the requirements of our industry. In conclusion, we would like to emphasize that we are aware of our responsibility and will continue our efforts towards sustainability. We are ready to use our expertise and resources to develop environmentally friendly alternatives while ensuring the performance and safety of our products, but currently see no possibility to completely abandon these products. We thank you for your attention and hope for a constructive collaboration to jointly create a sustainable future. 6695" "Dear ladies and gentlemen, we would like to emphasize that perfluorinated elastomers, due to their polymeric structure, do not release fluorinated compounds into the environment during use. These compounds are so composed that they do not emit any dangerous emissions during their service life. Furthermore, we would like to point out that perfluorinated elastomers can be safely recycled at the end of their life through thermal utilization. This process enables a safe and environmentally friendly disposal without negative impacts on human health and the environment. 6695" "We currently use approximately 300-400 kg of fluorinated elastomers and sealing materials such as PTFE per year for the production of special machinery 6695" "For bdtronic, fluorinated elastomers play a critical role. These materials are currently used in our process technology to process highly demanding adhesive and impregnating materials. The unique properties of fluorinated elastomers, such as their chemical resistance and flexibility, are crucial to the performance and service life of the pumps we use. Especially in the processing of complex adhesives, fluorinated elastomers are often the only option to ensure sufficient resistance and functionality. We estimate that approximately 50% of our total turnover depends on the availability of these materials. Currently, for most critical applications in our field, there is no alternative to fluorinated elastomers (FKM, FFKM) and thermoplastics (PTFE) 6695." "We strongly demand a targeted and carefully balanced exemption from the general ban on perfluorinated alkanes (PFAS) for certain highly specialized application areas, namely for fluorinated elastomers such as FKM, FFKM and their subtypes, as well as for fluorinated thermoplastics such as PTFE. These materials play an indispensable role in many critical industrial sectors, including mechanical and plant engineering, as well as in the chemical and process industries. Their extraordinary properties, such as high chemical resistance, temperature stability, and durability, are crucial for the integrity and performance of many products and processes. FKM, FFKM elastomers and subtypes, as well as fluorinated thermoplastics such as PTFE, offer unique technical solutions for challenges ranging from sealing in extreme environments to highly precise applications. A ban on these materials could have significant impacts on the safety, efficiency, and reliability of industries that rely on these materials. We therefore propose to create an exemption from the general PFAS ban that is carefully restricted to the above-mentioned fluorinated elastomers and thermoplastics. However, this exemption should be subject to strict environmental regulations and sustainability criteria. The affected industries should be obliged to take comprehensive measures for emission control and minimizing environmental impacts. In addition, continuous research and development efforts to explore more environmentally friendly alternatives should be promoted to reduce dependency on PFAS in the long term. This demand takes into account the real and essential need for fluorinated elastomers and thermoplastics in critical industrial sectors, while also prioritizing environmental protection and sustainability. It is of the utmost importance to find a balanced solution that meets both industrial requirements and environmental impacts, in order to ensure a sustainable and responsible future."

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: SEMI Europe welcomes that the semiconductor industry has been put forward for a potential derogation for reconsideration relating to “the semiconductor manufacturing process”.  Such a potential derogation needs to be understood as an umbrella term for what the industry needs to continue manufacturing semiconductors in the EU.  This includes not only the manufacturing process itself but all of the supply and value chains that are essential for such complex manufacturing to take place.  Core aspects of this include:
• Process Chemistries
• Semiconductor Manufacturing Equipment
• Semiconductor Manufacturing Infrastructure
• Semiconductor Manufacturing Support Equipment
• Semiconductor Devices
The Dossier Submitter developed Annex A Table A.49 as part of its initial research into the semiconductor industry’s uses of PFAS.  Since then, the semiconductor industry has conducted a much deeper and broader investigation into the industry’s uses of PFAS.  As a result, an updated version of the original table has been developed and is attached to this initial submittal as “Updated Annex A Table A.49”.  This updated table illustrates the depth and complexity of the industry’s uses of PFAS categorised by the five core aspects noted above.

Consequences of a Partial or No Derogation Outcome
Our research clearly demonstrates that if the semiconductor industry’s proposed derogation does not fully cover the uses captured in the updated Table A.49, then the ability to manufacture or import semiconductors in the EU will stop following the entry into force (EiF) and the expiration of the 18 month transition period (≈ 2028 timeframe).  Rather than being hyperbole, this is the only foreseeable outcome based on the fact that essentially all equipment, and most chemicals, required for the semiconductor manufacturing process depend on the use of PFAS substances, mixtures, and articles for which replacements are not currently known.  Such an outcome will be nothing short of a catastrophe for the EU economy and its citizens given the criticality and strategic position the semiconductor industry holds in enabling so many devices and industries such as automotive, electronics, communications, data storage & analysis, legal & regulatory infrastructure, remote education, scientific (including materials) research, medicine & medical devices, clean technologies for green energy etc.
In the absence of a comprehensive derogation, the proposal as it currently stands would lead to the EU inadvertently undermining not only its economic competitiveness but effectively threaten the success of flagship political initiatives such as the Green Deal, the Net-Zero Industry Act, REPowerEU Plan, 2030 Climate Target Plan. The EU’s digital transformation through its Digital Decade plan and its associated benefits for EU industry equally depends on a secure supply of semiconductors.  The EU Chips act would be fundamentally undermined as such a ban would decisively weaken the competitive position of the EU relative to competitors without similar restrictions.

PFAS Alternatives for the Semiconductor Industry
It is imperative that the decisions regarding derogations granted due to the inability to substitute PFAS must be based upon sound and factual data.  Our research shows that the data and related conclusions published in the Annex XV dossier concerning the semiconductor industry’s ability and timing to substitute PFAS is incomplete and therefore simply does not reflect the reality of the industry.
The Annex XV dossier was heavily focused upon two of four uses of PFAS – Photoacid generators (PAGs) and fluoroelastomers.  It concluded that a “High substitution potential at EiF for photolithography (photoacid generators), fluoroelastomers used for chip manufacturing” exists.  Bearing in mind that the assumed EiF timeframe will be 2026 or thereabouts, the feasibility of the proposed non-PFAS alternatives put forward by the Dossier Submitter was investigated.

Photoacid Generators
Between 100 to 150 PAGs are needed to manufacture semiconductors.  The Dossier Submitter has put forward seven non-PFAS PAGs, one of which is a patent and does not exist as a commercial product and will not be available to the industry by the EiF timeframe.  The remaining six non-PFAS PAGs were analysed by the industry and failed on numerous technical grounds.  Please refer to the SEMI comments attached for further details of the PAGs’ analysis.

Fluoroelastomers
Many semiconductor manufacturing processes are very complex, with most utilising elevated temperatures as well as aggressive and potentially hazardous chemistries that require special system design considerations.  Semiconductor manufacturing processes require high performance seal materials that have high operating temperature range capabilities.  The non-PFAS fluoroelastomers put forward in the Annex XV report were analysed by the industry to ascertain their viability for high volume manufacturing purposes.  The attached document containing SEMI’s assessment of proposed alternative fluoroelastomers illustrates why Ethylene propylene diene monomer (EPDM), Silicone rubbers, Aryl Ketone polymer (PEEK) and Hydrocarbon elastomers are not suitable alternatives.

Ability to Substitute and Derogation Timeframe
There are approx. 1,000 uses of PFAS in the semiconductor industry between the various core elements noted in the introduction.  Please refer to Q7 for several use cases that demonstrate the complexities involved.  Just a handful such as heat transfer fluids are sufficiently advanced in their research to be in a position to be substituted for high volume manufacturing (HVM) needs within the next 8 to 14 years.  The rest of the identified uses are dependent upon a non-PFAS invention in the first instance before being realistically developed for HVM.  Consequently, the proposed derogation timeframe of twelve years will not be sufficient for approximately 90% of the industry’s uses of PFAS.  This disparity in the proposed derogation timeframe and the actual timeframe to invent, qualify and deploy non-PFAS alternatives must be thoroughly considered in ascertaining an appropriate derogation timeframe.

The Semiconductor Industry and PFAS Emissions
While it is a known challenge to develop a comprehensive PFAS emissions profile for the semiconductor industry, SEMI has provided emissions information on polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), Perfluoroalkoxy (PFA), PAGS and lubricants in its Q5 response.

A Fair and Level Playing Field for the EU Based Semiconductor Industry
In recent years the EU and US established the EU-US Trade and Technology Council (TTC) as a transatlantic forum fostering cooperation on trade and technology related issues, based on shared democratic values.  The purpose of the TTC is to enhance trade and investment, strengthen technological and industrial leadership, boost innovation, promote emerging technologies and infrastructure, and encourage compatible standards and regulations.  Digitalisation is at the core of this council and the current EU regulatory pathway regarding PFAS will put the EU semiconductor industry at a significant competitive disadvantage that will give global competitors a significant structural advantage.  It is strongly requested that a comprehensive comparison is established between the EU and US PFAS regulatory landscape to ultimately recognise the overwhelming disadvantage being placed upon the EU based semiconductor industry as a result of the proposed scope of this PFAS Restriction.

The Need for Collaborative Research
The semiconductor industry has made amazing technological advances with the aid of PFAS since the 1980s.  Given the extreme complexity of our industry’s uses of PFAS, it will take a substantial collaborative effort to invent and further qualify non-PFAS alternatives for most of our current uses before they can be deployed.  Such an effort will require funding at the EU level to garner the range of solutions required at an industrial sector as the solution to PFAS use is beyond the capabilities of an individual company.

Summary
• The proposed derogation for reconsideration put forward for the semiconductor industry must capture all PFAS uses throughout its supply and value chain as noted in the updated Annex A Table A.49.
• The proposed derogation must consider the semiconductor industry’s research concerning the timeframe to substitute PFAS which is well beyond twelve years.
• A partial or no derogation outcome will disable many fundamental aspects of a well-functioning society and result in a catastrophe for the EU economy and its citizens.
• The proposed non-PFAS alternatives for PAG and fluoroelastomer use have been shown to be inadequate.
• The EU’s flagship strategies and initiatives are highly dependent upon the semiconductor industry.  To do the EU’s political ambition justice, the semiconductor industry needs a fully comprehensive derogation.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The responses in this Annex XV submittal refer to the use of Electronics and Semiconductor (Annex E.2.11.) with the sub use of Semiconductors as per Table 9.

5. Proposed derogations: At this point in time the semiconductor industry does not have a fully comprehensive PFAS emissions profile.  However, several uses of PFAS such as Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), Perfluoroalkoxy (PFA), PAGs and lubricants have been reviewed to illustrate usage and associated emissions.  PVDF - The average annual tonnage placed onto the market for the last 10 years for semiconductors in facility systems would be ~ 600 mt/year.  This material has a 25+ year service life.  It is not consumed or degraded during its use.  It may be replaced as needed for a factory retrofit.  Retrofit materials are collected in a segregated manner and can be landfilled or recycled.  An estimate of retrofit usage would be ~ 10%.  The EU market is estimated to be 6.9% of the global semiconductor market.  So, of the 600 mt/year, the EU portion would be 41.4 mt/year, of which 4.1 mt/year would be solid waste. There is no data on the volume of air or liquid waste resulting from the use of this material   Some of the 4.1 mt/year of PVDF in the EU is recycled, but not consistently.  PVDF can generally be recycled if it has not been exposed to chemicals. This number could be reduced by 90% if recycling is vigorously pursued.  PFA - The average annual tonnage onto the EU market for the last 10 years specifically for semiconductor usage is ~ 3700 mt/year, (out of 18.2 kt/year).  This is comprised of materials used in both consumed materials such as filters, fluoroelastomers, drum liners, etc. and “fixed asset components” such as tubing, valves, filter housings, tanks, etc. that would make up Fab production tools and production support equipment.  For this later segment these materials have a long service life (over 25 years).  There are more service-related replacements, like valves, that need to be repaired or replaced due to high usage, that will contribute to the waste stream.  The other reason that this material has a shorter than 25 year life is the change in process chemistries.  If a change to a process requires a new or different chemistry, then there will be whole system change outs.  This means that a percentage of material to waste would be as high as 20% annually.  3700 tonnes X 20% = 740 mt/year.  There is no knowledge of this material’s contribution to either air or liquid waste.   To summarise, PFA waste accounts for 740 mt/year in the EU. To date there is some recycling, but it is not consistent.  PFA can generally be easily recycled even if it has been exposed to chemicals. This number could be reduced by 90% if recycling is vigorously pursued.  PAG - The total amount of PFAS used in semiconductor photolithography is about 34 mt/year worldwide, of which 2.25 mt/year are used in Europe. Almost all of this amount can be disposed of in a controlled way, with wastewater emissions in Europe as low as 56 kg/year when all proper procedures are used. PFAS materials are used in photolithography mainly in five areas, all of which are critical to the functioning of a €534 billion industry.  Sub-use categories consist of Antireflection coatings, Topcoats and Embedded Immersion Barriers Layers, Surfactants, Dielectric Polymers (PBO/PI), Filters. To summarise, for photolithography PFAS chemicals approximately 56 kg/year are emitted through wastewater from semiconductor manufacturing facilities in the EU.    Lubricants - For the case of vacuum pumps used in manufacturing equipment for the wafer production process, there are ~ 7000 vacuum pumps per factory (varies with the size of the facility).  For each vacuum pump an average of 200 ml of Perfluoropolyether (PFPE) based lubricant oil is used per pump.  Vacuum pumps are serviced every two years hence an average number of pumps/year would be 3500. Calculating the annual tonnage per factory; 3500 X 200ml = 700l/year with a density of 1.8-1.9 kg/l = 1260-1330 kg/year of oil.  An average 100 grams/year of PFPE/Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) grease is used per Semiconductor Manufacturing & Related Equipment (SMRE) tool.  There are 1000 tools in a factory on average hence there is 100 kg/year of lubricant grease.  For the EU, there are approximately 45 semiconductor factories therefore there would be 56.7-59.8 mt/year of oil and approximately 4.5mt/year of grease on the EU market.  Used oils are recycled by the pump service companies and grease goes to segregated waste collection to be incinerated.  It must be noted that the data referenced above are current estimated values and are subject to further refinement as more accurate information is obtained by the industry.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: The unique properties simultaneously afforded by PFAS materials in terms of chemical resistance, temperature resistance, flexibility, low coefficient of friction, purity, non-flammability, etc., have led to thousands of applications in semiconductor manufacturing, where precision and purity of a wide range of highly complex equipment and a broad array of chemicals are required to deliver the exacting specifications demanded of advanced circuitry. The semiconductor industry has a long history of working toward more environmentally benign solutions including compliance with regulations on restricted materials. However, the ubiquitous nature of the applications space of PFAS in this industry, coupled with the lack of suitable alternative materials, makes substitution of PFAS an exceedingly difficult challenge, one whose magnitude cannot be overstated.  This response illustrates the numerous use cases of PFAS in semiconductors and the challenges posed when seeking alternatives by citing several examples where substitutions were evaluated but found to be insufficient. This is by no means intended by an exhaustive review of either all the applications of PFAS in semiconductor manufacturing, nor on the evaluations of alternatives. Rather it is meant to illustrate the expansive dependency that this multi-hundred-billion-euro industry has on this unique class of materials and how, despite wide-ranging efforts, alternatives do not meet the criteria required for safe and capable replacement. The examples attached in “Question 7 SEMI Use Case Examples” are arranged based upon the application space in which the PFAS material is used. For a more exhaustive description of the use of PFAS in the semiconductor industry, please see “The Impact of a Potential PFAS Restriction on the Semiconductor Sector”, an SIA PFAS Consortium- commissioned summary prepared by RINA, available on the SIA website or attached to this Annex XV consultation submittal.

General Comments: SEMICON APPLICATIONS FLUORTUBING TUBES

Fluortubing PTFE Tubings, known for its unique properties of chemical resistance, are widely used for delivering liquids in high-tech applications. These tubing are connected and installed to storage tanks that contain harsh chemicals such as hydrogen fluoride (HF) or hydrogen peroxide (H2O2). These chemicals are crucial for rinsing semiconductor processor chips used in computers and other semiconductor applications in order to purify their surfaces.

Purification and achieving ultimate purity, along with chemical resistance, are paramount in adopting PTFE tubing for these high-tech applications. Without these specialized tubes, the economical and efficient production of microprocessors would be jeopardized, as computer chips cannot be produced without thorough cleaning with hydrogen fluorides and/or hydrogen peroxides.

There are five objects that need to be purged from the semiconductor materials during the rinsing process:

Particles
Metal ions
Organic matter
Oil
Oxide film

None of these objects should be eluted or found before etching a microprocessor chip, as the purity of the chemicals and surfaces is crucial to ensure the quality of the final product.

Due to its unique characteristics, PTFE is the ideal solution for maintaining the purity of the chemicals during the delivery process. PTFE tubing does not react with the chemicals and does not release any metal ions, making it the only suitable material for this application. The delivery hose must also be pure and stable, as it should not introduce contaminants or react with the chemicals being transported.

In conclusion, Fluortubing PTFE tubing is essential for the safe and efficient delivery of harsh chemicals used in semiconductor manufacturing. Its unmatched properties of chemical resistance, purity, and non-reactivity make it the preferred material for ensuring the high-quality and purity of semiconductor materials during transportation and processing.

General Comments: Sennheiser develops and produces regulatory compliant and safe products for our customers. We support protecting the environment and avoiding release of environmental  hazardous substances. We strive to improve our processes to get sustainable products and decrease the environmental impact of our production and products.
In our products we only use very limited amounts of polymeric PFAS, where no alternative materials exist.
The polymeric PFAS are classified by OECD [1] as polymers of low concern safe for human health and the environment. They are non-toxic, bio-compatible, non-soluble and immobile.
Therefore, the polymeric PFAS should not be part of the restriction.
We suggest a risk-based and substance-based approach according to article 68 (1) and article 69 of the REACH process.
[1] OECD, 2006. OECD definition of polymer. OECD Environment, Health and Safety Publications. Available at: https://www.oecd.org/env/ehs/oecddefinitionofpolymer.htm

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: End of life The PFAS fraction of our products can be incinerated at above 850 °C so that no PFAS will be emitted. See attached research dossiers : uploaded document: Overview PFAS incineration studies.docx To ensure a safe recycling process, it is necessary to claim PFAS as Substance of very high concern (SVHC). This would ensure a) information along the supply chain on PFAS and b) a report of PFAS in the SCIP database and provision of any information needed for the recycling and safe use. The intention of the SCIP database is to enable recyclers to recycle the products without emitting SVHC.

6. Missing uses: Which PFAS are used by Sennheiser   PTFE,  FEP, FKM, PVDF, …      Applications in which PFAS are added   Electret foil in microphones; Isolators in Cables, Antennas and HF applications; micro electromechanical systems, sealings, batteries …      What is the function of the PFAS in the application?   An electret material possesses a permanent electrical dipole moment. When used in a condenser microphone, it provides the polarization voltage between the membrane and backplate in place of the external supply voltage. Electret materials are generally high-resistivity polymers, a prime example being PTFE. They are fabricated by heating a film of the material almost to its melting point and subjecting it to an intense electric field. The net dipole moment results from either rotation of permanent dipoles in polar materials or from migration of free charge carriers. In either case, when the material is cooled to room temperature the net dipole moment is “frozen-in.” The elimination of the external polarization voltage supply, however, has a significant advantage. The generation of a high-dc voltage and the extensive filtering needed to obtain a low noise floor, ripple, and hum require bulky components (except for battery-operated equipment). The absence of this requirement greatly enhances the miniaturization potential of electret-based instrumentation.   Cables with PTFE have an outstanding chemical performance and due to the low friction of the material a much better mechanical stability against bending and mechanical stress, which is therefore very sustainable in comparison to other materials.      Why is PTFE superior to alternative electret materials.   PTFE as electret material possesses excellent chemical stability and dielectric properties. In the manufacturing process of PTFE electrets, the material is electrically charged. The long-term stability of the charge is undisputed and maintains for decades, even under harsh environmental conditions. It is this long-term stability of the PTFE electret that prolongs the lifetime of the microphone. No alternative electret material is known to possess such long-term charge stability.   The high temperature stability of PTFE is of particular importance for this application, because the electret undergoes a soldering process at 250 °C. At this high temperature, the material must maintain its properties. No commercially available alternative electret material is stable above 200 °C [Electret Kapsel Entwicklungsreport.pptx].    Substitute materials that were tested by the internal research and development department are different poly(p-xylylene) polymers (Parylene N, Parylene C, Parylene D and Parylene HT). The most promising of these four materials was Parylene HT, which is unfortunately also considered a PFAS.   [Forschungsbericht Parylene als Alternative zu PFAS bei Sennheiser.docx]   Substitution of electret microphone capsules by other microphone types would be a technological step backwards. Other microphone types, for example dynamic microphones, require an external power supply to function. This requirement restricts the miniaturization potential of the devices. For energy consumption purposes, the electrically powered polarization needs more battery capacity and has less energy efficiency.

General Comments: Sentec AG is a medical device company and global leader in patient monitoring and respiratory care. The focus of our patient monitoring activities are the continuous and non-invasive measurement of transcutaneous carbon dioxide and oxygen, combined with pulse oximetry, providing crucial information about ventilation and oxygenation status at the point of care. An important benefit of the transcutaneous technology is its independence from lung function or lung impairments, reliable blood gas estimates can be obtained even in very sick patients. A particularly important patient group is the neonates, including the most vulnerable very preterm babies, that require ventilation or are otherwise in dire health conditions. Providing continuous information about carbon dioxide and its trending is crucial for the clinical decision and care for these young patients. There are currently no other non-invasive methods that can provide this information.
Technical Challenges and Requirements for transcutaneous measurement of gases:
1. The amount of gas diffusing out of the skin is extremely low, which requires very specific design considerations: a) minimized volumes above the skin for the detection of CO2/O2, b) reduction of diffusion barriers to the minimum, by proper material selection for membrane function and minimal thickness of such material, c) smart selection of membrane materials in regard to their gas solubility (perceived volume) and permeability.
2. The direct measurement on skin with a liquid (gel) between sensor and skin (used for sealing and optimized heat transfer) is a wet measurement with high humidity levels. For the electrochemical sensor design it is very important for the membrane material to have a low water vapor permeability, while, at the same time, having a high CO2/O2 permeability.
3. Mechanical robustness in clinical application: a) the device needs to withstand hospital cleaning and disinfection protocols (while fulfilling requirement 1.b – minimal thickness of membrane), b) impermeability to any liquid that could change behaviour of relevant sensing elements (e.g. electrolyte or optical properties).
4. Stable workflow for membrane change: for an electrochemical sensor the field exchange of electrolyte and membrane must be robust, so that clinical personnel can perform it without specific technical skills. This requires specific wetting properties on the sensor surface and membrane material itself.
5. Biocompatibility of patient interface

To meet these requirements the Sentec electrochemical (TC) sensors use a patient facing membrane that consists of fluoropolymers, specifically PTFE. Currently there are 2 models on the market:
• V-SignTM Sensor, for PCO2 and pulse oximetry (on the market since 2003)
• OxiVenTTM Sensor, for PCO2, PO2 and pulse oximetry (on the market since 2015)
The PTFE membrane confines a small amount of electrolyte to the surface of the sensor and provides the patient interface. The electrolyte has a specific composition to be sensitive to changes in CO2 that are reflected in a pH change in the electrolyte (Stow-Severinghaus electrochemical measurement principle). The current Sentec TC sensor designs are relying on some very specific and unique material properties of the PTFE membrane:
• High CO2 permeability
• Low water vapor permeability
• Ratio of water vapor to CO2 permeability (deeply embedded in short- and long-term behaviour of electrochemical measurement and linked to the stability of sensing and related algorithms)
• Liquid impermeable for water and most solvents (ensuring robust performance of electrolyte)
• Non-stick behaviour in cleaning action toward contact gel (patient application)
• Chemical resistance in cleaning action and resistance toward detergents (clinical handling)
• Importance of wetting behaviour and neutrality toward electrolyte (reliability of measurement, electrolyte replacement workflow (e.g., bubble free application of electrolyte))
• Biocompatibility (patient interface, supporting prolonged continuous monitoring)

Conclusion: So far, no other materials have been identified as suitable for membranes for TC sensors, even after considerable multi-year R&D efforts trying to substitute PTFE.

Impact:
The proposed ban means that Sentec would not be able to provide its clinical users state-of-the-art TC sensors for the continuous monitoring of the most vulnerable patients. Not being able to rely on TC monitoring for their clinical decisions, the care providers would be forced to use invasive and intermittent methods that are known to create pain and infections, also they would miss to detect critical events. Overall, the level of care would be reduced, which would lead to more adverse events and increased mortality.

Therefore, Sentec is soliciting a full exemption (time unlimited derogation) to the proposed ban. If this is not possible a maximum derogation time of 12 years is requested, in the hope that new materials become available to the market and that these could be a suitable replacement for the fluoropolymers.

General Comments: September 12th, 2023
Comments on Proposed PFAS Regulations

We have been molding and processing fluoropolymers for 70 years, producing and selling various products for a wide range of markets including science, automobiles, and semiconductor manufacturing, and thereby contributing to socio-economic development of society.
The PFAS restrictions recently proposed by the ECHA would include linear fluoropolymers because of their persistent property. However, we do not yet fully understand their impacts on human health and the aquatic ecosystem.
The scope of the proposal would place every PFAS substance under a single category. By doing so, it would restrict any number of PFAS substances, of which risk assessment has not been conducted and thereby acceptable/unacceptable risks are yet to be identified. It would breach Article 68(1) of REACH.
We support the statements of the Fluorochemical Products Council of Japan (FCJ) and the Japan Fluoropolymers Industry Association (JFIA) included in Attachments 1 and 2.
As described in the statements submitted by the two organizations above, fluoropolymers are used in a wide range of fields around the world, because they are “not easily degradable” and also “chemically stable” safe materials.

“Comments of Proposed Restriction of PFAS” by FCJ, April 25th, 2023 (Attachment 1)
https://www.cfcpj.jp/european-pfas-lp.html
“Comments on Proposed Restriction of PFAS” by JFIA, May 25th, 2023 (Attachment 2)
http://www.jfia.gr.jp/euroPFASinfo.html

Annex XV1.1.4.9. "Oligomeric and Polymeric PFASs" notes that there is a concern about the effects of pyrolysis products on human health. Also, Annex XV1.1.5.6. "Emissions Conclusions" notes that we do not fully understand the effectiveness of incineration to destroy PFAS nor a tendency to form fluorinated or mixed halogenated organic by-products. We understand recognize the ECHA's concerns from a material chemistry perspective, and if recycling or complete destruction of fluoropolymer waste is legally mandated, as was in the case of Fluorine gas regulation, we will follow such policies. Also, as a company, we are attempting to reduce waste by developing technologies to recycle PTFE waste generated during production processes.

1. Products Containing PFAS for Which We Propose Regulatory Exemption
We request a broad range of our products (PTFE, PFA molded or machined products) includ-ing both in-house and OEM to be exempt from, as they are yet to be risk-assessed. As described below, we, as a manufacturer, would face extreme difficulties in offering material solutions, if the following substances and product applications are to be substituted:
Substance name: PTFE / PFA
Product name: Bellows pump unit for air-driven bellows pumps

2. Structure and Features of Air-Driven Bellows Pumps
Pneumatically driven bellows pumps use pleated parts that expand and contract with air pressure inside a bellows case to suction and push fluid via the volume change during expansion and contraction. Cross-sectional and operating diagrams of the pump are shown in Appendix 1 and 2.
The structure uses a bellows pump unit that seals bellows parts and body parts with check valves. It avoids liquid leakage because there are no rotating shafts or sliding surfaces in the wetted parts.
Air-driven bellows pumps with PTFE bellows units have excellent chemical resistance, heat resistance, discharge stability, and leakage prevention, and are used for chemical transfer applications that require erosion resistance and purity, as typified in semiconductor manufacturing equipment.

3. Reasons why air-driven bellows pumps are selected for chemical supply pumps and chemical circulation pumps:
For chemical supply pumps and chemical circulation pump applications such as those for semiconductor manufacturing equipment, reciprocating-type positive displacement pumps are used because of their purity, leak-proof properties, practical pump life, ability to handle load fluctuations, and discharge stability specifications. The category of positive displacement pumps includes diaphragm pumps and plunger pumps in addition to bellows pumps. However, bellows pumps are selected because of their superior stability, purity, and heat resistance.
Diaphragm pumps are unsuitable for this context because of the low heat resistance of the seal portion of the diaphragm membrane, which is highly deformable. Plunger pumps with sliding parts are also unsuitable for this context, because they require a liquid seal at the sliding interface, which may result in contamination and leakage due to wear.
There are three types of drive systems: electric, hydraulic, and pneumatic. The pneumatic drive type is selected because the electric type may undergo insulation failure if exposed to corrosive gases and subsequently could ignite a flammable atmosphere, while the hydraulic type may cause contamination due to liquid leakage.

4. Material selection of bellows pump unit for air-driven bellows pumps for chemical supply pumps and chemical circulation pumps, typically for semiconductor manufacturing equipment:
The bellows pump unit consists of bellows parts, body parts, and a check valve. The check valve further consists of a valve case, valve, and coil spring.

Following are physical/mechanical properties required for a bellows pump unit:
① Suitable rigidity: Bellows parts should be rigid enough not to deform in any direction other than the expansion/contraction axis of the bellows at the air pressure required for chemical transport.
② Long life: PTFE bellows should not break for a long period of time even with repeated expansion and contraction.
③ Resistance to chemical contamination: No chemical contamination from the bellows itself.
④ Chemical resistance: No swelling, deterioration, or breakage due to contact with the chemical being transferred.
⑤ Heat resistance: Applicable to environments where chemicals are used at up to 180℃.
⑥ Leak-proof: Must be able to weld and have good sealing properties.

 The mechanical properties required for the bellows material of a bellows pump unit are firmness that does not deform in the radial direction under negative pressure during liquid suction and resistance to bending and deformation during repeated expansion and contraction. EPDM and FKM rubbers have good flexibility, but lack firmness, causing the bellows to cave in when negative pressure is applied, making liquid suction impossible. The evaluation results for resins are summarized in the “Flexibility” column of Appendix 3, Table 2, “List of material study results.” PET has good flexibility, but does not meet requirements of high-temperature properties and alkali chemical resistance. We have not found any suitable material for this application other than PTFE.

 Table 1 in Appendix 3 lists the chemical solutions and temperature conditions commonly used in semiconductor manufacturing equipment. The results of heat resistance and corrosion resistance evaluation for resins are shown in Table 2. PEEK and UHMWPE are corrosion resistant but lack flexibility and cannot be used for bellows parts.

 PTFE does not contain any additives and has a proven track record in semiconductor manufacturing applications as a pure material that does not contaminate chemicals. Although there is no data on other materials in this regard, it would be necessary to confirm whether purity can be assured before substituting PTFE.

 PTFE can be welded and is superior in preventing liquid leakage. It is also water and oil repellent and can be tightened in accordance with its creep resistance to prevent leakage. PVC is weldable and can be used for chemicals, temperature-limited containers, etc., but cannot be used for bellows due to its lack of flexibility.

 The body parts are sealed or welded to PTFE bellows parts, so nothing but PTFE can be used.

 Check valve cases and valves are sealed or welded to the PTFE body, so only PTFE can be used. Coil springs are required to have the same characteristics as bellows parts, so only PTFE can be used.

 In an operating environment where there is no compromise for chemical resistance, heat resistance, and bending resistance, if the material is changed, the function of the material may be impaired and damage may result in serious accidents such as leakage of chemicals or chemical injuries to workers due to exposure to the liquid.

5. Exemptions from PFAS regulations
There are no substitutes for PTFE in bellows applications for air-driven bellows pumps for chemical supply and air-driven bellows pumps for chemical circulation, especially those for semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and as such we recommend an indefinite exemption for PTFE for this application.

⑤ Heat resistance: Applicable to environments where chemicals are used at up to 180℃.
⑥ Leak-proof: Must be able to weld and have good sealing properties.

 The mechanical properties required for the bellows material of a bellows pump unit are firmness that does not deform in the radial direction under negative pressure during liquid suction and resistance to bending and deformation during repeated expansion and contraction. EPDM and FKM rubbers have good flexibility, but lack firmness, causing the bellows to cave in when negative pressure is applied, making liquid suction impossible. The evaluation results for resins are summarized in the “Flexibility” column of Appendix 3, Table 2, “List of material study results.” PET has good flexibility, but does not meet requirements of high-temperature properties and alkali chemical resistance. We have not found any suitable material for this application other than PTFE.

 Table 1 in Appendix 3 lists the chemical solutions and temperature conditions commonly used in semiconductor manufacturing equipment. The results of heat resistance and corrosion resistance evaluation for resins are shown in Table 2. PEEK and UHMWPE are corrosion resistant but lack flexibility and cannot be used for bellows parts.

 PTFE does not contain any additives and has a proven track record in semiconductor manufacturing applications as a pure material that does not contaminate chemicals. Although there is no data on other materials in this regard, it would be necessary to confirm whether purity can be assured before substituting PTFE.

 PTFE can be welded and is superior in preventing liquid leakage. It is also water and oil repellent and can be tightened in accordance with its creep resistance to prevent leakage. PVC is weldable and can be used for chemicals, temperature-limited containers, etc., but cannot be used for bellows due to its lack of flexibility.

 The body parts are sealed or welded to PTFE bellows parts, so nothing but PTFE can be used.

 Check valve cases and valves are sealed or welded to the PTFE body, so only PTFE can be used. Coil springs are required to have the same characteristics as bellows parts, so only PTFE can be used.

 In an operating environment where there is no compromise for chemical resistance, heat resistance, and bending resistance, if the material is changed, the function of the material may be impaired and damage may result in serious accidents such as leakage of chemicals or chemical injuries to workers due to exposure to the liquid.

5. Exemptions from PFAS regulations
There are no substitutes for PTFE in bellows applications for air-driven bellows pumps for chemical supply and air-driven bellows pumps for chemical circulation, especially those for semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and as such we recommend an indefinite exemption for PTFE for this application.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Siempelkamp Maschinen- und Anlagenbau GmbH welcomes the opportunity to contribute to the public consultation initiated by the European Chemicals Agency regarding potential restriction of Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) according to Regulation (EC) No. 1907/2006 (“REACH”).

Siempelkamp Maschinen- und Anlagenbau GmbH is an internationally active German family owned company. Sustainability and resource efficiency are the defining issues of our time. We bundle the answers to these challenges in our corporate claim “Intelligent engineering for future generations”. It stands for the energy with which we align our technologies with the future topics of digitalization and sustainability. “Engineering” refers to our core competence for which the name “Siempelkamp” has stood since 1883. As a technology supplier and systems provider for machinery and plant engineering, our core business is focused on the production of complete plants for the wood-based panel industry, as well as different types of press-systems. "Intelligent engineering" in summary illustrates our approach to continuously developing machines and technologies and thus shape the future of our industries. “For future generations” sums up our ambition to improve the world through our actions. Siempelkamp technologies are geared towards the careful use of resources and raw materials. We develop sustainable, durable products and future-oriented services. Our sustainability concept includes, for example, research and development in the areas of alternative raw materials and recycling or usage of our press-systems for future technologies e.g. in the area of light-weight components. Our portfolio is tailored to energy-efficient, sustainable production. In this way, we fulfill our corporate responsibility towards society.

We hereby provide additional information for a further use and refer to our previous consultation of September 4th, 2023.

With regard to the proposed restriction on the manufacture, placing on the market or use of PFASs we submit that for sealings under harsh conditions (Annex XV Restriction Proposal E.2.14. Lubricants) the proposed restriction does not adequately distinguish between the fields of application and service life time of the components/plants.

Request for exemption

We propose to approve the extended derogation of 12 years with a transition period of 18 months for sealings where the use takes place under harsh conditions or use is for safe functioning and safety of equipment. The extended derogation time will enable further research and development to identify alternatives.
Additionally, we propose that the following wording should be incorporated into the REACH Annex XV Restriction Report regarding PFASs as Lubricants and Sealings:

Annex XV Restriction Report E.2.14 Lubricants under harsh conditions:
• “In case of applications in a closed environment with defined human interactions an additional derogation period is possible if no alternatives have been established.”
• “In case of applications for plants/components which service life time extends the derogation period an additional derogation period is possible if no alternatives have been established”

Annex XV Restriction Report E.2.XX Sealings under harsh conditions:
• “In case of applications in a closed environment with defined human interactions an additional derogation period is possible if no alternatives have been established.”
• “In case of applications for plants/components which service life time extends the derogation period an additional derogation period is possible if no alternatives have been established”

We propose that there is a missing use of PFAS. Both points from above apply here as well. The materials are used in a closed environment and extend the service life time. PFAS or PFAS-containing materials are widely used in sealings for a variety of applications. Regardless of the fact that there are various mentions within the Annex, hydraulics are completely ignored. Hydraulic systems always work with (high) pressure and the sealings have to resist various influences (e.g., increased temperature) under dynamic conditions.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: This consultation for the Annex XV restriction report gives more specific information about the use of sealings under harsh conditions according Annex E.2.14. Table 9. Sealings which contain PFAS are used in a large number of Siempelkamp's products. The reasons for the use range from high temperatures to high pressures to a generally higher durability. To produce our sustainable wood-based materials (particleboards, MDF-boards, OSB-boards or even wood-fiber insulation boards), high-temperature sealings are used in our whole form- and pressing-line. Especially in our continuous press system (ContiRoll®), the operating temperature is around 270 °C. For finishing wood-based materials (particleboards, MDF-boards, plywood or multi-layer boards), produced by our ContiRoll® (see above) with coatings, our short-cycle coating systems are used. Special melamine-coated papers are applied under high pressure of up to 700 N/cm² and at a temperature of up to 220 °C. With our systems up to 250 cycles per hour (coatings per hour) under harsh conditions with high pressure and high temperatures are possible. Additionally, our systems can be used to produce wood-based insulations in various designs. These materials are widely used in the renovation or construction of buildings (also in accordance to the EU Green Deal).  Our rubber-press systems are used e.g. in the production of conveyor belts or tread pattern for tires. Both products cannot be produced without our press systems. Conveyer belts replace trucks and tread pattern help to increase the resource efficiency. These press systems use high pressures with up to 320 bar while reaching temperatures above 100 °C in the area of the sealing. Fiberglass and carbon-fibre-reinforced polymers are materials for which our press systems can be used. Both materials are used for the construction of light-weight systems to increase their efficiency (e.g., planes, vehicles or else). Additionally, the service-time and durability of these materials is higher compared to alternatives e.g. made from metals. With pressures up to 350 bar and temperatures with constant 100 °C and peak 120 °C combined with a friction-reduction the requirements towards the sealings are very high.  Since not every system can be improved using the above-mentioned materials, press systems for metal forming are still needed. Our systems can be used either in hot working or work hardening processes. With our variety of press systems our customers are able to produce chassis for planes, blades for turbines, parts for renewable energy systems, pipelines, and heat-exchanger. With pressures up to 350 bar and temperatures with constant 100 °C and peak 120 °C combined with a friction-reduction the requirements towards the sealings are very high. Some rare press systems generate pressures with up to 1,500 bar. Due to the high pressures and increased temperatures combined with e.g., short cycles the stresses on used seals are very high. The used high-temperature long-term synthetic sealings containing PFAS are used to reduce friction and prevent leakages. Currently, the high requirements cannot be fulfilled by other materials (please see DIN 3771-3, attached temperature-resistance-elastomers.pdf and Heinz K. Müller et al). They contain PFAS in a range of 40%-80% w/w. The sealings have a very limited weight reduction during use and most of the material (except of small amount of wear) is collected after maintenance. All of the sealings are made from solid material and contact is limited to trained staff during maintenance. Currently, there is no adequate PFAS-free alternative that would be reasonable for the plant operation of our customers. As stated by previous stakeholders in the Annex XV Restriction Report (E.2.1.14 Lubricants) there are no alternative sealings which could ensure the safe functioning, safety of equipment and a comparable service life time for the components under harsh conditions. Examples of used materials can be found in  attached “Materials_HydraulicSealings (German).pdf”, “productdatasheet double wiper (German).pdf” and “datasheet_ptfe-sealing_en.pdf”. As soon as PFAS-free alternatives become available that do not severely affect the customer in the operation and maintenance of the plant, we will switch to these alternatives.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: To be able to operate our different systems accurately and safely and to ensure our customers a long service life, our customers need to change the sealings regularly according to our guidelines. The number of sealings depends on the system and only for our ContiRoll product a 5-year-interval for changing is defined (see attached document “ContiRoll_-Cylinder-packing-change-interval.pdf”). For other systems the sealings are changed if a leakage occurs. In some cases, other sealings are renewed in this turnaround. As stated under no. 1, contact with people only occurs when changing the sealing. Since the sealings are solid, the handling is easy and uncontrolled emissions are expected to be extremely low. Apart from very minor wear and tear, all the material is replaced. By progressing wear of a sealing, the tightness decreases and leads to the need of replacement. It can be assumed that the amount of material wear out is far less than 1%. After usage the sealings are collected in a separate container and disposed as required by local regulations. To point this out: over 99% of the used material is collected without uncontrolled emissions.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: In our respectively our customers’ cases, the use of PFAS substances is restricted to a closed environment that is only accessible to humans during maintenance. After usage the sealings are collected in a separate container and disposed as required by local regulations. Depending on local regulations, this prevents the per- and poly-fluorinated alkyl substances from accumulating or uncontrolled emissions. The effectiveness of incineration under normal operational conditions with respect to the destruction of PFAS and the prevention of emissions was evaluated in the following study: Waste incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate potential formation of per- and poly-fluorinated alkyl substances (PFAS) in flue gas [Aleksandrov et al, 2019]. Additionally, the prevention of emission is regulated in the European industrial emission directive 2010/75/EU.

5. Proposed derogations: For over 200 ContiRoll® plants in operation worldwide, the amount of used sealings per system can be estimated to be around 65 kg. In total 13,000 kg sealing material is used. Every five years the sealings will be changed, resulting in an annual consumption of 2,600 kg. With a range of 40%-80% w/w the amount of PFAS is between 1,040 kg and 2,080 kg.  For our other press systems, the variety and thus also the variety of sealings is much higher and more individual. Our press systems for composite materials, multi-stack, short cycle, rubber and metal press systems are usually in operation for 25-30 years. Individual systems can produce for up to 50 years. A total of between 250-300 press systems are currently in operation and each system requires between 5 – 25 kg of sealing materials each year (estimate). In total 1,250 – 7,500 kg of sealing material and 500 – 6000 kg of PFAS. The consumption is highly dependent on the use of the systems, as there are no defined intervals for a renewal of the sealings. The sealings are renewed when oil leaks. According to our major supplier, we and our customers purchase approx. 3,850 kg per year. This results in a share for PFAS of 1,540 – 3,080 kg per year for this supplier. Together with our other suppliers our purchase of PFAS is between 2,000 kg to 4,000 kg per year. All of these purchased materials are solid and there is limited wear of less than 1% w/w.

6. Missing uses: In Annex XV of the restriction report the use of PFAS-materials for large hydraulic-components is missing. In such systems the sealings have two functions. First and foremost is the sealing function under high pressure and partially high temperatures. Additionally, the sealing is not embedded in a static system as the cylinder is in motion. The friction reduction of the used materials is the second function. The requirements for such a material in a non-static environment are much greater compared to static sealings. Often the materials are tested under static conditions and the assignment to thermal stability does not reflect the real conditions. For static resistance properties, please refer to the attached diagrams "Diagram Temperature and Oil Resistance (German).PNG" and "Temperature Resistance-Elastomers.pdf". For our products there is currently no PFAS-free alternative. From our point of view, the available materials are not suitable for the intended use based on the values in the data sheets. The stress under field-conditions exceeds the potential strength of the used materials. An internal example in file “Press cylinder sealing system in short cycle press system.pdf” shows the need of PFAS containing sealings for our systems. The use of hydraulic systems in warm to hot conditions is not specific to our product. From our point of view, there seems to be a missing use to be considered in the ECHA assessments.

8. Other identified uses: Since our plants are built to serve our customers for more than 30 years, we are proposing to approve the extended derogation of 12 years with a transition period of 18 months for sealings where the use takes place under harsh conditions or the use is for safe functioning and safety of equipment. Additionally, we propose that PFAS-containing sealings can continue to be used under harsh conditions if PFAS-free alternatives for harsh conditions do not enter the market within the extended transition period of 13.5 years, since the lifetime of our plants exceeds the derogation time. The sealings have to be replaced with exactly the same type. No other option like modification of the affected parts is possible. Thus, ensuring the operation of newly built plants or plants currently under construction until the end of its lifetime.  Furthermore, due to insufficient thermal stability – also for temperatures below the material-specific temperature – the sealings would degenerate faster. Please see attached “Diagram temperature and oil resistance (German).PNG” and “temperature-resistance-elastomers.pdf” as well as our internal example “Press cylinder sealing system in short cycle press system.pdf”. Additionally, the risk of a failure increases in a significant way. A total failure of such a sealing lead to unplanned downtimes. Attached is an internal confidential example (“Press cylinder sealing system in short cycle press system.pdf”) showing this inadequate stability. Regardless of whether the temperature is within the range of currently available PFAS-free alternatives, the material is not able to withstand the conditions. Switching the material to a PFAS-containing material which is suitable for much higher temperatures, the massive degradation of the sealings stops. The customer confirmed our expectations with the corresponding feedback. This internal example proves, that the test conditions for the classification of materials do not reflect the real conditions in operation. As such press systems usually are designed and produced for the needs of our customers, there is no back-up and a loss of a system could result in life-threatening situations for our customers like an unplanned long-term interruption in their operations. The research activity regarding PFAS-free sealings for harsh conditions is part of our suppliers. We use the sealings in hydraulic systems and currently there is no way to redesign our systems without them.

General Comments: Sigma Laborzentrifugen GmbH develops and markets laboratory centrifuges for application in dedicated medical applications, such as in-vitro-diagnostics and transfusion medicine, as well as life-science, biotech, pharma, food analysis and environmental analysis. The products are dedicated for professional use only. PFAS-containing components are vital in two functions relevant in centrifuges:
highly effective refrigerants (which are thus affected by the F-gases regulation at the same time), and
b) high-performance materials that have chemical resistant and anti-sticking properties, or have to withstand extreme conditions.

PFAS and F-Gas regulation both also deal with refrigerants relevant for centrifuges. Both regulations contradict each other considerably: PFAS provides for a transition period of 13.5 years for fluorinated refrigerant gases. The F-Gas Regulation wants to ban fluorinated refrigerant gases with a transition period of 18 months, preferably by Jan. 1, 2025. There are massive safety concerns for the use of natural, flammable refrigerants an alternative in centrifuges. Furthermore, the performance of known or also expected alternative refrigerants is not sufficient to adequately cool centrifuges with high performance, i.e., e.g., indispensable centrifuges for the separation of blood components for transfusion medicine will no longer be possible.

PFAS are high-performance materials that are among the most important industrial chemicals because of their special properties. "Many industrial products and applications that have to withstand extreme conditions or are manufactured under such conditions would no longer be possible with a blanket ban. The fact that these are indiscriminately and presumably unintentionally included in a blanket ban is a departure from the principle of proportionality, which was always upheld in previous substance bans.

Instead, room must be created for essential applications that will also allow technological progress in the future and within the framework of environmental regulations. While a ban of PFAS for mass production consumer items is the right step, instruments for professional use (which would include instruments with life-saving relevance) typically represent a very low risk of environmental emission and should remain possible, if performance requires the use of high-tech PFAS.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Ccomponents in high-tech instruments for professional, including medical, use.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Instructions for proper deposition and recycling are included with instruments for professional use, i.e. the risk of unwanted release into the environment is extremely low.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Instructions for proper deposition and recycling are included with instruments for professional use, i.e. the risk of unwanted release into the environment is extremely low.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Instructions for proper deposition and recycling are included with instruments for professional use, i.e. the risk of unwanted release into the environment is extremely low.

5. Proposed derogations: The amount of PFAS used in instruments such as centrifuges is extremely low (i.e. much less than 1 t per year from 600 t of total instruments weight.)
