General Comments: Specific Use case: Sulfuric Acid storage for water treatment on ships

Why Fluoropolymers for sulfuric acid?

Large ships, especially cargo ships for container, oil, ect…. , need to take up water for ballast when they cruse without loads. Releasing the ballast water in different locations than it was taken up, can cause wide-spread environmental damage to coastal ecosystems by invasive aquatic species carried in the ballast tanks of ships. Thus, since few years it is common to treat the ballast water and eliminate the worldwide transfer of invasive species. On 4. March 2023 the United Nations High Seas Treaty was finally signed by 190 member states requiring measures to avoid carrying invasive aquatic species onboard of ships across oceans.

Using sulfuric acid, chlorine dioxide disinfectant is produced on the ships for effectively treating the ballast water during intake (see Link). One key part of the chlorine dioxide production is a storage tank for sulfuric acid. To provide adequate corrosion protection of the H2SO4 tanks, they are lined using ECTFE sheets. The H2SO4 tanks on ships were subjected to a astringent approval process from DNV.

When it comes to safe handling of H2SO4, fluoropolymers like ECTFE provide the most efficient solutions. Production, storage, transport an use of chemicals and other hazardous materials can inevitably carry potential risks. Moreover, history has shown that accidents can not only have economic impacts, but also irreparable consequences on human lives and the environment. Mitigating such risks through rigorous safety management whilst simultaneously ensuring efficiency and availability is a major challenge for today’s worldwide chemical industry. Fluoropolymers play a key role in this aspect.

We strongly believe that the restriction proposal should differentiate between the various types of PFAS based of their chemical composition, their toxicological profile and the production method (e.g. the production of fluoropolymers without fluorosurfactants) as well as their specific uses. Not all PFAS are the same and there is no scientific basis to regulate them all the same. For detailed scientific information on the safety and environmental profile of fluoropolymers, we suggest to approach Cefic’s FFP4EU or Plastic Europe’s Fluoropolymer Group. Further information can also be found in Henry et al. (2018) and Korzeniowski et al. (2023), as well as in European Commission, Directorate-General for Environment, Bougas, K., Corden, C., Crookes, M., et al. (2020)

We request full exemption of fluoropolymers from the restriction proposal.

The Annex XV restriction report does not cover all relevant and essential uses of fluoropolymers in the critical sector “transportation”: Sulfuric acid storage tanks onboard of ships need to added to Annex XV.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The specific use of “fluoropolymers used for lining of H2SO4 tanks onboard of ships”,, which is necessary for the production of water disinfectants to purify ballast water is not listed in Table 9.R02 of Annex XV.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: For this specific use, currently mainly ECTFE sheets with a thickness of 2.3 mm is used and additionally also ECTFE welding rod, pipes and fittings are needed as accessories.  According to our supplier Solvay, ECTFE is already produced without the use of fluorinated polymerization aids, thus ECTFE has a very low potential for leaching of small molecular PFAS.    During manufacturing:   There is a certain amount of emissions when fluoropolymers are processes at elevated temperature in the thermoplastic state. While the majority of the emissions is HCl and HF, there is no detailed information available if the emissions contain small molecular PFAS. In our facility, the main parts of the extrusion line with the highest temperatures (thus the areas where emissions are most likely to occur) are covered with a ventilation hood to suck of fumes/emissions above the extrusion line. The off gases are then cleaned in gas scrubber, before released into the environment. Measurement have shown that some small molecular PFAS accumulate in the water of the gas scrubber, thus cleaning the off-gasses is a proven way to reduce emissions.  Precise work and proper work instructions avoid loss of fluoropolymers during the production in our facility. Material from the starting process as well as chips from cutting are collected and added again to the extrusion process (internal recycling). Material which cannot be processed again is stored in containers and sent for incineration following Austrian laws for handling waste (>850 °C effectively destroys PFAS during incineration).  Storage and handling  Proper Packaging avoids PFAS loss during the transportation and storage. After production, products are packed sold in sales units like: • Sheets: 12.5 m² and 25 m² • Pipes: OD 32 – 110 mm diameter; Length = 5 m • Welding Rod 3 -4 mm diameter (1 kg Spool)  During the production of semi-finished sheets, we therefore expect no environmental pollution processing the beforementioned Fluoropolymers.  The use-phase:   Products are used in the following specific sub-uses:  • ECTFE semi-finished products (sheets, welding rod, pipes, fittings etc.) are used for the lining of tanks onboard of ships in a well-controlled environment which ensured that ECTFE is not released into the environment. It must also be considered that ECTFE is on the inside of a steel tank only.  During the use phase at ambient temperatures, emissions from ECTFE do not occur (below detection limit), because the material is extremely stable, inert and does not degrade into small molecular substances over the whole life-time.   End-of-life:   Equipment which is decommissioned after service life (~10-15 years depending on the application) could be collected and deposited or incinerated according to the state of the art. There-fore it would be necessary to implement international regulations of dismantling and recycling ships. However, even at the end-of-life ECTFE remains very stable and does not degrade into small molecular PFAS, but it remains inert and is not expected to contaminate the environment.

6. Missing uses: The missing use discussed is related to the transportation industry. On board of large ships, sulfuric acid is need to for producing chlorine dioxide. For the safe and reliable storage of the sulfuric acid, the best solution is to line the tanks with ECTFE sheets for corrosion protection.  Onboard of ships the chlorine dioxide is needed for effectively treating the ballast water during intake. By treating the ballast water, it is ensured that invasive spices are not transported across the ocean causing wide-spread harm to costal ecosystems. Thus, today regulations are in place that treatment of ballast water needs to be done.  Further information about ballast water treatment onboard of ships can be found on the following website. This specific system is the best technology for large ships. b. The key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use.  Various chemical resistance lists (e.g. DVS Codes 2205-1) and the publication “Polymers in sulphuric acid service” (Sulphure Magazine, number 358, May-June 2015) confirm that ECTFE is chemically resistant to sulfuric acid um to 100 %. While other materials (e.g. PE, PP, rubber, …) can only handle lower concentrations. Also metals to not enable such a universal chemical resistance, at least not in cost effective way. • Long term chemical resistance of ECTFE against sulfuric acid (>98 %) at ambient temperatures in the H2SO4 storage tank. • Long-term leak prove lining for steel and FRP tanks • The ECTFE lining offers simple repair options since the sheet can be welded again after proper preparation in the case of mechanical or thermal damages. • Increasing the safety and reliability of the water treatment system on ships   c. The number of companies in the sector estimated to be affected by the restriction.  Apart from our suppliers for ECTFE (Solvay) and the companies producing the water treatment system, the largest impact is expected for the shipping industry and the companies operating the vessels.   d. The availability, technical and economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives for the relevant use, including information on the extent (in terms of market shares) to which alternative-based products are already offered on the EU market and whether any shortages in the supply of relevant alternatives are expected.  It is not our expertise to evaluate alternatives for treating ballast water of ships. There are other systems on the market that do not require sulfuric acid. However, especially for large ships, this specific system that uses sulfuric acid onboard of ships to produce disinfectant has proven to be reliable, most effective in treating the ballast water and also very cost effective. In order to protect the marine environment and avoid the transport of invasive species across oceans, it is essential to keep this systems on the market. Due to the arduous approval process at DNV that is expected to take several years and cost in excess of 1 Mio €, short term, no alternatives are available.  f. For cases in which substitution is technically and economically feasible but more time is required to substitute: • the type and magnitude of costs (at company level and, if available, at sector level) associated with substitution (e.g. costs for new equipment or changes in operating costs); • the time required for completing the substitution process (including any relevant certification or regulatory approvals); • information on possible differences in functionality and the consequences for downstream users and consumers (e.g. estimations of expected early replacement needs or expected additional energy consumption); • information on the benefits for alternative providers.  The steel tank for the sulfuric acid by itself is not resistant and would corrode and leak quickly. Alternatives or the lining would be available but are impacted by the PFAS restriction proposal as well. It would be possible to use PVDF, FEP or also PFA for the internal corrosion protective lining. Using PE or PP would not allow to use sulfuric acid with such a high concentration. Information about the corrosion resistance to sulfuric acid can be found in the attached paper in the Annex (Sulphur Magazine, number 358, May-June 2015). It clearly shows the that fluoropolymers are a superior solution at highly concentrated H2SO4.  We assume that it would be possible to use metal that is corrosion resistant to 96 % sulfuric acid. A detailed evaluation is not possible from our side, because metals are not our expertise. In any case, it would significantly increase the cost of the disinfecting system and it would require to start a new approval process. In total we assessed that it could take up 5-7 years to find an alternative for H2SO4 storage tank.  g. For cases in which substitution is not technically or economically feasible, information on what the socio-economic impacts would be for companies, consumers, and other affected actors. If available, please provide the annual value of EU sales and profits of the relevant sector, and employment numbers for the sector.  While the impact for our supplier, our company and our customers is not that big looking at the pure numbers, banning ECTFE and other fluoropolymers would increase the cost of water treatment onboard of ships and jeopardize the wellbeing of costal marine environment. The biggest impact is expected for international shipping companies and operators of vessels. In the end the transportation costs of all goods shipped in and out of Europe by sea would increase and impact our cost of living even further (e.g. increased inflation).

General Comments: Specificities and problematic of music strings production.
 INTRODUCTION :
Our company SAVAREZ sa produces high quality Music strings that are exported in more than 80 countries. We are worldwide leaders. Our reputation of highest quality strings has been built over 253 years of experience. SAVAREZ company is a 100% French company.
STRINGS AND INSTRUMENTS :
Music strings are dedicated to the category of instrument played with strings. The number of instruments played in the world is unlimited. There are many different categories using different way for creating sounds. Each instrument has specific characteristics and requirements for spare parts, raw materials and accessories. Strings are considered as accessories but play an essential role in the production of music.
In the category of stringed instruments there are many very different categories. They belong to the same family but present completely different characteristics, some are played with a bow, some are played with a plectra or a mediator, some are played with the fingers or even nails. Therefore it is impossible to use the same strings on all the existing instruments.
In addition very old instrument are still played like 500 years old instruments when at the same time contemporary and experimental instruments represent an important part of the instruments market.
We have to produce different strings with very specific raw materials for all stringed instrument from very old ones (five hundred years old) to the most recent contemporary ones. Instrument makers at the same time work on old instruments and create contemporary new one. We have to produce specific strings for these new contemporary instruments and most of the time we have to work with new raw materials.
As raw material has to present very high sounding characteristics and very special physical characteristics, when we are successful and achieve the very special strings required by instrument makers and musicians, it is always impossible to change the raw material. Only if there is a change in the requirements we have to find a new raw material. That means that musicians look for a  new sound, a new harmonic spectrum and a different playability. That means a fully new string.

- STRINGS
SAVAREZ company’s strategy is to produce very special strings for all possible instruments. In order to achieve this target Savarez uses 2200 different raw materials to produce 2300 different products due to the high diversity of instrument explained above. The number of used raw material demonstrates that each string is specific and requires very special raw materials to correspond to the requirements of the musicians and the music they play.
For this reason if an instrument has to be strung with metallic string it is impossible to change the metallic string by synthetic strings or gut strings. The opposite is true if an instrument is built to use synthetic strings it is impossible on this instrument to play metallic or gut strings. Example: electric guitar, classical guitar, Jazz guitars, violin, cello, double bass.

- PROBLEMATICS OF MUSICIANS
When a specific string is chosen by the musicians they do not want any changes because they cannot take a risk when they are on stage and play at their highest level. That means they chose the best raw material for them among 2200 products we already use. As a consequence it is obvious that changing even just a little a raw material creates an incredible difference not acceptable by the musician.
Any small change in the structure of the strings leads to very different properties, that means it can be considered as a new string. Most of the time this new string is rejected.

- OUR HISTORY WITH PVDF :
More than 35 years ago we discovered that some musicians were crazy about the quality of PVDF strings. We worked more than ten years to be able to offer on the market strings that very highly talented international musicians could accept to play.
Over the years the strings made of PVDF are more and more successful and used by an increasing number of musicians every year. For these musicians it has been a revolution, they adapted themselves to this material changing their way of playing. They did this effort because they recognized the incomparable characteristics of PVDF they cannot find with other raw material.
We speak about the big stars of the music well known worldwide playing concerts in front of several thousands of people. They cannot take any risk using a product of lower characteristics because of playing PVDF strings during more than 35 years. It is very difficult for a musician to change habits when they have been playing such strings for so long time.
So now our strings made of PVDF are well known all over the world and distributed in more than eighty countries.
Strings we produce with PVDF (Polyvinylidène difluoré ) represent a very big part of our activity (see ANNEX N°12 and 13).

 How do we use PVDF monofilament or multifilament, and risk of emission?
This PVDF is made of pure long chain PVDF ONLY.
We use mono filament or multi filaments. We receive directly from Japan monofilaments of pure PVDF in many different diameters and multi filaments of only one type made with the same pure PVDF. They are finished products that we do not transform, modify, or include in other products.
Absence of risk of emission :
We sell these PVDF monofilaments as we receive them. We just add the packaging. Multifilaments can be covered with a metallic thread without any frictions. So there is absolutely no risk of emissions during our production process.
During the use phase of our strings :
In fact when a string is made with multifilament pure PVDF covered with metallic thread the multifilament is not at all in contact with the fingers of the musicians or with the bow, because of the metallic thread in-between. So there is absolutely no risk that some thin microparticles can be removed from the strings.
Regarding the monofilaments there is no risk for another reason : One of the most important property of pure long chain PVDF is the solidity of the monofilament plus the quality of the surface. The surface is very smooth and hard. The most important is that the material is very resistant to the friction and do not get damaged very easily. This is one of the reasons why musician choose PVDF strings because they last much more than other material and do not get used when playing. All experience with musicians have demonstrate that after playing, the strings  were absolutely not damaged and no mark on the strings can be seen plus no particles could be find on the strings and on the fingers. The risk to transfer small particles in the water when washing hands is not significant and does not represent any danger.

 SPECIFIC PROPERTIES OF PURE LONG CHAIN PVDF MAKING IT IMPOSSIBLE TO REPLACE:
Pure long chain PVDF is the only material that has the following combined properties at the same time :
-  High density (1780 kg/m²) that allows the use of thinner strings with a tension similar to thick strings. All other synthetic material’s density is around 1000-1300kg/m², which makes a big difference for sensitive music strings
- Excellent vibrating ability due to the high homogeneity and very low internal friction : Very few materials have this ability to vibrate with a very low loss of energy, this allow the sound to last longer when the string is put under vibration. This explain why small particles cannot be observed.
-  Outstanding elasticity and stiffness characteristics (after long years of research on PVDF) compared with all other synthetic material (See comparison with Nylon in ANNEX n°1. Of course metallic strings cannot reach these standard of essential physical properties.
-  High mechanical tensile strength to support the tension on the instrument, and allow the string to stay in tune, These characteristics are essential for musical practice. See ANNEX N°1 + 2
-  Mechanical properties are not sensitive to high humidity conditions (NOT THE CASE OF POLYAMID). This is incredibly important when playing in hot and humid countries like Singapore, south American countries and other countries located close to the Equator.  No other material can pretend to offer this very important advantage. See ANNEX N°3
- Mechanical properties are not sensitive to high or very low temperatures, which is also very important.
-  Excellent resistance to nail abrasion (important for good string durability over time). No powder created while playing. See ANNEX N°4
-  Characteristic sound not imitable with other synthetic materials. See ANNEX N°5 + 6 (we can see that the harmonic spectrum of PVDF is richer than the Nylon’s one)
- Low friction coefficient of the surface to avoid noises when the fingers slide on the strings
- Good UV resistance avoid the string to become weak because of the sunlight (See ANNEX N°7)
Many musicians use these pure long chain PVDF strings and could not use other strings. They allow to give high level results, and make the public feel incomparable emotions.
Research of other materials for substitution:
Intense research are a major condition for our company to survive. For this reason we invest a lot of time and money in research. One of the most important direction is to test the biggest number of raw materials to try to find a new coming material on the market which could bring big advantages.
Because pure long chain PVDF is absolutely essential for the company (taking into account the involved turnover), we are very much concerned with the possibility of finding a new material which could replace PVDF, just in case some problem could appear with our suppliers: production capacity, technical problem, issue with sources of supply of raw material. New materials should precisely meet our specifications to be a possible substitute product or better.
From the time we have been so successful with pure a long chain PVDF we never stopped looking for substitute to the PVDF to ensure our future. That means a more than 30 years research.
After eliminating a huge quantity of material, we are still currently working on 15 new products. The results are absolutely not positive as it is the case since the beginning of the research.
According to our experience creating a new range of string for a specific instrument can take from 20 to 5 years. It has been the case for a new cello strings line we recently put on the market after almost 20 years working. This process is very long because we need to find a new raw material, wait long for the delivery of a special product, produce many different prototypes, check the durability (many month), work with many different musicians, then work on the packaging and the worldwide promotion.

 RECYCLING POSSIBILITY / POLLUTION :

PVDF is structurally classified as PFAS because it contains -CF2- group, but its properties are fundamentally different from those of low molecular weight PFAS: Long chain PVDF is stable, non-mobile, and do not enter the metabolic system of the human body. Therefore, it is basically harmless to human health and the environment. 2, 3

We think that the proposed restriction should not regulate all substances defined as PFAS, but rather identify more detailed substance groups which have similar toxicity profiles based on scientific evidence and should establish appropriate restrictions for each substance-groups based on their human health and environmental impacts.

The company who produces the resin and transformed it to monofilament or multifilament in Japan, informed us that during the production process of long chain PVDF resins, no small chains are generated and that our PVDF is stable in water, without decomposition.

“Now it is expected that close to 83 % of the global production of fluoropolymers will not require the use of short-chain PFAS such as fluorinated polymerization aids (FPAs). Especially, it is to be noted that the three main fluoropolymers by volume (PTFE, PVDF and FKM) will shortly be manufactured fully without the use of FPAs.1
In parallel, there has been progress in development of technologies to recover more than 99% of the emitted PFAS during fluoropolymer production”

During the next operation in our company we already  mentioned that there is absolutely no emission because of no transformation, physical or chemical, and no friction. And it is the case when playing the strings. No scientific evidence demonstrates the opposite.
About recycling, PVDF is a thermoplastic material that is easy to recycle.
Musicians are very sensitive to the environmental issue. At our initiative, supported by the music stores, we have been working together with the company VALOMATEX in France, to find the best solution for the recycling of musical strings made of PVDF. This company is used to recycle products made of PVDF. Today, we have the confirmation from them that we can send our strings to them to make them recycle. We already started to gather the used/rejected PVDF strings in our production factory, so that we can make them recycled in other useful products.
OFFER sent 24 May 2023 from VALOMATEX: “we can recycle PVDF. Send your sample for us to confirm.”  See ANNEX N°8
After sending samples of PVDF to this company we have been informed that they have been successful in recycling our rejected strings then we sent more quantities to be tested. Anyway they informed us we can start recycling all the PVDF we wish.
At this point we started exploring with musician how to get back used strings from them. They can take them to a shop or send them back to us. At the same time we are exploring how to proceed with music shops where the musicians can take back their used strings to be returned to us and sent to the company VALOMATEX able to recycle.
At the same time we study how to reward musicians and shops to return the string for recycling.
This is a realistic situation because we had a confirmation from the company VALOMATEX is that they accept to receive our PVDF for recycling already just now. It is not a possibility or a research it's a real fact in present days.
UNFAIR COMPETITION WITH OTHER MUSIC STRINGS PRODUCERS :
Most of our competitors (our main and bigger competitors) are located outside EUROPE and will not be affected at all by the restriction of the use of the PFAS in Europe. Therefore they are in a perfect position to take over 100% of  our worldwide market because they already sell PVDF strings and are known even if we cover more than 80 % of the market.
They are located in USA (more than 5companies) , in China, in Japan, South Korea, Russia……..
In Europe there are only 6 competitors for music strings which would be severely affected at the same time as us.
In Europe, our customers  (distributors, guitar makers, music shops, internet shops..)  will have no problem to buy PVDF strings from our competitors outside Europe. The result of the restriction of PVDF in Europe will severely affect only European string makers. That means that all European strings makers in Europe will be much weakened because they will lose 20 to 40% of their turnover. Foreign companies will be more than happy to receive this opportunity without paying anything. Unexpected outstanding gift from Europe. We wonder if it is really necessary to make European industry weaker than the international competition when we know that the emission regarding music strings cannot be considered like creating pollution.
Another terrible consequence will be that our foreign competitors outside Europe will increase the number workers they employ outside Europe, when European strings makers will have to fire so they will employ less people in Europe.
Savarez has created this PVDF string market since more than 35 years. Today, we hold about 80% of this market. In the musicians mind, PVDF strings = Savarez. Our brand is extremely famous and has a high quality reputation. But this sharpens the appetite of our competitors (including the Chinese competitors), who have been trying to copy our products for years. By chance their quality is lower than ours until now.
In case of restriction the result for SAVAREZ company would be a very significant loss of turnover which will greatly weaken the company. We would no longer be able to sell a product that is essential for us in terms of sales and image. In addition, all the years spent to study and develop these PVDF strings would be lost and the turnover given to our competitors in the world without compensation.
Our brand image would be damaged since these strings will no longer be available in France but exclusively outside Europe. The gain hoped by the European Commission in setting up these new restrictions will therefore be completely annihilated by this situation.

General Comments: SPECTARIS is the German industry association for optics, photonics, analytical and medical technology. The association represents 400 predominantly medium-sized companies operating on a global level. The optics, photonics, medical technology and analytical, bio- and laboratory technology sectors achieved a total turnover of over 84 billion euros in 2022 and employ around 342,000 people, only counting companies with more than 20 employees. In addition, one also has to take into account the many small and micro enterprises in these sectors that add to these figures.

*RISKED BASED APPROACH NECESSARY*
SPECTARIS supports the goal of the “Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability” that aims to better protect citizens and the environment from harmful chemicals. Within the framework of sustainable chemicals regulation, substances that pose unmanageable risks due to their properties and use profile should be restricted or regulated on the basis of scientific assessments, especially in regards to consumer products. However, SPECTARIS strictly rejects the broad regulation of entire substance groups regardless of their proven risk. It must be urgently considered whether a PFAS substance or its use poses an uncontrollable risk to the environment or human health, whether there is any environmental exposure at all, and whether suitable alternatives exist. The current restriction proposal risks to cause irreparable damage to Europe, its citizens and its industry, in particular, as there is no such comprehensive restriction of the PFAS substance group outside the EU. Moreover, the restriction proposal does not address the opportunities that some PFAS (e.g. Fluoropolymers of low concern) as high-performance materials offer for social and technological progress.

*ESSENTIAL USES AND NEED FOR DEROGATIONS*
Owing to the wide range of desirable physical and chemical properties PFAS offer, SPECTARIS members use and rely upon PFAS for a wide variety of manufacturing processes, components and essential products to our society which is outlined in a detailed report attached.
SPECTARIS members rely on fourteen proposed derogations and support the need for further five potential derogations outlined in the Annex XV report. A number of the derogations need to be adapted to cover additional uses and/or longer timeframes. SPECTARIS also underlines the need for additional (new) derogations. The additional derogations suggested by SPECTARIS highlight essential PFAS uses not covered by the currently proposed derogations. Moreover, the need for certain derogations in end uses such as medical and laboratory equipment requires clarification.
SPECTARIS members rely on the derogations for the manufacturing of their products as well as for the entire supply chain. It is therefore essential that the derogations be viewed holistically to comprise the production of PFAS to its use in the supply chain and production processes as well as in the final product. A product specific derogation will be of no use if the necessary raw material, components, production processes are no longer available to manufacture the product itself. This must be clearly and legally enshrined in the legal text of the restriction.
Also, it is important that a number of additional derogations are included. The additional derogations suggested by SPECTARIS highlight critical PFAS uses not covered by the currently proposed derogations and clarify needs for derogations in certain end uses.
In addition, SPECTARIS members would like to highlight the necessity for the continued use of PFAS in spare parts and repairs of products already placed on the market. SPECTARIS members not only manufacture new products but also service and maintain existing products, machines, and devices. Without the general consideration to permit the use of PFAS in these applications, this will cause the premature end-of-life and scrappage of products which otherwise could be serviced and maintained with PFAS-containing parts.

It is vital that the restriction does not impact products already placed on the market. It must be ensured that these products can continuously be made available on the market. With the current definition of “placing on the market” under REACH this would not be possible as any supply or making available to a third party, and hence any resale or lease, for example, is considered “placing on the market” under REACH.

Finally, a formal process for requesting new derogations as well as permitting existing derogations to be extended beyond the originally agreed time period should be established. This is important where PFAS-free alternatives are still either in the very early stages of their development, or do not exist as yet. As such the estimations of the minimum steps and time to be considered to qualify alternatives has a significant degree of uncertainty.

SPECTARIS members are not in a position to offer additional technical details on derogation ‘5b- Textiles used in personal protective equipment’ as the information is held by their supply chain, but SPECTARIS support the need for such a derogation.

*COMPLEX SUPPLY CHAINS AND LACK OF DATA*
It is necessary to understand that companies (downstream users) collaborate with (upstream) suppliers, in a complex supply chain with many tiers to identify PFAS uses. With the unprecedented large scope of the proposed restriction, the current disclosure requirements via safety data sheets and substances of very high concern (SVHC) declarations are insufficient to build the basis for identification and evaluation of all relevant PFAS uses. Although SPECTARIS members have undertaken great efforts to analyse their products and supply chains, it is impossible to identify all substances in all products, components, and manufacturing processes in the given time.

*ASSESSMENT OF ALTERNATIVES*
It is also crucial to understand that many SPECTARIS member products have to meet stringent quality, performance, safety and legal requirements with qualification of potential alternatives being a highly complex, multi-step, multi-year challenge. When considering if alternatives exist, it is essential that potential alternatives are researched and tested to determine whether they can be used in a functionally, safe and performance equivalent manner. Potential alternatives must be assessed within the context of already existing regulations (e.g. fire protection, efficiency requirements, safety standards) in order to avoid conflicting requirements. Also, potential alternatives may not be harmful to health or the environment, otherwise they will only lead to regrettable substitution. The level of technological maturity and availability of potential alternatives must also be considered and as such it is only when all of these factors have been assessed as suitable, that an alternative can be deemed viable. It is also important to note that even if in some cases other substances can be used or alternative processes applied, this does not mean that such an alternative is suitable for the entire range of similar applications. In some cases, it may ultimately be found that a non-PFAS alternative is not capable of providing the required technical function, essential performance or safety requirements. The examination of viable alternatives with regard to these mandatory criteria has not been done systematically in the present restriction proposal. It is not transparent in the report on which basis and how the evaluation of alternatives has been carried out by the authorities.

*CALCULATION OF TIME NEEDED FOR POTENTIAL SUBSTITUTION*
There is a great degree of uncertainty calculating minimum time needed for actual substitution. This is owed to the fact that for the vast majority of the PFAS uses outlined in the attached report, SPECTARIS members have up to date not yet been able to identify appropriate potential PFAS-free alternatives for substitution. Therefore, timelines outlined in the attached report do not and cannot comprise the time needed to identify a potential alternative itself. The timelines only outline some crucial steps within a substitution process and the time needed for them once a potential alternative has been identified.  The various steps in the substitution process include but are not limited to testing of the potential alternative, re-design (of product/manufacturing processes), tests for reliability and in-situ performance, as well as necessary regulatory approvals.
The minimum steps and time to be considered are also built on the assumption that it is possible to identify the parameter(s) in question the first time that tests are completed. If the test is not successful or if a potential alternative can no longer be considered part way through its development, the process of implementing PFAS-free alternatives can take much longer than outlined in the attached report as research and development steps may need to be repeated to find a different chemistry or technology that does not have the same issues. Many SPECTARIS member products have to meet stringent qualification requirements with qualification of alternatives being a highly complex, multi-step, multi-year challenge. Therefore, the minimum steps and time to be considered for derogations should assume and take into account that some potential alternatives will turn out to be unsuitable or even not available at all.
The PFAS restriction proposal should also provide for a revision of transition periods after an overall review of the monitoring data.

General Comments: Stadtwerke München (SWM) are planning and operating different plants working with gases targeted by the PFAS regulation, in particular Organic Rankine Cycles, cooling machines and heat pumps connected to district cooling or district heating grids. These machines are therefore part of the infrastructure of the city of Munich.

We wish to address the three main themes below:

Longer transition phase needed:
Switching to natural refrigerants for heat pumps in district heating and cooling systems involves adapting the buildings for bigger heating or cooling systems and not simply replacing the heat pumps or the cooling machines. Buildings need to be adapted for meeting safety and statics requirements.
This also means most of the time increasing the size of the building, since buildings often don't offer much extra space and heat pumps/cooling machines with natural refrigerants require more space for the same power output.

The investment costs of such installations are considerably high, and modifying the building in addition to replacing the heat pumps before the end of their service life would be difficult to manage in this short period of time and in addition is very expensive. This would lead to very substantial economic losses and we would be less of an economic position to invest in new installations, even though they are essential to the energy transition.

A derogation of 12 years for maintenance and refilling of existing HVACR equipment after EiF (Entry into Force) is suggested, but no clear definition of HVACR equipment is given. Equipment for district heating and cooling systems need to be specifically addressed by a derogation.
District cooling and heating systems have a service life of more than 30 years, therefore a transition phase of a minimum 20 years after EiF (Entry into Force) would be necessary, to avoid premature renewal of installations, which would be counterproductive to the preservation of environmental resources and also to the economical ability of energy service companies to invest in the energy transition with new installations.

Derogation for existing facilities where safety requirements could not be met:
Most of our district cooling systems are located right in city centres, underneath busy squares and in direct vicinity of subway stations with high traffic, where space is limited, and the adaptations needed to ensure safety would not be possible (e.g. dissipating air flows in the premises).
Because of such environmental requirements, it would not be possible to install natural refrigerants instead.

It is not clear, however, whether such installations are covered by the derogation linked to national safety standards and building codes, which seems to apply only to locations where specific national regulations apply and would not include locations where safety requirements could not be met, with regards to risks of explosion or toxicity and given the location of the existing installation.
Giving up completely the existing installations and relocating them at other locations can potentially lead to additional significant costs in district cooling and heating systems, as the piping infrastructure and distribution of energy within the grids was planned and installed based on the planned and installed generation capacity. If the generation units are installed at different locations in order to meet the requirements for natural refrigerants, new components might be needed in the system (e.g. pressure increase stations) and the piping might need to be significantly modified (additional costs, time and construction works in already packed city centres). For our applications, a change of working fluid in the machines does not only lead to a change in the surrounding buildings but also potentially in changes in the complete district heating infrastructure.
Existing generation units feeding district grids need to benefit from a derogation, if safety requirements cannot be met at the existing location and if a change of location leads to disproportionate costs.

Low leakage rates:
Fluorinated gases in these equipment are not consumables but operating fluids.
Heat pumps, refrigeration and air conditioning systems are designed with hermetically sealed systems to avoid leakage, and, at end of life, the fluorinated gas is collected under controlled circumstances to avoid releases. As a result, the release of fluorinated gases into the atmosphere from these equipment is very low or even negligible. Based on the evaluation of data from over 200 000 systems by the German organisation VDKF, the overall leakage rate is just 1,3%.
The F-Gas regulation already imposes very strict restrictions and controls on leakage, ensuring that this leakage rate remains very low.
Therefore, a longer transition phase for these equipment would not have a huge impact on the release of PFAS into the atmosphere but would ensure on the other hand the economic survival of investments that energy service companies have already made, to enable them to adapt in parallel to the new F-Gas and PFAS regulations and invest in new sustainable equipment.

General Comments: Statement of SBAO (Schweizerischer Verband für Augenoptik und Optometrie – Swiss Association of Ophthalmic Optics and Optometry) against PFAS ban and support for derogation proposal for the use of PFAS in Contact Lens Materials


It is with great concern that the Schweizerischer Verband für Augenoptik und Optometrie (SBAO - Swiss Association of Ophthalmic Optics and Optometry) has learned about the planned ban of Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) from 2025 onwards. We do recognize that these substances are harmful to the environment since they are non-degradable. We also agree that harmful substances for the environment should be avoided or substituted wherever possible, since environmental protection and safety are very important to us. Unfortunately, there are products/medical devices where small amounts of PFAS substances are an important ingredient that cannot be substituted easily.

One example that is of great importance for all Optometrists, Ophthalmic Opticians and Ophthalmologists are rigid gas permeable contact lens materials (RGP lenses). In theory, a switch from rigid lens wear to soft lens materials not containing PFAS substances should be feasible. Due to the presence of specific ocular diseases this is not achievable though. Examples are patients suffering from irregular astigmatism where it is for the most part not possible to perform a refit with soft contact lenses. Specialty rigid gas permeable contact lenses serve as means of optical and visual rehabilitation which cannot be achieved with a soft contact lens material.

Unfortunately, virtually all rigid gas permeable materials contain small amounts of substances of the PFAS category (e.g. trifluoroethyl methacrylate, hexafluoroisopropyl methacrylate or bis-hexafluoroisopropyl itaconate). All these substances make an essential contribution to properties such as oxygen permeability, biocompatibility, comfort, wettability, rigidity, lathability, durability, scratch resistance, shape stability and optical clarity of the material. Currently there are no alternative materials not containing PFAS substances for the production of safe rigid gas permeable contact lenses on the market. Without these small amounts of PFAS substances rigid gas permeable contact lenses as known today could not be produced anymore. Since many of RGP contact lens wearers depend on their lenses for reasons of visual rehabilitation this would mean a massive impact on their quality of life as well as on their ability to work. As a consequence, it can be expected that this would most likely lead to an assumed large socioeconomic burden.

A complete PFAS ban would affect all patients suffering from ocular diseases that affect the cornea and lead to irregular astigmatism, because soft lenses cannot conceal the corneal irregularity in the same fashion that rigid gas permeable lenses can.
Some examples of common corneal diseases are corneal ectasias (e.g. Keratoconus, Keratoglobus, Terriens Marginal Degeneration, Pellucid Marginal Degeneration), status post keratitis (e.g. herpetic, microbial, etc.) – in essence every disease that produces disturbance of the corneal surface. Patients with corneal post-traumatic corneal scarring also depend on rigid gas permeable lenses for visual rehabilitation.
In order to enhance the visual acuity, it is necessary to cover up any irregularity of the cornea which can only be achieved with a stable material that needs to be biocompatible and ideally highly oxygen permeable to keep the stress on the corneal tissue as minimal as possible. As mentioned above these properties are achieved with lenses that contain very small amounts of PFAS substances.

One very common reason for corneal irregularity is the disease of keratoconus. The prevalence of keratoconus in the population is highly variable and seems to depend on the geographic location and also (Daniel A. Godefrooij, 2017) race. (Jacinto Santodomingo-Rubido, 2022)
In a study performed in the Netherlands in 2016 the prevalence of keratoconus is reported to be as high as 265 per 100.000 patients. The study included 4.4 million patients from a mandatory health insurance database which represents approximately 30% of the Dutch population. (Daniel A. Godefrooij, 2017) Since the population of the Netherlands represents a good cross-section of patients with genetic origins in different parts of the world due to their colonial heritage, the crossover of various populations with different genetic backgrounds (races) is thought to be representative for other European Countries as well. Keratoconus is considered a type of irregular astigmatism and frequently affects both eyes. It can lead to major visual impairment up to legal blindness – treated and untreated. Irregular astigmatism cannot or only partially be corrected with spectacle lenses and often times, due to the extreme shape of the cornea, not at all with soft contact lenses. In Most cases a patient with keratoconus may only achieve visual acuities of approximately 0.10 (6/60 or 20/200) without visual correction but may well achieve 0.8 or higher (6/8 or 20/25 or higher respectively). With a “normal” visual acuity the patient can live a normal life. Their ability to work and participate in professional or social activities will not be affected as will their ability to drive. Without adequate optical correction in the sense of RGP contact lenses these patients would not meet the minimal visual acuity to perform certain professions or e.g. to drive. Good visual acuity is crucial to function in today’s society.

Another large group of RGP wearers that cannot be switched to soft lens options are children and young adults wearing orthokeratology lenses for myopia control. Myopia (“nearsightedness”) affects many people in need of optical correction and is a disease expected to become more prevalent in the world in the future. There are some alternatives with specialty soft contact lenses and specialty design spectacle lenses on the market – none of them as effective as orthokeratology lenses though.

As mentioned previously the modern RGP materials are highly biocompatible and oxygen permeable. This means that they should be replaced on a frequent basis – ideally annually, because they are prone to distortion of the material with long-term everyday use. Changes in shape of the lens will alter the fit and increase the risk for infections.

According to statistical data published by the European Council of Optometry and Optics (ECOO) there are around 25 million contact lens wearers in Europe. According to Data by OptikSchweiz from 2021 about 25% of the Swiss population are contact lens wearers. 2.7% of these only wear contact lenses.
In Switzerland there are approximately one thousand contact lens fitters who fit specialty RGP lenses. It is assumed that about 40% of all contact lens wearers in Switzerland are wearers of specialty RGP lenses. This number may vary from office to office between 20% to 60%.

Assuming that 80% of all RGP wearers cannot be switched to soft lenses or spectacles and assuming that each of the one thousand contact lens fitters cares for 1000 patients this would lead to 330 RGP wearers per office of which 80% (approximately 260 patients) would lose their ability to function in “normal” life.

Furthermore, this would most likely mean an expected socioeconomic burden of several Billion Swiss Francs (CHF) per year assuming that a patient who was previously able to work full-time will not be able to do so anymore. In a recent survey conducted by the European Council of Optometry and Optics (ECOO) a predicted value of more than EUR 5.68 billion per year has been assumed as the socioeconomic cost of negative impacts of a PFAS ban on RGP wearers. Several other scientific studies have evaluated the socioeconomic burden of patients with mild to severe visual impairment and blindness in regard to gross national income or productivity loss in different areas of the world. (Kristen A. Eckert, 2015) (Suni, 2020) (the Portugese visual impariment study group (PORVIS-group), 2019)
All studies show that a reduction in visual impairment (e.g., by patients being treated with specialty RGP contact lenses for visual improvement) can lead to a major gain in productivity and reduction in socioeconomic burden and their predicted numbers are comparable to the predicted value of ECOO.

As of today, there are not alternatives regarding RGP materials free of PFAS available. The development of new materials with similar properties in respect to biocompatibility and safety of contact lens wear will be a major encounter which will not be possible to be achieved in a short amount of time. The development and licensing of such materials would most likely take decades.
We hope the given examples can illustrate the importance of the continuous availability of rigid gas permeable contact lens materials for patients and society.

We highly recommend the consideration of a derogation for the use of PFAS substances in rigid contact lens materials and are fully support the explanations, concerns and suggestion on PFAS as well as the proposed derogation proposal handed in by the contact lens manufacturers association „EuromContact“.

General Comments: Statement of the district of Rastatt on the planned PFAS restriction at European level


On January 13, 2023, the Netherlands, Germany, Denmark, Sweden and Norway took the first formal step towards a European restriction on PFAS by jointly submitting a restriction proposal to the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA). The proposal aims to restrict both the use and manufacture of PFAS in order to reduce the risks posed by these substances to humans and the environment. Adoption would result in the most comprehensive substance restriction in Europe to date. The proposed restriction is highly complex because there are more than 10,000 different types of PFAS used in a wide variety of products. ECHA published the PFAS restriction proposal on February 7, 2023. The six-month public consultation is currently underway and is expected to end in September 2023. A final decision is not expected before 2025.

The district of Rastatt as well as the districts of Baden-Baden and Mannheim have had painful experiences with the PFAS group of substances. Due to application of paper sludge mixed with compost on arable land, about 1,100 hectares of soil in Central Baden are classified as contaminated. In addition to this considerable surface contamination, the groundwater from Rastatt to Ottersweier is also contaminated with PFAS. In total, an affected area of 200 km² has been delineated. The people in the district of Rastatt have to live with this pollution and are affected by it in many ways.

Due to the persistence of the pollutants, this problem will challenge the district of Rastatt and its population for decades. A comprehensive remediation is not possible and not financially feasible due to the dimension of the damage. Since 2013, an amount in the mid-double-digit millions has already been spent by the state, the district, the municipalities, the water suppliers and agriculture to protect the population. An ongoing financial burden will remain. These costs are essentially carried by the general public, but not by the producers and distributors of PFAS.

There is opposition to the planned PFAS restriction from industry associations. The Conference of Economics Ministers has endorsed these concerns (see attachment 1) , while the Conference of Environmental Ministers (see attachment 2), along with the Conference of Agriculture and Consumer Protection Ministers, has spoken out in favor of rapid implementation of the PFAS restriction.

From a scientific point of view, it is recognized that even PFAS with low acute toxicity pose a health risk in case of prolonged (chronic) exposure. The Special Report of the German Advisory Council on the Environment states that PFAS have already spread worldwide in the environment and accumulated in organisms including humans.

It is clear that mass production for countless consumer products for which substitutes already exist or for which there are no significant disadvantages in eliminating PFAS (e.g. cosmetics, food packaging or disposable cups) must be stopped as quickly as possible. The restriction proposal currently under consideration serves to protect humans and also grants industry long transition periods. In addition, substitutions with other substances are supported by research projects. Regular validation is planned to allow essential applications for which there are no substitute substances to continue, through derogations. In this way, industrial concerns are adequately taken into account in consideration of health and environmental protection.

The environmental administration of the district of Rastatt is committed to the EU restriction proposal in view of the dimension of the damage and the burden on the general public, the living conditions soil and water and the population in the district of Rastatt. It expressly welcomes the efforts of the Federal Republic of Germany to obtain a rapid and far-reaching PFAS ban in accordance with the restriction proposal at the European level for the protection of people and the environment.

An statement  with the same content by the Committee for Environment, Construction and Planning of the District of Rastatt is expected to be adopted on 26.9.2023.

Combined Comments: "Statement by Sodasan Wasch- und Reinigungsmittel GmbH on the PFAS prohibition 24.08.2023. As a producer of ecological washing and cleaning agents, we have been developing and producing high-quality products as resource-efficient and environmentally friendly as possible since 1982. Therefore, we welcome the proposal to restrict PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) and support a comprehensive ban on these chemicals. The protection of people, animals, and our environment has always been paramount in the production of our sustainable products. Therefore, we continuously deal with the latest findings on the potential toxicity of various ingredients. In this context, an intensive examination of PFAS was essential for us as well. An article by the European Environment Agency summarizes the risks associated with exposure to emerging chemicals, including PFAS, and emphasizes that exposure to PFAS is concerning, as it has the potential to cause kidney damage, liver damage, immunotoxic effects, reproductive disorders, endocrine disruptions, and carcinogenic effects. It is also noted that PFAS can cause neurological and developmental effects. Overall, this article reaffirms the need to understand and address the risks associated with PFAS exposure in Europe. These conclusions are consistent with our findings from comprehensive research on the effects of PFAS. Below, we would like to delve into some studies in more detail. One review paper addresses the current understanding of human exposure to PFAS and their effects on cancer, immune function, metabolism, and neurological development. It shows significant associations between PFAS exposure and adverse immunological effects in children, while dyslipidemia is the strongest metabolic effect associated with PFAS exposure. Another study investigated the potential pro-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects of PFAS. The results show that exposure to PFAS is associated with increased cytokine production, indicating chronic inflammation. In addition, decreased B-cell activation, altered T-cell subtypes, and immunoglobulin levels were found, suggesting PFAS-induced immunosuppression. All of this suggests that PFAS may have immunosuppressive and pro-inflammatory properties typical of carcinogens. The effects of exposure to PFAS on neurobehavioral and cognitive functions have also been studied. The study showed an association between PFOA exposure and increased sleepiness among adolescents and between PFOS exposure and gender-specific changes. Minor impairments in attention and memory were also observed in adolescents in relation to PFAS. A meta-analysis with 85 studies on rodents and 24 additional epidemiological studies found a consistent association between exposure to PFAS and liver damage, with elevated levels of liver enzymes observed in both rodent models and human studies. A Swedish study utilized biomonitoring data and performed a cumulative risk assessment for 17 PFAS individually and in combination. The results showed low concentrations of PFAS in the general population, but higher concentrations in professionally exposed ski waxers. Some well-studied PFAS congeners showed effects even at low doses. Concerns were raised about liver toxicity and reproductive toxicity in the professionally exposed group, indicating a need for reduced exposure. Immunosuppresssion and disrupted mammary gland development were identified as concerns in both study populations, emphasizing the need for additional toxicological data for many PFAS congeners. PFAS are also considered endocrine disruptors. They can interfere with the endocrine system and disrupt the normal function of hormones, leading to hormonal imbalances and other health effects. There is growing scientific evidence pointing to potential endocrine disruptions caused by PFAS. Experimental studies, for example, have shown that PFAS substances significantly affect the proliferation and function of Leydig cells in the testicles of rats. In another comprehensive meta-analysis, the relationship between exposure to perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and thyroid hormones was investigated. The results suggest that PFAS are associated with a reduction in the total T4 levels in the blood, with the effect varying depending on the PFAS concentration. A positive correlation between PFAS and free T4 as well as TSH was observed in the group with moderate PFAS concentrations. This review examines potential mechanisms by which poly- and perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) can contribute to carcinogenic effects. Although PFAS are not directly mutagenic, various mechanisms of the carcinogenic effect have been proposed, including metabolism, endocrine disruption, and epigenetic changes. These mechanisms are interdependent and sensitive to dose and timing of exposure. The review focuses on testicular and prostate cancer as examples to illustrate these mechanisms and emphasizes the need to consider the complex interactions between PFAS exposure and cancer development. A systematic review of the epidemiological literature shows that exposure to PFAS is associated with an increased risk of type 2 diabetes (T2DM). In particular, exposure to perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) shows a non-monotonic dose-dependent association with T2DM risk. Additionally, PFAS are persistent substances that accumulate in the environment and can cause extensive ecological damage. A study examined per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances in a coastal food web in the North Atlantic region of the United States. Twenty-four PFAS were analyzed in 18 marine species from the Narragansett Bay and surrounding waters, and significant relationships were found between PFAS concentrations and various ecological characteristics such as species, body size, habitat, feeding habits, and location. While PFAS exposure may have negative effects on the ecology of these organisms, many of these species are important fishery resources for recreational and commercial fishing, potentially leading to human exposure through the consumption of these organisms. This study found that fluorinated alternatives, especially short-chain PFAAs and perfluorinated ether carboxylic and sulfonic acids (PFECAs and PFESAs), have high environmental stability and mobility, indicating significant potential for global contamination. In addition, certain fluorinated alternatives were identified as toxic and pose global risks for humans and the environment. The knowledge deficit regarding the risks associated with fluorinated alternatives can be attributed to factors such as information asymmetry between the industry and other stakeholders. Based on existing case studies, the study suggests that a non-fluorinated substitution strategy, including chemical or functional substitutions, could serve as a long-term sustainable solution. However, further development and evaluation of this strategy are necessary. Overall, the study highlights the need to address the dangers associated with fluorinated alternatives, overcome knowledge gaps, and explore alternative solutions for a more sustainable transition from PFAS. Another study also suggests that groundwater contamination with PFAS, particularly PFOS, has been known since the 1990s but is only slowly being addressed. This contamination is hardly reversible, and the costs of remediation are high. The precautionary principle should be applied, as exposure to PFAS can hardly be reversed. All PFAS that enter the groundwater, regardless of their structure and bioaccumulation potential, lead to irreversible exposures and risks, as well as additional remediation costs. It is recommended to avoid highly persistent and mobile chemicals such as PFAS to protect groundwater resources for future generations. Given these (and many other) findings, it is of enormous importance that measures be taken to restrict the use of PFAS and ultimately achieve a reduction in their release into the environment. A comprehensive ban on PFAS would be an important step towards a more sustainable and healthier future. It would promote the development and use of more environmentally friendly alternatives and help reduce the burden of these harmful chemicals on human health and the environment. Furthermore, such a ban would provide incentives for companies to invest in innovative technologies and sustainable production processes, ultimately leading to positive changes in the overall economy. As GfaW, we are committed to ethical and sustainable business practices. A ban on PFAS would make it easier for us and our customers to realize these principles and ensure the protection of health and the environment. We fully support the proposal to restrict PFAS and encourage all affected stakeholders to express their support for such a ban and contribute relevant information to facilitate informed decision-making."

General Comments: STÖBER Antriebstechnik GmbH develops and produces drive systems in Pforzheim for the application of production machines and plants worldwide. Practically all our drive systems have the maximum possible efficiency according to the current state of the art. This applies to drive controllers as well as motors and gearboxes. The use of our products often replaces older production methods, which release far more CO2 than more modern ones. They are ergo suitable to counteract global warming even without deindustrialization.

The planned ban would threaten the existence of our company, as our products cannot do without PFAS-containing accessories altogether.

We only use PFAS-containing accessories where alternative products either do not exist or fall far short of the required technical properties. Thus, they are only used when technically necessary, as they are considerably more expensive than alternative products.

Special sealing materials such as fluoropolymers, in particular FKM, must be exempted from the ban, however, since these materials have so far been without alternative in terms of their chemical and thermal resistance. Alternatives are not in sight and hardly to be expected.

Furthermore, we use semiconductor modules in our products, for whose production PFAS is without alternative according to the current status. We demand an exemption or extension of the transition period for this.

General Comments: Subject: Concerns Regarding the Swift Prohibition of PFAS  (Per-/polyfluorinated alkyl substances)

We understand the concerns surrounding persistent substances and their accumulation over time. However, we consider the use of the ECHA process for a rapid ban of "substances of very high concern" in the EU to be questionable.

This approach contrasts sharply with other global regions (US& China), where substance bans are typically enacted following proven harm. The Eu-Strategy jeopardizes our competitiveness and risks driving away technologically advanced companies, which we consider our crown jewels.

It appears that the ban on PFASs was considered by five countries (Netherlands (NL), Germany (D), Norway (NOR), Sweden (S), and Denmark (DK)) mainly because of the persistence and feared accumulation of these substances over time. Jumping to conclusions without a solid basis cannot be justified. Persistence is not necessarily synonymous with harmfulness or toxicity, but rather implies a time horizon that can be compared to permanence.


For the PFAS family, which according to the status comprises about 10,000 chemical substances, harmful effects have been proven for only about 2% of the 10,000 substances. This raises questions about proportionality.

The procedure used is intended to quickly ban "substances of very high concern" according to Article 68 of the REACH Regulation. If it is used to ban an entire family at this low level of proven harmful substances, we consider this to be legally contestable.

It is important to recognize that PFAS materials play an essential role in several applications, including renewable energy generation, electromobility, communications, and smart energy use. Without PFAS, achieving a carbon-neutral economy will be significantly more difficult or impossible.

The consequences of such a ban are even far more reaching. Notably, NL has made substantial investments in companies like ASML, while Germany has provided billions in subsidies to INTEL and TSMC, aiming to attract them to our region, only to potentially impose work restrictions later.

The German Federal Environmental Agency has suggested in recent presentations (2023 Sept. 06 Fraunhofer IZM, Berlin AK-RKU) that there may be alternatives to the use of PFAS in semiconductor manufacturing. This is in contradiction to the very detailed elaboration of the SIA (semiconductors.org), which offers precise explanations for download.
This glaring contradiction raises concerns about the consistency of our regulatory decisions.





Providing substantial subsidies to companies like INTEL and TSMC and subsequently imposing bans on their operations within the EU, including Germany, seems counterproductive.
The United Kingdom could potentially benefit from BREXIT if many affected companies strategically choose to establish a presence in Europe, specifically in regions that do not enforce this regulation.

In conclusion, while we acknowledge the importance of addressing environmental concerns, we urge a more balanced and evidence-based approach to regulating PFAS. Rushing into bans without conclusive proof of harm could have adverse economic consequences and hinder our progress towards a sustainable future.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Subject: Objection to the Planned Ban on PFAS in the EU

Dear Ladies and Gentlemen of the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA),

I, Dr. Egbert Röhm, Managing Director of Theegarten-Pactec GmbH & Co. KG, hereby wish to participate in the public consultation on the proposed regulation of PFAS under the EU-REACH Regulation. The suggested measures could have significant implications for our company, our industry, and the economic position of Germany, while potentially creating competitive advantages for non-EU market participants.

Company Profile

Our company is a medium-sized manufacturer and distributor of high-performance packaging machines for confectionery and non-food products. We employ nearly 400 individuals and achieve an annual turnover of approximately 60-70 million euros. We produce high-performance packaging machines known for their precision and efficient processing of food and packaging materials. We export our machines worldwide, with about 90 percent of our turnover coming from exports, 80 percent of which are outside the European Union.
Our machines incorporate various components containing PFAS, such as cutting blades, scrapers, seals, hoses, chain guides, and articulating heads. Without the technical properties of the utilized PFAS, we would not be able to offer our machines in their current performance class. This jeopardizes our position as a global leader in international competition, particularly outside the European Union.

Socio-economic Impacts of a General PFAS Ban

A comprehensive ban on PFAS, particularly in applications involving seals and PTFE-coated materials, would have severe repercussions on our business operations. These components and coatings are essential for the functionality and performance of our machines, as they provide outstanding lubricating and separating properties, thereby ensuring precise processing. Presently, there are no alternatives that could offer comparable functions. A general ban would not only affect our entire product portfolio but also endanger the economic standing of Germany. Our industry significantly contributes to the success of the German economy and generates numerous jobs.

Specific Component: Seals

Due to requirements from the current Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC, operator protection against hazards during machine operation and strict separation of operating substances from the product area are demanded. Leaking lubricants like greases and oils potentially jeopardize both the food consumers and the machine operators. As manufacturers of machines for the food industry, we place utmost importance on hygiene and food safety.
Our machines extensively employ mechanical gears that require seals in large numbers due to manual setup procedures and associated safety risks for operators. The seals used in our machines contain PFAS according to the manufacturer, contributing to the machines' functionality and lifespan.
A ban on PFAS would significantly limit these functions as well as the performance of our machines and jeopardize our ability to maintain strict separation between operating substances and food.

Specific Component: PTFE-coated Blades

Another concrete example is the PTFE-coated blades used in our packaging machines for cutting (partially sticky) product masses and packaging materials. A research report from 2017 (attached, see pages 8ff) demonstrated the necessity of anti-adhesive coatings for cutting operations to ensure efficient processing. Adhering product residues (partially abrasive) on the blades disrupt the cutting process and lead to increased blade wear. The required coating systems derive some of their necessary properties from the included PFAS. Investigation of various coating systems revealed that specific systems must be selected to match the customer's product; otherwise, food processing might not be possible. Without these PFAS-containing coatings, for which there are currently no alternatives, the cutting process would be disrupted shortly after commencement, potentially rendering food processing entirely unfeasible.

Our Demands and Proposals

We strongly oppose a general ban on all PFAS and advocate for a differentiated assessment of individual fluoropolymers based on their specific hazard potential and ecological impacts. A comprehensive ban on PFAS would have drastic consequences for the global competitiveness of our industry and the overall European economic position.
We urge the European Union and the ECHA to conduct comprehensive scientific research on the potential risks and alternatives of PFAS before any ban or restriction is imposed. We are prepared to actively participate in this process, offering our expertise and years of experience to the discussion.
We sincerely thank you for considering our concerns and are available for further information or discussions.

Yours sincerely,

Dr. Egbert Röhm
Managing Director
Theegarten-Pactec GmbH & Co. KG

General Comments: Subject: Request regarding the proposed REACH restrictions on PFAS

We hereby submit a letter of request concerning the current situation where a proposal to ban the manufacturing, use, and entry into the EU market of all PFAS substances is being considered.

In Japan, an extensive social and private infrastructure has been constructed from the period of high economic growth to the stable growth  (around 1954 to 1991). Most steel structures are coated with anti-corrosion paint and are maintained through regular repainting. However, it is anticipated that the proportion of facilities that will exceed 50 years since construction within the next 20 years will increase significantly. Against this background, the maintenance of steel structures is becoming increasingly important each year. In order to reduce lifecycle costs, specifications for long-term durability coatings have been applied. These coatings allow for extended repainting intervals and reduce the generation of volatile organic compounds through a decrease in the number of repainting cycles. They play a crucial role not only in the economic maintenance of current social infrastructure but also in reducing environmental impact.

Regarding the anti-corrosion coating of steel bridges in Japan, a standard specification for long-term durability coatings has been established and implemented. This specification includes a sacrificial anode action effect zinc-rich paint for the anti-corrosion base, epoxy resin-based coatings with excellent corrosive substance blocking properties for the primer and intermediate coats, and weather-resistant fluororesin coatings for the topcoat. The fluororesin coatings used as topcoats inhibit UV degradation due to the high bonding energy of fluororesin, and it is not an exaggeration to say that they can maintain the performance of the coated structures for more than twice the lifespan compared to alternative polyurethane coatings. Fluororesin coatings are currently essential materials in Japan's anti-corrosion coatings.

With the regulation of PFAS in the EU, it is anticipated that global regulations on PFAS will expand. If these regulations are implemented in Japan, the standard specifications for steel structure coatings will no longer be applicable. Furthermore, the removal of existing coatings, including fluororesin coatings, during surface preparation for repainting work will affect waste disposal methods. Therefore, it is expected to cause significant disruptions to the maintenance of social infrastructure.

Regarding these regulations, unlike the previous regulations on PFOS and other substances, more than 10,000 types of fluorinated compounds are targeted, and there are objections due to the unclear basis for regulation. While PFAS is considered to have low biodegradability and poses unacceptable risks to human health and the environment, it is insufficient to categorize all 10,000 PFAS compounds collectively without providing data on their biodegradability. Thus, we must assert that the basis for such regulation is severely lacking.

Therefore, we would like to request the following:

１．Recognize that fluororesin coatings, including those used in Japan, are essential products for protecting various structures, including social infrastructure.
２．Acknowledge the lack of sufficient basis for regulating all 10,000 PFAS compounds.
Based on these two points, we respectfully request that you consider implementing measures to ease the restrictions on PFAS.
