General Comments: Subject: Statement on the planned exemption of PVDF, PTFE, ETFE, ECTFE, FPM and FFKM from a comprehensive ban on fluoroplastics in the chemical industry

Dear Sir or Madam

As a manufacturer of ventilation systems and equipment for the chemical industry, we would like to express our concern about the planned comprehensive ban on fluoroplastics.
We recognise and support the need to limit the use of harmful substances to minimize negative impacts on people and the environment. However, we would like to point out the essential role of fluoroplastics such as PVDF, PTFE, ETFE, ECTFE, FPM and FFKM in our industry and call for an exemption of these substances from the planned ban.
Fluoroplastics have proven to be indispensable in numerous applications, especially in chemically aggressive environments. These materials offer unparalleled chemical resistance, which is critical to the safety and efficiency of our products and applications. As a manufacturer of air handling equipment, we must demand the highest levels of reliability, durability and resistance from our products to prevent potential leaks and ensure the long-term safety of people and the environment.
Implementing the ban on fluoroplastics in our industry would inevitably lead to significant problems. For one thing, alternatives with comparable chemical resistance would not be available, which could lead to a weakening of safety standards. Greater leakage and a shortened life span of our products would be unavoidable consequences, which would significantly increase the danger to people and the environment.
We would like to emphasise that as a responsible company, we always strive to promote sustainable and environmentally friendly solutions. We support the research and development of environmentally friendly alternatives to fluoroplastics and are willing to help shape a long-term, gradual transition.
However, we must remain realistic and consider the current situation. Until reliable, safe and proven alternatives are available, we urge that PVDF, PTFE, ETFE, ECTFE, FPM and FFKM be exempted from the planned ban. This would allow us to continue to manufacture our products in compliance with the highest safety standards while providing time and space for research and implementation of more sustainable solutions.

We are open to a constructive dialogue and are at your disposal to find the best possible solutions for people and the environment together.
Thank you for your understanding and consideration of our concerns.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Subject: The draft restriction on the use of PFAS is causing concern. It is feared that surgical meshes made of PVDF could be banned after a short transition period.


For 30 years, the investigation of textile implants for the treatment of tissue defects has been a central focus of clinical and experimental research in the Department of Surgery at RWTH Aachen University. Within this framework, I have worked intensively with my colleagues on improving implant safety and have acquired numerous third-party funded research projects. With this research activity, which has now lasted 30 years, with more than140 publications (see Appendix 2) on the subject of mesh implants, more than 250 invited lectures on implants and numerous book contributions, it was possible to significantly improve the previously predominant oversized materials by introducing the concept of large-pored lightweight meshes. I was able to contribute this expertise as an expert witness for courts in the USA and Australia in numerous proceedings.

Medical implants must basically have a high stability and resistance to degradation if they have to function for years or decades in the tissue and the aggressive cellular environment of the biological foreign body reaction. This is all the more true if they have a large contact surface area, as is the case with "Surgical Meshes". These textile implants made of different materials are recommended for tissue reinforcement by all professional societies [Appendix 1: 1-4] as the therapy of choice and are routinely used as standard worldwide.

Among the currently used polymers, PVDF fulfils the requirements for textile medical implants in an outstanding way as it shows no signs of degradation after implantation and induces a low inflammatory and fibrous reaction due to its hydrophobic surface. In contrast, the alternative polymers available show dramatic disadvantages in some cases, which have led to over a hundred thousand documented court cases worldwide [Appendix 1: 6]. Among other things, the hydrophilic polymers made of polyester are subject to rapid hydrolytic degradation, while those made of polypropylene are subject to oxidative surface decay with the release of micro-particles and increased cellular activation of the inflammation and scarring processes [Appendix 2: 1,29].

In the past 30 years of intensive research activity with more than 140 publications (see Appendix 2) on the subject of "Mesh" it has become clear that PVDF is currently the best polymer for use in textile fabric reinforcement [Appendix 2: 1-140].
The production of PVDF mesh implants is currently a core technological competence built up over decades within the EU, a migration of production facilities to non-EU countries would be regrettable. A ban on PVDF as an implant material in the EU would mean an increased use of polypropylene (PP) or polyester (PET) meshes along with the increase of associated risks for thousands of patients if they do not have the option of obtaining PVDF implants outside the EU.

The development of hernia meshes made of PVDF began more than 20 years ago in 1998 which, with an increasing number of experimental and clinical studies (see ref. list Appendix 2 with the published results of our own studies), became increasingly clear when comparing implant materials that the conventional mesh implants made of polypropylene (PP) and polyester (PET) are associated with a pronounced inflammatory foreign body reaction, and with the millions of mesh implants in use, new, more compatible polymers were required. Initial trials confirmed the possibility of using PVDF for mesh constructions and also confirmed the superior compatibility after insertion into the tissue (see e.g. [Appendix 2: 118]). In the following years, more and more surgeons were convinced to the use of PVDF implants through publications and presentations at national and international conferences, even though large mesh manufacturers continued to stick to their standard materials of polypropylene (PP) and polyester (PET) against better knowledge and in part against the warning of the polymer manufacturer  [Appendix 1: 7].

The positive experience of surgeons, as well as first long-term registry studies with indisputable benefits for PVDF meshes in the long-term course [Appendix 1: 5] currently support the increasing use of PVDF mesh implants, and give hope that implants made of PVDF will increasingly replace implants made of risky polypropylene (PP) and polyester (PET) in the coming years.



Prof. Dr. U. Klinge

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Subject: There is no sufficiently strong enough evidence that technically and economically feasible alternatives existed for PVDF used in photovoltaic industry.

In the Energy Sector (Annex E.2.12.) of Table 8, ANNEX XV Restriction Report, it is claimed that there is sufficiently strong evidence that technically and economically feasible alternatives existed for PVDF replacement by using PET and EVA as backsheets of photovoltaic (PV) modules, though It also mentioned that the replacement could be less durable. Based on published scientific reports, field studies and our working experiences, we would like to argue that the so-called strong evidence is far away from strong and the concerns about less durable could be very true.

1. Fluoropolymers used in PV backsheet, still irreplaceable
Fluoropolymers, transformed to films, have been used as the exterior layer of PV backsheet for several decades since the born of PV industry, and they are still the only materials which have proven field service records in the real world. A joint research work project was conducted by the UL lab, the NREL lab, Northeastern Univ. and Case Western Reserve Univ. (sponsored by Department of Energy, Office of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy, under Award Number DEEE-000714) to investigate the correlation of long-term field reliability with accelerated laboratory testing. A comprehensive review has been published and one of their key findings is that the fluoropolymer based (PVDF and PVF) backsheets show the least yellowing and gloss loss in different climate zones, indicating the least degradation over years outdoor. Meanwhile, non-fluoropolymeric materials are seen with many failure modes, such as severe yellowing, gloss loss, delamination and cracking. An optical observation further reveals that the skin layer other than using fluoropolymers gets thinning several microns only after a limited service time period (Florida outdoor exposure test). Such a skin layer thinning issue has also been verified by in-house accelerated QUV weathering test [1, 2].

It is noteworthy to point out that there is a debate between PVDF and PVF producers. Engineers from Du pont argued that even PVDF based backsheet was not good enough since the cracking issue was observed through the so-called C-AST (combined) or MAST (sequential) weathering test [3]. Their observations may be correct but conclusions are misleading by wrong sampling. Apparently, Du Pont’s engineers are NOT aware of the state-of-the-art PVDF recipe and processing technique. In reality, commercialized high-quality PVDF films (certified by either UL or IEC) can easily pass either combined or sequential weathering test, and even more, PVDF film shows much better performance than PVF under super weathering test conditions (by using high pressure mercury lamp with heavy dose of UV irradiation). However, their proposed C-AST and MAST weathering test protocols are valid for screening outdoor weathering performers. By far, no non-fluoropolymer based backsheet could pass the aforementioned tests yet.

Due to the price soaring of PVDF resin in the past 2 or 3 years, another observation is that the FEVE coating has squeezed into the market and grabbed most of the share. Today, the situation is, the PV module manufacturing leaders found by themselves that the fluoropolymer based backsheet is still a must-to-have pertaining to PV module reliability and safe-to-use. Think about they need to sign off the insurance guarantee with so many compensation items listed thereon. Therefore, we would like to put our observations here: the PV backsheet, still needs fluoropolymers, irreplaceable with no solid substituent found yet.

2. Non-fluoropolymers used in PV backsheet, not prove themselves yet
In PV history, there were several non-fluoropolymers used for making backsheet. We give a brief overview below.

One of them is based on polyamide (PA), the so-called 3A backsheet (PA/PA/PA) developed by an European company. Although the 3A backsheet passed all rigorous in-house accelerated weathering tests, it led to massive field cracking failures in the end. The PV power plants requested skyrocketing compensation and even created a new market called backsheet repairing, unfortunately. Researchers from NIST analyzed the failure mode and made a conjecture that the acid release of EVA resin (encapsulation film used in PV module) at elevated temperature could be the critical factor leading to the disaster [4].

In Table 8 of ANNEX XV Restriction Report, there are two other polymers mentioned, namely PET and EVA, to replace PVDF. We do not want to expand talking about EVA here since it is a piece of wrong information. The EVA resin, having a melting point below 100℃, can never be used as the backsheet. As to the PET, we fear that it may likely repeat the similar story of PA if the NIST researchers were right about their conjecture. Comparing to the amide group (-CO-NH-) in PA, the ester group (-COO-) in the PET chain backbone is more vulnerable to water hydrolysis at elevated temperature. Either acid or base would accelerate the hydrolysis reactions. Meanwhile, PET absorbs UV light strongly due to its aromatic character, creating several cleavage sites vulnerable to oxidation and UV light irradiation attack. One may argue that PET could get weathering performance greatly enhanced by adding UV stabilizer, anti-oxidant and hydrolysis resistant agent. It is true but remember the PV module requests a working life of 25 years or even longer. Those additives are basically consumption ones, once exhausted, leaving no protection for PET chain molecules. It would not be a surprise to see the properties losing in an abruptly declining mode.

Recently a multi-layer co-extruded PP-type backsheet have appeared in the market place. It originates from a Chinese company, sold to a European company through acquisition. Unlike PET, PP does not absorb UV light strongly (though it does have UV sensitive bands) and also dose not hydrolyze. Through proper formulation by adding sufficient amount of UV stabilizers (HALS+UV absorbers) and anti-oxidants, one may achieve a fairly good UV weathering performance. However, the weakness of PP is due to its lower melting point (below 170℃ even for its homo-polymer). This triggers a field issue called hot spot. It says once a small part of PV module is shadowed by a certain unidentified article, the local temperature will rise high enough to see a possible PP melt-down. It might be a rare case, but there would be an unexpected chance to see that happen. Today, both IEC and the UL lab in the US have set codes for hot spot prevention. Unless those regulations abolished, the PP-type backsheet can NOT fulfill all customer needs. In the real world, the PP products find their niche place for small size PV modules where the hot spot may not be a concern.

3. Trend seen in the backsheet technology development
A very comprehensive market survey and report has been published by Shravan K. Chunduri and Michael Schmela recently [5]. The authors draw a picture illuminating the technology share of backsheet structure in 2022. And their observation is: even though PVDF type backsheet lost its dominance in backsheet market due to the price soaring of raw materials, the market still sticks to using fluoropolymers. The FEVE double-coating based backsheet products have started gaining prominence with market share over 50%, comparing to PVDF 22% and PVF 8%, respectively.

Meanwhile, the authors have a few other important findings. For instance, they found module production is not “made-to-order.” The major chunk of the modules is built with backsheet that needs to comply with universal climate conditions, no matter the PV module installed in the polar area or the dessert. And there is a trend for upgrading the module power warranty which requests the module life time extending from 25 to 30 years. Furthermore, the transparent PV front-sheet products start entering the arena with receiving UV irradiation dosage one order higher than that of the backsheet at least. All the above trends put a more rigorous demand on the durability and reliability of PV modules. Obviously, the fluoropolymer based backsheet or front-sheet is still the best candidate meeting such ever increasing rigorous demands, i.e. universal to all climate zones and longer module life time.

The authors also have noticed the trend about environment protection, sustainability and carbon footprint. The topics are intensely talked in China today as well. The EU sets a leading role evidenced by the EU Green Deal, and China actually takes steps even more rigorously and aggressively. Specific to the backsheet market, non-fluoropolymer type backsheet products, such as PET and PP, do have a better green image however lack of product reliability and durability. This exactly reflects the fact that the PFAS restriction proposal is opposed by many industry sectors and probably in a dilemma. A wise approach should never be a one-cut deal allowing no flexibility.

4. The PFAS restriction proposal: lack of sound scientific evidences
Limited to our knowledge, it seems that the driving force for drafting the PFAS restriction is entirely based on observations of the long-term misuse of PFOA and PFOS, which have been affirmed carcinogenic. The PFOA and PFOS should be banned immediately. We fully support this. However, not all PFAS matters are toxic, particularly fluoropolymers. This may make type alpha error: killing innocent. Meanwhile, it is doubtful that chemicals with only one fluorine atom attached is always safe. This may make beta type error: releasing guilty.

The fluoropolymers are generally non-toxic, chemically stable, durable and recyclable. Upon landfill, there is no evidence about their non-degradable nature leading to environment contamination and harmful effects to the biosphere. Recently, Hamaura J et al. have investigated the mineralization mechanism of PVDF, poly(VDF-co-HFP) and ETFE copolymers in superheated water in the presence of an alkaline reagent. Under experimental conditions, they show evidences that those fluoropolymers can convert to pure CaF2, i.e., artificial fluorspar [6].

5. Conclusion and proposals:
Up to today, the melt-processable fluoropolymers (such as PVDF and ETFE), used as exterior layers of PV backsheet and/or frontsheet, are still irreplaceable with no solid substituent found yet. Lack of them, the PV module products are at risk of losing durability and reliability, and the PV power station at risk of running unsafe. We propose that the fluoropolmers (such as PVDF and ETFE) should be exempted in the PFAS restriction act, at least for time being unless strong evidences are found them harmful to the environment and living beings. In most cases, the two fluoropolymers always play roles protecting us instead of making troubles.

General Comments: Submitting organisation

The Fire Industry Association (FIA) is the United Kingdom’s largest trade body related to fire protection matters representing well over 1000 companies (from small to the largest multi-nationals) involved in fire protection for residential, commercial and industrial applications in the UK, Europe and indeed worldwide. As such we primarily represent the interests of our members, but also try to encompass those of their customers and end users.

Position Statement and Concerns

We wish to make clear that we are supportive of the ECHA’s aim to reduce unnecessary exposure of the public and general environment to persistent PFAS compounds, particularly those known to be toxic (including potential breakdown compounds). However, we believe a blanket restriction applicable to all PFAS usage is unwise and may lead to many negative outcomes, particularly so if extended derogation periods are unavailable.

Article 68(1) REACH provides that substance(s) can be restricted only if they pose an unacceptable risk to human health or the environment. This unacceptable risk must be positively demonstrated by conducting a risk assessment that follows the conditions of Annex XV to REACH (and by cross-reference of Annex I and Annex XIII). Such risk assessment comprises hazard identification and characterisation, exposure assessment and risk characterisation.
By grouping all various PFAS substances together and restricting them as a single class, the proposed PFAS Restriction Proposal would restrict numerous PFAS substances that have not been risk-assessed and for which no unacceptable risk has been demonstrated, in breach of Article 68(1) REACH.
The extent of the problems that our industry will encounter should a blanket restriction be introduced can be illustrated by looking at these two examples.
The first example (out of thousands of products) relates to a device used in literally millions of homes, commercial and industrial premises, namely a smoke detector.

Most of the component parts which make up a smoke detector either incorporate a PFAS chemical or use one at some stage during the manufacturing process.
Circuit boards may use PFAS chemicals during manufacture and then also rely on them to provide effective protective coatings for difficult environments.
Components such as semiconductors, capacitors and optics all utilise PFAS chemicals, as does the insulation often used on wiring and terminations.
Even the plastic moulding for the detector may incorporate a PFAS as it will typically be required to offer certain flame retardant properties.
The PFAS used in these applications are generally fluoropolymers, which are generally not mobile in the environment, nor bio-accumulative or toxic. Other submissions to the ECHA consultation by those parties representing the Fluoropolymers Product Group (FPG)  manufacturers directly using such compounds can provide more detailed information on these PFAS.

However, a specific consideration for such components used in Fire Detection Systems is that any single change will generally require the product to be re-submitted for certification, often by numerous Notified Bodies, before being allowed back on to the market. Such a process can take more than a year and cost tens of thousands of Euros over and above the redevelopment effort of sourcing new components, changing manufacturing processes and likely product redesign.
Please consider that an average size fire protection system will utilise tens or sometimes hundreds of different products that will be affected by this proposed PFAS Restriction. Alternative chemical solutions can almost certainly be sourced for many, although probably not all product manufacturing and application requirements. However, to do so we as an industry and of course our suppliers, certainly need sufficient time to transition.
The second example relates to clothing used in the Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) sector, supplied as protective equipment for fire service personnel and those working in hazardous areas. The entire supply chain of PPE from raw material, textile weaving, coating and lamination are already working towards alternative solutions alongside the global standards committees however, there are several challenges in finding solutions which will meet the same level of protection.
For example, Durable Water Repellent’s are crucial in protecting firefighters from liquid threats such as water, oils/fuels, and chemicals. Currently, removing PFAS dramatically decreases the resistance from oil and chemicals to an unacceptable level, lower than the current European Standards.  Additionally, the inclusion of all fluoropolymers in a blanket restriction could be deemed as excessive as the fluoropolymer PTFE (which is fundamental in the breathability and chemical protection of a firefighting garment) has been confirmed to meet the 13 OECD criteria for polymers of low concern: those deemed to have insignificant environmental and human health impacts.
A firefighter’s PPE is their last line of defence and is constructed based on meticulous risk assessment. It is important to acknowledge the trade-offs and that removing all PFAS could be detrimental to the thermal stability, durability, breathability, and repellence of dangerous substances resulting in firefighters being exposed and vulnerable.
We recently as an industry experienced a real-world situation, caused by the UK’s exit from the EU, requiring most of our products to be re-certified for continuity of product approvals. This proved to be a rather chaotic logjam of applications for the thousands of products involved via the relatively small number of specialist Notified Bodies in the UK and across Europe.
However this was simply a paperwork exercise in most cases, but still took almost two years! The changes generated by the PFAS Restriction will be significant and also require re-assessment by the specialist test and certification bodies spread across Europe.
We strongly recommend you take these practical implications into consideration, particularly for life safety related products where third-party certifications are demanded.
In view of both the certification challenges and the safety aspects mentioned we request that the fire protection sector and its associated products be granted exemption, or the longest possible derogation period, from implementation of the proposed restriction largely due to the very real potential risks rapid introduction may cause. Although additionally there are likely to be very significant economic costs linked to the changes a blanket restriction will bring, our primary concerns relate to life safety implications if many of our fire protection products are effectively banned from the market with no near-term replacements available, potentially reducing fire safety for EU citizens.

We would be pleased to provide additional background and advise further if requested.
We also wish to endorse the views expressed in the Position Paper issued by Orgalim, dated 31st August 2023, titled “Orgalim position and recommendations on the proposed PFAS restriction”.

For and on behalf of the
Fire Industry Association

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Summary of the submission

Context

Biotherapeutic filters are process filters used during the manufacturing of bio-therapeutic drug products or samples such as therapeutic replacement of enzymes, antibodies, blood, derivatives of plasma, and biopharmaceuticals. There are two types of these kind of filters: nanofilters and microfilters (together referred as "biotherapeutic filters").

Biotherapeutic filters are made with hydrophilized polyvinylidene fluoride ("PVDF"). They ensure that biopharmaceuticals are safe, ultimately protecting human health and patient safety. Both types of filters do not impose any risk to human health or the environment and as such biotherapeutic filters fall unduly under the prohibitions laid down in the REACH restriction Proposal.
Biopharmaceuticals are vital for medicine and have advantages over synthetic drugs, including targeting specific molecules and causing fewer side effects. They are crucial for treating various diseases, and patients rely on their availability. Regulatory action should not undermine their supply in the EU.

Nanofiltration is an integral part of biopharmaceutical manufacturing, ensuring efficacy and safety as it effectively removes viruses, including those causing blood-borne diseases. Implementing parvovirus-reducing steps improves viral safety. Unlike virus inactivation which leaves residues and virus removal does not target non-enveloped viruses, nanofiltration has no significant disadvantage.
Nanofiltration, usually the last step before a drug substance becomes a drug product, enhances product safety by removing viruses, including small non-enveloped ones. It effectively removes relevant viruses such as HIV, HCV, and HBV. It is a crucial step in ensuring the safety of plasma-derived and recombinant products. Nanofiltration's virus removal capacity is based on size exclusion.

The PVDF filter is particularly used when the level of protein is in high concentration and is therefore, a nice application among the filtering processes in biopharmacy. The safety and efficacy of biopharmaceuticals in humans require drugs of highest purity, right concentration allowing the API to work effectively. Any change in the manufacturing process would require new authorisations and testing which would last years.
Microfiltration is an essential step in the manufacturing process to separate targeted antibodies from the animal cell in the biopharmaceutical manufacturing. PVDF membranes used in microfiltration are not replaceable as all alternatives have a lower transmission of the targeted protein of interest filterability and only PVDF can meet the various performances required for drug product applications.

Regulatory Context

Regulators in Germany point out that there are high requirements for viral shedding filters used in drug manufacturing. For example, the filter manufacturer must validate such filters to ensure virus clearance capacity and, for example, the drug manufacturer must perform virus validation studies as part of the approval process. Extensive regulations and guidelines exist to ensure the viral safety of biological medicinal products such as Directive 2002/98/EC, Directive 2004/23/EC, Guideline on plasma-derived medicinal products, EMA/CHMP/BWP/706271/2010, Guideline ICH topic Q5A (CPMP/ICH/295/95).

Universal REACH PFAS Restriction

On a general basis, it is important to note that the restriction of PFASs must be substance-related and risk-based (Article 68 para. 1 of the REACH Regulation). It is clear that not all PFAS pose an unacceptable risk that would justify a restriction. Especially, the restriction must differentiate between the different groups of PFAS and the risks, and the risks posed by their uses. ECHA, in particular RAC and SEAC members, should consider that fluoropolymers, such as PVDF, do not pose any risks to the environment and human health and should be generally exempted from the PFAS Restriction or benefit from a time-unlimited derogation.

Risk Analysis

Medical filters, made with substances like PVDF, have excellent properties such as temperature resistance, low permeability, and chemical resistance. They are operated by trained professionals, limiting exposure to workers and patients. No adverse events related to nanofiltration have been recorded, and regulators recognize it as a safe virus removal method.

Fluoropolymers, including PVDF, have heat resistance, biologically stable, and chemically stable. PVDF does not dissolve in water, immobile, insoluble (Water, Octanol, etc.), and too large to migrate to cell membranes and are not bioavailable or bioaccumulate. There are practically no alternatives that can replace the high performance provided by PVDF in in the biopharmaceutical sector.

PVDF, among other fluoropolymers is considered a polymer of low concern by OECD, do not bioaccumulate in living tissues. The fact that nanofiltration enabled by PVDF is used for many years without incident in a highly regulatory environment is a warrant of their safety of human health. Their overall safety is expressed by their use in the medicinal sector, Although not being considered a medicinal product, no biopharmaceutical product would be able to meet regulatory requirements should the use of PVDF in nanofiltration be restricted. After service life filters need to be incinerated due to their contamination with pathogens at special facilities as hazardous waste at high temperatures. Under these extreme conditions the C-F bond breaks down, thus completely destroying any PFAS.

Suggestions

Within that context, we kindly invite ECHA, in particular RAC and SEAC members, to consider the following options:

a) Option 1: biotherapeutic filters should be exempted from the REACH restriction Proposal a priori as they should not be covered by the REACH Regulation; or
b) Option 2: biotherapeutic filters should be exempted from the REACH restriction Proposal a priori as they are used in a closed system; in alternative,
c) Option 3: biotherapeutic filters should benefit from a time-unlimited derogation as the same rationale of plant protections products, biocides and human and veterinary medicines should apply.

In support of all three options, ECHA, in particular RAC and SEAC members, should consider that fluoropolymers, such as PVDF, do not pose any unacceptable risks to the environment and human health.

We ask ECHA, in particular RAC and SEAC members, to carefully take this information into account and reflect it in their opinions, in accordance with articles 70 and 71(1) REACH as well as the general principles of EU law, such as due process, right of good administration and right of defence.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Supplement to our first submission (31st of May, 2023)

99% of PFAS used in Europe is applied in non-energy transition related technologies and products (Note 1, Note 2). More precisely, electrolyzers are an overall industrial application with PFAS materials of low concern to the environment and human health. Environmental and human health risks of such PFAS are already even more limited across the hydrogen value chain (both in terms of environmental and human exposure). Furthermore, industrial electrolyzers are not foreseen for the consumer sector, there is no exposure to private individuals and almost all PFAS are within the closed loop of the electrolysis. (regarding polymers of low concern, please see further details in our first submission).

Thus, a blanket ban without differentiations between various PFAS substances shifts production facilities, supply chains, and sub-suppliers to outside of the EU.

First, regarding the important hydrogen sector, this deindustrialization of the chemical sector also has negative effects on hydrogen projects within the EU due to missing PFAS supply chain and leads to severe project delays. The technology is the DNA for hydrogen production electrolyzers and green-ready: Powered by renewable energy, the production of basic chemicals with industrial electrolyzers is green and emission free. Thus, no technology changes are required. Adapting the grey energy to green sources means to keep the European chemical market.

Precisely, the electrolyzer industry needs to grow rapidly to be able to deliver the (political) goals, e. g. 10 million tons green hydrogen by 2030 in the EU (Note 3). This is only possible with firm offtake commitments. Unfortunately, there are very few project Final Investment Decisions (FID) because of the uncertain markets and an uncertain regulatory framework (Note 4). The PFAS discussion alone, regardless of the outcome, introduces new uncertainties to the markets and will lead to further delay of the necessary FIDs. Hence, it directly endangers any 2030 green hydrogen goals.

If the currently planned PFAS ban is implemented, an increase in production capacities for electrolyzers is out of the question. A PFAS ban would massively endanger the business model of European electrolyzer specialists – and thus also the competitiveness of and the energy transition in Europe. You will find a density of electrolysis specialists in Europe like nowhere else in the world. With a PFAS ban, a technology exodus is almost guaranteed. Europe is in global competition for attracting green hydrogen (projects), and European leaders need to ensure that the EU remains attractive enough for investors. The US is already faster than the EU with their boosting Inflation Reduction Act. This in combination with a PFAS ban will create a pull effect for electrolyzer suppliers to expand their business there and building up the corresponding infrastructure instead of Europe.

Second, chlorine and alkali (potassium and sodium hydroxide) chemistry are essential building blocks for the manufacture of numerous products that we rely on every day across Europe and the world. Chlorine enables safe drinking water and healthy swimming pools. However, without it: many industrial and manufacturing value chains could not exist. Banned by the European Union, these production facilities will move outside Europe and force European producers of industrial and consumer products to import their raw material and higher their ecological Scope 3 footprint with potentially grey products.

To sum it up, electrolyzer applications and the electrolysis industry are highly relevant for the European industry and the European chemical market. Thus, they meet the criteria of essential use cases. And again: the used fluoropolymers meet the criteria of polymers of low concern.

Additionally, as we pointed out in our first submission, technically and commercially comparable alternatives are not available and will be hard to develop. This development might require changes in technology to guarantee continuous plant safety and could take decades of development. Our research and development regarding alternatives is only in the initial stages.

Request for exemption

Based on our descriptions and in line with suggestions by other affected companies in or organizations at the interface to our industry, we strongly insist on the electrolyzer industry (with fluoropolymers as essential and low-concern substances) with all types of AWE, PEM, solid oxide electrolyte cell or anion exchange membrane to be exempted from a ban and the overall PFAS restriction. More precisely, the industrial electrolyzers with all its technologies should be exempted – unlimited, as it seems to be unlikely to have PFAS free alternatives for membranes, even in 25 years. On this point, Europe needs derogations for low-concern PFAS such as fluoropolymers in industrial applications. A PFAS restriction should focus on potential hazardous PFAS substances with a clear exposure to human health and environmental risks.

The products concerned by this comment belong to a product range called SHT for Super-Hydrophobic and Transparent coatings. These patented products are the first products on the market that bring to transparent treated surfaces the superhydrophobic property allowing the water and mud to be totally repelled. The water drops bounce off the surface without even getting it wet.

This document describes our comments regarding the proposed restriction of PFAS under the REACH regulation and expresses our concerns regarding the absence of derogation for SHT products which are essential to ensure a clear vision obtained by different type of treated optics in degraded weather conditions (rains, snow).

General Comments: Swedenergy
• supports ECHA’s and the EU- commission’s ambition on ban of PFAS classified substances. Swedenergy agrees that the use of toxic PFAS substances must be minimized and in the long run completely phased out. Only applications that lack viable technical and economical alternatives, and are critical to society, shall be permitted in a transitional period.
• suggests that for essential industrial use of long-life products and solutions the legislation must focus on how to minimize and eliminate the environment and health impacts by avoiding, collecting, and destruction of leakages.
• believes that the capacity of the industry to provide alternatives must be assessed before phase-out of equipment and components in energy sector. To avoid adverse effects on the energy system, a proportionate legislation is needed. Considering technology and market situation there is need of a reassessment of the proposal as well as assessment of derogation needs. Ban on specific components must have a holistic view and the impacts on climate, environment, air pollution, circular economy and use of material must be considered regarding the life cycle of the installations and plants and the alternative solutions. It is not reasonable to demolish substantial investments with long lifetime due to lack of small but essential components. The impact of legislation in relation to the objective of EU’s decarbonisation strategy, circular economy, renewable energy, phase-out of fossil energy, etc must be evaluated.
• opposes the timeline for a ban on PFAS classified F-gases that are used in district heating and cooling, as there is currently no technological or economical viable alternative available on the market, able to deliver near 100% availability and the temperature ranges needed in Swedish and Nordic district heating networks.
• believes that future large-scale heat pump installations and chillers in district heating and cooling should be built with natural or other sustainable refrigerants, but more research and development are necessary to make this happen.
• suggests, due to the non-existence of technically and economically feasible alternatives, a 12-year derogation followed by an independent review and a possible prolongment, for new heat pump installations, in order not to slow down the transition away from fossil heating and cooling in Europe.
• proposes that derogation permits must be granted and supervised by a competent authority and renewed every five years, on the condition that there is sufficient evidence that drop-in alternative solutions are not available during the derogation period.
• argues for a level playing field in the heating and cooling market. For existing heating and cooling installations, we consider the proposed 12 years derogation for “Maintenance and refilling of existing HVACR equipment put on the market before [18 months after EiF] and for which no drop-in alternatives exist” as a minimum derogation period. Most industrial installations have up to 60 years lifetime and replacing them too early will have negative environmental and economic effects for both consumers and society. Instead, we strongly recommend, the derogation period to be extended for the remaining lifetime of existing installations, as long as operators can prove to have a strict customized leakage monitoring systems for refrigerants is in place to avoid PFAS leakages from district heating and cooling installations.
Seen from a socio-economic perspective, Swedenergy believes that measures for the phase out of PFAS should primarily and in the shorter term be aimed at the industries and areas that account for the largest leakage and emissions. For the reasons listed above, the energy sector needs a sufficiently long adjustment period to have the opportunity to reach the climate goals in a sustainable way while harmful substances such as PFAS are being phased out.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Energy sector

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Investments in energy industry are often heavy and have long lifetimes (in average 40-60 years). From environmental and health perspective, it is not wise to demolish large industrial facilities due to a lack of small components on the market. For existing installations and or projects, that are approved for installation before the regulation comes into force, consider and asses if there are efficient and feasible alternatives on the market. The repair and maintenance of operational equipment should be possible in accordance with circular economy and life cycle assessment principles. This would allow the reduction of waste and climate and environmental impacts until the completion of the entire lifespan of the plant or the equipment. The ban should only take effect after substantial repair or renewal of the existing installations, and if alternatives with equivalent technical properties (especially safety properties) are available on the market.  Swedenergy suggests that for essential industrial use of long-life products and solutions the legislation must focus on how to minimize and eliminate the environment and health impacts by avoiding, collecting, and destruction of leakages.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Ban on specific components must have a holistic view and the impacts on climate, environment, air pollution, circular economy and use of material must be considered regarding the life cycle of the installations and plants and the alternative solutions. It is not reasonable to demolish substantial investments with long lifetime due to lack of small but essential components. The impact of legislation in relation to the objective of EU’s decarbonisation strategy, circular economy, renewable energy, phase-out of fossil energy, etc must be evaluated.

5. Proposed derogations: Swedenergy argues for a level playing field in the heating and cooling market. For existing heating and cooling installations, we consider the proposed 12 years derogation for “Maintenance and refilling of existing HVACR equipment put on the market before [18 months after EiF] and for which no drop-in alternatives exist” as a minimum derogation period. Most industrial installations have up to 60 years lifetime and replacing them too early will have negative environmental and economic effects for both consumers and society. Instead, we strongly recommend, the derogation period to be extended for the remaining lifetime of existing installations, as long as operators can prove to have a strict customized leakage monitoring systems for refrigerants is in place to avoid PFAS leakages from district heating and cooling installations.  When heat pumps are installed at co-generation plants, it is possible to optimise the operation after the market’s needs of electricity, heat and cooling which means high total efficiency for production of energy. Besides, the production order of heat and cooling in district heating/cooling contributes to balancing the electricity and energy systems. In district heating and cooling, the heat pumps and sometimes cooling by free cold or absorption pumps are started when low price electricity is available on the market while operation of the heat pump and chiller installed at a building is generally a function of outside temperature.  In case of a rapid phase-out of PFAS classified F-gases in district heating and cooling, the Swedish power balance is weakened by larger electricity use in buildings for heating/cooling and less electricity production from cogeneration plants.

6. Missing uses: Assess the capacity of the industry to provide alternatives. An unrestricted ban on PFAS would mean that the energy transition would come to a standstill for some years, at a time when acceleration is necessary. The entire energy sector In Sweden is aware of its responsibility in dealing with PFAS and is already looking for alternative substances to substitute PFAS. In the short term, however, there is no guarantee that products with the necessary technical and safety requirements will be available at large scale. To avoid adverse effects on the energy system, a proportionate legislation is needed. Considering technology and market situation there is need of a reassessment of the proposal as well as assessment of derogation needs.   Furthermore, for all uses that will be derogated, a mechanism should be established to reassess the derogation period if no substitution meeting equivalent safety or production efficiency properties is available within the specified timeframe. Appropriate and adequate transition period must be defined for PFAS-containing installations.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Swedenergy suggests, due to the non-existence of technically and economically feasible alternatives, a 12-year derogation followed by an independent review and a possible prolongment, for new heat pump installations, in order not to slow down the transition away from fossil heating and cooling in Europe. For the existing district heating and cooling plants, we oppose the timeline for a ban on PFAS classified F-gases, for which there is no alternative available on the market. Instead, we suggest the strictest customized monitoring system to avoid leakage. Both small and large leakages must be quickly identified and stopped. A rough estimate is that a replacement of all Swedish heat pumps that today have a PFAS classified refrigerant amounts to 3.0-4.5 billion euro. Replacing these units requires careful analysis before the choice of technology can take place. For instance, one may question if it is better to build a new cogeneration plant and what environmental impacts building of new power plants will have. Assess the impact of PFAS restriction for articles or mixtures containing PFAS that contribute to facility safety, energy security and production of circular, renewable and low-carbon electricity, heat and cooling.

8. Other identified uses: Swedish District heating and cooling grids operates normally with a higher temperature (80-90 degrees) than often found elsewhere. Currently, there are no stable and well-functioning alternatives to PFAS based refrigerant blends working within this temperature range. Because the heat pumps are constructed according to the refrigerants’ physical properties, the revamping of the heat pump to use natural refrigerants is not possible.  As DHC is an energy solution particularly for urban areas, production sites are in many cases very close to where people live and work. Therefore, safety is one of the key priorities alongside sustainability for district heating companies.  National and local requirements will follow EU directives. What is unclear is how the fire protection authority and others will deal with having large amounts of flammable and sometimes explosive refrigerants near housing and premises. It is currently unclear what measures will be required to prevent fire and explosions from spreading to surrounding buildings, if it is permitted and what this may cost.  An immediate ban on use of PFAS classified F-gases is not manageable for energy companies in Sweden and would have major consequences for Swedish energy security. A production capacity of 1200 MW of heat would be at risk of disappearing, which currently cannot be replaced in the short term, nor achieved by the expected date which according to current proposal is scheduled by 2025. Also, a ban after 5 years is not manageable for the most district heating companies in Sweden as there is no alternative refrigernat on the market.   A transition period would provide a prerequisite for planning and projecting sustainable and long-term alternatives. For existing plants in district heating and cooling, Swedenergy suggest a derogation at least 12-years and at maximum the remaining lifetime of the facility conditioned that there is sufficient evidence that alternative solutions are not available during the derogation period.  Swedenergy suggests that it is better to guarantee the lifetime of investments that are already commissioned, conditioned that the strictest monitoring system must be installed to avoid leakage.   We also propose that derogation permits must be granted and supervised by a competent authority and renewed every five year, on the condition that there is sufficient evidence that drop-in alternative solutions are not available during the derogation period.

General Comments: Synetam is the union of manufacturers equipment and utensils for the catering, cookware and tableware.
Synetam brings together 87 leading manufacturers with sales of €1.5 billion and employing 7,000 people.
Founded in May 2023, Synetam is the result of a merger of 2 unions: Syneg and Unitam.

Synetam would like to make the following comments on the restriction report in touch with cookware and fluorinated gases.

The restriction report does not propose derogation for many uses of PFAS in our sector for which no alternative solution is available at this stage as fluorinated gases and cookware described in section 6 to 8 below.

1- REGARDING COOKWARE:

The proposed restriction of PFASs in Annex XV would have serious economic and social repercussions for our industry, and could put many companies out of business.

Annex XV lists presumed alternatives to current non-stick coatings. With the exception of ceramics, these technologies have insufficient resistance to heat, corrosion and chemicals, and insufficient non-stick properties, abrasion resistance and durability.

Ceramic is the only alternative currently identified, but it has significant limitations: inferior properties in terms of non-stick, non-stick durability and abrasion resistance, resulting in a shorter lifespan, requiring frequent utensil replacements.

If producers are forced to use this alternative, they will have to spend a great deal of money transforming their production tools to replace roller coating technology, which is mainly used for fluoropolymers, with spraying, the only technology compatible with ceramic coating.

Job losses will be permanent, as the closure of factories and the destruction of industrial know-how will make it impossible to turn back. This situation would benefit producers outside the EU.

On this basis, Synetam would like to alert on the following points:
- processing costs will be too high for some French companies, particularly small and medium-sized companies, to bear, leading them to cease trading; larger companies will probably be better able to bear the costs of R&D and industrial processing; but for all of them, costs will be much lower in Asia, which will encourage relocation outside Europe.
- it is not certain that appropriate alternatives can be found to enable French and European manufacturers to maintain their competitive edge and their presence in the industry in Europe.
- specifically for France, a first assessment shows that a ban of fluoropolymers will result in a loss of turnover of 76.5 million Euros by 2040 and a loss of 2200 jobs over the long-term in France.

Given the high economic risks associated with the restriction, Synetam requests the exclusion of fluoropolymers from the scope of the restriction for use in cookware and kitchenware, for the following reasons:
- Fluoropolymers have not been shown to have negative health effects and their use by the cookware and bakeware industries is unlikely to result in significant environmental emissions during the manufacturing, use and end-of-life phases.
- The restriction is not proportionate to the economic risks. Only the most resilient European producers will be able to continue manufacturing in Europe, while the others will have to close their facilities or relocate. Given the minimal risks posed by cookware coated with fluoropolymers, the economic disruption is disproportionate to the gains in protection afforded to EU citizens.

In conclusion, fluoropolymers should not be restricted because the absence of risks from fluoropolymers means that the proposed restriction is disproportionate to the very negative economic impacts of the proposal.

2- REGARDING FLUORINATED GASES:

The F-gas regulation provides for the phasing out of certain fluorinated gases with a high global warming potential (GWP) and the replacement by alternatives with a lower GWP. The definition adopted for PFAS applies in particular to HFOs and HFCs, which are the alternative to certain fluorinated gases that are banned or about to be banned under the F-gas regulation. The only known alternatives are CO2 and propane, which are either technically impossible to use in installations or create significant risks for installations and users (higher pressure or flammability).

Almost all manufacturing companies have no immediate alternative to refrigerant gases using PFAS, for technical and safety reasons.

In fact, only natural gases (R290 or R600a) would be PFAS-free, but they can only be charged in low-powered appliances that require small refrigerant gas charging. This type of gas presents other constraints (ATEX explosive atmosphere).

To comply with the F-GAS regulation, some companies have opted for HFO refrigerants such as R1234yf. This choice was made because it is a:
- validated by the European Commission for the automotive sector under the MAC Directive (Mobile Air Conditioning (MAC) Directive)
- studied and validated by the European Commission as non-persistent (11-12 day lifetime) and supposedly non-hazardous for the environment.
- included in the F-GAS regulation with a very low environmental impact: GWP less than 1 according to the IPCC5 report
- A2L type (low flammability), which is therefore satisfactory for the safety of equipment, establishments open to the public and installation and servicing technicians.

If the use of HFOs and HFCs were banned because of the presence of banned PFASs in their composition, and given that the use of other gases must satisfy both the requirements of the FGAS regulation and the restrictions on PFASs, these manufacturers would have no choice but to use so-called "natural" refrigerant gases. However, these gases are incompatible with their load requirements, and would not allow them to operate the appliances they manufacture under the whished safety conditions.

In the professional kitchen industry, the main alternative would be to change the regulatory and standards framework for hydrocarbon gases so that refrigeration equipment can be charged well above the loads currently authorized.

At the same time, this would require major industrial R&D work and investment in the refrigeration cycle. The question then arises as to whether these costs are disproportionate to the volume of appliances sold in the kitchen refrigeration industry.

In the specific case of refrigeration appliances installed or circulating in areas open to the public (e.g. hospital, canteens), manufacturers are required to supply appliances capable of transporting and keeping food cold whatever the outside temperature (maintain), and reheating it (regeneration) in less than an hour. This implies that in the same enclosure, these devices can cool and reheat above 130°C.

Some alternative gases exist, but they are not suitable for the applications in our sector:
- A3 hydrocarbon gases (highly flammable) such as R290a or R600: difficult to use in establishments open to the public such as hospitals. Above all, it will be difficult, if not impossible, for this explosive gas to coexist with electrical resistors, for example (mixed tank consisting of an evaporator for cold production and heating resistors for heat). The load limitation and safety conditions required for these A3 gases also make them particularly difficult to use.
- R744 (CO2): highly complex technology. High operating pressures, critical temperature of around 31°C, high power levels not compatible with medium-sized appliances such as those used in commercial and institutional catering. Very high manufacturing cost. They are complex to service and maintain.
- R717 (Ammonia) classified B2L (highly toxic, low flammability fluid): as with CO2, it will be very difficult to use in establishments open to the public, such as hospitals. NH3, unlike CO2, does not have a good image and can be synonymous with legitimate fears, given its level of danger. There are real constraints linked to the transport and export of materials.

In the context of our business, the social and economic impact of implementing these restrictions would have a destructive effect on our industrial tool bas and jobs.

On a panel of 10 companies that responded to our survey, i.e. 53% of refrigeration companies that are members of Synetam and represent more than 70% of the professional kitchen equipment market in France, a loss of turnover of between 10 and 80% is envisaged, with an average loss of around 25%.

Testimonials from leading companies in the sector:
- “If the law is passed in early 2024, we will no longer be able to sell appliances in France and Europe, which account for 80% of our turnover. The company will close down, with all its staff affected. Worse still, no solution will be found for the needs of our customers, because neither we nor our competitors will have solutions that comply with the regulations in the short term. A health risk is therefore to be expected.”
- “Without the possibility of using HFC and HFO refrigerants containing PFAS, we would lose 28% of our sales due to the cessation of production of appliances unable to switch to propane. This will have a major social impact on our company.”
- “Internationally, it will impact our export business outside the EU, which accounts for 10% of our sales. At the same time, it will distort competition with our competitors outside the EU.”

In conclusion, given the current use of our products and our current knowledge, Synetam do not believe it is possible to substitute the following refrigerant gases: R134a, R452A, R448A, R449A, R452, R454C, R455A, R1234yf, R32I. As such, we recommend to exempt F-gases especially for Catering Refrigeration applications from this restriction and we support and recommend a time-unlimited derogation with a review clause after 10 years to assess again the impacts and the availability of any new alternative.
