Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Thank you for giving us the opportunity to share our knowledge on the use of fluoroelastomers in the application of industrial automation. Fluoroelastomers are used predominantly in housing sealing and radial shafts sealing as well as for cable insulation in electric motors. In addition, fluoroelastomers are usedfor cable insulation and sealing for automation systems, which are used worldwide in a variety of different applications ranging from CNC-controlledmachines tools and wind turbines to intelligent building automation.
Fluoroelastomers such as Viton, FKM, PTFE or FEP are used in:
• seals for electrical motors (industrial use)
• cable insulation (industrial use)
• seals in connectors (industrial use)
Currently, fluoroelastomers are indispensable in high-temperature environments. Heat-resistant insulation is necessary for communication technology (EtherCAT) in machinery and drive technology. FKM insulation is used in cables for servomotors, as it has heat resistances, durability, and dielectric properties. Electromotors are used in applications for pharmatechnology and for machines which come into contact with food, where sealing materials have to withstand harsh environmental conditions due to necessary cleaning processes. Fluoroelastomers do not become brittle during the course of their use and have a long service life which minimizes maintenance work on the machine.
Other fluoroelastomers (FKM) are used for connectors, cables, and sealing. FKM is used because alternative materials do not demonstrate the same properties with regard to heat resistance or resistance to chemicals and oils.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Sub-use:   Beckhoff implements open automation systems using proven PC-based control technology which are used in in a variety of industrial sectors such as  photovoltaics, wind turbines, wind production machinery, the process industry, smart cities, tidal turbines, the semiconductor industry, the automotive industry, building automation, measurement and testing technology, packaging machinery, pharmaceutical processing and packaging, wastewater treatment, water treatment in general woodworking machines, and machine tools.  An overview of all applications can be found under “Industries” on following website:  Beckhoff | New Automation Technology | Beckhoff Worldwide Industrial control instruments contain sealing rings and cable insulation with fluoroelastomers

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Beckhoff Automation products come under the scope of the WEEE Directive 2002/19/EU, implemented through national German Electronics Act [ElektroG] in Germany.  Beckhoff Automation products are made available on a business-to-business basis. In accordance with the WEEE 2012/19/EU Directive, old devices and accessories are returned to us for professional disposal.  By the end of life phase old devices are prepared for recycling in a dedicated, approved facility. Emissions caused by the end of life phase are not expected due to high European standards for waste treatment.

5. Proposed derogations: In general, our products are made for industrial use only – therefore, they are handled by trained personnel under controlled conditions. They are constantly checked to assure their functionality over their service life and are often sent to our service for repairs to extend said service life further. This allows us to gain detailed information on the behavior of the materials used in our products. In total about max. 100 kg/a of sealing material is used in our electrical motors and 100Kg/a is used in sealing for connectors.  Due to the good resistance of the material to abrasion and the use of our products exclusively in closed industrial environments, we do not expect emissions into the environment under normal operating conditions. Emission during End of Life: The sealing material’s high durability guarantees that the products have a very long service life; very few sealings have had to be replaced in our motors to date. Old sealing materials are properly disposed of, and we implement our expertise to ensure that no PFAS Emissions are released into the environment during the life cycle of the product (motors, cables, connectors).  Usage in motors: The O-rings and radial shaft seals are set in place inside the motor housing during assembly in a controlled environment within our factory and after that, the motor remains assembled over the course of its service life. Therefore, we can also exclude any emissions into the environment within the normal service life of an electric motor for industrial use. Our very own service center has hardly seen any cases O-rings failure, meaning that the material of the ring does not leave the motor and is not emitted into the environment as they have almost no contact with the surrounding environment. If they need to be replaced, they are exclusively replaced at our service center in order to assure the warranty.   Usage in cables: In most cases, the connectors of a cable are only disconnected once or twice over their complete service life. When they are connected, the sealing material has minimal to no contact with the surrounding environment. Therefore, we can safely say that no emissions result from this part provided it is used as intended. As our cable contain valuable materials – mostly copper – we can ensure that they are disposed of or recycled appropriately so that the materials can be reused.   Conclusion: To our knowledge, no emissions occur from our products during their life cycle.

6. Missing uses: Use: Used as sealing and insulation material in industrial control instruments, not listed in the table.   a) The PFAS are bound into the polymer matrix of the fluorelastomers. Our cables or hardware products which are used to control machines are implemented in closed buildings or control cabinets. PFAS emissions into the environment are not expected under the described conditions. The amount of fluorelastomer (FKM, PTFE) used as sealing material in our servomotors is approx. 100 kg/a, the amount of fluorelastomer used in sealings for connectors and cables is a maximum of 100 kg/a.    b) FKM insulation is used in cables for servomotors due to its heat resistance, durability, and dielectric properties. Electromotors are used in pharmatechnology applications and in machinery which comes into contact with food, where sealing materials have to withstand harsh environmental conditions due to the required cleaning process. Fluoroelastomers do not become brittle over their period of use and have a long service life, and these factors which minimize maintenance work on the machine.  Other fluorelastomers (FKM) are used for connectors and in cables as sealing. FKM is used because alternative materials do not demonstrate the same properties with regard to heat resistant or oil resistance.   c) All customers worldwide would be affected as there is a lack of alternative materials that meet the same specifications as  fluoroelastomers do. Here is an overview of the affected industries: Industries and solutions | Beckhoff Worldwide   d) Alternative materials do not have the same properties with regard to durability and long service life in high-temperature environments. Heat-resistant insulation is necessary for communication technology (EtherCAT) in machinery and drive technology. Heat resistance enables copper to be saved in the cable industry. Cable cross-sections can be smaller yet still carry the same current load. Alternative materials such as NBR do not demonstrate the same qualities as fluoerelastomers in terms of acceptance of temperature fluctuations.  FKM is used because alternative materials do not demonstrate the same qualities with regard to heat resistance or oil resistance.  Oil resistance in particular is essential for industrial applications. Alternative sealing materials such as silicon cannot be used in automotive applications and for coating because silicon does not fulfill the “Free from paint wetting impairment substances” condition.  FKM is temperature resistant which permits it to be used in environments with great temperature fluctuations.  An appropriate sealing material is essential for assuring the service life of a product. In harsh environmental conditions, the material properties of the seals – along with the housing surface – are the main factors that determine whether the product can be operated for many years without any problems or has to be replaced after a short time. Abrasion resistance in industrial environments helps to ensure that our customers' machinery is very low-maintenance and the motors have a very long service life; ball bearings last longer if no dust penetrates them, and abrasive dust would otherwise lead to premature failure.

Content: Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Thank you for the opportunity to give feedback on the Restriction on the manufacture, placing on the market and use of PFAS. BASA, The British Adhesive and Sealants Association are concerned about some of the elements of the restriction proposal.

Firstly, we welcome the work of the European Chemicals Agency, and all their hard work in ensuring the safe use of chemicals and agree with the principal of removing PFAS that are hazardous to the environment.

After consulting our members, we are concerned that some products may contain low levels of PFAS or PFAS related substances that are below the threshold where they would be declared on the Safety Data Sheet (SDS).  We are not actively adding PFAS when formulating, but we now believe that some of the raw materials used may contain some PFAS. This makes it challenging for our members to identify products that contain PFAS, or PFAS related substances. We would therefore like to request a longer transition period for downstream users in the supply chain, particularly where very low levels of PFAS are present in the products placed on the market, as they will need to work with the complex supply chain to identify them and phase them out.

Due to the application of the products in our industry, we believe that PFAS are unlikely to be released into the environment or the levels of release are likely to be in very low level, and we feel that initial priority should be focussed on the larger volume applications, with larger impacts.

As we understand it, the restriction proposal is suggesting that the restriction shall apply 18 months from entry into force, but we feel that this time is unrealistic for our members to identify and formulate PFAS out of our products. We would welcome consideration of a longer time frame or a derogation for products containing very low amounts of PFAS where their use is smaller volumes, to aid this process.

Thank you for taking our comments into consideration.

Submitted on behalf of the Association.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Thank you for this consultation. FEA is willing to provide input on the use of fluorinated gases as aerosol propellant gases.
The raison d'être of the European Aerosol Federation (FEA, Fédération Européenne des Aérosols) since its establishment in 1959 has been to promote and advance the aerosol dispenser industry in Europe.
The FEA currently represents 18 European countries which include more than 350 small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and multinationals active in the aerosol dispenser industry. It has also close links with aerosol associations worldwide.
FEA is an accredited stakeholder of ECHA.
FEA’s public ID number in the EU Transparency Register is: 32814201372-84.
Website: https://www.aerosol.org/
FEA annual report: https://www.aerosol.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/2022_FEA_Annual_Report_interactive_final.pdf

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Applications of fluorinated gases (Annex E.2.8.), Propellants.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Certain technical aerosols use HFO-1234ze (1,3,3,3-Tetrafluoropropene, CAS: 29118-24-9) as propellant gas. 100% of propellant gas emissions occur during the use-phase. Reporting of HFCs quantities is mandatory under the F-gas II Regulation (EU) No 517/2014, which is under revision. The European Environment Agency (EEA) could be another source of information.  Extracted from the Annual European Union greenhouse gas inventory 1990–2021 and inventory report 2023 (EEA/PUBL/2023/044, 15 April 2023), submitted to the UNFCCC Secretariat: - F-gas emissions from 2.F Product uses as substitutes for ODS account for 2.4% of total EU-27 GHG emissions (without LULUCF) in 2021. - The subcategory 2.F.4 Aerosols/Metered Dose Inhalers contributes 2.3% from 2.F. - Combined 2021 HFCs emissions from Aerosols/Metered Dose Inhalers (2.F.4) in the EU-27 represents 1620 kt CO2 eq. - The HFCs reported in 2.F.4 are HFC-134a (medical and technical aerosols), HFC-227ea (medical aerosols only) and HFC-152a (technical and medical aerosols). - Emissions from technical aerosols have been playing a minor role from 2018 onwards due to EU F-gas Regulation bans.  For technical aerosols and associated aerosols, the aerosol industry already shifted the use of HFC-134a (GWP of 1430) to HFO-1234ze (GWP of 1.37). FEA estimates the quantities of HFO-1234ze in non-pharmaceutical aerosols (“Aerosols” under 2.F.4) below 1500 tons per year.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: 100% of propellant gas emissions occur during the use-phase. There is then no reason to prevent PFAS emission during the end-of-life phase. Those “post-users/empty” aerosols can be recycled like any other aerosols.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: 100% of propellant gas emissions occur during the use-phase. Those “post-users/empty” technical aerosols using HFO-1234ze should be recycled as any other aerosol. We do not foresee any impact on the recycling industry.

5. Proposed derogations: Certain technical aerosols use HFO-1234ze as propellant gas. 100% of propellant gas emissions occur during the use-phase. See also point 2. For technical aerosols and associated aerosols, the aerosol industry already shifted the use of HFC-134a (GWP of 1430) to HFO-1234ze (GWP of 1.37). So FEA estimates the quantities of HFO-1234ze in non-pharmaceutical aerosols (“Aerosols” under 2.F.4) below 1500 tons per year. The EEAP 2022 Assessment Report quotes estimated Trifluoroacetic Acid (TFA) yields for HFO-1234ze(E) at only 2%. It means less than 30 tons of TFA yielded per year for non-pharmaceutical aerosols (“Aerosols” under 2.F.4).  Reporting of HFCs quantities is mandatory under the F-gas II Regulation (EU) No 517/2014, which is under revision. The European Environment Agency (EEA) could be another source of information.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: HFO-1234ze is the sole remaining non-flammable liquefied gas propellant available to the aerosol industry, globally provided from a single manufacturer Honeywell. The high cost of HFO-1234ze, compared to previous HFC-134a or non-HFC alternatives, is a strong driver to switch to alternatives when feasible. Today tonnages of HFO-1234ze are lower than the previous tonnages of HFC-134a. For long time, ‘general’ aerosols already use alternative liquefied propellant gases (hydrocarbon or DME) – which are flammable – or compressed propellant gases when it is technically or economically possible while retaining product performance and user’s acceptance. By maintaining a constant pressure throughout the aerosol’s lifetime, liquefied gas propellants ensure that the pack performance is the same at the end of life as at the beginning. Compressed gas propellants such as nitrogen and CO2 cannot do this because as the product is used up the pressure within the container reduces and the spray rate varies. The aerosol dispenser industry already substituted HFC-134a (non-flammable liquefied gas, GWP 1430) by HFO-1234ze (non-flammable liquefied gas, GWP 1.37) in those technical aerosols which need to be non-flammable for safety reasons, while keeping high performance. The total industrial and technical aerosols segment (including both flammable and non-flammable products) only weighs 4% in volume, compared to the entire aerosol sector. Certain technical aerosols need to use HFO-1234ze to guarantee non-flammability while maintaining product performance. Examples are: - aerosol dispensers for the disinsection of aircrafts to prevent the spread of illnesses like malaria, zika or chikungunya in the EU. These products must be non-flammable but also follow other strict requirements of several international recommendations, standards and regulations (WHO, ICAO, Boeing/Airbus). This is a niche market in terms of volume of HFO-1234ze, but necessary to ensure the biosecurity of countries within Europe. - aerosol dispensers for testing fire detectors which alert people in case of fire at home, office, in hotels, restaurants... - aerosol dispensers for cleaning electrical equipment without disconnecting them. In this application, it is very important to use a non-flammable liquefied propellant to ensure constant pressure and non-flammability but also a good dielectric constant to be non-conductive. Other existing propellants do not have these three characteristics liquefied, non-flammable and non-conductive. As a matter of fact there are some studies and patents that analyse the option of using HFO-1234ze (GWP of 1.37) as a substitute of SF6 (GWP of 22800) which is the current insulating gas used in electrical switchgear. See some examples at https://theses.hal.science/tel-03524416/document or https://patents.google.com/patent/CN103782350B/en  - aerosol dispensers for cleaning devices in the neighbourhood of electrical equipment that cannot be switched off or disconnected need to have the same properties as aerosol dispensers used for cleaning electrical equipment that cannot be switched off. - aerosol dispensers for cleaning medical devices mainly for oxygen and nitrous oxide gases. In this case the absence of flammable products is mandatory. Fluorinated solvents are used – because they need to be non-flammable and non-combustible – and a fluorinated propellant gas is then needed in term of solubility / miscibility and non-flammability. - aerosol dispensers used for multipurpose lubricants or anti-seize applications on electronics or electromechanical assemblies that cannot be switched off need to be non-flammable. - aerosol dispensers with applications used on large isolating surfaces or in the neighbourhood of large surfaces that can get high electrostatic charging need to be non-flammable to avoid fires. - other aerosol dispensers used while there are ignition sources present need to be non-flammable. For those technical aerosols, which are niche applications, it is not feasible to use flammable alternatives due to safety reasons. Compressed gas propellants or compartmented technologies such as bag-on-valve cannot be used due to loss in performance.  Aerosol dispensers for entertainment and decorative purposes for the general public are also niche applications but not per se technical aerosols. However these products must be non-flammable (EU REACH Regulation, Annex XVII, entry 40). Those products are also covered by a restriction in the EU F-gas Regulation and use HFO-1234ze. Signal horns used for example on ships and boats, but also in other places for safety reasons, are also niche applications but not per se technical aerosols. However these products must be non-flammable due to the place (ship) and/or situation (fire or other sources of ignition) during use.  The two last examples demonstrate that some niche aerosol dispensers, which are not technical aerosols, must be non-flammable. For this reason, FEA suggests deleting the word “technical” in the proposed derogation for legal certainty: “z. propellants for [technical] aerosols for applications where non-flammability and high technical performance of spray quality are required until 13.5 years after EiF;”

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: See also point 5. The HFO-1234ze is not persistent as PFAS. Its Total Atmospheric Lifetime is 19 days. The Trifluoroacetic Acid (TFA) yield is estimated at 2%. Source: Environmental Effects of Stratospheric Ozone Depletion, UV Radiation, and Interactions with Climate Change: 2022 Assessment Report, Montreal Protocol Environmental Effects Assessment Panel (EEAP).

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The  Group is a group of companies who develop and manufacture high pressure valves, tube fittings and pressure regulators for almost all types of gas, in almost all application fields.
The products are used in just about any application field where gas is used
Just a short list of examples: Industrial gases, breathing and medical gases, food & beverage, fire protection, cryogenics & refrigeration, laboratories, semiconductor industry, aerospace, petrochemical, Chemistry, Laboratories, automotive, welding, transportation & storage, diving, leisure industry, paintball, barbecue and many more.

A large part of Group products contains PFAs(more than 90%). It seems to be important to separate the different places where PFAs can be used:
Depending on the different used of PFAs:
 PTFE tape
 Thermoplastics
 O rings
 Lubricants
 Coating
 Gases
PFAS are only use when no non fluorinated alternative solution exists.
PFAS stands for polyfluoroalkyl substances and comprises several up to 10.000 substances that are intended to become forbidden in the European Union due to their persistency.
Fluorinated polymers must be treated differently than other PFAs due to the low risk of toxicity, (when there are used in their stability range).  OECD assessment fluoropolymers (long chain PFAs) as polymers of low concern.

In  gas industry fluorinated polymers are used
1. PTFE tape (fluoropolymers)
PTFE tape is mandatory on tapered thread to avoid leaks and insure protection of the thread.  Millions of gas cylinders are already on market, with refurbishing. A solution which allows the use of tapered tread must be available.
On the request of interdiction, no derogation is allowed due to the fact 2 alternatives exist.
 Silicone tape
 Liquid/paste thread sealant


• Silicone tape, as external solution, is not applicable to tapered thread. Moreover it is a solution for low pressure. As PTFE tape is used at high pressures (up to 700 Bars) between the 2 threads it is not applicable
• Liquid/paste thread sealant is made with more than 30% of paraffinic distillate which are flammable . Moreover, it contains at least 25% of substances under particles form (Silica, talc, Titanium dioxide, Kaolin). This can be considered as toxic (depending on the particle size), and which is a potential non admissible pollutant in the valves (risk of gas pollution, risk of inflammation with oxidizing gases).
Consequently these 2 alternatives to PTFE tape are not usable in gas area.
For that reason, we require valves to comply with the conditions of restriction “until 13.5 years after EiF”, with the possibility of a continuation.
2. Thermoplastics
A thermoplastic, or thermosoft plastic, is any plastic polymer material that becomes pliable or moldable at a certain elevated temperature and solidifies upon cooling. In valves/regulators the thermoplastics can be used in 3 applications. First tightness applications (seats, Packing, Gasket), second friction application (Friction/back-up and sliding rings), then on external pieces (example caps)
A large part of such pieces is done with Polyamid 66, PEEK, Polyimid and PCTFE, PTFE, PVDF and PFA.  Depending on the application (temperature of use, mechanical properties, medical, semiconductors) and the gases in the valves some solution can be proposed.
In some Refrigerant applications, UHP applications, UHP gases applications, NO use for medical applications, only fluorinated polymers can be used. The risk to use another polymer is at least leak, then Inflammation.
In ISO 15001, and ISO 11114-2, we can check that for some gases, only fluorinated polymers are acceptable. For fluorine and high oxidizers it is mandatory.
In SEMICON industry, only fluorinated polymers are allowed for pollution/stability considerations.
Then the use of fluorinated polymers is mandatory for some applications. No alternatives are acceptable.
PTFE is known to have good friction properties. Then it can be used as a filler or a polymer for friction pieces. Depending of the application, it is possible to replace the materials by other plastics, or due to the forces, impossible.
For some devices, no alternatives exist.
In valves/regulators O ring can be used to make tightness.
It can be a primary tightness (with an O ring directly in gas contact), or a security tightness.
As for all the pieces in contact with gases or susceptible to be in contact with gas, material must be compatible with the used gases.
To our knowledge no solution will be available in a short time.
For that reason, we require valves to comply with the conditions of restriction “until 13.5 years after EiF”, with the possibility of a continuation.
3. Lubricants
A large majority of valves are homologated with PFPE lubricants. According to bibliography , this kind of lubricant is the only family of lubricant which is compatible with high pressure oxygen.
Moreover, the lubrification properties of PTFE and PFPE are necessary for hard application. Silicone lubricants are not chemically resistant, imply a decrease of lubrification and a decrease of self-life.
The quantities of lubricants in each valve are inferior to few milligrams. Such lubricants are compatible with food in Europe (according to European rules 1935/2004) and in USA (according FDA) Then the risk link to this PFA use is low.
For that reason, we require valves to comply with the conditions of restriction “until 13.5 years after EiF”, with the possibility of a continuation.
4. Coating
Each type of PTFE treatment is used for a specific application, when it is the best solution. For example:
a. PTFE painting is the only solution  to avoid salt accumulation on pieces submitted in marine atmospheres (salt spray). By this the self-life of the pieces increase, failures due to external corrosion decrease
b. Nickel+PTFE allows to protect carbon steel or ferritic stainless steel of corrosion in atmosphere with an acceptable friction coefficient of our devices.
c. Anodisation + PTFE
The aim of anodization+PTFE is to avoid galling and particles creation during screwing .
For these 3 coating the quantity of PTFE is low. It is used only to solve specific problematics.
5. Gases
Valves can be used for fluorinated gases in Refrigerant markets, in Industrial market, in semiconductor market and in Fire extinguisher application.
Some systems containing fluorinated gases are directly sold for fire extinguisher application. Gaseous fixed extinguishing installations can use 2 types of gas:
• Inert gas
• Halogenated gases, which are liquids and allow an active concentration lower than inert gases.
Halogenated gases are not toxic at the use concentration. In the case of non-controlled inflammation, some dangerous substances can be emitted. These dangerous substances are smelly before to be toxic, which allowed people to leave the area. The efficient concentration is low, which allow a liberation in few seconds (less than 10 seconds).
Halogenated gases are electrically neutral too. They are stocked as liquid under natrium over pressure. The action mechanisms are physical, as neutral gases, and chemical by inflammation reaction inhibition. They are not toxic at the use concentration. In the case of non-controlled inflammation, some dangerous substances can be emitted. These dangerous substances are smelly before to be toxic, which allowed people to leave the area. The efficient concentration are low, which allow a liberation in few seconds (less than 10 seconds)
The environmental properties (self life in atmosphere) where improved.  Really low for Novec 1230 (Cf enclosed document).
Conclusion and remarks

a. Release of PFAs due to presence of PFAs in Valves

• Manufacturers of Fluoropolymers assume that there is no release of PFAs during manufacturing.
• During machining/molding/injection/extrusion of PFAs there is no released. Scraps/chips can be recycled.
• As PFAs are fluoropolymer stable in condition of use there is no release during use.
• It is easily possible to treat waste to avoid release and to allow the recycling of all the components.
• The quantity of PFAs in valves is really low (100-500 mg/kg) but superior to 50 mg/kg
The risk to release eternal compound to due PFAs presence in valves is low, compared to the benefices to be able to use this compound for technical feasibility, and for security.
b. Chemical compatibility between gases and materials
In the interdiction request the problem of chemical compatibility is never approached.
But we assume that PFAs polymers are used in chemical industry for their low reactivity with high reactive chemicals. It is the only known solution to be able to use some chemicals/gases which can react with other Oring/plastics/metals.
For applications where high compatibility is required, no alternatives are available in short or middle term. An Interdiction would imply the impossibility to hand on more than 40 gases.
c. Maintenance of actual products/approval cycles
In the interdiction the problem linked to spare parts in order to repair existing products is never approached. The self-life of a valve can be more than 15 years, a cylinder must be tested each 15 years, and reused if successful.  Then it is important to be able to provide spare parts during the lifetime of the products.
Moreover, interdiction of PFAs polymers should imply to develop new technical solution without plastics. The necessary time to develop such a solution, then to test the security and homologate them will take many years (if we consider that some technical solution can be found). In the gas market, the changes are quite long to be accepted. By admitting some technical solution could be found, the time to put it on the market could be more than 10 years:
The alternatives which are presented in the interdiction request are underestimated. They consider only one part of the possible use. For example, for PTFE tape: the silicone tape alternative, or the sealant paste is applicable to liquids with low pressure, but unfortunately not to high pressure gas applications.
Probably, the PFAs interdiction will oblige to develop specific solutions (when it is possible) for each problematic, with the high risk of mistake and accidents (from leak of dangerous gases to inflammation of valves/regulators).
d. Extinguisher agent
As we saw previously, actual fluorinated extinguisher agent cannot be considered as non-biodegradable compounds in atmosphere. Moreover, the gas in released only in case of fire (ie accident) and not in day to day life.
The use of such agents allows to guaranty the security.
Then to our knowledge it does not have any short-term alternatives to fluorinated gases for fire extinguishers. As the new extinguisher agent doe does not have a long self-life in atmosphere, they cannot be considered as eternal pollutants.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Group is present in all applications involving gas/chemicals use.   PFAS manufacturing  Food contact and packaging.  Application of fluorinated gases  Medical devices  Transport  Electronic and semiconductors  Energy sector  Petroleum and mining In that case, valves and regulators are used to produce/deliver the final product. For technological and security reasons (compatibility between gas and material, pollution, temperature of use, mechanical properties) the use of PFAs is needed For firefighting some total systems containing fluorinated extinguishers are sold.  Some sectors of sub use are not present in the restriction demand:  Chemistry sector  Classical industrial application (welding)  Research  Pharmaceutical

General Comments: The Annex to the ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT include a section on Energy which also addresses the use of PFAS in the two applications Solar collector and Photovoltaic cells.

These two categories are very broad and imprecise and a risk will therefore be present, where (relevant) restrictions will be applied also to products which are not containing PFAS.

In specific the term Solar Collector refers to solar heat panels or concentrating solar systems, which importantly must not be understood as including the most dominating solar energy technology, namely double-glass Solar PV modules containing monocrystalline silicon solar cells of the architecture PERC, TOPCON or HJT used for building applied PV or utility scale ground mounted PV.

It's therefore suggested, that it's explicitly clarified, that such products shall not be included in the restrictions.

The misunderstanding may arise, since a niche application for silicon based solar cells may be car or boat roof integrated solar panels, where the front and back encapsulant may need to be flexible to follow the curvature of the roof. But such products are quite rare and can easily be distinctive from the large rigid products that's used for mainstream electricity generation.
Especially the type of modules which are build with heat strengthen soda-lime glass on both the front and backside, obviously will not be made with PFAS or have PFAS elements included. In specific the coatings of all standard solar PV modules is made by sintering a 120 nanometer thin layer of silicon dioxide to the glass surface at +700C, while at the same time performing the heat strengthening. Other coatings may have been proposed in the patent literature or scientific papers, but are not used for commercial PV modules where the focus will be on antireflective properties of the glass, since this directly translate into higher sales price of the product. Other coatings developed for antisoling properties are almost never used and will always be declared directly on the datasheet, since such coatings are more expensive and will only be added if the product can be sold as a premium module for some specific niche applications.

The other application mentioned in the Annex XV, related to tape fixation of cells. Such an application may have been used for products manufactured 5-10 year ago, but are not part of todays state-of-the-art PV module manufacturing process. This is evident from the Bill of Material supplied by the manufacturer and inspected by 3rd party quality inspectors during manufacturing.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The answers given below are short summaries for the information given in the confidential attachement. For detailed information on the answers and references please take a look at the confidential attachement.

Scope and restriction analysis
Fluorpolymers used as fluororubber and PTFE from us are handled in a very high range (such as Intake Manifold Gaskets, Oil Sumps, Valve Cover Gaskets, Sealing Elements for Cylinder Head Covers, Partial Coationgs for Cylinder Heat Covers, Sealing Lips of radial shaft sealing rings, O-Rings).

Hazard and exposure
Outgoing from fluoropolymers there are no exposures for human (can not cross cell membranes) and environment. Fluoropolymers fulfill the criterias for being classified as polymers of low concern and include negligible hazardous residual monomers. The only “hazard” outgoing from the fluoropolymers is the persistence which is expressly desired for the safe use of vehicles (and thus a benefit in that case).

Environmental emissions
There are no emissions outgoing from fluoropolymers used for automotive applications into the environment. In addition, fluoropolymers used in the transport sector as gaskets or sealings avoid the emission of non-polymeric hazardous substances because of their barrier function and inertness. Without the usage of fluoropolymers in this sector, the achievement of the climate protection targets will be endangered. Environmental emissions from PFAS in Li-Ion-batteries are not expected because in their function as a binder they are in a closed system and the batteries itself are getting recycled.

Information on alternatives
For the fluoropolymers which are used in the motor area for sealing applications are no alternatives available, because the material must have a very high stability/ persistent properties next to mechanical strength (higher 8 MPa), wear resistance, flexibility, resistance to high temperature (higher 200°C), fire retardancy, non-stick properties and a low coefficient of friction.

Information on benefits
Regarding fluoropolymers in the transport section: Less maintenance and lower risk of unexpected failure of propulsion systems. The lifetime of fluoropolymers is much higher than other elastomer classes especially for thermo-oxidative resistance, heat resistance and chemical resistance. A lot of existing propulsion systems in different sectors of the economy need to be replaced with new systems or can´t be operated anymore because the replacement gaskets might not be allowed to be produced anymore (disruption in transportation sector for people and goods, food sector because of agricultural equipment, resource mining and harvesting).

Other socio-economic (SEA) issues
Replacing fluoropolymers in the transport sector would lead to a huge frequency of maintenance and repair cycles. High costs and unclear timelines if and until when alternative solutions can be found.

Request for exemption
Fluoropolymers should be excluded from the PFAS-restriction.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Use Sector: Transport (Annex E.2.10.) • Use of PFAS in applications affecting the proper functioning related to the safety of vehicles, and affecting the safety of operators, passengers or goods, to the extent not addressed under other parts of this proposed restrictions (e.g. under lubricants, electronic equipment and TULAC)  Sub-uses: Sealing and hose applications in stationary and especially mobile propulsion systems as well as in fuel cells and electrolyser applications (e. g. PVDF is used as a cathode binder in Li-ion-cells); also power electronics, traction batteries. Examples for mobile propulsion systems are cylinder head gaskets for combustion engines for heavy duty trucks, ships, big construction, agcricultural and mining machines, fuel cells in various usages and electrolysers for hydrogen production ect.  More examples: Fuel management systems (spring energized seals); electric drive units (radial shaft seals); brake systems (guiding rings, special sealings).  Use Sector: Energy Sector (Annex E.2.12.) • PEM Fuel Cells, PEM Electrolyzers • Li-Ion-Cells: PVDF is used as cathode binder

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: For detailed information on the answers and references please take a look at the confidential attachement.  a) Regarding the fluoropolymer sector: • Manufacture & Processing Phase: approx. 0 % • Use Phase: approx. 0 % • End-of-life Phase: approx. 100 %  b) The fluoropolymer waste can be divided up into the groups “scrap” and “rubber waste”. The rubber waste-fraction goes to the thermal utilization and the scrap will be supplied to the scrap-recycling.  The BEST4Hy project deals with the recycling of end-of-life PEM and SOFC fuel cells. Producers of fuel cell stacks as well as recycling companies from the private sector and scientific institutions such as universities are involved. Publications show that it can be assumed that up to 80% of the ionomer (TRL3 - TRL5) in PEM fuel cells can be recycled.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: For detailed information on the answers and references please take a look at the confidential attachement.  The products formed by incineration of fluoropolymers depend (among others) on the incineration temperature. In general, the four main types of incineration products formed are fluoroalkanes, hydrogen fluoride, oxidation products and fluoropolymer particle matter. The formation of decomposition/ incineration products can be adjusted, so that the formation of PFAS can be reduced to a minimum in incineration processes.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: For detailed information on the answers and references please take a look at the confidential attachement.  Regarding Li-Ion-Batteries: The economic viability for PFAS-recycling in batteries is not given because the total amount is less than 1 %, especially regarding the concentration limits proposed in paragraph 2 of the proposed restriction entry.  Regarding fluoropolymers: Regarding the concentration limits proposed in paragraph 2 of the proposed restriction entry, recycling of fluoropolymer waste will only be economically viable – if at all – in a big scale.  Regarding PEM fuel cells, PEM electrolyzers: No information available.

6. Missing uses: For detailed information on the answers and references please take a look at the confidential attachement.  Fuel cells play a crucial role in zero-emission driving and – together with electrolysis – the key to storage of regenerative electricity for prolonged periods of time. If successfully introduced to the market, about 200,000 fuel cell vehicles (each 200 kW) are expected globally by 2030. Assuming a membrane area of 16 m² per car, about 128 t of PFSA materials would thus be needed to produce the proton exchange membranes. For a more optimistic scenario with 1 million vehicles on the road a total of 640 t results accordingly. This value represents only the membrane but does not yet include the proportions of additional PFAS materials in necessary components such as seals. In terms of membrane area, an annual expansion of electrolysis capacities of 10 GW per year by 2030 would require about 40 t/a of PFSA materials. On a maximum scenario of 40 GW per year, 160 t/a would be required.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: For detailed information on the answers and references please take a look at the confidential attachement.  Use Sector: Transport (Annex E.2.10.) • Use of PFAS in applications affecting the proper functioning related to the safety of vehicles, and affecting the safety of operators, passengers or goods (Paragraph 6 o))  Key functionalities: vehicle safety, reliability at high temperature fluctuations, all kind of resistances (chemical against a wide range of media, thermical up to 220 °C, biological), inflammability, resistance against friction and closure, high permeation density, low coefficient of friction, excellent mechanical properties, excellent barrier properties, non-stick properties. These functionalities are essential for the use in applications affecting the proper functioning related to the safety of vehicles, operators, passengers or goods. Consequences: high life cycle (up to 22 years), low damage rates, safe sealing and transport of several service liquids, low emissions of hazardous products and substances, achievement of the climate protection targets. In addition, PTFE should replace N-Methyl-2-Pyrrolidone as a coating material. In comparison to N-Methyl-2-Pyrrolidone, PTFE is not toxic to reproduction, so replacing N-Methyl-2-Pyrrolidone to PTFE would mean a substitution to a substance which is not harmful to human health. There isn’t known a fluorine-free alternative material with comparable properties and it is very unlikely that an adequate fluorine-free material alternative can be developed at all. Other polymers (e. g. PEEK, PU) do not allow the combination of the properties described above. If the use of fluoropolymers would be restricted this would directly or undirectly affect all the companies in the transport sector where in sum about 3.5 million people are employed. It is expected that the transport sector would be hit severly by such an act.

The ambitious targets for reducing CO2 emissions in the European Union towards climate neutrality in connection with the Green Deal and the Fit for 55 program require rapid and far-reaching measures with regard to the energy transition in almost all sectors, from the production of steel, for example, to heating in private households and mobility. The European Union has recognized that the transformation to climate neutrality can only succeed if a hydrogen economy can be successfully established in the EU. The EU Commission defined this in 2020 within the so-called hydrogen strategy for the vision of creating a hydrogen ecosystem, starting with research and innovation and extending to production and infrastructure. Hydrogen thus plays an important role in the decarbonization of industry and heavy transport in Europe. Specifically, the European Union aims to have a production capacity of 10 million tons of hydrogen per year by 2030 from 500 TWh of electricity produced by electrolysis. This is equivalent to about 14% of the EU's total electricity consumption and thus requires an enormous ramp-up of hydrogen technologies.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The appliances sector is driven by user expectations in terms of performance, low cost and durability. The properties provided by PFAS can be instrumental in fulfilling these objectives, whether PFAS content is introduced in the supply chain as part of the full product, or within spare parts.
The proposal for a restriction of PFASs detailed in “Annex XV restriction report” and its annexes do not mention spare parts.
Accordingly, the report suggests that it is not necessary to restrict the use of PFAS in spare parts. This exclusion should be made explicit in the relevant regulation.

It will be already a challenge to produce existing parts as the supply of PFAS is expected to decline.

From a practical perspective, once restrictions and/or derogations for the full product are in place, the availability of spare parts will follow the production trend.
So, if the use of PFAS in a product is restricted, spare parts with PFAS will gradually make room to spare parts without PFAS. This refresh process is favoured by efficient business models which aim at keeping the stock of spare parts as low as possible, by depleting the stock of old parts as soon as possible.
If, instead, the product benefits from a derogation, at the end of the derogation period spare parts with PFAS will also gradually make room to spare parts without PFAS, falling into the mechanism above described.

In conclusion, little gain will result from restricting PFAS in spare parts and therefore spare parts should be exempted from restrictions.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The comments are specific to the appliances sector. The appliances sector is not listed in table 9, except for appliances making use of fluorinated gases.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: The impact of spare parts on the feasibility and reliability of the recycling processes is included in the impact of recycling the whole product containing the parts. However, additional consideration can be made in terms of recycling capability by volume of products and parts treated. In particular: - Spare parts must provide a like-for-like replacement to keep the use of the product up to the operational standard it was originally designed and purchased for. If removing the PFAS is detrimental to the performance given by the part being replaced, the user will get less value from the product, ultimately be dissatisfied with it, and forced to discontinue its use. The product would reach its end of life earlier with an increased workload on recycling facilities. - Spare parts with lower performance and quality due to the removal of PFAS would lead to more frequent replacement, resulting in higher cost for the user, more waste and increased workload on recycling facilities.

6. Missing uses: The use of spare parts has not been identified by the restriction report. Spare parts are sub-assemblies of a product that can replace an original part to prolong the life of the product, whilst retaining same or similar function. Spare parts are typically complete sub-assemblies that allow for a relatively quick replacement to maintain the repair costs low. The installation of spare parts requires either a qualified repairer or be carried out by the user following the instructions for use of the product. Examples of spare parts for appliances are motor assemblies, heater assemblies, power supplies, cables, filters, light bulbs and battery pack assemblies.  Spare parts attract the same PFAS constraints of the product they are intended for. If they contain PFAS and alternatives to PFAS are not available for the intended operation of the host product, restricting their placing on the market will reduce the durability of the product.   The importance of spare parts is highlighted in the ongoing revision of the EU regulations supporting Ecodesign Directive 2009/125. The new regulations will include the objective of achieving a longer durability of products through the ability to repair them, when possible. Accordingly, spare parts are required to be made available for several years after each product unit has been placed on the market and started operation. Therefore, it is crucial not to disrupt the supply of spare parts. If spare parts are not exempted, parts with lower performance will enter the market, making products more likely to be repaired again, with higher maintenance cost to the consumer and increased delivery trips between warehouses and the customers’ address.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The application classification for lithium batteries and their related materials in which PFAS compounds are used might be not clearly stated in the proposed PFAS regulations for Annex XV. In addition, PFAS materials are used not only in high performance lithium rechargeable batteries, but also in general purpose primary lithium batteries which are indispensable products in our daily lives. For example, primary lithium batteries are used in watches, cameras, and vehicle keyless entry systems to make our daily lives more convenient. In the proposed regulation, many of the materials around the battery are not classified for use in detail, therefore, the respective regulation contents of them are unclear. We would like to focus on fluorinated electrolytes for primary lithium batteries and discuss application classification and exemption period in this public comment.
Fluorine generally has high chemical stability, and many fluorine compounds are used in battery material applications. In particular, disposable primary lithium batteries require a long service life, fluorine compounds with high heat resistance and excellent electrochemically stability are predominant as electrolytes. Primary lithium batteries require an electrolyte with high ionic conductivity to ensure high output, and the acidity derived from the strong electronegativity of fluorine is advantageous. Lithium primary batteries use non-aqueous solvents as, so lithium salt fluorinated compounds that are soluble in organic solvents are required. Among these, lithium trifluoromethanesulfonate (CAS No.: 33454-82-9) which utilizes the solvent affinity of fluorine is most suitably used. On the other hand, there are no non-PFAS alternative candidates that fully meet the performance requirements of electrolytes realistically, the research and development for alternatives will be very costly and time-consuming.
Lithium hydroxide, lithium carbonate, lithium fluoride, lithium sulfate, lithium nitrate, and lithium acetate have been considered as non-PFAS electrolytes for lithium primary batteries, but their very low solubility in non-aqueous electrolytic solution makes their application in lithium primary batteries difficult. Lithium hexafluorophosphate, which is also an electrolyte for lithium secondary batteries, is unsuitable for lithium primary batteries due to its poor thermal stability. Furthermore, lithium perchlorate has been used as an electrolyte for primary lithium batteries, but its use has been discouraged due to the high toxicity of perchloric acid.
As described above, fluorine is essential in electrolytes for lithium primary batteries which are general purpose products, and in particular trifluoromethanesulfonic acid derivatives are indispensable to achieve high performance in lithium primary batteries. We would like to request ECHA to issue an exemption period carefully, proceeding with the PFAS regulation on electrolyte applications for lithium primary batteries.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The application classification for lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) and their related materials in which PFAS compounds are used might be not clearly stated in the proposed PFAS regulations for Annex XV. Currently, development of LIBs for automotive use is being actively promoted to reduce CO2 emissions. However, the mainstream cells with an upper voltage potential of 4.1-4.2 V have reached the limit of capacity improvement, and there is a strong need for further higher potential shift. And to achieve a high potential shift of cells, high potential resistance of electrolyte is essential, where some PFAS compounds play a crucial role. In this public comment, we would like to focus on fluorine-containing compounds for LIBs and discuss the application classification and exemption period.
Fluorine increases the oxidation resistance of the molecule by incorporation due to its highest electronegativity effect. Replacing a portion of the solvent in an electrolyte with a fluorine-containing compound improves the oxidation resistance of the electrolyte. In general, as the number of fluorines in a molecule increases, the oxidation resistance increases, but at the same time the chemical stability increases, resulting in a lower degradation rate in the environment. Ester compounds containing hexafluoroisopropoxy (HFIP) groups combine both increased oxidation resistance and faster decomposition in the environment. The ester compound (specific structure is described in Section V) is hydrolyzed in the environment to form hexafluoroisopropanol and non-PFAS compounds (CO2, low molecular weight fatty acids, phosphoric acid, etc.). The decomposition rate of hexafluoroisopropanol in the environment is slow, but it has been confirmed that it does not bioaccumulate in the body. Borates, sulfates, and sulfonates compounds with perfluoropinacol skeleton coupled with hexafluoroacetone, the precursor of hexafluoroisopropanol, also have electrochemical oxidation resistance, but also hydrolysis in the environment. After hydrolysis, perfluoropinacol and non-PFAS compounds (boric acid, sulfuric acid, sulfonic acid) are formed.
Chlorine-containing compounds with chlorine substituted for fluorine are considered as oxidation-resistant solvents for non-PFAS. However, the use of chloride-containing compounds has been discouraged because they are not only highly toxic but also degrade battery performance other than oxidation resistance. At present, there are no alternative compounds other than fluorinated compounds that satisfy the oxidation resistance requirement, and the development of alternative candidates is likely to be very costly and time-consuming. As described above, a shift to higher potential is essential for LIBs, which are currently in strong demand for even higher capacity, and ester compounds containing HFIP are indispensable for this purpose.
As described above, LIBs, which are currently in strong demand for even higher capacitance, must shift to higher potentials, and fluorine-containing compounds, including HFIP-containing compounds, are essential for this shift. And through the careful use of these fluorine-containing compounds, we would like to contribute toward the realization of carbon neutrality. We would like to request ECHA to issue an exemption period carefully, proceeding with the PFAS regulation on electrolyte applications for lithium-ion batteries.

6. Missing uses: Electrolyte for lithium-ion batteries has no regulatory category in the PFAS regulation proposed by ECHA. We would like to request that electrolyte, which is essential to further improve battery performance, be exempted from the regulation.

General Comments: The applications of polyvinylidene fluoride ((PVDF) membranes for water treatment/wastewater filtration and for fruit juice filtration are not listed in the Annex XV PFAS Restriction Proposal.
PVDF is a high molecular weight fluoropolymer and it is produced without the use of PFAS polymerization aids. PVDF are considered not to pose risks to human health, have a favorable (eco)toxicological profile, and meet the OECD definition for polymers of low concern.
The adoption of PVDF as a membrane material has gained substantial popularity in recent years within the membrane filtration industry due to its exceptional properties and cost-effectiveness.
PVDF membranes offer a unique combination of attributes, including flexibility, durability, high tensile strength, impact resistance, and resistance to fouling.
Moreover, PVDF's robust chemical resistance enables frequent chemical cleaning procedures under a wide range of harsh conditions, which are both typical and necessary for maintaining efficient filtration operations.
Currently, there are no alternative membrane materials available that can match the longevity and properties of PVDF. A ban on PVDF would consequently have a significant and adverse impact on the membrane filtration industry.
In view of these considerations, we advocate for a general exemption or request a time-unlimited derogation for the use of PVDF as membrane material for water treatment/wastewater filtration and for fruit juice filtration.

Org. name: Association of Membrane Separation Technology, Japan
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The Association of Membrane Separation Technology of Japan (AMST) is pleased to provide its comments on the proposed PFAS regulation by the EU.

We strongly advocate to the EU that fluorine-based polymer and elastomer products should be made available for Water Treatment Plants, such as those used for drinking water, wastewater recycling for DPR (Direct Portable Reuse), IDR (Indirect Portable Reuse), and Power Plants, among others.
Since these products are essential to many people's lives, regulations should not group all PFAS materials together.
We believe that regulations should only apply to substances that may have an impact on human health and should be limited to specific applications where alternative products are available.

We are committed to three main goals: (1) improving public health, (2) protecting the global environment, and (3) ensuring a stable water supply.
The purpose of our activities is to contribute to the maintenance and improvement of social life, not only in Japan but also in the EU and the rest of the world, through the widespread adoption of membrane separation technology.

Only membrane products that have passed the certification test for membrane module standards for drinking water use (AMST certification), conducted by the evaluation committee for drinking water membrane modules of the association, are used in drinking water supply facilities in Japan. The required elution levels of AMST certification adhere to the same strict standards as those outlined in the Japanese Water Supply Law for water supply materials and equipment (Water Supply Materials and Equipment - Elution Test Method (JWWA Z 108), Ministry of Health and Welfare Notification No. 45).

Fluorine-based polymer products, such as filtration products like hollow fiber membranes and flat membranes, sealing materials for pumps and valves, and pipes, play an important role in water supply equipment due to their excellent properties, including high durability, chemical resistance, and heat resistance.
Due to their quality and reliability, these products are extensively used in water treatment plants and serve as essential components for ensuring the stable and uninterrupted operation of infrastructure facilities. They are crucial for supplying safe drinking water to numerous citizens, facilitating wastewater recycling, protecting the environment, and generating energy.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The percentages of emissions are as follows: The manufacture phase 0% The use phase 0% The end-of-life phase 100%

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: When iron is melted by the arc heat of an electric furnace (3000-7000 degrees Celsius), fluorinated resin is incinerated at the same time. Residue can be recycled into roadbed material. Fluorine dust is recovered as gas and used for steelmaking materials.

6. Missing uses: Fluorine-based polymer membrane products, such as microfiltration and ultrafiltration membranes, are among the top choices for water, wastewater, and wastewater recycling companies, thanks to their exceptional physical and chemical strength properties. These membrane products constitute a significant portion, approximately 50-80%, of the materials used in the water treatment field, making them a major component in the industry.  These membrane products are currently being used in numerous water treatment plants, sewage treatment plants, power plants, semiconductor facilities, and other companies across the EU. Thanks to their operational method that utilizes their unique characteristics, these products have a long service life of 5-15 years, making them environmentally friendly materials with low environmental impact.  In addition, unlike RO membranes, microfiltration and ultrafiltration membrane products are not interchangeable, and each product is utilized in specific operational methods (filtration and cleaning) to maximize its unique characteristics. As a result, there are currently no alternative products available on the market that can serve as immediate replacements.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: To replace fluorine-based polymer membrane products (microfiltration and ultrafiltration), mandatory system modifications of equipment and SCADA/PLC controls are required for water treatment plants, sewage treatment plants, and manufacturing processes in factories.  These modifications incur heavy burdens not only on entities and companies but also on the general public, take around a decade to complete, and cost significantly more than the initial implementation.  In particular, as fluorine-based polymer membrane products (microfiltration and ultrafiltration) are employed in water supply, wastewater recycling, power plants, and other critical infrastructure, there will be considerable health impacts on the lives of citizens and an economic burden on society during the modification period.  In addition, immediate replacement of these membrane products is challenging due to the need to navigate intellectual property rights (IPRs) related to the operation method and quality control of membrane products in order to provide retrofit products that can be directly used in the existing system.

General Comments: The attached report highlights the need for the modification of derogation 5n “Analytical equipment and laboratory equipment for at least 13.5 years after entry into force” and outlines the impacts that a restriction without derogation would have.

The modification of the derogation will allow critical measuring and control devices that feed in many different manufacturing and processing control applications to continue. Such devices support food production to raw material manufacturing, power generation and emission control and monitoring devices. Due to the large variety of applications analytical equipment are used in, the required technical performance can vary considerably, with indicative examples of specific product requirements outlined within the report but are characterised by harsh operating conditions over lifetimes of up to 20 years.

These specific characteristics for critical applications require extensive and specific qualifications to comply to current regulations while ensuring safe operations. Analytical devices are fundamental in the safe implementation of industrial processes where continuous monitoring is fundamental to ensure safety of operators and the environment. The use of an unsuitable PFAS-free alternative could result in severe health and safety repercussions.

Research has started into alternatives, but as yet has not found any suitable alternatives, therefore it is expected that a new material would require significant research effort, and then additional effort to implement into a manufacturable design. Due to the uncertainty in the timeline as to when viable alternatives will be identified, it is important that there is a proportionate process to allow derogations to be extended if needed.

It is important to note that PFAS are not only needed to manufacture new systems but also for servicing and maintaining existing products already placed on the market. Many applications will require redesign to use PFAS-free alternatives due to different inherent properties. It is critical that either this derogation or a general exception is made for the repair of systems to avoid the premature end-of-life and scrap of the systems which otherwise could be kept in service until the end of its expected lifetime.

Content: Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The attached report prepared by Ramboll presents findings of an independent socio-economic impact assessment conducted to assess the costs for the EEA society due to the inclusion of fluoropolymers in the scope of the universal PFAS restriction proposal.

These results are used in a proportionality assessment with a focus on PTFE to compare the costs and the benefits with respect to additional emissions avoided for the EEA society following the inclusion of PTFE within the scope of the PFAS restriction. The assessment is conducted for two separate cases (PTFE manufactured with or without the use of fluorinated polymerization aids) to account for the difference in terms of emissions additionally avoided depending on the technology used for the manufacturing of PTFE.

By comparing the results against previously reported benchmarks and cost-effectiveness ratios of further REACH restrictions, it could be concluded that an inclusion of PTFE manufactured without the use of fluorinated polymerization aid (as a representative of fluoropolymers) in the scope of the PFAS restriction under EU REACH would be disproportionate.

Furthermore, the cost-effectiveness ratios derived in the report could not account for the negative impacts associated with a potential restriction in relation to the EU Green Deal, decarbonization efforts through the hydrogen economy and electrification of vehicles, safety and well-being considerations and the strategic autonomy in sectors like semiconductors, nor could these ratios account for other environmental effects such as an increased consumption of energy and materials.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The BDH fully supports the European Commission's Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability launched on 14 October 2020. The implementation of the strategy is intended to improve the protection of people and the environment from risks posed by chemicals and at the same time increase the competitiveness of industry in the EU. However, the BDH rejects the published proposal for the restriction of PFASs in its current form, as all PFASs, based solely on their presumed persistence, fall under the proposed regulation of a broad restriction in form of a complete ban. Manufacturing, distribution and use would no longer be possible without appropriate exemptions. Only a few substances out of the entire group of more than 10,000 substances have been shown to have properties that have a proven negative impact on human health and the environment. These substances are usually already banned, restricted or otherwise regulated.

The broad restriction contradicts the basic idea of the sustainability strategy to define risk-based measures and in many cases leads to disproportionality, excessive regulatory complexity and serious disadvantages for European industry. We have summarised our general concerns below:

• The proposed assessment approach for blanket restriction of the entire PFAS substance group is inappropriate without a differentiated, substance- and application-related risk assessment. Restrictions should only be applied if the risks to humans and the environment are unacceptable. The risk-based approach should be maintained.
 PFAS, especially fluoropolymers, are high-performance materials and media that
play a major role in innovative processes and sustainable technologies. A simple replacement with other substances or materials is often not possible, as there are no practicable alternatives after considering all parameters. The consequence would be, on the one hand, a significant weakening of Europe as a technology and business location and, on the other hand, a threat to compliance with environmental and climate protection targets in Europe.
 Legal requirements ensure that emissions from industrial plants are and will be
minimised. For example, the use of PTFE seals is required by law. Plants without these seals cannot be approved. Other laws can also no longer be complied without the use of PFAS, e.g. TA-Luft in Germany, measures for energy efficiency and flame protection in buildings, ATEX, etc.
 PFASs are used in almost all industrial sectors. A blanket restriction on PFAS
would mean that future innovations and further developments of PFAS technologies would no longer be possible in the EU. De facto, this would mean deindustrialisation in Europe.

BDH member companies are affected in many ways by the PFAS restriction proposal, including manufacturers of hot water tanks for domestic hot water and energy storage in buildings and industry. PU foams containing HFOs are used for thermal insulation, for which there are currently no practicable alternatives (1233 zd, 1336mzz-Z/-E). No use exemptions are currently foreseen in the restriction dossier for these two HFOs.

The BDH calls for an exemption of 5 years after the end of the transition period for the two HFOs in foam blowing agents. The manufacturers would then also have sufficient time to examine alternatives and to change their manufacturing processes. It should also be noted that the two HFOs are not evaluated as (very) persistent under REACH in the respective registration dossiers. They have an atmospheric lifetime of days or months. They also do not decompose into TFA in a significant fraction. We estimate that the quantity of HFOs marketed as foam blowing agents for hot water storage tanks in Europe is relatively small, in Germany around 900 tons per year.

In particular, hot water storage tanks with a volume of more than 200 litres would be particularly affected by a ban on the two HFOs, as substitutes with poorer insulation properties lead to large insulation thicknesses that often cannot be implemented in practice in terms of space. This should also be seen against the backdrop of compliance with European climate targets and the planned tightening of energy efficiency requirements for hot water storage tanks through the revision of EU Ecodesign Regulation No. 812/2013 as of 1 September 2025.
