Introduction:
The British Valve and Actuator Association (BVAA) is a trade association that represents the interests of over 180 members involved in the supply of valves, actuators, services, components and materials to UK and European industry. Our members employ over 10,000 people and contribute sales revenue of $4bn annually to the economies of the UK and European Union, many members are subsidiaries of larger European or multi-national organisations.
The BVAA has recognised that the proposed PFAS restriction in its current form has the potential to cause significant damage to the manufacturing industry of the European Union by unnecessarily restricting the use of fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers in industrial valves and actuators. In response to the ECHA consultation the BVAA has collected industry specific data on this issue, which is presented in the document attached in section IV, in combination with an alternative proposal to exempt industrial valves and actuators that contain polymeric PFAS from the proposed restrictions.
It is outside of the scope of work of the BVAA, but it should also be recognised that much of the information presented here is equally applicable to all pressure equipment such as pumps, heat exchangers and instruments etc. The BVAA recommend that consideration is given to applying the exemption requested in this document to all pressure equipment.

Exemption of polymeric PFAS used in industrial valves and actuators:
Industrial valves are involved in the processing and creation of virtually every type of manufactured item in the world with a global market size of $70 Billion in 2021, nearly 25% of this being in Europe. Polymeric PFAS is expensive to manufacture, and so industrial valves and actuators employ these materials only where they are necessary to provide acceptable performance required by the process conditions. They play a vital sealing role by protecting humans and the environment from the potentially dangerous emission of process fluids across multiple industries therefore, it is not appropriate to group the restrictions and derogations to be applied to industrial valves and actuators by simply considering isolated end uses. In many of the applications in which polymeric PFAS are used there is no alternative material that will perform to the same level and protect the environment as effectively.
The BVAA propose that the use of fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers in industrial valves and actuators are considered as a single use case. Regardless of the industry or process that the valve is used in, the use of these materials in industrial valves should be excluded from the requirements of paragraphs 1 and 2, as stated on page 4 of the Annex XV restriction report. This exclusion is justified on the grounds that fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers are harmless to humans and the environment and they can be safely recycled at the end of life under the responsibility of the end user’s business.
The only area of potential environmental concern regarding fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers is the material manufacturer’s use of non-polymeric fluorinated PFAS surfactants in the polymerisation process. The material suppliers of fluoropolymer and fluoroelastomer materials are already taking steps to eliminate the use of any harmful non-polymeric PFAS material from the manufacturing process. As recognised in A.2.1.5.1 on p11 of Annex A of the restriction proposal, 50-60% of fluoropolymers are already manufactured without using these fluorinated polymerisation aids. Some material manufacturers in the market already claim to be manufacturing fluoropolymers without using fluorinated surfactants. The BVAA support the development of further controls to encourage, where possible, the global adoption of non-fluorinated polymerisation aids in the polymeric PFAS manufacturing process, within a timescale that is practically achievable by the industry.
Fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers are used as sealing, barrier, or load bearing components within the pressure envelope of industrial valves and actuators so they do not present any health or environmental risks during their operating lifetime because they have no contact with humans or the external environment. The only potential risk presented by polymeric PFAS used in industrial valves is the potential to persist in the environment during the end of life phase. A total, or time derogated ban, of polymeric PFAS used in industrial valves is not appropriate because the concerns regarding persistence in the environment raised in the Annex XV restriction report can be managed effectively by waste stream regulation.
At end of life, the PFAS used in industrial valves and actuators can, within the business to business waste disposal environment, be separated, controlled and then re-cycled, or alternatively incinerated by municipal waste incinerators. Both of these solutions are proposed in the UK HSE RMOA report recently published by the UK health and safety executive.
Refer to the BVAA PFAS in industrial valves-a special use case document attached in section IV for further information.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Comments apply to the following sectors: • Industrial food contact materials and processing  • Energy sector • Petroleum and mining- fluoropolymer applications Based on data supplied by BVAA members and presented in Figure 1 of the section IV attachment, 90% of industrial valves use polymeric PFAS, utilising their unique combination of properties in components for sealing, corrosion protection/hygienic operation, and low friction load bearing. These industrial valves are used in virtually all manufacturing industries including the use sectors highlighted above. The BVAA proposes that use of polymeric PFAS in all industrial valves and actuators should be considered a separate case for an exception to the annex XV restriction proposals. More detail on this proposal is outlined in the section IV attachment. Separate consideration of industrial valves and actuators by discrete sector or sub-use, as listed in Table 9 of the restriction proposal, would only capture some of the end uses of industrial valves. Many other valves and actuators make use of fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers for exactly the same reasons in different end uses and they should also be considered as exceptions to the proposed restrictions.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: As a downstream user of polymeric PFAS components, the BVAA has no information on emissions of polymeric PFAS during the material manufacturing phase.  Industrial valves and actuators that contain polymeric PFAS components do not have any PFAS emissions to the environment whilst these parts are in service as they operate within an enclosed pressurised system. The only polymeric PFAS emissions associated with industrial valves and actuators is in the end of life phase. The BVAA has supplied data in Figure 5 of the section IV attachment that estimates the expected annual emissions by end use sector, assuming that these are in the same proportion as the new sales volumes. This assumption is for indication only as the frequency and number of service interventions and valve replacements may fluctuate significantly from year to year.  This indicates that EOL emissions for polymeric PFAS from industrial valves in the petroleum and mining industry could be in the region of 800 tonnes or 24% of the total. Emissions from industrial valves in the food processing sector are contained in the general industry category of Figure 5. No specific information is available on the proportion of the 580 tonnes of emissions in this sector that come from the food processing industry.  The BVAA does not have data relating to how this waste is treated by the end user. However, please refer to sections 10 & 11 of the section IV attachment for further information on EOL treatment.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The safe incineration of fluoropolymers in conditions achievable by municipal incinerators has been the subject of several studies with positive results, demonstrating complete, effective decomposition of the material. One example of this is “Waste incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate potential formation of per- and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) in flue gas” - Municipal Incineration- W.L Gore et al 2019.

5. Proposed derogations: The BVAA have compiled information from members to estimate the typical PFAS content in an industrial valve. This information has been combined with the data in the Oxford Economics Global Valve and Actuator Market Outlook 2022 to give an estimate of the total polymeric PFAS emissions from industrial valves and actuators in the EU, based on 2021 sales volumes. PFAS emissions only occur from Industrial valves and actuators at the end of life and so this data is limited in accuracy by the loose relationship between new valve sales and volume of PFAS reaching end of life, but it may be considered indicative in terms of order of magnitude of emissions. The detailed estimate by valve type is shown within the section IV attachment in Figure 1 for all end uses of industrial valve and indicates potentially 3,360 tonnes per annum of polymeric PFAS emissions. This represents 1.2% of the total polymeric PFAS emissions stated in Table 3 of the annex XV restriction report taking the median value. As stated in the section IV attachment it is the BVAA view that emissions from industrial valves and actuators should be considered across all end uses, because the reasons to use polymeric PFAS in these valves are not dependent upon the end use sector. It is the type of fluid combined with pressure and temperature conditions that determines whether polymeric PFAS should be used. However, considering derogation 6f in the proposed restrictions for fluoropolymer applications in the petroleum and mining industry, the indicative EU annual emissions from industrial valves is in the order of 800 tonnes per annum taking the value for oil and gas refining in Figure 5 in the section IV attachment. This figure may be overstated as it includes all upstream, midstream and downstream activities in the oil and gas industry as well as refining however, the precise definition of petroleum and mining is not clear in the restriction report.

6. Missing uses: The missing use relevant to these comments is the use of polymeric PFAS components in the product group of industrial valves and actuators, as detailed in the section IV attachment. This use is partially represented within the restriction report by the following end uses:-  Industrial food contact materials and packaging, energy sector and petroleum and mining. a. The annual tonnage and emissions (at sub-sector level) and type of PFAS associated with the relevant use:  Figure 1 in section IV attachment estimates that the annual emissions by valve type total 3,370 tonnes all in the end of life phase. Figure 5 in the section IV attachment estimates the breakdown of emissions per year by end industries. 800 tonnes/y in oil and gas and refining is closest to the petroleum and mining end use. 440 tonnes/y power generation relates to the energy sector 580 tonnes/y general industry includes the food processing sector. b. The key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use: The key functionalities of fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers used in industrial valves such as PTFE and FKM are the inert chemistry of the materials and wide application temperature range, combined with excellent mechanical strength and a low coefficient of friction. Refer to sections 4 & 6 of the section IV attachment for further details.   c. The number of companies in the sector estimated to be affected by the restriction: There are estimated to be 1,000 valve manufacturers and suppliers in the EU, every one of these companies will be seriously, negatively impacted by this proposed restriction. However, as detailed in the section IV attachment, there are at least equally serious and wide impacts on environmental pollution through fugitive emissions, reduced plant efficiencies and ongoing spare parts and replacement costs that will adversely affect all branches of EU manufacturing industry if the restriction in its proposed form is adopted. d. The availability, technical and economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives for the relevant use, including information on the extent (in terms of market shares) to which alternative-based products are already offered on the EU market and whether any shortages in the supply of relevant alternatives are expected: See the attachment in section IV, BVAA PFAS in industrial valves-a special use case.  e. For cases in which alternatives are not yet available, information on the status of R&D processes for finding suitable alternatives, including the extent of R&D initiatives in terms of time and/or financial investments, the likelihood of successful completion, the time expected to be required for substitution (including any relevant certification or regulatory approvals) and the major challenges encountered with alternatives which were considered but subsequently disregarded: No suitable alternative material exists to replace all the desirable properties of fluoropolymers used in industrial valves and actuators as detailed in the section IV attachment. Polymeric PFAS are high cost materials therefore there have been considerable research efforts over the past years to identify “drop in” replacements with no success to date. Consequently, it is extremely likely that such material development would take a considerable period of time and be likely to exceed the arbitrary maximum 15 year derogation in the restriction period. Manufacturers of industrial valves and actuators are amongst many downstream users of these materials who can only begin development of new component designs for the many uses, detailed in section 4 of the section IV attachment, once the properties of the replacement material are known, still further increasing the timescales to a solution, assuming that an acceptable one can be found. A further consideration is the cost of qualification tests to prove that the new materials are suitable for the valve design. Section 5 of the section IV attachment details the implications of completing these qualification tests and estimates significant total costs to the valve industry of $267M or 2.2% of annual sales for the EU market. f. For cases in which substitution is technically and economically feasible but more time is required to substitute: i. the type and magnitude of costs (at company level and, if available, at sector level) associated with substitution (e.g. costs for new equipment or changes in operating costs); ii. the time required for completing the substitution process (including any relevant certification or regulatory approvals); iii. information on possible differences in functionality and the consequences for downstream users and consumers (e.g. estimations of expected early replacement needs or expected additional energy consumption); iv. information on the benefits for alternative providers: For some specific industrial valve applications existing materials are available that could replace PFAS materials but generally with reduced performance. An example of this could be the potential to use PEEK to replace a filled PTFE ball valve seat. This substitution would result in higher operating loads due to an increased coefficient of friction and higher sealing loads. Refer to section 6 in the section IV attachment for further details.  The valve design would need to be modified to accept the alternative PEEK material but it is not possible to quantify the time or cost at this point as too many variables are involved. Industry wide this activity would certainly consume thousands of engineering man hours to change the necessary 90% of total product designs that would be affected. The introduction of these materials would also still incur the qualification testing costs referenced above and estimated in section 5 of the section IV attachment. A ban on the availability of polymeric PFAS parts for industrial valves and actuators would mean that installed products would need to be modified to accept the new material as a spare part. The supply of spare parts for the existing installed base would be costly as detailed in section 7 of the section IV attachment.  The end user would be likely to see a reduction in plant performance and efficiency, increased environmental emissions and higher service and maintenance costs. International valve fugitive emissions testing standards state that the typical stem/shaft seal emissions performance of non PFAS alternatives such as graphite have a leakage rate 100 times greater than a material such as PTFE. No benefits to alternative providers have been identified as most suppliers to the industrial valve industry are also likely to supply the alternative material solution. g. For cases in which substitution is not technically or economically feasible, information on what the socio-economic impacts would be for companies, consumers, and other affected actors. If available, please provide the annual value of EU sales and profits of the relevant sector, and employment numbers for the sector: It is considered likely that, in the majority of cases, substitution of polymeric PFAS by existing materials to achieve the same level of product performance will not be possible. The socio-economic impact for more than 1,000 valve manufacturers and suppliers in the EU, with annual market sales of $12 Billion and estimated total profits of over $1 Billion, will be significant. There would also be a significant effect on the employment of an estimated 50,000 workers at these companies.  The time and investment necessary to find replacement materials for existing PFAS applications will also seriously deflect and delay existing R&D work. This is likely to result in delays in developing products for emerging technologies related to reversing climate change and the European Green Deal. A loss in the competitiveness of European manufacturers in the valve and actuator sector, compared to overseas competitors without the same reliance on the EU market, is extremely likely to result.  As detailed in the section IV attachment, industrial valves and actuators are used in all manufacturing sectors and the proposed restrictions are likely to have a significant impact on industrial output. This is due to deteriorating plant reliability, the requirement to invest in replacement units on a reactive basis where spare parts are no longer available, along with inevitable delays in the supply of replacement products due to the level of demand. There is also likely to be a significant cost to the environment in terms of increased pollution through fugitive emissions and increased maintenance costs.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Derogation 6a food contact materials for the purpose of industrial production, proposed for 6.5 years, and 6f fluoropolymer applications in petroleum and mining, proposed for 13.5 years after EIF are the only cases directly related to industrial valves and actuators contained in the annex XV proposal. It is the opinion of the BVAA that there are many other end use applications of industrial valves and actuators that use polymeric PFAS for the same reasons as these two end use cases, with little prospect of developing non-PFAS replacements for most of them. Therefore, these use cases should be expanded to include all polymeric PFAS used in industrial valves and actuators, not just food contact during processing and petroleum and mining.  Typical examples of the required extension in use cases would be energy, petrochemicals, chemicals, process, pharmaceuticals, food and beverage and water which effectively covers all the broad categories of use of industrial valves and actuators. It should also be recognised that a large number of these use cases are directly related to the supply of products to enable new technologies that form a vital part of the European Green Deal. Please refer to question 6 above and section IV attachment for further details.   The BVAA requests that the use case of industrial valves and actuators, if not all pressure equipment, should be granted an exception from inclusion in the Annex XV restriction proposal.

8. Other identified uses: It is the opinion of the BVAA that there are many other end use applications of industrial valves and actuators that use polymeric PFAS for the same reasons as the food processing and petroleum and mining industry. Therefore, these use cases should be expanded to include all polymeric PFAS uses in industrial valves and actuators, not just the two previously referenced. Please refer to the comments in section 6 above along with the comments in the section IV attachment.

General Comments: The cfbt.pl Foundation requests that PFAS agents not be excluded from the ban on use for firefighters' personal protective equipment, due to emerging information about their harmfulness to human health. Alternatively, the cfbt.pl Foundation takes the position that any exclusion from the ban on use should be as short as possible, as the best possible protection of firefighters' health should be sought. Firefighters are in an occupational group at particular risk of contracting cancer due to their work environment (IARC WHO 2022, Monograph 132) and shift work (IARC WHO 2010, Monograph 98).

Citing Appendix E of Report XV:
- “Information from one manufacturer of PPE suggested that an alternative weave construction could replace existing PFAS-based coatings in some PPE.”
- “There is sufficiently strong evidence that a derogation of PFAS use in PPE (either for 5 or 12 years) will cause substantial additional emissions which are below additional emissions under (worst-case) scenarios.”
- “Products, for which a full ban of PFASs is likely to lead to products not being available to EU customers as a result of technical feasibility considerations include, for example, Category III PPE for the protection against liquid and gaseous chemicals, including aerosols and solid particles, and microorganisms, and PPE for firefighting activities. A full ban of PFAS would also prevent maintenance, i.e. re-impregnation, of Category III workwear already in use. For these products, alternatives to PFASs are not able to provide the required functionalities at the level that is necessary to reach the requirements set out in EU legislation according to the assessment of the Dossier Submitters presented in Section E.2.2.2. As the provision of products of lower quality (below the set standard) is not acceptable for such products, a complete restriction of PFASs would actually result in the complete unavailability of suitable PPE for these types instead of changes to the quality of PPE on the market.”
- “A ban with a transition period of 18 months and a 12-year derogation is proposed for: Personal protective equipment (PPE) intended to protect users against risks as specified in Regulation (EU) 2016/425, Annex I, Risk Category III (a) and (c); Personal protective equipment (PPE) in professional firefighting activities intended to protect users against risks as specified in Regulation (EU) 2016/425, Annex I, Risk Category III (a) - (m); and Impregnation agents for re-impregnating of articles referred to above.”

In addition, consideration should be given to whether a more effective way to protect the health of firefighters would be to amend EN 469 to reduce the requirements for clothing water repellency and chemical resistance. In the firefighting community, there is a belief that the water repellency of special clothing is not enough to justify such high requirements for protective clothing that would justify the use of PFAS substances with all their negative effects. In addition, special clothing is used for protection against chemicals and therefore the requirement for chemical resistance of clothing intended for fighting fires in buildings may not be justified in view of the negative effects of PFAS substances on the health of the wearer and the environment. The same observation applies to firefighter gloves.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: The Chemours Company welcomes the opportunity to provide feedback to the ECHA public consultation on the universal PFAS restriction proposal submitted by Germany, Denmark, The Netherlands, Sweden and Norway (hereafter referred to as the Dossier Submitters).

PFAS are a large class of substances that have diverse and unique chemical properties. Given the range of relevant applications, it is not possible for Chemours to respond meaningfully to the consultation on a generic level. Rather, Chemours’ two business units specializing in fluoropolymers and fluorinated gases (F-gases): Advanced Performance Materials (APM) and Thermal & Specialized Solutions (TSS) have made separate submissions to the public consultation. Whilst TSS and APM have submitted separate comments, both business units share a common objective: to demonstrate, that a more tailored (differentiated) approach to the scope and conditions of a restriction, recognizing the different properties and conditions of use of different PFASs, would ensure the safe use of PFASs without imposing disproportionate costs or compromising the EU’s policy and strategic objectives.

As manufacturer, seller and downstream user of F-gases, Chemours’ TSS business unit recognizes the concerns raised by the Dossier Submitters with the safety profiles of some PFASs. TSS is aware of the increased scrutiny on PFASs as outlined in the EU’s Chemical Strategy for Sustainability. With expertise in the manufacture, properties and application of F-gases, TSS is committed to taking an active, responsible and constructive role in the public consultation on the proposed restriction to facilitate the development of a coherent approach to the regulation of PFASs.

The proposed restriction, as currently formulated, will have a disproportionate negative impact on EU society. This is because alternatives to F-gases cannot currently be implemented in applications for which there is no derogation currently proposed or may result in regrettable substitution. Equally, where alternatives can be implemented their technical performance will lead to very large societal costs associated with their greater energy demands and associated CO2 emissions.

TSS intends to demonstrate that F-gases can continue to be used safely and that an alternative restriction proposal that focuses on risk management via emission reduction and circularity would be more proportionate than the proposed restriction and would ensure that the EU is able to realize its policy ambitions whilst maintaining its competitiveness and strategic autonomy. The key elements of the submission are, as follows:
• The grouping approach used by the dossier submitters would lead to the restriction of some substances, specifically F-gases, which can be reliably demonstrated to be safe for human health and the environment.  Regulation which adequately deals with the differences in substance properties within the PFAS class, is critical for achieving EU ambitions and competitiveness; reading across the hazardous properties of some PFASs to all PFASs has not been justified based on sufficiently rigorous science.
• Further emission reduction of F-gases is possible without a ban through the use of an alternative risk management approach that is focused on emission minimization via improved mandatory risk management measures, refined technical standards for equipment (i.e., setting maximum leak rates) and establishing regulatory frameworks that ensure circularity.
• A ban of all PFAS would heavily impact a range of critical European industries, which are key to achieving the EU’s sustainability goals and which rely on the use of F-gases, as there are no suitable alternatives for several technical and/or economic reasons. A more proportionate phase-out, if ultimately preferred by the decision maker over alternative risk management approaches, would be to allow for transitional periods of appropriate duration per industry that recognize the applicable innovation cycle, the high effectiveness of risk management measures in certain uses and the enormous costs to society associated with the use of alternatives with lower technical performance (leading directly to increased energy consumption).

Combined Comments:
General Comments: The City of Stockholm has established a resource center with specialized expertise in chemistry. The Chemical Center is, among other things, a support function for the City with the vision of achieving a toxin-free Stockholm.

The Chemical Center at the City of Stockholm would like to contribute to the consultation on the proposed restriction of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). We support Restriction Option 1 (RO1) and firmly believe that a total ban on PFAS would greatly benefit the well-being of our citizens, the environment, and our municipal operations.

The Chemical Center conducts health-related environmental monitoring in indoor environments. As a part of this monitoring, PFAS levels in dust were assessed at 20 preschools, revealing considerable levels of PFAS in all 20 dust samples (see attached analysis results), in which some were exceeding the new proposed PFAS limits (i: 25 ppb, ii: 250 ppb). For example, in one dust sample, concentrations of a single PFAS substance (6:2 diPAP) reached 42,000 ppb. These findings indicate the presence of PFAS sources in these indoor environments, which may have direct or indirect implications for the well-being of children as well as staff. This is a matter of concern, as the City’s objective is to offer our citizens a good and safe indoor environment.

Furthermore, we have encountered challenges in determining whether our suppliers' products contain PFAS or not, as suppliers typically only analyse a few individual PFAS substances and may lack knowledge of the presence of PFAS in their products. This lack of information and transparency hinders our ability to verify compliance with our procurement requirements and prevent unintentional contributions to PFAS usage.

As a municipality, the City of Stockholm envisions no obstacles to completely phasing out PFAS from the municipality’s contracts and assortments, with some exceptions. These include, for example, electronic equipment such as computers, since PFAS might exist in the circuit boards. Although there are alternatives to PFAS in many sectors, further research and development is needed to identify and promote safer options where PFAS substitution remains challenging. A ban on PFAS would encourage innovation in this field and expedite the transition to safer alternatives. Additionally, a total ban on PFAS might encourage manufacturers and consumers to reassess the necessity of all functions provided by PFAS additives in products and materials.

A total ban on PFAS could also incentivize the development of standardized and commercially available analytical methods for measuring total PFAS content. This would simplify compliance verification of procurement requirements and enable more accurate monitoring of PFAS levels. Furthermore, it would facilitate informed decision-making regarding the products and materials procured, used, and produced. This, in turn, could lead to a more deliberate and proactive approach to eliminating PFAS and potentially drive innovation towards more sustainable alternatives that do not rely on harmful chemicals.

In sum, a total ban on PFAS would optimize the City’s efforts to prevent unintentional contributions to PFAS usage, encourage innovation, and expedite the transition to safer products and materials, ultimately creating a better and safer environment for our citizens.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: The Committee for European Construction Equipment (CECE) welcomes the opportunity to contribute to the public consultation organised by the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) on the PFAS restriction proposal. CECE represents the construction equipment sector’s durable and innovative machinery which are working tools to help build the houses, offices, factories, roads, railways and bridges that serve citizens across the globe. Manufacturers invest and innovate continuously to deliver equipment with highest productivity and lowest environmental impact.

In the same vein, efficiency, safety and high-precision technologies play a pivotal role. In that regard, as a forward-looking industry, we are contributing to the EU Green Deal and digital transformation. The PFAS restriction proposal may call the fulfilment of the objectives of the Green Deal into question and, if applied as is, would drastically affect our sector’s supply chains, halting the manufacturing of our products. The PFAS restriction proposal, if brought into force as is, would put the placing on the Single Market and the export of construction equipment, manufactured in EU-based plants, in jeopardy for several years. Many enterprises and their suppliers would be faced with dramatically high risks of economic or technical shutdowns and relocations overseas. The importance of PFAS in the EU economy should not be underestimated and a higher political debate should also be brought about, considering the social, economic, and cultural repercussions that the indiscriminate phase-out of PFAS will generate. Therefore, CECE calls upon the European Commission to ultimately take the most proportionate measures to safeguard our industry whilst fulfilling the EU Green Deal.

As an interested party, CECE would like to submit the following recommendations to ECHA and the European Commission:

1. Anticipating that an 18-month transition period will be conducive to impeding our supply chains with durable and severe repercussions on the Single Market in addition to imperiling the EU Green Deal and its circularity objectives, CECE requests ECHA to provide for transition periods of four to eight years in keeping with our industry’s specificities. On principle, applications of PFAS should be allowed until the full-scale availability of technically suitable, commercially viable and irrefutably safe alternatives can be demonstrated.
2. CECE calls upon ECHA to level the playing field between industries that share supply chains and technologies and request ECHA to grant the construction equipment industry, at the very least, the same derogations for the applications of refrigerants as the ones granted to the automotive industry.
3. Similarly, CECE calls upon ECHA to grant the construction equipment industry, at the very least, the same derogations for the use of PFAS in applications affecting the proper functioning related to its safety, its operators, workers/users, and goods in addition to proposing a 13.5-year derogation after entry into force.
4. CECE stands for an exclusion of fluoropolymers (including fluoroelastomers and polytetrafluoroethylene) from this restriction proposal or, at the very least, a 13.5-year derogation after entry into force for our essential fluoropolymers uses on O-rings, seals, coatings, hoses, clutch plates alongside brake friction disks. CECE invites ECHA to work on restrictions of high-risk PFAS instead of adopting the Dossier Submitters’ 'one-ban-fits-all’ approach.
5. In case of any fluoropolymers (including fluoroelastomers and polytetrafluoroethylene) restriction, CECE requests a general 13.5-year derogation after entry into force for all other essential PFAS uses on O-rings, seals, coatings, hoses, clutch plates alongside brake friction disks.
6. Having regard to the magnitude of this restriction proposal, CECE would like to invite the Commission to periodically exercise its implementing powers, conferred by Article 133 of Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 (‘REACH’), with the aim of reevaluating and redefining the duration as well as the scope of the derogations proposed or for reconsideration, following stakeholder consultations.
7. Considering that the revision of REACH is likely to take years, CECE calls upon the Commission to publish, at its earliest convenience, a Communication delineating the Essential Use concept and its methodology in future substance restrictions under REACH.
8. CECE stands for a cross-sector 13.5-year derogation after entry into force for uses of PFAS in Li-ion batteries.
9. Uses of PFAS in spare parts, remanufactured, refurbished, or second-hand products should benefit from a permanent derogation.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The company ENRX use PFA, FEP and PTFE as electric insulation materials because it has properties that is hard or impossible to achieve with other products. This will force the company in some cases to do expensive and time consuming redesigns, and in other cases to redraw our products from the market if PFAS materials is prohibited in the EU/EEC market.

ENRX produce and deliver induction heating converters for industrial use. They are typical from some few kW to up to 2 MW. The frequencies we use is normally from some kHz up to 500 kHz. Our challenge with electrical insulation material is that they are exposed for a mixture of high voltages, high current, high frequencies and in many cases water with temperature that can exceed 100’C. Over a time span of 40 years, we have developed the endurance of such materials that can stand all this challenges. Often the result has been fluor plastic, which is commonly used in our products. The path to what we have today has been long, and full of challenges. Lots of negative effects cannot be described with current theoretical knowledge and are based on experience.
Challenges are:
Partial Discharge (PD), which are an effect related to voltage, increasing with the electric frequency.
Water penetration into the insulation material because of temperature difference in cases where the insulation is exposed to water.
Weakness of the property to insulation related to long term exposure for high temperatures.
Capacitive heating of the insulation because of high frequency and strong electric fields.
Most of these effects are long term processes, that can develop over a long time before final insulation breakdown. Since some of this are difficult or even impossible to evaluate in a theoretic way, is experience important to find thresholds levels for the endurance of this materials. It may take years to evaluate the end result if we change the insulation of those materials. The new PFAS-directive don’t give us this time unless we get an extension of time to get new and fully capable replacement.

Most of our products would be influenced by this. This is products that have been in the marked the last 40 years and are well known by our customers.
All our products are delivered to the industrial marked, and the documentation describes to use professional disassembly with recycling and waste handling at end of life.
We expect this would be a common problem for the whole induction heating sector. ENRX is one of the biggest Induction heating companies in the world. There is a few big players in the business, and quite many smaller specializing in niches.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The sector of induction heating equipment is not mentioned in the table 9. Such equipment contains electronics which is mentioned as a sector. Other sectors which could not be found in the table 9, but that has would have the same concern, is electric cable producers and producers of electric power devices (Transformers, electric drives, power supplies etc) that are in need of materials with good electrical insulation characteristics.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The manufacturing phase a small amount of PFAS can result in scrap. There is very little emmision of the PFAS substances used in our equipments, since they are used as insulation materials within a fixed polymer. Total estimates is that 99% of the PFAS substances is still contained within the equipment after its lifespan of about 15 to 20 years. The documentation specifies at end of life to use professional recycling of the product, with disassembly and segmentation of components and materials for recycling or waste treatment

6. Missing uses: The induction heating equipment sector is not mentioned in the table 9. Neither is general electric industry that also has the same need for insulation materials with beneficial electrical properties.  I cannot estimate the use of PFAS for other then own organisation: In ENRX AS the use in our products of FEP and PFA is estimated to 2 tonn each year, and the use of PTFE estimates to 1.5 tonn per year. Approximately 1/3 of our products are sold to EU/EEC countries, resulting in a total use of  1.2 tonns of PFAS used in products sold within EU/EEC.  The key functionality for the PFA and FEP is as electrical insulating sorrounding electric cables used in direct watercooled electric devices.  The key functionality for the PTFE used is high electrical resistance and high temperature resistance material to create electric insulation between electric components. Replacement materials currently don’t exist or lead to significant restriction in functional properties, with the loss of sales as a possible outcome.

General Comments: The company I represent produces machinery/ production lines for sheet metal working. It is sensitive to environmental and human health protection issues and considers them of primary importance.
The company does not produce substances from the PFAS group, but in some cases, in order to satisfy particular specification requirements (for example resistance to high temperatures, low friction, high speeds) it uses components that inside have substances from the PFAS group. They are components such as hydraulic and pneumatic system components (in particular seals), lubricants, gearbox seals. There could also be also usage inside electrical, electronic devices/components.
We have consulted those suppliers who supply these components. All suppliers tell us that they have not completely clarified the situation that would arise from the introduction of the ban, but however they point out that unfortunately are not always possible/available on the market valid alternatives to components containing substances classified in the PFAS group.
We therefore believe it is our duty to inform you that a total and indiscriminate ban on the use of these substances will certainly lead to the following problems:
- In existing machines (already in operation at our customers), in the need for repairs/spare parts containing this type of substance, it will not be possible to restore the original performance level. In some cases it will not even be possible to restore a sufficient functioning level
- If a customer requests the supply of new machines with high demand needs, it will not be possible to propose satisfactory solutions.
- In these cases we will also find that our competitors (belonging to countries where the ban on PFAS is not willing to entry in force) will be instead able to propose the suitable machinery.
We therefore would like to underline that it is necessary to consider exemptions or limitations on the extent of the ban to avoid a critical impact on the activities of companies like the one I represent.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Baseline Information on alternatives Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The concerned dossier submitted by BAuA and four other governmental organizations from Sweden, the Netherlands, Denmark and Norway concerning the restriction procedure for so-called PFAS was published by the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) on the 07th Feb. 2023.

The restriction proposal also concerns all fluoropolymers, which are included in the large group of PFASs to be regulated via the definition of the presence of fluorinated carbon atoms (CF2 and CF3).

According to the submission, the background of this proposed regulation, which is intended to ban the manufacturing, placing on the market as well as the use of fluoropolymers, is the persistence of these substances, which is assessed as the "key hazardous property" in section 1.1.4 of the hazard assessment in the Annex XV Report.

The other potential hazards do not concern the fluoropolymers because they are not volatile, not mobile, not bioaccumulative, not toxic and no endocrine disruptors.

Thus, persistence is the main concern for regulation of these polymers (see Section 1.1.4.2. Annex XV Restriction Report "persistence as the core concern").

In order to be able to enforce an appropriate regulation also for fluoropolymers, alternatives were already asked for in the Calls for Evidence, which were intended to serve for the collection of information for the preparation of the dossier, and some information providers (stakeholders) also named some.

The alternatives for fluoropolymers mentioned in the dossier are essentially non-fluorinated polymers such as polyethylene (PE), polyetheretherketone (PEEK), or in the case of elastomers, ethylene-propylene-diene (monomer) rubber (EPDM).

In the restriction proposal, these polymers indicated as alternatives are not subjected at any point to a necessary hazard assessment, which is, however, already absolutely necessary in the preparation of such a dossier in order to determine whether alternatives may be named as such at all.

In Annex E, Appendix E2, with regard to all non-fluorinated polymers mentioned, "No data found" is stated for the PBT / vPvB assessment, or "Not sufficient data available for evaluation" is stated for Additional Information - which clearly does not correspond to an apropriate risk assessment, although sufficient meaningful data on this are publicly available. Please refer to the attachment in "SECTION IV. Non-confidential attachments", where you can clearly see that polymers in general are very persistent and even polymers considered as "bio degradable" in humus composting are very persistent in the sense of the definitions in Annex XIII REACH .
If you would have any doubts about the persistence of all plastics, as synthetic materials, please see the publications on persistent plastics in the world's oceans, which certainly do not lead to a PBT / vPvB assessment of "No data found".

Thus, demonstrably persistent polymers are given as alternatives to fluorinated polymers in this ANNEX XV Dossier, which leads to a nonsense of the whole process.

In addition, non-fluorinated alternatives are specified, although they do not match the properties of fluoropolymers, resulting in much higher wear and thus higher consumption of non-fluorinated polymers, which, as persistent materials, increase the environmental impact.
It should be noted that fluorinated polymers do not have a higher end-of-life impact than conventional polymers because they do not decompose into hazardous substances and do not release hazardous substances when disposed off as intended.

This is regulated separately in legal acts concerning waste management. Otherwise, substances such as dioxins or e.g. hydrochloric acid would still be generated and released, due to the uncontrolled incineration of municipal waste, or PVC that you listed as an alternative to fluoropolymers in Appendix E2.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: all sectors and (sub-)uses are concerned

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: fluoropolymers to not have higher emissions in the end-of-life phase, than non-fluorinated polymers - EU Waste Management Regulations are in force (do not double-regulate!)

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: fluoropolymers to not have higher emissions in the end-of-life phase, than non-fluorinated polymers - EU Waste Management Regulations are in force (do not double-regulate!)

5. Proposed derogations: Emissions of fluorinated production aids play and important role in this restriction process.  However, the substances relying on PFAS emulsifiers can be produced in closed loop systems, which is also what is demanded from the scientific circles you mentioned in the dossier: "The system would have to be changed so that persistent substances are not allowed to be used in open applications, but only in closed systems." (Prof. Martin Scheringer, ETH Zurich, 31.07.2023).  Derogations make no sense, as long as the production of needed fluoropolymers (PTFE, PVDF and FKM) with fluorinated production aids will be regulated. Example: what sense does a 13,5 years derogation for a stent covering with an expanded PTFE membrane make, if the polymer can't be produced any more from 18 months after EiF, because fluorinated processing aids must not be used any more!?

General Comments: The current proposal contains no derogations and a transition period of 18 months for coil coating applications of PVDF and FEVE fluoropolymers.
ECCA requests that these fluoropolymers are excluded from the proposed PFAS restriction on the basis that:
(a) They are manufactured and applied in carefully controlled industrial production units.  The resultant prepainted metal products are used on the external surfaces of buildings and are not sold directly to the consumer.
(b) The PVDF/FEVE coatings used in coil coated products are highly durable and offer the market a unique combination of properties.
(c) Whilst there are some alternative products e.g., polyurethane coatings that can be used to replace these fluoropolymers in some applications, there are no alternative products that will meet the performance of these fluoropolymers in those demanding market applications e.g., high UV or corrosive (marine/industrial) environments where they are specified by the architect.
(d) The PVDF/FEVE products are recycled at the end of life through established supply chains which result in the coating being incinerated at high temperatures in metal manufacturing processes.  These processes are subject to the Industrial Emissions Directive, and they deploy extensive abatement technologies to deal with a wide range of hazardous substances to minimise emissions to the environment.
This request is consistent with the approach of the UK Government who have recently published their detailed RMOA on the restriction of PFAS chemicals following detailed consultation with the various stakeholders.
Should ECHA decide to retain fluoropolymers within the proposed restriction then ECCA requests that a 12-year (+18 months) derogation is granted to these fluoropolymer applications.  This derogation should be reviewed every 5 years after the initial period  to assess whether the industry has been able to develop new polymer systems that meet the technical performance of the current fluoropolymer products.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The current restriction proposal suggests PFAS in fuel cells and electrolysers to be banned in the EU with an exclusive transition period of 5 years for fuel cell membrane electrode assemblies (MEA). In fact, the entire group of PFAS is proposed to be banned because they are assumed to be very persistent and to accumulate in the environment (cite 1). Besides fuel cell membranes with a derogation period of 5 years (RO1), no further exceptions on this ban related to hydrogen technologies are currently proposed for the energy and transport sector. In today’s form, the proposed regulation will thus fundamentally affect the upcoming transition of these sectors using carbon-free technologies based on hydrogen. Accordingly, the regulation will severely impact the achievement of the ambitious targets of EU’s climate carbon neutrality in the year 2050 and even the intermediate steps towards this goal (cite 2).

This contribution serves to supply the ECHA committees of RAC and SEAC with relevant information, ensuring that a broad range of perspectives from affected stakeholders of the energy and transport sector are recognized for the upcoming PFAS consultation. The contribution intents to ensure that RAC and SEAC receive substantial data from the affected stakeholders in relation to the current proposed restriction proposals database. The input will support and substantiate the upcoming consultation process and ratification, enabling an updated balanced regulation, carefully weighting the arguments of an ecosystem facing the contained use of persistent materials versus implementing the green energy deal and mitigating socio-economic impacts of the threat of a non-existing hydrogen energy transition within the European Union (cite 2-3).

Fuel cells and electrolysers are key applications in an upcoming hydrogen transport and energy sector. Correspondingly, hydrogen production and subsequent use are fundamental use cases for a secure and climate-neutral energy economy (cite 2-4). For this, fuel cells, electrolysers and hydrogen compressors are indispensable applications enabling hydrogen use as global future fossil-free energy carrier (cite 5).

All these fundamental technologies use PFAS functionally to produce hydrogen and convert hydrogen into usable power/energy. In fact, PFAS containing membranes represent the functional heart and core of fuel cells and electrolysers. Accordingly, these technologies use the entire spectrum of functional properties these materials offer: from fundamental physical properties to unique chemical properties (e.g., water conduction and transfer rates, durability of the membrane backbone versus chemical alteration, functional imbedding and grouping of scavenger ions, as well as a unique water swelling ratio).

Referring to these unique properties, no PFAS-free replacement materials are currently available which are in any way close to the product KPIs of the current materials and could be used in series production of fuel cells, electrolyser, and hydrogen compressors. Even worse, such materials are not expected to be available on an industrial level in the next 15 to 25 years (cf. to response to question 8). With this timespan for any alternatives to be developed and qualified, there would be - in Europe - no more financial investment made into fuel cells, electrolyser, and hydrogen compressor technologies in case a ban of PFAS will be installed. For fuel cells, even a 5-year exemption is not sufficient to maintain any further European investment for these technologies. This puts entirely at risk the overall climate-neutral energy transition in Europe through hydrogen production and use.

Based on scientific evidence, cellcentric requests an exemption for hydrogen fuel cells and electrolysers. This is needed as hydrogen represents a key technology for the energy and transport sector to enable the EU-wide energy transition of these sectors within the period of the next 10 years (cite 3). It will further allow the energy and transport sector to generally undergo the disruptive transition towards a circular, carbon-free economy based on hydrogen with the chance of reaching the ambitious climate carbon neutrality targets of the year 2050 countering the effects of global warming (cite 2).

Considering the low risk profile of fluoropolymers (“polymers of low concern”; cite 6-7), the lack of alternatives in a particularly demanding environment, and the potential socio-economic impact, we hold that fluoropolymer production and use for fuel cells and electrolysers should therefore be exempted from the overall PFAS restriction.

With these standards missing, it is difficult to build up statistics as there is currently no generally agreed reference the measurements can be commonly related to. Moreover, different applications of fuel cell systems and electrolysers demand a different choice of base materials, so there is a possible range of different configurations resulting in varying emission profiles. Additionally, even the individual trace of a specific emission profile is difficult to measure. The PFAS emission constituents vary according to the corresponding base properties and degradation cascades i.e., change over time. The degradation constituents under use are further strongly dependent on the specific use case, operating conditions, drive cycle, and installed materials.  With this variation in emission profiles, the emission products of individual fuel cell systems will vary and thus exhibit very different chemical and physical properties. The corresponding restriction proposal does not differentiate between any of these PFAS configurations, although they will be entirely different in the key properties of persistency and environmental accumulation which are the two general underlying assumptions of the restriction proposal. Fuel cells, electrolysers, and PFAS-free alternatives in the literature: In this section one will find data on PFAS-free fuel cell membrane alternatives that have been studied in the scientific world and at industrial level over the last 20 years. It should be noted that a literature search with the subliminal aim of “showing that there are no alternatives - through scientific sources” (i.e. “failing” PFAS-free alternatives) is rather challenging, as generally successes are more promoted (and thus published) than failures. Nevertheless, in order to support ECHA with appropriate data, the following approach is twofold – firstly with internal confidential data, and secondly with textbook literature from the period accordingly. This serves to show the connection between scientific discoveries and the corresponding painstaking – and unfortunately so far unsuccessful - steps to transform the initial scientific results into a commercially viable end product. At this level, it must be noted that despite decades of implementation attempts, a transfer of PFAS-free materials into a finished product has not succeeded to date. It is also difficult to provide internal data although it may be exchanged in a confidential environment. This follows from the fact that binding bilateral non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with suppliers or companies do not allow material to be shared on a confidential level with third parties (such as ECHA) unless a respective approval is given. Of course, the motivation for companies and suppliers to openly share "failed experiment" type information is generally low. This is true for research projects that did not lead to a successful outcome and did not lead to a finished product. Therefore, there is little data that industry can provide, and in any case only on a confidential level. In order to allow ECHA to properly assess the impact of the existing data and to reconsider the information in Table 8 of Annex XV, we provide the results of internal tests of five stacks (with 20 cells each) containing four different PFAS-free membrane alternatives and one PFAS-containing membrane as reference (see confidential note 1). The five stacks were assessed in the year 2017, with the life cycle test showing massive internal leakage of the various PFAS-free hydrocarbon membrane configurations after 400 hours of operation at the latest (see confidential note 1). The test was not an accelerated or increased life cycle test, but a standard real time test (where severe or elevated conditions were not even applied). The data is deliberately provided as an arbitrary example to show the status of (non)maturity of these materials on any pre-industrial level in relation to the reference material and the cited scientific material with the technological status of those days (see e.g., the upcoming section below). As the results were far from satisfactory in terms of durability, performance, lifetime and especially leakage, none of these configurations of PFAS-free membranes ever got beyond the 20-cell tests. Even after 10 years of scientific research (2008-2018) and mapping these technologies to industry standards, these membranes were still not able to meet the basic requirements at component level of an industrial application as passenger cars or in the heavy-duty transport sector. On scientific level in the year 2005, PFAS-free hydrocarbon membranes exhibited crossover leakage after up to max. 300 humidity cycles whereas PFAS-containing membranes as Nafion® NR111 allowed more than 4,000 cycles until crossover leakage under identical test conditions (cite 3). By industry, this factor of at least 10 represents the maturity of both technologies at that time in relation to each other and might to some extend still represent the maturity of these technologies - on an industrial level - with the materials (PFAS vs. non-PFAS) of today. The failure mechanism of these laboratory results is identical to the internal data on 20-cell stack level as shown above (cite confidential note 1); these types of PFAS-free membranes still failed due to brittleness and internal leakage, whether it be at single cell level (scientific experiments of 2005-2011) or on 20-cell stack level (internal results of the year 2017) with no fundamental progress despite intense research and development on these materials. Research time and time for maturation: In the past, fuel cell and electrolyser membranes - containing PFAS - have already seen a dedicated time of research and development until they themselves became a commercially available product. For example, a renowned paper of Laconti et al. (cite 10) in the year 2006 states 30 years of research and development time already for PFAS-containing membranes (“Polymer Electrolyte Membrane Degradation Mechanisms in Fuel Cells - Findings Over the Past 30 Years and Comparison with Electrolyzers”). This shows that at that time it already took science and industry over 30 years until the year 2006 to develop membranes – containing PFAS - to be matured and employed into upcoming fuel cell applications.  In addition to that, commercial availability of these membranes was still far from being in reach, with some of the described membranes implemented in fuel cell vehicles in the subsequent decade of the year 2010-2020. Taking this into account, an implementation period of 15 – 25 years starting with initial scientific demonstration at laboratory scale seems rather reasonable considering that the today existing prospects of PFAS-free alternatives are still one technology level before “proof-of-concept” status (TRL = 3).  Even in today’s literature, the alternatives are still on scientific laboratory level, and do not offer, e.g. any degradation or durability data for material tested above 1,000h. Citing an example of the year 2021, Nguyen et al., (cite 11), the alternatives described in this publication have been tested with stamp-size samples: “…The resulting catalyst-coated membranes were sandwiched between two 4 cm2 gas diffusion layers (H14C-Series, Freudenberg). The performances of the 4 cm2 active area MEAs were evaluated using a fuel cell test station (Scribner 850e). …” By numbers, the authors of this publication did test a sample number of two up to “a few” samples of membranes of the size of 4 cm² in their experiments. All samples were tested after production at Begin-of-Life (0h) of operation, so no durability or degradation data exist nor any End-of-Life data (e.g., after 5,000h of operation) are available. Interestingly, the used gas diffusion layers (GDLs) for the tested configuration MEAs used PFAS-containing GDLs as supporting layers (see H14C-Series), so the communication of this publication as an example of a “PFAS-free-MEA” alternative is presumably not justified.  Technology readiness level of alternative PFAS-free materials and implementation time: To additionally derive a dedicated timescale to implement these alternatives in accordance with the literature comparison above, the definition of technology readiness levels (TRLs) of new technologies (cite 9), and of the standard automotive development cycles provide a time perspective what it means to implement such an alternative from a “basic principles observed” (TRL = 1) up to an “actual system proven in operational environment” (TRL = 9). If PFAS-free alternatives with a sufficient technology readiness level of more than TRL = 1 will appear in the upcoming years, these materials – for automotive use - still have got to be qualified on component and system level, and to be integrated and certified in an automotive product like e.g., a fuel cell truck.  Kenley et al. estimate in a recent paper of the year 2023 based on data of successful implementations of NASA projects that on average the advance from a TRL = 1 to a TRL = 7 takes approximately 12.8 years with a 95% probability (cite 12; see Figure 1 therein). This holds for complex technologies (aviation, transport, energy systems) where a technology of a fuel cell or electrolyser might - by complexity - be related to. Even reaching a TRL of 7, these systems must still be qualified and certified for customers according to automotive development standards as e.g., DIN EN ISO 9001:2015, IATF 16949:2016, ISO 26262:2018, and (EU) 2018/858 (cite 13-16). Average development and certification cycles in the automotive industry in accordance with these standards can be approximated with a time of at least 5 years starting from TRL=7 until TRL=9 (actual system proven in operational environment).  Taking into account the maturation time according to the TRLs and the automotive development cycle, this yields an earliest market entry for PFAS-free alternatives in the automotive industry on the level of more than 15 years after finding first incidences of a possible alternative. The number of 15 years implies that in neither a proposed derogation period of 5 years nor of 12 years any automotive producer will be able to produce a PFAS-free fuel cell or electrolyser product even if the technical alternative would be “at hand” with a sufficient TRL of more than 1. Thus, already out of time perspective, we ask for a reconsideration of the restriction proposal for fuel cells and electrolysers leading to an exemption of these technologies from the proposed restriction. In this period of time it will also have to be researched and examined what type of environmental effects any of the PFAS-free alternatives may have as well as aspects of those new materials safety. Org. name: Zhonghao Chenguang Research Institute of Chemical Industry Co., Ltd.
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The definition in the proposal for PFAS is neither clear nor enforceable. It is more advisable to specify the CAS numbers of the PFAS substances that are specifically restricted and list the PFAS substances that are subject to restriction.

ECHA has made different interpretations for the definition of PFAS. For example, the restriction proposal submitted by five European countries published on February 7 suggested that there were about 10,000 PFAS substances, but the public consultation webinar held on April 5 indicated that there would be more than 10,000 PFAS substances. The specifically restricted PFAS substances should be more clear and clearly defined, so that the proposal can be operational and enforceable. For reference, Buck et al. defined PFAS in 2011 and gave a specific CAS number with clear directionality for each PFAS (supportive evidence: ieam0007-0513-SD1).

In summary, the definition for PFAS in the Proposal is not clear and the proposal's jurisdiction scope over PFAS is not clear since it is not known how many substances are covered. Neither specific list of the controlled substances nor the CAS number of the substance are available. The PFAS restriction proposal by ECHA does not comply with the objectivity and strictness of the regulation and is not enforceable.

General Comments: The definition of PFAS is too broad and overly simplistic
We believe that the proposed PFAS limitation of grouping all PFAS into one package is unacceptable, which includes approximately 10000 substances with significantly different molecular weights, physical, chemical, and biological properties. This grouping method is too broad. This grouping is only based on its chemical structure, not on its hazardous properties or risks, and is not applicable for the purpose of regulatory risk. It goes against the provision in Article 68 (1) that "restrictions can only be imposed when a substance poses an unacceptable risk to human health or the environment". Many of the more than 10000 substances have not been assessed for risk and have not been proved to have unacceptable risks. It can be clearly seen from the description on page 28 that “Yet in conclusion, considering the increasing lines of evidence from modelling, laboratory and monitoring studies, there is a justified concern for a subset of PFASs being bioaccumulative while large uncertainties remain for the majority of compounds due to lack of data.”
Also, for biological toxicity, on page 47, “Due to the high diversity of the PFASs the bioaccumulation potential and ecotoxicity/toxicityare expected to vary among the substances. Therefore, no overall conclusion on B/vB and T criteria was derived for each PFAS substance/(sub-)group (see also sections 1.1.4.6 and 1.1.4.7)”. We can see that the toxicity of different PFAS is also uncertain.

General Comments: The definition of PFAS series is too broad because it also includes substances that do not have hazardous characteristics or pose unacceptable risks, such as fluorosurfactants. Including fluorosurfactants in the restriction proposal violates the principle of proportionality. It is the perfluoroalkyl fluorosurfactants that should be restricted since their high stability is determined by C-C in the main chain and C-F in the side chain, and it is difficult to degrade. As an alternative to PFOA, perfluoropolyether fluorosurfactants are more easily degraded than perfluoroalkyl fluorosurfactants given by their C-O-C bond in the main chain. Compared with perfluoroalkyl fluorosurfactants such as PFOA, the usage of perfluoropolyether fluorosurfactants can be reduced by more than 30% in the recipe, therefore the fluorosurfactants should be defined differently. Because fluorine-containing surfactants are indispensable components in the emulsion polymerization of fluoropolymers, at present there is no feasible non-PFAS substitute, hence it will have a devastating impact on the whole fluoropolymer industry if perfluoropolyether surfactants are restricted.
At present, the research on non-PFAS surfactants in fluoropolymers has been going on, but there is no successful case of commercial application, especially in emulsion polymerization of fluoropolymers such as PTFE, FEP, PFA and FKM.
The perfluoropolyether fluorosurfactants are distinguished as a group of special substances compared against PFAS, as their molecular structure and properties are completely different from those of perfluoroalkyl surfactants. These substances are considered polymers of low concern, so their use will not pose a risk to human health or human health and the environment. Therefore, comprehensive exclusion of this group of substances should be considered under the PFAS restriction proposals.

Content: Hazard or exposure
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The detrimental impact of Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances on children

ESPE Statement

Existing peer-reviewed studies provide ample evidence for the association between child exposure to endocrine disruptors and the onset of numerous illnesses including endocrine cancer, obesity, disturbed timing of puberty, impaired fertility, neurodevelopment alterations and numerous rare diseases. Exposure is unavoidable and can take place through the placenta, breast milk, toys and plastic bottles as well as the floors babies crawl on.

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are a group of over 10,000 manmade chemicals used as oil and water repellents and coatings for common products including cookware, carpets, and textiles. These Endocrine-Disrupting Chemicals (EDCs) do not breakdown or very slowly over many years when they are released into the environment, and they continue to accumulate over time.1

PFAS are "forever chemicals", chemicals that are very persistent in the environment and in the human body.  They are transgenerational and can migrate via the placenta from mother to child during the prenatal period. 2-4 Postnatally PFAS will be taken up via breastmilk5 and later in life via inhalation of dust or by ingestion of PFAS in drinking water, soil, non-stick coating in pans, food packaging products and food, particularly from fish, fruit and eggs.6 New research also indicates that PFAS are dispersed through the air over long distances.7

As is the case for all EDCs in our environment, children are most vulnerable to the exposure to PFAS.
This is because of breathing space closer to the floor, lower body weight, differences in water and food intake, developing organ systems and longer lifespans during which toxic effects might manifest.8 Especially infants are extremely vulnerable as the first months of life are known to be a critical window for the programming of later adiposity and endocrine regulation, neurodevelopment and growth. 8-14 Higher serum PFAS levels in infants have also been associated with a lower vaccination response 15,16 Prenatal exposure has for example been associated with the timing of puberty in girls.17 A recent study showed that nearly 60% of children’s textiles labelled “waterproof”, “stain-resistant”, or “environmentally friendly” contained toxic PFAS substances.18

While decision makers including at the EU level have become more aware of the risks that PFAS pose for population health, ESPE has great concerns that current policies and legislation do not accurately address the specific impact PFAS and other endocrine disruptors have on children even before they are born. More should for example be done to avoid early exposure by focusing on the elimination of PFAS in all food, and other products including pans, clothing, toys, food packaging and floors. ESPE considers the recently published PFAS restriction proposal by authorities in The Netherlands, Norway, Germany, Sweden19 an important first step in the right direction.

As outlined in the restriction proposal as well as the EU Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability, PFAS should only be used in ‘essential’ products. Essential for ESPE means that PFAS should only be employed in those uses that are critical for the functioning of society and where no alternatives are available.20

Moreover, In principle only those essential chemicals should be allowed that have a relatively short half-life, meaning that the chemical leaves the human body relatively quickly after exposure. PFOA and PFOS, for example, do not meet this criterion.

Within the next 5 years all PFAS in the EU should be phased out entirely to stop further human exposure and the continuous contamination of our environment.

In addition to better policies, more research is needed to investigate the immediate and long-term effects of PFAS and other EDCs on the development of children from foetus to young adulthood,   particularly the impact on the endocrine system. This is essential to better protect and, where possible, mitigate current and future adverse health effects with lifelong impact.

Better tailored policy making and an improved understanding of the risks posed by PFAS in children are crucial to establish a safer environment for our children and society in general.
