Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Baseline Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The dossier submitter manufactures articles for integrated systems applied to industrial automation equipment. Such equipment is critical for ensuring an increased efficiency, productivity, and precision at industrial production level as well as workplace safety in a variety of sectors in the EEA ranging from manufacturing, energy, aerospace to pharmaceuticals, water treatment and waste management, to mention only a few. Thus, the use of such articles indirectly contributes to the provision of essential resources and products (i.e., safe water and food, reliable energy, medicines, and electronic products, etc.) for the EEA society and its consumers.

For the manufacturing, maintenance, repair and overhaul of these articles, PFAS-containing products are required, namely: semiconductors; capacitors, electromechanical and electronic devices, and electronic boards; seals and gaskets; lubricants; lithium-ion batteries; flame retardants; wiring and cable insulation; flat panel displays; PTFE plastics (particularly resins); as well as further articles manufactured with PTFE for performance requirements due to harsh operational conditions (e.g., washer or tubes).

For the use of fluoropolymer-containing products in the manufacturing and MRO of articles for industrial automation, the dossier submitter requests a time unlimited derogation, given the lack of alternatives to fluoropolymers in these applications and the classification of fluoropolymers as polymers of low-concern. Meanwhile, for the use of products containing short chain PFASs, derogations are requested in accordance with the downstream users manufacturing the respective products (e.g., semiconductors, flat panel displays). Indeed, no alternatives are currently available to replace short-chain PFASs in such manufacturing processes.  Overall, regarding the associated time derogations, the dossier submitter aligns with the derogations proposed by other industries active in the manufacture of the products in scope.

The dossier submitter would like to highlight that the omission of PFAS from the authorization list as a substance of very high concern, and the proposal to restrict it, significantly hinders the gathering of data on PFAS within the supply chain due to the constrained time period. Indeed, suppliers are not legally required to report information in their supply chain regarding PFAS substances. This leads to significant procedural challenges, as PFAS has so far remained unregulated, rendering the pertinent data virtually non-existent. The dossier submitter is conducting a survey throughout its upstream supply chain to gain a thorough understanding of the extent to which short-chain PFASs are used in products sourced from third-party suppliers. However, this is challenging due to the intricate nature of the supply chain and limited information from suppliers. Nonetheless, efforts are being made to collect as much data as possible.

With respect to the consequences that would be incurred within the EEA in case of a restriction scenario in which there would be no derogation for the use of PFAS-containing products for the manufacture and MRO of articles used in industrial automation, the present analysis reports on several socio-economic, sustainability and policy related implications. At the level of several stakeholders in the supply chain, such a restriction scenario would generate foregone profits, job losses as well as additional one-off investment costs for dismantling and clean-up of facilities following business shutdowns. Notably, for the purpose of monetization of impacts, due to data limitations, only foregone profits and the cost of unemployment associated with job losses at the dossier submitter could be quantified.

Beyond these monetized effects, the real impacts associated with a restriction scenario remain largely underestimated as broader societal and environmental consequences can only be qualitatively described due to lack of appropriate quantitative data. Such broader implications of a restriction include: a reduced operational productivity and safety coupled with reduced energy efficiency and consequently reduced market shares at the level of downstream industrial customers; a reduced shortage of essential products (clean water, medicines, safe food, renewable energy, electronics, etc.) on the EEA market as well as potentially increased prices for EEA consumers; significant delays for the electrification, sustainability and digitalization efforts and strategies at the EU level; a premature retirement of assets leading to a residual value of electrical and electronic equipment before end of life; an increased amount of electronic waste in the EEA; as well as foregone resources for producing equipment that does not reach end of life.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: This derogation request concerns the use of PFAS-containing products for the manufacture and maintenance, repair, and overhaul (MRO) of articles (electrical and electronic equipment) for integrated systems applied to industrial automation. The dossier submitter manufactures electrical and electronic equipment as well as supporting accessories, housings, connectors and software applied as integrated systems to industrial automation processes. Non-exhaustive examples of industrial sectors relevant to the industrial automation systems manufactured by the dossier submitter include the aerospace, automotive, and marine industries; the agriculture sector; the chemical sector; the fibers and textiles sector; the food and beverages sector; the life sciences sector, including the pharmaceutical industry; the metal industry; the mining sector; the oil and gas industry; the pulp and paper industry; the energy sector, including the renewables segment; the electronics and semiconductors sector; the waste management sector, including the wastewater segment. The dossier submitter’s products are used for discrete, process, motion, and safety applications. Importantly, these applications involve very demanding operational conditions in industrial automation. These non-exhaustively include high temperature, strong mechanical forces leading to tear and wear, high pressures, aggressive chemical environments, etc. Such environments require the use of materials that can withstand them, hence, the incorporation of PFAS (mainly fluoropolymers).

6. Missing uses: Semiconductors require PFAS functionalities such as thermal and chemical stability, low surface energy, and material compatibility. Photoresist, Antireflective coatings, and Photolithography benefit from low surface energy and non-stick properties, whereas Developers and Etching rely on chemical stability and compatibility. Rinsing solutions benefit from moisture resistance and low flammability, while Vacuum pumps and Vapor phase soldering require heat resistance. Capacitors, electronic circuits, and related parts and electronic boards utilize PFAS for their water and moisture repellency, chemical stability, dielectric strength, solder resistance, and heat resistance. These properties help maintain the performance and durability of the components. In Lubricants, PFAS provide low friction, high-temperature stability, chemical stability, damping, and heat conductivity, contributing to smooth operation and reduced wear and tear. For Lithium batteries, PFAS play a crucial role in electrode binder and separator coatings by ensuring electronic and ionic conductivity, energy efficiency, and high durability. Additionally, they serve as additives for electrolytes to enhance conductivity and prevent corrosion. Flame retardants utilize PFAS for their high thermal stability, chemical stability, low surface energy, and non-stick properties, which help in suppressing fires and minimizing damage to materials. Wiring and cable insulation benefit from the chemical stability, heat resistance, low surface tension, and electrical insulation of PFAS, ensuring safe and reliable energy transmission. Flat panel displays use PFAS for chemical stability, selected reactivity, and low boiling points, enabling efficient display technology with a long lifespan. Seals and gaskets rely on PFAS for their chemical stability, temperature resistance, sealing properties, and adaptability to irregular surfaces, resistance to ultraviolet radiation, elevated pressures, and swelling, providing a secure and long-lasting seal. Further PTFE-based materials like washers and tubes depend on PFAS for flexibility, temperature stability, chemical resistance, durability, and transparency for monitoring. Finally, PTFE plastics (resins) require PFAS for their chemical resistance, low friction, reliable adhesion, and durability, ensuring a long-lasting and reliable material for various applications.  Fluoropolymers (FPs) are crucial in various applications such as semiconductors, capacitors, electronic circuits, lubricants, lithium-ion batteries, flame retardants, seals, gaskets, wiring, and cable insulation. Their unique properties such as temperature and chemical resistance, low dielectric constant, and non-stick properties make it difficult to find alternatives. FPs are considered polymers of low concern, posing no health or safety hazards and contributing to economic growth. Industrial automation equipment relies heavily on FPs and short-chain PFAS due to their exceptional properties. Acquiring comprehensive data on short-chain PFAS usage is challenging since PFAS is not yet regulated, and suppliers are not legally obligated to report on PFAS substances. Given the difficulty of finding alternatives for certain applications and the potential negative impact on the EEA's industrial future, the dossier submitter requests a time-unlimited derogation for fluoropolymer-containing products. This approach allows industries to phase out PFAS, if possible, without imposing significant constraints, preventing potential shortages in essential goods. Meanwhile, for the use of products containing short chain PFASs, derogations are requested in accordance with the downstream users manufacturing the respective products (e.g., semiconductors, flat panel displays, etc.). Indeed, no alternatives are currently available to replace short-chain PFASs in such manufacturing processes. Overall, regarding the associated time derogations, the dossier submitter aligns with the derogations proposed by other industries active in the manufacture of the products in scope.  In the absence of a derogation from the upcoming PFAS restriction for the manufacture and MRO of electrical and electronic equipment relying on PFAS used in industrial automation, several stakeholders in the supply chain would be affected. This includes PFAS manufacturers, PFAS processors, companies manufacturing PFAS-containing products (e.g., capacitors, lithium batteries, electronic circuits, semiconductors, seals, gaskets, etc.) as well as manufacturers of PFAS-dependent electrical and electronic equipment for industrial automation, such as the dossier submitter. Without feasible alternatives to PFAS, these companies would have to shut down their PFAS-dependent operations in the EEA. Moreover, in such a scenario, all downstream sectors using PFAS-dependent electrical and electronic equipment for industrial automation would not have access at least in part to spare components and maintenance services for such articles. Consequently, such affected industrial facilities located within the EEA would either shut down automatic production processes depending on electronic and electrical equipment or implement changes to enable a downgrade from automatic to manual manufacturing processes, if economically justifiable.  Such a potential PFAS restriction scenario would therefore result in foregone profits, job losses, and additional one-off costs for dismantling and clean-up of facilities at the level of several stakeholders in the EEA, including manufacturers of PFAS-containing products, producers of PFAS-dependent articles for industrial automation, and downstream industrial sectors. Moreover, if businesses were to transition from automated to manual production processes, this would in turn lead to reduced operational productivity and safety, increased downtime risks, as well as reduced energy efficiency. This would in turn affect the competitiveness and market shares of the respective manufacturers, while there would be supply shortages of essential products on the EEA market (e.g., food products, medicines, semiconductors, energy, oil and gas, etc.) and potentially increased product prices for end customers. Furthermore, the non-availability of PFAS-containing products (e.g., semiconductors, lithium batteries, electronic circuits, etc.) could lead to severe implications for the digitalization and electrification efforts in the EEA, affecting European policies and strategies such as the Green Deal, the hydrogen strategy, and the digital transformation strategy, to mention only a few. Finally, the limited availability of MRO activities for PFAS-dependent articles in industrial automation would lead to premature retirement of assets, an increased volume of electronic waste, as well as higher resource consumption for waste treatment, resulting in additional carbon dioxide emissions in the EEA.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The draft PFAS regulation in Annex XV states that a 12-year exemption period for semiconductor materials that support the modern information society will be determined through public consultation. No use classification is indicated for Through this public consultation, we would like to confirm the application classification and exemption period for fluorine-based synthetic raw materials (precursors of photoacid generators) that are indispensable for the preparation of PFAS-containing semiconductor materials.
Fluorine compounds, defined as PFAS, support advanced semiconductor manufacturing technology through photolithographic techniques. In particular, PFAS has super strong acidity due to the strong electron-withdrawing property of fluorine, and is used as a strong acid anion for photoacid generators in photolithography technology. C1 or C2 short-chain perfluoroalkylsulfonic acid derivatives and perfluoroalkyltrifluorophosphoric acid derivatives are compounds useful as relatively less toxic photoacid generator precursors, such as trifluoromethanesulfonic acid (C1) anion, pentafluoro Ethylsulfonate (C2) anion, Tris(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)methide acid (C1) anion, Tris(trifluoromethyl)trifluorophosphate (C1) anion, Tris(pentafluoroethyl)trifluorophosphate (C2) anion are common used. The synthetic precursors of these strong acid anions, their salts (e.g. lithium, sodium and potassium salts) should also be industrially essential.
Photoacid generators composed of these strongly acidic anions are photoactive compounds that generate stable acidic substances through photoreactions caused by light irradiation. Currently, photoacid generators using strongly acidic fluorine-based anions defined by PFAS are used in various patterning materials and support the development of photolithography technology. In addition to strong acidity, the properties required for photoacid generator anions are 1) excellent stability, 2) excellent light transmittance, and 3) excellent solvent solubility. In general, fluorine compounds are the only compounds that can bring out these performances at a high level at the same time. In other words, the photoacid generator can be said to be one of the functional materials that bring out the properties of fluorine.
If a photoacid generator other than PFAS is designed as a substitute for the photoacid generator used in photolithography for semiconductor manufacturing, for example, as described in Reference 1, a sulfonic acid such as methanesulfonic acid TPS (TBNO, which is described as a substitute in Book E) also belongs to this) has a pKa of about -2, and the pKa of trifluoromethanesulfonic acid is about -14. The acid strength of the agent was overwhelmingly insufficient, and it was difficult to use it as a conventional patterning material.
In addition, as mentioned in reference 1, the semiconductor manufacturing industry also regards the toxicity of long-chain PFAS as a problem, and has developed shorter-chain (C1, C2) PFAS. Nonetheless, there are no non-PFASs in circulation, such as those listed as alternatives in Annex E. Photoacid generators used in photolithography suitable for current semiconductor materials have already been developed for more than 20 years. Therefore, in order to realize non-PFAS substitutes, new technological development will be required, and research and development is also expected to take several decades or more. Moreover, even if a non-PFAS alternative material overcomes the advanced technical problems, if it is used in a complicated semiconductor manufacturing process, it will take a lot of money and time to investigate the effects in the post-process.

On the other hand, as a raw material for the photoacid generator, a short-chain perfluoro compound is preferable to a long-chain perfluoro compound because of its better safety. For example, his LD50 (acute toxicity: oral) for C1 trifluoromethanesulfonic acid is 1,605.3 mg/kg and that for C4 nanofluorobutanesulfonic acid is 430 mg/kg. The former acid is about 1/4 less toxic than the latter acid.
Fluorine compounds subject to PFAS regulations are used as photo-acid generators useful in the manufacturing process of semiconductor materials, but some PFAS are classified as low-toxic compounds. If you follow the proper usage method according to the application of PFAS, it is possible to maximize the performance of fluorine. In the future, it will be inevitable that long-chain perfluoro compounds, which are relatively toxic, will be regulated, but we would like to seek exemptions for short-chain perfluoro compounds. Fluorine compounds are essential synthetic raw materials in the semiconductor industry, and compounds with trifluoromethyl or pentafluoroethyl groups are safer than other fluorine compounds, so they will continue to be used as photoacid generator precursors. I request you to use it.

　Reference：J. Micro/Nanopattern. Mater. Metrol. Vol. 21(1) 010901.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: The Earth is a remarkable planet, abundant in natural resources and diverse ecosystems that have sustained life for millions of years. As custodians of this planet, it is our responsibility to ensure its preservation for future generations. One crucial aspect of safeguarding the Earth is by avoiding the use of harmful chemicals such as PFAS. By doing so, we can protect our environment, maintain ecological balance, and secure a sustainable future for our children and their descendants.
Promoting Human Health by thinking long-term will be a challenge now but something that pays of both in the health and economical future.

Harmful chemicals not only pose risks to the environment but also impact human health. Exposure to toxic substances such as PFAS can lead to various health problems, including respiratory disorders, allergies, hormonal imbalances, certain types of cancer and probably more that stil is inte the unknown. By avoiding the use of harmful PFAS products, we can safeguard our well-being and that of future generations. There are sacrifices done now that will pay off down the road so please don't be like a company CFE and think ahead of the next quarterly report.

Content: Description of analytical methods
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The ECHA-PAFS detection method is not feasible.

It is not clear how many PFAS substances can be detected by the method published in the ECHA-PFAS restriction proposal. It is also unclear whether the test can cover the 10000 more substances in the scope of PFAS definition. After inquiring SGS, TUV and other international large-scale testing companies, it is shown that laboratory testing of PFAS substances can cover over 100 PFAS substances, this number is much lower than the 10000 more substances in the PFAS definition. The detection method of total fluorine is also proposed in the restriction proposal, but how does the detection method of total fluorine distinguish between inorganic fluorine and organic fluorine? At the same time, the detection of total fluorine is too simple and unreasonable, and all fluorine-containing substances will be counted among them, and other fluorine-containing substances that do not meet the ECHA-PFAS definition are mistakenly included therein. Taking PVF as an example, the structure of PVF does not belong to the definition of PFAS, but the detection method of total fluorine is bound to calculate the fluorine element in PVF. Similarly, it is unreasonable for other substances containing fluorine-containing elements not defined by ECHA-PFAS to apply total fluoride detection methods.

In summary, the ECHA-PFAS detection method cannot cover 10000 more substances in the scope of PFAS definition, and the total fluorine detection method cannot distinguish PFAS substances from substances containing fluorine-containing elements that are not defined by ECHA-PFAS. Is there a better solution for ECHA to regulate PFAS substances?

Content: Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The ECHA-PFAS restriction proposal regards persistence as a health risk, however the proposal lacks data on health risks.

The ECHA-PFAS restriction proposal considers high persistence to be a key hazard feature. But is persistence necessarily a health risk? The danger to human health mainly depends on whether harmful substances can enter the cells. Fluoropolymers are actually insoluble and do not migrate long distances, which are in line with the low concern polymers considered by Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). Additionally, fluoropolymers with molecular weights greater than 100,000 Da cannot penetrate cell membranes. Toxicological experiments on PTFE have also demonstrated that fluoropolymers are not bioavailable and bioaccumulative. Clinical studies have also shown that patients who receive permanently implanted PTFE cardiovascular medical devices suffer from no chronic toxicity or carcinogenicity, nor reproductive, developmental or endocrine toxicity. (supportive evidence: 11. A critical review of the application of polymer of low concern and regulatory）. PTFE is also listed in the EU10/2011 (Food Contact List) and has been proven to be used as food contact materials.

All of the above data indicate that not all PFAS pose health risks and the ECHA-PFAS restriction proposal does not provide health risk data for all PFAS, therefore it is unreasonable to restrict the use of all PFAS without distinction. It is recommended for ECHA to exempt PFAS having no health risk and restrict PFAS having health risks.

Content: Hazard or exposure
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The ECHA-PFAS restriction proposal violates the precautionary principle of REACH regulation.

The ECHA-PFAS restriction proposal fails to meet the premise principle (precautionary principle) of REACH regulation: the restriction must be based on the fact that such substance poses an unacceptable risk. The ECHA-PFAS restriction proposal neither demonstrates that all PFAS present unacceptable risks nor provides specific data to prove the PBT(persistent, bioaccumulative and toxic) characteristics of PFAS. We should not restrict the use of all PFAS only based on the biological toxicity and unacceptable risk of some PFAS and the assumptions and inferences that have not been verified by scientific research.

The ECHA-PFAS restriction proposal is unreasonable to a large extent at present. The proposal does not adequately assess their effects on human health and the environment and lacks toxicological data for most PFAS substances.

It is is unreasonable for the ECHA-PFAS restriction proposal to directly restrict the use of PFAS without specific data to support the unacceptable risk of PFAS, therefore the proposal violates the precautionary principle of the REACH regulation. It is recommended for ECHA to exempt PFAS that are not biotoxic and restrict PFAS that are biotoxict. And it is recommended for ECHA to conduct appropriate verifications for PFAS that lack biological toxicity data as soon as possible and then provide specific data based on such verifications. PFAS that are confirmed to have unacceptable risks are then included in the scope of restrictions.

General Comments: The EHEDG acknowledges the importance of addressing environmental and health concerns related to per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) under the REACH regulation. The EHEDG organisation is dedicated to promoting hygienic engineering and design practices, we understand the need to balance sustainability, safety, and innovation in the manufacturing sector.
We acknowledge the concerns surrounding the high persistence, mobility, bioaccumulation potential, long-distance transport potential, global warming potential, and ecotoxicity of certain PFAS substances.
EHEDG therefore fully supports the goal of preventing PFAS classified as very dangerous from entering the environment. However, we believe that a more differentiated and risk-based approach is necessary to address the potential ban of PFAS in materials used in (food) equipment and plant engineering. The current restriction proposal requires further refinement to ensure both environmental protection and the continuity of essential (food) industry processes.

This timeline is based on the process that includes development of alternative materials and testing by the supplier, integration and testing by the equipment manufacturers, testing, validation and acceptance of the food producing and processing industry. To facilitate the process and prevent unforeseen disruptions, EHEDG advocates for an uncomplicated and unbureaucratic application for the extension of exceptions beyond the initial period. EHEDG urges a thorough examination of available alternatives, considering technical maturity, safety aspects, energy consumption, and service life. Content: Scope or restriction option analysis
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The Electrolux Group would be affected by the upcoming PFAS restrictions in at least two main critical “clusters” of applications using fluoropolymers: (i) the electronics, semiconductors, and related electrical parts, as well as (ii) in lubricants. These key fluoropolymer-based applications are found from an overall assessment and across all our products’ portfolio, covering 100% of our (electronic) home appliances. Thus, any upcoming fluoropolymer-based restrictions under REACH would affect 100% of our product range, across all EU markets.

On the other hand, with regards to the use of fluoropolymers as non-stick coating for cooking purposes, the Electrolux Group may agree on that no-derogation would be provided for home cooking appliances, as well as in consumer cookware, following the 18-month transitional period, as alternatives are, or expected to become available.

However, as fluoropolymers are polymeric PFAS, we would like to bring forward that such polymeric substances do not share the same intrinsic substance properties as non-polymeric PFAS. Polymers generally have different physical, chemical and biological properties than non-polymer substances of low molecular weight.

Many fluoropolymers are distinctly different from other polymeric and non-polymeric PFAS due to their thermal, chemical, photochemical, hydrolytic, oxidative and biological stability, as well exhibiting negligible residual monomer and oligomer content and low-to-negligible leachability. They are non-mobile in the environment, not bio-accumulative and unable to bio-concentrate. Consequently, fluoropolymers show different safety and environmental considerations than other polymeric and non-polymeric PFAS.

In contrast, non-polymeric PFAS are more commonly detected in the environment and are often considered to be highly persistent and mobile. These have been used as processing aids in the polymerisation of certain fluoropolymers, thereby emitted to the environment during such production processes, during the production of articles-containing fluoropolymers, and during the disposal of such articles.

Considering the complete life cycle of fluoropolymers, environmental concerns may exist from the use of specific non-polymeric PFAS as polymerisation aid during the production process of such fluoropolymers, and from the presence of leachable residuals (polymerisation aid, monomers, oligomers and other by-products) in final fluoropolymers further used by downstream users and found in critical applications used in consumer products such as in our home appliances. The manufacturing process of fluoropolymers should thus be identified and considered as a critical “hotspot” phase of emissions of PFAS to the environment, and further risk assessed, controlled and managed adequately.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The Endocrine Society appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the restriction proposal and report for Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs). Founded in 1916, the Endocrine Society is the world’s oldest, largest, and most active organization of scientists and healthcare professionals dedicated to research on hormones and the clinical treatment of patients with endocrine diseases. Our membership includes nearly 18,000 clinicians and scientists from over 120 countries, including many researchers engaged in the study of the adverse effects of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) on endocrine systems.
We are pleased that the report acknowledges the ample evidence of harm to a variety of endocrine organs and systems due to PFAS exposure and we welcome the proposed group restriction on these well-studied endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs).  The documented effects on endocrine systems are well supported by the scientific literature. Peer-reviewed studies summarized in our Second Scientific Statement on EDCs (Gore et al., 2015) highlight the known effects of PFAS on pubertal timing, reproductive health, metabolism, and neurodevelopment; subsequent research has only expanded the scope of adverse effects to include impacts on bone health in children (Cawrile et al., 2022), thyroid hormone levels (Preston et al., 2021), and other endocrine endpoints.
Because PFAS are extraordinarily persistent in the environment and may cause effects at very low, biologically relevant levels for endocrine systems, including intergenerational effects, we urge ECHA to pursue a broad chemical scope consistent with the definition of PFAS as described in the report: “Any substance that contains at least one fully fluorinated methyl (CF3-) or methylene (-CF2-) carbon atom (without any H/Cl/Br/I attached to it).”  Further, the restriction should cover a wide range of uses, including manufacturing and consumer products.  Finally, we urge ECHA to strictly limit derogations, given the persistent nature of these chemicals and effects at very low levels.

Content: Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The engineering sector was not mentioned at all in your proposal, even though this sector is one of the largest in terms of employment and sales volume. The sector is very specific and has many different sub-sectors. For example, the pump sector (conveying elements/seals). Our pumps are used to pump various media, especially critical media. Currently, all of our pump types use various parts that contain PFAS substances, e.g. PTFE, FKM, FFKM, FVMQ. These items are used due to the unique chemical and physical properties of PFAS polymers, such as chemical stability, high temperature resistance and longevity in use in general (fewer replacements). Examples of PFAS items include stators for progressive cavity pumps, inserts and covers for rotary lobe pumps, O-rings and various seals. There is no known alternative on the market, especially for seals and O-rings. This was also mentioned in your proposal and an exception was proposed for the transport sector. There you mention that there are currently no alternatives on the market, and if there were alternatives, they would require a lot of time for the substitution to test and validate the performance of the pumps. Therefore, we propose to add pumps and especially conveying elements as a sub-sector and allow exemptions for the use of PFAS polymers until there are enough alternatives on the market. If this exemption is not added, then from now on we will no longer be able to bring pumps onto the market for our special applications.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Business area: Environment  For media that require conveying elements/seals in FFKM or FKM, we can no longer offer or sell pumps due to impending regulation. These include, among other things, pumps that are essential for pumping polymer concentrate in municipal and industrial sewage treatment plants, flocculants.  example applications: wastewater treatment and dewatering of sewage sludge.   Business area: Food In addition to the considerable chemical stability (resistance to fats and cleaning agents), the high temperature resistance is particularly noteworthy, which is required in order to always reliably clean/sterilize the machines and systems (food safety). FKM is therefore ideal for use in CIP/SIP cleaning processes and fatty products where EPDM can no longer be used. Due to the lack of suitable alternatives, the material FKM is indispensable not only for the pump industry, but for the food industry in general, a systemically relevant market segment. Another market segment is the cosmetic and pharmaceutical industries, which also use materials such as FKM and PTFE for the reasons mentioned above. The already existing shortage of certain medications would be exacerbated by restricting PFAS polymers. Our society should work to strengthen the security of supply of medicines in Europe by freeing ourselves from the dependence of other regions and producing more ourselves on the European market. The threat of relocation of corresponding industries to other regions due to a general restriction on PFAS polymers would be fatal. It's not just about economic effects; in the worst case, supply bottlenecks could also endanger social peace in the medium term.  Business area: Chemicals and  Electric  The operating principle of every eccentric screw pump is based on the use of elastomers/plastics. In addition to our operating principle, this also applies to static and dynamic seals! The elastic and chemical/thermal resistance are necessary in order to be able to pump critical media. There are currently no other technologies to replace these fluoroelastomers. For example:  • Battery manufacturing  • Promotion of polymers  • Acids and alkalis  • Solar industry  • Solvent-based materials  Several thousand different applications (media) would be affected and could no longer be supported if they were banned. Various system-relevant processes such as pharmaceuticals, renewable energies, wastewater recycling, chemical industry, oil and gas refineries would no longer be operable. It would have a massive impact on these areas. In addition to the technological regression, the economic damage would be unforeseeable.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: a.  No information available    b.  If PFAS were banned, the amount of waste would increase massively. We estimate that waste generation will increase to over 50%. The longevity of the products would be greatly reduced because the chemical resistance and temperature resistance of all other elastomers/plastics are significantly lower than fluorinated materials. The disposal route will not improve or change if PFAS is restricted.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Incineration disposal of PFAS, especially fluoroelastomers, is not desirable for this purpose and is exclusively disposed of in landfills in Japan.

6. Missing uses: The entire pump sector for pumping critical media does not exist. As a manufacturer, we use many purchased parts from the market and we also process a wide variety of fluorine materials. The most commonly used PFAS are PTFE and FKM.  We cannot currently estimate the tonnage of purchased parts such as elastomers/plastics. (PFAS per pump cannot be determined at this time) These parts must withstand critical physical (high temperature, friction, vacuum) and chemical conditions (acid, oxidative gases/liquids).  Currently, various parts made from PFAS are used in all of our pump types, e.g. B. PTFE, FKM, FFKM. These items are used due to the unique chemical and physical properties of PFAS polymers, such as: B. chemical stability, high temperature resistance and longevity in use in general (fewer replacements).  As far as the research and development of alternatives is concerned, we as manufacturers and end users cannot provide any information about the time frame. After the storage industry finds alternatives, we need approximately an additional 10 years to evaluate the new materials and ensure that they do not have a negative impact on the analytical capacity/quality and specifications of our equipment. The same time frame is required for the next topic: The most important component in conveyor elements for the topic of PFAS are stators and seals made of FKM. There is currently no alternative on the market because the specific properties of these fluoromaterials are unique. No other material can withstand such high temperatures and is so chemically resistant. When using silicone instead of FKM, the stators cannot guarantee the high temperatures required in modern materials research and development. Since silicone is also less chemical-resistant, changing service/spare parts for conveyor elements would become significantly more difficult. Special applications could no longer be operated! This would mean more waste and also more maintenance time. Since there are no alternatives on the market for the above-mentioned uses, the impact on the world would be massive!  The success of research and development cannot yet be estimated.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: The current restriction proposal is to collectively restrict PFAS including even a group of compounds, such as fluororesins, fluoroelastomers, and fluororubbers, with greatly different properties from other PFAS. If the restriction is applied without assessing risks of the aforementioned fluororubbers etc. in the consideration process, it will violate Article 68 of the REACH. The current restriction proposal is only based on the fact that fluorine (-F) is contained in the chemical structure, not based on a result of appropriately analyzing hazardous risks. We would have to say that the target of the restriction is broader than necessity. Being not readily degradable, that is a characteristic common among PFAS, is in other words having high durability. We believe that the fluororubbers are essential materials in applications where such a property is required. The fluororubbers such as FKM and FFKM are chemically stable, and insoluble in water. Thus, even if they are taken into a human body (e.g., stomach), they will be excreted without being accumulated in the body or in the blood. Therefore, it is believed that the likelihood of adverse influences on a human body is considerably low.

Org. name: European Alliance for Vision Research and Ophthalmology
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The European Alliance for Vision Research and Ophthalmology (EU EYE, EU Trans Reg ID: 221589017973-83, member of the Healthcare Professionals Working Party of the European Medicines Agency) is an interested party in the PFAS Chemical Restriction proposal and wishes to submit a use-specific derogation for specific PFAS products currently used to treat a number of eye conditions and preserve or restore visual function to patients.
This submission covers ophthalmic use of PFAS as Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs); as medicinal products; as medical devices for drug delivery and as medical devices in complex eye surgery and more specifically as intraocular tamponades in retinal detachment; macular holes; giant tears; ocular trauma; diabetic retinopathy; proliferative retinopathy; corneal transplant and glaucoma surgery.  The EU EYE believes that their use in eye surgery is not mentioned in Section 1.3.2.9  Medical devices nor listed among the sub-uses in the sector Medical devices (Annex E.2.9.) of ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT VERSION NUMBER: 2 DATE: 22.03.2023 (https://echa.europa.eu/documents/10162/f605d4b5-7c17-7414-8823-b49b9fd43aea).
 This submission is on the grounds of:
the societal necessity of these products and the associated significant socio-economic benefits with impact to patients of working age;
lack of available non-PFAS substitute materials even after research efforts for over 40 years due to the challenges of mimicking the natural properties of a healthy vitreous humor of the eye of humans and other vertebrates;
the miniscule quantities of PFAS materials used in the specific clinical application and therefore in emissions;
the controlled clinical conditions and disposal routes that are available.
These products are approved under other regulatory frameworks (medicinal products and medical devices) and they are already subjected to environmental risk assessment. Their limited use volume impose low environmental risk.
We propose therefore that any authorised products whether as Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs), as medicinal products and medical devices be exempted generally from the proposed ban on PFAS rather than individually and under an Essential Use derogation, to reflect their exemption in REACH Authorization procedures and prevent regulatory conflicts. It should be noted that gas and liquid tamponades of medical grade are in the WHO priority list of medical devices for ophthalmic surgery and clinical ophthalmology https://medevis.who-healthtechnologies.org/devices/OPH_259.
We assume that emissions in the manufacturing phase of these products are well controlled and regulated under the Good Manufacturing Practices and this may support an exemption also for  any raw materials, intermediates and auxiliaries involved in the manufacturing of the products in question. A ban in manufacturing of PFAS in the EU will not prevent sourcing the materials outside the region but this will create vulnerability on the supply chain.  We hope that manufacturing will be retained in EU to maintain autonomy and improve resilience of supply chains.

A new heavy internal tamponade in vitreoretinal surgery: an in vitro study. Eye 22, 1082–1088 (2008). https://doi.org/10.1038/eye.2008.144). Manufacture, storage and distribution of medical gases and liquids in cryogenic containers and mobile cylinders is normally assessed with respect to the conformity assessment procedure described in Annex II excluding section 4 of Council Directive 93/42/EEC on Medical Devices, as amended. Use as medical devices in clinical use for RETINAL DETACHMENT; MACULAR HOLES; GIANT TEARS; OCULAR TRAUMA; DIABETIC RETINOPATHY; PROLIFERATIVE RETINOPATHY; Rare use as tamponade after glaucoma surgery in aphakia to prevent/treat choroidal hemorrhage; improve graft adhesion in Descemet Membrane Endothelial Keratoplasty using SF6 https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29040116/ For details on indication and choice of agent for vitreous tamponades used in eye surgery https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK580519/ hexafluoroethane (C2F6) and octafluoropropane (C3F8) fulfil the criteria for vitreoretinal surgery as the ideal gas should be nontoxic, inert, insoluble in the aqueous humor, and have a lower water solubility than These gases are colourless, odourless and inert. When injected into the vitreous cavity, air does not expand, whereas pure SF6, C2F6 and C3F8 gases do.  Perfluorohexyloctane demonstrates strong spreading properties due to low surface tension, facilitating small drop sizes and interacting with the lipophilic part of the tear film to form a layer at the film–air interface and prevent evaporation. Perfluorobutylpentane F4H5 is a colorless liquid with high vapor pressure, and it is physically, chemically, and physiologically inert with no catabolism or metabolism in the human body. Additionally, low surface and interface tension permits dissipation of the drug within minutes from the ocular surface. The low viscosity and surface tension of SFAs result in droplets of around 15 μL—approximately one-third the size of standard aqueous drops. Thus, SFAs avoid the spillover effect and the subsequent loss of most of the administered dose, which increases their bioavailability. Further, the refractive index of SFAs is similar to that of water, so these formulations do not impair patients’ vision as emulsions and oily drops tend to do. Due to their amphiphilic nature, SFAs dissolve a number of therapeutically relevant, poorly water-soluble compounds such as cyclosporine A and tacrolimus. Moreover, the aqueous-free environment of this delivery system increases the stability of these drugs by preventing oxidation and hydrolysis. https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/medicine-and-dentistry/perfluorohexyloctane#:~:text=Perfluorohexyloctane%20(F6H8%2C%20NovaTears)%20 c. Market research platforms report activities in vitreous substitutes by five large companies (Novartis AG, Valeant Pharmaceuticals, Dutch Ophthalmic Research Center B.V., AL. CHI. MI.A srl, Flurn GmbH and Carl Zeiss Meditech AG.; https://www.valuemarketresearch.com/report/vitreous-tamponades-market#:~:text=For%20the%20year%202022%2C%20the,4.7%25%20between%202023%20and%202030. and about 28 smaller companies and SMEs which have innovated the field https://tracxn.com/d/companies/ophthafutur/__8ErCgINcbsRWnloV-uQzZK6mZ52DHOvto0ArTaFaNpk e. Despite the ongoing intensive research for the last 40 years for the ideal vitreous substitutes for the range of applications we have reported, the PFAs listed here are the closest vitreous substitute there is to today.  There are numerous challenges involving in mimicing the natural properties of a healthy human vitreous body, the clear gel that fills the space between the lens and the retina of the eyeball (the vitreous chamber) in humans and other vertebrates.  Any substitute requires a multi-aspect evaluation of the physical and biological parameters required to satisfy the needs of the surgeon and the anatomy and physiology of the eye.  An ideal vitreous substitute should have all the structural and functional qualities of the physiological vitreous: it should be biologically and chemically inert; optically transparent for light transmittance, in vitro and in vivo biocompatible, elastic, durable, non-biodegradable; hydrophilic, water-insoluble, with similar viscoelastic proprieties and refractive index; provide adequate support to the intraocular tissues; allow diffusion of ions and electrolytes; injectable through a small syringe, easily manipulable during surgery, and easily removable.  There are numerous experimental phases to test for such wide range of properties such as kinetics of hydration and water swelling, oscillatory and shear-stress analysis, shear-creep analysis, evaluation of solute diffusion.  Furthermore their classification as medical devices will require regulatory approval.  Although it general takes 12 to 16 weeks to get a CE marking for a medical device, considerable time is required for collection of clinical evidence on safety, quality and on achieving the intended clinical benefits when used as intended by the manufacturer. During such period the wellbeing of patients and health outcomes of eye services delivery will be compromised if the ban comes to force for the current medical devices. Since 2012 a variety of synthetic polymeric hydrogels and biopolymers, such as hyaluronic acid, collagen,gellan, chitosan,and alginate, have been under extensive evaluation in preclinical studies for their potential to act as vitreous substitutes and to allow both rapid and sustained release of a wide variety of therapeutics. For a list please look at Table 3 in Schulz A, Szurman P. Vitreous Substitutes as Drug Release Systems. Transl Vis Sci Technol. 2022 Sep 1;11(9):14. doi: 10.1167/tvst.11.9.14. PMID: 36125790; PMCID: PMC9508686.  Hydrogels should be designed to have appropriate physical, chemical, and biological properties, including the ability to gel in situ; however, to date, none has made it into clinical practice. Unlike silicone oils, they are not able to exert a significant tamponade effect (Liang et al., 1998), so are limited to conditions that require space filling and as drug delivery devices. Many of them are reported to degrade once implanted into the vitreous cavity. Hyaluronan- and collagen-based gels have been widely investigated, but even following the addition of other components and cross-linking, these materials do not have the required physical properties and have a lower density than water, limiting their use for tears in the upper area of the vitreous cavity or are still susceptible to degradation in vivo Work on various other natural and synthetic polymers, including polyacrylamide polyethylene glycol, and chitosan (Yang et al., 2008), has been reported. Williams R et all, Biomaterials in Ophthalmology in Encyclopedia of Biomedical Engineering, 2019https://doi.org/10.1016/B978-0-12-801238-3.11034-7 Despite their advantages, translation into clinical use continues to be hindered due to intransparency, deviating refractive indices, degradation, or insufficient biocompatibility, especially owing to low substance purity or toxic crosslinking agents. Non-crosslinked polymer solutions generally lack viscoelasticity and porosity and are mainly limited by degradation, short residence times, and a lack of tamponing effects. A variety of different crosslinked hydrogel systems, either pregelled or used as in situ gelling matrices, have been investigated using chemical or physical processes. Pregelled crosslinked hydrogels lose rheological properties owing to injection-induced fragmentation. The major drawbacks of chemically crosslinked in situ hydrogels are the toxicity of the monomers and/or crosslinkers remaining in the eye as well as the lack of precise control of the injection time. Physically crosslinked hydrogels degrade  relatively rapidly, as they do not exhibit permanent crosslinking. Whether any of these candidates can enter the clinical phase is not known as successful translation to the clinic requires addressing the limitations followed by assessment of the long-term safety and effectiveness of such systems for marketing authorisation by the EMA. The EU EYE believes that substitutions is neither technically nor economically feasible particularly given the niche use and market size: although the conditions requiring vitreous surgery (macular hole and retinal detachment) are not considered according to the definition of rare disease based on prevalence of disease, the use of the specific tamponades is only called for complex cases.  g. It is unlikely that a standardized effective model will be available in the future to replace them (at least not within the time limits proposed for derogations in the ban) given that 40 years of research has not produced an adequate replacement until now. Aside the time for R&D, consideration has to be given to the time required to collect the substantial clinical evidence for compliance with the new medical device regulations for efficacy and safety of product. Today, three vitreous substitutes are commonly used: intraocular gases, silicone oil and perfluorocarbon liquids. The global vitreous tamponade market outlook 2023-2033 indicates an increase at a CAGR of 3% during the next 10 years. Liquid tamponades are slightly more dominant than gaseous due to the widespread use for treatment of retinal detachment and enormous flow of tears, proliferative diabetic retinopathy and vitreoretinopathy in the European and Asian regions. https://www.factmr.com/report/vitreous-tamponades-market  The EU EYE will update our response with further technical and socio-economic information before the consultation deadline.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: The European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) is currently discussing the restriction of per- and polyfluoroalkyl (PFAS) substances.  We fully support efforts to minimize and mitigate the presence of substances which pose a threat to human health and the environment and we welcome the EU’s plans to gain a better understanding and oversight of PFAS uses and emissions. Due to the breadth of the proposed restriction (affecting over 10,000 substances and polymers) and the scale of the scoping challenge, Cytiva is calling on ECHA to take further time to analyze the risks and meaningfully consider the most proportionate approach by which to address them for the life sciences, bioprocessing and biopharmaceutical sectors so as to minimize unintended socio-economic costs to society. Specifically, Cytiva has identified 5 niche industrial uses of specific Polymers of Low Concern (PLCs) in critical equipment used in the manufacturing supply chain for pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical products that may require further time-derogations.

Cytiva is a supplier of hardware, specialized chemicals, consumables, and medical device products. Our products are used in applications ranging from fundamental biological research to making lifesaving vaccines, biologic drugs, and novel cell and gene therapies. We have 16,000 associates across 41 countries worldwide, including manufacturing sites in Sweden, Denmark, Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Austria. As a company our mission is to advance and accelerate therapeutics.
We welcome measures that help us understand, monitor, assess and address risks to human health and the environment. We supply the tools and services that help our customers do their work better, faster and safer. Some of our products, such as filters and membranes, can also support a range of applications in industries outside of biological research and manufacturing; these same types of membranes are also used in the manufacturing of semiconductors and in other cutting-edge manufacturing industries. We are finding ways to support our customers while respecting resource constraints and the effects of our industry on climate change and plastics waste. As we advance the development of therapies of the future, we are custodians for future generations and our ‘Designing in Sustainability’ strategy is business critical for us.
As it currently stands, the proposed restriction on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) did not specifically consider the life sciences and biopharmaceutical industry sectors and product groups where PFAS are used.  We are concerned that passage of the current proposal risks having significant unintended effects on the bioprocessing industry in the EEA with industry groups such as EFPIA and BPSA estimating that 94-100% of biopharmaceutical manufacturing campaigns in the EU will be impacted. Further, although used in small volumes, certain specific PFAS uses contribute to critical operational characteristics and performance functions: a proportional approach must therefore be taken to protect the development of new therapeutic medicinal therapies, drug availability, and ultimately the patients we serve.

As the life sciences and biopharmaceutical sectors are not significant PFAS users or emitters, our industry received insufficient consideration of costs and impacts and further analysis is required to identify the most effective approach to phasing out PFAS across our supply chains with the least socio-economic impact. At the very minimum, we believe additional time derogations are required for the 5 missing uses detailed below.
Cytiva’s consultation response:
 endorses related ECHA sector responses:  as a member of the bioprocessing industry committed to sustainable solutions, we also support related industry group sector responses, including those from the American Society of Mechanical Engineers: Bioprocessing Equipment (ASME-BPE) , Bioprocess Systems Alliance (BPSA) , BioPhorum , European Sealing Association (ESA) , European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA) , and MedTech Europe .
 seeks to outline the specific industry uses, impacts, benefits, and costs that must be proportionally considered; and
 addresses specific information requests for 5 key missing uses that merit careful consideration, largely associated with biopharmaceutical equipment manufacturing and the medical/biopharmaceutical supply chain:
1. Hydrophobic and/or oleophobic filtration membranes in pharmaceutical processing;
2. Fluoropolymer-based bioprocessing materials (e.g. membranes, gaskets, seals, fittings, etc.) in which no PFAS (C16 or shorter) chemicals or processing aids are used to manufacture the polymer;
3. Fluoropolymer-based bioprocessing materials (e.g.  membranes, gaskets, seals, tubing, O-rings, pumps, connectors) in which PFAS processing aides may be used in the manufacture of the polymer (e.g. PTFE filtration membranes, gaskets, seals, etc.);
4. Fluoropolymer used as auxiliaries on sites to manufacture chemicals vital to the bioprocessing industry;
5. Membranes used in medical device-related applications, including oleophobic, PTFE, and PVDF.

Org. name: American Chamber of Commerce to the European Union (AmCham EU)
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) is currently discussion the restriction of per- and polyfluoroalkyl (PFAS) substances. To secure long-term European manufacturing, this socio-economic analysis must not only include the impact on specific applications but also the impact on transatlantic trade and foreign long-term investments. Not taking these into account will ultimately have strong repercussions on the EU’s strategic autonomy and on many key policies, including the Green Deal ambitions.
Furthermore, ECHA, its committees, the European Commission and EU Member States should review the proposal’s current derogations and assess their enforceability. For many strategic sectors and technologies, derogations are too short or completely missing where no viable alternatives exist. In addition, the proposal does not adequately assess the availability and viability of relevant alternatives. By way of example, further derogations and exemptions are needed for important applications in medical technology, the high-tech sector (eg semiconductors), clean energy (eg hydrogen fuel cells and batteries) and industrial manufacturing. These are among the applications that ensure the continued operation of countless industrial plants that underpin entire value chains in Europe, supporting the green transformation of industry and the goals of the Green Deal.
The restriction’s framework should therefore take a proportionate approach to allow for both the achievement of the ambitions laid out in the Net-Zero Industry Act (NZIA), Green Deal and REPowerEU as well as the preservation of human health and the environment.
In summary, ECHA must amend the proposal to:
• Exclude from the scope of industrial/professional applications which are fundamental for European sovereignty and the implementation of the NZIA, as well as crucial for the cooperation established in the EU-US Trade and Technology Council (TTC) involving batteries, semiconductors/chips, heat pumps, electric vehicles, hydrogen and renewable energy.
• Ensure alignment with the main Green Deal principles including ‘Energy Efficiency First’, as embedded in the main legislative pieces of the REPower EU package.
• Exclude remanufactured/refurbished/repurposed products and components and allow repairability of products to further the goals of the Circular Economy Action Plan.
• Be coherent with other regulatory requirements and legislation, such as the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH) Regulation and the Classification, Labelling and Packaging of Substances and Mixtures (CLP) Regulation, Fluorinated Greenhouse Gases (F-Gas) Regulation and relevant sectoral legislation .
• Exempt those PFAS that have not been shown to pose an ‘unacceptable risk’ such as fluoropolymers, which should be regulated by separate regulation, for example by targeted emissions controls. The proposed outright ban is disproportionate to the risk substances such as fluoropolymers pose.
• Amend provisions based on incorrect technical assumptions. Accordingly, raw materials (eg fluorinated surfactants) required for the production of PFAS of low concern and which do not pose an ‘unacceptable risk’ (such as fluoropolymers) should be exempted.
• Include a more proportionate approach to thresholds, thereby ensuring an enforceable legislation.
• Include a general derogation for uses of PFAS at industrial sites to safeguard important value chains.
• Include a review clause for derogations in cases where no alternatives became available in the future.
• Consider new and ensure longer derogations that allow the industry to adapt or ensure the exclusion for some uses where alternatives are only at the research and development stage or not suitable in their current form.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis
Org. name: Advisory Committee of the German Society for Toxicology
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The European Commission (EC) is planning to phase out most uses of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) in the EU as a part of its Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability (CSS), The European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) has recently published a proposal under the EU chemicals regulation REACH to restrict the manufacture, use and placing on the market of PFASs.
The advisory committee of the German Society for Toxicology would like to contribute to the discussion on the proposal.
A critical problem of PFASs and their degradation products is the very high persistence, which clearly fulfils the criterion for the substance property Very Persistent (vP) according to Annex XIII of the REACH Regulation. Defining suitable subgroups of PFASs appears to be the approach to handle the restriction of PFASs which is scientifically sound. However, currently toxicity data are known only for few PFASs and for the majority of the PFASs, no toxicity data are available which would be needed for defining suitable subgroups. Large data gaps would have to be closed before subgroups could be defined which would clearly take up to centuries. This is in our view a time-frame which is not defendable with respect to potential irreversible harm and the very persistent property of PFASs. Because of the time pressure resulting from the potential irreversible harm, the precautionary principle has been selected to handle PFASs and in the restriction proposal PFASs are treated as one group. The advisory committee of the German Society for Toxicology sees the importance of precautionary strategies in risk management under conditions of uncertainty and in its view it is justified to apply this principle in the current situation.
ECHA's proposal received a lot of attention in the public. However, the advisory committee of the German Society for Toxicology has noted that the communication on the proposal, on its intention and on the underlying principle was not performed in a clear way because it has obviously led to the misunderstanding of a proven health hazard for all PFASs. In our view the communication should explain why the precautionary principle is applied and why the decision was made for a broad inclusion of PFASs. Data gaps versus current knowledge should also be clearly communicated and explained. Communication should also include that it is possible to derogate essential uses demonstrating that the proposal weights concerns against benefits which is inherent to the precautionary principle.
In summary whereas the advisory committee of the German Society for Toxicology see that applying precautionary strategies is justified for the PFASs it recommends to put more efforts in communicating why the precautionary principle is applied and why the decision was made for a broad inclusion of PFASs to avoid misunderstandings in the public.
