Combined Comments:
General Comments: The European Council of Vinyl Manufacturers (ECVM, www.pvc.org) represents 7 of the 11 producers of PVC resins and monomer (VCM) in Europe. The manufacturing capacity of the ECVM members amounts to ca. 85% of the total European VCM and PVC manufacturing capacities.  Between March and July 2023, ECVM has organised a Survey among its members to be able to provide information on PFAS used in the European VCM, suspension PVC (S-PVC) and emulsion PVC (E-PVC) plants to:

 Identify the uses of PFAS in the VCM and PVC plants
 Estimate tonnages of PFAS used per year
 Assess the process criticality and the feasibility of alternatives to PFAS
 Identify end of life destinations for each use category

Very high response rate could be obtained for the 16 VCM plants (100%), 19 S-PVC plants (95%) and 11 E-PVC plants (100%) run by the ECVM members.

Ca. 65 tonnes of PFAS have been found to be used per year by the ECVM members across 18 use categories.

The only 2 uses of low molecular weight PFAS by the European PVC industry are as industrial refrigerants (20 t/y) and air conditioning systems (0.03 t/y). All the alternatives to these two uses having their own challenges and being in any case costly to implement, a derogation of 12 years should be allowed to select environmentally and financially sustainable alternatives.

Fluoropolymers (45 t/y) meet essential uses of the European PVC industry, especially in the VCM plants. These plants deal with a combined mixture of acidic and hazardous medium including chlorine, HCl and chlorinated hydrocarbons and are in use at higher temperature. In order to comply with the tight requirements on environmental and worker exposure emissions, this demands special equipment that can withstand corrosion and ensure tight containment.

According to the Survey results, the 16 identified fluoropolymers uses include gaskets (13.9 t/y), lining in piping and industrial equipment (13.8 t/y), lining in valves (5.4 t/y), O-rings (3.5 t/y), sealants (2.8 t/y), hoses and tubing (1.4 t/y), personal protective equipment (1.3 t/y), column and internal packing (1.1 t/y), proton exchange membranes (0.6 t/y), analytical equipment (0.5 t/y), lubricants/grease (0.5 t/y), filter material (0.4 t/y), diaphragm/membrane in pumps (0.1 t/y), electrical heating conductor (0.1 t/y), reactor and compressor seals (0.06 t/y), and measurement devices (0.01 t/y).

There is generally no technically affordable and economically viable alternative material available to fluoropolymers to address these harsh conditions. Less resistant materials can't be used due to the high risk of failing, product release to the atmosphere, and potential harm to human life and the environment. For example, rubber lining can't be used in combination with high temperature and the presence of chlorinated hydrocarbons.

Without the use of fluoropolymers, the VCM and PVC plants cannot comply with the high plant safety standards and strict emission limits in place to protect people and the environment. Upper values for the environmental emission limits allowed for the VCM and PVC production in Europe are defined in three EU Best Available Techniques Reference Documents (LVOC, POL and WGC available on https://eippcb.jrc.ec.europa.eu/reference) issued by the European IPPC Bureau and enforced in the EU Industrial Emission Directive. Maximum limit values for occupational exposure for EDC (2 ppm) and VCM (1 ppm) are defined in Directive 2004/37/EC. Since the mid-nineties, the ECVM members have further committed to voluntarily abide with lower limits than those in the BREF or in 2004/37/EC and/or comply with the limits earlier than the date of implementation after publication. The latest version describing the voluntary commitment is available at https://pvc.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/ECVM-charter-pages.pdf.

At current production level, the few identified alternatives to fluoropolymers will not be available in large enough volume to meet the needs of the PVC and chemical industry. In most cases, there are no concrete substitution projects in place and as such the industry would need more than 10 years to replace fluorinated materials, given the vast use across the companies.

The vast majority of the fluoropolymer-containing equipment is mainly disposed of after use through low-emission processes (steel recycling, chemical incineration or recycling). A small uncontaminated fraction of the equipment is landfilled. In order to ensure that a safe and compliant production of important products can continue to be carried out in the EU in the future, the use of fluoropolymers in the VCM and PVC plants should be derogated for an unlimited time until technically and economically viable alternatives are found.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Four sub uses identified in Table 9 of the restriction report are relevant to the PVC industry:  • Application of fluorinated gases- Refrigeration. Refrigerants (20 t/y) are needed in VCM and PVC plants to achieve temperatures below those achievable with water from cooling towers, to reach condensation temperatures of some substances during distillations, or to achieve effective minimisation of gaseous emissions arising from vents or from incinerators. VCM polymerisation is highly exothermic and takes place at relatively moderate temperatures. Polymerisation temperature is an essential process parameter that cannot easily or not at all be ensured by cooling water refrigeration. All these processes require refrigerated water able to reach temperatures down to -20 °C for safety and quality reasons. F-gases are selected by the equipment manufacturers because they are highly effective, energy efficient and non-toxic. The current restriction proposal does not include any derogation for PFAS refrigerants used in industrial refrigeration. It only specifies derogations for low temperature (-50°C) refrigeration, refrigerants for laboratory tests and measurement equipment, and centrifuges. Alternative refrigerants have their own health and environmental risks and require high investments to convert to new industrial refrigerant equipment. Propane and propylene pose a risk of flammability, particularly when used in large quantities and in confined spaces; carbon dioxide is hazardous to human health, operates at high pressures and is less efficient at high ambient temperatures; ammonia is highly toxic, resulting in specific requirements for its use.  A derogation should be allowed to select environmentally and financially sustainable alternatives.  • TULAC-Professional apparels. Although representing a relatively low consumption of materials (1.3t/y), is obviously essential to ensure workers’ health and safety and to allow the execution of tasks necessary to protect the environment. Workers should be protected in the VCM and PVC plants against risks of Category III a) as defined in EU 2016/425 (substances and mixtures which are hazardous to health). Fluorinated substances are commonly used in fire, chemical and corrosion-resistant clothing. Despite strenuous efforts by manufacturers of protective personal equipment to find suitable options affording the same protection level, no commercially available alternatives achieving the performance standards of the VCM and PVC plants exist to date. The current restriction proposal does include a proposed 12-year derogation for PFAS-containing PPE protecting users against risks of Category III a); this is indeed the minimum time period necessary to develop, test and implement alternative solutions.  • Lubricants- Greases. Fluorinated lubricants are used (0.5 t/y) in the VCM and PVC plants for a safe functioning of equipment operated in harsh conditions. The current restriction proposal does include a proposed 12-year derogation for PFAS-containing lubricants when use takes place under harsh conditions or use is for safe functioning and safety of equipment; this time period should indeed be allowed to develop alternatives and implement them.  • Application of fluorinated gases- Air conditioning and heat pumps. Fluorinated gases (0.03 t/y) are present in air conditioning systems in some premises of the VCM and PVC plants. F-gases are subjected to a 12-year derogation for maintenance and refilling of existing HVCAR without drop-in alternatives. A time-unlimited derogation is proposed for refrigerants in HVCAR equipment in buildings where national safety standards and building codes prohibit the use of alternatives. All systems present in the VCM and PVC plants will fall under these derogations.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: No information could be obtained from the Survey on the share of emissions attributable to the manufacture, use and end-of-life phase for none of the 4 sub-uses listed in Request #1 (Request #2.a).  Information could be obtained on how waste is treated for 3 of the 4 sub-uses listed in Request #1:  • TULAC-Professional apparel (1.3 t/y): 91% chemical waste incinerator, 2% recycling, 1% landfill, 1% EoL management by third party, 6% unknown. • Lubricants- Greases (0.5 t/y): 90% recycling, 7% landfill, 3% unknown. • Application of fluorinated gases- Air conditioning and heat pumps (0.03 t/y): 87% chemical waste incinerator, 13% EoL management by third party.

5. Proposed derogations: Using the Survey results (representing ca. 85% of the VCM and PVC production in Europe), information can be provided for three derogated uses relevant to the VCM and PVC plants:  TULAC-Professional apparels: 1.3 t PFAS used per year. From the data obtained on the destination of the waste (question 2), it can be estimated as worst case, that 7% (91 kg) is emitted in the environment.   Lubricants- Greases: 500 kg PFAS used per year. From the data obtained on the destination of the waste (Question 2), it can be estimated as worst case, that 10% (50 kg) is emitted in the environment.   Application of fluorinated gases- Air conditioning and heat pumps: 30 kg PFAS used per year. As the F gases are incinerated or recycled (see Question 2), it can be assumed that there are negligible emissions to the environment for this use.

6. Missing uses: According to the Survey, 14 PFAS uses in the VCM and PVC plants could be identified as not being covered in the restriction report. All of these uses use fluoropolymers. Several internal studies from the ECVM members have put in evidence that fluoropolymers (especially the fully fluorinated, most chemically inert PolyTetraFluoroEthylene/PTFE and PerFluoroalkoxy Alkanes/PFA) show the best set of performances needed to cope with the harsh process conditions in the EDC/VCM production units:   • Chemical corrosion resistance vs. the great majority of metallic materials used in the chemical industry • Chemical permeation resistance to provide long-term protection • Temperature resistance (vs other thermoplastics) • Mechanical strength (vs other thermoplastics) • Excellent flexibility and sliding properties to secure tightness in rotating equipment (vs metallic materials) • Good wear resistance when a carbon filler is added to the fluoropolymer  External publications also mention that, for the conditions found in the EDC/VCM plants, fluoropolymer materials are the first-choice materials for corrosion resistance at high temperature. Volume 2 of the Dechema Corrosion Handbook mentions that fluoropolymers are the first-choice materials for hydrochloric acid equipment at elevated temperatures and concentrations (see extract in Annex 3 of the non-confidential attachment). Fluoropolymers are particularly resistant to hydrochloric acid in the presence of chlorinated hydrocarbons.   Less severe conditions are generally experienced in PVC plants, but various plant sections also require equipment with the outstanding set of performances provided by the fluoropolymers.  Use-specific information are provided below.  Gaskets and O-rings  According to the Survey results, fluoropolymer gaskets and O-rings are used in the VCM and PVC plants at levels of, respectively, 13.9 t/y and 3.5 t/y. For the gaskets, 68% of the volume is treated after use in a chemical waste incinerator, 29% is landfilled and 3% is managed by a third party. For the O-rings, 98% of the volume is treated after use in a chemical waste incinerator, 1% is landfilled, 3% is managed by a third party. PFAS is thermally destructed at the temperatures used (>800°C) during the incineration. The primary end products of PFAS combustion are CO, CO2, and HF. Air emissions of HF are strictly controlled by the 2010/75/EU Directive on industrial emissions.   Gasket and O-rings are critical piece of equipment to contain the dangerous substances present in the VCM and PVC plants and thus protect the workers and the environment.  Only polyfluorinated materials have sufficient resistance to handle EDC, VCM, and the various chlorinated by-products present in EDC and VCM streams. In VCM plants, there is, therefore, no real alternative, because of the combination of product type, pressure, and temperature. Metal (tantalum, high-quality stainless steel) / graphite seals could be used in PVC plants, but they require more space between flanges and hence significant and expensive adjustments as piping will have to be replaced. In very few cases in PVC plants, rubber seals could be used.  Lining in piping, valves and other industrial equipment (e.g. pump)  According to the Survey results, fluoropolymer lining in piping and industrial equipment is used by the ECVM members at a level of 13.8 t/y. This level is 5.4 t/y for the lining in valves. For the lining in piping and industrial equipment, 94% of the volume is treated after use through steel recycling, 6% is landfilled. For the lining in valves, 89% of the volume is treated through steel recycling, 1% is landfilled, 1% is managed by a third party and 9% has an unknown destination. As PFAS are thermally destructed at the temperatures used to melt down the metal scrap (>1500°C), minimum emissions of PFAS can be expected the end of life for these uses.  The corrosive substances and high temperatures in VCM manufacturing plants require highly mechanically and chemically resistant piping, valves and other equipment (e.g. pump) with an inner fluoropolymer lining.   It is very difficult to find suitable alternatives due to the high pressure, high operating temperatures, and types of transported fluids.   As illustrated in Annexes 3 and 4 of the non-confidential attachment, PTFE and PFA can be serviced at temperatures up to 250 °C (without mechanical load). This is much higher than other thermoplastics; PP and C-PVC have a maximum service temperature of 90-95°C; PE and PVC of 60 °C.  A study has been run by one ECVM member on the best material to use for an agitated storage vessel containing wastewater from flue gas cleaning of an incinerator for chlorinated hydrocarbons in a VCM plant. The wastewater is alkaline (pH 9.8-11.2) and the working temperature is 100°C. The combination of those two parameters excludes the use of all non-metallic materials. The use of a bisphenol A-based vinyl ester resin, PP and C-PVC is excluded due to their limited maximum operating temperatures (respectively, 85°C and 90-95°C). The use of a VE-NK resin is limited by the pH. As Polyvinylidene fluoride/PVDF is prone to stress corrosion cracking at this high pH, a PTFE-coated carbon steel was recommended as the best material.  As another example of the unique properties provided by fluoropolymer linings in corrosive environments, it is interesting to mention the case of a scrubber designed to scrub chlorine and acidic vapors with 22% caustic soda (Annex 5 of the non-confidential attachment). This scrubber was initially fabricated from fiberglass-reinforced plastic (FRP) and installed in 1977. Major repairs began in 1981 and continued at four-year intervals. After exploring several replacement materials, an ethylene-chlorotrifluoroethylene liner was selected for its excellent chemical resistance to caustic soda, chlorine and HCl, and high permeation resistance to chlorine and HCl. Installed in 1987, the scrubber remained in service until the plant shut down in 2001. Examination shortly after plant closing showed the liner to be in excellent condition.   Several other studies have also demonstrated the superiority of PTFE and/or PFA-lined pipes compared to conventional metallic materials in terms of chemical resistance.                                                                                                                                                                                        As stressed in the recent review article of Annex 6 of the non-confidential attachment, the selection of metallic materials resistant to hydrochloric acid corrosion is a very difficult task, especially under a high flow rate of acid making the material wear and corrode. Very often only titanium grade 7 (most corrosion resistant titanium alloy) or tantalum would be the only acceptable metallic alternatives for the conditions found in the VCM plants. However, these materials cannot meet the required performances in all cases and/or are far costlier than the fluoropolymers.  One ECVM member has reported that a connecting pipe section made of tantalum suffered from cracks after some years of operations. Other members reported several equipment failures with stainless steel:  • Stress cracking corrosion of the stainless-steel ball and stem of a valve due to HCl et chlorine. • Stress cracking corrosion on a stainless steel thermowell in the presence of HCl • Corrosion of stainless-steel bolts by HCl • Corrosion of the stainless steel outer support layer of bellows under high temperature  Beyond their reduced chemical and temperature resistance, the alternative materials often have  limited commercial availability. For instance, PFA-coated carbon steel is a standard material for pumps, and much more easily available than pumps lined with exotic metallic materials. Plastic material pumps are not (commonly) used. PTFE lining is also a standard solution for pipes.   Sealants  According to the Survey results, fluoropolymer sealants are used by the ECVM members at a level of2.8 t/y. 36% of the volume is treated after use in a chemical waste incinerator, 27% is treated after use through steel recycling, 14% is landfilled, 23% has an unknown destination. Almost 2/3rd of the volume of sealant is treated in high temperature processes where the PFAS is thermally destructed, minimum emissions of PFAS can be expected at the end of life for this use.  As the gaskets and O-rings, the sealants are critical pieces of equipment to contain the dangerous substances present in the VCM and PVC plants and thus protect the workers and the environment. Only polyfluorinated sealants have sufficient chemical resistance to handle EDC, VCM, and the various chlorinated by-products present in EDC and VCM streams. PTFE tapes are used between graphite blocks of heat exchangers for HCl stripping during the purification of VCM. In VCM plants, there exists, therefore, no real alternative, because of the combination of product type, pressure and temperature. In the PVC plants, silicone sealants could be used in sections with no exposure to chlorinated substances.  The current restriction proposal does not include any derogation of PFAS-containing sealants. A derogation should be allowed to develop alternatives and implement them.  Hoses and tubing  Hoses with an internal PTFE tubing and an external braid made of stainless steel, are mostly used in some sections of VCM plants when fixed piping is not the best option (temporary operation, lack of space). They are used for example to drain corrosive fluids such as HCl from condensers of distillation columns. These hoses offer excellent chemical resistance, and their structure provides a smooth bore to ensure clean, fast performance, resistant to high pressures and temperatures up to 260°C. PTFE has been proven to outperform rubber, silicone and PVC in these applications. Hoses with an internal PTFE lining can be used in PVC plants to provide low flow resistance and avoid wear.  According to the Survey results, these hoses are used by the ECVM members at a level of 1.4 t/y. 79% of the volume is treated after use in a chemical waste incinerator, 16% is recycled, 4% is managed by a third party, and 1% is landfilled. As most of the volume is treated in high temperature processes where the PFAS is thermally destructed, minimum emissions of PFAS can be expected at the end of life for this use.  The current restriction proposal does not include any derogation PFAS-containing hoses and tubing. A derogation should be allowed to develop alternatives and implement them.  Eight other smaller uses of fluoropolymers missing in the Annex XV restriction report have been identified from the Survey:   •  1.1 t/y of fluorinated column internals/packing are used by the ECVM members in fractionation or distillation columns to separate various chemicals in the VCM plants. 50% of the fluoropolymer for this use is treated in a chemical waste incinerator, 30% is landfilled, 14% is treated by a third party, 6% is recycled. • 0.6 t/y is used in proton-exchange membranes used for wastewater treatment stations of VCM plants. All the waste is treated in a chemical waste incinerator. • 0.5 t/y is used in different analytical equipment of the VCM and PVC plants. Most of the waste (81%) is treated in a chemical waste incinerator. A small fraction is recycled (7%). 12% of the waste has an unknown destination. • 0.4 t/y is used as filter materials in the VCM and PVC plants. 56% of the waste is treated in a chemical waste incinerator, 17% is landfilled, 13% is treated by a third party, 7% is recycled, and 13 % has an unknown destination.  • 0.4 t/y is used as membranes in positive displacement pumps used in the VCM and PVC plants. 57% of the volume is treated by a third party after use, 36% is recycled, and 7% is landfilled. • 0.1 t/y is used as coating on industrial electric heating elements used in reactors of VCM and PVC plants. All the fluoropolymer is recycled after use. • 0.06 t/y is used as mechanical seals for reactors and compressors from the VCM and PVC plants. 13% of the volume is treated in steel recycling according to the Survey. The rest has an unknown destination. • 0.01 t/y is used in various measurement devices from the VCM and PVC plants. All fluorinated waste is recycled according to the Survey results.  As the end of life of most of the fluoropolymers is managed through low emission processes, we recommend defining time-unlimited derogations with regular reviews for all these 14 fluoropolymer uses in PVC and VCM plants for which no alternative is currently available or in development. Once alternatives that are safer and technically and economically viable have been developed, such derogations could be revised.   Should these 14 fluoropolymer uses not become derogated, the restriction would directly affect the whole PVC manufacturing industry in Europe. 11 companies operate 21 VCM and 36 PVC production plants from the EU27 + Norway + UK area. Within these companies, an estimated number of ca. 8600 employees can be allocated to PVC production (including required upstream products like chlorine production) activities. The estimated turnover generated from the PVC sector (including upstream products like chlorine) accounts for an order of 6.6 bn Euros. This corresponds to an average turnover per employee of around 700000-800000 Euros (source: Polyglobe database owned by Kunststoff Information Verlagsgesellschaft mbH).  On top of this, the restriction would indirectly affect around 168000 employees working in EU27 + Norway + Switzerland + UK for 6300 companies converting PVC into rigid and flexible PVC articles.  In total, these 6300 companies generate a turnover of more than 35 bn Euros (source: EuroStat, UK Office of National Statistics, Statistics Norway, Statistical Office for Norway, Federal Statistical Office of Switzerland).  These data do not include the European producers of PVC plasticisers, PVC stabilisers, PVC additives and European PVC compounding companies.

General Comments: The European Data Centre Association (EUDCA) represents the community of European colocation data centre operators. EUDCA welcomes the proposed PFAS restriction as a crucial step to increase health safety in the European Union and improve the protection of the environment. However, EUDCA is concerned about this proposal’s potential disruptive and far-reaching implications for many industry sectors and supply chains, including the data centre industry.

Within the data centre industry, PFAS are most commonly used as refrigerants to cool the IT equipment located in data centre facilities, for the manufacturing of semiconductors and chips, and for the insulation of wires, cables and boards. Such equipment is essential to power these facilities and ensure the smooth operation of data centres, which facilitates the data transfers that enable many critical functions in today’s society and makes Europe fit for the digital age.

EUDCA is particularly concerned that this proposal may hinder the achievement of other sustainability and energy efficiency targets set by the EU and national governments for the data centre industry and to which many operators already committed voluntarily by certifying their adherence to the targets set by the industry under the Climate Neutral Data Centre Pact (CNDCP). Over the last few years, the colocation data centre industry has worked extensively to improve its sustainability performance and is coming under increasing scrutiny from European legislators to continue down this path. To create a coherent legislative framework, EUDCA would like to highlight some critical aspects of the current proposal and suggest possible solutions that could increase the safety of European citizens, whilst enabling data centres to support the digital and green transition.

Overall, EUDCA welcomes the goal of the proposal to phase out the use of PFAS in the data centre industry by eliminating path dependency for newly built data centres and ensuring that the industry follows a sustainability trajectory. However, EUDCA would like to stress that this proposal should not undo the EU’s sustainability achievements by applying a one-fits-all restriction to both existing and new data centres nor undermine data centres’ ability to comply with existing or upcoming restrictions and sustainability requirements.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: This comment applies to the following sector and (sub-)uses of PFAS relevant to the data centre industry: 1. Applications of fluorinated gases (Annex E.2.8.). Relevant uses:  o Refrigeration o Air conditioning and heat pumps o Insulating gas in electrical equipment  2. Electronics and semiconductors (Annex E.2.11.). Relevant uses and sub-uses: o Electronics (Heat Transfer Fluids); o Semiconductors (Heat Transfer Fluids, Data Centres - Immersion Cooling of Semiconductor Devices/Servers).  Though relevant to the data centres industry as a restriction on the use of PFAS for the following uses and sectors could have a significant impact on the efficient and safe operation of data centres, the following sectors and sub-uses are not directly covered by this response: 1. Electronics and semiconductors (Annex E.2.11.). Relevant uses and sub-uses: o Electronics (Wire insulation, Fire protection fluid, Lubricants (such as POEs)); o Semiconductors (Fluoroelastomers used for chip manufacturing).   2. Energy sector (Annex E.2.12.). Relevant uses: o Lithium-ion batteries o Batteries o Other: switchgears, High Voltage DC Converter Valves  3. Construction products (Annex E.2.13.). Relevant uses: o Coil Coating o PTFE – joining of pipework, bearings, etc o Insulating boards – insulation of buildings and services o Fire suppression systems – Using Halon/Novec/other, i.e. not carbon dioxide/ argonite/inergen (CO2/N2/AR2)  4. TULAC (Annex E.2.2.). Relevant use and sub-use:  o Professional apparel (PPE and clothing for operations/construction staff).

5. Proposed derogations: PFAS refrigerants currently used in data centres’ cooling and HVACR equipment (such as R-1234ze) have a very low Global Warming Potential (GWP) and allow data centres to operate at specific temperatures and pressure points. They create the perfect environment to achieve an ambitious level of Power Usage Efficiency (PUE), leading to low CO2 emissions even in high ambient conditions. Additionally, due to low risks of flammability and toxicity, the transport and in-facility application of these PFAS does not require additional mitigation measures, resulting in a lower embodied carbon footprint during construction.   For end-users, it is difficult to estimate the amount of leakage of PFAS deriving from their use. Typically, in end-products, PFAS are contained within a sealed and closed system, where the PFAS cannot escape. Compared to manufacturing processes, the instances and amount of gas leaked or released in the atmosphere by users are very limited, and when it occurs, it happens in controlled and safe situations. In data centres, due to the high level of security and compliance measures the systems using PFAS for operational purposes leakage to the outside is ensured to only occur in emergency situations. Typically, high-quality sealed HVACR systems need to comply with the standard EN378 on leak detection which limits the maximum allowed leakage. However, these gases are released exceptionally during emergency situations in case of overpressure to prevent catastrophic build-up which would release a small percentage in the atmosphere. Members of EUDCA estimate that the maximum average loss of gases in the data centre sector is below 2% of the mass of refrigerants deployed.

8. Other identified uses: In Annex XV report, several of the uses and derogations contained in Table 8 and Table 9 (such as refrigeration, air conditioning and heat pumps, fire suppressants, insulating gas in electrical equipment, electronics, semiconductors, and the energy sector) are relevant for EUDCA members. EUDCA welcomes the ban of PFAS for upcoming data centre projects, as the report accurately mentions that there might be some technically and economically feasible alternatives to PFAS, in particular for refrigeration and insulating gases in switchgear systems. However, even the 5 or 12-year derogations proposed for some PFAS applications do not account for the entire lifetime of a full-capacity data centre or of its equipment. For data centres specifically, the Uptime Institute White Paper on Life Expectancy of Facilities Infrastructure states that chillers have a life expectancy of 15-20 years; while MV switchgear has a life expectancy of 35 years. Furthermore, the analysis of alternatives to relevant uses and sub-uses gives insufficient consideration to their technical and economic feasibility for existing data centres.   1. Electronics and semiconductors (Annex E.2.11.) The Annex XV report predicts a 10% annual growth of PFAS use in the Electronics and semiconductor industry (1.3.2.11). Electronics and semiconductors are essential to deliver digital transformation and are crucial components of many of the IT and electronic equipment used in colocation data centres. Heat transfer fluids for the immersion and cooling of electronic equipment is an innovative technology which relies on PFAS (see Annex A, Table A.48). It allows for the optimal utilization of liquid cooling for servers and chips, without compromising the server’s efficiency. However, this is an emerging technology for which no data is available on whether there are economically available alternatives. Therefore, EUDCA recommends at least a 12-year derogation for the use of PFAS in chips and immersion cooling technologies to allow for alternatives to be developed.   2. Applications of fluorinated gases (Annex E.2.8.) Several uses and sub-uses in the application of fluorinated gases are relevant to data centre operation (e.g. insulating gas in electrical equipment, air conditioning and heat pumps, and refrigeration) as they support the equipment that is key to achieving the European Union’s sustainability goals. In the Fit for 55 agenda of the European Commission, several regulatory measures (such as the Energy Efficiency Directive) targeted the sustainability and energy efficiency of the ICT and specifically the data centre sector. Similarly, at the national level, some member states have already started considering mandatory energy efficiency targets (e.g. mandatory levels of Power Usage Efficiency (PUE)), to set the data centre sector on a track towards greater energy efficiency. However, the Annex XV report failed to account for these requirements.   a. Refrigerants Derogations for refrigerant equipment are provided already for the HVACR equipment put on the market before the entry into force of the ban and for which “no drop-in alternatives” currently exist. For industrial refrigeration, in the proposal (Table 8), it is mentioned that systems based on ammonia have been available for many years and could be a potential solution for large data centres. The proposal fails to consider derogations for other types of air-conditioning or cooling systems.  Currently, there are no technically available drop-in alternative solutions for HVACR systems for existing data centre plants. Similarly, for refrigeration based on the use of fluorinated gases, there are not sufficient available alternatives on the markets that would comply with this proposal and the upcoming restrictions under the F-Gases Regulation. Re-fitting existing data centres as well as implementing these technologies in new data centres would create significant market monopolies and a shortage of efficient solutions.  - Length and scope of derogation  The proposed 12-year derogation for HVACR systems for which no drop-in alternatives exist would be much less than the economic expected life of the majority of central cooling plants. Retrofitting will require the replacement of entire equipment and systemic changes to the cooling system infrastructure (e.g. pipework, structure, supports etc.). Data centre operators have already made great efforts to replace previous refrigerants that were not compliant with the requirements of the Fluorinated Greenhouse Gases Regulation (F-gases Regulation). Combined with the upcoming revision of the F-gases Regulation, an additional restriction on the use of alternatives to high GWP fluorinated gases may significantly impact the growth potential of many existing data centre facilities. Cost and energy efficiency are the two most important drivers to deliver sustainable growth within the data centre industry which are likely put at risk by the banning of PFAS refrigerants in the short term.   The proposed transition period and derogations for HVACR systems exclusively (18 months and 12 years) are not enough for a significant redesign of the entire air-conditioning cooling systems relying on PFAS refrigerants. Thus, EUDCA would suggest a more sustainable restriction for existing data centres applicable to all types of air conditioning cooling systems and refrigerants. A 12-year derogation would allow for the minimization of the amount of embodied carbon caused by the early replacement and associated project works to replace all chillers, VRF systems, and other cooling systems.  - Technical feasibility of alternatives A substitution of existing equipment with a new one capable of running on the proposed alternatives will have a potentially less efficient and decreased refrigeration performance and lead to a significant loss in energy efficiency not compatible with upcoming energy legislation at the national and EU level (e.g. the Energy Efficiency Directive and national ambitious PUE targets). In countries where the PFAS ban has already been in place for several years such as Denmark, in limited applications, CO2-based air-cooled or water-cooled chillers have been used instead of conventional PFAS refrigerants. However, these alternatives led to an estimated increase in carbon footprint that is approximately 50% larger than typical installations and 25-50% less energy efficient. Unlike the ban on the R22 gas and its CFC replacements, there are presently no ‘drop-in’ like-for-like replacements for conventional refrigerants. Proposed alternative refrigerants (such as CO2 and ammonia) have significantly different operating parameters which require increasing operating power in order to achieve the optimal ambient temperature, but reduce the overall energy efficiency of the data centres cooling systems.   The use of a non-PFAS medium may impose limits to the operation and design flexibility to elevate CHW temperatures or use CHW heat rejection in combination with immersion or raw cooling. This would reduce the possibility for data centres to improve efficiency as well are reduce the feasibility of reusing their waste heat due to lower CHW used. The majority of refrigerant systems within data centres are air-cooled, meaning that higher refrigerant condensing temperatures are required to provide cooling during extreme temperature events. In air-cooled ammonia systems, these temperatures cannot be achieved with air-cooled chillers. No manufacturer contacted was able to provide an air-cooled chiller rated for 40°C air temperature, which is the data centre air design condition for most of northern Europe (Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris, etc.). In southern Europe this value is even higher (Rome 42°C, Madrid 42°C, Athens 43°C, etc.). Therefore, in order to change to ammonia chillers for higher ambient temperatures, evaporative heat rejection is required. However, this technology will increase water use across the industry and reduce Water Usage Efficiency (WUE). Especially in water-scarce regions, these restrictions could have severe repercussions on the development of other industries relying on a large usage of water resources.   Furthermore, there is a high risk of chillers significantly derating or becoming non-operational at extreme ambient temperatures. This would significantly affect the accessibility of the internet for users. During peak ambient temperatures, the IT equipment might shut down as cooling would be insufficient. The lack of access to cloud services would lead to the loss of service for customers and EU citizens as well as massive revenue losses for businesses through downtime.   Moreover, alternative chillers often are larger than conventional ones. Ultimately, all considerations around the feasibility of switching to alternatives should be based on spatial planning to host larger ammonia chillers, while acknowledging that smaller data centres may be unable to host them. With a ban on the use of PFAS, redeveloping data centres and or replacing chillers with a significant weight and size difference would make the replacement of the chiller plant completely impracticable without significant structural works and extension, or construction of new facilities. The redesign and retrofitting of existing data centres to host new chillers might also lead to a premature replacement of existing PFAS-based cooling systems and other equipment. This would significantly increase the embodied carbon of any replacement brought about by the ban on PFAS refrigerants in data centres in contrast with industry-based and EU sustainability goals. For instance, ammonia-based chillers may not only be impossible to implant into existing smaller data centres but also in larger ones.   The following information provides indications of spatial, weight and energy efficiency differences between PFAS and ammonia refrigerants based on an indicative selection for a 4 MW water-cooled chiller from five manufacturers: - Spatial difference: PFAS refrigerants: 87-100%; Ammonia refrigerants: 128%-153%. - Weight difference: PFAS refrigerants: 100%; Ammonia refrigerants 179%-234%. - Energy Efficiency Difference: PFAS refrigerants: 100%-129%; Ammonia Refrigerants 98%-165%.  The proposed natural alternatives also have other less desirable properties that make their implementation not suitable for data centres. In particular: • Propane cannot be used as a solution in larger chiller systems due to the quantity of pressurized flammable gases and high explosivity risks. The use of propane and gases with flammability risks corresponding to A2L and A1 according to ISO817 are also banned in Italy in commercial areas where electronic equipment is located.  • Ammonia can be used only with care due to its flammability and toxicity (classified as class 3-highest toxicity under ASHRAE), increasing significantly the safety risks of the data centre operations as well as of the clients and employees. Moreover, ammonia chillers are often very big and operate at high operating pressures.  • CO2 can be used as an alternative but requires significant infrastructural investments and system changes due its to extreme operating pressures.  - Economic feasibility of alternatives  Expected costs are difficult to assess due to the uncertainty regarding the space, timing, weight and status of development. The magnitude of impact and change is dependent on the outcomes of each chiller manufacturer’s product development programmes. To make definite calculations on the cost of switching to the alternatives from a sustainability perspective, it will be relevant to consider the type of refrigerant, the scale of the implementation and the existing infrastructure.  For new installations, ammonia chillers are larger, heavier, and consequentially more expensive than conventional chillers. The following percentages provide indications of cost increases based on an indicative selection for a 4 MW water-cooled chiller from five manufacturers: PFAS refrigerants 100%; ammonia refrigerants: 130%-448%. Note that these figures are ONLY for the cost of the chiller. There are additional costs to allow for additional ventilation and leak detection requirements due to the flammability and toxicity of ammonia.  Even if available alternatives were considered technically feasible under an extended adjustment period for existing data centres, they may require mitigative measures to contain the higher level of flammability and toxicity. This would significantly increase the capital expenditures of data centres for emergency and safety measures including costs for training personnel and adoption of safety measures and equipment; emergency exits and ventilation systems; emergency showers and breathing apparatus. This could further increase the cost of the non-PFA chillers by between 25% -75%.  For existing facilities, alternatives may also require the substitution of existing equipment with larger ones and adjusting the facility to accommodate them. This would entail a significant cost for existing facilities given the scale of infrastructure changes required. Moreover, retrofitting or expanding data centre infrastructures in metropolitan areas will be very difficult due to heavy limitations on space and permitting plans. Therefore, requiring the transition to larger chillers, combined with the restrictions on land and space for new data centre developments, may heavily affect the achievement of the digitalisation goals set by the EU, as some smaller data centres may be forced to stop their operation.  The operating costs for large, water-cooled units, to keep lower ambient temperatures are also expected to increase.   Moreover, increased costs of warranty could be expected if the changes are not covered by the insurance policy. Similarly, plant replacement, such as the replacement of critical infrastructure like chillers or chiller components within the data centre environment might reduce resilience below client requirements and entail legal costs for an update to the service level agreement contractually agreed with the clients.  Finally, existing alternatives are not available in sufficient quantities on the market and already present higher procurement costs compared to PFAS. Ammonia chillers are available only in scarce quantities on the market and they cannot satisfy the growing demand from the expanding data centre industry in Europe. Similarly, CO2-based alternatives are only produced by a small number of producers. An 18-month transition period is insufficient to compensate for the scaling up of the production and for redesigns in the infrastructure. In case of the entry into force of the restrictions at the EU level, the impact on the supply chain due to the unavailability of products at scale could be massive. Industry might be incentivised to hoard PFAS leading to an increase in the prices due to speculation. In comparison, the CO2 and ammonia-based chillers and refrigerant alternatives market might also become more expensive. Therefore, while for existing facilities the cost could be very significant and not feasible without completely redesigning the entire data centre facility, for new data centres the costs could be lower but largely depend on the availability of the supply chain to keep up with the new demand. If there are any delays, the cost for new projects could be just as significant (estimated to be around tens of millions for a 16MW facility).   EUDCA thus recommends to: • Consider a derogation or a longer transition period for PFAS refrigerants of at least 5 years if the decision is taken to ban PFAS refrigerants outright, to allow for the research and development of new technologies equivalent to the ones currently relying on PFAS and alternative substances, or for a sector-specific assessment of the most appropriate alternatives for the data-centre industry; • Where the decision is not made to ban PFAS refrigerants outright, ensure that newer PFAS refrigerants (R1233zd, R1234ze, R1234yf) and their associated blends are reviewed holistically against the risk of their Persistence, Bioaccumalesence and Toxicity in comparison to Ammonia, and other ‘Natural’ refrigerants to determine whether there is a benefit to banning PFAS to replace them with more toxic alternatives; • Apply the derogations for the PFAS restriction in the air conditioning and refrigeration sectors to new data centre projects and extend the derogations or the transition period to at least 5 years; • Apply the derogations for PFAS restrictions in the air conditioning and refrigeration sectors to existing data centres and extend the derogations for the use of PFAS until the end of cooling plants' economic life expectancy or any case to at least 15 years;  • Set a measurable benchmark to determine the dimension of data centres below which the substitution may be feasible (define “large data centres”). The definition should be based on Megawatt capacity rather than turnover and could align with existing instruments applicable to data centres (e.g. Energy Efficiency Directive and EU Code of Conduct on Data Centre Energy Efficiency).   b. Insulating gas in electrical equipment   PFAS are also used as insulating gas in electrical equipment. While there are a few available natural-origin gas alternatives on the market to replace low to medium-voltage switchgear, their availability is insufficient to cover the large demand for switchgear technology expected to grow in the coming years to support the production of clean and renewable energy. Moreover, without adequate alignment of the entry into force of the restriction of this proposal with upcoming legislation, such as the revision of the F-gases Regulation, the availability of alternatives to PFAS gases on the market might be insufficient or not economically viable, especially for smaller data centres. EUDCA would recommend adding a derogation also for low to medium-voltage switchgear of at least 5 years to allow for the expansion of the market for alternatives, and to ensure fair competition and affordable prices to substitute the use of PFAS in switchgears. In any case, EUDCA would recommend aligning the PFAS restriction for insulating gases with the restriction on switchgear set under the revised F-Gases Regulation to avoid a compounded impact of these measures on the availability of switchgear.

Org. name: European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA)
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA) represents the innovative pharmaceutical sector in Europe. We welcome the proposed time unlimited derogation for active substances in human medicinal products within the scope of Directive 2001/83.  The proposed derogation for active substances is part of necessary mitigation measures to prevent medicine shortage.

We are concerned that development and/or supply of medicines in the EU will be severely impacted by the PFAS Restriction as presently drafted, based on a broadened definition of “PFAS” and the wide applicability across many different uses.
Regulatory scope: the restriction proposal aims at substances and articles without derogating products where marketing is subject to specific regulations. For medicinal products and medical devices, these are granted market authorisations under Directive 2001/83, or permissions under the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR) or EU In Vitro Device Regulation (IVDR), respectively. Restricting products under marketing authorisation or permission causes regulatory conflicts.
Substance scope: the substance group PFAS as defined in the regulation has no common hazardous properties. Fluoropolymers, for example, are non-hazardous, most are considered polymers of low concern by the OECD and some have food contact approval. Persistence of either the substance itself or its degradation products is the property of concern, but PFAS with demonstrated degradability are not derogated as such, so it cannot be claimed to be a common property of the regulated group.
Definition: the long-term goal of reducing emissions can only be achieved by a global restriction of PFAS, such as under the Stockholm convention. To facilitate this process, the definition of “PFAS” should be aligned as much as possible. The U.S. EPA working definition published in the fifth contaminant candidate list (CCL5) may serve as a blueprint.
Restriction option: If Restriction Option 1 is applied, all chemical, pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical manufacturing will have to move out of the EEA, as production and development depend on fluoropolymers and replacements are not available. Supply of medicines will be severely impacted, as approved active pharmaceutical ingredients (API) and medicines delivered within packaging and/or with drug delivery devices used to administer the medicinal products under market authorization are in scope of the restriction. The same is true, to a lesser degree, for Restriction Option 2. A socio-economic analysis (SEA) for the pharmaceutical industry sector is currently being conducted by EPPA (www.eppa.com) and will quantify and substantiate these claims. It will be submitted to the public consultation at a later timepoint upon finalisation.

Emissions depend on the use of the PFAS:
In case of fluoropolymers  in industrial use, PFAS are still part of the equipment at its end of life, and emissions can be controlled. In case of use of PFAS as chemicals or auxiliaries in Manufacture/Storage/Transport and Quality Control, substances can be used under controlled conditions to minimise exposure to the lowest level possible.  The use of substances should not be restricted if the goal of the restriction can be reached by other means. This would apply, for instance, to fluoropolymers in industrial use under inventory and end-of-life management as outlined in Article 8 of the Restriction Proposal.
For packaging of medicinal products or medical devices, the emissions depend on local waste management. Most European countries have implemented incineration of medical or municipal waste or are moving towards this goal. The typical packaging use is a thin fluoropolymer film (PCTFE, ETFE or other) laminated with other plastics or elastomers, facilitating incineration. As published, PFAS can be mineralized when incinerated: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0045653519306435
Data on PFAS emissions at the waste stage of actual pharmaceutical packaging materials will be submitted to this consultation at a later point in time.
In the case of PFAS API, the emission resulting from patient use is assessed as part of the marketing authorisation of medicinal products in an Environmental Risk Assessment (ERA). Pharmaceutical initiatives (Pharmaceuticals in the Environment, Innovative Medicines Initiative Premier) aim at increasing the environmental compatibility of all API. In the case of unused PFAS API, disposal schemes are established and improved.
Alternatives do not exist for API. Introduction of fluorine in the API molecule is an essential part of developing efficacious and safe candidates. Any changes to an API molecule would essentially require the development of a completely new candidate. Due to the unique properties of individual molecular structures containing fluorine, alternatives for API, development products and their starting materials and intermediates do not exist, as the function of the substances is on the chemical molecular level.
Alternatives for fluoropolymers in production, packaging and devices may exist in some cases. However, the sought after properties are outstanding resistance against heat, light, chemicals, time and abrasion, which is naturally linked to persistence. This means that alternatives are most likely persistent, too. In manufacturing and packaging, the use of fluoropolymers is closely linked to other sustainability considerations (recyclability, long service life or shelf life, production or transport resources/emissions, energy considerations etc.). These environmental trade-offs are not regarded when only the chemical nature of the material is regulated.
Benefits of fluoropolymers in production, packaging and devices include thermal and chemical stability, smooth hard surfaces that are easily cleaned and disinfected, and outstanding barrier properties protecting products from air, moisture, impurities, extractables and particles. This safeguards the safety and quality of products throughout their shelf life.
Other SEA topics: the ban of PFAS API as proposed in Restriction Option 1 has an expected impact on the industry of tens of billion Euros. The ban on manufacturing materials as outlined in both Restriction Option has an industry impact of hundreds of billion Euros. Both figures will be communicated and substantiated in the SEA study currently conducted by EPPA.
Transitional period: the established substitution timelines (5 or 12 years) are tailored to technical substitution. They do not factor in regulatory timelines such as mandatory stability testing or re-submission of market authorisations for regulated products.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: The European Federation of Pharmaceutical Industries and Associations (EFPIA) represents the innovative pharmaceutical sector in Europe. We welcome the proposed time unlimited derogation for active substances in human medicinal products within the scope of Directive 2001/83.  The proposed derogation for active substances is part of necessary mitigation measures to prevent medicine shortage.

We are concerned that development and/or supply of medicines in the EU will be severely impacted by the PFAS Restriction as presently drafted, based on a broadened definition of “PFAS” and the wide applicability across many different uses. If implemented as proposed, production may become impossible in the long run. This concern is not only based on “missing uses” in the proposal, but rather on the scope of the restriction. It appears unbalanced and out of proportion in the following aspects:

Regulatory scope: the restriction proposal aims at substances and articles without derogating products where marketing is subject to specific regulations. For medicinal products and medical devices, these are granted market authorisations under Directive 2001/83, or permissions under the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR) or EU In Vitro Device Regulation (IVDR), respectively. Restricting products under marketing authorisation or permission causes regulatory conflicts.

Substance scope: the substance group PFAS as defined in the regulation has no common hazardous properties. Fluoropolymers, for example, are non-hazardous, most are considered polymers of low concern by the OECD and some have food contact approval. Persistence of either the substance itself or its degradation products is the property of concern, but PFAS with demonstrated degradability are not derogated as such, so it cannot be claimed to be a common property of the regulated group.

Definition: the long-term goal of reducing emissions can only be achieved by a global restriction of PFAS, such as under the Stockholm convention. To facilitate this process, the definition of “PFAS” should be aligned as much as possible. The U.S. EPA working definition published in the fifth contaminant candidate list (CCL5) may serve as a blueprint.

Restriction Scope: the current proposal restricts the use of materials with certain structural properties, while the goal should be to reduce emissions of persistent chemicals. A re-adjustment of the scope from use to emissions would allow for innovative concepts, such as fostering circularity in the industrial use of fluoropolymers.

Restriction Options: if Restriction Option 1 is applied, all chemical, pharmaceutical and biopharmaceutical manufacturing will have to move out of the EEA, as production and development depend on fluoropolymers and replacements are not available. Supply of medicines will be severely impacted, as approved active pharmaceutical ingredients (API) and medicines delivered within packaging and/or with drug delivery devices used to administer the medicinal products under market authorisation are in scope of the restriction.

The same is true, to a lesser degree, for Restriction Option 2. A socio-economic analysis (SEA) for the pharmaceutical industry/EFPIA prepared by EPPA (www.eppa.com) is provided in Annex 1.


Emissions depend on the use of the PFAS:

In case of fluoropolymer in industrial use, PFAS are still part of the equipment at its end of life, and emissions could be controlled. In case of use of PFAS as chemicals or auxiliaries in Manufacture/Storage/Transport and Quality Control, substances can be used under controlled conditions to minimise exposure to the lowest level possible.  The use of substances should not be restricted if the goal of the restriction can be reached by other means. This would apply, for instance, to fluoropolymers in industrial use under inventory and end-of-life management as outlined in Article 8 of the Restriction Proposal.

For packaging of medicinal products or medical devices, the emissions depend on local waste management. Most European countries have implemented incineration of medical or municipal waste or are moving towards this goal. The typical packaging use is a thin fluoropolymer film (PCTFE, ETFE or other) laminated with other plastics or elastomers, facilitating incineration. As published, PFAS could be mineralised when incinerated (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0045653519306435). It is recognised however that the member companies of EFPIA do not operate incineration installations and therefore defer to the information provided by the waste sector federation(s) on the effectiveness of incineration methods.

In the case of PFAS API, the emission resulting from patient use is assessed as part of the marketing authorisation of medicinal products in an Environmental Risk Assessment (ERA). Pharmaceutical initiatives (Pharmaceuticals in the Environment, Innovative Medicines Initiative PREMIER - https://imi-premier.eu/) aim at increasing the environmental compatibility of all API. In the case of unused PFAS API, disposal schemes are established and continually improved (https://medsdisposal.eu/about-us/).

Alternatives do not exist for API. Introduction of fluorine in the API molecule is an essential part of developing efficacious and safe candidates. Any changes to an API molecule would essentially require the development of a completely new candidate. Due to the unique properties of individual molecular structures containing fluorine, alternatives for API, development products and their starting materials and intermediates do not exist, as the function of the substances is on the chemical molecular level.

Alternatives for fluoropolymers in production, packaging and devices may exist in some cases. However, the sought-after properties are outstanding resistance against heat, light, chemicals, time and abrasion, which is naturally linked to persistence. This means that close evaluation of alternatives is needed, as they may result in unintended consequences within the production process and may be persistent, too. In manufacturing and packaging, the use of fluoropolymers is closely linked to other sustainability considerations (recyclability, long service life or shelf life, production or transport resources/emissions, energy considerations etc.). These environmental trade-offs are not regarded when only the chemical nature of the material is regulated.

Benefits of fluoropolymers in production, packaging and devices include thermal and chemical stability, smooth hard surfaces that are easily cleaned and disinfected, and outstanding barrier properties protecting products from air, moisture, impurities, extractables and particles. This safeguards the safety and quality of products throughout their shelf life.

Other SEA topics: the ban of PFAS API as proposed in Restriction Option 1 has an expected impact on the industry of tens of billion Euros. The ban on manufacturing materials as outlined in both Restriction Option has an industry impact of hundreds of billion Euros (EFPIA SEA (Annex 1)).

Transitional period: the established substitution timelines (5 or 12 years) are tailored to technical substitution. They do not factor in regulatory timelines such as mandatory stability testing or re-submission of market authorisations for regulated products.

Requests for exemption or derogation:

- A time-unlimited derogation for PFAS API as laid out in Restriction Option 2, to keep the products in question on the EEA market. Note: A ban would restrict patients' access to safe and approved medicine in Europe, for which there is no alternative. This would result in a shortage of medicinal products.

- A time-unlimited derogation of non-EU API (not registered under 2001/83) for export and development products (PPORD) to the scope of this derogation. A ban at any point in time moves production and/or R&D out of the EEA, and has patient impact when the supply chain is disrupted or clinical trials cannot be conducted in the EEA.

Limiting the derogation to industry sectors (food and feed in 6a, petroleum and mining 6f) causes issues with definitions and justification. Emission can be controlled in the industry, and are limited to the waste stage.

- A time-unlimited derogation for packaging material of medicinal products and sterile barrier systems for drug delivery devices as in 6.l in Restriction Option 2, containing any fluoropolymers with approval instead of PCTFE only. General overview on a medicines environmental risk assessment:    In the EU a prospective Environmental Risk Assessment (ERA) is required since 2006 (CPMP/SWP/4447/00, 2006) when a marketing authorisation application (MAA) is submitted for a new Medicinal Product to be placed on the market or where there is potential for significant increase in environmental concentrations as a result of modifications to existing marketing authorisations (MAs), such as the addition of new indications. The EMA has scientific guidance on Environmental risk assessment of medicinal products for human use: https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/environmental-risk-assessment-medicinal-products-human-use-scientific-guideline.      On the 26 April, the Commission adopted a proposal for a new Directive (Directive on the Union code relating to medicinal products for human use) and a new Regulation (Regulation laying down Union procedures for the authorisation and supervision of medicinal products for human use and establishing a European Medicines Agency, amending Regulation (EC) No 1394/2007 and Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 and repealing Regulation (EC) NO 726/2004, Regulation (EC) No 141/2000 and Regulation (EC) No 1901/2006), which revise and replace the existing general pharmaceutical legislation.   As part of this revision, the Commission proposes to strengthen the ERA requirements by:   - Refusal of a Marketing Authorisation based on environment concerns.  - Manufacturing included in the environmental risk assessment of antimicrobials.  - Prioritisation of ERA for legacy active pharmaceutical ingredients, which were placed on the market before 2006.  - Increased interlinkage across non-pharma legislations.  - Restrictions on hazardous medicinal products.   As part of the revision, the industry (trade associations EFPIA, AESGP and Medicines for Europe) has proposed an extended environmental risk assessment (eERA) (https://www.efpia.eu/media/677261/interassociation-paper-on-extended-environmental-risk-assessment.pdf).    In summary the eERA aims to provide the following benefits:   - An API based ERA which better reflects the risks posed to environment from patient use.  - Strengthen the industry’s commitment to conduct robust and risk-based ERAs without compromising environmental protection or patient access to medicines.  - Provision for the ability to automatically cross-reference ERA data in marketing authorisation applications.   - Provide a mechanism for risk identification, refinement, and management during the MAA evaluation process .  - Provide clarity on appropriate well-defined follow-up responsibilities for ERAs with no need for independent and duplicative risk identification and prioritisation processes under different legislations (e.g. Water Framework Directive) .  - Updates to the ERA across the life cycle of the API in each MP in which it is contained that will ensure that each ERA reflects the latest environmental information.   - A focus on risk that reduces the burden on regulators (i.e. oversight) and industry.   - Reduction in the duplication of testing, delivering improved ERA consistency, proportionate use of testing resource, and bioethical benefits .  - Suggestions for mechanisms to increase the transparency of, and access to, ERA data.

An example of the impact to analytical testing would be the multiple components of an HPLC (High Performance Liquid Chromatography) system that are made of polymeric PFAS that enable analyses to be executed in a way that minimizes loss of compounds during analysis. In addition, there are a significant number of developmental, registered, and compendial HPLC methods (European pharmacopeia and other global compendia) that utilize trifluoroacetic acid as part of the mobile phase used for analysis. A primary source of PFAS in analytical are in the instruments and the vendors need to define and implement alternatives.  Additionally, the amount of time and personnel to successfully navigate any post-approval changes for registered methods would be significant to enable the development of new medicines as well as ensuring adequate supply of approved medicines. General Comments: The European materials handling industry manufactures technical equipment and systems delivering organisational solutions for complex production, storage and logistics requirements. Our companies support a sustainable logistic transformation and contribute directly to Europe’s green transition. Their personal commitment to reducing their environmental footprint takes various forms, amongst which a wide electrification process of their products.

PFAS are present in a variety of parts and components of all types of materials handling equipment. This is notably the case of hydraulic components where PFAS are found in seals, pipes, fittings, hoses, bearings and sliding elements, pumps and motors. Other uses include sealings in gearboxes, cooling agent in air conditioning systems, and binder/separator in Li-Ion batteries.

There are many more PFAS uses than those mentioned above. However, it is near to impossible to establish an exhaustive list because of the combined effect of, on the one hand, value chains’ complexity and materials handling equipment manufacturers position therein, and, on the other hand, identification issues due to insufficient harmonised classification of PFAS in the CLP Regulation.

The reasons behind such a widespread use are well-known, pertaining to PFAS’ unique and cumulative properties, such as performance, high temperature and oil resistance, chemical/electromechanical stability, sliding properties, high power density, etc. These properties are essential to materials handling equipment’s safe and efficient operation. According to our first findings, there are no or no comparable alternatives on the market capable to meeting those cumulative requirements for relevant uses in the materials handling industry.

Implementing a blanket ban without any differentiation would, as a direct consequence, essentially deprive our industry from components that are essential to produce materials handling equipment. Without suitable alternatives, this could simply put production chains to a halt, threatening our industry’s core business.

Given the materials handling industry’s enabling role, whether in production and distribution facilities, or to ensure logistic flows, indirect consequences would also be felt in many other sectors., some of which are absolutely critical, such as retail, food or health.

A risk-based and substance-based approach must be followed across the whole life cycle (including manufacturing and end-of-life stage) so that the actual risk of specific substances in each phase is the main driver for potential regulation, also taking into account the availability of alternatives that are suitable from a technical, economic and environment/health protection point of view.
In the absence of analytical and extraction method for PFAS and their uses, an information obligation for “intentionally added” PFAS should be introduced before any restriction is applied.
Given the time required to develop and approve alternatives that are suitable from a technical and safety point of view, and compliant with applicable EU regulatory requirements, much longer transition periods, of minimum 10 years, depending on the types of PFAS and their related use(s), should be provided.
Given the sheer number of substances and affected products, adequate market surveillance resources should be deployed to ensure proper enforcement of the future requirements.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Spare parts and refurbished parts should be excluded from the restriction, in line with Green Deal ambitions (e.g. Right to Repair) and to avoid premature obsolescence of many finished products.  Products already placed on the EU market for the first time should also be excluded from the restriction to allow them to be resold, repaired and maintained. General Comments: The European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity (ENTSO-E) represents 39 European Transmission System Operators (TSOs) from 35 countries. ENTSO-E is committed to collaborating with European authorities in gradually replacing the usage of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). ENTSO-E welcomes the European Chemicals Agency’s (ECHA) consultation, published on 22 March 2023, which seeks input on the draft restriction of PFAS proposed by Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden and Norway.

TSOs build and operate the critical power grid infrastructure to supply electricity to European industry and citizens. TSOs make sure to keep the environmental impact of the grid to a minimum and even enhance nature restoration and biodiversity in their corridors. PFAS may pose an environmental and health risk to the neighbouring and more distant populations, including to the workforce in grid operation and should be avoided whenever possible. Working towards PFAS-free grid equipment wherever possible is thus a goal shared by European TSOs and European Authorities.

The sophisticated high and extra high voltage equipment used in power grids is built to last 40+ years. It is designed to operate and withstand extraordinary and harsh conditions, such as high pressure, extreme voltage levels and temperatures, and to guarantee the functioning and resilience of the grid at any time. The use of PFAS in solid, liquid, and gaseous components of grid equipment is determined by manufacturers to ensure the highest requirements for its performance and reliability.

A restriction that does not take into account network-specific use cases could lead to the unavailability of critical assets and, thus, to unpredictable effects with regard to system security.

Due to a lack of data, TSOs do not yet have a comprehensive overview of the use of PFAS in the components of their electrical equipment, nor the PFAS used to manufacture this equipment. Furthermore, there is also insufficient information on possible alternatives to replace them. European TSOs are committed to protecting the public and workforce wherever risks stemming from PFAS are identified. Therefore, ENTSO-E would like to highlight typical use cases for PFAS where information exists and stress the need for use case-specific derogations in the restriction proposal in case no alternatives are available.

General Comments: The European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) https://home.cern/  is an intergovernmental Organization established in 1954.  The Organization has its seat in Geneva, but its site straddles the Franco-Swiss border.
CERN is funded by 23, mostly European, Member States, and its mission is to provide for collaboration in particle physics research of a pure scientific and fundamental character and in research essentially related thereto. At present, more than 10 000 scientific users from research institutes all over the world are using CERN’s installations for their experiments. To this end, it designs, builds and operates particle accelerators. CERNs flagship accelerator, the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) was approved in 1994 and went into operation in 2009. The LHC is part of a large complex of accelerators. Following a major upgrade to be completed around 2035 (High Luminosity LHC – HL-LHC), it is set to operate until the mid- 2040s.
The LHC serves several experiments, among them four worldwide scientific collaborations that use giant detectors to study particle collisions produced by the accelerator. These detectors were designed and built at the same time than the LHC.
CERNs scientific activities rely on the availability of efficient and reliable particle detection systems, i.e. particle detectors and associated cooling systems, that must operate in a particularly harsh environment of very low temperature and high ionizing radiation fields. These detection systems use F-gases (cf. section 6). Despite an extensive R&D program, focusing on the recirculation and recuperation of gases and more environmentally friendly particle detection solutions, no viable alternative can currently be implemented for this specific use.

CERNs operation further implies the use of various cooling systems using F-gases, such as hundreds of chiller units and heat pumps. For these units, CERN has already started to replace HFC by HFO to be in line with Kigali amendment.  Given the number of installations concerned and the fact that their refurbishment can only take place during extended maintenance periods (2 years every 5-6 years), this transition will take at least 12 years.  The cost of the refurbishment is currently estimated at least 50MCHF.

In the light of the above CERN requests the following to be considered for the future regulation:
- CERN research activities require an exclusion of F-gas restrictions until the end of the current physics program linked to the operation of HL-LHC, provided alternative detector technologies for future research programs are available in due time.
An additional derogation for research activities and, in particular particle detection and related cooling is required in this context.
- A clarification of scope and harmonization of objectives would also be welcome with respect to the current initiative and F-Gas Regulation EU No 517/2014. This would avoid un-necessary ambiguities and uncertainties.
