General Comments: The German Hospital Federation is the umbrella organisation of hospital operators in Germany. It represents the interests of its 28 members – 16 state associations and 12 central associations – in the Federal Republic of Germany and performs tasks assigned to it by law. The 1,887 hospitals treat about 17 million inpatients and about 21 million outpatients annually. With an annual turnover of 127 billion euros, German hospitals are an important economic factor in the growth market of healthcare.

The Annex XV Restriction Report stipulates that PFAS may only be used in areas where no suitable alternatives will be available in the foreseeable future or where the socio-economic advantages outweigh the disadvantages for humans and the environment. Time-unlimited, general derogations are envisaged, for example, for PFAS used as active substances in Plant Protection Products (PPP), Biocidal Products (BP) and human and veterinary Medicinal Products (MP).

We understand the concern behind the planned ban process and support the initiative to keep the use of PFASs to a minimum. However, we see that the use of PFASs in many products will be banned as part of the planned restriction process because it cannot be proven that equivalent alternatives do not exist or can be developed during the derogation period that may be granted.

Therefore, we suggest that, an impact analysis would be conducted before a final ban would be carried out, outlining the consequences  of discontinuing the products under discussion

Many of the products addressed in the Restriction Report that use PFASs in the development or manufacture are also used in hospitals. For the sake of simplicity, however, we would like to focus at this point on the medical devices that are intended for a ban according to the Restriction Report. These are predominantly used in hospitals and are indispensable for patient care. The discontinuation of these medical devices would lead to a catastrophic deterioration in patient care, and this against the background that it is already foreseeable that many medical devices will no longer be available on the market in the foreseeable future due to the high requirements of the MDR.

Hospitals are already feeling the effects of the MDR: if, on the one hand, rare medical devices / niche products and, on the other hand, proven, established existing products disappear from the market, this will have a significant impact on medical care. Hospitals are threatened with supply bottlenecks and obstacles to innovation. An additional loss of medical devices due to a PFAS ban would exacerbate the problem.

Against this background, the derogation periods until a ban (max. 12 years) are also to be regarded as insufficient, as the current situation shows that a prolongation of the medical device certificates takes years and a new certification is required in the case of a change to a medical device, which appears to be completely impossible within the specified period, since flawless, rule-compliant and reliable alternatives to PFAS must first be sought and tested.

Despite all our understanding of the effects of PFAS cumulating in the environment, we advocate that the use of PFAS in the manufacture of medical devices should not be banned until it is also certain that alternatives can be found and that the products can be recertified within the derogation period. The waiver of many medical devices would set back patient care by decades.

6. Missing uses: We refer to our general comments. Many of the products affected by a PFAS ban are also used in hospitals, especially medical devices. A discontinuation of these products, either because no adequate alternative to PFAS can be found during the transition period, or because the derogation period for the development of a PFAS alternative and re-certification of the device under the MDR is not sufficient, would have disastrous effects on patient care, which must be prevented at all costs.  We therefore demand that, before a PFAS is finally banned, an impact analysis be carried out to determine whether the ban will mean that a particular medical device will have to be withdrawn from the market and how this elimination of the medical device will affect patient care. If no comparable device from another manufacturer is available on the market, the PFAS ban shall not apply for the device in question.  In addition, we propose a declaration obligation for PFAS, also in order to be able to carry out such an impact analysis at all. Furthermore, the users would then also be informed about the use of PFAS during the manufacturing process and could, if necessary, look for alternative devices themselves or demand them (sustainable purchasing).

Content: Information on alternatives Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The Halon Alternatives Research Corporation (HARC) appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on an Annex XV Report that proposes a restriction on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) under REACH. HARC is a non-profit trade association that serves as an information clearinghouse and focal point for cooperation between government and industry on issues of importance to special hazard fire protection. HARC members encompass all levels of the fire protection industry including agent manufacturers, equipment manufacturers, distributors/installers, recyclers, and end-users.

Need for a time-unlimited derogation for clean fire suppressing agents

HARC supports the proposal in the Annex XV report for a derogation for clean fire suppressing agents. The information contained in the Annex XV report and its annexes along with detailed information submitted in response to the calls for evidence provide ample justification for such a derogation. The Annex XV report acknowledges that alternatives for many important uses of clean fire suppressing agents do not currently exist and are not in development. We understand the dossier submitters are assuming that 13.5 years is enough time for alternatives to be identified and developed, and while that may be a reasonable assumption for many uses of PFAS, it is unlikely to be the case for clean agent fire suppression.

The search for not-in-kind alternatives began over 30 years ago in anticipation of halon production for fire protection being phased out in the EU and other developed countries. It has continued with the regulation of HFC production and use. There is no indication or expectation within the fire protection community that new non-PFAS alternatives will suddenly be discovered. There have been strong economic and regulatory incentives to develop such products for many years. Millions of euros and extensive time has been spent in identifying, testing, and ruling out candidate alternatives before those now in use were commercialized. As all known candidate clean agent chemical groups have already been researched, discovering alternatives that are zero ODP, low GWP, and non-PFAS is highly unlikely.

As there will almost certainly be enduring critical uses of fluorinated clean agents well beyond 13.5 years after EiF, it will be necessary to include a time-unlimited derogation for clean fire suppressing agents in the PFAS restriction.

The use of fluorinated clean agents is small and decreasing, the emissions are low, and the rate of recycle is high. As such, the impact of a time-unlimited derogation for clean fire suppressing agents on overall emissions of PFAS should be relatively small.

Need for revised wording of the derogation for clean fire suppressing agents

The current wording of the clean fire suppressing agents derogation does not adequately reflect the multiple reasons that a non-PFAS alternative may not work in any specific fire or explosion hazard situation. While damage to assets and risk to human health are clearly important parameters, there are others including speed of extinguishment, time required for agent discharge, weight of the agent and equipment, and space required for the agent and equipment. Any of these factors, alone or in combination, can impact whether an alternative is suitable to protect a specific hazard.

One constant across all sectors of fire protection is the requirement to meet safety requirements such as those given in EN, ISO, NFPA, EASA and ASTM standards. In addition, fire suppression systems and agents are generally required to be listed by an approval agency such as LPCB, CNPP, VdS, BSI or CNBOP to EN standards. HARC would recommend incorporating the requirement to meet safety standards into the derogation by using the same wording as the prohibition on HFCs for fire suppression in the revised F-gas regulation. We believe this is appropriate as both regulations would cover some of the same clean agents. Tying the derogation only to situations where alternatives do not meet safety standards would significantly limit the size of the derogation.

Proposed time-unlimited derogation for clean fire suppressing agents

Column 2, 5.m. clean fire suppressing agents where required to meet safety standards

Justification for a derogation for clean fire suppressing agents

HARC commends the dossier submitters for the review of clean agent fire suppression contained in the Annex XV report and it’s annexes. They provide an accurate description of the need for halogenated clean agents for applications critical to society such as aviation, military, and telecommunications. They also correctly note the lack of current alternatives and alternatives in development. Below are excerpts from the Annex XV report and background documents that provide justification for a derogation for clean fire suppressing agents:

Annex XV Report, page 10

5m) The derogation applies to fire-suppressing agents in the form of fluorinated gases used for extinguishing fires in high-risk situations where alternatives pose significant risk to health or the assets to be protected. These situations may include aviation, data centres and cultural/historic resources. Such agents are different from fire-fighting foams which are aqueous mixtures.

Annex XV Report, Table 8, RO1

Alternatives available, but for some applications they have a range of drawbacks, for example risk of asphyxiation (e.g. CO2), potential to damage protected assets (e.g. water), slower speed of action than fluorinated gases. Critical applications include aviation and military vehicles.

Price already provides a mechanism favouring alternatives to fluorinated gases and has led to a significant shift in the market where they are not considered necessary. Remaining users which include safety critical applications such as fire prevention on aircraft and in military vehicles, and protection of cultural assets, consider the benefits of fluorinated gases sufficient to accept higher prices indicating potential for significant consumer surplus losses. [sufficiently strong evidence].

High substitution potential at EiF for some uses [sufficiently strong evidence] and low substitution potential at EiF for other applications [sufficiently strong evidence].

Annex XV Report, Table 8, RO2

Given the sufficiently strong evidence indicating the unavailability of alternatives at EiF for some applications, a derogation is proposed for: “clean fire suppressing agents where current alternatives damage the assets to be protected or pose a risk to human health”

Ban with a transition period of 18 months and a 12-year derogation, because the information provided in the consultation suggests the unavailability of alternatives. Current R&D development appears to focus on alternative fluorinated gases, rather than on non-PFAS alternatives [weak evidence base].


Annex XV Report, page 152

Potential alternatives are available, however, there are drawbacks (e.g. they can cause health effects, or may destroy equipment, or are not considered clean) and therefore fluorinated gases used as fire suppressants are not easily replaceable in the short-term.

Exponent F-gas Report, page 5

Such alternatives are available in some cases, but not all, including some ‘essential uses’ such as health care and fire control.

Exponent F-gas Report, page 13

In certain specialised situations, such as electronic fires affecting data centres, or museums containing sensitive cultural heritage, fast acting and ‘clean’ (i.e. non-residue forming) fire suppressants are required in order not to damage the items in the area in which they are used.

Criteria considered when determining the most appropriate fire suppressant for any application include a variety of factors such as local climate (temperature and pressure), occupation of the area to be protected, the type of asset to be protected, the type of combustible material present and the availability of a water supply.

The relevant Technical Committee to the Montreal Protocol notes significant problems in identifying alternatives that provide the same functionality as F-gas fire suppressants.

Exponent F-gas Report, page 14

Several options are available on the market, including the use of inert gases (nitrogen and argon), CO2, water mist technologies, inert gas generators, fine solid particle technology, dry chemical agents, water and aqueous salt solutions. However, these have several limitations:
• Several are not clean
• They tend to take longer to extinguish fires than F-gas equivalents
• Some are hazardous to health and cannot be used where there is a risk of human exposure

The problem of substituting away from F-gases in this sector is highlighted by continued use of substances that are not permitted for use in other sectors on account of their climate and other burdens.

Future Submission

HARC intends to submit additional information prior to the September 2023 comment deadline justifying the need for a time-unlimited derogation for clean fire suppressing agents and discussing the implications for future use and emissions of PFAS.

We are submitting this preliminary comment now to inform the dossier submitters and RAC/SEAC of this issue.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: The Hessian Ministry of the Environment, Climate Protection, Agriculture and Consumer Protection is increasingly concerned about the irreversible pollution of the environment with per- and polyfluorinated alkyl compounds (PFAS). Extensive data as well as contaminated sites show that the production of PFAS chemicals as well as the production, use and disposal of products containing PFAS lead to an increasing and ubiquitous impact on the environment. In Hesse the monitoring results of soils, ground and surface waters as investigated by the Hessian authorities show an extensive contamination with PFAS. The data includes results from the monitoring of ground and surface waters as well as results collected in context with contaminated sites where water or soil samples were analysed for PFAS compounds. The data can be found on the webpage of the Hessian Agency for Nature Conservation, Environment and Geology (https://www.hlnug.de/themen/wasser/fliessgewaesser/fliessgewaesser-chemie/spurenstoffe/pfas and
https://www.hlnug.de/themen/altlasten/altlastenschwerpunkte/pfc-per-und-polyfluorierte-chemikalien).
These pollutions already result in a problematic concentration of PFAS in various foods and in human blood serum. As a result, in many places problematic situations have arisen for the environment and human health, which lead to costly analysis, remediation and recommendation of consumption restrictions. This is illustrated by the results of the PFAS wildlife monitoring carried out by Hessian authorities. The data include a unique evidence of the specific exposure of different Hessian wild animals to PFAS. They show that ubiquitous exposure to PFAS alone has already led to irreversible damage and prevents the safe consumption of regional wildlife, in particular wildboar and freshwater fishes. The monitoring results collected by the Hessian State Laboratory from 2020 to the beginning of 2023 (Results - PFAS wildlife monitoring in Hesse_2020-1_2023.xlsx), as well as the summary report (summary report - PFAS wildlife monitoring in Hesse.pdf) can be found in the compressed archive in SECTION IV.
The Hessian Ministry of the Environment, Climate Protection, Agriculture and Consumer Protection considers the REACH restriction for the entire PFAS substance group with more than 10.000 individual substances as a historic opportunityto reduce the ubiquitous pollution with PFAS drastically. On such a scale, the Hessian Ministry of the Environment, Climate Protection, Agriculture and Consumer Protection does not consider it useful to continue to regulate only individual substances, as there is a risk of substitution by other non-regulated but also harmful individual substances of the same group (regrettable substitutions). In Hesse, various scientific work and research campaigns took place in the recent years to investigate the PFAS burden of the state. Studies of various environmental matrices, products and food show that the ubiquitous exposure to PFAS has already led to irreversible damage, preventing the safe consumption of food produced in the state of Hesse in some cases. It should be taken into account that most of the available studies so far only search for individual PFAS substances (usually by the analytical method LC-MS/MS). The majority of the PFAS-group cannot be found, even though it is present in a sample. The Hessian Ministry of the Environment, Climate Protection, Agriculture and Consumer Protection therefore tries to support the development and establishment of various analytical methods to determine PFAS-sum-parameters to solve this problem. The use of summary analysis (sum parameters) is the only way to analyse PFAS or their degradation products as a whole group of compounds and get a scope of their real impact to human health and the environment.
The Hessian Ministry of the Environment, Climate Protection, Agriculture and Consumer Protection expects the restriction proposal to provide incentives for a rapid transition to PFAS-free alternatives, especially for everyday products. Although suitable alternatives are already established on the market, PFAS are even used in coffee-to-go cups and other street food packaging intended for single-use applications. Exceptions to a PFAS restriction should only apply to a few strictly necessary uses for which there are no alternatives yet. On behalf of the Hessian Ministry of the Environment, Climate Protection, Agriculture and Consumer Protection the Hessian State Laboratory and the Goethe University Frankfurt, investigated if food contact materials sold in Hesse contain PFAS using various analytical methods. The studies show how fluorinated compounds can be identified in the products and that none of the investigated migrates were inconspicuous in terms of biological activity. A summary of the investigations carried out and their results (PFAS in food contact materials.pdf) can be found in the compressed archive in SECTION IV. Studies carried out in Hesse also show that the hazards resulting from the persistence of PFAS also apply to fluoropolymers. The degradation and mobilisation of dangerous substances as well as resulting harmful biological effects demonstrate the studies that can be found in the compressed archive in SECTION IV.

Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Adsorbable organically bound fluorine (AOF) method development and investigation results: In the Hessian State Laboratory, an analytical method has been developed as part of a PhD at the Justus Liebig University in Giessen. With the AOF PFAS can be measured as the sum of organically bounded fluorine. The new method is particularly suitable for water samples – especially wastewater. Org. name: The hydrogen and fuel cell center (ZBT)
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The Hydrogen and Fuel Cell Center ZBT welcomes the foundational endeavor to employ PFAS in an ecologically conscientious manner, with the aim of safeguarding human well-being and natural environment. However, a de facto impediment to the deployment of pivotal environmental technologies (and the PFAS containing components necessary for them) that are indispensable for ensuring a sustainable and reliable energy provision must be avoided. Here, a holistic view along the value chain from H2 production (electrolysis), transport, storage and refueling to the reconversion of hydrogen into electricity (fuel cells) is necessary.

Particular PFAS materials, specifically PFSA ionomers and ePTFE, remain essential components in energy and hydrogen applications. Electrolyzers and fuel cells are needed for sustainable energy supply within the EU's "Fit for 55" initiative: 10 million tons of green hydrogen are the annual production target to be reached by 2030. This implies an electrolysis capacity of 100 GW by 2030 for the European hydrogen sector. This makes upscaling of electrolysis production is imperative and urgent. For this upscaling, there are currently no alternatives to the PFAS materials required in electrolyzers and fuel cells. Proton conducting membranes, reinforcement meshes, electrodes, and gas diffusion layers rely on PFSA ionomers and ePTFE.

PFAS-free alternatives are subject of laboratory scale research, but their technical maturity may require as long as 25 years, if achievable at all. The suggested PFAS bans or excessively short derogation periods (like the proposed period of 5 years + 18 months for PEMFC application) in the Restrictions Proposal, pose a significant threat to the entire green hydrogen sector, which is vital for the attainment of the European Union's climate goals.

Our Recommendations:

- Include all hydrogen applications/sectors (fuel cells, electrolysis, storage, refueling & transport) in the "essential uses" section:
→ considered as an exception category
→ exemptions until appropriate affordable, environmentally friendly alternatives are available
→ regular review of the status quo of alternative materials and industrial feasibility

- compelling need for a substantial intensification of research efforts of alternative materials for PFSA ionomers (perfluorosulfonic acid – a proton conducting material)

- take-back obligation for products containing PFAS (e.g. fuel cell and electrolysis stacks)

- establish recycling system: Circular economy of PFSA ionomers (and PGM – Iridium and Platinum)

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Energy sector (Annex E.2.12.): Sector as a whole Proton-exchange membrane (PEM) fuel cells

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Use Phase: PFAS emissions in the water during the use of fluoropolymer-containing components in state-of-the-art electrolyzers and fuel cell stacks are so far assumed negligible. However, more detailed quantitative studies of such emissions with state-of-the-art materials under real-world conditions are needed. In the following, we provide an estimate of possible emissions based on older studies at older generations of materials.  In 2005 and 2009,  Healy et al. (Ref. 1) and Carlsson et al. (Ref. 2), respectively, studied the degradation products of PEMFC membranes (composed of PFSA ionomer) in fuel cells under operation. They found traces of PFSA side chain fragments by means of HPLC, MS, and F19 NMR. Those fragments were released during radical-induced mineralization (degradation) of the main chain (to CO2, H2O and HF).  In long-term measurements, Healy et al. (Ref. 1) determined a fluoride release rate of 1 x 10 8 g(F )/(h cm2) for a 15-cell stack under mild conditions. Extrapolating this rate to an automotive stack comprising 280 cells, each with an active area of 300 cm² (total: 84,000 cm²), the cumulative fluoride emissions amount to approximately 6.72 g after 8,000 h (equivalent to a driving distance of 300,000 – 400,000 km). According to the basic structure of Nafion (EW 1100) (Ref. 3), the molar ratio of ‘main chain fluoride’ to a ‘PFSA side chain’ is 31.4 : 1. If we make the assumption that the release of 31.4 fluoride ions (due to the mineralization of the main chain to CO2, H2O, and HF; “Backbone unzipping”) results in the release (without further mineralization) of one side chain (M = 342 g/mol), then we can estimate an approximate quantity of 3.85 g of PFSA side chain material to be emitted over an operating time of 8,000 h. Emissions from state-of-the-art systems should be even lower, because modern membranes are significantly more stable against degradation, e.g. due to the addition of radical scavengers.  Thorough quantitative analyses of product water from state-of-the-art PEMFC stacks are imperative to measure their level of PFSA fragment emissions. Based on these findings, additional technical measures can be developed to remove possible PFSA traces from the (fuel cell) product water.  End of life phase: The current standard is to incinerate fluoropolymers (e.g. PTFE and PFSA from gaskets, membranes and CCMs) at the end of their life and to treat the exhaust gases. This method can be considered a safe option for now, given that the exhaust emissions undergo meticulous processing, adhering to the highest standards and aligning with both EU and local regulations. Moreover, Aleksandrov et al. (Ref. 4) report that there is no evidence supporting the persistence of PFAS following incineration under these specific conditions. Page 419 of the Annex to the ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT states: “Information on emissions at the end of life of products is sparse, but it is the Dossier Submitters understanding that recycling of PEM fuel cells and electrolyzers is difficult and currently focused on recovering metal. Therefore, it is expected that PFAA and polymeric PFAS parts will be landfilled or incinerated, causing emissions during the end-of-life phase.”  The high costs of noble metals (Ir and Pt) and PFSA ionomers will naturally favor recycling and recovery over incineration or landfilling. Research by us and others demonstrates that recycling is feasible.  Xu et al. performed acid treatment of PEMFC CCMs (catalyst coated membranes) to produce recycled Nafion membranes with only small performance losses (Ref. 5): „The acid treatment approach to recycling the key materials of MEA (Membrane Electrode Assemblies) is simple and high efficient. The catalyst support (carbon black) was oxidized by the acid, and about 95% Pt as well as almost all the Nafion can be recycled. The fuel cell performance of the recycled Nafion is close to that of the pristine Nafion.“ In addition, Carmo et al. also showed promising results in relation to CCM recycling (Ref. 6): “We report the development of a facile recycling process for catalyst coated membranes (CCMs) used in polymer electrolyte membrane (PEM) water electrolyzers. After performance evaluation in an assembled electrolysis cell, ultrasonication is used to provide high-yield recovery of not only the noble-metal catalyst materials, but also of the fluoropolymer membrane itself, without the release of hazardous gases. […] A positive net benefit for nearly all CCM fabrication streams, very high recycling rates (>90%) and minimal loss in performance were obtained.” […] However, large amounts of collected PFSA membranes will not only prove beneficial to the environment, but also provide low-cost recovery of expensive membrane chemistry to be used as ionomers in the catalyst layer.”   Our institute (ZBT) studied the recyclability of PFSA ionomer from complete MEAs, i.e., real components of a PEM fuel cell, on behalf of an industry partner (3M/DYNEON). MEAs, including gas diffusion layers (GDL), were immersed in a water-isopropanol mixture (20 vol% isopropanol) while being stirred at 80 °C. The outcome was the separation of electrodes, dispersion of catalyst layers, and an optically pristine membrane.  In a first approach, the membrane was dispersed in DMSO at about 160 °C in a nitrogen atmosphere, resulting in a homogenous PFSA dispersion (alongside the ePTFE membrane reinforcement). This dispersion was then cast into new films or membranes with nearly unaltered proton conductivity. In the second approach, a non-reinforced membrane was cut into small pieces and then hot-pressed at 140-225 °C and 50 kN for 10 minutes. Again, the proton conductivity remained almost unaffected. Hence, PFSA ionomer can be effectively extracted from complex components and recycled via both dispersion and melting approaches, recovering virtually 100% of the original functionality.  Similarly, publicly funded projects indicate the reprocessing and reuse of PFSA ionomers and aim to advance this approach. The reusability of PFSA ionomer at the end of its lifecycle was demonstrated in the Frankenstack project (UK Research and Innovation) (Ref. 7): “FRANKENSTACK - Investigated re-using components of the ‘stack’ at the heart of hydrogen-producing electrolyzers, to reduce costs and open up new business models. The team built a ‘frankenstack’ using recycled components at 29% of the materials cost of a new stack, with average performance only 2% lower.”  Two projects (BReCycle and BEST4Hy) founded by Clean Hydrogen Partnership aim to develop end-of-life recycling for hydrogen technologies: • BReCycle project (2020 – 2023 | €1.5 million) (Ref. 8):  The aim of the project is to develop an efficient process for the reprocessing of fuel cells with which high-quality material fractions can be generated, in particular from the electrode coatings, and the polymer membranes can be safely separated. A general increase in the recyclability of fuel cells and the promotion of the use of secondary materials in the interest of resource conservation is being pursued.  • BEST4Hy project (2021-2023 | €1.5 million) (Ref. 9):  The aim of the project is to bring recycling approaches for PEMFC to TRL 5 and to demonstrate a high recovery yield of ionomers (80%), and the re-use of least 70% of ionomer for new cells/stacks.

5. Proposed derogations: PEM fuel cells: the ionomer requirement for a vehicle with a 100 KW PEMFC stack is 500 g. Hence, for 100,000 PEMFC vehicles (cumulative PEMFC power of 10,000 MW), a total of about 52.5 t PFAS ionomer would be required. Assumptions (PEM fuel cell stack): Voltage single cell: 0.65 V | current density: 2 A/cm² | membrane thickness: 22.5 µm |95 % of membrane is within the active area | Ionomer density: 0.20 kg / m² | Ionomer loading for anode / cathode: 1.0 mg/cm²    Electrolysis: the EU intends to grow electrolysis capacity by 17.5 GW annually (REPowerEU plan). This requires about 100 GW of electrolysis capacity by 2030, which would enable the production of 10 million tons of green H2 in 2030. Achieving 100 GW of electrolysis capacity via PEM technology would require 344 tons of PFSA ionomer. Assumptions (PEM electrolysis stack): Voltage single cell: 2.0 V | current density: 3 A/cm² | membrane thickness: 80 µm | 87 % of membrane is within the active area | active area per cell: 850 cm² | Ionomer density: 0.20 kg / m² | Ionomer loading for anode / cathode: 1.0 mg/cm²

6. Missing uses: PFAS materials are without alternatives for the development of the green hydrogen sector, which is essential to the European Green Deal. They are required for the production of H2 (PEM electrolysis) and its utilization for electricity generation (PEM fuel cell). Due to the similarity of PEM fuel cells and PEM electrolysis, corresponding details are discussed together in sections 2, 5, and 8. Apart from production and use of H2, it is also important to consider PFAS materials that are currently required for the H2 transport, storage and refueling.

8. Other identified uses: Alternatives to PFSA ionomers in membranes (PEM fuel cells and electrolysis): For decades, research has been ongoing in the field of hydrocarbon membranes (e.g. sulfonated polyphenylene sulfone (sPPS), polyetheretherketone (PEEK), or  polyarylene membranes) to replace PFSA ionomers (Ref. 10–13). While specific properties of hydrocarbons membranes may be very promising (e.g. proton conductivity), their durability is nowhere near the technical requirements. They are chemically attacked by hydroxy radicals (●OH) and hydroperoxy radicals (●OOH), which in turn originate from the degradation of H2O2. H2O2 is an omnipresent by-product of either fuel cell or electrolysis operations. PFAS-based membranes are sufficiently stable against those radical attacks, but so far no non-PFAS membrane achieved the durability thresholds for fuel cell applications (> 8,000 h for automotive; > 25,000 h for heavy-duty) or for electrolysis use (> 50,000 h). The notions pertaining to non-PFSA membranes primarily exist in the realms of laboratory or pilot-scale experimentation, lacking substantiation at an industrial magnitude and remaining in a nascent developmental stage. If at all achievable, industrial feasibility could transpire within a timeframe of 15 to 25 years. Thus, the proposed derogation period of 5 years + 18 month for PFAS ionomers as outlined in the restriction proposal, will seriously jeopardize the use of PEM fuel cells and PEM electrolyzers, which are imperative for the realization of the European Union's climate objectives.  The insufficient resilience of hydrocarbon membranes for PEM fuel cells and PEM electrolysis was reported in various publications and publicly funded research projects: Lai et al. showed that the examined hydrocarbon membrane exhibited a lifespan reduced by a factor ranging from 11 to 17 in comparison to commercial PFSA membranes (PEMFC application)(Ref.14): “Using the humidity cycling test described above, we compared four membranes: one noncommercial partially fluorinated hydrocarbon membrane and three commercial PFSA membranes, the homogeneous DuPont™ NR-111, the homogeneous Ion Power™ N111-IP, and the composite Gore™ GoreSelect® membranes. Significantly different crossover leak progression as a function of the number of humidity cycles was found, […]. Defining 10SCCM (SCCM denotes cubic centimeter per minute at STP) crossover as failure, NR-111 failed after about 4500cycles⁠, whereas there was no detectable leak in the N111-IP membrane even beyond 20,000cycles⁠. The composite Gore™ Primea® MEA failed between 6000cycles and 7000cycles⁠. On the other hand, the hydrocarbon membrane failed after only about 400cycles⁠. It should be noted that a wide variety of hydrocarbon proton-conductive membranes, with glass transition temperatures well above the test temperature, were tested with similar results.“ Such membrane leakage (gas crossover) not only reduces performance, but also poses a significant safety risk, as H2 and air can mix in the event of major membrane damage. Gubler et al. highlighted that numerous polyarylene membranes (PFSA free) also examined across various studies on proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) exhibited significantly heightened vulnerability to leakage (Ref. 10): “In all of these studies [referring to references 4, 6, 33, 34 of this publication (Ref. 10)], the homogeneous polyarylene membranes started leaking at or before the 20,000 RH cycle target, which is much earlier than state-of-the-art PFSA membranes.35” Alavijeh et al. compared the mechanical properties of hydrocarbon and commercial PFSA-containing membranes as membrane durability in wet-dry cycles is very important for PEMFC application not only in terms of lifetime but also for safety reasons. They demonstrated a notable susceptibility of hydrocarbon membranes to membrane damage due to swelling and shrinkage, which is further intensified by the application of a mandatory electrode layer onto the membrane surface (Ref. 15): “The hydrocarbon [HC] membranes analyzed in this work showed large residual stresses (severe contraction) during confined shrinkage at 80 °C that exceeded their yield stress, and are therefore deemed prone to failure after repeated wet-dry cycles. […] For the HC membranes at 80 °C, on the other hand, the addition of catalyst layers caused further reduction in elongation and increased shrinkage. The “contracting” behavior of the HC membranes was thus escalated in the presence of catalyst layers, which may limit the membrane’s ability to recover from shrinkage and further aggravate the constrained shrinkage stress, […].” Klose et al. investigated membrane electrode assemblies (MEA) based on sulfonated poly(phenylene sulfone) for PEM electrolysis and reported lower durability compared to PFSA ionomer-based reference (Ref. 13):  “An initial long-term stability test of sPPS (sulfonated poly(phenylene sulfone))-MEAs performed as constant current hold at 1 A cm−2 for 100 h showed lower durability for two sPPS-MEAs compared to the Nafion reference. It is theorized that the observed degradation partially originates from the high water content in the sPPS-membranes yielding a softening of the membrane and an increase of the gas crossover and thus, degradation via radical attack.” Beyond these scientific publications, three EU-funded projects, ELECTROHYPEM 2012 -2015; €1.3 million; Ref. 16), GAIA (2019-2022; €4.5 million; HORIZON2020; Ref. 17), and IMMORTAL (2021-2023; €3.8 million HORIZON2020; Ref. 18) also concluded that PFSA-free membranes are currently not stable enough or have reduced performance.  Alternatives to ePTFE reinforcement meshes in membranes:  The implementation of reinforcing materials in membranes is necessary to significantly increase their mechanical stability. These reinforcement meshes are 5 - 10 µm thick, highly porous and must have a high mechanical, thermal and chemical stability. State-of-the art materials for this purpose are ePTFE-based reinforcement meshes. Promising efforts are underway to substitute ePTFE with fluorine-free materials, such as electrospun polybenzimidazole (PBI), PEEK or PES as reinforcement materials. While electrospun PBI-type materials hold potential as a fluorine-free mechanical support, their effectiveness in PEM fuel cell systems has not yet been confirmed. Developing a PBI-based solution that meets performance and manufacturing standards for current and future needs could likely take 10-20 years.  Alternatives to PFSA ionomers in electrodes:  PFSA ionomers act as (necessary) ion-conducting additives in the electrodes (catalyst layers) and serve as binders. In addition to the fact of low long-term stability, a low gas permeability also has a negative effect on the functional efficiency of the electrodes. In contrast to PFSA ionomers, fluorine-free ionomers often have significantly lower permeabilities and solubilities for oxygen and hydrogen. These properties (favorable for electrolyte membranes) hinder their use in catalyst layers. Nguyen et al. showed that electrodes with non-fluorinated ionomers have significantly lower power densities (Ref. 19). Due to the significantly higher glass transition temperatures of fluorine-free ionomers (compared to PFSA ionomers), MEA production must be carried out via new GDE processes or direct membrane coating (both to be developed). The decal processes currently used are most likely not practical.  We estimate that full industrial feasibility of PFSA-free electrodes, if achieved (and suitable materials with sufficient oxygen gas permeability are successfully developed), could potentially take about 25 years.  Gas Diffusion Layer:  PTFE is currently the most commonly used material for gas diffusion layer (GDL) hydrophobization in industry. However, studies on the loss of PTFE during operation are rare. Ha et al. found in leaching and degradation tests that “the carbon structure, such as the carbonized resin, were more damaged than the PTFE, resulting in a reduction in mass as high as 0.5 – 1%.” (Ref. 20). This is in line with Yu et al. who studied the degradation of GDL under harsh conditions (H2SO4 for 1200 h) and found that the “relative content of PTFE decreased from 8.87% to 7.73% by TGA analysis.” (Ref. 21). Therefore, in the worst-case scenario, approximately 1% of the total PTFE content in the GDL is lost during operation and degradation in the PEMFC. A recent literature review by Lee et al. showed that other fluorinated polymers may be used as alternatives to PTFE or other treatments (Ref. 22) Nevertheless, there are currently no promising alternatives to fluorinated polymers to achieve the desired (and necessary) hydrophobization effect during the lifetime of the PEMFC under operating conditions.   Sealings: Sealings are essential within the stack to prevent any leakage of media and mixing of reactants. In industry, FKM or FFKM materials are commonly employed for this purpose due to their high chemical stability, durability, and minimal rates of H2 permeation. However, in stack manufacturing and research at ZBT, PFSA-free silicone-based sealing materials have been utilized for a considerable duration, showcasing sufficient stability and performance during long-term PEMFC operation (> 1000 h). In our perspective, PFAS-free alternatives for the low-temperature range (LT PEM; < 100 °C) in the sealing domain are already available, demonstrating adequate long-term qualification. Presently, the drawback of these silicone-based sealing materials lies in their slightly elevated H2 permeation rates compared to FKM or FFKM materials, which should be further reduced in future R&D efforts.   Socio-economic effects of a hastily implemented PFAS ban on PEM fuel cells and PEM electrolysis: Specific PFAS materials, particularly PFSA ionomers and ePTFE, are currently still indispensable in energy and hydrogen applications and thus belong to the category of "essential uses." Electrolyzers and fuel cells, along with their components, are expected to make a substantial contribution to achieving a more sustainable green energy supply, playing a pivotal role in the EU's "Fit for 55" program. By 2030, the EU aims to achieve an annual green hydrogen production of approximately 10 million tons. This implies an electrolysis capacity of 100 GW by 2030 for the European hydrogen sector. Consequently, the scaling up of electrolysis production must commence immediately. The industry relies on PFAS materials like PFSA ionomers and ePTFE for this purpose. The proposed bans or excessively short derogation periods (such as the suggested 5 years + 18 months for PEMFC application) in the Restrictions Proposal, could seriously jeopardize the use of PEM fuel cells and PEM electrolyzers, which are essential for fulfilling the European Union's climate objectives. Moreover, the proposed PFAS ban will undermine future innovations and the EU's standing as a hub for innovation in the burgeoning hydrogen sector. The European hydrogen market of the future, estimated to be worth 820 billion euros with the potential to create 5.4 million jobs by mid-century (Ref. 23), will be seriously jeopardized by this proposed ban.

General Comments: The Hydrogen Chemistry Company, HyCC, provides safe, reliable and affordable supplies of green hydrogen solutions to "hard-to-abate" industries, enabling them to achieve net-zero CO2 emissions. Our green hydrogen production by water electrolysis makes use of PEM and alkaline electrolysis technologies for which PFAS, particularly fluoropolymers are essential. HyCC joins the standpoint and proposals made by Hydrogen Europe regarding the PFAS use in the hydrogen industry. According to the information provided by Hydrogen Europe (submission no. 4144 on this public consultation and second input by Hydrogen Europe of 2023/09/25  on this public consultation), PFAS are essential to the proper functioning of PEM and alkaline electrolysers. There would be no alternative to PFAS in terms of KPIs, with no disruptive innovations expected. Using fluoropolymers in the hydrogen industry would come with limited emission risks and they would be ‘polymers of low concern’. To limit emissions and foster recycling, best practices and incentives should be installed. Without an exemption for both PEM and alkaline electrolysers, the hydrogen industry, and its competitiveness, as well as the REPowerEU targets would be threatened.

General Comments: The impact for banning Fluropolymers (PTFE ) in the sectors technical textiles, energy sector and architectural membranes would lead to a decrease of lifetime of the used textiles since almost all substitutes for PTFE have a smaller range of resilience in acidic and caustic environments. This would also increase waste since the same PTFE textile could be used again if the substances for filtration is changed. In addition its inherent UV resistance makes it a perfect fit for membranes which should last for a very long time. All other materials decompose after a certain time under UV radiation. This leads to less waste. Also due to disposal at a special facility the release of toxic residual substances can be reduced.
PTFE is widely used in technical textiles for different filtration usages. Finding a suitable alternative material that provides the same level of performance is challenging since the range of applications is always smaller then with PTFE. The innertness classifies this Fluropolymer as one with a much lower environmental concern than a lot of other PFAS substances. Therefore there should be an exemption for this Fluropolymer.

General Comments: The importance of PVDF for the manufacturing of surgical mesh implants
For more than 30 years I have worked as a clinical pathologist in close cooperation with clinical colleagues and industry in the field of surgical meshes for hernia and pelvic floor repair. During this time, I have for the first time worldwide investigated and detailed how surgical meshes behave in the body after long-term implantation and to what extent the tissue reactions I have observed correlate with the known clinical complications.
For this purpose, I have investigated countless mesh variants made of different polymers (including PP, titanised PP, PET, PVDF and others) and with different textile structures in preclinical models. Moreover, I have analysed thousands of explanted mesh samples from hernia, incontinence and prolapse patients from all over the world. As part of this work, I now have the world's largest databases of explanted surgical meshes. The results of my investigations have been published in more than 200 publications and lectures. For the last 15 years I have been an expert witness in mass litigations in the USA and Australia with more than 200,000 claims for damages following the use of hernia and pelvic floor meshes made of PP and PET.
The results of my studies on explanted surgical meshes significantly influenced mesh research over the last 30 years and led to new, significantly improved mesh modifications for the benefit of our patients. The textile structure, especially the pore size and the used polymer are critical parameters for optimal biocompatibility and long-term stability of these implants. The results prove higher complication rates in the long-term with mesh modifications made from polymers that are degradable and chemically unstable in the body. These include, in particular, the polymers polypropylene (PP) and polyethylene terephthalate (PET), which are by far the most commonly used polymers in terms of numbers. Both of these polymers exhibit a significant degree of degradation over time in the patient. The degradation process significantly influences the mechanical properties of the meshes as well as the extent of the inflammatory response and connective tissue induction or perifilamentary fibrosis. In the databases, perifilamentary fibrosis correlates positively and significantly with the rate of long-term complications.
An outstanding polymer in many aspects is PVDF. This special polymer remains stable for decades without signs of degradation or loss of function in the patient's body after long-term implantation. Thus, PVDF has entered many guidelines of surgical or uro-gynecological societies worldwide as an innovative polymer for sutures and mesh materials. A ban on PVDF for the manufacturing of implants and here in particular for the manufacturing of surgical meshes, which are indispensable in modern hernia and pelvic floor surgery, would be a serious mistake both medically and socio-economically. Therefore, I demand a time unlimited exemption for the use of PVDF in mesh implants.



Prof. Dr. med. Bernd Klosterhalfen

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The Element 9 GmbH&CoKG (E9) is a newly launched German enterprise; the consortia structure is open for partners. The mission of E9 is to bring circular economy for Fluoropolymers into reality (large scale). The business of E9 is the design and engineering of recycling plants, in a 1. step: for perfluorinated polymers (Upcycling) and in 2. Step: for partially fluorinated polymers; this also includes the implementation of proper waste management systems. E9’s expertise is based on the R&D results/assets of his partner InVerTec, (Institut für Innovative Verfahrenstechnik, Bayreuth, Germany, IVT). Aside from the upcycling of perfluorinated polymers (TRL 8), IVT has already explored additionally the recycling of partially fluorinated polymers, laminates, fluorinated gases/liquids and also polymers with functional groups for the fuelcell, water electrolysor applications (an overview is given in SKZ-Presentation [1]). All the technologies have TRL 4-8. The importance of Fluoropolymers and the numerous applications are appreciated in many statements. What is really missing and is not considered by ECHA so far, is the topic of recycling and establishing closed loops (circular economy). In Webinars from ECHA mostly incineration and the release of potential harmful gases were discussed so far. Obviously, the state of the art is not known by this community (references: [2], [3], [4], [5]). State of the art is the proven (on large scale) so called Upcycling Technology for perfluorinated polymers like PTFE, PTFE-Compounds, PFA, FEP (from the EoL-waste stream analysis these polymers represent more than 60% from > 20kT collected Fluoropolymer waste in Europe; [6]). This Upcycling technology enables the conversion of waste materials from manufacturing, processing and EoL back into the starting monomers Tetrafluorethylen (TFE) and Hexafluoropropylen (HFP). The savings in respect to resources, energy and CO2 reductions compared to the conventional R22-route are outstanding (savings per 1000 tons of TFE/HFP; [4], [7]): - 1,500 tons CaF2  - 2,000 tons sulfuric acid - 5,000 tons Chlorine;  - 10,000 tons HCl - 10,000 tons CO2 - up to 70% energy savings

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: In EU about 40 kT of Fluoropolymers are manufactured in 2020; about 23 kT of EoL materials are collected, this number does not include waste from Manufacturing or processing [6]. The EOL-products are easy to collecd, as they are dominated by industrial uses (>95%); consumer products are contributing to small portion only (<5%). See SKZ presentation of Thorsten Gerdes. The technical applications of fluoropolymers are in majority non-dispersive, this makes collecting them from the market very easy. Life cycle assessments show that these polymers are very energy demanding (220 MJ/kg for PTFE). Consequently recycling is a must to recover CaF2, anhydrous HF (aHF), the monomers Tetrafluoroethylene (TFE)/Hexafluoropropylene (HFP) or even the whole intact polymer [8].

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: During the incineration of perfluorinated polymers like PTFE no harmful fluorinated acids are generated; only the expected HF and CO2 are formed. From KIT results it is assumed that incineration of perfluorinated polymers is no source of PFAS [9], [10]. The HF can be recovered by proven technologies (References [11], [12], [13], [14]) and the incineration can be done by the so called smart incineration to generate anhydrous HF (aHF, the most valuable product). This study is in contrast to some statements in the literature that fluorinated acids are generated during incineration at high temperatures. The caloric value of fluorinated polymers is low (5400 kJ/kg [15]) and so oil/gas has to support the incineration which further increases the CO2-emissions. The alternative is the lab proven smart incineration to generate aHF [11], [16].  Incineration is in sharp contrast to the sustainable Upcycling technology for perfluorinated polymers including compounds based on these materials [4].

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: From all polymers, perfluorinated polymers are the ideal polymers to establish a closed loop recycling systems since these materials decompose back into the starting monomers TFE/HFP.  The Upcycling Technology was developed by E9’s partner IVT. The successful R&D efforts were financially supported by Deutsche Bundesstiftung Umwelt (DBU). This technology is based on a controlled thermal depolymerization of perfluorinated polymers. The results can be found in [17], [18] and it ended up in building a 500 to/year pilot plant at the Dyneon /3M side in Gendorf. Also this effort was supported by Umweltbundesamt (UBA /KFW). The opening of this 500 tons plant was in 2015; the final report about the performance of the 2 reactor systems [17], [18], [19] were provided to UBA/Dessau in 2020 (the confidential report can be found in the archives of UBA/Dessau). Meanwhile the process was further optimized by IVT. The plan of E9 is to use the experiences of this 500 tons plant to design /build large scale recycling units with capacities > 2000 tons and establish closed loops for perfluorinated polymers. The Upcycling technology would also allow the transformation of the present energy demanding R22 route to make TFE and HFP (about 220 MJ/kg) by using perfluorinated waste streams as secondary raw materials to produce the monomers. The savings in respect to resources, energy, CO2 reduction and environmental reliefs can be found in detail in [2], [8], [19]; [7].    The introduction of Upcycling technology into large scale (500 to/y) was awarded by Verband der chemischen Industrie (VCI, [20]) in 2017. For any remaining off-gases from the depolymerization process (e.g. C2F6, these amounts are quite small <2%) or perfluorinated acids during the quench step, modern technologies are available to destroy them or to reduce it the lowest levels. By using plasma technology also these byproducts can be recycled and converted into valuable products [21], [22]. Zero Emission strategy is mandatory for E9 when designing/engineering Upcycling units [4], [23]. E9 will now design larger scale upcycling units with 2000-3000 tons/year with partners from manufacturing, processors, and end users in order to establish a closed loop system. The available collected EoL waste in EU is more than 20 kT, additionally there are plenty amounts of PTFE/compounds in old landfills and significant amounts of manufacturing and processing streams (which can be used additionally and would provide an environmental relieve).  The target of Element 9 and partners will be to convert about 50% of the collected fluorinated Polymers in EU back into valuable monomers and generate new polymers without deficiencies in performance. The proposed ban or even a derogation for a few years on fluoropolymers (incl. the needed monomers) would deliberately destroy and eliminate the circular economy in EU and would contradict all efforts from the past, since E9 and their partners would not invest into Upcycling plants in EU and consequently the incoming waste per year would accumulate and the already landfilled perfluorinated materials would stay forever. For the remaining partially fluorinated polymers, mixtures perfluorinated polymers with hydrocarbon polymers or heavily contaminated materials, IVT also investigated recycling paths to recover at least the critical raw material (EU) CaF2 or anhydrous HF (aHF) ( [2], [11], [12], [5], [24], [14]).   The recovery of useable CaF2 from the incineration of fluorinated polymers in order to be used in HF-production is well advanced and also proven on larger scale; the plans for a 900 tons/year plant already exists (TRL>5) [25]. If incineration is the last option to handle the fluorinated waste streams one has to keep in mind that for (per)fluorinated polymers the caloric value is quite low and consequently additional oil/gas has to used and thus even increasing the CO2 emissions. IVT explored the smart incineration technology to convert the hot incineration gases into syngas (CO, H2) and aHF, thus avoiding the detour via CaF2 (TRL>4) [14]; [16]. On top, even for polymers with functional groups (so called ionomers) feasible recycling options were successfully developed and tested (TRL>4, [26]; [27]) Mechanical recycling exists for clean unfilled PTFE and for (per)fluorinated thermoplastics like PFA, FEP coming from processors or even End of Live (Eol) materials (this is a small recycling segment [4]). Additionally, the properties of the polymers are suffering. All in all, for fluorinated polymers the loops can be closed and sustainable technologies can be put in place. Consequently there is no argument left for the statement that these polymers are creating environmental burdens.  Element 9 with its partners from manufacturing, processing, end users and industry associations are willing to use and enlarge the proven Upcycling Technology in EU to close the loop for perfluorinated polymers. Depending on the fluorinated polymer/waste, Monomers TFE/HFP can be recovered, CaF2 or aHF can be obtained from incineration or even the whole polymer can be recovered. Zero emissions into air /water is mandatory. The authorities should help and support to put all these methods in reality.  It can be concluded that the activities of element9 are in good accordance with the goal of ECHA to close material cycles and protect environment from hazardous compounds. On the other hand forward looking industries like health care, green hydrogen, photovoltaics and computer technology can develop based in an environmental aware framework.  A ban would be detrimental to cope with the collected waste streams coming back in future. Fluoropolymers are indispensable materials for key applications and almost impossible to be substituted. Based on this and due to the fact, that sustainable recycling technology exists. Element 9 propose a complete and rapid exemption for all fluoropolymers.

5. Proposed derogations: With a few years of derogation, Element 9 and partners would not invest into Upcycling technology nor any other recycling technology in Europe. Consequently, the amount of collected waste >23 kT per year plus manufacturing and processing waste would accumulate.

10. Analytical methods: Invertec does have all know how about detection and control of emissions in hand, being necessary to run the UpCycling plants under save conitions.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: The International Union of Wagon Keepers (UIP), is the umbrella association of national associations from 14 European countries, representing more than 250 private freight wagon leasing companies and Entities in Charge of Maintenance (ECM), performing 50 % of the rail freight tonne-Kilometres throughout Europe. We are therefore representing down-stream users of PFAS when it comes to workshops maintaining and manufacturing freight wagons and tank wagons as well as end- consumers of PFAS when it comes to the companies leasing the freight/tank wagons. Our fleet counts around 234’000 freight wagons, of which around 82’477 are tank wagons, of which the majority are approved for the transport of dangerous goods. UIP members own most of the tank wagons operating in the EU market and are leasing them to shippers and railway undertakings who are operating them. Nevertheless, wagon leasing companies are also responsible to maintain the wagons (every 6 years) as well as the tanks in intervals of 4 and 8 years.

PFAS is used as sealing applications and sometimes as coating in tank wagons and is essential for the transportation of dangerous goods as there are currently no alternatives.  Seals and O-rings are of PTFE, FEP, PFA and fitted within the body of the valve and access hatch. Sealing elements can be found in the bottom valve assembly, the bottom outlet valves, top loading and discharge valves, in the airline assembly and in the access hatch seals.
Since this specific use case has not been properly identified in the Annex XV restriction report yet, we will provide more information under question 6.
PFA material is very performant because of their high thermal and chemical resistance and because they are water and oil repellent and wear resistant. This is why they are used in harsh environmental conditions such as sealings in tank wagons and can ensure the safe transportation of dangerous liquids and gases through the whole EU.

To our best knowledge and based on the position of the European Sealing associations and the ITCO report (see references in the Annex) there are currently no other alternatives on the market as performant and safe as PFAS sealings.
UIP is committed to the objectives of the REACH Regulation which are to protect human health and the emissions to the environment while guaranteeing the free movement of dangerous goods and freight in the internal market. UIP is supporting the attempt to limit the use of PFAS in non-essential consumer facing products. However, the use of PFAS in tank wagons needs to be exempted from the ban. Instead, there should be extra safety measures to limit emission during the manufacturing and end of life cycle phase.

To sum up our arguments below, given that: 1) there are no known health concerns of solid PFAS 2) there are no emissions during the use phase and that emissions during end of life phase can be avoided or better controlled through appropriate regulation how to recycle or dispose these sealings 3) there are no equivalent alternatives on the market for the sealings of tank wagons 4) any other less performing material used in sealings will have significant negative environmental and human health implications 5) a ban would have significant impact on the global chemical supply chain and the whole EU economy.

UIP is therefore considering that an exemption (or unlimited time derogation) for PFAS used in tank wagons would be needed. We could also support the inclusion of a review clause after 15 years to reexamine if appropriate alternatives are available on the market.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Our comments fall under the transportation sector and the sub-group : sealing applications.  Tank wagons are within the transportation sector a specialization for the transportation of liquids and liquefied gases of dangerous goods. Tank wagons are relatively standardized (see EN 12561 1-8) and are suitable for a range of cargo and approved by competent national authorities using a coding system described in RID – the International Agreement for the Carriage of Dangerous Goods.

6. Missing uses: PFAS used as sealing applications and sometimes as coating in tank wagons is essential for the transportation of dangerous goods has not been appropriately identified in the Annex XV restriction report. We are therefore providing you with more information under this section. Sealing elements are components within the metallic valves and equipment that are fitted to the tank operational openings and are crucial to the containment of the cargo of liquids and liquefied gases, most of which are regulated as dangerous goods (RID). But other substances are transported too, including food grade and non-regulated substances.  Seals and O-rings are of PTFE, FEP, PFA and fitted within the body of the valve and access hatch. Sealing elements can be found in the bottom valve assembly in the airline assembly and in the access hatch seals. For more information, please consult the ITCO IG09 Case study and see image 1 and 2 in the annex.  In very few tank wagons, PFAS is also used to coat tanks from within for the transportation of certain types of acids.  a.) the annual tonnage and emissions.  PFA material is essential for sealings at the tank wagon itself and its equipment e.g. valves. The main sealing materials are PTFE, FEP and PFA in solid form but as well as PFA envelope on an elastomer core. It is estimated that the materials used for tanks wagons are an average of 82% non PFAS and 18% PFAS (see ITCO study). UIP estimates that up to 8’500 kg of PFAS material is used per annum for sealing elements on tanks of rail tank wagons in Europe. [Explanation of calculation: We assume that a tank wagons has around 0.5 kg of PFAS per wagon which needs to be replaced every 6 years (average of the mandatory periodic revision time of 4 and 8 years for tank wagons) of the current tank wagon fleet of 82’477, 0.5 kg x 82’477/ 6= 6’873 kg) + (sealings in new built per year: 3’000 new tank wagons x 0.5 kg= 1’500 kg]   Based on the ITCO study, sealing elements use PFAS components in the solid form, primarily PTFE but similar materials too e.g., FEP, PFA, FFKM, FKM. The solid materials form does not allow for the materials to shred or degrade to particles as is the case with some other industries such as food packaging, clothing, and fire-fighting foams. Furthermore, the sealing element is incorporated into the tank and cannot get out into the environment. Mainly during the mandatory RID maintenance check, sealings are replaced at least every 8 years (full check-up), or even earlier if needed during the intermediate check-up after 4 years.  There is no emission during the use-phase since these sealing elements are compressed within the tank wagon valves and not exposed to the atmosphere. The material also does not wear out or shred or degrade into particles during its use. As regards the end of the life-cycle phase, maintenance facilities dispose the sealing materials as industrial waste since there is no recycling requirement. The percentage that is disposed of in landfill or municipal incineration is unknown. Given that sealing elements are solid materials and also given their persistency, they could be separated by our workshops for disposal of approved facilities if required. UIP would support rules on recycling and waste management of PFAS materials.  b.) The key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use.  Sealing elements of tank wagons are made of PFAS because of their high thermal and chemical resistance and the fact that they have very low surface tension and are thus water and oil repellent as well as abrasion and wear resistant at the same time (please see table 1 and 2 in the annex). There are up to date no alternatives that can offer the required chemical and thermal resistance combination. According to the chemical resistance chart PTFE is the most performing plastic against dangerous goods and allow the safe transportation of these goods across the whole EU.  To sum up: PFAS is used because of its following characteristics: Chemical resistance and compatibility for a wide range of chemicals. It has thermal stability in the required temperature range of usually -40 °C to +200 °C and needs to withstand standard pressure conditions of up to 30 bars or higher. When transporting refrigerated gases or compressed gases even lower temperatures or higher pressures are possible.  The sealings are capable of withstanding a degree of handling damage and do not absorb the substances transported. They withstand shrinkage, elastic recovery, vibration and are resistant to friction. It is also essential that the sealing elements remain leak tight during long-distance transportation. These characteristics are vital to ensure the safe transportation of dangerous liquids and gas around the EU. No currently available alternative material guarantees the same performance, safety and lifetime.  c.)The number of companies in the sector estimated to be affected by the restriction.  If it comes to a full ban, around 250 private Wagon leasing companies and their assets will be directly affected, most of them SMEs. Furthermore, over 80 workshops (see VPI-VERS data base) dealing with tank wagons maintenance and repairing will be affected as user of PFAS. However, given that the majority of dangerous good transportation is done by rail, a ban would lead to a disruption of the global chemical and liquefied gas transportation supply chain and be catastrophic for the chemical industry, all related industries that depend on chemical supplies and hence the whole European economy.  d.) The availability, technical and economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives for the relevant use  To our best knowledge and as well supported by the European Sealing Manufacturers and the ITCO study, there are currently no alternative materials that would perform as good as existing solid PFAS sealings as required for chemical thermal, plasma and radioactive resistance for seals. Less performing alternatives would significantly increase the risk of leakages and therefore pose a threat to the environment and also to human health due to the more frequent replacements of sealings and risk of contamination as well as leaks.  e.) For cases in which alternatives are not yet available, information on the status of R&D processes (...)  We are not in a position to comment on any R&D processes regarding PFAS sealings alternatives and will leave this to the sealing industry to comment. However, if an alternative was to be developed it does not necessarily mean that they can substitute easily the PFAS sealing with the current valves. Most likely an alternative (if then available) means also a change in the valve design which requires approval of the valves and in some cases even the re-approval of the tanks by the competent authorities.  If a PFAS alternative would become available UIP would recommend a transition time of 5 years for newly built tank wagons to provide the manufacturer with the relevant time to get the new tank wagons reapproved and to cover the time from ordering a tank to its delivery and then approval by the European Railway Agency. As for the existing tank wagon fleet, given its size (82’477 tank wagons) and their long-life cycle of 30 – 40 years and the fact that they must be revised on average every 4 – 8 years), UIP would request that they are exempted based on grandfather right entitlements. Changing the valves of each tank wagon could cost up to 10’000€ per tank wagon and would lead to the reapproval of each tank wagon, adding to administrative burden without any added value.  g.) For cases in which substitution is not technically or economically feasible, information on what the socio-economic impacts would be for companies, consumers, and other affected actors (...)  On Risk to environment and human health:  Safety is the prime consideration for tank wagons, especially since they are transporting a wide range of classified dangerous goods in liquid and gas form. Containment of these substances requires tank operational opening to be fitted with highly engineered valves, ancillaries, and access hatches, each requiring sealing elements between the metallic interfaces of the tank and valve. Since there are no real alternatives to PFAS for sealing applications that would provide the crucial performance range achieved by existing solid PFAS, a blanket ban of PFAS would mean a significant higher risk of leakages of dangerous goods into the environment. It would also mean higher emissions of toxic and dangerous products because before a sealing can be replaced, the tank needs to be cleaned from the product. Less performing alternative would also bring a much higher risk to human health, especially those working in workshops that would need to work with possible contaminated sealings and it means a higher exposure to dangerous goods during the activity of replacing the sealings.  On the Socio-Economic impact: A ban of PFAS for sealings used in tank wagons approved for the transport of dangerous goods would severely disrupt the global chemical and liquefied gas transportation supply chain. Some products could not even be transported any longer, implying a possible shortage of products of basic needs. Given that around 212 million tons/km of dangerous goods are transported alone by rail (see Eurostat link in annex) on a yearly basis, the effects would be catastrophic for the chemical industry, all related industries that depend on chemical supplies and hence the whole European economy. Since decades, rail freight has been the backbone of the chemical supply chain as certain products are forbidden to be transported on roads and road transport cannot offer the necessary capacity for the high volumes of chemicals and gas transports. Furthermore, a ban of PFAS, leading to the impossibility of using tank wagons, would undermine the European Green Deal and its objective to reduce CO2 emissions in transport by increasing rail freight’s market share. As alternatives for PFAS used in sealing do not exist, around 250 Wagon leasing companies and their assets will be affected, most of them SMEs. Furthermore, over 80 workshops dealing with tank wagons maintenance and repairing will be affected as user of PFAS.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: UIP would welcome an exemption under reconsideration under point 6 o. [applications affecting the proper functioning related to the safety of transport vehicles, and affecting the safety of operators, passengers or goods until 13.5 years after EiF]. Further clarification would be required as to what would fall under the scope of this exemption
