General Comments: The PFAS REACH restriction is expected to have a major impact on the automotive industry. This document is the second response of ACEA to the public consultation.
PFAS are mainly used in the automotive industry for their unique properties:
- High stability
- Resistance to high temperatures and high pressures
- Electrical insulation
- Resistance to aggressive chemicals
- Resistance to friction
- Surfactants properties
As of today, the restriction proposal includes fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers, which are fundamental to our industry. F-gases, also included in the restriction proposal, are also widely used as refrigerants and for testing methods.
As mentioned in our first contribution to the consultation (comment ID 4276) ACEA fully shares the desire to reduce the uses if PFAS in our industry. The current proposal by the dossier submitter is not appropriate as it would have a critical impact on our industry; mainly the impossibility to produce, approve and place on the market vehicles, as well as strongly negate the possibility to shift to better and greener technologies and electromobility.
We wish to explicit our position and give to the ECHA committees our proposal for relevant risk option management on PFAS. We also wish to give further details on the impact of the restriction proposal on the automotive industry, especially on the following subjects:
- Textiles in the automotive industry, as displayed in the answers to the ECHA online questionnaire
In the document attached
- PFAS in air conditioning as an addition to our first submission.
- PFAS used in the production process of vehicles, and in the production equipment.
- PFAS used in H2 technology in automotive industry.
- Electronics in the automotive industry.
- Lubricants in the automotive industry.
- PFAS used in paints, lacquers, and coatings.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Please note that our submission comes in two parts :  In the present questionnaire, we wish to provide information on :  - The TULAC sector, more specifically on the sub-uses “technical textiles”, focusing on filtration and separation media, and “textiles used in engine bays”. - Uses of PFAS in Lacquers. - Uses of PFAS in H2 technology.  In our attached document, we wish to provide further information on a proposed risk management option on PFAS. We also elaborate on several other topics : - Air conditioning systems. - PFAS in production of automotive – tools, machines, equipment and machinery. - PFAS in electronics used in the automotive industry. We also give further details on PFAS in lubricants, lacquers, paints and the applications of fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers in the automotive industry.  Sub-use: Technical textiles We welcome the derogation recommended for reconsideration by the Dossier Submitters. However, we would like to propose a series of modifications to the proposed wording. Firstly, we believe that referring to the functions of the textiles and not to their location in the vehicle allows to set an effective and enforceable limitation to the scope, while covering all the relevant applications. This is because the current wording leaves out textiles used for ignition protection, which constitutes a key safety feature in case of accident, providing more time to rescue people before the vehicle starts to burn out. With regard to NVH insulation, the current wording also leaves textiles used in other parts of vehicles e.g., as isolator between dashboard and engine compartment (front engine), between seats and the rear engine, or at the transmission tunnel. In addition, while this is not a primary concern for the automotive sector, we support the request of ATCS to extend the derogation to other types of vehicles, such as motorcycles or non-road mobile machinery that are used for construction or agriculture, in line with the position of the SEAC Committee in the context of the PFHxA restriction proposal. * * RAC & SEAC, Opinion on the Annex XV dossier proposing restrictions on Undecafluorohexanoic acid (PFHxA), its salts and related substances, June 9, 2021.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Sub-use: Technical textiles:  Volumes In the EU the annual consumption of C6 SFPs for initial textile finishing is estimated at 200-300 t/y, which translates to 10 kg of impurities (PFHxA) per year. This applies to all technical textiles and is not only limited to automotive applications. Emissions during textile production The European textile industry is committed to decrease emissions across its industry. Additionally, more stringent regulations, implementing measures to minimise releases of PFAS and other substances to the environment such as the Best Available Techniques (BREF/BATs), already significantly reduce emissions during textile production. The BREF/BATs determine that process baths should be reused to the highest extent possible, after which they should be collected separately and sent for professional waste management. As a result of the existing BATs, current measurements conducted by companies using C6 SFPs in textile finishing estimate emissions of 100-300 ng/l in water for all technical textiles (not limited to the automotive applications). Production scraps are incinerated in line with the European Waste Catalogue (CER 04 02 22). (1) Emissions during use of textile articles Technical textiles have an estimated C6 SFP concentration of 0.2-0.5%, as identified in the report by Ramboll and Wood on the use of PFAS in textiles. (2)   For further information on degradation of C6 SFPs, please refer to the studies cited by ATCS.  The end-of-life, removal and disposal are covered by the End of Life Vehicles (ELV) Directive (2000/53/EC), which ensures proper handling and treatment. (3) To the best of our knowledge, C6-treated technical textiles are subject to treatment in modern high-temperature incineration plants. High-temperature incineration is the most widely accepted method to handle PFAS-containing textile waste and is applied in the following manner: • 850ºC or higher for at least two seconds for non-hazardous waste; • 1100ºC or higher for at least two seconds in case of hazardous waste or co-incineration. (4) Incineration facilities commonly come outfitted with flue gas purification systems, which incorporate multi-stage wet scrubbers employing calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)2). Through this process, hydrogen fluoride is converted into calcium fluoride (CaF2). Hydrogen fluoride, a vital commodity chemical employed in the production of a diverse array of materials, primarily derives from this transformation into calcium fluoride. C6 SFPs provide several combined performance benefits to the sector, specifically:  • water repellence based on ISO 4920 and ISO 811; • oil repellence based on ISO 14419 (grade 3); • stain-resistance/soil protection based on AATCC 130; and • flame retardancy (5)  Approximately 300 automobile assembly and engine production plants operate in Europe today.  As discussed, C6 SFPs’ properties include a combination of stain, oil, grease and water repellence, which are imperative to manufacture the high-performance technical textile in these applications.  The Danish Environmental Protection Agency reported that many different agents providing water repellence are marketed, namely: Wax-based repellents consisting of paraffin-metal salt formulations, resin-based repellents consisting of fatty modified melamine resins, and hydrophobic modified polyurethanes. None of the identified agents provide efficient repellence against oil, alcohol and oil-based stains. Therefore, these agents cannot be considered as suitable candidates. (6)  In addition, the report by Ramboll and Wood concluded the following: For (textile) applications requiring repellency against blood, solvents, fuels (petrol, kerosene, diesel and resistance of components in motor to oil and diesel /gasoline) and liquid chemicals (Figure 5.3), PFAS-free finishing agents are not currently able to meet the same levels of performance.(7)  The lack of adequate performance by any of the alternatives examined suggests that removal of PFAS could lead to increased risks, with potential high societal costs. Complex products, including cars or non-road mobile machinery, undergo an extensive and meticulous validation phase, typically spanning a minimum of 5 years from the initial concept sketches to market release . (8) During this period, suppliers engage in testing to establish material specifications, while original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) undertake essential verification tests. In the case of novel materials, customers may also opt for third-party, independent laboratory testing and certification to enhance their confidence in the material's performance. No viable alternatives have become available. As such, we support a minimum transition period of 13,5 years after EiF to allow sufficient time to identify prospective candidates, conduct testing, gain approval, execute implementation, and subsequently introduce them into the market through novel products. We understand that no suitable candidates have been identified at this stage, and there is therefore not sufficient visibility as to when the transition from PFAS will be possible. Furthermore, C6 SFP-based filters used in automotive are expected to be collected separately and incinerated in line with waste codes 150202*, 150203 (both for i.e., absorbents, filter materials (including oil filters not otherwise specified), rags and protective clothing) and 160107 (applicable to oil filters).  (2) Finally, we would like to add a few comments on the proposed wording. Firstly, we understand that the reference to ‘high-performance’ raises enforceability questions. The concept “high performance” means the same as media “that require a combination of water and oil repellency”. We, therefore, suggest removing the terms “high performance” from the wording. In addition, the term ‘textiles’ should be removed, as filtration media does not only cover woven materials but also nonwovens, polyurethane membranes and cellulose-based media, which do not fit under the current wording. 6. Missing uses: Sub-use lacquers: During our discussion with our suppliers, it appears that PFAS are also used in lacquers. The main substance is PTFE, which is added to guarantee a low friction profile for horn and buckle spring, screws, and metal pillar loop. The durability of the lacquer is also increased by the addition of PTFE. Due to lack of available information, assessment need to be fine tuned in the years ahead. PFAS are also used directly in mixtures for painted parts, such as car’s interiors and lighting applications. Due to its property, currently no alternatives are qualified to substitute PTFE in lacquers for the automotive industry. More details about which substances are used can be found in the annex of the document. Sub-use H2 technology As mentioned by other professional associations, PFAS are also used in H2 technology. This also impact the automotive industry as H2 storage system are used for emerging new type of mobility. The details of the PFAS used and the parts are detailed in annex of the attached document.

Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Understanding the financial implications of such a wide-ranging restriction proposal are extremely difficult, given the wide variety of applications impacted, the availability of substitutes, the research and development that needs to be conducted. initial assessment indicate that costs will exceed 10 Billion of Euro’s/year for our industry , including refrigerants, Batteries, Powertrain. All other subjects will induce additional costs (research in joining technology / joint performance, research in membrane technology, research in coating / plating technology, research into textiles, unknown impacts etc)

Other identified uses: Sub-use: Technical textiles C6 SFP-treated technical textiles provide advanced insulation, compatibility with fire retardant products and resistance to water, fuels, extremes of temperature and abrasion. Overall, they contribute to extending the product lifetime and making cars safer, more cost-effective and more durable.

10. Analytical methods: As noted in the Restriction Dossier, it is currently not analytically possible to distinguish between PFAS and non-PFAS organofluorine substances when measuring the total fluorine content of a product . This would require highly sophisticated procedures that would be able to make the distinction which, to the best of our knowledge, are not yet available. In the SEAC Final Opinion on the restriction proposal on PFHxA*, its salts and related substances, the Enforcement Forum of ECHA drew attention to the need to come up with standard methods for the analytical testing of the content of the substances covered by a proposed restriction, i.e., PFHxA, its salts and C6 fluorotelomers, elaborating that some standard methods are currently only available for water matrices.  The measurement of C6 presents a notably greater challenge compared to measuring PFHxA, especially when these substances are bound within larger molecules or present in environmental mediums, biota, and similar contexts. Precursors inherently possess a notably higher level of complexity than singular substances like PFHxA or any PFCA. Consequently, this circumstance underscores the necessity for tests that are tailored to the specific characteristics of each substance. *https://echa.europa.eu/documents/10162/97eb5263-90be-ede5-0dd9-7d8c50865c7e

General Comments: The PFAS regulation covers about 10,000 substances. Only about 50 of these substances are fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers.
Fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers can be classified as PFAS based on their molecular structure. However, their toxicological and ecotoxicological behavior differs significantly from the most common PFAS.

Our company manufactures elastomer seals (O-rings, gaskets, etc.) made of PFAS polymers (FKM & FFKM).
These are mainly used in the following fields:
- Industrial applications
- Electronics
- Transportation
- Petroleum

The most important properties of fluoroelastomers for our products are:
- Thermal resistance at low and high temperatures.
- Chemical inertness to aggressive chemicals and other media.
This cannot be achieved by any other polymer.

All alternative elastomers that could replace FKM or FFKM have a lower heat resistance and are not stable at temperatures of over 170°C. Even high-temperature silicone elastomers cannot withstand combinations of aggressive media and high temperatures and consequently lose their strength and elastomeric properties. Only fluoroelastomers combine heat and chemical resistance with consistent elastic properties.

We would therefore like to clearly point out that there are no alternative materials for FKM & FFKM and a ban on these polymers will lead to a major problem in many areas of industrial manufacturing and the chemical industry.
Regulation of the monomers used may well be appropriate and the focus here should be on better controls and technologies. However, a complete ban on all PFASs does not seem to be effective and will set us all back years technologically.

General Comments: The PFAS regulation covers about 10.000 substances. Only approximately 50 substances of these are Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers.
Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers can be classified as PFAS based on their molecular structure. However, their toxicological and eco-toxicological profile is essentially different from the majority of PFAS substances.
Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers are recognised by the OECD as safe materials: "PLC" = polymer of low concern. They are non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water soluble and non-mobile molecules and are judged to have no significant impact on the environment and humans. They do not generate microplastics. For further details see studies of: pro-K Industrieverband Halbzeuge und Konsumprodukte aus Kunststoff e.V. Mainzer Landstraße 55 60329 Frankfurt am Main or The European Chemical Industry Council, AISBL Belliard, 40 - 1040 Brussels – Belgium

We produce products – mainly diaphragms - made of Fluoropolymers (mainly PTFE but PFA and ECTFE as well) and Fluoroelastomers (FKM and FFKM). These products are used in the production process of pharmaceuticals (including vaccines), semiconductors, photovoltaic cells, food and beverages, chemicals, in the water processing and many other industrial applications. In many of these applications the products have to meet the requirements of the FDA, the USP class IV, drinking water requirements and others. There are toxicological tests performed as well as leachability tests for these standards. There does not exist a viable alternative to these materials in these applications. Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers are very expensive and therefore they are already without any ban only used, if no other alternatives are available.

For our products the essential properties of the used Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers are:
a) High flexibility (for the movement of diaphragms in pumps, valves and pressure regulators)
b) Chemical inertness regarding a big variety of medias, including harsh chemicals like chlorine gas, hydrofluoric acid and others
c) thermal resistance against low and high temperatures (higher than 150°C)
d) resistance against steam for sterilization in steam
e) good cleanability, to avoid contaminations between production batches and growth of bacterias
These properties are all necessary within one product. There is no alternative material available, that combines all these properties.

We did check alternatives with the following result:
Substitution by other elastomers, for example EPDM: = not suitable
a) flexibility: better than now
b) chemical inertness: restricted
c) thermal resistance: lower (not sufficient)
d) resistance against steam: possible up to approximately 120°C, needed up to 145°C (not sufficient)
e) cleanability: worse
= not suitable

Substitution by other elastomers, for example Silicone: = not suitable
a) flexibility: better than now
b) chemical inertness: restricted
c) thermal resistance: sufficient
d) resistance against steam: not suitable
e) cleanability: worse
Silicone is not firm enough that the parts keep their form during operation
= not suitable

Substitution by PEEK: = not suitable
a) flexibility: not existing
b) chemical inertness: equivalent
c) thermal resistance: equivalent
d) resistance against steam: equivalent
e) cleanability: equivalent
= not suitable

Substitution by UHMW-PE: = not suitable
a) flexibility: equivalent
b) chemical inertness: restricted, problems with highly oxidizing acids (for example nitric acid, chromic acid, or halogens)
c) thermal resistance: significantly lower – not usable for our needs
d) resistance against steam: not given
e) cleanability: equivalent
= not suitable

For some uses the theoretically suitable substitutes are much more harmful than Fluoropolymers. For example former asbesto seals had been substituted by PTFE-seals.

Duration of the transition to replacement materials:
There is no replacement material available, so it will need an unforeseeable number of years for the research and development for such a material (if something can be developed). After a suitable alternative would be available, the validation in the pharmaceutical industry takes several years.
In 2015 we had to substitute an EPDM compound for pharmaceutical applications by another EPDM compound that already existed and was available at that time. Caused by the long and demanding tests this transition took more than 6 years till 2021 for a product for which the alternative was already known.
The transition to a product that still has to be developed and tested thoroughly might take far longer than 12 years.

Without Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers a vast range of industries would not be able to produce in Europe any more.  For many of these industries, it is the declared goal of the EU to establish them here or strengthen the existing companies, like the pharmaceutical industry, semiconductor production, renewable energies….. Production facilities for the transport of fluids could not be operated in Europe anymore. Numerous medicines, vaccines, chemicals, foods, beverages, semiconductors, photovoltaic cells… could only be produced outside of Europe and so Europe would get dependent on the import of these strategic products from outside Europe. The supply situation would be threatened much more and for a much longer time than during Corona times and it would effect a much bigger range of products. I don’t think that Europe can afford to get under such a strong dependency from other regions.

Even ecological and health reasons recommend to exempt the Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers from the PFAS regulation. It is sure that these raw materials will be needed and used in future, this will just be transferred to other countries outside of the EU. Nowhere else in the world the production, processing and usage of Fluoropolymers is so well regulated, clean and reliable and monitored by ecological standards than in Europe. A relocation of the production, processing and usage to other countries would give up these achievements and could lead to ecological and health threads in other regions of the world.

Based on the recognition by the OECD as safe materials: "PLC" = polymer of low concern we request to exempt the Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers from PFAS regulation or use restrictions.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: The PFAS Restriction proposal is flawed on three points:
1. The Annex XV report fails to demonstrate that PFAS fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers pose any environmental toxicity concerns beyond their basic property of persistence, nor that they are mobile in the environment, nor lead to bioaccumulation in the food chain, nor that these polymeric PFAS themselves or any breakdown product, if any, are associated with health effects on aquatic organisms, terrestrial organisms or humans. 2. Combined Comments:
General Comments: The PFAS restriction proposal submitted by five European countries to the ECHA in January, 2023 is to collectively restrict PFAS including even a group of compounds, such as fluororesins, fluoroelastomers, and fluororubbers (hereinafter, collectively referred to as “fluororubbers”), with greatly different properties from other PFAS.
PFAS materials like the fluororubbers described above have excellent properties in a chemical resistance (solvent resistance), a swelling resistance, a heat resistance, etc., and are used for fluid transfer equipment in many manufacturing facilities of the automobile manufacturing industry and the IT equipment industry, as described above.  If it is asked whether there are alternative materials for PFAS, we would not say never.  However, use of alternative materials would drastically shorten the life of the pump to increase life cycle costs, or damage the sealing performance due to early deterioration of the alternative materials to increase the risk of causing an unexpected leakage of transferred fluid, which would be harmful for people and environments.  Thus, if the current restriction proposal is applied, it would surely lower the production efficiency in the automobile manufacturing industry and the IT equipment industry, and cause the second, and third, worldwide shortage of semiconductors.
Therefore, regarding the current restriction proposal, we will give our views below, and request to exempt from the restriction the fluororubbers to be subject to the restriction at present.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The current restriction proposal is to collectively restrict PFAS including even a group of compounds, such as fluororesins, fluoroelastomers, and fluororubbers, with greatly different properties from other PFAS.  If the restriction is applied without assessing risks of the aforementioned fluororubbers etc. in the consideration process, it will violate Article 68 of the REACH.  The current restriction proposal is only based on the fact that fluorine (-F) is contained in the chemical structure, not based on a result of appropriately analyzing hazardous risks.  We would have to say that the target of the restriction is broader than necessity. Being not readily degradable, that is a characteristic common among PFAS, is in other words having high durability.  We believe that the fluororubbers are essential materials in applications where such a property is required.  The fluororubbers such as FKM and FFKM are chemically stable, and insoluble in water.  Thus, even if they are taken into a human body (e.g., stomach), they will be excreted without being accumulated in the body or in the blood.  Therefore, it is believed that the likelihood of adverse influences on a human body is considerably low.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Incineration disposal of PFAS, especially fluoroelastomers, is not desirable for this purpose and is exclusively disposed of in landfills.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: The PFAS restriction, as defined in the restriction proposal, will have a strong impact on all sectors where fluoropolymers are used.

Fronius International is divided into three business units - Perfect Welding, Perfect Charging and Solar Energy.

In our electric welders, battery charging systems and inverters, PFAS, mainly FLUORPOLYMERS, are used because of their excellent performance or unique combination of properties that contribute to the safety and durability of our products. The following properties are particularly important:
- Resistance to high temperatures
- Resistance to aggressive chemicals
- Resistance to high pressures
- UV resistance
- Low electrical conductivity
- Low frictional resistance
- Low water absorption
- Long-term stability

The following components contain PFAS and will be significantly affected by the proposed restriction:
- Insulations
- Seals (O-rings)
- Hoses
- Liners (wire guides)
- diaphragms
- Cables and connectors
- Electronic components

The uniqueness of PFAS and the proposal to restrict the entire group of substances in the EU would lead to an extremely challenging search for suitable substitutes in terms of the required technical properties and their impact on human health and the environment.
Based on current knowledge, it can be stated that for a large part of the applications of fluoropolymers, no alternatives exist or are known that meet the high requirements for efficiency, durability and safety.
Restrictions on these groups of substances should therefore not be imposed without a differentiated consideration of the intended uses and the associated consequences.

FLUOROPOLYMERS are generally considered to be chemically inert, non-soluble, non-bioaccumulative and non-toxic. They do not exhibit the environmental or toxicological properties associated with other PFAS of concern.

Due to the lack of alternatives, the lack of information requirements along the supply chain, and the lack of analytical methods to detect each of the substances of concern grouped under PFAS, it is not possible at this time to make a conclusive assessment of the use of PFAS in electrical welding equipment, battery charging systems, and inverters.
Negative indirect or direct effects on international competitiveness are very likely, and quantification of the expected impact is not possible at this stage.

For these reasons, and since the PFAS used in our products are mainly FLUOROPOLYMERS, we urge regulators to allow PFAS only in areas where there is a real risk from PFAS, and to introduce exemptions and special regulations where PFAS can be used safely and are also relevant to critical applications.

We therefore support the call for a GENERAL EXCEPTION for FLUOROPOLYMERS and call for a complete exclusion of polymeric PFAS from the scope of the present restriction proposal.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: The planned ban on several thousand chemical substances from the so-called PFAS group (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) threatens to have significant and disproportionately disadvantageous economic and social consequences due to the associated drop in tax revenues and the loss of jobs for the communities.
A ban would specifically endanger the existence of a Rotter company that works exclusively with these substances and has already made investments worth millions with state subsidies in the recent past and poses immense challenges to other companies that process these substances - not only in Rott a. Inn. There is a threat of macroeconomic damage, the scope of which is not foreseeable. Because the substances mentioned are used in countless production chains, including mechanical and plant engineering (application in seals, valves, hoses or compressors), in fuel cell technology, e-mobility, filtration or medical technology. Alternative materials are either not available at all or would mean a technological step backwards by decades.
Apparently, the proposed restriction assumes that the entire range of chemicals involved and their use is hazardous to health. Scientific studies do not prove this. Rather, there are PFAS substances that do not pose any relevant risk to humans or the environment, but are essential for the longevity and safety of many industrial products and production processes. These must be exempted from the ban.
In the case of the companies operating in the municipality of Rott am Inn, this relates in particular to the material PTFE, which is mainly used for applications in the chemical, pharmaceutical and food industry as well as for medical applications and has also been tested and classified as safe for this purpose in accordance with the requirements of the FDA, EC 10/2022 and in accordance with USP Class VI ( cytotoxicity according to USP 87 and in vivo implantation according to USP 88). Corresponding evidence can be found in "SECTION IV. Non-confidential attachment."
In the form now presented, the restriction poses a varying degree of threat to individual companies and sectors with all the consequences for jobs and municipal finances (trade tax), inhibits technological progress and also and especially endangers "green" technologies.
In the specific case of a specialized company in Rott am Inn, 20 permanent jobs are currently at risk in the event of a regulation of fluoropolymers. The company is one of only five European producers of expanded PTFE sealing and membrane materials, involved in the development of materials for future technologies, such as fuel cell membranes, which means that much greater impacts are to be expected in the foreseeable future. Combined Comments:
General Comments: The planned restriction of PFAS (per- and polyfluorinated alkyl substances) would have serious consequences for companies in the Neckar-Alb region in Baden-Württemberg in Germany. It affects companies in the automotive, medical technology, energy technology, industrial process equipment, functional surface coatings, membrane technologies and textile industries.
PFAS are used, among other things, for medical devices, functional surface coatings, wind turbines, photovoltaics, microsystems technology, e-mobility and fuel cells, for water treatment, filtration technology and food processing, as well as for textiles, especially technical textiles. The planned ban on the entire substance group of around 10 000 PFAS would have immediate economic consequences in the various industries. The companies depend on the further use of the PFAS substances, since in most cases there are no substance alternatives at present and in the medium term.

The proposed restriction on PFASs would have the following effects:
- No substitute available or on the research side foreseeable
- Relocation of production to non-EU countries
- Since the proposed restriction also includes placing on the market (including import), production abroad and import into the EU only would be possible to a limited extent
- Climate protection needs PFAS: Future industries in wind power, photovoltaics, microsystems technology, e-mobility and fuel cells are dependent on PFAS
- Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) and Polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) for instance have also proven to be extremely reliable over many years in the medical technology sector, for example in patient-friendly minimally invasive surgery
- Exemptions must be considered holistically and in some cases do not represent a sensible solution for the economy and industrial production

Based on a round table with affected companies on the PFAS restriction proposal, the Reutlingen Chamber of Industry and Commerce (Baden-Württemberg, Germany) issued a position statement with demands. The document is attached to this contribution. It asks for the following:

1. Differentiate PFAS - allow exemptions for fluoropolymers, such as PTFE, PVDF, which are classified by OECD as Polymers of Low Concern (PLCs).
2. Weighing the restriction against the social benefits of the applications, for example in the areas of patient care, future industries and climate protection
3. Consider the controlled use of PFAS substances and their waste management
4. Consider exemptions holistically and ensure appropriate transition periods
5. Safeguarding economic viability and international competitiveness in Germany and the EU as a business location
6. Strengthen climate protection: the PFAS ban contradicts the climate goals of the Green Deal, since fluoropolymers are needed for innovative energy technologies
7. Strengthen and subsidize research activities on alternatives

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Baseline Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The potential risks introduced by the broad restrictive measures on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) cannot be understated. GAMBICA's PIC sector and its members strongly support the goal of minimising environmental and human exposure to PFAS but believe that the proposed approach is not an appropriate method for doing this.

The document submitted along with this consultation submission emphasises the crucial role of PFAS in ensuring the safety and efficiency of key process industries, which are essential for the ongoing operation of modern society.

It elaborates on the significance of PIC equipment in process operations and underscores the socioeconomic impacts of downtime in process industries. The document offers an overview of PFAS characteristics that make them indispensable in process applications and the specific uses of PFAS in PIC equipment. It also discusses the challenges and concerns related to PFAS restrictions in the PIC equipment domain, from insurmountable certification issues to concerns about the understanding of PFAS emission risks. An illustrative overview of the potential costs associated with PFAS restrictions is also provided. This report aims to complement individual submissions from GAMBICA PIC members and industry suppliers to the ECHA consultation on the Annex XV restriction report.

GAMBICA's PIC sector makes the following recommendations:

1. A risk-based approach to restrictions - GAMBICA’s PIC sector advocates for a more nuanced and pragmatic approach to restrictions, recommending adopting a risk-based strategy on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) restrictions rather than broad restrictive measures. Restrictions in product areas with low emissions potential, where products are critical to the ongoing operation of critical infrastructure, and where PFAS have been proven to improve safety and performance should be assessed carefully to fully determine the suitability of restrictions.

2. Define ‘essential-use’ criteria - GAMBICA's PIC sector advocates for the establishment and application of universally accepted 'essential-use' criteria within REACH to exempt PFAS uses from restrictions when these criteria are fulfilled. GAMBICA recommends using the criteria outlined in the Montreal Protocol Decision IV/25: Essential uses, as a foundation.

3. Time-limited derogation if deemed necessary - After conducting a comprehensive impact assessment, if it is determined that restrictions are necessary for PIC equipment, the PIC sector of GAMBICA formally requests a 12-year derogation for PIC equipment to enable manufacturers to:
a) research alternatives to PFAS and assess their compatibility with PIC applications
b) implement necessary design modifications, and obtain re-certifications where required
c) prepare process industries for product design changes that could impact control schemes, overall performance, and safety.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Some sectors/sub-uses are relevant to the content of the GAMBICA PIC sector report submitted. The limited scope of the sector and sub-uses is a concern to GAMBICA's PIC members, who highlight the need for a new sector, “process instrumentation and control”, which is necessary to help ensure the continued operation of all process industries. Twelve key process industries/sectors have been highlighted in the report, and sub-uses are given broadly as this is a generic document. GAMBICA members will submit further details specific to their organisation.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Emissions during the manufacturing phase are covered by supplier submissions. Emissions during the use phase are minimal, but limited detail is available. Emissions at end-of-life are mostly understood and are covered in the submitted report. The risks associated with emissions throughout the PIC lifecycle are negligible, yet the risks associated with restrictions on PIC equipment are enormous and far-reaching.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Managed under the WEEE directive or hazardous waste regulations. The risks associated with emissions throughout the PIC lifecycle are negligible, yet the risks associated with restrictions on PIC equipment are enormous and far-reaching.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Limited impacts due to waste already being managed as already detailed.

5. Proposed derogations: Some of the proposed derogations are suitable for some uses of PIC equipment, however, not all uses are covered. Tonnage and emissions are negligible, as per end-of-life phase information.

6. Missing uses: For most applications, suitable alternatives are not yet available. GAMBICA members will submit further details specific to their organisation. See section 3 for socio-economic impacts on served industries. See section 5 for uses within PIC equipment. See section 6.1-6-5 for technical comments on substitution of PFAS within PIC equipment.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: None of the potential derogations are suitable for PIC equipment.

8. Other identified uses: Detail to be submitted by suppliers or in GAMBICA members’ individual submissions if appropriate.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: The Precious Metals industry supports the PFAS restriction. However, the current scope is far too broad and not based on hazard nor risk related to the different substances. This means that the impact on the precious metals industry using directly or indirectly the PFAS to produce and recycle precious metals will be significant. Indeed, the Precious Metals industry has identified direct (electroplating) or indirect (industrial equipment, PPE and analytical equipment) uses of PFAS but also some uses intrinsically related to the use of precious metals (green hydrogen). These uses occur in a well-controlled (industrial) environment, with negligible potential for release / exposure to humans and the environment.
It is worth noting that the PFAS is a huge group of substances with different levels of hazard. A lot of these substances are considered of low concern (cf. OECD ), such as the fluoropolymers.
For most of the uses related to precious metals, PFAS are selected because of their unique properties and there are no alternatives available today with a comparable performance. If these uses were no longer allowed and/or the exemption time is not sufficient to find alternatives, this might have significant impacts on the precious metals manufacturing and recycling activities in the EU, and thus be incompatible with e.g., the EU Green Deal.
PFAS are also present in recycling streams containing precious metals (‘PM’). The PFAS are all being destroyed during the recycling process, trapped from the flue gas and duly disposed of. Any limitation on the use of PM recycling streams containing PFAS will restrict PM recycling activities in Europe.
It is worth noting that the PGMs (Platinum Group Metals) have been identified at Critical Raw Materials. The Critical Raw Materials act sets targets to allow Europe to be resilient. The ban of all PFAS in the EU at short notice will for sure jeopardize the success of the Critical Raw Materials act.
Hence, the EPMF would like to request that:
- the hazard profile of the PFAS is considered to prioritize the PFAS included in the restriction.
- the scope of the restriction is limited and that substances of low concern (as per OECD criteria) are exempted from the restriction.
- if the exemption must be use driven, the uses of PFAS outlined above must be exempted for at least 12 years and a mechanism to renew these exemptions must be put in place.

Content: Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The present comment is made by a global company manufacturing in the EU components that are necessary for the safe functioning of various vehicles and mobility applications, such as synchronous belts used in propulsion systems.
The Annex XV Report includes the following derogation that is marked for reconsideration: ‘use of PFASs in applications affecting the proper functioning related to the safety of vehicles, and affecting the safety of operators, passengers or goods.‘  As follows from Annex XV Report (Table 8, page 131), this potential derogation is based on the fact that there is a ‘sufficiently strong evidence that alternatives for the full range of applications are not available‘.
The submitter is of the view that the wording of this derogation is too narrow. It excludes important mobility sub-sectors such as electric bikes and elevators, and it is ambiguous towards other applications, such as forklifts and earth-moving equipment.
The submitter proposes that the text of the derogation be changed as follows: „applications affecting the proper functioning related to the safety of transport, mobility, lifting appliances and material and earth-moving equipment, and affecting the safety of users, passengers or goods.“
A detailed reasoning is set forth in Section 6 below.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Transport (including mobility)

5. Proposed derogations: Please see last paragraph of Section 6

6. Missing uses: The Annex XV Report includes the following derogation that is marked for reconsideration: ‘use of PFASs in applications affecting the proper functioning related to the safety of vehicles, and affecting the safety of operators, passengers or goods.‘   The PFAS Q/A document published June 2023 provides that the term ‘vehicles‘ covers “regular conveyance of passengers, goods, animals etc as well as the transport vehicle itself. (…)” The derogation corresponds to sector ‘transport’ described in Annex A.3.11. of Annex A as including sub-sectors ‘automotive, maritime, aviation and railway‘.  These definitions are not covering the following sub-uses.   - Electric bikes and other mobility electric appliances The terms ‘vehicles’ and ‘automotive’ do not cover electric bikes, electric kick scooters and similar emerging mobility appliances. These appliances include a number of critical components that rely on fluoropolymers to ensure safe use. By way of example, electric bikes include synchronous belts that contain PTFE to handle extreme friction and wearing during the use. Currently, there is no alternative material that would be able to withstand such conditions without breaking.  Any unexpected rupture of synchronous belt would have serious safety implications on the user. For these reasons, the submitter proposes to add the term ‘mobility’ into the text of the derogation, with the intent to cover electric bikes, kick scooters and similar appliances.  - Elevators This important sub-sector is completely missing in the Annex XV Report, despite serious safety implications. Elevators include several critical components containing fluoropolymers, including synchronous belts. For such components, there is currently no viable alternative. Components with alternative materials known to date would lead to malfunctioning of the elevator with potentially fatal consequences. That is why the submitter proposes to add the term ‘lifting appliances’ to the text of the derogation.   - Forklifts  It is unclear whether the term ‘vehicles’ also includes material and earth moving equipment such as forklifts. These types of equipment also include several critical components containing fluoropolymers, including synchronous belts. Unexpected failure of a forklift or other heavy-duty appliances may lead to fatal injuries. Thus, in order to increase legal certainty, the submitter proposes to add the term material and earth-moving equipment.   Socio-economic analysis  As acknowledged in Annex XV Report (Table 8, page 131), for appliances containing fluoropolymers that are necessary to ensure safe functioning of transport-related appliances, there is a ‘sufficiently strong evidence that alternatives for the full range of applications are not available‘.  The submitter would like to second this conclusion. The submitter tested the most promising potential alternative material identified to date (Resorcinol Formaldehyde Latex (RFL) treated jacket material) in several tests and compared it to PTFE. The first test was a high-tension weight loss test. The test results revealed that whereas the weight loss of PTFE material remains relatively stable over run time, the weight loss of the alternative material becomes exponential after 100 hours of run time. In the motored engine test and in the High Torque Synchronous Belt life test, the alternative material achieved approximately 20% life span in hours as compared to PTFE.  [please see the attachment for detailed charts with test results]. This demonstrates that this alternative is not suitable and viable.   The socio-economic impact of the use of safety-critical applications without fluoropolymers would be as follows:  • High occurrence of unexpected failures during service life of transport and mobility appliances, leading to: (i) serious risk to users and passengers, with potentially fatal consequences, and (ii) damage to transported/lifted goods, • Significantly higher energy consumption due to higher friction, • Shorter service life of appliances, leading to higher consumption of raw materials and more waste. As a consequence, any transport/mobility products manufactured without fluoropolymers in critical applications would not be competitive globally.  Therefore, the manufacturing of the entire sector would have to move outside of the EU, which would lead to the loss of jobs and turnovers related to the entire mobility sector. Furthermore, non-availability of safe and viable electric mobility appliances on the EU market would have negative consequences to the achievement of the green deal goals as electric mobility is an emerging alternative to fossil-fuel vehicles.     The estimated overall weight of fluoropolymers in all submitter’s automotive/mobility belts manufactured in the EU is 23.6 tonnes per year. This translates in several million belt units/year. The portion of fluoropolymers in the mobility applications covered by this submission will be smaller by orders of magnitude (exact data is not available).

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The present proposal for the regulation of PFAS under the REACH Regulation would imply potential restrictions on the manufacture, placing on the market as well as the use of PFAS. The primary justification for the potential restriction is the very high persistence, as well as the high mobility, bioaccumulation potential, long-range transport potential, global warming potential, ecotoxicity, and human health effects of some PFAS substances. PFASs can enter the environment throughout the product life cycle during the manufacturing, use, and disposal phases without targeted protective measures, further increasing global concentrations.

Almost all manufacturers of machinery and equipment would be affected to varying degrees by a potential future PFAS restriction under the present regulatory proposal, either in the products or in production. For example, hydraulic components such as pumps, motors, valves, or cylinders, machine components that are essential to the operation of most industrial machinery and equipment, would be very significantly affected. PFASs, mostly fluorinated polymers, are often used, for example, in seals, hoses, pipes, valves and coatings, despite their generally much higher cost, because of their properties. A PFAS ban would in some cases lead to significant deterioration in the performance of the products. More drastic, however, would be the consequences of no longer being able to manufacture, import and market many machines at all, with the result that many companies would be completely or partially deprived of the basis for their business.

The chemical scope of the proposal is very broad and thus groups together different substances with different properties and risk profiles and regulates them equally. A sound risk assessment of the individual PFAS, taking into account not only hazard properties but also exposures from the various uses, has not been carried out. However, according to Article 68 of the REACH Regulation, applications of PFAS for which no risk could be identified should also be possible in the future.
F-gases fall under the universal PFAS restriction, whereas certain F-gases are already regulated under the EU F-gases Regulation. Thus, F-gases would be subject to double regulation.
As the classification of PFAS in the CLP Regulation is insufficiently harmonized, an analysis of concern is difficult to impossible, especially for machinery and equipment manufacturers in the middle of the supply chain. Traceability in formulations or intermediates can only be done using a final list of PFAS of very high concern (classified as CMR - carcinogenic, mutagenic, toxic for reproduction, PBT - persistent, bioaccumulative and toxic, vPvB - very persistent and very bioaccumulative, PMT - Persistent, mobile and toxic, vPvM - very persistent, very mobile; or as ED - endocrine disruptors, substances with endocrine-disrupting properties) with CAS numbers.
The use of PFAS-containing seals, hoses, pipes, valves and coatings is exempted from the ban in the restriction proposal only in certain industrial plants for a limited period of time. Yet these applications have a very high relevance for the entire industry. In addition, fluoropolymers are frequently used in industrial applications. Some of them have been scientifically evaluated as "polymers of low concern" (PTFE, EFTE, FEP, PFA, PVDF and VDF-co-HFP) because they are chemically stable, non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water soluble and non-mobile (see Henry et al (2018): A Critical Review of the Application of Polymer of Low Concern and Regulatory Criteria to Fluoropolymers. Integr. Environ. Assess. Manage. 2018, 14 (3), 316−334.). Since all fluoropolymers are considered polymers of low concern, any deviating classification would have to be scientifically justified.
Substitution options should be examined carefully and as part of a holistic approach. It must be ensured that suitable and equivalent alternatives are actually available for affected uses in terms of existing technical regulations, technological maturity, safety-related aspects, energy consumption, service life and other factors.
The transition periods formulated in the regulatory proposal conflict with the sustainability principle of repair-before-replace. Machines and systems are designed for decades-long periods of use. Repairs using spare and used parts to replace wear parts (such as seals and hoses) would no longer be possible after the transition period of 18 months. Even where exceptions exist, they are proposed only for five and twelve years. It is not clear whether and how an extension of the existing exemptions can be requested.

Such PFAS that are classified as very hazardous (e.g. CMR, PBT, vPvB, PMT, vPvM, or ED) should not be able to enter the environment. In this respect, regulation of these PFAS classified as hazardous is fundamentally correct if there is a risk of exposure. Likewise, it is understandable to group PFASs sensibly in terms of their risk potential so as not to have to regulate each of the potentially more than 10,000 substances individually. Nevertheless, we call for the extent of the regulation, the length of the transitional periods, the possibility of exemptions, the scope of application, as well as the demarcation from other regulations to be adjusted.
The restriction proposal includes F-gases, low molecular weight compounds as well as fluoropolymers. Regulation must be more differentiated and based on a comprehensive, scientific risk assessment. Substances assigned to substance groups must be shown to have comparable hazardous properties. The risk-based approach provided for in the REACH restriction procedure must be maintained so that uses that do not pose an unacceptable risk continue to be possible.
We call for a general exemption of fluoropolymers that are considered "polymers of low concern" according to the OECD definition. Substances, such as monomers and processing aids, which are necessary for fluoropolymer manufacture and production must be exempted from the ban, provided that safe use is ensured. Thus, groups with low risk (e.g. fluoroelastomers, fluoropolymers, assessed as "polymers of low concern") or uses without relevant risk (e.g. uses in closed systems) must be exempted.
In applications with extreme conditions (high or low temperatures, high pressure, UV radiation, high frictional resistance, aggressive chemicals or a combination of these) there are no suitable alternatives to PFAS-containing products. The use of fluoropolymers is anyway limited to applications where they are indispensable due to high prices. For example, the use of PFASs in industrial applications (e.g. seals, hoses, pipes, valves, compressors and coatings) contributes to safety, resource efficiency and longevity of industrial equipment, among others.
Some PFASs are mobile and enter the environment. However, the environmental pathway of various PFAS subgroups must be considered. Exemptions must apply where there is no relevant (environmentally hazardous) entry into the environment. A fluoropolymer seal located in the enclosed space of a machine definitely does not pose a relevant risk. Furthermore, an application in the B2B sector must be distinguished from one in the B2C sector. Industrial players can ensure that PFAS, PFAS-containing materials and products are handled professionally throughout the entire life cycle through professional risk management.
For industrial applications, the 18-month transition period formulated in the restriction proposal is too short. A period of several years is already needed to test the possible alternatives for functionality and safe applications, to qualify them for series use and, in many cases, to approve them under EU legislation. Thus, the general transition period must also be several years.
For the purpose of sustainability and economic efficiency, exceptions to the restriction are required for the placing on the market of spare, wear and used parts. These must be granted for an unlimited period or at least for a significantly longer period than the transitional periods currently provided for. In addition, it must be made possible to apply for future exemptions in an uncomplicated and unbureaucratic manner and to ensure that exemptions can be extended.
The chemical scope of the restriction must be communicated transparently by means of a clear list of affected substances (incl. IUPAC names, CAS numbers, EC numbers) so that companies can collect the information along the international and widely ramified supply chain.
It is unclear how universal regulation for PFAS will correlate with other regulations currently under discussion (in particular the EU F-Gases Regulation, (EU) No. 517/2014). Consistency and coherence with other EU regulatory frameworks must be ensured.

Content: Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The present submission is part of the submission of figawa e.V., DGMT and AE for the public consultation on the PFAS restriction proposal.
It describes the use of fluoropolymers (FPs) in products used for Gas and Liquid Fuels applications, which describe the use of highly flammable, combustible gases and short-chain molecules with high energy densities. The most commonly used GLFs are natural gas (mainly composed of methane, CH4), compressed natural gas (CNG), liquefied natural gas (LNG), liquefied petroleum gas (C3-C4 alkanes, LPG), and liquid mineral oils. In addition, renewable GLFs, such as hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO), fatty acid methyl esters (FAME), dimethyl ether (DME), and hydrogen (H2) in natural gas and pure H2 are gaining more relevance as energy carrier. Hence, storage, transport and measuring (for billing) of of all these energy carriers is included in GLF applications.
Combustion technology is of utmost importance in providing heat and energy for industrial, private and commercial purposes. Ensuring the safe and efficient operation of these applications relies on precise control and measurement of critical parameters. One such crucial aspect is the regulation of internal pressure, achieved through the use of gas pressure regulators incorporating fluoropolymers-based components. These fluoropolymers-based parts play a vital role in preventing overpressure build-up, safeguarding against potential environmental and economic disasters in the case of gas or liquid fuel releases.
Fluoropolymers-based sealings, including materials like FKM, PTFE, and PVDF, are currently indispensable in these installations. Their exceptional chemical and temperature resistance, along with robust mechanical properties, make them the preferred choice, as no other materials currently match their performance, lifetime and meet the stringent standards required for these critical applications. Fluoropolymers-based sealings also hold significant importance in the private, residential, commercial and industrial sectors in gas heating / applications, where they serve to prevent leaks and potential accidents.
FPs are high-performance materials with exceptional properties, such as chemical resistance, thermal stability, low flammability, material flexibility and anti-friction / gliding properties. There is no other available material that combines this wide range of functions and therefore no suitable alternatives exist at this time. Hence, figawa primarily supports an exemption of fluoropolymers by way of a time-unlimited derogation for the Gas and Liquid Fuels applications and distribution or at least the longest derogation period to perform the research necessary to find and implement alternatives that meet high standards, which would certainly require more than 20 years.
figawa members are mainly assembling end-products from components. During the assembly the exposure potential and emissions are very limited. Similarly, during the use phase emissions are considered controlled for most applications. For an assessment of end-of-life emissions, more research is required in the opinion of figawa and its members. This would also help to provide a foundation for more adequate regulatory measures in light of the low overall risks of FPs in the products’ different life-stages.
In summary, the consequences of a PFAS restriction, as outlined by the socioeconomic evaluation, amount to roughly 515.10 million Euros (NPV 2025) or 21.01 million Euros annually over a 45-year period. While this analysis predominantly focuses on input from figawa members and addresses issues related to gas and fuel shortages due to lack of impacted GLF components, it is crucial to highlight the far-reaching repercussions that a restriction, without the desired exemption, could have on the entire EEA society. Fast CO2-reduction by replacing hydrocarbons against hydrogen H2 would become with a high probability impossible.

For further details, please refer to the attached reports.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: a) During the manufacturing phase of end-products, the main task is assembly, which is conducted at room temperature. Overall, the potential for FP emissions during the manufacturing phase is considered limited as no or few tasks require heating or dissolving, or use components which are not purchased on the open market as ready-to-use. Nonetheless, figawa members are open to implementing monitoring programs and improving risk minimization measures if necessary.  In the use phase of FP-containing products, most components have minimal potential for emissions due to FPs' chemical and thermal stability. The long service-life and durability of these products also limit emissions from wear-and-tear effects. The main contact media for these components are air and gases, which makes wear-and-tear effects unlikely to contribute to environmental emissions. Some component groups, such as lubricants and coatings, may have emissions during use, but these are generally considered to be negligible, especially for components in direct contact with non-liquid media like gas or air. Overall, the emission potential of FPs from most components during the use phase is considered very low.  The disposal routes at end-of-life stage of products manufactured by figawa members depend on the product group. However, the disposal of end-products is often beyond the scope of manufacturers. Emissions from waste disposal can be challenging to standardize, as they depend on the waste disposal route, the proportion and type of PFAS in the product, and whether the end-product is dismantled before disposal. Landfilling FPs were reported, but there is uncertainty about the possibility of leaching and environmental impacts of landfilled FPs. Recycling is primarily focused on metals or valuable raw materials, rather than FPs. Despite the current difficulties regarding recycling, figawa members would like to highlight that FPs are important and valuable materials. Recycling is also an effective measure to reduce the amount of waste entering other waste-streams. The development of a regulatory framework for the recycling of FP materials should thus be emphasized. figawa members are in support of the development of legal requirements leading to the implementation of a recycling system for FPs. Incineration is considered the main waste disposal route in Europe, with both municipal and hazardous waste incinerators used. The incineration of FP-containing end-products may result in the formation of fluorinated by-products, but the extent is unclear. Knowledge on incineration and by-product formation and progress on abatement technologies is expected to be made available rapidly, allowing for the implementation of regulatory threshold values to minimize emissions. Figawa members support this approach.  While the emissions during manufacture and use phase are considered controlled, small emissions may occur during the use phase. The potential for emissions during the end-of-life phase, especially from incineration, cannot be excluded. However, further research on waste treatment options and abatement technologies is required as the extent and type of emissions is not well researched.  b) Based on end-products reported, an assessment on the distribution of disposal routes was assessed. However, information on disposal routes were collected from figawa members, which are manufacturers, and not from end-users. Due to this and the partly small sample size information may be subject to uncertainties. For a detailed breakdown, please refer to the attached CSR report.

There is no other available material that combines this wide range of functions and therefore no suitable alternatives exist at this time. Hence, figawa primarily supports an exemption of FPs by way of a time-unlimited derogation for the water supply applications or at least the longest derogation period to perform the research necessary to find and implement alternatives that meet high standards, which would certainly require more than 20 years.
figawa members are mainly assembling end-products from components. During the assembly the exposure potential and emissions are very limited. Combined Comments:
General Comments: The problematics of the proposed PFAS restriction -- science, law and policy

Summary

With the endorsement of the ideals of the toxic-free and pollution-free environment, EU chemical regulation is evolving rapidly and becoming more and more precautionary, moralistic, and, consequently, unhinged. The proposed restriction on thousands of diverse substances under the label of ‘all PFAS’ through the broadest ban on chemicals ever is illustrative of these trends.

The PFAS proposal flies in the face of science-based risk regulation, breaches the law, and deters innovation and investment in the EU. One of the most vexing problems associated with the PFAS Proposal relates to the unscientific use of the ‘grouping approach,’ which throws all subgroups of PFAS substances on the same pile based merely on a common moiety, without regard to hazard, risk, and exposure profiles. Another serious deficiency involves the equating of persistence (which is merely a pejorative way to characterize durability) with risk and even harm. The combination of persistence as harm with broad, open-ended grouping spreads and augments the adverse effects of the PFAS restriction.

This proposal would not only make a mockery of science-based chemical risk regulation, but also set aside the essential safeguards set forth in the REACH Regulation and imposed by EU law. In essence, the grouping based solely on structural similarity reflects dogmatic thinking inspired by the precautionary principle and the naturalistic fallacy — ‘only biodegradable is good’.  The main purpose of this paper is to explain how the proposal is neither science-based nor compliant with the applicable legal requirements.

The PFAS Proposal, which targets over 10,000 different substances, treats a known desirable property, durability, as an unknown potential harm that must be prevented at all costs and irrespective of the risks associated with the withdrawal of substances and the widespread introduction of alternatives. Undisciplined reading across from some hazardous PFAS substances, such as PFOS and PFOA, to all PFAS substances, however, would result in overly broad, unnecessary, and disproportionate regulation.

The default assumption under the REACH Regulation is that chemicals are regulated substance-by-substance, based on substance-specific careful risk assessment, assessment of alternatives, and socio-economic impact analysis, subject only to grouping under strict conditions. This fundamental principle is perverted in the PFAS proposal. Despite the proposal’s many pages and extensive annexes, risk assessments are unavailable for the vast majority of PFAS, assessments of alternatives are poorly supported with evidence or even entirely lacking, and the impact analysis is rudimentary at best.

The problematics of this proposed restriction are not limited to PFAS – it is indicative of the current trends in chemical risk regulation and would set a precedent that does not bode well for future regulatory proposals. As the PFAS Proposal demonstrates, European governments have discovered the potential of persistence as a vehicle to phase-out large groups of chemicals in pursuit of “toxic-free” society and “pollution-free” environment. Following incidents in the US and Europe, PFAS is an easy target and now serves as the test case for this novel approach. This proposal therefore should be of great concern to all stakeholders that care for balanced, science-based chemical risk regulation in accordance with the law.

Thorough analysis of the issues associated with the PFAS proposal suggests that the EU has incrementally moved towards chemical regulation based on an ideal of rooting out any chemical risk, and increasingly ignores the growing problem of false positives, risk/risk trade-offs (the risks of existing substances with which there is experience versus the risks of replacement substances that are largely unknowns) and the environmental, human health and economic consequences of the “zero risk” approach. Rather than preventing “regrettable substitution,” the proposal would result in regrettable stigmatization and, indeed, may increase, rather than prevent, risks of regrettable substitution.

Instead of the dogmatic approach reflected in the PFAS Proposal, the EU should follow the chemical risk regulation model embedded in the REACH Regulation, group PFAS in a way that reflects science and regulatory requirements, target risks that are unacceptable, and carefully weigh the costs and benefits of alternative regulatory measures and their real-world effects. In short, it should return to chemical risk management based on the tested principles of science-based risk assessment and relative cost-benefit analysis of available risk management options.

General Comments: The project, ‘Fluoropolymer Waste in Europe 2020’ was initiated by Pro-K and developed by Conversio provides information about the end of life fate of fluoropolymer applications, products and associated waste streams. The attached report delivers an in-depth description on how and where fluoropolymer containing products and corresponding wastes are generated and what happens to the collected fractions at the end of life that is identification of the waste treatment route such as incineration, landfill and recycling. Quantities of fluoropolymer waste are included as far as possible based on end-of-life of fluoropolymer lifetime assessment model.

From the study, it was concluded that in 2020, around 40 kilotons of fluoropolymer materials were sold to EU fluoropolymer product manufacturers. Out of which, 23.5 kilotons of fluoropolymer waste was collected, either in commingle waste streams or partly in source separated waste fractions. Almost, 84% of fluoropolymer applications were incinerated at the end of their life in energy recovery, 13% of the collected fluoropolymer waste was landfilled and around 3% was recycled. Overall, fluoropolymer waste is a tiny fraction of less than 0.01% by weight in comparison to the total plastic waste collected.

The Group is headquartered in Heidelberg, Germany. More than 2,800 employees in about 50 own sales and service companies as well as 11 production sites work hard to provide individual solutions and high-quality services to ProMinent customers in about 100 countries.

The ProMinent Group provides solutions for metering, water treatment and disinfection, measuring and control as well as digital fluid management for the following industries:
Chemical industry, industrial and municipal water treatment, food and beverage industry, treatment of swimming pool water, oil and gas industry and process industry.
The extensive product portfolio consists of metering pumps, peristaltic pumps, measuring and control technology and sensors to manage and meter fluids as well as metering systems for water treatment. For this purpose ProMinent provides all common systems, such as chlorine dioxide plants, chlorine gas metering systems, electrolysis systems, UV systems, ozone systems as well as systems for membrane filtration.

One of our base technologies is preparation, mixing and dosing of highly concentrated chemicals. By our devices, the highly concentrated chemicals are diluted into a process. Thus, we are dealing with the chemicals when they are most aggressive. Once the chemicals are diluted, they are usually much less aggressive. Environmental protection an operator safety is a must for us. We can only achieve this safety, using the most resistant materials available. These materials are fluoropolymers, which fall under the planned restriction.
If fluoropolymers become restricted for pumping/dosing applications, we significantly increase the risk, to spoil dangerous chemicals in our environment with the danger of injuring people.
In general, we require the availability of highly restistant tubing, seals, liners, pumpheads, valves, coatings, diaphragms.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: We cannot find our applications in the list of sectors. Our Company produces positive displacement systems for water and general fluid applications. They could contain pumps, valves, tubes, sensors etc. Below you can find a typical list of applications:   • Industrial food and feed production • Metal plating and manufacture of metal products  • Hydraulic fluids • Energy sector  • Lubricants • Petroleum and mining • Public and domestic drinking water plants  • Public and domestic swimming pool applications  • Industrial und public waste water treatment plants  • Public car, train or aircraft washing station • General industrial und public chemical process plants • Galvanic industry  This list of applications can for sure be extended, as our customers use our products, wherever they need to accurately adjust water quality.  We typically use polymer PFAS materials such as PVDF, PFA, PTFE as chemical resistant materials, tubing and diaphragms, but also coatings like ECTFE or elastomers on sealings like FKM or FFKM.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Production phase: On PVDF bulk components, the materials are used in moulding machines at temperatures way below the degradation temperatures. On PTFE diaphragms: During the production phase of composite PFTE diaphragms the maximum temperature during the vulcanization process is between 160°C and 180°C far less than the maximum usage temperature of PTFE ( 220°C ). Therefor no emission of PFAS are expected. On other components: Usually, fluorinated polymers used as seals, bearings, cables and coatings are supplied by specialized companies.  Usage phase:  The service lifetime of a diaphragm is between 3 and 10 years, depending on the intensity of usage, the type of chemistry to be dosed, the backpressure and the temperature of the chemical to be dosed. During the lifetime there is no indication of emission of PFAS. Also,the other components are not expected to show emissions because of their high stability.  End-of-life phase:  The composite diaphragms are thermically recycled at temperatures of 850°C or higher. Therefor we do not expect any formation of PFAS. Pure PFAS Polymers might be collected and used for chemical recycling.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: 95 % of our products (e.g. dosing pumps) are electrically driven and fall under directive 2012/19/EU ( WEEE ). Therefor all electrical products, containing a dosing diaphragm are collected and are recycled according this directive. Therefore it is easy to separate the diaphragm and the dosing head (may contain PTFE or PVDF or FKM ) in the recycling process and send these parts to special recycling facilities.
