Content: Information on benefits Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The proposed restriction of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) also affects the use of PVDF (Polyvinylidene fluoride) in medical applications.
PVDF (Polyvinylidene fluoride) was first investigated in Québec, Canada in the mid 1990s as an alternative suture material to polypropylene (PP) monofilaments in vascular surgery [Urban E, King MW, Guidoin R, Laroche G, Marois Y, Martin L, Cardou A, Douville Y. Why make monofilament sutures out of polyvinylidene fluoride? ASAIO J. 1994;40(2):145-56]. It turned out to feature advantageous physico-chemical and handling characteristics as well as superior biocompatability compared to polypropylene [Mary C, Marois Y, King MW, Laroche G, Douville Y, Martin L, Guidoin R. Comparison of the in vivo behavior of polyvinylidene fluoride and polypropylene sutures used in vascular surgery. ASAIO J. 1998;44(3):199-206].
The first animal studies of PVDF polymer as surgical mesh material were performed in Aachen, Germany in 2002 [Klinge U, Klosterhalfen B, Ottinger AP, Junge K, Schumpelick V. PVDF as a new polymer for the construction of surgical meshes. Biomaterials. 2002;23(16):3487-93]. Although approved as surgical mesh implant in humans since 2003 (in Germany) further studies underlined the favourable biocompatability of PVDF as mesh material for pelvic floor repair [Gerullis H, Georgas E, Eimer C, Goretzki PE, Lammers BJ, Klosterhalfen B, Boros M, Wishahi M, Heusch G, Otto T. Evaluation of Biocompatibility of Alloplastic Materials: Development of a Tissue Culture In Vitro Test System. Surg Technol Int. 2011;21:21-7].
Currently, PVDF surgical mesh implants are in use in hernia surgery (mostly in male patients), in pelvic floor repair in female patients to treat pelvic organ prolapse, and in stress urinary incontinence surgery both in male and female patients, a condition that costs the European society over 40 billion Euros per year. To date, no specific material-related complications have been reported in these indications over 20 years.
Recent data provided evidence that the clinical use of PVDF both in pelvic organ prolapse (POP) surgery and stress urinary incontinence (SUI) surgery had statistically significant lower rates of side-effects compared to polypropylene (PP). Typical side-effects are de-novo sexual dysfunction after POP surgery (with PVDF materials statistically significant lower rates compared to the PP group [OR = 0.12 (0.03, 0.46), p = 0.002]) and de-novo urinary urgency after SUI surgery (with PVDF materials statistically significant lower rates compared to the PP group [OR = 0.38 (0.18, 0.88), p = 0.01]) [Karalis T, Tsiapakidou S, Grimbizis GF, Mikos T. Surgical results in POP/UI surgery after using PVDF compared to other materials. A systematic review and meta-analysis. European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology 2023;284:110–119].
These findings are in line with the personal experience of more than 10 years of pelvic surgery with PVDF mesh implants in male and female patients. In the interest of high quality patient care I therefore call for an exemption for PVDF mesh materials in approved medical applications.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The proposed restriction of PFAS (Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl substances) proposed by 5 European countries is an excessive measure because it restricts more than 10,000 of organofluorine compounds (PFAS) on the grouping basis that they are equivalent in persistence to substances of concern. Polymer PFAS, compared with other PFAS, have very different physical, chemical, environmental, and toxicological properties, and they are thermally, biologically, and chemically stable, negligibly soluble in water, nonmobile, nonbioavailable, nonbioaccumulative, and nontoxic. Among other fluoropolymers, fluororesins, such as Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), are indispensable and irreplaceable due to its properties (e.g. resistance to heat, chemicals, resistance, corrosion, UV rays and oxidation resistance). They are used for and indispensable to wide range of products and situations. In addition, alternatives to polymerization aids for the production of the fluororesins have not beavailable. Therefore, we believe that Polymer PFAS as a whole, or at least fluororesins and fluororubbers, and polymerization aids for their production, should be excluded or exempted from the scope of the proposed restriction.

1. Polymer PFAS
A recent review(*1) states 16 unique families of commercially popular fluoropolymers meet the OECD Polymer of Low Concern criteria(*2). Abstract says below: Fluoropolymers possess a unique combination of properties and unmatched functional performance critical to the products and manufacturing processes they enable and are irreplaceable in many uses. Fluoropolymers have documented safety profiles; are thermally, biologically, and chemically stable, negligibly soluble in water, nonmobile, nonbioavailable, nonbioaccumulative, and nontoxic. Although fluoropolymers fit the PFAS structural definition, they have very different physical, chemical, environmental, and toxicological properties when compared with other PFAS. Even if the polymer is persistent, large molecule such as polymer cannot permeate to cell membrane.
*1.
Integr Environ Assess Manag - 2022 - Korzeniowski - A critical review of the application of polymer of low concern regulatory criteria to fluoropolymers II: Fluoroplastics and fluoroelastomers.pdf
*2.
https://www.oecd.org/env/ehs/risk-assessment/42081261.pdf

2. Fluororesins and fluororubbers
2-1. characteristics
Compared to conventional plastics, fluororesins, such as PTFE, PFA, FEP, ETFE, PVDF, PCTFE and ECTFE, and fluororubbers such as FEPM and FFKM, are chemically resistant, resistant to harsh conditions such as high and low temperatures, and have significantly longer lifespans, while at the same time being harmless to living organisms and the environment.Some fluororesins, such as PTFE and FEP, have additional properties: electrical characteristics, non-adhesiveness, abrasion resistance, corrosion resistance, UV rays resistance, oxidation resistance, cleanliness

2-2. use
Fluororesins are used for wide range of products and situations.
PTFE, for example, does not deform even at temperatures above 200℃, and is highly resistant to UV rays and oxidation. Therefore it is used for almost all process piping and sealing materials for pipe connection in chemical plants
PTFE seals are always used to connect high pressure gas cylinders and pipes such as oxygen, nitrogen and hydrogen.
Chemical resistance and heat resistance are important in laboratory synthesis experiments, and PTFE resins are used everywhere.
Chemical resistance and heat resistance are important for large-scale synthesis (780 L scale) at chemical manufacturing plants, and are essential for hydrolysis with high-concentration hydrochloric acid (heating and stirring at 50°C for 48 hours) For this reason, PTFE is used as a coating agent for SUS mechanical agitators.
We mainly use German-made diaphragm vacuum pumps. Diaphragms generally used in pumps are made of fluororubber for the flexible part and fluororesin for the wetted part. Spare parts are made of chemically resistant PVDF, PTFE and, FKM, FEPM.（Please see the Confidential Attachment in Section V.）

Fluororubber and fluororesin contribute to automobile safety, contribute to industrial decarbonization, and prevent environmental pollution. There is no suitable alternative material that meets all the required properties.
The characteristics and materials of PTFE such as chemical resistance, cleanliness, elasticity, non-adhesiveness, and heat resistance that will be used in various situations are also suitable for medical equipment, such as parts and tubes of various analyzers. Fluororesin tubing is used all over the world.
High-concentration, high-purity chemicals are used in semiconductor manufacturing equipment, which is indispensable to modern society, so PTFE, which has excellent heat resistance, chemical resistance, and abrasion resistance, is widely used. To date, no alternative materials have been found to replace PTFE, so we request an exemption.

2-3. alternatives and impact of the restriction
・Sealing materials and coating agents for process piping and piping connections in chemical plants
(1).No alternative.
PTFE is used for almost all process pipes in chemical plants, sealing materials for pipe joints, coating agents for SUS mechanical stirrers, coating agents for magnetic stirrers, etc. To date, no alternative materials have been found to replace PTFE.

(2).The impact of regulations on industry and society.
Most factories in the EU use Fluororesin, so they will have to move their factories out of the EU before the regulations start. It is inevitable that small and medium-sized enterprises such as European chemical factories, semiconductor factories and food factories, and power generation facilities in the EU will be seriously affected. In Europe, a serious impact on general consumers is inevitable.

・medical equipment, such as parts and tubes of various analyzers
(1).No alternative.
Fluororesin parts are used in all kinds of analyzers, such as gas chromatographs, caschromatograph mass spectrometers, liquid chromatographs, liquid chromatograph mass spectrometers, and spectrometers. The septum is also made of fluororesin such as PTFE to avoid organic contamination from the sample vial. Fluororesins are also used in laboratory equipment such as flasks and beakers to prevent contamination from glass in metal trace analysis.
Fluoropolymers and fluororubber such as PTFE, PVDF, PFA, FKM, and FEPM are widely used in the medical and pharmaceutical industries due to their functional properties and low reactivity. A fluororesin tube is used for the innermost layer of the catheter. PVDF is used to treat tissue defects and has excellent in vivo stability and durability. Fluoropolymers are highly capable of providing safe and effective treatments for many patients.

According to Annex XV Restrictions Report p99 and 128, there is currently no alternative and development will take more than 5 years, so a grace period of 1.5 years + 12 years is provided. We request a waiver, not a grace period, as we have no other alternatives.

(2).The impact of regulations on industry and society.
If the analysis equipment becomes unusable, it will not be possible to analyze controlled substances. Quality and safety inspections for products produced in all industries will not be verified. With the lack of medical equipment, medicines, and treatments for patients, companies in the EU are expected to suffer catastrophic damage, and it is predicted that the global economy will be adversely affected.

・semiconductor manufacturing equipment
(1).No alternative.
High-concentration, high-purity chemicals are used in semiconductor manufacturing equipment, which is indispensable to modern society, so PTFE, which has excellent heat resistance, chemical resistance, and abrasion resistance, is widely used.
In this semiconductor industry, fluoropolymers are used for transport of ultrapure water and other process media due to the excellent leach out behaviour, cleanliness, resistance against bio-film, high temperature resistance, chemical resistance, excellent mechanical properties and long lifetime performance.

According to ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT p105 and 135, it is subject to a grace period of1.5+12years because there is no alternative at present and it will take 3 to 10 years to develop it. We request a waiver, not a grace period, as we have no other alternatives and there is little prospect of development thereof within 3 to 10 years.

(2).The impact of regulations on industry and society.
If these fluororesin products are restricted, the semiconductor manufacturing process will be greatly affected, and DX, automobile EV, AI technology, IoT technology, etc. will be forced to retreat, and the world economy will be major impact on the global economy.

2-4.About spare parts
In addition to the above, separate consideration is required for fluororesin spare parts for products marketed before the regulation, as the life of the final product will be extremely shortened if it is not exempted, leading to the increased volume of the waste.
Products need the same spare parts as those used in the first production of each product. A re-design of spare parts often also requires a re-design of the products, because otherwise the original performance (i.e. safety and durability) can’t be guaranteed. Considering the supply chain and production processes of many manufacturers, such a re-design will be impossible in most cases.

We use diaphragm type vacuum pumps (made in Germany), and spare parts are made of PVDF and PTFE, FKM, FEPM, which have excellent chemical resistance. Diaphragm type vacuum pumps must be chemically resistant to all organic solvents, but only his fluororesins and his fluororubbers combinations meet this requirement.

If spare parts cannot be supplied, it will be impossible to procure them from within the EU. In the future, we will have no choice but to change to a diaphragm-type vacuum pump made outside the EU.

3. Polymerization aid in high molecular weight PFAS production
The transition period for PTFE, PVDF and FKM used as coagents is only 18 months, and for other coagents a period of 6.5 years (18 months transition period and 5 years grace period) is proposed (ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT, p.5 (Conditions of restriction 5 a) and p.116)
Published General Comments REF No.3960 contains a description of the importance and irreplaceability of coagents. As there is no alternative method for polymerization aids used in the production of fluororesin and fluororubber, exemption is requested.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: The proposed restriction of PFAS does not consider the sector of mechanical engineering. While medical products are exempted from the restriction, the machines which are needed to produce these products are not. Not only medical products but a variety of important products use machines and parts from the mechanical engineering industry. Therefore, it is important to consider the needs and boundaries of this sector in the restriction. We are a medium-sized company which produces weighing and labelling machines for the food industry. We use some articles which are suspected to contain PFAS, e.g. sealings, valves, hoses, electronic devices and parts etc. So, we are sure to be affected by the proposed restriction, but how big the impact is and how long it will take to find and test alternatives is not foreseeable. It should be noted that this applies not only to our headquarters in Germany, but also to our four subsidiaries (Spain, Netherlands, France and Belgium) and 19 distributors in the European region.
As a medium-sized company, we are one of the most common types of company in Europe. According to the IfM Bonn (Institut der Mittelstandsforschung), 99.8% of companies in Europe were SMEs in 2021.[1] SMEs are very important for the economy, as almost two-thirds of all employees in Europe work in SMEs. However, the average number of employees per SME in 2021 was 7.1 in Germany and only 3.6 in Europe.[1] It follows that the average company in Europe has limited personnel and financial capacities.
Especially in recent years, the number of regulations on product safety and sustainability has increased. Here it is important for companies to assess how they are affected, to be aware of their responsibilities and to act. This requires an ever-increasing amount of time and money. Until a few years ago, most SMEs were unaffected by such regulations and are now overwhelmed by the bureaucracy involved. According to an article in the "Haufe" newsletter, most SMEs do not have a dedicated compliance department, but only one part-time person who is responsible but often not specialised in these issues.[2] Our own experience in communicating with our suppliers also confirms this statement. In the future, the introduction of compliance management systems or departments will probably increase as SMEs are increasingly affected by such regulations. However, this will take a lot of time due to the limited personnel and financial capacities mentioned above.
As a manufacturer of complex machines, we do not produce raw materials or individual parts. We are a so-called downstream user. Therefore, we do not know the formulations of the materials we buy and depend on the information provided by our suppliers. This dependence creates several problems. First, we are not able to substitute raw materials, but have to wait for the market to adjust, e.g., we have been trying to source our purchased items lead-free for a year. This change was not possible for pneumatic connectors, for example, because there is no lead-free alternative due to the high costs. It was also not possible to obtain a custom-made product. Another problem is communication along the supply chain. Currently, the understanding of what PFASs are, is generally non-existent, and the capacity to identify PFAS is limited as many of our suppliers are also SMEs. Over the past month, we have been trying to get as much information as possible about PFAS in our products so that we can participate in this consultation. We asked 15 suppliers, not just SMEs, if they could provide us with information about intentionally added PFAS in their products. Only three companies responded. None of them could provide us with information that would meet the requirements of the proposed restriction. For this reason, we do not know what PFASs are in our products and in what quantity, with the exception of some parts that are made of PTFE. Therefore, we cannot apply for an exemption now and hope that our suppliers will be able to do so.
Even if there were a PFAS-free alternative for every material we use in our machines, the process of conversion is much more complicated. In the best case, the new item and the one it replaces are identical. This refers not only to the typical properties of PFAS, but also to the dimensions, tolerances, and so on. If there are changes here, the new article must be tested in all the applications used, and these may have to be redesigned. An article usually has more than one application, which makes it clear how complex such a changeover is. But even after this process, more problems follow. This time in the area of material logistics. If an alternative to an article containing PFAS is found and switched to, the inventory of the old article remains. The range of such an inventory can be more than 5 years. What should happen to the items in such a case? Does scrapping really make sense or is it allowed to use up old stock? There is no regulation on this yet, but it is urgently needed. The same problem applies to spare parts. We offer our customers spare parts for up to 10 years after the sale of a machine. Do spare parts in stock have to be scrapped or can they be used? What if the part needs to be redesigned to be PFAS-free? Then the part may no longer fit the customer's machine. If the proposed PFAS restriction also applies to spare parts, we will often not be able to repair the machines we have already sold. This goes completely against the principle of circular economy. We therefore request an exemption for spare parts, but also for existing stock. As a manufacturer of electronic equipment, we are subject to the WEEE directive, which means that we are obliged to take back our machines free of charge and dispose of them properly. As a result, targeted end-of-life processes can be carried out to minimise PFAS emissions. By expanding and specialization of recycling stations as well as making the transfer of information to them more transparent, it would be possible to use PFAS applications without alternatives, as well as existing items such as spare parts, etc. The continued use of spare parts and remaining stocks would also reduce the financial burden on companies already facing high costs from switching to PFAS-free products.
The proposed restriction sets very low limits for PFAS. However, there is no mention of whether these limits apply only to intentionally added PFAS or also to impurities etc. We see this as critical, as PFAS contamination of the environment is already a known problem. PFAS have been found in groundwater, plants, animals and even humans. The proposed limit values are in the range of 25-250 ppb, i.e. in the same range as the content in groundwater and plants. [3][4] Given this, the possibility of PFAS being present in plant-based plastics or materials above the proposed limits is very high.
Another concern is that recycled plastics may contain PFAS above the limits. The raw material may have been produced before the proposed PFAS restriction. However, the reuse of materials, especially plastics, is an important aspect of sustainability. In addition, some European legislation requires the use of a prescribed recycled content. The proposed restriction does not take these aspects into account. We therefore propose that the restriction on PFAS, and therefore the limits, should only apply to intentionally added PFAS. There would be no new PFAS emissions. At the same time, recycled and plant-based materials or plastics could be used safely and serve as an environmentally friendly alternative to petroleum-based plastics. Manufacturers would also not have to test all materials and components, which would also significantly reduce the burden on analytical laboratories and the regulatory control bodies.
We recognise the importance of reducing or eliminating PFAS emissions. However, the number of environmental regulations is increasing rapidly and the market needs to adapt. In particular, for most SMEs, a structural change is necessary to meet the requirements of these legislations. We therefore call for longer transition periods for SMEs. The engineering industry is largely made up of downstream users who cannot act until suppliers can offer PFAS-free alternatives. We therefore request that the mechanical engineering industry, in particular downstream users, be exempted from the PFAS restriction until raw material and component manufacturers can meet the demand for PFAS-free products. The aforementioned technical, logistical and human resource challenges for mechanical engineering companies must also be taken into account. We therefore call for an exemption for spare parts and remaining stocks, as scrapping them and the resulting irreparable machines would not be in the interest of a circular economy. Especially in the context of existing regulations for end-of-life processes in the B2B sector.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The proposed restriction on PFAS has a broad scope, grouping together substances with very different properties. One part of substances of this group has raised concerns due to their persistence and mobility, which can lead to accumulation in the environment. The removal from water is not easy and could be very difficult and thereby posing a risk to the safety of drinking water.

However, some applications are very specific and occur in very controlled areas, e.g. in the medical area as in hospitals. More specifically, if the PFAS containing article is used in hospitals or medical facilities, it is more likely that the PFAS containing article may come into contact with bacteria or other hazardous microorganism, like every other article used in such areas. Hospital waste is collected separately due to the risk of bacterial contamination, it cannot be disposed of with normal household waste. There are special requirements in Europe for the disposal of hospital waste.
Since this use and disposal occurs in a very controlled area, emission to the groundwater is not expected to occur.
Uses occurring in controlled areas with neglectable emissions and where no alternatives with similar performance properties are available, should be exempted from this proposal without any time-limitation.


A second general remark: This restriction proposal also includes substances that do not possess the characteristic of concern: namely persistence, mobility and bioaccumulation potential. One example for substances that not fulfilling all those criteria are per fluorinated polymers. Usually, under the conditions that perfluorinated polymers are used, they are non-toxic, non-bioaccumulative, non-mobile, insoluble in water, thermally, chemically and biologically stable, durable, hydrolytically stable, and are not degraded by hydrolysis, catalysis or metabolism. Consequently, they cannot bioaccumulate in water. The only characteristic they share with the PFAS mentioned above is their persistence. This persistence was taken as main argument for the restriction proposal including all PFAS, but persistence alone is not a hazard and other materials that are similarly persistent are widely used in various industries and are considered as safe (glass for example). For other materials persistence is seen “positively” and is also regarded as a key factor for durability and that the material does not become “unsafe” during its lifetime. If persistence is regarded as hazard without any other property, then a ban would be required for a lot of essential materials (glass, porcelain, stainless steel). These materials are immobile and inert and thereby no risk is associated with those materials. However, these materials are important for our economy and standard of living, and we need their continued availability to achieve the goals of the Green Deal and resource efficiency. If we switch to materials with a shorter durability, more resources will be needed to produce the articles made with these materials (due to the shorter life-span).
Additionally, the proposal does not include a proper risk assessment, which is a requirement of the REACH regulation (article 68). The proposal assumes that the hazards known for some of the PFAS mentioned above applies to the complete group and thereby all of them would have the same risk. As the mobile and soluble PFAS are quite different in their properties, it is very unlikely that perfluorinated polymers will possess the same risk in the same order of magnitude. Fluoropolymers are chemically stable and inert or relatively unreactive. Reactivity, in general, decreases as fluorine content of the polymer increases. This family of plastics has low toxicity and almost no toxicological activity. Excessive human exposure to fluoropolymer resin dust resulted in no toxic effects, although urinary fluoride content increased (Guide for the Safe Handling of Fluoropolymer Resins. Brussels, Belgium: Association of Plastics Manufacturers in Europe; January 2012). Because of the high molar masses and thermal, chemical, photochemical, and hydrolytic inertness and biological stability of fluoropolymers, it has been clearly evidenced that they satisfy the 13 accepted regulatory assessment criteria to be considered as polymers of low concern. (Recycling and the end of life assessment of fluoropolymers: recent developments, challenges and future trends).
Therefore, perfluorinated polymers should be exempted from this restriction.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The product affected by this consultation is a polyester film, which contains a PFAS component in its coating (needed to achieve the antifog property). The polyester film is used to manufacture medical face shields or surgical visors. Medical face shields and surgical visors provide additional face and eye protection for medical staff and others who work in close contact with patients. They can help reduce the risk of droplet infection and other disease transmission routes. In addition, they can also help protect the face from splashes of liquids and other potentially hazardous substances. During surgical procedures, there can be increased moisture in the visor, which can lead to fogging and reduced vision. An anti-fog coating can help reduce fogging and ensure a clear view of the surgical field. This can help improve the safety and effectiveness of the surgical procedure. The anti-fog coating is also useful for medical face visors. Medical face shields are often worn by medical personnel to protect the face and eyes from airborne infections and other disease transmission routes. If the visor fogs up, it can obscure the wearer's vision and increase the risk of injury or failure. An anti-fog coating can help reduce fogging and ensure a clear view of the surrounding area, which can improve the safety and effectiveness of medical staff.  The use is considered as derogation under paragraph 5 (b)/ (d) of the restriction proposal with a transition period of 12 years. The identified sector is “Personal protective equipment in the medicinal area”.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Manufacturing phase: see confidential annex regarding emission in the manufacturing phase.  The use-phase: The produced face shields and visors are used to protect against pathogens and to provide maximum vision (precision) during surgical procedures, the place of usage is in hospitals (and it could also be used in Europe, although we do not have any indications for that). The PFAS contained in the coating is a water-soluble anionic fluorosurfactant.   End-of life-stage: The end-of-life phase is very controlled in regard to release into the environment. When the face shields are worn in hospitals or medical facilities, at the end of life phase they are collected in separate bins and are collected by authorized disposal companies. It is important that medical face shields are not simply thrown away in the regular trash as they may have come into contact with potentially infectious materials and pose a potential public health hazard. It is also important that medical personnel wearing the visors take the proper steps to avoid contamination before discarding them. The disposal and collection of hospital waste are national or local requirements. In Germany, the bins containing the hospital waste are tightly closed to protect against humidity and the material should be in a manner that there will be no cracks, so no accidental release should occur. The bins are incinerated in special waste incineration plants or will be subjected to other approved thermal treatments (see: https://www.rki.de/DE/Content/Infekt/Krankenhaushygiene/Kommission/Downloads/LAGA-Rili.pdf?__blob=publicationFile).  When PFAS-containing materials are burned in incinerators, the PFAS can be released into the air. However, there are special technologies used in some incinerators to minimize the release of PFAS. These technologies include, for example, activated carbon filters and special emission control systems.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Face shields and visors are used to protect against pathogens in hospitals. Since they are disposed of as hospital waste with potential microbial contaminations, they are collected in separate bins and treated by special disposal companies.  We assume that incineration is the only way at the end-of-life because of the potential bacterial contamination of the personal protective equipment of medical stuff.  When PFAS-containing materials are burned in incinerators, the PFAS can be released into the air. However, there are special technologies used in some incinerators to minimize the release of PFAS. These technologies include, for example, activated carbon filters and special emission control systems.

5. Proposed derogations: See information in the confidential part.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: This input is regarding the manufacture of aluminum composite panels for façades of building  The identified sector is: "Construction products", whereas the use-sector is described as "Coil coating" in the Annex XV restriction report.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Manufacturing phase: The coating we use is based on FEVE (a copolymer of fluoroethylene and vinyl ethers) and polyurethane precursors. The coating is applied in industrial coil coating facilities. The FEVE is already in the form of a non-volatile polymer, so there are no PFAS emissions during coil coating.  During the coating process, pendant OH groups react with other components forming crosslinks. The crosslinked coating is very stable and cannot give off small PFAS substances to the environment. When manufacturing aluminum composite panels or aluminum plates, there is leftover material in the form of painted aluminum that is considered waste. This waste is collected and handled by aluminium recycling companies. The waste is shredded, grinded and incinerated and can be used in energy-intensive processes. Thereby the consumption of fossil fuels is reduced. The obtained dusts are not dangerous (they are mainly mineralic) and will be incorporated into an inert matrix. There are no residues from this incineration (for more details, please see confidential annex). Consequently, it can be concluded that no PFAS are released into the environment  Use-Phase: In the use-phase, the aluminum composite panels are applied to façades of buildings with the FEVE coated surface oriented to the outside of the building. The lacquer protects the panels against weathering and corrosion for decades and are extremely colorfast and resistant to dirt. Due to the inertness of the fluorinated polymer and by the fact that the polymer is not soluble in water, foreseeable and/ or accidental emission to the environment (e.g. the polymer is washed out by rain) is not expected. The use-phase of the aluminum composite panels is around 50 years. Further support for this is coming from a study, where the coating thickness degradation was investigated. In Japan, tests on bridges and sample panels were conducted in close proximity to the sea (duration was 25 years). The field tests shows that the degradation of the paints was very low over the observation time of 15 years (1.1 µm was the highest value observed). The degradation of other non-fluoropolymer-coating systems was much higher (22-28 µm) over the same period of time. (For more details see confidential information). In addition, a leaching test was performed. The leaching tests were conducted on the material before and after ageing and the PFAS content in the eluate was determined. The PFAS content was below the limit of quantification, which was less than 1 ppb. (also here more information can be found in the confidential information). Both tests let assure that no PFAS emission into the environment occurred during the use-phase of the aluminium composite panels. The same applies to an event of fire, where accidental release must be considered. Studies were conducted to check if toxic substances were emitted during combustion, but no hazardous components were detected, proofing no release of PFAS in significant amounts (For more details, please see confidential annex).  End-of-life phase:  At the end-of-life stage the aluminum panels can be brought to specialized recycling plants. A study by the Technical University of Delft showed an exceptionally high recovery rate of aluminum scrap in the construction sector. The Aluminum recovery rate was investigated at a large-scale sampling. Commercial and residential buildings in six European countries were checked and revealed that more than 92 percent (average 96 percent) was recycled, which shows clearly the importance of the recycling of Aluminum as a resource at the end of the life cycle. Aluminum products resulting from dismantling measures were sent for recycling or reused (Source: European Aluminium Association, 2011, website: https://alu-am-bau.ch/wp-content/uploads/2014/03/nachhaltigkeit_EAA_2011.pdf) In recycling plants, the paint is usually separated from the aluminum. This can be achieved be either thermal, chemical, or mechanical recycling. Recent work has shown, on a small scale, the ability to convert fluoroplymers back to their monomers (also called chemical recycling to monomer) (Sources: (a) M. Schlipf and T. Schwalm, Closing the recycling loop, Kunststoffe Int., 2014, 6, 58–60.; B) Invertec, Pilot project: Recycling of fluoropolymers (PTFE), https://www.invertec-ev.de/en/projects/environmental-care/ptfe-recycling.; c) D. A. Ellis, S. A. Mabury, J. W. Martin and D. C. G. Muir, Thermolysis of fluoropolymers as a potential source of halogenated organic acids in the environment, Nature,2001, 412, 321–324.). If the paint cannot be recycled, it is usually treated as hazardous waste and is incinerated. Approximately 85% of all fluoropolymers end up in waste-to energy incinerators. The incineration leads to degradation of the fluoropolymers into inorganic fluorides and into carbon dioxide. Studies under representative European municipal incinerator conditions have shown, that long-chain PFAS were not formed (< 1ng/m³) and also no short-chain PFAS (<14 ppb) were detected. This clearly shows that at the end-of-life stage fluropolymers do not generate measurable levels of PFAS. Instead, a complete mineralization of fluoropolymers could be shown, as also no organic fluorides were formed. (Research report from GFL in cooperation with the Fluoropolymers Group.: Pilot-Scale Fluoropolymer Incineration Study: Thermal Treatment of a Mixture of Fluoropolymers under Representative European Municipal Waste Combustor Conditions)   The PFAS containing paint is not only disposed without emission of PFAS into the environment, in addition there is also the possibility to use the formed waste-fuels to partly cover the energy demand of energy-intensive industries (40-50% energy coverage are currently achieved), when the PFAS containing paint is incinerated. This is already practiced by specialized waste disposal companies. The applied high temperatures minimize the formation of harmful substances. Thereby calcium carbonate or other fluorides are formed. These fluorides can be embedded in an inert matrix (more information is attached in confidential information. So, no foreseeable release in the environment occurs. In addition, the energy-coverage leads to a reduction of the CO2 emission and a reduced consumption of fossil fuels, which is fully in line with the goals of the European Green Deal.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: As technology continues to evolve, more and more remelting plants are now being designed so that the processing of coated and polymer-containing aluminum scrap requires no or limited preparatory processes. (Source: European Aluminium Association, https://alu-am-bau.ch/wp-content/uploads/2014/03/nachhaltigkeit_EAA_2011.pdf)

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: The FEVE (copolymer of a fluoroethylene and a vinyl ether) top coat on our high quality aluminium composite panels for facades and other architectural elements provides extreme durability, dirt resistance, weatherability, UV, oxidation and corrosion resistance, maintaining excellent appearance and performance for decades. Another key feature of our particular, high quality aluminium composite panel formulations is their fire safety. See: https://www.alpolic.eu/en  When used on building façades, the aluminium composite panels provide a durable, attractive appearance and reduce energy needs for cooling and heating. When retrofitting existing buildings, the panels are often combined with additional thermal insulation.  Alternatives to FEVE could be non-PFAS based polymers, but none of the alternatives have the required durability to meet demanding standards for maintenance of appearance. The best PFAS-free alternative lasts less than ¼ of the time in accelerated weathering tests, as demonstrated in the figures 1-3 in the non-confidential annex. Gloss retention is an important measureable indicator of weatherability. As the coatings weather, the surface becomes pitted and material is lost, causing the gloss values to be reduced.   For the coating process, the hazards of the non-PFAS and FEVE-based paints are similar, and entirely due to the non-polymeric components of the paints, primarily solvents. The non-PFAS paints degrade much more rapidly in weathering, losing components to the environment. It is well known that fluoropolymers have the best UV resistance. As this is an intrinsic physical property of the C-F chemical bond, it is unlikely to ever change.  Further support for this argumentation is coming from an OECD published comprehensive study on PFAS in coatings and their alternatives in 2022. The summary (at page 11) concludes: “FP-based paints are available for use on bridges and from the evidence reviewed here, their weatherability and durability performance is superior to that of alternatives such as PU. FP-based paints are significantly more expensive at the outset, although after 30 years PU coatings are more expensive than PFAS coatings because they require more frequent recoating, with associated labour, stoppage and material costs. ...” The following three key features were examined in the OECD study for PFAS coatings and alternatives: 1. Anti-soiling: “No non-PFAS alternatives have yet been identified as anti-soiling agents.” (3.4.2, page 31) 2. Performance in architectural applications: “From the above the weatherability and durability of PVDF and FEVE-based resins is better than alternatives, meaning they are likely to perform better in these respects for example in external architectural applications.” (7.2.1, page 58) 3. Total Cost of Ownership: "FP-based paints are commercially available for use on bridges and from the evidence identified in this study their weatherability and durability performance is superior to that of alternatives such as PU. An analysis on the costs over time of field painting a bridge with a FP-based paint (FEVE) system and a non PFAS alternative (polyurethane), paint system, was conducted (University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, 2013) and the conclusion was that per coating it would cost approximately 26 % more with the FPbased coating compared to polyurethane. However, after 30 years it was concluded that the total cost for the polyurethane coating would cost 16 % more than the FP-based coating, owing to the faster degradation of the non-PFAS coating and therefore a need for more frequent recoating, with associated labour and material costs." (9.3, page 63)  UV exposure tests for FEVE in comparison to a PFAS free alternative (HDPE) was done by our supplier. The tests revealed a noticeable difference in color shade and glass degradation after 3000 h (125 days) for the HDPE system in comparison to the FEVE system. For more information, please see the attached confidential information.

Combined Comments: General Comments: The proposed restriction on the manufacture, placing on the market and use of PFAS is an important initiative to safeguard health and wealth of humans and environment. The scientific evidence for the ecotoxicological impact of PFAS is getting solid, and therefore it is important that the proposed restriction is indeed pursued. As a way of mitigating the potential irritation in the general public on a potentially negative impact on e.g. rain coat water persistence could also be included in the proposal. Hence, by informing the public about the risks with PFAS and why a restriction could give a negative impact on a product that is dependent on PFAS for its intended use, a general understanding in the public may be settled. It may also be appreciated that a number of manufacturers have already found alternatives to PFAS in their manufacturing, which may mitigate negative impact on product availability in market areas where PFAS is currently used.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Information on benefits Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The proposed restriction options submitted by the Member States do not provide adequate scope for all of the required time-unlimited exemptions ourselves at SDC Technologies and the ophthalmic medical device industry believes are necessary for the risk-to-benefit profile of PFAS-containing substances and articles where used in essential use item(s). This is particularly important in cases where there is no pertinent risk of exposure or environmental emission during the intended use of the essential article, and where the PFAS is used in such low quantities (trace ppb in finished article as used) that the assumed hazard is negligible. For this, SDC Technologies requests that the criteria for time-unlimited exemptions for medical devices, namely in the eyewear market, is reviewed, broadened and incorporated into the proposal.

We believe the scope of the restriction is too broad, including fluoropolymers, which exhibit vastly different properties with regards to environmental and toxicological hazards. As fluoropolymers are the most widely-used PFAS subset for medical devices (Annex A.3.10.1.17), their inclusion in the restriction proposal would cause widespread disruption to the availability of resources in the medical professions. In this sector, availability of replacements will be slow to market, as replacement chemistries that exhibit similar performance properties are improbable, and will be subject to rigorous, time-intensive accreditation procedures, causing further delay before full-scale deployment in these applications. This is true for medical ophthalmic lenses, an essential-use item as millions of EU nationals rely on these daily. The presence of PFAS at ppb level in lens coatings helps to impart scratch-resistance, dirt-repellent and anti-reflective properties that make prescription eyewear safer to wear for the user, and allows for a longer life of service. General Comments: The proposed restrictions are extremely broad and the impact assessment of restrictions appear biased, superficial and/or incomplete, especially for more complicated use cases. This is probably most glaring in PPE and medical applications where Table 8 in ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT repeatedly mentions significant costs which also manifest as significant risks to life and health - this aspect is completely absent in section 2.4.2 where the impact of the restrictions on human health is (supposed to be) considered.

Also some fundamental assumptions appear blithely optimistic. Table 8 frequently mentions "Loss of producer surplus". More realistically it will mean increased prices, movement of production outside the EU or discontinuation of the product altogether, the latter with significant unmentioned impact if these products are somewhat important. Again, with medical equipment and PPE, this is a loss also manifesting in loss of lives.

Another area of optimism with limited foundation are the replacement options: Those replacement options have to exist in the first place, then both the substance and frequently the application have to be licensed and then those alternatives have to be competitive. Here the cost is both economical and the potential massive impairment of the adoption of heat pumps for home heating, something generally considered fairly important in the reduction of CO2 emissions.

General Comments: The province of Gelderland calls for a rapid and total ban of PFAS

This contribution reflects the position of the province of Gelderland on this consultation. The province of Gelderland supports the proposal for a complete ban on PFAS, to protect the environment and the health of our inhabitants. To avoid substitution of one PFAS for another, we support the fact that the restriction proposal targets the entire group of PFAS. Moreover, the province of Gelderland believes that it is irresponsible to postpone a ban.
Since PFAS are forever chemicals and won’t disappear from our environment, it is undesirable to take 12 years to phase out PFAS. Especially given that the quality of soil, air and water are increasingly under pressure. In Europe, there is increasing attention to a healthy living environment and stricter standards are being set for pollution of soil, air and water through the Soil Health Directive, the Air Quality Directive and the Water Framework Directive. Setting strict environmental standards for PFAS while at the same time letting new PFAS into the environment is counterproductive.

A cross border issue
Given the impact PFAS are already having on our living environment in combination with the uncertainties that still surround PFAS, the province also sees the importance of a European approach. The PFAS problem is transnational as is clear from the elevated PFAS concentrations in the river Westerschelde, which originate from a factory across the border in Belgium.
Since 2020, the Netherlands has been working with Germany, Denmark, Sweden and Norway on a proposal for a European ban on PFAS (Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances). On February 7th 2023, your agency published a proposal for a ban (restriction) on PFAS. In parallel, a consultation was issued to gather input on this proposal.

Why does the province of Gelderland support the restriction?
One of the tasks of the province, as a regional authority, is to ensure a clean and healthy environment for its residents. PFAS are increasingly known to have harmful effects on the health of humans and animals. PFAS are generally very stable, once in the environment PFAS compounds spread easily through soil, air and water. PFAS are used in countless products, which means that PFAS are present in the environment throughout the Netherlands (for illustration, see references 1, 2 and 3). Research shows that all kinds of (consumer) products and waste streams contain PFAS and that people are exposed to PFAS even in their own homes (4). As a result of this ubiquitous presence humans, animals and the environment are permanently exposed to PFAS with potential risks to human and animal health. Research by the RIVM, the Dutch national institute for health and environment, shows that people in the Netherlands already ingest too much PFAS through food alone (5). People living in close proximity to Chemours (a fluorpolymer plant in Dordrecht) are even advised against eating from their own gardens (6) and at several locations in the Netherlands people are advised against eating self-caught fish (e.g. 7). The drinking water companies in the Netherlands (see the reaction submitted to ECHA by VEWIN) point to the inability to completely remove these substances during the production of drinking water. Lastly, in a few recreational lakes around Dordrecht the province had to give a negative swimming advice due to excessive concentrations of PFAS (8).

The province of Gelderland is one of the twelve provinces in The Netherlands. We have 2 million inhabitants and a surface of about 5.000 km2. Currently we are carrying out a costly remediation project on a former industrial site. At this site the soil contamination was created in a couple of years. PFAS has been found already deep in the groundwater layer. Groundwater is our major drinking water source. We are concerned there are more of these sites in our province. Presently we are working on an inventory of PFAS-contaminated sites. Apart from these point sources there is a ‘background’ contamination level of PFAS which has major impact on the possibilities for transport and application of soil in housing construction and agricultural projects.

Social importance
Public concern about PFAS is high. This is mainly because the effects of PFAS on humans, animals and the environment are not yet clear. Residents living near a PFAS plant or near PFAS-contaminated land or water are rightly concerned about the effects on their health. Heightened media attention is increasing the public awareness of possible harmful effects and public support for these substances is decreasing.

The role of industry
To date, several industries are continuing to produce and use PFAS, thus releasing them into the environment. Moreover, PFAS are released not only during the production process, but also during use and at the end of their lifetime. In most waste incinerators PFAS are not completely destroyed, which means that even after phase-out, PFAS will continue to be released into the environment.
The province of Gelderland is aware that a total ban will demand a lot from the industry, but trusts in the inventiveness of the market to come up with sustainable, safe and circular alternatives. We believe that a rapid and total ban is a good incentive for companies to change their processes. Where exceptions are allowed, the risk assessment of PFAS should be handled more thoroughly. The province of Gelderland advocates a stricter burden of proof if companies want to continue using PFAS, as an exemption to the new regulation.
A rapid total ban is therefore the only correct course.

3. PFAS in seaspray, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam (2022)

RIVM, 2023-0011

Dordrecht, Papendrecht, Sliedrecht en Molenlanden, RIVM, 2022-0010

General Comments: The province of Zuid-Holland calls for a rapid and total ban of PFAS

This contribution reflects the position of the province of Zuid-Holland on this consultation. The province of Zuid-Holland supports the proposal for a complete ban on PFAS, to protect the environment and the health of our inhabitants. To avoid substitution of one PFAS for another, we support the fact that the restriction proposal targets the entire group of PFAS. Moreover, the province of Zuid-Holland believes that it is irresponsible to postpone a ban.
Since PFAS are forever chemicals and won’t disappear from our environment, it is undesirable to take 12 years to phase out PFAS. Especially given that the quality of soil, air and water are increasingly under pressure. In Europe, there is increasing attention to a healthy living environment and stricter standards are being set for pollution of soil, air and water through the Soil Health Directive, the Air Quality Directive and the Water Framework Directive. Setting strict environmental standards for PFAS while at the same time letting new PFAS into the environment is counterproductive.

A cross border issue
Given the impact PFAS are already having on our living environment in combination with the uncertainties that still surround PFAS, the province also sees the importance of a European approach. The PFAS problem is transnational as is clear from the elevated PFAS concentrations in the river Westerschelde, which originate from a factory across the border in Belgium. Since 2020, the Netherlands has been working with Germany, Denmark, Sweden and Norway on a proposal for a European ban on PFAS (Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances). On February 7th 2023, your agency published a proposal for a ban (restriction) on PFAS. In parallel, a consultation was issued to gather input on this proposal.

Why does the province of Zuid-Holland support the restriction?
One off the tasks of the province, as a regional authority, is to ensure a clean and healthy environment for its residents. PFAS are increasingly known to have harmful effects on the health of humans and animals. PFAS are generally very stable, once in the environment PFAS compounds spread easily through soil, air and water. PFAS are used in countless products, which means that PFAS are present in the environment throughout the Netherlands (for illustration, see references 1, 2 and 3). Research shows that all kinds of (consumer) products and waste streams contain PFAS and that people are exposed to PFAS even in their own homes (4). As a result of this ubiquitous presence humans, animals and the environment are permanently exposed to PFAS with potential risks to human and animal health. Research by the RIVM, the Dutch national institute for health and environment, shows that people in the Netherlands already ingest too much PFAS through food alone (5). People living in close proximity to Chemours (a fluorpolymer plant in Dordrecht) are even advised against eating from their own gardens (6) and at several locations in the Netherlands people are advised against eating self-caught fish (e.g. 7). The drinking water companies in the Netherlands (see the reaction submitted to ECHA by VEWIN) point to the inability to completely remove these substances during the production of drinking water. Lastly, in a few recreational lakes around Dordrecht the province had to give a negative swimming advice due to excessive concentrations of PFAS (8).

Social importance
Public concern about PFAS is high. This is mainly because the effects of PFAS on humans, animals and the environment are not yet clear. Residents living near a PFAS plant or near PFAS-contaminated land or water are rightly concerned about the effects on their health. Heightened media attention is increasing the public awareness of possible harmful effects and public support for these substances is decreasing.

The role of industry
To date, several industries are continuing to produce and use PFAS, thus releasing them into the environment. Moreover, PFAS are released not only during the production process, but also during use and at the end of their lifetime. In most waste incinerators PFAS are not completely destroyed, which means that even after phase-out, PFAS will continue to be released into the environment.
The province of Zuid-Holland is aware that a total ban will demand a lot from the industry, but trusts in the inventiveness of the market to come up with sustainable, safe and circular alternatives. We believe that a rapid and total ban is a good incentive for companies to change their processes. Where exceptions are allowed, the risk assessment of PFAS should be handled more thoroughly. The province of Zuid-Holland advocates a stricter burden of proof if companies want to continue using PFAS, as an exemption to the new regulation. A rapid total ban is therefore the only correct course.

General Comments: The REACH restriction proposal mentions that the worldwide market penetration rate of construction paints mainly using fluoropolymer is only 1% (OECD, 2022), and suggests Polyurethane as an alternative. However, in certain construction coatings for crucial infrastructure such as large steel structures (bridges and steel road bridges), the steel components supporting the structure must be repainted before corrosion sets in to avoid deterioration that leads to a decrease in structural integrity.
Therefore, specifically for steel structures within construction applications, it is desirable to adopt a coating system with fluoropolymer as the topcoat due to its excellent weather resistance.
In the proposed alternatives, polyurethane and fluoropolymer, the only difference lies in the topcoat of the coating specification. The primer and intermediate coat remain the same. Therefore, corrosion of the steel components, which are the substrate, progresses rapidly once the topcoat and intermediate coat thin out, exposing the epoxy coating of the primer. Thus, repainting needs to be carried out before corrosion of the steel components occurs, and the repainting cycle is primarily determined by the weather resistance of the topcoat.
As mentioned in the OECD report (2022), the repainting cycle for fluoropolymer coating specification is 20-25 years, while for the alternative polyurethane specification, it is 5-10 years. Therefore, if polyurethane is used as an alternative, it would require repainting twice as often compared to using fluoropolymer.
Furthermore, the OECD report (2022) provides a comparison of the cost incurred over a period of 100 years for repainting between the fluoropolymer coating specification and the polyurethane coating specification. According to this comparison, polyurethane shows an approximately 75% cost increase. Most importantly, in the estimation of repainting cycles, the fluoropolymer coating specification requires 3-4 repainting cycles over 100 years, while the polyurethane coating specification requires 9-10 repainting cycles. Repainting involves not only the production of the paint but also auxiliary materials such as painting tools, scaffolding, and protective nets, as well as the transportation of these materials to the painting site, resulting in the emission of carbon dioxide. Therefore, if the polyurethane coating specification is used as an alternative to the fluoropolymer coating specification, it would multiply carbon dioxide emissions over the long term, making it unsustainable as a viable alternative.

In addition, Japan Paint Manufacturers Association supports the statement made by FCJ on the issues of proposed restriction,as per attached in Section Ⅳ.

General Comments: The restriction describes the ban on the manufacture and use of over 10,000 substances, including fluoropolymers such as PTFE. In my view, this general ban does not sufficiently take into account the use of fluoropolymers, within the manufacturing processes of the (chemical) industry. To have highly stable and technically tight compounds is necessary to avoid diffuse emissions (of hazardous substances) to meet current emission restrictions for chemical plants. This application - especially fluoropolymers - contradicts a pragmatic, risk-based approach and endangers both the prosperity achieved in Germany and (and this is the more important aspect for me) the patient's well-being.  As a chronically ill person myself, I am dependent on the regular intake of medication and hereby express my concerns about the relocation of chemical drug production to non-European countries. In particular, the corona pandemic has shown massive delivery difficulties.
Last but not least, it still should be a goal to preserve jobs in Europe. The question of how European countries and their population want to live and interact with each other socially and socio-economically today and in the future continues to be ignored with such a ban on use and remains unanswered.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Description of analytical methods
Org. name: European Committee for Standardization CEN/TC 248 “Textile and textile products” WG 26 “Test methods for analysis of EC restricted substances”
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The restriction is not logical and clearly defined. Details are outlined in the following:

25 ppb for any PFAS as measured with targeted PFAS analysis
The unit ppb does not appear useful. The unit µg/kg would be much clearer and will not be subject to any discussions on how to interpret ppb. ppb is no SI unit.

A limit of 25 ppb (= 25 µg/kg) requires a test method with an appropriate Limit of Quantification (LOQ) that also takes the measurement uncertainty into consideration. For PFOA, PFOS and several other PFCA a sufficient low LOQ to verify compliance with 25 ppb in routine analysis is feasible. Using analytical instrumentation such as LC-MS/MS and GC-MS, GC-NCI-MS, GC-MS/MS available in market surveillance and third-party laboratories will not be sufficient to test for a number of PFAS because the LOQ for these substances is too high. For some substances it is above the proposed legal limit, e.g. LOQ of 4:2 FTOH: 400 µg/kg tested according to EN 17681-1:2022, see also the attached list PFAS including LOQ.
We recommend to follow the approach for PFOA in the POP regulation, setting a legal limit of 25 µg/kg for the PFCA and PFSA that can be tested with an acceptable LOQ, except HPFHpA CAS 1546-95-8 which has a LOQ of 100 µg/kg when tested according to EN 17681-1:2022, and a legal limit of 1000 µg/kg for single PFSA and PFCA related substances such as n:2 FTOH. The limit for the sum of PFSA and PFCA related substances should also be set to 1000 µg/kg.
It needs to be further outlined the only substances that are determined in a concentration above an LOQ as stated in a relevant EN standards should be included in the sum. In general, the legal text should reference to valid EN test standards for the related products groups because limits and especially limits of sums of substances are only useful with reference to the test method.


targeted PFAS analysis
It is outlined on page 9 that targeted PFAS analysis is “… the measurement of PFASs with an available analytical method for a specific set of substances and quantified against reference standards.” EN 17681-1:2022, EN 17681-2 and Fpr EN ISO/FDIS 23702-2:2023 contain lists of PFAS that are recommended to be tested for textiles, leather and footwear. Grounded in the text outlined on page 9, it appears to be sufficient to test for the PFAS listed in standards like the mentioned ones. This is useful because it is not possible to test for several hundred single PFAS that are of no technical relevance in textiles, leather and footwear for consumers. It would also give all involved parties legal certainty and harmonises the testing approaches. If it is the intention of the EU that “the measurement of PFASs with an available analytical method for a specific set of substances” shall be performed it is required to state this very clearly, e.g. with the order to use applicable EN standards, in the restriction text and not as a comment in a proposal or later in a guidance document. The latter will lead to legal uncertainty and issues in the free movement of goods.
It is highly recommended to initiate the development of standards of methods for PFAS testing in different matrices and for different product groups, ideally based on PFAS listed in EN 17681-1:2022.

polymeric PFASs excluded from quantification:
It is not defined in the restriction whether only polymers with a backbone that contains at least one fully fluorinated methyl (CF3-) or methylene (-CF2-) carbon atom (fluoropolymers), e.g. PTFE, count as polymeric PFASs or whether side-chain fluorinated polymers with hydrocarbon backbones also count as polymeric PFASs. A clear definition of polymeric PFASs in the restriction text needs to be provided in order to avoid confusion.
It appears only meaningful that polymers with a backbone that contains at least one fully fluorinated methyl (CF3-) or methylene (-CF2-) carbon atom count as polymeric PFASs since they cannot be analysed by targeted PFAS analysis whereas side-chain fluorinated polymers such as side-chain fluorinated polyacrylic polymers can often be degenerated and the released fluorinated side-chains, e.g. n:2 FTOH, can be analysed by targeted PFAS analysis.

It does not appear logical that for the sum of targeted PFAS analysis a prior degradation of precursors can be optionally applied but not for the analysis for the single substances. This would mean two different test methods have to be applied. It appears to be more useful to apply the degradation step for testing of the single substances (i.) and the sum (ii.). In this case the side chains of side-chain fluorinated polymers will also be covered by the limit of 25 ppb resp. the suggested 1000 µg/kg.

optionally with prior degradation of precursors:
It is stated that the prior degradation is an optional step. What means optional? In which cases should a degradation be performed and in which one not. Clearly define the cases in the restriction and not only in the proposal or later in a guidance document. On page 9, it is outlined: “The concentration limit for the sum of PFASs (250 ppb) may be calculated from targeted PFAS analysis either analysed directly as sample or after chemical degradation of the sample material. The latter may include degradation products from e.g. side-chain fluorinated polymers.” The use of may indicates an option and gives room for interpretation. How should market surveillance or third-party laboratories base any decision whether a product complies with the regulation on an option?
The outcome of the degradation depends on the degradation method. Without referring to a particular test method different results are to be expected. We strongly recommend to add a phrase that the degradation shall be performed as outlined in the relevant EN standard.
For example, CEN/TC 248/WG 26 “Textile and textile products - Test methods for analysis of EC restricted substances” is developing a standard that applies alkaline hydrolysis in order to degrade side-chain fluorinated polymers in order to test for compliance with the requirements of the POP regulation concerning PFOA related substances and the REACH regulation concerning C9-C14 PFCA related substances. Therefore, EN 17681-1:2022 is going to be revised. It is expected that the revised preliminary prEN 17681-1 will be published in the second half on 2023 and the final revised EN 17681-1 will be published in 2024.


Labware or parts of labware consisting of PTFE
Labware and parts of labware consist of PTFE. These labware or parts are required to analyse for several harmful substances. For instance, microwave digestion of samples for total metal analysis according to EN 16711-1:2016 which is done with aggressive acids, e.g. hydrofluoric acid, aqua regia, and oxidation agents such as hydrogen peroxide at temperatures above 200 °C and pressure above 200 bar cannot be done without PTFE containers.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: TULAC

6. Missing uses: Labware or parts of labware consisting of PTFE  Labware and parts of labware consist of PTFE. These labware or parts are required to analyse for several harmful substances. For instance, microwave digestion of samples for total metal analysis according to EN 16711-1:2016 which is done with aggressive acids, e.g. hydrofluoric acid, aqua regia, and oxidation agents such as hydrogen peroxide at temperatures above 200 °C and pressure above 200 bar cannot be done without PTFE containers.

Analytical methods: CEN/TC 248/WG 26 “Textile and textile products - Test methods for analysis of EC restricted substances” is developing a standard that applies alkaline hydrolysis in order to degrade side-chain fluorinated polymers in order to test for compliance with the requirements of the POP regulation concerning PFOA related substances and the REACH regulation concerning C9-C14 PFCA related substances. Therefore, EN 17681-1:2022 is going to be revised. It is expected that the revised preliminary prEN 17681-1 will be published in the second half on 2023 and the final revised EN 17681-1 will be published in 2024. The joined working group of ISO/TC 216/WG 2 and CEN 309/WG 2 “Footwear and environmental aspects” will also start a standardisation project for a PFAS test method applying alkaline hydrolysis.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Information on alternatives Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The restriction proposal baseline study for Petroleum and Mining sector, which focused on the use of PFAS substances in exploration, exploitation and offshore processing of oil, has not taken into consideration the use of PFAS substances in the onward processing of oil (petroleum refining) or refinery product distribution chains e.g. distribution of automotive fuels.
Refining operations are controlled chemical reactions which occur at high temperatures and / or pressures, often in the presence of a catalyst (which can be corrosive e.g. hydrofluoric acid) and may generate corrosive products which require onward reaction / transformation by secondary processes. These refining activities are not present in the upstream activities of petroleum and mining.
Refinery chemical reactions do not directly use or manufacture PFAS substances. However PFAS is present within industrial equipment, mostly in a solid form [e.g. PFAS components of dynamic and static seals, pump membranes/ diaphragms, PTFE linings in pipes and PTFE-coated bolts] or gaseous form [e.g. refrigerants]. This PFAS poses a low risk of exposure to the environment during operations.
Additionally, PFAS substances are used by manufacturers in the creation of raw materials which are then use in manufacture of process unit equipment such as seals, bushes and some electrical parts. Whilst these refining components do not themselves contain PFAS, the upstream manufacturing process for the raw material does. At present, information from a number of raw material manufacturers suggests that a viable alternative to PFAS is not likely to be available within the next 5 years.
The refinery supply chain is vast with many raw material and feedstock suppliers producing materials that do not contain PFAS, but where manufacturing processes utilise PFAS-containing substances in equipment designed for use at high temperatures and / or pressures and / or corrosive environments. A risk-based approach to restriction of PFAS is required especially for industrial applications where alternatives have not been developed.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The restriction proposal baseline study for Petroleum and Mining sector, which focused on the use of PFAS substances in exploration, exploitation and offshore processing of oil, has not taken into consideration the use of PFAS substances in the onward processing of oil (petroleum refining) or refinery product distribution chains e.g. distribution of automotive fuels. As a consequence, refinery operations (conditions and applications) are not exhaustively covered under the sector identified.  Petroleum refining transforms crude oil and other feedstocks (e.g. vegetable oils, pyrolysed waste plastics, used cooking oil, animal fats) and into fuels, petroleum intermediates and chemicals for use in industry and consumer sectors. Refining operations are controlled chemical reactions which occur at high temperatures and / or pressures, often in the presence of a catalyst (some catalysts are corrosive e.g. hydrofluoric acid) and can generate corrosive products which require onward reaction / transformation by secondary processes. These refining activities are not present or represented in the upstream activities of petroleum and mining sector.  Due to the complex nature of distinct refinery and secondary processes, each carried out within purpose designed equipment or process units, refining operations and refinery products distribution has multiple critical applications which contain PFAS substances or raw materials manufactured from PFAS precursors e.g. loading arm swivels, through to valves, gaskets, pump diaphragms etc.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: PFAS solids are not expected to breakdown during operations. During the operational phase, the risk of release would be due to product degradation over time from mechanical stress, erosion, chemical reaction. This could lead to the release of PFAS into product streams or leaching into secondary processing units. During the disposal stage, potential release of particles into the atmosphere would occur if incineration is below recommended temperatures.  PFAS gases (used for refrigeration) could be released to the atmosphere during the operational phase due to leaks in the equipment. Disposal of PFAS gases is in line with national disposal requirements and undertaken by a licensed disposal specialist.

5. Proposed derogations: The derogation proposed for fluoropolymer applications in petroleum and mining industry (until 13.5 years after EiF) does not apply to the refining operations and fuel distribution sector.

6. Missing uses: To date, the inventory of PFAS within refinery and fuel / chemical distribution equipment has determined that PFAS substances are present in gaskets and sealings, loading swivel arms, pumps/ compressors, pump diaphragms, PFAS-coated bolts and refrigerants. These core pieces of equipment are widespread around the various refinery processing units and distribution terminals. From experience, supplier information regarding these pieces of equipment primarily focuses on performance of equipment rather than on composition, meaning that percentage of PFAS present in these components is not often known. As yet, there are no known viable alternatives for these PFAS-containing equipment.  The types of PFAS identified are mainly fluoropolymers such as PTFE, FKM and FFKM but this does not mean that other types of PFAS are not present. One supplier highlighted that a seals manufacturer had no alternative product to replace the current PFAS-derived raw material and that an alternative was not likely to be available in the next five years. An exemption for all PFAS applications in refineries and fuels / chemical distribution within the industrial sector is requested, until proven replacement technology is available for each and every application.

8. Other identified uses: Please see statement 6.
