Combined Comments:
General Comments: The semiconductor industry is very reliant upon many applications of materials (solids, liquids, and gases) falling under the definition of PFAS as set out in the EU REACH PFAS restriction proposal. PFAS substances used in the semiconductor manufacturing process are not limited only to process chemicals, but they are also required in semiconductor manufacturing equipment, semiconductor manufacturing infrastructure, and support equipment. Therefore the proposed derogation “[the semiconductor manufacturing process (…)]” should not only cover PFAS used in the production of a semiconductor but also PFAS in the equipment used to produce semiconductors. UMS  supports the reduction of risks to human health and the environment out of conviction thereby searching for new alternatives. However, regulatory measures such as the restriction proposal for PFAS should be developed in an appropriate and, above all, holistic approach of the resulting consequences. Regarding to PFAS volume and application at UMS it is certain that it would be extremely demanding and in many case not even possible to substitute them. While UMS is eager to search for PFAS alternatives it must be clear that there is a high dependence on PFAS containing articles that are provided by suppliers for which no alternatives on the market exist.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Semiconductor   PFAS substances used in the semiconductor manufacturing process are not limited only to process chemicals but they are also required in semiconductor manufacturing equipment, semiconductor manufacturing infrastructure and support equipment. Most PFAS  specific uses in  semiconductor: • Machinery/ Tool • Photoresists  • Coolant  • Grease/oil/lubricant  • Process gases for etching • Refrigerant dryers •  Article/spare parts:  o Seals and Gaskets   o Wafer-holder o Process vessels o Pipes and fittings o Valves and pumps o Cables and wires o Storage and containers o Filters membrane

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Typical environmental emissions coming from the production process in semiconductor industry include emissions to air, water and the disposal of hazardous or non-hazardous waste.   Emission during use of  PFAS: PFAS solids: Fluoropolymers are polymers of low concern, which are chemically stable (no degradation to short chain PFAS) and no emissions are coming out of them if they are used properly during production.  Fluoriertes Gases (etch gases): During the plasma process, etching gases are transformed ions including CF3+ ions and highly reactive F radicals. Afterwards the converted gas can be filtered out using a gas reactor column (GRC) to safely remove hazardous gases from the exhaust. With additional treatment of the exhaust gas after the GRC with a higher amount of energy and nature gas the residuals finally can be burned into CO2 and HF/HCl, with will be washed out and can be lead to a standard water post treatment.  Refrigerants are only used in closed systems and are not released into the environment but are collected by qualified service personnel and is reprocessed or recycled.   Photoresist: The chemicals used in photolithography have relatively low vapor pressure so generally air emissions from photolithography are extremely small.  Coolant/Lubricants are only used in closed systems and due to their designed, to be long-lasting and do not need to often refill. Therefore, emission is only due to loss on leakages which are very rare.   End of life time: Air emissions Manufacturing facility exhaust systems are designed to remove chemical vapors or gases from equipment. There are already many national regulations regarding air emissions, which each company needs to comply with. F-gases:  By far the largest proportion of the PFAS gases that are used either already react in the plasma chamber or  decompose completely in the atmosphere in post-treatment processes due to their special short-chain chemical structures to substances that occur in nature Refrigerants are not released into the environment but are collected by qualified service personnel and is reprocessed or recycled.   Waste water treatment Semiconductor manufacturing facilities generate organic and aqueous waste streams, which are treated in accordance with local and federal waste and wastewater regulations. The main task of the precipitation-coagulation-clarification treatment processes is to remove dissolved metals and Fluorides from wastewater but so far not necessarily PFAS. However, some PFAS can be transformed into an organic form and be removed. The new EU Drinking Water Directive includes tests for perfluorinated and polyfluorinated alkyl substances (PFAS).  There is a national German standard DIN 38407-42 which allowed analyze in aqueous matrices only for 13 perfluorinated compounds (PFAS) with determination limits of 0.01 µg/L. There is also another Standard DIN 38414-S14 for determination of  13 polyfluorinated compounds (PFC) in sludge, compost and soil. Our company comply with water-related regulations as well as with voluntary standards, both above mentioned standards for PFASs analysis.    Chemical waste, like organic or anorganic compounds, solvents, resists potentially containing PFAS, are typically segregated, collected, and containerized to be treated at an offsite licensed treatment and disposal facility.  Waste Disposal Solid PFAS waste (like filter, seals, o-rings) are disposed at UMS according to legal requirements (chemical waste) so there is no emission into the environment. Equipment/Production Machinery including many PFAS containing spare parts are  decommissioned after  their service life, which can vary between 15-25 years depending on the application. This deposition take place under strict governmental rules (hazardous waste) in dedicated landfills or will be incinerated under controlled conditions and by dedicated companies.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The PFAS used in semiconductor production usually do not remain in the End Product /Chip/Wafer or only in very small atomic traces, which are strongly stable in cooperate in the thin film material stacks. As a result, PFASs do not have to be taken into account at the end of life of the products.

5. Proposed derogations: In our company necessary production and infrastructure facilities are equipped with highly standardized components made of fluoropolymers (like FKM, PFA, or PTFE). However, it is hard to estimate the existing volume of solid PFAS in our production machinery. Once purchased, a machine that contains PFAS is active in production for 20-30 years. Therefor the volume calculation of PFAS articles will be limited only to spare parts like O-rings, seals, valves etc. For example for one machine, working 24/7 there is a need to change approximately one time the rotary seal ring for the motor, around 3 times the PTFE Filter and only once/2 times the valve PFA per year. We estimate that the number of bought PFAs solid article can be less than 50kg per year. Solid PFAS waste (like filter, seals, o-rings) are disposed at UMS according to legal requirements (chemical waste) so there is no emission into the environment. Equipment/Production Machinery including many PFAS containing spare parts are decommissioned after their service life. This deposition take place under strict governmental rules (hazardous waste) in dedicated landfills or will be incinerated under controlled conditions and by dedicated companies.  The photoresists used in patterning must be able to produce highly miniaturized structures (nanometer structures). For this purpose, trace amounts of PFAS-containing fluorinated compounds are often added to the resists to ensure these properties and reduce the risks of defects. After evaluating the Safety Date Sheets (SDS)  and a contact with our supplier it turned out that two of our resists  (from more than 50) contain PFAS substance but in very small amount (less than 0,1%). Yearly consumption of those two resists is around 40L and taking into account that only 0,1% amount of them contain PFAS value then absolute yearly volume  of PFAS in resist is less than 400 ml. Chemical waste as photoresist typically are segregated, collected, and be treated at an licensed treatment and disposal facility.  Semiconductor wafer fabrication processes involve harsh, highly reactive and unique environments. For the semiconductor industries, PFAS containing coolant mainly base on PFPE products are used as heat transfer fluids during extreme conditions over a broad temperature range (-70°C-290’°C) to guaranty safety at work.  In UMS’s clean room PFAS containing coolant is used mainly based on PFPE products in the cooling thermostats or in circulation chillers in the plasma area. Yearly consumption of coolant is around  100L. Vacuum pumps play an important role in wafer fabrication, as they maintain safe, clean and effective working conditions. In the field of PFAS lubricants, there are PFPE (Perfluoropolyethers and their derivatives) and PTFE (Polytetrafluoroethylene) substances as raw materials of PFAS lubricants used in our more than 100 vacuum pump applications. Yearly consumption of lubricants combined for all 100 vacuum pumps is only 2-3L. Coolant/Lubricants  are only used in closed systems and due to their designed to be long-lasting and do not need to often replace.    Perfluorocarbons (PFCs) and hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) gases defined as PFAS, are widely used in the semiconductor manufacturing processes for the purpose of etching silicon and other silicon-based materials.  In our company we use very few F-gases where only one falls under the definition of PFAS as in the proposed restrictions. This PFAS containing gas is the key medium for every technology and product in our portfolio, thus critical and very difficult to replace. Nonetheless, the yearly use of our HFC gas (low-molecular-weight PFAS) is only 200 kg. During the plasma process, etching gases are transformed into ions including CF3+ ions and highly reactive F radicals. The reactive gas in the plasma reacts with the volatile atoms on the wafer surface, forming volatile compounds silicon tetrafluoride that are removed from the surface by the ion bombardment. Afterwards the converted gas can be filtered out using a gas reactor column (GRC) to safely remove hazardous gases from the exhaust. By far the largest proportion of the PFAS gases that are used either already react in the plasma chamber or  decompose completely in the atmosphere in post-treatment processes due to their special short-chain chemical structures to substances that occur in nature.   To maintain air condition in the clean room, primarily for keeping the temperature at 20°C and the relevant humidity at 40% we use refrigeration dryers and peak load dehumidifiers. Many refrigeration dryers use F- gases as refrigerants. Qualified external personnel carry out the exchange or refill of refrigerants typically over the entire lifecycle of the machine.  Therefore, refrigerants are not released into the environment but are refill or taken back by this personnel when the equipment is taken out of service and is then reprocessed or recycled. From that reason our company don’t have to buy  any of refriegents because they are purchased by service company. Most of the refrigerants in new equipment already consists of recycled refrigerants.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Proposed potential derogation [the semiconductor manufacturing process until 13.5 year after EiF], should not only cover PFAS used in the production of a semiconductor but also PFAS in the equipment used to produce semiconductors.  a) The annual tonnage and emissions: have been already answered at request 5 b) The key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use:  PFAS provide various characteristics that are required by the chip manufacturer: purity, chemical stability, durability and performance. Multiple relevant applications use a combination of two or more PFAS characteristics. If one of these characteristics is missing, it would have negative effects and consequences not only for the functionality of a product but especially for the safety of the workers and the environment.   Purity: Production in the semiconductor industry requires a high purity of the used materials. This starts from chemicals like acids or solvents and ends with process aids like carrier-holders and seals. The purity of the chemicals and surfaces is crucial to ensure the quality of the final product. Therefore, production of electronic chips – requires highly pure materials. Mostly these are fluoropolymers, which guarantee a high degree of purity for several steps in the semiconductor industry and are for those functions/purposes, irreplaceable. Fluoropolymers are totally inert materials, that means: a pump lined or container with a fluoropolymer like PVDF does not contaminate liquid, its purity remains unchanged.  High durability, chemical stability The stability of fluoropolymers (PFAS) results in unique and long lasting stable performance in many uses and applications. The high stability of fluoropolymers is based upon the carbon-fluorine bond - the strongest bond between carbon and another atom. As a result, fluoropolymers are highly inert and have an exceptional chemical stability which made them essential for the semiconductor industry. Fluoropolymers have far better durability and chemical stability than other materials. Thus, it helps users to reduce material and disposal volume but also in terms of work safety. Aggressive chemicals or extreme temperatures can destroy conventional O-rings, sealings, gaskets.  This ultimately leads to leakage, which can be prevented if these components contain / are mad of PFAS.   Stability in harsh conditions (low / high temperatures and mechanical strength)  Many PFAS are thermal resistant against low and high temperatures (higher than 150°C).  Good examples are lubricants which are used under harsh conditions and wide temperature ranges between -90 ºC to +300 ºC.  Increased sensitivity of the photoresists  Photoresists contain PFAS, as their chemical and physical properties (wetting agent, photoactive, low reflective index) are necessary in the exposure process of lithography to achieve the desired process result.  All these properties are achieved by using fluorinated copolymers either as photoresist itself or as a photosensitizer photo-acid generator quencher or as a contributor for antireflective coating.  Selectivity and performance of F-gases Plasma etching require precise control over the etched features like depth, shape, and selectivity. The main criterion for the selection of the etch gas is its ability to form a highly volatile reaction product with the silicon-based or metal-based wafer surface. Therefore, etching gases that ideally contain fluorine (PFAS like carbon tetrafluoride and octafluorocyclobutane) are generally used by etching structures. The better control  over the types and numbers of ions and radicals generated in the plasma  the  higher etching performance, level of uniformity, and reproducibility in process. Thus, the gaseous PFASs used are extremely difficult to substitute.   c) On the market:   UMS/our company is a strategic company for the space and defense industry in Europe with an essential function behind. A full ban on PFAS would affect the defense electronics business, due to disruption or even stop of manufacturing and thereby loss of Europe's political independence. UMS products are used in telecommunications (radio relay, satellite terminals and mobile radio base stations) automotive (adaptive cruise control, car sensors) defense (phased array radar, communication) and aerospace (satellite communication, earth observation). Many key companies in EU and non EU would be affected.  d) On Alternatives in general: Semiconductor company as UMS, are usually downstream user, means we use already available materials from our supplier. This is why we have no data or indicator if or how far they are with the research of alternatives. Although various PFAS-free alternatives were found and replacements were made, there are still a large number of applications in the semiconductor industry for which there are no alternatives. Especially PFAS that are used in equipment for process manufacturing or maintenance work are hard to replace.  e) On alternatives not yet available:  Semiconductor companies as downstream must rely on supplier and hope that they will develop PFAS-free solution in the next years. From intern research and contact with our suppliers, we know that are many PFAS applications with so far no alternatives available: For example, there is no alternatives for the pump/container material PVDF in the applications pumping of ultrapure water for semiconductor production. Due to the excellent leach out behavior, cleanliness, resistance against bio-film, high temperature resistance, chemical resistance, excellent mechanical properties and long lifetime performance PFAS containing product are irreplaceable At this moment no alternative materials for fluoropolymers, which could be compatible with semiconductor manufacturing. Even they are many PFAS free polymers of elastomers; unfortunately, they don't cover the chemical resistance and durability. For example, propylene diene monomer (EPDM) and silicone rubbers for sealing application cannot be used for various aggressive chemicals or gases. There are also no alternatives available for fluoropolymers sealing, applications. The reason for that the seal materials must have a very high stability/ persistent properties next to mechanical strength (>8 MPa), wear resistance, flexibility, resistance to high temperature (> 200°C). Photoresist contain PFAS: As it is have been reported in paper Journal of Micro/Nanopatterning, Materials, and Metrology, Vol. 21, Issue 1, 010901 (March 2022). https://doi.org/10.1117/1.JMM.21.1.010901 in almost all cases fluorine-free alternatives in optical lithography are either not current available or not fully tested and demonstrated. Lubricants: no alternative materials for lubricants used in semiconductor industry exist. PFPE and PTFE substances as raw materials of PFAS lubricants. These substances are necessary especially in the manufacturing process of semiconductor industry due to excellent temperature characteristics, chemical stability, heat resistance, low vapor pressure, low surface energy, and tribological properties like minimum outgas generation from the substances. To implement fluorine-free heat transfer fluids, it would be necessary to completely redesign semiconductor manufacturing-related equipment. Refrigerants: Although PFAS-free refrigerants are already available on the market, they are often flammable and therefore unsuitable for contact with higher temperatures or for system temperature control. In case, of finding  PFAS free  non-flammability alternatives simply using an existing dryer  to new refrigerant will not be technically possible  or  can be immensely expensive. In such cases a better option would be to invest in a new dryer.  f) On alternatives where substitution is technically and economically feasible but more time is required:  Potentially, we can imagine, that a PFAS-free alternative for PFCs semiconductor etching gases exists or will be explored in the coming years. But even if replacements of  PFC and HFCs gases in the semiconductor industry would be possible with e.g. mixtures of F2 or NF3, there are still many uncertainties. First, we expect very high costs for tool and infrastructure investments and a high additional workload of high skilled people for re-qualification of our products. Even despite these efforts, we cannot be sure that the performance and reliability of our products will not be affected. It can take over a decade to develop an alternative, with no guarantees that it will meet the requirements regarding performance of the product.

8. Other identified uses: Already answered in question 7 and attached document (IMAT PAPER) https://imat-ev.eu/wp-content/uploads/2023/06/2028_06_29-Positionspapier_PFAS_IMAT.pdf

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The Slovak Competent Authority for REACH and CLP Regulation (SK CA) appreciates the opportunity to provide general comments on the restriction report regarding per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) under REACH.
SK CA supports the aim of the REACH Regulation - to ensure a high level of protection of human health and the environment as well as the free circulation of substances on the internal market while enhancing competitiveness and innovation. In this context, we are also of the opinion if there is a legitimate need to regulate a group of chemicals, it requires a special approach and consideration of all possible regulatory measures, assessment of their proportionality, applicability and effectiveness, including the use of specific legislation aimed at human health and environment protection.
SK CA understands the importance of adopting actions to minimise releases of PFAS. However, the effectiveness of the proposed restriction on EU level we see disputable and relative, since emissions of PFASs to the EU environment do not origin exclusively from EU sources. The emissions originating from countries outside the EU cannot be ruled out, taking into account specific characteristics of concerned PFASs (persistency, mobility, bioaccumulation, toxicity, LRTP). If the given issue goes beyond the borders of the EU, we consider as more appropriate to start acting on a global level, due to the effectiveness and proportionality of the measures.
We would like to express our concerns about appropriateness of the proposed restriction as the best and most effective regulatory measure to minimise releases of PFAS into the environment for several reasons listed below:
• We believe that the proposed restriction should not regulate all substances defined as PFAS (according to OECD definition, 2021), but we rather prefer to identify more specific substance groups with similar toxicity profiles based on scientific evidence that would establish appropriate restrictions for individual substance group(s) to prevent their harmful effects on human health and the environment.

• Although the PFAS restriction report contains recommendations for the use of accredited, standard and validated test methods for PFAS, the methods summarized in the report (or its appendices) mostly do not meet these requirements. Well-established standards that focus exclusively on a targeted subset of PFAS (mostly 10-30 individual PFAS) represent a very small fraction of PFAS that are subject to restrictions. Standard methods are not available for the vast majority of PFAS, and even if scientific publications are available, it is questionable whether the proposed methods could be used for routine analyses of various products containing PFAS. In this context we have serious concerns about the feasibility and enforceability of the proposed restriction. If standard test methods for restricted PFAS are not available, it is questionable how affected entities will comply with restriction requirements and how enforcement authorities will check compliance with the restriction requirement. We share the opinion that the legal text should refer to valid EN test standards for the related product groups because limits and especially limits of sums of substances are only useful with reference to the test method. Regarding the scope and relevant EN standards we have a sympathy to the general comment of European Committee for Standardisation CEN/TC248 “Textile and textile products” WG 26 (Comment No 4130).

• The main concern for all PFASs and/or their degradation products that are in the scope of this comprehensive restriction proposal is according the dossier submitters the high persistence, exceeding excessively the criterion for very persistent (vP) according to Annex XIII of the REACH. Bearing in mind the broad scope of the restriction, lacking data regarding the substance identity for many substances included, data availability on persistency and degradability of PFAS only for a small group of them, the statement on very persistency for all PFAS we consider not sufficiently justified. As well as high mobility and bioaccumulation potential of some PFAS substances is insufficiently justified. The hazard profiles of the PFAS group differ significantly. Moreover, the fulfilment of the P/vP criteria as such is not a sufficient reason for adopting regulatory measures. SK CA supports scientific and well grounded restriction of specific, hazardous PFAS due to their harmful effects similarly as already regulated e.g. PFOS, PFOA or C8 - C14 PFCAs. We cannot agree to determine the scope of the restriction based on the chemical structure of PFAS substances according to the OECD definition, which does not inform whether a compound is harmful or not;  the definition only communicates that the included compounds share the same trait for having a fully fluorinated methyl- or methylene- carbon moiety. In light of the above, it cannot be concluded that all PFAS substances can be considered to be of concern and thus subject to the proposed restriction.
• We understand the REACH pays specific attention to substances with PBT/vPvB/PMT/vPvM concern or to substance considered “as if it is PBT/vPvB/PMT/vPvM and these substances / group of substances with such a special characteristics require specific regulatory measure approach.  The aim of the REACH is the substitution of such substances if suitable technically and economically viable alternatives are available. Until the substitution is achieved, substances need to be used and handled under strictly controlled conditions, and their releases and exposures need to be minimised.  The restriction addresses the manufacture, placing on the market, as well as the use of PFAS as such and as constituents in other substances, in mixtures and in articles above a certain concentration. According to proposed restriction approach - all uses of PFAS are covered by restriction proposal, regardless of whether they have been specifically assessed (i.e. it can be said that a complete ban is proposed), unless a specific derogation has been formulated and justified. The industry representatives and stakeholders are expected to provide justified reasons for derogations.  We believe that such an approach to create a restriction is not to be in accordance with the current rules under the provisions of REACH.
• PFAS are used in many diverse applications. Some of them are essential uses or uses critical for the European Green Deal objectives. Derogations should be made to not affect e.g. energy security, military or medical uses. Moreover, in case of uses in which PFAS do not become part of the finished products or releases from the product during the use are negligible and/or in which no alternatives with similar properties are available; these uses should be exempted, if it is shown that socio-economic benefits outweigh the risk to human health or the environment.

• A restriction should be combined with additional regulatory measures to reduce emissions from those applications with a derogation. Emission of PFAS coming from manufacture of these products as well as waste stage could be regulated via other special legislations e.g. for drinking water, waste and waste water. Substances used only in industrial settings could also be derogated with application of appropriate measures at manufacturing sites according to e.g. OSH legislation.

• We support development and implementation of mutual standards that industrial sector can use, a binding monitoring for PFAS lifecycle emissions, reporting and verification system harmonised across the EU as well as on global level. In this context, we consider useful to focus also on possible best available technique of disposal of PFAS emissions released to air, water, sediments and soil. Published scientific studies indicate that there are ongoing projects dealing with the mechanisms of degradation of various groups of PFAS in the environment and possible ways of disposing of PFAS, which indicate that PFAS substances could be degraded. (https://serdp-estcp.org/newsitems/details/cfea8916-49e5-421a-85c5-508f7cc56bf8/expanding-the-biodegradation-knowledge-base-of-pfas-in-the-subsurface).
To sum up, the restriction proposal should differentiate between the various types of PFAS on the basis of their chemical composition and hazard profile, manufacturing method and their particular uses. We are of the opinion that there is insufficient scientific data and evidence to justify a complete ban of PFAS. PFAS subject to the restriction should be limited to substances for which harmful effects on human health or environment have been demonstrated using scientifically sound and reliable data. The currently proposed PFAS restriction approach needs to ensure that the socio-economic costs arising from a general ban on PFAS do not outweigh their benefits. Banning all PFAS based on the persistence concern would have huge unintended consequences for European society, the economy and the competitiveness of EU industry and may create barriers to international trade. The restriction, as it is proposed will present a real challenge in terms of its transparency, feasibility and enforceability. We can support regulating PFAS for uses with large emissions for which alternatives exists or uses that are not essential, instead of complete ban of all PFAS uses (including essential uses) for which suitable technically and economically feasible alternatives are not available.

Content: Environmental emissions Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The submitter acts on behalf of its two German affiliates, who are global manufacturers of pumps and valves for industrial, food and pharma industry. The submitters would like to complement a previous submission with ID 4372 submitted by one of the submitters. In particular, the submitters have in the meantime conducted a socio-economic analysis of the impact of the proposed restriction, that is included in section 6 below. The submitters have analyzed their product portfolio and have identified the types of pumps that would not operate with alternative materials and would thus have to be phased-out. The reason for the phase-out would be that such pumps would not withstand the harsh conditions and would not pass the performance, safety and conformity requirements. These pumps are: horizontal and vertical pumps with fluoropolymer impellers and tubing that are designed for processing and manufacturing of hot and oxidizing chemicals such as ammonium nitrate, sulfuric and nitric acid and in chlorine-alkali- electrolysis.
Pumps and valves for the petrochemical, chemical, food and pharma industry containing PFAS (PTFE, PFA, ETFE) in the inert state as main parts material as well as sealing components material, which are irreplaceable, should be derogated for industrial applications.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Pumps and valves for the petrochemical, chemical, food and pharma industry containing PFAS (PTFE, PFA, ETFE) in the inert state as main parts material as well as sealing components material, which are irreplaceable.

6. Missing uses: Use of fluorpolymers in industrial pumps and valves is a missing use not adressed in the Annex XV Report. In the previous submission with ID 4372 the first submitter provided data on critical use in its pumps. By this submission the submitter would like to complement the data with the socio-economic analysis. As further documented in the confidential attachment, the first submitter would lose 35,7% of its overall turnover in plastic pumps and at least 34% in metal pumps. The second submitter would lose 60,7% of its overall turnover, with the biggest impact on centrifugal pumps (loss of 76,9%) and liquid pumps (loss of 88.1%).   This would, as a minimum, lead to an equivalent loss of EU jobs. Furthermore, it is possible that EU manufacturing operations would not be economically viable without the affected pump portfolios. Consequently, submitters’ manufacturing facilities would have to be moved outside of the EU.      The socio-economic impact downstream would be even more significant. Downstream chemicals manufacturing and processing industry is dependent on the use of the affected pumps (around 60% of submitters’ production is destined for EU industry).  Without these critical applications, EU chemical industries would not be able to operate any longer and would have to shut down their facilities.  This would also impact their customers, EU manufacturers of critical end-use applications. This would have immense societal impact that is not possible to estimate, or even imagine.   Consequently, the submitters request a derogation for fluoropolymers that would cover the critical uses in the case at hand, i.e. the use in pumps and valves that are intended for use in harsh conditions (temperature above 120C, acidic and corrosive chemicals).   Regarding the duration of such derogation, it is difficult to estimate the necessary time as currently there is no alternative material available, or even known. But even if there is an alternative material available today, the alternative would have to be tested in a trial-and-error testing and the pumps would have to be redesigned and re-certified according to EU standards. In an optimistic scenario that an alternative will be developed within next 5 years, the minimum duration of the derogation would be at least 13.5 years.   In addition, the submitters request a derogation for spare and replacement parts, otherwise all existing pumps would have to be scrapped prematurely because of the non-availability of a replacement part. The spare and replacement part derogation should be provided for the lifetime of the pumps which is at least 20 years. The spare parts derogation should apply to all fluoropolymer applications, not only to those that are in contact with harsh conditions. Content: Scope or restriction option analysis
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The Swedish Defence Industry Association (SOFF) represents 200 defense companies of various sizes. We've observed that the dossier submitters have not taken into account the utilization of aeronautic, space, security, and defense (collectively referred to as aerospace and defense) sectors. The proposed restriction option 2 (RO2) has been developed without considering the unique characteristics of our sector. The current proposed restriction would have severe consequences as it would halt aviation, space, and defense activities, including production, imports, and maintenance, just 18 months after its implementation.
In our comments, we emphasize the necessity of incorporating the specific needs of our sector in the proposed restriction options by the dossier submitters. Aerospace and defense products encompass both civilian and military aeronautics (comprising various aircraft and associated ground equipment), a range of security and defense products (including naval vessels, armored vehicles, weapon systems, and munitions), and space equipment such as satellites, launchers, and communication systems. These products share the common requirement of operating under extreme conditions and adhering to stringent safety and reliability standards.
Formal quality management systems, like AS9100, are in place to ensure compliance with these standards throughout the manufacturing, operation, and maintenance (Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul or MRO) processes. Any changes to product design are subject to rigorous formal change management procedures. MRO activities must use parts and components manufactured according to the approved design.
Regarding the use of PFAS chemicals in aerospace and defense products, we address this in our response to Q6. PFAS chemicals play an integral role in the production, operation, and MRO of these products. We provide 20 illustrative case studies, each outlining the application, the role of PFAS chemicals in performance, the availability of alternatives, and the impact of the proposed restriction on the application. Notably, fluoropolymers, used widely as seals, sealants, gaskets, lubricants, bearings, and more across these products, lack immediate drop-in alternatives due to stringent performance requirements. Substitution timelines depend on the identification, commercialization, and industrialization of new alternatives, which may take years.
We emphasize that the scale of substitution required is unprecedented, affecting thousands of parts, components, systems, etc., essential for production, operation, and MRO across aerospace and defense products. The economic impact extends beyond manufacturing jobs, potentially leading to the cessation of civilian aircraft production in the EEA, outsourcing of scheduled maintenance, and dependence on aging fleets. Defense forces would face critical challenges, including an inability to maintain existing products, procure new ones, or replenish weapon stocks, jeopardizing Europe's sovereignty.
Due to these reasons, we request that the dossier submitters modify their restriction proposal to explicitly consider our sector and its unique requirements. We ask them to take into account:
• Formal quality management systems, particularly stringent certification processes (e.g., AS9100 and NATO standards).
• The absence of suitable alternatives meeting safety and reliability standards.
• The lengthy substitution process.
• The extensive R&D activities needed.
• The complexity of products manufactured from numerous parts via global supply chains.
• Interdependencies across products.
• The need for adequate derogation coverage.
• The inadequacy of a 12-year derogation period.
• The necessity of a review clause.
• The prevalence of fluoropolymers in aerospace and defense products.
• The reporting requirements and administrative burden.
Specifically, we propose:
• Excluding fluoropolymers from the restriction.
• Implementing a sector derogation for non-polymeric PFAS chemicals.
• Exempting PFAS chemicals used for MRO.
• Providing a time-unlimited derogation for specific PFAS chemicals used in fire suppression systems.
Our sector's reliance on materials from various industries necessitates these measures to prevent widespread obsolescence and supply chain disruptions.
We argue that a blanket ban on fluoropolymers is disproportionate given the focus on conditions of use and risk management at manufacturing sites and end-of-life, not their inherent properties. There are more proportionate risk management options available, such as specific obligations under the Industrial Emissions Directive.
A blanket ban on PFAS chemicals carries significant implications for the European Defence Technological and Industrial Base (EDTIB). This ban has the potential to undermine the EDTIB's capacity to manufacture and maintain critical defense materials and capabilities. Several EU Member States, including Sweden, as well as NATO allies and the EU itself, have placed orders and rely on the EDTIB to develop, produce, and deliver these essential defense assets.
The EDTIB is currently grappling with unprecedented challenges in its supply chain and production processes. These challenges are particularly pressing as the EDTIB is actively working to provide critical equipment and materials to support Ukraine in its defense against Russia and to replenish depleted stocks. A PFAS ban would impede the EDTIB's ability to meet these demands, thereby placing the security of EU Member States and the EU itself at risk.
Furthermore, the adoption of a PFAS restriction in line with ECHA's recommendations could potentially lead to an increase in the import of defense material and equipment from third countries with lower environmental and health standards. Additionally, such a restriction may hinder the development of new European technologies and capabilities. This would put the EDTIB and EU Member States at a disadvantage when competing in the global market. These challenges are especially concerning at a time when the EU is actively seeking to reduce its reliance on third countries, promote innovation, enhance competitiveness, and foster economic growth.
Fluoropolymers possess unique properties ideal for high-performance applications with stringent safety and reliability requirements. Banning them compromises safety standards in aerospace and defense, as well as other industries.
Regarding fire suppression, PFAS chemicals are essential alternatives to Halon, particularly in aircraft. A time-unlimited derogation is requested to maintain ongoing activities without disruptions.
Lastly, we point out that reporting requirements, especially for ppb levels in articles, are impractical for aerospace and defense products, as they would necessitate testing thousands of components, which is not feasible given the current state of testing methods.
In summary, we seek an inclusive and tailored approach that considers the specific needs and challenges of the aerospace and defense sector in any restriction proposal involving PFAS chemicals.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The dossier in Table 9 did not encompass the usage within the aerospace and defense sector adequately. The listed applications fail to comprehensively consider the distinctive needs and requirements of aerospace and defense applications concerning safety and reliability. SOFF, therefore, urges the inclusion of aerospace and defense as a distinct sector, with specific attention given to their use of PFAS chemicals within the restriction dossier. The aerospace and defense sector comprises various end-products, including: • Commercial aircraft for passenger and cargo transportation, encompassing fixed-wing aircraft and helicopters. • Military aircraft, ranging from fast jets to training aircraft, large transports, and helicopters. • Naval vessels, such as surface ships (including aircraft carriers) and submarines. • Land vehicles, including tanks, armored vehicles, communication vehicles, weapons launchers, and military personnel and munitions transport vehicles. • Weapons, munitions, and ammunition. • Space launchers, satellites, and associated ground-based support equipment. • Other defense and security systems, such as radars, communication systems, cameras, Command & Control systems, protection, and surveillance systems. Further details on the aeronautics, defense, and space sub-sectors are provided below: Aeronautics: Aeronautics products encompass fixed-wing and helicopter aircraft, involving various technologies for wing controls, propulsion, communications, flight controls, cabin equipment, fuel systems, hydraulics, oil systems, and electrical systems. It also includes ground equipment, such as air traffic control and maintenance/inspection equipment. The stringent safety and reliability requirements in this sector subject the production, operation, and MRO of products to regulatory and industry standard controls. Defense & Security: This category encompasses military aeronautics and various other capabilities vital for national and European defense and security. It includes ships, submarines, munitions, land vehicles (tanks, artillery, armored personnel carriers), air defense systems, military aircraft, as well as ground platforms for surveillance, communication, critical infrastructure protection, and ground support equipment and maintenance/inspection equipment. Due to its sensitive nature, this sector operates under strict data security controls, especially concerning technology and materials. These controls are formalized through technology export controls and security classification, preventing information disclosure except under highly regulated conditions. This consultation response, therefore, cannot disclose sensitive details of PFAS uses in military products or their operation unless these technologies overlap with non-military applications. SOFF underscores that a case-by-case defense exemption mechanism, as defined in REACH Article 2(3) for each Member State, would not be practical for a restriction of this scope, as it would necessitate thousands of exemptions in each member state. Defense exemptions also pose limitations for applications with dual uses, such as shared supply chains with non-defense-related aeronautics, and cross-border supply. Space: The EEA boasts a robust space industry involved in satellite manufacturing, launch services, and space technology development. The space sector holds strategic importance for the EEA in terms of technological independence, supporting public policies, all economic sectors, and Europe's autonomous access to space.  PFAS chemicals play a fundamental role in the production, operation, and maintenance of aerospace and defense products, including the manufacture of component parts, sub-assemblies, and formulations within the aerospace and defense supply chains. Their unique properties render them well-suited for applications operating in harsh or extreme conditions with stringent requirements for reliability, performance, and safety over extended service lives. Comprehensive details regarding the widespread uses of PFAS chemicals within the aerospace and defense sector are provided in our response below.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Timeframe Concerns: SOFF expresses profound concerns regarding the proposed transition period and the absence of derogations for our intricate products and production equipment. Substituting PFAS compounds in our sector presents exceptional complexities, primarily driven by the imperative to employ certified and qualified materials to ensure the safety and reliability of products during their operational phase.  Considering the extensive and diverse applications of PFAS across thousands of articles within our society, with ongoing data collection efforts, it is imperative to allocate sufficient time for the qualification of PFAS-free alternatives. The vast number of PFAS-containing articles and materials that necessitate replacement, coupled with stringent qualification and certification requisites, demands an extended timeframe. This applies not only to older product designs but also to ongoing design and production projects.  The combination of the absence of derogations, the proposed transition periods, and the intricate verification and certification procedures specific to our sector creates an untenable situation where compliance with the draft regulatory text, if adopted as proposed, becomes nearly impossible.  Importance of Differentiated Consideration: In light of the crucial role PFAS play in our industry, it is imperative that their usage remains permissible as long as their associated risks can be effectively managed, or in instances where suitable alternatives are not readily accessible. Consequently, any legislation aimed at restricting substances should not be implemented without a differentiated assessment of their uses and the resultant implications.  SOFF advocates for a differentiated regulatory approach that aligns with Article 68(1) of REACH, focusing on risk-based considerations, and Article 69 of REACH, which is substance-based. Such an approach would enable a more nuanced and balanced approach to the regulation of PFAS compounds, taking into account their diverse applications and the complexities associated with their substitution.

6. Missing uses: The dossier submitters have overlooked the aerospace and defence sector, and the current restriction proposal inadequately addresses the uses within this sector. While some aerospace and defence uses might fall under proposed or potential derogations, the scope and duration of these derogations are deemed insufficient. Many aerospace and defence applications remain uncovered by any proposed or potential derogations. Therefore, we have provided insights into our sector's wide-ranging applications, along with information on alternative availability and socio-economic impacts, in the attached document. A summary of the key points is presented below.  PFAS chemicals play an extensive role in the production, operation, and maintenance of aerospace and defence products (refer to Table 1). Among PFAS types, fluoropolymers are the most commonly used, serving as parts (e.g., seals, cables, hoses), surface treatments (e.g., paints, coatings, sealants), and components of mixtures (e.g., lubricants). Our assessment of derogations reveals that there is limited coverage for the vast majority of aerospace and defence applications. Consequently, it becomes evident that the non-use scenario's impacts, as stipulated in the current draft, would become apparent as early as 18 months after implementation, given that roughly half of our reported application areas lack coverage under proposed or potential derogations.  We emphasize that the defence sector presents unique characteristics that warrant the dossier submitters' consideration. These include stringent safety and reliability requirements, the exceptionally high performance standards demanded of parts, components, systems, etc., due to harsh operational conditions, and the qualification and certification prerequisites in place to ensure safety and performance throughout a product's service life. Aerospace and defence products are also highly complex, consisting of numerous parts, components, sub-systems, and systems. A single major platform, such as an aircraft or ship, can comprise millions of parts, many of which are intricate assemblies (e.g., engines, landing gear, brake systems, fuel systems). These products boast extended service lives, necessitating the availability of spare parts consistent with the original design for decades. These sector-specific attributes render regulatory mandates for chemical substitution exceedingly challenging. In this context, the requirement to replace PFAS-containing materials would impact thousands of parts, components, formulations, and materials across diverse aerospace and defence products. Presently, there are no alternatives available that meet the stringent performance criteria demanded by these products. The list of potential alternatives presented in the restriction report (Annex E) is unsuitable for our sector, as the dossier submitters did not consider the specificities of our industry in their alternatives assessment. For example, the section outlining alternatives for the "transportation" sector does not account for varying performance requirements. Innovating new chemicals, formulations, and materials is necessary, followed by a lengthy qualification and certification process to ensure safety and reliability. For existing products, introducing new materials necessitates product redesign and recertification. To illustrate, in the case of a gas turbine engine, hundreds of PFAS-containing components would need replacement, requiring an alternative for each component before launching the recertification process for the redesigned engine. Adding to the challenge is the uncertainty surrounding R&D programs' ability to identify suitable alternatives, particularly for fluoropolymers, which are currently the sole materials possessing the requisite properties for aerospace and defence applications. It is improbable that a one-to-one alternative can be found for all current uses of PTFE, for instance. Considering the diversity of aerospace and defence products, it is crucial to recognize that the scale of the substitution requirement is unparalleled in our sector. Estimates suggest that a smaller short-haul commercial aircraft may contain approximately 400,000 - 500,000 PFAS-containing components (primarily fluoropolymers), while larger aircraft could have in excess of one million such components.  Regarding RO2, which entails a ban on all PFAS chemicals with time-limited derogations for specific sectors/applications, the impact hinges on the adequacy of derogations covering PFAS uses required for the production, operation, and MRO of aerospace and defence products. If derogation coverage is incomplete or derogation periods are misaligned, the impact can be as severe as RO1. Our use and derogation mapping demonstrates that the coverage is incomplete, and the derogation periods, when provided, are insufficient for our sector.  To shed light on the wider economic consequences of non-use scenarios, we refer to recent authorization applications submitted for continued use of a limited number of hexavalent chromium compounds in specific surface treatments of parts/components/systems/products by the aerospace and defence sector. This assessment provides an illustrative understanding of the economic ramifications of non-use scenarios (see Table 13 of the ASD response). Given the number of chemicals within scope and their pervasive use in aerospace and defence product production, operation, and MRO, the impact of RO2 would be catastrophic. RO2 would halt the production of new products, disrupt MRO of existing products, impede the import of products, components, and parts, and result in far-reaching economic consequences beyond job loss. For instance, considering civilian aviation, aircraft could operate within the EEA but could neither be produced, serviced, nor imported in the EEA. Similarly, in terms of national security, existing defence products (aircraft, naval vessels, land vehicles, munitions, weapons) could operate but not be serviced due to a lack of spare parts. Once existing stocks are depleted, replenishment would be impossible. New products/parts could neither be produced nor imported within the EEA, rendering defence forces unable to address security threats. It is implausible for these non-use scenarios to become a reality.  Based on our assessment, it is evident that the scale of the substitution requirement, coupled with the unique characteristics of our sector, has not been duly considered by the dossier submitters. Their proposed RO2 does not encompass our sector and is therefore incomplete. Consequently, we urge the dossier submitters to revise their proposal to include our sector and take into account our considerations and requests as outlined in our general comments.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: The Swedish Defence Materiel Administration, FMV, is a governmental agency acting under the Ministry of Defence. FMV's main assignment from the Government is to deliver materiel and services to the Swedish Armed Forces, SwAF. FMV procures equipment and services to the SwAF based short and long term capability requirements.
Within the scope of FMV´s mission we provide this response to the public consultation on the proposed EU restriction on PFAS. The response endeavors to bring attention to the SwAF dependence on PFAS, including many fluoropolymers, that are within scope of the current restriction proposal and for which there are currently no alternatives available. We conclude that there is a need for derogations within several areas of use to facilitate a controllable transition without compromising operational capability and effectiveness.
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine contributes to a deteriorating security policy situation in the vicinity of Sweden and in Europe. The invasion demonstrates that the Russian state leadership’s threshold for military violence is very low, and that it is prepared to take big risks to achieve their objectives. The overall deteriorating international security situation has decreased Sweden´s national ability to withstand even short periods of reduced readiness, including interruptions in our long-term preparedness to meet military threats to national sovereignty. In the light of the current events in the vicinity of Europe it is of outmost importance that defence materiel can be used and produced in the EU without disturbances.

FMV´s response regarding defence materiel is provided in the non-confidential attachments divided into the following (sub)-uses:
• Ammunition
• Fluorinated gases
• Fluoropolymers
• Medical devices
• Paints and cleaning fluids
• Lubricants
• Electronics, batteries and semi-conductors

In addition to information on PFAS-reliant uses for the SwAF and the need for derogations, FMV (below) takes the opportunity to inform on anticipated effects of the PFAS restriction on areas that can be considered unique to defence versus other sectors.

Long life-cycles of defence materiel and contracts
Defence materiel are generally designed for use in a demanding environment, posing a larger risk of fire and damages. It is also designed to be robust and resilient to minimize the need for service and maintenance. All time required for maintenance means less time in operation. Transition to PFAS free components may result in potential degradation in performance and the effect might be more time in a maintenance workshop. Hence, the choices made when designing defence materiel are often the more long-lasting and durable techniques that at the same time provide as much safety as possible. Another important feature is that materiel may be stored over time, ready for action for a fast transition into combat or a crisis situation.
Development of defence materiel is heavily regulated and has many product-specific requirements, which need to be given full attention when assessing alternatives and impact of withdrawal. Changes to the products and processes are subject to stringent contractual, qualification and certification requirements, which may be overseen by regulatory bodies and agencies such as the EASA (European Aviation Safety Agency) and the FAA (United States Federal Aviation Administration). Defence materiel are also subject to requirements in standards, both national and common standards as well as NATO standards. Products, components, or materials need to be examined, tested and meet all applicable standards or qualification requirements established by a certifying organization or government entity in order to be used by defence. This process can proceed for as long as 20-30 years.

Defence materiel tend to have longer life cycles than civil equivalence, 30-50 years is not un-common for vehicles developed for military use. Also ordinary trucks and smaller vehicles are operated and maintained by the SwAF for longer time than civilian equivalents. Development of new or modification of existing materiel is a process lasting several years. Due to the long processes as well as the need for supply security many of the contracts last for many years, sometimes over 10 years. A regulation as wide as the proposed PFAS restriction will strongly effect the outcome of the contracts between FMV and the defence industry when the design agreed upon has to be revised.

Limitation of Reach defence exemptions
Granting of a defence exemption (according to Reach article 2(3)) is a sovereign national responsibility, and a member state can only provide a defence exemption to the extent of its own jurisdiction. The Reach defence exemption process is often no option, or very difficult to manage, in cases in which defence industries in more than one member state are involved in a transnational supply chain. FMV is of the opinion that the granting of defence exemptions should be considered only after the following alternative methods have been examined; complying with the requirements of the Reach regulation and substitution of hazardous substance(s) with more benign alternatives. Another limitation of the Reach defence exemption is that it cannot be used to support the continued use of a dual-use substance outside the defence domain, i.e., for civil applications. Civil markets often include sectors with lower performance requirements and hence better substitution prospects. If a dual-use substance is withdrawn from the civil market due to Reach constraints (e.g., restriction or authorisation), it may become commercially unavailable or very expensive for military customers even if its use continue to be legally allowed for the defence sector due to a defence exemption. Hence, defence exemptions do not ensure the availability on the market of a dual-use substance. For a deeper understanding of the limitations of a defence exemption, FMV refer to the expected public consultation submission of the European Defence Agency (EDA).

Negative effects on interoperability and host nation support
The term "interoperability” can, from a military perspective, be defined as the ability for defence forces to work effectively together. This can be achieved through services being exchanged between and used by systems, military units or military forces. Interoperability is achieved through an international standardization process. An enhanced level of interoperability will greatly increase responsiveness and flexibility and hence the warfighting capability of European armed forces and international Partners or Allies (NATO). To achieve interoperability in certain areas of the military arena, all actors involved (European as well as international armed forces) agree to use standardized specific materiel/components/chemicals – which in many cases contain PFAS or fluoropolymers due to the ability for this group of chemicals to achieve high performance requirements and for which there are no substitutes today. The full ban on PFAS in the EU will have negative effects on interoperability between European armed forces as well as with international Partners or Allies (NATO), since the use and placing on the market (as well as import) of chemicals and articles containing PFAS in the EU will be prohibited (unless derogations apply). As pointed out in a previous section of this document, Reach defence exemptions do not ensure the availability on the market of dual-use substance. Hence, there is an absolute need to include derogations for manufacturing, use and placing on the market of PFAS and fluoropolymers for military purposes in the PFAS restriction in Annex XVII, when proposed derogations (already included in the PFAS restriction proposal or received in the public consultation) are deemed justified.
On the same note, the proposed ban on PFAS in the EU can be expected to have negative effects on European armed forces´ host nation support to non-EU NATO armed forces, if their national legislation does not impose the same restrictions on PFAS as in the EU. Simplified, host nation support entails providing support to foreign armed forces that are located on, operating on, from or in transit through the Host Nation’s territory. The Host Nation is expected to provide logistics and other support to foreign armed forces forces/organizations, which can include providing spare parts, goods and chemicals within the scope of the proposed restriction on PFAS. One concrete example is the Host Nation providing f-gases or lubricants for refilling in foreign armed forces defence equipment. The foreign armed forces can also bring their own supply of spare parts, goods and chemicals for use in the Host Nation’s territory. Since the scope of the proposed ban on PFAS in the EU cover a wide variety of chemicals and articles used in defence materiel globally, European armed forces´ host nation support to non-EU armed forces will be negatively affected due to the inability to provide necessary spare parts, goods and chemicals or for the non-EU armed forces to use supplies containing PFAS on (EU) Host Nation’s territory.

Org. name: Swedish Society for Nature Conservation (Svenska Naturskyddsföreningen)
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The Swedish Society for Nature Conservation warmly welcomes the proposal to restrict all PFAS as a group. These are our official comments to the annex XV restriction proposal on PFAS.
This restriction proposal is necessary to mitigate the invisible, yet ongoing crisis PFAS has imposed on our natural world. The irreversible emissions of PFAS to the environment that have been allowed to continue for decades has now polluted our food and drinking water to the extent that enormous resources are being spent every day by various authorities and institutions around Europe to investigate, evaluate, and decontaminate water, soil, and biota of PFAS. Enormous resources are and will be spent on the negative health effects from human exposure to PFAS, e.g., from cancer and infertility, lowered immune system, high cholesterol, and Thyroid issues. As a society it is completely unreasonable to continue pouring resources into remediation and decontamination and yet continue to use and emit the same substances that cause this crisis.
To really get rid of PFAS, incineration at 1400 ºC is required. At lower temperatures, PFAS degrade to shorter PFAS and eventually end up as extremely persistent ultra-short PFAS, of which some have high global warming potential. Municipality incineration contributes to the increasing environmental levels of PFAS. To minimize the emission, PFAS-containing products and materials should be handled as hazardous waste or be collected by those setting the products on the market in a extended producer responsibility program.
The producers knew already in the early days of the 1960s, that PFAS are extremely persistent with harmful health effects, yet they continued to push PFAS on the market. Hence, the industry has continued to develop product after product dependent on PFAS. They are now urging lawmakers to let them continue to pollute our world because they have failed to take moral action for decades, i.e., failed to shift towards developing products without using harmful and extremely persistent chemicals like PFAS. The use of PFAS has only increased despite common knowledge since the turn of the millennium of environmental and health issues. A recent investigation (Chemsec 2023) calculates that the costs for society (€16 trillion) hundreds of times exceed the profits for the industry (€26 billion) globally. This restriction is urgently needed.
Society can function well without PFAS. This restriction of all PFAS will favor companies that have already started the phasing out or do not use PFAS in their production (Chemsec 2023b). For some applications, alternatives to PFAS will be more difficult to find. Nevertheless, derogations should only be for specific, necessary applications, and not for groups of PFAS, groups of materials or groups of applications. As an example, the industry argues that fluoropolymers are essential and should be excluded, but only 8 % of the fluoropolymer production volume goes to necessary products like semi-conductors and pharmaceuticals (Chemsec 2023). Furthermore, the dossier already includes derogations or exclusions for many of the necessary applications.

Presence in the environment
PFAS are ubiquitous in the environment. PFAS are found around the globe, in the Antarctic (Garnett et al 2022) and the Arctic Environment and wildlife (Hartz et al 2023, Muir et al 2019), in forest soil far from any point sources (Sörengård et al 2022) as well as the Tibetan Plateau (Chen et al 2023), in sea turtles (Beale et al 2022), sharks (Chynel et al 2021), foxes (Riebe et al 2016), and many other animals, in drinking water and food, as well as  in the blood in virtually every human (Mørck et al 2015, Starling et al 2014, Kotlarz et al 2020, Toms et al 2019, Kotlarz et al 2023, Uhl et al 2023).
Scientists have concluded that PFAS now exceeds the planetary boundaries as the levels in rainwater exceed health advisory levels (Cousins et al 2022) and regulatory values for drinking- and surface water in several countries. Regarding PFAS being forever chemicals, hence never breakdown in the natural environment, this should be particularly concerning. PFAS in nature today does not only contaminate our drinking water and food but contributes to biodiversity loss (Sigmund et al 2023) and to climate change (i.e., the F-gases).
A restriction will be effective in limiting the presence in the environment. PFOS, one of the most well-known PFAS, was globally banned in 2009, and the levels of PFOS in biota are no longer increasing. However, PFOS is still one of the main PFAS found in the environment due to its persistency. Other PFAS are still increasing significantly in nature and biota, including the ultra-short PFAS (Hartz et al 2023). The cost of removing PFAS from drinking water and food will be extremely high in the foreseeable future, unless an effective and broad restriction is adopted and implemented within a few years.

Polymeric PFAS must be included in the dossier.
Polymeric PFAS (fluoropolymers, perfluoroethers, side-chain fluorinated polymers, and all other polymers fulfilling the PFAS-definition (Wang et al 2021)) should be within the scope of the restriction because they will decompose into shorter PFAS with time, and eventually end up as more bioavailable and toxic PFAS. Side-chain fluorinated polymers are also well known to release their perfluorinated side chains.
The full life cycle impact of polymeric PFAS on the environment and health is poorly understood (Lohman and Letcher 2023). Producers have argued that polymeric PFAS should be considered “polymers of low concern”, which results in lower regulatory oversight, less investigations, and a neglect of the impacts from the production and end-of-life phases. However, in the scientific context there has been no clear evidence that polymeric PFAS are of low concern and hence they should be regulated and restricted as other PFAS, as there is no indication that they pose a lesser threat than other PFAS. One of the main arguments for polymers to be recognized as “polymers of low concern” is that polymers in general are too big to penetrate the cell membrane and enter the bloodstream and organs. The same has been argued for other non-PFAS-polymers, but several separate studies have shown that polymers can pass through the cell membrane (Lohmann et al 2020) and polymers are found in human blood at concentrations as high as µg/ml quantities (Leslie et al 2022). Another argument is that polymers are insoluble in water and not mobile, but PTFE and other PFAS-polymers are found all over the world, both in waterbodies, soil, and biota, and are therefore obviously mobile, even though they are not soluble in water. The formation of low-weight-particular fluoropolymers at elevated temperature (Plastic Europe 2021, Wang et al 2022) is a probable source of fluoropolymers in the environment (from manufacturing, processing, recycling, and incineration), together with the spread of (micro)plastics/rubber made solely of or containing fluoropolymers (from products or scrapes of products/coatings). Polymeric PFAS is a substantial part of the microplastic found in biota and PTFE has been found in Mediterranean fish species (Capillo et al 2020), in the Arctic deep sea sediments (Bergmann et al 2017) as well as in the pristine international reference site for inland waters research in Antartica (González-Pleiter et al 2020). Microplastics and PFAS have overlapping properties and a wide coexistence in the environment (Kang et al 2023).
The industry themselves acknowledges that fluoropolymers can degrade, and they have published guides to safe usage (e.g., Plastic Industry 2018, Plastics Europe 2021), however the guides only state that emissions shall be treated accordingly to national/regional rules. The guides do not include information transfer in the supply chain, including consumers and waste managements.
The amount of PFAS released from fluoropolymer processing companies is unclear. Studies have shown PFAS emissions close to fluoropolymer manufacturers (Gerardu et al 2023, Dauchy 2023), and it is likely that the same pattern could be seen for processing companies as well. How consumers will know how to treat the great variety of products containing PFAS to not contribute to PFAS-emissions is unclear (e.g., not to over-heat the frying pan, not to spread the rubber granulate from the artificial turfs). Nonetheless, most emissions arise probably from waste management (Lin et al 2022, Stoiber et al 2020, Björklund et al 2023, Strandberg et al 2021, Wahlström et al 2021, Winchell et al 2021, Brunn et al 2023, U.S. EPA 2020, Bakker et al 2021, Liu et al 2022, Bulson et al 2023, Smallwood et al 2023).
The main risk of regarding polymeric PFAS as “polymers of low concern” is that the emissions during manufacture and end-of-life stage are neglected. The full life-cycle fate of polymeric PFAS must be addressed, including emissions at all stages and how the final waste should be handled to not pose any threat to society now or in the future.
SSNC agrees with the dossier authors that “Clarity on effects after repeated exposure of the diverse group of oligomeric/polymeric PFASs cannot be given on the basis of available data” and that polymeric PFAS at any point in their lifecycle “may generate and/or release non-polymeric PFASs”, and they “contribute to the overall exposure to and risks of non-polymeric PFASs” and should be included in this regulation.
Circular economy not possible without a uPFAS restriction
In a circular economy, used materials and products, should preferably be recycled into new products. Recycling involves various treatments (e.g., mechanic, heat, solvents) to separate parts and to reform them into something new. During this treatment, PFAS can be emitted (Bulson et al 2023, Guelfo et al 2023, Rensmo et al 2023, Lin et al 2022), adding to the increasing burden of PFAS. Also, since PFAS is difficult to remove, the recycled material will be contaminated by PFAS, making it less desired on the market. With the large amount of waste containing PFAS today (e.g., consumer products, building materials, sludge, electronics), that should be treated as hazardous waste, there will not be much left to recycle. Therefore, this PFAS restriction is a pillar stone to make the circular economy possible.

Ultra-short PFAS are increasing in nature.
The levels of short and ultra-short PFAS in the environment are rising and has been so since the ban of the ozone depleting freons, as suspected already in 1995 (Tromp et al 1995). There are several sources of short and ultra-short PFAS, e.g., F-gases, pesticides, pharmaceuticals, and degradation of longer PFAS including polymeric PFAS. Measurements close to hot-spot areas such as firefighting training sites, landfills and waste management facilities show very high levels; up to 84 000 ng/L of the sum of ultra-short PFAAs (Björnsdotter et al 2019).
It has been claimed that TFA found in the environment is of natural origin, but recent studies find little evidence for this claim (Joudan et al 2021, Pickard et al 2020). TFA levels in the environment have been increasing since the 1990s. TFA accumulates in the human food chain (Scheurer et al 2021) and is found in human blood in relatively high levels (Duan et al 2020), and even found in cord blood of newborn babies (Jia et al 2023).
Surface water and drinking water often contains ultra-short PFAS, contributing to a large proportion of the total amount of PFAS (Björnsdotter et al 2019, Sadia et al 2023) or at magnitudes above the normally measured PFAS-4 or PFAS-21 (Neuwald et al 2022). One example is the Netherlands, where ultrashort chain (C2−C3) PFAS (mainly TFA) dominate both raw and produced drinking water (TFA 30−1100 ng/L and PFPrA 1−66 ng/L), and with a relative mass contribution of 49− 99% (Sadia et al 2023). In a study were tap water from 31 sites in Sweden and Norway were analyzed, TFA concentrations between 70 – 720 ng/l were found, with the lowest concentrations in the north-west and the highest in south-east (van Hees et al 2023). Also in Germany, high levels of ultra-short PFAS have been found. In surface water TFA was the most dominate (with a median and maximum concentration of 900 ng/L and 12400 ng/L) followed by TFMS (median 8.0 ng/L, maximum 2100 ng/L) and PFPrA (median 12.6 ng/L, maximum 180 ng/L) (Neuwald et al 2022). Unfortunately, the most common technique to remove PFAS from water, granulated active carbon (GAC), does not remove ultra-short PFAS. Instead, an increase in levels can be seen for the ultra-short PFAS after GAC (Björnsdotter et al 2019).
Of the sources to ultra-short PFAS, pharmaceuticals and pesticides are excluded in the restriction proposal and need to be managed within their respective legalisation. But all PFAS eventually decompose to ultra-short PFAS, and thus the restriction scope must be broad and include both F-gases and polymeric PFAS (e.g., fluoropolymers). The F-gas regulation only regulates the greenhouse warming potential, not the amount used, nor the persistence in the environment.
Landfills, incineration facilities and waste-water treatment plants are hot-spots for PFAS emissions from e.g., consumer products, building materials, electronics, coatings/sealings and other liquids. To avoid emissions at end-of-life phase, all PFAS-containing waste (including liquids) should be handled as hazardous waste and incinerated at 1400 ºC. See question 3 for more information.
