3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Incineration of PFAS including polymeric PFAS contributes to environmental levels.  PFAS are used in a variety of consumer products, building materials and other products that sooner or later ends up in the waste streams. Waste treatment in all forms (incineration, wastewater treatment including sludge and landfill) are all hot spots releasing PFAS to the environment. Methods to remove and mineralize PFAS in the waste treatment stream are under development, but the treatment will be costly and should only be seen as a decontamination measure, and not as an excuse to continue the use of PFAS.  Fluorinated polymers degrade to other PFAS in municipality waste incinerators, with release of both volatile and water soluble PFAS (Wahlström et al 2021, Winchell et al 2021, Brunn et al 2023, U.S. EPA 2020, Bakker et al 2021). In Swedish waste incinerations, PFAS were found in the fly ash (less than LOD – 37,7 µg/kg), bottom ash (less than LOD – 12,8 µg/kg) and condensate water (less than LOD – 183 ng/L), even at temperatures above 1100 °C (Strandberg et al 2021). PFCA precursors were the dominating PFAS-class in bottom ash, in fly ash PFSA precursors were the dominating PFAS and in condensate water it was PFCA.  Another study on full-scale waste incineration from Sweden, concluded that short PFAS (C4-C7) are most abundant in the emission and that addition of 5-8 % sludge increased the emissions four-fold (Björklund et al 2023). The most abundant PFAS in the flue gas was PFBA (2.6 and 3.4 ng/m3 respectively for with and without addition of sludge), while in the treated process water it was PFHxA (70 and 154 ng/L respectively). The thermal destruction methods available demand a high energy consumption and often release greenhouse gases and other non-wanted by products. One study that analyzed ultra-short PFAS during combustion of PFOS shows that hexafluoroethane (C2F6) and tetrafluoromethane (CF3) are formed, both strong greenhouse gases (GWP 12 000 and 5 700 respectively) and extremely long lived (Verma et al 2023).  The C-F bond is very strong and difficult to break. Krug et al showed that a temperature of 1400 °C is needed to reduce 95% of CF4, at 1300 °C only 89% was depleted (Krug et al 2021). The C-H and C-C bonds in PFAS molecules makes them much easier to incinerate, a reduction by more than 99% is shown for C2F6 at 1060 °C and CHF3 at 930 °C. Still these temperatures are higher than in municipality waste incineration, indicating that a substantial amount of ultra-short PFAS, with strong greenhouse gas potential, are generated from PFAS-containing waste even at high temperatures. Bakker et al conclude that PFAS present in household, municipal and industrial waste degrade into other substances when this waste is incinerated in compliance with the legal requirements for waste incineration plants in the Netherlands, and that the new PFAS formed are strong greenhouse gases such as perfluoromethane and perfluoroethane (Bakker et al 2021).  Garcia et al showed that incineration of PTFE at 850 °C and inert conditions, C2F4 and C3F6 were formed. At increasing oxygen ratios, C2F4 and C3F6 decreased while fluorocarbons like C2F6 and CF4 increased. At typical incineration temperatures of 850-1050 °C a large portion of the PTFE was converted to C2F6 (12,5-60,9 weight%) and CF4 (5,5-9,3 weight%), both strong greenhouse gases (Garcia et al 2007). Another study shows that PTFE degrades to other PFAS like PFOA and PFNA in overheating situations on the stove, that also could be applied to unintended fires or incomplete waste incineration (Schlummer et al 2015). Flue gas from both waste and industry can hence contribute to PFAS in the environment and to the climate change. Products containing PFAS must be clearly marked to ensure proper use and waste management. The waste from a product containing PFAS must be treated as hazardous waste to minimize the emissions from the end-of-life phase. Therefore, PFAS-containing materials and products are not suited for recycling. Transparency is a must to be able to handle PFAS containing products in the waste management and ensure that PFAS are not incorporated into recycled materials. For references, see attached document.

Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Derogations in the dossier The SSNC acknowledges that some derogations from the restriction are necessary where the PFAS substance is crucial for the product or process and no alternatives for the same function exist AND that the product/process is essential for society. It is nevertheless of uttermost importance that a derogation is allowed only when no alternatives fulfil the same function, and that the performance is left outside the derogation criteria. Performance may not be 100 % of what PFAS can offer, since the wanted qualities of PFAS are also what make them extremely problematic in the environment, but if the function is reached the alternative should be deemed a good alternative.    A derogation should only be given under certain criteria: 1. Full disclosure of use (substances and amounts) and emissions. 2. Products containing PFAS should be labelled, to enable consumers to make an informed choice and ensure proper waste management. 3. Use case specific requirements for zero emission to the environment and zero exposure to workers, since the extreme persistency will allow even low levels of emissions to build up in the environment/human body. 4. Extended product responsibility, to ensure that the waste is treated responsibly, without any emissions. In particular, derogations for use of PFAS in protective wear must be made with cautionary rules, since exposure is difficult to avoid. Workers using and handling them must be informed and monitored. The washing of protective wear needs to be handled with zero emissions.

General Comments: The tank container fleet of 800,000 units, also commonly referred to as ISO tanks, operates in the global trade, safely  transporting liquids and liquified gases in bulk, most of which are classified as dangerous goods or are otherwise potentially hazardous.

Sealing element materials must provide a range of technical properties that ensure the materials function as reliable and safe containment of liquids and liquified gases. Fluoropolymers are widely used because of the proven properties of chemical resistance, temperature range, durability, shrinkage, and vibration resistance, and cutting and machining qualities.

It is paramount to maintain safety and leak-tightness tank containers. The consultation process is requested to recognise the importance of the tank container to the safety and efficiency of transport and grant an indefinite derogation for the use of fluoropolymer sealing elements.

However, there are certain situations where some alternative sealing elements might be usable with some of the substances being carried and in specific equipment applications, but alternative materials present risks.  For example, a fibrous material might be used as a gasket to seal the face between two flanges, but the material cannot be used in the manufacture of an “O” ring. In addition to being less reliable as a sealing gasket, fibrous material may become saturated with the dangerous substance transported in the tank e.g., a toxic chemical. The gasket would need to need to be handled by personnel undertaking maintenance, thus adding a health and safety issue along with an additional environmental disposal risk.  The restriction of fluoropolymers for manufacturing sealing materials would require a significant increase in the number of seals and gasket used manufactured for because alternative materials will not achieve the same range of substance compatibility and durable life expectancy. If a fluoropolymer sealing element is fitted abroad it might need to be replaced in Europe and adding to waste disposal.  Fundamentally, the chemical transportation industry is not able to cope with this dramatic change. It might cause a reduction in available cargo carrying capacity and an increase in costs. The material is not a viable like-for-like replacement because, as with all alternative materials, it is required by the tank approval regulations to undergo extensive type testing and field testing. Additionally, PVC-U may not be suitable due to the potential to emit corrosive chlorine gas which can cause chloride stress corrosion cracking in austenitic stainless steels, which is the material used for the tank and valve construction. PVC also contains SVHC which is likely to be restricted by environmental regulations.  6E3 Polypropylene  Polypropylene has a slightly wider temperature range of -10°C to +80°C but still not sufficient to satisfy most of our industry applications. Polypropylene has a wide chemical resistance at ambient temperature, but its chemical resistance reduces with increased temperature particularly with strong inorganic acids.  6E4 Elastomeric compounds  Some Silicone grades have a temperature range of -55°C to +300°C and can be used within sealing elements in certain applications but are not resistant to many of the chemicals transported including most solvents and Hydrochloric or Hydrofluoric acids. The lack of hardness also restricts the use of these material for some sealing elements. Elastomeric compounds such as silicone, nitrile, and neoprene, can also be regarded as bio-accumulative and toxic to the environment.  6E5 Natural Rubber  Natural rubber compounds provide elastic recovery properties and resist vibration. The material is  water-resistant as well as being tolerant to alcohols, acids and alkalis. There are limited applications for the material.         6 F  SUBSTITUTION IS TECHNICALLY AND ECONOMICALLY FEASIBLE but more time is required to substitute:  The tank container industry is a downstream user of flouropolymers and discussion with chemical manufacturers has offered no suitable alternative for future generation tank containers    6 G SUBSTITUTION IS NOT TECHNICALLY OR ECONOMICALLY FEASIBLE  information on what the socio-economic impacts would be for companies, consumers, and other affected actors. There are sealing elements, used for access hatches, that are  manufacture of a braided fibrous material with a PTFE coating which could be vulnerable to degradation, but preventative action is being taken to a) dispose only as licenced industrial waste and more importantly b) phase out the use of this sealing design.

General Comments: The TensiNet Association stands as a prominent force within the realm of membrane structures, bringing together professionals from various fields such as design, architecture, engineering, manufacturing, supply, and installation. This esteemed association operates primarily on a European scale, while also functioning worldwide, fostering collaboration, knowledge exchange, and innovation in the domain of tensioned membrane constructions. Through its diverse membership base and extensive expertise, TensiNet plays a pivotal role in advancing the development, understanding, and implementation of these unique architectural marvels.

Background:

The initial TensiNet project (2001-04) has been funded by the European Commission for three years. The consortium of TensiNet consisted of 22 participating organisations with representatives from 9 EU member states. The membership formed a complementary group representing multi-disciplinary industries (coater and weaver, manufacturer, producer, engineering and architecture offices), universities and other associations.
Within the thematic programme GROWTH (Promoting Competitive and Sustainable Growth) the partners made the knowledge of their specific domain available and exchanged know-how between different disciplines.
The publication of the first “European Design Guide for Tensile Surface Structures” (B. Forster, M. Mollaert (Eds.), European design guide for tensile surface structures, TensiNet Association, Brussel, 2004) was the result of these three years of assembling, structuring and analysing existing knowledge and data.

Mission/Aim:

The TensiNet Association is driven by the mission to empower its members to make meaningful contributions within their respective activities in the field of tensile membrane buildings. The association focuses on several key objectives to achieve this aim:
1. Providing Information and Advice in the field of tensile membrane buildings
2. Supporting Research and Technical Studies
3. Bridging the Gap between Research and Practice
4. Enhancing the Quality of Tensile Membrane Buildings
5. Expanding Architectural Applications
6. Facilitating the Translation of Scientific Results into Practice
7. Stimulating Research Initiatives

The association facilitates the exchange of information and encourages joint working among its members, creating a supportive network that enhances the overall quality of tensile architecture.

Objectives:

The TensiNet Association creates a platform for all parties interested in tensioned membrane structures.
TensiNet supports teaching, workshops and training activities in the field of tensioned membrane construction and provides information about these events.
TensiNet publishes the TensiNews newsletter twice a year. TensiNet organises every three year the TensiNet Symposium.
TensiNet continues to publish reference documents, Working Group publications and the proceedings of the TensiNet symposium.
TensiNet has launched several Working Groups (WG Sustainability and Comfort, WG Pneumatic structures, WG Specifications and EUROCODE, WG Specifications GOOD PRACTICE etc.). Each Working Group focuses on a specific topic and is responsible for its operation.
TensiNet maintains the website www.tensinet.com, containing a projects database, reference documents, research reports etc.

With respect to the PFAS Restriction Proposal, the TensiNet Association supports the statements and replies made by
o its members:
• Membrane and foil producers, coating and weaving companies: Sioen, AGC and Chukoh Chemical Industries
• Tensile architecture manufacturers and fabricators: Taiyo Europe GmbH and Vector Foiltec
o the Industrieverband Kunststoffbahnen e.V. (IVK Europe, answer uploaded 7/9, reference e6fabaeb-86f0-4292-aa5f-dc946e348491) representing Sioen, Mehler Texnologies, Sattler, Serge Ferrari and Verseidag,
o the FluoroPolymer Product Group (FPG, see https://fluoropolymers.eu/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/FPG-DRAFT-REACH-Restriction-Consultation-Response_FINAL.pdf) with member AGC.
For detailed information the TensiNet Association refers to their replies.

The TensiNet Association requests an exemption of all fluoropolymers from the PFAS Restriction Proposal under the REACH regulation.
By grouping all various PFAS substances together and restricting them as a single class, the PFAS Restriction Proposal would restrict numerous PFAS substances that have not been risk-assessed and for which no unacceptable risk has been demonstrated.

For now, there are no alternatives at hand and the restriction would mean the end of lightweight tensile structures in Europe.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Construction products / Architectural membranes and ETFE foils Membrane structures, also known as tensile surface structures or fabric structures, are architectural constructions that utilize flexible membranes ((un-)coated fabrics or foils) to create self-supporting roofs, canopies, and other types of enclosures (Ignasi de Llorens J. (Ed.), 2015, Fabric Structures in Architecture, Woodhead Publishing, Cambridge). These structures derive their strength and stability from the tension forces exerted in the surface (Stranghöner, N., Uhlemann, J., Bilginoglu, F., Bletzinger, K.-U., Bögner-Balz, H., Corne, E., Gibson, N., Gosling, P., Houtman, R., Llorens, J., Malinowsky, M., Marion, J.-M., Mollaert, M., Nieger, M., Novati, G., Sahnoune, F., Siemens, P., Stimpfle, B., Tanev, V., Thomas, J.-Ch., Prospect for European guidance for the Structural Design of Tensile Membrane Structures: Support to the implementation, harmonization and further development of the Eurocodes, JRC Science and Policy Report, European Commission, Joint Research Centre, Editors: M. Mollaert, S. Dimova, A. Pinto, St. Denton, EUR 31430 EN, European Union, 2023), which is typically made of materials like:  (1) PVC-coated polyester,  (2) PTFE-coated fiberglass, or  (3) ETFE and other films (more than 1500 buildings erected worldwide). (Gabler M., Cremers J., Knippers J., Lienhard J., 2010, Atlas Kunststoffe + Membranen: Werkstoffe und Halbzeuge, Formfindung und Konstruktion, De Gruyter; Detail, Berlin, München. Gabler M., Cremers J., Knippers J., Lienhard J., 2011, Construction Manual for Polymers + Membranes, Birkhäuser GmbH, Basel, ISBN: 3034607261) Advantages of membranes structures include:  - Lightweight: Membranes are significantly lighter than traditional building materials such as steel or concrete. This property allows for easier transportation, reduced foundation requirements, and overall cost savings (Monticelli C., Zanelli A., 2021, Material saving and building component efficiency as main eco-design principles for membrane architecture: case-studies of ETFE enclosures, Architectural Engineering and Design Management 17 (3-4), 264-280). Due to the ‘lightweight principle’ and the ‘lightweight nature of the cladding material’ the corresponding substructure can be significantly optimized leading to minimal quantities for the structure that is associated to a significant reduced carbon footprint / grey emissions of the building (Göppert K., Paech C., 2015, High-performance materials in façade design. Structural membranes used in the building envelope in Steel Construction, n. 8, No. 4, pp. 237-243). - Versatility of design: The flexible nature of membrane materials enables architects and designers to create unique and innovative shapes and forms that are challenging to achieve with conventional construction methods. Membrane structures offer great design freedom and aesthetic appeal (Xu J., Zhang Y., Yu Q., Zhang L., Analysis and design of fabric membrane structures: A systematic review on material and structural performance, Thin-Walled Structures 170 (2022) 108619; Zanelli A., Monticelli C., Mollaert M., 2021, Sustainable innovation in minimal mass structures and lightweight architectures, Architectural Engineering and Design Management 17 (3-4), 167-168; Forster B., Mollaert M. (Eds.), European design guide for tensile surface structures, TensiNet Association, Brussel, 2004). - Natural lighting: Membrane materials can be translucent or transparent, allowing natural light to penetrate the building. This feature reduces the need for artificial lighting during the day, resulting in energy savings and a more pleasant indoor environment (Forster B., Mollaert M. (Eds.), European design guide for tensile surface structures, TensiNet Association, Brussel, 2004). - Cost-effective: Compared to traditional construction, membrane structures can be more cost-effective due to reduced material requirements, shorter construction times, and simplified foundations. They can provide an economical solution for various applications. - Quick construction: Membrane structures are often prefabricated off-site, allowing for rapid installation and construction. This aspect makes them ideal for temporary or semi-permanent structures, public space canopies, event venues, and disaster relief shelters (Ignasi de Llorens J. (Ed.), 2015, Fabric Structures in Architecture, Woodhead Publishing, Cambridge). - Durability and weather resistance: High-quality membrane materials are designed to withstand challenging weather conditions such as wind, rain, and snow. They are often treated to be fire-resistant and UV-stable, ensuring long-term performance and reduced maintenance requirements (Beck P., 2021, Zum zeit- und temperaturabhängigen Werkstoffverhalten von Ethylen/Tetrafluorethylen—Folien im Hochbau - On time- and temperature-dependent material behaviour of ethylene—tetrafluoroethylene foiIs in building construction, Darmstadt, PhD- dissertation, Technische Universität Darmstadt, https://tuprints.ulb.tu-darmstadt,de/id/eprint/18560; Philip M., Al-Azzawi F., Effects of Natural and Artificial Weathering on the Physical Properties of Recycled Poly(ethylene terephthalate), J Polym Environ 26 (2018) 3139–3148; Mailler P., Nemoz G., Hamelin P., Long Term Behavior Characterization of Coated Fabrics for Architecture Membrane under Biaxial Loading, Journal of Coated Fabrics 26 (2016) 323–333, João L.S., Carvalho R., Fangueiro R., A Study on the Durability Properties of Textile Membranes for Architectural Purposes, Procedia Engineering 155 (2016) 230–237; Dezső Hegyi K.H., Long-term analysis of prestressed membrane structures, Journal of Computational and Applied Mechanics, 6 (2005) 219–235). - Sustainability: Membrane structures have the potential to be environmentally friendly. They require fewer materials, generate less waste during construction, and can be dismantled and reused in other projects. Coated fabrics or printed foils provide shade. The translucent membranes contribute to energy efficiency by reducing the need for artificial lighting (Monticelli C. et al., Life cycle assessment of textile façades, beyond the current cladding systems, Tensinet Symposium 2013 [Re]thinking lightweight structures, Proceedings, Mimar Sinan Fine-Art University, Istanbul, May 2013, 467-476; Monticelli C., Environmental assessment of ultralight roof structures built with new materials: the case of the ETFE cushions, Proceedings of IASS WG18 Colloquium, 2010; Tim C. R. Finlay, 2021, The Carbon Footprint of Long Span Structures: Review of the Millennium Dome and Subsequent Tensile Systems, Proceedings of the IASS Annual Symposium 2020/21 and the 7th International Conference on Spatial Structures, Inspiring the Next Generation, 23 – 27 August 2021, Guilford, UK, S.A. Behnejad, G.A.R. Parke and O.A. Samavati (eds.); Eryuruk, Z., & Mollaert, M. (2023, Apr), Canopy Wolke Marienfeld: Comparing the environmental performance of a short use, a reusable and a permanent membrane structure, (Newsletter Nr. 44 ed.) TensiNet Association; Eryuruk, Z., Mollaert, M., Van Hemelrijck, D., & De Laet, L. (2023, June), The environmental performance of membrane structure: OCMW Zoutleeuw case study, In Proceedings of the TensiNet Symposium 2023 TENSINANTES2023 (pp. 367-379); Cremers J., Environmental Impact of Membrane Materials and Structures – Status Quo., Tensinet Symposium 2013 [Re]thinking lightweight structures, Proceedings, Mimar Sinan Fine-Art University, Istanbul, May 2013, 447-456; Chilton J., Pezeshzadeh S., Afrin S., Embodied energy in ETFE foil construction, Tensinet Symposium 2013 [Re]thinking lightweight structures, Proceedings, Mimar Sinan Fine-Art University, Istanbul, May 2013, 457-466).  Membrane structures find applications in a wide range of industries and sectors due to their versatility, lightweight nature, and aesthetic appeal. Some common applications include (see also Rene Motro (Ed.), Flexible Composite Materials in Architecture, Construction and Interiors, Birkhäuser 2011): 1. Architectural Roofs and Canopies: Membrane structures are used in stadiums, convention centres, outdoor theatres, and shopping centres. They provide weather protection while creating visually striking spaces. 2. Exhibition and Event Spaces: Membrane structures are frequently employed as temporary or semi-permanent exhibition spaces, trade show pavilions, and event venues. They offer quick installation, flexibility in design, and can be easily customized to fit specific event requirements. 3. Transportation Facilities: Membrane structures are utilized in transportation infrastructure, including airport terminals, train stations, and bus terminals. 4. Sports Facilities: Membrane structures are used for tennis courts, swimming pool covers, indoor sports arenas, and practice fields. Their lightweight construction allows for clear-span spaces without columns, providing unobstructed views for spectators. 5. Commercial and Industrial Buildings: Membrane structures are employed for warehouses, storage facilities, manufacturing units, and distribution centres. 6. Hospitals: Transparent ETFE foils cover inner areas for surgery with (better cleaning and no bacteria). Membrane structures are used as roof systems and shade nets provide sun protection. 7. Environmental Structures: Membrane structures are used in environmental applications such as greenhouse covers, botanical gardens, zoos, and aviaries. They create controlled environments, allowing for optimal growth of plants or providing appropriate habitats for various species. 8. Military and Disaster Relief Shelters: Membrane structures are utilized in military applications as temporary barracks, command centres, or hangars. 9. Cultural and Recreational Facilities: Membrane structures are utilized in cultural and recreational projects such as museums, art installations, theme parks, and amphitheatres. They provide visually appealing spaces that enhance the visitor experience. 10. Educational Facilities: Membrane structures are employed as school playground covers, outdoor classrooms, and shade structures. They create comfortable and functional spaces. 11. Residential Structure: Membrane structures are used in residential applications as patio covers, shade sails, carports, and pergolas.  These are just a few examples of the diverse applications of membrane structures. Their lightweight, durable, and customizable nature makes them suitable for a wide range of architectural, commercial, and industrial projects.  The tendencies in architecture are going towards the relation of shapes of facades with the thermal and acoustic properties to reach the Net Zero Carbon request within 2023 /2050 and that lightweight and membrane-based building systems facilitate promising solutions to get more efficient and less-impacting building structures, due to the lightness. Beside an impact quantified around 14-30% (table 1 of use-phase of Construction products Table 1 of the annex XV restriction report), the end of the production of membranes for lightweight construction -  in comparison with its PFAS part of impact  -  will have the counter effect to stop the most promising research projects aimed at developing new membrane-based products, and consequently it will bring a detriment of the technological advancement of the entire construction sector, for which academics (on architecture, design and construction fields), public/private research institutions, companies, categories’ associations, architectural and engineering design societies and studios dedicated years of research, human resources and fundings and their activities have been in many cases financed by EU and national/regional fundings with demonstrated and recognized results.  For more literature references see Annex I.

(1) PVC-coated PVDF-top-coated polyester fabric: PVDF, providing protection for PVC, allows to improve the durability of the PVC-coated polyester fabric to 25 years or more (instead of 10 years). (2) PTFE-coated glass fabric: this is considered as an indispensable material for building roofs, especially large-span stadia. Taking the Tensinet Association as a representative group for Europe, it covers • Membrane and foil producers, coating and weaving companies: 11  • Tensile architecture manufacturers and fabricators: 36 • Architecture and engineering offices: 40 • Software companies and products: 4 • Steelwork and ropes producers: 2 • Universities: 21 • Other: 3  To get the opinion of the TensiNet members, the following was published on www.tensinet.com: Statement PFAS restriction:  The TensiNet Association, promoting the quality of tensile surface structures since 2000, formulates the following statement with respect to the PFAS restriction proposal:  For more than half a century, structural membranes, including PTFE-coated glass fabric, PVC-coated (with PVDF-top-coat) polyester fabric, ETFE-foils, and other variants, have found widespread use. These Fluoropolymers are classified as Polymers of Low Concern (PLC) (see Barbara J Henry, Joseph P Carlin, Jon A Hammerschmidt, Robert C Buck, L William Buxton, Heidelore Fiedler, Jennifer Seed, Oscar Hernandez, A critical review of the application of polymer of low concern and regulatory criteria to fluoropolymers, Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management, 2018). Bio-based Polymers: Bio-based polymers, such as polylactic acid (PLA) and polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs), are derived from renewable resources and are biodegradable. General Comments: The Toxics Use Reduction Institute (TURI) respectfully submits these comments to the European Chemicals Agency as input on their PFAS restriction proposal regarding electronics and semiconductor manufacturing. TURI is an independent government agency established by the Commonwealth of Massachusetts in the U.S. to help implement the state’s Toxics Use Reduction Act, assisting businesses with the transition to safer alternatives to hazardous substances.  We offer the following information based on our research and experience around the development and assessment of safer alternatives to PFAS chemistries. We are addressing one specific PFAS use in the manufacturing of electronics – as surfactants in etching solutions.
In addition to information on specific alternatives to PFAS, TURI would also like to offer information about methods we have found to be successful to facilitate the transition to safer alternatives.  TURI and our partner agency, The Office of Technical Assistance and Technology, assist manufacturing facilities in assessing their existing processes and materials, and examining alternatives that will reduce their use of toxic substances.  Where no feasible and safer options are available, TURI will connect university researchers to businesses, funding them to develop new solutions and materials. This partnership combines 1) TURI’s expertise in safer chemicals and assessing alternatives, 2) academic researchers’ deep expertise in chemistry and materials, and 3) businesses’ understanding of the technical and economic feasibility of their manufacturing processes and products.  TURI adds modest funding, project management, and communication assistance to spread the results to other businesses.  We have found this model to be successful in many instances, including the situation described here of identifying, testing, and commercializing safer surfactants for an electronics chemicals manufacturer.  The business owner has repeatedly said that the successful substitution would not have happened without this three-way collaboration and the funding provided by TURI.  We see tremendous opportunity to apply this model to the significant challenges presented by PFAS and its many discrete uses, and encourage ECHA to consider how this might be replicated on a larger scale to ensure the timely development and implementation of safer alternatives.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: The Toxics Use Reduction Institute (TURI) respectfully submits these comments to the European Chemicals Agency as input on their PFAS restriction proposal regarding semiconductors and electronics.  TURI is an independent government agency established in 1989 by the Commonwealth of Massachusetts to help implement the state’s Toxics Use Reduction Act, assisting businesses with the transition to safer alternatives to hazardous substances. TURI offers the following information based on research and experience around the assessment of alternatives, including their hazards, as businesses in Massachusetts face potential restrictions on products containing PFAS. TURI is pleased to share our experience in finding viable alternatives to PFAS in the electronics industry, specifically semiconductor production.  TURI’s objective is to provide holistic and objective information about available alternatives to assist EU Member States in crafting an appropriate PFAS restriction and businesses in assessing their alternatives.    This comment provides a brief overview of TURI’s experience with a collaborative research project with University of Massachusetts Lowell (UML) researchers and Transene Company (Transene), a manufacturer of chemical formulations for semiconductor and electronics processing.  Transene wanted to substitute PFAS-based surfactants in etching formulations with safer surfactants but needed assistance. In September 2021, a research project was initiated with the technical and financial assistance of TURI.   In less than two years, for a total investment of less than $50,000, researchers were able identify, develop and implement the near complete substitution of PFAS-based surfactants to a safer, non-PFAS alternative by Transene and over 90% its customers.  Below is a summary of the project and key observations. Further detailed information about this research is provided in the attached peer reviewed article:  "Safer and effective alternatives to perfluoroalkyl-based surfactants in etching solutions for the semiconductor industry;" (Sharma, et al 2023).  https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0959652623020371  • Surfactants based on PFAS such as fluoroalkyl sulfonamide, fluoroalkyl sulfonyl amino propane sulfonic acid, and potassium perfluorooctane sulfonate surfactants are widely used in etching solutions within the semiconductor industry to improve the wetting characteristics of the etchant and substrates. They are used because of their robust performance characteristics, including excellent stability in strongly acidic, alkaline, and oxidizing etching solutions.   • An interdisciplinary team of researchers at TURI and UML followed a methodology to identify and evaluate safer alternative surfactants using performance criteria provided by Transene, which were later validated experimentally. Transene produces multiple types of etching solutions, so significant testing was required. The etching solutions evaluated included tetramethyl ammonium hydroxide (TMAH), perchloric acid/ceric ammonium nitrate aqueous solution (chrome), ammonium hydrogen fluoride solution, or buffered oxide etchant (BOE) and a mixture of phosphoric, acetic, and nitric acid etchant (PAN).    • The researchers evaluated Hydrophilic-Lipophilic Balance (HLB) values, critical micelle concentrations (CMC), formulation compatibility, surface tension measurements, surface free energy, and contact angle measurements to determine the wetting characteristics of etchants on substrates of interest to the semiconductor industry. The substrates included in the testing were photoresist-coated silicon wafers, aluminum oxide-coated and chromium-coated silicon wafers, as well as glass substrates.  Once promising formulations were identified in the lab, industrial trials were performed using a quality-tracking method with consumers of Transene’s etching solutions, semiconductor manufacturers. The success of these industrial trials validated prototypes and greatly facilitated the drop-in substitution of PFAS-based surfactants with safer surfactants in etching solutions currently used by the semiconductor industry.    • The alternative surfactants evaluated were alkyl polyglucosides (trade names BG10 and CG50) and polyoxyethylene surfactants (trade names Brij35 and BrijS100).  Biobased alkyl polyglucoside surfactant (BG10) was selected as the preferred alternative in TMAH and PAN applications, while CG50 was the less toxic alternative in BOE etching solutions to replace PFAS based Novec4200 and Novec 4300 PFAS surfactants. Polyoxyethylene surfactants (Brij 35 and Brij S100) were determined to be less toxic alternatives for PFAS based FC95 in the chrome etching solution.   • Toxicity comparisons were conducted using TURI’s P2OASys chemical hazard assessment tool.  The comparisons indicated that these alternative surfactants are less hazardous for chronic human health effects than the PFAS surfactants.   • These safer alternatives have now been successfully implemented by over 90% of Transene’s customers in industries such as radio frequency and microwave chips, lasers, aerospace, and defense.  These companies have provided positive feedback with no reported deleterious effects on the final products. The remaining 10% of customers typically were larger companies where internal validation cycles were longer.  It is anticipated by Transene that the remaining customers will adopt the safer surfactants by the end of 2023.  • This successful approach opens new possibilities for the replacement of PFAS in numerous other commercial applications where PFAS is commonly used as a surfactant. It shows the power of a motivated company working with university researchers while supported by modest grants to innovate, quickly finding safer alternative and viable solutions to the use of PFAS. This research project was conducted with one company but has benefited many downstream users of their chemical product.  The project also could have been done with a consortium of electronics manufacturers, both within and across the electronics supply chain.  • TURI has also found that the formation of supply chain workgroups is a powerful tool to promote the development, testing and adoption of safer alternatives.  These workgroups include the collaboration of manufacturers throughout the supply chain, and are particularly effective where there are significant drivers to phase out a chemical use. The following are two successful examples of this supply chain approach: 1) Lead used for solder materials, printed circuit board surface finishes, and component finishes in the electronics industry.  In this case, there was a regulatory driver with the 2003 passage of the EU Restriction of Hazardous Substances (RoHS) directive. 2) Hexavalent chromium used for corrosion protection for various coating products such as bond primers, sealants, and conversion coatings in the aerospace and defense industry.  In this case, the market/customer driver was the 2011 Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation mandated by the U.S. Department of Defense to restrict the usage of hexavalent chromium.  In general, companies in the aerospace/defense industry have begun to adopt hexavalent chromium-free alternatives for certain applications of sealant and bond primer products.  The research on hexavalent chromium-free alternatives for conversion coatings remains ongoing as adoption by the aerospace/defense industry has been challenging.  For both the lead free and hexavalent chromium free supply chain workgroups, the sharing of the costs and resources among numerous companies throughout a supply chain helped to accelerate the identification, evaluation, and adoption of safer alternatives.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: The Toxics Use Reduction Institute (TURI) respectfully submits these comments to the European Chemicals Agency as input on their PFAS restriction proposal regarding fluorinated gases (F-gases). TURI is an independent government agency established in 1989 by the Commonwealth of Massachusetts to help implement the state’s Toxics Use Reduction Act, assisting businesses with the transition to safer alternatives to hazardous substances. TURI offers the following information based on research and experience around the assessment of alternatives, including their hazards, as businesses in Massachusetts face potential restrictions on products containing hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) and Per- and polyfluorinated alkyl substances (PFAS). TURI addresses F-gas concerns in Heating, Ventilation, Air Conditioning, and Refrigeration (HVACR) and shares data gathered about potential alternatives to HFCs and other F-gasses. TURI’s objective is to provide holistic and objective information about available alternatives, particularly the newer generation of refrigeration options, to assist EU Member States in crafting an appropriate PFAS restriction and businesses in assessing their alternatives.

The term “regrettable substitute” is used when an industry or society goes through an effort to eliminate a problematic chemical and switches to another chemistry or technology but then finds that the alternative is no safer than the original chemical.

Given recent technological progress and proven instances of success, the potential exists to completely transition from F-gas HVACR systems to alternative, non-fluorinated refrigerants. TURI carefully evaluated the substitution of HFCs with HFO refrigerants and has concerns based on the evidence of environmental hazards, such as their effective Global Warming Potential (GWP) and the likelihood of PFAS pollution throughout the lifecycle of HFOs.

For example, TURI believes that Figure B.41 of the Annex XV Restriction Report – PFAS is incomplete. There is evidence on the conversion of trifluoro acetaldehyde (CF3CHO; CAS number: 75-90-1) into HFC-23 (Fluoroform or Trifluoromethane; CHF3; GWP100=14800; CAS number: 75-46-7), with a GWP100 of 14,800.  In addition, there is evidence to suggest trifluoroacetic acid (CF3COOH; CAS number: 76-05-1) also converts into HFC-23 (fluoroform or trifluoromethane; CHF3; GWP100=14800; CAS number: 75-46-7). These pathways warrant consideration in the context of the proposed PFAS restriction.

The references provided herein are salient in an assessment of F-gas alternatives, in particular with respect to the hazard comparison of F-gas-based HVACR systems to non-fluorinated alternatives, and similar information was not observed in the current version of the EU’s Annex XV restriction report. TURI is pleased to share this information with you as you consider your restriction proposal.

Key points:
+ HFOs are potentially regrettable substitutes for HFCs.
+ The effective GWP of HFOs may be higher than regulatory thresholds because of their potential degradation into HFC-23 (trifluoromethane; HFC-23; GWP100=14800; CAS number: 75-46-7).
+ HFOs are often blended with HFCs to reduce the ‘average GWP’, which is a problematic indicator of GWP and progress toward climate mitigation objectives.
+ The patented pathways to produce the HFO refrigerants involve the use (and likely leakage) of Carcinogenic, Mutagenic, and Reprotoxic (CMR) chemicals and the production of PFAS as byproducts.
+ Heating, Ventilation, Air Conditioning, and Refrigeration (HVACR) equipment with non-fluorinated refrigerants are available on the market today at reasonable costs, and are safer than their fluorinated counterparts, including for Ultra Low Temperature (ULT) refrigeration.
+ Newer CO2, hydrocarbon (HC) and HC/CO2 designs present significant operating cost savings over F-gas systems.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: TURI offers information based on our research and experience around hazards, and alternatives to the application of fluorinated gases, including HFCs and HFOs, in:  • Annex E.2.8.: Heating, Ventilation, Air Conditioning, and Refrigeration (HVACR) systems. Sub-uses: Domestic refrigeration; Commercial and industrial refrigeration; Specialist applications: Low temperature refrigeration below -50⁰C; Refrigerants in laboratory test and measurement equipment; Refrigerants in refrigerated centrifuges.  • Annex E.2.10.: Transport refrigeration; Mobile air conditioning (MAC), excluding aircraft and military use.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The lifecycle of the HFO refrigerant family involves the use (and likely leakage) of known Carcinogenic, Mutagenic, and Reprotoxic (CMR) chemicals as precursors, as well as use and formation of HFCs:   Carbon tetrachloride (CTC) [1], perchloroethylene (PCE) [2], and HFCs [3] are precursors in the production of HFOs, and PFAS are by-products [4].   EPA determined that CTC presents an unreasonable risk [5] to workers from long-term inhalation and dermal exposures and liver toxicity from short-term dermal exposure, and has proposed risk management measures including an existing chemical exposure limit (ECEL) of 0.03 ppm as an 8-hour time-weighted average (TWA) [6]. This illustrates the concerns raised about the production phase of the HFO lifecycle in our alternatives assessment.  Comment on Figure B.41 of the Annex XV Restriction Report – PFAS:  There is scientific literature on various HFO degradation mechanisms pointing to the production of the high global warming HFC-23 (trifluoromethane or fluoroform; GWP100 = 14800; CAS number: 75-46-7) [7]. HFO-1234ze(E) is described in the literature as degrading quickly and quantitatively into trifluoro acetaldehyde (TFE; CF3CHO; trifluoroethanal; CAS number: 75-90-1) [8]. Similarly, studies describe that one molecule of HFO-1336mzz(E) produces one molecule of TFE and one molecule of TFA, quantitatively [8].  TFE is a well-known photochemical precursor of HFC-23 [7] in environmental conditions [9]. HFC-23 formation from TFE is not represented in the Figure B.41 of the Annex XV Restriction Report on PFAS. HFO-1234yf and HFO-1225ye quantitatively produce trifluoroacetic acid (CF3COOH; TFA; CAS number: 76-05-1) by oxidation in atmospheric conditions [8,10–12].  Although TFA is known for its chemical stability, it is not expected to remain intact indefinitely and may degrade into HFC-23 through diverse pathways (e.g.: [13,14]). These pathways for HFC-23 formation from TFA are not represented in the Figure B.41 of the Annex XV Restriction Report on PFAS. Given the above, TURI believes that the Annex XV Restriction Report on PFAS is missing important potential HFO degradation pathways. The potential degradation of HFOs to HFC-23 via TFE and TFA should be represented in Figure B.41, and these pathways warrant consideration in the context of the proposed PFAS restriction. The effective GWP of HFOs could be higher than regulatory thresholds, depending on the likelihood of them forming HFC-23.   While the Global Warming Potential (GWP) metric does not usually contemplate the greenhouse effect of degradation compounds, the effective GWP does consider GHG gas generation during environmental fate. There is evidence to suggest that commercially available HFOs, although having a low atmospheric lifetime, could decompose to HFC-23 (trifluoro methane or fluoroform; CHF3; GWP100 = 14800; CAS number: 75-46-7), increasing their effective GWP in a proportion worthy of consideration [7,9].  The eventual formation of HFC-23, with its very high GWP, undermines the climate change mitigation objective of phasing down HFC use globally under the Kigali Amendment of the Montreal Protocol. Therefore, HFOs may potentially be a regrettable substitute for HFCs in HVACR systems.   Many applications that use HFOs require blending with HFCs, with problematic hazards for toxicity, flammability, and the climate. With the exception of mobile air conditioning (MAC), pure HFOs have limited standalone applications, mostly serving as components in refrigerant mixtures with high GWP HFCs to reduce the ‘average GWP’ and the flammability of HFOs. These mixtures act as substitutes for R134a and R410a (both HFCs) refrigerants, retrofitting stationary AC, MAC, and heat pump units.  The use of ‘average GWP,’ as in the case of high-GWP HFC/HFO blends, misrepresents the hazard presented to the climate as it does not factor HFO degradation products into its calculus or prevent high-GWP HFCs emissions. In our view, more careful consideration is needed regarding the potential use of these PFAS to achieve climate change mitigation objectives [15–17]. Moreover, to mitigate the flammability risks of HFOs, companies are commercializing low-‘average GWP’ HFO blends with high-GWP HFC refrigerants. However, no commercial HFO/HFC blend classified as A1 also complies with a GWP lower than 450, while the GWP threshold for most applications is set at 150 [18]. HFOs such as R-1234yf are just slightly less flammable (A2L) than HCs [19] and produce highly toxic hydrogen fluoride (HF) and carbonyl fluoride (COF2) when burned [20–22], posing a serious risk to fire rescue teams. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Transformative technological progress and proven demonstration of success give us reason to see potential to completely transition away from F-gas HVACR systems to alternative, non-fluorinated refrigerants, including ultra-low temperature refrigeration. TURI has carefully evaluated HFOs and is very concerned with the evidence of significant environmental impact. HFOs may be regrettable substitutes to HFCs due to their elevated effective Global Warming Potential (GWP) and the likelihood of subsequent PFAS pollution.   Heating, Ventilation, Air Conditioning, and Refrigeration (HVACR) equipment with non-fluorinated refrigerants are available on the market today at reasonable costs, and are safer than their fluorinated counterparts, including for Ultra Low Temperature (ULT) refrigeration.  TURI’s assessment found that refrigerants such as carbon dioxide (CO2), ammonia (NH3), and hydrocarbons (HCs) can be efficiently implemented. Technological improvements have addressed historical concerns, such as the cooling capacity of CO2, corrosion from the use of CO2 and NH3, NH3 toxicity, and flammability of HCs [23–27].   The rising cost of new F-gas refrigerants is challenging the HVACR industry. HFOs are more expensive than HFCs [23]. However, high GWP refrigerants are capped for production and import in OECD countries, which caused a rise in their prices, partially explaining the competitiveness of HFOs and HFO/HFC blends to HFCs. R-32 is the only SNAP-approved HFC, being among the cheapest on the market. However, its GWP is higher than most of the oncoming regulatory thresholds, and its use is limited to retrofitting industrial equipment difficult to replace on short notice.  In this context, NH3, CO2 and HCs are becoming competitive. Commercial refrigeration equipment manufacturing based on hydrocarbons has reached economy of scale [25]. The price of refrigerant-grade HCs is comparable with novel HFOs, except that the equipment that works with HCs is designed to minimize the required refrigerant charge for safety purposes. CO2 (R-744) is the safest refrigerant gas, also offered at a very low cost. Ammonia is the cheapest and most abundant refrigerant, the main driver for its industrial applications.  Many HVACR manufacturing leaders are converting their sales portfolio to entirely non-fluorinated products by 2027 [23,26]. Specialized start-ups are successfully increasing their Market Readiness Level (MRL) to capitalize on the demand for systems using non-fluorinated refrigerants [28].  Equipment modernization could account for increasing in energy efficiency by 50%, expediting payback periods of new equipment acquisition by reducing energy use and related CO2 emissions. Strategic design improvement opportunities are: • The compressor is the heart of a vapor compression cycle. A more efficient compression can reduce CO2e emissions by up to 20% [29]. • The condenser is the part of the system that transfers heat from the refrigerant to the environment. Efficient condensers reduce energy usage about 15% [30]. • The evaporator is the part of the system that extracts heat from the environment. A more efficient evaporator can increase the intrinsic performance of the system by up to 10% [31].  • Integrating heat recovery systems greatly reduces heating costs and space demand [32,33], particularly for equipment operating with CO2.  Ammonia (R-717) is the most efficient refrigerant of choice for various industrial applications with typical cooling capacities above 1 MW. While new Ultra Low Charge (ULC) ammonia refrigeration systems are significantly more efficient and result in less risk to workers than traditional ammonia systems [27], leading us to consider them as favorable alternatives, it is crucial to recognize that the acute toxic hazard persists. EPA-SNAP authorizes new ULT equipment deployment using ethane (R-170), ethene (R-1150) and propane (R-290) for industrial ULT refrigeration (temperatures below -50⁰C). There are more than 700 available ENERGY STAR Certified Lab Grade ULT Refrigerators and industrial scale ultra-freezer models based on pure HCs, HC blends and CO2/HC cascade systems [34].  Solid-state refrigeration, such as thermoelectric or magnetocaloric refrigeration, are emerging technologies expected to be capable of meeting ULT refrigeration [35,36] as well as refrigerated centrifuges needs.  Newer CO2, HC and HC/CO2 designs present significant operating cost savings over F-gas systems. Despite CO2, HCs, or HC/CO2 based equipment being more expensive, newer designs present significant operating cost savings through performance monitoring digitalization and dedicated designs [25,37], such as adiabatic condensation that enables heat recovery in CO2 based systems [33,38].  Many grocery retailers are willing to invest in non-fluorinated refrigerant-based HVACR as an effective way to achieve GHG emission goals [39,40] while avoiding corporate liabilities related to using F-gas refrigerants. Equipment tailored to CO2 demonstrates up to 50% annual energy savings, resulting in short payback periods over the initial investment [41–43].   The ASHRAE standard 34 allows the use of slightly flammable refrigerants as drop in HFC substitutes. That also enables the growing adoption of hydrocarbons for new equipment, including domestic refrigeration and air conditioning, commercial refrigeration and industrial refrigeration. ASHRAE reclassified HFOs as slightly flammable (A2L) to encourage their use. Due to flame propagation and ignition probability, HC refrigerants are A3 ASHRAE safety class. Extensive testing results have shown that the risk of using A3 refrigerants in refrigeration can be mitigated if the system is improved using safety measures [20,25,44] such as proper electric insulation, sealed control units and leak detection sensors connected to feedback loop compressor controls, similar to those recommended for A2L refrigerants.  To mitigate the flammability risks of HFOs, companies are commercializing blends with high-GWP HFC refrigerants. However, no commercial HFO/HFC blend classified as A1 also complies with an ‘average GWP’ lower than 450 [18], while the GWP threshold for most applications is set at 150. HFOs such as R-1234yf are just slightly less flammable (A2L) than HCs [19] and produce highly toxic hydrogen fluoride (HF) and carbonyl fluoride (COF2) when burned [20–22], posing a serious risk to fire rescue teams.  A deterrent to a broader transition to non-fluorinated refrigerants is the lack of incentives to purchase newer equipment that works with such refrigerants.  Drop in substitutes for retrofitting purposes must possess very similar properties to the refrigerant to be replaced [45]. The similar properties of HFOs to HFCs in certain respects explains the market expansion of HFOs given the amount of deployed equipment currently utilizing HFCs.  While HFO refrigerants, particularly HFOs blended with HFCs or HCs, are currently used as a substitute, increasing regulatory and other pressures on the production and use of F-gases [23,46,47] and PFAS [48–50] will likely result in limitations on the availability of F-gas refrigerants.  It is important to note that retrofitted HVACR equipment generally exhibits lower efficiency compared to the latest models, contributing significant indirect CO2e emissions compared to a modernized HVACR scenario. Moreover, retrofitting has a typical payback period of 0.7 years due to low investment, while purchasing new equipment plus improving insulation of existing buildings can be as short as 2 years [51].  CO2, HC/CO2 cascade systems and Ultra Low Charge (ULC) ammonia systems are expected to dominate commercial and industrial refrigeration [52] in OECD countries by 2027 and in non-OECD countries by 2036. Moreover, numerous manufacturers and commercial operators have successfully switched to halogen-free refrigerants, particularly HC/CO2 cascade equipment [42], in several supermarket chains [26,53]. Peripheral measures such as heat recovery systems integrated with sanitary water heating enabled the adoption of CO2 refrigeration systems in medium and large food retail and storage facilities [33,43].  Trans-critical CO2 (R-744) has promising prospects for commercial refrigeration, including supermarkets [41,54]. It is expected that CO2 will achieve wider application in food storage (convenience stores and cold rooms) [55] and regular use in heat pumps [23], and be a major contributor to our ability to fully replacing HFCs before 2030. The number of self-contained HC-based refrigeration cabinets in U.S. stores was estimated to be 919,000 in December 2022, a 12% annual increase [56].  A new opportunity for ammonia is arising with the implementation of ULC units, paving the way for a resurgence of ammonia [25,27]. Novel ULC designs meet cooling capacity demands with lower ammonia charges. ULC ammonia systems have a specific charge that could go as low as 0.018 Kg/kW, representing a stark contrast to direct expansion systems [57] with a charge up to 2.6 Kg/kW, minimizing the refrigerant fill costs and potential liabilities related to acute toxicity and eutrophication. However, acutely toxicity and eutrophication hazards persist, so ULC ammonia systems still require robust process safety and engineering controls to prevent leaks and accidents.  Upgrading mobile refrigeration into using non-fluorinated refrigerants is within reach, considering that transportation has a long history of leveraging pressurized gases.  CO2-based transport refrigeration in Europe is expected to grow from 1% in 2018 to 20% by 2030 [37]. Particularly for global food transportation and fishing vessels, CO2 offers several advantages over HFC refrigerants [37,53,58].  CO2/HC cascade systems are increasingly employed in food transportation [26] and storage [25,27].  CO2 based Mobile Air Conditioning (MAC) systems debut in the 2023 European market. Most car makers now use the R-1234yf (HFO) refrigerant in their vehicles, implementing additional leak and fire safety measures that could also be used to reduce risk of using HC refrigerants.  The economic feasibility of non-fluorinated HVACR is translating into wider customer adoption. According to a recent report from ATMOsphere [56], market penetration of CO2, HC, and HC/CO2 based systems is steadily increasing in the US at an annual pace of 2.2%, while Europe is witnessing exponential growth driven by an expected increase of about 100% in cold storage revenue with respect to pre-pandemic levels, mainly due to perishable food storage, convenience stores and online grocery shopping. General Comments: The Toxics Use Reduction Institute (TURI) respectfully submits these comments to the European Chemicals Agency as input on their PFAS restriction proposal regarding fluorinated gases (F-gases). TURI is an independent government agency established in 1989 by the Commonwealth of Massachusetts to help implement the state’s Toxics Use Reduction Act, assisting businesses with the transition to safer alternatives to hazardous substances. TURI offers the following information based on research and experience around the assessment of alternatives, including their hazards, as businesses in Massachusetts face potential restrictions on products containing hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) and Per- and polyfluorinated alkyl substances (PFAS). TURI addresses F-gas concerns in Heating, Ventilation, Air Conditioning, and Refrigeration (HVACR) and shares data gathered about potential alternatives to HFCs and other F-gasses. TURI’s objective is to provide holistic and objective information about available alternatives, particularly the newer generation of refrigeration options, to assist EU Member States in crafting an appropriate PFAS restriction and businesses in assessing their alternatives.
The term “regrettable substitute” is used when an industry or society goes through an effort to eliminate a problematic chemical and switches to another chemistry or technology but then finds that the alternative is no safer than the original chemical.
Given recent technological progress and proven instances of success, the potential exists to completely transition from F-gas HVACR systems to alternative, non-fluorinated refrigerants. TURI carefully evaluated the substitution of HFCs with HFO refrigerants and has concerns based on the evidence of environmental hazards, such as their effective Global Warming Potential (GWP) and the likelihood of PFAS pollution throughout the lifecycle of HFOs.
For example, TURI believes that Figure B.41 of the Annex XV Restriction Report – PFAS is incomplete. There is evidence on the conversion of trifluoro acetaldehyde (CF3CHO; CAS number: 75-90-1) into HFC-23 (Fluoroform or Trifluoromethane; CHF3; GWP100=14800; CAS number: 75-46-7), with a GWP100 of 14,800.  In addition, there is evidence to suggest trifluoroacetic acid (CF3COOH; CAS number: 76-05-1) also converts into HFC-23 (fluoroform or trifluoromethane; CHF3; GWP100=14800; CAS number: 75-46-7). These pathways warrant consideration in the context of the proposed PFAS restriction.
The references provided herein are salient in an assessment of F-gas alternatives, in particular with respect to the hazard comparison of F-gas-based HVACR systems to non-fluorinated alternatives, and similar information was not observed in the current version of the EU’s Annex XV restriction report. TURI is pleased to share this information with you as you consider your restriction proposal.
Key points:
+ HFOs are potentially regrettable substitutes for HFCs.
+ The effective GWP of HFOs may be higher than regulatory thresholds because of their potential degradation into HFC-23 (trifluoromethane; HFC-23; GWP100=14800; CAS number: 75-46-7).
+ HFOs are often blended with HFCs to reduce the ‘average GWP’, which is a problematic indicator of GWP and progress toward climate mitigation objectives.
+ The patented pathways to produce the HFO refrigerants involve the use (and likely leakage) of Carcinogenic, Mutagenic, and Reprotoxic (CMR) chemicals and the production of PFAS as byproducts.
+ Heating, Ventilation, Air Conditioning, and Refrigeration (HVACR) equipment with non-fluorinated refrigerants are available on the market today at reasonable costs, and are safer than their fluorinated counterparts, including for Ultra Low Temperature (ULT) refrigeration.
+ Newer CO2, hydrocarbon (HC) and HC/CO2 designs present significant operating cost savings over F-gas systems.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: TURI offers information based on our research and experience around hazards, and alternatives to the application of fluorinated gases, including HFCs and HFOs, in:  • Annex E.2.8.: Heating, Ventilation, Air Conditioning, and Refrigeration (HVACR) systems. Sub-uses: Domestic refrigeration; Commercial and industrial refrigeration; Specialist applications: Low temperature refrigeration below -50⁰C; Refrigerants in laboratory test and measurement equipment; Refrigerants in refrigerated centrifuges.  • Annex E.2.10.: Transport refrigeration; Mobile air conditioning (MAC), excluding aircraft and military use.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The lifecycle of the HFO refrigerant family involves the use (and likely leakage) of known Carcinogenic, Mutagenic, and Reprotoxic (CMR) chemicals as precursors, as well as use and formation of HFCs:  Carbon tetrachloride (CTC) [1], perchloroethylene (PCE) [2], and HFCs [3] are precursors in the production of HFOs, and PFAS are by-products [4].   EPA determined that CTC presents an unreasonable risk [5] to workers from long-term inhalation and dermal exposures and liver toxicity from short-term dermal exposure, and has proposed risk management measures including an existing chemical exposure limit (ECEL) of 0.03 ppm as an 8-hour time-weighted average (TWA) [6]. This illustrates the concerns raised about the production phase of the HFO lifecycle in our alternatives assessment.  Comment on Figure B.41 of the Annex XV Restriction Report – PFAS:  There is scientific literature on various HFO degradation mechanisms pointing to the production of the high global warming HFC-23 (trifluoromethane or fluoroform; GWP100 = 14800; CAS number: 75-46-7) [7]. HFO-1234ze(E) is described in the literature as degrading quickly and quantitatively into trifluoro acetaldehyde (TFE; CF3CHO; trifluoroethanal; CAS number: 75-90-1) [8]. Similarly, studies describe that one molecule of HFO-1336mzz(E) produces one molecule of TFE and one molecule of TFA, quantitatively [8].  TFE is a well-known photochemical precursor of HFC-23 [7] in environmental conditions [9]. HFC-23 formation from TFE is not represented in the Figure B.41 of the Annex XV Restriction Report on PFAS. HFO-1234yf and HFO-1225ye quantitatively produce trifluoroacetic acid (CF3COOH; TFA; CAS number: 76-05-1) by oxidation in atmospheric conditions [8,10–12].  Although TFA is known for its chemical stability, it is not expected to remain intact indefinitely and may degrade into HFC-23 through diverse pathways (e.g.: [13,14]). These pathways for HFC-23 formation from TFA are not represented in the Figure B.41 of the Annex XV Restriction Report on PFAS. Given the above, TURI believes that the Annex XV Restriction Report on PFAS is missing important potential HFO degradation pathways. The potential degradation of HFOs to HFC-23 via TFE and TFA should be represented in Figure B.41, and these pathways warrant consideration in the context of the proposed PFAS restriction. The effective GWP of HFOs could be higher than regulatory thresholds, depending on the likelihood of them forming HFC-23.   While the Global Warming Potential (GWP) metric does not usually contemplate the greenhouse effect of degradation compounds, the effective GWP does consider GHG gas generation during environmental fate. There is evidence to suggest that commercially available HFOs, although having a low atmospheric lifetime, could decompose to HFC-23 (trifluoro methane or fluoroform; CHF3; GWP100 = 14800; CAS number: 75-46-7), increasing their effective GWP in a proportion worthy of consideration [7,9].  The eventual formation of HFC-23, with its very high GWP, undermines the climate change mitigation objective of phasing down HFC use globally under the Kigali Amendment of the Montreal Protocol. Therefore, HFOs may potentially be a regrettable substitute for HFCs in HVACR systems.   Many applications that use HFOs require blending with HFCs, with problematic hazards for toxicity, flammability, and the climate. With the exception of mobile air conditioning (MAC), pure HFOs have limited standalone applications, mostly serving as components in refrigerant mixtures with high GWP HFCs to reduce the ‘average GWP’ and the flammability of HFOs. These mixtures act as substitutes for R134a and R410a (both HFCs) refrigerants, retrofitting stationary AC, MAC, and heat pump units.  The use of ‘average GWP,’ as in the case of high-GWP HFC/HFO blends, misrepresents the hazard presented to the climate as it does not factor HFO degradation products into its calculus or prevent high-GWP HFCs emissions. In our view, more careful consideration is needed regarding the potential use of these PFAS to achieve climate change mitigation objectives [15–17]. Moreover, to mitigate the flammability risks of HFOs, companies are commercializing low-‘average GWP’ HFO blends with high-GWP HFC refrigerants. However, no commercial HFO/HFC blend classified as A1 also complies with a GWP lower than 450, while the GWP threshold for most applications is set at 150 [18]. HFOs such as R-1234yf are just slightly less flammable (A2L) than HCs [19] and produce highly toxic hydrogen fluoride (HF) and carbonyl fluoride (COF2) when burned [20–22], posing a serious risk to fire rescue teams. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Transformative technological progress and proven demonstration of success give us reason to see potential to completely transition away from F-gas HVACR systems to alternative, non-fluorinated refrigerants, including ultra-low temperature refrigeration. TURI has carefully evaluated HFOs and is very concerned with the evidence of significant environmental impact. HFOs may be regrettable substitutes to HFCs due to their elevated effective Global Warming Potential (GWP) and the likelihood of subsequent PFAS pollution.   Heating, Ventilation, Air Conditioning, and Refrigeration (HVACR) equipment with non-fluorinated refrigerants are available on the market today at reasonable costs, and are safer than their fluorinated counterparts, including for Ultra Low Temperature (ULT) refrigeration.  TURI’s assessment found that refrigerants such as carbon dioxide (CO2), ammonia (NH3), and hydrocarbons (HCs) can be efficiently implemented. Technological improvements have addressed historical concerns, such as the cooling capacity of CO2, corrosion from the use of CO2 and NH3, NH3 toxicity, and flammability of HCs [23–27].  The rising cost of new F-gas refrigerants is challenging the HVACR industry. HFOs are more expensive than HFCs [23]. However, high GWP refrigerants are capped for production and import in OECD countries, which caused a rise in their prices, partially explaining the competitiveness of HFOs and HFO/HFC blends to HFCs. R-32 is the only SNAP-approved HFC, being among the cheapest on the market. However, its GWP is higher than most of the oncoming regulatory thresholds, and its use is limited to retrofitting industrial equipment difficult to replace on short notice.   In this context, NH3, CO2 and HCs are becoming competitive. Commercial refrigeration equipment manufacturing based on hydrocarbons has reached economy of scale [25]. The price of refrigerant-grade HCs is comparable with novel HFOs, except that the equipment that works with HCs is designed to minimize the required refrigerant charge for safety purposes.  CO2 (R-744) is the safest refrigerant gas, also offered at a very low cost. Ammonia is the cheapest and most abundant refrigerant, the main driver for its industrial applications. Many HVACR manufacturing leaders are converting their sales portfolio to entirely non-fluorinated products by 2027 [23,26]. Specialized start-ups are successfully increasing their Market Readiness Level (MRL) to capitalize on the demand for systems using non-fluorinated refrigerants [28].  Equipment modernization could account for increasing in energy efficiency by 50%, expediting payback periods of new equipment acquisition by reducing energy use and related CO2 emissions. Strategic design improvement opportunities are: • The compressor is the heart of a vapor compression cycle. A more efficient compression can reduce CO2e emissions by up to 20% [29]. • The condenser is the part of the system that transfers heat from the refrigerant to the environment. Efficient condensers reduce energy usage about 15% [30]. • The evaporator is the part of the system that extracts heat from the environment. A more efficient evaporator can increase the intrinsic performance of the system by up to 10% [31].  • Integrating heat recovery systems greatly reduces heating costs and space demand [32,33], particularly for equipment operating with CO2.  Ammonia (R-717) is the most efficient refrigerant of choice for various industrial applications with typical cooling capacities above 1 MW. While new Ultra Low Charge (ULC) ammonia refrigeration systems are significantly more efficient and result in less risk to workers than traditional ammonia systems [27], leading us to consider them as favorable alternatives, it is crucial to recognize that the acute toxic hazard persists. EPA-SNAP authorizes new ULT equipment deployment using ethane (R-170), ethene (R-1150) and propane (R-290) for industrial ULT refrigeration (temperatures below -50⁰C). There are more than 700 available ENERGY STAR Certified Lab Grade ULT Refrigerators and industrial scale ultra-freezer models based on pure HCs, HC blends and CO2/HC cascade systems [34].  Solid-state refrigeration, such as thermoelectric or magnetocaloric refrigeration, are emerging technologies expected to be capable of meeting ULT refrigeration [35,36] as well as refrigerated centrifuges needs. Newer CO2, HC and HC/CO2 designs present significant operating cost savings over F-gas systems. Despite CO2, HCs, or HC/CO2 based equipment being more expensive, newer designs present significant operating cost savings through performance monitoring digitalization and dedicated designs [25,37], such as adiabatic condensation that enables heat recovery in CO2 based systems [33,38].  Many grocery retailers are willing to invest in non-fluorinated refrigerant-based HVACR as an effective way to achieve GHG emission goals [39,40] while avoiding corporate liabilities related to using F-gas refrigerants. Equipment tailored to CO2 demonstrates up to 50% annual energy savings, resulting in short payback periods over the initial investment [41–43].   The ASHRAE standard 34 allows the use of slightly flammable refrigerants as drop in HFC substitutes. That also enables the growing adoption of hydrocarbons for new equipment, including domestic refrigeration and air conditioning, commercial refrigeration and industrial refrigeration. ASHRAE reclassified HFOs as slightly flammable (A2L) to encourage their use. Due to flame propagation and ignition probability, HC refrigerants are A3 ASHRAE safety class. Extensive testing results have shown that the risk of using A3 refrigerants in refrigeration can be mitigated if the system is improved using safety measures [20,25,44] such as proper electric insulation, sealed control units and leak detection sensors connected to feedback loop compressor controls, similar to those recommended for A2L refrigerants.   To mitigate the flammability risks of HFOs, companies are commercializing blends with high-GWP HFC refrigerants. However, no commercial HFO/HFC blend classified as A1 also complies with an ‘average GWP’ lower than 450 [18], while the GWP threshold for most applications is set at 150. HFOs such as R-1234yf are just slightly less flammable (A2L) than HCs [19] and produce highly toxic hydrogen fluoride (HF) and carbonyl fluoride (COF2) when burned [20–22], posing a serious risk to fire rescue teams.  A deterrent to a broader transition to non-fluorinated refrigerants is the lack of incentives to purchase newer equipment that works with such refrigerants.  Drop in substitutes for retrofitting purposes must possess very similar properties to the refrigerant to be replaced [45]. The similar properties of HFOs to HFCs in certain respects explains the market expansion of HFOs given the amount of deployed equipment currently utilizing HFCs.  While HFO refrigerants, particularly HFOs blended with HFCs or HCs, are currently used as a substitute, increasing regulatory and other pressures on the production and use of F-gases [23,46,47] and PFAS [48–50] will likely result in limitations on the availability of F-gas refrigerants.  It is important to note that retrofitted HVACR equipment generally exhibits lower efficiency compared to the latest models, contributing significant indirect CO2e emissions compared to a modernized HVACR scenario. Moreover, retrofitting has a typical payback period of 0.7 years due to low investment, while purchasing new equipment plus improving insulation of existing buildings can be as short as 2 years [51].  CO2, HC/CO2 cascade systems and Ultra Low Charge (ULC) ammonia systems are expected to dominate commercial and industrial refrigeration [52] in OECD countries by 2027 and in non-OECD countries by 2036. Moreover, numerous manufacturers and commercial operators have successfully switched to halogen-free refrigerants, particularly HC/CO2 cascade equipment [42], in several supermarket chains [26,53]. Peripheral measures such as heat recovery systems integrated with sanitary water heating enabled the adoption of CO2 refrigeration systems in medium and large food retail and storage facilities [33,43].  Trans-critical CO2 (R-744) has promising prospects for commercial refrigeration, including supermarkets [41,54]. It is expected that CO2 will achieve wider application in food storage (convenience stores and cold rooms) [55] and regular use in heat pumps [23], and be a major contributor to our ability to fully replacing HFCs before 2030. The number of self-contained HC-based refrigeration cabinets in U.S. stores was estimated to be 919,000 in December 2022, a 12% annual increase [56].  A new opportunity for ammonia is arising with the implementation of ULC units, paving the way for a resurgence of ammonia [25,27]. Novel ULC designs meet cooling capacity demands with lower ammonia charges. ULC ammonia systems have a specific charge that could go as low as 0.018 Kg/kW, representing a stark contrast to direct expansion systems [57] with a charge up to 2.6 Kg/kW, minimizing the refrigerant fill costs and potential liabilities related to acute toxicity and eutrophication. However, acutely toxicity and eutrophication hazards persist, so ULC ammonia systems still require robust process safety and engineering controls to prevent leaks and accidents. Upgrading mobile refrigeration into using non-fluorinated refrigerants is within reach, considering that transportation has a long history of leveraging pressurized gases.  CO2-based transport refrigeration in Europe is expected to grow from 1% in 2018 to 20% by 2030 [37]. Particularly for global food transportation and fishing vessels, CO2 offers several advantages over HFC refrigerants [37,53,58].  CO2/HC cascade systems are increasingly employed in food transportation [26] and storage [25,27].  CO2 based Mobile Air Conditioning (MAC) systems debut in the 2023 European market. Most car makers now use the R-1234yf (HFO) refrigerant in their vehicles, implementing additional leak and fire safety measures that could also be used to reduce risk of using HC refrigerants.  The economic feasibility of non-fluorinated HVACR is translating into wider customer adoption. According to a recent report from ATMOsphere [56], market penetration of CO2, HC, and HC/CO2 based systems is steadily increasing in the US at an annual pace of 2.2%, while Europe is witnessing exponential growth driven by an expected increase of about 100% in cold storage revenue with respect to pre-pandemic levels, mainly due to perishable food storage, convenience stores and online grocery shopping.
