Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The use of seals made of fluoropolymers and fluororubber such as PTFE or FKM is state of the art in modern metal-cutting machine tools (e.g. milling machining centers). The materials used today are the result of decades of development in the field of materials science. Today, these seals ensure the tightness of the machine design against the escape of fluids such as oil or contaminated cooling lubricant into the environment or their mixing with each other. In addition to safety for people and the environment, this also increases the lifetime of components and assemblies and has a positive effect on friction behavior. These seals thus have a direct influence on the energy efficiency and sustainability of machine tools. These sealing materials have become particularly important since the EU chemicals regulation REACH (Regulation EC No. 1907/2006) came into force. Substance bans under REACH have greatly increased the incompatibility of seals and elastomers with new types of cooling lubricants containing only the permitted biocides. The machine tool industry has reacted to this and, through standardized insertion tests, has come to the conclusion in recent years that only PTFE and FKM are reliably resistant to these new types of cooling lubricants. Sealing materials previously used as alternatives, such as NBR or HNBR, are changing critically and leading to leakages and the premature failure of components and assemblies.
There are currently no alternative materials to the fluoropolymers and fluororubber currently in use that can be used without restriction. It is also not possible to estimate at present whether and when this will change in the future. For this reason, it must be possible to obtain an exemption for the continued use of fluoropolymers and fluororubber in order to protect people and the environment from leaking machine tools. To our knowledge, fluoropolymers meet the internationally recognized OECD criteria for "polymers of low concern" (PLC). They are chemically stable, non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water-soluble and non-mobile, so they are also suitable, for example, as materials for food contact, in medical applications or in the manufacture of high-purity active pharmaceutical ingredients (e.g. vaccines). We therefore call on the competent authorities of the European Economic Area (EEA) to agree with this scientific and only reasonable assessment and to follow, for example, the competent authorities of the United Kingdom, who see no need to restrict fluoropolymers including their manufacturing processes in any way.

General Comments: The Volvo Group welcomes the initiative to reduce the risks of long living and toxic per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances in the environment and wishes to provide comments on the consultation on the Annex XV restriction report related to the Restriction on the manufacture, placing on the market and use of PFASs.

The Volvo Group manufactures trucks, buses, construction equipment and power solutions for marine and industrial applications. Volvo Group also have a high pace in the transformation with a rapid expansion of the offer of electric vehicles and machines. The Volvo Group products often operate under harsh conditions and some of the materials and substances used in the Volvo Group’s products are potentially hazardous and cannot today be substituted to achieve the high safety and quality demands. Volvo Group works to reduce its dependency on such materials and substances with the aim to protect both people and the environment. In collaboration with partners, Volvo Group proactively evaluates alternatives in the design and supply processes to minimize and eliminate use of substances of concern.

The intention to reduce the risks of long living and toxic per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) is therefore in line with Volvo Group ambitions. At the same time, the Volvo Group is concerned by both the timeline and the scope of the PFAS restriction as proposed. Many applications in Volvo Group´s products, like e.g. batteries, refrigerants, sealings, internal combustion engines and fuel cells, are today unfortunately dependent on PFASs (mainly fluoropolymers) due to lack of alternatives that provide equal crucial function of durability, resistance to high temperatures and high pressures, electrical insulation, and chemical stability in order to secure safe products with a long operating lifetime.

Alternative solutions to PFAS use are still far from mature throughout our value chain. Our suppliers are investigating PFAS occurrences and alternative materials in parts they deliver to us and are today not able to give us a timeline for phase-out. Use of PFAS needs to be allowed as long as there is no full-scale availability of suitable and technically developed substitutes.

Volvo Group requests a formal process for extending already permitted derogations beyond the originally agreed time period.

An 18-months transition period, as provided for in the proposal, is not sufficient to phase out substances from our complex products with the required validations and verifications.

Volvo Groups considers that a transition period of at least 5 years is required to secure safe and high-quality products and to avoid non-sustainable substitutions.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Transport, TULAC, Application of Fluorinated Gases (Mobile Air-con), Electronics, Lubricants   Volvo Group appreciates that the FAQ published by ECHA (“Questions and answers – Answers by the five national authorities to questions on the content of the proposed restriction”) clarifies that the Transportation sector covers any kind of transport vehicle e.g., also maritime. However, the same components as used in vehicles are used in non-road mobile machinery (e.g. construction equipment, marine/industrial and auxiliary power generators) for the same technical reasons.   Volvo Group recommends that non-road mobile machinery (e.g. construction equipment, marine/industrial and auxiliary power generators), are included in the sector Transport and receive the corresponding derogation times.  Volvo Group wishes to refer to the technical information on use cases as submitted by European Automobile Manufacturers ‘Association (ACEA), Committee for European Construction Equipment (CECE), and the European Association of Internal Combustion Engine and Alternative Powertrain Manufacturers (EUROMOT).

5. Proposed derogations: Paragraph 5 (i) Maintenance and refilling of existing HVACR equipment, (p) Refrigerants in mobile air conditioning-systems, (s) Lubricants, (u) Technical textiles  Without adequate derogations for “Maintenance and refilling of existing HVACR equipment”, and “Refrigerants in mobile air conditioning-systems” Volvo Group foresee a period of time where no products will be available on the market due to lack of available alternative technologies for air conditioning systems. The current derogations cover mainly products within the definition of Vehicles, which excludes the sector non-road mobile machinery.  Volvo Group recommends the derogations to be extended also to non-road mobile machinery given the shared technologies and common supply chains.   Servicing of existing HVACR equipment must be untouched and remain possible without any time limit receiving an unlimited derogation.   Volvo Group furthermore wishes to refer to the technical information and timelines as submitted by European Automobile Manufacturers ‘Association (ACEA).  Regarding derogations for Lubricants and Technical textiles Volvo Group refers to the technical information on use cases as submitted by European Automobile Manufacturers ‘Association (ACEA), Committee for European Construction Equipment (CECE), and the European Association of Internal Combustion Engine and Alternative Powertrain Manufacturers (EUROMOT).

6. Missing uses: Volvo Group has a high pace in the green transformation with a rapid expansion of the offer of electric vehicles and machines. Availability of batteries and electronics is required in order to secure this transition.   Volvo Group recommends the longest possible derogation period for batteries and electronics.   For further technical information, Volvo Group wishes to refer to the submissions by European Automobile Manufacturers‘ Association (ACEA), Committee for European Construction Equipment (CECE), and the European Association of Internal Combustion Engine and Alternative Powertrain Manufacturers (EUROMOT).    Volvo Group has established procedures to request and assess substance information for parts used in Volvo Group products placed on the market. However, for suppliers of tools and equipment used in our factories or test facilities (but not placed on the market by Volvo Group), this is not in place. The presence of PFAS in these tools and equipment is therefore not known to us but it has to be assumed that equipment requiring, e.g. lubrication and sealants, contains PFAS. Based on the information submitted to ECHA during the stakeholder consultation so far, Volvo Group concludes that PFAS is used in equipment like robots that are used in factories and test facilities and believes that this could hold true also for our industry. The maintenance of these tools and equipment needs to be secured to ensure that we will be able to produce products for the future.   Volvo Group recommends a general exemption for parts used for maintenance of tools and equipment used in industrial settings.  Service, maintenance, and repairs of products are instrumental in the EU Green Deal and circularity. To support an extended lifetime for long-living products, it is necessary to secure the availability of spare parts. Our products often have extended lifespan, sometimes over 20 years. Assuming that PFAS-free alternatives are readily available on the market, which is not currently the case, it is likely that in many applications these will not be a drop-in replacement for the PFAS on a 1:1 basis due to different properties such as chemical inertness, tightness, and functionality. Systems will therefore need to be redesigned, reapproved, and replaced on the market. Therefore, the repair-as-produced principle should be applied to the placing of spare parts to allow legacy spare parts to be continued to be placed on the market.  Volvo Group recommends a general exemption of legacy spare parts (repair as produced).  Remanufacturing and refurbishment of products are instrumental in the EU Green Deal and circularity. Reused products are contributing to environmental sustainability by extending the lifespan of goods, reducing the need for new manufacturing and resource extraction.  Restricting PFAS in remanufactured, refurbished and repaired products will make it impossible to offer these alternatives as soon as PFAS was part of the original product as first placed on the market. This would lead to an increased demand for new products. In addition, this would create a higher amount of waste which would contradict the sustainability goal of resource efficiency.  As part of Volvo Group circularity ambitions the aim is to increase the remanufacturing business by 60% until 2025 (baseline 2018). This aim would be jeopardized by the current PFAS restriction proposal.   Volvo Group recommends that remanufactured and refurbished vehicles and non-road mobile machinery and parts thereof, are exempted from the restriction.  A general derogation is also needed for products that have already been placed on the market for the first time. Otherwise, they cannot be resold, or further processed and placed on the market again. Volvo Group products have a very long lifespan, sometimes over 20 years, and therefore products often have several owners over this time.  Without a derogation for second-life products, this will lead to unnecessary scrapping and increased waste.  Volvo Group recommends that vehicles and non-road mobile machinery and parts thereof, already placed on the market shall be exempted from the restriction.

7. Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Information on alternatives Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The Vorwerk Group is an international family company whose core business is the development, production and sale of innovative, high-quality household appliances. The Group pursues a strategy of sustainable growth. In 2022, it generated total sales of 3.2 billion euros. Vorwerk has been in business for 140 years and has always had its headquarters in Wuppertal, Germany.
Vorwerk is the number one direct selling company in Europe and the world's leading direct seller of premium household appliances with more than 90,000 independent sales consultants. Today, the Vorwerk Group sells directly to customers in 60 countries, mainly in Europe, but also in Asia and North and South America.
Vorwerk combines research, development and production in a single company. Vorwerk sets high standards in all areas and produces innovative products that are practical, useful and exceptionally durable.
In addition, sustainability has been an important part of Vorwerk's corporate strategy since 2016. Since then, the Vorwerk Group has reduced its own CO2 emissions by 52.9 percent (as of 31 December 2021). We therefore welcome the ECHA's initiative to further restrict the use of environmentally harmful substances such as the PFAS group.
Our contribution to this consultation focuses on the use of fluoropolymers in consumer cookware. We would like to point out that in the restriction dossier, the use of PFAS in consumer cookware is focused on non-stick coatings in simple pans or pots, however, what is not taken into account is that the consumer cookware sector also includes complex electrical appliances such as kitchen machines.
These machines consist of complex technical parts, some of which come into direct contact with food and are exposed to harsh environments such as high temperatures exceeding 200°C. For some of these parts, there are no known alternatives to the use of fluoropolymers. Here we have to use e.g. PTFE for some sub-parts such as seals, gaskets or as a lubricant. The choice of PTFE is made very carefully and we only use it when there is no technical alternative. However, it remains essential and without it, the core functions of our appliances would not be possible. We have conducted tests with alternative materials and the results clearly show that they do not meet the requirements of both the component and the Food Contact Framework Regulation (EC) No 1935/2004 and therefore cannot be used as replacement for PTFE. Data on this are deposited in the confidential attachment.
We therefore propose for the consumer cookware sector to grant a derogation for the use of fluoropolymers as food contact materials in complex electrical appliances where no alternative is known, e.g. gaskets, seals, etc. The conditions for this exemption should be the same as those defined for consumer cookware in the industrial and professional subsector.  The same should apply to lubricants used in complex electrical consumer products. As there are also no known alternatives for fluoropolymer-based lubricants in the consumer sector, the exemption should be extended to the consumer sector as well.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: - Food contact materials and packaging – Consumer cookware - Lubricants

6. Missing uses: For consumer products, derogations are needed in the sectors 'food contact materials and packaging' and 'lubricants'. In the restriction proposal, ECHA has focused on the use of PFAS in non-stick coatings, but has not sufficiently considered the use of fluoropolymers in complex electrical devices. Here, fluoropolymers play a crucial role in the functioning and (food) safety of electrical appliances. They are used in seals, gaskets and lubricants and there are currently no alternatives that combine their unique combination of properties in terms of chemical inertness, abrasion resistance, tribological properties and compliance with food contact regulations. Tests with various classes of other materials have shown that they are no viable alternatives because either their temperature resistance is insufficient or their abrasion resistance is too low, resulting in non-compliance with food contact regulations. If the strict ban on PFAS in consumer cookware were to come into force as proposed, it would no longer be possible to manufacture or place on the market high-tech electrical consumer products in Europe. For the entire sector of manufacturers of electrical household appliances, this ban would have fatal consequences and mean business closures and the loss of tens of thousands of jobs.

8. Other identified uses: In the sector of "food contact materials and packaging" for consumer cookware, only non-stick coatings on simple pots and pans seem to have been considered. This does not include electrical appliances that come into contact with food. Derogations have to be made for these appliances as the use of fluoropolymers such as PTFE is essential for their safe and reliable functioning.  In the case of lubricants in the explanatory notes, exemption 5s is limited to professional and industrial use. However, the safe functioning, durability and longevity of complex electrical consumer products also depend on the use of fluoropolymer-based lubricants. Therefore, consumer products should be included in the exemption.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: The watch industry uses lubricants containing the substances covered by the draft restriction. These molecules, used in small quantities, are necessary for the function and the long service life of the products.
Scope of the exemption request:
"By way of derogation, paragraphs 1 and 2 shall not apply to lubricants applied to internal watch parts, until 13.5 years after EiF."

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Our comments apply to the following sector: - Lubricants (sector as a whole).

6. Missing uses: a) The quantities of lubricants involved are extremely small. Indeed, one can count between 1.5mg and 6mg of fluorinated lubricant per watch, each containing approximately 30% of PTFE, which represents, at EU level for approximately 18-50kg of PTFE/year for the whole watch industry.  b) Mechanical assemblies generally require lubrication to function properly. This is particularly the case for timepieces with analogue displays, which means mainly mechanical watches and quartz watches. The watch industry produces complex objects, small in size, with very precisely toleranced dimensions (of the order of a micron) relying mainly on the mechanical and tribological properties of their components. The reliability, lifespan, precision of timekeeping instruments as well as the intervals between aftersale-services are highly dependent on the lubricants placed between the movement components. Watchmaking lubricants (solids and/or liquids) must meet several joint objectives: • Prevent wear • In some cases, due to their consistency, avoid untimely sliding of certain parts • Be easy to deposit industrially • Ensure the function for years without external intervention • Be compatible with on the one hand the epilame and on the other hand, the materials or their coating. Changing one of the substances of this trio has implications for the others In some cases, these lubricants may contain solid particles, such as PTFE for example, which allow their viscosity to be adjusted and thus guarantee the reliability of the watch, and to increase performance (better wear protection and lower friction coefficient). Replacing these particles with others thickeners involves significant technical qualification work that can go as far as changing parts' materials, or even completely redesigning the affected system. The excellent chemical stability of PFAS makes it possible to increase the inter-service period (performance product) which has the effect of reducing the logistics linked to the services and therefore the environmental impact. In addition, lubricants containing PFAS mainly have high molar masses (= long chains) because most often in the form of grease, and these inert long chains are less harmful than short chains.  c) The potential impact in the EU for the analogue watchmaking industry of the submitted restriction under consideration, without exemption, could be estimated at up to 188,000 jobs losses.  d) The use of substances covered by the draft restriction meets a technical need for which there is currently no suitable technical alternative.  e) Analogue watches have a very long lifetime, sometimes even exceeding that of an entire human life, passing from one generation to the next, thus limiting the PFAS-release into the environment. The consequences of a change in technology must therefore be assessed with such a sustainability objective in mind. By remaining in the same chemical family of molecules, substitution would certainly be simpler, but to be sure that a potential PFAS-based alternative is viable in the long term, it would therefore take years of research and development. In terms of benefits for the environment, considering the very small quantities of lubricants used, the impact would be marginal.  f) Substitution is not technically feasible yet. A substitution project would take approximately 8-10 years, including reliability testing as no accelerated test is available to shorten the development time.  g) With around 59,000 persons employed in the sector, the Swiss watch industry represents the bulk of the European watch industry. Moreover, it is a major client, possibly the largest, of the European watch component supply industry. Indirectly, tens of thousands of jobs in the retail trade in the European Union are dependent on the watch industry and the sale of its products. The EU is a traditionally important market for Swiss watch exports. In 2022, the Swiss watch industry exported over six million watches with a total value of CHF 5.4 billion to European Union Member States. These are almost exclusively analogue watches. In 2020, the watchmaking and jewellery industry and downstream sectors employed 167,000 workers in the EU and also 21,000 cross-border worker from EU in Switzerland, considering production, aftersales services and product distribution. These jobs are spread over many companies, mostly SMEs: in Germany only, there are approximately 7,600 enterprises in the retail segment. In the EU, the main manufacturing facilities are located in rural areas such as the Black Forest in Germany and the Jura in France. The potential loss of thousands of jobs would have a particularly hard social impact in these regions. The restriction would prohibit the placing on the market of watches and components containing substances covered by the draft restriction. The potential impact in the EU for the analogue watchmaking industry of the submitted restriction under consideration, without exemption, could be estimated at 188,000 jobs losses, €3.0 billion in lost export revenues, and €1.3 billion in lost taxes and social security contributions. When the lubricants are deposited on a component, exposure of the consumer and the environment to these substances is very unlikely, and the quantities used of substances covered by the draft restriction are very small. Considering the financial risks and the major potential impact on the employment of tens of thousands of people, the implementation of a restriction as proposed seems disproportionate without the implementation of the exemption for watchmaking lubricants. Both in terms of risk analysis and socio-economic impact.

General Comments: The WCC provides this comment in support of the position provided by VdL (Verban der deutschen Lackund Druckfarbenindustrie e.V.), the national German paint and coatings association, submitted on June 21, 2023. Briefly stated, VdL makes the following points:
• The ban on PFAS substances is overly broad, including critical raw materials that have no substitutes and are not toxic or hazardous to the environment under conventional criteria.
• The ban is beyond the scope of standard procedures under Article 68 of REACH banning substances that have not been shown to have an “unacceptable risk.” Persistence is not a hazard endpoint, and persistence, absent other characteristics, does not indicate unacceptable risk.
• The ban extends to fluoropolymers that are “polymers of low concern” under REACH, including polymers used in high-performance coatings that enhance safety. One example being intumescent coatings used on industrial buildings that delay the spread of fires during an explosion or accident.
• Considering the complex uses and chemical properties of fluorinated chemistries, companies and the Commission require additional time to compile and evaluate relevant information.
VdL provides further details and relevance to the paint and coatings industry, while identifying recommendations to the Commission. WCC adopts VdL’s comment and supports its recommendations. General Comments: The working environment for industrial automation / robotics calibration and measurement products, used within the overall industrial metrology sector, machine tool, grinding, automated cutting, electronic assembly, etc. is harsh, where products are expected to perform in multiple applications with high precision and reliability, at high speeds, at elevated temperatures and when potentially contaminated with aggressive fluids and solids. To achieve this, items such as cables, seals, O-rings, adhesives, labels and finishes must be resistant to a wide range of oils, coolants, and chemicals and solid materials. The stable properties of FKM and similar long chain PFAS are well suited to these applications.
Repeated evaluation of alternative materials has shown that the overall performance of PFAS is unmatched. Based on work carried out while selecting and qualifying materials, alternatives result in reduced reliability (an increased safety hazard) and shorter product lifetimes (resulting in higher levels of environmental waste).
Precision industrial automation / robotics / calibration / metrology system manufacturers are not adequately covered in section E.2.4 of the Proposal for Restriction and should be considered separately due to their broad impact on key precision manufacturing industries and their long life.
We recommend that consideration is given to the risk vs benefit of the use of larger fluoropolymers and that the ban targets high polluters and substances likely to cause environmental harm first, phasing in control of less harmful PFAS over a realistic timeframe.
We request that consideration is made to providing a derogation for the use of all PFAS types in the vitally important area of Industrial Automation (robotics) calibration and metrology and Industrial Metrology.
The timeframe for finding and qualifying alternative materials is unfeasibly short.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The industry sectors that use our industrial automation products are wide ranging and include manufacturers of all products where sub-micron and even nano-scale level measurements and very close tolerance position measurement and control is required. These include manufacturers of electronic assemblies on all scales, precision instrumentation manufacturers, automotive, aerospace, transport, (including motors for electric vehicles), medical products and oil and gas component manufacturing. In many of these cases it is also important that our products do not leach or ‘outgas’ contaminants that may affect critical processes or sensitive products. The resistant, passive nature of FKM and similar PFAS provide this.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: a) Usage phase: The service life of products typically exceeds 20 years and is supported by replacement by exchange packages. There are no emissions during this phase. b) End of life: PFAS are likely in many components within the product, where the main constituents are metals and cable materials, mainly aluminium, steel, copper and PTFE/PVC. Our products are recycled under WEEE type requirements. Thus, it is expected that any PFAS containing materials in our products will be separated and managed appropriately.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Recycling appropriately does not result in PFAS release or formation.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Due to the relatively low volume of PFAS and the long active life of this product type There are no significant impacts on the recycling industry. Our suggestion is that consideration is given to collection and recycling of items that include PFAS. Control of collection and recycling can be implemented easily in B to B environments. Regulations could be implemented through parallel legislation such as the Waste Framework Directive.

5. Proposed derogations: The annual consumption of PFAS is unknown. No PFAS is released to the environment during use. There is no foreseen release of PFAS to the environment at any stage and expected EOL treatment would prevent release at that stage.

6. Missing uses: Key functionalities provided by PFAS are based on the unique properties of PFAS materials including their stability in hostile environments, resilience, and low friction. To the best of our knowledge, and the results of our own testing and evaluation indicate that suitable alternatives are not yet available. For certain niche applications substitution is not technically or economically feasible. Use of PFAS in specific silicon wafer manufacturing equipment is important to ensure no contamination from components and that components are able to withstand use in a high vacuum environment.

8. Other identified uses: Alternative materials are being sought and further work is being done work to evaluate alternatives where they are found. To date no materials adequately meet the mechanical, thermal, and chemical stability offered by PFAS solutions. We request that consideration is made to providing a derogation for the use of all PFAS types in the vitally important area of Industrial Automation (robotics) calibration and metrology and Industrial Metrology.

General Comments: The world of construction and architecture has seen many developments in the last centuries. However, many of the main building materials concepts for the end-of-life have remained the same. Concrete, Steel, Bricks and Glass are proven building materials, but they are some of the main contributors to the devastatingly high CO2 footprint of the global construction industry.
One of the comparably new and very innovative construction systems is the use of ETFE film as a transparent building envelope. This system has been first introduced into architecture in 1982 and has since then continuously gained the interest of the construction industry, as it provides massive advantages for large scale transparent roof and façade cladding applications. These advantages lie among others in the technical features of the product, cost-efficiency factors, longevity and the massive reduction of material usage compared to other systems.
Prominent examples of the use of ETFE foil systems in modern architecture are:
a. Eden Project, Cornwall: A massive greenhouse with a UV-transparent shell of ETFE foils
b. Allianz Arena, Munich: Roof and façade provide stunning architecture and LED light
c. Neues Gymnasium, Bochum: Atrium roof for school and social buildings
By now, transparent roofs and facades made of ETFE foils are at a breakthrough point. After more than 40 years, the conservative construction industry has taken this product on as a viable and proven system. The drive for more sustainable and energy-efficient building solutions makes ETFE cladding the new go-to system. And the need to re-think construction in terms of creating sheltered living spaces for more and more people taps into the natural advantages of ETFE cladding materials.
The Vector Foiltec Group has pioneered ETFE foil systems around the world. By now, it is a proven system that many companies provide to an exponentially growing market. The future of architecture needs to cope with the challenge of using less materials, more lightweight solutions and reducing the use of CO2 heavy materials like concrete and steel (1). ETFE foil systems provide all these benefits and more. Also, ETFE foils are fully recyclable, as they are used in their pure form as a single copolymer – a rarity in the sphere of construction products. ETFE foils are chemically stable and do not emit any harmful substances during fabrication, use-life and recycling.
As ETFE foils fall under the category of the PFAS class of materials. Should ETFE foils be prohibited, we see an unjustified and devastating impact on the drive to make construction and architecture more sustainable.

General Comments: There are various applications of PFAS in food contact materials in consumer cookware, amongst others seals, O-rings, gaskets, tubing and pipes in consumer electrical equipment such as coffee machines (mentioned under the sixth bullet point on page 39 of Annex A where consumer cookware is divided in 7 different sub-uses). However, the Impact Assessment for consumer cookware in Annex E focuses exclusively on non-stick coatings (chapter E.2.3.2.2 on alternatives, chapter E.2.3.2.6 on substitution potential, chapter E.2.3.4.2 on impacts on consumers, impacts on society, cost-effectiveness, and practicability and monitorability). This is also reflected in the summary table on the assessment of costs and benefits for consumer cookware and home kitchen appliances (Table E.52 on p. 177 of Annex E) which states in the column “Alternatives” that “There is sufficiently strong evidence that technically and economically feasible alternative non-stick coatings are available for the domestic market, and already have significant market share” and in the row “Conclusion” that “A full ban after a derogation period of 18 months is concluded as feasible for the consumer non-stick coatings market”, not taking into account at all the sub-uses in consumer electrical equipment mentioned above.
In fact, the requirements for tubing and seals with food contact in electrical household appliances like coffee machines regarding temperature stability, pressure stability, chemical resistance (to cleaning and descaling agents) and food compliances are the same as in professional appliances and very similar to the ones for equipment for the industrial food and feed production. Accordingly, there are currently no alternatives available for the majority of the uses in this sub-sector, just as it has been concluded for industrial food and feed production equipment in Annex E.
In addition, even if alternative materials are found that fulfill the aforementioned requirements, it is very unlikely that 1:1 alternatives exist. As a consequence, if the affected components made from potential alternative materials are heavier, larger (e.g. because thicker tubes are necessary to achieve the same pressure stability) or slightly less resistant to pressure or temperature, the entire design of an appliance must be adapted. This will not be possible within the proposed transition period of 18 months, even if suitable alternative materials are found.
Therefore, we request that proposed derogation 6.a in RO2 for fluoropolymers and perfluoropolyethers for the use in food contact materials for the purpose of industrial and professional food and feed production is extended to electrical household appliances.
The environmental impacts of such an extended derogation have already been assessed in chapter E.2.3.3 of Annex E during the assessment of the environmental impacts of the proposed derogation for food contact materials for the purpose of industrial and professional food and feed production: As no data was available for quantifying the amount of additional emissions for this specific derogation, the environmental impacts were evaluated qualitatively in relation to a worst-case additional emission scenario, assuming a full derogation of fluoropolymers for the whole food contact materials and packaging sector. In relation to this reference scenario, which includes the use of fluoropolymers in electrical household appliances, additional emissions of the proposed derogation have been considered to be small. We therefore consider a derogation for fluoropolymers and perfluoropolyethers for the use in food contact materials in electrical household appliances justifiable.

Content: Information on alternatives Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: There has not been provided evidence that indicates that PFAS fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers present environmental toxicity concerns beyond their inherent persistence. Simply associating PFAS fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers with other PFAS types that do raise these concerns does not provide adequate justification for extending the Restriction proposal to include fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers.

Sufficient information is missing on existing PFAS-free alternatives that effectively substitute for fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers in the production of flexible packaging materials. Given the absence of presently viable alternatives and the need for a considerable timeframe to implement any potential solutions throughout the entire supply chain, we advocate for a justified extension of derogation times for food and feed packaging materials as well as for pharma packaging and packaging of medical devices.

Specific applications of PFAS fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers are missing, that are significant for Constantia Flexibles and our supply chains. Consequently, the availability of substitutes for these applications or the required timeline and resources for their widespread adoption across our supply chain have not been considered. Consequently, we are requesting exemptions or derogations for the following applications:
packaging materials for non-sterilised medical devices, packaging materials for pharmaceutical products for human and veterinary use, manufacturing equipment needed to make packaging materials for food, feed, medical devices, pharmaceutical products and other goods and for the equipment needed for the supply of raw materials to our production plants (e.g. vessels, tanks, etc...)

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: sector: Food contact materials and packaging, packaging for pharmaceutical (pharma packaging), medical devices, cosmetic and hygiene articles sub-uses: paper and board packaging, plastic packaging, other packaging applications

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: A significant portion of the PE and PP plastic films collected for recycling currently contain PFAS (fluoropolymers or fluoroelastomers). Plastic recyclers face practical challenges in determining whether the recycled plastic will fall below the 50 ppm limit (total fluorine content) without testing the finished product, which often leads to a high probability of exceeding the limit. Additionally, currently we don't know what happens to the fluoropolymer-based processing aids used for the production in PE and PP films during recycling. So not only the TOF value would have to be checked for recycled material, but also the other two limits for short chain PFAS. This situation will persist for a longer duration than the period during which virgin PE and PP materials are granted a derogation for continued PFAS use. This is because there is a delay until the last of those materials can no longer be reintroduced into the recycling process. To ensure the viability of the plastics recycling industry and to meet the sustainability goals of our sector, we therefore require an exemption or a sufficient long time derogation that allows for an extended transition period in plastic recycling loops.   Similar considerations apply to paper recycling streams. As long as PFAS-containing paper and board materials are introduced into paper recycling streams, recycled paper/board will continue to contain PFAS, potentially exceeding applicable limits. A time derogation is necessary to provide additional time for the paper recycling processes to phase out PFAS or to exempt the output-material from recyclers. Examples for the use of recycled paper/board by Constantia Flexibles include transport packaging and cardboard cores.

5. Proposed derogations: The following PFAS are used by Constantia Flexibles or may be present in our products:  - Fluoropolymers used in Polyolefin films for packaging applications (food contact materials, pharmaceutical packaging, packaging for medical devices, cosmetics and other health care applications) - PFAS-based coatings on fat-resistant paper - PTFE-additives in inks/lacquers   For information on tonnages, see confidential part.  We have no information on the resulting emissions to the environment.

6. Missing uses: Missing uses are: • packaging for pharmaceutical products • packaging for non-sterilised medical devices • manufacturing equipment used in the production of packaging materials for food, feed, medical devices, pharmaceutical products and other goods • equipment needed for the supply of raw materials to our production plants (e.g. vessels and tanks) • flexible polyolefin films for industrial application (e.g. stretch films to fix products on a pallet).

8. Other identified uses: In the Annex XV report, two alternatives have been identified for fluoroelastomer processing aids commonly used in flexible polyolefin-based packaging:  Boron Nitride and PE waxes.  Boron Nitride is not suitable for thin, flexible plastic films due to its inorganic, rigid nature. To achieve the same effect as a fluoropolymer-based processing aid, it needs to be added in larger quantities. Furthermore, it is unsuitable for producing transparent plastic films because it imparts a white color.  Polyethylene waxes have been experimented with, but the results indicated that they were largely ineffective for blow film extrusion of thin, flexible films.  In summary, neither of these alternatives proved to be viable replacements for fluoroelastomer processing aids in our production processes. Without a proper processing aid or with an inadequately functioning one, the produced PE films fail to meet the required technical and optical properties, specifically, transparent films without the undesirable "shark skin" effect (see attached pictures).  It's crucial to note that not only must the flexible films meet all technical and regulatory requirements, but the production process's efficiency must also be acceptable. This includes maintaining an acceptable production speed, avoiding an unacceptable increase in the scrap rate, and ensuring reasonable cleaning rates for the extruder. Otherwise, the production of thin, flexible plastic films would become economically unsustainable.  No alternatives have been mentioned in the Annex XV report for the use of PTFE waxes used as additive in inks and lacquers which are applied on packaging materials.  Generally, finding alternatives for these uses in packaging materials is a technical challenge. We are actively searching for functional alternatives, but this process is time-consuming. It involves development, validation, potential regulatory clearances (e.g., 10/2011/EC), authorisations for use in specific end markets (such as food, feed, medical devices, pharmaceutical products packaging), and implementation throughout the supply chain. For example, the approval process for sterilized packaging may take up to 2 years, as storage tests of the packaging material with the filling good have to be perfomed to check the suitability for long shelf-life products.  For the reasons listed above we request a time derogation of at least EiF + 6.5 years for the use of PFAS in food and feed packaging materials and for packaging materials used for cosmetics and other health care applications.  The change procedures/approval processes for pharma packaging and packaging of medical devices is even more challenging. A big challenge is the time that is needed for the regulatory approval or clearance for these applications in case the packaging system is changed. This requires e.g. new stability tests with the packed drug, time consuming extractable&leachable studies and the approval by authorities. Therefore,  we request a time derogation of at least EiF + 13.5 years for the use of PFAS in pharma packaging and packaging for medical devices.  Polymeric PFAS are used in manufacturing equipment for packaging materials for food and feed, pharmaceutical products, medical devices, and other healthcare items as well as in manufacturing equipment and vessels/tanks of the supplying industry (chemical industry). No alternatives are currently available for these applications, which is very similar to the manufacturing equipment for food and feed for which a derogation of EiF + 6.5 years is mentioned in the Annex XV report. We are requesting the same derogation for manufacturing equipment used for the production of packaging materials.  The same derogation is needed for manufacturing equipment and vessels/tanks of the supplying industry (chemical industry).  A potential ban on fluoropolymers in the production equipment would severely affect our operations. It has to be ensured that obtaining maintenance and repair parts for existing equipment, such as PFAS-embedded gaskets or seals, will be further possible and that supply chains will not be interrupted for theses uses. Otherwise, this would lead to last-time buys and eventually affect the ability to keep existing equipment (and manufacturing lines) running. Given the long service life of the equipment concerned, the huge investments required to replace all affected equipment, and the potential for significant disruption of key supply chains, it would be more appropriate to  even grant a time-unlimited exemption for these uses.

10. Analytical methods: To our current knowledge, there are no available analytical methods specifically designed for the precise quantification of fluoropolymers within materials and articles. The available analytical methods to determine PFAS in articles and materials are limited to volatile and semi-volatile substances, which can be effectively analyzed using liquid chromatography. To measure TF (total fluorine content) or TOF (total organic fluorine content), a procedure involves subjecting the sample to combustion within an oxygen-pressurized bomb (known as bomb calorimetry). After combustion, the fluorine content is determined through either ion chromatography or an ion-selective electrode. However, in cases where a sample cannot be placed inside the bomb calorimeter or cannot be completely combusted, such as with aluminum, it becomes impossible to accurately ascertain the fluorine or TOF content. This presents a significant challenge for enforcing and controlling these limits.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: There is an initial input to this consultation from May 2023.
415803ab-b01e-4cc4-8b85-c6f5393cc32e is the associated reference number..
The present input has been supplemented with additional information.
PFAS are a large and very heterogeneous group of substances and are defined as any substance that contains at least one fully fluorinated methyl (CF3-) or methylene (-CF2-) carbon atom (without any H/Cl/Br/I attached to it) in the Annex XV restriction report.
Due to their different and unique properties (e.g. water-repellent as well as temperature and chemical resistant), the use of many PFAS is crucial in the semiconductor sector, e.g. in the manufacturing process and in the production equipment. They can also occasionally be a component of finished semiconductor products.

A general prohibition on the use of PFAS would currently make semiconductor manufacturing in Europe impossible, as a majority of them cannot be replaced by alternatives according to current knowledge even in long term and it will be extremely difficult, to find chemical substances which are suitable and equivalent to PFAS in terms of their unique properties and which have no unknown or unforeseen hazards. This contradicts the target of the EU and the Member States, formulated in the EU Chips Act, to expand European capacity in semiconductor manufacturing and to strengthen Europe's competitiveness and resilience in semiconductor technologies and applications and also in the net-zero target. Semiconductors play a crucial role in the transition to a sustainable society and economy. Without them, renewable energy, electromobility and secure communication between connected devices are all inconceivable.

The restriction proposal by ECHA provides a potential exemption for semiconductor manufacturing, which would may be applied for 13.5 years from entry into force of the restriction. A temporary exemption from the restriction only makes sense if alternatives are available and this is more than doubtful even after the expiry of the proposed 13.5 years. Without an appropriate exemption, there is a risk that the proposed full restriction of PFAS will worsen the supply of the semiconductor industry with production materials required during semiconductor manufacturing or that these materials will no longer be available.

An appropriate exemption should be granted for the semiconductor manufacturing process, covering the entire semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem and including upstream and downstream supply and value chains. This should not only include the materials and precursors to manufacture the semiconductors. It must also be possible for the customers and users of the semiconductors to incorporate the semiconductors in turn into their products and thus to use the semiconductors over the longer term. Furthermore, the production equipment must not be forgotten, where e.g. also the spare parts supply must be possible in the future, as well as the devices which are necessary for R&D activities like e.g. evaluation boards.

In order not to jeopardize the important goals of the EU Chips Act and not to threaten an essential industrial basis in Europe, a general restriction of PFAS within the framework of the REACH regulation for the semiconductor industry and its supply chains should be avoided under all circumstances to eliminate a locational disadvantage for European semiconductor companies. For a strategic independence of the EU, it must be ensured that semiconductors can continue to be manufactured and sold in Europe and that stable and sustainable supply chains remain in place for this purpose.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Semiconductor products are the key enabler for improved energy consumption and performance across a wide range of everyday technology applications in society. The semiconductor sector depends on various application of materials (gases, solids, liquids) falling in scope of the PFAS definition. Thus, our following comments are related to the uses and sub uses identified in Table 9 in the Annex XV restriction report.  Use sector: Electronics and semiconductor (Annex E.2.11.) Sub uses: Semiconductors / Wires and cables / Coating, solvents and cleaning / Electronic components / Heat transfer fluids / Advanced semiconductor packaging / Photolithography   Use sector: Applications of fluorinated gases (Annex E.2.8.) Sub-uses: Refrigeration / Insulating gas in electrical equipment

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: End-of-life phase of PFAS-containing semiconductor products: Some of our sensor semiconductor products may contain PFAS to provide a safe connection to the environment while still protecting the sensor. In Europe, regulations were enacted years ago to facilitate the recycling of semiconductor products in order to minimize emissions to the environment. These are the WEEE Directive (European Parliament and Council, 2012) for consumer electronics and the ELV Directive (European Parliament and Council, 2000) for vehicles.  End-of-life phase of equipment and articles in semiconductor manufacturing: According to a 2023 ESIA publication, the end-of-life of semiconductor manufacturing sites is well over 25 years. The fundamental need for clean room manufacturing and the use of certain hazardous chemicals, which must also be highly pure, mean that in some areas only fluoropolymers can be used. For this reason, a fab may contain several tons of fluoropolymers in pipe linings, valves, seals such as O-rings, etc. (Source: PFAS Consortium - Articles Working Group, 2023). Due to the long life of fluoropolymers and the long use of semiconductor equipment, the emissions in the end-of-life phase of the PFAS-containing equipment are low compared to the quantities found in a fab. Any waste generated is collected according to the waste code numbers for mixed plastics and sent for proper disposal

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: production-phase: Using PFC gases (perfluorinated compounds) is still essential for semiconductor manufacturing. During these thermally highly demanding processes or also during chamber cleaning, a certain amount of the gas is already converted in the process and decomposed there into less harmful components (https://www.ipcc-nggip.iges.or.jp/public/2019rf/pdf/3_Volume3/19R_V3_Ch06_Electronics.pdf, see Table 6.11 there).  In order to increase reducing the remaining PFC emissions, the semiconductor industry has agreed ambitious targets for many years. For example, abatement tools have been installed on a voluntary basis. These abatement tools usually work with a destruction removal efficiency (DRE) that depends on the PFC used. For example, the PFAS C2F6 has a standard DRE of 0.95 according to Table 6.17 (https://www.ipcc-nggip.iges.or.jp/public/2019rf/pdf/3_Volume3/19R_V3_Ch06_Electronics.pdf). In these abatement tools the remaining PFC gases are further reduced by using high temperatures (e.g. natural gas burners or electric plasma systems) by first destroying the PFC gases in a combined burner/scrubber system through the chemical reaction of combustion, and then scrubbing and neutralizing them through subsequent washing processes. By applying these technologies, PFC emissions to the environment could be impressively reduced over the years.  Waste: The frequently expressed thesis that PFAS are indestructible is incorrect and has been impressively proven wrong by a number of papers. PFAS can be very well destroyed, preferably by incineration or pyrolysis. Conventional waste incinerators usually cover a temperature range of 600-1600 °C (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2095809917300796). At least 1,100 °C for two seconds results in a complete decomposition of most PFAS (Yamada T. et al. 2005) (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S004565350500425X).  Even under state-of-the-art domestic waste incineration conditions, PFAS are converted to inorganic fluoride at a minimum incineration temperature of 850°C (Aleksandrov K. et al. 2019). Investigation of incineration of PFAS substances PFOA, PFHxA, PFOS, recognized as problematic and therefore already regulated, at different temperatures (800 °C, 900 °C, 1000 °C) showed that at higher temperatures of 1000 °C no formation of fluorinated by-products occurred (Residual organic fluorinated compounds from thermal treatment of PFOA, PFHxA and PFOS adsorbed on granular activated carbon (GAC) | https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10163-016-0532-x).

5. Proposed derogations: The European Commission recently adopted a series of proposals aimed at, among other things, shaping EU climate, energy and transport policies to reduce net greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% by 2030 compared to 1990 levels. To achieve this goal, it is essential not only to maintain microtechnology in Europe, but to increase it strongly. The Chips Act of the European Union aims to reach this goal. It recognizes the importance of semiconductors and their manufacturing to achieve the above-mentioned goals. For this purpose, the German Infineon Technology AG has Frontend and Backend production sites in Regensburg and Warstein and Dresden (Germany), Villach (Austria) and Cegled (Hungary).  Semiconductors from Infineon Technology AG help to generate electricity from renewable energy sources. They also offer increased efficiency at all stages of the value chain in the energy sector: in generation, transmission, storage, and in particular, in the use of electricity. They form the basis for the intelligent and efficient use of energy: in industrial applications, power supplies for computers and consumer electronics,  as well as in motor vehicles.  Semiconductor manufacturing is characterized above all by the fact that it mostly takes place under clean room conditions and in closed systems. Any entry of impurities into our productions usually has a devastating effect on the quality of our products and is avoided wherever possible. Due to that the presence of employees in the clean room is reduced to the minimum. Under normal production conditions, there are no measurable emissions at the workplaces.  In general, the semiconductor manufacturing can be divided into two parts - "Frontend" and "Backend". In the Frontend, the raw wafer of silicon is processed, while in the Backend, the finished products are manufactured from the separated chip (circuits).  In the Frontend, PFAS are essential in the following areas: Photolithography and Plasma Etching.  Photolithography: Photolithography is one of the central processes for manufacturing integrated circuits. It involves using an exposure process to transfer the image of a photomask onto a photosensitive photoresist. Subsequently, the exposed areas of the photoresist are dissolved (alternatively, dissolution of the unexposed areas is also possible when the photoresist is cured under light). This creates a lithographic mask that allows further processing by chemical and physical processes, ultimately leading to the microchip integrated circuits. Photoresists and anti-reflective coatings for specific applications also contain mostly PFAS, as their chemical and physical properties (wetting agent and photoactive, combined with chemically inert behavior) are necessary in the exposure process of lithography to achieve the desired process result. Especially the generation of more advanced products with smaller and smaller structures require PFAS. These are, for example, photoacid generators (PAGs, such as sulfonium and iodonium acid salts with fluorinated anions), which are essential components of the chemically amplified resists (CARs) used today. When exposed to ultraviolet (UV) light, they generate so-called superacids, which cause the solubility change of the photoresist. All proven successful PAGs are fluorinated. The PAG content in the CAR is small (order of magnitude 1%, mostly smaller). Due to process control (spin coating, development, stripping or ashing), the main part of PFAS is destroyed or ends up in the solvent waste, which is properly disposed of. Only a very small proportion is ultimately found in wastewater. Top anti-reflective coatings (TARCs) require a very low refractive index, minimal surface energy and excellent barrier properties. All these properties are achieved by using fluorinated copolymers based on styrene, acrylate and methacrylate. At present, there are no suitable substances that can provide all the above-mentioned properties. If they can be developed at all in the future, their possible use in production will certainly take decades, since a large number of parameters will have to be optimized.  Plasma etching: Plasma etching is a material-removing, plasma-assisted dry etching process in which a high-frequency or electrodeless microwave discharge is ignited in a vacuum reactor filled with an etching gas (often low-molecular-weight PFAS), thus generating a highly reactive, etch-active plasma. The resulting plasma reacts with the wafer surface and cleans it or creates structures that have been prepared in previous steps (e.g. lithography). The main criterion for the selection of the etch gas is its ability to form a highly volatile reaction product with the silicon-based wafer surface (silicon or silicon dioxide). Therefore, etching gases that ideally contain fluorine (PFAS like carbon tetrafluoride and octafluorocyclobutane) are generally used when etching structures.  Since the chemical reactivity between fluorine and silicon is very high, the reaction product of the etching reaction is volatile silicon tetrafluoride, which has a high vapor pressure. These reactions can be controlled very well, while other etching gases (e.g. chlorine-containing etching gases) also give volatile silicon tetrachloride, but either react much more uncontrollably or less selectively, thus making it very difficult or in some cases impossible to generate the necessary fine structures on the wafers. Thus, the gaseous PFASs used are extremely difficult to substitute. By far the largest proportion of the PFAS gases used either already react in the plasma chamber or are systematically burned off in the downstream abatement process. This means that only a small proportion of PFASs is emitted via the exhaust air.  PFAS-containing materials are also used in the Backend, which cannot be easily replaced here either.  Adhesives:  PFAS can also be a component of semiconductor products, e.g. in some electrically insulating adhesives, 70-90 wt% filler content of the PFAS Polytetrafluorethylene (PTFE) may be present to reduce stresses. This filler also prevents moisture absorption, which also leads to the prevention of corrosion within the semiconductor product.  The PFAS remains in the product and does not change throughout the service life. At end-of-life, the semiconductor product is sent normally for proper disposal. Therefore, no emissions are observed.  PFAS-containing materials are also used in production equipment because PFAS-containing polymers have unique properties that are mostly not replaceable by other materials. Equipment: In our production, highly aggressive media (e.g. hydrofluoric acid, alkalis) have to be handled in some cases, or also highly pure media (such as ultrapure water). This requires the use of fluorinated polymers in our production equipment throughout the entire production process. Thus, many valves, seals and pipe linings are affected. Replacing all these materials would be a major challenge, since mainly the respective equipment manufacturers have the knowledge about the composition of the individual components / tools. The supply of spare parts could also become a problem. Although there is one of the most important equipment manufacturers, ASML in the Netherlands, many manufacturers are located outside the EU. The use of materials containing PFAS is very widespread, but we have no knowledge of any emissions via wastewater. In the case of equipment disposal, this is done by a certified disposal contractor. There are no other known emission paths.  A special case of semiconductor manufacturing is the production of power semiconductors. Infineon operates such a production site in Warstein. Power semiconductor chips are not intended for consumer use and require embedding in a controllable electrical structure - a power module. In these power modules, several semiconductor chips are mounted on boards and wired to control elements, which enables the conversion of current. Therefore, power modules represent an essential core in electric cars, charging stations, electric trains, wind turbines and solar farms; crucial elements for the green electrification of the EU.  Embedding power semiconductors in power modules that control thousands of volts requires sophisticated PFAS-based assembly techniques to produce safe and durable products. PFAS-related processes for power module assembly include the following: 1. Paste soldering relies on a partially organic paste. It requires thorough cleaning with the PFAS hydrogen fluoride ether (HFE) to remove paste residues that would prevent further assembly steps and fatally damage the sensitive semiconductor during operation. Reliable and complete removal is not possible with alternative cleaning methods. Previous developments to avoid this undesirable and costly cleaning step have not been successful. The failed attempts to establish alternatives to date indicate that a long transition period is required to find alternative methods. 2. In another application, PFASs are used as adhesion promoters to fix subcomponents of power modules before the next permanent assembly steps. Absolute residue-free evaporation of these adhesion promoters at elevated temperatures is critical and can only be guaranteed with chemically inert and non-adhesive PFASs without risk of ignition. 3. The assembly of power modules involves pressure-dependent processes. Whenever materials are permanently pressed together, a non-adhesive PFAS film is required as a demolding aid to allow removal of the components from the press cavity.  4. In another application, the use of PFAS in the manufacture of power modules is attributed to the electrically insulating and non-flammable properties of PFAS. To safely handle current up to 10000 V, defect-free module components are required. Only an initial test under these conditions in an insulating PFAS environmental bath enables a test that can function safely. To date, only chemically inert PFAS can be removed without leaving residues, allowing further assembly of the test components, and an insulating environment allows testing of these voltage classes without fear of ignition.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: A lot of different PFAS (gases, solids, liquids) are used in many applications in the semiconductor manufacturing process. Semiconductor manufacturing is a highly complex process and production times vary depending on the complexity of the products, but on average it can take several years from research and development to the final product.  The complexity of the products requires a smooth and coordinated workflow between the individual processes, whereby the materials used also work together and depend on each other, as is the case also with PFAS. The proven uniqueness of PFAS combined with the proposal to restrict or ban the entire group of substances in the EU would lead to an extremely large and unprecedented challenge for adequate substitution in terms of the required technical performance and the environmental and human health impacts ("Regrettable Substitution"). A majority of PFAS cannot be replaced by alternatives according to current knowledge even in long term and it will be extremely difficult, to find chemical substances which are suitable and equivalent to PFAS in terms of their unique properties and which have no unknown or unforeseen hazards. Thus, for many applications, it requires a great deal of effort and investment in basic research and development to find PFAS-free alternatives. Once a PFAS-free alternative exists and is available, this needs to be implemented and qualified within the associated processes. This process must be carried out again for each possible alternative, this requires both time and may lead to necessary changes (e.g. design requirements and properties of the product, manufacturing process and -equipment). Therefore, a temporary exemption from the restriction only makes sense if alternatives are available and this is more than doubtful even after the expiry of the proposed 13.5 years. For example, in photolithography, one of the major process steps, the potential timeframe for substitution is 15 to 20 years or more. The substitution time to be estimated depends heavily on the application of PFAS and whether a PFAS-free alternative can be found and made available at short notice by global formulators and their upstream chemical suppliers. Without an appropriate exemption, there is a risk that the proposed full restriction of PFAS will worsen the supply of the semiconductor industry with production materials required during semiconductor manufacturing or that these materials will no longer be available. An appropriate exemption should be granted for the semiconductor manufacturing process, covering the entire semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem and including upstream and downstream supply and value chains. This should not only include the materials and precursors to manufacture the semiconductors. It must also be possible for the customers and users of the semiconductors to incorporate the semiconductors in turn into their products and thus to use the semiconductors over the longer term. Furthermore, the production equipment must not be forgotten, where e.g. also the spare parts supply must be possible in the future, as well as the devices which are necessary for R&D activities like e.g. evaluation boards. Semiconductor manufacturing in Europe without the use of PFAS is therefore currently not possible. A general restriction of PFAS without an appropriate exemption would have very negative effects and consequences for European semiconductor companies as well as their suppliers and customers.  A general PFAS ban could have serious negative consequences for the entire industrial manufacturing landscape in Europe. A few months ago, the comparatively harmless shortage in the supply of semiconductors had a serious impact on e.g. the automotive industry, leading to major production reductions and stops. Future investments in Europe depends on legal certainty and the existence of stable supply chains and skilled workers. Infineon commits to Europe as an important business location and thus, e.g. operates a large part of its front-end manufacturing there, where Infineon recently announced plans to expand semiconductor production at its Dresden site with the largest single investment of €5 billion in the company's history.  A restriction on PFAS would have a direct negative impact on our revenue (FY 2022: €3.4 billion in Europe and €14.2 billion worldwide) and employees (FY 2022: 21,703 in Europe and 54,286 worldwide), as production with PFAS is not possible in Europe. The majority of Frontend sites are located in Europe, while the majority of Backend sites are located outside Europe. Since the Frontend sites are the suppliers of the Backend sites, if the Frontends stop production, the Backends would also have to stop production after a short period of time because they would run out of raw materials for their production.

10. Analytical methods: Currently there is no analytical methodology that would be applicable to all individual PFAS compounds as defined by the OECD and provide satisfactory results.  In the meantime, some analytical methods have been tested that can detect a few PFAS species in semiconductor manufacturing wastewater. However, this analysis by liquid chromatography together with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) quickly reaches its limits, since comparative standards are only available for a few substances used. Again, it has not been possible to find an analytical method that can detect all PFAS in a comprehensive manner. Therefore, it is very important to conduct extensive research to find and improve suitable analytical methods so that the semiconductor industry is able to provide analytical evidence that it can comply with the limits (e.g., US EPA 537.1 (modified)). Currently established is the determination of total fluorine in the sample. However, the detection limit here is 50 ppm. This is a value far above all limits (ppb, i.e. one one-thousandth below) that apply to PFAS. The proportion of inorganic fluorine can also be determined with the same accuracy, whereupon the amount of organically bound fluorine (i.e. total PFAS) can be calculated. All this, however, only in the ppm range mentioned above. The PFASs currently readily detectable were C4-C13 species in the aqueous phase (US EPA Draft 1633, EPA method currently under development). For the investigated wastewater from semiconductor manufacturing, the detection limit was about 1 ppt. However, it must be noted that almost all of the species included in the analytical interpretation library are not used at all in semiconductor manufacturing, with Perfluorobutane sulfonic acid (PFBS) being the only exception. Thus, the applicability of this method is mainly limited to the detection of PFAS by-products. Whether the existing laboratory capacity will be even slightly sufficient for the determination of all more than 12000 PFAS in the future may be highly doubted. The preparation of the measurements is relatively time-consuming and thus cost-intensive, which, together with the lack of capacities, is likely to lead to exponential price increases in analysis. It is likely that these increases can only be passed on partially, or not at all, to our globally acting customers. This represents a clear disadvantage for European semiconductor manufacturing in a global view of competition.

Content: Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits
Combined Comments:
General Comments: There is an urgent need to implement a ban on PFAS within the European Union.
First and foremost, the detrimental health effects associated with PFAS cannot be overlooked. Extensive scientific evidence has established the link between PFAS exposure and severe health conditions, including liver and kidney damage, hormonal imbalances, weakened immune systems, and even cancer. Moreover, PFAS have been associated with reproductive issues and developmental disorders in children. The well-being of our citizens should be of paramount concern, and banning PFAS is a significant step towards safeguarding public health.
The environmental impact of PFAS is equally alarming. These substances possess remarkable stability, rendering them resistant to natural degradation processes. Consequently, once released into the environment, PFAS can persist for prolonged periods, contaminating water bodies, soil, and even air. Widespread contamination of water sources and detection of PFAS in drinking water systems across the globe underscore the urgency of addressing this issue. The ecological risks posed by PFAS are extensive, as they accumulate in organisms, adversely affecting aquatic life and disrupting reproductive cycles. The long-term consequences of this bioaccumulation in the food chain further exacerbate the ecological imbalance.
It is important to note that viable alternatives to PFAS exist. By implementing a ban, we can actively promote the development and utilization of safer substitutes in various applications where PFAS have traditionally been employed. This shift will not only protect human health and the environment, but also foster innovation and drive the adoption of environmentally friendly practices.
In light of the substantial evidence regarding the negative health and environmental impacts of PFAS, it is essential to adopt the precautionary principle. This principle dictates that precautionary measures should be taken to prevent potential harm, even in the absence of complete scientific certainty. Implementing a ban on PFAS aligns with this principle and demonstrates our commitment to proactive and responsible decision-making.
In conclusion, I strongly urge the European Union to prioritize the protection of public health and the environment by swiftly implementing a ban on PFAS. The overwhelming evidence of the detrimental health effects, environmental contamination, and the availability of safer alternatives necessitates immediate action. By taking this decisive step, the European Union can lead the way in promoting the well-being of its citizens and safeguarding our fragile ecosystems. It is imperative that the voices of concerned individuals, scientific research, and environmental advocacy be taken into account in formulating policies that prioritize the long-term health and sustainability of our societies.
Thank you for your attention to this matter, and I trust that the European Union will act decisively in implementing a ban on PFAS to protect our health, environment, and future generations.

The geometry is very delicate and flexible, which is why e.g. PEEK material is not an alternative. Although this makes it possible to cover the temperature range, it greatly exceeds the cost framework as well as the ability to produce the delicate structures in question.

Another example, in addition to the application described in the medical sector, is the application of our materials in the automotive sector. In addition to applications in the ESP area, we are also represented here as a sealing ring directly in the brake system. Here, too, there is no possible replacement material that can guarantee both the high temperature requirements and the resistance to the various hydraulic oils.

With around 180 employees and an approximate processing capacity of around 250 tonnes of PTFE per year, we supply 100% of the material affected by the restriction. Furthermore, an outstanding feature of PTFE is its almost universal chemical resistance to a large number of chemicals used in industry.
