Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Information on alternatives Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Thies GmbH & Co. KG is a family-owned machine manufacturer from Coesfeld, with over 130 years of history. The core business is the development, production and related services around pressure vessels used for discontinuous washing, dyeing, bleaching, rinsing or other technical enhancement of textile materials. The company Thies is known to be the leading OEM with regards to innovative and sustainable solutions in textile wet processing for a customer range all over the world. Various features within our machinery, which guarantee high machine life time, low maintenance, low resource consumption and high operator safety regulations are based on the availability of fluoropolymers.

Thies GmbH & Co. KG fully support the goal of no longer allowing PFAS classified as very hazardous (for example: CMR, PBT, vPvB, PMT, vPvM or as ED) to enter the environment. In this respect, regulation of these PFASs classified as very hazardous is fundamentally correct when there is a risk of exposure.

The risk-based approach must be maintained so that uses that do not pose a relevant risk remain possible. The general exemption of fluoropolymers from PFAS regulation shall be made, which are considered "polymers of low concern" according to the OECD definition.
Fluoropolymers and substances, such as monomers and processing aids, which are necessary for fluoropolymer production must be exempted from the ban, provided that safe use is ensured. This is also what the study by the British Health and Safety Executive (HSE) envisages. In short, low risk groups (e.g. fluoroelastomers, fluoropolymers assessed as "polymers of low concern") or uses without relevant risk (e.g. contained uses) must be exempted1.

From the very large PFAS group of substances, fluoropolymers (FP) and PFPE are used in textile machinery construction.
The components made of FP and PFPE are mostly used inside a textile machine. Maintenance and disposal are carried out by qualified personnel.
The planned ban on the use of FP and PFPE in textile mechanical engineering would jeopardize the competitiveness of that industry sector in the EU as well as the technological sovereignty and security of supply of the EU textile industry.
At least, a long time period would be necessary, partly for the qualification and testing of alternative materials in textile mechanical engineering. In addition, a possible switch to other materials requires various certification processes (e.g. when used for pressure vessel components). These certifications can only be tackled by the suppliers after successful testing in textile mechanical engineering.
Therefore, it must be possible to use FP such as PTFE and FKM in the industrial applications in the textile machinery industry in the EU in the long term.

5. Proposed derogations: Please find the data in the confidential attachement

6. Missing uses: Sector and uses Sector: Textile machinery use: fluoropolymer applications in machines produced by the sector  Components made from fluoropolymers (FP) and PFPE are essential functional parts in several types of machines used in the textile industry: -              Textile machines for the production of textile materials (for the production of material for clothing, home textiles and technical textiles), e.g. machines for chemical fibre production, machines for nonwovens production, dyeing machines, impregnating machines, drying machines -              Pressure vessels for thermochemical treatment of textile recycling material in order to enable circular economy -              Fully automatic chemical dispensing systems (used in various industries apart from textile industry: chemical, pharma, food) -              Heat recovery systems for reduction of need for fossil fuel based thermal process energy -              Wastewater treatment technology  FP and PFPE are used in textile machinery due to their temperature, pressure and chemical resistance and sliding properties as -              sealing materials to maintain function, reduction of maintenance and prevent leakage, -              construction and coating materials for components to ensure energy efficiency of machines, material efficiency of components (reduction of wear) and highest fabric quality of processed textiles, -              part of lubricants: Lubricants with PTFE or PFPE are indispensable when used at high temperatures and in harsh conditions,  The sliding properties of PTFE components play a particularly important role in machines for nonwovens, dyeing machines and textile dryers, for example. This is particularly the case with water-saving dyeing machines and machines designed for flexible processing of different materials and carrying out different finishing processes. Both are among the core competencies of European manufacturers.  PTFE has been evaluated as "polymer of low concern". PTFE has been shown to be chemically stable, non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water soluble and non-mobile2. Furthermore, Henry et al. (2018) declare all fluoropolymers to be polymers of low concern (for these reasons, fluoropolymers are also approved, for example, as materials for food contact or in medical technology). In addition, fluoropolymers are used in textile machines in most cases inside the machines. They are replaced (spare parts case) or disposed of (dismantling of the machine) by skilled personnel.  On the one hand, FP in textile machines do not have any significant impact on the environment and people. On the other hand, there are no technically and economically feasible alternatives at EiF. Therefore, the use of FP in textile machines should be out of the scope of the PFAS regulation. If this will not be agreed, a transition period of 18 months and a 12-year derogation is necessary (i.e. until 2040).   2 Henry, B. J; Carlin, J. P; Hammerschmidt, J. A; Buck, R. C; Buxton, L W.; Fiedler, H.; Seed, J.; Hernandez, O. A Critical Review of the Application of Polymer of Low Concern and Regulatory Criteria to Fluoropolymers. Integr. Environ. Assess. Manage. 2018, 14 (3), 316-334.  a)            The annual tonnage and emissions and type of PFAS associated with the relevant use.  Due to their price, FP and PFPE are only used in textile machines where it is absolutely necessary.  For information about components, that are used in textile machines, please see the confidential attachment.   b)           The key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use  In addition to the key functionalities mentioned at the beginning, there are further reasons for the relevant use in dyeing machines, for example, with regard to sustainable textile production: -              PTFE semi-finished products ensure there a sliding and gentle contact with the textile fabric in ecologically important treatments with very little water and process chemicals. In the past, machines were flooded with so much water that the fabric floated during the process and there was no need for PTFE surfaces. By developing resource-saving and ecological processes, the use of water, energy and chemicals could be reduced by about 2/3. For example, in applications with little water (low filling level), the PTFE fabric slide is used to treat sensitive fabrics with high running smoothness, low abrasion in temperature ranges up to 140°C. Without the PTFE fabric slide, such an application would not be possible; much more water would be required for the sliding film. -              For a functioning circular economy, highly flexible textile machines are required that can process the recycled materials as gently as possible.  More detailed justifications why FP and PFPE are indispensable components in textile machines are given in the confidential attachment.   c)            The number of companies in the sector estimated to be affected by the restriction  The planned ban on the use of FP and PFPE in textile machinery would jeopardize the competitiveness of companies in that EU industry sector as well as the technological sovereignty and security of supply of the EU textile industry.  The estimated numbers of companies are given in the confidential attachment.   d)           The availability, technical and economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives  For many years, the core competencies of German textile machinery have included energy and resource efficiency as well as machines and processes for the production of textile materials that meet the highest quality standards. This applies not only to materials for the production of apparel and home textiles, but also to technical textiles as well as machines for textile recycling, wastewater treatment, heat recovery and chemical dosing systems.  To be able to offer this performance level to customers in the EU and worldwide, the use of FP and PFPE for certain machines and processes is necessary to ensure quality and efficiency in the textile industry (as explained above and in the confidential attachment).  There are limited alternatives to the use of FP and PFPE with considerable disadvantages: -              Possible alternatives for PTFE suffer from the fact that they are always inferior in at least one performance property, such as temperature resistance, temperature range or availability. This goes with early replacement needs, additional energy consumption and loss of quality of the processed textile material. -              Inconsistent and unreliable long-term mechanical integrity of other materials than PTFE do not meet the requirements of the textile industry (e.g. high velocities, the required long service life, high flexibility in production processes). Other design solutions – if even possible – would be associated with less flexibility and higher costs. Both cannot be considered as an alternative. -              For FKM, too, there are yet no alternatives in terms of their chemical and thermal resistance; they are not expected even in the medium term. -              Since PTFE and FKM are some of the most expensive materials, they are used in textile machinery only where there is a technical necessity.  e)            For cases in which alternatives are not yet available, information on the status of R&D processes for finding suitable alternatives, including the extent of R&D initiatives in terms of time and/or financial investments, the likelihood of successful completion, the time expected to be required for substitution (including any relevant certification or regulatory approvals) and the major challenges encountered with alternatives which were considered but subsequently disregarded.  It is hoped that new materials and coatings will come onto the market in the next few years so that textile machinery manufacturers will be able to use them for some components as alternative material. Qualification of alternative materials for FP and PFPE requires extensive testing and even longer trials for component testing and application engineering. However, regarding parts like for example seals, shut-off flaps and valves no alternatives are in sight.  i.             the type and magnitude of costs associated with substitution  If the EU were to implement the complete ban on all PFAS substances planned in the near future without exceptions for the textile machinery industry, textile machinery manufacturers would be faced with a great deal of additional work in R&D and application technology in the short term. The efforts in R&D have already risen sharply due to the supply chain problems caused by the Corona crisis and the Ukraine war, and still remain high. The additional effort required for material qualification, testing and trials would lead to a doubling of costs approximately due to the higher staffing levels required for R&D and technical center. Also in view of the non-given risk of PTFE, the predominantly medium-sized textile machinery industry in Germany (and Europe) should be granted a longer transition period for the realization of these R&D tasks.  ii.            the time required for completing the substitution process  In addition to a transition period of 18 months, a 12-year derogation is necessary (i.e. until 2040).  A transition period of 18 months is too short to develop alternatives for the required PFAS applications in the textile machinery industry. A period of several years is already required to test possible alternatives for functionality, safe application and textile-technological conditions of use. A possible conversion to other materials requires various certification processes (e.g. for pressure vessels). These certifications can only be tackled by the suppliers after successful testing in textile machinery.                  iii.           information on possible differences in functionality and the consequences for downstream users and consumers  Differences in functionality as explained under d). The service life of the parts varies depending on the type of machine and the textile processes carried out by the operator.   f)            information on the socio-economic impacts for companies If available, please provide the annual value of EU sales and profits of the relevant sector, and employment numbers for the sector.  Maintaining of competitiveness of European textile machinery industry and jobs in the EU The textile machinery industry has strong roots in the EU, especially in Italy and Germany. Besides, there is a significant industry in Belgium, France, The Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Sweden. Apart from local textile machine manufacturers in the Czech Republic, engineering companies in this country and in Bulgaria act as sub-contractors / extended workbench partners.  Production, placing on the market and putting into service of the parts mentioned in the confidential attachment would no longer be possible in the EU after a ban of FP and PFPE. The machines that need these indispensable parts could no longer be manufactured in the EU.  The additional high R&D costs explained under i) would put the predominantly medium-sized companies in the textile machinery industry at a disadvantage compared to non-EU suppliers. This would mean additional burdens to the already existing supply chain/sourcing problems and current shortage of skilled labor. A derogation until 2040 would permit a longer period for R&D.  Market surveillance cannot prevent non-EU import of textile machinery with FP components: There is no standardized analysis method to detect products containing PFAS. Thus, neither the import into the EU of FP and PFPE spare parts separately nor inside textile machines could be prevented. For example, Chinese manufacturers of man-made fibre equipment and dyeing machines would therefore be able to supply them with PFAS parts to customers in the EU without any problems. This would mean a distortion of competition for EU textile machine manufacturers.  For availabe statistical data please see the information in the confidential attachement.   Maintaining of competitiveness of European textile industry and jobs in the EU The Industrial Strategy of the EU values the textile industry as one of 14 strategic industrial ecosystems of the EU. The industry not only supplies the population with clothing, but also produces technical textiles for the medical sector, among other things, in addition to household and home textiles.  The EU Commission wants to make the European textile industry not only sustainable but more crisis-proof and resilient. The textile sector, especially dyeing and drying companies, are strongly affected by the high energy costs. The industry in the EU should not be saddled with additional costs and burdens. A ban of FP and PFPE use in textile machines would cause additional costs as a result of lower functionality of the affected components and machines.  The spare parts demand for machines on the market could not be covered from the EU: The EU textile industry would no longer be able to have the repair of machines already in use in the EU carried out with original FP and PTFE spare parts. It would have to accept losses in quality and efficiency or would try to source the spare parts in non-EU countries. Neither of these can be in the interest of the legislator. Non-EU textile companies are able to continue using FP and PFPE in textile machines and could gain significant competitive advantages.  A derogation until 2040 would permit to maintain production quality and costs in the textile industry and reduce the risk of job losses.

As it is industrial waste, temperatures >800°C are reached for more than 3 seconds and the fluoropolymer components are mineralized. These are converted into CaF2. Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Org. name: Robert Bosch GmbH - fuel cell and electroyser business unit
Combined Comments:
General Comments: This comment covers products and processes in the responsibility of the fuel cell and electrolyser area of Robert Bosch GmbH (PS-FM).
Please see in conjunction with Bosch input under 8fc8d7c5-213f-47de-b55a-b0ecede82a97
We would like to clarify that we fully agree with the intention to reduce PFAS in our environment to the greatest possible extend, reflecting the risks per respective PFAS subgroup.
Electrolyser and fuel cell technology are core elements of a hydrogen economy.  Due to the demanding requirements of hydrogen,  both technologies entirely rely on fluoropolymers (considered a PFAS subtype) for safe and reliable operation. For these highly specialised materials no alternatives with feasible substitution potential are foreseeable today. As hydrogen plays a central role in a decarbonized future energy system the use of fluoropolymers is crucial for the European pathway towards climate neutrality (Ref 1&2).

Henry (2019) and Korzeniowski (2022) (Ref 3&4) show that most fluoropolymers meet the OECD criteria to be defined as ‘polymers of low concern’ (PLC).  They are not water soluble, toxic and bioavailable and as such do not pose any substantial risk to human health or the environment. The restriction proposal’s approach of grouping fluoropolymers with all other PFAS types must be revised.

Our information from fluoropolymer producers indicates that fluoropolymer production is highly controlled and conforms to responsible manufacturing conditions. Furthermore, fluoropolymers in fuel cells and electrolysers remain in a confined industrial environment, where emissions and contact with workers or consumers are negligible. Due to their high initial price, achieving circularity is inherently encouraged and object to intensive research.

Instead of banning these essential, high-performing and low-concern substances, regulatory action should focus on monitoring, reporting and limiting potential PFAS emissions at all life-stages (manufacturing, use and end-of-life). Fluoropolymer production and use shall therefore be exempted from an overall PFAS restriction.

Incentivising best practices for the manufacturing, use and end-of-life stages of fluoropolymers, implementing circular economy practices and initiating research into alternative substances (fluorinated or not) that could ideally surpass the bandwidth of relevant fluoropolymer key performance indicators (KPI), or at least reach a comparable level should be the way forward. The current restriction proposal would push the fuel cell technology back to approximately TRL 2  (Ref 5) in terms of power density and durability.

Hydrogen Europe quantified what the consequences could be in terms of employment and investment for the European hydrogen industry.
For Bosch, this would put investments of more than 2 bn€ and more than 1200 jobs in development and production at risk in the period up 2030.

Global market distortion in case of an inadequate restriction also needs to be considered, as producers of fuel cells and electrolysers outside the EU – not covered by the restriction –  could gain significant competitive advantage.
The restriction proposal incomprehensively differentiates between PEM fuel cell and PEM electrolyser. Technically, all the arguments that justify an exemption or derogation for PEM fuel cell are also valid for PEM electrolyser as only the physical process is reversed. Possibly PEM electrolyser were deemed to be easily replaceable by other types of electrolysers. It is correct, how ever, that PEM electrolysers due to their uncontested performance in dynamic operation, are indispensable for an electricity grid relying on volatile renewable energy. We therefore call for PEM electrolysis to be reflected by the restriction proposal in the same way as PEM fuel cell.
Table E.134 also suggests that PEM fuel cells consist of individual, modular components (MEA, GDL, MPL and gaskets&seals). Physical requirements of these components are mutually dependent and define their respective specifications and system performance. There is no simple drop-in substitute for a component as a systemic re-development and optimization of cell, stack and balance of plant components is inevitable once a component is substituted. Even the gaskets in the harsh chemical conditions of fuel cell operation need to be durable and must not release decay products that poison the membrane and catalyst.
PFAS free electrodes currently only exist as technology concepts, which corresponds to TRL 2. The electrolyser or fuel cell system would consequently fall back on the level of the least developed component. It typically takes five years to bring a technology to TRL6 if the technology concept proofs to be viable. Other wise, the development clock is reset. Currently there is the risk, that no substitute for fluoropolymers PEM electrodes proofs to be viable. To promote a technology that is part of a complex system with many functional dependencies to TRL9 takes minimum another five years, as this requires adaption and redevelopment of additional components in the system. To achieve industrialization and market readiness with established and ramped-up supply chains another five years are required. A lead time of at least 15 years is thus justified for any restriction on fuel cell or electrolyser core components. Since the success of a technology development starting from TRL 2 can not be guaranteed, an exemption with regular review is the appropriate option.
It must be noted that restricting the use of fluoropolymers outside the stack in sealings, coating, valves and lining components all along the hydrogen infrastructure, will cause spill-over effects that can still jeopardise the European hydrogen industry.
It was mentioned by ECHA during the April 5 Q&A session that a derogation of a use brings about the same derogation for the entire upstream value chain of that use (including the use of monomers and polymerisation aids in the case of fluoropolymers). This must be clearly stated in the restriction dossier for legal certainty.
A general ban of substances which are necessary within the synthesis of ionomer materials would be equal to the ban of ionomer materials in general and PFSAs in specific.
Synthesising fluoropolymers like the Perfluoroalkane sulfonic acids (PFSAs) requires several small fluorinated molecules (Ref 6) as precursors or processing aids for the process.
As two of many possible processing aids for the microemulsion polymerization, substances like ammonium perfluorooctanoate and low molecular weight perfluoro polyether oils (i.e. Galden®) are mentioned here.
Necessary monomers include several perfluorinated vinyl ethers such as perfluoro butanesulfonyl fluoride vinyl ether, perfluoro-4-(fluorosulfonyl) butoxylvinyl ether or perfluoro(4-methyl-3,6-dioxa-7-octene-1-sulfonyl fluoride)vinyl ether, to name the most relevant.
Even in case of a derogation or exemption for a single application the consequences on the upstream value chain might be severe as business cases are impacted and production might be discontinued.
Clarity is also needed concerning spare parts. To allow for continued repair and maintenance we call for the “repaired as produced” principle, as the competitiveness would deteriorate rapidly if technology cannot be utilised up to the intended operation time.
Considering the low risk profile of fluoropolymers, the lack of alternatives and the potential socio-economic impact, we request that the production and use of fluoropolymers shall be exempted from the overall PFAS restriction.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: • Energy sector

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Producers of fluoropolymers are subject to rigorous environmental standards strictly controlling emissions. During further production steps any PFAS containing material that did not become part of the product is treated by the standard waste disposal process and thus incinerated. The use of electrolysers and fuel cells results to our knowledge in low, negligible or no PFAS emissions. The findings of a Master thesis indicate that fluorinated organic components accumulate at the fuel cell electrodes and cannot be detected in the condensate (Ref 7). This, however, is object of ongoing research which PS-FM pursues in cooperation with Bosch’s corporate research and external research institutes. PS-FM currently also joins a data gathering exercise across the whole hydrogen industry coordinated by Hydrogen Europe, that will provide robust, sufficient data supporting the claim that the amount of PFAS emissions in the effluent water or in the surrounding equipment is negligible. The goal is to provide results in a second submission to this ECHA public consultation in September, before the ECHA consultation phase deadline.  Concerning end of life PFAS emissions, please refer to our answer to question 2(b) of this questionnaire.  Incineration is currently the standard waste treatment for PFAS-containing material in the PEM fuel cell or electrolyser. Exhaust gases are treated at the highest standards and in line with EU and local legislation, and there is no indication that PFAS remains after incineration (Ref 8). There is currently no EU-level legislation on PFAS emissions regarding incineration. A binding standard on this should be a regulatory priority, rather than a complete ban on the materials.  At the end of life of fuel cell vehicles, fuel cells are dismantled, modules are removed and after that the stack itself is dismantled to collect the cells. The cells are then - as described above - incinerated to recycle the platinum group metals (PGMs), while the ionomers are fully destroyed resulting in hydrogen fluoride (HF) emissions only. HF emissions are then captured and treated, whilst the remnants are also measured against rigorous environmental standards.  Today no comprehensive PFAS emission data exist – hence there is need for a monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) system. Due to overwhelming economic PGM imperative, PEM fuel cells and electrolysers will be recycled specifically when sufficient end of life volumes are reached. Close to 100% of platinum recyclability can be reached (Ref 9). Additionally, fluoropolymer recycling could be another option. There are research tracks underway aimed at regaining functional ionomers through recycling. While precious metals separation from the membrane is an established process, right now the ionomers are altered so far that they cannot be used again in the production of new fuel cells.  As a nascent market, the recycling ecosystem for fuel cells and electrolysers is currently under development. This development of recycling of both PGMs and fluoropolymers could be jeopardised by the PFAS restriction proposal, as a market for secondary material would disappear.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The high value of the PGM contained in the MEA currently ensure that fuel cells and electrolysers do not go to landfill but enter recycling. To recover more substances besides only PGM is object of intense research. Information on this is provided by Hydrogen Europe and does not need to be restated here. The effectiveness of incineration to eliminate a PFAS like PTFE was recently documented in a peer-reviewed study by Aleksandrov et al. (2019, Ref 8). The study found that the combustion of PTFE under typical waste incineration conditions (municipal level) with Best Available Techniques (BAT) is essentially transformed to carbon dioxide and hydrofluoric acid. They thus concluded that the municipal incineration of PTFE should therefore be considered an acceptable form of waste treatment. The study confirms what was earlier found for fluorotelomers as well (Ref 10&11).

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Information provided by Hydrogen Europe

5. Proposed derogations: To provide an upper estimate of the tonnage of PTFE and PFSA required for fuel cell applications in the years until 2030, current state of the art cells can be analysed and used as calculation basis. This approach neglects the ongoing continuous development on the technology. It is also meaningful to differentiate PFAS in the cell gaskets from that in MEAs and GDLs, since the later ones are those where performant substitutes are not foreseen. Bosch’s assessment basically confirms the figures stated by Hydrogen Europe, where 41,67t/GW are stated for the gasket and 5,83t/GW for MEA and GDL. Our own analysis on competitor as well as our own stack results in 5t/GW for MEA and GDL. On the MEA and GDL side improvements up to 20% until 2030 are considered feasible. Bosch’s specific sealing concept allows for drastically lower (at least one order of magnitude less) gasket material requirement per stack than indicated by Hydrogen Europe.  Table 1 indicates the worldwide demand in fuel cell power according to Bosch expectation, which clearly is more optimistic concerning the role of fuel cells than IEA’s. This scenario results 2023 up to 2030 in ~1400 tonnes of PFAS in MEA and GDL. Year:2023;2024;2025;2026;2027;2028;2029;2030 FC power [GW]:5;8;14;22;35;48;64;80 PFAS [t] MEA & GDL:25;41;69;112;173;241;321;402  (evt. deviations due to rounding) Table 1: Worldwide demand in fuel cell power and resulting tonnage of PFAS use  The same estimate can be done for PEM electrolyser. Hydrogen Europe stated a PFAS demand of 12,5t/GW. Our own benchmark leads us to 7,5t/GW which is already a substantial improvement.  Table 2 indicated the worldwide demand in PEM electrolyser power according to Bosch expectation. This scenario results 2023 up to 2030 in ~550 tonnes of PFAS. Year:2023;2024;2025;2026;2027;2028;2029;2030 ELY power [GW]:0,7;2,0;3,1;4,4;7,0;12,5;17,3;28,5 PFAS [t] MEA & GDL:5,1;14,6;22,2;32,4;50,7;91,1;126,2;207,8 (evt. deviations due to rounding) Table 2: Worldwide demand in electrolyser power and resulting tonnage of PFAS use in PEM stacks  Due to the extended lifetime of fuel cells and electrolysers, there is only negligible end of life emissions to be expected before 2030 and the emissions during use phase which are orders of magnitude lower according to our knowledge as stated in question 2(a).  Overall PFAS emissions from fuel cells and electrolysers are by orders of magnitude lower than those assumed in the restriction proposal. This applies even more if emissions are narrowed down to PFAS from MEA and GDL!

8. Other identified uses: Additional input on alternatives in PEM electrolysers and PEM fuel cells: • Membrane o Ample information provided by Hydrogen Europe,  please refer to their contribution to this consultation o Bosch findings on PFAS-free substitutes is provided in Attachment 1&2a.  • Electrodes o Ample information provided by Hydrogen Europe,  please refer to their contribution to this consultation  o Bosch findings on PFAS-free substitutes is provided in Attachment 2b&3.  • Gas Diffusion Layer (GDL) o Ample information provided by Hydrogen Europe,  please refer to their contribution to this consultation  o Bosch findings on PFAS-free substitutes is provided in Attachment 4.  • Gasket o Ample information provided by Hydrogen Europe,  please refer to their contribution to this consultation  In essence, the material properties of perfluorinated polymers are unique and impossible to be replaced in the foreseeable future. Restrictions on fluoropolymers (mainly PTFE, ePTFE and PFSA) would make applications of water electrolysis & fuel cell technologies unfeasible, as it would dramatically reduce their service life, efficiency and robustness. Such lowering of the performance would drastically slow down the ramp up of this nascent hydrogen industry, potentially eliminating many industrial players in that business field and jeopardising both our climate objectives and industrial competitiveness.  Performance of all polymeric alternatives, such as that of hydrocarbon membranes, is still very low because they suffer from reduced thermal and chemical stability, reduced efficiency (e.g., higher ionic resistance) and/or inapplicable mechanical properties and have high deterioration rates and short life expectancies. Even if there is potential with respect to a single specific requirement the complete performance is no match to the material with fluoropolymers. Status of R&D, as described above, has shown that there is no business case for building electrolysers or fuel cells based on hydrocarbon membranes.

10. Analytical methods: As mentioned in our response to question 2(b) monitoring system for PFAS emissions is missing. A binding monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) system, ideally harmonised across industry and Member States, should be established and implemented. Where detected, PFAS emissions should be abated. This can be a far more effective tool in dealing with PFAS than a blanket restriction. Research in appropriate analytics of PFAS is required and PS-FM will engage in that research.

Content: Information on alternatives
Combined Comments:
General Comments: This comment covers the development of an alternative for fluoropolymers used in gas diffusion layers and microporous layers for electrochemical devices, specifically PEM hydrogen fuel cells.

Fuel cells are pivotal devices in the envishioned hydrogen economy of the European Union. Within these cells, fluoropolymers are integral to several components, including the membrane, gas diffusion layer, microporous layer and gaskets. Within the gas diffusion layer and microporous layer, fluoropolymers are used as a hydrophobizer and binding agent and facilitate water management in the cell.

It is known that the hydrophobicity of the GDL and MPL deminishes over the lifetime of a fuel cell, suggesting degradation of the PTFE polymer [ref. 1 and 2]. This degradation is particularly concerning for mobile applications, where it could lead to the release of PTFE or short-chain derivates into the soil, but it is also relevant for stationary applications. Aside from long-term operation, PTFE and more harmful derivatives can leach during incidents (e.g., device fire) or during improper decommissioning.

In our laboratory, we are developing an environmentally friendly alternative to PTFE for use as a hydrophobizer and binder in the gas diffusion layer and microporous layer of fuel cell devices. The coatings can also be relevant for applications in other electrochemical devices (cathode PTL of a PEM electrolyzer, CO2 electrolysis) or for use-cases in technical textiles, carbon fiber treatment, or other non-stick coating applications. We demonstrated that similar extrinsic (hydrophobic) contact angles are achievable with the new coatings compared to PTFE dipcoated samples, both when wetting with water and when wetting with a 20 wt% EtOH mixture.

The coatings are currently undergoing testing in lab-scale fuel cell devices (5 - 25 cm2) at technology readiness level 3-4. If regulatory requirements and market demand necessitate, we aim to bring these eco-friendly coatings to market as an alternative to PTFE. While we are actively working towards commercialization, we anticipate a development timeline of approximately 3-4 years to establish an industry-scale process and validate the coating's durability at timescales relevent for commercial fuel cell operation.

Further investigation is required to ascertain the long-term stability of these novel coatings, ensuring their reliability and effectiveness as sustainable alternatives to traditional fluoropolymers. We are expected to have more details in early 2024.

References on fluoropolymer degradation during fuel cell operation:
1. Wu, J. et al. A review of PEM fuel cell durability: Degradation mechanisms and mitigation strategies. J. Power Sources 184, 104–119 (2008).
2. Schulze, M., Wagner, N., Kaz, T. & Friedrich, K. A. Combined electrochemical and surface analysis investigation of degradation processes in polymer electrolyte membrane fuel cells. Electrochim. Acta 52, 2328–2336 (2007).

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Energy sector (Annex E.2.12.) - gas diffusion layer and microporous layer for electrochemical devices

5. Proposed derogations: Ca. 300 gram of fluoropolymer is used in a 160 kWnet heavy-duty fuel cell stack, assuming an average of 10 wt.% loading (typically GDLs have a PTFE loading of 5-30% and MPLs a PTFE loading of ~20 wt%). This results in 1.7 t/GW of fuel cell deployment. The emissions to the environment are heavily dependent on the operational conditions of the devices and under normal operation can be low.

Content: Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: This commentary concerns polymer optical fibre (POF) and optical fibers weaving solutions for lighting applications in health, automotive, safety, environment, communication and architecture.

The patented Lightex® technology uses optical fiber to obtain luminous optical fiber textile . However the use of fluorinated polymer is limited to gain of the optical fiber textile.  The manufacturing process of the textile consists of plastic optical fibers (FO; polymethylmethacrylate) around which textile yarn are wound. The FOs have an average diameter of about 500 µm. The core of the FO is a polymethylmethacrylate resin with an average diameter of 480 µm, coated with a 10 µm fluoropolymer. All FOs were collected at one end into an aluminum connector. These fibers are then connected to a light emitting diode (LED).

The role of this polymer is essential to maintain the optical properties of the optical fiber and  Fluorinated Polymer cannot be substituted today by any other material due to the specific requirement needed for the cladding in polymer optical fibre for optical signal transmission. It is mandatory to ensure a required and guaranteed stable luminous performance of the textile for the entire lifetime.The alternative according to our knowlage their does not exist yet but as soon as a alternative will be developed, we will need a transitional stage to validate the lightex performance and its durability.  This time estimated at  least 5 years of optmization once the alternative optical fiber will be proposed.  Regarding the release part : generraly realising of fluorinated polymer in the domain of textile is principaly due to the step of washing textile. For the majority of our applications the fabric is not washed because it is used for technical applications and therefore the risk of release hardly exists at all.

Thus we would like optical fibers with a PFAS coating to be exempted from this regulation because of their unique properties which cannot be replaced by other materials. We also want to create a new line in table 9 (annex XV): "Optical fiber" categories.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Our comment applies to the following sectors: - Home textiles - Professional apparel - Technical textiles - Medical - Vehicle  However, knowing that we use optical fibers as a raw material for the creation of our fabrics for the applications listed above, we would like a new sector to be created: "Optical fiber".  In fact, in the current version of Annex XV in “Table 2. PFAS main applications and sub-uses”, cables and wires are only mentioned in the table of sub-use of the section electronics and semiconductions (page 54). Since Polymer Optical Fibre is used in various applications like data cable, light-pipe, sensors, lighting and various sectors as e.g. medical devices, industrial devices and systems, construction products (e.g. lighting, light guide) and semiconductors (optical on-board data transmission, signal coupling etc…) we would like to recommend to create a main application optical fiber.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: We do not manufacture optical fiber. Concerning the phase of use we can distinguish two stages. The first corresponds to the weawing and the assembly in our premises and the second to the use by our customers. In both cases there is no emission during the use phase since we do not wash the products which have a technical use. Our textile products based on fiber optics have a lifespan of more than 15 years.  We cannot give a percentage at the end of its life given our low textile production. In order to obtain the the lighting textile which is a mix of textile yarn and optical fiber our annual consumption is 1 ton of optical fiber and the amount of PFAS used in the cladding of the POF is not more than 2% of optical fiber weight. The number of optical fiber reaching the end of their life is therefore much lower than these values.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: At present our scrap waste is treated by incineration. This may change in the future and this what we are looking for. During our participation in eco-design days, we asked waste managers about the possibility of recycling luminous fabrics at the end of their life. Their answer was that given the very low volume of annual waste, it is useless to set up a special mode of treatment or recycling.

5. Proposed derogations: Our annual consumption of optical fiber that contains PFAS is one ton. The amount of PFAS used in POF is less than 2%wt thus, the values become less than 0.02 T

6. Missing uses: Our suppliers have been working for some time on the search for alternative materials for the clad but no adequate alternative has been found until today. The role of this polymer is essential to maintain the optical properties of the optical fiber and  Fluorinated Polymer cannot be substituted today by any other material due to the specific requirement needed for the cladding in polymer optical fibre for optical signal transmission. Given the low rate of use (0.02T) and the current lack of alternatives, we would like a derogation for our application. If this is not accepted, we will have to cease our activity and therefore lay off all our employees. The activity of some of our customers and partners whose activity is based on our luminous textiles will also risk stopping in areas such as health and transport.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: At this time there is no alternative available.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Information on alternatives Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: This consultation submission supplements VDMA comment with reference number 4471 from the 2023/06/06 posted in the comments part 20.
The VDMA represents more than 3,600 German and European mechanical and plant engineering companies.
Scope: A broad chemical scope of the proposal. For the majority of PFAS no risk assessment has been taken. Although article 68 of the REACH Regulation stipulates: substances posing an unacceptable risk to human health, or the environment may be regulated under restrictions. A differentiated approach for different risk profiles of PFAS is needed. Not all PFAS pose an unacceptable risk that would justify a restriction. Therefore, individual substance groups, such as the fluoropolymer group, must be exempted from the restriction proposal altogether. Fluoropolymers are safe in use. They do not present significant toxicity concerns, cannot degrade into other PFAS, and are not “bioavailable”, “bioaccumulative” or water soluble.
Many uses and sub-uses have not been considered so far. Only a few and mostly very specific time-limited exemptions for industrial uses (e. g. refrigerants or lubricants in specially defined applications) have been proposed. Kindly find further information on missing uses in the attachment (Section IV).
The machinery and equipment manufacturing industry is missing as a sector in the restriction proposal. At the same time PFAS and PFAS-containing materials are needed here whenever extreme conditions (high or low temperatures, high frictional resistance, aggressive/corrosive/toxic chemical conditions, or a combination of these) prevail. Therefore, most existing industrial uses (e. g. seals, valves, pipes, gaskets) as well as future technologies (e. g. fuel cell, water electrolysis, heat pump, solar system) often do not have equivalent alternatives to the expensive PFAS.
It is necessary to distinguish applications in the consumer sector (B2C) from those in the B2B sector. Industrial actors can ensure that PFAS, PFAS-containing materials and products are handled professionally throughout the entire life cycle through professional risk management.
The lack of current information obligation for PFAS-substances (including IUPAC names, CAS numbers, EU numbers) leads to major challenges identifying the affected parts or technologies in the wide and often international supply chain of the machinery and equipment manufacturing industry.
In terms of circularity and sustainable products the issue of repairs is not addressed. As machines, equipment or plants are built to last for decades. Without derogation for spare, wear and used parts, a repair or a regular replacement of wear parts in long-lasting products, such as the replacement of seals or hoses in industrial plants or wastewater treatment plants, would no longer be possible.
