Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Description of analytical methods Information on alternatives Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: This submission covers a specific use in lithium ion batteries.

Fluorinated substances, including PFAS and inorganic fluorine, are used in various ways in Li-ion batteries.

A new develpment is the use of certain PFAS substances as additives to Li ion battery electrolytes that serve to extend the life of the batteries. These additives will increase lifetime of batteries by a factor of 2. In this application, the PFAS substance is mostly consumed, and is no longer present as "PFAS" at the end of life of the battery. Provisions for dealing with fluorine substances are already in place for battery recycling, which will eliminate any residual PFAS that was not consumed during battery use.

Thus, there should be a time-unlimited or permanent derogation for PFAS used in Li-ion battery electrolytes. Without such a derogation, the EU would forego an important development furthering the energy goals of the Green Deal, even though this use in the electrolytes would not cause any PFAS emissions.

While it would be theoretically possible to limit the derogation to the particular type of PFAS additive, in view of the inherent danger of fires that enforcement could face when trying to gain samples of the electrolyte from completed batteries, it would be more expedient to simply derogate the use of PFAS in the electrolytes as such. Inasmuch as current Li-ion battery recycling processes will convert any PFAS in the electrolyte to inorganic fluorine, which is then captured by absorbants, a simple derogation covering the use and any substances and mixtures destined for the use in Li-ion battery electrolytes would be sufficient."

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Automotive lithium-ion batteries  Electrolyte for lithium ion secondary battery

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Emissions in the end-of-life phase:  ・Manufacturing stage　0%(0t) ・Using stage　0%(0t) ・End of life (Emissions to the environment at the time of disposal)　0% (0t) The reasons are as follows.  Manufacturing:   No release of the PFAS additives into the environment due to high b.p. >90℃, with manufacture and  handling in closed systems.  No release during use. EVs (electric vehicles) and plug-in hybrid vehicles (PHVs) are highly safe because they are designed to prevent a large amount of electrolyte from flowing out of the battery body even if a collision occurs, mainly due to the fire hazard. Any PFAS in the electrolyte that did burn would be converted to HF. See highlighted text in attached reference 1a and 1b.  No release at end of life. As shown in attached reference 2, the additives are mostly consumed during the lifetime of the battery. At end of life, any remainder will be converted to inorganic fluorine compounds in battery recycling. The major portion of PFAS additive in the battery is consumed during charging and discharging, and little remains at the end of the battery's life,  which is 10-15 years.  Any residual amount of PFAS remaining  in the battery will be converted to HF during the thermal treatments in battery recycling, for example by ACCUREC Recycling GmbH (https://accurec.de/lithium?lang=en). Lithium ion batteries have other sources of fluorine (HF) as well, so they must be equipped with absorption equipment for HF, as shown in attached reference files 3 and 4.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Separate collection of batteries and recycling is required. By the end of the battery's life, the major portion PFAS has been consumed (see attached confidential reference 5), and any residual amount is converted to inorganic fluorine compounds and dealt with in battery recycling processes (see attached references 3 and 4).

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: a. Impact of the concentration limits:  At the beginning of battery life, the concentration of PFAS in the electrolyte would be well above the concentration limit, but the PFAS additive is consumed during the life of the battery,  as shown in attached confidential reference 5.  The concentration limit would not be practically relevant for recycling processes, even before end of life, because recycling processes for Li-ion batteries convert any remaining PFAS to inorganic fluorine compounds, which are already managed. Thus, concentration limits would not be relevant for battery recycling.  b. and c. recycling measures and costs: As described in attached reference 4, processes are already in place to deal with the fluorine compounds in Li battery recycling.

6. Missing uses: For the application as additive in electrolytes for Li-ion batteries. We have tried several PFAS-free alternatives as additives but none of those substances extended the life of Li-ion batteries. We are not aware of any possible alternatives, but can continue searching.  a. Annual tonnage and emissions: We anticipate about 800 t /a of the PFAS additives for Li-ion batteries. As already described, there would be no emissions.  b. Key functionality: "The key functionality is to extend the life of high capacity lithium ion batteries (also see ref.4) and support high rate charge. Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: This submission covers the use of polymeric PFAS, fluoropolymers and side chain fluorinated polymers, as cladding in polymer optical fibers (POF). (We are providing this information on behalf of our mother company in Japan.)

Generally, a restriction intended to prevent possible harm to drinking water and the food chain by substances with PBT or PMT properties should NOT be extended to polymers that cannot be bioaccumulative, mobile or toxic because the polymers are completely insoluble in water and fats. Persistence by itself is not a hazard. If persistence were a hazard, the EU should first ban glass and ceramics, as they are also man-made, also persistent, similarly inert and much more prevalent. If, on the other hand, glass and ceramics are not considered to be problematic, why ban fluorinated polymers?

The particular use covered by this submission, POF, is used in a variety of end uses in various sectors, but always dealing with the transmission of data or light itself. POF consist of a core fiber made of clear plastic, often polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA), surrounded by a cladding that consists of a fluoropolymer or side chain fluorinated polymer. PMMA is used as the core because it is highly transparent, amorphous, has low birefringence and can be formed to a flexible fiber with sufficient strength. The cladding is surrounded by a protective jacket of another material, such as PE or PVC.

In POF, the fluorine (PFAS) content of the cladding is essential because only with fluorine can a sufficiently low refractive index be achieved. The differential of refractive between the cladding and the core and the thickness of the cladding are what keeps the light traveling within the core, without loss to the outside. Fluoropolymers and side chain fluorinated polymers with a sufficiently lower refractive index than the core resin, often highly transparent PMMA, are chosen as the cladding.

(We already provided information on this use to the Dossier Submitters during the Call for Evidence. To our surprise, the Annex XV report does not mention the use in POF at all.)

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: In our understanding, the uses of polymer optical fibers (POFs) would fall into the following categories in Annex E of the Annex XV report, even though their uses were not mentioned in the report  (Annex E.2.2.) TULAC  - Technical textiles POFs are used for textile lighting in vehicles, costumes, disease treatment, and industrial applications.  This use is missing in the Annex XV report.  (Annex E.2.9.) Medical devices - Tubes and catheters POFs are used as light guides in catheters. Although the Annex XV report mentions PFAS in catheters, it does not mention this type of PFAS and this use.  - Diagnostic laboratory testing POFs are used for communication in endoscopes and medical equipment, sensors in PCR and other inspection machines, and local illumination in surgery. This use is missing in the Annex XV report.  (Annex E.2.10.) Transport - Use of PFASs in applications affecting the proper functioning related to the safety of vehicles, and affecting the safety of operators, passengers or goods, to the extent not addressed under other parts of this proposed restriction (e.g. under lubricants, electronic equipment and TULAC).  POFs are used for optical communications in vehicles such as automobiles, aircraft, and trains. This use is for data transmission in the vehicle, which is essential for the safe operation of the vehicle. This use is missing in the Annex XV report.  (Annex E.2.11.) Electronics and semiconductors - Electronics POFs are widely used in optical fiber sensors, optical communication cables for factory automation, robotics and other applications, inspection and industrial lighting devices, landscape lighting devices, medical surgical lighting devices, special scientific sensors, etc. These uses are missing in the Annex XV report.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: For the manufacturing and use phase of our POFs there can be no emissions in the EU as the POFs are manufactured outside the EU and in use the POFs are contained in a jacket material. For a worst case estimate at end-of-life assuming 100% were to go to landfill, see the Confidential Reference 1.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: POF should be incinerated or landfilled according to the disposal method determined for each use in each country and municipality in the EU. We do not have data on the percentages.  If it were determined that the POFs ought to be collected at end-of-life, this should be possible under the measures of the ELV or WEEE. For the medical uses, hygiene would dictate incineration as the proper disposal method.  Incineration: As shown by a study on the municipal incineration of PTFE, the conditions in such processes are sufficiently drastic to convert perfluorinated alkyl chains to HF and CO2.  Thus, incineration of our POFs will not lead to emission of PFAS substances. (See confidential reference 2, provided for your convenience.) no significant production of PFAS was observed and hydrofluoric acid and carbon dioxide were produced.  Landfilling: The PFAS cladding on the POFs is contained inside a jacket and thus will not be exposed to the environment at end of life. A chemical degradation test result of our PFAS polymer confirmed that fluorinated substances are not released to water even if were to be contacted in some unusual event. These tests covered neutral, strongly acidic and strongly basic conditions. (Report of the tests using the high molecular flow scheme method, which we did for the registration scheme for the country of our manufacturing site, is given in Confidential Reference 3.)

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: It would likely be quite difficult to disassemble the equipment that contains our POFs for dedicated mechanical recycling, due to the very small sizes and amounts. Incineration or potentially chemical recycling would be a better solutions.

5. Proposed derogations: 6. c. tubes and catheters in medical devices until 13.5 years after EiF: - Specific use:  POFs as light guides for catheters. This use was not explicitly mentioned in the Annex XV report, but it is our understanding that the derogation would apply. (The POFs are attached to the catheter.) See Confidential Reference 1 for tonnages  6. o. General Comments: Three different business units (BU) of Lehmann&Voss&Co. KG are having comments, these comments are clustered with respect to these business units:

BU Additives and Concentrates/ Masterbatches:
Lehmann & Voss & Co. produces polymer processing aids based on fluoropolymers (F-PPA), which are formulated as masterbatches. These masterbatches incorporate fluoropolymers like polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF), fluorinated ethylene propylene (FEP), or their copolymers, into a matrix of polymers like thermoplastics including polyolefins, polyamides, PET, and others. A specialized list of high-quality fluoropolymers is obtained from a roster of reliable suppliers.
In the context of polymer processing, fluoropolymers operate by establishing a protective layer that envelops the metal surface within the extruder barrel and encases the polymer melt. This interaction fosters a diminished surface energy between the metallic components and the molten polymer. As a result, an array of advantages is realized, encompassing decreased melt temperatures, alleviated pressure and machinery torque, alongside the mitigation of issues like melt fractures, the accumulation of material on dies, and the formation of gels or sharkskin.
Masterbatches are needed for numerous customers who struggle with handling complications and inaccurate dosing when working with pure substances. It is generally understood that polymer processing aids substantially enhance efficiency and production quality in plastics and rubber manufacturing . For our customers our masterbatch products guarantee the facilitation of seamless processes. Achieving optimal and efficient outcomes mandates precise additive dosing and thorough dispersion within the polymer matrix. Dealing with unfamiliar delivery forms like liquids, pastes, or powders, along with the challenge of accurately incorporating often minuscule quantities, can be both labor-intensive and prone to mistakes. This is where the significance of masterbatches becomes apparent. Tailored with carefully selected additives, including fluoropolymer-based PPA, masterbatches ensure optimal dispersion, rendering them a more dependable and cost-efficient choice for enhancing polymer processing.
As manufacturer of F-PPA masterbatches we find ourselves impacted by the prospective limitations on PFAS. Consequently, we would like to issue a comprehensive statement on this subject and actively participate in the ongoing consultation process. Our intention is to contribute to the discourse concerning the following sub-sectors detailed in the Annex XV Restriction Report for per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) :
• Plastic packaging
• Polymeric PFASs used as processing aids for production of non-PFAS polymers/plastics
We are advocating for a reevaluation of derogations and exemptions related to polymeric PFAS based on their non-toxic attributes, particularly when compared to the characteristics observed in non-polymeric PFAS substances. Henry et al. state: "[Fluoropolymers] have negligible residual monomer and oligomer content and low to no leachables. Fluoropolymers are practically insoluble in water and not subject to long-range transport. With a molecular weight well over 100 000 Da. Fluoropolymers cannot cross the cell membrane. Fluoropolymers are not bioavailable or bioaccumulative, as evidenced by toxicology studies on polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE): acute and sub chronic systemic toxicity, irritation, sensitization, local toxicity on implantation, cytotoxicity, in vitro and in vivo genotoxicity, hemolysis, complement activation, and thrombogenicity. Clinical studies of patients receiving permanently implanted PTFE cardiovascular medical devices demonstrate no chronic toxicity or carcinogenicity and no reproductive, developmental, or endocrine toxicity”.
In accordance with Regulation (EC) No. 1272/2008 , it is important to note that neither the employed fluoropolymer-based processing aids (F PPA) in our polymer processing aid masterbatches nor the polymeric carriers themselves are classified as hazardous substances or mixtures, provided that no other hazardous components are incorporated within the formulation. They contain no components recognized as meeting the criteria for persistence, bioaccumulation and toxicity (PBT), or very persistent and very bioaccumulative (vPvB) at levels of 0.1% or higher. They do not contain components considered to have endocrine disrupting properties according to REACH Article 57(f), Commission Delegated regulation (EU) 2017/2100  or Commission Regulation (EU) 2018/605  at levels of 0.1% or higher.
Additionally, our F PPA are incorporated into a polymeric matrix. As of Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008 of the European Parliament, hazardous properties of a product are drastically reduced if the substance is incorporated into a polymeric matrix and if its intended use is ensured. The fluoropolymer constituents are of macromolecular nature, which means they are not susceptible to migrating or otherwise being released into the environment.
In conclusion, the currently proposed restrictive regulations for fluoropolymers, a class of versatile synthetic materials, should be reconsidered due to their harmless safety profile regarding persistent, bioaccumulative, and toxic properties. Unlike some substances that may pose environmental or health concerns (e.g. non polymeric PFAS), fluoropolymers do not exhibit traits that lead to persistence in ecosystems, accumulation in organisms, or toxicity risks. Their inert nature and resistance to degradation ensure that they do not contribute to long-term environmental hazards.

BU Customized Polymer Materials (CPM):
With its Customized Polymer Materials (CPM) business unit, Lehmann&Voss&Co. KG has been helping designers, constructors and component manufacturers to define the most suitable thermoplastic compound for their application for almost 40 years now and thus to develop higher-performance components with lower system costs. Customers benefit from our in-depth knowledge of materials and applications, the independent selection of raw materials and the decades of experience of our product developers. From the very beginning, we have developed, produced, tested and commercialized thermoplastic compounds, always in close cooperation with our customers. As a result, we have developed many high-performance materials that are unique in their performance. One example is our extremely wear-resistant tribological compound with outstanding mechanical properties, as well as many others.
Polymer materials are the only possible alternative material for many tribological systems, especially if additional lubrication is not desired or cannot be realized. Most of the lubricants currently used are of fossil origin and cause enormous environmental pollution during production or disposal. Through integrated lubricants and reinforcing materials, we improve the wear, friction and run-in behavior of our polymer materials and thus of the complete tribological system. This enables maintenance-free or at least low-maintenance systems that function without additional lubrication. One of the most important tribologically effective additives is PTFE-micropowder.
The use of PTFE in its micropowder form as an additive for improving the tribological properties of plastics is crucial to maintain or reduce current energy consumption and global greenhouse gas emissions. A ban on PTFE, which has been shown to be non-bioaccumulative and chemically and thermally stable, would have a significant negative impact on various industries and the environment. Therefore, we would like to advocate here against a general PFAS ban or for an exemption of fluoropolymers from the currently proposed PFAS restriction ban.
PTFE micropowder is used as an effective anti-friction additive in plastics to reduce frictional resistance. The addition of PTFE-micropowder improves surface lubrication, resulting in lower frictional losses. This is particularly important in applications with moving parts, such as bearings, gears and slideways, which are also essential for safety-relevant components in vehicles. By reducing friction, energy losses are minimized, and the efficiency of machinery and equipment is improved. PTFE has an extremely low coefficient of friction, even when running dry, and thus offers excellent sliding properties. This enables low-friction movement of components, which significantly reduces energy requirements. In addition, PTFE has a high resistance to wear and abrasion, which extends the service life of components and reduces the need for replacements and repairs. This has a positive impact on the efficiency of machinery and equipment and contributes to cost savings. Reducing wear and eliminating the need for additional lubricants also leads to a reduction in the amount of waste and thus to a generally lower environmental impact. Fewer worn parts mean less waste to dispose of or recycle. Lubricants such as metal stearates and metal soaps are consumables and need to be renewed from time to time and usually disposed of as hazardous waste. Dispensing with additional lubricants and using dry-lubricated components therefore helps to conserve resources and reduce environmental impact. The following diagram shows the coefficients of friction of the various tribologically modified materials (blue) compared to the base polymers (grey). It illustrates the superior performance of PTFE compared to other materials and confirms its efficiency gains and environmental benefits in various applications. It also shows the potential for further research and development into tribological modifications to achieve even better sliding properties and lower friction losses.
Friction and wear of components contribute significantly to global energy consumption, which also releases a significant amount of greenhouse gas emissions. Our research and development in tribology, focuses on reducing friction and wear of our tribologically active products.
As previously mentioned, the use of PTFE-micropowder as an additive in plastics leads to the improvement of tribological properties. This minimizes energy losses in tribological contacts, which in turn leads to a reduction in energy demand and the associated greenhouse gas emissions. It is important to emphasize that the contribution of tribological contacts to global emissions is significant. It is estimated that tribological contacts cause about 23 % of the total global energy consumption. Of this amount, 20% is used to overcome friction and another 3% is used to refurbish worn parts and replacement equipment due to wear and tear and wear-related failures. This 3% alone is equivalent to the total CO2 emissions of global aviation before the COVID-19 pandemic.
Alternative tribologically effective additives, such as graphite or molybdenum disulphide (MoS2), tend to wear themselves out or fail to effectively reduce friction at high loads and speeds. This can lead to an increased abrasion rate and high heat generation, which affects the service life of components or tools and requires additional cooling. In some applications, the electrical conductivity of graphite may also be undesirable, especially when insulating materials are involved or electromagnetic interference is to be avoided. Geopolitical aspects should also not be neglected as the main mining areas for graphite are located in Asia and Africa.
It is crucial that research and development in this area continues in order to develop more sustainable solutions and further reduce energy consumption and emissions. PTFE plays an important role in improving the tribological properties of plastics and should therefore be considered as a valuable tool to promote energy efficiency and environmental protection. Furthermore, it is essential to consider the entire life cycle of products and materials when assessing environmental impacts. Banning PTFE without considering the potential impacts on energy consumption, emissions and waste generation could lead to unintended negative environmental impacts at other stages of the product life cycle. In recent years, considerable progress has been made in terms of sustainability and environmental compatibility. An important focus is on improving the recyclability of PTFE and developing processes to recover and recycle used PTFE. Through appropriate processes, PTFE can be reused and returned to the production process instead of ending up as waste. This helps to reduce the demand for new raw materials and to reduce the environmental impact of PTFE production.

BU Filtration:
Textiles for the use in filtration and separation media used in high performance air and liquid applications in industrial or professional settings that require a combination of water- and oil repellence.

Appropriate filtration with PTFE and PVDF high-performance filtration membranes reduces maintenance needs, extends service life and prevents failures of equipment and reduces energy consumption.

General Comments: Title: Preserving Patient Access and Industry Sustainability: A Pragmatic Approach to PFAS Regulation in Medicines Manufacturing
Introduction: As representatives of Medicines for Europe, we seek to address our deep concerns regarding the proposed restriction on Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) in industrial applications, including the manufacturing of medicinal products. While we acknowledge the environmental risks associated with PFAS, we believe that an outright ban on their use in pharmaceutical manufacturing could have irreparable consequences for both patients and the strategic autonomy of the European Union (EU) in the field of medicines manufacturing.
The Impact on Health Products and Technologies: The proposed PFAS restriction has far-reaching implications for the pharmaceutical sector:
• Essential Health Products at Risk: An across-the-board ban on PFAS stands to disrupt the production and availability of critical medicines, potentially leading to prolonged shortages.
• Life-Saving Products in Jeopardy: Many life-saving medications rely on PFAS technology in their manufacturing processes or may contain PFAS as active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), excipients, or components in packaging and drug delivery devices.
Contradiction to EU's Manufacturing Goals: We believe that the proposed ban contradicts the EU's current efforts to bolster medicines manufacturing and innovation within the region:
• Undermining Strategic Autonomy: The ban's approach is fundamentally misaligned with the European Commission's ongoing mission to strengthen the EU's medicines manufacturing capabilities.
• Threatening Investments: Members of Medicines for Europe have made substantial investments to establish new production sites for critical products such as antibiotics within Europe. However, there is an emerging realization that more extensive endeavors are needed to reestablish medicines production within the EU.
EU Initiatives and Recognition: Recent developments within the EU underscore the urgency of safeguarding medicines manufacturing:
• Urgent Measures: In June 2023, the European Council called upon the Commission to propose measures aimed at ensuring sufficient production and availability of critical medicines and components in Europe while diversifying international supply chains.
• Critical Medicines Act: This initiative builds upon previous requests from Member States to invest in stronger EU manufacturing, including the proposal for a Critical Medicines Act.
• European Parliament Support: In September 2023, 80 Members of the European Parliament, representing diverse nationalities and political groups, co-signed a letter urging the adoption of an Act to secure medicines supplies.
• Resilient EU2030 Report: The "Resilient EU2030" report, published by the Spanish Presidency ahead of the Informal European Council meeting in Granada, identifies health as a critical sector. The report emphasizes the need to reduce strategic dependencies in API manufacturing, increase investment in environmentally responsible API production, and foster research into more sustainable APIs.
The Case for a Prudent Approach: We advocate for a measured and balanced approach that takes into account the well-being of patients, the sustainability of the pharmaceutical industry, and the imperative of environmental protection:
• Prioritizing Patient Safety: Prohibiting all PFAS applications in medicines manufacturing poses risks to patients who depend on these products for their health and well-being.
• Alignment with Realities: Instead of an absolute ban, we propose a more nuanced approach that aligns the PFAS restriction agenda with the sector's practical challenges and the population's medical needs.
• Industry Commitment: The pharmaceutical industry remains steadfast in its commitment to adopting greener manufacturing practices and strengthening environmental protection standards. Initiatives like the AMR Industry Alliance and ongoing dialogues with Member States on integrating green manufacturing into national medicines procurement practices underscore this commitment.
Conclusion: While we acknowledge and share concerns about the environmental impact of PFAS, we implore decision-makers to consider the potential ramifications of an all-encompassing ban on medicines manufacturing. Achieving a balance between environmental preservation, patient well-being, and the sustainability of the pharmaceutical industry is paramount. In this critical sector, it is incumbent upon us to exercise prudence and wisdom to safeguard the environment without compromising patient access to essential medications or the EU's strategic autonomy in medicines manufacturing.
To allow for the continued manufacturing of life-saving medicines the products in scope of specific regulations should generally be derogated from a universal PFAS restriction, including all steps which are necessary for their manufacturing, packaging and delivery devices, in the EEA.

General Comments: To summarize, the unique properties presented by some of the materials in the PFAS family, specifically PTFE, FKM and FEP, are intrinsical to the existence and further development of the UV technology branch. Without them, inumerous issues regarding safety and lifetime will become prominent, impeding its success and setting back several environmental achievements already reached by the use of this technology.
It can be assumed that a limitation of the PFAS materials used will lead to a negative impact on the company's success and a negative impact on product sales. This ban influences the period of use of our products for our customers and drives up the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO). In the worst case, production process efficiency and safety of our customers decreases, and competitiveness deteriorates in comparison to non-EU sites.
The PFAS materials required for our end products are sourced externally. Some of them are further processed into components in our organization. Another part is sourced from suppliers who provide us with the required components for our end products. Therefore, our subsidiaries as well as our suppliers and their sub-suppliers will be affected if a ban of these materials is set in place. Since some components are outsourced and purchased through our suppliers, our suppliers and the whole supply chain will also be affected by the economic consequences.
It is not possible to give an exact number of the affected companies, because we do not know exactly the whole supply chain, competitors, recycling companies and our customers. We estimate that there will be approximately more than 1000 companies affected by a potential PFAS restriction EU wide. This way, a prohibition of PFAS will lead to a great amount of unemployment and loss of products and productivity in many different sectors of the industry.

For the above reasons we strongly recommend a derogation for our UV products/ - technology.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: There are several products in our portfolio that contain parts made out of PFAS materials. However, we do not manufacture PFAS components ourselves. The sectors and (sub-)uses mentioned in table 9 of the ANNEX XV restriction report would have to be expanded accordingly to reflect our product portfolio in the tables.

5. Proposed derogations: The listed derogations in paragraphs 5 and 6 of the proposed restriction entry text would have to be expanded accordingly to reflect our product portfolio. Nevertheless, we would like to comment on the waste management of the UV lamps, which constitute a considerable part of our products: The UV lamps and UV LEDs lamps fall under the (so called ElektroG) and must be disposed of separately, as required by law. The Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment Act (so called ElektroG) obliges manufacturers and importers of electrical and electronic equipment to, among other things, organize and finance the collection and recycling of waste equipment and to inform private and commercial users. Our recycler helps us, manufacturers, to meet these obligations. Our recycler is a take-back system created for the lighting industry and offers return points for private and commercial consumers nationwide. According to our recycler, approximately 90 % of the materials can be recycled by recovery of the materials. In this way, the materials are transferred to a material cycle and this ensures that no PFAS are released into the environment (source: homepage of our recycler).

6. Missing uses: Our organization has more than 50 years of experience in developing ultra-violet UV technology for industrial purposes. UV radiation can be applied to a wide range of applications, including curing of inks, adhesives and coatings as well as disinfection of water, air and surfaces, amongst others. The use of UV curing permits processes to be executed in faster times than conventional curing methods, allowing for more efficiency and savings in energy consumption. Water treatments based on UV radiation are free of chemicals, eliminating the damages these cause to the environment. In this business, the use of UV resistant materials is essential for the success of products, influencing not only their lifetime but also directly affecting their safety.  Our company develops, manufactures and distributes UV/LED-UV systems, UV lamps and UV measuring equipment, worldwide.  Our customers use our products all over the world. Our products are used for manufacturing processes in electronics, microelectronics, precision engineering and the optical industry, as well as in the printing, coating, automobile, aerospace, pharmaceutical, food and photovoltaic sectors.    The products are used for: - The cross-linking of photo-reactive substances, for instance the curing of coatings, inks and adhesives, applied to paper, wood and glass, amongst others - Disinfection of surfaces: sterilization of food packaging - Disinfection of air: disinfection of air conditioning and ventilation systems of different sizes - Disinfection of water: Disinfection of drinking water, ballast water disinfection of container ships - Disinfection of waste water: sewage treatment plants, cruise ships - Synthesis of vitamin D and components of medications - TOC (Total Oxidizable Carbons) reduction - Aquaculture / Fish farming - Ultra-pure water - Gas analysis systems The key functionalities of PFAS in UV-radiation devices are: - Coating of stranded wires (PTFE) - Lamp sockets (PTFE) - Sealings (FKM and PTFE) - Sealing stripes (PTFE) - Protection sleeves (FEP) - Hoses (PTFE and FKM) - Diffusion material (PTFE) - Electrically insulating materials (PTFE) - Connectors (PTFE) - Refrigerant (R407-C) This use of these materials is essential for our company due to the following properties: PTFE:  - Excellent UV resistance, which leads to long lifetimes - High dielectric strength, providing excellent insulation, that together with the great UV resistance guarantees safety throughout the product’s lifetime - High temperature resistance FKM: - High temperature resistance - No emissions that affect the curing process or vacuum process (this is not the case for silicone) FEP: - Excellent UV resistance and transmission - Maleable material, which together with its UV resistance and transmissivity is perfectly suited for use as protective sleeves for lamps R407-C: - Excellent cooling power UV lamps and their systems represent an established technology, providing high electric-to-optical conversion efficiencies in a cost and energy efficient matter. All peripherals like sensors, controls, lamp drivers have been optimized over decades to serve this technology. PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) is a material known for its excellent resistance to UV radiation, categorizing it as a crucial element in the development of UV-based devices. In our organization, PTFE is mainly used for the purpose of electrical insulation, particularly in PTFE-coated wires, in lamp sockets and as insulating material in different areas of the devices. It is used to assure that parts containing electricity and subjected to intense UV radiation remain safely insulated from its surroundings throughout the lifetime of the device. It is also widely used as sealing material in parts of the device directly under the influence of UV radiation. Due to the extreme conditions presented by high dosages of UV radiation, there are currently no other materials that can provide such a dosis of UV resistance, insulating and physical properties in the manner provided by PTFE. Therefore, a prohibition of its use constitutes an immense influence on the lifetime and safety of our products. Without a suitable replacement, the entire market of UV radiation devices is threatened, and their proper safety cannot be guaranteed. Furthermore, restricting PTFE will inevitably increase the cost of end products, which can cause problems, for instance, in municipal water treatment. Another material belonging to the PFAS family that is commonly found in our devices is FKM (fluorine rubber material), where it is widely used in higher temperature environments for the sealing of glass plates to housings, sealings in lamp production, in immersion tube systems and in immersion lamp systems. Silicone would be considered to be a suited material in many of these applications, as it is also resistant to higher temperatures. However, silicone cannot substitute FKM in most of these applications as it tends to influence the processes taking place around it.  As an example, silicone cannot be used to substitute FKM in sealings of UV lamp production because it is partially released from the sealing and penetrates the lamp discharge area, yielding an increase in voltage and thus failure of the lamp. Another example is the sealing of windows in curing devices. In this case, silicone present in the sealing is partially released into the enviroment and ends up coating the substrate to be cured, preventing the ink or adhesive from properly adhering to the surface and therefore hindering the success of the entire process. In such cases there are no suitable sealing materials besides PFAS-based ones. Here too, a ban of such substances would cause great damage to this line of business. Since the lamps are sometimes used in the presence of food, their packaging or in public facilities, in the event of lamp breakage no splinters should be released onto the goods to be treated or into the environment. In these applications, not only a high UV resistance but also a high UV transmittance is required to ensure that the useful UV radiation reaches its goal. FEP (Fluorinated ethylene propylene) posseses such properties and its maleability allows it to be used as protection sleeves that can be shrunk around indivdual lamps, providing the desired protection without hampering the UV dosage. To the best of our knowledge, there are no materials with these properties outside the PFAS family, which makes their prohibition raise additional safety issues. To summarize, the unique properties presented by some of the materials in the PFAS family, specifically PTFE, FKM and FEP, are intrinsical to the existence and further development of the UV technology branch. Without them, inumerous issues regarding safety and lifetime will become prominent, impeding its success and setting back several environmental achievements already reached by the use of this technology. It can be assumed that a limitation of the PFAS materials used will lead to a negative impact on the company's success and a negative impact on product sales. This ban influences the period of use of our products for our customers and drives up the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO). In the worst case, production process efficiency and safety of our customers decreases, and competitiveness deteriorates in comparison to non-EU sites.  The PFAS materials required for our end products are sourced externally. Some of them are further processed into components in our organization. Another part is sourced from suppliers who provide us with the required components for our end products. Therefore, our subsidiaries as well as our suppliers and their sub-suppliers will be affected if a ban of these materials is set in place. Since some components are outsourced and purchased through our suppliers, our suppliers and the whole supply chain will also be affected by the economic consequences.   It is not possible to give an exact number of the affected companies, because we do not know exactly the whole supply chain, competitors, recycling companies and our customers. We estimate that there will be approximately more than 1000 companies affected by a potential PFAS restriction EU wide. This way, a prohibition of PFAS will lead to a great amount of unemployment and loss of products and productivity in many different sectors of the industry. A negative effect on the job situation (e.g. fewer jobs in the future, termination of employees) in the organization cannot be ruled out. Furthermore, a negative corporate success would also have a negative impact on the prosperity of the region (lower tax revenues in the region, less spending, etc.). As of today, there exist no suitable non-PFAS materials on the market that are resistant to high dosages of UV radiation and have the insulating and physical properties of currently used PFAS. The prohibition of such materials for UV technology devices would represent a high threat to this technology’s existence and would have a direct impact in the lives of many people around the globe. In the case of water disinfection, for instance, the non-existence of UV technology would set back the advantages of a chemical-free process, with the need of replacement by the addition of chlorine or other chemicals to the water.  Identifying and testing suitable alternatives means increased time and costs, especially because the material must be suitable for the entire operating period intended for use. As an example, for UV lamps, this means a service life test of around 9,000 to 12,000 hours, on top of the time required for search and development of a suitable material. The desired transition period of just 18 months is therefore far too short, rendering a substitution of these materials.   For the above reasons we strongly recommend a derogation for our UV products/ - technology.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Today, fluorinated resins with PFAS are used in TULAC (Textiles, Upholstery, Leather, Apparel, Carpet) sector and more precisely in textiles to impart water, oil, and stain repellency for finished products.

Recent years developments bring new Fluor-Free chemistry treatments on the market that meet expectations for hydrophobicity property.
High level of performance is achieved for evaluation standards : spray test ISO 4920, Bundesmann ISO 9865, and promising Schmerber water column ISO 811 at new state.
Launderability could be comparable to Fluorine treatements products when only hydrophobicity and soft washes (30-40°C) only are needed.
It shows that fluorinated alternatives could be industrially used for water repellency with satisfying results if this is the only critical function.
From a physical view, textile hydrophobicity behaviour is obtained when the substance has a surface tension lower than that of water.
It could be done with silane, polyurethane, paraffin, wax materials that have high substitution potential for water repellency only.

Nevertheless, current Fluor-Free chemistry do not compete with fluorinated resin using PFAS for stain, oil repellency and chemical repulsions without possible discussion.
Surface tension of oil is so low that there is no identified alternative to PFAS despite the researchs of laboratories and chemical companies in surface engineering.
Hydrocarbon resistant test ISO 14419 achieve Grade 5/6 with PFAS chemistry (it means no wettability with low surface tension oils).
Fluor-Free struggle to overcome mineral oils which are easiest compositions used as references, and thus do not permit to pass requirements in oleophobicity.
This technical barrier here has to be investigated in future years as state-of-the-art today is not satisfying in terms of performances.
Requirements in PPE (EN 469 Firefighters, EN 13034 Protective Clothing against liquid chemicals, BS 7971 Protective clothing and equipment for use in violent situations and in training) could not be guaranteed without the usage of PFAS.
A typical example is the chemical repulsion and liquid penetration against very low surface tension substances (H2S04, NaOH, o-Xylene, Butane-1-ol) ISO 6530 for Risk Category III.
Textile have to be treated with PFAS to pass the repellency threshold and avoid all penetration during operating conditions where industrial washes 60°C are more stringent here than domestic conditions.

For all those reasons, PFAS usage is necessary for oil, stain, and chemical liquids repulsions because alternatives can not replicate those critical functionnalities.
Nowadays Fluorine is the only chemistry that fulfill requirements for special markets : professional apparel (PPE) and technical textiles.
In the case of PFAS restriction, a global review of requirements would be discussed as performance level will drop inevitably and current chemistry will fail to pass standards.
If PFAS are regulated, threshold values should be revise upwards to assure expected properties and technical specifications.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Today, fluoropolymers are used in numerous technologies, industrial processes and everyday applications from the aviation industry to transportation, including electrical vehicles, medical devices and energy production to technical apparel to name just a few. They are durable, chemically inert and mechanically strong in harsh conditions. These unique characteristics of fluoropolymers make them a critical material for a broad range of industries and sectors, playing a diverse and crucial role for society, with few, if any, viable alternatives.

Beyond their socio-economic value for European industry, their unique stability means that they are low-risk polymers for human health and their environment. Trying to replace them in their many applications would lead to substitution with alternatives (when available) that do not provide the same advanced performance and safety as fluoropolymers. Banning Fluoropolymers will be the wrong step into the future for our humanity.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: • Industrial food and feed production • Tubes and catheters • Hydraulic fluids

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Preliminary information from a recent project initiated by Gujarat Fluorochemicals Limited (GFL), a leading Fluoropolymer manufacturer, and executed by the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) in cooperation with Société Générale de Surveillance (SGS) demonstrates clearly that Fluoropolymers are converted to Inorganic Fluorides and Carbon dioxide at standard incineration conditions. The inorganic fluorides mainly include Hydrogen Fluoride and Silicon tetrafluoride. Total organic fluorides (PFAS) were non-detectable with a reporting limit of 0.08 ppm and Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) was also not detected with a reporting limit of 0.04 ppm. The results confirm that Fluoropolymers at their end of life when incinerated in waste to energy recovery plants do not generate any noticeable levels of PFAS emissions and therefore, pose no risk to human health and the environment.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The study involved application samples of the four most sold Fluoropolymers (PTFE, PVDF, PFA and FKM) provided by Pro-K (German association of polymer processors), which were incinerated under standard operating conditions for municipal and industrial waste incineration (850°C – 1100°C for two seconds residence time respectively) and consulted by the German Federal Environment Agency (Umweltbundesamt). Final data set and methodology used are being reviewed and validated by Environmental Standards Inc. The absence of organic fluorides and more specifically PFAS substances in incineration flue gas confirms complete thermal destruction of Fluoropolymers during incineration and therefore it should pave the way for exempting Fluoropolymers from the EU REACH PFAS restriction proposal.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: • The PTFE/PFA/FEP scraps resulting from manufacturing of hoses are sold to companies that recycle them.         •  2500 kg/year

5. Proposed derogations: • 100 tons/year of PTFE/FEP/PFA • no information on emissions

6. Missing uses: Chemical and pharmaceutical industry  Main properties of PTFE/PFA/FEP hoses: • excellent chemical resistance to almost all chemicals; • wide working temperature range (from -70°C to +260°C as a standard); • excellent resistance to ageing and weather conditions; • self-cleaning properties – non-stick surface. Nowadays, hoses made of PTFE/PFA/FEP are used in all sectors of the industry e.g. for steam, hot oil, fuel, paint, adhesives, high pressure gas transfer. In the chemical industry, they are used for loading and unloading of acids, bases, organic solvents and very aggressive chemicals. PTFE hose assemblies ensure highly hygienic transfer and perfectly suit food, cosmetic, pharmaceutical industry and biotechnology.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Fluoropolymers are high value chemicals that provide a wide variety of properties in key industrial sectors. These chemicals are indispensable to guarantee the adequate functioning of modern society, with key contributions in safety, decarbonization, and high-tech development. However, fluoropolymers show clearly differentiated properties from other PFAS, and the vast majority of these polymers have been identified as matching the definition of Polymer of Low Concern. Fluoropolymers are not expected to degrade during normal use or at their end of life, and the main concerns related to their manufacture are being successfully addressed by industry, with innovative developments in both safer designs and improvement of abatement techniques to control emissions.

8. Other identified uses: Fluoropolymers are used in a wide variety of highly critical applications due to their valuable properties, mainly by industrial actors.2 In the case that the use of fluoropolymers would be banned in Europe, a number of critical sectors would be significantly impacted, which could result in severe damage to the European society. The list below covers just a selection of examples of industries that could be damaged because of this. – Renewable Energy: fluoropolymers are key components in solar panels and wind turbines, where they protect against weather impacts of equipment exposed to e.g., rain and environmental contaminants. In photovoltaic cells, fluoropolymers improve electrical insulation. Furthermore, these materials are critical and absolutely necessary for optimal performance of lithium-ion batteries and hydrogen fuel cells. Without fluoropolymers, these devices will not work efficiently, and the goals of the European Green Deal would be seriously compromised. – Semiconductors: fluoropolymers provide properties that are essential in this use, such as resistance to harsh chemicals that need to be used in themanufacturing process while providing an environment completely free of impurities.No fluoropolymers available will mean that the semiconductor industry will not be able to produce the high-tech microchips that allowfor the development ofmodern (and reduced insize yet powerful) devices such as mobile phones, laptops and many other hightech equipment. – Chemical process industry: due to their unmatched properties in terms of resistance to chemical attack and optimumperformance under wide variations of temperature, fluoropolymers are the only available set of products on the market that allow for adequate performance of many chemical processes.While othermaterials could be used for handling chemical streams, these would need continued maintenance and replacement and what is worse, they would significantly increase the risk of failure and accidents, leading to higher probability of operators and the environment being unexpectedly exposed to highly hazardous chemicals. Fluoropolymers can be found in all kinds of tubing and industrial equipment, as well as joints and gaskets to secure operation and containment of chemicals. – Transport: fluoropolymers contribute to both fuel efficiency (as key components in combustion engines) and safety, playing a key role in systems such as brakes in cars or wing flaps in aircrafts. They are also the best option available (due to their high resistance but also high flexibility) to protect electrical cables in aircrafts, where high reliability of such cables,which can be exposed to thermal as well as chemical pressure, is fundamental. - Food and water treatment: wherever high purity is required, fluoropolymers play an irreplaceable role. These materials are present in water filtration systems (which avoids the need to use chemicals forwater treatment) and also in food processing systems to guarantee adequate sanitary conditions and avoid contamination which could otherwise reach consumers. – Pharmaceutical and medical devices: medical implants that are intended to be used in the human body (catheters, implants) due to their biological compatibility and inertness. Certainly, materials that are used for this purpose are not toxic for human health and, due to their high durability, can last for many years in the body without replacement. Furthermore, the production of medicines and vaccines by the pharma industry require as well ultra purity conditions which can only be achievedwith equipment based on fluoropolymer materials.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Transdermal Therapeutic Systems (TTS, also known as “transdermal patches”) are innovative drug delivery systems, allowing patients with conditions affecting the central nervous system or who need severe pain management to apply their medicine by themselves on a daily bases, with fewer side effects and higher adherence to their therapy. The release liner of these TTS can contain a fluoropolymer coating and are essential to the functioning of the product. The proposed PFAS restriction dossier, as currently envisioned, would ban the use of these TTS, as there is no derogation for this specific use and non-fluoropolymer release liners do not provide the same quality needed for the functioning of the product. This would greatly impact patients’ quality of care across the EU, with some even left without any other treatment options. In our confidential submission we therefore provide comprehensive information on the product and its uses, availability of alternatives and the impact on patients across the European Union.

LTS would like to highlight the missing use of release liners with a fluorosilicone release coating for Transdermal Therapeutic Systems (TTS). The release liners are coated on the adhesive-facing side with a highly hydrophobic dehesive coating to allow the release liner to be easily removed by the patient or caregiver. This is called low peel force. The intended function of the release liner is not achievable with other types of liners. The abovementioned low peel forces are essential and needed for patients using our products who suffer, e.g. from severe chronic diseases and pain management or in palliative care. The low peel forces enable the application of the patches by patients themselves.

Any alternatives to the currently used liners by LTS (mainly in combination with silicone based patches) are also based on fluoropolymer chemistry, specifically Fluorosilicone coatings. There are, therefore, no currently available PFAS-free alternatives which have the same features and provide similar benefits for patients in terms of ease of removal and skin impact, amongst others. This is especially true for pharmaceutical use.

PFAS-free alternatives mentioned in the literature comprise embossed plastic films, e.g. PVC (called “crimped liners”). The embossing reduces the contact area between the adhesive and the liner, which lowers the peel force slightly. However, these alternative liners do not work in combination with silicone BIO-PSA adhesives, and the peel forces are substantially higher when compared to fluoropolymer-coated release liners, which makes the application of the patches more difficult (if not impossible) for patients who suffer from severe chronic diseases and who are in pain management or in palliative care.
As no PFAS-free alternative liners are readily available to be used with the existing affected products, any efforts to bring alternative products to commercial roll-out would start at the R&D phase and therefore involve a lengthy process. This exercise can easily take 10 years or more. The process consists of the following phases:
• Inventing alternative liner materials
• Registration of alternative liner materials as a novel excipient
• Upscaling and commercialization of alternative liner materials
• Development of our TTS products with new liner
• Potential clinical trials
• Regulatory approval process

Please refer to our confidential submission for further data corroborating these claims and timelines.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) is formed in the atmospheric degradation processes for some HFCs and HFOs fluorinated gases. For most HFC/HFO refrigerants, degradation rates/yields into TFA are small, resulting in de minimis increases in overall TFA concentrations by comparison with pre-existing TFA levels. Only a few commercialized fluorinated gases decompose into fractions of TFA over 30% (including, HFO-1234yf, HFC-227ea, HFC-134a). Nevertheless, these emissions lead only to increases in TFA concentrations that safely remain at orders of magnitude below scientifically established DNEL/PNEC levels and/or food intake or water quality standards for TFA.

In addition to the abundant public scientific evidence on the non-toxicity of fluorinated gases (C2-C3
carbon range) and of their degradation product TFA (C2)3 compelling new scientific data has been
generated using ToxProfiler4, a unique human-based reporter assay that provides an extensive
quantitative toxicological profile of novel chemicals and drugs. The assay contains seven fluorescent
reporter genes to visualize the major cellular stress response pathways responsible for cellular/organ
toxicity.  It compares the toxicological activity and mode of action of Trifluoroacetic Acid (TFA) with longer-chain polyfluorinated compounds (PFAS).

This new study from September 2023 (Annex II to this submission - Toxys project code 23063) evaluated the toxicological activity and potency of a wide PFAS series, i.e., C2-C10, comprising TFA (C2). The study demonstrated not only the repeatability and the consistency of the ToxProfiler assay, but the data also irrefutably underlined that toxicological activity is observed only with PFAS having a carbon chain length of C4 or higher.

It clearly states that overall TFA was found to be non-toxic and did not trigger any of the 7 major toxicological pathways. A clear correlation was found between stress pathway activation and the carbon length of the tested PFAS. It was proved that C2/C3 molecules unequivocally do not trigger toxicological events in the ToxProfiler assay.

To summarize, short-chain polyfluorinated (less than C4) compounds do no exhibit toxicological activity, and hence it is demonstrated that TFA has biological properties that differ significantly from the longer-chain polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). Therefore, the inclusion of TFA, and the precursor fluorinated gases it degrades from, into the larger group of PFAS chemicals for REACH restriction purposes is not scientifically and legally justified.

This submission should be read in conjunction with the following two earlier Honeywell submissions: 76bb3d12-2101-4390-82cf-3498b47e8015 (May) and 145ab85b-73c2-49d7-81a6-5e2141b7d372 (August)​.

The four central pieces of data from these submissions are below:

1) According to the trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) REACH registration dossier and Chemical Safety Report (CSR), this substance does not fulfil the criteria for a PBT or vPvB substance under Annex XIII REACH. Neither does it raise equivalent levels of concern under Article 57(f) REACH. In this respect, ECHA already reviewed/evaluated the TFA dossier without concluding that further regulatory actions were needed.

2) Potential effects of HFC/HFO emissions on TFA concentrations and respective risks to humans and the environment were studied intensively worldwide. In this respect, highly qualified independent assessments of UNEP panels repeatedly concluded that “The current low concentration of trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) produced by the degradation of several hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) and hydrofluoroolefins (HFOs), is currently judged not to pose a risk to human health or to the environment.” and that “available evidence indicates that this breakdown product [TFA] is of minimal risk to human health”.

3) The most recent EEAP 2022 Assessment Report unequivocally cited a common agreement among the majority of experts that “all PFAS should not be grouped together, persistence alone is not sufficient for grouping PFAS for the purposes of assessing human health risk, and that the definition of appropriate subgroups can only be defined on a case-by-case manner” and that “it is inappropriate to assume equal toxicity/potency across the diverse class of PFAS”. According to the EEAP 2022 Assessment Report, this same argument applies to the inclusion of TFA, with a two-carbon chain and a single CF3 group, in a class with longer chain PFAS (e.g. PFOS). The Report concludes that “Trifluoroacetic acid has biological properties that differ significantly from the longer chain polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and inclusion of TFA in this larger group of chemicals for regulation would be inconsistent with the risk assessment of TFA” (page 25). This 2022 Report also concludes that “based on projected future use of these precursors of TFA [incl. HFC/HFO], no harm is anticipated” and that TFA “is unlikely to cause adverse effects out to 2100”.

4) Environmental fate and distribution modelling of TFA in the freshwater aquatic environment was conducted based on the assumption of constant and ongoing HFO emissions, which through atmospheric degradation in turn leads to a constant deposition of TFA. Initial modelling results demonstrate that within a short timeframe (months) a steady state concentration of TFA is reached, which does not further increase over time. This is illustrated in a case study for the Rhine basin (Germany, The Netherlands), for which TFA concentrations clearly below 10 µg/L are predicted. Importantly, this study invalidates the incorrect assumption in the Proposal that TFA concentrations in fresh water would keep increasing until “inevitably” a toxic level would be reached.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Honeywell International Inc.  is a global manufacturer and importer of various fluorinated gases to the European Union (EU), including hydrofluorocarbons (HFC) and This submission (HFO) and their mixtures (blends), primarily used in refrigeration, heating, ventilation and air conditioning (RHVAC), mobile air conditioning (MAC), thermal management systems (TMS) in electric vehicles (EV), as propellants in medical dose inhalers (MDI) and agents in insulation foam blowing applications.     Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) is formed in the atmospheric degradation processes for some HFCs and HFOs fluorinated gases. Only a few commercialized fluorinated gases decompose into fractions of TFA over 30% (including, HFO-1234yf, HFC-227ea, HFC-134a). General Comments: TRUMPF Laser- und Systemtechnik GmbH (henceforth referred to as TRUMPF Laser Technology or TLD) is a subsidiary of TRUMPF SE + Co. KG and engages more than 1000 employees worldwide. The Laser Technology business division has generated a turnover of 1,609 million euros in the financial year 2021/2022 with an increase of 21.7 percent in comparison with the previous financial year.
The branch “laser technology” achieved a global turnover of 21 billion US-dollars in 2021. (Source: Statista, “Umsatz mit Lasern weltweit in den Jahren 2006 bis 2021“). This number emphasizes the importance and the productivity of the laser technology in the worldwide economy.
Our product portfolio includes laser systems for cutting, welding and surface treatment of three-dimensional parts. We offer high-performance CO2 lasers, disk as well as fiber lasers, diode lasers, ultrashort pulse lasers plus marking lasers and systems. Our report here focusses on the marking laser TruMark which are used to identify, track, personalize and even modify all kind of metalic and non-metalic materials, mainly used in the automotive, medical and general industry.

In general, TRUMPF Laser Technology is aware of the concerns about PFAS and supports the substitution of hazardous substances for human health and the environment. A restriction should only concern a PFAS involving an unacceptable risk to human health or to the environment in accordance with Art. 68 of the REACH Regulation. In the restriction proposal, a profound risk assessment of every single PFAS with regard to its potential danger for human health or the environment has not been performed. As a consequence, applications of PFAS (such as fluorpolymers, so called “polymers of low concern”, and fluorelastomers) without a scientifically evidenced unacceptable risk to human health or to the environment, should still be used in the near future, until a suitable substitute with the same characteristics will be detected and tested (Source for “polymers of low concern”: Henry/Carlin/Hammerschmidt i.a., “A critical review of the application of polymer of low concern and regulatory criteria to fluorpolymers”, Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management – Volume 14, No. 3, pp. 316-334). With respect to the specific characteristics, the listed alternatives in the restriction proposal have only been assed for their technical feasibility in replacing some PFAS at a general level. In reality, the proposed substitutes are not feasible based on the specific needs to the same effect as the characteristics of the PFAS in question. Especially in the sector “mechanical engineering”, applications of PFAS are used under extreme conditions (e.g. ultrapure condition, very high/low temperature, chemical conditions).
Furthermore, we note that the sector of “mechanical engineering” with the focus on “laser systems for industrial applications” is not listed in the Table A.1 of Annex XV in the restriction proposal, although about 3.1 Mio. Europeans work in the branch “mechanical engineering”. The sector of “machinery and equipment” realizes a turnover of 748 billion euros, comprises circa 80 000 companies and represents one of the the largest branches measured in the EU (Source: VDMA, Mechanical engineering – figures and charts 2022, pp.12, 21).

Companies such as TRUMPF Laser Technology are situated near the end of the supply chain. We use PFAS in terms of parts in the production process of our lasers and laser systems. Therefore, we need detailed information of our suppliers to answer most of the specific questions. Almost all relevant suppliers are not able to collect that extent of information within six months (see responses of some suppliers in the confidential attachment) because there is no legal requirement which standardizes the information transfer of all PFAS to its customer. Besides, it would be nearly impossible to find a suitable substitute for most of the PFAS within 18 months or 6,5/13,5 years in case of an exemption. Normally, finding a substitute with the same specific characteristics in the product development process takes several years. That is why the legislative proposal should provide a formal mechanism to extend or renew exemptions in case a substitute for a PFAS is not feasible within set derogation times. Otherwise, a complete ban of PFAS would affect us because machine tools could not be built in the same quality as usual. In the high-tech sector, a market shakeout in the European industrial production is expected as a result of the significant competitive disadvantage.
Another point is that lasers and laser systems by TRUMPF have a product life cycle of about 20-30 years due to the high investment costs. Customers can demand and acquire spare or second-hand parts as long as a laser machine lasts on average. Therefore, the transition period of a specific substitute should be adapted to the availability of spare or second-hand parts based on the average life cycle of a machine. A general PFAS ban would lead to early depreciation of laser systems, associated with high economic plus ecological costs.
In the end, it is not clear how a restriction of a certain PFAS can be controlled by national or local authorities due to a lack of accountability of PFAS-free parts. Especially imported laser machines from third countries can contain PFAS in individual parts, while it would be not allowed to produce laser machines in the EU with parts including a PFAS.

6. Missing uses: Here are some of the major properties for TRUMPF laser technology  products which are critical: 1. Outgassing: Outgassing results in a release of contaminants that are damaging for mirrors and lenses used in state-of-the-art laser. Optical resonators have very strict cleanliness requirements as its essential for the process. Fluoropolymers are known to release much less of organic and inorganic contaminants than other polymers. In fact, it has been observed that the use of other materials can cause (permanent) damage to our optics. 2. Dielectric properties PTFE is an electrical isolator with high temperature resistance, good creepage and prevents arcing, so it is often used as holders, distance holders and other isolator parts for electronic parts. 3. Resistance to radiation (RF) High-frequency electromagnetic radiation is generated in the Laser Amplifier. The materials used must be resistant to this radiation to ensure both machine safety and human safety. 4. Thermal stability 5. Low friction  The listed substances in Appendix E2 are not in all applications (use cases) a technical alternative, because a combination of properties is required, e.g. outgassing and resistance to optical radiation. For more detailed examples, please check the confidential appendix for a list of selected use cases where we go into detail about the applications and alternatives.  If alternatives are not available, only an estimation can be given for the timeline: A time frame of 5 to 25 years is within the scope of possibility. „ For some applications, it is not currently possible to demonstrate that a non-PFAS alternative can fulfil the application-specific performance requirements. In these cases, it may be necessary to invent and synthesize new chemicals, and/or develop alternative approaches to device fabrication that provides the necessary electrical and computational performance. Invention is an open-ended endeavor without a fixed timeline or guarantee of success.” [SIA PFAS Consortium The Impact of a Potential PFAS Restriction on the Semiconductor Sector, RINA, 2023] Aspects such as the following further increase the uncertainty of the timelines. [SIA PFAS Consortium The Impact of a Potential PFAS Restriction on the Semiconductor Sector, RINA, 2023]: - Technical aspects: • The alternative may not be a drop-in replacement and alternative design changes need to be made, solution may not be backward compatible to designs of equipment which are already in service. • The technical requirements at each stage must be met, and may require multiple iterations of testing and development. • The solution may not address the long-term reliability of the alternative, which may only introduce additional design needs or technical limitations once the alternative has been used for a considerable length of time. • The solution may need to be qualified by a certified body which can add additional time. - Supplier factors: • Difficulties in identifying a new supplier and their qualification can add considerable additional time to envisaged timeline  • The alternative substance needs to be available in sufficient quantities to meet demand.  - Delays in testing: Unavailability of testing labs due to the expected increase in the demand for testing of other applications/alternatives, or delays in receiving test material from supplier or prototypes for testing. - Environmental: PFAS articles are exposed to hazardous substances during use which might contaminate the proposed alternatives differently, and thus impact recyclability. Therefore, alternative waste manage streams would need to be identified.  - Technical resources: Significant additional specialised highly educated technical resources will be required in the innovation and commercialisation of PFAS replacement materials. As such there may be additional time required to recruit and train additional people.  A sufficiently long transition time is crucial to ensure proper research into alternatives.

General Comments: Turbine based power plants play a key role in the European Electricity system, with more than 1.000 plants providing electricity and district heating all over Europe as of today. Therefore, it is worrying to see that power plants were not included in the Annex XV Report, underestimating their importance in the energy market.
The main European power plant manufacturers, represented by EUTurbines, ask in this response for a limitless derogation of the use of PFAS in order to be able to maintain their activities. As power plants producers, we are downstream users of PFAS containing components provided by specialised manufacturers -meaning we don’t directly handle the PFAS, but parts that have PFAS in their composition- for which we request as well an exemption of the restriction.
PFAS used in the power plant sub-sector are necessary to keep the operating conditions of power plants, such as extreme temperatures, high pressures, chemical resistances and high levels of friction. These same conditions oblige power plants to comply with very strict safety rules revised regularly, employ highly trained staff, and seal completely the environments where PFAS are present, preventing exposure. The PFAS used in our sector represents as well under 1% of the total used PFAS in the EU every year. Alternative materials have been and will be tested in the future to operate in this conditions, but to this day the substitution of the PFAS containing materials remains unfeasible, and it is calculated that it will be unfeasible at least for another 20 years.
A restriction of the PFAS use in our sector would ultimately lead to major disruptions in the electricity system and affect economically not only power plant manufacturers, but also industries and households all over Europe.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Energy sector - sector as a whole

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: A. Our members haven’t identified any emissions of PFAS during the manufacture and operation of their products. We therefore confirm that there are no emissions during any of the phases.  B. Our members provide the users of the power plants with the necessary information regarding the disposal of the products at their end-of-life. However, these instructions, compliant with EU regulations, don’t include details about separate substances used in components.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Our members are not accountable for the end-of-life of their products, which is a responsibility of the client, to whom instructions on the correct disposal of components is provided. However, the usual process is of municipal incineration for the adequate parts, and recycling by specialised companies in the case of metals and electronics. Due to the nature of power plants, this process is closely monitored by the relevant authorities, who define as well the rules for the waste management. About incineration, in the case of PTFEs, which are the main elements containing PFAs for our sector, Various studies have found that municipal burning, which is in many cases the usual method of disposal, effectively gets rid of the PFTE materials without degrading them to PFAS, thus preventing the contact with humans or the environment. More information on the subject in: Aleksandrov, K., et al. (2019), Waste incineration of polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate potential formation of per- and poly-fluorinated alkyl substances (PFAS) in flue gas, Chemosphere, Volume 226, pp. 898-906. Retrieved on: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0045653519306435
