However the restriction wouldn’t affect only the manufacturers of power plants, but the client companies (utilities) buying the turbines and operating said plants would be affected as well. In the EU there are around 87 main companies of this kind, a number that increases exponentially at a more local and regional level. These companies would no doubt be affected in case the turbine manufacturing is affected by the restriction, given that not only they wouldn’t be able to replace existing turbines by PFAS-free turbines (which for now aren’t economically or technically feasible) but would also be unable to keep the adequate maintenance of their currently installed turbines due to the inexistence of PFAS-free spare parts.  The affected companies in the sub-sector are the manufacturers of components as well. As downstream users, power plant manufacturers assembly parts manufactured by third companies, which are highly specialized and counted by hundreds all over Europe. As for the whole energy sector, it is not possible to provide with a single figure for companies affected by the restriction but taking into account that all electricity generating technologies use PFAS materials to some extent, the impact would be devastating for the whole sector, and thousands of companies. For further information check the attached paper  D) There are currently no feasible alternatives for PFAS in this sector and uses.  E) PFAS-free polymers have been tested recently in the turbine industry as potential substitutes. Particularly, silica-based coatings, PEEK, or UHMW-PE have been tested, as well as ceramic solutions, but have proved to have very poor chemical and friction resistance, thus being discarded as functioning. In some cases, the materials were able to withstand the conditions in the power plant, but for a very short period of time, which would require the periodical substitution of components to be done so often that it would render power plants completely inefficient in terms of electricity generation as well as financially. For further information check the attached paper  F) We don’t have any information in this topic  G) Should a derogation not take place for the power plant sector, EUTurbines members expect a loss of 100% revenue in the EU, ending operations immediately and causing the loss of thousands of jobs. Furthermore, if the PFAS ban is not derogated for the energy sector, there is a very high risk that the currently operational plants won’t be able to find spare parts needed for the normal maintenance due to the presence of PFAS in them. This would cause major disruptions in the European energy system, leading to a lack of offer to cover for the demand of electricity, causing shutdowns not only in homes and buildings, but industries all across Europe, potentially accounting for thousands of millions worth of losses. For further information check the attached paper

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: Tyrolit Schleifmittelwerke Swarovski AG & CO K.G. fully supports the protection goal of the EU Commission to keep potentially harmful substances out of environmental systems as well as human, animal and plant life.
However, the restriction proposal submitted to the European Chemicals Agency ECHA in February 2023 to regulate PFAS goes far beyond this.

Fluoropolymers (e.g. PTFE, fluoroelastomers) are part of the PFAS group due to their molecular structure. But their toxicological and ecotoxicological profiles differ substantially from the majority of PFAS substances. Fluoropolymers, including fluoroelastomers, are thermally,
biologically and chemically stable, non-bioaccumulative, non-toxic, non-mobile, non-bioavailable and have been shown to meet the globally recognized OECD criteria for Polymers of Low Concern (PLC).

We therefore request the exemption of fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers from the restriction as industrial production aids that do not become part of ready-to-sell finished articles, so that they may continue to be traded and used in the European Union. The approach of the restriction proposal to group all fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers with other PFAS types needs to be reconsidered.
Furthermore, we believe it is essential that an obligation to provide information within the supply chain for intentionally added/contained PFAS is implemented before general restrictions are introduced, as without knowledge of relevant uses it is impossible to apply for necessary exemptions.
On the current state of knowledge, in the abrasive industry polymers of low concern (fluoropolymers: PTFE) are used as auxiliary or operating materials. These materials are essential for the production process. As the abrasive industry is still auditing its supply chain to identify all details to
PFAS used in auxiliary and operating materials, we ask for a derogation for polymers of low concern from the restriction for the production of abrasive products. In case no time unlimited derogation/exemption can be given and considering the early stage of alternatives development, we request at minimum a derogation of 12 years plus transition period (13.5 years) for the use of PTFE-containing auxiliary and operating products in the production of abrasive products.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Currently, there are no adequate sectors and sub-uses available.  We propose to implement them:  Sector: „Industrial use/application of PFAS-materials“ Sub-uses:   - Industrial use/application of fluoropolymers as general auxiliary and operating materials during the production process.  - Industrial use/application of fluoroelastomers as general auxiliary and operating materials during the production process.  - Industrial use/application of fluoropolymers as component or machine element in production machinery.  - Industrial use/application of fluoroelastomers as component or machine element in production machinery.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Materials containing PTFE are used only as auxiliary and operating materials in the manufacture of abrasive products. The abrasive products themselves are free of PFAS. Due to very specific conditions in the production of especially resinoid bonded abrasive products –high temperature, high pressure, presence of resins – PTFE-coated glass fabrics, foils, fibres, metal plates or other PTFE products are used to resist these specific conditions. The PTFE  coated products are used for the handling of resin containing material during several manufacturing steps including the curing process in an oven. In addition, PTFE spray is used as release agent / lubricant. PTFE is used as it combines very specific properties like high temperature and pressure stability, non-stick properties, in some cases flexibility, chemical resistance and durability. A ban on these substances would have a severe impact on the production of abrasive products in terms of quality/ performance, safety and sustainability.  The PTFE products are used several times and will only be disposed when they do not fulfil the quality requirements anymore.  Due to the fact, that these PTFE products are only used at production sites a competent handling of the products by trained workers can be ensured.  When the products have reached the end of their life, they are collected separately and disposed of by certified disposal companies in accordance with national regulations.  Typically, most of the waste is incinerated which means that fluoropolymers will be destroyed during  this process. Furthermore, PFAS products are also used as components/safety equipment of production  machines. In all areas, the production lines include e.g. seals made of fluoropolymers, which  are essential to resist the production conditions and to ensure a safe production of abrasive  products.

6. Missing uses: Missing PFAS use: „Industrial use/application fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers as general auxiliary and operating materials during the production process “ Therefore, we propose to implement the sector "industrial application of PFAS materials", as well as the sub-uses:   - Industrial use/application von of fluoropolymers as general auxiliary and operating materials during the production process.  - Industrial use/application von of fluoroelastomers as general auxiliary and operating materials during the production process.  - Industrial use/application of fluoropolymers as component or machine element in production machinery.  - Industrial use/application of fluoroelastomers as component or machine element in production machinery.  TYROLIT Schleifmittelwerke Swarovski AG & Co. KG develops, manufactures and sells tools for surface finishing and cutting of materials. These tools are used in various industries, such as chemical, medical and process industry, railway, apparatus and tank construction, steel mills and foundries, wind and solar energy, vehicle construction, aerospace, mechanical engineering, and others. Especially most of the key industries for the implementation of the green deal goals of the EU as well as the sustainability goals of the UN directly depend on reliable and efficient processing of metals as construction materials provided by machining tools.  In the manufacture of resin bonded grinding tools, materials containing PTFE are used as auxiliary and operating materials, both in direct use and as part of components of the necessary manufacturing equipment. These include PTFE-coated glass fabric, metal plates and containers, PTFE hoses, etc., which are required due to the combination of various properties such as high temperature and pressure stability, non-stick properties, in some cases flexibility, chemical resistance and durability.  To expose the complexity of our sector, the abrasive industry has tens of thousands of products in its portfolio and produces a large segment of customized products for specific industrial applications. In most cases, the alternatives (e.g. silicones) did not fulfil the specific requirements of the abrasive production.  Silicone coated glass fabrics have been tested but the resistance against heat and pressure and the non-sticky properties are not sufficient for the production conditions in the abrasive industry applications.  The major problem is that there is no one-fits all solutions. This means that companies have to invest a lot of resources for the identification of possible substitutes and practical tests for products which are used as auxiliary products in the production process. This ties up resources  that are needed for the development of their core products – an effort that is completely disproportionate in view of polymers of low concern. With respect to seals or other products used as machines components in the production of abrasive products, abrasive companies do not have the scientific knowledge nor the expertise to decide if an alternative has the same quality and resistance than PTFE products which have  been used successfully for several years.  Tests with alternative materials resulted in more frequent product’s replacement which goes  against the very principles advocated by the Green Deal and the much-discussed Ecodesign  Sustainable Product Regulation: a drastic impairment of the product’s sustainability.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Considering the fact that PTFE/Fluoropolymers meet the globally recognized OECD criteria for  polymers of low concern, VDS asks for an exclusion of fluoropolymers from the restriction  proposal, or for an exemption by way of a time-unlimited derogation. Alternatively, in case  no time-unlimited derogation/exemption can be given. and considering the early stage of alternatives development, TYROLIT requests at minimum a derogation of 12 years plus transition  period (13.5 years) for the use of PTFE-containing auxiliary and operating products in the production of abrasive products.

8. Other identified uses: Although the abrasive industry is rather small compared to other sectors, the abrasive products are essential for the production of significant industrial sectors – for example in the energy sector, medical technology, the automotive, aerospace and defence industries and mechanical and plant engineering. Abrasive products have different functions: grinding, cutting, drilling and surface conditioning. Abrasive products have enormous importance and leverage in almost all industrial manufacturing processes. They are indispensable both for securing basic needs and maintaining system-relevant industrial productions.  At the moment, an exact estimation of the economic impacts of the PFAS restriction to the abrasive industry is difficult to make as the industry is still in the auditing process of their auxiliary and operating products. With the current restriction proposal almost all abrasive companies are concerned – at least with machine components.  PTFE is used as auxiliary and operating materials, therefore the final abrasive products do not contain PTFE which means that the import of products from outside the EU will not be impacted by the restriction proposal. This is a clear disadvantage of European producers compared to non-European producers who do not have to invest a huge amount of money in the  substitution of auxiliary and operating products. If no adequate substitute is available, European abrasives producers will be exposed to competitive disadvantages as they will no longer be able to produce with the same quality. Apart from the impact on the abrasive industry itself, the impact on other industry sectors must be taken into consideration. Abrasive products have key functions in the production processes of almost all industry sectors in all EU member states. This will have an enormous economic impact on the whole European industry and potentially lead to a great dependency on imports from outside Europe. Especially in times of fragile supply chains, this dependency  might result in a stop of productions in certain industry sectors in Europe. This will also impact the implementation of the Green Deal at European level. In addition, abrasive products are often individually designed for the customer in bilateral development processes and optimized for a specific process. The physical proximity to the customer is essential for this and is hardly possible with imported products. The result again is a possible lack of safety and quality.

General Comments: UCIMAC (Costruttori Italiani Macchine per Caffè Espresso ed Attrezzature per Bar, www.ucimac.org) is the Italian association of manufacturers of professional and commercial coffee machines and coffee grinders.
UCIMAC represents 16 member-companies, with a total turnover of more than 500 M€ and with a share of 75% destined for foreign markets and a share of more than 40% destined to European Union market.

In Italy there are 30 companies in this sector with a total turnover of more than 750 M€ and more than 3000 employees.

UCIMAC protects and promotes the interests of its member-companies through participation in the main technical committees, national and international, in the drafting of product technical standards, in supporting the interpretation and application of regulations and in the daily challenges of the world market through committees UNI (Italian Standardization Body), CEI (Italian Electrotechnical Committee), CEN (European Committee for Standardization), CENELEC (European Committee for Electrotechnical Standardization), ISO (International Organization for Standardization), IEC (International Electrothecnical Commission), NSF Food Equipment Joint Committee and its working groups (for USA market) and UL Standards Technical Panels (for USA market).

UCIMAC is part of ANIMA Federation (Confindustria Meccanica Varia).

UCIMAC supports the objective of avoiding emissions of hazardous substances into the environment and an appropriate regulation of uncontrollable risks posed by individual substances. Our industries are committed to continuously improving the environmental compatibility and safety of the products they place on the market.
UCIMAC’s technology industries offer a wide range of solutions, such as catering equipment, professional coffee machines and sustainable professional goods. All of these could only be produced today with the use of PFAS and would not work at all or work less efficiently without it. Therefore, restricting substances should not be done without a differentiated consideration of their uses and the consequences.
What is needed is a more differentiated regulatory approach that is risk-based according to Article 68(1) REACH and substance-based according to Article 69 REACH. The proposed blanket restriction of all PFAS, regardless of their toxicity and risk profile, does not meet this requirement. Given their enormous importance in industry, the safe use of PFAS must remain possible as long as their risks can be sufficiently "managed" by appropriate measures or no suitable substitutes are available.
It is important to distinguish between the different PFAS (groups) and the risks from each use.
It is also important to consider whether identified risks can be minimised through targeted measures, e.g. in occupational health and safety/emission control or waste legislation, rather than through a general ban under REACH. Only risky applications and those for which a technically suitable, economically proportionate and less environmentally and health damaging alternative exists should be restricted. Otherwise, we risk having an unmanageably long list of very specific exemptions or excluding certain products and processes from the European market.
Adequate transition periods of twelve years after entry into force (depending on product life and development times) for full conversion are needed, as provided for in other legislation, e.g. RoHS. An 18-month transition period for the full conversion of products and processes, as foreseen in the proposal, is insufficient.
Following the risk based approach we should consider that fluoropolymers are different to other PFAS for the reasons listed below:
• They do not exhibit the toxicological and environmental profiles associated with non-polymeric PFASs that could be considered of concern.
• They have unique physical-chemical properties, which let them very different from non-polymer PFAS and therefore should have a distinct class within them.
• They meet the OECD criteria of Polymer of Low Concern (PLC) and are non-toxic, biocompatible, insoluble and immobile molecules, which are deemed to have insignificant environmental and human health impact.

Industrial production of Fluoropolymers can and has to be handled safely in industrial facilities under controlled conditions.

Fluoropolymers are used for several use in the food and feed processing equipment to meet food contact safety, professional performance and durability.

Main implications for manufacturers, especially for UCIMAC members, of equipment are:
• No alternative allows a complete replacement with performances of equivalent quality; there are some possible alternatives for some properties but there’s no one material that present all the specific and unique properties of Fluoropolymers (no 1:1 alternatives are available)
• Costs will arise due to necessary amendments of machinery and equipment when switching to alternative substances. The industrial application process on products using non-fluoropolymers material is much more complicated.
• Due to the greater quantity of product necessary for this application and the reduced service life of the treated articles, a significant environmental impact must be considered in terms of nanoforms (microplastic) and CO2 emissions.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Main sector for UCIMAC is the production of professional devices for catering, hotellerie, restaurants and cafè, examples: • Coffee machines • Espresso coffee machines • Coffee grinders • Milk refrigerators • Soluble beverage machines

6. Missing uses: The fluoropolymers used in food and beverage industry are: • FKM for gaskets • PTFE for gaskets and steam circuit components • PVDF for milk circuits • FEP and PFA for hoses for milk, hot water and coffee  The above applications do not have alternatives with comparable performance in terms of corrosion resistance, durability and cleaning effectiveness. FEP and PFA do not have an alternative at all while the others could be replaced with existing materials with reduced mentioned performances. This could lead to the reduction of MTBF of the appliances for more than two times, increase the cost of maintenance of the same ratio, expose the product (beverage) to the risk of contamination due to poor cleanability which may expose human being (consumer) to hygienic risks.  point a)  Quantities of PFAS fluoropolymers used in the food and beverage industry are difficult to estimate because they are used only in a small fraction of the number of parts that make up the appliances.  point b)  Fluoropolymers are crucial for many applications in the food and beverage sector due to their unique properties. Their non-wetting and non-stick properties and high resistance to extreme temperatures provide a number of benefits and key functionalities including: • Increased lifetime of components • Lower cleaning and maintenance costs • Increased productivity by enabling production of multiple products with the same equipment, reducing failures and improving flow of process substances • Higher production yields and quality from improved purity of process substances • Health benefits from high purity and hygiene standards and lower health risks from cross contamination • Prolonged preservation of the product • Combination of steam, heat and chemical resistance enables efficient cleaning and sanitization of milk circuits  Point c)  Affected companies manufacturer of professional and commercial coffee machines and coffee grinders.: all, included most of their supply chain. In Italy there are more than 30 companies that will be affected by the restriction with a total turnover of 750 M€ and more than 3000 employees. In this estimation we do not consider the supply chain that produce the component based on PFAS used by the food and beverage industry.  Point d) For all the application of the fluoropolymers cited there are no alternatives yet having performance comparable to existing ones.  Point e) The R&D effort for develop new materials and test them on the appliances depends not only on the food and beverage industry itself but also on the supply chain of technological parts. This process will take place in two steps, first the development of new materials by the suppliers and, second, the test and developments of these new materials on the appliances by the food and beverage industry. This could take an amount of time that now it is not foreseeable and in any case it is not less than 12 years (see also reply to request No. 7, the next one).

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: In our view, for the reasons mentioned in the answer to the specific request No. 6, even if alternative substances are currently being developed, these would need to go through repeated demonstrations and evaluations and therefore they would take considerable time before they can be implemented. Moreover, for substances for which no alternatives have been identified yet, research and development will have to be promoted through trial and error in the future, and even a 12-year grace period may not be enough to confirm their availability. A risk analysis should be made for every single application of fluoropolymers and a more suitable period of derogations should be settled for each of them.  Because of that we propose to have a 12 year grace period and, during that, to conduct specific risk analysis to identify risks in order to take proper decisions based on that.

General Comments: Understanding Per-and Poly Fluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS)
PFAS stands for Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl substances and describes a wide range of chemistries with very different properties and uses. Because there are clear and important distinctions between the more than 4,700 materials often referred to as PFAS, it is a very complex topic. Therefore, when communicating about PFAS, we believe it is important to be specific about the particular chemistries or type of PFAS being discussed. There are significant differences between the chemical and physical properties of fluotopolymers like PVDF and ECTFE and other materials most often associated with the term PFAS. “PFAS” are, for example, described as mobile in the environment. PVDF and ECTFE, are fluoropolymers, are not mobile in the environment.

Semiconductor devices (“chips” or “integrated circuits”) are important components of many electronic devices. This “chips” are extremely complex to manufacture whereby up to 2000 process steps, which will require a production time up to 26 weeks.
In this semiconductor industry, fluoropolymers are used for transport of ultrapure water and other process media due to the excellent leach out behaviour, cleanliness, resistance against bio-film, high temperature resistance, chemical resistance, excellent mechanical properties and long lifetime performance.
PVDF is an inert material, and therefore absolute necessary to transport highest grades of ultrapure water required for the wet chemistry process in semiconductor factories to manufacture node sizes of 14,12,10,8,5, 3 nanometer. PVDF is intrinsically linked to the technology advances which has allowed the current node sizes to be achieved.
Ultrapure water in this industry is one of the most used media required in the wafer production, Ultra pure water is used in many process steps and the quality of water is most important for the chip factory output (yield)

Semiconductor fabs have a construction time of currently 2-3 years and run for 10-25 years after start up.
Considering that the Semiconductor industry was estimated having a global sale of 600 Billion$ (in 2022) and a further required growth up to 1 Trillion$ till 2030, because of the increasing demand on high quality chips in many applications (cars. KI, AI, data centers, 5G, etc,…) this industry plays a potential economical factor worldwide. Without PVDF the ability to produce semiconductor will be put at high risk.

UPW…Ultra pure water is a high-grade water that´s free from impurities like microbes, minerals and dissolved gases- It only contains H2O molecules and has a purity level very near to 100% and essential for the wafer cleaning process

Cold UPW… UPW with a temperature of ~20°C
Hot UPW… UPW with a temperature of ~ 75°C

Those products are included in the use category “semiconductors” as described in Annex XV, Table 8, of the proposed restriction, and identified with a 12 years derogation. We request on exemptoin for the category "semiconductors".

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: PVDF used for transport and storage of UPW (Ultra Pure Water) and other process media in the Semiconductor industry as well in pharmaceutical, bio-tech, hydrogen (H2) generation industry.  The specific Sector “PVDF Fluoropolymers used for transport and storage of UPW (Ultra Pure Water) and other process media in the Semiconductor industry” process is not listed in Annex XV.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: For the specific use-case mainly PVDF products are used. PVDF products like pipes, fittings, valves and sheets are solid products. We are using only PVDF raw materials without fluorinated polymerization aids. A controlled supply chain from resin manufacturing till installation in the UPW system is fully implemented and ensures zero emission.  Product manufacturing phase Our PVDF fittings and valves are produced by injection molding and pipes by extrusion. The complete production process is performed under cleanroom condition (class 9 and class 5 acc. DIN EN ISO 14644) - the production takes place in a complete contained environment.  Cleanroom: A cleanroom is a controlled environment that filters pollutants like dust, airborne microbes, and aerosol particles to provide the cleanest area possible. Class 0 would be the highest class. Semiconductor industry is working under clean room conditions 5. (cleanroom classes are defined in DIN EN ISO 14644)  All components are specially packed to ensure no contamination is taking place in the supply chain till the products are installed in the semiconductor fab.   During the production of PVDF components (process steps as mentioned before) no environmental pollution (no spraying, no microplastics, no Ionic or non-ionic PFAS from coatings etc.)/ emissions do appear. Measurements in the air (production environment) and process water are planned. The result will be published in a separate consultation later.  The use-phase:  Products are used in the following specific sub-uses:  PVDF-UHP piping systems (pipes, fittings and valves) are used for handling of Hot and Cold UPW (starting from UPW treatment plant, distribution loop, sub-main and hook-up piping to the process tools) as well for handling of other process media in this industry. PVDF piping system are used in waste water and chemical collection systems in semiconductor factories.  No emission are caused by using PVDF piping system for handling UPW, waste water and chemicals in a semiconductor fab. In actual fact this piping system ensures high life time and excellent and safe performances as required by this industry.  End-of-life:  Equipment which is decommissioned after service life (up to 30 years) will be stored under strict governmental rules (hazardous waste) in dedicated landfills or will be incinerated. PVDF Products are stable and will not degrade to PFAS.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: The process discusses is called Hot and Cold UPW  a) The industry especially semiconductor industry has a growing demand on PVDF piping systems because of the technical benefits PVDF offers for this high-grade production processes.  Specially for this application we are producing PVDF pipes, PVDF fittings and PVDF valves, PVDF sheets  b)  • Excellent leach out behaviour / cleanliness  • Very low particle shedding • High surface smoothness of piping components • Excellent temperature / mechanical properties • Optical transparency  • Low moisture absorption • Physiologically non toxic • Very good thermal stability and electrical properties • Excellent long term performance • Further analysis see attachement  c) Every state of the art semiconductor fab worldwide use PVDF piping systems and sheets in wet process systems. Detailed numbers are shown in the attached document.  d) PVDF has been introduced to this industry since 1980 and has become in the mean time the most suitable material for handling high quality Ultra Pure Water. In the past because of lower quality of water stainless steel and PVC piping systems were also used. Performance experience have shown that this materials the required quality level of UPW can by far not be reached and kept.  e) PVDF has become established over the last two decades and represents the required state of the art material.  f) From 5 to more than 25 years it is not currently possible to demonstrate that non PVDF alternative can fulfill the application specific performance requirement for UPW supply and storage. It may be necessary to invent new chemicals/polymers  as well develop alternative approaches in the manufacturing process that may or may not provide equivalent performance of the final Semiconductor devices.  g) See attachement

General Comments: Unfortunately, the proposed ban does not take into account at all the fact that PFAS are widely used in the pharmaceutical industry in facilities and equipment for the manufacturing and testing of medicinal products, in engineering and other fields of use.
The proposal text mentions such applications only for the food manufacturing industry (where, fortunately, exemptions are provided).
A short-term ban on PFAS poses the risk that the above-mentioned equipment and facilities in the pharmaceutical industry can no longer be operated which means that the supply of medicinal products to the population would no longer be guaranteed.
There are currently only very few substitute materials; the development of such substitute materials will certainly take years (with an uncertain outcome), if manufacturers are at all interested in making such a development effort.
Regardless of the consequences for the supply of pharmaceuticals, a short-term PFAS ban will also have an impact on the pharmaceutical companies themselves, primarily in form of a drop in sales and all the associated consequences (layoffs, company closures, relocations to non-European countries, etc.).
Exemptions and deferred entries into force are therefore requested.

As outlined in question 2 of this consultation, it is important to evaluate the sector of heating heat pumps on its own and not to aggregate all F-gas applications into one "application of fluorinated gases". To meet the variety of technical challenges, the use of PFAS for the numerous and different components used in heat pumps, as well as for the various systems and installation requirements, is crucial. With the help of our systems, blow-molded plastic products can be manufactured with minimal weight and energy input for energy and resource efficiency. Our systems are typically exposed to temperatures of up to 260°C, which place high demands on the sealing and lubricating materials used. We primarily use PFAS-containing components in the area of drive and fluid technology (seals, O-rings) and as lubricants during assembly. Since these components are very expensive, we only use them where the specific requirements necessitate their use. The PFAS group comprises many different substances, some of which are known to be dangerous to humans and the environment (e.g. perfluorooctanoic acid, perfluorohexanoic acid), while others, such as Teflon/PTFE, have no known negative effects despite decades of intensive use.

We clearly support the restriction of PFAS that are proven to be dangerous to humans and the environment. In the sealing technology, PFAS like PTFE, FKM, FFKM, or FPM are indispensable. The substances relevant to the sealing and lubricant industry are fluoropolymers, which the OECD has classified as "Polymers of low concern" and are considered non-toxic, non-bioavailable, and non-water soluble, therefore having no significant impact on the environment and people. When resistance to higher temperatures or higher tribological requirements at the sealing point are required, PFAS seals are used. The use of PFAS-free seals is not possible in many applications. Combined Comments: "Our machines and equipment are built to last for decades. In this context, it is important that replacement and used parts are taken into account in the restriction proposal. Neither fundamental exceptions to the regulation, nor longer transition periods are provided. This means that after the 18-month transition period, repairs, or the regular replacement of wear parts in durable products, such as the replacement of seals or hoses in industrial plants, would no longer be possible. Even where there are exceptions, these are proposed for only five and twelve years. It is not clear whether and how an extension of the existing exceptions can be requested. Due to the lack of standardized, simple analysis methods, it is not possible to control how the implementation of the restriction proposal, for example, especially with regard to imported PFAS-containing products, can be ensured in the future by market surveillance. This would lead to the fact that PFAS-containing products could no longer be manufactured in the EU, but they might still find their way into the EU. Uncontrolled import of PFAS-containing products would lead to significant competitive disadvantages. 8738" "We are a medium-sized, family-owned company in mechanical engineering. Combined Comments:
General Comments: Urenco is an organization headquartered in the United Kingdom with operating plants in the UK, Germany, the Netherlands and the USA.  This information is submitted by Urenco Deutschland GmbH on behalf of Urenco Ltd and the Urenco group of companies.
Urenco enriches natural uranium to produce Enriched Uranium Product (EUP), which is the precursor for uranium dioxide (UO2) fuel pellets used in commercial Nuclear Power Plants (NPP). Urenco provides EUP required to operate NPP’s in Europe, the USA , the Middle East and Asia from its enrichments production locations in Europe and the US. Orano, based in France, also provides enrichment services using the same technology as Urenco.
The two leading Western EUP suppliers are Urenco and Orano providing around two thirds of the enrichment services for European and US NPPs, with a fifth coming from Russia and the balance largely from existing inventories. Following the Ukraine crisis, the Urenco/Orano share will evidently increase as a result of the European and US  intention to become completely independent from energy supply provided by Russia and China.
The Urenco enrichment process uses so-called ultracentrifuge technology which involves processing of highly corrosive and hazardous uranium hexafluoride (UF6), the only existing volatile uranium compound that can be used for the enrichment process, as well as hydrogen fluoride (HF) and fluorine (F2) as by-products.  Due to their extremely high oxidation potential these compounds can only be safely and properly handled using fully fluorinated, polymeric materials. No alternative polymeric materials have been identified  that could reliably and safely replace the perfluorinated compound in use. Hence the use of perfluorinated lubricants (PFPE), polymers (e.g. PTFE, PTCFE) and elastomers (e.g. FKM) are essential for Urenco’s enrichment process, which cannot be operated without these materials.
In addition to uranium enrichment, Urenco’s Dutch subsidiary, Urenco Nederland BV, utilizes the same ultracentrifuge technology for production of, and research and development associated with, Stable Isotopes (SI).  Stable Isotopes are used across the globe by a large variety of organisations  for health services and industrial applications. A large share of Urenco Nederland’s Stable Isotope  product portfolio are precursors for radio-isotopes that are used for radio-diagnostic and radio-therapeutic application, contributing to the treatment of more than 2 million patients per annum in the western world, and  as precursors for advanced electronic materials in the semi-conductor industry. Similarly to UF6, the process media used for Stable Isotope enrichment are comparably corrosive and can only be handled in process equipment that uses perfluoropolymers.  The main alternative supplier for stable isotopes is Russia. Urenco supplies about one quarter of enriched heavy stable isotopes in the western world, with the remainder largely being supplied by Russia (other sources are below 3%). This means that in case of a ban of PFAS, there would be full reliance on Russian supply of these isotopes. However, even Russian capacity may be insufficient to supply the western market, therefore causing gaps in the supply of diagnostic and therapeutic health services and semi-conductor technology. Further, as a result of the war in Ukraine, dependence on Russian supply is now undesirable and so we expect that procurement of Stable Isotope products from Russia will reduce.
Urenco fully supports the aim of the Chemicals Strategy for Sustainability to improve the protection of human health and the environment against risks from chemicals and at the same time to increase the competitiveness of EU industry. However, Urenco rejects the broad regulation of entire groups of substances - in the case of PFAS, several thousand substances - irrespective of their actual risk. The PFAS regulatory approach being planned is contrary to generally accepted REACH principles, such as that there should only be restrictions in the case of unacceptable risks.
The proposed restriction asserts that there is sufficiently strong evidence for the adverse effects on the environment and the increased risk on human health damage for a number of specific PFAS compounds. However, with regard to fluoropolymers, the proposed restriction report provides no evidence to substantiate such effects.  On the contrary, although fluoropolymers are clearly persistent in the aquatic environment, there is strong evidence based on a number of scientific publications  that fluoropolymers are  completely insoluble in the aquatic environment  and therefore non-bioavailable. As such they are non-bioaccumulative and non-toxic.
These studies conclude that the majority of fluoropolymers meet the OECD criteria to be classified as ‘polymers of low concern’ (PLC), which are deemed to have insignificant environmental and human health impacts and based on that we propose they should be exempted from the restriction.
In the Urenco enrichment process perfluorinated polymers are used in completely closed production systems, in most cases for the life-time of the equipment.  The small number of perfluorinated components that are replaced based on preventative or corrective maintenance are generally radioactively contaminated. Disposal of radio-active waste materials is strictly regulated in the countries where Urenco operates, these materials are conditioned and immobilized (cemented) and transferred for long term storage in the appropriate national nuclear repositories, hence, PFAS from those materials have no transmission path into the environment.
Based on the arguments presented above, in summary:
• The unique properties of perfluorinated polymers make them indispensable for the safe processing of corrosive process media (UF6, HF and F2) used in Urenco’s enrichment process for the production of Enriched Uranium Product for global nuclear fuel production and the production of Stable Isotopes for health and industrial applications.
• There are currently no viable alternatives for handling these highly reactive chemical  compounds used in the front end nuclear fuel cycle, and it is highly unlikely that viable alternatives will be available in the future.
• There is no evidence that perfluorinated polymers have a significant harmful effect on the environment and human health.
• There is likely no transmission pathway of the perfluorinated polymers used by Urenco into the (aquatic) environment due to radio-active contamination, which requires treatment and storage in long-term national repositories.
• The proposed restrictions will result in the shut-down of the western enrichment industry and consequently nuclear power generation which will lead to incalculable and highly undesirable socio-economic consequences across the European community and the wider world due to lack of a secure and reliable energy supply.
• The proposed restrictions will terminate Western production of heavy stable isotopes as needed for medical and other purposes creating full reliance on Russian supply.
• The restrictions would also be likely to lead to loss of employment for a large number of people working in the enrichment industry, the wider nuclear fuel supply chain and nuclear power plants.

Urenco proposes a complete, time unlimited exemption for the production, use and import of any perfluorinated lubricants, polymers and elastomers from the currently proposed restriction with regard to the uses as mentioned above.
We have further detailed our justification for this proposal in the information below.

The main sector and use is the energy sector (annex E.2.12.). As described in 3.  general information section, Urenco is engaged in the enrichment of uranium. Urenco’s Enriched Uranium Product (EUP) is the precursor for uranium dioxide used as nuclear fuel in NPP’s across the western world and far east. Currently, around two thirds of the enrichment services for Western NPP’s is provided by Urenco (from plants located in Germany, the Netherlands, England and the US), and by Orano (based in France), a fifth is produced in Russia and the remainder is largely being sourced from existing inventories. The combined market share held by Urenco and Orano will evidently increase as a result of the current geopolitical situation with respect to Russia.  Implementation of the proposed Annex, as written, will mean Orano and Urenco are no longer able to produce enriched uranium products for about two thirds of the western NPPs, which will likely destabilize the entire global energy supply and market.  Source: https://world-nuclear.org/information-library/nuclear-fuel-cycle/conversion-enrichment-and-fabrication/uranium-enrichment.aspx In addition to front end supply of the nuclear energy sector, Urenco  is the main Western supplier for essential Stable Isotope products for industrial use,  specifically in the medical (Annex E.2.9.) and semiconductor (Annex E.2.11.) sectors, which Urenco would also no longer be able to produce as a result of the proposed ban. Moreover there are several other uses where the proposed restriction will at a minimum, have significant negative impact on Urenco’s operation and potentially a complete shut-down of Urenco’s ability to provide enrichment services for the nuclear fuel cycle and stable isotope production: • The enrichment process requires the use of coolants and refrigerants to achieve very low temperatures, and for this application fluorinated gases are essential (Annex E.2.8.). • Urenco’s process equipment can only use perfluorinated lubricants suitable for harsh conditions, to ensure safe functioning and safety of the equipment (Annex E.2.14.). • For safe transport of both natural UF6 feed material as well EUP, the valves of specially licensed transport cylinders are equipped with PTFE seals  (Annex E.2.10.). • And finally Urenco also uses construction materials (Annex E.2.13.) in its enrichment and auxiliary processes (e.g. PTFE thread sealants, PTCFE and PVDF construction materials)

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: For the perfluorinated polymers, elastomers and lubricant derogations are proposed by ECHA under the RO2 scenario: o Lubricants Annex E.2.14. Lubricants where the use takes place under harsh conditions or use is for safe functioning and safety of equipment; Ban with a transition period of 18 months and a 12-year derogation o Fluoropolymer applications, petroleum and mining Annex E.2.15.; Ban with a transition period of 18 months and a 12-year derogation. For Urenco’s enrichment process these proposed derogations will very likely only result in postponing the socio-economic impacts described under the RO1 scenario (see request 6) for the following reasons: o No viable alternatives have been identified to date for perfluorinated polymers to safely process the highly corrosive and reactive process media (UF6, HF and F2) and meet the other functional properties required. o The chances of successful identification, development and qualification of such alternatives are remote if not impossible for the reasons described in request 6.  o Replacement of perfluorinated polymers in all process equipment with alternative seals and lubricants will  be cost prohibitive and result in unacceptable downtime of the capacity as it will effectively require dismantling and rebuilding all equipment (centrifuges, pumps etc.). o Moreover the overall process of research, development, qualification, regulatory approval by the competent authorities and implementation of alternatives will, in the Nuclear sector undoubtedly stretch even beyond the a 12-year derogation period. Based above arguments Urenco applies for a time-unlimited exemption for the continued use of its complete perfluorinated polymer, elastomer and lubricant inventory. For the fluorinated gases the following derogation is proposed under the RO2 scenario  o Application of fluorinated gases Annex E.2.8.; Ban with a transition period of 18 months and a 5-year derogation.  The timeline for this derogation proposal appears to be roughly aligned with the existing legislation for the phase-out of 95% green-house F-gases by 2030 (EC regulation No 517/2014). However the latter regulation is aimed at restriction of supply, not use and makes an exception for F-gases for cooling < -50oC as the alternative development and qualification is not deemed feasible in this time frame.  The proposed derogation therefore conflicts with existing legislation.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Use of fluoropolymers in chemical industry was not considered as a derogation in the Restriction proposal.
In order to support the authorities with their evaluation, we provide substantial data on
- the indispensable need of fluoropolymers in chemical production,
- the chemical resistance and leaching behavior of PTFE,
- the incompatibility/lack of non-PFAS alternatives,
- the enormous impact of a potential ban, due to the ubiquitous presence of fluoropolymer components in production equipment,
- the range of PFAS emissions resulting from the use of fluoropolymers in production, namely:
o information on the very low turnover and disposal volumes of fluoropolymers,
o information on the disposal of our fluoropolymer components at a hazardous waste incineration plant,
- the immense potential impact on our company.
Considering the evidence provided, we ask for a time-unlimited derogation for the use of fluoropolymer materials in chemical manufacturing. This derogation must include all upstream processes to manufacture these fluoropolymers and articles to ensure resilience of the chemical industry in the EU market.

The restriction proposal contains a list of applications for which temporary exemptions are considered, but the use of fluoropolymers in chemical industry production has not been taken into account.
Industrial chemical manufacturing is highly integrated, often including multiple process steps, and using multipurpose facilities/plants. Fluoropolymers and other PFAS-containing articles are uniquely suited for use in these production steps. Use of these materials is critical due to their unparalleled chemical and permeation resistance, chemical durability, temperature stability and low leaching potential.
The restriction proposal in its current form would inevitably jeopardize the functioning of the European chemical industry, and critically impact downstream use sectors, such as the semiconductor and pharmaceutical industries.
Taken together, the use of PFAS in manufacturing plants is understood as essential to the chemical industry. The proposed ban will negatively affect its current innovative strength and the desired resilience of European industry.
Fluoropolymer components are used in chemical manufacturing facility equipment and infrastructure numbering in the many thousands. In order to bring clarity, we provide concrete examples of production usage.
Non-PFAS alternatives cannot fulfil the specific application requirements and thorough testing of alternatives has so far not resulted in viable alternatives – which is based on the unique properties of the C-F-bond in PFAS materials.
The lack of alternatives exists for many of the industry’s uses of fluorocarbon-containing articles and products and potential alternatives must be evaluated on a case-by-case basis.
With adequate risk management measures related to use and disposal of articles (including fluoropolymers), exposure to the environment or populations across all our product life cycle phases (service life, end-of-life, disposal) can be strongly limited.
The enormous impact of an implementation of the current draft restriction proposal on worker employment as well as on business figures of our company is described in a separate confidential document.

With the information provided (in more detail in the attachment) we hope to contribute to an appropriate regulation of PFAS including fluoropolymers while avoiding critical impacts on EU industry. Given the broad range and complexity of PFAS uses in this area, we are open to a direct exchange allowing us to give more detailed insights – which also includes the option to visit our site in Darmstadt.

Additional comments will be submitted separately by Merck to provide also regarding other PFAS uses a better basis for an adequate regulation of PFAS materials.
Merck is additionally actively contributing to industry association comments as e.g. from VCI, Cefic, SEMI, SIA and EFPIA – some comments are already submitted, others will be submitted later in course of the consultation phase.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Considering the points required: for some of our chemical plants we gathered information on the yearly replacement and the disposal of fluoropolymers: the estimated amount of fluoropolymers is 30-100 KG per plant per year. All fluoropolymers are treated at a hazardous waste incineration plant. More information is given in the attachment.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Fluoropolymer equipment waste is separately collected at its end-of-life phase and is subject to hazardous-waste incineration. Fluoropolymers waste is treated at a hazardous waste incineration plant using high temperature incineration. According to Regulation (EU) 2019/1021 and other publications high-temperature incineration is correlated to temperatures > 1,100 °C and 2 seconds contact time. Under these conditions, fluoropolymers are considered to be destroyed (RAC also proposes similar conditions in case of PFAS incineration in the opinion on the PFAS firefighting foam restriction Annex XV dossier: “If PFAS containing waste is incinerated or co-incinerated, the temperature shall be at least 1 100 °C”). These conditions are achieved in the hazardous waste incinerators used.  More information is given in the attachment.

6. Missing uses: The use of fluoropolymers in chemical manufacturing plants is not adequately addressed in the current Restriction proposal. In the attachment we provide information on the different aspects addressed in point a to g regarding this use. We demonstrate why chemical production with organic solvents and strong acids/bases is only possible with the use of fluoropolymers as only fluoropolymers fulfill the requirements regarding worker safety, environmental safety, and product quality. Thus, the entire chemical industry in the EU would be largely jeopardized by implementation of the current restriction proposal with critical impact also on downstream industries as e.g., semiconductor or pharmaceutical industry. The potential impact of the current restriction proposal on our company is described in the confidential attachment to this submission.

General Comments: Use of PFAS in cables

ZVEI e. V., the German Electro and Digital Industry Association, represents an industry with an annual turnover of about 225 bn. Euro and 906 thousand employees in 2022.
The proposed ban on the manufacture, use and placing on the market of PFAS (in substances, mixtures, and articles) would have a massive impact on almost all of our member companies, whose technologies are crucial for the energy transition, digitisation, European infrastructure, transport and logistics chains, healthcare, and process automation/measurement technology.
While ZVEI generally supports the objective of avoiding emissions of hazardous substances into the environment and the appropriate regulation of individual substances that pose uncontrollable risks, and our members are committed to continuously improving the environmental compatibility and safety of the products they place on the market, we see the production, research, and development locations of the German and European electro and digital industries, as well as their global competitiveness at serious risk in the event of a blanket ban and therefore call for a fundamental revision of the restriction proposal in key areas.

This comment focuses on the use of PFAS in cables. A more detailed description is available in the attached factsheet.

Sectors and (sub-)uses: The restriction dossier summarises the entire E&E industry in one short paragraph of the UPFAS restriction dossier, without taking into account the complexity of the E&E industry and the wide variety of  applications within it. Therefore, only a few examples can be given as representative of many other applications. (See Attachement for details)

General Comments: Usefulness of Fluoroelastomer
In Machine Tools which are used to machine metal parts that are incorporated into everything in the market, lubricating oil lubricates each moving machine element (Spindle, Ball Screw, Linear Guides, Slideways) in order to prevent wear and damage.

Lubrication is done using Centralized lubrication system(A system consisting of pump which pumps oil and valve that delivers appropriate amount to each lubrication point), and Fluoroelastomer are used in pumps and valves of centralized lubrication system in ensure a reliable seal.

The primary reason behind the use of Fluoroelastomer is its Oil resistance.

In the past nitrile rubber was used, but some lubricants used in various parts of the world caused the rubber to swell or shrunk, causing pumps and valves to malfunction, resulting in damage to Machine Tool in many cases.

We have mentioned regarding the oil to be used in our instruction manual, etc. However, its is very difficult to control the use of appropriate lubricating oil that is used in various parts of the world. Hence we have been using Fluoroelastomer which have superior chemical resistance for many years and there have been no major problems.

Availability of alternatives
Currently there is no equivalent to the performance of Fluoroelastomer, and even if there were, long term verification and confirmation would be required.

General Comments: Utility piping networks in Europe to convey either Natural Gas (with H2 being added in the future) or Drinking Water are today typically made from Polyethylene (PE) pipe due to the efficiency of installation (e.g. coiled pipe 100m long). The PE pipe ends are butt-welded to reach the 50-100 years life-time for the installation. The two heating plates in the welding machines are coated with PTFE to give the needed performance during butt-welding of PE piping (see discussion in attachment).
Utility products and installation procedures are heavily regulated (e.g. CEN and country standards) and 3rd party audited; any changes to the process will need serious validation time by public and private authorities. Moreover, there are estimated 50'000 welding machines in operation across Europe which will need to be replaced completely if the mirror get's damaged.
For this reason, a broad exemption for this group of FPs should be considered within the PFAS restriction proposal. Fluoropolymers (FPs) constitute a specific group of substances within PFAS, as their properties are completely different. These substances are considered polymers of low concern by OECD and therefore their use does not pose any proven risk to human health and the environment. The proposed PFAS restriction does not reflect these differences.

6. Missing uses: The missing use is for utility piping networks in the ground to convey natural gas (added H2 is in testing phase) and drinking water with PE piping. The PE pipe ends are welded with special butt-welding machines for which PTFE coated heating mirrors are being used. The advantage of the PTFE coating is the non-stick effect towards the soft PE ends and the high-temperature resistance with the needed welding temperatures (220° +/- 10°C). The welding process and parameters are given by German DVS Standards 2207/2208.  Although PE welding in Utility is the biggest user of butt-welding machines, many other polymers are butt-welded in Industrial or Building Technology Applications or Uses. Moreover, the "plane mirror" can have the shape of a socket called socket welding (mainly Building Technology uses).  Please refer to the confidental attachment.
