Combined Comments:
General Comments: Vaccines Europe (VE) represents major innovative research-based vaccine companies operating in Europe, including small and medium-sized enterprises. VE is a specialised group within EFPIA. VE concurs with the general response to the consultation supplied by our parent organisation the EFPIA. However, there are subtleties in vaccines production and supply that warrant a specific response to the consultation.
We are concerned that development and /or supply of vaccines in the EU will be severely impacted by the PFAS Restriction as presently drafted. This concern is based on the broad definition of “PFAS” within the restriction and the wide applicability across many different fields of use.

Regulatory scope: the restriction proposal aims at substances and articles without derogating products where marketing is subject to specific regulations. Vaccines are granted market authorisations under Directive 2001/83. Restricting products under marketing authorisation or permission causes regulatory conflicts.

Substance scope: the substance group PFAS, as defined in the regulation, has no common hazardous properties. Fluoropolymers, for example, are non-hazardous, most are considered polymers of low concern by the OECD and some have food contact approval. Persistence of either the substance itself or its degradation products is the property of concern.

Definition: the long-term goal of reducing emissions can only be achieved by a global restriction of PFAS, such as under the Stockholm Convention. To facilitate this process, the definition of “PFAS” should be aligned as much as possible. The U.S. EPA working definition published in the fifth contaminant candidate list (CCL5) may serve as a blueprint.

Restriction option: If RO1 is applied, all vaccines manufacturing will have to move out of the EEA, as production and development depend on fluoropolymers and replacements are not available. The supply of vaccines will be severely impacted, as approved vaccines delivered within packaging and/or with drug delivery devices used to administer the products under market authorization are in scope of the restriction. The same is true, to a lesser degree, for Restriction Option 2. A socio-economic analysis (SEA) for the pharmaceutical industry sector in general is currently being conducted by EPPA (www.eppa.com) and will quantify and substantiate these claims. It will be submitted to the public consultation at a later timepoint upon finalisation.

Transitional period: the established substitution timelines (5 or 12 years) are tailored to technical substitution. They do not factor in regulatory timelines such as mandatory stability testing or re-submission of market authorisations for regulated products.

Other SEA topics: The ban on manufacturing materials as outlined in both Restriction Options has an industry impact of hundreds of billion Euros. These figures are communicated and substantiated in the EFPIA SEA study.

Of utmost concern to vaccines manufacturers is the manufacture and supply products which meet their marketing authorisation obligations with respect to the products safety, efficacy, and stability. There are multiple challenges associated with the various vaccine technology platforms currently employed and the fact that vaccines are fragile biological substances. Some of the common challenges are:
• containment of the vaccine and its precursors to prevent contamination or degradation by environmental factors;
• need to protect workers from potential contamination during manufacture;
• need to have equipment which can be cleaned and sanitised;
• need to ensure sterile conditions;
• need to perform Quality Control testing in line with the testing approved by the competent authority (eg EMA or other authorities);
• need to be compliant with the European Pharmacopoeia;
• primary storage containers (vials, syringes) protecting the product and avoiding adsorption to contact surfaces;
• need to have products maintained at low temperatures (as low as -70°C) at stages during manufacture;
• ability to maintain a “cold chain” supply to the healthcare professional administering the product.
To meet these requirements the primary concerns of the vaccines industry are the accessibility of fluoropolymers (in production, packaging & testing), refrigerant gasses and QC materials (reagents & fluoropolymers).

The benefits of fluoropolymers in production, packaging and QC include thermal and chemical stability, resistance to adsorption, smooth hard surfaces that are easily cleaned and disinfected, and outstanding barrier properties protecting products from air, moisture, impurities, extractables and particles. This safeguards the safety and quality of products throughout their shelf life. Alternatives for fluoropolymers may exist in some cases, however, the required properties of outstanding resistance against heat, light, chemicals, time, and abrasion, are naturally linked to persistence. This means that alternatives are most likely persistent, too.
In manufacturing and packaging, the use of fluoropolymers is closely linked to other sustainability considerations (recyclability, long service life or shelf life, production or transport resources/emissions, energy considerations etc). These environmental trade-offs are not regarded when only the chemical nature of the material is regulated.
With respect to refrigeration and air conditioning fluorinated gases are commonly used heat transfer reagents. In general, the split in the overall use of fluorinated gases are air conditioning (41%) and refrigeration (34%) (for all applications, domestic, transport, industrial) with the remaining (25%) being general industrial uses. The key concern with fluorinated gases, in the proposed restriction, is their release into the atmosphere where they break down into trifluoroacetic acid (TFA).

In refrigerant applications fluorinated gases may be used either alone or in blends. Some materials which meet the definition of PFAS in the current restriction proposal are also included in the F-gas regulation, care should be exercised to ensure that any mismatch between regulations does not result in regrettable substitutions.
For example, a refrigerant that is outside the scope of the restriction is HFC-32 (difluoromethane) but since it still has a relatively high Global Warming Potential of 677, it may be banned under revisions to the F-gas regulation.  Obviously polymeric PFAS-containing materials are used in refrigeration equipment such as gaskets, tubes, lined piping and fittings, pump housings, impellors and filters for the benefits previously described for production equipment.
Refrigeration is used widely in vaccines industry throughout the supply chain in manufacture, storage and transportation and its criticality was highlighted during the rush to setup and maintain appropriate supply chains during the recent pandemic.

Fluorinated gases are commonly used in refrigeration equipment where extremely low, controlled temperatures are required (below -50 °C). They are also frequently used in refrigerated laboratory equipment that require precise temperature control over a large temperature range, e.g. test and measurement equipment and refrigerated centrifuges.

The above applications utilise equipment which is hermetically sealed and, during maintenance and during decommissioning, the fluorinated gas is normally collected under controlled circumstances to avoid release and leak detection and avoidance are now even more controlled under the current F-gas regulation. Reclaim and recycling or destruction of fluorinated gases plays an increasingly essential role in the pharmaceutical sector and promote a circular economy and reduce emissions. Specialist companies offer collection and regeneration service for used refrigerants.
Currently it is our understanding that the proposal will include derogations for specific refrigerants from proposed restrictions. These include :
• Low temperature refrigeration below –40°C (18 month transition, 5 year derogation)
• Laboratory test and equipment (18 month transition, 12 year derogation)
• Refrigerated centrifuges (18 month transition, 12 year derogation))
• Maintenance and refilling of existing HVACR equipment for which drop-in replacements do not exist (18month transition, 12year derogation)
• Mobile air-conditioning systems such as vehicles (18month transition, 5year derogation)
• Transport refrigeration other than in marine applications (18month transition, 5year derogation)
• HVACR equipment in buildings where national safety standards and building codes prohibit use of other alternatives (Unlimited derogation)

Whilst industry welcomes these proposed derogations it wishes to bring to the attention of the ECHA that, on the assumption that fluorine free technically viable alternatives exist for example carbon dioxide, hydrocarbons and ammonia, there will be potentially changes to plant, revalidations and relicensing of facilities to be factored into the derogation timing. The impact on regulatory agencies should also be evaluated.

Any restriction on QC reagents, equipment and consumables will have major regulatory impacts, on the assumption that alternatives with equivalent properties can be found and that the alternatives do not themselves have desirable properties. For example, trifluoro acetic acid (TFA) is a critical material in the quality control (QC) of most medicinal products, ubiquitous as a co-solvent or buffer in many pharmacopeial analytical methods.

Any restriction on TFA as a QC reagent would lead to wholesale revision of the Pharmacopoeia Europa, multiple changes to controls on pharmaceutical products, and a potential impact on global pharmacopeial harmonization.

As another example fluoropolymers, such as PTFE, are utilised in many product contact areas in analytical equipment and consumables due to the uniqueness of its chemical and physical properties. These properties of inertness, resistance to heat and aggressive environments, and low adsorption potential are essential to the performance of the extremely sensitive tests required in vaccines development and quality control.

Emissions depend on the use of the PFAS:
• In case of fluoropolymers in industrial use, PFAS are still part of the equipment at its end of life, and emissions can be controlled.
• In case of use of PFAS as chemicals or auxiliaries in Manufacture/Storage/Transport and Quality Control, substances can be used under controlled conditions to minimise exposure to the lowest level possible.
The use of substances should not be restricted if the goal of the restriction can be reached by other means. This would apply, for instance, to fluoropolymers in industrial use under inventory and end-of-life management as outlined in Article 8 of the Restriction Proposal.
For packaging of medicinal products, the emissions depend on local waste management. Most European countries have implemented incineration of medical or municipal waste or are moving towards this goal. The typical packaging use is a thin fluoropolymer film (PCTFE, ETFE or other) laminated with other plastics or elastomers, facilitating incineration. As published, PFAS can be mineralized when incinerated: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0045653519306435
Data on PFAS emissions at the waste stage of actual pharmaceutical packaging materials will be submitted to this consultation at a later point in time.
Requests for exemption or derogation:
- A time-unlimited derogation of fluoropolymers emissions that can be controlled in the industry and are limited to the waste stage
- A derogation for packaging material of medicinal products and devices as in 6.l in Restriction Option 2, but applicable to all fluoropolymers with approval rather than PCTFE only, and not limited by time.  Any substitution requires regulatory efforts in addition to the technical implementation, which must be regarded in the timeline to avoid disruption in the availability of medicines, and cannot be handled within 13.5 years.
- Additional derogations for identified specific PFAS uses in the pharmaceutical supply chain. These include starting materials, reagents, solvents, catalysts, and single or multiple use equipment necessary for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals or related processes such as quality control or diagnostic testing.
- Various types of fluoropolymers are used in the packaging of medicinal products, e.g. blister packs and PFAS coated elastomers used in vials, cartridges and syringes.  Also impacted are drug delivery devices e.g. prefilled pens used to administer medicines via subcutaneous injection.  Currently, there are no viable replacements for PFAS in primary packaging.  We believe it will take at least 10 - 20 years to find, test and implement replacements avoiding regrettable substitutions.  All primary packaging materials and drug delivery devices form part of the valid marketing authorisation and so any restriction will impact the supply of medicines in Europe and beyond.
- Generally, the transition periods proposed in the Restriction focus on the availability of potential substitutes and technical implementation complexity. They do not factor in regulatory efforts required in the pharmaceutical sector for validation and qualification of processes, or re-submission of market authorisations. Primary packaging changes require stability testing during the shelf life of the product. The requirements in regulated sectors add many years to any substitution timeline, even if the required capacity in authorities and industry is available.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: NEW proposal for a Sector: pharmaceutical and vaccines/biopharmaceutical industry.  This sector is missing from Table 9 of the Annex XV restriction report. Only the use as the active ingredient, can coating of pMDI and PCTFE packaging materials are covered in Restriction Option 2 of the draft restriction.  All (sub-)uses are missing for this sector, and are listed in 6: Missing Uses

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: As emissions depend on the use, information is included in the section 6: Missing Uses   Furthermore, close partnership across supply chains for medicinal products is needed to identify all sources of PFAS, to sufficiently manage emissions from waste streams, and where possible, to develop suitable alternatives that maintain the highly controlled environment required for efficacy and patient safety.  General overview on a medicines environmental risk assessment  In the EU a prospective Environmental Risk Assessment (ERA) is required since 2006 (CPMP/SWP/4447/00, 2006) when a marketing authorisation application (MAA) is submitted for a new Medicinal Product to be placed on the market or where there is potential for significant increase in environmental concentrations as a result of modifications to existing marketing authorisations (MAs), such as the addition of new indications. The EMA has scientific guidance on Environmental risk assessment of medicinal products for human use: https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/environmental-risk-assessment-medicinal-products-human-use-scientific-guideline.  On the 26 April, the Commission adopted a proposal for a new Directive (Directive on the Union code relating to medicinal products for human use) and a new Regulation (Regulation laying down Union procedures for the authorisation and supervision of medicinal products for human use and establishing a European Medicines Agency, amending Regulation (EC) No 1394/2007 and Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 and repealing Regulation (EC) NO 726/2004, Regulation (EC) No 141/2000 and Regulation (EC) No 1901/2006), which revise and replace the existing general pharmaceutical legislation. As part of this revision, the Commission proposes to strengthen the ERA requirements by: - Refusal of a Marketing Authorisation based on environment concerns. - Manufacturing included in the environmental risk assessment of antimicrobials. - Prioritisation of ERA for legacy active pharmaceutical ingredients, which were placed on the market before 2006. - Increased interlinkage across non-pharma legislations. - Restrictions on hazardous medicinal products.  As part of the revision, the industry (trade associations EFPIA, AESGP and Medicines for Europe) has proposed an extended environmental risk assessment (eERA) (https://www.efpia.eu/media/677261/interassociation-paper-on-extended-environmental-risk-assessment.pdf).  In summary the eERA aims to provide the following benefits:  - An API based ERA which better reflects the risks posed to environment from patient use. - Strengthen the industry’s commitment to conduct robust and risk-based ERAs without compromising environmental protection or patient access to medicines. - Provision for the ability to automatically cross-reference ERA data in marketing authorisation applications.  - Provide a mechanism for risk identification, refinement, and management during the MAA evaluation process . - Provide clarity on appropriate well-defined follow-up responsibilities for ERAs with no need for independent and duplicative risk identification and prioritisation processes under different legislations (e.g. Water Framework Directive) . - Updates to the ERA across the life cycle of the API in each MP in which it is contained that will ensure that each ERA reflects the latest environmental information.  - A focus on risk that reduces the burden on regulators (i.e. oversight) and industry.  - Reduction in the duplication of testing, delivering improved ERA consistency, proportionate use of testing resource, and bioethical benefits . - Suggestions for mechanisms to increase the transparency of, and access to, ERA data.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Effectiveness of incineration under normal operating conditions: The member companies of EFPIA do not operate incineration installations and therefore defer to the information provided by the waste sector federation(s) on the effectiveness of incineration methods.   Collaboration: The pharmaceutical industry is open to continued collaborations and is investing in partnerships to develop new and effective technologies, products and innovations that generate minimal waste throughout their lifetime of use in healthcare systems. These include pilot take back schemes and the @Medsdisposal (https://medsdisposal.eu/) campaign which raises awareness on how to dispose of unused or expired medicines appropriately in Europe.

5. Proposed derogations: As tonnage and emissions depend on the material and use, this information is included in  the EFPIA submission to '6: Missing Uses'

6. Missing uses: We highlight all presently identified uses in the vaccines sector below.  The vaccines industry identified the following uses of PFAS materials:    Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (API) production Vaccines, sterile production: fluoropolymers in production equipment (reactor lining, seals, gaskets, piping, anti-stick coating, surfaces, filtration units etc.) – fluoropolymers with product contact and quality impact, including spare or replacement parts  Vaccines sterile production: PFAS consumables and single-use material (filters, bioreactors, bags, tubes, etc.) – fluoropolymers with product contact and quality impact  Production general: fluoropolymers in complex equipment, such as insulation material, mechanical parts, including spare or replacement parts  Quality Control: PFAS materials and reagents used in quality control activities mandated by product licenses or regulations such as European Pharmacopoeia monographs. They include for example trifluoro acetic acid (TFA) in the mobile phase of high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), perfluoro butanoic acid (PFBA) as ion pair reagent in chromatography; N-methyl-bis(trifluoroacetamide) (MB-TFA), N,O-bis-trimethylsilyl-trifluoroacetamide (BS-TFA), and N-methyl-N-trimethylsilyl-trifluoroacetamide (MS-TFA) to derive silyl derivatives in gas chromatography or other methods.    Quality control and research and development: PFAS other than fluoropolymers in equipment, such as electrical components, diagnostic laboratory testing, refrigerants in laboratory equipment such as temperature-controlled centrifuges. Analytical laboratory equipment, e.g., Teflon tubing, valves, gaskets, and filters. Manufacturing, storage and transport: non-polymeric PFAS in equipment, such as electrical components, refrigerants in HVACR equipment, ultra-low temperature refrigeration, refrigerants in storage and transport, including spare or replacement parts. Packaging of Medicinal Products or Pharmaceuticals: Immediate packaging of medicinal products and API’s such as containers or closures with product contact, using approved fluoropolymer materials or coatings such as PCTFE, ETFE or PTFE. Applies to metal or plastic containers, vial stoppers or other coated elastomers. – NOT a missing use (§ 6. l), if “medicinal preparations” include pharmaceuticals (clarification on terminology required) and limited to PCTFE  Packaging containing fluoropolymer film for the protection of medicinal products or medical devices from air, moisture, other contaminants or to maintain sterility or stability as in § 6. m and, but not restricted to individual products or materials - not a missing use (mentioned in Table 2), but missing a general derogation.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: As socio-economic impact and potential alternatives depend on material and use, this information is included in the EFPIA submission.

8. Other identified uses: Although there is a time-unlimited derogation for the specific use of active substances used in human medicinal products in the EU, the sector was not identified in the restriction, including Table 8 and Table 9 of the draft proposal. Derogations for substances which do not cover their manufacture and development in Europe will initiate relocation outside of Europe. The current European share of global pharmaceutical revenue is 23.4%, and the estimated Research and Development spending is 41.5 bn Euro (2021, statista.com). The socio-economic impact analysis prepared for the innovative (bio)pharma industry (Annex 1 submission of EFPIA) substantiates the consequences of the proposed restriction on the pharmaceutical industry and the availability of medicines.

10. Analytical methods: Greater than 90% of all analytical testing on pharmaceutical ingredients and drug products utilize PFAS. These are present as reagents, consumables and in the instruments utilized throughout R&D, Manufacturing and Quality Control.  As currently drafted the PFAS restriction would limit the availability of replacement parts, necessary consumables, and reagents and would cause significant disruption to pharmaceutical company’s legal obligations to analyze and release its registered medicines. This would result in the disruption of the supply of approved medicines to patients and the progression of future medicines in clinical trials.  An example of the impact to analytical testing would be the multiple components of an HPLC (High Performance Liquid Chromatography) system that are made of polymeric PFAS that enable analyses to be executed in a way that minimizes loss of compounds during analysis. In addition, there are a significant number of developmental, registered, and compendial HPLC methods (European pharmacopeia and other global compendia) that utilize trifluoroacetic acid as part of the mobile phase used for analysis. A primary source of PFAS in analytical are in the instruments and the vendors need to define and implement alternatives.  Additionally, the amount of time and personnel to successfully navigate any post-approval changes for registered methods would be significant to enable the development of new medicines as well as ensuring adequate supply of approved medicines.  Therefore, any restrictions that do not include appropriate derogations either, time unlimited, or if time limited with a sufficient grace period to allow discovery, testing, validation and registration of alternatives to allow continued European and Global delivery of medicines to patients.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Vacuum cleaners give an essential contribution to a decent living standard. However, vacuuming dirt and dust in household and commercial environments must be carried out without any avoidable detrimental effects. For this purpose, the air used to collect dirt is filtered before being re-emitted in the surroundings.
The importance of this aspect is confirmed by the EU Ecodesign regulation for vacuum cleaners which insists on dust re-emission as one of the fundamental parameters to be controlled.

Nowadays, state-of-the-art filtration in vacuum cleaners is achieved with PTFE based membranes.
Substantial information about PTFE is available, with properties and use extensively reviewed and analysed in Annex A of the XV Restriction Report.
See for example general properties in A.3.2, with specific applications addressed in A.3.3 (Textiles, upholstery, leather, apparel and carpets). The review dwells on filtration and separation media efficacy, recognising that dust removal must be carried out in presence of challenging conditions (i.e. high air velocity). PTFE are also an obvious choice for air filtration of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) and medical devices in general (see A.3.10.1.17 – Polymeric PFAS for medical devices).

Overall, PTFE based filters score high when delivering filtration efficacy, lower energy consumption and long duration of the fibres, which also prevents frequent replacements.
These combined specifications are common to filtration in vacuum cleaners. However, the analysis in the Restriction Report is limited to professional and industrial use of PTFE. Table A.12 mentions the domestic sector, but only for fabrics, cookware and construction materials.

As stated in the Restriction Report, there are no technically feasible alternatives to PTFE membranes for high performance filtration applications for professional and industrial.
However, we strongly believe that high performance filtration in residential and commercial areas have an equally important function which benefits the entire population.
We ask that that the same conclusion reached for industrial and professional settings is extended to household and commercial use of vacuum cleaners.

In general filter media for vacuum cleaners can be produced without PFASs but such alternatives have not given encouraging results (see answer 6.d). The search for a suitable alternative to be successful requires a long sequence of trials, tests and validations both from material suppliers and vacuum cleaners manufacturers.

In conclusion, banning the use of PTFE in the filter media of vacuum cleaners without suitable alternatives in place would result in little gain in reducing PFAS emission (see 6a on tonnage) and be detrimental to consumers’ rights.

Accordingly, due to the current lack of suitable alternatives, a derogation of 12 years is necessary to provide sufficient time to the filters industry and its subsidiary customers to identify and implement alternative non-PFAS solutions for use in the filtration media of household and similar vacuum cleaners.

As a company advocating for the importance of good indoor air quality, we cannot compromise on this aspect of the design of our vacuum cleaners and we want to be able to continue to do so.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: These comments are specific to the appliances sector - vacuum cleaners. The appliances sector is not listed in table 9, except for appliances making use of fluorinated gases. Filters for vacuum cleaner can be considered under the TULAC category (Textiles, upholstery, leather, apparel and carpets).

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: No significant emission is expected in the manufacturing stage of a filter. No emission is expected during the life of a filter.  Regarding the end-of-life, the ePTFE membrane is part of a filter which is non-recyclable due to collection during normal use of aerosols of unknown origin or toxicity. For this special reason, the filter ends up either in landfill or domestic incineration waste streams. None of the materials making the filter are expected to be recycled and it is unlikely this can be done in the future, as for all PPE.  There is potential emission from the end-of-life phase because a percentage of filters will end up in the landfill through municipal waste. However, PTFE are long polymers, hence its filter efficiency characteristics, and it is not meant to breakdown easily in the ambient.  Extensive analysis has been carried out on the environmental impact of fluoropolymers, in particular PTFE, as documented by literature of the Society of Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry (SETAC). The paper and associated references available at the following link indicate that PTFE are polymers of low concern (PLC) and therefore the hazard assessment and restrictions on other polymers and non-polymeric PFAS are a separate matter. https://setac.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ieam.4035

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: When the filter goes to a municipal waste stream and onto incineration process which conforms to EU directive 2000/76/EC for combustion over 850°C, there is no expected PFAS emission.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: PTFE filters reach the recycling phase together with the whole vacuum cleaner. However, this filter is not a part that can be recycled (see answer 2) and we expect recyclers would appropriately direct the filter to incineration without further treatment costs.

5. Proposed derogations: The derogation proposed in 5e of the Summary of Annex XV is limited to PFAS used for filtration and separation media in industrial and professional settings. See answer 6a for an estimate of tonnage and emission of PTFE from filtration media in vacuum cleaners.

6. Missing uses: a) For vacuum cleaners the ePTFE membrane forms a very small percentage of the total product weight (0.003-0.004%) with the ePTFE about 1.4% by weight of the filter itself. Accordingly, depending on the various types of vacuum cleaners (e.g. cylinder, uprights, stick vacs) the ePTFE content can be between 35 and 70 mg per filter. Considering that the combined sales of household and commercial vacuum cleaners in the EU market are estimated to be approximately 43 millions for 2030 (see the report “Review study on vacuum cleaners” shared by the EU Commission in 2019, the amount of PTFE that would enter the market is between 1,5 and 3,0 tons per year. https://ekosuunnittelu.info/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/Vacuum-cleaner-review_Draft-final-report-_Nov-2018.pdf  Even if in most of the cases a PTFE filter, due to its durability, can reach the end-of-life phase together with the whole vacuum cleaner, for different reasons some users acquire an additional filter during the life of the appliance. A conservative estimate would quantify these additional filters in 50% of the total number of vacuum cleaners sold. This extra volume will likely end up in the landfill because not disposed of with the vacuum cleaner, whereas in the near future we can expect that all vacuum cleaners will end up in recycling centres with the filter inside properly sent for incineration. In summary, the likely scenario is that only a volume corresponding to the extra filters is expected to end in the landfill. Even assuming that such filters in a landfill are a significant source of emission, the potential emission should not exceed 1,5 tons per year.  b) Vacuum cleaners rely on high efficiency textile-based filters placed at the exhaust to trap dust and residual particles that otherwise would be released in the surrounding environment, typically indoor. Modern state-of-the-art filters for vacuum cleaners are based on the properties of PTFE, fluoropolymers that for this application are used predominantly in the expanded form (ePTFE). The characteristics given to the filter by the PTFE substrate enable unsurpassed performance at stopping microscopic dust that is known to have an adverse effect on allergy sufferers. High-performance ePTFE filters are commonly used to suppress these allergens down to 0.1micron particle size and provide similar benefit when applied to nano-aerosols, bacteria, mould, viruses and micro or nano-plastics. These filters allow high dust removal efficiencies in a single pass of the air, delivering filtration efficiency up to 99.99%. Vacuum cleaner filters commonly come with High Efficiency Particulate Air (HEPA) features, to sustain the importance that both manufacturers and ambient quality advocates give to this special use. In addition to operation at high temperature (~80°C), the benefits of PTFE based filters include wear and tear resistance when the filters are cleaned by the general user, requiring no specific skills (monthly, for ~7 years use in our applications). Accordingly, PTFE filters are long lasting, reusable, with a typical filter being replaced maybe once during the entire service life of the vacuum cleaner. Crucially, the performance of PTFE filters becomes critical for vacuum cleaners because both the velocity of the air required to achieve the necessary suction and the temperature of the exhaust are high.  c) It is estimated that 10 companies account for 95% of the EU market of vacuum cleaners for indoor use.  d) Known alternatives to ePTFE filters are: • Wet laid glass This alternative can reach high efficiency but results in higher energy consumption; It is also harder to maintain and must be disposed of once loaded as the material is very delicate and falls apart once washed or manipulated. If glass filters are manipulated, they can get easily damaged and scatter glass fibres which can be inhaled and cause health hazards; • Nano-fibres This alternative has a higher energy consumption and whilst they can be maintained, they are not durable and will degrade faster, becoming a health hazard when inhaled • Others Filter material types that allow high initial efficiency often possess an electrostatic charge, for example tribo-charged needlefelts or corona discharged melt blown media. The performance that they offer cannot be maintained as they lose charge throughout life if they are washed, with their filtration efficiency dropping by a factor of 10 or more, with a significant increase of the number of dust particles emitted into the environment.  Because of their drawbacks, these alternatives are not considered viable.  e) Suppliers of filters and membranes around the world have started R&D initiatives to engineer non-PFAS membranes with properties similar to those using ePTFE. However, there is still extensive work to be done. Any new membrane needs to be extensively tested for application into the vacuum cleaners’ industry, the materials approved for use (flame retardant materials also contain PFAS) and then the filter designed into a new generations of products. It is estimated that this would take at least 5 years.  f) As stated in the Restriction Report, currently there are no technically feasible alternatives for high performance filtration applications. The requirements met by ePTFE filters have not been found to be met robustly by any other known material alternatives on the market.  g) Banning the optimal method of filtering vacuum cleaners exhaust would affect the performance of the product and consumers. Nowadays, each household owns one or two vacuum cleaners and its performance affects the entire population, including people with pre-existing health conditions. As humans spend 90% of their time indoors (Diffey, 2010) (Roberts, 2016) a clean living and working environment is an important aspect of public health with health effects of poor indoor air quality highlighted in numerous studies around the world.

8. Other identified uses: If a vacuum cleaner is used without a PTFE high performance filter, dust particles remain airborne for a while and are inadvertently inhaled, increasing the risk of causing or worsening respiratory diseases for people exposed to them regularly. Alternatives to PTFE membranes in terms of filtering performance are more energy consuming or not durable (see answer 6d), thus compromising ecodesign objectives. Stopping the use of PTFE filters would reduce the ability of people to clean their house properly and be detrimental to their health. Considering that the EU has an ageing population (see Eurostat data) the cost to the society of not enabling a safe transition between equally performing materials would be long lasting.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Valmet

Valmet is a leading global developer and supplier of process technologies, automation and services for the pulp, paper and energy industries. With our automation systems and flow control solutions we serve an even wider base of process industries. Valmet’s net sales in 2022 were approximately EUR 5.1 billion.

Valmet’s technologies are used in the production of pulp, paper, tissue, board, bioenergy, biofuels, biochemicals and different bio-based materials in the bioeconomy. In addition to these, Valmet’s technologies also cover a range of processes used in the circular economy, such as fiber-to-fiber textile recycling, chemical plastics recycling and high-efficient energy recovery from waste. Our automation technologies and industrial internet solutions are used even wider, from the automation of food production lines and LGN terminals to balancing city wide electricity and heat production systems. Our intelligent valves are used from a wide variety of different process industries to the transfer of hydrocarbons and hydrogen in pipelines. Our emission control systems are used in industry and the marine sector. Our measurement systems are used in industry to ensure steady performance and quality. What is common to these technologies is that they are enabling and taking forward the green transformation in the society, and that to a large extent they rely on the use of fluoropolymers.

Valmet has, as part of a Bioeconomy Task Force already replied to the ongoing consultation as regards technologies used in the bioeconomy sector. In this additional contribution, we wish to highlight technologies we produce for other sectors, such as the chemicals industry, waste-to-energy sector, emission control equipment and automation.

PFAS chemicals

The first PFAS polymer (PTFE) was introduced to the market in 1946. Its industrial use began soon after, and several other important fluoropolymers were introduced in the coming decades (FEP in 1960, ETFE in 1970, and PFA in 1972). The era of fluoropolymers in the industry has today been ongoing already for well over 50 years. Due to their unique properties, such as low coefficient of friction, inertness to most chemicals, tolerance to high temperatures, they are today widely used, especially in different process industries.

Thanks to their properties, fluoropolymers have been one of the key innovations that have enabled the process industries to increase efficiencies in terms of resource use (machinery and use stage) and production (reliability and performance). Their properties have also been in centre stage in the minimisation of leaks and hazards, thus increasing the safety of the production processes to an unforeseen level.

Draft proposal

We agree with the principle to restrict any negative effects resulting from the use PFAS chemicals when and where necessary but have concerns about the proportionality of the draft proposal in its current format. We also fear that the ongoing consultation will not be able to identify all uses in the society, nor evaluate properly their essentiality. The restriction process was originally designed under the assumption that only a limited number of substances would be considered at one time, but now the ongoing consultation covers well over 10 000 substances at one go.

According to REACH Art 69.4:

“If a Member State considers that the manufacture, placing on the market or use of a substance on its own, in a mixture or in an article poses a risk to human health or the environment that is not adequately controlled and needs to be addressed it shall notify the Agency that it proposes to prepare a dossier which conforms to the requirements of the relevant sections of Annex XV. If the substance is not on the list maintained by the Agency referred to in paragraph 5 of this Article, the Member State shall prepare a dossier which conforms to the requirements of Annex XV within 12 months of the notification to the Agency. If this dossier demonstrates that action on a Community-wide basis is necessary, beyond any measures already in place, the Member State shall submit it to the Agency in the format outlined in Annex XV, in order to initiate the restrictions process.”

The material in Annex XV of the consultation clearly reveals serious gaps in knowledge on the substances that are nevertheless planned to be banned. It also gives only a small glimpse into the different uses, industries and value chains which are relevant to these chemicals. The material does not consider the possibility that some of the uses might be essential, or that measures might be in place - or could be set - to limit any exposure to emissions or the chemicals. These are prerequisites for determining if there is a risk to human health or environment that is not adequately controlled. Furthermore, the draft proposal is based on an optimistic assumption that the chemicals’ replacement would be doable in a rather short timeframe.

Control of the risks to human health or the environment

In our technologies, fluoropolymers are included in the components bought from suppliers. Even if fluoropolymers are used widely in our technologies, the amounts vary from extremely small (some µgs) to several kgs. Fluoropolymers are currently not considered as hazardous chemicals. Therefore, we do not get information on exact amounts from our suppliers.

Most components are inert material and placed in our technologies without further value adding. The components are placed in our technologies, used, and repaired or replaced in industrial environments and applying all existing health and safety requirements.

Most of our process technologies are based on the use of closed loops, thus minimizing the risk of emissions in the use phase. All emissions and sludges are treated according to requirements in legislation and environmental permits granted.

Any waste generated at our own production sites, or at our customer sites when installing new machinery/doing repairs or refurbishments, is disposed of by professionals and according to legislation and relevant permits. In locations where waste management companies can take sorted fluoropolymer waste for recycling, we sort them separately.

The waste is either sent to recycling or incinerated, according to the requirements in existing legislation. Landfilling is not likely but cannot be excluded, as fluoropolymers are not classified as hazardous waste.

Our customers do most of the regular maintenance work themselves but are professionals and operate in an industrial environment bound by the legislation and permits in force.

Impacts of the possible restriction

In process industries the production is an interlinked system, where all parts need to function properly and together, or nothing works.

Were the use of fluoropolymers be banned without the existence of properly working and tested alternatives, this would have grave consequences to the EU’s green and digital transformation, as well as the EU’s competitiveness, growth, and jobs. Considering the vital role fluoropolymers have had in increasing efficiencies and minimising health and safety risks, this would simply mean taking back the steps taken in the past 30 years. Already the threat that such a ban could take place and risk the operational capability of the industry would have extremely negative effects on any new investments in the region.

For the energy sector, in addition to bioenergy boilers, we produce high-efficient Waste-to Energy technologies (boilers, gasifiers) which utilise sorted waste. These technologies support and are an integral part of the circular economy. Gasification and combustion of waste involves high temperatures and chemicals that set high requirements for the technologies’ safe performance. Any alternative existing chemical does not include the properties needed in these technical environments, and the waste sector is an area where the high health and safety requirements do not allow for any compromises in materials used.

The same applies technologies used in the chemicals sector. There is no margin for deficient performance of the equipment, as the risk for environmental, health and safety hazards is obvious. In this sector, our latest R&I work involve for example recycling of textile fibers and chemical plastics recycling which have been subject to high expectations in the EU’s green transformation and political discussion.

In the terms of auxiliary systems, it is worth noticing that reaching the emission limits set in the EU legislation would not be possible if the performance of the emission control technologies is compromised. Fluoropolymers are used in these equipment widely due to their properties, and no well-functioning alternatives are available that would work in these harsh conditions. As for automation, the PFAS chemicals are in electronic components bought from our suppliers. We do not know what the status of alternative chemicals in them is, but all automation solutions are heavily reliant on the availability of these components.

The world is currently in an unforeseen technological race, and all major blocks try to secure their top position in innovations and strategic autonomy. These other regions are not planning any universal bans on the use of PFAS chemicals but understand their role as an enabler of competitiveness. E.g., the U.S. is focusing on restrictions on the use of PFAS chemicals in certain end-consumer applications with high risks and likely emissions. If the EU were now to introduce the planned universal restriction, this would mean that the EU would not only seriously risk any chance of reaching its climate targets and projections for the green transformation but would also willingly give the other blocks the leading role in industrial competitiveness and innovations.

The ban would also have serious implications to trade flows. In many sectors where the EU is a large exporter of goods, the trade flows would suffer a serious blow if the EU could no longer export the goods as much, and there would not necessarily be capacity outside the EU to directly meet with the demand. Whatever products that could still be manufactured in the EU would no longer be competitive, due to production reliability and speed going down, and the higher cost of energy due to increased reliance on fossil energy. The fluoropolymer containing technologies banned in the EU would continue to be used elsewhere, and the EU companies would for a large part continue serving these sectors but from production sites outside the EU.

Timeframes

The projected derogation periods, 13,5 years as a maximum, are not sufficient to ensure a smooth end to the use of fluoropolymers in technologies we produce. A lot of luck was involved when fluoropolymers were discovered, and it is far from certain that alternatives meeting the needs of the process industries will be found within the planned derogations’ time limit. In our sector for example, it is not uncommon that it takes 15-30 years from innovation to market uptake. In the case of the projected ban, creating alternative well-functioning chemicals is not all that is needed to substitute fluoropolymers. The new chemicals cannot be taken to use directly, but all the components and parts in the machinery would need to be redesigned, standardised, tested, certified, and this would need to be done to thousands and thousands of components and parts. The industry has used several decades to take all the current components and parts to use, and it would not be realistic to expect that their reintroduction to the market with the new requirements could be managed in just 13,5 years. Furthermore, the EU’s industry is using fluoropolymers so widely, that already the limited number of trained personnel, laboratories and certification bodies would not make this possible.

Should the ban on fluoropolymers apply spare parts, too, this would mean that the industries we serve would stop functioning in just a couple of months’ time. Without spare parts that are tested and certified, and which from a technical perspective also fit the existing design, we could not serve our customers, but the existing investments done by our customers would soon become stranded assets.

Proposal for measures to be taken

Any restriction on the use of fluoropolymers should be risk-based and substance-based. A universal restriction is not warranted, if adequate control of the risks to human health and environment is in place or could be reached with less drastic measures:

As a priority, the existing legal framework should be updated (classification as hazardous where necessary, new requirements to waste and industrial emissions legislation, etc.). before any restrictions.

Furthermore, before the introduction of any restrictions, an information obligation for "intentionally added" PFAS should take place, so that relevant uses and exemptions could be identified, and the used amounts of the chemicals reliably assessed.

The use of fluoropolymers in industry should remain possible before proven alternatives are in the market, and before proper redesign, testing, standardisation, and certification work for their uptake has been possible.

Either, a significantly longer transition period than 13,5 years should be given, as a minimum 25 years.

Or, a permanent derogation should be granted to industrial applications, coupled potentially with a clause to be included directly into the text of the restriction that the Member States or the Commission will review the state of alternatives and any new hazard data in, e.g. 10 years, and they will assess if a new Annex XV restriction proposal should be prepared for fluoropolymers in the derogated categories, depending on the state of alternatives.

Unless fluoropolymers are derogated in all critical industrial applications for an unlimited period, the repair-as-produced principle should be applied. The spare and replacement part derogation should be provided for the lifetime of the plants which is at least 30 years.

Note:

Valmet as a technology developer and provider buys the components including fluoropolymers from suppliers. Fluoropolymers are currently not considered as hazardous chemicals and there is no information obligation on them. The amounts used in most components bought is small. Therefore, we do not get information on exact amounts from our suppliers.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Valmet has, as part of a Bioeconomy Task Force already replied to the ongoing consultation as regards technologies used in the bioeconomy sector.    The comments in this additional contribution relate to critical technology applications related to chemicals industry, waste-to-energy, textiles and industrial auxiliary systems such as emission control equipment and automation. Although these involve some sectors mentioned in Table 9 of the Restriction Report (semiconductors, energy sector), the main sector, i.e. machinery and auxiliary systems are ‘missing uses‘, and are further described in Subsection 6.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: In our technologies, the fluoropolymers are included in the components bought from suppliers. Even if fluoropolymers are used widely in our technologies, the amounts vary from extremely small (some µgs) to several kgs. Fluoropolymers are currently not considered as hazardous chemicals. Therefore, we do not get information on exact amounts from our suppliers.   Most components in question are inert material and placed in our technologies without further value adding. The components are placed in our technologies, used, and repaired or replaced in industrial environments and applying all existing health and safety requirements.    Most of our process technologies are based on the use of closed loops, thus minimizing the risk of emissions in the use phase. All emissions and sludges are treated according to requirements in legislation and environmental permits granted.    Any waste generated at our own production sites, or at our customer sites when installing new machinery/doing repairs or refurbishments, are disposed of by professionals and according to legislation and relevant permits. In locations where waste management companies can take sorted fluoropolymer waste for recycling, we sort them separately.   The waste is either sent to recycling or incinerated, according to the requirements in existing legislation. Landfilling is not likely but cannot be excluded, as fluoropolymers are not classified as a hazardous waste.   Our customers do most of the regular maintenance work themselves but are professionals and operating in an industrial environment bound by the legislation and permits in force.   Our technologies include Waste-to-Energy boilers, waste gasifiers and emission control systems used in flue gas cleaning. Our technologies are based on the use of sorted waste. These technologies rely on the use of fluoropolymers, as only their properties offer the required performance levels in these harsh environments. We have not tested combustion of PFAS chemicals separately, but our deliveries made well meet the tight emission limits set for waste incineration.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Sufficient data has been provided in the public consultation so far on safe incineration of fluoropolymers.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Our technologies include Waste-to-Energy boilers, waste gasifiers and emission control systems used in flue gas cleaning. Our technologies are based on the use of sorted waste. These Waste-to-Energy technologies rely on the use of fluoropolymers, as only their properties offer the required performance levels in these harsh environments.    Should the use of fluoropolymers be banned in Waste-to-Energy technologies without equally well performing alternatives (not foreseen at the moment), this would risk the functioning of the EU’s ability combust waste, including PFAS waste, and securely manage them at the end-of-life.   We have not tested combustion of PFAS chemicals separately, but our deliveries made well meet the tight emission limits set for waste incineration.

5. Proposed derogations: Fluoropolymers used are included in components and parts we buy from our suppliers. We do not have the information on the amounts used, and the scale varies from a few µgs to several kgs.

6. Missing uses: In general, the use of PFAS in machinery and in auxiliary systems in industry are ‘missing uses‘. Set forth below is a description of sub-sectors ‘chemicals production, waste-to-energy, textiles, emission control, automation and valves, and related industrial applications’.      a) Type of PFAS, tonnage and emissions   Fluoropolymers are used in critical technology applications for the uses in question, such as: PTFE, modified PTFE, filled PTFE, FKM, PVDF, PTFE+C, FEP, TFM, PFA, FEP and FFKM.   We are unable to provide exact figure for the fluoropolymers used. This is because PFAS contained in our technologies in in components bought from our suppliers, and the size of the components and the concentration of fluoropolymers is variable. It can be stated that there are several thousands of critical components in our technologies, but their average size (weight) is rather small. The overall tonnage is likely to be in the range of kg rather than metric tons per a larger delivery.    The life cycle of critical components is also quite variable. For example, soft components in valves can be replaced every 3-5 years. Other components between 3-15 years.   Most of our process technologies are based on the use of closed loops, thus minimizing the risk of emissions in the use phase. All emissions and sludges are treated according to requirements in legislation and environmental permits granted.    Any waste generated at our own production sites, or at our customer sites when installing new machinery/doing repairs or refurbishments, are disposed of by professionals and according to legislation and relevant permits. In locations where waste management companies can take sorted fluoropolymer waste for recycling, we sort them separately.   There are data available (as also documented in the ongoing public consultation) that controlled incineration decomposes PFAS so that there are no PFAS emissions. Some fluoropolymers (such as PVDF) are recyclable. Some waste can in principle be landfilled (as fluoropolymers are not classified as hazardous waste), although this is not a typical mean of disposal of industrial waste so landfilling is not expected.         b) Key functionalities    The key functionalities of fluoropolymers feature in components such as seals, cylinders, coatings, hoses and O-rings that come in contact with harsh environment (high temperature above 120 °C, acidic and reactive chemicals and hydrogen, high friction).    Critical applications also include critical uses of fluoropolymers in electronic products in automated industrial processes. Any failure of the components would lead to the failure of the whole system in question.      c) The number of companies in the sector estimated to be affected by the restriction.   As we are only one technology provider, we do not have data on all our customer sectors. However, the following press releases of our deliveries in the EU may shed light on them.    d) The availability, technical and economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives for the relevant use   We are not aware of alternatives that withstand the harsh conditions in critical applications. Furthermore, legislation in force also requires a certain performance from technologies. For example, the Industrial Emissions Directive and environmental permits set harsh emission limits that the technologies need to manage. The Machinery Regulation requires that the technologies shall withstand extreme working environments (E.g., high temperatures, hot liquids e.g., oil (300C) hot steam and different harsh chemicals). In many cases the combination of heat, moisture and chemicals makes the working environment very corrosive, which adds durability requirements for fast-moving machinery parts where effective lubrication is mandatory.   Without fluoropolymers in critical applications, there would be leakage and emissions which would lead to penalties, and even closures of plants.   There are some alternative materials (as outlined in the Annex XV report) that can be used for some uses at hand. As already discussed in our reply with the Bioeconomy Task Force; The problem is that none of them has all critical properties. For example, stainless steel has poor friction resistance, leading to wearing of counterparts and consequently to the risk of unexpected breaks and H&S incidents, and also to significantly higher energy consumption. Stainless steel is also 250% more expensive than fluoropolymers. PEEK has 4 to 9 times higher coefficient of friction (with the consequences above). PEEK also has poor chemical resistance in sulphuric acid. NBR and HNBR have poor creep resistance already above 80⁰C. All alternative polymers have poor resistance to chlorine solutions. Silicone elastomer has high temperature resistance but cannot be used in contact with hydraulic or thermal oil.    In addition, there are no alternatives for sealing applications related to storage and transport of hydrogen (the hydrogen molecule is too small so there would always be a leak if alternative polymers are used).         e) For cases in which alternatives are not yet available, information on the status of R&D processes for finding suitable alternatives   We are not aware of any significant and credible steps in finding alternatives for fluoropolymers we use in critical places/harsh conditions.       f) For cases in which substitution is technically and economically feasible but more time is required to substitute:      (ii) The time required for completing the substitution process (including any relevant certification or regulatory approvals);   It may be that alternatives would be available for some uses involving no harsh conditions. Even so, a testing program, redesign and re-certification are required (e.g., electronic products), which is a lengthy process and involves many items. In our view, 25 years is also required for non-harsh conditions.    (iii) information on possible differences in functionality and the consequences for downstream users and consumers (e.g., estimations of expected early replacement needs or expected additional energy consumption):   Alternatives available to date even for non-critical applications are less performant than fluoropolymers. After replacement, we expect that they will have higher energy consumption, will require more maintenance, and will have a lower service life, leading to consumption of more raw materials and generation of more waste. We do not have exact data because components with alternative materials have not been developed, tested, and certified yet.    (iiiv) Information on the benefits for alternative providers.   Low benefits are foreseen, as the uses require low volumes of materials.      g) For cases in which substitution is not technically or economically feasible, information on what the socio-economic impacts would be for companies, consumers, and other affected actors.   For some limited critical applications, there may theoretically be an alternative (such applications are however not known as it would require testing and recertification of each component separately, which is not feasible). However, for many uses, viable alternative materials known to date would certainly not be suitable (as described above).   So first, a viable alternative will have to be developed. But this would be just a first step in the process.  After that, there would be a long step to redesign the components and technologies, test and standardize the alternative in all applications and to finally recertify the machinery (i.e., to carry out a testing against harmonized standards and a conformity assessment for the purposes of the CE marking) and plants (environmental and H&D standards + permits).    The time necessary for these steps is estimated between 5 years (alternative likely to be suitable, easy to implement) and 25 years (extensive testing, extensive re-certification requirements), or longer.    For example, for seals in valves, the minimum time necessary would be 25 years, due to the following reasons.   1) 99% of valve products have fluoropolymer components in them which would be a vast redesign job   2) Extensive certification testing is needed in valves. The most time-consuming certification testing is done for fugitive emission testing, according to ISO 15848. Furthermore, the valves need to comply with internal tightness tests according to ISO 5208 and others, such as fire-safe tests according to API 607. Due to the duration of a certification test (average 7 weeks for one valve) and a high number of fugitive emission certificate tests (over 150 pieces) the testing to re-certify valves with new material replacing PFAS will take approximately 20 years for the whole valve offering. This should happen after finding suitable substitute materials for PFAS and redesigning the whole product offering.    So, the derogation is requested for at least 25 years. However, this relies on an optimistic scenario that an alternative will become available shortly. But this is uncertain. Thus, unlimited derogation should be considered for critical uses, coupled with a sort of review period as outlined in the general comments section.    A socio-economic analysis of a situation where the restriction applies, but a viable alternative is not fully implemented yet, is described below.      1. Impact on technology developers and providers    The technology providers would be unable to deliver new plants without a significant redesign. Redesigned plants would be much less performant and more expensive. It is uncertain if such plants would pass conformity requirements (e.g., pressure equipment), or requirements in environment as well as health and safety legislation. In any event, such redesigned plants would not be competitive globally.   This would inevitably lead to significant shift of R&D and manufacture of these technologies outside the EU.   Without functioning spare parts, the customers would soon be at risk of the technologies invested in becoming stranded assets. Investment certainty would hit bottom, and also customers’ investments (where applicable) would be directed outside the EU.   The world is currently in an unforeseen technological race, and all major blocks try to secure their top position in innovations and strategic autonomy. China and the U.S. are not planning any universal bans on the use of PFAS chemicals but understand their role as an enabler of competitiveness.      2. Impact on the green and digital transition and EU’s leadership role in climate policies   If the EU were now to introduce the planned universal restriction, this would mean that the EU would not only seriously risk any chance of reaching its climate targets and projections for the green transformation but would also willingly give the other blocks the leading role in industrial competitiveness and innovations.   3. Health and Safety issues, risk of environmental damage   The use of alternative materials would significantly increase the risk of leakage of gases and liquids (hot, pressure, toxic, irritants) and pressurized media, leading to intoxication and injuries of personnel and explosions. Risk of crushing when sealing fails, and hydraulic systems start to move would increase.   Redesigned machinery would require more maintenance and repairs and would have more unexpected shutdowns, increasing further the risk of accidents and injuries.   Leakages of gas and liquid directly into the environment would increase because current protective measures are designed to fluoropolymer performance.    A lack of flue gas cleaning facilities would lead to direct emissions to the air.      4. Impact on energy consumption and waste   • Alternative materials would have a higher friction which would have significant energy efficiency impact.    • Impossibility to use waste from energy, and hydrogen. Leaks of methane and natural gas would increase.   • Shutdowns will lead to more waste. More frequent maintenance and more spare parts will also lead to more waste.    • It will be necessary to use fresh water to cool down moving contacts and to provide additional lubrication. Also, more fresh water and cleaning chemicals for cleaning of equipment.        5. Spare parts   Without a derogation for spare parts in existing machinery, all existing plants would have to shut down within months after the entry into force of the restriction, because replacement parts with alternative materials would not be compatible with existing machinery and re-design of existing plants is not feasible. The spare and replacement part derogation should be provided for the lifetime of the plants which is at least 30 years.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Vapor phase technology is used as a soldering process in electronics production worldwide. Our company is the market leader in this field.

This soldering process is increasingly replacing conventional soldering processes, as the soldering technology requirements of the new product generations can no longer be met with conventional processes. Electronics for the energy sector (production of energy, storage, power electronics), automotive (electromobility, charging infrastruc-ture), medical, aerospace and communication technology (5G, networks, data storage) are just a few examples. As a further effect, vapor phase soldering significantly in-creases the performance, reliability and durability of all products manufactured with it due to the particularly low temperature load.

The necessity and performance of this technology has already been proven very suc-cessfully during the conversion of electronics production to lead-free (RoHS).

Vapor phase technology stands for climate-friendly and sustainable electronics pro-duction. It can reduce electricity consumption in electronics production by up to 70%. Only considering the ASSCON vapor phase installation base a CO2 saving of approx. 75,000 t/year and a reduction in electricity consumption of 180 million kWh/year are currently achieved worldwide compared to conventional soldering processes. This compares with a consumption of operating material of 0.3% to 0.6% of the PFAS con-sumption assumed in the dossier.

This required operating material (heat transfer fluid) is currently covered by the planned PFAS regulation, which is already causing considerable uncertainty in the global electronics sector. However, it is not substitutable for vapor phase technology.

A ban on this resource means the "end" of vapor phase technology worldwide. All our customers who rely on vapor phase technology will have to stop their production as there are no alternatives to produce this type of electronics. Due to the lack of this type of highly engineered electronics, products such as electric vehicles, aircraft, power converters, satellites, renewable energy, and battery technology can no longer be manufactured.

However, vapor phase technology is one of the essential success factors for achieving and successfully implementing the goals of the EU Green Deal as well as the initiatives for environmentally friendly mobility and digitalization. If Europe does not want to jeopardize these goals and remain a leader in the development and production of future-proof electronics, vapor phase technology must be preserved for the future and especially for Europe, and an indefinite exemption / derogation of vapor phase soldering from any restrictions must be made!

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Our main application of heating / soldering of electronic and mechnanical components is completely missing. Our application is a production method using heat transfer fluids over a broad variaty of application and industries. If we have to specify to a listed sector, we can mention Electronics and Semiconductor (Annex E.2.11) but this are only two examples of application of our technology.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: There is no end-of-life because we are using a production method. If we talk about the end of operation of a production machine, that uses this technology, 100% of the heat transfer fluid (PFAS) will be recycled (only filtration / cleaning of the fluid is neccesary) and reused in the new production machine.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: There is no emission at end-of-life because we do not have a end-of-life scenario (see above point 2:)

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: None. The heat transfer fluid needs only to be filtered and cleaned (see above point 2:) and this can be done in a new production machine.

5. Proposed derogations: see attached statement

6. Missing uses: see attached statement

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: our technology is not even considered in the proposed restrction entry text (see above point 2:)

8. Other identified uses: our technology is not even considered in the proposed restriction entry text (see above point 2:). We have provided detailed information about (not existing) alternatives, socio-economic impacts on a broad variety of industries and applications in our attached statement.

General Comments: Various functions are imparted to printing inks and overprint varnishes, and various additives are blended in order to exhibit these functions. Various waxes are known for the purpose of surface protection, but PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) in particular has high heat resistance and is extremely difficult to substitute with other waxes. Therefore, we believe that 12 year derogation period is necessary.
Print methods that require 12 year derogation period include offset printing, UV coating, UV flexo, and UV letterpress. The reason for this is that these printing methods require a particularly high degree of surface protection due to the thin film thickness. In these printing methods, the film thickness is generally 1 to 3 μm.
End uses include packages and labels. If the description of the contents disappears due to abrasion during transportation, it is disadvantageous for consumers.
Furthermore, there are no particularly effective substitutes for applications involving temperatures of 200°C or higher. Applications include thermal paper and printed matter printed with a no-impact printer in the post-process. When the ink film melts due to high temperature, the print is damaged.
Additionally, in the metal sheet printing process, the specific gravity of the metal sheet used for metal containers is much higher than that of paper or plastic. Therefore, the magnitude of the frictional energy applied to the surface of the printed ink on metal is greater than on the paper or plastic. That means that the abrasion resistance required for metal decorating inks is much higher than that other uses.

General Comments: VDMA Fluid Power represents the interests of the hydraulic, pneumatic and sealing technology. With more than 230 member companies, we represent approximately 90% of the German market. In Europe, there would be more than 1000 fluid power companies affected by PFAS regulations.

6. Missing uses: Fluid power is included in many machinery products which are used to create a wide variety of essential products needed to support our life in modern society, for example food, pharmaceuticals, medical equipment and many other. A ban on the PFAS used (e. g. PTFE and FKM) would therefore have widespread socio-economic consequences beyond those affecting the industry.  A. We ask for a general exemption of fluoropolymers for hydraulic and pneumatic components and systems as well as for sealings. Used PFAS are: FKM, FFKM, FEPM, FVMQ, PTFE, PCTFE, TFM, PVDF, PFA, FEP, EPDM.  There is no alternative elastomer chemistry that allows the use at temperatures of more than 150 °C.  The characteristics of components using fluoropolymers are crucial for the safety of humans and the environment.   Any research, development, qualification and validation of suitable alternative materials requires longer transitional periods as foreseen in the restriction proposal. E. g. for very high temperatures and required flexible material, it is most likely that no alternatives will be found at all in the future.   In consequence, all risk assessments of machines and plants would have to be revised with alternative materials not providing the same properties as the used fluoropolymers of today. Experience with other materials does not exist as with fluoropolymers. This means that assessments need a long time. This would lead to interruptions in the supply chains in all industrial sectors including the medical, food or energy sector.   The following consequences have to be considered:  - The proposed restriction would be a severe obstacle for the technological development of the whole machinery and plant industry. As a result, parts of the industry would leave the EU and workplaces would be in danger. - In the EU, risks can be reduced by legislation. If the production would migrate to other parts of the world, the EU would have no influence on the safety requirements. - Fluoropolymers, for example in sealing solutions, contribute significantly to machinery and plant safety and therefore to human and environmental safety. They give an additional safeguard when normal operating conditions are exceeded in case of failures.  - An important parameter is the service life. If fluoropolymers were to be replaced by other substances (where temperature and chemical resistance requirements permit), a shorter service life must be expected. This in turn runs counter to the goals of the planned EU Ecodesign for Sustainable Product Regulation (ESPR), which in principle requires products to have a long service life.  The exemption should also include the production of fluorpolymers. If only fluoropolymers were exempted but not their production, dependence on countries outside the EU would arise. The consequences of supply bottlenecks have become clear in recent years.   B. Spare parts should be excluded from the restriction requirements for the following reasons: Long-life machines would have to be decommissioned if spare parts containing PFAS were needed. This is against the objectives of the planned Ecodesign Regulation (ESPR). PFAS-free alternatives that have shorter service lifes would lead to shorter maintenance intervals and thus more frequent shutdowns. From an environmental point of view, this would possibly lead to:   - higher energy costs for the more frequent maintenance - increased environmental impact due to additional transport/driving for the increased maintenance work - higher risks of leaks.  Production costs would increase, which in turn would have an impact on the prices of the end products.  For detailed information see attachment "PFAS applications in fluid power".
