General Comments: VDMA Textile Machinery represents around 150 manufacturers of machinery, equipment, components, accessories and software for the production of textile materials - from spinning to the production of textile fabrics and finishing. They represent about 90 percent of the total industry volume in Germany. About 14 percent of our members are based in Austria, France, the Netherlands, Italy, Portugal, Switzerland, Sweden and the UK.

VDMA Textile Machinery with its members fully support the goal of no longer allowing PFAS classified as very hazardous (for example: CMR, PBT, vPvB, PMT, vPvM or as ED) to enter the environment. In this respect, regulation of these PFASs classified as very hazardous is fundamentally correct when there is a risk of exposure.

The risk-based approach must be maintained so that uses that do not pose a relevant risk remain possible. The general exemption of fluoropolymers from PFAS regulation shall be made, which are considered "polymers of low concern" according to the OECD definition.
Fluoropolymers and substances, such as monomers and processing aids, which are necessary for fluoropolymer production must be exempted from the ban, provided that safe use is ensured. This is also what the study by the British Health and Safety Executive (HSE) envisages. In short, low risk groups (e.g. fluoroelastomers, fluoropolymers assessed as "polymers of low concern") or uses without relevant risk (e.g. contained uses) must be exempted1.

From the very large PFAS group of substances, fluoropolymers (FP) of low concern (PTFE, FKM, FFKM and PVDF) and PFPE are used in textile machinery construction.
The components made of these materials are mostly used inside a textile machine. Maintenance and disposal are carried out by qualified personnel.
The planned ban on the use of FP and PFPE in textile mechanical engineering would jeopardize the competitiveness of that industry sector in the EU as well as the technological sovereignty and security of supply of the EU textile industry.
At least, a long time period would be necessary, partly for the qualification and testing of alternative materials in textile mechanical engineering. In addition, a possible switch to other materials requires various certification processes (e.g. when used for pressure vessel components). These certifications can only be tackled by the suppliers after successful testing in textile mechanical engineering.
Therefore, it must be possible to use FP such as PTFE, FKM, FFKM, PVDF and PFPE in the industrial applications in the textile machinery industry in the EU in the long term.

V. is an association representing a wide range of manufacturers of chemical substances and mixtures, such as surfactants, textile, paper and leather auxiliaries, colorants, cosmetic raw materials, antimicrobial agents, polymeric flocculants and allied products. TEGEWA represents more than 100 member companies from Germany, Switzerland and the Netherlands – including globally active chemical companies as well as a large number of medium-sized companies.
TEGEWA member companies are mainly affected by this restriction proposal in the sectors textile and paper. Another relevant and important aspect for our member companies is the safe production of their chemical products which depends in many cases on fluorinated plant and component parts.
TEGEWA fully supports the comment submitted by the German association Verband der chemischen Industrie e.V. Especially TEGEWA supports the proposal to exclude the manufacturing process and the use in plants and machinery to allow safe production and reduction of emissions as well as uses like high-tech applications, energy uses, medical technology, safety clothing.
Furthermore, TEGEWA asks the Dossier submitters and ECHA to thoroughly consider the comments of EURATEX regarding textile uses, especially if these uses are necessary for protection and safety. In particular in cases where water, oil, and soil repellance at the same time is necessary and requested. For uses only need water repellancy and where alternatives are existing, TEGEWA supports the intention of the dossier submitters to restrict the use of PFAS.
Regarding the scope of the restriction proposal, we would like to point out that the huge number of more than 10,000 substances do have very different chemical and physical properties. Therefore, they are very diverse. So, we question the approach of the dossier submitter that all of them fulfill the prerequisites for a REACH restriction, thus the proposal goes beyond the basic principles of REACH and exceeds the given legal framework.  In particular, if there is no environmental exposure in specific applications and handling or it can be strongly minimised, a ban is not justified. So, we ask for a more differentiated assessment and regulatory approach that bans only uses that pose a risk is needed. A use for which no risk is identified must not be covered as a matter of principle.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Viega and Bode suggest a new sector (use) called infrastructure, since the application discussed in this comment exhibits many differences to the already established sectors in annex E of the restriction report.

The main features of infrastructure are its very long use phase compared to other sectors: Domestic and industrial installations are to be designed for a minimum of 50 years life span (see EN 806-2 standard) where the infrastructure requirements for supply grids outside buildings range up to 100 years. Studies exhibit, that these life spans are realistic and often even surpassed:  https://www.dvgw.de/medien/dvgw/gas/infrastruktur/1407-8wallerath.pdf and https://www.dvgw.de/medien/dvgw/wasser/netze/rohrwerkstoff-pe100-rc-eckert-2109.pdf

These extraordinary life expectancies, the use of pure fluoropolymers without any low molecular weight PFAS and installations being rigidly connected and therefore not allowing cleaning intervals with disassembly of the components makes it a sector with unique performance spectrum, which cannot be found in other sectors.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The sub-uses, which each are highly regulated by themselves and vary strongly with respect to their requirement portfolio, suggested by Viega are:  • Drinking water distribution installations (domestic & municipal) • High temperature and special media installations.  Viega and Bode reached the conclusion, that implementation of this new sector and its sub-uses is necessary, because of the unique properties of these PFAS polymer AND their applications, which are not covered by any other sector or sub-use.  Viega and Bode identified the following potentially relevant sectors in Annex E of the restriction proposal (X marks obvious incomparability):   1. Food contact and packaging E.2.3 a. From the sub-uses:   Short lived applications of low molecular weight PFAS (oil and grease resistance in food packaging), X  processing aids, X  cookware involving PFAS polymer powders in a binder, X  non-stick surfaces, X  emulsifiers X  The only remotely comparable aspect is the use of inert pipes and seals, where the differences in the application are huge: pipe connections in food processing have to be detachable for hygiene/cleaning reasons, seals are replaced on regular intervals, while PFAS polymer seals in infrastructural piping systems cannot be replaced or even reached after pipe connections have been made. Infrastructural seals are subject to harsher conditions and have to have the same life expectancy as the whole infrastructural installation.  2. Construction materials E.2.13 a. Schuster et al. published “Recycling of fluoro-carbon-elastomers – A review” (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aiepr.2022.08.002), stating the following:   “In fact, only two methods were found to be viably functioning for recycling FKM: 1. The milling of FKM to a fine powder to be added to virgin FKM 2. Mechanical devulcanization of FKM and addition to virgin FKM A comparative study for both methods has not been published yet. Chemical devulcanization works well for conventional rubber. For FKM, only patents were found. Cited papers in this regard often just refer to degradation and not to de-vulcanization.  It can be concluded that recycling of FKM is possible and leads to products with competitive properties to those produced with virgin material. However, as known from engineering design that deassembling is design aspect, elastomer and consequently also fluoro-elastomers shall be vulcanized with regard to facilitate devulcanization.”   Schuster et. Al. reach the conclusion, that recycling is possible and development of technologies is ongoing. To be able to develop and establish recycling technologies a derogation or preferably an exemption of the restriction are necessary.

We propose exemption from the PFAS restriction or at least a 12 year derogation with an 18 months transition period on this sub use. Initial emissions are expected in a few decades and the emissions are of low concern according to various OECD studies (see above). The tonnage of this emission cannot be estimated exactly but it is expected to be very low, because infrastructural installations are utilizing static sealing application with extremely long life spans. Recycling of the installations will cause incineration of the PFAS polymers and pose no threat to the environment (WDK incineration Study on fluoropolymer end of life – Gehrmann et al.; 2023). Furthermore Korzeniowski et al. (A critical review of the application of polymer of low concern regulatory criteria to fluoropolymers II: Fluoroplastics and fluoroelastomers, https://doi.org/10.1002/ieam.4646) prove that amongst others fluoroelastomers are in no way comparable to low molecular PFAS, because of their different properties in the area of mobility, persistence, bioaccumulation potential etc.:  “The data presented demonstrate the fluoropolymers in the study are thermally, biologically, and chemically stable, negligibly soluble in water, nonmobile, nonbioavailable, nonbioaccumulative, and nontoxic, and contain low levels of impurities. These results further demonstrate that the fluoropolymer class should be considered distinctly different and should not be grouped with other PFAS for hazard assessment or regulatory purposes.”

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Vienna, Austria 25. September 2023
Response of Cubicure GmbH to the efforts of ECHA to ban PFASs including fluoropolymers

After reviewing the “ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT - PROPOSAL FOR A RESTRICTION” it became clear that ECHA missed to add the uses of PFASs for 3D printing (also referred to as additive manufacturing) to the derogation list, in particular the use of fluoropolymers that represent a crucial part to operate 3D printers.

Compared to traditional subtractive or mould-based manufacturing technologies, 3D printing builds up its final products layer-by-layer. The use of fluoropolymers in 3D printing is particularly widespread in so-called light-curing or vat photopolymerization processes. The most widely used processes are stereolithography (SLA), digital light processing (DLP), and liquid-crystal display (LCD). In all cases, a liquid photoreactive resin is transformed into a cross-linked solid through a cross-linking reaction triggered by the local exposure to light of certain wavelengths. The reactive resins are located in a vat or are applied to the process zone via a film transfer systems. These vat or film transfer systems serve as a container (tub) or, in special cases, as carrier films for transferring the reactive resin into the process zone, where it is exposed to light and solidifies. The aforementioned vats or transfer films need to be highly transparent and colourless in order to let the light penetrate the exposure zone, where it triggers the crosslinking reaction.

After exposure, the cured layer needs to be separated from the vat surface. In order to obtain impeccable parts the separation forces between the cured material and the vat surface need to be as low as possible. The only known material that can meet the required technical prerequisites is FEP fluoropolymer. Moreover, the liquid resin must be prevented from diffusing inside the vat. Here, the FEP film serves as a diffusion barrier. Until now, there have been NO viable alternatives to fluoropolymers identified yet. However, the use of fluoropolymer film systems in 3D printing is only low in terms of quantity, but it is absolutely essential for the functionality of the vat or film transfer systems.

Today, 3D printing has established itself as a production tool for numerous applications and has become an indispensable part of everyday industrial life. 3D printing plays a particularly important role in the production of medical products. One example are dental aligners, which can be produced exclusively using 3D printing. Apart from medical products, 3D printing is also used in the automotive industry, medical technology, the electronics industry, telecommunications, aerospace, the defence industry and in many other promising areas.

A ban on fluoropolymers for use in 3D printing will therefore have immediate consequences for many important products, especially medical products, as no alternatives to fluorinated foils have yet been found and probably cannot be found due to their unique chemical nature.

A ban of fluoropolymers today equals a ban of new, low-energy consuming, decentralized manufacturing technologies that have proven to be of huge benefit during the covid crisis. When global supply chains collapsed, in many cases 3D printing remained one of the few technologies that was able to promptly produce desperately needed medical equipment. While traditional manufacturing technologies such as injection moulding require enormous amounts of energy, 3D printing and in special vat photopolymerization provides a low-energy alternative. Apart form that, there are approximately more than 1,000 high-tech jobs threatened by the planned legislation alone in Austria.

Therefore, Cubicure supports the demand of hundreds of other companies to grant a general exemption for fluoropolymers for an indefinite period of time. A general ban on fluoropolymers represents a competitive disadvantage for European companies in the harsh global competition that cannot be compensated and that will massively inhibit the continued existence, further development and new development of technical solutions to the problems of our times (e.g. climate change and global warming).

Thank you for considering our statement.

On behalf of Cubicure GmbH,

Dr. Markus Kury
Chief Product Officer

Combined Comments:
General Comments: VIK-Statement to restriction on the production, placing on the market and use of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)

General remarks:
Environment and health protection of flora and fauna is of high priority, also for German industry. A blanket ban of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) don´t do justice to this.
VIK remarks that it takes a case-by-case analysis rather than implementing a general ban. Measures affecting the lifecycle phases (production, placement on the market and use) should be done with a sense of proportion.

Current policy framework:
The german energy-intensive industry across all sectors is currently in a very challanging situation. Production has already shut down at many sites. Furthermore Germany possibly faces a longer lasting recession these days.
Currently many industries suffer under location disadvantages compared with other competitors worldwide.
Many companies are currently investigating the location conditions for further investment decisions in Europe.  Both to maintain local production facilities and with regard to important climate-neutral transformation projects.
The discussions of an EU-wide ban of PFAS or their comprehensive restriction, the discussions of substitution costs combined with the question of further availability of individual substances, substance groups or mixtures don´t ease the tense situation.

VIK remarks that climate protection, climate neutral mobility, green hydrogen, carbon management and the energy transition as a whole are only attainable with PFAS-substances.

A blanket ban on PFAS would hamper the targets of the European Green Deal, especially for technologies associated with the transformation of the energy system.
It must not come to an over-regulation of the economy where it inhibits sustainable growth and the developement of key technologies.

The fact is, that per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) play a key role in many technologies of the future. For example, PFAS are contained in electrochemical energy storage sites, energy infrastructure, fuel cells and hydrogen technologies. Their replacement, if possible at all, coheres capabilities which are not be available for the energy transformation; again, this will hamper the transition of our energy system and will jeopardize the ambitious targets.

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) – Relevance to the industry
The developement of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances together with their industrial use supported an advanced developement of industrial processes and technologies. Nowadays Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances are used in several industrial products.

The areas of application of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances within the industry results from their immanent properties, such as „resistance to extreme temperatures“, „resistance to aggressive chemicals” together with a “high abrasion resistance and wear resistance”

According to the mentioned specific properties devices and plant components can be manufactured in a more resource-efficient manner. The mentioned devices and plant components can be designed for example with less mass. Futher positive aspects are for example an increasement of service life as well as an extend of maintenance intervals.
Gaseous per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) function, for example, as insulating and protective gases in electrical switchgear.
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are essential for the innovative strength of modern industry, including when it comes to push climate-protection technologies to achieve the ambitious climate targets.

VIK stresses that a blanket ban on PFAS-based applications and products hamper the innovative strength of modern industry and jeopardizes jobs. Moreover, a blanket ban of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances jeopardizes Germany as a business location. If manufacturing chains in Europe break down, this may result in an unassailable lead of non-European-competitors, to a permanently and irreversible loss of market shares, sales revenues and technical know-how.

Aspects to be considered in the further course of the evaluation process:

 A general restriction of PFAS substances is disproportionate and like already explaind, does not lead to the desired results. Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances are not equally persistent nor mobile or bioaccumulative.
The implmentation of a general ban would have massive negative impact on the industry. For example, product diversity would be reduced significantly. Furthermore, the innovation capability of German industry would be considerably restricted.
 International value chains are of high complexity. In case of a restriction on many thousends of substances, we see a great risk of unforeseen disruptions to value chains. These effects can not be calculated in detail; a preparation to this situation is almost impossible. What we expect are incalculable economic effects.
 A lack of available PFAS-Alternatives would bind high socio-economic costs in trying to replace them in the short-term.

Recommendations:
General recommendations:
 VIK sees a further need for scrutiny after the end of the regular consultation phase. VIK therefore asks for an extension of the consultation phase, especially with regard to the impact on industries for a closer check regarding processes and applications that require purchased parts.
Currently the labeling is insufficient. Therefore it is difficult to assess along the supply chain whether alternatives are available on the market or not and which product may contain PFAS.
 Plant components such as seals, inlays, coatings and catalysts have to remain available on the market.
 In plants in which PFAS are currently used as operating and auxiliary materials, it must be ensured that technical alternatives can enable continued operation in the future.
For a continued operation in the future, regarding the normal service life, we recommend an orientation in accordance with the Electricity Grid Charges Ordinance (StromNEV), Annex 1.
 PFAS substitutes may bring along negative physical effects regarding e.g. material thickness and designs, mode of action, durability and UV-resistance.
The testing effort for proving safety-related requirements may increase; products could become more expensive.
 The impact of PFAS-substitutes on the environment are difficult to predict. From VIK perspective it would be helpful to draw up a whitelist. The mentioned whitelist should contain products and substances which are classified by ECHA as harmless for the environment in the long term. The whitelist can be seen as a starting point for the industry to develop PFAS-substitutes.

Specific recommendations:
 Ensure competition:
The Annex VI-Dossier mentioned that their is low substiution potenital to replace both SF6 and fluorinated gases as insulating gases in high-voltage switchgears. In this context VIK underlines that manufacturer-side monopolistic positions must be avoided; single-source solutions must not be allowed. In the interest of competitiveness and supply capability, there should be at least three different suppliers of insulating gases on the market. The example given here is representative of a large number of applications in the electrical industry.
 Close content coordination:
VIK recommends a close coordination of the following EU-Packages:
- Regulation on fluorinated greenhouse gases;
- ANNEX XV Restriction Report – propoal for a restriction of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)
F-gases can fall into both regulation schemes; VIK stresses, that double regulations should be avoided.
 PFAS labeling obligation:
VIK recommends mandatory PFAS labeling, with due regard to substance groups and quantities used.
Remaining PFAS substances that are indispensable for the community should be included in the REACH register in the same way as other chemicals. This ensures a responsible handling of PFAS substances and products. In line with the REACH regulation, it is ensured that in the long term the most hazardous substances are replaced by less hazardous or non-hazardous substances.
This may result in longer transition periods than five or twelve years. VIK recommends that ECHA reconsiders its specified transition periods according to the restriction dossier (Annex XV Report)
This approach ensures that industrial users can continue to participate in the market. The research-based industry receives time to research and develop innovative alternatives in line with EU requirements and to bring them to market maturity.
 Shortage of skilled workers aggravates the search for PFAS alternatives:
The current shortage of skilled workers makes it more difficult to develop new and PFAS-free substances and products. This situation also affects (high-performance) insulating gases.

General Comments: Vitens water company, the largest drinking water company in the Netherlands, strongly support the proposed PFAS restriction. PFAS measurements in drinking water, as reported by RIVM in October 2022, emphasize the need for action to protect the sources of our drinking water, the water system in general and our consumers.

PFAS is a serious risk for drinking water
Based on the 2020 EFSA report on “Risk to human health related to the presence of perfluoroalkyl substances in food”,  the Dutch national institute for Public Health (RIVM)  derived a health-based guidance value of 4,4 ng/l PFOA Equivalents.
In the mentioned study by RIVM, PFAS concentrations exceeded this threshold in over half of the measurements of  drinking water produced from surface water. For drinking water from groundwater, this was the case for 1 in 10 measurements. These concentrations need to be brought down to ensure people’s PFAS intake from drinking water does not become too high.
Areas with the highest PFAS concentrations in drinking water are located in the Western part of the Netherlands, where drinking water is mostly produced from river water. Concentrations the environment slowly decline because PFAS are widely present, do not or barely degrade and are difficult to remove in water treatment. Given this fact, a precautionary approach based on source-protection like a the proposed PFAS restriction, is the way forward.
Projections of future PFAS concentrations in ground- and surface water as a source for drinking water indicate that without tackling the source of PFAS  all drink water sources will eventually surpass these threshold values . KWR research in 2022 on PFAS in European waters   suggests that PFAS is raising similar high concern in other EU countries as well.

PFAS is a risk for the water system in general
In addition to the risks for drinking water specifically, it is important to stress that PFAS is a serious risk to the water system in its entirety. If people would only come into contact with PFAS through drinking water, the problem would be less serious. However, there are several other ways in which people are exposed to PFAS.
Furthermore, several examples can be mentioned in which PFAS has negative consequences for the water quality. Additional sources of PFAS in the water system, for example, are the supply of PFAS from upstream rivers and the deposition of PFAS through the air. PFAS has a negative effect on ecology, including toxic effects, accumulation in organisms and subsequently within the food chain.
PFAS also has a negative impact on other water functions like swimming, recreation in general on or close to the water, fishing, irrigation and livestock watering. We see waters in which the concentration of PFAS is already ten thousand times too high, and it is very difficult or even impossible to eliminate PFAS once it is present in the water system.
PFAS also contains  a risk to water soils and circular ambitions. Dredging activities are sometimes necessary to preserve the water system including the water quality. When PFAS accumulates within water soils, the dredge should ultimately be disposed which is very expensive. When it comes to sludge which can be derived from sewage treatment plants, it becomes impossible to reuse the wastewater. In reference a circular economy this is an undesirable effect.

TFA as an extreme threat
Especially the occurrence of the ultrashort PFAS TriFluoroacetic Acid (TFA) in surface water, groundwater and drinking water is an extreme threat. Data from Rijkswaterstaat and RIWA as stored in the Norman database (June 2023) show concentrations of TFA up to 3 microgram/l. The drinking water advisory threshold value for TFA as a single compound is set to 2200 ng/l (RIVM, 2023)  , but combined with other PFAS the proposed threshold-value is in the Netherlands is 4,4 ng PFOA Equivalents (PEQ)/l. In which TFA is given relative potency factor of 0,002.  Neuwald (2022) and Sadia (2023) found concentrations in the order of 1 microgram/l which exceed the limits as given by the European Drinking Water Directive    . In this directive,  which took effect on 12 January 2021,  a limit of 0.5 µg/l for all PFAS is included.  TFA alone exceeds this threshold. This TFA originate from various industrial use, domestic use and degradation products and are found in high concentrations in the environment and drinking water.  illustrating once more that only a (global) ban can be the way forward to prevent the ubiquitous emissions of this compound and its precursors  .
The claim that TFA is of natural origin is convincingly refuted by Joudan (2022)

Clean, deeper groundwater reserves for drinking water will be lost in the future without a ban
At this moment especially drinking water produced from river water is strongly affected by the PFAS pollution. Inevitability, drinking water from groundwater will also be affected without a ban.  Given the ubiquitous presence of PFAS from air-emissions and deposition at the soil-surface, this amount of PFAS will gradually and continuously infiltrate to the deeper aquifers, polluting  the previously unaffected reservoirs of clean drinking water for the Dutch and European costumers, leading to extreme purification costs and efforts. The infiltration-rate of PFAS to the deeper underground is modelled by KWR . This might take decades, but will, without a ban, eventually end up with the pollution of all existing European Groundwater bodies up to levels that exceed the threshold values for PFAS that are proposed in the current revision of the Water Framework Directive (WFD) and its daughter Directives on Environmental Quality Standards (WFD-EQSD) and Groundwater Directive (WFD-GD)), where Environmental Quality Standards (EQS) are proposed for a group of 24 PFAS on al level of 4,4 ng/l PFOA Equivalents.

Banning PFAS in is crucial for several reasons
Health Risks and Consumer Protection
PFAS have been associated with numerous adverse health effects, including developmental issues, liver damage, thyroid disruption, immune system impairment, and certain types of cancer. These substances can enter the human body through various routes, including drinking water. By banning PFAS in Europe, the aim is to reduce exposure to these harmful chemicals and protect public health. The Dutch National Public Health Institute (RIVM) has already calculated that Dutch citizens take in too much PFAS already. A ban on PFAS is absolutely necessary to ensure a safe living environment for European citizens now and in the future.
Water Treatment Challenges and Costs
Removing PFAS from water sources is challenging and costly for drinking water treatment facilities. Due to their unique properties, PFAS are resistant to traditional water treatment processes, making their removal extremely difficult, and moreover, advanced treatment methods, such as activated carbon filtration or reverse osmosis, require 5-20 % more source water, where (groundwater) sources of drinking water are becoming more scarce as a result of climate change and drought.
In addition to this, there are currently no efficient techniques available to eliminate PFAS from waste water through sewage treatment plants. In most cases, existing techniques to reduce PFAS are very expensive and little effective in case of a small source, especially considering the high contribution of additional sources of PFAS through the air and upstream supplies. These techniques are also require a huge amount of energy, which is not desirable in relation to climate change. It is much more effective and environmentally friendly to prevent PFAS from getting into the environment in the first place.  As the vast majority of PFAS in river water (Rhine and Meuse) entering the Netherlands is emitted somewhere in the international river-basin, a European, cross-border approach is the only logical approach to minimize this pollution.
PFAS removal techniques are insufficient and mostly moving PFAS from one medium to another
PFAS is a very persistent group of chemicals with no natural decay.  PFAS removal from drinking water is moving PFAS from one medium to another. Waste streams of PFAS containing activated carbon or membrane concentrate is the result. Removal of PFAS from water might be the solution for drinking water, but leads to extra pollution of (surface) water, air and landfills, as the waste-streams of standard purification (PFAS containing activated carbon, sludge or concentrate) ends up somewhere in the environment.  Verma at al. (2023)  described low performance of thermal and non-thermal treatment technologies in large scale applications.

The need for a ban on PFAS
Banning PFAS in Europe would lead to a reduction in their presence in water sources, easing the burden on water treatment facilities. This, in turn, can alleviate the costs associated with the specialized treatment required for PFAS removal. By preventing further contamination, it allows resources to be focused on enhancing overall water quality and improving treatment efficiency.
In conclusion, banning PFAS in Europe, particularly in the context of drinking water production, is essential for protecting public health, safeguarding the environment, and limiting public costs and even droughts. Droughts, because additional purification with for example membranes, requires  extra source waters from rivers and aquifers that are threatened for over-exploitation during long dry periods like the summer of 2023, where drinking water facilities throughout Europe feared for shortages.  Furthermore, banning PFAS aligns with global efforts to regulate and restrict these substances. It demonstrates Europe's commitment to environmental protection and encourages international harmonization in the control of PFAS. By taking decisive action, Europe can lead the way in creating a safer and more sustainable future, ensuring clean and healthy drinking water for its population and setting an example for the rest of the world.

All PFAS  are a  threat
As we have learned, PFAS are emitted along various pathways and are ubiquitous: everywhere in the world PFAS are found. Unwanted emissions occur during production, use, and disposal.
The total occurrence and emissions of lots of PFAS and precursors are not well known.  According to the Pubchem classification browser  , there are more than 6 million various PFAS that fit the OECD PFAS definition of the Restriction dossier. Removal and remediation is practically impossible. Even burning leads to smaller PFAS-fragments and transformation products like TFA.  Claims of industry that there are less harmful PFAS have led to regrettable substitutions, for example from PFOA to GenX (HFPO-DA). Similar claims of harmless PFAS-subgroups like fluoropolymers are refuted in literature by Lohmann et al.  .  Somewhere in the process of production, use and disposal PFAS will enter the environment and accumulate in water, soil, air and the foodchain. The supports the conclusion that the only way to prohibit further emissions and accumulation of PFAS in our environment is a complete ban.  Vitens water company strongly supports the broad scope of the PFAS definition in the restriction proposal.  The need for a broad scope is also necessary as the health based drinking water advisory level as derived by RIVM has no limitation and contains every PFAS (Including TFA) with an established Relative Potency Factor (RPF-value) translated to PFOA equivalents and should not exceed the level of 4,4 ng/l PFOA equivalents per litre. This list of PFAS is theoretically enormous.



The need of fast implementation and no exemptions
This restriction-proposal does not come as a surprise or unannounced. The societal risks and costs of the use of PFAS have been described many times, for example by Chemsec in 2023  . Given the time between the (announcement of the) proposal (2022) and suggested start of the implementation (2025), there will be enough time for industry to prepare. Therefore exemptions should not be tolerated and only be granted under very strict conditions and for a period as short as possible
Textile, paper and firefighting-foam industry have proven that there are always alternatives available for PFAS. It takes some years of a transformation period, but it is possible, as proven by the H&M group during the ZeroPM workshop in February 2023  .  Recently (june 2023), Martin Scheringer published a comment in science, with the same conclusion  .
Claims that PFAS are essential for societal favourable transitions like the energy transition should be critically assessed, The fact that PFAS are used for “essential” and high valued products, doesn’t automatically mean that PFAS are essential in these products. There will always be an alternative that will also better fit with the European ambitions of a circular economy. PFAS containing products are probably impossible to re-use. In order to prevent further pollution of the European environment and the sources of our drinking water a fast implementation with no exemptions is the way forward.

Only restriction of emissions is an illusion
Claims that the PFAS containing products are not the problem, but only the production, and that the emissions during production could be regulated is misleading. As stated by Lohmann (2020), emissions occur during production, use and disposal  . Removing of PFAS is an illusion. Removal of PFAS from air or water moves the PFAS from one phase to another, for example from water tot activated carbon or membrane concentrate. These PFAS containing waste-streams ends up in landfills or are burned at standard temperatures, leading to new/other and unmeasured smaller PFAS compounds that will re-enter the environment by leaching to soil and air. Again supporting the proposal for a complete ban.

Additional supporting documentation
Commissioned by Vewin (the Association of Dutch drinking water companies and the Dutch Water Association), KWR has compiled an overview of recent relevant scientific literature information that is important for the current restriction proposal. This report is attached as appendix 2. Relevant conclusions from this research are:
- PFAS have documented adverse effects on human health and the environment, and that (drinking) water is an important exposure route for humans to PFAS;
- The amount of literature and evidence on adverse health effects of PFAS is still growing;
- Many of reported removal methods have the potential to efficiently remove PFAS from water. Nevertheless, it should be noted that these findings are novel and sometimes promising, but it remains yet unclear if their implementation on a large scale is feasible;
- The restriction of PFAS can indeed result in lower exposure and thus risks to humans and the environment;
- It is argued that all PFAS, including fluoropolymers, give rise to emissions of harmful PFAS at some stage of their life cycle. Therefore, some authors support the broad definition of PFAS used in the restriction proposal and the resulting ban on fluoropolymers and other PFAS alike.
- It was noted that the authors supporting the exemption of fluoropolymers from a ban represent or are affiliated with PFAS-producing companies;
- 97 % of China’s PFOA/PFO emissions originated from the production of fluoropolymers;
- Emerging PFAS can induce toxicity like legacy PFAS like PFOS and PFOA;
- The justification for managing PFAS as a single chemical class to reduce PFAS-related risks is provided in the scientific literature. It is argued that a class-based approach can be implemented to eliminate non-essential uses of PFAS more effectively, develop safer alternatives, and clean up highly contaminated areas.
- A restriction of PFAS can indeed result in lower exposure and thus risks to humans and the environment;

The overall conclusion of Vitens water company is that there is strong scientific support for a complete ban of all PFAS according to the proposed PFAS definition, including subgroups as TFA and fluoropolymers.

General Comments: Vivisol UK is a European company producing and distributing industrial, medical and food gases.
The PFAS restriction as defined today will significantly impact all aspects of our industry (e.g., industrial/medical gas production, storage and both cylinder and bulk supply). This includes supply of gases to a range of critical industries including but not limited to:
• liquid and gaseous oxygen for hospital and healthcare facilities, such as was needed for Covid primary treatment.
• oxygen for industrial purposes like steel production
• pure gases and gas mixtures for food industry
• green hydrogen (cryogenic and gaseous) to enable delivery for the EU’s decarbonization targets.
• cryogenic and gaseous nitrogen for safety critical inert processing
• cryogenic helium for hospital MRI scanners.
• electronic gas (mixtures) towards the Semiconductor Industry.
• refrigerants.

For certain applications alternative solutions to PFAS materials could be available within derogation time.  These alternatives are under investigation with support from our equipment suppliers. The research, validation and potential implementation of alternatives will imply massive investment and time.

In addition, there are also very complex applications where alternatives seem to be not possible within derogation time or not at all, for example an alternative for the cryogenic properties of PFAS materials. The elasticity properties at cryogenic temperatures is acknowledged in Annex A section A.3.2.1.1, but impact of this proposed ban has not been considered in Annex E.  The lack of alternative can lead to a future risk to not be able to produce and supply these gases under the same safe conditions as today.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Construction products (Annex E.2.13.): PTFE thread sealing tape 1. It is widely used in gas industry as a protection of the connection between cylinder valve and cylinder. This is an essential functionality of PTFE tape as it provides lubrication of the thread, guarantee disassembly of the valve when necessary. Easy application and reliable performance in this application is not easy to replace. Historically used solution with cones based on silver and lead (alternatively including tin or aluminum) are not acceptable as they also contain problematic material. Gas companies run millions of cylinders globally and PTFE tape is used on almost every of these cylinders. If there is other solution like PTFE cones or PFPE based liquid lubricant, it is still based on PFAS.  We need further information from suppliers and development work with them to estimate the derogation period that we would need.  2. PTFE thread sealing tape is also used in equipment for cryogenic and low temperature service.  In this use we do not see any alternatives available yet and not under study.  3. PTFE thread sealing tape is used also in many other connections of gas production equipment where different design approach will need to be implemented to eliminate the use of PTFE. This will require time and investment into new equipment.  Availability of spare parts including PTFE tape will be essential for maintenance until the new equipment is available. We need further information from suppliers and development work with them to estimate the derogation period that we would need.    Lubricants (Annex E.2.14.): Sector as whole We appreciate that lubricants are selected in the group with 13,5 years derogation which highlights specifics characteristics of this products. PFPE based lubricants are widely used in gas equipment for great resistance in oxidizing atmosphere and high pressure. Introduction of these lubricants significantly reduced occurrence of oxygen ignitions (fire) and improved safety of our employees, customers and patients.  The applied quantities of the lubricant during manufacturing are very small and there is a high level of control for quantity applied to each piece of equipment to ensure functionality but not overdose lubricants.  Currently we see no evidence of availability for alternative guaranteeing adequate level of safety and expectation of successful development of such alternative is on very low probability within the proposed derogation time.

General Comments: We (SGL Fuel Cell Components GmbH) are one of the world’s leading manufacturers of carbon-based gas diffusion layers (GDL) and porous transport layers (PTL) for PEM fuel cells and PEM water electrolysers. Our products contain up to 20% (weight) fluorinated polymers (PTFE, optionally also FEP) which are applied solely by means of aqueous dispersions. The use of these fluoropolymers is indispensable for the functionality of our GDL/PTL products, namely hydrophobicity and resistance against (electro)chemical degradation. To date, there is no viable alternative to fluoropolymers for gas diffusion layers which can ensure the durability targets set for PEM fuel cells for use in transportation (especially for heavy-duty vehicles).

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Sectors: Water Electrolysis, Fuel Cells, Proton-exchange membrane fuel cells, Proton-exchange membrane water electrolysers, Anion-exchange membrane water electrolysers, carbon dioxide electrolysers

6. Missing uses: Although fluoropolymers belong to the PFAS group, they represent a very small sub-class and their properties differ significantly from the majority of per- and polyfluorinated alkyl compounds (PFAS). Depending on the definition, the entire group of chemicals includes more than 5,000 substances, less than 40 of which are fluoropolymers. In Ref. [1] and [2], toxicity, clinical, physical, chemical, thermal and biological data for a selection of fluoropolymers covering more than 95% of the current fluoropolymer market have been collated and critically reviewed.  Given their unique properties, fluoropolymers are important enablers for numerous key industrial and future topics and for achieving the goals set out in the EU Green Deal. This applies to the chemical process industry, mobility using fuel cells, green hydrogen production and many other applications. Potential “alternatives” to fluoropolymers are usually less safe, increase the carbon footprint and are inferior with respect to their performance. Due to the stringent EU chemicals legislation and other central environmental guidelines, there is no other region where fluoropolymer production and processing is as clean and reliable as in Europe. In addition, there are control mechanisms in place within companies that prevent environmental pollution from production and processing. The latter are key elements in the transformation of the energy and chemical industry in the EU that is currently under way – particularly for the following technologies:  • PEM fuel cells for zero-emission mobility • PEM and AEM water electrolysers to produce green hydrogen • Electrochemical production of base-chemicals from gaseous reactants (e.g. carbon dioxide)   [1] Henry et al., A Critical Review of the Application of Polymer of Low Concern and Regulatory Criteria to Fluoropolymers, Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management, Volume 14, Number 3, pp. 316–334, 2018  [2] Korzeniowski et al., A critical review of the application of polymer of low concern regulatory criteria to fluoropolymers II: Fluoroplastics and fluoroelastomers, Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management, Volume 19, Number 2, pp. 326–354, 2022  SGL Fuel Cell components use only polymeric PFAS such as PTFE (or FEP) in the form of aqueous dispersions (50-60 weight%) to manufacture coating dispersions. Mixing and feeding of the latter media is fully automated in order to minimise losses and spillage (attached document “Summary SGL FCC”). Any fluoropolymer-containing waste produced during cleaning of the manufacturing lines is collected in containers and subjected to incineration.  Our suppliers of fluoropolymer dispersions are required not to use any fluorinated surfactants (which we deem as critical substances) in their products and production processes.   Production processes within the attached “Summary SGL FCC” show how PTFE is processed at SGL Fuel Cell Components GmbH. Further, we have implemented measures so as to avoid emissions to the environment from PTFE raw materials, semi-finished and finished products. We ensure that the PTFE raw material is almost entirely transformed into products for our customers while a remaining minimal share of production waste is safely collected and sent for waste incineration. A recently conducted analysis of our wastewater (see attachement “Summary SGL FCC”) has shown that, currently, the total volume of PFAS that we release into the wastewater is already lower than 100 ng/L (which is the statutory limit for drinking water in Germany as of 2026, Ref. [3]). An even greater reduction in PFAS emissions could be accomplished by adding additional filtration processes.   Recycling concepts for waste and end-of-life products are available (solid waste incineration and reaction of released fluorine compounds with calcium hydroxide to form CaF2)  [3] https://www.lanuv.nrw.de/umwelt/gefahrstoffe/pfas/pfas-im-wasser#:~:text=F%C3%BCr%20die%20Summe%20von%2020,0%2C1%20%C2%B5g%2FL.  SGL Fuel Cell Components GmbH is one of the world’s leading manufacturers of carbon-based gas diffusion media (GDL) and porous transport (PTL) layers for PEM fuel cells and PEM water electrolysers. Our products contain up to 20% (weight) fluorinated polymers (PTFE, optionally also FEP) by weight which are applied by coating with aqueous dispersions. Accordingly, a 100 KW fuel cell vehicle contains around 200-300 g PTFE per stack.  The use of these fluoropolymers is indispensable for the functionality of  GDL/PTL products, namely hydrophobicity and resistance against (electro)chemical degradation. The latter property is also crucial for other fuel cell components such as proton exchange membranes (expanded PTFE) and catalyst layers (contain PFSA ionomers with a typical equivalent weight of 700 to 1200 g/mol).   The inherent physicochemical charateristics of fluorpolymers are crucial for the function of gas diffusion layers (GDLs) and porous transport layers (PTLs). Fluoropolymers suchs as PTFE or PTFE produce unrivaled superhydrophobic properties which are crucial for GDLs and PTLs, as their porous structures cannot be flooded by water formed during operation. In addition, the fluoroplastics serve as robust binder materials which hold the conductive carbon particles together and are highly stable against the corrosive conditions that tend to prevail in electrochemical environments of fuel cells and electrolysers.  In essence, fluoropolymers are indispensable for the development of highly efficient and stable electrochemical reactors involving gas phase reactions.   Fluorpolymer-containing fuel cell and electrolyser components are crucial for the following applications:  • Zero-emission propulsion of fuel-cell electric vehicles (forklifts, passenger cars, buses, trucks, ships, airplanes) • Fuel cells for combined heat and power (CHP) applications • Production of green hydrogen by means of PEM water electrolysis • Production of green hydrogen by via AEM water electrolysis • Metal-air batteries • Sustainable production of base chemicals (e.g. formic acid, lower alcohols, hydrogen peroxide) via electrochemical conversion of carbon dioxide or water  To date, our own efforts using non-PFAS hydrophobisation agents as well as published data [4] have clearly shown that to date, there is no viable alternative to replace fluoropolymers in gas diffusion layers which can ensure the performance and durability targets set for PEM fuel cells for use in transportation (especially for heavy-duty vehicles). Accordingly, a recently conducted patent search found not so much as a single patent claiming a PFAS-free gas diffusion layer material.  [4] Öztürk, A. Bayrakceken Yurtcan, Effect of calcination temperature on hydrophobicity of microporous layers prepared with two different molecular weights of PDMS polymer on PEM fuel cell performance with low Pt loading, International Journal of Hydrogen Energy, Vol 42, 2017, 6250-626, http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.ijhydene.2016.11.041  Hydrogen is widely seen as the most important pillar to facilitate the transformation of the energy supply and the chemical industry towards low/zero emissions. This is because hydrogen performs a number of different functions. The most relevant are the following:  1. Efficient way to store energy generated from wind and solar power 2. Zero-emissions fuels for mobility and power/heat production 3. Non-fossil-based industrial feedstocks (production of steel, glass, foods, etc.)  A ban on fluoropolymers will put entire sectors of new green and sustainbable industry which are just about to take off at serious risk.   We anticipate a loss of several hundred thousand jobs and economic output losses running into several hundreds of billions of euros.   PTFE is made up of polymerized tetrafluoroethene units forming a carbon backbone with 2 fluorine atoms covalently bound to each carbon atom. This chemical structure entails the nearly universal chemical stability.  • The C-F bond is the strongest (covalent) chemical bond. • In addition, the C-C chain (carbon backbone) is completely shielded by the large F atoms.  Hence, any alternative polymeric material is inherently inferior with regard to durability, corrosion resistance and hydrophobicity of fluoropolymers required in fuel cells and electrolyses. These limitations cannot be overcome with time – it is a matter of physico-chemical laws.   Moreover, fluoropolymers can be classified as "polymers of low concern" (PLC) according to the recognized OECD criteria. They rank among all those plastics that have successfully passed tests based on a total of 13 criteria defined by the OECD. PLCs pose no risk to the environment nor to human health.   Any premature ban (in the absence of commercially available alternatives demonstrated in the field for prolonged periods) of PTFE and other fluoropolymers for application in gas diffusion layers will foil any efforts to establish a clean energy economy based on hydrogen generation by water electrolysis, emission-free transportation based on PEM fuel cells, as well as new green chemistry concepts based on electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide to base chemicals.   In summary, we would like to emphasise that an exemption must be made for PTFE and other fluoropolymers (FEP, THV, PVDF, PFA) for application in gas diffusions layers (GDL) and porous transport layers (PTLs).

General Comments: We (the company VACUUBRAND) are manufacturer of vacuum pumps for rough and fine vacuum (atmospheric pressure down to 10-3 mbar absolute). In the previous entries (Table A.1 in Annex A of the Annex XV Restriction Report lists), the sector “Laboratory Equipment” and thus the entire laboratory industry was not considered in sufficient detail. In our understanding this also includes vacuum technology with its entire product portfolio (e.g. chemistry diaphragm pumps, diaphragm pumps, screw pumps, rotary vane pumps, chemistry hybrid pumps, vacuum controllers, vacuum gauges, vacuum networks, tubings, fittings and valves).

In vacuum technology fluoropolymers are used for all parts which are in contact with the media due to their many excellent properties. The most important of these are: excellent chemical resistance, low surface energy, durability, chemical inertness and temperature resistance (up to 200 °C). It is only because of these properties that vacuum pumps are able to maintain the qualitative standards required for the individual processes and the equipment.

Vacuum technology is a basic need of all laboratories in the world. Many processes carried out in the laboratory are performed under vacuum. A few examples of applications where vacuum is necessarily required are: Schlenk line (for handling samples under exclusion of air and moisture), filtration (for the separation of solids from liquids), fluid aspiration, freeze dryer (for a gentle drying process) and vacuum oven (for drying). Therefore, vacuum technology is needed in a wide range of academic and industrial areas, such as basic research, small scale production for example of chemicals, vaccines, medicines, flavors up to high scale production of solar cells. For this reason, more attention should be directed to the sector of laboratory equipment, as it seems that these relationships and the potential consequences have not been fully considered.

As of today, there is no adequate replacement for the fluoropolymers used, due to the high requirements for chemical resistance in combination with mechanical properties. The time required to identify alternative materials with similar properties is estimated to be at least 7 years. The combined cost of this operation will be immense and represent a significant part of our turnover. In addition, the overall chemical compatibility which is offered by the fluoropolymers will not be reproducible with other materials which will lead to restrictions for the users of these technologies.

6. Missing uses: Table A.1 in Annex A of the Annex XV Restriction Report lists - highlighted in blue - PFAS uses that have not been addressed in further detail, as among others laboratory equipment. This includes, in our understanding, all laboratory equipment, i.e. also vacuum technology: e.g. chemistry diaphragm pumps, diaphragm pumps, screw pumps, rotary vane pumps, chemistry hybrid pumps, vacuum controllers, vacuum gauges, vacuum networks, tubings, fittings and valves.  Vacuum is essential for a wide range of applications in laboratories and beyond, e.g.  • for clinical diagnostics and testing (integrated vacuum pumps in automated liquid handling stations for high throughput diagnostics and microplate washers: e.g. PCR-testing),  • for chemistry / pharma labs in research, universities and industry: in chemistry and pharma laboratories a lot of equipment/processes require vacuum. A large variety of partly highly aggressive chemicals are used in the labs   o for freeze dryers: freeze drying is a very gentle drying process for sensitive samples like medically active compounds such as vaccines. In freeze drying frozen samples are dried under vacuum without defrosting. o for filtration: filtration is used to separate liquids from solids. In filtration vacuum is needed to support and accelerate the process. o for Schlenk lines: Schlenk lines are used for processing samples under exclusion of air and moisture.  o for fluid aspiration in cell culture applications (e.g. media change, cell washing) in microbiology labs for basic research and diagnostics (universities, hospitals, life science and pharma companies). o for synthesis reactor systems (for sample and reactant feed, synthesis reaction process, purification, distillation, reflux, filtration, etc.),  • for the production of lithium ion batteries: in the production of lithium ion cells (for example for e-mobility) vacuum is used in the electrolyte filling line. It is needed in order to prevent foaming of the electrolyte and to fill the cells free of air. In addition, vacuum is of great importance for leak testing of battery cells, as these tests are performed in vacuum chambers. • for the production of solar cells: in the production process of solar cells the wafers are often doped in a low-pressure diffusion furnace with POCl3 or BBr3 (deposition from the gas phase). This process is performed under vacuum conditions (the vacuum is used to transport the carrier gas through the liquid). Despite the upstream high-performance cold trap, the vacuum pumps, gauges and controllers are highly exposed to the aggressive media. • as backing pumps for high vacuum pumping stations in PVD systems for semiconductor manufacturing: PVD (physical vapor deposition) is often used in the semiconductor manufacturing process. It is performed under high vacuum conditions. The vacuum technology might be exposed to harsh chemical conditions during this process.  In most of these cases partly highly aggressive chemicals are involved in the processes. The vacuum technology has to withstand those chemicals and therefore all parts which are in contact with media are made of fluoropolymers.   a) Based on the PFAS definition of the OECD, VACUUBRAND GMBH + CO KG only uses fluoropolymers. For our company, we process about 13.5 tons per year of different fluoropolymers. We use PTFE for hoses, tubings and diaphragms. FKM is used for diaphragms and sealings. ETFE is used for head covers and diaphragm clamping disks while ECTFE is used for valve heads. FFKM, FKM, FFKO and FKM/FEP are used for sealings like O-rings.   As the fluoropolymers are firmly bound in our products and therefore are not released, we cannot state any emission.   Our products are intended for B2B and are not suitable for private use. For products containing fluoropolymers sold to the market, VACUUBRAND fulfills its obligation to highlight the proper disposal of the product in its respective instruction manual.    b) Fluoropolymers are used in vacuum technology for all parts which are in contact with the media due to their many excellent properties. Starting with excellent, nearly universal chemical resistance to a wide range of chemicals (from organic solvents to strong acids and bases) used in chemical/pharmaceutical laboratories. This chemical resistance is irreplaceable in order to maintain the qualitative standards required for the individual processes and the equipment. Apart from that, the extremely low surface energy of fluoropolymers ensures low material adhesion and thus a reduction in chemical attack on the material. More precisely, chemical attack or corrosion on the vacuum technology without fluoropolymers would, on the one hand, lead to contamination of the processes on the customer side and, on the other hand, massively shorten the lifetime of the products. This can be extended even further, as the fluoropolymers used also lead to lower maintenance requirements and extended repair intervals due to their guaranteed durability, which is needed for the very often required continuous operation (up to 24/7). A change in material would therefore lead to a massive environmental impact due to the required regular replacement of the equipment. Another important function provided by fluoropolymers is their high temperature resistance. The internal temperatures in a vacuum pump may reach up to 200°C due to the internal compression and the materials must withstand these temperatures. The polymers are also characterized by a chemical inertness which is why they prevent contamination of the applications and thus a deterioration of the research results or samples or even products. At the moment, there is no adequate replacement for the fluoropolymers used. Due to the high requirements for chemical resistance, mechanical properties and all the characteristics described above, there are currently no alternatives.  In summary, it would make it impossible for our customers to carry out their processes in the actual way, which would besides the academic sector affect a wide range of industries. To give some examples: in many cases vaccine research and production, the manufacture of medicines or development of new medicines rely on chemistry resistant vacuum technology. In the same way the areas of virology and disease control would be faced with a major drawback and could no longer maintain todays standards and pursue future developments.  Also, in other areas from research in chemical industry over analytical instruments to the production of solar cells as well as batteries the ban of fluoropolymers for vacuum pumps would have a major influence.   c) The ban on fluoropolymers will have a strong negative impact on most of our customers, suppliers, and competitors.    d) For our products, we need flexible chemical resistant parts, such as diaphragms and valves. For diaphragms and valves, there is no known alternative to PTFE, FKM, FFKM as a flexible but in a wide range chemical resistant material.   We also have rigid chemical resistant parts, e.g. head covers, valve heads, diaphragm clamping disks, piping, tubing and flanges made of ETFE, ECTFE and PTFE respectively. Furthermore, sealings such as O-rings and rotary shaft seals made of FFKM, FKM or FFKO are used in our products  In future, a set of different material mixtures for different product variants for applications might be possible. As the universal chemical resistance that fluoropolymers bring with them will no longer be available, different products (vacuum technology) for different applications depending on the chemicals used will be needed. However, this will lead to a broader variety of products depending on the different chemicals used which then can lead to potential misuse and risks for users.   Estimated overall costs of substitution with alternatives will be immense and account for a significant amount of our turnover. The costs are distributed among the various development stages. For further details, see f.   The effects of the changed demand situation due to the elimination of PFAS cannot be estimated. It is very likely that the increased demand for non-fluoropolymer alternatives cannot be met in time through increased production build-up and that it therefore becomes problematic with regard to the procurement of non-fluoropolymer alternatives.     e) As the availability of alternative materials with the same properties is not yet given, the effects of the changed demand situation due to the elimination of fluoropolymers cannot be estimated.   For qualification, validation and implementation of possible alternatives which differ in their properties compared to fluoropolymers, please see f.   f) i) Estimated overall costs of substitution with possible alternatives which differ in their properties compared to fluoropolymers will be immense and account for a significant amount of our turnover. The costs are distributed among the various development stages and relate to the following tasks: • Research, endurance and fatigue tests, qualification und validation for material alternatives • Re-engineering and serialization for complete product portfolio • Recertification, cost for notified bodies • Marketing and sales efforts for new variants • Customer & service training  f) ii) For our products we use flexible and rigid chemical resistant parts as well as sealings for which it will need different time to develop possible alternatives:     For flexible chemical resistant parts like diaphragms and valves Total time to develop: 7 years (testing of alternative of materials / components, reliability testing, redesign of product for alternative solution)  For rigid chemical resistant parts e.g. vacuum chamber, piping, tubing, flanges Total time to develop: 5 years (testing of alternative of materials / components, reliability testing, redesign of product for alternative solution)  For sealings: O-rings, rotary shaft seal Total time to develop: 5 years (testing of alternative of materials / components, reliability testing, redesign of product for alternative solution)  f) iii) The way laboratories and research institutions have worked up to now would no longer be possible. The universal chemical resistance that fluoropolymer materials bring with them cannot possibly be replaced on a 1-to-1 basis. This will result in massive disadvantages for customers of vacuum technology. This has a direct impact on a large range of different sectors. The actual impact is not yet foreseeable, but one vacuum pump will no longer be sufficient to cover the various needs. It follows that different pumps are needed for different requirements. In addition, the replacement material used will not have the same durability. Thus, there will be a certain environmental impact due to the increased consumption of materials. Basic research is being carried out in so many different areas that universal reliability of vacuum technology is nearly irreplaceable in order to be able to cover the widest possible range of applications. In the future, customers in this sector will have to sacrifice some of the familiar advantages of universal vacuum technology. For example, a direct impact would be: significantly longer research times and thus a massive disadvantage in international competition and therefore also a weakening of the European economic area. This can also be transferred to other markets like universities and research institutions in the STEM sector, as well as major parts of the chemical, food and pharmaceutical industries.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We (The undersigned Finnish industry and trade organisations) support the goal of the restriction proposal to cease the emissions of PFAS substances to the environment. However we are concerned, that the wide overarching ban of substances and articles with unique properties would affect almost all business sectors in the EU and create uncertainty for future investments and the realisation of green transition in the EU.

The impact assessments, which are still to be finalized in companies, already strongly indicate that the following amendments to the restriction proposal are necessary:

Fluoropolymer products in industrial uses and in analytical devices, in R&D and in personal protective equipment and safety clothing should be excluded from the ban.
Fluoropolymer products are indispensable in almost all sectors and value chains. They are key components in safe and efficient operation of production plants as sealants, gaskets, hoses, pipes, valves, and coatings. They are also needed as lubricants, mould release agents, electrical insulations, fire resistant polymers and in personal protective equipment and safety clothing among others.
Many industrial processes could not be maintained in the EU in the future if safe coatings and sealants were not available. Replacing fluoropolymers with inferior alternatives would weaken environmental protection, energy, and resource efficiency, as well as process safety and occupational safety, even risking personal injury. In many analytical devices the inertness, non-reactivity, temperature durability and tightness of fluoropolymers are essential properties.

Substances covered in the Regulation (EU) No 517/2014 on fluorinated greenhouse gases should be exempted from the PFAS-regulation.
The PFAS restriction proposal is overlapping with F-gas regulation. Fluorinated gases are already strictly controlled in F-gas regulation, and companies have made their investments and planning according to provisions and transition periods in that regulation, also anticipating those in preparation.

Wider derogations are needed to maintain the competitiveness for the EU companies and value chains.
The derogations in paragraph 4 and 5 do not at present cover the precursors, raw materials, auxiliary agents, or intermediates of the final products. These need to be addressed in the derogations as well as R&D, so that EU manufacturing and innovations and development of products in the EU would still be possible.

The list of exemptions should remain open ended. The unique properties of PFAS substances, including their favourable toxicologial profile, make them challenging to replace. It should be possible to extend the list of exemptions or transition period, if no alternatives, which provide overall comparable or increased safety for the application is found and important value chain might be otherwise lost in the EU. In addition, for the sake of overall sustainability it is important that for example expensive equipment, facilities, and buildings can be used up to their anticipated end of life.

Better guidelines and, if necessary, regulations, should be prepared in cooperation with businesses for better control of environmental emissions and waste management. This would facilitate achieving the goal of ceasing the PFAS emissions to the environment.

Yours Sincerely,

Finnish Commerce Federation
Pharma Industry Finland
The Finnish Plastics Industries Federation
The Finnish Forest Industries Federation
Chemical Industry Federation Finland
Association for Finnish Paint Industry
Confederation of Finnish Industries
Finnish Textile and Fashion
Technology Industries of Finland
The Finnish Hardware Association, RASI ry
