General Comments: We (Venn Co., Ltd.) would like to thank you for the great opportunity to submit our comments on the proposed PFAS restrictions.
Venn Co., Ltd. was established in 1950 and has been contributing to the society as a leading valve manufacturer in Japan for approximated 75 years.
Since our foundation, the company has been consistently committed to designing, developing, manufacturing and selling self-regulated control valves, and has been positively addressing energy issues by controlling fluids without electricity or other energy sources.
Venn Co., Ltd. supports the statements made by FCJ on the issues of proposed restristion,as per attached in section IV.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: We have surveyed the industrial fields where the valves have been applied with fluoropolymers, fluororubber, fluorine-based grease and fluorine-based gaskets  Information on fields and applications is hereby provided. Our valves have been very widely used for fluid control purposes in the facilities such as chemical plant equipment, water supply and drainage equipment, water treatment equipment, gas supply equipment, boiler equipment, and the plant production equipment in various fields, air-conditioning and heating equipment, etc.  Upon our comprehension of Annex XV, it is difficult for us to give comment due to the fact no description has been accordingly given in the sectors listed in the restriction proposal.  For the valves used for fluid purposes in these industrial sectors and other equipment are requested to be fully described in the usage column of ANNEX XV.　　 　　　Chemical plant equipment includes chemical industry, chemical plant, plastics manufacturing, elastomer manufacturing, printing inks, photosensitive materials and fine chemical manufacturing. 　　　Water supply and drainage includes water supply equipment, buildings and residential applications. Water treatment includes drinking water treatment, water treatment, ultrapure water production, medical RO water production, hydrogen functional water production, ozone water production, carbonated water production, waste water treatment and chemical dilution and neutralization. 　　　The gas supply equipment sector includes fuel gas, nitrogen for analysis, hydrogen equipment for industrial plants, high-purity gas for semiconductor production, etching gas for glass production, raw material gas for agricultural production and the common air used for general purposes in the industrial plants, etc. Boiler equipment includes piping systems for steam-related supply, discharge and distribution, etc. 　　　Among plant production facilities in various industries, medical product manufacture also includes vaccine production, production of physiological saline solutions, nutriceuticals and functional beverages, and includes the transportation of gases, liquids and powders. Furthermore, it also involves the flow of H2O2 gas for sterilization. 　　　Paper mills have pipelines for bleaching agents, PH regulators, whitening agents and steam. 　　　In food factories, there are valves for sterilization, heating, container sterilization and equipment cleaning, as well as pipelines for water, hot water and steam for heating and cooling. 　　　In precision machinery manufacturing, there are ozone gas generators, plating solution production and analysis equipment, concentration equipment, fully automatic viscosity measuring equipment and high refractive index liquid supply equipment, etc. 　    As for the leisure equipment, valves are used to control hydraulic and pneumatic equipment and recreational water. Energy equipment also involve the fields that contribute to GHG reduction, such as the production of synthetic fuels from CO2, fuel cell production, hydrogen supply equipment, solar panel production and lithium-ion battery production, etc. 　    In terms of the medical equipment, control valves for steam usage are applied for temperature control of sterilizers. 　    In the semiconductor manufacturing sector, valves are divided into two categories: valves for chemicals and valves for gases. Valves for chemicals are used in cleaning process equipment, polishing equipment, wet etching equipment, immersion exposure equipment, fixture cleaning equipment, liquid quality analysis equipment and coater equipment, etc. Valves for gases are used in etching equipment, expanded process equipment and wafer inspection equipment, etc. Also, they are used as flow regulators. Fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers are used in these valves, as well as fluorogreases and fluorine-based gaskets where necessary. Thus, fluoroelastomers have been used throughout diverse fields and applications, and such applications are essential and important.　  The parts, materials and requirements for fluoroethlastomer used in valves are as the following. ・Main valve seat of solenoid valve: PTFE 　　Requirements: sealing performance on saturated steam is required. ・Main valve piston ring of solenoid valves: PTFE 　　Requirements: good sliding performance of the piston on saturated steam.  ・Main valve guide of solenoid valves: PTFE 　　Requirements: good sliding performance, corrosion resistance and durability of the main valve on saturated steam. ・Sealing gasket of solenoid valve body and cover: PTFE 　　Requirements: good sealing performance, corrosion resistance and durability on saturated steam. ・Main valve diaphragm of solenoid valve: Fluorine rubber. Requirements: Sealability, corrosion resistance and durability on high temperature water (90-100°C). ・Internal parts of pressure reducing valves and the piston sliding parts: PTFE ring. 　　Requirements: Effective sliding performance and durability of piston on saturated steam. ・Sealing gasket with body, cover, and lower cover of each valve: 　　　Requirements: sealing performance at high temperature, corrosion resistance, and durability. ・The gland seal of cylinder valves: PTFE 　  Requirements: Good sliding performance and durability against the temperature of saturated steam ・Diaphragms of pressure reducing valves: FKM 　　Requirements: Long-term (8 years) corrosion resistance and durability in hot fluid water. ・Main valve seat of pressure reducing valve: PTFE/FKM 　　　Requirements: sealing performance on various gaseous fluids, sealing performance on high temperature water, and corrosion resistance. ・Main valve seat of safety relief valve: FKM 　　　Requirements: sealability on various gaseous fluids, sealability on high temperature water, and corrosion resistance. ・Diaphragms of safety relief valves: FKM Requirements: Long-termed (8 years) corrosion resistance and durability on hot water with high fluid temperature. ・Seats of ball valves: PTFE 　　Requirements: corrosion resistance, good sliding performance and durability on hot fluids.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The PFAS used in the valves can easily be seperated and recycled at the end of the service life of a valve service.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Since the PFAS can be easily seperated and recycled, there will be no emiissions at the end of life phase

5. Proposed derogations: The fluoropolymers we use do not release to the atmosphere,volatilize or expose employees, or runoff to wastewater, and the risk of PFAS emissions from fluoropolymers is low. Therefore, we believe that fluoropolymers should not be included in the scope of the proposed PFAS limit.

6. Missing uses: Fluoropolymers, fluoro-rubbers, fluoro-greases, and fluoro-gaskets are used in 54% of the products we manufacture and sell. No other materials are currently available for replacing the multifunctional properties of fluoropolymers, fluoroethlamers and fluorogreases, which are widely used in valves. As for the mass-produced products, some manufacturers (such as FUJIKURA COMPOSITES Inc.) have stated that they are unable to establish alternatives that satisfy customers’ requirements. Loss of functionality of the sealing rings of valves may cause significant economic consequences, such as shortened operating life of the infrastructure, increased frequency and cost of maintenance, increased suspension time of operation, reduced product performance and economic losses due to the inability to supply products required by the customers.,etc. The following are some of the most important economic consequences of the use of valves. Valves in use nowadays are designed to last longer through maintenance. If the fluoropolymers, fluoroethlamers and fluorogreases required for valve maintenance were to become subject to regulation, it would definitely cause social and economic inconvenience and loss. It is easy to imagine that valves that cannot be maintained will have to be disposed of, which will consequently have a significant impact on the global environment and resources. Therefore, we would like to request that valves should be listed into the “exemptions without time limit “.

Combined Comments: General Comments: We admire the EU's continuous efforts in promoting environmental protection legislation, and we have sincerely complied with the requirements of EU chemical regulations, such as Regulation (EC) No 1907/2006 (REACH). PFASs are a group of thousands of substances primarily manufactured by humans, applied in many fields in Europe. These applications include textile industry applications, (food) packaging, lubricants, refrigerants, electronics industry, construction, and many more fields. These substances are used as their own state (non aggregated or aggregated), as components of mixtures, and as complex (articles) products for consumption, specialized, and industrial purposes. What are the specific risks mentioned in the report, what are the environmental risks, and what are the risks to human health? Does each substance have the same risk? The PFASs mentioned in the bill do not have a specific list indicating which risks are, and we believe it is not serious. Do you have any testing reports on the risks of PFASs to the environment and human health? Have you conducted a randomized double blind controlled trial? What PFASs substances pose specific risks to which group of people? 3. Persistence: The main concern for all PFASs and/or their degradation products within the scope proposed in this restriction is the very high persistence, which greatly exceeds the very persistent standard (vP, very persistent) specified in Annex XIII of the REACH regulation. PFASs and their degradation products may persist in the environment, longer than any other human made chemicals. Further supportive concerns are their bioaccumulation, mobility, long range transport potential, plant accumulation in plants, global warming potential, and ecological toxicological effects. PFASs enter the environment through emissions during production, use, and waste stages. What is the relationship between persistence and risk? Is there always a risk when there is persistence? Is worry a sufficient reason for restriction? Are these substances all possessing these negative characteristics? Is the persistence of all substances the same? Persistence alone is not sufficient to unify PFAS into a group and evaluate its risks to human health. Abstract：An expert panel was convened to provide insight and guidance on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) grouping for the purposes of protecting human health from drinking water exposures, and how risks to PFAS mixtures should be assessed. These questions were addressed through multiple rounds of blind, independent responses to charge questions, and review and comments on co-panelists responses. The experts agreed that the lack of consistent interpretations of human health risk for well-studied PFAS and the lack of information for the vast majority of PFAS present significant challenges for any mixtures risk assessment approach. Most experts agreed that “all PFAS” should not be grouped together, persistence alone is not sufficient for grouping PFAS for the purposes of assessing human health risk, and that the definition of appropriate subgroups can only be defined on a case-by-case manner. Most panelists agreed that it is inappropriate to assume equal toxicity/potency across the diverse class of PFAS. A tiered approach combining multiple lines of evidence was presented as a possible viable means for addressing PFAS that lack analytical and/or toxicological studies. Most PFAS risk assessments will need to employ assumptions that are more likely to overestimate risk than to underestimate risk, given the choice of assumptions regarding dose-response model, uncertainty factors, and exposure information. Part 5 Conclusion：Most of the applied assumptions (e.g., dose-additivity, equal potency) are more likely to overestimate risk than to underestimate risk (i.e., will err on the side of caution). Many experts agree that 'all PFAS' should not be classified together, and durability alone cannot be sufficient to classify PFAS into a group for evaluating human health purposes. Defining appropriate subgroups can only be done on a case by case basis. Many expert group members agree that it is inappropriate to assume that differentiated PFAS group substances have the same toxicity/virulence. Most of the assumptions used now have the problem of overestimating risks (erring on the side of being too cautious). 4.Low temperature mineralization problem： Original text: When these substances and their degradation products continue to be released into the environment, the environmental concentration will increase, as PFASs within the scope of this limitation proposal do not undergo mineralization under natural conditions. Once present in the environment, removing PFAS from surface water, groundwater, soil, sediment, and biota as much as possible is technically extremely difficult and costly. Environmental testing of PFASs indicates their widespread presence in the environment, including organisms and drinking water sources and food crops, as well as remote and primitive areas, which inevitably and irreversibly exposes contemporary and future generations. Human biological monitoring shows that PFASs are widely present in the human body, with high exposure communities showing the highest levels. Due to persistence and continuous emissions, as the environmental concentration of PFASs continues to increase, human exposure and the environment of these substances will inevitably lead to negative effects. Moreover, exposure to PFASs has high potential for intergenerational effects. Some scientists say that the geographical limitations of PFASs have been exceeded, and human biological monitoring studies have shown that mixed exposure to PFASs caused by partial leaks from different sources (such as food, drinking water, PFAS-containing products, dust, air) in the general population may already pose health risks. Low temperature mineralization can degrade perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids, which can be extended to degrade other perfluorinated and polyfluoroalkyl substances. The degradation rate is fast, and under mild conditions, defluorination will fundamentally solve the environmental problems of fluorinated substances. The thermal decomposition mechanism of perfluoroalkyl ether carboxylic acid and short chain perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acid demonstrates the effectiveness of pyrolysis degradation of PFAS.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We agree with the initiative to protect environment and health of humans and animals by a regulation of selected chemicals with high toxicity potential especially if combined with persistence and mobility. Objective of this contribution to the PFAS consultation is not to defend PFAS in general but to support the selection process regarding potential exemptions, addressing especially fluoropolymers.
It is very risky and expensive for the European Economy to announce a definitive ban of PFAS in general, with more than 10.000 substances, including the material group of 38 fluoropolymers. There are no real alternatives for a huge variety of applications in sight. Furthermore, already 50% of the fluoropolymers are produced without fluorinated processing aids (potential to be increased in 2024). The reputation of fluoropolymers (although considered products of low concern according OECD criteria) is already strongly negatively affected due to the undifferentiated announcement of a general PFAS ban and media. This affects sales, investments, material supply chain, fluctuation of employees, difficulties to hire new staff, etc. so that companies, that have been successful and healthy for decades, would be driven into bankruptcy in a short time. Sound investment decisions in product developments with fluoropolymers are impossible based on the current situation which seems to last for several more years. The proposed derogations are in general too short because of the lifetime of product generations:
• Automotive: 6 – 9+ years, Railway: 15 – 30+ years
• Medical: 10 – 15+ years
• Production Technologies including Mechanical Engineering: 10 – 20+ years

Additionally, new product introduction into the market takes between 2 and 8 years after necessary material choice decision depending on validation and certification requirements in the different sectors. E. g. in medical sector certification and clinical studies can take 5 - 8 years until successful new product introduction into the market.

Missing Uses + Request for Exemption
Several thousand companies and several 10.000 products in (new) mobility, (new) energy, health, food & pharma directly affected by proposed ban of fluoropolymers.

50 % share of products for production equipment enabling efficient processes in almost all industrial sectors with many more indirectly affected companies. Long term availability of spare parts is key.


Several million jobs under threat.

50 % of fluoropolymers (suspension S-PTFE) produced without fluorinated processing aids (surfactants)

Important and urgent request for exemption of responsibly manufactured fluoropolymers from “universal” PFAS ban because of valuable contributions regarding safety, sustainability, efficiency, and innovation in general.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We appreciate the opportunity to provide comments on an Annex XV Report that proposes a restriction on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) under REACH. The proposed EU restriction on PFAS raises legal concerns as it contradicts the principle of proportionality in REACH. Treating all PFASs as one group and imposing a general ban without considering specific risks is not appropriate. The broad restriction could disrupt critical value chains for products like batteries, semiconductors, electric vehicles, and renewable energy, potentially hindering climate neutrality goals. Regulating over 10,000 substances without a scientific basis and disregarding socio-economic consequences is problematic. Not all PFAS classes share the same hazards, so a risk-based approach is necessary. Fluoroelastomers and fluoropolymers are materials of low concern, and they should be excluded from the dossier.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Transportation, Industrial process/Process industry, Manufacturing

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Fluororubber gets irreversibly crosslinked and processed into rubber articles. These Fluoro-rubber components find application in various sectors, including transportation. These parts undergo meticulous end-of-life procedures during disassembly, where strict control measures are implemented. These measures ensure that the end-of-life parts are either recycled or subjected to incineration, in adherence to established protocols e.g., Federal Emission Control Act in Germany. In a specialized facility dedicated to waste disposal through incineration, the waste is treated at high-temperature (850°C – 1100°C). Recent scientific studies  clearly demonstrate that the incineration of Fluoroelastomers at their end of life in waste-to-energy recovery plants does not result in any detectable levels of PFAS emissions.

8. Other identified uses: Transportation:   The utilization of alternatives mentioned in table E.110 of Annex E like NBR, ACM etc may have detrimental effects on the safety of both vehicles and passengers. Manufacturing:  Our company acknowledges the significance of responsible manufacturing practices, even though our current manufacturing operations are not located in the EU. We have taken measures to use polymerization aids only when necessary and have implemented a comprehensive measure to prevent any emissions during the manufacturing process which includes targeted and non-targeted residue analysis, as well as an efficient waste management system. However, due to the extensive range of fluor elastomers in our portfolio, it is not feasible to completely switch to 100% non-fluorinated options within the designated timeframe for certain product groups.  We request the authorities to recognize the technical complexities and limitations associated with finding suitable non-fluorinated alternatives for these specific products. The development and validation of alternative materials require meticulous research, rigorous testing, and thorough evaluation to ensure they meet the stringent performance requirements and standards demanded by our customers.  The dossier mentions that strong evidence would be available if alternatives for non-polymeric PFASs as polymerization aids in FKM production exist. However, it is not yet clear about the performance of these "new" materials produced without PFAS aids and the environmental impact of substitution aids. Given the typical time needed for rigorous testing and evaluation in various industries such as automotive and aviation, it would be premature to assume that the alternatives without PFAS would perform identically. Rushing the substitution process without proper testing and data could potentially endanger people's lives, such as the use of fluor elastomers in sealing applications for cars or aviation. Therefore, we request the authorities reconsider the time frame allocated for the switch to a 100% flurosurfactant-free polymerization aid.  Furthermore, it is worth noting that fluoroelastomers, due to their indispensable nature, are not only prevalent in existing passenger car models but also in emerging vehicle and fuel technologies. Please find more information in the confidential attachment.  Process industry: Process industries like the chemical industry and F&B include multiple process steps and uses Fluoroelastomers containing articles are used. These fluoroelastomers like FKM, and FFKM has unique properties like chemical resistance, temperature stability, etc.  The current restriction proposal would jeopardize the functioning of the European process industries like chemical, food & beverage. Considering the evidence provided, we ask for a time-unlimited derogation for the use of fluoroelastomers materials in the process industries. Please find more information in the confidential attachment.

Content: Information on alternatives Information on benefits Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We appreciate the opportunity to provide scientific and technical information on the use of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in our air filtration products. Our company uses PTFE membrane, a type of PFAS, to enhance the filtration performance of our air filter media products, which play a critical role in ensuring the air quality and safety of various industrial and commercial settings.

Furthermore, in addition to the use of PTFE membrane, we have integrated treatments based on C-6 fluoroalkyl chemistry to further optimize the performance of our filter media. The integration of such treatments enhances the hydrophobic and oleophobic properties of the filter, ensuring improved resistance against water and oil-based aerosols. This hydrophobic/oleophobic treatment is indispensable in various air filtration applications, providing an additional layer of protection against a wider array of contaminants, thereby ensuring enhanced air quality and safety.

We want to emphasize that there is currently no alternative to PTFE membrane in the market that can match its performance and durability in air filtration applications. As such, it is crucial that a long-term derogation is granted to ensure the continued availability of PTFE membrane in our products.

The use of PTFE membrane in air filtration has proven to be effective in removing harmful particulates and contaminants from the air, including airborne viruses, bacteria, dust, and pollen. Its unique physical and chemical properties, such as high porosity, high surface area, and excellent chemical resistance, make it a reliable and durable material for air filter media.

While we acknowledge that PFAS have been identified as a class of substances of emerging concern, it is important to note that PTFE membrane, as a subclass of PFAS, exhibits a different set of physicochemical properties and environmental behaviors compared to other PFAS, such as perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS), which have been subject to regulatory scrutiny and restrictions.

PTFE membrane is a stable and non-reactive material that does not degrade under normal conditions and does not release PFOA or PFOS into the environment. Moreover, the manufacturing and disposal of PTFE membrane have been shown to have minimal environmental impacts compared to other PFAS-containing products, such as firefighting foams and surface coatings.

In conclusion, we believe that PTFE membrane plays an essential and irreplaceable role in air filtration and that a long-term derogation is necessary to ensure its continued availability. We welcome further dialogue and collaboration with ECHA and other stakeholders to ensure the safe and sustainable use of PFAS in our products and the environment.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Technical textiles - Textiles for the use in filtration and separation media used in high performance air and liquid applications in industrial or professional settings that require a combination of water- and oil repellence.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We appreciate the possibility to be part of public consultation to the PFAS restriction proposal. We would like to show that fluoropolymers should be completely exempted from this regulation and that the derogation time is too short, especially for medical applications. The proposed ban is very broad, covering many PFAS substances, but only 38 of them are fluoropolymers. However, banning these 38 substances will have a significant impact on Europe.
At Optinova, we hold the wellbeing and safety of our employees, customers, and communities in the highest regard. Our vision is “better life quality wherever we operate”. We are fully committed to conducting our business in strict adherence to our sustainability policies and local regulations. Based on our long experience of polymer processing, we have developed a deep understanding of various types of polymers, including high molecular weight fluoropolymers. These materials have distinctive characteristics in that, under normal conditions, they do not disperse in the environment and do not dissolve into components that migrate, accumulate or interact. This sets them apart from harmful and environmentally dispersive non-polymeric PFAS, where legislation and restrictions already apply.
Nowadays, fluoropolymers are extensively utilized in critical applications that are integral to our everyday life, including medical catheters and other medical devices, high-performance sensors, and various electronic equipment. We are exploring opportunities to expand our raw material portfolio, although viable alternatives for high molecular weight fluoropolymers are currently lacking.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Fluoropolymers are more costly to produce and process than other engineering polymers and therefore are often used where other substances cannot deliver the required performance. They are also prevalent where a small amount of fluoropolymer can be used while giving the same performance as a greater amount of a non-fluorinated chemical. Fluoropolymers operate over wide temperature ranges and in situations where extremely stable, non-reactive substances are required. The carbon-fluor bonds lead to very stable substances, a feature that also makes the terminal transformation products very persistent in the environment. Within Optinova fluoropolymers are used in the production of plastic tubing for customers producing the following applications: medical devices (all 3 classes) such as: intravenous catheters, ureteral access delivery and retrieval devices, endoscopic surgical devices, delivering fluid, medication, and pain treatment and industrial applications such as: transportation, food/beverage processing, sustainable energy solutions, semiconductors, electronics, cables, and chemical processing.  We work with customer specifications, meaning that our tubing solutions must be compliant with regulations and standards per application (for example: biocompatibility testing, barrier testing, FDA, and REACH registrations).

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Fluoropolymers lifecycle: We can provide indicative feedback about emissions on the usage phase of fluoropolymer raw material. We do not manufacture fluoropolymers but procure them from approved sources. Nor do we consider the end-of-life phase, we do however, seek to educate our customers on how to dispose of our tubing solutions. Processing phase: we convert fluoropolymers in our factories with approved technologies under controlled circumstances. We carry out inspections on incoming materials, check waste levels, production water quality, air quality, and soil quality around all factories.  For some fluoropolymers, we can recycle our production waste a few times, while maintaining the quality of industrial tubing produced. We also sell fluoropolymer waste to certified organisations for recycling purposes. Due to the outstanding performance of fluoropolymers in terms of biocompatibility and long-term stability with excellent long-term data (we can retest retained tubing samples) we have not observed any leachable or emissions during storage phase. (See attached documents, confidential).

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Within Optinova we reduce fluoropolymer waste as far as reasonably practicable and dispose of the remainder either through sales to certified organisations or through approved waste streams. There is a literature about recycling of fluoropolymers and some of the literature procedures are implemented, for example: when the iron is melted by the arc heat of an electric furnace during processing, the fluorinated resin is incinerated at the same time. Residue is recycled into roadbed material. Fluorine dust is recovered as gas and used for steelmaking materials. This greatly reduces the energy required to make steel. Other studies suggest that municipal waste incineration is an acceptable form of waste treatment, as no additional PFAS over baseline was detected after burning of PTFE. Given that the incineration is made at adequate temperatures. (See attached documents).

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Optinova’s fluoropolymer waste amounts to less than 15 % tonnes of material used per year (more than 75 % of it is for recycling) and we are actively seeking ways to reduce this further. To produce medical tubing, we must use virgin, non-recycled, raw materials.

5. Proposed derogations: We would like to see a permanent derogation of fluoropolymer materials for advanced applications as we believe this would avoid significant, negative impacts on European society.  Commercialization of fluoropolymers took place more than 70 years ago but satisfactory alternatives which possess all critical properties have still not been found. The possibility that acceptable new materials will be discovered and commercialised within the proposed derogation period is extremely unlikely.   Optinova uses following quantities of fluoropolymers per year (80 % of all materials Optinova uses):  for industrial applications (PTFE, FEP, PVDF, PFA, ETFE, EFEP): 70 %   for medical applications (FEP, PTFE): 30 % Total amount of waste from those industries is less than 1 % (disposal waste)

6. Missing uses: We believe that the strongest alternative candidates to fluoropolymers (FP) are silicone-based materials. These materials contain an Si-O bond which is the second strongest bond in chemistry, and it may be that in a few years these will also be labelled ‘forever chemicals’. In addition, PFAS substances are added to silicon-based materials to improve their properties or to be produced. Another potential alternative for FP substances is PEEK polymer. However, the biggest challenge with this material is that PEEK is not flexible meaning that fluoropolymers are often added, to virgin PEEK material to improve this property.  A further factor to consider with alternative raw materials is that we do not have long-term information on their impacts on the environment or human health. Fluoropolymers have some 70 years of data to draw upon in these matters, and to support claims of both positive and negative impacts on humans and the environment.  Examples of applications where FP are critical:    FP components for human implants: long term stability and excellent biocompatibility combined with flexibility and low friction - unique.  FP components for electronics (hydrogen electrolyser, semiconductor manufacturing): the success of the EU green deal and digital transformation is threatened due to a lack of suitable alternatives to fluoropolymers.  FP components for cables, for high frequency applications.  FP components for sealing devices: no other material can guarantee long term low emissions. All alternative materials will have shorter lifetime and higher leakage due to lower chemical and thermal resistance.   Our company have 700 employees and a turnover for 2022 of 50 million euro and would be significantly affected by the proposed regulation. We do not consider fluoropolymers to be in the same group as other PFAS, since they are safe and are polymers of low concern according to Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and scientific evidence. Fluoropolymers are compliant with existing restrictions.  Restrictions in the usage phase of FP are not relevant as FP are safe. In the manufacturing phase, the use of fluoro surfactants could be considered, and more effort should also be put into sustainable production. For the end-of-life phase a stricter way of decomposing should be deemed.  (See attached documents).

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: The proposed restrictions to prohibit fluoropolymers are out of REACH scope (persistence is not an indication of harm) and technically insecure because no other product on the market can perform the same functions.  Fluoropolymers are considered topologically safe for medical applications; therefore, they should not be considered harmful to human health.

8. Other identified uses: As a company, we work according to customer specifications. Our customers choose the materials for their device components. Fluoropolymers are not a cost-effective alternative, so the choice of these materials is based on performance and safety (for example: sterilization, chemical resistance, service temperature).

10. Analytical methods: According to our knowledge there is no practical measuring equipment and standards to robustly measure the current REACH restricted substances in reference to all PFAS emissions.

Org. name: Changshu 3F Zhenfu New Materials Co., Ltd
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a Chinese company that produces fluorine-containing fine chemicals VDF, TFA and fluoropolymers PTFE, FEP, FKM, PFA etc., and have been complying with various domestic regulations in China. The proposal to restrict PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances), compiled by the authorities of Denmark, Germany, Finland, Norway, and Sweden, was submitted to ECHA and aims to reduce the release of PFAS in the environment and make products and processes safer. The main reason for the restriction is that PFAS is extremely persistent in the environment and would have negative effects on human health and environment if unrestricted. We really appreciate the purpose of this proposal. However, we believe that the proposed restriction covers too broad a range of PFAS, which define PFAS as any fluorinated chemical (except for a few structures) that contains at least one fully fluorinated methyl (CF3-) or methylene (-CF2-) carbon atom (without any H/Cl/Br/I). The proposed PFASs are a group of thousands of mostly human-made substances that are used in many areas in EU. The proposal should specify the specific numbers involved, the specific molecular structure, and which ones are excluded.
In the context of this restriction proposal, the main issue with the safety of PFAS and/or their degradation products is the very high persistence of PFAS and/or their degradation products, which significantly exceeds the very durable standard (vP) set out in Annex XIII of the REACH regulation. FPASs and their degradation products are likely to persist in the environment longer than any other human-made chemical. Further concerns are their bioaccumulation, migration, long-range migration, plant accumulation, global warming potential, (ecological) toxicological effects. PFASs can enter the environment through emissions during production, use and waste. What is the risk mentioned in the report, is it that every PFAS substance has such a risk, and is the risk equivalent? If they are different, they should be treated differently, not one size fits all. For example, the environmental and toxicological characteristics of fluoropolymers are significantly different from most other PFAS, thus it is unscientific to treat them uniformly now.
According to the semiconductor industry’s prediction, the key PFAS derivatives for chip manufacturing, PFA fluoropolymers, are absolutely critical to semiconductor manufacturing. Denise Dignam, head of high-performance materials at Chemours, said, “If we didn’t have these, there would be a very serious mess around the world, and I can’t imagine how you would do these (semiconductor) manufacturing processes without these materials.” Thus, once the EU restriction is implemented, it will greatly affect the development of the semiconductor industry. Currently, the alternatives to PFAS mainly include two categories: one is short-chain PFAS, including short-chain perfluoroalkyl sulfonate (PFBS), short-chain perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFHxS), etc., These chemicals have less bioaccumulation and toxicity than long PFAS; The other category is non-PFAS alternatives such as bio-based polymers, alkyl silanes, alumina, etc., which do not contain PFAS elements and therefore have lower environmental and health risks. However, now the environmental and health effects of these alternatives require further research and evaluation. Meanwhile, the performance and cost of these alternatives need to be further improved and optimized to better meet market demand and environment and health requirements, which need to be repeatedly verified by the market and environmental protection. There may not be a perfect solution in 12 years, so it is necessary to recommend a longer time to facilitate implementation according to different situations, purposes and uses.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a company primarily engaged in the manufacturing of sliding bearings and functional components used in automobiles. We support the intention of your esteemed organization to limit the environmental release of PFAS in order to minimize impacts on people and the environment. We respect these efforts to reduce future risks.

In this regard, with a focus on economic viability, resource efficiency, and environmental preservation, we propose the following suggestions in response to the regulatory measures:

■ Exemption for PTFE
Various types of bearings with PTFE as their main component contribute to reducing CO2 emissions through excellent friction reduction effects in non-lubricated environments. The high stability of PTFE also contributes to long-term stable performance, leading to enhanced safety, reduced maintenance frequency, and waste reduction.
While we are exploring alternatives for PTFE, it currently remains irreplaceable as the main component in bearing materials, given its exceptional performance. Even if multiple alternatives were found, it is currently unclear whether any substitute material could meet all the diverse performance requirements for critical safety components like bearings. There is also a possibility that no suitable substitute material may be found even after continued exploration. Therefore, we request an exemption from PTFE regulations.

■ Exemption for the Use of Surfactants in Bearing Manufacturing
Surfactants used in the manufacturing of resin-coated bearings enhance the wetting properties of coating materials, enabling the application of smooth surface conditions on sliding surfaces during bearing assembly. Resin-coated bearings contribute significantly to friction reduction and CO2 emission reduction.
In the case of resin-coated bearings containing PTFE, the uniform dispersion of PTFE within the coating ensures consistent long-term sliding performance across all surfaces of the bearing. PTFE-containing resin-coated bearings demonstrate excellent friction reduction effects even in non-lubricated environments, contributing to CO2 emission reduction.
While we are committed to seeking alternatives for surfactants in line with the principle of reducing environmental impact, reproducing the pre-substitution performance of bearings remains a challenge. Ensuring all the diverse performance criteria for critical safety components like bearings are met has proven difficult due to the varying requirements of different management items.
We will continue efforts to explore alternatives for surfactants, but at this juncture, we request an exemption from the use of surfactants in bearing manufacturing that may affect appropriate functions related to vehicle safety, impacting drivers, passengers, or product safety.

■ Exemption for the Use of Defoaming Agents in Bearing Manufacturing
Defoaming agents used in bearing manufacturing contribute to suppressing the generation of defective products, such as peeling or poor appearance, leading to waste reduction. We understand the concept of reducing environmental impact and are actively pursuing alternatives for defoaming agents. However, while exploring alternatives for various defoaming agents, reproducing pre-substitution product quality remains a challenge.
While ensuring all the diverse performance criteria for critical safety components like bearings are met, stabilizing product quality remains necessary. However, we are facing difficulties meeting the requirements of various management items through substitution.
We will continue efforts to explore alternatives for defoaming agents, but at this juncture, we request an exemption from the use of defoaming agents in bearing manufacturing that may affect appropriate functions related to vehicle safety, impacting drivers, passengers, or product safety.

■ Exemption for Various Fluororesin Materials Used in Functional Components
Various fluororesins are used in functional components assembled in automobiles to ensure product functions, including sealing, heat resistance, flexibility, durability, and corrosion resistance. Currently, it is challenging to find resin materials with comparable capabilities to substitute for fluororesins, making substitution highly difficult.
Even if substitute materials were found, increased maintenance frequency and increased waste of discarded resin materials after maintenance could result in escalated safety, economic, and environmental concerns.
To mitigate these potential new issues, we request an exemption for various fluororesins used in functional components to secure product quality and safety. We support the declaration from Reference Nos. 3969, 3970, 3971, 3972, 3973, 4348, 4351, 5984.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a downstream user of fluorinated gases (“F-Gases”), specifically R-1336mzz(Z) and R-1233zd thermal management fluids that would be subject to the proposed restrictions. We therefore wish to provide evidence of the use of these substances.
Our two-phase direct on chip liquid cooling solution has substantial sustainability benefits – power reduction, optimized server operation, improved general Power Usage Efficiency and efficient heat reuse option leading to a reduction in carbon footprint.
The thermal management fluids we use have a very low global warming potential and zero ozone depletion potential, the closed-loop design keeps the refrigerant fully contained and uncontaminated and will properly be recycled at end of life by the manufacturers.
There are no alternatives currently or in sight, hence our application should be unlimitedly derogated, to allow for a more safe and sustainable data-center operation.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: F -Gases combine unique attributes, they are safe in terms of toxicological and physical properties, and they contribute to highly energy efficient Cooling.  We are a downstream user of fluorinated gases (“F-Gases”), specifically R-1336mzz(Z) and R-1233zd thermal management fluids that would be subject to the proposed restrictions. We therefore wish to provide evidence of the use of these substances. Our system is a direct-on-chip, waterless, dielectric liquid cooling solution to the mainstream with zero disruption to the data center.  One of the unique advantages of our dielectric direct-on-chip liquid cooling solution is its improved efficiency of removing heat away from the processors. As workloads cause the processors to heat, the dielectric liquid absorbs the heat causing the liquid to boil and vaporize. The state change from a liquid to a gas is a highly efficient mechanism to remove the heat, which is then expelled outside of the data center or used via heat re-use applications. We use the R-1336mzz(Z) and R-1233zd thermal management fluids. These thermal management fluids have a very low global warming potential and zero ozone depletion potential, making them an ideal choice for our closed-loop liquid cooling. Our comment applies to the sector applications of fluorinated gases, sub-uses air conditioning and heat pumps, specifically for datacenter direct on chip liquid cooling. Our system is functioning as HVAC for a single server.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The in-use and end-of-life emissions of F-Gases are regulated under a variety of EU legislation. For example, the EU F-Gas regulation (517/2014, currently under review) requires regular leak inspections and recovery at end-of-life. During the installation process of our cooling systems, the refrigerator is being pumped to a sealed system. During the use phase –our closed-loop design keeps the refrigerant fully contained and uncontaminated, ensuring no leakage occurs and maximizing utilization of the refrigerant’s virtually indefinite service life. End-of-life - when our system is finally upgraded or decommissioned, the refrigerant is uninstalled for reuse in a new system or properly recycled by the liquid manufacturers.

6. Missing uses: Following is information regarding the key functionalities and use of PFAS F-gases – specifically R-1336mzz(Z) and R-1233zd - for direct on chip liquid cooling of data-centers: According to statica (https://www.statista.com/statistics/878621/european-data-centers-by-country/) in 2022, there were 2,876 data centers in Europe.  We have developed a pool-boiling evaporator device, which efficiently moves large amounts of heat off the chip, evenly above all surface of the chip and provides on-demand responses. By using a self-regulated mechanism (patented) the system precisely supplies the amount of refrigerant needed to cool the heat generated by each component.  As mentioned above, R-1336mzz(Z) and R-1233zd thermal management fluids are being used in our two-phase direct on chip liquid cooling solution for data-centers.  The two-phase direct on chip liquid cooling solution allows for efficient cooling (free cooling) at any ambient temperature, efficient use of energy and space even under very high TDP’s, while posing no risk for the server. Furthermore, efficient heat reuse can be implemented with higher hot water temperature under any compute load.  By using a two-phase direct liquid cooling system, data-centers can use only about a quarter of the number of racks needed to provide the same power capacity as an air based cooling data-center. By using the said system, the data-center can achieve 75% saving of space, construction cost and annual renting cost, 25% saving in energy consumption and a reduction of the annual GHG emissions as well as decreasing heat waste by 100% when implementing waste heat reuse option.  Please see attached as PDF document a comparison table, demonstrating the saving that can be achieved for a 100MW data center when using a two-phase direct on chip liquid cooling solution instead of air-cooling solution.  Substitutions are not technically or economically feasible:  Water is not a viable liquid for two-phase direct on chip cooling since it has a relatively high T-sat (boiling point) of 100 °C at 1 atm (atmosphere). Most current CPUs have a T-case maximum limit below 100 °C. To achieve phase change from liquid water to vapor, the CPU will have to run excessively beyond its temperature limit, which will cause the CPU to throttle down and run at degraded clock speeds, shut down altogether, or suffer thermal damage. Hence water cannot be used for a two-phase direct liquid cooling. Furthermore, most water-based liquid cooling solutions must also include an ethylene or propylene glycol mixture to prevent the water from freezing and reduce corrosion.  Glycol-water mixtures potentially elevate the boiling point even higher, up to 129 °C, temperatures too hot for CPUs to approach.   Natural refrigerants such as ammonia, carbon dioxide, propane does not necessarily have a lower GWPs than certain F-gases, and in many cases, are far more energy intensive than F-gases. They are subject to corrosion, toxicity, high pressures, flammability, or in some cases lower operating efficiencies. As the entire system is located inside the data-centers, hydrocarbons, ammonia or CO2 cannot be used as alternatives, due to national safety standards and building codes for data-centers. Moreover, Ammonia and CO2 boiling points are quite below zero, which will require adding compressor to produce the needed high pressure for the two-phase direct on chip liquid cooling solution. Such an addition will increase the energy level needed, making the solution inefficient compared with the current solution.   As a result, the use of two-phase direct on chip liquid cooling solution for data-centers, should be considered under RO2- section (v) Proposed derogation: refrigerants in HVACR-equipment in buildings where national safety standards and building codes prohibit the use of alternatives – with time-unlimited derogation.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a European supplier of sealing elements, and our comments below primarily relate to fluoropolymers used in the compound of sealing elements.

With ECHAs proposed restriction on “Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)”, a broad group containing thousands of substances with vastly different properties will be effectively banned from the European market. The origin of this proposal is a concern about the identified human and environmental risks associated with several small molecular weight PFAS (such as PFOS and PFOA) combined with their persistence in the environment. The rationale behind ECHAs wide ban of all PFAS is that if only the substances that are confirmed to be dangerous are restricted, new, similarly dangerous PFAS substances will take their place until they too can be shown to be dangerous – thus continuing the emissions of persistent and harmful chemicals towards a point of no return. However, the PFAS sub-class fluoropolymers have documented safety profiles and are (Henry et al. 2018):
- thermally, biologically and chemically stable,
- negligibly soluble in water,
- nonmobile,
- nonbioavailable,
- nonbioaccumulative, and
- nontoxic.

18 of the most of the commercially used fluoropolymers (representing ~96% of the fluoropolymer market) have also been demonstrated to meet the criteria for “Polymer of Low Concern” (PLC) as defined by OECD (Korzeniowski et al. 2023, Henry et al. 2018, Bio by Deloitte 2015, OECD 1993). PLCs are by the OECD deemed to have “insignificant environmental health and human health impacts” (OECD 2009).

Thus, while fluoropolymers are persistent, they are inert, and research suggests that they are neither hazardous to human health nor to the environment. In the production stage, emissions can be controlled and limited to 99-99.99% (Daikin 2021, 2022). In the waste stage, incineration has been shown to completely combust fluoropolymers under normal waste-to-energy combustion circumstances (Aleksandrov et al. 2019, Bakker et al. 2021, Giraud et al. 2021a, 2021b).

In contrast, the socioeconomical cost of a ban would be immeasurable. Fluoropolymers are critical in many industrial sealing applications where no other materials can rival their temperature range and resistance to reactive chemicals, e.g., for:
- Biofuel mixes e.g., including ethanol and AdBlue (reactive chemicals)
- Liquified Natural Gas, liquified hydrogen (reactive chemicals, low temperature) (Campion et al. 2005)
- Chemical production (reactive chemicals)
- Gas turbine engines (high temperature) [Thomas E. 2003]
- Semiconductor manufacturing process (high temperature) (Legare et al. 2008)

In these applications, fluoropolymers are already the “last resort”– an o-ring in a specialty fluoropolymer compound can be a hundred times more expensive than one in nitril rubber. Thus, a time-limited derogation to find substitutes will have questionable effect on the motivation to find replacement materials, as the industry already has strong incentives to develop such substitutes. In addition, such substitutes will by definition also be persistent in the environment.

In summary, a general ban of fluoropolymers as sealing elements will not benefit human or environmental health but will cost billions of Euros for European companies and consumers.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a global company with leadership in sustainable technologies, operating in more than 30 countries with around 15% of our employees located in the EU across 7 major manufacturing sites. We are a downstream user of PFAS, in applications that require mechanical and chemical resistance and for which PFAS are uniquely suited. E.g. our noble metal refineries utilise fluoroelastomers and fluoropolymers in critical process equipment, and our current catalyst-coated membranes (CCM) technologies, which are key components of fuel cells (FC) and electrolysers (EL), employ polymeric PFAS. We also receive end-of-life FC and EL containing PFAS for processing to recover the platinum and iridium.

Our global expertise in these areas gives us a unique perspective on the troubling impacts of this proposed restriction, particularly on the energy transition and security of critical raw materials, and our comments seek to highlight these concerns. In particular, the evidence provided in the restriction proposal does not justify a universal PFAS restriction as the most appropriate option to address the putative risks from such a broad and variable group of substances. For example, most types of fluoropolymers have been demonstrated to meet the OECD ‘polymer of low concern’ criteria. The available data do suggest that enacting regulatory measures to limit emissions of non-polymer PFAS will meet the goals of the dossier submitters, without doing serious harm to other important EU policy goals.

The EU has dedicated itself to sustainable development and has set a very ambitious target of becoming the first climate-neutral continent by 2050. To meet this target, the EU put in place the European Green Deal, a hydrogen strategy and REPowerEU, with the development of the EU hydrogen economy a strong focus across all three. To achieve the hydrogen goals, the Commission outlined plans to produce 10 million tonnes of renewable hydrogen by 2030 domestically and to import a further 10 million tonnes. To meet the 10 million tonne domestic production, the vision is to install 6 GW of renewable hydrogen electrolysers by 2024 and at least 100-120 GW of renewable hydrogen electrolysers by 2030 (today Europe has less than 1.5GW).

One of the fastest growing means of generating hydrogen is from a proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyser. Their popularity is increasing because they can operate at high efficiency levels when paired with renewable electricity (converting the electricity that cannot be used at times of low demand into hydrogen). At their core PEM EL use a catalyst coated membrane (CCM) which is responsible for converting water into hydrogen; these CCMs rely on an ion conducting fluoropolymer (ionomer) to function. Under the proposed ECHA definition and restriction these essential components used at the core of PEM EL would be banned. The consequence would be that the European targets for domestic renewable hydrogen production could not be met. The EU would lose the potential to provide the continent with energy security and would therefore become dependent on energy imports.

It is anticipated that the 20 million tonnes of renewable hydrogen proposed in RePowerEU will be predominantly used in three main market sectors: chemicals, heavy industry and mobility. These sectors are positioned in the top five of greenhouse gas emitters in the EU (28% comes from mobility, 26% from industry, 23% from power, 13% from buildings and 13% from agriculture). Across these sectors, fossil fuel combustion is the biggest source of GHGs, accounting for 80% of emissions. Renewable hydrogen can and will play a key role in supporting decarbonisation across these hard-to-abate applications. 

Transportation is one of the most significant contributors to greenhouse gas emissions globally, and where electrification is more difficult, fuel cells are an attractive solution to support decarbonisation. Hydrogen fuel cell vehicles use hydrogen to generate power electrochemically without releasing any harmful emissions or particulates. Fuel cells have proven ideal for heavy duty and high usage applications, such as for trucks and buses, as they provide the range, low weight and rapid fuelling times required by commercial fleet operators, with a much lower critical/strategic material intensity than, for example, battery electric trucks and buses. As with electrolysers, a contributory fuel cell technology is also PEM-based, with fluoropolymers being key components (see the Hydrogen Europe position paper for a summary https://hydrogeneurope.eu/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/Hydrogen-Europe-position-paper-on-PFAS-ban_v12_FINAL.pdf), with no viable substitutes available today, or expected within the timeframes of the proposed derogation.

Beyond these sector-specific impacts (which are expanded on in the attachments), the restriction proposal does not acknowledge the criticality of fluoropolymers in the chemicals manufacturing and platinum group metal (PGM) refining sectors, where chemical-resistant industrial equipment, such as piping, gaskets, pumps etc. are required to support process safety.

The attachments elaborate on these general comments with supporting evidence, and we believe that fluoropolymers should be removed from the scope of the restriction. However, if this is not achievable, it is imperative the proposed derogations and exemptions consider the following:

1) A full exemption is given for fluoropolymers used in industrial equipment for chemicals manufacturing. In particular, for PGM refining applications, where fluoroelastomer and fluoropolymer industrial equipment is used in these refineries.

2) A time-unlimited derogation is permitted for uses of PFAS in the energy sector (placing on the market, use, repair and recycling) specifically in relation to PEM fuel cells and electrolysers, because the proposed 5-year derogation is not sufficient to allow development and qualification of alternatives in these essential applications, as well as to allow the suppliers of any identified alternatives to scale-up to meet demand (see attachment 06). PFAS emissions from use are negligible (See attachment 05) and at end-of-life can be well-controlled. There is a clear economic case to recover the PGMs from FC and EL and avoid loss of these valuable materials from the circular economy.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Metal plating and manufacture of metal products  (Manufacture of metal products not addressed elsewhere) Energy sector Chemicals manufacture (industrial equipment) is not listed in Table 9.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Detailed comments are provided in attachment 02.     At the heart of PEM EL and FC technologies is the PGM-coated catalyst membrane. At their end-of-life, recovery of the PGMs (critical and strategic raw materials, CRMs) will be a key factor whilst also ensuring the ionomer is not entering uncontrolled waste streams. Current PGM refining employs incineration to destroy the ionomer and control PFAS emissions. PGM recyclers are beginning to focus on new lower energy and higher value retention (ionomer recycle) routes to recycle FC and EL  related CCMs from production scrap and / or end-of-life materials, improving on existing incineration technologies.  Both old and new technologies control PFAS emissions in the recovery phase.     A ‘closed loop’ recycling model could help ensure that materials move from industry to a recycler and back to industry (for reuse), without loss to land disposal or other waste. The efficiency of both current incineration systems and the future (non-incineration) recycling of CCMs could be enhanced by, e.g., introducing “producer responsibility” regulations and/or regulations mandating end-of-life recycling.  These would significantly increase collection efficiency and help ensure high levels of recycling are achieved.    The proposed ban on PFAS materials would critically undermine the whole PGM refining industry because of the need for PVDF as a key refinery construction material and also its use in chemical seals that are essential to the aggressive processes needed to recycle PGMs. Clearly anything that undermines Europe’s well-developed PGM recycle industry will undermine European intentions to develop the clean hydrogen industry as well as the myriad of other PGMs applications in environmental clean-up, pharmaceutical, food and health etc. In addition, the PGM recycle industry makes a substantial contribution to climate change mitigation because recycled PGMs create 50-70 times less CO2 eq compared to the only other source of these CRMs (via hard rock mining).

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: A recent peer-reviewed study concluded that incineration is an acceptable disposal approach for end-of-life PTFE (Aleksandrov et al. (2019), https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chemosphere.2019.03.191). The use of best available scrubbing approaches suggests that such activities do not emit PFAS with PTFE, and that PTFE was virtually fully transformed to fluorine as hydrofluoric acid which can be easily scrubbed and collected.     See Attachment 03 for more details.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Please see answer to Specific Information Request 2 and in Attachment 04
