Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a global leader in thermal management solutions, with a large installed base that includes more than 1.8 billion feet of installed heat tracing cable.
Self-regulating electrical heat tracing cable is a common form of heat tracing cable. It is a specialized electric cable that is able to regulate its temperature, and, in turn, the temperatures of the items, vehicles, pipes, machinery, installations, and equipment into which it is incorporated. It has many applications. In addition to the cables, connecting components are needed to create a complete electrical system enabling a functional heat trace system.
One of these applications is that it can be used to maintain the heat of objects at controlled and high temperatures. These objects include, for example, pipelines, piping, valves, vessels, tanks, silos, antennas, electrical panels, safety sidewalks, stairs, guardrails.
This submission requests a derogation, until 13.5 years after EiF, for the use of fluoropolymers within jackets and cores of electric heat tracing cables which are designed to be used both:
a) at temperatures above 65°C but below 260°C; and
b) for process maintenance applications,
being “Process Maintenance Cables and Connections”.
We have separately submitted a derogation request for certain freeze protection cables, which are for use at temperatures below 65°C. The rationale behind the making of multiple submissions is because we see various distinctions between the two classes of products, how PFASs are used by them, and how they are used more generally (amongst other matters).
Form of cable and PFAS use
Self-regulating electrical heat trace cables, including Process Maintenance Cables, consist of two parallel conductors embedded in a heating core made of a fluoropolymer conductive polymer. The high temperature core is sometimes radiation-cross-linked to ensure long-term reliability. Heat is generated as electric current passes through the conductive polymer core between the cable’s conductors. As the ambient temperature drops, the number of electrical paths through the core increases and more heat is produced. Conversely, as the temperature rises, the core has fewer electrical paths and less heat is produced.
Other types of Process Maintenance cables are also important for high temperature heat trace: power-limiting cables, which are also two parallel conductors wrapped by a power limiting resistive element into zones which allow cut-to-length installation; constant wattage cables, which have a series resistive element which must be custom designed for applications; and skin-effect heat trace which utilizes a resistive heating in a ferromagnetic tube surrounded by the high voltage cable that induces current via electromagnetic interaction.  In all, cases, cable connection systems are temperature and physical property matched to create a complete heat trace system.
In Process Maintenance cables, all polymers used currently are fluoropolymers: core (self-regulating only), inner jackets, and outer jackets. The entire portfolio of fluoropolymer properties are needed to ensure the viability for these products, specific properties are addressed in the application descriptions.
Applications
Details of how Process Maintenance cables are used are set out in the “Sectors and (sub-)uses” part of the submission below. Key uses include, however:
(a) general maintenance of process temperatures of piping in industrial facilities (chemical, power, pharmaceuticals, food and beverage, and transport terminals)
(b) general freeze protection for outdoor water piping [(e.g. building connections, cooling towers, drainage lines, waste water applications, and other industrial water feed lines].

(c)temperature maintenance of long pipelines transporting temperature sensitive fluids;
(d) temperature maintenance of tanks, valves, pumps and measuring instruments associated equipment supporting process fluids,
(e) Heat tracing cables, heat trace components, and heat trace controllers work together with heat tracing cables as a system to play a vital role in the European Union’s ongoing efforts to secure energy supply as well as implementing the European Green Deal as they are used within LNG transport, decarbonization,  hydrogen production, storage and distribution just to name a few.
Substitutes
In our ongoing R&D-efforts we failed to find suitable replacements that show similar portfolio of properties of fluoropolymers and match our applications needs. This applies especially for applications that are not only subject to our industry standards for electrical heat tracing systems (e. g. IEC 62395) but for applications specifically for use in explosive environments (IEC 60079-30) posing even higher demands on material performance and safety.
For applications above 150°C, we believe that substitution of fluoropolymers in the cable construction (core, inner jacket, and outer jacket) of Process Maintenance electrical heat trace cables will not be possible. For example, there are currently no known non-fluoropolymer materials that have both a CTI≥ 600 V and temperature stability above 150°C.
We set out further details on the substitution analysis of the available alternatives in our response to information request 8.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: By reference to Table 9, the Process Maintenance Cables would most naturally fall within the sub-use “Electronics” in the “Electronics and semiconductors” sector.   In Table 2 (“PFAS main applications and sub-uses”) of the Annex XV report, the Process Maintenance Cables would most naturally sit under the sub-use of “wires and cables” in the “Electronics and semiconductors” sectors.  It should be noted, however, that the Process Maintenance Cables are used across multiple sectors and in multiple industries. Applications include complex chemical facility process piping, refinery process piping, energy terminal tanks / transport piping, food / pharmaceutical process piping, decarbonization process piping, and energy / chemical transport (long pipelines).   In the current version of Annex XV in “Table 2. PFAS main applications and sub-uses”, cables and wires are only mentioned in the table of sub-use of the section electronics and semiconductions and cables in the section petroleum and mining.  As a producer of electrical heat tracing systems, we use a variety of fluoropolymers in self-regulating, power limiting, constant wattage (polymer insulated), and skin-effect heat tracing cables. Electrical heat tracing systems are used for either freeze protection or to maintain a specific temperature.  While heat tracing systems are accurately included in the “Electronics and semiconductor” sector, it would be inaccurate to limit them solely to that sector as the fluoropolymers in heat tracing cables are present in numerous industries and applications, including without limitation: • Chemical and petrochemical industry: Electrical heat tracing is used to keep pipelines, tanks, vessels and other equipment at a constant temperature. This is done in order to prevent frost damage, maintain the viscosity of liquids and ensure the smooth operation of chemical processes.   • Oil and gas industry: Electrical heat tracing plays an important role in the transportation of oil and gases such as LPG/LNG or H2 through pipelines. It is used to control the viscosity of the media, prevent clogging due to wax formation or condensation and improve transport efficiency.  • Food and beverage industry: Electrical heat tracing is used for various applications, such as thawing food, maintaining proper storage temperatures, temperature control in fermentation processes, and handling of chocolate and fat (e.g. transportation through pipes).   • Pharmaceutical industry: Electrical trace heating is used to control the temperature in processes such as mixing, drying, distillation and fermentation. This ensures the quality and efficacy of the medicines produced and enables compliance with strict GMP guidelines.   • Building services: Electrical trace heating is used to prevent frost damage to water pipes, gutters, drainage systems and underfloor heating. It is also used for snow melting on pavements and driveways and for temperature control in heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems.   • Power generation: In power generation, especially in power plants and heat transfer facilities, electric heat tracing plays an important role in maintaining the operating temperature of piping, condensers, heat exchangers and turbines. This helps to improve efficiency and operational safety. Electrical heat tracing is used to protect critical components such as valves, pumps and measuring instruments from freezing or condensing. This ensures the smooth functioning of power stations, solar power plants, wind turbines, electrolysers, heat pumps, fuel cells and other energy generation systems.   • Personnel Safety:  Electrical heat tracing serves to protect safety systems such as fire sprinkler lines and enable safe passage of people on walkways, steps, stairways, and under eaves in industrial facilities, ship decks, helipads, and sea platforms.     • Transportation: Electrical trace heating is used for freeze prevention in rails and switch points to ensure safe railway traffic and for temperature maintenance of long-line pipelines for the transport of temperature sensitive fluids over long distances..   • Research and Development / Academics: Whenever specific temperature requirements have to be met during development, electrical heat tracing is used. This ranges from heating specific component (e.g. vacuum chambers or pipelines) to systems for the use in heated hoses in gas analysis. Another example in research is the use of electrical heating technology in particle accelerators.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: a) Usage phase: As under ordinary use cases Process Maintenance Cable is installed under insulation and/or cladding, there are not believed to be material emissions during the usage phase. b) End of life phase: A recent Conversio-study has shown that “at its end-of-life approximately 85 % of all fluoropolymers end up in waste-to-energy recovery incinerators” (Conversio-study can be acquired via “https://www.pro-kunststoff.de/fachwissen/conversio-studie-end-of-life-von-fluorpolymeren.html”).  Following on that study, the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) in cooperation with Société Générale de Surveillance (SGS) set out to investigate whether fluoropolymers get fully incinerated without any formation of short chain of long chain PFAS.  Preliminary results of that study demonstrate that (i) fluoropolymers are converted to Inorganic Fluorides and Carbon dioxide at standard incineration conditions; (ii) the inorganic fluorides mainly include Hydrogen Fluoride and Silicon tetrafluoride; and (iii) total organic fluorides (PFAS) were non-detectable with a reporting limit of 0.08 ppm and Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) was also not detected with a reporting limit of 0.04 ppm.  The study concluded that “fluoropolymers at their end of life when incinerated under representative European municipal incinerators conditions do not generate any measurable levels of PFAS emissions and therefore pose no risk to human health and the environment.” See Non-Confidential Annex 01. Additionally, Aleksandrov et al. already concluded in 2019 specific for PTFE that “municipal incineration of PTFE shows no significant generation of studied PFAS. See Non-Confidential Annex 02.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Concerning the effectiveness of fluoropolymer incineration, we would like to reference the ongoing research project by the Federal Institute for Materials Research and Testing (BAM) and the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT), funded by the German Federal Environment Agency:   “Basic investigations on thermochemical degradation of PFAS in laboratory and pilot plants to determine optimum combustion conditions for the thermal treatment of PFAS-containing waste materials.” See Non-Confidential Annex 03. The study involved application samples of the four most sold Fluoropolymers (PTFE, PVDF, PFA and FKM) provided by Pro-K (German association of polymer processors), which were incinerated under standard operating conditions for municipal and industrial waste incineration (850°C – 1100°C for two seconds residence time respectively) and consulted by the German Federal Environment Agency (Umweltbundesamt). The final data sets and methodology used are being reviewed and validated by Environmental Standards Inc. The absence of organic fluorides and more specifically PFAS substances in incineration flue gas confirms complete thermal destruction of Fluoropolymers during incineration and therefore it should pave the way for exempting Fluoropolymers from the EU REACH PFAS restriction proposal.

6. Missing uses: Please refer to Question 8 where we discuss alternatives and socio-economic impacts.

8. Other identified uses: a. Annual tonnage and emissions We use approximately 454 metric tons of fluoropolymers (being a combination of PFA, ETFE, ECTFE, and PVDF) annually in our process maintain products. As discussed in Question 2 above, there is not believed to be any material emissions from the intended use of our heat tracing products nor in their end of life recovery. b. Key functionalities provided by PFAS Process maintenance cables maintain the heat of objects at controlled and high temperatures. These objects include, for example, pipelines, piping, valves, vessels, tanks, silos, antennas, electrical panels, safety sidewalks, stairs, guardrails, and more.  As noted in General Comments section, there are four (4) types of process maintenance (high temperature) heat trace cables that use fluoropolymers: self-regulating, power-limiting, constant wattage (polymer insulated), and skin-effect systems.  There are three (3) ways in which fluoropolymers are used to enable the Process Maintenance Cables to function safely and robustly: (a) creation of self-regulating heating cores; (b) creation of inner dielectric jackets; and (c) creation of outer protective jackets.  In process temperature maintenance of industrial applications (including in the chemical, petrochemical, pharmaceutical, food, and energy transition sectors), fluoropolymers are used for high-temperature (> 65°C) self-regulating heating cores, within Process Maintenance Cables that rely on properties of high temperature resistance, high comparative tracking index (CTI), consistent and sharp semi-crystalline phase transitions which enable percolation physics that creates self-regulation and intrinsic temperature safety, high comparative tracking index (CTI), flame resistance, chemical resistance, impact resistance, flexibility, and durability for use in rugged and hazardous areas of industrial facilities. Many of these properties are required pursuant to industry standards for electrical heat tracing systems (e. g. IEC 62395) and (IEC 60079-30) for use in explosive environments, which poses even higher demands on material performance and safety.  Other properties are based on requirements that are market driven by customer values: e.g. durable heat-trace power output performance.    In process temperature maintenance of industrial piping, fluoropolymers are used for inner jackets of self-regulating, power limiting, constant wattage, and skin effect heat tracing providing dielectric resistance, high temperature resistance, high comparative tracking index (CTI), flame resistance, water resistance, impact resistance, flexibility, and durability for use in rugged and hazardous areas of industrial facilities.  In the case of skin effect heat tracing fluoropolymers also provide resistance to plasma discharge in the dielectric layer. Plasma discharge can occur in the operation of a skin effect heat tracing system between the dielectric layer and the ferromagnetic tube that surrounds the insulated skin effect cable.    In process temperature maintenance of industrial piping, fluoropolymers are also used for outer jackets and connection systems (heat shrink tubing, tubing, grease, and machined parts) of self-regulating, power limiting, and constant wattage Process Maintenance systems (cables and connections) providing high temperature resistance, chemical resistance, water resistance, flame resistance, UV resistance, impact resistance, abrasion resistance, flexibility, lubricity (anti-stick/slip), and durability for use in rugged and hazardous areas of industrial facilities.  c. # of companies in the sector affected  In the market, there are many direct competitors for our company’s [Process Maintenance Cables].  Based on market knowledge, we estimate >5 companies participate in producing similar products for the European market.    There are estimated more than 250 separate companies (commercial and industrial) that have purchased our products for process maintenance applications.    We anticipate that loss of fluoropolymer based high-temperature heat trace products (self-regulating, power-limiting, constant wattage, and skin-effect) will have a deleterious effect on the ability of the European Union’s ongoing efforts to secure energy supply as well as implementing the European Green Deal as they are used within heat pumps, LNG transport, decarbonization,  hydrogen production, storage and distribution just to name a few. Alternative heat-trace requires custom engineering / custom manufacture (lead-time), increased knowledge for successful install (craft sensitive), and has a lessor safety record resulting from installation errors.    d. Availability, feasibility, hazards/risks of alternatives Self-regulating cores: Our R&D team has evaluated alternatives to the use of fluoropolymers in the self-regulating heating cores of Process Maintenance Cables. They found through prototyping and testing that non-fluoropolymer alternatives that offer high temperature resistance have low comparative tracking indices (CTI) when used as a core material and inherently create extreme risk of electrical faults. See Confidential Annex 01.   Those historical efforts were abandoned. Although some higher CTI non-fluoropolymer materials have been identified for possible further consideration, their temperature capability is known to be compromised relative to the best fluoropolymers.  As such, it may be possible to create self-regulating heater cores for a subset of the current market applications potentially as high as 150°C, yet other (wider) properties of these alternatives are currently unknown (and could not be known without more development work). In particular, these characteristics of the alternatives are unknown at present: their ability to provide consistent and sharp semi-crystalline phase transitions (which enables percolation physics for self-regulation and intrinsic temperature safety), flame resistance, impact resistance, flexibility, and durability for use in rugged and hazardous areas of industrial facilities. Thus, the possible use of these alternatives moving forward presents an elevated risk of electrical faults when compared against the fluoropolymer constructions used today even in the potentially accessible <150° range.  The development of Process Maintenance self-regulating cables for use in the more commercially important regime of 150° - 260°C is currently believed by us to be non-achievable with non-fluoropolymer alternatives because high CTI non-fluoropolymers are not rated above 150°C  One approach to considering the alternatives is to ask what the position was for similar cables prior to the use of fluoropolymers. In this regard, it is important to recognize the historical perspective of how much safer electrical heat-tracing has become with the introduction of self-regulating technology for which high temperature process maintenance can only be done today with fluoropolymers.   Specifically, self-regulating cable (including Process Maintenance Cable) was awarded the 200th milestone because it solved two significant problems associated with constant wattage heaters:  IEEE Milestone: Polymer Self-Regulating Heat-Tracing Cable, 1972 (https://ethw.org/Milestones:Polymer_Self-Regulating_Heat-Tracing_Cable,_1972#Citation) See Non-Confidential Annex 04. More specifically, fluoropolymer containing Process Maintenance Cable:  • Can be cut to length in the field, which enables faster and safer installation (i.e. is less craft sensitive), and avoids the need for customization lead-times needed for factory design and fabrication.  Since “as-built” field piping is often not quite to drawing estimates, additional lead-time is required to support returns/redesign for different lengths. In short, “as-built” (non-fluoropolymer containing) piping can [materially] increase costs as it may not always be exactly right (which issue does not arise with fluoropolymer containing self-regulating Process Maintenance Cables, which can be cut on site).   • Are cross-over burn-out safe, enabling faster and safer installation (i.e. is less craft sensitive). Heat tracing cables are often placed in close proximity in complex piping (valves, elbows, flanges, etc.) or otherwise need to make use of multiple runs. If such cables are placed too close to each other, this could exceed the jackets’ design temperature due to too much power (causing an electrical short). The use of fluoropolymers that self-regulate addresses this issue, providing assurance that the cables will not fail in this way.       The use of fluoropolymers within the Process Maintenance Cables is expensive, with a mineral-insulated constant wattage heat-trace circuit roughly half the cost of a similar process maintenance self-regulating circuit. This notwithstanding, the vast majority of electrical trace heating is now done by self-regulating heaters with over 5 manufacturers all over the world making this type of heating cable, even though the material costs are much higher than an equivalent mineral insulated constant wattage circuit. In other words, the use of the known alternatives would, in fact, be cheaper (if cost was the only issue). However, if Process Maintenance Cables reverted to being fluoropolymer-free products, we would be repeating history; returning to a product that had a poorer safety record due to craft sensitivity, longer lead times needed for custom design / manufacture Inner dielectric jackets: In process temperature maintenance of industrial piping, fluoropolymer substitutions for inner jackets of self-regulating, power limiting, constant wattage, and skin effect heat tracing related Process Maintenance Cables must provide dielectric resistance, high temperature resistance, high comparative tracking index (CTI), flame resistance, water resistance, impact resistance, flexibility, and durability for use in rugged and hazardous areas of industrial facilities. Because non-fluoropolymer dielectrics used at high temperatures have a low comparative tracking index (CTI) [rating], a potential for defects that lead to arc faults is created.  This problem is well described in Kapton:  Miracle material with a Tragic History (https://hackaday.com/2018/04/04/kapton-miracle-material-with-a-tragic-history/).  Fluoropolymers replaced Kapton to enable safety.   In the case of a narrow range of self-regulating heat-tracing (<150°C) applications, it may be possible to identify inner jackets with higher CTI non-fluoropolymers, yet other properties of these alternatives are unknown, and could not be known without more development work. The unknown characteristics of these possible alternatives are the following:  flame resistance, impact resistance, flexibility, and durability for use in rugged and hazardous areas of industrial facilities. Thus, there is currently an elevated risk that the use of these alternatives would result in electrical faults when compared to fluoropolymer constructions used today even in the potentially accessible <150° range.  In the case of power limiting or constant wattage heat tracing related Process Maintenance Cables, because non-fluoropolymers have lesser temperature rating, there is a need to reduce the sheath temperature of the constant wattage heating wire, via a reduction of the design power output and improved heat transfer of to allow for a non-fluoropolymer inner jacket with a high CTI dielectric jacket (>600) to ensure safe operation.  A redesign strategy of this kind requires not only the redesign of the underlying product, but also a redesign of associated application and installation instructions. However, even if this is all done, this could still leave unresolved risks for electrical faults compared to the fluoropolymer solutions offered today because replacements have not been fully assessed.   In the case of skin effect heat tracing related Process Maintenance Cables, known higher CTI non-fluoropolymers do not have sufficient temperature resistance to operate above 150°C or known resistance to plasma discharge (being a quality needed for high temperature skin effect systems). As such, it is not possible to create high temperature skin effect systems with known non-fluoropolymers. See Confidential Annex 02.  Without high temperature skin-effect systems, it becomes more challenging to provide heat-trace for long pipelines that carry temperature sensitive fluids such as Sulphur, Asphalt, Vacuum Gas Oil, Phenol, Biodiesel feedstocks and more.  Skin-effect heat trace for process maintenance has been used successfully for more than 60 years.   Outer protective jackets and connection systems: The risk of introducing less mechanical durability to the outer jacket of Process Maintenance Cables (by removing the fluoropolymers) is the potential for an inadvertent breach of the jacket for which no detection is available. See Confidential Annex 03.  Should a breach occur, the inner jacket, which would also be non-fluoropolymer per the restriction proposal, would not likely have sufficient chemical resistance and, in turn, could become compromised if exposed to chemicals, which could lead to an electrical fault. We have evaluated alternative materials for chemical resistance finding no single solution to provide similar coverage especially against dilute acids, oils, and solvents.  The risk of introducing multiple offerings for chemical resistance when compared against a single offering is error in selection.  Should an error in selection occur, once the outer jacket has been compromised, then any non-fluoropolymer inner jacket will not likely have sufficient chemical resistance (and so could become compromised as a result of the resultant chemical exposure, which could lead to an electrical fault). For example, if a customer selects the chemically resistant protective jacket good for solvents, for which the application requires chemical resistance to hydraulic oil, it is likely that the protection could result in an arc fault in less than one year.    In the case of connection systems, high temperature resistance of non-fluoropolymers limits applications to below 150°C or the methods of splice, tee, and power connections will shift from low-profile on-pipe connections to off-pipe fluoropolymer free junction box connections.  The cost of shifting from on-pipe connections to off-pipe fluoropolymer free junction box connections will be borne by owners and operators, which may double or triple the cost.    e. For cases in which alternatives are not yet available  Multiple R&D projects over many years have considered how best to eliminate fluoropolymers from our products in an effort to reduce cost to customers, because fluoropolymers are the most expensive materials of the potentially suitable profiles. None of the substitution projects have been successful. Typical heat trace projects take 3-10 years to run including development of product requirements, iterative prototyping and testing, followed by system approvals expected by the market.  A recent project to increase the durability of one of our key products, took 7 years and cost roughly $1M.  f.   Cases for which substitution is feasible, yet more time is required   It is important to note that the duration of systems regulatory approvals is outside of our control and often doubles the development cycle of new products getting to market.   A recent project to increase the durability of one of our key products including systems regulatory approvals took 7 years to complete and cost roughly $1M. Given the breadth of portfolio changes needed, multiple projects would need to be run successively and could take decades. Self-regulating cores: As noted in d), and for Process Maintenance Cables to be used in process temperature maintenance of industrial piping, an iterative approach will likely be required to strike the requisite attribute balance required among heater cores (for a subset of the current market applications potentially as high as 150°C), such attributes to provide consistent and sharp semi-crystalline phase transitions (which enable percolation physics for self-regulation and intrinsic temperature safety), flame resistance, impact resistance, flexibility, and durability for use in rugged and hazardous areas of industrial facilities as well as market acceptance for applications only up to 150°C.  Due to the nature of iteration required in the marketplace, the detailed approvals needed to support systems regulatory approvals including components for electrical connections, we estimate that it may take 5-10 years to complete a non-fluoropolymer offering in industrial pipe freeze protection for applications only up to 150°C (and assuming that appropriate non-fluoropolymers can be promptly identified, which may not be the case). Furthermore, given the breadth of portfolio changes needed, multiple projects would need to be run successively and could take decades. As noted in d), the development of Process Maintenance Cables for use in process temperature maintenance via self-regulation-related operations in the more commercially important regime of 150° - 260°C is currently believed by us to be non-achievable with non-fluoropolymer alternatives.   These applications could potentially be served by metallic constant wattage heating with specific low sheath temperature products for hazardous locations, but this would require intrinsic temperature safety-related concerns to be addressed.  The cost of this change would be significant (>5x) in cost and lead-time to the facility owners and presents practical issues as described in (d) above that could give rise to safety issues not known with fluoropolymer self-regulating process maintenance heat trace.[  Inner dielectric jackets: As noted in d), and in relation to process temperature maintenance via power limiting or constant wattage applications, we anticipate that redesigning our applications to reduce heater power and increase heat transfer along with selection of non-fluoropolymer dielectrics with >600 CTI could take 4-7 years to complete including system regulatory approvals for inner jackets. These comments also apply to the development of inner jackets for self-regulating heater products for applications only up to 150°C (and assuming that appropriate non-fluoropolymers can be promptly identified, which may not be the case). Furthermore, given the breadth of portfolio changes needed, multiple projects would need to be run successively and could take decades. As noted in d), and in relation to Process Maintenance Cables that maintain temperature via skin effect], there is no known feasible alternative above 150°C.   Outer protective jackets and connection systems: As noted in d), and in relation to Process Maintenance Cables that maintain temperatures of industrial piping, an iterative approach will likely be required to strike the balance among mechanical ruggedness (of impact resistance, abrasion resistance, lubricity, and durability), chemical resistance, and market acceptance of multiple offerings (to cover the same product requirements) for outer jackets.  Due to the nature of iteration required in the marketplace, the detailed approvals needed to support systems regulatory approvals (including for components for electrical connections), we estimate that it may take 5-10 years to complete a non-fluoropolymer offering in industrial pipe freeze protection-related applications (and assuming that appropriate non-fluoropolymers can be promptly identified, which may not be the case). Furthermore, given the breadth of portfolio changes needed, multiple projects would need to be run successively and could take decades.  As noted in d), connection systems for process temperature maintenance will require application redesign and market iteration to shift to off-pipe fluoropolymer free junction box connections could take 4-7 years to complete including system regulatory approvals.  Given the breadth of portfolio changes needed, multiple projects would need to be run successively and could take decades  Reiterating, there are a multitude of projects needed to replace fluoropolymers in a large portfolio of products today, where it may be feasible.  Although any single project may take between 7-10 years, the capacity of business to support multiple projects is limited and a complete refresh of products without fluoropolymers (where possible) could take decades.    g. Cases for which substitution is impossible  As noted in d), the development of Process Maintenance Cables for process temperature maintenance via self-regulation-related activities for use in the more commercially important regime of 150° - 260°C is currently believed by us to be non-achievable with non-fluoropolymer alternatives for the reasons stated previously.    As noted in d) process temperature maintenance via skin effect, there is no feasible alternative above 150°C.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a Japanese chemical manufacturer, supplying fluorochemicals worldwide including European market.
We agree with the FCJ's opinion letter attached in section IV.

　 In this letter, we describe our opinion on a chain transfer agent, which is very important manufacturing aid for the production of fluoroelastomers.
　In Annex A restriction letter, the manufacturing process of fluoroelastomer, is described in A.2.1.5. As polymerizarion aids for fluoroelastomer, initiators, catalysts, surfactants, emulsifiers, and process aids are explained, however, a chain transfer agent to adjust molecular weights of polymers is not discussed.
　A PFAS compound, I(CF2)4I, is used as a chain transfer agent to adjust target and narrower molecular weight distribution of polymer by iodine transfer polymerization. This feature allows chain transfer agents to contribute to the excellent performance of fluoroelastomers, which in turn play an important role in society, for example, as materials that contribute to safe transportation by transport vehicles.
　In the production of fluoroelastomers, a chain transfer agent is incorporated into the polymer backbone, so it is not released into the environment through leaching, and its environmental impact is considered to be nothing.
　Therefore, we are proposing an exemption or deferral of the chain transfer agent used in the production of fluoroelastomers, as well as fluoroelastomers, from the proposed restriction.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Field of application: PFAS production Subcategory：Fluoroelastomer production aid Related application areas: 　The main field of application of the above chain transfer agent is PFAS production, specifically as a production aid for fluoroelastomers. More specifically, they are used as chain transfer agents in the production of FKM or FFKM. The specific compound I(CF2)4I is mainly used as a chain transfer agent. 　As stated in Annex A (page 25) of the proposed restriction, the recognized uses of fluoroelastomers (FKM and FFKM) are automotive (64%), chemical resin manufacturing (11%), aerospace industry (9%) and other (16%). Reference A (10.2.9 Applications of FKMs Page 192) identifies 60% as automotive, 10% as chemical, 10% as aerospace, and 20% as other. Furthermore, Reference A states that 30-40% of FKM is consumed in O-rings and gaskets, 30% in automotive shaft seals and oil seals, and 10-15% in hoses and profiles. 　This means that (I(CF2)4I) is mainly used as an essential raw material to supply fluoroelastomers used for the safe transportation of transport vehicles, whose socio-economic and non-substitutability is recognized in the restriction proposal (6. o.).

6. Missing uses: PFAS name: 1,4-Diiodooctafluorobutane, cas#375-50-8 Annual tonnage: See Section V Attachment. Annual emission: We believe that there is no environmental emission as a chain transfer agent. The rationale for this is shown below. 　The mechanism of chain transfer polymerization is described in Fig. 7 of Reference B and Scheme 11 of Reference C, etc. Iodofluorocarbons (IFCs) are highly reactive in iodine transfer polymerization (hereafter ITP); IFCs are readily attacked by radicals to form living polymers. The active living polymer can then undergo radical propagation and transfer reactions to produce even higher molecular weight living polymers. 　It is clear that in the above polymerization reaction, the chain transfer agent is consumed to form part of the polymer backbone. In Reference D (page 5775), it is shown that the chain transfer agent is completely consumed in the polymerization reaction using the chain transfer agent model compound C6F13I.  　The resulting living polymers are further radical cross-linked and used in various fluoroelastomer applications. As mentioned above, no unreacted chain transfer agent remains in the fluoroelastomer, so the chain transfer agent is not released into the environment at the time of use or disposal. In addition, the chain transfer agent, I(CF2)4I, is a liquid with a boiling point of 85°C, and it is recognized that it is unlikely to be released into the environment during transport from Japan to Europe in a sealed container or during the polymerization reaction. Therefore, the chain transfer agent I(CF2)4I is considered to have no environmental emissions during its total life cycle.  Living polymerization is one of the revolutionary methods in polymer synthesis because it allows control over the arrangement, composition, and length of molecules. The first example in fluoroelastomers is iodine transfer polymerization (ITP), which was commercialized 40 years ago by Tatemoto (Reference B). 　In Ref. B, it is shown that in this polymerization method, the number average molecular weight is equal to the ratio of polymer yield to amount of chain transfer agent (Fig. 3), and thus polymers of any molecular weight can be synthesized depending on conditions. 　In addition, a comparison of monoiodo and diiodo chain transfer agents shows that polymerization with I(CF2)4I yields a polymer with a narrower molecular weight distribution than that with (CF3)2CFI, as shown in Fig. 4 in Reference B. 　Furthermore, the resulting living polymer undergoes a process of radical cross-linking of the terminal iodine moiety with a multifunctional vinyl compound to obtain a fluoroelastomer. Especially when diiodides such as I(CF2)4I are used, radical crosslinked elastomers are obtained almost quantitatively because polymers without iodine moieties derived from the stopping reaction are not generated (Fig. 9). 　In this case, the method of radical cross-linking using iodine transfer polymerization also has the advantage of cross-linking without the use of an acid acceptor (base) as in amine and polyol cross-linking. 　As described above, iodine transfer polymerization using I(CF2)4I enables the provision of fluoroelastomers that meet various performance requirements, and most fluoropolymer manufacturers now employ ITP technology using I(CF2)4I in their product lineups (see Reference E Table1).  Since I(CF2)4I is a key material for manufacturing FKM and FFKM, the proposed restriction affects not only fluoropolymer manufacturers (11 companies) but also compound and sealant manufacturers that use fluoropolymers (see the European Sealing Association position paper. The association has 52 members). Downstream users in Europe are also expected to include the automotive, aerospace, rail and marine, chemical, food, construction, and electronics industries.  As mentioned above, polymerization using I(CF2)4I as a chain transfer agent yields a polymer with a very narrow molecular weight distribution.     On the other hand, it has been shown that when non-PFAS, hydrocarbon (isopentane) or chlorine compound (CCl4) was used as a chain transfer agent, a wider molecular weight distribution was obtained and the desired performance couldn't be obtained (Reference B, page 769). 　Also, when iodofluorocarbons such as (CF3)2CFI are used, polymers with a relatively narrow molecular weight distribution can be obtained, but there is the issue of by-products of the polymer that do not have an iodine moiety and do not contribute to radical cross-linking. Also, (CF3)2CFI is also a PFAS substance and is not a substitute for I(CF2)4I.   Since the automotive industry typically requires a service life of at least 10 years for related products, it is said that at least 10 years will be needed to change the specifications of fluoroelastomers. Therefore, it is assumed that at least 10 years will be required to develop alternative materials for chain transfer agents, which have a significant impact on the performance of fluoroelastomers. 　We insist that, as for the chain transfer agent (I(CF2)4I), which is such an important raw material, there should be an exemption or a deferment of restriction, as is the case with fluoroelastomers.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a leading international pump manufacturer. Our main industry sectors are dairy, food, pharma, personal health care. We cannot switch to PFAS free seal components and other PFAS free parts as they are simply as know PFAS free durable alternative options. A lot of products could automatically not be processed any longer.

Objection to the ban on use
We object to the ban on the use of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in elastomers and other materials.

Reason:
PFAS is present in the following parts in contact with the product:
Stainless steel no (99% of the surface in contact with the product).
Elastomers possible depending on the processed product
Sliding materials possible depending on the processed product
Lubricants possible on a product-specific basis

When pumping low-viscosity fluids in centrifugal pumps or when pumping higher-viscosity fluids in positive displacement pumps, the contact time between fluid and seals (elastomer) in the pump is very short. This means that the possibility of contamination of the fluid through diffusion from the elastomer into the fluid is very low. As long as there are no PFAS-free sealing components, it will be necessary to use a number of those components in contact with the product when assembling pumps. Our aim is  to minimize this number.

Our pumps are designed to be product-friendly and hygienic in every respect. We are always ready to use PFAS-free seals with the same chemical and mechanical resistance as soon as they are available. According to the current state of technology, there are no PFAS-free materials that are resistant to customer products for numerous customer applications.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a lithium thionyl chloride batteries manufacturer in Japan. We support the EU's ambitious attempts to reduce risks from hazardous substances and have taken real steps to meet the requirements of the EU chemical regulations, such as REACH.
However, the proposed restrictions on PFAS (Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl substances) this time aim to restrict more than 10,000 substances as substances of concern equivalent to the already regulated PFOS and PFOA on the grounds that they are difficult to decompose. We believe that it is an excessive measure to collectively restrict PFAS.
The high-molecular fluoropolymers (PTFE, PVDF, etc.) used in batteries are thermally, biologically, and chemically stable, are almost insoluble in water, do not migrate, and are too large to infiltrate cell membranes. As a result, it cannot be taken into the body and is considered to be a substance of low concern from the viewpoint of human and environmental health. Therefore, it should not be treated collectively in the same way as PFOS and PFOA, which are substances of very high concern. We endorse FCJ's   statement regarding the alleged restrictions.(See the attached documents in the Section IV)
We also believe that in order to comply with regulations, restricted substances should be identified individually with a unique identifier, such as a CAS number, rather than lumped together in a definition. The management of chemical substances contained in products is based on the communication of multiple and multi-layered supply chains. In general, electronic components and products are managed efficiently and reliably by comparing ingredient information from upstream suppliers with customers’ requirements using CAS numbers. However, if restrictions were enforced with a broad definition as in the proposed restrictions, it is highly likely that unintentional omissions would occur, and management would become inefficient, leading to deep concerns that restrictions would not be complied with.
The following references support the low toxicity of fluoropolymers.
1. The Impact Assessment in Annex E refers to the paper by J. Sales et al. (*1) , which cites the paper by B. J. Henry et al. (*2) making a case that high-molecular fluoropolymers  are low in toxicity and rather there are risks associated with low-molecular substances such as fluorinated polymerization aids.
2. The paper by S. H. Korzeniowski et al. (*3), which is also cited by the paper by J. Sales et al. (*1), also supports the paper by B. J. Henry et al.
*1 https://icrl.lexxion.eu/data/article/18603/pdf/icrl_2022_01-006.pdf
*2 https://setac.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ieam.4035
*3 https://setac.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ieam.4646
In this way, if the use of fluoropolymers is prohibited despite the low risk, it will be virtually impossible to supply lithium thionyl chloride batteries to the market, which will have a significant impact on society. As will be discussed later, it is not easy to develop alternatives, and we request derogation for 13.5 years. In addition, since there is a possibility that no substitutes can be found as a result of the search, we request that a provision for review of exemptions be included in the regulations.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: In the energy sector of the proposed restriction batteries are referred to as lithium ion batteries and "other batteries". But the scope of "other batteries" is too broad and ambiguous. Our batteries that we consider to be affected are lithium thionyl chloride battery.

8. Other identified uses: (Introduction)  We believes that the PFAS restriction proposal this time is an excessive measure, as it seeks to collectively restrict over 10,000 PFAS on the ground of persistence alone. PFAS are essential materials for batteries, and the impact of not being able to use them would be immeasurable. We requests derogation for 13.5 years by the following description about the actual use of PFAS in batteries, the alternatives feasibility, and the economic and social impacts.  a. Type of PFAS and annual tonnage for the relevant use. PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) is used as a positive electrode binder for lithium thionyl chloride battery. Our annual usage of PTFE is about 0.15 ton.   b. The key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use. PTFE used in positive electrode binder has the following functions.  ① A porous electrode is important for the positive electrode of ER battery because it traps and contains thionyl chloride, a liquid active material. When the carbon of conductive material and PTFE are kneaded, the PTFE fibrillates and integrates between the carbon powders, thus functioning as a binder that forms a suitable porous electrode.  ② In order to fully demonstrate the performance, it is important to make the battery as free from moisture as possible, and it is necessary to remove the moisture absorbed by the carbon at a high temperature of 200°C or higher when manufacturing the positive electrode. PTFE has heat resistance that does not degrade in this process.  ③ PTFE is chemically stable against highly reactive thionyl chloride. This makes it possible to maintain the mechanical strength of the electrode over the product life cycle.  c. The number of companies in the sector estimated to be affected by the restriction. As far as we know, there are more than a dozen lithium thionyl chloride battery manufacturers in the world, and if they are unable to produce batteries due to the regulation, many companies, including related companies, will be affected.  d,e,f. Regarding the technical feasibility of alternatives Rubbers (styrene-butadiene rubber, etc.), celluloses (carboxymethylcellulose, etc.), and polyolefins (polyethylene, etc.) can be considered as substitutes for PTFE used in the positive electrode binder. However, none of these have the functions described below, making it difficult to create an ER battery, making it difficult to replace them. ・Heat resistance and oxidation resistance that do not deteriorate when dried (baked) at 200°C or higher ・Chemical stability to thionyl chloride When considering alkaline batteries or carbon-zinc batteries as a replacement for lithium thionyl chloride battery, in addition to differences in battery voltage itself, there are significant differences in dischargeable temperature range, stability of discharge characteristics during long-term use, volume energy density (Wh/L), and weight energy density (Wh/kg), making it difficult to replace the applications for which lithium thionyl chloride battery are used. Furthermore other batteries use PFAS and are not substitutes.  g. Economic and social impacts caused by PFAS restrictions. It is very difficult to develop alternatives, and if the use of PTFE is banned, it will be virtually impossible to supply lithium thionyl chloride battery to the market. The numbers are for the global market, but lithium thionyl chloride battery-related companies will be at risk of losing at least the European market's worth of the 80 billion yen when the PFAS restrictions take effect(Source: Fuji Keizai '2022 Battery-related Market Report' (in Japanese). Moreover, this loss is only for the lithium thionyl chloride battery manufacturer, and the loss is further expanded with that of material manufacturers added. In addition to corporate losses, the impact on consumers and society is enormous. Lithium thionyl chloride battery is widely embedded, such as applications in the field of Internet of Things, Utility metering, security. If Lithium thionyl chloride battery cannot be supplied due to the PFAS restrictions, there is a risk of causing social confusion.  Based on the above, we request a 13.5-year derogation, as it will take at least 10 years to search for and commercialize alternatives to PFAS for batteries. In addition, since there is a possibility that a substitute product may not be found as a result of the search, it is requested that a provision for reviewing the derogation be included in the restrictions.

General Comments: We are a machine manufacturer and with regard of the supply and application of substances and products containing PFAS we are a “downstream user”. Our products are used in the automotive industry, mechanical engineering, photovoltaic industry, semiconductor industry, research and development, as well as the medical industry.
We fully understand and support the need of restrictions of environmentally dangerous and toxic substances. However, we find the current proposal to be not entirely thought out in certain use cases.
When it comes to a topic of this complexity, 6 months is not long enough for a thorough public consultation and 18 months is too short of a transition period.
PFAS are present in many of our products, the entire scope of which we cannot accurately predict yet, due to being a downstream user. This will be an initial challenge for all our parts manufacturers and a delayed challenge on our part, to see if the substituted parts still achieve the required specifications.

6. Missing uses: The following cases are currently known to us and affected by the proposed regulations: PTFE coated hoses for use in clean rooms, refrigerant, cables, paint rollers, lubricants, electrical components, coil coating, sealing rings, laser scanners, optical lenses, optical fibers, fiber lasers, coatings, PVDF membranes, chemical analysis tools, biomedical syringes.  If we use non-PFAS substances, the reduced longevity of certain simple parts such as sealants and hoses would significantly increase the amount of service required worldwide for our customers. This increases the costs as well as the environmental impact.    Specifically, we have hydrofluoric acid etching tools that are made of PTFE. PTFE wafer carrier are needed, the substitute (PU) would float in the chemistry due to a lower density. The hoses and sealing rings made of PTFE are exceptionally resistant to the corrosive and extremely toxic chemicals. Less resistant materials will lead to more exposure, possible accidents, possible spillage into the environment with devastating consequences. The currently proposed restrictions would make it impossible to get needed spare parts.    Fiber lasers consist of optical fibers that rely on fluorinated cladding to achieve low refractive index (n < 1.41 for industrial applications and n < 1.375 for most laser applications) and high Young’s modulus (E > 100 MPa).  Polyfluorinated silane coatings on glass give specific properties that have not been able to be reproduced with other silanes.  Finding replacements or substitutes will take years of development, the costs of which are unknown. The required resources will significantly obstruct current and new developments, especially due to the very short transition period.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a major manufacturer of rigid gas-permeable (RGP) contact lenses which are used for treating patients with complicated eye conditions. The maximum amount of PFAS released in the environment by our company is 5 kg per year. All RGP lens materials contain fluoropolymers, and there are no alternatives whatsoever, even at the experimental stage. The restriction on the use of PFAS in RGP lenses will make the use of RGP lenses impossible. This means that 250,000 patients in the EU, who now wear RGP contact lenses, would lose access to treatment. Based on the evidence-based impact assessment and analysis of alternatives presented in the attachment, a broad restriction for the use of PFAS in rigid gas permeable (RGP) contact lenses would lead to unacceptable costs for the European society and negatively impact the EU economy.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Medical devices (use sector); rigid gas permeable (RGP) contact lenses (sub-use).

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Our industrial waste is collected separately, packed in UN-approved plastic lidded drums and disposed of at an appropriate treatment facility (incinerated). The total volume of waste related to manufacturing of RGP lenses is 394.74 kg per year, including 152.06 kg of PFAS waste.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Menicon, founded in 1951 in Japan, is an industry leader and pioneer in contact lens research and production. The company’s main business areas are contact lenses, contact lens care products, medical instruments and supplies, and intraocular lenses.  Fluoropolymers are present in any commercially available material used for manufacturing rigid gas-permeable (RGP) lenses, and, consequently, in these lenses. The total amount of PFAS released into the environment is estimated at a maximum of 5.1 kg annually. Based on the estimated market share of 40%, one may extrapolate that the aggregate release of PFAS into the environment is 12.7 kg per year from the total EEA RGP lenses market.   PFAS are not used in any other products made by Menicon, and have no other part in the manufacturing processes.   Fluorinated compounds are used to produce polymer rods, which are then cut into standard-sized buttons. This is done outside the EU. The buttons are then imported within the EU, where they are cut into lenses, with material carved into a lens and then polished. To make 100,000 RGP lenses, one kilogram of PFAS is necessary. On the average, around 500,000 RGP lenses are made by Menicon on a yearly basis for an estimated number of 250,000 patients. The proposed PFAS restriction would affect all of these RGP contact lenses and, consequently, lens care products for RGP lenses.   The average annual volume of materials used to produce RGP lenses is 400 kg. The exact amount of PFAS processed in 2022 was 157.16 kg, including 5.1 kg used in lenses (equivalence: 100,000 lenses per kg PFAS) and 152.06 kg of PFAS waste. Only a small amount of PFAS end in finished lenses, due to specific lens geometry; all the rest is collected separately and treated at a dedicated facility.  The primary functions of PFAS in RGP contact lenses are to secure oxygen permeability of the finished product and to protect it from fouling. Other critical function provided is hardness, which allows a lens to retain its shape, therefore providing a quality of vision superior to soft lenses. This combination of characteristics is unique and can’t be reproduced in soft hydrogel lenses.  Menicon has a vast experience with developing and implementing new lens materials and new lens designs. However, all the RGP projects accomplished by Menicon up to now have been based on availability of fluorinated compounds. We are also not aware of any research projects involving fluorine-free RGPs conducted by other companies or researchers.  The reason for this is that all commercially available RGP lenses rely on a combination of a silicone-based compound (for oxygen permeability) and a fluorinated compound (oxygen permeability, stable shape, anti-fouling). Silicones are known to attract deposits, and lens deposits reduce quality of vision and provoke eye infections. Adding a fluorinated compound is necessary to address this safety concern. Therefore, to develop a PFAS-free RGP lens, one needs to phase out both fluoropolymers and silicone-based compounds, which would be a huge task.  To identify any overlooked alternative, Menicon asked support from a company specialized in AI-enabled technologies/innovations scouting. An AI search specially designed to explore all available scientific literature and patents for a possible substitute was conducted. However, it did not reveal newly appeared options worth investigating. The analysis of alternatives (see attachment) therefore concludes that no viable substitute is available now or will be available in the foreseeable future.  An impact assessment, encompassing social and economic impacts, was also conducted (see attachment). The key conclusion was that a potential restriction on the use of fluoropolymers in RGP lenses would have disproportionate socio-economic implications, with overall direct impact on our company monetised at more than 50 M (see confidential attachment for details). This is a conservative estimate (lower bound). There would also be significant adverse wider economic impacts (e.g., impacts on competition, innovations, and R&D).   In the most likely “non-use” scenario, Menicon will have no other option but to halt the production of RGP lenses in the EEA. This is because PFASs are integral components for the lens blanks that are used to manufacture RGP contact lenses. The market for RGP contact lenses will therefore become minimal and have no prospects for the future as a consequence of a PFAS ban. Lens care products will also be negatively affected.   A potential PFAS restriction would disturb the distribution of Menicon’s products and would therefore also negatively affect Menicon’s distributors and many downstream customers, which are located in the EEA countries.  This means that there would be significant reductions in the quality of life for RGP contact lens users. Despite the dominance of soft lenses in the market, RGP contact lenses are either the only viable option or offer superior visual outcomes for individuals with specific eye and medical conditions. In addition, a large group of current RGP contact lens wearers cannot switch to alternatives such as soft lenses because they do not sufficiently correct visual acuity.   Based on the impact assessment and analysis of alternatives (see attachment), there is a reasonable justification for requesting a time-unlimited derogation to continue using critical PFAS in RGP contact lenses.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a manufacturer and developer of hydraulic compo-nents such as pumps, valves, cylinders and volume flow me-ters as well as mass flow meters, for a wide range of applica-tions, such as regenerative power generation, chemical indus-try, machine tools, marine applications, mining, etc.
Since only certain group members of the PFAS group have been assessed in the proposal, but all of them have been classified as hazardous, we consider this disproportionate, particularly in the light of the fact that there is no possibility to extend the exemptions to be authorised for the duration foreseen until now if no marketable alternatives to PFAS are available.
The predicted concentrations in the environment also appear questionable in view of the proposal's authors' own assessment that there are no forecasting instruments. A well-founded scientific investigation at this point seems necessary, as the socio-economic effects of this ban in the EU are very far-reaching.


- Scope and restriction analysis
The present report proposal includes a large number of sectors and uses for products containing PFASs but lacks sectors and uses that affect our company and as many others. This has also been the case in previous consultations and has made it very difficult to provide information and data that only partially fit into the predefined categories.
PFAS are used in many machinery components such as seals, O-Rings, shaft seals, gaskets, hoses and pipes.
These components are used in a wide range of sectors in Report Annex XV and beyond.
For our company, seals made of fluoropolymers such as FKM, FFKM, FEP, PTFE and others of the PFAS group are of extreme importance. These seals are often used in contact with various mineral or synthetic oils and have to withstand extreme temperatures (high and low temperature) far beyond the thermal resistance of PFAS-free rubbers such as NBR. This also applies to use with chemicals such as hydrocarbons, acids and bases and their direct contact. These materials of the PFAS group are almost gas-tight and are therefore used in applications where either any leakage of the pumped medium into the environment or external contamination must be avoided. These safety aspects make materials of the PFAS group indispensable as sealing materials in pumps, valves, hydraulic measuring systems, cylinders and others.
PFAS Group materials are also used to reduce friction and wear, thus extending the life of products and improving efficiency (reducing energy consumption).
Furthermore, we use multi-material coatings in form of nickel hard coatings with embedded PTFE to reduce wear and thus extend product life and reduce waste.


- Hazard and exposure
Based on the use as seals, there is no exposure to humans or the environment.
As a component of coatings, they significantly reduce the coefficient of friction and thus contribute considerably to minimizing friction and thus to reducing the energy requirement of the pumps and likewise to minimizing wear and extending the service life of the products and thus to conserving resources.


- Environmental emissions
Fluoropolymers used in hydraulics and in components for conveying fluids in chemical plants do not emit any emissions into the environment .
With their high chemical resistance (inertness), thermal stability and good sealing function (barrier function), fluoropolymers ensure that no substances hazardous to humans or the environment can escape.
Thus, fluoropolymers make a significant contribution to the protection of humans and the environment.
Information on alternatives
See details/comments under "Information on benefits".
Information on benefits

-- Seals:
The sealing material FKM is the most commonly used for feed pumps, this can be explained by the unique properties of this sealing material. These seals can be used in a wide temperature range, which is only surpassed by PTFE at over 200°C for high temperatures. In the extremely low temperature range (-40°C) there is no substitute for FFKM, which is used as standard in oil supply systems in wind turbines. Silicone shaft seals cannot be used there because they are not compatible with the PAO oils used to protect the rotor bearings, as they show too much wear and are unsafe in sealing the shafts, which would mean a significant increase in maintenance measures. Other sealing materials cannot be considered due to the weather requirements of such wind turbines and were replaced by FFKM seals years ago.
Regardless of the application of the gaskets, we as users of gaskets from the PFAS group are dependent on the research and developments of the gasket manufacturers and their raw material suppliers and we can therefore not give any information on the time frame for the new development of alternative gaskets and materials. After the seal manufacturers have made such alternative seals available, we will need 3 to 5 years to test and release these seals in the individual applications. In addition, a trial phase, the duration of which is unknown to us, must be expected at our customers until the final release and market maturity, which is partly prescribed by EU directives.
Due to the universality of the materials from the PFAS group, it is to be expected that the alternative materials to be developed will no longer have the same broad properties of the fluoropolymers. Therefore, the products in which these alternatives are incorporated will also have less broad application capabilities, lower chemical and thermal resistance, which will lead to increased energy requirements and increased waste quantities, as these products will have shorter service life and application ranges.
Therefore, our customers have to expect earlier failures and higher maintenance requirements (shorter maintenance intervals). Likely our customers also have to implement the process changes in their plants and systems, as the advantageous properties of fluoropolymers will no longer be present.
An important aspect is also the future supply of spare parts for existing plants and systems. If future products equipped with alternative PFAS-free materials will no longer be 1:1 interchangeable, a considerable additional effort will be necessary when these products have to be replaced. For this reason, a special regulation regarding the supply of spare parts to our customers is absolutely necessary, as our products have a much longer service life than the transition periods provided for in the REACH regulation.
The safety aspect must also be kept in mind, as the available but functionally limited alternatives lead to higher risks for workers, users and the environment, for example in the case of leakage from plants by aggressive toxic and other volatile substances. Also the risk of fire, e. g. in the event of fuel leakage, including alternative fuels such as eFuils, especially on ships. The regulations in force from the IMO and the shipping registers speak a clear language and make the use of alternative materials impossible at the moment.

-- Bearings:
PTFE and PVDF are used as a running layer in plain bearings and are offered by various manufacturers worldwide in this type of design. These low-maintenance to maintenance-free bearing bushings are standard components for all pump manufacturers; we do not have a unique position here. Due to the special properties of PTFE and PVDF, permanent lubrication is achieved even at speeds at which no hydrodynamic lubrication occurs. Alternatives to these bearing bushings are, for example, lead-alloyed bearing materials, which are actually no alternative, as lead is carcinogenic and is regulated by the RoHS Directive. Similarly, lead is not an approved alloying metal in shipping by the IMO. For years, lead has been properly replaced as an alloying component in bearing bushes by PTFE and PVDF, but this has led to further dependence on these materials. Other oil-impregnated bearing bushings are not an alternative for feed pumps, as fluids are pumped that do not tolerate contamination. For example Applications are the chemical and pharmaceutical industries, the food industry, the plastics industry and others, and the manufacture of blades for wind turbines is affected in the same way. Thus, the regulation of PTFE in combination with PFAS would have a direct impact on the EU's Green Deal.
The same applies to bearings as to seals, we cannot give any information on the duration of research and development of alternative bearing materials as users and consumers of such bearings. After alternative materials are made available to us by the bearing industry, we would need 3 to 5 years in close cooperation with our customers to test them. As with the seals, we have to calculate with an unknown duration of the customer's testing on the component basis of the new materials and their approval for the bearings. Here the focus will be particularly on the service life of the bearings, since the usual long service life of up to 30,000 h and in more and more cases even 60,000 h of a plain bearing bush with PTFE no longer seem possible.
In this context, the mechanical efficiency of pumps and hydraulic motors will also have to be considered. The extremely good and low coefficients of friction of fluoropolymers improve the energy consumption of the systems in the area of bearings to an unattainable extent. This has to be seen especially in the context of the EU-wide Green Deal, as these hydraulic components are widely used and thus, even if they have only measurably small differences in energy consumption per component, will lead to a significant change in energy consumption across the multitude of products in the EU as well as worldwide. In short, the CO2 footprint will inevitably increase.
The safety aspect of bearings must also and especially be taken into consideration, as major damage is to be expected here in particular. The fuel pumps, and this also applies to alternative fuels such as ethanol, methanol, ammonia or hydrogen, require a high level of reliability, especially in ship propulsion systems, as a failure and the associated damage to the ship can lead to incalculable environmental damage. This also applies to pumps in the drive area of chemical plants, which can also cause serious damage.

-- Multi-material coating:
These nickel hard coatings with embedded PTFE are applied true to contour in a chemical process and thus without electricity. This unique process brings together the positive properties of the two components nickel and PTFE. Thus, the metal nickel provides the hard metal matrix to achieve the necessary structural robustness, and the embedded PTFE particles provide their characteristic non-stick, friction and heat resistance. Thus, this multi-material coating has a wide applicability due to its special characteristics of hardness and sliding properties, which are indispensable in many applications in hydraulic pumps, especially in feed pumps. At the moment, no materials are known that can replace these PTFE particles 1:1 in multi-component coatings.
In small sub-segments, MoS2 or graphite can substitute PTFE under certain conditions of use. However no industrial processes are known in which these alternative particles are used so that their direct use is limited.
At this point, as the end user of such coatings we must refer to the supplier industry of such coatings Considerable development and research efforts will be necessary to develop substitute multilayer systems and offer them on an industrial level. Therefore a realistic estimation of the time frame of such a development is not possible from our side. After the introduction of such coatings we will need between 3 and 5 years for testing and release in our company, and downstream our customers will need a time for component testing and series release that we cannot estimate.
Since these coatings are often used in the sector of bearings the same applies to them as already mentioned for the bearing bushings regarding energy consumption respectively the CO2 footprint and the safety aspects.


- Other socio-economic (SEA) issues
The socio-economic impacts are difficult or impossible to estimate due to the strong interdependence and mutual dependencies between manufacturers of hydraulic components and the chemical industry. Without the materials of the chemical industry, it would not be possible to manufacture the hydraulic components that are needed to produce these materials (PFAS-containing or PFAS-free). However, this does not only apply to the chemical industry as hydraulic components are used by all actors along the entire supply chain/manufacturing process.
Pumps and hydraulic components are also used in environmental protection and in waste and recycling management. The impact of limited availability of these components on these sectors of the economy and especially on environmental protection cannot be quantified because it cannot be predicted.
This assessment is applicable to all sectors of industry, so it is regrettable that the restriction dossier does not reflect this and that many sectors are not covered. Thus, the preferred approach of the restriction dossier to create application-oriented exemptions seems questionable. For such an approach, much more numerous and more detailed sectors need to be defined. The current proposal only represents European industry and the economy in a very rudimentary way. Therefore, it is unlikely that an economic and thus socially acceptable restriction of the PFAS group will be achieved, as the current layout of the restriction dossier will rather amount to a generalist ban. It is therefore of great importance that the restriction dossier is significantly revised in these areas.
In the current version of the restriction dossier the PFAS group will be effectively banned. Without sufficient alternative materials with the same properties, costs in Europe will increase significantly and will inevitably have an impact on consumer prices.
Similarly, without globally binding agreements on PFAS regulation, this increase in costs will make European industry less competitive, leading to a reduction in gross national product in Europe.
This cost increase is not limited to the hydraulic components industry. Due to the interdependencies described above and the very probable functional limitations of the substitute materials, there will be shorter component lifetimes and thus shorter maintenance intervals for plants and systems, with the consequences of longer production downtimes and increased production costs.
Directives such as the RoHS Directive can only be fulfilled with fluoropolymers in the case of bearings. Substitute materials such as lead banned by the RoHS Directive or oil-impregnated bearing materials are not alternatives. Here, as in the case of seals, science-based basic research with downstream industrial research must be carried out until these substitute products are ready for the market. The transitional periods proposed in the restriction dossier are very likely to be far too short, especially if component testing and their release have to be added.
The research and development capacities required for this will inevitably be lost for the Green Deal. The described increase in the CO2 footprint and the higher energy demand due to increased friction in the components even fundamentally counteracting to the Green Deal. This situation is further exacerinbated by the fact that PFAS-containing seals and bearings are essential for wind power and other renewable energy production. Thus, Europe is in double risk of not completing the Green Deal.
A similar picture can be seen in the shipping sector. Here there are regulations of the registry companies that prescribe the mandatory use of fluoropolymers in the drive train. Changing these regulations takes a very long time and is only possible through worldwide coordination. A quick ban on fluoropolymers would exclude the European shipbuilding industry and its suppliers from this market for the foreseeable future. This shows once again the extraordinary importance of a comprehensive agreement extending beyond the EU to ban the PFAS group.

Content: Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption

General Comments: We are a manufacturer and importer of medical devices and personal protective equipment for healthcare sector, whose customers include hospitals and healthcare providers allover the Europe (incl.WHO).
