Content: Baseline Information on alternatives Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a manufacturer of electrical heat tracing systems using a variety of fluoropolymers in all kind of specific heating solutions for the industry, e. g. heating cables/tapes, self-regulating trace heaters, heated hoses, and heating mats/jackets. These systems are used to heat pipes, valves, vessels, tanks, silos, antennas, etc. either to maintain a specific temperature or for freeze protection. In addition, heat tracing components play a vital role in the European Union’s ongoing efforts to secure energy supply as well as implementing the European Green Deal as they are used within heat pumps, during manufacturing of wind energy systems, they are vital for fuel cells and hydrogen production, storage and distribution just to name a few.

Often, very specific requirements have to be met, e. g. maintaining the process temperature of a medium within a certain range to either prevent the heated media from solidifying again, but also to prohibit overheating to prevent thermal degradation of the medium and to limit surface temperatures – which is especially important in explosive atmospheres.

Nearly all electrical heat tracing systems rely on fluoropolymers. Heating elements, electrical insulations and tubes made from PTFE, PFA, FEP, ETFE and PVDF. Obviously, these fluoropolymers are used because of their known outstanding temperature resistance in combination with their mechanical properties. Of course, there are polymers with similar temperature resistances, but they lack the mechanical properties needed, e. g. PEEK has similar continuous use temperatures as PFA or PTFE, but is way too rigid to be used for example as a cable insulation. Furthermore, electrical heating systems are often used in chemical of petrochemical plants and therefore rely on the chemical resistance properties of fluoropolymers. Moreover, some user applications additionally demand for non-flammability, UV-resistance, biological resistance, or safety for food contact.

In our ongoing R&D-efforts we failed to find suitable replacements that show similar thermo-mechanical properties of fluoropolymers and match our applications needs. This applies especially for applications that are not only subject to our industry standards for electrical heat tracing systems (e. g. IEC 62395) but for applications specifically for use in explosive environments (IEC 60079-30) posing even higher demands on material performance and safety.

Banning all fluoropolymers would affect all of our business segments, only a small fraction of our products would be unaffected, which anyhow would likely equate to going out of business for our company. Since electrical heat tracing is used in numerous applications throughout the whole industry, the production of an incalculable number of products would be affected or simply not be possible anymore. We therefore request an exemption of all fluoropolymer-based applications.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: As a producer of electrical heat tracing systems, we use a variety of fluoropolymers in heating cables/tapes, self-regulating trace heaters, heated hoses, heating mats/jackets. Electrical heat tracing systems are used for either freeze protection or to maintain a specific temperature.  Although heat tracing systems primarily may be subsumed into the “Electronics and semiconductor” and “petrol and mining” -sector according to the Annex XV restriction report (Table 9), their manifold use extends throughout the industry as a whole, to name but a few (non-exhaustive enumeration):  Chemical and petrochemical industry: Electrical heat tracing is used to keep pipelines, tanks, vessels and other equipment at a constant temperature. This is done in order to prevent frost damage, maintain the viscosity of liquids and ensure the smooth operation of chemical processes.  Oil and gas industry: Electrical heat tracing plays an important role in the transportation of oil and gases such as LPG/LNG or H2 through pipelines. It is used to control the viscosity of the media, prevent clogging due to wax formation or condensation and improve transport efficiency.  Food and beverage industry: Electrical heat tracing is used for various applications, such as thawing food, maintaining proper storage temperatures, temperature control in fermentation processes, and handling of chocolate and fat (e.g. transportation through pipes).  Pharmaceutical industry: Electrical trace heating is used to control the temperature in processes such as mixing, drying, distillation and fermentation. This ensures the quality and efficacy of the medicines produced and enables compliance with strict GMP guidelines.  Building services: Electrical trace heating is used to prevent frost damage to water pipes, gutters, drainage systems and underfloor heating. It is also used for snow melting on pavements and driveways and for temperature control in heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems.  Power generation: In power generation, especially in power plants and heat transfer facilities, electric heat tracing plays an important role in maintaining the operating temperature of piping, condensers, heat exchangers and turbines. This helps to improve efficiency and operational safety. Electrical heat tracing is used to protect critical components such as valves, pumps and measuring instruments from freezing or condensing. This ensures the smooth functioning of power stations, solar power plants, wind turbines, electrolysers, heat pumpos, fuel cells and other energy generation systems.  Transportation: Electrical trace heating is used for freeze prevention in rails and switch points to ensure safe railway traffic.  Research and Development / Academics: Whenever specific temperature requirements have to be met during development, electrical heat tracing is used. This ranges from heating specific component (e.g. vacuum chambers or pipelines) to systems for the use in heated hoses in gas analysis. Another example in research is the use of electrical heating technology in particle accelerators.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Emissions resulting from the end-of-life phase were topic of a study by Gehrmann et al. (see non-confidential annex 03 in Section IV). Their motivation was based on the Conversio-study which has shown that “at its end-of-life approximately 85 % of all fluoropolymers end up in waste-to-energy recovery incinerators” (Conversio-study can be acquired via “https://www.pro-kunststoff.de/fachwissen/conversio-studie-end-of-life-von-fluorpolymeren.html”).  The scope of their study was the question whether fluoropolymers get fully incinerated without any formation of short chain of long chain PFAS. The study “demonstrated that fluoropolymers are converted to inorganic fluorides and carbon dioxide” and they concluded that “the results confirm that fluoropolymers at their end of life when incinerated under representative European municipal incinerators conditions do not generate any measurable levels of PFAS emissions and therefore pose no risk to human health and the environment.  Additionally, Aleksandrov et al. already concluded in 2019 specific for PTFE that “municipal incineration of PTFE shows no significant generation of studied PFAS (see non-confidential annex 04 in Section IV).

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Concerning the effectiveness of fluoropolymer incineration, we would like to reference to the ongoing research project by the Federal Institute for Materials Research and Testing (BAM) and the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT), funded by the German Federal Environment Agency:   “Basic investigations on thermochemical degradation of PFAS in laboratory and pilot plants to determine optimum combustion conditions for the thermal treatment of PFAS-containing waste materials.” (see non-confidential annex 05 in Section IV)

6. Missing uses: As already has been proven by chemical analysis of our polymer supplier (see information request no. 2), fluoropolymers have no evidence of PFAS emission during the use in any application or at sub-sector level.  Estimated there will be around 100 of our customers in European industry with more than 100.000 employees in sum that will be directly affected.  Substitution is technically not feasible.  Alternatives to the fluoropolymers PTFE, PFA, FEP and ETFE will not be available for the usage of cable products in chemical industry applications. Further information s. information request no. 8.  The socio-economic value of electrical trace heating is manifold and depends on the respective application. Improving production output, safeguarding jobs, reducing environmental impact and maintaining infrastructure are some of the benefits that directly result from the use of electric trace heating.   Banning all fluoropolymers means also producing or using less safe, reliable and durable fluid handling equipment in chemical processes, pharmaceutical processes and in oil and gas industry, more prone to risk of leakages that can expose workers that operating on site to a major risk of serious injuries or short/long term health diseases, derived by came in contact with hazardous/dangerous media.  Leakage coming from fluid handling equipment (pumps) can have adverse effects also on the environment, when moving hazardous, corrosive or dangerous fluids. Banning all fluoropolymers and having thus less reliable equipment, lead to a major risk of fluid handling equipment (pumps and gaskets) leakage, worsening the environmental footprint of chemical, pharmaceutical and oil & gas process plants.  The scope of socio-economic impact cannot be estimated because the complete chemical industry will primarily be affected. Till today safe and effective industrial production processes have to be developed new from the beginning with the acceptance of big setbacks and company closures. In many cases no alternative way of safe trace-heating will be possible. The final impact on chemical industry will result in a dramatical socio-economic dismantling with the risk of a total collapse of the chemical industry and secondary branches.

8. Other identified uses: Our company provides industry with safety cable products for explosion-proof areas. Only the unique properties of fluoropolymers nowadays fulfil the high standards required by the DIN EN IEC 60079-0:2019-09 and DIN EN 60079-30-1:2018-04 (Explosive atmospheres - Part 30-1: Electrical resistance trace heating - General and testing requirements, see appendix) for trace heating in explosive areas.  Electrical heating in explosive areas (regulated by the ATEX/IECEx directives) will not be possible without usage of safety proofed self-limiting heating cables or resistance heating cables containing fluoropolymers. Banning fluoropolymers will result in unsafe and high-risks chemical industry when especially explosive areas are concerned. This reasons why in industrial environments electrical heat tracing ensures workplace safety.   By preventing frost damage or condensation, overheating of cables and consequently burning of plants only can be prevented by inflammable and temperature save heating cables containing PTFE, PFA, ETFE or FEP. Only the outstanding properties of fluoropolymers with a very low coefficient of friction and wear or rub makes them durable, especially in dynamic applications.  With the use of fluoropolymers accident and pollution risks are minimised. In addition, heat tracing enables the safe operation of equipment and components in extreme environments or during critical processes.  In many industrial processes where food or beverage needs to be heated to certain temperatures our cable products out of fluoropolymer play an important role: For electrical heating of chocolate, cooking oil or edible fats or other fluids that have to maintain a certain temperature to be processable our heating cables keep processes running. In contact with food or beverage, similar to medical applications, only fluoropolymers are suitable to meet the high hygienic requirements. Our products, especially in pharmaceutical and food industry, will not exist if PFAS and PFA, FEP and FEP will be banned. Many processes will have to be renewed to keep processes running and to keep the standards for hygiene and cleanliness in contact with food or medicals in future. We confirmed by our own research and tests according to IEC 60079-30-1:2015 that there is no suitable alternative material.   For industrial process-control it is necessary to analyse continuously samples of gases or liquids. We produce heated hoses containing tubes out of fluoropolymers that transport samples (of gas or liquid) to the analysing system. Using different materials as fluoropolymers will result in persistent contaminations inside the analytical tubes for sampling and this will consequently result in wrong analyses.  Therefore, a secure control of many industrial processes will not be possible in future without fluoropolymers. This firstly has an impact on producers of analytical instruments and finally on the entire chemical industry. Consequently, emission monitoring in industry has to be new developed from the start. Otherwise contamination of the environment cannot be hindered in future because processes and hazardous emissions get out of control.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a manufacturer of fluid control equipment established in 1982, and have contributed to the development of society by manufacturing and selling fluororesin precision equipment that enables the control of various chemical solutions required in the process of semiconductor manufacturing all over the world.
The PFAS restriction proposal issued by ECHA entirely restricts the use of various PFAS substances due to the persistent nature. It is clear that a blanket restriction of PFAS substances, which are indispensable for semiconductor manufacturing, would have a serious impact on the economy and society and we believe that, first of all, after carefully assessing the availability of alternatives, we should select from among more than 10,000 PFAS substances that are recognized to have an impact on human health and the environment through a risk assessment based on scientific evidence.
We support the statements of Conference of Fluoro-Chemical Product Japan (FCJ) and Japan Fluoropolymers Industry Association (JFIA), as shown in Attachments 1 and 2.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a manufacturer of fluorine resin films and earnestly comply with national chemical regulations while continuing our manufacturing and sales. We support the EU's efforts to reduce the risks associated with hazardous substances.
However, after having read carefully about contents of the restriction plan of PFAS proposed this time, we confirmed that there is not a concrete and detailed description about the fluorine resin films used for molding processing of the fiber reinforced plastic (FRP) as an important use in Annex A : manufacture and uses of Annex XV restriction report. Among the FRP, carbon-fiber reinforced plastic (CFRP) is used for the material of aircrafts because of its lightweight property together with high strength and modulus. CFRP is representative material contributing to light-weighting of the aircrafts, and CFRP greatly contributes to saving energy such as the fossil fuel in terms of the fuel economy improvement, and so it is thought as a material which is extremely important now and for the future.
The method to prepare the high-performance type of CFRP used in such aircrafts is called “autoclave method”, and the process to cure the matrix resin (represented by epoxy resin) of CFRP needs high temperature and pressure conditions (the autoclave method is known as a method to make high-performance CFRP among various CFRP molding methods). In the process of autoclave method, because the release film should be covered on the half-cured and so sticky article called prepreg and then prepreg is heat cured in autoclave after given shapes if necessary. The fluorine resin film has been used as release film because of its excellent mold release property and heat resistance. See the attached reference of the process figure.
The polymer types of the fluorine resin films used in this process mainly include ETFE, FEP and PFA. Development trials of the substitution to cheaper resin films have been attempted repetitively since before this PFAS restriction plan has been proposed because these fluorine resins are expensive, but it is the current situation that changes to other materials are not yet done. As a reason, the autoclave method is necessary to secure reliability such as the mechanical strength for the CFRP used in aircrafts, and the film having performance to endure the autoclave method is only the fluorine resin films.
Also, fluorine resin films applied for the autoclave method are not used by general customers　and are used indoors such as industrial factories and other facilities by manufacturers and disposed properly. Therefore, they are not released into the environment unless there is malicious intent. In addition, if the films are washed clean and re-melted, the obtained resins are reusable as fluorine resin films because of their excellent recyclability.
Based on the above, there is a very high possibility that alternative substances to this PFAS will not be a complete replacement due to their impracticality and so they should not be considered as viable substitutes in the CFRP process. Therefore, it is important to understand the significance of fluorine resin films in the CFRP process, and they should be exempted from this proposed restriction of PFAS.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a manufacturer of fluoropolymers (PTFE, PFA, ECTFE, etc.) and fluoroelastomers (FKM, FFKM, etc.).
We provide products made of fluoropolymers (PTFE, PFA and ECTFE, etc.) and fluoroelastomers (FKM, FFKM, etc.).
Our fluoropolymer products are used in many industries and for many different applications.

For example, the following are some of the areas in which fluorochemicals are used in equipment.
Fluorine products are used in:Petroleum refineries and petrochemicals, thermal and nuclear power plants, LNG terminals and other energy-related equipment, electronic components, environmental, medical, food, and electronics-related industries, semiconductor manufacturing, semiconductor manufacturing equipment peripheral equipment, automobiles and automotive parts, etc.

In addition, fluoropolymers and fluororubbers have superior characteristics to other general resins and rubbers, such as chemical resistance, heat resistance, and low permeability, making them one of the indispensable materials for each application, as there are no easy substitutes.

The characteristics of fluoropolymers and fluororubbers are shown in [Ref.1].

Reference 1: Properties of Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers

For example, even if we substitute general materials as described in [Ref.1], the long-term performance of equipment and facilities cannot be guaranteed due to their different characteristics, and the shortened life cycle may lead to an increase in waste related to the equipment and facilities, or in the worst case, a disaster due to damage or leakage accidents that may endanger human lives. In the worst case scenario, a disaster could occur due to damage or leakage, which could result in loss of life.

Therefore, if the proposed PFAS restrictions currently under consideration are enacted as is, it is expected to have a serious impact on many industries.

Therefore, we support JFIA and FCJ position [Ref.2] on the Proposed PFAS Restrictions.

And for the proposed PFAS restrictions being considered, we believe that the proposed PFAS regulations should distinguish between PFAS with specific hazards (PFAS that generate PFAAs and PFAAs) and non-hazardous fluoropolymers (fluoropolymers and fluoro-elastomers).

Reference 2: Position Paper on the Proposed European PFAS Regulation

Furthermore, fluoropolymers also meet the OECD's criteria of low concern [*1],
They are non-toxic and biocompatible and are therefore considered by the OECD to be safe for human health and the environment.
Therefore, we believe that fluoropolymers should be used without being restricted by PFAS regulations.

[*1] OECD, 2006 OECD Definition of Polymers OECD Environmental, Health and Safety Publications.
Available at: https://www.oecd.org/env/ehs/oecddefinitionofpolymer.htm


Therefore, we request a review of the proposed PFAS restrictions under consideration and an exemption for fluoropolymers from the proposed restrictions.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a manufacturer of medical devices and care for the wellbeing of our patients in every aspect. This covers our
direct role as a provider of products to facilitate diagnostics and therapy. But also as part of the
society and individual citizens we care for the environment and are concerned about chemicals accumulating in
nature and humans.
As medical device manufacturers we are part of an industry with long and complex supply chains. From what we
know it is very likely that among the many parts we purchase from our direct suppliers there are parts that either
contain PFAS or where PFAS are involved during the manufacturing process.
During the consultation period it was not possible for us to perform a complete and thorough analysis, which of our
parts and components would be affected by a potential ban of PFAS. We as a medium enterprise, order
very low volumes of materials compared to consumer product companies or the automotive industry, but
nevertheless require high quality products and many proofs for regulatory purposes. This results in a very low impact
and priority with our suppliers. As a manufacturer we do not purchase PFAS directly. As the knowledge which parts,
components or processes involve PFAS often is not available at our direct supplier but is only available further
upstream in the supply chain, gathering information is a time consuming and sometimes futile endeavor. This
absence of support is hard to show as supporting evidence.
Publicly available information show that metal parts (e.g. with friction reduction surface treatment), certain polymer
parts or electronics containing PTFE, PVDF, PFA or PFPE or using these polymers during manufacturing would be
subject to the ban. This will result in major efforts to replace these materials, while even the major chemical
companies do not provide or promise replacement materials in the foreseeable future. Even when those would be
available at some point in the future the effort to introduce the replacement within engineering is calculated by us
to be 2 to 3 years with further 3 years to validate their application in medical devices. The necessary change control
and gathering of clinical data is strongly enforced by the notified bodies following EU regulation. As there are presently
no replacement materials available the cost of engineering and validation cannot be calculated to be presented as
supporting evidence.
It is very likely that following a PFAS ban as planned many of the medical devices listed below under “1 Sectors and
(sub-)uses” will be discontinued and be no longer available for patients benefit. Even with the maximum derogation
time a timely replacement of PFAS and uninterrupted availability is far from sure.
For us as an SME medical device manufacturer it is impossible to give detailed substantiated information on the
alternatives and efforts needed after a complete ban of PFAS. However, the very likely consequence will be a
discontinuation of medical devices that are in daily use all over Europe!

This covers our direct role as a provider of in-vitro diagnostic PCR kits to facilitate diagnostics and therapy. But also as part of the society and individual citizens we care for the environment and are concerned about chemicals accumulating in nature and humans.
As medical in-vitro diagnostics PCR kit manufacturer we are part of an industry with long and complex supply chains. From what we know it is very likely that among the many instruments and parts we purchase from our direct suppliers there are parts that either contain PFAS or where PFAS are involved during the manufacturing process.

During the consultation period it was not possible for us to perform a complete and thorough analysis, which of our instrument parts and in-vitro diagnostic PCR kit components would be affected by a potential ban of PFAS. We as a small and medium enterprise, order very low volumes of materials compared to consumer product companies or the automotive industry, but nevertheless require high quality products and many proofs for regulatory purposes. This results in a very low impact and priority with our suppliers. As a manufacturer we do not purchase PFAS directly. As the knowledge which diagnostic instrument parts and PCR Kit components possibly involving PFAS often is not available at our direct supplier but is only available further upstream in the supply chain, gathering information is a time consuming and sometimes futile endeavor. This absence of support is hard to show as supporting evidence.

Publicly available information show that metal parts, certain polymer parts or electronics containing PTFE, PVDF, PFA or PFPE or using these polymers during manufacturing would be subject to the ban. This will result in major efforts to replace these materials, while even the major chemical companies do not provide or promise replacement materials in the foreseeable future. Even when those would be available at some point in the future the effort to introduce the replacement within engineering is calculated by us to be 2 to 3 years with minimum further 3 years to validate their application in medical in-vitro diagnostics products. The necessary change control and gathering of clinical data is strongly enforced by the notified bodies following EU regulation. As there are presently no replacement materials available the cost of engineering and validation cannot be calculated to be presented as supporting evidence.

It is very likely that following a PFAS ban as planned many of the medical in-vitro diagnostics products listed below under “1 Sectors and (sub-)uses” will be discontinued and be no longer available for patients benefit. Even with the maximum derogation time a timely replacement of PFAS and uninterrupted availability is far from sure.
For us as an SME medical in-vitro diagnostics PCR kit manufacturer it is impossible to give detailed substantiated information on the alternatives and efforts needed after a complete ban of PFAS. However, the very likely consequence will be a discontinuation of medical in-vitro diagnostics PCR kit for PCR diagnostics of e.g. new variants of SARS CoV19 and many other pathogenis viruses that are in daily use all over Europe!

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Sector: Medical in-vitro diagnostic PCR Kits. We request that  "In-vitro diagnostic PCR Kits /  ca. 10.000 Kits (100 PCR tests each) in 2019-2021"  be newly added to derogation as missing uses.

6. Missing uses: As already stated in the general comments, the medical in-vitro diagnostic PCR Kits listed under 1. Sectors and (sub-)uses are very likely affected by a PFAS ban, as their development, production and application requires plastic consumables and PCR instruments consist of parts and materials listed in many other sectors covered in the Restriction Report e.g. electronics or coated metal parts. Missing these products will very likely lead to a discontinuation of the listed medical in-vitro diagnostic PCR Kits and instruments after a PFAS ban. We therefore request the exemption or at least the maximum derogation period of 12 years for the products listed under 1. Sectors and (sub-)uses on the basis of the negative impact on patient care if said medical in-vitro diagnostic PCR Kits and instruments would be no longer available due to the non- availability of necessary pre-products and the time-consuming revalidation after technical changes.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a manufacturer of process control systems. High quality materials withstand the toughest process conditions including aggressive media, high-temperature and high-pressure applications. To withstand the toughest process conditions, we are also using fluoroelastomers for wetted seals such as Viton®, Kalrez®, Fluoraz® and Chemraz® made of FKM, FFKM and FEPM materials. Our process control systems play in vital role in:

1. Biotechnology and pharmaceutical industries
2. Chemical and petrochemical industries
3. Industrial food and food production
4. Diagnostic laboratory or industrial equipment
5. Petroleum and mining

Our customers' applications range from pharmaceutical research and production (insulin and vaccine production) to industrial and commercial food production. Here a general exception, which is independent of the target market, is desirable. As a producer and supplier, we cannot categorize our customers according to their end use in order to supply these customers with our products in accordance with a possible exception or, under certain circumstances, to no longer be able to supply these customers after possible exceptions have expired. The restriction proposal is too broad. A structuring or subdivision of the more than 10,000 substances concerned, which have different intrinsic properties, is not recognizable. This generic approach is incomprehensible. While previous restriction procedures mostly concerned individual substances posing a known unacceptable risk and their use, here any kind of use is prohibited for an entire group of substances (over 10,000 individual substances).
In our view, it is highly critical that the EU regulatory authorities would like to combine and restrict all PFAS in one group for the purpose of accelerating and simplifying their regulatory processes. A comprehensive ban on PFASs, as proposed here, will of course have no impact on the continued comprehensive need for these PFASs. The group-based restriction proposal chosen here is also legally questionable. According to Article 69 of the Reach Regulation (EC 1907/2006), a substance-based approach is generally required. In addition, the otherwise usual risk-based restriction proposal according to Article 68(1) was disregarded here. The restriction of a substance in applications from which no risk emanates (fluoropolymers) is therefore, in our opinion, also outside the legal framework specified for and by the REACH Regulation. This comprehensive and indiscriminate approach and the accompanying ban on all PFAS substances would have a massive impact on European companies and their ability to innovate, proving counterproductive towards the ongoing drive for European sovereignty and the goal of independent supply chains.

Fluoroelastomers are harmless in their use and have no emissions themselves during their intended use. However, they prevent emissions of hazardous substances from industrial plants and thus make a significant contribution to environmental protection.
The proposed restriction does not differentiate between fluoropolymers (such as PVDF, ECTFE, FEP, PFA and PTFE as wells as fluoroelastomers – FPM, FFKM, …) and other PFAS. Fluoropolymers as well as fluorelastomers have unique properties that distinguish them from other PFAS while they do not have the environmental and toxicological profiles associated with other PFAS that are of concern.
Sealings cannot be changed simply by other materials. Currently there are no other alternatives for these demanding process conditions available. Meaning long-term testing of other materials would be necessary. What will happen if a new sealing fails during the process application and who will take the responsibility?
Therefore, our objection is to completely exclude fluoroelastomers as well as fluoropolymers completely from this regulation, as they are polymers / elastomers of low concern according to the OECD scheme.
Moreover, the proposed exemption for use with a transition period of 6.5 years is not far-reaching enough. Rather, monitoring and control instruments used by industry should be exempted from a general ban, or the longest possible transition period of 13.5 years should apply here. This deadline is necessary given the lack of substitution options and very onerous validation and qualification requirements in the Medical and Pharmaceutical, Petroleum and Mining, and Food Contact Materials sectors.
Industries such as Medical and Pharmaceutical, Petroleum and Mining and Food Contact Materials are highly regulated themselves by the FDA and USP regulations, and use fluoropolymers for their special properties. Successful Tests according to (USP 87, USP 88, USP 85, ISO 11737) and Chemical-physical tests (USP 661) are mandatory and certify the harmlessness of these substances.

6. Missing uses: a.) As a manufacturer of production and packaging systems, we are in the middle of the supply chain. Identifying the exact extent of the impact therefore represents a major challenge for us and is very time-consuming or, in many cases, not possible for us. The number of products in which the use of relevant PFAS is directly evident from the material or coating of the product turned out to be small in our analyzes based on the total amount of all parts. For this reason, it is not possible for us to carry out a quantitative analysis or extrapolation of the total annual tonnage of PFAS used in products. b.) Production and packaging systems for the medical technology sector as well as the food and pharmaceutical industries are often exposed to extreme conditions and have the highest demands on their functionality and process reliability as well as safety and cleanability. PFAS materials play an important role in a variety of applications and component groups. They are always used when extreme conditions prevail. If the alternatives have lower performance compared to materials containing PFAS, additional maintenance costs will arise, for example due to higher wear. e.) Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a manufacturer of pumps and valves for the chemical and petrochemical industries, making us one of the market leaders in these types of pumps.
Fluoropolymers (PTFE, FFKM, FEP) are generally used as the material for seals in our pumps and valves. These seals ensure that as little as possible of the fluids in the piping leak to the environment. They therefore make a significant contribution to the safety, durability and resource efficiency of modern industrial plants.
Our pumps and valves must meet the requirements of the TA-Luft (2021 edition). The pumps with the mentioned seals are considered as "technically tight pumps" according to TA-Luft section 5.2.6.1. The flange connections of these pumps must not exceed maximum leakage rates according to 5.2.6.3 of TA-Luft. To our knowledge, this requirement in connection with highly aggressive liquids under high temperature and pressure loads can only be met with high-quality PFAS sealing materials.
The sealing materials used are so far considered polymers of low concern and have corresponding USP Class VI certificates (see examples attached) by way of evidence. Another study that supports the non-toxicity of these materials is: Henry, B. J; Carlin, J. P; Hammerschmidt, J. A; Buck, R. C; Buxton, L W.; Fiedler, H.; Seed, J.; Hernandez, O. A Critical Review of the Application of Polymer of Low Concern and Regulatory Criteria to Fluoropolymers. Integr. Environ. Assess. Manage. 2018, 14 (3), 316−334.)
The assessment must also take into account that the pumps and valves mentioned are industrial goods and are not used by the end consumer. It must therefore be assumed that the products are handled professionally and responsibly in all phases of the life cycle.

6. Missing uses: Missing uses: Fluoropolymers as sealing material in pumps and valves for the chemical and petrochemical industry. The seals and gaskets meet the high requirements for minimal leakage at high pressures and temperatures, even with acids and alkalis. Pumps and valves must meet the high requirements for emissions, for example, of the TA-Luft (edition 2021). The seals and gaskets extend the service life of the pumps and valves and reduce emissions. In our opinion, the minimization of leakages and thus also of the risk to the environment and to people is to be rated higher than the theoretical risk due to the uncontrolled release tot he environment of PFAS from the seals. During the use of the pumps and fittings, no emissions of PFAS are conceivable, as they are encapsulated in the pumps and fittings. The chemical and petrochemical industries are generally professional users and have appropriate disposal channels, so that uncontrolled disposal to the environment is almost impossible. According to our information, controlled disposal is possible without release to the environment, since fluoropolymers can be disposed of at temperatures above 1100°C without leaving residues. Reference: Aleksandrov, K.; Gehrmann, H.-J.; Hauser, M.; Mätzing, H.; Pigeon, D.; Stapf, D.; Wexler, M.: Waste incinertion of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate potential formation of per- and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) in flue gas, KIT Karlsruhe 2019 As users of the seals and gaskets, we cannot develop alternative materials. However, we are in constant contact with the gasket manufacturers in order to be able to use alternatives if necessary. So far, however, alternatives are not in sight.

General Comments: We are a manufacturer of Secondary battery parts, especially for high-performance rechargeable Lithium-ion cells and batteries to be used within the for electric vehicle industry for the EU/EEA.

We would like to disagree on the current proposal of the PFAS ban.

We use PFAS-based materials in our production of seal gasket.

Today, this is the only available material to be used to manufacture a seal gasket that can meet up to the specifications of sealing capability, high mechanical reliability and thermal resistance at the same time and it is used to protect heating or cooling systems in electroplating as well.

Please refer to the attached Chemical, Physical, Thermal, Electrical and Mechanical properties, Flammability, Gas and Moisture permeability, Light transmissivity, and Heat aging resistance from our supplier [CONFIDENTIAL].

Without utility of PFAS, above listed products will malfunction and eventually it will bring injuries for passengers.

Also in medical technology in endoscopic instruments used for operations and new areas of application are added every day, as fluoroplastics have a significantly longer service life compared to conventional plastics, but at the same time are harmless to the body and the environment.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a manufacturer of sliding bearings used in seismic isolators for buildings, water treatment machinery, dam gates and many other mechanical devices. Our sliding bearings use PTFE as a solid lubricant. The performance requirements for PTFE include low friction, insulation, chemical resistance and heat resistance and there is no alternative with these material properties. If the use of PTFE is banned, the performance of the sliding bearings will be reduced. Our concerns are below four points:
1. The life of the sliding bearings will be reduced and the number of bearing replacements will increase. The running time of the machinery used to manufacture the sliding bearings will be increased, resulting in increased CO2 emissions.
2. In the event of natural disasters such as earthquakes and floods, equipment will not function properly, causing serious damage to human life, such as collapsing buildings and overflowing rivers.
3. Engines require more power and use more fuel, increasing CO2.
4. There are currently no materials with low friction properties comparable to PTFE - lubricant consumption will be increased. It cause River pollution and environmental damage.
PTFE is an essential material for a safe life. PTFE should therefore be excluded from the proposed ECHA restrictions.
We support the two opinions of the FCJ and the JFIA.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a manufacturer producing components such as shock absorbing products or power steering gears for transportation equipment (automotive, motorcycle, railway vehicles), and hydraulic equipment components (cylinders, pumps, motors) for construction/agricultural machinery. Various types of PFASs have been used in our products to ensure the required performance and endurance. See the attached file for more detail of our products.
While 12-year derogation is proposed in Annex E.2.10 for transportation equipment, we believe that this application should be excluded from the scope of restriction as it is thought to be difficult to achieve replacement of PFASs with alternatives. This is because there is no available alternatives at this moment, and the material manufacturers has not been able to determine how long it will take to develop them. Also, even if any alternatives are developed, it will take a huge amount of additional time to complete a whole replacement process after the development, i.e. evaluating the performance, approval from the customers, preparation of mass production and consideration of the entire supply chain. In automotive industry in particular, as there are numerous numbers of auxiliary components including repair parts of existing vehicles, it is assumed that it will take more than 10 years to just complete the replacement. If the restriction is put into force, component manufacturers will not be able to place those repair parts using PFASs into market, which means the end users (consumers) cannot make a necessary repair, leading to a huge amount of economic loss.
With regards to hydraulic equipment components for construction/agricultural machinery, while the restriction proposal does not clearly mention how this application is dealt with, we believe that this application should also be excluded from the scope of restriction since the situation is similar to that for transportation equipment in terms of the types of PFASs in the products, the use and function of them, and the social structure related to the products.
If those applications are within the scope of restriction, the end users of transportation equipment and construction/agricultural machinery will be affected by deterioration in quality (performance, lifetime and safety). This will cause a huge socioeconomic loss in terms of the cost of more frequent parts replacement or elevated possibility of accidents.
With the all stated above taken into consideration, we strongly request to exclude the components for transportation equipment and hydraulic equipment components in construction/agricultural machinery from the scope of restriction.

Content: Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a manufacturing company in the chemical industry using PFAS as Downstream User. We use PFAS mainly in seals and valves in all process plants.
Exposure to the environment from parts installed within a machine/plant is practically non-existent (e.g. seals). On the other hand, the substances and fluids which are in the plants and are kept there safely due to persistent and durable seals, are partly toxic for the environment and the health and safety of humans. Banning PFAS in sealants would lead to an increased safety and environmental risk in machines, plants and systems. We are depending on extremely durable sealings as we use some strong solvents which might get out of process as a leakage. The effort to maintain and replace seals more frequently due to shorter lifetime and functionality is not economic and implementable.
There are currently no alternatives to FKM seals or PTFE-coated parts on the market, which could replace the seals with the same effectivity. According to our suppliers, this will not be the case in the long term either.
A general PFAS ban would make chemical industry and mechanical engineering in Europe uncompetitive and thus bring it to a standstill. In our opinion, the result would be at least a severe recession, and in the worst case a global economic crisis with unforeseeable consequences.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: None of the sectors and (sub)uses mentioned. The area of mechanical and plant engineering in the chemical industry has not been sufficiently considered here.  With our comments, we refer to the sectors and applications mentioned under 6.

6. Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a non-EU based manufacturer and supplier of an essential military defence technology that relies on non-emissive use of PFAS that will require a derogation from the proposed restriction in order to avoid severe adverse effects on EU and EU member state defence capabilities.

We manufacture expendable infrared countermeasure technologies – missile decoy flares -- used on military aircraft.  Military aircraft are high intensity infrared targets, threatened by infrared guided missiles.  To thwart those missiles, aircraft use pyrotechnic decoy flares, which generate a highly exothermic reaction.  That exothermic reaction exhibits a specific thermal signal.  These so-called Magnesium/Teflon/Viton (MTV) flares are designed to generate a thermal flare that will divert attacking heat-seeking missiles.  MTV-based aerial countermeasures flares provide essential protection for military operations.

The thermal signal that is essential to the performance of these products specifically depends on a reaction between two elements: magnesium and fluorine.  The presence of fluorine is therefor an unavoidable necessity in the performance of this essential national defence product.
That fluorine is in turn required to be supplied by the presence of fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers at the ignition site, via the presence of PTFE and FKM as part of the pyrotechnic composition.  The use of PTFE and FKM provides a safe source of fluorine in the demanding military aviation environment for the required reactions.

We know of no other technically feasible and operationally safe option for supplying fluorine to the countermeasure reaction site other than via PFAS-containing materials, specifically (in our case) PTFE and FKM. Fluoropolymers and fluorinated elastomers, due to their inherent stability, resistance to chemical and thermal degradation, and low coefficient of friction, are the only molecules chemically compatible with all families of pyrotechnic mixtures.  Their use is required in order to ensure military-specified precision performance at the moment of deployment.

For all these reasons, the defence industry has been using these materials in pyrotechnic compositions, and in components which are in contact with pyrotechnic compositions, since the 1980s.  We have no alternatives available today, and we know of no alternatives that could be developed in the foreseeable future.

Critically, moreover, there is virtually no environmental or human health exposure to PTFE and FKM materials used in these products from the use phase, because the perfluorinated compounds are – by design -- thermally destroyed during ignition of the product.  The modelled reaction products comprise of fluorometals, MgO, carbon, and HF.  This application is in effect a consumptive use of perfluoropolymer materials.  Extending a restriction on this socioeconomically valuable use of PTFE and FKM, with no meaningful or identifiable reduction of PFAS exposure or release, is clearly disproportionate and not justified.

A broad-based ban on PFAS that includes fluoropolymers, fluoroelastomers and the PFAS chemicals used to produce these materials by our upstream suppliers, without an appropriate derogation for these countermeasures applications, would put the security of the EU and EU Member States at risk.  We therefore join the other defence-related industries and trade associations that have submitted comments requesting a derogation for the use of PTFE and FKM in aerial countermeasures products and for the production of the PTFE and FKM materials needed to make these products.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The relevant use sector is “defence applications”, but this is not identified in Table 8 of the Annex XV report.   While the uses of pyrotechnic applications are briefly mentioned in Annex A to the restriction report dossier – the dossier notes briefly that “fluorine containing oxidizers, primarily polymers, are extensively used in pyrotechnic compositions” (Tables A1 – A77) -- they are not otherwise addressed in the restriction dossier, presumably due to limited information available.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Overview End of life of these products is typically coterminous with the use phase of the products – i.e., their end of life typically involves their deployment as aerial countermeasures and aerial disintegration and vaporization via high-temperature thermal ignition.  In both the typical use phase and typical end-of-life phase, virtually all of the PTFE and FKM is consumed in the reaction, which occurs at very high temperatures and thus is not expected to generate any PFAS by-products.  Background – Emissions in the production phase Our production takes place outside the EU/EEA. There are, accordingly, no PFAS emissions in the EU from production of our products.    PTFE and FKM are used as a binder during the production process of highly sensitive pyrotechnical compounds, and as controlled and stable source of fluorine for the magnesium-fluorine reaction.   Background -- Emissions in the Use Phase The PTFE and FKM used in the countermeasures devices are not accessible or replaceable by end users of the complex articles in which they are incorporated as components.  Needless to say, PFAS that is incorporated in those devices is likewise inaccessible to end users, and there are no consumer or occupational exposures at issue.    As described above, virtually all of the PTFE and FKM is consumed in the combustion reaction of the countermeasure flare upon release, which occurs at very high temperatures.  The high temperature exothermic reaction, ignited by ample fuel-to-oxidizer mixture, results in a reaction that consumes all available fluorine.  As a result, the use phase is not expected to generate any PFAS by-products.  See, e.g., F. Christo, Thermochemistry and Kinetics Models for Magnesium/Teflon/Viton Pyrotechnic Compositions, DSTO-TR-0938 (1999).  Emissions in the End-of-life Phase For unused pyrotechnics that are not destroyed during the use phase, safe handling requires that they be subjected to thermal treatment operations at disposal which also results in controlled destruction and transformation of PFAS molecules.  Disposal of these countermeasures-related pyrotechnics is -- like all other defence-related pyrotechnics and ammunition -- generally conducted through thermal treatment under highly controlled conditions.  In the case of these products in particular, disposal is effected via thermal treatment to initiate the reaction of magnesium and fluorine.  During the reaction and related high-heat reaction, fluorine is consumed from the PTFE and FKM source material and reacted into metal fluoride particles.  See, e.g., F. Christo, Thermochemistry and Kinetics Models for Magnesium/Teflon/Viton Pyrotechnic Compositions, DSTO-TR-0938 (1999).

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: See our reply to Question 2 above.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Unused products, due to their sensitivity as military defence articles and their explosiveness risks, are not subject to recycling operations at end of life.

5. Proposed derogations: Please see our reply to Question 2 above and Question 7 below.  A derogation is not currently proposed for PFAS used in MTV-based aerial countermeasures.  But for the reasons described elsewhere in our comments, such a derogation is required for national security purposes.  While fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers are major constituents of these products, the use and disposal of these products converts the fluorine to metal fluoride particles.  As a result, these products present only a de minimis risk of releases of PFAS into the EU environment, and negligible impacts on the environment and human health within the EU.

6. Missing uses: PFAS uses in aerial countermeasure flares is not adequately recognized or addressed in the Annexes with regulatory background material accompanying the PFAS Annex XV REACH Report.   Please see our reply to Question 7 below for details.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Introduction The use of PFAS in the MTV-based countermeasures devices is not currently covered by any applicable derogations under the proposed restriction.  We therefore provide information in this section that corresponds to each of the elements described in points (a)-(g) above, namely: - essential background on the devices; - annual tonnages and emissions of PFAS associated with this use; - the use of PFAS in the devices, and the use of devices in end products, and the key functionalities provided by PFAS; - information about alternatives; - the socioeconomic impact of the PFAS REACH Restriction Proposal that would occur in the absence of a derogation.  Essential Background:  What is a MTV-Based Countermeasure Device and Why Are They Important Military aircraft are high intensity infrared targets, threatened by infrared guided missiles.  To thwart those missiles, combat aircraft use pyrotechnic decoy flares, which generate an exothermic reaction.  That exothermic reaction exhibits a specific thermal signal, which mimics the airplane’s jet exhaust.  These so-called Magnesium/Teflon/Viton (MTV) flares are designed to generate a thermal flare that will divert attacking heat-seeking missiles.  MTV-based aerial countermeasures flares provide essential protection for military operations.    Why is PFAS Essential to the Operation of These Devices? We use PTFE and FKM in our pyrotechnic energetic compositions (i.e., explosive materials) for countermeasure flares because they provide unique functionality.  The PTFE and FKM act as a binder for the composition materials and also as a source of highly controlled and stable supply of fluorine. Fluorine provides enhanced oxidisation and reactivity for the product.  Most importantly, the functionality of these countermeasure flares – i.e., their effectiveness as missile decoys – depends on a precise chemical composition of the exothermic reaction, which generates a specific and carefully engineered thermal spectral “signature”, which mimics the infrared signatures of aircraft jet exhaust.  It is that unique chemistry that is required to attract and disrupt the attacking missile, and that unique chemistry that means that there are no viable alternatives.   Fluoropolymers are also used as the fluorine source for the magnesium reaction because their characteristics, in particular their excellent resistance to thermal or chemical attacks, are perfectly adapted to severe environments as required for defence applications.   How Much PFAS are Used in These Devices? We do not have an estimate of the amount of PTFE and FKM used in devices that are sold in the EU. As described above, virtually all of the PFAS materials are consumed and fully transformed during the ignition of the flare, meaning that PFAS emissions in the EU associated with the use of these essential safety measures are de minimis.  Analysis of Alternatives There are no known alternative substances or materials that provide this functionality in countermeasure flares other than PFAS.  To our knowledge, there has been little investment to date in the identification of alternatives, given the strict military tolerances and specifications required for safety and performance, the high performance of the current materials, and the absence of environmental emissions or human health exposures associated with these PFAS uses.   Nor, to our knowledge, are there alternatives to the MTV flares themselves, with respect to the specific functionality that they provide as an effective countermeasure against specific infrared-seeking missile threats.  The MTV countermeasure is an essential component of military combat aircraft.   Socio-economic analysis  A change would require invention and development of new substitute formulations with equivalent performance capabilities.  We are unaware of any chemical formula that could provide the functionality required in this exacting and essential application.  Even if an innovation led to the development of a new non-perfluorinated material as a source of fluorine for the essential magnesium-fluorine reaction signature, the use of that new material would require requalification of all related components, including updates to military procurement specifications and (potentially) changes in aircraft design.  It typically requires at least 10 years from the point of an innovation to requalify a pyrotechnical component such as these MTV based countermeasure flare products, with a direct cost to military purchasers (i.e., EU taxpayers) of hundreds of millions Euros. In the meantime, in the absence of a derogation, we (and other defence industry suppliers of these products) would be unable to fulfil military procurement contracts for the continued supply of these essential military defence products.  The results would be highly negative economic and security impacts.   Of greatest impact, without a derogation, military aircraft in the EU would be unable to be equipped with MTV flares, leaving them and their personnel at great vulnerability to certain heat-seeking missile attacks.    Conclusion and Derogation Request On the basis of the above, taking into account (a) the extremely low risk of environmental releases associated with this technology, and (b) the extremely high socioeconomic value of these applications, and because the use of PFAS in these devices is not covered by a derogation, we request an additional derogation to cover these uses. That derogation will need to extend for at least 13.5 years after entry-into-force of the future PFAS REACH Restriction.  Indeed for the reasons noted above, we believe that this derogation could be fully justified for inclusion as one of the non-time-limited derogations.

8. Other identified uses: Please see our reply to Question 7 above.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a pharmaceutical company focused on development, supply and licensing of generic drug products. Our portfolio includes hospital medicines of high value as oncological and parenteral drug products.
We welcome the chance to respond to the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) public consultation on the per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) REACH restriction proposal, because PFAS are used across many medicines’ lifespans and play a role in the research, development, and manufacturing of life-saving medicines.
We recognise the concerns raised about the potential adverse effects of PFAS on human health and the environment, and support efforts to minimise and mitigate the presence of these in our manufacturing processes and products.
The development and production of pharmaceutical products in European Economic Area is considered as a strategic priority for the European Union. For that reason, it is critical to approach this proposal with careful consideration of the impact on pharmaceutical manufacturing and supply of medicines, the development and production of which involve complex processes that requires quality standards, regulatory, and extensive testing compliance. Any significant changes in pharmaceutical industry can have consequences for patients, innovation, and industry supply chains.
In Annex XV restriction report, medical devices and APIs use in Medicinal Products are mentioned, but there are some missing uses that impact the pharmaceutical sector that are not detailed in.
Fluoropolymers such as PTFE or PVDF are present in our manufacturing processes such as equipment, tubes, seals, sterilization filters etc., including spare or replacement parts and are in contact with our pharmaceutical products. These materials are considered essential, adequate and inert (chemical and heat-resistance properties) to produce our medicinal products and are endorsed by European Medicines Agency (EMA) and national medicines authorities.
Our portfolio includes some parenteral drug products with chelating properties that avoid the use of some common materials used in the pharma industry as platinum silicone cured. To produce this type of product, the use of PTFE material accessories in the tubing and sealing of the production line is mandatory.
Replacement of these types of materials depends strongly on the suitability of the candidate alternatives in our manufacturing process. There are no universal substitutes that readily replace these materials, as each would require evaluation on a case-by-case basis.
The use of these materials in our manufacturing process is validated and is demonstrated that guarantees the quality of our medicines according to EMA requirements. A change in an in-contact product material will result in additional years of development, re-validation and regulatory activities that could impact in medicines supply.


We appreciate that we can submit some questions and requests about the restriction proposal:
- Since that pharmaceutical sector is a missing category, we will appreciate to clarify if the restriction applies to pharmaceutical industry. If on the contrary and this restriction includes pharmaceutical sector, due to the massive impact that would imply to our essential sector, we would like to include it as a detailed category and the derogations timelines.

- After a wide review, our experts did not find any alternatives to our PTFE or PVDF materials. Since the restriction proposal appoints that alternatives to these materials are available, we would like to know which materials are proposed and if the safety of them in the patients has been evaluated.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are a valve designing and manufacturing company in Japan.
Our valves are used in many industries such as food, chemical, pharmaceutical, and petroleum, not in Euro but mainly Asia country.
And our valves are used to close and control the flow of fluids and gases required in the production of food, chemical, pharmaceutical, and petroleum products.
These valves always use parts made of PTFE or fluoroplastic as raw materials.
The main parts of them are named Disc, Seat, Guide bushing, Gland Packing, and O-ring.
The most important functions required for each part are sealing, low-temperature and high-temperature resistance, chemical resistance, hygiene, low wear, low friction, and stability under many conditions.
While there are materials that have a single function or performance, such as closure or low friction, but valve components always need to have multiple functions.　For example, low friction and creep properties, low temperature performance and chemical resistance, high temperature performance and steam resistance, etc., must be combined in order to be used as valve components.
The reason why fluorine materials (PTFE, etc.) are used for those parts is because there is no other alternative material so far.
If PTFE materials are not available in the near future, the following damages and losses can be assumed, although they cannot be quantified.
1. deterioration of the work environment due to leakage of fluids or gases through valves, or injury to personnel due to such leakage.
2. fluid or gas leaks from valves or connected equipment, resulting in uncontrolled malfunction, loss of production efficiency, and potentially significant profit or economical loss.
3. if there are alternatives to PTFE parts, it is difficult to imagine that they would have the same durability under the same conditions, resulting in a large amount of material to be discarded as replacement parts.　This also means a tremendous environmental impact.
Currently, valves cannot function without PTFE and fluoropolymers.
PTFE and fluoropolymers are more difficult to obtain than ever before, and their prices have skyrocketed. Unless a revolutionary material is created to replace them, valves will not exist, and we will have no choice but to purchase them and produce valves.
The lack of functional valves in the manufacturing and production industry is similar to the lack of a water tap that cannot be shut off properly in the average home.
We must aggressively and quickly address the environmental, waste plastics, and marine microplastics issues, but it will take time, and PFAS alone is not a problem that can be solved in 18 months.
Therefore, we request a period of 13.5 years as a grace period to resolve the various issues.
I sincerely hope your consideration with our comments for our both problems should be solved.

General Comments: We are a worldwide leader in the production and sale of Oxo Intermediates and Oxo Performance Chemicals. Today, we employ more than 1,400 people worldwide at our plants in Germany, the USA, China and the Netherlands.
We produce more than 70 products. Our oxo products include aldehydes, alcohols, amines, carboxylic acids, polyols and ester.
Our products are used in various industry segments such as paints and coatings, lubricants and functional fluids, personal care, flexible packaging, etc. We produce also alcohols used as disinfectant for the health care market.
Our position within the value chain of Fluoropolymers:
We are using Fluoropolymers in our installations and safety clothes.
Fluoropolymers offer excellent properties that are currently not available as alternatives, such as resistance to aggressive media, temperature resistance, especially at high temperatures, and chemical protection for clothing.
From an environmental protection point of view, replacing seals made of fluoropolymer materials at a time X does not make sense, as it generates high amounts of waste. In addition, the equipment must be depressurized for shutdown and then flushed, which is an additional environmental burden.
Since the fluoropolymer materials are classified as PLC, they are to be exempted from the ban.
Scope:
• The substances jointly included in the proposal are very divers. Many of them behave absolutely differently. Not for all of them the prerequisites for a REACH restriction are fulfilled, thus the proposal goes beyond the basic principles of REACH and thus exceeds the given legal framework.
• In particular, if there is no environmental exposure in specific applications and handling or it can be strongly minimised, a ban is not justified.
• A more differentiated assessment and regulatory approach that bans only critical uses is needed. A use for which there is no risks must not be covered as a matter of principle.
• On the background of several existing legislation as the F gases regulation, the restriction of PFAS in firefighting foams and several restrictions in preparation (e.g. PFOS, PFOA) there already exist an efficient framework to ban certain uses with higher risks.
• The focus should be placed on the applications with the greatest environmental impact, whereby the entire, possibly global, value chain must be considered. We consider the differentiation between monomers and polymers to be a first target-oriented approach.
• In the legal text it must be made clear that the entire manufacturing processes of products exempted from the restriction or not falling under the restriction at all are not covered by the restriction.
• Raw materials, precursors and transported intermediate products for basic as well as temporary derogations must be explicitly exempted from the restriction in the legal text.
• The exemption of fully degradable PFASs must be clarified in the legal text. The description in the explanations on the scope of the restriction proposal is not sufficient. Fully degradable PFASs must not be covered by the restriction - regardless of the chemical structure.

Information on benefits
In many cases the use of PFAS has specific benefits due to the specific properties of the single compound.
• In certain cases, they enable safer and environment-friendly processes compared to former processes (e.g. sulfur and nitric acid, oleum).
• They allow to synthesise specific substances under moderate conditions and avoiding unwanted by-products.
• Due to their persistence, they ensure a long service life e.g. in plants or transport or enable the handling at all (harsh conditions, corrosive substances).
• In a lot of processes, the use of specific PFAS is required by other legislation.
• Especially many high tech applications, productions, and products are highly dependent on the use of certain PFAS as there are no alternatives.
Please see our detailed position, that contains more examples.

Other SEA issues:
• We have the impression that many more very important applications would have to be listed as exceptions.
• The approach of requiring specific information on potential derogations means a high burden to companies. They have to provide information (preferably in a level of detail equivalent to that of an authorisation dossier and also with a view to the entire value chain) for multiple applications within a very short time. This is not feasible for industry. We consider the approach to be disproportionate and, as we understand it, it contradicts the principle that in the case of a restriction, the responsibility for corresponding information lies with the authorities. The potential derogations must remain as real derogations, even if no extensive data can currently be submitted by industry in the context of the consultation.
• It has to be kept in mind that even if in some cases theoretically other substances can be used or alternative processes applied, this does not mean that such a possible alternative finally is “better”. In due time before the end of the time limit of a derogation, it must be carefully assessed whether suitable alternatives are available. If this is not the case, the derogation must be extended.

Transitional period
• Many applications and end products additionally underlay specific regulations. It has to be ensured, that in case of a ban the time for implementation of the transformation is sufficient.

Request for exemption
• The whole manufacturing process of the excluded products (whether they fall under the definition of PFAS or not) must be exempted. This has to be made clear in the legal text.
• The use of PFAS in plants should be excluded completely. Manufacturing processes and plants underlay multiple regulations and must fulfil strict requirements. A full ban of PFAS would cause severe problems without having positive effects on overall emissions. The production of necessary spare parts must remain possible in the EU as well.
• The use of PFAS in chemical synthesis, e.g. as catalysts or protective group should be excluded from the restriction. For industrial use a accurate socio-economic analysis should be carried out, including the final product as well as the whole production chain.
• PPORD has to be excluded to further enable research in the EU.
• All potential derogations (marked by [..]) should be kept as real derogations for the above-mentioned reasons.
