Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are reaching out to you to discuss the topic of PFAS (Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances) usage in the field of mechanical engineering and to emphasize the significance of these chemicals for our industry. PFAS, which include Teflon and other so- called "low concern PFAS," play a crucial role in achieving the desired properties and performance of mechanical components. It is essential to highlight that currently there are no practical alternatives that could equivalently replace the unique attributes of PFAS in many mechanical engineering applications.

Performance: PFAS are employed in mechanical engineering due to their exceptional characteristics. Teflon, for instance, is renowned for its excellent non- stick and frictionreducing properties. These attributes are critical in ensuring the longevity and efficiency of moving parts within machines. The application of PFAS leads to a significant reduction in friction and wear, thereby decreasing energy consumption and minimizing maintenance costs.

Temperature Resistance: PFAS exhibit exceptional temperature resistance. In applications where machines are exposed to extreme temperatures, these materials often stand as the sole option. From high- temperature ovens to aerospace applications, PFAS enable the handling of thermal stress and ensure reliable performance and acceptable lifespan. Chemical Resistance: The chemical resistance of PFAS is of paramount importance in many industrial environments. They withstand corrosion and degradation by aggressive chemicals, rendering them an irreplaceable component in many parts within chemical plants and related industries.

Years of Experience and Research: The utilization of PFAS in mechanical engineering is founded upon decades of experience and extensive research. Their attributes and application scopes have been thoroughly studied and optimized to ensure optimal performance. This knowledge and application contribute to the creation of durable and sustainable products, benefiting the environment in turn.

Sustainability and Research: We wish to underscore that the industry is acutely aware of the potential environmental impacts of PFAS. Therefore, we are consistently investing in research and development to discover more environmentally friendly alternatives that could genuinely serve as substitutes for our products.
It is vital to understand that current alternatives are incapable of meeting the specific requirements and performance attributes of PFAS. Despite concerns regarding the environmental impact of PFAS, we recognize their present indispensability in mechanical engineering. The industry is collaborating closely with regulatory bodies, research institutions, and scientific communities to drive the development of more sustainable alternatives. We are committed to gradually reducing the use of PFAS and adopting more environmentally friendly options, without compromising the performance and lifespan of
our products.

We hope that these insights help elucidate the significance of PFAS in mechanical engineering and underscore the urgency of seeking more sustainable solutions. We remain open to dialogue and collaboration, aiming to collectively find the best possible solutions.

6. Missing uses: The issue of PFAS usage holds significant importance, particularly when considering its application in the field of medicine. The criticality of this usage arises from the fact that, in certain medical contexts, technically or economically viable alternatives may not be readily available. This is largely due to the unique positive attributes of PFAS in terms of media fidelity.  Medical practices demand the utmost precision and safety, especially when dealing with sensitive medical fluids or substances. PFAS showcases its prowess in this arena, as its chemical resistance ensures that it does not contaminate the conveyed medium. This property guarantees the integrity of medical processes, contributing to patient safety. In situations where other materials might falter, the irreplaceable nature of PFAS becomes evident, as it contributes to upholding medical accuracy.  Nevertheless, it is imperative to take a holistic view and consider the socio- economic impacts on companies, consumers, and other relevant stakeholders when technical or economic substitution is not feasible. This necessitates a thorough analysis to strike a balance between the positive attributes of PFAS in medical applications and the potential societal repercussions.   The direct impact of the situation is substantial, affecting approximately 1,000 employees from KNF who are directly involved in the processes related to PFAS usage due to the use within the products . These productss play critical roles in various applications, particularly in the medical sector where its unique attributes are indispensable. Any potential changes or challenges related to the usage of PFAS could have significant implications for their job roles, responsibilities, and overall employment stability.   Moreover, the economic aspect cannot be understated, with an estimated revenue of around 220 million euros being tied to the utilization of PFAS. This financial figure underscores the importance of PFAS in the overall revenue stream of the relevant sector. Any disruptions or alterations to PFAS usage could potentially impact the financial performance of the companies involved, thereby influencing not only their profitability but also their ability to invest, innovate, and contribute to the broader economy.  In light of these figures, it becomes evident that the usage of PFAS goes beyond just a material choice; it has evolved into a significant component of operational and economic success. The complex interplay between its unique attributes, workforce dependence, and financial implications highlights the need for a comprehensive assessment of the situation to ensure that any potential changes are thoroughly evaluated and their consequences wellunderstood.   We, hereby advocate for the implementation of an exemption clause concerning the use of PFAS (Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances) within our sector. Our call is rooted in the unique technical requirements and critical functionalities that PFAS provide, which are often irreplaceable in the context of mechanical engineering.   The mechanical engineering industry is characterized by its intricate processes and diverse applications, where precision, reliability, and durability are paramount. PFAS, due to their exceptional chemical resistance and non- contaminating properties, have proven to be an invaluable component in various machinery and equipment. These attributes contribute to the longevity and effectiveness of components, thus ensuring the safety and optimal performance of the end products. It is crucial to acknowledge that the complexities and demands of our industry often render it challenging to identify suitable alternatives to PFAS. In many instances, the unique combination of attributes that PFAS offer cannot be replicated by other materials. The absence of PFAS could potentially lead to increased maintenance, reduced equipment lifespan, and compromised operational integrity, all of which could adversely affect the quality of our products and the safety of end- users. Furthermore, our industry's reliance on PFAS translates into the livelihoods of numerous employees, spanning from engineers and technicians to manufacturing personnel. These individuals have developed expertise and skills that are tailored to the integration of PFAS into our products. Any abrupt transition away from PFAS could not only disrupt these careers but also undermine the intricate knowledge base that has been cultivated over years. Furthermore the planed ban on PFAS would also have dramatic effects with downstream users and there field of operations.   We emphasize that our call for an exemption clause is not made lightly, but rather as a result of a comprehensive evaluation of the technical, operational, and socio- economic intricacies that define our industry. We firmly believe that, within the context of mechanical engineering, a judiciously crafted exemption would be a prudent step towards ensuring both the continued excellence of our products and the sustainability of our workforce. In conclusion, we urge regulatory authorities to consider the unique circumstances of the mechanical engineering sector and to grant an exemption clause for the use of PFAS where its attributes are genuinely irreplaceable. This approach will facilitate the ongoing advancement of our industry, the preservation of skilled jobs, and the provision of safe and reliable products to our global clientele.

6. Missing uses: The issue of PFAS usage holds significant importance, particularly when considering its application in the field of medicine. The criticality of this usage arises from the fact that, in certain medical contexts, technically or economically viable alternatives may not be readily available. This is largely due to the unique positive attributes of PFAS in terms of media fidelity.  Medical practices demand the utmost precision and safety, especially when dealing with sensitive medical fluids or substances. PFAS showcases its prowess in this arena, as its chemical resistance ensures that it does not contaminate the conveyed medium. This property guarantees the integrity of medical processes, contributing to patient safety. In situations where other materials might falter, the irreplaceable nature of PFAS becomes evident, as it contributes to upholding medical accuracy.     Nevertheless, it is imperative to take a holistic view and consider the socio-economic impacts on companies, consumers, and other relevant stakeholders when technical or economic substitution is not feasible. This necessitates a thorough analysis to strike a balance between the positive attributes of PFAS in medical applications and the potential societal repercussions.     The direct impact of the situation is substantial, affecting approximately 1,000 employees from KNF who are directly involved in the processes related to PFAS usage due to the use within the products . These productss play critical roles in various applications, particularly in the medical sector where its unique attributes are indispensable. Any potential changes or challenges related to the usage of PFAS could have significant implications for their job roles, responsibilities, and overall employment stability.     Moreover, the economic aspect cannot be understated, with an estimated revenue of around 220 million euros being tied to the utilization of PFAS. This financial figure underscores the importance of PFAS in the overall revenue stream of the relevant sector. Any disruptions or alterations to PFAS usage could potentially impact the financial performance of the companies involved, thereby influencing not only their profitability but also their ability to invest, innovate, and contribute to the broader economy.     In light of these figures, it becomes evident that the usage of PFAS goes beyond just a material choice; it has evolved into a significant component of operational and economic success. The complex interplay between its unique attributes, workforce dependence, and financial implications highlights the need for a comprehensive assessment of the situation to ensure that any potential changes are thoroughly evaluated and their consequences well-understood.     We, hereby advocate for the implementation of an exemption clause concerning the use of PFAS (Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances) within our sector. Our call is rooted in the unique technical requirements and critical functionalities that PFAS provide, which are often irreplaceable in the context of mechanical engineering.     The mechanical engineering industry is characterized by its intricate processes and diverse applications, where precision, reliability, and durability are paramount. PFAS, due to their exceptional chemical resistance and non-contaminating properties, have proven to be an invaluable component in various machinery and equipment. These attributes contribute to the longevity and effectiveness of components, thus ensuring the safety and optimal performance of the end products.  It is crucial to acknowledge that the complexities and demands of our industry often render it challenging to identify suitable alternatives to PFAS. In many instances, the unique combination of attributes that PFAS offer cannot be replicated by other materials. The absence of PFAS could potentially lead to increased maintenance, reduced equipment lifespan, and compromised operational integrity, all of which could adversely affect the quality of our products and the safety of end-users.  Furthermore, our industry's reliance on PFAS translates into the livelihoods of numerous employees, spanning from engineers and technicians to manufacturing personnel. These individuals have developed expertise and skills that are tailored to the integration of PFAS into our products. Any abrupt transition away from PFAS could not only disrupt these careers but also undermine the intricate knowledge base that has been cultivated over years. Furthermore the planed ban on PFAS would also have dramatic effects with downstream users and there field of operations.     We emphasize that our call for an exemption clause is not made lightly, but rather as a result of a comprehensive evaluation of the technical, operational, and socio-economic intricacies that define our industry. We firmly believe that, within the context of mechanical engineering, a judiciously crafted exemption would be a prudent step towards ensuring both the continued excellence of our products and the sustainability of our workforce.  In conclusion, we urge regulatory authorities to consider the unique circumstances of the mechanical engineering sector and to grant an exemption clause for the use of PFAS where its attributes are genuinely irreplaceable. This approach will facilitate the ongoing advancement of our industry, the preservation of skilled jobs, and the provision of safe and reliable products to our global clientele.

General Comments: We are representing with this input a German R&D institute which is in their department Hydrogen Technologies focused on PEM fuel cells and PEM electrolysers for more than 30 years. PFAS compounds of a PEM fuel cell or PEM electrolyser are in all membranes, gas diffussion layers or in ionomers which are act as binder materials to reach better perfomance and to reduce degradation effects. As the material is PFSA we use this abbreviation hereinafter.
Within the last decades we also had (in some national projects, especcially in micro fuel cell applications) occasionally tested PFSA-free membranes, but their electrochemical characteristics where in most of the cases below the PFSA-based. With a PFAS ban this market entry would be stopped. A PFAS ban in this field would be impossible to continue the ambitions to realise the European Green Deal with hydrogen technologies.
To find PFAS-free alternatives for all fuel cell and electrolyser components it takes more than 15 years of intensive R&D work to reach the TRL we have by now for this applications. Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are requesting a 12-year derogation from the proposed PFAS restriction for PFAS used as cooling fluids in Two-Phase Immersion Cooling systems for data centers in order to allow the manufacturers sufficient time to develop alternatives. Two-Phase Immersion Cooling is not identified and evaluated in the Annex XV dossier. More information and a detailed justification for the requested derogation can be found in the answer to the specific information request #6 (missing uses) and in the uploaded document.

6. Missing uses: Missing use: PFAS as cooling fluid in Two-Phase Immersion Cooling systems for data centers. Two-Phase Immersion Cooling is not identified and evaluated in the dossier. The energy consumption of data centers in the EU is currently 2.7 % of the total electricity demand and is expected to further increase by about 28 % by 2030. Therefore, it is essential to work on efficient data center cooling solutions to reduce the power consumption. Several solutions are currently available, but the most efficient solution is the Two-Phase Immersion Cooling (2-PIC), which would allow an additional reduction of approximately up to 2.94 TWh of the total electricity demand in the EU alone compared to the current most efficient data center cooling solution Single-Phase Immersion Cooling (1-PIC). In addition to energy savings, the use of Two-Phase Immersion Cooling systems offers other benefits, such as the potential to reduce total water consumption to zero and to reduce the overall footprint of the data center. To cool future generations of chips, the use of Two-Phase Immersion Cooling is indispensable to dissipate the increased heat generation. 2-PIC has different cooling fluid requirements than 1-PIC. The results of the evaluation of 1-PIC as described in the dossier and its annexes cannot be transferred to 2-PIC. This is especially true for the identification of non-PFAS alternatives. In order to evaporate the fluid on the chip surface and dissipate the heat, the working fluid must have very specific properties that are currently met only by cooling fluids that fall under the proposed PFAS restriction. There are currently no non-PFAS alternatives available for 2-PIC. However, manufacturers of cooling fluids are working on alternatives but these still need time to be commercially available. Therefore, we are requesting a12-year derogation from the proposed PFAS restriction for Two-Phase Immersion Cooling in order to allow the manufacturers sufficient time to develop alternative cooling fluids. More information and a detailed justification for the requested derogation can be found in the uploaded document.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are requesting an exemption for fluoropolymers, in particular fluoropolymer foams. Fluoropolymers such as PVDF meet the OECD definition of Polymers of low concern meaning scientific evidence of their toxicology does not support the need for restriction. They are not bio-available or bio-mobile and their end of life can be managed responsibly, negating persistence issues. The environmental impact of substitution would: substantially increase CO2 emissions (particularly in the aviation sector); reduce the durability of parts, increasing the need for regular replacement; substantially increase the use of alternative substances such as brominated flame retardants, which are not environmentally benign; negatively impact other human safety factors such as flammability resistance, some of which is legislated under FAA 25.856 and EASA CS 25.856.

We also request an extended transitional period for fluoropolymers. Use in aviation sector, for example, is highly regulated for safety reasons and changes are carefully controlled. This takes substantial time through R&D and Technical Readiness Levels to ensure continued safety. Expected transition would take 5-10 years and cost millions of pounds.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Aviation: fluoropolymer foams are extensively used because of their inherent flammability performance and lightweight thermal insulating performance. Direct alternatives do not exist. For example, return to thermoset composite structure with open cell insulation in hermetically sealed bags would typically give +30% weight penalty contributing to increased carbon emissions. The closest performing alternatives for flame retardance properties tend to have significant hazard profiles, and many are also under review such as halogenated flame retardants. Banning PVDF would encourage the use of hazardous substances in this respect.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: End of life, when using fluoropolymer foams in aircraft, comes after many decades of use. Durability and longevity is a key attribute reducing emissions during the use-phase. To our knowledge, no in-use foam will have reached end of life (supplied since 2008). Any end of life and manufacturing waste can be incinerated with energy recovery.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Incineration is effective in destruction of fluoropolymers, avoiding issues with persistence. Incineration emissions can be scrubbed to remove substances where possible.

General Comments: We are Semiconductor Equipment Association of Japan(SEAJ).
Semiconductor Equipment Association of Japan (SEAJ), founded in March 1985, promoted by the major semiconductor equipment manufacturers, is a nationwide organization of semiconductor manufacturing equipment, flat panel display (FPD) manufacturing equipment and equipment manufacturers that applied their technology and related equipment manufacturers.

0 Introduction
0.1 Agree with the purpose of EU REACH Regulation
The REACH Regulation has been carrying out the great role of contributing to human health by reducing the exposure risk to hazardous substances. This Regulation with foresight has been expanding globally due to the advantages and benefits to the Society. We fully understand the importance of the REACH Regulation which shall be respected and has been contributed to the REACH through our technologies. We also have highlighted the contribution to the safety, human health, and the environment through electric and electronic equipment.

0.2 Reasons for Submission of comments
If the current proposed restrictions would be applied, we will not be able to put our products on the EU market.
As described in Sections 1.1 and 1.2, our products support the social infrastructure of the EU and have a "critical" aspect that differs from general consumer products. Numerous alternative materials have been reported for PFASs that are being restricted, but unfortunately none are applicable for our product applications. As we have shown in some cases in section 1.2.2, if our products cannot be put on the EU market at all, it could have a significant negative impact on the environment and human health in the EU.
In order to continue to achieve the protection of the environment and human health that EU REACH aims to achieve, we would like to submit this opinion in the hope that the content of this opinion will be considered.

1 Products handled by this organization
1.1 What are our organization & Examples of products manufactured by its member companies
Examples of products manufactured by SEAJ member companies: Mask/reticle manufacturing equipment, Wafer processing equipment, etc. For specific details, see Section V “The survey result for the usage of PFAS in Semiconductor Manufacturing related Equipment”.
“Semiconductor manufacturing related equipment” should also be included in the definition of “semiconductor process” when considering transition and substitution periods. “Semiconductor manufacturing related equipment” is also an essential component of the semiconductor process, and the “semiconductor process” cannot be established without “semiconductor manufacturing related equipment”.
The derogation period, etc., needs to be considered for the “semiconductor industry” as a whole, which includes “semiconductor processes” and “semiconductor manufacturing related equipment”.
See also the opinion of SEMI Europe GmbH, “Consequences of partial or no derogation outcome”. (Part13-4304)

1.2 Features of our products
1.2.1  Our products are “Specialist equipment”
As described in Section 1.1, our products are highly specialized instruments used in laboratories, Research and Development, industrial sites, Universities, and academic institutions. Therefore, the user must undergo special training and education in order to use it safely and correctly. In this opinion we will refer to our product as "EEE specialist equipment" to distinguish it from general consumer products.
Semiconductor manufacturing equipment is installed in factory/laboratory clean rooms. As people are required to wear protective clothing, gloves, goggles, and other protective gear when in such rooms, there is almost no possibility of their bodies coming into direct contact with the equipment. The risk of exposure is very low.
See also the opinion of SEMI Europe GmbH. (part13-4304)

1.2.2  Critical for social infrastructure
We would like to emphasize strongly that EEE specialist equipment we manufacture plays a very important role in the social infrastructure. Below are some examples. We believe that you can understand that the nature is different from the product of "nice to have".
[ Case SEAJ1: Mask/reticle manufacturing equipment ]
Mask/reticle manufacturing equipment is used in the semiconductor manufacturing process to produce masks and reticles. High-resolution patterning and precise placement are important, which directly affects the performance and quality of semiconductor devices. Without the relevant equipment, it would be no longer possible to manufacture semiconductor devices themselves.
[ Case SEAJ2: Wafer processing equipment ]
Wafer processing equipment, with functionalities such as light exposure, mask alignment and photoresist development for creating circuit patterns on a semiconductor chip, is used in the semiconductor manufacturing process. High-resolution patterning and precise placement are important, which directly affects the performance and quality of semiconductor devices. Without the relevant equipment, it would be no longer possible to manufacture semiconductor devices themselves.

1.2.3  Low volume of production, long-life, long supply chain
The EEE specialist equipment is made in small numbers, is produced for long periods without modification or changes, and is a long-life product.
The instruments would have been replaced typically at least after 10-20 years or more from the release of the products. The supply chains are very long and take time to eliminate restricted substances from the supply chain.

1.2.4  Spare (Repair) parts are necessary
Spare parts are necessary to guarantee the expected lifetime (more than 20 years) of EEE specialist equipment. Especially since EEE specialist equipment requires high performance and high reliability, we would like to emphasize that the same spare parts are required throughout the life of the product as when it was first evaluated. Without spare parts, waste minimization according to the principles of “Right to repair” and “Repair as produced” cannot be achieved.

1.2.5  Long development cycle
Our products are required to be highly reliable because they are manufactured for a long period of time without modification. Along with this, long-term reliability tests are required. If there is a certification request, a longer period is required to obtain it.
As a result, development cycles are longer compared to other consumer products.
An example of development process is below:
- Searching of parts and materials: 1-2 years
- Reliability test: performance test of the product: 1-2 years
- Device design: 0.5-1 year
- Develop the production line /buy new production equipment: 1-2 years
- Create Technical Documentation: 0.5 year
- Training at the production site: a few months
- Production management (information to customers): 0.5-1 year
- Third-party certification: 1 year without clinical trial
a few years or more with clinical trial or customer approvals

1.3 Current status of PFAS applications and alternative technologies
Current status of PFAS applications and alternative technologies are described in Specific Information, Question 7. See Question 7 and the Annex.

2 Suggestions and requests from us
2.1 The long grace period and extension are required
If the alternatives are become available in the future, a long grace period is required until PFAS become restricted.
The instruments are made in small numbers, are produced for long periods without modification or changes, have to be reliable and need long term test for reliability.
The instruments would have been replaced typically after 10-20 years or more from the release of the products. The supply chains are very long and take time to eliminated restricted substances from the supply chain.
If the electric and electronic equipment mentioned above cannot use PFAS anymore and PFASs are to be substituted, the long grace period is required in order to test the product to comply with the safety requirements defined with IEC and other safety standards, and obtain the re-certificates according to the requirements.
An example of substitution process is below:
- Testing of alternative materials: 1-2 years
- Reliability test: performance test of the product: 1-2 years
- Device design change: 0.5-1 year
- Change the production line /buy new production equipment: 1-2 years
- Create Technical Documentation: 0.5 year
- Training at the production site: a few months
- Production management (information to customers): 0.5-1 year

As mentioned above, even if an alternative is found, the replacement takes a long time. EEE specialist equipment therefore needs a longer transition period.
If " Testing of alternative materials: 1-2 years " and " Reliability test: performance test of the product: 1-2 years " prove unusable to EEE specialist equipment, the process starts over. Then, it is not possible to predict when the replacement will be completed. It is necessary to check the status of alternative materials at regular intervals and extend the transition period if no alternative materials have been found.
Our equipment also uses general electronic circuit components (see application information in Japan 4EE Opinion RCOM Part 21, No. 4543, and comments to be submitted). In that case, too, the extension of the transition period is necessary.
“Semiconductor manufacturing related equipment” should also be included in the definition of “semiconductor process” when considering transition and substitution periods. “Semiconductor manufacturing related equipment” is also an essential component of the semiconductor process, and the “semiconductor process” cannot be established without “semiconductor manufacturing related equipment”.
The derogation period needs to be considered for the “semiconductor industry” as a whole, which includes “semiconductor processes” and “semiconductor manufacturing related equipment”.

General Comments: We are SME based in the UK manufacturing additive masterbatches and compounds.  Within our product range we supply fluoropolymer process aids (PPA’s) to UK and EU film manufactures – for both food contact and non-food contact applications, including recycled film.  The fluoropolymer process aid substances used are predominantly manufactured in Europe.
Details of the fluoropolymer used, including their CLP classification, usage and waste volumes are provided in confidential document:
“Fluoropolymer information and usage - CONFIDENTIAL – 230914.pdf”
According to our supplier SDS’ these substances are non-hazardous and have no CLP classification.
These substances do not have harmonised classifications on the ECHA database.
Detailed breakdown of PFAS usage is provided in the uploaded confidential document
“Anonymized customer PFAS tonnage - CONFIDENTIAL 230913.pdf”
As fluoropolymers are large, heat stable molecules none are lost as air emissions during compounding (at around 200oC). Degradation temperature given on SDS is 350oC.
This waste is solid waste with the fluoropolymers encapsulated within polyethylene or polypropylene.   This waste is disposed of by incineration for energy according to national regulations.
We are compliant with Operation Clean Sweep, conducting regularly audits to monitor and minimise lost pellets.  We also hold ISO 14001:2015 certification, are members of Ecovardis with a gold rating and monitor energy usage, water usage and waste generation.
Fluoropolymer process aids have found use in polyolefin films for strong commercial and increasingly environmental reasons.  Fluoropolymer process aids enable films to be processed either at low temperatures, so using less energy or throughput to be increased so more film is produced for the same energy input.
They have found increasing use due to the move to modern metallocene polymers which have narrow molecular weight distributions.  This narrow molecular weight distribution makes them difficult to process without a process aid but offers significant advantages in terms of physical and mechanical properties of the final film.  Metallocene polymers also have better barrier properties which is important for the development of monolayer packaging films – which in turn are desirable for increasing recyclability.
Fluoropolymers have dominated the polymer process aid market due to being non-hazardous, temperature stable, inert and effective at very low addition levels.  They are extremely effective at reducing friction between the barrel of the extruder and the polymer resulting in higher quality film produced with lower energy consumption.  The fluoropolymer also reduces die build up which enables film to be run for longer with fewer stoppages and thus less waste.

This film is primarily manufactured and used within the UK & the EU.  The mechanism by which they work is that the fluoropolymer has a high affinity for metal and so migrates out of the polymer melt to the metal surface forming a low friction coating. Once this coating has been established to sufficient level it just requires replacing as it slowly depletes. The consequence of this is that the level of fluoropolymer carried over in the produced film is significantly lower than the level of fluoropolymer process aid added to the process.
We are investigating alternatives, including those proposed in the restriction proposal. Our findings so far are that the potential current substances do not have any polymer processing aid effects. This is illustrated in the uploaded report:
“The evaluation of the efficacy of polymer process aid (PPA) additives - CONFIDENTIAL -  230913.pdf”
Our findings are in direct contrast to the statement in the restriction proposal that there is “ strong evidence pointing to the availability of alternative processing aids at EiF”.  We have been in the masterbatch business for over 30 years and in that time have not found an alternative to fluoropolymers that offer equivalent performance.
In our testing hexagonal boron nitride did not reduce melt fracture and costs 7 times more than fluoropolymers – meaning in practice film producers would not use it but would either run slower or consumer more energy (as the cost of doing this would probably be less than adding the boron nitride).  The result of this higher energy consumption per tonne of film produced would be increased CO2equ per tonne of film compared to using fluoropolymer PPAs.
The addition of polyethylene waxes would replicate the older wider molecular weight polymers, but the high addition required will negatively impact the properties the metallocene polymers are being used for.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Plastic packaging  Polymeric PFASs used as processing aids for production of non-PFAS polymers/plastics

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: We can only comment on the emissions during compounding the fluoropolymer into masterbatch. Typically fluoropolymers compound well and good yields are achieved.  Contained production losses are as solid waste. This waste is the fluoropolymers encapsulated within polyethylene or polypropylene.  No air nor water emissions. Detailed figures given in:   “Fluoropolymer information and usage - CONFIDENTIAL – 230914.pdf”  Waste is disposed of by incineration for energy according to national regulations via a certified waste company.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: The requirement of film to contain no more than 50 ppm organic fluorine will be challenging for the recycling industry.  How will this be measured?  It would be a significant cost (€50,000 to €90,000 for GC-MS – but will this be able to measure fluoropolymer levels?  How would you get the sample into solution?) to invest in equipment and personnel to carry out such testing. Note, cost effective recycling of mixed recyclate requires polymer process aids with high efficacy, to achieve commercial viability.

5. Proposed derogations: In the restriction proposal there is no derogation allowed for use in plastic packaging but there should be at least a long derogation or preferably an exemption for these non-hazardous fluoropolymers.  As outlined there is in reality no effective available alternative.  Stopping using fluoropolymer process aids in the plastic film industry will result in increased energy consumption and increased waste generation by this industry.  This will have a negative commercial effect on the companies and our shared environmental goal of reducing the impact of climate change. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: In case separate waste collection is not possible we assume that the remaining amount of blowing agent, the roughly 90% that was not released during spraying, is released at end of life.  We note that the lifetime of the sprayed LP SPF product is equal to the lifetime of the building/infrastructure and is commonly assumed to be at least 60 years.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Depending on the application type (construction or industrial OEM market) the end of life waste stream is incinerated with energy recuperation or, in rare cases where separated waste collection is not possible, landfill.

5. Proposed derogations: Given sufficiently strong evidence that technically and economically feasible alternatives are not available , foam blowing agents HFO-1234ze(E) and HCFO-1233zd(E) used in low pressure (< 20 Bar) spray polyurethane foam sprayed on-site are granted a time unlimited derogation.

6. Missing uses: Foam blowing agents in low-pressure spray polyurethane foam sprayed on site. 6a. During the production of the LP SPF products in a closed loop manufacturing process no emissions occur.  It is estimated a 10% loss of the HFO in the product during the on-site application and in worst case (landfill) a 90% loss of the remaining HFO in the product. If a separated waste collection is performed the remaining 90% will be destroyed during the incineration process. 6b. The key performance requirements for a LP SPF are as follows: • The product must be an effective barrier to heat (i.e., the product must have thermal resistance and be an effective insulator). One reason that consumers may choose to use LP SPF products in a building is because of the high thermal resistance (R-value per inch) compared to other insulation products. The unique application process allows builders to create architectural designs that could not otherwise meet required energy performance standards using other insulation products. • The product must be able to seal a wall assembly (where it is applied), serving as an effective barrier to air, vapor, moisture (closed-cell SPF), and sound. • The product must resist the spreading of flames and emission of smoke in the case of a fire. Mandatory criteria for surface burning characteristics have been established by building codes to help ensure fire protection.  • The product should have an appropriate reaction rate consistent with successful application of the product (in terms of seal, longevity, appearance, insulation capacity, etc.). For example, polyurethane-based spray foam polymerizes quickly, which: o Prevents slumping, thus providing a good seal for insulated cavities. Any alternatives would need to have equivalent performance properties in order to maintain the tight air barrier properties of LP SPF. o Reduces potential exposure to airborne pMDI. After application, the potential exposure is reduced to a level that allows other trades to enter the construction site in a timely manner. o Ensures that the product is fully reacted once it attains its final characteristics, which eliminates building occupants' exposure to pMDI. • The product must have good dimensional stability (<15% change by volume). LP SPF products should resist structural deterioration/decomposition and resist settling, which maintains insulation performance over time. The product must maintain minimum standards for shelf life in order to provide consistent quality of the product and hence meet the required performance standards. 6c. There are only two (2) manufacturers of low-pressure spray polyurethane foam (LP SPF) in the EU.  Fewer than five (5) comments are expected for this sub-sector use due to the limited number of manufacturers.  This should not be considered “weak evidence” since it will constitute the entire industry.  The number of companies/users, beyond manufacturers, affected by this restriction will expand into the thousands.  6d. There are no alternatives to the current blowing agents used in LP SPF. It is critical that blowing agents are considered viable alternatives only if they meet the requirements for manufacture and safety, as demonstrated below. Blowing agent alternatives must also meet environmental, hazard, economic and functional or performance properties to be considered a solution. Multiple building codes, industry standards and other certifications must also be met after the product is produced prior to commercialization. Therefore, research and development of commercially available blowing agent alternatives requires a complex product assessment that touches on a multitude of factors. 6e. All possible alternatives have been considered and have proven not to be feasible.  A new alternative will require invention by blowing agent technology developers.  6f. There are no technically feasible alternatives to the two HFOs used in low-pressure spray polyurethane foams.  6g. LP SPF foam systems serve a niche market in building, industrial and construction uses where no equally efficient alternatives are available. These systems take care of several applications that would otherwise impact negatively energy efficiency, safety, environment or fire behavior. Eliminating the use of HFO blowing agent without valid alternatives would heavily jeopardize our activities and more important the activities of thousands of end users, mostly SME’s, depending on this product.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: HFO ze & zd are required for LP SPF products, which play an important role delivering energy efficiency and GHG reduction benefits in their application.  The use of HFO ze & zd in LP SPF has resulted from research spanning more than a decade and considering an exhaustive set of blowing agents available today.  Because no other blowing agents available today meet the required performance needed for LP SPF applications, transition away from HFO ze & zd in LP SPF is not possible in the near term.  Transition out of these HFO blowing agents would require invention and development of new blowing agent materials, and the time to invent, develop, and ultimately implement a new technically viable LP SPF product is expected to be on the order of decades.   Without a time-unlimited derogation, LP SPF product would be eliminated from the market under the current proposal. Since no alternative products to LP SPF that meet the unique performance delivered by these products exist, there would be a market gap created where certain energy efficiency projects would terminate, making it difficult if not impossible for efficiency goals to be achieved.  In addition, as a result, value chain players, spanning manufacturers to distributors to professional installers would suffer significant loss of business and jobs including complete loss of business for many participants.

8. Other identified uses: We have identified a missing use. This question is addressed more thoroughly in Question 1 and Question 6.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: Regarding trifluoromethoxy, trifluoromethylamino- and difluoromethanedioxy derivatives, these compounds aren’t derivatives/degradants of HFOs.  There is a wealth of information regarding the degradation of HFO and relevant compartments in the public sector.  The emissions of TFA that can be expected to be released from HFO use broadly, including from many other uses in addition to use in LP SPF applications, have been recently reviewed by the UN EEAP, and are not expected to pose an environmental or health concern based on the exposures expected through the year 2100.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are the company with production facilities in Japan, capitalized at 100 million yen and less than 200 employees, manufacturing power, control and communication cables for manufacturing facilities, machinery and equipment at production plants and supplying them mainly to machinery equipment manufacturers, automotive manufacturing equipment manufacturers and semiconductor manufacturing equipment manufacturers.
We use fluoropolymers (ETFE, FEP), which are being considered as targets of PFAS regulations, in insulation materials for wires and cables for use in places where high durability is required, such as robot arms and cable carriers that are constantly operated and moved, and in harsh places where oil and chemicals are splashed.
We request that ETFE/FEP not be regulated because if ETFE/FEP cannot be used, it will cause inconveniences such as not being able to wiring to the above locations and shortening product life.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The subject wire and cable belongs to Electronics in Annex XV　Restriction Report – Per – and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) Table9. R02.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Disposal volume is approximately 2 tons per year. the respective quantities are unknown because we do not manufacture, use, or dispose of products containing fluoropolymers in  EU. However, , the annual disposal quantity is assumed to be 2 tons because the annual quantity of ETFE and FEP contained in products exported within EU is approximately 2 tons.

8. Other identified uses: a.  Fluoropolymers (ETFE, FEP) are used as insulation for wires and cables that require durability and are used under harsh environments. Annual consumption is approx. 30 tons and emissions are approx. 9 tons.  b.  Fluoropolymers (ETFE and FEP) are the only thermoplastic materials that simultaneously satisfy electrical (high insulation resistance, stable dielectric constant) physical (high heat resistance, high flame resistance, lubricity, excellent chemical resistance, oil resistance) and mechanical (high mechanical strength, high wear resistance) properties. These properties are required for cables and wires used in industrial applications where harsh wiring environments are common. In particular, they enable longer service life in moving parts of machines that are in constant operation and in wiring environments such as the following 1. environments where they are exposed to oil or chemicals 2. a wide range of temperature environments from -40°C to 150°C. 3. environments where high flame resistance is required, such as factories.  c.  we estimate that approximately 800 companies will be affected, mainly in the automobile manufacturing industry, manufacturers of machinery equipment and semiconductor manufacturing equipment, which has many locations that require high durability, such as in robot arms and cable carriers that are constantly in operation and moving, and in harsh locations where oil and chemicals are splashed If fluoropolymers (ETFE, FEP) can no longer be used as a material for cables and wires.  d.  An alternative material available on the market is cross-linked polyethylene. However, this alternative material has inferior heat resistance, flame resistance, and mechanical strength compared to ETFE/FEP, making it an imperfect substitute that cannot be wired as before. Comparative evaluation data of cross-linked polyethylene and ETFE are shown (detailed data are attached in Section IV). The requirements for a perfect substitute material for ETFE/FEP to be used for cable and wire insulation are a heat resistance temperature of 150°C or higher, a flame resistance of V-0 or higher at 0.4 mm thickness, and  tensile strength of 40MPa or  higher. Other than ETFE and FEP, which are PFAS materials currently in use, we have not found any alternative materials that can be used for electric wires and cable due to our lack of technical capabilities.  e.  We are considering alternative candidate materials with modified formulations such as flame retardant cross-linked polyethylene and polyester elastomer. A total of more than 10 years is expected for the development of cables using alternative materials (more than 6 years, budget of 50 million yen), commercialization study (3 years, budget of 100 million yen), and certification application (1 years, budget of 20 million yen). It will also require a huge budget of 170 million yen. Currently, no technically or economically substitutable candidate materials have been found among the materials that have been considered for formulation changes, and the likelihood of successful development is expected to be quite low.  According to the results of previous studies, flame-retardant polyethylene has not achieved the performance of heat resistance, flame resistance, and mechanical strength, and polyester elastomer has not achieved the performance of heat resistance and flame resistance, and no material that simultaneously meets these required properties has been found (detailed data is attached in the materials in IV). Under these circumstances, if ETFE/FEP is regulated and we enter an 18-month transition period, we will not be able to comply with the regulations and will likely be suspended from doing business with our customers, which is unacceptable. For the above reasons, please do not prohibit the use of ETFE/FEP in wires and cables until alternative materials with equivalent performance to ETFE/FEP are generally available in the world.  f.  At this time, there is no prospect for a techno-economically viable alternative material.  g.  Socioeconomic impacts on businesses, consumers, and other stakeholders are expected to include the inability to wire in special environments and increased replacement frequency and disposal volume due to reduced service life. Based on the above, we request that the ETFE/FEP replacement material currently under consideration be excluded from this proposed limitation because it cannot be a complete replacement material.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Information on benefits Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We are the manufacture of various valves used in HVAC&R products, e.g. four-way valve, stop valve, electronic expansion valve. Currently, over 50% of valves use PTFE as the sealing component. PTFE materials have the long-term reliability and durability as a maintenance-free feature, which is considered essentially for the design of hermetic systems. This requires the use of sealing elements with a critical range of properties and attributes. PTFE materials have excellent operational properties meeting the specific requirements in the application of valve product including:
1) Self-lubrication and low friction to ensure the sealing ability between moving parts without the requirement of maintenance.
2) Wear resistance to maintain the functional properties for long-term service life.
3) Chemical resistance against variety of refrigerant.
4) Thermal stability in the wide range of -40°C to 150°C for the operating ambient temperature.
5) High flexibility for the movement of diaphragms in valve and pressure regulator.
These properties are all necessary in our valve product. There is no alternative material available regarding the combination of all these properties.

We fully support all efforts to restrict the hazardous PFAS to circulate in the environment and ecosystem such as PFOA and PFOS. However, the very general definition of PFAS in the restriction proposal contains an extremely broad group of substances and not all of them are hazardous. For example, the proposed restriction does not differentiate between fluoropolymers (such as PVDF, ECTFE, FEP, PFA and PTFE as wells as fluoroelastomers - FPM, FFKM) and other PFAS. The PFAS regulation includes quite a large number of substances (more than 10,000). Only small amount of these substances (0.5%) are Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers. The molecular structure of fluoropolymers can be classified as PFAS based on the definition. However, they are quite different from the main part of PFAS substances. Fluoropolymers and Fluoroelastomers are classified by the OECD as safe materials: "PLC" = polymer of low concern. They are non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water soluble and non-mobile molecules and are judged to have no significant impact on the environment and humans. In addition, the combination of excellent favorable properties mentioned above makes PTFE materials the best adaption for dynamic and static sealings. No alternative materials with the same combination of properties are available. Regarding the persistence of degradation products in the environment, it would make more sense to not restrict fluoropolymers, but to focus on the measures of recycling.

We agree with the comments submitted by the Conference of Fluoro-Chemical Product Japan (FCJ), and see the attached report.

We request:
- It is not scientific and reasonable to regulate all PFAS the same. Various types of PFAS are to be differentiated based of their toxicological profile for the proposed restriction category.
- Fluoropolymers such as PTFE should be exempted.

Related information can be referred to the attached scientific report.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: PTFE material for valve seals in the HVAC&R application can’t be found in Annex A, A.3.2.1.1 Fluoropolymers and A.3.2.1.2 Fluoroelastomers sectors (P23-P25), and is not listed in Annex XV.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: When PFTE material is used in the final product such as air conditioning, PTFE’s excellent sealing performance matching the critical leakage standard for HVAC&R products. At the same time, PTFE hardly reacts with medium (refrigerants or other chemicals) and is chemically and thermally stable. In addition, PTFE is used in the hermetic system, and has no emission to the environment during the service time. At present, our valves are mainly used in the refrigeration industry, the product generally has a service life of more than 10 years, some of them are more than 20 years. The design life of the valve is even higher than that of the refrigeration unit. When the air conditioning reaches its end of lifecycle, components are generally collected, raw materials are classified under categories, and recycled separately. The PTFE part can be mechanically crushed and reused, and has limited emission to the environment.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: As the requirements from WEEE, components in many products at the end of service life such as white good shall be collected and recycled by the manufactures or other central collection station. Therefore, the strategy should be focused on the collection quantity and quality. Regarding the chemical composition, PFAS should be separated from other organic substance. In addition, further research on the recycling and reuse of fluorinated polymers should be performed, which will be important in the end to keep the fluorinated polymers in the recycling circle. Generally fluorinated polymers are polymers of low concern, which are chemically stable (no degradation to short chain PFAS) and no emissions are coming out of them if they are produced properly.   Scientific report on waste incineration and thermal recycling can be referred to the attached literature.

6. Missing uses: PTFE has excellent self-lubrication, wear resistance, high chemical resistance, wide thermal resistance and high flexibility for the dynamic and static sealing. PTFE materials have excellent combination of all these properties. In addition, there are a big various of refrigerant, and many refrigerants are good organic solvent. PTFE materials are quite stable to withstand most refrigerants, while achieving the aforementioned functions. Therefore, no better alternative solution has been found at present. All alternative material will have shorter lifetime and higher leakage due to lower chemical and thermal resistance.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We as FVEM- Fachvereinigung Edelmetalle e.V., the German Precious Metals Federation support the PFAS restriction. However, the current scope is far too broad and not based on hazard nor risk related to the different substances. This means that the impact on the precious metals industry using directly or indirectly the PFAS to produce and recycle precious metals will be significant. Indeed, the Precious Metals industry has identified direct (electroplating) or indirect (industrial equipment, PPE and analytical equipment) uses of PFAS but also some uses intrinsically related to the use of precious metals (green hydrogen). These uses occur in a well-controlled (industrial) environment, with negligible potential for release / exposure to humans and the environment.

It is worth noting that the PFAS is a huge group of substances with different levels of hazard. A lot of these substances are considered of low concern (cf. OECD1), such as the fluoropolymers.

For most of the uses related to precious metals, PFAS are selected because of their unique properties and there are no alternatives available today with a comparable performance. If these uses were no longer allowed and/or the exemption time is not sufficient to find alternatives, this might have significant impacts on the precious metals manufacturing and recycling activities in the EU, and thus be incompatible with e.g., the EU Green Deal.

PFAS are also present in recycling streams containing precious metals. The PFAS are all being destroyed during the recycling process, trapped from the flue gas and duly disposed of. Any limitation on the use of precious metals recycling streams containing PFAS will restrict precious metals recycling activities in Europe.

It is worth noting that the precious metals like PGMs (Platinum Group Metals) have been identified at Critical Raw Materials. The Critical Raw Materials act sets targets to allow Europe to be resilient. The ban of all PFAS in the EU at short notice will for sure jeopardize the success of the Critical Raw Materials act.

Hence, we would like to request that:

- the hazard profile of the PFAS is considered to prioritize the PFAS included in the restriction.
- the scope of the restriction is limited and that substances of low concern (as per OECD criteria) are exempted from the restriction.
- if the exemption must be use driven, the uses of PFAS outlined above must be exempted for at least 12 years and a mechanism to renew these exemptions must be put in place.

For further details we refer to the comments made under "Specific Information Requests" as well as to the attached statement of EPMF - European Precios Metals Federation.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: This submission relates to the use of fluoropolymers (fluoroelastomers and fluoroplastics) as seals, gaskets, vessel liners etc, within processing equipment used in the refining and recycling of precious metals. Such use is not recognised within the Annex XV restriction report (Table 9).

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: FVEM, the German Precious Metals Federation and its member companies do not possess empirical emissions data for PFAS.  The solid fluoropolymer-based articles, such as seals and gaskets used in precious metals refining processing equipment are used for their durability and ability to withstand the extremely aggressive conditions necessary to refine noble metals. Such fluoropolymer components typically undergo routine replacement only after many (e.g. 20-25) years, and even then the components are fully intact with no indication of degradation. Hence in-use emissions are expected to be zero.  Due to the high value of precious metals, it is common practice for end-of-life components such as the fluoropolymer seals and gaskets used in precious metals processing equipment to themselves be put through the precious metals recycling process to recover any adsorbed precious metals. Based on information published in the scientific literature (Aleksandrov et al, 2019; Taylor et al, 2014), it can be confidently expected that the fluoropolymers will be completely degraded and mineralised with negligible and likely zero emission of PFAS.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Precious metals do not possess any data on thermal degradation and mineralisation of PFAS under municipal waste incineration conditions. Scientific research papers (Aleksandrov et al, 2019; Taylor et al, 2014), though, support the view that such incineration does degrade PFAS and that any PFAS going through the Precious metals refining process will be thermally degraded and mineralised. Precious metals refining pyrometallurgy employs temperatures of over 900 °C and in most cases over 1,100 °C, and Best Available Techniques (BAT) dictate its air treatment systems achieve 1,100 °C for at least 2 seconds followed by several treatment steps to clean the air.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Annex E of the Restriction report acknowledges (page 196, Section E.2.4.2.2 Manufacture of Metal Products) that “there are other applications where other properties of PFAS are important, for example durability, resistance to chemical attack, thermal properties and sealing properties. Stakeholders did not identify alternatives that fulfil the performance of fluoropolymers e.g. for chemical and temperature resistance.”  The proposed Restriction would likely end the recycling of precious metals within the EU, due to the inability to obtain and use fluoropolymer components within processing equipment used in precious metals refining and the lack of any suitable alternatives. This would force the EU to become entirely dependent on imported precious metals and precious metals based products and contradict the EU’s strategic objective as outlined in the Critical Raw Materials Act.  PFAS as defined in the Restriction proposal may also be present in low concentrations within precious metals recycling feedstocks (e.g. within electronic wastes). Precise concentration ranges are not known – the heterogeneous nature of the feedstocks prevents practicable representative sampling until after thermal treatment which destroys any PFAS that was present (see responses to Questions 2 and 3) – but as those feedstocks are considered waste they themselves are exempt from Restriction under REACH.  It is vital that any future regulatory developments to embed the circular economy and invigorate the hydrogen economy and use of precious metals within electrolysers and fuel cells do not inadvertently alter the status of precious metals recycling feedstocks and inhibit the continued success story of precious metals recycling.

5. Proposed derogations: The use of PFAS (fluoropolymers) to which this submission relates is not covered by the derogations listed under Paragraphs 5 and 6 of the proposed Restriction.   Precise volumes of fluoropolymers used within componentry of processing equipment used in the recycling and refining of precious metals are not known. Data on environmental emissions are likewise not available, and we would welcome further research into analytical methodologies for detecting and quantifying PFAS in environmental media. Despite the lack of verifiable supporting data, it can be confidently expected (see answers to Questions 2 and 3) that environmental emissions of PFAS from the uses to which this submission relates will be negligible and likely zero.

6. Missing uses: The critical use of fluoropolymers within industrial chemical processing equipment, and specifically in the refining and recycling of precious metals – like platinum group metals (PGMs) identified as critical and strategic raw materials by the EU – is not recognised in the Restriction proposal.  Fluoropolymers are able to survive the extremely aggressive chemical conditions necessary for refining of noble metals. They are used inter alia as vessel linings, seals, and gaskets; their chemical stability ensuring the hazardous contents of the processing equipment remain contained and secure.  The annual tonnage of fluoropolymers used within precious metals processing equipment within the EU is not known but will be modest considering both the amounts required for the fluoropolymer components and their typically decades long service life. Specific fluoropolymers used in precious metals processing equipment include PFA (perfluoroalkoxy alkanes), PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride), ECTFE (ethylenechlorotrifluoroethylene / Halar), PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene), FKM (Fluorine Kautschuk Material / Viton), and FFKM (Kalrez).  Europe is a big player in the global precious metals supply chain, especially concerning recycling. Within Europe, there are four major precious metals refining and recycling companies that would be significantly affected by the Restriction – likely forcing them to relocate outside of Europe and causing the EU to become entirely dependent on import for these strategic critical raw materials.   In addition, there are an unknown number of additional and downstream companies that may require equivalent specification processing equipment to manufacture precious metals products.  It is expected that for some of these the use of fluoropolymers in processing equipment ancillaries is similarly necessary and not possible to substitute; hence the current Restriction proposal would also significantly impact the broader precious metals products industry in Europe.  No viable alternatives to the use of fluoropolymers in the described applications within precious metals processing equipment are known. Historically, gaskets requiring thermal and chemical stability were made of asbestos. Due to the well-known carcinogenicity of asbestos, these were replaced by fluoropolymer alternatives.  For some processes, use of glass equipment to replace fluoropolymer-lined vessels would theoretically be possible, but this presents its own hazards, and moreover even in those processes seals and other components would still need to be made from fluoropolymers.  Suppliers of industrial chemical processing equipment have engaged in R&D to identify suitable alternatives to fluoropolymers that could deliver the necessary performance, but no alternatives have been identified.  Annex E of the Restriction report acknowledges (page 196, Section E.2.4.2.2 Manufacture of Metal Products) that “there are other applications where other properties of PFAS are important, for example durability, resistance to chemical attack, thermal properties and sealing properties. Stakeholders did not identify alternatives that fulfil the performance of fluoropolymers e.g. for chemical and temperature resistance.”  Some precious metals like the platinum group metals (PGMs) are categorised as critical raw materials. PGMs provide a critical function within PEM electrolysers and fuel cells that are the basis of the hydrogen economy, and their unique properties have for a long time been utilised in numerous other important applications providing enormous health and societal benefits, including inter alia, anticancer drugs, medical devices such as pacemakers and cochlear implants, catalytic converters that prevent the emission of harmful chemicals from vehicle exhausts, electronic equipment, jet engines, and fertilizer production. The value chain for platinum group metals as precious metals in Europe (excluding complex end products) has recently been estimated at approximately €95 billion (Eftec, 2023). In the absence of any suitable alternatives to fluoropolymers within platinum group metals processing equipment, the Restriction proposal can be predicted to have the following socioeconomic impacts directly related to this: - Cessation of precious metals recycling and refining in the EU and the EU becoming entirely dependent on import of these strategic and critical raw materials - Closure of the bigger precious metals refineries sited in the EU, with the loss of business revenues in the single-digit billions of euros (Eftec, 2023), and the direct loss of jobs in the single-digit thousands (Eftec, 2023) - Cessation of production of precious metals products where dissolution of precious metals is necessary in the production process and the EU becoming entirely dependent on imports of those products - Closure of a larger number of sites and companies that utilise precious metals to make products that requires dissolving precious metals, with the loss of jobs in the thousands.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Not relevant.

8. Other identified uses: Not relevant. The specific uses of fluoropolymers that are the subject of this submission, i.e. their use in precious metals processing and recycling equipment, are not included in Table 8 of the Restriction Report.  The importance of fluoropolymers for metal plating and manufacture of metal products more generally is acknowledged in the report. Annex E of the Restriction report states (page 196, Section E.2.4.2.2 Manufacture of Metal Products) that “there are other applications where other properties of PFAS are important, for example durability, resistance to chemical attack, thermal properties and sealing properties. Stakeholders did not identify alternatives that fulfil the performance of fluoropolymers e.g. for chemical and temperature resistance.”

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: There is no data on the environmental degradation potential of any PFAS sub-groups. But as described earlier, though, environmental emissions of any form of PFAS from the use of fluoropolymers within precious metals processing equipment are expected to be zero both during use and at end-of-life.

Emissions in the end-of-life phase: A study by Conversio in 2022 prepared for Pro-K (Fluoropolymer downstream user association), has shown that at its end-go-life approximately 85% of all fluoropolymers end up in waste-to-energy recovery incinerators.  A recent project initiated and commissioned by Gujarat Fluorochemicals and executed by the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) in cooperation with Société Générale de Surveillance (SGS) was conducted to assess that fluoropolymers get fully incinerated without any formation of short chain or long chain PFAS.     The study clearly showed that fluoropolymers are converted to inorganic fluorides and carbon dioxide. The inorganic fluorides detected were hydrogen fluoride. The vast majority of samples indicated that long-chain PFAS were below 1 ng/m3 (>99% of samples associated with the 860°C condition and >98% of samples associated with the 1100°C condition). No short-chain PFAS were detected after incineration. TFA was undetectable in all samples with a reporting limit of 14 µg/m3. The results confirm that end-of-life fluoropolymers, when incinerated under representative European municipal incinerator conditions, do not generate measurable levels of PFAS emissions and therefore pose no risk to human health and the environment.   The study provides strong evidence that incineration of a mixture of fluoropolymers under representative municipal waste incineration conditions results in complete mineralization of the C-F bonds, no significant emissions of long-chain PFAS, and no significant emissions of TFA or light fluorocarbons such as CF4 or C2F6.   The main reason for including fluoropolymers in the EU PFAS restriction proposal was persistence (resistance to degradation in the environment) in the environment. The absence of organic fluorides, and more specifically PFAS, in tests representative of municipal waste incineration confirms complete mineralization of fluoropolymers and provides critical data to support the exclusion of fluoropolymers from the EU REACH PFAS restriction proposal. Combined Comments:
General Comments: We belong to the Japan Bearing Industry Association (JBIA) and we are a company that manufactures bearings.
Bearings support the rotating parts that are the central part of machinery, and lower energy consumption by reducing friction. As an extremely important element that determines the function of the entire machine, bearings are used in every product from the products related to regular life, such as washing machines, electronic devices and office machines, to the products related to human’s health and safety, such as production of food and medical machine etc.... They are also used in cutting-edge products such as robots and space rockets, not to mention in major industries such as semiconductor manufacturing equipment and automobiles. In order to maintain safe and proper rotational function in such a wide range of operating environments, it is essential to use seals, greases, sliding parts, and other components that contain PFAS with high heat resistance, lubricity, and other properties.
We support the opinions submitted by the JBIA and the statements made by Conference of Fluoro-Chemical Product Japan (FCJ) attached to IV section of this document.
Based on the above, we believe that this proposal, which collectively regulates over 10,000 PFAS, requires reconsideration because of the lack of appropriate risk assessment for individual chemicals and consideration of socioeconomic impact.
Therefore, we will submit our opinion.

[Exemption for PFAS-containing Materials Used in Bearing]
As mentioned above, bearings containing PFAS are extensively used to survive harsh conditions and to ensure safety functions. In addition, since there are no alternatives to PFAS, we believe that PFAS used in bearings are appropriate to be exemption, without limiting their use. For further details, please refer to Paragraph 2 of the SECTION V. Confidential Attachment.

[Exemption of Articles Marketed before the Implementation Date].
PFAS is used for a variety of applications in products, and the regulation is very broad in scope, leading to the generation of large quantities of waste whose products and components have all been put on the market before the start of their application.
Therefore, as in PFCA (C9-C14), we request the exemption of an article marketed before the date of application.

[Postponement of the Implementation Date]
Not limited to bearings, since the scope of regulations is very broad, appropriate response (evaluation and replacement for parts, etc.) is expected to be difficult for the period from the promulgation of the law to its enforcement of 18 months is too short. At a minimum, a transition period of at least 36 months is required, similar to PFCA (C9-C14).

[Postponement of the Implementation Date Considering the Analysis]
Since the restriction requires the contained amount should be less than 25 ppb for a single type of PFAS, it is essential for compliance whether industry can accurately analyze and measure even extremely small amounts of PFAS volumes. Therefore, we request regulating authority to provide an official method and guidelines for analysis and measurement in order that industry can comply with this regulation.
A certain preparation period is required for the company that is responsible for the analysis to establish a system, and for the company that manufactures the product to make an analytical decision before the start of the regulation.
Accordingly, it is requested to ensure a preparation period of at least 36 months from the time that the official method of analysis is agreed, the guideline for selection of analytical methods, and the flow of judgment is disclosed until the start of the regulation.

[Postponement of the Implementation Date for Articles]
Under the current proposed restriction, the implementation date is the same for articles, substances and mixtures. However, considering the broad scope of use of PFAS and the length of the supply chain, it is expected that switching substances and mixtures used in the manufacture of articles by the implementation date will take longer than in the case of other generally regulations. As a result, if the implementation date for articles, substances and mixtures were the same, substances and mixtures produced before the implementation date would remain in inventory on the market and in companies, and unused substances and mixtures would have to be disposed of. Therefore, we believe it is essential to set the implementation date of articles about one year later than the implementation date of substances and mixtures in order to avoid social disruption.

The coatings we apply fall under dangerous goods and are handled with special careunder designated waste key numbers. Our products are applied in very segregated areas by spray or dipping processes. During the application or production phase we emit mainly solvents and no polyfluorinated emissions to the air. The cabins have ventilations with filters which catch liquids, particles or none reacted products. The overspray which is not taken by the airstreams is solidifying on cardboard or foils in the cabinet or the rigid concrete floor. Those oversprays are broad to the general waste cycles in Germany and are burned or stored in specialized land fill. Liquid residues are collected and going to the special waste cycle and get thermally treated in waste plants. The material on the components for the industry is rigidized and cured in ovens. During use in production facilities during lifetime the coatings erode mainly, and emissions are banned locally in the productions sites and transferred into the waste stream cycles. After service life of the components those are sent back to us. The old coating is pyrolyzed and parts are getting recoated. Ther efore, the saving of resources for the manufacturing of the components for the chemical industry is high. Because of that those are metal based and mainly large and heavy. Some components are going to the metal scrap yards and will be recycled. In this process the PFAS containing coatingwill bepyrolyzed. Liquids form dipping and rinsing are sent to the wastewater purification system and the r esulting wastewater is transferred to the wastewater refurbish plant. Concentrations of critical substances are set as limit by the authorities. Concentrated bathes are part of the waste management according to the Kreislaufwirtschaftsgesetz(KrWG). Therefore, the end-of-life emissions arebelowa few kilograms per year in our sector. It is to be highlighted that fluoropolymers do not degrade, or they are not mobile, bio accumulative, or toxic and can be handled safely across the waste management and end-of-life cycle

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: During handling and production on our sites less than 1 % are emitted to the environment. The rest is cached or degraded fully to non PFAS in pyrolysis. Components which are landfilled are not leaching outdue to the rigid formand they arebound in other polymers.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: No impact due to the regulations in the Kreislaufwirtschaftsgesetz (KrWG) in Germany and respective laws in the European states. Furthermore, given the relatively large (up to hundreds or thousands) number of individual products supplied in this sector, all with different specific formulations,this would be a complex undertaking needing sufficienttime.
