Combined Comments:
General Comments: We certainly support efforts to limit persistent and bioaccumulative PFAS. However, we are very concerned about the current restriction proposal for various reasons and would like to take this opportunity to comment on it.
With the exception of a few single substances, PFAS substances are not yet regulated (e.g., listed as SVHC). For this reason, there is cur-rently no information on the presence of these substances in our complex supply chains. Therefore, we need a longer transition period.
Although fluoropolymers meet the definition of PFAS substances - they have CF3- or -CF2- groups - they are fundamentally different from low molecular weight PFAS. Fluoropolymers meet the OECD criteria of PLC (polymer of low concern) (OECD 2009 https://www.oecd.org/env/ehs/risk-assessment/42081261.pdf) and have well-documented safety profiles: they are thermally, biological-ly and chemically stable, poorly soluble in water, not mobile, not bioavailable, not bioaccumulative and not toxic (Korzeniowski et all, Integrated Environmental Assessment and Management; Volume 19, Number 2; pp. 326-354). This study, in conjunction with the Henry study (Henry et al, Integr Environ Assess Manag. 2018 May;14(3):316-334.), shows that approximately 96% of the global fluoropolymer market meets the criteria for PLC.
This considered, we require:
• transition period of at least 48 months, as there is currently no information obligation for PFAS within the supply chain and this time is needed even if substitutes are available for the changeover of complex products and processes
• risk-based approach (according to art. 68(1) REACH) and exclusion of fluoropolymers (including fluoroelastomers) classified by the OECD as polymers of low concern from the restriction proposal. Otherwise, an at least 12-year derogation period is indispensable for all industrial applications (B2B) of EEE according to the RoHS definition, including automation, monitoring and control technology (meaning both systems/machines and process technology)
• no reporting obligations during the derogation period for fluoropolymers as there are currently no alternatives for fluoropolymers and the information from the supply chain is insufficient
• a procedure for requesting new exemptions and a renewal option in case of continuous lack of PFAS alternatives (to be taken into ac-count in the REACH revision)
• a general exclusion for product that have been already placed on the market so that they can be resold or further processed and placed on the market again as a component of more complex products/articles. Otherwise, they would have to be disposed of as waste
• an at least 5-year derogation for the CF4 plasma etch process for polyimide in the use sector Electronics and semiconductors

We also support the submissions already made and in progress by ZVEI, VDMA, BDI, DIHK

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Our company does not manufacture PFAS substances, but buys PFAS-containing materials, components and process chemicals, which are used in the production of finished products. PFAS emissions during production are kept to a minimum. Scrap from internal assembly processes is collected and handed over to professional waste treatment/recycling companies in accordance with the legal waste regulations.   We manufacture automation and control technology for a wide range of industrial applications.  Our products are designed to be durable to ensure stable and reliable use by our customers. This equipment is installed in plants by qualified professionals. During the use phase, the fluoropolymers used in our products do not cause any emissions when used as intended After end-of-life, these products are collected, segregated, and recycled in accordance with European and local waste regulations.  Our products are mainly electrical and electronic equipment in the scope of RoHS and WEEE. Thus, proper collection and recycling is ensured and controlled.  There is a wealth of data showing that fluoropolymers such as PTFE do not degrade in the environment or release substances of toxi-cological or ecotoxicological concern (Hintzer & Schwertfeger; https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118850220.ch21).

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: No evidence was found that PFAS substances are released into the air during the incineration process of PTFE (Aleksandrov et all.;Chemosphere, vol. 226, July 2019, pages 898-906). Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) can be almost completely converted to fluorine (F) (as hydrofluoric acid (HF)) under typical waste incineration conditions at the BRENDA pilot plant at the Karlsruhe Institute of Tech-nology (KIT). Therefore, PTFE incineration should be considered an acceptable form of waste treatment. The second method is chemi-cal degradation. Production waste of various polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) compounds was pyrolyzed (Polymer Degradation and Stability Volume 62, Issue 1, 1998, Pages 1-7).  The almost complete conversion of PTFE to gases by pyrolysis provides an excellent feedstock for a TFE production plant and can be used to obtain monomers to produce fluoropolymers. Prof Nadagouda [Chemical Engineering Journal 457 (2023) 141235], in a comprehensive publication, presented a few known methods for the degradation of PFAS compounds. These include sonochemical/ultrasonic degradation, hydrothermal microwave treatment, subcritical or supercritical treatment, electrical discharge plasma technology, thermal destruction/combustion methods, low/high temperature thermal desorption process, vapour energy generator (VEG) technology and mechanochemical destruction. This review discusses in detail the background, degradation mechanisms/pathways and progression of each process.  In summary, PFAS degradation methods are known and large-scale research is currently being conducted to improve the processes. In our view, the sector should be adequately supported to develop methods for the safe and effective degradation of PFAS compounds Recycling of fluoropolymer products and fluoropolymer-containing products is difficult because separation of the fluoropolymer from the end products is not always possible (Hintzer & Schwertfeger; https://doi.org/10.1002/9781118850220.ch21). This is due to the fact that fluoropolymers are mainly used in small parts of larger finished products from a wide range of materials. There are sev-eral options for recycling fluoropolymer products. In primary recycling, solid fluoropolymer waste is milled and then reintroduced into the production cycle of some fluoropolymer products.  In secondary recycling, solid fluoropolymer waste is milled and then degraded to approximately 1% of the original degree of polymerisation. The recovered material can be used to manufacture new fluoropolymer products. Finally, in tertiary or upcy cling recy-cling, the solid fluoropolymer is milled and then decomposed into the starting monomers at temperatures higher than 600 °C (pyroly-sis) to obtain the same chemical components from which the fluoropolymer was produced; the monomers, such as tetrafluoroeth-ylene, are purified by distillation and can then be reused to produce new fluoropolymer (Schlipf & Schwalm, HIGH-PERFORMANCE PLASTICS Fluoropolymers 2014).  Regarding the CF4 (Tetrafluoromethane) process please refer to the attached report in section V.

8. Other identified uses: Article 68(1) of REACH states that substances may only be restricted if they pose an unacceptable risk to human health or the environ-ment. This unacceptable risk must be demonstrated in a risk assessment in accordance with Annex XV of the REACH Regulation.  Based on the OECD definition of PFAS in introducing a restriction on the use of this class of compounds, PFAS substances that have not undergone a risk assessment and for which no unacceptable risk has been demonstrated are restricted. This definition is based solely on chemical structure and does not take into account the hazardous properties or hazards of PFAS. As a result, it covers about 10 000 sub-stances with very different physical and chemical properties. Fluoropolymers are used in critical applications and in many areas, there is no substitute for fluoropolymers. Discontinuing the produc-tion and use of fluoropolymers would be a great loss for the innovation of the EU industry and economy. It would reduce the EU's glob-al competitiveness and also have a negative impact on the implementation of the EU Green Deal. It is crucial to develop a strategy that allows the EU to meet its commitments under the Green Deal, while implementing a balanced regulatory approach to PFAS.   Please refer to the attached report in section V!

10. Analytical methods: There are more than 10,000 PFASs, and specific analytical methods are available for only 40. If non-polymeric PFASs are known to be used in a product, a targeted analysis for PFASs can be performed. However, if polymeric PFASs are used in the product or if it is not known which PFASs are present in the product, a total fluorine analysis should be performed. Since the fluorine concentration may be from substances other than PFAS, e.g., fluorine outside PFAS, the results may not be objective. It is suggested that the legal text refers to the relevant EN test standards for the relevant product groups, as limits for total sub-quantities are only meaningful based on uniform test methods.  ppb or ppm are not an SI unit it would be better to use the unit µg/kg or mg/kg.   A limit value of 25 ppb (= 25 µg/kg) requires a test method with a suitable limit of quantification (LOQ), which also considers the measurement uncertainty  25 ppb and 50 ppm are extremely low limits that quickly push analytics to their limits in complex supply chains. Usual limits in regula-tions such as 0.1 mg /kg (1000 ppm) would be more suitable.

General Comments: We decided to submit a non-confidential and confidential report (attachments section IV an section V) to elaborate in detail on all the important topics addressed in the ECHA public consultation request. It is recommended to ECHA examiners to evaluate the confidential report, since more detailed and business related data could be provided. Please note that due to time constraints, this document may not include all detailed information about the ‘missing uses – Analysis of alternatives and socio-economic analy-sis’, but further submissions by Berghof Fluoroplastic Technology will provide this information during the course of the public con-sultation. A summary is given below, but note that all detailed information with supporting references and data is presented in the attachments!

Summary:

Scope or restriction option analysis:
The scope of our contribution is the processing of fluoropolymers in general, PTFE in particular and more specifically: suspension PTFE. It should be noted that Berghof Fluoroplastic Technology solely processes PTFE manufactured by suspension polymerization (i.e. sPTFE) to obtain sintered PTFE products to serve i) high-density/solid PTFE, ii) porous PTFE, iii) optical PTFE. It is known and confirmed by multiple sPTFE suppliers, that sPTFE does not require PFAS-based processing aids in their manufacturing process. Berghof Fluoroplastic Technology endeavor a supply chain, from raw material to shipped products, without PFAS-of-concern.
The consumption of all PTFE types worldwide and in western Europe is 190 and 35 Mio. kg respectively. The suspension PTFE mar-ket size is estimated to reach 1.500 Mio US$ by 2027 after growing at a CAGR of 7,2% from 2022 to 2027.
PTFE is a high performance polymer with a unique set of properties, e.g. temperature range from -250 to +260°C, universal chem-ical resistance, hydrophobic properties, excellent dielectric properties, amongst many others. This makes it an extremely valuable materials for the use in many different industries.

Hazard or exposure:
PTFE is a polymer of low concern (PLC) in terms of its potential environmental and human health impacts. To this, it is important that suspension PTFE is manufactured without the use of PFAS-of-concern. To confirm this, two other information sources are given related to hazard or exposure, i.e. i) safety data sheets and ii) statements of compliance (e.g. food contact material, USP class VI).

Environmental emissions:
During PTFE processing, emissions of PFAS-of-concern due to heating of the PTFE in the sintering process does not occur.
Berghof Fluoroplastic Technology has taken measures to further optimize the use of resources to meet the criteria of ‘Operation Clean Sweep’. Berghof Fluoroplastics Technology is an official partner of the 3M’s worldwide unique Fluoropolymer Up-Cycling Project. More than 95% of the generated waste of the production process is reused or recycled! Just a very small portion is too much contaminated (e.g. dirt) and leaves the factory for incineration. It is shown in scientific studies that municipal incineration of fluoropolymers using best available technologies is not a significant source of PFAS and should be considered an acceptable form of waste treatment. The relation between PTFE and its global impact as microplastic (MP) in marine environment was investigat-ed and it was concluded that PTFE plays a medium role when it concerns microplastics. sPTFE at Berghof Fluoroplastic Technology is used for industrial and high tech products only and is not directly applied as consumer goods. Therefore, the contribution of sPT-FE to microplastics is estimated very low. PTFE has a high molecular weight, no water solubility and volatility, therefore they are not expected to degrade to lower molecular weight PFAS.
 
Baseline:
Berghof Fluoroplastic Technology processes PTFE to make a wide variety of PTFE components consisting of high-density/solid PTFE, porous PTFE and optical PTFE for various industries: Semiconductor industry, laboratory equipment/technology, automotive, aerospace, chemical industry, industrial processing, electronics and electrical equipment, photonics (optical industry / light meas-urement), food & beverage, medical technology.

Information on alternatives:
PTFE is a high performance material and has many beneficial properties, especially the combination of these properties makes the difference in comparison to alternative materials. High performing polymers permit exceptional end-use-applications, special-ized products at high costs. In general, it can be stated, that PTFE will only be applied, when this is really required for the applica-tion, otherwise a less costly material will be chosen. PTFE is not used for conveniency, but for high-end products where a certain combination of properties is really necessary (essential use!).

Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues:
As soon as the restriction takes effect, it is expected that Berghof Fluoroplastic Technology will lose a very large share of the total revenue which is related to European business. Customer and industry/application demands cannot be met anymore and no com-petitive products can be offered. Relocating the production of Berghof Fluoroplastic Technology to outside Europe is the only al-ternative for the company to remain. This will result in losses of i. jobs, ii. taxes and iii technical/production knowhow in Europe. It will be a challenge (or an impossible mission) to compensate the revenue of the European market outside of Europe.
This does not have an impact solely on Berghof Fluoroplastic Technology but on whole Berghof Group as well. The existence of the total Berghof Group is highly endangered because of the entanglement of the PTFE products in the Berghof Group. Other subsidi-aries, i.e. Berghof Products + Instruments and Gigahertz Optik cannot apply these high-quality products with fit-to-purpose proper-ties anymore. The high-value products cannot be offered in the market anymore in a fair and competitive way. Berghof Fluoro-plastic Technology is a significant pilar for the Berghof Company. It can be concluded that the impact of a possible fluoropolymer ban will be devastating to the Berghof Group and its further existence is extremely doubtful.

Request for exemption:
Berghof Fluoroplastic Technology cannot comprehend the possible ban of fluoropolymers in general, PTFE in particular and more specifically: suspension PTFE. This fluoropolymer type is a polymer-of-low-concern and can be manufactured without using fluori-nated production aids, like fluorosurfactants. It is already confirmed by various sPTFE manufacturers that PTFE applied at Berghof Fluoroplastic Technology is manufactured with no such production aids. Berghof Fluoroplastic Technology endeavor a supply chain, from raw material to shipped products, without PFAS-of-concern.
We are not against a restriction/limitation of hazardous, persistent and mobile PFAS-of-concern, and support a scientific approach differentiating high and low risk substances based on risk assessment. In that way, it should be concluded that fluoropolymers should not be treated in a similar way as other PFAS and should be removed from the ECHA restriction dossier.
In general, it can be stated, that PTFE will only be applied, when this is really required for the application, otherwise a less costly material will be chosen. Furthermore, it is no discussion that the fluorine loop should be closed. This is manageable for PTFE ap-plied in industrial applications or in high tech products. These products are traceable and/or recyclable. The application of PTFE in consumer goods should be minimized and only applied if really necessary.
The socio-economical impact of a possible restriction or a ban of PTFE on Berghof Fluoroplastic Technology is severe. Relocating the production of Berghof Fluoroplastic Technology to outside Europe is the only alternative for the company to remain. This will result in losses of i. jobs, ii. taxes and iii technical/production knowhow in Europe. The existence of the total Berghof Group in Eu-rope is highly endangered because of the entanglement of the PTFE products in the Berghof subsidiaries. It can be concluded that the impact of a possible fluoropolymer ban will be devastating to the Berghof Group and its further existence is extremely doubt-ful. The uncertainty among various stakeholders, which is already evident in the initial reluctance to invest after the publication of the restriction dossier, already suggests how dramatically and quickly the Berghof Group would be hit by a possible fluoropolymer ban.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We develop, manufacture and market electronic components and systems focusing on fast-growing leading-edge technology markets, which include automotive electronics, industrial electronics and consumer electronics as well as information and communications technology. We have a global presence and are close to our customers. In the European Economic Area (EEA) alone, we already employ around 7,500 people at a total of 12 locations. In addition to the production of standard products, another of our core competence is working with our customers to implement solutions that meet their needs.

Our electronic components and systems are found in almost every electrical and electronic device, where they are indispensable for proper functioning. They perform important functions in conventional as well as electrically powered vehicles, industrial machinery, and electric trains, but also in wind turbines and photovoltaic systems, household appliances, LED lights, smartphones, notebooks, and entertainment devices. Everywhere, solutions from us secure the power supply, protect electronic circuits, capture measured variables, and ensure trouble-free operation.

We carefully reviewed the REACH Annex XV restriction proposal regarding Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) and have identified various use cases where PFAS are essential and not replaceable in both, our manufacturing processes as well as in our products. With this contribution we want to express our deep concerns regarding the proposed and universal restriction of PFAS. For our in-depth analysis please refer to the confidential attachment.

PFAS are crucial as an enabling material not only to sustain our European production and business, but also for the ability to achieve the targets of strategic EU policies set in terms of the European Green Deal, European Chips Act, digitalization and decarbonization of European industry as well as the European re-industrial policies.

PFASs are essential in a wide range of applications at the present time and for the foreseeable future. PFAS are used due to their unique combination of properties and their important characteristics for the wide range of our products and technologies.
- Environment-independent lifetime
- High temperature performance
- Electrical insulation; dielectric strength
- Chemical resistance against aggressive media
- Heat resistance at extreme temperatures and non-flammability
- Resistance against climatic influences (e. g. moisture, wetness, dust)
- Good mechanical properties (e.g. abrasion, surface tension, friction)

UNMANAGEABLE THRESHOLD

The proposed threshold of 25 ppb is far below any manageable reporting threshold for companies in the middle of supply chains. It is also about minor impurities for which even the manufacturer himself does not know the information, unless highly precise and costly measurements are made (for which, according to the information from the chemical industry, no analytical methods for PFAS have been established as international standard yet).

Even the smallest impurities lead to large quantities of raw materials and products (including those indented to be re-used/recycled and those already placed on the market for the first time) becoming hazardous waste.

POLYMERS OF LOW CONCERN

The vast majority of PFAS remaining in products belong to the polymeric PFAS group that is considered thermally, biologically, and chemically stable, negligibly soluble in water, nonmobile, nonbioavailable, nonbioaccumulative, and nontoxic.

In general, the commercially available and used fluoropolymers, which account for about 96% of the overall global fluoropolymer market, are deemed polymers of low concern, e. g. by OECD.

USAGE AND ALTERNATIVES (respectively the lack of thereof)

While some chemistries might offer a similar performance to PFAS for a particular parameter or property, it is the unique combination of properties that sets fluoropolymers apart and makes them vital for the electric components industry.

Alternative solutions are only partially available for some specific applications, for some no alternative is known at all.

- PTFE, FEP, ETFE, PVDF or PFA:
Exemplary use cases: electrical insulation on electronic components (cable sheath, shrink tubes, etc.)
Required characteristics: unique combination of heat resistance, electrical insulation, resistance to chemicals and mechanical properties (abrasion, flexibility, …),
Alternatives: PVC or PP are already in use as wire insulation for low temperature applications, but they cannot be used if high operating temperatures (above 105°C) are required. Polymers like PEEK or Polyimide are suitable for high operating temperature but have different mechanical and/or electrical properties compared with fluorinated polymers.

- FKM or FVMQ
Exemplary use cases: O-rings and sealings
Required characteristics: unique combination of heat resistance, resistance to chemicals and mechanical properties (flexibility)
Alternatives: EPDM rubber, Nitrile rubber (NBR) or Hydrogenated NBR as sealings are not suitable in most applications due to their insufficient media resistance.

- PFPE (example 1):
Exemplary use cases: glue for attaching sensitive MEMS to pressure ports
Required characteristics: unique combination of wide application temperature range, resistance to chemicals and mechanical properties (stability)
Alternatives: Substitution only partially possible by glass solders with lead (Pb) content. Also the substance lead (Pb) is affected by several regulations (RoHS, ELV, REACH) and should be avoided as PFAS-replacement for environmental reasons.

- PFPE (example 2):
Exemplary use cases: process aid in the manufacturing of film capacitors to define unmetallized area
Required characteristics: unique combination of electrical parameter and heat resistance
Alternatives: Not known.

- PFPE (example 3):
Exemplary use cases: heat transfer fluid for resistance measurement at NTC thermistors
Required characteristics: unique combination wide application temperature range, resistance to chemicals, dielectric properties
Alternatives: Not known for a general replacement. Only in some specific cases, silicone oil can be used. But silicone oil is a banned substance for certain applications (e.g., automotive) and by customers.

- PTFE tools
Exemplary use cases: jigs and tools in the production of electronic components (e.g. wafer carriers, sealing rings and handling tools).
Required characteristics: unique combination of heat resistance, resistance to chemicals (process aids) and mechanical properties (flexibility and stability) to prevent scratches on e.g. sensitive silicone-wafers
Alternatives: Not known.

- PFAS coatings
Exemplary use cases: coating/encapsulation of sensors in harsh environments
Required characteristics: unique combination of heat resistance up to 260°C, resistance to chemicals, resistance to moisture and wetness (hydrophobic properties), mechanical properties (stability), dielectric strength at high temperature.
Alternatives: It is very likely that alternatives do not exist at all (based on experience from extensive R&D efforts).

- C3F8, C4F8 (and CF4):
Exemplary use cases: used for MEMS Reactive Ion Etching (RIE) and Deep Reactive Ion Etching (DRIE) in order to passivate the silicon surface
Required characteristics: Achievable aspect ratio (defined as the total depth etched divided by the total elapsed time)
Alternatives: Not known at all. A sufficient aspect ratio is only known to be commercially achievable with fluorinated process gases.

IMPACT ON THE ELECTRONIC COMPONENTS SECTOR

For the electric components sector, the proposed restriction imposes a blanket ban on a huge number of substances in an undifferentiated manner and without proof of a specific risk. It is threatening production, research and development sites and activities in Europe and their competitiveness worldwide.

Also, the "hidden cross-section applications" such as seals, plain bearings and lubricants in components, machines and plant equipment are affected. Here, too, a ban would have far-reaching consequences even if PFASs were not added to the final product, so that the expected overall impact is likely to be much more serious and European sites and jobs are at stake.

In general, high efforts and time-consuming procedures are involved to test, approve and adopt alternative solutions for any of the PFAS uses. As for almost all known uses, no replacements are available yet, the actual fundamental material development or complete redesign of products takes longer than 5 years, provided that suitable solutions can be found at all. Once a possible replacement is identified, the time for validation, industrialization, customer and regulatory approval regularly takes another 2-3 years – at least; in difficult cases also more than 12 years is realistic.

EXEMPTION AND DEROGATION REQUEST

We call on the regulatory authorities to preserve the European production, labor and sales market. Restrict PFAS only in areas where there is a real risk from PFAS and establish exemptions and derogations where PFAS are safe to be used and crucial in critical-to-the-world applications:

1. Fully exclude polymeric PFAS from the scope of the upcoming restriction; at least fluoropolymers/-elastomers and perfluoropolyether.

2. Fully exclude PFAS in sensors and their manufacturing process from the scope of the upcoming restriction.

3. Establish a 13,5-year exemption for the use of PFASs in electronic components and their manufacturing, to be reviewed for renewal at least two years prior to expiration. In this context it is very important to choose a wording that allows PFAS as ingredient within the components as well as the use of PFAS as process aids in the production of electronic components.

4. Establishing a reasonable and practicable threshold for intentionally added levels of 0.1 percent by weight.

For no. 1 to 3 above we propose the following wording:
“By way of derogation, paragraphs 1 and 2 do not apply to:
- Polymeric PFAS such as fluoropolymers/elastomers and perfluoropolyether for use in and manufacturing of electrical and electronic equipment (EEE) or associated electronics and components such as control units, sensors, TVS diodes, capacitors, resistors, inductors, filters and electrical and electromechanical components such as MEMS and connectors.
- PFAS for use in and manufacturing of sensors (e.g., temperature sensors, pressure sensors, MEMS).
- Non polymeric PFAS for use in and manufacturing of electrical and electronic equipment (EEE) or associated electronics and components such as control units, sensors, TVS diodes, capacitors, resistors, inductors, filters and electrical and electromechanical components such as MEMS and connectors until 13,5 years after EiF. This derogation shall be reviewed and assessed by the commission no later than 11,5 years after EiF.”

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Our input mainly covers “Electronics and semiconductor (Annex E.2.11.)”. However, since other sectors also depend on the passive electric components, some of our contributions refers to e.g. Applications of fluorinated gases (Annex E.2.8.), Lubricants (Annex E.2.14), and “Plastics (other than packaging) and rubber/elastomer production (including flame retardant) [These are not listed in Table 9, but shown as “uses not researched in detail” in Table A1 of Annex A.].

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The amount of PFAS, which can theoretically be emitted in the End-of-Life treatment, is very limited. PFAS containing articles in electrical and electronic equipment are collected and dealt with in accordance with applicable regulations, e.g. Waste Framework Directive (WFD) 2008/98/EC, ELV Directive 2000/53/EC and WEEE Directive 2012/19/EU. If the components cannot be repaired or directly reused, they are sent for material or thermal recycling (a recent study by Conversio has shown that at its end-of-life approximately 85% of all fluoropolymers end up in waste-to-energy recovery incinerators). In these processes, the polymeric PFAS contained in our articles are either broken down into their original components or mineralized so that the PFAS properties are lost. Latest studies confirm that fluoropolymers at their end of life when incinerated under representative European municipal incinerators conditions do not generate any measurable levels of PFAS emissions and therefore pose no risk to human health and the environment.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Most of the technically used PFAS are stable for a long time and very resistant to chemicals. PFAS waste treatment technologies are mostly investigated and technically evaluated by energy assisted technologies. In the case of polymeric PFAS, incineration technologies were investigated with PTFE waste. Under test conditions in a waste incineration chamber, with a setup in compliance to the requirements of the 17th BImSchV, it was demonstrated that polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) can be almost fully transformed into fluoride (F-) (as hydrofluoric acid (HF)). Samples of the flue gas were analysed for the presence of 31 PFAS and found to be without significant measurable PFAS content.[1] At temperatures above 750°C PTFE decomposed to C2F4 and C3F6 in a pyrolysis process. During further combustion CF4 will be generated. At combustion temperatures above 1000°C CF4 formation is much reduced.[2] Based on this result a municipal incineration system according to the requirements according to §8 of the 17.th BImSchV (3) was sufficient to not detect any PFAS in the flue gas with exception of greenhouse gases like CF4 or C2F6 but with low evidence due to weak database. Technologies for CF4 decompositions are in operation and development with a focus on semiconductor processes.  A system for incineration of hazardous waste operates at about 200°C higher combustion temperature. A test facility for incineration of production PFAS waste was setup in Cooperation with the “Deutsche Bundesstiftung Umwelt” and company Dyneon. This facility is able to decompose more than 90% into its monomers.[4] Other test facilities investigated the incineration of PFOA treated fibers and observed decomposition at 1000°C without chromatographically detectable PFAS in the flue gas.[5] In a literature study PFOA and PFOS decomposition was successfully investigated at 350°C in supercritical water.[6] Incineration of Perfluoropolyether (PFPE) are less investigated but during development of PFPE fluids was observed that these fluids become instable at temperature above 290°C.[7] Other incineration systems for PFPE operate at 330°C with metallic iron reactants like aluminum powder for binding decomposed PFPE.[8]  For treatment of radioactive PFPE lubricants an incineration system with MnO2-catalyst and N12CO3 immobilizer was successfully tested. Impacts on the recycling industry: PFAS-containing products already placed on the EU market can no longer be supplied after the compliance enforcement date and have to be disposed of as hazardous waste. Also, existing stocks of PFAS-containing components and equipment already placed on the market for the first time have to be disposed of as hazardous waste, incl. almost all electric and electronic devices for second-hand use.  Recycling industry is working with high volume processing, such as shredding, of different types of products with different compositions on a ton scale and not on a single piece scale. Given the extremely low threshold of 25 ppb, even a few components containing PFAS would degrade extremely large quantities of recycled materials into hazardous waste.  High amounts of high-quality material as well as still fully functional devices must be treated as hazardous waste instead of being recycled, reused and conserving resources. General Comments: We disagree with the proposed PFASs restriction and request that fluoropolymers as well as the PFASs monomer feedstock are excepted from this proposal. PTFE as well as other fluoropolymers are “Polymers of Low Concern” (PLC) according to OECDs PLC criteria and that is because they are non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water soluble and non-mobile molecules and are judged to have no significant impact on the environment and humans. High molecular weight fluoropolymers, such as PTFE, do not degrade into persistent fluorinated chemicals that can contaminate water or cross a cell membrane. In fact, PTFE is used in many food, pharmaceutical, and medical applications. PTFE has unique properties and currently there are no alternatives with sufficiently similar properties. It has been already 70 years since the commercialization of fluoropolymers (including PTFE) and there has been no success in finding alternative materials which can serve to replace or improve on their performance. Thus the chances of discovering and commercializing new alternatives within a timespan of proposed derogations (up to 13 years) is extremely unlikely, if not impossible. General Comments: We do see the need of restrictions in order to protect the environment and peoples health, but we believe that PFAS with low hazard should be excluded from this restrictions. The fluoropolymers ar high molecular structures and they are not volatile and will not be solved in the human body or in drinking water and the environment at normall use. We therefore  believe that the fluoropolymers should not be a part of the scope of the restriction. Instead restrictions on emissions of the volatile PFAS used producing Fluoropolymers and producing products containing  fluorpolymers and restrictions on disposal, could be a solution in . In this case we could protect the environment and still take advantage of the fantastic properties that the fluoropolymers provides and that is used in many sectors with benefits for environment, Industry and the economic

6. Missing uses: We are a small company providing the service of applying coatings on Industry part that is widely used in the production Industry. A large part of our coatings are fluoropolymer coatings containing a high amount of fluoropolymer ( 50-100% fluorpolymer) We are using coatings containing different polymers for different applications and we also do a good job in finding the right solution for our customers. We normally do not recommend an expensive fluoropolymer solution if it is not nessecary. In general, we use PFA, ECTFE, PTFE, FEP and ETFE in our coatings.  We are using the unique properties of the fluoropolymers for coatings on many different parts and in many different sectors/applications and many applications that is not described in the restriction proposal:  Corrosion Protection: We are coating process equipment in many industries to protect the equipment against corrosion. A large sector for this is the chemical industry that utilises that the fluoropolymers can withstand harsh chemical environments. We are coating vessels and equipment to protect the steel from strong acids or alkali at temperatures up to 260°C. In some cases it is possible to manufacture the parts in a high alloy steel and still maintain the long lifetime of the part, however this is expensive and in some cases a high alloy steel is not even sufficient protection against corrosion. We have experienced that a good ECTFE or PFA coating can protect our customers parts in an environment of concentrated sulfuric acid at high temperature (260°C for PFA) for more than 20 years. Applications where we don’t see an alternative at the moment: • Desulfurization – corrosion protection of steel against concentrated sulfuric acid at temperatures up to 260°C.  • Equipment for Geothermic installations – corrosion protection • Equipment for pharmaceutical production – corrosion protection and non-stick • Equipment for Chemical industry – corrosion protection against harsh chemicals • Equipment for Electrolysis/production of Green Hydrogen – corrosion protection against electrolyte • Coating of measurement apparatus and thermo sensors for Industry • Machine parts for paint and varnish industry – both corrosion protection and non-stick applications. • Rollers for different industries. Corrosion protection and non-stick properties against chemicals, glues etc Since we are only a small company, we are using 7-12 tons of powder coating for these applications and most of this powder is fluoropolymer and mostly PFA of ECTFE  Non-stick and Low friction properties  We have many customers in production industry where Non-stick properties AND some of the other properties from fluoropolymers comes into use. We are providing coating solution to the following industries amongst others: food, medico, graphical Industry, Textile and paint/Varnish industry. Also we have customers in machine industry where we do not necessarily know the end user applications/sector.  For some of these applications we can find an alternative coating solution within for example ceramic coatings, we have in fact all ready changed in to ceramic coatings for some applications many years ago. However for many of our customers it is not possible with these alternatives because other properties from the fluoropolymers are needed. For example, the ductility is not the same for a ceramic as for a polymer, so our customers will not be able to bend the parts after coating or to machine/punch out parts of a coated panel. Another problem is that we don’t see as long lasting non-stick for the alternatives as for the fluoropolymer coating – the non-stick properties will wear faster for the ceramic coating than the polymer coating and our customers will therefor suffer economically since they need to have new coatings more often and therefore more down time in production. We have customers telling, that with new equipment coated with fluoropolymer coating they see a 30% higher output in their production that with worn equipment and a much higher need for cleaning with harsh chemicals. Another problem is that both the pot life and shelf life for these coatings are much shorter than for the fluoropolymer coatings, which can lead to larger scrap for a company like ours where we do not produce the same parts and the same coatings every day.  In spray applications we can come around this by planning, but we also have dipping process, where we use the same small amount of coating for a long period (1week or more). This is not possible with ceramic coatings of short pot life (1-2 days). Therefore, we will need to use more resources/coating material in order to coat the same number of parts. The coatings are also more expensive than most of the one-coat non-stick or low friction coating. Some coatings are 3-4 times the price of fluoropolymer coatings in purchase, and we as a coating company needs to add extra on this since the ceramic coatings do not come in an ready to use version.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We employ fluoropolymers within our hemodialysis devices due to their excellent chemical resistance and their resistance at temperatures up to 150°C. The hydraulic circuit contains sections of extreme pH and it has to be cleaned and disinfected for repeated use. Fluoropolymers such as PVDF, PTFE, FEP and PFA withstand the repeated reprocessing at acidic and alkaline pH without compromising the biocompatibility of the device. We consider the fluoropolymers superior to silicone which has similar mechanical properties but lower resistance and may be source of siloxane leachables classified as SVHC (Octamethylcyclotetrasiloxane, D4). It may be possible to replace some PVDF parts with PPSU or PEEK. However, no alternative materials are known for PTFE, FEP or PFA with equal thermic / chemical resistance and biocompatibility. Emissions from fluoropolymers that we apply for medical devices can be well controlled because they are only disposed of by service personnel. Since the emission is 100% coupled to end-of-life of the components during maintenance or end-of-life of the devices – 100% industrial waste, 100% can be incinerated or recycled. Waste management will be improved by the EU waste framework directive and fluoropolymers could be a specific group of waste. We request a permanent derogation for class IIb medical devices that are used for dialysis and their production tools, since fluoropolymers have an essential impact on the safety of these devices coupled to a very low emission.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Medical devices; Production of medical devices

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: 1) Manufacture phase: we use solid fluoropolymer components from qualified suppliers. 2) Use phase: Due to the outstanding performance of PVDF, PTFE, FEP and PFA in terms of biocompatibility and long term stability, PVDF, PTFE, FEP and PFA components are used in class IIb hemodialysis devices without any leachables or emissions in use phase. 3) End-of-life phase: Components are replaced during device maintenance after or are collected after end-of-life of the device. The lifetime of our devices under regular maintenance is about 8 years. The fluoropolymer components are disposed of as professional/industrial waste, mainly for incineration. They do not consist of several materials such as for coatings and could potentially be recycled with a good yield. Since the emission is 100% coupled to end-of-life of the components during maintenance or end-of-life of the devices – 100% industrial waste, 100% can be incinerated or recycled. Waste management will be improved by the EU waste framework directive and fluoropolymers could be a specific group of waste.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Scientific reports on waste incineration and thermal recycling:  2019 Aleksandrov et al. PTFE addition to waste incineration conditions showed no addition to PFOA contaminations 2023 Sormo et al. Decomposition of various PFAS under dry pyrolysis

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Impact of proposed concentration limits on recycling: 50 mg/kg would not enable us to use the fluorpolymers any longer. The fluorine content of PVDF, PTFE, FEP and PFA is about 50-75% fluorine and the components we need for application are larger than the proposed limit.  Fluorpolymer recycling is under development e.g. at OMV/Burghausen (Germany).

6. Missing uses: Fluoropolymers in the fluid-contacting circuit of hemodialysis devices (class IIb medical devices) and in the production of dialysis fluids (class IIb medical devices): a. <0,5 tonnes per year for production with emissions of about 10% due to end-of-life; type of PFAS: fluoropolymers. b. Fluoropolymers show excellent chemical resistance and excellent thermoresistance at temperatures up to 150°C, key properties to withstand extreme pH in the hydraulic circuit and extreme pH and temperature during cleaning and disinfection for repeated use at stable biocompatibility. c. Medical device manufacturers for dialysis devices plus their qualified suppliers for biocompatible fluoropolymers;  80.000 patients on chronical dialysis (Germany) and an estimated 10% of critically ill patients on intensive care with organ failure or sepsis: These would have no access or delayed access to the therapy and would eventually die (see ref. 2021 Willam). d. It may be possible to replace some PVDF parts with more expensive materials PPSU or PEEK. Similarly, fluoro rubber FKM could be replaced by EPDM. However, no alternative materials are known for PTFE, FEP or PFA with equal thermic / chemical resistance and equal biocompatibility. We consider the fluoropolymers superior to silicone which can have similar mechanical properties but lower resistance and may be source of siloxane leachables classified as SVHC (Octamethylcyclotetrasiloxane, D4). e. No technically feasible substitutions information by our suppliers for FEP, PTFE and PFA. f. Where it is possible to replace some PVDF parts with more expensive materials PPSU or PEEK, the material costs would increase  significantly. Very likely the cost increase would delay the availability of our devices leading to use of devices with greater patient invasiveness and multiple amount of disposables.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Description of analytical methods Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We fully agree with the wish of ECHA to ban the use of newly produced PFAS added to products. Our sector is processing the waste generated by our society and therefore we are confronted with PFAS in the waste that is discarded to our facilities.

Our members are active throughout the whole waste chain, from waste collection, recycling and processing - including composting and anaerobic digestion - to waste-to-energy and landfill operation. Some are active in sewer maintenance and hazardous waste. All facilities are contributing to recycling waste into new products. Recovering secondary materials prevents shortages and builds bridges to a sustainable future. Recycling is the pathway to a clean environment, contributes to the circular economy and protects the climate. And each kilogram of recycled waste delivers a guaranteed reduction in carbon-dioxide emissions.

The wide distribution of PFAS in society, the reason for this restriction proposal, is also reflected in the waste that is collected and processed in our facilities. And so it is inevitable that PFAS are also found in our recycled products. In contrary to the first addition of pure PFAS by the industry to products, our sector is not deliberately adding any   PFAS to the recycled products, only contamination during our processes can add PFAS, which will be in very limited concentrations.

At this point our sector has some knowledge of PFAS in the waste and has gained some experience with PFAS concentrations in the recycled products, but this knowledge is quite limited due to absence of regulation, clear standards, analytic methods and the broad variety of PFAS, which makes it very costly to examine.

Waste processing, treatment or incineration plants use acceptance criteria; for most members PFAS content is not part of the acceptance criteria, yet, because of the broad variety and the low concentrations in combination with absence of analytical methods and because of the inhomogeneity of waste materials.   Facilities do recognize the role they have to play in removing PFAS from the environment, so known waste streams with high concentrations PFAS are directed to those facilities who are able to handle these streams, mostly specialized incinerators.

Concerning the processing of waste: the waste sector will contribute to a certain amount of removal of PFAS from the environment either by incineration, physical separation or adsorption. It is however more of a side effect of the current processing methods. Only incineration –especially at very high temperatures- actively destructs the PFAS, but at this point it is not precisely known how effectively the PFAS is destructed for each type in the different waste streams. Processing in a rotary kiln and perhaps chemical recycling can destroy PFAS, but at this moment we don’t have any information on this subject. Any other processing step will concentrate the PFAS in a new waste stream but this will not definitely destruct the PFAS. At this moment we don’t see that landfilling of PFAS contaminated waste is an final solution, though it contributes to concentrating the PFAS in 1 place. It is inevitable that during the processing of the waste materials emissions to air and / or to water will occur.
Concerning recycled products: the waste sector is recycling waste into new resources that can replace primary materials in all ranges of products; recycled plastic, metals, granular materials, soil, compost, solvents, etc. In none of these processes we deliberately add any PFAS  to our products so restriction of PFAS will not impact our members in this manner,   but the effect it can have on the sales and use of our products can be enormous. The restriction proposal will set limits on the PFAS concentration in any material and makes no distinction between primary and secondary materials. Because of the broad range of PFAS it is impossible for the sector to guarantee that all of our streams are fulfilling the limits set by the restriction proposal and thus this may lead to refusal of our, from waste generated streams for recycling or re-use, due to the legal uncertainty and current lack of standardization methods. The impact this can have on the recycling industry is potentially enormous with a huge loss of jobs and companies going bankrupt. This will consequently lead to uncontrolled waste streams due to lack of capacity in other fields (landfills, incineration).

At this point, without the proper knowledge of the concentrations of the different PFAS in the different waste streams  , and the uncertainty and lack of standardization, it is not possible to foresee if the waste sector can meet the limits for the recycled materials, both for the individual limit of 25 ppb for PFAS as the sum of PFAS’s of 250 ppb or 50 ppm for polymeric PFASs.

Applying the same limits to the recycling industry as to products with added PFAS will harm the recycling industry and so also the aim of the  European commission to become a circular economy.  We point out that we have to reason from the position that the recycled materials have an end-of-waste status (since that is a core element of a circular economy which we strive to achieve) and henceforth the legal framework of REACH is applicable. When the limits will apply to recycling streams the goals of the restriction proposal will not be reached any faster. It will lead to more landfilling and no final destruction of PFAS, because there isn’t enough capacity to incinerate all waste streams   Off course the net environmental results will be negative with regard to greenhouse gas (carbondioxide) emissions, use of primary materials and so on.

We like to point out that at this stage no alternative techniques are available to extract PFAS from waste products. Also in the coming years PFAS will be allowed in some products, because no alternatives are available. This will extend the period in which waste management companies are confronted with PFAS in their streams.
Precisely because PFAS substances are so difficult to break down, it is vital to look at their presence in recycled raw materials in a different way than in virgin or primary raw materials. Even if primary use of PFAS is banned, society will still be confronted with PFAS for a very long time in our waste streams. Actually, producers at the beginning of the product chain have a lot of influence on the reduction of PFAS in products, the recycling sector however has little or no influence. Therefore, in our opinion, the focus of the restriction should be on product design and the application of primary materials in products. From this point of view a total ban of use of PFAS should be considered.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Incineration household waste At this point some research has been done to study the effectiveness of incineration, but it is very difficult, even impossible, to set-up a good mass balance with regards to PFAS and therefore it is impossible to calculate the effectiveness of incineration. It is known that PFAS can be destructed at higher temperature levels, but the effectiveness is highly dependent on the type of PFAS and the possibility that- with degradation - new, more resistant PFAS can be formed. There will be a difference between the effectiveness of incinerations for hazardous waste and incinerators for household and commercial waste, the first being more effective due to the kind of installation that is used and the higher operational temperatures. At this point some publications will give a range of up to 90% effectiveness or even higher.   Recently in the Netherlands analytical tests have been performed on the bottom ashes from household and commercial waste incinerators. Bottom ashes are used as building materials in construction works. There are however no standards for using building materials in construction works. For re-use of soil an 'Updated action framework for the reuse of PFAS-containing soil and dredging sludge (updated version of December 2021)(National PFAS advisory list) is in force. Although there are no standards for building materials, the standard of this framework is used as a reference for building materials. In the action framework 30+1 PFAS compounds included in the test requirements. The standard is 3 µg/kg for PFOS,  7 µg/kg voor PFOA en 3 µg/kg for all other PFAS, no sum parameters are defined. Compared to these standard, bottom ash complies in most cases (both untreated as treated). But exceedance does occur in several occasions.   The results from the analyses have a high uncertainty, for example due to the sample matrix, pre-processing, cross-contamination in laboratories, etc. Nevertheless, the results of analyses are almost always regarded as the hard truth. There is too little knowledge for a proper understanding of the situation and there is a lack of assessment frameworks/space for interpretation. We will submitted our database on PFAS in bottom ash. The dataset on polymeric PFAS is very limited, at this point it is not known how to determine this concentration. Analysing the Total Fluor content is not an option, this will lead to an overestimation due to the presence of other Fluor components, as the few results have shown.       Also the concentrations of PFAS in the flue gasses are hardly studied. Some test schemes are now starting to develop, but at this point little accurate results are available, the presence of PFAS in flue gases cannot be ruled out, also because some PFAS (especially short chains) are found in waste water of flue gases. We are aware that flue gasses have no relation to REACH, however it illustrates the complexity of proving the effectiveness of the destruction of PFAS.  For all other residues only very limited data is available in the Netherlands at this moment and therefore it is impossible to state something about the effectiveness of incineration. In the end incineration does destroy some PFAS, so it does contribute to the removal of PFAS from the environment, despite the fact that some residues that will be re-used can contain some PFAS.    Incineration waste water   A study has been carried out into the presence of PFAS in waste streams supplied for water purification (mapping). In a defined period of 4 weeks, a random regional test was carried out on all deliveries. Assumptions: - This random sample concerns the sampling of approximately 20% of the delivery of road transport and 100% of the deliveries by ship/water originating from ship cleaning. - Sampling and analysis has been performed by an independent third party. NEN 6600-1 was used as a guideline during the sampling. The samples have been analyzed in a NEN-EN-ISO 17025 accredited laboratory. - Analysis was carried out on the basis of the national PFAS advisory list (dated 12 July 2019). This list contains 30 PFAS connections, which has been supplemented with the GenX parameter. - The reporting limit of the PFAS compounds is 0.02 µg/l unless a sample has requested a different sample preparation, which means that different limits apply.  It follows from the results that: - Hardly any PFAS is found in sampled ship cargoes/washing waters. - In approximately 60% of the deliveries per truck, PFAS was found above the reporting limit. - In about 20% of the deliveries the concentration is >1 ug/l. It should be noted that 1 µg/l equals 1 ppb. - The results show that delivered loads of water (approx. 65%) contain on average more PFAS than ship deliveries (approx. 55%). The sampled oil deliveries (approximately 20%) contained PFAS compounds significantly less often than the water and ship deliveries. - Broken down by sector, PFAS is found in almost all cases in deliveries from waste processing. For other sectors, PFAS is detected in 20 – 50% of the deliveries.  Because PFAS is detected in the majority of loads, pre-treatment of PFAS-containing streams is not opportune, the bottlenecks in acceptance and analysis (such as availability of analyses, duration of analyses, influence by the matrix, lack of standards) are relevant factors in this. - The more complex the waste material, the more difficult the analysis and the higher the reporting limit. After treatment, the complexity of the water flow is lower, as a result of which lower reporting limits are used. This creates a situation where no PFAS is detected before purification, but after purification it is.  - Environmental quality standards are important for the compatibility of the discharge. These are (extremely) low or missing. Acceptance criteria are determined based on what can be allowed in the discharge. Given the low standards or lack of frameworks/clarity, a translation into acceptance criteria is complex.  Biological Physical treatment of water In effluent PFAS is detected in several cases. The sector follows developments with regard to PFAS, and specifically in relation to waste flows/processing. In practice, this is complex. There are two reduction techniques that are assessed in more detail, namely foam fractionation and activated carbon. Foam fractionation is hopeful on the basis of the laboratory tests, but is running into various bottlenecks in practice. The tests with activated carbon are running. The costs are high and this moment exact numbers cannot been given. And as a resultant another waste stream is created, which must be treated to prevent further emission.   The situation with regard to discharge of the effluent is complex. The suitability of the discharge of water is assessed by means of emission/immission tests. The environmental quality standards of the substances/parameters to be assessed are leading in this. For PFAS, environmental quality standards are only available for PFOS, PFOA and GenX. Draft environmental quality standards have been derived for a number of other PFAS (approximately 20), these are very low and have not yet been formally established. There are no environmental quality standards for all other PFAS. If the draft environmental quality standards are adopted, this will result in: - The standards for PFOS (0.007 ng/l), PFOA (0.3 ng/l) and GenX (10 ng/l) will then be tightened considerably. - Very low standards would then apply to various PFAS.  Based on current standards, adaptability already appears to be difficult. The trend is that standards are becoming stricter, which makes the whole thing even more complex and thus reducing the methods to extract PFAs from other waste streams.   Precursors At this stage the behaviour of precursors in the different waste processing streams is unknow. For literature it is known that the total amount of PFAs materials in the outgoing streams is higher that incoming due to the forming by precursors.   At this point the actual formation processes from the different precursors is unknown and thus also it is also unknown how to prevent the formation of PFAS during the processing. This means that at this stage a waste processing company cannot guarantee the end quality of the product even if an extensive sapling protocol has been performed. A total screening of all the materials entering the facility  on all possible precursors is impractical.   Concentration versus Emission At this point the proposal is aiming to reduce the content of PFAS in any material. For primary materials this is indeed the straightest and best way to the desired results. For secondary materials concentration limits is not the way to prevent PFAs distribution to the environment and still promoting re-use of secondary materials. As for other fields we would suggest a risk-based approach, which can be different for different kind of materials.   For example re-use as a building material the risk of emissions is very depending on the field of application. When used as a granular material as a foundation of in embankments the concentration will most likely  not be of interest, contact between people and animals is almost impossible. It will be more sense if one looks into the leaching of PFAS into the environment, this is also in accordance with standards that are developed in the Construction Product Regulation. Also we have found that high   Also we have found that high concentrations not automatically lead to enhanced leaching.    Finally, it is noted that the precise properties differ per specific PFAS. For example, one PFAS spreads faster or is more harmful than the other PFAS. There are also many PFAS about which little is known. PFOA, PFOS and GenX are usually labelled as the most hazardous  substances, but other PFAS are also more or less hazardous. To give a better interpretation of the risk, one idea is to work with so-called Relative Potential Factors (RPFs). These RPFs indicate how harmful individual PFAS are compared to PFOA. Using these RPFs, concentrations or exposures of different PFAS can be expressed in 'PFOA units'. The sum could then be compared with the available risk limits. The Dutch ‘RIVM’ (National Institute for health and environment) has previously published about this, but otherwise little attention is paid to individual assessment of the PFAS involved and the circumstances/application.   (lit. Per- and polyfluorinated substances in waste incinerator flue gases, RIVM report 2021-0143, J. Bakker | B. Bokkers | M. Broekman,

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: The recycling industry has very little influence on the concentration limits of PFAS in the waste they are accepting.   It is important to point out that the Recycling industry does not deliberately add any PFAS to the recycled products they create from the different waste streams. The impact the proposal will have on the recycling industry is hard to predict because it depends on several factors which are beyond the reach of the sector. Also it is very depending on the waste stream and the current processes that are used.  Not only the limits on the products can be challenging but also the reaction of manufacturers that are using our recycled streams is unpredictable. It is very well possible that some start to decline use of any recycled material because a complete PFAS free stream cannot be guaranteed. This will lead to an enormous setback for the circular economy. In the proposal/regulation it must be clear that recycled streams can be used in products to make sure that the goal of reaching an circular economy in 2050 is still possible. We like to indicate that the cross media en macro-economic effects must be weighed in restriction and not only focus on the direct environmental effects of PFAS. In addition to local interests/effects, there should also be an interest for the broader consequences/effects of a situation. We should avoid that certain measures to restrict PFAS can have other (significant) effects, for example: - Refusal of waste streams. However, the waste stream will still be released and another route is necessary. This does not mean that a better/more responsible route is found by definition. - Moving the contamination to a waste material, which then has to be processed again. - Moving the contamination from one to another compartment (e.g. from water to air) - Other environmental effects, for example CO2/nitrogen from transport and combustion    1. The recycling industry has no influence on the PFAS concentration in the waste streams that are collected. Only for certain special waste streams were high concentrations PFAS can be expected, a dedicated process must be applied and this method must focus on destroying the PFAS completely. For most streams the concentration PFAS is unknown, and if measures then only a specific incomplete set can be measured. There is no information at all on precursors and polymeric PFHC. Because of the heterogeneity of these streams and the distribution of PFAS in products it is not possible to separate streams with a higher concentration of PFAS. The current available methods are not suitable for screening the waste streams. This means that mixed waste stream will be processed in the current processes. Even if waste management company’s start to decline streams which may consist PFAS it still means that the stream must be processed at another facility or discarded in another way. This will not automatically means that the most environmental solution is chosen.  Fact is that waste streams with PFAS must be discarded and processed to new secondary materials, either by processing or incineration, or when these options can’t deal with the stream it must be landfilled. In general we have concluded that landfilling of waste is not favorable and not in line with the goals of European Commission to be Circular by 2050.   Also in summertime high PFAS concentrations in the air above landfills are measured, high with regard to incineration (* Lit. Literaturstudie om PFAS fra affaldsforbrænding, Miljøprojekt nr. 2246 September 2023).   At this point there is not enough information of the concentrations in the proposal will be problematic for the different sectors within waste management. Most sectors have done some analysis on the different streams but hardly enough to do an statistical analysis if the material can apply. Also it is not clear in which way the authorities want to enforce the regulation because at this moment no specific rules are known with regards to: - Sampling frequency - Sampling procedures - Pretreatment methods - Certified analytical methods - How to interpret the results and deviations (must all results comply or just the mean value),  -  2. For waste stream it is inevitable that the incoming streams and thus also the recycled products are somehow heterogeneous in the exact composition, which can result in an occasionally exceedance of the proposed limits. This uncertainty will also diminish the acceptance of the industry that uses the recycled products even if the chances on an exceedance are very limited. 3. The analysis that have been performed in the sector shows that mostly the concentration are below the proposed concentration limits, but only a very limited PFAS types have been analyzed (National PFAS advisory list). It can be assumed that most streams will comply with the limit of 25 ppb for any PFAS as measured with targeted PFAS analysis. If the limit of 250 ppb for the sum of PFASs measured as sum of targeted PFAS analysis, optionally with prior degradation of precursors (polymeric PFASs excluded from quantification) can be met is unknown due to limited information on the presence of all this types in waste streams. If the sector can comply with the limit of 50 ppm for PFASs (polymeric PFASs included) is unknown due to absence of information. Also there is current a lack of standardization methods to determine mPFAS, determination of Total Fluor will give an overestimation.    4. Norm setting versus detection limit; as shown in many analysis, there is a difference between detection limit and standard. The detection limit is in a lot of cases higher than the standard, due to the complex matrix of the waste stream. This means that it can never be proven with certainty that the standard will not be exceeded. When setting standards, one must stay far enough away from the detection limit (LoD Limit of Detection). Namely, if the true reading is just on or around the detection limit, there is a 50% chance of a false negative. The standard must therefore always be far enough above the detection limit to avoid a false negative. The measured value follows a gauss distribution, the standard deviation of which depends on the method of analysis, the equipment and the lab. The limit at which no false negative can be measured is called the LoQ (limit of quantification). Classically it is somewhere between 3 to 10 times higher than the LoD. The reporting limit of 0.01% therefore does not provide unambiguous information about whether products will be affected by the restriction proposal.    Instead of burden the sector with challenging limits, the waste management industry  is the only sector that can help to diminish the PFAS that already are produced and are used in products and are released into the environment. Despite the fact that it is not possible to remove all PFAS from the waste streams we certainly have a solid positive effect;- - Specialized incinerators are capable of destruction of PFAS by applying high temperatures and a guaranteed residence time . Even if some PFAS will stay intact, the current flue gas systems will extract a great part of this components; - Regular incinerators will destroy some PFAS, the efficiency will be less compared to the specialized incinerators but  contribute to destruction PFAS; - A lot of sectors have some sort of washing step in the process, the mobile PFAS will be washed out of the streams. Removing of PFAS from the water is still a challenging step, but research is ongoing. This will of course lead to a new waste stream contaminated with PFAS which must be treated by incineration. The total environmental benefit can be discussed. If the standards for discharging effluent become to strict it would mean that upgrading waste streams via washing processes become impossible. This will not only hit the goals for the circular economy, but will also hurt the ambition to remove PFAS from the current streams and the environment.  - Chemical recycling is developing in which waste streams are treated to become new chemical products. Exact information is unknown, but one can assume that PFAS will be destructed to some degree.  - A lot of recycling processes do have some separation steps in which the stream is separated into main stream and residues. Specific information about these residues is unknown, but one can imagine that PFAS will be concentrated in these residues. These residues could be treated, for example by incineration.    Summarizing, we recommend that the final regulation take into account the important role the waste management companies play in removing PFAS from waste streams (and so from the environment) and we ask that is recognized that the waste management industry, that has no part in the first distribution of PFAS, can’t be responsible for the PFAS already distributed in society. The sector can contribute to the greater environmental objective by directing specific known wastes with high concentrations of PFAS to specialized incinerators, the only option to breakdown PFAS components. For all other waste streams the existing routes must be recognized and the products that are produced must not be restricted by any kind of limits   to the concentrations of PFAS . At this point there is simply not enough information about the PFAS distribution in all kind of different waste streams to oversee the impact of the proposal. The waste management industry is the only sector that actively contributes to destruct existing PFAS (and thus remove it from the environment). To reach the goals of the European Union for a Circular Economy also it must be clearly stated that recycling products are exempt from any limit value  s, at least until there are cost effective technical methods to remove PFAS from the different products. . With introducing stringent limit values now Otherwise producers will avoid re-use just to avoid any risk and the circular economy will never become further away. a reality.    In some sectors of the industry is already confronted with PFAS restrictions, re-use of soil ('Updated action framework for the reuse of PFAS-containing soil and, Netherlands), discharging effluent. The limits set by these regulations are very strict and can have a negative effect on re-use . Standards for use of materials must be based on a good balance between safety for people and the environment and on technical and financial possibilities to comply. Naturally, the sector is willing to further implement new techniques in order to further reduce emissions in the coming years.  The waste management sector is willing to look into further options to enhance the removal of PFAS but research is needed to establish these steps.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We fully support the restriction of hazardous PFAS that pose a risk to humans, animals, and the environment. However, the very general definition of PFAS in the present restriction proposal results in an extremely broad group of substances with very different properties and not all of them are hazardous. Fluoropolymers such as PTFE, PFA, FEP and others belong to the group of PFAS but are not toxic, not water soluble, not bio available, not bio accumulative and are classified as polymers of low concern according to OECD.
Therefore, fluoropolymers should be completely excluded from the PFAS restriction proposal.
From our perspective, it would make more sense to not ban fluoropolymers, but to focus on recycling strategies and proper disposal concepts. More R&D work has to be done in this respect.
As a mechanical engineering company, we use fluoropolymers, mainly PTFE, for dynamic and static sealings and valves. The combination of extremely favorable tribological properties, outstanding chemical resistance, very broad temperature operating range and good shape adaptability makes PTFE-based materials the perfect match for dynamic sealings. All other polymer materials exhibit either poor tribological properties, lower chemical resistance, lower continuous operating temperatures or are too rigid or brittle for good sealing efficiencies.
As no alternative materials with the same combination of properties are available, a ban of PTFE and other fluoropolymers would lead to shifting our production of PTFE containing parts outside Europe. Existing machines in Europe could not be operated any longer and our customers from industry most probably also have to shift their production outside Europe.
Please find more details to our applications in the confidential section.

6. Missing uses: Mechanical and plant engineering represents an important economic segment in Europe and yet fluoropolymer applications within this segment are not considered in the PFAS restriction dossier from February 2023. Many machines or plants cannot be operated without sealings, bearings, valves, linings or other parts made of fluoropolymers and other materials are not available for a lot of this applications because of the unique properties of the fluoropolymers. We therefore propose the implementation of a sector for industrial application with sub-sectors for mechanical engineering, plant engineering, chemical/pharmaceutical industry and maybe others. More information is given in the confidential section.
