General Comments: We made an initial input to this consultation in 13th June 2023.
The associated reference number is bb3ca7a6-d243-4b52-b57d-f40c1087d9e7

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Semiconductor products are the key enabler for improved energy consumption and performance across a wide range, of everyday technology applications in society. The semiconductor sector depends on various application of materials (gases, solids, liquids) falling in scope of the PFAS definition. Thus, our following comments are related to the uses and sub uses identified in Table 9 in the Annex XV restriction report.  Use sector: Electronics and semiconductor (Annex E.2.11.) Sub uses: Semiconductors / Wires and cables / Coating, solvents and cleaning / Electronic components / Heat transfer fluids / Advanced semiconductor packaging / Photolithography   Use sector: Applications of fluorinated gases (Annex E.2.8.) Sub-uses: Refrigeration / Insulating gas in electrical equipment

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Some of our sensor chips may contain PFAS to provide a safe connection to the environment while still protecting the sensor. In Europe laws were enacted in the past to characterize the recycling of semiconductor products to achieve minimum environmental impact. For Example: the WEEE Directive (European Parliament and Council, 2012) for consumer electronics and the ELV Directive (European Parliament and Council, 2000) for vehicles.  End-of-life phase of equipment and articles in semiconductor manufacturing: According to a 2023 ESIA publication, the end-of-life of semiconductor manufacturing sites is estimated to be more than 25 years. The crucial need for clean room manufacturing and the use of special hazardous chemicals in high puritiy quality mean that for some use cases only fluoropolymers can fulfill the requirements. This is the reason why a production site may contain several tons of fluoropolymers in pipe linings, valves, seals such as O-rings, etc. (Source: PFAS Consortium - Articles Working Group, 2023). Due to the persistence of fluoropolymers and the long-term use of semiconductor equipment, the emissions in the end-of-life phase of the PFAS-containing equipment are low compared to the quantities found in a fab. Any waste generated is collected according to the harmonized European waste code numbers for mixed plastics (European Commission, 2002) and sent for proper disposal.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: During production: The use of PFC gases (perfluorinated compounds), some of which are considered PFAS as defined in the Restriction Report, is still essential for semiconductor manufacturing. During these thermally highly demanding processes or also during chamber cleaning, a certain amount of the gases is already converted in the process and decomposed there into less harmful components (https://www.ipcc-nggip.iges.or.jp/public/2019rf/pdf/3_Volume3/19R_V3_Ch06_Electronics.pdf, see Table 6.11 there).  In order to further reduce the remaining PFC emissions, the semiconductor industry has agreed ambitious targets for many years. For example, abatement tools have been installed on a voluntary basis. These abatement tools usually work with a destruction removal efficiency (DRE) that depends on the PFC used. For example, the PFAS C2F6 has a standard DRE of 0.95 according to Table 6.17 (https://www.ipcc-nggip.iges.or.jp/public/2019rf/pdf/3_Volume3/19R_V3_Ch06_Electronics.pdf). In these abatement tools, the remaining PFC gases are further reduced using high temperatures (e.g., natural gas burners or electric plasma systems) by first destroying the PFC gases in a combined burner/scrubber system through the chemical reaction of combustion, and then scrubbing and neutralizing them through subsequent washing processes. By applying these technologies, PFC emissions to the environment could be impressively reduced over the years.  Waste treatment: The frequently expressed thesis that PFAS are indestructible is incorrect and has been impressively proven wrong by a number of research results. PFAS can be very well degraded by incineration or pyrolysis. Conventional waste incinerators usually cover a temperature range of 600-1600 °C (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2095809917300796). At least 1,100 °C for 2 seconds results in complete decomposition of most PFAS (Yamada T. et al. 2005) (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S004565350500425X).  Even under state-of-the-art domestic waste incineration conditions, PFAS are converted to inorganic fluoride at a minimum incineration temperature of 850°C (Aleksandrov K. et al. 2019). Investigation of incineration of PFAS substances PFOA, PFHxA, PFOS, recognized as problematic and therefore already regulated, at different temperatures (800 °C, 900 °C, 1000 °C) showed that at higher temperatures of 1000 °C no formation of fluorinated by-products occurred (Residual organic fluorinated compounds from thermal treatment of PFOA, PFHxA and PFOS adsorbed on granular activated carbon (GAC) | https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10163-016-0532-x).

5. Proposed derogations: The European Commission recently adopted a series of proposals aimed at, among other things, shaping EU climate, energy and transport policies to reduce net greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% by 2030 compared to 1990 levels. To achieve this goal, it is essential not only to maintain microtechnology in Europe, but to increase it strongly. The Chips Act of the European Union aims to reach this goal. It recognizes the importance of semiconductors and their manufacturing to achieve the above-mentioned goals.  For this purpose, the German Infineon Technology AG has Frontend and Backend production sites in Regensburg and Warstein and R&D in Neubiberg near Munich. Within our group we also have production sites in various European countries: Dresden (Germany), Villach (Austria) and Cegled (Hungary).  Semiconductors from Infineon Technology AG help to generate electricity from renewable energy sources. They also offer increased efficiency at all stages of the value chain in the energy sector: in generation, transmission, storage, and in particular, in the use of electricity. They form the basis for the intelligent and efficient use of energy: in industrial applications, power supplies for computers and consumer electronics,  as well as in motor vehicles.  Semiconductor manufacturing is characterized above all by the fact that it mostly takes place under clean room conditions and in closed systems. Any entry of impurities into our productions usually has a devastating effect on the quality of our products and is avoided wherever possible. Due to that the presence of employees in the clean room is reduced to the minimum. Under normal production conditions, there are no measurable emissions at the workplaces.  In general, the semiconductor manufacturing can be divided into two parts - "Frontend" and "Backend". In the Frontend, the raw wafer of silicon is processed, while in the Backend, the finished products are manufactured from the separated chip (circuits).  In the Frontend, PFAS are essential in the following areas: Photolithography and Plasma Etching.  Photolithography: Photolithography is one of the central processes for manufacturing integrated circuits. It involves using an exposure process to transfer the image of a photomask onto a photosensitive photoresist. Subsequently, the exposed areas of the photoresist are dissolved (alternatively, dissolution of the unexposed areas is also possible when the photoresist is cured under light). This creates a lithographic mask that allows further processing by chemical and physical processes, ultimately leading to the microchip integrated circuits. Photoresists and anti-reflective coatings for specific applications also contain mostly PFAS, as their chemical and physical properties (wetting agent and photoactive, combined with chemically inert behavior) are necessary in the exposure process of lithography to achieve the desired process result. Especially the generation of more advanced products with smaller and smaller structures require PFAS. These are, for example, photoacid generators (PAGs, such as sulfonium and iodonium acid salts with fluorinated anions), which are essential components of the chemically amplified resists (CARs) used today. When exposed to ultraviolet (UV) light, they generate so-called superacids, which cause the solubility change of the photoresist. All proven successful PAGs are fluorinated. The PAG content in the CAR is small (order of magnitude 1%, mostly smaller). Due to process control (spin coating, development, stripping or ashing), the main part of PFAS is destroyed or ends up in the solvent waste, which is properly disposed of. Only a very small proportion is ultimately found in wastewater. Top anti-reflective coatings (TARCs) require a very low refractive index, minimal surface energy and excellent barrier properties. All these properties are achieved by using fluorinated copolymers based on styrene, acrylate and methacrylate. At present, there are no suitable substances that can provide all the above-mentioned properties. If they can be developed at all in the future, their possible use in production will certainly take decades, since a large number of parameters will have to be optimized.  Plasma etching: Plasma etching is a material-removing, plasma-assisted dry etching process in which a high-frequency or electrodeless microwave discharge is ignited in a vacuum reactor filled with an etching gas (often low-molecular-weight PFAS), thus generating a highly reactive, etch-active plasma. The resulting plasma reacts with the wafer surface and cleans it or creates structures that have been prepared in previous steps (e.g. lithography). The main criterion for the selection of the etch gas is its ability to form a highly volatile reaction product with the silicon-based wafer surface (silicon or silicon dioxide). Therefore, etching gases that ideally contain fluorine (PFAS like carbon tetrafluoride and octafluorocyclobutane) are generally used when etching structures.  Since the chemical reactivity between fluorine and silicon is very high, the reaction product of the etching reaction is volatile silicon tetrafluoride, which has a high vapor pressure. These reactions can be controlled very well, while other etching gases (e.g. chlorine-containing etching gases) also give volatile silicon tetrachloride, but either react much more uncontrollably or less selectively, thus making it very difficult or in some cases impossible to generate the necessary fine structures on the wafers. Thus, the gaseous PFASs used are extremely difficult to substitute. By far the largest proportion of the PFAS gases used either already react in the plasma chamber or are systematically burned off in the downstream abatement process. This means that only a small proportion of PFASs is emitted via the exhaust air.  PFAS-containing materials are also used in the Backend, which cannot be easily replaced here either.  Adhesives:  PFAS can also be a component of semiconductor products, e.g. in some electrically insulating adhesives, 70-90 wt% filler content of the PFAS Polytetrafluorethylene (PTFE) may be present to reduce stresses. This filler also prevents moisture absorption, which also leads to the prevention of corrosion within the semiconductor product.  The PFAS remains in the product and does not change throughout the service life. At end-of-life, the semiconductor product is sent normally for proper disposal. Therefore, no emissions are observed.  PFAS-containing materials are also used in production equipment because PFAS-containing polymers have unique properties that are mostly not replaceable by other materials. Equipment: In our production, highly aggressive media (e.g. hydrofluoric acid, alkalis) have to be handled in some cases, or also highly pure media (such as ultrapure water). This requires the use of fluorinated polymers in our production equipment throughout the entire production process. Thus, many valves, seals and pipe linings are affected. Replacing all these materials would be a major challenge, since mainly the respective equipment manufacturers have the knowledge about the composition of the individual components / tools. The supply of spare parts could also become a problem. Although there is one of the most important equipment manufacturers, ASML in the Netherlands, many manufacturers are located outside the EU. The use of materials containing PFAS is very widespread, but we have no knowledge of any emissions via wastewater. In the case of equipment disposal, this is done by a certified disposal contractor. There are no other known emission paths.  A special case of semiconductor manufacturing is the production of power semiconductors. Infineon operates such a production site in Warstein. Power semiconductor chips are not intended for consumer use and require embedding in a controllable electrical structure - a power module. In these power modules, several semiconductor chips are mounted on boards and wired to control elements, which enables the conversion of current. Therefore, power modules represent an essential core in electric cars, charging stations, electric trains, wind turbines and solar farms; crucial elements for the green electrification of the EU.  Embedding power semiconductors in power modules that control thousands of volts requires sophisticated PFAS-based assembly techniques to produce safe and durable products. PFAS-related processes for power module assembly include the following: 1. Paste soldering relies on a partially organic paste. It requires thorough cleaning with the PFAS hydrogen fluoride ether (HFE) to remove paste residues that would prevent further assembly steps and fatally damage the sensitive semiconductor during operation. Reliable and complete removal is not possible with alternative cleaning methods. Previous developments to avoid this undesirable and costly cleaning step have not been successful. The failed attempts to establish alternatives to date indicate that a long transition period is required to find alternative methods. 2. In another application, PFASs are used as adhesion promoters to fix subcomponents of power modules before the next permanent assembly steps. Absolute residue-free evaporation of these adhesion promoters at elevated temperatures is critical and can only be guaranteed with chemically inert and non-adhesive PFASs without risk of ignition. 3. The assembly of power modules involves pressure-dependent processes. Whenever materials are permanently pressed together, a non-adhesive PFAS film is required as a demolding aid to allow removal of the components from the press cavity.  4. In another application, the use of PFAS in the manufacture of power modules is attributed to the electrically insulating and non-flammable properties of PFAS. To safely handle current up to 10000 V, defect-free module components are required. Only an initial test under these conditions in an insulating PFAS environmental bath enables a test that can function safely. To date, only chemically inert PFAS can be removed without leaving residues, allowing further assembly of the test components, and an insulating environment allows testing of these voltage classes without fear of ignition.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: A lot of different PFAS (gases, solids, liquids) are used in many applications in the semiconductor manufacturing process. Semiconductor manufacturing is a highly complex process and production times vary depending on the complexity of the products, but on average it can take several years from research and development to the final product.  The complexity of the products requires a smooth and coordinated workflow between the individual processes, whereby the materials used also work together and depend on each other, as is the case also with PFAS. The proven uniqueness of PFAS combined with the proposal to restrict or ban the entire group of substances in the EU would lead to an extremely large and unprecedented challenge for adequate substitution in terms of the required technical performance and the environmental and human health impacts ("Regrettable Substitution"). A majority of PFAS cannot be replaced by alternatives according to current knowledge even in long term and it will be extremely difficult, to find chemical substances which are suitable and equivalent to PFAS in terms of their unique properties and which have no unknown or unforeseen hazards. Thus, for many applications, it requires a great deal of effort and investment in basic research and development to find PFAS-free alternatives. Once a PFAS-free alternative exists and is available, this needs to be implemented and qualified within the associated processes. This process must be carried out again for each possible alternative, this requires both time and may lead to necessary changes (e.g. design requirements and properties of the product, manufacturing process and -equipment). Therefore, a temporary exemption from the restriction only makes sense if alternatives are available and this is more than doubtful even after the expiry of the proposed 13.5 years. For example, in photolithography, one of the major process steps, the potential timeframe for substitution is 15 to 20 years or more. The substitution time to be estimated depends heavily on the application of PFAS and whether a PFAS-free alternative can be found and made available at short notice by global formulators and their upstream chemical suppliers. Without an appropriate exemption, there is a risk that the proposed full restriction of PFAS will worsen the supply of the semiconductor industry with production materials required during semiconductor manufacturing or that these materials will no longer be available. An appropriate exemption should be granted for the semiconductor manufacturing process, covering the entire semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem and including upstream and downstream supply and value chains. This should not only include the materials and precursors to manufacture the semiconductors. It must also be possible for the customers and users of the semiconductors to incorporate the semiconductors in turn into their products and thus to use the semiconductors over the longer term. Furthermore, the production equipment must not be forgotten, where e.g. also the spare parts supply must be possible in the future, as well as the devices which are necessary for R&D activities like e.g. evaluation boards. Semiconductor manufacturing in Europe without the use of PFAS is therefore currently not possible. A general restriction of PFAS without an appropriate exemption would have very negative effects and consequences for European semiconductor companies as well as their suppliers and customers.  A general PFAS ban could have serious negative consequences for the entire industrial manufacturing landscape in Europe. A few months ago, the comparatively harmless shortage in the supply of semiconductors had a serious impact on e.g. the automotive industry, leading to major production reductions and stops. Future investments in Europe depends on legal certainty and the existence of stable supply chains and skilled workers. Infineon commits to Europe as an important business location and thus, e.g. operates a large part of its front-end manufacturing there, where Infineon recently announced plans to expand semiconductor production at its Dresden site with the largest single investment of €5 billion in the company's history.  A restriction on PFAS would have a direct negative impact on our revenue (FY 2022: €3.4 billion in Europe and €14.2 billion worldwide) and employees (FY 2022: 21,703 in Europe and 54,286 worldwide), as production with PFAS is not possible in Europe. The majority of Frontend sites are located in Europe, while the majority of Backend sites are located in Asia. Since the Frontend sites are the suppliers of the Backend sites, if the Frontends stop production, the Backends would also have to stop production after a short period of time because they would run out of raw materials for their production. A general prohibition of PFAS for the semiconductor industry, its suppliers and customers must be avoided under all circumstances to eliminate a locational disadvantage for Europe.

10. Analytical methods: There is currently no analytical methodology that would be applicable to all individual PFAS compounds as defined by the OECD and provide satisfactory results. There are too many different PFAS compounds for this. In the meantime, some analytical methods have been tested that can detect a few PFAS species in semiconductor manufacturing wastewater. However, this analysis by liquid chromatography together with tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) quickly reaches its limits, since comparative standards are only available for a few substances used. Again, it has not been possible to find an analytical method that can detect all PFAS in a comprehensive manner. Therefore, it is very important to conduct extensive research to find and improve suitable analytical methods so that the semiconductor industry is able to provide analytical evidence that it can comply with the limits (e.g., US EPA 537.1 (modified)). Currently established is the determination of total fluorine in the sample. However, the detection limit here is 50 ppm. This is a value far above all limits (ppb, i.e. one one-thousandth below) that apply to PFAS. The proportion of inorganic fluorine can also be determined with the same accuracy, whereupon the amount of organically bound fluorine (i.e. total PFAS) can be calculated. All this, however, only in the ppm range mentioned above. The PFASs currently readily detectable were C4-C13 species in the aqueous phase (US EPA Draft 1633, EPA method currently under development). For the investigated wastewater from semiconductor manufacturing, the detection limit was about 1 ppt. However, it must be noted that almost all of the species included in the analytical interpretation library are not used at all in semiconductor manufacturing, with Perfluorobutane sulfonic acid (PFBS) being the only exception. Thus, the applicability of this method is mainly limited to the detection of PFAS by-products. Whether the existing laboratory capacity will be even slightly sufficient for the determination of all more than 12000 PFAS in the future may be highly doubted. The preparation of the measurements is relatively time-consuming and thus cost-intensive, which, together with the lack of capacities, is likely to lead to exponential price increases in analysis. It is likely that these increases can only be passed on partially, or not at all, to our globally acting customers. This represents a clear disadvantage for European semiconductor manufacturing in global competition.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We manufacture a lot of fluorinated intermediates and fluorine raw materials that are useful for the syntheses of pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals. Through our public comments, we would like to confirm contents of regulatory for fluorinated intermediates and fluorine raw materials that are subject to the PFAS regulations proposed by ECHA.
Organic compounds with fluorine atoms in their molecules are important for the fields of medical and agricultural chemistry. 30% of new synthetic pharmaceuticals and 70% of synthetic pesticides developed in the last five years are fluorine organic compounds. Most of the fluorinated pharmaceuticals and pesticides containing F atoms or CF3 groups, the roles of the fluorine atom are mimic effect, lipid solubility, electronegativity, and strength of C-F bond, which lead to beneficial effects and saving of the dose.
Methods for synthesizing organic fluorine compounds can be mainly divided into fluorination methods and building block methods. The former methods in which hydrogen and hydroxyl groups within organic compounds are directly substituted with fluorine was relatively required dangerous fluorinating agents and special equipment. Therefore, direct fluorination methods are unlikely to be applied to the industrial preparation of complex pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals. Conversely, the latter methods in which fluorinated organic compounds as intermediates are tolerant for functional groups and easily able to adapt general organic syntheses. The manufacturing of pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals using inexpensive and easily available fluorinated intermediates as starting materials take advantage of economic superiority.
Accordingly, fluorinated intermediates are indispensable in industrial production of pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals which are exempted to the PFAS regulations in the Annex XV report. Even if fluorinated intermediates have chemical structures specified in the PFAS restriction proposed by ECHA, it seems that these intermediates for pharmaceuticals and pesticides should be conditionally exempted from PFAS regulation as well as pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals are excluded from the proposed PFAS regulation.
On the other hand, fluorine raw materials for various catalysts are valuable in organic synthesis. To pick a well-known example, the super acid bearing CF3 groups of perfluoro sulfonic acids (e.g., trifluoromethanesulfonic acid (CAS Number: 1493-13-6)) due to the high electron-withdrawing property of fluorine is essential for efficient preparation of compounds. Especially, trifluoromethanesulfonic acid defined as a PFAS candidate is known to be 1,000 times more acidity than sulfuric acid. It is one of the strongest acids which is available at industrial scale. It is commonly used as a catalyst for many organic synthesis reactions such as alkylation, esterification, etherification, acylation, isomerization, cyclization, cationic rearrangement and cationic polymerization. Trifluoromethanesulfonic acid derivatives (e.g., trifluoromethanesulfonic anhydride (CAS Number: 358-23-6)) are also used for pharmaceutical and agrochemical applications as synthetic intermediate for a leaving group. It becomes possible to carry out reactions smoothly by using them.
Additionally, even if fundamental physical properties can be adapted by non-PFAS alternatives with weak acidity, the replacement of trifluoromethanesulfonic acid derivatives are likely to force poor yield and numerous unknown impurities in industrial production of pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals. In the manufacture of pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals, minute amounts of impurities are strictly controlled, and it is necessary to investigate effects of impurities to active substances carefully. When the manufacturing process of active substances was changing, that would be also requirements for development of re-synthesis, re-scale-up, customer’s re-evaluation and final re-qualification at specialized agencies in each country. In the worst case, re-production of active substances may be abandoned due to the influence of new impurities. Even if alternative compounds could be used in syntheses of pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals, it is conspicuously inefficient and uneconomical.
As we mentioned earlier, fluorinated intermediates and fluorine raw materials have been an enabling mass production of pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals. Fluorine material manufacturers fully understand not only the usefulness of fluorine, but also the toxicity and danger of fluorine, many fluorine manufacturers are proceeding with special care for the manufacturing environment. We manufacture fluorinated intermediates and fluorine raw materials that are essential for the syntheses of pharmaceuticals and pesticides for now while we firmly follow the water quality law and atmospheric law issued in Japan regarding the fluorine. We hope that we should continue to contribute to society in the future by productions of fluorinated compounds for syntheses of pharmaceuticals and pesticides. To accomplish this, fluorinated intermediates and fluorine raw materials for syntheses of pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals need to be deregulated by ECHA in the same way as active pharmaceutical and agrochemical products.

6. Missing uses: Although pharmaceuticals and agrochemicals are exempted to the PFAS regulations in the Annex XV report, fluorinated intermediates and fluorine raw materials for preparations of them have no regulatory classification within the PFAS restriction proposed by ECHA. We would like to demand that these intermediates and raw materials that are essential for the synthesis of active substances are exempted.

It seems that fluorinated regenerative medicines/materials should be conditionally exempted or do not hard restrict from PFAS regulation.
Fluorine material manufacturers fully understand not only the usefulness of fluorine, but also the toxicity and danger of fluorine. Furthermore, many fluorine manufacturers are proceeding with special care for the manufacturing environment. We manufacture fluorinated intermediates and fluorine raw materials that are essential for the syntheses for now while we firmly follow the water quality law and atmospheric law issued in Japan regarding the fluorine. We hope that we will continue to contribute to society in the future by production of fluorinated compounds for synthesis. To accomplish this, fluorinated intermediates and fluorine raw materials of three applications as our suggested above, need to be deregulated by ECHA in the same way as active pharmaceutical and agrochemical products.

General Comments: We manufacture and sell pressure sensitive adhesive tapes (PSTs) using PTFE as a carrier,  and a PTFE thread sealant which are used in aerospace applications pursuant to customers' requirements, industry-approved specifications, and regulatory requirements.

We understand that the EU proposes these PFAS/PTFE restrictions to reduce PFAS impact on the environment and human body  to create a sustainable future. We are also committed to these shared goals and to working collaboratively with the EU, our customers, the supply chain and all stakeholders  to find PFAS/PTFE alternatives that balance safety with environmental stewardship. Although the science, technology and socio-economic impacts of these objectives is complex and evolving, all stakeholders benefit from research and development into PFAS/PTFE alternatives while continuing to provide consumers access to products essential to modern life, including medications, medical supplies, devices, computers, alternative energy and transportation. Our company wants to be part of the PFAS/PTFE alternative solutions, innovations and emerging marketplace.  Consistent with EU's goals and objectives, we believe that, given enough time, we can develop an alternative with equal or better safety performance to PFAS/PTFE, and further ECHA's environmental initiatives. However, there are currently no alternative materials that provide industry safety and mechanical requirements of PTFE.

The purpose of this document is to provide ECHA with comments regarding our manufactured PSTs that use PTFE as a carrier and applied in the aerospace industry, specifically, anti-corrosion tape for cabin and cargo areas of aircraft.

Three of the most important properties of PTFE in these applications include:

1. Flame retardancy:  One of the indicators that explains the flame retardancy of a material is the oxygen index. The higher this number, the better the flame retardancy, and more than 40 materials are required. PTFE is significantly better than other materials.
2.Water vapor permeability: In order to prevent corrosion caused by condensation that occurs during takeoff and landing of aircraft, gasket materials must have small water vapor permeability. By choosing a material with low vapor permability,  moisture penetration due to condensation can be prevented.

3.Elongation: Another important function required of gasket base sheets is that they have moderate mechanical strength (especially elongation). This is because when the aircraft floor panel is fixed to the aggregate using bolts, it is necessary to ensure good sealing of the joint by extending the substrate appropriately.

Details of technical requirements are explained in the documents attached in Confidential Section V.

PTFE is considered a low concern polymer (Ref. 1, 2, 3).   Considering this and that there are currently no alternative materials that provide industry safety and mechanical requirements of PTFE, we request an Exemption from EU proposed rules to restrict the use of PTFE.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: "Some methods and processes used for PTFE recycling:  Mechanical Recycling: Mechanical recycling involves processes where PTFE waste is mechanically shredded or ground into smaller particles. These particles can then be mixed with new PTFE material to create a blend that can be used in certain applications. Mechanical recycling of PTFE is relatively limited due to the difficulty in processing PTFE's tough molecular structure.  Pyrolysis: Pyrolysis is a thermal decomposition process in which PTFE waste is subjected to high temperatures in the absence of oxygen. This process breaks down PTFE into its constituent elements, primarily fluorine and carbon. While pyrolysis can recover valuable fluorine for reuse, it's a more complex and energy-intensive method and may not be widely used for PTFE recycling.  Chemical Recycling: Chemical recycling involves breaking down PTFE into its basic components using chemical processes. This can include methods like hydrolysis, where PTFE is exposed to strong acids to break the polymer chain into smaller molecules. However, chemical recycling of PTFE is not as common due to the challenges associated with handling the strong acids required for the process.  Reprocessing PTFE Scrap: Some PTFE manufacturers offer reprocessing services for scrap PTFE materials generated during manufacturing. These materials are collected, reprocessed, and used in the production of new PTFE products. This closed-loop approach helps reduce waste in the manufacturing process.  Alternative Applications: In some cases, PTFE waste or scrap can be repurposed for applications where the material's unique properties are less critical. For instance, PTFE waste might find use in applications that don't require the same level of non-stick or high-temperature resistance, such as industrial fillers.  It's important to note that PTFE recycling is not as common as the recycling of other plastics due to the challenges posed by its chemical properties and molecular structure. The durable and chemically inert nature of PTFE that makes it valuable in various applications can also make it difficult to recycle using traditional methods applied to other plastics. As a result, recycling options for PTFE are relatively limited, and the focus often remains on reducing waste through proper manufacturing practices and responsible waste management."

General Comments: We manufacture APIs, their intermediates and FDF products. One of these APIs is used to treat hyperparathyroidism, another one is used for smoking cessation and  it is considered as essential medicine in the WHO Model Lists of Essential Medicines of the World Health Organization; another one is a medicine used to control blood glucose, another one is  used for obsessive compulsive disorder and it is considered as a therapeutic alternative for essential medicines for mental and behavioural disorders in the WHO Model Lists of Essential Medicines of the World Health Organization and a last one which  is an immunomodulating agent of the calcineurin inhibitor. We use intermediates that are under PFAS restriction to manufacture 20 tons per year of five APIs mentioned above, which represents around 25 M€ per year, 15% of our annual turnover. Alternatives do not exist for API. Introduction of fluorine in the API molecule is an essential part of developing efficacious and safe candidates. Any changes to an API molecule would essentially require the development of a completely new candidate. Due to the unique properties of individual molecular structures containing fluorine, alternatives for API, development products and their starting materials and intermediates do not exist, as the function of the substances is on the chemical molecular level. -  Production equipment: Fluoropolymers, such as polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE or Teflon), are highly used in pharmaceutical production equipment (reactor lining, seals, gaskets, piping, anti-stick coating, surfaces, filtration units etc.), and also in consumables and single-use materials (filters, bags, tubes, etc.) when the material is in contact with the product and have a direct impact on the quality of the product. According to the ISPE Guide (International Society for Pharmaceutical Engineering), in its Baseline Guide Volume 1, Chapter PRODUCT/PROCESS and point "3.3.1 Causes of Contamination and Preventative Measures", fluoropolymers are expressly recommended for process equipment, pipes and instrumentation in order to minimize the risk of contamination. Accordingly, Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and manufacturers of pharmaceutical equipment recommends the use of fluoropolymers in pharmaceutical production equipment. -  Quality control reagents: PFAS materials and reagents are used in quality control activities that are required by product licenses or regulations such as European Pharmacopoeia monographs. They include for example the use of trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) in the mobile phase of high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC).  Although pharmaceuticals are exempted from the PFAS regulations in the Annex XV restriction report, fluorinated materials in use of four applications such as, medicines intermediates, process materials (reactor lining, seals, gaskets, piping, surfaces, coating etc.), quality control analysis and medicines packaging material (container closure system), have no regulatory classification within the PFAS restriction proposed by ECHA. We would like to demand that these fluorinated materials which are essential in medicinal industries should be exempted.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We manufacture Bisphenol AF (BPAF, CAS No.; 1478-61-1) and its salts, which are quite useful as cross-link agents for fluoroelastomers (FKM) with excellent thermal resistance. The examples of BPAF salts are ammonium salts and phosphonium salts, and a representative example is benzyltriphenylphosphonium salt. We would like to issue the public comment to request for confirmation of ECHA's proposed regulation detailed and exemption from the regulation of BPAF and its salts.
FKMs are used in a wide range of industrial fields, including transport (e.g. aerospace and automotive), electronics and semiconductor manufacturing, oil and gas industries. FKMs are available for multiple applications as molded articles that should be sealing, O-rings, pump and engine components, or fuel hoses.
FKMs are compounds obtained by adding cross-link agents and additives to copolymers such as poly-VDF-HFP and poly-VDF-HFP-TFE, and they are cross-linked by heating and compressing to form various articles.

There are 3 types of cross-linking methods that include polyol-cross-link using BPAF and its salts, amine-cross-link using a polyamine compound, and peroxide-cross-link using triallyl isocyanurate and peroxy-radical initiators. Amine-cross-link and peroxide-cross-link are used by non-PFAS substances, but polyol-cross-link is used by BPAF and its salts defined as PFAS in the proposed regulation.
Amine-cross-link method is conventional system that does not use PFAS, but the use case is limited due to the foul odor with molding process, the long cross-link time, and the lack of thermal resistance in comparison to polyol-cross-link method. Peroxide-cross-link method does not use PFAS and is characterized by excellent chemical resistance. It is also shown as an alternative to BPAF and its salts in terms of chemical resistance, however it should be inferior to polyol-cross-link method in terms of cross-link time, compression set resistance, and thermal resistance.

That's why the cross-link agents such as amine and peroxide cannot completely replace BPAF and its salts in terms of economy and performance.

BPAF cross-linked FKMs are widely used in the electronics and semiconductor industries. The electronics and semiconductor sector is proposed 12-year derogation period (additional information from public comment is required). However, since there are no alternatives for polyol-cross-link agents, the derogation period of 12 years is not enough and full-exemption is suitable.
In addition, in the sectors listed Annex XV, it is quite difficult to find the reasonable alternatives for FKMs that can be used in a tough environment as the transport (automotive, railroad, ship, aerospace), petroleum and mining sectors.
On the other hand, BPAF should be essential as cross-link agent, but there are no specific descriptions of BPAF and its salts and the derogation proposals have not been shown in Annex XV.

The use cases for Transport sector, Electronics and semiconductor sector, and Petroleum and mining sector listed in Annex XV Table 9. are described as below.
In the list of Annex XV Table 9. 12-year derogation period is proposed for the semiconductors sector (with reconsideration), but there are no detailed mentions of specific articles and materials used for these applications.
12-year derogation period is proposed for fluoropolymer applications (containing FKM) in petroleum and mining sector.
No derogation is proposed in transport sector.
Application examples are described in Annex A, and proposals for alternatives are described in detail in Annex E. We would like to describe the use case and essentiality of BPAF and its salts using these annexes.

Transport (Listed in Table.9 Annex XV)
In Annex XV Table A.41 (p92), "Sealing applications" is listed as a sub-group, and described that 60% or more of the FKMs were used in sealing application in the transport sector. It seems to be the typical example for FKMs application.
The examples of PFAS use for transport are described in Annex E (p346), and the examples of non-fluorinated alternatives (e.g. NBR, ACM, CR) are described in Table E.113. (p349). However, it is difficult for non-fluorinated alternatives to achieve the same performance as FKMs in terms of durability. Therefore, it is affected that the replacement cycle will increase.
The fact means that the alternatives should causes economically disadvantage and the increasing amount of waste.
The use of ceramics causes high cost and is not reasonable.

Electronics and semiconductor- Electronics/Semiconductor (Listed in Table.9 Annex XV)
In Annex A Table A.49 (p114), "Bisphenol AF and its salts" are mentioned as cross-link agent in the category of "Fluoroelastomers, polymers including polyimides, polyamides, polyesters, polycarbonate" in the semiconductor industry.
Furthermore, fluoropolymer such as Viton (bland name of FKM) are mentioned as a use case of "Semiconductor Manufacturing Equipment & Infrastructure - Enabling Uses of Fluoropolymer Articles".
However, no descriptions are shown in electronics sub-use. FKMs are essential for not only manufacturing semiconductor but manufacturing electronic components (e.g. LED lighting, OLED display) .
In Annex E Table E.128 (p374), ethylene propylene diene monomer (EPDM) and silicone rubbers for sealing application are shown as alternatives for fluoroelastomers, however various poisonous chemicals (e.g. hydrogen fluoride, piranha solution) or specialty gases (e.g. fluorine based gases) are used in the actual electronics industry and the proposed alternatives seems to be lack of resistance to these chemicals.

Petroleum and mining (Listed in Table.9 Annex XV)
In Annex A Table A.61 (p148), the main uses of various fluoro-products are described in the field of the petroleum industry, for example seals, liners, valves, O-rings, gaskets and packer elements. The fluoroelastomers possess excellent durability and should be essential in the above use case. In addition, there is a description that acid chemicals are sometimes used in the mining industry.
In Annex E Table E.158 (p496), seals, liners, valves, O-rings, gaskets, packer elements are listed as actual use case of fluoroelastomers in the petroleum and mining industry. It is described that fluoroelastomers contribute some favorable properties for high temperature resistance, rapid gas decompression resistance, compression fluids resistance. Steel and other metal alloys, non-metal materials, fluorine-free polymers, and nylon are described as alternatives, however steel and other metal alloys make lack of flexibilities, and they are not suitable as alternatives. Others are constituted based on organic polymers and they have less resistance to PFAS for the fluids used in the petroleum industry.

The ban of BPAF and its salts makes polyol-cross-link FKMs to be lost in actual society, and it also brings extensive economic and environmental damage. From the above point, full-exemption of BPAF and its salts are suitable same as full-exemption of FKMs.
The above facts shows that there are currently no non-PFAS alternatives for the above uses, and they are strongly supporting our advocacy comments for BPAF and its salts.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We manufacture Bisphenol AF (BPAF, CAS No.; 1478-61-1), which is useful as a raw material for semiconductor materials and electronic components. We would like to issue the public comment to request for confirmation of ECHA's proposed regulation detailed and exemption from the regulation of BPAF.

BPAF is used in versatile applications for semiconductor and electronics.
First, BPAF is used as a raw material for photosensitive polyimides (PSPIs). PSPIs are quite essential to fabricate organic light emitting diodes (OLEDs) that are available for smartphones and TVs. PSPIs are also essential to fabricate high-performance semiconductor chips installed in data centers, personal computers (PCs), smartphones, etc.
Second, BPAF is a useful raw material engineering plastics such as polyesterimides, polyetherimides, liquid crystal polymers, polycarbonates, epoxy resins, acrylate resins, etc. These are quite useful materials that are possessing transparency, thermal resistance, moisture absorption resistance, and low dielectric property.
Finally, BPAF also acts as a raw material that is reacted with formaldehyde, trifluoroacetaldehyde, cyclopentadiene, etc., and the products can be used as phenol-novolac resins. Phenol-novolac resins are widely used as photoresists for manufacturing semiconductors. Furthermore, the derived phenol-novolac epoxy resins should be useful in the same manner as the engineering plastics.

Epoxy resins containing trifluoromethyl groups (CF3 groups) exhibit high thermal resistance, low water absorption, and low dielectric properties. They are essential materials in the advanced semiconductor packaging and substrate market, and they are certainly in actual demand. It is clear that these properties are derived from by the CF3 groups and they cannot be achieved with non-PFAS epoxy resins.
In addition, photoresists using PSPIs and/or novolac resins effectively have fine-pitch patternability, developability (alkali dissolution rate), and good insulation reliability. In particular, the CF3 groups work to control developability for the purpose of forming fine patterns.

In addition, there are no specific descriptions in Annex XV for other uses, however electronic devices and semiconductors are widely used in the transport (automotives, railroads, ships, aerospace) and energy sectors. Therefore, ban of BPAF should cause large social and economic risks and it is quite reasonable to exempt from BPAF.

The use cases for the Electronics and semiconductor sector listed in Annex XV Table 9. are described as below.
The lists in Annex XV Table 9. propose a 12-year derogation period for the semiconductor manufacturing process (with reconsideration), but there are no mentions of specific articles and materials used for these applications.
Application examples are detailed in Annex A, and proposals for alternatives are described in detail in Annex E. We would like to describe the use case and essentiality of BPAF using these annexes.

Electronics and semiconductors (Listed in Table.9 Annex XV)
In Annex A Table A.48. (p107-108), some use categories such as "Printed circuit boards", "Antennas and membranes", and "Organic light-emitting diode (OLED)" are listed in electronic components category.
In Annex A Table A.49. (p111-112), some use categories such as "Photolithography-Topcoats and Embedded Barrier Layers'' and "Advanced Semiconductor Packaging-Encapsulants and Thermal Interface Materials'' are also listed in Semiconductor manufacturing category.
Specifically, fluoropolymer is mentioned as examples of PFASs. Fluorinated phenol novolac resin, fluorinated epoxy resin, and fluorine-containing engineering plastics (fluorinated polyimide, etc.) seem to be used as PFASs.

In Annex E Table E.128. (p396), examples of non-PFAS alternatives are listed in the electronics component sector. The sub-use "Printed circuit boards", "Antennas and membranes", and "Organic light-emitting diode (OLED)" are included. The non-PFAS alternatives are not specifically indicated in the list.
Polyetheretherketone (PEEK) is described as an example of non-PFAS alternatives in the semiconductor industry (in case of chip manufacturing), however PEEK is a thermoplastic resin and is not suitable as a material for chip manufacturing that thermal resistance is required. In addition, the non-PFAS alternatives are not specifically indicated in the sub-use of "Photolithography-Topcoats and Embedded Barrier Layers" and "Advanced Semiconductor Packaging-Encapsulants and Thermal Interface Materials".

From the above points, engineering plastics and photoresists made from BPAF are important materials that make up semiconductors and electronic devices shown in the Annex XV., and it is difficult to find non-PFAS alternatives. Therefore, it is suitable to exempt BPAF from the proposed regulation.
The above facts shows that there are currently no non-PFAS alternatives for the above uses, and they are strongly supporting our advocacy comments for BPAF.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We manufacture hydraulic energy accumulators that are used in hydraulic systems worldwide and in a wide variety of applications. The energy storage consists of a cylindrical tube that is closed on both sides and in which a freely movable piston is installed, and which separates the cylinder space into 2 variable chambers. One of the chambers is filled with nitrogen. The other chamber is connected to the hydraulic system. If this chamber is filled with oil by the hydraulic system, the piston moves and reduces the gas space. This increases the pressure in the gas space and thus enables hydraulic energy to be stored, which can then be used for emergency supply or to cover energy peaks. The storage system thus also reduces the required electrical connection power and thus also contributes to stabilizing the power grids.
Among other things, these hydraulic accumulators are an indispensable part of the safety concept for regenerative power generation in wind power and hydroelectric power plants as an energy reserve for emergency shutdowns. Another large area of application is the use in machines and plants to cover a short-term high energy demand. Typical examples include die casting machines and hydraulic crash test benches in the automotive sector. To produce large components e. g. for battery-electric vehicles, the accumulators deliver the required hydraulic energy in the range of a few milliseconds, which enables parts to be produced at all or without errors in high quality. The testing of entire vehicles or individual components on hydraulic crash systems would also be unthinkable without hydraulic energy storage since an electric battery cannot provide the required power density.
The functionality of these hydraulic accumulators is essentially determined by the safe and leak-free separation between the gas and the oil space. Therefore, high demands are placed on the sealing materials:
- high wear resistance and service life
- high chemical resistance to the media used
- low friction - high piston speeds and number of load cycles
- low permeation
- wide operating temperature range
Seals made of NBR and HNBR rubber are used for many standard applications. Under extreme loads, which occur in accumulator systems for die casting machines and crash systems, among other things, safe operation with acceptable service lives is not possible with NBR or HNBR seals. No seal manufacturer guarantees the suitability of NBR-HNBR seals for the application parameters required for these applications. Based on decades of experience, only seals and guide elements made of PTFE compounds can reliably cover these requirements.

6. Missing uses: a) The annual tonnage of seals is less than 0,5t b) Key functionalities of seals made of PTFE compounds:    - high wear resistance and service life     - high chemical resistance to the media used     - low friction - high piston speeds and number of load cycles     - low permeation  c) In Europe, around 10 manufacturers of hydraulic accumulators are affected by the ban. d) At the moment there are no alternative materials for these seals that even come close to meeting the required operating parameters. e) not known f) not known g) If there is a ban on sealing materials that fall under the PFAS regulations, it can be assumed that customers will change their procurement methods and purchase hydraulic accumulator from manufacturers in North America and Asia, especially China. Many of our European customers already have production facilities in the USA and Asia. A ban will most likely lead to increased production relocations on the part of customers. A PFAS ban would affect approximately 25% of our sales. Due to the high internal value creation, it can be assumed that one in three jobs is at risk. Since we currently still have a technological advantage over foreign competitors in these products, a strategically important business area would disappear and our global competitiveness would massively deteriorate, which could endanger the company's existence in the medium term.

General Comments: We manufacture sealants and paints that fluor resin (PTFE, ETFE, FEVE, etc) and fluor rubber (FKM, FEPM, etc) are used as main raw materials. It is not limited to a wide range of applications, including automobiles, electronics/electricity, and chemistry. It is used in severe applications such as seals for water and chemical pipes, engine gaskets, and chemical-resistant seals for semiconductor manufacturing equipment. In addition, it is also used as a paint for the purpose of weather resistance and rust prevention, which has a longer life than acrylic and urethane do.
Since there are many user's trade secrets, and the specific contents are unknown, it is not possible to grasp the usage by restrictions for each use. Our products and processed goods are used all over the world, including Europe. Since our products are used in applications that cannot be maintained with other resins or rubbers, it is extremely difficult to replace them with non-fluorinated materials, and no alternative materials have been found. Because of the strict requirements, the product development period may take 5 to 10 years even with fluorine-based materials. More than 80% of our products contain fluoropolymers; so it is not easy to replace them in a short period of time. It can't be imagined how long it would take for our products to be developed with non-fluorine-based materials.
Proposals to collectively regulate more than 10,000 types of Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) as substances of concern equivalent to PFOS and PFOA, which are already regulated, based on the grounds that they are difficult to decompose, are excessive measures. Therefore, we believe that fluor rubber and fluor resin should be exempted from the regulation, and we support the two statements made by FCJ and JFIA on the issues of proposed restriction, as per attached in section IV.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We manufacture sealing parts for actuators that mainly use fluids, mainly hydraulic and pneumatic, and sell REACH-compliant products in the EU, we sell REACH compliant products within the EU. The applications range from public transportation such as automobiles, construction machinery, and railroads to various industrial components such as agricultural machinery, food machinery, and semiconductors, as well as control equipment for power plants, including nuclear power plants.
These industrial machines are used in the manufacture of all the essentials needed to support daily life in the modern world. Our sealing components are the parts that support the foundation of these industrial machines. Therefore, the impact on various social activities in general can be judged to be enormous.
　 It is therefore proposed that a permanent derogation or a permanent exemption be granted for this use case, referred to as ‘industrial automation components and equipment.'

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: We manufacture and sells sealing parts for actuators that use mainly fluids, mainly hydraulic and pneumatic. Its applications range from public transportation such as automobiles, construction machinery, and railroads to various industrial parts such as agricultural machinery, food machinery, and semiconductors, as well as production plants such as steel mills and control equipment for power plants including nuclear power plants. Therefore, the impact on various social activities in general is enormous and difficult to deal with. In view of this, we request that permanent exemptions or exemptions be granted for all components.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: We have maintained ISO14001 certification since 2003 and are committed to fulfilling our social responsibility to the environment. These efforts include compliance with the revised RoHS Directive, and the "Revised RoHS Directive Compliance Regulations" have been issued and incorporated into the management system. 　All PTFE and fluorine rubber emitted during our manufacturing processes are disposed of appropriately in accordance with legal regulations and in a manner that is currently considered to have the least impact on the environment. In addition, since items shipped as products are used by organizations, not individuals, and since items such as automobiles are subject to disposal based on laws and regulations, we believe that disposal in accordance with laws and regulations is being properly implemented.

5. Proposed derogations: We supply PTFE products as seals for power steering and gas dampers for automobiles. 　Chips emitted from cutting operations are properly collected by dust collectors, and environmental measurements confirm that there is no exposure to workers. In addition, materials spilled into the water during cleaning are separated in a sedimentation tank within the factory and disposed of appropriately as industrial waste.

6. Missing uses: The missing use for PFAS is 'industrial automation components and equipment'. Sub-uses are almost unlimited. Restricting or inhibiting the supply of these "industrial automation components and equipment" will adversely affect the manufacturing and process industries in the European Union.  Fluoropolymers are often used in industrial applications such as the automotive, machinery and semiconductor industries. These polymers have been assessed as being of low concern (PTFE, FEP, PFA, and ETFE).  These polymers have proven to be chemically stable, non-toxic, non-bioavailable, non-water soluble and non-migratory. For these reasons, in addition to factors such as safety, energy consumption and service life, fluoropolymers are also approved as materials for food contact and medical technology. The use of fluoropolymers is highly relevant to the whole industry, as a wide range of components and equipment are used to manufacture industrial machinery across the European Union. This machinery is used in the manufacture of almost all the essentials needed to support the daily lives of modern society.  a.  I don't have information on this topic. b.  The main features of the PFAS materials used are their physical properties. Chemical resistance, temperature resistance and general mechanical properties uniquely provide the functionality required for many industrial automation components and equipment. Many applications in components and equipment cannot be satisfied by alternative materials, making corresponding industrial machinery and processes impossible. “Seals" (packing) are used in industrial machinery as sealing systems (sealing components) to prevent fluid leakage and intrusion of foreign substances from the outside. Since seals seal fluids, the materials used must have appropriate elasticity, so various elastomers and resin materials are used. In seals (packings) used under high-pressure conditions, seals tend to protrude from the overhang gap of sliding parts and are easily damaged. Therefore, "backup rings" are used in combination to fill the gap, thereby extending the life of the seal. Since the material of this backup ring must have adequate rigidity and elasticity, resin materials are mainly used. Fluorine rubber and PTFE, which are the subject of the proposed regulation, are used as important materials in the construction of various sealing systems, including hydraulic and pneumatic cylinders.　  【Fluorine rubber】 Fluorine rubber is used for seals that are used under high temperature conditions. Silicone rubber and HNBR are also available as rubber materials that can be used under high temperature conditions. However, silicone rubber and HNBR have significantly inferior mechanical strength and abrasion resistance compared to fluorine rubber, so they can be used for seals for fixed applications. Although it is possible, it is difficult to use silicone rubber, especially in reciprocating seals, so fluorine rubber is used instead.　 Furthermore, fluorine rubber is resistant to various fluids including acidic and alkaline solutions, so fluorine rubber is used not only under high-temperature conditions but also as a sealing material in environments with special fluids.  【PTFE】 PTFE is used as a back-up ring material as well as a sealing material because of its heat resistance and flexibility. PTFE is used as a material for backup rings as well as sealing materials. There are backup rings made of synthetic resins such as polyethylene and nylon, but these materials do not have any of the characteristics of PTFE, such as “heat resistance”, “flexibility”, and “low friction properties”. However, since it does not satisfy all requirements, it can only be used for limited purposes. Currently, it is difficult to establish an existing sealing system without a PTFE backup ring. c.  I don't have information on this topic. d. There are currently no known alternative materials to fluoropolymers used in the industry to manufacture components and equipment for industrial automation. Since the development of alternative materials that meet the usage conditions and environment of regulated fluorine rubber and PTFE is extremely difficult considering the history of material development, the grace period for application of regulations to fluorine rubber and PTFE has been extended. I think this should be a special measure with no time limit. e. f. g. I don't have information on this topic.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We manufacture, process and supply films using fluorine raw materials such as PTFE according to the customers' applications.
Fluoropolymers have various characteristics and functions, so they are used in a wide range of applications in various industries. Therefore, we manufacture and supply the most suitable processed fluoropolymer products for many different applications.
Regarding the European PFAS regulation proposal, we understand that it is being proposed in consideration of the environmental impact and the impact on the human body in order to create a sustainable future and we sympathize with that way of thinking.
On the other hand, we think that there are several uses that would affect the European society and economy if they are restricted without providing any alternatives.
This is the case of the PTFE mold-release sheets used as process materials in the semiconductor manufacturing process, we would like to share our comment about.
The semiconductor manufacturing process is divided into two main processes: the `front-end process' , where electronic circuits are designed on wafers, and the `back-end process' where the patterned wafer is cut into chips and then packaged; fluoropolimers like PTFE and ETFE are used as mold-release sheets in the die-bonding and in the molding processes, part of the back-end process,
The main properties required to the mold-release sheets are heat resistance, releasability and flexibility. Fluoropolymers are the only materials that can satisfy all of the characteristic specifications that express these functions; furthermore, if there is just one property not meeting the specifications, the material cannot be used with this function in the semiconductor manufacturing process. Details can be checked in the file named "Mold-release sheet for the semiconductor manufacturing process"., attached to Section V.
Also attached to Section V is a document "Reference material 1" which indicates that PTFE is of low concern.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: >Sectors and uses: Semiconductors　　 >Field/Application: Mold-release sheets used in the die bonding and molding processes in the back-end semiconductor manufacturing process.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Comparative data on the properties required for this application of PTFE, ETFE and other materials currently used as release sheets are attached to SECTION V is  (file name: ”Mold-release sheet for the semiconductor manufacturing process”). At present, there are no materials that can replace PTFE, so if restrictions are imposed, it will be impossible to manufacture semiconductors in Europe. Also, even if a grace period is granted, if, within the same period, no materials that can satisfy the release sheet forementioned properties are developed, it will be impossible to manufacture semiconductors in Europe. Since there are now no alternatives, It is not possible to estimate how the material can be developed and, as a consequence, to estimate the necessary development time and cost implications.  On the other hand with regard to socio-economic impacts, many companies such as PTEF raw material manufacturers, PTFE film  manufacturers, Semiconductor manufacturing equipment manufacturer and Semiconductor manufacturer would be seriously affected. We are a PTFE film manufacturer and our operations will be affected by the work of approximately 60 employees involved. We have no knowledge of the specific impact of other manufacturers. Therefore, we ask for unlimited derogation for these specific applications.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We manufacture, process and supply films using fluorine raw materials, such as PTFE, according to the customers' applications.
Fluoropolymers have various characteristics and functions so they are used in a wide range of applications in various industries. We manufacture and supply the most suitable processed fluoropolymer products for many different applications.
Regarding the European PFAS regulation proposal, we understand that it is being proposed in consideration of the environmental impact and the impact on the human body in order to create a sustainable future and the company sympathize with that way of thinking.
There are several uses that would affect the European society and economy if they are restricted without any alternatives. As one of them, we consider that a derogation is appropriate for the internal pressure adjustment applications of electrical and electronic devices installed in vehicles.
Vehicles are equipped with various electrical and electronic devices such as ECUs (electric control units), millimeter wave radars and lights. If these devices are broken, this will affect the vehicle main driving control features such as "running", "turning" and "stopping" and, in the worst case, people might be injured due to the loss of the driving control. Therefore, electrical and electronic devices are installed in a housing and protected from any external elements, chemicals and liquids, such as rainwater and oil, that may adhere to the device and cause a short circuit.
During driving a pressure differential between the inside and the outside of the housing is usually generated by the heat of the device and by the changes in the altitude.
If the housing is sealed, it is unlikely that external elements or liquids might adhere to the electrical and electronic parts of the internal device. However, if differential pressure is generated repeatedly, the sealed part of the housing may break and external elements or liquids may enter into the device and cause a failure into the system. Therefore, the generated differential pressure is alleviated by making holes on the housing and installing a filter to prevent external elements and liquids from penetrating through the holes.
Filters must be made of materials/components that can withstand the harsh environment that vehicles are exposed to, the high-temperature environment in the engine room and oils and washer fluids. Therefore, filters made of a PTFE porous membrane coated with a perfluoropolymer oil-repellent agent are used for this purpose. As a matter of fact, there is no other material than PTFE that can function as a filter for the housing of vehicles electric and electronic parts, being provided with air permeability (internal pressure adjustment), waterproofness (prevention of water penetration) and long-term durability, as PTFE prevents the adhesion of oil and other chemicals and so the deterioration of the device.
If a non-PFAS material is used for this application, it will not be able to meet the required durability. For this reason, it is expected that the frequency of vehicle electronic circuit board failures will increase significantly and every electronic circuit board will be discarded.  As a result, the discarded weight of this product will increase tens or hundreds of times and this will have a huge impact on the environment.
The unique features of PFAS materials make them suitable to fulfill the function of a filter for internal pressure adjustment and all the other various functions hereinabove. In addition, there are currently no alternative ideas to PFAS materials for the described use.
The above details are added text 'Supporting data are provided in section III-7'

Both the PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) porous membrane and the fluoropolymer liquid-repellent coating material that makes up the filter correspond to OECD polymers of low concern.
In addition, the PFAS used in this application is of low concern and used in small quantities.
I expect that vehicles will still be used but alternative products will cause a safety risk (due to requirements in the application that can not be met fully by current non-PFAS products).
Also, use of precious resources (rare earth metals needed to manufacture replacement electronics, etc.) might generate significant environmental impact.
Therefore, we believe that a derogation to this regulation is appropriate and we agree with (FCJ)'s opinion attached in Section IV.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We offer chillers for precise cooling and heating of a wide range of temperature zones, and air dryers for dehumidifying compressed air in industrial applications.
They use HFC and HFO refrigerants and are incorporated in many user sectors.
Examples include factories, life science applications such as MRI and CT scanners, semi-conductor industries such as wafer fabrication, and processes requiring precise temperature control.
They have many other applications where a wide temperature range and accurate temperature control are essential for executing processes and operations.
We support the statement made by FCJ(4102) and JRAIA(4292) on the issues of proposed restriction, as per attached in Section IV.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: We consider our products to fall under the refrigeration sector (Annex E.2.8) of the Applications of fluorinated gases. In this sector, deferral is considered for refrigeration below -50°C and laboratory testing and measurements. Our products are not intended for use by the general public or in building installations, they are primarily intended for use in factories, hospital machine rooms, laboratories and clean rooms. All our products consist of hermetically sealed refrigeration circuits. As the products are handled by specialised engineers in companies, laboratories and hospitals, the potential for refrigerants emissions to the environment and human exposure is considered to be very low, but no derogation has been considered.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The respective life cycle emissions of the refrigerants used in our products are as follows; a)-1 Emissions to the environment during the production of the refrigerant itself, filling of cylinders, etc. We do not have precise data. a)-2 Emissions to the environment when filling our products with refrigerants There is a slight emission to the atmosphere after use from the coupler for connection during refrigerant filling. The internal volume of the largest coupler is less than 10 cc. Even if 10 cc of R410A (approx. 0.065 g/cc), the most dense refrigerant we use, leaks out, the emissions would be 0.65 g/unit, which is estimated at 0.65*12800 units ≈ 8.32 kg/year. In addition, there is no exposure to employees as refrigerant filling is carried out under adequate (local) ventilation (exhaust air). a)-3 Emissions during operation of our products All our products are shipped with a confirmed leakage volume of less than 3 g/year (for sealed circuits) in accordance with EN 378. The highest estimated emissions are 12800 units x 3g/year = 38.4 kg/year. b) Emissions during disposal of our products. Emissions in the end-of-life phase are of little concern for the following reasons; In the end-of-life phase, our products are managed by the Regional Programme for Industrial Recycling. We already comply with the F-Gas Regulation and its stringent requirements for best practice, leak checking, operator record keeping training and proper waste disposal.  The new F-Gas regulation proposal will prevent emissions through legal applications and enforce ODS recovery. Our products are used in professional and industrial environments where proper handling, use and disposal can be ensured.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: It is not expected that our products would ever be intentionally incinerated. All refrigerants used by our company are recovered in dedicated recovery cylinders and transferred to specialised companies for destruction

Therefore, the amount of PFAS that our company places on the EU market is approximately 4500 kg. Specialist applications listed in the exclusions:. Three specialised applications have been identified for which no alternatives are currently available. 'Refrigerants in low temperature refrigeration below -50 °C' - Refrigerants in laboratory tests and measurement equipment - Refrigerants in refrigerated centrifuges: These are used e.g. in medical laboratories, where natural refrigerants are flammable or pose a hazard through the use of high pressure due to rotor failure, which can damage the refrigerant system.  In addition, Annex e, 2.8.2 explains as follows; 'In industrial, laboratory and medical, test and measurement refrigeration equipment, fluorinated gases provide highly dynamic and precise temperature control over the entire range from -100 °C to +300 °C. This temperature range can also be achieved with other refrigerants than PFAS, but no other refrigerant than PFAS seems to have the same wide operating range. Fluorinated gases may therefore be advantageous in equipment where the temperature changes frequently over the entire temperature range. Such equipment can be designed with sealed systems that have been found not to leak under normal use.'  This explanation precisely describes how our chillers and air dryers function. Therefore, for the avoidance of doubt, we request that this professional application is clearly understood as follows; It is recommended to add "Refrigerants used in industrial, laboratory, medical, test, measurement, and all other refrigeration equipment" for a 12-year derogation. This would include all industrial, laboratory and medical, test and measurement equipment and all other refrigeration equipment as described in Annex E, 2.8.2. At present, it is not possible to compile a complete list of all applications that may require precise temperature control. Not to mention future technologies that may require this functionality. General Comments: We produce rigid PU foams are used mainly as insulating material in the building industry for spray, discontinu sandwich panel, packaging applications. In these formulas we have to use HFO-1233zd as a physical blowing agent to have excellent isolation value.
We did formulation development trials by using another blowing agents instead of HFO-1233zd. However, it is not possible to use other blowing agents for spray foam formula. For example; pentane has a problem with boiling, evaporation point, flammable, needs special storage conditions.
