Customers who want to use pentane need to make serious payments to machine manufacturers in order to make their machines pentane compatible.
In addition, one of the most important points; In all these different alternative blowing agent trials, we achieved the best insulation value with the HFO-1233zd.
In today's energy crisis, covering the buildings with HFO-1233zd-based polyurethane spray foam to increase energy efficiency, and saving energy is another important benefit of HFO-1233zd.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: We are working as a polyurethane systems house developing innovative solutions for the insulation sector.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: In France, it is obligatory to obtain a certificate from the organization called CSTB in order to use polyurethane spray foam as insulation material in buildings. CSTB is also in charge of drawing up Environmental and Health Data Sheets. An analysis of the product's life cycle will be carried out to calculate its environmental impact. The environmental impact of construction products is used to determine a building's environmental performance, and is one of the focuses of the 2020 Environmental Regulations (RE 2020). Data will be required for all stages of the life cycle, from extraction of raw materials to end-of-life, including transport, installation and use of the insulation. The result of the calculations made for our product based HFO-1233zd was determined in accordance with FDES.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: After the spray foam application, there is no waste sent to burning. Spray foams applied in France must have a VOC A+ value. In addition, emission values are calculated in the FDES file. You can look at this site: https://www.base-inies.fr/iniesV4/dist/recherche-fdes

5. Proposed derogations: We are usi,g around 100 tons HFO-1233zd per year.

HFO are safe in terms of physical properties, it contributes to highly energy efficient Heating, Air Conditioning, Cooling and thermal insulation.

We, the undersigned producers and users of fluoropolymers, encourage the treatment of fluoropolymers separately from other PFAS substances regulated by REACH restrictions, depending on the risk profile and use.
In view of the fact that the use of fluoropolymers has been confirmed to be safe through rigorous prior testing and that many of their uses are critical, it is proposed that fluoropolymers be exempted from any Reach regulation.

Fluoropolymers are classified as PFAS only by molecular structure, but their environmental and toxicological data differ significantly from most other low-molecular PFAS.

In general, most fluoropolymers (fluoroplastics and fluororubbers) do not have the worrisome environmental and toxicological characteristics of other PFAS substances.
Specifically, the latest research shows that the 16 most commercially popular fluoropolymers meet the OECD criteria of low concern because they are chemically stable, non-toxic, bioineffective, insoluble in water, non-mobile materials, and are recognized to have no significant impact on the environment and human health.
Through the use of fluoropolymers, significant benefits are generated throughout the value chain. They offer unmatched chemical and temperature resistance as well as unique electrical properties and their stability, combined with these characteristics, translates into unique, durable, long-lasting performance in applications and helps to extend product life. In addition, the durability of fluoropolymers makes them ideal materials for developing innovative technologies.
Evaluation of alternative materials has shown that, even when available, they do not meet the key performance characteristics of fluoropolymer based materials and lack the combination and range of properties required to differentiate fluoropolymer based materials for applications.

Restrictions on a wide range of PFAS, including fluoropolymers, could result in:
Environmental, health and safety impacts, such as increased safety risks to employees, medical staff and consumers; and increased emissions from modes of transport due to technological regression;
The use of less durable and reliable materials leads to high maintenance costs and increased replacement frequency, resulting in more waste;
Negative impact on emerging and growing technology markets such as energy storage, electrification, renewables and hydrogen;

In addition to the need to redesign products, it also limits the variety of products that need to meet stringent standards, such as safety standards
Therefore, it is recommended to implement different restriction control proposals for different types of PFAS according to their risk profile and functional characteristics, to recognize the safety and importance of fluoropolymers, and to exempt fluoropolymers from any restriction action under REACH.

Besides, from the fluoropolymer itself, this kind of substance is a class of high molecular weight macromolecular polymer, its molecular weight is far more than 100000Da, which cannot cross cell membranes, is widely considered a "low concern polymer" (PLC) and should be considered significantly different from other categories of PFAS (effectively grouping all PFAS into one substance, unsupported by scientific data, which is lacking in this EU bill). Data show that fluoropolymers have thermal, chemical, photochemical, hydrolytic and biological stability, and because of their strong chemical stability, it is difficult to pose a threat to the environment and human health. In the case of polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), toxicological studies have demonstrated that fluoropolymers do not have bioavailability or bioaccumulation: acute and subchronic systemic toxicity, irritation, sensitization, local toxicity at implantation, cytotoxicity, in vitro and in vivo genotoxicity, hemolysis, complement activation, and thrombosis. Clinical studies of patients receiving permanently implanted polytetrafluoroethylene cardiovascular medical devices have shown no chronic toxicity or carcinogenicity, and no reproductive, developmental or endocrine toxicity. These fluoropolymers cannot be classified as substances of high concern (SVHCs) under REACH, do not meet the PM (persistent mobile) and PMT (persistent mobiletoxic) standards proposed by UBA, and do not meet the criteria for the inclusion of POP under the Stockholm Convention.

Countries have issued prohibition and replacement directives for preparations that may be PFAS in the manufacturing process, such as the Prohibition of Certain Hazardous Substances Regulations of Canada, 2016 (SOR/2012-285). In 2019, the Ministry of Ecology and Environment of China issued the Announcement on the Prohibition of the Production, Circulation, Use, Import and Export of Persistent Organic Pollutants such as Lindane, the 2019 EU POPs Regulation ((EU) 2019/1021) and its amendment Regulation (EU) 2020/784, etc. At present, there are no substances that may belong to PFAS in the preparation of fluoropolymers.




Above all, it can be seen that fluoropolymers do not ring in terms of their production process and use and their downstream applications Environmental and human hazards, there is no related substitute, should be exempted, allowing production and use.

General Comments: We provide different case studies for our contribution to the PFAS consultation phase. Therefore, we submit general feedback in addition to the case studies.
This case study provides the influence of PFAS ban or restriction for high vacuum pumps for different application. High vacuum is for example needed to generate the needed atmosphere for the vaporing and coating processes. Due to the high-performance requirements on the bearings and the need for these properties to be retained for the life of the vacuum pump to ensure continued safe operation. Suitable alternatives need to be created and these then need to be proven to work over a suitable qualification period. The bearing grease enables a very long lifetime of the pumps and less bearing exchanges. The qualification for bearing grease is very complex and needs extended lifetime test in laboratory and field tests.
This makes a decoration for PFAS-containing bearing grease needed. In case of a timely limited derogation, 20 years are proposed to get, qualify, and approve new materials in these applications.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Referring to Table 9 of the Annex XV restriction report this case study applies on several applications in the provided sectors. The attached Vacuum Market Segmentation provides a good overview of applications in which vacuum is used. As vacuum pumps are used in very brought field of application many sectors are influenced by PFAS-containing vacuum pumps. As vacuum pumps are not a separate Sector or sub-uses all answers take also linked applications into account. Proposed Sector: Industrial Process Equipment, Vacuum pumps, Pressure blowers and similar.  Proposed Sub Uses: Used for Vacuum drying, vacuum degassing, vacuum concentration, vacuum distillation, vacuum impregnation, and other processes in industries such as chemical, food, pharmaceutical, textile, papermaking, and electrical engineering. The attached Vacuum Market Segmentation provides a good overview of applications in which vacuum is used.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The overall impact over the lifetime is neglectable as PFAS-contaminated emissions do not occur. Only exception could be abrasion of coatings in the gas flow. Emission while maintenance where PFAS-containing parts are replaced and reach their end of lifetime as a part.  <5% in regular usage, >95% end of life/service replacement

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Vacuum pump is a combination of mainly steel, ion casts, aluminum, electronics and other materials (plastics). Electronics and other materials can be separated from the reusable metals. Declaration could ensure separation and limit release of PFAS-containing products to environment. PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) are widely used, long lasting chemicals, components of which wear very slowly over time. We aim to comply with any legislation which apply to our products such as REACH and ROHS. For this purpose, we keep lists of prohibited and restricted substances that are communicated to our suppliers.  Although certain groups of PFAS substances have already been phased out (for example PFOA and PFOS), the majority of PFAS chemicals have not yet been regulated. Nevertheless, regulations and restrictions on PFAS are currently being introduced in different countries.  We are currently working with our suppliers to find viable alternative materials to those containing PFAS that will be prohibited in accordance with upcoming legislation.

6. Missing uses: Proposed Sector: Industrial Process Equipment, Vacuum pumps, Pressure blowers and similar.  Proposed Sub Uses: Used for Vacuum drying, vacuum degassing, vacuum concentration, vacuum distillation, vacuum impregnation, and other processes in industries such as chemical, food, pharmaceutical, textile, papermaking, and electrical engineering. The attached Vacuum Market Segmentation provides a good overview of applications in which vacuum is used.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: We propose derogations for industrial process equipment (especially the use for vacuum applications). Apart from the use in electronics, in oil (e.g. PFPE oil) and coating (e.g. PTFE), used PFAS-containing components are mainly used in sealing applications with low wear and very limited emissions while operating. Proposal therefore is a derogation regarding the use in PFAS-sealings taking a possible declaration into account. This makes the use of PFAS transparent but without any limitations of products or applications. This would especially ensure the use in applications with aggressive processes gases or high temperature, where, for now, no alternatives are available. It would also avoid the risk of having extensive pollution due to highly increasing maintenance (e.g. 10 times high rate of oil exchanges) or a higher fail and scrap rate of industrial process equipment in harsh applications.  In case of a ban or restriction we propose a derogation period of 20 years.

Content: Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Baseline Information on alternatives Information on benefits Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We recognise the importance of the proposed PFAS restriction and the concerns of the regulators and agree that materials containing PFAS should not be used where there is a suitable alternative or the environmental impact is high such as firefighting equipment, fluoropolymer coatings on clothing and cook ware, lubricants and make up are a few examples, where alternative solutions could be found.
PTFE, FEP and PFA (fluoropolymers) once extruded fall into the category of ‘polymers of low concern’ and are chosen for their unique properties for critical applications such as medical, aerospace, automotive and green technologies.  The loss of these materials from the market will significantly impact quality of life for those requiring lifesaving operations using medical devices, the development of EV’s, aviation safety and meeting the demands for implementing green technologies.
Adtech Polymer Engineering Ltd is an SME employing 25 team members across 2 production sites in the UK & Scotland.  We work with PTFE, FEP and PFA in an extruded form and are a DU of extruded tube and sheet. We produce FEP heat shrink sleeving, custom fluoropolymer fabrications, gas sample bags and chambers, fluoropolymer covers for level detection and temperature sensing.  Protective Heat shrink covers for UVA and UVC lamps, heat shrink roll covers.  We supply a wide range of metric and imperial FP tube to end users and distributors worldwide.
As DU we’re using on average 765,000 metres of extruded fluoropolymer tube per annum.
These polymers are chosen for their unique properties, lubricious surface, biocompatibility, chemical and UV resistance and high working temperature and insulative properties.
We work in many critical sectors.
o Medical devices
o Aerospace
o Automotive
o Environmental monitoring – emission testing
o Green energy and EV development.
o Food & Beverage
o Chemical
o UVC sterilisation
o UVA insect control
o High voltage
o Coding and marking
If the PFAS restriction was applied to fluoropolymers this would significantly impact our business and that of our customers.

Manufacturing Phase
Equipment
• Our manufacturing equipment does not use any fluoropolymers as part of its design and maintenance.

Product produced
• Down stream user of extruded PTFE, FEP and PFA tube, sheet and film.
• We produce FEP heat shrink sleeving, custom fluoropolymer fabrications, gas sample bags and chambers, fluoropolymer covers for level detection and temperature sensing.  Protective Heat shrink covers for UVA and UVC lamps, heat shrink roll covers.  We supply a wide range of metric and imperial FP tube to end users and distributors.
Emissions at the production phase
• A large proportion of our manufacturing processes do not require the fluoropolymer to be taken above its decomposition temperature.  It’s at this point that fumes can be created.
• For processes that require processing temperatures above the decomposition temperature then portable LEV extraction is in place.
• Employee safety is ensured by written works instructions with exact requirements for extraction, risks and control measures.
o This is followed up with toolbox talk (generally annually), all new starters are made aware of the requirements for the use of LEV equipment.
o Signage is in place.
• Occupational Hygiene Survey was carried out to evaluate the Organic and Inorganic Vapours under COSHH regulations.  The survey results concluded that the processes were all well below the respective workplace exposure limits, indicating the current control measures are satisfactory.
• A procedure is in place for the safe removal and disposal of the HEPA filters from the portable LEV equipment.
• No processing fumes are vented to atmosphere.

Tooling maintenance
• We do not use any fluoropolymer lubricants.

Use Phase
Function and benefits
• FP are chosen by our clients for its chemical resistance, lubricious surface, inert, biocompatibility, insulation properties and high working temperature.
• These functions are chosen as our clients are working in the following markets.

Alternatives
• FP deliver the best performance for these critical applications, particularly where several of the key properties are required.
Chemical, sensors
o Lubricious surface, high temperature and chemical resistance.
 Some alternative materials may cope with the temperature range, but do not have the chemical resistance or the lubricity required.
UV applications
o UVC, UVA applications – for glass free environments the lamps must be coated and FEP does not embrittle and allows a high UV transmission rate which is essential for the performance of the device, it also contains glass fragments should the lamp be damaged.
 PET heat shrinkable sleeving does not withstand this UV application and quickly breaks down and dramatically affects the transmission output of the lamps.
Medical
o Biocompatibility and lubricious surface
Transition to alternatives
• Currently there are no suitable alternatives for FEP, PTFE, PFA raw polymer that are made without polymerisation aids that don’t contain PFA’s.
• A transition period is dependent upon how quickly fluoropolymer manufacturers can develop a new grade of raw polymer without the use of PFAS as a polymerisation aid.
• If lesser grade polymers are chosen as a less effective alternative, this would lead to a shorter life span for products in aggressive and critical environments. Leading to a less sustainable product and increased waste streams.
Transition steps
• All new polymer grades would need to be tested within each application by our clients.
• Medical, aerospace and automotive have longer testing and implementation requirements to ensure the compliance, safety and performance criteria are met.  This could take 3-5 years as an estimation based on a usual R&D to market lead time.
• With current FP grades there is historical data for their performance over many decades.

End of Life
• PTFE, FEP and PFA tube, film and heat shrink can be re-cycled, provided it is not contaminated.
o These are polymers of low concern as once processed do not deteriorate.
• We actively re-cycle scrap generated within our own processing.
• Clients have been made aware that it is possible to re-cycle these polymers.
• Main concern is the number of re-cycling providers and the volume of material that they will accept.
o Smaller users may struggle to find a re-cycler prepared to take their products.

Socio Economic impacts
• The supply and processing of FP is our core business and we have been trading since 1982.  A complete European ban on PTFE, FEP and PFA would significantly impact the business and would result in job losses and loss of turnover.

Org. name: Switching Gears for Net Zero Alliance
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We represent the Switching Gears for Net Zero Alliance. We are six leading power equipment manufacturers with a commitment to support the EU to set global standards for a cleaner future by phasing out of harmful chemicals used in insulating gases in electrical equipment. We have been relentless in our quest for alternatives to SF6, an insulating gas with a high global warming potential, using new technologies based on natural-origin gas and free of F-gases. We support the restriction proposal for the use of PFAS in insulating gases for electrical switchgear. Multiple European manufacturers are successfully operating switchgear based on natural-origin gases. This technology is tried and tested and has been in operation for medium and high voltage for over 10 years.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: This consultation response applies to insulating gas in electrical switchgear in all voltage-levels. This response specifically considers PFAS insulating gases used as alternatives to SF6 in switchgear:   •Fluoronitrile (hereafter referred to as C4-FN) which has a GWP of 2750; (CAS 4532-60-5) and when used in a mix has a GWP < 1000; •Fluoroketone (hereafter referred to as C5-FK) which has GWP 0.29 (CAS 756-12-7); and  •Some HFO’s (hereafter referred to as HFOs) such as HFO1336mzzE, HFO1234yf, HFO1234zeE or HFO1233zd which have a GWP between 1 and 20)  Although our member companies are active in other sectors and may submit comments on these as well as on other uses of the transmission & distribution sector, our joint comments do not apply to these other uses.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: For PFAS used as insulating gases in electrical switchgear, leakages are of great concern given their impact on the climate and human health. Insulation gas technologies for electrical switchgear using PFAS like Fluoronitrile will never reach zero direct emissions as the gas itself will always contribute to the emission level.    With respect to C5-FK, when escaped or leaked into the air, it is demonstrated that under the light energy it can be decomposed in air as illustrated in figure 1 in our attachment. The main element of its degradation is trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) and perfluorocarboxylic acid: i-PFBA. The TFA in particular is rapidly separated into water droplets and reach the land and oceans via rain, snow and fog, thereby entering our ecosystems and harming human health. TFA is classified as “harmful to aquatic life with long lasting effects” in its material safety datasheet. In addition, as TFA is a strong acid, it readily forms trifluoroacetate salts with minerals in soils and surface water.  All decomposition paths of (C5-FK) end up in HF (hydrofluoric acid) (LC50: 630ppm) or CF3COOH (Trifluoroacetic acid - TFA) (Inhalation rat LC50: 10 g/m3. Investigated as a mutagen). The molar yield of TFA for C5-FK is 100%, whereas the molar yield of HFO1336mzzE is "up to 20%". However, 2.5 times more HFO gas is needed with respect to C5-FK to meet same dielectric withstand at same temperature range.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: As C4-FN, C5-FK, and HFOs are used in mixtures in order to avoid liquefaction at low temperatures, they are impossible to recycle at the end of life or after maintenance. As the destruction process of the mixture is expensive, there is a non negligeable risk that emissions can occur during maintenance or end of life in countries where these gases are not regulated.

5. Proposed derogations: Regarding the proposed derogation times mentioned in the PFAS ANNEX XV report (Annex E.2.8, Table E.106. Insulating gas in electrical equipment - Summary table on assessment of costs and benefits, based on a general transition period of 18 months):  - Full ban 18 months transition period: up to and including 145kV: Our Alliance supports this restriction proposal as the majority of European medium-voltage manufacturers (<52kV) already decided to use PFAS-free insulating gases. For high-voltage (above 52kV): enough European and global manufacturers have PFAS free insulating gas products already available.   - Ban with use-specific derogation (5 years): above 145kV: Our Alliance supports a restriction in EiF+ 5 years as multiple European and global manufacturers will have PFAS free insulating gases available.   - Ban with use-specific derogation (12 years): a derogation of 12 years is not applicable (see above: max 5 year derogation is sufficient).

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Regarding the proposed derogation times, a derogation of 12 years is not applicable as a maximum of 5 year derogation is sufficient. Over 70% of the medium voltage (MV, ≤52 kV) market uses NOG technology, including European champions such as Schneider Electric, Siemens AG, and Nuventura. For high voltage (HV, > 52 kV), 75% of original equipment manufacturers in Europe have this technology available such as Siemens Energy, Hitachi Energy, Trench, Pfiffner, and HSP.  Change for others is technically feasible within the proposed timelines. For example, our alliance member Nuventura is an SME which was able to develop natural-origin gas technology in an 4 year period. In addition to the feasibility of timeframes for original equipment manufacturers to make the switch to NOG technology, multiple suppliers can provide natural-origin gases in Europe (e.g., Linde, Air Liquide), thereby allowing for a smooth transition.

8. Other identified uses: Natural-origin gas (NOG) technology can be used as an alternative to PFAS as insulating gases in electrical switchgear. NOG technology is based on a mix of nitrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide resulting in emissions that are harmless to the environment. NOG technology has sufficient dielectric strength even at low operating temperatures, good arc quenching and current interruption capability for load current switching, displays stable behaviour over its lifetime, even under electrical stress and is compatible with switchgear materials. NOG technology also has a minimal environmental impact, showing no ozone depletion potential (ODP) and no water pollution potential. Natural-origin gases are non-toxic or have a low acute toxicity, are non-carcinogenic, nor mutagenic, nor reprotoxic, and generate no toxic metabolites. In addition there is reasonable availability of the gas by multi-sourcing on the market and at affordable costs. Lifetime costs show natural-origin gas solutions are more cost-effective as there is no need for special gas handling tools or trainings and no costs related to reporting and other requirements.   Unlike some PFAS insulating gases for use in electrical switchgear, there is no patent on this commodity. Natural-origin gases can be produced by many suppliers and demand for these gases to replace PFAS insulating gases for use in electrical switchgear will keep prices low, resulting in no extra costs to households. Additionally, net costs to society are negative when considering avoided costs to the climate.  Only natural-origin gases enable climate neutrality in switchgear. NOG is a technology capable of the lowest carbon footprint and are toxic free including its decomposition products as the energy supply becomes decarbonized.   On the other hand, PFAS insulating gases for use in electrical switchgear are not very stable and decompose quickly in the atmosphere. For instance, the atmospheric lifetime of fluoroketone is 14 days. This gas will decompose during arc breaking or partial discharge and will not recombine. Tests made with a 14 liter tank with load break switch have shown that after 100 CO at 630 A / 24 KV, 51% of the fluoroketone initially present in the mixture (C5-FK + air) disappeared, generating 25 different Fluorine by-products and an overpressure of 0.5 bar in the tank. All these by-products are toxic and protection of people should be made in case of leakage or end of life handling. In addition, PFAS insulating gases for electrical switchgear are restricted by their high boiling points at lower pressures when compared with natural-origin gases, posing challenges for use in lower temperatures and in cold countries. 10,000 tons Flournitrile-mix are needed annually. A further roll-out of Fluoronitrile in switchgear would create 50+ tons of highly potent climate drivers and ‘forever chemicals’ leaking into the environment. This outcome can and must be avoided.    Furthermore, there is no European gas producer of PFAS insulating gases for use in electrical switchgear, leading to supply chain and energy security issues because original equipment manufactures are forced to turn to foreign providers. On the other hand, multiple European suppliers can provide natural-origin gas technology.

General Comments: We request an exemption of the restriction for the use of food contact materials, especially for the devices producing alkaline ionized water.

Enagic is a manufacturer of alkaline ionized water apparatus for household use. Our products generate purified and alkaline ionized water for drinking through the electrolysis of water. We provide our apparatus with customers around the world, Asia, EU, North and South America, producing more than 15,000 apparatus every month.

Alkaline ionized water is slightly alkalized, ph9-10, containing molecular hydrogen. Since alkaline ionized water is expected to improve gastrointestinal conditions and help stomach and intestine function, alkaline ionized water apparatuses are officially approved as household-use medical device in Japan.
Not only alkaline ionized water, but the apparatus can also generate acidic ionized water which can be used effectively for applications other than drinking such as washing dishes and clothes, sweeping and cooking.

PFAS, PTFE membrane plays an essential role for the process of generating alkaline ionized water. The alkaline ionized water apparatus has electrolytic tank and PTFE membranes separate it into 2 sections with electrodes. PTFE membrane has its excellence in high permeability with high porosity and the feature “allows the passage of the various ions in the water but prevents the free passage of the water itself” during electrolysis process.

We tested several alternatives for the PTFE membrane in the past years, but their performance is far from what PTFE membrane do. Not only the poorer performance in permeability and porosity, but some alternatives are also too thick to put on our device. The manufacturer of the PTFE membrane also has no idea about alternatives for PTFE membrane for this purpose and have not done enough research and development. Our devices produce drinking water and partly used for medical purpose, the alternative requires safety, and it should be developed carefully. Given the situation, we believe that 5 years is too short to prepare alternatives. If the proposed restriction put into effect on the purpose of our use after 5 years without no valid alternatives, we would lose about 30% of our sales.

• Make a delineation between substances of particular danger and substances that pose less to no danger, such as PTFE, PVDF, and FEP
• Consider a time unlimited derogation for medical devices – 12 years is not sufficient and such a limit could cause shortage of medical devices
• Expanded derogations to include all medical devices with exceptions to specific unsafe substances / devices which are of particular danger

Content: Information on alternatives Information on benefits Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We request that polymer fluoride be exempted from this restriction for the following reasons.

(1) No alternative
Fluoropolymer is a unique material with various properties such as high heat resistance, chemical resistance, low dielectric properties, and water absorption resistance. Low-dielectric CCL is one of the essential elements for high-speed data transmission and must be used in 5 and 6G high-speed communication areas (Attached file Figure 1). To transmit large amounts of data at high frequencies, low dielectric and low dissipation factor characteristics such as fluoropolymer are required, and lead heat resistance (300 ℃) must also be excellent. Even if a certain grace period is given, an alternative material will not be found, and these properties can only be found in fluoropolymers to date. As mentioned above, no material can replace fluoropolymer (low-dielectric properties) in the field of PCB raw materials (Attached file Table 1).

(2) Energy saving and Waste Reduction
Our company measured the dielectric properties of materials used in low-dielectric FCCL. As a result, we confirmed that PTFE (fluoropolymer) had the lowest dissipation factor value among various materials (Attached file Figures 2, 3). In terms of energy savings, this can reduce energy consumption and extend the product’s lifespan, depending on which low-dielectric material is selected and used. For this reason, using excellent low-dielectric materials in electronic products is an efficient way to save energy. From an environmental perspective, the impact of reducing waste can also be expected. According to estimates by the Japan Agency for Science and Technology’s Low Carbon Society Strategy Center, reducing the dissipation factor is expected to help reduce total electricity consumption by 10% in 2030 and 12% in 2050 compared to the current level when using the same amount of electricity.

(3) Effects of fluororesin on the human body and environment
Additional verification is needed to determine whether fluoropolymer harms the human body. Fluorine compounds can be classified into polymer resins and non-polymer resins. Currently, some non-polymers have been confirmed to be harmful to the human body and the environment. However, for polymer fluorosis (non-volatile, non-soluble in water), it is not known precisely what adverse effects they have on the human body. Additionally, some have proven that most fluoropolymers meet OECD standards for being defined as ‘low-risk polymers’ [Ref 1, 2]. Nevertheless, regulating all fluorine compounds in a comprehensive scope is a standard that does not consider the different characteristics of fluorine compounds. Polymer fluoropolymers should be exempt from restrictions until their effects on humans and the environment are proven.

[Reference]

To be used in the 5,6G high-speed mobile communication area (generally in the 6GHz frequency band (sub 6) and 24~100 GHz frequency band (mmWave) above 6GHz), materials with low dissipation factor must be used. The most suitable material in this field is fluoropolymer, primarily because of its electrical properties (Dielectric constant: 2.1, Dissipation factor: 0.0002), low water absorption, non-flammability, and high heat resistance. Fluoropolymer is an essential material in the high-frequency, high-speed mobile communication industry. c. Since there is still no alternative to fluoropolymer if it is included in regulatory restrictions, it is expected that there will be restrictions on numerous companies in fields such as IoT and AI (automotive, manufacturing, healthcare, aerospace, semiconductors, etc.) that will be applied to high-speed 5G networks. d. In the case of PI and LCP, materials currently applied to circuit boards, the dissipation factor at 10 GHz are 0.018 and 0.002, respectively. The dissipation factor of PTFE is 0.0002, which is equivalent to 1/90 and 1/10 of PI and LCP, respectively. In addition to PTFE, materials with low dielectric constants include polyethylene, polypropylene, and olefin. However, when applied to circuit boards, they are not applicable because the materials cannot withstand the high heat generated during soldering and laser processing. No alternative material can match the dielectric properties, low water absorption, and high heat resistance of fluoropolymers. Developing materials with the same properties as fluoropolymers with current scientific technology is also problematic. e. Additionally, I understand that research and innovation are underway in various fields, such as batteries and clean hydrogen, to achieve CO2 emissions and climate neutrality in the European Union. It is impossible to replace it due to selective light blocking, dielectric constant characteristics, water repellency, etc.

If other materials are used, the lifespan of the equipment will be greatly reduced, and the risk of use will increase. This will lead to increased other material usage.
This will work against reducing carbon emissions.

2) The unique properties of ETFE materials, such as chemical resistance, heat resistance, flexibility, low coefficient of friction, purity, non-flammability, etc., lead to thousands of applications in communications and semiconductor manufacturing.
Fluoropolymers are very stable and durable and can maintain long-term stability when used in tough conditions such as high corrosion, high temperatures and long UV exposure. If substitutes are available, they are expected to have the same stability and durability to meet the requirements of use.
However, due to the ubiquity of ETFE in this industrial application and the absence of suitable alternative materials,
ETFE replacement technology poses an extremely difficult challenge. This bill only proposes several possible substitutes and does not provide a detailed comparison and evaluation of the various properties and applications of the alternatives and ETFE materials, which in no way can be used as a justification or basis for banning ETFE materials.
Conversely, this lack of detailed justification demonstrates the indispensable position that ETFE currently holds in many sectors of manufacturing.

The tensile strength at the elastic/plastic limit is 21~23N/mm2, but the tensile strength up to the breaking point is 52N/mm2. For structural calculations, a conservative limit of 15N/mm2 is used. 6. Missing uses: 1) Fluorine-based polymers are mainly used, and the name of the PFAS material most commonly used is ETFE (Cas No. 25038-71-5).  2) In 2022, global annual consumption of fluoropolymers is expected to be approximately 500,000 tons, and the industry itself is expected to generate revenue of 10 billion euros. Although the fluoropolymer content in the end product is very low, they provide the end product with a specific, irreplaceable combination of performance, creating social and economic value that far exceeds the impact of the industry itself.  3) In general, some of the alternative materials may have similar properties to fluoropolymers in terms of parameters or performance, but the combination of properties required for the application is what distinguishes fluoropolymers from other alternative materials. Economic impacts include setbacks in advanced technology, loss of efficiency, and higher capital and maintenance costs. Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We request two additional exemptions and recommend the wording:
i) “PTFE as insulation material in coaxial cables for uses other than in private households until 13.5 years after EiF”
ii) “Spare parts for i) until 10 years after expiration of i)”



Executive Summary

This exemption request is connected to our exemption request for PTFE in insulation bodies of coaxial connectors. The findings in the exemption request for coaxial connectors apply analogously for this request.

Cable assemblies as enablers for basic societal functions and transformations intended by the EU Green Deal.

A cable connector is in itself a useless product as a raw cable is also. Only in connection, forming a cable assembly, they get the basic piece of basic societal functions and transformations intended by the EU Green Deal. The applications are the same as referred in our other exemption request and are for example:

1) Data transfer in cars where small space and low weight is of very high importance: Autonomous driving is only possible with fast and reliable data connections.

2) Mobile phone antennas to connect cables to cables or printed circuit boards: Mobile radio and 5G expansion is a basic societal need.

3) Test equipment for semiconductors: Semiconductors are the basic piece of uses 1) to 3) and subject of the European Chips Act

4) Connectors used in aerospace applications: Satellites wont work without ESA approved connectors.

The cable junction is essential for the combination of connectors and cables

As we explained in our other exemption request for connectors the mating face is very important so they will fit to other connectors. The same applies to the other end of the connector: the cable junction. Here the connector is fit to the cable (see pictures in the non-public annex).

PTFE shows unique properties as insulation material in coaxial cables

The structure of a coaxial cable is usually (Please see the non-public annex for pictures and examples):
- Inner contact
- Inner dielectric insulator
- Outer contact, often with shielding
- Outer plastic sheath

The outer plastic sheath can be made from different materials like polyolefins, PVC or fluoropolymers like FEP. For this exemption request the inner dielectric insulator is of essence. As it separates the inner contact and the outer contact, its relative permittivity (εr) is very important. Usually, foamed PTFE is used as material as it has an extremely low permittivity. As there is no other material that can be used for cables and has a similar low permittivity a change from PTFE to non-PFAS material would always require an increase of the diameter of the inner dielectric insulator. This would mean that also a higher diameter in the cable junction is required which usually goes hand in hand with a complete re-design of the connector.
Besides the re-design of the connector, also it is hard to find an alternative cable due to the very high requirements: The cables used in the named applications must be very flexible as usually several cable assemblies are turned together at very limited space and must show all required electrical requirements.

Sufficient time must be given for substitution

We are not able to estimate how long it takes the cable manufacturers to develop a PFAS-free cable with the required properties. This is not topic of this exemption request. The process outlined in the following starts with the situation that a market-ready cable exists.
The steps for re-design of the connector are similar as explained in our other exemption request for connectors. But the required changes are much more complex than in case of changes in the mating face (We further elaborate on this in the non-public attachment).

1 Qualification of a new cable (1 year)
2 Design and manufacture of prototypes (3 years for cable connectors)
3 Test of prototypes, this usually includes several iteration steps to adjust the prototype according to the test results (2 year)
4 Standardization of the new connectors and test methods (3 years, can be partially parallel to 5: for 4 and 5 together 5 years)
5 Approval test: Sample production, test at customer site, inhouse test, third party certification (3 years, included in the 5 years for 4 and 5)
6 Change of production from PTFE to an alternative material first in pre-series and then in series-production (3 years)
7 Market acceptance of the new connectors and complete change to connectors without PTFE (3 year)

The process starts with the qualification of the new cable. As the cable is determining factor in this substitution, the qualification must be accounted as at least one year because it must be sure that the cable is suitable, at least one second source exists, and the cable is accepted by the manufacturer of the final equipment. The design and manufacture of prototypes is expected to take about 3 years because the connector must be completely re-designed (we further elaborate on this in the non-public attachment). It should be considered that a company will not manufacture only one specific connector, but hundreds of different kinds of connectors would be subject of substitution. As test and production facilities are limited, they cannot run in parallel for all these connectors. This fact is considered in this discussion and very optimistic numbers for the duration are given.
In step 2 prototypes with the adjusted cable junction are designed and manufactured. The prototypes are then tested according to standards, customer requirements and the inhouse experience of the connector manufacturer. This step is considered to take minimum two years. We are not experts in the standardization of cables but the same processes in the international standardization bodies as for connectors apply and so steps 4 and 5 are estimated to take 5 years. The further steps, 6 and 7, until the substitution is finalized will take as long as in the case of changing the mating face. In sum the duration until substitution is possible is estimated as more than 12 years from the time on when a PFAS-free cable exists. Thus 13.5 years for the exemption are still optimistic.

Conclusion

The use of connectors and cables is linked to each other. If the material of the inner dielectric insulator in coaxial cables is changed, its diameter will increase. To fit to this cable a complete re-design of the connector is necessary. This requires the full re-design of the connector. The duration of the single steps for the substitution is similar as explained in our other exemption request for connectors. Overall, an exemption for 13.5 years is requested. The possibility for renewal of the exemption should be given. For spare parts additional 10 years should be granted.

Content: Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We request two additional exemptions and recommend the wording:
i) “PTFE in insulation bodies of electrical and electronic connectors for uses other than in private households until 13.5 years after EiF”
ii) “Spare parts for i) until 10 years after expiration of i)”

Executive Summary

Electrical and electronic connectors are enablers for basic societal functions and transformations intended by the EU Green Deal.

In this exemption request we refer to connectors with very complex geometries that allow the transfer of signal, data, and power with a minimal size of the connector. These connectors have not much in common with household connectors neither according to their function nor their shape. Examples are:

1) Data transfer in cars where small space and low weight is of very high importance: Autonomous driving is only possible with fast and reliable data connections.

2) Mobile phone antennas to connect cables to cables or printed circuit boards: Mobile radio and 5G expansion is a basic societal need.

3) Professional design of printed circuit boards to connect board to board: Transformation to a CO2 neutral society will only be possible with smart infrastructure.

4) Test equipment for semiconductors and calibration equipment for vector network analysers: Semiconductors are the basic piece of uses 1) to 3) and subject of the European Chips Act; no smart devices or infrastructure would work without calibration.

5) Connectors used in aerospace applications: Satellites won’t work without ESA approved connectors.

Electrical and electronic connectors base on a standardized mating face

The obvious function of a connector is to connect cables to cables, circuit boards to circuit boards, or a mixture of both. In all cases this means that on both sides, cable or circuit board, a connector must be placed, and the connection is established by locking both connectors to each other. This is of course only possible when both connectors fit together. They fit together if the geometry of the single contacts and the insulation body is the same, which is called the mating face. Usually, connectors of different manufacturers are used together in the same final equipment. They can only work together if they have the same mating face. To allow this, technical standards are applied.  In other cases, customer specific connectors are developed for a specific project. But also, these connectors are based on technical standards and existing geometries. The development of new technical standards takes three to four years. Usually when the material of the insulation body is changed also the mating face is changed as the substitute material has different technical properties (see below).
Examples of standards that define the mating face or materials of connectors:
- ISO-20860-1
- MIL-STD-348
- IEC-61169 Series
- ESCC 3402

Properties of PTFE are unique

PTFE is an expensive material with a unique combination of technical properties:
- Low relative Permittivität (εr)
- Very high temperature resistance
- Very high resistance against environmental impacts like heat, cold, UV light
- High flame resistance
The permittivity describes the electric polarizability of a dielectric. In the case of a connector, it is the basic material property to define the minimum thickness of insulator material between two pins. As further described in the non-public annex a higher permittivity of the material means that a higher thickness of the insulator material is required. This usually changes the geometry of the mating face with the consequences as described above. The relative permittivity depends on temperature and frequency. Other materials may have a similar permittivity at a specific temperature or frequency but while the permittivity of PTFE stays relatively constant over a high range of temperature and frequency this is usually not the case for these other materials.
Other materials with a low relative permittivity like polyolefins are in case of connector manufacturing usually not mechanically processed but injection moulded. While this is a very widely used technique, PTFE is currently usually mechanically processed because injection moulded parts often have small defects like blowholes and injection moulding is not economically feasible in case of small batches.


Sufficient time must be given for substitution

The substitution of PTFE in electrical and electronic connectors will usually require a re-design of the connectors. As overview the steps until such a re-design leads to a market-ready connector are (with rough estimation of required time):
1 Literature search and prioritization of possible alternatives as well as computer-based design/simulation of prototypes (3 – 6 months)
2 Manufacture of prototypes (6 - 12 months for PCB connectors; 3 years for cable connectors: see also our other exemption request for cables)
3 Test of prototypes, this usually includes several iteration steps to adjust the prototype according to the test results (2 year)
4 Standardization of the new connectors and test methods (3 years, can be partially parallel to 5: for 4 and 5 together 5 years)
5 Approval test: Sample production, test at customer site, inhouse test, third party certification (3 years, included in the 5 years for 4 and 5)
6 Change of production from PTFE to an alternative material first in pre-series and then in series-production (3 years)
7 Market acceptance of the new connectors and complete change to connectors without PTFE (3 year)

The first step (1) of substitution is literature search and consultation of material manufacturers to identify potential alternatives. After this, prototypes are manufactured (step 2). The manufactured prototypes are tested according to standards (see above), customer requirements and the inhouse experience of the connector manufacturer. This is quite time consuming as some tests cannot be shortened, e.g. specific environmental impacts like heat or cold have to be tested for several weeks. As it is very unlikely that the prototypes already pass all tests, several iteration cycles will be required. As soon as at least some prototypes passed the tests, the standardization process can be started. Product standards, defining the mating face must be adjusted or newly issued and the existing test standards must be adjusted. Due to the complex interplay between international product standards, international test standards and private product or test standards (usually owned by a certification company like UL) three years for standardization is very optimistic. Step 4 can happen partially in parallel to step 5 (approval test) but time saving of more than one year is not realistic for steps 4 and 5 because both processes are highly iterative, and standardization cannot be finalized when step 5 is not finalized. While in step 3 the connectors are tested in laboratory environment they cannot be used until all approval tests under field conditions have been passed in step 5.
After step 5 pre-series and then series production is changed to the new material, which takes at least three years. Pre-series production and especially series production have quite different requirements than sample production. In series production of course much higher amounts of material are required, at least one second source supplier must be qualified, enough machines must be ready for production, eventually new machines have to be bought, staff has to be trained and many further details have to be fulfilled.
As the connectors with PTFE-insulator will usually not fit to the connectors using an alternative material a smooth transfer using for some time both connectors in parallel is not possible, accordingly the market will need three years to prepare and implement this change.

At least additional ten years for spare parts are required

As explained above, an interruption of basic societal functions may not happen and past or current equipment that is based on PTFE-connectors will usually not work with connectors using alternative materials. It is neither ecologically nor economically feasible to replace functioning connectors from functioning equipment. But spare parts are needed for the connectors that will lose their function over the next years. Thus, after the expiry of the exemption for PTFE in connectors further ten years for spare part will be required. Especially to the end of this ten years, there will be only a few spare parts that apply this exemption.

Conclusion

Electrical and electronic connectors that use PTFE-insulation bodies are enabler for basic societal functions and transformations intended by the EU Green Deal. A change from PTFE to an alternative material usually requires a re-design. The re-design requires several development steps and is not possible in the 18 months transition period recommended by the annex XV dossier but at least 13.5 years are required. The possibility for renewal of the exemption should be given. For spare parts additional 10 years should be granted.

Org. name: DuPont de Nemours, Inc., Country: USA
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We respectfully submit our information in response to the per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) restriction proposal. It is our view that an additional derogation for the military sector is critical for European society and will not diminish the potential for the proposed restriction to achieve its aim of protecting human health and the environment.
Our evidence will show that PFAS, specifically fluorosilicones, used in the military sector cannot be replaced with alternative materials because the differential in performance of these materials is so great that the viability of certain current and future technologies that enable military applications, specifically aerospace applications of use, will be compromised or even extinguished entirely.  We would also note that while this response is focused on military applications, these materials are used in non-military aerospace applications as well.  Many of the same requirements noted in military specifications (MIL Specs) are the same reasons these materials are selected for civilian aircraft.
Our submission will also seek to demonstrate that emissions arising from uses within the military sector can be adequately controlled through appropriate disposal technologies at the end of life and during manufacture.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Our comments apply to uses in the missing use: military applications.  Other proposed derogations have mentioned being “related to the safety” of transport vehicles.  The qualification of an application that is ‘related to [the] safety’ may be difficult to define. Any application that impacts the proper functioning of a military application can lead to unsafe situations. For example, equipment failures on a military fighter jet can be catastrophic. Something as seemingly small as a frayed gasket can easily lead to something as significant as critical equipment failure or even enemy detection. So, when the seal for a crucial pod mounted against the outside of a jet’s fuselage leaks or tears, it not only compromises the jet’s electromagnetic shielding but also puts the vital equipment within the pod at risk of damage from air pressure and physical debris. [1] Therefore, we propose the following wording for a derogation to ensure that uses of PFAS without which military vehicles would be inoperable within the context of acceptable risk are covered by the derogation: By way of derogation, paragraphs 1 and 2 shall not apply to fluoropolymers, perfluoropolyethers, and fluorosilicones for the use in: [applications affecting the safety and proper functioning of military vehicles, and affecting the safety of operators, passengers, or goods].  [1] Shielding the War fighter Laird White Paper – https://www.laird.com/resources/shielding-warfighter-novel-seal-solution

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Emissions during manufacture, use and final disposition of fluorosilicones used in military applications should be considered separately. Processing of fluorosilicones into product that may be used in military/aerospace currently results in waste streams that are disposed by incineration and, for solid bulk forms, by landfill. Incineration is employed to ensure that liquid waste discharges to the environment are prevented. Waste is collected and processed by facilities licenced and permitted to process such wastes. At the end of their useful lives, components of military vehicles such as aeroplanes are not disposed of as municipal waste by consumers. Instead, professional companies manage the final disposition. In the case of aircraft, the aerospace industry has created several schemes developing and promoting dismantling practices [1-3]. TARMAC-Aerosave (https://www.tarmacaerosave.aero/) was set up following the conclusion of the PAMELA-Life project (Process for Advanced Management of End-of-Life Aircraft). The Aircraft Fleet Recycling Association (AFRA https://afraassociation.org/) was founded in 2006 as a member-driven organisation whose mission is to develop and promote the safe and sustainable management of circularity of components and aircraft in the aviation sector. In 2012 it was reported that around 1/3 of aircraft are dismantled by its members [4]. These facts are pertinent because they demonstrate that the organisations and infrastructure are already in existence to manage waste streams arising from the recycling of aircraft and other military applications, and even though at the current time specific requirements relating to the disposal of fluorosilicones do not exist, it is self-evident that once an imperative were issued, existing organisations and practices could readily adapt to ensure that fluorosilicones were disposed by incineration when deemed necessary. Therefore, given that fluorosilicones emissions in the military sector occur during production and final disposition, where comprehensive infrastructure, best practices and regulations already exist, a more proportionate way of effectively preventing fluorosilicones from being dispersed into the environment would be to capitalise on such existing facilities. In the independent RMOA prepared for Fluoropolymers Group (FPG) of PlasticsEurope by Chemservice, use of existing waste regulations was concluded to represent an effective approach to adequately control risks from polymeric PFAS disposal [5].The Industrial Emissions Directive (IED 2010/75/EU), the ELV directive (2000/53/EC as amended) and the Waste Framework Directive (WFD 2008/98/EC) constitute a strong regulatory system that could be used to enforce containment of fluorosilicone emissions arising from the manufacture of or disposal of military vehicles. 3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Incineration has proven to be an effective method of disposal. General Comments: We respectfully submit our information in response to the Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) restriction proposal. We are aware that trade associations representing the aerospace and automotive industries (among others) intend to advocate for removal of fluoropolymers from the scope of the restriction proposal. We would endorse that proposal because it aligns with our understanding of the socioeconomic benefits of the use of polymeric PFAS in essential applications, they can be fully mineralized by incineration and polymeric PFAS are not toxic and do not bioaccumulate. Our submission below is not intended to detract from such arguments. Instead, in the event that the evidence submitted to justify removal of polymeric PFAS from the scope of the restriction proposal altogether is insufficient, we would like to demonstrate how the proposed derogation o. under paragraph 6 of the proposal can, with a small alteration, enable wire and cable insulation applications in the transport sector to continue to bring socioeconomic benefits to European society without diminishing the potential for the proposed restriction to achieve its aim of protecting human health and the environment.
Our evidence will show that PFAS used in applications in the transport sector described in section A.3.11 (and by reference A.3.12) of Annex A of the Annex XV Restriction Report cannot be replaced with alternative materials because the differential in performance of these materials is so great that the viability of certain current and future technologies that enable air, rail and road modes of transport will be compromised or even extinguished entirely.
Our submission will also seek to demonstrate that emissions arising from uses within the electrical engineering and information technology sub-group of transportation can be adequately controlled through appropriate disposal technologies at the end of life and during manufacture.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Our comments apply to uses in the transport sector E.2.10, under the electrical engineering and information technology subgroup. The proposed derogation o, listed under paragraph 6 of the restriction proposal is: By way of derogation, paragraphs 1 and 2 shall not apply to fluoropolymers and perfluoropolyethers for the use in:… [applications affecting the proper functioning related to the safety of transport vehicles, and affecting the safety of operators, passengers or goods until 13.5 years after EiF]. (original wording) The qualification of an application that is ‘related to [the] safety’ may be difficult to define. Any application that impacts the proper functioning of a vehicle can lead to unsafe situations. For example, a malfunction of the propulsion system of a locomotive may not be intrinsically unsafe, but it could result in the obstruction of the track and potentially the need for passenger disembarkation between stations. This would be unsafe, as it would place passengers into an unsafe environment. Therefore, we propose a small adjustment to the wording of the derogation to ensure that uses of PFAS without which vehicles would be inoperable are also covered by the derogation: By way of derogation, paragraphs 1 and 2 shall not apply to fluoropolymers and perfluoropolyethers for the use in:… [applications affecting the safety and proper functioning of transport vehicles, and affecting the safety of operators, passengers or goods until 13.5 years after EiF]. (proposed alternative wording) The evidence that we provide about the comparative performance of alternative materials relates to the sub-use of Wires and Cables, under the Electronics and Semiconductor sector (E.2.11). This application is referenced in Table 8 of the Annex XV Restriction Report under the Electronics use sector.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Emissions during manufacture, processing, use and final disposition of polymeric PFAS used in electrical applications should be considered separately. Processing of polymeric PFAS into product that may be used in transport and electrical applications currently results in waste streams that are disposed by incineration and, for solid bulk forms, by landfill. Incineration is employed to ensure that liquid waste discharges to the environment are prevented. Waste is collected and processed by facilities licenced and permitted to process such wastes. Studies have been conducted that demonstrate that under industrial incineration conditions, polymeric PFAS can be fully mineralized back to its natural form as fluoride salts. A comprehensive study has been planned and is being executed by the American Chemistry Council’s Performance Fluoropolymer Partnership (PFP), who have described their work in their own consultation response. The electronics applications in transportation require that the fluoropolymer encapsulate wiring, either narrow gauge, low power wires and cables most frequently used in aerospace applications, or heavy gauge wires used in the powertrain of land-based vehicles. The proper function and the safety of vehicles depends on the integrity of the encapsulation, which is required to endure service conditions for at least 20 years in the case of rail and automotive applications and at least 30 years in aerospace. Therefore, during the entirety of the 30-year service life, negligible ablation, degradation or emission of the fluoropolymer would be taking place. In many implementations this is assured by entirely encapsulating the fluoropolymer in a non-PFAS material such as polyimide, silicone or epoxy. At the end of their useful lives, components of vehicles are disposed of. Vehicles such as aeroplanes and trains are not disposed of as municipal waste by consumers. Instead, professional companies manage the final disposition. In the case of aircraft, the aerospace industry has created a number of schemes developing and promoting dismantling practices [1-3-]. For example, TARMAC-Aerosave (https://www.tarmacaerosave.aero/) was set up following the conclusion of the PAMELA-Life project (Process for Advanced Management of End-of-Life Aircraft). As another example, the Aircraft Fleet Recycling Association (AFRA https://afraassociation.org/) was founded in 2006 as a member-driven organisation whose mission is to develop and promote the safe and sustainable management of circularity of components and aircraft in the aviation sector. As a result of these initiatives, in 2012 it was reported that around 1/3 of aircraft are dismantled by its members [4]. The rail industry has long recognised the importance of recycling rolling stock at the end of its useful life. The value of scrap materials is significant. Therefore, the REUSE project (https://uic.org/projects/article/reuse) was established to promote recycling practices amongst companies involved with the end of life stage of rolling stock [5]. A regulatory framework already exists to manage waste generated from road vehicles. The ELV directive (2000/53/EC as amended) sets minimum targets for recycling and mandates the improvement of the environmental performance of all economic operators involved in the life-cycle of vehicles. These facts are pertinent because they demonstrate that the organisations and infrastructure are already in existence to manage waste streams arising from the recycling of aircraft and land-based vehicles, and even though at the current time specific requirements relating to the disposal of polymeric PFAS do not exist, it is self-evident that once an imperative were issued, existing organisations and practices could readily adapt to ensure that polymeric PFAS were disposed by incineration rather than landfill. Therefore, given that PFAS emissions in the transport sector occur almost exclusively during production and final disposition, where comprehensive infrastructure, best practices and regulations already exist, a more proportionate way of effectively preventing polymeric PFAS from being dispersed into the environment would be to capitalise on such existing facilities. In the independent RMOA prepared for Fluoropolymers Group (FPG) of PlasticsEurope by Chemservice, use of existing waste regulations was concluded to represent an effective approach to adequately control risks from polymeric PFAS disposal [6].The Industrial Emissions Directive (IED 2010/75/EU), the ELV directive (2000/53/EC as amended) and the Waste Framework Directive (WFD 2008/98/EC) constitute a strong regulatory system that could be used to enforce containment of polymeric PFAS emissions arising from the manufacture of or disposal of vehicles of all types. 3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Incineration has proven to be an effective method of disposal. Peer-reviewed publications can readily be found that describe how suitable incineration parameters can reliably prevent emission of PFAS in flue gas or fly ash. Alexandrov et al. [7] studied typical municipal waste incineration and found no statistically significant difference in the PFAS content of flue gas and fly ash between model PFAS-free waste and waste doped with PTFE. Taylor et al. [8] have also published results demonstrating that incineration of fluoropolymers results in no detectable emissions of PFAS. A comprehensive study has been planned and is being executed by the American Chemistry Council’s Performance Fluoropolymer Partnership (PFP), who have described their work in their own consultation response. Operators of incinerator plants who have expertise in the disposal of hazardous wastes are accustomed to maintaining suitable operating conditions that prevent emissions of organic carbon and fluorine. The combustion temperature is important, obviously. Temperatures in excess of 850 °C with higher temperature after-burners are routine. Less widely discussed is the relevance of H+ radicals in the combustion zone, since it is the presence of hydrogen radicals that results in the splitting of C-F bonds. Hence, incinerator conditions may be tuned to maximise the destruction of C-F bonds and result in complete mineralisation of PFAS in incinerators [9] [7] “Waste incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate potential formation of per- and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) in flue gas” by Krasimir Aleksandrov et al., Chemosphere 226 (2019) p898-906 DOI: 10.1016/j.chemosphere.2019.03.191 [8] “Investigation of waste incineration of fluorotelomer-based polymers as a potential source of PFOA in the environment” by P.H. Taylor et al. Chemosphere 110 (2014) p17-22 DOI: 10.1016/j.chemosphere.2014.02.037 [9].
