7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: a. Tonnage and emissions: One large aircraft may contain around more than 500km of wires and cables, in around 100,000 individual lengths [10]. Re-qualifying this quantity of components in each of the dozens of designs of commercial aircraft would be an incredible undertaking but it would avoid the use of only around 1 tonne of polymeric PFAS from the wiring system of each aircraft Over the past five years an average of 330 aircraft were delivered to Europe per year [11,12], therefore this derogation applied to aircraft wiring would account for only 330 tonnes out of a total market size of 40,000 tonnes for polymeric PFAS [13]. The quantity of polymeric-PFAS insulated wiring used in the construction of railway rolling stock each year is similarly modest. Based on our understanding of the specifications of wiring used in magnetic wire wraps in traction motors and other powertrain applications, if polymeric PFAS were to be entirely eliminated from this application then the quantity avoided may be estimated to be around 22 tonnes per year [14]. The polymeric PFAS that are used in wiring applications in aerospace and transport wire insulation applications are PTFE, FEP and PFA. These materials can be used individually or in combination. b. Key functionalities For electrical insulation of wire and cables in both aerospace and rail/road powertrain applications, a combination of properties is essential due to the challenging operating conditions. For aerospace, wires are specified according to heat resistance and voltage rating, as described in standards such as Standard SAE AS4372C [15]. Other critical properties include •arc resistance •flame resistance •low smoke emission •30+ year service life The essential requirements for wiring used in powertrain applications are •High continuous operating temperature •Broad chemical resistance •Low moisture uptake •Corona resistance • 20+ year service life c. Number of companies involved ASD, the trade association representing the aerospace and defence industries, has around 3000 members. They estimate that 600,000 people are employed in the aerospace industry in Europe [16], ranging from aircraft manufacturers to manufacturers of parts for assembly or repair. There are many more companies further up the supply chain who provide materials and components to ASD-member companies. d. The availability, technical and economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives: Different temperature standards ranging from 135°C to 260°C apply for different applications in an aircraft. There are only a few polymer chemistries that are capable of service in excess of 200°C. Arc tracking is the ability for electrical discharges to scorch the insulating material and leave an electrically conductive carbon deposit. Such defects have been implicated in air disasters that have resulted in heavy loss of life (see [19]). Therefore, high resistance to arc tracking is an essential property. Below is a list of polymers that are capable of 200°C service, along with an indication of whether they are arc-tracking resistant (rated IMG 0 when measured according to IEC 60112:2020). PFA – Perfluoroalkoxy alkane – IMG 0 PTFE – Polytetrafluoroethylene – IMG 0 FEP – Fluorinated Ethylene Propylene – IMG 0 PI – Polyimide – Not resistant PAI – Polyamide-Imide – Not resistant PEEK – Polyetheretherketone – Not resistant LCP – Liquid Crystal Polymer – Not resistant PPS – Polyphenylene Sulfide – Not resistant PPSU – Polyphenylene Sulfone – Not resistant The only wire insulation materials that combine the essential thermal and arc resistance properties for aerospace applications are fluoropolymers. Land-based transport powertrain applications also require >200°C service capability. The insulation must also be robust and resistant to dust, grit, oil, water and cooling fluids. Rail motor technology is moving towards higher operating voltages and switching speeds which enables greater power handling for faster and more efficient trains [21] but requires wire insulation which must withstand corona discharge degradation. To ensure that motors can continue to operate, the corona resistance of the wire insulation must be improved either by increasing the thickness or decreasing the dielectric constant [22]. When polymeric PFAS are compared to the other 200°C-capable polymers, it can be noted that non-PFAS polymers have dielectric constants 50% higher than PFAS polymers (data collected from a variety of publicly accessible datasheets and databases): PFA – Perfluoroalkoxy alkane – 2.1 FEP - Fluorinated Ethylene Propylene – 2.1 PTFE – Polytetrafluoroethylene – 2.1 PEEK – Polyetheretherketone – 3.2 LCP - Liquid Crystal Polymer – 3.2 PPSU - Polyphenylene Sulfone – 3.2 PPS - Polyphenylene Sulfide – 3.3 PI – Polyimide – 3.4 PAI - Polyamide-Imide – 4.5 Using thicker insulation instead of low dielectric constant insulation means that there is less room for copper in the motor windings so that the motor would have a lower maximum power. Additionally, cooling is less effective, so motors could not run at their full rated power. These two effects would mean that vehicles which are designed and specified to use high power density motors with fluoropolymer-insulated wire would need to run more slowly or carry a lower load. Although there are many designs of motor for different types of rail application (including locomotives, metro vehicles, very high speed and high speed trains) and the designs of these motors use different combinations of materials to constitute a composite insulation, all major manufacturers of motors worldwide are understood to use polymeric-PFAS coated polyimide film as the first insulation layer. This means that almost all rail vehicles in service depend on motors that utilise polymeric PFAS [14].  Annex E of the Annex XV Restriction Report lists a number of alternative materials for wire and cable insulation. These are listed below along with the criteria by which they fail to provide adequate performance in transport applications: Silicone materials – lose mechanical properties on ageing, outgas during service, leading to delamination and weaknesses in the insulation layer. Cannot achieve required service life [20] PEEK – not resistant to arc tracking EPDM – not resistant to oils or hydrocarbon fluids Mica – mica is a mineral filler and requires a polymeric matrix to act as a flexible cable insulator PVC – maximum operating temperature only around 100°C PE (polyethylene) – maximum operating temperature only around 120°C Ceramic – not flexible, susceptible to mechanical (impact) damage e. Status of R&D processes for finding suitable alternatives Due to the inescapable need for a combination of properties that can only be fulfilled by fluoropolymer materials (as described in part d, above), there is no scope for development of alternative PFAS-free materials for all aerospace wire insulation applications. To address the needs of wire insulation for traction motors, evaluation of PFAS-free insulation materials has been initiated. Research has identified several candidate materials for investigation in pilot trials. Once a solution is identified (taking around 2-3 years), scale-up to commercial manufacturing volumes must follow, which would take a further 2-3 years. Downstream evaluations by wire manufacturers and then motor fabricators would then follow, before locomotive and vehicle designers could begin to specify those motors into vehicle designs or consider approving the use of the new material in existing designs. Considering the minimal potential for identifying an alternative material for polymeric PFAS in aerospace electronics, and the early stage of candidate development and long development cycle for land-based transport, a derogation of at least 13.5 years is necessary to ensure that existing transport modes will not be compromised by the PFAS restriction proposal. At the expiry of the derogation there needs to be a process to assess whether viable replacement materials exist so that vehicles that are already in service can continue to be repaired and maintained, otherwise perfectly viable vehicles would need to be scrapped due because of unavailability of spare parts. f. For cases in which substitution is technically and economically feasible: At this time, no alternatives that can be used as immediate replacements for current deployments of polymeric PFAS in the discussed aerospace and rail/road are available. g. Information on what the socio-economic impacts: All civil and military aircraft that are currently approved utilise polymeric PFAS extensively in their design, therefore the restriction would mean that no new aircraft could be manufactured, sold or repaired with PFAS-containing spare parts in the EU. While the impact of a polymeric PFAS ban on the aircraft industry would be significant given the number of companies and employees directly involved, the downstream impact to society and the economy of not having access to air travel would be profound. A socioeconomic assessment has not been conducted for this eventuality, but the scale of impact could be appreciated by considering the breadth of industries and economic sectors that depend heavily on air transport, as described in [17] and [18]. References are provided in the non-confidential attachment.

8. Other identified uses: Our comments apply to uses in the transport sector E.2.10, under the electrical engineering and information technology subgroup. Nevertheless, much of the information pertaining to the analysis of alternatives can be applied to sector E.2.11 Electronics & Semiconductor under the Electronics sub-use for Wires and Cables insulation.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We respectfully submit this information in response to the Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) restriction proposal.  It is our view that the proposed potential derogation for “the semiconductor manufacturing process” should be maintained after reconsideration, as the industry is currently unable to make cutting-edge, energy efficient microprocessors without the use of PFAS substances.  “The semiconductor manufacturing process” is a highly complicated, international set of interlinked processes involving chemical producers, semiconductor manufacturing equipment producers, producers of semiconductor manufacturing infrastructure and support equipment, and finally the producers of the semiconductor devices themselves.  This industry has been on the forefront of innovation for decades, and is essential for enabling modern society.  Without semiconductor devices, there is no precision farming, no electric vehicles, no efficient electric rail systems, no fly-by-wire aircraft, no cellular telephones, and the list goes on.
In the absence of a comprehensive derogation, the proposal as it currently stands would lead to the EU inadvertently undermining not only its economic competitiveness but effectively threaten the success of flagship political initiatives such as the Green Deal, the Net-Zero Industry Act, REPowerEU Plan, 2030 Climate Target Plan. The EU’s digital transformation through its Digital Decade plan and its associated benefits for EU industry equally depends on a secure supply of semiconductors.  The EU Chips act would be fundamentally undermined as such a ban would decisively weaken the competitive position of the EU relative to competitors without similar restrictions.
We support and endorse the evidence submitted by industry trade associations and consortia in favor of the proposed derogation for the semiconductor manufacturing process.  We also wish to provide additional information on our own efforts attempting to identify alternatives to PFAS process chemistries currently produced by our organization.  We have previously researched and voluntarily adopted replacements for long-chain PFAS materials in our lithography product lines.  In addition to general research over the past few decades, we have dedicated several scientists to researching PFAS alternatives for the remaining short chain and polymeric PFAS in specific subcategories of process chemistries for the past ~3 years, and continue to dedicate these resources.  These highly skilled scientists have yet to discover any non-PFAS solutions which can approach the performance required in current semiconductor manufacturing processes.
In summary, while the semiconductor industry is highly innovative and constantly focused on improving the efficiency and environmental footprint of our sector, we have been unable to identify or develop alternative chemistries which work around the fundamental physical-chemical properties of PFAS materials which are so essential to semiconductor manufacturing.  The likelihood of identifying, developing, scaling, and implementing alternatives to all of the different PFAS uses throughout the semiconductor industry prior to EIF of the restriction proposal is essentially non-existent.  While we will continue to research the possibility of replacements for PFAS process chemistries, we cannot escape the fact that the semiconductor industry has optimized its processes for decades to deliver the cutting edge, efficient chips upon which modern society is based.  Without PFAS chemistries, the EU chipmaking capabilities will be decades behind what EU society currently requires, let alone the future chips needed to drive the climate and productivity ambitions of the Union.
We request that a derogation be established for the semiconductor manufacturing process for a minimum of 12 years.  In many cases, even 12 years is unlikely to be sufficient for the sector to identify and implement alternatives, if such alternatives are even possible under the fundamental laws of chemistry and physics.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: This submission applies to the Semiconductors use sector as identified in the restriction proposal (proposed derogation 5.ee).  We are commenting specifically on the use of process chemistries in this sector.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Calculated emissions from the semiconductor fabrication process are included in an attachment.  Actual data is not currently available due to a lack of appropriate analytical methods.  Projects are underway to develop new analytical methods to close this data gap.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: The process chemistries covered in these comments (with rare exception) are consumed at the semiconductor device maker’s facilities, and do not remain in the finished semiconductor device.  As such, we do not foresee significant impacts on the electronics recycling industry from a derogation for the use of PFAS as process chemistries in the semiconductor manufacturing process.

5. Proposed derogations: PFAS-based technologies have been used in the semiconductor industry to develop smaller and more advanced products as they enable cutting-edge developments in photolithography. Several subclasses of PFAS chemicals are used within the semiconductor production process.  Photoacid generators (PAGs) are essential components of the Chemically Amplified Resists (CARs) which are used in advanced photolithography. When exposed to ultraviolet (UV) light, they generate strong acids. The chemistry requires sulfonium or iodonium- salts with PFAS-containing sulfonate anions. The solubility change of the photoresist is caused by the super acids which are created by the strong electronegativity of the fluorine atom. All PAGs that have been demonstrated to be successful in modern photolithography applications are fluorinated. Top antireflective coatings (TARCs) need a very low refractive index, low surface energy and outstanding barrier properties. Fluorinated acrylate / methacrylate / styrene-based copolymers provide these properties. PFAS surfactants’ unique properties, i.e., very low surface tension and a combination of hydrophobic and oleophobic behaviour, are used in numerous photolithographic materials. Fluorinated acrylate / methacrylate / styrene-based copolymers provide immersion top coatings and embedded barrier layers with the necessary low surface energy, outstanding barrier properties and a lack of intermixing with the photoresist. Key photolithography uses of PFAS and technical criteria Photoresists and Bottom Antireflective Coatings (BARCs)  – PAGs and thermal acid generator (TAG) - Function: Precursor for the photoacid catalyst or thermal acid needed for CARs and BARCs. - Types of compounds used: These chemicals are complex and to obtain the required performances they contain several lower chain length PFAS sulfonates. - PFAS provide: Strong electronegativity of Fluorine atom in the complex resist/BARC matrix allows for controlled generation of strong acid upon exposure to UV light, or under thermal baking processes. Photoresists – polymers - Function: Control pattern profile in extreme ultraviolet (EUV). - Types of compounds used: lower chain length PFAS polymer. - PFAS provide: Increases EUV absorbance, improves the dissolution properties, increases resolution. Immersion barriers - Function: Protection of the resist from immersion liquid and of the exposure tool from contamination. Prevent water film pulling and resist component leaching in immersion topcoats. - Types of compounds used: Spin-on barriers: Water insoluble and developer soluble PFAS polymers with fluorinated side chains. Embedded barriers: oligomeric or low molecular weight polymeric highly fluorinated materials. Fluoroalcohol methacrylate polymers with high water contact angles (in the order of >90°). - PFAS provide: Barriers that are soluble in casting solvents, insoluble in water but soluble in developer, and that show no intermixing with photoresists. Hydrophobicity and control of contact angle, inert under 193nm radiation, and transparency. Spin-on photolithography formulations – surface levelling agent  -Function: to make angstrom level flatness of organic thin film coating, including photoresists, various underlayers and overcoats, rinsing solutions, developers etc. -Types of compounds used: fluorinated low glass transition polymer or oligomers, to give low surface tension, with good organic solvent and/or developer solubility -PFAS provide: surface leveling reagent to make flat surface even at minimum amount of loading. Control of contact angle, reduce resist swelling for rinsing solution, improve developer spreading uniformity  Dielectric Polymers [Polyimides (PI) / polybenzoxazoles (PBO)] - Function: Provide electrical, thermal, moisture, chemical, and mechanical protection for the semiconductor device. - Types of compounds used: Water-insoluble PFAS polymers. - PFAS provide: PFAS groups attached to the polymer backbone provide solubility in environmentally friendly casting solvents and enable aqueous development. Overall, it is estimated that the total PFAS used for photolithography described above in Europe amounts to 2248 kg per year (see RINA paper attached). The estimated emissions amount to 1161 kg/year.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: This submission relates to a subset of proposed derogation 5.ee, “the semiconductor manufacturing process”.  We support and endorse the evidence submitted by industry trade associations and consortia in favor of the proposed derogation for the semiconductor manufacturing process.  We also wish to provide additional information on our own efforts attempting to identify alternatives to PFAS process chemistries currently produced by our organization.  In addition to general research over the past few decades, we have dedicated several scientists to researching PFAS alternatives for the remaining short chain and polymeric PFAS in specific subcategories of process chemistries for the past ~3 years, and continue to dedicate these resources.  These highly skilled scientists have yet to discover any non-PFAS solutions which can approach the performance required in current semiconductor manufacturing processes. As shown in the confidential attachment, we have invested resources in seeking alternatives to PFAS process chemistries used in semiconductor manufacturing.  There has been clear customer interest in potential replacements, and we have considered alternatives research to be in our own economic best interest.  However, as shown in the confidential attachments, we have yet to identify replacements for several existing process chemistry functions which function comparably to existing PFAS materials.    The semiconductor manufacturing industry relies on peak performance of every aspect of the production process to ensure a viable yield of functional chips.  Each processing step introduces the potential for errors, and those errors accumulate over the manufacturing cycle.  Even a slight increase in manufacturing defects in each cycle rapidly compounds and results in a significant number of failed chips.  This failure rate in turn leads to an increase in raw material usage to deliver the number of working chips demanded by the market, increasing costs, waste generation, energy usage, and several other factors. The semiconductor industry has been researching PFAS-free alternatives for 25 years. There may be some instances where substitution is possible, in most photolithography applications, PFAS-free materials have been found to be unsuccessful or ineffective. For many applications it would be necessary to reinvent potential PFAS-free alternatives. Identifying and implementing is a lengthy process that involves academic research, material supplier research, development (validation), scale-up, and subsequent efforts by the semiconductor manufacturer to demonstration (verification), integration, implementation, and scale-up to high-volume manufacturing. Even though all PFAS uses have their specific challenges and timelines for development, it will take 15 to more than 20 years to develop PFAS-free alternatives for most of the photolithography uses, while for photoacid generators (PAGs), it is expected that this process will take more than 25 years to replace the existing PFAS PAGs. Semiconductor technology development cycles often take a long time. Because of the complexity of the products and associated production processes, a major innovation can take years to bring to market. Manufacturers of electronic devices, working in conjunction with their materials and equipment suppliers, must typically proceed through multiple stages of research, technology integration, prototyping, and manufacturing ramp-up to achieve a process change effectively. One technology development cycle typically takes around 10 years from fundamental research to production ramp-up.  Many materials are unique and have specific technical requirements making it extremely challenging to find a viable alternative. For many of the uses of fluorocarbon-containing materials by the semiconductor manufacturing industry, no known alternatives exist. It is possible that in some cases it is found that a PFAS-free alternative is not able to provide the necessary chemical function. Where it is not possible to invent a PFAS-free alternative, it may be necessary to abandon the integrated circuit device structure and replace it with an alternative device structure that has the same performance. In some cases, the use of non-PFAS alternatives is prevented by the fundamental laws of chemistry and physics. The socioeconomic implications of eliminating semiconductor manufacturing in the EU are difficult to quantify.  In a best-case scenario, the impact to broader EU society would be minimized through the import of chips manufactured in other regions.  Even this best case scenario would lead to the loss of hundreds of thousands of direct jobs in the EU between semiconductor device manufacturers and the associated supply chain.  It also directly contradicts the EU’s strategic objective to locate additional semiconductor manufacturing within the region. In a worst-case scenario, prohibiting the import of electronic products containing PFAS would leave the EU at a significant disadvantage to the rest of the world, as the acquisition of efficient vehicles, modern computers, cell phones, and other modern essentials would then be required to be stopped at the EU border.

10. Analytical methods: Specific analytical methods to detect and quantify the minute concentrations of PFAS waste in semiconductor manufacturing process water streams have not yet been standardized.  However, the Semiconductor PFAS consortium is funding research to develop analytical techniques for future use.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Org. name: International Pharmaceutical Aerosol Consortium IIPAC) AND International Pharmaceutical Aerosol Consortium-Regulation and Science (IPAC-RS)
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We share here an executive summary of our 20 September submission.  Please see the attached document and appendices for relevant data, evidence, references, and survey results.  IPAC and IPAC-RS respectfully submit further data and evidence supplementing our 10 May 2023 submission and in support of two requests:

o 12-year derogation for HFC-134a (CAS number 811-97-2) and HFC-227ea (CAS number 431-89-0) as medical propellants (“existing medical propellants”) and
o a permanent exemption or time-unlimited derogation from the proposal of HFO-1234ze(E) (CAS number 29118-24-9) as a medical propellant (“future medical propellant”).

Please note that this submission addresses two categories of propellants – existing and future.  The issues and considerations are similar in some aspects, but distinguishable in others, as we outline below.  One important distinction is that the two existing medical propellants – HFC-134a and HFC-227ea – are already subject to policies and regulations aimed at phasing them down over the next several years in light of their carbon footprint and impacts to climate.   Therefore, their use by 2030 should be substantially reduced in the European Union and on the decline, globally.   HFO-1234ze(E) and HFC-152a (CAS number 75-37-6) are new propellants and are potentially important solutions to delivering lower carbon footprint respiratory care for the foreseeable future.  HFC-152a is not in the scope of the ECHA REACH PFAS proposal.
• The ECHA REACH proposal states in Table 8 (pages 100-101) that alternatives/substitutes are readily available for MDIs (also known as pressurised MDIs, or pMDIs) and the ban of medical propellants would have “likely very small costs” and would not lead to “additional administrative costs for industry or authorities.”  The proposal further concludes that “drop in substitute[s]” exist for HFC-134a and HFC-227ea as medical propellants in pMDIs (page 100).  These statements and conclusions are not supported by experience, evidence or data.  The two future alternative propellants (HFO 1234ze(E) and HFC-152a) are not currently available for patient use.  Further, pMDIs are complex devices and medical propellants must meet a specific range of technical performance characteristics to be safe and effectively deliver consistent doses of life-saving medicines for patients.  A new propellant cannot simply be “dropped in.”  As indicated by the number and complexity of the studies discussed in Section 2 of the attachment, significant development work is required in order to use alternative propellants.  This results in regulatory burden for which sufficient time and certainty must be given.  Developing pMDIs to use a new propellant requires careful review and testing of a range of several aspects and is subject to comprehensive preclinical and clinical studies, extensive product development studies inclusive of product stability and product characterisation tests as well as regulatory review and approval by the EMA and other regulatory agencies.  In addition, a comprehensive package of several toxicological studies on propellant should be provided to exclude safety issues and should be part of the application for marketing authorisation of new drugs.  Finally, the approach outlined in the proposal is inconsistent with the direct experience of the European Commission in the earlier propellant transition due to phase out of chlorofluorocarbon (CFC) MDIs.
• To reiterate, the current proposal recommends a 12-year derogation for MDI coatings given “the lack of technically feasible alternatives and the high societal value of the medicinal products indicates that a full ban would be associated with high socio-economic costs.”  Table 8 of the proposal further states: "Sufficiently strong evidence that technically and economically feasible alternatives are not generally available.” The precise same rationale applies to the existing medical propellants for MDIs and an inconsistent conclusion is not justified.  In addition, although commercially available alternatives are present, since the type of material is different, a broad series of screening experiments should be planned to find compatible materials providing suitable drug product profile in terms of chemical and physical stability.  In the worst case scenario, new materials or customised ones should be developed impacting development time and costs.
• In this submission, we detail technical and performance characteristics, regulatory requirements and other considerations for medical propellants for pMDIs with supporting literature and documentation.  These data and evidence demonstrate the importance of having a minimum of two options for medical propellants (i.e., HFC-152a and HFO-1234ze(E)) to ensure flexibility so that a range of medicines with varying physiochemical and clinical properties remain available for patients.  It is also important to note that moving to one medical propellant would reduce supply options to a single source of pharmaceutical-grade medical propellant for Europe, the United States, Canada, and the UK.  This presents significant supply risks.  These data and information support why it takes several years (typically 6-10) to develop pMDIs with future propellants and time is also required to enable multiple products to transition as there will be a staggered process.  It must be understood, as detailed herein, that this transition impacts a significant portfolio of products around the world (perhaps in the hundreds).  Not all products will be submitted to or approved at once by EMA and other global regulatory authorities.  Note that HFC-152a is not in scope of the ECHA REACH proposal.
• We also elaborate on the points made in our initial submission regarding respiratory patient care considerations and socio-economic impacts.  Switching patients to new medicines is not a trivial matter and must be handled carefully and driven by clinical factors.  For certain patient groups a pMDI device is the only means of effectively delivering an inhaled medicine to the lungs.  Moreover, changing a patient’s prescribed inhaler when their condition is stable on their current device risks loss of disease control and is inconsistent with clinical guidelines.  Evidence demonstrates it can have variable clinical consequences. These points are supported by peer-reviewed literature (see below and reference list) and data collected in a recent industry survey conducted by IPAC and IPAC-RS (see Appendix C in attachment).

Please see attached document for further details and data.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Propellants in Metered Dose Inhalers (MDIs).

Content: Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We specialise in the development and production of Multi-laser Powder Bed Fusion Additive Manufacturing Machines.
These machines combine the power of laser technology with fine powder in an atmosphere of Argon to allow production of metallic 3-D printed parts in a safe environment.
It is imperative that the machine works and contains its internal environment to ensure powder and Argon do not escape, to prevent the risk of an explosive atmosphere and Argon asphyxiation. In addition to the integrity of the products produced, which serve many industries, including medical products, aerospace components and multiple other manufacturing applications.
To achieve this, Seals, O-rings, adhesives, and finishes must be resistant to escape of powder and Argon. The stable properties of FKM and similar long chain PFAS are well suited to these applications.
Repeated evaluation of alternative materials has shown that the overall performance of long-chain PFAS is unmatched. Based on work carried out while selecting and qualifying materials, alternatives result in reduced reliability (an increased safety hazard) and shorter product lifetimes (resulting in higher levels of environmental waste).
We recommend that consideration is given to the risk vs benefit of the use of larger fluoropolymers and that the ban targets high polluters and substances likely to cause environmental harm first, phasing in control of less harmful PFAS over a realistic timeframe.
The timeframe for finding and qualifying alternative materials is very short and does not recognise the increased strain on the supply chain during the investigation, development and implementation phases.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The industry sectors that use our Additive Manufacturing are wide ranging and include manufacturers of many products that have far reaching environmental improvements, due to reduced material input, architecture unobtainable by conventional machining, reduced weight, reduced waste, increased strength and longevity of use. The machines are only used in a B2B industrial environment. This encompasses automotive, aerospace, transport and medical products. In many of these cases it is also important that our products do not leak or leach contaminants that may affect critical processes or sensitive products the resistant, the passive nature of FKM and similar PFAS provide this. It is a conservative estimate that the division consumes over 1 million items/substances a year that contain PFAS, where the PFAS content is expected to be a fraction of a %. Typical items in the machine, or that are used during manufacture, that contain PFAS are: Cleaning fluids  Adhesives & primers  Sealants Heat Transfer Fluids Inks for Printing Lubricants - Oils and grease (also used in bearings) Air & Fluid Filters Batteries Electrical items e.g., cables, connectors, Sensors, switches, lcd screens Pumps Electrical Actuators Fasteners  Bearings, shields and lubricants Metal coatings - Chrome anodizing, plating, paints Springs Bushes Tapes e.g., PTFE, Polyester, double sided Pneumatic & Hydraulic fittings Seals, O-Rings & Gaskets

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: a) Usage phase: The service life of machines typically exceeds 20 years and is supported by repair and upgrade packages. There are very low to negligible levels of emissions during the usage phase, typically through loss of PFAS contained in certain lubricants.   b) End of life: PFAS only form a very small percentage by weight of the machines, the prime constituents are metals, mainly steel. Our machines are recycled as scrap metals (Electronical and Electricals are managed under WEEE). PFAS are not separated from metal parts and processed at high temperatures along with the metals. Processing temperatures exceed the temperature at which PFAS will be destroyed.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Recycling does not result in PFAS release or formation. PFAS are recycled with metals and incineration >800C destroys the PFAS. Recycling of B2B products can be controlled to enable safe recycling. Work should be done to improve recycling process to ensure PFAS are captured and recycled or destroyed.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: The company manages the recycling chain and due to the relatively low volume of PFAS and the long active life of this product type there are no significant impacts on the recycling industry. Our suggestion is that consideration is given to collection and recycling of items that include PFAS. Control of collection and recycling can be implemented easily in B2B environments. Regulations could be implemented through parallel legislation such as the Waste Framework Directive.

5. Proposed derogations: The annual consumption of PFAS is unknown at this point, but is a low % of the overall product. Very limited amounts of PFAS emissions in manufacturing – industrial cleaners (derogation). Aside from recycling at end of life, there is negligible release of PFAS.

6. Missing uses: Key functionalities provided by PFAS are based on the unique properties of PFAS materials including their stability in hostile environments, resilience, and low friction. The unique characteristics of PFAS thermal, mechanical and chemical stability results in the inability to find suitable alternatives. Following an initial analysis, and to the best of our knowledge, there are a number of technology critical constituent components that would be virtually impossible to replace; based on previous searches our own testing and the results of evaluation trials. For certain niche applications, such as powder circulation seals and powder modules, substitution is not technically or economically feasible. The identification of all uses requires major efforts as not only is it smaller components that contain PFAS, but a whole range of bought-out products that get integrated, such as Pumps, Motors, Chillers. Where the supply chains have to be educated and declarations have to be sought. Smaller supply chains are likely to just disappear and dispose on non-compliant stock, which will affect the socio-economic balance and put a major strain on all industries and waste streams. There are a large number of components, where there is no immediate alternative that is obvious, so research, trials and evaluations would be required. There are a low number of components that could be exchanged with low risk, but potential reduction in life and increase in waste streams. Use of PFAS in seals is important to ensure no contamination from the seals themselves and that the seals are able to withstand use in a powder intensive, gas tight and vacuum environment. Alternatives offer inferior performance leading to shorter product life, leading to more waste and increased safety issues such as leakage of harmful substances and catastrophic failure. PFAS are very expensive and are only used as a last resort, where suitable alternatives cannot be found. However, it is going to further increase costs in the Global market to develop, test and implement alternatives, that are not totally suitable. Ironically without the use of components that contain PFAS (were no alternatives exist) the machine would not be able to recirculate powder, making a huge impact on the need to clean and recycle dirty, potentially explosive, powder.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: As a minimum the scope of ban should be reduced to align with the OECD definition of PFAS. A scientific approach should be taken to focus on harmful PFAS with the argument that long chain polymers are stable, non-mobile and not harmful. If there has to be a ban it should focus on high risk, high volume short lifetime uses of PFAS – Scotchgarde, fast food wrappers etc. An 18-month transition is far too short, which would result in excess pressures throughout the supply chain and leading to severe economic pressures, employment risks and the stifling of technology and potential a retrograde step to all manufacturing industries. A minimum of 12 years should be applied to such a monumental proposal.

8. Other identified uses: Alternative materials are being sought and further work is being done work to evaluate alternatives where they are found. To date no materials adequately meet all the mechanical, thermal, and chemical stability offered by PFAS solutions. Wiring is a major part of the electrical construction in the machine, it is likely that this could be changed for PVC/silicone outer, but will require a probable design change, plus significant testing, verification and validation. All of which would take several years resulting in major economic expense, risk and harm.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: A scientific approach should be taken to focus on harmful PFAS with the argument that long chain polymers are stable, non-mobile and not harmful. If there has to be a ban it should focus on high risk, high volume short lifetime uses of PFAS – Scotchgarde, fast food wrappers etc.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Baseline Information on alternatives Information on benefits Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We strongly support the ban of hazardous PFAS, where a negative impact on humans and environment is given.
A total ban of more than 10000 substances with strongly differing properties, and where only for few of them strong evidence on hazardous properties is available, is not proportionate. Especially for fluoropolymers, a lot of evidence is existing that no negative impact for humans and environment is given during the use phase (approval for food contact, drinking water contact,…), if the risk within the manufacturing process and end-of-life is appropriately managed.
Although initiated under the ECHA Chemical Strategy for Sustainability (CSS)*, the proposal is – and can only be – adopted under the current REACH rules, which must be demonstrated to be met. We believe that there is not enough scientific data and evidence which would justify the complete ban of more than 10000 PFAS.

A complete ban of PFAS (including fluoropolymers) would mean a de-industrialization of Europe, as the fluoropolymers are required along the complete supply chain for many industry sectors.
Starting at the beginning of the supply chain with the production of basic chemicals, where the fluoropolymers are needed due to safety aspects (humans could be hurt by the pumped medium in case of leakage), over the processes to manufacture materials (moulding of polymer parts), components (manufacture of electronics) and products (fluoropolymers as part of the machinery equipment to produce the products), they are also needed for many other reasons.
High performance technologies need high performance materials. Renewable energy, which should also be used by industry, does only work with fluoropolymers. Development of new technologies require (in some cases) such kind of materials as they make things possible, which is impossible with other materials.

What should also be taken into account is, that if all PFAS are banned, other regulations, which are required to place a product on the market, (e.g. energy efficiency, hygienic requirements, ATEX, food contact, drinking water contact…) cannot be fulfilled for specific products anymore. Generally, PFAS are only used, where really required and in very small quantities, as in most cases other (cheaper solutions) are well performing.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: During the previous consultation it became clear already that it is difficult, if not to say impossible, to find a suitable sector for pumps. We thought about transport, lubricants, electronics and semiconductors, food contact materials and finally gave information in different sectors, but nothing really fitted. Essential sectors like machinery and chemical industry have not been taken into account at all, but even that would not be sufficient as there are so many more applications. Therefore, we propose to add further sectors. But even by doing that, it will not be possible for all economy operators to sort their products in any of the proposed sectors. For the pump industry, a sector pumps and pump applications is recommended, as they are used all over the industry to pump media.    Typical examples of fluoropolymers containing pump components are:  1. Pump seals: Fluoropolymer materials such as PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene) or PFA (perfluoroalkoxy) are used as pump seal components. These materials offer excellent chemical and temperature resistance and low friction, which helps to reduce energy consumption, extends the service life of the pump and also assures a higher tightness level along the service.   2. Product lubricated bearings: Fluoropolymer materials like PTFE or mixtures of fluoropolymers with other materials such as metals, ceramics and other polymers are used as product lubricated bearings, as they offer excellent chemical resistance and low friction, which helps to reduce wear and extend the life of the pump.  3. Pump linings: Fluoropolymer linings are used in pumps to protect the internal components from corrosive chemicals or other aggressive fluids. These linings can be made from materials such as PTFE, PFA, FEP (fluorinated ethylene propylene), or PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride).  4. Diaphragms: Fluoropolymer diaphragms are commonly used in pumps that handle aggressive chemicals or other fluids that can attack traditional elastomer diaphragms. PTFE and FEP diaphragms are often used in applications that require high purity or resistance to aggressive chemicals.  5. Coatings: Fluoropolymer coatings are applied to pump components such as impellers, casings, and fasteners to provide protection against chemical attack, corrosion, or abrasion. These coatings can, for example, be made from materials such as PFA (perfluoroalkoxy) or ETFE (ethylene tetrafluoroethylene).  6. Cable sheaths: Fluoropolymers are applied to high voltage cable sheaths of submersible pumps because of their resistance to UV radiation, the excellent insulating properties and the resistance to moisture and water uptake.  7. Gaskets: Fluoroelastomers, also known as FKM or FFKM, are preferred for gaskets, because they offer high resistance to chemicals, such as hydrocarbons, acids and bases, and can withstand temperatures up to 200°C. Furthermore, they provide a low gas permeability, which makes them mandatory for applications where either the fluid being pumped must be kept free from contamination, or where the release of the pumped fluid to the environment must be avoided in any case. In addition to their chemical and thermal resistance, fluoroelastomers also offer good compression set resistance and excellent aging characteristics. These properties make them a reliable and long-lasting choice for use in industrial pumps, especially for applications where safety is crucial.  Overall, the excellent chemical resistance and durability of fluoropolymers make them essential for many pump applications in for example: 1. Chemical processing, where highly aggressive chemicals are present, because they can withstand the corrosive effects of these chemicals, considering also higher temperature behavior. 2. Oil and gas production, because of their resistance to hydrocarbons, high temperatures, and high pressures encountered in drilling and production operations. 3. Energy production because of their high temperature stability even in the presence of air borne oxygen. 4. Pharmaceutical applications in conventional as well as biotechnological processes, because they are inert and non-reactive and can be sterilized.  5. Food and beverage processing applications, because of their non-sticking properties and chemically inertness, which is relevant for the regular cleaning and disinfection processes, and that the quality of the contacting food and beverage is not negatively changed. 6. Water and wastewater treatment applications, where highly corrosive chemicals are present e.g. water electrolysis for hydrogen and oxygen separation or water purification for the electronic industry. 7. Pumping and circulation of drinking water.   This list of applications is for sure incomplete, as the use of PFAS containing components in a pump is not related to the sector, but more to the fluid being pumped. As such a derogation for pump applications is mandatory to safeguard the production of essential raw materials and goods, or the even better solution would be a complete exclusion of fluoropolymers from the PFAS restriction.   Many more sectors are in the end relevant, as pumps are on the one hand used as equipment during the complete supply chain, and on the other hand are dependent on the working supply chain to get the components which are required for their production. We are not able to give detailed information. This can only be given by the respective actors in the supply chain. A (non-finished) list of examples:  - Electronics: pumps are using semiconductors and other electronics to be able to work properly  PFAS required in production. - Delivery of energy: PFAS are required in the energy sector, especially for the production of renewable energy. - Machinery: to produce any kind of materials and components, machines are necessary. Those machines, e.g. pressure moulding or compression moulding equipment for any kind of thermoplastics, need fluorinated polymers and in some cases other PFAS (high temperatures other materials cannot deal with, non-sticking, temperature changes…). - Spare parts: existing production equipment, which is often used for 20, 30 or even more years, contain e.g. sliding parts from PTFE; the further use of those machines should be ensured life extension and not to dispose all machining equipment (consistent with the targets of the requirements of the Ecodesign directive and resources efficiency targets).  - Air conditioning of production sites (e.g. electronic production) contain fluorinated gases due to safety reasons.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Pumps requiring PFAS materials are typically maintained by specialized companies, which means by professionals. To avoid improper disposal of PFAS and PFAS containing components a system for proper tracking during service and at end of life can be implemented and will be consistent with already existing recovery processes (WEEE, …). The Digital Product Passport will allow a better traceability of the pumps and the components in question. At the moment, it is difficult to provide any figures, but such recovery organisation is feasible.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Due to the requirements coming from WEEE, many products are coming back to either the manufacturers or other central collection centres already. The quantity of collection should be further improved. Furthermore, processes for the separate collection of the PFAS containing materials from those collected products should be established and their recycling or, in case necessary, disposal under suitable conditions must be improved  As far as we know under certain conditions (burning at specific temperature range), no PFAS are released to environment, but the details are not known by pump industry. Additionally further research on the recycling and reuse of fluorinated polymers should be done, which will be important in the end to keep the fluor in the material flow.  Dependent on the use, another problem appears with a possible (unsuitable) substitute. Within industry, fluorinated polymers can be in use for many years; sometimes 20, 30 years or longer, whereas a substitute material could require much more frequent replacement (few days or weeks). The waste stream of these replacement materials, including their contamination, would be substantially higher. More frequent change of substitute materials could, dependent on the pumped medium, present additional hazardous for the worker and/or create extensive safety measures for maintenance and handling. Generally fluorinated polymers are polymers of low concern, which are chemically stable (no degradation to short chain PFAS) and no emissions are coming out of them if they are produced properly.

Consumers:  - The disruption of the supply chains lead to absence of essential goods, not only PFAS containing, but also all other kind of goods where PFAS are required anywhere in the supply chain for their production.  d) What could be an alternative for PTFE, which is used due to its sliding properties- providing an example:  In case PTFE is used due to its sliding properties, an alternative could, from practical/ technical aspects be lead (Pb). This could e.g. be used as filling in other materials (e.g. metals, carbon, …) As lead (Pb) is proven to be hazardous, it is in fact no alternative. PTFE has been implemented as substitute for applications, where formerly lead (Pb) has been used.  If materials seem to be a potential alternative at the first look, most of them finally identify not being suitable, if ALL aspects are taken into account. Finding an alternative is always means finding something which can in the end fulfil many different requirements, such as mechanical properties, chemical resistance, producibility, availability, HSE aspects, fulfilling other regulations, energy efficiency, and further more.   In most cases, the (very) expensive fluoropolymers are only used, where either all alternatives would quickly fail and lead to safety problems in many cases, the fluorinated polymer ensures function of the product/part (for an acceptable and longer duration) or where the conditions are not exactly known (e.g. composition of wastewater changes regularly (oil, water, bacteria, antibiotics, other drugs, rainwater, pesticides, fertilizer…)).  e) As the process to find and establish an alternative is dependent on the chemical industry (if they find alternative materials), a forecast is absolutely impossible.  We can estimate a timeline for R&D regarding integration of alternatives in pumps after they are developed and made available by the chemical industry. Finding a substitute was not in focus until now, and no suitable alternatives, with almost identical properties are currently known by us.  As for fluoropolymers it was possible in many cases to unify different properties in one part and this is not possible with other existing materials, a complete new design concept will be necessary for those cases.  A design change, if possible at all, means on the one hand a long time to find a new suitable design, which fulfils intended function(s), and on the second hand a long test duration, especially if different properties need to be qualified. For most trials a decreased performance is expected, and different approaches will need to be assessed. It may also lead to an extension of pump range complexity because of replacement by many new designs instead of one.  An example are sealings: if metals are used as seals instead of fluorinated polymers, a design change is required. Much higher forces need to be applied to achieve the same tightness level. Additionally the machining tolerances must be more precise to be able to produce those functioning surfaces. The chance that looseness appears in a shorter time clearly increases. After dismantling, the re-use of such metallic seals is impossible.  In case polymer alternatives are identified, production process adaptions are required. New moulding processes including new tools would need to be established. As in current processes PFAS are usually required (either as material or as production aid), these new “PFAS free” moulding processes would need to be developed before new parts from fluropolymer-alternatives could be produced. Where a fluoropolymer needs to be replaced by multiple polymers, the qualification time and the investments increase significantly.  f) In general customers demand solutions, which fulfil their requirements. If there are different options available, which can, from technical aspects, satisfy the customer’s need, they will always take the least expensive solution. That means, if there is a suitable solution without a fluoropolymer (which is very expensive), it will be used.  Where PFAS (fluorinated polymers) is used, it is the only solution for that case. It brings increased the life-time, better functionality (including energy efficiency), and safety (work safety, safe use, tightness, …), which are substantially better than other material solutions. g) The effect on the pump industry includes both upstream and downstream concerns. The complexity of the pump industry supply chain makes it impossible to quantify the socio-economic impact on the creation of pumps. The complete industry is affected. Where parts of the supply chain are not working, the complete pump economy breaks down. Pump manufacturers will not get materials from their supply chain (as well PFAS containing and NOT-PFAS containing materials), and will not be able to produce pumps   Downstream, pumps are used within the complete supply chain as part of the manufacturing process and are vice versa getting their parts, materials, and energy from many actors along the supply chain, who also use the pumps. Therefore, it would be a highly complex exercise to estimate the costs given the web of interaction between downstream and upstream aspects of the pump industry.   Pumps are used within and/or pump production is dependent on: - Manufacture of basic chemicals - Manufacture of materials (PFAS containing and NON-PFAS containing) - Manufacture of components (including multi-material components like electronics) - Manufacture of (assembled) products - Manufacture of machines for the different production steps - Water treatment (including industrial wastewater treatment) - Energy production and transport (esp. renewable energy) - Recycling and disposal - Other industry sectors (food and feed production where disinfection is required, pharmaceutical industry, …) -   It is quite apparent that the effect of a ban or a severe restriction on PFAS use goes far beyond any one industry or market sector.  Essentially this will take a number of technologies relating to sealing, chemical resistance, heat resistance, environmental contamination, product purity, process contamination, and friction reduction, back to where they were in the 1950s.  There are more than 10,000 of compounds affected and there are certainly many times this number of processes and applications involved.  This completely precludes any practical attempt to set up a “by exception” regulation.  Such a ban or restriction of PFAS compounds will have the effect of making large swaths of European industry, such as chemicals, pharmaceuticals, aircraft, and automotive, to name a few, uncompetitive in many international markets.  The social and economic ramifications in Europe of this are simply beyond imagination and clearly must be avoided.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We submit different case studies regarding the restriction of use cases.
As a developing and manufacturing company for vacuums pumps the Table 9 of the Annex XV does not provide a suitable sector and sub use. Therefore, we propose to a new sector and sub use with respect to industrial process equipment and vacuum technology.

30-40% of the components of products of our products are affected by PFAS material. Therefore, the whole product portfolio needs a redevelopment in case of a PFAS ban or a brought restriction. This affects more than 10 product platform and over 100 products. Mainly affected are sealings (O-Rings, shaft sealings, flat gaskets, etc.), electronics (frequency converter, controllers, drives, motors etc.) as well as oil and grease.
The proposal for a derogation timeframe regarding the use of PFAS affected components is 20 years. This is taking into account that some applications, that for some applications the development of new material has be taken into account. Not all pumps could be redeveloped at the same time and the requalification in the application itself is needed. A shorter derogation time generates a risk for industrial process manufacturers in Europe as well as for some applications where vacuum is needed.
Independent from the timeframes, the ban of PFAS in industrial process equipment would lead to a number of variants and increased costs of products, as the qualification of e.g. sealing concepts has to be done for single applications. Furthermore, electronics are a high risk for now.
From an economical point of view, a ban or restriction of PFAS affected products regenerates a risk to lose markets with PFAS affected production processes but PFAS-free products (e.g. production in countries without PFAS restrictions but import to European market while European companies cannot provide these products anymore).
From a strategical perspective, a ban or restriction of PFAS affected products limits the possibilities in the EU to get the lead in upcoming complex technologies like semiconductors, battery production, coating process for technical surfaces, etc.). For these processes, vacuum or controlled atmospheres are mandatory. Furthermore, a very high number application is affected already only by possible limitations in the vacuum industry.
Sustainability is affected by a possible ban or restriction, as the PFAS restriction conflicts with other EU goals, like the transformation from fossil energy to renewable. Furthermore, field population is at risk to be scrapped because of minor issues when simple PFAS-affected spare parts are not long available. The generated industry scrap is avoidable by wisely chosen derogations.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Referring to Table 9 of the Annex XV restriction report this case study applies on several applications in the provided sectors. The attached Vacuum Market Segmentation provides a good overview of applications in which vacuum is used. As vacuum pumps are used in very brought field of application many sectors are influenced by PFAS-containing vacuum pumps. As vacuum pumps are not a separate Sector or sub-uses all answers take also linked applications into account. Proposed Sector: Industrial Process Equipment, Vacuum pumps, Pressure blowers and similar.  Proposed Sub Uses: Used for Vacuum drying, vacuum degassing, vacuum concentration, vacuum distillation, vacuum impregnation, and other processes in industries such as chemical, food, pharmaceutical, textile, papermaking, and electrical engineering. The attached Vacuum Market Segmentation provides a good overview of applications in which vacuum is used.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The overall impact over the lifetime is neglectable as PFAS-contaminated emissions do not occur. Only exception could be abrasion of coatings in the gas flow. Emission while maintenance where PFAS-containing parts are replaced and reach their end of lifetime as a part.  <5% in regular usage, >95% end of life/service replacement

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Vacuum pump is a combination of mainly steel, ion casts, aluminum, electronics and other materials (plastics). Electronics and other materials can be separated from the reusable metals. Declaration could ensure separation and limit release of PFAS-containing products to environment. PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) are widely used, long lasting chemicals, components of which wear very slowly over time. We aim to comply with any legislation which apply to our products such as REACH and ROHS. For this purpose, we keep lists of prohibited and restricted substances that are communicated to our suppliers.  Although certain groups of PFAS substances have already been phased out (for example PFOA and PFOS), the majority of PFAS chemicals have not yet been regulated. Nevertheless, regulations and restrictions on PFAS are currently being introduced in different countries.  We are currently working with our suppliers to find viable alternative materials to those containing PFAS that will be prohibited in accordance with upcoming legislation.

6. Missing uses: Proposed Sector: Industrial Process Equipment, Vacuum pumps, Pressure blowers and similar.  Proposed Sub Uses: Used for Vacuum drying, vacuum degassing, vacuum concentration, vacuum distillation, vacuum impregnation, and other processes in industries such as chemical, food, pharmaceutical, textile, papermaking, and electrical engineering. The attached Vacuum Market Segmentation provides a good overview of applications in which vacuum is used.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: We propose derogations for industrial process equipment (especially the use for vacuum applications). Apart from the use in electronics, in oil (e.g. PFPE oil) and coating (e.g. PTFE), used PFAS-containing components are mainly used in sealing applications with low wear and very limited emissions while operating. Proposal therefore is a derogation regarding the use in PFAS-sealings taking a possible declaration into account. This makes the use of PFAS transparent but without any limitations of products or applications. This would especially ensure the use in applications with aggressive processes gases or high temperature, where, for now, no alternatives are available. It would also avoid the risk of having extensive pollution due to highly increasing maintenance (e.g. 10 times high rate of oil exchanges) or a higher fail and scrap rate of industrial process equipment in harsh applications.  In case of a ban or restriction we propose a derogation period of 20 years.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We support the opinion for the Annex XV restriction report as stated in the document issued by the Conference of Fluoro-Chemical Product Japan (FCJ), which is attached in Section IV.
We manufacture flowmeters and liquid level gauges for equipment used in a wide range of industries, including semiconductor manufacturing and various chemical-related industries.
Fluoropolymers are used in these flowmeters and liquid level gauges.
Fluoropolymers are extremely useful materials with a variety of excellent properties such as non-leaching, heat resistance, chemical resistance, electrical properties, and non-adhesiveness.
As a result, they are in high demand from the semiconductor industry as well as the automotive, electronics, chemical, medical, and aerospace industries, and their unique performance and characteristics contribute to the development of each industry.
Although numerous alternative materials have been reported for fluoropolymers with the various characteristics described above, unfortunately none of them are substitutable for the applications in our products.
The restriction for fluoropolymers is expected to have a significant negative impact on industrial development in Europe, therefore we request that fluoropolymers be completely exempted from the scope of the restriction.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Electronics and semiconductors (Annex E.2.11.)  Petroleum and mining (Annex E.2.15.) fluororubber/perfluoroelastomer/fluorosilicone rubber, which has high corrosion resistance, is often used to transfer petroleum, organic solvents, corrosive liquids, chemicals, etc.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The flowmeters using fluoropolymers that we manufacture cannot be purchased by general consumers but are handled by people with specialized knowledge.  Therefore, used flowmeters will be properly disposed of by specialized companies.  In the future, we think that the spread of PFAS substances can be prevented by further clarifying rules on disposal methods by industry groups and other organizations that use PFAS related products including our flowmeters.

6. Missing uses: The packings and O-rings assembled in the flowmeters and piping we manufacture are widely using fluororubber/perfluoroelastomer/fluorosilicone rubber. Depending on fluids, the use of the materials above is mandatory.  Immersion tests with alternative materials have shown that they cause leakage under pressurized conditions, and no alternative materials have been found at this time.  The restriction for the use of fluororubber/perfluoroelastomer/fluorosilicone rubber in these applications makes it impossible to operate various devices and equipment safely, and the impact on various industries will be enormous.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Fluoropolymers, mostly PFA, PTFE and PVDF, are essential materials for manufacturing flowmeters used in semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and they are used in all semiconductor manufacturing equipment used in wet processes.  As the performance of semiconductors increases, extremely high cleanliness is required for semiconductor manufacturing equipment. Therefore, the piping material in the equipment must be completely non-leaching substances. In addition, liquids that are extremely aggressive to other substances are also used, and the piping material must be able to withstand such aggression. Furthermore, semiconductor manufacturing equipment installed in a limited space such as a clean room requires a small footprint as much as possible. Therefore, the piping in the equipment has a very complicated shape, and if the piping cannot be bent, it cannot be assembled.  Fluoropolymers are the only piping materials that can meet these conditions, and no alternative materials have been found. In addition, it is highly unlikely that usable alternative material will be found in the future, and even if one were to be found, it is highly likely that the characteristics of persistence at issue under this restriction will be similar.  For the flowmeters we manufacture, semiconductor manufacturers require the use of fluoropolymers. This is due to particularly high non-leaching requirements. To comply with the requirements from semiconductor manufacturers, we have no choice but to use semiconductor-grade fluoropolymers, so if the use of fluoropolymers is restricted, we will not be able to manufacture flowmeters. Since fluoropolymers are necessary to continue manufacturing semiconductors that support all technological innovations in recent years, we request that fluoropolymers be completely exempted from the scope of the restriction.

General Comments: We support the PFAS group restriction of non-essential uses of PFAS, where no human and environmentally safe alternatives exist.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: PFAS emissions to the environment stem from point sources (industrial sites, landfill sites, accidental release) or from diffuse pollution, leading to ubiquitous pollution of the aquatic environment. This feed-back is provided by the drinking water sector. With the view to better identifying sources, it would be useful to introduce a well-structured system of PFAS-containing products with regards to their users (for example medical devices for use in hospitals or textiles for outdoor use or textiles for fire fighters). The proposal lists PFAS sinks including drinking water treatment. This should be specified more, including contamination levels, sources and impacts on natural cycles. We feel particularly concerned as removing PFAS from raw waters is extremely costly and not sustainable as it only shifts the pollution from one environmental media to another. Reliance on end-of-pipe solutions creates a substantial stumbling block on the water sector’s journey towards climate neutrality.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: As described by Lohmann et al. (2022), in the process of production, use and disposal PFAS will enter the environment and accumulate in water, soil, air and the foodchain. This supports a ban of PFAS as a group to avoid further emissions and accumulation of PFAS in our environment.

8. The costs of PFAS to the world are estimated to be €16 trillion, per year.

9. Degradation potential of specific PFAS sub-groups: Under specific circumstances long-chain PFAS degrade to short-chain PFAS like TFA. TFA is highly mobile and persistent and can lead to contamination of water resources (German Environment Acency, 2021: Reducing the input of chemicals into waters: trifluoroacetat (TFA) as a persistent and mobile substance with many sources)

10. Analytical methods: Directive (EU) 2020/2184  stipulates that ‘by 12 January 2024, the Commission shall establish technical guidelines regarding methods of analysis for monitoring of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances under the parameters ‘PFAS Total’ and ‘Sum of PFAS’, including detection limits, parametric values and frequency of sampling.’ The development of a valid analytical method for eluates is of utmost importance for valid and sound analysis and comparable results.

(Not suitable for use in dry areas) - There is a risk of short circuit or electric leakage when water leaks.
