Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We would like to draw your attention to products using the Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) and specifically such products having working fluids containing PFAS. Organic Rankine Cycle power systems are an emission-free technology suitable for the conversion of thermal energy into electricity. ORC systems can be used to harvest waste heat, generated from industrial processes and engines for example, which would otherwise be wasted to the environment. There is a tremendous potential for the utilization of stationary waste heat from the energy intensive industry. The association KCORC has estimated the technical potential of waste heat utilization from industry to 150 TWhel/yr in EU27[1]

This input supplements the comments made from our European association KCORC on products and systems using the Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC). Our core business, using the ORC cycle, is within systems for low temperature (waste) heat recovery.

Technical details on ORC can be found on KCORC web page https://www.kcorc.org/en/science-technology/, or at our web page https://climeon.com/how-it-works/. For your convenience, the position paper from KCORC on PFAS working fluids in ORC systems can be found here: https://kcorc.org/media/medialibrary/2023/08/20230616_PFAS_statement_KCORC_Final.pdf

We fully support all comments from KCORC, but as products with ORC do have variances, and could be used in many applications, we here submit specific comments and proposals related to our type of products. Under question 6 below we propose a derogation for “fluorinated gases used as working fluid for the operation of products using the Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) to convert low temperature heat (less then 200 °C) into electricity” (for details and justification see under question 6 in submitted confidential document)

Further to the proposed derogation we also have some additional topics to comment.

Exemption time and exemption process
From what we understand, the draft legislation act is not indicating any procedure on extending or renewal of derogations. In general, the proposal is suggesting different derogation on 5 and 12 years respective, and because of a general 1,5 year derogation the actual derogation time for the specific applications will be 6,5 and 13,5 years respectively.

Although, we fully support the intension to replace PFAS working fluids, it is most difficult to predict how successful a conversion to non-PFAS working fluids actually will be. We already now see significant issues mainly because of safety and additional product costs (see more on this below). Furthermore, we face issues related to compliance mainly on the marine side, where flammable refrigerants cannot be used today. It is most difficult to predict how fast these obstacles could be handled. We therefore propose an exemption process similar with e.g. the RoHS Directive, where it would be possible to apply for renewal or modification of exemptions for certain application, if that would be needed. Such application would be then assessed before being approved. We take note that Orgalim, representing Europe’s technology industries, also bring this topic up in their position paper on the proposed PFAS restriction: (https://orgalim.eu/sites/default/files/attachment/Orgalim%20PFAS%20position%20paper_310823.pdf)

Servicing of products with long life time
The proposal contains a 12 year derogation for maintenance and refilling of existing HVACR equipment drop-in use of service refrigerants on products already placed on the market. For products with a long life time – like product using ORC – we believe this time is too short. We foresee an active product lifetime of 20-30 years where the products would save significant CO2 emissions by harvesting waste heat. It would be counterproductive to take products out of service because of this limitation. We do not see a real drop-in (from PFAS to a non-PFAS working fluid) alternative to be realistic.

Furthermore, and with reference to the European Green Deal and the Commission proposal on promoting the repair of goods, we believe the proposed derogation for service must be calculated from the time a product is actually placed on the market or put into service. For products under a 12 year derogation, and sold in the later part of this period, the remaining time to benefit from the drop-in service derogation would be dramatically reduced. It will not be possible to sell this type of products if service could not be offered for the whole remaining life time.

Also this topic is addressed by Orgalim, who stresses the importance of possibility to maintain and service products on the market in order to avoid too early disposal in environmental perspective.

Content: Hazard or exposure Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We would like to explain the hazard information regarding fluorinated gas used as SF6 alternative for molten magnesium cover gas. This fluorinated gas CAS No. is 756-13-8 (chemical name: 1,1,1,2,2,4,5,5,5-Nonafluoro-4-(trifluoromethyl)-3-pentanone) and has a boiling point of 40℃. This fluorinated gas is produced by various manufacturers including 3M (Novec612), Zhejiang Noah Fluorochemical (Noah5112), Fanda Chemical (FK649), and Waysmos (FK 5-1-12). Based on OECD301B biodegradation test, 1,1,1,2,2,4,5,5,5-Nonafluoro-4-(trifluoromethyl)-3-pentanone is not readily biodegradable as the amount of CO2 generated biologically within 28 days was calculated to be 3%. Regarding atmospheric degradation, 1,1,1,2,2,4,5,5,5-Nonafluoro-4-(trifluoromethyl)-3-pentanone reacts with OH radicals, and the half-life in the air is estimated to be 5.11 days, with a Global Warming Potential (GWP) of less than 1. For bioaccumulation, 1,1,1,2,2,4,5,5,5-Nonafluoro-4-(trifluoromethyl)-3-pentanone was tested under OECD305 procedure, and was found to have a very low concentration, below 4.8. On the other hand, this gas decomposes under ultraviolet light, producing TFA and HF in the process. Mutagenicity was assessed using the AMES test, and no mutagenicity was observed. Acute toxicity evaluation involved exposing rats to vapor of 1,1,1,2,2,4,5,5,5-nonofluoro-4-(trifluoromethyl)-3-pentanone for 4 hours, resulting in an LC50 of more than 1,227 mg/L, and an LD50 of more than 5,000 mg/kg in oral ingestion, making it a safe liquid.

[Request for Exemption]
1,1,1,2,2,4,5,5,5-nonofluoro-4-(trifluoromethyl)-3-pentanone is used as a fire-resistant cover gas when casting magnesium alloys. Magnesium is the lightest among practical metals, and it has higher specific strength and specific stiffness compared to aluminum, iron, and plastic materials. Therefore, it is applied to the casings of mobile phones and laptops, and it is expected to expand its application to automotive components where weight reduction is required, such as electric vehicles in the future. Moreover, it is recyclable, and the energy required for recycling is only 4% of that for new block manufacturing, making it an eco-friendly material.

However, molten magnesium burns with a flash when it reacts with air, so 1,1,1,2,2,4,5,5,5-nonofluoro-4-(trifluoromethyl)-3-pentanone and a mixture of CO2 or N2 are supplied as a cover gas to the surface of molten magnesium to form a protective film and prevent combustion. While some regions use SO2 as a cover gas, SO2 pollution in the atmosphere can irritate the respiratory system and lead to disorders such as coughing, asthma, and bronchitis. The Minamata disease, which occurred around 1961 in Japan, is a famous example of the health hazards caused by SO2, making it a challenging substance to use in Japan. The SO2 environmental standards require a daily average of 0.04 ppm or less for a one-hour value, and 0.1 ppm or less for a one-hour value. When SO2 is used as a cover gas, it is highly likely to leak out of the magnesium dissolution furnace, posing significant risks to workers.

In contrast, 1,1,1,2,2,4,5,5,5-nonofluoro-4-(trifluoromethyl)-3-pentanone is non-flammable, low in toxicity, has a GWP of 1. Furthermore, the Ozone Depletion Potential (ODP) of 1,1,1,2,2,4,5,5,5-nonofluoro-4-(trifluoromethyl)-3-pentanone is 0, indicating that it does not contribute negatively to environmental issues such as ozone depletion or global warming.

Based on all the hazard information provided, 1,1,1,2,2,4,5,5,5-nonofluoro-4-(trifluoromethyl)-3-pentanone is assumed to be a cover gas that is friendly to both health and the environment thus we strongly request 1,1,1,2,2,4,5,5,5-nonofluoro-4-(trifluoromethyl)-3-pentanone to be exempted from PFAS regulations.

We believe that regulatory targets should be limited to substances where a risk assessment based on scientific evidence recognizes an impact on human health or the environment, taking into consideration economic and societal impacts and kindly ask ECHA to reconsider 1,1,1,2,2,4,5,5,5-nonofluoro-4-(trifluoromethyl)-3-pentanone from restriction target.

General Comments: We would like to express the gratitude of having the opportunity of stating our opinion to the proposed restriction on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances(PFASs).
The proposed restriction of PFAS materials currently under consideration covers more than 10,000 types of PFAS materials, and the safety and hazardousness of each and every material has not been fully discussed. Therefore, PFAS should be sub-categorized and their risks should be evaluated appropriately.
In addition, PFAS materials have already been applied to a wide variety of functional products and have contributed significantly to the prosperity of mankind throughout the world. The figure in attached file shows the imports of PTFE, the major PFAS material, into the EU from both within and outside the region1). Its importance as a material has grown significantly, with an increasing trend in both weight and value over the last three years. In addition, PTFE has the best properties of all industrially available materials, including low dielectric properties, low surface tension, low coefficient of friction, and chemical resistance, positioning it as an essential and difficult-to-replace material in many product categories. In terms of weight, the imports exceed 40,000 tons/year, and it is believed that PTFE is incorporated into a variety of functional products and shipped around the world. Furthermore, the import value of PTFE alone exceeded 500 million euros in 2022, and it is estimated that the market size of applied functional products is even larger, which has a significant economic impact not only on the EU region but also on the world, and it is not difficult to imagine the supply chain disruption it would cause.
These statistics also suggest that the proposed PFAS restriction should not be a comprehensive restriction, but that the proposed restriction should be discussed on a case-by-case basis, allowing time for sufficient safety and risk assessment, so that the impact on human health and the global environment can be balanced with the development of the technology.

General Comments: We would like to speak out against a general ban on PFASs, which excludes the fluoroplastic PTFE from the restriction proposal. Specifically, we are talking about welding shoes made of PTFE, which is essential for the welding process while ensuring the required, qualitative standards.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The "welding" sector is not listed separately in the ANNEX XV Report. This is a necessary process for joining thermoplastics, which is used in various industries. Applications range from drinking water structures to sewers and storage tanks to landfill liners and special applications such as chemical storage tanks, etc. All these linings could not be produced without these welding shoes.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: FRANK GmbH distributes the welding shoes and is not a manufacturer. Accordingly, no data are available regarding PFAS emissions during production and the end-of-life stage. However, monomer units, for example, may be released during the production of the granules, but these are typically removed via degassing and a fume hood. Purification can take place in the downstream process by means of a gas scrubber. No PFASs emissions occur during use. Based on free-radical polymerization, macromolecules are produced which are highly resistant thanks to the strong bonding (due to the high electron negativity of fluorine). Under typical conditions of use, no degradation takes place that could lead to PFASs emissions.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Chemical recycling of the welding shoes is possible, as this is a single-grade semi-finished product. Emissions would be negligible.

6. Missing uses: As noted in the previous section "Section III. Non-confidential comments", welding is used as a joining/connection technique for various sectors. The areas of application range from drinking water structures, sewers and storage basins to landfill linings and special applications such as chemical storage tanks, etc. All these linings would not be producible without these welding shoes. A separate sector for this is not indicated. A possible designation could be as follows: Sector: Welding Subsector: Welding nozzle  a. No information is available on annual tonnages or emissions.  b. The essential functions guaranteed using PTFE welding shoes include the following: I. Excellent non-stick properties: This ensures a uniform weld while avoiding contamination. II. High temperature resistance: Since the welding process can only take place above the melting temperature of the respective polymer, temperatures of at least 220 °C are not unusual, depending on the material. The material must be able to withstand this continuous thermal stress over a longer period without, for example, undergoing degradation. III. Durability: Thanks to the strong bond between carbon and fluorine, a long service life can be guaranteed. Under the intended operating conditions of the polymer, there is no decomposition or release of PFAS. This also pleases the user, as it eliminates the need for frequent replacement of the welding shoes.  c. It is not possible to determine the exact number of companies affected. However, it is a fact that all companies involved in the extrusion welding business suffer from the effects of a general PFAS restriction.  d. Silicones can be an alternative material to produce welding shoes. However, substitution is accompanied by qualitative losses, since PTFE has properties that are in some cases unsurpassed. The non-stick properties mentioned in the previous subsection and the outstanding friction values cannot be achieved by silicones. PTFE is unsurpassed in these properties. Both properties are essential for ensuring high welding quality. Furthermore, the degree of wear and thus the wear is higher with silicones. The consideration regarding to an alternative material may also be to rely on metals. However, this also means that the non-stick and sliding properties of PTFE cannot be achieved. Furthermore, heat conduction is significantly more pronounced with metals, so that excessive heat input occurs in undesirable areas of the joining zone during the welding process.  e. This section is skipped, as it has already been dealt with in the previous section.  f. Same as section e.  g. The socio-economic influences/consequences in the event of a ban on PTFE for the application case studied will be outlined below: Price development: A ban on PTFE would lead to the search for alternative materials being pushed forward as quickly as possible. Due to the reduced supply, as a shortage takes place, this would result in higher prices for end customers, making the market steadily more expensive.   Qualitative impact:  For many years, PTFE has proven itself as a material for welding shoes due to its excellent properties in terms of anti-stick properties, sliding properties as well as heat resistance. Based on these properties, optimal welding can be ensured. With an alternative material, the welding quality could be impaired.  Jobs/market: The ban on PTFE would cause the entire sector to collapse, which would ultimately lead to the loss of numerous jobs. The development as well as the substitution of a new alternative material requires a long time, which especially the small and medium-sized companies cannot afford. Furthermore, if an alternative material were successfully developed, there would be disruptions in the supply chain. The prices of the "new" welding shoes would literally skyrocket.   Environment:  As described in advance, PTFE is a very resistant plastic thanks to the strong bond between fluorine as well as carbon atoms. As a result, the longevity of the product can be guaranteed. With alternative materials, the potential risk could be having to replace them more frequently. The frequent production of new plastics due to low durability is more harmful to the environment than the use of PTFE.

General Comments: We would like to state here our objection to the broad ban of all materials that have been grouped under the PFAS designation.  There are significant differences in how fluoropolymers are used, as well as significant differences in the potential environmental or human impact in comparison to other low molecular-weight PFAS materials such as Perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids and Perfluoro sulfonic acids (number of carbons: 4 – 14).  For example, PTFE is among the safest materials for use in medical implants (minimal foreign body response in comparison to other polymers such as polyester), no known harm for humans or the environment, yet are being lumped in the same classification as other materials which do have known human health concerns.  Banning fluoropolymers may lead to use of materials that are worse for the environment and society.  We should propose to give industry the proper health, safety and environmental tools and guidelines, then allow industry to consider the full impact and choose the best materials for a given application.

Finally, a ban of fluoropolymers will discourage or delay new product or technology innovations that don’t exist today, but would benefit from the unique properties of fluoropolymers.  This regulation is basically banning (or at a minimum heavily discouraging) future development with fluoropolymers, a material with unique properties and no known harm.  As stated above, we should use tools to know the environmental impact (CO2, longevity in use, impacts from RM sourcing, etc.) when selecting the best material for a product, but this type of blanket ban for future use is short-sighted and bad for society.

Content: Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We write this submission to the ECHA PFAS Public Consultation as co-Chairs of the Global Asthma Network (GAN) - a network established in 2012 to improve asthma care globally, with a focus on low- and middle income countries, through enhanced surveillance, research collaboration, capacity building and access to affordable, quality-assured, essential medicines - and on behalf of the GAN Steering Group.

Asthma is a major global health problem affecting approximately one in ten children and one in fifteen adults.1-4 It causes considerable morbidity and is a cause of avoidable death across the life course.4 Recent studies published by GAN and others demonstrate the ongoing burden of this disease and difficulties that children, adolescents, and adults with asthma face in accessing affordable asthma care.4-8 Limited access to affordable inhaled medicines including inhaled corticosteroids is a major contributor to the avoidable global morbidity and mortality due to asthma.

GAN is currently working to try to address the challenges around access to affordable asthma inhalers particularly in low- and middle-income countries. This is where the greatest burden of avoidable asthma morbidity and mortality is seen.

There are two main options for the delivery of inhaled asthma medicines - pressurised metered dose inhalers (pMDI) and dry powder inhalers (DPI) – and it is important that the inhaled rather than oral route is used to maximise local (lung) medication deposition and to minimise systemic effects. Both inhaler options are important as patients with asthma differ in their ability to use these devices. Although largely older children and adults can use DPIs, many are unable to use them, for example due to disabilities (people of all ages) and any reason for difficulty generating the sufficient inspiratory effort. This latter is THE reason younger children with asthma need to use a pMDI with spacer, as DPIs are ineffective – they can’t voluntarily breathe in rapidly enough.

Major progress in treating preschool wheeze and asthma in children under 6 has been due to the availability of the pMDI and spacer combination – introduced in the 1990s. Before this the only option for inhaled drug delivery in younger children was a compressor-driven nebuliser, an expensive delivery system and only available for people with ready access to electricity and the equipment. Many studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of the pMDI with spacer in treating all severities of asthma symptoms in the community. All asthma management guidelines and the Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) strategy make it clear that the DPI has no place under 6 years of age.9

Without access to pMDIs, these more vulnerable groups would be left without access to inhaler medication for asthma treatment, placing them at greater risk for asthma morbidity and mortality. Furthermore, patients with poorly controlled asthma have greater healthcare resource utilisation and increased need to use inhalers which further aggravates the financial and carbon-emissions costs.10

We recognise that there are important opportunities to address the environmental consequences associated with the treatment of patients with asthma noting that the most environmentally friendly patient with asthma is one with optimal control on the lowest possible individualised level of treatment. This is a topic we covered in our Global Asthma Report 2022, and an area that we plan greater advocacy efforts for over the coming years.4

We are in strong support of efforts to reduce the global warming and other environmental consequences associated with inhaled medicines for asthma, however, we appeal on behalf of children, adolescents, and adults with asthma around the world that these efforts take into consideration their needs for available, affordable, and usable inhalers including pMDIs to help keep them well. And in so doing, to keep global warming and other environmental consequences of asthma as low as possible.

We are concerned about the proposed ban on the use HFO1234ze(E), which we understand has near zero global warming potential (GWP) and which is in clinical development as a replacement for propellants with higher GWP currently authorised for use in pMDIs. Such a ban would limit options to just one other alternative (HFA-152a) which we understand is itself subject to restriction in the coming years due to its GWP. Taken together, these bans/restrictions pose a substantial risk that patients with asthma will have greatly limited or no access to pMDIs and that those more vulnerable patients living in low-resourced areas of the world (where most people with asthma live) would be particularly badly affected as prices are likely to rise for them. These inhaled medicines are on the World Health Organization (WHO) Essential Medicines List, a list of the medications considered to be most effective and safe to meet the most important needs in a health system. They are already of limited affordability in low- and middle-income countries and any increase in prices would put them further out of reach.5

We request therefore that the needs of children, adolescents and adults with asthma are taken into consideration through this consultation and that the case of HFO1234ze(E) specifically is examined from the perspective of; 1) the need to improve and save lives of people with asthma, 2) the opportunities to minimise the overall environmental consequences of asthma by maximising asthma control through access to affordable essential inhaled medicines for all and 3) to ensure continued access to inhalers for people living with asthma especially children and the elderly.

2. Introduction

The purpose of this report is to inform the national authorities, with regard to the EU-REACH PFAS restriction proposals and highlight that there is an existing and viable alternative to PTFE (and other fluoropolymers such as PCTFE, PVDF) in some critical applications and in particular, in cookware and sealing applications.  The existing and available alternative is PolyEtherEtherKetone Polymer, referred to as PEEK.

Regarding consumer cookware, the current restrictions proposal provides: “There is sufficiently strong evidence that technically and economically feasible alternatives are widely available on the market. These include ‘ceramic’coatings, anodised aluminium and stainless steel (recognising that the preferred option may vary across applications). Conclusion: High substitution potential [sufficiently strong evidence}”.  Thus, PEEK has not been mentioned in respect to consumer cookware.

As we further elaborate on below, PEEK has better mechanical properties than PTFE and it is also economically viable, refer to Section 7. This is demonstrated by the fact that there is an increasing number of cookware and sealing applications using PEEK on the EU market. PEEK is not hazardous, it is not a PBT/vPvB and it has additional environmental benefits compared to PTFE, such as recyclability and a better life cycle performance.






3. Chemical Identity of PEEK

PEEK like PTFE, is classified as a high-performance polymer. These materials exhibit high levels of performance across a range of properties, including physical, thermal, mechanical and chemical characteristics. PEEK belongs to a family of high-performance polymers called polyaryletherketones (PAEKs), which are also sometimes referred to as aromatic polyketones. Since the industrial commercialisation of PEEK polymer by ICI in the 1980s, PEEK has become the best-known and most widely-available polymer in the PAEK family.

PEEK is a homopolymer, made from a predominantly linear chain of a single repeat unit with a typical average molecular weight range of 70-120,000 g/mol. The PEEK molecule contains aryl groups connected via ether bonds (-O-) and carbonyl groups (-C=O-). The polymer is semi-crystalline. This crystallinity gives rise to properties such as creep and fatigue resistance, mechanical strength at elevated temperature and generally good chemical resistance.

The polymerisation of PEEK is a polycondensation reaction which takes place via a nucleophilic aromatic substitution mechanism. Two monomers, 4,4’-difluorobenzophenone and hydroquinone are reacted together in the presence of alkali metal carbonate(s).  The nucleophile is created in situ via deprotonation of the hydroquinone by the alkali metal carbonate. The reaction takes place in a polar aprotic solvent, diphenylsulphone, which keeps the growing PEEK polymer in solution with the monomers as the reaction proceeds.

PEEK is not classified as a PFAS, nor are PFAS or PFOA used in the polymerisation process to make PEEK.

7. Economic viability assessment

Historically, the fluoropolymers have often been favoured based on low costs. However, recently for PTFE there have been supply chain challenges post-Covid and particularly due to difficulties in obtaining a mineral used in their manufacture, called fluorspar, which is mined in Mongolia and China. Consequently, pricing for PTFE/PCTFE has fluctuated with price increases reflecting periods of high demand. When the total cost of solution is considered, then PEEK often becomes a lead candidate in material selection – since the increased performance, capability or duration of use, can off-set any initial higher cost of material.

In Cookware, there is potential to reduce overall system costs with PEEK as an alternative coating to PTFE.  Given the durability and abrasion properties highlighted above, a PEEK coating system may succeed with a thinner coating layer compared to PTFE, thus saving costs by using less material and reducing processing costs from building thickness with multiple coating layers. Even at the same coating thickness, less PEEK material is used due to the density of the polymers:  PEEK density 1.3 gcm-3 / PTFE density 2.16 gcm-3.


8. Hazard and Risk Assessment of PEEK

8.1 Hazard Assessment

As follows, from the biocompatibility data and food contact test data outlined in Section ‘Risk Assessment’ below, PEEK is not deemed to be toxic. PEEK is not classified under the CLP Regulation.

Persistent (P) and Bioaccumulation (‘B’) modeling of PEEK polymer using OECD QSAR ToolBox v.4.5 SP1

P and B modelling of a low molecular weight oligomer structure of PEEK (that consists of one unit of the benzophenone and two units of the benzoquinone) using the OECD QSAR ToolBox v.4.5 SP1 (latest version) has been evaluated. This oligomer provides a reasonable worst-case representative structure for estimating the potential for PEEK polymers to bioaccumulate. The results of the predictive modelling provide indication that PEEK is not likely to fulfill the criteria for “Bioaccumulative” (B) or “Very Bioaccumulative” (vB) defined in Annex XIII of the EU 1907/2006 REACH regulation. Regarding persistence, the model profile suggests that PEEK will fulfill the criteria for the “Very Persistent” (“vP”) designation (and therefore, also meet the criteria for “Persistent” (“P”) chemicals).

Thus, it is possible to conclude that the PEEK polymers will not be classified as either PBT (“Persistent, Bioaccumulative and Toxic”) or vPvB (“Very Persistent, Very Bioaccumulative”), because PEEK does not meet either B or vB criterion. In addition, it is not deemed to meet the T (toxic) criterion.

A Detailed Assessment of P and B properties of PEEK is included in the Annex to this paper.

In addition, the PEEK polymerization process does not intentionally add or use any PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) during the manufacturing process.

This is possible when the composition and structure of the polymer is known. In order to complete the assessment, find a reasonable representative structure of MW less than 1,000 and use this in the P2 modeling programs.”

• “Category 2: Polymers with high molecular weight (MWn more than 1,000) and large low molecular weight (LMW) material composition (≥25% with MW less than 1,000; more equal 10% with MW less than 500). These polymers can be assessed for environmental fate and toxicity as the polymer; however, oligomers may need to be assessed in addition to account for any increased toxicity due to these lower molecular weight compounds.”

• “Category 3: Polymers with high molecular weight (MWn more than1,000) and minimal LMW material (less than 25% with MW less than 1,000; less than 10% with MW less than 500). These are generally assessed solely as the polymer. However, as stated above, if a high percentage of unreacted monomers with potential health concerns are present, additional assessment may be required to address concerns for the monomer.”

As noted in ECETOC (2019) (https://www.ecetoc.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/10/ECETOC-TR133-1CF4Polymers.pdf):

“…specific properties of polymers also provide opportunities to streamline the RA process. For example, the molecular weight (Mw) distribution of a polymer product allows determining if internal bioavailability is likely. If the polymeric substance and/or polymer product are too large to pass through biological membranes, it is not meaningful to conduct higher-tier in vivo testing (while testing for local effects on e.g. skin or eyes may still be necessary). Similarly, for LMW components of the polymer product, diffusivity and migration potential from the polymer matrix determine external bioavailability e.g. at the eyes and skin, and internal (systemic) bioavailability (Step 7).”

It is possible that, once absorbed, the larger molecules may be more resistant to metabolism or biotransformation and elimination than the short PEEK. Thus, the potential for a PEEK to bioaccumulate may be positively correlated with the rate of its absorption from the gastrointestinal tract and positively correlated with the MW of the polymer molecules that may be absorbed to any significant extent.  However, in the absence of experimental data, the short PEEK profiled here provides a reasonable worst-case representative structure for estimating the potential for PEEK polymers to bioaccumulate.”

Furthermore, there is no reason to believe that longer PEEKs would be less persistent in the environment that the short PEEK profiled here

Combined Comments:
General Comments: We, Japanese four electric and electronic equipment industry (JP4EE, that is: JEITA (Japan Electronics and Information Technology Industries Association), CIAJ (Communications and Information Network Association of Japan), JBMIA (Japan Business Machine and Information System Industries Association) and JEMA (Japan Electrical Manufacturers’ Association)) have been vigorously committed complying with chemical regulations set by many countries. We have consistently supported the ambitious attempt of EU to reduce the risk caused from the hazardous substances and sincerely and diligently taken actual measures to meet the requirements under the EU chemical regulations such as REACH.
The electrical and electronic equipment (EEE) are manufactured via supply-chain extending over the world, and chemical legislations in the EU, one of the big markets in the world, would have big influence over the world. Under such situation, we believe it essential that proposed requirements would not hamper the smooth international circulation of the products including EEE and would be implementable as a law reasonably.
From the point of view above, we would be very happy if you consider the following opinions carefully.
Our general comments are attached to this input as JP4EE Annex_1-2_Japan 4EE Comments on restriction dossier on PFAS Part 2. We summarise our input here, but please see our JP4EE Annex_1-2 and other Annexes relating to each topic.

(1) The restriction should be considered based on the risk evaluation. Especially, it would be appropriate for ECHA to reconsider the proposed restriction for fluoropolymers, if ECHA cannot provide scientific justification for such measures.
We have consistently supported the ambitious attempt of EU to reduce the risk caused from the hazardous substances and sincerely and diligently taken actual measures to meet the requirements.  However, it is unfeasible to legislate the PFAS restrictions in this dossier as they stand, and we are deeply concerned that, if enforced, they will not only hollow out EU industry, but also make existing infrastructure unsustainable.

(a) About the risk assessment of the substances themselves.
PFAS are a huge group of substances that include many different substances with varying levels of risk. However, we believe that a blanket restriction on all PFAS may lack a risk-benefit balance and is not scientifically or socio-economically sound. As PFAS are not even SVHCs, it is impossible to provide accurate information on their use in articles within the input deadlines for dossiers, so we have to guess based on speculation (See (6) below for Explanation of Difficulties in Obtaining Information on Chemical Substances Contained in EEE.). Risk assessments based on such guesses may lack credibility.
Highly hazardous PFAS such as PFOS and PFOA are already restricted under REACH. If other PFAS for which a hazard classification has not yet been identified are to be restricted, a proper risk assessment should be conducted and the regulation should focus on applications with high exposure potential and well-established alternative technologies.　
Especially for the risk of fluoropolymers, Chemical industry explains as follows: Fluoropolymers do not pose a risk to human health or the environment as they are non-toxic, not bioavailable, non-water soluble, non-mobile and do not bio accumulate. If ECHA cannot provide more reasonable justification, it would be appropriate for ECHA to reconsider the proposed measures for fluoropolymers.

(b) About the assessment of the risk caused by the substances in the articles.
During the use of articles like EEE, it is presumed that an exposure amount of PFAS is generally negligibly low compared with the exposure of the PFAS as chemicals own. The blanket restriction on PFAS will affect many industries. We hope that you will consider our recommendations and information in the following sections and make a scientific and technical decision about the need for and feasibility of regulation.

(2) The possible risk caused from the articles should be properly considered, and convincing justification should be provided to show why the uniform restriction of PFAS in the articles is the most appropriate Union-wide measure to address the identified risks.
In the course of risk assessment, the fact that the end-of-life stage of EEE is managed according to WEEE Directive should be well-recognised and evaluated. We would like to ask the researchers and law-makers to evaluate the industry’s effort and diligence to meet the sector-specific EPR legislation properly.
We believe that emissions relating to EEE are quite well managed and are quite limited. If there are any concerns on the EOL stage of EEE, requirements for separate treatment under the recycling legislation such as Article 8 of WEEE or occupational safety regulations would be more effective ways to manage them with better cost-benefit than reflecting them to the threshold of PFAS under REACH which does not cover waste in principle.

(3) The regulation for the substances which are currently and widely used in the global supply-chain should be gradually introduced.
If the uniform restriction of PFAS in the articles is really planned by ECHA after the proper risk assessment, all the issues described in our following comments should be carefully considered for establishing the feasible and enforceable measures.
For complex articles such as electrical and electronic equipment (EEE), even a single substance survey will not work unless the entire global supply-chain responds appropriately to the survey. In such context, the collection of SVHC information is a well-established tool for understanding the presence of substances of concern, and through SVHC surveys, end-product manufacturers can make concrete estimates of the amount of the substance used and the potential impact if the substance is regulated.

However, as the restriction of PFAS is proposed not via the route via SVHC and authorization, end-product manufacturers are unable to estimate the exact amount of use or potential impact. Forcefully requesting information on the proposed restrictions in this situation would have little chance of gathering reliable data.

In addition, even if we had been able to gather more data, we consider that the separate date of the restriction of the articles should be set as a date later than that for chemicals. For EEE, complex articles, necessary transition period would be at least 5 years or more after the feasible substitutes are available as substances or mixtures. For EEE for industrial and social infrastructures would need longer time. From this perspective, it makes practical sense to establish an "Authorisation" step before restricting a substance. Please also see our Comment (5) below.

(4) About the appropriate thresholds and denominator for the articles: The management at the level of 1,000 ppm in the article would be practical and feasible.
We consider that the feasible denominator for the restriction of substances in the articles should be “article” and not be “homogeneous material”, especially for the proposed thresholds is at ppb order. What can be surely managed by the article manufacturers are threshold value on the order of 1,000 ppm.
Please see our Comment 4 in JP4EE Annex_1-2 attached to this input for the details.

(5) Necessity of sufficient time until the enforcement of the restriction. In the case of restricting substances contained in articles according to the REACH, we would like the Dossier Submitter to set sufficient time until the enforcement of the restriction. For the very small amount of PFAS in complicated EEE, it would take 48 months only to complete the investigation of containment.
We are continuously investigating and reviewing the PFAS applications in EEE after the submission of our 1st input, and we consider that most of the applications found out would need applicable derogations. The reasons why are that many of substitutable applications of PFAS have already been replaced in response to the recent trend of regulating fluoro-substances and PFAS materials with high-performance are relatively expensive.

However, it takes very long time to investigate the substances which have not become even SVHCs through the whole supply-chain and to check whether there are any other unknown applications using PFAS than those currently known or not. Based on the experience of compliance with the RoHS Directive, even in the case when replacement exists, a period of at least 4 years is necessary to implement substitution in the article, even if the restricted substances are clearly identifiable and the threshold value is on the order of 1,000 ppm. PFAS is very huge group of substances, we cannot even assume the necessary transitory period, but we estimate that at least 4 years would be needed only to complete the investigation of containment. Please see our Comment (6) for the difficulties in the investigation of such products.

In considering the above, the first four years had better to be set as a kind of “checking point” for the complex articles. If any application becomes known during this period and no feasible substitutions are found out at present, a mechanism to set a new derogation for such application should be established.

(6) Explanation of Difficulties in Obtaining Information on Chemical Substances Contained in EEE.
We would like to explain again about the difficulties in obtaining information on chemical substances contained in EEE, as the reason why that it takes long time to investigate very small amount of substance(s) in the complex articles, as described in the comment 5 above. This is because we feel it would be difficult to have the law-makers, who have mainly covered chemicals, understand truly how the material investigation in the complex article is difficult. Please see our Comment 5 in JP4EE Annex_1-2 attached to this input for the details.

(7) The period and the way of setting and maintaining a “derogation” should be further considered and established. The criteria for setting a derogation for the essential use for the complex articles should be similar to those of RoHS, and the date set for a derogation should not be an expiry date of the derogation but be a date for reviewing it.

(a) About the criteria for setting a derogation for the essential use for the complex articles.
As PFAS is the huge group of the industrial chemicals taking indispensable uses on complex articles at present, the conditions set in the Article 5(1)(a) of RoHS DIRECTIVE 2011/65/EU should be considered in determining appropriate derogations for the PFAS in the complex articles as follows:
(a) inclusion of materials and components of EEE for specific applications in the lists in Annexes III and IV (note: exempted applications from the restriction under RoHS), … where any of the following conditions is fulfilled:
‑ their elimination or substitution via design changes or materials and components which do not require any of the materials or substances listed in Annex II (note: restricted substances) is scientifically or technically impracticable,
‑ the reliability of substitutes is not ensured,
‑ the total negative environmental, health and consumer safety impacts caused by substitution are likely to outweigh the total environmental, health and consumer safety benefits thereof.

(b) About the procedures relating to applying, setting and reviewing a derogation.
Current PFAS dossier proposes three types of the duration, that is, five years, twelve years, and without limitation, for the listed derogations.
However, we feel uncertain whether the duration of five years plus transitory period would be feasible for the substitution. Such duration would be feasible when there are practical substitutes which can be used in the actual products with a certain reliability, but we have experienced many cases where some non-substitutable applications are inevitably found out in pushing forward the actual substitution. In addition, we also feel concern about the duration of twelve years plus transitory period, because there is no guarantee that some alternative technology is developed and that the substitution becomes practically feasible within such duration for PFAS applications relating to semi-conductors, for example.
The complex article manufacturers consider that the date set for a derogation should not be an expiry date of the derogation but be a date for reviewing it.
For your reference, under current RoHS Directive, all the exemptions (derogations) are checked by the industry every five years. Then, for the applications which have not become substitutable yet, the Commission technically reviews them in response to the requests for renewal of the exemption from the industry. However, the review and renewal of many exemptions at five years’ interval would not be practical, because the burden for such actions is so heavy not only for the industry but also for the authority. We consider twelve years’ interval would be practical and feasible to review the derogations, in considering the broad coverage of PFAS group, the time for the chemical industry to develop the new materials and wide-variety of the final applications in EEE.

(8) Necessary PFAS derogations in EEE. (Relating to the Questionnaire 6 to 8).
There are currently no feasible substitutes for PFAS which can attain the performance needed for EEE for the applications listed in Column E of our revised JP4EE Annex 3. We would like to request ECHA to set the derogations for them, as the feasibility in EEE becomes assessable only after the viable substitute materials are established.

The end-of-life stage of EEE is strictly and properly managed according to WEEE Directive. No e-wastes are dumped into environment without necessary care. Other complicated products such as vehicles are also managed under their sector-specific waste legislations. Such legislations apply extended producer responsibility (EPR) to the manufacturers, and the industry has taken big effort to meet the requirement with spending huge cost and resources. We would like to ask the researchers and law-makers to evaluate such effort and diligence properly. If there are concerns on the risk of substances and mixtures, it may be more effective to cover them by occupational safety standards or the like. We consider that the methods of management should be flexible if there are other effective options to be considered.   We believe that emissions relating to EEE are quite well managed and are quite limited. In the first place, at design and manufacturing stages, the use of PFAS in EEE is limited to the places where the functions of PFAS are really necessary, because PFAS materials are more expensive in exchange for high-performance than non-PFAS low-performance ones.  In addition, in use phase, EEE must keep their quality and performance in their durable life. The PFASs used in products have a very low vapour pressure and therefore do not volatilise at room temperature, and are designed to remain where they are applied to in order to provide the required function during the product life time, and to perform well under more severe conditions than the rated operating conditions. We therefore believe that it is unlikely that PFASs will be released into the atmosphere from the products during the use phase.  EEE will enter into end-of-life stage with keeping the above conditions, and the emission at EOL stage has been adequately and legally controlled because waste EEE is covered under EU recycling legislations such as WEEE Directive 2012/19/EU or Battery Directive 2006/66/EC. Therefore, we consider that PFAS contained in the products from the volume of PFAS use, 4,860t, for EEE (Electronics and semiconductor), as described in the baseline, would not be discarded to the environment. If there are any concerns on the EOL stage of EEE, requirements for separate treatment under the recycling legislation such as Article 8 of WEEE or occupational safety regulations would be more effective ways to manage them with better cost-benefit than reflecting them to the threshold of PFAS under REACH which does not cover waste in principle.

General Comments: We, NECA, Nippon Electric Control equipment industries Association, provide parts and products that assembled into various types of final products.
Therefore, quality requirement depends on requirement from customers that produce final products. Our main customers are: social infrastructures, industry automation, factory automation, process automation, semiconductor manufacturers, automotive industries etc that are required so much severe quality and safety.

Our parts and products are repeatably assembled into the social infrastructure and various types of industrial instruments of the EU and have a "critical" aspect that differs from general consumer products. Numerous alternative materials have been reported for PFASs that are being restricted, but unfortunately almost none are applicable for our product applications. As we have shown in the cases listed below, if our products cannot be put on the EU market at all, it could have a significant negative impact on the environment and human health in the EU.
In order to continue to achieve the protection of the environment and human health that EU REACH aims to achieve, we would like to submit this opinion in the hope that the content of this opinion will be considered.

Our customer’s products are “Specialist equipment”
They are highly specialized instruments used in laboratories, specialized institutions, industrial sites, and medical sites etc. Therefore, the user must undergo special training and education in order to use it safely and correctly. In this opinion we will refer to our product as "EEE specialist equipment" to distinguish it from general consumer products.
We would like to emphasize strongly that EEE specialist equipment plays a very important role in the social infrastructure. Below are some examples. We believe that you can understand that the nature is different from the product of "nice to have".

- Low volume of production, long-life, long supply chain
- The EEE specialist equipment is made in small numbers, is produced for long periods without modification or changes, has to be reliable and need long term test for reliability. The instruments would have been replaced typically after 7-10 years or more from the release of the products.  The supply chains are very long and take time to eliminate restricted substances from the supply chain.
- Table 5-4 Amount of EEE (tons) put on the EU market, per year and product category, “Support for the Evaluation of Directive 2011/65/EU on the restriction of the use of certain hazardous substances in electrical and electronic equipment Final Report” shows the percentage of category 8 and 9 products is only 3.5 of all amount of electric and electronic equipment(EEE) (tons) put on the EU market.
- Long development cycle
- Our customer’s products are required to be highly reliable because they are manufactured for a long period of time without modification. Along with this, long-term reliability tests are required. If there is a certification request, a longer period is required to obtain it.
- As a result, development cycles are longer compared to other consumer products

Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The EU has legislations requiring proper collection and disposal for all products, but adding an obligation to do something based on whether or not they contain PFAS will undoubtedly bring up management costs. Rather, it is more efficient to designate PFAS as SVHC, utilize the scheme that provides information to waste disposal companies, and technically standardize beneficial treatment methods when PFAS is contained. Waste EEE is controlled by WEEE Directive.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: Spare parts are necessary to guarantee the expected lifetime (more than 20 years) of EEE specialist equipment. Especially since EEE specialist equipment requires high performance and high reliability, we would like to emphasize that the same spare parts are required throughout the life of the product as when it was first evaluated. Without spare parts, waste minimization according to the principles of “Right to repair” and “Repair as produced” cannot be achieved.

If other non-PFAS materials are feasible for the requirements, we would choose them. The materials are carefully selected, and used only for inevitable uses.  Emissions of use of Specialist equipment are strictly controlled. Many measurement instruments are used for the control of emissions and occupational safety. The instruments cannot cause the leak or emission, otherwise they cannot be used for the control of emissions and occupational safety. EEE is controlled by WEEE Directive in the end of life. End of life shall be controlled by sector-specific legislations, such as, WEEE Directive.

If the alternatives are become available in the future, a long grace period is required until PFAS become restricted   The instruments are made in small numbers, are produced for long periods without modification or changes, have to be reliable and need long term test for reliability. The instruments would have been replaced typically after 7-10 years or more from the release of the products. The supply chains are very long and take time to eliminated restricted substances from the supply chain. If the electric and electronic equipment mentioned above cannot use PFAS anymore and PFASs are to be substituted, the long grace period is required in order to test the product to comply with the safety requirements defined with IEC and other safety standards, and obtain the re-certificates according to the requirements. An example of substitution process is below: - Testing of alternative materials: 1-2 years  - Reliability test: performance test of the product: 1-2 years - Device design change: 0.5-1 year - Change the production line /buy new production equipment: 1-2 years - Create Technical Documentation: 0.5 year - Training at the production site: a few months - Production management (information to customers): 0.5-1 year  - Third-party certification: 1 year without clinical trial    a few years or more with clinical trial or customer approvals  As mentioned above, even if an alternative is found, the replacement takes a long time. EEE specialist equipment therefore needs a longer transition period. If " Testing of alternative materials: 1-2 years " and " Reliability test: performance test of the product: 1-2 years " prove unusable to EEE specialist equipment, the process starts over. Then, it is not possible to predict when the replacement will be completed. It is necessary to check the status of alternative materials at regular intervals and extend the transition period if no alternative materials have been found.

General Comments: We, Shanghai Huayi 3F New Materials Co., Ltd., are a high-tech enterprise specializing in the R&D, production and sales of fluoropolymer (PTFE, PVDF, FKM, FEP, PFA, etc.), fluorine fine chemicals, fluorine refrigerants and other fluorine-containing chemicals. Our company's products are widely used in new energy, information technology, semiconductor, 5G, environment protection, data center and other fields. For many years, we have been adhering to the development concept of "GREEN CHEMICAL FOR BETTER LIFE". Regarding the proposed restriction of PFAS proposed by 5 European countries, we are shocked and unable to understand the proposed limit of more than 10,000 organic fluorine compounds (PFAS), we believe that this is a very excessive restriction measure.
Therefore, we intend to present the following views at the public consultation of ECHA.
1. The proposed restriction needs to consider the efforts of PFAS production enterprises to continuously reduce the environmental impact during the production process
In the proposed restriction, it is mentioned that“For the EU, this resulted in an estimated amount of 140 000 to 310 000 t of PFASs introduced to the market in 2020, which – due to the expected economic growth in several sectors – is expected to increase even further under the baseline scenario. Over a 30-year period the expected mean PFAS tonnage in the EEA is 49 million tonnes, leading to emissions of about 4.5 million tonnes during the manufacture and use phase when no action is taken.”。In recent years, we know that the development of science and technology has been continuously accelerating, and in the future speed of development can be even faster. Therefore, in five or ten years, due to the development of science and technology, we will have stronger control technology and capabilities for the production and usage of PFAS, which will go beyond our imagination. Perhaps some technology developments may be contributed by some PFAS products. We believe that these developments and changes also need to be considered in the Proposed Restriction. For example, in the past decade, advanced equipment, advanced control technology, advanced testing instrument technology, digitization and intelligent have gradually been applied to the production process of the fluorine chemical industry. Since 2020, our company has invested 300 to 500 million RMB annually in advanced production equipment, precision testing instruments, artificial intelligence, big data analysis, and other advanced technologies for factory intelligent optimization and transformation. We have gradually reduced the emissions of waste gas and wastewater from the production process and optimized the waste treatment, we are making our effort to reduce the impact on the environment during PFAS production. We also firmly believe that PFAS production enterprises will achieve near zero emissions in the production stage in the future.
Explanatory notes Column 1–Substance identity refers to“All PFASs subject to this restriction proposal are either persistent themselves or degrade to persistent PFASs, except for a few specific PFAS subgroups with combinations of key structural elements for which it can be expected that they will ultimately mineralize in the environment”. We do not agree with the viewpoint. During our production process, some PFAS waste gas and other fluorinated substances are generated, but after being incinerated in an incinerator above 1000 degrees Celsius, the generated waste gas is washed with water and alkali, and almost all fluorine elements are collected in the form of hydrofluoric acid or calcium fluoride, at last, there is no PFAS in the emission gas, only carbon dioxide, nitrogen, and oxygen. In addition, we believe that it is easier for companies and research institutions to develop mineralizing technologies for most PFAS than to find alternatives.

2. The proposed restriction will cause significant damage to the global semiconductor industry
We agree and support the “Financial Times” report on restrictive measures published on February 7, 2023, titled 'Chip suppliers warn on EU plan to bar for ever chemicals', which stated that Chip suppliers have warned that a European effort to impose a ban on “forever chemicals” will cause widespread disruption to already tight semiconductor supply chains. Our company's products (PFA and FFKM) are widely used in semiconductor manufacturing equipment and process. Through communication with a lot of our customers of PFA and FFKM, we unanimously believe that it will be difficult to find suitable alternatives to apply semiconductor manufacturing processes in the future. Therefore, if the proposed restriction is implemented, it will cause significant damage to the semiconductor industry.
We know that semiconductor integrated circuit chips are made from thousands of processes, and any minor defects caused by manufacturing equipment or processes can lead to the ultimate failure of chip manufacturing. During the wafer manufacturing process, strong acids, strong alkalis, corrosive electronic gases, and chemicals are formed and used, as well as local high-temperature and high-pressure. Metal ions, organic particles, etc. in the integrated circuit chip manufacturing production process have an impact on chip manufacturing, which is a PPB and PPT level control. Because of the high purity, super stability, as well as easy processing and shaping, PFA are widely used in semiconductor pipelines, valves, components, containers, equipmen. PFA has become an irreplaceable material in semiconductor processing. In addition, FFKM has excellent chemical resistance, high and low temperature resistance, and low precipitation, and it is also regarded as an indispensable sealing material in the semiconductor manufacturing industry.

3. According to the main hazardous concerns about PFAS in the proposed restriction, fluoropolymers should not be restricted.
According to proposed restriction Concern, “PFASs and their degradation products may persist in the environment longer than any other man-made chemical. Further supporting concerns are their bioaccumulation, mobility, long range transport potential (LRTP), accumulation in plants, global warming potential and (eco)toxicological effects”. Fluoropolymers can remain stable and difficult to degrade under conditions such as high temperature, ultraviolet radiation, chemical corrosion, biological degradation and other conditions. Fluoropolymers do not have mobility and long range transport potential, and will not be absorbed by the human body. Although fluoropolymers are PFAS, they are completely different from PFOA and PFOS from the above-mentioned hazardous concerns, fluoropolymers should not be combined with PFOA and PFOS for risk assessment.
Fluoropolymer has excellent physical and chemical characteristics such as chemical resistance, high and low temperature resistance, weather resistance, water resistance, lubricity, flame retardant, high dielectric and so on, and has been widely used in the field of energy (fuel cells, lithium-ion batteries, energy storage batteries, photovoltaic), electronic communication, 5G, semiconductor, environmental protection, non-stick cooking, medical, aerospace and other fields. It has become an indispensable and irreplaceable material in many fields. It should be noted that because of super stable physical and chemical properties, fluoropolymers are widely used in non-stick pans, semiconductor fields with strict conditions, medical fields (catheters, arterial stents, sterilized medical device packaging), etc., these applications also prove that people do not need to worry about the toxicological effects of fluoropolymers on organisms. In summary, we advocate the proposal to exempt fluoropolymers for unlimited time.

Org. name: Water Processing Division, Sumitomo Electric Industries, Ltd.
Combined Comments:
General Comments: We, Water Processing Division, Sumitomo Electric Industries, Ltd.  insist that fluorocarbon polymers including PTFE and PVDF, used as filtration media for solid-liquid separation, liquid-liquid separation and gas separation can be used without any safety and health concerns.  We insist, based on our argument, that fluorocarbon polymers should be exempted from PFAS restriction against deployment of fluorocarbon polymers like PTFE and PVDF to be PFAS restriction.

In particular, fluorocarbon polymers like PTFE do not show any environmental and toxicological concerns which are observed in low molecular weight PFAS such as PFOS, PFOA, PFNA, PFHxS and others.  Additionally fluorocarbon polymers satisfy standards of low concerned substances specified by OECD.

Filtration membranes which can remove solid particles from turbid water or liquids are essential products for human life.  Our argument is that substances, which affect health and environment, are the only chemicals to be restricted and not all chemicals of similar structures.

Filtration membrane products help
-improvement of public health for healthy and safe life
-improvement of environment and conservation of water body not only in EU but on our whole planet
-Stable supply of water to areas of water shortage

and contribute improvement of human life.  Furthermore, recently these filtration membrane products are expected to show outstanding performances in distillation as an alternative to current water or liquid treatment processes which consume a big volume of heat, and in carbon neutral technology to separate CO2.

At this moment, fluorocarbon polymers including PTFE and PVDF share more than 70% of the total polymeric membrane market which is a clear evidence that the market evaluates high performance of such products and relies on such products.

As a conclusion, inclusion of fluorocarbon polymers into PFAS restriction just because chemical structures belong to PFAS group, seriously affect improvement and conservation of water environment and water supply.

And we supports the statement made by FCJ on the issues of proposed restriction, as per attached on Section Ⅳ.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: [Products and Uses] Filtration membranes are used to remove turbidity from water or liquid which contain particles, and/or turbid substances like oil and to gain purified water or liquid.  The products contribute improvement and conservation of global water environment.  PFAS like PTFE and PVDF are used as raw materials for such filtration membranes.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Filtration membranes made of PTFE are described as follows.  [Manufacturing of PTFE-made filtration membranes]  In manufacturing processes of PTFE-made filtration membranes, raw material is PTFE powder.  PTFE is categorized as a low concern substance by OECD.  Such PTFE powders are manufactured by PTFE manufacturers which production processes do not contain any restricted substances like PFOA, PFOS.    Emissions from PTFE-made filtration membrane manufacturing processes are described as follows: (1) In any manufacturing processes, PTFE is not emitted or discharged outside of the factory or to atmosphere, or water.   (2) No evaporation occurs as no heating processes above PTFE decomposition temperature are applied. (3) Some chances exist that production workers may contact with PTFE resins, semi finished products and/or finished products but these workers always wear gloves due to quality control reasons and direct exposure to skins is always avoided.  Used gloves are incinerated by authorized waste management contractors. (4) No water cleaning is applied to production facilities including those having direct contacts with PTFE.  No PTFE is discharged to water body.  Clothes are used for cleaning when needed.  Used clothes are incinerated by authorized waste management contractors. (5) Loss of PTFE during manufacturing processes is delivered to authorized waste management contractors and disposed by one of the following manners. -Pulverization – incineration – landfill Heat during incineration is recovered (thermal recycling) Ashes of incineration are land filled in controlled landfill sites. -Reuse After pulverization, PTFE is used as additives for paints, lubricants, coating for traffic signs to prevent dirt and others. PTFE is inert, non toxic and not mobile.  It is not hazardous in landfill and reuse.    [Use of PTFE-made filtration membranes]  As PTFE is far inert, no dissolution of PTFE into permeate water is observed.  PTFE-made membranes are used also in potable water applications in water supplying facilities.  In case in Japan, only approved products by The Association of Membrane Separation Technology, Japan can be used.  The dissolution level permitted in this approval process is strictly controlled in a similar manner as that applied for equipment used for water supply in Japan (JWWA Z108, Notification No. 45 of the Japanese Ministry of Health, Labor, and Welfare).   In general, use of PTFE-made filtration membranes is limited to water applications and then is always below 100°C which is far below PTFE decomposition temperature of 500 – 600°C.  No decomposition of PTFE occurs during use.   Those are also used for filtration of solvents. As PTFE is resistant to almost all kinds of solvents used for industrial applications, dissolution of PTFE into solvents do not occur also in solvent filtration.

8. Other identified uses: (a) The annual tonnage and emissions (at sub-sector level) and type of PFAS associated with the relevant use  Relevant use : filtration membranes used for solid-liquid separation and those modules  For this relevant use -Name of PFAS:  PTFE, PVDF -Annual tonnage : Although no information of tonnage of PTFE- and PVDF-made filtration membranes is available, more than 70% of polymeric filtration membranes are made of PTFE and PVDF.  It is assumed that similar market share is also seen in EU and the share is considered to be very high.   Emissions;  No relevant information in EU is available.  (b) The key functionalities provided by PFAS for the relevant use  Filtration membranes used for liquid-solid separation have tiny pores in micron meter range and produce purified liquids out of liquids containing solid and/or turbid substances including oil by filtration of these substances.  Specifically, removal of turbidity from surface water like river water, production of safe drinking water by removing dirt and germs, purification of industrial and domestic wastewater for discharge to rivers and others or for reuse.  This contributes conservation of global water environment and protect water resources.  PTFE and PVDF filtration membranes offer high filtration performance to highly separate and remove turbidity as well as durability which keep high performance for a long period.  (c) The number of companies in the sector estimated to be affected by the restriction  Affected companies include (1) filtration membrane manufacturers which manufacturing plants locate in EU, (2) out-of-EU filtration membrane manufacturers which export products to EU, (3) any importers/exporters of such products.  However, no information is available of these companies.   In addition, any EU users who already use PFAS filtration membranes are affected.  Although no information on number of such users is available, quite a number of users are there along with increasing environment awareness and social mission for environment.  (d) The availability, technical and economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives for the relevant use, including information on the extent (in terms of market shares) to which alternative-based products are already offered on the EU market and whether any shortages in the supply of relevant alternatives are expected.  Market share of PFAS membranes among organic membranes are more than 70%.  The remaining can be considered as alternatives.  However, there is a background.  At the beginning of market growth, available materials for filtration membranes were non PFAS substances like PE or PP.  Along with recognition of membrane filtration technology as well as market growth, issues of non PFAS filtration membranes like inability of long-term operation due to breakage of fibers caused by poor tensile strength of fibers are raised.  The market has called for high durable and long-life products.  To meet such requirements, PFAS type membranes including PTFE- or PVDF- made membranes have been developed and have been launched into the market.  Therefore, use of non PFAS materials means that the market goes back to the era of the beginning when low-durable membranes are used.  Increase of water treatment costs by an increased frequencies of membrane replacements or increase of waste management costs caused by increase of wastes may deteriorate appetite of users to buy or to introduce membranes. It ultimately moves back water environment measures.  (e) For cases in which alternative are not yet available. ….  N.A.  (f) For cases in which substitution is technically and economically feasible but more time is required to substitute:  i) Interchangeability of products among filtration membrane manufacturers is low.  Furthermore, operation conditions of each product are different.  Therefore, modification of system and/or additional civil works may be needed if alternatives should be adopted by current PTFE, PVDF membrane users.  PTFE and PVDF filtration membranes are widely adopted by municipal water and wastewater facilities which means that additional social burden by taxpayers are raised.  If introducing alternatives to new facilities and not a retrofit to existing facilities, -Demerits shall be observed as described in article d if currently available non PFAS membranes. -Inorganic membranes can be substitutes but these are several times more expensive compared to organic membranes and, therefore, it is not socio economically feasible.  Only a limited supply of inorganic membranes is available due to smaller number of manufacturers.  -New materials, which are not yet available in the market, are not feasible as it takes time for development and commercialization as well as evaluation and approval for safety.  ii) The above mentioned modification of systems or civil works needs a year-level working period though it varies depending on size of such facilities.  If such works fall on a certain period, additional work period may be needed due to unavailability of construction working forces.  Even if only replacements of filtration membranes shall be done without any modifications and or civil works, it is also difficult for users as users should avoid intellectual properties for operational and maintenance conditions owned by existing companies,   iii) PFAS-made membranes are used for social infrastructures including water and wastewater networks, power plants, waste management plants, wastewater recycling facilities. General Comments: Weiss Technik GmbH manufactures environmental simulation systems in which products from all over the world are tested. These products can be environmentally friendly and sustainable alternatives to replace their current predecessors.

Environmental simulation systems are equipped with components which partly consist of materials or gases containing PFAS. In part, PFAS-containing refrigerants are used in environmental simulation systems, which benefit from their safety properties and cannot be replaced so easily.  These PFAS-containing refrigerants allow safe operation at test room temperatures as low as - 70 °C.  Developments have already taken place to replace high-GWP refrigerants with more environmentally friendly alternatives (e.g. R-469A, R-472B and R-473A for R-23).

If these refrigerants were now banned, the alternatives would be flammable refrigerants, which cannot be used due to their easy flammability.

Furthermore, some of the other components in environmental simulation systems would contain PFAS. For example, it is possible to produce PFAS-free compressors for PFAS-containing refrigerants, but it is not possible to produce PFAS-free compressors for natural refrigerants.

Also other components to withstand the different thermal loads within an environmental simulation system (e.g. + 180 °c to - 70 °C) are PFAS containing. For example, Teflon coatings and Teflon hoses are used where there are no alternatives. This ultimately means that sustainable and more environmentally friendly products can only be tested if components containing PFAS continue to be permitted for environmental simulation.

Furthermore, our facilities are used to perform a wide range of internationally prescribed tests. These include tests according to IEC-60068-FF and IEC-60721-FF, but also test standards that measure the VOC emissions of products. If components containing PFAS were to be banned for our application, there would no longer be any data on VOC emissions.  This data is used by you to seek a PFAS ban.

General Comments: When molding resin or elastomer, melted resin or elastomer is poured into a mold and molded. When the molded article is demolded from the mold, the molded article may not be smoothly removed from the mold and may break.
In many cases, the molded product can be smoothly peeled off by using various release agents.
However, when a release agent other than a fluorine-based compound is used, there are often cases where the resin adheres to the mold, making it impossible to release the mold.
Fluorinated compounds have the lowest surface tension among solid substances. As a result, it exhibits non-adhesiveness and is less likely to adhere to substances such as resins.
　When the fluorine-based compound is applied to the mold for molding, the surface of the mold becomes non-adhesive. As a result, the molded product can be smoothly removed from the mold.
Also, realistically speaking, fluorine-based compounds are much more expensive than other mold release agents, but the reason why fluorine-based compounds are still used is that they cannot be released from molds without fluorine-based compounds. This is a case where the quality is greatly deteriorated.
For these reasons, the fluorine compound is an essential use as a release agent.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Release agent for mold.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Since the discarded mold is finally melted at a high temperature, it is presumed that the fluorine compound adhering to the mold decomposes and becomes HF.
