General Comments: While the Annex XV report is very detailed and considers a wide range of uses and sectors, we are missing the consideration of general machinery products and in particular Compressor systems. Compressors are widely used for industrial production but also for other processes like water treatment or within the transportation sector. PTFA play an important role for reliable seals under difficult conditions, especially high temperatures. More details see §6 below.

6. Missing uses: Industrial machinery and especially Compressor Systems have obviously not been researched in the ANNEX XV Restriction Report and it is difficult to consider them as a sub-use of any of the researched uses. With currently about 12 Billion € sales volume in Germany alone, the compressor and pump industry is certainly not a niche market or niche use. Our comments below are related specifically to screw compressors, where PFAS are used in different areas. For other types of compressors there are similar uses and considereations From our assessment the seals are the most critical use and most difficult to substitute. (On coatings and lubricants there are already alternatives available).  Especially PTFE and FKM have become a standard for seal materials for e.g. lip seals and O-rings. It is possible to find substitutes for some of the uses quickly, where temperatures are limited. But especially on oil free compressors (which are advantageous in regards to environment to oil injected screw compressors) there are areas with temperatures above 150°C, where substitutes are not yet available. A full ban of PFAS will require more research with the suppliers, redesigns for alternative solutions and extensive qualification testing to ensure reliable function of the alternatives.  With the same arguments which are applied for the (potential) derogation for applications related to the safety of vehicles (see table 8 on page 101 of ANNEX XV Restriction report, Version 2) we advocate a 12-year derogation for Compressors to have sufficient transition period to find alternative solutions. As suppliers for seals are often identical to those suppling the automotive industry it will be a common approach to find and qualify alternatives. The requirements for seals used in compressors are very similar to those used in combustion engines (high temperatures, chemical stability). With the very long use period of compressors, which can be 20 years or longer, it is also important to have replacement parts available for repairs and maintenance. Otherwise entire compressor systems have to be taken out of service even in case of some very limited defects, which would have a big economic impact for the users but also in terms of sustainability. Only an unlimited derogation for replacement parts for compressors can avoid this very negative effect. The environmental impact will be extremely low, as the long-term availability of spare parts will trigger transition to PFAS-free materials and solutions wherever possible. (Besides the increasing cost disadvantage of e.g. PTFE and FKM.)

Combined Comments:
General Comments: While the following information pertains to us, we also support the submissions made by Flexible Packaging Europe (FPE).

1. Widening the definition of PFAS restrictions to include all fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers has placed vented packages under this restriction.
2. The introduction of the use of expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) into packages has allowed for significant advances in safe and effective packaging across multiple industries – Food, Life Sciences, Personal Care, Agrochemicals, Cleaning & Sanitation. The advancements of ePTFE to provide safe and effective packages has supported industry efforts to increase the efficacy of products, increase the concentration of active ingredients (to reduce transportation waste), and to reduce the weight and the complexity of plastic containers.
3. The specific characteristics of ePTFE are unmatched by any alternates available today. Removing ePTFE as a functional component to packaging will eliminate the benefits ePTFE provides – lighter weight packages, higher concentration of active ingredients, more effective products, and the use of less complicated packaging.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: a. Other packaging applications i. The use of ePTFE in packages to allow for pressure equalization (package venting). ii. The use of ePTFE membranes in packaging allows for the safe equalization of pressure inside a package. A package can require venting for several reasons – the degradation of high concentrations of ingredients (bleach and hydrogen peroxide) that off-gas and build pressure inside of packages; the expansion and contraction of containers due to elevation changes; the expansion and contraction of containers due to temperature changes; the contraction of containers due to oxygen scavenging; the contraction of packages due to product migration. iii. Higher concentrations of bleach and hydrogen peroxide have been introduced to plastic packages over the last 10-15 years. The use of venting has allowed these packages to remain safe without the risks associated of product off-gassing. Off-gassing products can cause packages to expand (bloat) to the point of tipping and/or rupture. Venting has allowed these packages to remain light (thin-walled bottles). The increase in concentrations of active ingredients have allowed for a reduction in shipping excess water in solutions and have allowed for more effective products for cleaning and sanitation especially in food service and medical environments. The elimination of ePTFE to vent these packages will put these products at risk. iv. Over the last 4 years 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2023 to date we have processed over 2,000,000,000 package vents. v. We have spent 3 years in research with membrane manufacturers and we have not found effective alternatives. Some materials are available that can provide package venting of dry goods, but nothing has been identified for liquid products, especially low surface tension liquid products. vi. Since there are no current effective alternatives to for safe and effective vented packages a 12-year derogation will be required to allow time to identify alternatives to ePTFE for use in package venting. b. Diagnostic laboratory testing i. The use of ePTFE in life sciences laboratory products for Bioprocessing and Cell Culture. ii. The use of a cap, vented with ePTFE, on a cell culture flask allows sterile air into the flask without having to open the cap which can contaminate the flask. iii. Over the last 4 years 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2023 to date we have processed over 110,800,000 laboratory vents. iv. Currently we have not identified effective alternatives to ePTFE that allow for the required sterile air flow. v. The stated 12-year derogation will be necessary to identify alternatives. c. Membranes used for venting of medical devices i. The use of ePTFE in medical devices allows for sterile venting. ii. The use of ePTFE membranes for medical devices such as insufflation filters, blood/liquid collection canisters, and protecting vacuum pumps is necessary to assure that the air passing through the filter remains sterile and eliminates prevents the fouling of medical air and vacuum systems.  iii. Over the last 4 years 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2023 to date we have processed over 3,300,000 package vents. iv. The stated 12-year derogation will be necessary to identify alternatives.

6. Missing uses: e. We have spent 3 years in research with membrane manufacturers and we have not found effective alternatives. Some materials are available that can provide package venting of dry goods, but nothing has been identified for liquid products, especially low surface tension liquid products in packaging applications. Currently we have not identified effective alternatives to ePTFE that allow for the required sterile air flow in diagnostic laboratory testing and venting of medical devices. The stated 12-year derogation will be necessary to identify alternatives.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: While we see the need to regulate critical substances, such as some low molecular weight PFAS that are known or likely to be harmful, we believe that a broad and undifferentiated approach as used in the current proposal is not appropriate. In particular, the inclusion of fluoropolymers that are considered polymers of low concern (PLC) according to the OECD definition [2,3] cannot be understood. They are not harmful to humans or nature and are even used as medical implants.

Fluoropolymers are very important materials for plain bearing and other sliding element applications. We use PTFE, PVDF, PFA, FEP and ETFE. Fluoropolymers (especially PTFE) are used in these cases because they offer unique properties. They show low friction, excellent damping (low stiffness) and very good thermal and chemical stability. There are no non-fluorinated materials that combine all these properties. Especially PTFE, which has the lowest friction of all solid materials [4] plays the most important role for plain bearings. Even though there are plenty of different materials for plain bearings, applications using PTFE-based materials are not replaceable (see attachment, section 6).

In 2022 our total consumption of fluoropolymers sums up to about 60 tons. Thereof, PTFE has the largest share with 45 tons. Using these fluoropolymers, over 240 million parts are produced by us yearly, supplying various applications and industries. Our market share in Europe is approx. 30% for these high-performance products. The market for simple PTFE bearings is even several times larger (see attachment, section 4).

About 80% of the fluoropolymers containing products produced by KS Gleitlager are for the in-use-phase in the transportation (automotive) sector. Energy consumption and related emission of CO2 of this sector is highly relevant and it is known that friction itself is responsible for one third [5,6] of this energy consumption. Therefore, bearings with low friction play an important role in making this sector more energy efficient and thereby reducing the carbon footprint.

In addition, machines and systems in other industrial sectors are also supplied. While it is difficult to assign every application to specific sectors, it is clear, that a replacement in all these applications would have an immense impact also on many industries. One example is the control and regulation technology (e. g. solenoid valves), where stick-slip-free sliding elements are very important. These are used, for example, in respirators, the importance of which became clear during the Corona pandemic. In addition, the chip industry also requires dry-running stick-slip-free sliding guides in wafer cutting systems. Of course, also the low friction which is important for energy efficiency is an important criterion for many applications. For example, the efficiency of a radial piston motor (e. g. used in drives for construction machinery or in the food industry), which is currently around 80%, can be estimated at only 60% using bearings with standard polymers; similar considerations can be made for hydraulic pumps, which are used in heat pumps.

Apart from these enormous effects on energy consumption and related reduction of the carbon footprint, maintenance-free bearings, and the possibility to use these bearings without lubrication (oil or grease) causes further positive ecological and economical effects. In case of maintenance-free bearings, the after-market expenditures can be omitted.

While a ban of fluoropolymers would of course also have an impact on sales and workers at our company, it would have an immense impact on the entire economy. Even though plain bearings are inconspicuous components, fluoropolymer-based plain bearings are key parts in many applications, as we have shown.

We therefore request a general exemption of fluoropolymers for plain bearing applications. A sector-by-sector approach is impossible due to the complex value chains.

More details, also on the above stated comments can be found in the attached document.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Our comment applies mainly to the sectors transportation, medical devices, energy sector, construction products and defence technology.  Our products are also used in other sectors, like machinery and industrial applications. However, a clear assignment to specific sectors and uses is not always possible for us. Further information can be found in the attachment (section 3).

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Estimations on emissions during the different stages of the life-cycle result overall in low and uncritical emissions.  Further information can be found in the attachment (section 5).

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Plain bearings are part of metallic constructions and are following the metallic recycling route. At the applied conditions, fluoropolymers should be completely mineralized to non-toxic substances.  Further information can be found in the attachment (section 5.3).

5. Proposed derogations: Assignment to sectors and sub-uses as defined by the restriction proposal is not trivial and not always possible in our case. Based on the unique properties presented and the important benefits for a wide range of applications, we request a general exemption for fluoropolymers for sliding element applications.  Further information can be found in the attachment.

6. Missing uses: Our products are widely used in different applications, which are obviously not completely considered in the current proposal. However, an assignment to sectors and specific sub-uses and a respective evaluation is hardly manageable. Based on the unique properties presented and the important benefits for a wide range of applications, we request a general exemption for fluoropolymers for sliding element applications.  Further information can be found in the attachment.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Based on the unique properties presented and the important benefits for a wide range of applications, we request a general exemption for fluoropolymers for sliding element applications.  Further information can be found in the attachment.

8. Other identified uses: Our products are widely used in different applications, which are obviously not completely considered in the current proposal. However, an assignment to sectors and specific sub-uses and respective evaluation is hardly manageable. Based on the unique properties presented and the important benefits for a wide range of applications, we request a general exemption for fluoropolymers for sliding element applications. General Comments: While we understand the concern regarding the so called 'forever chemicals', we would consider positive to determine which chemicals included in PFAS are considered substances of high concern.

We are a manufacturer of plastic plated products and a small amount of our processes have chemicals with PFAS, such as mist suppressants for chromic acid etching processes and preliminary surface treatment. Trials were performed in the past using PFAS free chemicals for preliminary surface treatment and their performance was not up to par. As for chromic acid etching, at the moment there is not a single PFAS free mist suppressant in the market. Without the necessary chemicals, our defect rates would increase noticeably, thus causing an considerable economic impact in our company and other enterprises in the same industry. It has to be considered too that defective products can be recycled at a certain extent. However, non-recyclable materials are a burden to the environment. Producing massive amounts of waste in order to get rid of a minimum amount of chemicals is not likely to solve the environmental issue but to worsen it.

It is for the previously stated reasons that we would request a thorough description of those chemicals in PFAS whose usage should be restricted and not to apply the restriction generally until there are feasible solutions. We agree progress and a better environment are for the better but not at just any cost.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Who is ABB Robotics?
ABB is a global technology leader in electrification, robotics, automation, and motion. With a history of innovation stretching back over 130 years, ABB’s success is driven by about 105,000 talented employees in over 100 countries, more than a third of which are based in Europe. One of the 4 main divisions is ABB Robotics & Discrete Automation.

ABB Robotics is a pioneer in robotics, machine automation and digital services, providing innovative solutions for a diverse range of industries, for example automotive, electronics, logistics, life science & healthcare and food & beverages. More information can be found in Figure 1 in the attachment. As one of the world’s leading robotics and machine automation suppliers, we have shipped over 500,000 robot solutions. ABB Robotics provides services to the EU, and its products are produced both inside and outside the EU. Factories and developmental centres for a wide range of products are located in Europe, including in Sweden, Germany, Norway and the Czech Republic with a total of several thousand employees. In addition to the direct jobs created by ABB, there are also a number of indirect jobs established as a result of the wide supplier base in the EU which provides ABB Robotics with components. ABB Robotics plans to expand this number alongside the growth of the robotics market in the coming years.

ABB Robotics helps our customers of all sizes to increase productivity, flexibility and simplicity and to improve output quality.  We aim to make robotics as familiar and useful in the workplace as a laptop or smartphone is today. The product portfolio of ABB Robotics can help customers with welding & cutting, handling & machining, press automation, packaging, assembly & testing, and producing automotive products, as can be seen below. We enable our customers to see the possibilities and unlock new opportunities with flexible automation.

Why is ABB contributing to the ECHA consultation on PFAS
ABB Robotics supports the dossier submitters and ECHAS proposed restrictions on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). We acknowledge the concerns surrounding the high persistence, mobility, bioaccumulation potential, long-distance transport potential, global warming potential, and ecotoxicity of certain PFAS substances and the various environmental and health issues and risks they pose to society.

Reassessing the crucial part PFAS has in our products, ABB Robotics would be strongly affected by the proposed restriction and is therefore contributing to the ECHA consultation of the restriction.
We have analyzed our products and prepared a few contributions where we see the need for specific exemptions from the restriction, to be able to find long term sustainable solutions and the continuity of providing reliable products for essential industries. We ask the ECHA technical experts to review these contributions carefully and consider them in the preparation of the final regulation, especially regarding the exemptions we are asking for.
We recommend that ECHA creates a new main application titled “Robotics” as a new sector (Main applications in Table 2 in Annex XV Report). This is because robots are important for shaping up the future of human civilization and because several sub-uses have been identified on PFAS that are critical to Robotic industry. We therefore propose to add the following sub-uses under Robotics sector: Cable & Harness, Seals in Gears & Motors and Food and Medical Robots. Overall, we request 3 exemptions, one for Cable & Harness, the second for Seals in Gears & Motors and finally for Fluoropolymers Seals in robots in the medical & food industry. We also ask that you consider the spare parts of these components to be included in the exemption as well.

Executive summary:
Fluoropolymers including fluoroelastomers are vital high-engineering materials that improve the performance of industrial robots/manipulators and enhance the durability of our components. Removing fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers from our products will result in poor-performing robots with much-reduced longevity and an increased cost to customers. One use of fluoropolymers is in seals which enables robots to work in harsh applications that require extreme chemical compatibility and various types of resistance. For example, Food and Medical production is subjected to strict hygiene requirements and daily washdown with high pressure water and strong detergents. Therefore, the robots need to be able to meet these strict requirements as well, which is only possible with fluoropolymers.
We request that fluoropolymers seals used in robots for Food and Medical applications be removed from the scope of the Restriction.
Alternative risk management options such as controlling emissions during the manufacturing, use and end-of-life phase should be implemented as an alternative to the restriction on fluoropolymers which includes fluoroelastomers.
To promote sustainability and cost-effectiveness, we also request the same exception to the restriction on placing spare, wear, and used parts on the market. We request that this exemption, both for new parts and spare, wear and used parts should be valid for an unlimited time, and then ECHA should review the exemption again in 5 years.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: An appropriate Use sector or sub-use in Table 2/Table 9 for this contribution was not found. Therefore, we recommend that ECHA creates a new main application titled “Robotics” as a new sector (Main applications in Table 2). This is because robots are important for shaping the future of human civilization and because several sub-uses have been identified as containing PFAS that are critical to the Robotic industry. We then propose to add the following sub-uses under Robotics: Cable & Harness, Seals in Robotic Gears & Motors, Food and Medical Robots. Under the sector "Robotics", this specific contribution is a sub-use of "Fluoropolymer seals used on robots for Food and Medical applications".  Additionally, this specific contribution could also apply to the existing Sector of "Food contact materials and packaging" in Table 2, but as a new sub-use "fluoropolymer seals used on robots for food contact applications". This specific contribution can also be seen as a special case in "Industrial food and feed production" listed in Table 8.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: According to the ACEA (the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association) consultation, the European fluoropolymer industry is one of the best-controlled industries from an environmental standpoint. The manufacturing phase has the greatest risk of emissions during its lifetime, as PFAS monomers and processing aids are required for fluoropolymer and fluoroelastomer production. Non-PFAS processing aids are becoming available, according to manufacturers, but final polymer properties can be adversely impacted.  During robot manufacturing/assembly, fluoropolymer seals will not emit any PFAS substances, nor are they necessary for assembling the robot. During the robot application stage in the Food and Medical industry, dynamic fluoropolymer seals will wear down. The PFAS debris will be handled by a hygienic risk management system from the food/pharmaceutical producers, for example by being cleaned away by a daily cleaning regime.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The disposal of fluoropolymers under the conditions common in European waste incineration plants does not produce PFAS of concern:   Studies (for example, Gehrmann, H.-J. et al., Pilot-Scale Fluoropolymer Incineration Study, 2003) confirm that fluoropolymers at their end of life when incinerated under representative European municipal incinerators conditions do not generate any measurable levels of PFAS emissions and therefore pose no risk to human health and the environment.   When fluoropolymers are incinerated, the resulting fluorine compounds are decomposed and the evolving hydrogen fluoride gas is separated in gas scrubbers; so no PFAS are released into the environment.   These fluoropolymers have a carbon polymer backbone with fluorine atoms attached directly to the carbon backbone. These polymers do not lead to the formation of long-chain PFAS or PFAC as a result of degradation. (ref. Bougas, K., et al., Final report for the DG Environment, European Commission, Brussels, https://data.europa.eu/doi/10.2779/890644, 2020)   Further work is needed though to understand the full impact of fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers. A comprehensive scientific risk assessment should be conducted to identify if restricted substances within specific groups have comparable hazardous characteristics. For example, within the fluoropolymer's family, do they all have the same environmental and health impacts? Or are some of them worse, and others better? This approach will allow fluoropolymers which do not pose a significant risk to human health or the environment to be used as seals and packaging materials in the food industry.  Ref "EHEDG position paper on the potential ban of PFAS on food contact surfaces in Food manufacturing/processing equipment"

6. Missing uses: As previously stated in Question 1, we have proposed “Robotics” as a new main application and "Fluoropolymer seals used on robots for Food and Medical application" has been identified as a missing sub-use that has not been covered in detail in the original Annex XV restriction report.  a. Industrial robots have just started to be deployed in Food and Medical applications where there is a hygienic concern. This is due to a lack of labour in general in Food and Medical applications that has been intensified with the COVID-19 pandemic. The tonnage today is still quite low (roughly 500kg/year globally), but it’s expected that it will grow 10-20% annually according to CGAR.  b.Industrial robots/manipulators have been traditionally deployed mainly in the Automotive and Electronic industries. Today, they are more needed in Food and Medical applications due to a lack of labour, harsh environments, and automation.     The food industry is large and complex, encapsulating every process involved in supplying food to the world’s population. This includes production, processing, preservation, packaging, distribution, certification, and other activities. With the many diverse elements involved in such large-scale operations, most tasks in the food industry are highly intensive in terms of labour and capital. From rising labour costs and supply chain disruptions to food and workplace safety, the number of problems plaguing the food industry only seems to multiply. With an expected compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 12.80%, between 2022-2028, robotic technologies are rapidly revolutionizing the global food industry. Riding on the wave of demand created during the pandemic, many areas of the food industry are now competing to integrate AI and automation technology into their operations.   Many segments in the Food and Medical industry (for example protein industry that suffers most from lack of labor after COVID) have strict hygiene requirements and must wash down equipment on a daily basis using high-pressure water and strong detergents. The use of chemical agents and cleaning regimes is totally dependent on food producers. They typically use alkaline (pH can be 10), chlorine, and strong acid (pH can be 1), all of which are highly corrosive towards metals and polymers. Figure 2 shows some equipment in a food-processing plant. Figure 3 shows some examples of corroded robot and motor under such environments if they are not properly designed. Both of these can be found in the non-confidential attachment.  The most important key enabler for industrial robots to work in such harsh environments is the use of fluoropolymer seals. These robots with fluoropolymer seals can be used in industrial robots in hygienic environments.  Functional uses of Fluoropolymer seals  There are two types of fluoropolymer seals which are required for hygienic purposes.  1. Fluoroplastic seals for dynamic robot joint Fluoroplastic seals serve several key functions for dynamic robot joint:   • One important function of the dynamic seal is to protect the robot joints against the high-pressure water jet, such as an IP69K water ingression level, which is common to clean the robot. The seal protects the key components such as the motor or gearbox from corrosion.   • Resistant/compatible with harsh detergents including strong acid, strong alkaline, and disinfectants. Which needs to be used in a hygienic environment. Fluoropolymer is excellent here and beats all other polymer materials.  • In addition to being corrosion-resistant, it also needs to have low friction. In hygienic environments, it is often necessary to run the robot without any lubrication on the joints. This means that there needs to be very small friction even with a harsh robotic motion and torsional load. PTFE is currently the best material for this because it has a lower friction coefficient than any other plastic material.   2. Fluoroelastomer seals for static robot joint Fluoroelastomer seals serve several key functions for static robot joints:  • Sealing the metal-to-metal joint against high-pressure waterjet, protecting the key components such as the motor and gearbox inside the robots from corrosion. Compared to plastic materials, elastomer materials are vulnerable to hydro erosion from high-pressure waterjet. Here fluoroelastomer has much better resistance compared to other elastomer materials.   • Resistant/compatible with harsh detergents including strong acid, strong alkaline, and disinfectants which need to be used in a hygienic environment. Fluoropolymer is excellent here and beats all other polymer materials because other plastic materials will corrode or age much faster, resulting in a very poor service lifetime.   • No gap with metal counterpart, allowing easy to clean, meeting design guideline of EHEDG (European Hygienic Engineering and Design Group)   Based on these functions which are needed for robots to be able to be deployed in Food and Medical applications, there is no alternative seal material other than fluoropolymer to the knowledge of the author. The current Restriction proposal (RO2) listed a 6.5 years derogation after EiF for food contact materials (FCM) for the purpose of industrial and professional food and feed production (page 7 in EHHA restriction report). Industrial robots for this application could be considered in direct contact with food or indirect contact with food (splash zone). But, the timescale is woefully insufficient to try to find alternative materials, since nothing currently exists and suppliers do not have a time estimate of when an alternative will become available. Therefore, we request an unlimited time exemption from the restriction and then request ECHA to review the exemption again in 5 years. During that time, ABB Robotics will continue to push suppliers to find equivalent replacement materials.   c. More robot manufacturers enter this market which has the potential to become the biggest market for industrial robots. The estimated number of companies is between 20-100 by the author.  d. It has been difficult with the limited time to research the availability, technical and economic feasibility, hazards and risks of alternatives for the relevant use of PFAS in Sealings within Robotics and Automation.  No alternative materials/technology are available for this specific use. The key requirements have already been discussed in 6b, which also discusses the lack of other materials  e.  ABB Robotics relies on the suppliers' expertise to propose alternative materials, since this is not knowledge that we possess in-house, in addition to the testing from the suppliers' side to find the best solution. Before ECHA’s ban in February 2023, there was a lack of awareness of PFAS and the potential ban, which means it was not considered as part of the design criteria in the material selection process. Thus, the use of fluoropolymers has never been doubted. Based on this, no alternative materials have been evaluated, so it is impossible to confidently state any substitutes without testing, both at our supplier's site and in ABB Robotics products.  The next step would be for seal suppliers to find/develop alternative materials that are chemically resistant to different types of detergents used in Food and Medical applications. After that, the alternative materials need to be sent to a 3rd party lab to check compliance as food contact materials for different regions/authorities (FDA, EC, GB, NSF, 3A, USP, etc.). This process could potentially take 2-3 years.  After seal suppliers are confident in the chemistry and compliance of alternative materials, seal prototypes need to be manufactured and tested on robots. Typically, it will take 2 years to validate seals on specific robot variants. Normally it will take a few seal design iterations before it can be mechanically validated on robots.   Considering the tough requirements both mechanically (robotic motion) and chemically (against harsh detergents in Food and Medical applications), the likelihood of successful development of seals based on alternative materials is not high. It is impossible to give a plausible estimation of how many years it could take to come up with alternative seal materials/technology for this specific application.    g.The Food and Medical industry currently suffers from a lack of labor due to the harsh environment, such as the high hygienic requirements, high injury risk, highly repetitive workload, etc.). This situation is only getting worse during and after the COVID pandemic. Fluoropolymer seals are the KEY to enable industrial robots to work in that kind of harsh environment. Without fluoropolymer seals, industrial robots will not be able to be hygienic enough (easy to clean) and will corrode very fast (in ~2 months).    The high price of PFAS, especially the fluoropolymer seals used on robots for Food and Medical applications, ensures their limited use, indicating that they are employed only when necessary. It is essential to thoroughly evaluate the availability of equivalent alternatives before imposing a complete ban, as these unique materials contribute to the safety, resource efficiency, and longevity of industrial plants.   What we propose as derogation/exemption: Fluoropolymers including fluoroelastomers are vital high-engineering materials that improve the performance of industrial robots/manipulators and enhance the durability of our components. Removing fluoropolymers and fluoroelastomers from our products will result in poor-performing robots with much-reduced longevity and an increased cost to customers. One use of fluoropolymers is in seals which enables robots to work in harsh applications that require extreme chemical compatibility and various types of resistance. For example, Food and Medical production is subjected to strict hygiene requirements and daily washdown with high-pressure water and strong detergents. Therefore, the robots need to be able to meet these strict requirements as well, which is only possible with fluoropolymers.   We request that fluoropolymers seals used in robots for Food and Medical applications be removed from the scope of the Restriction.  Alternative risk management options such as controlling emissions during the manufacturing, use and end-of-life phases should be implemented as an alternative to the restriction on fluoropolymers which includes fluoroelastomers. To promote sustainability and cost-effectiveness, we also request exceptions to the restriction of placing spare, wear, and used parts on the market. ABB Robotics has a large business of repairing, updating and refurbishing our products. It’s estimated that ABB refurbishes around 5% of ABB robots in the field, and then many 3rd parties also purchase ABB robots to repair and refurbish as well.  There are also ABB robots which have been used for over 25 years. All spare parts use the same materials as newly sold products, which means that if there are no alternative materials for newly developed parts, there will be the same for the spare parts.  To promote sustainability and cost-effectiveness, we also request the same exception to the restriction on placing spare, wear, and used parts on the market. We request that this exemption, both for new parts and spare, wear and used parts should be valid for an unlimited time, and then ECHA should review the exemption again in 5 years.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: This specific sub-use can also be seen as a special case in "Industrial food and feed production" listed in Table 8 where 6.5 years grace period has been proposed. However, this is not sufficient for the industry to develop commonly usable safe alternatives.  We request that fluoropolymers seals used on robots for Food and Medical applications are removed from the scope of the Restriction, with the same reasoning listed in question 6.

General Comments: Why Fluoropolymers for power plants and waste incineration?

The combustion of wastes of diverging qualities or fossil energy sources leads to the formation of gases with a high content of sulfur, chlorine and fluorine compounds. When the dewpoint of these gases is underrun in heat exchangers, housings and ducts in order to re-cycle more heat out of the combustion gases, this leads to a heavy condensation of hydrochloric, hydrofluoric and sulfuric acid on the involved equipment and in consequence to one of the strongest types of corrosion known, called dewpoint corrosion. The latter even corrodes the most resistant steel grades and thus requires other technical solutions. A lining of the condensing heat-exchangers, their housings and the flue gas ducts with the fully-fluorinated thermoplastic PFA (tetrafluoroethylene-perfluoroalkylvinylether) renders possible a service of the heat exchangers under condensing conditions and consequently increases the total power production efficiency of the waste-incineration plant, even having a positive environmental effect due to a positive influence on the overall energy mix. The suitability of this technical principle had already been demonstrated in multiple successful examples in fossil- and waste-fired power plants.

In our view, the Annex XV restriction report does not cover relevant and essential uses of fluoropolymers in the critical sector “chemical industry”: Semi finished products like sheets, welding rods or caps are mechanically solid, chemically resistant and stable even in harsh and corrosive environments

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The specific Sector “PFA products for Heat Exchangers and ducts of waste incineration and fossil power plants.” is not listed in Annex XV.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: For the specific use-case mainly PFA products are used. PFA products like foils (thickness of 1.5 mm and 2.3 mm), pipes (from 20 mm up to 110 mm), welding rods and PFA covering caps etc. are solid products.  Today most PFA raw materials are produced using fluorinated polymerization aids that may remain in extremely small amounts (ppm) within the PFA and have the potential to leach-out during the use phase. To reduce the risk of small molecular PFAS to be emitted from fluoropolymers, it is desirable to produce them without fluorinated polymerization aids. For example, Gujarat Fluorochemicals has already announced that by July 2023 they will change their production process to eliminate the need for fluorinated polymerization aids for the production of PFA. We have the goal to use only PFA resins that are produced without fluorinated polymerization aids after 2025. Thus, already today, we are selecting and shifting more and more quantity to PFA suppliers that use the new technology that can produce the PFA without fluorinated polymerization aids.    During manufacturing:   From literature it is possible to asses the emissione of fluoropolymers during thermoplastic processing (e.g. extrusion of sheets at 370 °C) as well as at the maximum opperating temperature (260 °C). In the book Technology of Fluoropolymers (Drobny et al. 2009; Link-to-Drobny-2009) presents a study where loss of weight due to thermal degradation of PTFE is evaluated. Loss of weight is mainly HF, but also low molecular PFAS could cause the weight loss. One can assume that this findings are also valid for PFA, because PFA has exactly the same molecular structure, the only difference is, that PFA has shorter molecules.   Table according to Drobny et al 2009, page 171-172  During the extrusion of sheets, pipes and welding rods, the PFA is heated up to about 370 °C and kept at this temperature for about 10 Minutes, before it is cooled down again. According to Drobny et al, we can calculate the emissions of PFA at the extrusion temperature of 370 °C as follows:  33500 kg * 0.004 %/h /100 *10/60 = 0,22 kg  Extruding products from about 33500 kg of PFA, is expected to lead to about 0.22 kg of low molecular emissions according to Drobny at al. One should not forget these emission are mainly composed of HF, thus only a fraction of the 0.22 kg/year have the potential to be PFAS.  In our facility critical production areas like extruder, extrusion die and calender-rolls are covered with a ventilation hood to suck off possible low molecular substances and HF. The processing gases are afterwards cleaned via a gas scrubber before released into the atmosphere. Measurement show, that low molecular PFAS accumulate in water used in the gas scrubber, thus it is proven that they are removed from the off gases collected above the extrusion line.  Precise work and proper work instructions avoid loss of fluoropolymers during production. Material from the starting process as well as chips from cutting are collected and added again to the extrusion process. Material which cannot be processed again is stored in containers and sent for incineration following Austrian laws for handling waste.  Storage and handling  Proper Packaging avoids PFAS loss during the transportation and storage. After production, products are packed sold in sales units like: • Sheets: 12.5 m² and 25 m² • Pipes: OD 32 – 110 mm; Length = 5 m • Welding Rod 3 -4 mm (1 kg Spool)  During the production of semi-finished sheets, we therefore expect no environmental pollution processing the beforementioned Fluoropolymers (no spraying, no microplastics, no ionic or non-ionic PFAS from coatings etc.)   The use-phase:   Products are used in the following specific sub-uses:  • PFA semi-finished products (Foils, welding rod, pipes etc.) are used for the lining of the heat exchanger and plant equipment which are in direct contact with the condensating sulfuric acid (260 °C, 98 % Sulfuric acid) and flue gas. • Semi-finished products are installed in a controlled environment (chemical plant, workshop) which ensures that fluoropolymers are not released into the environment. Unusable cuttings, shavings, etc. are collected and sent for incineration or recycling.  During the use phase the PFA is used at a maximum temperature of about 130 - 230 °C. Assuming the worst case of 260 °C, the following emissions can be expected from PFA according to Drobny at all during the lifetime of 15 years:  33500 kg * 100*10^-11 %/h /100% * 24 * 365 * 15 = 0.044 kg Considering that this is the worst-case scenario at the topmost application temperature and that not all of the 0.044 kg are PFAS, but mainly HF, the release of PFAS into the environment is negligible during the whole use phase. Additionally, it is expected that the emission are not constant, but are slowly decreasing during the life-time.  That the emissions caused by PFA are negligible becomes very obvious when looking at the data presented by ECHA during the webinar on April 5th 2023: Emissions from fluorinated gases, emissions from textiles or emissions from medical devices are expected to be in excess of >>1000 t each year. Thus, restriction need to focus on applications that cause most of the emissions.    see Table from ECHA webinar, April 5th 2023   End-of-life:   PFA Fix Point lining which is decommissioned after service life (~ 10-years depending on the application) will be deopsited under strict governmental rules (hazardous waste) in dedicated landfills or will be incinerated. PFA Products are stable and will not degrade to small molecular PFAS.

Due to the increasing environmental regulations the demand of waste incineration plants is constantly growing. The condensing heat exchangers are furthermore upstream of the flue gas de-sulfurization. Upstream of the condensing heat exchangers the gas temperatures are high and no flue gas condensation occurs. Therefore, metals are the appropriate material for these regions in the flue gas stream. In the flue gas desulfurization section, the flue gases are less corrosive and the gas temperatures lowered to a point, where often cheaper materials like polypropylene (usable to approx. 90°C) can be used. PFA lining has become established over the last few years and represents the current state of the art. Currently for this application no other solution based on polymeric products seams feasible due to the extreme operating conditions, that require a special combination of temperature and chemical resistance. General Comments: Why Fluoropolymers used in the food industry?


Even in areas that, at first glance, are not associated with highly hazardous chemicals, it is inconceivable to make safe processes without fluoropolymers. Such areas are the food industry and the fertilizer industry. Inorganic acids (e.g. nitric acid, hydrochloric acid, sulfuric acid, phosphoric acid), alkalis (e.g. sodium hydroxide) and cleaning agents containing active/free chlorine in high concentrations are indispensable in these fields of application. Critical, dangerous chemicals are used in many processes directly related to the food/fertilizer industry.
Pipes, fittings, components and tanks must be cleaned between cycles to avoid residues from the previous production. For these processes (CIP process -Cleaning In Place) the below described chemicals are absolutely necessary:

Acid cleaning
(sulfuric acid, phosphoric acid, nitric acid, hydrochloric acid in high concentrations)
Alkaline cleaning (mixtures of sodium hydroxide up to 50%/ sodium hypochlorite 15% concentration, chlorine bigger 3 mg/l)
Mixed cleaning with acids and alkaline chemicals

Inorganic and high concentrated acids (hydrochloric acid up to a concentration of 37%, nitric acid up to a concentration of 65%, phosphoric acid up to concentration of 95%, sulfuric acid up to a concentration of 96-98%,..) are absolutely necessary ingredients in many process areas of the food industry and are used in fields as for the production of sugar, fruit juices, marinades (e.g. organic fats cannot be dissolved in water, by cleaning with acids the developed salts are soluble in water and can be cleaned/removed).

For the treatment of the waste water in certain areas of the food industry high quantities of waste products from the process are, e.g.  "white water" residues developed by processes in the dairy industry, that must be treated with large amounts of caustic soda and sulfuric acid.
Laboratories in the food industry need an effective rinsing solution against all irritating or corrosive chemicals. From raw material to final product, various tests are performed and there is a large number of different chemicals that vary from low to high concentration.
The most stringent hygiene and purity standards have to be met when manufacturing and packaging food. This of course also applies to all materials coming into contact with foodstuff during the production process. Products with high purity are essential, again this requirement is only fulfilled by fluorinated polymers, the reasons for the use are the outstanding properties like excellent leaching behavior, purity, resistance to biofilm, high chemical and temperature resistance. Fluoropolymers are inert from the chemical point of view (due to the fluorine in the molecular chain). Inertness of a material is a requirement of highest priority for the transport of ultrapure water.
Last but not least fluoropolymers like PVDF have also the approvals for food applications, to get direct in contact with food (e.g. FDA, EU 10/2011, drinking water approvals like WRAS).

The production of phosphate fertilizers goes hand in hand with the production of mineral acids. The most important are phosphoric acid, sulfuric acid (as the main reagent) and nitric acid (as a reagent or additive).  Sulfuric acid is used primarily in the production of phosphoric acid and ammonium sulfate. These, in turn, are the main ingredient in most chemical fertilizers. Ammonium sulfate fertilizers are made by reacting sulfuric acid with ammonia. In the production of phosphate fertilizers, large quantities of sulfuric acid are required to break down the rock phosphate, and the reaction produces superphosphate Ca(H2PO4)2/CaSO4. Sulfuric acid is used primarily in the production of phosphoric acid and ammonium sulfate. These are the main ingredient in most chemical fertilizers. Ammonium sulfate fertilizers are made by reacting sulfuric acid with ammonia.

The production of acids and their use in the production process requires special care in the selection of materials for the process equipment.
Another challenging aspect of phosphate fertilizer production is the handling of solids, powders and media containing suspended solid particles are abrasive and can cause severe damage to piping and valves.
Abrasion resistance, high flame resistance and food-safe compliance are some of the material properties that make fluorinated thermoplastics perfect suitable for the use in this industry.
Pipes, fittings, tanks made from PVDF and ECTFE have turned out to be this solution and have been showing an excellent performance since many decades.

Production, storage, transport and use of chemicals and other hazardous materials can inevitably carry potential risks. Moreover, history has shown that accidents can not only have economic impacts, but also irreparable consequences on human lives and the environment. Mitigating such risks through rigorous safety management whilst simultaneously ensuring efficiency and availability is a major challenge for today’s worldwide chemical industry (in this case production of food and fertilizers).

In our view, the Annex XV restriction report does not cover relevant and essential uses of fluoropolymers in the critical sector “chemical industry” or chemicals necessary in the food/fertilizer industry: Pipelines, storage tanks and transportation containers for the handling of chemicals. Fluoropolymers are mechanically solid, chemically resistant and stable even in harsh and corrosive environments.

We request full exemption of fluoropolymers used in industrial applications from the restriction proposal.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The specific Sector “Systems in PVDF and ECTFE for applications in the food industry” is not listed in Annex XV.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: For this specific application extruded PVDF and ECTFE pipes, injection molded PVDF and ECTFE fittings and valves are used. Furthermore, semi-finished products in PVDF and ECTFE in form of extruded sheets (up to 20 mm thickness), pressed sheets (up to 40 mm thickness) round bars (up to OD = 340 mm) are needed to make tanks for storage/for the process and to make machined fittings. Welding rods (circular profile: 3 and 4 mm) are needed as accessories. Sheets are used for construction and inside lining of storage tanks and transportation containers.  According to our supplier of the raw material for pipes, fittings, valves and main semi-finished products, PVDF and ECTFE are already produced without the use of fluorinated polymerization aids, thus PVDF and ECTFE have a very low potential for leaching of small molecular PFAS.    During manufacturing:   For the specific use-case mainly PVDF and ECTFE products are used. PVDF/ECTFE products like pipes, fittings, valves and sheets are solid products. We are using only PVDF and ECTFE raw materials without fluorinated polymerization aids. A controlled supply chain from resin manufacturing till installation of the systems in PVDF and ECTFE is fully implemented and ensures zero emission.   Product manufacturing phase  Fittings and valves are produced by injection molding and pipes by extrusion. Semifinished products are produced by extrusion or by a pressing process. All components are specially packed to ensure no contamination is taking place in the supply chain till the products are installed.   During the production of PVDF and ECTFE components (process steps as mentioned before) no environmental pollution (no spraying, no microplastics, no Ionic or non-ionic PFAS from coatings etc./ emissions do appear). Process water analysis of our production water do not show any PFAS contamination.   There is a certain amount of emissions when fluoropolymers are processes at elevated temperature in the thermoplastic state. While the majority of the emissions is HCl and HF, there is no detailed information available if the emissions contain small molecular PFAS. In our facility, the main parts of the extrusion line with the highest temperatures (thus the areas where emissions are most likely to occur) are covered with a ventilation hood to suck of fumes/emissions above the extrusion line. The off gases are then cleaned in gas scrubber, before released into the environment. Measurement have shown that some small molecular PFAS accumulate in the water of the gas scrubber, thus cleaning the off gasses is a proven way to reduce emissions.  Precise work and proper work instructions avoid loss of fluoropolymers during the production in our facilities. Material from the starting process as well as chips from cutting are collected and added again to the extrusion process (internal recycling). Material which cannot be processed again is stored in containers and sent for incineration following Austrian laws for handling waste (>850 °C effectively destroys PFAS during incineration).  Storage and handling  Proper Packaging avoids PFAS loss during the transportation and storage. After production, products are packed sold in sales units like:  • Pipes: OD 20 – 315 mm diameter; Length = 5 m; packed in plastic foil • Fittings and valves: OD 20 – 315 mm diameter; packed in plastic foil and proper cardboard • Round bars: OD 20 – 340 mm diameter; Length = 1 m; packed in plastic foil • Welding Rod 3 -4 mm diameter (2 kg Spool); packed in plastic foil and proper cardboard • Sheets from 2 mm up to 50 mm thickness, wrapped in plastic foil, packed in cardboard boxes  During the production, storage and handling of PVDF/ECTFE pipes, fittings, valves, semi-finished products no environmental pollution is expected. The material is inert and very stable, especially at ambient temperature.  The use-phase:   Products are used in the following specific sub-uses:  • PVDF piping systems (pipes, fittings, and valves) and semi-finished products are used for handling for handling of most aggressive process media in food/fertilizer industry. No emissions are caused by using PVDF piping system for handling chemicals in the pickling processes. In fact this piping system ensures high lifetime and excellent and safe performances as required by this industry.   • ECTFE piping systems are used for the transport of most aggressive chemicals in its different forms. Components made of ECTFE ensure the safe transport of most critical media for human beings and environment. All these different media do not leach out any elements, which belong to the group of PFAS. During the use in the temperature range from 20-120°C emissions from ECTFE do not occur (below detection limit), because the material is extremely stable, inert and does not degrade into small molecular substances over the whole lifetime.   End-of-life:   Equipment which is decommissioned after service life (~25 years depending on the application) could be collected and deposited or incinerated according to the state of the art and according to laws in place for handling waste. Incineration destroys PFAS substances.

6. Missing uses: The highest standards of hygiene and purity must be maintained in the food industry, which means, that also critical chemicals with strong acid or basic character have to be used in many processes. This also applies to all materials that come into contact with food during the production process and are needed for all processes (including cleaning, waste water treatment).  By using thermoplastic components made of fluorinate polymers  in production equipment, downtime can be reduced, manufacturing processes significantly accelerated and production runs significantly extended. The safety for employees and the environment is only ensured using fluoropolymers and this for a long period of application. Abrasion and impact resistance, high flame resistance classification and certificates for food contact  are some of these material properties that make these thermoplastics perfect  for use in the food industry and related fertilizer industry.  a)  The industry has a growing demand on ECTFE and PVDF piping systems/semifinished products because of the technical benefits these fluoropolymers offer for this high-grade production processes.  Specially for this application we are producing PVDF/ECTFE pipes, fittings and valves, PVDF/ECTFE semi-finished products with the following approximate demand per annum:  Further details see attached document.  b) Various, reliable, internationally accepted chemical resistance lists/tables (e.g. DVS Codes 2205-1, DIBt media list 40.1-1-4, ISO TR10358) , information supplied by the raw material supplier confirm that PVDF and ECTFE are the only safe and long term solution for the handling of inorganic acids, lyes and processing additives , these fluoropolymers are chemical resistant no matter how the temperature (up to 120°C) and pH value are, while other materials (e.g. PE, PP, PVC, ABS, PA, …) are only for short term solutions) including the risk of unexpected immediate  failures.  Also, metals (steel, copper) do not enable such a universal chemical resistance, at least not in a cost effective way. In addition to the outstanding chemical resistance PVDF/ ECTFE systems meet all further requirements for such applications:  • Internal pressure resistance of pipes and fittings • Temperature resistance  • UV resistance  • Flexibility  • Weldability • Suitability for below ground applications  • Availability of pipes, fittings, valves and special parts (complete supply range)  c) Apart from our suppliers for PVDF and ECTFE and the companies producing the PVDF/ECTFE products used in the food industry, fertilizer industry for the transport and storage, the largest impact is expected for the shipping industry and agricultural companies.   Affected industrial applications in general: Whole chemical industry, agricultural industry, refinery and petrochemical industry, metallurgy industry, power industry, semiconductor industry, the whole human mankind is affected.  d) Only high grade piping systems made of high grade thermoplastics, such as PVDF, ECTFE, offer safety, reliability and significant improvements in performance, installation and safety during operation. Alternatives like PE, PP, PVC, ABS, PA and metal pipes can only handle low concentrations or higher concentrations for a very limited lifetime including the risk of unexpected failures, which would have dramatic influence on the environment. Furthermore, it must be taken into account that the chemicals vary in processes in the food industry or in fertilizer factories, i.e., plastics must be resistant to both acids and alkalis. Again, for such critical chemical loads, only fluoropolymers are a safe solution for long term.  e) PVDF and ECTFE have become established over the last decades and represents the current state of the art, as the old systems has been replaced due to the large number of problems. Currently for this application no other solution based on polymeric products seams feasible due to the extreme operating conditions, that require a special combination chemical resistance (in special the handling of various chemicals with different character), high purity, approvals for food contact. Furthermore, it must be taken into account that the chemicals vary in processes in the food industry or in fertilizer factories, i.e., plastics must be resistant to both acids and alkalis. Again, for such critical chemical loads, only fluoropolymers are a safe solution for long term:  f) Alternative piping systems do not offer a sufficient resistance, especially if its special chemical behavior in watery solutions is considered (changing pH-value, strong oxidizers). Other piping systems than the ones made of PVDF and ECTFE are not resistant in the same way and would corrode and leak. Alternatives would be available but are impacted by the PFAS restriction proposal as well. It would be possible to use FEP or also PFA. Using PE, PP, PVC, ABS, PA, steel, copper would never have the same performance for these media.   We are in permanent contact with raw material suppliers, and we are always considering to include products made of new developments (regarding the raw materials with better resistance against chemicals used in the process of surface treatment, the same high flame resistance properties by keeping a purity and having approvals/certificates for food applications) in the product range. Concerning raw materials with improved resistance to critical in these treatment processes are not available, which are competitive from the technical point of view. Based on this fact/example a material, that withstand these chemicals, having the same high flame resistance by keeping a high purity and having approvals/certificates, excellent abrasion properties, will not be available within the next 15-20 years.  g) Detailed informaiton see document attached.  At first glance the impact for our company, the competitors, the customers and the suppliers seems to be not drastically, banning ECTFE and other fluoropolymers would increase the cost of water treatment/disinfection.   During food production, microorganisms can survive the thermal preservation process. Contamination is also possible during processing. In fact, food is one of the most common sources of serious illness worldwide (caused by listeria, salmonella, EHEC). Almost one in ten people on earth, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates in a recent report, is affected each year by infections or poisoning caused by contaminated food (600 million people, 420 000 of whom die). The numbers are very conservative estimates. "These estimates are the result of a decade of work, involving more than 100 experts from around the world," says Dr. Kazuaki Miyagishima1), director of WHO's Department of Food Safety and Zoonoses.  Process equipment, which is suitable for the transport and storage of food stuff on the one hand and which withstands the absolutely necessary cleaning process with critical chemical media on the other hand are only available in fluoropolymers like PVDF and ECTFE (including certificates for food contact).  Production of fertilizers and the availability of them is in direct relationship to the hunger of the world. According to the WHI 2022 the number of people without regular access to adequate calories is increasing, affecting as many as 828 million in 2021 (91% of these people lived in Asia and Africa). The fertilizer crisisis in many ways very worrisome, as it could inhibit food production in the rest of the world. If the fertilizer problem is not resolved and fertilizer trade does not continue, there will be a very serious food supply problem in the next years. Without a fundamental change in direction, neither the world as a whole nor some of the  most affected  countries are projected to achieve even low levels of hunger as defined by the WHI for 2030. 44 countries currently have serious or very serious hunger situations. For 20 countries with moderate, serious, or very serious levels of hunger, the 2022 WHI scores are higher than those for 2014.These countries are in different regions of the world, not just those with the worst overall levels of hunger. Even in stable regions and countries, there remain areas of food insecurity where increased and targeted efforts are needed.  Global fertilizer prices were already high before Russia invaded its neighboring country on the 24th of February 2022, as natural gas and coal prices forced some fertilizer producers to cut production in the energy-intensive sector.  As already described, based on further global crises (as conflicts, climate change and the economic impact of the COVID-19 pandemic,..) the situation regarding the shortage of fertilizers is likely to worsen, and this is a very strong driver of hunger, this development is expected to be ongoing.  A further increase of the shortage of fertilizers caused by failures in the facilities by not using proper piping systems would exacerbate this global humanitarian crisis even more. Fertilizers are key to high yields of corn, soybeans, rice, and wheat.  Banning PVDF and ECTFE would not only cause harm to our business and the business of competitors and suppliers, but to all companies and end users in the chemical, agricultural industry, better a dramatic influence on the whole world. Such industries depend on PVDF and ECTFE as a safe material for the most important process of food production for the mankind.  1) Dr. Kazuaki Miyagishima studied medicine and received his Doctor of Medicine degree from the University of Tokyo, Japan. He also received an international diploma of public administration from the Ecole Nationale d’Administration, France, and a Ph.D degree in medical sciences from Showa University, Japan. After a postgraduate study in physiology, he joined the Japanese Ministry of Health and Welfare as medical officer, where he was responsible for health policy and planning, maternal and child health, medical personnel training, and mental health, among others. From 1994 to 1998, he worked in the Food Safety Programme at the WHO headquarters, Geneva. In 1998 he became Associate Professor in public health and health policy at Kyoto University, Japan. In 2003, he was appointed Secretary, Codex Alimentarius Commission, by the Directors-General of FAO and WHO.

General Comments: Why semiconductor machine use pfpe lubricant ?

Perfluoropolyether (PFPE) lubricants are commonly used in the semiconductor industry for various applications due to their unique properties and characteristics. Semiconductor manufacturing processes involve intricate machinery and equipment that require precise and controlled movements. PFPE lubricants offer several advantages that make them suitable for such applications:

Chemical Inertness: PFPE lubricants are highly chemically inert, which means they are resistant to reacting with various chemicals and gases used in semiconductor fabrication processes. This is crucial because semiconductor manufacturing involves exposure to corrosive and reactive chemicals, and traditional lubricants might degrade or react with these substances, leading to equipment malfunction or contamination.

Thermal Stability: Semiconductor manufacturing often involves high-temperature processes, and PFPE lubricants have excellent thermal stability. They can maintain their lubricating properties at elevated temperatures without breaking down or evaporating, ensuring consistent performance and preventing equipment damage due to overheating.

Vacuum Compatibility: Many semiconductor processes are performed in vacuum environments, where traditional lubricants can vaporize and contaminate the vacuum chamber. PFPE lubricants have low vapor pressures, meaning they have minimal tendencies to evaporate and contribute to vacuum contamination. This property helps maintain the integrity of vacuum conditions during manufacturing processes.

Low Outgassing: Outgassing refers to the release of volatile compounds from a material under vacuum conditions. PFPE lubricants exhibit low outgassing characteristics, making them suitable for use in cleanroom environments where even minor contaminants can have a significant impact on semiconductor quality.

Nonflammability: PFPE lubricants are nonflammable, which is crucial in industries where fire safety is a concern. Their nonflammable nature adds an extra layer of protection when used in equipment that generates heat or operates in high-temperature environments.

Longevity: PFPE lubricants have a longer lifespan compared to many traditional lubricants. They have excellent resistance to degradation, ensuring that lubrication intervals can be extended, reducing maintenance frequency and downtime.

Compatibility with Materials: PFPE lubricants are compatible with a wide range of materials commonly found in semiconductor equipment, such as metals, ceramics, and polymers. This compatibility prevents material degradation or damage, ensuring the long-term functionality of the equipment.

In summary, the semiconductor industry requires lubricants that can withstand harsh chemical, thermal, and vacuum conditions while maintaining stable performance and minimizing contamination risks. PFPE lubricants offer these benefits, making them a preferred choice for lubricating critical machinery and equipment in semiconductor manufacturing processes.

General Comments: Winning the War against PFAS: A Path to a PFAS-Free Future with
Ceramic Membranes

CERAFILTEC applauds the position of the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) with regards to restricting all PFAS in all applications in the EU. As a major player in the water and wastewater treatment industry and developer of ceramic flat membrane technology, CERAFILTEC is keenly aware of the deleterious and “forever” issues associated with PFAS and widely used polymeric membranes. As fellow humans, we are—and should be—committed to winning the war against PFAS and their potentially devastating effect on human and environmental health.
Much has been written about the dangers of PFAS, and as the world becomes increasingly aware of the environmental and health impacts of industrial materials, the mounting concerns surrounding the PFAS issue cannot be ignored.
We stand with our colleagues at the ECHA in waging an important war against these materials. And every battle, no matter how small, is important to our winning this ‘good fight.’ For this reason, we feel compelled to enlighten the ECHA about the available alternative to PVDF membranes used for water and wastewater filtration.
The dawn of a new era
For those of us in the water industry, the dawn of a new era is upon us—one illuminated by the superior, sustainable and inescapable promise of ceramic membranes.
There was a time, not too long ago, when doctors described cigarette smoking as harmless, and wearing seatbelts in cars was seen as an overcautious act. In hindsight, these notions seem ludicrous, even dangerous. Today, with our evolved understanding, we recognize these once-accepted practices as harmful and recognize PFAS as a class of molecules that are serious environmental contaminants.
Just as the world transitioned from the soot-stained era of coal to the clean, boundless promise of renewable energy, from the rattle and hum of diesel trains to the smooth, whisper-like glide of electric engines, and from the energy-intensive process of thermal desalination to the sleek efficiency of reverse osmosis, so too is the shift from polymeric UF membranes to ceramic UF membranes underway. Thus transition is not a matter of 'if', but 'how soon'.
Ceramic membranes are more than an 'alternative'; they are a leap forward in membrane technology. These innovative solutions are fully capable of replacing polymeric membranes entirely. And as demand increases, the resulting economies of scale will lead to cost advantages for ceramics that are unparalleled and unimaginable. This shift is already happening today, as ceramic membranes are already fully cost competitive. We believe that the scale will continue to tip even more in favor of ceramic membranes, not only for providing more cost-effective solutions for industry participants, but also myriad benefits for sustainability and technical superiority.
Advantages of ceramic membranes
Ceramic membranes come with a raft of advantages. At the top of this list is the fact that they present no PFAS issue and in fact, are capable of removing PFAS from water with proper process solutions.
Clay, silica, and alumina constitute materials from which ceramic membranes are typically made. The sustainable sourcing of these materials reduces the environmental footprint associated with membrane production.
They are sustainable, known for their durability and long lifespan, and they produce minimal to no waste. Highly resistant to chemical degradation, they are suitable for treating water and wastewater containing aggressive chemicals or high levels of contaminants and reducing the need for chemical pretreatment or the use of additional chemicals, which also can have environmental implications.
At their end-of-life, ceramic membranes can be reused or recycled, a testament to their environmental virtues.
In addition, the potential for waste reduction is enormous. If we replaced all polymeric membranes with ceramic ones, we would save plastic waste equivalent to 3 billion plastic bottles annually. Imagine these bottles spread out on the ground, occupying an area of 7,000 football fields—year after year. A transition to ceramic membranes could render this haunting scenario obsolete.
Summary
Historically, regulations or consumer shifts have led to the replacement of harmful or outdated products with safer, more efficient alternatives. We've bid farewell to lead-based paints, moved beyond the era of ozone-depleting CFCs in aerosols, and replaced single-use plastic bags with reusable shopping bags. Each shift, though initially challenging, brought with it enormous benefits, making it difficult to fathom why we ever persisted with older methods.
In the same vein, it will soon be unimaginable that we ever used anything but ceramic membranes in filtration systems. The transition we are discussing is not just about reducing waste or eliminating a potential source of PFAS contamination; it is about embracing progress. It is about acknowledging the inherent human drive to innovate, to strive for better—more efficient, less harmful solutions—that will help win the war against PFAS.

About the Author
Julius Glöckner, MBA, CPA, CIA, CFE, is Chief Commercial Officer of CERAFILTEC. He can be reached at julius@cerafiltec.com.

They do not present significant toxicity problems and do not degrade into other PFAS. Fluoropolymers are also expensive. Therefore, they are only used where no other products/materials offer viable alternative solutions. Their chemical purity and resistance to harsh conditions, corrosion, and extreme temperatures (hot and cold) are unique properties needed in a variety of applications. The assessment of alternative materials has shown that they cannot meet the critical performance characteristics of fluorinated materials and are not safe. The use of fluoropolymers brings significant benefits along the value chain and is essential and indispensable for numerous technologies, industrial processes, and everyday products. 6701" "As a company with main areas of work in fluid technology, mechanical engineering, mobile hydraulics, and food technology, our industry is not included in the 3,500 companies organized in the VDMA as the largest industry association. The same applies to FKM materials, which must be used at high operating temperatures and with more aggressive media. Even the use of these materials (FDA approval/USP Clas VI) for food contact shows that they are safe. FKM fluoropolymers are equally safe and, in our opinion, must continue to be used without exceptions. 6701" "- Machine and plant engineering accounts for approximately 40% of the sales volume of seals in the mechanical engineering, food technology, and other fluid power industries of our company.
