Combined Comments: "We have been manufacturers of O-rings and special seals for over 60 years, mainly made from the materials FKM, FFKM, and PTFE, all of which belong to the group of fluoropolymers. We demand the exclusion of fluoropolymers from the PFAS definition due to their high importance for the industry and their low risk to the environment and health, so that they do not fall under the draft restriction. This demand is detailed below. According to the OECD criteria, fluoropolymers are considered Polymers of Low Concern. They have been extensively tested and approved for safety-critical areas (see Appendix B and C). This can be seen in the approvals we have, for example, for our material VR1 (base polymer FKM). This has passed a BAM test as well as the DVGW 549 and 682. This material has been tested and approved for use with oxygen as well as in gas applications. The documents are attached. Due to their special properties, fluoropolymers are of high importance to the industry. They have high thermal stability, chemical inertness (against solvents, oils, water, acids, and bases), low values of refractive index, permittivity, abrasion, and water absorption, as well as excellent weather resistance, oxidation resistance, and durability (see Appendix D). In the case study we conducted (Appendix A), the companies surveyed from process technology and the energy sector also confirm that chemical and thermal resistance, low friction and aging, pressure resistance, low abrasion and wear, and high tightness are the properties that only fluoropolymers can meet their applications with (see Appendix A). Furthermore, there are approvals that can only be met by fluoropolymers in combination with the requirements of the seal. If these were to be banned, these standards could no longer be met, which could pose a danger to health and the environment. Furthermore, there are no materials that can substitute for the functionality of fluoropolymers. A ban on fluoropolymers would have an impact on the entire value chain and system-relevant industries and thus on the end consumer. To illustrate this, the results of the case study are explained below. Without the use of fluoropolymers, plants for energy generation and chemical plants for the production of raw materials for paints, adhesives, and plastics could not be operated. In addition, increased wear, short service lives, and production downtime could result. Without seals made of fluoropolymers, a secure shut-off of gas, oil, and heating water pipes would no longer be possible. Many process plants could only be operated for a short time with increased, dangerous emissions and significantly higher production costs. Finally, many products in the energy supply sector, particularly district heating, would no longer be manufacturable (see Appendix A). Also affected is the food industry. For example, filling systems need to be cleaned with aggressive media in order to ensure hygienic filling according to standards. For this, fluoropolymers are necessary, as only these materials are resistant to the media used there. The bureaucracy that would arise from exemptions and transition periods would not be feasible for SME business processes. Our individual items are delivered to many different customers. In addition to direct users, the majority (about 60%) goes through technical trade, and the final use of the seal is therefore not known to us. The same item could therefore still be delivered to customers in the transportation sector, but not to the chemical industry. With this limitation, we would no longer be marketable, as low production volumes would no longer allow us to generate market-sensitive prices. A continuation of business for our group of companies, consisting of six companies with around 400 employees and an annual turnover of approximately €65 million, would no longer be possible. Fluoropolymers generate around 85% of our total sales. Maintaining production would no longer be economically viable. A ban would therefore result in machines and equipment from system-relevant sectors no longer functioning. Furthermore, there is a risk that due to unsuitable seals, dangerous media could enter the environment or pose a direct danger to workers. For these reasons, we demand the exclusion of fluoropolymers from the PFAS definition. Supporting evidence can be found in the appendix. 8055" "Manufacturer of FKM, FFKM, and PTFE seals Production process: Waste products during manufacturing are sorted and recycled in a pure form o Use: Long lifespan compared to other sealing materials 8055" "Featuring industries: - Process technology - Pumps and valves industry  - Automotive industry - Shipping industry - Chemical industry  - Medical technology - Food industry  - Oil and Gas industry"

Combined Comments: "We strongly support the proposal of the Restriction report to restrict PFAS as a group of substances and to only continue using PFAS for essential applications in exceptional cases. Based on the extraordinary persistence of all PFAS that meet the definition, the group approach is the only possible measure to prevent contamination of humans and the environment. Previous experience shows that the ban of individual PFAS such as PFOA or PFOS has led to their replacement by other PFAS with a comparable hazard profile (regrettable substitutions). With more than 10,000 individual PFAS compounds, a regulation of individual substances cannot be effective. We support the proposal (Option 2) to allow applications for which suitable alternatives are not currently available for a longer transition period. However, we reject indefinite exceptions. Manufacturers and users should be obliged to regularly report on research and development efforts undertaken to replace the current PFAS application with a fluorine-free application with lower risk in cases of exceptions. In addition, holders of exceptions should be required to report on measures they have taken to minimize PFAS emissions. The necessity of exceptional use of PFAS should be examined. For example, PFAS-treated outdoor clothing certainly has higher performance than alternative products. However, extraordinary performance is only required for polar and high mountain expeditions, not in the usual use case, for which numerous PFAS-free products are already on the market. We explicitly support the regulation of polymeric PFAS as well. The need arises in particular from significant emissions during production (use of non-polymeric PFAS as emulsifiers) and during use at high temperatures. Disposal is also a problem, as waste incineration temperatures are usually not high enough to completely destroy PFAS. Problems also exist, for example, when coated products such as frying pans or baking molds are heated for metal recycling, leading to uncontrolled emissions of fluorinated decomposition products. Also, a recent OECD analysis of side-chain fluorinated polymers such as acrylates, oxetanes, urethanes, ethoxylates, and siloxanes in various applications should be considered. The existing data is incomplete, but it indicates significant risks, e.g. through hydrolysis of the fluorinated side chains (https://www.oecd.org/chemicalsafety/portal-perfluorinated-chemicals/synthesis-report-on-understanding-side-chain-fluorinated-polymers-and-their-life-cycle.pdf). We ask for a re-evaluation of the exceptions for active substances of agricultural and non-agricultural pesticides, as well as for pharmaceuticals. We, like SEAC, do not believe that the exclusion of these substances is mandatory. If exceptions are maintained, we urge the Commission to take appropriate measures in plant protection, biocidal, and pharmaceutical law to ensure that the use of PFAS active substances remains restricted to essential applications. We welcome the fact that manufacturers of such active substances are supposed to have corresponding reporting obligations. Regarding the list of exemption regulations (pages 4-8 of the Restriction Report), we would like to point out that exemption regulations should be as specific as possible. For most of the uses mentioned in the table, this is the case, but not for uses 5p and 5q (coolants in combustion engines and transport vehicles: Here, the coolant for which the exception applies should be named more specifically: Coolants such as R 1234yf and R 1234ze, which rapidly degrade to trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), should not be subject to the exception, taking into account the individual case against the climate impact of the gas). Exceptions 5v (hard chromium plating) and 5w (foam blowing agents) are also too broadly formulated. The specific PFAS compound for which the exception applies should be specified here. We also see the exception 6a (food contact materials) as problematic, as it practically allows the continuation of PFAS coating in all cases. It should be noted that a legal regulation in Denmark from 2020 has successfully led to the circulation of only PFAS-free food contact materials there https://arnika.org/en/publications/throwaway-packaging-forever-chemicals-european-wide-survey-of-pfas-in-disposable-food-packaging-and-tableware. The exception 6g (non-stick coatings in industrial and professional baking molds) is also incomprehensible to us. The most questionable to us seems to be exception 6o: Applications for safety in transport vehicles, which is supposed to last for even 13.5 years. This exception, if it has any justification at all, is completely unspecific and should be limited to a few justified applications of specific PFAS. The duties of commercial users are not well-defined. Although they are supposed to create a management plan according to No. 8 (page 8) and make it available to the enforcement authorities, they do not have an active role in informing the authorities. It is to be feared that the examination of the management plans will fall victim to enforceable deficits, and in light of the vested interests of manufacturers and importers, they will endlessly extend their exceptions because, allegedly, the users have no alternatives to PFAS." "We are adding two publications that make it clear that in many areas where PFAS currently appear to be indispensable, fluorine-free alternatives will be available at least in the foreseeable future: - Mirfarsi S.H. et al. (2023) High-temperature stability of hydro carbon-based Pemion® proton exchange membranes: A thermomechanical stability study, Hydrogen energy https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijhydene.2023.07.236 - Xiao Zhi Lim (2023): Can the world leave ‘forever chemicals’ behind?, Nature Vol. 620, 24-27 Also, at a webinar by ChemSec on June 19, 2923, it was demonstrated that fluorine-free alternatives have been developed in the following areas: F-gases, semiconductor production, fuel cells and electrolyzers (ionomers), and technical textiles, which will make PFAS dispensable in the future. The attached publication by Brunn et al. lists several publications on page 4 that illustrate a possible PFAS substitution. 9477" "The information in the 'Restriction Report' on waste, recycling, and sludge is scarce and incomplete. It should be noted that the contamination will only decrease very gradually, even with a very effective restriction on the use of PFAS, since many PFAS-containing products have a longer lifespan and only reach the waste phase with a delay. The restrictions on recycling (risk of PFAS transfer, especially in paper/cardboard and textiles), waste treatment, and sludge utilization due to PFAS contamination further demonstrate the essential need for a comprehensive restriction of the entire group of substances. General Comments: WirtschaftsVereinigung Metalle e.V. (WVMetalle) fundamentally rejects the group restriction procedure for PFAS.

The restriction proposal must do justice to this group of substances' critical economic and social role. PFAS are crucial in countless critical modern applications such as semiconductor production, (alternative) energy, climate or medical technology and biotechnology. Non-ferrous metals play an essential role in enabling these products. Therefore, exemptions from the restriction for using PFAS in the non-ferrous metals industry should be granted, particularly for critical and strategic raw materials, as defined by the Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA).

According to the REACH Regulation, a differentiated assessment of the risks to humans and the environment associated with these substances (hazards + exposures), including already established
protective measures/use, occurs. Instead of a general restriction under REACH, targeted regulations, e.g., occupational health and safety, could be more practical.

A distinction between industrial uses and consumer products would be necessary. Where PFAS do not enter the product, and safe use is already proven, their use should be allowed indefinitely. Safe PFAS substances, which are used as process chemicals and have no exposure, should be exempted indefinitely from the
REACH restriction.

The transition periods must be set appropriately and industry-related. A generic regulation cannot consider the specifics of the industry, e.g. for the semiconductors industry, such as development periods, qualification and certification phases at customers.

Even though we cannot provide quantitative information and data (we would need more time), by submitting our position, we would like to address the importance and the challenges of using PFAS in the non-ferrous metals sector.

Content: Baseline Transitional period Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: With regard to the PFAS restriction proposal, we express our concerns about the following aspects:

• Socio-economic: The health sector (here focusing on medical devices and pharmaceuticals) helps to diagnose, to cure and to care. Lives and wellbeing of hundreds of thousands of patients depend on the availability of state-of-the-art medical products, each day and worldwide. Any missed, too small or too short exemption of a PFAS use in healthcare puts these lives in danger.

• Data gaps: Due to the broad relevance of PFAS in industry and the unprecedented large scope of the proposed restriction, current disclosure requirements via safety data sheets, SVHC declaration or other means are fully insufficient to build the basis for identification and evaluation of all relevant PFAS uses in time within this legislative process.

• Complexity: Tight, detailed exemptions cannot cover all relevant uses of PFAS in medical devices and pharmaceuticals and its supply chain. With the current approach it can be expected that relevant uses will be (unintentionally) banned with serious impact on the availability of these products, i.e. putting patients’ lives at risk. Much broader, generic exemptions for medtech/healthcare are needed.

• No alternatives: PFAS, especially fluoropolymers, are often intentionally used due to their unique chemical/material properties. Alternatives are missing, would not fulfill required technical criteria or would have equal environmental properties.

• Time: The medtech sector is strictly regulated, has very high quality standards and is already today facing huge challenges, e.g. due to the implementation of new sectoral legislation (Medical Device Regulation) and complex multi-tier supply chains. The transition and therefore the re-registration of all medical devices across Europe to this new MDR was prolonged to 2027/2028 due to limited Notified Body capacities. During this period and as long as medical devices are still registered under the former sectoral legislation (Medical Device Directive) significant material changes are not allowed anyway.

• Supply gaps: Medtech is also dependent from upstream suppliers, notified bodies and competent authorities. An uncoordinated sudden stop of supply of PFAS containing materials puts the supply of medical devices at risk. A phase-out of PFAS (if feasible at all) will require much more time, even in those few cases where an alternative might already exist from a technical point of view. The registration of these material changes under the MDR will require years beyond 2025 + 18 months.

• Competition: The restriction puts high pressure only on EU-based manufacturers using fluoropolymers. This causes a significant disadvantage for the European MedTech and pharmaceutical industry at international markets and opposes efforts to increase the strategic autonomy of the EU.

A non-PFAS alternative or a no-derogation scenario would likely result in significant consequences, such as an inability to manufacture critical medical devices and pharmaceuticals. This could lead to the discontinuation of life-saving technologies, medicines, and services, including procedures for stenting, heart valve repairing, renal replacement, catheters, implants, and capital equipment used in related procedures. Additionally, there could be an impact on in-vitro diagnostic (IVD) uses, including instruments and testing kits.

Alternative medical technologies could reduce medical or technical performance. Medical procedures could have to be replaced with much more invasive and higher-risk procedures (such as open-heart surgery) which would significantly increase patient trauma.

What we ask for:

Considering the above-mentioned aspects and the critical function the healthcare sector has for the well-being and functioning of society we ask for a full derogation for at least 13.5 years of medical devices and pharmaceuticals from the PFAS restriction including intermediaries and the use of PFAS in the manufacturing process of pharmaceuticals and medical devices and/or the medical technology’s upstream supply chain. An additional review procedure before the end of this derogation should assess the need for further medical exemptions. Furthermore, spare parts for mentioned products and production facilities require an even longer exemption. Thereby, quality and continued access to essential medicines and medical technologies containing PFAS for patients and practitioners are guaranteed.

While we appreciate the proposed derogations for certain applications, we are concerned that many crucial medical applications remain disregarded or uncovered. If no drop-in alternative is available, as this is the case for all medical uses, or a PFAS is discovered in a medical device in future, the absence of derogation would adversely affect not only PFAS manufacturers and medical technology producers but especially patients and practitioners throughout Europe. The medical device and pharmaceutical sector is also dependent on its supply chain for alternative materials and components, which, when available, still need to pass lengthy regulatory approval processes.

Where available, a transition to non-PFAS medical technologies should be done in a realistic timeframe ensuring sufficient time to move to alternatives in a safe and controlled manner.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: With the proposed ban of PFAs (incl. proposed derogation periods from ECHTA) the chips and semiconductor device supply of the EU is highly endangered. Additionally, the dependency on foreign chips and semiconductor devices will increase to nearly 100%. The main European societal challenges cannot be resolved in time!

The European Union names seven main challenges  to be solved within the next fifteen years:
• Health, demographic change and well-being
• Nutrition and food safety
• Safe and clean energy
• Intelligent, sustainable and integrated mobility
• Climate protection, environment, resource efficiency and natural resources
• Europe in a changing world: inclusive, innovative and reflective societies
• Secure societies - protecting the freedom and security of Europe and its citizens

To resolve these challenges, data mining and data processing are one essential building block. Only in a digitally connected and smart society, the above-mentioned challenges can be resolved within the proposed time frame. Digital devices are the base for a connected and smart society to do the data mining and data processing. All these devices depend on a safe, efficient and responsible semiconductor industry. European lawmakers understand the importance of semiconductor devices and launched the European Chips Act  in 2022. Semiconductor devices have high strategic value and have the potential to help to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 50% within the next seven to eight years .

In 2021, the semiconductor industry generated a global revenue of $550 billion. Projected is an annual growth of 12% . Roughly, a third of all semiconductor devices are used for communication applications, another third for data processing applications and the last third splits evenly into automotive, industrial and consumer electronics . Within the semiconductor supply chain, European equipment suppliers provide 23% of globally required semiconductor production equipment . Within this supply chain, PFAs are used for process chemicals, manufacturing equipment and production facilities. PFAs are widely used in semiconductor production equipment for their specific and unique chemical and physical properties . A sudden ban of PFAs would set semiconductor performance approximately back by at least 10 years.

SUSS Microtec is a provider of semiconductor production equipment with an annual revenue of 300 Mio. Euro (2022) and 1.250 employees worldwide. All research and development, as well as most of the production is located within the European Union . As a market leader in photomask cleaning equipment, SUSS Microtec facilitates the EUV applications as the current cutting edge exposure technology (provided by ASML), by gently cleaning the photomask for the 5nm structures in front end semiconductor production.
A broad variety of PFAs are used in these photo mask-cleaning tools. Core properties are the chemical, thermal and physical stability of PFAs to avoid particles above 10nm in the cleaning process. PFA and PCTFE are used in tubes and valves. ETFE, ECTFE and PVDF are mostly used for processing chambers, housing and frames covers. PTFE and PFA are often used for passivation of parts, FKM and FFKM for seals and gaskets. A typical photomask cleaner consists of approximately 10% of PFAs in mass but nearly 100% of the parts in direct contact the photomask and/or the cleaning medias are made of PFAs. Substitutes would need to have the same properties, which would probably lead to the same problems seen with PFAs today. Those substitutes are not available yet!

The wide spectrum of chemical resistance of PFAs allows SUSS to provide Coater / Developer and Wafer Cleaning equipment for the advanced backend semiconductor production. The chemical stability of PFAs enables customers to run a wide range of applications and processes on SUSS tools. This flexibility saves space, preserves resources and saves energy. A typical advanced backend tool consists of 4% of PFAs in mass. Nearly 100% of the parts in direct contact the Semiconductor devices are made of PFAs. Substitutes would need to have the same properties, which would probably lead to same problems seen with PFAs today. Those substitutes are not available yet.

Ahead of the European Green Deal, SUSS Microtec supports its tools longer than 25 years with service and upgrades, even provides remanufacturing . A derogation period much shorter than 20 years would be a severe disadvantage and a major economic threat to SUSS Microtec and the rest of the European Semiconductor Equipment suppliers.

Since the entire semiconductor industry in Europe is responsible for less than 1% (mid-range estimation) of all PFAs used in the European Union , a total ban including semiconductor industry is unreasonable considering the importance of the industry to tackle the societal challenges mentioned above. The semiconductor industry has a long history of proactively substituting unhealthy and toxic substances. A substitution of PFAs for most applications is possible, just not within the ECHTA proposed time line. For applications such as mentioned above, new materials need to be developed, qualified and mass-produced to cover current needs for chemical stability and cleanliness. For some PFAs such as PVDF and PTFE expert cannot yet foresee a timeline for a replacement development .

Current expert evaluations estimate a timespan of minimum 15 to 20 years to replace most PFAs with less hazardous materials. This ensures that substitutes does not lead to higher energy consumption or other kind of additional resource consumption or higher equipment downtime .
As a part of the European society, and a hidden champion within Europe’s high-tech industry, a hasty ban of PFAs would be a technological and economical threat to SUSS Microtec. Therefore, SUSS Microtec would require a 20 years derogation period to participate in the development of PFAs substitutes, to implement these substitutes into products and to qualify their performance within our customer’s processes. Additionally, SUSS Microtec would require an incentive or subsidy for material makers to start working on substitutes immediately.

General Comments: Within the pest control industry, a range of UVA (black light, typically at 365nm) emitting lamps, in both fluorescent & LED form, are used to attract insects into traps to prevent the risk of bacteria transport are placed in areas where hygiene levels are paramount. These places such as food preparation, processing, sales areas, laboratories & medical facilities to name a few. To maintain a suitable catch rate, a certain intensity of UVA output at 365nm is required (figure 1.), however, these areas also have a requirement to be glass free due to the risk of breakage. The UVA emitting lamps are coated to offer protection from glass & foreign bodies escaping in the event of breakage. Typically, fluoropolymers (such as FEP, PFA & THV) are used as the preferred coating family due to the properties comprising of UV stability, UV transmission, impact resistance, tensile strength & temperature stability which in turn has been the only proven material type to pass testing to meet IEC:61549 on UV emitting lamps.

Other industries such as water & air purification require the use of UVC lamps. These lamps also require a coating similar to the pest control industry with high levels of UVC output to fulfil the purification objectives while also in case of accidental breakage & foreign body release. The UVC output is more aggressive than the UVA output previously mentioned so fluoropolymers are the only product group suitable for this application.

Generally speaking, no other plastic group offers the properties that are required within these fields of use listed above. PET (figure 3.), PMMA & PC (figure 2.) are commonly used in general lighting (white light) purposes due to the lack of UV, any band width emitted from the light source does not cause degradation or blocks the UV output required.

Content: Information on alternatives Request for exemption
Combined Comments:
General Comments: WMF is a member of Industrieverband Haus-, Heiz- Und Küchentechnik (HKI) and the Federation of the European Cookware, Cutlery and Houseware Industries (FEC). We are committed to providing safe, affordable, and high-quality products to our customers, and refer to the FEC responses to this consultation regarding our confidence in the safety of fluoropolymers, distinct from non-polymeric PFAS. Accordingly, we request a full exemption of fluoropolymers from the scope of the restriction.

WMF is a leading premium brand of household products, hotel equipment and a world market leader in offering solutions for professional coffee machines. We have a wide spectrum of machines, cookware, cutlery products for consumers and professionals in the fields of hospitality, restaurants, quick service restaurants, coffee chains, convenience stores…
Beside the development, production and sales, the after-sale service, to keep the machine over their intended lifetime in professional work, is key to our value proposition.
The application is linked to commercial dispensing appliances for preparation or delivery food and drinks.

Fluoropolymers should be fully exempted from the scope of the restriction proposal, and especially for uses in professional and cookware sectors:
- The continued availability of certain fluoropolymers for use in hoses, seals and plastic injection moldings for which there are no substitute materials is a specific interest of the professional sector.  Specifically, PTFE and PFA hoses, FKM seals and PVDF injection molded parts. Without substitute materials, 100% of the Professional Coffee Machine (PCM) business is affected. There is no machine existing for our sector without these materials.
- The continued availability of certain fluoropolymers for non-stick coatings for cookware, bakeware and kitchen equipment is a specific interest of the household equipment sector. A ban on fluoropolymer coatings will lead to concerning socioeconomic side-effects on European cookware businesses, especially in Germany, France and Italy, as detailed in the FEC contribution, and in a study commissioned to an independent consultant, Ricardo.
- The significantly longer lifespan of fluoropolymer-based coatings cookware results in less frequent replacement by the consumer, meaning a decreased environmental impact by avoiding additional manufacture and transport, and a lower total waste volume. As such, fluoropolymer-based coatings cookware provides substantial benefits to consumers, particularly in a context of consumer price inflation and towards achieving the objectives of the European Union’s Waste Framework Directive with regards to waste hierarchy.
- There are studies to which we can refer, indicating there are minimal emissions through the lifecycle of cookware, bakeware and electrical appliances.
- In most applications, the use of fluoropolymers is due to the unique combination of material properties such as temperature and pressure resistance as well as the approval for contact with food and the easy cleanability (hygiene). The reason for the use of the materials is also due to the unique properties of high temperature and chemical resistance as well as the friction behaviour (which fulfils clean-in-place needs). The fluoropolymers are therefore deliberately used to achieve the material properties required for the intended use of the products.

A full exemption of fluoropolymers is the appropriate course for professional and cookware sectors, given their established safety, lack of appreciable emissions into the environment of non-polymeric PFAS, and their essentiality for important economic sectors. Furthermore, the disposal and thus safe destruction of harmful substances at the end of the life cycle can be organized in a targeted and verifiable manner.

Additionally, accommodations for the availability of spare parts will be critical:
- In the B2B area, we are committed to supplying spare parts for at least 8 years after the last series delivery. A ban on further materials would massively damage our after sales service and mean a high additional investment for our customers due to reduced useful life and thus higher depreciation periods or earlier new investments.
- Spare parts and remanufactured/refurbished products must be excluded from the restriction as a matter of principle. The repair-as-produced principle must be applied to the placing on the market of spare parts, wear parts and used parts for the purposes of sustainability and economic efficiency.
Spare and wear parts must be exempt without limitation for all products purchased by customers prior to the validity date of the restriction until the equipment reaches its practical end of life.

-Finally, a PFAS restriction could affect other components than hoses and seals in the professional sector. Due to the lack of information within the supply chains, the complete extent of the impact cannot be determined. Therefore, we also propose an information disclosure requirement.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Concerning the professional sector, derogation 6a is already mentioned for materials in contact with food for equipment used in industrial food and feed production. This includes hoses and gaskets as well as cable sheathing with food contact used in commercial kitchen and catering equipment, such as professional coffee machines. In professional applications, fluoropolymers are used because of the requirements for temperature and pressure resistance and chemical resistance (against organic oils and greases, cleaning agents and descaling agents). Furthermore, requirements for food safety materials have to be fulfilled. Likewise, for the use of hoses in contact with food, high pressure properties are required that are temperature-resistant, resistant to chemicals and grease, and provide elastic properties to use the hose in a complex machine with more than 1000 components. For seals used in food contact, durability plays an important role in addition to temperature resistance, chemical and grease resistance. Without PFAS components, the service life of seals in the devices is very limited and the seals wear out very quickly.  PFA (Perfluoro alkoxy polymer, CAS 26655-00-5 / 31784-04-0),   FEP (Fluoroethylene propylene CAS: 25067-11-2) and   PTFE (Polytetrafluoroethylene 9002-84-0) are used for hoses (or tubes) in commercial coffee machines  FKM (Vinylidene fluoride-hexafluoropropylene copolymer, CAS 9011-17-0) is used for O-rings (seal- ing rings) und   PVDF (polyvinylidene fluoride, CAS 24937-79-9) is used for plastic parts.  Currently, there are no alternatives available with the required properties for these uses.  The use of these materials is very limited in numbers and weight in relation to the complete coffee machine.   Manufacturers, in collaboration with suppliers, are searching for alternative materials. Furthermore, even if alternative materials that meet the required specifications are found, it is not possible that there will be one-to-one alternatives for these applications.   The dossier states that alternatives for the various uses of PFAS in industrial food and feed production are not immediately technically and economically feasible. In section E.2.3.4.4 "Other uses", the dossier writers state that there is sufficient evidence of low substitution potential for industrial applications such as the use of fluoropolymers in seals, tubing etc. in production equipment where the components need to address from, for example, high temperatures and pressures and strong cleaning agents so that a derogation is therefore considered. The mentioned applications of fluoropolymers in seals, hoses, etc. are comparable in the industrial and commercial sectors. The proposed derogation of 6.5 years after EiF in derogation 6a for food contact materials for the purpose of food production for the professional kitchen equipment will not be sufficient as suitable alternative materials have not been identified yet. There won’t be any one-on-one alternatives and fluoropolymers are in usage harmless. In addition to the evidence submitted by FEC attesting to the safety of the class, this gives further evidence that they should be entirely exempted.   The environmental impact of the extended derogation 6a was assessed in chapter 2.4.3.3 in the evaluation of the environmental impact of the proposed exemption provision for food contact materials for industrial and commercial food and feed production: As no data was available to quantify the amount of additional emissions for this specific exemption, the environmental impacts were assessed qualitatively in relation to a worst-case scenario for additional emissions, assuming a full exemption provision for fluoropolymer for the whole food contact materials. In relation to the reference scenario, the additional emissions of the proposed derogation are considered to be small.  Fluoropolymer-based coatings (PTFE) are also widely used for cookware, bakeware and electrical appliances, due to their unique combination of properties (e.g. non-stick, high-temperature resistance, durability, heat conductivity, and resistance to abrasion). A restriction on fluoropolymer-coated cookware is not justified, due to the fact that proposed alternatives are not of sufficient durability. Besides, a ban on fluoropolymer coatings will lead to concerning socioeconomic side-effects on European cookware businesses, especially in Germany, France and Italy, as detailed in the FEC contribution, and in a study commissioned to an independent consultant, Ricardo.   Fluoropolymers should be fully exempted from the scope of the restriction proposal.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Commercial kitchen appliances, such as commercial coffee machines, fall under the WEEE directive due to electronic components and are properly disposed of at the end of their life cycle. The high proportion of stainless steel and plastic materials as well as rare earth metals can be recycled and reused. The PFAS-relevant components are sent for thermal recycling.    Fluoropolymer coated cookware and bakeware can be handled properly at their end of life, with minimal risk of environmental emissions of non-polymeric PFAS. Incineration, recycling and landfilling all adequately address the possibility of PFAS emissions, and consequently fluoropolymer-coated food contact items are unlikely to represent a risk to human health or the environment.    Furthermore, studies on incineration has concluded on the safety of the end-of-life phase:   The study "Pilot-Scale Fluoropolymer Incineration Study: Thermal Treatment of a Mixture of Fluoropolymers under Representative European Municipal Waste Combustor Conditions" executed by the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT) concludes that at the end of their life cycle, fluoropolymers do not generate measurable PFAS emissions during incineration under representative European incineration plant conditions and therefore do not pose a risk to human health and the environment.  Similarly, the publication "Waste incineration of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) to evaluate potential formation of Per- and Poly-Fluorinated Alkyl Substances (PFAS) in flue gas" (at https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0045653519306435) concludes that municipal incineration of PTFE using the best available technologies is not a significant source of the investigated PFAS and should be considered an acceptable form of waste treatment.

General Comments: Woodward L’Orange has been developing and manufacturing injection systems in the industrial and off-highway segment. We also manufacture common rail technology for power-to-x and heavy fuel oil applications. Our injection systems are used in power units for ships, power plants, emergency power supply, railroad applications and other heavy-duty machinery.

In the present restriction proposal, PFAS are defined as substances with at least one fully fluorinated methyl or methylene carbon atom. Due to this the chemical scope of the proposed restriction is very broad, containing over 10 000 substances. Different substances with different applications and risk profiles are grouped together based on their chemical structure alone.

Article 68 of the REACH Regulation stipulates that substances which pose an unacceptable risk to the environment may be regulated by restrictions. Using that logic, any application using PFAS for which no risk could be identified must remain possible to do in the future.

Our company only uses so-called “Polymers of low concern” by definition of the OECD (PTFE, ETFE, FEP, PFA, PVDF and VDF-co-HFP). PFAS containing parts would be mainly seals used in high-temperature and/or high-pressure environments.
The reasons we use PFAS materials are that in the high-temperature and high-pressure environments where our products operate, no other substances have similar properties, especially temperature resistance, chemical resistance and service life. PFAS / Polymers of low concern in the seals are present in a solid state. The materials are chemically inert.

A survey on a significant part of our supply chain showed that over 50% of our suppliers would be affected by the proposed restriction. Some of them have reported that they would no longer be able to manufacture and sell their products in the EU at all.
80% of suppliers do not have an alternative ready as of now. Realistically, qualifying new materials would take anywhere from 12-15 years. Even if a supplier has an alternative to the current materials used, the alternative material does not have the same properties in temperature resistance, chemical resistance and service life.
This poses a significant safety risk when applied to our products in emergency power supply units. We would no longer be able to deliver injection systems of the same capacity to hospitals, data centers and power plants looking for an emergency power supply option.

Combined Comments:
General Comments: Xylem is a downstream user of PFASs and a global provider of high technology products and systems designed to effectively meet the demands and challenges of treating water and wastewater and of premium field, portable, online and laboratory analytical instrumentation serving water, wastewater, ocean/coastal, food & beverage, environmental, chemical and pharmaceutical markets. Xylem recognizes the concerns raised by the Dossier Submitters on the safe use of some PFAS and is aware of the increased scrutiny on PFAS substances in line with the EU’s chemical strategy for sustainability and goals of the Green Deal for a toxic-free environment.
Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs) are a broad class of different, but structurally related, chemical substances that have diverse and special properties. For instance, fluoropolymers, a sub-group within the large PFAS family, are high molecular weight polymers that have, not only specific toxicological and environmental profiles but also unique physicochemical properties. These properties have led to fluoropolymers, being used in applications where they enable high levels of product performance.
In 2020, the European Commission published the Chemical Strategy for Sustainability (CSS)1 and announced an intention to ban non-essential uses of PFASs in the EU. In 2023, five European Countries2 proposed a far-reaching ban on the entire PFAS class across industrial, professional and consumer uses and/or subsequent article service life under the EU REACH regulation. This proposal is known as the ‘universal’ PFAS restriction3. To avoid significant (i.e., disproportionate) negative impacts on EU society, the proposed PFAS restriction acknowledges that it will be necessary to continue to use PFASs in specific (derogated) uses, at least for the time needed until safer alternative substances or technologies become available.
Under REACH, a restriction is any measure on the manufacture, placing on the market or use of a substance (on its own, in a mixture or in an article) used to address an ‘unacceptable’ risk. REACH restrictions, therefore, are not limited to bans but can comprise, for example, requirements for use of risk management measures, training or certification. Before a restriction can be implemented, the European Commission and the EU member states must have concluded that it is the most appropriate way to address the identified risk. To inform this decision, restriction proposals (also called Annex XV restriction reports) should include a comprehensive restriction and regulatory management option analysis (RMOA).
The European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) is currently considering the Annex XIV report for the universal PFAS restriction, including the restriction and regulatory management option analysis performed. Specifically, ECHA’s scientific committees for risk assessment (RAC) and socio-economic analysis (SEAC) are developing ‘opinions’ on the proposal for the European Commission, who will then decide on whether to implement the proposal after discussions with EU member states. The RAC and SEAC opinions will be informed by the public consultation on the proposal, which is open until the 25th of September 2023. The RAC and SEAC opinions are expected in 2024.
Xylem, as an expert stakeholder on the applications of PFASs in water, wastewater and analytical technologies for industrial and professional uses, intends to engage constructively in the public consultation on the proposal and would like to take this opportunity to inform ECHA that it is currently developing a detailed response to the public consultation with the aim of facilitating better, more proportionate, regulation of PFASs. Xylem will provide a more detailed submission in September and through this initial submission, Xylem will outline the approach it will take to contribute to the public consultation.
Xylem has over 30 specific brand companies that specialize in water products and services that move, treat, analyze, monitor and return water to the environment, in public utility, industrial, residential and commercial building services settings. Xylem’s products cover every aspect of water, from pumping, piping, measuring, analyzing, cleaning, and pipe inspections. Fluoropolymers are used in these applications to provide essential functionality such as chemical and thermal resistance, elasticity, abrasion resistance, dirt- and hydrophobic functions, as well as excellent electrical resistance.
Xylem considers that because the Annex XV report does not assess a complete range of potential restriction or regulatory management options (it only assesses the appropriateness of a ban), it has not been clearly demonstrated that the proposed restriction is the most appropriate means to regulate the potential risks of PFASs. Specifically, the Annex XV report should include a comprehensive comparative restriction and regulatory management option analysis based on the criteria given in Annex XV of REACH of effectiveness, practicality and monitorability.
As currently proposed, a ban on all PFASs will have significant negative impacts on the water and wastewater industry and, as a result, European society. The impacts of a ban on many critical uses in the water and wastewater industry, as outlined above, have not yet been identified and assessed in the Annex XV report. This is a significant limitation of the Annex XV report and is not consistent with evidence-based decision-making and the principle of better regulation.
For example, Xylem’s ultraviolet (UV) and ozone systems are used to sterilize and disinfect contaminated water to independently verified drinking water standards, internationally recognized certification and regulatory processes- and meet World Health Organization (WHO) standards and European (Drinking Water Directive) legislation. PFAS polymers are used in UV disinfection and ozone oxidation systems in articles such as seals and connectors to hold parts in place or provide low friction and anticorrosion properties. No viable alternative has been identified for these uses and failure to use PFAS polymers would result in these parts disintegrating from the UV rays. A ban on PFAS would, therefore, lead to potential substitution with lesser suitable materials, lowering the water quality and subsequently causing harm to many people’s health and safety.
Xylem intends to demonstrate that an alternative restriction proposal, including a derogation for the continued use of PFASs, more specifically fluoropolymers and perfluoropolyethers, in industrial and professional applications where safe use for human health and the environment are assured over their complete lifecycle) would be a more appropriate regulatory measure than a ban.
Xylem is currently undertaking assessments that will address two main aspects:
i) whether restriction options other than a ban, for example the mandatory use of specific risk management measures that control or minimize emissions and exposures would be a more appropriate approach to regulation; allowing essential uses to continue;
ii) under what circumstances, a ban on the use of fluoropolymers and perfluoropolyethers could be designed to ensure that critical functions (and benefits) are not lost to society.
Specifically, the assessments will explore the scope (i.e., applications) and duration of any transitional periods needed to avoid disproportionate social impacts by using information on alternatives (technical and economic feasibility) and socio-economic analysis.
Following this high-level submission, Xylem will submit a detailed submission in September bas
Xylem’s technologies enable a zero-pollution future and is committed to contributing to evidence-based chemical policy and regulation. Xylem is confident that a coherent, regulatory approach for PFASs that ensures their safe use whilst also ensuring that critical technologies remain available can be achieved.

PFAS can be important precursor chemicals for various end products. Other, especially fluoropolymers, have important functions in facilities and manufacturing processes, such as seals, valves, linings, or membranes; without them, a facility cannot be operated safely. Both the production and use of necessary precursor chemicals (e.g. transported isolated intermediates) and plant engineering aspects must be taken into account. Important aspects here include both the availability of products and the preservation of jobs.  • Resilience in the EU must be ensured. With an extensive ban on polyfluorinated substances and polymers, the production and availability of important products such as pharmaceuticals, medical devices, and electronic components such as semiconductors and chips in the EU are at stake. There are concerns that production sites may have to be shut down and that investments in new facilities will no longer be made in Europe. It must be ensured that Europe's dependence on imports does not increase.  • The use of fluoropolymers in facilities should generally be exempted. The current form of the restriction proposal will inevitably lead to the shutdown of essential parts of the European pharmaceutical and chemical industry, which rely on materials made of fluoropolymers for which there are currently no alternatives. This affects not only the processes associated with the production of fluoropolymers, but also almost the entire pharmaceutical and chemical production, including all downstream manufacturing processes in other sectors. Therefore, the use of fluoropolymers [as materials] in the (pharmaceutical-chemical) process industry including disposal facilities must be exempted from the restriction, and subsequently, the associated production processes of these fluoropolymers for industrial applications and research purposes as well. In the production processes for fluoropolymers, any release of PFAS into the environment must be avoided according to the state of the art (strictly controlled conditions), which cannot be guaranteed to the same extent in the production outside the EU.  • Functional facilities must be able to continue operating. It must be taken into account that wear and maintenance materials must be provided for sufficiently long periods of time. In many cases, there are no alternatives. Consequences such as the absence of basic chemicals and raw materials, the necessary supply of spare parts for operation, and the repair and maintenance of existing facilities throughout the entire downstream value chain must also be taken into account. The resulting premature decommissioning and disposal would be disproportionately and inexorably burdensome for the environment and society.  • Safe conditions for handling and transportation must be ensured. The use of hoses, valves, or coatings made of PFAS can also be important under certain conditions in the transport of products. It must be ensured that the restriction does not have safety-relevant negative effects when goods are transported and handled.  • A holistic approach is necessary in the evaluation of alternatives. The use of PFAS can offer advantages over alternative processes or substances in terms of energy consumption, environmental protection, plant safety, or occupational safety. The current restriction proposal includes only a few exceptions, and it is questionable whether these will continue to be available in the future, as the socio-economic analysis does not examine whether the operation of production facilities that produce only a few exempted products will still be profitable in the future. Thus, there is a risk that essential applications that are actually exempt from the restriction may no longer be available in the future.  • Research, development, and innovations must continue to be possible in Europe. In order to maintain innovative developments in Europe, it must be possible to use substances and products falling under the PFAS definition within the scope of research and development, as well as in production and process-oriented research and development (PPORD). The use of necessary devices and apparatus in those areas must also continue to be permitted. A specific exemption for PPORD is needed in the restriction proposal. • For many industrial applications of fluoropolymers, there are currently no substitutes for use in compliant facilities. Replacing the installed plant components is neither reasonable nor possible due to the resulting waste and the high costs and production losses. If a ban on immobilized PFAS polymers were to come into effect, this would have far-reaching implications for the entire industry. • The few exceptions point to the following scenario: The replacement of plant components during ongoing operations is technically and personnel-wise hardly possible, and if so, only associated with high costs without any added value. It is evident that the fittings and components for chemical production plants that do not use PTFE are demonstrably more expensive - up to a factor of 10. • If a medium-sized company had to replace ball valves with PTFE seals at all its German locations with other equivalent shut-off valves, this would entail an investment requirement of at least 10% of annual turnover. In addition, there would be plant shutdowns for several weeks. In an era of skilled labor shortages and supply bottlenecks, production shutdowns of several months would accumulate. This would mean, without wanting to calculate further, the ultimate end for production at the German locations and thus an unwarranted interference with the entrepreneur's fundamental rights. • Therefore, we demand that fluoropolymers be excluded from the scope of the restriction. Furthermore, the production and disposal of these polymers must be secured in the EU under appropriate conditions. • The same applies to the entire research and development sector of the German industry, wherein labs almost exclusively use PTFE seals, hoses, and components. Only through these materials can the demanding safety and quality requirements for modern research activities involving changing substances be met. • This ultimately means that not only will industrial operations come to a standstill, but also all research and innovation in Germany. • Today, the production of PFAS polymers is only carried out abroad in non-European countries with environmental impacts that are not known there. In any case, increased climate impacts result from the transportation of plant components to Europe. • The regulations for the Green Deal in Europe and the simultaneous threat of a ban on important PFAS polymers lead to the industry relocating and consumer goods no longer being manufactured and used under high European environmental standards. • This entails a complete de-industrialization of the European continent with unforeseen consequences. A loss of prosperity can be expected for the population, with disadvantages for the entire society, especially in the supply of people, including and especially in the healthcare sector. • The production of these goods shifts to less regulated foreign countries, and importers dictate the prices. This also leads to further dependencies on other, sometimes undemocratic countries. This is precisely what the political agenda is intended to prevent. Negative effects, such as those experienced during the Ukraine conflict, should not be repeated. • In the end, there will be a disadvantage for the entire global population without any added value for the environment and health protection, but with negative effects on global climate and biodiversity protection due to relocated production." From the perspective of the chemical pharmaceutical industry, the following applications are of great importance: Material use: I. Synthesis: Due to their specific reactivity, certain fluorinated alkyl compounds are used as protective groups in chemical synthesis to carry out targeted reactions and avoid undesirable by-products. II. Catalysis: Certain fluorinated alkyl compounds can support specific reactions as catalysts. Used products: I. Seals: Seals based on fluoropolymers play an important role in the entire processing industry, such as in the production of (bio)pharmaceutical-chemical products. Due to their chemical resistance (safety aspect) and physiological safety (FDA approval/USP Class), fluoropolymer-based seals are used as standardized industrial products in the chemical and pharmaceutical environment. PFAS-based seals are often essential for ensuring safe and compliant operation of facilities for the production of basic chemicals or certain pharmaceutical-chemical products under extreme conditions or requiring high purity. In addition to manufacturing, the use of fluoropolymer-based seals also affects chemical handling facilities and the transport vehicles they handle (rail tank cars, tank trucks, tankers, containers, etc.). Valves and pressure-bearing accessories (e.g. valves, strainers): Valves and pressure-bearing accessories in chemical and pharmaceutical industry facilities are often exposed to aggressive and corrosive media, requiring them to withstand stress reliably and permanently. A material that does not withstand the given stresses in the long term results in very high safety risks. Almost all valves with high requirements for tightness are either made entirely of fluoro-polymers, are lined with them, or at least require fluoro-polymer seals. In addition, many pharmaceutical processes require membrane valves with PTFE membranes due to their chemical resistance and are specifically specified and prescribed. I. Lined pipelines and hoses: Many processes in the chemical and pharmaceutical environment place high requirements (e.g. corrosion resistance) on the material to be used. In these cases, lined pipelines made of fluoropolymers (PTFE/PFA) are used to prevent corrosion or other reactions with the material of the pipelines or hoses and to prevent contamination in the product. In addition to these special requirements, these pipelines and packaging materials must meet the legal requirements for tightness (WGC, BREF ex IED). Hoses made of fluoropolymers (e.g. PTFE) are used, for example, in the pharmaceutical industry and in the filling of material medical products. They are also relevant for filling chemicals, sampling, and analysis technology, and are irreplaceable, especially due to the high purity requirements. II. Membranes made of fluoropolymers are also used as filter membranes for sterile filtration in the production of medical products and pharmaceuticals, as well as in biotechnology. They are also important components in membrane pumps and (pressure) sensors. III. Flame retardancy in sensitive areas: For safety reasons, certain components must be equipped with flame retardants. Many electrical and electronic applications are necessary for the implementation of digitalization and the energy revolution, extending to renewable energies; network infrastructure, digital end devices, and electric vehicles are just a few examples. For the functionality and service life of these products, flame-retardant cables, plastic enclosures, and components may be required. A restriction must not lead to the inability to comply with fire protection regulations or insurance requirements. Pharmaceutical-chemical industry facilities in Europe are subject to a licensing procedure in which it is officially examined whether operating these facilities is safe. This process is time-consuming and expensive and must be repeated for relevant changes and planning. Therefore, changing existing facilities is not readily possible. It must be ensured and demonstrated that even without the use of PFAS polymers, the necessary protection of the environment against gaseous and liquid leaks is guaranteed with alternative sealing and valve systems, and that, for example, the requirements set by TA-Luft are met. If suitable alternatives are not available, facilities may need to be shut down, and if possible, converted to other processes, as soon as PFAS-containing spare parts are needed.  Changing processes in the chemical and pharmaceutical industry, where this should be technologically possible, requires a sufficiently long planning phase and very high investments due to the time-consuming licensing procedure. It is only feasible if application-specific substitutes are available that at least demonstrate the same performance and service life, especially under harsh conditions, to continue to operate facilities safely. The longevity, i.e., the persistence of the materials, is an important property for the safety of the procedures. In addition, process changes in chemical reactions usually result in a changed composition of the resulting reaction products. Targeted intermediate and final products would have to be newly specified and approved for the respective intended use in lengthy investigations. According to experts, there are currently no adequate substitutes to operate the numerous affected facilities in a future-proof manner, justifying the effort of going through the facility licensing process again. In cases where an alternative is not available, a complete redesign of materials would be necessary, the success of which is in no way guaranteed. Chemical processes that are indispensable, e.g. on PTFE-lined pipes and reactors, would be discontinued in the EU in the future, and production would be completely relocated to non-European countries. This would lead to increased dependency of the EU on imports and contradict efforts for European sovereignty. In the event of a PFAS restriction, the impact on facilities and production processes must be considered and exemptions must be taken into account. It is also important that spare parts for the facilities are available to ensure a long useful life in terms of sustainability. Many regulations demand the purity and tightness of production facilities, requirements that are defined in corresponding regulations. These binding and increasingly stricter requirements, for example, for the tightness of facilities, can only be met according to the recognized state of the art by using PTFE and other PFAS polymers. The same applies to purity requirements in the production of certain pharmaceuticals or food products as well as in medical technology. The production of renewable energies also depends on these polymers.  The constructive implementation according to the recognized state of the art has been carried out for decades using PTFE and other PFAS polymers:  1. The American Food and Drug Administration (FDA) values the low elution and prescribes the use of PTFE sole approval as a sealing material for the food industry within the framework of GMP regulations.   2. In medical technology, products made of PTFE are prescribed for the following applications: analytics and laboratory applications, degassing, feed lines, disinfection.  3. General Comments: Zeus requests an exemption from regulations as they pertain to PTFE, FEP, PFA and PVDF in their uses for medical devices, aerospace safety enhancements, green energy initiatives and semiconductor manufacturing.  The use of fluoropolymers in these applications are the result of their unique properties and are used as the polymer of last resort by design engineers due to their expense and difficulty in processing.  The solution to PFAS in the environment is to control and regulate the manufacturing of the polymers concerned, not in their processing or uses.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Please see the lists below provided in an effort to completely cover all product Sectors and (sub-) uses Zeus is involved in globally.    Tubing, heat shrink, and roll cover utilizing various fluoropolymers PTFE, FEP, PFA, PVDF, ETFE, ECTFE, THV  Used in Medical Devices including: Catheters for electrophysiology, cardiovascular, peripheral, neurovascular, structural heart, endoscopy, colonoscopies, endometrial and atrial fibrillation ablation, vitreoretinal microsurgery of the eye, and insulin infusion,  Heat shrink tubing used in manufacturing catheters, Diagnostic equipment  Industrial applications for fluid handling in: Analytical chemistry equipment Chemical and fertilizer manufacturing and handling Electrical,  Food and beverage,  Mining,  Pharmaceutical manufacturing,  Petroleum production and processing,  Semiconductor manufacturing,  Water and wastewater,  Automotive, Aerospace and Electrical systems:  including fuel lines, batteries, sensor protection, wire coating, tubing and heat shrink for wire protectors and conduits, Machinery roll covers,  Gas recovery in animal waste and landfill systems, Air pollution control systems Fluoropolymer monofilament, beading, ribbons, and profiles  Primarily PTFE used in medical devices as floss, manufacturing aids, and as sutures.   PTFE nonwoven membranes Medical devices for structural heart devices, cardiovascular and peripheral stent coverings, and gastric bypass device coverings. Industrial filtration applications. The way derogations were assigned is not consistent. Some unlimited derogations apply to products under other EU regulations (biocidal products within Regulations (EU) 528/2012, plant protection products within Regulation (EC) 1107/2009, and human and veterinary medicinal products within Regulation (EC) 726/2004, Regulation (EU) 2019/6 and Directive 2001/83/EC). While others such as production of medical devices covered under Regulation (EU) 2017/745 have a time limited derogation and then only for specific applications within medical devices, not all medical devices.  The same logic and general derogation discussed in the Proposal Sections 2.2.3 Active Substances in Plant Protection Products (PPP), Biocidal Products (BP) and Medicinal Products (MP) and 2.2.4 Conclusion on the Most Appropriate Regulatory Risk Management Options should be applied to medical devices regulated under Regulation (EU) 2017/745.  All medical device components we manufacture with fluoropolymers that are used in medical devices have undergone extensive clinical evaluations to ensure safety to humans.  In addition, the design and manufacture are controlled to exclude or justify inclusion of any carcinogenic, mutagenic or toxic to reproduction (‘CMR’), of category 1A or 1B , in accordance with Part 3 of Annex VI of Regulation (EC) No 1272/2008 which includes the nonfluoropolymer PFAS that have shown to potentially be a CMR.  The regulation also limits substances having endocrine-disrupting properties relevant to human health. USP and ISO Data on the compatibility and safety of components used in our manufacture of fluoropolymer products is presented in the table below.    In addition, the use of polymerization aids in the production of some fluoropolymer has a time limited derogation for some, but not PTFE, PVDF and FKM.  However, PTFE is the most common fluoropolymer used in medical devices (tubes and catheters, stent wraps) and in automotive and aerospace applications. A timed derogation for the manufacturer of all fluoropolymers including and especially PTFE must granted otherwise most medical devices will cease to be manufactured between the Entry into Force (EiF) and the proposed 18 month transition period for PTFE. The Proposed 12 year derogation for medical devices is useless if PTFE is not available. These medical devices have a longer derogation time because of the lack of alternatives.  How will PTFE medical devices, tubes and catheters be manufactured after 18 months if no one is making PTFE? Carl Dannenberg (Scientific Officer, BAuA) suggested in the Chemwatch PFAS Meeting on April 25th that the intention was that if an application is derogated, the supply chain would be as well. The issue with that statement is it is not in the Proposal’s original or current version.  This intent needs to be added to the proposal or provide a derogation for the manufacture of PTFE.  Tubing in others to economic sectors and applications don’t appear to have derogations, but are needed for the same properties and lack alternatives, just as they do in medical devices.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Zeus has tested its incoming fluoropolymer resins, its scrap, and articles produced for the target PFAS compounds without finding any in the scrap or articles tested. This testing was prompted by Regulation (EU) 2017/745 for medical devices and applies to all other applications since we use the same process and polymers. Therefore, there is no risk from the disposal of the scrap which is at the end of its life and no risk from the articles to release target PFAS compounds at the downstream end of its life. See attached data (PFAS Data Summary). We currently recycle 35% of PTFE scrap materials.  The remainder is currently landfilled.  The recycled PTFE scrap is purchase by a company that breaks the PTFE down into a very fine powder for use in inks , paints and other coatings. That path of recycling may disappear as an option if fluoropolymers are banned from these applications. Previously we recycled almost 100% of our PTFE scrap materials, but fear of this proposal and proposed changes to US laws caused the recycler to change what they would accept. We are currently evaluating a waste-to-energy option through cement kilns. Landfilling of some scrap will probably continue for some time. We currently recycle 90% of our melt processed fluoropolymers with the remainder landfilled. The melt process scrap is sold to recyclers that clean and re-process the resin for use in making products that do not require virgin resin.  Contrary to the cited documents and opinions of the dossier submitters, we can find no studies or evidence that any of our fluoropolymer materials will release any target PFAS to the environment while in a landfill. Especially PTFE because there is no non-fluorinated part to degrade. To the contrary we have found document EOL2 that supports our claim that fluoropolymers do not release target or arrowhead PFAS while in a landfill. Our fluoropolymer articles are not soluble, mobile, or bioavailable at any time during use or in a landfill and do not form micro-plastic particles in a landfill.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: While some of our waste is incinerated, Zeus is not involved directly in any design or ownership of incineration facilities or processes.  However, we have found several studies that suggest that fluoropolymers are completely destroyed in municipal incinerators, industrial kilns and hazardous waste incinerators without releasing any products of incomplete combustion. Therefore supporting our position that fluoropolymers are not a threat to human health or the environment at the end-of-life. We have received no indication or guarantee that suitable PTFE resins will be available to replace all grades currently in use. Even if one or more resin suppliers are able to provide a resin within the eighteen months after EiF it will take us at least two years to develop the processing for the different grades and work with our customers to approve the conversion of their products. Medical device and tubing and catheter customers will need three years to revalidate and an additional three years following resubmittal for their devise(s)’approval by government agencies. The above indicates a minimumt eight years for transition after the successful PTFE resin is provided by resin manufacturers.  A timed derogation for the manufacturer of all fluoropolymers including and especially PTFE must granted otherwise most medical devices will cease to be manufactured between the Entry into Force (EiF) and the proposed 18 month transition period for PTFE. The Proposed 12 year derogation for medical devices is useless if PTFE is not available. These medical devices have a longer derogation time because of the lack of alternatives.  How will PTFE medical devices, tubes and catheters be manufactured after 18 months if no one is making PTFE? Carl Dannenberg (Scientific Officer, BAuA) suggested in the Chemwatch PFAS Meeting on April 25th that the intention was that if an application is derogated, the supply chain would be as well. The issue with that statement is it is not in the Proposal’s original or current version.  This intent needs to be added to the proposal or provide a derogation for the manufacture of PTFE. Tubing in others to economic sectors and applications don’t appear to have derogations, but are needed for the same properties and lack alternatives, just as they do in medical devices.

10. Analytical methods: The proposed total fluorine (TF) analysis of articles should be reconsidered since it is not specific to PFAS and will be biased extremely high due to the numerous inorganic and organic fluorine containing compounds in the environment.  The test is at best a screening tool.  TF is not a proxy for PFAS or a substitute for target analysis and should not be used for conclusions on articles or polymeric materials. Fluorine is the 13th most common element on the planet. Toothpaste contains 1350 – 5000 ppm of inorganic fluoride.  Natural microorganisms and plants produce organofluorine compounds (Murphy, 2003; O’Hagan, 2002; Proudfoot, 2006).  Twenty percent of commercially available human and veterinary pharmaceuticals contain fluoro-compounds (ACS Omega, 2020). These pharmaceuticals along with the biocidal and plant protection products containing fluoro-compounds are derogated from this proposal yet they will show up in this analysis.  Numerous inorganic and organofluorine containing materials that are not PFAS will be detected in this method.  While they have their limitations, Fourier Transformed Infra-red (FT-IR) and or Raman spectroscopy could be used to detect surface coatings and identify polymers as a more targeted analysis.  Even the Extractable OrganoFluorine (EOF) compared to mass balance of target compounds has shown 45% - 92% unknown fluorine compounds (Koch, 2019). In addition, data in Karrman, 2019 indicated EOF could be biased high (102%) or low (2%) when compared to target analysis. TF would have a much higher bias than even EOF.
