General Comments: Zhejiang Noah Fluorinechemical Co., Ltd. mainly produces high-efficiency and environmentally friendly perfluorohexanone fire extinguishing agent, fluorinated cooling fluid and high-end electronic cleaning agents containing fluorine.
Hexafluoro-propylene dimer (CAS:3709-71-5) and hexafluoropropylene trimer (CAS:2107-25-7) were applied as coolant for supercomputing center, date center,because of excellent environmental performance, good safety performance, efficient electrical insulation properties, low dielectric constant and nonflammable.
Information on hexafluoro-propylene dimer (CAS:3709-71-5) was retrieved from the registered substances database on the ECHA website, where a comprehensive evaluation of its PBT properties was conducted and reliable conclusions were given. The REACH chemical assessment showed no PBT or vPvB characteristics.
All impurities identified as present in HFP kinetic dimer at  0.1% or bigger than 0.1% are isomers or homologues of HFP kinetic dimer, with physical/chemical properties essentially the same as HFP kinetic dimer. Impurities therefore have PBT characteristics equivalent to HFP kinetic dimer. The ultimate degradation products are expected to be hydrofluoric acid, trifluoroacetic acid, isoperfluorobutyric acid and carbon dioxide. HF and CO2 are inorganic substances not needing a PBT assessment and TFA and PFBA are not bioconcentrating or toxic.
By screening and definitive REACH PBT criteria, HFP kinetic dimer is very persistent, “vP”. An evaluation of its fate in water or soil concludes that HFP kinetic dimer is rapidly removed to the atmospheric compartment by volatilization, and it will not partition into water or soil from the atmosphere. Therefore, this substance is non-persistent in the aquatic and terrestrial environments. It is very persistent only in the atmosphere and is subject to long-range transport in the atmosphere but is not subject to deposition in remote or pristine environments. Due to mixing in the atmosphere and lack of partitioning out of the atmosphere, concentrations in the biosphere will be negligible. Widespread exposure to HFP kinetic dimer will not occur.
Based on the expected partitioning behavior of HFP kinetic dimer, additional laboratory studies on the biodegradation and bioaccumulation in the water, sediment and soil compartments are not relevant for the evaluation of PBT properties of this substance. The “B” criterion in aquatic organisms is not met due to lack of exposure. The calculated log Koa value indicates that HFP kinetic dimer cannot bioaccumulate in air-breathing animals. Collectively, the log Kow, the HLC, and the calculated Koa indicate that HFP kinetic dimer is not expected to bioaccumulate in aquatic, sediment or soil organisms. HFP kinetic dimer does not fulfill the criteria for bioaccumulative (“B”) or very bioaccumulative (“vB”).
Based on available data, HFP kinetic dimer is not classified as carcinogenic, mutagenic, or toxic to reproduction or specific target organ toxic after repeated dose. HFP kinetic dimer does not meet the REACH “T” criteria for mammalian toxicity. This information combined with the lack of acute aquatic toxicity can be used to conclude that HFP kinetic dimer does not fulfill the screening criteria for toxic (“T”).
The data show that the properties of the substance do NOT meet the specific criteria in Annex XIII Section 1, or while not allowing a direct comparison with all the criteria, nevertheless indicate that the substance would not have these properties. Substance is NOT PBT or vPvB.
The hexafluoropropylene trimer (CAS:2107-25-7) will be decomposed in the atmosphere to produce hydrofluoric acid, trifluoroacetic acid, isoperfluorobutyric acid and carbon dioxide. HF and CO2 are inorganic substances not needing a PBT assessment and TFA and PFBA are not bioconcentrating or toxic.
The experimental results are consistent with the calculated bond dissociation energies and UV-vis excitation spectra of the radical. Additional calculated C-C BDEs for a number of fluorocarbon radicals show that radicals can be designed with very low C-C BDEs for the generation of CF3.radicals.The ultimate degradation products are expected to be  trifluoroacetic acid (TFA, CAS# 76-05-1) and hydrofluoric acid (HF, CAS# 7664-39-3).  These acids are miscible in water and are completely ionized in rainwater.  They are expected to undergo wet deposition with no further significant transformation.
The LC50/ppwv of hexafluoropropylene trimers is larger than 10000，it can be inferred from the bioaccumulation and toxicity of hexafluoropropylene dimers that hexafluoropropylene trimers also do not have PBT properties.
Trifluoroacetic acid is a strong organic acid with a pKa of 0.23.  It is miscible with water, and its low octanol/water partition coefficient (log Pow= -2.1) indicates no bioaccumulation potential.  TFA does not accumulate significantly in lower forms of aquatic organisms such as bacteria, small invertebrates, oligotrichoworms, and some aquatic plants (including duckweed).
The definition of PFAS in the proposal is very broad and therefore covers thousands of substances with different (ecological) toxicity characteristics, which is inconsistent with science and ECHA's own reading policy guidelines. In addition, the OECD Expert Group on PFAS issued the following position in 2021 in support of more targeted restrictions: "As PFAS are a chemical class with multiple molecular structures as well as physical, chemical and biological properties, it is strongly recommended that this diversity be appropriately identified and communicated in a clear, specific and descriptive manner." The term "PFASs" is a broad, generic, non-specific term that does not inform whether a compound is harmful, but merely indicates that the compound under the term has the same structure with a fully fluorinated methyl or methylene carbon portion. This statement was again supported by the majority of experts in the UNEP Environmental Impact Assessment Panel in 2022. In other jurisdictions around the world, such as the Health and Safety Executive in the United Kingdom and the Environmental Protection Agency in the United States, efforts to regulate PFAS do not target the above substances, but focus on certain groups of substances and certain applications (e.g. PFOS/PFOA, etc.).
Hexafluoropropylene dimers and trimers have a vital role in semiconductors, precision electronics, power, new energy (lithium-ion battery vehicles, energy storage, etc.), data centers, transportation, construction and other fields. Banning the substances in question will now have a significant impact on the corresponding industry in Europe. According to current knowledge, they cannot be replaced by substitutes even in the long run, and it is difficult to find suitable and equivalent chemicals because they have unique properties and no unknown or unforeseen hazards.
In 2019, the EU issued the European Green Agreement, proposing that the first is to formulate and publish the European Climate Law as soon as possible, aiming to formally incorporate the EU's goal of achieving carbon neutrality by 2050 into EU law. The second is the development of the European Climate Convention, which aims to attract the attention and participation of citizens and all sectors of society in climate action. The third is to update the 2030 Climate Target Plan, raising the previous goal of reducing emissions by 40% from the 1990 level by 2030 to 55%.
Regulation (EU) No 517/2014 (F-gas regulation) is a regulation that aims to reduce emissions of fluorinated greenhouse gases in the EU by 2030 to one-third of 2014 emissions.
The inclusion of the above hexafluoropropylene dimer and trimer substances in the scope of PFAS regulation contradicts the objectives of the relevant legislation enacted by the European Union. The development of data centers, semiconductors, renewable energy, electric vehicles, transportation and other areas is essential to achieve the European Green Deal's energy saving and emission reduction targets.
In order not to endanger the important objectives of the relevant act and not to threaten the important industrial base of Europe, the general restriction of the above-mentioned fluorides in the framework of the REACH regulation should in any case be avoided, and it is proposed that the above-mentioned fluorides be completely excluded from the scope of the restriction proposal.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Hexafluoropropylene dimers (CAS:3709-71-5) and trimers (CAS:2107-25-7) belong to the field of electronics and semiconductors(Annex E.2.11.) and are used as heat transfer cooling working medium for supercomputing center, date center, semiconductor dry etching, wafer testing, packaging, etc. As well as high temperature electronic products cleaning treatment agent, insulating liquid, solvent diluent, etc. In addition to the above fields, hexafluoro-propylene dimer (CAS:3709-71-5) also can used as foam blowing agents mentioned in the Applications of fluorinated gases (Annex E.2.8.).

6. Missing uses: The draft restrictions do not mention the application of liquid cooling for thermal management in supercomputing center, data centers, semiconductors, precision electronics, lithium-ion batteries. In the context of the new industrial revolution, the rapid iteration of big data, computing power, algorithms, etc., is driving artificial intelligence to enter a new stage, which also promotes the continuous innovation of AI architecture, and thanks to this, the scale of AI servers continues to expand and the number of clusters continues to increase. At present, there are three types of architecture types: small and medium size, medium size, and large size, which correspond to 1000, 2000, and 2000-18000 clusters respectively. According to statistics, the global AI server market size is $12.2 billion in 2020, and the global AI intelligent server market is expected to reach $28.8 billion by 2025, with a five-year CAGR of 18.8%. Since the beginning of this year, the development of AI has ushered in a small climax, first ChatGPT landed in the Apple Store and became the fastest application in history to break through the million users; After that, Google, Huawei, Baidu, iFlytek and other companies have launched their own large language models; Second, the strong launch of Apple Vision Pro marks the formal entry into the era of spatial computing; At the NVIDIA COMPUTEX 2023 conference just past, the full-scale mass production of supercomputer GH200 undoubtedly provided strong hardware support for the continued development of AI. In the case of NVIDIA DGX H100, a single 8GPU DGX H100 server consumes 10.2kW, which is higher than the power consumption of an entire rack in a traditional data center. In view of the carbon neutrality targets set out in the European Green Deal issued by the European Union, finding ways to save energy and reduce emissions of cooling is key. Common cooling methods can be divided into: air-cooled and liquid-cooled according to the refrigerant. As one of the alternative cooling methods, the air cooling system works by blowing the hot air out of the room through the fan, so as to achieve the cooling effect. Specifically, an air-cooled system completes the process by drawing air in from the front of the rack and, after passing through an internal radiator, expelling hot air from the back of the rack. The advantages of air-cooled systems are lower cost, easy maintenance and management, and no additional water resources are required. They will not dissolve in the human body, drinking water, and environment under normal use, and have no significant impact on the environment or humans. At the same time, fluoropolymers play an irreplaceable role in various industries due to their excellent durability, low dielectric loss, and dielectric resistance. The ECHA-PFAS proposal to restrict the use of fluoropolymers will have a huge negative impact on European society, seriously leading to the disappearance of many important industries in the EU. Therefore, we suggest that fluoropolymers should not be included in the PFAS restriction range.

In the 5G high-frequency transmission industry, PTFE, FEP, and ETFE are suitable for low attenuation data transmission cables due to their excellent electrical insulation, particularly low loss factor, low dielectric constant, and moisture absorption. Fluoropolymers have excellent high-temperature and pressure resistance properties, and can be used as insulation media for RF cables, greatly improving the transmission signals. If fluoropolymers cannot be used, the companies in Europe that process fluoropolymers, which account for 90% of revenue will have the risks to shut down.

Looking at other communication cable materials that we know, considering the comprehensive performance advantages provided by fluoropolymers, there is no substitute that can replace fluoropolymers. For example, in terms of heat resistance, fluoropolymers have excellent thermal stability and can maintain performance stability under high temperature conditions. They can be used normally under high temperature conditions up to 200 ℃. However, PE and PVC cable insulation is generally only suitable for external environments of 70-90 ℃. PEEK may be another alternative in terms of durability and usage temperature, but the cost of use is about 5-8 times that of PTFE; In terms of flame retardant, fluoropolymers (limit oxygen index 60-95%) have a higher limit oxygen index and flame retardancy compared to PVC (limit oxygen index 36-47%) and PE (limit oxygen index 18-26%). At the same time, PVC cables will release HCl gas and black smoke during combustion, causing "secondary damage" after a fire; In terms of electrical performance, if wants to have the same insulation performance as fluoropolymers, no other material can provide the same low dielectric properties. The dielectric constant and insulation resistance of fluoropolymers are significantly better than other substitutes, and compared to substitutes such as PE and PVC, the signal attenuation of fluoropolymer insulated cables is smaller.

In summary, the complete substitute of PFAS in high-frequency transmission and communication cables is highly unlikely to exist, or it cannot be replaced in practical applications. Therefore, we suggest that fluoropolymers used for this purpose should be exempt from regulations.

Unfortunately, the focus on permit issuance, supervision, and enforcement does not result in a proportional reduction of the negative effects of PFAS. Completely reducing the emission and discharge of PFAS is a process that has been ongoing for many decades, and so far has not led to a reduction to zero emissions/discharge. Another concern is that products containing PFAS end up as waste at the end of their life1). PFAS cannot be separated in such cases. Also, PFAS is not destroyed in incineration plants. As a result, even after a ban, PFAS will remain in our living environment for a very long time, with possible harmful effects. We cannot reverse what has already occurred. Worldwide, PFAS is present in the environment and in humans, as a result of years of emission of PFAS by factories. What we can and want to achieve is to prevent PFAS from causing new damage in the future. In this context, the current restriction proposal is seen as a good step towards a global ban on this group of substances. Because PFAS does not respect the boundaries of a continent, contamination from other continents will continue. The next step should be a global ban. An important factor is that (in the Netherlands) applying the precautionary principle in the permitting and enforcement of PFAS production processes has not been approved by the court up to now2) Furthermore, removing PFAS from soil, groundwater, and surface water - if it is even possible - is technically extremely difficult and very costly. Based on the foregoing, the restriction of the entire group of PFAS is seen as the most appropriate and effective way to eliminate the negative effects on the environment, nature, humans, and animals. Below, this standpoint is further substantiated with specific (local and supra-local) information and various research results.  2 Source of local and regional PFAS contamination In the municipality of Dordrecht, there is a chemical industrial complex. This complex includes the location of Chemours Netherlands B.V (formerly DuPont; hereinafter: Chemours). This factory uses various PFAS types in its production process. Since 1967, Teflon PFTE, Teflon FEP, and Viton have been produced. Also located at the complex are Dow Chemical Dordrecht (polymers) and Delrin Netherlands B.V. (thermoplastic plastics). From 1967 to October 2012, DuPont, later Chemours, used the auxiliary substance PFOA in the production of various fluorine compounds (namely fluoropolymers, homopolymers/copolymers, and fluoroelastomers) in, among others, the Teflon factory. The use of PFOA was terminated because PFOA has been classified as a Substance of Very High Concern (SVHC) at the European level since 2013. The GenX technology (HFPO-DA) has been developed to replace PFOA in the production of fluorinated plastics, including Teflon, since the end of 2012. In this process, the auxiliary substances FRD-902 and FRD-903 are emitted to air and water, and E1 to the air. GenX substances - belonging to PFAS - were identified as a potential SVHC at the national level on 2 February 2018 and as a SVHC at the European level on 26 June 2019.  3 Local concerns about PFAS The municipalities of Sliedrecht, Papendrecht, Dordrecht, and Molenlanden have a close collaboration when it comes to dealing with and combating PFAS. Since 2015, the municipalities of Dordrecht, Sliedrecht, and Papendrecht, and since 2018, the municipality of Molenlanden have investigated the harmful effects of the PFAS group of substances and have also signaled to the national government that the problem is greater than just our municipalities. It is now widely known that, due to their persistence, bioaccumulation, and poor degradability, PFAS have caused irreparable harm that is difficult and in many places impossible to remove. Soil, groundwater, and surface water are contaminated in our area. Swimming is no longer possible everywhere. People cannot eat home-grown produce from their gardens everywhere without concern, and PFAS in nature leads to the accumulation of the substance in animals. The municipalities and residents of our municipalities are deeply concerned about this.  4 Research on the consequences of PFAS Below is a chronological overview of the most important research on (the consequences of) PFAS. This research supports our position to move towards a total ban of PFAS as soon as possible. Since 2018, the Waterschap Rivierenland has been conducting measurements of surface water in its work area. Based on these measurements, the National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM) has advised against consuming fish caught in surface water, due to exceeding the risk threshold value for fish.3) In 2022, the RIVM conducted research on crops from vegetable gardens in Dordrecht, Sliedrecht, Papendrecht, and Molenlanden. Based on this research, the RIVM advised vegetable garden owners in Sliedrecht within 1 kilometer of Chemours not to consume crops from their own gardens. Other vegetable garden owners located within approximately 1 to 10 kilometers to the northwest, northeast, or east of Chemours, or about 2.5 kilometers to the southwest, are advised not to consume vegetables and fruit from their own gardens year-round, due to the high PFAS concentration in these crops. The consumption of own crops should be regularly alternated with those from a store.4) The research agency Arcadis concludes in a study conducted in 2022 on soil and water in vegetable gardens in the municipalities of Dordrecht, Papendrecht, Sliedrecht, and Molenlanden5) that in these municipalities, crops from own gardens can be eaten without restrictions up to a maximum contamination of 4.6 µg/kg PFOA. Above this level, there may be a risk in consuming crops from own gardens. In the immediate vicinity of Chemours, the use of ditch water and shallow groundwater for irrigation of vegetable gardens is not recommended. The agricultural sector in the area of the four municipalities also has concerns about the consequences of PFAS for growing crops and the quality of grassland as food for livestock. Although two studies in 2020 and 2021 of meat samples and agricultural products (meat, eggs, milk) by the Dutch Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) found hardly any exceedance of the current European norms for PFAS in eggs, meat, and fish,6) our farmers are concerned about the real consequences of PFAS in the soil, grassland, and air for their livestock, the grass and silage from their own land that they eat, and for the products they grow on their land. This ongoing uncertainty is having a significant impact on the livelihood security of the agricultural sector in the region. The Safety Board (OVV) published the report "Industry and residents" on 13 April 20237). One of the industries investigated is Chemours. This report provides answers to how residents surrounding industry will be protected against adverse health effects and exposure to industrial emissions, and which measures offer better protection. The Safety Board concludes that the health of residents surrounding industry deserves better protection. The board also calls for competent authorities to act from the precautionary principle. To date, the Dutch courts have not approved the application of this principle. In its report "Risk assessment of exposure to PFAS through food and drinking water in the Netherlands,"8) the RIVM has examined the intake of food and drinking water. It appears that people in the Netherlands are already ingesting more PFAS through food and drinking water than the health-based limit. If people ingest more PFAS than this health-based limit for a longer period of time, harmful health effects cannot be ruled out, according to the RIVM and the Public Health Service. The recreation sector also experiences the consequences of PFAS pollution. Recently (July 2023), the RIVM conducted research on PFAS in swimming water in the region9). Although it was found that the majority of the analyzed swimming water in the municipalities is safe enough for swimming, at one location (Dordrecht, Merwelanden), the advice was not to swim pending further research.  5. Sub-conclusion 1 We endorse the concerns about PFAS expressed in the restriction report. As municipalities, we are confronted daily with the consequences of PFAS for our residents, our businesses, the environment, and nature. PFAS is not only present in the soil of our territory, but also in surface water and groundwater. The consequences of exposure to PFAS are irreversible and are not limited to the boundaries of our municipality or the Netherlands. This calls for action at the European level, and certainly an initiative for, in our view, a much-needed global ban.  6. Response to the contents of the restriction proposal Specific comments on the contents of the restriction proposal are provided below. They are addressed by topic, and, if necessary, the relationship with the restriction proposal is made.  6.1 Scope of the restriction The proposal (pages 50, 68) states that the restriction applies to the manufacture, trade, and use of PFAS in the EU as such and as a component of other substances, in mixtures, and in products above a certain concentration. We note that the ban should also apply to the import of PFAS (in all its forms and product forms) from a country outside the European Union for further processing, production, or transit to or through another EU country. Furthermore, the ban should also oversee the production, trade, and transit between a factory with a location in the EU and one or more locations outside the EU. This is to ensure a comprehensive ban on PFAS.  6.2 Essential use"

Org. name: ZVEI e. V. - German Electro and Digital Industry Association
Combined Comments:
General Comments: ZVEI e. V., the German Electro and Digital Industry Association, represents an industry with an annual turnover of about 225 bn. Euro and 906 thousand employees in 2022.

The proposed ban on the manufacture, use and placing on the market of PFAS (in substances, mixtures, and articles) would have a massive impact on almost all of our member companies, whose technologies are crucial for the energy transition, digitisation, European infrastructure, transport and logistics chains, healthcare, and process automation/measurement technology.

While ZVEI generally supports the objective of avoiding emissions of hazardous substances into the environment and the appropriate regulation of individual substances that pose uncontrollable risks, and our members are committed to continuously improving the environmental compatibility and safety of the products they place on the market, we see the production, research, and development locations of the German and European electro and digital industries, as well as their global competitiveness at serious risk in the event of a blanket ban and therefore call for a fundamental revision of the restriction proposal in key areas.

This consultation article focusses the use of PFAS contained in electrical connectors. A more detailed description is attached in a PDF document.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The restriction dossier summarizes the whole E&E industry in a short paragraph without respecting the complexity of the E&E industry or applications. Nearly every complex technical article is somehow related to E&E from a small bicycle lamp to complex industrial tools. Hence only individual examples can be provided as representatives for a lot of other applications.  (Details in Attachment)

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The PFAS based substances are used in a controlled industrial environment. Management processes like ISO 9001 and ISO14001 ensure the proper and safe handling of these substances.  Connectors are typically collected and treated/milled in the waste stream. Metal components are recycled by melting and reused for creation of new metal alloys. Melting on brass happens at temperature over 1000°C that PFAS lubricants will be decomposed. In any case the PFAS content adhering to connector pins is negligible and impossible to be measured in the exhaust gas during the melting process.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The literature offers different sources on investigations on the incineration of PFAS. In summary PFAS decompose in municipal incineration facilities at BAT level. More details in attached PDF.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: From today’s point of view the recycling industry isn’t impacted because the PFAS adhering to the metal parts decompose during metal recycling. The plastic components of electrical connectors are typically incinerated in case of waste coming from end-of-life goods goods. Production waste is treated single graded with technically and economically reasonable processes.

5. Proposed derogations: We are requesting an exemption for electrical connectors for a period of 12 years plus a reasonable transition period of at least 4 years for all types of electrical connectors. In addition, it must be possible to apply for a further derogation in case no suitable alternative is available on the market. The exemption methodology should be in line with the current RoHS Directive.

Org. name: ZVEI e. V. - German Electro and Digital Industry Association
Combined Comments:
General Comments: ZVEI e. V., the German Electro and Digital Industry Association, represents an industry with an annual turnover of about 225 bn. Euro and 906 thousand employees in 2022.

The proposed ban on the manufacture, use and placing on the market of PFAS (in substances, mixtures, and articles) would have a massive impact on almost all of our member companies, whose technologies are crucial for the energy transition, digitisation, European infrastructure, transport and logistics chains, healthcare, and process automation/measurement technology.

While ZVEI generally supports the objective of avoiding emissions of hazardous substances into the environment and the appropriate regulation of individual substances that pose uncontrollable risks, and our members are committed to continuously improving the environmental compatibility and safety of the products they place on the market, we see the production, research, and development locations of the German and European electro and digital industries, as well as their global competitiveness at serious risk in the event of a blanket ban and therefore call for a fundamental revision of the restriction proposal in key areas.

We are therefore submitting our position and key proposals to this public consultation on the UPFAS restriction proposal. In the coming weeks, we will submit further product-specific contributions to substantiate our proposals and the need for further derogations and an adequate transition period.

Facts and figures:
According to an internal ZVEI survey (see attached), fluoropolymers (including fluoroelastomers and perfluoropolyethers) account for more than 75 % of PFAS uses known to ZVEI members by 2021. Taking into account the companies' production facilities , we estimate that almost 100% of our member companies will be affected by the planned PFAS restriction, although the overall impact will vary from company to company.

In addition, around three quarters of the companies that responded to the questionnaire indicated a medium or high relevance of PFAS to their products. Therefore, a broad PFAS restriction will have a significant negative impact on most companies.

About two thirds of the companies reported, that the PFAS-containing articles are for B2B purposes and three quarters of the affected products contain fluoropolymers (including perfluoropolyethers and fluoroelastomers).

Under normal/intended conditions of use, PFAS contamination of the environment is considered negligible during the lifetime of the products, as these PFAS-containing parts and articles remain in the products without contaminating the environment. At the end of life, typical products of the electro and digital industry are collected separately and treated as WEEE, i.e. they are dismantled and recycled under controlled conditions.

PFAS are used for their unique properties, such as resistance to harsh conditions, water and substance repellency and the friction behaviour. Most fluoropolymers are used in seals, cables, as lubricants or non-stick coatings but also to support a stable technical functionality when working at high temperatures. Thus, PFAS are therefore deliberately used to achieve the necessary material properties required for the intended product use.

For the majority of PFAS applications, there are no known substitutes. It will be extremely challenging to find chemicals with adequate properties without relevant or unforeseen hazards.

In any case, in most cases substitution cannot be achieved in a short transitional period of a few months, as assumed in the restriction dossier. For some industries, it is already clear that even a derogation of well over ten years will not be sufficient. In the semiconductor industry, for example, even the 13.5 year exemption period (12 years plus 18 months transition period) will not be enough to identify and qualify new alternatives.

As a result, the discontinuation of many products which are relevant for the European economy and society or to products which don’t meet the customer expectations in function, reliability and safety is to be expected. Alternative materials need to be evaluated on a case-by-case basis and can’t be easily transferred from one application to another.

PFAS other than fluoropolymers are also used in our industries, although to a lesser extent, e.g. F-gases as refrigerants in existing building and machinery equipment, as process gases (semiconductor manufacturing) or as insulating gases in T&D equipment.

In summary, the results of the questionnaire show the widespread use of PFAS in the E&E industry and the current lack of technically equivalent and economically viable alternatives with fewer negative impacts on human health and the environment.

Based on our current knowledge, the majority of technical articles containing PFAS cannot be replaced by suitable/equivalent PFAS alternatives even in the long term. Where alternatives are available, they must first be qualified in the manufacturing process, which may result in redesign or unavailability of the final product.
It is not only the manufacture and placing on the market of end products that will be affected by the proposed restrictions. The use and placing on the market of mixtures containing PFAS (e.g. as process chemicals) and manufacturing equipment will also have an impact on our industry's ability to produce.

The lifespan of products in the electro and digital industry varies widely and can be up to 40 years (e.g. infrastructure for electricity transmission and distribution).

According to the restriction dossier and the German UBA, the electronics/semiconductors and energy sectors currently contribute less than 2 % of total PFAS emissions in the EU.

Reflection of the current UPFAS restriction proposal:
The dossier only provides for a small number of mostly temporary derogations, which ZVEI considers insufficient. In particular, the proposal lacks broad exemptions for polymeric PFAS and important  uses of PFAS in the electro and digital industry.

The subgroup of fluoropolymers in particular is used in many products, production processes and equipment in our industry because of its outstanding properties (e.g. resistance to extreme conditions (temperature, pressure or chemically aggressive media), low dielectric constant and low coefficient of friction). As a result of decades of development towards smaller, more efficient, and safer products, it is usually the unique combination of several of these properties that requires the use of PFAS.

For many applications, no suitable substitutes are known. Consequently, no timeframe can be given for when substitutes will be available. A temporary derogation would therefore send the wrong investment signal for key technologies that should be strengthened in Europe (e.g. semiconductors, lithium-ion batteries, CO2-neutral energy production and distribution, etc.).

Where PFAS-free alternatives are known, they are often no drop-in alternatives: the specific combination of properties of PFAS materials can often only be replaced by a combination of materials or components, which requires more development effort and time than a 1:1 replacement. Changes in product dimensions, design and possibly the entire manufacturing process may be required.

Electronic devices are often made up of thousands of individual components sourced through complex international supply chains. Changes to key components or product design require intensive testing, re-qualification and, where necessary, recertification of products through sometimes complex testing procedures. The time-consuming redesign of products and subsequent testing must be carried out at every stage of the value chain. If the tests are not passed, the whole process starts all over again. Such iterations can take years. For products that require certification or (mandatory) conformity assessment, limited testing capacity (both in terms of personnel and laboratory equipment) is often the speed-determining step.

Our position (see attachement):
Our society is facing major challenges in the energy transition: Mobility and energy supply must become climate-neutral within a few decades. The electro and digital industry offers a wide range of solutions, such as semiconductors, lithium batteries, heat pumps and technologies for energy transmission and distribution. All of these could not be produced today without the use of PFAS or would not work at all or work less efficiently. (see attachement). Restricting substances should therefore not be done without a differentiated consideration of the uses and the consequences for them.

Key requirements:
Regarding the restriction approach/procedure:
A more differentiated regulatory approach is needed that is risk-based according to Article 68(1) REACH and substance-based according to Article 69 REACH. The proposed blanket ban on all PFAS, regardless of their toxicity and risk profile, does not meet this requirement. Given their enormous importance in industry, the safe use of PFAS must remain possible as long as their risks can be well "managed" by appropriate measures or no suitable substitutes are available.
It is important to distinguish between the different PFAS (groups) and the risks from each use.
It is also important to consider whether identified risks can be minimised through targeted measures, e.g., in occupational health and safety, emission control or waste legislation, rather than through a general ban under REACH.

Only risky applications and those for which a technically suitable, economically justifiable, and less environmentally and health damaging alternative exists should be restricted. Otherwise, we risk having an unmanageably long list of very specific derogations or the exclusion of certain products and processes from the European market.

Where substitution is possible, appropriate transition periods of four to eight years after entry into force (depending on sector, product life and development times) are needed, as provided for in other legislation, e.g. RoHS . Even in the case of known substitutes, the 18-month period foreseen in the proposal is insufficient for the conversion of complex products and processes.

Only the introduction of an information obligation for "intentionally added" PFAS (e.g. through inclusion in the REACH Candidate List) prior to the introduction of targeted restrictions will allow all relevant uses to be included in the assessment in due time and any necessary derogations to be applied for.
There is currently no legal basis for the dissemination and communication of information on PFAS in products along the supply chains. Most PFAS are neither classified in a harmonised way according to CLP nor included in the REACH Candidate List. Information on PFAS in products is therefore only fragmentarily available in the complex international supply chains. It will take years to fill these information gaps.

Derogations:
In general, a clearly defined process for applying for new derogations and for renewing and reviewing those already granted is needed, especially in the case of a broad restriction of previously non-declarable substances. The current derogations are insufficient and do not take into account the relevance of PFAS for a wide range of uses and possible innovations in the electro and digital industry.

Spare parts and remanufactured/refurbished products must be excluded from the restriction as a matter of principle. The repair-as-produced principle must be applied to the placing on the market of spare parts, wear parts and used parts for the purposes of sustainability and economic efficiency.

A general derogation is also needed for products that have already been placed on the market for the first time.  Otherwise, they cannot be resold or further processed and placed on the market again as a component of more complex products/articles. The only option would be disposal.

Fluoropolymers meeting the criteria for "polymers of low concern" and industrial applications in closed systems and equipment components generally do not cause relevant emissions to the environment when used as intended. Due to the high industrial importance, general and long-term derogations are necessary, especially if no technically suitable and environmentally safer alternatives are known. Risks in the manufacturing and waste phase are better addressed in the relevant legislation (emissions/occupational health and safety, waste legislation).

Monitoring/conformity:
Transitional periods must take into account existing laboratory capacity, availability/usability of analytical methods and the burden on businesses (staff, time, equipment).

Compliance with the proposed restriction cannot be verified for all uses with currently available methods and in the absence of a complete substance list. Practical and standardised analytical and extraction methods must be available for all restricted substances and uses before a legal restriction is imposed.

To create a level playing field for all market participants and to reliably detect any infringements market surveillance needs to be strengthened, in particular at external borders, but also within the EU.

Org. name: ZVEI e.V. - German Electro and Digital Industry Association
Combined Comments:
General Comments: ZVEI e. V., the German Electro and Digital Industry Association, represents an industry with an annual turnover of about 225 bn. Euro and 906 thousand employees in 2022.
In 2022 the EMEA market size of passive components was 5.7 bn Euro. Passive Components are used in the market segments of Telecommunication, Consumer & Home Appliances, Micromobility, Medical & Healthcare, Industrial & Energy and Automotive.

Passive components, such as capacitors, resistors, inductors or filters, are crucial to make the (electronics) world “go round”. There is no semiconductor component and no electronic circuitry which can work properly without passive components.
With this contribution the leading manufacturers for passive electric components organized in the ZVEI want to express their deep concern regarding the proposed and universal restriction of PFAS.

PFAS are crucial as an enabling material not only to sustain our European production and business, but also for the ability to achieve the targets of strategic EU policies set in terms of the European Green Deal, European Chips Act, digitalization and decarbonization of European industry as well as the European re-industrial policies.

PFAS are essential in a wide range of applications at the present time and for the foreseeable future. PFAS are used due to their unique combination of properties and their important characteristics for the wide range of our products and technologies.
- Environment-independent lifetime
- High temperature performance
- Electrical insulation; dielectric strength
- Chemical resistance against aggressive media
- Heat resistance at extreme temperatures and non-flammability
- Resistance against climatic influences (e. g. moisture, wetness, dust)
- Good mechanical properties (e.g. abrasion, surface tension, friction)

UNMANAGEABLE THRESHOLD

The proposed threshold of 25 ppb is far below any manageable reporting threshold for companies in the middle of supply chains. It is also about minor impurities for which even the manufacturer himself does not know the information, unless highly precise and costly measurements are made (for which, according to the information from the chemical industry, no analytical methods for PFAS have been established as international standard yet).

Even the smallest impurities lead to large quantities of raw materials and products (including those indented to be re-used/recycled and those already placed on the market for the first time) becoming hazardous waste.

POLYMERS OF LOW CONCERN

The vast majority of PFAS remaining in products belong to the polymeric PFAS group that is considered thermally, biologically, and chemically stable, negligibly soluble in water, nonmobile, nonbioavailable, nonbioaccumulative, and nontoxic.

In general, the commercially available and used fluoropolymers, which account for about 96% of the overall global fluoropolymer market, are deemed polymers of low concern, e. g. by OECD.

USAGE AND ALTERNATIVES (respectively the lack of thereof)

While some chemistries might offer a similar performance to PFAS for a particular parameter or property, it is the unique combination of properties that sets fluoropolymers apart and makes them vital for the electric components industry.

Alternative solutions are only partially available for some specific applications, for some no alternative is known at all.

- PTFE, FEP, ETFE, PVDF or PFA:
Exemplary use cases: electrical insulation on electronic components (cable sheath, shrink tubes, insulators for HF applications, insulating films in capacitors, etc.)
Required characteristics: unique combination of heat resistance, electrical insulation, resistance to chemicals and mechanical properties (abrasion, flexibility, …),
Alternatives: PVC or PP are already in use as wire insulation for low temperature applications, but they cannot be used if high operating temperatures (above105°C) are required. Polymers like PEEK or Polyimide are suitable for high operating temperature but have different mechanical and/or electrical properties compared with fluorinated polymers.

- FKM or FVMQ
Exemplary use cases: O-rings and sealings
Required characteristics: unique combination of heat resistance, resistance to chemicals and mechanical properties (flexibility)
Alternatives: EPDM rubber, Nitrile rubber (NBR) or Hydrogenated NBR as sealings are not suitable in most applications due to their insufficient media resistance.

- PFPE (example 1):
Exemplary use cases: glue for attaching sensitive MEMS to pressure ports
Required characteristics: unique combination of wide application temperature range, resistance to chemicals and mechanical properties (stability)
Alternatives: Substitution only partially possible by glass solders with lead (Pb) content. Also the substance lead (Pb) is affected by several regulations (RoHS, ELV, REACH) and should be avoided as PFAS-replacement for environmental reasons.

- PFPE (example 2):
Exemplary use cases: process aid in the manufacturing of film capacitors to define unmetallized area
Required characteristics: unique combination of electrical parameter and heat resistance
Alternatives: Not known.

- PFPE (example 3):
Exemplary use cases: heat transfer fluid for resistance measurement at NTC thermistors
Required characteristics: unique combination wide application temperature range, resistance to chemicals, dielectric properties
Alternatives: Not known for a general replacement. Only in some specific cases, silicone oil can be used. But silicone oil is a banned substance for certain applications (e.g., automotive) and by customers.

- PTFE tools
Exemplary use cases: jigs and tools in the production of electronic components (e.g. wafer carriers, sealing rings and handling tools).
Required characteristics: unique combination of heat resistance, resistance to chemicals (process aids) and mechanical properties (flexibility and stability) to prevent scratches on e.g. sensitive silicone-wafers
Alternatives: Not known.

- PFAS coatings
Exemplary use cases: coating/encapsulation of sensors in harsh environments
Required characteristics: unique combination of heat resistance up to 260°C, resistance to chemicals, resistance to moisture and wetness (hydrophobic properties), mechanical properties (stability), dielectric strength at high temperature.
Alternatives: It is very likely that alternatives do not exist at all (based on experience from extensive R&D efforts).

- C3F8, C4F8 (and CF4):
Exemplary use cases: used for MEMS Reactive Ion Etching (RIE) and Deep Reactive Ion Etching (DRIE) in order to passivate the silicon surface
Required characteristics: Achievable aspect ratio (defined as the total depth etched divided by the total elapsed time)
Alternatives: Not known at all. A sufficient aspect ratio is only known to be commercially achievable with fluorinated process gases.

IMPACT ON THE ELECTRONIC COMPONENTS SECTOR

For the electric components sector, the proposed restriction imposes a blanket ban on a huge number of substances in an undifferentiated manner and without proof of a specific risk. It is threatening production, research and development sites and activities in Europe and their competitiveness worldwide.

Also, the "hidden cross-section applications" such as seals, plain bearings and lubricants in components, machines and plant equipment are affected. Here, too, a ban would have far-reaching consequences even if PFASs were not added to the final product, so that the expected overall impact is likely to be much more serious and European sites and jobs are at stake.

In general, high efforts and time-consuming procedures are involved to test, approve and adopt alternative solutions for any of the PFAS uses. As for almost all known uses, no replacements are available yet, the actual fundamental material development or complete redesign of products takes longer than 5 years, provided that suitable solutions can be found at all. Once a possible replacement is identified, the time for validation, industrialization, customer and regulatory approval regularly takes another 2-3 years – at least; in difficult cases also more than 12 years is realistic.

EXEMPTION AND DEROGATION REQUEST

German manufacturers of electrical components are calling on the regulatory authorities to preserve the European production, labor and sales market. Restrict PFAS only in areas where there is a real risk from PFAS and establish exemptions and derogations where PFAS are safe to be used and crucial in critical-to-the-world applications:

1. Introduce a reporting requirement to ensure sufficient data on use along the supply chain.

2. Fully exclude polymeric PFAS from the scope of the upcoming restriction; at least fluoropolymers/-elastomers and perfluoropolyether.

3. Establish a 13,5-year exemption for the use of PFASs in electronic components and their manufacturing, to be reviewed for renewal at least two years prior to expiration. In this context it is very important to choose a wording that allows PFAS as ingredient within the components as well as the use of PFAS as process aids in the production of electronic components.

4. Establishing a reasonable and practicable threshold for intentionally added levels of 0.1 percent by weight.

For no. 2 and 3 above we propose the following wording:
“By way of derogation, paragraphs 1 and 2 do not apply to:
- Polymeric PFAS such as fluoropolymers/elastomers and perfluoropolyether for use in for use in and manufacturing of electrical and electronic equipment (EEE) or associated electronics and components such as control units, sensors, capacitors, resistors, inductors, filters and electrical and electromechanical components such as connectors.
- Non polymeric PFAS for use in and manufacturing of electrical and electronic equipment (EEE) or associated electronics and components such as control units, sensors, capacitors, resistors, inductors, filters and electrical and electromechanical components such as connectors until 13,5 years after EiF. This derogation shall be reviewed and assessed by the commission no later than 11,5 years after EiF”

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Our input mainly covers “Electronics and semiconductor (Annex E.2.11.)”. However, since other sectors also depend on the passive electric components, some of our contributions refers to e.g. Applications of fluorinated gases (Annex E.2.8.), Lubricants (Annex E.2.14), and “Plastics (other than packaging) and rubber/elastomer production (including flame retardant) [These are not listed in Table 9, but shown as “uses not researched in detail” in Table A1 of Annex A.].  Almost all industrial sectors are affected by regulation of electrical and electronic equipment because they use electrical and electronic parts as components. Therefore, some of our contributions also refer to e.g. Medical devices (Annex E.2.9.) and (ii) Transport (Annex E.2.10.).

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The amount of PFAS, which can theoretically be emitted in the End-of-Life treatment, is also very limited. PFAS containing articles in electrical and electronic equipment are collected and dealt with in accordance with applicable regulations, e.g. Waste Framework Directive (WFD) 2008/98/EC, ELV Directive 2000/53/EC and WEEE Directive 2012/19/EU. If the components cannot be repaired or directly reused, they are sent for material or thermal recycling (a recent study by Conversio has shown that at its end-of-life approximately 85% of all fluoropolymers end up in waste-to-energy recovery incinerators). In these processes, the polymeric PFAS contained in our articles are either broken down into their original components or mineralized so that the PFAS properties are lost. Latest studies confirm that fluoropolymers at their end of life when incinerated under representative European municipal incinerators conditions do not generate any measurable levels of PFAS emissions and therefore pose no risk to human health and the environment.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Most of the technically used PFAS are stable for a long time and very resistant to chemicals. PFAS waste treatment technologies are mostly investigated and technically evaluated by energy assisted technologies. In the case of polymeric PFAS, incineration technologies were investigated with PTFE waste. Under test conditions in a waste incineration chamber, with a setup in compliance to the requirements of the 17th BImSchV, it was demonstrated that polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) can be almost fully transformed into fluoride (F-) (as hydrofluoric acid (HF)). Samples of the flue gas were analysed for the presence of 31 PFAS and found to be without significant measurable PFAS content.[1] At temperatures above 750°C PTFE decomposed to C2F4 and C3F6 in a pyrolysis process. During further combustion CF4 will be generated. At combustion temperatures above 1000°C CF4 formation is much reduced.[2] Based on this result a municipal incineration system according to the requirements according to §8 of the 17.th BImSchV (3) was sufficient to not detect any PFAS in the flue gas with exception of greenhouse gases like CF4 or C2F6 but with low evidence due to weak database. Technologies for CF4 decompositions are in operation and development with a focus on semiconductor processes.  A system for incineration of hazardous waste operates at about 200°C higher combustion temperature. A test facility for incineration of production PFAS waste was setup in Cooperation with the “Deutsche Bundesstiftung Umwelt” and company Dyneon. This facility is able to decompose more than 90% into its monomers.[4] Other test facilities investigated the incineration of PFOA treated fibers and observed decomposition at 1000°C without chromatographically detectable PFAS in the flue gas.[5] In a literature study PFOA and PFOS decomposition was successfully investigated at 350°C in supercritical water.[6] Incineration of Perfluoropolyether (PFPE) are less investigated but during development of PFPE fluids was observed that these fluids become instable at temperature above 290°C.[7] Other incineration systems for PFPE operate at 330°C with metallic iron reactants like aluminum powder for binding decomposed PFPE.[8]  For treatment of radioactive PFPE lubricants an incineration system with MnO2-catalyst and N12CO3 immobilizer was successfully tested. 4. Impacts on the recycling industry: PFAS-containing products already placed on the EU market can no longer be supplied after the compliance enforcement date and have to be disposed of as hazardous waste. Also, existing stocks of PFAS-containing components and equipment already placed on the market for the first time have to be disposed of as hazardous waste, incl. almost all electric and electronic devices for second-hand use.  Recycling industry is working with high volume processing, such as shredding, of different types of products with different compositions on a ton scale and not on a single piece scale. Given the extremely low threshold of 25 ppb, even a few components containing PFAS would degrade extremely large quantities of recycled materials into hazardous waste.  High amounts of high-quality material as well as still fully functional devices must be treated as hazardous waste instead of being recycled, reused and conserving resources. Instead, high amounts of virgin materials are required to cover the needs with the related environmental impact and the dependance on the sources, which are often outside of the EEA.

Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Request for exemption
Org. name: ZVEI e. V. - German Electro and Digital Industry Association
Combined Comments:
General Comments: ZVEI e. V., the German Electro and Digital Industry Association, represents an industry with an annual turnover of about 225 bn. Euro and 906 thousand employees in 2022.
The proposed ban on the manufacture, use and placing on the market of PFAS (in substances, mixtures, and articles) would have a massive impact on almost all of our member companies, whose technologies are crucial for the energy transition, digitisation, European infrastructure, transport and logistics chains, healthcare, and process automation/measurement technology and production technology.

While ZVEI generally supports the objective of avoiding emissions of hazardous substances into the environment and the appropriate regulation of individual substances that pose uncontrollable risks, and our members are committed to continuously improving the environmental compatibility and safety of the products they place on the market, we see the production, research, and development locations of the German and European electro and digital industries, as well as their global competitiveness at serious risk in the event of a blanket ban and therefore call for a fundamental revision of the restriction proposal in key areas.

This consultation paper focuses on the use of PFAS-containing substances such as PFPE fluids and PTFE greases required for advanced industrial applications. A more detailed description is attached in a PDF document.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The restriction dossier summarises the entire E&E industry in one short paragraph, without taking into account the complexity of the E&E industry or applications. Nearly every complex technical article is somehow related to E&E, from a small bicycle lamp to complex industrial tools. Therefore, only a few examples can be given as representative of many other applications.

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: The PFAS-based substances are used in a controlled industrial environment. Management processes such as ISO 9001 and ISO14001 ensure that these substances are handled properly and safely. In general, the liquids containing PFAS are extracted from the tools and returned to the manufactures for cleaning and reuse or are sent to qualified waste stream operators.   In applications where PFAS-based liquids are used as process fluids (i.e., vapor phase soldering or fluid heating processes) the PFAS-based liquids do not have an end of life through contamination or chemical destabilisation. At the end of the life of the process equipment, these PFAS-containing process fluids are drained, filtered and then 100% reused in new production equipment. The PFAS containing process fluids are NOT disposed of or destroyed.  Gaseous PFAS emissions, e.g., from etching processes, are treated in qualified abatement systems using thermal incineration.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: There are different sources in the literature for studies on the incineration of PFAS. In summary, PFAS decompose in municipal incineration facilities at BAT level. See attached PDF for more details.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: From today's point of view, the recycling industry won't be affected because the materials will be collected in single grades.

5. Proposed derogations: The use of PFAS-containing lubricants is suggested by the entry "s" for a derogation, but this only refers to specific applications where they are used as lubricants.  However, there are applications, where PFAS-containing "lubricants" are used for purposes other than lubrication. In vapour phase soldering systems, the substances are used for the process itself - heat transfer to heat various products for electronics or other applications. There are no PFAS-free alternatives for the vapour phase soldering process.  The same is true for the etching process and the liquid heating process.  We see a need for these substances to be made available for an unlimited period of time due to their wide range of uses. A time limit on the exemption should only be imposed in individual cases where substitutes are already known and under further development.  Examples of uses of these substances are described in the attached PDF file.

6. Missing uses: The physical and chemical properties of the PFAS heat transfer liquid are essential for the process of vapor phase soldering and fluid heating. Only these properties make this process possible and applicable for the production. The properties are immanent to PFAS, they are based on this chemical structure and are conditioned by it.  The properties of the heat transfer liquid required for vapor phase soldering and fluid heating can only be guaranteed by PFAS. No other material offers the properties required for this process. If the production or composition of this heat transfer fluid is changed, this process no longer works. The PFAS cannot be substituted by any other material as a heat transfer liquid. There has been permanent searching for alternative substances that are not based on PFAS and have the properties of PFAS as a heat transfer liquid. Regular and repeated contacts with the chemical industry, research and development and universities brought the only result: there are no alternatives and they are not even imaginable! A ban on PFAS for use in vapor phase soldering systems and heat transfer liquids therefore inevitably leads to the "end" for the technology. Many existing products in the E&E industry can no longer be processed without these processes and the machines that run these processes. If these processes and the respective production machines are not derogated, Europe will not only lose all this E&E production but also experience a significant step backwards related to the use of products of important sectors such as electronics for the energy sector (production of energy, storage, power electronics), automotive (electromobility, charging infrastructure), medical, aerospace and communication technology (5G, networks, data storage) - just to name a few examples. The significant impact on daily life is self-explanatory.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: The uses of the PFAS as described in the attachement are technically very advanced industrial applications that are needed to keep Europe attractive as a high-performing, innovative location for future technologies.  However, these processes are not only indispensable for future processes. Many existing products in the E&E industry can no longer be manufactured without these processes and the machines that run these processes. If these processes and the respective production machines are not derogated, Europe will not only lose all this E&E production but will also experience a significant setback in the use of products in key sectors such as electronics for the energy sector (production of energy, storage, power electronics), automotive (electromobility, charging infrastructure), medical, aerospace and communications (5G, networks, data storage) - just to name a few examples. The significant impact on everyday life is obvious.  The applications are described in more detail in the annex.

Content: Description of analytical methods Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues
Org. name: ZVEI e. V. - German Electro and Digital Industry Association
Combined Comments:
General Comments: ZVEI e. V., the German Electro and Digital Industry Association, represents an industry with an annual turnover of about 225 bn. Euro and 906 thousand employees in 2022. It is one of the most important industrial associations in Germany and represents the interests of a high-tech sector with a very wide and extremely dynamic product portfolio. Our more than 1,100 member companies employ around 90 per cent of the electro and digital industry´s workforce in Germany. Our members include global players, medium-sized and family-owned businesses.
As a first step in preparing for a replacement of PFAS in products and materials, the industry is investigating the uses of PFAS in the upstream supply chain, from the complex product level to the material level, in close cooperation with suppliers, sub-suppliers and material manufacturers. As there is currently no legal obligation to provide information for most PFAS substances, this information is not available and needs to be prepared individually for each material and article. Even for specific PFAS substances that are already restricted, the threshold level in these regulations is significantly higher than the proposed threshold in the proposed regulation, meaning that compliance with existing regulations would not result in a compliance with the new regulation.
In our industry, PFAS are used because of their outstanding performance or unique combination of properties, despite the high costs of these materials. In this sense, the labelling of the respective items as containing “intentionally introduced” PFAS is suitable for declaring the presence of said substances. Under various environmental protection and product safety regulations, directives, standards and initiatives "intentionally introduced" means "deliberately utilised during the manufacture of the components and/or in the formulation of a material or component where its continued presence is desired in the final product to provide a specific property, appearance or quality“. With this definition, it would be possible to identify PFAS substances in products based on the bill of material (BoM) or the material recipes. The identification process would be drastically simplified. In addition, it is also very unlikely that such low concentrations as proposed would have the intended impact. Here, practically concentrations of above 0.1%wt or above 0.01%wt are valid according to [European Commission, (2022). Microplastic Act - amending Annex XVII to Regulation 1907/2006. Official Journal of the European Union].
Analyses for trace impurities in the products are not conducted as part of routine lot certification procedures. The analytical process is complex due to the practically not limited list of PFAS substances and the extremely low threshold level.
Additionally, due to the inherent properties of polymeric PFAS, namely a high molecular mass with a broad molecular mass distribution, their characterisation is fundamentally different from the low-molecular equivalents. Standard chromatographic and mass-spectrometry-based techniques are not suitable, so direct quantification is not possible without very sophisticated methods and detailed a-priori knowledge about the substances. The proposed measurement of organic fluorine content is only an indirect measure and provides insufficient information on PFAS content.
The requested analysis to certificate PFAS free materials would lead to high costs and a critical number of requests for analysis in the limited number of available laboratories. For complex technical articles it’s practically impossible to analyse even all relevant commercially used PFAS.
The identification of contaminations in products would not lead to any additional environmental benefits, since the detection and cleaning of already contaminated areas is not in the impact area of REACH restrictions. Detecting contaminated areas would also be possible with much less extensive measures than testing every raw material. Lower concentrations calculated to the mass of the complete article are typically observed when PFAS are used as an additive layer to improve surface properties, or as remaining traces of a release agent in demoulding processes and are part of the BoM or documented in the production process, which can also be identified and stated by the supplier. In such cases, PFAS are used in higher concentrations in the production process, which are covered by the regulation on its own if not exempted. Both cases would make the analysis of the article obsolete.

A higher threshold of 0.1 wt% PFAS in articles combined with the "intentionally introduced" principle would allow for a simplified and more realistic detection. This approach would facilitate and speed up the search and implementation of alternative materials for PFAS without a noteworthy impact on the residual amount of PFAS in articles. “PFAS-free” would be defined as ”below 0.1 %wt of PFAS”, which gives suppliers the possibility of product statements regarding PFAS.

There is currently no general approach for detecting PFAS. This is due to the wide range of PFAS compounds. SGS has published a multi-step method for the identification of a very limited amount of PFAS (1).
The German "LANUV" from NRW published analytical methods for PFAS identification based on HPLC methods for 19 PFAS substances (2), which is far from identifying the whole group of PFAS substances.
The German BAM published analytical methods for the detection of PFAS in the environment (3), (4) which clearly state that it is impossible to identify individual PFAS compounds.
The German BMUV published guidelines for the assessment of PFAS in 2022 (5). The guidelines focus on the identification of PFAS in soil and water, are limited to certain detectable PFAS compounds and provide a summary of the legal requirements for PFAS content in soil and water. This study is limited to PFAS compounds that dissolve in water.
ASTM E3302-01 (6) offers a summary about PFAS detection methods with focus on environmental analysis.
Available publications present studies on dissolvable PFAS, but no information about investigation of complex technical articles is available. In summary, we conclude that PFAS can be identified in homogenous materials but it is technically not feasible to identify unknown PFAS compounds especially in complex assembled articles.
An enforcement, in particular in an international supply chain is impossible.
For this reason, we propose for the segment of electronics (electrical equipment and electronic components - if not in general applicable) the infatuation of the following principle:
Articles and materials can be declared as “PFAS-free” if PFAS are not “intentionally introduced” and/or the threshold level of PFAS is below 0.1 %wt (or if preferred by ECHA below 0.01 %wt).

Literature:
(1) https://sgs-institut-fresenius.de/fileadmin/Media/Industry_Environment/Environment_Health_Safety/Downloads/Leaflet_PFASafe-German__1_.pdf
(2) https://www.lanuv.nrw.de/umwelt/gefahrstoffe/pfas/analytik
(3) https://www.bam.de/Content/DE/Paper-des-Monats/2022/Umwelt/2022-05-01-paper-des-monats-umwelt.html
(4) Philipp Roesch et. al; “Investigation of per‑ and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in soils and sewage sludges by fluorine K‑edge XANES spectroscopy and combustion ion chromatography”; Environmental Science and Pollution Research, Band 29, Heft 18, Seiten 26889 - 26899, 2021
(5) https://www.bmuv.de/fileadmin/Daten_BMU/Download_PDF/Bodenschutz/pfas_leitfaden_2022_en_bf.pdf
(6) https://www.astm.org/e3302-21.html

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The comment does not apply to a specific sector listed in the Annex XV restriction report (Table 9) but will be valid for all sectors and products.

4. Impacts on the recycling industry: In most cases, articles without intentionally added PFAS will be "PFAS free". If the material is unintentionally contaminated with PFAS, the concentration will be very low. The extremely low thresholds as proposed in the universal PFAS restriction dossier would hamper, if not prohibit, the circular economy, which relies on the reuse of even contaminated materials to upcycle them, e.g., into recycled plastics. This would lead to an increase in waste (Commission, A new Circular Economy Action Plan for a cleaner and more competitive Europe, 2020) and the need of additional virgin materials.

8. Other identified uses: The process of identification whether a material or an article contains PFAS, is very much influenced by the proposal we are making here. If only intentionally added PFAS had to be identified, the identification would be straightforward. Intentionally added substances have to be declared on the bill of material (BoM) or in the recipe of a material. Identification would therefore require little additional efforts as it would not require chemical analysis. In the case of the 25 ppb threshold, chemical analysis is the only way of verification and proof. The effort (time and cost) would be immense given the huge amount of materials on the market, as there is no information on whether materials contain PFAS. In most cases there is an infinite number of articles which can be generated out of few (raw) materials. As contamination does not follow clear rules, in most cases the analytic test would only cover a single moment in time and the “same” (raw) material might be PFAS-free in one sample and PFAS-contaminated in the next. The validity of chemical analysis is therefore highly questionable.

10. Analytical methods: After reviewing the analytical methods proposed by ECHA in Annex E of the restriction proposal, it is unclear whether adequate "commercially available analytical methods" approved for measuring the concentration of a substance or pollutant are available to determine the amount of PFAS with the very low proposed threshold limit of 25 ppt. It should be emphasised that no suitable test method has yet been established or developed to determine the content of PFAS in a non-homogeneous product or article. As recently as March 2023, the White House National Science and Technology Council released a study on PFAS compounds, acknowledging that only a limited number of methods have been developed to detect PFAS, most of which focus on PFAS in different media (National Science and Technology Council, 2023). There are no methods for detecting PFAS in articles, products or product components.  The analytical methods that are already available include a distinct list of PFAS target analytes with specific chemical structures for which the methods have been validated, which may differ among methods. The quantity of PFAS that can be identified by targeted analysis is extremely limited. Only about 1% of the proposed number of  restricted PFAS can be accurately determined by the commercially available targeted analysis methods, which are optimised for homogeneous materials and solutions.  Our proposal applies to all materials and articles. It does not deal with exemptions of PFAS substances or applications, but with the replacement of a threshold level from material analysis by a restriction of intentionally added substances. As amounts above 0.1% are usually added to influence a technical performance, we propose a threshold of 0.1% or 0.01% as sufficient to demonstrate that no PFAS have been intentionally added.
