Content: Scope or restriction option analysis Environmental emissions Information on alternatives Other socio economic analysis (SEA) issues Transitional period
Org. name: ZVEI e.V. - German Electro and Digital Industry Association
Combined Comments:
General Comments: ZVEI e. V., the German Electro and Digital Industry Association, represents an industry with an annual turnover of about 225 bn. Euro and 906 thousand employees in 2022. It is one of the most important industrial associations in Germany and represents the interests of a high-tech sector with a very wide and extremely dynamic product portfolio. Our more than 1,100 member companies employ around 90 per cent of the electro and digital industry´s workforce in Germany. Our members include global players, medium-sized and family-owned businesses.
ZVEI Battery Section supports the objective of avoiding emissions of hazardous substances into the environment. In our view mobility and energy supply must become climate-neutral within a few decades. The German industry offers a wide range of solutions in the area of batteries to reach this goal. Batteries are essential for the success of the EU Green Deal and to meet the goals of the EU Fit For 55 program. All state-of-the-art batteries of today – irrespective of the electrochemical systems – benefit from or even cannot be produced without the use of PFAS. No non-PFAS alternative materials that meet the standards of efficiency, durability and safety are currently known. PFAS used in the battery industry are crucial as their chemical resistance and tolerance to a high range of working temperatures are necessary properties for the safe and proper functioning of the batteries. PFAS are used in key components and/or production of most high-performance battery technologies such as lead-, nickel-, alkaline metal-air- and especially lithium-based systems as needed for future electromobility and energy storage applications. Even if alternative solutions exist or can be developed, they are expected to lower the efficiency and durability of batteries in most cases, which would also mean that much more batteries need to be produced to achieve the planned energy transition, leading to higher consumption of energy and material and more waste at the end of life. Restricting substances for batteries should therefore not be done without a differentiated consideration of the uses and the consequences for them. Moreover, a more differentiated regulatory approach that is risk-based according to Article 68(1) REACH and substance-based according to Article 69 REACH should be applied. The proposed use-ban of PFAS in the battery industry regardless of their toxicity and their potential to emit into the environment does not meet these criteria. Most PFAS substances that are relevant for batteries (such as PVDF and PTFE as electrode binders) are fluoropolymers, which are not toxic and have a much more benign environmental profile than monomolecular PFAS regarding their bio accumulative properties and mobility in the environment as defined by OECD and shown in numerous studies (e.g.: A critical review of the application of polymer of low concern regulatory criteria to fluoropolymers II: Fluoroplastics and Fluorelastomers, Stephen H. Korzeniowski et al, 2022. A critical review of the application of polymers of low concern and regulatory criteria to fluoropolymers, Barbara Henry et al, 2018). Fluoropolymers should therefore not be in the scope of the planned regulation. For all PFAS substance used in batteries that will eventually be restricted, the German battery industry requests derogation periods of 13.5 years due to the fact that suitable non-PFAS alternatives are not known so far. On top of that, downstream industries such as manufacturers of equipment powered by batteries will need further 2-3 years (and even much longer in case of some especially safety-sensitive applications such as explosive atmospheres) for testing and adapting of PFAS-free batteries in their products.
Finally, we would like to stress the need for timely and frequent reviews during the derogation periods and the possibility to extend them in case that potential alternatives still have not been found after a certain time.”

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: The comments apply for the following sectors: - energy and here as sub sector batteries, specifically downstream user industries (e.g., manufacturers of equipment, vehicles and products powered by batteries).

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Regarding 2a: Emissions during battery manufacturing: No unintended and uncontrolled PFAS emissions are foreseen during manufacturing of batteries or battery components (see section 4.2.1 of the RECHARGE paper).   Emissions during battery use: Batteries are defined in the REACH regulation as "an article with no intended release" meaning that, under normal and reasonably foreseeable conditions of use, no end-user of the Batteries will be exposed to any chemical substances. No PFAS emissions are foreseen during battery use (see section 4.2.2 of the RECHARGE paper).    Emissions during battery recycling: In general, the new battery regulation and the existing battery directive stipulates that no batteries should end up in the environment at the end of their life cycle.   Regarding 2b: No adequate information available.

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: No adequate information available.  Battery recycling is mandatory in Europe since 2006 according to the Battery Directive and will remain mandatory with higher recycling targets in the upcoming Battery Regulation.

5. Proposed derogations: No adequate information available for our industry. For any general information: see Recharge Paper.

6. Missing uses: Regarding 6a: There are no national sector figures for the German battery industry available. Therefore, we refer to section 4.1 of the Recharge paper for the PFAS consumption in tons in the EU.  Emissions during manufacturing – we refer to section 4.2 and 5 of the RECHARGE Paper  Regarding 6b: PFAS (in particular PTEF and PVDF) are used in batteries as binder materials in active material mass of electrodes. Even if a battery system does not benefit from PFAS in active material, PFAS are used in electrolytes, valves, gaskets, washers, permeable membranes (more details in section 2 of the Recharge paper).  In addition to the PFAS contained in the batteries, we would also like to point out the importance of using PFAS, especially fluoropolymers like PTFE, in manufacturing equipment for batteries. Depending on the kind of battery, parts like mixers, pipes and coaters used in related processes are often exposed to extreme conditions like high temperatures and corrosive chemicals, for which no other suitable materials are available. In this respect, we support the contribution of VDMA (Verband Deutscher Maschinen- und Anlagenbau) to this consultation.  Regarding 6c: It is difficult to say which companies in Germany are specifically affected by the regulation. In addition to battery manufacturers, there are a large number of battery users who source cells or batteries from manufacturers and assemble them into battery packs. These are adapted for special products and applications and then placed on the market. Roughly speaking, every company (machinery industry, vehicle industry, transformation industries, ...) that uses batteries in its products is affected by PFAS restrictions.   Regarding the battery industry as such, we do not have the exact number of battery companies in Germany, but only the number of employees who are directly employed in the German battery industry. In 2022, this number was 14,561 employees in Germany. The number has increased by 67 percent in the last 5 years (2018: 8.715 employees).   Regarding 6d: Contrary to what is stated in Annex E (page 416), solid state batteries and lead based batteries are not potential non-PFAS alternatives to Lithium-Ion batteries. This is because: Solid state batteries use PFAS, specifically PVDF and PTFE in the binder within the active material, in solid electrolytes and in gel polymer electrolytes. Although lead based batteries do not use PFAS in active materials, they use PFAS containing valves and membranes. The performance and durability characteristics of lead-based batteries are specific to their specific application, which are different to Lithium based batteries.   Regarding 6e: We refer to section 3.1 and table 2 of the Recharge paper. For most of the uses in the battery industry there are as of today no alternatives existing. Therefore, we request for these uses a minimum derogation period of 13.5 years and a review clause if it is foreseeable that after 13.5 years no alternatives will exist.    Reviews should be conducted timely and frequently e.g., every 3 years to give industry adequate time for adaptation.  On top of that, downstream industries such as manufacturers of equipment powered by batteries will need further 2-3 years for testing and adapting PFAS-free batteries in their products. Besides incorporation into battery packs (manufacturing aspects), this would make need of cells/packs testing and qualification such as water repellence and temperature of operation (systems level qualification). This also includes testing of compatibility with all tool types developed and sold in the past (whole product platform), especially with focus on safety aspects. Even longer testing and qualification periods of up to 6-7 years will be needed in case of some especially safety-sensitive applications such as batteries installed in aircraft and battery powered equipment for use in explosive atmospheres (ATEX Directive 2014/34/EU). This is also due to the expectation that the very demanding test requirements in place for such application, which are intended to prove the inherent safety of the batteries, are much harder to fulfil without PFAS, which often provide the key properties for passing these tests especially due to their chemical stability.   Regarding 6f: We refer to section 3.3 of the Recharge paper. In table 2 of section 3 of the Recharge paper. Section 3 mentions a few applications where an alternative would be technically possible. However, a transition requires more than 6.5 years of transition time because the development process for batteries is more complicated. Org. name: ZVEI e. V. - German Electro and Digital Industry Association
Combined Comments:
General Comments: ZVEI e. V., the German Electro and Digital Industry Association, represents an industry with an annual turnover of about 225 bn. Euro and 906,000 employees in 2022. It is one of the most important industrial associations in Germany and represents the interests of a high-tech sector with a very broad and extremely dynamic product portfolio. Our more than 1,100 member companies employ around 90 per cent of the workforce in the German electro and digital industry. Our members include global players as well as medium-sized and family-owned companies.

Most of the electrical equipment covered by ZVEI´s members has a long service life and is therefore very well prepared for the sustainable goals currently being developed by the EU. For example, electrical equipment for transmission and distribution has for decades been designed for a service life of 40 years, and in many cases it is technically, economically and ecologically possible to extend this service life further, in some cases with some maintenance or refurbishment.

The original design of the installed base, as well as the products actually manufactured and installed, contain PFAS in various areas based on specific functions and needs verified by type testing.
Maintenance and repair require spare parts to restore the product to a condition that meets the technical requirements and performance needed for the task. In the majority of cases, it is necessary to apply the “repair-as- produced-principle”, as otherwise the technical performance might change and/or test certificates may become invalid, which would revoke the permission of use.

The exclusion of the use of PFAS-containing spare or wear parts from the restriction is crucial because of the serious risk of a sudden end-of-life for a wide range of long-lived products, manufacturing equipment and infrastructure after the date of application of the restriction. The current restriction proposal prevents the transition to a circular economy and undermines fundamental sustainability goals, such as the “repair-as-produced" principle enshrined in EU product legislation such as Directive 2009/125/EC, which allows products already placed on the EU market to be restored to their original condition without undergoing a new conformity assessment.

As an example, the segment of transmission and distribution of electricity is strongly affected. The service life of more than 40 years is practically achieved through well planned and executed maintenance. In gas circuit breakers, for example, a PTFE nozzle has a very specific and extremely important technical function. There is no known substitute material that can replace PTFE. When this component needs to be replaced during maintenance or repair due to wear or failure, there is no alternative to the original part. If a new PTFE part cannot be used, the circuit-breaker cannot be repaired and is not allowed to be energized again. As a result, not only will a breaker or bay out of service, but an entire substation may have to be removed from the network. The replacement of a switchgear by a new one will take 5 years or more of planning and execution. The small defect will therefore have a long-term disruption of the network as result.  If several such cases occur in the network in close proximity (n-1 principle), the consequence would be a long-term blackout with catastrophic consequences for the society and the industry and dramatic costs. A total blackout of just one hour in a city such as Frankfurt am Main costs around 600 million euros. Critically, PTFE nozzles are also used in auxiliary circuit breakers in power laboratories where maintenance is very frequent. A ban including spare and wear parts would lead to a loss of testing capacity in Europe, which would also affect the establishment of new PFAS free T&D equipment.

Another example is household appliances: So far, no technically and economically feasible alternatives have been found for tubes with food contact made of fluoropolymers in household appliances such as coffee machines, and even if alternative materials are found within the next few years, it is very unlikely that there will be 1:1 alternatives. As a consequence, a tube made of a potential alternative material might be heavier, larger, have a larger bending radius etc. than the FEP or PFA tubes currently used, which means that it would not fit into the appliances currently on the market which are designed to be as compact as possible. An exemption for spare parts is therefore urgently needed, as otherwise whole appliances may no longer be repairable because simple parts such as tubes could no longer be replaced.

For this we ask for the segment of electrical equipment covered by the members of the ZVEI (if not in general):

Spare parts and wear parts used for the maintenance and repair of products already placed on the market prior to the validity date of the restriction, taking care of any exemption for components or technologies, need to be exempted from the regulation without time limitation until the equipment has reached its practical end of life.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Oil seals used in engines of transportation equipment  a. Type of PFAS FKMs, bisphenol AF  b. Major functions of PFAS It prevents leakage of lubricating oil while maintaining the lubricating performance of the bearings as a rotary shaft seal for vehicular engines. It provides functionality and safety until the product life of the vehicle (approximately 20 years) without deterioration by heat or lubricating oil in an environment reaching 200 deg.C.  g. Substitution is not technically or economically feasible The ambient temperature of the engine part is usually around 150 deg.C, but oil seals have sliding heat generation, so heat resistance of around 150 ~ 200 deg.C is required. Also, contact with engine oil requires the oil resistance class of ASTM D 2000 to be at least "E." The heat resistance evaluation results for materials of oil resistance class "E" or higher are, for example, 1/100 to 1/500 for NBR, 1/40 to 1/80 for ACM and HNBR, and 1/10 to 1/20 for VMQ in comparison with FKM at 175 degrees C. This value is proportional to the life, and even the most heat-resistant VMQ has a life of 1/10 to 1/20, which means that parts must be replaced about once every 1 to 2 years. Thus, the number of 0 replacements increases to more than 10 over the life of the product, and the amount of waste with environmental impact increases more than 10 times. Replacing seal parts requires removing the engine from the engine bay, which is a significant financial burden. Failure to do so will result in increased environmental pollution from oil leaks and, in the worst case, an accident resulting from engine failure and the fatal impact of engine fire. Thus, FKM (perfluoro and polyfluoropolymers) is an important material to reduce environmental impact and protect human lives. Therefore, FKM (perfluoro and polyfluoropolymers) is not subject to regulation and its continued use in Time-unlimited is essential. The above is exactly the same for engines of construction, industrial and agricultural machinery. It can be said that the proposed regulations have established upper limits for the release of bisphenol AF into the environment and that the environmental impact has been sufficiently examined. The threshold for bisphenol AF in molded products should be in accordance with the values in this proposed legislation. The use of FKM (perfluoro and polyfluoropolymers) is exempted from PFAS regulations, and its continued use with Time-unlimited is essential. The above is exactly the same for engines of construction, industrial and agricultural machinery.

6. Missing uses: Fuel cells play a crucial role in zero-emission driving and – together with electrolysis – the key to storage of regenerative electricity for prolonged periods of time. If successfully introduced to the market, about 200,000 fuel cell vehicles (each 200 kW) are expected globally by 2030. Assuming a membrane area of 16 m² per car, about 128 t of PFSA materials would thus be needed to produce the proton exchange membranes. For a more optimistic scenario with 1 million vehicles on the road a total of 640 t results accordingly. This value represents only the membrane, but does not yet include the proportions of additional PFAS materials in necessary components such as seals. In terms of membrane area, an annual expansion of electrolysis capacities of 10 GW per year by 2030 would require about 40 t/a of PFSA materials. On a maximum scenario of 40 GW per year, 160 t/a would be required. (https://www.now-gmbh.de/aktuelles/pressemitteilungen/nationaler-wasserstoffrat-nimmt-stellung-zu-den-auswirkungen-des-verbots-der-per-und-polyfluorierten-chemikalien-pfas/#:~:text=Der%20Nationale%20Wasserstoffrat%20hat%20am,Konkrete%20Handlungsempfehlungen%20werden%20genannt.)

8. Other identified uses: The ambitious targets for reducing CO2 emissions in the European Union towards climate neutrality in connection with the Green Deal and the ‘Fit for 55’ program require rapid and far-reaching measures with regard to the energy transition in almost all sectors, from the production of steel, for example, to heating in private households and mobility. The European Union has recognized that the transformation to climate neutrality can only succeed if a hydrogen economy can be successfully established in the EU. The EU Commission defined this in 2020 within the so-called hydrogen strategy for the vision of creating a hydrogen ecosystem, starting with research and innovation and extending to production and infrastructure. Hydrogen thus plays an important role in the decarbonization of industry and heavy transport in Europe. (https://germany.representation.ec.europa.eu/news/eu-kommission-legt-definition-von-erneuerbarem-wasserstoff-vor-2023-02-13_de). Specifically, the European Union aims to have a production capacity of 10 million tons of hydrogen per year by 2030 from 500 TWh of electricity produced by electrolysis. This is equivalent to about 14% of the EU's total electricity consumption and thus requires an enormous ramp-up of hydrogen technologies. The intended PFAS ban for the PEM fuel cell and for PEM electrolysis with a transition period of 6.5 years would now have the consequence that companies involved in this technology and currently in the industrialization and thus in the ramp-up of these products with the PFAS-containing state of the art would no longer be allowed to pursue them due to the ban. This would result in an abrupt halt to all activities, as these companies would first have to re-enter a development stage for a fluorine-free product. This would make the goals of the EU's Green Deal and hydrogen strategy untenable.

These hoses and tubings are commonly used in the production of chlorine gas using alkaline electrolysis, which is a more energy-efficient and environmentally friendly method of production. In alkaline electrolysis for chlorine production, Fluortubing's PTFE tubing is used in the construction of the anode compartment and for transporting the chlorine gas. This material is resistant to chemical attack by the alkaline electrolyte, which can be up to 30% NaOH or KOH, and is also resistant to the highly reactive chlorine gas produced at the cathode. Additionally, PTFE tubing is flexible and can be easily formed to fit the desired shape and length of the anode compartment and the chlorine gas transport line. Using Fluortubing's PTFE tubing in alkaline electrolysis for chlorine production has several advantages, including durability, longevity, and sustainability. PTFE tubing has a long flex life, which means that it can withstand repeated bending and flexing without degrading, making it a durable and long-lasting material for use in the construction of chlorine production cells. In summary, Fluortubing's flexible hoses and tubings made of PTFE are essential for the European Green Deal's objective of creating a more sustainable and energy-efficient future for Europe. In general if POF was no longer there would be several issues and challenges that could arise in various industries and applications. Here are some potential consequences:      Limited Data Transmission Options: POF provides a cost-effective and reliable solution for high-speed data transmission. Without POF, industries relying on its benefits may face limited options for efficient and affordable data transmission. This can impact areas such as telecommunications, automotive networking, industrial automation, and medical diagnostics.      Increased Reliance on Traditional Copper Cables: In the absence of POF, industries may have to rely more heavily on traditional copper cables for data transmission. Copper cables have limitations such as limited bandwidth, susceptibility to electromagnetic interference (EMI), and greater signal loss over longer distances. This could lead to decreased performance, slower data speeds, and potential reliability issues in critical applications.      Reduced Flexibility and Maneuverability: POF's lightweight and flexibility are advantageous in applications that require routing through tight spaces or around moving parts, such as robotic systems. The unavailability of POF could limit the design and implementation of flexible and agile systems, impacting industries such as robotics, industrial automation, and medical devices.      Compromised Immunity to Electromagnetic Interference: POF is immune to EMI and radio frequency interference (RFI). Without POF, industries may face challenges in maintaining reliable and interference-free data transmission, particularly in environments with high EMI/RFI levels. This can result in decreased signal quality, potential data corruption, and increased susceptibility to external noise sources.      Higher Costs and Complex Installations: POF is known for its cost-effectiveness and ease of installation due to its simpler manufacturing process and compatibility with existing infrastructure. The unavailability of POF could lead to higher costs associated with alternative optical fiber solutions, as well as more complex installation processes. This can impact industries such as telecommunications, data centers, and consumer electronics.      Potential Performance Limitations: POF offers advantages such as low attenuation, low dispersion, and wide acceptance angles. Alternative optical fiber solutions may not provide the same level of performance or may have limitations in terms of distance, bandwidth, or signal quality. This could result in compromised system performance and reduced capabilities in various applications.      Slower Technological Advancements: The absence of POF may slow down the pace of technological advancements in industries that heavily rely on fiber optic solutions. POF has been a driving force behind innovations in areas such as high-speed data transmission, medical imaging, and industrial automation. Without POF, research and development efforts in these fields may face challenges in finding suitable alternatives and making progress.  It's important to note that these issues are hypothetical and based on the assumption of POF no longer being available. However, they highlight the potential impact of losing the benefits and capabilities that POF currently offers to industries and applications.

Missing uses: 2L filling of HFO-1336mzz-Z per 60kWh battery cooling system; Forecast of car sales with 2phase immersion cooling for year 2030: 5’000’000 cars/year;  Forecast of Emissions: 1.0 g/year/System Fast charging for battery cooling remains a technical challenge. Standard coolant-based cooling circuits suffer from high thermal resistance and capacity limitations that make them unsuitable for 6C+ charging rates. The use of dielectric and non-flammable fluids allows for a full immersion of the battery cells in cold liquid. This technology reduces thermal resistance by direct contact of the fluid with the battery cells and larger cooling surfaces at the same time. The non-flammability is essential to a safe operation in direct contact with the high voltage parts, and potentially prevents thermal runaway (‘explosion’) of the battery packs. When employing a dielectric and non-flammable liquid with a standard boiling point in the range of the optimized battery temperature (30-40°C), the phase change of the fluid from liquid to vapor can even be employed to increase heat transfer and cooling capacity by evaporation while keeping the absolute pressure in the battery housing low. Such systems can be referred to as 2-phase immersion cooling systems. Keeping internal pressure low is favorable for a performance-effective design of the battery housing as the large footprint of the battery housing would be very prone to deformations by high internal pressures. Suitable refrigerants for this application include the Hydrofluoroleofins (HFOs) and Hydrofluoroethers (HFEs) R1233zd, R1336mzz or Novec 7000 that feature non-flammability, dielectricity and low vapor pressures. While dielectricity and low vapor pressures could also be achieved with hydrocarbons, the requirement of using non-flammable fluids makes the usage of HFOs essential.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: All 2phase immersion cooling fluids non-flammable on the market are only feasible with Hydrofluoroleofins (HFOs) and Hydrofluoroethers (HFEs), otherwise cooling fluids would be flammable and explosive

Combined Comments: 6. Missing uses: Missing use The EU restriction report is incomplete as is missing the use of PTFE in "Electroless Nickel-PTFE (EN PTFE) Composite Plating”.  This process has crucial implications in various sectors, notably in automotive, textile, and machinery. EN PTFE plays a pivotal role in enhancing the durability and life span of mechanical parts in these sectors. By providing a robust anti-corrosion layer and reducing wear, EN PTFE directly contributes to the longevity and reliability of components, thus reducing the frequency of part replacements. This not only has economic benefits but also promotes sustainability by reducing waste. The absence of EN PTFE in these applications would severely impact the functionality and efficiency of various machines and vehicles, thereby affecting industries at large. Therefore, its exclusion from the restriction report suggests a significant gap in understanding the wide-ranging applications of PTFE.  Annual tonnage and emissions The "Electroless Nickel-PTFE (EN PTFE) Composite Plating" process annually utilizes approximately 20 tons of PTFE. The emission distribution is distinct across different stages of the process. During the manufacturing phase (20-40% of emission), emissions primarily come from spent baths and drag-out to rinsing tanks. Spent baths typically undergo D9 physio-chemical treatment, and the resulting PTFE-containing sludge is likely landfilled. In the use phase (1-5% of emission), emission sources stem from the gradual wear of the coating, introducing potentially diffused emissions into the environment. End-of-life emissions (50-70% of emission), interestingly, are practically non-existent in terms of PFAS. Given that the components plated with EN PTFE are metallic, they typically undergo recycling through smelting at their end-of-life stage. This process incinerates the PTFE particles, which does not result in PFAS emissions. A comprehensive understanding of emission sources and stages is crucial in forming an effective PFAS regulation policy.  Key functionalities provided by PFAS EN PTFE Composite Plating is a unique process that leverages the beneficial properties of both its constituent elements: Nickel and PTFE. In this composite coating, the hard metal matrix provided by nickel offers the necessary structural robustness, while the embedded PTFE particles contribute their characteristic anti-stick, low friction, and heat resistance properties. This distinctive blend of hardness and functional features is at the heart of EN PTFE's wide applicability and effectiveness. Importantly, no other particles currently known share the same unique combination of properties that PTFE offers. This makes PTFE not merely an additive but an integral part of the composite, rendering it essential for the "Electroless Nickel PTFE Composite Plating" process. It is this unparalleled combination of properties that makes the proposed restriction on PTFE use potentially disruptive to numerous industries.  Companies affected The proposed PTFE restriction will have broad implications, impacting an estimated 200 plating companies directly. However, the effects of this restriction reach much further, potentially affecting up to 5000 downstream industries across the EU. EN PTFE is employed in a diverse array of applications where the unique combination of electroless nickel's hardness and PTFE's anti-stick, low friction, and heat resistance properties are integral. From automotive to textile, machinery, and beyond, the use of EN PTFE composite plating is widespread. Consequently, any restriction on PTFE use would not only disturb the operations of these direct users but also have a ripple effect on countless businesses and industries reliant on products produced using EN PTFE. Such a far-reaching industrial and economic disruption underscores the significance of a well-considered, comprehensive assessment of the proposed restriction.  Alternatives The unique combination of properties offered by EN PTFE in composite plating currently has no complete alternative. While particles like MoS2 or graphite may replicate some of PTFE's properties, they fall short of fully matching its unique combination of anti-stick, low friction, and heat resistance characteristics. Additionally, processes employing these alternative particles are not yet established at an industrial scale, limiting their immediate usability and feasibility as substitutes. Regarding the end use, alternative technologies might be adopted for some applications, but this is not a universal solution. Certain uses might necessitate design changes to avoid reliance on EN PTFE coatings, introducing additional costs and potential performance compromises. In some cases, there may be no viable alternative at all, leading to unavoidable impacts on both the industries and consumers. This lack of complete alternatives, coupled with the potential implications of substituting PTFE in various uses, illustrates the challenges that a restriction on PTFE would pose. It underscores the need for extensive research and development efforts to identify or create a material that can match the broad applicability and effectiveness of PTFE in EN composite plating.  R&D on alternatives The search for viable alternatives to PTFE in EN composite plating is a challenging task. While some downstream applications might be adaptable to use alternative technologies or substances, a significant proportion of these applications may find it extremely difficult or outright impossible to locate suitable substitutes. This stark disparity in the feasibility of substitution underscores the critical role of PTFE in these applications. To overcome these challenges, substantial investment in research and development initiatives is needed. But it's not just about finding alternatives - these alternatives must also be economically viable, sustainable, and capable of fulfilling the specific technical requirements that PTFE currently meets. Furthermore, they must be able to be scaled up to industrial levels without significant barriers. However, as of now, the progress of such R&D initiatives is uncertain. There are also inherent challenges related to time, costs, and the potential risks associated with exploring new, untested materials or technologies. The lack of current alternatives to PTFE underlines the significance of its role and the urgency of further investment and focus in the development of suitable and sustainable alternatives.  Substitution costs and time The feasibility of substitution is highly variable across different uses of EN PTFE Composite Plating. Upstream, substitution is currently not feasible due to the unique properties of PTFE. Downstream, the situation ranges from difficult to impossible, depending on the specific application. This variability underscores the challenge of finding a one-size-fits-all solution to replacing PTFE. For some applications, the transition could be costly and time-consuming, involving significant redesigns, testing and certification of new materials, adjustment of manufacturing processes, and potential changes in performance or lifespan of the product. Even in cases where substitution appears possible, the time frame for a successful transition might be substantial, potentially leading to temporary disruption of production and services. These factors could have ripple effects throughout the supply chain, potentially leading to increased costs for downstream users and consumers. All these considerations highlight the complexity of moving away from PTFE usage and the need for a nuanced, industry-specific approach to substitution, where the costs, risks, and benefits are carefully weighed.  Socio-economic impacts The data provided is an estimation based on the knowledge of the process and the EU market. The data may be inaccurate. The proposed restriction on PTFE could have substantial socio-economic repercussions. For plating companies that directly employ EN PTFE composite plating, the financial impact is estimated at approximately 60 million €/year. However, this is only the tip of the iceberg. The downstream industries, which utilize the products from these plating companies across a myriad of applications, could face an even greater economic challenge. The impact here is estimated at a significant 600 million €/year. These figures reflect not only the loss of revenues and increased costs for businesses but also potential job losses and the cost of transition to alternative materials or processes. Beyond the direct financial impacts, there are potential consequences for product quality, performance, and lifespan. Some industries might have to compromise on these aspects if they switch to inferior or less suitable materials. This, in turn, could impact consumer satisfaction and trust. Moreover, the effects could be more pronounced for certain industries or regions, leading to a disproportionate impact. Therefore, a comprehensive socio-economic impact assessment is crucial to understanding the full ramifications of the proposed restriction. This would help inform a balanced and equitable policy decision, considering both environmental goals and socio-economic realities.

7. Potential derogations marked for reconsideration: Oil seals used for drivetrains in the undercarriage of transport vehicles Produced by NOK CORPORATION and supplied to the EU.  a. Types of PFAS FKMs, bisphenol AF  b. Major functions of PFAS It prevents leakage of lubricating oil while retaining the lubricating performance of the bearings as a rotary shaft seal around the vehicle's foot. It provides functionality and safety until the product life of the vehicle (approximately 20 years) without deterioration by heat or lubricating oil in an environment reaching 150 deg C.  g. Substitution is not technically or economically feasible Oil seals are essential for sealing lubricants because the drivetrain around the vehicle's foot has bearings and uses lubricants. Since the temperature around the bearings increases due to sliding resistance and reaches 150 deg C or higher, especially in large vehicles with large shaft diameters, oil seals must be both oil-resistant and heat-resistant. NBR, ACM, and VMQ other than FKM can ensure function and safety until the product life (20 years) when the normal temperature is around 100 deg C. However, with the increasing size and performance of modern transportation equipment, the temperature of these products reaches over 150 deg C. As the attached data shows, the product life is shortened by 1/10 at 150 deg C compared to 100 deg C. That is, the parts need to be replaced once every 2 years. Thus, the number of 0 replacements increases to more than 10 over the life of the product, and the amount of waste with environmental impact increases by more than 10 times. Replacing seal parts requires the removal of the drivetrain from the undercarriage, which is a significant financial burden. Failure to do so can lead to increased environmental pollution from oil leaks and, in the worst case, to vehicle fires resulting and fatal accidents from damaged drivetrains. Thus, FKM (perfluoro and polyfluoropolymers) is an important material for reducing environmental impacts and protecting human lives. Therefore, FKM (perfluoro and polyfluoropolymers) is not subject to regulation, and its continued use with Time-unlimited is essential. The above is exactly the same for the drivetrains of construction, industrial and agricultural machinery.  Prohibiting the marketing of vehicles that have been type-approved after a certain period of time hinders the recovery of vehicle development costs, so it can be said to be against the concept of the ELV Directive. Banning supply parts from coming to market after a certain deadline violates CE principles and Green Deal goals because it prevents the repair and inspection of vehicles already on the market. Type certification systems and supplies should be recognized as important requirements for exemptions.  In addition, the use of FKM (perfluoro and polyfluoropolymers) to form molded products with rubber elasticity requires the use of bisphenol AF, a type of PFAS, as a cross-linker. Proposed regulations for bisphenol AF have been published in the "ANNEX XV RESTRICTION REPORT - BPA and bisphenols of similar concern for the environment". It can be said that the proposed regulations have established upper limits for the release of bisphenol AF into the environment and that the environmental impact has been sufficiently examined. The threshold for bisphenol AF in molded products should be in accordance with the values in this proposed legislation. The use of FKM (perfluoro and polyfluoropolymers) is exempt from PFAS regulations and its continued use with Time-unlimited is mandatory. The above is exactly the same for the drivetrains of construction, industrial and agricultural machinery.

Missing uses: While F-gases used in foaming agents are discussed in the current draft regulation, additives (not gases) containing PFAS are also used in foam products for insulation and other molded products.  An example is a PTFE-based processing aid represented by Mitsubishi Chemical's METABLEN (https://www.m-chemical.co.jp/products/departments/mcc/metablen/product/1202132_7202.html).  It is added to foam resins to significantly improve the moldability of the base resin or to meet thermal insulation specifications.  The use of alternative processing aids has been shown to result in inability to mold itself or poor thermal insulation specifications.  The reduction in home thermal insulation performance is directly related to environmental and economic impacts.  It also reduces the risk of fire because melted resin is less likely to drip on another location (drip prevention).  In many cases, resins that are sufficiently drip-prevention reduce the amount of flame retardant required, and decreasing the amount of flame retardant has a positive impact on the environment.  Unlike F-gases used for foaming, there is little risk of release into the environment.

1. Sectors and (sub-)uses: Proposed derogation 5s: lubricants where the use takes place under harsh conditions or the use is needed for safe functioning and safety of equipment. Here: medical device sector, optometry devices (tabletop devices for eye care professionals). In optometric devices, PTFE (polymeric PFAS, CAS: 9002-84-0) greases, tapes, or coatings are used as dry, i.e., oil-free, lubricant. They are used to ensure lubrication and low friction moving optical parts, thus contributing to both safety and functionality of the devices where the unhindered, contamination-free movement of optical parts over lifetime is essential for correct eye exams. PTFE-based lubricants (greases, tapes, coatings on moving parts) are used to reduce friction and wear between surfaces. They meet critical needs in mechanical applications due to their excellent tribological properties, neglegible stick-slip behaviour, very low coefficients of friction (<< 0.1). Due to their chemical inertness, early corrosion of lubricated metallic parts is prevented to guarantee life-long movement. They show no to very low outgassing or creeping. As a consequence, they are ideal candidates for use in optical pathways of medical devices, where deterioration of the optical performance is inadmissible. Typical alternatives do not present the advantages of PTFE grease. They are typically prone to creeping and higher outgassing or show lower stability against UV irradiation, resulting in contamination risks of optical parts (lenses, mirrors, cameras, photosensors). They are also inferior in tribological characteristics, thus potentially adversely affecting safety and functional features of moving parts.

5. Proposed derogations: To satisfy the above mentioned uses, very small amounts of PTFE (polymeric PFAS, CAS: 9002-84-0) are required in our optometry products. Per se, PTFE qualifies as polymer of low concern: PTFE is a fluoropolymer with a very high molecular weight so that it cannot cross cell membranes. PTFE is non-toxic, chemically inert, durable and flexible. It is long-term stable in ambient applications,  and resistant to UV radiation in particular. It has neglegible residual monomer and oligomer content and low to no leachables. Fluoropolymers are negligibly soluble in water and not prone to creeping. PTFE is not bioaccumulative, as evidenced by toxicology studies on polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE).  For an overall assessment see : J. Sales et al., Fluoropolymers: The Safe Science That Society Needs; International Chemical Regulatory and Law Review, Vol. 5, No. 1 (2022), pp.  13-23, and references therein.  During production, any PTFE lubricant is applied in controlled production environment by trained personnel. The lubricants are applied in solid state either as tapes, thin coatings or layers of grease. Over the entire product range, overall annual usage of PFAS-based lubricants (polymeric PTFE) during production stays well below 10 kilograms (i.e., 0.01 tons). Calculated per device, the mass-specific PFAS content stays below 20 ppm (parts per million, polymeric PFAS lubricant). Calculation example (worst case estimate): typically 0.1 grams of grease are applied to a final device of > 20 kg weight. For thin coatings and tapes, the amounts used are even lower. Our optometry products are medical devices that are exclusively used in professional environments (eye care specialists). They qualify as electromechanical systems subject to controlled disposal following local restrictions (eg.WEEE).  During use, the mechanical moving parts are covered fully in a housing. Given the high stability of solid PTFE, environmental exposure over lifetime is tending to nil.

Sectors and (sub-)uses: SYMBIO, a joint venture of MICHELIN and FORVIA, designs, produces and sells a complete range of StackPacks®, prevalidated and preintegrated hydrogen fuel cell systems, mostly for road transportation applications. We would be therefore classified under 2 sectors   - Energy sector (Proton-exchange membrane (PEM) fuel cells)  - Transportation

2. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Fuel Cell systems are mainly using 2 fluoropolymers among the ~10,000 substances covered by the restriction proposal: PTFE and PFSA ionomer, which are contained in the Membrane Electrode Assembly and the humidifier.   - Manufacturing: The polymers are supplied in liquid (ionomer dispersion) and solid state (membrane, GDL) to our plant. The liquid ionomer is mixed with precious material to coat the membrane film to obtain the Membrane Electrode Assembly. There is no emission of PFASs during our process in normal operation. Manufacturing scraps are recycled in dedicated channels (see End-of-Life). Containments are set-up to prevent any emissions (dust or liquid) if any incident occurs. The functioning and controlled temperature of the fuel cell stack (around 80-90°C) is well below the known degradation temperature of PTFE or PFSA ionomer (260°C)  , granting chemical and mechanical stability to our products.   - Use: The fuel cell systems are integrated into vehicles, typically light and heavy commercial vehicles. Membranes contained in the fuel cell stack and humidifier are concealed in their sealed casing. Except during maintenance, there would be no access to this component in normal use.  Degradation of the membrane during the life time of the vehicle is closely studied as it influences directly the performance (durability, power output, efficiency, etc.) of the fuel cell. R&D projects are ongoing to analyze the degradation in typical use operation (e.g. durability tests for light commercial vehicles including many starts and stops of the system). The degradation materials released during operation is today assumed to be neglectable, but measurements will be conducted as part of ongoing R&D projects. Defective systems are generally replaced during maintenance and either recycled and reused or sent to appropriate professional recycling companies.  - End-of-Life: Fuel cell recycling is a relatively new and emerging field, but there are several methods that have been proposed and tested for recycling these components. Industrial-scale recycling exists in Asia (Japan, China) but also in Europe (Belgium). After being dismantled, the whole membranes  are pre-shredded or directly sent in a plasma oven to be burnt under extreme temperature (1400-1700°C). This step aims mostly to recover the precious metal inside the MEA, but it also leads to the burning of the PFASs (Balva, 2017). No PFASs emission occurs during the recycling process as the PTFE and PFSA ionomer are then completely destroyed and can no longer be released in the environment (Aleksandrov et al. , 2019) .  See attached document of section V for further information

3. Emissions in the end-of-life phase: Fuel Cells will be collected to recover precious metals, namely Platinum, as the recycling process creates value and participates to circular economy and reduces dependency on raw material suppliers and therefore reduces our overall CO2 footprint by a factor of 50 over the life cycle according to International PGM Association Shredded MEAs are burnt in a plasma oven under very high temperature (1400-1700°C). All the PFASs are burnt and no release in the environment occurs. All our components and scraps containing PFASs are sent to professional recycling channels. Other identified uses: The proposed derogation duration of 6,5 years for the use of fluoropolymers in Fuel Cell applications will not be sufficient to find alternatives that fulfill Key Performance metrics (Power, Density, cost, etc.) required for fuel cells to be able to replace incumbent (internal combustion engine) technologies.  The fuel cell industry has already invested massive amounts of both private and public funds (including national and European-level subsidies) to develop the technology and at the same time its mass-market industrialization, based on the current generation PFAS-containing components.  A too short derogation period will put an end to the emergence of hydrogen fuel cells as a zero-emission technology, thereby making Europe’s “Fit for 55” targets in the transport sector, notably its hardest to abate segments (heavy duty transport, light commercial vehicles, buses & coaches, rail, marine etc.), impossible to achieve.  Moreover, such a derogation would destroy the nascent and still fragile European Fuel Cell ecosystem and leave the global market for fuel cells to non-European competitors. This would be contrary to the ambitions set by the European Union regarding the development of strategic industries, notably via its ongoing hydrogen IPCEI.  None of Europe’s major trading partners (in particular North America, China, Japan, South Korea) has engaged in a general PFAS ban, and none of them is targeting the technologies necessary to enable the decarbonization of the transport sector. 6. Missing uses: PTFE powders have very important role as a wear resistance agent for coating film of paints to be used for Automotive Interior and Exterior Parts.  Although some candidate materials as althernative to PTEF providing certain wear resistance are available, those materials feature less heat resistance and shorter duration of effectiveness in heat resistance than PTFE.  In this sense, there is no material can feature the same performances to the conventional type of PTFE at present.

6. Missing uses: At our company, a wide variety of Fluoropolymers (e.g. PTFE, Viton, Gylon, PVDF) are used as production plant components in the manufacturing of pharmaceuticals as well as in analytical equipment for testing those pharmaceuticals. Moreover, TFA (trifluoro acetic acid) is a critical component used in chemical analysis of our active pharmaceutical ingredients.  At one of our affiliated companies, PFA (Perfluoralkoxy polymers) is used for the storage of pharmaceutical products (drug substance) at the site.   Fluoropolymers are used in the above-mentioned applications due to their unique properties, namely the resistance to high temperature and aggressive chemicals. In detail, these are: • Ozone, which is used for the production of WFI (Water for injection) which is e.g. necessary for the production of parenteral drugs • Steam (with temperatures ranging between 140 and 200°C) • Solutions of sodium hydroxide and citric acid used for cleaning purposes In case of the storage of pharmaceutical products, chemical inertia as well as temperature stability are critical material properties. TFA (trifluoro acetic acid) is used in testing of active pharmaceutical ingredients. The relevant procedures are mandatory from a regulatory perspective for release of the substances to the market.   Due to the unique properties of fluoropolymers, replacement in pharmaceutical manufacturing context is – at least in the short term – impossible. Membranes or seals made of EPDM (Ethylene-Propylene-Diene-Monomer rubber) are not suitable as alternatives in these applications. This is due to their limited stability in hot and / or corrosive environments which can lead to degradation of the material and – worst case – contamination of pharmaceutical products. Moreover, the lifespan of EPDM under the prevalent conditions would be very limited. This would not only potentially compromise product quality, it would also pose a serious risk of exposure of staff to aggressive chemicals. Furthermore, it would drive up costs as well as waste quantity due to a higher replacement frequency.  TFA used for analytical purposes cannot be replaced. If this were necessary, it would imply the development of a completely new analytical method which would also be subject to approval by the FDA (US Food and Drug Administration). Analytics carried out according to guidelines from pharmacopoeias require the use of the specified reagents which cannot be changed without the underlying pharmacopoeia being changed. Concerning the storage of pharmaceutical product, a replacement of the material is currently impossible. Apart from required properties (e.g. inertia), any change of the material would be subject to lengthy validation procedures and approval by the relevant regulatory authorities.  The planned ban would thus have massive consequences on our company, since fluoropolymers are used in the media production and distribution virtually throughout the whole company site including various production plants. They are also used in a variety of analytical equipment. The new development of analytical methods for our major product would not only be very costly and time-consuming, but also subject to approval by the FDA. In consequence, the ban would result in a shutdown of nearly the whole site with 500+ jobs affected and the inability to supply important pharmaceuticals to markets in the EU, Northern America and others. As the restrictions would not apply to producers outside the EU, this could ultimately lead to dependence on non-EU producers for the supply of the aforementioned pharmaceuticals.   In conclusion, a replacement of fluoropolymers in addition to a ban of TFA in the manufacturing of pharmaceuticals is neither technically nor economically feasible for our company and would put the company as a whole at risk.

Combined Comments: 6. Missing uses: Fittings for plumbing applications (gas, sprinkler, sanitary and heating) a. Type of PFAS: Fluoropolymer (PVDF) b. Key functionalities provided by PFAS: PVDF • Chemical inert, making it resistant to chemicals too which it can be exposed at a construction site (for example other plastics are susceptible to foaming agent, specific seals) without decreasing the expected lifetime of the product. • Corrosion resistance as it is a plastic making it suitable for the transportation of water. • High thermal stability, making it suitable for high temperature (95°C) applications such as the transport of hot sanitary water. • It complies with the strict European drinking Water regulations and certifications, making it a safe material to be used in contact with drinking water. • Excellent long term creep resistance, making it possible to resist pressures of up to 10 bar at an elevated temperature during its lifespan of 50 years. • Ductile material, making it suited to be connected by deforming the fitting material to the pipes making a watertight connection. It also makes it very robust when handled by an installer. This ductility is maintained during the entire life cycle of the product as these ductile properties remain after aging under influence of the constant load and temperature shocks (20°C – 95°C) that occur during the life span of the product. c. Number of companies:  Between 10-20 companies (piping systems producers & MB/compounds suppliers for piping systems) in Europe are impacted by the PFAS restriction proposal.  d. Available alternatives:  • Brass CW617N* and CW602N: both types of brass have phase out plans in place as they have a high lead content making it not suited for the ever-stringent drink water regulations. As a replacement the more expensive and CW724 (or ecobrass) is proposed. This material is 50% more expensive as standard CW617N* as the material is more expensive and harder to produce due to the higher hardness of the material impacting the machinability. At the current price level of brass CW617N*, brass is double as expensive as PVDF. This price gap is expected to rise to almost 3 times as expensive when the regulations require the use of ecobrass.  Brass is not corrosion resistant, making it less suitable for water applications.  Copper is known to become scarcer as there is a big demand due to the energy transition.  https://www.cnbc.com/2023/02/07/there-isnt-enough-copper-in-the-world-shortage-could-last-until-2030.html. • PPSU: This is another polymer which is more brittle as PVDF making it more prone to failures when handled by the installer as it has a lower impact strength.  The material is not chemical inert towards 100 + chemicals known to be used at a construction site. A contact with the chemical can cause the bonds between the polymers to break and initiate a crack which gradually grows when the fitting is exposed to alternating cycles of hot and cold water. This causes a failure with big damages as a result of water leakage. Detailed description of the tests performed and chemical resistance of PPSU to known substances at the construction site are added in attachment. The price of PPSU is in normal market circumstances similar to a fitting produced from PVDF. PPSU however has a limited supply chain and only a very limited producers. BASF and Solvay are the only manufacturers of drinkwater approved PPSU. Solvay has stated to be sold out PPSU in 2024. BASF was not accepting new customers for PPSU in 2022 due to capacity constraints. e. / f. The change over to a different material for fittings is comparable to a completely new product development as the behavior of the material is different making it necessary to develop a connection that is watertight, determining the dimensions and design of the press profile.  PPSU is also known from literature to be a difficult material to process. Fitting development is due to the design lifetime of 50 years and the demanding application of 10 bars internal pressure at elevated temperature time consuming. Accelerated aging tests are performed to simulate the lifetime of 50 years. Although the tests are accelerated the duration of a single test is 3,5 months up to 7 months for the larger diameters (>=63 mm). These extensive tests to verify the product quality lead to long development times. 5 -7 years of development are common in the industry. This effort is enlarged by the need to redevelop the complete Henco product range as in Q1 2023 the complete fitting and manifold product range is made of PVDF. Since the shrinkage factor is different for PPSU (0,7%) compared to PVDF (2,7%); the existing molds can’t be used to injection mold PPSU. Based on a rough estimate that it costs between 35.000 EUR (Chinese mold) and 65.000 EUR (European mold); the total cost for the case of Henco to replace +/- 500 injection molded articles in PVDF can add up to 17.500.000EUR to 32.500.000EUR not including the additional costs needed in production equipment to process the material.  The mold temperatures are higher (+/- 180°C) compared to PVDF (+/- 90°C) causing the need for high temperature control units to stabilize the mold temperature. For example, dryers are needed to dry PPSU resin before transporting it in the injection molding machines. These dryers are not required for PVDF. Also, a post treatment step is advised to get rid of residual mold-in stresses in the product. This requires the installation of an annealing oven. It is estimated that these elevated temperatures and pre- and post-processing steps result in a worsening of the environmental footprint of the synthetic fittings produced by Henco. In total the investment would be 20.000.000EUR to 35.000.000EUR which is very heavy compared to the sales in the PVDF fitting product line which equaled 37.000.000 EUR in 2022.  All these adjustments replace other R&D efforts, for example efforts to go to a full circular economy and add no new value to the product as the switch from the very performant PVDF to a less performant PPSU is seen by Henco as a step back in the quality and features of the product. Since there is no evidence that fluoropolymers are a hazard to human health and the material is tested and found to be compliant with the very strict drinkwater approvals (NSF 61,KTW, W270/DVGW, ACS, WRAS) the question can be raised if the ban on PVDF is in proportion to caution principle.
